## Series title page

# COMPLETE COURSE OF PATROLOGY, OR UNIVERSAL, COMPLETE, UNIFORM, CONVENIENT, AND ECONOMICAL LIBRARY OF ALL THE HOLY FATHERS, DOCTORS, AND ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS WHO FLOURISHED FROM THE APOSTOLIC AGE DOWN TO THE TIME OF INNOCENT III; A CHRONOLOGICAL REPRINT OF ALL THE MONUMENTS OF CATHOLIC TRADITION THAT HAVE SURVIVED FROM THE FIRST TWELVE CENTURIES OF THE CHURCH, ACCORDING TO THE MOST ACCURATE EDITIONS, CAREFULLY COLLATED WITH ONE ANOTHER AND WITH VARIOUS MANUSCRIPTS, AND MOST DILIGENTLY CORRECTED; CONTINUALLY ILLUSTRATED BY DISSERTATIONS, COMMENTARIES, AND VARIANT READINGS; ENLARGED BY ALL WORKS DISCOVERED AFTER THE EXTENSIVE EDITIONS PRODUCED DURING THE LAST THREE CENTURIES; FURNISHED WITH PARTICULAR ANALYTICAL INDICES FOLLOWING EACH INDIVIDUAL VOLUME OR EACH AUTHOR OF SOME IMPORTANCE; ADORNED WITH CHAPTERS PROPERLY ARRANGED WITHIN THE TEXT ITSELF, AND ALSO WITH TITLES DISTINGUISHING THE UPPER MARGIN OF EACH PAGE AND INDICATING THE SUBJECT MATTER BELOW; ENLARGED BY WORKS BOTH DOUBTFUL AND APOCRYPHAL, as well as by those possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; ENRICHED WITH TWO GENERAL INDICES: THE FIRST, OF SUBJECTS, BY CONSULTING WHICH WHATEVER EACH FATHER HAS WRITTEN ON ANY TOPIC MAY BE SEEN AT A GLANCE; THE SECOND, OF SACRED SCRIPTURE, FROM WHICH IT IS EASY for the reader to discover which Fathers, and in what passages of their works, have commented on the individual texts of the books of Scripture. A MOST ACCURATE EDITION, AND EASILY PREFERABLE TO ALL OTHERS IF ONE TAKES INTO ACCOUNT THE CLEANNESSS OF THE TYPE, THE QUALITY OF THE PAPER, THE INTEGRITY OF THE TEXT, THE PERFECTION OF THE CORRECTIONS, THE VARIETY AND NUMBER OF THE WORKS REPRINTED, THE EXTREMELY CONVENIENT FORM OF THE VOLUMES, CONSISTENTLY SIMILAR THROUGHOUT THE ENTIRE WORK, THE LOW COST, AND ABOVE ALL THIS COLLECTION—A SINGLE, METHODICAL, AND CHRONOLOGICAL GATHERING OF SIX HUNDRED FRAGMENTS AND OPUSCULES HITHERTO SCATTERED HERE AND THERE, BUT BROUGHT TOGETHER FOR THE FIRST TIME IN OUR LIBRARY FROM WORKS RELATING TO EVERY AGE, PLACE, LANGUAGE, AND FORM.

FIRST SERIES, IN WHICH ARE PUBLISHED THE FATHERS, DOCTORS, AND WRITERS OF THE LATIN CHURCH, FROM TERTULLIAN TO GREGORY THE GREAT. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the *Complete Courses* in the several branches of ecclesiastical learning.

## [THE COMPLETE WORKS OF SAINT AMBROSE.]

[Col. 0009]

# PREFACE TO THIS SECOND VOLUME

[Col. 0009]

[Col. 0009A] Whatever relates generally to the correction of the works of Saint Ambrose, and especially to those books contained in the first volume, we set forth in the preface to that volume with sufficient care that it does not seem possible to repeat it here without justly wearying the reader. What remains, therefore, in this place is only to examine somewhat the treatises that make up this volume—both those that are genuine and truly Ambrosian, and those that are spurious and forged—and also to say something about those that have perished through the injury of time.

Having published in the preceding volume those books which, by a certain right of their own, belong to the divine Scriptures, in this one we present the remaining writings of our Doctor: namely, those in which the virtues and practices proper to certain distinguished forms of Christian life are taught, and in which Catholic doctrines are either explained [Col. 0009B] to the less instructed or defended against the impiety of heretics. When we have appended to these writings the letters of the same Bishop, as well as the Orations delivered by him at the funerals of his brother Satyrus and of the emperors Valentinian and Theodosius, the result is a volume that is most pleasing both for the variety itself and for its account of the various changes of the Ambrosian age, whether in the Church or in the empire; and most useful for the weight of its subjects, which contain a great many points of faith and discipline. In reading it, one scarcely knows whether one should admire more Ambrose’s piety in forming sacred ministers and virgins, his learning in defending the divinity of Christ and of the Holy Spirit, or his skill and steadfastness in carrying out [Col. 0009C] the greatest affairs.

Since, as in the first volume, each work in this one is preceded by its own *Admonition*, in which we have examined the same matters as far as our ability allowed, it would be superfluous to linger longer here over their investigation. As for the order in which they have been placed, since it was in no way possible to follow considerations of age and chronology, we have adopted that which seemed demanded by the affinity of their subjects and which we judged least contrary to the arrangement of earlier editions. But so that the necessary change should cause no one difficulty, we have appended to this Preface a complete list, in a single sequence, of all the treatises that make up this volume, together with the initial page noted for each.

[Col. 0009D] With regard to our notes, which are more frequent and longer in this volume, we shall again warn the reader that they were not written for the learned; for we readily confess that it is more fitting for us to take the part of pupils than of teachers. Yet when we saw that, in subjects of the greatest importance, serious difficulties and byways of no small consequence repeatedly arose, we hoped to win some gratitude from modern theologians if, for their sake, we smoothed those rough places which veterans habitually tread without injury to their feet. Although we are truly conscious that we have striven with all our strength not to depart even by a fingernail’s breadth from the Catholic faith, nevertheless, if anywhere—as human weakness may cause us—we have expressed something less consonant with it, we are prepared to erase it not only with tears but also with blood. Indeed, we may also profess this: even in those opinions concerning which everyone is especially free to decide which he prefers, we have carefully taken precautions lest, carried away by any prejudices, we should ever deviate from the right path.

[Col. 0010A] In this volume we have corrected and restored a great many passages through the benefit of ancient codices; but many more items that had long since crept [Col. 0010B] into the number of the Ambrosian works we have either omitted or relegated to the Appendix, judging that it would be unjust for spurious offspring, wholly unworthy of him, to usurp the glorious name of so great a Father together with his legitimate children. Indeed, we cannot sufficiently wonder that so many books and sermons have been attributed to the holy Doctor which are entirely alien to his genius, style, and age, and some of which are also circulated among the works of other writers. But this causes us even greater astonishment: that certain ill-employed men should have so deceived the public trust as to interpolate in various places certain compositions whose first reading clearly showed not to be Ambrose’s, so that they might more safely pass them off as Ambrosian. No one would say that this kind of imposture is less serious than the crime of those who mix counterfeit coins struck by themselves with genuine ones. [Col. 0010C]

Accordingly, as we have already indicated, those spurious offspring have been arranged in two categories: those omitted and those included in the Appendix. We judged that the former should be passed over because, having been published elsewhere with the writings of other authors, as has been said, they would easily be found by anyone diligent in searching; or else because, being in themselves extremely slight and useless, they were equally unworthy of the labor of editors and the attention of readers [Note: [Col. 0009D] See the editor’s Notice, vol. XV, col. 1961.]. As for those from which we composed the Appendix, they likewise fall into two classes. For earlier editions had either advertised them as Ambrosian—the larger number—or had gathered them at the end as though stolen works, or at least works highly suspect of being [Col. 0010D] spurious. From this latter class we retained certain treatises: namely, those that we judged neither useless nor to have been published anywhere else. Concerning all these, as also concerning certain little works published for the first time in this edition, we add nothing; for the *Admonition* prefixed to each writing sufficiently explains whatever the reader needs to know beforehand.

[Col. 0011A] To come now to the works not admitted into our edition from the earlier ones: those which the Romans had already rejected from Gillot’s edition, we likewise repudiated as manifestly spurious. Such is the fragment *On the Faith of the Resurrection*, which Gillot had appended, though not without some hesitation, to Ambrose’s genuine book on the same subject. He would never have taken care to publish it, however, if he had discovered that it had been pieced together from Jerome’s letter to Pammachius against the errors of John of Jerusalem.

The same is true of the meditations taken, as Gillot himself testifies, from the archives of the Paris Charterhouse. They are all found among the meditations that may be read in Augustine, volume IX of the Louvain edition, though not in the same order. These very pieces appear [Col. 0011B] in the Appendix to volume VI of the new edition, and are preceded by an *Admonition* which anyone can readily consult. Nor are the following writings unlike them; indeed, they depart still further from Ambrose’s character: brief letters of philosophers, which Gillot, following Gilbert Cognatus, published as having been translated by the holy man from Greek into Latin. With these the Romans likewise rejected the second of the two letters concerning a possessed monk, which the Gillot edition had reproduced from a single German manuscript, where the three books *On Duties* immediately follow them. That letter was rightly removed beyond doubt, since it is none other than Gregory the Great’s letter to Januarius, bishop of Cagliari. But since the other is a fragment torn from the end of the book *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues*, there was no reason for the [Col. 0011C] Roman edition to retain it. In addition, neither letter bears Ambrose’s name inscribed in our manuscript; hence it is clear that both were wrongly attributed to him merely because they were appended to the books *On Duties*.

Now, to discuss those treatises which, although not rejected by the Roman edition, we nevertheless decided to exclude from ours, the books *On the Calling of the Gentiles* will lead the way. These books have indeed been published until now among the Ambrosian works, but critics agree with equal consistency that they are not Ambrose’s, even while they disagree about their true author. To avoid recounting here the individual opinions about them, there are the dissertations of two learned men, Quesnel and Antelmi. The former, having published these [Col. 0011D] books among the works of Saint Leo, brought forward the arguments by which he thought they could be attributed to that Pontiff; the latter, believing that his own Prosper was being wronged, recently defended Prosper’s claims against Quesnel. We shall speak again about this matter in the Letter to Demetrias, where we shall deal with the rejected letters.

We also omitted the book *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues*, which they had published at the end of volume V of the Roman edition. Some manuscripts attribute it to our Ambrose, others to Augustine, and others even to Leo—but all with equal falsity. Best of all, however, one codex [Col. 0012A] of the abbey of Saint-Ebrulf bears it under the name of Ambrose Autpert. To Autpert it has already been vindicated by arguments of no little force in the Appendix to volume VI of the final edition of Augustine, where that same discussion is found.

[Col. 0012A] Moreover, in the Appendix to Ambrose’s works there are certain little pieces which in this edition we have thought it superfluous to reprint: for example, the *Exposition of the Faith of the Nicene Creed against Arius and Photinus*, which has been entirely stitched together from several passages of the first book of Saint Ambrose’s *On the Faith*; likewise the *Exhortation to Undertake Repentance*, since it is found in almost identical words in Sermon 393 among Augustine’s works, so that it is plainly evident that it must be denied to Ambrose. Add also the treatise *On the Customs of the Brahmans*, whose omission no one would complain about, since it is wholly unworthy of Ambrose. Finally, the order of the works rejected is closed by the *Sermon on the Purification of Saint Mary*. Although not a few codices attribute it to Ambrose, and the distinguished Baluze published it from an old manuscript in which it bore the name of Alcuin, in the first volume of his *Miscellanies*, it nevertheless seems more probable that this sermon belongs to Ambrose Autpert. For, apart from the fact that the most ancient codex of Fleury presents it under his name, Peter the Deacon testifies that the same author wrote most beautiful homilies on the saints and on this feast of the most blessed Virgin (*On the Illustrious Men of Cassino*, chap. 13).

[Col. 0012B] Let what has been said suffice concerning the works that at some time held a place among the Ambrosian writings or in their Appendix. We shall now examine [Col. 0012C] those that are nowhere found in the editions of the holy Doctor’s volumes. A *Book of the Physiologus* is cited in the Decree from the Roman Synod held under Pope Gelasius; it was written by heretics and marked with the name of Blessed Ambrose, and is apocryphal (*Distinctio* 15, chapter “Holy Rome”). Hormisdas likewise prohibited it in a decretal; but this treatise has long since vanished.

In the library of Saint Gall in Switzerland there are preserved two codices a thousand years old. In one of them there is a treatise under this heading: “Book of Saint Ambrose, bishop, against the heretics,” whose opening is: “David, with a single stroke of a stone,” and in the other there is another treatise entitled: “Book of Saint Ambrose, bishop, composed in praise of the saints,” whose first words are: “It is our concern, beloved brothers.” At our request, our Mabillon had both [Col. 0012D] copied while he was examining the libraries of Germany. But when we had reexamined the former—which we also possess copied from a Paris manuscript and which is cited as Ambrosian in the *Milleloquium* of Urbino—we discovered that it is only part of a work that was published once and again in the *Library of the Fathers*: first under the heading “Bishop Faustinus against the Arians,” and again under this one: “Gregory of Baetica, bishop of Illiberis, to Galla Placidia Augusta.” Although some, led by this inscription, have attributed the work to Gregory, it is more correctly assigned by others to Faustinus; but pressing this matter is not relevant here.

As for the second of these treatises, [Col. 0013A], you may understand that it too is foreign to Ambrose from the following fact: it is a sermon delivered by an anonymous bishop who plainly relates that he had returned from Britain, where he had stayed for a long time for the purpose of restoring peace. What seems to have deceived those who thought this writing should be attributed to our Doctor is that its author mentions the saints Protasius and Gervasius, and even addresses Ambrose himself. But this last point sufficiently proves that it is not an address by the holy Bishop.

[Col. 0013A] In the codices of the Ambrosian Library at Milan there are also several little works prefaced with the title of our Doctor. Some of these were discovered and copied by the Mabillon mentioned above and his companion, Dom Michael Germanus, while searching through the museums of Italy with their customary diligence. The first is entitled the [Col. 0013B] *Confession of Faith of Saint Ambrose*, and begins: “The faith written down at Nicaea was sufficient.” But Father Jacques Homey, an Augustinian theologian, published it from a Colbert manuscript in the *Supplement to the Fathers*; Father Quesnel had already published it in volume II of the works of Saint Leo, page 138, where it bears the name of Faustinus at its head. Nothing conflicts with the arguments by which Quesnel vindicates it for Faustinus and asserts that it was written between the years 379 and 381; but nothing supports our regarding it as Ambrose’s.

To this little document our Mabillon and Germanus also added two others, namely a *Little Book of Faith* and a *Letter on Modesty and Chastity*. The little book is acephalous, while the letter is truncated at the end; and, in addition, both are so broken up [Col. 0013C] by frequent lacunae that, even if they departed less from Ambrose’s character, they would scarcely be worth the paper and labor required to publish them. The same judgment should be made concerning certain other writings said to be found in the same library under these titles: *On Offering Firstfruits*, *On Those Who Quarrel over Superior Things*, and *Against the Astronomers*. Our associates mentioned above were unable to investigate these little works because of the limited time they spent in Milan.

In the Vatican Library, besides a few writings that we published in the Appendix, there are others attributed to Ambrose: namely, *On Blessed Peter and Simon Magus*, which is a fragment of book II of Eusebius Pamphilus’s *Ecclesiastical History*, translated into Latin; also *On Peter’s Repentance*, *On the Slaughter of Agag*, *On the Faith [Col. 0013D] to Blessed Jerome*, and *A Sentence on a Penitent Man*. This *Sentence* is also found in a Cistercian manuscript under the heading “Treatise of Saint Ambrose, bishop, on Repentance,” while in the Appendix to Jerome’s works it is prefaced as follows: “Letter of Saint Jerome to a certain man who was doing penance in the world.” Perhaps those with sufficient leisure will find the remaining treatises mentioned above among other authors; for us, however, it is enough that from reading the copies we possess here we have ascertained with certainty that they are not Ambrose’s.

[Col. 0014A] The Gallican libraries likewise boast certain little writings never published among Ambrose’s works, but falsely claiming the Ambrosian designation. Thus, in the Royal Library there are sermons *On the Eucharist*, *On the Man Born Blind*, *On Peace*, *On the False Friend*, and *Against Those Who Do Not Confess That the Soul Was Created, or Who Say That It Is Derived by Descent*; in the Colbert Library, sermons *On the Nativity of Blessed Mary*, *To Those Living in Monasteries*, and *On the Malice of the Flesh*; and in certain provincial libraries similar pseudonymous writings are found, such as the *Letter of Saint Ambrose to Hilary*. But since none of these, or similar writings, could deceive learned men who happened to encounter them, and their spuriousness is immediately recognized, we think nothing need be added here.

Nevertheless, two compositions must not be passed over in silence. They have never been published in the body [Col. 0014B] of the Ambrosian works, but elsewhere they have been published under Ambrose’s name. One is found in Bolland on 20 January under the heading: “Acts of Saint Sebastian the Martyr, by Saint Ambrose, bishop.” But all critics of more refined judgment have easily recognized this inscription as false. Indeed, they display far less of the Ambrosian genius than do the Acts either of Saints Protasius and Gervasius or of Saints Vitalis and Agricola—although their proper place in the Appendix will clearly show that we were not wrong to relegate those works there. It is therefore surprising that so learned a man could have erred in this matter.

The other of the two works we mentioned is the history of Hegesippus concerning the Jewish war and the destruction of Jerusalem. Certain editions attribute this history to Ambrose, and so do some manuscripts. For example, the fourth [Col. 0014C] of its five books is entitled as follows in a codex of the Carmelite house at Clermont: “The fourth chapter of Saint Ambrose, bishop, on the dispersion of the Jews, from Flavius Josephus the historian.” To this may be added the testimony of Cassiodorus, who asserts that in his own time there existed a version of Josephus attributed by some to Saint Jerome, by others to Rufinus, and by others to Ambrose (*On Divine Literature*, chap. 17).

Yet we learn from Jerome’s own letter to Lucinius of Baetica that it is not Jerome’s, since there he declares that he translated nothing from Josephus’s history. Nor does the wording itself seem to allow us to assign it to Rufinus; and thus all probability returns to Ambrose. One may also add several expressions [Col. 0014D] common to the author or translator of this history and to our Bishop, which Gronovius claims to have carefully collected for comparison.

It is easy, however, to answer that such an argument from comparison is deceptive, since anyone can readily cut out and assemble similar formulas of speech from entirely different authors. The authority of Cassiodorus can also be dissolved without difficulty. Either he did not indicate this history, since it consists not of seven books but only five, and is not so much a translation of Josephus’s books as an abridgment, with narratives often inserted from elsewhere; or, even if he did designate this very work, no one will deny that it happens every day that, when the true author of some work is unknown, several people are popularly substituted for him, all equally falsely.

[Col. 0015A] It is credible that, from that same popular rumor, some audacious person inscribed Ambrose’s name in certain codices, after which the error was propagated still further. Certainly, there is nothing Ambrosian in this work, neither in style nor in judgment. Nor will anyone easily force us to believe that Ambrose had as much leisure for serious matters as would have been necessary to write not only these five books but also the other four that the author says he composed from the same number of Kings.

As for the word *Hegesippus*, we hold that this was done *παρὰ τοῦ Ἰοσηποῦ*—“from Josephus”—but that scribes, in place of *Josephus* or *Josippus*, beneath which the author intended to remain concealed, corruptly substituted *Hegesippus* or *Egesippus*.

[Col. 0015B] But to bring this section to an end, it would be desirable that, in place of so many little books wrongly inscribed with Ambrose’s name, antiquity had preserved and transmitted to us all the genuine offspring of his mind with greater fidelity and care. Among the works we miss, the first place must be given to the *Commentaries on the Prophet Isaiah*. From them Augustine is able to read and cite many passages against the Pelagian heresy; and Ambrose himself mentions them in his *Exposition of the Gospel according to Luke* (book II, no. 56).

Another outstanding work of our Ambrose has likewise perished, although Augustine mentions it with great praise. Writing to Paulinus of Nola, he says: “I believe that Your Holiness possesses the books of the most blessed Pope Ambrose; but I desire those which he wrote with the greatest care and fullness against certain exceedingly ignorant and exceedingly proud men who maintain that the Lord derived His learning from Plato’s books” (*Letter* 31, new edition). The same work is cited by him in various places under different titles. At times he calls it *On the Sacraments*, or *On Philosophy*; at times *On the Sacrament of Regeneration*, or *On Philosophy*; sometimes simply *On Regeneration*; and elsewhere *On Philosophy against Plato*. We deeply regret that this most beautiful disputation has perished. Yet it is no small consolation to us that many works still remain in which he never fails to refute and crush those rash men whenever an opportunity arises, as we have shown in the proper places.

[Col. 0015D] We do not sufficiently understand in what sense Ambrose’s statement should be taken: “We have already arranged a great many things concerning the deeds of Elijah in the frequent discourse of various books” (*On Elijah and Fasting*, chap. 3, no. 5). For if the holy man means nothing else by this than that his books frequently mention the deeds of Elijah, scarcely anything will appear to have been lost in this respect. But if he testifies that he treated that subject expressly in several books, we must say that those books perished many centuries ago.

There is less reason for doubt concerning the treatise that he wrote about the boy Pansophius, whom he had raised from the dead, as Paulinus the deacon relates in these words: “For that little child [Col. 0016A] also he composed a little book, so that what he could not know because of the infancy of his age he might learn by reading” (*Life of Ambrose*, no. 28). But it is an established fact that this little book has nowhere been found for a very long time.

That same most faithful deacon of Ambrose has handed down to memory that he composed and sent to Fritigil, who was queen of the Marcomanni, an instruction in the Catholic faith. He says of it: “For her, namely Fritigil, he wrote a distinguished letter in the form of a catechism” (*ibid.*, no. 36). We have no doubt that this little jewel has completely vanished. For those who wish a certain fragment cited in Greek by Theodoret (*Polyhistorical Dialogues*, dialogue 2), and to be cited below by us as well, to have been taken from that letter are simply guessing.

Although Ambrose himself appears to have arranged his letters into a book [Col. 0016B], it is beyond dispute that many are absent from the collection that now survives (*Letter* 48, no. 7), including very important ones, as may be inferred from the persons to whom they were written. Nevertheless, we believe that the letter to Irenaeus, in which mention is made of a speaking partridge and which some claim was lost through the injury of time, has survived intact. What misled those learned men will be explained more clearly elsewhere.

It is also highly probable that certain works of the holy Doctor that have perished were composed against the sect of Apollinaris, since Paternus, bishop of Braga, who had given his name to that heresy, is said to have been converted to the true faith by reading books against the Apollinarists published by Ambrose.

[Col. 0016C] Many believe that Cassiodorus’s words refer to some lost sermon: “Saint Ambrose, bishop of Milan, delivered a sermon on the judgment of Solomon” (*On Divine Literature*, chap. 2). We nevertheless believe that nothing else is indicated there than the opening of the book *On Virginity*, which until now had been connected in a single sequence with the third book *On Virgins*. Its opening words are: “It is reported among the ancients that Solomon’s judgment was noble …” We shall show that this opening has little affinity with the rest of the book and is perhaps some homily that the scribes joined to that work.

The same Cassiodorus, when discussing the Book of Wisdom, speaks as follows: “Concerning it both Father Augustine and Saint Ambrose said certain things under the name of homilies” (*ibid.*, chap. 5). If Senator truly saw these homilies, and if the title truthfully attributed them to Saint Ambrose, it will have to be said that they did not reach our age. For apart from those sermons from which we have often shown that many of the holy Doctor’s books are composed, no others now remain; this will be proved by us in the appropriate place.

Finally, in that same Cassiodorus we read [Col. 0017A]: “It is also said that Saint Ambrose composed commentaries on the prophets in the usual sweetness of his eloquence. I was wholly unable to find them, and I leave them to you to seek with great diligence” (*ibid.*, chap. 3). It is not sufficiently clear which commentary is meant, unless perhaps the *Commentaries on Isaiah*. Since, however, the phrase “it is said” asserts nothing, and since Cassiodorus himself, as already mentioned, was accustomed to devote every effort to seeking the books of the ancients, you may infer that he was deceived by common report, or that those writings had already disappeared in his own age.

There are some who think that Ambrose also expounded Proverbs, and who interpret the opening words of the book *On the Mysteries* in that sense: “We delivered a daily discourse on moral matters, when either the deeds of the Patriarchs were being read or the precepts of Proverbs.” It is indeed certain that at that time the blessed Bishop was engaged in explaining the histories of the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and others. If he likewise devoted similar labor to elucidating the Book of Proverbs, it must be admitted that that commentary is missing. [Col. 0017B]

But since at that point Ambrose is speaking only of the sermons that he delivered daily to the people, nothing prevents our supposing that, after composing books from his discourses on the Patriarchs, he changed nothing in those that were in the form of expositions of Proverbs. These, like loose and scattered leaves, may have been lost; or perhaps they were never committed to writing at all, which is certainly known to have happened with other sermons of the same Ambrose.

They further say that he himself testifies to having discussed at length the marriage of the Blessed Virgin with Saint Joseph, and from this they infer that the holy man wrote some book on this subject which no longer survives. Yet since we find him treating this very matter several times—for example, once and again in the *Exposition of the Gospel of Luke* [Col. 0017C] (book II, no. 1 and following, and book X, no. 133), in the *Book on the Institution of a Virgin* in equally many places (chapters 6 and 7), and more briefly in the third hymn (stanza 5)—there is no need to understand Ambrose’s statement as referring to a lost book. This is especially so since he could have treated the same subject again in the commentaries on Isaiah and in other works that truly have perished.

Here too is the passage that we read in Ambrose: “Thus that Samson—as a summary of the history; for the arrangement of the entire reading must be reserved for its proper time” (*Prologue to the Book on the Holy Spirit*, no. 12). This has led [Col. 0018A] some to suppose that our Doctor promised to publish a commentary on the deeds of Samson. Although he continued the same history in his letter to Vigilius (*Letter* 19), they say that he nevertheless failed to fulfill his pledge: not only is there no explanation of that history there, but the promised work, they claim, was to be a public writing, whereas the letter was private.

But, leaving aside the fact that Ambrose was not unaware that his letters quite frequently became public, who does not see that nothing certain or definite is promised in Ambrose’s words, and that they may indicate a sermon rather than a treatise? Moreover, it often happens that a similar promise is forgotten when its author is distracted and occupied by other concerns.

Leontius of Byzantium [Col. 0018B] cites an Ambrosian testimony from a book, he says, *Against Apollinaris* (book II, *Against Nestorius and Eutyches*), which is denied to be found among the works now circulated under Ambrose’s name. But there is no reason to have great confidence in this author’s care in citation, since in book I *Against Nestorius and Eutyches* he produces two passages under the same heading, although they are found in the book *On the Mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation*, and not in precisely the same words. What, then, if we believe that this third passage, which we read cited in the following book as though taken from the same source as those two, was likewise drawn from *On the Incarnation*, even though the same words were not preserved?

Finally, there are those who maintain, on the basis of a splendid passage in Augustine (*Soliloquies*, book II, chap. 14)—which we shall not quote because it is somewhat [Col. 0018C] longer—that our Ambrose published a separate work *On the Immortality of the Soul*. Yet for Augustine’s words to have a full and complete sense, it seems sufficient that Ambrose discussed that immortality in various books. If someone should insist that the passage signifies a treatise expressly composed on that subject, we do not resist the claim, provided that it be understood as referring to the letters written by our Doctor to Horontianus on the same matter (*Letter* 34 and following).

# [ON THE DUTIES OF MINISTERS.]

[Col. 0017D]

# ADMONITION TO THE THREE BOOKS *ON THE DUTIES OF MINISTERS*

[Col. 0017]

Since the sacred ministers hold an honored place among the other faithful in the Lord’s flock, Ambrose—who was ever intent on instructing every order of the parish entrusted to him—could not leave the conduct of that distinguished portion without precepts by which it might both attain the sanctity appropriate to its office and lead the people along the same path by the example of its virtues. Hence the origin of these books. For after he had diligently endeavored to instruct his clergy orally in piety, he later resolved, lest the precepts given should gradually slip from their minds, to collect them into the body of a proper work and hand them over to them as something they might always carry, as it were, in their hands and bosoms. He therefore rightly entitled the work *On the Duties of Ministers*, a title which we have restored from nearly all the manuscripts and from the better class of witnesses.

In the first book (chapter 1), after immediately setting forth the reasons that had induced him to write, not without an ingenuous humility concerning himself, he shows (chapter 2 and following) that silence is the best teacher of speech and must especially be maintained in anger; and that the king and prophet had given us its rules before Pythagoras, and far more excellently (chapter 10, no. 31). Then, taking up his subject, he skillfully explains the origin of the word *duty* (*officium*) (chapters 8 and 9), its meaning, and the parts into which it is divided (chapter 11). Above all, he warns the Christian man to beware of thinking, after the manner of philosophers, that the honorable or useful is to be measured by the present life rather than by the future one. He says that the intermediate duty consists in observing the commandments, while the perfect duty consists in observing the evangelical counsels; and that the philosophers had known this only through barren speculation. Next (chapter 12 and following), after refuting certain errors, he proceeds to the individual classes of duties. In young men especially he commends (chapter 17 and following) that modesty which governs not merely outward appearance and shines forth in movement, gait, speech, and food, but also orders the inner faculties—namely, through fear of God, reverence for parents, and moderation of the mind’s disturbances. He declares that these qualities are particularly required in clerics, since they ought to be so rightly constituted in every respect that, offering no opening for the slanders of the envious, they may shine before all by the example of a good way of life. Later (chapter 25 and following), after undertaking a discussion of the virtues commonly called cardinal, he establishes that they are the sources of everything honorable and seemly, which is the subject of this book. Although he admits that these virtues cannot be separated from one another, he nevertheless treats them individually. First, after defining prudence (chapter 27), he demonstrates that the pagan sages fell into vices which they nevertheless knew to be at war with prudence itself. In the same way he treats justice (chapter 28 and following), examining its various parts, especially generosity and benevolence. Speaking of fortitude (chapter 35 and following), he teaches that it consists in two things: contempt for external circumstances, and the undertaking and execution of great, difficult, laborious, and dangerous enterprises. On this occasion he proves by examples the excellence of the men produced under the Old Covenant (chapter 40 and following), by whom pagan heroes are surpassed in military glory; but he asserts that Christian fortitude consists in contempt for earthly things, endurance of injuries and calamities, and the suffering of the most savage punishments for the sake of Christ’s faith. Finally, beginning to speak of temperance (chapter 43 and following), he explains all its parts, among which the chief are tranquillity of mind, devotion to gentleness, care for what is honorable, and consideration of what is seemly. To these he adds the principle that the greater moral good must always be preferred to the lesser.

After demonstrating at the very beginning of the second book that the honorable gives rise to happiness (Book II, chapter 1), he refutes (chapter 2 and following) the errors of the philosophers and of Cicero concerning the highest good of this life, showing that it is situated in knowledge of the divinity and in the fruit of good works. Since the same honorable end is attained through the useful good, he discusses the useful throughout the whole book. Since the useful itself both consists in piety and is inseparable from the honorable (chapter 6 and following), he teaches that it cannot be attained except through those virtues which win us esteem and affection among human beings. He then sets forth three ways of winning people over (chapter 8 and following): namely, that one may bind their love to oneself by beneficence, their trust by justice and prudence, and their admiration by distinguished and outstanding deeds. He illustrates all these points with highly appropriate examples, drawn for the most part from divine authority. Yet nothing more pious can be imagined than those precepts by which he instructs us in works of mercy (chapter 15 and following) and in all the duties belonging to the mutual fellowship of human beings, while at the same time proscribing the vices opposed to them.

In the third book the holy Bishop compares the honorable good with the useful. Yet he does not fail to warn us (Book III, chapter 2) that these two kinds of good are joined by an indissoluble bond in righteous men, and therefore that this comparison is undertaken only on the basis of the popular opinion that separates them. From this he establishes the following general principle: a good man should think that he ought to deprive no one else of anything, nor wish to increase his own profit through another’s disadvantage (ibid., no. 13). He proves this both by natural and human laws and by divine laws drawn from both Testaments (chapter 3 and following). To the objections raised against these principles he gives this answer: Christian men must not depart from the example of Christ, who never preferred his own advantage to that of another. From this he concludes that in every action and transaction, in every circumstance, the honorable must always be preferred to the useful (chapter 5 and following), even if it were entirely certain that our deceit would be hidden from God no less than from human beings. He adds that this law was sanctioned by God himself, and that there is no need to resort to ancient fables in order to establish so certain a matter. For the Christian religion supplied examples of it (chapter 9 and following) in those great men who truly carried out what among the pagans was regarded as miraculous. Finally, he shows that even the greatest examples among the Romans are in every respect inferior to the sacred heroes (chapter 15 and following).

We do not deny that Ambrose proposed to follow Cicero’s arrangement in his own *On Duties*; but we boldly affirm that Cicero himself imitated the books of Panaetius and Hecato far more closely. For the holy Bishop plainly indicates that he undertook to imitate the Orator for no other reason than that, in the case of the man who above all others professed exact laws of morality, he might more forcefully refute the false precepts of pagan ethics, and at the same time openly show by how great a distance Christian teaching surpassed whatever had ever been most excellent among the gentiles. Everywhere he rejects that empty affectation of eloquence which Cicero never ceases to display. At various points, moreover, he labors to demonstrate clearly that whatever the philosophers taught that was more excellent in moral discipline had been wholly taken from our own authors. Above all, he overturns the arrogance of that same Tullius and completely abolishes his doctrines concerning revenge and ambition. But he strives with the greatest insistence to establish a point which Cicero scarcely touched upon: namely, that our principal duties concern God and that all our deeds and words must be referred to his glory. He also vigorously proves the further point of which the Orator had not even the faintest notion: that the present life is a road to immortality and that one reaches it through good works. In addition, he commands that the mind be withdrawn from earthly goods, that the body’s wantonness be restrained by stricter discipline, that offenses and injuries inflicted by enemies be forgiven, and that greater benefits be bestowed upon those who have harassed us with greater cruelty and injustice. [Col. 0021]

But so that the curious reader may more easily recognize in what matters our Ambrose agrees with Cicero or differs from him, we have displayed in the lower margin all the passages both of the *Duties* and of the other works of the same author to which the holy Bishop appears to have referred. In this way it will immediately become clear that Ambrose departs from Marcus Tullius wherever the affinity between the two is not indicated by a marginal reference. It will also become evident with what judgment Augustine called these same books filled with the most useful precepts (Letter 82, to Jerome, no. 21), and how deservedly everyone has valued them down to the present day, as may be understood from manuscripts of every age that one finds in libraries.

Who, then, could endure a Christian author’s daring to say of these books: “Saint Ambrose also wrote *On Duties*, I believe, in order to inculcate religion in children. For my part, I think religion should be drawn from the divine Scriptures; on civil morals I would rather hear Cicero”? It is not easy to determine whether this opinion inflicts the graver injury upon Ambrose or upon the sacred pages. For since these civil morals are nothing other than human actions to be ordered by prudence and the other cardinal virtues, is it not monstrous insolence to prefer profane ethics to those precepts which the Holy Spirit breathed concerning this subject through the prophets, or which Christ himself dictated with his own mouth to his apostles? It is therefore no longer surprising if a heterodox writer holds in contempt these books, in which this holy Doctor interprets Christ’s moral teaching; contempt for the Fathers is familiar to such people.

The same author himself, moreover, supplies grounds for doubting whether he ever read these books, when he writes: “I believe it was to inculcate religion in children.” For Ambrose himself, in quite a few passages, and the title of the work in very many manuscripts—as has already been said—testify that they were intended not for children but for the ministers of the Church of every age. Nevertheless, although the author’s purpose was to educate the clergy, no one will deny that the work is useful to every condition of life. For since clerics have superiors whom they obey and inferiors whom they govern, it has consequently come about that the work contains very many precepts rich in benefit for everyone.

This same usefulness was the reason why these books were not only copied so many times, but also reduced by many people into the form of abridgments or excerpts. Excerpts from them survive in one manuscript of the monastery of Lérins; an abridgment survives in one codex of the Church of Chartres, skillfully arranged with connections and transitions. A copy of this was transcribed through his own efforts and sent to us by D. Le Feron, a canon of that distinguished church and a doctor of the Sorbonne. We do not deny that this exemplar was produced by an ancient hand, but many others available to us are older still. For, to pass over the Benignian manuscript of eight hundred years, the three Vatican manuscripts, the Laon, Crespi, and Bigot manuscripts of approximately seven hundred years, the Colbert manuscript alone—otherwise called the Thuaneum—was unquestionably produced more than a thousand years ago and exceeds the Chartres manuscript by at least four centuries. Moreover, since in all those codices our *Duties* are divided into three books, this is clear evidence that the Chartres manuscript is nothing other than an epitome. The work could readily be condensed in this way, since examples and digressions may be removed without loss of meaning.

As for the age of the work itself, some maintain that our Ambrose first set his hand to writing it at the very beginning of his episcopate. Baronius seems to support this opinion when, under the year 377, he says of it: “Afterward he undertook to write those three excellent books, when he had instructed the people for some time.” But if the great Cardinal had held this opinion, he would not have agreed with himself; for he himself assigns to events occurring at some considerable interval after the aforementioned year 377 certain facts that are mentioned in this work. For example, Ambrose there recalls that he sold Church vessels for the redemption of captives (Book II, chapters 15 and 28). Baronius refers this to the war waged against the tyrant Maximus in the year 387, although it seems more probable to us that it concerns the barbarian invasion which, in the year 379, after the death of Valens, devastated Thrace and Illyricum and advanced as far as Italy, from which they carried away countless captives.

This same opinion concerning these books is refuted by the fact that in them he clearly directs the reader to consult his own book *On Noah and the Ark*, published in the year 379, as has been demonstrated. In addition, he repeatedly says that he is speaking there to those clerics upon whom he himself had laid hands. From this it is evident that his clergy was already sufficiently numerous and had therefore been established for several years. He also indicates that Justina’s persecution had continued for many years when he says that, because of the deposits of widows, he had suffered many attacks from the imperial court (ibid., chapter 29, no. 150). Nor does the account of the two clerics who fell away from the faith during the time of the Arian assault (Book I, chapter 18, no. 72) seem to refer to any persecution other than Justina’s, around the year 386.

Furthermore, the holy Bishop complains that all foreigners had been driven out of Rome by an unusual scarcity of grain; Baronius states that this famine occurred in the year 383. Others, however, maintain that the Romans suffered from a shortage of grain once and again: first toward the end of the life of Damasus, the pontiff whom Ambrose calls “the most holy old man” (Book III, chapter 7), and secondly after his death, which is placed in the year 384. On this view, Baronius spoke only of the earlier famine, although our Ambrose indicated both.

What is also said about the deposit of the widow of Ticinum seems capable of being applied to no other event more appropriately (Book II, chapter 29, no. 150) than to a certain law issued by Valentinian the Younger in the city of Pavia on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March. For from the place where it was issued it may sufficiently be inferred that, while the emperor was passing through that city, his mother Justina—who was relentlessly hostile to the Catholic bishops—induced him to attempt to cause such trouble for the bishop of Ticinum.

All these considerations lead us to believe that these books were composed only after Justina’s persecutions, the war against the tyrant Maximus, and his assassination very shortly thereafter—that is, around the year 391. At that time, having experienced a more peaceful condition for his Church, he resolved to arrange into the body of a proper work those precepts which he had taught his clergy from the sacred pulpit during the first years of his episcopate, and to hand them over to them for constant use. For there is no room for doubt that these books consist for the most part of sermons delivered publicly, since in the first book passages of Scripture are expounded which he himself recalls as having been read in the assembly. Perhaps he wished to treat them there again because, having once seen the minds of his hearers moved by them, he hoped for the same fruit if they were read through attentively by those very people.

[Col. 0023B]

SAINT AMBROSE, BISHOP OF MILAN, THREE BOOKS ON THE DUTIES OF MINISTERS [Note: [Col. 0023B] The word “ministers” was missing in the earlier editions and in several more recent manuscripts; we have restored it from the best and most numerous witnesses. On this matter, see what was said above in the introductory notice.] [Note: [Col. 0023B] Written around the year 391.] (C)

[Col. 0023]

BOOK ONE.

1. CHAPTER ONE.

[Col. 0023A]

The bishop’s proper duty is to teach; but he must learn in order to teach; indeed, he must even teach what he has not learned, or at least must both learn and teach at the same time.

1. I do not think it arrogant if, among my children, I assume the desire to teach, since the Teacher of humility himself said: “Come, children, listen to me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord” (Psalm 33:12). In this saying one may observe both the humility of his modesty and his graciousness. [Note: [Col. 0023B] Several manuscripts read, “for by teaching the fear,” and so forth. More numerous and better manuscripts, as well as all the editions, have the reading given in the text. Again, where the old edition, together with some manuscripts, reads “a distinguished lesson in modesty,” the Roman edition, with by far the greater part of the manuscripts, more correctly reads “a distinction of modesty,” that is, a sign and, as it were, a banner of modesty.] For by saying “the fear of the Lord,” which seems to be common to everyone, he expressed a mark of modesty. Yet since fear itself is the beginning of wisdom [Note: [Col. 0023B] One Vatican manuscript reads, “and of accomplished blessedness.”] and the cause of blessedness—for those who fear God are blessed—he clearly showed himself to be a teacher of wisdom and a guide toward attaining blessedness. [Col. 0023B] [Note: [Col. 0023B] Thus read the old edition and a large number of written codices. The Roman edition, however, and several of those same old manuscripts have in the margin *pudenter significavit* (“he indicated modestly”); the latest Paris editions and not a few manuscripts read *prudenter* (“wisely”); one manuscript even has *potenter significavit* (“he indicated powerfully”).]

2. Therefore, being diligent in imitating his modesty and not arrogating to ourselves the imparting of the grace [Note: [Col. 0023C] Several manuscripts read, “which that Spirit [imparted].”] of wisdom which that Spirit infused into him, we, through him, hand over to you as children what has been made manifest to us through sight and example, [Col. 0024A] since we can no longer escape the duty of teaching which the necessity of the priesthood imposed upon us against our will. For “God appointed some as apostles, some as prophets, others as evangelists, and others as pastors and teachers” (Ephesians 4:11). [Note: [Col. 0023C] The editions of Erasmus and those following him, together with three or four manuscripts, read *usu comperta* (“discovered by experience”); the edition of Amerbach, with at least twenty-five manuscripts, more correctly reads *visu comperta* (“discovered by sight”). For how could he say that these things had been discovered by experience, at the very point where he professes himself such a novice in ecclesiastical knowledge? Rather, “discovered by sight,” that is, by reading: he evidently indicates that he will transmit examples of virtues which he observed recorded in the Scriptures. Moreover, he indicates none too obscurely that scarcely anything binds bishops more closely or more sacredly than the duty of teaching. It is true that from the earliest centuries of the Church this responsibility was entrusted by certain bishops to priests; among these were Augustine and Chrysostom, who performed that office with great benefit to the Church, unlike the notorious Arius, who performed it to the Church’s great ruin. Nevertheless, Saint Ambrose himself continually fulfilled this part of his episcopal office, instructing not only the clergy but also his people, speaking publicly every Sunday, as Augustine testified in *Confessions*, Book VI, chapter 3; we too observed this in the preceding volume, in the introductory notice to the exposition of the Gospel according to Luke.] 

3. I do not therefore claim for myself the glory of the apostles. [Note: [Col. 0024C] Some manuscripts and Gill in the margin read, “the vigilance of the apostles.”] For who could do this except those whom the Son of God himself chose? Nor do I claim the grace of the prophets, the power of the evangelists, or the watchfulness of pastors. I desire only to attain the apostles’ attention and diligence concerning the divine Scriptures, which he placed last among the duties of the saints, and I desire to learn this very thing so that I may devote myself to teaching. For there is one true Teacher, who alone did not first learn what he was to teach everyone; human beings, however, learn first what they are to teach, and receive from him what they are to hand on to others.

4. Yet even this did not happen to me. For I was snatched from the tribunals and the insignia of public administration [Note: [Col. 0025D] The *infula* was a head ornament made of woolen thread. It was appropriate not only to magistrates but also to suppliant speakers, priests, and even the victims themselves. When Ambrose says that he was snatched from the tribunals into the priesthood, Paulinus explains the matter more fully in his life of Ambrose; later writers borrowed the same account from him.] into the priesthood, and I began to teach you what I myself had not learned. Thus it happened that I began to teach before I began to learn. I must therefore learn and teach at the same time, since previously I had no leisure to learn. [Note: [Col. 0025D] All editions continue after the word “learn” as follows: “And however much anyone may have progressed, no one lives who does not need to be taught.” But since these words are entirely absent from the manuscripts—with the exception of one Laon manuscript, scarcely older than the editions themselves and interpolated with not a few additions of this kind—it is clear that they are nothing more than some marginal note which was carelessly introduced into the text.]

CHAPTER TWO.

There are many dangers incurred by speaking, and Scripture shows that their remedy lies in silence.

5. What, above all else, ought we to learn except to be silent, so that we may be able to speak? Otherwise my own voice may condemn me before another’s voice absolves me; for it is written: “By your words you will be condemned” (Matthew 12:37). Why, then, should you hasten to incur the danger of condemnation by speaking, when by remaining silent you can be safer? I have seen very many fall into sin by speaking, but scarcely anyone by keeping silent; and therefore it is more difficult to know how to be silent than how to speak. I know that most people speak because they do not know how to be silent. It is rare for anyone to keep silent when speaking would do him no good. He is wise, therefore, who knows how to be silent. Finally, the Wisdom of God said: “The Lord has given me a learned tongue, that I may know when I ought to speak” (Isaiah 50:4). Rightly, then, is he wise who receives from the Lord knowledge of the time when he ought to speak. Hence Scripture says well: “A wise man will be silent until the proper time” (Ecclesiasticus 20:7).

6. Therefore the holy men of the Lord, knowing that the human voice is often [Note: [Col. 0025D] The old edition, with some manuscripts, reads “an announcement of sin”; the same editions in the margin, and the Roman edition in the text with one or two manuscripts, have “is joined to sin”; many other codices agree with us.] an announcement of sin and that human speech is the beginning of error, loved to keep silent. Finally, the holy man of the Lord said: “I said, I will guard my ways, so that I may not sin with my tongue” (Psalm 38:2). He knew and had read that it belongs to divine protection for a person to be hidden from the scourge of his own tongue and from the testimony of his own conscience (Job 5:21). We are beaten by the silent reproach of our thoughts and by the judgment of conscience; we are also beaten by the blow of our own voice when we say things whose sound strikes our spirit and wounds our mind. Who possesses a pure heart free from the filth of sins, or does not sin with his tongue? Therefore, because he saw that no one could preserve a holy mouth from the uncleanness of speech, he imposed upon himself, through silence, a law of innocence, so that by keeping silent he might avoid the fault which he could scarcely escape by speaking.

7. Let us therefore listen to the teacher of caution: “I said, I will guard my ways”—that is, I said to myself, by a silent command of thought I charged myself to guard my ways. There are some ways which we ought to follow and others which we ought to guard: we should follow the ways of the Lord and guard our own, lest they lead us into guilt. You can guard them if you do not speak too quickly. The Law says: “Hear, Israel, the Lord your God” (Deuteronomy 6:3). It did not say, “Speak,” but “Hear.” Eve therefore fell because she spoke to the man what she had not heard from the Lord her God. The first voice of God says to you: “Hear.” [Note: [Col. 0026D] Thus read the manuscripts, except three: one reads *custodias* (“you should guard”), another *cito corrigas* (“you should quickly correct”). The edition, together with the Fullingen manuscript, reads: “If you hear, you guard your ways”; the Roman and Fullingen manuscripts read “guard”; “and if you have fallen, quickly correct yourself.” Below, where we have restored from nearly all the manuscripts “so that you may not sin,” the edition, with a few manuscripts, reads “and you will not sin.”] If you hear, you guard your ways; and if you have fallen, you quickly correct yourself. “With what does a young man correct his way?”—with the keeping of your words, Lord (Psalm 118:9). Be silent, then, first, and listen, so that you may not sin with your tongue.

8. It is a grave evil for someone to be condemned by his own mouth. For if each person must give an account for an idle word (Matthew 12:36), how much more for a word of impurity [Col. 0026B] and shamefulness! Words spoken rashly are more serious than idle words. Therefore, if an account is demanded for an idle word, how much more is punishment exacted for speech of impiety!

CHAPTER THREE.

Silence ought not to be perpetual or idle; and how the heart and mouth must be guarded against disordered passions.

9. What, then? Are we to be mute? Certainly not. There is a time for keeping silent and a time for speaking (Ecclesiastes 3:7). Further, if we give an account for an idle word, let us take care that we do not also give an account for idle silence. [Note: [Col. 0026D] The editions of Gill and Rome read, “for there is also a great and burdensome silence.”] For there is also a busy silence, as in the case of Susanna, who accomplished more by keeping silent than she would have by speaking (Daniel 13:3). By keeping silent before human beings, she spoke to God, and she found no greater indication of her chastity than silence. Conscience spoke where no voice was heard; nor did she seek human judgment on her behalf, since she possessed the Lord’s testimony. She therefore wished to be acquitted by him whom she knew could in no way be deceived. The Lord himself, while silent in the Gospel, was working the salvation [Note: [Col. 0026D] Many written codices read “the salvation of all”; some, as well as all the editions, read “the salvation of human beings.”] of human beings (Matthew 26:63). David therefore rightly imposed upon himself not perpetual silence, but watchfulness.

10. Let us therefore guard our heart; let us guard our mouth. Both commands are written: here, that we should guard our mouth; elsewhere it is said to you, “Guard your heart with all vigilance” (Proverbs 4:23). If David guarded his heart, will you not guard yours? If Isaiah had unclean lips—he who said, “Woe is me, for I am pierced, because I am a man and have unclean lips” (Isaiah 6:5)—if the prophet of the Lord had unclean lips, how can we have clean ones?

11. And to whom but each one of us is it written: “Hedge your property with thorns . . . bind your silver and your gold, and make a door and a bar for your mouth, and a yoke and a balance for your words” (Ecclesiasticus 28:28–29)? Your property is your mind; your gold is your heart; your silver is your speech: “The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tested by fire” (Psalm 11:7). A good mind is also a good possession. Indeed, a pure person is a precious possession. Hedge this possession, therefore, and surround it with thoughts; fortify it [Note: [Col. 0027D] The old edition reads “with thorns of anxieties”; some copies in the margin and a few manuscripts in the text read “with pious anxieties,” which the Roman edition admitted into the text. Other manuscripts, not a few, read “with thorns, with anxiety”; the more numerous and better witnesses, however, read “with thorns, with anxieties.” The Bigot manuscript has both: “with thorns, with pious anxieties,” which is not unreasonable.] with thorns and anxieties, lest irrational passions of the body burst into it and carry it away captive; lest violent impulses invade it; lest they plunder its vineyard [Note: [Col. 0027D] Some manuscripts and Gill in the margin read “lest they tear apart the vintage.”] as they pass along the road. Guard your inner person. Do not neglect or despise it as though it were worthless, because it is a precious possession. And rightly precious, since its fruit is not fleeting and temporal but enduring and brings eternal salvation. Cultivate your possession, therefore, [Note: [Col. 0027D] Thus read the old edition and nearly all the manuscripts. The Roman edition, with several other codices, reads “so that they may be lambs for you,” which it also notes in the margin as referring to Proverbs 27:26, although it is not sufficiently clear whether the holy Bishop had that passage in mind.] so that it may be fields for you.

12. Bind your speech, lest it grow luxuriant, become wanton, and gather sins to itself through excessive talking. Let it be restrained and held within its banks. A river in flood quickly gathers mud. Bind your mind; do not let it be slack or drifting, lest it be said of you: “It is not possible to apply a remedy, or oil, or a bandage” (Isaiah 1:6). Sobriety of mind has its own reins by which it is guided and governed.

13. Let there be a door for your mouth, so that it may be closed when necessary, [Col. 0027C] and more carefully barred, lest anyone provoke your voice to anger and you return insult for insult. Today you heard the reading: “Be angry and do not sin” (Psalm 4:5). [Note: [Col. 0027D] The latest Paris edition and some manuscripts read: “Therefore we also become angry, because it is an effect of nature.”] Therefore, even if we are angry—for anger is an affection of nature, not of willful power—let us not bring an evil word out of our mouth, lest we fall into guilt. Let there be a yoke and a balance for your words—that is, humility and measure—so that your tongue may be subject to your mind. Let it be restrained by the bonds of a bridle and have its own reins, by which it may be drawn back to proper measure. Let it produce speeches weighed on the scales of justice, so that there may be gravity in thought, weight in speech, and moderation in words.

CHAPTER FOUR.

The same watchfulness ensures that speech proceeds not from perverse impulses but from right reason; and it is chiefly in this matter that the devil lies in wait for us.

14. If someone guards these things, he becomes gentle, meek, and modest. For by guarding his mouth, restraining his tongue, and not speaking before he has questioned, weighed, and examined [Note: [Col. 0028D] Not a few manuscripts read “his words, if this should be guarded.”] his words—whether this ought to be said, whether it ought to be said against this person, whether this is the proper time for such speech—he truly practices modesty, gentleness, and patience. Thus he does not burst into speech out of indignation and anger, does not reveal in his words any sign of passion, does not show in his speech that the fire of lust is burning, nor that the goads of anger are present in what he says. In the end, speech—which ought to commend a person’s inner character—does not disclose and betray some vice in his conduct.

15. It is then above all that the adversary lies in wait, when he sees that some passions are arising in us; then he stirs up kindling and prepares snares. Therefore, not without reason, as you heard read today, the Prophet says: “For he himself has delivered me from the snare of the hunters and from the harsh word” (Psalm 90:3). [Note: [Col. 0028D] Thus read all the editions and the more numerous and better manuscripts, together with the Roman Psalter and the Vulgate. Some, however, read “he will deliver me,” and are supported by many of the old Psalters and by Augustine. Jerome, on the basis of several Greek codices, has “he will deliver you.” But for *quod est* (“which is”) in the phrase “harsh word,” Symmachus wrote *λόγον ἐπήρειας*, “a word of violent insult, abuse, or injury”; Theodoret wrote *τὸν λόγον ταραχώδη*, “a turbulent and disturbing word.”] Symmachus rendered it “the word of irritation”; others, “of disturbance.” Our speech is the adversary’s snare, but it is also no less our own adversary. We often say what an enemy may seize upon and use, as it were, our own sword to wound us. How much more tolerable it is to perish by another’s sword than by our own!

16. The adversary therefore examines our weapons [Note: [Col. 0028D] The Roman edition and a few manuscripts read, “and sharpens his arrows.”] and brandishes his own. If he sees me agitated, he inserts his barbs, so as to stir up the seeds of quarrels. If I utter an indecorous word, he tightens his snare. Sometimes he sets before me, as bait, the possibility of revenge, so that while I desire to avenge myself, I may insert myself into his snare and tighten the knot of death around me. If, then, anyone senses that this adversary is present, he ought at that moment to exercise greater watchfulness over his mouth, so as not to give the adversary an opening. But not many people see him.

CHAPTER FIVE.

Even against the visible adversary, when he incites us, we must employ silence; by its sole aid we prevail and preserve the humility that must be displayed toward everyone.

17. Yet we must also beware of the one who can be seen—of anyone who insults, incites, exasperates, or suggests incentives to luxury or lust. Therefore, whenever someone abuses us, challenges us, provokes us to violence, or summons us to quarrel, let us then practice silence; let us not be ashamed then to become mute. For the one who provokes us is a sinner, one who does us an injury and desires to make us like himself.

18. Finally, if you remain silent and pretend not to notice, he is accustomed to say: “Why are you silent? Speak, if you dare. But you do not dare; you are mute; I have deprived you of speech.” If you remain silent, he is even more enraged: he thinks himself defeated, mocked, slighted, and ridiculed. If you answer, he thinks himself superior because he has found an equal. For if you remain silent, people will say: “That man abused him; this man despised him.” If you return the insult, they will say: “Both of them abused each other.” Both are condemned; neither is acquitted.

His aim, therefore, is to provoke me so that I may say and do things like him. But it belongs to the righteous person to pretend not to notice, to say nothing, to retain the fruit of a good conscience, to entrust himself more to the judgment of good people than to the insolence of an accuser, and to be content with the dignity of his own conduct. For this is to be silent concerning good things: being conscious of one’s own uprightness, one ought not to be moved by false accusations, nor to consider that another’s abuse carries more weight than one’s own testimony.

19. Thus it comes about that he also preserves humility. But if he does not wish to appear humbler, he turns such thoughts over in his mind and says to himself: “So then, he is to despise me and say such things against me in my presence, as though I could not open my mouth against him? Why, then, should I not also say things with which I could distress him? So then, he is to insult me, as though I were not a man, as though I could not avenge myself? He is to accuse me, as though I could not bring forward still graver charges against him?”

[Note: Hence the Gill and Roman editions, on the authority of one or another manuscript, removed the threefold particle *ut* (“so that”), which, however, the other editions and the very numerous manuscripts present more elegantly. There is here an ellipsis to be supplied with the verb *patiar* (“I shall endure”), *ferendum est* (“it must be endured”), or something similar.]

[Col. 0029C] 20. Whoever says such things is neither gentle nor humble; he is not without temptation. The tempter harasses him and inserts such thoughts into his mind. Often he employs a man and sets an evil spirit beside him to say these things to him: but you should keep your footing fixed upon the rock. Even if a servant utters abuse, the just man remains silent; even if a weak man offers an insult, the just man remains silent; even if a poor man brings an accusation, the just man does not answer. These are the weapons of the just man: to conquer by yielding. Just as skilled javelin-throwers commonly conquer while retreating, and, when fleeing, wound their pursuer with heavier blows.

[Note: The Roman edition alone has: “he employs a wicked man.”]

[Note: Not a few manuscripts read here and below, “let the just man remain silent”; and shortly afterward, “let the just man not answer.”]

## CHAPTER VI

That in this matter David’s silence and humility are to be imitated, so that we may not appear worthy of insult.

[Col. 0029D] 21. Why, indeed, should we be disturbed when we hear abuse? [Col. 0030A] Why do we not imitate the one who says: “I became mute and was humbled, and I kept silent from good things” (Psalm 38:3)? Did he merely say this, and did David not also do it? Indeed, he did so (2 Samuel 16:6 ff.). For when Shimei, the son of Jemini, was reviling him, David remained silent; and although surrounded by armed men, he did not return the insult or seek revenge, even to the point that he did not permit the son of Sarvia, who said that he wished to avenge him, to do so. Thus he went along as one mute and humbled; he went silently and was not disturbed when he was called a man of blood, though he was conscious of his own gentleness. He was therefore not disturbed by insults, for he possessed an abundant consciousness of good works.

[Note: Several manuscripts have here: “When Shimei, the son of Gera, was reviling him, David remained silent”; a few others: “When Shimei, the son of Gera, son of Jemini, was reviling him, David remained silent.” The Roman edition reads: “Shimei, the son of Gera, son of Jemini,” and so forth.]

[Note: The Codex Theodosianus reads: “for he possessed an abundance of honor and consciousness of his works.”]

22. Accordingly, the person who is quickly moved by an insult makes himself appear worthy of abuse, while wishing to prove himself unworthy of it. Better, therefore, is the person who disregards an insult than the one who is pained by it. For the one who disregards it despises it as though he did not feel it; but the one who is pained is tortured as though he had felt it.

[Note: Most manuscripts omit *torquetur* (“is tortured”) after *quasi senserit* (“as though he had felt it”); in its place the Laudian manuscript reads: “he is as though he had felt it.”]

8

## CHAPTER VII

How beautifully Psalm 38 was employed as a preface, by which the holy man was led to resolve to write *On Duties*; and with better right than Cicero formerly wrote to his son, and for what reason.

23. It was not without forethought, then, that, writing to you, my sons, I used the preface of this psalm (Psalm 38:1). The prophet David gave this psalm to the holy Jeduthun to sing; I urge you to hold fast to it, delighted by the depth of its meaning and the force of its statements.

[Note: Compare this passage with what is said in the preceding volume, page 841, numbers 1 and 2, in the heading of this very psalm; you will observe considerable affinity between the two passages.]

For from the points we have briefly touched upon, we perceive that this psalm teaches both patience in keeping silent and the proper occasion for speaking, and, in its later verses (ibid., verse 8), contempt for riches—things that are the greatest foundations of the virtues. As I was therefore considering this psalm, the thought arose in my mind to write *On Duties*.

24. Although some students of philosophy have written on these matters—Panaetius and his son among the Greeks, and Cicero among the Latins—I did not consider it foreign to my office to write on them myself as well. And just as Cicero wrote to educate his son, so I too write to instruct you, my sons; for I love you no less, whom I have begotten in the Gospel, than if I had fathered you in marriage. Nature is not more vigorous in loving than grace.

[Note: Panaetius, whom Tully mentions in more than one place, is reported by Vossius, in his book *On Philosophical Sects*, chapter 19, page 103, to have been a Rhodian; consult that work. As for a son of his who wrote something, you will perhaps find no one besides Ambrose, unless one understands Posidonius, his pupil and successor, concerning whom Cicero speaks in book 3 of *On Duties* and in letter 16 to Atticus, or Hecato, also a pupil of Panaetius, whom the same Tully states wrote six books on this very subject.]

Certainly we ought to love more those whom we think will remain with us forever than those who will remain with us only in this world. The former are often born degenerate, bringing disgrace upon their father; you we chose beforehand, that we might love you. Thus the former are loved by necessity—a necessity that is not a sufficiently suitable or lasting teacher for loving eternally; but you are loved by judgment, by which a great weight is added to the power of love: approving those whom you love, and loving those whom you have chosen.

[Note: An old edition, together with a few manuscripts, reads: “a weight of love.”]

## CHAPTER VIII

That the term *duty* is customary not only among philosophers but also among sacred writers; and from what it is derived.

25. Since, then, the persons are appropriate, let us see whether the subject itself is appropriate for writing about duties, and whether this term belongs only to the school of philosophers or is also found in the divine Scriptures. Thus, while we were reading the Gospel today, the Holy Spirit—almost as though encouraging us to write—offered us a reading by which we might be confirmed that *duty* can also be spoken of among us.

For when Zechariah the priest had become mute in the temple and could not speak, it says: “When the days of his duty were fulfilled, he departed to his own house” (Luke 1:23).

[Note: This is how the Vulgate edition reads. The Greek text, however, has τῆς λειτουργίας αὐτοῦ, “his ministry” or “his service.” But since a duty is what is appropriate to each person, which is expressed in Greek by καθῆκον, and since nothing is so appropriate to a sacred minister as the ministry itself, you may understand from this that the Ambrosian meaning of *duty* can not unreasonably be defended.]

We therefore read that *duty* can be spoken of by us.

9. 26. Nor is the reasoning itself inconsistent with this, since we think that *officium*—“duty”—is derived from *efficiendo*, “bringing about,” as though it were *efficium*; but, for the elegance of speech, one letter having been changed, it is called *officium*.

[Note: Several manuscripts read: “they thought it should be called,” which is incorrect.]

Or certainly, it means that you should do those things which harm no one and benefit everyone.

## CHAPTER IX

That duty is derived from the honorable and the useful, and also from comparison between the two; but that Christians recognize nothing as honorable or useful which does not contribute to the life to come, and therefore that this treatment of duty will not be superfluous.

27. They thought, then, that duties were derived from the honorable and the useful, and that one should choose between those two whatever is preferable.

[Note: Cicero, book 1 of *On Duties*, page 351: “There is therefore a threefold division,” and so forth.]

[Note: Not a few manuscripts read *deinde indicere* (“then to impose”); some read *incedere* (“to proceed”).]

Then it happens that two honorable things and two useful things come into comparison, and one asks which is more honorable and which more useful. Duty is therefore first divided into three parts: the honorable, the useful, and the question of which is preferable. Then these three are divided into five categories: two honorable things, two useful things, and the judgment of choice.

They say that the first belong to the dignity and honor of life, the second to life’s advantages, resources, wealth, and capacities; and that judgment must be applied to the choice between them. So much for them.

28. We, however, measure and define nothing whatever except what is seemly and honorable, using rather the standard of what is to come than of what is present; and we define as useful nothing except what benefits the grace of that eternal life, not what contributes to the enjoyment of the present life. Nor do we place any advantages in possessions and resources of wealth; rather, we consider these disadvantages if they are not rejected; and we regard them as more of a burden when they are possessed than a loss when they are expended.

[Note: The Erasmian and later editions, together with one or two manuscripts, read: “and since these are more burdensome, they are to be valued more than when they are expended,” and so forth. But this transposition, which is contrary to the other manuscripts and the edition of Amerbach, does not remove the obscurity of the passage. To remove it, supply the verb *putamus* (“we consider”), and interpret *cum sint* (“since they are”) as standing for *cum adsint* (“when they are present”), so that it is set in opposition to the following clause, “when they are expended.”]

29. Our writing, therefore, is not a superfluous work, because we assess duty by a different standard from theirs.
