They count the advantages of this age among good things; we count them even among losses, since the person who receives good things here, like that rich man, is tormented there, while Lazarus, who endured evil things here, found consolation there (Luke 16:25).

Moreover, those who do not read those writings may read ours if they wish—those who seek not an accumulation of words or an art of speaking, but the simple value of the subject matter.

## CHAPTER X

That the fitting was frequently treated in the sacred writings before it was treated in the books of philosophers; that Pythagoras borrowed his law of silence from David, but that David’s discipline is superior; and that the first duty is moderation in speaking.

30. From reading we are instructed and taught that the fitting—called πρέπον in Greek—was given first place in our Scriptures, when we read: “Praise is fitting for you, O God, in Zion” (Psalm 64:2); or in Greek: Σοὶ πρέπει ὕμνος, ὦ Θεός, ἐν Σιών, “To you, O God, a hymn is fitting in Zion.” The Apostle also says: “Speak the things that are fitting for sound doctrine” (Titus 2:1). And elsewhere: “It was fitting for him, through whom all things exist and through whom all things exist, to bring many sons to glory and to perfect the leader of their salvation through suffering” (Hebrews 2:10).

31. Was Panaetius, then, earlier than this? Was Aristotle, who himself also discussed duty, earlier than David, when even Pythagoras himself, who is said to have preceded Socrates, followed the prophet David (Psalm 38:2 ff.) and gave his disciples a law of silence?

[Note: When Aristotle is said to have discussed duty, this should not be understood as though he published a separate treatise under that title, but rather that he transmitted much concerning the duties of individuals in his books *Politics* and *Economics*, and especially in the three volumes of his *Moral Works*, which are in everyone’s hands. As for the assertion that David was older than these philosophers, we have already observed that it agrees with chronology in volume 1, pages 766 and 982. Panaetius flourished only around 625 years after the founding of the City, that is, 126 years before the restoration of salvation; Aristotle around 3570 years after the creation of the world, that is, approximately 380 years before Christ; Socrates in the year of the world 3525; and Pythagoras, finally, approximately 550 years before the Virgin’s childbirth, that is, about 500 years after David. Whoever desires more about these philosophers should consult, concerning Pythagoras, Diogenes Laertius, Porphyry, the Anonymous author cited by Photius, Augustine, *The City of God*, book 18, chapter 37, Vayerius, *On the Virtue of the Pagans*, and Naudé, *Apology for Illustrious Men*; concerning Socrates, besides several of those already mentioned, Diodorus Siculus, Aristides, oration 2, Eusebius, Suidas, and others. We have already touched upon Panaetius to the extent sufficient here.]

But Pythagoras did so in order to prevent his disciples from speaking for five years; David, however, did not do so to diminish nature’s gift, but to teach restraint in bringing speech forth. Pythagoras taught by not speaking how to speak; David taught us, by speaking, to learn to speak more effectively. For how can there be doctrine without practice, or progress without use?

32. Whoever wishes to acquire military discipline exercises himself daily with weapons, rehearses battle as though stationed in the line of battle, and, as though an enemy were stationed before him, practices against him. In order to acquire skill and strength in throwing javelins, he either tests the strength of his own arms or avoids the blows of his opponents, and with watchful gaze gets out of the way of the blow.

[Note: This is how the old edition and nearly all the manuscripts read. The Roman edition, however, has “receives it with watchful gaze.” Nothing should be changed. For why should it not correctly be said that a blow “goes out” or “goes outside the blow,” just as, conversely, we say that a missile or blow comes “within the range” or “within the striking distance” of a weapon?]

Whoever strives to steer a ship at sea with the helm, or to propel it with oars, first practices on a river. Those who seek sweetness in singing and excellence of voice first gradually strengthen their voices by singing. Those who seek a crown through bodily strength and a lawful contest of wrestling harden their limbs through daily practice in the training ground, nourish endurance, and accustom themselves to toil.

33. Nature itself teaches us this in little children: before they learn to speak, they first practice sounds. Thus sound is a kind of exercise and training ground for the voice.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “the sound is an arousal”; the old edition reads: “and nature itself.”]

So too those who wish to learn caution in speaking should not reject what belongs to nature, but should practice what belongs to restraint, so that those who are on watch may increase their attention by keeping watch, not by sleeping. For every undertaking grows through exercises proper and native to it.

34. David therefore kept silent, not always, but at the proper time—not continually and not toward everyone; but he did not answer an irritating adversary or a provoking sinner. And, as he says elsewhere (Psalm 38:13–14), he did not hear those who spoke vanity and devised deceit, as though he were deaf, nor, as though mute, did he open his mouth to them; for elsewhere also you have: “Do not answer a fool according to his folly, lest you become like him” (Proverbs 26:4).

35. The first duty, then, is moderation in speaking. By this sacrifice of praise is offered to God; by this reverence is shown when the divine Scriptures are read; by this parents are honored.

[Note: We have already read this sentence in chapter 2, number 5, in the same words. One Vatican manuscript and the Tellerian manuscript do not have it here; nevertheless, since it occurs in all the others and in the editions, we did not wish to move it from its place, especially since it is not unusual for Ambrose sometimes to repeat the same statements.]

I know that most people speak because they do not know how to keep silent. It is rare for anyone to remain silent when speaking is not advantageous to him. Before speaking, the wise person considers many things: what he should say, to whom he should say it, and in what place and at what time. There is therefore a proper measure both for keeping silent and for speaking; there is also a proper measure in action. It is beautiful, then, to maintain the measure of duty.

## CHAPTER XI

That every duty is either intermediate or perfect, as is shown by testimonies of Scripture; to this is added praise of mercy and an exhortation to it.

36. Every duty, moreover, is either intermediate or perfect, as we can equally establish by the authority of the Scriptures.

[Note: Cicero, book 1 of *On Duties*, page 531, line 36: “There is also another division,” and so forth. Observe meanwhile Ambrose’s teaching concerning the distinction between commandments and counsels, which modern heterodox writers so stubbornly attack and reject.]

For we have the Lord saying in the Gospel: “If you wish to enter into eternal life, keep the commandments.” The man said to him, “Which ones?” Jesus said to him: “You shall not murder; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness; honor your father and mother; and, you shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matthew 19:17 ff.). These are intermediate duties, to which something is lacking.

37. Finally, the young man says to him: “I have kept all these things from my youth; what do I still lack?” Jesus says to him: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you possess, give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me” (ibid., 19:21).

And above (Matthew 5:44–45) it is written that we are to love our enemies, pray for those who slander and persecute us, and bless those who curse us. We must do this if we wish to be perfect, like our Father who is in heaven, who commands his sun to shine its rays upon the good and the evil and causes the earths of all to be enriched by rain and dew without distinction. This, then, is perfect duty, which the Greeks called κατόρθωμα, “right action,” by which all things that may have involved some falls are corrected.

[Note: Ibid., page 351, line 37: “Perfect duty, however,” and so forth.]

38. Mercy also is good; it too makes people perfect, because it imitates the perfect Father. Nothing so commends the Christian soul as mercy.

[Note: Book 2 of *On Duties*, page 383, line 12: “In that other kind,” and so forth.]

First, mercy should be shown to the poor, so that we may share in common the offspring of nature, which produces the fruits of the earth for everyone’s use. Give what you possess to the poor and help one who is your companion and your equal. You give a coin; he receives life. You give money; he values it as his substance. Your denarius is his capital.

39. In this respect he confers more upon you, since he becomes the debtor of your salvation. If you clothe the naked, you clothe yourself with righteousness. If you bring a stranger beneath your roof, if you receive one in need, he obtains for you the friendship of the saints and eternal dwellings. This is no ordinary grace. You sow bodily things and receive spiritual ones.

Are you astonished by the judgment of the Lord concerning holy Job? Marvel at his virtue, for he could say: “I was eyes to the blind and feet to the lame. I was a father to the weak; the shoulders of my lambs were warmed by their fleeces. No stranger stayed outside; my door was open to everyone who came” (Job 29:15–16).

Truly blessed is the person from whose house the poor never went away empty-handed; for no one is more blessed than the one who understands the need of the poor and the distress of the weak and needy. On the day of judgment he will have salvation from the Lord—the one who will have the Lord as debtor to his mercy.

## CHAPTER XII

That no one should be turned away from practicing mercy: it is shown that God cares about human actions, and, on the authority of Job, that every wicked person is miserable amid the very abundance of his wealth.

40. But many are turned away from the duty of administering mercy because they think that the Lord does not care about human actions, or that he does not know what we do in secret and what our conscience holds; or because God’s judgment seems in no way just when they see sinners abounding in riches, rejoicing in honors, health, and children, while the just live in poverty, without honor, without children, and in bodily weakness, surrounded by continual grief.

41. The question is no small one, since Job’s three friends pronounced him a sinner for this reason: they saw him, once rich, reduced to poverty; once the father of a fruitful household, deprived of his children; covered with ulcers, bristling with bloody marks, and scored with wounds from head to foot (Job 4:3, 11, 14 ff.).

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “and bristling with vile food”; others, “with varicose veins.” Neither reading is sufficiently suitable, and the word familiar to our Author should not be changed.]

To them holy Job offers this assertion: “If I suffer these things because of my sins, why do the wicked live? They grow old, and their offspring are in riches according to their desire; their children are before their eyes; their houses are abundant, and fear is nowhere. The scourge of the Lord is not upon them” (Job 21:7 ff.).

42. Seeing this, the weak man is agitated and turns his attention away. Before holy Job was about to state this man’s words, he first prefaced them, saying: “Bear with me, and I will speak; then look upon me. For even if I am reproved, I am reproved as a man. Bear, therefore, the burden of my words” (ibid., 1 ff.).

For I am about to say something I do not approve; but I shall bring forward unjust words in order to refute you. Or perhaps, because it has been turned thus.

[Note: *Versus* is used here for *conversus* (“changed”), since Ambrose, as elsewhere often, proposes another version of the same passage.]

What then? “Am I perhaps reproved by man?” That is: man cannot reprove me because I have sinned, even if I deserve to be reproved; for you do not accuse me on the basis of evident guilt, but judge the merits of my sins from my misfortunes.

[Note: The Tellerian manuscript reads: “A lying man cannot reprove.”]

Thus, when the weak person sees the wicked prospering through favorable successes while he himself is in an inferior condition, he says to the Lord: “Depart from me; I do not wish to know your ways” (ibid., 14). “What does it profit that we served him? Or what advantage is there in our approaching him? Everything good is in their hands, but he does not see the works of the wicked.”

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “the unjust through prosperous successions.”]

43. Plato is praised because in his *Republic* he introduced the person who had undertaken the role of arguing against justice as asking pardon for statements he did not approve, and saying that this role had been assigned to him for the sake of discovering the truth and examining the argument.

[Note: In book 2 of the *Republic*, Plato introduces Glaucon as speaking among those who said that injustice should be preferred to justice, and as excusing the task imposed upon him in this way: Ἐπεὶ ἔμοιγε, ὦ Σώκρατες, ἔτι οὐ δοκεῖ οὕτως, “For, Socrates, it still does not seem so to me.” And below: Μὴ ἐμὲ οἴου λέγειν, ὦ Σώκρατες, ἀλλὰ τοὺς ἐπαινοῦντας, πρὸ δικαιοσύνης ἀδικίαν ἐροῦσι δὲ τάδε, “Do not suppose, Socrates, that I am saying this, but rather those who praise injustice instead of justice; they will say the following.”]

Cicero approved this to such an extent that he himself thought it necessary to speak in this vein in the books he wrote *On the Republic*.

44. How much older than those men is Job, who was the first to discover these things and judged that they should be prefaced not for the sake of embellishing eloquence but for the sake of establishing the truth?

[Note: Job is commonly believed to be the oldest of all writers, born approximately 2330 years after the creation of the world, whereas Plato flourished scarcely before the year 3550. Nevertheless, there are some who attribute the book bearing his name not to him but to Moses. See the history of Job, worked out with considerable learning by Spanheim.]

He immediately made the question clear himself, adding that the lamp of the wicked would be extinguished and their downfall would come (Job 21:17); that God, the teacher of wisdom and discipline, is not deceived but is the judge of truth (ibid., 22); and therefore that the happiness of individuals is not to be assessed according to outward abundance, but according to the inner conscience, which distinguishes the merits of the innocent and the wicked and is the true and incorruptible judge of punishments and rewards.

The innocent person dies in the power of his simplicity, in the abundance of his own will, carrying a soul filled as with fat (ibid., 23 ff.). But the sinner, although he abounds outwardly, overflows with pleasures and is fragrant with perfumes, drags out his life in bitterness of soul and closes his final day, bringing with him none of the good things with which he feasted.

[Note: A few manuscripts read: “He receives his food in the bitterness of his soul.”]

[Note: The old edition and some manuscripts read: “bringing back nothing of what he had feasted upon, no good things,” and so forth.]

He takes away nothing with him except the price of his crimes.

45. Considering these things, deny, if you can, that the recompense belongs to divine judgment. The one is blessed according to his own disposition, the other miserable; the one acquitted by his own judgment, the other guilty; the one joyful at his departure, the other grieving. How can the person be acquitted who is not innocent even in his own eyes?

“Tell me,” he says, “where is the protection of his tents?” (Job 21:28). No sign of it will be found. For the life of the criminal is like a dream. He opened his eyes; his rest passed away; his pleasure vanished. Indeed, even while the wicked live, the rest they appear to possess is itself in hell; for while alive they descend into hell.

46. You see the sinner’s banquet; question his conscience. Does it not stink more foully than all tombs? You observe his joy and marvel at the health of his body, his children, and the abundance of his wealth; look within at the ulcers and bloody marks of his soul and at the sorrow of his heart.

For what should I say about wealth, when you have read: “His life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions” (Luke 12:15); when you know that, although he may seem rich to you, he is poor to himself, and his own judgment refutes yours?

What should I say about the multitude of his children and his freedom from pain, when he himself mourns and judges that he will be without an heir, when he does not wish his successors to be imitators of him? For the sinner has no inheritance.

Thus the wicked person is himself punishment for himself; the just person, however, is himself his own grace.

[Note: The edition and several manuscripts read: “he is himself his own glory”; but the majority and the best manuscripts read: “he is himself his own grace,” that is, his own rest and delight.]

And for each of them the reward of good or evil works is paid out from himself.

## CHAPTER XIII

The opinions of the philosophers who deny God’s care either of the whole world or of some of its parts are refuted.

47. But let us return to our subject, lest we seem to have passed over the division already made, because we have encountered the opinion of those who, seeing criminals wealthy, joyful, honored, and powerful, while most of the just are needy and weak, think either that God cares nothing for us, as the Epicureans say, or that he does not know human actions, as the wicked suppose, or, if he knows everything, that he is an unjust judge, since he allows the good to suffer poverty and the wicked to abound.

It was not a superfluous digression, as it were, that the disposition of such people should be answered—people whom they judge happy, although they themselves consider themselves miserable. For I thought that they would believe themselves more readily than they would believe us.

[Note: Epicurus taught that divine happiness could not subsist together with providence and the administration of the world, and human happiness still less. Accordingly, he attempted by every means to tear the fear of deity from human minds, as may be seen in the learned Petrus Gassendus, *Epicurean Philosophical Syntagma*, part 2, sections 2, chapters 5 and 6, and part 3, chapters 20 and 21. Because of this impiety, his disciple Lucretius extols him with remarkable praises, both at the very beginning of books 1 and 2 and especially in book 3, where he sings that for this reason Epicurus should be counted among the gods.]

48. Having covered this ground, I think it easy to refute the remaining points. First, let us refute the assertion of those who think that God has no care whatever for the world, as Aristotle maintains, saying that his providence descends only as far as the moon.

[Note: Diogenes Laertius attributes the same opinion to this philosopher in these words: διατείνει δὲ αὐτοῦ (θεοῦ) τὴν πρόνοιαν μέχρι τῶν οὐρανίων, τὰ δὲ ἐπίγεια κατὰ πρὸς ταῦτα συμπάθειαν οἰκονομεῖσθαι, “He says that God’s providence extends to the heavenly things, while earthly things are governed in accordance with their sympathy with them.” But this opinion is not found in the surviving writings of Aristotle.]

And what craftsman neglects the care of his work? Who abandons and forsakes what he himself judged should be made? If governing is an injustice, is it not a greater injustice to have made something, since doing nothing is no injustice, whereas failing to care for what one has made is the height of cruelty?

49. If they either deny God as their creator or consider themselves to belong to the number of beasts and animals, what shall we say about those who condemn themselves by this insult?

[Note: No one is unaware that Epicurus denied that God was either the creator of the world or, as we said above, its governor. On this subject one may consult the learned Gassendus, *Epicurean Philosophical Syntagma*, part 2, section 1, chapter 3, and section 2, chapters 2–6. Moreover, the statement that the Epicureans held that God is involved in all things seems to refer to Lucretius, who signifies this very idea under the name and veil of Venus at the beginning of book 1. From this, it is clear, the two famous passages of Virgil were taken, one in the *Georgics*, book 4, and the other in *Aeneid* 1; consult them.]

They themselves assert that God pervades everything and that all things stand in his power; that his force and majesty penetrate all the elements, the earth, heaven, and seas. Yet they think it an insult to him if he penetrates the human mind—than which he himself has given us nothing more excellent—and enters into the knowledge of divine majesty?

50. But the philosophers who are thought sober mock the teacher of these doctrines as a drunkard and a patron of pleasure.

[Note: Here he calls Epicurus drunk, since, as some have reported, he used to vomit up his drunkenness three times a day before voluntarily dying in a bath: Τὸν ἄκρατον ἔσπασεν, “he drained the unmixed wine,” as Diogenes Laertius says in his life. As for his advocacy of pleasure, those who say that he meant the pleasure of the soul are mistaken, since his words, recorded by the same Diogenes, demonstrate the contrary: Οὐ γὰρ ἔγωγε ἔχω τί νοήσω τὸ ἀγαθόν, ἀφαιρῶν μὲν τὰς διὰ χυλῶν ἡδονάς, ἀφαιρῶν δὲ τὰς δι’ ἀφροδισίων, καὶ τὰς δι’ ἀκροαμάτων, καὶ τὰς διὰ μορφάς, “For I myself cannot understand what the good is if I remove pleasures derived from flavors, pleasures derived from sexual intercourse, pleasures derived from sounds, and pleasures derived from forms.” His association with the most debauched young men and women proves this no less. Nevertheless, it should not be concealed that the same Laertius writes in the same place that this madness was attributed to him by his rivals in order to stir up envy against him, and that great men were not lacking who professed themselves defenders of Epicurus; among them we rightly name the highly learned Gassendus, because of the very learned life of that philosopher which he wrote. But since Tully says in book 3 of the *Tusculan Disputations* that these very things are contained in Epicurus’s book *On the Supreme Good*—a book that no one denied was his—and since the holy Fathers attribute the same doctrine of pleasure to him, it is more credible, as Tully indicates, that Epicurus’s disciples, when pressed, fled for refuge to the pleasure of the soul as to a sacred anchor, in order to lessen the envy directed against him.]

For what should I say about Aristotle’s opinion? He thinks that God is content with his own boundaries and lives according to the prescribed limits of his kingdom, as the tales of the poets relate. They say that the world was divided among three gods, so that one received heaven, another the sea, and another the underworld to rule; and that they were careful not to provoke war among themselves by taking an interest in the regions belonging to others.

[Note: All editions and quite a few manuscripts read: “they bear it in three”; others more correctly read: “among three.” Again, the same editions and several manuscripts read: “what had fallen to them by the lot of the kingdom that had to be restrained”; more and older manuscripts read: “what had fallen to them to restrain by imperial authority,” which is better, since *imperio* (“by authority”) belongs with *coercenda* (“to be restrained”). As for the division by which the world is said to have been divided among three—Jupiter, Neptune, and Pluto—the works of the philosopher transmitted to us contain nothing about it.]

He therefore asserts in the same way that God has no care for the earth, just as he has no care for the sea or the underworld. And how do they exclude the poets whom they follow?

[Note: Aristotle, in book 1 of the *Metaphysics*, chapter 2, denies that poets who tell unworthy tales about the gods should be heard, and in book 14, chapter 8, he attacks their stories. But this subject is treated much more fully by Plato, in various places and especially in books 2, 3, and 10 of the *Republic*.]

## CHAPTER XIV

That nothing escapes the knowledge of God, proved both by testimonies of Scripture and by the example of the sun, which, although a creature, nevertheless penetrates everything by its light or heat.

51. The next question is whether, if God’s care has not overlooked his work, his knowledge can overlook it. Therefore, does the one who planted the ear not hear? Does the one who fashioned the eye not see and observe?

52. This empty opinion did not escape the holy prophets. David, accordingly, represents as speaking those whom he declares to be puffed up with pride. For what is more arrogant than for people who themselves are under sin to resent that other sinners live, saying: “How long, O Lord, how long will sinners exult?” (Psalm 94:3).

And below: “They said, ‘The Lord will not see, nor will the God of Jacob understand.’” To them the prophet replies: “Understand now, you senseless among the people; and you fools, become wise at last. He who planted the ear, does he not hear? He who fashioned the eye, does he not observe? He who chastises the nations, does he not rebuke—the one who teaches human beings knowledge? The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings, for they are vain” (ibid., 7 ff.).

Who detects all things that are vain, yet does not know the things that are holy and does not know what he himself has made?

[Note: The edition, together with some manuscripts, reads: “the things that have been made.” But in the majority and most trustworthy manuscripts one reads: “the things that are holy.” In this reading there is an elegant antithesis.]

Can a craftsman be ignorant of his own work? A human being detects what is hidden in his work, yet God does not know his own work? Thus the work would contain a deeper mystery than its author. Did he make something superior to himself, whose worth the author did not know and whose purpose the judge did not understand? So much for them.

53. For us, however, the testimony of the one who says, “I am he who searches hearts and kidneys” (Jeremiah 17:10), is sufficient. In the Gospel the Lord Jesus also says: “Why are you thinking evil in your hearts?” (Luke 5:22). For he knew that they were thinking evil. Finally, the Evangelist testifies, saying: “For Jesus knew their thoughts” (Luke 6:8).

54. Their opinion cannot fail to move us sufficiently if we consider their deeds. They do not want above them a judge whom nothing escapes; they do not want to grant knowledge of hidden things to one whom they fear will expose their secrets. Yet the Lord, knowing their deeds, handed them over to darkness. “At night,” he says, “the thief will be there. And the eye of the adulterer watches for darkness, saying: ‘No eye will see me’; and he places a covering over his face” (Job 24:14–15). [Note: The Roman edition reads, “everyone who does evil flees the light,” and so forth.]

For everyone who flees the light loves darkness, striving to remain hidden, although he cannot remain hidden from God, who knows, within the depths of the abyss and within human minds, not only what has been done but also what is being contemplated. Finally, even the man who says in Ecclesiasticus, “Who sees me? Darkness surrounds me, and the walls conceal me; whom should I fear?” (Sirach 23:25–26)—although he thinks these things while lying in his bed, where he supposes he will not be discovered—is caught. “And there will be disgrace,” he says, “because he did not understand the fear of God” (ibid., 31).

55. What could be more foolish than to suppose that anything escapes God, when the sun, which is the minister of light, penetrates even hidden places, and the force of its heat breaks into the foundations of a house and its secret chambers? Who would deny that the inner parts of the earth, which winter ice has bound, are warmed by the mildness of spring? Trees therefore know the hidden force of heat and cold, to such an extent that their roots are either scorched by cold or invigorated by the sun’s warmth. Finally, when the gentleness of heaven has smiled upon it, the earth pours itself forth in various fruits.

[Note: Some manuscripts: “it pours forth various lands into fruits.”]

56. If, then, a ray of the sun pours its light over the whole earth and inserts itself even into enclosed places, and neither iron bars nor the barriers of massive doors prevent it from penetrating, how could the intelligible splendor of God not insert itself into the thoughts and hearts of human beings, which he himself created? And yet are we to suppose that he does not see what he himself made—indeed, made so that created things would be better and more powerful than their maker, able, whenever they wished, to hide the knowledge of their creator from him? Did he therefore insert such power and capacity into our minds that, whenever he wishes to comprehend it, he himself is unable to do so?

## CHAPTER XV

Those who are displeased that the good suffer evil and the wicked enjoy good are shown, by the example of Lazarus and the authority of Paul, that punishments and rewards are reserved after this life.

57. We have settled two matters and, as we think, this discussion has proceeded in a manner not inappropriate. A third kind of question remains, as follows: Why do sinners abound in wealth and riches, feast continually, without sorrow or mourning, while the just are in need and are afflicted either by the loss of spouses or of children? The parable of the Gospel ought to have satisfied them: the rich man was clothed in linen and purple and displayed lavish banquets every day, while the poor man, covered with sores, gathered the scraps from his table. But after both had died, the poor man was resting in Abraham’s bosom, while the rich man was in torments (Luke 16:25). Is it not clear that rewards or punishments for merits remain after death?

58. And rightly so, because in a contest there is labor, and after the contest victory for some, disgrace for others. Is a palm ever given to anyone, or a crown awarded, before the race has been completed? Paul rightly says: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith. What remains is the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the just judge, will award me on that day—not only to me, but also to those who love his coming” (2 Timothy 4:7–8). “On that day,” he says, “he will award it,” not here. Here, however, he struggled amid labors, dangers, and shipwrecks, like a good athlete, because he knew that “through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God.” Therefore no one can receive a reward unless he has competed lawfully; nor is victory glorious except where the contests have been arduous.

## CHAPTER XVI

After confirming what was said above about rewards and punishments, it is added that it is not surprising if those for whom no future reward is destined do not labor or contend here; and it is further shown that temporal goods are granted to them so that no excuse may remain.

59. Is he not unjust who gives a reward before the contest has been completed?

[Note: The Erasmian and later editions read, “who first seeks a reward.” The Amerbach edition and all the manuscripts read, “who first gives a reward.” This is not unreasonable, for both actions ought to be attributed to injustice.]

Therefore the Lord says in the Gospel: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5:3). He did not say, “Blessed are the rich,” but “the poor.” Thus blessedness begins with divine judgment, where human hardship is valued. “Blessed are those who hunger, for they will be satisfied. Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted. Blessed are the merciful, for God will have mercy on them. Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God. Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are you when they curse you and persecute you and speak every evil against you for righteousness’ sake. Rejoice and exult, for your reward is abundant in heaven” (ibid., 5 and following). He promised that the reward would be given in the future, not in the present; in heaven, not on earth. Why do you seek elsewhere what is owed elsewhere? Why do you demand a crown prematurely, before you have conquered? Why do you wish to wipe away the dust? Why do you desire rest? Why do you long to feast before the stadium has been closed? The crowd is still watching; the athletes are still in the arena, and you are already asking for leisure.

[Note: The ancient edition, together with a few manuscripts, reads “in the arena” (*in stemmate*); the Roman edition, together with more numerous manuscripts, reads “in the arena” (*in scammate*). The meaning of *scamma* has been explained in the work *On Elijah and Fasting*, chapter 13, page 550.]

60. But perhaps you say: Why do the wicked rejoice? Why do they live in luxury? Why do they themselves not labor with me? Because those who have not signed up for the crown are not held to the labor of the contest; those who have not entered the stadium do not bathe in oil or smear themselves with dust. Those for whom glory awaits are met by injury. Those anointed men customarily watch, not compete; they do not endure the sun, the heat, the dust, or the rain. Let the athletes therefore say to them also: “Come, labor with us.” But the spectators will reply: “For the time being we judge you here; but without us you will claim the crown and glory, if you win.”

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “Anointed spectators are accustomed to watch.” A few others immediately afterward read, “they are not accustomed to endure the heat,” and so forth.]

61. These people, then, who have devoted their pursuits to pleasures, luxury, robbery, profits, and honors, are spectators rather than combatants. They have the benefit of labor, but not the fruit of virtue.

[Note: “The benefit of labor” means exemption from labor, not the profit that arises from labor.]

They cultivate leisure and heap up piles of riches through cunning and wickedness; but, even if late, they will pay the penalty for their wickedness. Their rest is in hell; yours, however, is in heaven. Their house is in the tomb; yours is in paradise. Hence Job aptly said that they keep watch in the tomb (Job 21:32), because they cannot have the sleep of rest that was enjoyed by the one who rose again.

62. Do not therefore think like a child, speak like a child, think like a child, or demand like a child the things that belong to a later age. The crown belongs to the mature. Wait until what is perfect comes, when you can recognize the very form of the revealed truth—not through an image in a riddle, but face to face. Then it will be revealed why that rich man was rich, though he was wicked and a robber of another’s property; why another was powerful; why one abounded in children and another was supported by honors.

63. Perhaps the robber will be told: “You were rich; why did you rob what belonged to others? Poverty did not compel you, want did not force you. Did I not make you rich for this very reason, so that you could have no excuse?” The powerful man will also be told: “Why did you not assist the widow, or those orphans who were suffering injustice? Were you weak? Were you unable to help? I made you powerful for this reason: not to inflict violence, but to repel it. Is it not written to you: ‘Rescue the one who is suffering injury’ (Sirach 4:9)? Is it not written to you: ‘Deliver the poor and needy from the hand of the sinner’ (Psalm 81:4)?” The prosperous man will also be told: “I endowed you with children and honors and granted you bodily health; why did you not follow my commands? My servant, what have I done to you, or how have I grieved you? Did I not give you children, confer honors upon you, and grant you health? Why did you deny me? Why did you suppose that what you did would not come to my knowledge? Why did you keep my gifts while despising my commandments?” (Micah 6:3 and following).

64. Finally, from the case of Judas the betrayer we may gather these points. He was chosen as an apostle among the Twelve, and he was entrusted with the money-box containing the funds to be distributed to the poor, so that he would not appear either dishonorable or needy when he betrayed the Lord. For this reason the Lord bestowed these things upon him, so that the Lord might be justified in him: Judas was not provoked by an injury, but had violated grace and thus become liable to a greater offense.

## CHAPTER XVII

The duties of the young man and examples suited to his age are proposed.

65. Since it has therefore become sufficiently clear that punishment awaits wickedness and reward virtue, let us begin to speak about duties—duties that we must observe from adolescence, so that they may increase with age.

[Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, book 1, page 368, line 4: “And since duties are not assigned alike to unequal ages, some belong to young men,” and so forth.]

[Note: All editions read, “together with the pursuits of good deeds.” But the words we have removed are absent from the manuscripts and do not seem necessary to the sense. Again, the editions and a few more recent manuscripts read, “to show honor to parents, to show reverence to elders.” But the more numerous and better manuscripts, with the word *reverentiam* truncated, place *deferre* absolutely. The same occurs in two places below: in the first they omit the word *honorem*, which had been placed before *deferens* in the editions; in the second they read *sedulo tamen obsequio* instead of the editions’ *sedulum tamen obsequium*.]

It is therefore characteristic of good young men to fear God, honor their parents, show respect to elders, preserve chastity, not disdain humility, and love kindness and modesty, which are ornaments of youth. For just as dignity belongs to old men and liveliness to the young, so modesty commends adolescents, like a certain natural endowment.

66. Isaac feared the Lord, being, as was fitting, Abraham’s offspring; he honored his father to such an extent that he did not refuse even death against his father’s will (Genesis 22:9 and following). Joseph likewise, when he had dreamed that the sun, moon, and stars worshiped him, nevertheless showed his father dutiful obedience (Genesis 37:6 and following). He was chaste, unwilling even to hear anything except what was pure; humble even to servitude; modest even to flight; patient even to imprisonment; forgiving injury even to the point of granting a reward. His modesty was so great that, when seized by a woman, he preferred to leave his garment in her hands as he fled rather than abandon his modesty (Genesis 39:8 and following). Moses and Jeremiah, too, chosen by the Lord to proclaim God’s oracles to the people, excused themselves on the grounds of modesty from what they were able to do by grace (Exodus 4:10; Jeremiah 1:6).

## CHAPTER XVIII

On the aspects of modesty: how it regulates speech and silence, accompanies chastity, commends our prayers to God, and governs bodily movements. The story of two clerics, by no means unworthy of notice, is related; then it is explained how one’s walk should be composed according to the same virtue, and how great care must be taken that nothing immodest be uttered by the mouth or exposed on the body. All these matters are illustrated with highly appropriate examples.

67. Modesty, therefore, is a beautiful virtue and a gracious charm, which is observed not only in deeds but also in speech itself.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “The virtue of mercy and gracious kindness is beautiful.”]

[Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, book 1, page 369, line 43: “Above all, they take care that speech not indicate that some defect is present in one’s character,” and so forth.]

Do not go beyond the proper measure in speaking; let your speech utter nothing unbecoming. The mind’s mirror usually shines forth in words. Even the sound of the voice is balanced by modesty, so that a louder voice may not offend anyone’s ear. Finally, in singing itself the first discipline is modesty—indeed, in every use of speech: one should begin gradually either to chant, sing, or finally speak, so that modest beginnings may commend what follows.

68. Silence itself also, in which the other virtues find repose, is the greatest act of modesty. If it is thought to arise from childishness or arrogance, it is reproached; if from modesty, it is counted as praise. Susanna remained silent in danger and considered the loss of modesty more serious than the loss of life; she did not think that her safety should be preserved at the cost of her modesty. She spoke only to God (Daniel 13:35), to whom chaste modesty could express itself. She avoided looking upon the faces of men; for there is modesty even in the eyes, so that a woman neither wishes to look at men nor to be looked at by them.

69. No one, however, should think that this praise belongs only to chastity. Modesty is the companion of purity, and through its companionship chastity itself is safer. A good sense of shame is the companion of preserving chastity; if it places itself before the first dangers, it prevents purity from being violated.

[Note: This is the reading of the editions and a very few manuscripts. The more numerous manuscripts read, “if it place itself before the first dangers, and does not permit what is first to be attempted”; one manuscript reads, “if it place itself before the first [dangers],” and another, “as though it place itself before the first [dangers].” The latter reading is quite attractive.]

At the very beginning of knowledge, this modesty commends the Lord’s mother to readers and, like a trustworthy witness, establishes her as worthy to be chosen for such a task: while in her chamber, while alone, while greeted by the angel, she remains silent and is troubled at his entrance; her Virgin’s eyes are disturbed by the unfamiliar appearance of a male sex (Luke 1:20 and following).

[Note: Some manuscripts, neither few nor of inferior quality, read *speciem peregrinatur*; some have *peregrinatus*, others *aspectus*, and so forth. Later, where the editions and a few manuscripts read *sermonem refelleret*, the rest read partly *sermonem praeferret*, some *proferret*, and partly *sermonem referret*. The last reading seems more consistent with the sense.]

Thus, although she was humble, out of modesty she did not return the greeting of the one who greeted her, nor did she give any answer until she learned about the birth of the Lord that she was to receive; she wished to learn the nature of what was to happen, not to continue the conversation.

70. In our very prayer, modesty is highly pleasing and greatly wins favor with our God. Did it not give preference to the tax collector and commend the one who did not even dare to raise his eyes toward heaven? For this reason he was more justified in the Lord’s judgment than the Pharisee, whom presumption disfigured (Luke 18:13–14). Therefore let us pray in the incorruptibility of a quiet and modest spirit, which is precious before God, as Peter says (1 Peter 3:4). Great, then, is the modesty that, although more restrained even in exercising its own rights, appropriating and claiming nothing, and in a certain way contracted within its own strength, is rich with God, before whom no one is rich. Modesty is rich because it is God’s portion.

Paul also commanded that prayer be offered with modesty and sobriety. He wishes this to be the first and, as it were, the preliminary quality of the prayer that follows, so that the sinner’s prayer may not boast; but, as though covered with the color of modesty, the more it displays modesty through remembrance of sin, the more abundant grace it may deserve (1 Timothy 2:9).

[Note: Many manuscripts read, “may cover it with the color of modesty.”]

71. Modesty must also be maintained in movement, gesture, and walking.

[Note: Cicero, book 1 of *On Duties*, page 368, line 28: “But since that propriety is discerned in all deeds and words, and finally in bodily movement and posture.”]

For the disposition of the mind is seen in the body’s posture. From this the hidden person of our heart is judged either frivolous, boastful, or agitated—or, on the contrary, more serious, steadfast, pure, and mature. Thus the body’s movement is, as it were, a voice of the soul.

72. You remember, sons, a certain friend who seemed to recommend himself through diligent services. I nevertheless did not admit him to the clergy for this one reason: his gestures were exceedingly unbecoming. I also remember another whom I had found among the clergy and whom I ordered never to walk ahead of me, because, as though by the blow of an insolent gait, he struck my eyes. I said this when he was restored to office after an offense. I made this the sole exception, and my judgment was not mistaken: both men withdrew from the Church, so that the treachery of their minds might be shown to be of the same character as that revealed by their walk. For one deserted the faith during the Arian disturbance; the other, out of desire for money, denied that he was ours, lest he undergo a priestly judgment.

[Note: The manuscripts agree almost unanimously on *subiret, sacerdotem se nostrum*, except for two, which, like the old edition, read *subiret sacerdotem se nostrum*. The Roman edition alone reads *subiret sacerdotum se nostrum*, a meaning not wholly incompatible with our reading. He seems to have fled to the Arians to avoid rendering an account of some administration he had accepted, or perhaps of some theft. Ecclesiastical judgments and the administration of Church property will be discussed more suitably elsewhere.]

The image of frivolity shone forth in their walk, a certain appearance of wandering buffoons.

73. There are also those who imitate theatrical gestures by walking slowly, as though they were some sort of ceremonial trays or the movements of swaying statues, so that whenever they move a step they seem to preserve certain rhythms.

[Note: Cicero, book 1 of *On Duties*, page 369, line 8: “For even gymnastic movements,” and below, line 14: “But care must be taken lest either by slowness,” and so forth. Among the ancients there were various kinds of ceremonial objects. Some were used in triumphs, when the spoils of conquered peoples—precious garments, gold, crowns, weapons, engines, and finally images of captured cities—were carried on wagons before the chariots of the triumphing generals. Others belonged to games and spectacles and were not very different from the former. Others, finally, belonged to religious ceremonies, in which images of the gods were carried. Ambrose seems to be speaking chiefly of the last kind, as he himself appears to explain below. Funeral biers, on which the corpse of the deceased was carried out while images of his ancestors were borne before it, were also not very different from these. Since all these objects were carried with considerable solemnity and slowness of movement, they could readily give rise to Ambrose’s comparison, as well as to Cicero’s.]

74. Nor do I consider it honorable to walk at a run, except when some danger or just necessity requires it.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “or a just necessity.”]

For we often see those who hurry twisting their faces and gasping; if they lack a necessary reason for haste, this is a blemish deserving just reproach. I am not speaking of those whose occasional haste arises from a reason, but of those for whom constant and continual haste becomes habitual. In the former I do not approve the appearance of statues, nor in the latter the appearance of things violently shaken apart.

75. There is also a commendable manner of walking in which there is a mark of authority, the weight of dignity, and the trace of tranquility—provided, however, that there is no striving or affectation, but that the movement is pure and simple; for nothing artificial is pleasing. Nature should shape the movement. If there is some defect in nature, let effort correct it, so that art may be absent but correction not be lacking.

76. If even these matters are examined more deeply, how much more must we beware lest anything shameful come out of the mouth; for this gravely defiles a person. It is not food that defiles, but unjust slander and obscene words.

[Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, book 1, page 368, line 39: “And those parts of the body whose functions are necessary, neither the parts themselves,” and so forth.]

These things are shameful even in ordinary society. In our office, however, no word that falls dishonorably should fail to arouse modesty. We must not only refrain from saying anything unbecoming ourselves; we must not even lend an ear to such words, just as Joseph, lest he hear what was incompatible with his modesty, fled while leaving his garment behind (Genesis 39:12). For whoever takes pleasure in listening provokes another to speak.

77. Even to understand what is shameful is a matter of the greatest modesty. But to look upon something of this kind when it happens accidentally—what horror it arouses! Therefore, what displeases us in others—can it possibly please us in ourselves? Does nature itself not teach us this?

[Note: Ibid., line 32: “At the outset, nature itself seems to have taken great care of our body,” and so forth. In Ambrose’s text, the Erasmian and later editions prefer, “This very nature teaches us”; the manuscripts, with remarkable consistency, read, “nor does nature itself,” while Amerbach has, “nor does this very nature.” This is not unreasonable, for it continues the question that has begun.]

Nature perfectly arranged all the parts of our body, both to provide for necessity and to adorn grace. Yet those parts that are appropriate to see—those in which the summit of beauty is placed, as though on a certain citadel, and in which the sweetness of form and the beauty of the face are diffused, and whose practical use is more readily available—she left exposed and open. But those in which the service of natural necessity exists, lest they present an ugly spectacle of themselves, she partly removed and concealed within the body itself, and partly taught and urged us to cover.

78. Is nature itself not therefore the teacher of modesty? Following its example, human modesty—which, I believe, is named from *modus*, “measure,” because it knows what is fitting—covered and concealed what it found hidden in the structure of our body. Thus there is that opening which was commanded to be made transversely in Noah’s ark (Genesis 6:16), in which there is a figure either of the Church or of our body, through which the remains of food are expelled. The maker of nature therefore showed such care for our modesty, and preserved what is fitting and honorable in our body with such concern, that he relegated certain channels and outlets of our bodily passages behind us and turned them away from our sight, lest the cleansing of the bowels offend the eyes.

The Apostle beautifully says of this: “Those members of the body that seem weaker are more necessary; and those members of the body that we think less honorable, we surround with greater honor; and those that are unpresentable among us have greater dignity” (1 Corinthians 12:23). Indeed, by imitating nature, human effort increased grace. We have interpreted this more fully elsewhere (*On Noah and the Ark*, book 1, chapter 8), so that we should think it improper not only to conceal from the eyes but even to name by their proper terms the signs and functions of those bodily members that we have received as things to be concealed.

79. Finally, if these parts are exposed by accident, modesty is confounded; if deliberately, it is judged shamelessness. Hence Noah’s son Ham incurred offense, because he saw his father exposed and laughed; those who covered their father, however, received the grace of blessing (Genesis 9:22 and following).

[Note: Cicero, book 1 of *On Duties*, page 369, line 3: “According to our custom, when sons have reached puberty, they do not bathe with their parents,” and so forth. That this commendable custom did not prevail in Africa is indicated by Saint Augustine, *Confessions*, book 2, chapter 3. Otherwise, we understand from numerous testimonies of writers that ancient Christians were not forbidden the use of public baths: not only because Marcian and other Christian and pious emperors built bathhouses, but also because we read in Irenaeus, book 3, chapter 3, and in other ecclesiastical writers, that the apostle John once went to bathe and, finding Cerinthus inside, departed without bathing, lest the bathhouse collapse in which the enemy of truth was bathing. Gregory the Great certainly did not regard bathing as so sinful—provided it was done from necessity, not luxury—that he replied in book 11, letter 3, that one should not abstain from it even on the Lord’s Day. Health was the reason the Evangelist John used the bath, according to Theodoret, book 2 of *The Fables of Heretics*, although Epiphanius tells the whole story differently in *Heresy* 30; consult him. Augustine also records that he sought a bath to ease the grief caused by his mother’s death, in *Confessions*, book 9, chapter 12. Only luxury in bathing is therefore forbidden. Accordingly, Athanasius, in his book *On Virgins*, and Leander, *On the Institution of Virgins*, chapter 10, forbade baths to virgins—not to all, but to those who were healthy—whereas Saint Benedict, in Rule 36, permitted them to sick monks. Yet there were some who would not use them even when ill, as Egesippus and Jerome relate of the apostle James, Palladius of Isidore and Evagrius, and Gregory of Nazianzus of Basil. Nor were there lacking philosophers who claimed this same distinction for themselves, as Seneca records of himself in Letter 108, and Porphyry of Plotinus.]

From this arose the old custom, both in the city of Rome and in many cities, that adult sons did not bathe with their parents, nor sons-in-law with their fathers-in-law, lest the authority of paternal reverence be diminished. Nevertheless, most people cover themselves as much as they can even in the bath, so that even where the entire body is naked, this particular part may remain covered.

80. Priests also, according to the ancient custom that we read of in Exodus, wore undergarments, as the Lord said to Moses: “You shall make linen undergarments for them, to cover the shame of nakedness. They shall extend from the loins to the thighs, and Aaron and his sons shall wear them when they enter the tent of testimony; and when they approach to sacrifice at the altar of the sanctuary, they shall not bring sin upon themselves, lest they die” (Exodus 28:42–43).

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “to cover the shame of sweat”; many others, as well as the old edition, read more appropriately, “the shame of modesty.” The Roman edition has replaced this with “the shame of the body,” evidently following the Septuagint, which reads: **Καλύψαι ἀσκημοσύνην χρωτὸς αὐτῶν**—“to cover the indecency of their flesh.” The Hebrew text has “nakedness”; the Vulgate reads, “to cover the shameful flesh.”]

Some of our people are still said to observe this. Most, however, judge that it was spoken spiritually, as a warning concerning modesty and a safeguard of chastity.

## CHAPTER XIX

How the Orator describes propriety; whether and to what extent physical beauty contributes to virtue; and finally, with what care we must ensure that nothing affected or effeminate appears in us.

81. I have taken pleasure in lingering at greater length over the aspects of modesty because I was speaking to you, who either recognize its benefits in yourselves or are unaware of its losses. Although it is appropriate to all ages, persons, times, and places, it especially suits adolescents and the years of youth.

82. At every age we must preserve what is fitting and suitable to what we do, so that the order of our life may correspond and harmonize with itself. Hence Tullius also thinks that order must be preserved in that propriety; he says that it consists in beauty, order, and adornment suited to action—things which, he says, are difficult to explain in speech, and therefore sufficient to understand.

[Note: Cicero, book 1 of *On Duties*, page 368, line 29: “And this is situated in three things: beauty,” and so forth.]

83. I do not quite understand why he included beauty, although he also praises bodily strength. We certainly do not place the substance of virtue in bodily beauty, but neither do we exclude grace, because modesty often suffuses the face itself with shame and makes it more pleasing. Just as an artisan generally works better with a more suitable material, so modesty stands out more in bodily beauty itself—provided that the beauty of the body is not affected, but natural, simple, and careless rather than sought after; not aided by expensive and dazzling garments, but ordinary, so that nothing is lacking to propriety or necessity and nothing is added merely for brilliance.

[Note: Ibid., line 49: “In these matters two things especially must be avoided,” and so forth. It is generally acknowledged that white garments were once regarded as signs of joy. Numerous testimonies of writers report that the Romans customarily wore this color at festivals and banquets. Sacred interpreters likewise connect it with the same meaning because Christ’s garments became white at the Transfiguration and because angels appeared clothed in white after the Resurrection. The same meaning may not implausibly be assigned to the custom by which the newly baptized wore white garments throughout the octave of Easter, though this also displayed a sign of innocence. Yet white was not so exclusively associated with joy that it could not also serve mourning; we know that Roman women once wore white at funerals, and some say that this custom was also preserved in Gaul by widowed queens. Black or dark clothing was otherwise thought appropriate to sorrow; hence monks, whose task is to mourn both their own sins and those of others, chose it. For this reason Antony the Great, inflamed with desire for martyrdom, put on white so that, if recognized by the sign of monastic color, he would not be prevented from approaching the judge, as Rosweidus relates in his life of him. Baronius writes that sacred virgins likewise customarily wore this color, under the year 57. From a certain passage in Jerome’s letter to Nepotian, which he assigns to the year 393, he also concludes that clerics in ancient times wore neither dark nor white garments, but chestnut-colored and violet ones. He adds that the color black first entered the Church when monasticism was adopted by clerics in certain Churches and monks were made bishops. In this latter point, at least, he seems to agree with the learned Cardinal, since the life of Saint Martin says that, after he had been raised to the episcopal see, he retained the black cloak that he had previously worn as a monk. In explaining Jerome’s passage, however, he disagrees with Peter of Cluny. The latter interprets it as merely warning Nepotian to avoid vanity in the use of either color. Although Baronius’s explanation may seem less forced, it is nevertheless certain that Ambrose forbids the clergy here nothing except an affected and excessively bright whiteness of clothing, as what follows clearly shows: nothing should be added to its brightness. This agrees remarkably with what Basil commands in Letter 1 to Gregory of Nazianzus. You may consult that letter yourself.]

84. The voice itself should be neither languid nor broken, sounding feminine in no way, as many are accustomed to feign under the appearance of gravity; rather, it should preserve a certain form, rule, and virile vigor. For this is what it means to maintain the beauty of conduct: to render to each sex and person what is appropriate. This is the best order of actions; this is adornment suited to every activity. But just as I do not approve of a soft and weakened tone of voice or bodily gesture, so neither do I approve of one that is harsh and rustic. Let us imitate nature: its likeness is the pattern of discipline and the form of propriety.

## CHAPTER XX

To preserve modesty, the company of intemperate people, banquets with outsiders, and dealings with women must be avoided; our leisure at home must instead be spent in pious and honorable pursuits.

85. Modesty certainly has its own reefs—not reefs that it itself brings forward, but those upon which it often runs aground if we fall in with the company of intemperate people, who, under the appearance of pleasure, pour poison into the good. If such people are frequent companions, especially at banquets, games, and jokes, they weaken that manly gravity. Let us therefore beware lest, while wishing to relax the mind, we dissolve the whole harmony, as it were, the concord of good works; for habit quickly bends nature.

86. Hence I think it particularly prudent and appropriate to ecclesiastical conduct, and especially to the duties of ministers, to avoid the banquets of outsiders: either so that you yourselves may be hospitable to travelers, or so that, through this precaution, no opportunity for reproach may remain. Banquets with outsiders involve occupations and distractions, and they also reveal a desire for feasting.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “they produce a desire for feasting.”]

Stories about worldly affairs and pleasures also frequently creep in; you cannot close your ears, and to prevent them is thought arrogant. Cups too slip in, even against one’s will. It is better to make an excuse once at your own house than frequently at another’s; and even if you yourself rise sober, your presence ought not to be condemned because of another’s insolence.

[Note: [Col. 0049D] The Church has always exercised great care for the reputation of its ministers. Hence Ambrose, in this passage, restricts the contact of younger clerics with widows and consecrated virgins by so many conditions. Moved by the same prudence, the bishops of the fourth Council of Carthage, wishing to indicate that every occasion for this kind of intimacy should be removed, decreed in canon 102: “It pertains to the bishop’s guilt . . . if, for the sake of supporting their present life”—although scarcely any reason could be more just—“widows or religious women are subjected to the familiar association of clerics.” Since the holy Doctor nowhere prescribes how such women who approach clerics are to be received, one may infer that they were not accustomed to leave their homes very frequently to visit anyone. Nevertheless, we find that the Church as a whole made provision that no woman should approach a deacon without a deaconess. If such caution was established concerning the access of an ordinary woman to a deacon, who would be surprised that the cohabitation of priests with women was prohibited by so many canons?]

87. There is no need for younger men to visit the homes of widows and virgins except for the purpose of visitation; and even this should be done with elders—that is, either with the bishop or, if the matter is more serious, with priests. Why should we give secular people an opportunity for slander? Why should we lend authority to those frequent visits as well? What if one of them should happen to fall? Why should you incur the odium arising from another’s fall? How many strong men have been deceived by temptation! How many have given no place to error, yet have given occasion for suspicion!

88. Why not devote to reading those periods during which you are free from ecclesiastical duties? Why not visit Christ again, address Christ, hear Christ? We address him when we pray; we hear him when we read the divine utterances. What have we to do with the homes of others? There is one house that receives everyone. Let those who seek us come to us instead. What have we to do with stories? [Col. 0050B] We have received the ministry of serving Christ’s altars, not the duty of serving human beings.

89. It is fitting that we be humble, gentle, meek, serious, and patient, and that we observe moderation in everything, so that no vice in our character is announced even by our silent expression or by our speech.

## CHAPTER XXI

Anger must be guarded against before it arises; if it has arisen, it must be restrained and calmed. If we cannot even accomplish this, at least the tongue must be restrained from abuse, so that our emotions may resemble the disturbances of children. The saying of Archytas is recalled, and it is shown that David preceded him in this matter both by his deeds and by his writings.

90. [Note: [Col. 0050D] Cicero, *On Duties*, book I, p. 363, line 12: “Anger must especially be prohibited,” etc. Here our Ambrose differs from Cicero, since Cicero, following the Stoics, places virtue in freedom from the emotions, whereas Ambrose, according to Christian teaching, places it in their moderation.] Let anger be avoided; or, if it cannot be prevented, let it be restrained, [Col. 0050C] for indignation is an evil enticement to sin, and it so disturbs the mind that it leaves no room for reason. The first thing, then, if possible, is for tranquility of character, through habitual practice, [Note: [Col. 0050D] Some manuscripts read *affectione propositi*, “by the attachment of one’s purpose,” instead of *in naturam vertatur*, “to be turned into nature.”] disposition, and determination, to become part of one’s nature. Then, since this impulse is usually so firmly implanted in nature and character that it cannot be uprooted [Note: [Col. 0050D] Several manuscripts and the Gill edition in the margin and Roman edition in the text read *atque evinci non queat*, “and cannot be overcome.”] or avoided, if it can be foreseen, let it be restrained by reason. Or if the mind has first been seized by indignation before reason could look ahead and take precautions against its seizure, consider how you may overcome the movement of your mind and moderate your anger. Resist anger if you can; yield if you cannot, [Col. 0051A] because it is written: “Give place to wrath” (Rom. 12:19).

91. Jacob piously yielded to his enraged brother (Gen. 27:42 and following), and, instructed by the counsel of Rebekah—that is, by patience—he preferred to remain away and live as an exile rather than arouse his brother’s indignation. He would return when he thought that his brother had been appeased. And for this reason he found such great favor with God. By what acts of obedience, by how many gifts, did he reconcile his brother to himself, so that the brother no longer remembered the blessing that had been taken from him, but remembered the satisfaction that had been offered (Gen. 32:3 and following)!

92. Therefore, if anger has overtaken and seized your mind, and has risen up within you, do not abandon your position. Your position is patience; your position is wisdom; your position is reason; your position is the calming of indignation. Or if the obstinacy of someone answering you has provoked you, and perversity has driven you to indignation, then, if you cannot calm your mind, restrain your tongue. For it is written: “Keep your tongue from evil, and your lips from speaking deceit. Seek peace, and pursue it” (Ps. 33:14–15). Consider that peace of the holy Jacob, by which you should first calm your mind: [Note: [Col. 0051D] The Roman edition alone reads: “Jacob, consider how great the calming of the mind was at first.” The old edition and a few manuscripts read: “Jacob, consider how, when the mind had first been calmed”; several others: “Jacob, consider how great it was; first, etc.” The remaining witnesses read as in the text, except that some have *quanto*, “how greatly,” instead of *qua tu*, “by which you.” The latter is erroneous.] if you cannot prevail, put a bridle on your tongue; then do not neglect the pursuit of reconciliation. The secular orators have appropriated these ideas from our writers and set them down in their own books; but the meaning has its true grace in the one who first uttered it.

93. Let us therefore avoid or moderate anger, so that it may neither make exceptions in our praises nor exaggerate our faults. It is no small thing to calm anger; it is no less than not to be disturbed at all. The former is our achievement; the latter belongs to nature. Finally, the disturbances of children are harmless, and have more charm than bitterness. Even when children quickly become angry with one another, they are easily calmed and return to one another with greater affection. They do not know how to manipulate one another deceitfully and cunningly. Do not despise these children, of whom the Lord says: “Unless you turn and become like this child, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 18:3). Thus the Lord himself—that is, the power of God—like a child, when he was cursed, did not curse in return; when he was struck, he did not strike back (1 Pet. 2:23). So shape yourself that, like a child, you do not retain an injury or practice malice; let everything proceed from you innocently. Do not consider what may return to you from others. Preserve your position; guard the simplicity [Col. 0051D] and purity of your heart. Do not answer an angry person in kind, or an imprudent person with imprudence. A fault quickly provokes another fault. If you rub stones together, does not fire break out?

[Col. 0052A] 94. The pagans report—for they are accustomed to magnify everything in words—[Note: [Col. 0051D] Valerius Maximus reports the same story about Archytas in book 4, chapter 1. It is nevertheless certain that Archytas lived much later than David, for the common reckoning of chronologists establishes that his teacher Pythagoras lived only in the year 3389 after the creation of the world, whereas David had already flourished from the year 2887. Others, however, have attributed this very saying to different persons: Laërtius to Plato, Plutarch to Charillus, and Stobaeus to Theano.] the saying of the philosopher Archytas of Tarentum, who said to his steward: “How unfortunate you are—I would have punished you, had I not been angry!” But David had already restrained his armed hand in his indignation (1 Sam. 25:32). And how much greater is it not to curse in return than not to take revenge? Abigail had recalled the warriors who were prepared to avenge themselves upon Nabal by her entreaty. From this we understand that, when timely intercessions are made, we ought not merely to yield but even to take delight in yielding. He was so delighted that he blessed the woman who intervened, because he had been recalled from his pursuit of vengeance.

95. He had already said concerning his enemies: “For they have turned iniquity against me, and in anger they troubled me” [Col. 0052B] (Ps. 54:4). Let us hear what he said when disturbed by anger: “Who will give me wings like a dove, and I will fly away and rest?” (ibid., 7). They provoked him to anger; he chose tranquility.

96. He had already said: “Be angry, and do not sin” (Ps. 4:5). As a moral teacher who knew that the natural emotion should be redirected by the discipline of reason rather than eradicated, he teaches moral conduct; that is: “Be angry where there is wrongdoing, at which you ought to be angry.” [Note: [Col. 0052D] Cicero, *On Duties*, book I, p. 370, line 4: “Rebukes also sometimes become necessary,” etc.] For it cannot happen that we are not moved by the shamefulness of things; otherwise what is judged is not virtue but sluggishness and indifference. [Note: [Col. 0052D] The old edition and part of the manuscripts read *lenitudo*, “mildness”; Gill in the margin and the Roman edition in the text, along with other manuscripts, read *lentitudo*, “sluggishness,” which is more suitable, since this is a vice; there is no other reading.] Be angry, then, in such a way that you abstain from sin. Or understand it this way: If you are angry, do not sin, but overcome anger by reason. Or certainly in this way: If you are angry, be angry with yourself because you have been disturbed, and you will not sin. For whoever is angry with himself because he has been quickly provoked ceases to be angry with another; but whoever wishes to prove his anger just becomes more inflamed and quickly falls into wrongdoing. According to Solomon, the one who restrains anger is better than the one who captures a city (Prov. 16:32), because anger deceives even the strong.

97. We must therefore take care not to fall into disturbances before reason has composed our minds; for anger, grief, or fear of death often deprives the mind of life and strikes it with an unforeseen blow. It is therefore admirable to anticipate this through reflection, exercising the mind by turning matters over in thought, so that it is not aroused by sudden disturbances but, bound by a kind of yoke and reins of reason, grows calm.

## CHAPTER XXII

[Col. 0052D] Concerning thoughts and appetite, and concerning the decorum of speech to be maintained in conversation and debate.

98. There are two kinds of movement, namely, of thought and of appetite: one belonging to thought, the other to appetite; [Note: [Col. 0052D] Cicero, book I, p. 369, line 19: “The movements of the mind, however, are of two kinds: some belong to cognition, others to appetite,” etc.] they are not confused but distinct and different. Thoughts have the task of seeking out the truth, [Note: [Col. 0053C] Some manuscripts read *et quasi emoliri*, “and, as it were, to work it out.”] and, as it were, of bringing it forth; appetite impels and rouses us to do something. Thus, according to the very character of their nature, thoughts instill tranquility and calm, while appetite shakes us into action. Let us therefore be so formed that the thought of good things enters the mind and appetite obeys reason—if indeed we wish to direct our minds toward preserving that decorum—so that affection for some matter does not exclude reason, but reason examines what accords with moral goodness.

99. [Note: [Col. 0053C] Cicero, book I of *On Duties*, p. 369, line 23: “And since speech has great power,” etc. Below, line 39: “Let this speech, in which the Socratics excel, be gentle,” etc. Likewise, line 40: “But since in all of life,” etc. Ambrose presents the entire subject matter of ecclesiastical sermons as contained in two parts: either it concerns faith or it concerns morals, that is, the moral virtues; and he includes these under justice, namely, universal virtue. Thus Christ himself says to John the Baptist, “It is fitting for us to fulfill all justice,” that is, every virtue. The holy bishop likewise distributes this same general justice below, as it were, into its proper members: continence, which concerns ourselves; particular justice, which concerns our neighbor; and diligence, which is especially directed toward the worship and service of God. When he adds that there should not always be one fixed discourse, but that the subject should be taken up according to the reading completed in the church’s assembly, he indeed directs that the sermon should be composed differently when Scripture deals with continence and when it deals with justice or piety. Yet he does not remove meditation or preparation; rather, he requires it, when he forbids a discourse to be made too brief and gives as the reason that it might reveal laziness and carelessness. Perhaps there will again arise an occasion to speak of this matter.] And since we have said that the preservation of decorum requires us to know what measure belongs to deeds and words, while the order of speaking comes before that of acting, speech is divided into two kinds: familiar conversation, and exposition and debate concerning faith and justice. In both, we must ensure that there is no disorder; speech should proceed as gentle and calm, full of goodwill and grace, without any insult. Let stubborn contention be absent from familiar conversation, for it generally arouses empty questions rather than contributing anything useful. Let debate be without anger, pleasantness without bitterness, admonition without harshness, and exhortation without offense. And just as in every action of life we must take care that excessive emotion does not exclude reason, but must retain the place of deliberation, so in speech also it is fitting to preserve that rule, lest we arouse anger or hatred, or reveal any signs of our own greed or laziness.

[Col. 0053C] 100. Let speech of this kind concern the Scriptures above all. For what ought we to speak about more than the best way of life, exhortation to observance, and the safeguarding of discipline? Let its beginning have a rationale and its conclusion due measure. [Note: [Col. 0053D] Ibid., line 49: “And as the manner of beginning has been, so let the manner of ending be.”] Tedious speech arouses anger. How unbecoming it is that, although every conversation ought ordinarily to increase grace, it should contain a blemish of offense!

101. We must also take up discourses on the doctrine of faith, instruction in continence, debate concerning justice, and exhortation to diligence—not always one fixed subject, but whatever the reading presents, both taking it up and pursuing it as we are able; neither excessively prolonged nor quickly interrupted, lest it either leave behind weariness or reveal laziness and carelessness. Let the speech be pure, simple, clear, and comprehensible, full of seriousness and weight—not affected elegance, but grace that is not allowed to lapse.

## CHAPTER XXIII

[Col. 0054B]

Jokes, although sometimes respectable, are nevertheless altogether prohibited among ecclesiastical men; the voice, however, ought to be pure and simple.

102. [Note: [Col. 0053D] Above, line 25: “The rhetoricians give many rules concerning contention,” etc.] Secular writers also offer many instructions concerning the art of speaking, which I think we may pass over, [Note: [Col. 0053D] Page 365, line 13: “They may indeed use play and joking,” etc. Thomas Aquinas, *Summa Theologiae* II-II, question 168, article 2, reply to objection 1. Saint Thomas intends Ambrose’s words to signify nothing other than that jokes should be rejected by Christian orators when expounding sacred doctrine to the people. Yet, with due respect to so great a doctor, the statement that jokes are contrary to ecclesiastical discipline does not seem identical with saying that jokes must be avoided in teaching sacred doctrine; rather, there appears to be no rule in the sacred books or canons permitting clerics to joke. But even if this passage is understood specifically of teaching Christian doctrine to the people, that does not resolve the force of the objection. For the objector had set against it the words of the same doctor in the following section, where, speaking of stories—that is, familiar conversation—and introducing Christ’s threat against those who laugh, he condemns absolutely every kind of joke.
