Nor is it surprising that Ambrose forbids clerics the use of jokes, since Basil universally denies that it is lawful for a Christian to laugh, *Shorter Rules*, question 31. Consult also his letter 411 and *Ascetic Constitutions*, chapter 12; in this teaching as well, Saint Benedict imitated him in chapter 6 of his Rule. These matters indeed apply to ascetics, but they also suit all who are devoted to virtue, and especially priests, of whom Bernard rightly and piously says in book II, chapter 13 of *On Consideration*: “Among secular people, trifles are trifles; in the mouth of a priest, they are blasphemies.” See likewise the *Treatise on the Order of Life and the Institution of Morals*, wrongly attributed among Saint Bernard’s works, where in chapter 3 the text of Ambrose with which we are concerned is copied word for word. It must moreover be admitted that, in this category, those sin most gravely who transfer theatrical jests to the sacred platform and dissolve and defile evangelical seriousness with histrionic and buffoonish wit. See our Mabillon’s note on the passage of Bernard cited above, as well as J. B. Thiers and others.] when considering the discipline of joking. For although jokes may sometimes be respectable and pleasant, they are nevertheless contrary to ecclesiastical rule; for how can we make use of things that we do not find in the sacred Scriptures?

103. We must also take care, even in stories, that they do not bend the seriousness of a stricter purpose. “Woe to you who laugh, for you shall weep” (Luke 6:21), says the Lord. And are we to seek material for laughter, so that, laughing here, we may weep there? I think that not only excessive but every kind of joking should be avoided, unless perhaps it is not unbecoming for speech to be full of pleasantness and grace. [Note: [Col. 0054D] The old edition and some manuscripts read: “yet full of pleasantness.”]

104. What should I say about the voice? I think it is enough for it to be simple and pure. [Note: [Col. 0055D] Cicero, book I of *On Duties*, p. 369, line 29: “In the voice, however, let us pursue two things: that it be clear and pleasant,” etc.] For it to be melodious belongs to nature, not to technique. Let it certainly be distinct in its manner of pronunciation and full of vigorous, manly substance, so that it avoids a rustic and semi-rustic sound, yet does not strive after theatrical rhythm; rather, let it preserve the mystical character. [Note: [Col. 0055D] “Mystical” means appropriate to the holiness of the mysteries.]

## CHAPTER XXIV

Three things must be observed in the actions of life: that appetite be subjected to reason; that proper moderation be maintained in our pursuits; and finally, that each thing be done at its proper time and in its proper order. All these qualities shone forth so greatly in the holy men of the Old Testament that it is clear they were excellently equipped with the virtues commonly called cardinal virtues.

105. I think enough has been said concerning the art of speaking. Let us now consider what is fitting in the conduct of life. [Note: [Col. 0055D] Cicero, book I, p. 370, line 37: “In undertaking every action, three things must be observed,” etc.] In this matter we see three things to be considered. First, that appetite not resist reason; for only in this way can our duties accord with decorum. If appetite obeys reason, what is fitting can easily be preserved in all duties. Next, we must not appear to undertake a small and insignificant matter with excessive ceremony, or to abandon a great matter with too little care—neither with greater zeal than the matter itself warrants, nor with less. Third, I think we must not pass over the moderation of our pursuits and labors, nor the order of things and the suitability of times.

[Col. 0055C] 106. The first of these is, as it were, the foundation of everything: that appetite obey reason. The second and third are the same, namely, moderation in both. For among us there is no room for the contemplation of liberal form—that is, beauty—and dignity. What follows concerns the order of things and the suitability of times. Accordingly, there are three matters that we must see whether we can show to have been perfected in any of the saints.

107. First, the patriarch Abraham himself, who was formed and instructed for the teaching of the future succession, was commanded to leave his land, his kindred, and his father’s house (Gen. 12:1 and following). Although he was bound by the affection of multiplied ties, [Note: [Col. 0056D] Several manuscripts and editions read “multiplied”; some read “bound by the affection of manifold kinship.”] did he not nevertheless present his appetite obedient to reason? [Col. 0055D] Who would not be delighted by the affection for his land, his kindred, and even his own household? Their sweetness therefore soothed him, but the consideration of the heavenly command and eternal reward moved him more powerfully. Did he not consider that his wife was weak for labor, vulnerable to injury, and beautiful in a way that might incite the insolence of others, and that she could not be led away without the greatest danger? Yet he judged it wiser to undergo everything than to make excuses. Then, when he was going down into Egypt, he instructed her to say that she was his sister, not his wife.

108. Consider how powerful his appetite was. He feared for his wife’s chastity; he feared for his own safety; he suspected the lusts of the Egyptians. Yet reason for carrying out his devotion prevailed with him. He considered that, with God’s favor, he could be safe everywhere, but that, if the Lord were offended, he could not remain unharmed even at home. Thus reason conquered appetite and made it obedient to itself.

109. [Note: [Col. 0056D] The Roman edition, together with one or two manuscripts, reads: “When his nephew had been captured, he recovers him by war.”] When his nephew had been captured, he was neither terrified nor thrown into confusion by so many peoples and kings, but took up war; after winning the victory, he refused a share of the spoil, although he himself had been its author (Gen. 14:14 and following). When a son had also been promised to him, although he considered that the strength of his body had died away, that his wife was barren, and that he was of extreme old age, he nevertheless trusted God even against the course of nature (Gen. 15:6).

110. Consider how everything agrees: appetite was not absent, but was restrained; a mind evenly suited to its tasks, which regarded neither great things as trivial nor lesser things as great; moderation appropriate to his affairs; order in things; suitability of times; measure in words. First in faith, outstanding in justice, vigorous in battle, not greedy in victory, hospitable at home, attentive to his wife.

111. His holy nephew Jacob also found it pleasing to live securely at home; but his mother wished him to go into exile, so that he might make way for his brother’s anger (Gen. 27:24 and following). The soundness of this counsel conquered his appetite. An exile from home and a fugitive from his parents, he nevertheless everywhere observed a fitting measure in his affairs and reserved each action for its appropriate time. At home he was acceptable to his parents: one, challenged by the maturity of his obedience, gave him a blessing, while the other inclined toward him with loving affection (Gen. 25:34). Preferred even in his brother’s judgment, when he thought his food ought to be yielded to his brother, he was naturally pleased by nourishment, but in accordance with filial devotion he yielded to the request. A faithful shepherd to the master of the flock, an attentive son-in-law to his father-in-law, tireless in labor, frugal at table, foremost in making satisfaction, generous in reward (Gen. 31:6 and following). Finally, he so calmed his brother’s anger that he obtained the favor of the man whose enmity he had feared (Gen. 33:1).

112. What shall I say of Joseph? He certainly desired freedom, yet he accepted the necessity of servitude. How submissive he was in servitude, how steadfast in virtue, how kind in prison, wise in interpretation, moderate in power, provident in abundance, just in famine—adding the order of praise to events, suitability to times, and equity to peoples through the moderation of his office (Gen. 39:1 and following)!

[Col. 0057A] 113. Job likewise was blameless amid prosperity and adversity, patient, grateful and acceptable to God. He was afflicted by pains, but consoled himself (Job 2:3 and following).

31 114. David too was brave in war, patient in adversity, peaceful in Jerusalem, gentle in victory, sorrowful in sin, provident in old age. Through the individual sounds of the stages of life he preserved the proper measures of circumstances and the turns of time, so that he seems to me to have poured forth to the immortal God a song of his merit, sweet not less in his manner of living than in the sweetness of his singing. [Note: [Col. 0057C] This is found in the most numerous manuscripts and in the Era edition and Gill’s margin. Several others, as well as all editions in the text, read “moral to God”; Benignus has “of himself to the immortal God,” etc.]

115. What duty belonging to the chief virtues was lacking in these men? The first of these virtues, [Note: [Col. 0057C] Cicero, book I, p. 352, line 36: “But everything honorable arises from one of four parts,” etc.] they placed prudence, which is occupied with the investigation of truth and instills a desire for fuller knowledge. Second, justice, which assigns to each person his own, does not seize what belongs to another, and neglects personal advantage in order to preserve common equity. Third, fortitude, which is conspicuous both in warfare through greatness of spirit and at home, and which prevails through the strength of the body. Fourth, temperance, which preserves the proper measure and order of everything that we judge should be done or said.

## CHAPTER XXV

Having explained why the discussion did not begin with the virtues just mentioned, it is now shown more closely that those same virtues existed in the patriarchs of old.

116. Perhaps someone will say that these matters ought to have been placed first, since the various kinds of duties arise from these four virtues. But this belongs to method, [Note: [Col. 0057D] Page 351, line 27: “Since the whole discussion will concern duty, it pleases me first to define it,” etc.] in that duty should first be defined and afterward divided into its distinct categories. We, however, avoid technical procedure and present the examples of our ancestors. These neither obscure understanding nor introduce subtlety into the treatment. Let the life of our ancestors therefore be for us a mirror of discipline, not a contrivance of cleverness; an object of reverent imitation, not an occasion for argumentative ingenuity.

117. In holy Abraham, then, prudence was present in the first place, as Scripture says: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Gen. 15:6). [Col. 0058A] No one is prudent who does not know God. Finally, “The fool has said in his heart, ‘There is no God’” (Ps. 13:1), for the wise person would not say this. How can one be wise who does not seek his creator, who says to a stone, “You are my father” (Jer. 2:27): [Note: [Col. 0057D] The statements attributed here to Manichaeus and Arius are clear. No one is unaware that Arius attributed imperfection to Christ, whom he cast down into the order of created beings, while Manichaeus assigned the creation of bodily things to the devil. Yet someone might perhaps find difficulty in the fact that Eunomius is joined to Marcion rather than to Arius. For it is established that Eunomius was a disciple of Aetius and associated with the Arians, as Socrates testifies in book II, chapter 15, saying that he shared their beliefs and expressions; Eunomius himself later gave his name to that sect, as the same Socrates indicates in book I, chapters 7 and 13. Sozomen may likewise be consulted, book IV, chapter 25, and book VI, chapter 26, along with others. Theodoret, however, resolves the difficulty. In book II, chapter 29 of his *Ecclesiastical History*, he had merely written that Eunomius compounded the blasphemy of Arius with a new addition of impiety; but in book IV of his *Compendium of Heretical Fables* he explains the matter more fully, saying: “When baptizing, they wet the upper parts of the body with water as far as the chest, but forbid water to be applied to the remaining parts as though they were accursed . . . . They are also said to dare another thing, which I would not entrust to writing,” etc. From this it is plainly inferred that he admitted a dual principle: one good, from which the upper parts of the body, whose goodness they did not deny, proceeded; and another evil, from which the lower parts, which they maintained were evil, proceeded. We are therefore surprised that those who recorded Eunomius’s collected errors in writing—among the ancients, Epiphanius and Augustine, and among later writers, Baronius, Petavius, and all the others—failed to notice the impiety of which the blessed Doctor speaks here. Perhaps the very atrocity of this error explains why certain imperial laws, such as that of Gratian mentioned by Sozomen in book VII, chapter 1, while freely allowing everyone to follow whatever religion or assembly he wished, added the exception of Manichaeans, Photinians, and Eunomians. It seems certain that Ambrose himself refers to this blasphemy in book II, chapter 5 of *The Hexaemeron*, where the Eunomians are called “offspring of a degenerate root,” namely, the inferior fruit of the Arians.] who says to the devil, like Manichaeus, “Are you my creator?” How can Arius be wise, preferring to have an imperfect and degenerate creator rather than a true and perfect one? [Note: [Col. 0058D] Many manuscripts read: “How can one be wise, like Arius . . . like Marcion.”] How can Marcion and Eunomius be wise, since they prefer to have an evil God rather than a good one? How can one be wise who does not fear his God? “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110:9). And elsewhere you have: “The wise do not depart from the mouth of the Lord, but discourse in their confessions” (Prov. 24:7). Scripture also says at the same time: “It was reckoned to him as righteousness”; [Col. 0058B] thereby it bestowed upon him the grace of another virtue.

118. Our forefathers therefore first defined prudence as consisting in the knowledge of truth. For who among them came before Abraham, David, and Solomon? Next, they held that justice concerns the fellowship of the human race. Finally, David says: “He has distributed; he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures forever. The righteous shows mercy; the righteous lends” (Ps. 111:9). For the wise and righteous person, the whole world is a possession of riches. The righteous regards common things as his own and his own things as common. The righteous accuses himself before others. For he is righteous who does not spare even himself and does not allow his hidden faults to remain concealed. See how righteous Abraham was. In old age he had received a son by promise (Gen. 22:3 and following), yet, when the Lord demanded that he be offered in sacrifice, he did not think that he should refuse—not even though the son was his only one.

119. Observe here all four virtues in a single deed. It belonged to wisdom to believe God and not to place the favor of his son before the command of the creator. It belonged to justice to return what had been received. It belonged to fortitude to restrain appetite by reason. The father led the sacrificial victim; the son asked questions; the father’s affection was tested, but not overcome. The son repeated his filial appeal; the father’s heart was pierced, but his devotion was not diminished. [Col. 0059A] The fourth virtue, temperance, was also present. The righteous man preserved both the measure of piety and the order of execution. Finally, while he carried what was necessary for the sacrifice, while he arranged the fire, while he bound his son, while he drew the sword, he earned by this order of sacrifice the preservation of his son.

120. Who was wiser than holy Jacob, who saw God face to face and merited a blessing (Gen. 32:1 and following)? Who was more just, since he divided with his brother what he had acquired by offering gifts? Who was more courageous, since he wrestled with God? Who was more modest than the man who displayed modesty in both place and time, preferring to cover his daughter’s injury by marriage rather than avenge it, because, being among foreigners, he thought it better to protect love than to accumulate hatred?

121. How wise was Noah, who built so great an ark (Gen. 6:14 and following)! How just, since he was preserved as the seed of all and alone among all was made both the survivor of the former generation and the founder of the future—born for the world and for all things more than for himself! How brave, that he overcame the flood! How temperate, that he endured the flood—recognizing when he should enter, with what moderation he should live, when he should release the raven, when the dove, when he should receive them back on their return, and when he should seize the opportunity to leave?

## CHAPTER XXVI

The philosophers sinned against their own principles in investigating truth, whereas Moses showed himself wiser than they. We must strive all the more earnestly to acquire wisdom because of its greater dignity, toward which all people are impelled by nature itself.

122. In the investigation of truth, therefore, they discuss the decorum that must be observed: we should seek with the greatest zeal what is true, not take falsehoods for truths, not envelop truths in obscurity, and not occupy the mind with superfluous, confused, or ambiguous matters. What is more unbecoming than to worship wood, as they themselves do? What is more obscure than to investigate astronomy and geometry, as they approve; to measure the spaces of the deep air; to enclose the heavens and even the sea within numbers; and to abandon the causes of salvation while seeking errors?

123. But Moses, instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, did not approve these things. Rather, he judged that wisdom to be loss and foolishness; turning away from it, he sought God with the deepest affection. Therefore he saw, questioned, and heard him speaking. Who was wiser than the man whom God himself taught, who emptied all the wisdom of the Egyptians and all the powers of their arts through the force of his work (Exod. 3:1 and following)? He did not regard the unknown as known or rashly assent to such things. Those who do not judge that it is contrary to nature or shameful to worship stones and seek aid from images that have no sensation should learn that these are precisely the two things to be avoided above all in this natural and honorable matter.

124. Therefore, the more exalted the virtue of wisdom is, the more earnestly, I think, we must strive to attain it. Thus, so that we may think nothing contrary to nature and nothing shameful or unbecoming, we must devote both time and diligence to examining matters carefully. Nothing distinguishes human beings more from the other animals than participation in reason: human beings seek the causes of things and judge that the creator of their race must be investigated—the one in whose power lies the power of our life and death, who governs this world by his will, and to whom we know that an account of our actions must be rendered. Nothing contributes more to an honorable life than believing that he will be the judge whom hidden things do not deceive, unbecoming things offend, and honorable things delight.

125. It is therefore inherent in all human beings, according to human nature, to investigate the truth, which draws us toward the pursuit of knowledge and learning and instills in us the desire to inquire. To excel in this seems beautiful to everyone, but only few attain it: those who, by turning over their thoughts and examining their plans, expend no small effort so that they may reach the point of living happily and honorably and draw near to it through their works. For, he says, “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the things that I say” (Matt. VII, 21). Indeed, studies of knowledge without deeds, I scarcely know whether they do not involve one even more deeply.

## CHAPTER XXVII

[Col. 0060C]

That prudence is the first source of duty, from which the other three virtues are derived, and that they are so interconnected with it and with one another that they cannot be separated or divided from one another.

126. The first source of duty [Note: [Col. 0059D] In the same place, p. 353, line 4: “But from the four places into which,” etc.] is therefore prudence. For what is so full of duty as to devote zeal and reverence to the Author? Yet this source also flows into the other virtues; for justice cannot exist without prudence, since examining what is just and what unjust requires no small degree of prudence. In both cases the error is extreme. For whoever judges what is just to be unjust, and what is unjust to be just, is accursed before God. “What use is wealth to a fool?” says Solomon (Prov. XVII, 15–16). [Note: [Col. 0059D] Thus the old edition, with several and indeed older manuscripts; the Roman edition, with others, reads “wealth to a fool.” The Septuagint reads, “Why does a fool have money?” [Col. 0060D] The other versions do not differ, except that Aquila and Theodotion write, “Why is this price in the hand of a fool?,” which is closer to the Hebrew text.] Nor, again, is prudence without justice; for piety toward God is the beginning of understanding. [Col. 0060D] From this we perceive that saying—more transferred than discovered by the wise of this age—that piety is the foundation of all virtues.

127. The first form of justice [Note: [Col. 0060D] Cicero, same work, line 22: “But of the remaining three, that principle extends most widely,” etc. At this point Saint Ambrose teaches that piety is joined to justice, a point also maintained by the Angelic Doctor, *Summa Theologiae* II–II, q. 8, a. 1. This piety is the gift of the Holy Spirit, as the same Thomas teaches, II–II, q. [Col. 0061D] 121, art. 1. Regarding the piety owed to parents, which he himself calls a virtue, he differs from Ambrose in this respect: Ambrose commands that the fatherland be preferred to parents, whereas Thomas prefers parents to the fatherland. Cicero preceded the holy Bishop in this, *De officiis*, p. 353, line 32: “But since, as Plato has splendidly written, we were not born for ourselves alone, and our country claims a share of our origin, our parents another share, and our friends another,” etc. Likewise, p. 358, line 35: “But when you have surveyed everything with reason and spirit, no association is more pleasing or dearer to each of us than that which we have with the republic. Parents are dear, children are dear,” etc. Also Book III, p. 400, line 30: “What if a father should attempt to seize tyranny or betray his country? . . . Finally, if the matter should concern the destruction of the country, he will put the safety of the country before the safety of his father.” The words which the Orator says he transferred from Plato are found in the same philosopher’s ninth letter, which is addressed to Archytas I, in this form: “But you must also bear in mind that each of us was not born for himself alone, but that our country receives one part of our origin, those who begot us another, and our other friends another.”] is piety toward God, the second toward the fatherland, the third toward parents, and likewise toward everyone; and this too accords with the teaching of nature. For from the beginning of life, as soon as the senses begin to be infused, we love life as God’s gift; we love our country and our parents, and then our peers, with whom we desire to associate. From this arises charity, which places others before oneself and does not seek its own interests; in this lies the preeminence of justice.

128. [Note: [Col. 0062D] Cicero, *De officiis* I, p. 352, line 4: “To begin with, nature has bestowed upon every kind of living creature the instinct to protect itself, its life, and its body, and to avoid those things,” etc.] In all living creatures as well there is implanted, first, the preservation of their own safety, avoidance of what harms them, and pursuit of what benefits them—such as food and hiding places in which they may protect themselves from danger, rain, and sun—which is a matter of prudence. It follows also that all kinds of living creatures are naturally inclined to gather together: first with those that share their kind and form, and then with others as well. Thus we see cattle delighted by herds, [Note: [Col. 0062D] Some manuscripts read “horses or rams by flocks.”] horses by herds, and especially like creatures by their equals; deer likewise with deer, and often joining themselves to human beings. What should I say now about the desire to beget and about offspring, or even about the love of those who generate, in which the chief form of justice is found?

129. It is therefore clear that these virtues, and the remaining ones akin to them, are related to one another. For fortitude also—[23, question 3, chapter “Fortitude”] whether it protects the fatherland from barbarians in war, defends the weak at home, or protects companions from robbers—is full of justice. To know by what plan one should defend and assist, and also to seize the opportunities of times and places, belongs to prudence and moderation. Temperance itself cannot know measure without prudence; to recognize the appropriate occasion and to give according to due measure belongs to justice. In all these matters magnanimity is necessary, as is a certain strength of mind, and often of body, so that one may be able to accomplish what one wills.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

[Col. 0061C]

That society consists of justice and beneficence; that Christians do not acknowledge as its two parts vengeance and private possession; and that what the Stoics teach concerning the common ownership of things and mutual assistance they borrowed from the Holy Scriptures. The great splendor of justice, and the obstacles that impede access to it.

130. Justice, therefore, is directed toward the fellowship of the human race and toward commonality. For the principle of society is divided into two parts: justice and beneficence, which they also call generosity and kindness. Justice seems to me the loftier, generosity the more pleasing: the former maintains strict judgment, the latter goodness.

[Col. 0062A] 131. But the very first duty which philosophers assign to justice is excluded among us. For they say that the first form of justice is that no one should harm anyone unless provoked by injury; but this is annulled by the authority of the Gospel (Luke IX, 56). Scripture wills that the spirit of the Son of Man be in us: he came to confer grace, not to inflict injury.

132. Next, they regarded it as a form of justice that one should treat common things as common—that is, public things as public—and private things as one’s own. But this too is not according to nature; for nature poured everything forth in common for everyone. For God commanded all things to be generated [Note: [Col. 0062D] Some manuscripts read, “so that offspring might be common to all. And the earth, therefore, would be,” etc. Others, and the edition, read better as in the text.] so that nourishment might be common to all, and so that the earth might be a kind of common possession for everyone. Nature therefore produced common right; appropriation made right private. [Col. 0062B] At this point they say [Note: [Col. 0062D] Cicero, *De officiis* I, p. 353, line 32: “But since, as it has been admirably written,” etc.] that the Stoics approved the view that everything produced on earth is created for human use, while human beings are generated for the sake of human beings, so that they might benefit one another.

133. From where did they take this, unless they adopted it from our Scriptures? For Moses wrote that God said: “Let us make man in our image and according to our likeness, and let him have dominion over the fish of the sea, the birds of heaven, the cattle, and all the creeping things upon the earth” (Gen. I, 26). And David says: “You have subjected all things beneath his feet, all sheep and oxen, moreover the beasts of the field, the birds of heaven, and the fish of the sea” (Ps. VIII, 8–9). Thus they learned from our Scriptures that all things were subjected to human beings, and therefore they believe that they were generated for the sake of human beings.

[Col. 0062C] 134. We also find in the books of Moses that human beings were generated for the sake of human beings, when the Lord said: “It is not good for man to be alone; let us make him a helper like himself” (Gen. II, 18). The woman, therefore, was given to the man as a help, so that she might bear children and so that one human being might be a help to another. Finally, before the woman was formed, it was said of Adam: “There was not found a helper like him” (ibid., 20); for a human being could not receive help except from another human being. Among all living creatures, therefore, no animal like him—and, to speak plainly, no helper for man—was found; hence a helper of the female sex was awaited.

135. [Note: [Col. 0062D] Ibid., line 36: “In this we ought to follow nature as our guide,” etc. Also p. 357, line 37: “But the fellowship of human beings is best,” etc.] Therefore, according to God’s will, or according to the bond of nature, we ought to assist one another, compete with one another in the performance of duties, place all advantages as though in the midst for common use, and, to use the word of Scripture, bring help to one another—whether by zeal, service, money, works, or in whatever way—so that the grace of fellowship among us may increase. Let no one be recalled from duty [Note: [Col. 0063D] Cicero, *De officiis* I, p. 354, line 35: “For the care of other people’s affairs is difficult; although Terence,” etc.] by fear of danger; but let each regard both adversity and prosperity as his own. Finally, holy Moses did not shrink from undertaking difficult wars for the people of his fatherland; he did not tremble before the weapons of the most powerful king, nor did he fear the ferocity of barbarian savagery. Rather, he cast aside his own safety in order to restore liberty to the people.

136. [Note: [Col. 0063D] Ibid., p. 553, line 23: “In which the splendor of virtue is greatest.”] Great, therefore, is the splendor of justice, which is born for others rather than for itself and assists our common life and fellowship. [Note: [Col. 0063D] Ibid., p. 352, line 25: “From this arises greatness of spirit,” etc.] It maintains loftiness, so that by its own judgment it holds everything subject, brings aid to others, contributes money, refuses no service, and undertakes dangers on behalf of others.

137. Who would not desire to hold this citadel of virtue, unless avarice first weakened and bent the strength of so great a virtue? For while we desire to increase our wealth, accumulate money, seize lands as possessions, and surpass others in riches, we strip off the form of justice and lose common beneficence. For how can someone be just who strives to take away from another what he seeks for himself?

138. The desire for power also makes the manly form of justice effeminate. For how can one intervene on behalf of others who strives to subject others to himself? How can one bring aid to the weak against the powerful who himself seeks a power oppressive to liberty?

## CHAPTER XXIX

[Col. 0063C]

That justice must be preserved even in war and toward enemies themselves, as is shown by the examples of Moses and Elisha; that the ancients received from the Hebrews the practice of calling enemies by a gentler name; and finally, that the foundation of justice is faith and its form is found in the Church.

139. How great justice is can be understood from the fact that it makes no exceptions for places, persons, or times, and is reserved even for enemies. [Note: [Col. 0063D] Cicero, *De officiis* I, p. 355, line 23: “And in the republic the laws of war must especially be preserved,” etc.] Thus, if a place or day for battle has been fixed with an enemy, it is considered contrary to justice either to anticipate him in place or to forestall him in time. For it matters whether someone is captured in a particular battle and serious engagement, [Note: [Col. 0064D] “With superior advantage,” that is, with some greater opportunity of time or place, as the context clearly demonstrates.] or by superior advantage or by some circumstance. A more severe vengeance is returned upon fiercer and treacherous enemies, and upon those who have inflicted greater injury. Thus it was with the Midianites, who through their women had caused many of the Jewish people to sin, and hence God’s anger had been poured out upon the people of their fathers. Therefore Moses, after his victory, allowed none of them to survive (Num. XXXI, 3 ff.). But the Gibeonites, who had attempted the people of their fathers more by deceit than by war, Joshua did not destroy; rather, he subjected them to the penalty of the condition imposed upon them (Josh. IX, 20 ff.). As for the Syrians whom Elisha had led into the city after they had besieged it and struck with momentary blindness so that they could not see where they were entering, he did not consent to the king of Israel’s desire to strike them, saying: “You shall not strike those whom you did not capture with your lance and sword. Set bread and water before them, so that they may eat and drink, and then let them return and go to their lord” (IV Kings VI, 14 ff.), so that, won over by kindness, they might repay the favor. Finally, afterward the Syrian raiders ceased coming into the land of Israel.

140. If justice therefore prevails even in war, how much more must it be observed in preserving peace? The prophet extended this grace even to those who had come to seize him. For we read that, after the Syrian king learned that Elisha was the one who opposed all his plans and [Note: [Col. 0064D] “Plans” here does not have the same sense as an explanation of an argument or reasoning; rather, it means precisely a cleverly or shrewdly devised stratagem.] counsels, he sent his army to besiege him. When Gehazi, the prophet’s servant, saw the army, he began to tremble at the danger to their safety. The prophet said to him: “Do not be afraid, for there are more with us than with them.” When the prophet prayed that the eyes of his servant might be opened, they were opened. Gehazi therefore saw the entire mountain filled with horses and chariots around Elisha. When these descended, the prophet said: “Strike, O God, the Syrian army with blindness.” When this had been granted, he said to the Syrians: “Come after me, and I will lead you to the man whom you seek.” And they saw Elisha, whom they had eagerly desired to seize; yet, although they saw him, they could not hold him. It is therefore clear that faith and justice must be preserved even in war, and that nothing can be honorable if faith is violated.

141. Finally, the ancients also called their adversaries by a gentler name, calling them foreigners; for in ancient usage enemies were called foreigners. We may likewise say that even this practice was taken from our Scriptures: the Hebrews called their adversaries *Allophyles*, that is, “foreigners,” using the Latin term. Thus we read in the First Book of Kings: “And it came to pass in those days that the foreigners assembled for battle against Israel” (I Kings IV, 1).

142. [Note: [Col. 0064D] Ibid., p. 353, line 39: “But the foundation of justice is faith,” etc.] Faith, therefore, is the foundation of justice; for the hearts of the just meditate upon faith. And when a just person accuses himself, he places justice above faith; for his justice appears when he confesses the truth. Finally, the Lord also says through Isaiah: “Behold, I lay a stone as the foundation of Zion” (Isa. XXVIII, 18), that is, Christ as the foundation of the Church. [Col. 0065A] Christ is the faith of all; but the Church is a certain form of justice. It is the common right of all: [Note: [Col. 0065D] The ancient Fathers always urged the Christian people with the greatest insistence to attend the Church’s assemblies and to pour out prayers to God in common, as we learn not only from that very ancient letter published under the name of blessed Barnabas, but also from Ignatius’ letter to the Ephesians, from chapter 39 of Tertullian’s *Apologeticus*, and from innumerable other testimonies of the Fathers and canons of councils. It is nevertheless more probable that public prayers of this sort are not meant here. Rather, when it is said, “he prays in common,” etc., this signifies only that he prays, works, and is tested on behalf of all, or for the benefit of all; in this consists the communion of the saints. Yet the Church does not pray in common in such a way that it fails also to offer prayers for individuals. For in the preceding volume we saw Ambrose more than once urging sinners to flee to the prayers of the Church. These very prayers, however, although composed for the benefit of individuals, also flow, through the benefit of charity, to the advantage of all. It is also useful to note here that immediately afterward the holy Doctor attributes justification not to faith alone, as the heterodox do, but also to works proceeding from faith and charity.] in common he prays, in common he acts, in common he is tested. Finally, whoever denies himself to himself is himself just and himself worthy of Christ. Therefore Paul laid Christ as the foundation (I Cor. III, 11), so that we might place works of justice upon him; for faith is the foundation, while in works there is either injustice if they are evil, or justice if they are good.

## CHAPTER XXX

On beneficence and its parts, benevolence and generosity; how these are to be joined together; and what accompanying qualities are required for someone to exercise generosity with praise and merit.

143. But now let us speak of beneficence, which is itself divided into benevolence and generosity. Beneficence is complete when it consists of these two things. For it is not enough to wish well, [Dist. 86, chapter “It is not enough,”] but one must also do good; nor again is it enough to do good unless it proceeds from a good source, that is, from good will: “For God loves a cheerful giver” (II Cor. IX, 7). For if you act unwillingly, what reward is there for you? Hence the Apostle says generally: “If I do this willingly, I have a reward; if unwillingly, I have been entrusted with a stewardship” (I Cor. IX, 17). In the Gospel also we have received many instructions concerning proper generosity.

144. It is therefore beautiful to wish well and to give with the intention [Note: [Col. 0066D] Cicero, *De officiis* I, p. 356, line 37: “For one must first see that kindness does not harm those very people whom,” etc.] of doing good, not harm. For if you think you should give to a man of luxury for the dissipation of luxury, or to an adulterer for the payment of adultery, that is not beneficence, [Col. 0065C] where there is no benevolence. It is harm, not help, if you give to someone who conspires against his fatherland, who wishes at your expense to gather together the depraved who will attack the Church. This is not commendable generosity, if you assist someone who wages a serious dispute against a widow and orphans, or who attempts by force to seize their possessions.

145. Generosity is not approved [Note: [Col. 0066D] Cicero, *De officiis* I, p. 356, line 42: “And those who harm some in order to be generous toward others are involved in the same injustice,” etc.] if one person is given what someone extorts from another; if he seeks it unjustly and thinks it should be distributed justly—unless perhaps, like Zacchaeus (Luke XIX, 8), you first restore fourfold to the one whom you defrauded, and compensate the vices of paganism by the zeal of faith and the action of the believer. Let your generosity therefore have a foundation.

146. The first thing required is that you give with faith and do not defraud anyone in what you offer, lest you say that you are contributing more while contributing less. Why is it necessary to say this? It is fraud against a promise; it is in your power to give whatever you wish. Fraud destroys the foundation, and the work collapses. Did Peter burn with indignation in such a way that he wished Ananias or his wife to be destroyed (Acts V, 3 ff.)? Rather, by their example he did not wish the others to perish.

147. Nor is generosity perfect [Note: [Col. 0066D] Ibid., p. 357, line 3: “It may also be seen that many are not generous so much by nature as driven by a certain desire for glory,” etc.] if you give more for the sake of display than of mercy. Your disposition gives its name to your deed; it is judged according to the source from which it proceeds. You see what a moral judge you have. He consults you about how he should receive your work; first he questions your mind. “Let your left hand not know what your right hand is doing” (Matt. VI, 3). He is not speaking only of the body; let even your like-minded companion, your brother, not know what you are doing, lest, while you seek the reward of display here, you lose there the fruit of recompense. Generosity is perfect when someone conceals his work in silence and secretly assists the needs of individuals—when the mouth of the poor praises him, not his own lips.

148. Further, perfect generosity [Dist. 86, chapter “It is not enough,” § “Perfect generosity”] is commended by faith, cause, place, and time, so that you first act toward those who belong to the household of faith. It is a grave fault if, while you know it, a believer is in need; if you know that he is without resources, [Note: [Col. 0066D] Some manuscripts and the old edition read, “suffering from hunger.”] enduring hunger and suffering hardship, especially if he is ashamed to be in need; if he has fallen into the misfortune either of the captivity of his relatives or of false accusation, and you do not help him; if he is in prison and a just man is being tormented by punishments and penalties because of some debt—for although mercy is owed to all, it is owed more abundantly to the just—if at the time of his affliction he obtains nothing from you; if at the time of danger, when he is being dragged to death, your money has more value with you than the life of the dying. Concerning this Job said beautifully: “May the blessing of the perishing come upon me” (Job XXIX, 13).

149. God is not a respecter of persons, because he knows everything. We, however, owe mercy to all; but because many seek it deceitfully and fabricate their misery, when the cause is revealed, the person identified, and the urgency of the moment presses, mercy ought to pour itself forth more generously. For the Lord is not miserly, as though he sought the most. Blessed indeed is the one who gives up everything and follows him; but blessed also is the one who does what he has from affection. [Note: [Col. 0066D] The latest Paris editions, with one or two manuscripts, read, “the one who does what he owes”; better are the other editions and the remaining codices: “the one who does what he has,” supply, “in his power,” as in Mark XIV, 8: “What she had, she did.”] Finally, he preferred the widow’s two small coins to the gifts of the rich (Luke XXI, 3), because she contributed everything she had, while they contributed a small part from their abundance. Affection therefore makes a rich contribution poor or a poor contribution rich, and assigns value to things. The Lord, however, does not want wealth to be poured out all at once, but to be distributed [Note: [Col. 0067D] Cicero, *De officiis* I, p. 356, line 49: “Another point required caution,” etc. Also p. 358, line 9: “But since resources are limited,” etc.] (Dist. 86, chapter “The Lord does not wish this”): unless perhaps, like Elisha, you kill your oxen and feed the poor from what you have (III Kings XIX, 21), so that no domestic concern may hold you, but, having left everything, you may devote yourself to prophetic discipline.

150. That generosity is also to be approved [Note: [Col. 0067D] Cicero, *De officiis* I, p. 358, line 40: “But if a certain contest and comparison be made,” etc.] [Dist. 86, chapter “Generosity is to be approved”] by which you do not despise your relatives if you discover that they are in need. For it is better that you yourself assist your own people, who are ashamed to ask others for money or to seek assistance for some necessity. [Col. 0067B] Yet it should not be so that they wish to become richer through what you could contribute to the needy; for the cause takes precedence over favor. You did not dedicate yourself to the Lord for this reason, so that you might make your relatives rich, but so that you might acquire everlasting life for yourself through the fruit of good work and redeem your sins at the price of mercy. Do they think they are asking for little? They are seeking your price; they are trying to deprive you of the fruit of your life, [Note: [Col. 0067D] “And they think they are acting justly”—these words are absent from the ancient editions and from the great majority of manuscripts, although they are found not only in the Roman edition but also in four manuscripts. Below, where all editions read “We prefaced the advice,” almost all manuscripts read “We expressed the advice.” Observe in passing how much Ambrose’s prudence shines forth here: he assigns to piety what belongs to it without taking anything away from justice. For it belongs to piety, when beneficence is being distributed, not to pass over relatives and relations, but to count them among the first of the poor; it belongs to justice not to enrich them from what is owed to other poor people. Nor should this advice be regarded as a kind of greater perfection; otherwise it would certainly not be added, and he would not accuse the person because he had not made him rich, when that person wishes to defraud him of the reward of eternal life. Let the foolish disguises of human greed therefore be dismissed. It has never been the purpose of the Church to satisfy either the luxury of a priest or the ambition of his relatives.] and yet they think they are acting justly. And he complains that you have not made him rich, when he wishes to defraud you of the reward of eternal life.

151. We have expressed the advice; let us seek authority. First, no one ought to be ashamed to become poor from being rich while giving to the poor, because Christ became poor although he was rich, so that he might enrich everyone by his poverty. He gave us a rule to follow, so that the reduction of one’s patrimony might be a sound accounting if someone has driven away the hunger of the poor and relieved their need. Hence, in this matter I offer the advice which the Apostle gives: “For this is useful to you, so that you may imitate Christ” (II Cor. VIII, 10). Advice is given to the good; correction restrains those who err. Finally, as though speaking to the good, he says: “Because you began not only to do, but also to will, from the previous year” (ibid.). Both are required of the perfect person, not merely one part. Thus he teaches that generosity without benevolence, and benevolence without generosity, are not perfect. Therefore he urges perfection, saying: “Now, therefore, complete the act as well, so that just as your willingness to do was ready, so also may your accomplishment be according to what you have. For if the will is ready, it is accepted according to what one has, not according to what one does not have. Not so that there may be relief for others but distress for you, but according to equality at this time: your abundance for their need, so that their abundance may be for your need, and equality may be achieved, as it is written: ‘The one who had much did not have too much, and the one who had little did not have too little’” (ibid., 11 ff.).

152. We have observed how he includes benevolence, generosity, measure, fruit, and persons. He includes measure because he was giving advice to the imperfect; for only the imperfect suffer distress. [Note: [Col. 0068D] Lest anyone suppose that every measure in giving is always connected with imperfection, on the basis of what he had just said—“He includes measure because he was giving advice to the imperfect”—he explains his meaning more clearly by asserting that someone established in the priesthood or in a ministry who retains some part of his patrimony lest he burden the Church, but works honorably to the extent sufficient for his office, should by no means be considered imperfect. From this we learn that Augustine added a certain severity to the opinion of our Ambrose: he wanted clerics entirely stripped of their patrimony to live a common life, as can be learned from many passages of his works, but especially from the book *On the Common Life of Clerics*.] But if someone established in the priesthood or in some ministry does not wish to burden the Church and therefore does not contribute everything he has, but works honorably to the extent sufficient for his office, he does not seem imperfect to me. And I think that here he spoke of distress not of the mind but of the household.

153. Regarding persons, I think this was said: “So that your abundance may be for their need, and their abundance for your need”—that is, so that the people’s abundance in good works may relieve their need for nourishment, and their spiritual abundance may assist the people in their lack of spiritual merit and confer grace upon them.

154. Therefore he offered an excellent example: “The one who had much did not have too much, and the one who had little did not diminish.” He rightly urges all people to the duty of mercy by this example, because the one who possesses a great deal of gold does not have too much, since whatever exists in this age is nothing; and the one who has little does not diminish, because what he loses is nothing. A thing is without loss when the whole of it is loss.

155. There is also this good interpretation: the one who has much, even if he does not give, does not have too much, because however much he acquires, he is always in need if he desires more; and the one who has little does not diminish, because what feeds the poor is not much. Likewise, the poor person who contributes spiritual things in exchange for monetary things, even if he possesses a great deal of grace, does not have too much; for grace does not burden the mind but lightens it.

156. It can also be understood in this way: You do not have too much, O human being. For how much is what you have received, even if it seems much to you? John, than whom no one is greater among those born of women, was nevertheless lower than the one who is least in the kingdom of heaven.

157. It can also be understood thus: God’s grace does not abound corporeally, because it is spiritual. Who can comprehend its greatness or breadth, which he does not see? If faith is like a mustard seed, it can move mountains, yet no more than a mustard seed is given to you. If grace abounds in you [Note: [Col. 0069D] The negation is absent from all editions and from some manuscripts; nevertheless it is found in many more and better codices. If you take the sentence with us as a question, the meaning is not inappropriate.]—need you fear that your mind will begin to be puffed up by so great a gift, since many have fallen more disastrously from the height of their hearts than they would have fallen had they possessed no grace of the Lord? And the one who has little does not diminish, because it is not corporeal, so that it can be divided; and what seems little to the one who possesses it is very great to the one who lacks nothing.

158. When giving, one must also consider age and weakness [Note: [Col. 0069D] Cicero, *De officiis* I, p. 357, line 6: “The third consideration is that in beneficence,” etc. Also Book II, p. 382, line 12: “In that other kind of giving,” etc.] (Dist. 86, chapter “To be considered”), and sometimes even modesty, which reveals a free-born origin. Thus you should give more to the elderly, who can no longer obtain their livelihood by their own labor. Likewise, bodily weakness should be assisted more readily. Then consider one who has fallen from wealth into poverty, especially if he lost what he had not through his own fault but through robbery, confiscation, or false accusation.

159. But perhaps someone will say: “The blind man sits in one place and is passed by, while the strong young man frequently receives.” And it is true, because the latter intrudes through persistence. That is not a matter of judgment but of weariness. For the Lord also says in the Gospel (Luke XI, 8) concerning the man who had already closed his door, that if someone knocks at his door more shamelessly, he rises and gives to him because of his persistence.

## CHAPTER XXXI

[Col. 0069C]

By the example of the earth it is taught that a benefit received should be repaid with a more generous hand; the passage of Solomon about a banquet, introduced for the same purpose, is later explained in a spiritual sense.

160. It is also beautiful to show greater consideration for someone who has given you either [Note: [Col. 0069D] Cicero, *De officiis* I, p. 357, line 20: “But if there are merits, so that gratitude is not to be entered into but repaid,” etc.] a benefit or a gift if he himself falls into need. For what is more contrary to duty than not to return what you have received? I think it should be returned not in equal measure but more abundantly, and that the use of the benefit should be repaid, [Note: [Col. 0069D] The editions and a few manuscripts read: “the use of the benefit should be weighed, so that you may assist to the extent that,” etc.] so that you too may help to the extent that you relieve his hardship. For to be no greater in returning than in conferring a benefit—that is, to be lesser—is wrong, since the one who first conferred it is superior in time and prior in kindness. [Note: [Col. 0069D] “Than in conferring” is absent from two manuscripts and the Roman edition, but appears in the others and in no way obstructs the meaning.]

[Col. 0070A] 161. Hence in this also we must imitate the nature of the earth, which customarily returns the seed it has received in a multiplied quantity, greater than what it received. Therefore it is written for you: “As a field is a foolish man, and as a vineyard is a man lacking sense. If you leave him, he will be desolated” (Prov. XXIV, 30–31). The wise person, therefore, should be like cultivated land, returning the seeds it has received as though they had been lent to it, in greater measure. Thus the earth either brings forth spontaneous fruits or pours back and returns entrusted seed in a richer heap. You owe both by a kind of inherited practice from your parent, lest you be left like an unfruitful field. Even if someone might excuse himself for not having given, how can he excuse himself for not having returned? [Note: [Col. 0069D] Cicero, *De officiis* I, p. 357, line 24: “Should we not imitate fertile fields, which produce much more than they have received?”] It is scarcely permissible not to give to someone; but it is not permissible not to return what one has received. [Note: [Col. 0070D] Ibid., line 27: “Whether we give is in our power; but it is not permissible not to return what is owed to a good man.”]

[Col. 0070B] **162.** Therefore Solomon beautifully says: “If you sit down to dine at the table of a powerful man, understand wisely what is set before you; and put your hand to it, knowing that you ought to prepare such things. But if you are insatiable, do not desire his delicacies; for these things lead to [Note: [Col. 0070D] All editions and a few manuscripts read, “a false life.” Others, many more in number, read, “a deceptive life.” The Septuagint has, ταῦτα γὰρ ἔχεται ζωῆς ψευδοῦς, “for these things belong to a false life.” Aquila and Theodotion have, Καὶ αὐτὸς ἄρτος ψευσμάτων, “and he himself is bread of deceit.” Immediately afterward the Amerbach edition has *quam nos*, “than we”; the other editions, *quem nos*, “whom we”; nearly all the manuscripts, *quas nos*, “which we,” etc.] a deceptive life” (Prov. XXIII, 1 ff.). Desiring to imitate these sayings, we have written them down. To confer a favor is good; but he who does not know how to return one is most hard-hearted. The earth itself offers an example of humanity: it supplies spontaneous fruits which you have not sown, and it returns, multiplied, what it has received. You may not deny money that has been counted out to you; how, then, may you lawfully fail to return the favor you have received? [Note: [Col. 0070D] The Roman edition alone has, “In Solomon also you have this”; but Ambrose either quoted the passage from memory, or indicated not the title of the book but its subject matter; for it is certain that the work is *Ecclesiasticus*, a collection of proverbial sayings. Immediately below, the same edition says: “That banquet in Proverbs does not concern food,” etc.]

In Proverbs also you find that this repayment of gratitude is accustomed to have such great value with God that it finds favor even on the day of ruin, when sins may be outweighed. And why should I use examples from others, when the Lord himself promises in the Gospel a more abundant reward for the merits of the saints and exhorts us to perform a good work, saying: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you; [Note: [Col. 0070D] The Roman edition alone has, “a good measure, pressed down.”] a good measure, shaken together, overflowing, they will pour into your lap” (Luke VI, 37, 38)?

**163.** Thus Solomon’s banquet too concerns not foods but good works. For by what are minds better feasted than by good deeds? Or what else can fill the minds of the righteous so readily as the consciousness of a good work? And what food is more pleasing than to do the will of God? The Lord himself declared that this food abounded for him alone, as it is written in the Gospel: “My food is to do the will of my Father who is in heaven” (John IV, 34).

[Col. 0071A] **164.** Let us delight in this food, of which the Prophet says: “Delight in the Lord” (Ps. XXXVI, 4). Those delight in this food who have grasped the higher pleasures with wondrous understanding, who can know what that pure and intelligible delight of the mind is. Let us therefore eat the bread of wisdom and be satisfied with the word of God; for human life, made in the image of God, is not sustained by bread alone but by every word of God. Concerning the cup, holy Job says quite explicitly: “As the earth awaits rain, so they await my words” (Job XXIX, 23).

## CHAPTER XXXII

After explaining what gratitude should be returned for the dishes of the banquet just mentioned, various ways of repaying a benefit are reviewed; benevolence, its effects, and its order are also discussed.

[Col. 0071B] **165.** It is therefore beautiful that we should be moistened by the address of the divine Scriptures, and that God’s words should descend upon us like dew. When, then, you sit at the table of that powerful man, understand who this powerful man is; and, placed in the paradise of delight and seated at the banquet of wisdom, consider what is set before you. Sacred Scripture is the banquet of wisdom: its individual books are individual dishes. 44 First understand what delicacies the dishes contain, and then put out your hand, so that you may carry out in works what you read or receive from the Lord your God, and repay by your duties the grace conferred upon you. Thus Peter and Paul, who by preaching the Gospel returned something in exchange for the gift bestowed, could each say: “By the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me was not in vain; but I labored more abundantly than all of them” (1 Cor. XV, 10).

**166.** One therefore repays the fruit of the benefit received—as gold for gold, silver for silver; another repays labor; another, I do not know whether more richly still, [Note: [Col. 0071D] Cicero, *On Duties*, Book II, p. 384, line 26: “For plainly that poor man, if he is a good man, even if he cannot return a favor, can certainly possess gratitude, and suitably so,” etc.] returns affection alone. For what if no ability to repay is available? In returning a benefit, the disposition accomplishes more than wealth; benevolence weighs more heavily than the ability to return the gift. Gratitude is returned in the very fact that it is possessed. Great, therefore, is benevolence, which, even when it contributes nothing, gives more; and, possessing nothing in its patrimony, bestows upon many, doing so without any loss to itself and to the profit of all. For this reason benevolence surpasses liberality itself. It is richer in character than liberality is in gifts; for more people are in need of a benefit than abound in them.

**167.** Benevolence is sometimes joined to liberality, from which liberality itself proceeds, when the disposition to give is followed by the practice of giving; and sometimes it is separate and distinct. For where liberality is absent, benevolence remains—a kind of common parent of all, which joins and unites friendship: [Note: [Col. 0071D] Cicero, *On Duties*, Book I, p. 358, line 46: “Counsels, conversations, exhortations,” etc.] faithful in counsel, joyful in prosperity, sorrowful in grief; so that each person considers himself more guided by the counsel of the benevolent than by that of the wise. Thus, although David was more prudent, he nevertheless followed the counsels of the younger Jonathan. [Note: [Col. 0071D] This sentence is translated from Cicero, *On Friendship*, p. 425, line 18, where it reads: “For those who remove friendship from life seem to remove the sun from the world.”]

Remove benevolence from human society, and it will be as though you had removed the sun from the world, because human society cannot exist without it; [Note: [Col. 0071D] Cicero, *On Duties*, Book I, p. 358, line 5: “From this arise those common duties: not to block flowing water, to allow fire,” etc.] thus one shows a traveler the way, calls back one who has gone astray, offers hospitality—“for this was no mediocre virtue,” of which Job prided himself when he said [Col. 0072B] (Job XXXI, 32): “The stranger did not remain outside; my door was open to every traveler”—gives water from flowing water, and lights one lamp from another.

Benevolence is present in all these things, like a spring of water refreshing the thirsty and like a light that shines also upon others and is not diminished for those who have kindled a light for others from their own.

**168.** There is also this liberality of benevolence: if you possess a debtor’s bond, tear it up and return it, having received nothing from the debtor in repayment of the debt. Holy Job admonishes us that we should do this by his example (ibid., 35 ff.). For he who has something does not borrow; he who has nothing does not release the bond. Why, then, even if you do not demand it yourself, should you reserve it for greedy heirs, when you can present it, with the praise of benevolence and without loss of money, to the debtor?

45 **169.** And, to examine the matter more fully: [Note: [Col. 0072D] Cicero, *On Duties*, Book I, p. 357, line 37: “The fellowship of human beings is best,” etc. Also p. 358, line 16: “The closer bond of fellowship among relatives . . . the first fellowship is found in marriage itself,” etc. And line 40: “But if some conflict should arise,” etc.] benevolence, having first proceeded from members of the household—that is, from children, parents, and brothers—reaches, through the degrees of kinship, to the sphere of cities, and, leaving paradise, fills the world. Finally, when God had placed a benevolent affection in man and woman, he said: “The two shall be one flesh” (Gen. II, 24), and one spirit. Hence Eve trusted the serpent, because she who had received benevolence did not suppose that there could be malevolence.

## CHAPTER XXXIII

Benevolence is to endure especially in the Church and among people joined by the same or related virtues.

**170.** Benevolence is increased by the assembly [Note: [Col. 0072D] Ibid., p. 358, line 24: “For it is a great thing to have the same things,” etc. The relationship by which grace is received seems chiefly to signify the bond contracted between the one who ordains and the one ordained, the baptizer and the baptized, and also the catechizer and the catechized; to this may likewise be referred the sacred kinship that arises between sponsors and those sponsored. The origin of these terms of relationship is the fellowship of the Church. First is the reverence shown by children, by which not only lay Christians but also clergy addressed bishops by the title of father; thus below, in chapter 41, Saint Lawrence calls the blessed Sixtus “father” three times. Second is the authority and paternal affection of fathers, by which Sixtus in the same place in turn calls Lawrence his son, and Ambrose, throughout this work and elsewhere, calls his clergy, as well as sacred virgins and widows, his daughters. He himself sufficiently indicates that this involves no less affection than authority in chapter 7, where he says: “For I do not love you less, whom I have begotten in the Gospel, than if I had received you in marriage,” etc. Finally, third is the brotherhood of brothers; that the first Christians were accustomed to be called by this name is clear from the many passages of the Acts of the Apostles and the canonical Epistles.] of the Church, fellowship in faith, association in initiation, the relationship of receiving grace, and communion in the mysteries. These too claim for themselves the names of relationships: the reverence of children, the authority and affection of fathers, and the brotherhood of brothers. Relationship in grace therefore contributes greatly to the increase of benevolence.

**171.** The practices of equals in virtue also contribute to it. For benevolence produces similarity of character as well. Thus Jonathan, the king’s son, imitated the gentleness of holy David, and therefore loved him (1 Kings XIX, 2 ff.). Hence also the saying, “With the holy man you will be holy” (Ps. XVII, 26), seems to apply not only to conduct but also to benevolence.

The sons of Noah, certainly, lived together, but there was no harmony of character among them (Gen. IX, 22 ff.). [Col. 0073B] Esau and Jacob also lived in their father’s house, but they differed (Gen. XXV, 27). Benevolence did not exist between them, causing one to put the other before himself; rather, there was rivalry, which seized the blessing (Gen. XXVII, 14 ff.). For since one was harsh and the other gentle, benevolence could not exist between differing characters and conflicting pursuits. Add to this that holy Jacob could not prefer one who had degenerated from his father’s virtue.

**172.** Nothing is so conducive to fellowship as equity joined with justice, which, like the equal and companion of benevolence, causes us to love those whom we believe to be our equals. [Note: [Col. 0073C] Ibid., line 28: “And although every virtue attracts us to itself and makes us love those,” etc.] Benevolence also contains fortitude; for since friendship proceeds from the fountain of benevolence, it does not hesitate to endure grave dangers to life for a friend: “Even if evils befall me through him,” he says, “I endure them” (Ecclus. XXII, 31).

## CHAPTER XXXIV

Some further benefits of benevolence are mentioned.

[Col. 0074A] **173.** Benevolence also habitually wrests the sword of anger from the hand. Benevolence makes the wounds of a friend preferable to the voluntary kisses of an enemy (Prov. XXVII, 6). [Note: [Col. 0073C] Ibid., line 32: “And that comes about which Pythagoras,” etc.] Benevolence makes many become one; for if there are several friends, they become one in whom there is one spirit and one judgment. We also observe that reproofs in friendship are welcome, since they have sharp points but no pain. We are pierced by censorial words, but we delight in the diligence of benevolence.

**174.** In sum, the same duties are not always owed to everyone, nor are the preferences always those of persons; rather, they are generally determined by circumstances and times, so that someone may sometimes help a neighbor more than a brother. For Solomon also says: “A neighbor nearby is better than a brother far away” (ibid., 10). Therefore people often entrust themselves to a friend’s benevolence rather than to a brother’s relationship. Benevolence is so powerful that it often surpasses the bonds of nature.

## CHAPTER XXXV

Fortitude is divided into military and domestic fortitude; the former is not a virtue without justice and prudence, while the latter consists chiefly in endurance.

**175.** We have treated the nature and force of moral beauty at sufficient length in the section on justice. Now let us discuss fortitude, [Note: [Col. 0073D] Ibid., p. 359, line 11: “It must be understood that, when the matter proposed,” etc. Ambrose, while making clear that the handling of weapons is unlawful for clerics, uses the particle *iam* (“now”) here once and again. It is evident that he distinguishes clerics in this way either from the priests and Levites of the former covenant, for whom bearing arms was not forbidden, or rather from Christian laymen, whom the evangelical law does not prohibit from military service. We know, however, that Erasmus is criticized by Sixtus of Siena, *Bibliotheca*, Book VI, note 156, and by several others, as though in his *Annotations*, especially on chapter III and most particularly on chapter XXII of the Gospel according to Luke, he wished to assert that it was unlawful for Christians to wage war and branded the contrary opinion as impious. Yet Erasmus himself explains his position in such a way that he condemns only wars among Christians, while saying that he approves, with Ambrose, of Christians’ wars against barbarians to the extent that he simultaneously warns that such wars do not belong to evangelical purity. That this should not be taken otherwise may also be understood from the fact that the emperors whom Erasmus reports Ambrose to have praised for their wars did not always fight against barbarians. For Theodosius, who stands first among those rulers, waged war against the tyrants Maximus and Eugenius, who were nevertheless Christians. Certainly below, in Book III, chapter 3, the holy Doctor openly indicates that he does not disapprove of war, where he says: “When it is considered glorious for each person to seek the tranquility of all at the cost of his own dangers,” etc.

What Saint Martin, as soon as he became a Christian, is said by Sulpicius Severus to have said while contemplating renouncing military service—“I am Christ’s; it is not lawful for me to fight”—must be referred to the singular impulse of the Holy Spirit, by which he was called to a more perfect kind of warfare. Hence emperors who by their edicts forbade soldiers this spiritual warfare were rebuked more freely by the holy Fathers. Otherwise, that the use of arms was always permitted to those who had given their name to Christ is demonstrated by the fact that, in the earliest times, even the armies of pagan emperors were filled with Christian soldiers. See Tertullian, *On the Crown of the Soldier*, chapter 11; Augustine, *On Free Will*, chapter 5; *Sermon* 303, on Saint Lawrence; *The City of God*, Book I, chapter 21, and many other passages; and, above all, Saint Thomas, II-II, question 40.]

which, as though higher than the others, is divided into military and domestic matters. But the pursuit of military affairs now seems foreign to our office, since we devote ourselves more to the duty of the mind than of the body; our use no longer concerns arms but the work of peace. Our ancestors, however—Joshua, Jerubbaal, Samson, and David—won the highest glory even in military affairs.

**176.** Fortitude is therefore, as it were, higher than the other virtues, but it is never an unaccompanied virtue; for it does not commit itself to itself. Otherwise, [Note: [Col. 0075D] Cicero, *On Duties*, Book I, p. 359, line 22: “But that elevation of spirit which is seen in dangers and labors, if it lacks justice,” etc.] fortitude without justice is material for wrongdoing. For the stronger it is, the more ready it is to oppress the weaker; and even in military affairs it is considered necessary to examine whether wars are just or unjust.

**177.** David never waged war unless provoked. Thus he had prudence as the companion of his fortitude in battle. When he was about to fight Goliath, a man of enormous bodily size, in single combat, he rejected the armor with which he would have been burdened (1 Kings XVII, 40); for virtue relies more on its own strength than on the protection of others. Then, so that he might strike with greater force from a distance, he killed the enemy with a stone’s blow. Afterward he never undertook war except after consulting the Lord (2 Kings V, 19 ff.). Therefore victorious in all his battles, ready with his hand even into extreme old age, he entered the fierce ranks of warriors when war was undertaken against the Titans, eager for glory and careless of safety (2 Kings XXI, 15 ff.).

**178.** But this alone is not splendid fortitude. We also recognize the glorious fortitude of those who through faith, by greatness of spirit, stopped the mouths of lions, quenched the power of fire, [Note: [Col. 0075D] Thus Gill’s and the Roman editions, with part of the manuscripts. The older editions, with another group, have “they escaped the edge of the sword.” The Greek text reads, ἔφυγον στόματα μαχαίρας, “they escaped the edge of the sword,” etc., to which various translations agree. Further below, where all editions and several manuscripts have “girded with legions,” other manuscripts read “subject to legions,” and some “with legions subjected,” etc.] escaped the edge of the sword, and from weakness became strong (Hebr. XI, 33, 34): who, not girded with an escort and legions to share a common victory with many, but by the naked virtue of the mind, won an individual triumph over the faithless.

How invincible was Daniel, who did not fear the roaring lions around him! [Note: [Col. 0075D] Several manuscripts have “with ropes around his sides.”] The beasts were growling, and he was feasting (Dan. XIV, 38).

## CHAPTER XXXVI

The duty of fortitude is, first, to drive injury away from the weaker; second, to restrain improper movements of the mind; and finally, both to despise low things and to pursue honorable things with an unbroken spirit. These duties are shown to be required of all Christians, but especially of ecclesiastical persons.

**178\*.** The glory of fortitude does not consist only in bodily strength and physical sinews, but rather in the virtue of the mind; [Note: [Col. 0075D] Cicero, *On Duties*, Book I, p. 361, line 38: “In general, that which is morally honorable, which proceeds from a lofty spirit,” etc.] [Note: [Col. 0076D] Ibid., p. 353, line 42: “But there are two kinds of injustice,” etc.] nor does the law of virtue lie in inflicting injury (23, q. 2, c. *Non in inferenda*), but in driving it away. For whoever does not repel injury from a companion, when he can, is as much at fault as the one who commits it.

Thus holy Moses first began his trials of military fortitude here (Exod. II, 11 ff.). When he saw a Hebrew being injured by an Egyptian, he defended him, striking down the Egyptian and hiding him in the sand. Solomon likewise says: “Rescue the one who is being led away to death” (Prov. XXIV, 10).

48 **179.** Whence, then, Tully, or Panaetius, or Aristotle himself derived this teaching is sufficiently clear. Yet Job, who was older than all three, also said: “I rescued the poor man from the hand of the powerful, and I helped the orphan who had no helper. May the blessing of the perishing come upon me” (Job XXIX, 12, 13). Was he not most courageous, who so bravely endured the assaults of the devil and conquered him by the virtue of his mind? Nor should we doubt the fortitude of the one to whom the Lord says: “Gird your loins like a man; receive height and strength; [Col. 0076B] humble every one who inflicts injury” (Job XL, 2). The Apostle also says: “You have the strongest consolation” (Hebr. VI, 18). He is therefore strong who consoles himself in some pain.

**180.** And rightly indeed that is called fortitude when each person conquers himself, restrains anger, is softened and bent by no enticements, is not disturbed by adversity, is not lifted up by prosperity, and is not carried about, as by some wind, through the changing circumstances of life. What is more elevated and magnificent than to discipline the mind, afflict the flesh, and bring it into servitude, so that it obeys command, submits to counsels, and in undertaking labors diligently carries out the mind’s resolve and will?

**181.** This, then, is the first force of fortitude, since [Col. 0076C] fortitude is discerned in two kinds of matters: [Note: [Col. 0076D] Several manuscripts have “fortitude is bent”; some, “the mind is bent.” Cicero, *On Duties*, Book I, p. 359, line 49: “In general, a brave and great spirit is especially discerned in two things,” etc.] first, that it regard external bodily things as insignificant and consider them, as superfluous, more worthy of contempt than desire; second, that it pursue with splendid intensity of mind, even unto affection, all those things that are supreme—everything in which moral goodness and that which is fitting (*πρέπον*, *prepon*) are discerned. What is so splendid as to shape your mind in such a way that you do not regard riches, pleasures, or honors as among the greatest things, nor expend all your efforts upon them? When your mind has been so disposed, you must judge that which is honorable and fitting ought to be preferred, and direct your mind toward it in such a way that, whatever happens by which people are usually broken in spirit—loss of patrimony, diminution of honor, or the slander of the faithless—you may, as though superior to it, remain unaffected. [Col. 0076D] Then too, dangers to life itself, undertaken for justice, must not move you.

**182.** This is the true fortitude possessed by Christ’s athlete, [Note: [Col. 0077C] Some manuscripts have: “unless he has competed lawfully.”] who is not crowned unless he competes lawfully. Does this commandment of fortitude seem insignificant to you: “Tribulation produces patience, patience produces proof, and proof produces hope” (2 Cor. VII, 5)? See how many contests there are, and yet one crown. This command is given only by the one who has been strengthened in Christ Jesus, whose flesh had no rest. Affliction was everywhere: battles outside, fears within. Although he was placed amid dangers, very many labors, prisons, and deaths, he was not broken in spirit but fought on, so that he became stronger than his weaknesses.
