**183.** Consider, then, how he teaches that those who approach the offices of the Church ought to possess contempt for human things. “If you have died with Christ to the elements of this world, why, as though living in the world, do you still submit to decrees? Do not touch, do not defile, do not taste”—things which all lead to corruption through their use (Col. II, 20 ff.). And below: “If therefore you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, not those that are upon the earth” (Col. III, 1). And again: “Put to death, therefore, your members that are upon the earth” (ibid., 5).

These words are still addressed to all the faithful. But to you, son, he recommends contempt for riches and avoidance of profane and old-womanish fables, permitting nothing except what exercises you toward godliness; for bodily exercise is useful for nothing, but godliness is useful for everything. [Note: [Col. 0077C] Some manuscripts have “for their own corruption”; and below, “My son,” he says, “Timothy,” followed by “contempt for riches . . . I urge,” etc.]

**184.** Let godliness therefore exercise you in justice, self-control, and gentleness, so that you may flee youthful pursuits and, strengthened and rooted in grace, undertake the good contest of faith. Do not entangle yourself in secular affairs, since you serve as a soldier of God. For if one who serves as a soldier under an emperor is prohibited by human laws from undertaking or conducting lawsuits, from carrying out forensic business, and from selling merchandise, how much more should one who serves in the warfare of faith abstain from every practice of commerce, content with the produce of his little farm, if he has one; and, if he does not, with the fruit of his stipends! [Note: [Col. 0077C] Ambrose shows that three activities were formerly forbidden to soldiers: defending or managing the causes of others; pursuing in court business matters, whether one’s own or another’s; and selling goods. Concerning commerce, which Chrysostom likewise reports as forbidden to soldiers by law in his *First Epistle to Timothy*, the words of our author are clear. The first two matters must be interpreted in the sense we have given them; this can be understood from the laws that survive on the same subject. For what Ambrose calls the undertaking of lawsuits, who does not see to be precisely what is expressed in the law *De Cognitoribus et Procuratoribus*, enacted under the consuls Olybrius and Probinus by Arcadius and Honorius, in these words: “Let no soldier become an undertaker or defender of lawsuits, nor an advocate in the examination of another’s dispute,” etc.? How well the words “the conduct of forensic business” correspond with law 3, *De Commeatu*, issued under the same consuls and by the same emperors, where we read: “Those who have obtained temporary leave . . . shall assume no obligation for themselves and shall not involve themselves in the affairs of anyone,” etc.; likewise with laws 15 and 17, *De Re Militari*. The former, under Arcadius and Honorius as consuls, states: “If anyone hereafter is found to retain a soldier in a private business,” etc.; the latter, under Honorius and Eutychianus as consuls, says: “If any soldier . . . is found either at leisure or occupied with another’s business, let him immediately be reported to us,” etc. These provisions clearly exclude soldiers from domestic as well as external business. Nevertheless, we should not suppose that Ambrose had these laws in view, since they are much later than this treatise; rather, we think that they were written to confirm other similar laws that have since perished. This may also be inferred from Vegetius, Book II, chapter 19.

Ambrose, moreover, sufficiently proscribes forensic activities in the words “from every practice of commerce,” since these correspond to the preceding words, “Do not entangle yourself in secular affairs,” which plainly include contentious business in the courts. His words concerning other kinds of commerce, however, should not be interpreted so rigidly or literally. It is certain that not only priests and deacons were customarily entrusted with the administration of Church property, but also that Saint Felix, stripped of all his possessions for Christ, leased, as Paulinus writes, three *jugera* of land so that he might provide for his own life and for that of others poorer than himself. Moreover, canon 3 of the Fourth Council of Carthage orders clerics to procure food and clothing for themselves either by a craft or through agriculture. None of these things could be accomplished without some form of commerce. See on this matter Sozomen, Book III, chapter 17, Valesius’s edition; *Decretum*, distinctions 88 and 89; Godefridus on the law of Arcadius and Honorius mentioned above; Spence, *Digressions*, Book II, chapter 15; Renatus a Valle, *On Hipparchus, or On Religious Commerce*; Thomassinus and others.]

For there is a good witness who says: “I was young, and now I am old, and I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his offspring seeking bread” (Ps. XXXVI, 25). Such is the tranquility and moderation of mind that it is neither distressed by the desire to seek wealth nor troubled by fear of poverty.

## CHAPTER XXXVII

Equanimity of mind is to be preserved in prosperity as well as in adversity; yet evils are sometimes to be avoided.

**185.** This is also what is called freedom of mind from anxieties: we should be neither too soft in pains nor too elated in prosperity. [Note: [Col. 0078D] Cicero, *On Duties*, Book I, p. 360, line 20: “We must be free from every disturbance of mind,” etc. Also p. 363, line 17: “And even in prosperous circumstances and those flowing according to our wishes,” etc.] If those who urge some people to undertake public office give these instructions, [Note: [Col. 0078D] Cicero, *On Duties*, Book I, p. 360, line 45: “Those who undertake public affairs, no less than philosophers,” etc. Also p. 362, line 34: “In general, those who will benefit the state,” etc.] how much more ought we, who are called to the office of the Church, to do those things that please God, so that the virtue of Christ may be displayed in us and we may be approved by our commander in such a way that our members are weapons of justice—not carnal weapons in which sin reigns, but powerful weapons of God by which sin is destroyed? Let our flesh die, so that every fault may die in it; and, as though living from the dead, let us rise again to new works and ways of life!

**186.** These are the full rewards of fortitude, worthy and honorable. [Col. 0079A] But because in everything we do we seek not only what is honorable but also what is possible, [Note: [Col. 0079D] Here the Roman edition had suppressed the little word *quia* (“because”) and replaced *quaerimus* (“we seek”) with *quaeramus* (“let us seek”), evidently because the ancient reading seemed to produce a somewhat suspended sense. Since all the other editions and all the manuscripts present the same reading, however, we have thought it should be restored in full. Interpret the sentence so that its final part is: “lest we perhaps undertake something,” etc.; these words have the same force as if it were written, “let us beware lest we undertake,” etc.] let us beware that we do not undertake something we cannot carry out. Therefore, during persecution, the Lord wishes us to withdraw from one city to another—or, to use the very word, to flee (Matt. X, 23)—lest someone rashly, while desiring the glory of martyrdom, offer himself to dangers that weaker flesh or a less steadfast spirit might perhaps be unable to bear and endure. [Note: [Col. 0079D] Ibid., p. 361, line 3: “But one who approaches the conduct of affairs must beware lest he consider only this,” etc.]

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

The mind is to be strengthened by exercise against future troubles and confirmed by foresight; the difficulties that arise here are also discussed.

**187.** Nor, on the other hand, should anyone, through cowardice, yield and abandon the faith because of fear of danger. [Note: [Col. 0079D] Ibid., line 4: “In this very matter one must consider,” etc.] For this reason the mind must be prepared, the intellect exercised, and firmness established, so that the mind may be disturbed by no terrors, broken by no hardships, and made to yield by no punishments. These things are indeed difficult to endure; but because fear of greater punishments overcomes every punishment, if you strengthen your mind by deliberation, do not think you should depart from reason, and set before yourself the fear of divine judgment and the torments of everlasting punishment, you can undertake the endurance required of the mind.

**188.** This therefore belongs to diligence: that a person prepare himself in such a way. It belongs to intellectual power if someone can foresee by the vigor of his mind what is to come, place before his eyes what may happen, and determine what he ought to do if it happens; at times to turn over in his mind two or three possibilities simultaneously, which he may conjecture could occur either singly or together, and to arrange, for each separately or for all together, the actions he understands will be beneficial. 51 [Note: [Col. 0079D] Ibid., line 6: “But in all affairs,” etc. Also line 47: “It belongs to a brave and steadfast spirit not to be disturbed,” etc.]

**189.** It is the mark of a brave man not to disguise the approach of some danger, but to anticipate it, as though surveying it from a watchtower of the mind, and to meet future events with provident thought, [Note: [Col. 0079D] Cicero, Book I, *On Duties*, p. 362, line 1: “And not to allow it ever to be said: ‘I had not thought so.’”] lest he later say: “This happened to me because I did not think it could happen.” Indeed, unless adversities are reconnoitered, they quickly take possession. As in war an unexpected enemy is scarcely withstood, and if he finds people unprepared, he easily overwhelms them, so evils that have not been examined beforehand break the mind all the more.

**190.** In these two matters, then, the excellence of the mind consists first in this: that your mind, trained by good thoughts and pure in heart, should see what is true and honorable—for “blessed are the pure in heart, because they too will see God” (Matt. V, 8)—and should judge that only what is honorable is good; then, that it should be disturbed by no occupations [Note: [Col. 0079D] Three manuscripts have “disturbed by thoughts.”] and fluctuate under the sway of no desires.

191. Yet hardly anyone does this easily. For what is more difficult than to discern, as though from some citadel, the resources of wisdom and all those other things which seem great and lofty to most people? Then, to confirm one’s judgment by steadfast reasoning, and to despise as useless whatever one has judged to be trifling? Then, if something adverse occurs and is thought grave and bitter, to bear it in such a way that one considers nothing to have happened contrary to nature, when one has read: [Note: Codex Fisc., “Naked I came forth from my mother’s womb.”] “Naked I was born, and naked I shall depart. The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away” (Job 1:21)—for certainly he had lost both his children and his possessions. And in all things to maintain the character of a wise and just man, as he maintained it who said: “As it pleased the Lord, so it has happened; blessed be the name of the Lord” (ibid.). And below: “You have spoken as one of the foolish women speaks. If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, shall we not endure evil things?” (Job 2:10).

## CHAPTER XXXIX

Fortitude must fight against all vices, especially against avarice; this is shown by what was done in holy Job.

192. Fortitude of soul, then, is neither mediocre nor distinct from the other virtues—a fortitude that wages war alongside the virtues—but rather that which alone defends the adornments of all the virtues and guards their judgments; that which engages in an unappeasable battle against every vice, unconquered in hardships, courageous in dangers, sterner toward pleasures, and firm against enticements, to which it does not know how to lend an ear or, as the saying goes, even to say “hail”; [Note: Benignus and certain other witnesses read “in an inexhaustible battle”; Codex Fisc. reads “in an insuperable battle.”] that which neglects money, [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, book 1, p. 360, line 15: “Therefore these things too must be avoided, as must money,” etc.] flees avarice as a kind of stain that makes virtue effeminate. For nothing is so contrary to fortitude as being overcome by profit.

Often, after the enemies have been driven back and the enemy line has been thrown into flight, [Note: In the same sense Polybius, *Histories*, book 10: “And many, after successfully carrying out their attacks … not only fell away, but were completely defeated.” He himself supplies an example of this in book 5, in the destruction to a man of Xenoetas, Antiochus’ prefect, by the stratagem of Molon, the rebel. Justin supplies other examples in book 1, in the defeat and beheading of Cyrus by the cunning of Tomyris; Cornelius Tacitus in book 1 of the *Annals*, in the defeat of the Armenian leader by Caecina, Germanicus’ lieutenant; and others in other authors. We would scarcely note these matters were it not for the simultaneously mournful and shameful disaster of the Christians who, within the memory of our fathers, recalled the Turks upon themselves after they had been routed and laid low near Erlau in Hungary through greed for plunder—a disaster that warns our commanders that they are made no more cautious by the misfortunes of others. Thus the king of Israel wisely took precautions in 2 Kings 8, so that no treachery might be prepared for him under cover of the opportunity for plunder. The Romans likewise observed that custom mentioned by Polybius in the tenth book cited above.] while the warrior is seized by the spoils of the slain, he has met a pitiable death among those whom he had struck down; and when the legions, their triumphs cast down, are occupied with booty, they have recalled upon themselves the enemy who had fled.

193. Fortitude, therefore, must repel and crush so monstrous a plague; it must neither be tested by desires nor broken by fear. For virtue remains consistent with itself, so that it vigorously pursues every vice as though they were poisons of virtue. Let it repel anger as with certain weapons, since anger removes deliberation, and let it avoid it as a disease. [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, book 1, p. 359, line 46: “But one is most easily led to unjust actions,” etc. Likewise, p. 360, line 18: “The desire for glory must also be avoided,” etc.] Let it also beware of the appetite for glory, which, when pursued without restraint, has often caused harm, and which is always harmful when arrogated to oneself.

194. What was lacking in holy Job, either in virtue, or what vice crept into him? How did he endure the hardship of illness, cold, and hunger? How did he disregard the danger to his health? Were his riches accumulated through plunder, from which such abundance flowed to the needy? [Note: Almost all manuscripts have this wording; the printed editions, however, read: “Did avarice, wealth, or the pursuits and desires of pleasure …?”] Did wealth arouse in him avarice, or the pursuits and desires of pleasure? Did the insulting quarrel of the three kings, or the insolence of servants, stir him to anger? Did glory, as though he were a lightweight, exalt him—he who called down severe penalties upon himself if he had ever concealed an involuntary fault or, out of respect for the multitude, refrained from proclaiming it before everyone? For virtues are not compatible with vices, [Note: Several manuscripts: “But they remain consistent with themselves”; Benignus and several others: “But they oppose themselves.” This reading would not be objectionable if *sibi* were punctuated separately.] but remain consistent with themselves. Who, then, was as strong as holy Job? Who can be assigned second place to him, when he scarcely found anyone equal to himself?

## CHAPTER XL

Our people too were not lacking in martial virtue, as is shown by examples of the ancients, and especially by the renowned deed of Eleazar.

195. But perhaps some are held fast by a passion for military glory, so that they think martial fortitude alone is fortitude; [Note: Some manuscripts read “the fortitude of combatants.”] and therefore they suppose that I have turned to these matters because such fortitude was lacking among our people. How courageous was Joshua son of Nun, who in a single battle struck down five captured kings together with their peoples (Joshua 10:5ff.)! Then, when battle pressed against the Gibeonites [Note: The old edition and many manuscripts read, “when battle arose.”] and he feared that night might impede victory, with greatness of mind and faith he cried out: “Let the sun stand still”; and it stood still until the victory was completed. Gideon, with three hundred men, carried off a triumph over a vast people and a fierce enemy (Judges 7:8ff.). Jonathan, though a young man, displayed valor in a great battle (1 Samuel 14:1ff.). What shall I say of the Maccabees (1 Maccabees 2:35ff.)?

196. But first I shall speak of the people of the Fathers, who, being prepared to fight for the temple of God and for their lawful institutions, were deceitfully attacked by their enemies on the Sabbath. They preferred to offer their defenseless bodies to wounds rather than fight and violate the Sabbath. Thus they all joyfully offered themselves to death. But the Maccabees, considering that by this example the whole nation might perish, avenged the slaughter of their innocent brothers even on the Sabbath, when they themselves were challenged to battle. Thereafter King Antiochus, provoked by this, kindled war through his commanders Lysias, Nicanor, and Gorgias; but with his Eastern and Assyrian forces he was so crushed that forty-eight thousand men were laid low in the middle of the field by three thousand.

197. Consider the valor of the commander Judas Maccabaeus from the deed of one of his soldiers (1 Maccabees 6:43ff.). For when Eleazar noticed an elephant surpassing the others, clothed in royal armor, and supposed that the king was upon it, he rushed headlong into the midst of the legion [Note: The Gill and Roman editions, together with several manuscripts, read “he burst forth”; other editions, with more and better manuscripts, read “he slipped away.” Again, where the earlier edition and several manuscripts read “he was killing the beast,” the Roman edition and some other, though fewer, manuscripts more elegantly read “he kept killing it until he reached the beast” (the Roman edition: “until he should reach the beast”).] and, throwing aside his shield, killed with both hands until he reached the beast. Then he went beneath it and, thrusting his sword upward, killed it. Thus, as the beast fell, it crushed Eleazar, and he died.

What great courage of soul! First, that he did not fear death; then, that, surrounded by the legions of his enemies, he rushed upon the massed foe, penetrated the center of the army, and, rendered fiercer by his contempt for death, threw aside his shield, faced the bulk of the wounded beast with both hands, and bore its weight upon himself; afterward, that he went beneath it so as to strike it with a fuller blow. Enclosed by its fall, he was less crushed than enclosed, and was buried in his own triumph.

198. His judgment did not deceive the man, although the royal appearance had deceived him. For the enemy, stunned by so great a spectacle of valor, did not dare to attack the unarmed man while he was occupied, [Note: How could he be “unarmed,” since he was armed with a sword and was killing enemies with both hands? This must refer to his having thrown aside his shield, in accordance with Cicero’s speech *For Caecina*, p. 45: “Weapons are called by their proper names: some are for defense, others for inflicting harm. Those who do not possess the former are said to be unarmed,” etc.] and after the fall of the collapsing beast they were so terrified that they all considered themselves unequal to the valor of one man.

Finally, King Antiochus, called the son of Lysias, who had come with one hundred and twenty thousand armed men and thirty-two elephants— [Note: The Gill edition and the Amerbach edition in the margin, with by far the greater number of manuscripts, read “the son of Lysias”; other editions, with some manuscripts, omit it, since it seems contrary to Scriptural authority. But here *son* means the ward or foster-child of Lysias: this Antiochus had been entrusted by his father to Lysias’ fidelity and, as it were, guardianship.]so that from sunrise, around each beast, the brilliance of the armor flashed like mountains, shining as though with burning lamps—was so frightened by the courage of one man that he begged for peace. Thus Eleazar left peace as the inheritance of his valor. But let these matters belong to the triumphs.

## CHAPTER XLI

The greatness of spirit of Judas and Jonathan is praised, and the steadfastness of the martyrs in endurance—the very important part of fortitude—is set before our eyes.

199. But since fortitude is proved not only in prosperity but also in adversity, let us now consider the end of Judas Maccabaeus (1 Maccabees 9:8ff.). After he had defeated Nicanor, the commander of King Demetrius, he felt secure against the king’s army of twenty thousand. He nevertheless undertook battle with nine hundred men. When they wished to withdraw lest they be overwhelmed by the multitude, he urged them to choose a glorious death rather than a shameful flight: “Let us not,” he said, “leave a charge against our glory.” Accordingly, when battle had been joined and they had fought from the first rising of day until evening, he attacked the right wing, where he saw the enemy’s strongest force, and easily routed it. But while pursuing the fugitives, he exposed his back to a wound; thus he found a death more glorious than triumphs. [Note: Erasmus and subsequent editions, together with two manuscripts, read: “a place of death more glorious than triumphs.”]

200. Why should I add Jonathan, his brother? Fighting with a small force against royal armies, abandoned by his own men and left with only two companions, he renewed the battle, routed the enemy, and recalled his fleeing men to share in the triumph.

201. Here you have martial fortitude, in which there is no ordinary form of honor and propriety: it prefers death to slavery and disgrace. But what shall I say about the sufferings of the martyrs? And, not to wander farther afield, the Maccabean boys won no lesser triumphs over the proud King Antiochus [Note: It is worthwhile comparing this account of the martyrdom of the Maccabean brothers with their history in book 2 of *Jacob and the Blessed Life*, chapter 11, where it is more fully expounded, and also with the following chapter, no. 53, in the words: “What lyre could produce sweeter songs,” etc. You will see that each was set before the other as a model.] than their own parents had won. The parents conquered while armed; the boys, without arms (2 Maccabees 7:1ff.).

The band of seven boys stood unconquered, surrounded by royal legions. Punishments failed, torturers yielded, but the martyrs did not fail. One, after the skin of his head had been stripped away, had altered his appearance but increased his courage. Another, ordered to bring forth his tongue to be cut off, replied: “The Lord does not hear only those who speak; he also heard Moses when he was silent” (Exodus 14:15). He hears the silent thoughts of his own more than the voices of all. Do you fear the scourge of the tongue but not the scourge of blood? Blood too has its own voice, with which it cries out to God, as Abel’s blood cried out (Genesis 4:10).

202. What shall I say about the mother, who joyfully watched as the number of her sons’ deaths became the number of their trophies, and delighted in the voices of the dying as though in the songs of singers? She saw in her sons the most beautiful lyre of her womb, and a harmony of piety sweeter than every measure of the lyre (2 Maccabees 7:20ff.).

203. What shall I say about the infants [Note: He means the children from two years old and under who were slaughtered at Herod’s command, whom the tradition of the Church has always counted among the martyrs. It was not unreasonably believed that, just as another’s will had been sufficient to make them liable for sin, so another’s will—that is, Christ’s will—and the grief of their parents would also be sufficient to make them worthy of glory: when Rachel wept for her children so as to offer infants, washed in her tears, to Christ, as Ambrose himself says in his letter to Horontianus, formerly numbered 39 in the old editions, which the Roman edition detached from that collection and placed among the *Expositions on Genesis*. Various holy Fathers delivered sermons for the feast of the Holy Innocents, especially Augustine and Bernard; consult them.] who received the palm of victory before attaining the capacity of nature? What shall I say about holy Agnes, who, placed in danger regarding two greatest things—chastity and life—protected her chastity and exchanged life for immortality?

204. Let us not pass over Saint Lawrence, who, when he saw his bishop Xystus being led to martyrdom, began to weep—not over Xystus’s suffering, but over his own being left behind. Thus he began to address him in these words:

“Where are you going without your son, father? Where are you hastening, holy priest, without your deacon? You were never accustomed to offer sacrifice without a minister. What, then, have you found displeasing in me, father? Have you judged me degenerate? At least test whether you have chosen a suitable minister. To whom you entrusted the consecration of the Lord’s blood, [Note: The old editions, followed by all manuscripts except one Vatican manuscript and ten Gallican manuscripts, read “the consecration of the Lord’s body and blood.” The Roman edition, departing from all manuscript and printed Ambrosian copies, replaced *consecrationem* with *dispensationem*. From this alteration, quite a few heterodox writers thought they had legitimate grounds for most vehemently accusing the editors of corruption and bad faith. But this accusation was insufficiently considered: they ought to have remembered that Hospinian, in book 5, chapter 6 of his *Sacred History*, attributed this corruption not to the Roman edition, which had already been published for many years, but to Eutropius. Nor is Hospinian’s own insinuation necessarily free from rashness. For not only in the life of blessed Xystus in Lipomanus, Venetian edition of 1554, but also in the life of Saint Lawrence, as it appears in the Lombardic Legend of Jacob of Genoa, printed at Nuremberg in 1487, we read “the dispensation of the Lord’s blood.” This is no slight indication that somewhere there exists a copy in which it is read in this way. Nevertheless, we must stand by the older and genuine reading, which, to use Cardinal Bona’s expression, is not at all to be feared. For *consecration* may mean either the act of consecrating itself or its effect—that is, consecration already completed—and neither sense conflicts with Catholic understanding. If the first sense is preferred, what is surprising about attributing consecration to a deacon, when Abbot Guerric, sermon 5, *On the Purification*, even says that the people consecrate? Certainly the deacon cooperates in this action not as one among the congregation of the faithful, but as the principal minister of the priest who consecrates, in a manner that we may call concelebration. This is relevant to canon 3 of the Roman synod addressed to the bishops of Gaul, in Sirmond, volume 1 of the *Gallican Councils*. We think that two passages should be understood in this sense: one in Peter of Blois’s letter 123 to the bishop of London, the other in Peter of Cantor’s book *On the Miraculous Word*, chapter 41. Hallerus, book 3 of *The Hierarchy*, p. 375, interprets both as referring only to dispensation, while Cardinal Bona, book 1 of *Liturgical Matters*, chapter 25, no. 4, interprets the first as referring only to presence; consult those works, as well as our Menardus in his edition of the *Sacramentary of Saint Gregory*. Moreover, the second sense of *consecration*—namely, the distribution of the consecrated thing—is wholly free of difficulty and especially appeals to us. The word “you entrusted” signifies something already completed, and the other words, “a share in the sacraments that are to be completed,” can beautifully be referred to the same dispensation. Furthermore, it was the proper duty of deacons to administer the Lord’s blood to the people, as the Council of Aachen, chapter 7, says: “For just as consecration belongs to the priest, so the dispensation of the sacrament belongs to the minister. The former sanctifies what has been offered; the latter distributes what has been sanctified.” These words are also found in Isidore, book 2 of *Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 8, and in an ancient author who falsely bears Jerome’s name. This explanation will not seem forced to one who, with Anthony Godellus, *Ecclesiastical History*, volume 1, p. 579, considers that in the very sacrifice of the Mass, when a portion of the sacred host is placed in the chalice, *consecration* is used for the consecrated thing. Add what Cardinal Bona says in the cited passage: that a deacon is said to consecrate insofar as he distributes the blood, which is our consecration and sanctification, and the source and essence of all sanctification. Away, then, with the vain invention of certain writers, following Hospinian, who in the cited passage and in book 1, chapter 23 of the same *Sacred History*, try to infer from these words of Ambrose that formerly deacons were permitted to celebrate the Eucharist in the absence of priests. For, apart from the fact that in more than twenty-four manuscripts and in all writers who cite this same passage the mention of the Lord’s body is omitted, the holy Levite himself professes that he is not the celebrant but the celebrant’s minister; nor does he speak of the priest’s absence but of participation. Therefore, wherever we read that deacons consecrated in another sense, this must be attributed to proud and rash usurpation.] to whom you entrusted a share in completing the sacraments, do you deny me a share in your blood? Take care lest your judgment be endangered while fortitude is being praised. The disciple’s rejection is a loss to the teacher. What is more, illustrious and excellent men are surpassed by the struggles of their disciples rather than by their own. Abraham offered his son (Genesis 22:9); Peter sent Stephen ahead (Acts 7:57). And you, father, display your valor in your son; offer him whom you instructed, so that, confident in your judgment and attended by noble company, you may reach the crown.”

205. Then Xystus said: “I am not leaving or abandoning you, my son; but greater contests are owed to you. We, like old men, take up the course of a lighter battle; you, like a young man, await a more glorious triumph over the tyrant. Soon you will come; stop weeping; after three days you will follow me. [Note: All editions and some manuscripts read, “Between the priest …,” whereas more manuscripts omit *between*. Since the bishop is understood by “priest,” and the deacon by “Levite” (for, as the Council of Aachen later defined in chapter 7, drawing on book 2, chapter 25 of the *Apostolic Constitutions* and Jerome’s letter 85, “the order of deacons derives its beginning from the tribe of Levi”), it is appropriately asserted that an interval of three days comes between the two. For there are three distinct grades in the hierarchy: bishops, presbyters, and deacons, as the Fathers of Trent, adhering to the tradition of the ancients, confirmed.] The middle number is fitting between priest and Levite. It was not your role to conquer under your teacher, as though you were seeking an assistant. Why do you desire a share in my passion? I leave its entire inheritance to you. Why do you seek my presence? Let weak disciples precede their teacher; let the strong follow, so that those who no longer need instruction may conquer without their teacher. Elijah likewise left Elisha. To you, then, I entrust the succession of our valor.”

206. Such was their contest, truly worthy of a contest between priest and minister: which of them should suffer first for Christ’s name. In tragic dramas, they say that great applause arose in the theater when Pylades claimed to be Orestes, while Orestes insisted that he was Orestes, as he truly was: Pylades so that he might be killed in Orestes’ place, and Orestes so that Pylades might not suffer death on his behalf. But they were not permitted to live, since both were guilty of parricide: one because he had committed it, the other because he had helped. [Note: “The one who had committed it” means Orestes, who killed his mother Clytemnestra to avenge his father Agamemnon, whom she had murdered. “The one who had helped” means Pylades, Orestes’ kinsman and friend, so faithful that both were regarded as a model of true friendship. This passage was taken and adapted not from Euripides’ *Iphigenia in Tauris*, as the Roman edition noted in the margin, but from Cicero, book 5 of *On the Ends of Good and Evil*, p. 109, and the *Dialogue on Friendship*, p. 422, where he relates that this applause arose in a tragedy by Marcus Pacuvius.]

No one compelled Saint Lawrence to do this except the love of devotion. Yet after three days, when he had deceived the tyrant and was placed upon a gridiron to be burned, he too said: “This side is cooked; turn it over and eat.” Thus by the courage of his soul he conquered the nature of fire.

## CHAPTER XLII

Authorities must not be provoked, nor should ears be given to flattery.

207. I also think we must beware lest, while some are driven by an excessive desire for glory, they abuse their powers too insolently and often stir up the minds of the pagans, already hostile to us, toward persecution and inflame them to anger. Thus, so that those people may be able to persevere and overcome punishments, how many do they cause to perish?

208. We must also take care not to open our ears to flatterers. To be softened by flattery seems not only inconsistent with fortitude but also characteristic of cowardice. [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, book 1, p. 363, line 30: “We must beware lest we open our ears to flatterers or allow ourselves to be flattered,” etc.]

## CHAPTER XLIII

On temperance and its principal parts, namely tranquility and moderation of soul, care for moral goodness, and consideration of propriety.

209. Since we have spoken of three virtues, [Note: Same work, line 44: “It follows that we must speak of that remaining part of moral goodness, in which modesty …,” etc.] it remains for us to speak of the fourth virtue, which is called temperance and moderation. In it, tranquility of soul, the pursuit of gentleness, the grace of moderation, care for what is honorable, and consideration of propriety are especially observed and sought.

210. We must therefore maintain a certain order of life, so that its first foundations may be drawn from modesty. Modesty is the companion and intimate associate of a tranquil mind; it flees insolence, shuns every immoderate luxury, loves sobriety, fosters moral goodness, and seeks that which is proper.

211. Let the choice of one’s associates follow, [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, book 1, p. 368, line 5: “It is therefore proper for a young man to associate with his elders,” etc. Likewise, book 2, p. 380, line 38: “Young men are very easily recognized, and in the best sense,” etc.] so that we may join ourselves to the most approved of our elders. For although the companionship of equals is sweeter, that of old men is safer. Through a kind of instruction and direction in life, they give color to the character of the young and dye it, as it were, with the purple of integrity. If those who are unfamiliar with a place, when they desire to undertake a journey, seek to travel with experienced guides, how much more should young men undertake the new path of life with old men, so that they may be less able to go astray or turn aside from the true path of virtue! For nothing is more beautiful than to have the same people as both teachers and witnesses of one’s life.

212. In every action we must also seek what is appropriate to persons, times, and ages, and what suits the character of each individual. [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, book 1, p. 365, line 42: “The other [kind of propriety] is attributed specifically to individuals; for just as in bodies,” etc.] For what suits one person often does not suit another. One thing is appropriate for a young man, another for an old man; one thing in dangers, another in prosperity.

213. David danced before the ark of the Lord (2 Samuel 6:14); Samuel did not dance. Yet David was not therefore censured; rather, Samuel was praised more. David changed his appearance in the presence of King Achish (1 Samuel 21:13). [Note: Some editions and manuscripts read “before the king”; other, no fewer but older, witnesses read “against the king,” that is, opposite the king.] But if he had done this after the fear of being recognized had been removed, he could by no means have escaped the reproach of frivolity. Saul too, surrounded by a choir of prophets, himself prophesied; but of him alone, as though of one unworthy, it was said: “And Saul among the prophets” (1 Samuel 19:24).

## CHAPTER XLIV

Each person ought to devote himself to the office suited to him; but many are hindered by imitating their fathers’ pursuits, contrary to the practice of men of the Church.

214. Let each person, therefore, know his own character [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, book 1, p. 366, line 16: “Each person’s own qualities must be carefully preserved,” etc. And below, line 40: “Let each person therefore know his own character,” etc. Likewise, p. 367, line 30: “In this deliberation, all counsel must be referred to each person’s own nature,” etc.] and apply himself to what he has chosen as suitable for him. Let him first consider what he should pursue. [Note: A few manuscripts and the old edition read: “Let him not only know,” etc.] Let him know his strengths, but also recognize his faults; let him show himself an impartial judge of himself, so that he may devote himself to his strengths and avoid his faults.

215. One person is considered better suited to reading that requires distinction, another more pleasing in psalmody, another more diligent in exorcizing those troubled by an evil spirit, and another more suitable for the sacristy. [Note: Although the acolyte and doorkeeper are not mentioned here, it by no means follows that their orders did not then exist in the Church, since the four listed are mentioned merely by way of example. As for the fact that the psalmist and keeper of the sacristy are listed alongside the reader and exorcist, although among us they are no longer orders, we think this happened because the minor orders of the clergy are merely ecclesiastical institutions and are found to have been increased or diminished by the Church according to varying needs. The Council of Carthage III, canon 21, and IV, canon 10, as well as Gregory the Great, book 11, section 54, the Roman *Ordo*, and others speak of the psalmist or cantor. We shall speak of the keeper of the sacristy and his office in chapter 50 of this book. Meanwhile, observe that the several orders were not ordinarily assigned all to everyone, but one to each individual; and that it was placed in the bishop’s discretion whom he should assign to which order.] The priest should consider all these things and assign to each person the office suited to him. For whatever a person’s character leads him toward, or whatever office suits him, he fulfills it with greater grace. [Note: The better manuscripts read “he fulfills it with greater grace”; other manuscripts and the printed editions read “it is fulfilled with greater grace,” with only a very slight difference of sense.]

216. But this is difficult in every area of life and most difficult in our own calling. [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, book 1, p. 367, line 5: “But most of those whose fathers or ancestors excelled in some glory,” etc.] For everyone loves to follow the life of his parents. Thus most are drawn into military service because their parents served, while others turn to different activities.

217. In ecclesiastical office, however, you will find nothing rarer than one who follows the discipline of his father. [Note: “Father” means, of course, a spiritual father—that is, an instructor and teacher. Or, if you insist that a natural father is meant, we shall certainly not object, provided that you understand this to refer only to a father established in the minor orders, and to one initiated into the greater orders only insofar as he had children before his ordination. For we shall later show most clearly, in its proper place, that Ambrose taught that continence must necessarily be observed by the latter.] This is either because the seriousness of the calling frightens him away, or because abstinence is more difficult at an unstable age, or because ecclesiastical life seems too obscure to energetic youth; and therefore they turn to pursuits that they consider more likely to win applause. For most people prefer present things to future things. They serve the present; we serve the future. Therefore, the more excellent the cause, the more attentive our care ought to be.

## CHAPTER XLV

On the beautiful and the honorable: what distinction exists between them both among secular authors and among sacred ones.

218. Let us therefore maintain modesty, and that moderation which raises up the adornment of the whole of life. For it is no small matter to preserve measure in individual things and to assign each its order, [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, book 1, p. 363, line 47: “This contains what may be called *decorum* in Latin,” etc.] in which that quality truly shines forth which is called propriety. It is so joined to moral goodness that it cannot be separated from it. For what is proper is honorable, and what is honorable is proper; thus the distinction lies more in language than in any separation within virtue. It can be understood that they differ from one another, but it cannot be explained.

219. To attempt to draw out some distinction, [Note: Same work, p. 364, line 10: “For just as the grace and beauty of the body cannot be separated from health,” etc.] moral goodness is like good health and a certain soundness of body, while propriety is like grace and beauty. Just as beauty seems to surpass soundness and health, yet cannot exist without them or be separated from them in any way—for unless there is good health, there can be neither beauty nor grace—so moral goodness contains propriety within itself, so that propriety appears to proceed from it and cannot exist without it.

Moral goodness is therefore like the soundness of our whole work and action, while propriety is like its appearance. Although propriety, when mingled with moral goodness, is distinguished in opinion, and although it may appear to excel in some respect, it nevertheless lies at the root of moral goodness, as its outstanding flower: without that root it withers, while in it it flourishes. For what is moral goodness except that which flees disgrace as though it were death? And what is dishonor except that which brings dryness and death? When, therefore, the substance of virtue is green, propriety shines forth like a flower because the root is sound; but when the root of our purpose is diseased, nothing sprouts. [Note: Some manuscripts read “in the virtue of our purpose”; in others, and in the printed edition, *in virtute* is absent, making the wording more convenient.]

220. You have this expressed somewhat more clearly in our own writings. David says: “The Lord reigns; he has clothed himself with beauty” (Psalm 92:1). And the Apostle says: “Let us walk honorably, as in the day” (Romans 13:13). [Note: The editions and some manuscripts add: “which in Greek is said …”] What the Greeks call *euschēmonōs* (εὐσχημόνως) properly signifies “with good bearing” or “with a good appearance.”

When God therefore formed the first human being, he fashioned him with good bearing and a fine arrangement of his limbs, and gave him an excellent appearance. He had not granted remission of sins; but afterward, when he renewed him by the Spirit and infused grace into him—he who had come in the form of a servant and had assumed the appearance of a human being—he took upon himself the beauty of human redemption. And therefore the Prophet said: “The Lord reigns; he has clothed himself with beauty.”

Then elsewhere he says: “Praise is fitting for you, O God, in Zion” (Psalm 64:2). This is to say: It is honorable that we fear you, love you, beseech you, and honor you; for it is written: “Let all your things be done honorably” (1 Corinthians 14:40). But we can also fear, love, ask, and honor a human being; praise, in a special sense, is said to God. This is what we offer to God as something more excellent than all the rest, and it is called propriety.

It is also fitting for a woman to pray in an adorned manner; but it is especially fitting for her to pray veiled and to profess chastity with good conduct (1 Timothy 2:9–10). [Note: The Roman edition reads “in orderly dress”; the other editions, together with the manuscripts and the Vulgate, read “in adorned dress,” from the Greek *en katastolē kosmiō* (ἐν καταστολῇ κοσμίῳ). The same Roman edition, where the others and most manuscripts read “with good conduct,” substituted, with some manuscripts, “through good conduct,” evidently referring to the Apostle’s phrase from the cited passage, “but through good works,” namely, “professing piety through good works.” Ambrose has also changed “piety” into “chastity.”]

## CHAPTER XLVI

The twofold division of propriety is proposed; then, after it has been shown that what accords with nature is honorable and what does not is disgraceful, this same division is illustrated with examples.

221. Propriety is therefore that which takes precedence, and its division is twofold. [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, book 1, p. 364, line 13: “Its description is twofold. For there is a certain general propriety,” etc.] For there is a kind of propriety that is general, which is diffused throughout the whole of moral goodness and is viewed, as it were, in the entire body. There is also a special kind, which shines forth in some particular part.

The general kind is present when one’s entire life has a harmonious and consistent form of moral goodness in every action, when all of one’s life agrees with itself and differs in no respect. The special kind is present when some particular action stands out among one’s virtues.

222. Observe also that it is seemly to live according to nature and to conduct oneself according to nature, while what is contrary to nature is shameful. For the Apostle says, as though asking: “Is it fitting for a woman to pray to God unveiled?” And does not nature itself teach you that, if a man wears his hair long, it is a disgrace to him, since it is contrary to nature (1 Cor. XI, 13)? And again he says: “But if a woman has long hair, it is a glory to her” (ibid. 15). This is according to nature, since hair serves as a covering; for this is the natural veil. Nature itself therefore supplies us with our appearance and form, which we ought to preserve. If only we could also preserve its innocence and not alter what we have received through our own wickedness!

[Note: [Col. 0089D] Ibid., line 15: “That is seemly which accords with human excellence,” etc. Likewise below, line 40: “But the duty which derives from it first,” etc. Ibid., p. 367, line 31: “For since in all things that are done,” etc.]

[Note: All editions read, “does not nature teach us that a man,” etc.; but this is contrary to the authority of the manuscripts, which is also supported by the apostolic text: διδάσκει ὑμᾶς ὅτι ἀνήρ, “it teaches you that a man,” not διδάσκει ἡμᾶς, “it teaches us,” etc.]

223. You have here this general seemliness, because God made the beauty of this world. You have it also in its several parts: when God made the light and distinguished day from night (Gen. I, 3 ff.), when he founded heaven, when he separated earth and sea, when he appointed the sun, moon, and stars to shine upon the earth, he approved each thing individually. Thus the seemliness that shone forth in the several parts of the world gleamed in the whole, as Wisdom proves when it says: “I was the one whom he applauded . . . when he rejoiced in the completed world” (Prov. VIII, 30–31).

Similarly, in the construction of the human body, the portion belonging to each member is pleasing; but the harmonious arrangement of the members taken together gives still greater delight, since they appear so well fitted and suited to one another.

CHAPTER XLVII

How that seemliness ought to shine forth in our life: what we should provide and what desires we should restrain.

224. If, then, someone preserves uniformity throughout his life and in the manner of his individual actions, and also guards order, consistency in words and deeds, and moderation, that seemliness excels in his life and shines forth as though in a mirror.

[Note: Cicero, On Duties, book I, p. 364, line 33: “Thus this seemliness, which shines forth in life, moves,” etc.]

225. Let gracious speech also be added, so that it may win the affection of those who hear, and make him pleasing to his relatives, fellow citizens, or, if possible, to everyone. Let him neither display himself as a flatterer nor make himself available to be flattered by anyone; the one is a mark of cunning, the other of vanity.

[Note: Ibid., p. 370, line 3: “Above all, care must be taken that we appear both to respect and to love those with whom we converse.”]

226. Let him not despise what each person, and especially a truly good man, thinks of him; for in this way he learns to show respect to the good. To disregard the judgments of good men is either arrogance or irresponsibility: the former is attributed to pride, the latter to negligence.

[Note: Cicero, On Duties, book I, p. 364, line 35: “A certain reverence must therefore be shown toward human beings,” etc.]

227. Let him also beware of the movements of his soul; for he must both observe himself and keep watch around himself. Just as he must guard against himself, so also he must protect himself from himself. There are movements in which that desire is present which bursts forth, as it were, in a sudden rush; hence it is called ὁρμή in Greek, because it suddenly tears itself away with a certain force.

[Note: Several manuscripts read, “with a force that creeps along.”]

There is no insignificant force of soul and nature in these movements. Yet this force is twofold: one part lies in desire, the other in reason, which restrains desire, makes it obedient to itself, and leads it wherever it wishes; and, as though by diligent instruction, teaches it what ought to be done and what avoided, so that it may obey a good mistress.

[Note: All editions and several manuscripts read, “so that it may obey a good female ruler”; many others, and better ones, read, “so that it may obey a good female tamer.” The latter is more appropriate, since it refers to what precedes—namely, that reason restrains desire, etc.]

228. We must be anxious lest we act rashly or carelessly, or do anything for which we cannot give a credible account. The cause of our actions, even if it is not explained to everyone, is nevertheless examined by everyone. Nor do we have any ground on which we can excuse ourselves. For although there is a certain force of nature in every desire, desire itself is nevertheless subject to the law of nature’s reason and obeys it.

[Note: Cicero, book I of On Duties, line 1: “It must, however, be brought about that desires obey reason,” etc.]

Therefore it belongs to a good watchman to keep such vigilance in his mind that desire neither run ahead of reason nor abandon it: it must not, by running ahead, disturb and exclude reason, nor, by abandoning it, leave it helpless. Agitation removes steadfastness; abandonment reveals cowardice and exposes laziness.

When the mind is disturbed, desire spreads itself more widely and farther, and, as though driven by an unbridled rush, does not accept reason’s reins or perceive any of the driver’s controls by which it might be turned back.

[Note: Cicero, ibid., p. 365, line 6: “By which not only souls are disturbed, but bodies also. One can see the very faces,” etc.]

Hence it is often not only the mind that is thrown into agitation and reason that is lost; the face too becomes inflamed, whether by anger or lust; it grows pale with fear, cannot contain itself in pleasure, and exults with excessive joy.

229. When these things occur, that natural kind of judgment and dignity of character is cast aside, and steadfastness—the one quality that can preserve its authority in actions and deliberations and retain what is seemly—can no longer be maintained.

[Note: Cicero, ibid., line 11: “For we were not so constituted . . . but rather for severity,” etc.]

230. A more serious desire arises from excessive indignation, which is usually kindled by the pain of an injury received. The psalm whose teaching we placed in the preface instructs us sufficiently concerning this (ch. II, 6–7). It is fitting that this should have happened: when writing about duties, we could make use of the assertion in our preface, which itself also pertains to the instruction of duty.

[Note: Cicero, On Duties, book I, p. 370, line 12: “It is right even in those disputes which arise with our bitterest enemies,” etc.]

231. But since above, as was appropriate, we briefly touched upon how each person can take care not to be provoked by an injury received, and since we feared that the preface might become too long, I now think that the matter should be discussed more fully. The opportunity is suitable for explaining, in the section on temperance, how anger is to be restrained.

CHAPTER XLVIII

After the subject of restraining anger is taken up again, three classes of those who suffer injuries are explained; the Apostle and David are said to have reached the most perfect of them. From this occasion certain distinctions between the present and the future life are handed down.

232. We wish, if we can, to demonstrate from the divine Scriptures that there are three kinds of people who receive an injury. One kind consists of those whom a sinner insults, reviles, and spurs onward.

[Note: Several manuscripts read, “the wicked reviler”; one, “the reviler of wickedness”; quite a few others, “wickedness reviles”; some editions, including the Amerbach edition, “he reviles with wickedness”; several, including Erasmus and Gill, “he reviles and disturbs”; two, “he reviles and incites wickedness”; finally, the others and the Roman edition, “he reviles, he rides over.” The word was scarcely understood by the scribes, and this produced such diversity. Here *inequitat* means nothing other than that he urges and harasses as though with spurs.]

Because justice is lacking in such people, shame increases and pain grows. There are many like them among those of my own order and number. For if someone does me, a weak man, an injury, perhaps, although weak, I may forgive my injury. If he brings a charge against me, I am not so great that I can be content with my own conscience, even if I know myself innocent of what is alleged; rather, like a weak man, I desire to wash away the mark of wounded honor. Thus I demand an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth, and repay insult with insult.

[Note: Codex Bigotianus reads: “Knowing that I have not done what he alleges, I am not so great . . .”; “even if I know that what is alleged against me is foreign to me.”]

233. But if I am one who is making progress, though not yet perfect, I do not return the insult. Even if he pours out abuse and floods my ears with insults, I remain silent and make no reply.

[Note: The edition and a few manuscripts read, “even if he pours out abuse”; many other manuscripts read, “and floods my ears with insult.” Again, where the edition and most manuscripts read, “I make no reply,” some manuscripts have, “I repay nothing.”]

234. But if I am perfect—for I speak by way of example, since in truth I am weak—then, if I am perfect, I bless the one who curses me, as Paul also blessed, when he says: “We are cursed, and we bless” (1 Cor. IV, 12).

[Note: Two manuscripts read, “We are cursed, and we bless; we suffer persecution, and we endure.”]

For he had heard the one who said: “Love your enemies, pray for those who slander and persecute you” (Matt. V, 44). Therefore Paul endured and bore persecution, because he conquered and subdued human feeling through the prospect of the promised reward, so that he might become a son of God if he loved his enemy.

235. Yet we can also show that holy David was not inferior to Paul in this kind of virtue. At first, when Shimei, the son of Gera, cursed him and brought accusations against him (2 Sam. XVI, 7 ff.), he remained silent, humbled himself, and kept silence concerning his own good deeds (Ps. XXXVIII, 3)—that is, concerning the consciousness of his good works. Then he desired to be cursed, because by that curse he was acquiring divine mercy.

[Note: One manuscript reads, “because that curse . . .”]

236. Observe how he preserved humility, justice, and prudence in order to merit grace from the Lord. First he said: “He curses me because the Lord told him to curse” (2 Sam. XVI, 10). Here you have humility: he judged that whatever is divinely commanded should be borne with equanimity, as though by a servant. Again he said: “Behold, my son, who came forth from my body, seeks my life” (ibid. 11). Here you have justice: if we suffer more grievous things from our own people, why do we bear with indignation what is inflicted by strangers?

Third he said: “Let him alone, let him curse, for the Lord has told him to do so, so that the Lord may see my humiliation and repay me with good for this curse” (ibid. 12).

[Note: Two manuscripts read, “that the Lord may give a blessing for this curse.”]

He not only endured the one who reviled him, but also left unharmed the one who stoned and pursued him (2 Sam. XIX, 22); indeed, after his victory he willingly forgave him when he asked pardon.

237. I inserted this so that I might show, in the spirit of the Gospel, that holy David was not only unoffending but even pleasing to the one who reviled him, and that he was more pleased than angered by the injuries for which he believed a reward would be returned to him. Yet although he was perfect, he still sought more perfect things. As a human being, he grew hot with the pain of injury; but he conquered like a good soldier and endured like a strong athlete.

[Note: Thus read the greater number of the more reliable manuscripts; some others, and the edition, read: “But he conquered the spirit as a good soldier,” etc.]

The end of patience is the expectation of the promises, and therefore he said: “Make known to me, Lord, my end, and the number of my days, what it is, that I may know what I lack” (Ps. XXXVIII, 5).

He seeks that end of the heavenly promises, or that end when each person will rise in his own order: “Christ the first fruits, then those who belong to Christ, who have believed in his coming, then the end” (1 Cor. XV, 23). For when the kingdom has been handed over to God and the Father and all powers have been abolished, as the Apostle said, perfection begins.

Here, therefore, there is impediment; here there is weakness even among the perfect; there, perfection is complete. Therefore he asks for those days of eternal life which are permanent, not those which pass away, so that he may know what he lacks: what land of promise bears perpetual fruits, what the first dwelling with the Father is, what the second and what the third are, in which each person will rest according to the measure of his merits.

238. Those things, then, are what we ought to desire in which perfection and truth are found. Here there is shadow, here image; there, truth. Shadow in the Law, image in the Gospel, truth in the heavenly realm (Heb. X, 1 ff.). Formerly a lamb was offered, and a calf was offered; now Christ is offered. Yet he is offered as man, as one receiving suffering; and he offers himself as priest, so that he may forgive our sins: here in image, there in truth, where he intervenes for us before the Father as an advocate.

[Note: The Thuaneus manuscript reads, “Here, therefore, we appear in image.”]

Here, then, we walk in image and see in image; there, face to face, where perfection is complete, because all perfection is in truth.

[Note: The Codex of Thierry and three others read, “Here there is image; truth is in the heavenly places.” But the other reading is supported not only by far more manuscripts and by all the editions, but also by the agreement of another passage in the Exposition of Psalm XXXVIII, no. 25, where these same words can be read without any variation. Moreover, Edmund Albertinus, book II, chapter 2, p. 505, imposes on these words of Ambrose—“image in the Gospel, and now in image,” etc.—the meaning that the holy man denies that Christ is offered here except in image, whereas in heaven he offers himself in truth; thus image and truth are set against each other in such a way that one excludes the other. But unless he had been blinded by partisan zeal, he would certainly have perceived that Christ is said to be offered in image for no other reason than that he is offered as man, as one receiving suffering. Therefore, so that the mind of the holy Doctor may be clearly understood, it must be noted that by these words, “Here there is shadow, here image,” etc., he describes the Church as a certain intermediate state between the Synagogue and heaven: in the Synagogue there was only shadow, while in heaven there is only truth; but in the Church both are joined together. Indeed, it is so true that Ambrose signifies truth joined with image in the Gospel covenant that he could not separate them without completely overturning the truth of the bloody sacrifice itself, and therefore of the Lord’s incarnation, since in his understanding these mysteries cannot be referred either to the Synagogue or to heaven, but to the Church. Ambrose himself expresses his meaning in the cited passage from the Exposition of Psalm XXXVIII in words so clear that they leave no room for sophistry: “Now we see good things through an image and hold the good things of the image. We saw the High Priest coming to us; we saw and heard him offering his blood for us. We follow as best we can . . . for although Christ is not now seen to offer, he himself is offered on earth when Christ’s body is offered,” etc.]

CHAPTER XLIX

The image of the virtues must be preserved in us, while the image of the devil and of vices—and especially of greed—must be erased. Greed deprives us of freedom and, by troubling us with various vanities, strips us of the image of God.

239. Therefore, while we are here, let us preserve the image, so that there we may arrive at the truth. Let the image of justice be in us; let the image of wisdom be in us, because that day will come, and we shall be judged according to the image.

240. Let the adversary not find his own image in you—not rage, not fury—for in these is the image of wickedness. The adversary, the devil, seeks someone to kill and devour like a roaring lion. Let him not find in you a desire for gold, heaps of silver, or images of vices, lest he take away from you the voice of freedom.

For the voice of freedom is that by which you say: “The ruler of this world is coming, and he will find nothing in me” (John XIV, 30). Therefore, if you are confident that he will find nothing in you when he comes to search you, you will say what the patriarch Jacob said to Laban: “Search and see whether you have anything of yours with me” (Gen. XXXI, 32). Blessed indeed is Jacob, with whom Laban could find nothing belonging to him! For Rachel had hidden the golden and silver images of his gods.

241. Therefore, if wisdom, faith, contempt for the world, and your grace conceal every form of faithlessness, you will be blessed, because you do not look toward vanities and false insanities (Ps. XXXIX, 5). Is it a small thing to silence the adversary, so that he cannot possess the authority to accuse you? Thus the one who does not look toward vanities is not troubled; for whoever looks toward them is troubled, and very vainly indeed.

What is it to gather wealth except vanity? For it is altogether vain to seek things that perish. But when you have gathered them, how do you know whether you will be permitted to possess them?

242. Is it not vain for a merchant to travel day and night in order to accumulate heaps of treasure, gather merchandise, be troubled about the price lest he sell for less than he bought, and watch the prices of different places—only for jealousy arising from his notorious trading to stir up robbers against him, or, while seeking profit and unwilling to delay for calmer winds, to suffer shipwreck?

[Note: Several manuscripts read, “so that he may heap up”; some, “so that he may increase.”]

[Note: The edition and a few manuscripts read, “he may pile up merchandise.”]

[Note: One manuscript reads, “lest the love of trade, avenging itself, stir up envy against him.”]

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “suffering shipwreck at sea”; one, “falling into death.”]

243. Is not that man also vainly troubled who, with the greatest labor, accumulates what he does not know to which heir he will leave? Often the luxurious heir tears apart with reckless extravagance what the miser had amassed with the utmost anxiety.

[Note: Some manuscripts and the edition read, “the luxurious heir squanders it.”]

The disgraceful glutton, blind to the present and careless of the future, often swallows what was sought for so long in a kind of whirlpool. Often, too, the heir one had hoped for acquires the envy attached to the inheritance received and, by dying quickly, transfers to strangers the advantages of the succession he had entered upon.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “he acquires the envy of the inheritance divided among them.”]

244. Why, then, do you weave a spider’s web in vain, a thing empty and fruitless, and hang up, as it were, useless nets of accumulated wealth? Even if wealth flows in, it is of no benefit; indeed, it strips you of the image of God and clothes you with the image of the earthly.

[Note: Compare, if you wish, what is said here with what appears in volume I, book IV of *On the Interpellation of Job*, no. 24, and in the *Exposition of Psalm XXXVIII*, no. 27. Apart from these two passages, to which the subject itself shows that Ambrose was referring, he also mentions imperial images elsewhere, for example in book VI of the *Hexaemeron*, chapter 9, no. 57, and in Sermon 10 of the *Exposition of Psalm CXVIII*, no. 25. This is not surprising, for it is certain that Roman emperors were accustomed to be honored with no other form of homage more ostentatious. To say nothing of the small images that some private individuals carried with them and, producing them, used to frighten those who threatened them with harm, as Cornelius Tacitus records in book III of the *Annals*, it can be gathered from many ancient monuments that the emperors—especially after they had recently been proclaimed or had won some notable victory—were customarily honored with golden or silver statues, or statues made of some other precious material, erected not only in the cities where the imperial seat was located and in private and public buildings, but also sent to more distant provinces. See Zosimus, *History*, book IV; Libanius, Letter 841, to Severus; and what we noted in the preceding volume, p. 1095.]

If someone possesses the image of a tyrant, is he not liable to condemnation? You remove the image of the eternal Emperor and erect in yourself the image of death. Rather, cast out from the city of your soul the image of the devil and raise up the image of Christ. Let this image shine in you and in your city—that is, let it shine in your soul—and let it erase the images of vices.

Concerning these David says: “Lord, in your city you will bring their images to nothing” (Ps. LXXII, 20). For when the Lord has depicted Jerusalem according to his own image, then every image of the adversaries is erased.

CHAPTER L

Levites must be especially alien to earthly desires. What their virtues are according to the Apostle, and how much chastity is required of them; likewise, their dignity and office, for which the primary virtues are necessary. These virtues were not unknown to philosophers, but they erred in their arrangement. Some things are according to nature and duty in themselves, yet because of accompanying circumstances become contrary to duty. From this is inferred how many qualities the dignity of the Levites demands. What follows is an exposition of the words of Moses blessing the tribe of Levi.

245. If even the people themselves have been instructed and trained by the Lord’s Gospel to despise wealth, how much more ought you Levites, whose portion is God, not to be held by earthly desires? For when Moses divided the earthly possession among the people, the Lord excluded the Levites from participation in earthly property, because he himself was to be their portion of inheritance (Num. XVIII, 23). Hence David says: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and my cup” (Ps. XV, 5).

[Note: The same interpretation appears in volume I, column 210, no. 11, and more fully in column 1056, no. 4.]

Therefore the Levite himself is called “mine” or “for me.” Great, then, is his office, so that the Lord says of him: “He is mine”; or, as he said to Peter concerning the stater found in the fish’s mouth: “You shall give it for me and for yourself” (Matt. XVII, 26).

[Note: Two manuscripts read, “as sharers in eternal possession,” but less appropriately.]

Hence, when the Apostle had said that a bishop ought to be sober, chaste, respectable, hospitable, able to teach, not greedy, not quarrelsome, and ruling his own household well, he added: “Likewise deacons must be serious, not double-tongued, not addicted to much wine, not pursuing dishonest gain, holding the mystery of the faith with a pure conscience” (1 Tim. III, 8). “And let these also first be tested, and then let them serve, having no accusation against them.”

246. We see what qualities are required of us: that the minister of the Lord be abstinent from wine and supported by a good reputation not only among the faithful but also among those who are outside.

[Note: Several manuscripts read, “but also among unbelievers,” that is, those who are outside.]

For the public estimation of our actions and works ought to bear witness to them, lest the office suffer dishonor; so that whoever sees a minister of the altar adorned with appropriate virtues may praise the author and revere the Lord who has such servants. The praise of the Lord is present where the possession is clean and the discipline of the household innocent.

247. What shall I say of chastity, when only one marriage is permitted, and a marriage repeated is not allowed? Therefore even within marriage there is a law not to repeat the marriage and not to enter into union with a second wife.

[Note: Cicero, On Duties, book I, p. 368, line 8: “But this age must especially be kept from lust,” etc. Because of Ambrose’s words, the Magdeburg Centuriators, century IV, chapter 10, accused our Doctor of seeming to condemn second marriages. They either thought that the words referred to Christians generally and thus failed to perceive the author’s meaning, or understood them as referring only to clerics, as they truly must be understood; in that case the accusation falls not upon Ambrose alone but upon the whole Church. For the impediment of digamy to sacred orders is the most ancient of all, having been established in the Apostle’s commands to Timothy and Titus. It may seem astonishing that this has been understood in this way not only by heterodox writers but also by certain Catholics, as though sacred ministers were forbidden nothing except the simultaneous use of several wives. As if such polygamy had ever been permitted in the Church even to laymen! There is no need to linger in refuting an error decisively overthrown by the entire succession of ecclesiastical tradition.

There is, however, another matter that divided the ancient Doctors into differing opinions: whether a man who had one wife before baptism and took another after baptism was bound by the law of digamy. Ambrose affirms this here and in his letter to the Vercellenses; Jerome, however, denies it in book I against Jovinian, in Letter 83 to Oceanus, and in his commentary on Titus I. The former view was followed by his most faithful disciple Augustine, *On the Good of Marriage*, chapter 18, no. 21; by Innocent I in his letter to Macedonius, preserved in the collection of canon law edited by Quesnel; and also by Leo I in two letters, one to Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica, and the other to the metropolitan bishop of Illyricum. The decision of these great pontiffs subsequently prevailed throughout the Western Church, with one or two exceptions.

There are learned men who think that Jerome’s opinion prevailed in the East, relying chiefly on the annotations of Zonaras and Balsamon on canon 17 of the Apostles, which they themselves openly believe to favor Jerome. Yet that canon makes no mention of a marriage entered into before baptism. Even if we grant that these authors—who speak not of marriage but of sins committed before the sacrament of regeneration—held the opinion attributed to them, we shall insist that they testify only to what they themselves think, not to the position of the entire Eastern Church.

Who could believe that the Doctor just mentioned, if he had been supported by so many auxiliary forces, would have responded so timidly in his first *Apology against Rufinus* that, although in his reply to Oceanus he nearly classed the opposing opinion among the heresy of the Cainites, in the work cited above, lowering his tone, he wrote: “When asked by the brothers what we thought, we replied without prejudging anyone, allowing each to follow what he wished, and without overturning another’s decision by our own judgment”? Nor, after previously asserting that the whole world was full of such ordinations, would he here restrict his words to certain priests.

Francis of Messana accomplishes nothing when he attempts to reconcile this disagreement between Ambrose and Jerome by means of certain metaphysical distinctions; so obvious a discrepancy cannot be removed by subtleties. Moreover, we can scarcely find another Father older than Ambrose who wrote about this digamy. It is not sufficiently clear on what grounds Spencaeus traced this question back to Tertullian, since that same Father, in book 11 of *On Monogamy*, did not wish a digamy contracted with a husband before baptism to prejudice widows.]

What could be said of chastity, when only one union is permitted, and a repeated union is forbidden? There is therefore, even within marriage itself, a law not to repeat marriage or enter into a second union. Many people find it astonishing that even a marriage repeated before baptism should create an impediment to election to office and to ordination, since sins ordinarily cease to be obstacles when they have been forgiven through the sacrament of washing.

But we must understand that guilt can be forgiven by baptism, whereas a law cannot be abolished. In marriage there is not guilt but law. Whatever belongs to guilt is therefore released in baptism; whatever belongs to law in marriage is not dissolved. How can someone encourage widowhood who has himself entered into marriages repeatedly?

248. You know that the ministry must be presented without offense and undefiled, and must not be violated by any marital intercourse. You received the grace of sacred ministry with bodies intact, with incorrupt chastity, and even apart from marital relations.

[Note: This passage of Ambrose concerning clerical continence is so clear and explicit that the Centuriators, in the century and chapter cited above, were forced to resort to their usual devices—namely, to accuse the author himself of false doctrine. Yet here the holy Bishop is not acting as a legislator imposing a new yoke upon the necks of clerics; he is bearing witness to an established and long-standing custom. How universal and firm that custom was is sufficiently shown by the fact that only in the more secluded places, where vices habitually seek refuge, were there people who attempted to violate it.

Furthermore, these men did not cite in their defense any authority from the New Covenant, any canon of a council, or the practice of particular Churches, but only the custom of the Old Testament. The holy Doctor admirably dismantles this covering of incontinent clerics. Compare also what he argues on this same subject in his letter to the Vercellenses.]

I have not passed over this because in many more secluded places men, while exercising the ministry or even the priesthood, fathered children and defended this as an ancient practice, since the sacrifice was offered at intervals of days. Yet even the people were purified for two or three days so that they might approach the sacrifice clean, as we read in the Old Testament (Exod. XIX, 10), and they washed their garments.

If there was such observance in the figure, how much greater should it be in the reality? Learn, priest and Levite, what it means to wash your garments, so that you may present a clean body for the celebration of the sacraments. If the people were forbidden to approach their offering without washing their garments, do you, unwashed in mind as well as body, dare to plead for others and dare to minister to others?

[Note: The edition, together with several manuscripts, reads “to offer praise for others”; in many other and better manuscripts the preposition is omitted. Again, where the old edition and all the manuscripts read, “Behold, I choose the Levites,” etc., only the Roman edition reads: “Behold, I have taken the Levites in the midst of the children of Israel; they shall be their redemptions, and they shall be mine. For from the day when I struck down the firstborn in the land of Egypt, I sanctified every firstborn in all Israel.” The sacred pages agree sufficiently with us, except that they expand the final portion, which Ambrose gives in abbreviated form, as follows: “For every firstborn is mine. On the day when I struck down every firstborn in the land of Egypt, I sanctified every firstborn in Israel for myself.”]

249. The Levites have no insignificant office. Concerning them the Lord says: “Behold, I choose the Levites from among the children of Israel in place of every firstborn who opens the womb among the children of Israel; they shall be their redemptions, and they shall be mine. For I sanctified the firstborn for myself in the land of Egypt” (Num. III, 12–13).
