We have learned that the Levites are not counted among the rest, but are preferred to all, chosen from among all and sanctified, like the firstborn fruits and first fruits assigned to the Lord, in which there is the fulfillment of vows and the redemption of sins.

“You shall not count them,” he says, “among the children of Israel; but you shall appoint the Levites over the tabernacle of testimony, over all its vessels, and over everything that is in it. They shall carry the tabernacle and all its vessels, and they shall minister in it. Around the tabernacle they shall pitch their camps. When it moves forward, the Levites shall take down the tabernacle; and when the camp is established, they shall set up the tabernacle again. Any stranger who approaches shall be put to death” (Num. I, 49 ff.).

[Note: Erasmus in the margin and Gill in the text, together with several manuscripts, read, “its vessels, the altar, and over”; the Roman edition reads, “its vessels, and over.”]

250. You, then, have been chosen from the entire number of the children of Israel, counted among the sacred fruits as a firstborn, placed in charge of the tabernacle so that you may stand guard in the camps of holiness and faith. If a stranger approaches them, he will die. You have been placed there to cover the ark of the covenant.

For not everyone sees the heights of the mysteries, because they are covered by the Levites, lest those who ought not see should see, or those who cannot preserve them should take them. Moses, finally, saw spiritual circumcision, but covered it, so that he might prescribe circumcision in a sign. He saw the unleavened bread of truth and sincerity; he saw the passion of the Lord. He covered the unleavened bread of truth with bodily unleavened bread, and covered the passion of the Lord with the sacrifice of a lamb or calf.

[Note: Two manuscripts read, “so that the mystery of his faith might be preserved for the good Levite under its covering”; one reads, “and the good Levite . . . preserved the coverings”; the others agree with us, except for a few and those written by a younger hand, which, together with the edition, read: “And the good Levites . . . under this covering.”]

And the good Levites preserved the mystery under the covering of their faith. Do you think that what has been entrusted to you is insignificant? First, that you should see the heights of God, which is wisdom; then, that you should maintain watch for the people, which is justice; that you should defend the camp and guard the tabernacle, which is fortitude; that you should present yourself chaste and sober, which is temperance.

251. These men also, though outsiders, established the principal categories of virtues; [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, Book I, p. 372, line 22: “For since all moral worth … Therefore those duties which arise from fellowship are more agreeable to nature,” etc. Our Ambrose blames the philosophers because they placed justice, which concerns the community and society of human beings, before wisdom, although wisdom’s beginning, or first part, concerns faith and the worship of God. Nevertheless, in this passage Saint Ambrose does not seem to have sufficiently considered Cicero’s teaching. Cicero here places justice before that prudence alone which the Greeks call *phronēsis* (φρόνησις), not before that first of all virtues which the Greeks call *sophia* (σοφία): the knowledge of divine and human matters, which contains the community of gods and human beings, and fellowship between them. Here one sees that the knowledge of divinity and the duties of religion are counted by the Orator as belonging to wisdom. That he orders *phronēsis* to be placed after justice should not seem strange, since he also includes divine worship under justice [Col. 0100C], etc. Indeed, Ambrose himself, above, in chapter 27, subjects piety toward God to justice. But when he elevates the dignity of prudence above justice on the ground that prudence is justice’s foundation—and that Christ is the foundation—this is pious and Christian; yet Cicero, not unreasonably, on p. 372, line 30 and following, concludes that fellowship surpasses all duties in this way: “For,” he says, “considered action follows knowledge and prudence; thus acting thoughtfully is more valuable than thinking prudently.” The disagreement can easily be reconciled if we say that prudence has superiority in origin and necessity, while justice has superiority in dignity and usefulness.]

but they judged the order of fellowship to be higher than that of wisdom; although wisdom is the foundation, and justice is the work that cannot endure unless it has a foundation. The foundation, however, is Christ (1 Cor. 3:11). [Note: Several manuscripts read this way, but we have changed the earlier order, which is less suitable. Immediately afterward, where the printed editions and a few manuscripts read, “since it is the foundation, justice is the work,” etc., others have partly “since it is the foundation, justice’s work,” and partly “since the foundation is justice, it is the work”; three have “and it is the work which,” etc.]

252. Faith, therefore, is first—the faith that belongs to wisdom—as Solomon says, following his father: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Prov. 9:10). And the Law says: “You shall love the Lord your God; you shall love your neighbor” (Deut. 6:5). [Note: Erasmus and later editions, together with a few manuscripts, read “which is wisdom.”] For it is admirable that you should devote your grace and services to the fellowship of the human race. [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, Book I, p. 373: “Within the community itself there are degrees of duties … so that the first are owed to the immortal gods,” etc.] But the first moral obligation is this: that what you possess most precious—namely, your mind, than which you have nothing more excellent—you should dedicate to God. When you have paid your debt to the Creator, you may devote your works to benevolence and assistance to human beings, and bring aid to their needs, whether with money, service, or any other gift. This extends widely in your ministry: with money, so that you may help; by discharging a debt, so that you may release one who is bound; with service, so that you may undertake to preserve what the person who entrusted it fears to lose.

253. It is therefore a duty to preserve and return a deposit. [Note: Ibid., p. 354, line 41: “But circumstances often arise when those things which most …,” etc.] Yet sometimes a change is required, whether because of circumstances or necessity, so that it is not a duty to return what you have received. For example, if an open enemy should demand back money from someone who was aiding the barbarians against his country; or if you were to return something to a person while someone else was present to extort it; or if you were to return a sword to a madman when he could not keep it safe; or if you did not refuse a deposited sword to a person out of his mind, with which he would kill himself—is it not contrary to duty to have returned it? If you knowingly receive goods acquired by theft, so that the person who lost them may be defrauded, is that not contrary to duty?

254. It is also sometimes contrary to duty (Distinction 22, question 4, chapter “Est etiam”) to fulfill a promise and keep an oath. [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, Book I, line 47: “A promise can also arise,” etc.] Thus Herod, who swore that he would give Herodias’s daughter whatever she asked, granted John’s death so as not to break his promise (Matt. 14:7 ff.). For what shall I say of Jephthah, who sacrificed his daughter, who had first come out to meet him as he returned victorious, in order to fulfill the vow he had made: that he would offer to God whatever first came out to meet him (Judg. 11:39)? It would have been better never to promise anything of the kind than to fulfill a promise by parricide. [Note: The final Paris editions read, “whatever she was going to ask.”]

255. You are not unaware how much deliberation this requires. And therefore the Levite who is to guard the sacristy is chosen, [Note: Saint Ambrose had said above, in chapter 44, “another is more suitable for the sacristy.” These words have caused no small difficulty to distinguished men who either had not read this passage or did not remember having read it. Some thought that the custody of the sacristy was at times entrusted even to those who had received no ecclesiastical order, not even the lowest; others, although they did not think that the name denoted an order distinct from others, nevertheless maintained that this duty was customarily entrusted to subdeacons or doorkeepers. Since by “sacristy” the secretarium, or sacristy, and especially the sanctuary are understood, some might object to canon 20 of the Council of Laodicea, by which subdeacons are forbidden both entry into those places and contact with the sacred vessels. It could nevertheless be answered, with Balsamon and Zonaras, that entry into the sacristy was forbidden only when the sacred mysteries were being celebrated there, and contact with consecrated vessels only when they contained Christ’s blood or were being carried in processions—if this passage did not settle the matter in favor of those who wish the care of the sacristy to have been assigned to deacons. Hence they teach that the sacristy was the same as what the Greeks call the *diakonikon* (διακονικόν) and *skeuophylakion* (σκευοφυλάκιον), although I find that not only deacons but also presbyters and chorepiscopi were appointed to this office at Constantinople. The sacristy was also the same as what in the Eastern Church was called a *martyrion*, whether one understands by this a cemetery situated outside the basilicas, where the bodies of martyrs were buried; the basilicas themselves, which were built only over the relics of martyrs; or the sanctuary itself, and even the holy altar, beneath which the sacred ashes of the saints were deposited. This was properly called the confession and memorial of the martyrs. See further Haller, *On Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, chapter “On the Number of Ecclesiastical Orders”; Morinus, *On the Sacred Orders*, Exercise II, chapter 1; Cardinal Bona, *On Liturgical Matters*, Book I, chapter 24; Thaumassinus, Part I of *Ecclesiastical Discipline*, Book I, chapter 36; and the learned Cangius, under the word “Sacrarium.” Moreover, there is no doubt that our Saint wished this responsibility to be entrusted chiefly to deacons, so that they might guard the holy place with greater authority from violation, especially from those profane banquets of which we have already said something in the book *On Elijah and Fasting*, and perhaps will add more later when the opportunity arises.]

so that he may not be deceived in counsel, may not abandon faith, may not fear death, and may do nothing immoderate, so that in his very appearance he may display gravity; [Note: Cicero, Book I, p. 357, line 10: “Pericles was right … But, Sophocles, a magistrate ought to have not only restrained hands but also restrained eyes.”] and he should be one who possesses not only a restrained mind [Col. 0101B] but also restrained eyes, lest even an accidental encounter violate the countenance of sobriety; for it is written: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5:28). Thus adultery is committed not only through the pollution of the deed but also through the intention of the gaze.

256. These requirements may seem great and excessively severe, but they are not excessive in a great office, since the Levites enjoy such favor that Moses said of them in his blessings: “Give to Levi his men, give to Levi his manifest ones, give to Levi the lot of his vote, and his truth to his holy man, whom they tested in temptations and cursed at the waters of contradiction. He said to his father and mother, ‘I do not know you’; he did not acknowledge his brothers, and he disowned his sons. He has kept your words and observed your covenant” (Deut. 33:8 ff.). [Note: All the editions read “his true men”; the manuscripts, on the contrary, read “his men.” It is possible that later manuscripts followed an older exemplar in which *i* had been written for *e*, as we have observed in Thuaneus, who teaches that for more than a thousand years people wrote forms such as *docit*, *studit*, *quodlibit*, *mercidem*, and similar words. Nevertheless, it is more probable that “his men” is genuine, and that the editors restored *viros* (“men”) so that it might serve almost as a synonym for *manifestos* (“manifest ones”), since the Septuagint has only: “Give to Levi his manifest ones” (Δότε Λευὶ δήλους αὐτοῦ), “and truth,” etc. You may understand that this conjecture is false from the fact that when Saint Ambrose, in his book *On the Blessings of the Patriarchs*, chapter 3, wrote only, “Give to Levi the lot of his portion and truth,” etc., Flaminius Nobilius inferred that the holy Doctor had read *klērous* (κλήρους) instead of *dēlous* (δήλους), whereas this passage shows that he read both. The Hebrew text, however, has: “Your perfections and illuminations to your pious man.” The Vulgate: “Your perfection and your doctrine to your holy man.” The Chaldean paraphrase: “With perfection and light you clothed the man who was found holy before you.”]

257. Those, then, are his men and his manifest ones who have no deceit in their hearts and conceal no fraud, but guard his words and ponder them in their hearts, as Mary also pondered them (Luke 2:19); who do not consider their own relatives preferable to their duty; who hate violators of chastity and avenge the injury done to modesty; who know the proper times for duties—what is greater, what is lesser, what is suited to each occasion—and follow only what is honorable. [Note: Cicero, Book I of *On Duties*, p. 372, line 20: “But among the very things that are honorable,” etc.] Indeed, when two honorable courses are before them, they should judge that the more honorable is to be preferred. These men are rightly blessed.

28. If, therefore, anyone makes God’s just ordinances manifest, let him place incense: [Note: Several manuscripts read this way, and some editions agree, except that in the second part they offer a slightly altered reading, “and let him place incense.” The Thuaneus manuscript and several others of good antiquity read, “let him openly place the righteous deeds of God as incense.” This is not at all bad if interpreted as follows: “If, removing all dissimulation, he offers the righteous deeds of God as incense, or as a kind of incense.” Again, several more numerous and older manuscripts end the first book after the word “find”; others, as well as the editions, add “with him”; the Bigot manuscript has “with the God who lives and reigns”; four manuscripts have “with you who live and reign,” etc.] “Bless, Lord, his strength; accept the works of his hands” (Deut. 33:11), so that he may find the grace of prophetic blessing with him who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 0103]

### CHAPTER I

[Col. 0103A]

The blessed life is acquired through moral excellence, since the Christian, scorning human glory and favor, desires that his works please God alone.

1. In the preceding book we discussed the duties that we judged to be consistent with moral excellence, in which everyone has agreed that the blessed life is situated—the life that Scripture calls eternal life. [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, Book II, p. 373, line 45: “How duties are derived from moral excellence … I believe I explained in the preceding book.”] So great is the splendor of moral excellence that tranquility of conscience and the security of innocence produce the blessed life. [Note: The final Paris editions read, “we judged to belong to moral excellence; we were by no means uncertain that it was situated,” etc.] And therefore, just as the rising sun conceals the light of the moon’s sphere and of the other stars, so the radiance of moral excellence, when it shines with true and incorruptible beauty, overshadows the other things that are considered good according to bodily pleasure or according to the world, which appear bright and splendid.

2. Truly blessed is the person who is not judged by the opinions of others but experiences blessedness through inward perceptions, as his own judge. For he neither demands popular approval as a reward nor fears it as punishment. Thus, the less he pursues glory, the more he rises above it. For those who pursue glory receive it as the reward of the present, a shadow of future things that hinders eternal life; as it is written in the Gospel: “Truly I tell you, they have received their reward” (Matt. 6:2)—namely, those who, as though a trumpet were sounding, delight in publicizing their generosity toward the poor. The same is true of the fasting they undertake for display: “They have,” he says, “their reward.”

3. It is therefore characteristic of moral excellence either to show mercy or to fast in secret, so that you may appear to seek your reward from your God alone, and not also from human beings. For the one who seeks it from human beings has his reward; but the one who seeks it from God has eternal life—which only the author of eternity can bestow, as in the saying: “Truly I tell you, today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43). Hence Scripture more explicitly called the eternal life that which is blessed, so that the matter might not be left to human opinion but entrusted to divine judgment. [Note: The editions read, “so that it might be left to be judged”; the manuscripts, “so that the matter might be left to be judged”—with the implied addition, “the matter.”]

### CHAPTER II

The various opinions of philosophers concerning blessedness; it is first proved from the Gospel that blessedness consists in the knowledge of God and the pursuit of good works; then, so that it may not seem to have been borrowed from the philosophers, it is confirmed by the testimonies of the prophets.

4. Thus some philosophers placed the blessed life in freedom from pain, such as Hieronymus; others in knowledge of things, such as Herillus, who, hearing Aristotle and Theophrastus wonderfully praise knowledge of things, made knowledge alone, as though it were the highest good, his supreme principle, although they had praised it as a good, not as the only good. [Note: What is said here about the various philosophical opinions concerning natural blessedness is taken from Cicero—not from *On Duties*, but from other philosophical works of his, such as the surviving books of the *Academic Questions*, the *On Ends of Good and Evil* (especially Book V), and the five books of the *Tusculan Disputations*, especially the last. The similarity of expressions, doctrine, and often even order between those works and what is presented in this and the next two chapters is so great that there can be no doubt that Saint Ambrose had them in view.]

Others identified it with pleasure, such as Epicurus. Others, such as Callipho and, after him, Diodorus, interpreted it in such a way that one associated moral excellence with pleasure and the other with freedom from pain, since without moral excellence the blessed life cannot exist. The Stoic Zeno held that the only and highest good is what is honorable. Aristotle, Theophrastus, and the other Peripatetics held that the blessed life consists in virtue—that is, in moral excellence—but asserted that its blessedness is also completed by bodily and external goods. [Note: Some editions and a few manuscripts read, “by bodily pleasures and external goods”; several others, “by excellent bodily pleasures,” etc. But the Thuaneus manuscript, two Vatican manuscripts, two Laon manuscripts, and several others read, “by bodily and external goods.” This is best, since “bodily” agrees with “goods,” as is expressed more clearly below. A little later, where the editions read, “the blessed life in knowledge,” one manuscript reads, “in conjunction,” etc.; all the others read, “eternal life.” This must be the correct reading, as is shown by the scriptural testimonies immediately cited and by what is said below: “Faith therefore possesses eternal life.” From the whole passage it is readily understood that the eternal life spoken of here is not the life that will follow the resurrection, but the life that the righteous live even during this present light; hence it is called eternal life that which is blessed, as is explained near the end of chapter 1. The editions therefore did not err in meaning.]

5. But divine Scripture placed eternal life in the knowledge of divinity and in the fruit of good works. Finally, the Gospel supplies testimony for both claims. Concerning knowledge, the Lord Jesus said: “This is eternal life: that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3). And concerning works he replied: “Everyone who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or fields for my name’s sake will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life” (Matt. 19:29).

6. But lest anyone think this to be a recent teaching, and that it was treated by the philosophers before it was proclaimed in the Gospel—for the philosophers were earlier than the Gospel, namely Aristotle and Theophrastus, or Zeno and Hieronymus, but later than the prophets—let them consider how long before the name of philosopher was heard both elements were clearly expressed through the mouth of holy David. For it is written: “Blessed is the one whom you instruct, O Lord, and whom you teach from your law” (Ps. 93:12). We also read elsewhere: “Blessed is the man who fears the Lord; he greatly delights in his commandments” (Ps. 112:1). We have spoken of knowledge, whose reward he recalled to be the fruit of eternity, the Prophet adding that in the house of the one who fears the Lord, or who has been instructed in the Law and delights in the divine commandments, “glory and riches are in his house, and his righteousness endures forever and ever” (ibid., 3). [Note: Many more and better manuscripts read this way; others, as well as the editions, read, “which are in his house … ‘Glory,’ he says, ‘and riches are in his house,’” etc.]

In the same psalm he also added, concerning works, that the reward of eternal life belongs to the righteous man. Finally he says: “Blessed is the man who shows mercy and lends; he will order his words with judgment, because he will not be shaken forever. The righteous will be held in everlasting remembrance” (ibid., 5–6). And below: “He has distributed; he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures forever” (ibid., 9).

7. Faith therefore possesses eternal life, because it is a good foundation; good deeds possess it as well, because the righteous man is proved both by words and by actions. For if he is practiced in speech but idle in works, he refutes his wisdom by his deeds. [Note: The editions and several manuscripts read, “he rejects it by his deeds.”] And it is more serious to know what one ought to do and not to have done what one has recognized ought to be done. Conversely, to be energetic in works but faithless in disposition is like trying to raise beautiful rooflines upon a defective foundation: the more you build, the more collapses, because good works cannot endure without the protection of faith. An insecure mooring in a harbor punctures a ship, and sandy ground quickly gives way and cannot bear the weight of the building placed upon it. The fullness of reward is therefore where there is perfection of virtues and a certain equality of sobriety in deeds and words.

### CHAPTER III

The definition of blessedness drawn from Scripture is examined, and it is shown that nothing is added to it because of external goods, nor taken away because of misfortunes.

8. Since the claim that knowledge of things alone suffices has been rejected—either as empty according to the superfluous disputes of philosophy, or as a half-complete opinion—let us consider how divine Scripture resolves the question concerning which we see philosophical discussions to be so numerous, complicated, and confused. [Note: Cicero, in *On the Ends of Good and Evil* and in the *Tusculan Disputations*, acknowledges that there are so many opinions concerning the natural blessedness of this life that, to avoid confusion, he is compelled to reduce them to a certain order and a number of headings. Saint Augustine, *City of God*, Book XIX, chapter 1, writes that Varro reported that they could be reduced to as many as 288. This same chapter, as well as the two immediately following it, should be consulted, since it can add considerable light to what Ambrose teaches here.]

For Scripture asserts that nothing is good except what is honorable, and judges virtue to be blessed in every condition of things: it is neither increased by bodily or external goods nor diminished by adversity. Nothing is so blessed, moreover, as what is free from sin, full of innocence, and filled with the grace of God. For it is written: “Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the wicked, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of pestilence; but his delight was in the law of the Lord” (Ps. 1:1–2). And elsewhere: “Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord” (Ps. 119:1).

9. Innocence and knowledge therefore make a person blessed. We observed above that the blessedness of eternal life is also the reward of good works (above, chapter 2). It remains, then, that, once the support of pleasure and the fear of pain have been rejected—the former as broken and soft, the latter as unmanned and weak—we should show that the blessed life stands firm even amid pains. [Note: The editions, with one or two manuscripts, read, “it despises … it demonstrates”; many manuscripts, in large number and agreement, read, “it despises … it demonstrates.” This is not unsuitable, provided that these two words are referred to the Scripture mentioned in the preceding section.] This can easily be taught when we read: “Blessed are you when they revile you and persecute you and say every evil thing against you on account of righteousness. Rejoice and exult, because your reward is great in heaven. For so they persecuted the prophets who were before you” (Matt. 5:11–12). And elsewhere: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him take up his cross and follow me” (Matt. 16:24). [Note: The editions read, “whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself and take up”; the manuscripts read, “whoever wishes to come after me, let him take up.”]

### CHAPTER IV

The same argument—that blessedness is neither diminished nor increased by external circumstances—is illustrated by examples from antiquity.

10. Blessedness therefore exists even amid pains, which virtue, full of sweetness, suppresses and restrains, being itself rich in its inward resources, whether in conscience or in grace. [Note: Some manuscripts read, “either for steadfastness,” etc.] For was Moses not greatly blessed when, surrounded by the armies of the Egyptians and shut in by the sea, he found through the waves a path on foot for himself and the people of his ancestors by his pious merits (Exod. 14:13)? When was he stronger than at that moment, when, surrounded by the gravest dangers, he did not despair of salvation but demanded triumph?

11. What of Aaron? When did he consider himself more blessed than when he stood between the living and the dead and, by placing himself in the way, stopped death from passing from the corpses to the ranks of the living (Num. 16:48)? What shall I say of the boy Daniel, who was so wise that, among lions enraged by hunger, he was not broken by fear of any bestial savagery? He was so free from fear that he could feast without dreading that the beasts might be provoked to feed by his example (Dan. 14).

12. There is therefore virtue even in suffering, which offers itself the sweetness of a good conscience; and this proves that suffering does not diminish the pleasure of virtue. Just as suffering causes no loss of blessedness to virtue, so bodily pleasure or the abundance of material advantages adds nothing to it. Concerning these the Apostle beautifully says: “What was gain to me, these things I counted as loss for Christ” (Phil. 3:7–8). And he added: “For his sake I have counted everything as loss, and regard it as refuse, so that I may gain Christ” (Heb. 11:26).

13. Finally, Moses considered the treasures of the Egyptians to be his loss, and preferred the reproach of the Lord’s cross. He was neither rich when he abounded in money nor later poor when he lacked food—unless perhaps someone should think him less blessed at that time when, in the desert, daily nourishment was lacking for him and his people. But what no one would dare deny was the highest good and blessedness was supplied to him from heaven: manna, that is, the bread of angels; and a daily rain of meat overflowed for the feasts of the entire people (Exod. 16:13 ff.).

14. The holy Elijah also lacked bread for food, if it were sought [or: if one looked for it] (1 Kings 17:6); but it did not seem to be lacking because it was not sought. Thus, through the daily service of ravens, bread was brought in the morning and meat in the evening. Was he therefore less blessed because he was poor with respect to himself? Not at all. Rather, he was more blessed because he was rich toward God. He preferred to be rich for others rather than for himself, as was the case with him who, during a famine, asked food from a widow, yet would grant that her jar of flour would not fail for three years and six months, and that the widow’s vessel of oil would suffice and provide for her daily needs (ibid., 14). Rightly Peter wished to be there where he saw these men (Matt. 17:4). Rightly they appeared on the mountain with Christ in glory, because he himself became poor although he was rich.

15. Riches therefore provide no assistance toward the blessed life. The Lord clearly demonstrated this in the Gospel, saying: “Blessed are the poor, for yours is the kingdom of God. Blessed are those who now hunger and thirst, for they will be satisfied. Blessed are those who now weep, for they will laugh” (Luke 6:20 ff.). [Note: Some manuscripts read, “Blessed are the poor in spirit”; in the following verse the editions alone read, “and thirst for righteousness.”] Thus it has been most clearly declared that poverty, hunger, and suffering—which are considered evils—not only do not hinder the blessed life but even assist it.

### CHAPTER V

What are considered good things are often an impediment to the blessed life, while what are considered evils provide material for virtue; this is confirmed by examples of blessedness and by other examples.

16. But it is also clear from the Lord’s judgment that those things which appear good—riches, satiety, and joy free from pain—are harmful to the fruit of blessedness, since it is said: “Woe to you who are rich, for you have received your consolation! Woe to you who are filled, for you will hunger” (ibid., 24 ff.)! And woe to those who laugh, for they will mourn. Thus bodily pleasures or external goods are not merely no assistance toward the blessed life but are even a loss. [Note: Four manuscripts read, “bodily pleasures”; other manuscripts more suitably read, “bodily or external goods,” as above, p. 71.]

17. Hence Naboth was blessed even when he was stoned by the rich man (1 Kings 21:13), because, poor and powerless against royal wealth, he was rich only in devotion and religion, and would not exchange the inheritance of his father’s vineyard for royal money. He was therefore perfected because he defended the rights of his ancestors with his own blood. Hence also Ahab was wretched, even by his own judgment, because he had caused a poor man to be killed in order to possess his vineyard.

18. It is certain that virtue alone is the sole and highest good, and that it alone is sufficient for the fruit of the blessed life; that life is made blessed not by external or bodily goods but by virtue alone, through which eternal life is acquired. For the blessed life is the fruit of the present; eternal life, however, is the hope of the future.

19. Yet there are some who think the blessed life impossible in this body, so weak and fragile, in which one must necessarily suffer anguish, pain, lamentation, and sickness. [Note: Some manuscripts read, “to be distressed by pain, to lament.”] As though I were saying that the blessed life consists in bodily exultation, and not in the height of wisdom, the sweetness of conscience, and the sublimity of virtue! For blessedness does not consist in being subject to suffering but in conquering suffering, nor in being broken by the temporal movement of pain. [Note: Some Paris editions read, “through fear of pain”; others, together with the manuscripts, “through the movement of pain.” Immediately afterward, where all the editions and two manuscripts read, “fearing that it might happen,” several manuscripts have “that punishment might happen,” incorrectly; others, “nor that punishment might happen here.” The latter is better, but best of all is the reading of the Thuaneus manuscript and many others: “Suppose it should happen”—that is, “grant, assume, imagine”—words serving a rhetorical concession.]

20. Suppose that these things, which are said to bear heavily upon the force of pain, should occur: blindness, exile, hunger, the violation of a daughter, and the loss of children. Who would deny that Isaac was blessed, though he did not see in his old age and bestowed blessings on his descendants (Gen. 27:1 ff.)? Was Jacob not blessed, although he fled from his homeland, endured exile as a hired shepherd, lamented that his daughter’s chastity had been violated, and suffered hunger (Gen. 31:1 ff.)? Are those not blessed whose faith receives God’s testimony when it is said: “The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob” (Gen. 34:1 ff.)? Slavery is wretched, but Joseph was not wretched; rather, he was plainly blessed when, placed in slavery, he restrained his mistress’s lust (Gen. 39:8 ff.). What shall I say of holy David, who lamented the deaths of three sons [Note: The manuscripts agree almost unanimously in this reading; the editions, however, add, “the death of Amnon and Absalom, and of the little child born from her who had been Uriah’s [lacuna] of his daughter Tamar.”] and, harder still, the incest of his daughter (2 Sam. 18:33)? How could he not be blessed, from whose succession the author of blessedness arose, the one who made many blessed? For “blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed” (John 20:29). They too were in a condition of weakness, but they became strong through weakness. What was more grievous for holy Job than the burning of his house, the sudden death of his ten children, and bodily pains? Was he therefore less blessed than if he had not endured these things, through which he was tested all the more (Job 1:14 ff.; 2:7 ff.)?

21. Grant, nevertheless, that there was some bitterness in those things, and that the strength of his spirit did not conceal the pain. For I would not deny that the sea is deep because its shores are shallow, nor that the sky is bright because it is sometimes covered with clouds, nor that the earth is fertile because in some places it is barren gravel, nor that the crops are flourishing because they commonly contain sterile oats mixed among them. [Note: *Glarea* means sandy earth, filled with small stones and pebbles. Virgil, *Georgics* II, verse 212:

“Nor indeed does the gravel of the sloping field, though barren,  
scarcely provide low-growing cassia and dew for the bees.”]

Likewise, suppose that the harvest of a blessed conscience is interrupted by some bitter pain. If anything adverse or bitter should happen to the whole sheaf of the blessed life, is it not hidden like sterile oats, or is not the bitterness of darnel covered over by the sweetness of grain? [Note: Thus all the editions and most manuscripts; some others read partly “a blessed conscience,” and partly “to be the conscience of the blessed.” Where the same editions and a few manuscripts read “with bitter pain,” more manuscripts read “with a heap,” some “a blessed conscience,” and some “to be the pain of the blessed.” The reading of the Thuaneus manuscript and the others is more suitable: “with bitter pain.”] But now let us proceed to the matters proposed. [Note: Cicero, Book II, p. 374, line 49: “But now let us proceed to our established principles.”]

## CHAPTER VI

Concerning usefulness—not the profitable kind, but the just and honorable kind—which is also pursued through losses; and it is divided into bodily usefulness and usefulness connected with piety.

22. In the preceding book we made the division in such a way [Note: Ibid.: “Since five methods have been proposed for pursuing duty, two of which belong to honor,” etc.] that moral excellence and propriety came first, from which duties were derived, and usefulness second. And just as we said in the first case that there is a certain distinction between moral excellence and propriety, a distinction more easily understood than explained, so, when we discuss usefulness, it seems necessary to consider what is more useful.

23. We do not calculate usefulness by estimating financial profit, but by the acquisition of piety, as the Apostle says: “Piety is useful for everything, holding promise for the present life and for the life to come” (1 Tim. 4:8). [Note: Ibid., p. 375, line 4: “What is called useful—a word in which custom has slipped,” etc.] Therefore, if we search the divine Scriptures carefully, we often find that what is honorable is called useful: “All things are lawful for me, but not all things are useful” (1 Cor. 6:12). He was speaking above about vices. This, then, is what he means: It is permitted to sin, but it is not proper. Sins are within one’s power, but they are not honorable. It is easy to indulge in luxury, but it is not just. For food is gathered not for God but for the belly.

24. Therefore, since what is useful is also just, it is just that we serve Christ, who redeemed us. Hence those who offered themselves to death for his name are just; unjust are those who turned aside. Of them he says: “What profit is there in my blood?” (Ps. 29:10)—that is, What advantage has my righteousness brought? Hence also the words concerning them: “Let us bind the just man, because he is useless to us” (Isa. 3:10)—that is, the unjust man who reproves, condemns, and corrects us. This may also be applied to the avarice of wicked men, which is close to perfidy, as we read in the case of Judas the betrayer: through devotion to avarice and desire for money, he incurred and fell into the snare of betrayal.

[Note: An allusion is made to what is said in the same place, p. 376, line 48: “Men even submit themselves to another’s rule and power,” and so forth.]

[Note: The editions read: “of whom it is said … while I descend into corruption”; that is, “who …?”]

[Note: Six manuscripts read “that is, to the unjust,” a reading to which a learned man has added the weight of his conjecture. Twenty-eight others and all the editions, however, read “that is, the unjust man.” This is more appropriate: the word “unjust” should be referred not to “us,” but to “useless,” since the holy Doctor is here demonstrating that “useful” is taken for “just,” and conversely “useless” for “unjust.”]

25. We must therefore discuss that usefulness which is full of moral worth, just as the Apostle defined it in these very words: “I say this for your benefit, not to lay a snare for you, but for what is honorable” (1 Cor. 7:35). It is therefore clear that what is honorable is useful, and what is useful honorable; that what is useful is just, and what is just useful.

[Note: All the manuscripts, with the exception of two in which there is some confusion, read: “that what is honorable is useful and just; and that what is useful is honorable and just; and that what is just is useful and honorable.”]

For I am not addressing merchants greedy for profit, but sons; and my discourse is about the Duties which I desire to impress and instill in you, whom I have chosen for the ministry of the Lord, so that what has become deeply rooted and impressed in your minds and conduct through practice and instruction may also be made explicit through speech and discipline.

26. Therefore, since I am going to speak of usefulness, I shall use that prophetic verse: “Incline my heart to your testimonies, and not to avarice” (Ps. 118:36), lest the sound of “usefulness” awaken a desire for money. Indeed, some have: “Incline my heart to your testimonies, and not toward usefulness”—that is, not toward the usefulness that hunts after markets for profit, that has been bent and diverted by human practice toward the pursuit of money.

For common usage calls only that profitable which yields gain. We, however, are speaking of the usefulness that is sought through losses, so that we may gain Christ, whose profit is “godliness with contentment” (1 Tim. 6:6). Great indeed is the profit by which we acquire godliness, which is rich before God—not with fleeting possessions, but with eternal gifts, in which there is not slippery temptation but enduring and perpetual grace.

[Note: Cicero, Book II, p. 375, line 18: “Let piety and holiness render the gods propitious,” and so forth.]

27. There is therefore one usefulness that is bodily, and another that belongs to godliness, as the Apostle distinguished them: “Bodily exercise,” he says, “is useful for a little, but godliness is useful for all things” (1 Tim. 4:8). What is as honorable as integrity? What is as seemly as preserving the body pure, and chastity inviolate and undefiled? What is also more seemly than that a widowed wife should remain faithful to her deceased husband? What is more useful than this, by which the heavenly kingdom is obtained? For there are those who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 19:12).

## CHAPTER VII

That usefulness is the same as moral worth; and that nothing is more useful than affection, which is acquired through gentleness, courtesy, beneficence, justice, and other virtues; as may be understood from the histories of Moses and David; and finally, that faith arises from affection, and affection again from faith.

28. Usefulness is therefore not merely the familiar companion of moral worth; usefulness itself is also identical with moral worth. Thus the one who wished to open the kingdom of heaven to all was seeking not what was useful for himself, but what was useful for everyone. We must therefore establish for ourselves a certain order and series of degrees, proceeding even from familiar and ordinary matters to those that are pre-eminent, so that from the several forms of usefulness we may gather their full benefit.

29. First, let us recognize that nothing is so useful as being loved, and nothing so useless as not being loved; for I consider being hated ruinous and utterly fatal.

[Note: Cicero, Book II, p. 377, line 2: “Of all things, nothing is better suited to preserving power than being loved,” and so forth.]

Let us therefore act so that, with every diligence, we may commend our reputation and good name, and first, through calmness of mind and kindness of spirit, insinuate ourselves into human affection.

[Note: The editions read: “and by ease of spirit, moderation in instruction, and courtesy of speech and dignity of words.” Cicero, Book II, p. 378, line 24: “But there is another avenue to the multitude, namely, to flow, as it were, into the minds of all,” and so forth.]

Kindness is popular and pleasing to everyone, and nothing so readily enters the human senses. If it is assisted by gentleness of character and ease, by moderation in instruction, by courtesy of speech, by dignity of words, and also by patience in conversation and the graciousness of modesty, it advances incredibly far toward increasing affection.

[Note: Cicero, Book II, p. 380, line 48: “Yet it is difficult to say how greatly it wins the minds of men,” and so forth.]

[Note: Ibid., line 49: “There survive letters of Philip to Alexander … in which they instruct him to win the minds of the multitude by gracious speech,” and so forth.]

30. We read that not only among private persons but even among kings, the effectiveness of gracious courtesy has been immense, or that arrogance and inflated speech have caused great harm, so that they weakened kingdoms themselves and dissolved power.

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads “the usefulness of courtesy.” And below, “inflicted by the people of God,” and so forth.]

Now, if someone wins popular favor through advice, experience, service, duties, and acts of office; or if someone offers his own danger on behalf of the whole people, there is no doubt that such affection flows back upon him from the people in such abundance that the people place his safety and favor before their own.

[Note: Some manuscripts read “by the use of counsel in service.”]

31. How many insults Moses absorbed from the people (Exod. 32:11 and following)! And when the Lord wished to punish their insolence, he repeatedly offered himself on behalf of the people, so as to withdraw them from the divine indignation!

[Note: Several manuscripts read “he was absolving insults.”]

How gently he addressed the people after their injuries; how he consoled them in their labors, soothed them with oracles, and encouraged them by his deeds! And although he spoke constantly with God (Gen. 33:8 and following), he was nevertheless accustomed to address human beings with humble and gracious language. Thus he was rightly judged superior to men: they could not gaze directly upon his face (Gen. 34:29 and following), and they believed that his burial place had not been found (Deut. 34:6), because he had so bound the minds of the entire people to himself that they loved him more for his gentleness than they admired him for his deeds (1 Sam. 10:12, and elsewhere).

[Note: The latest Paris edition reads: “how gentle he was in speech.”]

32. And what of holy David, the imitator of Moses, chosen from among all to rule the people? How gentle and gracious he was, humble in spirit, diligent in heart, and readily sympathetic! Before he became king, he offered himself on behalf of everyone. As king, he made his service equal to that of all, and shared their labor: strong in battle, gentle in command, patient under insult, more ready to endure injuries than to repay them.

Therefore he was so dear to everyone that, although still a young man, he was sought for the kingdom even against his will; while resisting, he was compelled to accept it; and when old, his people asked him not to take part in battle. Everyone preferred to risk danger for him rather than have him risk danger for all.

33. Thus, through his freely given services, he had bound the people to himself (2 Sam. 2:2 and following). First, during the people’s dissensions, he preferred to live in exile at Hebron rather than reign in Jerusalem. Next, he loved virtue even when it appeared in an enemy, and thought that justice should be shown equally to those who had taken up arms against him and to his own men.

Finally (2 Sam. 3:32 and following), when Abner, the strongest champion and leader of the opposing side, was bringing on battles, David admired him; when Abner pleaded for peace, David did not reject his request but honored him with a banquet. When Abner was killed by treachery, David grieved and wept; he honored him by accompanying his funeral. By avenging his death, he demonstrated his fidelity of conscience, which he transmitted to his son along with the hereditary rights, being more concerned that the innocent man’s death should not go unavenged than with grieving his own death.

34. This was no ordinary conduct, especially in a king: to perform the duties of humility in such a way as to show himself accessible even to the lowest; not to seek food at another’s peril, and to refuse drink (2 Sam. 23:13 and following); to confess his sin and offer himself to death on behalf of the people, so that the divine indignation might be turned upon him. To the destroying angel he offered himself, saying: “Behold, here I am; I have sinned, and I, the shepherd, have done evil. What has this flock done? Let your hand be against me.”

35. What more should I say—that when men were plotting deceit, he did not open his mouth, and, as though he had not heard, judged that no word should be returned; he did not answer insults; when he was disparaged, he prayed; when he was cursed, he blessed?

He walked in simplicity, avoiding the proud and following the undefiled; he mixed ashes with his food while lamenting his own sins, and tempered his drink with tears (Ps. 37:14, and elsewhere).

[Note: One edition and two manuscripts read “fleeing arrogance”; a somewhat larger number read “avoiding gatherings”; the great majority of manuscripts, and those of greatest authority, acknowledge neither “arrogance” nor “gatherings.” No manuscript at all contains the word found in the printed editions after “following.”]

He was therefore rightly desired by the whole people, so that all the tribes of Israel came to him and said: “Behold, we are your bones and your flesh. Yesterday and the day before, when Saul was king over us, you were the one who led Israel out and brought it in. And the Lord said to you: You shall shepherd my people” (2 Sam. 5:1 and following).

And what more shall I say of one concerning whom God gave this judgment: “I have found David according to my heart” (Ps. 88:21)? For who walked in holiness of heart and righteousness like him, fulfilling the will of God? On his account pardon was granted to his sinful descendants, and a privilege was reserved for his heirs (1 Kings 11:12–13).

36. Who, then, would not love one whom he saw so dear to his friends? Because he sincerely loved his friends, he believed that he was loved equally by them. In the end, parents preferred him to their children, and children to their parents. Hence Saul was deeply angered and wished to strike his son Jonathan with a spear, because he judged that David’s friendship meant more to Jonathan than either filial piety or paternal authority (1 Sam. 20:30 and following).

37. Indeed, as a powerful incentive to common affection, it is highly effective when someone returns the love shown to him and proves that he loves no less than he is loved; and this should be evident through examples of faithful friendship.

[Note: Some manuscripts read “let him make it evident through examples”; others, “an example.”]

For what is more popular than favor? What is more implanted in nature than loving the one who loves you? What is more deeply rooted and impressed in human affections than being moved to love someone whom you wish to love you?

The wise man rightly says: “Spend your money for your brother and friend” (Sir. 29:13). And elsewhere: “I will not be ashamed to greet my friend, nor will I hide myself from his face” (Sir. 22:31). For the teaching of Ecclesiasticus testifies that the remedy of life and immortality is found in a friend (Sir. 6:16). No one will doubt that the supreme protection lies in love, since the Apostle says: “It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things; love never fails” (1 Cor. 13:7 and following).

38. David therefore did not fall, because he was dear to everyone and preferred to be loved by his subjects rather than feared.

[Note: Cicero, Book II, p. 377, line 8: “For fear is a poor guardian of lasting security,” and so forth.]

Fear preserves vigilance for a time, but it knows nothing of lasting security. Therefore, when fear has departed, boldness creeps in, since faith is not compelled by fear but displayed by affection.

39. Affection is therefore the first means of winning approval.

[Note: Cicero, Book II, p. 378, line 13: “Let this therefore be certain, and both the first and most necessary point: to have trustworthy friendships,” and so forth.]

It is good, then, to have the testimony of the affection of many. From this arises faith, so that even strangers do not fear entrusting themselves to your affection when they have observed that you are dear to many.

Similarly, one arrives at affection through faith: when someone has shown faithfulness to one or two persons, it is as though that faith flows into the minds of all, and he wins the favor of everyone.

## CHAPTER VIII

That nothing is more effective for winning favor than advice; but that no one can be trusted with it unless he relies upon justice and prudence; and that the extent to which these two virtues shone in Solomon is made clear by his celebrated judgment.

40. Two things therefore contribute greatly to winning approval: affection and faith; and a third, if you possess something which most people consider worthy of admiration in you and rightly deserving of honor.

[Note: Cicero, Book II, p. 376, line 38: “Whatever men …,” and so forth. Also p. 378, line 21: “The highest and perfect glory consists …,” and so forth.]

41. Since the use of counsel wins people over above all, prudence and justice are therefore desired in each person, and many look for them, so that the person who possesses them may be trusted as someone able to give useful and reliable advice to one who seeks it.

[Note: Cicero, Book II, p. 378, line 34: “Faith can be obtained through two things,” and so forth.]

For who would entrust himself to someone whom he did not think wiser than the person seeking advice himself? It is therefore necessary that the one from whom advice is sought be superior to the one who seeks it. Why would you consult someone whom you did not believe capable of discovering something better than you yourself understand?

42. But if you find someone who excels in quickness of intellect, vigor of mind, and authority; who is also more prepared through example and experience; who resolves present dangers, foresees the future, announces what is impending, clarifies the issue, supplies a remedy in time, and is prepared not only to give advice but also to come to the rescue—such a person is trusted so completely that the one who seeks advice may say: “Even if evil should happen to me through him, I will bear it” (Sir. 22:31).

43. To such a man we entrust our safety and reputation—one who is, as we said above, just and prudent. Justice ensures that there is no fear of fraud; prudence ensures that there is no suspicion of error.

[Note: Cicero, Book II, line 39: “For in just and trustworthy men—that is, good men …”; “of these two, justice is more powerful for producing trust,” and so forth.]

Yet, speaking according to common usage, we entrust ourselves more readily to a just man than to a prudent one.

[Note: Cicero, Book II, line 46: “But lest anyone wonder why, although all philosophers agree … that one who possessed one [virtue] …,” and so forth.]

According to the definition of the wise, however, where one virtue is present, the others are present as well; prudence cannot exist without justice. We find the same in our own writings, for David says: “The just man shows mercy and lends” (Ps. 36:21). Elsewhere he explains what the just man lends: “The good man is gracious and lends; he orders his affairs with justice” (Ps. 111:5).

44. Is not that celebrated judgment of Solomon itself full of wisdom and justice? Let us therefore examine it, if this is so.

“Two women,” he says, “stood before King Solomon, and one of them said to him: ‘Hear me, my lord. I and this woman live in one room. Three days ago, after giving birth, we each bore a son, and we were together; there was no judge in the house, nor any other woman with us, except us two alone. This woman’s son died during the night, because she had lain upon him. She arose at midnight, took my son from beside me, placed him in her bosom, and put her dead son in my bosom. When I arose in the morning to nurse the child, I found him dead. At daybreak I examined him, and he was not my son.’

“The other woman replied: ‘No, but my son is the one who is alive, and your son is the one who is dead’” (1 Kings 3:16 and following).

45. This was the dispute: each claimed the surviving child for herself, while denying that the dead child was hers. Then the king ordered a sword to be brought and the child divided, with each woman receiving a portion—half for one and half for the other.

The woman whose maternal affection had been stirred cried out: “By no means, my lord; do not divide the child. Give him to her instead, and let him live; do not kill him.” But the other replied: “Let him be neither mine nor hers; divide him.”

Then the king ordered that the child be given to the woman who had said, “Do not kill him, but give him to that woman,” because, he said, “her maternal feelings have been stirred for her son.”

46. It was therefore not without reason that people judged the understanding of God to be in him: for what is hidden is [known] to God. What is more hidden than the testimony of the inward organs, into which the understanding of the wise descended as an arbiter of compassion, as it were, and from which it drew forth a kind of voice from the womb? The maternal affection was revealed: it preferred that her son live with another woman rather than be killed before his mother’s eyes.

[Note: All the editions and a few manuscripts read “because the hidden things of God are in him.” Six or seven others read “because the things hidden by God have been made manifest to him.” Most of the rest have “because he is powerful in the things hidden by God.” Since the verb “are evident” is omitted in the oldest manuscripts, which did not recognize that the sentence was to be expressed in the form of a question, each editor supplied from his own judgment what seemed necessary to the meaning.]

47. It was therefore the work of wisdom to distinguish hidden consciences and draw out the truth from concealed things; and, as with a sword, to penetrate by the sword of the spirit not only the inward parts of the womb but also those of the soul and mind.

It was also the work of justice that the woman who had killed her own child should not take another’s, but that the true mother should receive her own. Finally, Scripture itself pronounced this judgment: “All Israel heard of the judgment which the king had judged, and they feared before the king, because they saw that the understanding of God was in him to administer justice” (1 Kings 3:28).

Solomon himself therefore asked for wisdom so that he might be given “a prudent heart to hear and judge with justice” (ibid., 9).

## CHAPTER IX

Although justice and prudence are inseparable, one should accommodate the understanding of the common people, who distinguish the cardinal virtues.

48. It is therefore clear, even according to the divine Scripture, which is more ancient, that wisdom cannot exist without justice, because wherever one of these virtues is present, both are present.

How wisely Daniel, too, by means of a searching interrogation, exposed the falsehood of the fraudulent accusation, so that the responses of the accusers did not agree! It was an act of prudence to betray the guilty through the testimony of their own words; it was also an act of justice to hand over the guilty to punishment and rescue the innocent (Dan. 13:54 and following).

49. There is therefore an inseparable fellowship between wisdom and justice. But common usage divides one particular form of the virtues in this way: temperance is seen in despising pleasures; fortitude in labors and dangers; prudence in the choice of good things, knowing how to distinguish advantages and adversities; justice as the good guardian of another’s right and the defender of property, preserving to each person what is his.

Let this fourfold division therefore be accepted for us by the favor of common opinion. Withdrawing our step from that subtle philosophical discussion of wisdom, which is drawn out, as it were, from some inner shrine for the purpose of refining truth, let us follow forensic usage and popular understanding. Maintaining this division, let us return to our subject.

## CHAPTER X

That one’s safety is more readily entrusted to the counsel of a just man than of a prudent man; that everyone seeks one who unites justice and prudence in himself; and that Solomon, Joseph, and Daniel provide examples of this.

50. We entrust our affairs to the most prudent person, and seek advice from him more readily than from others. Yet the faithful counsel of a just man is superior, and frequently outweighs even the genius of the wisest man.

[Note: Cicero, Book II, On Duties, p. 378, line 41: “Of these two, justice is more powerful for producing trust,” and so forth.]

“For the wounds of a friend are useful, more than the kisses of others” (Prov. 27:6).

[Note: The editions, together with a few manuscripts, read: “For the wounds of a friend are more useful than the kisses of strangers.” Many more and older manuscripts read: “useful … than the kisses of others.” This verse, which is found only in the Septuagint, is frequently cited by Ambrose. He always expresses it so that the more reliable manuscripts have “useful” rather than “more useful,” with the adverb “more” understood; and for “the kisses of others,” one everywhere finds “the voluntary kisses of an enemy,” as in the Septuagint: ἐκούσια φιλήματα ἐχθροῦ, that is, “voluntary kisses of an enemy.”]

Furthermore, because judgment belongs to the just man, while argument belongs to the wise man, the former has the authority of deliberative judgment, the latter the ingenuity of discovery.

[Note: Up to this point Chapter 9 extended in the old editions; whether this was correct, any reader can easily judge.]

51. If you join the two together, there will be great healthfulness in their counsels, which everyone regards with admiration for wisdom and love of justice. Thus everyone seeks to hear the wisdom of the man in whom the bond of both virtues exists.

So all the kings of the earth sought to see Solomon’s face and hear his wisdom. The queen of Sheba came to him and tested him with questions: “She came and spoke to him about everything that was in her heart, and she heard all Solomon’s wisdom, and no word escaped her” (1 Kings 10:2–3).

52. Who is this woman, whom nothing escaped and to whom true Solomon announced everything? Learn, O man, from these words that you hear her speak:

“True is the report which I heard in my land concerning your words and your wisdom. I did not believe those who told me until I came and my eyes saw; and now not even half is according to what they announced to me. You have added good things above everything I heard in my land. Blessed are your women, and blessed are your servants who stand before you and hear all your wisdom” (ibid., 6 and following).

Understand the banquet of the true Solomon, and understand wisely what is set forth at that banquet. Consider in what land the assembly of the nations heard the fame of true wisdom and justice, and with what eyes it saw him—eyes contemplating the things that are not seen. For “the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal” (2 Cor. 4:18).

53. Who are the blessed women, except those of whom it is said that they hear the word of God and bear it (Luke 11:28)? And elsewhere: “Whoever does the word of God is my brother and sister and mother” (Matt. 12:50).

Who are your blessed servants who stand before you, except Paul, who said, “To this day I stand bearing witness to small and great” (Acts 26:22), and Simeon, who waited in the temple to see the consolation of Israel (Luke 2:25)?

For how could he have asked to be dismissed, unless, standing in attendance upon the Lord, he could not depart until he had obtained the Lord’s will? Solomon has been set before us as an example, one whose wisdom everyone eagerly sought to hear.

54. Joseph also was not idle even in prison, so that people did not cease consulting him about uncertain matters. His counsel benefited all Egypt, so that it did not experience the seven years of famine and he relieved other peoples from wretched famine through fasting (Gen. 41:10 and following).

[Note: In earlier editions this point began Chapter 11, but incorrectly. For this example and the following one clearly belong to Chapter 10; only afterward does he treat that third element proposed at the beginning of Chapter 8.]

55. Daniel, taken from among the captives and made the arbiter of royal counselors, corrected present circumstances by his counsels and announced future events. From the things which he had frequently interpreted, showing himself to be a true announcer, confidence was placed in him in all matters (Dan. 2:10 and following).

[Note: Some manuscripts read “he announced that they were true.”]

## CHAPTER XI

The third condition that wins someone’s trust is shown to have shone forth in Moses, Daniel, and Joseph.

56. The third element, concerning those who are considered worthy of admiration, seems to have been traversed through the example of Joseph, Solomon, and Daniel.

[Note: Cicero, Book II, p. 379, line 3: “There were therefore three things belonging to glory, this third one,” and so forth.]

For what should I say of Moses, whose counsel all Israel awaited daily, whose life gave proof of his prudence and increased admiration for him? Who would not entrust himself to the counsel of Moses, to whom the elders reserved for judgment whatever they thought exceeded their own understanding and ability?

57. Who would reject Daniel’s counsel, concerning whom God himself said: “Who is wiser than Daniel?” (Ezek. 28:3). Or how could people doubt the minds of those to whom God granted such great grace?

Wars were brought to an end through Moses’ counsel; through Moses’ merits nourishment flowed from heaven and drink came from the rock.

58. How pure was Daniel’s mind, so that he softened barbarous customs and calmed lions (Dan. 14:39)! What temperance was in him! How great the restraint of his mind and body!

It was not without reason that he became an object of wonder to everyone. Although supported by royal friendships—a thing people greatly admire—he did not seek gold, nor did he value the honor bestowed upon him more highly than fidelity. Indeed, he preferred to risk danger for the law of the Lord rather than bend for the favor of a human being.

59. What should I say of the chastity and justice of holy Joseph, whom I had almost passed over? By the former he rejected his master’s enticements and refused rewards; by the latter he despised death, cast off fear, and preferred prison (Gen. 39:8 and following).

Who would not judge him fit to give counsel in a private matter, whose fruitful spirit and fertile mind made the barren season fruitful through a kind of abundance of counsel and heart (Gen. 41:25 and following)?

## CHAPTER XII

That no one seeks counsel from a person contaminated by vices, nor again from someone morose and difficult; but rather from one whose model we possess in Scripture.

60. We observe, then, that the integrity of one’s life, the pre-eminence of virtues, the practice of benevolence, and the grace of accessibility contribute greatly to acquiring counsel.

[Note: All the editions read “the grace of frugality.” Nearly all the manuscripts more elegantly read “the grace of accessibility”; for frugality is already included above under integrity of life, while Saint Ambrose will also discuss accessibility below.]

For who would seek a spring in mud? Who would ask for drink from turbid water? Wherever there is luxury, intemperance, or confusion of vices, who would think that anything should be drawn from there? Who would not despise the filth of such character? Who would judge someone useful to another’s cause whom he sees to be useless to his own life?

[Note: Cicero, Book II, On Duties, p. 379, line 8: “But they despise and scorn those in whom there is no virtue,” and so forth.]

Who, again, would not flee a wicked, malevolent, abusive person, one prepared to do harm? Who would not avoid him with every effort?

61. Who would court someone, however well equipped to provide counsel, if he were difficult to approach—like someone who blocks access to a spring? What good is it to possess wisdom if you refuse counsel? If you block the opportunity for consultation, you have closed the spring, so that it flows neither to others nor benefits you.

62. The same saying aptly applies to someone who possesses prudence but defiles it with the filth of vices, since he contaminates the outlet of the water.

[Note: Translated from Virgil, Aeneid 4:

“Degenerate spirits are exposed by fear …”]

“Life exposes degenerate spirits.” How can you judge superior in counsel someone whom you see inferior in character? The person to whom I am preparing to entrust myself must be above me.

Or shall I consider someone fit to give me advice who does not give it to himself? Shall I believe that he is available to me who is not available to himself—whose mind pleasures occupy, lust enslaves, avarice subdues, desire disturbs, and fear shakes?

How can there be a place for counsel here, where there is no peace?

[Note: The editions and a few manuscripts read “lust enslaves”;]

63. The counselor whom the gracious Lord gave to the fathers and, when angered, took away is worthy of admiration and reverence (Isa. 3:3). Whoever is able to give counsel ought to imitate him and preserve prudence free from vices, since nothing defiled enters into it.

## CHAPTER XIII

Having demonstrated the beauty of wisdom by divine testimonies, the discourse proceeds to prove its fellowship with the other virtues.

64. Who, as though displaying beauty in his face, would present the appearance of beauty and then dishonor the grace of his superior form with the hindquarters of beasts and the claws of wild animals? Yet the form of the virtues is so admirable and splendid, and especially the beauty of wisdom, as the sequence of Scripture indicates.

[Note: Erasmus and the editions following him read “such a beauty of face”; Amerbach, together with all the manuscripts, reads “as though displaying beauty in his face.” This is not inappropriate. Compare this passage with the beginning of the Horatian treatise On the Art of Poetry.]

For “she is more beautiful than the sun, and, compared with the arrangement of the stars, she is found to be prior to light” (Wis. 7:29). Night receives this light, but wickedness does not overcome wisdom.

[Note: Cicero, Book II, On Duties, p. 379, line 19: “Who would not admire the splendor and beauty of virtue?” and so forth.]

[Note: Erasmus and the later editions, together with certain manuscripts, read “is found to be more equal.”]

65. We have spoken of its beauty and confirmed it by the testimony of Scripture. It remains to teach, on the authority of Scripture, that wisdom has no fellowship with vices, but an undivided union with the other virtues. Its spirit is articulate, undefiled, sure, holy, loving what is good, keen, preventing nothing good from being done, benevolent, steadfast, secure, possessing every virtue, and seeing all things (Wis. 7:22 and following).

[Note: Amerbach and the manuscripts read thus, except that some read “truth” rather than “virtue.” Since Erasmus and Gill had excised the sentence, the Roman edition restored it in this altered form: “And elsewhere: For it teaches sobriety and prudence, justice and fortitude.”]

And further: “It teaches sobriety, and justice and virtue” (Wis. 8:7).

## CHAPTER XIV

That prudence is joined with all the virtues, but especially with contempt for wealth.

66. Prudence therefore accomplishes everything, since it has fellowship with all good things. For how can it give useful counsel unless it possesses justice, so that it may put on steadfastness; does not fear death; is not recalled by any terror or fear; and does not consider itself permitted to turn away from the truth through flattery?

[Note: Erasmus and the later editions, together with some manuscripts, read “unless it possesses justice and puts on steadfastness.”]

Let it not shun exile, since it knows that the world is the homeland of the wise; let it not fear poverty, since it knows that the wise man lacks nothing, for the whole world is his wealth.

[Note: Cicero, Book II, On Duties, p. 379, line 22: “For no one can be just who fears death,” and so forth.]

What is more elevated than the man who cannot be moved by gold, who holds money in contempt, and, as though from a certain citadel, looks down upon human desires? Those who have done this are judged by men to be above humanity: “Who is this,” he says, “and we will praise him? For he has done wonders in his life” (Sir. 31:9).

How could one not admire the man who despises riches, which most people have preferred even to their own salvation?

### 67. [Note: Several Paris editions read: “Therefore he teaches all”; and below, “That teaches more,” etc.] It is fitting, then, that all should display the dignity of frugality and the authority of self-restraint, and especially one who excels in honor, lest a prominent man possess treasures of his own and one who presides over free men serve money. It is more fitting that his mind should be above his treasure and that he should be below his friend in service. Humility, after all, increases favor. [Col. 0120C] These qualities are full of praise and worthy of a leading man: not to share the shameful desire for dishonest gain with Tyrian merchants and Gileadite traders; not to place every good in money; and not, like a hired laborer, to count up daily profits, [Note: All editions read *calculari compendio* (“to calculate profit”); the manuscripts, however, read *calculari compendia* (“to calculate profits”), which is much more suitable.] to calculate profits.

## CHAPTER XV

### On generosity: to whom it should chiefly be distributed, and in what way people of modest means may exercise it through their efforts and advice

### 68. If it is praiseworthy to maintain a sober attitude toward these matters, how much more excellent is it if you acquire the affection of the multitude through generosity, being neither extravagant toward the importunate nor restrictive toward the needy! [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, Book I, p. 378, line 26: “That goodwill is chiefly won by benefits.” Also p. 382, line 1: “Sometimes, however, one must give generously,” etc.]

### 69. There are, moreover, many kinds of generosity. [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, Book I, p. 383, line 12: “In that kind of giving,” etc. Several matters in the Ambrosian text appear to deserve careful, rather than cursory, attention. First, it is clear from this passage that those ancient bishops were greatly concerned that no needy person should be deprived, openly or secretly, of the assistance necessary to sustain life. Second, they regularly appointed persons to whom this responsibility was entrusted—either choosing them from among the priests, which was more frequent in the Eastern Church but also occurred at times in the West, as we learn from this and the following chapter, or taking them from the order of deacons. The latter practice seems generally to have prevailed throughout the West, as is evident not only from what the holy Bishop frequently relates in this work concerning blessed Lawrence, and from what Prudentius records in his hymn about the same martyr, but also from Sulpicius Severus, who states in the *Life of Saint Martin* that Martin had appointed his archdeacon to this office. Finally, one should observe that these dispensers did everything not according to their own inclination, but at the direction and pleasure of the bishop, to whom they regularly referred everything, so that nothing was outside his authority. This agrees very well with Apostolic Canons 39, 40, and 41, Canon 57 of the Council of Laodicea, and the definitions of innumerable subsequent councils.]

Not only must one arrange and distribute daily support to those who need it in order to sustain their lives, but one must also care for and assist those who are ashamed to admit publicly that they are in need, so that the common provision for the poor may not be exhausted. I am speaking of one who presides over some office, whether he exercises the priestly ministry or serves as a dispenser: he should report such cases to the bishop and should not hold back if he learns that someone has fallen into necessity or, deprived of his resources, has been reduced to poverty—especially if he has not fallen into this condition through youthful extravagance, but through someone’s plunder or the loss of his inheritance, so that he is unable to meet his daily expenses. [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, Book I, p. 378, line 14: “A more generous kindness … unless perhaps they are deserving,” etc.]

### 70. The highest generosity is to redeem captives, snatch people from the hands of enemies, rescue human beings from death, and, above all, rescue women from disgrace; to return children to their parents, parents to their children, and citizens to their country. These things are all too well known from the devastation of Illyricum and Thrace. [Note: Baronius maintains that this devastation of Illyricum and Thrace occurred in the year 387 after the birth of Christ. But the most learned Cardinal does not speak consistently here. For if the sacred vessels were melted down and sold by Ambrose in that same year, it necessarily follows that these books of *Duties* were published only after that year, whereas elsewhere he has affirmed that they were published a full decade earlier, around the year 377. It seems much more probable that the calamity mentioned here by Saint Ambrose followed the violent death of the emperor Valens. After his commanders Trajan and Sebastian had been killed and the entire army had been destroyed, the Goths and other barbarians ravaged Illyricum as far as the Julian Alps and the region of the Veneti, laying everything waste with fire and sword. Baronius himself has recorded this after Ammianus Marcellinus, Socrates, Sozomen, and Theodoret. See also the distinguished Hermann, *Life of Ambrose*, Book II, chapter 12.]

How many captives were being sold everywhere throughout the whole world! Yet even if you gathered them together, they would not fill the number of one province. There were nevertheless people who wanted to return to slavery those whom the Church had redeemed—people more grievous than captivity itself, who begrudged another’s mercy. If they themselves had fallen into captivity, they would serve as free men; if they had been sold, they would not refuse the service of slavery. Yet they wish to destroy another’s freedom, although they could not destroy their own slavery unless perhaps the buyer chose to receive the price. Even then, however, slavery is not abolished but redeemed.

### 71. The foremost generosity, therefore, is to redeem captives, especially from a barbarous enemy who contributes nothing humane toward mercy except what greed has reserved for ransom; to assume another’s debt when the debtor cannot pay and is pressed for payment of what is legally owed, while poverty has deprived him of the means; to nourish little children and protect orphans. [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, Book II, p. 382, line 15: “Those are generous who, from their resources, redeem captives from pirates … or assist in providing dowries for daughters,” etc.]
