### 72. There are also people who marry off girls deprived of their parents, for the sake of preserving their chastity, and assist them not only with their efforts but also with financial support. There is also that form of generosity which the Apostle teaches: “If any faithful person has widows, let that person provide for them, so that the Church may not be burdened with their support, and so that it may suffice for those who are truly widows” (1 Tim. 5:16).

### 73. Such generosity is useful, therefore, but it is not possible for everyone. For there are many good men who possess only modest means: they are content with little for their own use, but are not capable of relieving another’s poverty. Nevertheless, another kind of beneficence is available by which they can help someone who is inferior in circumstances. [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, Book II, p. 381, line 33: “Next we must speak of beneficence, which has two forms,” etc.]

For generosity is of two kinds: one assists through material support—that is, through the use of money; the other is expended through the contribution of one’s efforts, and is much more often splendid and much more illustrious. [Note: Erasmus and the editions following him read: “which is expended through the contribution of efforts.”]

### 74. How much more illustriously Abraham recovered his nephew by force of victorious arms (Gen. 14:16) than if he had redeemed him! How much more usefully did holy Joseph assist Pharaoh through wise foresight than if he had contributed money! Money could not redeem the abundance of one city; the foresight of all Egypt drove back the famine for five years (Gen. 41:33 ff.). [Note: Gill, in the margin, and the Roman edition in the text read “for seven years.” But since all the other editions and the manuscripts prefer “five years,” it is credible that the holy Bishop wrote this because he thought that the Egyptian people had lived at least through the first two years on private produce, before famine forced them to take refuge in the royal granaries. This interpretation seems to be supported by the reading: “And there was famine throughout all the land, but throughout all the land of Egypt there was bread”—καὶ ἐγένετο λιμὸς ἐν πάσῃ τῇ γῇ, ἐν δὲ πάσῃ τῇ γῇ Αἰγύπτου ἦσαν ἄρτοι (“and there was famine in all the land, but in all the land of Egypt there was bread”). It should not be concealed, however, that some manuscripts read οὐκ ἦσαν ἄρτοι (“there was no bread”), a reading with which the Syriac version also agrees. But the agreement of all the other versions, as well as of the Hebrew text itself and of the sequence of the discourse, supports the other reading.]

### 75. Money is easily consumed, but counsel does not know how to be exhausted. Counsel increases through use; money diminishes, quickly runs out, and even abandons generosity itself, so that the more people you wish to give to, the fewer you help, and often you lack what you had thought to give to others. [Col. 0122C–0123A] But the contribution of counsel and effort, the more widely it is distributed, the more abundantly it remains and returns to its own source. The richness of wisdom flows back into itself; and the more widely it has flowed, the more thoroughly practiced becomes everything that remains.

## CHAPTER XVI

### The measure to be observed in generosity, so that what was owed to the more deserving is not squandered on the undeserving; yet alms should not be distributed too sparingly or timidly. Blessed Joseph is to be imitated, whose prudence is commended at greater length

### 76. It is therefore clear that generosity must have a measure, lest giving become useless. Sobriety must be maintained, especially by priests, so that they distribute not for display but for justice. [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, Book II, p. 382, line 7: “Therefore one’s property must not be so closed that kindness cannot open it,” etc.]

Nowhere is there a greater eagerness for requests. Strong people come; people come who have no reason except to wander about; and they wish to drain the resources of the poor and empty the fund. Not content with little, they seek greater things, winning support for their requests by the display of clothing and bargaining for increased profits through false claims of noble birth. If anyone readily believes them, he quickly exhausts the savings that ought to benefit the poor. Let there be a measure in giving, so that they do not depart empty-handed, but neither is the life of the poor transferred as plunder to frauds. Let there be a standard, therefore, so that humanity is not abandoned and necessity is not left without help.

### 77. Many pretend to have debts. Let their claims be examined for truth. They lament that they have been stripped through robbery: either the wrong itself should establish their credibility, or knowledge of their character, so that they may be helped more readily. [Col. 0123C] Provision should be allotted to those exiled from the Church, if they lack the means of support. [Note: All editions, and the larger and better part of the manuscripts, read “those exiled from the Church.” Some manuscripts, however, have a variant reading that is materially uncertain in the supplied text. The question with the first reading is: who are those “excluded from the Church”? Some have wanted this to refer to people who had been forced into exile from their churches on account of the faith. But the holy Doctor would never have spoken of them so briefly and faintly. We understand them, therefore, as those who had been separated from the Church’s sacred rites for the sake of penance. Although Augustine testifies that ecclesiastical alms were customarily withheld from them, Christian generosity was nevertheless not absent in extreme necessity. The passage may also be explained by taking “from the Church” with “to be distributed,” rather than with “those excluded,” that is, exiles.]

Thus the person who observes the proper measure is miserly toward no one but generous toward all. We ought not merely to lend our ears to the voices of those who pray, but also our eyes to their needs. Weakness cries out more loudly to the good worker than the voice of the poor. It cannot happen that the importunity of shouting people does not extort something more; but there is not always room for shamelessness. [Note: Some Paris editions read: “there should be room for imprudence.”] The one who does not see you must be seen by you; the one who is ashamed to be seen must be sought out by you. Let the one shut up in prison also come before you; let the one afflicted by illness, who cannot speak to your ears, resound in your mind.

### 78. The more the people see you at work, the more they will love you. I know that many priests, the more they gave, the more abundantly they possessed, because whoever sees a good worker gives to him what that worker will distribute according to his office, confident that his mercy will reach the poor. [Note: This praiseworthy custom of the ancient Christians should not be passed over hastily: they placed their money in the hands of the Church’s steward or dispenser, who afterward distributed it among the groups of poor believers. There is a notable passage on this subject near the end of blessed Justin’s *Second Apology*, whose words are worth reproducing here: “Those who are wealthy,” he says, “and are willing, each according to his own choice, contribute whatever they wish; and what is collected in this way is deposited with the president. He then assists orphans and widows, those who are in need because of illness or any other cause, those who are in bonds, and visiting strangers; and, to speak simply, he is the guardian of all who are in need.”]

For no one wishes his contribution to benefit anyone except the poor. [Note: Some manuscripts read “his consolation.” But the reading found in the others and in the editions—“his contribution,” that is, his alms, which the Apostle calls the collection—must certainly be preferred. Below, where the editions and many manuscripts read “he will despise both,” the Thuanus manuscript and several others prefer “both are displeasing.”] If anyone sees a dispenser who is either immoderate or excessively stingy, he will despise both: whether the dispenser squanders the fruits of another’s labor through excessive distributions or hides them away in moneybags.

Just as a measure of generosity must be maintained, so also a spur must usually be applied. [Note: The Thuanus manuscript and many others read “a spur is usually [needed].” The words “a measure must be applied” seem to be required.] A measure is needed so that you can do daily what you do well, lest through lavishness you withdraw what you have granted to necessity. A spur is needed because money works better in a poor person’s food than in a rich person’s purse. Beware of enclosing the salvation of the needy within your own purses and, as though in tombs, burying the life of the poor. [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, Book II, p. 382, line 3: “What is more foolish than something you do gladly,” etc.]

### 79. Joseph could have given away all Egypt’s wealth and poured out the royal treasures; yet he did not wish to appear lavish with another’s property. He preferred to sell grain rather than give it to the hungry, because if he had given to a few, it would have been lacking for many. He approved that generosity which would provide abundance for everyone. He opened the storehouses so that all might buy a supply of grain (Gen. 41:56–57), lest by receiving it for free they abandon the cultivation of the land, since whoever uses another’s property neglects his own.

### 80. Therefore he first amassed money, then the remaining resources, and finally acquired the rights over the land for the king—not to strip everyone of what was theirs, [Note: Some manuscripts read: “but to support the public treasury,” or “for the public treasury.”] but to support it. He established a public tax by which they could possess their own property more securely. [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, Book II, p. 385, line 3: “One must take every possible care, if it can be done,” etc. Also line 15: “Care must also be taken lest … a tax have to be imposed,” etc.]

This was so pleasing to all those whose lands he had taken that they thought it not a sale of their rights but a redemption of their lives. Finally, they said: “You have saved us; we have found favor in the sight of our lord” (Gen. 47:14 ff., 25). For they had lost nothing of their property, since they had received back the right to it; nor had they lost anything of their advantage, since they had acquired permanence.

### 81. O great man, who sought not the temporary glory of excessive generosity but established an enduring benefit through foresight! [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, Book II, p. 386, line 33: “O great man, and worthy of …,” etc.] He made the people assist themselves through their own taxes and ensured that, in time of necessity, they would not require another’s aid. It was better to contribute something from their produce than to lose everything concerning their rights. He established a fifth as the contribution, being more farsighted in provision and more generous in taxation. [Note: Some manuscripts read: “He established the contributory portion.”] In the end, Egypt never again suffered a famine of this kind.

### 82. How splendidly, moreover, he gathered what was to come! First, how skillfully did the royal interpreter express the truth of the dream! The king’s first dream was this: Seven heifers came up from the river, beautiful in appearance and fat in body, and grazed along the bank of the river. Other heifers, ugly in appearance and lean in body, [Note: Many manuscripts read: “and emaciated in body.”] came up from the river after those heifers and grazed beside them on the very bed of the banks. These heifers appeared to devour those superior in both beauty and grace.

The second dream was this: Seven fat, choice, and good ears of grain rose from the earth. [Note: Some manuscripts read: “rose from the bosom of the earth.”] After them, seven thin ears, corrupted and withered by the wind, [Note: The Thuanus manuscript and some others read “corrupted and soaked”; many others read “corrupted and moldy,” which is not implausible.] attempted to follow; and it seemed that the barren and thin ears devoured the flourishing and abundant ears.

### 83. Holy Joseph explained this dream in such a way that the seven heifers represented seven years, and likewise the seven ears represented seven years, interpreting the periods by the offspring and produce. For the offspring of a heifer represents a year, and the produce of a harvest completes a full year. They came up from the river because days, years, and seasons pass like rivers and flow swiftly onward.

Thus he declared that the first seven years would be years of fertile, fruitful, and productive soil; but that the following seven years would be sterile and unproductive, their barrenness destined to consume the abundance of the preceding years. For this reason he warned that provision should be made so that, during the more abundant years, a supply of grain might be collected capable of sustaining the poverty of the future barrenness.

### 84. What should I admire first? His intelligence, by which he descended into the very dwelling place of truth; or his counsel, by which he foresaw so grave and prolonged a necessity; or his vigilance and justice, one of which, after he had undertaken so great a responsibility, gathered such abundant supplies, while the other preserved equality among all?

What shall I say of his greatness of spirit—that, having been sold into slavery by his brothers, he did not retaliate for the wrong but drove away famine? What shall I say of his kindness, by which he sought the presence of his beloved brother through a pious deception, pretending through an artfully arranged theft to establish him as guilty of robbery, so that he might keep him as a pledge of affection (Gen. 44:2 ff.)?

### 85. Hence his father rightly says to him: [Note: These two testimonies from Genesis and Deuteronomy are cited somewhat differently in *On the Blessing of the Patriarchs*, chapter 11, sections 46 and 53. Here the ancient editions agree sufficiently with the manuscripts, except that they read “my zealous son, my younger son.” “May my God help you … and bless you … in the bush; may it come upon your head,” etc. We have corrected these variations, as well as those added by the Roman edition on the basis of written codices, especially the Thuanus manuscript.]

“Joseph is my son, greatly increased; Joseph is my son, greatly increased, my zealous younger son … . My God helped you and blessed you with the blessing of heaven from above, and with the blessing of the earth, of earth possessing all things, because of the blessings of your father and mother. He prevailed over the blessings of the enduring mountains and the desires of the everlasting hills” (Gen. 49:22 ff.).

And in Deuteronomy: “You who were seen in the bush, come upon the head of Joseph and upon his crown. Honored among his brothers, the firstborn of the bull is his glory; the horns of the unicorn are his horns. With his horn he shall toss the nations together to the ends of the earth.” [Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “He himself has ten thousand of Ephraim, and he himself has thousands of Manasseh.” All the others, together with the manuscripts, agree with us; the Hebrew text also supports them. The Septuagint instead prefers: Αὗται μυριάδες Ἐφραὶμ, καὶ αὗται χιλιάδες Μανασσῆ (“These are the tens of thousands of Ephraim, and these are the thousands of Manasseh”); the remaining versions agree with this.]

“To him belong the tens of thousands of Ephraim, and to him the thousands of Manasseh” (Deut. 33:16 ff.).

## CHAPTER XVII

### What virtues ought to be present in one whom we consult, and in what way Joseph and Paul were adorned with them

### 86. The person who gives counsel to another ought therefore to be such that he offers himself as an example of good works to others—in teaching, integrity, and dignity—so that his speech is wholesome and irreproachable, his counsel useful, his life honorable, and his judgment noble.

### 87. Such was Paul, who gave counsel to virgins (1 Cor. 7:25 ff.) and instruction to priests (Tit. 2:7), first presenting himself as a model for our imitation. Therefore he also knew how to humble himself, just as Joseph did. Joseph, born from the highest line of the patriarchs, did not disdain degrading slavery; he expressed it through his service and ennobled it by his virtues.

He knew how to humble himself, having endured both a seller and a buyer, and having called the buyer his master. Hear him humbling himself: “Since my master knows nothing in his house because of me, and has placed everything he possesses in my hands, nothing has been withheld from me except you, because you are his wife, how can I do this evil thing and sin before the Lord?” (Gen. 39:8 ff.). [Note: The old edition and some Paris editions, with a few manuscripts, read: “My master, apart from me, knows nothing … you who are his wife.” The Roman edition, with the stronger portion of the manuscripts, reads as in the text, and more suitably, since it renders what is found in the Septuagint: οὐ γινώσκει δι’ ἐμὲ οὐδὲν … διὰ τὸ σὲ γυναῖκα αὐτοῦ εἶναι (“he knows nothing through me … because you are his wife”).]

This is a voice full of humility and full of chastity: humility, because he showed honor to his master; honor, because he returned gratitude; and chastity, because he considered it a grave sin to be defiled by a shameful crime. [Note: The best and most numerous manuscripts read this way; some editions and manuscripts, however, read “he showed honor because he returned gratitude.”]

### 88. The counselor, therefore, ought to be such that there is nothing obscure in him—nothing deceitful, nothing pretended that could contradict his life and character; nothing wicked or malicious that could turn away those seeking counsel. [Note: All editions read: “nothing deceitful, nothing fabricated.” But “nothing fabricated” is omitted in very many manuscripts, including the oldest.]

There are some things that are avoided and others that are despised. We avoid those that can cause harm, those that can maliciously creep toward injury—for example, if the person consulted is of doubtful loyalty and greedy for money, so that he could be changed by a price; or if he is injurious, in which case he is avoided and shunned. But a pleasure-seeker, an intemperate person—even if free from deceit—who is nevertheless greedy and excessively desirous of shameful profit, is despised. For what evidence of diligence can such a person provide? What fruit of labor can he produce? How can he receive responsibility and concern into his mind if he has surrendered himself to sluggishness and idleness?

### 89. Therefore the good man of counsel says: “I have learned to be sufficient in the circumstances in which I find myself” (Phil. 4:11). For he knew that avarice is the root of all evils, and therefore he was content with his own and did not seek what belonged to another (1 Tim. 6:10). “It is enough for me,” he says, “that I have; whether I have little or much, it is much for me.”

Something more precise should perhaps be said. He used a carefully chosen word: [Note: The most ancient manuscript reads: “He makes it enough for me, he says … because they made it enough for them.”] “It is sufficient for me,” he says, “in the circumstances in which I am”—that is, it is neither lacking nor excessive. It is not lacking, because I seek nothing more; it is not excessive, because I possess it not only for myself but for many. This concerns money.

### 90. Moreover, it can be said of everything that the present was sufficient for him: he did not desire greater honor or more abundant service; he was not greedy for excessive glory or seeking favor he did not deserve. Rather, patiently enduring labor, he awaited the end of a rightful contest and secure reward: “I know,” he says, “how to humble myself” (Phil. 4:12).

It is not an uneducated humility, then, but one possessing modesty and self-knowledge, that is praised. There is a humility born of fear, and there is one born of inexperience and ignorance; therefore Scripture says: “He will save the humble in spirit” (Ps. 33:19). He spoke excellently, then: “I know how to humble myself”—that is, I know in what place, with what moderation, toward what end, in what office, and in what responsibility.

The Pharisee did not know how to humble himself, and therefore he was cast down; the publican knew how, and therefore he was justified (Luke 18:11 ff.).

### 91. Paul also knew how to abound, because he possessed a rich spirit, even though he did not possess a rich man’s treasure. He knew how to abound because he did not seek a gift of money but sought the fruit found in grace. We can also understand it in this way: he knew how to abound because he could say, “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians; our heart is enlarged” (2 Cor. 6:11).

### 92. He was instructed in everything, both in being filled and in being hungry. Blessed is the one who knew how to be filled in Christ. This, then, is not bodily but spiritual fullness, which knowledge produces. Knowledge is rightly required, because “man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God” (Deut. 8:3).

Therefore, whoever knew how to be filled and to hunger in this way knew how always to seek new things; he hungered for God and thirsted for the Lord. [Note: All editions read: “to hunger and thirst for the Lord.” Some manuscripts read “to hunger for God, he thirsted,” or “to hunger and the Lord,” while many others read “to hunger for God, to thirst in the Lord.” In some of these, however, the preposition *in* is absent.]

He knew how to hunger because he knew that “those who hunger shall eat their fill” (Matt. 5:6). He knew how to abound and could do so though he possessed nothing, because he possessed everything (2 Cor. 6:10).

## CHAPTER XVIII

### How much harm wicked counselors cause, as can be sufficiently understood from the example of the ten tribes that revolted from King Rehoboam

### 93. Justice, therefore, splendidly commends men who preside over some office; injustice, by contrast, abandons and attacks them. Scripture provides us with an example when it says that, after Solomon’s death, the people of Israel asked his son Rehoboam to lighten their necks from harsh slavery and moderate the severity of his father’s rule. But, rejecting the counsel of the elders and following the prompting of young men, he gave them an answer of this kind: he would add to his father’s burden and replace lighter punishments with heavier ones (1 Kings 12:4 ff.).

### 94. Enraged by this answer, the people replied: “We have no portion with David, nor inheritance in the son of Jesse. Return, each man to your tents, O Israel” (1 Kings 12:16), [Note: The words “because this man …” are not found in the biblical books, nor are the final words “he shall be to us” in most of the better manuscripts. Some of these also read “neither as leader” rather than “neither as judge.”] because this man will be neither prince nor leader for us. Thus, abandoned and deserted by the people, he could scarcely retain the allegiance of two tribes, and that only because of David’s merit.

## CHAPTER XIX

### Justice, kindness, and friendliness win over many; but these must be sincere

### 95. It is therefore clear that equity strengthens authority, while injustice dissolves it. For how can wickedness possess a kingdom when it cannot govern even a single private household? The greatest kindness is therefore necessary, so that we may protect not only public authority but also private rights. Goodwill is of the greatest assistance: it seeks to embrace everyone with benefits, bind them through service, and secure them through gratitude. [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, Book II, p. 378, line 8: “If these things are unjustly done to the Roman people,” etc. Also p. 379, line 43: “Since the power of justice is so great,” etc.]

### 96. We have also said that friendliness in speech is highly effective in winning favor. But we wish it to be sincere and sober, without any flattery, lest the flattery of speech disgrace the simplicity and purity of conversation. [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, Book II, p. 380, line 9: “How excellently Socrates followed this path … so that he was such as he wished to be considered. But if some people, through pretense,” etc.] For we must be examples to others not only in our actions but also in our speech, in purity and in faith. Let us be what we wish to be considered, and let us reveal the feeling we possess. Let us not say in our heart an evil word that we think can be hidden by silence, because the one who made hidden things hears what is said in secret, and the one who infused thought into the inward parts knows the secrets of the heart. Let us therefore consider ourselves placed before the eyes of the Judge, and regard whatever we do as set in the light, so that it may be made manifest to all.

## CHAPTER XX

### The great benefit to everyone of association with good people, and especially to the young; proved by the examples of Joshua son of Nun, Moses, and others. To this is added that those unequal in age may sometimes be equal in virtue, as Peter and John show

### 97. It is therefore of the greatest benefit for everyone to associate with good people. [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, Book II, p. 380, line 38: “Most easily, however … young men who attach themselves to distinguished and wise men,” etc.] It is also useful for young people to follow distinguished and wise men, because “whoever walks with the wise is wise, but whoever associates with the foolish is recognized as foolish.” Thus such association is of great benefit both for instruction and for the testimony of uprightness. Young people show that they are imitators of those to whom they cling; and the opinion grows that they have received from them a likeness of life, since they have drawn from them the desire for companionship. [Note: Earlier editions read: “Therefore association with good people is of great benefit.”]

### 98. Hence Joshua son of Nun became so great: the association with Moses not only instructed him in knowledge of the Law but also sanctified him for grace (Exod. 24:13). Finally, when the divine presence appeared to shine in Moses’ tent and the majesty of the Lord was seen there, Joshua son of Nun alone was in the tent. Moses spoke with God, and Joshua likewise was covered by the sacred cloud. The elders and the people stood below; Joshua ascended with Moses to receive the Law (Exod. 33:11). The entire people remained inside the camp, while Joshua was outside the camp, in the tent of testimony. When the pillar of cloud descended and spoke with Moses, Joshua stood there like a faithful servant; nor did the young man leave the tent while the elders, standing far away, trembled before the divine miracles.

### 99. Everywhere, therefore, amid marvelous works and awe-inspiring mysteries, he clung inseparably to holy Moses. Hence it came about that the one who had been his companion in daily life became his successor in authority (Deut. 34:9). It was deservedly granted to such a man that he should stop the courses of rivers (Josh. 3:15 ff.) and say, “Let the sun stand still,” and the sun stood still (Josh. 10:12–13), as though, watching his victory, he delayed the night and prolonged the day. What is more, he alone—something denied to Moses—was chosen to lead the people into the promised land. He was a great man in faith and miracles, great in triumphs. The works of the former were more majestic; those of the latter more prosperous. Both, therefore, supported by divine grace, advanced beyond the human condition (Exod. 14:21): the one commanded the sea, the other the heavens.

### 100. The bond between elders and young people is therefore beautiful (Gen. 12:4). Some are a source of example, others of comfort; some of instruction, others of delight. I omit the fact that the young Lot clung to Abraham even when Abraham was setting out, lest this be thought to have resulted more from kinship and necessary than voluntary association.

What shall we say of Elijah and Elisha? Although Scripture does not explicitly indicate that Elisha was young, we nevertheless notice and infer that he was younger (1 Kings 19:21). In the Acts of the Apostles, Barnabas took Mark, Paul took Silas, Paul took Timothy, and Paul took Titus (Acts 12 and elsewhere).

### 101. In those earlier examples, however, we see duties divided, with the elders prevailing in counsel and the younger in service. Often those unequal in age but equal in virtue take delight in one another’s association, as Peter and John did. We read in the Gospel—and on his own testimony—that John was a young man; [Note: The Roman edition cut out the words “and by his own voice,” but they are found in the other editions and in all the manuscripts.] yet in merits and wisdom he was second to none of the elders. For venerable old age of character and gray-haired wisdom were present in him. An unstained life is the reward of a good old age.

## CHAPTER XXI

### The great value, for one’s commendation, of defending the weak, welcoming strangers, or performing similar services, especially for men of proven character. A condemnation of avarice follows, and prodigality is particularly censured in priests
102. This also contributes to the advancement of a good reputation: if you rescue a poor man from the hands of the powerful, or free one condemned to death, insofar as this can be done without disturbance; lest we seem to act more for the sake of ostentation than of mercy, and, while wishing to heal lesser wounds, inflict more serious ones. [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, book II, p. 381, line 29: “Glory and favor are gained above all by acts of defense,” etc. As for what Ambrose says about rescuing someone condemned to death, one may consult what we noted in volume I of our *Exposition of Psalm 118*, sermon 8, no. 41. Here I wish only to add that the caution inserted at this point arose from the fact that bishops, clerics, and even monks sometimes attempted, with zeal more fervent than prudent, to rescue defendants from punishment; by riots, or at least by giving occasion for serious complaints from imperial judges. Add that it could also happen that those whom they themselves had freed through bribery were accused of having been violently abducted from the bishops. To remove this abuse, therefore, certain laws were enacted by the emperors—for example, by Theodosius and Arcadius, in books XV and XVI, *On Punishments*. Moreover, Cujacius, in his *Paratitlon* on the Code, title “On Episcopal Hearings,” supposes that this custom, by which clerics and monks sometimes exempted the condemned from punishment, originated in the example of pagan priests; he asserts on the authority of Tacitus, Suetonius, and Plutarch that they possessed this right. A vestige of this ancient custom still remains among us: at Rouen, each year on the feast of the Ascension, one of those guilty of homicide is acquitted after ceremonially carrying on his shoulders the sacred bier of the Roman bishop. Likewise, at Orléans, whoever meets the new bishop as he enters the city, if he is burdened with guilt deserving capital punishment, receives the same grant of impunity. Ivo of Chartres mentions this privilege in letter 53.] Now, if you have freed someone oppressed by the wealth of a powerful man, and burdened more by faction than by the weight of his crime, this greatly strengthens the testimony to your excellent reputation.

103. Hospitality also commends many people. [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, book II, p. 386, line 37: “Theophrastus also rightly praised hospitality,” etc.] For it is a public form of humanity that a stranger should not lack lodging, that he should be received courteously, and that the door should be open to the newcomer. It is highly honorable, in the judgment of the whole world, to receive strangers with respect; not to let the grace of a hospitable table be lacking; to meet them with acts of generosity; and to inquire about the arrival of guests. [Note: Some manuscripts read “the door.” What grace and reward belong to one who receives guests and strangers! Great indeed is this, etc.]

104. This praise was bestowed upon Abraham, who kept watch before his door lest some stranger perhaps pass by; and he diligently maintained his lookout so that he might meet him, anticipate him, and ask him not to pass on, saying: “Lord, if I have found favor before you, do not pass by your servant” (Gen. 18:1 ff.). And therefore, as the reward of his hospitality, he received the fruit of posterity.

105. Lot also, his nephew, close to him not only by relationship but also by virtue, because of his hospitality turned away the punishments of the Sodomites from himself and his own household (Gen. 19:1 ff.).

106. It is therefore fitting to be hospitable, kind, and just, not desirous of what belongs to another; indeed, when provoked, to yield something of one’s own right rather than attack the rights of others; to avoid lawsuits, shrink from quarrels, and purchase concord and the blessing of tranquility. [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, book II, p. 383, line 30: “In every transaction ... equitable and accommodating, yielding much to many from his own right,” etc.] For a good man to relax something of his own right is not only an act of generosity but often also an advantage. First, to escape the expense of litigation is no small gain; then there is the further benefit that friendship is increased, from which many advantages arise—advantages that, though despised for a time, will later prove fruitful. [Note: All editions read: “which, if despised at some time, may later prove fruitful”; all manuscripts, however, read as in the text, except one or two, which have: “which, though he despise them for a time, will later prove fruitful.”]

107. In acts of hospitality, humanity should indeed be extended to everyone; but greater honor should be shown to the just. [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, book II, p. 384, line 22: “And so people commonly say that, when benefits are distributed, they follow the character of men,” etc.] For whoever receives a just man in the name of a just man will receive the reward of a just man, as the Lord declared (Matt. 10:41–42). So great, moreover, is the favor of hospitality with God that not even a cup of cold water is without the reward of recompense. You see that Abraham received God as a guest when he sought guests? You see that Lot received angels? [Note: Many editions and some manuscripts read: “How do you know whether, when you receive a guest, you may be receiving Christ ... since Christ is in the guest?”] How do you know whether, when you receive a human being, you may be receiving Christ? For Christ is in the guest, because Christ is in the poor, just as he himself says: “I was in prison, and you came to me; I was naked, and you clothed me” (Matt. 25:36).

108. It is therefore a pleasant thing to pursue not money but grace. [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, book II, p. 384, line 23: “But who, in the end, would not prefer the cause of the poor and excellent man,” etc. Also line 43: “But morals have been corrupted and depraved by admiration for wealth.”] Yet this evil has long since flowed into human minds: that money should confer honor, and that people’s minds should be captivated by admiration for riches. From this avarice insinuated itself, as a kind of barrenness of good works, so that people regard as a loss whatever is spent beyond custom. But even against avarice in this matter, lest it should be able to cause any hindrance, venerable Scripture has taken precautions, saying: “Hospitality with vegetables is better” (Prov. 15:17). And below: “Better is bread with sweetness in peace” (Prov. 17:1). Scripture does not teach us to be spendthrifts, but generous.

109. For generosity has two kinds: [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, book II, p. 382, line 12: “There are altogether two kinds of generous people, one of which is called extravagant,” etc. The examples of extravagance that Saint Ambrose adds here he had already attacked frequently in the preceding volume. Indeed, the luxury and wastefulness of banquets are described in their true colors not only elsewhere but in many passages of the book *On Elijah and Fasting*. On circus and theatrical spectacles, see especially *Exposition of Psalm 118*, sermon 5, p. 1025. As for his attacks on gladiatorial games, one may perhaps rightly infer that this cruel form of entertainment was not common at Milan; the ancient Fathers never failed to condemn it with the utmost disgust. Among later authors, besides the ancient writers, J. Lipsius discusses such contests most carefully in his two books of *Saturnalia*. Rosinus collected some material in *Roman Antiquities*, and Laurentius much in his *Polymathia*. Finally, he gives hunting spectacles as the last example of extravagant expenditure—namely, the circus displays in which unusual wild beasts, procured at enormous cost throughout Africa and other very distant regions, were exhibited to the people. Martial has many epigrams about this manner of hunting; Suetonius and others also have some material. Above all, however, one should consult Tertullian’s *On Spectacles* and Cassiodorus, book V of the *Variæ*.] one of liberality, the other of extravagant expenditure. [Note: The Bigot manuscript adds after the word “kinds”: “On the two kinds of generosity.” But this is written in the margin.] It is generous to receive a guest, clothe the naked, redeem captives, and assist those who have nothing by one’s resources; it is extravagant to overflow with lavish banquets and abundant wine, whence you have read: “Wine is extravagant, and drunkenness is insulting” (Prov. 20:1). It is extravagant to squander one’s own wealth for the sake of popular approval—as those do who dissipate their patrimony on circus games, theatrical shows, gladiatorial contests, or even hunts, in order to surpass the public celebrations of their predecessors, although all that they do is empty. For it is not fitting to be immoderate even in expenditures on good works.

110. Beautiful generosity toward the poor themselves is also to maintain moderation, [Note: Gratian: “It is also beautiful generosity, in the very gift given to the poor, to maintain moderation.”] so that you may have enough for more people: not to pour yourself out beyond measure for the sake of winning favor. [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, book II, p. 383, line 34: “Care must also be taken of one’s household resources,” etc.] Whatever proceeds from pure and sincere affection is honorable; [Note: Ibid., line 3: “Those expenditures are also better which concern walls, shipyards, harbors,” etc.] do not undertake unnecessary constructions, nor neglect necessary ones.

111. This is especially appropriate for a priest: to adorn God’s temple with fitting beauty, so that through this worship also the Lord’s palace may shine; to undertake works of mercy appropriate to the occasion; and to give as much as is proper to strangers—not what is superfluous, but what is suitable; not what overflows, but what accords with humanity. He must not seek favor for himself at the expense of the poor, nor show himself either too restrictive or too indulgent toward the clergy. The former is inhuman, the latter extravagant: either expense is lacking for the needs of those whom you ought to draw away from sordid schemes of commerce, or it exceeds what pleasure requires.

## Chapter XXII

A proper measure must be established between excessive leniency and severity; for those who attempt to insinuate themselves into the minds of others through calculated leniency achieve nothing solid or lasting, as the example of Absalom clearly demonstrates.

112. There should also be a measure in the very words and instructions, lest either excessive leniency or excessive severity be apparent. Many prefer to be more lenient so that they may seem good; but it is certain that nothing simulated or fabricated belongs to true virtue, and indeed it is not usually lasting. At first it blooms; as time proceeds, it is scattered and dissolves like a little flower. What is true and sincere, however, is established on a deep root. [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, book II, p. 380, line 11: “But if some, through pretense and empty display,” etc. Also p. 382, line 27: “And that very winning over of the multitude,” etc.]

113. And to prove our assertions by examples, since what is simulated cannot last but, flourishing only for a time, soon falls away, let us produce from the same family from which we have drawn many examples for moral improvement one testimony to simulation and deceit (2 Sam. 14:25).

114. Absalom was the son of King David (2 Sam. 15:1 ff.), distinguished in appearance, outstanding in beauty, and excellent in youth, so that no such man was found in Israel: immaculate from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head. He made for himself chariots and horses, and fifty men to run before him. He rose early and stood beside the gate on the road. If he noticed anyone seeking the king’s judgment, he approached him and said: “From what city are you?” He would answer: “I am from one of the tribes of Israel, your servant.” Absalom would reply: “Your words are good and straightforward, but no one has been appointed for you by the king to hear you. Who will appoint me judge? Whoever comes to me, whatever judgment he needs, I will vindicate.” With such words he caressed each person. And when they approached to bow before him, he would stretch out his hands, seize them, and kiss them. Thus he turned everyone’s hearts toward himself, while such flatteries touch the deepest feelings of those close to him.

115. But these pampered and ambitious men chose what was honorable and agreeable for the moment, and pleasant. When only a short delay had passed—the delay that the prudent prophet of them all thought should be introduced by yielding for a little while—they could not tolerate or endure it. Finally, though confident of David’s victory, he commended his son to those who were about to fight, so that they would spare him (2 Sam. 18:5). For that reason he preferred not even to take part in the battle, lest he should seem to raise arms against his son, even though he was a parricide. [Note: The Roman edition reads: “He did not wish to take part, lest he should seem to raise arms against him.”]

116. It is therefore clear that what is true is perpetual and solid, and that what is gathered sincerely rather than deceitfully endures; but what is prepared through simulation and flattery cannot continue for long.

## Chapter XXIII

Those whose loyalty has been purchased either with money or through influence have an unstable faith.

117. Who, then, would regard as faithful either those who are bought into obedience with money or those who are enticed by flattery? [Note: Ibid., p. 376, line 45: “For the situation is bad when what ought to be achieved by virtue,” etc. Also p. 381, line 42: “Philip rightly accuses his son Alexander in a certain letter,” etc.] The former frequently wish to sell themselves, while the latter cannot endure harsh commands. They are easily caught by a slight little compliment; if you touch them with a word, they murmur, abandon you, depart hostile, and leave in indignation. They prefer to command rather than obey, as though they thought that those whom they ought to have as their superiors should instead be indebted to them for the favor and subject to them.

118. Who, then, would consider faithful those whom he has believed he must bind to himself either with money or with flattery? For the man who has received money considers himself cheap and despised unless he is frequently bought again. Thus he is constantly awaiting his price; and the man who appears to have been won over by entreaty always wants to be asked.

## Chapter XXIV

One should strive for honors, especially ecclesiastical honors, by honorable means; but once office has been attained, it should be administered moderately and wisely. Inferior orders must not detract from the bishop through simulated virtues, nor should the bishop be envious of the clergy; rather, he must be just in all things, and especially in judgment.

119. I therefore think that one should strive for honor through good actions and a sincere purpose, especially ecclesiastical honor; so that there may be neither arrogant carelessness nor slack negligence, neither shameful affectation nor unbecoming ambition. Direct simplicity of heart is sufficient for everything and commends itself well enough.

120. In the office itself, neither harsh severity nor excessive leniency is fitting, lest we appear either to exercise authority or altogether to fail to fulfill the office we have undertaken. [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, book I, p. 363, line 5: “In exercising equality of justice, accessibility must also be practiced ... and yet gentleness must be approved in such a way,” etc.]

121. We must also strive to bind many to us through benefits and services, and preserve the favor that has been conferred, lest those who feel themselves gravely injured become forgetful of a benefit to which they are entitled. [Note: Cicero, book II, p. 376, line 12: “I hold this to be characteristic of virtue: to win people’s hearts,” etc. Also p. 384, line 12: “It is nevertheless possible by one’s efforts to benefit many,” etc.] For it often happens that those whom you have favored with your gratitude, or whom you have raised to some higher rank, you turn against you if you judge that someone unworthy should be placed above them. But it is fitting also for a priest, through his benefits or judgments, to show favor in such a way as to preserve equity, and to show deference to a presbyter or minister as to a parent.

122. Nor, because they have once been approved, should these men become arrogant; rather, as mindful of the favor shown them, they should maintain humility. Nor should the priest be offended if a presbyter, minister, or anyone from the clergy increases his reputation through mercy, fasting, integrity, teaching, or reading. [Note: Some manuscripts read: “For the praise of a teacher is pleasing to the Church,” etc.] For the praise of a teacher is a grace to the Church. It is good for someone’s work to be praised, provided it is not done with any desire for ostentation. Let the lips of one’s neighbors praise each person, and not his own mouth; let his works commend him, not his own efforts.

123. [Note: Blessed Ignatius repeatedly commands in many passages of his letters that clerics should obey their bishop just as God himself, especially in his letters to the Ephesians, Magnesians, and Trallians. Cyprian, in letters 55 and 65, teaches that heresies and schisms ordinarily arise from no other source than the clergy’s refusal and reluctance to obey their bishops. Theodoret presents a grievous example of this in Arius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book I, chapter 2; others present it elsewhere.] But if someone does not obey the bishop and wishes to exalt and elevate himself, to obscure the bishop’s merits through a feigned display of teaching, humility, or mercy, he proudly deviates from the truth. For this is the rule of truth: that you do nothing for the sake of commending yourself by which another is diminished; nor, if you possess something good, should you use it to deform or disparage another. [Note: The Thuanus manuscript reads: “so that there is no deceit in commending yourself,” etc. This is not a bad reading if one supplies a verb that may have been omitted by the scribe.]

124. Do not defend an evil person or think that holy things should be entrusted to one who is unworthy; nor, on the other hand, press and attack someone whose crime you have not discovered. [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, book II, p. 381, line 21: “This precept of duty must also be carefully observed: never to summon an innocent person to a capital trial ... Yet just as this must be avoided, so it should not be regarded as contrary to religious duty,” etc.] For although injustice quickly gives offense everywhere, it does so especially in the Church, where equity ought to exist and equality ought to be maintained, so that the more powerful may claim nothing for himself beyond what is due, and the richer may usurp nothing more. Whether poor or rich, people are one in Christ. Let no one who is holier arrogate more to himself; for he ought to be more humble.

125. Nor should we accept anyone’s person in judgment: let favoritism be absent; let the merits of the case decide. [Note: All editions and some manuscripts read: “let the merits of the case determine”; some manuscripts have “discern.” The Thuanus manuscript and all the most ancient copies, however, read: “let the merits of the case contend and compete,” that is, let them decide the matter.] Nothing weighs so heavily upon one’s reputation, indeed upon one’s faith, as to favor the more powerful in judgment by handing over the cause of the inferior; or to accuse a poor innocent person while excusing a rich person guilty of wrongdoing. It is indeed characteristic of humanity to favor those of higher rank, lest they think themselves injured or grieve at defeat. But first, if you fear giving offense, do not accept the judgment—if you are a priest, or anyone else, do not provoke it. You may remain silent in a merely financial matter, although it is a mark of steadfastness to stand by equity. But in God’s cause, where the danger concerns communion, even to conceal the sin is no small offense. [Note: Ambrose seems clearly to imply in these words that bishops were permitted to decline arbitration in secular causes and lawsuits, although others maintain that this office was imposed upon them by the Apostle in 1 Cor. 6:1 ff. Augustine nevertheless observes in *On the Work of Monks*, chapter 15, that Paul himself was unable to obtain exemption from such duties. Indeed, Christ himself refused to accept a complaint brought before him concerning an inheritance that one of two brothers did not wish to divide with the other. What wonder, then, if we find even the holiest bishops so often and so seriously complaining of the necessity of deciding lawsuits, forced upon them by the shamelessness of the people?]

## Chapter XXV

Benefits should be bestowed upon the poor rather than the rich. The rich either think that the return of the benefit was already owed by them, or resent appearing thereby to have become debtors; whereas the poor make God himself their debtor on their behalf and gladly acknowledge the benefits they have received. An exhortation to despise money is added.

126. What advantage is it to you to favor a rich man? Is it because he will repay his benefactor more quickly? [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, book II, p. 384, line 24: “From whom a quicker and more immediate repayment seems likely,” etc.] We more often favor those from whom we hope to receive a return of gratitude. But for that very reason we ought to devote ourselves more to the weak and needy, because on behalf of one who has nothing we hope for recompense from the Lord Jesus (Luke 14:12–13), who, under the appearance of a banquet, set forth a general pattern of virtue: we should bestow our benefits rather on those who cannot repay them, teaching that the rich should not be invited to banquets and feasts, but the poor. The rich appear to be invited so that they may in turn give us a banquet; the poor, because they have nothing with which to repay, make the Lord our recompense when they receive, and he has offered to make himself the debtor on behalf of the poor.

127. Even according to ordinary worldly practice, a benefit conferred upon the poor is more useful than one conferred upon the wealthy; [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, book II, p. 384, line 29: “But those who regard themselves as wealthy and honored,” etc.] for the rich disdain a benefit and are ashamed to be indebted for a favor. Indeed, he claims for his own merits what has been bestowed upon him, as though he had received it as something owed to him, or as though the giver had thought that the rich man would return it to him with greater abundance. Thus, in receiving a benefit, the rich, simply because they have received it, think that they have given more than they have accepted. [Note: Ibid., line 33: “But the poor man, when whatever has been done, thinks that he has been regarded,” etc.] The poor person, although he has no money with which to repay, returns gratitude. In this respect it is certain that he gives back more than he has received: money is discharged coin for coin, but gratitude is never exhausted. Money is emptied by repayment; gratitude, however, is repaid by receiving it and retained by repaying it. Moreover, what the rich man rejects, the poor man acknowledges: he confesses that he is bound by a debt, and considers that he has been assisted, not honored. He thinks that children have been given back to him, life restored, and his household preserved. How much better, then, to place a benefit with the good than with the ungrateful?

128. Therefore the Lord said to his disciples: “Do not possess gold, silver, or money” (Matt. 10:9), because, as with a sickle, he cuts down the avarice sprouting in human hearts. Peter also said to the lame man who had been carried from his mother’s womb: “I have neither silver nor gold; but what I have, I give you. In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise and walk” (Acts 3:6). Thus he did not give money; he gave health. How much better it is to have health without money than money without health! The lame man rose, receiving what he had not hoped for; he did not receive the money he had hoped for. Yet such things are scarcely found even among the Lord’s saints: that riches should be despised.

## Chapter XXVI

How ancient an evil avarice is is clear from many examples in the Old Testament; from these it is also evident how empty the possession of money is.

129. Human morals have been so overcome by admiration for riches [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, book II, line 43: “But morals have been corrupted and depraved by admiration for wealth,” etc.] that no one is thought worthy of honor unless he is rich. Nor is this a recent custom; rather, what is worse, this vice has long taken root in human minds. For when the great city of Jericho had fallen at the sound of the priests’ trumpets and Joshua the son of Nun had gained the victory, he learned that the strength of the people had been weakened by avarice and the desire for gold. For when Achan had taken from the spoils of the burned city a golden garment, two hundred didrachmas of silver, and a golden tongue—or gold plate—when brought before the Lord, he could not deny it, but disclosed the theft (Josh. 7:19 ff.). [Note: Erasmus and the later editions, together with the better manuscripts, read “tongue”; Ambrosius’ edition reads “line,” and many manuscripts read “rod,” while some have “golden plate.” Below, where we read “the law was delivered” with the better ancient manuscript, some copies have “the law of God was given,” and the Roman edition has “the law of God was enacted.”]

130. Avarice is therefore old and ancient: it began together with the oracles of the divine law—or rather, the law was delivered in order to restrain it. Because of avarice, Balak thought that Balaam could be tempted by rewards to curse the people of his fathers; and avarice would have prevailed had not the Lord commanded him to refrain from the curse (Num. 22:7 ff.). Because of avarice, Achan was put to death and had brought the whole people of his ancestors into destruction. Thus Joshua, who was able to make the sun stand still so that it would not move forward (Josh. 10:12–13), was unable to stop human avarice from spreading. At his voice the sun stood still; avarice did not stand still. With the sun standing still, Joshua completed his triumph; but while avarice advanced, he almost lost the victory. [Note: Erasmus and the later editions read “to make the sun stand still.”]

131. And what of Samson, strongest of all—was he not deceived by the avarice of the woman Delilah? Thus the man who tore apart a roaring lion with his hands; who, bound and handed over to foreigners, alone and without any helper, broke his bonds and killed a thousand of them; who tore apart ropes woven from sinews as though they were soft threads of flax—this man, with his neck bent upon a woman’s knees, was shorn and lost the adornment of his unconquered hair, the privilege of his strength. Money flowed into the woman’s lap, and favor departed from the man (Judg. 16:5 ff.).

132. Avarice is therefore savage, and money seductive: it contaminates those who possess it, but does not help those who do not possess it. [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, book II, p. 384, line 45: “Perhaps it helps the one who has it,” etc.] Suppose, nevertheless, that money sometimes helps; it helps one who is nonetheless inferior and desires it. What is it to one who does not desire it, who does not seek it, who does not need its assistance, and who is not swayed by the pursuit of it? What does it matter to others if the one who has money is richer? Is he therefore more honorable? For through possessing money honor is often lost, since one has more to guard than to possess. For we possess what we use; but what exceeds use does not have the benefit of possession, only the danger of custody.

## Chapter XXVII

In contempt for money there is a form of justice. Clerics and bishops ought to pursue this virtue, as well as several others; in particular, excommunication must not be imposed precipitately.

133. In sum, we know that contempt for money is a form of justice; and therefore we ought to avoid avarice and devote every effort to ensuring that we never do anything contrary to justice, but preserve it in all our actions and works.

134. If we wish to commend ourselves to God, let us have charity, be of one mind, pursue humility, and consider one another superior to ourselves. For this is humility: that no one arrogate anything to himself, and that he consider himself inferior. Let the bishop employ the clerics as his members, especially the ministers, who are truly sons; let him assign each person to the office for which he sees him to be fitted.

135. With pain even the part of the body that has become rotten is cut away, and it is treated for a long time to see whether it can be healed by medicines; if it cannot, then a good physician cuts it off. So it is the mark of a bishop’s good disposition to desire to heal the infirm, remove spreading ulcers, and cauterize some things rather than cut them off; finally, what cannot be healed, to cut it off with pain. Hence that most beautiful precept stands out all the more: that we consider not our own interests, but those of others (Phil. 2:4). In this way there will be nothing by which, whether angry, we indulge our own feeling, or, showing favor, grant something to our own will more than is just.

[Note: Here our Ambrose shows himself moved by the same feeling of piety with which the Church, the most loving mother of her children, declares herself affected when she is compelled in general councils to cut someone off from her body. The Synod of Ephesus, act 1, in the sentence passed against Nestorius, speaks thus: “Compelled by the sacred canons and by the letter of our most holy father and fellow-minister Celestine, bishop of the Roman Church, and shedding tears continually, we necessarily came to this mournful sentence against him.” Likewise, the Council of Chalcedon, act 1, and the seventh Council of Constantinople lament against Eutyches: “Therefore, weeping and groaning over his complete destruction, we decreed,” etc. See likewise in the Council of Chalcedon, act 3, the subscriptions of the Fathers against Dioscorus, especially those of Maximus, Cyrus, Constantine, Patricius, and Epiphanius.]

## Chapter XXVIII

Mercy is to be exercised more generously even at the cost of one’s own unpopularity. In this connection is related the memorable history of the sacred vessels broken by Ambrose for the redemption of captives, together with a most beautiful account of the lawful use of the gold and silver possessed by the Church. Then, after the deed of Saint Lawrence has shown who the true treasures of the Church are, rules are set forth for melting down and spending consecrated vessels.

136. This is the greatest incentive to mercy: that we sympathize with the misfortunes of others (Distinction 86, chapter *Pulchra*, § *Compatiamur*) and, as far as we can, aid the necessities of others—sometimes even beyond our means. For it is better, for the sake of mercy, to furnish grounds for accusation or to endure unpopularity than to display cruelty. Thus we once incurred unpopularity because we broke up sacred vessels in order to redeem captives; the Arians could have disliked this, though they disliked the deed less than having something with which to reproach us. For who is so hard, unfeeling, and iron-hearted as to dislike the redemption of a man from death, a woman from the defilements of barbarians—which are worse than death—or young women, boys, and infants from the contagion of idols, by which they were polluted through fear of death?

[Note: From this entire chapter we learn that, from the earliest centuries onward, there were precious vessels in the Church: some dedicated and consecrated for the use of the sacraments, others not so dedicated, but intended only for splendor and ornament. Both kinds existed in such abundance that they sufficed to redeem an innumerable multitude of captives. We further understand that Ambrose by no means disapproved of the Church’s golden furnishings, since he allows that they may lawfully be disposed of only in specific and defined cases, when other means are lacking. Thus, wherever some holy Fathers—Jerome, letter 2 to Nepotian; Chrysostom, homilies 52 on Matthew and 60 to the people of Antioch; Isidore of Pelusium, book II, letter 88; and Bernard, chapter 11 of the *Apology*—seem to condemn the use of gold or silver ornaments in churches, their meaning must be understood as condemning not legitimate use, but abuse: namely, either clearly profane luxury and pomp, or the perverse religious scruple of those who would more readily endure many poor people to perish than allow a golden vessel to leave the treasury. We recognize that those Arians were of this disposition, who sought, on the occasion of this deed—never sufficiently praised—to stir up prejudice against our saint. Compare what appears above, p. 86, no. 70, where we noted when these events occurred, as also in our admonition to these books *On the Duties of Ministers*.]

137. Although we acted in this matter not without some reason, we nevertheless dealt with it before the people in such a way as to confess, and to demonstrate at length, that it was far more expedient to preserve souls for the Lord than gold (Matt. 10:9). He who sent the apostles without gold gathered Churches without gold. The Church possesses gold (12, question 2, chapter *Aurum*), not in order to store it up, but to distribute it and provide aid in necessities. What need is there to keep what is of no help? Do we not know how much gold and silver the Assyrians carried off from the temple of the Lord (2 Kings 24:13)? Is it not better that priests melt it down for the nourishment of the poor, if other resources are lacking, than that a sacrilegious enemy carry it away after it has been profaned? Will not the Lord say: “Why did you permit so many needy people to die of hunger? You certainly had gold; you ought to have supplied them with food. Why were so many captives led away into commerce and not redeemed, and slain by the enemy? It would have been better for you to preserve vessels of the living than vessels of metal.”

[Note: Erasmus and the subsequent editions, with some manuscripts, read: “a priest melts them down for the nourishment of the poor” (the Roman edition, “for the nourishment”); some manuscripts read, “an enemy profanes and carries them off.” The Roman edition reads: “than that a sacrilegious person profane and carry them off,” etc. The Amerbach edition, with by far the greater number of others, reads as in the text, except that some manuscripts read *sacrilegiis* (“by sacrileges”) for *sacrilegus* (“a sacrilegious person”).]

[Col. 0140C] 138. No answer could be brought against these objections. For what would you say: “I was afraid that the temple of God would lack its ornaments”? He would reply: “The sacraments do not seek gold, nor are those things pleasing through gold which are not purchased with gold. The ornament of the sacraments is the redemption of captives. Truly, those are precious vessels which redeem souls from death. That is the true treasure of the Lord which accomplishes what his blood accomplished.” Then the vessel of the Lord’s blood [Col. 0141A] is recognized when redemption is seen in both, so that the chalice may redeem from the enemy those whom the blood redeems from sin. How beautiful it is that, when throngs of captives are redeemed by the Church, it may be said: “Christ redeemed these!” Behold gold that can be approved; behold useful gold; behold Christ’s gold, which delivers from death; behold gold by which chastity is redeemed and purity preserved.

[Note: [Col. 0141D] Erasmus’s edition and the editions following it, together with some manuscripts, read “I acknowledge,” with “when I see in both,” etc.]

139. Therefore I preferred to hand these men over to you as free rather than to reserve the gold. This number of captives, this order of persons, is more excellent than the appearance of cups.

[Note: [Col. 0141D] Some manuscripts read “the appearance of the vessels.”]

Gold ought to have served this purpose of the Redeemer: to redeem those in danger. I recognize that the blood of Christ poured into gold not only made it glow, but also impressed upon it, through the gift of divine action, the power of redemption [Col. 0141B].

140. Such gold the holy martyr Laurence [104] reserved for the Lord. When the treasures of the Church were demanded from him, he promised that he would show them. On the following day he led out the poor. When he was asked where the treasures were that he had promised, he pointed to the poor and said: “These are the treasures of the Church.” And truly they are treasures, in whom Christ is, in whom faith is. Finally, the Apostle says: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (II Cor. 4:7). What better treasures does Christ have than those in whom he said that he was? For it is written: “I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink; I was a stranger, and you welcomed me” (Matt. 25:35). And below: “Whatever you did for one of these, you did for me” (ibid., 40). What better treasures does Jesus have [Col. 0141C] than those in whom he loves to be seen?

141. Laurence displayed these treasures [Note: [Col. 0141D] Some manuscripts read: “Laurence, and he saw those whom he…”] and conquered, because even the persecutor could not take them away. Thus Joachim, who kept gold during the siege and did not distribute it to purchase provisions, both saw his gold snatched away and was led into captivity (IV Kings 24:13). Laurence, who preferred to distribute the Church’s gold to the poor rather than reserve it for the persecutor, received the sacred crown of martyrdom for the exceptional vitality of his interpretation. Was it ever said to Saint Laurence: “You ought not to have distributed the treasures of the Church or sold the vessels of the sacraments”?

142. What is required is that someone carry out this duty with sincere faith and discerning prudence. Certainly, if someone diverts the proceeds to his own use, it is a crime; but if he distributes them to the poor or redeems a captive, it is mercy. For no one [Note: (12, q. 2, chapter “Gold,” § “No one can”)] can say: “Why does a poor man live?” No one can complain that captives have been redeemed; no one can accuse anyone because the temple of God has been built; no one can be indignant because space has been enlarged for burying the remains of the faithful; no one can grieve because the dead find rest in Christian burials. For these three purposes it is lawful even to break up, melt down, and sell vessels of the Church that have been consecrated.

143. Care must be taken that the form of the mystical cup does not leave the Church, lest the service of the sacred chalice be transferred to impious uses. Therefore vessels that had not been consecrated were first sought within the Church; then they were broken into pieces; finally they were melted down and distributed in small portions to the needy, and they also contributed toward the ransom-price of captives.

[Note: [Col. 0141D] The edition and many manuscripts read “through small distributions”; the Thuanus manuscript and several others of good authority read “through the minutiae of the distribution.”]

If new vessels are lacking, and if there are none that plainly appear never to have been consecrated, I think that all things may lawfully and piously be converted to the uses mentioned above.

105 CHAPTER XXIX.

[Col. 0142B] The deposits of widows—and indeed of all the faithful—ought to be defended in the Church even at personal risk; this is illuminated by the examples of the priest Onias, Ambrose, and the bishop of Ticinum.

144. This must certainly be carefully observed: the deposits of widows must remain inviolate and be preserved without any violation—not only those of widows, but those of everyone. Faith must indeed be shown to all, but the case of widows and orphans is the more important.

145. Indeed, as we read in the Books of the Maccabees (II Macc. 3:10 ff.), everything deposited in the temple was preserved under the designation of widows. For when information had been given about the money—of which Simon, that wicked man, disclosed to King Antiochus that enormous sums could be found in the temple at Jerusalem—Heliodorus was sent [Note: [Col. 0141D] All editions and most manuscripts read “sent to Jerusalem”; but the better and older manuscripts consistently read “sent to the matter,” with “the present matter” understood, that is, sent to the very place.] to deal with the matter [Col. 0142C]. He came to the temple, disclosed to the high priest the envy aroused by the report, and explained the reason for his arrival.

146. Then the priest said that provisions belonging to widows and orphans had been deposited there; he also showed him certain property belonging to Hyrcanus son of Tobias, a holy man.

[Note: [Col. 0142D] The words “but some … and two hundred talents of gold” are absent from the Thuanus manuscript and many other manuscripts that are older and of better quality. We therefore strongly suspect them. Nevertheless, since they appear in some manuscripts and in all editions, we have not thought it appropriate to remove them. Four manuscripts read “some belonging to the orphan Tobias.”]

There were forty talents of silver and two hundred of gold. When Heliodorus wished to take these away and claim them for the king’s interests, the priests threw themselves before the altar, wearing their priestly robes, and tearfully called upon the living God, who had given the law concerning deposits, asking him to show himself the guardian of his commandments. The altered face and color of the high priest revealed the anguish of his spirit and the anxious concern of his mind. Everyone wept, because the place would be brought into contempt if the security of trust were not preserved even in God’s temple. Women girded their breasts and virgins shut themselves in and beat upon the door; some ran to the walls, others looked out through the windows; all stretched their hands toward heaven, praying that the Lord would assist his own laws.

147. But Heliodorus, undeterred by these things, pressed on with what he had undertaken [Col. 0143A] and surrounded the treasury with his attendants. Suddenly there appeared to him a terrifying horseman shining in golden armor; his horse was adorned with a magnificent covering. Two other young men also appeared, renowned for their strength, pleasing in beauty, radiant with glory, and splendid in dress. They surrounded him and, striking the sacrilegious man from both sides, scourged him continuously without interruption. What more need be said? Enveloped in darkness, he fell to the ground and lay there lifeless, struck down by this evident sign of divine action, with no hope of recovery remaining in him. Joy arose among those who had been afraid, and fear among the arrogant.

[Note: [Col. 0143C] Some editions read “and some of Heliodorus’s friends, chosen from among them.” Thereafter all editions and a few manuscripts read “so that he might ask that his life be spared.” Finally, the Roman edition alone reads “he was gasping out his life.”]

Some of Heliodorus’s companions, now cast down, begged Onias to grant him life, since he was breathing his last.

148. When the high priest made this request, the same young men appeared again to Heliodorus, clothed in the same [Col. 0143B] garments, and said to him: “Give thanks to the high priest Onias, through whom your life has been restored. But you, having experienced the scourges of God, go and announce to all your people how great a reverence for the temple and how great a power of God you have learned.” After saying this, they disappeared. Heliodorus, having recovered his breath, offered a sacrifice to the Lord, gave thanks to the high priest Onias, and returned to the king with his army, saying: “If you have any enemy or any plotter against your affairs, send him there, and you will receive him back scourged.”

149. Therefore, my sons, trust must be preserved regarding deposits, and diligent care must be applied. Your ministry shines forth splendidly in this matter if the pressure of a powerful person—pressure that neither a widow nor orphans can withstand—is restrained through the Church’s assistance; if you show that the commandment of the Lord has greater force with you than the favor of the rich.

150. You yourselves remember how often we have entered the struggle against royal assaults on behalf of the deposits of widows—or rather, of everyone [Col. 0144A]. This is a matter we share together. I shall offer a recent example from the Church of Ticinum, which was in danger of losing a widow’s deposit that it had accepted. For when the man who wished to claim it for himself by an imperial rescript brought the matter before the Church,

[Note: [Col. 0143C] Many and ancient manuscripts read “the clerics were asserting authority”; four read “were despising authority”; one reads “were putting forward”; another “were not holding, but asserting authority.” Nevertheless, the reading of the others and of the editions seems preferable, unless one wishes to understand by “were asserting” that the clerics were emphasizing and enlarging upon the imperial authority because they yielded to it; this fits well with what follows. Below, where the editions of Amerbach and Erasmus, together with some manuscripts, read “the form of the rescript was being read more directly: the master of offices, acting through the agentes in rebus, was pressing the matter,” Gill and the Roman edition, together with some manuscripts, read “the form of the rescript was being read: the direction of the master of offices,” etc. Some manuscripts read “the form of the rescript was directed, the master”; some others, “the form of the rescript, the plunder of the master”; finally, the remaining manuscripts—including the Thuanus and others of more approved quality—read as we have in the text. We have already explained in the previous volume what a rescript was and by what names it was called; on this matter one may also consult the jurist Bulenger, On the Roman Empire, book III, chapter 12. There are also certain other terms which, so that they may not delay the reader, we shall explain. In this passage, interpellare means the same as compellare: to summon, bring an action, and make a legal claim. By honorati are meant those who, having previously discharged public offices, possessed the distinction of honorary rank. Thus the word is to be understood not only here and in book III, chapter 7, but also in writers contemporary or nearly contemporary with Ambrose, as well as in the Theodosian Code, under the title “On the Office of the Judge.” See Cassiodorus, Variae, book II, letters 3, 4, 8, 29, and 40. Consult also the same Bulenger, On the Roman Empire, book II, chapter 16. Intercessores, according to Gothofredus in book I, On Pledges, were those whom the governors of the provinces appointed as executors. The Master of Offices presided over the palace offices. Agentes in rebus were so called because they acted under the Master of Offices, as Gothofredus explains under the title “On the agentes in rebus”; Bulenger treats both offices in On the Roman Empire, book III, chapter 14, and book VI, chapter 42. Finally, “the form of the rescript was read more directly” means plainly and openly, without any convoluted wording. We have discussed that widow’s deposit held by the Church of Ticinum in the Admonition to these books On the Duties.]

the clerics were not maintaining their authority; and the honorati and intercessores who had been assigned maintained that the emperor’s commands could not be resisted. The form of the rescript was read more directly: the regulations of the Master of Offices were in force, and an agens in rebus was pressing the matter. What more is there to say? [Note: [Col. 0144C] The Divion manuscript reads “it was believed”; the Feron and Laud manuscripts read “it was to be handed over.” But nothing should be changed in the reading of the other manuscripts and editions, since we often express by the past tense what we indicate as immediately future—for example, when we say “consider this done,” or “the city had been captured, unless help had arrived,” etc.] It had been handed over.

151. Nevertheless, after taking counsel with me, the holy bishop surrounded those rooms to which he had learned that the widow’s deposit had been transferred. When it could not be taken away, it was received under a written acknowledgment. Later it was again demanded under that acknowledgment: the emperor had repeated his command that he himself should come to us in person. This was refused. The emperor, having been shown the authority of divine law [Col. 0144B], the sequence of the reading, and the danger of Heliodorus, finally accepted the explanation. Later an attempt had also been made to proceed by stealth; but the holy bishop forestalled it and returned to the widow what he had received. Meanwhile trust remained safe:

[Note: [Col. 0144D] An old edition reads “oppression is not a matter of fear.” Elsewhere the same editions as the Roman edition, together with many manuscripts, read “because now the property, not the trust, is in danger”; the Thuanus manuscript and several others read “because the property is not in danger, trust was in danger.” Perhaps “is not” was written by scribal error for “and not,” or “not even”; unless here too there has been a transposition of “and not.”]

pressure is not a cause for fear, because now the property, not the trust, is in danger.

CHAPTER XXX.
