Conclusion of the book by an exhortation to avoid the envious and to pursue prudence, faith, and the other virtues.

152. My sons, flee wicked men; beware of the envious. There is this difference between a wicked man and an envious man: the wicked man takes pleasure in his own good, while the envious man is tormented by another’s; the former loves evil, the latter hates good. Thus the one who wishes well to himself is almost more bearable than the one who wishes evil to everyone.

153. My sons, think before you act; and when you have thought for a long time, then do what you approve. When an opportunity for an honorable death is given, it should immediately be seized.

[Note: [Col. 0144D] All editions, together with some manuscripts, read “An honorable death, when an opportunity,” etc. The Thuanus manuscript and other more authoritative copies read “An opportunity for an honorable death,” etc. This is more appropriate: not every death is honorable, and therefore not every opportunity for death should be seized.]

Delayed glory slips away and is not easily grasped.

108 154. Love faith, because through faith and devotion Josiah acquired for himself great affection from his adversaries; for he celebrated the Lord’s Passover when he was eighteen years old, as no one before him had done (IV Kings 23:21 ff.).

[Note: [Col. 0145A] Thus read many manuscripts, and the better ones; nevertheless, not a few manuscripts and all editions read “from all.” It is more probable, however, that Ambrose is alluding here to what is recorded in II Chronicles, chapter 35: that he engaged the king of Egypt in battle only reluctantly, and after he had tried affectionately to dissuade him.]

Therefore, just as he surpassed his predecessors through zeal, so you also, my sons, take up zeal for God. May zeal for God seek you out and consume you, so that each one of you may say: “The zeal of your house has sought me out” (Ps. 68:10). The Apostle was called a zealot of Christ (Luke 6:15). Why do I speak of the Apostle? The Lord himself says: “The zeal of your house has consumed me” (John 2:17). Let it therefore be God’s zeal, not that human zeal [Note: [Col. 0146A] The Carnutus manuscript reads “which produces envy.”] which envy produces.

155. Let there be peace among you, the peace that surpasses all understanding. Love one another. Nothing is sweeter than charity; nothing is more welcome than peace. You yourselves know that I have always loved you and still love you more than others: you have grown together in affection as sons of one father, into the bond of brotherhood.

156. Hold fast to what is good, and the God of peace and love will be with you in the Lord Jesus—to whom belong honor, glory, majesty, and power, with the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

BOOK THREE.

[Col. 0145]

107 CHAPTER ONE.

What David and Solomon taught us about how we should converse with our own heart; consequently, Scipio should not be regarded as the first author of the saying attributed to him. How beautifully the holy prophets spent their leisure; their leisure is compared with that of others, and it is shown that the righteous person is never alone or confined.

1. The prophet David taught us to walk about in our heart as though in a spacious house and to converse with it as with a good companion, so that he might speak to himself and converse with himself, as in the saying: “I said, I will guard my ways” (Ps. 39:2). Solomon, his son, likewise says: “Drink water from your own vessels and from the springs of your own wells” (Prov. 5:15); that is, use your own counsel. For “deep water is counsel in a man’s heart” (Prov. 20:5). “Let no stranger,” he says, “share you. Let the spring of your water belong to you alone, and rejoice with the wife who has been yours from your youth. Let the stag of friendship and the fawn of graces converse with you” (Prov. 5:17–18).

2. Therefore Scipio was not the first to know that one is not alone when one is alone; [Note: [Col. 0145D] Cicero, On Duties, book III, at the very beginning: “Publius Scipio, Marcus’s son, who was the first,” etc. Ambrose discusses this opinion much more fully in Letter 3 to Sabinus.] nor was he the first to know that he was no less occupied when he was at leisure. Moses knew it before him: although he was silent, he cried out (Exod. 14:15); although he stood idle, he was fighting. Indeed, he was not merely fighting but also triumphing over enemies whom he had not touched (Exod. 17:11 ff.). He was so at leisure that others supported his hands, yet he was no less occupied than the others: with idle hands he conquered the enemy whom those who were fighting could not defeat. Thus Moses spoke even in silence and worked even in leisure. Whose occupations were greater than this man’s leisure, who, stationed on the mountain for forty days, embraced the whole Law, and in that solitude was not without one who spoke with him (Exod. 24:15 ff.)? Hence David also says: “I will hear what the Lord God speaks within me” (Ps. 85:9). And how much greater it is if God speaks with someone than if he speaks only with himself!

3. The apostles passed by, and their shadow healed the sick. Their garments were touched, and healing was conveyed (Acts 5:16).

4. Elijah spoke a word, and the rain ceased and did not fall upon the earth for three years and six months. Again he spoke, and the jar of flour did not fail, nor was the vessel of oil emptied throughout the entire period of the daily famine (III Kings 17:1 ff.).

5. And since warfare delights many, what is more excellent: to accomplish a battle through the strength of a great army [Note: [Col. 0146D] Amerbach, Gill, and not a few manuscripts read “with great muscles”; “with great strength,” as in the others, is better. Immediately afterward, the editions following Erasmus, together with very few manuscripts, read “by their own merits”; Amerbach, together with many more and very authoritative manuscripts, reads “by his own merits.”] or through merits alone?

Elisha was sitting in one place, while the king of Syria brought a great mass of war against the people of the fathers, accumulated various stratagems of counsel, and sought to surround them with ambushes. But the prophet detected all his preparations and, present everywhere through the strength of his mind by God’s grace, announced the enemy’s plans to his own people and warned them of the places where they should be on guard. When this was disclosed to the king of Syria, he sent an army and surrounded the prophet. Elisha prayed and caused all those men to be struck with blindness; then he led them captive into Samaria, although they had come to besiege him (IV Kings 6:8 ff.).

[Col. 0147A] 6. Let us compare this leisure with the leisure of others.

[Note: [Col. 0147D] Cicero, On Duties, book III, p. 387, line 47: “But neither is this leisure like the leisure of Africanus, nor is this solitude,” etc.]

Others usually withdraw their minds from affairs in order to rest and remove themselves from the gathering and company of human beings; they either seek the seclusion of the countryside and pursue the solitude of fields, or, within the city, give their minds free time and indulge in quiet and tranquility. But Elisha either, in solitude, divides the Jordan by his passage, so that the lower part flows away while the upper part runs back toward its source (IV Kings 2:8); or, on Carmel, having removed the difficulty of conception, unexpectedly makes a barren woman fruitful in conception [Note: [Col. 0147D] Several manuscripts read “through difficulty and inability to bear, he makes conception fruitful”; some read “he makes conception fruitful.”]; or he raises the dead; or he moderates the bitterness of food and makes it sweet through the addition of flour; or, after distributing ten loaves, he gathers the leftovers once the people have been fed; or he makes iron that has fallen from an axe and sunk into the depths of the Jordan float upon the water by throwing wood into it [Col. 0147B]; or he cleanses a leper, changes drought by rains, or famine by fruitfulness (IV Kings 4:16 ff., and elsewhere).

7. When, then, is the righteous person alone, who is always with God? When is he solitary who is never separated from Christ? “Who,” he says, “will separate us from the love of Christ? I am confident that neither death nor life nor an angel…” (Rom. 8:35). When is he released from work who is never released from merit, by which the work is brought to completion? By what places is the one confined for whom the whole world is the possession of riches? By what estimation is he defined who is never encompassed by opinion? For he is, as it were, unknown and known; as it were, dying, and behold, he lives; as it were, sorrowful, and always more joyful; as needy, yet enriching others; as having nothing, and possessing everything (II Cor. 6:8). For the righteous man regards nothing except what is steadfast and honorable. Therefore, even if he appears poor to others, he is rich to himself: he is measured not by the worth of things that perish, but of things that are eternal.

CHAPTER II.

What philosophers discuss concerning the comparison of the honorable and the useful has no place among Christians, for whom nothing is useful except what is just. Which duties are perfect, and which intermediate? The same words apply differently to different persons; finally, the righteous man never seeks his own advantage at another’s expense, but always strives for the benefit of others.

8. Since we have spoken of the two preceding topics in which we treated the honorable and the useful, it follows that we must compare honorableness and usefulness with one another and ask what ought to be pursued.

[Note: [Col. 0147D] Cicero, On Duties, book III, p. 388, line 30: “Panaetius, therefore, having proposed three kinds,” etc.]

For, as we discussed above, whether something was honorable or shameful, and in the second place whether it was useful or useless, so here some think that we must inquire whether it is honorable or useful.

[Col. 0147D] 110

9. We, however, are moved by the concern that we might appear to set these things against one another as though they were in conflict, although we have already shown above that they are one: that nothing can be honorable unless it is useful, nor useful unless it is honorable.

[Note: [Col. 0148D] Cicero, On Duties, book III, p. 389, line 3: “For whether the honorable alone is good, as the Stoics hold,” etc.]

For we do not follow the wisdom of the flesh, in which pecuniary advantage is valued more highly, but the wisdom that is from God, in which the things highly esteemed in this age are regarded as loss.

10. For this *katorthōma* [κατόρθωμα], which is a perfect and complete duty,

[Note: [Col. 0148D] Ibid., line 15: “For what the Stoics call the highest good, appropriately,” etc.]

proceeds from the true source of virtue. Second to it is the common duty, which its very wording indicates is not a matter of difficult or exceptional virtue, but something that can be shared by very many. For to seek monetary gains is familiar to many, and to take pleasure in a more refined banquet and more agreeable meals is commonplace; but to fast and be self-controlled belongs to few, and not to be desirous of another’s property is rare. By contrast, the desire to take something from another and not to be content with one’s own is widespread, since in this most people share. Thus some duties are primary and others intermediate.

[Note: [Col. 0148D] Ibid., line 23: “All these duties the Stoics call intermediate duties, common duties,” etc.]

The primary are shared with few; the intermediate with many.

11. Finally, even in the same words there is often a distinction. We call God good in one way and a human being good in another; we call God just in one way and a human being just in another. Likewise, we call God wise in one way and a human being wise in another. The Gospel also teaches us this: “Therefore you also must be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect” (Matt. 5:48).

I read that Paul himself is both perfect and not perfect. For after saying, “Not that I have already received it, or am already perfect; but I pursue it, if I may apprehend it” (Phil. 3:12), he immediately adds: “Therefore, as many as are perfect…” (ibid., 15). There are two forms of perfection: one has intermediate numbers, the other complete numbers; one belongs here, the other there; one corresponds to human possibility, the other to the perfection of the future. But God is just in all things, wise above all things, and perfect in everything.

12. There is also a distinction among human beings themselves. Daniel is wise in one way, of whom it was said, “Who is wiser than Daniel?” (Ezek. 28:3); other wise men are wise in another way; and Solomon in yet another, for he was filled with wisdom beyond all the wisdom of the ancients and beyond all the wise men of Egypt (III Kings 4:29 ff.). It is one thing to possess wisdom in an ordinary way and another to possess perfect wisdom.

[Note: [Col. 0148D] Ibid., line 48: “But those who measure everything by profits and advantages, and do not desire them,” etc.]

The one who has ordinary wisdom is wise for temporal things and wise for himself, so that he may take something from another and add it to himself. The one who is perfectly wise does not know how to regard his own advantages [Col. 0149A], but directs his whole affection toward what is eternal, what is beautiful and honorable, seeking not what is useful to himself but what is useful to everyone.

13. Therefore let this be the rule by which we cannot go wrong between those two things, the honorable and the useful: the righteous person thinks that nothing should be taken from another and does not wish his own advantage to be increased through another’s loss.

[Note: [Col. 0149D] Cicero, On Duties, book III, p. 390, line 11: “Therefore, so that we may judge without error … some formula must be established,” etc. And below, line 21: “To take something from another, and to deprive a human being,” etc.]

The Apostle prescribes this rule for you when he says: “All things are lawful, but not all things are expedient; all things are lawful, but not all things build up. Let no one seek his own, but the other’s” (I Cor. 10:22); that is, let no one seek his own advantage, but the other’s; let no one seek his own honor, but the other’s. Hence elsewhere he says: “Considering one another superior to yourselves, each of you not looking to his own interests, but to those of others” (Phil. 2:3–4).

14. Let no one seek his own favor, and let no one seek his own praise, but the other’s. We can also observe this clearly declared in Proverbs, where the Spirit speaks through Solomon: “My son, if you are wise, you will be wise for yourself and for your neighbors; but if you turn out wicked, you alone will bear the evil” (Prov. 9:12). For the wise person counsels others, as the righteous person does, since both share the same form of virtue.

CHAPTER III.

The foregoing commandment—not to seek one’s own advantage—is pressed more insistently, first by the example of Christ, then by an interpretation of the name, and finally by the very structure and functions of the limbs. From this he shows how disgraceful it is to diminish another’s advantage, since by this crime both natural and divine law are violated, and in addition that which makes us superior to other living creatures is lost; finally, civil laws are trampled underfoot with the utmost disgrace.

15. If anyone therefore wishes to please everyone, let him seek in all things not what is useful to himself but what is useful to many, as Paul also sought. For this is to be conformed to Christ: not to seek what belongs to another, not to take anything away from another in order to acquire it for oneself (Phil. 2:6 ff.).

For Christ the Lord, although he was in the form of God, emptied himself in order to take the form of a human being and enrich it with the virtues of his works. Do you, then, strip the one whom Christ clothed? Do you remove the garments from the one whom Christ dressed? You do this whenever you desire to increase your own advantages through another’s loss.

[Col. 0149D] 16. Consider, O human being, from where you have taken your name: surely from *humus*, the earth, which takes nothing away from anyone but gives everything generously to all and supplies various fruits for the use of all living creatures. From this comes the name *humanity*, the distinctive and domestic virtue of a human being, which helps one’s companion.

17. Let the very form of your body and the functions of your limbs teach you.

[Note: [Col. 0149D] Cicero, On Duties, book III, p. 390, line 27: “For if each individual limb possessed this perception,” etc.]

Does one of your limbs claim for itself the functions of another limb? Does the eye claim the function of the mouth, or the mouth that of the eye, or the hand the service of the feet, or the foot that of the hands? Indeed, even the right and left hands have most of their functions divided between them, so that if you exchange their uses, it is contrary to nature. You would first strip the whole person before changing the functions of your limbs: for example, if you were to offer food with the left hand, or use the right hand to perform the left hand’s service of washing away food remnants—unless necessity should demand it.

18. Suppose you gave the eye the power to take away from the head its sense, from the ears their hearing, from the mind its thoughts, from the nostrils their sense of smell, and from the mouth its taste, and to gather all these faculties into itself. Would it not dissolve the whole structure of nature? Hence the Apostle beautifully says: “If the whole body were an eye, where would hearing be? If the whole body were hearing, where would smell be?” (I Cor. 12:17).

[Col. 0150B] We are all therefore one body and different members, but all are necessary to the body. For one member cannot say to another:

[Note: [Col. 0150D] The edition and a few manuscripts read “the member say to the member: ‘I do not need you,’” etc.]

“I have no need of you.” Indeed, those members that seem to be weaker are all the more necessary and generally require greater care for their protection. And if one member suffers, all the members suffer with it.

19. Therefore how serious it is that we should take something away from the one with whom we ought to sympathize, and that we should become a fraud and a source of harm to the one with whom we owe a shared service! This is surely the law of nature, which binds us to every form of humanity, so that as parts of one body we may show mutual consideration for one another. Let us not think that anything should be taken away, since it is contrary to the law of nature not to help.

Thus we are born so that the members may agree with one another, one may adhere to another, and they may serve one another through mutual service. If one fails in its duty, the others are hindered. If the hand tears out the eye, has it not denied itself the use of its own work? If it wounds the foot, how much benefit from its activities has it begrudged itself?

And how much more serious it is for the whole human being to be deprived than for one member! If the whole body is violated in one member, then surely in one human being the fellowship of all humanity is destroyed. The nature of the human race is violated, as is the congregation of the holy Church, which rises as one connected and compact body through the unity of faith and charity. Christ the Lord also, who died for all, will grieve that the reward of his blood [Col. 0150D] has been made void.

20. What is more, even the law of the Lord teaches that this rule must be observed: you must take nothing away from another in order to preserve your own advantage.

[Note: [Col. 0150D] Ibid., line 37: “And this is required much more by the very principle of nature, which is divine and human law,” etc.]

It says: “You shall not move the boundaries that your fathers established” (Prov. 22:28); it commands that you return your brother’s stray calf (Exod. 23:4); it orders the thief to die (Exod. 22:2); it forbids defrauding a hired worker of his due wage; it decrees that money be returned without interest (Lev. 19:13). For it is an act of humanity to assist one who has nothing; but it is harshness to extort more than you have given (Deut. 23:19).

[Note: [Col. 0151C] Thus read by far the greatest number of manuscripts, and the oldest; nevertheless, some manuscripts and all editions read “if for this reason the poor man needed your help,” etc.]

If he needs your help because he had no means of repaying from his own resources, is it not impious to demand more from someone who had no means of paying even a smaller amount, under the pretense of humanity? You therefore release another person’s debtor in order to condemn him to yourself, and you call this humanity, when it is an increase of injustice?

21. This is what makes us superior to other living creatures: other kinds of creatures do not know how to contribute anything, whereas wild animals seize and human beings give. Hence the Psalmist says: “The righteous man is compassionate and gives” (Ps. 37:21).

There are nevertheless some things to which even wild animals contribute. For they nourish their offspring by giving to them, and birds satisfy their young with their own food; but to the human being alone it has been granted to feed all as though they were his own. This is owed by the very law of nature. If it is not permissible to refuse to give, how is it permissible to take away?

Do not the laws themselves teach us this? They order that what has been taken from someone, together with compensation for the injury to the person or to the property itself, be restored, so that they may deter the thief from taking things either by penalties or by fines [Col. 0151B].

[Note: [Col. 0151D] Cicero, On Duties, book III, p. 390, line 36: “For this is what the laws look to, this is what they desire,” etc.]

22. Yet suppose that someone could either not fear punishment or evade the fine: is it worthy that one person should deprive another? [Note: The Roman edition reads, “that one should deprive another.”] This is a slavish vice, characteristic of the lowest condition; so contrary to nature that poverty seems rather to extort it than nature to recommend it. Yet the secret thefts of slaves are the public robberies of the rich.

[Col. 0151C] 23. What is so contrary to nature as to injure another for one’s own advantage, when natural affection persuades us to keep watch for everyone, endure hardships, and undertake labor on behalf of all; and when each person considers it glorious to seek the tranquility of everyone through his own dangers, and judges it far more gratifying to himself to have averted the destruction of his country than his own dangers, and esteems it more excellent to have devoted his services to his country than, living in leisure, to have led a tranquil life amid the abundance of pleasures?

## CHAPTER IV

Having shown more strictly that the person who harms another for his own advantage will pay a heavy penalty to his conscience, it follows that nothing is advantageous to one person which is not likewise advantageous to everyone; and therefore that the philosophers’ question concerning two shipwrecked men has no place among Christians, for whom charity and humility must be practiced everywhere.

24. From this, then, it follows [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, Book III, p. 391, line 1: “From which it follows that a person obedient to nature cannot harm a person.”] that a person who has been formed according to the guidance of nature, so as to obey it, cannot harm another; and that if he harms someone, he violates nature. Nor is the advantage he thinks he gains as great as the disadvantage that consequently befalls him. For what punishment is more severe than the wound of an inward conscience? What judgment is stricter than the domestic judgment by which each person is guilty before himself, and himself charges himself with having wrongfully inflicted an injury upon his brother? [Col. 0152B] Scripture commends this in no ordinary way [Note: All editions and a few manuscripts read, “Scripture condemns”; other manuscripts more elegantly read, “Scripture commends.” The reference is to the domestic judgment of conscience under discussion.], saying: “From the mouth of fools comes the staff of insult” (Prov. 14:3). Folly, therefore, is condemned because it commits insult. [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, Book III, p. 391, line 1: “But if he thinks that this must indeed be avoided, yet also those much worse things—death, poverty,” etc.] Is this not more to be avoided than death, than loss, than poverty, [Note: Some manuscripts add, “than exile, weakness, pain.”] than exile, than the pain of weakness? For who would not regard bodily defect or the loss of property as lighter than a defect of the soul and the loss of reputation?

114 25. [Note: Ibid., line 8: “Therefore there ought to be one thing common to all,” etc.] It is therefore clear that all ought to seek and hold to this: that the advantage of each individual should be the same as that of everyone, and that nothing should be judged advantageous unless it benefits the common good. How can something benefit one person [Note: All editions, along with a few manuscripts, read, “benefit one person which is useless to everyone?” Some somewhat more numerous manuscripts read, “benefit one person which harms everyone?” A few have both: “which is useless and harms everyone?” The reading adopted in the text is more suitable. Again, where all editions, together with one or two manuscripts of a later hand, read “the advantage of everyone,” the remaining manuscripts omit the words we have excised: “if the advantage of everyone is one, we are bound by nature’s law to consult,” etc.] if it is useless to everyone? What is useless harms. Certainly, it does not seem to me that someone who is useless to everyone can be useful to himself. For if there is one law of nature for all, then there is likewise one common advantage for everyone, and by nature’s law we are bound to consult the interests of all. Therefore, a person who wishes to benefit another according to nature cannot harm him contrary to nature’s law.

26. For if those [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, Book III, p. 393, line 26: “Chrysippus cleverly says … that those who run races,” etc.] who run in a stadium are so guided and instructed by the rules that each competes through speed, not fraud, and hastens toward victory in the race as much as he can, yet dares not trip or knock down another with his hand, how much more must victory in this course of life be pursued without fraud or deception of another [Note: Thus Ambrosius’ edition, together with very many of the oldest manuscripts. Erasmus and later editions, with others, read, “which we must seek,” etc.]?

27. Some ask [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, Book III, p. 391, line 24: “Perhaps someone might say: ‘Then must the wise man not…?’” Also p. [Col. 0153C] 400, line 20: “If a fool seizes a plank from a shipwreck,” etc.] whether, when a wise man is in a shipwreck, he may wrest a plank from a foolish shipwreck victim, and whether he ought to do so. For my part, although it might seem more beneficial to the common good for the wise man rather than the fool to escape the shipwreck, nevertheless it does not seem that a Christian, just, and wise man ought to seek life through another’s death. Thus, even if he encounters an armed robber, he cannot strike back at the attacker [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, Book II, p. 376, line 22: “If some disadvantage is brought upon us, let us repel and avenge it,” etc. [Col. 0153D] Also, *Pro Milone*: “If our life should fall into some ambush … every honorable means of saving our life ought to be employed.” Compare with Ambrose’s teaching here what Tertullian teaches on the same subject in his *Apology*; Cyprian, *Letter to the Thebans*, in the Priorian edition 56 and 57, to Pope Cornelius; the Council of Ancyra, canon 22, on involuntary homicide; and Basil, *Letter to Amphilochius*, canon 11. From these sources you will easily understand that our Doctor was instructed not in the school of Cicero and the other, admittedly more honorable, pagans, but in that same school of Christ in which those holy Fathers were taught.], lest, while defending his safety, he stain his piety. Concerning this there is an open and evident saying in the books of the Gospel: “Put your sword back in its place; for everyone who strikes with the sword will perish by the sword” (Matt. 26:52). What robber is more detestable than the persecutor who had come to kill Christ? Yet Christ did not wish to be defended by wounding his persecutors, though he wished to heal everyone by his own wound.

[Col. 0153B] 28. Why, then, should you judge yourself superior to another, when it is the mark of a Christian man to put another before himself, claim nothing for himself, assume no honor for himself, and demand no reward for his merit? Furthermore, why do you not accustom yourself rather to bear your own disadvantage than to seize another’s advantage? What is so contrary to nature as not to be content with what you have, but to seek and disgracefully covet what belongs to another? For if honor is according to nature—for God made all things very good—then disgrace is surely contrary to it. Honor and disgrace cannot therefore be compatible, since by nature’s law they are distinct from one another.

## CHAPTER V

The just person does nothing contrary to duty, even when he hopes to remain concealed; to signify this very point, the philosophers devised the tale of Gyges’ ring, which is dismissed and replaced by the certain and true examples of David and John the Baptist.

29. [Note: Some manuscripts read, “But lest we now make this book tedious.” Cicero, *On Duties*, Book III, p. 392, line 2: “But since the work we have begun … as though bringing it to a summit,” etc.] But now, to bring this book also to its culmination, as though directing our judgment toward the conclusion of our discussion, let nothing be sought except what is honorable. [Note: All editions read, “For the wise man does nothing except what is honorable”; but the words omitted here are absent from all manuscripts. Cicero, *On Duties*, Book III, p. 392, line 33: “Therefore let this class of deliberations be removed from consideration,” [Col. 0154C] etc. And below, line 37: “And likewise, in every deliberation, the hope of concealing and hiding,” etc.] The wise man does nothing except what is done sincerely and without fraud; nor does he do anything by which he would bind himself to any crime, even if he could remain hidden. For he is guilty before himself before he is guilty before others; and in his judgment the public disclosure of disgraceful conduct is not so shameful [Col. 0154A] as the conscience itself is. [Note: The Roman edition reads, “than the disclosure of conscience.” This is not quite correct; for the meaning here is not that public disclosure of disgraceful conduct is less shameful than disclosure of conscience, but less shameful than conscience itself—that is, than the inward awareness of the disgraceful deed. Below, the same Roman edition reads, “whom, when a great storm of rains had arisen, he made into earth, and into whom,” etc. We do not sufficiently understand the purpose of that alteration.] We can teach this not through fictitious tales, as the philosophers argued, but through the truest examples of just men.

30. Therefore I shall not invent a chasm in the earth that split open after being loosened by great rains [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, Book III, p. 392, line 40: “From this Plato introduces that Gyges who, when the earth had opened,” etc.], into which Gyges is said, according to Plato, to have descended and there encountered that fabulous bronze horse [Note: The Ambrosian and Erasmian editions read, “that fabulous horse”; Gill’s and the Roman editions read, “fabled,” etc.] which had doors in its sides. When he opened them, he noticed a golden ring on the finger of a dead man whose lifeless body lay there, and, greedy for gold, took the ring. But when he had returned to the royal shepherds, one of whom he himself was, it happened that he had turned the bezel of the ring toward his palm [Note: All manuscripts read, “the bezel”; three of them, for clarification, add in the margin: “Alternatively, the setting”—for this is what he calls the upper part of the ring in which the stone is set.], and he saw everyone while no one saw him. Then, when he turned the ring back into its proper position, he was seen by everyone. Having learned the power of this marvelous object, through the ring’s opportunity he committed adultery with the queen, killed the king, and, after putting to death the others whom he thought should be killed lest they hinder him, gained the kingdom of Lydia.

31. “Give,” he says [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, Book III, p. 392, line 49: “If the wise man himself possesses this very ring,” etc.], “this ring to a wise man, so that by its power he may remain hidden when he has committed a crime.” For he will flee the contagion of sin no less than if he could not remain hidden. Concealment is not the wise man’s hope of impunity, but innocence. Finally, the law was established not for the just but for the unjust (1 Tim. 1:9), because the just man has the law of his own mind and the standard of his equity and justice. Therefore he is recalled from guilt not by fear of punishment but by the rule of honor.

[Col. 0154C] 32. Therefore, to return to the subject, I shall offer true examples in place of fables, not fables in place of truth. What need have I to invent a chasm in the earth, a bronze horse, and a golden ring found on the finger of a dead man—whose power was so great that the person wearing it appeared whenever he wished, while, whenever he did not wish, he withdrew himself from the sight of those present so that, though present, he could not be seen? [Note: Ibid., p. 393, line 3: “This is the power of this ring and of this example,” etc.] Surely the point is this: whether a wise man, even if he used such a ring by which he could conceal his own crimes and gain a kingdom, would refuse to sin and regard the contagion of crime as more grievous than the pain of punishment—or whether he would use the hope of impunity to commit crime. Why, I ask, do I need the fiction of a ring, when I can demonstrate from historical events that a wise man, seeing that if he committed a sin he would not only have to hide but would also have to reign, while, if he avoided the crime, he would face danger to his life, nevertheless chose the danger to his life in order to remain free from crime rather than the crime by which he could secure a kingdom?

33. Finally, when David was fleeing from King Saul, who was seeking him in the wilderness with three thousand chosen men in order to kill him, he entered the king’s camp and found him sleeping. He not only did not strike him himself but also protected him from being killed by one of those who had entered with him. For when Abishai said to him, “Today the Lord has delivered your enemy into your hands; shall I now kill him?” he replied: “Do not destroy him, for who can stretch out his hand against the Lord’s anointed and be guiltless?” [Note: The Roman edition adds, “And David said: ‘As the Lord lives.’”] And he added: “As the Lord lives, unless the Lord strikes him, or his hour comes that he should die, [Note: The old editions and the Roman edition do not differ here except that the latter punctuates the passage as follows: “and it is appointed to me, let it not be from the Lord,” etc. This evidently corresponds to the words of the Septuagint: Καὶ προστῇ, μηδαμῶς μοι—‘and should it happen, far be it from me,’ etc. The manuscripts agree more closely with the old editions, except that the latter prefer ‘into battle,’ while the manuscripts have ‘for battle’; and, instead of ‘descend,’ Thuanus reads ‘withdraw.’ Shortly afterward, where all editions read, ‘and he took the flask of water, and while they slept,’ etc., the manuscripts have the wording found in the text.] or he departs into battle and [death] be added to him—far be it from me to stretch out my hand against the Lord’s anointed” (1 Sam. 26:8 ff.).

34. Therefore he did not permit him to be killed, but took only the spear that was beside his head and the flask. Then, while everyone was sleeping, he left the camp, crossed to the summit of the mountain, and began to rebuke the king’s guards, especially Abner, the commander of the army, [Col. 0155C] because he had not provided a trustworthy guard for the king and his lord. Finally, he pointed out where the king’s spear and the flask beside his head were. When the king called to him, he returned the spear and said: “May the Lord repay each person according to his righteousness and his faithfulness. As the Lord delivered you into my hands, I did not wish to stretch out my hand against the Lord’s anointed.”” [Note: All editions read, “stretch out my hand against the Lord’s anointed”; some manuscripts read, “lay my hand upon,” etc.; all the others have the wording of the text.] Though he said these things, he nevertheless feared Saul’s ambushes and fled, changing the place of his exile. Yet he did not put his safety before innocence, since, when the opportunity to kill the king had been granted to him for a second time, he refused to make use of it—although it offered both security to one fearful for his life and a kingdom to an exile.

35. What need did John have of Gyges’ ring, if he could have remained silent and thus not been killed by Herod (Mark 6:18)? [Col. 0156A] His silence could have preserved him, so that he would both have remained alive and not been killed. But because he not only refused to permit himself to sin for the sake of defending his life, but could not even tolerate or endure another’s sin, he provoked the cause of his own death. Certainly those who deny that it could have happened that Gyges might have hidden himself through the ring’s power cannot deny that John could have kept silent.

36. But although the fable lacks the force of truth, it nevertheless has this purpose: that if a just man can conceal himself, he should nevertheless avoid sin as though he could not conceal himself; [Note: Some manuscripts read, “and hide himself not by putting on the ring but by putting on Christ.” Thus the Apostle says to the Romans.] and he should conceal his life not by putting on the ring but by putting on Christ, as the Apostle says: “For your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. 3:3). Therefore let no one here seek to shine, let no one claim distinction for himself, let no one boast (Luke 9:36). Christ did not wish to be known here; he did not wish his name to be proclaimed in the Gospel while he lived on earth. He came in order to remain hidden from this world. Let us, then, likewise hide our life after Christ’s example, flee boastfulness, and not seek to be proclaimed [Note: Erasmus and later editions read, “let us not desire to be proclaimed”; the Ambrosian edition and some manuscripts, “let us not expect to be proclaimed”; others more elegantly, “let us not expect it.”]. It is better to be in humility here and in glory there. “When Christ appears,” he says, “then you also will appear with him in glory” (Col. 3:4).

## CHAPTER VI

Advantage must not prevail among us. What those who seek profit from grain customarily allege, and what should be answered to them. The Gospel parable and Solomon’s sayings are set before them.

[Col. 0156C] 37. Let advantage therefore not overcome honor, but honor advantage [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, Book III, p. 394, line 26: “Let it remain, then, that what is disgraceful can never be advantageous,” etc.]—by advantage I mean what is judged according to popular opinion. Let greed be put to death; let covetous desire die. The holy man denies that he has entered into commerce, because seeking increases in prices is a matter not of simplicity but of cunning. Another says: “Whoever hoards grain is cursed among the people” (Prov. 11:26).

38. The judgment has been decisively stated, leaving nothing for debate, [Note: [Col. 0156D] All editions and some manuscripts read, “what kind of controversial argument”; others, more numerous and older, “what kind of disputed argument.” Below as well, where the same editions and few manuscripts read, “to be threefold simple,” the very many and best manuscripts omit “threefold.”] concerning the sort of controversial argument that commonly arises when one person claims that agriculture is universally regarded as honorable, that the fruits of the earth are simple, and that the person who has sown more will be more deserving of approval; [Note: Someone might reasonably conjecture that this entire passage was taken from Cicero’s *Oeconomica*, which no longer survives. For what is said here—“The more abundant returns of industry,” etc.—corresponds most plainly with these words of Xenophon, whose work on the same subject we know Cicero translated: Τοὺς γὰρ ἄριστα θεραπεύοντας αὐτὴν πλεῖστα ἀγαθὰ ἀντιποιεῖ, “For it repays those who care for it best with the greatest benefits,” and with these: ἀνὴρ οὐ λαμβάνει σῖτον ἐκ τοῦ ἀγροῦ, οὐ γὰρ ἐπιμελεῖται ὡς αὐτῷ σπείρηται ἢ ὡς κόπρος γίνηται, “A man does not obtain grain from the field, for he does not take care that it be sown for him or that it become manure.” You may observe other similar passages for yourself.] and that the more abundant returns of industry are not defrauded, while negligence and carelessness in uncultivated land are usually censured.

39. “I plowed,” he says, “more diligently; I sowed more abundantly; I cultivated more carefully; I gathered good yields; I stored them with greater care; I preserved them faithfully; I guarded them prudently. Now, at a time of famine [Note: The Roman edition had removed the word “I sell” here, but this was done to the injury of the other editions and all the manuscripts.], I sell and assist the hungry. I sell grain that is not another’s but my own, not for more than the others, indeed even for less. What fraud is there in this, when many could perish if they had nothing to buy? Is industry being called a crime? Is diligence being censured? Is foresight being blamed? Perhaps he will say: ‘Joseph also gathered grain in abundance and sold it during the famine.’ Is anyone compelled to buy it at a higher price? Is force used against the buyer? The opportunity to buy is offered to everyone; no injury is inflicted on anyone.”

40. After these arguments have been made as each person’s ability permits, another rises and says: “Agriculture is indeed good: it supplies fruits to everyone, and through simple industry it accumulates the fertility of the earth, introducing neither deceit nor fraud. Finally, if any defect occurs, it results in greater loss; for if someone sows well, he reaps better, and if he sows pure and sound grain, he gathers a purer and sounder harvest. Fertile earth returns multiplied what it has received; a faithful field customarily repays its yields with interest.”

41. From the revenues of rich soil, therefore, you ought to expect the reward of your labor; from the fertility of productive land [Col. 0157C] you ought rightly to hope for returns. [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, Book III, p. 394, line 31: “If a good man should bring a great quantity of grain from Alexandria to Rhodes,” etc.] Why do you turn nature’s industry to fraud? [Note: Some editions and manuscripts read, “nature’s industry and generosity.”] Why do you begrudge humanity the common fruits? [Note: Some manuscripts here and below read not *partus* (“fruits”) but *pastus* (“nourishment”). Elsewhere shortly afterward, some codices read, “when you auction it and store the grain because of the price.”] Why do you diminish abundance for the peoples? Why do you seek to produce scarcity? Why do you make the poor wish for barrenness? When they do not experience the benefits of fertility, because you raise the price and store away the grain, they prefer that nothing be born rather than that you trade upon the public hunger. You court a shortage of grain and a scarcity of food; you lament the abundant fruits of the soil; you mourn the public fertility; you deplore granaries full of crops; you investigate when the yield will be more barren, when the harvest will be poorer. You rejoice that your curses have succeeded, so that nothing has been born for anyone. Then you are happy that your harvest has arrived; then you pile up wealth for yourself from everyone’s misery. And you call this industry, you name this diligence—when it is the cunning of craftiness and the cleverness of fraud—and you call this a remedy when it is an invention of wickedness. Shall I call it robbery or usury? You lie in wait for the times of robbery, when you creep like a harsh ambusher into people’s very entrails. The price is increased as though by accumulated interest, by which the danger to people’s lives is heaped up. Interest multiplies for you on the stored grain; you conceal grain like a moneylender and raise the price like a seller. Why do you pray evil upon everyone, wishing the famine to become greater, as though no grain remained, as though a less fertile year were approaching? Your profit is the public loss.

42. The holy Joseph opened his granaries to everyone; he did not close them. He did not seek to raise the price of provisions, but established a lasting source of aid. He acquired nothing for himself; instead, through prudent organization, he arranged how the famine might be overcome even in the future (Gen. 41:56).

43. You have read how the Lord Jesus exposes this hoarder of grain and seeker of profit in the Gospel. [Note: Erasmus and later editions read, “the lands reserved for the price of grain.”] His estate had produced rich crops, and he, as though in need, said: “What shall I do? I have nowhere to store my harvest. I will pull down my barns and build larger ones” (Luke 12:17–18), [Col. 0158B] though he could not know whether his soul would be required of him the following night. He did not know what to do; as though he lacked food, he remained perplexed. His barns could not contain the provisions, and he thought himself in need.

44. Solomon therefore rightly says: “Whoever withholds grain will leave it to the nations” (Prov. 11:26)—not to his heirs, because the profit of greed does not come into the rights of successors. What is not acquired legitimately is scattered, as though by certain winds, with outsiders seizing it. And he adds: “Whoever hoards provisions is cursed among the people, but blessing belongs to the one who shares” (ibid.). [Note: All editions and a few manuscripts read, “but his blessing is on his head.” Erasmus and later editions read, “on the head of the one who shares.” This reading agrees with the Hebrew text and the principal versions; nevertheless, the oldest codices, together with the Chaldean Paraphrase, omit the words “on the head,” without any inconvenience to the meaning.] You see, therefore, that one ought to be a distributor of grain, not a seeker of profit from its price. This, then, is not true advantage, when more is taken away from honor than is added to profit.

## CHAPTER VII

Those who expel foreigners from the city in a time of famine are by no means to be approved. An outstanding decision of a Christian old man on this matter is reported; an unworthy deed committed at Rome is set against it; and, by comparing the two, it is shown that the first was joined with honor and advantage, while the second was not.

45. Nor should those who prohibit foreigners from the city be approved [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, Book III, p. 394, line 6: “Those also act wrongly who prevent foreigners from using the cities,” etc.]. To expel them at the time when they ought to be helped, to separate them from the common parent’s markets [Note: Many manuscripts, and not the least authoritative, read “common parents.” This is not entirely unsuitable, since it may refer to the words below, “[Col. 0159C] most of them are also our parents.” Yet “common parent”—that is, Rome, which was like the mother of the whole empire, or rather the earth, which is the common mother of all—is more harmonious.], to deny them the fruits that have been spread abroad for everyone, and to undo the partnerships of life already established: with those who have shared common rights, to refuse to share assistance in a time of need. Wild animals do not expel wild animals, yet a human being excludes a human being. Even beasts and animals regard as common to all the food that the earth supplies. They also help creatures of their own kind; a human being attacks one who ought to regard nothing human as alien to himself.

46. How much more rightly did that man act who, when he had advanced to old age, the city was suffering famine, and—as commonly happens in such circumstances—the people were demanding that foreigners [Note: The Roman edition reads, “be expelled from the city.” It is difficult to determine who that pious old man was on whose advice the foreigners were not expelled from Rome. Yet it seems certain that he was devoted to the Christian religion, since Ambrose calls him a most holy old man. Moreover, he appears to have been in charge not of the grain supply but of the city; the former was under the latter’s authority, and both had responsibility for the civic grain supply, as J. C. Bulengerus states in Book VI, chapter 2, of *On the Roman Empire*. We would not say that Ambrose’s words point elsewhere: “bearing the responsibility of the urban prefecture, greater than the others”; these words include not only the lesser offices but especially the grain prefecture, as well as the distribution of grain, concerning which Bulengerus likewise writes in Book V, chapter 13. As for Baronius’s opinion that this event should be attributed to Gracchus, although it rests on no evidence from any authority, it at least involves no contradiction. Since he places the second famine mentioned immediately afterward in the year 383, what prevents the earlier one from having occurred in 376 or 377, during which years Gothofredus reports that Gracchus held the prefecture in Book III of *Questions*, where he also explains two passages, one from Jerome and one from Prudentius, concerning the same prefecture? On this point, however, Hermann, in Book I, chapter 6, of his *Life of Ambrose*, does not agree with Gothofredus, nor does he agree with Baronius concerning the famine of 383; for in Book III, chapter 8, he thinks it exceedingly likely that the first occurred in that year.] should be expelled from the city—he, bearing the responsibility of the urban prefecture, greater than that of the others, summoned the honorable and wealthy men and asked them to deliberate together. [Note: Erasmus and later editions read: “saying how monstrous it would be to expel foreigners, how inhuman it would be to strip a human being of humanity,” etc. The Ambrosian edition and nearly all manuscripts have the wording of the text, except that some read “from a human being” instead of “by a human being”; others combine both readings.] He said how monstrous it was to expel foreigners, how one human being would be stripped of humanity by another who denied food to one who was dying. We do not tolerate unfed dogs before our tables, yet we exclude human beings. How unprofitable it would also be for so many peoples to perish in the world, peoples whom dreadful wasting disease was consuming; how many would perish to the loss of their own city, though they had been accustomed to assist it either by contributing aid or by conducting commerce; [Note: Thus the Ambrosian edition and the manuscripts, with greater agreement. Erasmus and later editions read, “helping no one through another’s hunger”; that reading avoids ambiguity but does not preserve the author’s words.] how no one could relieve another’s hunger; how they could at most prolong a day, but not drive away poverty; indeed, once so many inhabitants had perished and so many farmers had died, the supplies of grain would disappear forever. “Are we therefore excluding those who have been accustomed to bring us food? Do we refuse to feed in a time of need those who have fed us throughout our whole life? How much is supplied to us by them even at this very time! ‘Man does not live by bread alone’ (Deut. 8:3). There is our household there; most of them are also our parents. Let us repay what we have received.”

47. “But we fear that we may increase the scarcity.” First of all, mercy is never diminished but increased. [Col. 0159C] In addition, let us redeem the grain supplies that must be distributed to them by collecting contributions; let us restore them with gold. Surely, when these people are gone, do we not seem to need to redeem other cultivators for ourselves? [Note: Gill’s marginal note and certain Paris editions in the text read, “How much more advantageous it is,” etc. Incorrectly: here “more cheaply” means “at less cost and expense.”] How much cheaper it is to feed a cultivator than to purchase one! Once they are gone, where will you recover them, where will you find someone to restore? And even if you find someone whom you can replace in number, though inexperienced and unaccustomed to the land, you cannot replace him in cultivation.

[Col. 0160A] 48. Why say more? Gold was contributed, and grain was collected. Thus he neither diminished the city’s abundance nor deprived foreigners of food. How great a commendation this brought the most holy old man before God, and how great a glory before human beings! Truly great was this man who could truly say to the emperor, pointing out the peoples of the whole province: “I have preserved all these for you; they live through the benefit of your senate; your council has rescued them from death.”

49. How much more advantageous this was than what was recently done at Rome: that people who had spent most of their lives there were expelled from that vast city, leaving with their children in tears, as though they were lamenting the exile of citizens who had to be removed; relationships among many were broken, and marriages and family ties were severed. And certainly the fertility of the year had been favorable; the city alone lacked imported grain. It could have been helped if grain had been requested from the Italians, whose children were being expelled. Nothing is more disgraceful than to exclude someone as though he were a stranger and demand from him as though he were one’s own. Why do you expel the person who feeds himself from his own resources? Why do you expel the person who feeds you? You retain the slave and drive out the parent? You accept the grain but do not offer affection? You extort food but do not repay gratitude?

50. How disgraceful and how useless this is! For how can what is unbecoming be useful? 121 How many resources of the corporate associations [Note: “Corporations” are those enrolled in societies and guilds of various crafts, such as sculptors, painters, and others. Symmachus discusses them in Book X, letters 27 and 58. See Gothofredus on Book II of *On the Privileges of Corporations* in the *Theodosian Code*, as well as Scaliger and others.] has Rome recently been deprived of? It could both have retained them and escaped famine, while waiting for favorable winds and the arrival of the hoped-for ships’ supplies.

51. How honorable and useful, by contrast, was that earlier action! [Col. 0160C] What is so proper and honorable as to assist the needy through the contributions of the wealthy, provide food for the hungry, and ensure that no one lacks nourishment? What is so useful as to preserve cultivators for the fields [Note: The editions and a few manuscripts read, “to preserve cultivators of the fields.”], rather than allow the rural population to perish?

52. Whatever is honorable is therefore useful; and whatever is useful is honorable. Conversely, whatever is useless is unbecoming; and whatever is unbecoming is also useless.

## CHAPTER VIII

Those who prefer what is honorable to what is useful are approved by God, as is clear from the examples of Joshua, Caleb, and the other scouts.

[Col. 0161A]

53. When could our ancestors have escaped slavery unless they had believed that serving the king of the Egyptians was not only disgraceful but also useless (Exod. 12:34 ff.)?

54. Jesus and Caleb, sent to reconnoiter the land, reported that it was indeed fertile but inhabited by extremely fierce peoples. Terrified by war, the people recoiled and refused to take possession of that land (Num. 13:28 ff.). The scouts Jesus and Caleb urged that the land was advantageous; they regarded it as dishonorable to yield to the nations. They preferred to be stoned, as the people threatened, rather than abandon what was honorable. [Col. 0161B] Others tried to dissuade them; [Note: Some manuscripts read, “the people objected, saying.”] the populace protested, saying that war with those savage and harsh peoples would be unavoidable, that they would fall in battle, and that their wives and children would be given over to plunder.

55. The Lord’s indignation blazed up, and he wished to destroy them all. But at Moses’ entreaty he moderated his sentence and postponed vengeance, judging that it was sufficient punishment for the faithless that, although he spared them for the time being and did not strike down the unbelievers, they would nevertheless not enter the land they had refused because of the price of their unbelief. The children and women, however, who had not murmured, and who were pardonable by reason either of sex or of age, would receive the promised inheritance of that land. Finally, all those who were twenty years old and above fell dead in the wilderness, though the punishment of the others was delayed. But those who had gone up with Jesus and had advised against it [Note: The editions, together with one or two manuscripts, read, “immediately died from a severe plague,” etc.] died at once from a great plague, while Jesus and Caleb entered the promised land with those who were innocent by reason of age or sex (Num. 14:6 ff.).

56. The better party therefore preferred glory to safety; the worse preferred safety to honor. The divine judgment approved those who thought that honorable things should be preferred to useful ones; but it condemned those for whom what seemed advantageous to safety outweighed what was suited to honor.

122 ## CHAPTER IX

Fraud and dishonorable profits are especially unbecoming to clerics, whose duty is to serve the advantage of all. They must by no means intervene in monetary cases, though they should do so in capital cases. They must harm no one, even when provoked: David is offered as an example. Nor should they prefer life to honor: the killing of Naboth is set before them.

57. Nothing, therefore, is more disgraceful than to have no love of honor, to be enticed by ignoble gain through a kind of degenerate commercial practice, to burn with avarice in one’s heart, to gape day and night for the ruin of another’s estate, and not to lift one’s mind toward the splendor of honor or contemplate the beauty of true praise.

58. [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, Book III, p. 398, line 2: “To me, indeed, even genuine inheritances do not seem honorable,” etc.] From this arise inheritances sought by hawking and solicited through a pretended appearance of restraint and dignity—[Note: Thus the great majority and oldest manuscripts; some, however, and all printed editions read: “inheritances sought by angling.”]—a practice abhorrent to the purpose of a Christian man. For everything elicited by contrivance and arranged by fraud lacks the merit of simplicity. Even among those who have accepted no office in the ecclesiastical order, an affected ambition for an inheritance is judged unbecoming. Those placed at the final limit of life have their own judgment, so that they may freely testify to what they think, since afterward they will not amend it. Yet it is not honorable [Note: Erasmus and the subsequent editions removed *competentia*, although the word occurs in Amerbach’s edition and nearly all the manuscripts. What is said here concerning both pecuniary and capital cases should be compared with what occurs above, pp. 93 and 100.] to divert from others advantages [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, Book III, p. 398, line 11: “A just man … will take away from no one anything that he may transfer to himself,” etc.] that are either owed or prepared for them, since it belongs to a priest or minister to benefit everyone, if possible, and harm no one.

59. Finally (14, Question 5, chapter “Denique”), if one person cannot be helped without another being harmed, it is better for neither to be helped than for one to be burdened. Therefore it is not the priest’s business to intervene in pecuniary cases, in which it cannot happen that the defeated party is not frequently harmed, since he considers himself defeated through the intercessor’s favor. It is therefore the priest’s duty to harm no one and to wish to benefit everyone; but to be able to do so belongs to God alone. For in a capital case, to harm someone whom one ought to help when he is in danger is not without grave sin. In a pecuniary case, however, to incur hatred is foolish, since serious troubles frequently arise for a man’s safety—and in such a cause even to face danger may be glorious.

Let the pattern set before us therefore be maintained in the priestly office: [Note: Ibid., line 14: “Let him now teach himself that the good man is one who benefits those whom he can and harms no one unless provoked by injury.” See also what we have noted on this subject above, p. 114, no. 27.] that he harm no one, not even when provoked or offended by some injury. For the man who said, “If I have repaid those who repaid me with evil” (Psalm 7:5), is a good man. What glory is there if we do not harm one who has not harmed us? But virtue consists in forgiving when one has been harmed.

60. How honorable it was [Note: Ibid., p. 396, line 28: “Whether the good man is one who benefits those whom he can and harms no one,” etc.] that, although he could have harmed an enemy king, he preferred to spare him (1 Samuel 24:5 and following)! How useful it was as well, since this benefited his successor, so that all might learn to preserve loyalty toward their own king, not to usurp power, but to show reverence! Thus honor was preferred to usefulness, and usefulness followed honor.

123

61. It was not enough that he spared him: he added that, although the man had been killed in war, he grieved over him and lamented him tearfully, saying:

“Mountains of Gilboa, let neither dew nor rain fall upon you. Mountains of death, for there the protection of the mighty was taken away—the protection of Saul. [Note: Thus the majority of the more authoritative manuscripts, to which the editions also conform, except that they read: “but by blood”; other manuscripts read: “as though he had not been anointed with oil and with the blood of the wounded.”] He was not anointed with oil and the blood of the wounded, nor with the fat of warriors. The arrow of Jonathan did not turn back, and the sword of Saul did not return empty. Saul and Jonathan, handsome and most beloved, inseparable in life, were not separated in death; swifter than eagles, stronger than lions. Daughters of Israel, weep over Saul, who clothed you in scarlet garments with your ornaments, who placed gold upon your apparel. How have the mighty fallen in the midst of battle? Jonathan was wounded in death. I grieve for you, my brother Jonathan; you were exceedingly dear to me. Your love had fallen upon me, like the love of women.” How have the mighty fallen, and the weapons of war perished” (2 Samuel 1:21 and following)?

62. What mother would mourn an only son in such a way as this man mourned an enemy? Who would pursue the author of his favor with such praises as this man bestowed upon the one who had plotted against his life? How piously he grieved, with what depth of feeling he groaned! The mountains withered under the prophetic curse, and divine power fulfilled the sentence of the one who pronounced the curse. Thus, in response to the spectacle of the king’s death, the elements themselves discharged their punishment.

63. What, then, was the cause of death for holy Naboth, if not his contemplation of honor? When the king asked him for his vineyard, promising to give him money in return, Naboth refused an ignoble price for his ancestral inheritance, and preferred to avert such disgrace by death. “Far be it from me,” he said, “that the Lord should give you the inheritance of my fathers” (1 Kings 21:3)—that is, “May God not permit such dishonor to be inflicted upon me; may he not allow such a disgrace to be extorted from me.”

He is certainly not speaking about vines—for God is not concerned with vines, nor with a piece of land—but about the right inherited from his fathers. He could indeed have received another vineyard from the king’s vineyards and become his friend; and in this the usefulness of the present age is commonly thought to consist. But what was disgraceful he judged not to be useful. He preferred to face danger with honor [Note: Erasmus and the subsequent editions read: “with honor rather than usefulness.”] rather than usefulness with disgrace. I speak of ordinary usefulness, not that usefulness in which there is also the grace of honor.

64. Finally, the king himself could have extorted the vineyard, but he considered the act shameless and grieved when Naboth was killed. The Lord also announced that the woman’s savagery [Note: The Roman edition reads, “the savagery of the woman’s mouth”; many manuscripts read, “the savagery of the woman’s audacity”; others, more numerous, as well as Amerbach’s and Erasmus’s editions, read as in the text.]—who, forgetful of honor, preferred disgraceful gain—would be punished with a fitting penalty.

[Column 0163D] 65. Every fraud, therefore, is disgraceful. [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, Book III, p. 396, line 29: “It is never useful to sin, because it is always disgraceful,” etc.] Finally, even in matters of little value, the falsification of the balance and fraudulent measurement are detestable. If fraud is punished in the marketplace of saleable goods and in commercial dealings, can it appear blameless among the duties of virtue? Solomon cried out: “A large weight and a small one, and differing measures, are unclean before the Lord” [Note: All printed editions read “before God”; all manuscripts read “before the Lord”; some, “before God.”] (Proverbs 20:10). Above he likewise says: “A deceitful balance is an abomination to the Lord, but a just weight is acceptable to him” (Proverbs 11:1).

## CHAPTER X

That fraud is to be avoided in every contract, and that this is commanded not only by civil law but also in the sacred Scriptures, as the example of Joshua and the Gibeonites makes clear.

66. In all things, therefore, fidelity is honorable, justice pleasing, and a measure of equity delightful. [Note: Some manuscripts read: “a measure of equality.”] But why should I speak of other contracts, especially the purchase of estates, or settlements and agreements? [Note: All editions include: “Are these not formulas of honor?” The phrase “of honor” is absent from all manuscripts.] Are not these the formulas: that fraud be absent, and that the one whose fraud has been detected be liable to a double penalty? [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, Book III, p. 396, line 5: “And this bad fraud too was punished by the laws,” etc. Also below, line 31: “And as for the law concerning estates … he would incur a double penalty,” etc.]

Everywhere, therefore, the consideration of honor prevails: it excludes deceit and drives out fraud. Hence the prophet David rightly expressed this general judgment: “He has done no evil to his neighbor” (Psalm 14:3). Not only in contracts—where defects in the things being sold are also required to be disclosed, and, if the seller has not revealed them, even though he has transferred them into the buyer’s legal possession, they are voided by an action for fraud [Note: Ibid., line 34: “Whatever defect is present in an estate, they held that it ought to be disclosed,” etc.]—but generally in all things deceit must be absent: simplicity must be made manifest and truth declared.

67. Divine Scripture clearly presented this ancient rule concerning deceit—not as a formula of jurists, but as the judgment of the patriarchs—in the book of the Old Testament that bears the title *Joshua son of Nun*. For when news had spread among the peoples that the sea had been dried up during the Hebrews’ crossing; that water had flowed from a rock; that daily nourishment from heaven had been supplied in abundance to so many thousands; that the walls of Jericho had collapsed under the sacred sound of trumpets, the blows and shouting of the people [Note: Thus nearly all manuscripts; all editions, however, read “struck by sound and shouting,” though “by blows” refers to the striking together of jars.]; that the king of the Hittites had been defeated and hanged upon a tree until evening—the Gibeonites, fearing the powerful hand of the Hebrews, came by stealth, pretending that they were from a distant land. They had traveled for a long time, they said, and had split their sandals and worn away their clothing, displaying the signs of their age. They claimed that the reason for all this labor was their desire to obtain peace and enter into friendship with the Hebrews. They began asking Joshua son of Nun to establish an alliance with them.

Because he was still unfamiliar with the region and ignorant of its inhabitants, he did not recognize their fraud, nor did he consult God; instead, he believed them quickly.

68. So holy was their faith in those days that it was not thought possible for anyone to deceive them. Who would criticize this in holy men, who judge others according to their own disposition, and, because truth is dear to them, think that no one lies, while they do not know what it means to deceive? They readily believe what they themselves are, and cannot suspect what they are not.

Hence Solomon says: “The innocent believes every word” (Proverbs 14:15; 22, Question 4, chapter “Innocens”). This readiness is not to be blamed, but goodness is to be praised. To be innocent is to be unaware of what may cause harm; and even if someone is deceived, the person who believes that there is faithfulness in everyone nevertheless judges everyone favorably.

[Column 0165B] 69. Inclined by this devotion of mind to believe them, he arranged the covenant, granted peace, and confirmed the alliance. But when they came into their lands and the fraud was discovered—that although they were neighbors, they had pretended to be foreigners—the people began to resent that their ancestral community had been deceived.

Joshua, however, did not think that the peace he had granted should be revoked, because it had been confirmed by the sanctity of an oath. He did not wish, while accusing another’s faithlessness, to break his own faith. Nevertheless, he punished them by assigning them the lower service of menial labor. The sentence was more merciful, but also more lasting; for the penalty of their ancient craft remains in their services, assigned to them by hereditary obligation even to this day (Joshua 9:15 and following).

## CHAPTER XI

By introducing certain examples of fraud through rhetorical reticence, it is shown that these and all other frauds are condemned more openly in Scripture.

70. I shall not mark out the finger-snappings involved in acquiring inheritances, nor the naked successor’s dances [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, Book III, p. 398, line 7: “Suppose that a good man possessed this power: that if he snapped his fingers … But if Marcus Crassus were given this power … in the marketplace, believe me, he would dance.” The striking or snapping of the fingers is used for something utterly trivial; hence the proverb, “I would not buy it for a snap of the fingers.”]—for these things too are commonly noticed—nor the carefully arranged retinue of a pretended fishing expedition, designed to entice the buyer’s interest. Why, indeed, was he found to be so devoted to luxury and refinement that he was willing to practice such a fraud?

71. Why should I speak of that pleasant and secluded retreat near Syracuse, and of the Sicilian’s craft [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, Book III, p. 395, line 30: “Gaius Canius, a Roman eques … when he had gone to Syracuse for leisure, not for business,” etc.]? When he had encountered a foreigner and learned that the man desired to purchase gardens, he invited him to dinner in the gardens.

[Note: Erasmus and the subsequent editions, with two recent manuscripts, read: “The guest promised that he would come the next day; when he came, he encountered,” etc.]

The guest came the next day and found a great crowd of fishermen, a banquet splendidly prepared, and, in full view of the diners before the little gardens, fishermen arranged where they had never before cast their nets. Each man eagerly offered whatever he had caught to the banqueters. Fish were heaped upon the table and sprang back, striking the eyes of those reclining there. The guest marveled at such an abundance of fish [Note: Some manuscripts read, “and at the great number of guests.”] and such a multitude of boats.

When he asked the reason, he was told that there was a water source there, and that countless fish gathered there because of the fresh water. What more is there to say? The host enticed the guest into taking the gardens from him. Wishing to sell them, he was compelled to accept the price reluctantly. [Note: Amerbach and a number of manuscripts read “when asked, he accepts”; other editions read “with difficulty”; manuscripts read “burdened, he accepts.”]

72. The next day the buyer came to the gardens with his friends and found no boat. When he asked whether the fishermen had some festival holiday that day, he was told that they did not, and that they had never been accustomed to fish there except on the previous day.

What authority would this man have to rebuke deceit, when he himself had pursued so disgraceful a deception for the sake of luxury? Anyone who rebukes another for sin must himself be free from sin. I shall not, therefore, bring such trifles before the authority of this ecclesiastical judgment, which condemns generally every desire for disgraceful profit and, in a brief summary, excludes frivolity and craft.

73. What shall I say of the man who, having learned that a will was false [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, Book III, p. 395, line 41: “Certain men from Greece [made] the false will of L. Minucius Basilius, a wealthy man,” etc.], although legally made by others, claims for himself an inheritance or legacy and seeks profit through another’s crime? Even the public laws bind the person who knowingly uses a false document as guilty of a criminal act. The rule of justice is clear: it is not fitting for a good man to depart from truth, to inflict unjust loss on anyone, or to attach any deceit to a transaction or contrive any fraud.

[Column 0166C] 74. What is clearer than the case of Ananias (Acts 5:1 and following)? He defrauded the proceeds of the field he himself had sold and placed part of the price at the apostles’ feet as though it were the whole amount; as guilty of fraud, he perished. He was certainly permitted to offer nothing, and he could have done so without fraud. But because he mingled fraud with the act, he gained not the grace of generosity but paid the penalty of deceit.

75. In the Gospel, the Lord also rejected those who approached him deceitfully, saying: “Foxes have dens” (Matthew 8:20), because he commands us to live in simplicity of heart and innocence. David likewise says: “You have practiced deceit like a sharp razor” (Psalm 52:4), accusing the evildoer and traitor, since such an instrument is used to adorn a person but often wounds him.

If anyone professes favor while weaving deceit after the example of a traitor, so as to betray to death the person whom he ought to protect [Note: Thus the manuscripts with great agreement, except one or two, in which, as also in the editions, one reads: “of Doeg the traitor … whom he ought to conceal and protect.”], he is judged by comparison with this instrument, which, through the fault of a drunken and faltering hand, is accustomed to wound. [Note: The Laudian manuscript reads: “Just as that Doeg, drunk with wine, acted maliciously.”] Thus, drunk with the wine of malice, Doeg brought death upon the priest Abimelech by the evidence of his deadly betrayal, because he had received the Prophet as a guest, whom the king, inflamed and goaded by envy, was persecuting (1 Samuel 22). [Note: Erasmus and subsequent editions read “Ahimelech.”]

## CHAPTER XII

Nothing dishonorable is to be promised, nor, if one has sworn to something unjust, is it to be observed; Herod is shown to have sinned in this way. The vow made by Jephthah is also censured, together with all other things that God does not wish to be fulfilled. Finally, Jephthah’s daughter is compared with and preferred to two Pythagoreans.

76. The disposition must therefore be pure and sincere, so that each person (22, Question 4, chapter “Unusquisque”) may speak plainly, possess his own vessel in holiness, and not lead his brother astray through verbal trickery; [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, Book III, p. 400, line 47: “What if a wise man were asked by someone who intended to make him his heir … to dance openly in the marketplace before entering upon the inheritance,” etc.] he must promise nothing dishonorable. And if he has made such a promise, it is more tolerable not to fulfill the promise than to do what is disgraceful.

77. Very often people bind themselves by the sacrament of an oath. Even after realizing that they ought not to have made the promise, they nevertheless fulfill what they pledged out of regard for the oath—just as we wrote earlier concerning Herod (above, chapter 9), who disgracefully promised a reward to a dancing girl and cruelly paid it. It was disgraceful that a kingdom was promised for a dance; it was cruel that a prophet’s death was given as the reward for the sanctity of an oath.

How much more tolerable would perjury have been in such a case! Yet it could be called perjury only if what a drunken and unmanned man had sworn amid wine and the chorus of dancers could be called an oath. The prophet’s head was brought in on a platter, and this was judged to be fidelity when it was actually madness.

78. Nor can I ever be persuaded that Jephthah made his promise without recklessness [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, Book III, p. 401, line 11: “What of Agamemnon, when he had vowed,” etc.]—that he would sacrifice to God whatever first met him upon his return within the threshold of his house—since he himself regretted his vow after his daughter came out to meet him.

Finally, he tore his garments and said: “Alas, my daughter! You have hindered me; you have become a goad of grief to me” (Judges 11:35).
