[Note: Older editions read: “You have hindered me, you have hindered me; you have become an impediment to me, a goad of grief.” The Roman edition reads: “You have deceived me, an impediment before my eyes; you have become a goad of grief to me.” The manuscripts agree among themselves except that some read “You have hindered me, a goad,” etc., while the others read “You have hindered me; a goad,” etc.]

Although he fulfilled the harshness of the sacrifice out of pious fear and dread, he nevertheless established and left to posterity an annual mourning to be lamented by succeeding generations. A harsh promise, and a harsher fulfillment, which even the one who made it had to mourn.

Finally, this became a command and decree in Israel, observed year after year: “The daughters of the people of Israel went to mourn the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite for four days each year” (ibid., 40). I cannot accuse the man who was compelled to fulfill what he had vowed; yet it was a pitiable necessity when it was fulfilled by parricide (22, Question 4, chapter “Unusquisque,” section “Miserabilis”).

79. It is better not to make a vow than to vow something whose fulfillment the one to whom it is promised does not wish. In Isaac, finally, we have an example (Genesis 22:13): in his place the Lord appointed a ram to be sacrificed to him. Not every promise, therefore, is always to be fulfilled (22, Question 4, chapter “Non semper”).

Indeed, the Lord himself frequently changes his decision, as Scripture indicates. In the book called *Numbers*, he had resolved to strike and destroy the people by death; but afterward, when Moses pleaded with him, he was reconciled to his people (Numbers 16:12 and following). Again he said to Moses and Aaron: “Separate yourselves from the midst of this congregation, and I will destroy them all at once” (Numbers 16:21). When they withdrew from the assembly, the earth suddenly split open and swallowed the impious Dathan and Abiram.

80. The example of Jephthah’s daughter is more excellent and more ancient than the example regarded as memorable among philosophers [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, Book III, p. 393, line 43: “They say that Damon and Pythias, the Pythagoreans, were so disposed toward one another,” etc. See also Book V of the *Tusculan Disputations*, p. 186, line 48; Valerius Maximus, Book IV, chapter 7; and Ambrose, *On Virgins*, Book II.] concerning two Pythagoreans. One of them had been condemned to death by the tyrant Dionysius. When the day of execution had been appointed, he asked permission to go home so that he might make arrangements for his family. To ensure that his faithfulness in returning would not be doubted, he offered a pledge for his death, on the condition that if he himself did not return by the appointed day, his guarantor would acknowledge that he must die in his place. The guarantor did not refuse the terms of the pledge, but awaited the day of execution with steadfast courage.

Thus one did not withdraw himself; the other received him on the appointed day. [Note: All editions and some manuscripts read “the other returned on the appointed day”; the remaining manuscripts variously read “he returned,” “he withdrew,” or “he was received.” The reading “the other received” found in the Thuanus manuscript and several others of better quality is not bad if it is referred to the guarantor; the meaning would then be precisely the same as if the text read: “The other promised that, unless the accused returned by the appointed day, he would undergo death.”]

This was so remarkable that the tyrant took into his friendship the men whose danger he had been pressing.

81. What, then, is a miracle in men distinguished by learning and reputation is found to be far more magnificent and illustrious in a virgin, who said to her grieving father: “Do for me as it has gone forth from your mouth” (Judges 11:36 and following). But she asked for a period of two months, so that she might go with her companions into the mountains, where they would lovingly mourn her virginity, destined for death. Neither the tears of her companions moved the girl, nor did grief bend her, nor did groaning delay her; no day passed her by, no hour deceived her. She returned to her father as though returning to a vow, and by her own will urged on his hesitation, making what had happened accidentally through impiety into a sacrifice of piety by deliberate choice.

## CHAPTER XIII

Judith, after undergoing many dangers for the sake of honor, is shown to have gained manifold benefits.

82. Behold Judith, remarkable in herself, who approached Holofernes, a man feared by the nations and surrounded by the Assyrians’ triumphant host. First she struck him by the charm of her beauty and the grace of her countenance; then she outwitted him with the elegance of her speech (Judith 10:12 and following). Her first triumph was that she brought back unimpaired modesty from the enemy’s tent; her second was that a woman won victory over a man [Note: Some manuscripts read: “She drove away the peoples with her son.”] and, by her strategy, routed the peoples (Judith 13:20).

83. The Persians shuddered at her boldness. What those two Pythagoreans are admired for, she did not fear: neither the danger of death, nor—what is more serious for good women—the danger to her modesty. She did not tremble before the blow of a single executioner, nor before the weapons of an entire army. A woman stood among the battle formations, amid victorious arms, secure in the face of death. As far as the magnitude of the danger was concerned, she went forth prepared to die; as far as faithfulness was concerned, prepared to fight.

84. Judith therefore followed honor, and in following it found usefulness. It belonged to honor to prevent the people of God from surrendering themselves to the profane; to prevent them from betraying their ancestral rites and sacred obligations; to prevent holy virgins, dignified widows, and chaste matrons from being subjected to barbarian impurity; and to prevent the siege from being ended by surrender. It belonged to honor to prefer risking herself for everyone so that she might rescue everyone from danger (Judith 8:10 and following).

85. How great was the authority of honor, that a woman should claim for herself counsel concerning the gravest matters [Note: The Thuanus manuscript reads: “nor presume upon assistance from the leaders of the people.”] and not entrust it to the leaders of the people! How great was the authority of honor, that she should presume upon God as her helper; how great the grace, that she should find him so!

## CHAPTER XIV

How honorable and useful Elisha’s deed was. Its comparison with the celebrated deed of the Greeks. John laid down his life for the sake of honor, and Susanna likewise exposed herself to mortal danger for the same reason.

86. What else did Elisha pursue but honor when he brought the Syrian army, which had come to besiege him, into Samaria as captives, after covering their eyes with blindness, and said: “Lord, open their eyes so that they may see.” And they saw (2 Kings 6:18 and following).

When the king of Israel entered intending to strike them and asked the prophet for permission to do so, Elisha replied that they should not be struck, since he had not captured them by his own hand or by weapons of war; rather, they should be helped with food. Finally, after being refreshed by a banquet, they decided never afterward to return as raiders into the land of Israel.

87. How much more sublime this was than the deed of the Greeks [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, Book III, p. 394, line 17: “After the victory in the war that was fought with the Persians, Themistocles,” etc. The same account is found in Plutarch’s *Aristides*.], when two peoples were competing with each other for glory and power, and one of them had the opportunity to burn the other people’s ships secretly, but considered the act dishonorable and preferred to have less power honorably than more power disgracefully.

Those men, indeed, could not do this without committing a crime: they would have deceived those who had gathered in alliance for the completion of the Persian war. Although they could deny the deed, they could not avoid blushing at it. Elisha, however, did not wish to destroy men who, though deceived, had been struck not by fraud but by the power of the Lord; he preferred to preserve them rather than destroy them, because it was honorable to spare an enemy and grant life to an adversary whom he could have killed had he not shown mercy.

88. It is therefore clear that whatever is honorable is always useful. Judith, through the honorable contempt of her own safety, ended the danger of the siege [Note: Some manuscripts read: “and acquired public honor and personal usefulness”; several others: “and acquired public honor through personal usefulness.” The remaining manuscripts and editions, more aptly, read as in the text.], and through her personal honor acquired public usefulness. Elisha likewise forgave more gloriously than he struck, and more usefully preserved the enemies whom he had captured.

89. What else did John consider but honor? He could not endure an illicit marriage even in a king, saying: [Note: The Roman edition reads: “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife.”] “It is not lawful for you to have her as your wife” (Mark 14:4). He could have remained silent unless he had judged it dishonorable, from fear of death, not to speak the truth; to bend prophetic authority before the king and cloak it with flattery. He knew, of course, that he would die because he opposed the king; yet he preferred honor to safety. And what could have been more useful than that his suffering brought glory to the holy man?

90. Holy Susanna too, when threatened with the terror of a false accusation and seeing herself pressed on one side by danger and on the other by disgrace, preferred to avoid disgrace through an honorable death rather than, out of a desire for safety, accept and endure a shameful life. Thus, while she devoted herself to honor, she also preserved her life. If she had chosen what appeared useful to her life, she would not have gained such glory; indeed, she might not have escaped the punishment of a crime that would have been not merely useless but dangerous (Daniel 13).

We therefore perceive that what is disgraceful cannot be useful, nor, conversely, what is honorable useless, because usefulness is always joined with honor, and honor with usefulness.

## CHAPTER XV

After recounting the noble decision of the Romans, it is shown from Moses’ deeds that he had the greatest concern for honor.

91. Orators relate as a memorable deed that, when the physician of an enemy king came to a Roman commander and promised that he would give the king poison, the commander bound him and sent him back to the enemy. Truly, it was a splendid act: the man who had entered into a contest of virtue did not wish to win by fraud. For he did not place honor in victory; rather, he declared that victory itself was disgraceful unless it had been sought through honor. [Note: Some manuscripts read: “he declared it disgraceful.”]

92. Let us return to our Moses and go back to what came before, so that we may bring forward examples that are both more excellent and more ancient. The king of Egypt did not wish to release the people of their fathers. Moses told the priest Aaron to stretch out his staff over all the waters of Egypt. Aaron stretched it out, and the water of the river was turned into blood; no one could drink the water, and all the Egyptians were dying of thirst, while clear streams abounded for the patriarchs (Exodus 7:20).

They cast soot toward heaven, and sores appeared, together with burning blisters on humans and quadrupeds (Exodus 9:10 and following). [Note: Older editions and some manuscripts read “falling blisters,” perhaps “hot” ones; some read “bursting” ones.] They brought down hail amid flaming fire, and everything upon the earth was crushed. Moses prayed, and everything was restored to favor: the hail ceased, the sores were healed, and the rivers supplied their customary drink (ibid., 30).

93. Again, when Moses had raised his hand, the earth was covered with darkness for three days, and the darkness was poured over it (Exodus 10:22). Every firstborn of Egypt was dying, while the entire offspring of the Hebrews remained unharmed. When Moses was asked to put an end to these further calamities, he prayed and obtained it (Exodus 12:29 and following). In this he is to be praised because he abstained from sharing in fraud; in the other matter he is admirable because, by his own power, he turned away from the enemy the punishments divinely threatened against him—truly, as it is written, exceedingly meek and gentle.

He knew that the king would not keep faith with his promises; nevertheless, he considered it honorable, when asked, to pray; when injured, to bless; and when assailed, to forgive (Numbers 12:3). [Note: Manuscripts and older editions differ only in that, where the text reads “when asked,” many manuscripts read “when he had been asked,” and where it reads “calamities,” some manuscripts have “endings.” The Roman edition, after “give,” added “and bless,” removing the words “he prayed and obtained it.”]

94. He threw down his staff, and it became a serpent that devoured the serpents of the Egyptians (Exodus 7:12), signifying that the Word would become flesh, which would empty the venom of the dreadful serpent through the remission and forgiveness of sins. For the staff is the direct, royal Word, full of power and the insignia of rule.

The staff became a serpent because he who was the Son of God, born from God the Father, became the Son of man, born from the Virgin. Raised up like a serpent on the cross, he poured healing into the wounds of humanity. Hence the Lord himself says: “Just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of man be lifted up” (John 3:14).

95. Finally, another sign performed by Moses also pertains to the Lord Jesus: “He put his hand into his bosom and brought it out, and his hand became like snow. Again he put it in and brought it out, and it was like the appearance of human flesh” (Exodus 4:6–7). This signified first the radiance of the Lord Jesus’ divinity, and afterward his assumption of flesh, in which all nations and peoples were to believe by faith.

He rightly put in his hand, because Christ is the right hand of God. Whoever does not believe in his divinity and incarnation is scourged like a reprobate—like that king who, because he did not believe the evident signs, was afterward scourged and prayed that he might deserve forgiveness.

How great, then, the disposition toward honor ought to be is demonstrated by these examples, and especially by the fact that Moses offered himself for the people, saying that God should forgive the people or else erase him from the book of the living.

## CHAPTER XVI

[Column 0172B]

After a brief introduction of Tobias, it is proved that Raguel surpassed the philosophers in honor.

96. Tobit also presented a clear pattern of moral excellence when, leaving the banquet, he buried the dead and invited the poor to the food of his modest table (Tobit II, 2 ff.). Raguel especially showed this concern for moral excellence: when he was asked to give his daughter in marriage, he did not conceal even her faults, lest by keeping silent he should seem to deceive the suitor. Thus, when Tobit’s son asked that the girl be given to him, he replied that by law she was indeed owed to him as a kinsman, but that he had already given her to six men, all of whom had died. This righteous man therefore feared more for others and preferred that his daughter remain unmarried rather than that strangers be placed in danger because of her marriage (Tobit VII, 13 ff.).

97. In a few words he resolved all the philosophers’ questions. [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, Book III, p. 395, line 4: “Let a good man sell a house because of certain defects that he himself knows,” etc.] They discuss the defects of houses, asking whether they ought to be concealed or disclosed by the seller; but our man here judged that even his daughter’s faults ought not to be concealed. And certainly he was not himself seeking to give her away, but was being asked to do so. We cannot doubt how much more morally upright he was than they, if we consider how much more important a daughter’s welfare is than the price of a saleable object.

## CHAPTER XVII

The great moral concern with which the ancient fathers, about to go into captivity, concealed the sacred fire

98. Let us consider another event that took place in captivity and possessed the highest moral beauty. For moral excellence is impeded by no adversity; indeed, it stands out and excels more in adversity than in prosperity. Amid chains, weapons, flames, slavery—which is more grievous to free people than any punishment—amid the punishments of the dying, the destruction of their country, [Note: Amerbach, with not a few manuscripts, reads “the fear of the men.”] the fear of the living, and the blood of the slain, the concern for moral excellence nevertheless did not perish from our ancestors. Rather, amid the ashes [Col. 0173A] and embers of their overthrown homeland, [Note: “It shone and gleamed in pious affections” is absent from several manuscripts, including some of inferior quality; in some of these, *nec inter* (“nor amid”) is read instead of *sed inter* (“but amid”), not without justification. The reading of the other manuscripts and of all the editions is preferable.] it shone and gleamed in their pious affections.

99. For when our fathers, who at that time were worshipers of almighty God, were being led away to Persia, the priests of the Lord secretly hid the fire taken from the altar in a valley. There was there something like an open well, infrequently visited because of the withdrawal of its water, inaccessible to common use, in an unknown and secluded place. There they concealed the hidden fire, marking it with a sacred sign and keeping silent about it (II Maccabees I, 19 ff.). [Note: Several manuscripts read: “like a well that was by no means open, rarely visited because of the withdrawal of its water”; one reads: “like a well that could not hold water”; another: “unable to hold water and rarely visited.”] [Note: “With a sacred sign,” that is, with some mystical mark by which the place could later be recognized.]

They did not take pains to bury gold or hide silver for preservation for their descendants. Rather, amid their extremity, they cared for moral excellence and judged that the sacred fire had to be preserved, lest either the impure contaminate it, or the blood of the dead extinguish it, or a heap of disfigured ruins destroy it.

100. Thus they went to Persia free in religion alone, since captivity could not extort that alone from them. But after a very long time, when it pleased God, he put it into the mind of the king of Persia to order that the temple in Judea be restored and the legitimate rites be reestablished in Jerusalem. To accomplish this favor, the king of Persia sent the priest Nehemiah. He brought with him the descendants of those priests who, when departing from their native land, had hidden the sacred fire so that it would not perish.

When they arrived, as the account handed down by their fathers relates, they found not fire but water. Since there was no fire with which to burn the altars, Nehemiah the priest ordered them to draw water, bring it to him, and sprinkle it over the wood. Then—an astonishing sight!—although the sky was covered with clouds, the sun suddenly shone out and a great fire was kindled, so that everyone, amazed at this manifest act of the Lord’s favor, was filled with joy. Nehemiah prayed, and the priests sang a hymn to God. [Note: The editions and a few manuscripts read: “a hymn to God until it was consumed,” etc.] When the sacrifice had been consumed, Nehemiah again ordered the remaining water to be poured over the great stones. When this had been done, a flame was kindled, [Note: So read the manuscripts and old editions with broad agreement, except that some manuscripts and editions read *consumptum est* (“was consumed”), whereas the most authoritative read *consummatum est* (“was completed”). The Roman edition alone reads: “which then, when the light had shone forth, was immediately consumed by the altar.”] and the radiant light from the altar was immediately completed.

101. When this sign had been revealed, the king of Persia ordered a temple to be built at the place where the fire had been hidden and where water had later been found; many gifts were brought to it. Those who were with holy Nehemiah called it *ephthar*, which means “purification”; many call it *nephthē*. [Note: The Roman edition, following the Septuagint, has *nehpthar*; the old edition, together with Aldus’s manuscript of the same Septuagint, has *ephthar*, a reading also supported by the manuscripts, except that many of them, through the ignorance of copyists, give *epathar*, others *ephatar*, and some even *phatur*. Below, where all editions and many manuscripts read *nephthē*, several manuscripts prefer *nephē*. See Pliny, Book II, chapter 118, and Book XXXV, chapter 15.]

It is also found in the accounts of the prophet Jeremiah that he ordered those who would live afterward to take some of the fire. This is the fire that fell upon Moses’ sacrifice and consumed it, as it is written: “For fire went out from the Lord and consumed all that was upon the altar, the burnt offerings” (Leviticus IX, 24). This fire was required to sanctify the sacrifice; and therefore, when the sons of Aaron attempted to bring strange fire, fire again went out from the Lord and consumed them, so that they were carried out dead beyond the camp (Leviticus X, 1 ff.).

101*. [Note: See column 204, note [“With a sacred sign,” that is, with some mystical mark by which the place could later be recognized]. If the same number occurs twice consecutively, even without an asterisk, let the reader understand that in such or similar cases we have changed nothing, unless perhaps a larger lacuna, caused by a more serious error, had intervened between the two numbers.]

When Jeremiah came to the place, he found a house shaped like a cave, together with a tent and an ark, and he brought in the altar of incense and blocked up the entrance. When those who had come with him searched more carefully in order to mark the place for themselves, they were entirely unable to comprehend or find it. When Jeremiah learned what they had intended, he said: “The place shall remain unknown until God gathers the assembly of the people and becomes reconciled to them. Then the Lord will reveal these things, and the majesty of the Lord will appear” (II Maccabees II, 5 ff.).

## CHAPTER XVIII

The preceding event, and especially the account of the sacrifice offered by Nehemiah, signifies the Holy Spirit and Christian baptism; likewise, the sacrifice of Moses and Elijah, and the history of Noah, are referred to the same mystery

102. We have the gathering of the people; we recognize the reconciliation of the Lord our God, which the Reconciler accomplished in his Passion. [Note: Several manuscripts read: “we do not recognize the reconciliation.” This is not inappropriate, provided it is expressed with the force of astonishment or a question.] I think that we cannot fail to recognize this fire either, when we read that the Lord Jesus baptizes with the Holy Spirit and with fire, as John said in the Gospel (John I, 33).

The sacrifice was rightly consumed, because it was for sin. That fire, however, was a type of the Holy Spirit, who was to descend after the Lord’s ascension and remit the sins of all, and who, like fire, inflames the faithful soul and mind. Hence Jeremiah, after receiving the Spirit, says: “And it came to pass in my heart as a burning fire, flaming in my bones; and I was dissolved on every side, and I cannot bear it” (Jeremiah XX, 9).

Moreover, in the Acts of the Apostles, when the Spirit had descended upon the apostles and upon many who were awaiting the Lord’s promises, we read that tongues appeared divided among them like fire. [Note: The Roman edition reads: “tongues appeared distributed.”] Finally, the spirit of each person was so inflamed that those who had received the diversity of languages were thought to be filled with new wine. [Note: Nearly all the manuscripts read: “they were thought to be filled with the diversity of languages.”] (Acts II, 4 ff.)

103. What, then, does it mean that fire became water and water kindled fire, unless it is because spiritual grace, through fire, burns away our sins, and through water cleanses them? Sin is both washed away and burned up. Hence the Apostle says: “The fire will test the quality of each one’s work” (I Corinthians III, 13); and below: “If anyone’s work is burned, he will suffer loss, but he himself will be saved, yet as through fire” (ibid., 15).

104. We have introduced this to prove that sins are burned away through fire. It is therefore clear that this truly is the sacred fire which then descended upon the sacrifice as a type of the future remission of sins.

105. This fire, then, is hidden during the time of captivity, when guilt reigns; but in the time of freedom it is brought forth. And although it has been changed into the appearance of water, it nevertheless preserves the nature of fire, so that it may consume the sacrifice. Nor should you be surprised when you read that God the Father said: “I am a consuming fire” (Deuteronomy IV, 24); and elsewhere: “They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water” (Jeremiah II, 13). The Lord Jesus himself, like fire, inflamed the hearts of those who listened (Luke XII, 49), and, like a fountain, refreshed them; for in his Gospel he says that he came in order to cast fire upon the earth and to provide living water to the thirsty (John VII, 37 ff.).

106. In Elijah’s time also fire descended, when he challenged the prophets of the nations to kindle the altar without fire. When they were unable to do so, he himself drenched his sacrifice with water three times, and the water flowed around the altar. Then he cried out, and fire fell from the Lord out of heaven and consumed the burnt offering (III Kings XVIII, 38).

107. You are that sacrifice. Consider each detail silently. [Col. 0175C] The breath of the Holy Spirit descends upon you; it seems to burn you when it consumes your sins. Finally, the sacrifice that was consumed in Moses’ time was a sacrifice for sin. Hence Moses says, as it is written in the Book of Maccabees (II Maccabees II, 11), that because what was for sin had not been eaten, it was consumed.

Does it not seem to you that the whole outer person is consumed when, in the sacrament of baptism, he perishes? [Note: All editions read: “our outer man is crucified.”] “Our old man has been nailed to the cross,” the Apostle declares (Romans VI, 6). There, as the examples of the Fathers teach you, [Note: All editions and several manuscripts read: “Egypt is submerged.”] the Egyptian is submerged and the Hebrew rises again, renewed by the Holy Spirit, who also passed unharmed through the Red Sea, where the fathers were baptized under the cloud and in the sea (I Corinthians X, 1 ff.).

108. In the Flood, too, in the time of Noah, all flesh died, yet the righteous man was preserved with his offspring (Genesis VII, 21 ff.). Is a person not consumed when this mortal life is brought to an end? [Note: Thus read the more numerous and better manuscripts; others, along with the editions, read: “when he is swallowed up.”] Finally, the outer person is corrupted, but the inner person is renewed.

This death of the flesh occurs not only in baptism but also in repentance, for the advancement of the spirit, as we are taught by apostolic authority, when Saint Paul says: “I have decided to hand over the one who has done this to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ” (I Corinthians V, 3–4).

109. The longer digression seems to have been made out of wonder at the mystery, while we strive to disclose more fully the sacrament that has been revealed—a sacrament so full of moral excellence that it is also full of religion.

## CHAPTER XIX

The outrage committed by the citizens of Gibeah against the wife of a certain Levite is related, and from its punishment it is inferred how deeply those ancient people cared for moral excellence

110. How great was our ancestors’ concern for moral excellence is shown by the fact that they pursued by war the injury inflicted upon one woman through sexual violence and, after defeating the people, swore to the tribe of Benjamin that they would not give them their own daughters in marriage. The tribe would have remained without any means of continuing its descendants unless it had been granted permission for the necessary fraud. Yet this indulgence does not seem to have been without a punishment appropriate to their intemperance, since they were permitted only to enter marriages by seizure, not with the solemnity of marriage. And indeed it was fitting that those who had violated another’s household should themselves lose the solemnity of marriage.

111. How full of compassion the story is! The man, it says (Judges XIX ff.), a Levite, had taken a wife—[Note: A few manuscripts read: “whom he called his concubine.”] whom I believe is called a concubine because of sexual relations. [Note: Observe how beautifully this confirms what we said in our discussion of Abraham, Book I, chapter 4, column 290, volume I, no. 23: namely, that a legitimate wife is quite often called by the name “concubine.”] After some time, having been offended by certain matters, as commonly happens, she withdrew to her father, and remained there four months.

Her husband then arose and went to his father-in-law’s house to restore relations with his wife, call her back, and bring her home. The woman met him and brought her husband into her father’s house.

112. The girl’s father rejoiced. He came out to meet him and sat with him for three days; they feasted and rested. On the following day the Levite rose early, but his father-in-law detained him so that he would not so quickly abandon the pleasure of the feast. On the second and third days, too, the girl’s father did not permit his son-in-law to depart, until all their joy and goodwill had been completed.

But on the seventh day, when the day was already declining toward evening, after the meals and cheerful banquets, when he pleaded the nearness of the coming night, thinking that he ought to rest among his own people rather than among strangers, he could not keep him and sent him away together with his daughter.

113. But after they had advanced some distance, when evening was already pressing near and they had approached the city of the Jebusites, the servant advised his master to turn aside to it. His master did not agree, because it was not a city of the children of Israel; instead, he aimed to reach Gibeah, which was inhabited by the people of the tribe of Benjamin.

There was no one to receive the travelers as guests except an elderly foreigner. When he saw them, he asked the Levite, “Where are you going, or from where have you come?” When the Levite replied that he was a traveler returning to Mount Ephraim and that no one had taken him in, the man offered him hospitality and prepared a banquet.

114. When they had eaten their fill and the tables had been removed, wicked men rushed upon the house and surrounded it. Then the old man offered his virgin daughter and the Levite’s wife, her equal, with whom she was accustomed to sleep, to the men of iniquity, merely so that violence would not be inflicted upon the guest. [Note: The editions and a few manuscripts read: “his wife, with whom he was accustomed to sleep.” The best and most numerous manuscripts, however, read as in the text.]

But when this reasoning accomplished little and violence prevailed, the Levite surrendered his wife to them. They had intercourse with her and abused her throughout the night. Overcome by the atrocity, or by the pain of the injury, [Note: Some manuscripts read: “before the guest’s lodging.” Erasmus and later editions read: “before the door of the lodging.”] she threw herself before the door of the host with whom her husband had lodged and breathed out her spirit. Even in her final act of life she preserved the proper affection of a good wife, leaving at least the rites of her burial to her husband.

115. When this became known—I will not delay over the details—nearly the whole people of Israel rose in fury for war. Although the battle remained uncertain and its outcome doubtful, on the third occasion of fighting the people of Benjamin was handed over to the people of Israel and, by divine judgment, paid the penalty for its intemperance.

Benjamin was also condemned so that no one would give his daughter to one of its men in marriage. This was confirmed by the oath of a sworn covenant. But when they were pierced with remorse because they had passed so harsh a sentence upon their brothers, they tempered its severity in this way: they took as wives virgins who had been deprived of their parents, whose fathers had been killed for the offense, or they joined themselves to them by seizure. For those who had violated the right of another’s marriage had shown themselves unworthy of obtaining marriage because of the disgraceful deed they had committed. Yet, so that the tribe might not perish from the people, connivance in the fraud was granted.

116. Thus it is revealed how great our ancestors’ concern for moral excellence was: forty thousand men drew the sword against their brothers of the tribe of Benjamin while seeking to avenge the injury to chastity. [Note: Some editions read “the injury of immodesty”; the others, and the manuscripts, more appropriately read “the injury to modesty”—namely, the injury suffered by chastity.] For violators of chastity were not tolerated. [Note: Gill, in the margin, and the Roman edition in the text read: “the violators of chastity were not offered up.”]

In that war sixty-five thousand warriors were killed on both sides, and the cities were burned. [Note: So read the editions and several manuscripts; others give forty thousand, or forty-five thousand. But unless Ambrose quoted the passage from memory, one must read sixty-five thousand, as is known to be found in the sacred books when the dead in each battle are reckoned.] Although the people of Israel had initially been defeated, even the fear of an adverse war did not shake them from their grief over the chastity that had to be avenged. They rushed into battle, as though preparing to wash away the stain of the crime with their own blood.

## CHAPTER XX

After the dreadful siege of Samaria had been lifted according to Elisha’s prophecy, the concern for moral excellence shown by the four lepers is related

117. And what wonder is it if that dignity and moral excellence were a concern to the people of God, when, as we read in the Books of the Kings (IV Kings VI), even the lepers did not lack consideration for moral excellence?

118. There was a great famine in Samaria, because the army of the Syrians had besieged it. The king anxiously inspected the military guards above the wall. A woman addressed him, saying: “This woman persuaded me to bring my son, and I brought him, and we cooked him and ate him. She promised that afterward she too would bring her son, and we would eat his flesh together. But now she has hidden her son and does not wish to bring him.” [Note: Several manuscripts read: “she denies having her son and hides him.”]

The king was moved because it appeared that the women were being fed not only on human corpses but even on the corpses of their own children, and, terrified by the example of so terrible a calamity, he announced the death of the prophet Elisha. He believed that it lay within Elisha’s power to lift the siege and drive away the famine—or perhaps he was angry because Elisha had not permitted the king to strike the Syrians whom he had afflicted with blindness.

119. Elisha was sitting with the elders [Note: The editions read: “in his house.” And below, two lines later: “this son of a murderer.” The manuscripts, however, almost unanimously read as in the text.] in Bethel. Before the king’s messenger entered, he said to the elders: “Have you seen that the son of that murderer has sent to take away my head?” Then the messenger entered and delivered the king’s order, announcing the immediate danger to his head (IV Kings VI, 32–33).

The prophet answered him: “At this hour tomorrow, a measure of fine flour will cost a shekel, and two measures of barley will cost a shekel at the gate of Samaria.” When the messenger sent by the king did not believe this, saying, “Even if the Lord should rain an abundance of grain from heaven, could this possibly happen?” Elisha said to him: “Because you did not believe, you shall see it with your eyes, but you shall not eat of it” (IV Kings VII, 1–2).

120. Suddenly there was in the Syrian camp something like the sound of chariots [Note: The editions and one or two manuscripts add: “and the sound of a multitude.” Other manuscripts, though not many, read: “and many voices,” or “as well as the voice of great strength.” The remaining manuscripts agree with us. Again, where we, together with the old editions and all the manuscripts, read “the king of the Amorites,” the Roman edition substituted “the king of the Hittites.”] and the sound of a multitude of horsemen, a mighty sound, and a great tumult of war. The Syrians thought that the king of Israel had summoned the king of Egypt and the king of the Amorites as allies into the battle. They fled at dawn, abandoning their tents, because they feared that the sudden arrival of new enemies would overwhelm them and that they would be unable to resist the united forces of the kings.

This was unknown in Samaria, since the people there, weakened by fear and exhausted by hunger, did not dare to come out or even to look out (ibid., 6–7).

121. There were four lepers at the city gate, for whom life was a punishment and death a gain. They said to one another: “Look, we are sitting here and dying. If we enter the city, we shall die of hunger; if we remain here, no means of sustaining life is available to us. Let us go to the camp of the Syrians: it will either be a swift death or a remedy for our survival.”

They went on their way and entered the camp. And behold, everything belonging to the enemy had been abandoned. They entered the tents and, first finding food, drove away their hunger; then they seized as much gold and silver as they could. Although [Note: Thus read by far the greater number of manuscripts, and those of better authority; some manuscripts, however, and all the editions read: “when they alone could lie upon the spoil, they decided,” etc.] they alone were enjoying the spoil, they nevertheless decided to report to the king that the Syrians had fled, because they judged this to be morally right rather than, by suppressing the information, to foster a fraudulent robbery.

122. At this report the people went out and plundered the Syrian camp. The abundance of the enemy’s provisions made grain cheap, in accordance with the prophetic saying: a measure of fine flour would cost a shekel, and two measures of barley would cost the same price.

Amid this joy of the people, the messenger on whom the king was resting [Note: All editions, together with a few manuscripts, read: “stationed at the gate among” the people, etc.] was crushed amid the haste of those going out and the exultation of those returning, trampled by the people, and died (IV Kings VII, 3 ff., 8 ff.).

## CHAPTER XXI

Esther is shown to have pursued the glory of moral excellence at the risk of her life; likewise, the barbarian king, by putting to death a very close friend. Friendship must always be joined to moral excellence, as the examples of Jonathan and Alchimelech prove

123. What of Queen Esther? In order to rescue her people from danger, did she not offer herself to death, acting in a dignified and morally excellent manner, and did she not refuse to tremble before the wrath of the cruel king? (Esther IV, 16.) The king of Persia himself, fierce and proud of heart, nevertheless judged it morally right to repay with gratitude the informer who had revealed the plots prepared against him, to free the people from slavery and rescue them from death, [Note: All editions read: “and not spare the man who had suggested such disgraceful things.”] and not spare the one who had proposed such disgraceful acts (Esther VI, 3 ff.).

Finally, he handed over to the cross the man whom he had regarded as second to himself and chief among all his friends, because he had perceived that he had been dishonored by that man’s treacherous counsels (Esther VII, 9).

124. That friendship is worthy of approval which protects moral excellence and is rightly preferred to wealth, honors, and powers. But friendship is not ordinarily preferred to moral excellence; rather, it follows it. Such was the friendship of Jonathan, who, out of filial devotion, shrank neither from his father’s displeasure nor from danger to his life (I Kings XX, 29 ff.). Such was that of Abimelech, who, in return for the duties of hospitality, judged that he ought to undergo his own death rather than betray his fleeing friend (I Kings XXI, 6).

## CHAPTER XXII

Moral excellence must not be abandoned for the sake of a friend; nevertheless, if testimony must be given against a friend, caution must be exercised. Among friends, what openness is required in laying bare the heart, what generosity in enduring, what freedom in reproving? Friendship is the guardian of the virtues and is found only among people of similar character. It must be gentle in correction and detached from personal advantage; hence how rare true friends are among the rich! How great is the dignity of friendship: the greater it is, the more detestable is a friend’s treachery, as is shown by the examples of Judas and Job’s friends

125. Nothing, therefore, is to be preferred to moral excellence. Yet Scripture also warns us concerning friendship, lest moral excellence be neglected out of devotion to a friend. Philosophers have raised many questions: [Note: Ibid., line 33: “But whether one ought to act against the republic,” etc. Also *On Friendship*, p. 424, line 1: “Let us therefore consider, if you please, how far love in friendship ought to proceed,” etc.] Should anyone take a position against his country for a friend’s sake, in order to obey his friend? Should one abandon loyalty while indulging and attending to his friend’s interests?

126. Scripture indeed says: “A club, a sword, and a sharpened arrow is the man who gives false testimony against his friend” (Proverbs XXV, 18). But consider what it asserts. It does not condemn testimony given against a friend, but false testimony. What if someone is compelled to testify for God’s sake, or for the sake of his country? Should friendship outweigh religious devotion, [Note: The Roman edition reads: “should vice outweigh charity.”] should it outweigh love for one’s fellow citizens?

Even in these circumstances, however, the truth of the testimony must be sought, lest a friend be attacked through the treachery of another friend, when his faithfulness ought to acquit him. A friend, therefore, must neither gratify a guilty person nor plot against an innocent one.

127. Certainly, if it is necessary to give testimony and one has discovered some fault in a friend, one should reprove him privately; if he does not listen, reprove him publicly. There are good corrections, and they are often better than silent friendship. If a friend thinks he is being injured, nevertheless correct him; if the bitterness of correction wounds his spirit, nevertheless correct him—do not be afraid. [Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “The wounds of a friend are more useful.” The old edition and the manuscripts read “tolerable,” or “more tolerable”; some read: “the wounds of a friend are more acceptable,” etc.]

“For the wounds of a friend are more bearable than the kisses of flatterers” (Proverbs XXVII, 6). Correct a friend who is going astray, therefore; do not abandon an innocent friend. [Note: Cicero, *On Friendship*, p. 428, line 1: “For friendships ought not to have, as other things do, satiety,” etc.] Friendship must be steadfast and persevere in affection; we must not change friends in a childish manner through some fickle judgment.

128. Open your heart to your friend, so that he may be faithful to you [Note: Ibid., p. 426, line 15: “Let there be among them a sharing of all things, counsels, and desires,” etc.] and that you may receive from him the joy of life. A faithful friend is a medicine of life and a gift of immortality (Ecclesiasticus VI, 16). [Note: Cicero, *On Friendship*, p. 427, line 38: “To say nothing of these matters, how burdensome and difficult the sharing of misfortunes seems to most people,” etc.]

Treat your friend as an equal, and do not be ashamed to anticipate him in acts of kindness; friendship knows no pride. Hence the Wise Man says: “Do not be ashamed to greet a friend” (Ecclesiasticus XXII, 31). [Note: Ibid., p. 428, line 20: “But the greatest thing in friendship is that the superior should be equal to the inferior,” etc.]

Do not abandon a friend in need, do not leave him, and do not desert him, because friendship is a support in life. Therefore let us bear one another’s burdens, as the Apostle taught (Galatians VI, 2); he says this to those whom charity has embraced as members of the same body. [Note: The editions and a few manuscripts read: “those whom the same charity has embraced.”] If a friend’s prosperity helps his friends, why should support not also be available to a friend in his adversity? Let us help with counsel, contribute our efforts, and share his feelings in compassion.

129. If necessary, let us endure hardships for a friend. Often enmities must be faced for a friend’s innocence, and frequently slanders, if you resist or reply when a friend is criticized and accused. Do not regret such an offense; for it is the voice of the righteous: “Even if evils have befallen me because of a friend, I endure” (Ecclesiasticus XXII, 31).

A friend is tested in adversity, for in prosperity everyone seems to be a friend. But just as patience and endurance are necessary in a friend’s adversity, so in prosperity appropriate authority is necessary, so that it may restrain and rebuke a friend’s arrogance when he exalts himself.

130. How beautifully Job, placed in adversity, says: “Have pity on me, my friends, have pity” (Job XIX, 21). These words are not those of a man abjectly pleading, but of one passing judgment. [Col. 0181C] For when he was unjustly reproved by his friends, he replied: “Have pity on me, my friends”—that is, you ought to show mercy; yet you oppress and attack a man whose afflictions you ought, out of friendship, to share.

131. Therefore, my sons, preserve the friendship you have begun with your brothers; nothing in human affairs is more beautiful. [Note: Cicero, *On Friendship*, p. 421, line 39: “What is sweeter than to have someone with whom you dare to speak about everything as with yourself,” etc.] It is the comfort of this life to have someone to whom you may open your heart, with whom you may share your secrets, to whom you may entrust the hidden things of your heart; to have a faithful man who rejoices with you in prosperity, sympathizes with you in sadness, and encourages you in persecution.

How good were the Hebrew youths as friends, whom not even the flame of the burning furnace separated from their mutual affection (Daniel III, 16 ff.)! We have spoken of this above (chapter 9). Saint David rightly says: “Saul and Jonathan, beautiful and beloved, inseparable in life, and in death they were not divided” (II Kings I, 23).

132. This is the fruit of friendship: that faith is not destroyed for the sake of friendship. [Note: Cicero, *On Duties*, Book III, p. 393, line 41: “For if everything is to be done that friends wish,” etc. Also *On Friendship*, p. 424, line 15: “But if we decide that what is right should be granted to friends,” etc.; line 27: “This, then, is the first law in friendship,” etc.] [Note: Erasmus and later editions, together with several manuscripts, read: “that faith is not abandoned for the sake of friendship.”]

A person cannot be a friend to someone who has been unfaithful to God. Friendship is the guardian of devotion and the teacher of equality: the superior should show himself equal to the inferior, and the inferior to the superior. Among people of dissimilar character there can be no friendship; therefore the goodwill of both must correspond.

The inferior should not lack authority if circumstances demand it, nor the superior humility. Let the superior listen as to an equal, as to a companion; and let the friend advise and rebuke as a friend—not out of a desire for display, but out of an affection born of charity. [Note: Cicero, *On Friendship*, p. 425, line 45: “Therefore this, at least, is established, as I think: among the good, friendship exists among the good,” etc. Also p. 429, line 49: “But it is fitting first to be a good man, and then to seek another like oneself,” etc.]

133. Let the admonition not be harsh, nor the rebuke insulting. Just as friendship must flee flattery, so it must also be free from arrogance. [Note: *On Duties*, Book I, p. 370, line 9: “For the most part, one may make use of gentle correction,” etc. Also *On Friendship*, p. 430, line 48: “For friends often must be admonished and rebuked,” etc.]

For what is a friend except a partner in love, to whom you join and attach your spirit, mingling it with his so that you wish the two to become one; one to whom you entrust yourself as to another self, from whom you fear nothing, and from whom you ask nothing dishonorable for the sake of your own advantage? [Note: Cicero, *On Friendship*, p. 429, line 41: “For he is indeed a friend who is as another self,” etc., “and acquires another whose spirit he so mingles with his own,” etc.] [Note: Ibid., p. 425, line 50: “And it seems to me that those who form friendships for the sake of advantage,” etc.]

Friendship is not a source of revenue, but is full of dignity and full of grace. Friendship is a virtue, not a business; for it is not produced by money [Note: The editions and several manuscripts read: “it is not sought through money.”] but by grace, not through bidding up prices, but through a contest of goodwill.

134. Finally, friendships are generally better among the poor than among the rich. [Note: Cicero, *On Friendship*, p. 426, line 12: “For this is the life of tyrants, namely, one in which there is neither trust nor affection,” etc.; “yet they are courted through the appearance of friendship,” etc.; “the great wealth of powerful men excludes faithful friendships,” etc.] The rich are often without friends, while the poor possess an abundance of them. There is no true friendship where there is deceitful flattery. Many flatter the rich in order to win their favor; toward a poor man no one is a flatterer. Whatever is offered to the poor is genuine; his friendship is free from envy.

135. What is more precious than friendship, which is shared by angels and human beings? Hence the Lord Jesus also says: “Make friends for yourselves from the unrighteous mammon, so that they may receive you into their eternal dwellings” (Luke 16:9). God himself makes us friends out of servants, just as he himself says: “Now you are my friends, if you do what I command you” (John 15:14). He gave us the pattern of friendship that we should follow: we are to do our friend’s will, to open to our friend all the secrets we hold in our hearts, and not to be ignorant of his hidden thoughts. Let us show him our breast, and let him open his to us. “Therefore,” he says, “I have called you friends, because everything that I heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15:14). A friend therefore conceals nothing, if he is a true friend: he pours out his soul, just as the Lord Jesus poured out the mysteries of the Father.

136. Therefore, the one who keeps God’s commandments is a friend, and is honored by that name. The one who is of one mind is a friend; for unity of souls belongs among friends. No one is more detestable than the person who has violated friendship. Hence the Lord found in the betrayer this gravest offense, by which he condemned his treachery: he had not returned the favor of grace, and had mixed the poison of malice into the banquets of friendship. [Note: [Col. 0183B] The Benignian manuscript, concerning which place—as we said above—Saint David aptly says: “But you,” etc.] Thus he says: “But you, a man of one mind with me, my leader and my familiar friend, who always shared sweet food with me” (Psalm 54:14)! That is: this cannot be endured, because you, as his intimate friend, attacked the one who had granted you favor. “For if my enemy had cursed me, I would certainly have endured it” (ibid., 13); and I would have hidden myself from the one who hated me. An enemy can be avoided; a friend cannot, if he wishes to lie in ambush. We are on guard against the person to whom we do not entrust our counsels; but we cannot guard against the person to whom we have entrusted them. Therefore, to heap up the odium of his sin, he did not say, “You, my servant, my apostle,” but “My intimate friend”—that is, you are a betrayer not only of me but also of yourself, since you betrayed your intimate friend.

137. When the Lord himself had been offended by the three kings who had failed to show proper respect to holy Job, he preferred to forgive them through a friend, so that the intercession of friendship might become the remission of sins. Accordingly, Job prayed, and the Lord forgave them. Friendship benefited those whom insolence had harmed (Job 42:7 ff.).

## CONCLUSION

138. I have entrusted these matters to you, my sons, so that you may preserve them in your hearts. Whether they offer any benefit, you will judge; meanwhile, they provide a great abundance of examples. For almost all the examples of our ancestors, and very many of their sayings as well, are contained in these three books. Thus, even if the discourse itself contributes little charm, the sequence of antiquity, expressed in a kind of compendium, nevertheless supplies a great deal of instruction.

# [ON VIRGINS]

## PREFATORY NOTICE TO THE FOLLOWING BOOKS, IN WHICH THE ORIGIN OF SACRED VIRGINS IS ALSO DISCUSSED

Since the institution of virginity has been established in the very words of Christ the Lord and in the counsels of the Teacher of the nations, and has always been held in the highest esteem in the Church, we shall not linger in refuting those heretics who, against the manifest authority of Scripture and universal tradition, either placed celibacy after marriage or proscribed vows of continence as rash, impious, and unlawful. But since among Catholics some have maintained that, from the very beginnings of the Church, there existed virgins who both professed solemn vows of continence and embraced common life in monasteries; while others allow them only private vows and a life either spent in the secular companionship of many women or lived individually in their fathers’ homes; while still others recognize in them merely a simple intention, which they displayed by the modesty of their veils and clothing, attributing to our Ambrose the first institution of communities of virgins—it has seemed to us worthwhile to speak somewhat more fully on the subject.

It is clear that the first opinion has been adopted by many who, attempting to defend it in dissertations and even enormous volumes, have collected testimonies of the Fathers and of certain councils, together with the Acts of many martyrs. Nevertheless, it seems to encounter serious difficulties. Roman laws strictly prohibited and punished celibacy; the idolaters by no means permitted even the smallest gatherings of Christians, and, driven by the utmost frenzy of their lust, raged especially against virgins. The authority of what is read in the Acts of very many martyrs would remove these obstacles, were it not weakened by a strong suspicion—not to say almost manifest indications—of corruption. As for the passages cited from the Fathers or councils, others readily interpret them in such a way as to bring them over to their own side as well.

Accordingly, we gladly agree with Innocent I that there were two classes of sacred virgins: namely, some who were specially married to Christ and deserved to be veiled by a priest; and others who, although not yet covered by the sacred veil, nevertheless promised always to remain in their virginal intention (Letter to Victricius of Rouen). We contend, however, that both groups were bound by a perpetual vow of virginity. Certainly we see that the Fathers, and Augustine above all, habitually use the words “intention” and “vow” in the same sense. Nor, even among the scholastics, does “vow” signify anything other than an intention confirmed by words. Those sacred virgins certainly did this when they openly declared their commitment by changing their clothing and occupying a separated place in the church.

If they appeal to a passage of Cyprian, where he commands: “Those who do not wish, or are unable, to persevere should marry rather than fall into the fire through their sins” (Letter to Pomponius), the answer is that this was established on account of the lapse of certain virgins who, even while being tormented by the cruelty of tyrants, continued to bring scandal upon the Church. Consequently, although he condemned such marriages in the strongest terms, he judged that they should be tolerated as lesser evils in order to avoid greater ones, rather than truly approving them. Indeed, Saint Epiphanius (Heresy 61), and after him Augustine (Book on the Good of Widowhood, chapters 10 and 11)—whose times, the adversaries do not deny, saw vows of virgins in customary use—forbid the dissolution of a marriage contracted after vows had been made, on account of the husbands, who would have bound themselves by a greater crime if they had brought other wives into their homes. Yet they declare the women’s offense to be a very great one and worthy of ecclesiastical penalties. What other intention, we ask, could Cyprian have had? Does he not say that those corrupted and defiled virgins had firmly resolved to maintain continence and had devoted themselves to Christ? How, then, can it be denied that a vow had been made in their case? Hence that same Father, together with Augustine, expressly asserts that these women were guilty of adultery (Expositions on Psalms 83 and 75), since they had broken the faith they had given to Christ the Lord.

Let it therefore remain established that the manner of life of virgins and continent women is not later than Christianity itself; that from apostolic times there existed girls who consecrated their virginity to God, whether by a vow or by a firm promise of perpetual continence; and finally, that these vows were customarily declared before bishops, priests, parents, or all Christians by those external signs that we have already mentioned. During the most difficult periods, when the Church was devastated and groaning under the bitterest tyranny, these same virgins lived in the seclusion of their paternal homes. But after, through the help of divine kindness, tranquility began to be granted to the faithful, those brides of the Man of God themselves undertook to establish monasteries in the East. Athanasius, compelled by the persecution of the Arians to flee to Rome, provided the occasion for some to be established there as well. At Rome this way of life initially found less favor among the nobility (Jerome, On the Praises of Marcella); but when certain distinguished matrons had embraced it, it was gradually propagated among other religious communities through the zeal of their foremost leaders.

In assisting so holy and useful an institution, the great Ambrose showed himself inferior to no one. He not only supported and enlarged it with all his strength after it had been adopted in his own diocese, but also extended it through the neighboring provinces and even across the sea, as far as Africa and Mauritania. Hence one may acknowledge that, even if the praise of being the first father of communities of religious women among the Italians is not owed to the holy Bishop, it cannot be denied him without injustice that he was at least their patron and propagator. To make clearer the manner in which the profession of virginity was extended, let us undertake an analysis of the books that we publish here.

Since the holy man had nothing more important at heart than to instruct the people entrusted to him in salutary doctrine, at the beginning of his episcopate he judged that he would perform a worthwhile service if, by demonstrating the holiness of virginity, he encouraged Christian girls, so far as he could, to profess it. He therefore delivered sermons on this subject with such eloquence and force that they crossed even the seas. His blessed sister Marcellina, stirred by reports of them, congratulated him by letter on so joyful and successful an outcome. She also begged him to commit to writing what he had spoken aloud, since she could not hear it in person. Therefore, in order to comply with so just a request, he resolved to arrange his sermons into those three books that we still possess.

In the first book he examines the dignity of virginity and, after the singular humility displayed at the very beginning, reveals what moved him to write. Then, after first praising blessed Agnes, whose feast had fallen on that day, he asserts that virginity descended to us from God the Father together with the Word. From this he concludes that among the Gentiles that virtue had never existed, while among the Hebrews it had existed only in shadow. Although it was by no means commanded, he makes clear that it was nevertheless far superior to marriage when the two are compared. Taking this opportunity, he lovingly rebukes parents, and widows in particular, because they prevented their daughters from even hearing him preach on the subject. To make clearer how greatly they sinned in this matter, he places before their eyes the example of girls who came to Milan from Piacenza and Bologna, and even from lands across the sea, in order to be married to Christ. Finally, after recounting the most beautiful deed of a certain virgin who could not be dragged away by her family from the altar before professing continence, the book is brought to a close.

In the second book he undertakes to form the character of virgins, declaring that he could do this more effectively by examples. His first and principal example is taken from the Mother of God, the leader of all virgins. He describes her virtues briefly, but with the greatest ornament and eloquence. To her he adds Thecla, Paul’s disciple and the patroness of the Church of Milan, whom the virgins should endeavor to reproduce in themselves as an absolute model. But lest those examples seem greater than their strength, he sets before them a third example, one of more recent memory. This was a Christian virgin who, while voluntarily exposing herself to martyrdom, was condemned by a tyrant to a brothel. Through the help of a Christian soldier she escaped by divine intervention and ultimately obtained the palm of martyrdom together with him. Then the holy Bishop turns his mind to the consideration of idolatry and argues that, in the famous story of Damon and Pythias, nothing can rightly be compared with the constancy of that noble virgin. Finally, excusing the perhaps somewhat excessive artistry and eloquence he had employed in his speech, he asserts that he did so in order to draw souls to God with greater force and sweetness.

He begins the third book with the exhortation that Pope Liberius gave to Marcellina when she was veiled in Rome, in the Basilica of the Apostles, on the very feast of the Lord’s Nativity, in the presence of an innumerable multitude of the faithful. She had often discussed this very sermon with her brother; accordingly, he sent her its entire text here, where it seemed especially appropriate, set down in his own words rather than those of its author. Her ardor of spirit, however, was such that it could not be confined within the limits of Liberius’s instructions. Accordingly, her loving and prudent brother advises her to relax her fasts for a time and devote herself more intensely to prayer and to the inward cultivation of the remaining virtues. Since he wished this to benefit not only his sister but also the instruction of other virgins, he prescribes what they ought to follow and what they ought to avoid; above all, he dissuades them from banquets and dancing. Finally, after answering Marcellina’s question about virgins who had voluntarily taken their own lives, he recounts the martyrdom of Sotheris, a woman related to him by family ties, and at last places the crown upon the book. Whatever is read thereafter in the printed editions, since it constitutes a distinct treatise in all the manuscripts, should be assigned after the book On Widows.

Ambrose himself testifies that he composed these books in the third year of his episcopate, that is, in the year 377 after the restoration of peace (Book II, chapter 7). Nevertheless, the sermons of which, as we have said, they consist must have been delivered some time earlier, since their fame had traveled through places separated by immense stretches of sea. In this respect, we cannot fail to admire that a man scarcely removed from the administration of a province and from secular tribunals showed himself so thoroughly trained in sacred letters and Christian eloquence that he composed books deserving the accumulated praise of Jerome (Letter to Eustochium and Apology against Jovinian), Augustine (Book IV of On Christian Doctrine, chapter 21), and all those who flourished in the Church during the succeeding centuries.

# THREE BOOKS OF SAINT AMBROSE, BISHOP OF MILAN, ON VIRGINS, TO HIS SISTER MARCELLINA [Note: [Col. 0187B] Written in the year 377.] (C)

## BOOK ONE

### CHAPTER I

Ambrose, understanding that each person must render God an account of his words and talents, applies his mind to writing. After reviewing several examples of divine mercy, he encourages himself to hope; but soon confessing himself unequal to the task, he wishes to be treated like the barren fig tree of the Gospel. Nevertheless, to silence the censure of his critics, he declares that he hopes words will not fail him, since he is speaking of Christ.

1. If, according to the judgment of heavenly truth (Matthew 12:36), we must render an account of every word we have spoken, whatever idle word it may be; or if each servant has hidden within the earth the talents of spiritual grace entrusted to him—talents that were to be distributed among the bankers so that they might be multiplied by accruing interest—whether like a timid moneylender or like a greedy possessor (Matthew 25:14 ff.), he will incur no slight offense when his master returns. We must rightly fear this, since, although our talent is small, we have nevertheless been entrusted with the very great necessity of lending the words of God to the minds of the people, lest the interest on our own speech also be demanded—especially since the Lord requires zeal from us, not success. Hence I resolved to write something. Our voice is heard with greater danger of embarrassment than a book is read, for a book does not blush.

[Note: [Col. 0187B] A few manuscripts read *praesentare rationem* (“to present an account”).]

2. Distrusting my own talent, yet encouraged by examples of divine mercy, I dare to prepare a discourse; for, if God wills, even a she-ass has spoken (Numbers 22:28). If an angel should stand beside me, burdened as I am beneath the weights of this age, I too shall open my long-silent mouth. The one who loosed the bonds of nature in that she-ass can loosen the impediments of inexperience. In the ark of the Old Testament the priest’s rod blossomed (Numbers 17:8); it is easy for God to make a flower spring even from our knots in the holy Church.

[Note: [Col. 0187B–0188B] All editions and not a few manuscripts read “even from our own knots”; some others read this as well, but not quite correctly. For it is clear that our Ambrose, in his humility, compares himself with a rod unpolished and rough with knots.] Why should we despair that the Lord will speak through human beings, when he spoke through thorns (Exodus 3:4 ff.)? God did not disdain even the bush. Would that he also illumine my thorns! Perhaps some will admire a certain brightness shining even among our thorns; there will be others whom our thorn does not wound; and there will be those for whom the voice they hear from the bush causes the sandal to fall from their feet, so that the mind’s progress may be freed from bodily impediments.

3. But these are the merits of holy men. Would that Jesus, in some way, looked upon me as I still lie beneath that barren fig tree (John 1:48)! Would that our fig tree too, after three years, should bear fruit (Luke 13:6 ff.). But whence comes such hope for sinners? Would that the Gospel cultivator of the Lord’s vineyard, perhaps already ordered to cut down our fig tree, might spare it this year also, until he digs around it and casts a basket of manure upon it; perhaps to raise the poor from the earth and lift the needy from the dung heap! Blessed are those who tie their horses beneath vine and olive (Genesis 49:11), consecrating the course of their labors to light and joy. But me the fig tree still overshadows—that is, the itching of worldly pleasure, alluring to greatness, weak for labor, soft for use, barren for fruit.

[Note: [Col. 0189C] The editions read “for perhaps from the earth”; some manuscripts read “for perhaps,” etc.]

[Note: [Col. 0189D] All editions, with a few manuscripts, read: “consecrating the labor of their courses to peace and joy, lest the fig tree … overshadow.” Other manuscripts, greater in number and authority, have the reading given in the text.]

4. Perhaps someone wonders why I dare to write when I cannot speak. Yet if we recall what we read in the Gospel Scriptures (Luke 1:63–64) and in priestly deeds, and if holy Zacharias serves as our example, we shall find that there is something the voice cannot explain but the pen can mark. If the name of John restored a voice to his father, I too should not despair of receiving a voice, even though I am mute, if I speak of Christ. For who shall recount his generation, according to the prophetic saying (Isaiah 53:8)? Therefore, like a servant, I shall proclaim the household of the Lord; for the immaculate Lord has consecrated to himself an immaculate household even in this body, full of the defilements of human frailty.

[Note: [Col. 0189D] The Roman edition and some manuscripts read “the handmaid of the Lord … an immaculate handmaid”; the older edition, together with the remaining manuscripts, rightly reads “household” in both places. Here he is speaking generally first about the state and order of virgins, and then proceeds to praise one of them individually.]

## CHAPTER II

He teaches that the beginning of his book is appropriately introduced because it was the birthday of a virgin, namely blessed Agnes. He praises her most elegantly for her name, her modesty, and her martyrdom, but above all for her age: although only twelve years old, she overcame terrors, promises, tortures, and finally death itself with wholly manly constancy.

5. It is fitting that, since today is the birthday of a virgin, we should speak of virgins, and that the book should begin with praise. It is the birthday of a virgin: let us follow her purity. It is the birthday of a martyr: let us offer sacrifices. It is the birthday of holy Agnes: let men marvel, and let children not despair; let married women be astonished, and unmarried women imitate her. But what worthy thing can we say of her, whose very name was not without the light of praise? Devotion beyond her age, virtue beyond nature: so that it seems to me that she had not the name of a human being, but the oracle of a martyr, by which she indicated what she would become.

[Note: [Col. 0189D] The Roman edition alone reads “her name is empty of praise”; we have restored “full of light” from the older edition and all the manuscripts. This name is said to be praiseworthy because “lamb,” *agna*, and “pure,” Greek ἀγνή (*hagnē*), are both symbols of innocence and of religion, since that animal was once especially appointed for sacrifice.]

6. Nevertheless, I have a means by which I may obtain assistance. The name of a virgin is a title of modesty. I shall call her a martyr; I shall proclaim her a virgin. The praise is sufficiently ample when it is not sought but possessed. Let intellectual skill therefore withdraw; let eloquence fall silent: a single voice is enough for proclamation. Let old men, young men, and children sing her. No one is more praiseworthy than one who can be praised by human beings. As many people as there are, so many heralds are there praising the martyr while they speak.

[Note: [Col. 0189D] All editions, with the Teller manuscript, read: “I shall call the martyr. I have praised enough. The praise is lengthy,” etc. The other manuscripts have the more elegant reading given in the text, except that several read “I have proclaimed” instead of “I shall proclaim.” Again, after two lines, the Roman edition alone reads “There is one voice of heralds,” which is less appropriate.]

7. She is said to have suffered martyrdom at the age of twelve.

[Note: [Col. 0189D] The Roman edition reads: “This girl of thirteen years,” etc. The same is found not only in the Acts of this holy martyr, which were wrongly attributed to blessed Ambrose among his letters—as we shall show in its proper place—but also in Augustine, *Sermon on Various Subjects* 101, 273 in the new edition, although the words “thirteen years” are entirely absent from the Floriac manuscript. Nevertheless, the reading found in all the manuscripts and in the older edition should by no means be changed. We customarily call those who have not yet completed their thirteenth year either twelve or thirteen years old indiscriminately. The writers, together with Baronius, agree that she suffered in the last persecution. Her feast is celebrated among the Greeks on January 14 and 21, and also July 15; among the Latins, on January 21 and 28.]

How much more detestable the cruelty that spared not even so tender an age! Rather, how great the power of faith, which found a witness even in that age. Was there a place for a wound in that little body? And she who had no place to receive the sword had a place from which to conquer the sword. Yet girls of that age cannot even bear the stern looks of their parents, and, when pricked by a needle, habitually cry over the punctures as though they were wounds. She, among the bloody hands of executioners, stood fearless; she remained unmoved amid the harsh dragging of clanking chains; now she offered her whole body to the raging soldier’s sword, not yet knowing how to die but ready to do so; or, if she were unwillingly dragged to the altars, she stretched out her hands to Christ amid the flames and, in the very sacrilegious fires, marked the Lord’s trophy as a victor.

[Note: [Col. 0190D] “To mark the Lord’s trophy” means to form the sign of the cross with the arms raised aloft, a practice familiar to the earliest Christians during prayer.]

Now she placed her neck and both hands into iron chains; but no chain could enclose such slender limbs.

8. A new kind of martyrdom? Not yet fit for punishment, and already mature for victory; difficult to fight, easy to be crowned. She fulfilled the discipline of virtue, though she anticipated the judgment of age. No bride would hasten to the bridal chamber as happily as this virgin, advancing swiftly toward the place of punishment in the success of her cause—not with her head adorned by braided hair, but for Christ; not crowned with little flowers, but with virtues. [Note: [Col. 0190D] Some manuscripts read: “All her relatives could weep.”]

Everyone could weep; she alone was without tears. Many marveled that she so readily gave away, as though already finished with it, a life whose first breath she had scarcely drawn. All were astonished that she had already become a witness to divinity, although at that age she could not yet, by reason of her years, be regarded as legally independent or competent to give testimony.

[Note: [Col. 0191D] Someone might ask why Ambrose denies that Agnes, at thirteen years of age, could have been regarded as legally independent or competent to bear witness, when it is clear from Tertullian’s *On the Veiling of Virgins*, chapter 11, that among the Gentiles it was customary for girls at twelve and boys at fourteen to be entrusted with their own affairs. Her commentators observe, however, that although wards were released from guardianship in business matters, they were not yet freed from the guardianship of authority. Thus, although they were permitted to conduct their own affairs, because they still remained under female guardianship many things were forbidden to them, as may be found in those authors. Later, Constantine the Great issued a law granting full age to males at twenty and girls at eighteen. See the Theodosian Code under this title, and Cassiodorus, *Variarum* III, form 41, together with the observations of Godefroy and Fornerius on the same passages.]

Ultimately, she caused people to believe in God when they still would not have believed in her as a human being. For whatever is beyond nature comes from the author of nature.

9. With how much terror did the executioner act in order to make her afraid, and with how many blandishments in order to persuade her! How many men sought her consent so that she might reach marriage! But she said: “This too is an insult to the Bridegroom: to wait for one who may please [me]. He who chose me first will receive me. Why do you delay, executioner? Let the body perish that may be loved by eyes I do not wish to love it.” She stood, prayed, and bent her neck. You would have seen the executioner tremble as though he himself had been condemned; the executioner’s right hand shake, his face grow pale as he feared danger to another, while the girl did not fear danger to herself. Thus, in one victim, you have a double martyrdom: of modesty and of religion. She remained a virgin, and she obtained martyrdom.

[Note: [Col. 0192D] All editions and several manuscripts read: “‘It is an insult,’ she says, ‘to wait for one who is destined to please him’” (some manuscripts omit “she says”). Other manuscripts read: “to wait for one who is destined to please”—which is more fitting. But what if we read “to look upon” instead of “to wait for”? Certainly the manuscripts consistently display this final reading in place of the former.]

[Note: [Col. 0192D] Most manuscripts read “he chose me first”; nevertheless, “the one who chose me first,” found in the other manuscripts and all editions, is better.]

### CHAPTER III
