The praises of virginity are drawn from various sources, but especially from the fact that virginity itself deserved to bring the Word down from heaven to earth. Hence the practice that had flourished under the ancient covenant among a few was later propagated among countless people.

10. The love of purity now invites us—and you also, holy sister, by your silent and speechless conduct—to say something about virginity, lest a virtue that is primary appear to have been touched only in passing. Virginity is not praiseworthy for the reason that it is also found among martyrs; rather, it is praiseworthy because it makes martyrs.

[Note: [Col. 0192D] Two manuscripts read “or by silent conduct of gentle manners”; the remaining manuscripts and all editions read “or by mute conduct,” etc. The Roman edition adds “you ask,” but there is no reason for this, since “you invite” is plainly understood. He is addressing his sister Marcellina, mentioned in the Prefatory Notice.]

11. Who could comprehend by human intelligence that which nature itself has not confined within its laws? Or who could embrace in natural speech what lies above the ordinary course of nature? Virginity summoned from heaven what it was to imitate on earth. Nor did it seek its manner of life from heaven without reason, since it found its bridegroom in heaven. Crossing beyond clouds, air, angels, and stars, it found the Word of God in the very bosom of the Father and drank him in with its whole heart. For who, having found so great a good, would abandon it? “Your name is ointment poured out; therefore the young women have loved you and drawn you” (Song of Songs 1:1). Finally, this is not my own statement: “Those who neither marry nor are given in marriage will be like the angels in heaven” (Matthew 22:30). Let no one therefore wonder if those who are joined to the Lord of angels are compared with angels. Who, then, would deny that this way of life flowed from heaven—a way of life that we do not readily find on earth until after God descended into these limbs of an earthly body? Then a virgin conceived in her womb, and the Word became flesh, so that flesh might become God.

[Note: [Col. 0192D] The Roman edition omitted the word “virgin,” contrary to the testimony of all the others and of all the manuscripts.]

12. Someone may say: “But Elijah too is found to have been free from the desires associated with bodily intercourse. For that reason he was carried up to heaven in a chariot; for that reason he appears with the Lord in glory; for that reason he is to be the forerunner of the Lord’s coming (Malachi 4:3). And Mary took a tambourine and, with virginal modesty, led the dances (Exodus 15:20).” But consider whose figure she then bore. Was she not a figure of the Church, which joined to itself with an immaculate virginal spirit the devout gatherings of the people who were to sing divine songs? For we also read that virgins had been assigned to the temple at Jerusalem. But what does the Apostle say? “These things happened to them figuratively, so that they might be signs of things to come” (1 Corinthians 10:11). For a figure exists among the few, but the reality among the many.

13. But afterward, when the Lord came into this body and joined the fellowship of divinity and body without any stain of intermingled confusion, then the practice of heavenly life, spread throughout the whole world among human bodies, took root. This is what the angels ministering on earth declared would be the future order: a people that would offer service to the Lord through the worship of an immaculate body. This is that heavenly army which the host of praising angels promised on earth. We therefore have the authority of antiquity from the beginning of the age, and the fullness of the profession from Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0192D] A few manuscripts read: “and of the body, lest he wounded [it] with any … stain.”]

## CHAPTER IV

It is denied that the glory of virginity ever existed among any of the Gentiles—whether in the sacred rites of Vesta, the Phrygian goddess, and Liber Pater, or among philosophers. The case of the Pythagorean virgin is also discussed: although greatness of spirit is praised in her, continence is lacking, whereas both qualities shine forth in our virgins.

14. Certainly virginity is not something I share with the Gentiles, something common among barbarians, or something customary among the other living creatures. Although we draw one and the same breath of this vital air with them, share the common condition of an earthly body, and do not differ from them in the practice of generation, we nevertheless avoid the reproach of an equal nature in this one respect: virginity is sought by the Gentiles, but it is violated once consecrated; it is attacked by barbarians and unknown to the rest.

15. Who will set before me the virgins of Vesta and the priestesses of Pallas? What sort of chastity is this—not the chastity of morals, but of years—which is prescribed not by perpetuity but by age? Such integrity is all the more wanton because its corruption is reserved for old age. They themselves teach that their virgins ought not and cannot persevere, since they have put an end to virginity. What sort of religion is that in which young women are ordered to be chaste and old women unchaste? Nor is she chaste who is restrained by law, nor is she unchaste who is released by law. O mysteries! O morals! Necessity is imposed upon chastity, while authority is granted to lust. Thus she is not chaste who is compelled by fear, nor honorable she who is hired for a reward, nor is that modesty genuine which, exposed daily to the reproach of intemperate eyes, is beaten by shameful gazes. Exemptions are granted; prices are offered—as though selling chastity were not the greatest indication of wantonness. What is promised for a price is paid for a price; it is sold for a price and counted out for a price. Chastity does not know how to redeem itself when it habitually sells itself.

[Note: [Col. 0193C] Ambrose repeatedly contrasts and prefers Christian virgins to the Vestals elsewhere, but especially here and in the *Report against Symmachus*. If the passages are compared with one another, they will receive light from their mutual comparison. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Book II; J. Lipsius, *On the Vestals*; and Joseph Laurentius discuss at length their institution, number, office, privileges, and manner of life.]

[Note: [Col. 0193D] Some manuscripts read “not the prudence of morals.”]

[Note: [Col. 0193D] Some manuscripts read “let it be an indication of wantonness.” A little later they read: “it is sold for a price, it is rewarded for a price.”]

16. What shall I say about the Phrygian rites, in which unchastity is a discipline—and would that it were merely the unchastity of the weaker sex! What shall I say about the orgies of Liber, where the mystery of religion is an incentive to lust? What sort of life, then, can the priests have where the violation of the gods is worshiped? They therefore do not have a sacred virgin.

[Note: [Col. 0193D] The Phrygian rites were celebrated in honor of Cybele, the mother of the gods. Her priests were certain castrated rogues called Galli. Lucian reports much about the institution of these rites in *The Syrian Goddess*, and in *The Ass* he describes the obscene and unspeakable lusts and frauds of these Agyrtae, or Galli—material that Apuleius later adapted and expanded. On this subject, besides Servius on Book IX of the *Aeneid*, see Arnobius, Book V; Augustine, *City of God* VI, chapter 7, and VII, chapter 25; and others. The orgies were the same as the Bacchanalia. They were called by this name from the verb ὀργίζεσθαι, meaning “to be angry” or “to rage,” since no one is unaware that this was characteristic of these rites. They are discussed by Livy, decade 4, Book IX; Augustine, *City of God* II, chapter 9, and even more fully VII, chapter 21; Joseph Laurentius in various places; and others.]

[Note: [Col. 0194C] The Roman edition, with the Teller manuscript, reads “they do not have the sacred virgin.” This reading would not be objectionable if it rested on somewhat stronger support.]

17. Let us see whether perhaps even the precepts of philosophy, which is accustomed to claim for itself the mastery of all virtues, have formed some woman. A certain Pythagorean virgin is celebrated in a story: when a tyrant forced her to disclose a secret, she bit off her tongue, lest he have any means—by torture or otherwise—of extracting a confession, and spat it into the tyrant’s face; so that, since he did not cease questioning her, he had no one left whom he could question.

[Note: Thus all the manuscripts, except Teller’s, with which the editions read: “she is celebrated in stories, because, when …” Rome reads: “she is celebrated in stories, because, when … she is said to have cut out her tongue from a tyrant.” But “is said” seems to have been added by those who failed to observe that the infinitive *abscidisse* (“to have cut off”) refers to *celebratur* (“is celebrated”), not to *fertur* (“is said”). By that Pythagorean virgin, Saint Ambrose seems to indicate Leaena, the friend of Harmodius and Aristogeiton. She was aware of their conspiracy against Hipparchus; when discovered, she maintained silence even after her tongue had been cut out, and earned a statue represented in the form of a lioness, with open mouth and no tongue. Consult Herodotus, *Terpsichore*; Thucydides, Book I; Plutarch, *On Talkativeness*; Pliny, Book XXXIV, chapter 8; and others.]

18. Yet this woman, strong in spirit but with swelling womb, an example of silence and a flood of unchastity, was overcome by desires that torture could not overcome. Thus she who was able to conceal the secret of her mind did not conceal the reproach of her body. She conquered nature, but did not preserve discipline. How she would have wished her voice to become a defense of her modesty!

[Note: Quite a few manuscripts read “a moment of her modesty”; one has “a memorial,” and so forth.]

And perhaps patience had trained her for this, so that she might deny her guilt.

[Note: All the editions read “repentance had instructed her”; but all the manuscripts most correctly read “patience.” The form “patientiam” found in some witnesses must be attributed to the ignorance of the scribes.]

She was therefore not unconquered on every side; for although the tyrant could not discover what he was asking about, he nevertheless discovered what he was not asking about.

19. How much stronger are our virgins, who conquer even powers they cannot see; who gain victory not merely over flesh and blood, but also over the very prince of the world and ruler of the age! Agnes was certainly younger in age, but greater in virtue, richer in triumph, and more confident in steadfastness. She did not cut out her tongue through fear, but reserved it for the sake of her trophy. For she had nothing whose disclosure she feared: her confession was not criminal but religious. Thus the former merely concealed a secret; the latter bore witness to the Lord, whom, because her age was not yet able to confess, nature confessed.

# CHAPTER V

*That heaven is the homeland of virginity, but the author is the Son of God, who, though himself a virgin before the Virgin, was nevertheless born from a virgin and took the virgin Church as his bride. That we were all received from her, and some of her dowries are recalled. That her daughters surpass others because virginity is not subject to a command, and because it provides a most readily available opportunity for the cultivation of piety.*

20. In encomiums, a person’s homeland and parents are customarily praised, so that the dignity of the succession may be magnified by recalling its founder. Although I have not undertaken a panegyric of virginity but an exposition, I nevertheless think it relevant to make clear what its homeland is and who its author is. Let us first determine where its homeland lies. For if one’s homeland is where one’s generative dwelling is, then the homeland of chastity is certainly in heaven. Thus it is a stranger here, but a citizen there.

21. What, moreover, is virginal chastity except integrity free from contamination? And whom can we regard as its author except the immaculate Son of God, whose flesh did not see corruption and whose divinity did not experience contamination? See, therefore, how great are the merits of virginity. Christ before the Virgin, Christ from a virgin: born from the Father before the ages, but born from a virgin for the sake of the ages.

[Note: Several manuscripts read “born again for the sake of the ages.”]

The former belongs to his own nature; the latter was for our benefit. The former always was; the latter he willed.

[Note: Four manuscripts read: “he willed this toward the end”; the rest, except one reading “he willed this to happen,” give simply “he willed this.” All the editions likewise have “he willed this,” except the Roman edition, which reads “he willed this to be.” The same Roman edition adds *virgin* after the next occurrence of *Christ*, although the word appears neither in the older edition nor in any manuscript.]

22. Consider another merit of virginity: Christ is the bridegroom of the virgin and, if one may say so, the Christ of virginal chastity; for virginity belongs to Christ, not Christ to virginity. She who married is a virgin; she who carried us in her womb is a virgin; she who gave birth is a virgin; she who nourished him with her own milk is a virgin. Of her we read: “What great things the virgin Jerusalem has done!”

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “How great things the virgin Israel has done.”]

“Breasts will not fail from the rock, nor snow from Lebanon, nor will water carried by a mighty wind turn aside” (Jeremiah XVIII, 13 and following). What sort of virgin is this, watered by the fountains of the Trinity; for whom waters flow from the rock, breasts do not fail, and honeys are poured forth? The rock, according to the Apostle, is Christ. Thus from Christ the breasts do not fail, brightness comes from God, and the river from the Spirit. This is the Trinity that waters its Church: the Father, Christ, and the Spirit.

23. But let us now descend from the mother to her daughters. “Concerning virgins,” says the holy Apostle, “I have no commandment of the Lord” (I Corinthians X, 4). If the Teacher of the Gentiles had none, who could have one? He had no commandment, certainly, but he had an example. Virginity cannot be commanded, but it can be desired; for things that are above us are matters of aspiration more than of instruction. “But I wish you,” he says, “to be without anxiety. He who is unmarried is concerned with the things of the Lord, how he may please God … and the virgin thinks about the things of the Lord, so that she may be holy in body and spirit. But she who is married thinks about the things of the world, how she may please her husband” (I Corinthians VII, 32–34).

# CHAPTER VI

*The holy man declares that he by no means condemns marriage. Nevertheless, in comparing the good of married women with that of virgins, he first sets before us the evils that accompany fertility: the pains of childbirth, the burdens of rearing children, subjection to a husband, and excessive concern for beauty and adornment. He then sets against these the greater beauty and more fruitful fertility of virgins, whom he asserts to become very like the Church.*

24. I do not, indeed, discourage marriage, but I add to it the benefit of virginity. “Let the one who is weak eat vegetables,” he says (Romans XIV, 2). I demand one thing, but admire another. “Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek release. Are you released from a wife? Do not seek a wife” (I Corinthians VII, 27). This is the commandment for those joined in marriage. But what does he say about virgins? “He who joins his virgin in marriage does well; and he who does not join her does better” (ibid., 38). “She does not sin if she marries; but if she does not marry, she is eternal.”

[Note: Four manuscripts read: “But she, if she does not sin, is eternal”; four others: “But she, if she does not marry, does not sin; she is eternal.” The remaining witnesses and the editions have the reading given in the text.]

In the one case there is a remedy for weakness; in the other, the glory of chastity. The former is not censured; the latter is praised.

25. If you please, let us compare the good things of married women with the least of the good things of virgins.

[Note: Two manuscripts read: “with many good things of virgins.”]

Let a noble woman boast that she is fruitful in childbirth: the more children she has borne, the more she labors. Let her count the consolations of her children, but let her count the troubles as well. She marries and weeps. What sort of vows are those that are wept over? She conceives and becomes heavy. Fertility begins to bring impediment before it brings fruit. She gives birth and falls ill. How sweet is a pledge that begins in danger and ends in dangers, destined to bring pain before pleasure! It is bought with dangers and is not possessed at one’s will.

26. Why should I recount the troubles of nursing, educating, and marrying off children? These are the miseries of the fortunate.

[Note: Thus the edition and part of the manuscripts; another, not much smaller, portion reads: “and marrying off a son.” That is less appropriate.]

A mother has heirs, but she increases her sorrows. For one ought not to speak of adversities, lest the hearts of holy parents tremble. See, my sister, how grievous it is to suffer what ought not to be heard. And these things belong to the present age. But days will come when they will say: “Blessed are the barren, and the wombs that have not borne children” (Luke XXIII, 29). For the daughters of this age are born and give birth; but the daughter of the kingdom abstains from the pleasure of a man and from the pleasure of the flesh, so that she may be holy in body and spirit.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “but the daughter … from the will of a man and from the will of the flesh,” and so forth. The older edition and the manuscripts agree sufficiently among themselves, except that quite a few read: “but the daughters of the kingdom abstain,” and so forth. Some even read “sons” instead of “daughters,” and, in order to restore the construction of the whole passage, conclude it thus: “as John says: those who are not born from the pleasure of man or from the pleasure of the flesh, but from God.”]

27. Why should I rehearse the heavy servitude and subjection to husbands of women, whom God commanded to serve before he commanded servants to serve (Genesis III, 16)? I mention these things so that they may obey more indulgently; for if they are virtuous, this is the reward of love, and if they are wicked, the punishment of sin.

28. From this arise those incentives to vice by which women paint their faces with artificial colors, while they fear to displease their husbands, and, through the adultery of their appearance, meditate the adultery of chastity. What madness is this: to alter the image of nature, to seek a painted likeness, and, while fearing their husband’s judgment, to betray their own! For she who desires to alter what she was born as first passes judgment on herself. Thus, while striving to please others, she first displeases herself. What judge, woman, can we seek who is truer concerning your deformity than you yourself, who fear to be seen? If you are beautiful, why do you hide it? If you are deformed, why do you pretend to be beautiful, possessing neither the favor of your own conscience nor the favor of another’s error?

[Note: Most manuscripts read: “and you will possess neither the favor of your own conscience nor the favor of another’s face.”]

For he loves another woman, while you wish to please another man. And you become angry if he loves another, although he is being taught by you to commit adultery against you? You are a bad teacher of your own injury. Even a woman who has endured a procurer refuses to act as a procurer; and although she is a degraded woman, she sins not against another but against herself. Crimes are almost more tolerable in another:

[Note: All the editions, with a few manuscripts, read: “in adultery crimes are …”; likewise Augustine in the passage cited in the margin, where he reports these words as a splendid example of elevated diction. A large number of witnesses instead read “in another,” namely, in what this woman admits, since she sins against herself, not against another.]

there, modesty is adulterated; here, nature.

29. How much expense is required so that even a beautiful woman may not be displeasing! From one side, expensive necklaces hang from the neck; from the other, a gold-embroidered garment trails along the ground. Is this appearance therefore purchased, or possessed? What is more, various enticements are even employed for scent.

[Note: The editions and a few manuscripts read: “even various enticements of perfumes,” and so forth.]

The ears are weighed down with gems, and another color is poured over the eyes. What remains one’s own when so many things are changed? A woman loses her own senses—and thinks she can live?

30. But you, blessed virgins, who know such things as torments rather than ornaments; whose modest faces are suffused with holy shame, and whose good chastity is your adornment; who are not enslaved to human eyes and do not measure your merits by another’s error—you too have, indeed, your own service of beauty, in which the beauty of virtue serves, not that of the body: a beauty that no age extinguishes, no death can take away, and no illness corrupt. Let God alone be sought as judge of beauty, for he loves more beautiful souls even in a less beautiful body. You know neither the burden of the womb nor the pain of childbirth; yet the offspring of a devout mind is more numerous, since it regards all people as children: fruitful in successors, barren of bereavements, it does not know funerals but knows heirs.

[Note: Several manuscripts read: “does not know the funerals of an heir.”]

31. Thus the holy Church, undefiled by intercourse and fruitful in childbirth, is a virgin in chastity and a mother in offspring.

[Note: Several manuscripts read: “Thus the virgin gives birth to us, not with pain”; the others and the editions agree entirely, except that the Roman edition has “conceives” instead of “gives birth.”]

The virgin gives birth to us, therefore, not impregnated by a man but filled with the Spirit. The virgin gives birth to us not with the pains of her members but with the joys of angels. The virgin nourishes us not with bodily milk but with that of the Apostle (I Corinthians III, 2), with which he suckled the still-weak age of the growing people. What married woman, then, has more children than the holy Church, which is a virgin in her mysteries and a mother among the peoples, whose fertility Scripture also testifies to when it says: “For more are the children of the deserted woman than of her who has a husband” (Isaiah LIV, 1)? Our Church has no husband, but she has a bridegroom; for whether it is the Church among the peoples or the soul in each individual, she is joined as a bride to the eternal Word of God, without any deviation from modesty, barren of injury but pregnant with reason.

[Note: Thus the old edition and nearly all the manuscripts; the Roman edition, with one or two manuscripts, reads “with a flow of modesty.”]

# CHAPTER VII

*He urges parents to educate their daughters for virginity, and sets before their eyes the many troubles that arise from the pleasure they seek in grandchildren. Nevertheless, he denies that he prohibits marriage; indeed, he defends it against heretics who oppose it. In other respects, preferring virginity to marriage, he explains how beautiful the Bridegroom of virgins is and with what gifts they are endowed by him. Then, after expounding several passages from the Song of Songs for this purpose, he draws from them moral and virtuous instructions suited to the condition of virgins.*

32. You have heard, parents, with what virtues you ought to educate your daughters and with what disciplines you ought to form them, so that you may have daughters whose merits can redeem your faults. A virgin is God’s gift, a parent’s offering, the priesthood of chastity. A virgin is a mother’s sacrifice, by whose daily offering divine power is appeased. A virgin is an undivided pledge of her parents, one who does not trouble them with a dowry, does not abandon them by moving away, and does not offend them by injuries.

[Note: This could scarcely prove more clearly that monasteries for virgins had not yet been established at Milan, though they had been at Bologna, as is shown below, chapter 10, section 57.]

33. But someone desires to have grandchildren and acquire the name of grandfather. First he gives away his own children while seeking those of others; then he begins to be deprived of certainties while hoping for uncertainties. He contributes his own wealth and is still asked for more; unless he pays the dowry, he is subjected to demands; if he lives long, he is burdensome.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “He strives to purchase a son-in-law.”]

This is buying a son-in-law, not acquiring one: he sells her parents the sight of their daughter. Was she carried in the womb for so many months so that she might pass into another’s power? Is care taken to commend the virgin merely so that she may be taken away from her parents more quickly?

[Note: The Roman edition, with a few manuscripts, reads “the care of the virgin to be entrusted”; the other editions, with the remaining witnesses, read “the care of the virgin to be commended”; two manuscripts read “the commended virgin.”]

34. Someone will say: “Then you discourage marriage?” On the contrary, I commend it, and I condemn those who are accustomed to discourage it, since I regularly cite the marriages of Sarah, Rebecca, Rachel, and the other women of ancient times as examples of singular virtues. For whoever condemns sexual union also condemns children, and condemns the human fellowship of the race, which is transmitted through successive generations. For how could an age destined to endure forever succeed one age after another, unless the grace of marriage stirred the desire to beget offspring? Or how can it be proclaimed that the immaculate Isaac approached the altars of God as a victim of paternal devotion (Genesis XXI, 2), or that Israel, placed in a human body, saw God (Genesis XXXII, 27), and gave the people a religious name, if their origin is condemned? Sacrilegious men—the Manichaeans, to be sure—have this one point in common with the wisest, that by condemning marriage they declare that they ought not to have been born.

[Note: The Manichaeans are meant here. Augustine speaks of them in *On Heresies*, chapter 46, as follows: “Hence they unquestionably condemn marriage and, insofar as it lies in their power, prohibit it, since they prohibit begetting, for the sake of which marriages are joined.”]

35. I do not, therefore, discourage marriage, but enumerate the fruits of consecrated virginity. The latter is a gift for the few; the former belongs to all. Nor can virginity exist unless it has a source from which it is born. I compare good things with good things, so that what one surpasses may more readily become clear. Nor do I introduce any opinion of my own, but repeat what the Holy Spirit uttered through the prophet: “Sterility with virtue is better,” he says (Wisdom IV, 1).

36. The first thing that women about to marry desire above all else is to boast of the beauty of their bridegroom. By this they must acknowledge that they are inferior to holy virgins, who alone can say: “You are beautiful beyond the sons of men; grace has been poured upon your lips” (Psalm XLIV, 3). Who is this bridegroom? He is not devoted to base services, nor proud of fleeting riches, but his throne is forever and ever. “The daughters of kings are in his honor. The queen stood at your right hand in a garment of gold, clothed round about with variety of virtues. Hear, therefore, daughter, and see, and incline your ear, and forget your people and your father’s house; for the King has desired your beauty, because he himself is your God” (ibid., 30 and following).

37. Observe also how much the Holy Spirit has conferred upon you through the testimony of divine Scripture: kingship, gold, and beauty. Kingship—either because you are the bride of the eternal King, or because, bearing an unconquered spirit, you are not held captive by the allurements of pleasure but rule over them like a queen.

[Note: These words are omitted in many more manuscripts, perhaps because you are the bride of the eternal King.]

Gold—because, just as that material becomes more precious when tested by fire, so the beauty of the virginal body, consecrated to the divine Spirit, gains an increase in its form.

[Note: All the editions read as above; some manuscripts instead have: “but you do not slip away as a captive.”]

But what greater beauty can one imagine than that of her who is loved by the King, approved by the Judge, called by the Lord, and consecrated to God—always a bride, always unmarried, so that neither love may have an end nor modesty suffer loss?

38. This is truly the beauty that lacks nothing, which alone deserves to hear from the Lord: “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no reproach in you. Come here from Lebanon, bride; come here from Lebanon. You shall pass over and cross from the beginning of faith, from the summit of Sanir and Hermon, from the dens of lions and the mountains of leopards” (Song of Songs IV, 7–8). By these indications the perfect and irreproachable beauty of the virginal soul is displayed. Consecrated to the divine altars, amid the attacks and hiding places of spiritual beasts, it has not been bent by mortals but has remained intent upon the mysteries of God, and has deserved to be loved by him whose breasts are full of joy: “For wine gladdens the heart of man” (Psalm CIII, 15).

[Note: The great majority of manuscripts read “not bent by moral things”; one has “by customs.”]

39. “The fragrance of your garments is above all perfumes” (Song of Songs IV, 10). And below: “The fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of Lebanon” (ibid., 11). See, virgin, what progress you grant us. Your first fragrance is above all the perfumes that were brought to the burial of the Savior (John XIX, 39), and it smells of the death of the body’s movements and the pleasures of the limbs. Your second fragrance, like the fragrance of Lebanon, exhales the integrity of the Lord’s body and the flower of virginal chastity.

# CHAPTER VIII

*He expounds the following passage of the Song of Songs, “A dropping honeycomb,” and so obtains an occasion for comparing holy virgins with bees.*

40. “Let your works compose a honeycomb” (Song of Songs IV, 11); for virginity is worthy to be compared with bees: so laborious, so modest, so self-controlled. The bee feeds on dew, knows no sexual intercourse, and composes honey. The virgin’s dew likewise is the divine word, because God’s words descend like dew. The virgin’s modesty is undefiled nature. The virgin’s offspring is the fruit of her lips, free from bitterness and fertile in sweetness. The labor is shared, and the fruit is shared.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “Let your work compose a honeycomb … The virginal dew also …”; the Roman edition has “for the virgin.”]

41. How I would wish you, daughter, to imitate this little bee, whose food is a flower, whose offspring is gathered by the mouth and composed by the mouth! Imitate her, daughter. Let your words present no covering of deceit and contain no wrapping of fraud, so that they may possess purity and be full of dignity.

42. Let eternal posterity of your merits also be produced for you by your mouth.

[Note: Many manuscripts read: “Let it be produced by your work.”]

Gather it not for yourself alone but also for many—for who knows when your soul will be required of you?—lest, leaving behind storehouses heaped with grain, useful neither for your life nor for your merits, you be snatched away to where you cannot carry your treasure. Be rich, therefore, but toward the poor, so that those who share your nature may also share your resources.

43. I also point out to you the flower that you must pluck, the one who said: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys. Like a lily among thorns” (Song of Songs II, 1–2). This clearly indicates that virtues are surrounded by the thorns of spiritual wickedness; hence no one gathers fruit unless he approaches with caution.

# CHAPTER VIII*

*He continues to adapt other passages from the Song of Songs to his subject. First he urges the virgin to seek Christ and explains where he may be found. Then, after describing his excellence according to both natures, he discloses with what perfections the Bride is adorned by him and with what defenses she is protected. Finally, he compares her chastity with that of the angels and prefers her even to that portion of them whom intemperance cast down from heaven.*

44. Take wings, therefore, virgin—but wings of the spirit—so that you may soar above vices if you desire to touch Christ: “He dwells on high and looks upon the lowly” (Psalm CXII, 5). His appearance is like the cedar of Lebanon, which extends its foliage to the clouds and fixes its root in the earth. For its beginning is from heaven, its later growth is on earth, and it produces fruits near to heaven. Search more diligently for so good a flower, lest perhaps you find it in the valley of your breast; for it is frequently breathed upon the lowly.

45. He loves to be born in gardens, where Susanna found him while walking—ready to die rather than be violated (Daniel XIII, 7). What these gardens are, he himself demonstrates when he says: “A garden enclosed is my sister, my bride; a garden enclosed, a sealed fountain” (Song of Songs IV, 12). In such gardens, because the image of God is stamped with seals, the water of a pure fountain shines forth, lest streams scattered amid the wallows of spiritual beasts be disturbed by mud. Hence modesty is enclosed, surrounded by a spiritual wall, lest it lie open to plunder.

[Note: Several manuscripts read: “surrounded by a moral spirit.”]

Thus, like a garden inaccessible to thieves, it gives off the fragrance of the vine, burns with the olive, and glows with the rose, so that religion may grow in the vine, peace in the olive, and the modesty of consecrated virginity in the rose. This is the fragrance with which the patriarch Jacob was fragrant when he deserved to hear: “Behold, the fragrance of my son is like the fragrance of a full field” (Genesis XXVII, 27). For although the field of the holy patriarch was full of almost every fruit, the former produced crops through greater labor of virtue, while this one produces flowers.

46. Gird yourself, therefore, virgin; and if you wish such a fragrance to breathe from you as from a garden, close it with prophetic commandments. “Set a guard over my mouth, and a door around my lips” (Psalm CXL, 3), so that you too may say: “As an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved among the sons. I desired and sat in his shadow, and his fruit was sweet in my throat” (Song of Songs II, 3). “I found him whom my soul loved; I held him and will not let him go” (ibid. III, 4). “My beloved has descended into his garden, to eat the fruit of his apple trees” (ibid. V, 1).

[Note: Thus most manuscripts; several manuscripts and all the editions instead read: “Let him descend … and eat,” which also agrees with the sacred text.]

“Come, my beloved, let us go out into the field” (ibid. VII, 11). “Set me as a seal upon your heart and as a seal upon your arm” (ibid. VIII, 6). “My beloved is white and red” (ibid. V, 10). It is fitting, virgin, that you should fully know the one whom you love and recognize in him the whole mystery both of his innate divinity and of his assumed embodiment. He is white with good reason, because he is the Father’s splendor; red, because he is the offspring of a virgin. The color of both natures shines and glows in him. Yet remember that the signs of his divinity are more ancient than the mysteries of his body, because he did not begin from the virgin; rather, he who already was came into the virgin.

47. He was separated from the soldiers; he was wounded by the spear (Matthew XXVII, 29 and following), so that he might heal us with the blood of his sacred wound.

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “He was despised by the soldiers.”]

He will surely answer you—for he is gentle and humble of heart (John XIX, 34), gracious in appearance—“Arise, North Wind, and come, South Wind; blow upon my garden, and let my perfumes flow” (Song of Songs IV, 16). For from every region of the world the fragrance of consecrated religion has grown, and the limbs of the beloved virgin have given off their fragrance.

[Note: All the editions and a few manuscripts read: “the fragrance of the beloved virgin has grown and her limbs have given off their scent”; the remaining manuscripts agree with us, except that many read “will give off their fragrance,” and one “gave off their fragrance.”]

“You are beautiful, my beloved, as a good reputation; fair as Jerusalem” (Song of Songs VI, 3). It is not the beauty of a fragile body, destined to perish through sickness or age, but the reputation of good merits, subject to no accidents and never to die, that adorns virgins.

48. And since you are now worthy to be compared not with human beings but with heavenly beings, whose life you live on earth, receive from the Lord the commandments you are to observe. “Set me,” he says, “as a seal upon your heart and as a seal upon your arm” (Song of Songs VIII, 6), so that the marks of your prudence and deeds may emerge more clearly, in which Christ, the image of God, may shine forth. He, equaling the breadth of the Father’s nature, expressed everything of divinity that he received from the Father. Hence the Apostle Paul also says that we have been sealed in the Spirit (Ephesians I, 13), because we have the image of the Father in the Son and the seal of the Son in the Spirit. Sealed with this Trinity, let us take the greatest care lest fickleness of conduct or the deceit of any adultery unseal the pledge we have received in our hearts.

49. But let fear depart from the holy virgins, to whom the Church first grants such great defenses. Concerned for the growth of her tender offspring, she herself grows like a wall, with breasts increasing abundantly like towers, until, once the hostile assault of the siege has been broken, she secures peace for vigorous youth through the protection of maternal virtue (Song of Songs VIII, 10). Hence the Prophet also says: “Let peace be in your strength, and abundance in your towers” (Psalm CXXI, 7).

50. Then, when the Lord of peace himself has embraced the vineyards entrusted to him with stronger arms and has seen his branches budding, he tempers the air around the emerging fruits with a protective countenance, as he himself testifies: “My vineyard is before me: a thousand for Solomon, and two hundred for those who guard its fruit” (Song of Songs VIII, 12).

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “A thousand, Solomon”; others: “a thousand, says Solomon.”]

51. Above he says: “Sixty mighty men surround his offspring, armed with drawn swords and trained in the disciplines of warfare” (Song of Songs III, 7–8).

[Note: All the editions read: “armed with drawn weapons.”]

Here he speaks of a thousand and two hundred. The number increased where the fruit also increased, because the holier a person is, the more fortified he is. Thus the prophet Elisha showed that the defenses of angelic armies were present with him (IV Kings VI, 17); thus Joshua son of Nun recognized the commander of the heavenly host (Joshua V, 14). Those who can fight for us can therefore guard fruit in us as well. But for you, holy virgins, there is a special defense, since you preserve undefiled the sacred chamber of the Lord. Nor is it surprising that angels fight for you, since you fight with the habits of angels. Virginal chastity deserves the protection of those whose life it deserves.

52. Why should I pursue the praise of chastity further? Chastity even makes angels. Whoever preserves it is an angel; whoever loses it is a devil. Hence religion also received its name.

[Note: The Theodoret and Teller manuscripts read: “Hence a legion also is called …” If this reading appeals to anyone, it would have to be referred to the devil, whom our Saint indicates in Book VI on Luke, section 47, to have been called a legion in the Gospel because of his impurity. The remaining manuscripts and the editions more correctly read: “Hence religion …” But do not suppose that Ambrose derives the word *religio* from chastity. What kinship is there between these words? Rather, he means “received a name,” that is, “received a title,” so that a virgin is called religion, as he immediately indicates. Cicero, in Book II of *On the Nature of the Gods*, derives *religio* from *relegere* (“to reread”); Lactantius, in Book IV, chapter 28, from *religare* (“to bind”); and Augustine, finally, from *reeligere* (“to choose again”).]

A virgin is one who marries God; a prostitute is one who makes gods. What shall I say of the resurrection, whose rewards you already possess? “In the resurrection,” he says, “they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven” (Matthew XXII, 30). What is promised to us is already present in you, and the fulfillment of our vows is found among you. You belong to this world, yet you are not in this world. The age has deserved to possess you, but it has not been able to hold you.

53. How remarkable, moreover, that angels fell from heaven into the world because of their intemperance, while virgins passed from the world into heaven because of their chastity!

[Note: Ambrose accepted as probable a threefold opinion concerning the sin of the angels, which he found in other Fathers. First, the interpretation concerning good angels of the passage read according to the Septuagint—“The angels of God saw the daughters of men”—is presented here and in *Apology of David*, page 675, following Philo and almost all the Fathers. The second interpretation, which explains the same passage as referring to evil angels who had already fallen from heaven because of pride, is presented from Philo and several others in *Noah and the Ark*, chapter 4, page 23. The third, which explains the passage as referring to the marriages of the sons of Seth with the daughters of Cain, is preferred in the sermon on Psalm CXVIII, sermon 4, page 1011. On all these passages, see our observations. Meanwhile, observe that the opinion which seems to have arisen in the fourth century on the authority of Ambrose, Jerome, and Augustine subsequently became the sole prevailing view.]

Blessed are the virgins whom no enticement of bodies solicits and no mire of pleasures casts down! A diet of moderation and a drink of abstinence teach them not to know vices, because they teach them not to know the causes of vices. The cause of sin has often deceived even the righteous. Hence, after God’s people sat down to eat and drink, they denied God (Exodus XXXII, 6). Hence Lot unknowingly endured intercourse with his daughters (Genesis XIX, 33). Hence the sons of Noah, walking backward, once covered their father’s nakedness (Genesis IX, 22): what the shameless man saw, the modest man blushed at, and the devout man covered—he would have offended had he too looked. How great is the power of wine, that the waters of the flood did not strip the man whom wine stripped naked!

# CHAPTER IX

*The final praise of virginity is presented: namely, its freedom from avarice. On this occasion the holy Bishop recalls to his sister how great is the happiness of one who is not forced to accommodate herself to the luxury and vanity to which women about to marry are enslaved.*

54. What of this? How great a happiness it is that no desire for possessions inflames you! The poor man asks for what you have; what you do not have, he does not demand. The fruit of your labor is a treasure for the needy, and two coins, if they are all you possess, are the wealth of the giver.

54*. Listen, then, sister, from how many things you are free. For it is neither my task to teach you what you must avoid nor yours to learn it; the practice of perfect virtue does not require instruction but itself forms it.

[Note: In the Benedictine edition the number 54 is used twice. We have transcribed both, marking the later one with an asterisk. The same asterisk, whenever attached to a number, has the same meaning. —Editor.]

You see how she who arranges herself in order to please proceeds like the trays borne in a procession, turning everyone’s eyes and faces toward herself; and by that very effort to please she becomes more deformed. For she displeases the people before she pleases her husband. But among you, the rejection of concern for adornment is more becoming; and the very fact that you do not adorn yourselves is itself an adornment.

[Note: The editions read: “having rejected concern for beauty, she pleases more.”]

55. [Note: All editions, together with one or two manuscripts, read: “Behold ears torn by wounds, and miserable necks bowed under the weight”; the result is not an alleviation of punishments, etc. Quite a few manuscripts read: “Pity the flesh torn by wounds, the ears, and the burdens pressing down the neck. They are not…” The remaining manuscripts have the better reading, as in the text. Moreover, if one wishes to compare this entire passage with what is read on the same subject in Clement of Alexandria, *Paedagogus*, book II, chapter 12, and Tertullian, *On the Adornment of Women*, chapter 6, one will readily observe that these early Fathers were by no means unknown to Ambrose.]

Behold ears torn by wounds, and pity the burdens of the bowed, wretched neck. The differences among metals are not alleviations of punishments. Here a chain constricts the neck; there an iron shackle encloses the foot. It makes no difference whether the body is weighed down with gold or with iron. [Note: Thus a large number of manuscripts read; some, however, as do the editions: “If the neck is weighed down, if movement is burdened, what good is value…”] Thus the neck is weighed down, thus movement is burdened. Value is of no help—except that you women tremble lest your punishment be wasted on you. [Col. 0204B] What difference does it make whether another’s judgment or your own condemns you? In this respect you are even more pitiable than those condemned by public law: they wish to be stripped, whereas you wish to be bound.

56. How pitiable, too, is that condition in which, like the form of a slave offered for sale, a bride-to-be is put up for auction, so that whoever wins by his price may purchase her. Yet slaves are sold under more tolerable conditions, since they often choose their masters. If a virgin chooses, it is a crime; if she does not choose, it is an insult. Although she may be beautiful and attractive, she both fears and desires to be seen: she desires it so that she may sell herself at a higher price; she fears that the very fact of being seen may bring her disgrace. What mockeries of hopes there are, and what anxious fears at the outcome of the suitors’ efforts: lest the poor man mock her, lest the rich man disdain her, lest the handsome man ridicule her, lest the nobleman scorn her!

## CHAPTER X

[Col. 0204C] To those who object that Ambrose’s frequent exhortations to virginity have produced no result sufficient to satisfy them, he introduces examples both of other virgins and of those from Mauretania and Bologna; but he especially praises the virtues of the latter and their zeal in promoting virginity.

57. Someone will say: “Every day you sing the praises of virgins to us. What am I to do, when I sing the same thing every day and accomplish nothing?” But it is not my fault. Indeed, consecrated virgins come from Placentia, [Note: A few manuscripts read, “great virgins come from Placentinosa”; incorrectly.] they come from Bologna, [Note: In almost all manuscripts, “They come from Bologna” is missing.] they come from Mauretania, to be veiled here. You see a great thing. Here I treat the subject, and elsewhere I persuade. If that is so, let us treat it elsewhere, [Note: Some manuscripts read, “so that I may persuade elsewhere.”] so that we may persuade you.

58. What of the fact that even those who do not listen to me follow, while those who listen do not follow? For I have known many virgins who wished to do so but were forbidden even to come forth by their mothers—and what is more serious, by widows, with whom I am now speaking. Surely, if your daughters wished to love a man, they could choose by law whomever they wished. If they are permitted to choose a man, are they not permitted to choose God?

59. Consider how sweet is the fruit of chastity, since it has taken root even among barbarian hearts. Virgins brought here from the remotest regions of Mauretania [Col. 0205B] desire to be consecrated; and although all their households are in chains, [Note: This refers here to the tyranny of Gildo, not of Firmus, as some maintain. Firmus was defeated in A.D. 373 by Count Theodosius, father of Theodosius the Great. Gildo, although he had fought on the Roman side against his brother Firmus, after Firmus had been killed himself seized Africa and supported the Donatists, who savagely harassed the Catholics. As for the law said to have been issued in this year in the Theodosian Code, by which the repetition of baptism was prohibited: since it was addressed to Flavianus, vicar of Africa, who was himself infected with this same heresy, it should not be thought to have brought any assistance to the Church. See Augustine, *Against Petilian*, book II, chapter 83, and letter 87 in the new edition, section 8; also Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXVIII, and Claudian, *On the War against Gildo*.] chastity nevertheless does not know how to be captive. She professes the kingdom of eternity, though she mourns the injury of slavery.

60. For what shall I say of the virgins of Bologna, a fertile army of modesty, who renounce worldly pleasures and dwell in the sanctuary of virginity? Without a companion of the male sex, [Note: That is, masculine companionship, since at that time it was unusual for women to live without the company of men.] advanced through modesty to the number of twenty and to the fruit of a hundredfold, and having left their parents’ dwelling, they make their way into the tents of Christ, tireless soldiers of chastity. Now they resound with spiritual songs; now they earn their sustenance by their labors; they even seek with their own hands the means of supporting generosity.

61. And if the scent of seeking out virgins should become habitual—for beyond all else they hunt out and investigate modesty’s quarry—then with every trace of their concern they pursue the hidden prey even to its very bedchambers. Or if the freer flight of one of them should appear, you may see them all rise on every wing, beat their feathers, and leap forth with applause, so that they may surround the flying one with the chaste choir of modesty, until, delighted by the shining company, and forgetful of her father’s house, she enters the snares of modesty and the enclosure of chastity. [Note: Thus all the manuscripts read; the edition has instead: “forgetful of home and family.”]

## CHAPTER XI

It is desirable that a virgin’s parents should favor her, yet she is worthy of greater praise when divine love has impelled her toward this purpose despite their opposition. Therefore neither the force of parents nor the loss of patrimony is to be feared; this is confirmed by the memorable deed of a noble and devout virgin.

62. [Col. 0205D] It is good, then, if the attentions of parents breathe upon a virgin like breezes of modesty; but it is more glorious if the fire of tender youth, even without the nourishment of the old, spontaneously hurries itself toward the fuel of chastity. Her parents will deny her a dowry; but you have a rich bridegroom, and, content with his treasure, you will not seek the benefits of an ancestral inheritance. How much more valuable than dowry payments is chaste poverty!

63. And yet, have you ever heard that anyone was made an outcast from a lawful inheritance on account of a devotion to purity? Parents object, but they wish to be overcome. At first they resist because they fear believing; they are often indignant, so that you may learn to conquer; they threaten disinheritance, to test whether you can avoid fearing the loss of worldly goods; they flatter you with seductive enticements, to see whether the various blandishments of pleasures can soften you. You are being trained, virgin, while you are being compelled. These are your first contests, presented by the anxious wishes of your parents. Conquer your filial affection first, girl. If you conquer your household, you conquer the world.

64. [Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “But what does it matter whether the losses of your patrimony remain with you or with your family?” And below: “and does not receive much more … eternal life.” “Believe,” etc.]

But let us suppose that the losses of your patrimony remain with you: will not the losses of possessions that are fleeting and fragile be compensated by the future kingdoms of heaven? Yet if we believe the words of heaven, there is no one who has left house, or parents, or brothers, or wife, or children for the sake of the kingdom of God, and who does not receive seven times as much in this present age; and in the age to come he will possess eternal life (Matt. 19:29). Entrust your faith to God; lend to Christ what you entrust to a human being as money. The good guardian of a deposited hope pays out the talent of your faith with multiplied interest. Truth does not deceive, justice does not circumvent, virtue does not cheat. But if you do not believe the oracle, believe at least the examples.

65. A girl who until recently was noble in the world, but is now nobler before God, is within our memory. When her parents and relatives were pressing her into marriage, she fled to the most holy altar. Where could a virgin turn better than to the place where the sacrifice of virginity is offered? Nor was that the end of her boldness. She stood at God’s altar as a sacrifice of modesty, a victim of chastity: now placing the priest’s right hand upon her head and asking for prayer, now impatient of a fitting delay and placing the crown of her head beneath the altar. [Note: Amerbach and Erasmus read: “Will the altar veil me better?” Gill and the Roman edition, “Will my mother veil me better than the altar?” The manuscripts, however, unanimously have the best reading: “Will the maforte veil me better?” *Maforte*, or *mavorte*, as in Cassian, book I, chapter 7, was a kind of veil with which a virgin’s head was covered at her consecration, just as the *flammeum* or *flammeus* covered the face of girls when they were joined in marriage; hence the words *nubere* and *nuptiae* are derived. Nevertheless, *flammeus* is sometimes also used of a virgin’s veil, as in this passage, and as will be seen in several places below.]

“Will the maforte veil me better,” she said, “than the altar, which itself sanctifies the veils? Such a bridal veil is more fitting, in which Christ, the head of all, is consecrated daily.”

[Col. 0206D] “What are you doing, relatives? Why do you still trouble my mind by seeking a marriage? I have long since made provision for myself. Are you offering a bridegroom? I have found a better one. Heap up whatever riches you wish, boast of nobility, proclaim power: I have one whom no one can equal—rich in the world, powerful in authority, noble in heaven. If you have such a one, I do not reject your proposal; if you cannot find him, parents, you are not providing for me but envying me.”

66. While the others were silent, one spoke more abruptly: “What if your father were alive? Would he permit you to remain unmarried?”

Then she, with greater religious devotion and more measured filial reverence, replied: “Perhaps that is why he has died: so that no one might be able to offer an impediment.” [Note: The Roman edition, with a few manuscripts, reads: “so that he could offer no impediment.”]

By her reply concerning her father, she uttered an oracle concerning herself, and proved it by the timely end of her own life. Thus the others, each beginning to fear the same thing for himself, began to favor what they had sought to prevent. Virginity brought no loss of the possessions owed to her; rather, she also received the benefit of purity. You have here, girls, the reward of devotion; parents, beware of the example of offense.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0207]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0207B]

Ambrose explains that, recognizing the need to form the character of virgins in this book, he has chosen the path of examples; he modestly deflects from himself the charge of presumption, and explains why he undertook the work in writing rather than orally.

1. In the preceding book I wished—not that I was able—to explain how great is the gift of virginity, so that the heavenly grace of the gift might itself invite the reader. In the second book it is fitting that the virgin should be instructed and educated, as though by the teaching of suitable precepts.

2. But since we are weak in giving admonition and unequal to teaching—for the teacher ought to excel the one being taught—we thought that the virgin should be imbued by examples rather than by precepts, lest we appear either to have abandoned the task we had undertaken or to have claimed too much for ourselves. An example, indeed, accomplishes more, since what has already been done is not judged difficult, what has been proved is useful, and what has been transmitted into us by a kind of hereditary succession through the practice of a father’s virtue is religious.

3. If anyone accuses us of presumption, let him accuse us rather of diligence, because, when virgins asked, I thought that not even this should be denied them. For I preferred to be led into the danger of modesty than not to comply with the will of those whose devotion our God also graciously accepts.

4. Nor can this be called presumption, since, although they had resources from which to learn, they sought my affection rather than my instruction. [Note: All editions read, “and diligence cannot be excused,” with no sense that removes the negation; but the verb is also absent from the manuscripts and must be supplied. Again, where the old edition and some manuscripts read “the authority of the mother,” the Roman edition and other manuscripts have “the authority of the martyr.” Finally, for *derivarent*, found in all editions and some manuscripts, several others more elegantly read *derivarem*.]

Nor need diligence be excused, since, having the authority of a martyr for the observance of discipline, I did not judge it superfluous to channel the charm of my speech toward the attractiveness of their profession. It is easy for one to teach who restrains vices with stern feeling; but we, who cannot teach, shall flatter.

5. And since many of them, being absent, longed for the use of our speech, I composed this volume, so that, having received the gift of my voice sent to them, they would not think that the one they might hold was absent. But let us pursue the subject before us.

## CHAPTER II

The example of Mary is proposed to virgins; her various virtues are enumerated: chastity, humility, austerity of life, and love of solitude. Once these virtues have been established by evangelical testimony, her devotion toward her relatives, her diligence in learning, and her eagerness to visit the temple are also commended. Finally, it is related how she, adorned with so many gifts, will go to meet countless virgins and lead them, with a magnificent triumph, to the Bridegroom’s chamber and to the heavenly altars, to which they were made like by their chastity.

6. Let the virginity and life of Mary be set before you as though depicted in a portrait, from which, as from a mirror, the appearance of chastity and the form of virtue may shine forth. From this model you may take examples for living, since it displays, as in a pattern, the lessons of goodness and shows what you ought to correct, what to reproduce, and what to retain. [Note: Thus several of the more authoritative manuscripts read; the other manuscripts and all editions have: “the virginity and life of blessed Mary, from whom, as in a mirror, the appearance of chastity shines forth,” etc.]

7. The first stimulus to learning is the nobility of the teacher. Who is nobler than the Mother of God? Who is more splendid than she whom Splendor chose? Who is more chaste than she who bore a body without bodily contamination? For what shall I say of her other virtues? She was a virgin not only in body but also in mind, and no deceitful artifice corrupted her sincere affection; humble in heart, weighty in speech, prudent in spirit, sparing in conversation, more devoted to reading; placing her hope not in the uncertainty of riches but in the prayer of the poor; diligent in work, modest in speech, accustomed to seek as judge of her mind not a human being but God; harming no one, wishing well to all, rising before her elders, not envying her equals, fleeing boasting, following reason, loving virtue.

When did she ever offend her parents even by her expression? When did she disagree with her relatives? When did she disdain the lowly? When did she mock the weak? When did she avoid the needy? She was accustomed to visit only those gatherings of men at which compassion would not blush and modesty would not pass by. There was nothing harsh in her eyes, nothing brazen in her words, nothing immodest in her actions; no excessively languid gesture, no overly relaxed walk, no wanton voice. Thus the very appearance of her body was an image of her mind, a figure of her goodness. For a good house ought to be recognized at the vestibule itself, and at its first entrance it should show that no darkness lies within, so that our mind, unimpeded by any bodily barriers, may shine outward like the light of a lamp placed within. [Note: The Roman edition, with one or two manuscripts, reads: “unimpeded by any bodily restraints.”]

8. Why should I describe her frugality in food and her abundance in duties—the one extending beyond nature, the other almost falling short of nature itself: there, no periods of time left without activity; here, days doubled by fasting? And whenever the desire for refreshment arose, the food was usually whatever came to hand, enough to ward off death, not to provide delicacies. The desire to sleep never came before necessity; and yet, when the body rested, the mind remained awake. Often in dreams it either repeated what it had read, continued what sleep had interrupted, carried out what it had planned, or foretold what was to be done. [Note: Some manuscripts read: “or repeats pleasant things.”]

9. She knew no reason to go out of the house except when she went to church, and even then with her parents or relatives. At home she was industrious in solitude; in public she was accompanied by a retinue, yet she had no better guardian of herself than herself. Venerable in walk and speech, she lifted not so much the footprint of her step as the degree of her virtue.

Let the virgin have others as guardians of her limbs, but let her herself be the guardian of her conduct. There will be more from whom she may learn if she teaches herself, since she has virtues as her teachers: whatever she does is instruction. Thus Mary paid attention to everything as though she were being admonished by many; thus she fulfilled every duty of virtue, so that she seemed not so much to learn as to teach.

10. Such did the evangelist show her (Luke 1:27); such did the angel find her; such did the Holy Spirit choose her. Why should I linger over each detail, as though she were loved by her parents and praised by strangers, when she was found worthy to give birth to the Son of God? She was found at home, in the inner chamber, at the very entrance of the angel, without a companion, lest anyone interrupt her attention or disturb her. For she did not desire female companions, since she had good thoughts as companions. Indeed, she seemed less alone when she was alone. For how could she be alone, when so many books were with her, so many archangels, so many prophets?

11. Finally, Gabriel found her where he used to visit her; and Mary, as though the angel had assumed the appearance of a man, trembled, as though, hearing his name, she recognized someone not unknown (ibid., 28ff.). Thus she was disturbed by a man, though she was not disturbed by an angel, so that you may recognize religious ears and modest eyes. When greeted, she fell silent; when addressed, she replied. Yet she who had first been disturbed in her feelings afterward promised obedience. [Note: All editions read “had been hesitant at the sight”; all manuscripts, “had disturbed her feelings.”]

12. How devout she was toward her relatives is shown by divine Scripture (ibid., 45). For she became humbler when she learned that she had been chosen by God, and immediately went to her kinswoman in the hill country—not, of course, so that she might believe by an example what she had already believed through an oracle: “Blessed is she who believed” (ibid., 56). And she remained with her for three months. In so long an interval, faith was not being sought but devotion was being shown. This occurred after the child, leaping in his mother’s womb, had greeted the mother of the Lord, being more mature in devotion than in nature.

13. Then, amid so many successive signs—when the barren woman gave birth, the virgin conceived, the mute spoke, the magus worshiped, Simeon waited, and the stars announced—Mary was swift at the arrival and steadfast before the miracle: “She kept all these things in her heart” (Luke 2:19). Although she was the mother of the Lord, she nevertheless desired to learn the Lord’s commandments; and she who had given birth to God still desired to know God.

14. What of the fact that every year she also went to Jerusalem on the solemn day of Passover, and went with Joseph? (ibid., 41.) Everywhere, modesty is the companion of each virtue in a virgin. It must be inseparable from virginity, without which virginity cannot exist. Therefore Mary did not go to the temple without the guardian of her modesty.

15. This is the image of virginity. Such was Mary that the life of this one woman is the instruction of all. If, then, the author is pleasing, let us approve the work, so that whoever desires her reward for herself may imitate her example. How many forms of virtue shine forth in one virgin! The secret of modesty, the standard of faith, the obedience of devotion: a virgin within the house, a companion in service, a mother at the temple.

16. O how many virgins she will meet, how many she will embrace and lead to the Lord, saying: “These are the ones who guarded the bed of my Son, these are the ones who kept the nuptial chambers with unblemished modesty!” How the Lord himself will commend them to the Father, repeating that saying of his: “Holy Father, these are the ones whom I guarded for you, in whom the Son of Man rested, laying down his head. I ask that where I am, they also may be with me” (John 17:24).

But if they did not live for themselves alone, they ought not to benefit themselves alone. Let them redeem their parents; let them redeem their brothers. “Righteous Father, the world did not know me, but these knew me and did not wish to know the world” (ibid., 25). [Note: Some manuscripts read: “They ought not to be able to benefit themselves alone.” And below: “the world did not know you.”]

17. [Note: Thus the old edition and nearly all the manuscripts read, except for a few, which have “What a good thing that is!” instead of “What a splendid spectacle that is!”—not very correctly. Gill and the Roman edition, after “What a spectacle that is, without that bridegroom,” add “what joy!”]

What a splendid spectacle that will be, what joy among the angels applauding that she deserves to dwell in heaven, she who lived a heavenly life in the world! Then Mary too, taking up the tambourine, will raise up choirs of virgins singing to the Lord because they crossed the sea of the world without the waves of worldly things (Exod. 15:20). Then each will exult, saying: “I will go to the altar of my God, to God who gives joy to my youth” (Ps. 42:4). “I will offer to God a sacrifice of praise, and I will fulfill my vows to the Most High” (Ps. 49:14).

18. For I would not hesitate to say that God’s altars stand open to you, whose minds I would confidently call altars, on which Christ is sacrificed daily for the redemption of the body. If the virgin’s body is God’s temple, what is the spirit, which, as though the ashes of the limbs had been stirred, covered by the hand of the eternal priest, exhales the vapor of divine fire? Blessed virgins, who breathe forth such immortal grace that you are like gardens in your flowers, like temples in your holiness, like altars in your priest!

## CHAPTER III

As Mary is said to be the model for shaping one’s life, so Thecla is the model for facing death. She was condemned to the beasts, yet not only suffered nothing from them but, on the contrary, was cherished and worshiped by them. And lest the preceding examples frighten anyone, a more recent example is now proposed.

19. Therefore let holy Mary form the discipline of life, and let Thecla teach the lesson of being sacrificed. She, fleeing the marriage bond and condemned through the rage of her bridegroom, changed even the nature of beasts through their reverence for virginity. For when she was prepared for the wild beasts, and even turned her gaze away from men, offering her very vital parts to a savage lion, she caused those who had brought lustful eyes to return with chaste ones.

20. It was possible to see the beast licking her feet and lying on the ground, bearing witness with mute sound that it could not violate the virgin’s sacred body. Thus the beast worshiped its prey; forgetful of its own nature, it had assumed the nature that human beings had lost. You might have seen, by a kind of transfusion of nature, human beings clothed in savagery commanding the beast’s ferocity; the beast kissing the virgin’s feet and teaching what human beings ought to do.

Virginity possesses so much power to inspire wonder that even lions marvel at it. Food did not soften them though unfed, their roused impulses did not carry them away, anger did not inflame them when provoked, habit did not deceive them when accustomed to it, nor did their natural savagery take possession of them. [Note: Some manuscripts read: “nor did accustomed practice deceive them.”]

They taught reverence while worshiping the martyr; [Note: He calls blessed Thecla a martyr because she endured torments for the faith which, by their nature, should have brought death, although it is thought more probable that she was divinely delivered from them and died peacefully. See Baronius, Appendix to volume X.] they also taught chastity, since they kissed nothing but the virgin’s feet, their eyes lowered toward the earth, as though ashamed lest any male—or beast—should see the virgin naked.

21. Someone will say: “Why did you introduce the example of Mary, as though a mother of the Lord who could be imitated might be found? Why also that of Thecla, whom the Teacher of the Gentiles instructed? If you seek a disciple, provide a teacher of this kind.”

I present to you a recent example of this kind, so that you may understand that the Apostle is not the teacher of one person only but of all.

## CHAPTER IV

When a virgin of Antioch refused to sacrifice to idols, she was condemned to a brothel, but through the intervention of a Christian soldier she escaped without any loss of modesty by exchanging clothes with him. When he was consequently led to execution, she returned immediately and steadfastly contended with him for the crown, which at last was bestowed upon them both.

22. Not long ago there was a certain virgin in Antioch [Note: Some manuscripts read: “avoiding the sight of public life”; others, and the editions, as in the text, except that the editions prefer “she avoided being seen,” whereas all the manuscripts have “she avoided eyes.” Many have thought that the virgin mentioned here is the same as Theodora of Alexandria, whom the Martyrology formerly circulated under the name of Bede the Venerable reports to have been delivered from a similar punishment through the aid of the Christian soldier Didymus. This error led not only Molanus, Surius, and many others astray, but even Baronius himself; accordingly, in his notes on the Martyrology for April 28, he writes that the occurrence is said by Ambrose to have taken place at Antioch through the ignorance of the writers. Yet the same cardinal withdrew his opinion in the *Annals* under the year 309, chiefly because Didymus is not recorded as having suffered with Theodora in the cited Martyrologies. The continuators of the Bollandists propose two further considerations: that this virgin is described as having recently been alive, and that her conversation with her deliverer is absent from some Acts of Theodora. One might answer the first point by saying that, in comparison with Thecla, who lived in apostolic times, she lived recently; and the second by saying that the conversation was omitted merely for the sake of brevity. But what they think is something in Ambrose’s narrative that he transferred from the so-called proconsular Acts seems to us much more likely to have been transferred from Ambrose into those Acts. Who, then, should that virgin of Ambrose be considered to be? We believe that it is neither easy nor particularly necessary to determine this.]

She avoided public notice; but the more she avoided men’s eyes, the more she inflamed them. For beauty heard of but not seen is desired all the more, through two goads of desire, love and curiosity: nothing is encountered that might displease, and what is pleasing is thought to be even greater when it is not examined by a judging eye but longed for by a loving mind. Therefore the holy virgin, lest the desires for possession should be nourished any longer by hope, professed the integrity of her modesty and so extinguished the torches of the wicked that she was no longer loved but denounced.

23. Behold persecution. The girl, unaccustomed to flee and certainly afraid of falling among those lying in wait for her modesty, prepared her spirit for virtue: so devout that she did not fear death, so modest that she awaited it. The day of the crown arrived. Everyone’s expectation was immense. The girl was brought forth, professing a twofold contest, both of chastity and of religion. But when they saw the steadfastness of her profession, her fear of violating modesty, her readiness for torture, and her shame before being seen, they began to devise a way to destroy religion under the appearance of chastity, [Note: Several manuscripts read: “to destroy the appearance of chastity”; one has: “to destroy the appearance of chastity and religion.” The more elegant reading, found in the other manuscripts and editions, is as in the text. They expected her to sacrifice to idols rather than endure being taken to prostitution.] so that, once they had taken away what was greater, they might also snatch away what remained. They order the virgin either to sacrifice or to be prostituted in a brothel. How do those who avenge their gods in this way worship them? Or how do those who judge in this manner live themselves?

24. Here the girl, not because she doubted about religion but because she trembled concerning her modesty, said to herself: “What shall we do? Today I shall be either a martyr or a virgin; one of the two crowns is begrudged us. But the name of virgin is not acknowledged where the author of virginity is denied. For how can you be a virgin if you worship a prostitute? How can you be a virgin if you love adulterers? How can you be a virgin if you seek love? It is more tolerable to have a virgin mind than a virgin flesh” (22, question 5, chapter *Tolerabilius*). “Both are good, if it is permitted; if it is not permitted, then at least let us be chaste not before human beings but before God. Rahab was a prostitute, but after she believed in God, she found salvation” (Josh. 2:9ff.). “Judith adorned herself to please an adulterer” (Judith 9:1ff.); yet because she did this out of religious devotion, not love, no one judged her an adulteress.

The example turned out well. For if she who entrusted herself to religion preserved both her modesty and her country, perhaps by preserving religion we too shall preserve chastity. But if Judith had wished to place chastity before religion, she would have lost both her country and her chastity.

25. Thus, instructed by such examples and holding in mind the Lord’s words—“Whoever loses his life for my sake will find it” (Mark 10:39)—she wept and remained silent, lest the adulterer hear her even speaking. She did not choose the violation of modesty; she rejected Christ’s denial. Consider whether she could have adulterated her body when she did not even adulterate her voice.

26. For a long time now my speech has been ashamed, and, as though afraid to approach and explain the succession of shameful events, it hesitates. Close your ears, virgins. The girl of God is led to a brothel. But open your ears, virgins. The virgin of Christ may be prostituted; she cannot be adulterated. Wherever the virgin of God is, there is the temple of God. Brothels do not stain chastity; rather, chastity removes even the infamy of the place.

27. A huge crowd of wanton men gathers at the brothel. Learn the miracles of the martyrs, holy virgins; unlearn the names of places. [Note: Quite a few manuscripts read: “Shut the dove inside … who will first attack the dove?”]

The dove is shut inside; hawks shriek outside. Each contends to be the first to seize the prey. But she, lifting her hands to heaven as though she had come to a house of prayer, not to a place of lust, said:

“Christ, you who subdued the savage lions for the virgin Daniel (Dan. 14:39), can also subdue the savage minds of human beings. For the Chaldeans fire rained dew (Dan. 3:50); for the Jews the water held itself suspended (Exod. 14:21)—through your mercy, not by their own nature. Susanna knelt for punishment and triumphed over the adulterers (Dan. 13:42); the hand that violated the gifts of your temple withered (3 Kings 13:4). Now your temple itself is being touched. Do not permit the sacrilege of incest, you who did not permit theft. Let your name be blessed now also, so that, having come here for adultery, I may depart a virgin.”

28. She had scarcely finished the prayer when a man burst in, terrifying in the appearance of a soldier. How the virgin trembled at him before whom the trembling crowd gave way! But she had not forgotten her reading: “Daniel had come to witness Susanna’s punishment, and the one whom the people had condemned was acquitted by one man” (Dan. 13:45ff.).
