A sheep may also lie hidden beneath the appearance of a wolf. Christ too has his soldiers, and he even has legions (Matt. 26:53). Or perhaps an executioner has entered. Do not be afraid, soul; such men often make martyrs. O virgin, your faith has saved you!

29. The soldier said to her: “Please, sister, do not be afraid. I have come here as a brother to save your soul, not to destroy it. Save me, so that you yourself may be saved. I entered as an adulterer; if you wish, I shall leave as a martyr. Let us exchange clothing: yours suits me, and mine suits you—but both belong to Christ. Your garment will make me a true soldier; mine will make you a virgin. You will be well dressed, while I shall be better stripped, so that the persecutor may recognize me. Take the clothing that conceals the woman; give me what consecrates the martyr. Put on the cloak that hides the virgin’s limbs and preserves her modesty. Take the cap that covers your hair and conceals your face.

“Those who enter a brothel usually blush. When you have come out, be careful not to look back, remembering Lot’s wife, who lost her nature because, although with chaste eyes, she looked back at something impure (Gen. 19:26). Do not fear that anything will be lost from the sacrifice. I will offer the victim to God on your behalf; you will offer the soldier to Christ on my behalf. You possess the good warfare of chastity, which serves for everlasting pay; the breastplate of righteousness, which encloses the body with spiritual protection; the shield of faith, with which you may repel the wound; the helmet of salvation—for there is the defense of our salvation where Christ is, since the head of a woman is a man, but the head of a virgin is Christ.”

30. And as he speaks these words, he removes the cloak. Yet his appearance still arouses suspicion both as persecutor and as adulterer. The virgin offers her neck; the soldier offers his cloak. What pomp, what splendor, when in a brothel they contended for martyrdom! Let the characters be added: a soldier and a virgin—that is, by nature unlike one another, but alike through God’s mercy—so that the oracle may be fulfilled: “Then wolves and lambs shall feed together” (Isa. 65:25). Behold, the ewe-lamb and the wolf not only feed together but are also sacrificed together. What more? With her clothing changed, the girl flies out of the snare, no longer on her own wings, since she was borne along on spiritual ones; and—something no age has ever seen—a virgin emerges from the brothel, but now Christ’s virgin.

31. But those who saw with their eyes and did not see [Note: Thus all the manuscripts, except that two have *fremuere* (“they roared”); the Roman edition, however, after “they saw” and “did not see,” adds only *corde* (“with the heart”), while, with the other editions, it removes the particle *ceu* before *lupi* (“as wolves”).] raged like predators against a lamb, like wolves over prey. One who was more shameless entered. But when he had taken in the whole situation with his eyes, he said: “What is this? A girl entered; a man appears. Behold, this is not the fabulous stag substituted for the virgin [Note: Understand the hind substituted in the sacrifice for Iphigenia, the virgin daughter of King Agamemnon. Dictys of Crete, Book I; Euripides, *Iphigenia at Aulis*; Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, Book XII; and others speak of it.], but what is true: a soldier from a virgin. Yet I had also heard, and had not believed, that Christ changed water into wine (John 2:9); now he has begun to change sex as well. Let us go away from here while we are still what we were. Have I myself also been changed, since I see something other than I believe? I came to the brothel; I see a surety [Note: Properly, *vadimonium* is a promise to appear on an appointed day before judges; but here it means that the soldier established himself, as it were, as the virgin’s surety.]. Yet I shall leave changed; I shall depart chaste, although I entered as an adulterer.”

32. As proof of the matter, since a crown was owed to so great a victor, the man who had been seized for the virgin was condemned in her place. Thus from the brothel not only a virgin but also martyrs emerged. It is said that the girl ran to the place of execution, and that both contended over who should die, while he said: “I have been ordered to be killed; the sentence absolved you when it seized me.” But she began to cry out: “I did not choose you as the surety of my death [Note: Some manuscripts read: “but I feared the seizure of my modesty.” More manuscripts, however, together with all the editions and a few others, preserve the connection and prefer the more elegant reading: “but I desired you as the pledge of my sex.”]. I sought you as the pledge of my modesty. If modesty is at issue, my sex remains; if blood is demanded, I do not need a guarantor—I have the means by which I may discharge the debt. This sentence has been pronounced against me, and it was pronounced for me. Certainly, if I had made you guarantor for a debt of money, and, while I was absent, a judge had assigned your property to the creditor, you would bring the same action against me, and I would settle your obligations from my estate. If I refused, who would judge me undeserving of an undeserved death? How much greater is the interest on this head! Let me die innocent, so that I may not die guilty. There is no middle course here: today I shall either be guilty of your blood or a martyr because of me. If I returned quickly, who dares exclude me? If I delayed, who dares absolve me? I owe more to the laws, being guilty not only of my own flight but also of another’s slaughter. The limbs that were insufficient for the outrage are sufficient for death. There is a place in a virgin for a wound where there was no place for insult. I avoided disgrace; I did not change my martyr’s profession. If you snatch death from me, you have not redeemed me but deceived me. Beware, I beg you, lest you contend [Note: Some manuscripts read: “Beware lest you be heard contradicting.”]; beware lest you dare to contradict me. Do not take away the benefit you gave. While you deny me this sentence, you restore the former one. For one sentence is changed by the sentence previously pronounced. If the later one does not hold me, the earlier one does. We can both satisfy the sentence, if you first allow me to be killed. In your case they have no other punishment to inflict; in the virgin, modesty is liable to punishment. Therefore you will be more glorious if you appear to have made a martyr from an adulteress than to have made an adulteress from a martyr.”

33. What are you waiting for? Two contended, and both conquered; the crown was not divided but increased. Thus the holy martyrs, conferring benefits upon one another, the one gave martyrdom its beginning, the other its completion.

## CHAPTER V

The memorable deed of two friends of the Pythagorean school is recounted with praise, yet shown to be inferior to the preceding example. The discussion also treats of Dionysius’ mockery in stripping the idols, and of the weakness of the gods in tolerating his sacrileges; set against this is the severe vengeance with which God once proceeded against Jeroboam.

34. The schools of philosophers likewise raise Damon and Pythias, the Pythagoreans, to heaven [Note: This pair of friends is discussed by Cicero, *On Duties*, Book III, in the passage already cited by us and elsewhere, as well as by Valerius Maximus, Book IV, chapter 7, and others.]. When one of them had been sentenced to death, he asked for time to settle his affairs. But the exceedingly clever tyrant, thinking that no one could be found, required him to provide a surety who would be killed in his place if he himself delayed. I do not know which of the two was more noble. Both were noble. One found a guarantor for his death; the other offered himself. Thus, while the condemned man delayed his punishment, the guarantor did not refuse death, but faced it with a serene countenance. When he was being led away, his friend returned, presented his neck, and submitted his throat. Then the tyrant, astonished that friendship was dearer to the philosophers than life, asked to be received into friendship by those whom he had condemned [Note: All the editions read: “Such is the grace of virtue.” All the manuscripts read: “that the grace of virtue is so great,” with *constat* (“it is evident”) or something similar understood.].

Such is the grace of virtue that it even bends a tyrant.

35. Worthy of praise, but inferior to our examples. There both were men; here there is one virgin, who first even conquered her sex. They were friends; these were strangers. They offered themselves to one tyrant; these to several tyrants, and to tyrants more savage because the former spared, while the latter killed. Among those two, only one was subject to necessity; among these, the free will of both was involved. These were also wiser, because the goal of the others’ devotion was the favor of friendship, while for these it was the crown of martyrdom. The former contended for men; these for God.

36. Since we have mentioned this matter, it is fitting to weave in what he thought about his gods, so that you may judge them all the weaker, since their worshipers mock them. For when he had entered the temple of Jupiter [Note: On these mockeries of Dionysius directed against his own gods, consult Diodorus, Plutarch, Valerius Maximus, and others.], he ordered the golden garment covering the statue to be removed and a woolen one to be put on, saying that gold was cold in winter and burdensome in summer. Thus he mocked his god, thinking that he could bear neither weight nor cold. Likewise, when he saw that Aesculapius had a golden beard, he ordered it removed, declaring it inappropriate for the son to have a beard when his father did not [Note: All the editions read: “while his father Apollo still did not have one”; these words are found in none of the manuscripts.]. He also took away the golden bowls held by the statues, alleging that he ought to receive what the gods gave: “For,” he said, “these are the prayers of human beings: that they may obtain good things from the gods. Nothing, however, is better than gold. Yet if it is evil, the gods ought not to possess it; if it is good, human beings ought rather to possess it, since they would know how to use it.”

37. They were so mocked that Jupiter could not defend his garment, Aesculapius his beard, Apollo could not yet have begun to grow one, and all those called gods could not draw back the bowls they held—not so much because they feared the charge of theft as because they had no understanding. Who, then, would worship gods who can neither defend themselves as gods nor hide themselves as human beings?

38. But in the temple of our God, when Jeroboam, a most wicked king, was removing the gifts his father had placed there and pouring libations to idols over the holy altar, did not his right hand, which he stretched out, wither, and did not the idols he invoked benefit him at all? Then, turning to the Lord, he asked forgiveness, and immediately the hand that had withered through sacrilege was healed through religion (1 Kings 13:2 and following). So timely an example of both divine mercy and indignation was given in one man: as he sacrificed, his right hand was suddenly taken from him; as he repented, forgiveness was granted.

## CHAPTER VI

Conclusion of the Second Book. The very modest author testifies that, if he has written anything good thus far, it must all be attributed to the merits of virgins. He declares that it was his duty, before delivering sterner precepts, to soothe their minds with the sweetness of prayer and examples; he demonstrates this both by ordinary human practice and by the authority of the divine books.

39. I, a priest not yet three years in office, have prepared these little gifts for you, holy virgins, inexperienced though I am through practice but instructed by your conduct. For how much experience could have grown in so short a period of initiation into religion? If you see any flowers here, read them as gathered from the bosom of your life. These are not precepts for virgins but examples drawn from virgins. Our discourse has painted an image of your virtue; in this speech, as in a mirror, you see the likeness of your gravity shining back [Note: Some manuscripts read: “If you have breathed any grace into my talent.”]. If you have breathed any grace into my talent, whatever fragrance this book gives off belongs to you. And since there are as many opinions as there are people: if anything in our speech has been purified, let everyone read it; if anything has been refined, let the more mature approve it; if anything is modest, let it cling to their hearts and color their cheeks; if anything is flowery, let a flower-filled age not reject it.

40. We ought to kindle love in the bride; for it is written: “You shall love the Lord your God” (Deut. 6:5) [Note: The Roman edition reads: “We ought at the wedding to adorn the bride’s hair with certain curling-irons, or at least with the curling-irons of speech.” The old editions do not depart from the manuscripts, except that, instead of *in nuptiis* (“at the wedding”), nearly all of them have *innuptis*, that is, “for the unmarried,” or virgins. This is not unfitting, but the editions seem preferable in view of what follows. Again, the Roman edition alone reads *perpetuis spargere* (“to scatter perpetual [roses]”); the others and the manuscripts more suitably read *perpetuos*, so that the “perpetual bridal chambers” may be set against the temporal ones mentioned in the following verse. Incidentally, observe that Ambrose regards only vows of perpetual chastity as legitimate.]. We ought at the wedding to adorn the hair with certain curling-irons, at least with the curling-irons of discourse; for it is written: “Clap your hands and stamp your foot” (Ezek. 21:14). We ought to scatter roses over perpetual bridal chambers. Even in these temporal marriages, the bride is applauded before she is commanded, lest harsh commands offend before love, fostered by endearments, grows mature.

41. The strength of horses learns to love the sound of a stroked neck [Note: Some manuscripts read: “The young heifer learns to love the sound of a certain applause, so that she does not refuse the yoke.” Recognize the clear imitation of Virgil, *Georgics* III, where we read:

“Then more and more to rejoice in the master’s gentle  
Praises, and to love the sound of her stroked neck.”],

so that it will not refuse the yoke. In the end, one becomes accustomed to the word of playful encouragement before the blow of discipline. But once it has submitted its neck to the yoke, the bridle constrains it, the goad urges it, its companions pull, and the yoked partner invites it [Note: That is, the animal yoked beside it, or the driver.]. Thus our virgin ought first to play in holy love, to admire the golden supports of the heavenly marriage bed at the very entrance of the wedding chamber, and to see the doorposts crowned with garlands of foliage, and inwardly drink in the delights of the resounding choir [Note: He touches upon an ancient wedding custom, by which doors were adorned with wreaths and garlands on such joyful occasions, and groups of singers and flute players were hired. Lucian writes of this, mentioning that he saw something “all decked with garlands” (*πάντα κατεστεμμένα*), along with flute girls and commotion, and so forth.], lest, frightened by the Lord’s yoke, she withdraw before she bows when called.

42. “Come here from Lebanon, bride; come here from Lebanon; you shall pass over and pass through” (Song 4:8). This little verse must often be sung again by us, so that she may follow when called by the Lord’s words, if she does not believe human ones. We did not discover this teaching ourselves but received it. Thus the heavenly doctrine of the mystical song instructs: “Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth, for your breasts are better than wine, and the fragrance of your perfumes is above all spices. Your name is poured-out perfume” (Song 1:1–2). This entire passage of delights sounds like play, arouses applause, and provokes love. Therefore, it says, “the young women loved you and drew you along; we shall run after the fragrance of your perfumes” [Note: Some manuscripts read: “we shall run.”] “The king brought me into his chamber” (ibid., 3). She began with kisses in order to reach the chamber.

43. Yet she was so patient of hard labor and so trained in virtue that she opens barred gates with her hand, goes out into the field, and remains in fortresses; at the beginning, however, she runs after the fragrance of the perfume. Soon, when she has entered the tabernacle, the perfume changes from the fortresses [Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “the perfume is to be changed in the fortresses.” With the others, it then adds: “Finally, see where she is to escape.” The manuscripts, however, read in both places as in the text, except that one punctuates it: “the perfume changes; from the fortresses, finally, [see] where she is to escape,” and so forth. This reading is not objectionable.]. Finally, see where she goes: “If she is a wall,” she says, “let us build upon her silver towers” (Song 8:9). She who was playing with kisses now raises towers, so that, crowned with the precious heights of the saints, she may not only thwart hostile attacks but also build secure defenses of good merits.

# BOOK THREE

## CHAPTER 1

The speech of Liberius, who consecrated Marcellina by giving her the virginal veil, is reported. Its opening derives both from the crowd flocking to the wedding of that Bridegroom, by whom he says they are to be fed, and from the appropriateness of the day on which Christ was born of a virgin. By an elegant description of his perfections, he inflames her love for him.

1. Since I have arranged what we had in the preceding two books, it is time, holy sister, to review the teachings of Liberius of blessed memory, the teachings that you are accustomed to discuss with me, so that the more holy the man, the more welcome the speech may be [Note: This Liberius, the supreme pontiff, is indeed the same man who in the year 357 subscribed to the formula offered to him by Demophilus at Sirmium—whether, as Petavius and Blondel maintain in their notes on Epiphanius, to the later formula, or, as Baronius and certain more recent writers, equipped with new arguments, prefer, to the earlier one—in order to obtain his return from exile. He had nobly repaired his lapse when, at the Council of Rimini, he refused with the greatest steadfastness to give his assent and vote. It is therefore not surprising that Ambrose calls him “of blessed memory” and “a holy man,” since Basil the Great, in Letter 74; Epiphanius, *Heresy* 75, chapter 7; and finally Siricius, in his letter to Himerius of Tarragona, canon 1, awarded him titles of honor and veneration not unlike these. Liberius died, according to Baronius, on September 9, 367; according to other, more exact writers, on September 24, 366. His name is recorded among the saints in the additions to Usuard, in Bede’s martyrology, and also in the work written in verse by Wandelbert and published in volume V of the *Spicilegium*.]. For when, on the birthday of the Savior, he marked your profession of virginity at the Apostle Peter’s church by a change of clothing—what better day could there be than the day on which a virgin acquired offspring?—and when many maidens of God stood by, each contending for your companionship, he said: “You have desired a good marriage, daughter. You see how great a crowd has gathered for the birthday of your Bridegroom, so that no one departs unfed. This is he who, when asked to a wedding, changed water into wine” (John 2:9). In you too he will bestow the true sacrament of virginity, though previously you were subject to the lowly elements of material nature [Note: Observe the antiquity of publicly professed vows, which certainly were performed with certain ceremonies. The Magdeburg Centuriators seem to acknowledge this in several places, especially *Cent.* 4, chapter 7, where they derive the rite of consecrating a monk from the *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy* of Dionysius. See also Mabillon, *Ancient Gallican Lectionary*, Book II, chapter 76: “Reading at the Veiling of Virgins”; and the Frankish Missal, Book III, chapter 10: “Blessing over Virgins,” and chapter 11: “Blessing of a Widow’s Garment.” See also Gregory, *Sacra*, p. 173 and following.].

This is he who fed four thousand people in the desert with five loaves and two fish (Luke 9:13 and following). He could have fed more, if there had then been more people to feed. Finally, he has called more people to your wedding; but now it is not bread from barley that is served, but a body from heaven.

2. Today, indeed, according to his humanity, a man has been born from a virgin, but before all things he was generated from the Father: one who in bodily form reflects his mother, but in power reflects his Father. The Only-begotten on earth, the Only-begotten in heaven; God from God, born from a virgin; righteousness from the Father, power from the Powerful One, light from light; not unequal to the one who generated him, not separated in power; not confused by an extension or utterance of the Word, as though mingled with the Father, but distinct from the Father by the right of generation [Note: Thus all the editions, together with some manuscripts. Others, however, and more of the manuscripts read: “so that, being mixed with the Father, he may be distinct in person, confused in unity” (or: “confused by the unity of the person”), “so that both may be one, not each one”; for *indifferentis*, some read *indifferenter*. “For he himself is your brother.” Most of these readings, however, taste as much of interpolation as does the one given above.]. He is your brother, without whom neither heavenly, nor marine, nor earthly things subsist (Song 5:1). He is the good Word of the Father, which, he says, “was in the beginning”: you have his eternity. “And the Word was with God” (John 1:1 and following): you have his power, undivided from and inseparable from the Father. “And the Word was God”: you have his uncreated divinity. For your faith must be drawn from this concise account.

3. Love him, daughter, because he is good: “No one is good except one, God” (Luke 18:19). If it is not doubted that the Son is God, and God is good, then certainly it is not doubted that the Son, God, is good. Love him, I say. He is the one whom the Father begot before the morning star, as eternal; “from the womb he generated him” (Ps. 109:3), as Son; “from his heart he uttered him” (Ps. 44:2), as Word. He is the one in whom the Father was well pleased (Matt. 17:5); he is the Father’s arm, because he is the creator of all things; the Father’s wisdom (Col. 2:3), because he proceeded from the mouth of God; the Father’s power (1 Cor. 1:30), because the fullness of divinity dwells bodily in him. The Father loves him so greatly that he carries him in his bosom and places him at his right hand, so that you may learn wisdom and recognize power.

4. If, therefore, Christ is the power of God, was God ever without power? Was the Father ever without the Son? If he was always the Father, then surely the Son was always also the Son. Therefore, the perfect Son belongs to the perfect Father. For whoever diminishes the power diminishes the one whose power it is. Perfect divinity admits no inequality. Love, therefore, the one whom the Father loves; honor the one whom the Father honors: “Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father. And whoever denies the Son does not have the Father” (John 5:23). So much concerning faith.

## CHAPTER II

He undertakes the instruction of the virgin, prescribing what moderation is to be observed in drink and food and how the movements of the soul are to be restrained. On this occasion, after recounting and censuring the fabulous death and restoration of Hippolytus, he finally warns that hot foods and banquets must be avoided.

5. But sometimes, even when faith is secure, youth is suspect. Therefore use wine sparingly, not to increase bodily weakness but not to arouse pleasure; wine and youth alike kindle the same fire. Let fasting also bridle tender age, and let frugality restrain untamed desires with certain reins. Let reason recall them, hope soften them, and fear confine them. For one who does not know how to govern desires, like someone carried away by untamed horses, is rolled about, trampled, torn apart, and afflicted.

6. This is said to have happened once to a young man because of his love for Diana [Note: Virgil, Book VII of the *Aeneid*; Servius on the same book; Ovid, Book XV of the *Metamorphoses*; Hyginus, and others, tell this story of Hippolytus, torn apart by maddened horses.]. But the story is colored by poetic falsehoods, so that Neptune, provoked by the grief of the rejected rival, is said to have driven the horses into madness, thereby magnifying his great power: he did not conquer the young man by strength but deceived him by trickery. Hence they also renew a sacrifice to Diana every year, so that a horse may be sacrificed at her altars. They call her a virgin, though she—something even prostitutes usually blush to do—was able to love one who did not love her. But let their fables retain their authority, for all I care; for although both alternatives are wicked, it is nevertheless less serious for a young man to have burned with love for an adulterous woman until he perished than for two gods, as they themselves say, to have contended over adultery: Jupiter, moreover, avenged the grief of his lustful daughter upon the physician-adulterer because he had healed the wounds of the man who had committed adultery with Diana in the woods—Diana, certainly an excellent huntress, not of wild beasts but of lusts, though also of wild beasts, so that she might hunt naked.

7. Let them therefore grant Neptune dominion over madness, so that they may establish the crime of incestuous love. Let them grant Diana sovereignty over the woods she inhabited, so that they may confirm the adultery she committed. Let them grant Aesculapius the power by which he restored the dead, provided they admit that he himself did not escape the thunderbolt. Let them also grant Jupiter the thunderbolts he did not possess, so that they may bear witness to the disgraces he did possess. But let us return from fables to our subject.

8. I think that all foods which generate heat in the limbs should likewise be used sparingly; for even meats bring down flying eagles. Let that inner bird within you also, of which we read, “Your youth will be renewed like the eagle’s” (Ps. 102:5) [Note: Thus nearly all the manuscripts; some manuscripts and all the editions, however, read: “as the youth of the eagle.”], holding itself aloft and swift in virginal flight, know no desire for excessive flesh [Note: Some manuscripts read: “soaring aloft, borne on a virginal wing,” and so forth.]. Avoid the gatherings of banquets; avoid greetings.

## CHAPTER III

He urges the avoidance of visits, the preservation of modesty, and silence, following the example of Mary by observing the mysteries. For this purpose he recalls the deed of a pagan youth and a saying of a profane poet, and adds the miracle of a certain holy priest.

9. I want visits among younger women to be less frequent, except perhaps when deference is owed to parents or equals. Modesty is worn away by social duties, boldness emerges, laughter creeps in, and restraint is loosened while urbanity is being sought: not answering the one who asks is childishness; answering is conversation. Therefore I would rather that a virgin lack words than have an excess of them. For if women are even commanded in church to keep silent concerning divine matters, and at home to ask their husbands (1 Cor. 14:34), what do we think is required of virgins, in whom modesty adorns their age and silence commends their modesty?

10. Is it not a remarkable example of modesty that Rebecca, when she came to her wedding and saw her bridegroom, took a veil (Gen. 24:65), so that she would not be seen before she was joined to him? Certainly the beautiful virgin feared not for her appearance but for her modesty. What of Rachel? How, after a forced kiss, she wept and groaned, and would not have ceased weeping unless she had recognized her kinsman (Gen. 29:11–12) [Note: The Vulgate and other versions, together with the Hebrew text, read: “he kissed her”; “and he lifted up his voice and wept”; “and he told her,” and so forth. From these words, the account here of the modest kiss followed by weeping is elegantly and appropriately attributed to Rachel, although it ought to be referred to Jacob. And even if there were some ambiguity in other languages, the Septuagint clearly reads: “and he cried out with his voice, and wept” (*καὶ βοήσας τῇ φωνῇ αὐτοῦ, ἔκλαυσε*).]? Thus she preserved the duty of modesty and did not neglect the affection owed to family. If it is said to a man, “Do not look upon a virgin, lest she cause you to stumble” (Sir. 9:5), what should be said to a consecrated virgin, who, if she loves, sins in her mind, and, if she is loved, sins in deed?

11. Silence is the greatest virtue, especially in church. No divine saying will escape you in the readings if you lend your ear and restrain your voice. Do not utter from your mouth any word that you might wish to recall; let confidence in speaking be sparing. For there is abundant sin in much speaking. To the murderer it was said, “You have sinned; be silent” (Prov. 10:19), so that he might sin no more; but to a virgin it must be said: “Be silent, lest you sin.” For Mary, as we read, kept in her heart everything that was said about her Son (Luke 2:19). When something is read in which Christ is announced as coming or shown to have come, do not interrupt by chattering, but apply your mind. Is anything more unworthy than for divine oracles to be surrounded by noise so that they are not heard, not believed, and not revealed; for the mysteries to resound amid confused voices, so that prayer drawn forth for the salvation of all is impeded [Note: All the editions read: “of all, although the pagans … offer”; the manuscripts, however, agree in large numbers with our reading. The following story of the barbarian youth is recounted by Valerius Maximus, Book III, chapter 3, under “Patience.”]?

12. Pagans show reverence to their idols by keeping silent. Hence the following example is reported. While Alexander, king of the Macedonians, was sacrificing, a young barbarian who was tending the light received the fire upon his arm; though his body was burned, he remained motionless, neither revealing his pain by a groan nor indicating his punishment by silent tears. Such discipline of reverence was present in the barbarian boy that nature itself was overcome. Yet he feared not gods, who did not exist, but the king. For what would he have feared in those whom, if the same fire had touched them, it would have consumed?

13. How much better is the case of a certain young man who, at his father’s banquet, was ordered not to reveal his love for prostitutes by conspicuous signs? And you, virgin of God, in the mystery, refrain from groaning, throat-clearing, coughing, and laughter. If he can do this at a banquet, can you not do it in the mystery? Let virginity first be marked by the voice; let modesty close the mouth; let religious devotion exclude weakness; let habit train nature. Let a virgin’s gravity announce her to me first, with modesty visible, a measured step, and a restrained expression; let signs of virtue precede and announce integrity. A virgin who must be sought out when she is seen is not sufficiently commendable [Note: The editions read: “What if someone … ?” and below: “in the service … cough, abstain from laughter … you cannot in the service of God.” The manuscripts, however, read as in the text, except that some, with the editions, read *ministerio* (“service”) instead of *mysterio* (“mystery”). Here Ambrose is referring to the comedy of Terence entitled *The Self-Tormentor*, Act II, where near the end of Scene 3 the young Clinias is warned to maintain modesty at table in his father’s presence. From the same passage the holy bishop transferred the words: “Refrain from groaning, throat-clearing, coughing, and laughter.”].

14. It is often said that when the many croakings of frogs were disturbing the religious ears of the congregation, a priest of God ordered them to be silent and to show reverence to the sacred prayer; immediately the surrounding noises ceased. The marshes are silent, then, but human beings will not be silent? An irrational animal recognizes through reverence what it does not know by nature. Is human immodesty so great that most people do not know how to show the mind’s religion the deference they show the pleasure of the ears?

## CHAPTER IV

After repeating Liberius’ exhortation, Ambrose praises his sister’s virtues, especially her fasting. Yet he urges her to relax it for a time and to cultivate the mind through alternating exercises, adducing especially elegant examples for this purpose. He also presses her to frequent prayer, to repeat the Lord’s Prayer and the psalms even at night, and to recite the Creed in the hours before dawn.

15. These teachings came to you from Liberius of holy memory; among others they are greater than truths, but before you they are lesser than examples [Note: All the editions and a few manuscripts read: “greater than words”; the rest read: “greater than truths,” except one, which has: “you are considered greater.” The latter does not fit very well.]. In this way you have not only equaled every discipline in virtue but surpassed it in emulation. We have fasting among our precepts, but fasting for individual days; you, however, by multiplying nights and days, pass innumerable periods without food. And whenever you are asked to take food or to put down your book for a little while, you answer immediately: “Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word of God” (Matt. 4:4). The use of food is such that, when food is present, fasting is desired [Note: Thus several manuscripts, except that instead of “so that, through distaste for eating,” they read “so that, through distaste for use,” which is not pleasing. Others and the editions read: “use; food is at hand, so that, through distaste for eating,” and so forth.]. Drink comes from a spring, tears in prayer, sleep in a book.

16. These practices suited your younger years, until the mind, ripened by age, began to grow white. But once the virgin has raised the trophy of a disciplined body, labor must be moderated, so that it may be suited to her corresponding age [Note: Some manuscripts read: “so that it may be preserved in a corresponding age”; others more appropriately, together with the editions, read: “suited to age,” that is, to those who are more advanced in years.]. A vine of mature age, burdened too quickly with fruitful branches, cracks unless it is sometimes restrained. Yet while it is growing, it should abound, and when it has grown old it should be pruned [Note: A few manuscripts read: “and be planted when already old.” Shortly afterward all the editions read: “die when emptied.”]. Otherwise it will become wild through its shoots or die, exhausted by excessive fruit. A good farmer both restrains the finest vine by nourishing the soil, protects it from the cold, and takes care that it is not scorched by the midday sun. He also works the field by turns; or, if he does not allow it to lie fallow, he alternates different seeds, so that the fields may rest after changing their produce [Note: From Virgil, *Georgics* I:

“The fields rest after their varied offspring,” and so forth.].

You too, veteran virgin, sow the hills of your heart with at least varied seeds: now with moderate nourishment, now with more sparing fasts, with reading, work, and prayer, so that the change of labor may be periods of rest.

17. Not every field produces every crop [Note: Virgil, in the same passage:

“Not every soil bears everything,” and so forth.]. From one place vineyards rise over the hills; elsewhere you see purple olives; here, fragrant roses. Often, too, after leaving the plows, the sturdy farmer himself scratches the soil with his finger, so that he may set down the roots of flowers [Note: Some manuscripts read: “so that he may set down the roots of a flower.”], while with the rough hands by which he bends struggling bullocks among the vineyards, he gently presses the udders of sheep. For the better the field, the more abundant its fruit. Therefore, following the example of the good farmer, do not cleave your soil with perpetual fasts as though with lowered plowshares. Let the rose of modesty bloom in your gardens, the lily of the mind, and let beds of violets drink from the spring of sacred blood. There is a common saying: “What you intend to do at length, do not do continuously.” Something should be added to the days of Lent [Note: Many manuscripts read: “and so that nothing … may be increased.” But if you compare this precept with the stanza of the Lenten evening hymn in which we are commanded to use food and drink more sparingly, you will readily acknowledge that Ambrose was inspired by the same Spirit by which the Church is governed.], but in such a way that nothing is done for display, only for religious devotion.

18. Frequent prayer should also commend us to God. If the prophet says, “Seven times a day I have praised you” (Ps. 118:164), though he was occupied with the responsibilities of a kingdom, what ought we to do, who read: “Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation” (Matt. 26:41)? Certainly, solemn prayers with thanksgiving should be offered when we rise from sleep, when we go out, when we prepare to take food, when we have taken it, at the hour of incense [Note: The holy Luke mentions the hour of incense in chapter 2, verse 10. Maldonatus, Jansen of Ypres, and others write in their comments on this passage that it was customary among the Jews for incense to be burned every day, morning and evening. Ambrose seems to have in mind the evening offering of incense, since mention of going to bed follows shortly afterward.], and finally when we go to bed.

19. But even in bed I want you frequently to intertwine the psalms with the Lord’s Prayer, whether when you wake or before sleep moistens the body, so that, at the very beginning of rest, sleep may find you free from concern for worldly matters and meditating on divine things. Finally, even the man who first devised the name of philosophy ordered a flute player to play softer melodies every day before he went to bed, so that he might soothe hearts troubled by worldly cares [Note: Many writers report that Pythagoras and his followers were especially devoted to music—for example, Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, Book IV; Macrobius, *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio*; Aulus Gellius, Book I, chapter 14; and Quintilian, Book IX. The latter confirms very clearly what Ambrose teaches here.]. But he, like someone washing a brick, foolishly tried to erase worldly things with worldly things; indeed, he smeared himself more deeply with mud by seeking a remedy in pleasure. We, however, after washing away the filth of earthly vices, should cleanse the inner mind from every pollution of the flesh.

20. We must also recite the Creed every day at the hours before dawn, as the seal of our heart; to it we should also turn in spirit whenever we are seized by fear of anything. For when is a soldier without the oath of service, a soldier in his tent, a warrior in battle?

## CHAPTER V

[Col. 0225D]

Having urged the shedding of tears by means of a verse of David, he teaches here that the word “bed” may be understood simply, or figuratively, as signifying our body; and he approves and confirms this interpretation. How did Christ assume a body of pain and turn over the bed in his sickness? Everything must be referred to Christ’s honor, and one must rejoice with spiritual gladness, not in the things that, through frenzied feasting, brought about the death of John the Baptist.

21. Who would not understand as spoken for our instruction what the holy Prophet says: “Every night I will wash my bed; I will drench my couch with my tears” (Ps. VI, 7)? For whether you understand “bed” literally, it shows that such an abundance of tears ought to be poured out that the bed may be washed, [Note: Not a few manuscripts: “that the couch may be drenched with weeping.”] the couch drenched with the tears of one beseeching. For weeping over present things is the reward of future things, since “blessed are you who weep, for you shall laugh” (Luke VI, 21). Or, if we understand the prophetic saying as referring to the body, let us wash away the sins of the body with tears of repentance.

“For Solomon made himself a bed from the wood of Lebanon; its columns were of silver, its back-rest of gold, its couch adorned with gems” (Song III, 9–10). What is this bed except the form of our body? For in the gems is displayed the appearance of bronze shining with radiance, in the gold fire, in the silver water, and through the wood earth. The human body consists of these four elements, and in it our soul reclines. [Note: Thus the printed editions and a few manuscripts; many others read: “if it does not exist rough with mountains, if it is not dry upon the ground,” though this is less suitable.] Let it not exist without rest, rough with mountains or dry upon the ground, but, raised above vices and supported by the wood, let it rest.

Hence David also says: “May the Lord bring him help upon his bed of pain” [Col. 0226C] (Ps. XL, 4). [180] How can it be a bed of pain when one who has no sensation cannot suffer? Yet the body of pain is like the body of his death: “Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death?” (Rom. VII, 24).

22. Since we have introduced a verse in which we mentioned the Lord’s body, lest what the Lord assumed—a body of pain—trouble any reader, let him remember that he both grieved and wept over the death of Lazarus (John XI, 35), and that in his Passion he was wounded, and from the wound there came forth blood and water (John XIX, 34), and he breathed out his spirit. Water for washing, blood for drinking, spirit for resurrection. For Christ alone is our hope, faith, and charity: hope in the resurrection, faith in the washing, charity in the sacrament.

23. Yet, just as he assumed a body of pain, so also he turned the bed in sickness (Ps. XL, 4), because [Col. 0227A] he transformed the troubles of human flesh into an advantage. For through the Passion sickness was dissolved, and through the resurrection death. Yet you ought to grieve for the world and rejoice in the Lord: sorrowful for repentance, joyful for grace; although the Apostle to the Gentiles has prescribed in a salutary command that we ought both to weep with those who weep and rejoice with those who rejoice (Rom. XII, 15).

24. But whoever desires to unravel completely every remaining scar of the question [Note: He calls the remnant of the difficulty a “scar,” using a metaphor drawn from wounds whose mark remains in the flesh even after they have been healed.] should have recourse to the same Apostle: “Whatever you do in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, giving thanks to God the Father through him” (Col. III, 17). Let us therefore refer all our words and deeds to Christ, who made life from death and created light from darkness.

For just as a sick body is at one time warmed by hotter remedies and at another moderated by colder ones, and a change of remedies, if made according to the physician’s prescription, is salutary but, if undertaken against his command, increases the illness, so whatever is administered to our physician Christ is a remedy, while whatever is taken up without his sanction is harmful.

25. Joy ought therefore to belong to a mind conscious of its goodness, not to be aroused by disorderly banquets or wedding music. For modesty is unsafe there, and temptation is suspect where extreme dancing accompanies delights. I want God’s virgins to remain far from this. For, as a certain teacher of secular matters said [Note: Cicero is intended; the same statement is found in *Oration for L. Murena*.], no sober person dances unless he is insane.

If, according to secular wisdom, either drunkenness or madness gives rise to dancing, what should we suppose the divine Scriptures have warned us by their examples, when John, Christ’s forerunner, was beheaded at the dancer’s request? The example shows that the allure of dancing has done more harm than the madness of sacrilegious rage.

[181] ## CHAPTER VI

Having introduced the mention of the holy Forerunner, he describes and amplifies with the greatest eloquence all the circumstances of his murder, so as to deter his readers from the dancing and banquets of the impious.

26. Since the memory of such a man must not be passed over briefly, we ought to consider who he was, by whom and for what reason, how, and at what time he was killed. The just man is killed by adulterers, and the punishment of a capital crime is turned against the judge by the guilty. Then the prophet’s death is the reward of a dancing girl. Finally—something which even all barbarians are accustomed to shudder at—the order for completing the cruelty is issued amid food and banquets; and from the banquet to the prison, and from the prison to the banquet, the service of a deadly crime is carried about. How many crimes are contained in a single offense!

[Col. 0228A] 27. A deadly banquet is prepared with royal luxury. When it has been ascertained that a crowd larger than usual has gathered, the queen’s daughter, having received secret instructions [Note: The Roman edition reads *amandanda secretis*; other editions and the manuscripts read *mandata secretis*; two manuscripts read *commendata secretis*. Below, where the edition reads “the daughter learning from her adulterous mother,” the words “daughter” and “mother” are absent from all the manuscripts.], is brought into the presence of the men to dance (Mark VI, 21).

What could she have learned from an adulteress except the loss of modesty? Is anything so inclined to lust as to expose, through disorderly movements, what nature has hidden or discipline has veiled; to play with the eyes, twist the neck, scatter the hair? It is rightly from this that an insult to divinity proceeds. For what modesty can exist where there is dancing, shouting, and clattering?

28. “Then,” he says, “the king, being pleased, said to the girl, ‘Ask me for whatever you wish.’ And he swore to her that he would grant her even half his kingdom if she asked for it” (ibid., 22–23). [Col. 0228B] See how secular people themselves judge their secular authorities, so that kingdoms are given even for dancing.

But the girl, prompted by her mother, asked that John’s head be brought to her on a platter. [Note: Some manuscripts add: “At this saying the king was distressed.”] When it says, “The king was distressed” (ibid., 25ff.), this is not the king’s repentance but a confession of wickedness. Divine judgment has this custom: those who have committed impious deeds condemn themselves by their own confession.

“But because of those reclining at table,” he says. What could be more disgraceful than ordering a murder so as not to displease the diners? “And because of the oath,” he says. What strange religion! He would have perjured himself more tolerably. Hence the Lord not without reason commands in the Gospel that one should not swear, lest an oath become a cause of perjury and a necessity of sinning. Thus, so that the oath might not be violated, the innocent man is struck down (Matt. V, 34). I do not know which I should shudder at first. Perjuries are more tolerable than the sworn pledges of tyrants.

[182] 29. Who, seeing the prophet being hurried from the banquet to the prison, would not have thought that he had been ordered to be released? Who, I ask, hearing that it was Herod’s birthday, a solemn banquet, and that the girl had been given the choice of asking for whatever she wished, would not have supposed that someone had been sent to release John? [Note: All editions read “sent to John for his release”; the manuscripts read partly “sent to John’s release,” partly “sent for John’s release.” The latter is more suitable, unless *missam* (“sent [woman]”) is substituted for the preceding *missum* (“sent [man]”).] What has cruelty to do with delights? What has pleasure to do with funerals?

The prophet is dragged to punishment at banquet time, by a banquet command [Note: “At banquet time” occurs in all editions but is absent from the manuscripts.], though he would not have wished even to be released. He is killed by the sword, and his head is brought on a platter (Mark VI, 27ff.). This dish was owed to cruelty, so that savagery, still unsated by the feast, might feed upon it.

[Col. 0228D] 30. Look, most savage king, upon spectacles worthy of your banquet. Stretch out your right hand, so that nothing may be lacking from your cruelty; let streams of holy blood flow between your fingers. Since hunger could not be satisfied by food, nor the thirst of unheard-of savagery quenched by cups, drink the blood still flowing from the severed head, its veins yet gushing.

See the eyes, even in death, bearing witness against your crime and resisting the sight of your pleasures. The eyes are closed not so much by the necessity of death as by horror at luxury. That golden mouth, whose judgment you could not endure, falls silent, [Note: All editions read “and you are still feared”; nearly all manuscripts read “and you still fear.”] and you are still afraid. Yet the tongue, which commonly continues even after death to perform the office of the living, condemned the incest, though it moved with a quivering motion.

This head is carried to Herodias. She rejoices and exults as though she had escaped her crime, because she had slaughtered her judge.

31. What do you say, holy women? [Note: Several manuscripts read: “See what you ought to teach.”] Do you see what you ought to teach your daughters, and also what you ought to unteach them? She dances—but she is the daughter of an adulteress. Let the woman who is modest and chaste teach her daughters religion, not dancing.

But you, serious and prudent men, [Note: All editions and a few manuscripts read: “avoid. If such are … of the treacherous.” Below they likewise read: “what concerning the deserts … of those who,” whereas the far more numerous manuscripts read as in the text. It is also clear that, when a sister asked the holy Doctor what he thought of those who laid violent hands on themselves, he praised women who, in order to preserve chastity, voluntarily took their own lives under a special inspiration of God. Augustine, however, in *City of God*, book I, chap. 19 and following, discussing the same matter, states his opinion with some hesitation—perhaps because of the Circumcellions, as Baronius supposes for the year 309. The same cardinal reasonably conjectures that these martyrs, of whom Ambrose speaks here and also in the letter to Simplician, are the same women whom Augustine mentions without names in the passage cited. Whether Ambrose’s Pelagia is distinct from the woman mentioned in the *Acts of Saint Lucian*, martyr and presbyter of Antioch, in Eusebius, *History*, book VIII, chap. 12, Valesius’s edition, and in two homilies of John Chrysostom, is a question of no small difficulty, since the principal circumstances of their histories differ. Consult Cardinal Baronius’s notes on the Roman Martyrology for the fifth day before the Ides of June, and his *Ecclesiastical Annals* for the already cited year 309; also Fronton du Duc on Chrysostom’s Homilies 41 and 51 to the people of Antioch.] learn to avoid the banquets of detestable people. If such are the banquets, what must the judgments of the treacherous be?

## CHAPTER VII

When Marcellina asks what should be thought about those who inflict violence upon themselves so as not to fall into the hands of persecutors, he responds and sets before her eyes the example of the virgin Pelagia, together with that of her mother and sisters, described with singular elegance. He adds the martyrdom of blessed Soteris, from whom he and Marcellina traced their descent.

32. Now, as the end of the discourse is opening before us, you rightly suggest, holy sister, what should be thought of those women who threw themselves from a height or plunged into a river so as not to fall into the hands of persecutors, although divine Scripture forbids Christians to inflict violence upon themselves. Indeed, we have a clear assertion concerning virgins placed in the necessity of guarding themselves, since an example of martyrdom exists.

33. Holy Pelagia once lived near Antioch. She was about fifteen years old, the sister of virgins, and herself a virgin. At first she was shut up at home by the trumpet-call of persecution. When she saw that she was surrounded by robbers of faith and modesty, while her mother and sisters were absent, she was without human protection but filled more fully with God.

“What shall we do,” she said, “unless you look to yourself, captive virginity?” [Note: All editions, together with some manuscripts, read *captiva virginitas* (“captive virginity”); a large number of others read *captiva virginitatis* (“captive of virginity”). This is not at all unsuitable, for it is an apostrophe in which, addressing herself, she uses a mixed construction, employing now the plural and now the singular.]

There is both a vow and a fear in dying, because death is not merely received but embraced. Let us die, if it is permitted; or, if they do not permit it, let us die. God is not offended by the remedy, and faith lightens the deed.

Certainly, if we consider the very force of the word, what voluntary violence is there? [Note: Some manuscripts read: “What is more truly voluntary violence? I wish to die, and yet I cannot.”] Rather, that is violence: to wish to die and yet be unable to do so. Nor do we fear the difficulty. For who wishes to die and cannot, when there are so many easy paths to death?

Now I shall cast down and overturn the sacrilegious altars by throwing myself upon them, and extinguish the kindled fires with blood. I do not fear that my right hand, growing weak, will fail to complete the blow, or that my breast will shrink from the pain. [Note: A few manuscripts read: “I shall leave no sin of the flesh.”] I shall leave no sin to the flesh. I shall not fear that a sword will be lacking. We can die by our own weapons; we can die without the executioner’s service, in our mother’s embrace. [Note: Thus the more numerous and better manuscripts. The others, along with the editions, differ only in punctuation, reading: “by the kindness of her mother. She is said to have carried it,” and so forth.]

[Col. 0230B] 34. She is said to have adorned her head and put on bridal clothing, so that you would not say that she was going to her death but to her bridegroom. But when the detestable persecutors saw that the prey of her modesty had been snatched from them, they began to search for her mother and sisters.

But the women, by a spiritual flight, were already holding the field of chastity. Suddenly, with persecutors threatening on one side and the torrent of the river blocking escape on the other, they were shut in for the crown.

“Why should we fear?” they said. “Behold the water; who prevents us from being baptized?” (Acts VIII, 36). This too is baptism, by which sins are forgiven and kingdoms sought. This too is baptism, after which no one sins. Let the water receive us that is accustomed to regenerate. Let the water receive us that makes virgins. Let the water receive us that opens heaven, [Note: The Roman edition alone adds: “covers the underworld.”] shelters the weak, conceals death, and makes martyrs.

“We beseech you, God, creator of all things, that the water not scatter bodies emptied of spirit; that death not separate the corpses whose affection did not separate their life. Let there be one steadfastness, one death, and also one burial.”

[184] 35. Having spoken these words, [Note: All editions read “with their bosoms raised slightly”; some manuscripts read “with their girded bosoms raised slightly”; the remainder read “with their bosoms raised slightly into a girdle,” that is, “in the manner of a girdle,” which agrees beautifully with what follows.] and having lifted and girded the folds of their garments slightly, so that they might cover their modesty without impeding their steps, they advance with clasped hands, as though leading a chorus, into the middle of the riverbed, directing their steps toward the place where the current was swifter and the depth more precipitous.

None drew back her foot; none suspended her advance; none tested where she might set her step. They were anxious when the earth came toward them, hindered by the shallow water, joyful at the deep.

You would have seen the devout mother binding their hands together in a knot, rejoicing in her pledge, yet fearful of the danger lest the waves carry her daughters away from her.

“These,” she said, “I sacrifice to you, Christ, as guardians of chastity, leaders of the journey, companions in suffering.” [Note: Amerbach, Erasmus, and the Roman edition, with two manuscripts, read: “leaders of virginity, guides of chastity, companions in suffering”; Gill and the remaining witnesses read as in the text.]

36. But who would rightly marvel that such steadfastness belonged to the living, when even in death they secured the immovable position of their bodies? The water did not strip the corpse; the rapid current did not whirl them about.

Indeed, although the holy mother was without sensation, she still preserved the embrace of affection and did not loosen in death the devout bond she had clasped, so that she who had fulfilled her duty to religion might die with affection as her heir. [Note: Most manuscripts read “she might die as the heir of affection”; others, together with the editions, read “she might die as the heir of piety”; the old edition reads “might be moved.” Both readings are to some extent suspect.] For those whom she had joined together for martyrdom she claimed even to the tomb.

37. But why, sister, do I use examples from foreigners with you, when an inspired inheritance of hereditary chastity, infused by the parent of a martyr, instructed you? From where did you learn what you had no opportunity to learn, stationed in the field, with no virgin companion and no teacher to form you? You did not therefore act as a pupil—for that cannot happen without instruction—but as an heir of virtue.

38. For how could holy Soteris [Note: This blessed Soteris, also called Soteres in some manuscripts and Sothera, as the continuators of Bollandus prefer, may be so named. Since she is called a virgin not only in the martyrologies but also by Ambrose himself in the *Exhortation to Virginity*, the reader may reasonably wonder why the author here calls her the founder of his lineage and above Marcellina’s ancestor. The same continuators of Bollandus reply that writers of those times commonly called not only grandfathers from whom someone directly descended but also all ancestors from whose stock he originated by the name “parent.” This holy martyr suffered in the year 304 from the Incarnation, if we believe Baronius; others place her martyrdom in 293 or 287. There is also considerable disagreement among authors about the place of her martyrdom, and those who assign Rome to her seem farther from the truth. Her feast is reported from the Roman Martyrology on the fourth, and from others on the eighth, day before the Ides of February.] not be the author of your character, when she is the author of your lineage?

In the age of persecution, she was raised to the summit of suffering even through servile insults. She gave to the executioner that very face which, amid the tortures of the whole body, is usually free from injury and more accustomed to look upon torments than to endure them. [Note: Most manuscripts read: “she gave it bravely and patiently to the executioner, so that when she offered her tender cheeks to punishment…”] She was so brave and patient that, when she offered her tender cheeks to punishment, the executioner grew weary from striking before the martyr yielded to the insult.

She did not bend her face or turn her countenance; [Note: The same manuscripts read: “not overcome by groaning, she shed no tear.”] she gave neither groan nor tear. Finally, when she had overcome every other kind of punishment, she found the sword she had sought. [Note: Since the treatise ends with these words in all the manuscripts, we have judged that what follows in the editions should be placed under its own title after the book *On Widows*.]

## [ON WIDOWS]

[Col. 0231]

### INTRODUCTORY NOTICE TO THE BOOK *ON WIDOWS*, IN WHICH SOMETHING IS ALSO TOUCHED UPON CONCERNING THE INVOCATION OF THE SAINTS

[Col. 0231]

At the very beginning of this Commentary (No. 1), Ambrose declares that it should be joined to the three books on Virgins because he was led to write it by the authority and example of the Apostle, who frequently couples the praises of both conditions in his letters. Yet in the course of the work (chap. 9, no. 57ff.) we find an occasion that moved him more sharply to undertake and commit this treatise to writing.

After her husband’s death, a certain matron, who still had several daughters, some of marriageable age and others already married, had recourse to the common refuge of all mourners—namely, Ambrose. The holy man consoled her as best he could and also advised her, with the intensity of her grief moderated, to put aside her mourning garment, since perhaps the appointed period of mourning had already elapsed.

That widow, who had concealed her love of pleasure beneath a dark mourning cloak, interpreted Ambrose’s words to suit her desire and was thinking of nothing but arranging a new marriage. This did not escape the holy Bishop. Since he clearly understood how many evils, quarrels, disputes, and hostilities would necessarily arise from it, he began both to dissuade her from that marriage and to remove any suspicion that he had approved it by proclaiming the excellence of Christian widowhood and exhorting widows to cultivate it.

At the outset, therefore, he asserts that the profession of widowhood comes immediately after virginity and is far superior to marriage (chap. 1). As evidence for this he offers not only apostolic testimony but also the example of the widow of Sarepta (no. 3ff.), whose chastity, he teaches, was not solitary but accompanied by many other virtues, such as hospitality and piety.

After interpreting this story according to its moral and mystical sense, he passes to Anna the prophetess (chap. 4), and from her proceeds to the widow whom Luke records as having cast two small coins into the treasury (chap. 5). Then, after reviewing several examples from the Old Testament—namely, Naomi (chap. 6), Judith (chap. 7), and Deborah (chap. 8)—he explains their histories both morally and mystically, though Anna’s only mystically.

Finally, after explaining the story of Peter’s mother-in-law, he brings the book to its conclusion (chap. 9, no. 53) and compels widows, with all the power of his language, to persevere in the celibate life, whose holiness, gifts, and distinctive virtues he describes there (chap. 10ff.).

[Col. 0233] Moreover, when he mentions blessed Peter’s mother-in-law, he addresses the widow mentioned above (chap. 9, no. 57ff.), though he spares her name. He teaches that all the reasons by which she concealed her desire to enter a new marriage were slight and specious, since in reality she was pursuing only love of pleasure and worldly delights.

He acknowledges that the marriage bond (chap. 12ff.) is good and holy, and compares the Church with a fertile field (chap. 14, no. 87) that produces flowers of different beauty in virgins, widows, and married women. He therefore adorns them all with the name “flowers,” but asserts that the Church’s soil abounds more in grain than in lilies—that is, that married women greatly outnumber virgins.

Finally, after assigning first place to virginity over marriage and showing (chap. 14, no. 84) that only idolaters ever inflicted penalties upon widowhood, he concludes that all Christian women who have been freed from the marital obligation ought not to withdraw from so religious a purpose. At the end of the book (chap. 15, no. 86), after examining the disguised arguments commonly used by widows who wish to marry, he presses them forcefully. Yet it is clear that he used so impassioned a peroration for no other reason than to deter this woman’s troubled mind more easily from the plan she was considering.

Nothing could have been said either more prudently or in greater agreement with sound doctrine, since he neither condemned second marriages nor failed in the duty by which he was bound to prefer widowhood to them and to urge the souls entrusted to his care always toward greater perfection.

He intended the opening of this book to remove every doubt about its author—unless someone also wishes to deny the books on Virgins to Ambrose, an absurdity that no one can fail to recognize.

Nevertheless, the Centuriators, having mentioned this same book, write with no little disdain: “Ambrose, if indeed it is Ambrose’s, contains much that is gross concerning the invocation of departed saints” (*Centuries* IV, chap. 4). What could be more foolish than this doubt? If what we have already said is not sufficient for them, and if they wish to be taught explicitly by Ambrose on this matter, let them consult his Commentary on the Gospel according to Luke. There they will find this very work cited by him at least four times and the reader referred to it.

To make the authority of such critics appear still more clearly worthless, let anyone consider Jerome’s testimony in Letter 50 to Pammachius: “Let him read,” he says, “the book of Saint Ambrose *On Widows*” (*Apology against Jovinian*).

Why, then, did the Magdeburgians conceal these facts? Clearly so that they might call “gross” with somewhat greater boldness what the devout Doctor teaches concerning the invocation of the saints (chap. 9, no. 55). But those ingenious men accomplished nothing. Everyone understands that what they call gross appeared orthodox to Ambrose; for he did not wish to forge a new dogma but to bear witness to Catholic truth.

Indeed, the most prudent Bishop would never have proposed from the pulpit to the people the things they attack solely because they openly agree with the teachings of the Roman Church, if he had thought that anything impious or in any way liable to offend the weak was contained in this doctrine.

Nor need we bring forward what Perkins wrote, namely, that the book *On Widows* conflicts with the Commentary on chapter 1 of the Epistle to the Romans, since Rivet himself (*Sacred Criticism*), belonging to the same sect and order, judged his argument so futile as to deserve no consideration at all.

From all that we have examined thus far, it can be understood that this book was composed from sermons in which the holy Doctor addressed the widow who was aspiring to a second marriage. He subsequently committed them to writing and published them not long after the books on Virgins—that is, after the year 377—as the very beginning of the work sufficiently declares.

[Col. 0233]

## ONE BOOK OF SAINT AMBROSE, BISHOP OF MILAN, ON WIDOWS

[Note: Written around the year 377.] (C)

[Col. 0233]

[185] ## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0233A]

After treating of virgins, it is appropriate to discuss widows, since the Apostle has associated them with virgins, as in a certain sense teachers of virginity and far superior to married women. How glorious it is for widows that Elijah was sent to a widow! Yet they are not worthy of praise unless they imitate that woman’s virtue, especially her hospitality. How great that virtue was in this woman is explained; but first the avarice of men is briefly touched upon, since, by claiming common things for themselves, they have deprived themselves of the divine promises.

1. It has worked out well, brothers, [Note: The Royal manuscript and one Cologne manuscript read: “brother, that, since …”; some manuscripts read “the four preceding books.”] that, since we have discussed the praises of virgins in the three preceding books, a treatise on widows has followed. For we ought not to dishonor and separate from the praise of virgins those whom apostolic authority has joined with virgins, according to what is written: “The unmarried woman and the virgin think about the things of the Lord, so that she may be holy in body and spirit” (1 Cor. VII, 34).

In a certain sense, widows’ example possesses the authority of a teacher of virginity. Those who preserve a chaste bed with a husband serve as a lesson to virgins that integrity must be preserved for God. And it is almost no less a virtue to abstain from a marriage that once gave pleasure than never to have known the delights of marriage.

They are strong in both respects: they neither regret the marriage to which they remain faithful nor become bound to marital pleasures, lest they appear weak because they cannot do without them.

2. Yet even in this virtue the rewards of freedom have been established: “A woman is bound for as long as her husband lives; but if her husband sleeps, she is free. Let her marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord. But she will be happier if she remains as she is, according to my counsel; for I think that I too have the Spirit of God” (ibid., 39–40). [Note: Some manuscripts read: “I say this according to my counsel.”]

The Apostle therefore clearly expressed the difference when he said that one woman is bound and mentioned that another is happier. [Note: Thus all editions and some manuscripts; some others read “has shown that she is happier,” while others add immediately afterward: “and this no longer according to his own judgment but according to the divine.”] He taught this not so much as a judgment of his own as something drawn from the infusion of the divine Spirit, so that this might appear to be a heavenly rather than a human judgment.

3. But what of the fact that, at the time when famine was pressing upon the whole human race in every form, Elijah was sent to a widow (1 Kings XVII, 9)? And observe how a particular grace is reserved for each [Note: Many manuscripts read: “how each one’s own grace is reserved by its seals.”]: an angel to a virgin, a prophet to a widow (Luke I, 27–28). Add that there it was Gabriel, here Elijah, so that the most eminent leaders from the ranks of angels and prophets appear to have been chosen.

But the praise of widowhood is not simple unless the virtue of widowhood is also present. There had certainly been many widows before, but one is preferred above all; this does not so much call the others back from striving as summon them forward by the example of virtue.

4. The preface therefore makes attentive ears [Note: All editions read “makes attentive ears by its forewarning”; all manuscripts read “makes attentive ears by its preface.”], although the simplicity of the meaning itself is moral, since it exhorts widows to the example of virtue. Each woman appears to excel not by profession but by merit, and the grace of hospitality before God does not perish. He rewards a cup of cold water, as he himself declared in the Gospel (Matt. X, 42), with the richest reward of eternity, and compensates a small measure of flour and oil with the abundance of unfailing and overflowing supplies (1 Kings XVII, 16).

For if one of the Gentiles said [Col. 0235D] that all things ought to be common among friends, [Note: Diogenes Laertius attributes this saying to Pythagoras in his life of him. It is also quoted by Plato, Aristotle, Cicero, and others, and explained by Erasmus in *Adages*, collection 1, century 1, proverb 1.] how much more ought they to be common among relatives! For we are relatives, joined together in one succession of bodily descent.

5. Yet we are not confined by some prescribed limit of hospitality. Why do you think that what exists in the world is private, when the world itself is common? Or why do you assign the fruits of the earth to private owners, when the earth is common?

“Consider,” he says, “the birds of the air, for they neither sow nor reap” (Matt. VI, 26). Indeed, those who possess nothing as their own lack nothing, and God, the arbiter of his own judgment, knows how to keep his promise.

Finally, the birds “do not gather,” yet they eat, because the heavenly Father feeds them. [Note: All editions, together with the Tell manuscript, read: “they do not gather, and they abound … monuments of the saying”; the other witnesses read as in the text. In the Roman edition the following words had been partly inverted and partly altered, reading: “Every tree that has in itself the fruit of sowable seed shall be for you as food … upon the earth,” and then: “by directing them to private uses, through gathering we become needy, and through gathering …”]

But we turn the general warning of the saying toward our own uses: “Every tree that has in itself the fruit of seed-bearing seed shall be food for you, and for all the beasts, and for all the birds, and for all the serpents upon the earth” (Gen. I, 29–30). By gathering we become needy, and by gathering we are emptied. We cannot hope for the promise if we do not keep the oracle.

It is therefore a salutary command also to heed the law of hospitality, so that we may show respect to guests, because we too are guests in the world.

6. How holy was that widow who, although pressed by the extremity of famine, preserved the reverence owed to God! She did not claim food for herself alone but shared it with her son, so that the flesh might not outlive its pledge. [Note: Some manuscripts read: “so that she might not exalt herself over the pledge.”]

A great duty of piety—but one even greater in religion. For just as no one ought to be placed before a son, so the prophet of God ought to be placed before her son and his safety.

She should be considered to have offered him not a small amount of food but the whole support of her life, since she left nothing for herself: so hospitable that she gave everything, so faithful that she believed immediately. [Note: Some manuscripts read “but superior in religion.” This is wrong, for Ambrose here teaches what he had already taught in Book VII on Luke, no. 146: that religion takes precedence over duties of human affection. Although this should be understood of religion directed immediately toward God, rather than of religion directed to him through some creature, it is nevertheless credible that the widow observed such manifest signs of the divine will in the holy prophet that she could not doubt the truth of his words. Nor should anyone say that, according to Chrysostom, she was devoted to the worship of idols; for he himself continues as follows: “But she was a religious woman who, with God going before her, had as much faith in her heart as she had little flour in her jar.”]

## CHAPTER II
True widowhood is prescribed from the Apostle: namely, that she should raise children, honor her parents, desire to please God, show herself irreproachable, display maturity of merits, and have been married to one man. Yet he denies that second marriages were condemned by Paul; finally, he adds that widows ought to possess a distinguished reputation for virtue in the eyes of all. Why younger widows are to be avoided, and in what way it is said to be better to marry than to burn. Finally, the dignity of widows is demonstrated by the fact that divine anger is most gravely aroused by injuries inflicted upon them.

[Col. 0236D] **7.** Therefore a widow is defined not merely by abstinence of the body, [Col. 0237A] but designated by virtue. The prescriptions are not mine, but the Apostle attributes them to her. I am not alone in conferring honor, 188 but the Teacher of the Gentiles first bestowed it, saying: “Honor widows who are truly widows. But if any widow has children or grandchildren, let her first learn to govern her own household and to repay the reciprocal obligation to her parents” (1 Tim. 5:3–4). Hence it is also understood that both forms of pious affection must belong to a widow: she must love her children and defer to her parents. Thus, while she repays obedience to her parents, she exercises authority [Note: [Col. 0237C] Some manuscripts read, “let her defer honor to her parents.”] over her children and rewards herself by her own service; [Note: [Col. 0237C] So read Amerbach and all the manuscripts except a few, in which one finds, “over her own children: she rewards herself.” The editions of Erasmus and those that follow differ from Amerbach only in that in them the word “herself” has been omitted. They evidently did not notice that Ambrose regularly uses the verb *remunerari* in the active sense.] for what she gives to others benefits herself.

**8.** “For this is acceptable,” he says, “in the sight of God” (ibid.). Therefore, if you consider this, widow, since you belong to God, you must pursue what you have learned is pleasing to God. Earlier, indeed, the holy Apostle, exhorting widows to devote themselves to continence, said that they should consider the things of the Lord (1 Cor. 7:34). Elsewhere, when a widow who has been tested is being chosen, she is commanded not merely to consider, but also to hope in the Lord: “She who is truly a widow and desolate,” he says, “let her hope in God and continue in supplications and prayers night and day” (1 Tim. 5:5). Not without reason does he show that such women must be irreproachable: just as the work of virtue is enjoined upon them, so also abundant honor is conferred upon them, so that they may even be honored by bishops.

**9.** What sort of woman should be chosen is described [Note: [Col. 0237D] The older edition reads, “in the very words of the Teacher”; the Roman edition, “in the very words of the Teacher of the Gentiles.”] in the words of the Teacher himself: “Not less than sixty years old, having been the wife of one man” (ibid., 9). [Note: [Col. 0237D] Ambrose explains this passage of the Apostle as though it required not so much an age of sixty as gravity and the other virtues that ought to be present in a woman of sixty; consequently, if these are found in a younger woman, she should not be excluded from the profession of widowhood. Jerome likewise, in his letter to Furia, denies that Paul rejects younger widows, teaching that Paul requires sixty years only of those who were to be supported at the Church’s expense; he confirms this also in his commentary on Isaiah, chapter 3. Nor would it perhaps be unreasonable to refer both these words of Ambrose and the earlier ones—“so that they may even be honored by bishops”—to this consideration, for among ecclesiastical writers the words “honor” and “honorificence” signify the support by which someone is assisted in sustaining life.
