Father Morinus, however, in *On Sacred Orders*, Exercise 10, chapter 2, prefers the view that this number of years need not apply to all who profess widowed continence, but only to those who were appointed to the office of deaconess. Hence, he says, women are to be chosen who had previously been married to one man. Thaumassinus, in *Ecclesiastical Discipline*, part I, chapter 53, denies that the Fathers can be reconciled in any more convenient way here than by saying that those who require widows to be sixty years old are speaking of widows chosen for some ecclesiastical office, whereas those who do not reject women younger than that age are speaking of widows who profess chastity alone. Surely no one should persuade himself that the Apostle prohibited the Church from supporting weak widows under sixty, since this was later decreed in the Fourth Council of Carthage, canons 101 and 102.] Not that old age alone makes a widow, but that the merits of widowhood should be the recompense of old age. For certainly more excellent is the woman who subdues the heat of youth and the burning ardor of early age, desiring neither a husband’s affection nor the richer delights of children, than one whose body is already exhausted, whose old age is cold, whose years are mature, and who can neither burn with pleasures nor hope for childbirth.

**10.** Nor, if a woman has entered a second marriage—which the Apostolic precepts certainly do not condemn [Note: [Col. 0238D] Observe that our Teacher is here much more moderate not only than those who entirely proscribed second marriages contrary to the judgment of the Church, such as Tertullian and others, but also than quite a few of the ancient Fathers, who seem to have spoken of these marriages somewhat too severely.]—is she, if she is again widowed, to be shut out from the affection of widowhood as though she had abandoned the fruit of chastity. She will indeed possess the merit of chastity, even if attained late; but the woman who has not experienced another marriage will be more highly approved. In the former, the devotion to chastity stands out; in the latter, either old age or modesty seems to have imposed a limit upon marriage.

**11.** Yet bodily chastity alone is not the widow’s strength, but a great and abundant discipline of virtue: “Let her have testimony in good works, if she has raised children, if she has received strangers in hospitality, if she has washed the feet of the saints, if she has supplied those suffering tribulation, if, finally, she has followed every good work” (ibid., 10). You see how many disciplines of virtue he has included: first, the duty of piety; second, devotion to hospitality and the service of humility; third, the ministry of mercy and the aid of generosity. In short, he demands the execution of every good work.

**12.** And for this reason he thinks that younger women should be avoided (ibid., 11), since they cannot undertake so great a work of virtue. For youth is near to falls, because the various heats of desire inflame an age already burning with ardor. [Note: [Col. 0238D] The editions read, “the heat of desires inflames the fervor of a burning age”; all the manuscripts more appropriately read as in the text, except that the Tellier manuscript has: “[lacuna] fervor inflames the age.”] It is the task of a good teacher to keep the material of sin at a distance. The first discipline of instruction is to avert guilt; the second is to instill virtue.

Nevertheless, since the Apostle knew that Anna, an eighty-year-old widow, had from her youth been a herald of the Lord’s works (Luke 2:36–37), I do not think that he intended younger women to be recalled from the affection of widowhood, especially since he said: “It is better to marry than to burn” (1 Cor. 7:9). He certainly recommended marriage as a remedy, so that what was perishing might be healed; he did not prescribe it as a choice, lest a woman who possessed continence pursue chastity. For it is one thing to assist someone who is falling and another to commend virtue. [Note: [Col. 0238D] All the editions, together with the Tellier manuscript alone, read: “he prescribed what the chaste and continent woman should follow”; the other manuscripts agree substantially with us.]

**13.** And why should I speak of human judgments, when the Jews are reported to have offended the Lord in no matter more gravely, according to the divine judgments, than by violating the dignity of the widow and the rights of minors? This is proclaimed in prophetic voices as the cause that brought rejection upon the Jews. This alone is mentioned as a reason capable of mitigating the reproach of their offense, if the widow is honored and equitable justice is rendered to minors. Thus you read: “Judge for the orphan, justify the widow; and come, let us reason together, says the Lord” (Isa. 1:17–18). And elsewhere: “He will receive the orphan and the widow” (Ps. 145:9). And elsewhere: “Blessing I will bless her widow” (Ps. 132:15). In this, too, a figure of the Church is set forth. You see, therefore, holy widows, that the duty entrusted to you, honored by the supports of divine blessing, must by no means be abandoned through careless negligence.

## CHAPTER III

He returns to the widow of Sarepta, in whom he demonstrates that the figure of the Church was present, and confirms this by Isaiah’s testimony; from this he concludes that in her there is an example for virgins, married women, and widows. Turning to the prophet, he says that Christ also was signified in him, since he promised the divine mysteries and the future watering by rain. The twofold sign of Gideon is likewise related and explained. From these matters he infers that the power of performing miracles does not belong to everyone, and that Christ’s incarnation and the rejection of the Jews are there foreshadowed.

**14.** But, to return to what came before, what does it mean that, although there was a very great famine throughout the whole land, God’s care was not absent from the widow, and the prophet was sent to her [Note: [Col. 0239D] All the editions, together with the Tellier manuscript alone, read, “to sustain her.”] to sustain her? (1 Kings 17:14). In this, since the Lord reminds me (Luke 4:25) that he is about to speak in truth, he seems to summon our ears to a mystery. For what could be truer than the mystery of Christ and the Church? It is not without purpose, therefore, that one widow is preferred among many. For what woman was such that so great a prophet, who was taken up to heaven, should be directed to her—especially at a time when heaven had been closed for three years and six months, when a great famine had arisen throughout the whole land? Everywhere, then, there was famine, yet this widow still had no need. What are these three years? Perhaps those during which the Lord came into the world and could not find fruit on the fig tree, according to what is written: “Behold, these three years I have come seeking fruit on this fig tree, and I do not find any” (ibid., 7).

**15.** This is surely that widow of whom it was said: “Rejoice, barren woman who do not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail, because the children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband” (Isa. 54:1). And rightly is she called a widow, to whom it is fittingly said: “You will not remember your shame and your widowhood, because I am the Lord who make you” (ibid., 4–5). And perhaps for this reason she is a widow: she indeed lost her husband according to the suffering of the body, but on the day of judgment she will receive again the Son of Man whom she seemed to have lost. “For a brief time,” he says, “I abandoned you” (ibid., 7), so that, having been abandoned, she might preserve her faith all the more gloriously.

**16.** All, therefore, have an example to imitate—virgins, married women, and widows. And perhaps for this reason the Church is virgin, married, and widowed, because these are one body in Christ. This, then, is that widow for whose sake, while the dryness of the heavenly word prevailed on earth, prophets were sent. For she was a widow who was barren, but reserved her childbirth for its appointed time.

**17.** Hence the person of that man, too, does not seem insignificant to us: he watered the dry earth with the dew of the heavenly word and opened the closed heaven—not, certainly, by human power. For who is able to open heaven except Christ, for whom food is daily gathered from sinners—an increase for the Church? [Note: [Col. 0239D] So read most manuscripts; the editions and the Tellier manuscript, however, have “the food of the Church into a heap”; another has “the food of the Church in heaps,” and so forth.] For it is not within human power to say: “The jar of flour shall not fail, and the vessel of oil shall not fail until the day when the Lord gives rain upon the earth” (1 Kings 17:14). Although it is customary for prophets to preface their words in this way, this is nevertheless the true voice of God. Therefore it was stated beforehand: “For thus says the Lord” (ibid.). It belongs to the Lord to pledge the perpetuity of the heavenly sacraments, to promise that the grace of spiritual rejoicing will not fail, to grant defenses of life and pledges of faith, and to bestow gifts of virtue.

**18.** But what is meant by “until that day when the Lord gives rain upon the earth” (ibid.) except that he will also descend “like rain upon the fleece, and like drops that drip upon the earth” (Ps. 72:6)? In this the mystery of the ancient history is disclosed: holy Gideon, a warrior in the mystical combat, receiving a sign of future victory, recognized through the strength of his mind the spiritual mystery—that the rain was the dew of the divine Word. First it rained upon the fleece, while the whole earth burned with perpetual drought; then, in a second sign, it drenched the threshing floor of the whole earth with poured-out rain, while there was dryness upon the fleece (Judg. 6:37 and following). [Note: [Col. 0239D] The Tellier manuscript has “the whole expanse of the lands”; several others and the editions have “the whole earth.”]

**19.** For the prophetic man perceived the sign of the future, growing Church. At first the divine dew began to moisten within Judea—for “God is known in Judea” (Ps. 76:2)—while the whole earth of the world remained dry in faith. [Note: [Col. 0240D] All the editions read, “while the entire world, dry in faith, was scorched”; all the manuscripts except the Tellier, as in the text, and shortly afterward all the editions read “with an audacious crime,” whereas all the manuscripts have “with a varied crime.”] But when Joseph’s flocks began to deny God and, with varied daring, to heap up the offense of monstrous sins against the Godhead, then, when the dew of heavenly rain had been poured throughout all the lands, the Jewish people began to dry up in the heat of their faithlessness, while prophetic clouds and apostolic saving rain watered the holy Church gathered from every region of the earth. This is that rain, not formed from the moisture of the earth or condensed from the mist of mountains, but spread throughout the whole world in the salutary rainfall of the heavenly Scriptures. [Note: [Col. 0240D] Some manuscripts read “gathered from the mountains.”]

**20.** It is shown, therefore, by this example that not everyone is worthy to obtain the miracles of divine power, but only those whom the zeal of religious devotion supports; and that those who are deprived of heavenly reverence are excluded from the fruit of divine work. It is also shown in the mystery that, in order to restore the Church, the Son of God assumed the sacramental realities of a human body [Note: [Col. 0241D] Not a few manuscripts read, “assumed sacred mysteries.”], while the Jewish people were rejected, from whom the Counselor and the Prophet (Isa. 3:1 and following) and the miracles of the Lord’s benefits were taken away, because they refused to believe in the Son of God through a certain civic stain of envy. [Note: [Col. 0241D] Some manuscripts read, “because of a certain stain of envy among the citizens.”]

## CHAPTER IV

He reveals what the life of widows ought to be by the example of Anna, whom he demonstrates to have displayed an example of chastity in each period of her life. From these examples he establishes that there are three degrees of the same virtue, all of which the Church embraces; he also sets before each state examples in Mary, [Col. 0241B] Anna, and Susanna. Nevertheless, he adds that the state of virginity surpasses the other two, while a widow ought to exercise greater care in preserving her reputation.

**21.** Scripture has therefore taught [Note: [Col. 0241D] All the editions and the Tellier manuscript read, “how great a contribution”; the Tellier manuscript in its first hand has “the consolation of grace”; the other manuscripts read, “how much grace a contribution confers.” Here “contribution” means beneficence and almsgiving.] how much grace a contribution confers, and how great is the gift of divine blessing upon widows. Since God bestows such honor upon them, we must observe what sort of life is fitting for them. Anna teaches what sort of women widows ought to be: deprived by her husband’s premature death, yet finding the mature reward of praise, [Note: [Col. 0241D] The older editions read, “she finds from God a reward of praise”; the Roman edition, together with all the manuscripts, reads *adoream*, and so forth. *Adorea* was a military reward consisting of a type of grain on which the Romans lived for three hundred years from the founding of the City. Hence, by transference, *adorea* signifies praise and honor, especially military honor.] she devoted herself no less to the duty of religion than to the pursuit of chastity. “A widow,” he says, “eighty-four years old, a widow who did not depart from the temple, a widow who served with fastings and supplications day and night” (Luke 2:36–37).

**22.** You see what sort of widow is praised: the wife of one man, already proved by the progress of her years, vigorous in religion though her body was now exhausted. [Note: [Col. 0242D] Quite a few manuscripts read, “a widow, and now exhausted in body.”] Her lodging was in the temple, her conversation in prayer, her life in fasting. Through the days and nights, by the service of unwearied devotion, though she recognized the old age of her body, she did not know old age in her piety. Thus a widow is formed from youth; thus she is praised in seasoned old age: she who preserved widowhood not through the opportunity afforded by time, nor through bodily weakness, but through the greatness of her virtue. For when he says that she had been with her husband for seven years from her virginity, he declares that the supports of old age had begun with the pursuits of youth.

**23.** We are therefore taught that there are three virtues of chastity: one conjugal, another widowed, and a third virginal. We do not praise one in such a way as to exclude the others. These are suitable to each of their respective professions. In this consists the Church’s rich discipline: it has those whom it prefers, but it does not have those whom it rejects—and would that it could never have any! [Note: [Col. 0242D] “Discipline” here means nothing other than the institutions, laws, and customs that prevail in the Catholic Church, since the word is often used for doctrine and instruction.] Thus we praised virginity without rejecting widows; thus we honor widows while reserving its proper honor for marriage. It is not our precepts but divine testimonies that teach this.

**24.** Let us therefore recall how Mary, how Anna, and how Susanna are praised. But since we must not only proclaim their praises, but also follow their disciplines, let us recall where Susanna (Dan. 13:7), where Anna (Luke 2:38), and where Mary (Luke 1:28) were found; and let us observe how each is praised with appropriate commendation and where each dwells: [Col. 0242B] the married woman in paradise, the widow in the temple, the virgin in seclusion. [Note: [Col. 0242D] One Colbert manuscript reads, “the married woman in the garden”; read “in the orchard,” and understand that in this manuscript the Latin word was used for the Greek word meaning “paradise,” with the same sense.]

**25.** But in those women the fruit is slower, whereas in the virgin it is more mature. Old age proves the former; virginity is the praise of youth. She does not seek the assistance of years who is the fruit of every age. Virginity suits adolescence, adorns youth, and enlarges old age; and in every period of life it possesses the gray hairs of justice, the maturity of gravity, and the veil of modesty; it does not impede devotion but increases religion. [Note: [Col. 0242D] All the editions read, “which impedes devotion”; all the manuscripts read, “which [namely, virginity] impedes devotion.”] We learn from what follows that every year, on the solemn day of Passover, holy Mary went with Joseph to Jerusalem (Luke 2:41). Everywhere there is energetic devotion; everywhere the constant companion of modesty is joined to the Virgin. Nor is the Lord’s mother puffed up as though secure in her merits; rather, the more she recognized her merit, the more abundantly she fulfilled her vow, the more generously she rendered her service, the more devoutly she carried out her duty, and the more fully she completed the mystical time.

**26.** How much more, then, is it fitting for you to be attentive to the pursuit of chastity, lest you leave room for an unfavorable opinion, since you possess the testimony of purity only in your conduct! A virgin, although in her the excellence of character is also greater than that of the body, nevertheless rejects slander by the integrity of her flesh. A widow, who has lost the support of virginity by which she might prove herself, possesses the test of chastity not in the voice of a midwife but in her own conduct. Scripture has therefore taught how attentive and devout the widow’s disposition ought to be.

193

## CHAPTER V

The Gospel widow is presented as an example of generosity toward the poor; her two small coins are shown to be worth more than the larger gifts of the rich. It is also taught that the two Testaments are signified by these two small coins. What is the treasury from which we are commanded, after the example of the Magi, to draw three gifts, or, in imitation of the Gospel widow, two coins? After this comes an exhortation intended to inflame widows with zeal for good works.

**27.** In the same book, though in another place, he also taught how merciful and generous one ought to be toward the poor, and that one should not be deterred by consideration of poverty, because generosity is defined not by the amount of one’s patrimony but by the disposition to give. Finally, by the Lord’s own voice, that widow is placed before all others, of whom it is said: “This widow has put in more than all” (Luke 21:3). In this the Lord morally instructs everyone, so that no one may be held back from contributing to the ministry by shame over poverty, nor the rich flatter themselves that they seem to contribute more than the poor. A coin from little is more abundant than a treasure from much, because what is measured is not how much is given, but how much remains. No one gives more than the woman who left nothing for herself. [Note: [Col. 0243D] Some manuscripts read, “who left nothing for herself”; one reads, “who retained nothing for herself.”]

**28.** Why do you, rich woman, boast in comparison with the poor? When you are burdened with gold and drag a costly garment along the ground, why, as though you were inferior to your own wealth and small beside it, do you desire to be honored because you have surpassed the poor woman in your contribution? Rivers overflow when they are swollen, yet a drink from a stream is more pleasing. New wine foams while it ferments, and the farmer does not regard what has spilled as a loss. When the harvest is cut and the threshing floors groan, grain leaps forth; [Note: [Col. 0243D] All the editions read, “the grain sheds its leaves”; all the manuscripts read, “the grain leaps forth”; some have “bursts apart.”] yet when harvests fail, the jar of flour does not fail, and the vessel full of oil continues to pour. Nevertheless, drought emptied the rich men’s jars, while the widow’s little oil overflowed (1 Kings 17:15). Therefore it is not what you spit out in disgust but how much you contribute in devotion that must be assessed. In the end, no one gave more than the woman who fed the prophet from the food intended for her children. And because no one contributed more, no one merited more. This is the moral interpretation.

**29.** Yet do not despise, in the mystical sense, this woman putting two coins into the treasury. She was plainly a great woman, since by divine judgment she deserved to be placed before all others. Perhaps she is the one who contributed two Testaments from her faith for the support of humankind, and for this reason no one did more. No human being could equal the quantity of her contribution, since she joined faith with mercy. You, therefore, whoever are exercising your life in the pursuit of widowhood, do not hesitate to bring two coins to the treasury, full either of faith or of grace.

[Col. 0243D] **30.** Blessed is the woman who brings forth from her treasure the complete image of the King. Your treasure is wisdom; your treasure is chastity and justice; your treasure is sound understanding. It was like that treasure from which the Magi brought gold, frankincense, and myrrh when they worshiped the Lord (Matt. 2:11): by gold declaring the King’s power, by frankincense venerating God, and by myrrh confessing the resurrection of the body. [Col. 0244A] You too possess this treasure, if you seek within yourself: “For we have this treasure in earthen vessels” (2 Cor. 4:7). You have gold to contribute. God does not demand from you the price of unwilling metal, but that gold which fire cannot consume on the day of judgment. He does not ask for costly gifts, but for the fragrance of faith exhaled by the altars of your heart, and for the devotion of a religious mind breathed forth.

**31.** From this treasure, therefore, not only the three gifts of the Magi but also the widow’s two coins are drawn, in which the complete heavenly image of the King shines forth, together with the radiance of his glory and the image of his substance. Good, too, are those laborious wages of chastity which the widow contributes from her own work and daily task, [Note: [Col. 0243D] This is an obvious imitation of the following passage of Virgil, from Book VIII of the *Aeneid*, where, concerning a chaste woman, after several preceding lines he continues:

[Col. 0244D] “Adding night to her work, she exercises her maidservants by the light of lamps at the long task, so that she may preserve her husband’s chaste bed and be able to raise her little children.”] working constantly at her tasks by night as well as by day and gathering, through her vigilant labor, the reward of profitable chastity, so that she may guard the undefiled bed of her deceased husband, nourish her beloved children, and minister to the poor. She is to be preferred to the rich; she is the one who will not fear Christ’s judgment.

**32.** Imitate her, daughters: “For it is good to imitate what is good. Imitate the better gifts” (Gal. 4:18). The Lord always watches you—Jesus watches, I say, when he approaches the treasury [Note: [Col. 0244D] Thus all the manuscripts except the Tellier manuscript, with which all the editions agree: “you approach . . . you carry to the needy,” etc.; the Pratensis manuscript reads, “he approaches. But concerning . . .”] and you suppose that the alms derived from your good works should be contributed to the needy. How great a thing it is, then, to contribute your coins and acquire Christ’s body! Do not, therefore, come forth empty into the presence of the Lord your God—empty of mercy, empty of faith, empty of chastity. For Jesus the Lord is accustomed to look upon and praise not the empty, but those rich in virtues. Let him see you, young woman, laboring; let him see you ministering. This is the reward you owe to God: that from the progress of other women as well you contribute your reward to God. No reward is better for God than one that possesses the gifts of piety.

## CHAPTER VI

The example of Naomi is placed before us: a widow who receives fruit from the daughter-in-law whom she herself formed in virtue. From this it is inferred that the necessary supports of a good widow will never be lacking. And if her life appears more sorrowful, she is then more blessed, since joys have been promised her by the Lord; in this connection, certain points are discussed concerning the usefulness of tears.

**33.** Or does that widow Naomi seem insignificant to you, who sustained her widowhood with the sheaves of another’s harvest, and whose daughter-in-law, advanced in age, supported her? (Ruth 2:2 and following). For this too contributes both to the support and to the grace of widows: that they should train their daughters-in-law in such a way that they may possess in them a support for their mature old age, and may receive, as the wage of their instruction, the reward of their own discipline. For if a woman has trained her daughter-in-law well and educated her well, Ruth cannot fail her: Ruth, who preferred her mother-in-law’s widowhood to her father’s house. Even when her own husband had died, she nevertheless did not abandon her; she supported the needy woman, consoled the grieving one, and did not depart when she was dismissed. For a woman of excellent discipline knows no need. Thus Naomi, deprived of two sons and a husband, who had lost the fruits of fertility, did not lose the benefits of piety; she found both consolation in grief and support in poverty (Ruth 1:5).

**34.** You see, therefore, holy women, how fruitful a widow is in a progeny of virtues and in offspring of merits that cannot perish. A good widow, then, knows no need. Even if she is weighed down by age and extreme poverty, she is accustomed to possess the reward of her instruction. Although her relatives may be absent, she nevertheless finds strangers who honor her as a mother, revere her as a parent, and desire to acquire the reward of their own commendation through the small expense of providing food. [Note: [Col. 0245D] The Vallière manuscript reads, “a good commendation of her material.”] For they repay the widow’s merits more abundantly. [Note: [Col. 0245D] All the editions, together with the Tellier manuscript, read, “they repay her merits more than food requires”; the other manuscripts read as in the text.] For she seeks food, while they provide the expense.

**35.** But she seems to lead sorrowful days and pass her time in tears. She is more blessed for this reason: with brief weeping she purchases everlasting joys for herself, and with short moments she acquires eternal times. To such women it is rightly said: “Blessed are those who mourn, for you shall laugh” (Luke 6:21). Who, then, would prefer the false appearances of present joys to the pleasure of future security? Does that author seem contemptible to us, the chosen author of the Lord’s body, who “ate ashes like bread, mingled his drink with weeping, and with evening tears acquired for himself the morning joy of redemption” (Ps. 102:10)? From where did he deserve such great joy, unless because he wept so greatly and, as though by the price of his tears, purchased for himself the grace of future glory?

**36.** A widow therefore possesses good material for commendation: while she mourns her husband, let her weep for the world; and let redeeming tears be ready at hand, tears which, while poured out for the dead, will benefit the living. [Note: [Col. 0245D] The editions and the Tellier manuscript read, “the weeping of the mind is ready” (the Roman edition deleted “is”); the other manuscripts, more elegantly, read as above.] Tears of the eyes are ready for the sorrow of the soul: they win mercy, lessen toil, lighten grief, and preserve modesty. Nor does the woman who possesses consolation in tears, in which are the wages of charity and the duties of piety, any longer seem wretched to herself.

## CHAPTER VII

It is shown that a good widow does not lack courage, in the person of Judith. After her clothing and fasts have been recalled, her preparation against Holofernes is described. Her chastity and wisdom in devising a pious stratagem are displayed, as are her temperance and sobriety. Finally, after it has been shown that she shines no less in the praise of prudence than in that of courage, her great modesty amid such success is made clear.

**37.** Nor is courage ordinarily absent from a good widow. For this is true courage: to surpass the limitations of nature and the weakness of her sex through the devotion of her mind. Such was the woman named Judith, who alone was able to recall men broken by siege, struck with fear, and wasted by hunger from destruction, and to defend them from the enemy. For, as we read, when Holofernes, made terrifying by the success of many battles, had forced countless thousands of men within the walls, while the armed men trembled and were already deliberating their final fate, she went forth beyond the wall. She was superior to the army that she freed, and stronger than the army that she put to flight (Judith 8:6 and following).

**38.** But, if you wish to learn the disposition of mature widowhood, follow the entire sequence of the Scriptures. From the days of her husband’s death, she put off the garment of joy and took up one of mourning. She devoted herself to fasting throughout all the days, [Note: [Col. 0245D] The Roman edition alone reads *sola confoderat, et dominica*; but since all the other editions and manuscripts have *dominicam*, what prevents *dominica* here from meaning, as it does in so many passages of Scripture, the Lord’s solemnity?] except on the Sabbath, the Lord’s day, and the times of the sacred festivals, not indulging in refreshment but deferring to religious observance. For this is what it means that “whether you eat or drink, you should do everything in the name of Jesus Christ” (1 Cor. 10:31): even bodily refreshment must be subordinated to the worship of sacred religion.

Strengthened, therefore, by long-continued mourning and daily fasts, holy Judith (Judith 10:3 and following), who sought none of the world’s pleasures, heedless of danger and made stronger by contempt for death, put on, in order to devise a stratagem [Note: [Col. 0245D] The older edition reads, “that she might construct a deceit by a contrivance”; Gillot, the Roman edition, and the Tellier manuscript read, “that she might construct a fabricated deceit”; the remaining manuscripts give our reading.], that garment of joy in which she had been accustomed to dress while her husband was alive, as though she would please her husband if she freed her country. [Col. 0246C] But she was looking toward another husband, whom she sought to please—namely, the one of whom it was said: “After me comes a man who was made before me” (John 1:30). And rightly did she resume the ornaments of marriage for the battle, because the memorials of marriage are weapons of chastity; for otherwise the widow could neither have pleased nor conquered.

**39.** Why should we pursue the rest, when she remained chaste among thousands of enemies? Why should we praise her wisdom, since she devised a plan of this kind? [Note: [Col. 0246D] The manuscripts agree almost unanimously on this reading; the editions, however, have: “she devised a stratagem, so that, while she drew out the powerful man through intemperance, she might keep the inferior men away from her, prepare an opportunity for victory, reserve the reward of abstinence, and carry back no lesser—Amerbach has ‘no smaller’—trophy of preserved chastity.” The Tellier manuscript partly agrees with the other manuscripts and partly with the editions.] She chose a powerful man in order to ward off the intemperance of the inferior one and to prepare an opportunity for victory. She preserved the merit of abstinence and the grace of chastity. For, as we read, neither stained by food nor by adultery, she brought back from the enemy a triumph of preserved chastity no less than that of a liberated homeland. [Note: [Col. 0246D] The Vallicellian manuscript reads, “than the liberation of her homeland.”] (Judith 12:1 and following.)

**40.** Why should I speak of sobriety? Temperance is a virtue particularly suited to women. While the men were drunk with wine and buried in sleep, the widow took away the sword, [Note: [Col. 0246D] The later Paris editions, together with the Tellier manuscript, read, “she exercised her hand.” And below, all the editions and some manuscripts read, “the drunken men, having been exercised.”] put forth her hand, cut off the warrior’s head, and passed undefiled through the midst of the enemy ranks (Judith 13:4 and following). You perceive, therefore, how much drunkenness can harm women, when wine so weakens men that they are defeated by women. Be temperate, then, widow: chaste first from wine, so that you may be chaste from adultery. He will not tempt you at all if wine does not tempt you. For if Judith had drunk, she would have slept with the adulterer. But because she did not drink, the sobriety of one woman was able both to overcome and to outwit a drunken army. [Note: [Col. 0247C] Quite a few manuscripts read, “the awakened drunken army of one,” and so forth.]

**41.** Nor was this work accomplished by her right hand alone; it was far more a trophy of wisdom. For while she conquered Holofernes with her hand alone, she conquered the whole enemy army by her counsel (Judith 14:1 and following). For, when Holofernes’ head was hung up, she raised the courage of her people and broke that of the enemy—arousing her own people through shame and striking the enemy with terror. Thus they were slaughtered and put to flight. In this way the temperance and sobriety of one widow not only conquered her own nature but, what is greater, made even men more courageous (Judith 15:1 and following).

42. Yet not elated by these successes—though she had every right to rejoice and exult in victory—she did not abandon the duty of widowhood. Rather, scorning all who sought her in marriage, she put off the garment of delight and resumed that of widowhood. Nor did she love the adornments of her triumphs, judging those victories better in which the vices of the body are conquered than those in which the weapons of enemies are overcome (Judith XVI, 26 ff.).

## CHAPTER VIII

The holy bishop says that many other widows existed who approached Judith in virtue, but that he will now speak only of Deborah. What great examples she left to widows! They chose her to govern and defend the men. Her greatest glory also proceeded from the fact that she placed at the head of the war her son, whom she herself had trained; yet he declared that he would not lead the troops unless she were present. Thus she both commanded the army and foretold the outcome of the war. In her are signified the Church’s struggles and triumphs, as well as her spiritual weapons; historically, however, every excuse of weakness is taken away from women.

43. And lest this achievement seem to have been accomplished by only one widow, it must certainly be supposed that many others possessed equal or nearly equal virtue; for a good field ordinarily produces many ears full of grain. Nor should you doubt that she made that ancient harvest of the former ages fruitful in the character of many women.

[Note: Several manuscripts read, “that she amassed that ancient harvest”; but since …]

But since it would be tedious to include them all, learn of some of them, especially Deborah, whose virtue Scripture has handed down to us (Judges IV, 4).

44. For she taught not only that widows did not need a man’s help, but even that they could be a support to men. Neither deterred by the weakness of her sex, she undertook the duties proper to men and increased what she had undertaken. Finally, when the Jews were governed by judges—because they could be governed neither by justice nor defended by courage, while wars were raging everywhere—they chose Deborah to govern them by her judgment. Thus one widow ruled many thousands of men in peace and defended them from the enemy.

There were many judges in Israel, but no female judge before her; many judges after Joshua, but no prophetess. Therefore, I think that her judgment was read aloud and that her deeds were recorded, lest women be held back from the duty of virtue by the weakness of their sex. A widow rules peoples, a widow leads armies, a widow chooses commanders, a widow orders wars, and assigns triumphs. Nature, therefore, is not guilty of fault, nor subject to weakness: it is virtue, not sex, that makes people vigorous.

[Note: Quite a few manuscripts read, “but no woman before Judith; one … woman before Deborah.” Ambrose and Jerome agree that Deborah presided over the judgments of the Israelites; but they do not agree whether she was the same woman who was a widow and the mother of Barak. Jerome writes in Letter 10, to Furia: “Some incompetently include Deborah among widows and suppose that Barak was Deborah’s son, although Scripture reports otherwise. She is mentioned here because she was a prophetess and is counted among the judges.” Spencaeus thinks that by these words Ambrose is accused of incompetence. His opinion is indeed supported by the fact that this letter was written not long after Jerome’s Letter 50 to Pammachius, dated A.D. 393, which mentions this very work of Ambrose. In this matter, therefore, that holy Father sometimes followed his own temperament, which was somewhat too vehement, or at least indicated only an ignorance of the Hebrew language.

That Spencaeus seems to award Jerome the palm in this question, however, other interpreters will not so readily concede. For although Scripture calls Deborah the wife of Lapidoth, they maintain that she can rightly be called a widow either because she had been separated from Lapidoth, whom they think to have been the same person as Barak, so far as their marital relationship is concerned, or because Lapidoth was not a man’s name but the name of a craft. Accordingly, they think the phrase should be translated not “the wife of Lapidoth,” but “the woman who tends lamps,” which is the much more common opinion.

We, however, think with Ambrose that Lapidoth was the name of Deborah’s husband, but that he was dead; hence “the wife of Lapidoth” is used for “Lapidoth’s widow,” a usage not uncommon among writers. As for Ambrose’s calling Barak Deborah’s son, many agree with him, despite Jerome’s denial. On all these matters, one may consult the entire company of interpreters.]

45. In peace, indeed, no complaint or error is found in the woman, although many who were responsible for no slight sins had served as judges over their people. But when the Canaanites—a fierce race in battle, and prosperous through the success of their abundant forces—raised hostile minds against the Jewish people, the widow, above all others, equipped the preparations for war. And so that you may learn that domestic necessities did not depend upon public resources, but that public office was governed by domestic discipline, she brought forth from her own household a son as commander of the army, so that you may recognize what a widow can do in training a warrior. As a mother she instructed him; as a judge she appointed him; as a courageous woman she trained him; as a prophetess she sent him forth as one assured of victory (ibid., 6).

[Note: “So that you may recognize what a widow can do in training a warrior” is found only in the editions and in the Tellier manuscript. A little later, where those same editions, together with that manuscript, read “as though she were a prophetess sending him forth to certain victory,” the other manuscripts have the wording found in the text.]

46. Finally, that the whole victory lay in the hand of a woman is shown by Barak, her son, when he says: “Unless you come with me, I will not go, because I do not know the day on which the Lord will direct his angel with me” (Judges IV, 9). What great was the virtue of this woman, to whom the commander of the army says, “Unless you come, I will not go”? What great, I say, was the courage of the widow, who did not hold back her son from danger out of maternal affection, but rather, with a mother’s devotion, urged her son toward victory, declaring that the whole victory lay in the hand of a woman?

47. Deborah, therefore, prophesied the outcome of the battle; Barak, at her command, led out the army; Jael seized the triumph. For she acted in accordance with this prophecy in Deborah, [Note: All editions read, “Deborah’s prophecy served her”; the Tellier manuscripts read, “the prophecy of Deborah served her”; the other manuscripts support our reading.] which mystically revealed to us the rise of the Church destined to arise from the Gentiles, for whom the triumph over Sisera—that is, over spiritual adversarial powers—was to be won.

The oracles of the prophets fought on our behalf; on our behalf those judgments and weapons of the prophets conquered. Therefore it was not the Jewish people, but Jael, who sought victory over the enemy. Unhappy, then, is the people that was unable, through the power of faith, to pursue the enemy whom it had put to flight. Thus, through their offense salvation came to the Gentiles; through their negligence victory was preserved for us.

48. Jael therefore struck down Sisera, whom the hand of the ancient Jews had already put to flight under a flashing commander—for this is what the name Barak means.

[Note: Several manuscripts read, “the interpretation of Balak is ‘hand,’ but the joy of the Jews had put him to flight.”]

For, as we frequently read, heavenly assistance came to the patriarchs through the prayers and merits of the prophets. Yet even then victory was being prepared for them over spiritual wickedness, to whom it is said in the Gospel: “Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew XXV, 34). Thus the beginning of victory comes from the ancestors; its completion is in the Church.

49. The Church, however, conquers hostile powers not with worldly weapons but with spiritual weapons, which are powerful before God for destroying strongholds and every height of spiritual wickedness (II Corinthians X, 5). Therefore Sisera’s thirst is quenched with a cup of milk (Judges IV, 19), because he is overcome by reason; for what is salutary to us as food is deadly to the hostile power as weakness.

[Note: All editions read, “he is overcome by prayer,” not improperly, since below it says, “the weapon of the Church is prayer.” Yet all manuscripts read, “he is overcome by reason.” In the same place, the words “The weapon of the Church is faith,” which occur in all editions and in several manuscripts, are absent from many more and older manuscripts.]

The weapon of the Church is faith; the weapon of the Church is prayer, which conquers the adversary.

50. Thus, according to the historical meaning, to rouse the courage of women, a woman judged, a woman ordered, a woman prophesied, a woman triumphed; and, mingling with the troops engaged in battle, she taught men to fight under a woman’s command.

[Note: Several manuscripts read, “the woman teaches how to fight”; … “the victory of the Church is the soldier of faith.”]

According to the mystery of faith, however, the warfare of the Church is victory.

51. You therefore have no excuse in nature, women. You have no excuse, widows, for attributing your weakness to the weakness of your sex or to the loss of your husband’s support.

[Note: The editions read, “you may assert your own …”]

Each person has sufficient protection if virtue is not lacking in the soul. In widows, advancing age itself is a defense of modesty; the grief of losing a husband, the practice of work, care of the household, and concern for children ordinarily keep harmful wantonness away from modesty. Even the mourning dress, the funeral procession, constant weeping, and the sadness impressed upon the sorrowful brow by deeply furrowed wrinkles restrain the eyes of the insolent, extinguish lust, and turn away immodest glances.

[Note: The same manuscripts read, “the constant weeping destined to provide the pomp of the funeral, and the wrinkles furrowing the mixed brow …”]

Grief born of devotion is a good guardian of modesty: guilt does not creep in if vigilance is not lacking.

## CHAPTER IX

He answers the objection of women who used to say that they would be better off if they abounded in prosperous circumstances, showing from the sacred writings that widows possess support in their children and sons-in-law. After confirming this by the example of Simon’s mother-in-law, he urges them to have recourse to the Apostles as their neighbors and relatives, where he discusses most beautifully the invocation of the saints. Then, after refuting certain complaints about loneliness and the necessity of preserving their property, he demonstrates how utterly unbecoming it is for a widow whose daughters are already marriageable or already married to marry again.

52. You have learned, therefore, widows, that you do not lack nature’s support and can preserve the healthfulness of your decision; nor do you need domestic assistance, since you can even claim the summit of public power.

53. But perhaps some woman says that widowhood is bearable for one whose circumstances are prosperous, whereas widows are quickly broken and easily overcome by adversity. Although experience itself teaches us that cheerfulness is more slippery for widows than seriousness,

[Note: All editions and some manuscripts read this way; many others instead read, “that cheerful widows are more wanton than serious ones.”]

we are nevertheless instructed by examples from Scripture (I Timothy V, 16) that widows’ weaknesses too ordinarily do not lack support, and that divine and human assistance is more readily available to them than to others if they train their children well and choose good sons-in-law.

Finally, when Simon’s mother-in-law was confined by a severe fever, Peter and Andrew entreated God for her: “And standing over her, he commanded the fever, and it left her; and immediately she rose and served them” (Luke IV, 38–39).

[Note: “And immediately she rose and served them” is absent from most manuscripts.]

54. “She was,” he says, “held by a severe fever, and they entreated him for her.” You too have neighbors who may plead for you. You have the Apostles as neighbors; you have the martyrs as neighbors, if, by approaching them in the fellowship of devotion, you also approach them through works of mercy—for the one who shows mercy is a neighbor.

Show mercy yourself, and you will be near to Peter (Luke X, 37). Kinship of blood does not make neighbors, but kinship of virtue, because we do not walk in the flesh but in the spirit. Love, therefore, Peter’s closeness and Andrew’s relationship, so that they may pray for you and your desires may depart. Struck by the word of God, you will rise immediately—you who were lying on the earth—in order to serve Christ.

“For our citizenship is in heaven, from which we also await the Savior, the Lord Jesus” (Philippians III, 20). No one who is lying down serves Christ. Serve the poor, and you have served Christ: “Whatever you did for one of these,” he says, “you did for me” (Matthew XXV, 40). You therefore have assistance, widows, if you choose for yourselves such sons-in-law, patrons for your descendants, and such neighbors.

55. Peter and Andrew, then, entreated God for the widow. Would that someone existed who could so quickly pray for us—or rather, those who pray for their mother-in-law, Peter and Andrew his brother; for then they were able to pray for a relative,

[Note: All editions read, “they were able because of their relationship”; all manuscripts read, “they were able because of their in-law relationship,” and similar forms.]

but now they can obtain blessings for us and for everyone. For you see that one burdened by great sin is less fit to pray for herself—certainly less fit to obtain anything for herself.

Let her therefore bring other petitioners to the physician. The sick cannot pray for themselves unless the physician has first been summoned to them by the prayers of others. The flesh is weak, the mind is sick and impeded by the bonds of sins, and in its weakness it cannot advance a step toward the seat of that physician.

The angels, who have been given to us for our protection, must be entreated for us. The martyrs must be entreated, whose patronage we seem in a certain way to claim for ourselves through the pledge of their bodies. They can pray for our sins, having washed away with their own blood whatever sins they may have possessed. These are God’s martyrs, our guardians, observers of our life and actions. Let us not be ashamed to employ them as intercessors for our weakness, since they themselves knew the weaknesses of the body even when they conquered them.

[Note: Some editions read, “even while they were alive.”]

56. Simon’s mother-in-law therefore found those who would pray for her. You too, widow, will find those who will plead for you if, as a true widow and one desolate, you hope in God, persist in entreaties, persevere in prayers, and afflict your body as though dying every day, so that by dying you may live again; if you flee pleasures, so that even when sick you may be healed. “For she who lives in pleasures is dead while she lives” (I Timothy V, 5–6).

[Note: Most manuscripts read, “if, as a true widow and desolate, you persist in spiritual entreaties to God.”]

57. The reason for marrying has been removed from you; you have those who intercede for you. Do not say, “I have been abandoned.” That is the complaint of one who wants to marry. Do not say, “I am alone.” Chastity seeks solitude; the modest woman seeks privacy, the immodest a crowd.

[Note: All manuscripts read this way except the Tellier manuscript, which, like the editions of Amerbach and Erasmus, places the following wording here: “But you have a case, and you fear the intercessor of your adversary before the judge …” The Gill and Roman editions give the text most badly in this form: “But you have a case, and an intercessor; you fear the adversary before the judge. For you …”]

But you have a case, and you have an intercessor. You fear the adversary: the Lord intervenes for you before the judge, saying: “Judge for the orphan, and justify the widow” (Isaiah I, 17).

58. But you also wish to preserve your property. There is a greater property of modesty, which a widow governs better than a married woman. A servant has sinned. Forgive him; for it is better that you bear another’s fault than expose your own.

[Note: The editions of Amerbach and Rome read, “But you wish to marry. It is permitted. A simple desire does not possess guilt; I do not ask the reason,” and so forth. This is less elegant.]

But you wish to marry. It is permitted. A simple desire is not a crime. I do not ask the reason: why conceal it? If you think it honorable, admit it; if unsuitable, be silent. Do not accuse God or your relatives, saying that you lack support; would that you did not lack the will!

Nor should you say that you are consulting your children, when you are taking their mother away from them.

59. There is also something that one’s means permit, but one’s age does not permit. Why are a mother’s marriage preparations made between her daughters’ weddings, and often after their weddings? Why does a grown daughter first learn to blush at her mother’s bridegroom rather than her own? We urged you, I admit, to change your clothing, not to take up the bridal veil; to withdraw from the tomb, not to prepare a bridal chamber. What does a new bride after her sons-in-law mean? How unbecoming it is to have children younger than one’s grandchildren!

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads, “It is as unbecoming … as grandchildren.” Although this change is slight, it distorts the meaning, which anyone of even moderate intelligence can understand for himself.]

## CHAPTER X

He returns to Christ, praising his supreme kindness in approaching all kinds of suffering people and saying that, through the favor of the Gospel, this kindness has been placed before our eyes. He then recounts various methods known to have been used by this same physician in healing; next he praises the speed of the cure, provided that we do not neglect to call upon the physician. To these matters he appends a moral interpretation of the will, which he teaches was expressed in Peter’s mother-in-law. Finally, after explaining what sort of minister of Christ—and especially what sort of bishop—one ought to be, he says that it is proper to them to rise through grace.

60. But let us return to our subject, and let us not abandon the physician while grieving over the wounds of our own sins; while healing the ulcers of others, let us not multiply our own wounds.

This physician, then, is entreated. Do not be afraid, because the Lord is great, and perhaps he may disdain to come to a sick woman; for he often comes to us from heaven. He is accustomed to visit not only the rich but also the poor and the servants of the poor.

He came even now, when summoned, to Peter’s mother-in-law; “and standing over her, he commanded the fever, and it left her; and immediately she rose and served them” (Luke IV, 39). As worthy of remembrance as it is worthy of desire, worthy also of love is the Lord’s gracious affection and his wondrous deeds toward each person.

[Note: The Vallian manuscript reads, “And he deigns to visit widows.”]

He does not disdain to visit widows or to enter the narrow recesses of a poor cottage. As God he commands; as man he visits.

61. Thanks be to the Gospel, through which even we, who did not see Christ coming into this world with our own eyes, seem to be present with him when we read of his deeds. Just as those whom he approached drew faith from him, so may he approach us while we believe in his actions.

62. Do you see how many kinds of healings he possesses? He commands the fever; he commands unclean spirits; elsewhere he lays on his hands himself. He therefore customarily heals the sick not only by his word but also by touch.

And you, therefore, who are burning with various desires of the world—whether captivated by the appearance of some man or by money—entreat Christ, bring in the physician, extend your right hand to him. May the hand of God touch your inward parts, and may the grace of the heavenly Word examine the inner veins of your souls; may God’s right hand probe the hidden places of the heart.

To others he smears their eyes with clay so that they may see (John IX, 6–7), and the Creator of all teaches us that we must remember our nature and perceive the baseness of the body. No one can see divine things more fully than one who, conscious of his own humility, does not know how to exalt himself.

[Note: The editions and a few manuscripts read, “conscious of his own humility.”]

Another is ordered to present himself to the priest so that he may be rid forever of the vestiges of leprosy (Luke V, 14). For only one who knows that he must present himself to that priest whom we have received as our advocate for our sins can preserve purity of mind and spirit—to the one of whom it is said: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm CIX, 4).

63. Do not fear any delay in healing. The one who is healed by Christ knows no impediment. You must apply the remedy you have received. As soon as he gives the command, the blind sees, the paralytic walks, the mute speaks, the deaf hears, the fever-stricken serves, and the lunatic is set free.

[Note: A few manuscripts read, “And you, therefore, who are wasting away disgracefully with desire for something … entreat God. If you defer faith …”]

And you, therefore, whatever you are who are wasting away disgracefully through desire for some thing, entreat the Lord, offer faith, and fear no delay. Where prayer is present, the Word is present; desire is driven away, lust departs. Do not fear the offense of confession; rather, claim its privilege. You who previously suffered from a bodily illness will immediately begin to serve Christ.

64. At this point one may also understand the disposition of Peter’s mother-in-law’s will, from which she had taken up for herself, as it were, the seed of a future posterity; for each person’s will is the author of his or her posterity. From the will wisdom is born, and the wise person takes it in marriage, saying: “I determined to take her to myself as my bride” (Wisdom VIII, 2).

Thus the will that at first languished, drenched by the surges of various desires, later rose strong through the duty of apostleship into the service of Christ.

65. At the same time, the passage shows what sort of person one who serves Christ ought to be. First, it is necessary to be free from the allurements of various pleasures and to avoid the inward sickness of body and soul, so that one may administer Christ’s body and blood.

[Note: All editions, together with the Tellier manuscript, read, “who serves Christ, is shown. For she must …” All the other manuscripts read, “who serves Christ … for it is necessary …” The latter reading is clearly preferable. The holy bishop is adapting his discourse to bishops, as the following makes explicit. For nowhere in the Church is it found that women were permitted to administer Christ’s body. On the contrary, this is prohibited not only in the Apostolic Constitutions, Book III, chapter 15 and following, and Book VIII, chapter 28, but also by Epiphanius, Heresy 79, and at the end of the Panarion. In these places the ministry of deaconesses is almost entirely confined to undressing and dressing women in the baptistery.]

No one who is sick from his sins and far from being healthy can administer remedies that grant immortal health. Consider what you are doing, priest, and do not touch Christ’s body with a feverish hand. First heal yourself, so that you may be able to minister.

If Christ orders those who had previously been lepers to present themselves to the priests once cleansed (Luke XVII, 14), how much more fitting is it that the priest himself should be clean! That widow, therefore, has no reason to resent my having spared her nothing, since I spare myself nothing either.

66. “Peter’s mother-in-law,” he says, “rose and served them” (Luke IV, 39). And rightly did she rise, for she was already ministering the type of the sacrament through apostolic grace. It is proper for Christ’s ministers to rise, according to what is written: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead” (Ephesians V, 14).

## CHAPTER XI

After rejecting the reasons commonly offered for repeating marriage, he declares that he does not condemn second marriages. Although he reviews their disadvantages from the Apostle, he nevertheless affirms that the condition is approved in the Church; here he chastises the heretics who prohibited them. Since different people possess different strengths, he writes that this is why chastity was not commanded but advised.

67. We say, then, that widows do not need resources, since they are accustomed to give; nor support, since their forces have often defended men in the greatest dangers. Marital duties can also easily be restored to them either by their sons-in-law or by their relatives. Divine mercy is also more readily available to them. Therefore, when no sufficient reason for marrying seems to exist, the desire to marry ought to be absent.

68. Yet what we say is offered as advice, not imposed as a command. We encourage the widow rather than bind her. For we do not prohibit second marriages, but we do not advise them. One consideration concerns weakness; another concerns the grace of chastity.

I say more: we do not prohibit second marriages, but we do not approve of marriages repeatedly entered into.

[Note: All manuscripts except the Tellier manuscript read this way. The Tellier manuscript, together with all the editions, prefers: “For not everything that is permitted is fitting.” What Ambrose says here—that he does not approve of marriages repeatedly entered into—is milder than the language of many other Fathers, who, as was noted in Book I, On Abraham, chapter 4, scarcely fail to regard such marriages as equivalent to fornication. Nevertheless, the present passage abundantly proves that he does not condemn them as unlawful.]

For not everything that is permitted is beneficial: “All things are permitted to me,” the Apostle says, “but not all things are useful” (I Corinthians VI, 12). It is permitted to drink wine, but excessive drinking is not fitting.

69. It is therefore permitted to marry, but it is more beautiful to abstain; for marriage involves bonds. Do you wish to know what bonds? “The woman who is under a husband is bound by the law while her husband lives; but if her husband dies, she is released from the law of her husband” (Romans VII, 2).

It has therefore been proved that marriage is a bond by which a woman is bound and released.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “The grace of love is a good thing”; some others, “Do you wish to have a good grace?” Other manuscripts and the editions have the better reading, “The grace of mutual love is good,” and so forth.]

The grace of mutual love is good, but servitude is greater. For “the woman does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does” (I Corinthians VIII, 4). And lest you perhaps think that this servitude belongs not to marriage but to sex, it likewise says: “The husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does.”

What necessity marriage imposes, when it subjects even the stronger party to the other! Each serves the other’s needs. Even the temperate person may not withdraw his head from the yoke when he must serve the other’s intemperance.

“You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of men” (ibid., 13). You see how evident is the definition of conjugal servitude. I do not say this, but the Apostle; nor does he, but Christ, who spoke through him.

And he certainly defined this servitude in the case of good marriages. For above you read: “The unbelieving husband is sanctified through the believing wife, and the unbelieving wife is sanctified through the believing husband” (ibid., 14). And below: “But if the unbeliever departs, let him depart. The brother or sister is not enslaved in such cases” (ibid., 15).

If, therefore, a good marriage is servitude, what is a bad marriage, when the partners cannot sanctify one another but instead destroy one another?

[Note: Most manuscripts read, “what is a bad thing, since they cannot sanctify one another?” But in accordance with the discipline of the Church … Immediately afterward, where all editions read, “And although Christ’s flock consists of all … yet the flock in some …,” all manuscripts have the reading that we have received into the text.]

70. Just as we exhort widows toward the grace of virtue, so we also summon women to ecclesiastical discipline, because the Church consists of everyone.

[Note: The editions read, “And although Christ’s flock consists of all, yet the flock …”]

Although Christ’s flock consists of everyone, some feed on solid nourishment, while others are still nourished on milk. They must beware of those wolves who hide in sheep’s clothing, pretending to abstinence while provoking the disgrace of intemperance.

For because they know how heavy are the burdens of chastity, and cannot themselves so much as touch them with their fingertips, they demand them excessively from others, while they themselves are unable to observe even moderation and collapse beneath an unjust burden.

[Note: “Unjust,” that is, excessive and greater than their strength. The expression is taken from Virgil, Georgics III: “While he makes his way beneath an unjust burden,” and so forth.]

The weight of the load must correspond to the strength of the bearer; otherwise the load collapses when the bearer is weak. A stronger food also chokes the throats of infants.

71. Therefore, just as a multitude of bearers is not judged by the strength of only a few, nor are the stronger nevertheless prescribed by the weakness of others, but each person is allowed to undertake as much of the load as he or she wishes, while the full reward remains in the increase of virtue, so women too must not be ensnared, nor forced to undertake a burden of more severe abstinence beyond their strength. Each woman should be left to weigh herself—not compelled by the authority of a command, but encouraged by an increase of grace.

Therefore different rewards have been assigned to different virtues. One thing is not condemned so that another may be praised; everything is praised, so that what is better may be preferred.

## CHAPTER XII

Certain distinctions between commandment and counsel are presented. To make them still clearer, the story of the rich young man mentioned in the Gospel is recounted, together with the diversity of rewards proposed for counsels and commandments.

72. Marriage is therefore honorable, but integrity is more honorable; for “he who joins his virgin in marriage does well, and he who does not join her does better” (I Corinthians VII, 38).

What is good, then, must not be avoided; what is better must be chosen. It is therefore not imposed but preferred.

[Note: Quite a few manuscripts read, “but it is proposed.” The same manuscripts also read below, where counsel calls forth grace. “And therefore …” The other manuscripts and all the editions agree with our text.]

And therefore the Apostle rightly said: “Concerning virgins I have no commandment of the Lord, but I give advice” (ibid., 25). A commandment is issued to subjects; counsel is given to friends. Where there is a commandment, there is law; where there is counsel, there is grace.

A commandment recalls one to nature; counsel summons one to grace. Thus the law was given to the Jews, while grace was reserved for the more elect. The law recalled those straying from the limits of nature through a desire for sin to the observance of nature by the fear of punishment; grace, however, summoned the elect not only through their zeal for good works but also through the rewards set before them.

73. Behold the difference between commandment and counsel, if you remember the man to whom the Gospel first prescribes that he must not commit murder, commit adultery, or bear false witness (Matthew XIX, 18 ff.).

[Note: This is the reading of every manuscript without exception; all the editions, however, read: “And that you may understand the difference between counsel and commandment, remember that man.”] There is a commandment wherever there is punishment for sin.

But when he had recalled that he had fulfilled the commandments of the law, counsel was given to him: that he should sell everything and follow the Lord. These things are not imposed as commandments but offered as counsel.

There are therefore two forms of command: one obligatory, the other voluntary. Hence in one place the Lord says, “You shall not kill,” where he commands; in another, “If you wish to be perfect, sell all that you have.” Here, then, the person is free from commandment, since the decision is left to his judgment.

[Note: A few manuscripts read, “to whose judgment it is entrusted”; all the editions read this.]

74. Thus those who fulfill the commandment can say: “We are unworthy servants; we have done what we were obliged to do” (Luke XVII, 10).

The virgin does not say this; nor does the one who sold his possessions. Rather, he awaits the rewards laid up for him, like the holy Apostle who says: “Behold, we have left everything and followed you; what, then, shall we have?” (Matthew XIX, 27).

He did not say that, like an unworthy servant, he had done what he was obliged to do; rather, like a useful servant to his master, who had multiplied through profitable investment the talents entrusted to him, he confidently awaits the reward of faith and virtue, conscious of his merits.

And therefore it is said to him, together with the others: “You who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (ibid., 28).

To the one who had preserved his talent, however, he promises rewards, though lesser ones, saying: “Because you were faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things” (Matthew XXV, 21).

Faith, therefore, is owed; mercy is in the reward. The one who believed well, so that he might be believed, earned this; the one who distributed well, because he did not seek his own, obtained what is heavenly.

## CHAPTER XIII

After introducing the Gospel passage concerning eunuchs, he says that those who became such either by nature or through human violence are not for that reason greatly to be praised. Those who turned their own hands against themselves, however, are to be condemned. He shows that this action is neither useful, since it does not remove the mind’s desire, nor honorable, since it leaves no room for struggle. Therefore only those are to be praised who have conquered themselves through continence. Yet no one is to be compelled to this, since neither the Apostle nor Christ himself bound this virtue by a commandment. From this one understands that marriage vows are not disapproved, but that chastity is preferred.

75. Therefore no commandment is given, but counsel is offered. The commandment concerns chastity; the counsel concerns integrity. “Not all receive this word, but those to whom it has been given.”

There are eunuchs who were born so from their mother’s womb (Matthew XIX, 11–12), in whom human beings possess the necessity of nature, not the virtue of chastity.

[Note: All editions read, “in whom it is not the virtue of chastity.” And there are eunuchs …]

And there are eunuchs who made themselves eunuchs, by will, certainly, not by necessity. And there are eunuchs who were made so by men.

Therefore there is great merit of continence in them, because it is the will, not weakness, that makes a person continent.

[Note: Most manuscripts read, “because the grace of continence, since it is the work of God …” But there is clearly a lacuna, of the kind frequently left in the manuscripts of this little work through the carelessness of copyists.]

For it is fitting to preserve intact the gift of the divine work. Nor should it perhaps be considered little that they are not held by the slippery weakness of the body. For if they have been deprived of the palm of entering this contest, they have also been deprived of the material for danger; and although they cannot be crowned, they nevertheless cannot be defeated.

They possess other kinds of virtues by which they ought to commend themselves, provided that their faith is firm, their mercy overflowing, their freedom from coveting what belongs to others complete, and their grace abundant. But in these matters there is no fault, because their condition was not brought about by their own choice.

76. The case of those who use a sword against themselves is not the same—a matter into which we have digressed not without reason. For there are those who regard restraining sin by the sword as a virtue. [Note: A Virgilian imitation from the same book, Book III of the *Georgics*: “Immediately restrain guilt with the sword,” etc. The holy Doctor here testifies that, in his own memory, there were people who thought that dishonorable bodily impulses had to be resisted not only by prayer, fasts, and vigils, but also by force and armed hand. Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* 58, records that he had frequently heard that the Valesians were accustomed to inflict this violent amputation not only on themselves but also on travelers. Nevertheless, since, according to his testimony, they separated themselves from the Church, and since this heresy does not appear to have spread widely, it is more probable that Ambrose is indicating certain Catholics and treating them more gently for that reason—unless one prefers to think that this was done out of respect for Origen, whose writings many esteemed highly. In any event, it is clear that Ambrose himself condemned this crude interpretation of the Gospel passage by which they had been led into error, no less than did other Fathers, such as Basil, in *On Virginity*; Chrysostom, in his commentary on Matthew 19; and Jerome, Letter 65. It is not sufficiently clear which statutes of the ancients are cited here. We have, on this subject, Apostolic Canons 21, 22, 23, and 24, which the learned Thomassin asserts were renewed by the Council of Nicaea. Nor does it matter that some prove these canons not to belong to apostolic times, since nothing prevents their being said to be later than Origen’s self-castration and earlier than the Council of Nicaea. Concerning Origen’s deed, besides Eusebius, Book VI, chapter 8; Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* 64, no. 3; and Theodoret, Book II, chapter 24, see also Peter Halloix, Book IV of his *Defense of Origen*, and Huet, Book I, chapter I, no. 13.]

As for these people, although we do not wish to state our own judgment—although there are statutes of the ancients—we nevertheless ask them to consider whether anyone may draw this toward a profession of weakness rather than toward the glory of strength. [Note: A large number of manuscripts read: “lest it be something pertaining to a profession of weakness. Therefore let no one,” etc.] Therefore let no one serve as a soldier, lest he someday be defeated; let no one use the service of his feet who fears the danger of walking; let no one employ the function of his eyes who fears the fall of desire. But what good does it do to cut away the flesh when there is even guilt in the very act of looking? For whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart (Matthew 5:28). And a woman who looks at a man in order to desire him likewise commits adultery. We ought therefore to be chaste, not weak; to have modest eyes, not incapacitated ones.

77. No one, then, as many suppose, ought to cut himself off, but rather to conquer himself; for the Church receives victors, not the defeated. Why should I use arguments when the form of the apostolic prescription is at hand? For you have this:

“Would that those who want you circumcised would also be cut off” (Galatians 5:12)! [Note: The sense, not the Apostle’s exact words, is cited. The Greek reads: ὄφελον καὶ ἀποκόψονται οἱ ἀναστατοῦντες ὑμᾶς—“Would that those who are disturbing you would cut themselves off,” as the Vulgate editions have it; or, according to the proper force of the verb, “those who are agitating you toward innovations.” Ambrose’s reasoning is this: the Apostle plainly shows that voluntary amputation of the genitals is a great evil, since he invoked it as a punishment against those who were trying to impose circumcision upon the faithful as a necessity. Ancient interpreters, such as Jerome, Chrysostom, and others, commonly understood the Apostle’s curse to refer to the cutting off of the male organ. Those who, with more recent interpreters, prefer to understand the passage as separation from the Church must attribute the following sense to Ambrose: If the Apostle wishes those who merely commanded circumcision of the foreskin to be separated from the Church, how much more would he wish this of those who attempted to emasculate a man completely!]

For why should the opportunity for a crown and the exercise of virtue be taken away from a man who was born for praise and prepared for victory—one who can rather castrate himself by the virtue of his soul? For there are eunuchs who have castrated themselves for the sake of the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 19:12).

78. Yet this is not commanded to everyone; it is, however, demanded of everyone. For the one who gives commands must always observe the measure of decrees, and the one who distributes weights must preserve fairness in judgment: “A false balance is an abomination to the Lord” (Proverbs 11:1). There is therefore a lesser weight and a greater weight; but the Church accepts neither: “A greater weight and a lesser, and double measures, both are unclean in the sight of the Lord” (Proverbs 20:10). Wisdom distributes weights, and distributes them in such a way as to assess the virtue and strength of each person. Therefore it says: “Let him who is able to receive it receive it” (Matthew 19:12).

79. The Creator of all things knows that the dispositions of individuals are diverse; therefore he called virtue forth by rewards, rather than binding weakness with chains. The teacher of the nations (Romans 7:23 and following), that excellent charioteer of our morals and ruler, as it were, of our inward affections, also knew this. He had learned from himself that the law of the body resists the law of the mind, yet yields to the grace of Christ. He knew, I say, that the various assaults of the mind resist one another; therefore he did not press the exhortation to integrity so far as to abolish the grace of marriage, nor did he prefer marriage in such a way as to extinguish the pursuit of integrity. Beginning with persuasion toward continence, he descended to remedies for incontinence; and when he had displayed the prize of the heavenly calling to the stronger, he nevertheless allowed no one to fail on the road. He applauded those who went ahead without despising those who followed behind. For he himself had learned that the Lord Jesus supplied barley bread to some, lest they fail on the way (John 6:5 and following), and his own body to others, so that they might strive toward the kingdom (Matthew 26:26).

80. The Lord himself did not impose a command, but invited the will; nor did the Apostle establish a command, but gave counsel (1 Corinthians 7:25). Yet this human counsel does not claim to possess the measure of human strength; it confesses that the gift of divine mercy has been bestowed upon it, so that it might faithfully know how to prefer the first things and arrange the second. Therefore, he says: “I think”—not “I command,” but “I think”—“that this is good because of the present necessity” (ibid., 26).

81. Marriage, then, is not to be avoided as though it were a fault, but as a burden of necessity. For the law bound the wife to bear children in labor and sorrow, and her turning would be toward her husband, who would rule over her (Genesis 3:16). Thus the married woman, not the widow, is assigned to labor and pain in the bearing of children; and the married woman, not the virgin, is subjected to the rule of a husband. The virgin is free from all these things: she has pledged her affection to the Word of God and awaits the bridegroom of blessing with lamps (Matthew 25:4), with the light of a good will kindled. Therefore she is summoned by counsels, not bound by chains.

## CHAPTER XIV

Although the widow has not received a command, she has received such frequent and useful counsel that it should not seem contemptible.
