He does not wish to cast a snare upon anyone, since the field of the Church is enriched even by marriage; nevertheless, the widowhood praised by the Apostle cannot possibly be denied to be good. Hence he does not deal superficially with those whose laws he knew had proscribed it.

82. The widow, too, receives not a command but counsel—and counsel given not once but repeated often. First he said: “It is good for a man not to touch a woman” (1 Corinthians 7:1); then: “I wish that all people were as I myself am” (ibid., 7); third: “It is good for them if they remain as I do” (ibid., 8); fourth: “It is good because of the present necessity” (ibid., 26). He defined this as pleasing to the Lord and honorable, and finally determined that perseverance in widowhood is happier—not merely by his own counsel, but also by the Spirit of God. [Note: All editions, with the Tell manuscript, read *perseverantem* (“the one persevering”); the others read *perseverantiam* (“perseverance”). Below, where the Gill and Roman editions, together with the manuscripts, read “not easy to grasp, nor wearisome to equal,” the Amerbach and Erasmus editions had printed “not easily grasped, nor equal to the wearisome.”]

Who, then, would reject the kindness of such a counselor, one who gives free rein to the will and advises others to pursue what he has judged useful from his own experience—something not easy to grasp, nor wearisome to equal? Who, then, would refuse to become holy in body and spirit, when the reward is above labor, grace above practice, and recompense above work?

83. I say this not to cast a snare upon the others, but so that, as a worker assigned to the field entrusted to me, I may see this field of the Church fertile—now green with the flower of integrity, now rich with the dignity of widowhood, and now overflowing with the fruits of marriage. For although they are different, they are nevertheless the fruits of one field. The lilies of gardens are not so numerous as the ears of grain; nor are the rows of harvest fields, prepared to receive many seeds, so abundant as the fallow lands that rest after yielding their fruits. [Note: “Ears of the harvest” is found in the printed editions alone and in the Tell manuscript.]

84. Good, therefore, is widowhood, which is so often praised by apostolic judgment; for it is a teacher of faith and a teacher of chastity. Hence even those who venerate the adulteries and disgraces of their gods established penalties for celibacy and widowhood, so that, as rivals of their crimes, they might punish the pursuits of virtue. Their apparent purpose was to seek fertility, but their real aim was to abolish the resolve of chastity. For when his service has been completed, the soldier lays down his arms; and once the office he held has been left behind, the veteran is released to his own fields, so that he may obtain rest from a life worn down by labors and may make others more ready to undertake their tasks through the hope of future repose. The more mature farmer likewise entrusts the plow to others, and, weighed down by youthful labor, tests the care of old age. It is easier to prune the vine than to press it, so that he may restrain luxuriant growth and cut down youthful wantonness with the sickle, teaching that a certain frugality of fruitfulness is also to be desired in vines. [Note: Several manuscripts read: “He entrusts the plow, which others must drag, to others … it is easier to prune the vine,” etc. This is erroneous.]

85. Similar to him is the widow, as a veteran who has completed the campaigns of chastity. Although she lays down the arms of marriage, she nevertheless governs the peace of the whole household; although free from the task of carrying burdens, she is provident in arranging marriages for younger women. With the gravity of old age, she decides where the more useful cultivation and the more abundant fruit may be found, and which union is more suitable. Therefore, if the field is entrusted to the more mature rather than the younger, why should you think a married woman more useful than a widow? And if the persecutors of the faith were also persecutors of widowhood, then widowhood is certainly not to be fled by those who follow the faith as though it were a punishment, but to be held as a reward.

## CHAPTER XV

He removes the excuse of those who put forward the desire for children, but he dwells especially on those who have children from a previous marriage. He finely describes their heavy servitude, the future hostility among the children, and, finally, the rare concord between the spouses themselves. At the end he takes care that no one should misuse examples from Scripture in this matter.

86. But perhaps some may think that marriages should be repeated for the sake of having children. If the desire for children is the reason for marrying, then where the fruit of children already exists, there is no reason. [Note: A few manuscripts read: “Although it is not a matter of counsel.”] Yet what kind of counsel is it to wish to try again a fertility that was unsuccessfully attempted, or to undergo again the bereavement that you have already endured? This is the reason for repeating marriage among those who have no children.

87. Therefore, a woman who has had children and lost them—for her struggle is the greater, since she has hope of bearing children—does she not seem, amid the very bonds of a repeated marriage, to display the funerals of the children she has lost? Will she not again suffer what she seeks to repeat, and, at the very tombs of her wishes, shudder at the images of the bereavements she has endured and the din of lamentation? [Note: The Tell manuscript and certain Paris editions read “the tumult of vows,” incorrectly. Below, where the same Paris editions read “with funeral torches kindled,” and several manuscripts read *funabulis*, the other manuscripts and editions more appropriately read *funalibus*, that is, torches made from ropes smeared with pitch, which were customarily used at funerals.] Or, when the night is passed with torches lit, does she not think that a funeral procession is being prepared rather than a bridal chamber? Why, then, daughter, do you seek again the sorrows you fear more than you seek the children you no longer hope for? If the pain is grievous, its cause should be avoided, not sought.

88. What counsel, then, should I offer you, who already have children? What reason have you for marrying? Perhaps an error of frivolity, the habit of intemperance, or the consciousness of a wounded heart drives you. But counsel is given to the sober, not to the intoxicated; therefore I speak to a free conscience, for whom both alternatives remain open. Let the wounded have a remedy, and the honorable woman counsel.

You, then, daughter, what are you attempting? Why do you seek foreign heirs when you have heirs of your own? You do not desire children, whom you already have, but servitude, which you do not have. This is true servitude: a love less vigorous, which is not commended by the pledge of an unflowered virginity, and in which the first period of life is not full of holy modesty and grace; a situation in which offense is more serious, insolence more suspect, and concord less frequent, since love rooted in time and beauty flourishing with the years do not bring the spouses together. What a burdensome affection—to fear loving your children and to be ashamed to look upon them; and for discord to arise from the very source from which mutual love ordinarily softens the feelings of parents. You wish to produce children who will not become brothers to your own, but adversaries of your children. What, then, is it to produce other children except to strip the children you already have—depriving them alike of the duties of affection and of the advantages of property? [Note: Most manuscripts read: “so that she may be ashamed to love her children … from which it ordinarily softens mutual affection,” etc. This is less appropriate.]

89. Divine law bound husband and wife together by heavenly authority, and mutual love remains difficult. For God took a rib from the man and formed the woman in order to join them to one another, saying: “And the two shall be one flesh” (Genesis 2:24). He did not say this of second marriages but of the first; for Eve did not take a second husband, nor did holy Church acknowledge a second husband: “For this is a great sacrament, in Christ and in the Church” (Ephesians 5:32), and therefore it must be guarded. Isaac, too, knew no wife other than Rebecca (Genesis 24:67), nor did Abraham the father bury any wife other than Sarah (Genesis 25:10). [Note: Erasmus and Gill, and with them the Roman edition, read in the text: “nor did Abraham the father bury another except Sarah as his wife”; the Roman edition reads, “except Sarah, he buried her as his wife.” In the margin, however, and in Amerbach’s text, together with all the manuscripts, our reading is given. The Roman edition also changed “in holy Rachel … in her also” to “in holy Jacob … in him also”; this conflicts equally with the other editions and with all the manuscripts. Nevertheless, the ellipsis of the word “Jacob,” understood before the verb “loved,” admittedly makes the meaning somewhat obscure.]

90. In holy Rachel there was more a figure of the mystery than an example of the order of marriage (Genesis 29:28 and following). Yet even in her we have something that can be referred to the grace of a first marriage: the bride whom he first had, he loved more; fraud did not exclude affection, nor did the intervention of another marriage destroy love for the first bride. Thus the holy patriarch taught us how much deference we owe to first marriages, since he himself showed so much deference to his first betrothal. Beware, therefore, daughters, lest you be unable both to preserve the grace of marriage and to increase its burdens.

# [ON VIRGINITY]

## INTRODUCTORY NOTICE TO THE BOOK ON VIRGINITY

We have separated this treatise from the Third Book *On Virgins*, with which all editions until now had joined it. We were led to do so by considerations which, as we think, make not only the necessity of this distinction evident but also make us wonder at so obvious and yet so long-unrecognized a confusion.

In every manuscript, absolutely, that same Third Book *On Virgins* ends with the very words at which we have ended it. Moreover, the distinct commentary not only begins everywhere in this manner—“Noble among the ancients,” etc.—but also occupies, in most of those same manuscripts, a position immediately after the Book *On Widows*. Furthermore, Ambrose himself, after discussing Saint Pelagia, her mother, and her sisters in the aforementioned Book *On Virgins*, clearly indicated that he was bringing that book to an end when he said: “Now, as I spread my sails toward the conclusion of my speech,” etc. (Book III *On Virgins*, chapter 7, no. 32). He certainly would never have said this if he had intended to append a much longer discussion on another subject, in the part of the work already treated in that same book.

There is also a very clear difference both in subject matter and in manner of expression. Throughout this whole work he nowhere addresses his sister Marcellina, but almost everywhere addresses virgins collectively, and sometimes widows as well. Finally, a passage from the Book *On Widows*, which is known to be later than the Books *On Virgins*, is explicitly indicated in this little work (Book *On Widows*, chapter 8, no. 46). Since this did not escape the Roman editors, it is astonishing that they failed to notice the absurd compilation of different works.

To make the matter clearer, let us examine the individual parts of this work somewhat more attentively.

Beginning with that famous judgment of Solomon, the holy man explains its mystical meaning (chapter 1, no. 1 and following). Yet, to acknowledge the truth, this first part has little connection with the remainder of the composition. Later, after elegantly describing Jephthah’s sacrifice—which he expressly declares to be in no way approved by him (chapter 2, no. 5 and following)—he says that he is astonished that no one was found to oppose the killing of a virgin (chapter 3, no. 10), whereas everyone finds fault with him because he forbade an unlawful marriage for a virgin. He then undertakes the defense both of his own conduct and of the virginal state (no. 11), chiefly defending his action by the example of the Forerunner; and he elevates the condition of virginity (nos. 14, 15, and following) on the ground that Christ chose virgins to whom he would first appear after rising again.

After dealing as modestly as possible with his accusers, he presses the matter more forcefully (chapter 5, no. 24 and following), demonstrating (chapters 6 and 7) that he had persuaded no one to do anything shameful, novel, or useless. He then responds beautifully to the objections raised (chapter 7, no. 35 and following). But when he reaches the objection that the consecration of virgins of tender age should not be permitted (no. 39 and following), he dissolves it with the greatest prudence and finally declares that age alone should in no way be an obstacle, since children too have steadfastly shed their blood for Christ (chapter 8, no. 42 and following), and since Christ himself wished children to have free access to him. Finally, even at the very beginnings of the Church, a multitude—that is, people of every sex and age—followed him.

Then, as though the subject had naturally arisen, he explains when and where Christ should be sought by virgins, using certain verses from the *Song of Songs* (no. 45). After turning to the widow whom he says he had treated elsewhere, namely in the Book *On Widows* (no. 46), he warns, for the sake of reconciliation, that sluggish teachers and those too lax should be avoided (nos. 47 and 50). Continuing his exposition of the *Song of Songs* (nos. 48 and following), he teaches what the soul must do so that it may seek Christ and itself be sought by Christ (chapters 9 and following), and also what it must do to receive and retain him within.

After skillfully revealing the virtues to be desired and the vices to be avoided there (chapter 15 and following), he offers a method for restraining the four movements of the soul which Plato imitated from Ezekiel’s image of the flying chariot. He promises that by this way the soul will certainly arrive at Christ. When it had been publicly read in the Gospel, on the same day that was sacred to the chief Apostles, that Christ had entered Peter’s boat and urged him to let down the nets, he makes clear what it means to put out into the deep and what it means for the Apostles to labor (chapter 19, no. 131 and following). Finally, after predicting that his fishing would prosper through the presence of the Bishop of Bologna, and exhorting virgins and widows alike to let themselves be enclosed in the apostolic nets (chapter 20, no. 129), he crowns the work with a commendation of Peter and Paul, to whom he adds John (no. 130 and following).

What has been said thus far clearly demonstrates that this composition ought to be placed after the Book *On Widows* and detached from the Books *On Virgins*. But what title should be assigned to it is not immediately clear. It appears that a leaf was removed from the autograph manuscript, thereby both causing the work to be joined incorrectly and allowing later scribes to prefix whatever title each preferred. Hence those who wished to place the same treatise immediately after the three Books *On Virgins* called it the Fourth Book *On Virgins*; those who preferred to put it after the Book *On Widows* prefixed the title Second Book *On Widows*.

But Jerome attributes only one book *On Widows* to Ambrose (Letter 50, *Apology Against Jovinian*), and this work discusses widows only briefly and incidentally in a few passages; therefore that title cannot be imposed upon it. Nor is it any more permissible to call it the Fourth Book *On Virgins*. Jerome himself recognizes only three Ambrosian books under that title (*ibid.*, *Apology*, page 392, column 2), and Ambrose himself testifies that he composed only three (Book *On Widows*, chapter 1, no. 1).

In this uncertainty, nothing seemed better to us than to title it *On Virginity*, judging that this would both sufficiently distinguish it from the other treatises on the same subject and indicate the nature of its argument. Nor would this depart greatly from the manuscripts, since most of them end with the words: “Here ends Saint Ambrose’s *On Virginity*”; for when those same manuscripts add “Fourth Book,” they add it on their own authority.

It is also clear, both from the form of the language itself (chapter 5, no. 24) and from the citations of Scripture that had been read publicly in the Church (chapter 3, no. 14, and chapter 19, no. 21), that this book was delivered as a sermon. Nevertheless, we do not think that it was completed in one single address, since, besides the sermon delivered on the feast of the Apostles (chapter 19, no. 124), namely on the third day before the Kalends of July, at least one other sermon can be distinctly recognized. It also seems no less certain that this book is later than the work *On Widows* and was therefore composed, in all probability, in the year 378, specifically after the month of June had ended.

## SAINT AMBROSE, BISHOP OF MILAN, ONE BOOK ON VIRGINITY

[Note: Written around the year 378.]

## CHAPTER I

Having narrated historically the judgment of Solomon pronounced between two women, he adds that this very event was committed to writing so that we may know that even the most hidden things can be brought to light. Then, turning to its mystical meaning, he explains the false mother as temptation, the true mother as faith, and the sword as the word of God. Finally, he prepares the reader for the history of Jephthah.

### 1

The famous judgment of Solomon among the ancients is said to have taken place when he was appealed to by two women who were in dispute (1 Kings 3:16 and following). One of them, having turned over in sleep and crushed her own infant, claimed the other woman’s child; the other, conscious of true love and innocent of guilt, claimed her son by rightful ownership. Since both persisted in their claims, the judge’s mind was at a loss; for Solomon could not penetrate the inner secret, since the mind of each petitioner was more hidden than the facts before him. When their encounter had reached an ambiguous outcome, he ordered a sword to be brought out and commanded the servants to pretend that they were performing a grim duty. He ordered the infant to be divided, so that each woman might receive one part. On hearing this, the woman who was claiming another’s child not only consented but demanded that the little one be divided, unmoved by any maternal feeling. [Note: Thus all manuscripts and the Amerbach, Erasmus, and Gill editions in the body of the text; Erasmus and Gill in the margin, and the Roman edition in the text, read “moved by maternal feeling.”]

But the woman who knew that the infant was hers, fearing not to be defeated but to be deprived of her child, and now concerned not for her own comfort but for the safety of her offspring, began to beg that the boy be handed over alive to the other woman rather than returned to his true mother cut into pieces. Therefore Solomon, who was questioning the hidden affection not with divine majesty but by human reasoning, judged that the child should rather be given to the woman whose own grief had betrayed her as the true mother. But the other, whom compassion for the dying child did not move, he pronounced excluded from nature, since he saw her excluded from affection. [Note: Several manuscripts read “not with divine majesty.” This is not unsuitable if it is referred to the verb “questioned”; the meaning would then be “he did not consult God, as the prophets commonly do.”]

### 2

The truth, then, was not concealed; yet it wavered through the pretence of the other woman. For a long time the good mother too remained caught in an uncertain outcome, while the judgment was being tested by an uncertain result. Although these things took place figuratively in former times, they were nevertheless written for our correction, so that we may understand that everything fictitious can be exposed and everything contrived can be revealed. [Note: All editions and a few manuscripts read “everything that was done”; the other manuscripts more correctly read “everything that was fabricated,” so that the reference is to the feigned mother.]

### 3

These two women, then—for our purpose here is not to discuss women—these two, I say, are faith and temptation. Temptation, I say, is the universal author of error from the beginning. After losing its offspring through the carnal fault of its conduct and through the sleep of the mind, it tries to take away the fruit of another’s offspring. Thus, while temptation argues, faith wavers, until the sword of Christ distinguishes the hidden affections.

What is this sword of Christ? The one of which it is written: “I have come to bring a sword upon the earth” (Matthew 10:34). It is the sword of which it is written: “And your own soul a sword shall pierce” (Luke 2:35). But learn what this sword, this weapon, is: “The word,” he says, “is sharp and powerful, and more penetrating than every very sharp sword, piercing even to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow” (Hebrews 4:12). The word of God is a good sword—a good sword because it searches heart and kidneys, distinguishes falsehood from truth, and does not destroy those whose soul it has pierced, but preserves them.

## CHAPTER II

The vow made by Jephthah during battle, his return after gaining victory, and the meeting with his daughter are recounted. Although the act itself is to be condemned, faith in fulfilling the vow is not to be disapproved. The question is discussed why God, having forbidden Abraham’s sacrifice, did not prevent Jephthah’s act of homicide.

### 4

Let this much be said about the Book of Kings: it has been taken up because of the subject, reviewed as history, appropriated to conscience, and drawn forth from faith. Now let us examine the sequence of the reading taken from the Book of Judges. For this parricide was not to be heard with idle ears. Let us therefore repeat the history.

### 5

Jephthah was a judge of the Jews. Troubled by the uncertain outcome of the war and fearing the uncertainty of battle, he made the following vow (Judges 11:30–31): if he defeated his adversaries, he would sacrifice to God, the author of his victories, whatever first met him at the threshold of his house. [Note: Some manuscripts read: “whatever met him at the doorway of his house.”]

Having therefore prevailed in battle and routed the enemy, he returned home. At the very entrance his daughter, mindful of her affection but unaware of the offering, came out to meet him. But the father immediately remembered and, reminded of his own pledge, groaned at the prospect of fulfilling his vow.

“Alas for me, my daughter,” he said, “you have destroyed me; for I have opened my mouth concerning you to the Lord.”

Then she replied: “Father, if you have opened your mouth concerning me to the Lord, do to me as the word that came from your mouth requires” (ibid., 35 and following).

She asked only for a delay of two months, until she might climb the mountain and mourn her virginity. When the two months had passed, she returned to her father. He fulfilled his vow. These are the words we must use, since divine Scripture did not disclose the outcome of the matter but avoided mention of the killing. [Note: Several manuscripts read: “since Scripture, which avoids mentioning parricide, had not disclosed the outcome of the matter.”]

### 6

What, then? Do we approve this? Certainly not. Yet although I do not approve of the killing, I observe the fear and dread of violating the pledge. Finally, Abraham was told: “Now I know that you love the Lord your God, because you have not spared your only son” (Genesis 22:12). You therefore have an indication teaching that a promise must not rashly be violated. Yet the same reading asserts that God does not approve of homicide, since a sheep was substituted for the son (ibid., 13), so that the animal rather than the son might be struck.

### 7

Jephthah therefore had an example that he ought to have followed, because the Lord takes no delight in human blood. In one oracle given to Abraham he taught that the safety of children must be placed after religious obedience: children should be offered to God by their parents, but they should not be slaughtered. Certainly, if the daughter was so anxious about her father’s vow, why did the father not hesitate over the killing of his daughter? And if she guarded against a falsehood on her father’s part, why did he not guard against his daughter’s destruction?

### 8

Someone may say: Why did God not permit the killing to take place there, yet allow it to be fulfilled here? Is God a respecter of persons? No, but he is a respecter of merits and virtues. While the issue was still uncertain, an oracle ought to have shown what should be done both in the present case and in the example to follow. But once the example had already gone before, he did not judge an oracle necessary, since the form of the earlier act had shown what ought to be done.

### 9

Or perhaps, because the forms of merit were not the same, the forms of action were not the same either. The father grieved; the daughter wept. Both doubted God’s mercy. Abraham did not grieve, nor did he consult parental affection. When he heard the divine oracle, he did not delay the sacrifice but hastened to obey. Isaac did not doubt (ibid., 3 and following) when he followed his father with unequal steps; he did not weep when he was bound; he did not ask for delay when he was offered. Therefore mercy is more abundant where faith is more prompt. And rightly did he not weep at his father’s deed, because he was the laughter of his mother (Genesis 21:6). In place of this joyful devotion, a ram was commanded to be sacrificed for him, because he himself had not delayed to be sacrificed—uncertain neither of God’s mercy nor of his own devotion.

No one, therefore, was found to recall the father’s bloodstained affection, because the fulfillment of the promised offering was wholly consistent with the obligation of the vow. [Note: All editions read: “because every promised offering corresponded to the duty.” Many manuscripts read: “because the duty corresponded to everyone’s promised offering.” Others, more suitably, read: “because the duty of every promised offering corresponded,” where *officium* means the fulfillment or execution of the promise.]

## CHAPTER III

The holy man wonders that, although no one prevented Jephthah’s act of homicide, some people tried to prevent the fulfillment of a vow of virginity, and even accused him because he forbade a consecrated virgin to marry. He proves that this was part of his duty not only by the example of the Baptist and the commands of Scripture, but also by the institutions of the pagans themselves. Finally, he praises virginity because virgins were the first to see Christ risen.

### 10

A sacrifice of blood is offered, and no one resists; a sacrifice of chastity is offered, and someone is found to forbid it. [Note: The negation is absent before the words “and someone is found to envy” in all editions, where it was read incorrectly; we have removed it on the authority of all the manuscripts. At this point, too, some manuscripts differ from the others: where the text reads “the father vowed his daughter’s integrity,” they read “the daughter knew her integrity.”]

The father promised homicide, and the promise is fulfilled; the father vowed his daughter’s integrity, and the devotion of so pious an offering is begrudged. There the daughter, grieving, offered her blood for her country’s pledge; here so pious a promise is fulfilled neither by hereditary obligation nor by the will of the person herself.

11. In this matter we too are called to account. For what, exactly? Because we have prohibited illicit marriages? Then let them call John the Baptist to account for the same offense. And if there is nothing else in us that can perhaps be approved, let this alone be condemned in us which was approved in the prophet. Or have we brought forward an author of whom we ought to be ashamed? Recall what other cause he had for martyrdom. Certainly this was the cause of his suffering: “It is not lawful for you to have her as your wife” (Matt. XIV, 4). If this was said concerning a man’s wife, how much more concerning a consecrated virgin! If it was said to a king, how much more must it be said to private persons! Let us therefore give thanks to the divinity that there is no Herod here—and would that there were no Herodias either!

217

12. Was it therefore not lawful to speak in defense of virginity? And why is it written: “Judge the orphan, and justify the widow” (Isa. I, 17)? And why is it written: “Father of orphans and judge of widows” (Ps. LXVII, 6)? Shall we then abandon those devoted to chastity and integrity, or even condemn them?

[Col. 0269B] [Note: Most manuscripts read: “Fathers of orphans and judges of widows.”]

13. Yet among the Gentiles themselves virginity is customarily held venerable amid altars and hearths; and although among them there is no piety arising from merit, no integrity of mind, nevertheless bodily virginity is praised. Will no one therefore prevent virgins from profane ceremonies, while virginity is driven away from the Church of God? There they are compelled to do what they are not taught; here what may not go untaught is forbidden? There they are recalled from marriage by rewards; here they will be forced into marriage by injuries? [Note: Gellius, Book I, chapter 12: “A Vestal virgin seems to be called captured because, having been taken by the hand of the chief pontiff from the father under whose authority she is, she is led away as though captured in war.” For more about the Vestals, see Book . . . . . , On Virgins, chapter 4, no. 15.] There violence is used so that they may be taken; here violence will be used so that they may not make their profession? And can the priests be so patient that the sacrifice of integrity is not vindicated—even by offering death, if that is necessary? [Col. 0269C]

14. Consider that virgins were deemed worthy to see the Lord’s resurrection before the apostles. Certainly today’s reading, which has just been read, taught this; for when the body of our Lord Jesus Christ had been placed in a new tomb, as John said (John XIX, 41–42), and Joseph had placed the Lord’s body in his own tomb, according to the Gospel of Matthew, as it stands in that book (Matt. XXVII, 25 and following), the virgins were watching. Matthew rightly also called the tomb new, lest anyone believe that another person had risen from an old tomb. Rightly also, in the spiritual sense, he was placed in the tomb of the righteous, because Christ rises from the dead in the new disposition of the righteous. Rightly, too, in the literal sense, it was another’s tomb, because the Lord did not seek his own tomb. Let those who are under the law of death have a tomb; the victor over death had no tomb of his own. For he who returned bearing trophies from death did not desire death’s sepulcher. Thus Mary saw the Lord’s resurrection: she saw it first, and believed. Mary Magdalene also saw it, [Note: Many manuscripts read “although she was still wavering”; one manuscript has “although she was still noting this”; another has “although she was still changing”; the remainder, together with the editions, have the reading more aptly found in the text. It will not be useless to compare what is said here about the virgins as witnesses of the Lord’s resurrection with what is found in Book VI of the Exposition of the Gospel according to Luke, p. 1387, no. 14, and also to consult the observation appended to that passage. Meanwhile, observe either that Ambrose has suffered a lapse of memory when, contrary to the explicit testimony of Mark XVI, 9, he affirms that Christ appeared to Magdalene only in the second place; or that we must subscribe to the pious opinion of those who, as Estius says, wish the Mother of God to be signified here by “Mary.” But what if the holy Doctor is hinting here that there were two Magdalenes? Compare this with the final chapter of the work on Luke and resolve the difficulty.] although she was still wavering.

## CHAPTER IV

Taking occasion from the doubting Magdalene, he encourages virgins to faith; and he most delightfully works through, in a spiritual sense, what is read in the Evangelist John concerning Christ’s conversation with her.

15. At this point take careful note of a considerable question, [Col. 0270B] lest you, virgins, should doubt the Lord’s resurrection. Observe that merit is produced not by bodily virginity alone, but also by integrity of mind. In fact, Mary Magdalene is forbidden to touch the Lord [Note: Several manuscripts add: “because she was doubting.”] because she was wavering [218] in faith concerning the resurrection. It is therefore she who touches Christ who touches him by faith.

16. “Mary, however, stood outside at the tomb, weeping” (John XX, 11). [Note: Most manuscripts read: “She who is outside is weeping”; for “she who is inside,” and so forth. A little later they again read “she wept”; “she who did not believe thought that he had been taken away by trickery,” and so forth.] She who is outside weeps; for she who is inside does not know how to weep. She weeps because she does not see Christ’s body, and thinks it has perished because she herself does not see it. Thus Mary is outside—but not Peter, not John. They ran in and entered; and therefore they did not weep, but departed rejoicing. She who did not enter wept, did not believe, thought that he had been taken away by trickery, and, even when she saw the angels, did not think that she ought to believe. And therefore the angels say to her: “Woman, why are you weeping? Whom are you seeking?” (ibid., 13). The angels say this, and afterward the Lord repeated it in the same words, so that you may know that the angels’ words are the Lord’s commands.

17. Finally, as I said, the Lord also repeated the same words, saying: “Woman, why are you weeping? Whom are you seeking?” She who did not believe is a woman; for he who believes rises into a perfect man, into the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ (Eph. IV, 13). “Woman,” he says: this is not an insult concerning sex, but concerning hesitation. And rightly “woman,” [Note: Several manuscripts read: “she who was being reproached.” This is not inappropriate, since it has the same meaning as “was being rebuked,” which is suitably placed after the words “this is an insult.” Refer also to Book X on Luke, no. 161.] since she was wavering, because the virgin had already believed. “Why are you weeping?” That is: You yourself are the cause of your weeping; you yourself are the author of your tears, since you are an unbeliever in Christ. You weep because you do not see Christ: believe, and you will see him. [Col. 0271A] Christ is present and is never absent from those who seek him. “Why are you weeping?” That is, tears are not needed, but ready faith worthy of God. Do not think about mortal things, and you will not weep; do not think about things that perish, and you will be unable to have cause for weeping. Why do you weep over what causes others to rejoice?

18. “Whom are you seeking?” That is: Do you not see that Christ is present? Do you not see that Christ is the power of God, that Christ is the wisdom of God, that Christ is holiness, that Christ is chastity, that Christ is integrity, that Christ was born of a virgin, that Christ is from the Father, with the Father, and always in the Father, born, not made, and not degenerate, [Note: Thus several manuscripts; others, together with all the editions, omit the word “beloved.”] but always beloved, true God from true God?

19. “They have taken the Lord from the tomb,” she says, “and I do not know where they have placed him” (John XX, 15). You are mistaken, woman, in thinking that others have taken Christ from the tomb and that he was not raised by his own power. But no one has taken away the power of God; no one has taken away the wisdom of God; no one has taken away venerable chastity. Christ is not taken from the tomb of the righteous, nor from the secret place of his virgin or the hidden chamber of a devout mind; and if some wish to take him away, they cannot.

20. Then the Lord said to her: [Note: This text is found neither in the Greek manuscripts of the Evangelist nor in any Latin manuscripts. It is also referred to in Book X on Luke, no. 161.] “Mary, look toward me” (ibid., 16). When she does not believe, she is “woman”; when she begins to turn, she is called Mary—that is, she receives the name of her who gives birth to Christ; for there is a soul that spiritually gives birth to Christ. [219] “Look,” he says, “toward me.” Whoever looks toward Christ is corrected; but he errs who does not see Christ.

[Col. 0271C] 21. And so, having turned, she looked and said: “Rabbi,” which means “teacher.” Whoever looks turns; whoever turns looks more fully; whoever sees makes progress. And therefore she calls him “teacher” whom she believed to be dead; she addresses him whom she thought she had lost.

22. “Do not touch me,” he says (ibid., 17)—that is, although these are the beginnings of correction, the wavering disposition nevertheless does not touch Christ. “Do not touch me,” he says; that is, do not touch the power of God, the wisdom of God, revered integrity, honorable chastity.

23. “But go to my brothers.” What else does this mean than: “Now stop weeping outside”? Go to the elect and the most observant priests, and say to them: “I am ascending to my Father and your Father, my God and your God.” What else does this mean than: “Do not raise this question, woman”? Certainly, ask those who are more perfect; they will tell you what distinction there is between “my Father” and “your Father.” For he who is my Father according to divine generation is your Father according to adoption. By saying “my Father,” the Son of God separates himself from creatures; by saying “your Father,” he designates the grace of spiritual adoption. Likewise, by saying “my God,” he reveals the mystery of his Incarnation, so that he calls him whom he has naturally as Father “God” because of the sacrament of the body he assumed; and when he says “your God,” he shows the progress of his working in us.

## CHAPTER V

He returns from his digression to his own defense, and not only acknowledges what has been charged against him but presses it further, openly professing that he wishes even to recall those who intend to marry to the pursuit of virginity.

24. And indeed God became our God from the time Christ suffered, when, to omit other matters, virgins were ready to die in order to preserve their integrity. I speak neither of a cause nor of a person; for where the Lord’s grace is, there the Lord’s peace ought to be. Nor do I publicly accuse anyone; I come to defend myself. [Note: Some manuscripts read: “I come defended”; others: “I find myself defended.”] For we have been accused, and, unless I am mistaken, most of our accusers are among you. I prefer to rebuke their sentiments rather than expose their persons. The odium of the charge is this: that I recommend chastity. Whoever does not gladly receive this exposes himself.

25. “You teach virginity,” he says, “and persuade very many.” [Note: Four manuscripts read: “Would that I were not overcome.”] Would that I were convicted! Would that the effect of so great a charge were proved! I would not fear the odium if I recognized its effectiveness. And would that you accused me by examples rather than struck me with words! But I fear that I may seem to have had false advocates assigned to me, who commend me by the praises of others. [Note: Some manuscripts read “preachers,” which, although not altogether without sense, is less elegant. A “false advocate” is one who secretly and deceptively praises and defends the person whom he is believed to be censuring and accusing. Cicero uses this expression in Philippic II, not far from the beginning; Ambrose seems to have imitated him here.]

26. “You prevent girls initiated into the sacred mysteries and consecrated to integrity from marrying.” [220] Would that I could recall those intending to marry! Would that I could exchange the bridal veil for the devout veil of integrity! Does it seem unworthy that consecrated virgins should not be led away from the most sacred altars to marriage? And if they are permitted to choose a bridegroom, [Note: We have already noted in the letter to Sisinius that we shall say something about this freedom to choose a bridegroom.] are they not permitted to prefer God? Thus the nature of the deed is changed in my case, so that what has always belonged to the grace of priests—sowing the seeds of integrity and calling forth the pursuit of virginity—becomes a reproach to me.

## CHAPTER VI

To call people to virginity is neither shameful, nor new, nor useless. Having briefly dealt with the first point in the opening chapter, he demonstrates that the second—that it is not new—is proved by Christ’s teaching, the judgment of the apostles, and the example of children. Then, while warning that marriages are not to be condemned, he explains their many serious difficulties and wisely advises that no one disparage either condition.

[Col. 0273A] 27. For I ask whether this is censured as something shameful, or as something new, or as something useless. If as something shameful, then the vows of all are shameful, and the life of angels is shameful, which the grace of the resurrection imitates; for “those who neither marry nor are given in marriage will be like the angels in heaven” (Matt. XXII, 30). Whoever censures this, therefore, condemns the vows of the resurrection. Accordingly, what has been established for human beings as a reward cannot appear shameful; nor can the character of something displease whose truth lies both in its fruit and in its vow.

[Col. 0273B] 28. But suppose it is not shameful: is it then new? We rightly condemn everything new that Christ did not teach, because Christ is the way for the faithful. If, therefore, Christ did not teach what we teach, we too judge it detestable. Let us examine, then, whether Christ taught integrity or thought it ought to be rejected: “There are eunuchs,” he says, “who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XIX, 12). There is therefore a splendid campaign that serves the kingdom of heaven. Thus even then the Lord taught that the pursuits of chastity ought to remain undefiled.

29. And so, seeing that it surpasses all else, the apostles say: “If such is the case of a man with his wife, it is not expedient to marry” (ibid., 10). By this statement they judged the burdens of the marital bond to be weightier and preferred the grace of true integrity. But the Lord, knowing that integrity was to be proclaimed to all but imitated by few, says: “Not all receive this word, but those to whom it is given” (ibid., 11). That is, integrity is not common to the many or an ordinary possession; it is not granted because of weakness, but permitted because of virtue. Finally, after saying, “There are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven” (ibid., 12), to show that this belongs to no ordinary virtue, he says: “Let the one who is able to receive it receive it.”

30. And therefore, after this saying, children are brought forward to be blessed, so that, free from corruption, they may preserve the gift of integrity in an unstained age. [221] For the kingdom of heaven belongs to those who have returned to childlike chastity, as though to the nature of infants, through ignorance of corruption. Virginity is therefore also approved by the heavenly voice and is to be sought according to the Lord’s commands.

31. At this point let us imitate the teaching of the divine voice. For after mentioning above that marriage was not to be dissolved except on account of fornication, he then connected to it the grace and gift of integrity (ibid., 9), to teach that marriages are not to be condemned but approved, while nevertheless the pursuit of integrity is to be preferred to marriage itself. Who is so opposed to truth as to condemn marriage? But who is so alien to reason as not to feel the burdens of wedlock? “The unmarried woman and the virgin,” indeed, “think about the things of the Lord, so that she may be holy in body and spirit. But the married woman thinks about the things of the world, how she may please her husband” (I Cor. VII, 34).

32. In addition to these difficulties, although she does not sin by marrying, she will nevertheless have the affliction proper to this fleshly condition: for the labors of childbirth are severe, as is the burden of bearing and educating children. He previously prescribed that no one should be turned away from such injuries; for many, placed amid the pains of childbirth, say that they renounce marriage, and many others, unable to bear the burdens of matrimony, turn their affection away from their wives. [Note: Some manuscripts read: “alienated from the marital relationship,” and so forth.] And therefore the Apostle first said: “Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek release” (ibid., 27). And rightly he says “bound”; for a husband and wife are joined to one another by a certain bond of affection, and are mutually fastened by certain reins of love.

33. The bonds of marriage are therefore good, but still bonds; marriage is good, but nevertheless drawn from a yoke, and from the yoke of the world, so that one wishes to please a husband rather than God. The wounds of charity are good as well, and are to be preferred to kisses: “The wounds of a friend are more useful than the voluntary kisses of an enemy” (Prov. XXVII, 6). Peter wounds (Matt. XXVI, 51), while Judas kisses (ibid., 49); kisses condemn the former, while a wound corrects the latter. Through the kisses of the one, the poisons of betrayal are poured out; through the tears of the other, guilt is washed away. Thus, to show that the prophetic utterance speaks of the good wounds of charity, the Church says in the Song of Songs: “For I am wounded by charity” (Song II, 5).

34. Let no one, therefore—whether one who has chosen marriage—criticize integrity, or whether one who pursues integrity—condemn marriage. The Church long ago condemned the interpreters who opposed this judgment, namely those who dared to dissolve the conjugal bond. For hear what the holy Church says: “Come, my brother, let us go out into the field; let us rest in the villages; let us rise early and go into the vineyards; let us see whether the vine has blossomed” (Song VII, 11–12). [Note: Only the Roman edition reads: “Many fields bear fruit.”] The field has many fruits, but that one is better which overflows with both fruits and flowers. The field of the Church is therefore fertile with varied abundance. Here you may see the shoots of virginity blooming in flower; there, as in forested fields, widowhood flourishing in dignity; elsewhere, like a rich crop of marriage, filling the Church’s [222] granaries with the harvest of the world; and, like a married vineyard, filling the winepresses of the Lord Jesus with its produce, in which the fruit of faithful marriage abounds.

## CHAPTER VII

Having undertaken the third point—namely, that virginity is not useless—he denies that it brings any harm to the commonwealth; on the contrary, he teaches that wherever this condition flourishes most, there the population of citizens is most abundant. Even if the opposite were true, however, it would still not make virginity reprehensible, since this is not censured in wives who live chastely. After demonstrating the emptiness of the objection that marriage is thereby made more difficult for the young, he responds to those who contend that virgins should receive the veil only later, explaining that the bishop’s prudence is required; but he proves by examples of martyrs and of children coming to Christ that age alone is not to be considered.

[Col. 0275A] 35. The pursuit of integrity is therefore neither shameful nor new. Let us see whether it may perhaps be judged useless; for I have heard some say that the world has perished, the human race has failed, and marriages have been weakened. I ask: who has sought a wife and not found one? [Col. 0275B] When have wars been fought for a virgin? Who has ever been killed for a virgin? But from marriages arise the deeds by which a wife’s adulterer is killed and a ravisher is attacked in battle. [Note: Under the Julian law on the punishment of adultery, a father was permitted to kill his daughter and any adulterer of hers if they were caught in the offense, wherever it occurred. A husband had the same right, but subject to a precise definition of the persons and places involved. As for battles provoked against the ravisher of another man’s wife, who does not know the famous war in which Europe and Asia clashed for ten whole years, and which could be ended only by the destruction of the Trojan kingdom and the entire people? It was undertaken for no other reason than Helen, carried off by Paris. Besides Homer, see the historians Dictys of Crete and Dares the Phrygian, although in many respects they are no less fabulous than Homer himself.] These things have always harmed the commonwealth. No one has been condemned for a sacred virgin, because chastity is not restrained by punishment but increased by religion and preserved by faith.

36. If anyone therefore thinks that the consecration of virgins diminishes the human race, let him consider that where there are few virgins, there are also fewer human beings; where the pursuit of virginity is more frequent, there too the number of human beings is greater. [Note: The Codex Regius and the Codex Fiscianus read: “Say how many the Alexandrian Church consecrates.”] Learn how many the Alexandrian Church, and how many the Church of the entire East and of Africa, customarily consecrate each year. Fewer human beings are born here than virgins are consecrated there. From the very practice of the whole world, therefore, virginity is judged not useless, especially since salvation came through a virgin, destined to make the Roman world fruitful.

37. If anyone forbids this, let him also forbid chaste wives to live as such, since incontinent women can give birth more frequently. Let no woman remain faithful to a husband who is traveling, lest she harm the future offspring and lose the season of more frequent childbirth.

38. “But the way to obtain marriage becomes more difficult for young men.” What if it has perhaps become easier? For I ask to have some discussion with those who hold the view that virginity should be prevented. We must therefore examine who these people are: whether they are men who have wives or men who do not. If they have wives, they need not be afraid; their wives can no longer be virgins. If they do not have wives, let them not do themselves an injustice by having hoped for marriage only with a woman who was not going to marry. Or perhaps fathers, anxious about their daughters’ marriages, are distressed when virgins are consecrated? They too have no cause for fear, if they follow the advice. Among the few, their daughters will be chosen more quickly.

39. Many also say that virgins should receive the veil at a more mature age. I do not deny that priestly caution is required, so that a girl is not veiled rashly. Let the priest certainly consider her age—but the age of her faith and modesty. Let him consider the maturity of her reserve; let him examine the gray hairs of her seriousness, the old age of her conduct, the years of her chastity, and the dispositions of her purity; then also whether she has the safe guardianship of her mother and the sober attentiveness of her companions. If these things are present, the virgin is not lacking in advanced age; if they are absent, let the girl be delayed because of her character, though she may be younger in years.

40. It is not therefore a more flourishing age that is rejected, but the mind that is examined. Certainly it was not old age but virtue that proved Thecla. And why should I add more, when every age is suitable for God and perfect in Christ? Finally, we do not call virtue an appendage of age, [Note: The Fiscian manuscripts read: “We speak of the virtue of the mind.”] but age an appendage of virtue. Nor should you be surprised at a profession among adolescents, when you read of suffering among little children; for it is written: “Out of the mouth of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise” (Ps. VIII, 3). Do we doubt whether adolescence can follow in continence the one whom infancy confesses even unto death? And do we regard it as incredible [Note: Many manuscripts read: “if noble girls”; others, more suitably, together with the editions, have “marriageable girls.” Since virgins are commonly thought mature for a husband at twelve years of age, this may raise some difficulty, since the holy Bishop was satisfied with so tender an age. Not long afterward, the Third Council of Carthage, canon 4, assigned twenty full years for the consecration of virgins; Leo I in the ancient Pontifical and the emperor Majorian, Constitution 8, later extended this to forty years. Nevertheless, one must remember that there were formerly two kinds of consecration, clearly distinguished by Innocent I, whom we cited in the Preface to the work On Virgins; by Leo I in his letter to Rusticus of Narbonne; and by Gelasius in his letter to the bishops of Lucania—namely, solemn and private. Thus there is no contradiction if the canon of Carthage and the constitutions of Leo and Majorian are understood of the former, while this passage of Ambrose and another in Jerome’s letter to Marcella concerning the consecration of Asella at only twelve years of age are understood of the latter. Basil’s testimony might also be added: in Epistle, Canon 18, he requires no more than sixteen or seventeen years for the profession of virginity. If you insist that Ambrose’s words must also be understood of solemn consecration, we shall not strongly object, since it has always been within the Church’s power to change her discipline for just reasons and according to the needs of the times. Meanwhile, marvel that those very objections against virginity which Ambrose refuted so wisely and forcefully in this work have been revived in our own time by heretics,] if marriageable girls follow Christ to the kingdom, whom even children followed in the desert; as we read that four thousand men were satisfied with five loaves, “apart from,” he says, “the children and women” (Matt. XIV, 21).

41. Do not therefore keep infants away from Christ, since they too suffered martyrdom for Christ’s name: “For to such belongs the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XIX, 14). The Lord calls them, and you forbid them? For the Lord himself says of them: “Let them come to me.” Do not keep young girls away, concerning whom it is written: “Therefore the young women loved you” (Song I, 2), and “They brought you into the house of their mother” (Song VIII, 2). Finally, do not separate even little children from Christ’s charity, since they confessed him with prophetic exultation while they were still enclosed in their mother’s womb (Luke I, 41).

224

## CHAPTER VIII

Above he taught that every age is suitable for seeking Christ; here he shows that no place is unsuitable for this purpose. Why are the sick brought to Christ when the sun is setting, while he is sought only after day has dawned? He also gives instruction about avoiding ostentation. He exhorts them to follow Christ by day, and declares that he is found neither in the forum nor in the streets, where the Bride is said to be wounded and stripped.

42. At the very beginnings of the Church the crowds sought him. Why? Because, it says, “laying his hands on them, he healed them” (Luke IV, 40). Neither time nor place is sought for healing. For medicine must be neglected in no place and at no time. Mary is blessed by the angel inside a house (Luke I, 28); David is anointed as a prophet inside a house (I Kings XVI, 3). Jesus heals everywhere, everywhere he makes whole: on the road, in the house, in the desert. On the road the woman who touched his fringe is healed (Matt. IX, 20); in the ruler of the synagogue’s house his daughter is raised (Mark V, 41); in the desert the crowd is healed. Thus you have it: “When the sun had set, all who had the sick with various diseases brought them to him. And he laid his hands on each one of them and healed them” (Luke IV, 40). He healed, therefore, both in the desert and after the sun had set, and he healed by laying on his hands, so that he might show himself both God and man. It was therefore not without reason that, when day had dawned, the crowds sought him.

43. I see the order of events. At sunset the sick are brought to Christ; when day has come, the crowds seek him. For when is Christ sought except by day? Whoever walks in the light does not depart from Christ. Thus night still had the groans of the sick, while day already had the faith of the people and the joy of those who had been healed, so that what is written might be fulfilled: “At evening weeping will remain, and in the morning joy” (Ps. XXIX, 6). For what greater grace could the crowds have than to follow Christ even into the desert?

44. In this he teaches that ostentation must be far from the perfect person; for he avoided not an abundance of people to be healed but ostentation concerning his works. Therefore, if we desire to be saved, or if we already deserve healing, let us follow Christ, who flees bodily pleasures as though amid the arid and barren soil of this life, [Note: Thus all editions and several manuscripts; some others read: “and, fasting alone in a certain thirst, fleeing the delicacies of the body”; one has: “and, fasting alone, since he is in bodily appetite”; another: “and, fasting alone, by which we now flee the wantonness of the body.” Nothing sound is found in the remainder.] with a certain bodily thirst.

45. Let us follow him by day. There is a day of the Church, which Abraham saw and rejoiced (John VIII, 56). Let us therefore follow Christ by day; he is not found in the nights. “In my bed,” she says, “by night I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought him and did not find him; I called him, and he did not answer me” (Song III, 1). [225]

46. Christ is not found in the forum or in the streets. Indeed, even she could not find him in the forum and in the streets who said: “I will rise; I will go around the city, through the forum and the streets, and seek him whom my soul loves. I sought him, and did not find him; I called him, and he did not answer me” (ibid., 2). Let us therefore by no means seek Christ where we cannot find him. Christ is not a street-corner seller. Christ is peace, whereas in the forum there are quarrels; Christ is justice, whereas in the forum there is injustice; Christ is a worker, whereas in the forum there is idle leisure; Christ is charity, whereas in the forum there is slander; Christ is faith, whereas in the forum there are fraud and treachery; Christ is in the Church, whereas in the forum there are idols. And so that the widow whom I rebuked in another book [On Widows, chapter 9 and following] may recognize that I did not speak out of a desire to slander her, but to admonish her, and that I am not harsh but concerned; [Note: All editions and some manuscripts read: “may receive the grace of reconciliation.” The other manuscripts have the better reading: “may receive, as the grace of reconciliation, what I am about to say.” The meaning is the same as if he had written: “may accept what I am about to say as a testimony of reconciliation, namely, that in the Church . . . .”] let her accept this as a grace of reconciliation: in the Church the widow is justified; in the forum she is deceived. [Col. 0278C] Let us therefore flee the forum; let us flee the streets.

47. “Take prudence as your acquaintance,” so that it may guard you from a foreign and wicked woman . . . . “For through the window she looks out from her house upon the streets” (Prov. VII, 4 and following). Let us flee the streets. For it is not merely an injury not to have found the one whom you seek; often even to have sought where one ought not is a wound: to have sought in the houses of men who falsely assume the name of teachers; to have sought more boldly than modestly. [Note: Observe the danger faced by those who consult priests either deprived of ecclesiastical learning, corrupted by secular desires, or excessively indulgent because of some innate softness of character. Whoever seeks the way of salvation from such people is undoubtedly seeking where he ought not. We note incidentally that many manuscripts have a lacuna at this point, extending for nearly three complete columns.]

48. Let us therefore beware, following the example of that Church, lest the watchmen who go around the city find us: “The watchmen who go around the city found me; they struck me and wounded me, and the watchmen of the walls took away my mantle” (Song V, 7). [Col. 0278D] Not in herself, daughters; [Note: “Not in herself, I say, daughters”—the Roman edition too had removed this phrase, contrary to the evidence of all the other editions and manuscripts.] not, I say, in herself, daughters, but in us the Church is wounded. Let us therefore beware lest our fall become a wound to the Church, lest someone take away our mantle—that is, the covering of prudence, the emblem of patience, by which the ambition of softer clothing is stripped away: “Those who wear softer clothing are in the houses of kings” (Matt. XI, 8). But Christ gave us a mantle, with which he himself clothed his apostles and his body. Finally, when he commands you, if someone asks you for your tunic, to let him have your mantle as well (Matt. V, 40), this means that you should hand over the emblem of your philosophy and, as though with the covering of your prudence, clothe all around the person who previously was naked.

## CHAPTER IX

Christ is to be sought in the mountains of spices and in the desert. The fruitfulness of the desert is described, with an explanation of why Christ is called the flower and the lily; and the Church is said to desire to be brought into the house of wine and to have charity ordered within her.

49. Let us therefore seek Christ there, daughters, where the Church seeks him: in the mountains of good fragrance, which, by the heights of their exalted deeds, breathe forth the sweet fragrance of life in proportion to the summits of their merits. For he flees the streets, he flees gatherings and the tumult of the forum, in accordance with what is written: “Flee, my brother, and become like a gazelle or a fawn of a gazelle on the mountains of spices” (Song VIII, 14). Hated by serpentine vipers, fleeing dogs, and hostile to creeping snakes, he does not know how to dwell except in the heights of virtues; he does not know how to remain except among such daughters of the Church as can say: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God” (II Cor. II, 15)—but to some, a fragrance of death unto death, namely, to those who are perishing; to others, a fragrance of life unto life, namely, to those who breathe the fragrance of the Lord’s resurrection with living faith.

50. These are the mountains of spices that received the body of the Lord Jesus and bound it in linen cloths with spices (John XIX, 40). For all who have believed that Jesus died, was buried, and rose again have raised the lofty summit of true faith to the heights of virtues. Where, then, is Christ sought? Surely in the breast of the prudent priest.

51. And since this discourse is drawn from the desert, he himself also shows where Christ is to be sought, saying: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys. Like a lily among thorns” (Song 2:1–2). Behold another place where the Lord is accustomed to dwell—not, indeed, in one place only, but in several. “I,” he says, “am the flower of the field,” because he frequents the open simplicity of a pure mind. “And the lily of the valleys”: Christ is the flower of humility, not of luxury, pleasures, or wantonness, but the flower of simplicity, the flower of humility. “Like a lily among thorns.” Does not the good-smelling flower rise amid the hardships of labor and the contritions of souls, since God is pleased by a contrite heart?

52. This is the desert, daughters, which leads to the kingdom; this is also the desert that blossoms like a lily, according to what is written: “Rejoice, barren woman, and exult, desert, and let it blossom like a lily” (Isa. 35:1). In this desert, daughters, that good, fruit-bearing tree which produces good fruits (Matt. 7:17) begins to spread out the branches of its deeds and to raise up the summit of its divinity [Col. 0280A]. Beside it let the trees of our forest put forth fruit, for “as an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved among the midst of the sons” (Song 2:3). And seeing this, let the Church rejoice and be glad, saying: “In his shade I desired and sat, and his fruit was sweet in my throat.”

53. Seeing this, I say, and already rejoicing in the success of our faith, let the Church say: “Bring me into the wine-house and order love in me” (ibid., 4). Love cannot exist without faith; for there are, as it were, three guarantors of the Church: hope, faith, and love. When hope has gone before and faith has been founded, love is ordered and the Church is joined together.

227 CHAPTER X

That, in order that we may deserve Christ’s coming to us, the Holy Spirit ought to be invoked; for he does not always come, nor does he come to everyone, but to the soul that has so removed its earthly garment that afterward it does not put it on again. What the washing of the feet signifies; and what the Bride says, “How shall I put them on again?” Finally, it is demonstrated that the spiritual feet of the soul are to be understood here, and what the Bride means when she says, “How shall I soil them?”

54. You have therefore learned where to seek Christ; learn also how you may be worthy for him to seek you. Stir up the Holy Spirit, saying: “Rise, North Wind, and come, South Wind; blow upon my garden, and let my spices flow forth” (Song 4:16). “Let my beloved descend into his garden and eat the fruit of his fruit trees” (Song 5:1). The garden of the Word is the disposition of a soul in bloom, and in its fruit trees there is the fruit of virtue.

55. He comes, therefore; and whether you eat or drink, if you invoke Christ, he is present, saying: “Come, eat my bread and drink my wine” (Prov. 9:5). Even if you sleep, he knocks at the door. He comes, I say, frequently, and through the lattice extends his hand; but not always, nor to everyone, only to the soul that can say: “At night I have put off my tunic” (Song 5:3). For in this night of the world, you must first remove the garment of bodily life; the Lord stripped himself of flesh in order to triumph on your behalf over the dominions and powers of this world.

56. “How shall I put it on again?” (ibid.). See what the soul devoted to God says. It has so stripped itself of bodily actions and earthly ways that it does not know how, even if it wished, it could put them on again. “How shall I put it on again?” That is: with what shame, with what modesty, with what memory, finally? For the practice of the good has lost the habit of its former perversity.

57. “I have washed my feet; how shall I soil them?” (ibid.). You have learned in the Gospel that washing the feet is a distinguished mystery of humility, according to what is written: “If I, the Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, how much more ought you to wash one another’s feet?” (John 13:14). But this pertains to humility. As for the mystery itself, the one who wishes to have a share with Christ must wash his feet: “For if I do not wash your feet,” he says, “you will have no share with me” (ibid., 8). When this is said to Peter, what judgment is made concerning us?

[Col. 0281A] 58. Therefore, the one who has washed his feet does not need to wash them again; and so let him beware of soiling them. And rightly does holy Church say: “I have washed my feet.” She does not say, “How shall I wash them again?” but “How shall I soil them again?”—as though forgetful of the former stain, forgetful of contamination. Thus, in the bodily ministry, she teaches how we ought to wash away the spiritual trace of our actions. Therefore, when you have once washed your feet with the irrigation of the eternal fountain and cleansed them by the sacrament of the mystery, beware lest they again be soiled by the flood of bodily desire and by actions befouled with earthly filth.

[Note: [Col. 0281D] All editions, with a few manuscripts, read: “Beware lest again the mire of bodily desire [soil them], lest they be stained by the filth of muddy actions”; many other and better witnesses have the reading used in the text.]

59. These are the feet that David washed in the Spirit, teaching you how you may not soil them when he says: “Our feet were standing in your courts, Jerusalem” (Ps. 121:2). Here, certainly, understand not the feet of the body, but those of the soul. For how could an earthly human being have the feet of the body in heaven? Jerusalem, as Paul taught you (Heb. 12:22), is in heaven. And he likewise taught you how you can stand in heaven when he says: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20)—the citizenship of conduct, the citizenship of deeds, the citizenship of faith.

CHAPTER XI

That it is good to tremble and hasten at Christ’s approach; that he is accustomed to bring a reward not only when he has come but even before he comes, so that myrrh flows from the fingers and hand—that is, so that we may believe that Christ did not see corruption, since his name is poured-out ointment. This ointment, which always burned fragrantly with the Father, the Son poured out in time; but it was poured out among the Jews and gathered up by the Gentiles. Since it still flows daily, it must be carefully received, so that it may penetrate our whole soul.

60. Whoever lives in this way can say: “My beloved put his hand through the lattice, and my belly was troubled because of him; I rose to open to my brother” (Song 5:4). It is good that one’s inward parts should be troubled at the Lord’s coming. If Mary was troubled at the coming of an angel (Luke 1:29), how much more are we troubled at Christ’s coming! For when divine things flow in, the bodily disposition wanders away, and the use of the outward person grows old. You too, then, be troubled; you too, hasten. Those who hasten are commanded to eat the lamb (Exod. 12:11). Rise and open: Christ is at the door; he is knocking at the vestibule of your house. If you open, he will enter—and he will enter with the Father.

61. Nor does he leave a reward only when he has entered; he sends a reward ahead even before he enters. The soul is still troubled; it still feels along the walls of its house; it is still seeking the door where Christ is; it is still loosening the bond of flesh and the restraints of the body; Christ is still knocking outside. “But my hands,” he says, “dripped with myrrh, and my fingers were full of myrrh on the handles of the bolt” (Song 5:5).

What myrrh do the hands of the soul drip, except that which was offered by that righteous Nicodemus, a teacher in Israel (John 3:1 ff.)—the one who deserved first to hear the mystery of the washing, who brought a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred pounds, and placed it in the body of Jesus (John 19:39)? He brought, certainly, the perfect fragrance of faith.

62. This is the fragrance that the soul exhales when it begins to open to Christ, so that it may first receive the fragrance of the Lord’s burial and believe that his flesh did not see corruption and did not wither through any odor of death, but rose embalmed with the fragrance of that eternal and ever-green flower. For how could the flesh of him whose name is “poured-out ointment” (Song 1:2) wither? [Col. 0282B] He emptied himself so that he might breathe forth for you.

63. This ointment always existed, but it was with the Father; it was in the Father. It gave off its fragrance only to angels and archangels, as though within the vessel of heaven. The Father opened his mouth, saying: “Behold, I have appointed you as a covenant of my people, as a light of the nations, that you may be salvation to the end of the earth” (Isa. 49:6). The Son descended, and all things were filled with the new fragrance of the Word. “The heart of the Father poured forth the good Word” (Ps. 45:2); the Son gave forth fragrance, the Holy Spirit exhaled, and he spread himself through the hearts of all. “For the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit” (Rom. 5:5).

64. The Son of God himself, in the body as in a vessel, at first held back the fragrance, awaiting his appointed time, as he says: “The Lord gives me a learned tongue, that I may know when it is necessary to speak a word” (Isa. 50:4). The hour came [Note: [Col. 0281D] Most manuscripts read as in the text; some manuscripts and editions read: “He opened his mouth; the ointment went out.”], and he opened his mouth and poured out the ointment, when power went out from him.

65. This ointment was poured out upon the Jews and gathered up by the Gentiles; poured out in Judea, it gave its fragrance throughout all the lands. Mary was anointed with this ointment, and the virgin conceived; the virgin gave birth to the good fragrance, the Son of God. This ointment was poured out upon the waters and sanctified the waters. With this ointment the three young men were anointed, and the flame sprinkled them with moisture (Dan. 3:23). Daniel was anointed with it, and it softened the mouths of the lions and soothed their fierceness (Dan. 6:22).

66. This ointment flows daily and never fails. Take your vessel, virgin, and draw near, so that you may be filled with this ointment. Take the ointment valued at three hundred denarii, but given freely, not sold, so that all might have it freely. Virgin, anoint yourself. Do not grieve like Judas (John 12:5), because this ointment is poured out, but bury Christ within yourself. Close your vessel, certainly, lest the ointment run out. Close it with the key of integrity, with modesty in speech, and with abstinence from boasting.

[Note: [Col. 0282D] One Paris edition reads only: “but bury yourself with Christ,” improperly. Below, where all editions and several manuscripts read, “Close with the key of integrity,” and so forth, others have partly: “Close the door of integrity; close the modesty of speech by abstaining from boasting”; partly: “Close with the key of integrity the modesty of speech and abstinence from boasting.” Neither of these readings, however, is entirely satisfactory.]

67. Whoever possesses this ointment receives Christ; and therefore she who possessed it says: “I opened to my brother; my brother passed by” (Song 5:6). How did he pass by? That is, he penetrated the inward parts of the mind, as it was said to Mary: “And a sword will pierce your own soul also” (Luke 2:35). For the living Word of God, like a sharp sword, penetrates and examines both the barriers of bodily thoughts and the inner places of the heart (Heb. 4:12).

CHAPTER XII

That Christ is to be awaited by all, and especially by virgins; but if he delays, as through the soul’s habitual sluggishness, one must rise and invoke the Holy Spirit by contemplating the gifts already received from him, for the Bridegroom will answer immediately. What it means when she says that her head and locks are wet; where the warning against curling the hair is inserted. Then, after urging the soul again to preserve innocence and to acquire spiritual fragrance from deeds and faith, he promises that she will thus be pleasing, that Christ will approach her, and that he will withdraw from her only for the sake of testing her; therefore tempters are to be despised.

68. And you therefore, soul, one of the people, one of the common multitude—for Christ is not astonished by any worldly distinctions of rank, nor does he admire a gilded garment, a precious necklace, or noble wreaths of glittering gems, for the expense of these things often provokes strife in the Church and drives peace away—certainly you, one of the virgins, who illumine the beauty of your body with the splendor of the mind—for you are nearer to the one compared with the Church—you, I say, established in your chamber and at night, always meditate on Christ and hope for his coming at every moment.

69. If he seems to you to delay, rise. He seems to delay when you sleep too long; he seems to delay when you are absent from prayer; he seems to delay when you do not raise your voice in psalms.

[Note: [Col. 0283D] We understand this as referring to the private singing of psalms at home, since public psalmody does not yet appear to have been instituted at that time in the Church of Milan. Alternatively, “voice” may signify any other sacred and spiritual song, to which the holy Apostle exhorts us.]

Dedicate the first fruits of your vigils to Christ; sacrifice the first fruits of your actions to Christ. You heard above that he called you, saying: “Come from Lebanon, Bride, come from Lebanon; you shall pass over and pass through from the beginning of faith” (Song 4:8). You shall pass over into the world to contend; you shall pass through to Christ to triumph over the world. You heard that he separated you from lions and leopards—that is, from the attacks of spiritual wickedness. You heard that the beauty of your virtues pleases him. You heard that he preferred the fragrance of your garments—that is, the good odor of integrity—to every other fragrance. You heard that you are a locked garden, filled with the sweet fruits of fruit trees. Ask, therefore, that the Holy Spirit breathe upon you, breathe upon your chamber, and increase the fragrance of a devout mind and spiritual grace. He will answer you: “I sleep, but my heart is awake” (Song 5:2).

[Col. 0284A] 70. You hear the voice of one knocking at the door and saying: “Open to me, my sister; rise, my near one, my dove, my perfect one” (ibid.): near through love, a dove through simplicity, perfect through virtue; “for my head is filled with dew.” For just as the dew of heaven removes the dryness of night, so the dew of our Lord Jesus Christ has dripped moisture of eternal life amid the nights and darkness of the world. This is the head that did not know how to wither in the world’s heat; hence he says: “For if they do these things in the moist wood, what will they do in the dry?” (Luke 23:31). This head, then, sprinkles others and abounds for itself. And rightly does the head of Christ abound, because Christ is your head; he is always full and is neither exhausted by his generosity nor diminished by his long-continued giving. Upon this head iron did not ascend, the instrument of war and emblem of discord [Col. 0284B].
