71. Now look and see what kind that dew is—not, certainly, ordinary moisture: “but my locks are drops of night” [Note: [Col. 0283D] The Roman edition alone reads: “But my locks are drops of night.”]. Do not, my near one, take the locks to mean bodily hair (Song 5:2). To him they are not ornaments but crimes: allurements of beauty, not commands of virtue. The Nazirite has other locks, upon which iron does not ascend and which no one cuts. They are not arranged with curling irons or ordered by art, but, curling with the manifold grace of shining virtues, they gleam. Learn from the history what sort of locks the Nazirite has—locks which, as long as Samson possessed them untouched, made him impossible to conquer (Judg. 16:17). He lost his locks and lost the merit of his virtue.

231 72. Having therefore heard the voice of the Word, do not seek to put on again the tunic you removed at night [Col. 0284C]; “for it encounters you,” and is frequently presented through spiritual wickedness [Note: [Col. 0283D] Amerbach and Erasmus read “for it is poured out”; Gill and Rome, with a few manuscripts, “for it is offered”; other manuscripts, finally, “for it is offended,” and so forth. This is not inappropriate, since it has the same sense as “encounters.” But what if one should read “it is displayed”? Certainly we would consider this reading much preferable if it had any support besides conjecture.]. Forget, I say, and do not know how to put it on again; and as though the Lord were already standing near, rise in agitation, freed from bodily bonds [Note: [Col. 0284D] Several manuscripts read: “rise up on the ground,” preparing the mind through prayers.]. As you rise, prepare your inner mind through prayers, so that from humble things you may strive toward heavenly things and endeavor to open the doors of your heart. As you stretch out your hands toward Christ, your deeds will give forth the fragrance of faith.

73. Bring your hands, therefore, to your nostrils, and with tireless and wakeful eagerness of mind examine the fragrance of your deeds. The fragrance of your right hand will soothe you, and your limbs will exude the aroma of the resurrection; your fingers will sweat myrrh—that is, spiritual deeds will give off the grace of true faith. Thus, virgin, you take pleasure from your inner self, and you yourself are sweet and pleasant to yourself; and, as often happens to sinners, you do not begin to displease yourself. For naked simplicity, stripped of the coverings of bodily deceit, will please you more.

[Col. 0285A] 74. Christ desired you to be such; Christ chose you to be such. Therefore he enters through the open door, for the one who promised that he would enter cannot deceive. Embrace, then, the one whom you sought; draw near to him, and you will be illumined. Hold him fast; ask him not to leave quickly; entreat him not to depart. For the Word of God runs swiftly; it is not seized by weariness, nor held by negligence. Let your soul attend to his word, and press on the track of heavenly speech; for it passes quickly.

75. Finally, what does she say? “I sought him and did not find him; I called him, and he did not answer me” (Song 5:6). Do not think that you, who called, pleaded, and opened, displeased him because he went away so quickly: he allows us often to be tested. Finally, when the crowds asked him not to depart, what does he say in the Gospel? “I must preach the word of God to the other cities” [Note: [Col. 0285D] The Roman edition alone reads “the kingdom of God.” Again, the same edition, together with others and several manuscripts, reads “search again”; some manuscripts read “search outward”; others more suitably have “go out,” and so forth.] “because for this I was sent” (Luke 4:43). But even if he seems to you to have gone away, go out and search again (Song 5:7).

76. Now, devoted to God, do not fear those formidable spiritual guards who roam about outside; do not fear those who go around the city; do not dread wounds, which cannot harm those who follow Christ. Even if they take away your body—that is, the life of your body—Christ is near. When you have found him, recognize where you ought to dwell with him, lest perhaps he depart from you; for he quickly abandons the negligent.

232 CHAPTER XIII

That we must learn from the Church how the Bridegroom can be held: namely, by the bonds of love and through the benefit of sufferings. He must also be brought into the inner house, but one first adorned with virtue. Through which window the Bridegroom is said to put out his hand, and how windows are to be prepared for a virgin. She must also put the bolts of silence upon her door, which Eve failed to do to her great loss. Then she will sweat the myrrh of mortification and resurrection, provided that she is such a virgin as the Apostle commands her to be; but she must desire to seek Christ and hate loquacity.

77. Who, then, except holy Church, ought to teach you how to hold Christ? Indeed, she has already taught you, if you understand what you read: “How briefly it was, when I passed by them, until I found him whom my soul loved; I held him, and I will not let him go” (Song 3:4). By what, then, is Christ held? Not by bonds of injury or knots of ropes, but he is bound by the bonds of love, by the reins of the mind, and held by the soul’s affection. If you too wish to hold Christ, seek him continually and do not fear punishment; for amid bodily sufferings, amid the very hands of persecutors, Christ is more readily found. “How briefly it was,” he says, “when I passed by them.” For after you have escaped the hands of persecutors within a short space and brief moment, and have not yielded to the powers of the world, Christ will meet you and will not allow you to be tested for long.

78. She who seeks Christ in this way, who finds Christ, can say: “I held him, and I will not let him go, until I bring him into my mother’s house and into the chamber of her who conceived me” (ibid.). What is your mother’s house and her chamber except the inward and secret recess of your nature? Preserve this house; cleanse the inner rooms of this house, so that, when it has been made immaculate and stained by no filth of an adulterous conscience, the spiritual house may rise, joined together by the cornerstone into a holy priesthood, and the Holy Spirit may dwell in it. She who seeks Christ in this way, who entreats Christ in this way, is not abandoned by him; rather, she is frequently revisited, for he is with us “until the consummation of the world” (Matt. 28:20).

79. Christ, then, has been found and is held; and he has been found who put his hand through your window. What is our window (Song 5:4) except that through which we see the works of Christ—the eye of the soul and the gaze of the mind? Therefore, virgin, let Christ enter through your window; let Christ put out his hand through the window. Let the love of the Word, not of the body, come to you. If, then, the Word of God puts out his hand through your window, see how you should prepare your windows; see how you ought to wipe them clean from every dust of sin. Let the virgin’s window contain nothing foul, nothing adulterous [Note: [Col. 0286D] A few manuscripts read: “let it contain nothing earthly.”]. Far from it be rouge and the other trifles of studied adornment; far from it be the enticements of adulterous love. The closure of the ears is similar: no burdens are to be hung upon them, no wounds inflicted; their one adornment is to hear what is beneficial.

233 80. Learn also to close your door at night; let no one easily find it open. The Bridegroom himself wants it to be closed when he knocks. Our door is our mouth; it ought to be opened almost exclusively to Christ, and it should not be opened unless the Word of God has first knocked. Hence it is written: “A locked garden is my sister, Bride; a locked garden, a sealed fountain” (Song 4:12), so that she may not easily open her mouth or mark it with ordinary speech. For you ought not to answer concerning divine matters unless you have been addressed by the Word of God. What have you to do with others? Speak to Christ alone; converse with Christ alone. For if it is written that women should be silent in the Church (1 Cor. 14:34), how much more is it unfitting for a virgin’s door to stand open, unfitting for a widow’s doors to stand open! The ambusher of modesty quickly slips in; quickly a word falls out that you may wish to recall [Note: [Col. 0286D] The Roman edition alone reads: “quickly he catches the word.”].

81. If Eve’s door had been closed, neither would Adam have been deceived, nor would she have answered the serpent when questioned (Gen. 3:2 ff.). “Death entered through the window” (Jer. 9:21)—that is, through Eve’s door. Death enters through your door if you speak falsely, shamefully, or brazenly; finally, if you speak where you ought not. Let the doors of your lips therefore be closed, and let the vestibule of your voice remain barred. Perhaps it should then be unbarred when you have heard the voice of God, when you have heard the word of God.

82. Then myrrh will sweat for you (Song 5:5); then the grace of baptism will breathe upon you, so that you may die with Christ to the elements of the world and rise with Christ. “Why,” he says, “as though living in the world, do you submit to ordinances?” Do not touch, do not handle, do not taste things that perish through use itself” (Col. 2:20 ff.). Corruption must be far from the chaste; therefore bury the care of the flesh and of the world. Since you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is (Col. 3:1). When you seek Christ, you see God the Father; for Christ sits at the right hand of God.

83. But she who seeks Christ ought not to be ordinary; she ought not to be in the marketplace, nor in the streets, with a plaintive voice, an unsteady step, readily lending an ear [Note: [Col. 0287D] Thus the old edition and several manuscripts; but the Roman edition and some manuscripts read: “easy of access.”], cheap in appearance. The Apostle denies you earthly companionship and teaches that you must fly with spiritual wings toward heaven, almost beyond the limits of nature. “Think on the things that are above,” he says, “not on those that are upon the earth” (ibid., 2). But because this was impossible for those shut up in what is like a prison of the body, and because when the bodies have died the soul is borne to fly back to higher things, while during life we are bound by a certain law of our nature, he therefore added: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (ibid., 3). If it is hidden with Christ in God, let it not appear to the world; for Christ died to the world and lives to God.

84. See now how Christ loves to be desired, but does not love conversation. That virgin therefore opened her doors to the Word of God; but “he passed by,” she says, “and my soul went out at his word” (Song 5:6). She went out from the world, went out from the age, and remained in Christ. “I sought him,” she says, “and did not find him” (ibid.); for Christ loves to be sought for a long time.

CHAPTER XIV

That the Bride is found by the guards of the heavenly Jerusalem, into which she must enter, and by what manner. The light, walls, gates, and citizens of that same city are explained. How the soul is understood to be stripped by the holy angels; and how she who has found Christ sought in the marketplace and in the mystical streets is wounded by those same angels. To this is joined another explanation of the cloak usefully removed.

85. “The guards of the walls found her.” Perhaps there are other guards whom we ought to understand more fully. There is a city whose gates are not closed by day, of which it is said: “Its gates shall not be shut by day” (Rev. 21:25), for night will no longer be in it; the nations will bring glory and honor into it. That, then, is the city of Jerusalem which is in heaven (Heb. 12:22), within which you are already preserved as one perfected and immaculate; for nothing common enters it.

[Note: [Col. 0287D] In the common usage of Scripture, “common” has the same meaning as “unclean,” as we have already noted elsewhere.]

Common chastity is not there; common purity is not there, which is written in the book of life (Rev. 21:27).

86. If, then, we have found the city, let us enter it; let us see its light, its walls, its tribes, its wall foundations, and also the guards of its walls. But how shall we enter it? In this city there is life, and there is one way that leads to life; the way is Christ. Therefore let us follow Christ. But the city itself is in heaven. How, then, shall we ascend to heaven? The Evangelist teaches us, saying: “And the Spirit carried me onto a great and high mountain and showed me the holy city Jerusalem descending from heaven” (Rev. 21:10).

[Note: [Col. 0287D] Among heretics, both ancient and modern, there were those who denied that the Apocalypse had been written by John the Evangelist; some even went so far in their impudence as to attribute it to Cerinthus. Such were the Alogians, whom Epiphanius refuted. There were also Catholics who attributed the same book either to another John of the same age as the Evangelist or believed that it could rightly be doubted whether the Evangelist should be called its author. Nevertheless, whatever they bring forward to the contrary is weak when set against the entire host of the ancient Fathers. For the common opinion is supported by Justin, Dialogue with Trypho; Irenaeus, Books IV and V; and, in Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, Book III, chapter 23, by Clement of Alexandria, likewise in that book, chapter 25; again, in the same author, Book V, chapters 18 and 28, by Apollonius; and finally, in Book VI, chapter 25, by Origen, to whom Tertullian, Against Marcion, is added. With these and all the others our Ambrose agrees here, as also in Psalm 1, no. 54; Psalm 40, no. 26; and elsewhere.]

Let us ascend, then, in spirit, because the flesh cannot ascend to it. In the meantime let us ascend to heaven, so that afterward it may descend from heaven to us—the city in which there is a light like that of a most precious stone, like jasper and crystal (ibid., 11). It has a great and high wall.

87. You have learned about the light; you have learned about the wall. Learn about the gates; learn about the guards. “It has,” he says, “twelve gates, and at the gates twelve angels, upon which are written the names of the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel” (ibid., 12).

[Note: [Col. 0288D] Several manuscripts read “twelve corners,” contrary not only to the authority of all the others and of all the editions, but also to that of the sacred text.]

The names of the patriarchs are contained in the gates; the apostles are in the wall, for the foundations of the city are the apostles (ibid., 14), and Christ is the cornerstone, in whom the whole structure rises. God is outside, God is inside, God is everywhere; for, he says, “the city has the majesty of God” (ibid., 11). Therefore you also, holy virgins, and all you who are righteous and preserve the chastity of an immaculate soul [Note: [Col. 0288D] Many manuscripts read: “and bear an immaculate soul in chastity”; some: “and bear chastity with an immaculate mind”; the others and the editions agree with our text.], are fellow citizens of the saints and members of God’s household. But you will possess this nobility of your homeland only if you seek Christ within the boundaries of this city, entering through faith and precious deeds, illumined by the light of the patriarchs, founded upon the apostles, and dwelling among the angels.

88. How, then, are these guards angels, who take away the cloak of the chaste soul (Song 5:7)? One cloak belongs to virgins; another to worldly youth [Note: [Col. 0289D] Thus the old edition and all manuscripts except three, which read “another belongs to adolescence.” “The worldly woman who…” The Roman edition differs from the others only in replacing adolescentiae with adolescentulae.]. She who seeks Christ in the marketplace has lost even the cloak she had; for prudence is possessed not in the marketplace or streets, but in the Church. And perhaps—in order that we may also win their favor and teach that God is merciful toward all, since they too sometimes find Christ, provided that they seek him continually—this cloak is the garment of the body.

89. Therefore, the one who has sought Christ in the chamber—provided she sought him as the one who said, “Thus I remembered you upon my bed” (Ps. 63:7); if she sought him in the nights, according to what is written, “In the nights lift up your hands to the holy places” (Ps. 134:2); if she sought him in the city, in the marketplace and in the streets: “in the city of our God”; perhaps in the marketplace where that judge sits according to divine law [Note: [Col. 0290D] Several manuscripts read: “sits by divine right.”], and in the streets from which those who gathered for the Lord’s supper were collected—may, while the angels guard the city of God, encounter him as she searches for a long time.

90. Indeed, from the heavenly nature of the guards we can understand a heavenly city, a heavenly marketplace of eternal justice—not mean streets, but perhaps those in which that fountain is accustomed to overflow, concerning which it is written: “Let your waters flow forth from your own fountain, and let your waters be poured out in your streets” (Prov. 5:16). Whoever seeks Christ in this way reaches the angels.

91. But if good merit is the way by which one reaches the angels, why is the one who has reached them wounded? There is also a good sword whose wound is good. The Word of God wounds but does not fester. There is the wound of good love; there are the wounds of love. Therefore she said: “I am wounded with love” (Song 2:5). She who is perfect has been wounded with love. The wounds of the Word are therefore good; the wounds of the one who loves are good: “The wounds of a friend are more useful than the voluntary kisses of an enemy” (Prov. 27:6). Rebecca was wounded with love when she left her parents and migrated to her bridegroom (Gen. 24:58 ff.); Rachel was wounded with love when she envied her sister and loved her husband (Gen. 30:1). Her sister had an abundance of children, while she herself was still barren, and she envied her because she represented the type of the Church, to which it is said: “Rejoice, barren woman who do not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who are not in labor” (Isa. 54:1).

92. The guards therefore found her, wounded her, and took away her cloak—that is, they removed the covering of bodily action, so that the naked simplicity of the mind might seek Christ; for no one can see Christ clothed in the garment of philosophy, that is, in the dress of secular wisdom. And rightly is the garment of philosophy taken away from her, lest someone plunder her through philosophy (Col. 2:8). Her cloak is rightly taken away as she approaches Christ, so that she may enter with a pure heart to see God: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8). Finally, when she had cleansed her heart, she found the Word and saw God.

236 CHAPTER XV

That the soul is aroused to seek God; and, after explaining why it is designated by a feminine term, he urges that divine favor be implored, so that the soul may be governed by him like a certain chariot. For it has four movements, as though they were four horses, by which it is carried away; he teaches that they are to be controlled by reason and prudence.

93. Seek him, therefore, virgin—or rather, let us all seek him; for the soul has no sex. But perhaps it received a feminine name because a more violent heat of the body drives it, while it itself soothes the impulse of the flesh by love of itself, with a certain gentle and pleasing rationality.

[Col. 0290B] 94. Therefore, by prayers and supplications we must invite God to deem it worthy to breathe upon us like a good south wind. May the breath of the heavenly Word breathe upon us, which is accustomed to stir fruit-bearing trees not with a heavy wind but with a gentle breath and soft blowing. Hence it is written: “He set me as the chariots of Amminadab” (Song 6:11), because our soul, when it is joined to the body, like a kind of chariot of neighing horses, seeks a charioteer to guide it. For Amminadab was the father of Nahshon, as we read in Numbers (Num. 1:7), who was a prince of the people of Judah. His figure refers to Christ, who, as the true prince of the people, mounts the soul of the righteous as a charioteer mounts a chariot and governs it with the reins of the Word, lest it be carried headlong into precipices by the fury of violent horses.

95. For they are, as it were, its four horses: the four affections—anger, desire, pleasure, and fear. When these, raging, begin to drive it, it does not know itself at all; for “the corruptible body weighs down the soul,” and, like a chariot of irrational animals, it drags the unwilling soul along, as though rushing headlong under the force of cares, until the bodily passions just mentioned are calmed by the power of the Word. This is the providence of the Word as a good charioteer: lest the mortal body joined to that soul, which in itself is not subject to death, make its movement difficult.

[Note: The edition and a few manuscripts read *irrationabilium* (“of irrational animals”). The Roman edition has *irrationalium animalium cursus* (“the course of irrational animals”); many others have “[lacuna] currus” (“chariot [lacuna]”).]

96. First, then, let it master these swift movements of the body and restrain them with the bridle of reason. Then let it beware lest, through unequal movement, it become entangled like a horse, so that what is good is either disfigured by the vicious, hindered by the sluggish, or disturbed by the turbulent. The horse of wickedness neighs, injures the chariot by throwing itself about, and burdens its yoke-fellow. The good charioteer soothes this horse and sends it out onto the plain of truth; he avoids the winding path of deceit. The course upward is safe; the descent downward is dangerous. Hence, like veterans who have borne the yoke of the Word well, they are led as far as the Lord’s manger, in which the food is not hay but the bread that came down from heaven.

97. The wheels of this chariot are those of which the prophet said: “And the spirit of life was in the wheels” (Ezek. I, 20), because the chariot of the soul rolls smoothly and roundly, without any hindrance.

## CHAPTER XVI

The Word is invited into the garden of the nut tree, which is a figure of temptation, so that it may gather the fragrances of faith and virtues and eat honey. In Christ everything is supplied to all; therefore one must approach him with firm faith, following the example of the woman with the issue of blood, whose marvelous effects are proclaimed. Humble confession must also be added to faith; and one must not answer those who disparage Christ, but, following the example of that same woman, say: “I have not labored,” and so forth. Finally, in order to give authority to the confessing woman, the examples of Peter and Paul, pertaining to the same virtue, are offered.

98. But, lest we wander farther afield, the Word of God is invited into the garden of the nut tree (Song VI, 10), in which there is the fruit of prophetic reading and priestly grace—bitter in temptations, hard in labors, but fruitful in inward virtues. Hence Aaron’s staff also blossomed as a nut tree (Num. XVII, 8), no longer by its own nature but by a hidden power. Let him therefore descend into his garden,

[Note: Three manuscripts read: “to gather myrrh, to receive faith’s fragrance, and to find heavenly food.”]

to gather faith, to receive fragrances, to find heavenly nourishment, and to feast upon the sweetness of our honey, saying: “I gathered my myrrh with spices; I ate my bread with my honey” (Song V, 1). The holy Church stores in honeycombs this mixture of various virtues, gathered by the harmonious work

[Note: Several manuscripts read: “gathered with harmonious voice.”]

of those bees that proclaim wisdom (Prov. VI, 8), so that it may be Christ’s food.

99. Thus we have everything in Christ. Let every soul approach him, whether sick with bodily sins, or fastened as though by certain nails of worldly desire, or still imperfect but nevertheless advancing through diligent meditation,

[Note: A few manuscripts read: “but nevertheless advancing through shining meditation.”]

or already perfected in many virtues. Everything is in the Lord’s power, and Christ is everything for us. If you desire to heal a wound, he is the physician; if you burn with fevers, he is the fountain; if you are burdened by iniquity, he is righteousness; if you need help, he is power; if you fear death, he is life; if you desire heaven, he is the way; if you flee darkness, he is light; if you seek food, he is nourishment. “Taste, then, and see that the Lord is sweet; blessed is the man who hopes in him” (Ps. XXXIII, 9).

100. She who suffered from an issue of blood hoped in him, and was immediately healed,

[Col. 0291D]

because she approached in faith (Luke VIII, 43 and following). And you, daughter, touch his fringe with faith. The flow of worldly pleasures, now surging like a torrent, will be dried up by the warmth of the saving Word—provided that you approach with faith, provided that with equal devotion you grasp at least the outermost fringe of the divine discourse, provided that, trembling, you fall before the Lord’s feet.

Where are the feet of the Word, if not where the body of Christ is? O faith richer than all treasures! O faith stronger than all bodily virtues! O faith more health-giving than all physicians! As soon as the woman approached, she felt the power and obtained healing; just as, if you bring an eye near the light, it is illuminated before you are aware of it, and the operation of the light precedes the preparation. An old, incurable affliction—which had defeated every invention of medical skill and exhausted the supply of money—was healed by the sole touch of the fringe. Therefore, virgin, you must preserve that woman’s modesty in approaching and imitate her devotion in faith.

101. What grace it was that she who was ashamed to be seen was nevertheless not ashamed to confess her infirmity! Do not conceal your falls, then; confess what he already knows. Do not be ashamed of what the prophets were not ashamed. Hear Jeremiah say: “Heal me, O Lord, and I shall be healed” (Jer. XVII, 14). So she also said when she touched the fringe: “Heal me, O Lord, and I shall be healed; save me, O Lord, and I shall be saved,”

[Note: “Save me, O Lord, and I shall be saved” is omitted in several manuscripts.]

“because you are my glory”; for she alone is healed whom you have healed.

102. If someone nevertheless says to you—for this is how the faithful are often tempted—“Where is the word of the Lord? Let it come” (ibid., 15), for it was also said to the Lord: “Let him come down now from the cross, and we will believe him; he trusted in the Lord, let him deliver him now, if he wills” (Matt. XXVII, 42–43). If anyone therefore insults you by saying this and wants to draw you into idle tales, do not answer him; Christ did not wish to answer such people. Ask Christ alone. If you speak to them, they will not believe; if you question them, they will not answer you.

[Note: A Paris edition reads: “Speak by the word alone.” This is very poor.]

Say to the Word alone: “I have not labored by following after you, and I have not desired the day of man” (Jer. XVII, 16).

103. That woman said this, and the bleeding stopped. Although exhausted, although sick, although she had long sought Christ, she nevertheless said: “I have not labored by following after you.” For she does not labor who follows Christ, since he calls those who labor to himself so that they may rest (Matt. XI, 28). Let us therefore follow him. As long as we follow him, we do not labor, because “there is no labor in Jacob” (Num. XXIII, 21). And in Isaiah: “Those who wait for the Lord … shall run and shall not labor” (Isa. XL, 31).

104. Then, when Christ asked who had touched him (Luke VIII, 45), does she not seem to have said to you: “Why do you ask, Lord? You know. What comes forth through my lips is before your face, and therefore I am not ashamed to confess my own sins. Let those who persecute me be ashamed, but let me not be ashamed” (Jer. XVII, 18)?

105. Peter was not ashamed to say: “Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man” (Luke V, 8). He was a wise and serious man, in whom there was the foundation

[Note: Some manuscripts read “foundation.” This is not wrong. Hence those Catholics who deny that the Fathers ever understood Christ’s words, “Upon this rock I will build my Church,” of Peter can be refuted from this passage of the holy Doctor alone; for it is clear that he alludes here to Peter.]

of the Church and the teaching of discipline. He saw that nothing was more useful for him than not to be exalted by the outcome of a successful undertaking. And therefore he says: “Depart from me, Lord” (II Cor. XII, 7). He does not ask to be abandoned, but not to be puffed up.

106. Paul too glories in the thorn of the flesh, because provision was made for him lest he be exalted. It is seductive boasting, which even Paul fears; slippery, which is guarded against even in Paul. Yet he was not one easily moved by a trivial fall: he feared being exalted by revelations, and therefore, like a strong athlete, he rejoices that he had learned to purchase the soul’s health at the price of a wound to the body.

## CHAPTER XVII

He advises the avoidance of boastfulness by various examples, especially that of the little bee. For our soul has its own flights, by which, rising above the world, it is joined to God and to eternal virtues. He teaches that these virtues are above the world by the example of Christ, and urges the soul to imitate him and the apostles. Yet, lest the model seem too exalted, he encourages it to become Christ’s disciple, so that it may be helped by prayer; meanwhile, it should apply diligence and leave various vices outside.

106. Therefore, if you recognize that divine gifts overflow and abound in you, measure your virtue, give thanks to God, and receive contemplation of the body as the ballast of a ship,

[Note: The Roman edition reads “the contention of the body”; other editions and manuscripts more correctly read “the contemplation of the body,” that is, consideration of bodily frailty and worthlessness. *Saburra*, mentioned immediately afterward, is sand placed in the bottom of ships so that they may neither roll excessively nor incline to one side. What follows concerning the bees was plainly taken from Virgil, *Georgics* IV:

“... and often they lift little stones  
as ballast for their unstable boats,  
tossed about by the wave;  
with these they balance themselves through the empty clouds.”]

lest, amid the great waves of the world, some breeze of boastfulness carry you about. That wise bee, when it suspects movements in the air, often lifts little stones and balances itself through the empty clouds, lest the light oarage of its wings be driven headlong by the blasts of the winds.

[Col. 0293C]

Paul and Barnabas thought themselves burdened when they saw themselves being worshiped (Acts XIV, 12–13). And you, virgin, beware, like that little bee, lest the breeze of this world raise up the flight of your wings.

107. The soul has its own flights. Therefore it is said: “Who are these who fly like clouds and like doves with their young?” (Isa. LX, 8). The soul therefore has spiritual flights, by which it traverses the whole world in a brief moment; for the thoughts of the prudent are free. The higher and more divine the things toward which they raise themselves, the more freely they are borne, without any impediment from earthly weight. Thus, clinging to God and bearing within itself the likeness of the heavenly image, once it has quieted its course after the disturbance of the horses, it is carried into that ethereal and pure place by the beating of spiritual wings and looks down upon everything in this world. Intent upon eternal virtues, it glides above the world.

Justice is above the world; love is above the world; chastity is above the world; goodness is above the world; wisdom is above the world. And although it may be in this world, it is nevertheless above the world.

[Note: “Love is above the world” is lacking in most manuscripts.]

108. Justice was above the world when the devil offered all the kingdoms of the world and all their glory (Matt. IV, 8). He was above the world who touched nothing of the world. Finally, he says: “The prince of this world is coming, and in me,” he says, “he will find nothing” (John XIV, 30). Learn, then, to be above the world while in this world; and although you bear a body, let the inner bird fly within you. He is above the world who lifts up God in his body.

109. But we cannot imitate God. Let us imitate the apostles, whom the world hated because they were not of this world (John XV, 19). Imitate them; follow them. But you think it difficult to rise above the world by human strength. You are right; for the apostles too deserved to be above the world by following the Lord, not as his companions but as his disciples. Be Christ’s disciple and Christ’s imitator; and he who prayed for them prays for you. “For I do not pray,” he says, “for the apostles only, but for those who will believe in me through their word, that they may all be one.” The Lord therefore wishes us all to be one, so that we may all be above the world: so that there may be one chastity, one will, one goodness, and one grace. For by these the soul’s flight is nourished and increased.

110. Therefore let us not grow sluggish, but rise up from earthly things; for the nature of wings is such that, by exercising themselves, they acquire strength.

[Note: All editions read: “Let us not grow sluggish in abandoning earthly things; for this is …” Some manuscripts, however, read: “Let us not grow sluggish while seated on earthly things; for this is …” The remaining manuscripts, many more in number, have the reading adopted in the text.]

Flight is aided by the very thing in which the soul delights. If it always follows God, desires to dwell in the house of the Lord, feeds upon his delight, and is nourished by the miracles of heavenly virtues, it will leave outside envy, which is outside the choir of angels, and outside the desires of the body, which ought not to defile the temple of God. Therefore, because we are the temple of God, let us cast away material anxieties from ourselves.

## CHAPTER XVIII

The fact that poets attribute a chariot, horses, and wings to the soul was taken from the prophet Ezekiel. The forms of the four living creatures, by which the four Evangelists are represented, are also shown to be figures of the four cardinal virtues. David too spoke beautifully of the soul’s wings. The holy Bishop therefore kindles us to flight and reveals to us what must be avoided by recounting Icarus’s fall. Then, having set forth the difficulty of flying, he teaches that, if our actions are in harmony with one another, we shall see Christ upon the throne guiding us. Since Christ is also read to have sometimes gone up a mountain and sometimes entered a ship, he takes this occasion to unfold the mystical meaning of the ship and of Peter’s fishing.

111. And lest we should seem to have borrowed the language of philosophy or poetry when we speak of the soul’s chariot, horses, and wings—for they rather borrowed these things from us—the sequence of prophetic reading shows that we have used our own household resources. It is written in this way by the holy Ezekiel:

“And the hand of the Lord came upon me there, and I saw, and behold,

[Note: Nearly all manuscripts have this reading. The editions, however, read “a rushing spirit,” following the Septuagint, *pneuma exairon* (πνεῦμα ἐξαῖρον), that is, “a carrying-away, stormy spirit.” Yet there is nothing to prevent Ambrose from having translated “a rising spirit,” since after *exairon* he may have understood *heauton* (ἑαυτόν), that is, “raising itself.” Again, where our text and most manuscripts read “and a flashing fire, and light around it,” some manuscripts have only “and a flashing fire, and light in it, and in the midst something like a likeness,” where there is clearly a lacuna. The editions differ from our reading only in preferring “and light in it, and in the midst like light” to “and light around it like the light.” Neither reading differs greatly from the prophetic words.]

a rising spirit was coming from the north, and there was a great cloud in it, and flashing fire, and light around it like the appearance of amber in the midst of the fire, and light in it, and in the midst something like the likeness of four living creatures” (Ezek. I, 3 and following).

112. You see, then, that four living creatures have already been described. We must attend to what sort of living creatures they are: “The likeness,” he says, “of their faces was the face of a man; and the face of a lion was on the right of the four; and the face of a calf was on the left of the four; and the face of an eagle was above the four; and their wings were spread out” (ibid., 10–11).

113. Here too we understand the soul to be described. Its four living creatures are its four affections, but not in the same way as those we described above; for those affections are still being educated and are receiving progress, whereas here the soul is already described as perfected. Indeed, the former are invited toward heaven, while this one is in heaven with the Word of God.

It has four affections comparable to the likeness of a man, a lion, a calf, and an eagle. We understand these forms to have been represented according to the distinct character of the Gospel books. Thus here too, through the figures of the living creatures, the species of affection is expressed: rational in the man, impetuous in the lion, desirous in the calf, and perceptive in the eagle.

114. For the Greeks have stated that every wise man possesses *logistikon* (λογιστικόν), *thymētikon* (θυμητικόν), *epithymētikon* (ἐπιθυμητικόν), and *diorat̄ikon* (διορατικόν)—the rational, spirited, appetitive, and perceptive faculties. The Latins, however, speak of prudence, fortitude, temperance, and justice.

Prudence belongs to human reason. Fortitude possesses something of the force of a raging virtue and contempt for death. Temperance, bound by sacred love and contemplation of heavenly mysteries, disregards bodily pleasures. Justice, placed upon a lofty platform, sees and examines everything; since things are born for others rather than for itself, it investigates not so much its own advantages as the benefits of the community.

And rightly the soul that practices justice receives the form of an eagle, because, fleeing earthly things and raised wholly toward the heavenly mystery, it gains the glory of the resurrection as the reward of righteousness. Therefore it is said to it: “Your youth shall be renewed like the eagle’s” (Ps. CII, 5).

[Note: A few manuscripts read “which are more familiar to others”; others, more correctly, together with the editions, read “which are more naturally born for others,” and so forth. You will find the same sentence in the same words in Psalm XXXV, column 768, no. 7.]

115. Thus, according to David also, the soul is supported by spiritual wings. He wished to show us how winged it is when he said elsewhere: “Our soul has been rescued like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters” (Ps. CXXIII, 7). And elsewhere: “I trust in the Lord; how can you say to my soul, ‘Flee to the mountain like a sparrow’?” (Ps. X, 2).

The soul therefore has its own wings, by which it can rise freely from earthly things. The rowing of its wings is not a material arrangement of feathers but the continual order of good works, like that of the Lord, to whom it is rightly said: “And in the shadow of your wings I will hope” (Ps. LVI, 2). For not only were those hands of the Lord, fastened to the cross, stretched out like the wings of a flying creature; his heavenly deeds also, like a cooling shadow of eternal salvation, tempered the burning fires of the world.

116. Therefore, since the opportunity to fly has been given to us, let each person stir up within himself the grace of God; forgetting what lies behind and reaching toward what lies ahead, let him press on toward the goal (Phil. III, 13). Far from the honors of military service, far from the heats of the world,

[Note: “Military service” is understood not only of service in a camp but also of the legal profession. Symmachus writes in Book VII, Letter 124: “He will perform his service in the offices of letters,” and so forth. Indeed, we commonly use this word for any kind of office, examples of which occur everywhere.]

lest what the fables relate should happen—that the heat of the sun melt the wax and, the feather of the Icarian flight slipping away, leave the flight helpless. For although poetic authority may be absent,

[Note: Certain Paris editions and some manuscripts read “although the weight of the sayings is harmful.” Other editions and more manuscripts read correctly: “[let the poetic authority] be absent”; for here “weight” means authority or truth, which Ambrose denies to poets. Again, where all editions and some manuscripts read “they wished to show the maturity of the prudent,” many manuscripts read “they wished to show prudence through maturity,” which is less satisfactory. Finally, the Gillot edition in the margin and the Roman edition in the text, together with some manuscripts, read “flights through heaven,” whereas the older edition and many more manuscripts correctly read “flights through the world.”]

nevertheless, with poetic wit they wished to show that flights through the world are safe for mature wisdom, while youthful levity is exposed to worldly desires, with its wings driven backward and, through forgetfulness of the truth, the structure of its merits dissolved, so that it falls back to earth with greater destruction.

117. Flight is not easy for everyone. The course of human life is difficult even when its inward living creatures are at variance.

[Note: All editions read “when the living creatures on earth are at variance.” Some manuscripts read simply “when they are at variance.” In the four living creatures, the reference is to the life of … The remaining manuscripts have the more elegant reading adopted in the text.]

But if the order of our actions agrees with itself, the prophet will also see in us that one wheel upon the earth joined to the four living creatures. Ezekiel will therefore see again—for he still sees, is still alive, and will continue to live—the wheel rolling without hindrance in the midst of another wheel upon the earth (Ezek. I, 15–16).

The wheel upon the earth is the life of the body, adapted to the virtue of the soul and shaped in harmonious course according to the Gospel command. The wheel within the wheel is, as it were, life within life: either because the life of the saints is not discordant with itself, but what the earlier age has been, so also is the later; or because, in this bodily life, the practice of eternal life is set in motion.

118. When these things are in harmony, then the divine voice will resound; then “above the likeness of a throne there appeared a likeness as the appearance of a man” (Ezek. I, 26). This man is the Word, because “the Word became flesh” (John I, 14). This man is the driver of our living creatures, the ruler of our conduct, who, according to the measure of our merits, usually ascends either a chariot, a mountain, or a ship—but a ship in which either the apostles sail or Peter fishes (Luke V, 3 and following). Nor is the ship contemptible that is led into the heights (Matt. XVII, 1), that is, separated from unbelievers.

Why is a ship chosen for Christ to sit in and for the crowd to be taught, unless because the ship is the Church, which, with the full sail of the Lord’s cross and by the breath of the Holy Spirit, sails well through this world?

119. In this ship Peter fishes. Sometimes he is commanded to fish with nets, sometimes with a hook. A great mystery! For the fishing appears to be spiritual: he is commanded to cast the hook of teaching into the world, so that it may raise Stephen, the first martyr,

[Note: The edition reads “may sweep him from the sea”; some manuscripts read “[lacuna] may rescue him,” others “[lacuna] may lift him up.” Stephen is discussed not only here but also in *Hexaemeron* V, 6, no. 16, and in *Commentary on Luke* V, no. 75. What is added shortly afterward—“minister of the altar”—clearly signifies that deacons were regarded not merely as administrators of the Church’s resources and alms, as was decreed at the Council in Trullo against the Council of Neo-Caesarea and, indeed, against the universal tradition of the Fathers, but as true ministers of the altar, as we have already noted elsewhere.]

from the sea, who held Christ’s wealth within himself; for a martyr of Christ is the Church’s treasure. That martyr, then, who first rose from the sea to heaven, captured by Peter and made a minister of the altar, is lifted up not by a net but by a hook, so that he might be raised to heaven by the stream of his blood. A treasure was in his mouth, since he spoke of Christ in his confession.

For what treasure is in us except the Word of God? The perfect fisherman therefore fishes with both nets and hook: with the net he encloses; with the hook he burns. The crowd is enclosed by the net; by the hook the individual is chosen.

O that I might be permitted to swallow that hook which would burn my mouth and give salvation through a gentle wound!

[Note: A few manuscripts read: “and smooth salvation with a wound”; several others: “and at least smooth the wounds.” The remaining manuscripts and the editions have the better reading adopted in the text.]

## CHAPTER XIX

He urges virgins to enter the nets of wisdom, that is, the kingdom of heaven, into which Peter is commanded to lead them. Another interpretation of the same command is given, in which we are to understand the heart of a man as the deep and as the Church. A third interpretation, concerning Christ himself, is then proposed; hence the same apostle replies that he has labored in vain through the night. The way in which Christ and Peter still say the same things is also explained. Finally, an exhortation follows: if we cannot fully pay the price we owe Christ, we should at least show ourselves not unworthy of his benefit, lest he complain that he shed his blood and entered the place of corruption in vain.

120. Enter, then, daughters, into the apostles’ nets, which are let down not by human authority but by God’s command. For the net of spiritual wisdom and teaching is the kingdom of heaven, because it is written: “The kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea” (Matt. XIII, 47).

121. Today you heard the Lord Jesus say to Simon: “Put out into the deep, and let down your nets for a catch” (Luke V, 4). Before this Peter did not put out into the deep when he was fishing in the lake. Although it was a sea, it was not deep (ibid., 5); Scripture does not recognize a deep sea.

Understand, then, what “deep” means: “Deep water is counsel in the heart of a man” (Prov. XVIII, 4). The heart of a man is deep where there is nothing shallow. Put out, then, the oars of your discussion and faith into the deep; put out into the heart of man.

Here he calls Peter to the Church by a parable, whereas according to Matthew he called him in simple words, saying: “Come, and I will make you fishers of men” (Matt. IV, 19).

122. There is another mystery: “Put out into the deep,” because previously he was on the shore, when he was in the Synagogue. The water of Judea was not deep. Indeed, the Samaritan woman also thought the well was deep when she said: “The well is deep; where then do you have the living water to give me?” (John IV, 11).

Therefore he could not put out into the deep when he believed together with the Jews, who could not even draw water from the well.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “He could put out into the deep. When could he? When he believed as a Jew. For also …” This is erroneous.]

Therefore it is said to Peter: “Put out into the deep,” that is, “Lead to Christ.” For Christ is high, of whom the Father says to John: “And you, child, shall be called the prophet of the Most High” (Luke I, 76). Lead, then, to Christ. And rightly “deep,” in whom there is “the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God” (Rom. XI, 33).

“Put out into the deep,” who, high above the high,

[Note: This is the reading of the Amerbach and Erasmus editions, together with many more manuscripts, except that they have “will guard and exalt.” Gillot and the Roman edition, together with some manuscripts, read “because he is high,” while another edition has “the high”; the text is “he guards and exalts above the high.”]

guards and exalts.

123. Therefore there are deep waters where Christ is—that is, faith. They are deep waters that fear the Lord, such as these: “The waters saw you, O God; the waters saw you and were afraid” (Ps. LXXVI, 17).

Among the Jews there was no deep water,

[Note: An old edition reads: “The water was not deep in the heart of man.” The Roman edition, more elegantly, together with all the manuscripts, has the reading used above.]

because there was no depth in the heart of man. Therefore the Lord says: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Matt. XIV, 8). Christ loves to be in the heart: “For just as Jonah was in the belly of the whale three days and three nights, so will the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth three days and three nights” (Matt. XXII, 40).

124. Finally, so that you may know that he is speaking of faith when he says “Put out into the deep,” Peter says: “Master, having labored throughout the whole night, we caught nothing; but at your word I will let down the nets” (Luke V, 5).

Peter had night before he saw Christ. The day had not yet come for him, because he had not yet seen the true light. The Synagogue is night; the Church is day. Hence Paul also says: “The night has passed; the day has drawn near” (Rom. XIII, 12).

A good light, which shook off the darkness of faithlessness and made the day of faith. Peter became day; Paul became day. Therefore today, on their feast day, the Holy Spirit cried out, saying: “Day pours forth the word to day” (Ps. XVIII, 3)—that is, from the innermost treasure of the heart they proclaim the faith of Christ. Both are good days, for they have poured forth the true light for us.

125. We read these things in the Gospel. And perhaps today in heaven this is the conversation of Christ and Peter concerning us. Every day Peter fishes; every day the Lord says to him: “Put out into the deep.”

I seem to hear Peter saying: “Master, having labored throughout the whole night, we caught nothing.” It was night;

[Note: Here we learn that the feast day of the apostles, which was always celebrated on the same day, was observed from the earliest centuries of the Church with the greatest solemnity, since it was kept with vigils and fasting beforehand. We do not, however, think that this fast imposed as great an obligation as the Lenten fast, since Ambrose rebukes those who broke it rather mildly.]

fewer people gathered for the vigils. Peter labors in us when our devotion labors; Paul labors too. Indeed, today you heard him say: “Who is weak, and I am not weak?” (II Cor. XI, 29).

[Note: Several manuscripts read: “Do not fail; labor so that you may make progress. Therefore the apostles …”]

Do not make the apostles labor on your behalf. Therefore they say to him: “Having labored throughout the whole night, we caught nothing.” Certainly none of the wealthier people fasted.

Peter rightly answered them today: “Conduct yourselves in fear during the time of your sojourn, knowing that you were not redeemed from your futile way of life inherited from your fathers with perishable silver or gold, but with the precious blood, as of an unblemished and spotless lamb, Christ Jesus” (I Pet. I, 18–19). It was not gold and silver that freed you, but the testing of faith, much more precious than gold, which perishes.

126. A good servant strives to repay his Lord the price that was paid for him. Do not prepare gold, daughter; do not prepare silver. Christ did not redeem you with these riches. Have the price ready. You will not always be required to pay, but you always owe it. He paid blood; you owe blood. He paid for you; render it for yourself.

We were pledged to an evil creditor by our sins; we contracted a bond of guilt; we owed the penalty of blood. The Lord Jesus came and offered his own for us—but you cannot repay blood.

127. A good servant ought to repay his Lord the price owed to him. If he cannot repay the price, let him at least do this: let him not appear unworthy of the price. Therefore, conduct yourself as worthy of such a price, lest Christ, who cleansed and redeemed you, come and find you in sins and say to you: “What profit is there in my blood?” (Ps. XXIX, 10). What benefit did it bring you when I descended into corruption?

128. But do not wonder how he descended into corruption, although, as it is written elsewhere, his flesh did not see corruption (Acts II, 24 and following). He did descend into the place of corruption—he who penetrated the realms below—but, being incorruptible, he excluded corruption.

[Note: In explicit words the holy Bishop here states his view concerning Christ’s descent to the dead. Since some deny that this should be regarded as an article of faith, it will be necessary to discuss it somewhat in the treatise on the Apostles’ Creed.]

## CHAPTER XX

He asks for prayers, recognizing that his fishing cannot prosper without God’s favor, and gives thanks to God for having deigned to send him help. He indicates that he is not using his own nets but those of Peter and Paul, by whom he hopes the virgins will be brought to life. He explains how useful it was for John to have abandoned everything for Christ; the more humble his person was, the greater authority he ought to have. He also shows the significance of Christ’s joining fishermen with Moses and Elijah. A pleasant comparison is drawn between these fishermen and Moses.

129. But, to return now to higher things, pray that it may also be said to me: “Put out into the deep, and let down your nets for a catch.” For who can fish for this people without God, especially when such great storms and tempests of this world oppose us?

But whenever the Lord wills, he commands the nets to be let down, and a multitude of fish is caught. Not only one ship but another also is filled, because several Churches are filled with an immaculate people. And this happens well, because the Lord knew that we would labor, and he supplied assistance through our companions.

A fisherman of the Church of Bologna is present, suited to this kind of fishing.

[Note: Baronius says that Eusebius, bishop of Bologna, is meant here. Nothing at all undermines his opinion, since that holy man attended the Council of Aquileia in 381 together with Ambrose. What the same cardinal adds—that this Eusebius is the one to whom Ambrose’s treatise *On the Institution of a Virgin* is dedicated—requires fuller examination and will therefore be discussed in the preface to that treatise on the following page. The feast of Blessed Eusebius is recorded in the ecclesiastical calendars on the sixth day before the Kalends of October.]

Give fish, Lord, because you have given helpers.

130. Yet we use not our own nets, but those of the Apostles. May your company, O daughters, be driven into those folds and certain recesses of apostolic discussions [Note: A considerable number of manuscripts read “the recesses of arrangements.”]. May Peter give you life, daughters—for he also intervened for a widow (Acts 9:39–40), and how much more for a virgin! [Col. 0300D] He, unwilling that widows should continue long in mourning, moved by their tears, restored their benefactress to life. [Col. 0301A] May Paul give you life, he who commanded you to be honored (1 Tim. 5:3), who says: “It is good if they remain as I am” (1 Cor. 7:8). By honor he provokes you; by his teaching he instructs you; [Note: According to Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* III.30, there were some who maintained that Paul’s celibacy had been denied by Clement of Alexandria; some even associated Ignatius with Clement in this opinion, citing his *Epistle to the Philadelphians*. Influenced by their authority, several Catholics in our own time have expressed a doubtful judgment on the matter; but above all, many heterodox writers have eagerly seized upon it to attack and disparage the condition of the celibate life. Yet although they also produce certain passages from Paul’s letters—such as those from 1 Corinthians 9 and Philippians 4:5—misunderstood in their favor, these have no force against the other very clear testimonies of the same Apostle and against the common agreement of the whole tradition. Certainly this passage sufficiently indicates that Ambrose never favored their opinion. See also Baron[ius], under the year 57; Bellarmine, *On the Clergy* I.20; Pamel[ius] in Tertullian, *On Monogamy*, note 13; Leo Allatius, *On the Methodii*; and the multitude of commentators on the Apostle’s disputed passages.]. he invites you by his example (Matt. 4:20 and following). [p. 246] May he give you life who, leaving all that was his, followed the Lord: Peter followed; John followed.

131. See what this fisherman also achieved. While seeking his profit in the sea, he found life for all. He abandoned the small boat and found God; he left the oar and found the Word; [Note: “He loosened the line, he bound faith; he folded the nets, he lifted up men”—these words are absent from several manuscripts.] he loosened the line, he bound faith; he folded the nets, he lifted up men; he despised the sea, he gained heaven. Thus this fisherman, while himself being tossed upon the troubled waters, established minds wavering in their unstable state [Note: Several manuscripts read “in the mobile station of the mind.”] upon the rock. [Col. 0301B]

132. Let us therefore more frequently set forth the art of the fisherman, so that we may believe more fully in his virtue. Let him have been an obscure servant, so that he might be a more renowned evangelist; poor in poverty, so that he might be richer in virtue; seemingly worthless in honor, but precious in faith. The less a fisherman is believed, the more he is believed, because what he has spoken is not his own, [Note: All printed editions have this reading; some manuscripts instead read, “he spoke divine things.” Others read, “he spoke divine service: the condition of the common people.” Neither reading is entirely satisfactory.] but divine. His humble condition serves; it removes the expectation of secular wisdom and increases the esteem of spiritual wisdom. He who did not learn the Law, yet understands the things of the Law, is himself a law to himself; he who did not learn the Law and speaks beyond the Law received it from him from whom the Law itself came (Rom. 2:14–15). [Col. 0302A]

133. What sudden dignity this is! Two fishermen on the Lord’s mountain (Matt. 17:1 and following) are associated with one as bearer of the Law and the other as its executor. See what kind of fisherman this is. Moses indeed, having surpassed all earthly things and the heights of worldly wisdom, ascended by the understanding of his mind even to heaven and the stars. But the mind of this fisherman is not darkened by clouds, confined by ages, or excluded from the mysteries of heavenly nature; having surpassed all corporeal matter, it saw the Word with God and perceived that the Word itself was God (John 1:1 and following). Nor did it tremble, weakened by the sight of the flesh in Peter; rather, it recognized the Son of God even in a human being (Matt. 16:17), so that the assumption of the body, taken up into the right of the divinity that assumed it, might pass into the name of its author. [Note: Several manuscripts read, “taken up from the divinity of the one who assumes it”; some others, “adopted for the right of divinity, acquired for the use of the mind”; the remaining manuscripts and the printed editions, which we follow here, have the more suitable reading.]

134. When Moses says, “And God said … and God made” (Gen. 1:3 and following), he signified the Father and the Son; but he was not ignorant, while I was still ignorant. In the end, after the Law the people went astray; after the Gospel they believed. Great is God’s grace in differing virtues. In Moses, because he described the world; in Peter, because he did not know the world. [Note: A few manuscripts read, “in different ages.” This is not an unsuitable reading.]

# [ON THE INSTITUTION OF THE VIRGIN.]

## INTRODUCTION TO THE BOOK ON THE INSTITUTION OF THE VIRGIN.

This work does not bear the same title in handwritten and printed manuscripts. In the former it is prefaced by the heading: “Sermon on the Perpetual Virginity of Saint Mary”; in the latter: “Institution to Eusebius,” or “On the Institution of the Virgin.” Each title has its own rationale. Those who placed the former title before it seem to have been influenced chiefly by the fact that the greater part of this composition is devoted to refuting the adversaries of that same Mary. We also think this is why, although numerous manuscripts of all the other treatises concerning the virginal calling are found, so few and imperfect manuscripts of this work exist. They evidently judged it to pertain less to the formation of virtue and morals than to the refutation of a heresy not merely obsolete but overthrown and utterly extinguished. That this is not a recent condition of those manuscripts may also be understood from the fact that in the *Exposition of the Canticles* compiled from Ambrose’s works by William, abbot of Saint-Thierry (*Appendix* to volume I, p. 1545), nothing drawn from this same book has been inserted. As for the editions, those who gave them their title more accurately grasped the work’s purpose and end. Therefore, since the breadth of the summary pages could not accommodate both titles in full, we decided to place only the latter at the head of the book.

In the editions it also reads “To Eusebius.” Although this name is absent from our manuscripts, it must nevertheless have existed in the codices from which that text was committed to the press; the question is only who this Eusebius was. Some, with Baronius (under the year 377), have thought him to be the same as Saint Eusebius, bishop of Bologna. Yet it seems much more probable that another Eusebius is meant: a citizen of Bologna whose close friendship with Ambrose is sufficiently demonstrated by a letter of that saint addressed to him. He was the head of a very noble family and had a son, Faustinus, the father of a large and beautiful family. That devout grandfather used to send his grandchildren to Ambrose so that he might care for their education. Among them the holy Bishop numbers a girl, Ambrosia, whom he calls “the spiritual dove … anointed with the olive of integrity”; he identifies her together with her brother of the same name when he says that both were Ambrose’s pledges, and so forth. Thus, when Eusebius earnestly commended his granddaughter to the holy Bishop (chapter 1, no. 1), Ambrose received her at Milan with no ordinary spiritual joy. Having learned her desire and obtained the consent of her parents, he consecrated her with solemn rite. Before she was veiled, he exhorted this victim of virginity at the altar in a grave and devout address, as was customary; he then sent the same address, adding only two chapters, to that religious man (chapters 1 and 2).

First, therefore, he praises Eusebius for having shown that Ambrosia was dearer to him than his other children (chapter 1, no. 1 and following), demonstrating that the virginal state is far superior to marriage in many respects. Then, after teaching that silence and prayer must always accompany continence, he explains the qualities of prayer (ibid., no. 4 and following, and chapter 2, no. 8 and following). Soon afterward he declares that, although he has often treated that eminent virtue, he nevertheless willingly devoted the labor of this work to Ambrosia’s sake (chapter 2, no. 15). After these preliminaries, he reports the sermon he delivered while that same Virgin was being veiled. At the beginning he testifies that virginity is an adornment to both sexes (chapter 3, no. 6); returning to events from the beginning, he proves that women are unjustly brought into disrepute as the causes of human error and sin. He also answers the customary accusation by which women are said to be stumbling blocks to men (chapter 4, no. 25 and following), where he recounts very beautifully the devotion and fasts of many women of that age (ibid., nos. 30 and 31). From the old Eve he then turns to the new—namely, Mary—and asserts that she was the first to raise the standard of sacred virginity (chapter 5, no. 32 and following). He consequently adds that he is amazed that some Christians have dared to deny perpetual integrity to this mother of God and likewise of all virgins. He says that this sacrilege ought indeed to be suppressed in eternal silence; but since a bishop—Bonosus, namely, who presided over the diocese of Sardica, or rather of Naissus, as we shall explain elsewhere—had fallen into this impiety, it no longer seemed permissible to conceal it (ibid., no. 35 and following). Therefore, fearing that episcopal authority might harm the true faith, he attacks him in a public assembly to which an immense crowd had flocked for the consecration of a foreign and most noble virgin (chapters 6, 7, and 8). First he brings forward the sophisms of these heretics and then applies his own solutions to each of them (chapter 9, no. 58 and following). For the most part he gives the same answers as Jerome gives to Helvidius, that Arian disciple of Auxentius. The principal difference between them is that, whereas the latter is content to refute the fallacies of the opponents, Ambrose additionally supplies arguments by which Mary’s perpetual virginity may be demonstrated. There, exhorting virgins to imitate their own standard-bearer because of the Bridegroom’s jealousy (chapters 10, 11, and 12), he proves the divinity of this same one, which the heretics had arrogantly attacked (chapters 13, 14, and 15). After again urging virgins to imitate the chastity of the Mother of God, he explains what virtues are required in them (chapter 16, no. 100 and following). Finally, returning by name to Ambrosia, he briefly discloses what she must accomplish (chapter 17, no. 104 and following). After giving thanks to God for having established in the new covenant the angelic profession of virginity through Mary’s example (ibid., no. 107 and following), he offers Ambrosia, who is now to receive the sacred veil, to her; and he prays with the most ardent affection that she may not disdain to admit her, enriched by God with virtues, into the bright choir of her brides (chapter 2, no. 15).

It remains now to investigate the date of this composition. Observe that Ambrose not only says that he had already published several books before undertaking this work (chapter 6, no. 43), but that this work also has a close affinity with the books *On the Faith*, with the treatise *On the Mysteries*, and even—with this especially noteworthy—with the work *On the Sacraments*, with the letter of the Council of Milan, and with the letter of Siricius. Above all, it is closely related to the *Exposition of the Gospel according to Luke*, whose teaching and expressions it reproduces in many passages and to which it directs us to refer in unmistakable words. Accordingly, this book is later than the same Commentary, to which we assigned the year 386. Finally, the heresy of Bonosus, whose two principal tenets the holy Doctor refutes so clearly, and the letter that Siricius sent from the Synod of Capua, where Bonosus’s case had been examined, a letter in many respects very similar to this little work—these two facts make it necessary to consider that this work appeared no earlier than the year 391. Nevertheless, it is not evident that a date much later than that should be assigned to it, since the author testifies that it was then for the first time that he spoke publicly against that heresy. Therefore, if he followed here the custom of those times, according to which sacred virgins were veiled especially during the Paschal celebration, one may rightly say that the sermon was delivered at Easter in the year 392.

# SAINT AMBROSE, BISHOP OF MILAN, ON THE INSTITUTION OF THE VIRGIN AND THE PERPETUAL VIRGINITY OF SAINT MARY, TO EUSEBIUS. ONE BOOK

[Note: Written around the year 392.]

## CHAPTER ONE

Parents rightly take greater care for a sacred virgin than for their other children. How excellent that consecration is; especially concerning silence, which commends the modesty of virginity no less than it does the Church, whose entire glory is within, and whom we ought to imitate in prayer.

1. You commend to me your pledge, which is equally mine, Ambrosia, consecrated to the Lord [Note: Two manuscripts read “Ambrose’s sacred pledge,” or “the Lord’s sacred pledge.”]; and in devout affection you assert that you are more solicitous for her than for the rest of your offspring. And truly this is so in the mind of a faithful man. You educate the others so that you may send them from home and unite them to strangers; but you will always have this one with you. In the others, too, you exercise the obligation of a father’s devotion; in her you go beyond fatherhood and advance in vow and zeal so that she may please God. Although this is the more excellent object of your vows, she alone nevertheless fulfills whatever you owe on her own behalf and on behalf of all your children.

2. This is the sacrifice that Abel offered from the firstborn of his sheep (Gen. 4:4). The Apostle also praises it above all others when he says to the Corinthians: “He who stands firm in his heart and has decided in his heart to keep his virgin, does well.” [Note: Some manuscripts read, “who stands firm in his heart,” corresponding to the Greek text, ὃς καὶ ἕστηκε (*hos kai hestēke*), “who has stood”; other manuscripts and editions, with the Vulgate and other versions, read “who has decided,” and so forth.] Therefore he who joins his virgin in marriage also does well; and he who does not join her does better (1 Cor. 7:37–38). Accordingly, after David had described the grace of the Church, whose entire glory is within, not without—for her highest praise consists in good thoughts, an undefiled affection for chastity, and the intention of a sincere conscience—he added: “Virgins shall be brought to the King after her” (Ps. 44:15–16). Then, turning to the Lord the Father, he says: “They shall be brought to you, close after her; they shall be brought in joy and gladness, they shall be led into the temple of the King.”

3. Who is the one who is “close after her,” unless it is she who draws near to Christ, to whom the Word says: “Arise, come, my near one, m[lacuna]e[lacuna]mosa, my dove; for behold, the winter is past” (Song 2:10–11)? Before she received the Word of God, winter was dishonorable and fruitless; when she received the Word of God, and the world was crucified to her, summer came. At last, warmed by the heat of the Holy Spirit, she began to be a flower and to breathe the fragrance of faith, the perfume of chastity, and the sweetness of grace.

4. Elsewhere he also adds: “Your eyes are doves, apart from your silence” (Song 4:1), because, wholly spiritual and simple like a dove—in whose form the Holy Spirit was seen by John to descend—she sees spiritual things and knows how to keep silent about the mysteries she has seen. To be silent is no ordinary virtue; there is a time for silence, just as there is a time for speaking, as it is also written: “The Lord gives me a tongue of instruction, that I may know when it is necessary to speak” (Isa. 50:4). [Col. 0306B]

5. Thus modesty is a kind of adornment of virginity, and silence commends it. Therefore the glory of the Church is also within, not in an excess of words, but in her dispositions and in the inner chambers of the mysteries, as she herself says to the Bridegroom: “Who will grant you to be my brother, nursing at the breasts of my mother? Finding you outside, I shall kiss you, and indeed they shall not despise me. I shall take you and lead you into the house of my mother, and into the secret place of her who conceived me” (Song 8:1–2). And above she says: “The king brought me into his chamber” (Song 1:3).

6. Outside, [Note: Four manuscripts read, “Christ kisses the Church.”] the Church kisses Christ, and is brought by him into the chamber. He kissed her outside “when, like a bridegroom coming forth from his bridal chamber, he rejoiced like a giant to run his course” (Ps. 18:6). He is a giant outside, because, “though he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but took the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:6–7). Therefore he who was within became outside. See him within, when you read that he is in the bosom of the Father; recognize him outside, when he seeks us in order to redeem us. He became outside himself so that he might be within me, [Note: All printed editions read, “and might become our physician …,” since Christ is the physician; all manuscripts have the reading translated in the main text.] and might be in our midst.

7. Let us therefore be where Christ is the mediator, rooted and established in our hearts. And therefore, as he himself commanded: “When you pray, enter into your chamber” (Matt. 6:6), and pour out your soul upon yourself. Your chamber is the secret place within; your chamber is your conscience. Thus Ecclesiastes says to you: “Do not curse the king even in your conscience, and do not curse the rich in the inner chambers of your bedchamber” (Eccles. 10:20). Pray there, then, and pray in secret, so that he who hears in secret may hear you; and pray without anger and dispute, “having renounced the hidden shame” (1 Tim. 2:8). [Note: All editions, together with one or two manuscripts, read “having renounced hidden shame”; other manuscripts, more appropriately, read “having renounced the hidden shame,” that is, having rejected even hidden disgrace or guilt.] For the righteous man fears not the exposure of his crime but its contamination.

## CHAPTER TWO

Prayer must begin with the praises of God and, after our petitions have been set forth, end in thanksgiving. It is commended by peace and tranquility; on this occasion the Gospel passage concerning the conduct commanded of virgins is explained with exceptional clarity.

8. How good is prayer together with mercy! Good is the prayer that observes its order, so that we begin first with divine praises. If, when we plead before a human being, we wish to make the judge favorably disposed, how much more when we entreat our Lord! Let us therefore first offer God the sacrifice of praise; hence the Apostle also says: “I urge, first of all, that supplications, prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings be made” (1 Tim. 2:1).

9. Let the eighth Psalm of David teach you. It begins with the praises of God: “O Lord, our Lord, how wonderful is your name in all the earth! For your majesty has been exalted above the heavens. From the mouth of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise” (Ps. 8:2 and following). Up to this point it is prayer; then comes supplication, that the enemy may be destroyed; petition, that he may see the moon and the stars—the moon signifying the Church, the stars the children of the Church, shining with the light of heavenly grace—and what he asks he promises, in the prophetic spirit, that he will see; thanksgiving, because the Lord watches over the human being and strengthens this clay of our body by divine visitation, [Col. 0308A] or because he subjected to humanity all the classes of living creatures.

10. Likewise the Lord’s Prayer embraces everything, and it is not necessary to explain it in ordinary fashion. But you who read this, recognize how you ought to distinguish its parts. Above all, however, prayer must be commended, as I said before, by calmness and tranquility of spirit, so that each person may be consistent and harmonious with himself, and that what is written may be fulfilled: “If two of you agree on earth about anything whatever that they ask, it will be done for them by my Father who is in heaven. For where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them” (Matt. 18:19–20). [Note: These words indicate that the Lord’s Prayer was among those mysteries that the Church once concealed from catechumens. Chrysostom gives this reason in *Homily 21 on Matthew*: one who has not been reborn through holy baptism may not call God “Father.” Thus, from the *Roman Order* and Amalarius Fortunatus, *On Ecclesiastical Offices* 8, we learn that, with a brief interpretation according to Roman custom, it was accustomed to be delivered to the candidates on Wednesday of the fourth week of Lent. Augustine testifies that in the African Church this was customarily done only on the Monday after Palm Sunday (*Homily 42 of 50*, now Sermon 58 in the new edition). Yet both agree that these candidates had to recite the same prayer from memory on Holy Saturday. Moreover, when explaining the qualities of prayer, Ambrose uses a passage from 1 Timothy 2:1, the Lord’s Prayer, and Psalm 8; and in the same Psalm he says that the moon signifies the Church and the stars the faithful. Similar material may be read in *On the Sacraments* VI.5, so similar that it seems doubtful whether, if different authors wrote these works, one did not use the other; or, if one and the same author wrote them, whether Ambrose did not reproduce his own material—which is by no means unusual for him.]

11. Who are these two, unless the soul and the body? Hence Paul also “disciplined his flesh and brought it into servitude” (1 Cor. 9:27), so that the flesh might be subject to the soul as to its queen and obey the commands of the mind; lest there be dissension in one person, and he wage war within himself, and the law of the body resist the law of the mind. Thus he joined these two, distinct in a certain respect, in peace, according to his own assertion: “For Christ is our peace, who made both one and broke down the dividing wall of hostility in his flesh” (Eph. 2:14), so that he might not do what he did not wish, nor do what he hated. These two, then, are soul and flesh. Hence David also says: “I will not fear what flesh can do to me” (Ps. 55:5), since he knew flesh to be the adversary of his soul.

12. Yet, to express these two more clearly, they are not merely two, but also two human beings: one inward, the other outward.
