[Note: The editions read, “If these two, when set before themselves in equality, meet”; the latest Paris edition reads “in inequality”; but all the manuscripts, which we follow here, more suitably have the reading translated in the main text.] If these two meet in equal accord, so that thoughts agree with deeds and deeds with thoughts, the wheel of our life will revolve without any stumbling, so that what is written may be fulfilled: “The sound of your thunder was in the wheel” (Ps. 77:19). These two, then, are one—not merely one, but one human being. Hence the Apostle says: “That he might create the two in one human being, making peace, and reconcile both in one body to God through the cross, killing the hostility in himself … so that through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father” (Eph. 2:15 and following).

13. There are also two human beings: the old and the new. [Note: The Codex Vallensis reads, “that old man subject to sin … worn away by anxiety.”] The old man is subject to sin and worn out, worn and torn like an old garment; we fasten him to the cross in baptism. Hence the Apostle says: “Our old man was crucified with him, so that the body of sin might be destroyed, and we might no longer serve sin” (Rom. 6:6). The old man is therefore fastened to the cross so that he may die to sin, so that the new man may rise, renewed by grace. We have spoken of the two.

14. Perhaps someone may say: What do you say about three, since Scripture says: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them” (Matt. 18:20)? Here too the explanation is clear, because the same Apostle says: “May the God of peace himself sanctify you completely, and may your spirit and soul and body be kept blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Thess. 5:23). [Note: On these three elements of which Ambrose teaches that the human being consists, see what we observed in book I of the *Exposition of Luke*, column 1277, and book VII of the same *Exposition*, column 1460.] Where these three are complete, there Christ is in their midst: he governs and rules these three within and composes them in faithful peace.

15. Let the virgin therefore guard these three things intact within herself above all else, so that she may give no cause for complaint against sacred virginity and may be blameless, without wrinkle and without stain. Although we have spoken of it in numerous books, we have nevertheless judged it fitting, for the sake of the aforementioned pledge, to compose this book for you. [Note: “The aforementioned pledge” means Ambrosia, mentioned at the very beginning of the book: “You commend to me your pledge, Ambrosia,” and so forth. As for the books in which Ambrose says that he has discussed virginity, we do not understand him to mean only those that he composed on this subject and under this title; we include other works as well, wherever the occasion arose to discuss this very virtue, which he never failed to take up eagerly. So deeply was he committed to acting everywhere as a teacher of virginity.]

## CHAPTER THREE

The female sex must not be blamed, since God has bestowed such gifts upon it. God did not approve the human being immediately upon creating him, both because human dignity consists not in the body but in the soul and in the divine image, and because the human being is to be praised only at the completion of the whole work; furthermore, woman had not yet been created, although she was formed from man and was to express with him the figure of a great sacrament, from which she is also shown to have received her name.

16. Excellent is virginity, which not only absolved both sexes from guilt but also summoned them to grace. We usually accuse the female sex because it introduced the cause of error, without considering how much more justly the reproach may be turned back upon us. For, returning to the beginning and questioning the origins of things, we shall investigate how much honor was bestowed upon woman and how, even in the miserable condition of human frailty, she nevertheless found grace.

17. When God had praised all his works—heaven, earth, the seas, night and day, the latter having been made for the use of labor and the former for the fruit of rest—and had praised the wild beasts, when he came to the human being, the one for whose sake all things were generated, he alone does not seem to have been praised (Gen. 2:10 and following). What is the reason, unless perhaps it is that other things exist in their outward form, while the human being is hidden? In animals you find nothing greater than what is seen; in the human being nothing is lower than what is seen. Although he consists of soul and body, what is visible in him serves; what is invisible rules in him. [Note: Some manuscripts read, “since he consists of soul,” and so forth.]

18. Therefore the others are rightly praised at the beginning, while the praise of the human being is not brought forth but reserved, because the grace of the others is outward, whereas his is inward; theirs is in birth, his in the heart. For what is as high and as deep as the human mind, which is covered and concealed as if by a kind of bodily wrapping, so that no one can easily look within and contemplate it? Therefore the human being is not praised beforehand, because he must first be tested and then proclaimed—not in his outward skin, as in a public forum, but in the inner person. The Apostle Peter beautifully defined him when he said that the person of the heart is hidden in the incorruptibility of a quiet and gentle spirit, which is precious before God (1 Pet. 3:4). [Col. 0310B]

19. It is rightly delayed, so that his praise may follow after it has earned interest; its delay is not loss but increase. Let no one therefore despise himself [Note: All editions, together with four manuscripts, have the reading translated in the main text, except that those manuscripts read “the slight” instead of “the worthless,” and “to be” instead of “himself”; other manuscripts read, “as if worthless, and let him not consider himself contemptible.”] as worthless, nor value himself by the appearance of his body. Even though holy Job said: “Naked I came from my mother’s womb, and naked shall I return there” (Job 1:21), he nevertheless possessed something by which he could be found rich not only among human beings but also before God.

20. What is richer than being made in the image and likeness of God? The human being made in the image is the inward man, not this outward one; he is evaluated by understanding and cannot be grasped by the eyes. He, therefore, is the one we must contemplate, though he is investigated only later. God therefore did not think the making of the human being should be praised, because his greater portion lies in virtue. His appearance is indeed splendid and superior to that of the other living creatures; but irrational creatures should be judged by the beauty of their bodies, whereas those filled with reason should reserve a common praise.

21. Let the human being therefore stand out and excel for me not so much in face as in disposition, so that he may be praised in those things in which God also is praised by prophetic judgment. Of God it is written: “Terrible in counsels above the sons of men” (Ps. 66:5). Let his works shine before God, as he weaves together good things through constant works; and therefore his praise is not at the beginning but at the end, for no one is crowned unless he has competed lawfully. Hence the Wise Man says to you: “Before death, praise no one” (Eccles. 11:30). The reason for this he taught above when he said: “For at the end of a person his works are revealed” (ibid., 29).

22. Let us consider the third point, in which God made his judgment manifest. When he had made the human being and placed him in paradise to work and guard it, he said that it was not good for the human being to be alone. “Let us make,” he said, “a helper corresponding to him” (Gen. 2:18). Without woman, therefore, man has no praise; in woman he is proclaimed. For when he says that it is not good for the human being to be alone, he certainly confirms that it is good for the human race if the female sex is joined to the male.

23. We must also consider that man was made from earth and clay, while woman was made from man. The flesh, indeed, is clay; but the former was still unformed, while the latter was formed.

24. Let us now summon that splendid Apostolic example written in Scripture: “A man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh. This is a great mystery; but I speak of Christ and the Church” (Eph. 5:31–32). [Note: Some manuscripts read, “Therefore we have heard.” In the older editions this was the beginning of the following chapter. Let the discerning reader judge how beautifully the passage fits.] We therefore perceive that through woman that heavenly mystery of the Church was fulfilled, and that in her the grace was represented for whose sake Christ descended and completed the eternal work of human redemption. Hence Adam called his woman “Life” (Gen. 2:23), for through woman the succession and offspring of the human race are spread among peoples, and through the Church eternal life is conferred. [Note: Three manuscripts read, “and through the Church the regenerated children of God are increased”; the other manuscripts and editions differ only in that the former read “is conferred,” while the latter read “is acquired.”]

## CHAPTER FOUR

That woman’s sin was lighter than man’s is demonstrated by the difference of sex, the circumstances of the temptation, the divine sentence, and the responses of both. After this, remedies are prescribed for men against women’s temptations, especially imitation of women who fast.

25. Certainly we cannot deny that the woman erred. [Note: Some manuscripts read, “What wonder, then, if the weaker sex fell?”] Yet why are you surprised that she erred, if the weaker sex fell, when the stronger also fell? The woman has an excuse in her sin; the man has none. She, as Scripture declares, was deceived by the wisest of all serpents; you were deceived by a woman. That is, a superior creature deceived her, but an inferior one deceived you. A woman deceived you; an evil, though nevertheless angelic, creature deceived her. If you could not resist an inferior, how could she have resisted a superior? Your guilt absolves her. [Note: It may be noted in passing that the doctrine defended by Ambrose throughout this chapter—that Eve’s sin was lighter than Adam’s—is in a certain respect opposed to what Saint Thomas teaches in *Summa Theologiae* II–II, question 163, article 4. Although he admits that Adam’s guilt must be considered graver than Eve’s because of the condition of his person, he nevertheless asserts that, in itself and by its nature, it was lighter. Consult him, together with Nicholas’s notes on the same passage.]

26. If you doubt the relative merit of the guilt, let us question the sentence. To her it was said: “In sorrow you shall bear children, and your turning shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule over you” (ibid., 16). But to the man it was said: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (ibid., 19). And truly it was a just sentence. For if Adam could not preserve what he had heard from the Lord God, how could the woman preserve what she heard from the man? If the voice of God did not strengthen him, how could a human voice strengthen her? [Note: All editions read, “And truly, according to this sentence”; all manuscripts more suitably have the reading translated in the main text.]

27. Finally, when Adam was summoned to account because he had tasted contrary to the divine commands he had heard with his own ears, he had nothing to say except that the woman had given him the fruit and he had eaten. But the woman said: “The serpent deceived me, and I ate” (ibid., 13). How much greater is the woman’s acquittal! He is accused; she is questioned. Add to this that he first confesses his guilt; for she who says that she was deceived testifies to her error. Confession, therefore, is the medicine of error.

28. In the judgment itself, how much more lenient was the woman than the man! He accused his wife; she accused the serpent—that is, she did not, even when accused, turn the charge back against him. Rather, she preferred, if she could, to absolve her accuser than to bind him.

29. You have, therefore, both the absolution of guilt in the confession [Col. 0312B] and the execution of the sentence in its fulfillment. “In sorrow,” he says, “you shall bear children.” [Note: The Roman edition has *commendationis suae* (“of her commendation”). This is indeed a typographical error, but one that was subsequently propagated in all the Paris editions.] She acknowledges the weight of her condemnation and carries out the duty of her penal condition. For your sake the woman struggles through her pains, ^256 and finds a reward through punishment, so that through the children by whom she is afflicted she may be set free. Thus grace came from injury, salvation from weakness; for it is written: “She will be saved through the bearing of children” (1 Tim. 2:15). Thus she gives birth with salvation to those whom she brought forth in sorrow, and raises to praise those whom she bore in pain.

30. But you say, O man, that the woman was a temptation to the man. It is true. If she is beautiful, then here is another temptation. Yet the beauty of Abraham’s wife did not harm him when he went down into Egypt; rather, it benefited him greatly. He was honored through his wife, not made a laughingstock on account of her (Gen. 12:16, 20). Why do you seek beauty of face in your wife rather than beauty of character? Let your wife please you more by her uprightness than by her beauty. Let her be chosen who resembles Sarah in character. It is not the woman’s fault that she is what she was born to be; but it is the man’s fault to seek in his wife what so often becomes a temptation to him. If he is the weaker, the woman herself may stumble; if he is the stronger, the man is endangered. We cannot criticize the work of the divine craftsman; but if bodily beauty delights anyone, let that inner beauty delight him much more—the beauty made in the image of God, more adorned within than without.

31. If, therefore, your wife is a temptation, be more cautious and seek a remedy against the danger of temptation: “Watch and pray,” he says, “lest you enter into temptation” (Matt. 26:41). The Lord said this; the man heard it; the woman fulfilled it. [Col. 0312D] Every day women fast, and observe fasts that were not imposed upon them: they acknowledge their sin and summon a remedy. Once the woman ate of what had been forbidden, [Col. 0313A] and every day she makes amends by fasting. [Note: The editions and certain manuscripts read *jejunium solvit* (“she makes amends by fasting”).] [Note: Paulinus wrote in the Life of Ambrose that Ambrose used these very words against Theodosius when he barred him from entering the Church after the massacre at Thessalonica. Yet this statement cannot be found elsewhere in Ambrose’s works.] You who followed the one who was wandering, follow the one who is correcting herself. Both of you ate; why does she alone fast? That is, both of you sinned; why does she alone seek a remedy for the error?

## CHAPTER V

The sentence of condemnation is shown to have been released in Sarah, and much more so in Mary, who gave birth to God while preserving her virginity intact; she also displayed the sign of that same virtue. The impudence of the heretics who denied that she remained a virgin is exposed, and their arguments drawn from the Gospels are refuted.

32. Come, Eve, now sober; come, Eve, although once intemperate in yourself, now fasting in your offspring. Come, Eve, now such that you are not excluded from paradise but carried up to heaven. Come, Eve, now Sarah, who bears children not in sorrow but in rejoicing, not in grief but in laughter. A manyfold Isaac will be born to you. Come again, Eve, now Sarah, of whom it is said to the man: “Listen to Sarah your wife” (Gen. 21:12). You may indeed be subject to the man, as is fitting for you; yet you have quickly canceled the sentence, so that the man is commanded to listen to you.

^257 33. If Sarah, by giving birth to the type of Christ, deserves to be heard by the man, how much does the sex that gave birth to Christ—while preserving virginity—advance! [Note: It is better known than to require proof that Isaac, destined by his father’s will for sacrifice, was a type of Christ.] Come, therefore, Eve, now Mary, who brought us not only the incentive to virginity but also brought God himself. Hence Isaiah, joyful and exultant at so great a gift, says: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isa. 7:14), which is interpreted as “God with us” (Matt. 1:23). Whence came this gift? Certainly not from earth. Rather, from heaven he chose and consecrated for himself this vessel through which Christ would descend, and he sanctified the temple of chastity. He descended through one woman, but called many. Hence Mary alone among women found this special designation of the Lord, which means: “God from my lineage.” [Note: The interpretation of the name *Maria* is not especially successful. But since Ambrose, as we have often seen, customarily consulted those skilled in Hebrew in similar matters, it should be thought that some half-learned person whom he mistakenly considered learned imposed it upon him. The etymology of the same word that follows immediately is preferable.]

34. Many women were also called Mary before Mary: for Mary, the sister of Aaron, was so called (Exod. 15:20, 23). But that Mary was called “bitterness of the sea.” The Lord therefore came into the bitterness of human frailty, so that the bitterness of our condition might be sweetened, tempered by the sweetness and grace of the heavenly Word. This was signified by the spring of Marah, sweetened by means of wood; for the people of the nations, previously bitter through sins, or our flesh, through the tempering of the Lord’s Passion, was to be changed into other uses. [Note: All editions read *fons Mara* (“the spring of Marah”), evidently following the Hebrew text and all versions except the Septuagint. In the latter we read: “They came to Marah, and they could not drink from Marah” (Ἦλθον δὲ εἰς Μερρᾶ, καὶ οὐκ ἠδύναντο πιεῖν ἐκ Μερρᾶς). Our manuscripts differ from this only in displaying *Mirra* instead of *Merrha*, through the scribes’ ignorance.]

35. Mary, therefore, is extraordinary: she raised up the sign of sacred virginity and erected for Christ the devout standard of undefiled integrity. Yet although all are summoned to the observance of virginity by the example of holy Mary, there were those who denied that she remained a virgin. We have long preferred to remain silent about so great a sacrilege. But since the matter has brought it into the open, so that even a bishop may be accused of this lapse, we do not think that he should be left uncondemned. [Note: It is beyond dispute that the bishop indicated here without being named was Bonosus, whose case the Council of Capua had referred to neighboring bishops. It is less clear, however, what episcopal see he held. Garnerius repeatedly claims—in his notes on Marius Mercator, pp. 115 and 130, and in Dissertation 1, *On the Heresy and Books of Nestorius*, §6—that Bonosus presided over the metropolitan see of Sardica. Baron(ius), under the year 389, Petavius in vol. 4 of *Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, book 14, and other distinguished writers confess that this was unknown to them, and that they learned it from a work prepared by Mercator and first published by Garnerius. Garnerius is supported by the fact that he says Bonosus’s case was entrusted to Anysius of Thessalonica and the Macedonian bishops as neighboring authorities, because the canons did not permit suffragan bishops to judge their own primate. Nevertheless, Lucas Holstenius, in his *Geographical Notes on the Roman Patriarchate*, pp. 122–123, maintains that Bonosus held the see of Naissus, a city that he places here and in his notes on Hortellius in Dacia. One might object to Holstenius that, if Bonosus had been a suffragan of the metropolitan see of Sardica, the Fathers of Capua ought, according to the canons, to have referred him to his own primate—unless it is considered highly plausible that he had appealed from a condemnation already imposed by that primate, and that the Capuan assembly entrusted the Macedonians with hearing the appeal. For the letter of Innocent cited by Holstenius must be of the greatest weight: it states that priests and deacons were ordained by Bonosus in the Church of Naissus, something the canons granted only to the proper bishop, not to the primate. We may therefore believe that, in Garnerius’s manuscripts, some word—perhaps *provinciae* (“of the province”) or another similar term—was omitted after *Sardicensis*. The learned Hermannus, who also followed Holstenius, may be consulted on this matter in *Life of Ambrose*, book 7, chapter 7. Nor should it be omitted that Augustine does not appear to have known this heresy, since he makes no mention of it in his *Catalogue*. Indeed, when discussing the heresy of Jovinian, whose follower Bonosus was, he denies that any bishop who had allowed himself to be infected by the same error had ever been found.]

We read that the woman herself was also called such, just as the Lord himself said at Cana of Galilee when she said to him, “They have no wine,” and he replied: “Woman, what is that to me and to you?” (John 2:3, 5). Elsewhere we read what Matthew said about Joseph and Mary: “She was found to be with child before they came together, having conceived from the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 1:18). And below: “He did not know her until she had given birth” (ibid., 1:25). And again concerning Joseph: “He did not wish to expose her” (Matt. 1:19). The brothers of the Lord also seem to indicate that they were born from Mary. And the Apostle says: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law” (Gal. 4:4). Each of these points must be unraveled for us, [Note: The edition reads *notanda nobis sunt* (“they must be noted by us”); the manuscripts more appropriately read *enodanda* (“they must be unraveled”), and so forth. Moreover, the objections collected here were not new, nor were they peculiar to the Bonosians, as may be understood from Jerome, *Against Helvidius*, and Epiphanius, *Against the Antidicomarians.] so that anyone who reads them may not be bound by arguments of this kind. Let us therefore answer them in order.

36. Why should we be troubled by the word “woman”? It refers to sex; it is not a word for corruption but for sex. Common usage does not prejudice the truth. Indeed, virginity first received this name. For when God had taken one of Adam’s ribs and filled in flesh in its place, Scripture says: “He built it into a woman” (Gen. 2:22). Certainly she did not yet know a man, and already she was called “woman.” Scripture did not conceal the reason for the name either, saying: “Because Adam said: ‘Bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh. She shall be called woman, because she was taken from her man’” (ibid., 2:23). “Because she was taken,” it says, “from her man,” not because she had experienced a man. Thus, as long as she was in paradise, she was called woman, and she had not been known by a man. But after she had been expelled from paradise, we read that Adam knew Eve his wife, and then she conceived and bore a son (Gen. 4:1). The first knot, therefore, has been untied.

37. The second question arises because it is written: “Before they came together, she was found to be with child” (Matt. 1:18). But it is the custom of divine Scripture to establish the matter that has been undertaken and defer an incidental matter. [Note: An incidental cause, or question, is a secondary and less important heading.]

38. This also resolves the third question, where it is said: “He did not know her until she had given birth to her Son” (ibid., 1:25). What then? Did he know her afterward? Certainly not. For you have it written: “I am God, and until you grow old, I am” (Isa. 46:4). Did God, then, cease to be God after those to whom “until” was spoken had grown old? Likewise, in the prophecy of David we read: “The Lord said to my Lord: ‘Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet’” (Ps. 109:1). After the peoples of the nations had been subjected—those who had previously seemed enemies because they denied the author of salvation and served idols—did the Son cease to sit at the Father’s right hand, or will he not sit there forever?

39. What prejudice is there against Mary if Joseph did not understand the mystery of the heavenly plan and thought that the virgin was not a virgin when he saw that she was pregnant? The angels did not know his resurrection either, as the verses signify: “Lift up the gates, ^259 your princes, [Note: The Roman edition, following one Vatican manuscript, reads *principes vestri* (“your princes”), which Augustine also read, evidently following the Septuagint, where we find οἱ ἄρχοντες ὑμῶν (“your rulers”). The other Ambrosian manuscripts and the old editions read *principes vestras*, as does the Vulgate and the Arabic version. The Hebrew text and the other versions, however, have: “Lift up your heads, O gates.” That the angels are said not to have known the Lord’s resurrection was already taught by Ambrose in book 2 of his *Commentary on Luke*, no. 15. He presents the same doctrine in book 4 of *On the Faith*, chapter 1, and in *On the Sacraments of Initiation*, chapter 7, in very similar language. The author of *On the Celestial Hierarchy*, chapter 7, §3, explains it at greater length; the Angelic Doctor raises and resolves the same difficulty in part 1, question 107, article 4, reply to objection 4; consult him.] and be lifted up, eternal gates, and the King of glory shall enter. Who is this King of glory?” (Ps. 23:7–8). They ask as though they do not know, and others answer: “The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle; he is the King of glory.” The Prophet repeated the same verses, and nevertheless they again asked as though they did not know; for it is written: “Lift up the gates, your princes, and be lifted up, eternal gates, and the King of glory shall enter. Who is this King of glory?” (ibid., 9–10). How, then, could a human being know the divine secret that the angels did not know? In the book of Isaiah you also have: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with the red of his garments from Bosor?” (Isa. 63:1). Yet it was certainly less remarkable for a man to rise again than for a virgin to give birth. For the dead had already risen through Elijah’s prayers and Elisha’s supplications (1 Kings 17:22; 2 Kings 4:17); but never before, and never afterward, did a virgin give birth.

40. Joseph formed this opinion because he intended to expose her as though she were guilty, before he was warned by the angel (Matt. 1:20). Afterwards, as a faithful man without doubt, he preserved the angel’s declaration concerning her virginity.

## CHAPTER VI

After two other objections concerning the same matter have been resolved, it is added that it would have been absurd if Christ had chosen a mother who would not remain a virgin, or had denied her the most glorious gifts of virginity.

41. Nor should the statement trouble us that “Joseph took his wife and departed into Egypt” (Matt. 1:24). A woman betrothed to a man received the name “wife.” For when a marriage is initiated, the name of marriage is assumed (27, q. 2, *Cum initiatur*, 1 and 2). [Note: It is clear from this passage that Ambrose places the nature of marriage not in consummation but in mutual consent. Jerome, Augustine, and the other Fathers agree with him in this; Gratian later followed them in the *Decree*, as did Peter Lombard in book 4 of the *Sentences*, distinction 27, and other canonists and theologians.] It is not the deflowering of virginity that makes a marriage, but the marital agreement. Thus, when a girl is joined to a man, there is a marriage—not when she is known through intercourse with a man.

42. Although we have discussed elsewhere at greater length the fact that she was betrothed in marriage, it is enough for the present to touch upon the reason for the heavenly mystery: so that those who saw Mary pregnant would believe not that her virginity had been violated by adultery, but that the child of a betrothed woman was legitimate. For the Lord preferred that some should doubt his own birth rather than his mother’s chastity. [Note: The Roman edition alone reads *cum alibi plenius dixerimus* (“although we have said more fully elsewhere”), but the word should be retained on the authority of the other editions and manuscripts. More is signified here than is expressed; after the words “we shall say more fully,” the sense seems to require a mental supplement. The reference is to book 2 of the *Exposition of Luke*, where not only this objection but the others as well are answered at length. This also shows that when the holy man above said, “we have long preferred to remain silent,” he meant not the doctrine itself but only the persons whom he had deliberately left unnamed there.]

[Col. 0317A] 43. The Lord himself teaches that relatives by nation and lineage, and even members of a people, may be called brothers, when he says: “I will declare your name to my brothers; in the midst of the Church I will praise you” (Ps. 21:23). Paul also says: “I could wish that I myself were accursed for the sake of my brothers” (Rom. 9:3). They could have been brothers from Joseph, not from Mary. Whoever pursues this matter more carefully will discover the point. We have not thought it necessary to pursue it, since it is clear that the name “brother” is common to many relationships. [Note: Jerome reports and refutes this opinion in his commentary on Galatians 1; the theological school generally agrees with him on this point.]

44. Would the Lord Jesus choose for himself as mother a woman who could defile the heavenly dwelling with male seed, as though she were incapable of preserving the guardianship of virginal chastity? By her example other women are summoned to pursue integrity, while she herself would depart from the very gift that was set before the others as their model.

45. And what greater merit than that of a mother would the Lord have esteemed, what reward would he have reserved for her? [Note: Those who defend Mary’s inviolate conception customarily extend this Ambrosian principle as widely as possible; proponents of the opposing view maintain that it must be restricted within definite limits. Certainly it cannot be denied that limits must sometimes be assigned to it; on this matter see Théophile Raynaud, *Diptycha Mariana*, in more than one place.] For he assigned no more abundant gifts to anyone than to virginity, as Scripture teaches us. Thus the Lord spoke through Isaiah: “Let not the eunuch say, ‘Behold, I am a dry tree.’ Thus says the Lord to the eunuchs: Whoever keeps my commandments, chooses what I desire, and embraces my covenant, I will give them in my house and within my walls a named place, better than sons and daughters; I will give them an everlasting name, and they shall not fail” (Isa. 56:3ff.). He promises others that they shall not fail; would he have allowed his mother to fail? But Mary does not fail; the teacher of virginity does not fail. Nor could it happen that she who had carried God should think that a human being was to be carried by her. Nor would Joseph, a just man, have plunged into such madness as to join himself to the Lord’s mother in bodily intercourse.

## CHAPTER VII

After it has been proved that Mary remained in virginal integrity because she was given as mother to the disciple, her purpose of virginity is confirmed by the fact that she could not have changed it: such was her steadfastness during her Son’s Passion and her virtue during the Baptist’s exultation.

46. Yet Mary should be defended by her own character, not by that of others. She did not fail, as I said. The Son of God himself is witness: while he was on the cross, he commended the disciple to his mother as her son and entrusted her to the disciple as his mother (John 19:26–27). John, who wrote more mystically, teaches this. [Note: If one compares nearly everything said in this chapter with book 2 of *On Luke*, no. 130ff., and with the corresponding passage in the letter to the Vercellans, one will find such agreement that it cannot be denied that the three works have the same author.] The other Evangelists wrote that during the Lord’s Passion the earth trembled, the sun withdrew, and pardon was requested for the persecutors (Matt. 27:51ff.). But this beloved disciple of the Lord, who had drawn from the Lord’s breast the secrets of wisdom and the mysteries of his gracious will, passed over what the others had related and pursued this point more carefully, so as to confirm by his own judgment the continuance of his mother’s virginity (John 13:23), like a son concerned for his mother’s chastity, lest anyone stain her with the great reproach of violated integrity.

47. For it was fitting that the one who granted pardon to the thief should absolve his mother from every doubt concerning her chastity. He says to his mother: “Woman, behold your son.” And he says to the disciple: “Behold your mother” (Luke 23:43; John 19:26–27). The disciple is the one to whom the mother is entrusted. How could he take a wife from her husband if Mary had been joined in marriage or had known the use of the marital bed? [Note: Two matters must be noted here. First, whether Ambrose, who at the beginning of the preceding chapter seemed to acknowledge a true marriage between Mary and Joseph, contradicts himself here. Second, whether the scholastics rightly derive from this Ambrosian teaching their distinction between a ratified marriage and a consummated marriage. The holy Doctor does not contradict himself. Here he denies only that a wife from whom a husband has fathered children, or with whom he has had marital relations, can be taken away from him without injury. But a woman who has always lived with her husband as with a brother may rightly be separated from her husband’s companionship, provided the purpose for which they were joined has been removed. It does not follow at all that the marital bond is dissolved in this way or that those so separated may enter a new marriage with others, although the theologians mentioned defend the possibility of deriving that conclusion from this passage.]

48. [Note: This was the beginning of chapter 7; but since it is clear that it had been placed here, as had the beginnings of the next two chapters, in an inappropriate location, we did not hesitate to transfer it, like the other chapter openings mentioned, to a more suitable place; and this is what we have done.] Close your mouths, impious men; open your ears, devout ones; hear what Christ says. The Lord Jesus gives testimony from the cross (John 19:26), and for a little while postpones the salvation of the world so as not to leave his mother dishonored. John is added as witness to Christ’s testament. Let the defense of his mother’s chastity be read; let the testimony of her integrity be read. Let the disciple’s guardianship of his mother also be read, a sign of filial devotion. “And from that hour the disciple took her into his own home” (ibid., 19:27). Certainly Christ was not divorcing her, nor was Mary abandoning her husband. But with whom should the virgin live, except with the one whom she knew to be the heir of her Son and the guardian of her integrity?

49. The mother stood before the cross, and while the men fled, she stood without fear. Consider whether the mother of Jesus could have changed her chastity when she did not change her courage. She gazed with devoted eyes upon the wounds of her Son, through whom she knew redemption would come to all. She stood before a spectacle worthy of a mother, not fearing the executioner. The Son hung upon the cross; the mother offered herself to the persecutors. If the only purpose had been to cast herself before her Son, her devoted affection would be praiseworthy, since she did not wish to outlive him. But if she desired to die with her Son, she also longed to rise with him, not ignorant of the mystery that she had given birth to one who would rise again. At the same time, since she knew that the death of her Son had been offered for the benefit of the world, she awaited the possibility that her own death might add something to that public gift. But Christ’s Passion needed no assistance, as the Lord himself had foretold long before: “I looked, and there was no helper; I searched, and no one supported me; and I delivered them by my own arm” (Isa. 63:5).

50. How, then, could Mary’s integrity have been wrested from her? When the apostles fled, she did not fear punishment but offered herself to danger. So great was her grace that she not only preserved in herself the grace of virginity but also bestowed the mark of integrity upon those whom she visited. She visited John the Baptist, and he leaped in his mother’s womb before he was born (Luke 1:41). At Mary’s voice the infant leaped, obeying before he had been born. And not without reason did he remain pure in body, whom the mother of the Lord had, for three months, exercised by a kind of oil and ointment of her presence and integrity. Afterwards she was entrusted to John the Evangelist, who knew nothing of marriage. Therefore I am not surprised that he spoke of divine mysteries more than the others, since the dwelling of heavenly sacraments was present with him.

## CHAPTER VIII

The testimonies of Ezekiel, especially the one concerning the gate that was not to be opened, are applied to Mary: through her Christ alone passed without opening it, and he strengthened it so that afterward it was not opened even to Joseph.

51. Now let those who raise this question tell me what the Lord says through the prophet: “Now I will restore the captivity of Jacob and have mercy again upon the house of Israel” (Ezek. 39:25). [Note: This is the reading of the old editions and manuscripts, supported by the Syriac version. The Roman edition reads *reducam* (“I will bring back”), with the Hebrew text and the remaining versions; the Septuagint has *Ἐν τῷ ἀποστρέψαι με* (“when I turn back …”).] And below: “I will gather them from the nations, and I will gather them from the lands of the peoples, and I will be sanctified in them before the nations. And they shall know that I am the Lord their God, when I appear to them among the nations. And I will no longer turn my face away from them, because I poured out my anger upon the house of Israel, says the Lord” (ibid., 27ff.).

52. Further on the prophet says that he saw, upon a very high mountain, a city being built (Ezek. 40:2ff.), whose many gates are described; one, however, is described as closed. Concerning it he says: [Note: The Roman edition, following the Hebrew text and all the versions, reads “And he turned me”; the old editions and manuscripts read “And I turned myself.” Perhaps Ambrose’s manuscript had ἐπέστρεψα (“I turned”) instead of ἐπέστρεψε (“he turned”), an easy alteration.] “And I turned according to the way of the gate of the sanctuary on the outside, which faces east, and it was closed. And the Lord said to me: ‘This gate shall be closed; it shall not be opened, and no one shall pass through it, because the Lord God of Israel shall pass through it. And it shall be closed, because this leader shall sit in it to eat bread before the Lord. He shall enter by the way of the vestibule of the gate and shall go out by the same way’” (Ezek. 44:1ff.). [Note: We have restored from the manuscripts the word *Aelam*, absent from all the editions. It is also found in the Septuagint; the other versions render it “the way of the gate’s vestibule” or “portico.”] What is this gate except Mary? It was closed because she was a virgin. Mary, therefore, is the gate through which Christ entered this world when he was poured forth in a virginal birth, and he did not break open the closed barriers of virginity. The enclosure of chastity remained undefiled, and the seals of integrity remained inviolate, when he came forth from the virgin whose greatness the world could not contain. [Note: This passage completely resolves the difficulty raised by another passage in book 2 of the *Exposition of Luke*, where Christ is said to have opened his mother’s womb. There Ambrose shows that he spoke in that manner only to adapt his language to Moses’ wording. He intended to signify nothing except Christ’s emergence, while the barriers and signs of virginity remained as they had been before the birth, during the birth, and afterward. See what we noted in the cited book of the *Exposition of Luke*, col. 1300, no. 57.]

53. “This gate,” he says, “shall be closed, and it shall not be opened.” Mary is a good gate, which was closed and was not opened. Christ passed through it, but did not open it.

54. And to show that every human being has a gate through which Christ enters: “Lift up,” he says, “your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, eternal gates, and the King of glory shall enter” (Ps. 23:7). How much more, then, was there a gate in Mary, in whom Christ sat and from whom he came forth? For there is also a gate of the womb. Hence holy Job says: “Let the stars of that night be darkened, because it did not close the gates of my mother’s womb” (Job 3:9–10).

55. There is, therefore, also a gate of the womb, but it is not always closed. Yet one alone could remain closed: the gate through which the birth came forth without loss to the virgin’s bodily barriers. Therefore the prophet says: “This gate shall be closed; it shall not be opened, and no one shall pass through it”—that is, no human being—“because the Lord God of Israel shall pass through it.” “And it shall be closed,” that is, it shall be closed both before and after the Lord’s passage. It shall not be opened by anyone, nor has it been opened, because it always had Christ as its door, and he said: “I am the door” (John 10:7), whom no one could tear away from it. [Note: The edition reads: “but not every one is always closed.”]

56. This gate faced east, because it poured forth the true light: it gave birth to the East and bore the Sun of righteousness. Let the foolish hear, then: “This gate shall be closed,” he says, “which receives only the God of Israel.” Could the one of whom it was said to the Church, “For he has strengthened the bars of your gates” (Ps. 147:13), not strengthen his own gate? Certainly he strengthened it and preserved it intact. Indeed, it was not opened.

57. Let them therefore hear the prophet saying: “It shall not be opened, and it shall be closed”—that is, it shall not be opened by the man to whom she was betrothed. For it would not be permitted that the gate through which the Lord would pass should be opened. “And after him,” he says, “it shall remain closed”—that is, Joseph shall not open it, because it will be said to him: “Do not fear to take Mary your wife; for what has been born from her is of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 1:20).

## CHAPTER IX

How virginity is signified by various symbols, and what sacred virgins should learn from each of them.

58. A closed gate, therefore, is virginity; and a closed garden is virginity; and a sealed fountain is virginity. Hear, virgin, with attentive and open ears, and with chastity closed, open your hands so that the poor may recognize you. Close your door, lest an invader enter. Open your mind; preserve the seal.

59. Virginity is also a branch from the root, for it is written: “A branch shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root” (Isa. 11:1). This branch is not hollow but solid. Let no one, therefore, burn your branch, so that you may guard your flower. You are a branch, O virgin; do not bend, do not curve toward the earth, so that the flower of your ancestral root may rise in you.

60. You are a closed garden, O virgin; preserve your fruits. ^264 Let thorns not grow up in you, but let your grapes flower. You are a closed garden, daughter; let no one remove the hedge of your chastity, for it is written: “Whoever breaks through a hedge will be bitten by a serpent” (Eccles. 10:8). Let him remove only that hedge of which it was said: “Why has the hedge been cut down?” (Gen. 38:29). Let no one destroy your wall, lest you become a place of trampling. You are paradise, O virgin; beware of Eve.

61. You are a sealed fountain, O virgin; let no one pollute your water, let no one disturb it, so that you may always behold your image in your fountain.

62. You are a closed gate, O virgin; let no one open your door, which the Holy and True One once closed—he who holds the key of David, who opens and no one closes, who closes and no one opens (Rev. 3:7). He opened the Scriptures to you; let no one close them. He closed your chastity; let no one open it.

## CHAPTER X

Virginity is suggested to be a crown in the Lord’s hand; Scripture reveals him as one, not second, just as it reveals the Father and the Spirit. The heretics raise an objection from the Gospel text, but when it is resolved by other testimonies, the Catholic faith concerning the Trinity is confirmed.

63. “I am coming quickly,” he says; “hold fast what you have, so that no one may take your crown” (Rev. 3:11). What is your crown except that of which it was said: “And you shall be a crown of beauty in the hand of the Lord” (Isa. 62:3)?

64. Who says this except the one of whom Ecclesiastes said: “There is one, and there is not a second” (Eccles. 4:8)? Who is this except the one of whom it was said: “Your teacher is one, Christ” (Matt. 23:10)? He is one because he is the only-begotten Son of God; because he alone, as it is written: “He alone stretches out the heavens and walks over the sea as on land” (Job 9:8).

He, therefore, is not second because he is first; he is not second because he is one: “One God the Father, from whom are all things, and we in him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through him” (1 Cor. 8:6). One God the Father, [Note: The edition reads “and one Son of God”; the manuscripts read, more appropriately, “and one God the Son.”] and one God the Son, and one Holy Spirit, as it is written: “All these things one and the same Spirit accomplishes, distributing to each one as he wills” (1 Cor. 12:11). “One,” he says, because there is one God. There is no second, because he does what he wills, not what is commanded. One, therefore, is God the Father, and one is the Son of God. One and one, because there are not two gods. The Son is one, because he is one with the Father, as he himself said: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:29). And the Spirit is one, because he is the unity of the Trinity, distinguished neither by order nor by time.

65. But [Note: [Col. 0321D] A question may arise here whether by the word “they say” the Bonosians are to be understood. Certainly neither Ambrose above, in chapter 5, nor Bonosius, in the letter in which he referred his own judgment to the bishops of Macedonia, attributes this heresy to them. Yet it is not difficult to reply that, in a work undertaken for the instruction of a virgin, the error diametrically opposed to virginity had first of all to be refuted; whereas at the Council of Capua there was need to deal only with the doctrine proper to those heretics, since the doctrine they shared with the Arians had already been sufficiently and more than sufficiently pierced through by the authority of the Church. Nevertheless, the same bishop does not at all neglect to refute it incidentally here, because one who has denied Christ’s divinity will scarcely ever hold a correct opinion concerning Mary’s perpetual virginity. Moreover, you may understand that the Bonosians are designated here, and not without reason, from the fact that the Photinians—whom it is agreed arose from the Arian heresy as the most bitter enemies of Christ’s eternity—were afterward so confused with them that, having lost their own name, they passed into the designation “Bonosians,” as Gennadius testifies in his *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 14. The Second Council of Arles, canons 16 and 17, likewise teaches that the Bonosians derive from the error of the Photinians, although what is reported there concerning the baptism of the two groups indicates that there was some difference in their doctrine. See also the decree of Gelasius concerning prohibited books, where the two heretics appear to be joined together.] they read: “Go, baptize the nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19); and they object that the Father is named first, the Son second, and the Holy Spirit third. Does the Gospel, then, by saying, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God” (John 1:1), signify that the Father is inferior, because it first recalled that the Word of God always is and always was in the beginning? Or, when the Apostle said, “In the kingdom of Christ and of God” (Ephesians 5:5), did he establish an order? Or, when the Lord Jesus himself says, “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to evangelize the poor, to preach release to captives” (Luke 4:18), did he testify that the Spirit is more exalted than the Son of God?

66. You see, virgin, how these matters are resolved. Open your ears to them; close your mouth. Open your ears, so that you may hear the faith; close your mouth, so that you may preserve [Note: [Col. 0322D] The manuscripts read “the reverence of God.” They read “Concerning him they read,” etc. The latter is less elegant.] reverence.

67. Next, they read that he said, “In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,” and they do not understand that he first said, “In the name,” as he says. He signified three persons, indeed, but asserted one name of the Trinity.

68. Therefore there is one God, one name, one divinity, one majesty. Hence there is no second: for the Trinity is the beginning of all things, and the primacy of the Trinity is over all things. Therefore, “there is one and there is no second.” He is one who has no second, because he alone is unique without sin, alone without a helper; he says: “I looked, and there was no helper” (Isaiah 63:5).

## CHAPTER XI

Since Christ labored so greatly for us, we ought to labor for him alone. He is not to be read as “second,” except insofar as he is man, in which sense he is also called “last.” The passage from Ecclesiastes and the example of Elisha are adapted to this point.

69. “There is no end to his labor” (Ecclesiastes 4:8), because he is our advocate with the Father on behalf of all, and he took upon himself our infirmities; he grieves for us and is weakened for us, as he says: “I was sick, and you did not visit me” (Matthew 25:43).

70. “His eye is not satisfied with riches” (ibid.), because he himself is the height of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God, in whom are the treasures of heavenly mysteries. Why, then, do we labor for the world instead, and defraud our soul at the cost of so great a goodness, when we ought to serve no other Lord but this one?

71. He, therefore, is not second. I certainly offer this testimony: I read that he is first; I read that he is not second. Let those who call him second prove it from Scripture.

72. But someone says that it is written: “The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man is from heaven, heavenly” (1 Corinthians 15:47). [Note: [Col. 0323D] Thus the manuscripts; the editions, however, read, “But first let us see of whom he is speaking.” Moreover, according to Epiphanius, Photinus also raised this objection; hence it is very well confirmed that the holy teacher is here replying to some disciple of Photinus, such as we showed above Bonosius to have been.] But attend to what he says. “The second man,” he says—as though he had said “a second man.” And I say that he is first according to divinity, before whom there was no one; but second according to the flesh, because he came after Adam.

73. I say more: not only “second” according to man, [Col. 0323C] but also “last.” Thus you have it written: “The first man, Adam, was made a living soul; the last Adam, a life-giving spirit” (ibid., 45). See Christ’s mercy: he is both first and last. He who was first made himself last for our sake. He is first because all things are through him; last because resurrection is through him. For he descended and cast himself down, making himself lower than all, so that he might raise up all who were lying prostrate.

74. Hence Ecclesiastes also says: “For if one falls, the other will raise up his companion; and woe to that one when he falls and there is no second to raise him.” [Note: [Col. 0323D] The edition reads, “woe to him who, being alone, falls”; the manuscripts, “woe to the one when he falls.” The latter is more apt, for the Septuagint reads, “Woe to him, to the one, when he falls,” etc.] And indeed, “if two sleep, they have warmth; but one, how will he be warmed?” (Ecclesiastes 4:10–11). This means that the one who has Christ with him, even if he falls, will rise again; even if he has died, he will live again, because he is present to him; he who came to cast fire upon the earth (Luke 12:49). [Note: [Col. 0323D] All the editions read, “he is present”; the manuscripts, “he is present to him.” This is preferable, so that it refers to the one who has fallen, and the antecedent of the implied relative is “he” or “another.” Below, where the old editions and manuscripts read, “This young man, therefore,” the Roman edition has removed the final word. Not rightly.] Finally, when Elisha raised the boy from the dead, he breathed upon him (2 Kings 4:34), so that he might infuse him with the warmth of life. Keep this fire, therefore, with you in your breast, so that it may raise you up; let not the chill of everlasting death creep over you.

[Col. 0324A] 75. This young man, therefore, cast himself down: he came through Mary and infused the warmth of life into the breasts of those who listened. Hence they say in the Gospel: “Was not our heart burning within us when he opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24:32).

## CHAPTER XII

That Christ is designated by Ecclesiastes as the second young man is understood both from other passages and from the continuation of this very passage: namely, that he is the one who is described as having passed through the gate and as having sat in it and eaten.

76. This is the second young man, as Ecclesiastes says: “I saw all the living who walk under the sun with the second young man; who will rise up for him?” [Note: [Col. 0324D] The Roman edition alone reads, “Who will rise up with him?” But the reading of the other editions and of the manuscripts is also supported by the Septuagint, whose words are: “who will rise up after him” (*hos anastēsetai autou*), and the other versions do not differ from this.] (Ecclesiastes 4:15). For who will rise up for Christ, when he has risen for all, and all have risen in him, since they have received the hope of resurrection?

77. It is clear that this was said of Christ when you observe that the passage corresponds to the blessing or prophecy of Jacob, who said concerning Judah: “Who will raise him up?” (Genesis 49:9). Certainly not another, because he raised himself, as he himself says: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19). He was speaking of the temple of his body.

78. This also truly applies to Christ alone, which he added: “There is no end to all his people” (Ecclesiastes 4:16), because Christ’s innumerable people have no end, and faith in the resurrection of eternal life obtains for them the age of perpetuity. Therefore it is beyond doubt that according to the flesh he was called both a young man and one who could fall or rise. Finally, he added this also: “The good child is poor and wise” (ibid., 13), for he became poor although he was rich.

79. Therefore that king of Israel himself passed through this gate; that leader himself sat in it, when the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14), like a king sitting in the royal court of the virginal womb, or in a boiling pot, as it is written: “Moab is the court of my hope,” or “the pot of my hope” (Psalm 59:10). Both readings are found in different manuscripts. The virgin is a royal court, for she is subject not to a man but to God alone. The womb of Mary is also a pot, for when the Spirit, who came upon her, was fervent within it, she filled the whole world by giving birth to the Savior.

80. He ate while sitting in the gate (Ezekiel 44:3), namely that food of which he says: “My food is to do the will of my Father who is in heaven” (John 4:34).

## CHAPTER XIII

Mary’s virginity is beautifully signified by the pot and the light cloud; the rain of this cloud was foreshadowed in many types in the Old Covenant and ought to be gathered by virgins, just as the most powerful ointment of that pot ought to be received. No one should plead poverty, but preparation should be made.

81. O the riches of Mary’s virginity! She boiled like a pot, and like a cloud she rained Christ’s grace upon the earth; for it is written of her: “Behold, the Lord comes, seated upon a light cloud” (Isaiah 19:1). Truly light, for she knew nothing of the burdens of marriage; truly light, for she lifted this world from the heavy debt of sins. She was light who carried forgiveness of sins in her womb. Finally, she lifted John, who was in the womb, and at the sound of her voice he leaped; the infant exulted with joy, animated first by the perception of devotion and only afterward by the infusion of vital spirit (Luke 1:41).

[Col. 0325B] 82. Receive, therefore, receive, sacred virgins, the spiritual rain of this cloud, the tempering of bodily heat, so that you may extinguish all the fires of the body and the inner recesses of your mind may be moistened. The fathers who preceded us announced that the rain of this consecrated cloud would bring the world’s future salvation (Psalm 71:6). They signified that this rain would come as falling drops descending upon the earth, which Jerubbaal requested and obtained. Follow the good cloud, which produced within itself a spring by which it watered the whole world (Judges 6:36 and following). Receive, then, the voluntary rain, the rain of blessing, which the Lord poured out upon his inheritance. Receive the water, and do not let it run away from you; for it is a cloud—let it dissolve you and drench you with sacred moisture; for it is a pot—let it steam with eternal Spirit.

[Col. 0325C] 83. Receive, therefore, from this Moabite pot the ointment of heavenly grace, and do not fear that it will fail: what has been emptied out overflows all the more, because its fragrance has gone out into all the earth (Psalm 59:10), as it is written: “Your name is an ointment poured out; therefore the young women have loved you” (Song of Songs 1:2). Let this ointment descend into the innermost recesses of the heart [Note: [Col. 0325D] The editions read “into the depths of the soul”; the manuscripts, “into the deepest recesses.”], into the secret places of the viscera, where holy Mary breathed forth not the fragrances of delights but the inspirations of divine grace.

84. This rain extinguished Eve’s desire; this ointment wiped away the stench of hereditary error; this ointment Mary, the sister of Lazarus, poured upon the Lord’s feet, and the whole house was filled with its devout fragrance (John 12:3).

[Col. 0325D] 85. Let no woman consider herself poor, let none think herself needy, let none fear that she cannot buy this precious ointment or suppose that this spring is for sale. “You who thirst,” he says, “go to the water; and whoever has no money, go, buy, and drink without money” (Isaiah 55:1). And above he says: “You were sold for nothing, and you shall be redeemed without money” (Isaiah 52:3). Therefore the Lord became poor although he was rich, so that all might buy him, and so that especially through his poverty he might enrich the needy.

86. Prepare, therefore, the vessels of the Lord, so that you may receive this fountain of living water, the fountain of virginity, the ointment of integrity, the fragrance of faith, and the grace of gentle mercy, flowering abundantly [Note: [Col. 0325D] The manuscripts read, “may you clothe yourselves with the flowering grace,” etc.]. Put on the innocence of his Lamb, who, when he was cursed, did not curse in return; when he was struck, did not strike back (1 Peter 2:23).

## CHAPTER XIV

To impel virgins more ardently to imitate Mary, it is shown that much which is mystically said of the Church also applies to the virgin Mother of God.

87. Imitate her, daughters, to whom beautifully applies what was prophesied of the Church: “Beautiful are your steps in sandals, daughter of Aminadab” (Song of Songs 7:1) [Note: [Col. 0325D] Thus the editions; the manuscripts, “to whom it was said: ‘Beautiful …’”]. This is because the Church proceeded beautifully through the preaching of the Gospel [Note: Two manuscripts read, “because the Church is beautiful.”]. The soul proceeds beautifully when it uses the body as a sandal, so that it can carry its foot wherever it wishes without any impediment [Note: In one manuscript the sentence is rearranged so that it reads, “so that it may wish to carry its own foot,” etc.].

88. In this sandal Mary proceeded beautifully, for, without any union of bodily intercourse, the Virgin gave birth to the author of salvation. Hence John excellently says: “I am not worthy to loosen the strap of his sandal” (John 1:27)—that is, I am not worthy to comprehend the mystery of the Incarnation within the narrow limits of the human mind or to explain it with the poverty and weakness of speech. Hence Isaiah also says: “Who will declare his generation?” (Isaiah 53:8). Beautiful, therefore, are the steps either of Mary or of the Church, because beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim the Gospel.

89. How beautiful also are those things which were prophesied of Mary under the figure of the Church, provided that you consider not the members of the body but the mysteries of her generation! For it is said to her: “The curves of your thighs are like necklaces, the work of the hands of an artist. Your navel is a turned bowl that never lacks mixed wine. Your belly is like a heap of wheat enclosed among lilies” (Song of Songs 7:1 and following) [Note: [Col. 0325D] The old edition reads, “the work of an artist’s hands”; the Roman edition, “by the work of an artist’s hands”; the manuscripts, “the work of an artist’s hands.” The Septuagint generally supports these readings: some of its manuscripts read *ergon technitē*, others *ergō cheirōn technitē*. Below, where the old edition and the manuscripts read “small among lilies,” the Roman edition restored “fenced,” etc.; this seems to be the true reading, since the Septuagint consistently prefers *pephragmenoi en krinois*, “enclosed among lilies.”]. This is because Christ’s birth from the Virgin was in every respect self-consistent and coherent, just as victors in worldly battles customarily honor the necks of brave men with bestowed necklaces; so he lightened our yoke that he might crown the necks of the faithful with the insignia of virtue.

[Note: [Col. 0326D] The manuscripts read *onerare*, “to burden,” in place of *honorare*, “to honor,” which we have retained from the editions. The editions present the whole passage as follows: “containing within itself the birth of Christ in all things. Just as victors …” Here “containing within itself” means “corresponding to and cohering with itself”; the holy Doctor intended to signify that Christ possessed in his birth such a connection among his perfections that they might in some way appear to form a crown. As for the fact that victors in contests were customarily presented with necklaces, this is established by so many frequent testimonies of writers that it is unnecessary to cite them here. Anyone desiring more may consult Vegetius, Book II, chapter 27, and Lipsius, *On Roman Military Affairs*, Book V, p. 209, where he traces the modern necklaces of equestrian orders back to this custom.]

90. Truly, Mary’s womb was that turned bowl, in which there was Wisdom, who mixed her wine in the bowl, supplying the unfailing grace of devout knowledge from the fullness of her divinity (Proverbs 9:2).

91. In that virgin womb there simultaneously germinated both a heap of wheat and the grace of the lily’s flower, because it gave birth both to a grain of wheat and to a lily. It was a grain of wheat according to what is written: “Amen, amen, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone” (John 12:24). But because a heap was made from one grain of wheat, the prophetic word was fulfilled: “The valleys will abound with grain” (Psalm 64:14), because that dead grain brought forth abundant fruit. This grain, therefore, filled all human beings with the perpetual food of heavenly gifts; and the utterance of the prophetic mouth was fulfilled, as the same David says: “He fed them with the fat of wheat, and he satisfied them with honey from the rock” (Psalm 80:17).

92. Divine oracles also testify that the lily was present in this grain, because it is written: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys; like a lily among thorns” (Song of Songs 2:1). Christ was a lily among thorns when he was in the midst of the Jews.

## CHAPTER XV

Virgins may in a certain distinctive way be called Christ’s lilies; Christ himself, moreover, is rightly represented by a heap of wheat surrounded by lilies, since he both made the Church fruitful and bore the crowns of various struggles.

93. Hear, virgin, what he says: “The lily of the valleys,” he says, is Christ—that is, of humble and gentle souls. Be gentle, therefore, humble, and meek, so that Christ may germinate in you like a lily. Of him you also have elsewhere: “His lips are lilies dripping first-rate myrrh” (Song of Songs 5:13) [Note: [Col. 0327D] The edition reads, “dripping full myrrh,” for so the Septuagint has *stazonta smyrnan plērē*. The manuscripts and the Vulgate, however, read “dripping first myrrh”; the Hebrew text has “flowing myrrh.”]. Those who speak of Christ’s passion and celebrate it with their own mouths, and who carry his mortification in their bodies, are Christ’s lilies; especially sacred virgins, whose virginity is radiant and undefiled. Hence many understand the Church to appear to say: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys”—she who in this valley of the world exhales the grace of a good fragrance through diligent confession of devotion. Finally, she says elsewhere: “My brother has gone down to his garden, to the beds of spices, to pasture in the gardens and gather lilies. I belong to my brother, and my brother belongs to me, who pastures among the lilies” (Song of Songs 6:1–2).

94. From that womb of Mary, therefore, there was poured into this world a heap of wheat enclosed among lilies, when Christ was born from her, to whom the prophet David says: “You will bless the crown of the year of your goodness, and your fields will be filled with abundance. The boundaries of the desert will grow rich, and the hills will gird themselves with exultation. The rams of the sheep are clothed, and the valleys abound with grain; indeed, they will cry out and sing a hymn” (Psalm 64:12 and following).

95. What is the year of the Lord’s goodness except that of which it was said: “At an acceptable time I heard you, and on the day of salvation I helped you” (Isaiah 49:8)—when the Church abounded in the faith of the peoples and clothed the priests with righteousness? Hence the Apostle also says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians 6:2)—when the Lord came to proclaim “the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of retribution,” as he himself recalled in his Gospel, saying: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me,” and so forth (Luke 4:18).

[Col. 0328B] 96. Then the Lord crowned the time of his coming by his works, glory, and honor. For that whole year of his life in this world contained struggles of various passions. As a child he conquered Herod (Matthew 2:16), over whom he triumphed in the passion of the infants. He hungered, thirsted, was scourged for us, endured for us insults unworthy of him, ascended the cross, and died for us.

## CHAPTER XVI

Virgins must go out to meet Christ, and in what manner. He was indeed crowned by his mother, yet his divinity must not be doubted. Perfect faith must therefore be taken in the food prepared by Jacob and in the garment woven by the prudent woman, which were prefigured, so that the virgin, having received blessings from Christ, may see God in the human being—or rather, may put on Christ—and likewise all the adornments of virtue.

97. You see how many struggles there were! Yet he was not a grasping exactor of reward, for one heavenly crown of virtue was sufficient for him [Note: [Col. 0328D] The editions add *passus est*, “he endured,” after *certamina*; in the manuscripts it is more elegantly understood]. Therefore, daughters of Jerusalem, go out, as divine Scripture exhorts you in the Song of Songs: “Go out and behold King Solomon in the crown with which his mother crowned him on the day of his betrothal and on the day of the joy of his heart” (Song of Songs 3:11). For, it says, “he made for himself love from the daughters of Jerusalem.” That is: Go out from these bodily anxieties and cares; go out from this carnal pleasure, and make your pilgrimage away from the body, so that you may be present with the Lord, since those who are in the flesh cannot please their Lord. Therefore it is said to you that you are not in the flesh but in the spirit (Romans 8:8–9), if you can grasp the love of that true and peace-making Solomon, which he made for himself; and therefore he received a crown from his mother.

98. Blessed is the mother Jerusalem, and blessed is Mary’s womb, which crowned so great a Lord. It crowned him when it formed him; it crowned him when it gave birth to him; for although [Note: [Col. 0329D] Do not suppose that Ambrose is here denying that the most pure Virgin must truly be regarded as the Mother of God. Interpret the passage in relation to the heretics whom, as we have seen, he undertook to refute. To prove both that Mary’s virginity remained undefiled and that Christ’s divinity must not be denied, it is enough if he teaches that the same Mother of God conceived by the work of the Holy Spirit, without any sexual union. Otherwise, how could Mary be denied to have contributed as much to Christ’s birth as other mothers contribute to the birth of their children, since, in Ambrose’s words, she formed him, gave birth to him, conceived him, and bore him? But more on this in Book III, *On the Faith*, chapter 7.] she formed him without any action of her own—for the Holy Spirit came upon the virgin; hence he himself also says: “Your eyes saw my unformed substance”—yet precisely because she conceived and bore him for the salvation of all, she placed upon his head the crown of eternal devotion, so that through the faith of believers Christ might become the head of every man. The flesh of Christ, therefore, was unformed by human agency; when Mary the Virgin conceived him, by an unusual and new mystery of the Incarnation, without any admixture of male seed, divine grace took from the Virgin what belonged to flesh and formed in her the members of the last Adam, the spotless man.

99. You hear “man,” but understand what is above man, because it is written: “You shall not boil a kid in its mother’s milk” (Exodus 34:26). And elsewhere you read: “He is a man, and who will recognize him?” (Jeremiah 17:9). Therefore you must not estimate that Lamb, in whom the fullness of divinity dwells bodily (Colossians 2:9), by the powers of human condition, nor confine the majesty of incomprehensible power within the weakness of base understanding [Note: [Col. 0329D] The Roman edition alone reads, “by the weakness of an inferior kinship.” This is not unsuitable.]. For Jacob did not cook that food of perfect faith in milk, by which Isaac the father was so delighted that, with prophetic sobriety, he bestowed upon him the entire prerogative of blessing (Genesis 27:25). And therefore the Apostle wrote that the thin fluid of milk is the food of doctrine, saying: “Everyone who is fed on milk is inexperienced in the word of righteousness” (Hebrews 5:13); for he is a little child, whereas solid food belongs to the mature.

100. Therefore you too, daughter, take that garment of the woman [Note: [Col. 0330D] The edition reads, “woven by the woman through the zeal of pious action”; the manuscripts read as in our text.] woven by pious action, who opens her hands to the poor and whose lamp is not extinguished throughout the night (Proverbs 31:19 and following). Put it on, and bring such delicacies to your father, so that he may say: “How is it that you found it so quickly, my daughter?” (Genesis 27:20 and following), praising wisdom still tender in age and also the affection of devout dedication. And may he say to you: “Come near to me, daughter”; and, smelling the fragrance of your garments, may he bless you, saying: “Behold, the fragrance of my daughter is like the fragrance of a field which the Lord has blessed; and may God give you dew from heaven above and abundance from the richness of the earth.” And may he add: “Whoever curses you shall be cursed, and whoever blesses you shall be blessed.”

101. Clothed in this garment, Jacob saw a man and asked a blessing from him as from the Lord God, and he called the place “Vision of God” (Genesis 32:26 and following). Clothed in this garment, he saw that garment of Christ concerning which he says: “He will wash his garment in wine” (Genesis 49:11). He also blessed Joseph, saying: “Joseph is my son, grown great; Joseph is my son, grown great, my younger son, a son who has been envied; return to me” (ibid., 22), signifying the mark of the Lord’s resurrection. And he added: “The blessing of your father and of your mother has prevailed over the blessings of the everlasting mountains and the desires of the eternal hills” (ibid., 26)—that is, “over the king of grace” [Note: [Col. 0330D] All the editions read thus; the manuscripts, “over the king, grace.” What if we read “over the law, grace”? The sense seems to support this conjecture, although the other two readings are not absurd.].

102. Take this garment, so that you may put on Christ and be renewed in knowledge of him. Put on, therefore, as God’s chosen one, compassion, kindness, humility, patience, modesty, and love, which is the bond of unity (Colossians 3:12 and following), so that you owe no one anything except to love your sister mutually; and do not envy her grace, but imitate the one whom you see to be more approved, so that Christ’s peace and grace may be in you, and the word of God may dwell in your heart, while you flee the thoughts of this world [Note: [Col. 0330D] Gill’s edition in the margin and the Roman edition in the text read, “flee the contagions”; the other editions and the manuscripts, “flee the thoughts,” with no inferior sense.].

103. Once dead to the world, do not, I beg you, touch or handle what belongs to this age. Rather, always withdraw yourself from the conduct of this world through psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing not to man but to God (Colossians 2:20 and following). And, as holy Mary used to do (Luke 2:19), ponder these things in your heart. Like a good little lamb, chew the divine commandments in your mouth, so that you too may say: “I will meditate on your wonders” (Psalm 118:27). Let your soul neither sleep nor drip [Note: [Col. 0330D] The manuscripts read, “Your precious soul”; this is not sufficiently correct. Moreover, if you compare this passage with what is discussed in *Commentary on Psalm 18*, sermon 4, number 15, the latter will receive considerable illumination from it.] from weariness. For drops of rain drive a person from his house in winter; but the perfect soul does not drip, since there is no crack of more serious sin in it. It remains in its house and rejoices in and enjoys the freshness of an unbroken dwelling. But if something should perhaps waver, say: “Strengthen me in your words” (Psalm 118:28).

## CHAPTER XVII

Thanks are given to God because the life of angels, once lost in paradise, now shines in virgins; and because virginity was worthy to bring forth Christ for the world and to lead the Hebrews out through the sea. After this, Ambrosia herself is commended and offered to God, so that he may protect his gift in her and join her in heavenly marriage to spiritual births; may grant virtues in place of dowry and ornaments, through whose benefit she may deserve to hold her Bridegroom. Finally, Christ is entreated to receive his handmaid joyfully.

104. Now, when all has been traversed, I turn my prayers to you, Father of grace [Note: [Col. 0330D] The edition reads, “Father of glory … we give unceasing thanks.”], to whose mercy we give innumerable thanks, because in sacred virgins we see on earth the life of angels that we once lost in paradise. For what more could you have contributed either to encouraging the efforts of virgins and strengthening their virtue, or to celebrating the glory of virginity, than that God should be born from a virgin? [Note: [Col. 0331D] In the same sense, see *On Jacob and the Blessed Life*, chapter 6, number 21: “My fault became for me the reward of redemption, through which Christ came to me,” etc. Likewise *On Psalm 39*, number 20: “Happy is the fall that is restored to something better.” Similar expressions occur frequently elsewhere.] Our fault benefited us more than it harmed us: in it our redemption found a divine gift.

105. But your only-begotten Son himself, coming into the world to take up what had been lost, could find no purer generation of his flesh than by dedicating to his own dwelling the heavenly court of a virgin, in which there would be both the sanctuary of immaculate chastity and the temple of God.

[Col. 0331B] 106. What more should I append—that by your divine gift, together with the holy Moses and Aaron (Exodus 15:20), the virgin Mary led the army of the Hebrews on foot through the waves? I leave ancient things aside; I seek no private examples. This nobility of the virgin family is sufficient.

107. I ask you to protect this handmaid of yours, who has dared to serve you, dedicate her soul to you, and devote herself to the pursuit of her purity. I offer her in priestly service and commend her with a father’s affection, so that, gracious and protective, you may bestow on her the grace by which she may rouse the Bridegroom who dwells in the inner chambers of the heavenly bridal rooms, deserve to see him, and be brought into the chamber of her God and King. May she deserve to hear him say to her: “Come here from Lebanon, Bride; come here from Lebanon; you shall cross over and pass through from the beginning of faith” (Song of Songs 4:8), so that she may pass beyond the world and pass over into those eternal things.

108.
