Therefore, Father, look upon your gift, for whose sanctification you sought no one’s counsel; but without any petitioner or mediator you bestowed upon her so great a grace that, before the divine oracles, no one could have believed it: that a virgin should carry God in her womb. Stirred by the prerogative of this gift, the practices of virginity and the examples of sacred purity multiply. Having been summoned by them to the grace of such virtue, may this handmaid of yours also stand beside your altars [Note: [Col. 0331D] Concerning the various ornaments of brides and wedding rites, Baron, Brissonius, Antoine and François Hotman, and Joseph Laurentius in *Polymathia*, Book III, synopsis 8, “On Betrothals and the Marriages of the Ancients,” and synopsis 15, “On Nuptial Laws,” contain much material not unworthy of knowledge, etc.], not carrying golden hair flowing from a shining head, dedicated to a wedding veil, but that hair with which that Gospel woman, holy Mary, diligently wiped Christ’s feet and filled the entire house with the ointment poured out, offering it under a sacred veil to be consecrated (John 12:3).

[Col. 0331D] 109. The maiden is present, whom neither wedding celebrations, nor rewards, nor the burden of a pregnant womb with its anticipated pain trouble; rather, she asks for the immaculate offspring of faith and devotion, so that she may conceive in her womb from the Holy Spirit and, pregnant, bring forth for God a spirit of salvation. But so that this may proceed through the grace of merits, you, God the almighty Father, add the support of commendation; for modesty is not the only dowry. Let modesty, sobriety, and restraint gird the hair of sacred virginity [Note: [Col. 0332D] Two manuscripts read, “the hair of the sacred virgin.”], so that, girded with the company of virtues and bound with the purple covering of the Lord’s blood, she may carry the mortification of the Lord Jesus in her flesh. These are the better coverings: they are the garments of virtues, by which guilt is covered and innocence is revealed.

110. Clothe your handmaid, then, in these garments, which are clean at all times; for whatever no intervening fault has darkened remains clean, so that it may rightly be said to her: “Your works have pleased God” (Ecclesiastes 9:7–8). “Let your garments be white at all times, and let oil never be lacking on your head,” so that she may be able to kindle her mystical lamps; and when the Bridegroom comes, may she be counted worthy of the heavenly bridal chamber among those wise virgins (Matthew 25:10), whose light of devotion, faith, and dignity illuminates the gift of her sacred profession.

111. Therefore protect your handmaid, Father of love and glory [Note: [Col. 0332D] The same manuscripts read, “Father of brightness and glory.”], so that, as in a locked garden and a sealed spring, she may keep the enclosures of chastity and the seals of truth. Let her know how to cultivate her field, which holy Jacob cultivated [Note: [Col. 0332D] The Roman edition reads, “which holy Isaac cultivated.”], and let her gather from it sixtyfold and hundredfold fruit. In the virtues and strengths of this field, awaken and revive grace and love in her. Let her find the one whom she loved, hold him, and not release him until she receives those good wounds of love which are preferred to kisses. Always ready, by night and by day, let her keep watch with the whole spirit of her mind (Song of Songs 5:7), lest the Word ever find her sleeping. And because her beloved wishes to be sought repeatedly, in order to test her affection, let faith and her soul follow him as he returns; let her go forth into your Word and journey away from the body, so that she may be present with God. Let her heart keep vigil, while the flesh sleeps, lest it begin to keep vigil in sins.

112. You, Lord, add other ornaments of sacred virginity; add diligent devotions, so that she may know how to possess her vessel, and know how to humble herself; let her hold fast love, the wall of truth, the enclosure of modesty. Let her veil not be of pine, nor let cypresses surpass her; let turtledoves not surpass her chastity, nor doves her simplicity. Let there be simplicity in her heart, restraint in her words, modesty toward all, devotion toward relatives, and mercy toward the needy and the poor. Let her hold fast what is good and abstain from every appearance of evil; let the blessing of one who is dying come upon her, and let the mouth of the widow bless her (Job 29:13).

[Note: Is. Casaubon, in his *Notes on Trebellius Pollio*, p. 207, no. 12, discussing certain less modest verses of the emperor Gallienus, cites this passage of Ambrose and adds: “I do not doubt that this holy and eloquent man imitated this passage of Gallienus and transferred it from a less honorable meaning to an honorable and devout one.”]

[Col. 0333A] 113. Set your word as a seal upon her heart, as a seal upon her arm (Song 8:6), so that Christ may shine forth in all her senses and works; let her fix her attention upon Christ and speak of Christ. Let many waters not be able to extinguish her love, nor persecution, nor the sword, nor danger.

[Note: All the editions read: “to extinguish love, neither persecution nor the sword.”]

But, strengthened in every good work and word, let her put on your glory and live in your grace in this world. Sanctify her in truth, strengthen her in virtue, bind her together in love, and lead her by your divine favor to that heavenly glory of chastity and integrity, that undefiled and spotless crown; so that there she may follow the Lamb’s footsteps, feed at midday, remain at midday, and not walk among the flocks of companions; but, mingled with your lambs, may she live blamelessly as a companion of virgins and a follower of Marys (Rev. 14:4; Song 1:6).

[Note: Thus the manuscripts; the editions, however, read: “and may she not fall among the flocks of companions.” [Col. 0334B] This is by no means a bad reading.]

[Col. 0334A] 114. Come forth, therefore, Lord Jesus, on the day of your espousals; receive her who has long been devoted to you in spirit and now also in profession; fill her with knowledge of your will; take her from the beginning into salvation, in sanctification of spirit and faith in the truth, so that your handmaid may say: “You have held my right hand; you have led me according to your will, and in glory you have received me” (Ps. 67:24). Open your hand and fill her soul with blessing (Ps. 144:16), so that you may save her who hopes in you (Ps. 85:2), and so that she may become a vessel sanctified for honor, useful to the Lord, approved for every good work.

Through that eternal cross, through that venerable glory of the Trinity—to whom belong honor, glory, and eternity, to God the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit, from ages past, now, and always, and throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Note: All the editions and some manuscripts read: “prepared for every good work.”]

[EXHORTATION OF VIRGINITY.]

[Col. 0333]

AN INTRODUCTION TO THE EXHORTATION OF VIRGINITY.

[Col. 0333]

That the all-good and all-great God never permits his own to be afflicted except for his greater glory and for their benefit and that of the Church is made clear by that journey of Ambrose which gave occasion to this work. The holy man had heard that the tyrant Eugenius was hastening into Italy and indeed to Milan, as Paulinus relates (*Life of Ambrose*). Therefore, thinking that the man who was attempting to restore idolatry under the pretext of the Christian religion ought not to be awaited, he came to Bologna. While he was staying there, he solemnly celebrated the translation of the bodies of the martyrs Vitalis and Agricola, whose divine revelation to him seems to be indicated by Paulinus (*ibid.*). When the people of Florence learned this, they invited him with immense enthusiasm to visit them and not refuse to dedicate their new church. The holy Bishop granted their request, although he had decided to go elsewhere (ch. 1, no. 1, and Paulinus, *Life of Ambrose*).

Since he had brought with him some relics of the Bolognese martyrs, he deposited them in that church, which he himself consecrated there with splendid ceremony. On that solemn occasion he delivered the discourse from which this book consists.

He himself declares this at the beginning of the work (ch. 1, no. 1). After briefly describing the martyrs’ suffering and the exhumation of their relics (no. 2 and following), he adds that he had brought to them a portion gathered with his own hands—namely, the nails, the triumphant blood, and the wood of the cross (ch. 2, no. 9). For he denies (*ibid.*, no. 10) that it would have been right for the widow Juliana to suffer rejection from him, since she had built the sacred church which, according to Paulinus (*Life of Ambrose*), was called Ambrosian because Ambrose himself inaugurated it.

Since that devout and truly Christian mother was not content to consecrate her resources to Christ in building a noble basilica, she also determined to devote herself, together with her entire family, to him. Indeed, while her husband was still alive, she had already, as it were, offered the first fruits of her sacrifice. For although he did not yield to his wife in the praise of devotion, shortly before his death—and despite bearing the sufficiently heavy burdens of marriage, namely one son and three daughters—he nevertheless did not refuse, for the sake of ecclesiastical usefulness, to enter the sacred orders with his wife’s consent (ch. 2, no. 12). Thus he had already made a beginning in continence; but after her husband had completed his mortal course, she wished to place the finishing touch upon her work.

Therefore, to kindle her children to embrace the profession of continence, she urged them in the discourse which the holy Doctor, adorning it with his own style and eloquence, presents to all who had gathered there, in this sense (ch. 3 and following).

At the outset, addressing her son, who had not yet passed beyond the years of childhood, she asserts that he was given the name Laurentius for this reason: when his parents had already despaired of producing a male child, they obtained him through the patronage of so great a martyr (ch. 3, no. 14 and following). From this she concludes that he belongs to that martyr, since, just as Hannah vowed Samuel to God, she had vowed him to the same martyr, in order to fulfill his mother’s promises before that martyr’s shrine. Then, turning her speech to her daughters (ch. 3, no. 17 and following), she presses them to consecrate their chastity to Christ by setting the disadvantages of marriage against the benefits of celibacy. Finally (ch. 4, no. 25 and following), sometimes addressing the son, sometimes the daughters, and sometimes all together, she leaves nothing unattempted in order to induce them to fulfill the vows which their parents had made in their name. Nor was that pious desire of the mother fruitless. Laurentius was enrolled among the readers (ch. 8, no. 54), while his sisters, having professed chastity in the customary solemn manner (ch. 14, no. 93), preserved it in their mother’s house.

[Col. 0335] Moved by these circumstances, Ambrose wished to continue Juliana’s discourse with an exhortation of his own (ch. 9 and following). There he teaches those same virgins what their duty is, what exercises they ought to pursue, and what they ought to accomplish, so that they may live with their mother according to the rules of their profession. Subsequently he also instructs other Christian virgins (ch. 10, no. 71, and following), to whom he transfers his discourse from those three victims of integrity. Then, after proposing various examples for them to imitate, he does not omit the holy Soteris (ch. 12, no. 81), their relative, as we have seen elsewhere (*On Virginity*, book 3, no. 39); from her sufferings he describes the incident in which she willingly endured having the executioner strike and bloody her face with his fist.

He also adds certain other precepts (ch. 13, no. 83 and following). When these are concluded, he promises the widow who had vowed herself, her children, and all her possessions to Christ that an exceedingly abundant reward awaits her from him (ch. 14, no. 92). Finally, he entreats God (*ibid.*, no. 93) that, ever present and favorable in the church she had consecrated, he may receive the prayers of the faithful and the sacrifice of the Lord’s body, but above all may accept the complete offering of this entire family.

Since this treatise, as we have seen, was delivered in a public assembly, it is probable that it contains nothing beyond a single discourse. Yet although the holy Doctor was prolix in speaking on that occasion, he could scarcely persuade himself, amid so joyful a celebration, to curtail his discourse further. Nor shall we depart from probability if we believe that the discourse is preserved in the manuscripts exactly as it was delivered at Florence. For whenever he himself formed books from his sermons, he almost always inserted something by which that transformation could be recognized.

Hence the work is more appropriately entitled in the manuscripts *Exhortation of Virginity*, and in the older editions *Exhortation to Virgins*, than in the Roman edition, *A Treatise on Exhortation to Virginity*. Nevertheless, what we have explained above abundantly proves that each of these titles fits the subject of the work without impropriety.

It may, however, seem strange that Ambrose should have introduced a widow addressing her daughters while she and her daughters were listening, and should have adapted for her a discourse which one might infer had been delivered by the woman herself. But he undoubtedly did this so that greater force might be added to his exhortation.

Since he delivered this discourse while fleeing Eugenius, and also after the sacred relics of the saints Vitalis and Agricola had been revealed, it follows that the event occurred not before the rebellion of the aforementioned tyrant, but while our Bishop had not yet returned to his own see, which he regained on the Kalends of August in the year 394. Baronius indeed assigns the year 392 to this work (*Annals*, under the year 392), but it must certainly be assigned to the following year. It also seems no less certain that the discourse was composed and delivered as Easter was approaching; this is plainly indicated by what the holy man says: “The day of Easter has come,” and so forth (ch. 7, no. 42).

[Col. 0335]

THE EXHORTATION OF SAINT AMBROSE, BISHOP OF MILAN, ON VIRGINITY, ONE BOOK [Note: Written around the year 393.] (C)

277 CHAPTER ONE.

[Col. 0335A]

Ambrose, coming from Bologna to those who had invited him, relates that he brought gifts, namely the relics of the martyrs Agricola and Vitalis. Although one of them had been a master and the other a slave, a comparison is nevertheless drawn between them; and since the latter preceded the former to martyrdom, it is shown that servitude is no impediment in Christ. Their contest is then described; the saint illuminates it by the omen contained in each man’s name. Finally, after recalling the burial which they had received in Jewish tombs, he relates with what joy they were discovered and brought forth.

1. Those who are invited to a great banquet customarily take gifts home with them. I was invited to your Bolognese banquet, where the translation of a holy martyr was celebrated; therefore I have reserved for you gifts full of holiness and grace.

[Note: By metaphor he calls the translation of the saints’ bodies a banquet, because it was an assembly full of solemnity and joy, such as banquets are accustomed to be.]

Gifts, moreover, are customarily associated with the triumphs of princes; and these gifts are triumphal, for the martyrs’ palms are the triumphs of Christ, our Prince. I was not actually directing my journey here; but since I was summoned by you, I ought to bring with me what had been prepared for others, lest I come to you with less than expected, so that what is less in me might be found greater in the martyr.

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads, “to possess the triumphs of princes.” Properly speaking, *apophoreta* were little gifts which those who had been invited to a banquet customarily carried home, such as fruits, roasted birds, or something of that kind. The word was also used of gifts which newly appointed magistrates sent to their friends. There were also triumphal *apophoreta*, distributed by emperors celebrating a triumph. The term is found used for the vessels in which sacred relics were stored, but only in later Latin. On these meanings consult Turnebus, *Adversaria*, book 19, ch. 23; Lipsius, *Saturnalia*, book 1, ch. 16; Rosweidus in his notes on St. Paulinus’s fifth letter; Du Cange under the same word; and others.]

2. The martyr’s name is Agricola; Vitalis was formerly his slave, but now is his companion and fellow in martyrdom.

[Note: Thus the editions and a few manuscripts; many others read: “he was a slave.” Before him, the slave, his companion and fellow in martyrdom, went ahead. This is by no means a bad reading. Baronius reports that these Bolognese martyrs were crowned under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, in the year 303; Hermannus embraces Baronius’s opinion, although it rests upon a letter that is undoubtedly spurious, as he himself acknowledges.]

The slave went ahead to prepare the place; the master followed, confident that through the faith of his little slave he would already find it prepared. We do not praise what belongs to another, for the slave’s passion is the master’s instruction. One taught; the other fulfilled. Nothing is taken away from him. For how can what Christ bestowed be diminished? The former, by serving a man, learned admirably how to please Christ; the latter, however, acquired a double distinction: in the former, that of a teacher; in himself, that of a martyr. Yet after they had deserved to become equals, they competed with one another in benefactions. The one sent him ahead to martyrdom; the other summoned him there.

3. Therefore no social condition creates an impediment to a man’s commendation; nor does noble ancestry bring merit, but faith does. Whether slave or free, we are all one in Christ: “Each person will receive back from the Lord whatever good he has done” (Eph. 6:8). Slavery does not detract, and freedom does not help. See how little importance condition has in this matter. “Were you called as a slave?” he says. “Do not be concerned . . . for whoever was called in the Lord as a slave is the Lord’s freedman. Likewise, whoever was called as a free person is Christ’s slave” (1 Cor. 7:21–22).

[Note: Quite a few manuscripts read: “See,” he says, “the force of the Apostle. He seems to have lowered the one called as a slave more than the one called as a free person.”]

See, I say, the force of the Apostle. He seems to have given more to the one who was called as a slave than to the one who was called as a free person: from a slave he makes Christ’s freedman; from a free person, a slave.

[Note: Several manuscripts read: “For once he has become Christ’s freedman, he becomes a slave from a free person.”]

But he gave more to neither; rather, he distributed to both by an equal measure. For in Christ slavery and freedom are weighed on an equal scale, and the merits of good slavery and freedom are not divided by any distinction, because no dignity is greater than serving Christ. Thus Paul is “a slave of Christ Jesus” (Rom. 1:1); for this slavery is glorious, and in it the Apostle also glories. Is it not the highest glory when we have been valued at such a price that we were redeemed by the Lord’s blood? But let us now proceed to the rest.

4. When the holy Vitalis was compelled by his persecutors to deny Christ, and he confessed the Lord Jesus Christ all the more, they inflicted every kind of torture upon him, so that there was no place on his body without a wound. He poured out a prayer to the Lord, saying: “Lord Jesus Christ, my Savior and my God, command that my spirit be received, for I now desire to receive the crown which your holy angel has shown me.” When he had completed the prayer, he gave up his spirit.

[Note: From the words “When the holy Vitalis” to “he gave up his spirit,” almost all the manuscripts lack everything that is contained here. Nor is the whole passage without considerable suspicion, especially because the words “inflicting every kind of torture upon him” fit poorly with what precedes and follows. In its place, however, the Roman edition substituted, on the authority of several manuscripts, a passage from letter 55, which reads more smoothly: “so grievously tortured by every kind of torture.” Since our manuscripts fail us, we have changed nothing in the edition.]

5. Saint Agricola was considered gentler in character, so that he was loved even by the enemies themselves. For this reason they delayed his passion. But this honor shown by his persecutors was more bitter than any savagery, because it begrudged him martyrdom. Finally, when the holy Agricola did not yield, he was crucified, so that we may understand that their flattering words were not an expression of diligence but of deceit. They wished to terrify the master by the punishment of the slave. Christ turned this into an occasion of grace, so that the master might imitate the slave’s martyrdom.

[Note: All the editions and some manuscripts read: “so that the master might be invited by the slave’s martyrdom”; many others, by far the majority, read as in the text.]

6. Each man’s name was suited to martyrdom, so that they seemed designated for martyrdom by the names themselves. The one was called Vitalis, as though he were to acquire true eternal life for himself by despising this present life; the other Agricola, as one who would sow the good fruits of spiritual grace and, by the shedding of sacred blood, water the plantations of all his merits and virtues.

7. They had been buried in Jewish ground, among the Jews’ own tombs. The Jews had allowed themselves to share a burial place with those whose Lord they had denied. Thus Balaam also once said: “Let my soul die among the souls of the righteous” (Num. 23:10); yet while he lived he did not share in the works of those among whose souls he desired to die. These men whom they had persecuted while alive they honored when dead. There, then, we sought the martyrs’ remains, as though gathering a rose among thorns.

8. We were surrounded by Jews as the sacred relics were carried out; the people of the Church were present with applause and joy. The Jews said, when they saw the martyrs: “Flowers have appeared on the earth” (Song 2:12). The Christians said: “The time of pruning has come” (*ibid.*). “Already the reaper is receiving his wages” (John 4:36). Others sowed, and we reap the fruit of the martyrs.

Again, when they heard the voices of the applauding Church, the Jews said among themselves: “The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land” (Song 2:12). Hence it is rightly written: “Day pours forth the word to day, and night reveals knowledge to night.” Day to day (Ps. 18:3): Christian to Christian; night to night: Jew to Jew. The Jews therefore indicated that they possessed knowledge of the martyrs, but not knowledge of the Word—that is, not knowledge according to the knowledge of what is solely good and solely true. “For, being ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish their own, they did not submit to God’s righteousness” (Rom. 10:3).

CHAPTER II.

First he magnifies the value of the relics; then he declares the widow Juliana worthy to receive them, since she ought to be honored on the authority of the Apostle and praised because she grieved the losses of the Church more than her own.

9. I have therefore brought you gifts which I gathered with my own hands: the trophies of the cross, whose grace you recognize in its works. Certainly the demons themselves also confess it. Let others store up gold and silver and extract them from hidden veins; let them gather precious chains of jewels. That is a temporal treasure, and often harmful to those who possess it. We gather the martyr’s nails—and many of them, so that there were more wounds than limbs. You might say that the martyr was crying out to the Jewish people when we gathered his nails: “Put your hands into my side, and do not be unbelieving but believing” (John 20:27). We gather the triumphant blood and the wood of the cross.

10. We could not deny these things to the holy widow when she requested them. Receive, therefore, the gifts of salvation, which are now being placed beneath the sacred altars. That widow, then, is the holy Juliana, who prepared and offered this temple to the Lord, which we dedicate today: worthy of such an offering, since in her offspring she has already consecrated temples of chastity and integrity to the Lord.

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads, “That holy widow is Judaea.” The fact that *Judaeam* is inserted when I intend to say *Julianam*—“I wished to say Juliana, but said Judaea”—does lend some support; nevertheless, without manuscripts or at least an old edition, we place no confidence in conjecture. In a few manuscripts one finds: “That widow, then, saw and offered what [is done] today,” and so forth. Here observe how ancient is the custom of dedicating churches with solemn ceremony. A letter of this same saint of ours to Felix of Como also provides evidence of this practice. Certain Catholics and the heterodox Magdeburg Centuriators state, in their second century, that this rite was not adopted until after the reign of Constantine, while others wish it to have been transferred into the emerging Church from the ancient Synagogue. Cardinal Bona reconciles both opinions, *Liturgical Matters*, book 1, ch. 20, no. 3.]

When I wished to say “Juliana,” I said “Judaea.” My tongue did not err but defined the matter; for Judaea is the soul that confesses Christ. Finally, “God is known in Judaea” (Ps. 75:2)—that is, where he was acknowledged, not where he was denied. Judaea therefore exists in the spirit, where there is a greater portion and a purer understanding, because “salvation is from the Jews” (John 4:22). Thus the error of the tongue found testimony to holiness.

11. Let us therefore honor this widow, because it is written: “Honor widows who are truly widows” (1 Tim. 5:3). She does not seek the honor of our words, since she has fulfilled the Apostle’s command, possessing a testimony in good works: she raised her children well and instructed them better.

12. Who did not mourn her as abandoned and pitiable when she lost her husband? But she grieved more deeply that a minister had been taken from the sacred altars than that she herself had lost a husband or her children a father. For although she had been widowed of her husband’s protection and consolation, the cause of the Church outweighed all else in her devout mind.

281 CHAPTER III.

Juliana’s exhortation to her children. At the beginning she tells her son that he is not called Laurentius without reason, but because he was conceived through the patronage of the martyr of that name and promised to him. He must therefore fulfill his parents’ vows. Nothing should hold him back, since divine service is superior to all other things, while human life is most wretched. Yet there is an escape from its evils, provided they choose chastity, which is here set against the servitude of marriage.

13. She therefore girded up the inward parts of her mind, and seeing herself surrounded by three daughters and one son—by whom other women are commonly intimidated—she was made stronger and addressed her children in these words:

“My children, you have lost your father, but you have a mother. That exchange would indeed have been better if your father were alive and your mother absent. Nevertheless, although I am weak and desolate, I show you that, if you wish to follow where I indicate, you may consider that your father has not died. For you have a better parent in heaven. He is the one who has also sustained these earthly fathers.

“What hope is left now? Your father was rich in grace, not money; wealthy in ministry, not in inheritance; his inheritance is faith. He was rich toward God but poor in the world. He left you sufficiently rich if you follow his purpose. Faith alone is undivided between the sexes: the wealth of men, the dowry of virgins.”

14. “And you, my son, being somewhat closer to your father, acknowledge what you owe your mother and restore the name to the household. Your age excuses you, but your inheritance summons you. Let father and mother rejoice in you, my son (Prov. 23:25). Do not despise your mother as though she were foolish. ‘A king’s admonition,’ he says, ‘which his mother taught him.’ What is the son who preserves God’s sayings? Firstborn, I say this to you, my son: ‘What is the son of my womb? What is the child of my vows? Do not give your honor to a woman’ (Prov. 31:1 and following). Hear what the wise man says; hear what Scripture asserts.”

[Note: The old edition reads: “What is she who is his mother, and what is the son who preserves God’s sayings?” Gill’s edition and the Roman edition read: “What did his mother teach him? What will you preserve, my son? God’s sayings.” The manuscripts, however, agree overwhelmingly with our text.]

15. “Consider who helped you to be born: you are the son of my vows more than of my sorrows. Consider to what offering your father designated you by giving you that name—when he called you Laurentius.

[Note: From this passage let innovators learn how ancient is the practice of making vows to saints who have been received into heaven, so that through their intercession the faithful may more readily obtain from God what they desire.]

“There we laid down our vows, from which we took your name. The fulfillment followed the vows. Repay the martyr what you owe the martyr. He obtained you for us; restore what we promised concerning you by giving you this name.”

[Col. 0341A] 16. “What else, my son, is there that you should choose except the God of your fathers?

[Note: Several manuscripts read: “What else do you think should be loved?”]

“He makes the poor and the rich, the humble and the exalted.

[Note: Many good manuscripts read: “He is poor, and he makes the rich humble and raises up the exalted.”]

“He raises the poor from the earth, lifts the needy from the dung heap, and makes him sit with the powerful in the tribunal of honor and inheritance. He grants a vow to the one who makes a request and blesses the years of the righteous.

“What is more excellent than this, my son? Or what is human life on this earth except a swift runner?

[Note: The old edition and the manuscripts read as in the text, except that some manuscripts have *levior cursor* (“lighter than a runner”), while the Roman edition reads *nisi levior cursore* (“unless lighter than a runner”). They passed by and saw nothing.]

“Behold, we have passed by and seen nothing. Would that we imitated this runner (Job 9:25), so that we saw nothing and carried no burdens! But what is more serious is that the race is empty and the burdens are futile. They are indeed futile, but not light, nor free from sin; for the interest of sin is a heavy burden.

“Hence holy Job cries out: ‘Is not the life of man upon earth a trial, or is his life not like that of a day laborer? And as a slave who fears his master, who has found shade, and as a day laborer awaiting his wages, so I have waited in vain; nights of sorrow have been assigned to me. If I lie down, I say, “When will it be day?” When I rise again, “When will it be evening?” I am full of pain from evening until morning. My life is lighter than ash. It has perished in empty hope’ (Job 7:1 and following).

“Therefore man is nothing unless you, Lord, turn your attention to him, visit him until morning, and lead him into rest. If a tree is cut down, it sprouts again and flowers at the scent of water; but when a human being falls, he is nothing.

[Note: A considerable number of manuscripts read: “sorrows press upon him forever.”]

“Pains come upon him.”

17. “If you wish, then, my children, to avoid this trial of so many necessities, you must seek bodily integrity (32, q. 1, ch. *Integrity*), which I recommend as counsel, not impose as a command.

[Note: That is, it can only be recommended, unless a vow intervenes.]

“For virginity alone can be recommended; it cannot be commanded. It is a matter more of a vow than of a precept. What belongs to grace is not commanded but desired; it is more a matter of choice than of servitude. Hence the Apostle also says: ‘Concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord, but I give advice, as one who has obtained mercy from the Lord’ (1 Cor. 7:25).

“For he had read that the Lord said to eunuchs: ‘Those who keep my commandments and choose what I desire and embrace my covenant—I will give them in my house and within my walls a place and a name better than sons and daughters; I will give them an everlasting name, and it shall not fail’ (Isa. 56:4–5). ‘A better place,’ he says, ‘I will give you,’ addressing eunuchs—namely, those who have cut themselves off by removing their sexual organ.

[Note: See *On Widows*, ch. 13, no. 76.]

“These, therefore, are the ones who possess rewards in heaven superior to those of others.”

18. The Son of God proclaims these people in his Gospel. When the Apostles said, “If that is the situation of a man with his wife, so that it is not lawful for him to dismiss her except on the ground of fornication, it is not expedient to marry,” the Lord replied: “Not everyone can receive this word, but only those to whom it has been given” (Matt. 19:10–11)—that is, the weakness of human nature cannot grasp this so that it is open to everyone; but it is easy for those alone to grasp it upon whom divine grace has shone, so that they can make themselves eunuchs in order to obtain the kingdom of heaven.

CHAPTER IV.

After briefly setting forth the dignity of integrity, she explains what losses marriage will bring upon her daughters. To rouse them to avoid those losses, she introduces the Apostle’s judgment and example. Then, recalling both the miseries she endured in marriage and those she would have to endure in widowhood, she asserts that all of them will be repaired by their virginity and that she herself will thereafter need no protection.

[Col. 0342B] 19. “You have heard, my children, how great is the reward of integrity. The kingdom is acquired, and the heavenly kingdom displays the life of angels. I recommend this to you, since nothing is more beautiful: that among human beings you may be angels, who are bound by no marital union (Matt. 22:30). For those who do not marry, and those who do not take wives, are like angels on earth. Thus they do not experience the tribulation of the flesh, they do not know servitude, they are lifted away from the pollution of worldly thought, and they devote their minds to divine matters; as though stripped of the weakness of the body, they think not about the things of man but about the things of God.

20. “Consider, daughters, if you wish to marry, how much you lack, since you lack a father. You lack a rich dowry; and even if that were abundant, you would purchase servitude at a high price. But now who would not despise women deprived of their father? Where will you flee? From whom will you seek help against the injuries of men? How many hardships there are in marriage itself! How serious are the insults commonly inflicted! How many chains!

21. “First, marriage itself is a bond by which a married woman is tied to a man and bound in subjection to him. It is indeed a good bond of love, but still a bond, from which a married woman cannot free herself when she wishes, nor possess free control of herself. The Apostle says: ‘The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does’ (1 Cor. 7:4). And why is this surprising concerning the woman, when the husband likewise does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does? If the stronger does not have authority over himself,

[Note: Most manuscripts read: “when the weaker does not.”]

“how much less the weaker! Common servitude therefore does not set the woman free but binds her more grievously.”

22. “See, then, what Scripture says and what the Apostle recommends. Who can give you better counsel than that vessel of the Lord’s choosing? Listen carefully to what he says:

[Note: Thus the old edition and all the manuscripts, agreeing properly with the apostolic text. The Roman edition, however, follows the Vulgate version: “But I wish all people to be as I myself am.” Compare *On Virginity*, ch. 20, no. 130.]

“‘I wish all people to be as I myself am’ (1 Cor. 7:7). And again, concerning the unmarried and widows, he says: ‘It is good for them if they remain as I am’ (*ibid.*, 8). I want you to be imitators of so great an Apostle, so that you may follow his life. He rejected the bond of marriage in order to be bound to Christ Jesus. He could not have attained such great apostolic grace if he had been tied to the companionship of marriage.

23. “If he who was outstanding in teaching and possessed so great a gift of Christ judged it so important to abstain from marital intercourse—and therefore remained as he was, lest anything be taken away from his ministry, since the care of marriage would prevent him from always devoting himself to prayer and always attending to divine commands, requiring him to please his wife—what ought you to choose, for whom virginity alone can provide freedom? For a woman who marries is sold into servitude for her own money.

“Slaves are purchased on better terms than marriages: in the case of slaves, the price buys the status of servitude; in marriage, a price is added to the servitude. A married woman is burdened with gold and valued by gold.”

284 24. “I have experienced, my children, the labors of intercourse and the indignities of marriage; and even under a good spouse I was not free under a good husband. I served my husband and labored to please him. The Lord had mercy, made him a minister of the altar, and immediately he was taken from both me and you—and perhaps, through the Lord’s mercy, so that he would not be called a husband.”

[Note: The word “altar” was absent from all the editions, but is found in by far the majority of manuscripts. This passage makes it clear that the obligation of continence had already been imposed from the earliest times even upon married men who had been admitted to the order of ministers, that is, deacons.]

25. “You see a mother advanced in years because of sorrows, and still immature in the service of widowhood.

[Note: Most manuscripts read “immature in the rewards of virtue,” but the other manuscripts and all the editions more correctly read “immature in the service of widowhood”—perhaps meaning not yet sixty years old. This passage, and *On Widows*, ch. 2, no. 9, seem to require that age, so that a widow’s old age might be supported by the services of the Church.]

“You see that every protection and adornment has been taken away. I have neither the help of a husband nor the grace of virginity. I am of little concern to myself; you are my grief, you are my concern. The burdens of marriage remain with me, while its supports have departed. How much better it would have been never to have entered into these experiences!

[Note: Several manuscripts read “into these things”; some have the better reading, “into this,” and never “we would have come.”]

26. “Yet you can excuse your father and ease your mother if what has been lost in us is restored in you. Our marriage will not have displeased us for this one reason: if our labor benefits you. I shall think it the next best thing to be the mother of virgins, as though I myself possessed virginity.

“Consider, my children, what kind of mother the Lord Jesus chose for himself when he came to these lands. He came through a virgin to give salvation to the world, and by the birth of a virgin he healed the fall of woman. May your integrity also heal my errors.”

27. Consider what good virginity is. It is certain that I am left destitute and in need of protection; but if you wish to remain thus, I shall require no one’s help: the crown of your integrity will abound for me in every kind of assistance [Note: All printed editions and some manuscripts read, “for every assistance”; a much larger number of other manuscripts read, “for every aid”; one has “wealth.” This is by no means bad.]. Who would not call me blessed, whom they now consider wretched? Who would not honor the mother of so many virgins? Who would not venerate the sanctuary of modesty?

## CHAPTER V

The palm of public salvation is attributed to virgins under both covenants, and various praises of mystical virgins are celebrated; virginity is also represented by the figure of a garden and vineyard, while marriage is represented by the type of vegetables. Hence he admonishes his sons that, having rejected the spiritual Ahab and Jezebel, they should embrace the true Naboth, who was accused and killed for our sake. Why, therefore, is it foretold that he came upon a light cloud, and why did he also commend his mother to John? How, finally, did this man, who as mystical Levi possessed nothing, come to be said to have received her “as his own”?

28. Holy Scripture has brought many women into the light, but it has given the palm of public salvation to virgins alone. In the Old Testament, a virgin led the Hebrew people, shut in by land and sea, on foot through the sea (Exod. XV, 20); in the Gospel, a virgin gave birth to the author and redeemer of the world (Luke I, 27). The Church is a virgin (II Cor. XI, 2), and the Apostle took care to present her to Christ as a chaste virgin; the daughter of Zion is a virgin (Isa. XXXVII, 22); that city, Jerusalem, which is in heaven, is a virgin (Rev. XXI, 27), into which nothing common or unclean enters; and she too whom Jesus calls is a virgin, to whom he also says: “Come here from Lebanon, Bride, come here from Lebanon; you shall pass over and pass through from the beginning of faith” (Song IV, 8). The virgin not only passed over, but also passed through: she who hastens to the Bridegroom passes through the world and passes over to Christ; or because she who has dedicated herself to Christ, passing over to heavenly things, passes beyond earthly things. For the Bridegroom himself comes to his Bride in such a way that he leaps over the mountains and bounds over the hills (Song II, 8).

29. He adds still further to the praise of virginity: “A garden enclosed is my sister, my Bride, a garden enclosed, a sealed fountain” (Song IV, 12). Thus virginity, enclosed within the fortress of modesty, produces better fruits, and the seals of chastity remain undefiled within it. Preserve this garden of your souls, preserve this fountain of pure water, so that no one may disturb or mark it in you—the fountain which your generative origin has sealed in you. Let no one take away the vineyard of your soul and plant worthless vegetables. For the vineyard is a kind of virginal fruit; marriages are like vegetable gardens, in which there is frequent frost [Note: Thus a great many manuscripts; others, however, and all printed editions read, “frequent jealousy.”]. Therefore, just as vegetables and herbs quickly fall and wither unless old age brings them to an end or continence raises them to perfection [Col. 0344D].

30. Therefore let no Ahab come among you, desiring to destroy and extinguish your vineyard; nor let Jezebel come among you—that vain and worldly outpouring. For this is what the name signifies: vain and empty overflow [Col. 0345A]. But let Naboth come, who “comes from the father,” as the interpretation of his very name indicates; let him defend the vineyard with his own blood and offer his life for it. He is the one who was stoned for us, who died for us, who was falsely sought through fabricated testimonies; who, though rich, came here poor, so that we might be enriched by his poverty [Note: The printed editions and some manuscripts read, “so that you might be enriched by his poverty.”] (III Kings XII, 2 ff.). He is the vine which, with the overflowing fruits of his grace, filled the whole world. May he remain deeply rooted in your breasts, so that your fruit may abound and the heat of the bodily vapor may be tempered by the fluid of spiritual grace.

31. He is the one who came in a cloud, as the prophet said: “Behold, the Lord sits upon a light cloud, and he will come into Egypt” (Isa. XIX, 1), signifying that he would come into Egypt—that is, into the affliction of this world—upon a virgin [Note: Some manuscripts read, “upon the virgin”; the printed editions, “through the virgin.”]. He therefore called Mary a cloud because she bore flesh; a light one because she was a virgin, burdened by no obligations of marriage. She is the rod producing the flower, because virginity is pure and directed toward the Lord with a free heart, not bent back by any winding paths of worldly cares (Num. XVII, 8).

32. Therefore the Lord, from the cross, entrusted her to his beloved disciple, Saint John (John XIX, 27), who said to father and mother, “I do not know you” (Deut. XXXIII, 9). Indeed, when called by Christ, he left his father (Matt. IV, 21), following the Word. The virgin is entrusted to him who does not know his own; she is entrusted to him who draws wisdom from Christ’s breast; she is entrusted to him who did not acknowledge his brothers and did not know his sons. Therefore the Law blesses him: “Give Levi his true ones; give Levi his lots” (Deut. XXXIII, 8) [Col. 0345C].

33. Thus he himself also received the Lord’s mother; for we read that “from that hour the disciple took her into his own” (John XIX, 27). What does “into his own” mean, since he had left father and mother and followed Christ? Or how could she be “into his own,” when the apostles themselves had said, “Behold, we have left everything and followed you” (Matt. XIX, 27) [Note: Some manuscripts read, “when the disciples themselves had said.”]? What possessions did John have, who had no worldly or secular possessions, and who was not of the world? What, then, did he have as his own except what he had received from Christ? He was a good possessor of the word and of wisdom, a good receiver of grace. Hear what the apostles received from Christ: “Receive,” he says, “the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven; and whose you retain, they are retained” (John XX, 22–23). For the mother of the Lord Jesus would not have moved to anyone other than a possessor of grace, where Christ had his dwelling place [Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “For the mother of the Lord Jesus would not have moved to a possessor of grace unless where Christ had his dwelling place.” This is scarcely appropriate.].

## CHAPTER VI

He applies the preceding statements to his sons, teaching how they too can be light clouds through virginity, and give Levi his true ones, if they remain such as their first parents were before sin. He compares them with the sons whom their parents begot after being expelled from Paradise and, on the occasion of the first son, urges his own sons not to seek worldly possessions, which the daughters of Zelophehad desired. What is signified by this, and what lots are we commanded to give to Levi? What difference is there between the Lord’s and Moses’ casting of lots? By the one marriage is signified; by the other, virginity, which is followed by the freedom of Christ’s ministers.

34. Therefore you too, my sons, give true ones to that true Levi. Be clouds, but light ones. You will certainly be so if virginity lightens the burdens of your condition and illumines the darkness of this muddy flesh. Therefore she says: “I am black and beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem” (Song I, 4)—black through the flesh, beautiful through virginity. Thus those who marry are clouds, and heavy clouds; for I think that the word for those who marry is derived from “clouds.” Indeed, when those who are about to marry receive the bridal veils, they are covered like clouds. And truly they are heavy clouds, bearing the burden of marriage. For they are also said to become heavy in the womb when they receive the seeds of conception.

35. Therefore give Levi his true ones [Note: The manuscripts everywhere have “his men”; but that “his true ones” is the genuine reading is demonstrated by the nearby words, “What is so true?” and by other words occurring not much later, “For that is true which we are born as,” and so on. The same passage above, column 69, no. 266, should consequently be corrected, as should the note appended there—unless one prefers to suppose that Ambrose read the passage differently in different manuscripts, a practice which can readily be observed elsewhere in him.]. What is as true as undefiled virginity, which guards the seal of modesty and the enclosure of integrity through its natural birthright? But when a young woman is deflowered through marital intercourse, she loses what is her own when what belongs to another is mingled with her. For that is true in which we are born, not that into which we are changed; what we received from the Creator, not what we assumed from a sexual union. Therefore give true ones to true Levi, that leader of the priests; to true Aaron, to true Melchizedek—true ones such as he himself created, not such as the custom of this world produces—so that he may recognize in you his work and that generative seal undefiled and whole.

36. Give him, present to him, that Adam who existed before sin, and that Eve who existed before she drank the serpent’s slippery poison, before his plots brought about her downfall—when they had nothing for which to be ashamed. For now, although marriages are good, married couples nevertheless have something of which they themselves are ashamed. Therefore, my sons, be such as Adam and Eve were in Paradise (Gen. IV, 2). Of them it is written that after Adam had been expelled from Paradise, he knew Eve his wife, and she conceived [Col. 0346D] and bore a son whom she called Cain; and again she conceived and bore a son whose name was Abel [Note: All printed editions read, “and bore a son, whose name was Abel.” Since what follows clearly shows the passage to be incomplete, Latinius, following Bandinius, declared that it should be supplemented thus: “and bore Cain, and said, ‘I have acquired a man through God.’ And again she conceived,” and so on. But it is thanks to all the manuscripts that we have no need of this conjecture.]. The second fruit was therefore better than the first, because the one was undefiled, the other stained. The one clung to God and was wholly the Lord’s; the other was a worldly and earthly possession. Indeed, in the one the redemption of the world is announced, while from the other came the world’s ruin; in the one is Christ’s sacrifice, in the other the devil’s murder of his brother. Therefore, my sons, let nothing belonging to worldly possession be yours, and do not think that you have been allotted any earthly or Jewish possession to vindicate [Note: Many manuscripts read, “to vindicate those possessions”; some, more suitably, “to judge them.” It would be absurd to think that such possessions had been allotted to you for judgment.].

37. We do read that Moses—that is, the Law—decreed that lands acquired by war and slaughter should be distributed by lot to the Hebrew people (Num. XXVI, 53), and that the daughters of Zelophehad asked for their possession, because they were the daughters of Zelophehad (Num. XXVII, 1 ff.). Yet Moses did not divide the land among the Levites (Deut. XVIII, 1 ff.), whose dwelling was not earthly but higher; instead, without earthly labor, he assigned to them the support of sacred ministry. But what are the daughters of Zelophehad who ask for land, except—as the interpretation teaches—“the shadowing of the mouth”? This is found in those whose mouth has no word and whose speech contains no truth (Ps. V, 10), as among the Jewish people who refuse to confess Christ Jesus as God’s Son. Such people therefore seek land and ask for this kind of possession, in which they toil throughout their whole lives and, instead of fruit, reap thorns of cares and anxieties [Note: Most manuscripts read, “and reap anxieties.”].

38. Therefore flee, daughters, the shadow of the mouth, since you believe in the eternal light that illumines every human being; confess Christ not as though he were in shadow, but in the light. “The people who sat in the shadow of death: a light has risen for them” (Isa. IX, 2). We too were in the shadow, but now we are no longer, because we confess Christ. Would that I too had been permitted to say, “we who profess Christ”! Nevertheless, let us profess: I, widowhood; you, virginity. May confession with the mouth be made for salvation in us.

39. Therefore give to that saving Levi his lots [Note: Several manuscripts read, “his lots.” “His lot is Levitical; it is a widow,” which is thoroughly corrupt.]. His lot is Levitical; his lot is virginity; his lot is widowhood, because not only a virgin but also an unmarried woman thinks about the things of the Lord. Hence the Apostle also said: “In whom we have also been allotted a portion” (Eph. I, 11). For just as in the Old Testament the land was divided by lot (Josh. XVIII, 10), so in the Gospel we are assigned to the Lord by a kind of lot. Hence it is also written of the evangelists: “They divided my garments among themselves, and over my clothing they cast a lot” (John XIX, 24) [Note: Certain Paris editions read, “Hence it was also said by the evangelists.” This is incorrect; Ambrose means nothing else here than that the evangelists were prefigured by the soldiers dividing Christ’s garments. See *Exposition on Luke*, Book X, column 1528, no. 115 ff.]. And when a twelfth apostle had to be chosen in Judas’s place, the apostles thought that the office of the apostleship should be assigned by lot. Accordingly, after prayer that the Lord would choose whichever of the two he wished, the lot fell upon Matthias (Acts I, 26).

40. That former allotment, then, was earthly; this one is spiritual. In the former is the material wealth of the world; in this, the duty belonging to a person. There is possession of cares; here, a division of graces. There we possess fields full of labor and sorrow; here, we are possessed by Christ. Hence holy David says: “You have possessed my kidneys” (Ps. CXXXVIII, 13) [Note: All printed editions read, “the holy one of the Lord”; all manuscripts read, “holy David.”]. May he possess your kidneys, my sons, so that the seeds of chastity and the incentives to virtue may remain in them. Therefore dedicate yourselves to Christ and confess him, so that you may say: “The Lord is my portion” (Ps. CXVIII, 57). A married woman cannot say this, but an unmarried one can; the married woman seeks to please her husband, the unmarried woman Christ. The one is the possession of the world, the other of Christ.

41. Christ’s possession is the Levite, who claims nothing for himself from earthly things. He who seeks a wife cannot say, “The Lord is my portion.” What, then, does Christ’s minister say? “Silver and gold I do not have; but what I have, I give you: in the name of Jesus the Nazarene, rise and walk” (Acts III, 6). For he had received this, because he did not desire gold. Indeed, he had been sent without a staff, without a bag, without money (Luke IX, 3). And therefore he gloried because he did not possess what he had not received; for he was not ashamed of poverty, since the poor man had redeemed him. Therefore he said, “Rise and walk,” because he had read: “This poor man cried, and the Lord heard him” (Ps. XXXIII, 7).

## CHAPTER VII

Virginity is shown to be better than the fertility of others, since it imitates the abundant births of the Church, which are produced by lot—that is, by grace and not by works. Lots are therefore to be given to Christ, who pays a reward beyond the labor; truth too—that is, virginity—is to be given. How many and how great are the temptations by which it is attacked! But when we have learned from the Apostle that chastity is good, the holy Widow indicates that we must have recourse to a remedy. Through an elegant allegory of that ancient Mary, she signifies that the remedy lies in the mortification of the flesh and in the merit of the Lord’s Passion, by which we are led to victory. Afterwards wisdom is to be sought in the heavens and drawn into the interior, so that we may live.

42. Therefore let the Lord be your portion—the Lord who makes the barren woman and the one who bears children. He makes both: but one gives birth in sorrow, while the other rejoices in barrenness, to whom it is said: “Rejoice, barren woman who do not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail” (Isa. LIV, 1). For she has children without the pain of childbirth. Hence it is said of the Church: “Who has heard such a thing? If the earth has travailed in one day, and a nation has been born all at once” (Isa. LXVI, 8) [Note: The Roman edition reads, “Who has heard such a thing, if she has travailed,” and so on.]. Yet the earth does not give birth in one day; grace gives birth. Easter comes, the sacraments of baptism are celebrated throughout the whole world, and sacred virgins are veiled. Thus in one day, without any pain, the Church regularly gives birth to many sons and daughters [Col. 0349A]. Therefore it is beautifully said: “And a nation has been born all at once,” from a consecrated people.

43. You see the mysteries; you see the grace of Christ, the grace of the Holy Spirit, which is conveyed as though by a kind of lot, because each person is justified by the Lord not from works but from faith. For just as the outcome of a lot is not in our power, but is determined by whatever chance brings, so the Lord’s grace is conveyed not as though on the merit of a payment earned, but as though according to his will. Hence the Apostle also speaks of the divisions of graces, which are conveyed in different ways to God’s servants: “All these things one and the same Spirit works, distributing to each one as he wills.” He says, “as he wills,” not “as is owed” (I Cor. XII, 11). Finally, the Lord also says to those who demanded a greater reward for their work and complained that they had received the same as those who came later: “If I am good, why is your eye evil?” (Matt. XX, 15).

44. Therefore, my sons, give your lots to him who is accustomed to grant his own a reward beyond the merit of their labor. Give his truth to the holy man (Deut. XXXIII, 8)—that is, integrity; for integrity belongs to him who came undefiled. Truth, therefore, is virginity; corruption is falsehood. Stand firm in your heart, like a good vine on its branch.

45. There are many temptations; therefore Scripture says: “They tempted him with temptation and cursed him beside the waters of contradiction at Kadesh” (Deut. XXXII, 51). Virginity is tempted by many suitors; and when a virgin wishes to persevere, there arise those who oppose her. The suitor contradicts, and when rejected, curses. An unmarried woman, whether virgin or widow, appears to be an object of reproach. For Kadesh is the unmarried woman who is holy in body and spirit and has dedicated herself to the Lord; she has left her parents and does not do the will of those who are accustomed to say: “You owe us grandchildren, daughter.” Kadesh is she who knows no children. If she prefers the reproach of Christ to the riches of the world—the reproach which one who seeks to please Christ must necessarily undergo—how much more ought you, whom your father urges toward integrity and your mother encourages to follow what is fitting, to do so?

46. Virginity is therefore good. Hence he says: “He who has decided in his heart [Note: Some manuscripts read, “to preserve his virginity.”] to keep his virgin unmarried does well.” Therefore he who gives his virgin in marriage also does well, and he who does not give her in marriage does better (I Cor. VII, 37–38). The former does well because of the snare; the latter does better because of the advantage. The former is for a remedy, the latter for a reward. But happier is the one who remains thus, according to my counsel—“for I think that I too have the Spirit of God” (ibid., 40). Therefore follow the Apostle’s counsel, my sons, the gift of the Holy Spirit.

47. Therefore you too, like Mary, the sister of Moses and Aaron, take the tambourine in your hands and go forth, saying: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously exalted; horse and rider he has cast into the sea” (Exod. XV, 20). Mortify your members in the manner of a tambourine: let no wantonness of the flesh boil up in them, and let every sensation of bodily burning perish. Let the spirit alone resound in them amid the dead pleasures of the body. For if you have died to sin, you will live to God; and you will live if no desire reigns in your dead body.

48. Turn the cross of the Lord Jesus in your hands, and lifting it up through your works, trample the depths of this world and pass through. Let that horse, neighing in lust, find no place in you; and whoever wishes to pursue and seize you, let him be drowned. Let water be a wall around you on the right and on the left, so that every vapor of the body may be tempered, until divine favor leads you to those intelligible twelve springs and seventy palm trees, to that great rest of the Sabbath, and deigns to plant you on the mountain of his inheritance, where holy Mary leads the choirs [Note: Understand this as the repose of the blessed resurrection, which Ambrose commonly teaches is signified by the number seven. Among the Jews there were three “great Sabbaths,” concerning which see *Exposition on Luke*, Book VIII, no. 25, where we make some observations. Consult the passage itself if convenient.].

49. Therefore put on the Lord Jesus, my sons; seek true wisdom, of which Job says: “But wisdom—where has it been found, and where is the place of understanding? … The abyss said, ‘It is not in me.’ The sea said, ‘It is not with me’” (Job XXVIII, 12 ff.). The abyss rightly said, “It is not in me,” because he has risen; for it does not possess the one whom it could not hold. Indeed, in the Gospel you find that the angels said to the women who came to the tomb: “You seek Jesus who was crucified. He is not here, but has risen” (Matt. XXVIII, 5–6). What does “he is not here” mean? It means that he is not in the tomb, not in the underworld, but in the heavenly places. The sea too—that is, the world—says, “He is not with me,” because he is above the world, and the fall and allurements of human life did not change him; because he committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth (I Pet. II, 22). Thus the abyss said, “He is not in me”; the sea said, “He is not with me.” But heaven did not say that he was not with it, for it had received him when he rose. Paradise did not say, “He is not in me,” for it knew him reigning within it, once even the thief had been released, just as the Lord himself said: “Today you will be with me in Paradise” (Luke XXIII, 43).

50. Draw wisdom, my sons, into the inner chambers of your heart, for it is more precious than all gold and silver; death does not know it, because “the dead will not praise you, Lord, but the living” [Note: All printed editions, with some manuscripts, read, “will praise the Lord”; a great many other manuscripts read, “they will praise you, Lord.”]. Therefore, so that you may live, praise the Lord, and praise him day and night (Ps. CXIII, 17–18). You will praise him if no desire for marriage or care for the world turns you away from him, since those who enter marriage are troubled by the affairs of this world.

## CHAPTER VIII

To press more vigorously upon her offspring, who had already been promised to God by their parents, she recounts the obedience of Jephthah’s daughter in fulfilling her father’s vow. Then, turning to her son, she recalls to him how he had been obtained from God through prayers, and therefore cannot be denied to him without guilt. Having said these things, the holy woman, seeing the eagerness of her pious offspring, pours herself out in thanksgiving; Ambrose narrates her progress into the Church, where she found her son performing the office of reader.

51. Consider, my sons, what you owe to your parents’ vows. We have opened our mouth to God [Note: Above, through Juliana’s words, he had already reminded Laurentius, the brother of those three virgins, of vows made by parents, as though they ought to carry the greatest weight with him. Here he teaches still more explicitly the power of those vows to bind children. There is no doubt that formerly children offered by their parents to monasteries were compelled—at least in the Western Church—to observe the monastic life permanently. This is expressly prescribed by the Council of Toledo, canon 48, where we read: “Either paternal devotion or one’s own profession makes a monk. Whichever of these there has been will keep him bound,” and so on. Likewise canon 50: “The same applies to those who have been tonsured by their parents,” and so on. Isidore lays down the same rule; he is cited not only in *Decretum* 20, question 1, chapter “Quicumque relatus,” but also by Saint Benedict of Aniane in the *Concordance of Rules*, chapter 45, § 3, and by Smaragdus in chapter 49 of the *Rule of Saint Benedict*. The synod of Orléans V, canon 19, and the first Council of Mâcon, canon 18, likewise prescribe this. Pope Gregory II may also be added, in letter 9 to Boniface of Mainz, cited in *Decretum* 20, question 1, chapter “Addidistis.” Besides the Rules of Saint Benedict, the Master, and others, the same matter is confirmed by the formulas used by parents when offering their children, which our Menard presents in the *Concordance of Rules*, chapter 66; and, besides Acherius in his notes on Lanfranc and elsewhere, our Mabillon presents them in volume III of the *Analecta*, p. 469. See also the most learned Thomassin, *Ecclesiastical Discipline*, part II, chapter 45, who attributes that custom to the Spanish councils—though it might perhaps more properly be referred to this exposition of Ambrose, or at least to the Rule of Saint Benedict, which is a century older than the fourth Council of Toledo. Thomassin, however, maintains that the opposite custom prevailed among Eastern Christians, and even among Western Christians during the first four centuries of the Church.]. A vow is the will of the parents. We have vowed; you fulfill. The daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite ought to teach you how great is the power of parents’ vows: so that she would not frustrate her father’s offering, she even offered her own death. For when he, anxious about the danger of war, had vowed that if the outcome of the battle were favorable he would sacrifice to God whatever first met him on his return home, once he had won the victory his daughter met him, joyful above all others in the joy of victory and in the fulfillment of piety. The father groaned, not remembering affection, but remembering his vow [Note: All printed editions and a few manuscripts read, “not mindful of affection”; many more manuscripts read, “mindful of affection.” The latter seems preferable, so that the sense is that he burst into groans not so much from the recollection of paternal affection as from the recollection of the bloody vow.]. His daughter asked the reason; he told her what he had promised to the Lord. Then she encouraged him to fulfill the gift promised to God. Thus she discharged her father’s rash offering with her own blood (Judg. XI, 31 ff.).

52. These things are common to you [Note: Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read, “These things, daughters, are common to you”; the Roman edition, “let them be commended to you.” Below, where the printed editions read “intercourse,” the manuscripts read “assembly,” with the same meaning.]. But you, my son, whom the true Elkanah gave me (I Sam. I, 1 ff.)—that is, whom God’s possession gave me; my petition, my request—for Samuel also received his name from this; you, I say, my obtained and vowed son, of whom I do not know how you came into my womb, for I had already despaired of offspring of the male sex; you whom my vows, not the secret practices of any solemn assembly, formed [Col. 0351C]; you, I say, my son, acknowledge from whom you were given to me. He fashioned your face; he marked out your limbs; he received my prayers. To his temple and service I consecrated you before you were born. You were born not for your parents, nor for yourself, but for God, whose you began to be before you came out of your mother’s womb. Indeed, we all belong to him, but you, who were specially promised to your Lord, are returned to him, because it is written: “Vow and render to the Lord your God” (Ps. LXXV, 12). I, wretched and unworthy, yet like Hannah, promised that throughout all the days and nights of your life you would not depart from the sight of the Lord. I promised; you fulfill it. The Lord himself will complete for himself the gift of his sacrifice.

53. Thus and in other ways the pious mother spoke. When she had seen the fitting affection of her sons, leading her weaned child by the breasts of spiritual grace into the temple of the Lord, she turned to prayer and said: “My heart has been established in the Lord; my horn has been exalted in my God. My mouth has been enlarged over my enemies; let it rejoice in your salvation, because there is none holy like the Lord, and there is none just like our God, and there is none holy besides you” (I Sam. II, 1–2).

54. Thus the mother spoke to her sons, bringing into her household at once the titles of widowhood in herself and of integrity in her children, as though they were certain feminine dignities. Truly she was an outstanding woman, who kept nothing for herself: she offered to God everything she possessed. Her life is an instruction in discipline and a kind of pattern of chastity through good purpose and better teaching. For an example of widowhood and virginity is itself a lesson.

55. She proceeds into the church of her virgin daughters, surrounded by an accompanying retinue [Note: Many manuscripts read, “surrounded by domestic company, a great distinction.”], bringing with her the honor of her household. In the Church she finds what she may call her own: her son sounding forth the oracles of the sacred readings, so that when the brother is heard, the sisters seem to themselves to be learning at home. The mother too, in imitation of the heavenly example, rejoices that she is advancing through her son; she entrusts every word of the reader to her pious affection and preserves it carefully in her heart.

## CHAPTER IX

To add his own holy exhortation to the mother’s, the bishop urges those virgins to seek Christ in the divine Scriptures. He asserts that when he is sought, he is already present; he teaches them to ask where he dwells at midday—that is, in the Father’s light—and to seek him also in the light of good works and in nightly prayers. When he has passed by, they are to follow him; for he delights in being sought repeatedly, so that he may revive grace and wound the soul with love. He proves the nature of these wounds through various examples of the saints.

56. Yet although the maternal exhortations lacked nothing, I too will address you, my sons, in a few words. Seek the Lord Jesus, who urges us to seek the kingdom of God: “And behold,” he says, “all things will be supplied to you” (Matt. VI, 33). But I prefer you to bring the reward before the merit and thus demand payment. The reward is good, but the dispenser of the reward and author of the gift is more divine. The reward is in the kingdom; in Christ lies the power to reward. Seek her in the divine Scriptures, where Christ is found, and say as she said: “Tell me where he is whom my soul has loved” (Song I, 6). The Synagogue too sought the one whom it had lost; seek the one whom you will not lose. But why, Synagogue, do you say “the one whom I loved,” and not “the one whom I love”? You do not hold him because you say that you loved him. Why do you not love him still, so that you may be able to hold him?

57. But let us leave her aside. You, virgin, when you begin to seek him, find him present; for he cannot be absent from those who seek him, since he made himself manifest to those who did not seek him and was found by those who did not inquire after him (Isa. LXV, 1) [Note: Most manuscripts read, “while she thinks that she has treated the matter.”]. While you ponder and reflect, he is at hand. Learn to ask, when he comes, where he feeds and where he dwells, as she said: “Where do you feed? Where do you dwell at midday?” (Song I, 6). For where does Christ dwell except where the midday of righteousness shines? This is taught by the testimony of sacred Scripture, which says: “He placed his tabernacle in the sun” (Ps. XVIII, 6). Hence the same Prophet says elsewhere: “In your light we shall see light” (Ps. XXXV, 10). The Son is light, and the Father who is seen in the Son is also light, because the Son is “the splendor of the Father’s glory and the image of his substance” (Heb. I, 3).

58. But seek Christ also in your own light, virgin—in good thoughts and good works that shine before your Father who is in heaven. Seek him in the nights; seek him in your chamber [Note: The printed edition reads, “seek him in your bedchamber.”], because he comes by night as well and knocks at your door. He wishes you to keep watch at every moment; he wishes to find the door of your mind open. There is also that door which he wishes to stand open, so that your mouth may be opened and resound with the praise of the Lord, the grace of the Bridegroom, and confession of the cross, while you recite the creed and sing psalms in your chamber. Therefore, when he comes, let him find you watchful, so that you may be ready. Let your flesh sleep, but let faith keep watch; let the allurements of the body sleep, but let the prudence of the heart keep watch. Let your limbs give off the fragrance of Christ’s cross and of burial, so that sleep may pour no heat into them and arouse no agitation [Note: Most manuscripts read, “so that no fear may arouse him … When this comes, the Bridegroom will pass by, so that the soul may …”; but other manuscripts and the printed editions have the reading given in the text.]. She is the soul that opens herself to Christ, whom no vapors of the flesh disturb.

59. When the Bridegroom finds these things, he will pass by. Let your soul follow him; let it leave its chamber and go forth in his word, as it is written: “My soul went forth at your word” (Song V, 6)—that is, let it be a pilgrim away from the body, so that it may be present with God, because while it is in the body it is a pilgrim away from Christ. Hence the Apostle says: “Therefore we dare and consent rather to be pilgrims away from the body and to be present with the Lord” (I Cor. V, 8 ff.) [Note: Thus all the manuscripts without exception; all printed editions instead read, “and we strive more earnestly.” In Greek: θαῤῥοῦμεν δὲ, καὶ εὐδοκοῦμεν, “we are confident and approve”; the Vulgate has, “we dare and have good will”; other versions have, “we are confident and desire.”]. And therefore we strive, whether absent or present, to please him. For we must all appear before Christ’s tribunal, so that each may receive back what belongs to his body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil. How quickly he has proved the case for the resurrection of the body! For the flesh must rise again, since it is destined to obtain the reward of its deeds, so that what we have done in the body we may receive back in the body.

### 60 [Col. 0354B–D]

The Lord therefore wishes to be sought more often: [Note: The reading of not a few manuscripts is *discedit*, “he departs.” Why? “That he may revive,” etc. It is not inappropriate.] he departs and runs away in order to revive the grace which he wishes also to be revived by you and in you, as we read written to Timothy: “For which cause I remind you that you revive the grace of God which is in you through the laying on of my hands” (2 Tim. 1:6). Once grace has been revived, the soul becomes wounded by love, as she says: “For I am wounded by love: if you have awakened and stirred up love” (Song 5:8). What this means we shall be able to understand if we recall that the Lord Jesus is an arrow, to whom the Father says: “I have set you like a chosen arrow” (Isa. 49:2). And since he himself is love, there are certainly darts of love by which he wounds those who seek him. Finally, those bound with fetters follow him, because he binds those whom he wounds. Thus there are also bonds of love, by which Paul was bound when he said: “Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ” (Philem. 1).

### 61 [Col. 0354C–D; p. 294]

Job teaches that these are wounds of love—Job, than whom no one loved Christ more, for he loved him even amid the torments of his own body. Hence he said: “The arrows of the Lord are in my body; their fury has drunk up my blood. When I begin to speak, they pierce me” (Job 6:4). They are therefore wounds of love, and good wounds. Indeed, “the wounds of a friend are better than the voluntary kisses of an enemy” (Prov. 27:6). Jeremiah too was burning, and could not endure the fire of love with which he was inflamed for the prophetic ministry (Jer. 20:9). Finally, he was thrown into a pit (Jer. 38:6), because he announced to the Jews the disasters that were to come and could not keep silent. Stephen was being stoned (Acts 7:58), and received those wounds for Christ with devout affection, as wounds of love. The apostles were scourged and rejoiced together (Acts 5:40). How good is the Lord, for whom insults are sweet and death welcome! And welcome indeed is that death which acquires immortality.

## CHAPTER X [Col. 0354D–0355A]

A passage from Ecclesiastes concerning clothing is appropriate to virginity; but what he adds about carrying oil on the head is also to be understood of humility of mind and modest composure of body, since interior ornaments are chiefly required in us, and the wealth of the poor is the simplicity of innocence. How does the Synagogue say to the Church, “Where do you feed?” and so forth? And how does the Church receive these words as Christ’s: “Unless you know yourself,” and so forth? This signifies that the divine image resides in our soul, and that the greatest care must therefore be taken of it. Accordingly, he urges the young man to delight in innocence of heart; and virgins to avoid the eyes of men, after the example of Mary, and to shun every occasion for gossip.

### 62 [Col. 0355A–B]

“Let your garments,” he says, “be white at all times” (Eccles. 9:8). What is whiter than virginity? [Note: The editions read, “What is brighter than an untouched garment.”] What is whiter than an undefiled garment of chastity? Conjugal chastity is good, as is the chastity of widowhood; all chastity is pure, but perhaps not all is white, or not white at all times (1 Cor. 7:4–5). It is not white when one does not have authority over one’s own body, when prayer is set aside for a time. Of virginity, therefore, it is beautifully said: “Let your garments be white at all times, and let oil be upon your head” (Eccles. 9:8), so that your lamps may always be able to shine and not be extinguished when that heavenly Bridegroom begins to come (Matt. 25:6 ff.).

### 63 [Col. 0355B–C; p. 295]
