By what reasoning Ecclesiastes spoke of oil on your head we shall gather from Proverbs, because “the eyes of a man are in his head” (Eccles. 2:14)—that is, the perceptions of your wisdom. [Note: So read all the manuscripts. Conversely, all editions read: “But what anointing Ecclesiastes said was on your head we gather from Proverbs”; the Roman edition has “from other passages.” The words quoted by Ambrose are indeed found at the place indicated in the margin. It is possible, however, that he was referring to Prov. 17:24, *πρόσωπον συνετὸν ἀνδρὸς σοφοῦ*, “the understanding face of a wise man,” a saying which, as he sometimes does, he may have quoted only from memory.] Perhaps for this reason also that woman in the Gospel is praised who wiped the Lord’s feet with her hair (Luke 7:38 ff.), because she humbled herself by faith, lest she seem exalted through the wisdom of the flesh, which Paul, the true interpreter of hidden things, declared not to be subject to the Law (Rom. 8:7), because it was subject to Christ. [Note: The editions all read as in the text; some manuscripts have *ut homini*, “as to a man,” followed by corrupt wording. Another has *ut homini, quam Lege subditam viro*, “as to a man, whom he declared subject to the Law and to a husband,” and so forth; nothing else is sound. Below, all editions omit the particle *si*, “if,” after *quoniam*, although it is found in all the manuscripts; they also destroyed the structure of the whole sentence through faulty punctuation.]

### 64 [Col. 0355C–D; p. 295]

We can also understand this beautifully in a bodily sense. In the prophetic writings the daughters of Zion are reproved because they walked with uplifted necks, casting glances with their eyes, dragging their robes along with the movement of their feet, and playing with their feet (Isa. 3:16 ff.). Therefore the Lord says that he will take away the glory of their clothing and their ornaments, their hair and their curls. Rightly, then, this woman spread out her hair (Luke 7:38), so that the discipline of the Gospel might loosen the knots of her locks. Hence the apostles said: “Not with the plaiting of hair, as Peter taught” (1 Pet. 3:3), nor “with braided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly clothing,” as Paul asserted (1 Tim. 2:9); rather, women should seek the ornaments of the inner person, “for that hidden person of the heart, who is poor in the world, is rich with God.”

### 65 [Col. 0355D–0356A; p. 295]

“You have heard,” children, you who think yourselves poor. [Note: All editions read, “You have heard, daughters, because you call yourselves poor”; all manuscripts read as in the text.] But who is a rich man, when he lacks so many things, except the one whose conscience is not burdened by sin? For, he says, “Good is the substance of the man who has no sin in his conscience” (Eccles. 13:30). You have heard, I say, in what way you may be rich with God: “Let there be in you,” he says, “an incorruptible and modest spirit” (1 Pet. 3:4). The riches of innocence and simplicity are good riches; sin is not charged against them, because there is no deceitful or fraudulent cunning in them. The simple person knows no slander and does not know how to envy; he is content with his own and does not seek what belongs to another. Even if he is poor, he seems rich to himself if he has enough for food. Hence the apostle Paul says beautifully: “Their deep poverty abounded in the riches of their simplicity” (2 Cor. 8:2).

### 66 [Col. 0356A–B]

And because the Church was adorned with fitting ornaments and, receiving light from Christ, shone forth, the passage may also be understood in this way: the Synagogue says to the Church, “Where do you feed? Where do you rest at midday? Lest I become as one who is veiled among the flocks of your companions” (Song 1:6). She desires to be a hireling, although previously she claimed dominion for herself. How destructive is unbelief!

### 67 [Col. 0356B–C]

But because she is unbelieving, harsh, and sacrilegious, Christ separates her from the flocks of his Church, saying: “Unless you know yourself, O beautiful among women” (ibid. 7)—that is, first recognize who you yourself are, and then ask to draw near to my flocks. The Synagogue is rightly called beautiful among women, not among virgins, because she followed Eve the woman, through whom the Fall came. The Church, however, is beautiful among virgins, because she is a virgin without wrinkle. [Note: Some Paris editions read, “beautiful among men.” Below, all editions and two manuscripts have “and the likeness.” “For in what are we made in the image of God, except in the substance of the soul?” The remaining manuscripts preserve our reading.]

### 68 [Col. 0356C–D; p. 296]

Therefore, whether man or woman, one must know that one is made in the image and likeness of God, so as to pursue the beauty of the soul, not of the body. In what do we consist? In the substance of the soul and the vigor of the mind. This is our whole portion. Hence David says: “I will hope in God; I will not fear what flesh can do to me” (Ps. 55:4). We are not flesh, then, but spirit. Of the Jews it was said: “My spirit shall not remain in them, because they are flesh” (Gen. 6:3). We are not gold, nor money, nor an abundance of riches; those things are external to us. Therefore Moses says to you: “Pay attention to yourself” (Deut. 15:9)—that is, to your soul—lest you perish, lest you become carnal. “Pay attention to yourself”: that is, to the image you received from Christ, to the likeness according to which you were made. Preserve that image which Christ painted in you by his works, as he himself says to Jerusalem—that is, to the peaceful soul: “Behold, I, Jerusalem, have painted your walls” (Isa. 49:16).

### 69 [Col. 0357A; p. 296]

Pay attention, then, and you especially, child; pay attention to yourself, so that you may rejoice in your youth, to whom Scripture says: “Rejoice, young man, in your youth” (Eccles. 11:9). [Note: Four manuscripts read, “He does not say to you alone: ‘The season of life is as it were…’”] It does not speak to you merely of one period of life. It is, as it were, the flower of life and the age of good works, of which it is written: “Your youth shall be renewed like the eagle’s” (Ps. 103:5). “Let your heart delight you,” he says, “in the days of your youth, and walk in the ways of your heart without blame, and in the sight of your eyes”—but not in the boldness of your eyes (Eccles. 11:9), that is, in spiritual sight, not worldly presumption. And know that for all these things God will bring you into judgment. “Remove anger from your heart, and put away wickedness from your flesh” (Eccles. 12:14).

### 70 [Col. 0357A–B; p. 296]

Pay attention to yourself, virgin, so that you may persevere in prayer and your face may grow pale through continual supplication. But before prayer, prepare your soul (Eccles. 18:23), lest you seem to tempt God when you entreat him; let your conduct speak what you pray for, let faith assist, and let your works commend it. Pay attention to yourself—what I say to every virgin. For you, the devout, do not lack a teacher of instruction. [Note: All editions read, “what I say to you, to whatever virgin I speak”; the manuscripts omit the word without any loss of meaning. Again, the old edition and all manuscripts read *praesertim professionis*, “especially of the profession”; the Roman edition restored *praesertim professioni*, “especially to the profession.” This is not satisfactory, for it does not refer to *attende*, “pay attention,” but contrasts sacred virgins here with other virgins mentioned shortly before. Finally, where all editions have *ab hominis irreverentis*, “from an irreverent man,” two manuscripts read *ab omni irreverentia*, “from every irreverence,” two others *ab omnis irreverentis*, and the rest *ab omni irreverenti*. The entire passage is read in Greek as follows:]

*Ὀπίσω ἀναιδοῦς ὀφθαλμοῦ φύλαξαι, καὶ μὴ θαυμάσῃς ἐὰν εἰς σὲ πλημμελήσῃ ὡς διψῶν ὁδοίπορος τὸ στόμα ἀνοίγει, καὶ ἀπὸ παντὸς ὕδατος τοῦ σύνεγγυς πίεται.*

“Guard yourself from the shameless eye, and do not be surprised if he transgresses against you: like a thirsty traveler, he opens his mouth and drinks from every water that is near.” The Vulgate version does not depart from this. From this it may also be confirmed, as we have noted elsewhere, that Ambrose used a sacred text differing in no small degree from ours.

### 71 [Col. 0357B–C; Col. 0358D; p. 297]

Pay attention, I say, virgin, especially one of sacred profession, and beware of every irreverent eye. And if he passes by for a time like a traveler, nevertheless he opens his mouth and drinks from every nearby water, so that he may intoxicate you (Eccles. 26:14 ff.). [Note: Many manuscripts read, “drink the nearest water”; others and the editions read, “he will drink.” Observe how much love of solitude the holy Doctor demands from virgins, since he wishes even their more frequent attendance at church to be restricted.] Let no journey of yours take place without your mother, who is an anxious guardian of chastity. Your going even to church should be less frequent, young women. Consider how great Mary was, and yet, when she is sought, she is found nowhere else except in her chamber (Luke 1:28). Let her teach you what you should follow. She saw an angel in the form of a man and trembled in heart, withdrawing her gaze. Hence the angel says to her: “Do not be afraid, Mary.” [Note: All manuscripts except two read, “Solitude teaches modesty”; the two, together with all editions, have “Solitude is fitting.” The latter is less well connected, as what follows—“and a school”—sufficiently shows.] Solitude teaches modesty, and a secluded place is a school of chastity.

### 72 [Col. 0357C–D; Col. 0358A; p. 297]

For what need have you even of approaching a neighbor easily? “The foot of a fool is quick to enter his neighbor’s house, but the wise man is ashamed” (Eccles. 21:25). From this arise stories and gossip, against which you are beautifully warned to guard yourself when the wise man says to you: “Who will set a guard over my discipline and a sure seal upon my lips, lest I fall by them and my tongue destroy me?” (Eccles. 22:33). [Note: The Roman edition reads, “lest I fall away from it,” referring to discipline, as in the Septuagint: *ἵνα μὴ πέσω ἀπ’ αὐτῆς*. The remaining editions, together with all manuscripts and the Vulgate, have “lest I fall by them,” namely, by the lips—lest they drive me into ruin.] If the male sex is commanded to remain silent before elders (Eccles. 11:8), how unbecoming it is for virgins to speak and to sow various conversations!

### 73 [Col. 0358A]

Suppose you command yourself to keep silent: can you command others not to speak so that you will not hear? A person can sometimes put a bridle on his mouth and a balance on his words; he cannot do so with his ears. Speaking is within our own control, but hearing depends on another’s power; often we hear what we do not wish to hear.

## CHAPTER XI [Col. 0358A–B]

He joins new admonitions to those above: they are to avoid readiness to swear and to prefer tears to merriment; they are to abstain from laughter, through which the Synagogue perished; they are to moderate anger, even if they cannot extinguish it entirely; finally, if they have not maintained proper restraint, they are to repent with compunction.

### 74 [Col. 0358B]

Let us next consider what else Scripture admonishes us. “Do not swear readily” (Eccles. 23:9), because many circumstances commonly arise that prevent us from fulfilling what we have sworn. Whoever does not swear certainly does not commit perjury; whoever swears must at some time fall into perjury, because “every human being is a liar” (Ps. 116:11). Do not swear, therefore, lest you begin to perjure yourself.

### 75 [Col. 0358B–C; p. 298]

Even freer merriment is not fitting in virgins. If they have nothing to weep over, let them weep for the world; let them weep over the falls of sinners, for whoever weeps over the falls of others will beware of her own. [Note: The words *fleant saeculum*, “let them weep for the world,” are absent from all editions but have been added from nearly all written manuscripts, except two.] Finally, let them weep even in contemplation of this: by weeping here, they may receive consolation there, lest, like that rich man who lived luxuriously here and, according to the Lord’s declaration, suffered severe punishments there, they hear: “You received good things during your life” (Luke 16:25 ff.). How much happier Lazarus, who wept here and rejoices there; who hungered here and feasts there! If you too wish to pursue good joy, the book of Ecclesiastes shows you the joy you should pursue, saying: “Come, eat your bread with joy, because your deeds have already pleased God” (Eccles. 9:7).

### 76 [Col. 0358C–D; Col. 0359A; p. 298]

Let us consider what the same Ecclesiastes has warned us all about immoderate laughter. “As the crackling of thorns under a pot, so is the laughter of fools” (Eccles. 7:7). Thorns, when they burn, crackle and are quickly consumed, so that no warmth results. Hence it was also said of the Jews: “They burned like fire among thorns” (Ps. 118:12). Consumed by their own laughter, they were burned up in the Lord’s Passion, when they made sport of the conflagration of their own souls, saying: “He hoped in the Lord; let him deliver him; let him save him, since he wants him” (Ps. 22:8). And while mocking him, they struck his head with a reed; because they crowned him with thorns and offered him vinegar to drink, that laughter set the Synagogue on fire forever. [Note: Some manuscripts read, “and they crowned him with a crown of thorns.”] Such, then, is the laughter of fools, which makes a sound without grace and burns the pot of its own body. Sarah rightly denied that she had laughed (Gen. 18:15), lest she seem, by laughing, to have doubted the fulfillment of the heavenly promises; yet that laughter had been full of seriousness and modesty, and no witness except God alone, who is not deceived by hidden things, knew it.

### 77 [Col. 0359A–B]

How beautiful too is this saying: “Do not hasten in your spirit to become angry, because anger rests in the bosom of fools” (Eccles. 7:10). That is, even if there is a cause that arouses indignation, let revenge not be hasty, lest the heat of indignation boil over without measure. He cannot therefore remove the movement that is natural, but he inserts delay, so that the medicine of deliberation may temper anger. Thus David had already said: “Be angry, and do not sin” (Ps. 4:5)—not because he commanded anger, but because he could not remove what belonged to nature; rather, like a good physician, he gave a remedy so that anger itself might not do harm.

### 78 [Col. 0359B]

Finally, even if someone has slipped in heart, since anger does not know how to keep within bounds, he advises that the person be pierced with remorse in his bedchambers and that each one condemn his own error. Thus it is written: “What you say in your hearts, and be pierced with remorse in your beds” (ibid.). He therefore wished all people to be judges of their own offenses, so that one who is not held by public testimony might blush before himself, judging in secret where he has fallen, and restrain himself with a kind of goad of bitterness and shame.

## CHAPTER XII [Col. 0359C–D]

He passes to frugality, by which the body may be worn down; he commands that a good reputation be acquired; above all, he requires sobriety in a virgin—that is, abstinence from wantonness and vain bodily ornaments, which he grieves to see sought even by certain sacred virgins. Against them he sets the example of holy Soteris, who took so little care of her appearance that she willingly offered her face to be disfigured by the executioners’ blows. He compares her with the Etruscan youth who, they say, disfigured his face with scars.

### 79 [Col. 0359D]

Why should I speak of frugality, when the Wise Man says: “Take away from me the desire of the belly, and do not let the desire for sexual intercourse seize me” (Eccles. 23:6)? [Note: The editions read, “and the desire for intercourse.”] Do not fear the weakness caused by fasting and abstinence; serious weakness makes the soul sober.

### 80 [Col. 0359D–0360A]

How the Proverbs of Solomon also teach that one must strive for a good reputation is shown by their saying: “A good name is better than great riches” (Prov. 22:1). For what is an inheritance unless it is governed by good administration and action? [Note: All editions, with a few manuscripts, read, “unless that good administration and work”; the majority of manuscripts read as in the text.] Hence holy Job says: “Let the blessing of the one who was dying come upon me, and let the widow’s mouth bless me. I was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame, a father to the weak” (Job 29:13 ff.). “If I saw a naked person passing by and did not clothe him; if the needy did not bless me, and I did not warm their shoulders with the fleeces of my sheep; if I ever hid my sin, even one I had committed unintentionally rather than willingly; if I ever allowed the poor person to leave my door with an empty lap” (Job 31:19 ff.)—for by such deeds a good name is acquired.

### 81 [Col. 0360A–C; p. 299]

Above all, however, the pursuit of sobriety excels in a virgin. By sobriety I do not mean abstinence from wine, but from bodily wantonness and worldly display, by which we are intoxicated more grievously than by wine; for it gives the cup of ruin and the goblet of wrath. Hence the Lord also says to Jerusalem: “Hear, humbled one, drunk not with wine. Behold, I have taken from your hand the cup of ruin, the goblet of wrath” (Isa. 51:17). Though the Synagogue has drained this cup, let the daughters of the Church not drink it. For it was said of the Jews: “Their daughters are adorned, embellished, like the likeness of a temple” (Ps. 144:12). But you are the temple of God, daughters of him who is not transformed into an angel of light, but is the true light who is from the true light. Therefore in you let there be not a likeness but the truth. Many, although they profess the pursuit of chastity, seek aids to beauty, so that they may appear more elaborately adorned, with a brighter face than is fitting for the sacred women of the Lord. To them I reply with that apostolic saying: “Since you have died with Christ to the elements of this world, why, as though living in this world, do you make regulations? ‘Do not touch, do not defile, do not taste’—things which are all unto corruption” (Col. 2:20 ff.). [Note: The words “and worldly display,” absent from all editions, have been restored from almost all manuscripts. The Roman edition reads, “the cup which he emptied”; the other editions and all manuscripts more elegantly use a concessive construction: “the cup which he will have emptied,” and so forth.]

### 82 [Col. 0360C–D]

But not so holy Soteris, to offer a household example from a devout relative. We priests have a nobility that ought to be preferred to prefectures and consulships; we have, I say, the dignities of faith, which cannot perish. But Soteris, as I said, did not care for the appearance of her face. Though exceedingly beautiful in countenance and a noble virgin descended from ancestors who had held consulships and prefectures, she preferred sacred faith to the honors of her parents and refused to obey when commanded to sacrifice. A savage persecutor ordered her to be struck on the face, so that the tender virgin might yield either to pain or to shame. But when she heard this command, she uncovered her face, unveiled and exposed solely for martyrdom, and willingly met the outrage, offering her face so that the sacrifice of martyrdom might take place where the temptation to modesty usually lies. She rejoiced that the danger to her integrity was removed at the expense of her beauty. [Note: A certain Paris edition has “at the cost of beauty,” which is unsuitable.] The executioners could indeed inscribe her face with the livid marks of wounds, but they could not in any way disfigure the face of her virtue or the grace of her inward beauty.

### 83 [Col. 0360D–0361A]

Ancient stories tell of an Etruscan youth who, because his remarkable facial beauty inflamed women with love for him, scarred his face with marks so that no woman could love him. [Note: Valerius Maximus calls this youth Spurinus, Book 4, chapter 5, “On Modesty.”] Whether his mind was chaste I leave aside; his motive was nevertheless not innocent, since he punished himself on its account. He, however, merely endured wounds so as not to cause harm; she carried back the triumphal scars of martyrdom in order to preserve the image of God that she had received.

## CHAPTER XIII [Col. 0361A–B]

He urges virgins to preserve the divine image in themselves, so that, instructed by God himself, they may not fear the scourge of another’s tongue. He explains how and to what extent this is not to be feared, and also how they must guard themselves from their own tongue. In this connection the examples of Susanna, Joseph, Daniel, and Job are introduced.

### 84 [Col. 0361B–C; p. 300]

Preserve this image also, daughters; preserve the divine commandments of Scripture: “That every mouth may be stopped” (Rom. 3:19). For it is written: “Blessed is the man whom you instruct, Lord, and teach from your law” (Ps. 94:12). The good Lord instructs and teaches, and often reproves; but he also makes blessed the one whom he reproves: “Blessed is the man whom the Lord reproves” (Ps. 94:12). Therefore do not reject his rebukes, because they arise from love and grace; he himself strikes, and, because he is a good physician, he heals with his own hands (Deut. 32:39). “Seven times he will deliver you from troubles, and at the seventh no evil will touch you. In famine he will rescue you from death; in battle he will snatch you from the hand of the sword; from the scourge of the tongue he will hide you” (Job 5:19 ff.). [Note: The Roman edition reads, “six times from troubles.” In far more manuscripts the following words are missing: “he will hide you.” If you judge that no one should be disparaged, you will not fear the tongue of another. Anyone can readily admit that a lacuna exists here.] If you consider no one worthy of disparagement, you will not fear the scourges of another’s tongue.

### 85 [Col. 0361C–D]

He wonderfully expressed the words of slanderers by calling them the scourge of the tongue, whose sound resounds far and wide. The apostle Peter, wishing to separate us from it, warns us not to return evil for evil or abuse for abuse (1 Pet. 3:9), but, when we are cursed, to return the grace of blessing. Hence it says: “Restrain your tongue from evil” (Ps. 34:13), as from the scourge of the tongue; and do not fear the sound of words if your conscience is clean. It is indeed good, if possible, to give no opportunity for slander; but since many attack not vices but virtues, let them criticize what is worthy of praise, and not find what is worthy of blame.

### 86 [Col. 0361D]

But what is worse, we are scourged not only by another’s tongue but also by our own. These are the more serious blows, when we incur sin through excessive speech. Therefore guard your ways, virgin, so that you do not sin with your tongue (Ps. 39:2). Often even speaking good things is a crime for a virgin. But why are you surprised about a virgin, when a woman is commanded to learn in silence (1 Tim. 2:11)? Good is the modesty commended by silence.

### 87 [Col. 0361D–0362A]

Susanna was in danger, and she remained silent (Dan. 13:35), so that her silent modesty might speak more effectively. At last, modesty found a defender who would defend her chastity. Of her it is rightly said that the Lord hid her from the scourge of the tongue.

### 88 [Col. 0362A]

What shall we say of women? Joseph remained silent when accused (Gen. 39:20), so that innocence might defend him better than speech. Daniel, wiser than them all, remained silent and closed the mouths of lions (Dan. 14:29 ff.). Hence holy David says beautifully: “I set a guard over my mouth while the sinner stood against me” (Ps. 39:2).

### 89 [Col. 0362A–B]

What do you want to say? Are you afraid that, if you remain silent, the accusations will be believed? But listen to the good teacher, holy Job, saying: “Behold, I laugh at insults and do not speak; I will cry out, and nowhere is there judgment” (Job 19:7). That is: an accuser casts insults? You have reason to laugh inwardly if your conscience does not acknowledge the charge. Why should you answer words with words? Judgment has not yet come; and even if you cry out, it does not draw near. Many struggles are owed to you in this world.

### 90 [Col. 0362B; p. 301]

Holy Job had conquered the pain of loss; he had conquered—or rather, shut out—the bitterness of mourning over the loss of his children; he had conquered the harshness of his wounds. [Note: All manuscripts read as in the text, except one. All editions, however, have “the harshnesses,” “the livid marks of the body”; the wording continues, “were applied to the woman’s trials,” and so forth.] The temptations of his wife were added to the livid marks on his body, and he himself did not feel them. The rebukes of his friends were still reserved for his final contest. He had wrestled with paternal affection (Job 1:18), wrestled with bodily pain and sickness (Job 2:7); he had to undergo also the trial of words.

## CHAPTER XIV [Col. 0362C–D]

One must not judge anyone’s merit from the misfortunes of this world, since this is a place of struggle, not of crowns. Paul asserted that the crown is reserved both for himself and for those who love Christ’s coming. Among these must also be counted the widow who, after consecrating to God all the children whom she herself had raised, offered a double sacrifice: that of her widowhood and that of her children’s virginity. Ambrose concludes with a deeply devout prayer.

### 91 [Col. 0362D–0363A; p. 301]

Therefore, when you see a widow suffering through some losses, or through the misfortune of her children; when you see a just person afflicted by death or injuries, do not weigh that person’s merits by the misfortunes of this world, or wonder whether he has been abandoned by the Lord. Here we struggle, but elsewhere we are crowned. I have spoken not only about myself but about all people in common. For where would I have so much merit, when indulgence is my crown? Here is the struggle, there the prize; here is military service, there the pay. Therefore, while I am in this world, I still struggle, still contend, still am driven toward falling; but powerful is the Lord, who receives the one who has been pushed, steadies the one who is slipping, and raises the one who is wavering. Why then are you surprised that someone suffers? As long as one is in this life, there will be no lack of struggle, and there will be no crown. No one is proved except the one who perseveres to the end, so that afterward the one who has contended lawfully may be crowned. [Note: The editions read *adhuc decerto*, “I still fight”; the manuscripts read *adhuc decerno*, “I still contend.”]

### 92 [Col. 0363A–B; p. 302]

Who was stronger than Paul, who more blessed? Yet that chosen vessel of the Lord did not claim the crown for himself before he had completed the whole contest. Therefore he says: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith; as for the rest, the crown of righteousness is reserved for me” (2 Tim. 4:7–8). He says that it is to be given not only to himself but also to all who love the Lord’s coming. Beautifully he says, “to those who love Christ’s coming,” for no one hastens toward judgment except one who is secure in innocence, or one who relies upon his labor, aided either by the Lord’s grace or by devout struggles for Christ.

### 93 [Col. 0363B–0364A]

That privilege will certainly also belong to the widow who has raised her children well, who rejoices in her children, and especially to her who has given to the Lord all those whom she received. Hence the widow in the Gospel is placed before the rich (Luke 21:3–4), not only because she put all she had toward the support of the poor, but also because, having brought two small coins, she is praised by the Lord’s own voice—that is, for her complete faith. Indeed, for the healing of the man, that Samaritan also gave two coins to the innkeeper, so that he might care for the wounds of the man injured by robbers (Luke 10:35). Therefore, because she imitated, in her devotion to her offspring, both the virginity of Mary, the sister of Aaron, according to the Old Testament (Exod. 15:20), and the purity of holy Mary, the mother of the Lord, according to the New (Matt. 1:23), she will receive the reward of faith in the divine judgment. She kept nothing back for herself as a support in this world, but devoted everything to the Lord as the devout offering of her children.

### 94 [Col. 0364A–B]

Now I entreat you, Lord, to look down continually upon this house of yours, upon these altars which are dedicated today, upon these spiritual stones by which a tangible temple is consecrated to you in each person; and in your divine mercy receive the prayers of your servants poured out in this place. Let every sacrifice offered in this temple with wholehearted faith and devout diligence become for you a fragrance of sanctification. [Note: The old editions and a few manuscripts read, “into the fragrance of sanctification”; many others read, “into the honor of sanctification”; only the Roman edition has “into the fragrance of sweetness.”] And when you look upon that saving sacrifice through which the sin of this world is wiped away, look also upon these devout sacrifices of chastity, and protect them with your enduring assistance, so that they may become for you acceptable sacrifices, a pleasing fragrance, pleasing to Christ the Lord. May you deign to preserve their whole spirit, soul, and body blameless until the day of our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son.

# ON THE FALL OF A CONSECRATED VIRGIN [Col. 0363]

## PREFATORY NOTICE TO THE BOOK ON THE FALL OF A CONSECRATED VIRGIN [Col. 0363]

This work contains a vehement rebuke in which the same bishop, with the greatest anguish of spirit, reproaches a girl who, after promising virginity at the altar, had repeatedly allowed herself to be defiled by an unchaste young man (ch. 4, no. 11), and was said to have killed the child conceived by him (ch. 8, no. 53). The crime was enormous by its very nature, but it had been made much graver both by many other circumstances and by the offense it subsequently caused among people (ch. 1, no. 3).

Susanna—for that was her name—came from a noble family (ch. 1, no. 3). When she had resolved to preserve perpetual chastity, she could not overcome the opposition of her parents’ wishes until she devoutly affirmed that certain terrifying visions had moved her to this decision (ch. 4, no. 16). On the very feast of the Lord’s resurrection, in the principal basilica, near the altar to which groups of neophytes had led her with lighted candles (ch. 5, no. 18), she pronounced her vows, with the whole people responding, “Amen” (ibid., no. 19). Soon afterward, after the customary exhortation, the same bishop placed the veil upon her and admitted her, together with the other women religious, into the monastery (ch. 7, no. 27 ff.), where he did not neglect to instruct her frequently with suitable precepts (ibid.).

There she did not lead a life so entirely removed from every appearance and likeness of wrongdoing that, not long afterward, her chastity was not attacked by hostile rumors (ch. 6, no. 24). Susanna bore this with the greatest impatience. The bishop, joining his efforts to those of her parent, labored in vain to discover the authors of the slander and subject them to canonical penalties. Although this should have made her more cautious, nevertheless, after three years had passed (ch. 7, no. 29), she truly committed the crime whose false accusation had previously troubled her, and did so not without causing great scandal among Jews and Gentiles.

She moved heaven and earth to conceal it and could not be brought by any means to confess it. At last, convicted before the bishop, she was assigned to public penance (ch. 6, no. 25). When she had already begun to perform it (ch. 8, no. 37), the same bishop began to address her in the most forceful speech, from which this writing is composed. Having set before her eyes the enormity of the crime both by enumerating its circumstances and by removing her excuses, he teaches that only one remedy remains for her: penance equal to the sin (ch. 8, nos. 33 and 35). If she nobly endures its labors and disgrace to her final breath, he promises that she will escape the punishments of hell that she has deserved (ch. 8, no. 35).

He also addresses the seducer of the same pseudonymous virgin (ch. 9, no. 38), and by the example of Belshazzar, as well as of the Sodomites and Gomorrhans (no. 40), shows him what punishments await him unless he displays similar fruits of repentance. He urges him toward such repentance (no. 41), setting before him the unavoidable necessity of the final judgment. Finally, turning back to Susanna, he prescribes for her the daily recitation of Psalm 50 (ch. 10, no. 42) and further suggests various dispositions of mind (no. 43 ff.) by which she may move herself to sorrow and God to mercy.

[Col. 0365] This work is cited by the Second Synod of Douzy under the names of Ambrose and Jerome, and it is in fact found among the works of both. Erasmus, in his editions of these Fathers, subjects it to radically different judgments. For, whereas in the edition of Jerome he declared that the style plainly proves it not to be Jerome’s, but that its flavor of diction approaches Augustine’s manner of speaking, in the Ambrosian edition he asserts—together with Perkins and Hospinian—that it is a declamation of the sort represented by St. Jerome’s work on the reconciliation of mother and daughter. If by this similarity he means similarity of expression, nothing could be more inconsistent than those two judgments. Perhaps, however, he meant that the similarity consisted solely in his supposing both compositions to be declamations—that is, writings composed on a fictitious subject for the practice of style. Accordingly, Marianus Victor, unmoved by this similarity, relegated the work in question to the appendix of his edition of Jerome. Yet, content merely to touch upon Erasmus’s judgment concerning its affinity with Augustine’s diction, he altogether omits to say why Erasmus believed it should be denied to Jerome. The reason for that denial, however, could readily have been derived from a reading of the work itself, and one beyond all reasonable objection. For the author repeatedly indicates that he is a bishop, which no one is unaware is incompatible with Jerome.

Although there does not appear to be so great a conflict if the same treatise is attributed to Ambrose, there are nevertheless some who think it should be removed from the catalogue of the legitimate fruits of the holy Doctor. Robert Cocus (*Censurae scripturarum*, etc.) therefore denies that it is Ambrosian because the author writes that, if this girl had met death while her virginity was still intact, she would have become a living victim for her parents’ sins, an atoning offering to the Lord (Chapter 4, no. 15). But what else do we read in Book I *On Virgins*, where Ambrose addresses the parents of virgins as follows: “So that you may have those whose merits redeem your sins . . . a virgin, the mother’s offering, by whose daily sacrifice divine power is appeased” (Chapter 7, no. 32). Accordingly, Rivet (*Sacred Criticism*, Book III, chapter 16), disregarding this reasoning of his associate, raises nothing against the Ambrosian attribution of the same work except what certain Catholic authors (Bellarmine and Possevin) object: namely, that in chapter 8, no. 40, the work contains a thoroughly Novatian sentence, which Ambrose attacks in his two books *On Penance* (no. 37). But if the author of this writing had been infected with that heresy, how could he have urged the fallen woman so strongly toward public penance, while at the same time relieving her with the hope of avoiding the eternal punishments owed to her crime? Add that it was once the custom of the Church not to grant pardon and reconciliation even at death to those guilty of certain atrocious crimes; consequently, the Author could have included this offense of Susanna among those crimes without any error. Therefore, we think that the somewhat harsher expressions found there were employed for no other purpose than to instill a greater horror of the disgrace committed, to urge the guilty woman more sharply to works of penance, and to ensure that she would not at some time be drawn back from the austerity once undertaken either by her own softness or by the indulgence of some more lenient teacher.

This being so, nothing now militates against Ambrose except the style. For although the expression of this work may seem to some not greatly different from Ambrose’s, it must nevertheless be admitted that the holy Bishop, even when employing speech at its most impassioned, uses less dense and abbreviated clauses. It may also be added that this little work contains certain sentences and examples quite familiar to Ambrose. We do not deny that this carries some weight, but it should not for that reason be regarded as an “Achillean,” as they call it, argument, since it is not unusual for different authors to agree in similar matters. Yet even if it were established beyond doubt that the author of this work was not Ambrose, it would still be no less certain that our Doctor had to be assigned as its father someone not inferior to him in age; for it is clear that even then there were many who practiced idolatry, and not a few who were initiated into the sacred Easter festival, while the error of those who admitted some intermediate state between eternal punishments and glory was also flourishing (Chapter 8, no. 35).

We are not unaware that, according to Gennadius (*On the Catalog*), Nicetas, bishop of Dacia, wrote a little book to a fallen virgin, an incentive to amendment for all who fall; and hence there are learned men who maintain that this very book should be restored to him as its true owner. But what prevents an occasion from arising for Ambrose also to be led to treat the same subject? Certainly there exists a letter of Basil (*To a Fallen Virgin*) on the same subject and with the same title. And in Ambrose himself, if the virgin Indicia could be accused of a false crime, another could also be accused of a true one (*Letter to Syagrius*). Accordingly, nothing seems more consonant with reason than that, on the authority of all the printed editions and manuscripts—if one recent manuscript is excepted, which wrongly attributes it to John Chrysostom—we should retain this treatise among Ambrose’s other compositions concerning virginity. Indeed, no one fails to admit that it is worthy of Ambrose and filled with much evidence concerning the discipline of the ancient Church. But nearly all who have transmitted anything about it regard it as a letter, and in this they are certainly mistaken. For that it is a sermon is made clear even by the apostrophe to the corrupter (Chapter 9, no. 38 and following).

[Col. 0365]

## ONE BOOK OF ST. AMBROSE, BISHOP OF MILAN, ON THE FALL OF A CONSECRATED VIRGIN. (C, G, S)\*

### 305 CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0367A]

The Author breaks his silence and summons everyone to sympathize with the Church as it mourns the corruption of the sacred virgin; then, setting before them the disgracefulness of the crime, he declares his own grief concerning it.

[Note: [Col. 0367C] All this down to the following number, which was lacking in the earlier editions, has been added in our text from the Fleury and Königsberg manuscripts. The same material also occurs in the letter of Pseudo-Jerome; but there it is preceded by these words: “I think a crime is lighter when a man voluntarily confesses his sin than when, concealing his evils, he is detected unwillingly and exposed against his will.” Yet everyone sees that these words conflict with the author’s intention; for here he reveals not his own crime but another’s. For what is said below, “the crime conceived,” means nothing other than a crime known and thus far suppressed by silence. Moreover, the same words are found almost without change in chapter 8, no. 36, whence it is highly credible that some unskilled person transferred them to this place.]

**1.** Why are you silent, O soul? Why do you seethe with thoughts? Why do you not burst forth into speech and disclose the ardor of your mind, so that you may obtain some consolation? This plainly—this will be, as it were, the remedy for your sickness, if with open mouth you digest the crime conceived. For even a swelling ulcer, when opened, though full of pus, gives relief from the inflammation as it evaporates.

[Note: Pseudojerome has: “when it has become swollen, although suppurated, evaporating, etc.” This is less elegant.]

**2.** Hear me now, you who are near and you who are far away, you who fear the Lord, who rejoice with the joy of His Church and mourn with its sorrow, as it is written: “Rejoice with those who rejoice, and weep with those who weep” (Romans 12:15). I address you, I say, who retain the truest charity of Christ and do not rejoice over iniquity, but rather groan over it.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “From the truth are the words of my mouth, etc.” The printed editions and a few manuscripts read: “. . . and whether they proceed from righteous grief.”]

Pay attention to the words of my mouth, judge those that proceed from righteous grief, and together with me shudder at the character of the crime that has been exposed.

**3.** A noble virgin, dedicated to Christ, wise and learned, has fallen into the pit of shame; she conceived grief and gave birth to iniquity; she has destroyed herself and stained the Church. Hence every Christian soul has received a grievous wound, because what is holy has been given to dogs, and pearls have been thrown before swine (Matthew 7:6). For by ravenous men the name of holiness has been torn apart, and by the unclean and filthy the precious purpose of chastity has been trampled underfoot.

[Col. 0368A] 306

**4.** Hence the heat within my spirit; hence an incurable grief, because one evil drags many good things along with it, and one sinful cloud has almost obscured the Church’s entire light.

[Note: Several manuscripts read: “an insane grief”; one: “an insatiable grief.” The reading is less elegant, though the former is not at all displeasing.]

I shall therefore take up the prophetic voice and say tearfully: “Hear me, all peoples, and see my sorrow” (Lamentations 1:12): “my virgins and my young men have gone into captivity.” Truly, this is captivity, where souls captive to sin are led to death and possessed by the devil’s domination.

## CHAPTER II

He addresses the corrupted woman and sets before her eyes how honorable and blessed she had been before committing the crime, and into what calamity and disgrace she afterward fell.

**5.** Let my speech now be directed to you, who are the head and cause of these evils, who, wretched in so many ways, have lost even the name of virginity along with the glory of virginity. It is forbidden to call Susanna unchaste; it is not permitted to call you a lily, since you are not one.

[Note: All printed editions and many manuscripts, together with Pseudojerome, read: “It is not permitted to name what is”; several others: “it is not permitted to name a lily, which is not.” But it is clear that the verb must be supplied from the other witnesses and the printed editions to complete the sentence. The mention of the lily occurs because, in the name Susanna, that flower—as well as the rose—was signified.]

Where shall I begin? What shall I say first, and what last? Shall I recall the good things you have lost, or mourn the evils you have found?

**6.** You were a virgin in God’s paradise, truly among the flowers of the Church; you were Christ’s bride, God’s temple, the dwelling place of the Holy Spirit.

[Note: The printed edition reads: “And whenever I say it.”]

And when I say “you were” again and again, you must groan again and again, because you are not what you were. You walked in the Church like that dove of which it is written: “The wings of the dove are silvered, and the hind parts of its back are like the appearance of gold” (Psalm 67:14).

[Note: The same printed editions read: “in the pallor of gold.”]

You shone like silver and gleamed like gold when you came forth with a sincere conscience. You were like a star shining in the Lord’s hand; you feared neither any wind nor any clouds of war.

**7.** What is this sudden reversal? What is this sudden change? From God’s virgin you have become Satan’s corruption; from Christ’s bride, an accursed harlot; from God’s temple, a shrine of uncleanness; from the dwelling place of the Holy Spirit, the devil’s hovel. You who once walked confidently like a dove now hide in darkness like a lizard. You who shone like gold because of the honor of virginity have now become more worthless than the mud of the streets, so that you may even be trampled under the feet of the unworthy.

[Note: The printed edition and several manuscripts read: “the beauty of virginity.”]

You who were a star shining in the Lord’s hand—as though falling from the high heavens—have had your light extinguished and have been changed into a coal.

## CHAPTER III

How wretched she is, since she now has no access to God, and indeed not even to human beings themselves; from this the magnitude of the confusion she will one day suffer before the saints and angels may be understood.

**8.** Woe to you, wretched woman, and again woe, because you have lost such great goods for the sake of a brief period of lust! What hope have you left yourself with Christ the Lord, whose members you took and made members of a prostitute (1 Corinthians 6:15)? Will the Holy Spirit visit you when you have rejected Him who keeps Himself far even from filthy thoughts?

**9.** But let us come to human beings, so that through them divine things may be recognized. Consider which holy man or which holy woman would not shudder to approach you. Open your eyes, if you can; lift your brow, if you dare; look confidently upon some holy person.

[Note: Thus read not a few manuscripts and Pseudojerome; the others and all printed editions read: “Does not the consciousness of your deed incline and press down your face . . .?” Below, where all printed editions and four manuscripts read “perhaps on account of some offense,” the greatest number of manuscripts omit “perhaps.”]

Does not the consciousness of what you have done incline and press down your face like lead? Will not darkness and dreadful gloom move before your eyes? Will not fear and trembling shake your soul and limbs?

**10.** If, then, buried beneath such great confusion, you cannot look upon human beings living in the flesh and liable to some offense, what will you do before the chaste apostles? What will you do before Elijah, Daniel, and so great an army of prophets? What will you do before John? What will you do before Mary, Thecla, and Agnes, and the spotless choir of purity?

[Note: The Amerbach, Gill, and Roman editions, together with several manuscripts, read: “and the undefiled marriage-bed”; Erasmus and more manuscripts read: “and the undefiled choir”; some: “. . . clergy.”]

What, finally, will you do before the holy angels? Will you not be burned, struck as though by lightning by the splendor and brightness of the undefiled?

## CHAPTER IV

[Col. 0370A]

After refuting the excuses that corrupted women are accustomed to offer, he returns to the crime, pities her parents and the whole family, and teaches that it would have been more desirable for them if she had died beforehand. He shows that no consolation remains for them except that they had consented to her choosing the profession of virginity solely in hope of divine reward; but she had deceived their expectation.

**11.** But perhaps you will say: “I could not endure it, because I carried about fragile flesh.” Blessed Thecla will answer you with her innumerable companions: “We too were clothed in the same flesh, yet neither the frailty of the flesh could stain or mutilate the full purpose of our chastity, nor could the cruelty of tyrants cast us down through various tortures.” Truly (Gratian, *Decretum* 32.5, chapter *Revera*), the flesh cannot be corrupted unless the mind has first been corrupted. The soul, therefore, which precedes the flesh in desire, will remain guilty.

[Note: Quite a few manuscripts read: “could have stained.”]

**12.** But you will say: “I did not want this evil; I suffered violence.” That exceedingly brave Susanna, whose name you falsely bear, will answer you: “Placed between two presbyters—between two judges of the people, certainly—and alone amid the woods of paradise” (Daniel 13:20 and following), “I could not be overcome, because I did not want to be.” How could you endure violence from one most foolish young man, and in the middle of the city, unless you willingly wanted to be violated?

[Note: The printed editions and a few manuscripts read: “you wanted to be violated.”]

Who, finally, heard your cries? Who perceived your struggles? But, to pass over these matters, certainly after the violence had been inflicted you ought to have exposed the crime, if not to others, at least to your parents or your sisters. It would have been an excuse for your misfortune, a complete purification of your conscience, if you had brought the enemy of your chastity into public view.

**13.** But perhaps you were ashamed that many should learn that you had been violated. And what did you fear where there was no cause for fear, except that by keeping silent about the crime you might be joined to the adulterer more often?

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “But shame prevented this.”]

Let us suppose that shame prevented you from confessing. What do you say about the second intercourse, the third, and the frequent commerce of vileness? Let the fiction of violence cease, cease now; let the evidence of shame cease, when so many times you offered those members dedicated to Christ to be polluted in their own substance by the most wicked adulterer.

**14.** My spirit shudders, shudders; my mind wastes away when we come to the entrance of the crime. For even a physician, however brave in spirit, when he cuts a wound more deeply, will, I think, endure some measure of horror. Alas, ruined woman, do you now understand that every path of excuse has been closed to you in every way? Do you now feel how much evil wicked desire has brought upon you, both in body and in soul?

**15.** Your father, who counted you his singular glory, had not expected this disgrace from you. Your mother had not believed that this mourning and these tears would arise from you for her, since through your virginity she consoled the groaning of her childbirth.

[Note: Similar passages are found in *Exhortation to Virginity*, chapter 4, no. 26.]

Your brothers and sisters had not expected this dishonor from you, although you have gravely wounded them all, as though with a single sword of your crime.

**16.** If you had died according to the common lot, your parents would have mourned you briefly out of longing; but they would have rejoiced greatly because they had sent forth an undefiled virgin, a living offering to the Lord, namely, an atoning sacrifice for sins. But now they mourn one who is dead and not dead; they grieve for one who is alive and not alive: dead, certainly, in the glory of virginity, alive in the disgrace of shamefulness.

**17.** Your father is angry with the flesh from which you were sown; your mother curses her womb, from which you unhappily came forth into this light. Yet they cannot find any limit to their grief, except that they seem plainly to have this one consolation: neither your father compelled you nor your mother forced you to profess virginity, which you professed willingly and of your own accord. For I know that when your father set many difficulties before you and impressed upon you how arduous was the path of preserving virginity, you not only resisted stubbornly,

[Note: From Ambrose’s own *Life* and from other contemporary authors it can be learned that revelations were not rare in that age. The fact that heterodox writers reject some of them as frivolous or superstitious in no way weakens the truth of those that were holy and divine. If the revelations mentioned here really occurred, Susanna polluted herself by a still graver crime.]

but also said that terrifying revelations had been given to you.

**18.** Therefore, to the extent that they hoped for a reward because they did not resist your purpose, understand, wretched woman, that the weight of judgment increases for you to the same extent, because you did not preserve what you willingly promised. With what snares did that most wicked serpent bind you? With what poisons did he infect you—the one who deceived Eve—so that he might strike you with such blindness and cause such forgetfulness in your soul?

## CHAPTER V

He recalls to her memory on what day, by what rite, and amid what gathering of the people she was consecrated, adding that her blood ought rather to have been shed than her fidelity violated; he heightens the point by comparison with secular marriages. He then resolves an objection drawn from the Apostle’s words.

**19.** Do you not remember the holy day of the Lord’s resurrection, on which you offered yourself at the divine altar to be veiled?

[Note: The Roman edition alone, from Pseudojerome, reads: “the holy day, the day of the Lord’s resurrection.” Shortly afterward, with the old edition and most manuscripts, it reads: “among those splendid lights of the heavenly kingdom.” We have restored the passage from the same Pseudojerome and from the Flavian and Riom manuscripts, although in the Riom manuscript, after the word “neophytes,” “the lights of the angels” is added; we did not think this should be admitted into the sequence of the text. Much is found in this passage concerning the discipline of the ancient Church. First, we learn that it was customary for the newly baptized to carry lighted candles in their hands. Next, Ambrose had already taught in *Exhortation to Virginity*, chapter 7, no. 42, that the Easter festival, as well as the feast of the Lord’s Nativity, was formerly appointed for the veiling of virgins, as he had likewise stated above in Book III *On Virgins*, chapter 1, no. 1; Pope Gelasius of Rome added the birthdays of the Apostles. We also learn that a gathering of the people took place for such consecration, and finally that an address was customarily delivered to the virgin. On this subject see the Book III *On Virgins* cited above.]

In so great and solemn an assembly of the Church of God, amid the splendid lights of the neophytes, you came forth as though about to marry the King, among the candidates of the heavenly kingdom. Do you not remember what address was made to you on that day: “Look, daughter; behold, virgin, and forget your people and your father’s house, and the King will desire your beauty, for He is the Lord your God” (Psalm 44:11–12)?

Remember, then, how great a crowd gathered for the marriage of your Bridegroom and Lord.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “and of the Lord’s marriage.”]

You ought to have kept the fidelity you promised before so many witnesses, always to remember to whom you pledged your virginity. You ought more readily to have poured out blood together with spirit than to lose your chastity.

**20.** After these words had been spoken on the day of your consecration, and after many praises had been pronounced over your chastity, you were covered with the sacred veil. There the whole people, subscribing to your dowry not with ink but with the spirit, cried out together, “Amen.”

I am overcome by tears when I remember these things; I am pierced by goads when I consider these human examples.

[Note: The printed edition and a few manuscripts read: “when I consider these examples . . . What do you think will happen if among . . .”]

For if among ten witnesses, once the betrothal has been made and the marriage completed, any woman joined to a mortal man commits adultery, she does so not without great danger,

[Note: Perhaps a definite number is being used for an indefinite one, or a greater number for a lesser. Nevertheless, Franz Hotmann, in *On Betrothals*, chapter 3, interprets the passage so as to maintain that formerly precisely this number of witnesses was necessary for the validity of betrothals. Brissonius also shows in *Selections from Ancient Civil Law*, Book II, that this number was once required for lawful acts, citing a passage from the edict of the praetor written in the notes of Valerius Probus. As for what is added shortly afterward concerning the danger faced by adulterers, for a long time no capital punishment was established for them among the Romans, as Augustine testifies in *The City of God*, chapter 5. Jurists consider this so certain that whenever they find a capital or blood penalty imposed on adulterers by the early emperors, they understand it as referring to civil death—deportation, condemnation to the mines, or simple exile. Constantine the Great, defender of religion and chastity alike, was the first to enact a law subjecting adulterers to the ultimate penalty. His son Constans increased this penalty by a law reported by Baronius under the year 339, ordering that such criminals be punished as parricides, by the sack or by fire. We understand, however, from Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XXVIII, chapter 1, that this law was not long observed to the letter. In addition, many private punishments were permitted against adulterers caught in the act: confiscation, flogging, rhaphanism, mutilation, and even killing, as we observed in our *On Virginity*, chapter 7, no. 35.]

what shall we say when, among countless witnesses of the Church, before the angels and the armies of heaven, a spiritual union is dissolved through adultery? I do not know whether a death or punishment worthy of it can be imagined.

**21.** Someone will say: “It is better to marry than to burn” (1 Corinthians 7:9).

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “I would rather marry.” Ambrose had already disposed of this objection, proposed to him elsewhere, in exactly the same way.]

This saying applies to one who has not made a promise, to one who has not yet been veiled. But she who has pledged herself to Christ and received the sacred veil has already married; she has already been joined to an immortal husband. If she now wishes to marry according to the common law of marriage, she commits adultery and becomes a servant of death. If this is so, what must be said of one who is defiled by secret and furtive shamefulness and pretends to be what she is not?

[Note: The printed editions and manuscripts read: “a virgin in appearance.”]

A virgin in appearance, not in deed: twice an adulteress, both in conduct and in appearance.

## CHAPTER VI

He continues to recall the considerations by which she ought to have been deterred from her shamefulness. Since she had already been laboring under an evil reputation for three years, he marvels at her madness: she despised enemies, friends, and God Himself alike, and broke through every barrier.

**22.** But I return to you, who, having forgotten such great blessings, have become the receptacle of such great evils.

[Note: Four manuscripts read: “and the spectacle of such great evils, etc.” Again, where our text reads “with the Apostle crying out to you,” others read “attend to the crying Apostle”; the printed editions have “from this point especially crying out to you,” etc.]

How, in that shameful act, did the virginal habit not come to mind—the procession into the Church amid choirs of virgins? How did the light of vigils not flash before your eyes? How did the singing of spiritual hymns not enter your ears? How did the power of heavenly readings not fan your mind? Above all, the Apostle crying out to you from this point: “Flee fornication; every sin that a person commits is outside the body, but the one who fornicates sins against his own body” (1 Corinthians 6:17). And when he says, “against his own body,” he nevertheless shows that such a person sins against Christ. For he adds: “Or do you not know that your bodies are a temple of the Holy Spirit, whom you have from God, and you are not your own? For you were bought at a great price; glorify God and bear God in your body” (ibid., 20).

[Note: The Riom manuscript alone has “Do you not know” through “you are not your own”; since these words fit the sequence of the speech perfectly, and since scriptural passages are not rarely found considerably abridged in manuscripts, we have not hesitated to receive them into the text.]

And again he says: “But fornication and every impurity must not even be named among you, as is fitting for saints” (Ephesians 5:3). And setting aside all flattery, the Apostle fixes the sentence: “Know this and understand it: no fornicator, or impure person, or covetous person will have an inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God” (ibid., 5).

**23.** Did such great and terrifying matters not come to your mind when your members were being sought for that wicked deed? But a deadly forgetfulness was plunging you down as into a bottomless whirlpool, and execrable desire was leading you away as a captive.

**24.** Ought you not at least to have remembered that place enclosed by screens where you stood in the Church, to which religious matrons and noblewomen, competing with one another, hurried to seek your kisses, though they were holier and more worthy than you?

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “as though she were holier and more worthy”; the old edition and manuscripts differ only in that many of them have “you were” where, through a scribal error, they read “you had stood.” The matters contained in this chapter that concern the ancient discipline should not be passed over cursorily. At its very beginning it teaches that virgins had their own distinctive clothing and that they proceeded to the Church from the monastery not singly but in groups. Here it teaches that a place was assigned to them in the Church, separated not only from men but also from other women; that, as a mark of honor, noble matrons customarily sought from them the kiss of peace; and finally, that scriptural sentences were inscribed on the wall, reminding these same virgins of their duty.]

Ought you not at least to have remembered those commandments that the written wall itself placed before your eyes: “The married woman and the virgin are divided: the unmarried woman thinks about the things of the Lord, how she may be holy in body and spirit” (1 Corinthians 7:34)? But you turned the saying into its opposite, thinking and acting in such a way that you were holy neither in body nor in spirit: in body, by fornicating; in spirit, by pretending to be a virgin.

**25.** Oh, shame! Ordinarily reputation follows the deed, but in your case evil reputation preceded the deed.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “It is grievous that reputation should follow the deed, but your evil reputation advanced . . . and there would have been mockery concerning you.”]

For when, three years earlier, some rumor and whisper had arisen concerning you, you pretended to be innocent and publicly demanded punishment for the slanderers in the Church. What anguish I endured! What labors your father endured on account of your reputation, seeking out each person and binding each one to his testimony, until we could reach the author of the infamy! It was grievous and intolerable to me and to all good people that anything shameful should be said or believed about God’s virgin.

**26.** You did not fear this, nor did you keep it before your eyes, lest you become a source of joy to your enemies and find hostile those who were laboring on behalf of your reputation. How bold, how reckless you were, that your conscience did not terrify you; but, with a feigned virginity, you thought you could even deceive God. But He who said, “There is nothing hidden that will not be revealed” (Matthew 10:28), and “You did this in secret; but I will do it openly” (2 Samuel 12:12)—He who does not lie—brought the furtive crime into public view and exposed the works of your darkness in the sight of this sun.

**27.** O, whatever the speech may attempt to present, still harsher things arise; and while wishing to moderate himself, he finds no measure.

[Note: The Roman edition and Pseudojerome read: “O, he who introduces the speech encounters harsher things”; Pseudojerome has “encounters,” which is better. The Paris edition reads: “a harsher thing encounters him,” which is not unsuitable; nevertheless, nothing should be changed in the reading of the other editions and manuscripts.]

You have forgotten your purpose; you have forgotten your parents; you have forgotten the whole Church; you have forgotten the glory of virginity; you have forgotten the honor of your dignity; you have even forgotten the promise of the kingdom; you have forgotten the terrifying judgment. You embraced corruption; you brought forth the fruit of confusion; and the end is a most savage death and everlasting destruction.

[Note: “A most savage death,” that is, death through anguish of soul and despair, unless it produces worthy fruits of penance—indeed, a complete death. For among Christians, vow-breaking virgins were never put to a violent death, as pagan Vestals were buried alive in the earth.]

## CHAPTER VII

[Col. 0375A]

He asserts that he had discharged toward her every responsibility of episcopal office; but she had not merely gained nothing from it; she had also presented others with grave scandal. The Gospel shows that such scandal is condemned to the severest punishment.

**28.** Certainly, you have no reason to complain of our negligence; for whatever belongs to the office of a shepherd was denied neither to you nor to anyone else.

[Note: The Riom manuscript reads: “spiritual reading”; immediately afterward Pseudojerome has: “holy communion.” Although she is said to have entered a monastery, since at that time men were permitted to enter women’s monasteries as visitors, it is certainly not surprising that the crime could have penetrated even this place through the audacity of depraved men.]

Spiritual love was provided, and holy admonition was not lacking. Having forgotten your father’s house, as it is written (Psalm 44:11), you passed into the virginal monastery. Set among so many women, you should not merely have been safe, if you had wished; you could even have provided protection for others. But these and other precautions were taken in vain.

**29.** In vain I set forth the hymn of virginity, so that you might sing together both the glory and the observance of your purpose.

[Note: We have already noted in *On Flight from the World*, chapter 4, no. 20, that “hymn” may sometimes be taken for all Scripture, but especially for the psalms of David. Hence it may perhaps rightly be said that the hymn of virginity here means nothing other than either those sentences inscribed on the wall, mentioned above, or, more probably, the final part of Psalm 44. For from verse 10 to the end it contains many things pertaining to the glory and observance of the virginal purpose—namely, the dignity of Christ’s brides and the endowments and virtues with which they ought to be adorned. If someone prefers to understand it as a hymn composed for that use, we will not resist too obstinately; for above, in chapter 5, where at no. 18 he recalled that certain words from this psalm had been recited, he shortly afterward adds: “After these words had been spoken, and after many praises had been pronounced over your chastity.” These words can be applied to such a hymn without excessive strain.]

I sowed beside the road; I sowed among thorns; I sowed on rocky ground. Either the birds—that is, demons—snatched my words from your heart (Luke 8:5 and following), or they were choked by your evil thoughts, or they withered in the excessive heat of lust. Alas for me, because where I thought I was building gold, silver, and precious stones, I find that I had labored on wood, hay, and straw—materials destined to burn (1 Corinthians 3:12)! I too shall say with the prophet: “Alas for me, because I have become like one who gathers straw at harvest” (Micah 7:1)!

[Note: A few manuscripts read: “a thorn at harvest?” And indeed, if you alone, etc.]

**30.** And certainly, if you had inflicted harm only upon yourself, it would have been a sorrow, but perhaps a bearable one. Now, however, how many souls have you wounded by your crime, and how many souls have you caused to repent of their purpose because of you! How many lips even of the faithful have been polluted by blaspheming the way of the Lord! The Gentile world has opened its mouth against us; through your disgrace the synagogue of the Jews has exulted against the holy Church.

[Note: The majority of manuscripts read: “will exult in perpetual disgrace”; some: “exulted.”]

**31.** And if the one who causes a single person to stumble must have a millstone tied around his neck and be thrown into the sea (Matthew 18:6), what sentence will you pronounce against yourself, through whose crime every soul has been wounded and the name of the Lord has been blasphemed among the nations? Is it not true that whenever people say, “O virgins,” the heap of your iniquity increases? Here you lie wounded; here you lie prostrate.

## CHAPTER VIII

[Col. 0376A]

What is the nature, difficulty, and rationale of the remedy he wishes to apply? He urges her to have recourse to repentance—not repentance of just any kind, but appropriate repentance—whose inward act, as well as its outward signs, he here describes. Moreover, through its benefit she will obtain immunity from eternal punishment, provided that she is the more severe toward herself in proportion as she confessed her sin less freely. He also inflames her to this by recalling the terror of the future judgment.

### 32

I wish to help, but I cannot come to your aid, because the whole head is in pain and the whole heart in sorrow: from the feet even to the head, as Isaiah says, there is no remedy to be applied (Isaiah 1:5–6). Your illness has excluded every aid of human medicine. [Note: The Floriac manuscript and Pseudo-Hieronymus read: “disgraced by devastation.”] And although both the good and the wicked, moved by righteous indignation, judge you worthy of every kind of devastation, to be tormented by every sort of punishment, to be condemned to death or burned by fire, nevertheless I, who know that more grievous torments are reserved for criminals and that ungodly souls remain in suffering without end—not temporal sufferings, but eternal ones—wish you to undergo other punishments, punishments that will be profitable and will not destroy your soul.

### 33

Therefore, in accordance with the divine judgment, I shall give counsel; for that one and only remedy must be attempted [Note: Some manuscripts read: “that aid must be attempted.”] which the divine voice offers through Ezekiel to the wretched: “I do not desire the death of the sinner,” he says, “so much as that he should turn and live” (Ezekiel 33:11). And again, after this, the Lord says: “I said, ‘Turn back to me.’ Is there no balm in Gilead, or is there no physician there? Why has the health of the daughter of my people not arisen?” (Jeremiah 8:22). These words plainly concern repentance; these judgments of God call sinners to repentance [Note: After the word *peccatores* (“sinners”), the Roman edition, following Pseudo-Hieronymus, inserted into the text *revocant ab errore* (“they recall them from error”), which is absent from the earlier editions and from our manuscripts.]. For repentance is necessary for those who have fallen, just as medicines are necessary for the wounded.

### 34

But how great and of what kind do you think the necessary repentance must be? It must either equal the crimes or certainly exceed them. Consider, then, whether this sin of adultery is a simple one, or whether it is doubled by that death which is said to have been secretly inflicted; and the magnitude of the repentance must correspond to the weight of the conscience.

Repentance, therefore, must not be enacted in words only, but also in deed. It is enacted thus: place before your eyes from what great glory you have fallen and from what book of life your name has been erased; and believe yourself already set near those outer darknesses where there will be weeping of the eyes and gnashing of teeth without end. When you have conceived these things in your mind with firm faith, as they truly are—since it is necessary that the transgressing soul be handed over to Tartarean punishments and the fires of Gehenna, and since, after the one baptism, no other remedy has been established except the solace of repentance—be content to undergo whatever affliction, whatever labor, provided that you are freed from eternal punishments.

### 35

Therefore, considering and reconsidering these things within yourself, be yourself the harsher judge of your deed. First of all, every concern for this present life must be ended for you [Note: All editions, together with many more manuscripts, read *interimenda tibi est* (“must be ended for you”); Pseudo-Hieronymus, however, together with two manuscripts, has *intermittenda tibi est* (“must be interrupted for you”). The latter is less elegant. Here, in summary, the exercises of repentance, both inward and outward, are proposed. If anyone is surprised that mournful clothing and the cutting of the hair are counted among them, let him consult Morinus, *De Administratione Poenitentiae*, book IV, chapter 17, no. 7 and following, where he will find that these same things were then prescribed to penitents. But since the passage concerns a virgin consecrated to God, another difficulty arises from current usage, according to which the hair of sacred virgins is ordinarily cut. It is nevertheless certain that formerly discipline in this matter varied according to place. For, in addition to canon 17 of the Council of Gangra, held, as is generally thought, in the year 324—a canon which Gothofredus, with substantial arguments against Baronius, defends as referring to veiled virgins, whereas Baronius, in his notes on the Roman Martyrology under 20 September, understands it of certain heretical women—there is, besides this canon forbidding the tonsure of virgins under anathema, the law 27 of Theodosius, *De Episcopis et Clericis*, which, as Baronius himself admits, prohibits the same thing to the same virgins. That law was issued in the year 390, and indeed with the consent of the bishops, since the same penalty of anathema was imposed. Optatus of Milevis reports that sacred maidens grew their hair and wore it loose like brides. Ambrose also, in *De Institutione Virginis*, chapter 17, and Augustine, in letter 109, sufficiently show that among their countrymen it was not customary for virgins to cut off their hair. Jerome likewise indicates this rather clearly in letter 48, to Sabinianus, when he says that he received locks of hair as pledges of love from the nun whom he had corrupted in the monastery at Bethlehem, into which she had withdrawn after receiving the veil at Rome. On the other hand, in the same letter Jerome reports that in the monasteries of Egypt and Syria it had become customary for both virgin and widow who had consecrated themselves to God “to offer their hair to the mothers of the monasteries to be cut.” Add to this Palladius, in the *Lausiac History*, chapter 41, where he writes that the habit of such virgins was to be tonsured and hooded. Canon 66 of the Council of Nicaea, according to Alphonsus of Pisa, is also cited, as is Athanasius’s *On True Virginity*, in support of the same practice. This practice ultimately alone prevailed, when nuns wished, in pious rivalry, to show that they gloried in the insignia of repentance no less than monks. Besides the authors mentioned, Spencaeus treated these matters fully in book V, chapter 3 of *De Voti Redempt.*; our Menardus in *Sacram. Gregor.*, p. 212; Heeften in *Disquis. Monast.*, book V, discussion 7; and Thomassin in *Discipl. Eccles.*, part I, book I, chapter 50.], and, considering yourself dead—as indeed you are—think how you may come to life again. Next, you must take mournful clothing, and both mind and every limb must be punished with a chastisement they deserve. Let the hair be cut which, through vain glory, provided an occasion for lust. Let the eyes flow with tears which did not look upon a man innocently. Let the face grow pale which once blushed immodestly [Note: All editions and several manuscripts read *viruit impudice* (“flourished immodestly”). This is by no means bad; *viruit* can elegantly mean “flourished,” in which sense Cicero speaks of “having vigor” and Horace of “knees growing green.” Nevertheless, more and better manuscripts read *irrubuit impudice* (“blushed immodestly”). Nor is this reading less plausible; besides the more fitting antithesis between *pallescat* (“let it grow pale”) and *irrubuit* (“blushed”), redness in the face is an indication both of good health and of intense emotion. Again, some manuscripts read *incuria et jejuniis* (“neglect and fasts”) instead of *injuriis et jejuniis* (“harsh treatment and fasts”). This is not unreasonable, but *injuriis* should not be changed: it means rigid and severe chastisement, as in book II of *On Abraham*, chapter 8, no. 51, where a heifer is said to be tamed *injuriis*. Finally, where all editions and manuscripts except the Florentine read *de pulchritudine placuit* (“was pleased with its beauty”), the Florentine has *de turpitudine placuit* (“was pleased with its ugliness”).]. Finally, let the entire body be worn down by harsh treatment and fasting; let it shudder, sprinkled and covered with ashes, under sackcloth—because it once took pleasure in its beauty. But let the heart melt like wax, distressing itself through fasts and tossing itself about in thought, asking why it was overthrown by the enemy. Let the senses also be tormented, because, although they held dominion over the bodily members, they yielded to an evil rule.

### 36

Such a life and such an exercise of repentance, if it perseveres, will dare to hope—even if not for glory, certainly for release from punishment. For God says: “Turn back to me, and I will turn back to you. Turn back with all your heart, in fasting, weeping, and mourning; tear your hearts and not your garments, for I am gracious” [Note: The editions and some manuscripts read “and I am merciful” (*et misericors sum*).] “and merciful” (Joel 2:12–13). Thus that great David, when he turned back, was justified; thus that sinful city, Nineveh, escaped the destruction hanging over it (2 Kings 12:13). Therefore, if the sinner does not spare himself, God will spare him (John 3:5 and following). And if, during this brief span of life, he compensates for the future punishments of everlasting Gehenna, he will free himself from eternal judgment.
