[Note: The Regensburg manuscript reads “even if not the crown, nevertheless pardon and a certain remission of punishment”; the other manuscripts and editions differ in no respect except that where the editions and a few manuscripts prefer *vacuationem* or *evacuationem* (“emptying,” “remission”), many other manuscripts read *vacationem* (“release”). Some, moreover, infer both from these words and from others in letter 2 to Horontianus that Ambrose approached the opinion held by certain ancients, according to which they admitted an intermediate state between the glory of the blessed and the punishments of the damned; this will be discussed in connection with that same letter. Here we merely note that the Author touches upon the difficulty but leaves it unexamined. This is an oratorical concession, as though he were saying: “Even if it should not happen that you attain glory”—a matter I do not discuss—“at least you will obtain immunity from punishments.” If anyone nevertheless insists that the Author declares this virgin destined to be excluded from glory, provided that “glory” is not understood in its entirety but rather as that particular glory promised to virgins who preserve their pledged fidelity to the heavenly Bridegroom, we shall concede the point.]

### 37

A great wound requires deep and prolonged medicine; a great crime has a great satisfaction as its necessary counterpart [Note: No one will deny that the sentence which follows, said to occur at the very beginning of this book in Pseudo-Hieronymus, properly belongs here. It also shows that in ancient times the discipline was such that those who were accused by others before the bishop of secret crimes were condemned, after careful investigation, to more severe punishments than if they had voluntarily accused themselves. Whoever wishes may consult Morinus, *De Administratione Poenitentiae*, book I, chapter 10, and book II, chapter 6.]. For there is no doubt that a crime is lighter when a person voluntarily confesses his sin and repents; but when he conceals his wrongs, is exposed against his will, and is made public unwillingly, the crime is more serious. You cannot deny that this has happened to you. Therefore you must grieve more intensely, because the sin is more serious.

### 38

If sinful human beings could perceive in their minds what judgment God will bring upon the world, and if human understanding were not scattered by worldly vanity or weighed down by unbelief, they would gladly endure any kind and any amount of suffering in the present—even if life were prolonged—provided only that they did not fall into those punishments of eternal fire [Note: All editions and some manuscripts read *homines peccatores* (“sinful human beings”); the Roman edition, following Pseudo-Hieronymus, removed *peccatores*. “Judgment is impending upon the world; the human sense …” If the phrase is read with *non infidelitate gravaretur* (“were not weighed down by unbelief”), the Roman edition and Pseudo-Hieronymus have *gravarentur* (“were not weighed down”), while the other manuscripts have the more appropriate singular, as in the text.].

But you, who have now entered the contest of repentance, persist, wretched woman: cling firmly, as to a plank in a shipwreck, hoping through it to be freed from the depths of your crimes [Note: All editions and some manuscripts, together with Pseudo-Hieronymus, read “like a shipwrecked person to a plank, hoping to be saved through it”; the other manuscripts read “as in shipwrecks,” except that the Florentine omits *per ipsam* (“through it”). Below, where the same editions, together with a few manuscripts, read “that pardon can be granted by a human being,” and again “seek the remedy from that one alone,” the more numerous manuscripts agree with us, except that in the final part many have “seek the remedy from him himself.” The Florentine and Regensburg manuscripts, however, read “it is fitting for you to seek from him alone,” and so forth. Since scribes are more accustomed to shorten than to expand, we prefer this reading. Moreover, it has been demonstrated in the *Admonition* that those who attribute the Novatianist heresy to this Author on the basis of these final sentences rely upon no certain reasoning.]. Cling to repentance until the end of life, and do not presume that pardon can be granted to you by a human being; for whoever wishes to promise you this is deceiving you. Since you have sinned specifically against the Lord, it is fitting that you await the remedy from him alone on the day of judgment [Note: Many manuscripts, together with Pseudo-Hieronymus, read “seek the remedy from him himself on the day of judgment.”].

## CHAPTER IX

He rebukes the virgin’s corrupter and terrifies him by the example of Belshazzar. Then, since he is not content with inward anguish, he admonishes him to embrace legitimate repentance; finally, lest he flatter himself because of the multitude of sinners, he brings before him the burning of Sodom and of other cities and urges him to break the snares of the enemy.

### 39

But what shall I say of you, son of the serpent, servant of the devil, violator of God’s temple—who in one crime committed two offenses, adultery and sacrilege? It was plainly sacrilege when, with insane rashness, you polluted the vessel offered to Christ and dedicated to the Lord. That king Belshazzar of the Persians, who used the vessels of the Lord—which his father had taken from the temple at Jerusalem—to drink with his friends and concubines, was struck down that very night by the hand of an angel and punished by a cruel death (Daniel 5:30). What do you think will happen to you, at once ruined and ruinous, who with impious recklessness profaned and sacrilegiously polluted a rational vessel consecrated to Christ and sanctified for the Holy Spirit [Note: The Florentine and Regensburg codices read “sanctified by the Holy Spirit”; Pseudo-Hieronymus reads “sanctified with the Holy Spirit”; Regensburg alone, consistently, has “you polluted it by rash and impious sacrilege.”], forgetful of your calling and a despiser of divine judgment? It would have been better for you never to have been born than to have been born in such a way that Gehenna would claim you as its own son [Note: The Florentine manuscript reads thus; the other manuscripts and editions read “than that Gehenna should claim you as its own son.” In many manuscripts the words “its own son” are absent.].

### 40

And although the very consciousness of your crime drives you headlong in every direction—for “the wicked flee when no one pursues” (Proverbs 28:1)—and although dreadful images of your sin terrify you even when asleep, not only when awake, nevertheless, lest anything be withheld from a diseased or dying sheep by its shepherd as a remedy, I offer counsel. Voluntarily seek the prison of repentance [Note: Several manuscripts read “the tower of repentance.” This is by no means inappropriate, since repentance, like a fortress, keeps us safe from divine anger. But it may also refer to something familiar to Ambrose: he says that after his expulsion from paradise Adam was confined in a fortress, perhaps because it was customary to keep criminals in a fortified place. This agrees in sense with the reading of the other manuscripts and all the editions.]; bind your inward parts with chains; torture your soul with groans and fasts; seek the help of the saints; lie beneath the feet of the elect, so that your unrepentant heart may not store up wrath for you on the day of wrath and of God’s righteous judgment, when he will repay each according to his works (Romans 2:5–6). Nor should you number yourself among those whom Paul laments: “Those who sinned before and did not repent of the uncleanness, fornication, and lust which they practiced” (2 Corinthians 12:21).

### 41

Nor should you flatter yourself because of the multitude of similar sinners and say: “I did not do this alone; I have many companions.” Rather, reflect that a multitude of companions does not make crimes go unpunished. For in Sodom and Gomorrah and throughout all five cities there lived innumerable peoples, and all alike who lustfully used their bodies were consumed by fiery rains (Genesis 19:25). Lot alone escaped that unavoidable conflagration (ibid., 29), because he had shown himself separate from that disgrace.

### 42

Therefore, unhappy man, even now drive from your heart the serpent’s flatteries, and amid mourning and continual tears, while that dark soul remains in your unclean body, obtain for yourself a remedy for the day of necessity [Note: Several manuscripts and Pseudo-Hieronymus read “obtain for yourself the remedy of necessity.”], always keeping before your eyes the Apostle’s sentence: “We must all be manifested before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive what belongs to him through his body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil” (2 Corinthians 5:10).

## CHAPTER X

Returning at last to the fallen virgin, he supplies her with certain urgent prayers and various expressions of repentance gathered here and there from Scripture.

### 43

Who will console you, virgin daughter of Zion? For your devastation has become great, like the sea. “Pour out your heart like water before the face of the Lord” (Lamentations 2:13, 19); lift your hands to him for the remedy of your sins [Note: All editions read “for the remedy of your soul and sins,” whereas all manuscripts, together with Pseudo-Hieronymus, read as in the text.]. Receive, then, this lamentation. First of all, let the fiftieth psalm never be omitted from any day, since it was sung for such a situation; and proceed through it with tears and groaning as far as the verse: “A contrite and humbled heart God will not despise” (Psalm 50:19).

### 44

Moreover, pour out this lamentation, not without contrition of heart, in the sight of God the Judge:

“Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes” (Jeremiah 9:1), “that I may mourn the wounds of my soul? My feast days have been turned into mourning, and my songs into lamentation” (Amos 8:10). The sound of hymns has departed, and the joy of psalms; the gnashing of teeth and weeping of eyes have taken their place. I was silenced, humbled, and kept silent concerning good things, and my pain was renewed. My heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation the fire will blaze. Fear and trembling came upon me, and darkness covered me (Psalm 38:3–4). The abyss surrounded me and finally drowned my head in the fissures of the mountains (Jonah 2:6) [Note: Some manuscripts read “in the fissures of the mountains”; the Regensburg manuscript, together with Pseudo-Hieronymus, reads “in the clefts of hell.” Below, that same manuscript alone has “he will have mercy on my crimes.”].

### 45

“Woe is me, for I have become like Sodom and have been burned like Gomorrah” (Genesis 19:24). Who will pity my ashes? I have offended more grievously than Sodom, because it transgressed without knowing the law, whereas I, having received grace, sinned against the Lord. “If a man sins against a man, there will be someone to intercede; but I have sinned against the Lord—whom shall I find as my intercessor?” (1 Samuel 2:25) [Note: The words “If a man sins against a man …” are almost entirely absent from the manuscripts; nevertheless they are found in some manuscripts, in all the editions, and in Pseudo-Hieronymus.].

I conceived sorrow and gave birth to iniquity; I opened a pit and dug it, and I fell into the pit which I had made. Therefore my sorrow has turned back upon my head, and my iniquity has descended upon my crown. My uncleanness is before my feet; I did not remember the last things, and I fell miserably (Psalm 7:15 and following).

### 46

There is no one to console me. Oh, how bitter is the fruit of lust—more bitter than gall, more cruel than a sword! How have I become desolate? Suddenly I failed; I perished because of my iniquity, as one rising from sleep. Therefore my image has been destroyed in the city of the Lord (Psalm 72:19–20) [Note: All manuscripts read thus; the editions and Pseudo-Hieronymus have “like a dream of one awakening.” In the following verse, where all editions and several manuscripts had *vilificata est* (“has been made contemptible”), other manuscripts read *nullificata sum* (“I have been brought to nothing”), partly as in the text.].

My name has been erased from the book of life. I have become like an owl in a dwelling, like a solitary sparrow on a roof; there is no one to console me. I look to the right and see that there is no one who recognizes me (Psalm 101:7 and following). Escape has vanished from me, and there is no one who seeks my soul (Psalm 141:5). I have become like a lost vessel; I have heard the reproach of all who dwell around me.

“Woe to that day on which my mother bore unhappy me, and this cruel light received me!” It would have been better for me not to have been born than to become, among the nations, a spectacle of shame” (Psalm 30:13–14). Because of me, disgrace has come upon all the servants of the Lord and upon those who worship him worthily (Job 3:3).

### 47

Mourn for me, mountains and hills; mourn for me, springs and rivers, because I am a daughter of weeping. Mourn for me, beasts of the forests, reptiles of the earth, birds of heaven, and every living soul that enjoys life. For blessed are you, wild beasts and birds, who have no fear of hell and will not have to render an account after death. For us there remains the cruel punishment of Tartarus, because, possessing understanding, we sin; therefore there is no peace for sinners.

### 48

“My sin, my iniquity—human offenses are not comparable to these, because this is impiety. Having promised to preserve my flesh as a virgin and having publicly professed chastity, I lied to the Lord. Therefore I have no confidence to call upon the Most High Lord, because the mouth of those who transgress is obstructed” [Note: The old edition reads: “It is my sin; it is my iniquity. Human offenses are not comparable, because this impiety is dreadful: having promised, with respect to the flesh, to preserve a virgin, and having publicly professed chastity, I have lied to God.” The Roman edition reads: “to pollute virginity in the flesh, and having publicly professed chastity,” and so forth. The manuscripts agree with our reading except that two have *carnem pollutam* (“polluted flesh”), one *carne polluta* (“with polluted flesh”), and another *carnem pollicitam* (“promised flesh”); it is obvious that these are scribal alterations. Notice again the explicit reference to publicly professed virginity.].

For the Prophet sang of my evil: “Those who distance themselves from you will perish; you destroy everyone who fornicates away from you” (Psalm 72:27). And again: “My tongue has cleaved to my jaws, and I have been brought down into the dust of death” (Psalm 21:16) [Note: The Regensburg codex reads “the mouth of those who speak iniquity.” Again, where all editions read “My soul has cleaved to my throat,” all manuscripts have “My tongue has cleaved,” a reading confirmed by the text of Scripture and by all its versions.].

### 49

Nevertheless, I shall cry out to the Lord while there is still time, while an interval is granted, because “in death there is no remembrance, and in hell there is no confession”:

“Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor correct me in your fury. For your arrows are fixed in me, and there is no health in my flesh because of the face of your anger; there is no peace for my bones because of the face of my sins. For my iniquities have risen above my head, and like a heavy burden they have weighed heavily upon me. My scars have become foul and have rotted, because of my folly. I am afflicted and bowed down to the end; I roar because of the groaning of my heart” (Psalm 37:1, 9).

“My heart is troubled within me; my strength has left me, and the light of my eyes is not with me” (Psalm 37:1–9). “God, you have rejected me and destroyed me; you have shown me hard things; you have given me wine of compunction” (Psalm 59:4–5). “I have been driven from your sight; I shall no longer rise to your holy temple” [Note: All editions read “to look again,” whereas all manuscripts have partly “to rise” and partly “to rise again.”], “and I have become an object of destruction.”

### 50

“What profit is there in your blood, when I descend into corruption?” (Psalm 29:10). “Will you work wonders for the dead, or will physicians raise them up?” (Psalm 87:11). Yours is the word; yours is the promise:

“I do not desire the death of the sinner, but conversion, and that he should live” (Ezekiel 33:11) [Note: Two manuscripts alone read “but conversion, so that he may turn”; the old edition has “but conversion, so that he may be able to live.” The Roman edition reads: “but conversion, and I shall live so that I may be able to live; to you, God, I turn, who alone …” Pseudo-Hieronymus has simply “but conversion. My conversion is to you, God, so that I may be able to live; for you alone …”]. To you, my God, is my conversion, for you alone can renew all things and recall souls from the underworld. You release those in chains; you, God, raise up the oppressed, give sight to the blind, and raise the dead.

### 51

“I have strayed like a lost sheep” (Psalm 118:176); seek your handmaid, lest the cruel wolf swallow me. Many say to my soul: “There is no salvation for him in his God” (Psalm 3:3). But your counsel is with you (Psalm 108:84). “How many are the days of your handmaid? When will you execute judgment with me?” But “do not enter into judgment with your handmaid” (Psalm 142:2). My soul has failed in your salvation; my eyes have failed through tears; my glory has been poured out upon the earth (Psalm 118:81). “When will you look upon me and restore my soul?” (Psalm 34:17). “Because of my iniquity you have chastised me, and you have made my soul waste away like a spider” (Psalm 38:12). Remember, Lord, that I am dust; see my humility and my labor, and forgive all my sins (Psalm 24:18). Forgive me, that I may be refreshed, before I depart and shall be no more, “and in hell there will be no confession” (Psalm 38:14).

[Note: Here the treatise ends in Jerome. The Roman edition alone had excised “and in hell there will be no confession”; the Paris edition restored it incorrectly as “and confession will not be lower.” Accordingly, after the words “You are able, Lord,” all the editions lacked “to tear my sackcloth and gird me with gladness”; we have restored these words from nearly all the manuscripts, since they are entirely appropriate here.]

### 52

You are able, Lord, to tear the sack and gird me with gladness (Psalm 29:12); to break my bonds, with which I am bound and constricted—you who did not disdain Rahab the harlot (Joshua 6:17). Take your anger away from me, Lord, because I have sinned against you cruelly, until you justify my cause and lead me into the light. God of hosts, grant effectiveness to my repentance and perseverance in confession, lest the deceiver of my soul harden me [Note: Three manuscripts read: “Grant the effect of patience.” Below, where all editions and some manuscripts read, “I desire, O God, that this be granted, that I may confess you forever,” many more manuscripts contract the passage to: “I desire this to be granted, O God, who reign in the Trinity forever and ever.”]. I desire this gift and this grace to be granted to me from your fountain, O God: that I may confess you forever, who live and reign in the Trinity forever and ever. Amen.

# [ON THE MYSTERIES]

## ADMONITION ON THE BOOK ON THE MYSTERIES, IN WHICH THE SAME BOOK IS ALSO ASSERTED TO BE BY AMBROSE

The author of this work declares at its very beginning (chapter 1, no. 2) that he is laboring for the newly baptized as well, and is undertaking the sacraments that had until then been unknown to them. For it was the custom of the bishops of ancient times to conceal those sublime mysteries as carefully as possible from the uninitiated. While these candidates still remained among the catechumens and those preparing for baptism, they were prepared for baptism by frequent prayers, exorcisms, and other ceremonies. They were admitted to sermons, in which, as this very author openly teaches, they were chiefly accustomed to be instructed in the strict principles of Christian ethics (ibid., no. 1). In their discourses, however, the bishops interwove arguments against the false and impious teachings of pagans and heretics. Nor did they omit to insert instruction concerning the unity of the divine substance, the persons of the Trinity to be worshiped, and other points that were customarily explained to them from the Creed.

They entirely abstained, however, from a more inward discussion of the other sacraments, and above all of the Eucharist. Those good candidates of our religion were, moreover, so teachable in mind that they did not extend their curiosity toward matters which the Church did not wish to make manifest to them. They reasoned, evidently, that nothing false or superstitious could be contained in a religion which, supported by so many miracles and wonders, erected the worship of the one God upon the ruins of idolatry, which it overthrew, and which required the conduct of its followers to be brought into conformity with a standard so strict and so consistent with reason.

Ambrose marks the instructions for the ordering of life that he had delivered to the unbaptized in these opening words: “We have given a daily discourse on moral matters,” and so forth (ibid.). It can scarcely be doubted that the books on Abraham and the others which we have shown to have been delivered by him before catechumens and those preparing for baptism are intended here (see the *Admonition* to those books). He then adds that, since he is now addressing those who have been regenerated by holy baptism, it is incumbent upon him to explain to them both the nature and the ceremonies of that sacrament and of the others.

First, therefore, after explaining the opening of the mouth and ears (chapter 1, no. 3), and mentioning the renunciation made in the baptistery (chapter 2, nos. 5–6), he treats the blessing of the font (chapters 3, 4, and 5). There, in order to prove that regeneration is accomplished not by the efficacy of ordinary water but by the present power of the divine Spirit, he examines various symbols by which the same sacrament was prefigured in the Old Law. From this he also concludes that the sacred washing always obtains the same effect, since the worthiness or unworthiness of the minister contributes nothing to it.

He next describes the approach of those who had emerged from the life-giving bath to the bishop, from whom, after the anointing of the head and the washing of the feet (chapter 6, no. 29 and following), they received a white garment (chapter 7, no. 34 and following). Then, after explaining the meaning of each ceremony, he expresses, drawing sentences from the Song of Songs, how greatly Mother Church rejoices at the enlargement of her household (ibid., no. 35 and following). Finally, after affirming that the neophytes had been enriched and adorned by the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit through the assistance of Confirmation (ibid., no. 42), he explains at length how they proceeded in solemn procession from the baptistery to the altar, where they were to be refreshed by the sacrament of the Lord’s body (chapter 8, no. 43). It is certainly not surprising that he dwells much longer on this point, since it is the end and completion of the others.

He therefore declares that it is his intention, with the greatest diligence (ibid., no. 44), to establish that this sacrament is to be preferred to all the sacraments of the ancient Synagogue both in antiquity and in excellence. He first demonstrates this from the fact that the bread and wine offered to Abraham by Melchizedek were a figure of the Eucharist (ibid., no. 45). He demonstrates the second point by showing that this mystery surpasses the manna, which the Israelites regarded as nothing more sacred, as light is superior to shadow, truth to figure, and the Author’s body to manna (chapter 8, no. 49).

Indeed, because it was easy for the neophytes to object: “I see something else; how do you assert to me that I receive the body of Christ?” (chapter 9, no. 50), he proceeds to answer the objection. Accordingly, so that they might hold with certainty that the bread is converted into the Lord’s body by the priestly blessing, after rejecting the testimony of the bodily senses, he brings forward not only the clearest miracles by which the records of the Old Testament relate that nature was changed or even created from nothing (chapter 9, nos. 51–52), but also cites the greatest of all miracles, namely, the incarnation of Christ (ibid., no. 53). Then, as though every occasion for doubt had been completely removed, he exhorts this innocent flock, using certain appropriate verses from the Song of Songs (ibid., nos. 55 and following), to honor the mystery by keeping it secret and, feeding Christ within themselves on the various fruits of virtue, to gladden the Church; nor should they ever afterward doubt their regeneration.

Here, however, we cannot refrain from making a few observations on the occasion of the Eucharist. The bishop instructs the neophytes, still wet from baptism, by giving them their first knowledge of the sacraments hitherto unknown to them. This catechesis is simple and entirely free from every embellishment and rhetorical adornment. Accordingly, the author of the work proposed to prove that the Eucharist is as much superior to the manna as the body surpasses the shadow and the truth the figure. To demonstrate this, he repeatedly teaches that Christ’s flesh, into which the bread is changed by the Lord’s words, is contained in the sacrament. To assert this change, he employs examples that are, above all, extraordinarily miraculous. Finally, having exerted every effort to discredit the testimony of the eyes, he maintains that there is not even the slightest room for doubt that from the bread which the senses announce as present there comes to be—not a figure of the body, but the very body conceived in the Virgin’s womb and delivered over to the most extreme sufferings for us. Who, then, could deny that our Bishop recognized here a true and substantial conversion? Since he wishes to establish and confirm this conversion by the Lord’s words, “This is my body” (Matt. XXVI, 26) (Chapter 9, no. 52), is it not manifestly clear that he understands those words in their simple and proper sense, not figuratively?

We admit that he also employs certain examples of miracles by which he would persuade his hearers that baptism possesses the power of regeneration. But there the subject is the power of producing effects, not any substantial change; nowhere, after all, will you find him saying that the nature of the water is changed into the Spirit. On the contrary, he testifies in words so explicit and so frequently repeated that the water always remains in existence, and remains even after the blessing, that he seems in a certain sense to have taken precautions lest anyone should conceive such an opinion.

Furthermore, everyone can see how different the position of Catholics and that of the heterodox is here. Any one of our priests would most gladly commend and follow Ambrose’s method in instructing the unlearned in the knowledge of this mystery; but which minister of the sectarians would not consider that he ought to adopt a method plainly opposed to it? We may add that this little work supplies explicit and positive supports, as they are called, for establishing orthodox doctrine, whereas Albertinus Carentonius, formerly a minister, draws from it no argument at all for proving his own opinion. He merely sets forth objections (Book II, *On the Sacraments*, chapter 2), to which he gives only utterly futile and empty answers.

Yet fair-minded judges must recognize that from this work, in which Ambrose familiarly imbued newly converted Christians with their first principles, one should learn what his opinion was concerning the Eucharist rather than from his other books. In those other works, he deliberately spoke more obscurely on account of the unbelievers and catechumens who listened to him together with the baptized.

Those who have mentioned this writing always attributed it to Ambrose with great unanimity. At last, however, in the preceding century certain heterodox writers appeared who thought that the holy Doctor should be deprived of a possession so long enjoyed. We find, indeed, a letter of Heinrich Bullinger to Joachim Vadianus, dated at Saint Gall on 7 July 1535, in which, embracing this book together with the following work *On the Sacraments*, he indicates that he agrees with him concerning both works—namely, that these dull productions could by no means be the offspring of an excellent author and exceptionally keen judgment.

He gives three reasons for this conclusion: the difference in style; the different method of explaining the Eucharist here and in Ambrose’s acknowledged books; and the colder treatment of the subject than would befit Ambrose’s acumen and diligence. He adds that Erasmus, although he concealed his view and veiled his judgment so as not to seem to follow their opinion concerning the sacraments, nevertheless, by relegating these books to the final volume of his edition of Ambrose, showed that he had no doubt that they were the work of some literary impostor. As though Erasmus had composed his fourth volume solely from spurious works! But since this is merely a conjecture about Erasmus’s opinion, it ought rather to be dismissed than refuted.

To the three arguments just mentioned we shall reply in a single word: this is a catechesis and therefore, by its own distinctive character, ought to have been published simply, clearly, and without rhetorical flourishes. Meanwhile, Bullinger does not appear to be a particularly suitable judge of Ambrosian writings when, at the point where he expels a legitimate offspring on such slight grounds, he accepts the commentaries on the Epistles of Paul as unquestionably genuine.

The writer whose work was printed at Helmstedt together with the *Censure of Robert Cocus* (1655) also removed this work from the catalogue of Ambrosian writings; in this he was followed by Dallaeus in his book *On Confirmation*. He first gives the following reason for his judgment:

> “The author,” he says, “asserts that Scripture testifies that, at the prayers of Jerobaal, fire descended from heaven. Yet nothing of this kind is read in Scripture concerning Jerobaal.”

But who does not see that here nothing else is meant except what is related in Judges, chapter VI: Gideon begged the angel to permit him to offer a sacrifice; when the angel consented, Gideon poured the broth over the unleavened cakes and the boiled meat, and the angel touched these with the tip of his staff, whereupon fire burst forth divinely from the rock upon which they had been placed? We must therefore say that what Scripture recounts at greater length is reported more briefly by Ambrose.

It could also have happened that he found this story recounted somewhat differently in his manuscripts from the way it is found in ours. We have observed that this happened to him more than once elsewhere, and especially in the final chapter of the book *On Naboth*. Nor will this seem surprising to anyone who has noticed how great was formerly the diversity of Old Testament manuscripts, so that as many different copies circulated as there were churches, as Jerome repeatedly testifies in his Prefaces. Saint Augustine has much the same point in *On Christian Doctrine*, Book II, chapter 11.

The second reason for expunging the work is stated as follows:

> “This same author,” he adds, “explains the paralytic’s words, ‘I have no man,’ as though by ‘man’ the paralytic understood Christ the mediator; this is extremely trivial” (John V, 7).

But extremely trivial is the person who argues in this way. For either he does not understand, or pretends not to understand, that the holy Bishop is doing precisely this in the same passage: showing that in the pool there was a figure of baptism, in the man who lowered the sick person into it a type of Christ himself, and in the sick man finally a symbol of sinful humanity. The paralytic, therefore, is to be understood mystically—or, to use the word employed by our saint, intelligibly. What could be more consonant with Ambrose’s method of interpreting Scripture?

He expresses the third objection in this way:

> “This author says that personal sins—that is, actual sins—are forgiven through baptism, but hereditary sins—that is, original sins—through the washing of the feet. This is certainly heretical and does not agree with theology or the teaching of the Church, as Maldonado testifies.”

This argument appeared so strong and irresistible to Dallaeus (*On Confirmation*, Book III, chapter 8) that, although he had thought it sufficient merely to indicate the other objections as if with a finger, he wished to reinforce this one with his own support. After asserting that both the author of this work and the author of the books *On the Sacraments* had speculated about the washing of the feet in an improper and utterly absurd manner, he quotes the relevant passages and adds:

> “That each dream, being wholly or almost the same, is foolish and insulting to the baptism instituted by Christ sufficiently demonstrates that Ambrose is the author of neither little work.”

This is a very serious accusation, we do not deny it. But the accusers themselves have made an unfortunate mistake: the very teaching to which these Aristarchuses attach so black a theta is found not only in other extant and undisputed works of Ambrose, but also in lost works whose passages are preserved by his most faithful disciple Augustine in his controversies against the Pelagians. There Ambrose would never have advanced a doubtful doctrine, much less a heretical one, with impunity.

Had these writers considered this, they would not have attacked a position fortified by the authority both of so many great doctors and of the ancient Church with such confidence. We shall demonstrate, in the appropriate passage (Chapter 6, no. 32), that they were led into error because they entirely failed to understand the words “hereditary sins,” by which nothing is meant except concupiscence—or, as Ambrose himself says, “the inclination to sin.”

The final argument of Cocus’s editor is so futile that it scarcely deserves to be reported. He says that this author teaches here that the three divine persons must be expressed in baptism, whereas this conflicts with what is asserted in the books *On the Holy Spirit*: namely, that for baptism the invocation of only one divine person is sufficient.

But if this inference were admitted, all books in which the three divine persons are said to be invoked in baptism would have to be denied to Ambrose—something even his opponents would be ashamed to assert. What contradiction is there, then, if someone, speaking of the ordinary manner of administering this sacrament, says that the three divine persons are to be invoked, while, when discussing whether baptism conferred under the invocation of only one person ought sometimes to be regarded as valid, he maintains the affirmative position? We shall address that matter in its proper place.

Meanwhile, let those be ashamed who go about snatching a sound writing, wholly unworthy of being denied to Ambrose, from its rightful parent on such slight grounds—and do so not only against the manuscripts of all kinds, but also against the testimony of so many and such eminent men, Catholic and sectarian, ancient and modern, so that if they do not wish to be persuaded by their authority, they may at least be overwhelmed by their number. We do not doubt that many writers of great reputation within the Calvinist communion perceived this—Blondel, Falcar, Albertinus, and others—for, disregarding the censures of a few of their own party, they did not withhold their assent from the truth.

Since, then, nothing deprives Ambrose of possession of this book, we must now inquire to which year it should be assigned. The holy Bishop himself seems to indicate its date at the very beginning of the work. For there he says (Chapter 1, no. 1) that he had held daily discourses on moral subjects while the deeds of the patriarchs or the precepts of Proverbs were being read. It is certainly most likely that by this he means his books on Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, together with others. We admit, however, that some difficulty arises from the fact that he preached on the same subject in different years, as we have indicated in the appropriate places (*In the Admonition*). Nevertheless, since it is plausible that he refers only to the principal discourses, we do not think that the same words can more properly be referred to any others than to those just mentioned. Accordingly, we have assigned approximately the year 387 to this little work.

Its title, moreover, is found elsewhere in different forms. In Amerbach it reads, *On the Mysteries to Be Initiated Into*; in Erasmus and Gillotius, *On Those Who Are Initiated into the Mysteries*; in the Roman edition, *On Those to Be Initiated*; in very many manuscripts, *On the Mysteries, or on Those to Be Initiated*—that is, on the first knowledge of those same mysteries, for otherwise the title would have to be *On the Initiated*. Finally, in the oldest manuscripts it is entitled *On the Divine Mysteries*, or simply *On the Mysteries*. We follow these manuscripts.

# ONE BOOK OF SAINT AMBROSE, BISHOP OF MILAN, ON THE MYSTERIES

[Written around the year 387.]

## CHAPTER ONE

He promises to append an exposition of the mysteries to the discourses he had previously delivered on moral subjects. Then, having explained why he had not disclosed them earlier, he undertakes their mystical exposition, showing that they were once celebrated by Christ himself.

### 1

We held daily discourses on moral subjects while either the deeds of the patriarchs or the precepts of Proverbs were being read, so that, instructed and formed by these teachings, you might become accustomed to walking in the paths of your ancestors, following their course, and obeying the divine oracles. Thus, renewed through baptism, you might adopt the conduct of life appropriate to those who have been cleansed.

**Note:** The Alnet manuscript reads, “so that you might not become accustomed to entering the ways of evil.” Below, where the old edition and nearly all manuscripts read “to obey the oracles,” the Roman edition, together with a few manuscripts, has “to obey the commandments.”

### 2

Now the time admonishes us to speak about the mysteries and to set forth the very order of the sacraments. If we had thought that this should be disclosed before baptism to those not yet initiated, we would have been judged to have betrayed rather than revealed it. Moreover, the light of the mysteries has poured itself more effectively into those who were unsuspecting than it would have done if some speech had run ahead of it.

**Note:** Some manuscripts read, “if something had preceded it.” A little later, many manuscripts have “with the gift of the sacraments having been brought to you,” some “with the gift having been brought to you,” instead of the reading found in the others and in all editions: “with the gift of the sacraments having been breathed into you.”

### 3

Open, therefore, your ears and draw in the good fragrance of eternal life breathed into you through the gift of the sacraments. We signified this to you when, celebrating the mystery of the opening, we said: “Ephphatha,” which means “Be opened” (Mark VII, 34), so that each person coming to grace might understand what he was being asked and remember what he ought to answer.

**Note:** Gregory the Great, in the *Sacramentary*, the Roman Order, Albinus, and others have written about this ceremony. Menardus, our own scholar, observed in the *Sacramentary*, p. 139, that it was unknown to the Greeks. When Christ is said below to have celebrated the same ceremony, understand this not to mean that he actually instituted it, but that he provided the occasion for its institution, since it was celebrated in imitation of that miracle. Valerius Strabo rightly observes that various ceremonies were instituted by others (*On Ecclesiastical Matters*, chapter 26). When it was performed and according to what rite is explained more fully in the book *On the Sacraments*, chapter 1.

### 4

Christ celebrated this mystery in the Gospel, as we read, when he healed a mute and deaf man (ibid.). He touched his mouth, because he was healing both a mute and a man: in the one case, so that he might open his mouth to the sound infused into it; in the other, because this touch was suitable for a man and not suitable for a woman.

**Note:** The editions of Erasmus, Gillotius, and Rome read, “but he touched his mouth.” Amerbach and all the manuscripts read, “but he touched,” and so forth. Consequently, where several manuscripts and all editions read, “he was healing a man,” some manuscripts read, “he was healing a deaf man.” Finally, instead of “the sound of the voice,” which is found in all editions and in not a few manuscripts, other manuscripts more correctly read “by the sound of the voice,” that is, “for emitting the sound of the voice.”

## CHAPTER TWO

What those entering the Church to be initiated promised, in the presence of what witnesses, and why they turned toward the East.

### 5

After this, the Holy of Holies was opened to you, and you entered the sanctuary of regeneration. Recall what you were asked; recognize what you answered. You renounced the devil and his works, the world and its luxury and pleasures. Your voice is preserved—not in the tomb of the dead, but in the book of the living.

**Note:** “The Holy of Holies” means the sanctuary of regeneration, the baptistery, the sacred font. Both Ambrose and other Fathers call that place by these names. Since Paulinus, in Letter 22, is also found to have called the relics of the saints “the Holy of Holies,” and since from Ennodius of Ticinum, in his letter to Utalis, and Gregory of Tours, *History*, Book X, chapter 31, we understand that those sacred pledges were customarily kept in baptisteries, perhaps someone may think that Ambrose called this place by that name for the same reason. Nevertheless, it is more probable that the term is used here only metaphorically. On all the matters mentioned in this passage, consult Cyril of Jerusalem, *Mystagogical Catecheses* I, and others.

**Note:** Although Ambrose does not recount all the ceremonies of baptism, he did not wish to omit this one, of which scarcely any Father fails to make mention, since it was numbered among the principal ceremonies.

### 6

There you saw a Levite; you saw a priest; you saw the high priest. Do not consider the bodily forms, but the grace of the mysteries. You spoke in the presence of angels, as it is written: “For the lips of the priest guard knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord Almighty” (Malachi II, 7). There is no deceiving and no denying: he is the angel who announces the kingdom of Christ and eternal life. He should not be judged by his appearance, but by his office. Consider what he has handed down, weigh the use made of it, and recognize his status.

**Note:** The Roman edition alone reads, “you saw priests.” In Book I of *On the Sacraments*, chapter 2, a presbyter is indeed mentioned in the singular. By this word the holy Bishop does not designate a bishop, as he usually does, but a priest of the second order; in contrast to him, the bishop is immediately afterward called “the high priest.” Again, Erasmus, together with the following edition and several manuscripts, reads “the grace of the mysteries”; Amerbach, with more numerous and better manuscripts, has the reading found in the text.

**Note:** Some manuscripts, together with the Hebrew text and the Vulgate and Chaldean versions, read “of the Lord of hosts.” The remaining manuscripts and all the editions, together with the Septuagint, Syriac, and Arabic versions, read “of the Lord Almighty.”

### 7

You entered, therefore, in order to see your adversary, whom [the reading is uncertain] you are thought to renounce openly. You turned toward the East; for whoever renounces the devil turns toward Christ and looks directly upon him.

**Note:** All the editions read, “whom you soon thought you ought to renounce.” All the manuscripts read, “whom you ought to renounce to his face”; some have “you thought,” most “you have thought,” and one even “you have been spat upon.” To renounce someone “to his face” means the same as openly and plainly. Thus *εἰς πρόσωπον* is used in Didymus and in the Greek scholia in the sense of *φανερῶς*, “openly.” In other scholia it is used in the sense of *ἀναισχύντως*, “shamelessly”; perhaps it occurs in this sense in Job I, 11. Nor is the reading found in the Royal manuscript, “you have been spat upon,” entirely displeasing—namely, that your mouth is smeared with spittle. But then the clauses should be divided as follows: “whom you ought to renounce. You have been spat upon in the face,” and so forth. From this passage we learn that it was customary for those who renounced the devil to turn toward the West, since afterward they turned toward the East in order to look upon Christ.

## CHAPTER THREE

He teaches that the presence and operation of the divinity must be considered in the water and in the sacred ministers, through several figures by which baptism was foretold from the creation of the world and afterward.

### 8

What did you see? Certainly, water—but not water alone. You saw Levites ministering there, and the high priest questioning and consecrating. The Apostle first taught you that we must not contemplate the things that are seen, but the things that are not seen; for the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal (II Corinthians IV, 18). Elsewhere also you have: “For the invisible things of God are understood from the creation of the world through the things that have been made; his eternal power and divinity are likewise discerned through his works” (Romans I, 20). Hence the Lord himself also says: “If you do not believe me, believe at least the works” (John X, 38). Believe, then, that the presence of the divinity is there. Do you believe in the operation but not in the presence? From where would the operation proceed if presence did not precede it?

**Note:** The consecration of the font is discussed in Book I of *On the Sacraments*, chapter 5. It is clear that this was known not only to the authors of the *Apostolic Constitutions*, Book VII, chapter 4, and of the work *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, chapter “On Baptism,” but also to Saints Cyprian, in the synodical letter to Januarius and the other bishops of Numidia; Basil, *On Psalm LXX*; Gregory of Nyssa; and others. Therefore the English editor of Cyprian’s works, at the passage cited, rightly denies that those formulas are as recent as the innovators try to persuade themselves and others.

### 9

Consider how ancient this mystery is, prefigured at the very origin of the world. In the beginning itself, when God made heaven and earth, Scripture says, “the Spirit was borne over the waters” (Genesis I, 2). He who was borne over the waters—was he not working upon the waters? But why should I say merely “working”? As far as presence is concerned, he was borne over them. Was he not working, he who was borne over them? Recognize that he was working in the making of the world, when the Prophet says to you: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power” (Psalm XXXII, 6). Both points are supported by prophetic testimony: that he was borne over the waters and that he was working. Moses says that he was borne over them; David testifies that he was working.

**Note:** The Roman edition alone reads: “But I shall say that he was working. As regards presence, he was borne over them. But as regards the fact that he was working, recognize that he who was borne over them was working in the making of the world, when he says to you …”

### 10

Receive another testimony. All flesh had been corrupted by its sins. “My Spirit,” God says, “will not remain in human beings, because they are flesh” (Genesis VI, 3). By this God shows that spiritual grace is turned away by carnal impurity and the stain of more serious sin. Therefore, wishing to restore what was lacking, God brought about the flood and commanded the just Noah to enter the ark (Genesis VII, 1 and following). When the flood had receded, Noah first sent out a raven, which did not return; then he sent out a dove, which, as we read, returned with an olive branch (Genesis VIII, 7–8). You see the water, you see the wood, you behold the dove—and do you doubt the mystery?

**Note:** Some manuscripts read, “when the flood had descended.”

### 11

The water, therefore, is that in which the flesh is immersed so that every carnal sin may be washed away. Every disgrace is buried there. The wood is that to which the Lord Jesus was fastened when he suffered for us. The dove is the form in which the Holy Spirit descended, as you learned in the New Testament (Matthew III, 16); he inspires in you peace of soul and tranquility of mind. The raven is a figure of sin: it goes out and does not return, provided that in you also the guardianship and pattern of the righteous are preserved.

**Note:** All editions and several manuscripts read, “so that sin may be washed away.” Every vice is buried; the remaining manuscripts, greater in number and antiquity, have the reading found in the text. One manuscript, however, reads, “so that sin may be washed away by charity.”

### 12

There is also a third testimony, as the Apostle teaches you: “For all our fathers were under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea” (I Corinthians X, 1–2). Finally Moses himself says in the Canticle: “You sent your Spirit, and the sea covered them” (Exodus XV, 10). You perceive that already then, in the passage of the Hebrews, the figure of holy baptism went before us: the Egyptian perished and the Hebrew escaped. For what else are we taught daily in this sacrament except that guilt is submerged and error is abolished, while piety and innocence remain secure?

**Note:** The old edition and a few manuscripts read, “piety and innocence remained wholly”; the Roman edition has “remain secure”; several manuscripts, “remain safely”; and more, “remained safely.”

### 13

You hear that our fathers were under the cloud—and a good cloud, which cooled the flames of carnal passions. A good cloud overshadows those whom the Holy Spirit visits. Finally, he came upon the Virgin Mary, and the power of the Most High overshadowed her (Luke I, 35), when she gave birth to the redemption of the human race. That miracle, too, was performed through Moses as a figure (Exodus XIV, 21 and following). If, then, the Spirit was present in figure, is he not present in reality, when Scripture says to you: “The law was given through Moses, but grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John I, 17)?

### 14

Marah was a spring of the greatest bitterness. Moses cast wood into it, and it became sweet (Exodus XV, 23 and following). Water, unless consecrated beforehand by the proclamation of the Lord’s cross, is useful for no purpose of future salvation. But once it has been consecrated through the mystery of the saving cross, it is made suitable for the use of the spiritual bath and the saving cup. Just as Moses therefore cast wood into that spring—that is, the prophet—so the priest casts the proclamation of the Lord’s cross into this font, and the water becomes sweet for grace.

**Note:** The Roman edition removed the words “that is, the prophet,” although they are set in a certain antithesis against the word “priest.”

**Note:** Someone might perhaps think that Ambrose is saying here that water is entirely unfit for baptism unless it has first been sanctified by prayer. It must be observed, however, that the issue here is not what they call the legal requirement or validity, but merely the customary practice, to which the ancient figure is applied.

### 15

Do not, therefore, trust only the eyes of your body. What is not seen is more truly perceived, because the one is temporal, while the other is eternal; it is not grasped by the eyes but discerned by the soul and the mind.

### 16

Finally, let the reading of the Books of Kings instruct you (IV Kings V, 1 and following). Naaman was a Syrian and had leprosy, nor could he be cleansed by anyone. Then a young girl from among the captives said that there was a prophet in Israel who could cleanse him from the contagion of leprosy. Taking gold and silver, he went, as the text says, to the king of Israel. When the king learned the reason for his arrival, he tore his garments, saying that he was being challenged, since things beyond royal power were being requested of him. Elisha, however, informed the king that he should send the Syrian to him, so that he might learn that there was a God in Israel. When Naaman arrived, Elisha ordered him to immerse himself seven times in the Jordan River.

### 17

Then Naaman began to reason with himself that his homeland had better waters, in which he had often immersed himself, and had never been cleansed of leprosy. Recalled by this thought, he did not obey the prophet’s commands. But, persuaded by the exhortation and entreaties of his servants, he consented and immersed himself. Immediately cleansed, he understood that the cleansing of a person does not come from the waters but from grace.

**Note:** The editions read, “and had never been cleansed from leprosy.”

### 18

Now recognize who that young girl from among the captives is: plainly, the gathering from the nations—that is, the Church of the Lord—previously weighed down by captivity to sin, when she did not yet possess the freedom of grace. Through her counsel that vain people of the nations heard the prophetic word, about which it had long been doubtful. Later, when it believed that the command ought to be carried out, it was cleansed from every contagion of vice. Naaman doubted before he was healed; you have already been healed, and therefore you must not doubt.

## CHAPTER FOUR

It is shown, by the testimony of John and by the very words used in administering this sacrament, that water does not cleanse without the Spirit. This is also signified by the Gospel’s pool and by the paralytic healed there by the Lord. In this passage it is demonstrated that the Holy Spirit truly descended in Christ’s baptism, and what is to be understood in this mystery.

### 19

For this reason it was said to you beforehand that you should not believe only what you saw, lest you too should say: “Is this the great mystery of which eye has not seen, ear has not heard, and which has not entered into the human heart?” (I Corinthians II, 9). I see waters such as I saw every day. Are these waters to cleanse me—waters into which I have often descended and have never been cleansed? From this recognize that water does not cleanse without the Spirit.

### 20

Therefore you have read that the three witnesses in baptism are one: water, blood, and Spirit (I John V, 7). For if you remove one of these, the sacrament of baptism does not stand. What, after all, is water without the cross of Christ? A common element, without any sacramental effect. Nor, again, is there a mystery of regeneration without water: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John III, 5).

Even the catechumen believes in the cross of the Lord Jesus, with which he too is signed. But unless he has been baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, he cannot receive the forgiveness of sins or draw upon himself the gift of spiritual grace.

**Note:** Two points are to be observed from these words. First, they affirm the necessity of baptism for the washing away even of the sins of catechumens; the same is taught in Sermon 3 on Psalm CXVIII, p. 911. From this we infer that Ambrose by no means held the opinion attributed to him concerning the Emperor Valentinian. Second, they affirm that the three divine persons must necessarily be expressed in the form of baptism. From this we conclude that the opinion that the same sacrament administered only in the name of Christ is valid has been wrongly attributed to him. We shall treat both matters in their proper places.

### 21

That Syrian, then, immersed himself seven times under the Law (IV Kings V, 14). But you have been baptized in the name of the Trinity: you confessed the Father; remember what you did. You confessed the Son; you confessed the Holy Spirit. Maintain the order of the realities in this faith. You died to the world and rose again to God. And, as though buried in that element of the world, you died to sin and were raised to eternal life. Believe, therefore, that the waters are not empty.

**Note:** The Roman edition, together with one or two manuscripts, adds, “but you have been baptized in grace.” The old edition and the remaining manuscripts more correctly omit the words “in grace.”

### 22

For this reason it was said to you: “An angel of the Lord descended at a certain time into the pool, and the water was stirred; and whoever first descended into the pool after the stirring of the water became well from whatever sickness afflicted him” (John V, 4). This pool was in Jerusalem, and one person was healed each year. But no one was healed before the angel had descended. So that it might be a sign that the angel had descended, the water was stirred for the sake of unbelievers. For them there was a sign; for you, faith. For them an angel descended; for you, the Holy Spirit. For them a created thing was stirred; for you, Christ himself, the Lord of creation, works.

### 23

Then one person was healed; now all are healed—or at least, the one Christian people. For in some there is also deceptive water (Jeremiah XV, 18). The baptism of the faithless does not heal (*I, q. 1, canon “Non sanat”); it does not cleanse but defiles. The Jew baptizes jugs and cups (Mark VII, 4), as though things without sensation could receive either guilt or grace. You, baptize this sensible cup of yours, in which your good works shine and in which the splendor of your grace gleams. Therefore that pool too was a figure, so that you might believe that divine power descends into this font.

**Note:** By “the faithless,” one might first understand those who broke the promise made to Christ in baptism to observe his commandments. More narrowly, it might mean those separated from the mystical body of Christ through heresy. Finally, it might mean those who rejected the light of faith offered to them. Nothing suggests that the first meaning should be attributed to the holy Bishop. Certainly, on that interpretation he could not be denied to be a heretic, since the Council of Constance, session 8, and the Council of Trent, session 7, canon 17, condemned Wycliffe’s fourth article: “If a bishop or priest is in mortal sin, he neither ordains, confects, consecrates, nor baptizes.” On this matter see William Estius, *Commentary on the Sentences*, distinction I, and Mabillon, in Sermon 66 of Saint Bernard.

As for the reception of baptism administered by heretics, everyone knows that there was formerly a great controversy on this subject between Cyprian and Stephen; nor is it less well known what the position of Cyprian and the Africans was. As for Stephen’s opinion, in our own time there have been those who argued, contrary to the principles of the ancients, that Stephen forbade baptism to be repeated for all who returned from heresy, even if they had not been baptized in the name of the Trinity. Their principal evidence is Stephen’s decree, reported by Cyprian in opposition to his letter: “If anyone, therefore, comes to us from any heresy, let nothing be innovated,” and so forth.

They also cite Augustine, *On the One Baptism against Petilianus*, chapter 14, who says: “Stephen judged that the baptism of heretics ought in no way to be repeated.” But perhaps they did not sufficiently observe that the words of both men must be understood according to the practice prevailing in those times, as Eusebius, Book VII, chapter 3, and Vincent of Lérins, *Commonitorium* I, chapter 19, sufficiently indicate. According to the nearly universal tradition, it was customary to rebaptize only those heretics who had not been baptized under the invocation of the Trinity. This is established not only by the authority of the authors mentioned above, but also repeatedly by Augustine in his writings against the Donatists, Optatus of Milevis, Facundus of Hermiane, and others.

Indeed, Leo the Great would not escape the same charge unless his statement in Letter 89 to Nicetas were understood in a similar way: “Those who have received baptism from heretics are to be confirmed by the invocation of the Holy Spirit alone through the imposition of hands.” There no distinction among heretics is expressed. Yet it is even more probable that Stephen wrote that condition in his letter—namely, that baptism is sufficient provided it was administered in the name of the Trinity.

For what else did Firmilian mean when he wrote as follows? “It is also absurd that they do not think it necessary to ask who the person was who baptized, on the ground that the one who was baptized could obtain grace by the invocation of the Trinity, of the names of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.” Later, after relating the story of a certain demon-possessed woman, he adds: “What, then, shall we say of this woman’s baptism … especially since she lacked neither the confession of the Trinity nor anything else?”

Add to this that neither the Fathers of Arles nor Augustine, while openly condemning the position of Cyprian and the Africans, said anything against Stephen and the Roman Church. Indeed, Facundus explicitly states that Cyprian was rightly censured by Stephen.

However the matter may stand, it is certain that this passage of Ambrose is wrongly cited in this controversy. For it does not concern the baptism of heretics, but the baptism of Jews—or even of unbelievers, which is the third possible interpretation. This is made clear both by the entire sequence of the discourse and by the author of *On the Sacraments*, Book II, chapter 1, no. 2.

24. Finally, that paralytic was waiting for a man [Col. 0396A] (John 5:7). And who was that man, if not the Lord Jesus, born of a Virgin? At his coming it was no longer a shadow that healed individuals, but the Truth that healed everyone. He, therefore, is the one who was expected to descend, of whom God the Father said to John the Baptist: “Upon whom you see the Spirit descending from heaven and remaining upon him, he is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit” (John 1:33). Of him John testified, saying: “For I saw the Spirit descending from heaven like a dove and remaining upon him” (ibid., 32). And why did the Spirit descend in the likeness of a dove, unless so that you might see, unless so that you might recognize that the dove which righteous Noah sent out from the ark was also a likeness of this dove, so that you might recognize the type of the sacrament (Gen. 8:8)?

[Col. 0396B] 25. And perhaps you will say: Since that which was sent out was a real dove, whereas here he descended “like a dove,” how can we say that there it was a likeness, but here the reality, when according to the Greeks it is written that the Spirit descended “in bodily form, as a dove” (σωματικῷ εἴδει ὡσεὶ περιστερὰν) (Luke 3:22)?

[Note: [Col. 0396D] In Luke, this passage is expressed in Greek as: σωματικῷ εἴδει ὡσεὶ περιστερὰν, “in bodily form, as a dove.”]

But what is as true as the divinity which always remains? A creature cannot be the reality, but only a likeness, which is easily dissolved and changed. Moreover, those who are baptized ought not to possess merely the likeness, but true simplicity. Hence the Lord also says: “Be wise as serpents and simple as doves” (Matt. 10:16). Rightly, therefore, the Spirit descended like a dove, to admonish us that we ought to possess the dove’s simplicity.

[Note: [Col. 0396D] Most manuscripts, and the Amerbach edition, punctuate this passage differently, namely: “ought to possess the likeness, but it is to be accepted in place of the reality.” We also read this concerning Christ: “And being found in appearance [Col. 0397A] as a man” (Phil. 2:7); and concerning God the Father: “Nor have you seen his appearance” (John 5:37). The following clearly shows, however, that the other punctuation is preferable.]

We also read that a likeness is to be understood in place of the reality concerning Christ: “And being found in appearance as a man” (Phil. 2:7); and concerning God the Father: “Nor have you seen his appearance” (John 5:37).

## CHAPTER V

Christ’s presence in baptism is confirmed, and therefore its ministers are not to be considered. Finally, the confession of the Trinity customarily made by the baptized is briefly examined.

26. Is there still anything about which you ought to doubt, when the Father speaks loudly to you in the Gospel, saying: “This is my Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3:17); when the Son speaks, upon whom the Holy Spirit manifested himself like a dove; when the Holy Spirit also speaks, who descended like a dove; when David cries out: “The voice of the Lord is over the waters; the God of majesty has thundered; the Lord is over many waters” (Ps. 28:3)?

And when Scripture testifies to you (1, q. 1, c. *Cum Script.*) that, when Gideon prayed, fire descended from heaven (Judg. 6:21), and again, when Elijah prayed, fire was sent which consumed the sacrifice (1 Kings 18:38)?

[Note: [Col. 0397C] The Roman edition alone adds: “which consumed the sacrifice.” Concerning the fire descending upon the sacrifice of Gideon, see what we said in the *Admonition*. This passage is cited by Alger of Liège, *On the Sacraments*, book III, chapter 10, to prove that true sacraments exist among heretics. Gratian likewise employs this very passage for the same purpose in the *Decree*, but corrupts it, preferring “Jeroboam” in place of “Gideon.” His commentator observes, however, that the passage does not concern wicked priests and therefore is wrongly cited in that case as testimony.]

27. Consider not the merits of the persons, but the offices of the priests. And if you do consider merits, then, just as you consider Elijah, consider also the merits of Peter or of Paul, who handed down to us this mystery received from the Lord Jesus. Visible fire was sent to them so that they might believe (1, q. 1, c. *Cum Script.*, § *Ignis*); an invisible fire operates for us who believe. It was given to them as a figure, but to us as an admonition.

[Note: [Col. 0397D] A few manuscripts of no inferior authority read “as a warning.”]

Believe, therefore, that the Lord Jesus is present, invoked by the prayers of the priests. He said: “Where two or three are gathered, there am I also” (Matt. 18:20). How much more, then, where the Church is, where his mysteries are: there he deigns to grant his presence!

28. You descended, therefore; remember what you answered—that you believe in the Father, that you believe in the Son, that you believe in the Holy Spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0397D] The ancient Fathers demonstrated the complete equality of the divine Persons against the Arians and other ancient heretics by no more effective proof than that drawn from the form of baptism. The Socinians are still pierced by this weapon. Observe here that baptism is performed by immersion.]

You do not say there: “I believe in the greater, the lesser, and the last”; rather, you are bound by the same pledge of your voice to believe in the Son just as you believe in the Father, and to believe in the Holy Spirit just as you believe in the Son. The sole exception is that you confess that you must believe in the cross of the Lord Jesus alone.

## CHAPTER VI

Why, after emerging from the baptismal font, anointing is performed on the head; why also the feet are washed after baptism; and what sins are forgiven by each rite.

29. After this, naturally, you went up to the priest. Consider what followed. Was it not what David says: “Like the ointment on the head, which ran down upon the beard, the beard of Aaron” (Ps. 133:2)? This is the ointment of which Solomon also says: “Your name is poured-out ointment; therefore the maidens loved you and drew you” (Song 1:2).

[Note: [Col. 0397D] The Roman edition alone adds: “Draw us after you.” And below: “into the fragrance of your ointments.” As regards the first phrase, the Hebrew text and the Vulgate agree with one another, whereas the Septuagint and the other versions agree with us. As regards the second, all the idioms of Scripture favor the same reading. Nevertheless, we think that Ambrose cited this passage while also alluding to the fragrance of Jacob’s garments when he secretly obtained his brother’s blessing from his father.]

How many souls renewed today have loved you, Lord Jesus, saying: “Draw us after you; we will run into the fragrance of your garments” (ibid., 3), so that they might inhale the fragrance of the resurrection!

30. Understand why this is done, because “the eyes of the wise man are in his head” (Eccl. 2:14). Therefore it flows down upon the beard, that is, into the grace of youth; therefore upon Aaron’s beard, so that you may become a chosen race, priestly and precious. For we are all anointed by spiritual grace into the kingdom of God and into the priesthood.

[Note: [Col. 0398D] Quite a few manuscripts read: “into the kingdom of God and the co-priesthood.”]

31. You ascended from the font; remember the Gospel reading. For our Lord Jesus washed the feet of his disciples in the Gospel.

[Note: [Col. 0398D] The Roman edition alone reads: “Jesus washed feet,” omitting “in the Gospel.” Below, where all editions and some manuscripts read “he refused the service,” the other manuscripts read “he refused the mystery.” The latter is not entirely correct.]

When he came to Simon Peter, Peter said: “You shall never wash my feet” (John 13:8). He did not understand the mystery, and therefore refused the service, because he thought that he would burden the servant’s humility if he patiently accepted his Lord’s service.

[Note: [Col. 0398D] Several manuscripts read: “because the servant thought that he was being burdened by humility.”]

The Lord answered him: “If I do not wash your feet, you will have no part with me.” On hearing this, Peter said: “Lord, not only my feet, but also my hands and my head.” The Lord answered: “He who has been washed needs only to wash his feet, but is entirely clean” (ibid., 9).

32. Peter was clean, but he had to wash the sole of his foot; for he possessed the sin inherited from the first man, when the serpent tripped him up and persuaded him into error (Gen. 3:6).

[Note: [Col. 0398D] This passage has long caused difficulty for many. In the margin of the Claromontane manuscript, written by the same hand as the text, one finds the following remark: “It is strange that he says that personal sins are washed away in baptism, but that original sins are removed in the foot-washing performed by the Lord for his disciples.” Hugo of Saint-Victor was referring to the same matter when, in his commentary on John 13, he wrote that some had asserted that original sin is forgiven after baptism through the washing of the feet.

Some heterodox writers, inflamed by this opinion—as we said in the *Admonition*—went much further and chiefly for this reason rejected the book as not being by Ambrose. Yet it did not occur to them to consider two passages in which the holy Doctor teaches something plainly parallel.

The first is taken from the lost commentary on Isaiah, which Augustine cites in book IV, chapter 11, of *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, in these words: “And in another place in the same work, speaking of the apostle Peter, he says: He offered himself, asking that not only his feet and head be washed, which he had previously thought to be a sin; for he immediately understood that by the washing of the feet the dirt of the culpable succession inherited from the first man is removed.”

The second passage, cited by Augustine against Julian in his *Exposition of Psalm 48*, verse 6, no. 8, reads as follows: “Our iniquity is one thing, and the iniquity of our heel another, in which Adam was wounded by the serpent’s tooth and left, through his wound, an inherited succession subject to guilt, so that we all limp from that wound. Hence the Lord washed the disciples’ feet, to wash away the serpent’s poisons; and Peter is rebuked because he excused himself lest the Lord wash his feet. … The Lord answers him: ‘He who has been washed does not need to wash except his feet, but is entirely clean.’”

What could be found more closely corresponding to these three passages? Nevertheless, although Augustine also uses them there to prove original sin, it must not be supposed that Ambrose held the opinion that original guilt is removed by such a washing. For who would believe that Augustine would set against his own opponents and those of the Church testimonies that departed from truth and faith, especially when that same ceremony was not practiced in Africa, as will be said elsewhere? Or who, again, would think that Ambrose—who everywhere attributes perfect righteousness and regeneration to baptism, and who in this very passage, as in many others, acknowledges that Peter was clean—could have held that the stain of original sin was washed away by a foot-washing which he knew was omitted in many churches?

But conjecture is unnecessary here, for he himself sufficiently reveals his meaning in the cited *Exposition of Psalm 48*, no. 9, in these words: “Hence I think,” he says, “that the iniquity of the heel is rather the slipperiness of sinning than some guilt belonging to our offense. And rightly the Lord says: … ‘Let us wash the feet,’ so that we may remove the slipperiness of the heel, so that our standing in virtue may be firm; and so that no one may fall through ancestral error who is prepared to stand by his own resolve; and so that he who desires to keep the path of virtue may not fear the slipperiness of inheritance.”

What could be clearer than that by “the slipperiness of sinning,” “the slipperiness of the heel,” and “the slipperiness of inheritance” nothing else is indicated—as we noted on this same passage—than concupiscence? Although concupiscence is not truly and properly sin in those who have been reborn, nevertheless, because it arises from sin and inclines toward sin, it is called sin by the Apostle.

Thus Ambrose believed that a particular grace was conferred in the washing of the feet, so that these inherited sins—or that sin of the first man which Peter possessed by succession—might be removed. His faithful interpreter calls this a greater aid to sanctification, if indeed the interpreter is not Ambrose himself, in book III, chapter 1, no. 7, *On the Sacraments*.

We are not unaware that certain Catholic theologians think that Ambrose calls these slight sins—sins which Augustine calls natural—“inherited.” But since faith teaches that venial sins, no less than mortal sins, are cleansed in baptism, we must adhere entirely to the interpretation supplied by the holy Doctor himself.]

Therefore his sole is washed so that inherited sins may be removed; for our own personal sins are forgiven through baptism.

33. At the same time, understand that the mystery consists in the very service of humility. For he says: “If I, Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, how much more ought you to wash one another’s feet?” (John 13:14). Since he himself, the author of salvation, redeemed us through obedience, how much more ought we, his little servants, to offer the service of humility and obedience!

[Note: [Col. 0400C] Some manuscripts read: “the mystery consists in the service.”]

## CHAPTER VII

The washing away of sins is signified by white garments; through whose work the Church came to call herself black yet beautiful. The angels marveled at her brightness, as also at that of the Lord’s flesh; indeed, Christ himself commended his Bride’s beauty under various figures, and the mutual affection between them is described.

34. After this you received white garments (Decretum, *On Consecration*, distinction 4, chapter *Accepisti*), so that they might signify that you had put off the covering of sins and had put on the chaste veils of innocence, concerning which the Prophet said: “You shall sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be clean; you shall wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow” (Ps. 51:7).

[Note: [Col. 0400C] Anyone who remembers the white garments customarily worn by the newly baptized will scarcely find an ancient Father or ecclesiastical historian who does not mention them.]

For the one who is baptized appears to have been cleansed both according to the Law and according to the Gospel: according to the Law, because Moses sprinkled the blood of the lamb with a bundle of hyssop (Exod. 12:22);

[Note: [Col. 0400D] The Roman edition alone reads: “the blood of the bird,” noting Leviticus 14 in the margin. But the agreement of all the older editions and manuscripts makes it more probable that the allusion is to the passage assigned by us.]

according to the Gospel, because Christ’s garments were white as snow when he displayed the glory of his resurrection in the Gospel (Matt. 17:2). He is therefore made whiter than snow whose guilt is forgiven. Hence the Lord also says through Isaiah: “Though your sins be as scarlet, I will make them white as snow” (Isa. 1:18).

35. Possessing these garments, which it has assumed through the bath of regeneration, the Church says in the Song of Songs: “I am black but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem” (Song 1:5).

[Note: [Col. 0400D] Thus all editions, together with several manuscripts. Many others read “daughter of Jerusalem,” but this conflicts with the authority of all the sacred manuscripts.]

Black because of the frailty of human condition, beautiful because of grace; black because she is made from sinners, beautiful through the sacrament of faith. Seeing these garments, the daughters of Jerusalem, astonished, say: “Who is this that comes up whitened?” (Song 8:5). She was black—how has she suddenly been made white!

36. The angels also were uncertain when Christ rose; the heavenly Powers were uncertain when they saw that flesh was ascending into heaven. Finally they said: “Who is this King of glory?” And while some said: “Lift up the gates of your Prince, and be lifted up, eternal gates, and the King of glory shall enter,” others doubted, saying: “Who is this King of glory?” (Ps. 24:8–9).

[Note: [Col. 0400D] Some manuscripts read “the gates of your Prince”; some “your princely gates”; and several others “the gate of your Prince.” This reading was discussed in *On the Institution of the Virgin*, chapter 5, no. 39, where we also added something concerning this ignorance of the angels. Ambrose treats the matter elsewhere as well, especially in book I, chapter 6, *On the Faith*.]
