In Isaiah, too, you find the heavenly powers expressing their uncertainty: “Who is this who comes up from Edom, whose garments are red from Bozrah, beautiful in a white robe?” (Isa. 63:1).

37. But Christ, seeing his Church in white garments—for her sake he had assumed filthy garments, as you find in the book of the prophet Zechariah (Zech. 3:3)—or seeing the soul cleansed and washed by the bath of regeneration, says: “Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved; behold, you are beautiful; your eyes are like doves” (Song 4:1). It was in the likeness of a dove that the Holy Spirit descended from heaven (Luke 3:22).

[Note: [Col. 0401C] The older editions, together with most manuscripts, read, as we said above: “because he descended like a dove.”]

Beautiful are the eyes like those of a dove, because the Holy Spirit descended from heaven in the dove’s likeness.

38. And below: “Your teeth are like a flock of shorn sheep, which have come up from the washing; all of them bear twins, and none among them is barren; your lips are like a scarlet thread” (Song 4:2–3).

[Note: [Col. 0401C] The Roman edition alone reads: “An apt comparison.”]

This is no ordinary praise. First, there is the pleasing comparison with shorn sheep; for we know that goats can graze safely in high places and take their food securely on steep slopes; then, when they are shorn, they are relieved of what is superfluous.

[Col. 0401B] The Church is compared with their flock, possessing within herself many virtues of souls which through the washing lay aside superfluous sins, which bring to Christ mystical faith and moral grace, and which speak of the cross of the Lord Jesus.

39. In these things the Church is beautiful. Therefore the Word of God says to her: “You are altogether beautiful, my beloved, and there is no reproach in you, for guilt has been submerged.”

[Note: [Col. 0401C] A Gembloux manuscript reads: “Come here from Lebanon, bride; come here from Lebanon,” and so on.]

“Come here from Lebanon, Bride; come here from Lebanon. You shall pass over and cross over from the beginning of faith” (ibid., 7–8), because, renouncing the world, she has passed beyond the age and crossed over to Christ.

And again the Word of God says to her: “How beautiful and how delightful you have become, love, in your delights! Your stature has become like a palm tree, and your breasts like clusters of grapes” (Song 7:6–7).

40. The Church answers him: “Who will grant that you be my brother, nursing at the breasts of my mother? Finding you outside, I shall kiss you; indeed, they will not despise me. I shall take you and lead you into the house of my mother, into the inner chamber of her who conceived me. You shall teach me” (Song 8:1–2).

Do you see how, delighted by the gift of graces, she longs to reach the innermost mysteries and consecrate all her senses to Christ?

[Note: [Col. 0401C] Thus the Roman edition, together with part of the manuscript tradition. The older manuscripts instead read: “she seeks the one who awakens, and asks that she be awakened,” and so forth. That reading is less suitable.]

She still seeks, still awakens love, and asks that it be awakened for her by the daughters of Jerusalem. Through their grace—that is, through the grace of faithful souls—she desires the Bridegroom to be stirred to a fuller love of her.

41. Therefore the Lord Jesus himself, invited by such great devotion of love, by beauty of appearance and grace, and because no sins now stained those who had been washed,

[Note: [Col. 0401C] The Roman edition alone reads: “because those who had been washed were no longer stained by any sins.” Perhaps it feared that innovators might misuse Ambrose’s words to assert that sins are not removed but merely covered. Their argument would be futile, however, for sins do not stain where they do not exist.]

says to the Church: “Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm” (ibid., 8:6). That is: You are beautiful, my beloved; you are altogether beautiful; nothing is lacking in you.

“Set me as a seal upon your heart,” so that your faith may shine with the fullness of the sacrament.

[Note: [Col. 0401C] The same Roman edition alone added here after “sacrament”: “As a seal upon your arm, so that your works … you were made. Many waters will not be able to extinguish love, so that your love … cannot. Why? Repeat it, because …”]

Let your works also shine and bear the image of God, in whose image you were made. Let your love not be diminished by any persecution, which many waters cannot extinguish and rivers cannot overwhelm (ibid., 7).

42. Therefore repeat it, because you have received the spiritual seal, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety, the spirit of holy fear (Isa. 11:2); and preserve what you have received. God the Father has sealed you; Christ the Lord has confirmed you; and he has given the pledge of the Spirit in your hearts, as you learned from the apostolic reading (2 Cor. 1:22).

[Note: [Col. 0401C] It is beyond doubt that this refers to Confirmation. Yet because no mention of chrismation is made here, it produces many and considerable difficulties. P. Sirmond argued that in the first centuries no anointing other than the one described in the preceding chapter was used for the newly baptized in administering this sacrament—that is, the anointing by which the priest anointed the head of those emerging from the sacred font—and that only the laying on of hands was reserved to the bishop.

His most vigorous opponent on this point was Pierre Aurelius, who argued that the chrismation customarily performed by the priest was an anointing of the crown of the head, and therefore that another anointing—namely, of the forehead—must have been added by the bishop.

Dallaeus defends Sirmond’s position and, in book III, chapter 8, *On Confirmation*, explicitly denies that any anointing is signified either here or in book III, chapter 2, *On the Sacraments*. He maintains instead that these authors recognize only two seals: one of the body, discussed above in chapter 6 and in book III, chapter 1, *On the Sacraments*; the other of the spirit, discussed in the passages just cited. The first was performed with chrism by the same presbyter who had anointed the crown, upon the forehead in the form of a cross; the second, by the laying on of the bishop’s hands, by which the heart is sealed with sevenfold grace.

But first that writer is mistaken about the minister, since he teaches that the anointing signified in chapter 6 of this book and in chapter 1 of book III, *On the Sacraments*, was performed by a presbyter, whereas a simple inspection of the passages makes it clear that this is attributed to the bishop alone.

Next, when he infers that the same sealing is to be counted among the ceremonies of baptism, by the same reasoning one could conclude that the same is true of the sacrament of the Eucharist—something he himself would never concede.

We shall not pursue this matter further here. We will add, however, that Sainte-Beuve, who attributes the effect and grace of Confirmation to chrismation in dissertation 3, article 21, never discusses the laying on of hands without attaching to it the anointing mentioned in the preceding chapter.

If anyone should say that these two things are too sharply separated both here in Ambrose and in book III, chapters 1 and 2, *On the Sacraments*, for them to constitute one sacrament, the answer is readily given that things which are not separated in administration may nevertheless be separated in exposition. For it is certain that not everything is related here in the order in which it was performed; indeed, quite a few things are omitted.

This favors the opinion of those who, with Pierre Aurelius, think that a distinct chrismation is included here. But whatever the heterodox may say, since it is probable that anointing is, as Sainte-Beuve teaches in the cited proposition 6, merely an integral part of Confirmation, we shall always retain intact the substance of that sacrament.

Besides, Gregory’s *Sacramentary* notes two distinct chrismations, whereas the Gallican *Sacramentary* and Missal, and likewise the Gothic Missal, mention only the one performed on the forehead. The anointing of the crown, which they attribute to Pope Sylvester, was probably commanded to be received by the Council of Orange in places where it had not yet been admitted, although P. Morinus maintains that the intention of that council was either to abolish that anointing or to declare it unnecessary. As for his further claim that the council assigned the frontal anointing to the deacon, this should not seem surprising if it is not essential to that sacrament.]

## CHAPTER VIII

On the mystical banquet of the Lord’s altar: lest anyone undervalue it, it is shown to be more ancient than the sacred rites of the Synagogue, since it was expressed in the sacrifice of Melchizedek; and to be far superior to the manna, since it is Christ’s body. A very elegant comparison is made between the two.

43. This people, cleansed and rich in such insignia, hastens to Christ’s altars, saying: “And I will enter the altar of God, to God who makes my youth joyful” (Ps. 43:4). For, having laid aside the garments of ancient error and renewed the youth of the eagle, it hastens to approach that heavenly banquet.

[Note: [Col. 0403C] This indicates the procession of the newly baptized from the baptistery to the altar—that is, from the lowest part of the church to the sanctuary—so that they might there be nourished by the holy Eucharist. This was not done without a certain devout ceremony filled with majesty. Each person carried a lighted candle in his hand; and throughout the entire octave, when they approached the sacred assembly in the same attire, any girls who had professed virginity during the Easter festival were also led among these innocent flocks. The final book, *On the Fall of a Virgin*, bears witness to this. The lights are discussed in the short work *On the Mystery of Easter*, chapter 5; near the end of Gregory of Nazianzus’s Oration 40; in Cyril of Jerusalem’s *Procatechesis* and *Catechesis* 1; by Venantius Fortunatus; and by others. We may add that almost whenever Ambrose mentions the sacrament of the Eucharist—and he mentions it quite often—he employs Psalm 42, but especially Psalm 23. See what we observed above, in the volume on the earlier *Apology of David*, chapter 12, no. 59.]

It comes, therefore, and, seeing the most holy altar prepared,

[Note: [Col. 0403D] “Prepared,” that is, adorned. From the very beginning of the Church, it was customary to adorn the sacred altars with double coverings, curtains, various gifts of gold and silver, candles, and finally flowers. This is attested by Optatus of Milevis, book VI; Victor of Vita, book I, *On the Persecution*; Paulinus of Nola, poem 14, *On Saint Felix*; Jerome, letter to Nepotian; Augustine, book XXII, chapter 8, *On the City of God*; Theodoret, book I, chapter 31, *Ecclesiastical History*; and others.]

it exclaims: “You have prepared a table before me.” David represents her as speaking when he says: “The Lord feeds me, and I shall lack nothing. In a place of pasture he has settled me; beside waters of refreshment he has led me” (Ps. 23:1–2).

And below: “For even if I walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I shall fear no evil, for you are with me. Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me. You have prepared a table before me against those who afflict me. You have anointed my head with oil, and your cup, making drunk—how excellent it is!”

[Note: [Col. 0404D] All editions and a few manuscripts, together with the Hebrew text and the Vulgate, read “and my cup”; many other, much older manuscripts read “and your cup.” So also do the Septuagint and the other versions. Below, the Roman edition alone reads “nor have they entered into the heart of man”; the Arabic version agrees there.]

44. Let us now consider this, lest someone, seeing visible things—for invisible things are not seen and cannot be grasped by human eyes—should perhaps say: God rained manna upon the Jews; he rained quail (Exod. 16:13). But for that beloved Church he has prepared these things of which it is said: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart—what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2:9).

Therefore, lest anyone say this, we wish with the greatest care to prove both that the sacraments of the Church are more ancient than those of the Synagogue and that they are more excellent than the manna.

45. The reading from Genesis that has been expounded teaches their antiquity (Gen. 14:18). For the Synagogue took its beginning from the law of Moses (Exod. 34:1 and following). Abraham, however, was much earlier. After he had defeated his enemies and recovered his own nephew, when he had gained the victory, Melchizedek met him and brought forth the things which Abraham received with reverence.

It was not Abraham who brought them forth, but Melchizedek, who is introduced as being without father, without mother, without beginning of days and without end, made like the Son of God. Concerning him Paul says to the Hebrews: “He remains a priest forever” (Heb. 7 and following). In Latin interpretation he is called “king of righteousness” and “king of peace.”

46. Do you not recognize who this is? Can a man be king of righteousness when he is scarcely righteous himself? Can he be king of peace when he can scarcely be peaceful?

[Note: [Col. 0404D] Some manuscripts read: “since he himself, having been defeated, is righteous”; several others: “since he himself, as king of peace, is scarcely righteous.”]

He is without mother according to his divinity, because he was begotten from God the Father, of one substance with the Father. He is without father according to his incarnation, because he was born from a Virgin. He has neither beginning nor end, because he himself is the beginning and end of all things, the first and the last.

The sacrament you received is therefore not a human but a divine gift, brought forth by him who blessed the father of faith, Abraham, whose grace and deeds you admire.

47. It has been proved that the sacraments of the Church are more ancient; now learn that they are more excellent. Truly,

[Note: [Col. 0404C] The Roman edition begins chapter 9 with these words in the earlier editions. Everyone can see how unsuitable that is. From this point to the end of the work there are so many arguments, and such powerful ones, for proving Christ’s real presence in the sacrament—as it is called—that the most vigorous defenders of Eucharistic truth, Lanfranc, Guitmund, Alger, Peter of Cluny, and others, eagerly strove to draw them out and set them against the rash novelty of Berengar.

Nor did the heterodox exert less effort in attempting to weaken or evade these proofs. Yet the prudent reader will readily detect that their arguments and quibbles are empty, not to say foolish. Consult Cardinal du Perron, *On the Eucharist*, book II, section 14, and volume II of the work *On the Perpetuity of the Faith*, published in the vernacular. There you will read this matter demonstrated so clearly that you will be inclined to affirm that anyone who does not see the faith of the Roman Church expressed in these same testimonies is suffering from no ordinary blindness.]

it is wonderful that God rained manna upon the fathers, and that they were nourished daily by food from heaven. Hence it is said: “Man ate the bread of angels” (Ps. 78:25).

Yet all those who ate that bread died in the desert. But this food which you receive, this living bread which came down from heaven, supplies the substance of eternal life; and whoever eats it will not die forever. It is the body of Christ.

48. Consider now whether the bread of angels is more excellent, or the flesh of Christ, which is certainly the body of life. That manna was from heaven; this is above heaven. That was of heaven; this is of the Lord of heaven. That was subject to corruption if it was kept for another day; this is free from all corruption, so that whoever devoutly tastes it cannot experience corruption.

[Note: [Col. 0404D] In the earlier editions, these words began chapter 9. No one fails to see how inappropriate that is. From this very place to the end of the work there are so many arguments, and arguments so effective, for proving Christ’s real presence in the sacrament, as it is called, that the most vigorous defenders of Eucharistic truth—Lanfranc, Guitmund, Alger, Peter of Cluny, and others—vied with one another in bringing them forth and opposing them to Berengar’s rash novelty. Nor did the heterodox labor less diligently to weaken or evade these proofs. Nevertheless, the prudent reader readily recognizes their arguments and quibbles to be empty, not to say foolish. See Cardinal du Perron, book II, section 14, *On the Eucharist*, and volume II of the work *On the Perpetuity of the Faith*, published in the vernacular. There you will read this point demonstrated so clearly that you will be ready to affirm that anyone who does not see the faith of the Roman Church expressed in these same testimonies is suffering from extraordinary blindness.]

For them water flowed from the rock (Exod. 17:6); for you, blood flows from Christ (John 6:55 and following). The water satisfied them for an hour; the blood washes you forever. The Jew drank and thirsts; when you have drunk, you cannot thirst. The former was in shadow; the latter in truth.

49. If that which you admire is a shadow, how great must this be, whose shadow you also admire! Hear that what took place among the fathers was a shadow: “They drank,” he says, “from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ. But God was not pleased with most of them, for they were struck down in the desert” (1 Cor. 10:4–5).

These things were done in figure for us. You have learned which things are more excellent: light is superior to shadow, truth to figure, and the body of the author to manna from heaven.

## CHAPTER IX

Lest anyone, struck by the outward appearance, waver in faith, it is demonstrated by many examples—through which it is established that nature has been changed or overcome—that true flesh of Christ is made from bread. Finally, the treatise is brought to a close with several matters concerning its effects, the dispositions of those who use it, and related questions, presented figuratively.

50. Perhaps you will say: “I see something else; how do you assert to me that I receive Christ’s body?” This, then, still remains for us to prove.

How many examples, therefore, do we employ! Let us prove that this is not what nature formed, but what blessing consecrated; and that the power of blessing is greater than that of nature, because through blessing nature itself is also changed.

51. Moses was holding a staff; he threw it down, and it became a serpent (Exod. 4:3–4). Again he seized the serpent by the tail, and it returned to the nature of a staff. You see, then, that by prophetic grace the nature both of the serpent and [Col. 0406A] of the staff was changed twice? The rivers of Egypt were flowing with a pure stream of water; suddenly blood began to gush from the veins of the springs, and there was no drink in the rivers (Exod. 7:20 ff.).  

[Note: [Col. 0405D] All editions, and some manuscripts, read “at the prophet’s prayers”; several others, and Lanfrancus with them, “at the prophet’s words”; the oldest of all, “from the prophet’s prayer,” that is, immediately after his prayer had ended.]

Again, at the prophet’s prayer, the blood ceased in the rivers, and the nature of the waters returned. The Hebrew people were hemmed in on every side: on one side surrounded by the Egyptians, on the other shut in by the sea. Moses raised his staff; the water separated and froze in the form of walls, and a road for walking appeared between the waves (Exod. 14:21 ff.). The Jordan, turned backward contrary to nature, returned to the beginning of its source (Josh. 3:16). Is it not clear that the nature either of the sea’s waves or of the river’s course was changed? The people of the fathers were thirsty; Moses touched the rock, and water flowed from the rock. Did grace not operate beyond nature, so that the rock poured forth water which nature had not given it?  

[Note: [Col. 0405D] The old editions, together with not a few manuscripts, read “the river Marah”; the Roman edition alone, “the spring of Marah”; the other, much more numerous manuscripts, as in the text.]

[Col. 0406B] The river Marah was exceedingly bitter, so that the thirsty people could not drink. Moses cast a piece of wood into the water, and the nature of the waters laid aside its bitterness (Exod. 15:23 ff.), which grace, suddenly infused, tempered. In the time of the prophet Elisha, the iron blade of an axe fell from one of the sons of the prophets and immediately sank. The man who had lost the iron asked Elisha for help. Elisha too cast a piece of wood into the water, and the iron floated (2 Kings 6:6). We certainly recognize that this also occurred beyond nature; for the nature of iron is heavier than the fluidity of water.

[Note: [Col. 0405D] “The nature of iron,” that is, the nature and substance of iron. Ambrose himself has already taught above that the word species is sometimes used in this sense.]

52. We therefore observe that grace is of greater power than nature [Col. 0406C]—and yet we continue to count this as the grace of prophetic blessing? If a human blessing had such [Col. 0406C] power that it changed nature (1 Kings 18:38), what shall we say of divine consecration itself, where the very words of the Lord the Savior operate? For this sacrament which you receive is brought about by Christ’s word. If Elijah’s word had such power that it brought fire down from heaven, will Christ’s word not have power to change the species of the elements? You have read of the works of the whole world: “For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. 148:5; De Consecratione, distinction 2, chapter *In quibus*, section *Cujus* [Col. 0407A], clearly). The word of Christ, then, which was able to make from nothing what did not exist, cannot change what exists into what it did not previously exist as? For it is no less to give new things to things than to change natures.

[Note: [Col. 0407C] Thus all editions read, as do all but one or two manuscripts; Algerus likewise reads it this way in book 1 of *On the Sacraments*, chapter 9: “Is it not greater to give new things to things,” and so forth. A little later, however, where the Roman edition, together with several manuscripts and with Lanfrancus, Guitmundus, and Algerus, agrees with our text, the old edition and many more manuscripts omit the word *exemplo* (“by example”); several manuscripts also have *veritate* (“by truth”) instead of *veritatem* (“truth”).]

53. But why do we use arguments? Let us use his own examples, and establish the truth of the mystery by the example of the incarnation. Did the ordinary course of nature precede when the Lord Jesus was born from Mary? If we look for the usual order, a woman joined to a man is accustomed to bear children. It is therefore clear that the Virgin gave birth beyond the order of nature. And this body which we consecrate is from the Virgin. Why do you seek the order of nature in Christ’s body, when the Lord Jesus himself was born from a Virgin beyond nature? It is truly the flesh of Christ that was crucified and buried; therefore it is truly the sacrament of that flesh.

[Col. 0407B] 54. The Lord Jesus himself cries out: “This is my body” (Matt. 26:26). Before the blessing of the heavenly words, one species is named; after the consecration, the body is signified.

[Note: [Col. 0407C] In the Roman edition the word *alia* (“another”) had been deleted, although it is found in the other editions and in all the manuscripts, as also in Guitmundus and Algerus [Col. 0407D]. Conversely, the words *vox Christi* (“the word of Christ”), which appear in all editions and in Algerus before the verb *significatur* (“is signified”), are absent from the manuscripts and from Guitmundus.]

He himself says that it is his blood. Before consecration it is called something else; after consecration it is named blood.

[Note: [Col. 0407D] In the earliest beginnings of the Church, as we learn from the liturgies of Saints James and Mark, it was customary for the canon of the Mass to be recited aloud. After the words of consecration had been pronounced, the people—and in later times, according to the liturgies of Basil and Chrysostom, the choir—responded, “Amen.” Menardus proves that this practice also existed in the Ambrosian Church, in his *On the Sacramentary of St. Gregory*, p. 385, on the authority both of this passage and of another in book 4 of *On the Sacraments*, chapter 5. Cardinal Bona likewise teaches this concerning the Eastern Churches in *On Liturgical Matters*, book 2, chapters 13 and 25, citing in this connection the letter of Dionysius of Alexandria to Pope Sixtus and Tertullian, *On Spectacles*, chapter 25. Their testimonies, however, do not clearly explain whether “Amen” was sung immediately after the consecration or only after other prayers had been recited. Florus’s passage, which the same author cites, is clearer. As for the practice by which individuals receiving the Eucharist responded “Amen,” it is mentioned by the author of the *Apostolic Constitutions*, chapter 13; Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechesis* 5; Augustine, *Sermon to the Newly Baptized*; and the author of *On the Sacraments*, in the books and chapters cited above. It is especially worthy of notice that the faithful, at the very moment when the Lord’s body was either consecrated by the priest or received by them, gave explicit testimony to its true presence. More on these rites may be found both in the writers already mentioned and in Baronius under the year 57, Pamelius, and others.]

And you say, “Amen”—that is, “It is true.” Let what the mouth speaks be acknowledged by the inward mind; let the heart feel what the spoken word expresses.

55. By these sacraments, then, Christ feeds his Church, and by them the substance of souls is strengthened. Rightly, therefore, seeing her progress rich in grace, he says to her: “How beautiful are your breasts, my sister, my bride! How beautiful they have become from wine, and the fragrance of your garments is beyond all spices! Your lips, O bride, drip with honeycomb [Col. 0407C]; honey and milk are under your tongue, and the fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of Lebanon. A garden enclosed is my sister, my bride; a garden enclosed, a sealed spring” (Song 4:10 ff.).

[Note: [Col. 0408D] The old edition, together with many of the better manuscripts, reads *favus distillans* (“a dripping honeycomb”); the Roman edition, with the others, *favum distillant* (“they drip with honeycomb”). The first reading is supported only by the Vulgate, but perhaps scribes adjusted the passage to its form, as anyone can readily detect has often happened in manuscripts.]

This signifies that the mystery ought to remain sealed with you, lest it be violated by the deeds of an evil life and by adultery against chastity; lest it be disclosed to those for whom it is unsuitable; lest it be scattered [Col. 0408A] among the faithless by loquacious chatter. Your guardianship of the faith must therefore be good, so that the integrity of life and silence may remain undefiled.

56. Hence the Church, preserving the height of the heavenly mysteries, drives away from herself the violent storms of the winds and invites the sweetness of springtime grace. Knowing that her garden cannot displease Christ, she calls upon the Bridegroom himself, saying: “Rise up, north wind, and come, south wind; blow upon my garden, and let my perfumes flow” (ibid., 16). “Let my brother come down into his garden and eat the fruit of his fruit trees” (Song 5:1).

[Note: [Col. 0408D] The Roman edition alone reads: “I shall eat my bread . . . I shall drink my wine . . .” The faithful understand why I have said “bread and wine.” The old edition and all the manuscripts read as in the text, except that some prefer *partim dixerunt* (“some said”) and others *partim dixerim* (“some may say”); two have *fideles intelligite* (“understand, faithful ones”); one has *fidelis intelligis* (“you understand, faithful one”).]

For she has good and fruitful trees whose roots have been steeped in the irrigation of the sacred font and which have sprouted into good fruits through the shoot of a new fertility, so that they are no longer cut down by the prophetic axe but are made fruitful by evangelical abundance (Matt. 3:10).

[Col. 0408B] 57. Finally, the Lord, delighted by their fertility, responds: “I have entered my garden, my sister, my bride; I have gathered my myrrh with my spices; I have eaten my food with my honey; I have drunk my drink with my milk” (Song 5:1).

[Note: [Col. 0408D] Some manuscripts read “the fruit of his apples.”]

Why he said “food and drink,” understand, faithful one. There is no doubt that he himself eats and drinks in us, just as you have read that he says he is in prison in us (Matt. 25:36).

58. Therefore, seeing such great grace, the Church urges her children and urges those near at hand to hasten to the sacraments, saying: “Eat, my neighbors, and drink; drink deeply, my brothers” (Song 5:1). What we should eat and drink, the Holy Spirit has expressed elsewhere through the Prophet [Col. 0408C], saying: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet; blessed is the man who hopes in him” (Ps. 33:9).

In that sacrament Christ is present, because it is Christ’s body; it is therefore not bodily food but spiritual food.

[De Consecratione, distinction 2, chapter *In illo sacramento*.]

Hence the Apostle says of its type: “Our fathers ate spiritual food and drank spiritual drink” (1 Cor. 10:3). For the body of God is a spiritual body; the body of Christ is the body of the divine Spirit, because Christ is Spirit, as we read: “Christ the Lord is the Spirit before our face” (Lam. 4:20).

[Note: [Col. 0409A] Several manuscripts of no inferior quality read “because it is the Spirit of Christ.”]

And in Peter’s Epistle we have: “Christ died for us” (1 Pet. 2:21). Finally, this food strengthens our heart, and this drink gladdens the human heart, as the Prophet recalled (Ps. 103:15).

59. Having therefore received everything, let us know that we have been reborn; let us not say, “How have we been reborn? Did we enter into our mother’s womb and were we born again?” I do not recognize here the ordinary operation of nature. But here [Col. 0410A] there is no natural order, where the excellence of grace is present.

Finally, the ordinary course of nature does not always produce generation. We confess that Christ the Lord was generated from a Virgin, and we deny the order of nature. Mary did not conceive from a man; rather, she received him in her womb from the Holy Spirit, as Matthew says: “She was found to be with child from the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 1:18).

[Note: [Col. 0409A] All editions and some manuscripts read “makes regeneration” [Col. 0410A]; the others, which are also the more reliable, read “makes generation.” The latter is better, as the sense itself plainly shows, since what follows is an example not of regeneration but of generation.]

If, then, the Holy Spirit came upon the Virgin, effected conception, and fulfilled the work of generation, there can be no doubt that, coming upon the font—or upon those who receive baptism—he effects the reality of regeneration.

[ON THE SACRAMENTS.]

[Col. 0409]

PREFACE TO THE BOOKS ON THE SACRAMENTS, IN WHICH THE AUTHOR OF THE SAME WORK IS DISCUSSED.

[Col. 0409]

The subject of this work is plainly the same as that of the preceding book *On the Mysteries*. For here there is nothing except sermons by which the bishop instructs the newly baptized in the sacraments they had received on the preceding day, that is, baptism, confirmation, and the Eucharist.

Here you will find only three matters worthy of consideration that are not found in the discussion *On the Mysteries*: namely, in book 3, chapter 1, that the washing of the feet, which had been instituted in his own church, is reported as unfamiliar in the Roman Church; in book 4, chapters 5 and 6, that, so that it might become more plainly known by what words that remarkable transformation of bread into the Lord’s body is effected, he explains the part of the liturgy which we call the canon; and finally, in book 5, chapter 4, he continues the exposition of the Lord’s Prayer, whose explanation he had promised to give them.

Having returned to this subject again toward the end of book 6, chapter 5, he sets forth the rule of prayer, presenting the same Lord’s Prayer and Psalm 8 as models of perfect examples, and explaining individually how one ought to begin, in what order to distinguish the petitions, what to append, what to cite, how to conclude, and for whom to pray (chapter 3).

This final section, where prayer is treated generally, was taken from Ambrose’s work *On the Institution of the Virgin* (chapter 1, no. 7, and chapter 2, no. 8 ff.). Where, however, the author borrowed what is said in book 5, chapter 4, concerning the prayer commended to us by Christ, we entirely fail to discover. Although it is established that our Doctor explained it more than once, this exposition is nevertheless not found among his legitimate surviving works.

In the rest, the author imitates the discussion *On the Mysteries* so closely that, apart from a few ceremonies which he either condenses after Ambrose had treated them at greater length or discusses after Ambrose had omitted them, he generally does little more than expand the arguments and statements of that little book.

But just as he imitated Ambrose, so others have also reproduced him. Thus, in the Appendix to the sermons of Augustine in the new edition, sermon 84 was copied wholly from this work, almost in the same words.

The question of the author of this work has been highly controversial in our own age and in the preceding one. Since, moreover, our institution does not permit us to leave the question undiscussed, we shall examine the matter with such candor that all partisan zeal will be set aside entirely.

We are persuaded of this: whoever may be called the author of these books, Catholic truth will suffer no injury from the matter. For we are certain that, if the writer were pushed back to the seventh century, as Albertinus wishes (*On the Sacrament of the Eucharist*, book 2, p. 509), or even to the eighth, as Dallaeus argues (*On Confirmation*, book 3, chapter 8), we would thereby possess two episcopal witnesses to tradition: Ambrose preaching *On the Mysteries*, and another bishop preaching *On the Sacraments*. Since they would be separated from one another by three or four centuries, they would furnish an argument stronger than all the quibbles of the heterodox.

We shall therefore examine the matter, laying aside every prejudice, just as if the question were now being raised for the first time. To make the procedure clearer, we shall set the arguments and replies of both sides against one another, and add whatever our reading of Ambrosian writings has supplied or whatever we have happened to gather elsewhere concerning this same subject.

Some of the heretics portray both the work itself and its author in extremely lurid and offensive colors. Bullingerus, in his letter to Joachim Vadianus, calls these books stupid and does not hesitate to suggest that Erasmus thought the work to be that of some kind of huckster.

The editor of Coccius’s *Censura*, also describing the books, says: “For in these books there are many falsehoods, some ridiculous things, one unmistakable heresy, and another statement that conflicts with Ambrosian doctrine” (*Helmstedt*, 1655).

Albertinus likewise treats the same author with no gentler hand. In the vast work he compiled *On the Sacrament of the Eucharist*, he writes as follows (book 2, chapter 1, p. 507):

“He is an ape of Ambrose; he teems with barbarisms; he contains many things, some of them ridiculous and wholly unworthy of Ambrosian dignity, some contradictory, some simply false. He draws inept conclusions and pours forth a gross lie. Would Ambrose have spoken so foolishly?”

These are the encomiums bestowed upon our author by those ministers; we present them collected together before the eyes of our readers [Col. 0411]. However much Calvinists may admire Albertinus and his work, we certainly do not think that their more moderate members will approve the excesses of this and similar writers.

For although that minister wishes to appear to have been led to this position by love of the truth alone (ibid., column 1), no one who reads these words can fail to perceive that he was moved by a much more vehement desire to assist his sect in whatever way he could.

If this author were really as he is depicted in that portrait—ignorant, deceitful, absurd in intellect, and ridiculous—what should we conclude about all those great men who for so many centuries attributed the same discussions to our Doctor, when not one of them perceived that the author’s alleged gross lies, serious contradictions, and ridiculous inventions were utterly unworthy of Ambrosian candor, acumen, and judgment?

Should not Albertinus himself have been ashamed that he labored so strenuously to drag into his opinion an author whom he represented not merely as a nobody but, because of so many crimes, as deprived of civil status, if he is to be believed?

He ought plainly and openly to have rejected him. For no one will ever persuade Calvinists that any advantage can come to them from a witness whom they wish to have lied in the Gospel words and who therefore could clearly have lied in the matter of the Eucharist as well.

Yet because even from the mouths of those who most passionately serve their own emotions truth is sometimes uttered, we shall examine Albertinus’s objections—as though they had been proposed with a calm and completely impartial mind. In them he gathered together many of the principal objections of the editor of Coccius, cited above, Rivetus (*Sacred Criticism*, book 3, chapter 18), and others.

Accordingly, he presses the objection drawn from these words, “Therefore at Rome the faithful are called ...,” as follows (book 2, p. 507, column 2): “As though this designation were peculiar to Rome. It was common everywhere—in the East, in the South, in the North, and in the West. Ambrose himself used it at Milan in his genuine writings.”

The distinguished Nathanael Alexander replies (*Ecclesiastical History*, fourth century, part 1, section 2, p. 503) that neither in manuscripts of better quality—such as those he himself was able to consult—nor in the more accurate editions, namely those modeled on the Roman form, is the word *Romae* found.

In the manuscripts where it does occur, he says, this happened because, in some of them, certain readers interpreted the syllable *Rae* as *Romae*, when they should have read it correctly. Nor does anything prevent a diphthong from being written in place of a simple vowel, since interchangeable usage of this kind occurs in written books.

We do not deny that this part of the reply is entirely correct. Indeed, we add that the whole solution receives considerable support from the fact that, in place of *Romae*, three manuscripts—the Vatican, the Regius, and the Thuaneus—read the proper name *recto*; the Roman edition preferred to substitute the adverb *recte*.

Nevertheless, we cannot wholly adopt this opinion because of the number and antiquity of the manuscripts in which the complete word *Romae* appears.

For from the entire multitude whose variants we have collected, apart from the three just mentioned and two others in which the copyist’s error produced *rotome*, sixteen others—including the Benignianus, Remensis, and Claromontanus, all more than eight hundred years old—display the word *Romae* in its proper letters.

Furthermore, we have nowhere found the abbreviation in question in a similar form.

We therefore believe that the same word has been placed here *ἐμφατικῶς* (*emphatikōs*, emphatically), so that more is signified than is expressed. Thus “at Rome the faithful are called” will mean the same as if he had said: “Not only in this or any other Church, but even in the most distinguished of all, those who have been baptized are called faithful.”

Our interpretation is supported also by the conjunction *et* (“and”), which Alexander observed to precede the word *Romae* in several manuscripts and which we have found in many of ours.

The objections Albertinus raises against the exposition of the Lord’s words, “For we must fulfill all righteousness,” as well as against the doctrine concerning secret prayers proposed by the same author (cited place, p. 508, column 1), are so slight that mere inspection of the passages can establish that the author neither draws an inept conclusion nor speaks foolishly, as Albertinus derides him for doing.

More serious, certainly, is the accusation that follows concerning these words: “He pours forth a gross lie, for he says that the Lord did not say in the Lord’s Prayer, ‘Do not lead us into temptation,’ but, ‘Do not permit us to be led into temptation’” (ibid., column 2).

What more serious charge could be brought against a preacher of the Gospel? Yet the accuser was unfortunate in that the blow he aimed and launched with such effort fell entirely ineffectual and useless.

For when he himself acknowledges that Cyprian read the same way—as he adds in that very passage—his statement, “But it is one thing to read in this way and another to affirm that the Lord spoke in this way and no other,” is pure slander.

For when, recalling the prayer instituted by Christ, he expresses its sixth petition in these words, “And do not permit us to be led into temptation,” does he not deny, if not with his mouth, at least abundantly in the thought of his mind, that the same petition was expressed in a different form?

Nor, surely, should this author have been charged with rashness or falsehood, since he had the support of a considerable number of Latin manuscripts, as is evident from Augustine’s authority (*On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 6).

Perhaps someone will object: Since the author elsewhere testifies that he consulted the Greek language (book 5, chapter 4), why did he here either neglect to examine it or disregard what he found upon examination?

Augustine, in the same book cited above, professes that he was unable to find anything in the Greek copies except “Do not bring us into temptation.”

Although this objection may appear somewhat more plausible, the answer is nevertheless straightforward. Augustine is speaking only of the manuscripts that he himself was able to read. What prevents the manuscripts of another province from having this petition differently?

Nor was there any reason for this author to resort to the Greek copies, since the agreement of so many Latin witnesses was entirely sufficient to persuade him.

The same minister, after transcribing at greater length the author’s passage concerning the washing of the feet, adds the following (cited place, p. 508, column 1):

“But in this discussion, apart from the barbarism of the expression”—we admit that there is barbarism in this discussion, but it is Albertinus’s barbarism—“there is first of all falsehood. For who could say that Ambrose followed the type and model of the Roman Church in everything, when it is clear from Augustine that Rome and Milan differed from each other in many ceremonies? [Col. 0413]

“Then there is contradiction. For after saying, ‘In everything I desire to follow the Roman Church,’ he immediately, as though making a recantation—and how Latin this is in the speech of so severe a critic!—says, ‘Yet we too are human beings; therefore, because what is observed elsewhere is more correct, we too observe it correctly.’

“And again, after saying, ‘I say this not because I criticize others,’ he suddenly criticizes them.”

Yet in all this you will find no contradiction if you are willing to interpret the words candidly and according to ordinary human speech.

Who can deny that when he says, “I desire to follow the Roman Church, yet we too are human beings,” the sentence is not simple or absolute, as they call it, but conditional? Accordingly, the words “as far as may be permitted” or “as far as it may seem expedient” must be supplied in thought.

Likewise, in the words that precede—“to follow in everything the type and model of the Roman Church”—there is nothing false, provided one does not distort them from their proper sense, namely, their moral sense.

Finally, the charge that he criticized those whom he had denied criticizing is nothing but empty faultfinding. What is more consistent with common speech than for someone, when unable to repel an accusation from himself unless he transfers it to another, to soften the accusation in the same way?

Let us now consider what answer can be made to this charge. “The author of these books,” Albertinus says (cited place, p. 508, column 2), “follows a version different from the one used by Ambrose.”

We do not deny that this is very true. But, as Alexander aptly replies in the passage cited above, a reading of Saint Ambrose’s works shows that he did not always quote the same passages of Sacred Scripture in the same words.

To this very brief and certain response we need add only this: Since it is beyond doubt that our author wrote without extensive preparation, it should not seem at all surprising if he quoted Scripture not always in its precise wording but in the words that memory supplied to him at the moment.

It is also clear that, since he nowhere used what is called the Vulgate, he must be judged older than the Vulgate, according to Albertinus’s own position.

Finally, they bring forward certain other trifles—for example, that the author plays with empty allegories. But what they call empty allegories are precisely what makes him more closely resemble Ambrose’s manner of expression.

They add that the testimonies which Ratramnus cites as though they came from the work *On the Sacraments* are found only in the little book *On the Mysteries*.

But what if an incomplete manuscript misled him? What if his memory failed? This mistake would certainly have been especially easy because the two treatises are usually joined together in manuscripts.

Finally, they loudly insist that the diversity of style itself reveals and proves a diversity of authors. But this objection is denied to possess any real weight, because “the Fathers use different styles of speaking according to the diversity of their subjects” (Alexander, cited above).

The extent to which this reply may rightly be applied will be considered below. For now, let us hear the champions of the opposing opinion.

First, they produce numerous and very ancient manuscripts written by hand, together with all the printed editions in which these same books were published after the invention of printing.

Then, as an auxiliary force, they bring forward men of the greatest reputation: Hincmarus of Reims, Deoduinus of Liège, Paschasius Radbertus, abbot of Corbie, Ratramnus, a monk of the same monastery, Florus the deacon of Lyon, Lanfrancus, Berengarius, Algerus, Guitmundus, Durandus of Troarn, Hugh of Langres, Ivo of Chartres, Gratian, the Master of the Sentences, and finally all who from the beginning of the ninth century down to our own memory or that of our fathers have mentioned these same books—not even excluding dissenting heterodox writers, apart from a few recent ones.

Although there can be no doubt that this argument is the strongest of all those usually brought forward on the matter, it does not nevertheless establish the conclusion invincibly or necessarily.

How many works, after circulating for a very long time under the name of certain authors, have ultimately been stripped of that attribution—and are stripped of it every day?

Besides, those writers did not themselves investigate the matter independently and deliberately. Some followed one another; others trusted their manuscripts, in which they found the same little work inscribed in one place with the name of Ambrose, and in another joined to a treatise bearing the same title.

For since the oldest manuscripts display no author’s name, those who took the trouble to copy them, knowing that Ambrose had written on this very subject, did not hesitate to assign them to him. Others, although they did not think the works were Ambrosian, nevertheless judged that they should be appended to the book *On the Mysteries* because of the similarity of their subject.

Second, they propose the character of the diction, which they insist is extremely similar in the writing *On the Mysteries* and in this work. Their opponents vigorously deny this.

They do so with good reason. The author attempts to imitate that little book in such a way that he transfers and converts nearly everything into his own style—that is, into a much inferior one.

Yet from this same passage the opponents draw an argument exactly contrary to the one just described. “Who,” they ask, “would find it plausible that Ambrose should reproduce and rework in another book what he had already treated in his discussion *On the Mysteries*?”

Nevertheless, this argument is no stronger or more effective than the other. It is by no means unheard of for the Fathers to explain the same subject in two sermons or books; indeed, we have observed this very thing elsewhere in Ambrose.

The third argument is framed in these words: Augustine testifies that Ambrose published a work *On the Sacraments* (book 2 of *Against Julian*, chapter 5 ff., and *Retractions*, book 2, chapter 4). Therefore, they say, either that work should be produced for us, or it must be admitted that it is the very work under discussion.

The answer is readily available. The subject of the two works is not the same, nor is the title the same. The work mentioned by Augustine was not simply entitled *On the Sacraments*; the title also included *On Philosophy*. Since, according to Augustine’s testimony, it was composed against the Platonists, it is not obscure that a different subject was treated in it.

Finally, certain other points may be brought forward. One might say that the author discusses the weakness of his voice (book 1, chapter 6) and that Ambrose himself complains of the weakness of his voice in the second *Apology for David* (chapter 5, no. 28), while the disciple mentioned above testifies that his voice was easily exhausted (*Confessions*, book 6, chapter 3, no. 3).

One might add that the same author admits (book 6, chapter 5) that he teaches what he himself has not learned—something also quite familiar to Ambrose.

Finally, one might press the exposition of the Lord’s Prayer, which Ambrose’s commentary on Luke demanded, but which was omitted there for no other reason than that he remembered having explained it elsewhere. Since this same prayer is explained in only this one of all the works circulated under Ambrose’s name, why should we not acknowledge that this explanation is his?

The first objection may be answered by observing that, apart from the fact that the other *Apology for David* is probably wrongly attributed to Ambrose, there have been and still are many people who admit, while preaching, that they suffer from weakness of voice and lungs.

Since there are also people who, out of modesty, confess that they are unequal to explaining the subject they have undertaken, the same point provides an answer to the second difficulty.

As for the third, a reply may likewise be made: deny that Ambrose committed to writing everything he pronounced orally, and deny that everything he committed to writing has survived to our time.

Perhaps this may also be added: since the works of Tertullian and Cyprian, Latin Fathers, on that prayer were already available, he was drawn away from this labor as unnecessary, just as Hilary himself testifies concerning his own work in his *Commentary on Matthew*, canon 5.

From the matters we have discussed thus far, two conclusions emerge.

The solutions we have applied to the sectarians’ arguments plainly show that the insults and reproaches which they pour out upon this author in wagonloads prove nothing except that his doctrine is exceedingly troublesome and hateful to them.

On the other hand, the replies we have made to the arguments of the Catholics who vindicate this work for Ambrose show that the negative position is no less probable than the affirmative one. Thus some orthodox writers have not unreasonably remained doubtful on the matter (Cardinal Bona, *On Liturgical Matters*, book 1, chapter 7, no. 4; Arnauld, *On Frequent Communion*, part 1, chapter 13; Hermann, and others).

But so that we do not remain uncertain about everything, we have proposed three matters for investigation at this point: what rank the author possessed, when he lived, and in what region.

The definition of the first question is readily available. It is clear that he was a bishop who instructed the newly baptized and the people entrusted to his care. This rank appears openly everywhere.

Even if there were no other evidence by which it could be proved, that famous passage alone would suffice, namely where he says: “In everything I desire to follow the Roman Church, but we ...” For who would speak in this way except a bishop?

As for the second point, from the authors mentioned it becomes probable that the writer whom we are investigating flourished before the eighth century; but from the Saint Gall manuscript, written in capital letters approximately a thousand years ago—as Mabillon (Museo Italico, p. 7) is our most authoritative witness— it is established that he is even older than the seventh century. Moreover, this same work itself claims a more remote date by arguments of its own. For since it is clear that these sermons were delivered to neophytes—and indeed not to a few, since this bishop calls them both “the many” and “the candidate congregation” (Book V, ch. 3)—one may infer that the custom of baptizing infants had not yet been entirely adopted. And it seems to us that this points to a period not much later than the age of Augustine. Further, he sufficiently intimates (Book VI, chapters 4 and 5) that pagan worship was still flourishing in his diocese at that time. This is also confirmed by the fact that no heretics are refuted except the Arians and those who attacked Christ’s divinity, and by the version used by this author, which sufficiently indicates that the Vulgate had not yet acquired authority everywhere at that time.

Regarding the third question, we determine the matter as follows. It is beyond dispute that the author of these books was not subject to the Roman metropolitan see; nevertheless, it is no less certain that his own see was not far distant from Rome, since he both knew and followed its ceremonies in many respects. Since, moreover, the ceremonies mentioned in this work have a very close affinity both with those of the ancient Gallican Church and with those of Milan, we infer that his diocese was adjacent to both. We shall not, however, object if anyone prefers, with the very learned scholar Hermann (Vitae Ambrosianae elucidatio, p. 30), to attribute these same sermons to Venerius or to some other disciple of Ambrose who presided over the Church of Milan not long after him. We add only this: from what the author records about Holy Communion—namely, that among both the eastern peoples and his own people it was customary to receive it only once each year (Book V, ch. 4)—one may prudently conclude that he certainly lived after the time of Chrysostom, but before the Roman order and ceremonies were received in the West.

Nevertheless, the following considerations chiefly prevent us from giving our full support to those who attribute this work to Ambrose. First, there is a difference in expression. Although we recognize that authors vary their style and that, according to the subject and the occasion, they sometimes raise it and sometimes lower it, the author’s character nevertheless always appears and, as it were, intermittently shines through. A writer accustomed to noble and elegant diction never lowers himself to the level of those cold and childish questions that are occasionally scattered through this work; Ambrose did not do so in his book *On the Mysteries*, although the subject is the same. It must also be added that we do not think Ambrose would have imitated his own books so slavishly. For this entire commentary was drawn almost wholly from the earlier work *On the Mysteries*, and partly also from the book *On the Institution of Virginity* (ch. 1, no. 7, and ch. 2, no. 8). We add, too, that the Milanese are nowhere censured by the holy bishop in his certain books for receiving Communion so infrequently. Finally, the fact that the author attacks the Roman Church so vehemently over the washing of the feet does not seem to us at all characteristic of the Ambrosian discipline. We know that Ambrose wished the usages and rites of each Church to remain so free to it that, wherever he happened to arrive, he adapted himself to that Church, as Augustine reports (*Letter* 54, formerly 118).

[Col. 0417] Nevertheless, since we do not wish to detract in this matter from anyone’s opinion, and since we are not unaware that many would be displeased if a writing regarded for so long, by almost universal agreement, as Ambrosian were deprived of its customary place, we have been all the more inclined to preserve it in its order and possession because, having been composed from Ambrose’s opinions and, for the most part, even from his words, it is at least for that reason not unworthy to be numbered among the Ambrosian works.

It is clear, moreover, that these six books are six sermons, one of which the Author delivered on each day. For he repeatedly says that he spoke on the previous day or would speak on the following day. Beginning on the Tuesday after Easter Sunday, he continued in this manner through the octave of the same feast. For at the end of Sermon 4 (ch. 6) he promises that he will address those who remained on the following day, Saturday, and on Sunday—namely, Low Sunday, *in albis*. But if anyone prefers to follow the authority of the Saint Gall manuscript, which divides the last book into two, it will be necessary to say that the first sermon was delivered on the Monday after Easter. Since that division seems rather inconvenient—for by it a new book is formed from only a few verses of Book VI, beginning with the words “Another matter, David’s Psalms,” and so forth—we think that its scribe was guided by nothing other than understanding the words “on the following day, Saturday” as referring to two days, whereas he would have understood them more correctly as referring to a single day by apposition, or rather by a grammatical ellipsis. It may also have resulted from this that a sermon numbered 247 in the new edition of Augustine’s works, printed under the name of Ivo of Chartres, although one of the manuscripts in our library attests that it too is Ivo’s, was placed in the Alnetine manuscript (the Alnetine Monastery of the Cistercian Order), under the title of Book VII *On the Sacraments*, after these sermons of ours. It is also not far from the truth that those by whom these sermons were copied intended to assign one to each day through the octave, omitting only Easter Sunday because its solemnity made it more occupied. Nor does it seem to have arisen from any other cause that in several manuscripts *On the Mysteries* is called the First Book *On the Sacraments*; that which is actually the First Book *On the Sacraments* is demoted to the second position, and so forth.

[Col. 0417]

SIX BOOKS OF SAINT AMBROSE, BISHOP OF MILAN, ON THE SACRAMENTS (C, G, S)*

[Col. 0417]

BOOK ONE.

349 CHAPTER ONE.

[Col. 0417A]

After announcing that he will speak about the sacraments, whose explanation ought not to have been given beforehand, he proceeds to the mystery of the opening, which he teaches was signified by Christ in the healing of the deaf and mute man.

1. I begin my discourse on the sacraments which you have received, the explanation of which ought not to have been given beforehand; for in a Christian man faith comes first. That is why those who have been baptized are called “the faithful” at Rome; and our father Abraham was justified by faith, not by works (Rom. 4:3). Therefore you received baptism; you believed. For it would be impious for me to think otherwise. You would not have been called to grace unless Christ had judged you worthy of his grace.

[Note: [Col. 0417B] Some more recent manuscripts read *whose reason*; the Roman edition has *the reason for this*; the remaining manuscripts and editions have *whose reason*. This is not wrong, for *ratio* is often used for the thing itself, and the meaning is therefore the same as if one read, “the discourse which ought not to have been given,” or, as some manuscripts have it, “which I did not think should be given,” and so forth. Consequently, the latest Paris edition restored: “For in a Christian man the best thing is faith,” instead of what is found in the other manuscripts and in all the other editions: “For in a Christian man faith comes first.” These words clearly indicate that the habit of supernatural faith is first infused in baptism. Finally, concerning what follows—“Therefore at Rome also the faithful,” and so forth—it has already been discussed in the Preface, which should be consulted.]

[Col. 0417B] 2. What, then, did we do on Saturday? The opening, of course: the mysteries of the opening were celebrated when the priest touched your ears and nostrils. Our Lord Jesus Christ signifies this in the Gospel when a deaf and mute man was brought to him and he touched his ears and his mouth: his ears because he was deaf, his mouth because he was mute, and he said, “Ephphatha” (Mark 7:34). This is a Hebrew word which in Latin means “Be opened.” Therefore the priest touched your ears so that your ears might be opened to the discourse and address of the priest.

3. But you say to me: Why the nostrils? There, because the man was mute, he touched his mouth, so that, since he could not speak the heavenly mysteries, he might receive a voice from Christ. But there it was because the person was a man; here, because women are baptized, and a servant does not possess the same purity as the Lord—for since he grants sins, whereas sins are forgiven to this one, what comparison can there be?—therefore, on account of the grace of the work and gift [*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter “Propter gloriam”], the bishop does not touch the mouth but the nostrils,

[Note: [Col. 0418B] Here the edition and Gratian repeat: “Why the nostrils?”; but without manuscript support.]

so that you may receive the good odor of eternal piety and say: “For we are the good odor of Christ to God,” as the holy Apostle said (2 Cor. 2:15); and may there be in you a fragrance full of faith and devotion.

CHAPTER TWO.

He explains the anointing of the Christian athlete. In order to stir him to preserve the faith of his renunciation, he magnifies the dignity of the witnesses in whose presence it was made; finally, he illuminates the matter by an example.

4. You came to the font [*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter “Venisti ad fontem”]; you entered. Consider whom you saw; consider what you said; repeat it carefully. A deacon met you, a presbyter met you.

[Note: [Col. 0419D] This anointing is not mentioned in the little book *On the Mysteries*.]

You were anointed like Christ’s athlete, like one who was about to engage in the struggle of this age, and you professed the contests of your struggle. Whoever struggles has something to hope for: where there is a contest, there is a crown. You struggle in this world, but you are crowned by Christ; and for the contests of this world you are crowned? For although the reward is in heaven, the merit of the reward is stored up here.

[Note: [Col. 0419D] Gill in the margin, the Roman edition in the body of the text, and a few manuscripts read “the merit of the reward is gathered.”]

5. When he asked you, “Do you renounce the devil and his works?” what did you answer? “I renounce.” “Do you renounce the world and its pleasures?” what did you answer? “I renounce.” Remember your words, and never let the sequence of your pledge slip from you. If you give a written bond to a man, you are held liable to repay his money; you are bound by an obligation, and the lender binds you even when you resist. If you refuse,

[Note: [Col. 0419D] This is found in the Gill and Roman editions and in the majority of the more authoritative manuscripts; in the remaining editions and manuscripts, the words “if you refuse, you go to the judge” are omitted.]

you go to the judge, and there you are convicted by your own bond.

[Col. 0419C] 6 and 7. Consider where you made your promise, and to whom you made it. You saw a deacon, but he is Christ’s minister. You saw him minister before the altars. Therefore your written bond is held not on earth but in heaven. Consider where you receive the heavenly sacraments. If this is Christ’s body, angels also are stationed here. “Where the body is, there the eagles will be,” you have read in the Gospel (Matt. 24:28). Where Christ’s body is, there eagles are accustomed to fly, so that they may flee earthly things and seek heavenly things. Why do I say this? Because all human beings who proclaim Christ are angels and seem to be enrolled in the place of angels. How so?

[Note: [Col. 0419D] Codex Claromontanus: “Understand: John was the Baptist, born of a man.”]

Consider the case of the Baptist. John was born of a man and a woman; yet hear that he too is an angel: “Behold, I send my angel before your face, and he will prepare your way before you” (Matt. 11:10). Consider another passage from the prophet Malachi:

[Note: [Col. 0419D] Most manuscripts have “Malachiel”; some, but more recent ones, read “the prophet Malachiel says.”]

“For the lips of the priest guard knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth; for he is the angel of the almighty God” (Mal. 2:7). These things are said in order that we may proclaim the glory of the priesthood, not that anything should be claimed on the basis of personal merits.

8. Therefore you have renounced the world; you have renounced this age. Be vigilant. Whoever owes money always considers his bond; and you, who owe faith to Christ, preserve the faith, which is far more precious than money. For faith is an eternal inheritance, whereas money is temporary. Therefore always remember what you promised, and you will be more cautious. If you keep your promise, you will keep your bond.

[Note: [Col. 0419D] When we know God through faith only obscurely and, as Paul says, “in part,” and when, according to the same Apostle, what is “in part” must be brought to an end, how can faith be called an eternal inheritance? The answer is straightforward. Faith contains two things within itself: knowledge and obscurity. The latter is certainly to be expelled when the clear and intuitive vision, as it is called, arrives. But knowledge will not be destroyed; rather, it will be perfected by the addition of beatific light. This is sufficiently shown by the example proposed in the same place, namely 1 Corinthians 13, where a child who has put away the faults of childhood finally attains mature perfection.]

CHAPTER III.

[Col. 0420B]

Although the neophytes saw only the font and the ministers, the author shows that the greater realities are those which are not seen.

9. Then you came closer: you saw the font, and you saw the priest above the font. Nor can I doubt that what happened to the Syrian Naaman fell into your minds as well (2 Kings 5:11 ff.), because although he was cleansed, he first hesitated. Why? I shall tell you; listen.

10. You entered; you saw water; you saw the priest; you saw the deacon. Lest someone should say, “Is this the whole thing?” Indeed, it is the whole thing. Truly the whole thing, where there is complete innocence, complete piety, complete grace, complete sanctification. You saw what you could see with the eyes of your body and with human sight; you did not see those things which produce their effects,

[Note: [Col. 0420D] Some manuscripts read “which work,” rather than “which produce their effects”; but “which are seen” is also found.]

because they are not seen. The things that are not seen are much greater than those that are seen, because the things that are seen are temporary, while the things that are not seen are eternal (2 Cor. 4:18).

CHAPTER IV.

The sacraments of Christians are more divine and more ancient than those of the Jews; and here he discusses the meaning of the word “Passover.”

11. Let us therefore begin. Hold me to the pledge of my word and demand its fulfillment. We admire the mysteries of the Jews which were given to our fathers, outstanding first in the antiquity of their sacraments and then in their holiness.

[Note: [Col. 0420D] This is how some manuscripts of better quality read. Among them, however, the Claromontanus manuscript has “outstanding in holiness besides”; the others and the old edition have “first in the antiquity of the sacraments, then outstanding in holiness.” Since no intelligible meaning could be expressed by this—what could “the antiquity of outstanding sacraments” mean?—the Roman edition attached to the word “outstanding” the phrase “the word of virtues,” with little greater success. Consequently, where all editions have *praemitto* (“I put forward”), the manuscripts more appropriately read *promitto* (“I promise”).]

I promise that the sacraments of Christians are more divine and more ancient than those of the Jews.

[Col. 0421A] 12. What is more remarkable than that the Jewish people passed through the sea? Let us speak for the moment about baptism. Yet all the Jews who passed through it died in the desert. But whoever passes through this font

[Note: [Col. 0421C] Erasmus and the editions that followed read, “passes from earthly things to heavenly things; for this is the Passover, that is, the passage.” Gratian likewise has this, except that for *transit* he reads *transitus est*, “it is the passage.” Amerbach and all the manuscripts, however, have the reading in the text.]

passes from earthly things to heavenly things. For this is the passage—therefore it is called Passover (*pascha*), that is, his passage: a passage from sin to life, from guilt to grace, from defilement to sanctification. Whoever passes through this font does not die but rises again.

CHAPTER V.

In the story of the leper Naaman, the water that possesses Christ’s grace is shown to be the only water that heals. Christ wished to be baptized solely for our sake. Therefore the Holy Spirit, appearing in the form of a dove, did not descend upon him until he had entered the water of the Jordan; and he explains how the whole Trinity was present there.

13. Naaman was therefore a leper. A certain girl said to his wife, “If my lord wishes to be cleansed, let him go to the land of Israel; there he will find one who can remove his leprosy.” She told this to her mistress, and the wife told her husband, Naaman, king of Syria, who sent him, as one especially dear to him, to the king of Israel. The king of Israel heard that he had been sent to him so that he might cleanse his leprosy, and he tore his garments. Then the prophet Elisha sent word to him: “Why have you torn your garments, as though there were no God able to cleanse a leper? Send him to me.” He sent him. When Naaman arrived, the prophet said to him:

[Note: [Col. 0421C] The edition reads, “Go down into the Jordan.”]

“Go into the Jordan, immerse yourself, and you will be healed.”

14. He began to think to himself and say: “Is this the whole thing? I came from Syria to the land of Judea, and I am told: ‘Go and descend into the Jordan, immerse yourself, and you will be healed,’ as though there were not better rivers in my own country.” His servants therefore said to him: “Master, why do you not obey the prophet’s word? Do it, rather, and put it to the test.” Then he went to the Jordan, immersed himself, and rose up healed (2 Kings 5:1 ff.).

15. What, then, does this signify? You saw water, but not every water heals;

[Note: [Col. 0421C] Water is a work; the operation is that of the Holy Spirit. This was absent from the ancient editions and from not a few manuscripts, but was restored in the Roman edition and is found in more manuscripts. Here *opus* means the natural thing, or element; elsewhere it more commonly signifies the effect.]

water heals when it possesses Christ’s grace. One thing is the element, another the consecration; one thing is the work, another the operation. Water is the work; the operation is that of the Holy Spirit. Water does not heal unless the Spirit descends and consecrates that water, just as you have read that when our Lord Jesus Christ was giving the form of baptism, he came to John, and John said to him: “I ought to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?” Christ answered him: “Allow it now. For thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness” (Matt. 3:14–15). See that all righteousness has been established in baptism.

[Note: [Col. 0421C] We said above in the Preface that this is one of the passages used by the minister Albertinus to prove that the book should be attributed to someone other than Ambrose. After reporting this very interpretation of the Lord’s answer, he adds: “But the true Ambrose, when considering this same answer in various places, does not draw such a foolish conclusion.” To prove this, he points to several passages, including this one from *Apology of David*, chapter 8: “Therefore he hastens with complete purpose toward that perfection in which all righteousness is fulfilled, which is the sacrament of baptism . . . but after Christ had been baptized . . . all righteousness was fulfilled.” Yet observe how foolishly he argues with a few manuscripts when he tries to force a distinction between the two passages.]

[Col. 0422B] 16. Why, then, did Christ descend, unless so that this flesh might be cleansed—the flesh which he assumed from our condition? For Christ did not need the washing away of his own sins, since he committed no sin; but it was necessary for us, who remain subject to sin. Therefore, if baptism was for our sake, its form was established for us and the pattern of our faith was set before us.

[Note: [Col. 0421D] Gill in the margin and the Roman edition in the body of the text have “the abolition of sins.” But shortly afterward, where all the editions have “the form of baptism has been established,” the manuscripts prefer *baptismum* (“baptism”); more recent manuscripts have *baptismus*. We have retained “its form has been established.” Here “form” seems to mean the manner and order of celebrating the sacrament, as also below in no. 18.]

17. Christ descended; John stood by baptizing; and behold, the Holy Spirit descended as a dove. It was not a dove that descended, but something like a dove. Remember what I said: Christ assumed flesh, not something like flesh, but the reality of this flesh; Christ assumed true flesh. The Holy Spirit, however, descended from heaven not in the reality of a dove but in the form of a dove. Therefore John saw and believed.

[Note: [Col. 0422C] The edition, together with not a few manuscripts, reads “Christ truly assumed flesh”; some of these omit “flesh”; the remaining manuscripts give “true flesh.” Again, immediately afterward, where the editions and many manuscripts read “in the form of a dove, not in the reality of a dove but in the form,” several others, and those of better age, have the reading found in the text. The statements made here about the Lord’s flesh are absent from the treatise *On the Mysteries* and seem to be directed against certain heretics who denied its reality. Since it is likely that the ancient disciples of Cerdo and Marcion had already died out—those to whom, as may be learned from Tertullian, *On the Prescription against Heretics*, chapter 5, *On the Flesh of Christ*, chapter 1, *Against Marcion*, and elsewhere, a phantom flesh was attributed—we may believe that the Author perhaps alludes to the Manichaeans, or rather to the Priscillianists. For Pope Leo the Great testifies in his *Letter* 15, chapter 4, of the new edition, that they survived until his time and held the same madness concerning the Lord’s flesh as those ancient heresiarchs.]

[Col. 0422C] 18. Christ descended, and the Holy Spirit also descended [*De Consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter “Per aquam,” section “Descendit”]. Why did Christ descend first and the Holy Spirit afterward, when the form and practice of baptism require that the font first be consecrated and then the one who is to be baptized descend? For as soon as the priest enters, he performs the exorcism

[Note: [Col. 0422D] All editions and some manuscripts read: “he performs, secondly over the creature of the water, an invocation afterward,” and so forth. Many more manuscripts have: “he performs an invocation over the creature of the water a second time”; some have “through an invocation,” and so forth. The remaining manuscripts, although fewer, more appropriately have the reading in the text. It is clear that the cause of the variation lay in the adverb *secundum*, which in not a few codices was incorrectly abbreviated by an arithmetical sign. Here *secundum* is neither an adverb of number nor of order, but simply of place; it means precisely “nearby” or “next to,” as children know. In the baptismal ceremonies mentioned here, the account does not always agree with the *Sacramentary of Saint Gregory* or with the Gothic missal, but comes closer to the old Gallican missal and likewise to the Gallican *Sacramentary* published by Mabillon. We have already said something about this in the Preface to these books.]

over the creature of the water, and afterward offers invocation and prayer, so that the font may be sanctified and the presence of the eternal Trinity may be present. But Christ descended first, and the Spirit followed. Why? So that the Lord Jesus would not appear to need the mystery of sanctification, but that he himself would sanctify, and the Spirit would also sanctify.

19. Christ therefore descended into the water, and the Holy Spirit descended like a dove (Matt. 3:16). God the Father also spoke from heaven. You have the presence of the Trinity.

CHAPTER VI.

It is demonstrated, by adapting each of its elements, that the figure of baptism preceded in the Red Sea. The same is also shown more briefly in the Flood; after the first sermon has been concluded, the next is promised.

[Col. 0423B] 20. The Apostle says that the figure of this baptism existed in the Red Sea: “For our fathers were all baptized in the cloud and in the sea” (1 Cor. 10:1–2). And he added: “All these things happened to them as a figure” (ibid., 6)—as a figure to them, but in reality to us. At that time Moses held the staff; the Jewish people were shut in; the Egyptian was pressing upon them with weapons on one side,

[Note: [Col. 0423C] “And on the other side” is missing from all editions and from not a few manuscripts; we have restored these words from many other codices.]
