and on the other side the Hebrews were enclosed by the sea. They could neither cross the sea nor retreat before the enemy, and they began to murmur (Exod. 14:21 ff.).

21. Observe: do not be offended because their prayer was heard. Although the Lord heard them, those who murmured were nevertheless not free from guilt. When you are hemmed in, it is your task to believe that you will escape, not to murmur; to invoke and ask, not to give voice to complaint.

[Col. 0423C] 22. Moses held the staff and led the Hebrew people: at night in a pillar of light, by day in a pillar of cloud. What is light except truth, since it pours forth clear and full illumination?

[Note: [Col. 0424C] Some manuscripts have “open and plain.”]

What is the pillar of light except the Lord Christ, who drove away the darkness of unbelief and infused the human affections with the light of truth and spiritual grace? But the pillar of cloud is the Holy Spirit. The people were in the sea, and the pillar of light went before them; then the pillar of cloud followed, as though it were the shadow of the Holy Spirit. You see that through the Holy Spirit and through water he displayed the type of baptism.

23. In the Flood, too, there was already a figure of baptism, although the mysteries of the Jews did not yet exist.

[Note: [Col. 0424C] All editions and most manuscripts read: “Thus the form of this baptism preceded. You see, therefore,” and so forth; but the most ancient manuscripts agree with us.]

If, then, the figure of this baptism preceded, you see how much earlier the Christian mysteries were than those of the Jews.

24. But for the moment, in view of the weakness of our voice and the limitation of time, let it be enough today to have taken a taste of the mysteries of the sacred font. Tomorrow, if the Lord grants me the power or opportunity to speak, I shall explain them more fully. It is necessary that your holiness have attentive ears and a more ready mind, so that you may be able to retain what we can gather from the sequence of Scripture and communicate to you, and so that you may possess the grace of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. To this Trinity belongs an everlasting kingdom, from age to age, now and always, and for ever and ever.

[Note: [Col. 0424C] This complaint about the weakness of his voice seems indeed, as was said in the Preface, to give some support to those who seek to ascribe these books to Ambrose. Yet it tells no little against them that this author, shortly below and in Book VI, chapter 5, addressing his hearers, says: “Your holiness [must have] ears,” and so forth. They will not easily prove this form of address Ambrosian, any more than the clipped questions scattered throughout.]

BOOK TWO.

[Col. 0423]

355. CHAPTER ONE.

[Col. 0423D]

He resumes his explanation of the Flood, in which he asserts that true baptism was prefigured; he adds a few remarks about other baptisms.

1. Yesterday we began to discuss how the figure of baptism also preceded in the Flood.

[Note: [Col. 0423D] Only the Roman edition reads “to discuss in a sermon.” For the sense is no worse if one supplies “on the previous day” than “in a sermon.”]

What is the Flood (Gen. 7:23) except that in it the just man is preserved as seed for righteousness, while sin dies?

[Note: [Col. 0424D] Not a few manuscripts have “the sinner dies.” Below they have only “the mind of the just.”]

Therefore, when the Lord saw the sins of human beings multiplying, he preserved the just man alone with his offspring; and he commanded the water to rise even above the mountains. Thus in that Flood all corruption of the flesh perished, while only the lineage and form of the just man remained. Is this not the Flood which is baptism, by which all sins are washed away, while only the mind and grace of the just person are raised again?

2. There are many kinds of baptism, but there is one baptism, the Apostle cries (Eph. 4:5). Why? There are baptisms of the nations, but they are not baptisms. They are washings; they cannot be baptisms. The flesh is washed, but guilt is not washed away; rather, in that washing it is contracted. There were also Jewish baptisms (Mark 7:8), some superfluous, others figurative. The figure itself benefits us because it announces the truth.

CHAPTER II.

He explains the Probatica Pool, stirred by an angel and restoring health to the first person who descended into it; he also explains the paralytic’s answer to Christ.

3. What was read yesterday?

[Note: [Col. 0425D] No liturgy or sacramentary records this Gospel reading as customarily recited during the octave of Easter. It may nevertheless perhaps be indicated in the book *On the Mysteries*, where it says: “Therefore it was said to you that the angel of the Lord descended,” and so forth. But this may have been a special practice of certain Churches, or these words may have been inserted into some baptismal prayer. In that case it would have to be said that this same sermon was delivered on Easter Day; the opinion may be supported by the heading in the Gallican codex: “Here begins the first day at Easter.”]

“The angel,” he says, “descended into the pool at a certain time, and whenever the angel descended, the water was stirred; and whoever descended first was healed of whatever illness afflicted him” (John 5:4).

[Note: [Col. 0425D] The old edition and most manuscripts read: “This signifies the figure of the Lord who was to come,” while several others have: “This was done as a figure of the coming Lord,” and so forth. The latter reading is not entirely unacceptable, provided that *figura* is taken in the ablative and *ventura* in the plural accusative. The Roman edition, however, changed the meaning in this way: “This was done as a figure of our Lord Jesus Christ who was to come,” giving a clear sense. Nevertheless, the authority and number of the manuscripts lead us to prefer the ancient reading and interpret it in the same manner as the edition: it signifies, or, as the edition has it, it signified, a figure of the Lord who was to come—as though it read, “which signified the coming presence of our Lord.” For figure and appearance are often confused with one another, and *species* may be taken for the thing itself, or for the outward appearance of a thing; this we have noted above from Ambrose and can establish from various passages of Scripture. It should not, however, be concealed that one Vatican codex has “a figure of the one who was to come,” and so forth, which is not inappropriate.]

4. Why an angel? For he is the Angel of great counsel (Isa. 9:6). “At a certain time”—the time reserved for the final hour—so that at the very setting of the sun he might catch the day and delay its setting. Whenever, therefore, the angel descended, the water was stirred. Perhaps you say: Why is it not stirred now? Hear why: signs are for unbelievers, faith for believers (1 Cor. 14:22).

5. Whoever descended first was healed of every infirmity. Who is first: first in time or first in honor? Understand both. If first in time, the one who descended first was healed before the others—that is, from the Jewish people rather than from the nations. If first in honor, the one who descended first—that is, the one who possessed fear of God, zeal for righteousness,

[Note: [Col. 0426D] Some manuscripts have “the love of grace.”]

the grace of charity, and an inclination toward chastity—was healed more fully. Yet at that time only one person was healed; at that time, I say, in the figure, only the one who descended first was cured. How much greater is the grace of the Church, in which all who descend are saved?

6. But observe the mystery. Our Lord Jesus Christ came to the pool, where many sick people were lying. It was easy for many sick people to lie there, since only one was healed. Then he said to the paralytic: “Descend.” He replied: “I have no man” (John 5:7).

[Note: [Col. 0426D] Some manuscripts have: “He said to the paralytic, ‘Do you wish to be healed?’ But he replied, ‘I have no man,’” and so forth. We said in the Preface that an objection against the author of this work has been constructed from this passage; the Preface should be consulted.]

See where you are baptized. From where does baptism come, except from Christ’s cross, from Christ’s death? There is the whole mystery, because he suffered for you. In him you are redeemed; in him you will be saved.

7. “I have no man,” he says—that is, because “by a man came death, and by a man the resurrection of the dead” (1 Cor. 15:21). He could not descend; he could not be saved, because he did not believe that our Lord Jesus had assumed flesh from the Virgin. But this man, who was awaiting the mediator between God and human beings, the man Jesus Christ, expecting the one of whom it was said, “And the Lord will send a man who will save them” (Isa. 19:20), said: “I have no man.” And therefore he deserved to attain healing because he believed in the one who was coming. Yet he would have been better and more perfect if he had believed that the one he hoped would come had already come.

CHAPTER III.

[Col. 0426B] After recounting certain details from the story of Naaman, he briefly touches on several other figures of the same sacrament.

8. Now consider the individual elements. We said that the figure preceded in the Jordan, when that leper Naaman was cleansed. What was that little girl from among the captives (2 Kings 5:5) except one who bore the appearance of the Church and represented its figure? The people of the nations were captive—captive, I do not mean in the captivity established under some hostile people,

[Note: [Col. 0426D] Some manuscripts have “placed under a hostile people”; the rest and all editions have the reading in the text, except that in the Roman edition the word *populo* was corrupted.]

but the captivity I mean is the greater one: when the devil, with his cruel dominion, rules over his own, and subjects the necks of sinners to himself as captives.

9. Therefore you have one baptism: another in the Flood; a third kind when the fathers were baptized in the Red Sea; a fourth kind in the pool, when the water was stirred. Now I ask you whether you ought to believe that the presence of the Trinity exists in this baptism, in which baptism is administered in the Church.

[Note: [Col. 0426D] The Claromontanus manuscript has “in which Christ baptizes”; some others have “in which the Church baptizes.”]

CHAPTER IV.

The Author sets forth two other figures of baptism: in the iron that floated at Elisha’s prayer, and in the spring that was made sweet when wood was thrown into it.

10. Thus our Lord Jesus Christ himself says to the Apostles in his Gospel: “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19). This is the word of the Savior.

11. Tell me, O man! Elijah called down fire from heaven, and fire came down from heaven (3 Kings 18:38). [Col. 0427A] Elisha invoked the name of the Lord, and from the water the iron of the ax, which had sunk, rose up (4 Kings 6:6). Behold another kind of baptism. Why? Because every person before baptism is pressed down and submerged like iron; but once baptized, he is lifted up not like iron, but like a lighter piece of fruitful wood. Here too, then, there is another figure. The ax was used to cut wood. The ax-head fell from its handle—that is, the iron was submerged. The prophet’s son did not know what to do; but he knew only that he should ask the prophet Elisha and seek a remedy. Then Elisha threw in a piece of wood, and the iron was lifted up. Do you see, then, that in the cross of Christ the weakness of all human beings is lifted up?

12. There is another example, even though we are not keeping the order—for who could comprehend all the deeds of Christ?—as the apostles said (John 21:25). When Moses had come into the desert, the people were thirsty, and they came to the spring of Merrha and wanted to drink its water: when they first drew it, they sensed its bitterness and began to be unable to drink. Therefore Moses threw a piece of wood into the spring, and the water, which had previously been bitter, began to grow sweet (Exodus 15:23 ff.).

[Note: [Col. 0427D] Nearly all the manuscripts have this wording: “and wanted to drink the water: when they first drew it, they sensed its bitterness and began,” etc. The editions, however, read “and wanted to drink the water, and when he first drew it, he sensed its bitterness, and he began,” etc. Hence the Roman edition removed the final “and.” Below, where the same phrase was alone liable to corruption, it added “Marath” after “the spring.”]

13. What does this signify except that, since every creature is subject to corruption, water is bitter to everyone? Even if it is sweet for a time, even if it is pleasant for a time, it is nevertheless bitter, because it cannot take away sin. Once you have drunk, you will thirst; once you have begun to experience the sweetness of the drink, you will again feel bitterness. The water is therefore bitter; but when you receive the cross of Christ, when you receive the heavenly sacrament, it begins to be sweet and pleasant—and rightly sweet, because in it guilt is recalled.

[Note: [Col. 0427D] Several manuscripts read “in which guilt is cut away”; the others and the old edition have the reading in the text, except that some corruptly have “in the water” or “into the water” instead of “in which.” The Roman edition, instead of “is recalled,” printed “is devoured.”]

If baptisms were so powerful merely in figure, how much more powerful is baptism in reality?

### CHAPTER V

He gathers from what precedes that the Trinity is present at the priest’s prayer, and confirms this from the bodily figures by which the Holy Spirit is said to have descended upon Christ and the disciples.

14. Let us consider this, then. The priest comes, says a prayer at the font, invokes the name of the Father, and the presence of the Son and the Holy Spirit; he uses heavenly words.

[Note: [Col. 0427D] Not a few manuscripts read “heavenly words, which belong to Christ”; the others and the old editions have the wording in the text, while the Roman edition has “heavenly.” [Col. 0428D] What are the heavenly words? They are Christ’s words: that we baptize “in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” In the ancient reading nothing need be changed except the punctuation, which may nevertheless be retained, provided that the verb “are” is supplied once in this form: “The heavenly words are those which belong to Christ,” etc.]

What are the heavenly words? They are Christ’s: that we baptize in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. If, then, at the word and invocation of a human being the presence of the Trinity was present, how much more is it present where the eternal Word is at work? Do you wish to know that the Spirit descended? You heard that he descended “like a dove” (Matthew 3:16).

[Note: [Col. 0428D] The editions read: “Hear that he came down as if,” etc.]

Why “like a dove”? So that unbelievers might be called to faith. At the beginning there had to be a sign; later there must be perfection.

15. Take another example. After the death of our Lord Jesus Christ, the apostles were in one place and were praying on the day of Pentecost. Suddenly there was a great sound, as though the Spirit were being carried along with mighty force, and tongues appeared, divided like fire (Acts 2:2–3).

[Note: [Col. 0428D] Some manuscripts add “after the Lord’s ascension,” etc.]

What does this signify except the descent of the Holy Spirit, who wished to reveal himself bodily even to unbelievers—that is, bodily through a sign, spiritually through the sacrament? Thus his coming received a manifest testimony; but for us the privilege of faith is now conferred, because at the beginning signs were given to unbelievers, whereas for us, now in the fullness of the Church, the truth must be grasped not by a sign but by faith.

[Note: [Col. 0428D] The old edition and some manuscripts read not “not by signs, but by faith”; the Roman edition has “not by signs but by faith.” Several manuscripts more correctly read “not by a sign,” etc.; this is also the conjecture of Latinius.]

### CHAPTER VI

When the sentence of death had been pronounced upon human beings on account of sin, he asserts that baptism was devised in order to raise them again.

16. Let us now discuss what is meant by the term baptism. You came to the font, descended into it, and saw the high priest, the Levites, and the presbyter in the font. What is baptism?

17. In the beginning our God made the human being so that, if he did not taste sin, he would not die by death. He contracted sin, became liable to death, and was expelled from paradise. But the Lord, wishing his benefits to endure and to abolish all the serpent’s snares, and also to undo everything that had caused harm, first pronounced the sentence upon the human being: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Genesis 3:19); and he made the human being subject to death. It was a divine sentence and could not be dissolved by human condition. A remedy was given: that the human being should die and rise again. Why? So that what had previously resulted in condemnation might result in benefit. What is that, except death? Do you ask how? Because death, intervening, brings sin to an end. For when we die, certainly we cease to sin.

The sentence therefore seemed to have been satisfied, because the human being, who had been made to live if he did not sin, was beginning to die. But so that God’s perpetual grace might endure, the human being died; and Christ discovered the resurrection—that is, a way to restore the heavenly benefit which had been lost through the serpent’s deceit. Both things, then, happened for our sake: death is the end of sins, and resurrection is the restoration of nature.

18. Yet, so that the devil’s fraud and snares might not prevail in this world, baptism was devised. Hear what Scripture—or rather, the Son of God—says about this baptism: the Pharisees, who refused to be baptized with John’s baptism, “rejected the counsel of God” (Luke 7:30). Baptism, therefore, is the counsel of God. How great is the grace where the counsel of God is present!

19. Listen, then. So that the devil’s bonds might also be loosed in this world, a way was devised for a living person to die and to rise again alive.

[Note: [Col. 0429C] The Roman edition alone reads: “a living person should die and rise again alive.”]

What does “alive” mean? It means that he is living with bodily life when he comes to the font and is submerged in the font.

[Note: [Col. 0429C] Some manuscripts read: “Therefore water is earth.”]

What is water except something from the earth? The heavenly sentence is therefore satisfied without the terror of death. When you are submerged, that sentence is dissolved: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Genesis 3:19). The sentence having been fulfilled, there is room for heavenly benefit and remedy. Water, then, is from the earth; but the possibility of our life did not allow us to be covered with earth and to rise again from the earth. Moreover, it is not earth that washes, but water washes; therefore the font is like a tomb.

### CHAPTER VII

The example of a threefold questioning and immersion is found in Peter’s threefold response. Why, when the whole Trinity forgives sins, is it said that there is one name in which we must be saved? And in what manner do we die with Christ in baptism and are anointed unto eternal life?

20. You were questioned: “Do you believe in God the Father almighty?” You said, “I believe,” and you were immersed—that is, you were buried. Again you were questioned: “Do you believe in our Lord Jesus Christ and in his cross?” You said, “I believe,” and you were immersed; therefore you were also buried with Christ. For whoever is buried with Christ rises with Christ. A third time you were questioned: “Do you also believe in the Holy Spirit?” You said, “I believe”; a third time you were immersed, so that the threefold confession might absolve the manifold fall of your former life.

[Note: [Col. 0429C] Since no mention is made here of the formula pronounced by the priest, someone might wonder whether those three questions and answers themselves took its place. Yet the author sufficiently indicates below that the formula was not omitted, where he says: “He commanded us to be baptized in one name, that is, in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,” etc. It must therefore be said that individual questions were not inserted into the individual immersions, but that all of them were pronounced beforehand together, as we learn was customary from Gregory’s Sacramentary, the Roman Ordo, the Sacramentary and Gallican Liturgy, Tertullian’s Against Praxeas, Cyril of Jerusalem’s Mystagogical Catechesis 2, and many others. Accordingly, nothing else is indicated here except that the questions and immersions correspond to one another—not in the order of celebration, but, so to speak, in the intention of those celebrating.]

21. Finally, to offer you an example, after the holy apostle Peter had appeared to have fallen during the Lord’s passion through the weakness of human condition—he who had previously denied him—Christ questioned him three times afterward about whether he loved Christ, so that he might erase and undo that fall. Then Peter said: “Lord, you know that I love you” (John 21:15 ff.). He said it three times, so that he might be absolved three times.

[Note: [Col. 0429D] The Roman edition reads: “because he had denied him three times.”]

22. Thus the Father forgives sin just as the Son forgives it, and so does the Holy Spirit. Yet he commanded us to be baptized in one name, that is, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Do not be surprised that he said “one name,” where there is one substance, one divinity, and one majesty. This is the name of which it was said: “In which it is necessary for all to be saved” (Acts 4:12). In this name you have all been saved; you have been restored to the grace of life.

23. Therefore the Apostle cries out, as you heard in the reading just given: “Whoever is baptized is baptized into the death of Jesus” (Romans 6:3 ff.). What does “into death” mean? It means that, just as Christ died, so you too should taste death; just as Christ died to sin and lives for God, so you too should die, through the sacrament of baptism, to the former allurements of sins, and rise again through the grace of Christ.

It is therefore death, but not in the reality of bodily death; it is death in likeness. When you are immersed, you receive the likeness of death and burial; you receive the sacrament of that cross on which Christ hung and his body was fastened with nails. When you are crucified, therefore, you cling to Christ; you cling to the nails of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that the devil may not be able to pull you away. May Christ’s nail hold you fast—the nail that recalls the weakness of human condition.

[Note: [Col. 0429D] The Claromontane manuscript reads “receive the sacraments.” A little later, instead of “you cling to Christ,” it reads “you adhere to Christ,” perhaps “you are added,” that is, “you are joined.”]

24. You were immersed, then, and came to the priest. What did he say to you?

[Note: [Col. 0430C] This prayer is found in Gregory’s Sacramentary and in the Gallican Sacramentary, as well as in the old Gallican Missal. From it it is clear that the formula of confirmation, if that is what is being discussed here, is supplicatory. This can also be established from Tertullian’s On Baptism, Cyprian’s Letter 73, Jerome’s Dialogue Against the Luciferians, Augustine’s fifteenth book On the Trinity, Isidore’s second book On Ecclesiastical Offices, chapter 26, and sixth book of the Origins, final chapter, together with other works.]

“God,” he said, “the almighty Father, who regenerated you from water and the Holy Spirit and forgave you your sins, may he himself anoint you unto eternal life.” See where you have been anointed: “unto life,” he says, “eternal life.” Do not prefer this life to that life.

[Note: [Col. 0430D] Latinius conjectures that the reading should be “to any life”; but we do not see why that alteration is necessary.]

For example, if some enemy should arise, if he should wish to take away your faith, if he should threaten death so that someone might apostatize, consider what you should choose. Do not choose that in which you have not been anointed; choose that in which you have been anointed, so that you may prefer eternal life to temporal life.

[Note: [Col. 0430D] Nearly all the manuscripts, omitting “in which he has not been anointed” and the final words “through Christ,” etc., read as follows: “Do not choose it; the Benignian manuscript reads, ‘do not neglect it’; but choose that in which you have been anointed, life,” etc. Since the Claromontane manuscript and all the editions prefer our reading, it is credible that the lacuna should be attributed to some ancient copy from which the other manuscripts were transcribed.]

Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 0431]

## CHAPTER I

Why those who have been immersed and given life in baptism receive ointment on the head, and what regeneration is; why we too must imitate the nature of a fish in the sea of this present age. Also, concerning the mystery of the washing of the feet, whose usefulness is explained, although the practice does not prevail in the Roman Church.

1. Yesterday we discussed the font, whose appearance is like a kind of form of a tomb. Into it we are received, immersed, and raised again—that is, resurrected—when we believe in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. You receive μύρον (myron), that is, ointment, upon your head.

[Note: [Col. 0431C] All the editions and by far the majority of the manuscripts read “the mystery, that is, the ointment”; the Gemetian, Pratellian, Coenomanian, and first Tellerian manuscripts partly prefer “myrrh,” partly “myrron,” etc. But μύρον should be read, and no sensible person will deny that this is the genuine reading. Below, instead of “but when wisdom has received grace,” not a few manuscripts contract the passage as follows: “but when grace has begun to be perfect, this is called regeneration.”]

Why upon the head? “The sense of the wise is in his head,” says Solomon (Ecclesiastes 2:14); for wisdom is cold without grace. But when wisdom has received grace, then its work begins to be perfect.

[Note: [Col. 0431D] Not a few manuscripts read: “but when grace has begun to be perfect, this is called regeneration.”]

This is called regeneration.

2. What is regeneration? In the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 13:33) you have the verse that is spoken in the second psalm: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you,” which appears to refer to the resurrection. For the holy apostle Peter interpreted it in the Acts of the Apostles in this way: when the Son rose from the dead, the Father’s voice resounded: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Psalm 2:7). Hence he is also called the firstborn from the dead.

[Note: [Col. 0431D] The Roman edition alone has “the apostle Paul.” Again, near the end of this section, it has “the Apostle’s interpretation,” as it does here. But we would rather attribute a lapse of memory to the author than suppose that all the manuscripts and old editions are corrupt. Immediately afterward, where all the editions and some manuscripts read “just as that resurrection was regeneration,” more and better manuscripts have a lacuna followed by “regeneration was.” Other manuscripts invert the second part as follows: “so also this regeneration is resurrection”; the others and all the editions have the reading in the text.]

What, then, is resurrection except when we rise from death to life? Thus also in baptism, since it is a likeness of death, without doubt, when you are immersed and rise again, a likeness of resurrection is produced. Therefore, rightly, according to the interpretation of the apostle Peter, just as that resurrection was regeneration, so this resurrection is also regeneration.

3. But what do you say, since you are immersed in water? Is that why you feel yourself to be a stranger, why doubt holds you? We have indeed read: “Let the earth produce from itself fruit that sprouts” (Genesis 2:11). Likewise you have read about the waters: “Let the waters bring forth living creatures” (ibid., 20), and living creatures were born. Those things happened at the beginning of creation; but for you it has been reserved that water should regenerate you unto grace, just as it generated other creatures unto life.

Imitate that fish which indeed received a lesser grace, yet ought to be a wonder to you. It is in the sea, and above the waves; it is in the sea, and swims upon the billows. A storm rages in the sea, squalls roar; but the fish swims and is not submerged, because it is accustomed to swim.

[Note: [Col. 0432C] The Claromontane manuscript reads: “because nature has made it accustomed.” This is one of those passages which the heterodox mocked. Let them learn from Augustine that God’s common and daily works deserve in themselves as much admiration as extraordinary works.]

So this present age is also a sea for you. It has various waves, heavy billows, and savage storms. Be a fish, then, so that the wave of the age may not submerge you.

Beautifully, the Father says to the Son: “Today I have begotten you” (Psalm 2:7)—that is, when you redeemed the people, when you called them to the kingdom of heaven, when you fulfilled my will, you proved yourself to be my Son.

4. You have come up from the font. What followed? You heard the reading.

[Note: [Col. 0432C] Gill’s and the Roman edition, as well as the second Tellerian manuscript, read: “The high priest is girded.” Amerbach and Erasmus have: “The priest is girded.” All the manuscripts omit the verb “is”; most of them, including the oldest, also do not recognize the adjective “high” here or below. Nevertheless, in those centuries it was customary for a bishop to be called “high priest,” and the episcopate “the high priesthood.” [Col. 0432D] Ambrose supplies early examples of the first usage in his Exposition of Psalm 118, sermon 2, and in On the Mysteries, chapter 2, section 6. The second is established by his life written by Paulinus, who says: “He wept most bitterly whenever it happened to be announced to him that some priest had died . . . because it was difficult to find a man who was considered worthy of the high priesthood.” Again, in this very passage, where all the editions and many manuscripts have “the beginning of the ministry,” other manuscripts give “the completion of the mystery,” which is less suitable.]

The high priest is girded. Although the presbyters also performed the washing, the beginning of the ministry comes from the high priest. The high priest, I say, being girded, washed your feet.

What is this mystery? You certainly heard that when the Lord had washed the feet of the other disciples, he came to Peter, and Peter said to him: “Are you washing my feet?” (John 13:8). That is: You, the Lord, wash the feet of a servant? You, the spotless one, wash my feet? You, the creator of heaven, wash my feet?

You find the same thing elsewhere. He came to John, and John said to him: “I ought to be baptized by you, and you come to me?” (Matthew 3:14). I am a sinner, and you come to me, a sinner, as though to lay aside your sins, although you committed no sin?

See the whole of righteousness; see humility; see grace; see sanctification: “Unless I wash your feet,” he says, “you will have no part with me.”

5. We are not unaware that the Roman Church does not have this custom.

[Note: [Col. 0432D] The matters mentioned concerning this rite in book On the Mysteries, chapter 6, are explained here somewhat more fully. For the author, not content merely to touch upon the reason for this institution—namely, the imitation of the Lord’s humility set forth in the preceding Gospel reading—and its particular effect, the weakening of concupiscence, further explains not only the order in which it was performed by the bishop and presbyters, but also refutes the Roman Church, where the practice was not observed. Moreover, it is clear that the interpretation by which the Romans maintained that the Gospel passage should be understood as referring to the washing of travelers’ feet was not accepted by others in the sense that they thought it could be omitted in baptism, but in the sense that baptized persons were obliged to wash travelers’ feet. See in the Appendix to the sermons of St Augustine, p. 288, the third of those published by Sirmondus from the Remigian manuscript under Augustine’s name; also Caesarius’s sermon, numbered 257 in the same Appendix, as well as two other anonymous sermons published there, namely 149 and 158. The former attributes to the same washing power to remit not only minor but even deadly sins. Furthermore, we learn from the Gothic Missal, p. 249, and the Old Gallican Missal, p. [lacuna], published by our Mabillon, that the custom of washing feet in baptism was also observed in the Gallican churches. Another missal published by the same scholar in the Italian Journey does not differ from these, except that it places the same washing after the white garment has been given. This washing, after having flourished for some time in Spain, was abolished by the Council of Elvira, canon 48. Concerning the African Church, Augustine gives much information bearing on the same ceremony in Letter 54, section 10, and Letter 55, section 35; from this one may learn how greatly that Church differed from the Ambrosian or Gallican Church in this matter. Berosus, in the Ambrosian Ceremonial, testifies that the use of this washing had not yet disappeared in his own time.]

Although in all things we follow its type and model; nevertheless, it does not have the custom of washing the feet. Consider, then: perhaps it withdrew from the practice because of the multitude. Yet there are some who say and try to excuse it, claiming that this should not be done as a mystery, nor in baptism, nor in regeneration, but that it is like washing the feet of a guest. Humility is one thing; sanctification is another.

Finally, hear that it is a mystery and sanctification: “Unless I wash your feet, you will have no part with me” (John 13:8).

[Note: [Col. 0432D] The Claromontane manuscripts read: “it is a mystery of sanctification.”]

I say this not to criticize others, but to commend my own duties. In all things I desire to follow the Roman Church; yet we too are human beings and have understanding. Therefore, where something is observed more correctly elsewhere, we too preserve it more correctly.

[Col. 0433B] 6. We follow the apostle Peter himself; we cling to his devotion. What does the Roman Church say to this? Peter the apostle himself, who was a priest of the Roman Church, is certainly the author of this assertion for us. Peter himself says: “Lord, not only my feet, but also my hands and my head” (ibid., 9). See his faith. What he first refused was an act of humility; what he afterward offered was an act of devotion and faith.

[Note: [Col. 0434C] All the editions read “he offered himself”; all the manuscripts read simply “he offered,” with “his feet,” etc., understood. Likewise, where all the editions and many manuscripts have “of devotion and faith,” some manuscripts prefer “devotion of faith.”]

7. The Lord answered him, because he had mentioned his hands and head: “Whoever has bathed does not need to wash again, except to wash his feet” (ibid., 10). Why this? Because in baptism every sin is washed away.

Sin therefore departs. But because Adam was tripped up by the devil (Genesis 3:6), and poison was poured out upon his feet, you wash the feet so that, in the part where the serpent lay in wait, a greater aid of sanctification may be added, whereby it may not afterward be able to trip you up. You wash the feet, therefore, so that you may wash away the serpent’s poisons.

It also contributes to humility, so that in the mystery we may not be ashamed of what we disdain in ordinary service.

[Note: [Col. 0434D] The Claromontane manuscript reads: “so that we may not be ashamed in the ministry.” Immediately afterward, instead of “which we do not disdain,” as found in all the editions and the Claromontane manuscript, the manuscripts read without the negative: “which we disdain.” This is plainly the correct reading.]

### CHAPTER II

The baptized person is sealed with the Holy Spirit. Although all the virtues belong to him, seven belong to him by a special right. When the baptized person has approached the altar, his eyes are smeared with clay, like those of the blind man described in John’s Gospel; this signifies the confession of sins. The author refutes those who deny that they are sinners and shows that, through the imposition of this clay, their eyes are opened to see spiritual things.

8. There follows the spiritual seal, which you heard read today, because after the font perfection remains to be accomplished, when, at the priest’s invocation, the Holy Spirit is poured in: the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and strength, the Spirit of knowledge and piety, the Spirit of holy fear—seven virtues, as it were, of the Spirit (Isaiah 11:2).

[Note: [Col. 0434D] Some manuscripts read: “seven virtues, as it were seven spirits.”]

[Col. 0434B] 9. All the virtues indeed belong to the Spirit; but these are, as it were, cardinal and principal virtues. What is more principal than piety? What is more principal than knowledge of God? What is more principal than strength? What is more principal than the counsel of God? What is more principal than fear of God? Just as fear of the world is weakness, so fear of God is great strength.

10. These are the seven virtues when you are sealed. For, as the holy Apostle says: “The wisdom of our God is manifold” (Ephesians 3:10). And just as God’s wisdom is manifold, so the Holy Spirit is manifold, possessing various and diverse virtues. Hence he is also called the God of virtues, which can be applied to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. But that belongs to another discussion and another time.

11. What follows after this? You must come to the altar (Psalm 79:5).

[Note: [Col. 0434D] All the editions and most manuscripts have this reading; two, however, read “who have just come,” and two others “to which you did not come before.” This reading is very attractive. Below, where the editions and many manuscripts have “if you have not read,” the negative is absent from not a few manuscripts. Finally, what follows concerning the blind man is entirely omitted in the treatise On the Mysteries.]

Since you have come, you must see what you did not see before—that is, the mystery which you read about in the Gospel; and if you did not read it, certainly you heard it.

The blind man presented himself to the Savior to be healed. He who healed others merely by word and speech and restored the light of their eyes by command nevertheless wanted to prefigure this mystery in the Gospel written according to John. John truly saw and recorded great mysteries more than the others, and he explained them.

All the holy evangelists were indeed holy, as were all the apostles except the betrayer; yet the holy John, who wrote his Gospel last, as though specially summoned and chosen by Christ, poured forth the eternal mysteries with a kind of greater trumpet. Whatever he said is a mystery.

Another evangelist said that a blind man was healed—Matthew said it, Luke said it, Mark said it. What does John alone say? “He took clay, and smeared it upon his eyes, and said to him: ‘Go to Siloam.’ And he rose, went, washed, and came back seeing” (John 9:6–7).

[Note: [Col. 0435C] All the editions and some manuscripts have: “Go, wash in Siloam.” A little later they likewise have “with the eyes of your heart”; in both places, however, many more and better manuscripts have the reading given in the text.]

[Col. 0435B] 12. Consider also the eyes of your heart.

[Note: [Col. 0435C] The editions read: “the eyes of your heart.”]

You saw bodily things with bodily eyes; but you were still unable to see the things that belong to the sacraments with the eyes of your heart. Therefore, when you gave your name, he took clay and smeared it upon your eyes.

[Note: [Col. 0435C] Catechumens gave their names for baptism when they were admitted to the order of those preparing for it. It has also been observed that the custom of confessing sins before baptism was ancient, as shown in the Exposition of the Gospel according to Luke, book 6, column 1383. From this it may be understood that the statement below, suggesting that the confession could be omitted, is not entirely characteristic of Ambrose. For although that opinion is true—as theologians teach after the Angelic Doctor, part III, question 8, article 6—it is scarcely believable that Ambrose, who was accustomed to exhort his people to such preparation from the practice of the ancient Fathers, would say something that might draw them away from it. Indeed, since the sense of the entire passage seems to be that those who were to be baptized customarily confessed their sins not in any other way than by fleeing to the remedy and declaring themselves sick and wounded through a certain silent and implicit confession, we believe this can be established quite clearly: these homilies were delivered somewhere other than in the Church of Milan.]

What does this signify? That you should confess your sin, recognize your conscience, do penance for your offenses—that is, acknowledge the condition of the human race. For even if the person who comes to baptism does not confess his sin, nevertheless by this very act he fulfills a confession of all sins: he asks to be baptized in order to be justified, that is, to pass from guilt to grace.

[Col. 0436A] 13. Do not think this an idle matter. There are some people—I know that there was certainly one—who, when we said to him, “At your age you ought rather to be baptized,” replied: “Why should I be baptized? I have no sin. Have I contracted sin?”

[Col. 0436C] The old edition and some manuscripts read “which he had not washed”; the Roman edition and the second Tellerian manuscript more correctly read “which he had not smeared”; but the remaining manuscripts most correctly read “which he had not lifted.” The final Paris edition alone, instead of “he flees to baptism” two lines later, substituted “he rises up to baptism,” departing from all the other editions and manuscripts. That was a typographical error.]

This man had no clay, because Christ had not lifted it from him—that is, had not opened his eyes. For no human being is without sin.

14. Therefore the person who flees to the baptism of Christ acknowledges that he is human. Thus he also placed clay upon you—that is, shame, prudence, and consideration of your weakness—and said to you: “Go to Siloam.”

What is Siloam? It means, he says, “sent.” That is: Go to the font in which the cross of the Lord is proclaimed; go to the font in which Christ has redeemed the errors of all.

[Col. 0436B] 15. You washed, you came to the altar, and you began to see what you had not seen before. That is, through the Lord’s font and the proclamation of the Lord’s passion, your eyes were then opened. You, who previously seemed to be blind in heart, began to see the light of the sacraments.

Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, we have come as far as the altar, toward a fuller treatment. And because the time does not permit us to begin a complete discussion—for the treatment is longer—let what has been said today suffice. Tomorrow, if it pleases the Lord, we shall discuss the sacraments themselves.

[Note: [Col. 0436C] The Claromontane manuscript alone, and that by a correction made by the same hand, reads: “because it is not the time to begin the entire discussion.”]

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0435]

[Col. 0435D] 365

## CHAPTER I

The Tabernacle of the old law and the practices customarily observed there are applied to the baptistery and to the effects of baptism.

1. In the Old Testament the priests regularly used to enter the first tabernacle; into the second tabernacle the high priest entered once a year (Leviticus 16:2 ff.). Recalling this clearly in the Letter to the Hebrews, the apostle Paul explains the order of the Old Testament (Hebrews 9:1 ff.). In the second tabernacle there was manna; there was also Aaron’s staff, which had withered and afterward blossomed again; and there was the incense-burner.

[Col. 0436D] 2. To what does this refer? So that you may understand what the second tabernacle is, into which the priest has introduced you, into which the high priest used to enter once a year: it is the baptistery, where Aaron’s staff blossomed (Numbers 17:8). Before, it was dry; afterward, it blossomed again. You too were dry, and you began to blossom again in the watered font. You had withered through sins; you had withered through errors and offenses; but you have now begun to bear fruit, planted beside streams of water.

3. But perhaps you will say: What does this have to do with the people, if the priest’s staff had withered and blossomed again? Who are the people themselves except a priestly people? To them it was said: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation,” as the apostle Peter says (1 Peter 2:9). Each person is anointed for priesthood and anointed for kingship; but it is a spiritual kingship and a spiritual priesthood.

4. In the second tabernacle there is also an incense-burner (Hebrews 9:4), which is accustomed to give off a good fragrance. So now you too are the good fragrance of Christ; now there is no lot of offenses in you, no odor of a grave error.

[Note: [Col. 0437D] Gill’s edition, the Roman edition, and the second Tellerian manuscript read “no stains in you”; some others, “no stain in you”; the far more numerous and superior manuscripts, as well as the editions of Amerbach and Erasmus, read “no lot in you.” This is a good reading, which we noted already in volume 1, column 61, in Ambrose, and which would often have been worth noting again. From this one may infer either that this author was especially devoted to Ambrosian books, or that both authors lived in places and times not very different from each other.]

## CHAPTER II

Human condition in baptism is a source of wonder even to the angels, for through baptism it is restored to the grace of innocence and youth.

5. It follows that you should come to the altar. You have begun to come. The angels watched; they saw you arriving; and they saw that human condition which had previously been filthy with the dark squalor of sins suddenly shine again. Therefore they said: “Who is this who comes up from the desert, made white?” (Song of Songs 8:5).

[Col. 0437B] The angels therefore marvel. Do you wish to know that they marvel? Listen, then, to the apostle Paul saying that things have been bestowed upon us which angels desire to see (1 Peter 1:12). And again: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard . . . what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Corinthians 2:9).

[Note: [Col. 0438D] Here, as in several other places, the author’s memory has misled him.]

6. Then recognize what you have received. The holy prophet David saw this grace in figure and desired it. Do you wish to know that he desired it? Hear him again saying: “You shall sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed; you shall wash me, and I shall become whiter than snow” (Ps. 50 [51]:9). Why? Because although snow is white, it quickly becomes blackened and spoiled by some dirt; this grace which you have received, if you hold fast to what you have received, will be enduring and perpetual.

7. You were therefore coming to the altar desiring it, since you had seen such great grace; you were coming to the altar desiring to receive the sacrament. Let your soul say: “And I shall go in to the altar of my God, to God who gives joy to my youth” (Ps. 42 [43]:4). You laid aside the old age of sins and took on the youth of grace: the heavenly sacraments accomplished this for you. Finally, hear David saying again: “Your youth shall be renewed like the eagle’s” (Ps. 102 [103]:5). You have begun to be a good eagle, one that seeks heaven and scorns earthly things. Good eagles are around the altar: “For where the body is, there also are the eagles” (Matt. 24:28). The form of the body is the altar, and the body of Christ is on the altar: you are eagles, renewed by the washing away of sin.

## CHAPTER III

The author, intending to show that our sacraments are both older and more divine than those of the Jews, completes the first part by comparing the institutions of Melchizedek and Abraham [Col. 0438A]; there he makes it clear that Melchizedek was both the author of our mysteries and a figure of Christ.

8. You came to the altar, you saw the sacraments placed upon the altar, and you were indeed astonished at the created thing itself; yet it was a solemn and familiar created thing.

9. Perhaps someone will say: “God granted the Jews such great grace: he rained manna upon them from heaven” (Exod. 16:13). What more did he give to his faithful? What more did he grant to those to whom he promised more?

[Note: The Claromontane manuscript reads, “granted them such a benefit that manna rained upon them.”]

10. Understand that I am saying that the mysteries of Christians are earlier than those of the Jews, and that the sacraments of Christians are more divine than those of the Jews. How so? Understand. When did the Jews begin to exist? Certainly from Judah, the great-grandson of Abraham; [Note: All editions and some manuscripts read *aut*, “or”; if you wish, understand it also in this way: “from the Law which the Jews were deemed worthy to receive.” The great majority of the others, as in the text.] or, if you wish to understand it in this way, from the Law—that is, from the time when the Jews were deemed worthy to receive the Law. Thus the Jews were so called either from Abraham’s great-grandson or from the time of holy Moses. And if at that time God rained manna from heaven for the murmuring Jews, whereas for you the figure of these sacraments came beforehand, when Abraham existed, when he gathered three hundred and eighteen retainers [Note: Some manuscripts read, “gathered three hundred and nineteen,” and went forth and pursued them.], and pursued your enemies for you, rescuing his nephew from captivity—then, having conquered, he came, and Melchizedek the priest met him and offered him bread and wine (Gen. 14:18).

Who had bread and wine? Abraham did not. But who had them? Melchizedek. He, therefore, is the author of the sacraments (Heb. 7:1 ff.). Who is Melchizedek? He is signified as the king of righteousness, the king of peace. Who is this king of righteousness? Can any human being be king of righteousness? Who, then, is the king of righteousness, except the righteousness of God, who is the peace of God and the wisdom of God? He was able to say: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John 14:27).

11. Understand, then, first of all, that these sacraments which you receive are earlier than the sacraments of Moses—whatever the Jews claim to possess—and that the Christian people began before the Jewish people began: but we exist in predestination, while they exist in name.

12. Melchizedek therefore offered bread and wine. Who is Melchizedek? “Without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life”: so says the Epistle to the Hebrews. “He is without father and without mother.” Like whom? Like the Son of God. The Son of God was born without a mother through a heavenly generation, because he was born from God the Father alone; and again he was born without a father when he was born from the Virgin, for he was not generated from male seed, but was born from the Holy Spirit (Matt. 1:20) and the Virgin Mary and brought forth from a virginal womb. In all these respects Melchizedek is like the Son of God. Melchizedek was also a priest [Col. 0439A], because Christ too is a priest, to whom it is said: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109 [110]:4).

## CHAPTER IV

To persuade his hearers that this sacrament should be regarded as more divine than manna, he asserts that Christ’s very body is made from bread by the word of Christ himself. After confirming this by various effects that reveal the efficacy of that word, he explains why the blood is given under another form.

13. Who, then, is the author of the sacraments except the Lord Jesus? These sacraments came from heaven, for every plan comes from heaven. Truly it is a great and divine miracle that God rained manna from heaven upon the people, and the people did not labor, but ate.

14. Perhaps you say: “My bread is ordinary bread.” But this bread is bread before the sacramental words [*On Consecration*, distinction 2, chapter “Bread Is”]; when consecration has been added, from bread it becomes [Note: Many manuscripts, together with Lanfranc and Alger, read “becomes the body of Christ”; other manuscripts, and all printed editions, read “becomes the flesh of Christ.” The following words are again quoted by Blessed Alger with the entire intervening verse omitted, followed by “Therefore, consecration”; but what Alger immediately cites from this chapter clearly shows that the passage was presented by him in abbreviated form. The manuscripts and editions differ only in one respect: many manuscripts have *we affirm*, omit the word *by consecration*, and several read “But consecration”; the editions agree among themselves, except that the older ones punctuated the passage as follows: “Let us therefore affirm this: how can what is bread be the body of Christ by consecration? Therefore, consecration,” and so forth. This is less graceful.] the flesh of Christ. Let us therefore affirm this. How can what is bread be the body of Christ? By consecration. But by what words is the consecration accomplished, and whose words are they? The words of the Lord Jesus. For all the other things [Note: All editions and eleven manuscripts omit *in what precedes*, “are said by the priest”; we have restored these words on the authority of other codices, especially the Benedictine and Claromontane manuscripts. But where the text has “praises are offered to God,” the Roman edition inserts “prayer is offered.” Other editions and all the manuscripts read “praise is offered to God,” but in the following clause they divide among themselves in three ways. The old editions and some manuscripts read “it is requested by prayer”; the Gembloux, Pratelles, Alnet, and Teller manuscripts read “prayer requests”; finally, the Benedictine, Rheims, Claromontane, Sorbonne, and Colbert manuscripts read “prayer is requested.” We prefer the latter reading because of the antiquity of the three manuscripts, without rejecting either of the others. It should incidentally be observed that the preface of the Mass, as it is called, and the sacred *Trisagion* are signified by the words “praise is offered to God”; while the following prayer, which we call the first prayer of the canon, is signified by the words “prayer is requested.” Nor does it pose any obstacle that the author wrote “for kings,” not “for emperors.” Apart from the fact that good authors, and Ambrose himself, use “king” for “emperor,” he may perhaps have employed this word to conform more closely to Paul’s wording in 1 Tim. 2:1. We should further note that Gregory the Great, in book VII, letter 7, indiction 2, and Cyprian, in *On the Unity of the Church*, call the canon a prayer; and Augustine, in letter 149 of the new edition, establishes this distinction between prayer and supplication: that the things preceding consecration should be called supplications, while those following it should, according to ecclesiastical usage, be called prayers. But no one who has observed that the author omitted entire prayers from the canon he cites will be surprised that he is not exact in every individual word.] that are said in what precedes are said by the priest: praises are offered to God, and prayer is requested for the people, for kings, and for the rest. But when the time comes to effect the venerable sacrament, the priest no longer uses his own words, but uses the words of Christ. Therefore Christ’s word effects this sacrament.

15. What is Christ’s word? The word by which all things were made. The Lord commanded, and heaven came to be; the Lord commanded, and earth came to be; the Lord commanded, and the seas came to be. The Lord commanded, and every creature was brought forth (Gen. 1:1 ff.). You see, therefore, how effective Christ’s word is. If there is such power in the word of the Lord Jesus that things began to exist which did not exist, [Note: Thus read the old editions and the manuscripts, except the Illidan manuscript, which omits the entire phrase “how much more … which existed.” The final part is rendered in the Roman edition as “so that what existed might be changed into something else.” Lanfranc had preceded that edition: he testifies that he found this passage so read in some manuscripts. Yet Edmund Albertinus, in book II of *On the Sacrament of the Eucharist*, p. 510, brings a grave charge against both Lanfranc and the Roman edition, as though they had corrupted the same passage. But neither can the Romans be blamed for following the authority of so great a man, nor can Lanfranc himself be accused of falsification. Apart from the fact that the same words are omitted above in the Illidan manuscript and could likewise have been omitted in some others, who could believe that Lanfranc sought an escape by corruption, when (1) he does not conceal that the other reading exists in several manuscripts, but explains it and clearly demonstrates that it can be understood only in a thoroughly Catholic sense; (2) he suitably confirms the different reading which he prefers by a passage from the treatise *On the Mysteries*—for since this same testimony of Ambrose could only absurdly be twisted away from the sense of real presence, it is scarcely plausible that the writer whom Albertinus calls “Ambrose’s ape” would teach something contrary to Ambrose’s views; and (3) it would be inconsistent with Lanfranc’s gravity and prudence to corrupt a position which he showed had been corrupted by his opponent. Let this suffice to free Lanfranc from every suspicion of bad faith. As for the passage itself, Lanfranc in the work cited, and Alger in book I, chapter 7 of *On the Sacrament*, reply that bread and wine, according to their external appearance, are “what they were,” but according to their internal substance are changed into the body of Christ. Although they reinforce this interpretation with Ambrosian words and examples so strongly that nothing more seems necessary, Mornay du Plessis nevertheless brought the same argument forward again against Cardinal Perron. The cardinal replied two things: first, that the words themselves are not free from suspicion of corruption, namely because of the authority of Lanfranc just mentioned; second, that their meaning is by no means that bread and wine are said to be “what they were,” or “that which they were,” since in the first part of the sentence there is no mention of bread or wine; rather, “what existed” is simply said to exist and not to be destroyed, because the matter of the sacrament is not stripped of being in its universal extent through transubstantiation, but is transferred from one specific being to another specific being. It does not terminate simply in non-being, but in another being, to which it is joined and connected by succession, contiguity of existence, and the unity of the accidents in which both terms had been grounded. These words, truly and wisely spoken, could satisfy all who love sincerity more than contention. Albertinus nevertheless still objects, denying that things of whose substance nothing remains, and which are simply non-being, can remain within the breadth of being. He adds that it is said of bread and wine that they should be “what they were”; but they were, he says, in the specific being of bread and wine, from which he concludes that the change cannot be called substantial but accidental. He thinks this reasoning of his is excellently confirmed by what our author adds: “You yourself existed, but you existed …” Who, Albertinus continues, would think that the author deliberately selected an example of accidental change to confirm his thesis if the discussion concerned substantial change? The first of these arguments is answered in volume III, book VII, chapters 6 and 7 of *The Perpetuity of the Faith*; there it is shown most clearly that our author in this passage departs not in the least from ordinary usage and custom of speech. The examples of air and running water, which are constantly changing yet are always called by the same names, illustrate this admirably. The same point could also disperse Albertinus’s inference about the specific sense, if Perron had not above disclosed and dissolved the trap in the argument, which this minister carefully concealed. But, he says, only one example of accidental change is offered here; therefore the passage concerns only accidental conversion. But many examples of substantial changes are supplied here; therefore, we conclude with far greater right that the passage concerns substantial conversion. Thus we acknowledge a twofold conversion in the Eucharist: one substantial, by which the entire substance of bread is changed into the body of Christ; the other accidental, by which the species of bread, naturally appointed to signify his presence, become figures and antitypes of the Lord’s body. We contend that this is entirely true and invincible for defending the Catholic dogma against Calvinist cavils. Yet what if we affirm that the words “so that they may be what they were, and be changed into something else” contain a division? No one will deny that the particle *and* is sometimes used in place of *or*. What is more common than these formulas: “The Lord kills and gives life; he leads down to the underworld and brings back. The Lord makes poor and makes rich; he humbles and raises up”? Certainly the Lord does not do both simultaneously, but does whichever he wills. Consider the entire passage under discussion, and you will find three effects of divine power proposed there: the creation of things that do not exist, and, in the case of things that do exist, either their preservation or their conversion, as God sees fit.] how much more effective is it, so that they may be what they were and be changed into something else? Heaven did not exist, the sea did not exist, the earth did not exist; but hear David saying: “He himself spoke, and they came to be; he himself commanded, and they were created” (Ps. 148:5).

16. Therefore, to answer you: the body of Christ did not exist before consecration; but after consecration I tell you that it is now the body of Christ. He himself spoke, and it came to be; he himself commanded, and it was created. You yourself existed, but you were an old creation; after you were consecrated, you began to be a new creation. Do you wish to know how new a creation? “Everyone,” he says, “in Christ is a new creation” (2 Cor. 5:17).

17. Understand, then, how Christ’s word has been accustomed to change every created thing, and changes the institutions of nature whenever he wills. How, you ask? Understand. First of all, let us take an example from his generation. It is customary for a human being to be generated only from a man and a woman, and through the custom of marriage. But because the Lord willed it, because he chose this mystery, Christ was born from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin—that is, “the man Christ Jesus, mediator between God and human beings” (1 Tim. 2:5). You see, then, that he was born contrary to established practice and order: a human being was born from a Virgin.

18. Consider another example. The Jewish people were being pressed by the Egyptians and were shut in by the sea. At the divine command, Moses touched the waters with his staff, and the wave divided—not according to the ordinary course of its nature, but according to [Note: The Claromontane manuscript reads, “according to the command of heavenly grace.”] the grace of the heavenly command (Exod. 14:21 ff.).

Consider another example. The people were thirsty and came to a spring. The spring was bitter; holy Moses threw a piece of wood into the spring, and the spring that had been bitter became sweet. That is, it changed the ordinary course of its nature and received the sweetness of grace (Exod. 15:23 ff.).

Consider a fourth example. The iron of an axe had fallen into the water; as iron naturally does, it had sunk. Elisha threw in a piece of wood, and immediately the iron rose and floated upon the water (2 Kings 6:6)—contrary, certainly, to the nature of iron, for iron is a material heavier than the element of water.

19. From all these examples, then, do you not understand how greatly the heavenly word operates? If the heavenly word operated in an earthly spring, if it operated in other things, does it not operate in the heavenly sacraments? You have therefore learned that from bread the body of Christ is made, and that wine and water are poured into the chalice; but it becomes blood [Note: The Claromontane manuscript reads, “by heavenly consecration.” The following objection is twisted by Albertinus against orthodox doctrine so that he wants Christ to be received by us in the Eucharist only in the manner in which we are said to put him on in baptism and to be stained with his blood. The reply is that the comparison between the Eucharist and baptism is established on this point: according to this author, Christ placed a likeness in each sacrament so that in one we would not be affected by the horror of death, and in the other by the horror of body and blood. These two likenesses differ in that one concerns the reality only through its effects, while the other concerns the reality also as present through its substance. As for the objection that the appearance of blood is placed here instead of the reality, in opposition to the likeness, we admit that *appearance* is sometimes taken in this sense, namely when it is understood concretely, to speak with the philosophers; but here we rightly insist that it is used abstractly. First, the opposition between appearance and likeness is thus fully preserved, since appearance is the external form and, as Perron says, the proper manifestation of a thing, whereas likeness in these passages signifies nothing other than a remote analogy. Second, throughout this chapter the author clearly presupposes that Christ’s body and blood are present, as will be evident to anyone who examines it with an open mind. Third, when he undertakes in book II, chapter 6, to teach that a human being dies and rises again in baptism, it is not enough for him to say, “A way was found for a living human being to die and a living human being to rise again”; as though he feared that someone might believe that the person had not truly died in baptism, he immediately adds, “What does ‘living’ mean? It means living with the life of the body when he came to the font and was plunged into the font.” Yet in this book, although he repeatedly says that bread and wine become body and blood, he never states that their natural substance remains. Finally, the horror of a thing is no more removed by its absence than by its being concealed; horror arises from the affection of the senses, which is moved only by external form.] by consecration through the heavenly word (De Consec., dist. 2, ch. “Bread,” §§ “Therefore” and “But perhaps”).

20. But perhaps you say: “I do not see the appearance of blood.” Yet it has a likeness: just as you received the likeness of death, so also you drink the likeness of the precious blood, so that there may be no horror of gore, while the price of redemption nevertheless operates. You have therefore learned that what you receive is the body of Christ.

## CHAPTER V

The body and blood of Christ are consecrated and truly effected by the Lord’s own words. Hence it rightly follows that this sacrament surpasses manna; its reality is sealed by the word “Amen.”

21. Do you wish to know that it is consecrated by heavenly words (De Consec., dist. 2, ch. “Bread,” § “Do you wish to know”)? Hear the words. The priest says: “Make this offering for us,” he says, “approved, [Note: The word *ratam*, “approved,” was absent from all editions and some manuscripts; it has been restored from several others. The Roman edition alone inserts, between two words, “which is made as a figure of the body,” and so forth. But the common reading is legitimate and does not deviate by a hair’s breadth from pious and Catholic doctrine. For it is clear that the passage concerns not the offering of the Lord’s body and blood already consecrated, but the preparation of the offering. At this stage Catholics commonly teach from the holy Fathers that there is a certain analogy and likeness between the bread and the body, and between the wine and the blood. Moreover, even if the effect of consecration—or consecration itself as already completed—were being contemplated here in anticipation, as Albertinus holds, this would still do nothing against Catholic doctrine. For what orthodox child, having merely tasted the first elements of religion, would not immediately answer that in the Eucharist there are two things: the sign and the thing signified, or the sacrament and the sacred reality? Neither excludes the other. Perron’s firm and complete answer therefore remains intact. As for Albertinus’s malicious charge that the Roman editors corrupted this passage, we first ask how he knows that no manuscript exists reading “is made as a figure.” But, he says, all the old editions, all the manuscripts, Paschasius, Durandus, and others present the passage differently. We admit this, but the alleged corruption of so famous a passage seems all the less probable because it can so easily be demonstrated. Add that such a severe charge of corruption should not be affixed where, with very slight changes in wording, the same meaning plainly remains; and that is clearly what has happened here.] rational, acceptable”—which is a figure of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ. “On the day before he suffered, he took bread in his holy hands, looked up to heaven toward you, holy Father almighty, eternal God, giving thanks; he blessed it, broke it, and gave the broken bread to his apostles [Note: “And to his disciples” is omitted only in the Roman edition. Below also, where all editions together with all the manuscripts read “will be broken for many,” the same Roman edition changes it to “is given for you,” perhaps to adapt the author’s words to the liturgical canon. Although the same canon is cited here, as noted above and in the *Admonition*, anyone who compares the two will readily recognize that it is presented neither in full nor always in the same words found in the missal books. This must be attributed either to the author’s unreliable memory or to variations among the manuscripts.] and to his disciples, saying: ‘Take and eat from this, all of you; for this is my body, which will be broken for many’” (Luke 22:19).

22. Likewise, after supper, on the day before he suffered, he took the chalice, looked up to heaven toward you, holy Father almighty, eternal God, giving thanks; he blessed it and gave it to his apostles and disciples [Col. 0444A], saying: “Take and drink from this, all of you; for this is my blood” (Matt. 26:27–28). Observe all these things. The evangelist’s words continue up to “Take,” whether concerning the body or the blood. From that point onward, the words are Christ’s: “Take and drink from this, all of you; for this is my blood.” And observe each detail.

23. “On the day before he suffered,” he says, “he took bread in his holy hands.” Before it is consecrated, it is bread; but when Christ’s words have been added, it is the body of Christ. Finally, hear him saying: “Take and eat from it, all of you; for this is my body.” And before Christ’s words, the chalice is full of wine and water; when Christ’s words have operated, it becomes the blood of Christ, which redeemed the people. See, therefore, by how many kinds of power Christ’s word can transform all things. [Col. 0444B] Moreover, the Lord Jesus himself testifies to us that we receive his body and blood. Should we doubt his faithfulness and testimony?

24. Now return with me to my original proposition. It is indeed a great and venerable thing that manna rained from heaven upon the Jews (Exod. 16:13); but understand this. Which is greater: manna from heaven, or the body of Christ? Surely the body of Christ, who is the author of heaven. Moreover, the one who ate manna died; but the one who eats this body will receive forgiveness of sins and will not die forever (De Consec., dist. 2, ch. “Before,” § “Who eats”).

25. Therefore [Note: Gill and the Roman edition, together with a few manuscripts, read “you say, not idly, when you receive it”; some manuscripts read “you answer, ‘Amen.’” Ambrosian and Erasmian editions, together with by far the greatest number of the most reliable manuscripts, omit “when you receive it.” Immediately afterward, where all editions and several manuscripts read “confessing in the spirit,” a few other manuscripts prefer “trusting in the spirit.” Finally, before the words “the priest says to you,” some manuscripts add “when you have asked,” which is absent from the others and from all editions. The conversion of bread and wine into Christ’s body and blood, and the real presence, as it is called, are asserted so clearly and openly throughout this chapter that anyone who wished to add some new light to it would seem to be trying to attach additional rays to the sun.] you say, not idly: “Amen,” confessing in your spirit that you receive the body of Christ. The priest says to you, “The body of Christ,” and you say, “Amen,” that is, “It is true.” Let the heart retain what the tongue confesses.

## CHAPTER VI

The excellence of this sacrament is demonstrated from the fact that through it the Lord’s Passion is renewed. The discourse ends with a brief notice of matters to be treated in the coming days.

26. So that you may know that this is the sacrament, its figure came beforehand. Then learn how great the sacrament is. See what he says: “Whenever you do this, you will make a commemoration of me until I come again” (1 Cor. 11:26).

27. And the priest says: “Therefore, remembering his most glorious Passion, his resurrection from the dead, and his ascension into heaven, we offer you this spotless victim, a rational victim, an unbloody victim, this holy bread, and the chalice of eternal life; and we ask and beseech you to receive this offering upon your exalted altar through the hands of your angels, just as you deigned to receive the gifts of your righteous servant Abel, the sacrifice of our patriarch Abraham, and that which Melchizedek, the high priest, offered to you.”

28. Therefore, whenever you receive, what does the Apostle say to you? “Whenever we receive, we proclaim the death of the Lord” (De Consec., dist. 2, ch. “If whenever”). If we proclaim his death, we proclaim the forgiveness of sins. If, whenever blood is poured out, it is poured out for the forgiveness of sins, I ought always to receive it, so that my sins may always be forgiven. Since I always sin, I must always have the medicine.

29. Meanwhile, today we have explained as much as we could. But tomorrow, Saturday, and on Sunday we shall speak, as best we can, about the order of prayer. May the Lord our God preserve for you the grace he has given and deign to illuminate more fully the eyes he has opened for you, through his only-begotten Son, our king and Savior, the Lord our God, through whom and with whom praise, honor, glory, majesty, and power belong to him, with the Holy Spirit, from ages past, and now, and always, and throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

# BOOK FIVE

[Col. 0445]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0445C]

He first repeats what was previously said: that the figure of the sacrament, and therefore of Christ himself, preceded in Melchizedek and his sacrifice. Then he brings forward two reasons why water is mixed into the chalice.

1. Yesterday our discourse and treatment proceeded as far as the sacraments of the holy altar. We learned that the figure of these sacraments preceded in the time of Abraham, when holy Melchizedek offered sacrifice (Gen. 14:18), having neither beginning nor end of days. Hear, man, what the Apostle Paul says to the Hebrews. Where are those who say that the Son of God is temporal? [Note: Erasmus and the subsequent editions read, “is temporal? Concerning Melchizedek,” and so forth. The Ambrosian edition and the manuscripts read, “is temporal? Melchizedek,” and so forth, but with less suitable punctuation. We believe that our author is referring to those heretics who were called Melchizedekians. They repeatedly asserted that this priest was an outstanding power of God and superior to Christ himself both in time and dignity, since Christ appeared many centuries later and was invested with the same priestly order. Epiphanius reports and refutes their errors in *Heresy* 35; Augustine treats them more briefly in his Index, *Heresy* 34.] It was said that he has neither beginning nor end of days. If Melchizedek has no beginning of days, could Christ have one (Heb. 7:1 ff.)? But the figure is not greater than the reality. You see, therefore, that he is himself the first and the last (Rev. 1:8). [Note: “The first, because he is the author of all things; the last”—these words are omitted in almost all the manuscripts.] The first, because he is the author of all things; the last, not because he comes to an end, but because he encompasses all things.

2. We said, then, that the chalice and bread are set upon the altar. [Note: A few manuscripts read, “In the chalice, I mean, wine is poured”; many others and the old editions read simply, “in the chalice.” Erasmus and Gill read, “Wine is poured into the chalice, he says.” Since the word “he says” rightly displeased the Roman editors, they removed it on their own authority; but the Claromontane manuscript restored the true reading for us, as in the text. Concerning the admixture of water, which Ambrose omits in *On the Mysteries*, most of the Fathers speak in a way that indicates it was instituted by Christ himself, including Irenaeus, book IV, chapter 57; Cyprian, letter 63; Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, book IV, chapter 21; the Third Council of Carthage, canon 24; and various Liturgies of James, Mark, Basil, and Chrysostom, together with John of Damascus, book IV of *On the Orthodox Faith*. In this matter the Eastern Church differs from the Western: the former pours water into the chalice twice, cold water before consecration and warm water before communion. There were also heretics who held that only water should be offered; concerning them, see Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, book I; Irenaeus, book V, chapter 1; Augustine, *On Heresies*, chapter 74; Theodoret, *Haereticarum fabularum*, chapter 20; and others.] What is put into the chalice?
