Wine. And what else? Water (De Consec., dist. 2, ch. “Into the Chalice”; Exod. 17:6). But you say to me: How, then, did Melchizedek offer bread and wine? What does the admixture of water mean? Hear the reason.

3. First of all, what does the figure that preceded in the time of Moses contain? When the Jewish people were thirsty and murmured because they could not find water, God commanded Moses to touch the rock with his staff. He touched the rock, and the rock poured forth a great stream, as the Apostle says: “They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them; and the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4). It was not an immovable rock that followed the people. You too drink, so that Christ may follow you. See the mystery. Moses—that is, the prophet; the staff—that is, the word of God. The priest touches the rock with the word of God, and water flows, and God’s people drink. The priest therefore touches it, water overflows into the chalice, springs up into eternal life, and the people of God drink—the people who have obtained God’s grace. You have learned this.

4. Consider another example. At the time of our Lord’s Passion, when the great Sabbath was approaching, because our Lord Jesus Christ—or the thieves—was still alive, men were sent to strike them. But when they came, they found the Lord Jesus Christ dead. Then one of the soldiers touched His side with a lance, and from His side water and blood flowed (John XIX, 33 ff.). Why water? Why blood? Water, to cleanse; blood, to redeem. Why from His side? Because grace comes from the same source as guilt. Guilt came through a woman; grace through the Lord Jesus Christ (*On Consecration*, distinction 2, chapter *In calicem*, § “From His side”).

[Note: The Roman edition reads, “because the Lord hung . . . among the thieves, men were sent to strike Him . . . [and] opened His side with a lance”; the other editions and all the manuscripts read as in the text, except that one Tell. manuscript reads, “they were sent to strike the living men; they found,” etc.]

## CHAPTER II

How it is shown, through a mystical interpretation of certain passages from the Song of Songs, that the one who has been cleansed, invited by Christ, also aspires to the immeasurable sweetness of the sacrament.

5. You have come to the altar. The Lord Jesus calls you—or your soul, or the Church—and says: “Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth” (Song of Songs I, 1). Do you wish to apply this to Christ? Nothing is more pleasing. Do you wish to apply it to your soul? Nothing is more delightful.

6. “Let him kiss me.” You see that you are clean from every sin, because your offenses have been wiped away; therefore He judges you worthy of the heavenly sacraments, and therefore invites you to the heavenly banquet: “Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth.”

[Note: All editions read, “He sees you”; all manuscripts, “You see yourself.” A little later, where the old edition and not a few manuscripts read, “from the earth,” Gill. in the margin and the Roman edition in the body of the text, together with many more manuscripts, more aptly read, “they have been wiped away.” Finally, the Roman edition alone had added the word “banquet,” reading “and for these words, ‘Nevertheless, because of what follows, ‘your soul,’ it had substituted merely, ‘then your soul,’” etc.]

7. Yet, because of what follows, your soul—or human nature, or the Church—seeing itself cleansed from all sins and worthy to approach the altar of Christ—for what is the altar except the form or image of Christ’s body?—saw the wondrous sacraments and said: “Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth,” that is, “Let Christ impress a kiss upon me.”

[Note: Here, and above in Book I, chapter 2, section 7, the altar is called the form or image of Christ’s body, because in His body, as upon a sacred altar, Christ the Lord offered to the Father a perpetual and continual sacrifice.]

8. Why? “For your breasts are better than wine” (Song of Songs I, 1); that is, “Your meanings, your sacraments, are better than wine.” That wine, although it has sweetness, joy, and grace, contains worldly gladness; in you, however, there is spiritual delight. Thus Solomon introduces the marriage either of Christ and the Church, or of spirit, flesh, and soul.

9. And he added: “Your name is oil poured out; therefore the maidens have loved you” (ibid., 2). Who are these maidens except the souls of individuals who have laid aside the old age of this body and have been renewed through the Holy Spirit?

10. “Draw us; we shall run after the fragrance of your perfumes” (ibid., 3). See what he says. You cannot follow Christ unless He Himself draws you. Thus, so that you may know this, He says: “When I have been lifted up, I will draw all things to Myself” (John XII, 32).

11. “The King brought me into His chamber.” The Greek has: “into His storehouse” (*εἰς ταμεῖον αὐτοῦ*), that is, into His provision-room or pantry. There are good libations, good fragrances, sweet honey, diverse fruits, and varied dishes, so that your meal may be seasoned with very many courses.

[Note: That is, *εἰς ταμεῖον αὐτοῦ*, into His provision-room or pantry.]

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “where there are honeys of good fragrance.”]

## CHAPTER III

How abundant are the fruits that return to those who have received the Lord’s body; how Christ responds to the Church, which rejoices in the multitude of her guests; and, finally, how great is the delight that the faithful, brought back from Egyptian slavery, experience in this food.

12. You have therefore come to the altar and received the body of Christ. Hear again what sacraments you have received. Hear holy David speaking; he too foresaw these mysteries in the Spirit, rejoiced, and declared that nothing was lacking to him. Why? Because whoever has received the body of Christ will never hunger.

13. How often have you heard the twenty-second Psalm and not understood it? See how fitting it is for the heavenly sacraments (*On Consecration*, distinction 2, chapter *In calicem*, § “Hear the psalm”):

“The Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing. He has placed me there in a pastureland. He has led me beside waters of refreshment; He has restored my soul. He has led me along paths of righteousness for His name’s sake. For even if I walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, because You are with me. Your rod and Your staff—they themselves have comforted me” (Psalm XXII, 1 ff.).

The rod is authority; the staff is suffering—that is, Christ’s eternal divinity, but also His bodily suffering. The former created; the latter redeemed.

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads, “the suffering is”; the eternal divinity of Christ is, while the suffering is temporal.]

“You have prepared a table before me in the sight of those who afflict me. You have anointed my head with oil, and my cup, making me drunk, is exceedingly excellent.”

14. You have therefore come to the altar, received the grace of Christ, and obtained the heavenly sacraments. The Church rejoices in the redemption of many and delights, with spiritual exultation, that a white-clad household stands before her. You have this in the Song of Songs. Rejoicing, she summons Christ, having prepared a banquet that seems worthy of heavenly feasting. Therefore she says: “Let my brother come down into his garden and gather the fruit of his fruit trees” (Song of Songs V, 1). What are these fruit trees? You had become a dry tree in Adam; but now, through Christ’s grace, you have burgeoned as fruit-bearing trees.

[Note: All editions and some manuscripts read, “You have sprouted as a fruit-bearing tree”; two manuscripts read, “you sprout,” and two others, “he has sprouted.” The oldest and most numerous, however, prefer the reading given in the text. Although this does not quite agree with the preceding clause, it is nevertheless not unlike the author’s style, which is always simpler than precise.]

[Note: From this passage and from chapter 8 of *On the Mysteries*, it may be observed that in those churches the newly baptized were accustomed to communicate in the sacred mysteries at the altar. As for the other faithful, however, the practice was not everywhere the same. At Constantinople it was customary for laymen, at least those holding higher rank, after approaching the altar to offer bread for consecration, to remain in the choir until they had become participants in the sacraments. At Milan, however, after making the offering, these same laymen immediately withdrew from the choir and then presented themselves again at the altar to partake of the sacrifice. There Ambrose observed this rule so strictly that he ordered Theodosius himself, who had remained inside the enclosure of the clergy after offering the customary gift, to withdraw; the most pious emperor immediately obeyed, as we shall relate in its proper place. Moreover, the Council of Laodicea had likewise ordered this practice to be observed in the Eastern Church in canon 19, and in later times the Council of Toledo IV established the same rule for Spain in canon 17. Nevertheless, it may be learned not only from Gregory of Tours, Book IX, chapter 3, and Book X, chapter 8, but also from the cited Council of Toledo, that the contrary practice prevailed in the Gallican churches; for in canon 4 the same rite is established and approved.]

15. The Lord Jesus gladly receives this and, with heavenly condescension, answers His Church: “I have come down,” He says, “into my garden; I have gathered myrrh with my perfumes; I have eaten my bread with my honey, and I have drunk my wine with my milk. Eat, my brothers,” He says, “and drink deeply” (ibid.).

16. “I have gathered myrrh with my perfumes.” What is this vintage? Recognize the vineyard, and you will recognize the vintage. “You brought a vine out of Egypt” (Psalm LXXIX, 9), that is, the people of God. You are the vineyard; you are the vintage. Planted as a vineyard, you have yielded fruit as a vintage. “I have gathered myrrh with my perfumes,” that is, in the fragrance which you have received.

[Note: Quite a few manuscripts read, “and acknowledge the vintage.” Again, in the following verse, instead of “that is, the people of God,” some manuscripts have, “this is the people of God.” This is not inappropriate.]

17. “I have eaten my bread with my honey.” You see that there is no bitterness in this bread, but complete sweetness. “I have drunk my wine with my milk.” You see that this is a joy undefiled by the filth of any sin. For whenever you drink, you receive remission of sins, and you become drunk in the Spirit (*On Consecration*, distinction 2, chapter *In calicem*, § “Whenever”).

[Note: This sentence is expounded at length and elegantly in Book I, *On Cain and Abel*, chapter 5, section 19, from which it was perhaps transferred to this passage.]

Therefore the Apostle also says: “Do not become drunk with wine . . . but be filled with the Holy Spirit” (Ephesians V, 18). For one who becomes drunk with wine staggers and reels; one who becomes drunk with the Spirit is rooted in Christ. And therefore it is an excellent drunkenness that produces sobriety of mind. These are the things that we have briefly reviewed concerning the sacraments.

## CHAPTER IV

To instruct the newly faithful in a pattern of prayer, he briefly expounds the Lord’s Prayer, set before them as in a mirror.

18. What remains now except prayer? And do not think that it is a matter of little importance to know how you ought to pray. The holy Apostles said to the Lord Jesus: “Lord, teach us to pray, just as John taught his disciples.” Then the Lord said: “Our Father who are in heaven, hallowed be Your name; Your kingdom come; Your will be done, as in heaven so also on earth; give us this day our daily bread; and forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors; and do not allow us to be led into temptation, but deliver us from evil” (Luke XI, 1 ff.). You see how brief the prayer is, yet full of every virtue. What grace there is in its first utterance!

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads, “When you pray, say: ‘Father,’” etc. The Lord’s Prayer, which the author here explains to the neophytes, was customarily expounded by bishops in many churches to catechumens before baptism, as we have noted in Book I, *On the Duties of the Clergy*, chapter 2, section 10. From this one may infer that in such ceremonies practices also differed according to locality. Indeed, we find that the same practice was not always preserved even in the same church. For example, Augustine, sermon 227, which is counted as the fourth on Easter Day, expressly says that the newly baptized, after the sanctification had been completed, “returned” the Lord’s Prayer; whereas in sermon 58 he plainly says that on the vigil of the same feast they were to return not the Prayer but the Creed. We may therefore believe that this was left to the bishops, so that they might establish these rites according to circumstances, time, and the number of those being baptized. It is also possible that the passage in sermon 58 was corrupted by scribal transposition and should be corrected to read, “not the Creed, but the Prayer”; examples of such transpositions are frequent in manuscripts. Nor would it be unreasonable to understand the words of sermon 227—“we speak of the Lord’s Prayer which you received and returned”—not of the recitation that the neophytes made before the presbyter, but of that in which they pronounced the Prayer together with the celebrating bishop and the entire people present at the sacred rites.]

19. O man! You did not dare to lift your face toward heaven; you directed your eyes toward the earth; and suddenly you received the grace of Christ—all your sins were forgiven you. From an evil servant you became a good son. Therefore have confidence, not in your own works but in the grace of Christ; for the Apostle says: “By grace you have been saved” (Ephesians II, 5). This, then, is not arrogance but faith; to proclaim what you have received is not pride but devotion.

Therefore lift your eyes to the Father who begot you through the washing; to the Father who redeemed you through the Son; and say: “Our Father.” It is a good confidence, but a moderate one. You call Him Father as a son, but do not claim anything for yourself in a special sense. The Father is specially the Father of Christ alone; He is the common Father of us all, because He alone begot Christ, whereas He created us. Therefore you too, by grace, say: “Our Father,” so that you may deserve to be a son. Commend yourself to Him through the Church’s regard and consideration.

20. “Our Father who are in heaven.” What does “in heaven” mean? Hear Scripture saying: “The Lord is exalted above all the heavens” (Psalm CXII, 4).

[Note: Thus read the majority and the better manuscripts. Others, together with the old edition, read, “The Lord is exalted above all the nations,” to which the Roman edition adds, “and His glory above the heavens.” We think, however, that our author reported from that verse only the words that served his purpose.]

And everywhere you find that the Lord is above the heavens of heavens—as though the angels were not in heaven, as though the Dominions were not in heaven. But He is in those heavens of which it is said: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Psalm XVIII, 2). Heaven is where sin has ceased; heaven is where crimes are punished; heaven is where there is no wound of death.

21. “Our Father who are in heaven: hallowed be Your name.” What does “hallowed” mean? Is it as though we wish Him to be sanctified who says, “Be holy, because I am holy” (Leviticus XIX, 2), as though some sanctification were added to Him through our prayer? No. Rather, may He be sanctified in us, so that His sanctification may reach us.

[Note: The old edition, together with some manuscripts, reads, “from our preaching.” Later, after the words “I was born for this,” the Roman edition adds, “and for this I came into the world.”]

22. “Our Father who are in heaven: hallowed be Your name; Your kingdom come.” Is God’s kingdom not eternal? Jesus Himself says: “For this I was born” (John XVIII, 37), and you say to the Father: “Your kingdom come” (Luke XVII, 21), as though it had not come. But God’s kingdom comes when you have obtained His grace (*On Consecration*, distinction 2, chapter *In calicem*, § “Your will be done”). For He Himself says: “The kingdom of God is within you.”

[Note: All editions and manuscripts read as in the text, except that in some of the latter, and in the Roman edition, the words “the Lord” are omitted. This passage, like the one below—“How? You have this in the Song of Songs”—is found without a question mark in not a few manuscripts.]

23. “Your kingdom come; Your will be done, as in heaven so on earth; give us this day our daily bread.” All things have been reconciled through the blood of Christ, whether in heaven or on earth. Heaven has been sanctified; the devil has been cast down.

[Note: All editions read “the devil.” It occurs there where the man does also; but all manuscripts, as in our text—with one or two exceptions, in which “the devil, where the man also occurs” is read.]

Where does he move about? Where also the man whom he deceived is. “Your will be done” means: let there be peace on earth, just as in heaven.

24. “Give us this day our daily bread.” I remember my discourse when I was treating the sacraments (above, Book IV, chapter 4). I told you that before Christ’s words, what is offered is called bread; but once Christ’s words have been pronounced, it is no longer called bread but is named the body (*On Consecration*, distinction 2, chapter *In calicem*, § “I told you”). Why then, in the Lord’s Prayer that follows, does He say, “Our bread” (John VI, 35)? He did say “bread,” but *ἐπιούσιον* (*epiousion*), that is, “supersubstantial.” This is not the bread that passes into the body, but that bread of eternal life which supports the substance of our soul (*On Consecration*, distinction 2, chapter “This is not the bread”).

[Note: Thus read all editions and a very small number of manuscripts. In the others, as also in Augustine’s sermon 84 of the Appendix, the phrase “which the Greeks call coming” is absent. Joseph Scaliger denies that *ἐπιούσιον* can be rendered by *supersubstantial*, since, he says, it is not derived from *οὐσία*; one would have to say *ἐπούσιον*. Rather, it comes from *ἐπί* and *ἰών, ἰόντος, ἰοῦσα, ἰούσης*, from *ἔω*, whence *ἄπειμι*; hence later *ἐπιοῦσα*, with *ἡμέρα* understood, “the following day,” or “tomorrow.” This is correct and suitable for illuminating this passage of our author. But we shall discuss it again in Book III, *On the Faith*, chapter 7.]

Therefore it is called *ἐπιούσιος* in Greek. The Latin, however, called this bread “daily,” whereas the Greeks call it “coming,” because the Greeks say *τὴν ἐπιοῦσαν ἡμέραν*, “the coming day.” Thus both expressions—the Latin and the Greek—seem useful: the Greek signified both meanings in a single word, while the Latin said “daily.”

25. If the bread is daily, why do you take it only after a year, as the Greeks in the East have been accustomed to do? Receive daily what benefits you daily. Live so that you may deserve to receive it daily. Whoever does not deserve to receive it daily does not deserve to receive it after a year. How did holy Job offer sacrifice daily for his children, lest perhaps they had sinned either in their heart or in their speech? Therefore you hear that whenever the sacrifice is offered, it signifies the Lord’s death, the Lord’s resurrection, the Lord’s ascension, and the remission of sins; and yet you do not receive this bread of life daily (I Corinthians XI, 26)? Whoever has a wound seeks medicine. The wound is that we are under sin; the medicine is the heavenly and venerable sacrament.

[Note: As we indicated in the Preface, one may not rashly conclude that Ambrose instituted in certain of his works this kind of complaint about the negligence of his people in receiving Christ’s body. He does indeed imply in Book III, *On Penance*, chapter 9, that some abstained from Holy Communion under the pretext of penance; but the passage, when examined carefully, proves abundantly that this abstinence was neither universal nor so prolonged. It must nevertheless be admitted that by that century the former practice of daily communion had grown cold, as we understand from Jerome’s letters 50, *Against Jovinian*, and 28, *To Lucerius*, as well as Augustine’s letter 54 to Januarius. Yet they did not condemn the later practice in such a way as to conceal that they preferred the earlier one; indeed, Augustine, sermon 227 of the new edition, attempts to lead the neophytes to the daily Eucharistic banquet by the same reasoning as the present author. As for the Greeks, it is true that Chrysostom rebukes the distaste and negligence of his people in receiving the Eucharist in homily 3 on the Epistle to the Ephesians, and speaks still more openly in homily 5 on the First Epistle to Timothy about the annual reception of the Lord’s body. Nevertheless, it is sufficiently clear from the same homily 3, cited above, that this lack of devotion did not belong to everyone, and consequently was no greater in the East than in the West. For this reason Ambrose does not seem to have reproached the Greeks rather than the Latins with this custom; indeed, one may reasonably infer from this that the accusation is more appropriate to some later author.]

26. “Give us this day our daily bread.” If you receive it daily, each day is “today” for you. If Christ is “today” for you, He rises for you daily. How? “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Psalm II, 7). Today, then, is the day when Christ rises. “He is the same yesterday and today,” the Apostle Paul says (Hebrews XIII, 8). But elsewhere he says: “The night has advanced, and the day has drawn near” (Romans XIII, 12): yesterday’s night has advanced, and today’s day has drawn near.

27. It follows: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” What is a debt except sin?

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “Therefore, if you do not receive it, you will not need it”; others partly, “Therefore, if you had not received it, you would not have needed it”; and partly as in the text. The editions do not differ from these except that they have “even if” instead of “if,” which is less suitable. Immediately afterward, where the old edition and many manuscripts read, “you are born rich,” while some others read, “you were born rich,” the Roman edition, although supported by only a few manuscripts, more aptly reads, “you would be born rich.”]

Therefore, if you had not taken the money of another’s interest, you would not be in need; and for this reason sin is imputed to you. You possessed the money with which you might have been born rich. You were rich, made in the image and likeness of God (Genesis I, 26); you lost what you possessed—that is, humility—when you sought to claim arrogance. You lost your wealth, just as Adam was made naked (Genesis III, 7); you accepted from the devil a debt that was unnecessary. And so, though you were free in Christ, you became the devil’s debtor. The enemy held your bond, but the Lord crucified it and erased it with His own blood (Colossians II, 14); He removed your debt and restored your freedom.

28. He therefore rightly says: “And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” Consider what you are saying: “As I forgive, so also forgive me.” If you forgive, you deal rightly so that you may be forgiven. If you do not forgive, how do you appeal to Him so that you may be forgiven?

[Note: All editions read, “you deal rightly”; all manuscripts, “you appeal rightly,” which makes excellent sense, as the following words show: “how do you appeal to Him,” that is, “how do you compel Him by your address,” etc.]

29. “And do not allow us to be led into temptation, but deliver us from evil.” Consider what He says: “Do not allow us to be led into temptation that we cannot bear.” He does not say, “Do not lead us into temptation,” but, as though He were speaking of an athlete, He wants such temptation as human nature can bear; and may each person be delivered from evil—that is, from the enemy, from sin.

[Note: The latest Paris edition reads, “from vice”; the other editions and all manuscripts more suitably read, “from the enemy.” What is found in Greek, *ἀπὸ τοῦ πονηροῦ*, is commonly rendered in Latin “from evil” or “from the evil one,” expressions by which the evil spirit is usually designated by the holy Fathers, although the phrase may also be understood in the neuter gender as referring to any calamity or disadvantage.]

[Note: The editor says that these words cannot be an exposition of the preceding petition, as the author himself clearly indicates, since not only here and at the beginning of the chapter, but also in the following book, chapter 5, after the words “to be led into temptation,” he immediately adds the final petition, “but deliver us from evil.” St. Hilary, on the other hand, in Psalm CXVIII, verse 8, seems to have wished to refer the same words to the biblical text, saying: “This too is contained in the order of the Lord’s Prayer, when it says: ‘Do not abandon us to temptation which we cannot bear.’” Yet these words are found neither in the Gospels of Matthew and Luke nor in any other Fathers.]

30. The Lord is powerful: He has taken away your sin and forgiven your offenses. He is able to protect and guard you against the hostile snares of the devil, so that the enemy who habitually generates guilt may not creep upon you. But whoever entrusts himself to God does not fear the devil. “If God is for us, who can be against us?” (Romans VIII, 31). To Him, therefore, be praise and glory from the ages, and now, and always, and forever and ever. Amen.

## BOOK SIX

### CHAPTER I

Since Christ’s true flesh and true blood are present in the sacrament, consecrated, that is, by the omnipotence of the divine Word and concealed under an alien appearance lest they cause offence, we may understand from this that in that food we participate in the divine substance.

1. As our Lord Jesus Christ is the true Son of God, not as other human beings are sons by grace, but as Son from the substance of the Father, so the flesh which we receive is true flesh, as He Himself said, and His drink is true (*On Consecration*, distinction 2, chapter *Sicut est verus*).

[Note: Lanfranc read this passage as follows: “other human beings by grace, but as Son by nature,” that is, from the substance of the Father. The continuation found in Amerbach, Erasmus, and by far the greater number of manuscripts is read as in the text; Gill likewise reads it thus, except that before “is drink” he wished the word “blood” to be supplied. But the Roman edition, with the same Lanfranc, three French manuscripts, and one Vatican manuscript in the margin, restores the text thus: “so His flesh is true . . . and His blood, which we drink, is true.” Were not the number and antiquity of the opposing manuscripts an obstacle, we should most willingly adopt this reading. Observe, moreover, that from this comparison it rightly follows that Christ’s flesh and blood are substantially in the sacrament.]

2. But perhaps you say—as the disciples of Christ also said at that time when they heard Him saying, “Unless anyone has eaten my flesh and drunk my blood, he will not abide in me and will not have eternal life” (John VI, 54)—perhaps you say: “How is it true? I see a likeness; I do not see the reality of blood” (*On Consecration*, distinction 2, chapter *Forte dicas*).

[Note: Thus the old edition and all manuscripts read, except a few in which “flesh” is added. This is less elegant, since the word “true” is referred at once to both flesh and blood. The Roman edition, with Gratian, states this more explicitly: “How is the flesh true? How is the blood true?”]

3. First of all, I told you above (Book IV, chapter 4) about Christ’s word, which works so as to be able to change and transform the kinds and established ordinances of nature (John VI, 67). Then, when His disciples could not bear Christ’s saying that He would give them His flesh to eat and His blood to drink, they departed; Peter alone, however, said: “You have the words of eternal life, and how can I depart from you?” (ibid., 69). Therefore, lest more should say this, as though there were some horror at blood, while the grace of redemption remained, you receive the sacrament indeed under a likeness, but truly attain the grace and power of its nature.

[Note: Erasmus and Gill read, “to transform the general ordinances of nature”; the Roman edition differs from them only by adding “into another” after “transform.” Amerbach and all the manuscripts agree with our text, except that some, including Lanfranc, read “the kinds and ordinances.” The author in this chapter states his answer to the objection drawn from sensory evidence—which he had already proposed in Book IV, chapter 4, section 14—in such a way as to cut off every evasion. First he recalls that substantial transformation has already been adequately proved; then he gives the reason why the sacrament was instituted under an alien appearance, which he calls a likeness.]

4. “I,” He says, “am the living bread which came down from heaven” (ibid., 41). But flesh did not come down from heaven; that is, He assumed flesh from the Virgin on earth. How, then, did bread come down from heaven, and living bread? Because our Lord Jesus Christ Himself shares both divinity and body; and you who receive the flesh participate, in that food, in His divine substance (*On Consecration*, distinction 2, chapter *Sicut est verus*, § “I am”).

### CHAPTER II

That in all the sacraments the operation of the Trinity and the equality of the divine persons may be observed; with a brief attack on the error of the Arians.

5. You have therefore received instruction concerning the sacraments; you have learned everything most fully: that you were baptized in the name of the Trinity. In all that we have done, the mystery of the Trinity has been preserved. Everywhere are the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit: one operation, one sanctification, although certain things may seem, as it were, special to particular persons.

6. How? God anointed you, the Lord sealed you, and placed the Holy Spirit in your heart (II Corinthians I, 21–22). You have therefore received the Holy Spirit in your heart. Receive another point: as the Holy Spirit is in the heart, so Christ also is in the heart. How? In the Song of Songs you have Christ saying to the Church: “Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arms” (Song of Songs VIII, 6).

[Note: Thus all editions and manuscripts read, except that in some manuscripts and in the Roman edition “the Lord” has been omitted. Not a few manuscripts present this passage, as also the one below, “How? You have this in the Song of Songs,” without a question mark.]

7. Therefore God anointed you and Christ sealed you. How? Because you have been sealed to the form of His very cross, to His passion; you have received a seal in His likeness, so that you may rise in His form and live according to His pattern—He who was crucified to sin and lives to God; and your old human being, immersed in the font, was crucified to sin but rose again to God (Romans VI, 4 ff.).

8. Then elsewhere you have something special: God called you, while in baptism you are, as it were, specially crucified together with Christ. Then again, when you receive the spiritual seal, as it were specially, see that there is a distinction of persons, but that the whole mystery of the Trinity is connected.

9. Then what did the Apostle tell you, as was read the day before yesterday? “There are divisions of gifts, but the same Spirit. There are divisions of ministries, but the same Lord. There are divisions of operations, but the same God, who works all things in all” (I Corinthians XII, 4 ff.). “God,” he says, “works all things.” But concerning the Spirit of God it was also read: “One and the same Spirit, distributing to each as He wills” (ibid., 21). Hear Scripture say that the Spirit distributes according to His own will, not according to obedience. Therefore the Spirit distributes grace to you as He wills, not as He is commanded; especially since the Spirit of God is the Spirit of Christ. And hold fast that He is the Holy Spirit, the Spirit of God, the Spirit of Christ, the Paraclete Spirit.

[Note: All editions and some manuscripts read “divisions of mysteries”; the others, with the apostolic text, more rightly read “divisions of ministries”; some also read “administrations.”]

10. The Arians think that they disparage the Holy Spirit if they call Him the Paraclete Spirit. What is “Paraclete” except “comforter”? As though it had not also been read of the Father that He is the God of consolation (II Corinthians I, 3). You see, therefore, that they think the Holy Spirit is disparaged in that in which the power of the eternal Father is proclaimed with devout affection.

### CHAPTER III

Intending to teach the manner of prayer, he reconciles Christ’s words with those of the Apostle, declaring that the chamber of which Christ speaks must be understood as the secrecy and silence of the heart.

11. Now receive how we ought to pray. The powers of prayer are many. Where we ought to pray is neither an insignificant nor a trivial question. The Apostle says: “I desire men to pray in every place, lifting up pure hands without anger and disputing” (I Timothy I, 8). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “But when you pray, enter into your chamber; and when you have shut the door, pray to your Father” (Matthew VI, 6). Does it not seem contradictory for the Apostle to say, “Pray in every place,” while the Lord says, “Enter into your chamber and pray”? But it is not contradictory. Let us therefore resolve this; then how you ought to begin prayer, in what order to arrange it, what to weave into it, what to plead, how to close prayer, and then for whom you ought to pray: let us discuss all these things.

[Note: Not a few manuscripts, and not inferior ones, read: “Let us learn all these things.”]

12. First, where you ought to pray. Paul seems to say one thing, the Lord another. Can Paul teach contrary to Christ’s commands? Certainly not. On what ground? Because he is not Christ’s opponent but His interpreter: “Be imitators of me,” he says, “as I also am of Christ.” What then? You can pray everywhere, and you can always pray in your chamber. You have your chamber everywhere. Though you are placed among Gentiles or among Jews, you nevertheless have your secret place everywhere. Your chamber is your mind. Though you are in a crowd, you preserve your hidden and secret place in the inward human being.

13. “But when you pray, enter into your chamber.” He rightly says, “enter,” lest you pray as the Jew does, to whom it is said: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isaiah IX, 13). Therefore let your prayer not proceed merely from your lips. Attend wholly with your mind; enter into the recess of your breast; enter wholly. Let Him, whom you desire to please, not see you as perfunctory. Let Him see that you pray from the heart, so that He may deign to hear you as one praying from the heart.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “into the chamber of your breast.”]

14. “But when you pray, enter into your chamber.” You have this elsewhere also: “Walk, my people, and enter into your inner rooms; shut your door; hide yourself for a little while, until the Lord’s wrath has passed” (Isaiah XXVI, 20). The Lord spoke this through the prophet; but in the Gospel He said: “But when you pray, enter into your chamber; and when you have shut the door, pray to your Father.”

15. What does “with the door closed” mean? [Note: All editions and many manuscripts read this correctly as above; nevertheless, several others prefer: “Hear what door you have to close”; one even reads: “What door do we have? Hear what you ought to [close],” etc. Albertinus, however, accuses the Author of absurdity on the basis of this passage, because he immediately adds: “Would that women would listen!”—as though it could seem absurd to any sane person that women should be reminded of modesty when they appeared to have forgotten it so completely that they made themselves intolerable in the Church, as the Author indicates in the following chapter. By the same reasoning one could certainly say that Ambrose himself was being absurd, since similar remarks are found in Book III of *On Virginity*, chapter 3, section 11 and following.] Hear what door you have, what door you ought to close when you pray. Would that women would listen! You have already heard; holy David taught you, saying: “Set, O Lord, a guard over my mouth, and a door around my lips” (Psalm 140:3). There is another door, of which the Apostle Paul speaks, saying: “That a door of the word may be opened to me for speaking the mystery of Christ” (Colossians 4:3). This means: when you pray, do not cry out in speech, do not pour out your prayer, and do not parade it before the crowds. Pray in your secret place, confident that the One who sees all things and hears everything can hear you in secret. And pray to your Father in secret, [Note: Old editions and not a few manuscripts read: “and hears”; Erasmus and Gill: “he will hear you pleading”; the Roman edition: “where he hears you pleading”; the other manuscripts read as in the text—except the Claromontanus manuscript, which has: “for he who sees in secret sees you pleading.”] who hears you pleading in secret.

# CHAPTER IV

Why one ought to pray in secret rather than with loud cries; why men ought to pray in every place, but women ought not; and what the following words refer to: “lifting pure hands,” and so forth.

16. Let us ask what benefit there is in this, and for what reason we ought to pray more in secret than with loud cries. Listen: let us take an example from human custom. If you ask someone who hears quickly, you do not think shouting is necessary; you ask quietly, in a measured voice. If you ask someone who is deaf, do you not begin to shout so that he may hear you? Therefore, whoever cries out thinks that God cannot hear him in any other way than by his shouting; [Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “And whoever asks him with a cry.” This passage also belongs to the number of those impaled upon Albertinus’s “spit.” Yet if the one who supplied the passage is being absurd by implying that the person who cries out thinks he will never be heard by God unless he cries out, who does not see that an impious person could bring a similar charge against Christ himself—as though, in Matthew chapter 6, he had supposed that those who pray at length were convinced that they would obtain nothing except through many words? But although it is probable that the Author had this Gospel passage in mind, he also seems to allude to the cries of the prophets of Baal, as well as to Elijah’s words mocking them in 1 Kings 18.] and when he asks Him in that manner, he detracts from His power. But whoever prays in silence places faith in God and confesses that God is “the searcher of heart and inward parts” (Psalm 7:10), and that He hears your prayer before it is poured forth from your mouth.

17. Therefore let us consider the words: “I desire, then, that men pray in every place” (1 Timothy 2:8). Why did he say “men”? Certainly prayer is common to women and men alike. I find no explanation except perhaps that the holy Apostle said “men” so that women would not usurp the command, misunderstand “in every place,” and begin shouting everywhere—women whom we cannot tolerate in the Church.

18. “I desire, then, that men”—that is, those who are able to keep the command—“pray in every place, lifting pure hands.” What does “lifting pure hands” mean? Are you really supposed, in your prayer, to display the Lord’s cross to the Gentiles? That sign is indeed a sign of virtue, not of shame. [Note: Several manuscripts read: “It is a sign of virtue, not of shame.” Again, very many offer: “You lift pure hands … you lift them,” whereas some others and all editions read: “Lift,” and so forth. The latter is more elegant. The fact that he previously stated that the Lord’s cross should not be ostentatiously displayed to the Gentiles points to the ancient Christian practice by which suppliants raised their arms in the form of a cross. See Book I of *On Virginity*, chapter 2, and Book II, chapter 4.] Yet there is a way in which you can pray without displaying the figure, but by lifting up your deeds. If you wish to perform your work, lift pure hands through innocence. Lift them not every day: once you have lifted them, there is no need to lift them again.

19. “I desire, then, that men pray in every place, lifting pure hands without anger and disputation.” Nothing is truer: “Anger,” he says, “destroys even the wise” (Proverbs 15:1). Therefore, at all times, insofar as possible, a Christian man ought to restrain his anger, and especially when he approaches prayer, lest indignation disturb your spirit, lest a kind of furious rage obstruct your prayer. [Note: All editions and some manuscripts read: “when he approaches, lest indignation disturb his mind, lest a kind of fury of anger obstruct his prayer.” This is smoother, etc. But several other and better manuscripts read as in the text.] Rather, approach with a calm heart. Why are you angry? Has a servant sinned? You are approaching prayer so that your own sins may be forgiven you, and yet you are indignant. This is what it means to pray “without anger.”

# CHAPTER V

On the disordered disputation of those who pray, and on the modesty with which women ought to pray; likewise, on the beginning, middle, and end of prayer, with a repeated exposition of the Lord’s Prayer, carrying the treatise to its conclusion.

20. Now let us consider disputation. Often a businessman or a miser comes to prayer: one thinks about money, another about profit, another about honor, another about desire—and he thinks that God can hear him. Therefore, when you pray, it is fitting that you prefer divine things to human things.

21. Likewise, he says, “I desire women to pray, not displaying themselves in ornaments or in pearls,” as the Apostle Paul says (1 Timothy 2:9). But the Apostle Peter also says: “The grace of a woman is of the greatest value, so that her husband’s affection may be converted through his wife’s good conduct, and the unbeliever may be converted to the grace of Christ” (1 Peter 3:1–2). The dignity, modesty, and good conduct of a woman have this power: they call her husband to faith and devotion, just as the speech of a prudent man often accomplishes the same. Therefore, he says, “let a woman not have her adornment in the decoration of her hair or in braided tresses, but in prayer from a pure heart,” where there is “the hidden person of the heart,” who is always rich before God (ibid. 3–4). You therefore possess the means by which you may be rich. In Christ, your riches are modesty and the insignia of chastity, faith, devotion, and mercy. These are the treasures of righteousness, as the prophet recalled (Isaiah 33:6).

22. Next, let us consider where you ought to begin. Tell me: if you wished to ask a person for something and began in this way—“Give me; here is what I am asking you for”—would not the prayer seem arrogant? Therefore prayer ought to begin with praise of God, so that you may ask the almighty God, for whom all things are possible and who has the will to grant them. Supplication follows, as the Apostle taught when he said: “I urge, then, first of all, that prayers, supplications, petitions, and thanksgivings be made” (1 Timothy 2:1). The first prayer, therefore, ought to contain praise of God; the second, supplication; the third, petition; the fourth, thanksgiving. You ought not to begin like a starving person by asking first for food, but first with the praises of God.

23. For this reason these wise advocates also follow this discipline: they make the judge favorable to them. They begin with his praises in order to make the judge well disposed toward them. Then gradually they begin to ask the judge graciously to listen patiently. Third, they dare to set forth their petition and state what they are asking. Fourth, just as they began with praises of God, so they ought to end in praise.

24. You have this pattern in the Lord’s Prayer: “Our Father who art in heaven” (Matthew 6:9). [Note: This is how the great majority of manuscripts and the ancient editions read. Some manuscripts and old editions, however, do not have *est* (“is”), and Gill, with two manuscripts, reads *nova* (“new”) instead of *in eo* (“in him”), not implausibly. A few others, together with the Roman edition, read: “Here is the praise of God, because he is proclaimed as Father,” and so forth. Whereas all editions present “and on earth,” all manuscripts, with two exceptions, prefer “not on earth.”] It is praise of God that He is proclaimed Father; in this lies the glory of His loving kindness. It is praise of God that He dwells in heaven, not on earth. “Our Father who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name”—that is, so that He may sanctify His servants; for His name is sanctified in us when Christian people are proclaimed. Thus “hallowed be thy name” is the expression of a wish. “Thy kingdom come” (ibid. 10): this is a petition, that the kingdom of Christ may be in us. If God reigns in us, the adversary cannot find a place. Guilt does not reign; sin does not reign; rather, virtue reigns, chastity reigns, devotion reigns. Then: “Thy will be done, as in heaven and on earth. Give us this day our daily bread” (ibid. 11). This is the greatest of the petitions that are made. “And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (ibid. 12). Therefore receive it daily, so that daily you may ask forgiveness for your debt. “And do not permit us to be led into temptation, but deliver us from evil” (ibid. 13). What follows? Hear what the priest says: [Note: These words seem to indicate that the concluding formula was customarily recited by the priest alone. In the Greek Church, according to Arias Montanus, the priest likewise alone pronounced: “For thine is the kingdom,” and so forth—ὅτι σου ἔστιν ἡ βασιλεία—which was transferred from the liturgies of James, Basil, and Chrysostom into the Gospel text of Matthew and into the Eastern versions, as Erasmus, Grotius, and others have observed. Since the mentioned conclusion is used in no Latin churches, it is certain that the church governed by this Author was in that rite more closely aligned with the East.] “Through our Lord Jesus Christ, in whom is to you, with whom is to you, honor, praise, glory, majesty, and power with the Holy Spirit, from the ages, and now, and always, and unto all ages of ages. Amen.”

25. [Note: This is how all editions and many manuscripts read. Others have, in part, “This Psalm of David,” and in part, “Another Psalm of David,” and so forth. In the preface we noted that a new sermon begins with these words in the Saint Gall manuscript. We add that the same words are written in one Reginensis manuscript as though they were the beginning of a new treatise; in the Claromontanus manuscript, however, they are entirely omitted together with the rest of the section.] Another point: although the Psalms of David are one little book containing the forms of prayer whose virtues we described above (above, section 22), nevertheless all these parts of prayer are often found in a single psalm, as we find in the eighth psalm. It begins in this way: “O Lord, our Lord, how wonderful is thy name in all the earth!” (Psalm 8:2). This is therefore the first prayer. Then comes supplication: “For I shall see thy heavens, the works of thy fingers”—that is, “I shall see the heavens, the moon and the stars which thou hast founded” (ibid. 4). [Note: The Roman edition had cut the words “that is, I shall see the heavens.”] Certainly he does not say, “I shall see heaven,” but “I shall see the heavens,” in which grace and heavenly splendor begin to grow bright. The Prophet was then promising himself that these heavens would be given to him, for those who deserved heavenly grace from the Lord. [Note: Several manuscripts read this way; the others and the ancient editions differ in having: “the stars of heavenly grace rising.” This is less suitable. The Roman edition alone reads: “he would deserve … the stars, men shining with heavenly glory.”] “The moon and the stars which thou hast founded”: by the moon he calls the Church, and by the stars he calls the saints shining with heavenly grace. Then observe his petition: “What is man that thou art mindful of him, or the son of man that thou visitest him? Thou hast made him a little less than the angels; thou hast crowned him with glory and honor, and hast set him over the works of thy hands” (ibid. 6–7). Then there is another thanksgiving: “Thou hast subjected all things beneath his feet, all sheep and oxen, and moreover the beasts of the field,” and so forth (ibid. 8 and following).

26. We have taught, according to the measure of our understanding, perhaps what we have not learned; and we have expressed it as best we could. [Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “perhaps what we have learned from the Lord.”] Your Holiness, instructed in priestly observances, should labor to hold fast what you have received from God, so that an offering, like a pure sacrifice, may always recognize its own seal in you. [Note: Several manuscripts read: “so that the offering, like a pure sacrifice, may recognize its own seal in you,” which is quite suitable. Several others agree with us, except that the Vallilucensis manuscript reads *sit ut* (“may be as”) instead of *sicut* (“like”), not implausibly. The remaining manuscripts and all editions also agree with us, except for the word *et* (“and”), which they place before *in vobis* (“in you”), thereby completely corrupting the sense.] Thus you too may attain grace and the rewards of virtue, through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong glory, honor, praise, and perpetuity from the ages, and now, and always, and unto all ages of ages. Amen.

# [ON PENANCE]

[Col. 0461]

## INTRODUCTION TO THE TWO BOOKS ON PENANCE

Since these two books were written against the Novatians, and since it will be easier to grasp Ambrose’s purpose, the order and progression of the work, and the force and weight of his arguments, we thought it would not be unwelcome to the reader if we set before him the origin of that heresy, its development, and the condition in which it stood when these books were composed.

The Novatians were named after the founders of the sect, Novatus and Novatianus. Although most of the ancients, especially the Greeks, improperly confuse them with one another, Ambrose invariably distinguishes them. The former was a presbyter of the Church of Carthage, but never attained episcopal dignity; in this matter Baronius, Petavius, Labeus, and several others were mistaken. He was restless and wicked in spirit, and suited for nothing so much as the creation of innovations. He had joined himself to Felicissimus, who foolishly maintained that peace should be restored to those who had lapsed into idolatry without imposing any penalty upon them. To lend his heresy a little more authority, he pushed Felicissimus forward by every artifice and intrigue toward the diaconate, although the bishop himself, Cyprian, not only did not consent but was not even consulted. They added to this crime others full of both shamelessness and savage cruelty, on account of which a day was appointed for him to answer before Cyprian. But the persecution that had meanwhile been renewed prevented further investigation of him. Novatus used this opportunity to flee to Rome. When he arrived there near the beginning of the year 251, he found the clergy and people divided over the appointment of a pontiff in place of Fabian, who had recently suffered martyrdom.

Two presbyters, Cornelius and Novatianus, had drawn the divided factions of the Romans to themselves. Novatianus professed the doctrines of the Stoic philosophers. He was a man of exceptionally sharp intellect, extensive learning, and no ordinary eloquence. Yet, apart from the fact that he had been subjected to exorcisms, he had been baptized in bed because of illness, and the bishop had not confirmed him with sacred anointing. Nevertheless, the same prelate overlooked these deficiencies and honored him with priestly dignity, thereby arousing considerable offense in the minds of the people. Thus, when the greater and more just number of votes had given the pontificate to Cornelius—a man of outstanding virtue who had been exercised in every rank of the Church—Novatianus, unable to bear rejection, resolved with himself to overturn that election. To accomplish this, he wrote a notorious pamphlet against Cornelius; finally, he denied that Cornelius’s ordination was legitimate because he did not exclude from his communion those Christians who, during the raging persecution, had burned incense to idols. He drew not a few of the people into his faction. Novatus, judging this opportunity favorable to his own affairs, attached himself to Novatianus. Thus, in order to advance Novatianus’s cause with all his strength, he contrived that Novatianus should be ordained pontiff by three bishops whom he had summoned for this purpose from a small and extremely obscure part of Italy, men who were inexperienced and simple. It was then that the name “antipope,” previously unknown to the established religion of Christ, first began to be heard. Novatianus announced his ordination by letters and envoys sent to the African and Eastern Churches, but it was rejected everywhere.

Meanwhile, in order to continue stirring up hatred against Cornelius and to acquire authority under the pretext of discipline, Novatianus taught that the Church lacked the power by which the crime of those who had lapsed could be forgiven. These people were divided into *Libellatici*, *Thurificatores*, and *Apostates*, although he did not at all deny that they should be exhorted to works of penance. At first they confined themselves within these limits. But when they were pressed hard by Cyprian and the other Fathers—who demonstrated that it was a supreme injustice to grant pardon for graver sins, such as murder and adultery, while denying it only to the lapsed—they were finally driven to assert that all sins were equally incapable of forgiveness. Their followers were nevertheless ashamed of this madness; later there were some who wished to restrict the position to the more serious crimes alone.

Many were attracted by this appearance of severity, and within a short time a numerous sect arose from them. To distinguish themselves from the orthodox, they arrogated to themselves the extremely presumptuous name Καθαρῶν, that is, “of the pure.” Socrates composed, with considerable praise, an extensive catalogue of the bishops of this sect (Book IV of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 21). He also describes the struggles undertaken by its adherents on behalf of Christ’s divinity, and reports that their constancy under punishment was so conspicuous that even Catholics, moved by it, wished to join their prayers with theirs in their churches. These accounts would be less suspect if they had not come from a writer so favorably disposed toward them. Various councils condemned this heresy and prescribed what was to be observed regarding those who returned to the Church. Although the most learned of the Fathers directed their pens against it, the sect nevertheless persisted for a very long time, spreading through nearly every region of the Christian world.

Ambrose encountered the heresy in this condition when he attacked it in these two books (chapter 1). He begins most appropriately with a commendation of moderation, a virtue certainly lacking among the Novatians. He then asserts the power entrusted to the Church to absolve crimes of every kind (chapter 2), demonstrating that God is more inclined toward mercy than toward severity (chapters 3 and 4). After answering the objection drawn from divine immutability (chapter 5), he in turn presses them sharply with various testimonies from Scripture, especially with Christ’s promise to Peter of the keys of heaven (sections 32 and 33). He joins to these other considerations drawn from their principles and practices (chapter 8). Then, proceeding to other objections (chapter 9), he dwells especially on refuting their claim concerning the “sin unto death” (chapter 10). Having shown that orthodox teaching is clearly asserted by John the Evangelist (chapter 11), he completely overturns their futile answers (chapter 12). Finally, from the history of the Corinthian who had been separated from Paul and then restored to the sacred communion, he constructs a most powerful argument in confirmation of the Catholic doctrine (chapter 13 and following).

In the second book, after teaching that penance must be undertaken carefully and at the proper time (chapter 1), he attacks the two principal supports of the Novatians. Their first support (chapters 2 and 3) was supplied by the Apostle’s words asserting that those who had fallen could not be renewed to penance. Their second (chapter 4) was drawn from John’s Gospel, where it is said that the sin against the Holy Spirit will be forgiven neither in this age nor in the age to come. He treats and dissolves both difficulties with such force of reasoning that he illuminated almost all later theologians who dealt with their solution, as we have noted in the appropriate places. Finally, he proves that the Novatians themselves drive sinners to repeat baptism (chapter 5, section 36), so that by its benefit they may obtain the forgiveness which the Novatians denied them through works of penance, whereas the apostles everywhere promise us forgiveness of sins. Taking this opportunity, he invites Christians to penance (chapter 6), setting before their eyes its individual parts and qualities. He adds that Christ, moved by their tears and by the prayers of Mother Church, will come to them to bring about a spiritual resurrection, whose form he recalls as having been displayed in Lazarus (chapter 7). He confirms this raising and the banquet at which Lazarus took part together with the Lord as an argument against the Novatians, again using as an example the forgiveness Paul granted to the Corinthian. Then, turning his eyes upon himself (chapter 8, section 67 and following), he prays to God with the greatest possible submission of spirit that he may receive both absolution from his own sins and mercy toward the sins of others. Finally, after examining the vices that commonly insinuate themselves into penance (chapter 9 and following), and after indicating the caution to be observed in choosing the proper time for public penance, he brings the book to a close.

As for the date of this work, it seems to us that it can reasonably be inferred by comparing two passages with one another: first, the words “I wrote two little books on Penance long ago,” found in the *Exposition of Psalm 37*, which we have shown was written in the year 393 (section 1); and second, the statement in Book II of this commentary, “We elders also sin” (chapter 8, section 74), especially when compared with the preceding words, “I have undertaken some labor for your holy Church” (section 73). Since there can be no doubt that public labor, known to everyone, is designated in the latter passage, it must be understood as referring either to the struggle undertaken against Justina, the leader of the Arians, or against Symmachus, the defender of idols. Therefore, some intervening year must be assigned to this work, perhaps 384. On this reckoning, when the year 393 was passing, the holy man could have said, “I wrote long ago.”

These final words sufficiently reveal to whom this commentary should be attributed. But when, in Book II, he speaks of being carried away from the tribunals and undertaking labor on behalf of the Church, the passage is so thoroughly Ambrosian that we are greatly surprised that Petrus Sotus wished to deprive our Doctor of this work (*Institutiones sacerdotales*, “On the Necessity of Confession,” lesson 9), on account of passages by which anyone ought to be persuaded that it belongs to Ambrose himself. We shall examine his arguments in due time, if they prove worth the effort. Here we shall add only this: Augustine cites these books repeatedly, as genuinely Ambrosian, in *On Original Sin*, chapter 31; Book II against Julian, chapters 3 and 9; and Book IV against the Two Letters of the Pelagians, chapter 11. This authority alone ought to outweigh all conjectures, however much such conjectures are accustomed to mislead even learned men; an example of this is found in the theologian just mentioned. Rivetus was unquestionably more seriously at fault (*Sacred Criticism*, Book III, chapter 16), for after reporting Sotus’s arguments, he maliciously suppressed the opposing arguments. It is not difficult to perceive the reason for this silence in a work that promises to censure books of this kind. For nowhere else is it scarcely made clearer that Christ entrusted to the Church the authority to forgive sins, the necessity of confessing them, and finally the merit of good works and bodily chastisements.

[Col. 0465]

## SAINT AMBROSE, BISHOP OF MILAN: TWO BOOKS ON PENANCE

[Note: Written around the year 384.]

[Col. 0465]

## [BOOK ONE]

### CHAPTER I

The praise of moderation. How necessary this virtue is for the leaders of the Church, demonstrated especially by the example of the Lord’s charity and gentleness. Since the Novatians have departed from this virtue, they are not to be regarded as disciples of Christ; their pride and lack of mercy are rebuked.

1. If the greatest end of the virtues is that which looks to the improvement of the greatest number, moderation is nearly the most beautiful of all. It does not offend even those whom it condemns, and those whom it has condemned it usually makes worthy of absolution. Indeed, it alone has propagated the Church purchased by the Lord’s blood; it imitates the heavenly beneficence and tempers the redemption of all with a wholesome conclusion that human ears can bear, minds do not reject, and spirits do not fear. [Note: One German manuscript, from around the year 800, begins as follows: “When God terrifies us, he does not wish to break us, but he does not wish to punish us. A certain psalm says: ‘Thou hast given a sign to those who fear thee, that they may flee from the face of the bow.’ For when a bow is drawn, the farther backward the hand is pulled, the more forcefully the shot is propelled. So too the threats of God come with greater severity the longer they are delayed. Yet it is an act of mercy when punishment is delayed, so that the penitent may be healed and the healed person may not be condemned. Hear the Apostle: ‘Do you despise the riches of his goodness and patience? Do you not know that the kindness of God leads you to repentance?’ But so that we may correct the vices of our weakness,” and so forth. Other manuscripts and editions agree with one another, except that some of them read: “If the end of the prophets,” and below, instead of “for the redemption of all,” one manuscript has “of the Redeemer,” and two have “in the redemption of all.” Instead of “tempering with a wholesome conclusion,” some have “a wholesome and temperate conclusion,” while others have “with a wholesome conclusion and temperance.”]

2. For whoever strives to correct the vices of human weakness ought to bear that weakness itself and, in a certain sense, weigh it upon his shoulders (Luke 15:5), not cast it away. For that Evangelical shepherd is said to have carried the weary sheep, not to have thrown it away. [Note: Three manuscripts read *quoquo modo vensare* (“to carry in whatever manner” [reading uncertain]); the Claromontanus manuscript has *quodammodo pausare* (“to pause in some manner”).] Solomon says: “Do not be excessively righteous” (Ecclesiastes 7:17), for moderation ought to temper righteousness. For how can someone who regards you with disgust present himself to you for treatment, someone who thinks that he will be an object of contempt rather than compassion to his physician?

3. Therefore the Lord Jesus had compassion on us, in order to call us to himself, not to frighten us away. He came gentle; he came humble. Finally, he said: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matthew 11:28). The Lord Jesus therefore refreshes; he does not exclude or cast away. It was fitting, then, that he chose disciples such as these—interpreters of the Lord’s will—who would gather the people of God, not reject them. Hence it is clear that those are not to be regarded as disciples of Christ who think that harshness should be followed instead of gentleness, and pride instead of humility; who seek the Lord’s mercy for themselves but deny it to others. Such are the teachers of the Novatians, who call themselves “the pure.” [Note: The authorities for the statement that the Novatians arrogated to themselves the title Καθαρῶν, “of the pure,” in order to distinguish themselves from the Catholics, whom they regarded as impure, are Eusebius, Book IV of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 23; Epiphanius, Heresy 79; Augustine, *On Heresies*, 38; Theodoret, Book III of the *Compendium of Heretical Fables*; and others. Augustine makes a particularly witty play on them in chapter 2 of *On Christian Combat*: “If they wished to acknowledge their own name, they would call themselves ‘worldly’ rather than ‘pure.’” As can be learned from Cyprian, Pacianus, Augustine, and many others, they called the Catholics “Apostates” and “Capitolines,” because the Catholics communicated with those who had offered sacrifice to Jupiter in the Capitol. In turn, they were called “Montenses,” either after some place bearing that name or because Novatus had supported Felicissimus, who, as we learn from Cyprian’s Letter 41, had withdrawn with his followers to a mountain. They were also called *scaevae* (“left-handed”), perhaps for no other reason than that, since they exercised the power of binding sins but not of loosing them, they in some way imitated those who, neglecting the right hand, use only the left for service. See the Council of Labbe, volume II, page 951.]

4. What could be more presumptuous than these people, when Scripture says: “For no one is pure from sin, not even an infant of one day” (Job 14:4), and David cries out: “Cleanse me from my sin” (Psalm 50:2)? Are these people holier than David, from whose family Christ chose to be born through the mystery of the Incarnation—he whose offspring is the heavenly palace, receiving the world’s Redeemer in a virginal womb? [Note: This is how the old editions and many manuscripts read. The Roman edition, together with others, has: “the heavenly court is the womb of the Virgin”; the manuscripts have “of the virginal womb.”] What, moreover, could be harsher than for them to prescribe penance while refusing to release the penitent from it? By denying forgiveness, they remove the incentive to penance. For no one can perform penance well unless he has hoped for pardon.

### CHAPTER II

What the Novatians say—that they deny communion only to those who have lapsed—is inconsistent both with Scripture and with their own teaching. As for the reverence for divine power which they put forward as a pretext, by this very claim they wrong that power, since a person does injury when he refuses to exercise the office entrusted to him, or some part of it. The power of binding and loosing cannot be attributed to heresy, but is rightly vindicated by the Church, since she received it from the Holy Spirit, against whom these people act arrogantly.

5. But they deny that communion ought to be restored to those who have fallen through transgression. If they excepted only one crime—that of sacrilege—to which they denied forgiveness, they would indeed appear harsh, but they would at least be refuted only by divine pronouncements and would remain consistent with their own assertions. For the Lord excepted no crime when he forgave all sins. But since they think, after the manner of the Stoics, that all sins are to be judged by equal measures, they assert equally that the man who kills a rooster, as they say, and the man who strangles his father are to be forever excluded from the heavenly mysteries. [Note: The passage may seem internally contradictory: here the Novatians are said to regard all sins as equal, while below the same people are said to introduce an evident distinction between more serious and less serious faults. But there the holy Doctor indicates clearly enough that the response he mentions was made by later Novatians; the earlier ones held the equality of sins in the way stated here. It is nevertheless quite plausible that Novatian was initially accused of treating all sins alike because he excluded the *libellatici* from reconciliation just as he excluded the *thurificatores*. Then, compelled by the consequences of his teaching, he rejected every distinction among sins, also in order to evade the objection by which Cyprian argued that adulterers were admitted to penance while the lapsed were denied it. When that equality of crimes later made the sect too odious, its more recent adherents withdrew from that doctrine. As for the example drawn from the killing of a parent and of a rooster, Cicero himself presents it in the speech *For Lucius Murena*, and another example involving the killing of both a father and a slave in *Paradox* 3. But Cicero does not seem entirely consistent with himself, for although he defends the equality of sins there, he is nevertheless forced to confess that the person who killed his father commits many sins. Horace therefore rightly says of this Stoic opinion:

> Those who have nearly judged all sins equal  
> Struggle when they come to the truth:  
> Their sense and moral feeling resist.

And below:

> Nor will reason prevail here—that the one who breaks  
> The tender shoots in another’s garden  
> And the one who by night steals the sacred things of the gods  
> Sin equally and in the same way, and so forth.]

How then do they accuse people of a single crime, when they themselves cannot deny that it is utterly unjust for the punishment of a few—the lapsed, that is—to fall upon many, namely, those guilty of every sort of crime? [Note: The order of these somewhat more intricate words is as follows: since they themselves cannot deny that it is most unjust for the punishment of a few to reach many, namely, those guilty of whatever crimes.]

6. [Elsewhere chapter II.] But they say that they show reverence to the Lord by reserving to Him alone the power to forgive crimes. On the contrary, they do the greatest injury to the very One whose commands they wish to rescind and whose entrusted office they refuse to exercise. [Note: The Roman edition alone reads, “than to him whose will they wish [to rescind].” This is incorrect, since the preceding *nulli* (“to no one”) is in the first plural, not the third singular, as will be clear on examination.] For since the Lord Jesus himself said in his Gospel: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain, they are retained” (John 20:22–23), who, then, honors him more: the one who obeys his commands, or the one who resists them?

7. The Church preserves obedience in both respects, so that it both binds sin and releases it; heresy is harsh in one respect and disobedient in the other: it wishes to bind what it does not release; it does not wish to release what it has bound—thereby condemning its own position. For the Lord wished the right of both releasing and binding to be equal, since he permitted both under the same condition (*On Repentance*, distinction 1, chapter “The Word of God,” § “The Lord”). Therefore, whoever does not possess the right of releasing does not possess the right of binding either.

[Note: For, according to the Lord’s judgment, whoever possesses the right of binding also possesses the right of releasing; so likewise their assertion strangles itself: since they deny that they possess the right of releasing, they ought also to deny that they possess the right of binding. In the manuscripts of Laon, the Sorbonne, and Michael, the words “and possesses the right of releasing” are omitted, with no worse sense.]

How, then, can one of these be permitted and the other not permitted?

[Note: This is the reading of Gill and all the manuscripts except two of Albinus, which read: “To those to whom both have been granted, it is certain that both are permitted; and to the Church, etc.” Amerbach and Erasmus instead read: “If some have been granted permission for both, or permission for neither, it is certain that the Church is permitted both, while heresy is permitted neither.” The Roman edition alone reads: “To whom it has been granted, both are permitted; but to whom it has not been granted, it is certain that neither is permitted,” etc., as in Amerbach.]

For those to whom both have been granted, it is clear that both are permitted; or, if both have not been granted, it is certain that neither is permitted. The Church is permitted both; heresy is permitted neither, for this right has been entrusted to priests alone. The Church therefore rightly claims this right, since she possesses true priests.

[Note: The latest Paris edition reads “which the true Priest possesses.” A few lines later, instead of “priests of God,” the Roman edition, together with two manuscripts, has “true priests.” In this passage Ambrose argues from the supposition of his opponents and teaches nothing other than that the acts of the bishops or presbyters of the Novatians are illicit. For the Fathers of the Council of Nicaea plainly indicated that their ordination had been valid, since they decreed that all clerics returning from that heresy to the Church should retain their rank and order. Thus the priests of heretics are denied to be true priests in the same way that we commonly deny that a king who does not legitimately use his power is a true king.]

Heresy cannot claim this right, since it does not possess priests of God. By failing to claim it, it pronounces judgment upon itself: since it does not possess priests, it ought not to claim priestly authority for itself. Thus we see shameless obstinacy making a modest confession.

8. Consider also this: whoever received the Holy Spirit received both the power of releasing sin and the power of binding it. For it is written: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven; and whose sins you retain, they are retained” (John 20:22–23). Therefore, whoever cannot release sin does not possess the Holy Spirit. The ministry of the priest is the office of the Holy Spirit, while the authority of the Holy Spirit consists in releasing and binding offenses. How, then, do they claim his ministry when they distrust his right and power?

9. What is more, they are even more insolent. For since the Spirit of God is more ready for mercy than for severity, they refuse what he says he wishes and do what he says he does not wish, since punishment belongs to the judge, while forgiveness belongs to the merciful. It would therefore be more tolerable, Novatian, for you to release than to bind: in the one case you would be assuming something as though sparing sinning; in the other, you would be forgiving as though moved by compassion for distress.

[Note: Amerbach and Erasmus read “sparing the act of sinning”; Gill and not a few manuscripts read “sparing the part of sinning”; one manuscript has “the part”; the Roman edition and the remaining codices read “sparing sinning,” except the Cistercian manuscript, which has “sparing the sinner.”]

### CHAPTER III

In response to the Novatians’ claim that they deny pardon only for the more serious offenses, Saint Ambrose replies that by this position they once again condemn the founder of their sect and offend God himself, who granted the power to forgive every kind of sin. Yet greater sins require greater repentance. He further adds that they show themselves perverse in this matter because such a distinction among faults leaves the grounds for severity to God, whose mercy, shining forth so wonderfully in Christ’s incarnation, they refuse to imitate.

10. But they say that, apart from the more serious offenses, they grant pardon for lesser ones. This was not the teaching of Novatian, the author of your error, who held that repentance should be granted to no one. He adopted this position so that, since he himself could not release what he had bound, he would not bind it—lest, by binding, he should make people hope for release.

[Note: The Roman edition everywhere made “Novatus” out of “Novatian”; misled by this alteration, Petavius counted our Ambrose among those Fathers who confuse the two heresiarchs with one another. Yet that learned man would have judged otherwise if he had consulted another edition or any handwritten codex.]

In this respect, therefore, you condemn your father by your own judgment, because you distinguish sins into those which you think should be released by you and those which you consider beyond remedy. But God makes no distinction, since he promised his mercy to all and granted his priests the authority to release without any exception (*On Repentance*, distinction 1, chapter “God”). Yet whoever has aggravated the fault should also increase the repentance, for greater crimes are washed away by greater tears.

[Note: Some manuscripts read “greater crimes are overwhelmed by greater weeping … nor are you disciples and imitators”; the sense is that greater crimes are washed away by greater tears.]

Thus neither is Novatian approved, since he shut off pardon from everyone, nor are you, his imitators and condemnors, approved: for you diminish the efforts of repentance precisely where they ought to be increased, although Christ’s mercy has taught that more serious sins must be supported by greater aids.

11. What perversity is this, that you claim for yourselves what is possible by concession, while reserving for God what, as you say, is impossible? This is to choose for yourselves the occasions for forgiveness and to leave God the opportunity for severity. And where is the saying: “Let God be true and every man a liar,” as it is written, “so that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged” (Romans 3:4)?

To acknowledge, then, that God is more inclined to mercy than tenacious of severity, he himself says: “I desire mercy rather than sacrifice” (Hosea 6:6). How, then, can your sacrifice be acceptable to God, when you deny mercy, although he himself says that he does not desire the death of the sinner but his correction (Ezekiel 18:32)?

[Note: The Roman edition, together with two manuscripts, reads “what is possible, granted by God”; the other manuscripts read partly “what is possible, granted to God,” and partly, with the ancient edition, “what is possible, granted to God,” etc. One manuscript also reads “what can be granted to God,” etc. Shortly afterward, where Amerbach, Erasmus, and the Roman edition, together with the Tellian manuscript, read “material for striking,” Gill and the other codices read “material for raging.”]

12.
