The Apostle, interpreting this, says: “Because God, sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and on account of sin, condemned sin in the flesh, so that the justification of the Law might be fulfilled in us” (Romans 8:3–4). He does not say “in the likeness of flesh,” because Christ truly assumed human flesh; nor does he say “in the likeness of sin,” because he committed no sin but became sin for us. Rather, he came in the likeness of sinful flesh (2 Corinthians 5:21)—that is, he assumed the likeness of sinful flesh.

[Note: Some manuscripts read “not merely a likeness, but in the likeness of sinful flesh—that is, he assumed,” etc. Several others likewise omit only the word “merely”; the remaining manuscripts and editions have the wording found in the text.]

He therefore says “likeness” because it is written: “And he is man, and who will recognize him?” (Jeremiah 17:9).

[Note: All the editions and most manuscripts read as above; several others instead have: “This was not in the flesh according to man, who is not recognized.” The latter reading is less appropriate.]

He was man in the flesh according to humanity, so that he could be recognized; but in power he was above humanity, so that he could not be recognized. Thus here also he possesses our flesh, but he does not possess the faults of that flesh.

13. For he was not generated, as every human being is, from the mingling of male and female; rather, born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin (Matthew 1:18), he assumed an immaculate body, which not only had no faults to stain it, but which no injurious mingling of generation or conception had darkened.

(Saint Augustine, *Against Julian the Pelagian*, book II, at the beginning and end; *On Original Sin*, book II, chapter 40; and *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, book IV, chapter 11.)

For we are all born under sin, and our very origin is affected by fault, as you find written when David says: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother brought me forth” (Psalm 50:5). Therefore Paul’s flesh was a body of death, as he himself says: “Who will free me from this body of death?” (Romans 7:24). But Christ’s flesh condemned sin: sin did not experience it at his birth, and he crucified it at his death, so that justification by grace might exist in our flesh, where previously there had been a flood of guilt.

14. What, then, shall we say to these things except what the Apostle said: “If God is for us, who is against us? He who did not spare his own Son but delivered him up for us all, how will he not also, with him, grant us all things? Who will bring an accusation against God’s elect? God, who justifies? Who is he who condemns? Christ Jesus, who died—indeed, who also rose again, who is at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us” (Romans 8:31–34).

Those for whom Christ intercedes, Novatian accuses. Those whom Christ redeemed for salvation, Novatian condemns to death. To those to whom Christ says, “Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle” (Matthew 11:29), Novatian says, “I am harsh.” To those to whom Christ says, “You will find rest for your souls, for my yoke is easy and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:29–30), Novatian imposes a heavy burden and a harsh yoke.

### CHAPTER IV

He continues proving the divine mercy and demonstrates through an exposition of the Gospel testimony that it is greater than severity. He plainly shows, by the example of athletes, that those who denied Christ before men should not all be treated in the same way.

15. Although these statements sufficiently show how inclined the Lord Jesus is toward mercy, let him himself also teach you. When he wished to instruct us against the pressure of persecution, he said: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather, fear him who can cast both soul and body into Gehenna” (Matthew 10:28). And below: “Everyone who confesses me before men, I also will confess before my Father who is in heaven; but whoever denies me before men, I also will deny before my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 10:32–33).

16. Where he confesses, he confesses on behalf of all and embraces everyone; where he denies, he does not deny everyone. For above he says: “Everyone who confesses me, I also will confess him”—that is, every such person. Since he says “everyone,” no one who has confessed is excluded from the reward. It would consequently have been appropriate for him to say below as well: “But everyone who denies me.” Yet, so that he would not appear to deny everyone, he added: “Whoever denies me before men, I also will deny him.” He promises grace to all; he does not threaten all with condemnation.

[Note: This entire passage is abbreviated in the Claromontane manuscript as follows: “He heightens this expression of his mercy not only in that book of the Gospel of the Lord Jesus written according to Matthew, but we also find it read in that written according to Luke.” The other manuscripts and the editions agree among themselves, except that some of them read “is entitled” instead of “is written.”]

He magnifies what concerns mercy and diminishes what concerns vengeance.

17. Thus it is written not only in the book of the Gospel of the Lord Jesus that is written according to Matthew, but it is also found in the one that we recognize as written according to Luke (Luke 12:8), so that you may know that both evangelists included it deliberately.

18. [Elsewhere chapter III.] We have stated what is written; let us gather its meaning. “Everyone,” he says, “who has confessed me” (Matthew 10:32)—that is, whoever, from whatever life or condition, has confessed me—will have me as the rewarder of his confession. When “everyone” is said, no one who has confessed is excluded from reward. It does not similarly say, “Everyone who has denied will be denied,” for it may happen that someone, overcome by tortures, denies God with his speech but worships him in his heart (*On Repentance*, distinction 1, chapter “It Can Happen”).

19. Is the case of one who denies willingly the same as that of someone whom tortures have bent toward sacrilege, though his will did not? How utterly unworthy it would be for the merit of the contest to have force among human beings but not, it is claimed, before God! For often, even in the secular contests of athletes, the common people have been accustomed to crown with the victors those who were defeated, provided their contests had been honorable—especially those whom they saw to have been excluded from victory, perhaps through trickery or fraud.

[Note: Some manuscripts omit “perhaps”; for it, several have “or by lot.” In place of “excluded,” Erasmus, the Roman edition, and certain manuscripts read “shaken off”; Amerbach and Gill read “cut off.”]

Will Christ, then, allow his athletes, whom he sees to have yielded for a little while to severe tortures, to remain without pardon?

20. Will he not take account of their labor, since even those whom he casts down he does not cast down forever?

[Note: Some manuscripts read “the reward of labor.”]

For David says: “God will not cast off forever” (Psalm 76:8). And against this we hear heresy saying: “He casts off forever”? “Nor will he cut off his mercy to the end, from generation to generation, nor will God forget to show mercy,” the Prophet cries (Psalm 76:9–10). Yet there are people who introduce a kind of forgetfulness into the divine mercy?

### CHAPTER V

An objection based on God’s immutability is answered by adducing testimonies of Scripture in which God promises mercy to sinners emerging from their mire. It is added that indulgence is more readily prepared for those who sinned in a certain sense unwillingly; this is illustrated by the elegant example of prisoners of war and by a speech placed in the mouth of the devil himself.

21. But they say that they maintain these positions so as not to make God appear mutable if he forgives those with whom he had been angry. [Elsewhere chapter IV.] What then? Shall we reject the divine oracles and follow their opinions? God is to be judged not by the assertions of others but by his own words.

What more striking testimony of his mercy could we offer than this: through the prophet Hosea, he immediately grants indulgence to those whom he had threatened as though angry?

[Note: The Albinus and Thuane manuscripts read “for presenting his mercy”; other manuscripts and the editions more appropriately read “a distinction of his mercy,” that is, a sign, testimony, or proof of it.]

For he says: “What shall I do for you, Ephraim? What shall I do for you, Judah? Your mercy is like,” etc. (Hosea 6:4). And below: “How shall I make you? Shall I make you like Admah and set you like Zeboiim?” (Hosea 11:8).

In the very midst of his indignation, he clings to something like a father’s affection, considering how he might hand the sinner over to punishment; and although Judah deserves it, God nevertheless continues to deliberate with himself.

[Note: The old edition reads “even if a Jew should marvel,” incorrectly. The Roman edition and several manuscripts read “even if he threatens the Jews,” more appropriately. The remaining manuscripts have the reading found in the text.]

But immediately, after saying, “I will make you like Admah and set you like Zeboiim”—two cities that shared in a similar destruction because of their proximity to Sodom—he says: “My heart has been changed within me; my compassion is stirred. I will not act according to the fierceness of my anger” (Hosea 11:8–9).

22. Is it not evident that the Lord Jesus is indignant with us sinners for this reason: that the terror of his indignation may convert us? His indignation, therefore, is not the execution of vengeance but rather the work of absolution. Thus he says: “If you turn and groan, you will be saved” (Isaiah 30:15). He awaits our temporal groans, so that he may remit eternal punishments; he awaits our tears so that he may pour out his compassion.

Thus in the Gospel, moved by compassion for the tears of a widowed mother, he raised her son (Luke 7:13).

[Note: Many manuscripts read: “He regards our groans … he regards our tears … he regards,” etc.]

He awaits our conversion so that he too may return to grace, which would remain in us if no lapse entered into us. But because by our sins we incur offense, he is indignant so that we may be humbled; we are humbled so that we may be more worthy of mercy than of punishment.

23. Let Jeremiah certainly teach you, saying: “For the Lord will not reject forever; for when he has humbled, he will have mercy according to the multitude of his mercies. For he has not humbled from his whole heart, nor rejected the children of men” (Lamentations 3:31–32).

[Note: The ancient German manuscript reads “because he does not humble for that reason.”]

We certainly read this in the Lamentations of Jeremiah, and from these and the other words that follow we understand that he humbles all the captives of the earth beneath his feet so that we may avoid his judgment (Psalm 112:7).

Yet he does not humble the sinner entirely from his heart, even to the ground, since he also raises the needy from the earth and lifts the poor from the dungheap. For he does not humble from his whole heart the one whom he reserves for pardon.

24. If, then, he does not humble every sinner from his whole heart, how much less does he humble from his whole heart the one who did not sin with his whole heart! For just as he said of the Jews, “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isaiah 29:13; Matthew 15:8), perhaps he may also say of certain fallen ones: “These denied me with their lips, but in their hearts they are with me.” Punishment overcame them; treachery did not turn them away.

Some people deny pardon without cause to those whose faith their persecutor has so far acknowledged that he sought to conquer it by tortures.

[Note: All the editions read “having pursued it so far”; all the manuscripts read “having confessed it so far.” Certainly persecutors in a certain sense confess that those whom they attack with tortures possess faith in Christ. For if they believed that those people were devoid of the same faith, they would treat them as friends.]

They denied once, but confess every day. They denied with speech, but confess with groans; they confess with cries; they confess with tears; they confess with free, not forced, voices. For a time they yielded to the devil’s temptation, but afterward the devil also withdrew from those whom he could not claim for himself. He yielded to their tears; he yielded to their repentance. Those whom he had invaded as strangers, he lost as his own.

25. Is this not like someone who leads away a captive population from a conquered city?

[Note: Some manuscripts read “the population of a captured city.”]

The captive is led away unwillingly: he goes to foreign lands out of necessity, yet inwardly he does not depart in affection; he carries his homeland with him in his heart and seeks an opportunity to return.

What, then? When such a person returns, is there anyone who persuades us that he should not be received? He should be received with less honor, certainly, but with greater eagerness, so that the adversary may have nothing in which to exult.

[Note: Some manuscripts read “not, of course, with lesser honor but with greater eagerness.”]

If you forgive the armed man who was able to fight, will you not forgive the one in whom faith alone was fighting?

[Note: Some editions and several manuscripts read “who was able to resist.”]

26. If we inquire into the devil’s own opinion concerning such fallen people, does he not seem to say: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me”? For how can he be with me who does not depart from Christ? They appear to worship me for no reason, since they preserve the teaching of Jesus; yet I thought they were teaching mine. They condemn me more when they abandon what they have learned. Certainly Jesus is glorified more greatly in them when he receives them as they return.

All the angels rejoice, because there is greater joy in heaven over one sinner doing penance than over ninety-nine righteous people who do not need repentance (Luke 15:7). A triumph over me is celebrated in heaven and on earth. Christ loses nothing when those who came to me with weeping return to the Church with longing. By their example even some of my own are put at risk, those who will learn that there is nothing here, where people are enticed by present rewards, but much there, where groans, tears, and fasts are preferred to my feasts.

### CHAPTER VI

When the Novatians exclude sinners from Christ’s banquet, they show themselves to be imitators not of the pious Samaritan but of the proud lawyer, as well as of the priest and Levite who are criticized in the Gospel—or rather, even more pitiless than they.

27. Do you therefore exclude these people, Novatians? For what else is exclusion than denial of the hope of pardon?

Yet the Samaritan did not pass by that half-dead man abandoned by robbers. He treated his wounds with oil and wine, first pouring in oil to soothe them; he placed the wounded man upon his own beast, carrying all his sins upon it (Luke 10:33–34). Nor did the shepherd despise the sheep that had gone astray (Luke 15:4).

28. But you say: “Do not touch me.” You speak as though wishing to justify yourselves: “He is not our neighbor.” You are more arrogant than that lawyer who wished to test Christ. He asked, “Who is my neighbor?” (Luke 10:29); he asked, whereas you deny.

You are like that priest descending, and like the Levite passing by, refusing to receive for healing the one whom you ought to have taken in, and refusing hospitality to the one for whom Christ counted out two bronze coins, whose neighbor Christ commands you to become so that you may show him mercy.

[Note: All the manuscripts read as above; all the editions, by contrast, read “he counted out two denarii,” with the same sense, since all small-denomination coins were formerly made of bronze. Hence the name *chalkologoi* (χαλκολόγοι), “bronze-collectors,” for those who gathered alms from others. Hence also Jerome rendered the two *lepta* (λεπτά) of the widow, which Christ the Lord commended above the offerings of the rich who put much into the treasury, as “two bronze coins.” The books are full of such expressions. Below, instead of “so that you may show him mercy,” as all the editions and several manuscripts read, others prefer “so that you may more easily have mercy on him.”]

For he is the neighbor whom not only a shared nature has joined to you but whom mercy has also united. You make yourself alien to him through pride, vainly puffed up in the mind of your flesh and not holding fast to the Head. For if you held fast to the Head, you would understand that you must not abandon the one for whom Christ died. If you held fast to the Head, you would understand that the whole body must grow through the bond of love, being joined together rather than torn apart, toward the increase of God and the redemption of the sinner.

29. Since, then, you remove every fruit of repentance, what else are you saying but this: “Let none of the wounded enter our lodging; let none be healed in our Church”? Among us the sick are not treated. We are healthy and have no need of a physician, because he himself says: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Matthew 9:12).

### CHAPTER VII

Having appealed to Christ, who invites everyone to his supper, he indicates that the Novatians neither enter it themselves nor permit others to enter, a practice that the holy Church does not imitate. He then makes clear that these same heretics can have no part with Christ, who desires the salvation of all.

30. Therefore, Lord Jesus, come in your entirety to your Church, since Novatian makes excuses. Novatian says: “I have bought a yoke of oxen” (Luke 14:19)—he who does not accept Christ’s easy yoke but places a heavy burden upon his own neck, which he cannot bear.

Novatian detained your servants who had invited him, and killed them after subjecting them to insult, having defiled them with the stain of repeated baptism.

[Note: Cyprian, in Letter 73, Eusebius in his *Ecclesiastical History*, and others likewise charge the Novatians with repeating baptism; but Cyprian himself in Letter 76 in turn rejected their baptism. Indeed, it is clear that even Saint Basil, in Letter 1 to Amphilochius, canon 1, and Letter 3, canon 47, was uncertain about it, although it was approved by the eighth canon of the Council of Nicaea and by the judgment of all the other Fathers.]

Go out, then, to the crossroads and gather the good and the bad (Luke 14:21); bring the weak, the blind, and the lame into your Church. Command that your house be filled; bring everyone to your supper, because whoever you summon you will make worthy, if he follows.

The one who lacks the wedding garment is indeed rejected—that is, the garment of love, the covering of grace. Send, I say, to everyone.

31. [Note: This is the reading of the old edition and most manuscripts, except that some preface it with “Novatian himself.” The Roman edition, together with a few manuscripts, reads: “Those whom your Church does not excuse from your supper, Novatian excuses.”]

Your Church does not excuse people from your supper; Novatian excuses them. Your household does not say, “I am healthy; I do not need a physician”; rather, it says: “Heal me, Lord, and I shall be healed; save me, and I shall be saved” (Jeremiah 17:14).

Finally, the figure of your Church appears in that woman who came up behind you and touched the fringe of your garment, saying within herself: “If I touch his garment, I shall be saved” (Matthew 9:21). This Church therefore confesses her wounds; this Church desires to be healed.

32. And you, Lord, wish to heal everyone, but not everyone wishes to be healed. Novatian does not, because he thinks himself healthy.

You, Lord, say that you are sick, and in the least of us you feel our infirmity, saying: “I was sick, and you visited me” (Matthew 25:36). Novatian does not know how to visit that least one in whom you desire to be visited.

You say to Peter, when he made excuses so that you would not wash his feet: “Unless I wash you, you will have no part with me” (John 13:8). How, then, can these people have fellowship with you, when they do not receive the keys of the kingdom and deny that they ought to forgive sins?

33. They rightly confess this about themselves, for they do not possess Peter’s inheritance, since they do not possess Peter’s seat, which they tear apart through impious division.

[Note: All the editions and some manuscripts read “Peter’s faith”; many more and better manuscripts read “Peter’s seat.”]

But they act wickedly in denying that sins can also be forgiven in the Church, when Christ said to Peter: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you release on earth will be released also in heaven” (Matthew 16:19); and when the chosen vessel of the Lord himself says: “If you have forgiven anything to anyone, I also have; for what I have forgiven, I have forgiven for your sake in the person of Christ” (2 Corinthians 2:10).

Why, then, do they read Paul if they thought that he had erred so impiously as to claim for himself the right of his Lord? But he claimed what he had received; he did not usurp what was not due to him.

### CHAPTER VIII

What Christ bestowed upon his disciples. When the Novatians lay on hands and confer baptism, they are refuted by their own practice, since sins are forgiven by the same authority in repentance as in baptism. Finally, their arrogance is especially chastised by the Lord’s own example.

34. [Elsewhere chapter VII.] The Lord wishes his disciples to possess great power; he wishes his servants to do in his name what he himself did when he was on earth (John 14:12). Finally, he says: “You will do greater things than these” (Matthew 10:8).

He gave them power to raise the dead. And although he could have restored Saul’s sight himself, he nevertheless sent him to his disciple Ananias, so that through Ananias’s blessing the eyes Saul had lost might be restored to him (Acts 9:17).

He also ordered Peter to walk with him upon the sea, and when Peter wavered, he immediately rebuked him because he had diminished the grace of the gift through smallness of faith (Matthew 14:29–31).

[Note: All the editions read “gifts of graces”; a few manuscripts read “the gift of grace”; the rest read “the grace of the gift.” The latter is best, since the passage concerns only the grace or favor of that gift by which Peter was permitted to walk upon the waters. Again, where the old edition and all the manuscripts read “the light of the world,” the Roman edition alone added “by nature.”]

He also gave his disciples the grace to be the light of the world (Matthew 5:14), although he himself was the light of the world. And because he was about to descend from heaven and ascend into heaven, he lifted Elijah up to heaven (2 Kings 2:11), intending to restore him to earth at the appointed time. Likewise, since he was to baptize in the Holy Spirit and fire (Matthew 3:11), he first anticipated the sacrament of baptism through John.

35. Finally, he gave his disciples every gift, concerning which he says: “In my name they will cast out demons; they will speak in new tongues; they will take up serpents; and if they drink anything deadly, it will not harm them. They will lay hands upon the sick, and they will be well” (Mark 16:17–18). He gave everything, therefore, but in all these things there is no human power when the grace of the divine gift is at work.

36. Why, then, do you lay on hands and believe in the efficacy of a blessing if perhaps a sick person recovers?

[Note: Here “the work of blessing” means the effect of blessing. It seems, moreover, that this refers to the blessing by which the sick are anointed by presbyters and commended in prayer to God Almighty, according to the command of the Apostle James, which we call extreme unction. Besides the fact that the effect of this sacrament is also the sick person’s recovery, we have already observed that the Novatians paid no attention to the laying on of hands by the bishop, that is, confirmation.]

Why do you presume that some people can be cleansed through you from the defilement of the devil? Why do you baptize if sins may not be forgiven through a human being? In baptism there is certainly forgiveness of all sins. What difference does it make whether priests claim for themselves this authority through repentance or through the washing?

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “There is one ministry in both.”]

There is one mystery in both.

37. But you say that in the washing the grace of the mysteries is at work. What, then, in repentance? Does not the name of God operate there? What, then? Wherever you wish, you claim for yourselves the grace of God; wherever you wish, you reject it? But this is the arrogance of insolence, not the fear of holiness: you are disgusted by those who wish to do penance. You cannot endure the tears of those who weep.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “to do penance, namely to endure it by weeping; you cannot bear to hear tears.” Less suitably.]

Your eyes cannot tolerate the cheap clothing, the filth of the soiled; my delicate ones, with proud eyes and swollen hearts, say indignantly, each one: “Do not touch me, for I am clean.”

38. The Lord does indeed say to Mary Magdalene, “Do not touch me” (John 20:17), but he did not say “because I am clean”—he who was clean. You dare, Novatian, to call yourself clean, although even if you were clean in your deeds, you would become unclean by this one statement?

Isaiah says: “Woe is me, for I am pierced in heart; because I am a man and have unclean lips, and I dwell among a people having unclean lips” (Isaiah 6:5). Yet you say, “I am clean,” although, as it is written, not even an infant of one day is clean (Job 14:4).

David says: “Cleanse me from my sin” (Psalm 50:4)—David whom the grace of the merciful Lord often justified. Yet you call yourself clean, although you are so unjust that you do not show mercy; you see the speck in your brother’s eye but do not consider the beam that is in your own eye (Matthew 7:3).

For every unrighteous person is unclean before God. What is more unjust than wanting your sins to be forgiven while you yourself think that sins should not be forgiven for one who asks? What is more unjust than justifying yourself while condemning another, even though you commit more serious offenses?

39. Finally, when the Lord Jesus was about to celebrate the remission of our sins, John said to him: “I ought to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?” He replied: “Let it be so for now; for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness” (Matthew 3:14–15).

The Lord came to the sinner, although he himself had no sin, and wished to be baptized although he had no need to be cleansed. Who, then, can tolerate you, who think that you have no need to be cleansed through repentance because you say that you have already been cleansed by grace—as though it were already impossible for you to sin?

### CHAPTER IX

By comparing similar passages of Scripture, the words, “But if a man sins against the Lord, who will pray for him?” are shown not to mean that no one will pray, but that a worthy intercessor must be sought—such as Moses and Jeremiah, by whose prayers God is recorded to have spared the people of Israel.

40. [In some editions, chapter VIII.] But you say: “It is written: If a man sins against another man, they will pray for him to the Lord; but if a man sins against the Lord, who will pray for him?” (1 Kings 2:25). First, as I have already said above, I would tolerate your bringing this objection forward if you did not grant remission of penance only to apostates. Yet what difficulty does this question really raise? For it is not written, “No one will pray for him,” but “Who will pray?” That is, the question is what sort of person can pray in such a case; no one is excluded.

[Note: [Col. 0478D] What Ambrose says, “I would tolerate,” should not be understood as though he judged this crime of apostasy unforgivable, since throughout this entire work he proves the contrary. Rather, he concedes only this: that they would employ the Evangelist’s words with a somewhat more plausible appearance of truth if they confined themselves within the limits of apostasy.]

41. Finally, you have in the fourteenth Psalm: “Lord, who will dwell in your tabernacle, or who will rest upon your holy mountain?” (Psalm 14:1). It does not mean that no one will dwell there, but that a tested person will dwell there; nor does it say that no one will rest, but that the chosen person will rest. To show that this is true, not long afterward, in the twenty-third Psalm, he says: “Who will ascend the mountain of the Lord, or who will stand in his holy place?” (Psalm 24:3)—that is, not just anyone from the common crowd, nor someone of ordinary and plebeian worth, but a person of outstanding life and exceptional merit. And to show that when “who” is said, it does not mean “no one,” but signifies “someone,” after saying, “Who will ascend the mountain of the Lord?” he adds: “The innocent in hands and pure in heart, who has not received his soul in vain” (ibid., 4). And elsewhere: “Who is wise and will understand these things?” (Hosea 14:10). Does he mean that no one will understand? And in the Gospel: “Who is the faithful and prudent steward whom the Lord will set over his household, to give them their measure of wheat at the proper time?” (Luke 12:42). And so that you may understand that he was speaking of one who certainly exists, not of one who does not exist, he adds: “Blessed is that servant whom, when his lord comes, he will find doing so” (ibid., 43). I think the same is meant by: “O God, who is like you?” (Psalm 83:1)—certainly not that no one is like him, since the Son is the image of the Father (On Repentance, distinction 1, chapter “Si sacerdos,” § “Deus”).

42. “Who will pray for him?” (1 Kings 2:25) must therefore be understood in the same way: someone of exceptional life ought to pray for the person who has sinned against the Lord. The greater the fault, the greater the intercessions that must be sought (1 Kings 2:25). It was not just anyone from the common people who prayed for the Jewish people, but Moses, when they worshiped the calf’s head, forgetful of the faith (Exodus 32:31). Did Moses err? He certainly did not err, since what he asked for, he both deserved and obtained. For what would such devotion not obtain, when he offered himself on behalf of the people, saying: “And now, if you forgive their sin, forgive it; but if not, erase me from your book of life” (ibid., 32)? You see that he did not, like a pampered and fastidious intercessor, concern himself with avoiding offense, as Novatian says he fears; rather, mindful of everyone and forgetful of himself, he did not fear to incur offense in order to strip and free the people from the danger of offense.

43. [Col. 0480A] Rightly, therefore, it is written: “Who will pray for him?”—that is, someone like Moses, who offers himself for sinners; someone like Jeremiah, to whom, although he was a prophet, our Lord God said: “Do not pray for this people” (Jeremiah 7:16), yet he prayed and obtained forgiveness.

[Note: [Col. 0479C] Some manuscripts read, “to whom, since he was a prophet, it was said.”]

Finally, moved by the prophet’s intercession and by the entreaty of so great a seer, the Lord speaks to Jerusalem—for she too had done penance for her offenses—and says: “Lord Almighty, God of Israel, the soul in anguish and the anxious spirit cry out to you: hear, Lord, and have mercy” (Baruch 3:1–2).

[Note: [Col. 0479C] The Claromontanus manuscript alone reads, “since she too had done penance for her offenses.”]

And he orders the garments of mourning to be put aside and the lamentations of repentance to be cast off; for it is written at the end of the book: “Take off, Jerusalem, the robe of your mourning and affliction, and put on forever the beauty of the glory given to you by God” (Baruch 5:1).

## CHAPTER X

John did not absolutely and simply prohibit prayer from being made for those guilty of a sin unto death; for he knew that Moses, Jeremiah, and Stephen had prayed for similar people, and he himself also indicated that forgiveness was not to be denied to them.

44. [In some editions, chapter IX.] Such intercessors, then, must be sought in the case of grave offenses; for if just anyone from the people were to pray, they would not be heard.

45. Hence that question of yours, which you derive from John’s letter, will not be able to carry any weight: “Whoever knows that his brother is committing a sin not unto death, let him ask, and God will give him life, because it is not a sin unto death. There is a sin unto death; I do not say that he should pray for it” (1 John 5:16). For John was not speaking to Moses and Jeremiah, but to the people, who ought to employ another intercessor for their sins; it is enough for such a person to entreat God for lesser offenses, while he thinks that forgiveness for graver ones must be reserved for the prayers of the righteous.

[Note: [Col. 0479C] Some manuscripts read, “another propitiator.”]

[Note: [Col. 0479D] You may perhaps ask what is meant here by the word “righteous.” To understand it more easily, observe that it cannot be taken of just any righteous people. There is no doubt that many such people existed among the people, yet the blessed Doctor teaches that they were granted nothing more than the ability, through their prayers, mutually to obtain forgiveness for lesser faults. Thus the reference may be to those who were conspicuously righteous, such as the prophets and martyrs here designated in Moses, Jeremiah, and Stephen; or at least to priests alone, who themselves are often symbolically represented under the person of the prophets.

It is not in dispute that Ambrose is alluding to the passage in James: “Confess your sins to one another”—that is, to one another mutually—“your sins … for the continual prayer of a righteous person is very powerful.” Many, both among the ancient Fathers and among more recent theologians, teach that these words contain a command to confess sins to priests. Accordingly, they believe that the phrase “to one another” is defined by “the righteous person,” signifying the priest, to whom alone the absolution of offenses belongs.

Nor is this alien to our Doctor’s teaching concerning the priestly power to forgive crimes. On this subject, consult Commentary on Psalm 118, sermon 10, no. 17, and Exposition of Luke, book V, no. 11.

As for the expiation of lesser faults, besides the prayers which people offered for one another out of inward devotion, certain psalms, the Lord’s Prayer, the Creed, and especially the general confession customarily made at the beginning of the sacred liturgy could also be recited. Morinus, On Penance, book V, chapter 32, judges that this passage should be understood of that confession. But since neither here nor in several other passages which he says should be understood in the same way is any mention made of such a confession, it is more credible that the subject is solely the prayers of the faithful who pray for one another.]

For how, then, would John say that one ought not to pray for a more serious offense, when he had read that Moses prayed and obtained his request where there had been deliberate apostasy, and when he also knew that Jeremiah had prayed (Jeremiah 14:13)?

46. How would John say that one ought not to pray for a sin that was unto death, when he himself wrote in the Apocalypse a command to the angel of the church at Pergamum (Revelation 2:12)? There you have people holding the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to place a stumbling block before the children of Israel, to eat sacrifices offered to idols, and to commit fornication. “So you also have those who hold the teaching of the Nicolaitans; in the same way, repent. Otherwise I am coming to you soon.” You see that the God who demands repentance promises forgiveness! Finally, there too he says: “Let anyone who has ears hear what the Spirit says to the churches: To the one who conquers I will give to eat of the hidden manna” (Revelation 2:7).

47. Had John himself not known that Stephen had prayed for his persecutors, who could not bear even to hear Christ’s name, when he said concerning those who were stoning him: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them” (Acts 7:59)?

[Note: [Col. 0479C] Several manuscripts read, “the effect of whose prayer”; some read, “the devotion of whose prayer.”]

We see the effect of that prayer in the Apostle: for Paul, who was guarding the garments of those who stoned Stephen (Acts 9:15), shortly afterward, through the grace of Christ, became an apostle, although previously he had been a persecutor.

## CHAPTER XI

John’s preceding statement is illuminated by another testimony of his, in which salvation is promised to believers in Christ. From this the Novatians are refuted, since they urge the lapsed to faith while denying them forgiveness. It is added that many martyrs, after their fall, obtained a double grace; and the example of the devout Samaritan likewise shows that those in whom even the faintest faith breathes are not to be abandoned.

48. [In some editions, chapter X.] Since, then, the discussion concerns John’s general epistle, let us ask what John himself wrote in the Gospel and whether it agrees with your interpretation. For he records that the Lord said: “God so loved this world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life” (John 3:16). If, therefore, you wish to restore someone who has fallen, do you urge him to believe or not to believe? Certainly, to believe. But whoever believes, according to the Lord’s statement, will have eternal life. How, then, will you forbid prayer for one to whom eternal life is owed? Faith is a gift of divine grace, as the Apostle teaches in his distribution of graces: “To one is given faith in the same Spirit” (1 Corinthians 12:9); and the disciples say to the Lord: “Increase our faith” (Luke 17:5). Whoever therefore has faith has life; whoever has life is certainly not excluded from forgiveness. “Everyone,” he says, “who believes in him should not perish.” When “everyone” is said, no one is excluded, no one excepted; he does not except the one who has fallen, provided that afterward he believes rightly.

[Note: [Col. 0481D] Some manuscripts read, “Do you urge him to believe?”]

[Note: [Col. 0481D] The First Epistle of John is called “general” because it is addressed not to one particular person, as the Second and Third are, but to the whole Church at once.]

49. We have discovered very many who restored themselves anew after their fall and suffered for the name of God.

[Note: [Col. 0482D] Three manuscripts read, “armed themselves”; one reads, “renewed themselves.”]

Can we deny these people fellowship with the martyrs, when the Lord Jesus did not deny it to them? Do we dare say that life was not restored to those to whom Christ restored the crown? Therefore, just as after a fall the crown is restored to many if they suffer, so, if they believe, faith is restored. This faith is God’s gift, as it is written: “It has been granted to you by God not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him” (Philippians 1:29). Can one who has God’s gift fail to have forgiveness?

50. There is not merely one grace, but a double grace: that everyone who believes should also suffer for the Lord Jesus. Whoever believes therefore has his own grace; but he has another if his faith is crowned by suffering. For Peter was not without grace before he suffered; but when he suffered, he acquired another. And many who did not receive the grace to suffer for Jesus nevertheless received the grace to believe in Jesus.

51. Therefore it is said: “So that everyone who believes in him should not perish” (John 3:16). “Everyone,” he says—that is, whatever his condition, whatever his fall, if he believes, he need not fear perishing. For it can happen that the Gospel Samaritan, who is the guardian of our souls—for “Samaritan” means “guardian”—finds someone descending from Jerusalem to Jericho (Luke 10:33), that is, falling back from the contest of martyrdom into desire for this life and worldly favor,

[Note: [Col. 0482D] Some manuscripts read, “worldly grace.”]

wounded by robbers, that is, by persecutors, and left half-dead; and that he does not pass him by, but cares for and heals him.

52. Perhaps he does not pass him by for this reason: because he recognizes something living in him, from which he may be able to recover life. Does it not seem to you that the one who has fallen is half-dead, if faith breathes something vital in him?

[Note: [Col. 0482D] Several manuscripts read, “if he hopes through faith.” This is less suitable. Perhaps one should read, “if he breathes through faith.” Cyprian, in Letter 52, speaks in the same way of those who, while preserving faith inwardly, offered incense to idols out of fear of torture; Ambrose may have had this passage in mind.]

For the person who utterly casts God out of his heart is dead. The person who does not cast him out entirely, but temporarily denies him under the pressure of torture, is half-dead. Or if he is dead, why do you tell him to do penance, when he can no longer be healed? If he is half-dead, pour in oil and wine—not wine without oil, of course, but what both soothes and stings. Take him up on your beast, hand him over to the innkeeper, spend two denarii on his care, and be his neighbor (ibid., 34–35). But you cannot be his neighbor unless you show mercy; for no one can be called a neighbor except one who has cared for him, not killed him. If you wish to be called his neighbor, Christ says to you: “Go, and you do likewise” (ibid., 37).

## CHAPTER XII

To the passages already cited from John’s Gospel another passage from the same Gospel is added. When the necessity of keeping God’s commandments is objected to, it is readily answered that life is promised not only to the person who has always kept them, but also to the person who keeps them after a fall. This is then confirmed from David, although a certain difference between the two is nevertheless explained.

53. [In some editions, chapter XI.] Let us consider another similar passage: “Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; but whoever does not believe the Son will not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him” (John 3:36).

[Note: [Col. 0483D] The Roman edition reads, “is unbelieving toward the Son”; the Claromontanus manuscript, “does not believe in the Son.”]

What “remains” has already begun, and it began because of some offense, since previously he did not believe. When, therefore, someone believes, the wrath of God departs, while life approaches (ibid., 36). To believe in Christ is therefore gain of life; for whoever believes in him is not judged.

54. But at this point they reply that the person who believes in Christ must keep his word; for, they say, it is written, with the Lord saying: “I have come as light into this world, so that everyone who believes in me may not remain in darkness; and if anyone hears my word and keeps it, I do not judge him” (John 12:46–47). He does not judge, and you judge? He says: “So that the one who believes in me may not remain in darkness”—that is, even if he has been in darkness, he must not remain in it; he must correct his error, amend his fault, and keep my commandments. For I said: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but correction” (Ezekiel 33:11).

I said above: “Whoever believes in me is not judged”; and this I maintain: “For I did not come to judge the world, but so that the world might be saved through me” (John 3:17). I willingly forgive; I readily pardon:

[Note: [Col. 0483D] The Claromontanus manuscript reads, “I desire mercy.”]

“I prefer mercy to sacrifice” (Hosea 6:6), because through sacrifice the righteous person is commended, while through mercy the sinner is redeemed. “I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners” (Matthew 9:13). In the Law there is sacrifice; in the Gospel there is mercy: “The Law was given through Moses, grace through me” (John 1:17). What could be clearer?

55. Finally, below he says: “Whoever despises me and does not accept my words has one who judges him” (John 12:48). Does the person who has not corrected himself seem to you to accept Christ’s words? Clearly, he does not. Whoever therefore corrects himself accepts his word; for this is his word: that each person should call himself back from sin. Either, then, you must exclude this statement of his, or, if you cannot deny it, submit to it.

56. The person who ceases to sin and renounces his offenses must also keep the Lord’s commandments.

[Note: [Col. 0483D] The edition reads, “who has ceased to sin and renounced his offenses.”]

You must not therefore interpret this as referring only to someone who has always kept them. For if that were what he meant, he would have added “always.” By not adding it, he pronounced judgment concerning the person who keeps what he has heard; and he heard it in order to correct his error. Therefore he kept what he heard.

57. [In some editions, chapter XII.] How harsh it would be for someone who afterward keeps the Lord’s commandments to be summoned to everlasting punishment, let the Lord himself teach you—he who did not deny forgiveness even to those who did not keep his commandments, as you have it in the body of the Psalm: “If they profane my ordinances and do not keep my commandments, I will visit their iniquities with the rod and their offenses with blows; but I will not destroy my mercy from them” (Psalm 88:32–33). He therefore promises mercy to everyone.

58. But lest you think that this mercy exists without judgment, there is a distinction between those who have rendered perpetual obedience to the heavenly commandments and those who have fallen at some point, whether through error or necessity. And lest you think that you are being confined by my argument, hear Christ’s judgment. For he says: “If the servant knew his master’s will and did not do it, he will be beaten with many blows; but if he did not know it, he will be beaten with few” (Luke 12:47–48).

[Note: [Col. 0483D] The Claromontanus Codex reads, “Accept Christ’s judgment … but whoever did not know, with few.”]

Both, therefore, are received if they believe, because God chastises every son whom he receives (Hebrews 12:6); and the one whom he chastises he certainly does not hand over to death, since it is written: “The Lord chastising has chastised me, but he has not handed me over to death” (Psalm 117:18).

## CHAPTER XIII

From Paul it is shown that those who have committed a sin unto death are not to be abandoned but subjected to penance. It is explained what it means to be handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, and how desirable this is. Satan inflicts weakness upon the body, but these weaknesses are turned to the benefit of the spirit. Thus the great power of God shines forth: he compels Satan, against his will, to harm himself and benefit us.

59. Finally, Paul teaches that those who have committed a sin unto death are not to be abandoned, but rather restrained with loaves of tears and made to drink sorrowful draughts, yet in such a way that the sadness itself remains measured. This is what is meant by: “You will give them drink with tears in measure” (Psalm 79:6), so that sorrow itself may have a limit, lest the person doing penance be swallowed up by excessive grief (2 Corinthians 2:5 and following), as he wrote to the Corinthians: “What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or with love and a spirit of gentleness?” (1 Corinthians 4:21). Yet the rod is not severe, since he had read: “You will indeed strike him with the rod, but you will save his soul from death” (Proverbs 23:14).

60. What it means to come with a rod is shown by the denunciation of fornication, the accusation of incest, and the rebuke of arrogance—for they were puffed up, when they ought rather to have mourned—and finally by the condemnation of the offender, so that he might be removed from communion and handed over to the adversary, not for the destruction of the soul but of the flesh (1 Corinthians 5:1 and following).

[Note: [Col. 0484D] Another German manuscript reads, “the answer of arrogance.” Below, where all the editions and many manuscripts read “the condemnation of the offender,” some have “the condemnation of the error,” and some “the condemnation of the community.”]

For just as the Lord did not give Satan power over the soul of holy Job, but permitted him freedom with regard to his flesh (Job 2:6), so here also the person is handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the serpent may lick his earth but do no harm to his soul (Micah 7:17).

61. Let our flesh, then, die to its desires; let it be captive and subject, and let it die subjected to good servitude, without resisting the law of our mind. This is what happened in Paul, who disciplined his body (1 Corinthians 9:27) in order to bring it into servitude, so that his preaching might become more credible if the law of his flesh agreed and conformed to the law of his mind.

[Note: [Col. 0485D] Some manuscripts read, “Let our flesh therefore be bitten … and, subjected, be adorned.” This is not quite correct.]

The flesh perishes when its wisdom passes into the spirit, so that it no longer thinks about the things of the flesh but about the things of the spirit. Would that I might see my flesh grow weak! Would that I were not dragged captive into the law of sin! Would that I might not live in the flesh but in the faith of Christ (Romans 7:23)! Therefore grace is greater in bodily weakness than in health.

Finally, Paul, whom Christ loved greatly (Galatians 2:20), he did not wish to free from weakness of the flesh. When Paul asked that the weakness depart from him, he answered: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness” (1 Corinthians 12:8–9). And Paul takes greater pleasure in his weaknesses, saying: “When I am weak, then I am powerful” (ibid., 10); for the strength of the soul is brought to completion through the weaknesses of the flesh.

62. [In some editions, chapter XIII.] We have explained Paul’s statement; now let us consider the very words and the reason why he said that he had handed the person over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh.

[Note: [Col. 0485D–0486D] Among the ancients there were two interpretations of this statement. The first explained it as referring to works of penance by which the body is afflicted and brought low; this was the interpretation of Origen, Homily 24 on Leviticus, Basil, Letter to Amphilochius, canon 7, and others. The second, adopted by several Greek Fathers—Chrysostom, Theodoret, Oecumenius, and others—held that the Church handed people separated from communion over to Satan, giving him leave to rage against their bodies. Estius proves that this latter is not the Apostle’s meaning in this passage; Morinus adds further reasons in On Penance, book VI, chapter 11.

These great men erred: the former in believing that Ambrose followed only the second interpretation; the latter in judging that here the same Father explained Paul’s words solely as the chastisement of the flesh employed to restrain the passions of the mind, although he indicates that he would not disagree with those who understand this Ambrosian passage as referring to works of penance. It must, however, be admitted that our Doctor embraced both explanations of the Pauline passage. For he explicitly sets forth here the latter interpretation, which we said was held by Chrysostom and certain other Greeks, as Job’s example alone abundantly proves. Nor is this surprising, since, as the deacon Paulinus attests, he himself had experienced this power of the demon in the pitiable case of a man whom he had excluded from the sacred rites. He sufficiently suggests the former interpretation in this very chapter, no. 59, where he says that those who commit a sin unto death are to be assigned the labors of penance; and still more plainly at the end of chapter 7, which should be consulted.]

Because the devil is our tempter. He inflicts weakness upon individual limbs and is accustomed to bring illnesses upon the whole body. Finally, he struck holy Job with a grievous ulcer from the soles of his feet to the crown of his head,

[Note: [Col. 0486D] The Roman edition reads, “because he had received power for the destruction.”]

because he had received power over the destruction of his flesh, as God said: “Behold, I hand him over to you; only preserve his soul” (Job 2:6). The Apostle transferred this in the same words, saying that he had handed such a man over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, “so that the spirit may be saved on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 5:5).

63. Great is the power, great is the grace, which commands the devil to destroy himself. For he destroys himself when he makes the person whom he attempts to overthrow by tempting him stronger out of weakness.

[Note: [Col. 0486D] The Claromontanus Codex reads, “makes him holier out of weakness.”]

For while he weakens the flesh, he strengthens the mind. Bodily illness repels sin; the lust of the flesh, however, nourishes guilt.

64. The devil is therefore mocked, so that he wounds himself with his own bite and arms against himself the person whom he thought he would weaken. Thus he also loved holy Job more after he had wounded him. Though Job, whose entire body was covered with terrible ulcers,

[Note: [Col. 0486D] The same Codex reads, “struck with dreadful ulcers.”]

endured the devil’s bite, he did not feel its poison. Therefore it was rightly said to him: “You will draw out the dragon with a hook; you will mock him like a bird; you will bind him like a sparrow for a child, placing your hand upon him” (Job 40:24).

65. You see how Paul mocks him, so that he may put his hand into his cavern, like that prophetic child (Isaiah 11:8–9), and the serpent may do him no harm; so that he may drag him out of his hiding places and make a spiritual antidote from his poison; so that what is poison may become medicine. What is poison for the destruction of the flesh becomes medicine for the salvation of the spirit. What harms the body benefits the spirit (On Repentance, distinction 1, chapter “Potest,” § “Quod nocet”).

66. Let the serpent therefore eat my earth; let him drive his tooth into my flesh and crush my body.

[Note: [Col. 0486D] Some manuscripts read, “let him crush the body with the tooth of the flesh.”] Let the Lord say even of me: “I hand him over to you; only preserve his soul” (Job 2:6). How great is the power of Christ, that even the devil, who always wishes to harm, is commanded to guard a human being! Let us therefore make the Lord Jesus propitious to us. When Christ commands, the devil himself becomes the guardian of his own prey; even against his will he obeys the heavenly commands. Though savage, he nevertheless obeys gentle orders.

67. But why should I commend his obedience? Let him always be evil, so that God may always be good, who turns his malice toward our benefit. He wants to harm, but he cannot if Christ withstands him; he wounds the flesh but guards the soul; he devours the earth,

[Note: [Col. 0486D] The Benedictine Codex reads, “but preserves Christ.”]

but preserves the spirit. Finally, it is written: “Then wolves and lambs will feed together; the lion and the ox will eat straw; but the serpent will eat earth like bread. They will not harm or destroy on my holy mountain, says the Lord” (Isaiah 11:6 and following). This is the sentence passed upon the condemned serpent: “Earth will be your food” (Genesis 3:14). What earth? Certainly that of which it was said: “You are earth, and to earth you will go” (ibid., 19).

## CHAPTER XIV

What Ambrose said above—that the flesh is handed over to Satan for destruction and eaten by the serpent—he now teaches takes place only if the soul is freed from carnal desires. Accordingly, he gives many necessary instructions for guarding the eyes and the mind, confirming them by the example of the most chaste Joseph. He then urges everyone to avoid the nets by which we are dragged into the fire of pleasure, and persuades us not to fear that our flesh might be eaten by the serpent.

68. The serpent eats this earth if the Lord Jesus is favorable to us, so that the soul does not share in the weakness of the flesh and is not inflamed by the vapor of the flesh and the heat of the limbs.

[Note: [Col. 0487D] Many manuscripts read, “so that the soul does not suffer the weakness of the flesh and is not kindled by the body’s heat. It is good …”]

“It is better to marry than to burn” (1 Corinthians 7:9); for there is a flame that burns inwardly (Proverbs 6:27). Therefore let us not bind this fire in the bosom of the mind and in the recesses of the heart, lest we burn the inner garments of our being and the devouring flame of lust consume this external clothing and carnal covering of our soul. Instead, let us pass through the fire (Isaiah 43:2).

If someone falls into the blaze of love, let him leap over it and pass through it. Let him not bind adulterous desire with the chains of his thoughts or fasten any knots for himself through continual meditation. Let him not gaze repeatedly upon the form of a prostitute, nor let a young woman raise her eyes to the face of a young man. And if she happened to look and was captivated, how much more will she be captivated if she looked out of curiosity!

69. Let custom also teach us. A woman covers her head with a veil so that even in public her modesty may be secure; her face does not easily meet the eyes of a young man, but is covered by a bridal veil, lest even accidental encounters expose her to a wound, whether another’s or her own. Yet both are her own wound. If she veils her head (1 Corinthians 11:5 and following) so that she may neither rashly be seen nor see—since, when the head is veiled, the face is concealed—how much more ought she to veil herself with the covering of modesty, so that even in public she herself may possess her own privacy!

70. Let it be granted that the eye has fallen upon something, but let the affections not fix upon it. For it is not a crime to have seen, but one must beware lest the sight become the beginning of a crime. The bodily eye sees,

[Note: [Col. 0487D] This is found in the old edition and in several manuscripts; the Roman edition differs only in not retaining the verb “remain.” Other manuscripts read, “let the modesty of the mind remain, restraining the eyes of the body”; but in some there is no sound reading.]

but let the eyes of the heart be restrained; let modesty of mind remain. We have a moral and merciful Lord. The prophet indeed said: “I do not want you to gaze upon the form of a promiscuous woman”; but the Lord nevertheless said: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Proverbs 5:2).

He did not say, “If anyone looks, he has committed adultery,” but, “If anyone looks in order to desire her,” he has not bound the sight but sought the affection.

[Note: [Col. 0487D] Amerbach and Erasmus, with many manuscripts of lesser authority, omit “has bound”; perhaps without a worse meaning.]

Yet good is that modesty which habitually restrains the very eyes of the body, so that often we do not even see what we see. For we seem to look at whatever presents itself by its outward appearance; but if the mind’s attention is not joined to it, our sight too, in accordance with the function of the flesh, fades away. Thus we see more with the mind than with the body.

71. And if the flesh sees fire, let us not bind that fire in our bosom—that is, in the secrecy of the mind and the hidden place of the heart. Let us not entangle this fire in our bones; let us not cast knots upon ourselves; let us not mingle conversation with anything from which adulterous fire might boil up. The speech of a young woman is a knot for young men; the words of a young man are bonds of love.

72. Joseph saw this fire when a woman eager for adultery addressed him (Genesis 39:7). She wanted to capture him with her speech and cast the snares of her lips, but she could not bind the chaste man. The woman’s bonds were loosed by the voice of modesty, words of gravity, the reins of caution, the guardianship of faith, and the discipline of chastity.

The shameless woman therefore could not capture him in her nets. She stretched out her hand and seized his garment in order to bind him with a knot. The words of a wanton woman are nets of desire; her hand is a knot of love (Proverbs 7:21). But the chaste mind could be captured neither by the nets nor by the knot: the garment was shaken off, the knot was loosened.

[Note: [Col. 0488D] A few manuscripts read, “with the garment shaken off”; some, “with the clothing shaken off.”]

And because he had not bound the fire in the bosom of his mind, he did not burn his body.

73. [In some editions, chapter XIV.] You see, then, that our mind is the author of guilt. The flesh is innocent, but often the servant of sin. Therefore, do not let the beauty that arouses desire conquer you.

[Note: [Col. 0488D] Several manuscripts of sufficiently good authority read, “let not the form of desire conquer you,” and so on. For “the lover’s snare,” many also read “the snare of love.”]

The devil stretches out many nets and many snares. The eye of a prostitute is the lover’s snare. Our own eyes are nets for us; therefore it is written: “Do not be caught by your own eyes” (Proverbs 6:25). We ourselves therefore stretch out the nets in which we are entangled and ensnared. We ourselves tie our own bonds, as we read: “Each person is bound by the bonds of his own sins” (Proverbs 6:2).

74. Therefore let us pass through the fire of adolescence and the heat of youthful age; let us pass through the water and not remain in the water, lest deep rivers enclose us. Let us pass through, rather, so that we too may say: “Our soul has passed through the torrent” (Psalm 123:5); for the one who passes through is safe.

Finally, the Lord says: “If you pass through the waters, I am with you; the rivers will not enclose you” (Isaiah 43:2). And the Prophet says: “I saw the wicked exalted above the cedars of Lebanon; and I passed by, and behold, he was no more” (Psalm 36:35–36). Pass beyond worldly things, and you will see the heights of the wicked brought down.

[Note: [Col. 0488D] Some manuscripts read, “and you will see all the glory of the wicked fallen.”]

Moses too, passing beyond the worldly rivers, saw a great vision and said: “I will pass over and see this great vision” (Exodus 3:3). For if he had been immersed in the vices of the body and the slippery pleasures of this world, he would not have seen such great mysteries.

75. Let us too pass through this fire of lust, which Paul feared—but feared for us. By disciplining his body, he had made himself no longer afraid for himself; he says to us: “Flee fornication” (1 Corinthians 6:18). Let us therefore flee it as though it were pursuing us—not following behind us, but pursuing us within ourselves. Let us take care, then, lest while fleeing it we carry it along with us. Often we want to flee, but if we do not shake it completely out of our mind, we carry it away rather than leave it behind.

Let us therefore leap over it, lest it be said to us: “Walk in the fire of your flame, which you have kindled for yourselves” (Isaiah 50:11). For just as the person who binds fire in his bosom burns his garments (Proverbs 6:27), so the person who walks upon fire must necessarily burn his feet; for it is written: “Can someone walk upon burning coals without scorching his feet?” (Proverbs 6:28).

[Col. 0489B] **76.** The fire is intense, and therefore let us not supply it with the fuel of luxury. Lust is fed by banquets, nourished by delicacies, kindled by wine, and inflamed by drunkenness. More serious than these are the provocations of words, which intoxicate the mind with a kind of wine from Sodom’s vine. Yet let us also beware of an excess of this wine; for where the flesh is drunk, the mind staggers, the spirit totters, and the heart is tossed about. Therefore the command given to Timothy is useful in both respects: “Use a little wine because of your frequent infirmities” (I Tim. V, 23). When the body is hot, it draws in vapor; when the flesh grows cold with the chill of illness, your soul is cooled; when your body suffers, your mind is sad—but your sadness will turn into joy.

**77.** Do not therefore fear if your flesh is eaten: your soul is not devoured. For this reason David says that he does not fear, because his enemies were eating his flesh, not his soul, as we read: “When evildoers draw near against me, to eat my flesh—those who trouble me, my enemies—they themselves were weakened and fell” (Ps. XXVI, 2). Thus the serpent brings ruin only upon itself. Therefore the one who has been crushed by the serpent is handed over to the serpent, so that the one whom it cast down may be raised up; and the serpent’s ruin may become man’s resurrection. Scripture shows Satan to be the author of this bodily crushing and carnal weakness, when Paul says: “There was given to me a thorn of my flesh, an angel of Satan, to buffet me, so that I might not be exalted” (II Cor. XII, 7). Thus Paul learned how to heal in the same manner in which he himself had been healed.

## CHAPTER XV

[Col. 0489D] Returning from his digression, he explains what it means to come “with a rod” or “in a spirit of gentleness.” One who has fallen grievously must be separated, but restored to the sacred rites after being cleansed by the prayer and tears of the devout congregation. The old leaven must be purged when the harshness of the letter is tempered with the flour of a gentler interpretation. How all in the Church must be kneaded together with its flour and nourished with the food of love, lest they become like that envious brother whom the Novatians imitate; their pride is indicated here.

**78.** Thus the good teacher, while promising one of two alternatives, granted both. He came with a rod, because he removed from sacred communion the man who had been convicted. And it is rightly said that he was handed over to Satan who is separated from Christ’s body. He also came in love and in a spirit of gentleness, either because he handed him over in such a way as to save his spirit, or because he later restored through the sacraments the man whom he had previously separated.

**79.** For one who has fallen grievously must indeed be separated, lest a little leaven corrupt the whole lump; and the old leaven must be purged—either in each individual, the old man, that is, the outward man with his deeds; or in the people, grown old in sins and hardened by vices. And he rightly said “purged,” not “thrown away.” For what is purged is not judged wholly useless; it is purged so that what is useful may be separated from what is useless. But what is thrown away is believed to contain nothing useful.

**80. [In some editions, Chapter XV.]** The Apostle therefore judged that he should then be restored to the heavenly sacraments, if he himself wished to be purged. And he rightly says, “Purge out”; for it is as though he is purged by the works of the whole people and washed by the tears of the congregation—redeemed from sin through the prayers and weeping of the people, and cleansed in the inner man. For Christ granted this to his Church: that through all it might redeem one, the Church which merited the coming of the Lord Jesus, so that through one all might be redeemed.

[Note: Thus the Roman edition and all manuscripts; but the old edition incorrectly preferred the addition “to be restored to the sacraments,” and the later Paris edition no more correctly had “to be entrusted to the sacraments.” Moreover, Ambrose, both in his other books and especially in these, so frequently urges those guilty of serious crimes to seek refuge in the prayers of the Church and of all Christians that there can be no doubt that he valued those intercessions no less than Tertullian. Tertullian says on this subject in *On Repentance*, chapter 10: “When you cast yourself at the knees of the brothers, you touch Christ, you entreat Christ; likewise, when they shed tears over you, Christ suffers, Christ is wounded for you,” and so forth. Those interested in the ceremonies by which those public prayers and tears were poured out for penitents may learn about them from the author of the *Apostolic Constitutions*, Book II, chapter 18, and especially Book VIII, chapter 9; likewise from canon 19 of the Council of Laodicea. If they wish, they may add what can be read concerning this rite in Chrysostom, Homily 72 on Matthew and Homily 18 on II Corinthians; it will become clear that the rite was established and customary in the Eastern Church. In the Western Church as well it prevailed no less. Besides the Ambrose cited above, witnesses include Pacianus, *Exhortation to Repentance* and Letter 1 to Sympronianus, among others; also Sozomen, Book VII of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 16, and the Roman Order, in the passage describing the rite of absolution on Thursday of Holy Week.]

**81.** This is Paul’s meaning, though his words make it less clear. Let us consider the Apostle’s own statement: “Purge out,” he says, “the old leaven, so that you may be a new kneading, just as you are unleavened” (I Cor. V, 7). This may mean that the whole Church takes upon itself the burden of the sinner, for whom it must feel compassion in weeping, prayer, and sorrow; and, as though with his leaven, kneads itself entirely together, so that through all, while one person practices repentance, what is superfluous may be purged by a kind of collective contribution of manly mercy or compassion.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “while someone exercises patience in respect of another.”]

[Note: Erasmus and later editions read, “individually, by mercy.” This is very appropriate and well suited to the words “by a kind of shared admixture.” For there is no doubt that this alludes to the highly commended custom of the ancients: when one of their friends had been ruined in his fortunes by some mischance, his friends individually contributed an *eranōn* (ἔρανον), that is, a collected sum of money, to relieve his misfortune, as Casaubon explains in his commentary on Theophrastus’ *Characters*, under the chapter “On Self-Will” [Greek title uncertain in the supplied text]. The charity of the first Christians greatly expanded this beneficence, so that, as the Apostle himself testifies more than once, collections were made to assist brothers pressed by poverty not only in the same city but also in different and distant places. The holy Doctor transferred this custom from bodily matters to spiritual ones. Nevertheless, although the adverb “individually” has a particular force here, since *virilis* is found in all the manuscripts and in Amerbach, we have decided to retain that reading. Nor does it lack its own elegance: through it he shows that serious and generous mercy is required, not a soft and womanish kind, such as even a foolish cause often arouses.]

Or it may mean what that Gospel woman teaches (Luke XIII, 21), who represents the type of the Church because she hides leaven in her flour until the whole is leavened, so that the whole world may be taken in.

**82.** The Lord taught me in the Gospel what leaven is when he said: “Do you not understand that I did not speak about bread? Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees” (Matt. XVI, 11). Then, he says, they understood that he had not told them to beware of bread, but of the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees. Thus the Church hides this leaven—that is, the teaching of the Pharisees and the disputation of the Sadducees—in her flour, when she softens the harsher letter of the Law by a spiritual interpretation and breaks it, as it were, with the mill of her own exposition. She brings forth, as it were, from the husks of the letters the inner secrets of the mysteries, and establishes faith in the resurrection, through which God’s mercy is proclaimed and the restoration of the life of the dead is believed.

[Note: The grains of seeds are enclosed in husks, like a covering.]

**83.** The adoption of this comparison does not seem inappropriate here. For the kingdom of heaven is the redemption of the sinner; and therefore let all of us, good and bad, be kneaded together with the flour of the Church, so that we may all be a new kneading.

[Note: An ancient German manuscript reads, “the forgiveness of sinners.” A little later, where all editions read, “so that we may be in a new kneading,” all manuscripts more appropriately have, “so that we may be in the new kneading.”]

[Note: The editions read, “so that we may be in a new kneading.”]

But lest anyone fear that the admixture of more defective leaven might discolor the lump, he therefore said: “So that you may be a new kneading, just as you are unleavened” (I Cor. V, 7). That is, this kneading will make you such as the pure sincerity of your innocence was. Thus, if we show mercy, we are not darkened by another’s sin; rather, we obtain that person’s redemption as a gain to our own grace, so that the purity that existed may endure.

[Note: A few manuscripts read, “through his redemption we obtain the grace of our own salvation”; some read, “we obtain the grace of his redemption.”]

And therefore he added: “For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (ibid.). That is, the Lord’s Passion benefited everyone and granted redemption to sinners who repented of the crime they had committed.

**84.** Let us therefore feast on good food, practicing repentance and rejoicing in redemption; for no food is sweeter than goodwill and devotion. Let no envy of a saved sinner be mingled with our feasts and our joy, lest he exclude himself from the Father’s house, like that envious brother described in the Gospel, who grieved that his brother had been received—the brother whom he had been glad to see excluded forever (Luke XV, 28).

**85.** You cannot deny, Novatians, that you resemble him. For this reason, as you say, you do not assemble in the Church: because through repentance hope of returning was granted to those who had fallen.

[Note: In order to defend their separation, the Novatians maintained that the Church had perished through the reception of the lapsed, as Cyprian testifies in Letter 52 and Pacianus on page 57; and thus they turned schism into heresy, as Augustine says of the Donatists, who in this respect showed themselves zealous imitators of the Novatians. They deliriously claimed that the Church had utterly perished because it communicated with Caecilianus, who had been ordained by, as they loudly alleged, traditors of the sacred books. But the grief over the loss of the episcopate distressed Donatus no less than Novatianus. On this subject see our Ambrose here and our *Admonition*, which should be consulted.]

But this was only a pretext. In fact, Novatianus, inflamed by grief over the episcopate he had lost, organized a schism.

**86.** But do you not understand that the Apostle prophesied concerning you also, and says to you: “And you are inflated, and did not rather mourn, so that the one who did this deed might be removed from your midst” (I Cor. V, 2)? He is truly removed completely when his sin is abolished. The Apostle does not say that he should be excluded from the Church; he urges that he should be purged.

## CHAPTER XVI

The Novatians are compared with the Apostle. How aptly the Lord’s words apply to them: “You do not know whose spirit you are.” Their zeal for repentance is extinguished when they remove its fruit. In this way sinners are deprived of Christ’s promises, although they should not be admitted to the mysteries too quickly. Finally, examples of certain penitents are proposed.

**87.** Since, then, the Apostle remitted the sin, by what authority do you deny that it should be remitted? Who is more reverent toward Christ, Novatianus or Paul? But Paul knew that the Lord was merciful; he knew that the Lord Jesus was more offended by the severity of his disciples than by mercy (II Cor. II, 10).

**88.** Finally, when James and John said that they would call down fire from heaven to consume those who refused to receive the Lord, Jesus rebuked them, saying: “You do not know whose spirit you are; for the Son of Man did not come to destroy human souls but to save them” (Luke IX, 55–56). To them he said, “You do not know whose spirit you are,” although they belonged to his spirit. But to you he says: “You are not of my spirit”—you who do not possess my clemency, who reject my mercy, who exclude repentance, which I wished to be preached in my name through my apostles.

**89.** For you say in vain that you preach repentance when you remove the fruit of repentance (Luke XXIV, 47). People are moved to pursue something either by rewards or by benefits; but every endeavor grows sluggish through delay. Therefore, so that the devotion of the disciples might be enriched by a present reward, the Lord said that whoever had left all his possessions and followed God would receive sevenfold both in this life and in the future (Matt. XIX, 29).

[Note: This is the reading of the old edition and many more manuscripts. The Roman edition, with some other codices, has “a hundredfold,” which corresponds aptly to the Gospel passage. Nevertheless, Latinius observed that “sevenfold” is cited four times by Cyprian and three times by the author of *Questions on the Old and New Testaments* preserved in Augustine.]

He first promised it in this life, to remove the distaste caused by delay; then he added “and in the future,” so that here you might learn to believe that rewards would also be paid to you in the future. The reward of present things, therefore, is testimony to future things.

**90.** If someone, then, possessing hidden sins, nevertheless earnestly practices repentance for Christ’s sake, how is he received if communion is not restored to him? I want the guilty person to hope for forgiveness; let him seek it with tears, seek it with groans, seek it through the weeping of the entire people. Let him beg to be pardoned. And when his communion has been deferred a second and a third time, let him believe that he pleaded too mildly; let him increase his weeping, return later in greater misery, clasp the feet with his arms, kiss them with kisses, wash them with tears, and not let go, so that the Lord Jesus may say of him: “Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much” (Luke VII, 47).

[Note: This passage caused Dallaeus extraordinary difficulty.
