In Book III, chapter 11, of *On Confession*, passing over it very lightly as something Perronius had brought against him, he says: “These words are directed against the Novatians, and signify that the penitent ought to be reconciled, which we do not deny; they do not signify that no sin is forgiven except to one who has secretly confessed his sins to a priest, which we deny.” But an intelligent man could not fail to see that the obvious conclusion against him was: “If one who has hidden sins and repents because of them ought to be reconciled, then hidden sins were subject to public repentance, and therefore also to the authority of priests.” On this point he says nothing here.

In Book IV, chapter 22, of the same work, however, he does not deny that it could sometimes happen that people burdened in conscience by secret crimes voluntarily and without compulsion from any law unburdened themselves before a priest, and willingly and gladly submitted to public repentance on the priest’s advice. After discussing this at greater length, he adds: “It seemed appropriate to preface this here, lest anyone be disturbed or led away from the truth if he should encounter, either in his own reading or in what Arnauld has cited, some unusual example of this kind of repentance among the ancients.” From these words it is easily and reasonably inferred that such examples were not considered wholly rare or unique, since he did not dare deny that examples of this sort could be found both in Arnauld and elsewhere.

We would now ask that minister whether it would be less scandalous for someone who had voluntarily confessed a hidden offense to perform public penance than for someone who had confessed it under compulsion of law. Indeed, the scandal would be greater in proportion as those who performed public penance for hidden offenses were rarer. Since such scandal did not prevent pastors from admitting to public penance those who voluntarily confessed hidden sins, neither could it deter them from establishing a law that even concealed crimes should be publicly confessed.

We would ask him again whether the distance between a public sin and one voluntarily and freely disclosed in secret is smaller than between a public sin and one disclosed under legal compulsion. No one could say this, since the opposite is perfectly evident. Since this difference alone did not prevent those who voluntarily confessed hidden sins from being subjected to the same public penalties imposed upon those guilty of manifest crimes, it likewise should not have prevented laws from being established by which hidden offenses would be expiated through the same public repentance by which manifest offenses were cured.

Hence it is clear that the principal difficulties he raises against the necessity of confessing hidden sins, which he rejects, apply no less against voluntary confession, which he admits. Thus the answer did not satisfy its author without good reason. He brought forward a third argument, much more futile than the earlier ones, when he claimed that all printed manuscripts were corrupt in the word “hidden.” We expected him to set handwritten manuscripts against the printed ones—not all, perhaps, but at least some, or even one. Since he neither did nor could do this, the agreement of the printed and unprinted books, both ancient and recent, is more than sufficient to preserve the authority of this passage fully and clearly.

Let us nevertheless hear his conjectures. First he asks the Catholics why hidden rather than manifest sins are mentioned here. As though, he says, the Novatians had asserted that forgiveness should be denied only for hidden sins, or Ambrose had shown that only hidden sins could be absolved by the Church. But who would not marvel that so sharp-sighted a man is here so blind that he does not see why only secret sins are mentioned? First, because anyone could easily infer *a fortiori* that the same applied to manifest sins, which are amply treated elsewhere in this work; and second, because the cruelty of the Novatians was thereby shown to extend more clearly and broadly, since even secret sinners were excluded from the hope of forgiveness.

Yet Dallaeus presses the matter further, believing that “many” rather than “hidden” should be read. He thinks this is proved especially by the fact that it would have been easy for scribes to err here and read two c’s for an m. He supports the claim by the similarity of the two letters, by the antithesis between many sins and repentance undertaken for Christ, and finally by the relation that these words bear to the Gospel passage that follows.

First, he would have done us a great favor if he had produced some examples of such an error; for we can affirm that we have not yet observed any. Next, what prevented scribes from making the same mistake in the cited passage from Luke, or at least from being warned at the same place about the corruption they had introduced? Why did no one before him detect the error from arguments that seem so obvious to Dallaeus?

In fact, Ambrose’s words relate no less well to the testimony just mentioned if one reads “hidden” than if one reads “many”—unless, perhaps, hidden crimes cannot be committed in numbers equal to manifest ones. As for the antithesis, our reading is certainly much more elegant, since sins secretly committed are thereby contrasted with public repentance.

“Be that as it may,” he says, “is it right to prefer this single passage, on the basis both of its arguments and of the contrary testimonies of the other Fathers?” But this is flight, not an answer. For we deny that the other Fathers are opposed to Ambrose here, and we maintain that many passages both of Ambrose and of other ancient writers support him. We noted some in the previous volume—for example, Book VII on Luke, page 1465, Book X, page 1525, and elsewhere. More will also be supplied in the published books on this subject by Alexander, Bibaqueus, and our Sammarthanus; consult them.]

**91.** I have known some who, in repentance, furrowed their faces with tears, carved their cheeks with continual weeping, and laid their bodies down for all to trample. With fasting mouth and pallid face, they continually displayed in their living bodies the appearance of death.

## CHAPTER XVII

Severity must be joined to compassion, as the Apostle is shown to have done in the case of the Corinthian. It is maintained that this man had been initiated through baptism, against the cavils of the Novatians. It is further shown that “destruction of the flesh” signifies not its annihilation but its chastisement, a point also confirmed by the comparison with the earth.

**92.** What do we expect the dead to deserve forgiveness for, when they inflicted death upon themselves while they were alive? “This rebuke,” he says, “which is inflicted by the majority is sufficient for one who is such, so that, on the contrary, you should rather forgive and console him, lest perhaps he be swallowed up by excessive sorrow” (II Cor. II, 6). If the rebuke inflicted by the majority is sufficient for condemnation, then the entreaty made by the majority is likewise sufficient for the remission of sin. The moral teacher, conscious of our weakness and interpreter of divine compassion, wishes the sin to be forgiven and consolation to be offered, lest sorrow swallow up the penitent through the weariness of prolonged delay.

[Col. 0495B] **93.** Therefore the Apostle forgave him; and he not only forgave him but also wished love to be confirmed toward him. Whoever is loved does not encounter harshness but gentleness. Nor did he forgive only himself: he wished everyone to forgive him as well, and said that he had forgiven for the sake of the others, lest the many should remain sorrowful for the sake of one.

“If anyone,” he says, “has been forgiven by you, I also have; for I too, for your sake, in the person of Christ, have forgiven, lest we be deceived by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his devices” (ibid., 10). One may rightly guard against the serpent if one is not ignorant of his devices, which are many and directed toward harm. He always wishes to harm and always to deceive, so as to inflict death. But we must beware lest our remedy become his triumph; for we are deceived by him if, through excessive sorrow, the one who can be freed through indulgence perishes.

[Note: An ancient German manuscript reads, “through excessive obstinacy.”]

[Col. 0495C] **94.** And so that we might know that he is speaking of one who had been baptized, he added: “I wrote to you in the letter not to associate with fornicators of this world” (I Cor. V, 9). And below he continued: “But now I have written to you not to associate with anyone who is called a brother if he is a fornicator, or greedy, or a servant of idols” (ibid., 11). Those whom he joined together for punishment, he also wished to belong together for forgiveness. “If anyone is such,” he says, “with such a one you should not even eat” (ibid.). How severe he is toward the obstinate, how indulgent toward those who plead! Against the former, Christ’s injury is armed; for the latter, the invocation of Christ gives support.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “the invocation of Christ gives support.”]

**95.** But lest anyone perhaps be disturbed because it is written: “I handed such a man over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh” (ibid., 5), and say, “How could he belong to forgiveness when all his flesh had perished?”—since it is clear that in both cases the man is redeemed and in both cases saved, neither the soul without the flesh nor the flesh without the soul, since they are joined as partners in their deeds and cannot be without a shared punishment or reward—let him have this answer: “Destruction” does not signify the complete consumption of the flesh but its chastisement.

For just as one who is dead to sin lives to God, so the allurements of the flesh perish, and the flesh dies to its desires, so that it may live again for chastity and the other good works.

[Note: Several manuscripts read, “as partners joined together in deeds and works.”]

**96.** And what more fitting example could we take than that of a mother? The earth itself, from which we have been taken, when cultivation and care are interrupted, appears abandoned; and dies, whether the field has been planted with vineyards or with olive trees. Yet it does not lose its proper sap, as though it were a kind of soul belonging to it. Finally, when cultivation is renewed and seeds are entrusted to it, it rises more fruitful in crops, judged suitable for them. It is therefore not inappropriate to say that our flesh also dies in this way, so that it may be understood to have been restrained rather than destroyed.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0495] ## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0495C]

Ambrose is about to append new instructions to those of the preceding book. He allegorically indicates the necessity of undertaking repentance promptly and also urges that it be undertaken. Then, by proposing the form of repentance found in the Apostle for imitation, he briefly presents its various fruits.

**1.** Although quite a few things useful for exhorting people to repentance have been written in the preceding book, nevertheless, since many more can be added, let us continue the banquet we have begun, lest we seem to have left behind a meal of our words only half-consumed.

**2.** Repentance must be undertaken not only carefully but also promptly, lest perhaps that Gospel householder who planted a fig tree in his vineyard should come and, seeking fruit on it, fail to find any and say to the keeper of the vineyard: “Cut it down. Why does it even occupy the ground?” (Luke XIII, 7). And unless the keeper of the vineyard intervenes, saying: “Lord, let it remain this year also, until I dig around it and put a basket of manure on it; and if indeed it bears fruit—but if not, cut down the fig tree” (ibid., 8–9)—

**3.** Let us therefore manure this field that we possess, and imitate the industrious farmers who are not ashamed to fill the earth with rich manure and scatter unclean ash over the field, so that they may gather more abundant fruits.

[Note: An imitation of those verses from Book I of the *Georgics*:

“Do not be ashamed to saturate the fallow ground with rich manure, nor to scatter unclean ash over exhausted fields.”]

**4.** The Apostle teaches us how to manure it when he says: “And I count everything as dung, so that I may gain Christ” (Phil. III, 8)—he who, through dishonor and good repute, deserved to please Christ. For he had read that Abraham, when he confessed himself to be dust and ashes, found God’s grace through the highest humility (Gen. XVIII, 3). He had read that Job, sitting in dung, recovered everything he had lost (Job XXIV). He had read in David’s prophecy that God raises the needy from the earth and lifts the poor from the dungheap (Ps. CXII, 7).

**5.** Let us therefore not be ashamed to confess our sins to the Lord.

[Note: That confession is made to God in the presence of a priest who acts as His vicar in this respect is made clear by what immediately follows: “It is shameful,” etc. For who would be ashamed to confess sins to Him alone, when he knows that they are more clearly known to Him than to himself? Certainly there can be shame in having committed them, but not in confessing them. Again, the statement that each person exposes his crimes sufficiently shows that the subject is not merely public crimes connected with scandal, but also hidden and secret ones voluntarily reported to a priest. See what is said below, chapter 4, no. 27, concerning one accused of a lesser fault.]

It is shameful for each person to expose his crimes; but that shame plows his field, removes its perpetual thorns, cuts down its brambles, and brings forth fruits that he had believed to be among the dead. Follow the one who, by plowing his field well, sought eternal fruits.

“We are cursed,” he says, “and we bless; we suffer persecution and endure; we are blasphemed and we entreat; we have become as the refuse of this world” (I Cor. IV, 12–13). If you too plow in this way, you will sow spiritual things. Plow, so that you may remove sin and acquire fruit. He plowed so that he might root out in himself the disposition of a persecutor.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “so that he might eradicate in himself the effect of the persecutor.”]

What more could Christ have contributed to our pursuit of correction than to convert us and give us a teacher who had been a persecutor?

## CHAPTER II

He answers the passage from the Apostle used by heretics against repentance, showing through an exposition of each of its parts—and through the prior mention there of the legal baptisms—that it must be understood of the repetition of baptism, although he adds that it may also be referred to the idea that what is impossible for human beings is by no means impossible for God.

**6.** Although they are refuted by so clear an example both of the Apostle himself and of his writings, they nevertheless still wish to resist. They claim that the authority of the Apostle’s statement supports them, citing what is written in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “For it is impossible for those who have once been enlightened, who have tasted the heavenly gift, who have become participants in the Holy Spirit, who have tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come, and who have fallen away, to be renewed again unto repentance, crucifying again for themselves the Son of God and triumphing in display” (Heb. VI, 4 ff.).

[Note: The Novatians produced no other passage that seemed more favorable to their heresy than this one. This was also the reason why the Epistle was accepted more slowly among the Latins as canonical, as can be learned from Eusebius, Book III of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 3, and Book VI, chapter 20; from Philastrius, *On Heresies*, 41; and from Jerome in various places. Epiphanius likewise records, when speaking of the same heresy, that this passage was the principal stronghold of the Cathari. Ambrose’s answer, however, is entirely correct, and it was embraced by the most distinguished writers equal or later than our teacher, although some, interpreting the passage of repentance, preferred to understand it as signifying a moral impossibility. That interpretation is also indicated at the end of the chapter.]

**7.** Could Paul preach against his own action? He forgave the Corinthian his sin through repentance (II Cor. II, 10). How could he himself here criticize his own judgment? Therefore, since he could not destroy what he had built, we recognize that he did not say something contrary but something different. What is contrary attacks itself; what is different ordinarily has a distinct rationale. It is not, however, so contrary that one does not support the other.

For since he preached that repentance brings forgiveness, he also had to speak about those who think baptism should be repeated; and first our anxiety had to be removed, so that we might know that after baptism, if anyone sinned, the sin could still be forgiven. Otherwise, deprived of the hope of forgiveness, they might be corrupted by the false idea that baptism should be repeated. Then it was necessary to demonstrate by rational argument that baptism must not be repeated.

**8.** The words themselves make clear that the passage was spoken about baptism, since he signified that those who have fallen cannot be renewed unto repentance. For we are renewed through the washing, by which we are reborn, as Paul himself says: “We have been buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life” (Rom. VI, 4). And elsewhere: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who has been created according to God” (Eph. IV, 23–24). And elsewhere: “Your youth will be renewed like the eagle’s” (Ps. CII, 3).

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads, “as the eagle, when it has died … so through the sacrament of baptism.” It should be observed in passing that Ambrose attributes to the eagle what is commonly said of the phoenix, which many writers imagine to be reborn from its own ashes.]

The eagle too, when it has died, is reborn from its remains; so, through the sacrament of baptism, when we have died to sin, we are reborn to God and restored. Thus he teaches that there is one baptism, as elsewhere: “One faith; one,” he says, “baptism” (Eph. IV, 5).

**9.** It is also evident that in the one who is baptized the Son of God is crucified, because our flesh could not abolish sin unless it had been crucified in Christ Jesus. Thus it is written: “Whoever among us has been baptized in Christ Jesus has been baptized into his death” (Rom. VI, 3). And below: “If we have been united with the likeness of his death, we shall also be united with his resurrection, knowing that our old man has been crucified with him” (ibid., 5–6). And to the Colossians he says: “You have been buried with him through baptism, in which you also rose with him” (Col. II, 12).

This was written so that we might believe that he himself is crucified in us, so that through him our sins may be cleansed, so that he himself may fasten our bond of indebtedness to the cross—he who alone can forgive sins. He himself triumphs in us over principalities and powers, since it is written of him: “He displayed principalities and powers, triumphing over them in himself” (Col. II, 15).

**10.** Therefore, when he says in this Epistle written to the Hebrews that it is impossible for those who have fallen to be renewed unto repentance, “crucifying again the Son of God and triumphing in display” (Heb. VI, 6), we must understand this as having been said about baptism. In baptism we crucify the Son of God in ourselves, so that through him the world may be crucified to us. We triumph, in a certain sense, when we take on the likeness of his death—he who displayed and triumphed over principalities and powers on his cross—so that we too may triumph, in the likeness of his death, over the principalities whose yoke we cast off.

Christ was crucified once and died to sin once; therefore there is one baptism, not several.

**11.** Moreover, did he not also introduce above the doctrine of baptisms? Since there were many baptisms in the Law, he rightly reproved those who abandon perfection and seek the beginning of the word.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “who abandon and seek the beginnings of the Word”; others, “who abandon and seek the principal words.”]

He teaches us that we ought to know that all the baptisms of the Law have been abolished, and that there is one baptism in the sacraments of the Church.

[Note: Some manuscripts and editions add, “that there is one baptism in the Church.”]

He exhorts us, however, that, leaving the beginning of the word, we should strive toward perfection: “And this we shall do,” he says, “if God indeed permits” (Heb. VI, 3). For no one can be perfect without God’s favor.

### 12

I could indeed say this also to anyone who thinks that the foregoing was said about penance: “What is impossible with human beings is possible with God”; and God is able, whenever he wills, to forgive us sins—even those which we think cannot be forgiven. Therefore, what appears impossible for us to obtain is possible for God to grant. For it also seemed impossible that sin could be washed away by water; indeed, Naaman the Syrian did not believe that his leprosy could be cleansed by water. But God made what was impossible possible, granting us so great a grace (2 Kings V, 11).

Similarly, it seemed impossible that sins could be forgiven through penance. Christ granted this to his apostles, and from the apostles it was transmitted to the ministry of priests (John XX, 22). Thus what seemed impossible became possible. Nevertheless, he makes clear by sound reasoning that the saying concerned baptism, so that no one should repeat it.[^c0048-1]

### CHAPTER III

[Col. 0499D]

He confirms the preceding solution by the parable of the prodigal son proposed from the Gospel. Explaining each of its parts, he turns them against the Novatian assertions in such a way that he necessarily concludes from them that reconciliation must not be denied even to one guilty of the gravest offense, provided that he has truly repented.

### 13

For the Apostle would not act against Christ’s manifest teaching when, speaking of the sinner who practices repentance, he made the comparison with the man who went abroad, squandered all the property he had received from his father by living dissolutely, and afterwards longed for his father’s bread while eating husks. He deserved a robe, a ring, sandals, and also the slaughter of the calf, which bears the figure of the Lord’s Passion, through which the heavenly sacrament is bestowed upon us (Luke XV, 13 and following).[^c0048-2]

### 14

It is rightly said that he went abroad, since he had been separated from the sacred altars. For this means being separated, as a citizen and member of the household, from that Jerusalem which is in heaven, the dwelling-place of the holy. Hence the Apostle also says: “Therefore you are no longer strangers and sojourners, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household” (Ephesians II, 9).

### 15

“And he squandered,” he says, “his property.” He rightly squandered it, since his faith faltered in works: “For faith is the substance of things hoped for, the proof of things not seen” (Hebrews XI, 1). And faith is a good possession, in which our hope has its patrimony.[^c0048-3]

### 16

Nor is it surprising that he was perishing from hunger, since he needed divine nourishment. Driven by his longing for it, he said: “I will arise and go to my father and say to him: Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you” (Luke XV, 18). Do you not clearly perceive that this has been explained to us: that, in order to obtain the sacrament, we are impelled to pray—and that you wish to take away the very thing for which penance is performed?[^c0048-4]

Take away from a helmsman the hope of reaching his destination, and he will wander uncertainly amid the waves. Take away the crown from a wrestler, and he will lie inert in the stadium. Take away from a fisherman the effectiveness of his catch, and he will cease to cast his nets. How, then, can one whose soul is suffering hunger pray more earnestly to God if he despairs of sacred nourishment?

### 17

“I have sinned,” he says, “against heaven and before you.” He certainly confesses a sin deserving death, lest you think that anyone practicing penance for any crime may rightly be excluded. For the one who has sinned against heaven—or against the heavenly kingdom, or against his own soul, which is a sin unto death—has also sinned before God, to whom alone it is said: “Against you alone have I sinned, and I have done evil before you” (Psalm L [LI], 6).

### 18

He so quickly obtains pardon that the father runs to meet him while he is still coming and still far away, gives him a kiss—which is the distinctive sign of sacred peace—and orders a robe to be brought, the wedding garment, without which anyone is excluded from the wedding feast. He gives a ring on his hand, which is the pledge of faith and the seal of the Holy Spirit. He orders sandals to be brought (Exodus XII, 11); for one who is about to celebrate the Lord’s Passover and feast upon the lamb must have protection against every assault of spiritual beasts, and must have a foot protected against the serpent’s bites. He orders the calf to be slaughtered, because “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians V, 7). For whenever we receive the Lord’s blood, we proclaim the Lord’s death (1 Corinthians XI, 26). Therefore, just as he was sacrificed once for all, so whenever sins are forgiven we receive the sacrament of his body, so that forgiveness of sins may be effected through his blood.[^c0048-5]

### 19

Thus, by the Lord’s preaching, it has been most clearly commanded even to those guilty of the gravest crime that, if they practice penance with their whole heart and with open confession of sin, the grace of the heavenly sacrament is to be restored to them.[^c0048-6] Therefore, it is certain that nothing remains for you by which you can excuse yourselves.[^c0048-7]

### CHAPTER IV

He turns against the Novatians themselves another objection drawn from blasphemy against the Holy Spirit. He shows that by this blasphemy one must understand an unsound faith. After confirming this by Peter’s judgment against Simon Magus and by Gospel testimony, he urges the same heretics to return to the Church and asserts that the Lord’s clemency is so great that he would not have denied pardon even to Judas the betrayer, had he repented before Christ.

### 20

Nevertheless, it has come to our ears that you are accustomed to bring forward this further objection: you say that it is written: “Every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven to human beings; but blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven to human beings. And whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come” (Matthew XII, 31 and following).

By this example your entire assertion is destroyed and dissolved; for it is written: “Every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven to human beings.” Why, then, do you not forgive? Why do you bind the chains which you do not loose? Why do you tie knots which you do not release? Forgive others; deal with those whom, because they sin against the Holy Spirit, you think are bound forever by the authority of the Gospel.

### 21

And yet let us consider whom he binds, repeating the preceding words of the passage itself, so that we may understand it more clearly. The Jews were saying: “This man casts out demons only by Beelzebul, the prince of demons.” Jesus answered: “Every kingdom divided against itself will be destroyed, and every city or house divided against itself will not stand. If Satan casts out Satan, he is divided against himself; how, then, will his kingdom stand? And if I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out?” (Matthew XII, 24 and following).[^c0048-8]

### 22

Here we plainly see that he was speaking of those who said that the Lord Jesus cast out demons by Beelzebul. The Lord answered them in this way because Satan’s inheritance belonged to those who compared the Savior of all with Satan and placed Christ’s grace in the devil’s kingdom. And, so that we might know that he was speaking of this blasphemy, he added: “Brood of vipers, how can you speak good things when you are evil?” He declares, therefore, that those who say such things do not belong to pardon.

### 23

Finally, Peter says to Simon (Decree, part I, question 1, chapter “Peter”), who, corrupted by his habitual practice of magic, had thought that he could acquire Christ’s grace by money through the laying on of hands and the infusion of the Holy Spirit: “You have neither part nor share in this faith, because your heart is not right before God. Repent, therefore, of this wickedness of yours and pray to the Lord, if perhaps this thought of your heart may be forgiven you; for I see that you are in the bondage of iniquity and the bitterness of gall” (Acts VIII, 21 and following).[^c0048-9]

You see that apostolic authority condemns this man, who blasphemed against the Holy Spirit through magical vanity, and all the more because he did not possess a pure conscience of faith. Yet Peter did not cut off his hope of pardon; instead, he invited him to repentance.

### 24

The Lord’s response, therefore, concerned the blasphemy of the Pharisees. For this reason he denies them the grace of his power, which consists in the forgiveness of sins, because they claimed that his heavenly power was supported by the devil’s assistance. He also declares that those who separate the Lord’s Church use a diabolical spirit, thereby including heretics and schismatics of every age. He denies them indulgence because, whereas every sin is directed against individuals, this one is directed against the whole body. For they alone wish to dissolve Christ’s grace—those who tear apart the members of the Church, for whose sake the Lord Jesus suffered and the Holy Spirit was given to us.

### 25

Finally, so that you may know that he is speaking of those who scatter, we have it written: “Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters” (Matthew XII, 30). And so that we might know that he was speaking of these people, he immediately added: “Therefore I tell you: every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven to human beings, but blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven to human beings” (ibid., 31). When he says, “Therefore I tell you,” did he not clearly wish us to understand that this applied above all to them?

With good reason he added: “A good tree produces good fruits, but an evil tree produces evil fruits” (Matthew VII, 17), for an evil assembly cannot produce good fruit. The tree, therefore, is the assembly, and the fruits of the good tree are the children of the Church.

### 26

Therefore return to the Church, you who have impiously separated yourselves. For he promises pardon to all who turn back, since it is written: “Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved” (Joel II, 32). Finally, even the Jewish people, which said of the Lord Jesus, “He has a demon” (John VIII, 48), and said, “He casts out demons by Beelzebul” (Luke XI, 15), and crucified the Lord Jesus, is called by Peter’s preaching to baptism, so that it may lay aside the guilt deserved for so great a crime.

### 27

But what is surprising if you deny salvation to others, when you refuse your own salvation, although those who seek penance from you differ in no respect from you?[^c0048-10] I think that Judas also could not have been excluded from pardon by so great a mercy of God, if he had practiced penance not before the Jews but before Christ. “I have sinned,” he said, “because I betrayed innocent blood” (Matthew XXVII, 54). They answered: “What is that to us? You see to it.” What other response do you give when someone guilty of a lesser sin confesses his own deed to you? What else do you answer but: “What is that to us? You see to it”? The noose follows this speech—the punishment becoming more savage because the guilt is lesser.

### 28

But if those people do not turn back, then you at least return, you who through various falls have fallen from the lofty height of innocence and faith. We have a good Lord, who wishes to pardon everyone, who called you through the prophet, saying: “I am, I am he who blots out iniquities; and I will not remember them. But you, remember, and let us enter into judgment” (Isaiah XLIII, 25).

### CHAPTER V

They deny that Peter explicitly promised pardon to Simon Magus. First, it is argued that the apostle may have used an equivocal expression because he knew the magician’s faithlessness. Second, it is shown from several passages of the Old Testament, from the usage of profane authors, and finally from the evangelists themselves that the adverb “perhaps” (*forsitan*) can also signify affirmation. He then adds that the apostles transmitted to us the practice of penance, whose fruits are displayed by David. Finally, he adduces the example of the Ephraemites, teaching that we should practice penance after their manner so that divine mercy and the sacraments may be granted to us.

### 29

Nevertheless, they raise the question concerning the words of the apostle Peter. Because he said, “Perhaps” (Acts VIII, 22), they think that Peter did not affirm that sin would be forgiven to one who practiced penance. But they should consider whom he was discussing—namely Simon, who did not believe from faith but was devising a fraud. Indeed, when a man said to the Lord that he would follow him, although the Lord saw that his sincerity was incomplete, he answered: “Foxes have dens” (Matthew VIII, 20). If, before baptism, the Lord prevented this man from following him because he saw that he was deceitful, should you be surprised that, after baptism, the Apostle did not absolve him when he persisted in wrongdoing, declaring him to remain in the bondage of iniquity?

### 30

But let this be their answer. For my part, I say neither that Peter doubted nor that so important a matter should be strangled by the prejudice of a single word. For if they think that Peter doubted, did God also doubt? He says to the prophet Jeremiah: “Stand in the court of the house of the Lord, and you shall give an answer to all Judah, to those who come to worship in the house of the Lord, all the words that I have commanded you to answer them; do not take away a word. Perhaps they will listen and turn back” (Jeremiah XXVI, 2–3). Let them then say that God also did not know what would happen.

### 31

But ignorance is not expressed by that word. Rather, this kind of usage is frequently found in the divine Scriptures, because the expression is simple. Thus the Lord also says to Ezekiel: “Son of man, I am sending you to the house of Israel, to those who have provoked me—them and their fathers—even to this day; and you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord God: Perhaps they will listen and be afraid” (Ezekiel II, 4–5). Did he not know, then, whether they could or could not turn back? This expression, therefore, does not always indicate one who is doubting.

### 32

Finally, even the wise men of this world, who place all their glory in the expression of words, did not always use what we call *forsitan* in Latin and τάχα (*tacha*) in Greek to express doubt. Thus they say that the first of their poets said: “Ἦ τάχα χήρα ἔσομαι,” which means: “Soon I shall be a widow.” And elsewhere: “τάχα γάρ σε κατακτανέουσιν Ἀχαιοὶ πάντες ἐφορμηθέντες” (Homer, Iliad, Book III). For he would not be doubting that, if all attacked together, one man could easily be struck down by everyone.

### 33

But let us use examples from our own sources rather than from others. Thus you have in the Gospel that the Son himself said of the Father, when he had sent servants to his vineyard and they had been killed: “I will send my most beloved son; perhaps they will respect him” (Matthew XXI, 37). And elsewhere the Son says in his own person: “You know neither me nor my Father. If you knew me, you would perhaps know my Father also” (John VIII, 19).

### 34

If, then, Peter used the same words that God used without prejudice to his knowledge, why should we not accept that Peter also used such language without prejudice to his faith? For he could not doubt Christ’s gift, since Christ had given him the power to loose sins (Matthew XVI, 19), especially since he ought not leave room for the schemes of heretics, who wish to destroy human hope in order more easily to persuade the despairing to repeat baptism.

### 35

But the apostles, possessing this authority, taught penance according to Christ’s instruction; they promised pardon and released guilt, just as David also taught when he said: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not reckoned sin” (Psalm XXXI [XXXII], 1–2).[^c0048-11]

He called both blessed: the one whose iniquity is forgiven through the washing, and the one whose sin is covered by good works. For one who practices penance must not only wash away his sin with tears, but also cover and conceal his former offenses by more upright deeds, so that sin may not be reckoned against him.[^c0048-12]

### 36

Therefore, let us cover our falls by subsequent deeds and cleanse them with tears, so that the Lord our God may hear us groaning, just as he heard Ephraem weeping, as it is written, God saying: “I have surely heard Ephraem weeping” (Jeremiah XXXI, 18). He also expressed the very words of the lamenting Ephraem, saying: “You chastised me, and I was chastised, like an untrained calf” (ibid.).

A calf plays and leaves the manger. Therefore Ephraem was like an untrained calf, far from the manger, because he had abandoned the Lord’s manger and, following Jeroboam, worshiped calves (Tobit I, 5), just as prophecy through Aaron had foretold that the Jewish people would fall. Accordingly, in practicing repentance he says: “Convert me, and I shall be converted, for you are the Lord my God. For after I had repented at the end of my captivity, and after I came to know you, I groaned over the days of my confusion and submitted myself to you; for I received reproach and made you known” (Jeremiah XXXI, 19).

### 37

We have observed how penance should be practiced, with what words and with what tears, so that the day of sin may be called a day of confusion. For it is confusion when Christ is denied.

### 38

Therefore let us submit ourselves to God and not be subject to sin. Recalling our offenses, let us blush as though they were a reproach; let us not proclaim them as a kind of glory, as some boast after chastity has been conquered and justice overthrown. Let our conversion be so complete that we who did not acknowledge God may now ourselves make him known to others.

Then, moved by such a conversion of ours, the Lord will answer: “Ephraem is a beloved son to me from his youth, a cherished child; for whenever my words are in him, I shall surely remember him. Therefore I hastened toward him; I will surely have mercy on him, says the Lord” (Jeremiah XXXI, 20).

### 39

What mercy he promises us he shows below, saying: “I have given drink to every thirsty soul, and I have filled every hungry soul. Therefore I arose, and I looked, and my sleep was sweet to me” (ibid., 25–26). We perceive that the Lord promises his sacraments to those who sin; therefore let us all turn back to the Lord.[^c0048-13]

### CHAPTER VI

Those who have fallen from faith or innocence are again urged to repent. From Isaiah he teaches what they should expect from God and what they themselves must do. Then, recalling Christ’s proverbial rebuke of the Jews, and taking that occasion to criticize dancing and theatrical movements, he transfers the same proverb to a spiritual meaning. Next, from Jeremiah’s practice of repentance on behalf of Jerusalem, he explains what conditions this virtue requires. Finally, to show more clearly how effective this medicine is, he enumerates many who wished to use it either for themselves or for others.

### 40

But if those people do not turn back, then you at least return, you who through various falls have fallen from the lofty height of innocence and faith. We have a good Lord who wishes to pardon everyone, who called you through the prophet, saying: “I am, I am he who blots out your iniquities, and I will not remember them; but you, remember, so that we may enter into judgment” (Isaiah XLIII, 25).

“I,” he says, “will not remember; but you, remember.” That is: I do not recall any of the offenses that I have forgiven you, as though they had been covered by a kind of forgetfulness; but you remember. “I,” he says, “will not remember because of grace; you remember for the sake of correction. Remember, so that you may know that your sin has been forgiven. Do not glory as though you were innocent; do not make yourself more guilty by justifying yourself. But if you wish to be justified, confess your offense.” For a shamefaced confession of sins truly loosens the bonds of crimes.[^c0048-14]

### 41

You see what your God requires of you: that you remember the grace you have received and not glory as though you had not received it. You see by what promise of forgiveness he urges you to confess. Take care lest, by resisting the heavenly commands, you fall into the condition of the Jews, to whom the Lord Jesus says: “We played music for you, and you did not dance; we lamented, and you did not weep” (Luke VII, 32).

### 42

The saying is commonplace, but the mystery is not commonplace. Therefore, let no one, deceived by a merely ordinary interpretation of this saying, think that we are commanded to perform the slippery movements of public dancing or the delirium of the stage; such things are vicious even in adolescence. Rather, he commanded the dance that David danced before the ark of the Lord. Everything that is offered to religion is fitting, so that we may not be ashamed of any service that advances the worship and observance of Christ.[^c0048-15]

### 43

Thus it is not the dance associated with pleasure and luxury that is being praised, but one by which each person raises the body actively, does not allow the limbs to lie sluggishly on the ground, and does not let the feet grow numb through slow steps. Paul danced spiritually when he stretched himself out for us, forgetting what lay behind, reaching toward what lay ahead, and pressing on toward Christ’s prize. You too, when you come to baptism, are instructed to raise your hands and to have swifter feet with which to climb toward eternal things (Philippians III, 13–14). This is a dance accompanied by faith and attended by grace.

### 44

This, then, is the mystery: “We played music for you”—that is, the new song of the Testament—“and you did not dance,” that is, you did not raise your soul to spiritual grace. “We lamented, and you did not weep,” that is, you did not practice penance. Therefore the Jewish people were abandoned, because they neither practiced penance nor accepted grace. John brought penance; Christ brought grace. The one he announces as a servant; the other he bestows as Lord. The Church therefore preserves both, so that it may obtain grace and not cast aside penance. Grace is the gift of the giver; penance is the remedy of the offender.

### 45

Jeremiah knew that penance was a great remedy. He undertook it in his Lamentations on behalf of Jerusalem and introduces Jerusalem itself as practicing it, saying: “Weeping, she wept in the night, and her tears were on her cheeks, and there was no one to comfort her among all those who loved her. The roads of Zion mourn” (Lamentations I, 2). And he added: “For these things I weep; my eyes have grown dim with weeping, because the one who comforted me has gone far from me” (Lamentations I, 16).

We perceive that she considered this the bitterest accumulation of her misfortunes: that there was no one to comfort the mourner. How, then, do you take away that very consolation when you deny the hope of obtaining the release of penance?

### 46

But let those who practice penance hear how they ought to practice it: with what zeal, what emotion, what intention of mind, what shaking of their inmost entrails, and what conversion of heart. “See, Lord,” she says, “for I am afflicted; my belly is troubled by my weeping; my heart is turned within me” (ibid., 20).

### 47

You have learned the intention of the soul; now learn the faith of the mind and the posture of the body. “The elders of the daughter of Zion sat on the ground and kept silent; they put dust on their heads and girded themselves with sackcloth. They brought down the princes to the ground. The virgins of Jerusalem fainted in tears. My eyes have grown dim; my belly is troubled; my glory has been poured out upon the ground” (Lamentations II, 10–11).

### 48

The people of Nineveh also wept in this way and escaped the destruction announced against the city (Jonah III, 5). For the medicine of penance is so powerful that God seems to change his sentence. It is therefore in your power to escape. The Lord wishes to be entreated; he wishes hope to be placed in him; he wishes supplication to be made to him. You are a human being, and you wish to be entreated so that you may forgive; yet you think that God will not forgive you when you do not entreat him?

### 49

The Lord himself wept over Jerusalem (Luke XIX, 41), so that, because Jerusalem did not wish to weep, it might reach pardon through the Lord’s tears.[^c0048-16] He himself wishes us to weep so that we may escape, as you have it written in the Gospel: “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves” (Luke XXIII, 28).

### 50

David wept, and deserved that divine mercy should remove the death of the perishing people (2 Samuel XXIV, 10), when, having been offered three choices, he nevertheless chose the one in which he would experience the greater mercy of the Lord. Why are you ashamed to weep over your sins, when God even commanded the prophets to weep for peoples?

### 51

Finally, Ezekiel too was commanded to weep for Jerusalem, and he received a book at whose head was written: “Lamentation, a song, and woe” (Ezekiel II, 9)—two mournful things and one delightful one. For the person who will be saved in the future is the one who weeps more in this world: “The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning, and the heart of fools is in the house of feasting” (Ecclesiastes VII, 5). The Lord himself also says: “Blessed are you who weep now, for you will laugh” (Luke VI, 21).

### CHAPTER VII

Since the older edition and the remaining manuscripts, which are much more authoritative, have another reading, the verb “persuades” should be referred to Paul himself: he quotes the cited passage in such a way that it persuades us that the passage must be understood only of the repetition of baptism.

[^c0048-2]: The Roman edition alone reads: “he placed it in the one who went abroad,” and so forth.

[^c0048-3]: A few manuscripts read: “in which our hope has its support.”

[^c0048-4]: The examples he offers here are entirely similar to those proposed by Cyprian in Letter 55, to Antonianus. Hence someone might easily think that our Teacher imitated him.

[^c0048-5]: “In the same way as he was sacrificed once for all” (On Penance, distinction I, chapter “It Can Be Done,” section “As Once”).

[^c0048-6]: Some manuscripts read: “the restoring grace … it is certain that he returned.”

[^c0048-7]: How strongly he regarded this Gospel passage as directed against the Novatians may readily be learned if one does not hesitate to compare this entire chapter with his exposition of the same passage in the Commentary on Luke.

[^c0048-8]: In this extraordinarily important objection, Pacianus also gives an answer in Letter 3 to Sympronianus, near the middle, using the same two responses that Ambrose employs here. Morinus, led by these very passages, argued in Book IX of *On the Administration of Penance*, chapter 28, that both Fathers attributed to the passage the doctrine that some sin is truly unforgivable. Nevertheless, concerning Pacianus, he is forced to admit that Pacianus expressed his meaning in such a way that he considered nothing to be signified by these passages as unforgivable except persistence in the crime, or final impenitence.

As for Ambrose’s position: after saying, “He confesses,” Morinus adds that Ambrose evidently means that those who blaspheme directly, like the Pharisees, should not hope for pardon. A little later he continues: “To lessen the force of the argument, he extends that sin to heretics and schismatics, to whom grace is not denied when they repent, thereby implying that mercy would not be lacking to others either, if they could practice penance.” This is Morinus’s view. Yet he certainly had to prove that the holy Teacher thought repentance impossible for blasphemers of this kind, and Ambrose did not establish that.

For a clearer understanding of the question, observe that, in the passages brought forward by the heretics concerning blasphemy against the Spirit, the response here proceeds in two ways: first, by a rhetorical concession through which their argument is turned back against them; second, by examining those same passages more closely and asking what that sin against the Spirit finally is.

Thus, to illustrate the matter by examples, all those people are declared guilty of this crime: those who slanderously said that Christ cast out demons by Beelzebul; Simon and those who, with him, thought that the gifts of grace could be bought; and finally heretics and schismatics. Since Ambrose commonly promises pardon to the last group when they return—a point Morinus himself does not deny—and since, in the following chapter, Ambrose demonstrates that grace would truly have been promised even to Simon had he repented, there is no reason why we should not think that he held the same view concerning the first group as well.

This is especially so because in Book I, chapter 2, he declares generally: “The Lord excludes no crime, since he forgave all sins.” The theologian mentioned above, who argues that Ambrose treated blasphemy as an exception to this universal rule, offers no adequate proof for his opinion.

Let it therefore remain established that, for Ambrose, no sin was simply beyond hope of pardon except final impenitence. Augustine likewise, in this question—which he declares in *The Enchiridion*, chapter 8, and in *On the Words of the Lord*, sermon 71, number 38, to be the most difficult of all—followed the same opinion in Book I of the *Retractations*, chapter 19.

If someone says that all sins may in the same way be called unforgivable, we shall admit this, but we shall add that blasphemy is so called because it contains more malice and pride than weakness and is therefore forgiven much more difficultly; it is designated in this particular way. See Maldonado on the relevant passage in Matthew; Alexander, Dissertation 22 in the *Ecclesiastical History of the Third Century*; and the other interpreters of the cited Matthean text, as well as the scholastics on Book II of the *Sentences*, distinction 43, and on Thomas, *Summa Theologiae* II–II, question 14, article 3.

[^c0048-9]: The Claromontanus manuscript reads: “from this folly of yours.” Again, where all manuscripts and the old edition read “the remembrance of your heart,” the Roman edition alone has “the thought of your heart.”

[^c0048-10]: All editions and many manuscripts read: “although they have no difference from you,” a wording to which we think no meaning can be assigned. The remaining manuscripts read better: “although they differ in nothing,” that is, they should be considered sinners to the same degree as you yourselves.

[^c0048-11]: These words of David have been explained once and again in the preceding volume, namely in *Noah and the Ark*, chapter 31, number 117, and in *An Apology for David*, chapter 9, number 49. In those passages the holy Teacher teaches that the prophet signifies baptism and penance. In the second passage, it is worth observing that Ambrose includes among the works by which David covered his sin even works that preceded his fall. Hence this provides considerable authority for the opinion of theologians who think that good works, once killed by some mortal sin, revive through penance.

Here, however, while arguing against the Novatians, he examines the matter more carefully. Thus he distinguishes two things in penance: washing away sin with tears and covering it with more reformed deeds. All Catholics will readily agree that the former concerns contrition and the latter satisfaction. Indeed, even Dallaeus himself, in Book VII of *On Penance and Satisfaction*, chapter 8, does not differ from us concerning the first.

Concerning the second, however, arguing there against Cardinal Bellarmine, he maintains that the holy Bishop is speaking in the sense that the sinner should shade and cover, by good works as by ointment and plaster, the scars still clinging to sins already forgiven. But the sequence of the discourse plainly shows the contrary. Consider it, especially the example of the Ephraemites that follows, and you will understand for yourself that he is speaking altogether of tears and works—not merely works that apply plaster to sins already forgiven, but works that also turn divine mercy toward sinners so that they may obtain forgiveness for the offenses committed.

As for the first part of the cited Psalm 31, which Ambrose explains of baptism, interpreters of Paul, who presents the same words in Romans IV, 7, commonly understand it in the same way.

[^c0048-12]: Some manuscripts read: “cover his former offenses by deeds of amendment.”

[^c0048-13]: The Gill and Roman editions read: “what he promises to those practicing penance”; Amerbach, Erasmus, the marginal reading of Gill, and all manuscripts read: “what he promises to those who sin,” with the qualification understood: provided that they practice penance.

At the beginning of the following chapter, all editions read: “If those people do not turn back,” while all manuscripts have: “But if those people do not turn back,” as also occurs at the end of chapter 4, number 29. This repetition of several verses sufficiently indicates that the material contained in the preceding chapter was inserted as a digression, and that the chapters were consequently not distributed correctly in the earlier editions. It is also clear that Sotus had this passage in mind when he sometimes objected in this work that the same points were repeated word for word, as though repetitions were unusual in Ambrose.

[^c0048-14]: A number of orthodox theologians insist that sacramental confession is being discussed here, and some declare that this is clearer than daylight. Nevertheless, we must admit that such complete evidence is lacking here, since the discussion rather concerns confession made before God concerning sins already forgiven.

Their opinion is nevertheless probable because of the preceding words, “If you wish to be justified, confess your offense,” and because of the earlier statement, “Then you return, you who through various falls have fallen from innocence,” and so forth. It is entirely certain, however, that here and throughout the work confession is presupposed. These books teach everywhere that its three parts—contrition, declaration, and satisfaction—are necessary for the remission of sin.

[^c0048-15]: The Claromontanus manuscript reads: “of public dancing.” Latinius conjectures that “of playful dancing” should be read, evidently because of what follows, “and the delirium of the stage.” But with no worse sense, and with all the manuscripts and editions, we read “of slippery dancing,” that is, impure dancing inclined toward luxury, as is described below. The holy Teacher interprets this verse of Luke in a similar manner in Book VI, number 5, of his Commentary on that Gospel.

[^c0048-16]: The Roman edition reads: “might reach pardon.” This is not a bad reading, except that it stands alone.

He urges people to weep over and confess their sins, asserting that Christ is moved by the tears of the sinner and of the Church so that he may justify him. This is wonderfully illustrated by the fitting story of Lazarus raised from the dead. After showing that the Novatians are successors of those Jews who plotted to kill Lazarus, he teaches that the complete justification of every kind of sin is represented by the fragrance of the ointment poured by Mary upon Christ’s feet; and again he shows that the same heretics are marked out in the person of Judas, who was envious while the others rejoiced.

[Col. 0510B] **52.** Let us therefore weep for a time, so that we may rejoice for eternity. Let us fear the Lord; let us forestall him by confessing our sins; let us correct our falls and amend our error, lest it also be said of us: “Alas for me, my soul! For the reverent one has perished from the earth, and there is no one who corrects among human beings” (Micah VII, 2).

[Note: [Col. 0509D] The old edition has *periît timor tuus*, “your fear has perished”; some manuscripts have *periit timoratus*, “the fearful one has perished”; others, *periit reverens*, “the reverent one has perished.” We have followed the latter reading, as does the Roman edition.]

**53.** Why are you afraid to confess your sins before a good Lord? “Declare your iniquities,” he says, “so that you may be justified” (Isaiah XLIII, 26). Even while he is still guilty, the rewards of justification are offered to the sinner; for the one who willingly acknowledges his own crime is justified. Indeed, the just person is, at the beginning of his speech, his own accuser (Proverbs XVIII, 17). The Lord knows everything, but he awaits your voice—not in order to punish, but in order to forgive. He does not want the devil to insult you and accuse you because you conceal your sins. Anticipate your accuser: if you accuse yourself, you will fear no accuser; if you yourself disclose your guilt, then, even if you have died, you will live again.

[Col. 0510C] **54.** Christ will come to your tomb. And if he sees Martha, that good woman of service, weeping for you, and Mary, who listened attentively to the word of God, like the holy Church that chose for herself the better portion, he will be moved by compassion when he sees the tears of many at your death, and he will say: “Where have you laid him?” (John XI, 34)—that is, in what condition of guilt is he, in what order of penitents? “Let me see the one for whom you are weeping,” so that he himself may be moved by your tears. Let me see whether he has already died to that sin for which forgiveness is being sought.

[Note: [Col. 0509D] The Roman edition, with two manuscripts, reads: “if he himself moves him by his tears.” Other editions, with the remaining manuscripts, read as in the text. Moreover, what Saint Ambrose teaches in this and the following number makes it perfectly clear that whatever was said above about confession made secretly to God alone is to be understood in the sense that the confession itself was also made before a priest. On this point even Dallaeus does not disagree with us, except insofar as he maintains that the same *exomologesis*—confession—had to be made publicly before the Church. Since he thinks that this assertion is proved by chapter 10 of this book, we shall examine his arguments there.

In the meantime, since the stations of the penitents, each of which is touched upon in various places in this work, are here indicated in general, we have thought it useful to represent them here in the words of Matthew Blastares in the *Nomocanon*: “The penitents,” he says, “are divided into four orders: the weepers, the hearers, the prostrate, and the standers. The weepers are those who stand outside the door of the oratory and ask from the faithful entering and leaving both the assistance of their prayers and forgiveness of their sin. The hearers are those who stand outside the door, in the place called the *narthex*, and listen to the divine Scriptures and the explanation of the common teaching; afterward they leave with the catechumens. The prostrate are those who stand inside the church, but behind the ambo; they too leave with the catechumens when the deacon proclaims that solemn formula, ‘All catechumens, depart.’ Finally, the standers pray and sing psalms with the faithful, but they are nevertheless excluded from participation in the holy mysteries until, after the appointed period has elapsed, the fullness of divine communion receives them.” Thus far he. Since he explains the whole matter most clearly, we have transcribed him here.]

**55.** The people will say to him: “Come and see” (ibid.). What is “Come”? It means: Let the forgiveness of sins come; let the life of the dead come; let the resurrection of the deceased come; and let your kingdom also come upon this sinner.

[Col. 0511A] **56.** He will come and command the stone to be lifted—the stone which the fall of the sinner has laid upon his neck. He could have removed the stone by the command of his word, for when Christ commands, even insensible nature usually obeys. By the silent force of a hidden operation he could have transferred the stone of the tomb, in whose Passion, when the stones were suddenly removed, [429] many tombs of the dead were opened. But he commanded human beings to remove the stone: literally, so that unbelievers might believe what they saw and look upon the dead man rising; figuratively, so that he might grant us to lift the burdens of sins, certain masses weighing down the guilty. It is our task to remove the burdens; it is his to raise up, his to lead out of the tombs those freed from their bonds.

[Col. 0511B] [Note: [Col. 0511D] Some manuscripts read, “freed from the weight.”]

**57.** Seeing, then, the sinner’s heavy burden, the Lord Jesus weeps; for he does not allow the Church alone to weep. He suffers with his beloved, and says to the dead man: “Come outside” (John XI, 43)—that is: You who lie in the darkness of conscience and in the filth of your sins, in a kind of prison of the guilty, come outside; disclose your own sin, so that you may be justified. “For with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans X, 10).

[Note: [Col. 0511D] Thus the manuscripts unanimously. All the editions, on the contrary, read: “Why do you lie … in some prison of the guilty? Come outside.” This is not at all a bad reading.]

**58.** [Note: [Col. 0512D] Some manuscripts read, “If you have been converted.”] If you have confessed, once called by Christ, the barriers will be broken and all bonds will be loosed, even if the stench of bodily corruption is severe. The one whose flesh stank in the tomb had been there four days; but the one whose flesh did not see corruption was in the tomb for three days. For it did not know the vices of the flesh, which is composed of the substances of the four elements. However great, then, the stench of the dead may be, it is all removed when the sacred ointment gives forth its fragrance (De Poenit., dist. I, cap. *Quantuslibet*). The dead man rises, and his bonds are ordered to be loosed, though he is still in sin. The veil is removed from his face, the veil that obscured the truth of the grace he had received. But since he has been granted forgiveness, he is ordered to uncover his face and open his countenance; for the one whose sin has been forgiven has nothing of which to be ashamed.

**59.** Yet amid such great grace of the Lord and such a miracle of divine generosity, when everyone ought to have rejoiced, the impious were stirred up and gathered a council against Christ. They also wanted to kill Lazarus (John XI, 47). Do you not rightly recognize that you are successors of those whose hardness you have inherited (John XII, 10)? For you too are indignant and gather a council against the Church, because you see the dead come to life again in the Church and sinners raised up after receiving forgiveness. Thus, so far as lies in you, through envy you want to kill again those who have been raised.

**60.** But Jesus does not withdraw his benefits; rather, he increases them by heaping generosity upon generosity. He carefully visits the one who has been raised, and, rejoicing in the grace of the celebrated resurrection, comes to the supper which his Church has prepared for him. There the one who had been dead is found among those reclining at table with Christ.

[Col. 0512A] **61.** Then all who look with a pure gaze of mind—those who do not know how to envy—are astonished. Such are the children whom the Church possesses. They are astonished, as I have said, that the one who lay in the tomb yesterday and the day before (ibid., 3) is one of those reclining at table with the Lord Jesus.

**62.** Mary herself pours ointment upon the feet of the Lord Jesus. Perhaps upon his feet because one of the lowliest has been snatched from death; for we are all the body of Christ, though some may be its higher members (I Corinthians X, 17). The Apostle was Christ’s mouth, who said: “Do you seek proof of the Christ who speaks in me?” (II Corinthians XIII, 3). [430] The prophets were his mouth, through whom he spoke of things to come. Would that I too might deserve to be his foot, and that Mary might pour her precious ointment upon me, anoint me, and wipe away my sin!

**63.** [Also chapter VIII.] What we therefore read about Lazarus, we ought to believe of every converted sinner: although he may have a stench, he is nevertheless cleansed by the precious ointment of faith.

[Note: [Col. 0512D] All editions and some manuscripts read, “he is corrected by the ointment of precious faith”; the other manuscripts, which are more elegant, read as in the text.]

For faith possesses such great grace that where the dead man had stunk before, the whole house is filled there with a good fragrance.

**64.** The house of Corinth stank when it was written concerning it: “It is actually reported that there is fornication among you, and such fornication as is not found even among the Gentiles” (I Corinthians V, 1). There was a stench because a little leaven had corrupted the whole lump. It began to smell sweet when it was said: “If you have forgiven anyone anything, I have forgiven him also. For what I have forgiven—if I have forgiven anything—I have forgiven for your sake in the person of Christ” (II Corinthians II, 10). Thus, when the sinner had been freed, great joy arose in it, and the whole house was fragrant with the sweetness of grace. Therefore the Apostle, well aware that he had poured the ointment of apostolic forgiveness over them all, says: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God among those who are being saved” (ibid., 15).

**65.** Everyone therefore rejoices at the outpouring of this ointment; Judas alone objects (John XII, 4). So now too the transgressor objects; the betrayer rebukes. But Christ himself rebukes the man who does not understand the remedy of the Lord’s death and does not grasp the mystery of so great a burial. For the Lord both suffered and died in order to redeem us from death. This most excellent price of his death indicates that the sinner is absolved and received into new grace, so that all may come and marvel at how he reclines with Christ and, praising God, say: “Let us eat and make merry, because this man was dead and has come to life again; he was lost and has been found” (Luke XV, 24). But if some unbeliever objects, asking why he eats with tax collectors and sinners, the answer is given to him: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Matthew IX, 12).

## CHAPTER VIII

He continues to urge confession and tears, turning his prayer toward himself. After indicating his desire to cleanse the Lord’s feet like the woman in the Gospel, in whose action he says that the pattern of penitence was given, he asks that, even if someone does not attain the perfection of this example, Christ will nevertheless come to his tomb. With the deepest humility he asks Christ to visit and raise him in his own tomb; above all, he asks to be granted compassion for sinners, whose offenses he is convinced are lighter than his own. Therefore one must not insult those for whom Christ died; from among the straw which he does not neglect, the speaker also desires to be gathered.

**66.** Show your wound to the physician, so that you may be healed. Even if you do not show it, he knows it; but he desires to hear your voice. Wipe your scars with tears. Thus the woman in the Gospel wiped away the sin and stench of her error; thus she washed away her guilt when she washed the feet of Jesus with her tears (Matthew IX, 22).

**67.** Would that you also reserve for me the mud of your feet, [431] Jesus, which, as you walk about in me, you have dirtied! [Note: [Col. 0513C] The latest Paris editions read, “while you walk on earth”; most incorrectly, as what follows shows.] Would that you offer me the filth of your footprints to wipe away—the filth that I have fastened upon your steps by my conduct! But where shall I obtain living water with which I can wash your feet? If I have no water, I have tears; and as I wash your feet with them, would that I might wash myself as well! How may I obtain from you the words: “Her sins, which are many, are forgiven, because she loved much” (Luke VII, 47)? I confess that I ought to have been forgiven more, and that more has been forgiven me, since I have been called to the priesthood from the noise of lawsuits in the forum and from the terror of public administration. Therefore I fear that I may be found ungrateful if I love less, when more has been forgiven me (ibid., 44).

[Note: [Col. 0513C] All editions and some manuscripts read as in the text. The others read, “I cannot equal this woman in all things”; one has, “not in all things,” and another, “not in everything.” This is certainly not a bad reading, for the prayer about himself, composed by the holy man, is not thereby interrupted; indeed, it continues below at greater length in the utmost humility.]

**68.** But not everyone can equal this woman, who was rightly preferred even to Simon, who was giving the Lord a meal. She provided a lesson to all who wish to obtain forgiveness: she kissed Christ’s feet, washed them with her tears, wiped them with her hair, and anointed them with ointment.

**69.** In the kiss there is a remarkable sign of love. Therefore the Lord Jesus says: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song of Songs I, 1). What do the hair signify except that, having bowed down every dignity of worldly office, you should know that indulgence must be earnestly begged; that you should prostrate yourself weeping upon the ground; that, lying upon the earth, you should move compassion?

[Note: [Col. 0513D] All editions read, “unless you are moved … to implore indulgence”; all the manuscripts, on the contrary, read as in the text.]

The fragrance of good conversion is also expressed in the ointment.

[Note: [Col. 0513D] All editions and some manuscripts read, “of good conduct”; the other manuscripts, which are also the better ones, read, “of good conversion.” This is more appropriate, as the example of the penitent David below makes clear.]

David, of course, was a king, and he said: “Every night I wash my bed; I drench my couch with my tears” (Psalm VI, 7). Therefore he merited such great grace that from his family a virgin was chosen who would give birth to Christ for us through her own childbirth. For this reason that woman too is proclaimed in the Gospel.

**70.** Yet if we cannot equal her, the Lord Jesus knows how to help the weak as well, where there is no woman who can prepare a banquet, bring ointment (John XII, 7), or carry with her a spring of living water. He himself comes to the tomb.

**71.** Therefore, Lord Jesus, would that you deign to approach this tomb of mine (John XI, 34) and wash me with your tears, since, with my hardened eyes, I do not have tears enough to wash away my sins! If you weep for me, I shall be saved. If I am worthy of your tears, I wipe away the stench of all my sins. If I am worthy for you to weep over me for a little while, you will call me out of the tomb of this body and say: “Come outside” (ibid., 43), so that my thoughts may not be held enclosed within the narrow confines of this body, but may go forth to Christ and live in the light; so that I may think not about works of darkness, [432] but about works of light. For the one who thinks about sin strives to shut himself up within his own conscience.

[Note: [Col. 0513D] Thus all the editions and most manuscripts. Of the rest, two read *absterges*, “you will wipe away”; two, *absterge*, “wipe away”; two others, *abstergebis*, “you will wipe away”; and the same number, *abstergam*, “I shall wipe away”—a reading also conjectured by Latinius. But perhaps neither here nor elsewhere did those who introduced such alterations sufficiently notice that nothing is more frequent in authors than present tenses used for future ones.]

**72.** Call your servant out, then. Although bound by the chains of my sins, with my feet fettered and my hands tied, already buried in dead thoughts and works, at your call I shall go out free. I shall be found among those reclining at your banquet, and your house will be filled with precious ointment—if only you have deigned to redeem me, you will preserve me. For it will be said: “Behold that man…”

[Note: [Col. 0513D] Do not understand Ambrose’s words, “not nourished in the bosom of the Church,” as though he were admitting that he had ever lived among idolaters, heretics, or schismatics. He merely indicates that he was not brought up among those who, destined for ministry at the altar, were instructed in the Church from childhood.

On this ecclesiastical instruction of children, see the first letter of Siricius, chapters 3 and 9; also the Third Council of Carthage, canon 19; Paulinus the bishop, *On Saint Felix*, poem 4; Paulinus the deacon, speaking of himself in the *Life of Ambrose*; Ambrose himself, in *Exhortation to Virgins*, concerning Laurence, and elsewhere; Augustine, *On the Morals of the Catholic Church*, book I, chapter 33; and others.

Ambrose also adds here, “but snatched away from the tribunals.” He uses the same words in book I of *The Duties*, chapter 1, number 4. He also rather aptly contrasts with the psalmist’s song the shouting of the herald, who usually suppresses the tumult and secures a hearing in the forum by his cries—that is, the melodies of ecclesiastical singers. Below, when he testifies that he undertook certain labors for the Church, it is probable that he refers to nothing other than the conflicts he entered into against Symmachus or the empress Justina.

All these things, together with the signs of profound humility repeatedly scattered throughout the work, speak so clearly of Ambrose as their author that it is surprising what Sotus intended when, for these same reasons, he denied this work to our bishop.]

not brought up in the bosom of the Church, not disciplined from childhood, but snatched away from the tribunals, taken away from the vanities of this world, trained from the herald’s voice to the psalmist’s song, remains in the priesthood not by his own merit but by Christ’s grace, and reclines among the guests at the heavenly table.

**73.** Preserve, Lord, your gift; guard the gift you bestowed even upon one who fled from it.

[Note: [Col. 0515D] The Benedictine manuscript reads, “guard the house which you have bestowed.”]

For I knew that I was not worthy to be called a bishop, since I had given myself to this world; but by your grace I am what I am. Indeed, I am the least and lowest in merit of all bishops. Yet because I too have undertaken some labor for your holy Church, protect this fruit; do not allow the one whom you called, though lost, to the priesthood, to perish as a priest.

[Note: [Col. 0515D] All editions and all but two manuscripts read, “and first of all, so that I may know how to have compassion.” The Laon manuscript reads, “and first of all, so that we may have compassion.” The ancient German manuscripts have the best reading: “and first of all, grant that I may know,” and so forth.]

And first of all grant that I may know how to have deep compassion for sinners. This is the highest virtue, because it is written: “You shall not rejoice over the children of Judah on the day of their destruction, nor speak proudly on the day of their distress” (Obadiah 12). But whenever the sin of someone who has fallen is disclosed, let me have compassion; let me not rebuke arrogantly, but mourn and weep, so that while I weep for another I may weep for myself, saying: “Tamar has been more justified than I” (Genesis XXXVIII, 26).

**74.** Perhaps the young woman fell, deceived and thrown headlong by circumstances that kindle sins; but we elders also sin. The law of this flesh wars against the law of our mind and leads us captive into sin, so that we do what we do not wish (Romans VII, 23). She has an excuse in her age; I have none now: she ought to learn, whereas we ought to teach. Therefore “Tamar has been more justified than I” (I Timothy VI, 10).

**75.** When we accuse someone’s greed, let us remember whether we ourselves have done nothing greedily. And if we have, since greed is the root of evils and, like something hidden beneath the earth, creeps through our body, let each of us say: “Tamar has been more justified than I.”

[433]

**76.** If we have been gravely angered against anyone, a layman has a lighter case than a bishop, since he acted while angry.

[Note: [Col. 0515D] Some manuscripts read, “because he acted more suitably.”]

Let us reconsider the matter with ourselves and say: “This man who is accused of anger has been more justified than I.” For if we say this, we guard ourselves, lest the Lord Jesus—or one of his disciples—say to us: “You see the speck in your brother’s eye, but you do not see the beam in your own eye. Hypocrite, first remove the beam from your own eye, and then you will see how to remove the speck from your brother’s eye” (Matthew VII, 4–5).

**77.** Let us not be ashamed, then, to say that our guilt is heavier than that of the person whom we think ought to be accused, because Judas, who accused Tamar, said this; and remembering his own guilt, he said: “Tamar has been more justified than I” (Genesis XXXVIII, 26). In this there is both a profound mystery and a moral instruction. His guilt was therefore not reckoned against him, because he accused himself before he was accused by others.

**78.** Let us not rejoice, then, over anyone’s sin, but rather mourn, because it is written: “Do not rejoice over me, my enemy, because I have fallen; but I shall rise again. For if I sit in darkness, the Lord will be my light. I shall bear the Lord’s anger because I have sinned against him, until he justifies my cause, executes my judgment, brings me out into the light, and I shall see his righteousness. My enemy shall see it, and shame shall cover her, who says to me, ‘Where is the Lord your God?’ My eyes shall see her, and she shall be trampled like mud in the road” (Micah VII, 8 and following).
