And rightly so, because the one who rejoices at another’s fall rejoices in the devil’s victory. Therefore let us grieve all the more when we hear that a human being has perished, one for whom Christ died, who does not neglect even a straw in the harvest.

**79.** Would that he not cast away this straw in the harvest—that is, the empty oats of my fruit—but gather it, as someone says: “Alas for me, for I have become like one who gathers straw in the harvest and a grape-cluster in the vintage” (Micah VII, 1)—so that he may eat in me at least the first fruits of his grace, even if he does not approve the later ones.

[Note: [Col. 0515D] All the manuscripts read as in the text; all the editions, however, read, “even if I do not approve.”]

## CHAPTER IX

How necessary is faith for penitence? What resources for obtaining forgiveness are available to each person? Prayer, tears, and fasting are more valuable than money. After confirming this with examples, and adding that generosity contributes greatly to forgiveness but must be joined with faith, he recounts several defects of that same generosity. He then joins to them certain other failures in penitence, namely, those of people who immediately seek reconciliation while giving up none of their customary luxury; those who place penitence merely in abstaining from the sacraments; and finally those who, relying on the hope of penitence, give themselves over to lust.

**80.** We must therefore believe both that penitence is to be performed and that forgiveness is to be granted; [434] yet we must hope for forgiveness as something received through faith, not as something owed. For it is one thing to deserve; another to presume.

[Note: [Col. 0515D] Several manuscripts read, “as from an ungrateful person”; one, “as from an intact whole”; the rest, “as from a written obligation” (*syngrapha*), for which the edition has *ex syngrapha*. A few lines later, where all editions and some manuscripts read, “so that you do not charge interest,” one manuscript has, “so that you do not act craftily,” while the others have, “so that you do not make a transfer of debt,” and so forth. To make such a transfer is to change creditors, so that, in order to pay a sum owed to one person at moderate interest, one receives from another the necessary amount at a higher interest.]

Faith obtains it as though from a written contract; presumption, however, is closer to arrogance than to petition. First pay what is owed, so that you may deserve to obtain what you hope for. Pay the debt of a good disposition, so that you do not transfer the debt elsewhere, but by the capital of your faith extinguish the interest on the debt you have contracted.

**81.** The one who owes God has more resources for repayment than the one who owes a human being. A human being demands money for money, and money is not always available to the debtor; God demands a disposition, which is in your power. No one is poor who owes God, unless he has made himself poor. And if he has nothing to sell, he has something with which to pay. Prayer, tears, and fasting are the good debtor’s capital, and much richer than if someone were to bring money from the sale of estates without faith.

**82.** Ananias was poor, then, when he brought money to the apostles after selling his field; hence he could neither discharge his debt, but entangled himself instead (Acts V, 1–2). The widow who put two small coins into the treasury was rich; of her it was said: “This poor widow has put in more than all” (Luke XXI, 2). For God seeks not money but faith.

**83.** [Also chapter IX.] I do not deny that sin can be diminished by generosity shown toward the poor, provided that faith commends the expenditure. For what does the contribution of one’s property profit without the grace of love?

**84.** There are people who seek the praise of generosity merely for display, wishing to appear approved by the public because they have kept nothing for themselves. But while they seek the reward of the present age, they do not store up anything for the future; and because they have received their reward here, they cannot hope for it there.

**85.** There are people who, after giving their wealth to the Church in a sudden impulse of mind rather than by enduring judgment, later think it should be reclaimed. For them neither the first reward nor the second is valid: the first lacked judgment, and the second involved sacrilege (17, q. 4, canon “Sunt qui opes”).

[Note: [Col. 0517C] Most manuscripts read, “the acceptable reward”; one has, “there is grace.” It is difficult not to marvel here at how far our Ambrose was from greed, since he declares himself so ready to restore gifts once offered and handed over to the Church when their owner asks for them back. His disciple Augustine admirably imitated this freedom from desire, as Possidius testifies in chapter 24 of his life. Ambrose also displays a similar contempt for wealth elsewhere; see his discussion of the same matter in the commentary on Luke’s Gospel, book VIII, number 79, and in the letter concerning the basilicas that were not to be surrendered.]

**86.** There are people who regret having divided their wealth among the poor. But those who practice penitence ought not to regret this alone, lest they repent of their very penitence. For many, conscious of their sins and afraid of future punishment, ask for penitence; and when they have received it, they are recalled from their public supplication by shame. They seem to have asked to repent of evils and to perform good deeds.

[Note: [Col. 0517D] Thus the old edition in the text and all the manuscripts. Erasmus and Gill, in the margin, read, “this alone must be feared,” and the Roman edition transferred that reading into the text.]

**87.** Some ask for penitence for this reason: they want communion restored to them immediately. Such people desire not so much to loose themselves as to bind the priest. They do not divest their own conscience of guilt, but clothe the priest's conscience with it, though he has been commanded: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor throw [435] your pearls before pigs”—that is, do not grant the fellowship of sacred communion to unclean impurities.

[Note: [Col. 0517D] Some manuscripts read, “they clothe the priests with whom…”] [Col. 0518A]

[Note: [Col. 0517D] Erasmus and Gill in the margin, and the Roman edition in the text, have “to unclean spirits.” The Roman edition alone adds, “not to be readily imparted”; all the other manuscripts omit these words.]

**88.** Thus you may see people [Note: [Col. 0517D] The latest editions read, “walking in a white garment.”] walking about in changed clothing, when they ought to mourn and groan, because they have defiled that garment of cleansing and grace.

[Note: [Col. 0517D] The more ancient manuscripts read, “of offering and grace.” This is not an absurd sense, for Ambrose may have alluded to the custom of the ancients, according to which those who were to perform sacred rites put on clean clothing. In the received reading, however, there is an allusion to the baptismal garment, mentioned above.]

You may see women burdening their ears with pearls and bending their necks, which they ought rightly to bow to Christ, not to gold. They ought to weep for themselves because they have lost the pearl that comes from heaven.

**89.** There are also people who think that this is penitence: abstaining from the heavenly sacraments.

[Note: [Col. 0518D] The Roman edition alone reads, “These are more severe judges of themselves”; below, with one or two manuscripts, it has “if they avoid,” and so forth.]

These are harsher judges of themselves: they prescribe punishment for themselves and avoid the remedy, though they ought rather to grieve over their punishment because they are deprived of heavenly grace (De Poenit., dist. I, cap. *Sunt qui arbitrentur*).

**90.** Others, having set before themselves the hope of performing penitence, think that they have acquired permission to sin. Yet penitence is a remedy for sin, not an incentive to sin. A wound requires medicine, not medicine a wound; medicine is sought because of the wound, not a wound desired because of the medicine. Moreover, hope that is deferred to time is weak, since all time is uncertain and no hope survives every moment of time.

## CHAPTER X

He seeks to remove the shame that keeps people from public penitence. By presenting the practice of the profane, he demonstrates the usefulness of prayers offered simultaneously by the whole Church and adduces examples of mourning saints. Then, after censuring those who think that the same penitence should be undertaken repeatedly, he explains how difficult it is to perform penitence well and how it ought to be carried out.

**91.** Would anyone tolerate your being ashamed to ask God, when you are not ashamed to ask a human being? Would you be ashamed to beseech God, whom you do not hide from, when you are not ashamed to confess your sins to a human being whom you do hide from?

[Note: [Col. 0518D] All editions and a few manuscripts read as in the text. The rest, with broad agreement, read, “the leaders of prayer,” except for two, which have “of preaching,” a less suitable reading. The expression “leaders” is not altogether displeasing, since it may refer to priests or deacons whom the bishop ordered to preside over the prayers of the penitents.

A more serious difficulty concerns the sense in which the earlier words—“when you are not ashamed to confess to a human being whom you hide from”—are to be understood. Bellarmine and other Catholic writers with him interpret them as referring to what they call auricular confession. Dallaeus, Albertinus, and other non-Catholics, on the contrary, obstinately transfer them to the public declaration of a public sin, which they say was expressed not with the tongue or mouth, but by tears, gestures, and the whole bearing of the body.

It is obvious that they are vainly laboring against the clear truth. First, Ambrose uses the singular: “to confess,” he says, “to a human being whom you hide from.” No one can fail to see that if he had intended to signify public *exomologesis*, his argument would have been much more effective if expressed with the plural. Second, the entire sequence of the discourse shows that penitents were called away from public supplication for no other reason than that, by its external acts, they disclosed themselves to be sinners. Third, a clear distinction is expressed between satisfaction and confession. The words just quoted belong to confession; the following words belong to satisfaction: “when satisfaction must be made to a human being,” and so forth.]

Do you avoid witnesses to your prayer and those who share your knowledge, when, if satisfaction must be made to a human being, you have to approach many people, implore them, and ask them to deign to intervene; to prostrate yourself on your knees, kiss their footprints, and offer children who are still ignorant of the guilt as petitioners for their father’s forgiveness? [436] Do you find it burdensome to do this in the Church—to beseech God and seek the protection of the holy people in your supplication—where there is nothing that ought to cause shame except failure to confess, since we are all sinners? There the more praiseworthy person is the more humble; the more righteous is the one who is more abject in his own eyes.

**92.** Let the mother Church weep for you (De Poenit., dist. I, cap. *Fleat*) and wash away your guilt with her tears; let Christ see you mourning, so that he may say: “Blessed are those who mourn, for you shall rejoice” (Luke VI, 21). He loves it when many pray for one.

Finally, moved by the tears of the widow, because many were weeping for her, he raised her son from the dead (Luke VII, 13). For this reason he heard Peter more quickly, so that Dorcas might rise again (Acts IX, 36), because the poor were mourning the woman’s death. For this reason he immediately forgave Peter himself, because he wept most bitterly. And if you too weep most bitterly, Christ will look upon you and your guilt will depart (Luke XXII, 62).

[Note: [Col. 0519C] Some manuscripts read, “For habit”; the Claromontane manuscript, “For the wound of pain banishes”; some have “binds,” “luxury,” and so forth.]

For the practice of grief banishes the pleasures of crime and the delights of error. Thus, while we grieve over what has been done, we exclude what might otherwise be done, and a kind of discipline of innocence is formed from the condemnation of guilt.

**93.** Let nothing, then, call you back from penitence; this is something you share with the saints. Would that your penitence might be such as the lamentation of the saints, worthy of imitation. David ate ashes like bread and mixed his drink with tears (Psalm CI, 10). Therefore he now rejoices more, because he wept more: “My eyes have flowed down in streams of water,” he says (Psalm CXVIII, 136).

**94.** John wept greatly, and says that the mysteries of Christ were revealed to him (Revelation V, 4). But that woman who, though she was in sins and ought to have wept, rejoiced, and was clothed in purple and scarlet and adorned herself with much gold and precious stones, now mourns the misery of eternal weeping (Revelation XVII, 4).

### 95

[Note: [Col. 0519C] Quite a few manuscripts, and not inferior ones, have *Merito reperiuntur* (“They are rightly found”); somewhat better are those which, with Gratian, distinguish *merito* from *reperiuntur*. Yet other witnesses and the editions are to be preferred. Here it is clearly declared that formerly public penance, once performed, was not customarily repeated any more than baptism was. The same is indicated at the end of the following chapter. That this opinion of Ambrose was shared by other Fathers may be learned from Tertullian, *On Penitence*, chapter 7; Pope Siricius, Letter 1 to Himerius, canon 4; Augustine, Letter 157 in the new edition; and others. Indeed, these passages of Ambrose are understood in no other way by the Master of the Sentences, Book IV, distinction 14; by Saint Thomas, Part III, question 80, article 10, reply to objection 2; and by other theologians after them. Yet they were mistaken in this matter, because they supposed that those who, having completed public penance, had fallen again into sin were admitted to secret penance. For those who returned to their former crimes like dogs to their vomit were left to themselves, so that they might appease God by whatever better way seemed appropriate; nevertheless, at the end of life they were reconciled through absolution and fortified with the sacred viaticum of Communion. On this matter see Morinus, *On the Administration of Penance*, Book IX, chapter 29, and Alexander, third century, *Church History*, dissertation 10. Besides that penance for more serious crimes, there was also another for lighter and daily faults. Although Ambrose properly distinguishes the two kinds of sin, since he does not explain which faults are to be regarded as light and which as serious, we refer the reader to the author of that sermon which was published among Augustine’s doubtful works as number 352, section 7.]

They are rightly censured (*On Penance*, distinction 3, chapter *Reperiuntur*) who think that penance should be performed repeatedly, because they are indulging themselves in Christ. For if they truly performed penance, they would not later think it necessary to repeat it, because, just as there is one baptism, so there is one penance—which, however, is performed publicly. We ought to repent of our daily sins; but the latter penance is for lighter offenses, the former for graver ones.

### 96

I have more easily found those who preserved their innocence than those who performed penance properly. Or does anyone regard that as penance where there is ambition for acquiring office, where wine is poured out, where there is even the use of marital intercourse? [Note: [Col. 0520C] A few manuscripts read *culpae conjugalis* (“of marital fault”). This is not sufficiently correct, for the subject here is not adultery, which is permitted to no one, but marital intercourse, from which penitents alone are ordered to abstain. You may perhaps wonder why Ambrose requires such abstinence, since it is not mentioned in those works in which other Fathers prescribe the observances incumbent upon penitents. Nevertheless, it seems possible to infer that this practice of continence prevailed in those times from the fact that Pope Siricius, in his letter to Himerius, section 5, excludes those who had performed public penance from Communion—except at the point of death—if they subsequently entered a new marriage. The same is true of the Council of Arles II, canon 21; and its canon 22 further forbids public penance from being imposed on a married person without the consent of the spouse. Add that this severity seems to have been mitigated by Pope Leo in his letter to Rusticus of Narbonne, by the Council of Toledo VI, canon 8, and also by the Second Council of Toul, which allow public penitents, if they are unable to remain continent, to seek intercourse with their lawful wife, lest they be exposed to the danger of fornication. Nor is it surprising that continence was imposed in public penance, since it was likewise required even of the innocent during the Lenten fast; on this matter one may consult the learned Thaumassinus. As for the other practices of public penitents described here by Ambrose, these too may be found set forth by other Fathers, for example Tertullian, *On Penance*, chapters 9–12; Cyprian, in his own letters and those of the Roman clergy concerning the Lapsed; Gregory of Nyssa, *Homily on Penance*; Pacian, *Exhortation to Penance*; Caesarius, homily 8; and others.]

The world must be renounced; even sleep must be indulged less than nature demands. One must be interrupted by groans, broken by sighs, and set apart for prayers. One must live in such a way as to die to the use of this present life: a person must deny himself and be wholly changed. Thus, as the story goes, a certain young man, having gone abroad because of his love affairs with prostitutes and having returned after his passion had been extinguished, later encountered his former beloved. When she, finding that he did not interrupt her, supposed that he had not recognized her, she approached him again and said, “It is I.” He replied, “But I am not myself.” [Note: [Col. 0520D] The old edition and some manuscripts read *post amores meretricios* (“after his love affairs with prostitutes”); the Roman edition and others, which we follow here, read *propter amores meretricios* (“because of his love affairs with prostitutes”); some have *amorem meretricium* (“a prostitute’s love”). Again, the editions and a few manuscripts read *veteri occurrisse dilectae, quae ubi non interpellatam* (“he encountered his former beloved, who, when she had not been addressed…”); the Roman edition reads *non interpellata, mirata putaverit* (“not having been addressed, she supposed in amazement…”); certain manuscripts have *postea vero ei occurrisse dilectam, quae ubi se non interpellatam mirata* (“afterward he encountered his beloved, who, when she was amazed that she had not been addressed…”); some read *admirata sit, putaverit* (“she was amazed and supposed”); the remaining manuscripts, including the better ones, read as in the text.]

### 97

Hence the Lord rightly says: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matthew 16:24). For those who have died and been buried in Christ ought not again, as though living, engage in the affairs of this world. “Do not touch, do not handle,” he says, “things which all perish through use” (Colossians 2:20), because the very use of this life is corruption of integrity.

## CHAPTER XI

He first explained why baptism is not to be postponed until death: the reason is penance. By adducing testimonies from Scripture, he presses those who postpone penance. Nevertheless, he adds that it should not be undertaken while desires are still burning; rather, one should wait until they have subsided.

### 98

Good, therefore, is penance; if it did not exist, everyone would postpone the grace of cleansing until old age. To such people the sufficient answer is that it is better for me to have something to mend than to have nothing to wear: yet, just as things repaired once are restored, so things repeatedly patched come apart.

### 99

The Lord himself sufficiently warned those who postpone penance when he said: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matthew 4:17). We do not know at what hour the thief will come; we do not know whether our soul will be demanded from us during the coming night. After Adam’s sin, God immediately expelled him from paradise; he did not delay, but at once separated him from its delights so that he might do penance. He immediately clothed him in a tunic of skins, not silk (Genesis 3:21).

### 100

Why do you delay? Is it so that you may commit more sins? Since God is good, are you therefore evil, and do you despise the riches of his goodness and patience (Romans 2:4)? Rather, the Lord’s goodness ought to lead you to penance. Therefore holy David says to everyone: “Come, let us worship and fall down before him, and let us weep before the Lord our Maker” (Psalm 94:6).

But concerning the sinner who dies without penance—since nothing remains except to mourn bitterly and to weep—you have him himself weeping and saying: “My son Absalom, my son Absalom!” (2 Samuel 18:33). For one who is wholly dead is mourned without exception.

### 101

As for those who, exiles and strangers beyond the boundaries of their ancestral land prescribed by the holy law of Moses, have become entangled in worldly errors, hear the psalmist singing: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept, when we remembered Zion” (Psalm 136:1). He introduces the groans of the fallen, who, still placed amid the present age and its passing realities, ought to come to their senses—following the example of those who, because of the price of their sin, had been led into the misery of captivity. [Note: [Col. 0521D] Amerbach and Erasmus read: “He introduces the groans of the fallen, placed amid the present age and passing realities,” and so forth. Gill and the manuscripts read as in our text, except that five of them have *genus* (“kind”) instead of *gemitus* (“groans”), not incorrectly. For by synecdoche that word may be referred to the adjective placed here, so that the sense is: “He introduces fallen people, placed …,” and so forth. The Roman edition reads: “He introduces the groans of the fallen and, amid the present age and passing realities,” and so forth.]

### 102

There is nothing so profoundly painful as for someone held captive beneath sin to remember from where he fell and from what height he collapsed, because he turned away from that splendid and beautiful contemplation of divine knowledge toward bodily and earthly things. [Note: [Col. 0521D] Thus the old edition and several manuscripts read; one of them has *pura* (“pure”) instead of *pulchra* (“beautiful”), and quite a few have *defluxerit* (“flowed down”) instead of *deflexerit* (“turned aside”). The Roman edition and the other manuscripts differ from us only in having changed *cognitionis* (“of knowledge”) into *conditionis* (“of condition”).]

### 103

Thus you have Adam hiding himself when he learned that God was present, wishing to remain concealed when he was sought, and being called by the Lord with a voice that pierced the feelings of the one in hiding: “Adam, where are you?” (Genesis 3:9). That is: Why do you hide yourself? Why do you lie concealed? Why do you flee from the one whom you desired to see?

So grievous is the guilt of conscience that, without a judge, it punishes itself and wishes to cover itself; yet before God it is naked.

### 104

Therefore no one living in sin ought to arrogate to himself or usurp the authority of the sacraments (*On Penance*, distinction 1, chapter *Sunt qui*, section *Nemo*), because it is written: [Note: [Col. 0521D] Although throughout these books Ambrose repeatedly urges sinners not to postpone penance any longer, nevertheless, since—as has been said—it was not repeated, he wisely warns that its time should by no means be hastened for those who are still so carried away by the heat of youth and desire that there is scarcely hope that they will not relapse into their former habits. This was also the reason why Monica delayed the baptism of her son Augustine. Meanwhile, the holy Doctor prescribes what such persons must especially observe: first, he deters them from usurping—that is, unworthily receiving—the Eucharist. He aptly applies this very passage from Genesis, just as God by the word “rest” removed Cain from the sacrifice; and in Book II of *Cain and Abel*, chapter 7, he cleverly transfers the same word to the prohibition against excusing or defending sin.]

“You have sinned; be still” (Genesis 4:10). In the present psalm David says: “Upon the willows” (*On Penance*, distinction 3, chapter *In salicibus*), “in its midst we hung up our instruments”; and below: “How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?” (Psalm 136:1–2).

For if the flesh resists the mind and is not subject to the governance and command of the spirit, it is a foreign land—a land not subdued by the labor of its cultivator—and therefore it cannot bear the fruits of charity, patience, and peace.

It is better, then, to be still when you are unable to perform the works of penance, lest in penance itself something occur that later requires penance. If penance has once been usurped and not rightly celebrated, it neither obtains the fruit of the former nor permits the use of the later (*On Penance*, distinction 3, chapter *Si quis*, section *Poenitentia*). [Note: [Col. 0522D] Some manuscripts read: “when you do not seek to practice.”]

[Col. 0523A]

### 105

Certainly, even when the flesh resists, the mind ought to be intent upon God; and if works do not follow, faith must not abandon us. [Note: [Col. 0523B] Amerbach and Erasmus read *fides desiderat* (“faith desires”); Gill and some manuscripts, which are also the better witnesses, read *fides deserviat* (“faith should serve”); the Roman edition has *fides non deseratur* (“faith must not be abandoned”); the remaining manuscripts have *non deserat* (“it must not abandon”), evidently referring to sinners of this kind.]

And if either the enticements of the flesh or hostile powers attack us, the mind must remain devoted to God (Romans 7:23). For we are most strongly pressed when the flesh gives way; and there are those who assail the wretched soul with great force, seeking to take away every source of protection. Hence the words: “Lay it waste, lay it waste, down to its foundations” (Psalm 136:7).

### 106

David, taking pity on her, says: “Wretched daughter of Babylon” (ibid., 8). Wretched indeed, because she is Babylon’s daughter, having ceased to be God’s daughter.

Yet he invites a physician for her, saying: “Blessed is he who will seize and dash your little ones against the rock” (ibid., 9)—that is, he who crushes weak and slippery thoughts against Christ, who by reverence and discernment shatters all irrational movements of the soul. Thus, if someone is carried away by adulterous love, he may extinguish the fire and the intercourse of the prostitute, and renounce himself through disciplined effort in order to gain Christ. [Note: [Col. 0523B] Some manuscripts read *reverentia et discretione* (“by reverence and discernment”); one has *et discerptione* (“and by tearing apart”).]

### 107

We have therefore learned both that penance must be performed and that it must be performed at the time when the wantonness of sin has cooled; and that those placed in captivity under sin must be more reverent, not usurpers. [Note: [Col. 0523B] Many manuscripts, and not inferior ones, read *Dicimus ergo* (“Therefore we say”); one has *Discimus ergo* (“Therefore we learn”); the remaining manuscripts and the old edition, with Gratian, have the reading found in the text. Again, for *culpae defervescat luxuria* (“the wantonness of sin may cool”), some manuscripts reverse the words: *culpa defervescat luxuriae* (“sin may cool toward wantonness”). Finally, where the editions read *usurpatores* (“usurpers”), the manuscripts, with one exception, have *usurpatiores* (“more presumptuous usurpers”). Perhaps *usurpantiores* should be read.]

For if Moses, when he eagerly desired to draw nearer in order to receive knowledge of the heavenly mystery, was told, “Remove the sandals from your feet” (Exodus 3:5), how much more ought we to strip the feet of our soul of bodily bonds and release all our steps from the entanglement of this world?

## [ON THE FAITH]

[Col. 0523]

# INTRODUCTORY NOTICE TO THE BOOKS ON THE FAITH

[Col. 0523]

When Auxentius, after driving out the holy bishop Dionysius, relying on the support of the Arian emperor Constantius, seized the Church of Milan by force and mutilated and disfigured it with every crime, there is no doubt that Ambrose, as soon as he was elected in the place of the deceased bishop, had nothing more urgent than to repair the ruins inflicted under the tyrannical domination of the Arians. Divine favor assisted such pious efforts. Although he had been transferred from secular offices to the episcopate, he immediately aroused such universal admiration that everyone regarded him as a teacher and oracle of truth.

Moved by this, Caesar Gratian, when he was preparing to depart for the East to bring assistance to his uncle Valens, who was waging war against the Goths, asked Ambrose for a treatise establishing the divinity of Christ (*Book I on the Faith*, prologue; *Book III*, chapter 1, section 1), so that he might fortify himself against the Arian plague, which was then raging savagely in those provinces, as though with an immediate antidote. Ambrose praised the emperor’s faith (*Book I*, prologue, section 4), and declared that he would prefer to write an exhortation to faith rather than a disputation about faith; nevertheless, he wished to obey the emperor’s will by arguing briefly and on the authority of the councils (*ibid.*, section 5), above all that of Nicaea.

After dividing the work into two books, he states at the outset the difference between Catholic faith and Arian perfidy (*Book I*, chapter 1, section 6 and following). There he also asserts the unity of nature in God (*ibid.*, section 8 and following) as well as the Trinity of persons, and consequently proves that Christ is the Son of God and that worship is owed to him as true God (chapter 2, section 13). For he possesses divine attributes (*ibid.*, sections 14–15), and in Scripture he is signified by four names of divinity (section 16 and following).

Then, from Isaiah and Jeremiah, he teaches (chapters 3–4) that this is what the common nature of things proclaims. Next, after placing before the reader the chief points of Arian error—namely, the claims that the Son is unlike the Father, began in time, and was created (chapter 5)—he attacks and overturns each of them in these two books. The Arians denied, on the other hand, that he was good, almighty, the true Son of God, and one in divinity with the Father.

Accordingly, after first warning (chapter 6) that, although he knew the leaders of the Arian faction disagreed among themselves, he would attack no one privately but would oppose all of them collectively under the name of heretics, he demonstrates that the Son is like the Father in all things (chapter 7) and coeternal with him (chapter 8 and following), and consequently neither made (chapter 14 and following) nor created. From this he concludes that the definition of the Fathers of Nicaea—which was also approved by the first and third confessions of Rimini—must be embraced (chapters 18–19). Finally, he prays to God (chapter 10, section 122) to inspire his readers, and especially the emperor, with a disposition that would cause them to prefer nothing to the sacred deposit of faith (*ibid.*, section 136).

In Book II, after explaining the twelve titles by which Scripture designates the Son of God (*Book II*, prologue), he continues the struggle against the Arians. He teaches (chapter 1 and following) how great is the impiety of denying the Son’s goodness. Then he proves that the same Son is omnipotent and, although sent by the Father—whom he called greater—and subject to him, nevertheless entirely free (chapter 4 and following). He adds that, overcome by his infinite goodness, the Arians ought to have been led by those weaknesses and miseries which Christ had assumed (chapter 7) to healthier views; otherwise they should fear him as judge, whose sentence will instill as much despair in heretics as confidence in Catholics (chapter 11 and following). At this point, turning his address to Gratian (chapter 15), he says that he wrote these books briefly and without polish; nevertheless, they would suffice for all who sincerely sought the truth. Finally, he promises the emperor certain victory and asks God to grant him the triumph due to his faith (chapter 16).

Ambrose sent these two books to Gratian as he was preparing to travel east. Caesar approved them so highly that, after returning to his homeland, he begged the holy bishop by letter (*Letter to Ambrose*) to arrange for them to be sent to him again and to add to them a disputation on the divinity of the Holy Spirit. Yet this same little work had received no greater approval from Catholics than offense from heretics, who had tried by every device to diminish its authority. They could find nothing in it to criticize except that they repeatedly claimed Ambrose had deliberately aimed at excessive brevity (*Book III*, chapter 1, section 2), so that he might evade the necessity of answering their arguments, which were stronger than any possible refutation.

Ambrose wished to block the way to such accusations, which, however unjust, could nevertheless trouble the weaker. Therefore, after asking the emperor to allow him to postpone his work on the Holy Spirit (*Letter to Gratian* and *Book V*, chapter 2, section 34 and following), he composed three additional books by which the Arians would be forced into silence.

In the first of these, after immediately dissolving certain complaints of his opponents (*Book III*, chapter 1), he explains that the source of Arian error (chapter 2) is their attribution to Christ’s divinity—whose character as Creator and Most High cannot be denied—of things belonging solely to his humanity, in which he is rightly called Redeemer and created man. Once this foundation is established, all their schemes collapse, and their futile insistence that Scripture says the Father alone is powerful and alone possesses immortality becomes clear (*ibid.*, section 11 and following); likewise their claim that the Son was made and created (chapter 4 and following).

Afterward (chapter 7 and following) he demonstrates that the same Son is true God, just as the Father is, since they have one kingdom (chapter 12), one majesty (chapter 13), and one glory. He adds that, since the Arians cannot deny that the word “substance” is used in Scripture (chapter 14), the Son must be proclaimed consubstantial with the Father (chapter 15), while the impiety of Rimini is condemned (chapter 16). Finally, several other testimonies to the Son’s divinity, together with answers to the objections raised against them, bring the book to its conclusion (*ibid.* and the following chapter).

In the next book, although he declares it astonishing that human beings should abolish faith in Scripture (*Book IV*, chapters 1–2), he says that it is not astonishing that they should remain uncertain about Christ’s divinity, since even the angels professed their uncertainty on this matter at his ascension. He then turns to the objections of the heretics and explains the sense in which their cited words—“God is the head of Christ” (chapter 3), and likewise, “The Son can do nothing of himself” (chapter 4)—are to be understood.

After demonstrating that all things are truly possible for him (chapter 5 and following), he makes it clear that he cannot be accused of imperfection because he cannot generate (chapter 8), nor of temporality because he is begotten (chapter 9). Finally, after unraveling the difficulty drawn from the Son’s mission and glorification (chapter 10, section 130 and following), he refutes several other sophistries (chapters 11–12).

The final book, beginning with a brief introduction, first explains the reasons why these five books were written and what the author hopes readers will derive from them (*Book V*, prologue, section 8 and following). The objections are immediately repeated, and the passage “That they may know you, the true God” is explained at length to show why it does not undermine Christ (chapter 1 and following). Another passage, “We worship what we know,” is treated more briefly (chapter 4); but our Doctor devotes considerable attention to the statement attributed to the Lord, “To sit at the right hand,” and so forth (chapter 5 and following). He then turns to the words, “You loved them as you loved me,” where he again discusses the Lord’s mission briefly (chapter 7).

After these points have been debated, he explains in what sense Christ called the Father “Lord” (chapter 8), and on that occasion proves that all heresies are extinguished by this one verse of David: “The Lord said to my Lord,” and so forth. Then, after showing (chapter 9) how useless are the heretics’ efforts to evade the words of baptism, he demonstrates (chapter 10) that the passage “Whoever believes in me does not believe in me,” and so forth, in no way favors the abolition of Christ’s divinity; rather, he confirms that divinity there by various weighty arguments (chapter 11).

Finally, after smoothing whatever seemed difficult in the statement “When he has handed over the kingdom to God,” and likewise in the other statement, “Of that day and hour no one knows,” he professes his faith (chapter 12, section 19). He also attacks Arius’s arrogance in claiming for himself knowledge of divine secrets that had not been revealed even to Moses or Paul, explicitly declaring that that impious man was more swollen with pride than Lucifer himself.

Many authors—the Master of the Sentences, Gratian, and Saint Thomas—cite these books under the title *On the Trinity*, and they are likewise so entitled in quite a few manuscripts. Nevertheless, it is certain that Ambrose prefixed to them the common title *On the Faith*. They are not only cited under that name by Pope Leo of Rome (*Letter to the Emperor Leo*) and others, but Ambrose himself frequently refers to them by the same title (*Letter to Gratian*; *Book I on the Faith*, prologue, section 4).

Although Manichaeus, Sabellius, Photinus, and other leaders of ancient heresies are frequently attacked in them (*Book I*, chapters 1 and 6; *Book II*, chapters 5 and 9; *Book IV*, chapter 3; *Book V*, chapter 8), nevertheless both the objections reported above and the entire work clearly show that these books were composed chiefly against the inventions of the adherents of pure Arianism.

From what we have observed thus far, it is clear that the first two books were written at the time when Gratian was preparing an expedition against the Goths, by whom Valens was being hard pressed—that is, toward the end of the year 377 or the beginning of 378. As for the three later books, since it is beyond doubt that they were composed only after the same emperor had returned to the West, everyone will understand that they must be assigned to the year 379.

Although they were written at different times, they nevertheless readily coalesced into a single body, both through the unity of their subject and through the author’s own design, which he made clear not only by the arrangement of the work but also by his frequent citation of earlier books in the later ones (*Book III*, chapter 12, section 93; chapter 13, section 103; *Book IV*, chapter 1 and elsewhere). [Col. 0527]

It is no more evident that he distributed the entire treatise among five books than that he did not himself divide those books into chapters. This is proved both by the older manuscripts, in which the individual books are presented in continuous discourse, and by the more recent codices and editions, where chapter summaries appear so ineptly and are placed in such inappropriate locations that it has been necessary not only to substitute new ones—as we have done throughout this work—but also, something rarely required elsewhere, to divide the discourse itself differently here almost everywhere.

Since polemical works ordinarily bring a certain unpleasant satiety to readers, especially to rulers, Ambrose decided to forestall this problem by confining his disputation within the narrow limits of two little books. He enlivened these considerably through skill and diligence in treatment. But when he realized that the subject required fuller discussion, he took much greater care to remove anything that might produce boredom. With this purpose he worked diligently to weave proofs and objections together, employed apt and ingenious transitions, inserted prefaces, and from time to time mixed in and sprinkled moral precepts and even certain pointed sayings.

Everywhere he arranges the objections with such art that the reader can anticipate their solutions with no little pleasure. The answers he himself supplies, however, are so carefully considered and so solid that all who later labored over the same subject judged that none could be preferred to them.

We have already observed how highly Gratian valued the earlier books of this work. Yet, not content with the common testimonies of his judgment, Ambrose wished to add a more illustrious indication of it (*Book I on the Holy Spirit*, chapter 1), when Gratian ordered the Church, which the wickedness of the heretics had seized and isolated, to be restored to the Catholics.

The supreme pontiffs—Leo I, Agatho, and others—the Doctors—Jerome, Augustine, Theodoret, Vincent of Lérins, and others—and the ecumenical councils—Ephesus, Chalcedon, Constantinople III, and others—not only adorned these books with the highest praise, but also employed their testimonies in vigorous combat against heresies that arose in later ages.

For this reason we cannot sufficiently marvel that in our own time and in that of the Fathers there have been men who, trampling underfoot the universal tradition of the whole Church and of all ages—established by the authority of the divine books, confirmed by the Fathers in all the councils, asserted by the blood of so many martyrs and by the labors of so many confessors, as Ambrose himself testifies (*Book III*, chapter 15, section 128), proven by the books of so many highly learned Doctors, and embraced in a single voice by countless men distinguished for genius, learning, and piety—have undertaken to revive that old and obsolete heresy.

You may be even more astonished that these rash men oppose all of this with nothing but the very objections which the holy Doctor so decisively demolished in this work. Even if the other books of the Socinians were not witnesses to this fact, Crellius’s impious treatise *On the One God the Father* alone would suffice to make the matter certain and evident to everyone.

[Col. 0527]

# THE FIVE BOOKS OF SAINT AMBROSE, BISHOP OF MILAN, ON THE FAITH, TO GRATIAN AUGUSTUS (C, S)

[Col. 0527] [Note: [Col. 0527B] The first two were written toward the end of the year 377; the three later ones in the following year.]

# BOOK ONE

## 443 PROLOGUE

[Col. 0527A]

Ambrose praises Gratian for his ardor in learning the faith while humbling himself. Although he denies that Gratian needs human instruction, since he has been taught by God himself, he nevertheless adds that by this piety Gratian is preparing a path to victory for himself. Then, having suggested the difficulty of the work, Ambrose declares that he will follow not so much argument as authority, especially that of the Council of Nicaea.

### 1

The Queen of the South came to hear Solomon’s wisdom, as we read in the Book of Kings (1 Kings 10:1 and following). King Hiram also sent to Solomon in order to know him (1 Kings 5:1). You too, holy Emperor Gratian, imitator of ancient history, have wished to hear my faith. But I am not Solomon, whose wisdom you might admire; nor did you, Augustus not of one nation but of the whole world, judge that the faith should be expressed in a little book—not in order to learn it, but in order to approve it.

### 2

For what could you learn, Emperor Augustus, when from your very beginnings you have always cherished a pious devotion? [Note: [Col. 0527B] All the editions, together with two manuscripts, read: “since from your very beginnings you have been pious,” and so forth. The remaining manuscripts, as in the text, are more elegant.]

“Before I formed you in your mother’s womb, I knew you; and before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you” (Jeremiah 1:5). Sanctification, therefore, is not handed over but infused; and so preserve the divine gifts. For what no human being taught you, God himself, certainly, infused as its author.

### 3

You ask me, holy Emperor, for a little book on the faith as you prepare to go into battle; for you know that victory is ordinarily sought more through the faith of an emperor than through the valor of soldiers.

Abraham led three hundred and eighteen men into battle and carried away trophies from countless enemies. [Note: [Col. 0529B] The sign of the cross is represented by the letter T, which Jerome, following Origen, asserts had this very form in the ancient Hebrew characters, in his commentary on Ezekiel 9:4; Grotius defended this opinion against Scaliger in his discussion of the same passage. As for the number 318, among the Greeks it was expressed arithmetically by the letters τ and ιη, the latter two letters being the initials of the sweetest name, Jesus. Hence the basis of Ambrose’s allusion is clear. He proposes it again in this same book, chapter 18, just as he had already expressed it in Book I of *On Abraham*, chapter 9. Nor is it peculiar to the holy Bishop: the same interpretation is found in Book I of *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 1, by Paschasius the deacon, a contemporary of Pope Gelasius, as also in Prudentius, *Preface to the Psychomachia*, though less clearly. Before all these came Clement of Alexandria, who lucidly explains the same interpretation as having been received from ancient theologians, in Book VI of the *Stromata*, page 656. Hence it is evident that the ancients by no means believed that God had wished the mysteries of religion to be so bound to Hebrew letters that they could not also be indicated in Greek, just as Tertullian asserts that Ezekiel designated the Lord’s cross by the Greek letter T in Book III against Marcion, chapter 22.]

By the sign of the Lord’s cross and name, after subduing the strength of five kings and their victorious armies, he avenged his kinsman and gained both his brother’s son and a triumph (Genesis 14:14 and following).

Jesus, son of Nun, likewise defeated by the sound of seven priestly trumpets enemies whom he could not overcome with the powerful hand of the whole army, when he recognized the commander of the heavenly host (Joshua 6:6 and following).

Therefore you too are preparing to conquer because you worship Christ; you are preparing to conquer because you defend the faith whose little book you have requested from me.

### 4

I would indeed prefer to undertake the task of exhorting people to faith rather than disputing about faith. In the one there is a religious confession; in the other, rash presumption. But since you need no exhortation, and since I cannot evade the task of writing when piety requires it, I shall undertake this bold business on a modest occasion: I will dispute briefly about the faith and weave together more testimony.

### 5

Concerning the councils, I shall follow above all what the three hundred and eighteen priests, chosen in the judgment of Abraham, carried forth as a trophy: victorious through their harmonious strength in the faith and having subdued the perfidious throughout the whole world. [Note: [Col. 0529D] Ambrose again gives this number of the Nicene Fathers in chapter 18 of this book. He is supported not only by Hilary, *Against Constantius*; Jerome, *Chronicle*; Rufinus; and others, but also by Athanasius himself in his letter to Jovian. Therefore there was no reason for Valesius, in Eusebius, *Book III on the Life of Constantine*, chapter 8, to deny that the number of those bishops could be established; rather, he ought to have acknowledged the corruption of the Eusebian passage that assigns only 250, a corruption now generally recognized. Socrates and Eustathius make this clear by quoting the same text of Eusebius: the former gives “more than three hundred,” the latter “three hundred or thereabouts.” This cannot in any way refer to the 250 of the Vulgate reading of Eusebius, but fits 318 perfectly—although in that number we do not include the few Arians who attended the synod.]

It therefore seems to me divine that in the councils we possess an oracle of faith in the same number in which history gives us an example of piety.

## 445 CHAPTER ONE

He distinguishes the Catholic faith from the errors of the pagans, Jews, and heretics. After explaining the meaning of the words “God” and “Lord,” he demonstrates the distinction of persons and the unity of nature. By separating these, the Arians introduce not merely three gods but also destroy the kingdom of the Trinity.

6. This, then, is the assertion of our faith: that we say there is one God; that, unlike the Gentiles, we do not separate the Son; that, unlike the Jews, we do not deny that he was begotten from the Father before the ages and afterward born from the Virgin; that, unlike Sabellius, we do not confuse the Father and the Word, asserting that the Father and the Son are the same; that, unlike Photinus, we do not argue that the Son began from the Virgin; and that, unlike Arius, by believing in several and unlike powers, we do not make several gods according to the error of the Gentiles, since it is written: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deut. 6:4).

[Note: [Col. 0529D] Ambrose here mentions the authors of the principal heresies concerning the Trinity and the divine persons: Sabellius, Photinus, and Arius. According to Eusebius, *Hist.* VII, 6, the first of these began spreading his errors in the city of Ptolemais, in the Pentapolis, around the year 257. He taught that there was only one person in God, but that this person was expressed under three different names, as Epiphanius, *Heresy* 62; Basil, Letter 64; Philastrius; Augustine; and others report.

Photinus was born in the province of Galatia and became bishop of Sirmium, as we noted in our fifth book of the *Commentary on Luke*, no. 4. After acquiring for himself exceptional learning and eloquence, he began publishing new doctrines around the year 343. He denied that Christ had existed before Mary and blasphemously maintained that Christ had been born from Mary and Joseph through marital intercourse, as Marius Mercator relates. Hence, when Ambrose is reported to say that Photinus taught that the Son of God originated from the Virgin, or when Epiphanius says “from the Virgin Mary,” this must be understood as a kind of license—as when Virgil, *Eclogue* 6, calls Pasiphae, the mother of three children, a virgin—or, more properly, as an antonomasia, so that she may not be deprived of the honor attached to her customary name.

Epiphanius also adds that Photinus, when pressed, was accustomed to say: “The Word was in the Father, but he was not yet the Son . . .”; that the Son did not exist, but that there existed only that which would at some time be given the name “Son,” and so forth. These statements seem not to deny the eternity and divinity of the Word. This may perhaps explain why Augustine, in *Heresy* 44, after saying that Photinus believed the same things as Paul of Samosata, from whom the beginning of Christ from the Virgin was derived, immediately adds: “Nevertheless, in some respect he is said to have opposed him.” For this reason Garnerius’s conjecture could reasonably be confirmed, had he not asserted that Photinus consistently maintained the faith in the ὁμοούσιον [*homoousion*, “consubstantial”]. In this way, too, passages in the Fathers that seem mutually contradictory may be reconciled. Wherever Photinus is said to have denied that the Word was consubstantial, this may be referred to his true opinion; but wherever the opposite is attributed to him, it may be understood of the second answer to which he resorted when compelled.

Consult the same Garnerius, *Dissertation I on Heresies* and *On the Book of Nestorius*; and, if you wish to know the arguments against him, Alexander. As for Ambrose’s joining Arius to the two preceding heretics, since this entire work is directed against Arius’s heresy, he has been treated in the Preface.]

7. For “God” and “Lord” are names of magnificence, names of power, as he himself says: “The Lord is my name.” And, as the Prophet declares elsewhere: “The Lord Almighty is his name” (Isa. 42:8). Therefore, “Lord” and “God” mean either that he rules over all, or that he beholds all, and is feared by all.

[Note: [Col. 0530D] In this passage and in the following scriptural text, the Roman edition had added “God” after the word “Lord,” although this is absent from other manuscripts. As for the etymologies given below, the first is clear. The second derives the word from ἀπὸ θεᾶσθαι, “to behold,” as indicated by Gregory of Nyssa in his work addressed to Ablabius, Basil in Letter 141, Dionysius, Damascene, and others. The third derives it from the word δέος, which means “fear,” because God inspires fear. Hence Petronius and Statius say: “Fear first made gods in the world.” See Vossius, *Etymologicon*, under that word.]

8. If, then, there is one God, there is one name and one power of the Trinity.

[Note: [Col. 0531D] So read the greater number of the more authoritative manuscripts; some others read, “one name of power, one of the Trinity”; finally, certain manuscripts and all the editions read, “one name, one power, one Trinity.” Below, only the Roman edition has “certainly, not in names,” so that the unity of essence may be shown; while by the three things he has posited he declares that there are three persons. The source from which this was taken has not yet been discovered.]

Finally, he himself says: “Go, baptize the nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19). In the name, certainly, not in names.

9. He himself also says: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). He said “one,” so that there might be no distinction of power and nature; he added “are,” so that you might recognize the Father and the Son. Thus the perfect Father is believed to have begotten a perfect Son: the Father and the Son are one, not through confusion of person but through unity of nature.

10. [Elsewhere, chapter II.] We therefore say that there is one God, not two or three gods—an impious heresy into which the Arians fall even while accusing others of it.

For the man who separates the divinity of the Trinity says that there are three gods, although the Lord, by saying, “Go, baptize the nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit,” showed that the Trinity possesses one power. We confess the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, so that in the perfect Trinity there may be both the fullness of divinity and the unity of power.

11. “Every kingdom divided against itself will quickly be destroyed,” says the Lord (Matt. 12:25). The kingdom of the Trinity, therefore, is not divided. If it is not divided, it is one; for what is not one is divided.

[Note: [Col. 0531D] When nature is divided, power is likewise divided and consequently diminished. Hence Tertullian’s celebrated saying: “If God is not one, he is not God.” Gregory of Nazianzus also writes elegantly in *Poem* 3:

> For to me, rule by many is equal to rule by none at all,  
> when they contend; division is strife, and it hastens toward dissolution;  
> far from divinity, rule by many is for me.

]

They therefore wish the kingdom of the Trinity to be such that it could easily be destroyed by its own division. Rather, because it cannot be destroyed, it is clear that it is not divided. Unity is neither divided nor split apart; therefore it is not subject to corruption or decay.

## CHAPTER II

Having exhorted the emperor to zeal for the faith, Ambrose demonstrates that Christ is God by the unity of will and operation that exists between Christ and the Father. After setting forth the divine attributes, he affirms that they also belong to Christ; and, having pursued his various appellations, he teaches that by them substantial unity and personal distinction are proved. He then adduces several examples to explain that unity and denies that God’s unity can be defended in any other way.

12. “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 7:21). Faith, therefore, ought not to be merely superficial, revered Emperor; for it is written: “Zeal for your house has consumed me” (Ps. 68:10). Let us therefore invoke Jesus the Lord with faithful spirit and devoted mind, and believe that he is God, so that whatever we ask of the Father in his name we may obtain.

[Note: [Col. 0532D] A few manuscripts read: “For the Father always wishes the Son to be asked.”]

For the Father wishes the Son to be asked, and the Son wishes the Father to be asked.

13. The grace of piety is in harmony, and the works of power do not conflict. For whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does. The Son both does likewise and does the same things; yet he wishes the Father to be asked for what he himself is going to do, so that you may recognize this not as an indication of inability but of unity of power. The Son of God, therefore, is rightly to be adored and venerated: by his divinity he founded the world, and by his piety he shaped our disposition.

14. We must therefore believe God to be good, eternal, perfect, almighty, and true, as we have received in the Law, the Prophets, and the other divine Scriptures, because without these attributes God is not God. He who is God cannot be other than good, since the fullness of goodness exists in the nature of God. Nor can God be temporal, since he made time. Nor can God be imperfect; for whoever is lesser is necessarily imperfect, lacking something by which he might be equaled to one greater. This, then, is the proclamation of faith: God is not evil; nothing is impossible for God; God is not temporal; God is not lesser.

[Note: [Col. 0532D] Several manuscripts read: “If I err, not even badly.”]

If I am mistaken, let them refute me.

15. Since, then, Christ is God, he is also good, almighty, eternal, perfect, and true; for these qualities belong to the nature of divinity. Either, therefore, let them deny the nature of divinity in Christ, or they cannot deny to God the things that belong to the divine nature.

16. Certainly, so that no one may be able to err, let him follow those things by which Holy Scripture has indicated that we should understand the Son.

[Note: [Col. 0532D] Some manuscripts read: “Let them follow those things that Scripture indicates.”]

He is called the Word, he is called the Son, he is called the Power of God, he is called the Wisdom of God.

[Note: [Col. 0532D] In the same sense, St. Thomas, *Summa Theologiae* I, q. 32, a. 2, ad 3: “To show that he was immaterially begotten, he is called the Word.”]

He is the Word because he is without stain; Power because he is perfect; Son because he is begotten from the Father; Wisdom because he is one with the Father—one in eternity, one in divinity.

[Note: [Col. 0532D] Several manuscripts have *unus* three times instead of *unum*, incorrectly.]

For the Father himself is not the Son; rather, there is an explicit distinction of generation between the Father and the Son, so that from God there is God, from one who remains there is one who remains, and the full comes from the full.

17. These, then, are not empty names but signs of operative power. There is a fullness of divinity in the Father, and a fullness of divinity in the Son—not a different divinity, but one divinity. What is one is not confused; what is undifferentiated is not multiple.

18. For if, as it is written, the soul and heart of all believers were one (Acts 4:32); if everyone who clings to the Lord is one spirit, as the Apostle said (1 Cor. 6:17); if husband and wife are one flesh; if all human beings, as far as nature is concerned, are of one substance; if Scripture says this of human beings, that many are one, although no comparison with divine things is possible—how much more are the Father and the Son one in divinity, where there is no difference at all either of substance or of will?

19. For otherwise, how shall we call God one? Difference produces plurality; unity of power excludes numerical multiplicity, because unity is not a number but the very beginning of all number.

## CHAPTER III

Ambrose proves the unity of the Father and the Son by testimonies from Scripture. First, by comparing different passages, he expounds a text from Isaiah in such a way as to assert that there is no difference in the Son from the Father’s nature, except insofar as concerns the flesh, and consequently that the two possess one divinity. After confirming this with the authority of Baruch, he teaches that the prophets must be believed in this matter.

20. How greatly divine Scripture has expressed the unity of the Father and the Son according to divinity is attested by the prophetic oracles. For thus says the Lord of hosts: “Egypt has labored, and the commerce of the Ethiopians and the Sabaeans; tall men will pass over to you and will be your slaves. They will follow you bound in fetters; they will worship you and pray to you, because God is in you, and there is no God besides you. For you are God, and we did not know it, the God of Israel” (Isa. 45:14).

21. Hear the prophetic voice: “God is in you,” he says, “and there is no God besides you.” How does this agree with the Arians? They must necessarily deny either the divinity of the Father or that of the Son, unless they believe the unity of the same divinity.

22. “God is in you,” he says, because the Father is in the Son. For it is written: “The Father who remains in me, he himself speaks”; and: “The works that I do, he himself also does” (John 14:10). But elsewhere, too, the Son is in the Father, for he says: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 14:10). Let them dissolve this unique property of nature and unity of operation, if they can.

23. God, therefore, is in God, but there are not two gods; for it is written that there is one God (Deut. 6:4). The Lord is in the Lord, but there are not two Lords, since it is likewise written: “You cannot serve two lords” (Matt. 6:24). The Law also says: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deut. 6:4). And yet in that same Testament we read: “The Lord rained from the Lord” (Gen. 19:24): “The Lord,” it says, “rained from the Lord.”

So also in Genesis you have: “And God said,” and “God made”; and below: “And God made man in the image of God” (Gen. 1:3, 26). Yet it was not two gods, but one God who acted.

Thus both the unity of operation and the unity of the name are preserved. For when we read “God from God,” we certainly do not say that there are two gods.

24. Finally, in the forty-fourth Psalm you have the Prophet both calling the Father God and declaring the Son to be God, when he says: “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever”; and below: “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. 44:7, 8).

[Note: [Col. 0533] Several manuscripts read: “The Prophet called him God, and did not deny the Son when he said.”]

The one who anoints is God, and the one who is anointed according to the flesh is the Son of God. Indeed, whom does Christ have as companions of his anointing except those who share in his flesh? You see, therefore, that God is anointed by God; but in the assumption of human nature the Son of God is designated as anointed, and the form of the Law is not violated.

25. Here, therefore, when it is said, “The Lord rained from the Lord,” recognize the unity of divinity. The unity of operation does not produce a plural divinity, as the Lord himself shows when he says: “Believe me that I am in the Father and the Father is in me; or else believe because of the works themselves” (John 10:38). Here, too, we observe that he indicated the unity of divinity through the unity of works.

26. To prove that the Father and the Son have one divinity and one dominion, and to prevent us from falling into the error of Gentile or Jewish impiety, the Apostle prudently showed what we ought to follow, saying: “There is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and we in him; and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and we through him” (1 Cor. 8:6).

Just as, by saying “one Lord, Jesus Christ,” he did not deny that the Father is Lord, so, by saying “one God, the Father,” he likewise did not separate the Son from the truth of divinity. Thus he showed not a plurality of divinity but a unity of power, because in dominion there is divinity and in divinity there is dominion, as it is written: “Know that the Lord himself is God; he made us, and not we ourselves” (Ps. 99:3).

27. God, therefore, is in you through unity of nature; and there is no God besides you through the distinctiveness of substance, difference having been excluded.

28. In the Book of Jeremiah also Scripture speaks of one God, yet confesses both the Father and the Son. Thus you have: “This is our God, and no other will be reckoned beside him. He discovered the whole way of discipline and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved. After this he appeared on earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch 3:36, 37).

29. He speaks of the Son: “For he himself lived among human beings”; and he says: “This is our God, and no other will be reckoned beside him.” Why do we scrutinize the one of whom so great a prophet says that no other can be reckoned beside him? For what other reckoning can there be where there is unity of divinity? The people confessed this while placed in danger; those who feared religion did not know how to sow questions.

30. Be present, Holy Spirit, with your prophets, in whom you have been accustomed to dwell,

[Note: [Col. 0535D] Amerbach, Erasmus, and several manuscripts read: “in whom you established yourself.”]

with whom we believe. If we do not believe the prophets, shall I believe the wise men of this world? But “where is the wise man? Where is the scribe?”

[Note: [Col. 0535D] Ambrose is not designating another rustic, but Jeremiah; he is alluding to the baskets of figs mentioned in that prophet, chapter 24 and following.]

Our rustic, while grafting fig trees, discovered what the philosopher did not know. For “God chose what is foolish in the world to confound what is strong” (1 Cor. 1:27). Do we believe the Jews because “God was once known in Judea” (Ps. 75:2)? Yet they deny precisely that for which we believe, because they do not know the Father, having denied the Son.

## CHAPTER IV

After collecting and presenting several arguments for proving the unity of God, Ambrose shows that Christ’s divinity and humanity are foreshadowed in the three gifts of the Magi, just as the truth of divinity and of the Trinity is foreshadowed in the angel who walked among the three youths amid the flames.

31. [Note: [Col. 0535D] Most manuscripts read: “One Lord . . . Faith signifies one Lord.”]

One God is attested by the common nature of things, because there is one world. One God is signified by faith, because there is one faith of the New and Old Testaments. One Holy Spirit is testified to by grace, because there is one baptism in the name of the Trinity. The Prophets speak of one God; the Apostles hear of one God. The Magi believed in one God, and as suppliants brought gold, frankincense, and myrrh to Christ’s cradle: with gold confessing him to be king, with frankincense venerating him as God. Gold is the treasure of kingship, frankincense the sacrifice of God, and myrrh the sign of burial.

32. What, then, did the mystical gifts placed among the lowly manger signify, except that we should understand in Christ a distinction between divinity and flesh? As man he is seen; as Lord he is adored. He lies in swaddling clothes, but shines in the stars. The cradle indicates one who is being born, and the stars one who rules. It is flesh that is wrapped; it is divinity that is served by angels. Thus neither is the natural dignity of majesty lost, nor is the reality of the assumed flesh left unconfirmed.

[Note: [Col. 0535D] Amerbach, Erasmus, the Roman edition, and several manuscripts read: “is hidden in the cradle”; Gill, with many more and more authoritative manuscripts, reads: “lies,” and so forth.]

33. This is our faith. Thus God wished to be known by all. Thus the three youths believed and felt none of the surrounding flames, while the destructive fire consumed the faithless and the harmless flame refreshed the faithful, for whom the fires that burned others became cooling, because by the merit of faith the punishment had lost its natural character. For an angel was present in visible form,

[Note: [Col. 0535D] The Roman edition and several manuscripts read: “who protected”; with no bad sense. The remaining editions and many manuscripts read: “who admonished,” which is also acceptable. The sense, therefore, is that the angel indicated that the Trinity of the divine persons was signified in the three youths, just as unity of power or nature was indicated in the angel himself, who was one; for Ambrose uses these terms interchangeably in this work.

As for the teaching that the Son of God was present in the angel, this is not Ambrose’s opinion alone but also that of several ancient Fathers. Among them, the author of *Questions on the Old Testament* goes further. In question 18 he says of Nebuchadnezzar: “By the merit of his kingdom he saw Christ in the furnace.” Yet it seems that our saint preceded him below, in chapter 13, no. 80. See the commentators on Daniel and the Scholastics on *Sentences* II, distinction 8, as well as St. Thomas, *Summa Theologiae* I, q. 51.]

who admonished them that, in the number of the Trinity, there should be praise of the one power.

[Note: [Col. 0536D] Some manuscripts read: “the praise of majesty.”]

God was blessed; the Son of God was seen in the angel; holy and spiritual grace spoke through the youths.

## CHAPTER V

The various blasphemies of the Arians against Christ are recounted. Before answering them, Ambrose warns Catholics to beware of the sophistries of philosophers, since the heretics placed their chief hope in them.

34. [Elsewhere, chapter III.] Let us now consider what arguments the Arians bring against the Son of God.

35. They say that the Son of God is unlike the Father. If this were said of a human being, it would be an insult.

36. They say that the Son of God began in time, although he himself is the creator of time. We are human beings, and we do not wish to be temporal. We began in time, and we believe that we shall exist without time. We desire to become eternal; how, then, can we deny that the Son of God is eternal, whom nature, not grace, teaches and demonstrates to be eternal?

37. They call him created. Who would count an author among his own works, so that he might appear to be what he himself made?

38. They deny that he is good. The sacrilegious statement condemns itself, so that it cannot hope for pardon.

39. They deny that he is the true Son of God; they deny that he is almighty, although they confess that all things were made through the Son and that all things were created by the power of God. For what is power if not perfect nature?

40. They also deny that he is one with the Father in divinity. Let them therefore erase the Gospel; let them erase Christ’s words. For he himself said: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). I am not the one saying this; Christ said it. Was he deceitful, so as to lie? Was he impious, so as to claim what was not his? These matters will be set out more fully in their proper places.

41. Now, since the heretic says that the Son is unlike the Father and attempts to establish this through crafty arguments,

[Note: [Col. 0536D] Hilary also, after citing this same passage of the Apostle, forewarns us against the arguments and deceptions of philosophers. Other Fathers likewise command that they be avoided, especially Augustine in *Against Faustus* XIII, 15. Epiphanius explicitly singles out Aristotle’s dialectic; we may reasonably believe that Ambrose also had this in view. Perhaps this gave rise to the story reported by Cardinal Nicholas of Cusa in his *Apology of Learned Ignorance*: “It is read,” he says, “that the blessed Ambrose added to the litanies: ‘From the dialecticians”—some have “from dialectic”—“of Aristotle, deliver us, O Lord.’”]

we must say what is written: “See that no one despoils you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition and according to the elements of this world, and not according to Christ; because in him the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. 2:8–9).

42. They place all the force of their poisons in dialectical disputation, which philosophical opinion defines as possessing not the power to establish but the practice of destroying. Yet it did not please God to save his people through dialectic: “For the kingdom of God is in simplicity of faith, not in contention of speech” (1 Cor. 4:20).

## CHAPTER VI

Ambrose is about to prove that Christ is not unlike the Father. After naming the more celebrated leaders of the Arians, he reveals how poorly they agree among themselves and, against them—as against certain monsters—displays the protection of the Scriptures.

43. [Elsewhere, chapter IV.] They say, then, that he is unlike the Father; we deny it—indeed, we shudder at the word. But I do not want you, holy Emperor, to believe an argument or our disputation. Let us question the Scriptures; let us question the Apostles; let us question the Prophets; let us question Christ. What more is needed? Let us question the Father, whose honor they claim to pursue, if the Son is judged to be degenerate.

[Note: [Col. 0537B] In Ambrose’s writings generally, a *degenerate* person is one who departs from his origin not only in perfection but also in nature and substance. Hilary uses the word in the same way in *On the Trinity* VIII: “While God, by begetting, becomes degenerate in nothing within him—that is, in the Son.” Hilary also frequently uses the word *genus* for nature, agreeing here with the author of the work *On Definitions* cited by Athanasius, where we read: “Nature and substance are therefore also genus.”]

But it is not an honor to a good Father to insult the Son. A good Father cannot be pleased if the Son is believed to have degenerated from the Father rather than equaled him.

44. Forgive me, holy Emperor, if I turn my words for a little while to the heretics themselves. But whom should I read above all—Eunomius, Arius, or Aetius, his teachers?

[Note: [Col. 0537C] All editions and several manuscripts here and in two passages below read “Eudoxius, Eunomius,” and so forth; but the greater number of manuscripts, and those of greater authority, everywhere omit Eudoxius. We recognize that this is certainly the genuine reading, not only because all editions and manuscripts have “his teachers,” where “their teachers” would be required, but also because, with Eudoxius omitted, Eunomius is discussed a few lines later.

Someone may have added Eudoxius here after reading either in Athanasius, *On the Councils*, p. 913, that Aetius was called the teacher of Eudoxius, or in Theodoret, book II, chapter 27, that Aetius found at Antioch Eudoxius, who had seized the bishopric of that city and afterward that of Constantinople, and who agreed with him in doctrine.

Aetius, commonly called “the atheist,” was, according to Epiphanius, ignorant of letters into advanced old age, but devoted himself to dialectic. His principal teaching consisted in Aristotle’s categories, and he spent entire days treating, defining, and dividing divine matters by syllogisms and geometrical rules. He came to Alexandria after George had intruded into the patriarchal see; George seems also to have admitted him to ecclesiastical duties. This may perhaps explain why Athanasius thought that George had ordained him deacon, although he had actually received that order from Leontius, the eunuch and Arian bishop of Antioch.

Aetius roundly asserted that the Son was ἀνόμοιον [*anomoion*], that is, unlike the Father. Hence his followers, who were sometimes called Aetians after their author, were more frequently called Anomoeans. The other Arians harassed Aetius, not because he held a different opinion, but because, by revealing his mind more openly, he brought hatred upon the entire faction through his blasphemies.

Accordingly, Constantius exiled him to Amblada, situated on the borders of Pisidia and Phrygia, where he published a book filled with 300 arguments—or, more accurately, fallacious arguments. St. Epiphanius refutes forty-seven of them; he treats both the author himself and his followers at considerable length. See also Valesius’s edition of Sozomen, book III, chapter 5, and Socrates, book, chapter 35.

Eunomius had Aetius as his teacher. When he met him at Alexandria in the year 356, he accompanied him in 358 as he traveled to Antioch to Eudoxius, as we have said. Not long afterward, having become bishop of Cyzicus from being Aetius’s secretary, he preached his errors with such vehemence that Eudoxius, at a council held in Constantinople by order of the emperor, was forced to strip him of his dignity.

Philostorgius tells the matter differently, but because of his declared enthusiasm for Eunomius he is entirely unworthy of being believed. After being deposed from the episcopate, Eunomius carried out a secession, ordaining bishops and presbyters, although he does not seem to have publicly renounced his friendship with Eudoxius until the reign of Jovian.

Those who knew that both bishops held the same opinion, judging it unworthy that Eudoxius had defected from Eunomius through cowardice, joined Eunomius’s faction under the name of Eunomians. Among them were George of Alexandria, Acacius of Caesarea, and many other Eastern bishops; and among Westerners, nearly all who had joined the Arian party. The remaining Arians and Semi-Arians rejected them.

Gregory of Nyssa and Basil wrote against Eunomius. He is also mentioned by Epiphanius, *Heresy* 76; Augustine, *On Heresies*, chapter 24; and, besides Theodoret, Socrates, and Sozomen, many others.]

There are many names, but one treachery; they do not differ in impiety, although they disagree in fellowship; they are not unlike in fraud, but differ in their association.
