[Note: [Col. 0538D] The old edition and one or two manuscripts read: “but in thought.” The Roman edition, together with the others, reads: “but in association,” which is much more elegant, since it corresponds to the preceding “they disagree in fellowship.” One manuscript of Thuaneus has “but in contention,” which is not an unsuitable sense.]

For I do not understand why they do not wish to agree among themselves.

45. The Arians avoid the person of Eunomius, but affirm his treachery and carry on his impiety. They say that he disclosed more openly what Arius had written. What a lavish display of blindness! They approve the author but reject the executor. Thus they have now divided themselves into several forms.

[Note: [Col. 0538D] All editions and a few manuscripts read: “Some follow Eudoxius, some Eunomius”; many others omit these words, as noted above; others have “Eudoxius”; and some, instead of “or Aetius,” have “or Euticius” in both places, which is not sufficiently correct. Below, where we, with the other editions and a considerable portion of the manuscripts, read “others hold different views,” the rest more aptly have “others think otherwise.”

As for the three heretics who are here added to those mentioned above, since there will be occasion to speak at length of the first two at the Council of Aquileia and of the last in many passages to come, we shall add nothing about them here.]

Some follow Eunomius or Aetius; others, Palladius or Demophilus and Auxentius, or the heirs of this treachery; others hold different views. Is Christ divided? But those who divide him from the Father tear themselves apart.

46. And therefore, since they have conspired together against the Church of God, although they do not agree among themselves, I shall designate them by the common name “heretics,” to whom an answer must be given. For heresy, like a certain Hydra of the fables,

[Note: [Col. 0539D] The monsters celebrated in the poets’ fables and known to everyone. How aptly heresy and heretics are compared with them is sufficiently demonstrated both by the Hydra’s poison and its seven heads, which multiplied as they were cut off, and by the barking and rage of Scylla’s dogs, as well as by the frequent shipwrecks of the imprudent upon the same reef. The holy author will speak of these again in book III, chapter 1.]

grew through its own wounds; and, though repeatedly cut down, sprouted again, destined for fire and doomed to perish in flames. Or, like a monstrous Scylla, a portent divided into various forms of treachery, it presents the superfluous name of a Christian sect; but those whom it finds miserable, wavering amid the shipwrecks of faith in that sea of impiety, it tears apart with the savage tooth of a beast, girded about with monstrous horrors.

47. Its cavern, holy Emperor, which sailors say is dreadful in its blind hiding places, and whose entire neighborhood resounds with blue dogs among the rocks of treachery, we ought somehow to pass by with our ears closed. For it is written: “Hedge your ears with thorns” (Ecclus. 28:28). And elsewhere: “Beware of dogs; beware of evil workers” (Phil. 3:2). And again: “Avoid a heretical person after the first admonition, knowing that such a person is perverted and sins, being condemned by his own judgment” (Titus 3:10–11). Therefore, like good helmsmen, so that we may pass by more safely, let us spread the sails of faith and reread the order of the Scriptures.

## CHAPTER VII

From Paul, the Prophets, and the Gospel, Christ is asserted to be like the Father, especially from the creation of the human being according to the divine likeness.

48. The Apostle says that Christ is the image of the Father; for he says that Christ is “the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation” (Col. 1:15). “Firstborn,” he says, not “first-created,” so that he may be believed to be begotten according to nature and first according to perpetuity.

Elsewhere also the Apostle asserted that the Father “appointed him heir of all things, through whom he also made the ages; he is the radiance of his glory and the impress of his substance” (Heb. 1:2–3). The Apostle says “image,” while Arius says that he is unlike the Father. Why “image,” if he does not possess likeness? In paintings, human beings do not wish the figures to be unlike their subjects; yet Arius contends that the Son is unlike the Father and wants the Father to have begotten one unlike himself, as though the Father were unable to beget one who was like him.

49. The Prophets say: “In your light we shall see light” (Ps. 36:9). The Prophets say: “For he is the brightness of eternal light, and the spotless mirror of God’s majesty, and the image of his goodness” (Wis. 7:26).

See how many things are said. “Brightness”: because the radiance of the Father’s light is in the Son. “Spotless mirror”: because the Father is seen in the Son. “Image of goodness”: because what is wholly perceived in the Son is not body in body but power. “Image” teaches that he is not unlike the Father; “impress” signifies that he is an expressed likeness; “brightness” indicates that he is eternal.

The image is certainly not a bodily face, not composed of pigments or wax, but simple, proceeding from God, coming forth from the Father, expressed from the source.

50. Through this image the Lord showed the Father to Philip, saying: “Philip, whoever sees me sees the Father also. How then can you say, ‘Show us the Father’? Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?” (John 14:9–10). For the one who sees the Son sees the Father in the image.

Do you see what kind of image he calls it? This image is truth; this image is justice; this image is the power of God. It is not mute, because it is the Word; it is not insensible, because it is Wisdom; it is not empty, because it is Power; it is not void, because it is Life; it is not dead, because it is Resurrection.

[Note: [Col. 0540D] Quite a few manuscripts read “not mutable”; the others and the editions read “not mute,” which is better, as the following explanation shows, because he is the Word.]

You see, therefore, that when he is called “image,” the Father is indicated as the one whose image the Son is, because no one can himself be his own image.

51. I could say more about the testimonies of the Son,

[Note: [Col. 0540D] All editions and a few manuscripts read “testimonies concerning the Son”; the others more suitably read “the Son’s testimonies,” that is, testimonies given by the Son himself, as the immediately following words clearly show.]

but, lest he be thought to have favored himself excessively, let us question the Father. For he himself said: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26). The Father says to the Son, “in our image and likeness”; and you call the Son of God unlike the Father?

52. John says: “Beloved, we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when it is revealed, we shall be like him” (1 John 3:2). O heedless madness! O shameless obstinacy! We are human beings, and insofar as we are able, we shall be in the likeness of God; yet we dare to deny that the Son of God is like the Father?

[Col. 0540C] 454

**53.** Therefore the Father said: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.” At the beginning of the world itself I hear of the Father and the Son, and I see one work. I hear the one speaking, I recognize the one making; but I also read of one image and one likeness belonging to both the Father and the Son. This likeness is not one of difference but of unity. Therefore, whatever you claim for yourself, you detract from the Son of God, since you cannot exist in the image of God except through the image of God.

## CHAPTER VIII

From the demonstrated likeness of the Son to the Father, it is readily shown that he is likewise eternal; this is also asserted by the prophecy of Isaiah and by the Gospel of John, whose authority is shown to crush the leaders of heresy.

[Col. 0540D]

**54. [Elsewhere, Chapter V.]** It is therefore clear that he is not unlike the Father, and for that reason the way is more readily open for us to acknowledge that he is also everlasting, since one who is like the everlasting must certainly be everlasting. But if we call the Father everlasting and deny this same quality to the Son, we say that he is unlike him; for what is temporal is unlike what is everlasting. The Prophet cries out that he is everlasting, and the Apostle cries out that he is everlasting: the Old Testament is full of testimonies to the everlasting Son, and so is the New.

**55.** Let us therefore maintain the sequence. It is written in the Old Testament—to mention just one passage among many: “Before me no other God existed, and after me there will be none” (Isa. 43:10). I shall make no argument; I ask you yourself. Who says this—the Father or the Son? Whichever you say, you will understand that you are convicted by it—or, if you believe, instructed. Who, then, says this—the Father or the Son? If the Son: “Before me,” he says, “there was no other God.” If the Father: “After me,” he says, “there will be none.” The one has no predecessor, the other no successor: each is known in the other, the Father in the Son and the Son in the Father. For when you name the Father, you have also designated his Son, since no one is his own father; when you name the Son, you also confess his Father, since no one is his own son. Therefore neither can the Son exist without the Father, nor the Father without the Son. The Father, then, is always, and the Son also is always.

[Col. 0541D]  
*Note:* Some manuscripts read, “Behold, understand that you are convicted.” All editions and some manuscripts read *non obloquendi* (“not for contradicting”); others, and indeed more of them, read *non colloquendi* (“not for conversing”).

**56.** “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God; he was in the beginning with God” (John 1:1). “He was,” he says, “with God.” He was, he was, he was, he was—behold, four instances of “was.” Where did the impious find something that was not? Elsewhere John also says in his epistle: “What was from the beginning” (1 John 1:1). The verb “was” extends indefinitely: whatever you may conceive, the Son was.

**57.** Our fisherman has excluded all heresies in this brief chapter. For what “was in the beginning” is not enclosed within time and is not preceded by a beginning. Therefore let Arius be silent. But what “was with God” is not confused by commingling; rather, it is distinguished by the solid perfection of the Word remaining with the Father, so that Sabellius may be silenced. “And the Word was God.” Therefore this Word is not a word in the utterance of speech, but belongs to that heavenly designation of power, so that Photinus may be refuted.

[Col. 0541D]  
*Note:* The older editions and some manuscripts read “as he confesses,” which is preferable. The Roman edition and a greater number of manuscripts, including older ones, read “so that he may be refuted.” Photinus, when he disclosed his true opinion, maintained that the Word was not substantial and *ἐνδιάθετον* (“inwardly conceived”), but passing and *προσφορικόν* (“uttered” or “expressed”), as has already been stated.

[Col. 0542D]  
But when it is said that he “was in the beginning with God,” the inseparable unity of eternal divinity in the Father and the Son is taught, so that Eunomius may blush.

[Col. 0542D]  
*Note:* Editions read, “so that Eudoxius and Eunomius may blush.”

Finally, since all things are said to have been made through him, he is clearly designated as the founder of both the New and the Old Testament, so that Manichaeus can find no occasion for temptation. Thus the good fisherman enclosed them all within one net, making them incapable of fraud, even though they were unfit for the catch.

## CHAPTER IX

The holy man questions the heretics; and, after setting out their answer—that the Son is earlier than all time, but later than the Father—he concludes that change is being introduced into God and that eternity must be attributed to both persons.

[Col. 0541D]

**58.** Tell me, heretic—for the most merciful emperor grants me permission to address you briefly, not out of a desire to contradict or a hunger to hear, but for the sake of explanation—tell me, I say: was there ever a time when God the almighty Father did not exist, while God did exist?

“You do not assert a time,” you say. Good—and cleverly said. For if you assert a time, you convict yourself, because you must claim that there was a time before the Son, although the Son is the author and creator of time. He cannot himself have begun after his work; therefore you must confess that he is the author of his own work.

**59.** “I do not deny the Son before the ages,” you say; “but when I call him Son, I show that the Father is prior, for the Father is prior to the Son.” What is this? You deny that there is a time before the Son, yet you wish something—I know not what—to have preceded the Son, something belonging to time; and you show that certain intermediate efforts at begetting existed, in which you signify a temporal generation of the Father. For if the Father began to exist, then God existed first and afterward became Father. How, then, is God immutable? If he was first God and afterward Father, he was certainly changed by the addition of generation.

**60.** But may God avert this madness. We have raised this question only to refute their impiety. A pious mind asserts generation without time, so that it may call the Father everlasting with the Son and never assert that he was at any point changed.

**61.** Let honor therefore join to the Father the Son whom divinity has joined; let impiety not separate him whom the distinct property of generation has united. Let us honor the Son, so that we may also honor the Father, as it is written in the Gospel (John 5:23). The Son’s eternity is the mark of the Father’s majesty. If the Son did not always exist, then the Father was changed; but the Son always existed, and therefore the Father was never changed, because he is always immutable. Thus we see that those who wish to deny the Son’s eternity wish to teach that the Father was changed.

[Col. 0542D] 456

## CHAPTER X

Having confirmed Christ’s eternity from the Apostle, he declares that divine generation must not be measured or scrutinized according to the pattern of human generation; and, having avoided the difficulties arising from this, he explains that whatever is said of this generation in bodily terms must be understood spiritually.

[Col. 0542D]

**62.** Take another proof that clearly establishes the Son’s eternity. The Apostle says that God’s eternal power is also his divinity (Rom. 1:20).

[Col. 0542D]  
*Note:* The Ebrul. manuscript reads: “and wisdom.”

But Christ is the power of God, for it is written that Christ is the power and wisdom of God (1 Cor. 1:24). Therefore, if Christ is the power of God, and the power of God is eternal, Christ too is eternal.

[Col. 0543A]

**63.** Therefore, heretic, do not construct an accusation from the practice of human generation, nor fashion one from our speech. For we cannot contain the immensity of divinity within the narrow confines of our words—of that greatness of which there is no end (Ps. 144:3). If you attempt to define human generation, you point to time; but divine generation is above all things: it extends far beyond and rises above every thought and perception. For it is written: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14:6). Therefore, whatever you may think about the Father, however great an eternity you attribute to him, you cannot think anything about him except through the Son; nor can any understanding pass to the Father except through the Son.

“This is,” he says, “my beloved Son” (Matt. 17:5).

[Col. 0543D]  
*Note:* The old edition, together with very few manuscripts, reads: “He is, he says, that which exists continually.”

“He is,” he says, “who always is what he is.” Hence David also says: “Forever, O Lord, your word remains in heaven” (Ps. 118:89). For what remains does not fail either in substance or in eternity.

**64.** You ask me how the Son can exist if the Father is not prior to him. I ask you in turn when or how you think the Son was generated. For I cannot know the secret of generation: the mind fails, the voice is silent—not mine alone, but that of the angels as well. It is above the Powers, above the Angels, above the Cherubim, above the Seraphim, above every perception, because it is written: “The peace of Christ, which is above every perception” (Phil. 4:7).

[Col. 0543D]  
*Note:* Many manuscripts read: “which surpasses every perception.” If Christ’s peace surpasses every perception, and so forth.

If Christ’s peace is above every perception, how can so great a generation not be above every perception?

[Col. 0543C]

**65.** You too must place your hand over your mouth: it is not permitted to scrutinize heavenly mysteries.

[Col. 0543D]  
*Note:* Ambrose was not the only one to condemn excessive curiosity in investigating divine matters, especially the Son’s generation; nearly all the Fathers proscribed it in the same way. Thus Athanasius, *Oration* 3 *Against the Arians*; Basil, *Homily* 29; Gregory of Nazianzus, *Oration* 1; Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechesis* 11; Cyril of Alexandria, *Dialogue* 2 *On the Trinity*; Hilary, Book II; and others. Nevertheless, our theologians who debate the same generation in the schools should not for that reason be condemned. Their discussions do not arise, as they do among the heretics, from the vice of a restless and proud mind, but from a humble and pious desire to learn.

It is permitted to know that he was born; it is not permitted to investigate how he was born. I may not deny the former; fear forbids me to inquire into the latter. For if Paul calls ineffable the things he heard when he was caught up into the third heaven, how can we express the mystery of the Father’s generation, which we could neither perceive nor hear?

**66.** But if you draw me toward the custom of human generation, so that you may call the Father prior, consider whether earthly examples of generation apply to the generation of God. If we speak according to human experience, you cannot deny that in a human being the father’s experiences precede those of the son. He grew first, grew old first, suffered first, wept first. If, therefore, one is younger in time, the other is older in suffering. If one entered the age of generation, neither did the other escape the shame of begetting.

[Col. 0543D] 457

**67.** What pleasure do these tortures of questioning give you? You hear “Son of God”: either erase the name or acknowledge the nature.

[Col. 0544D]  
*Note:* Some manuscripts read: “You hear the truth; acknowledge … these things are not to be judged according to bodily realities.”

You hear “womb”: acknowledge the evident truth of generation. You hear “heart”: understand the Word. You hear “right hand”: acknowledge the power. You hear “mouth”: acknowledge the wisdom. These things are not to be evaluated corporeally in God. The Son is generated incomprehensibly; the Father generates without suffering; and yet God truly generated God from himself and generated him beyond every understanding. The Father loves, and you investigate; the Father is well pleased, and you envy along with the Jews; the Father honors, and you revile along with the Gentiles.

## CHAPTER XI

It cannot be proved from Scripture that the Father is prior to the Son, nor from arguments drawn from human generation, since innumerable absurdities would follow from them; and the bold assertion that Christ was born in time is the height of impiety.

[Col. 0544B]

**68.** You ask me whether the one who is Father cannot be prior. I ask you to teach me when the Father was prior, and to gather the truth from testimonies or arguments. If from testimonies, you have certainly received the teaching that God’s power is eternal. You have also read him saying: “Israel, if you listen to me, there will be no new god among you, and you shall not worship a foreign god” (Ps. 80:10).

One of these statements signifies eternity, the other the distinctness of an undifferentiated substance, so that we believe the Son to be neither later than the Father nor of another divinity. For if he is later than the Father, he is new; and if he is not of one divinity, he is foreign. But he is neither later, because he is not new, nor foreign, because he was born from the Father—because God, blessed above all things, is forever (Rom. 9:5), as it is written.

[Col. 0544D]  
*Note:* The Roman edition alone reads: “the unity of substance.”

**69.** But if they consider him foreign, why do they worship him, since it is written: “You shall not worship a foreign god” (Ps. 80:10)? Or if they do not worship him, let them confess it, and the matter is ended, so that they do not deceive anyone under the profession of a religious name. These, then, are the testimonies of Scripture. Or if you have another, you must produce it.

[Col. 0544D]  
*Note:* This objection pressed those heretics with considerable force, and Ambrose repeatedly did not fail to bring it against them. Nevertheless, they replied that the Father is worshiped and honored in the Son as a king is worshiped and honored in an image of himself, as can be learned from Athanasius, *Oration* 4 *Against the Arians*. But since this answer would imply that the same veneration could also be offered to a human being created in the image of God, Athanasius himself, in *Orations* 3 and 4 against them, together with Basil, *Homily* 27 *Against the Sabellians*, Gregory of Nyssa, and others, assigned the authors of this evasion almost to the category of pagans. See also Valesius’s notes on Book II of Theodoret’s *History*, chapter 23.

**70.** It remains, then, that the truth be established also by arguments. Although arguments ordinarily yield to human testimonies, argue nevertheless, heretic, as you wish.

“You see,” you say, “we accept by custom that the one who generates is prior to the one who is born.” Follow, then, every trace of this custom; and if the rest agrees, I will not object to your requiring this also. But if nothing else agrees, how can you demand this one point when the rest is absent?

Therefore, since you require custom, when the Son was generated from the Father, he was a little child. You saw an infant wailing in a cradle; he passed through successive stages of age. For if he experienced the weakness of generation, he must have fallen into the weakness not only of birth but also of life.

[Col. 0545A] 458

**71.** But perhaps you will sink into such madness as not to deny these things of the Son of God, measuring him by human weakness. What if you cannot deny him the name of God, yet wish to prove him human by his weakness? What if, while you scrutinize the Son, you accuse the Father; and while you prejudge Christ, you condemn the Father?

**72.** For if divine generation was subject to time, and this is appropriated from the custom of human generation, then the Father also carried the Son in a bodily womb and bore the burden for the course of ten months. But how can the practice of generation exist without the other sex? You see that the customary sequence of generation did not begin, yet you suppose that the customary requirements of a bodily birth were present.

[Col. 0545D]  
*Note:* All editions, together with a few manuscripts, read: “the requirements of some bodily birth”; many other, better manuscripts read: “the requirements of some bodily necessity of birth,” that is, they suppose that birth was subject and bound to the necessity of bodily condition.

You seek custom; I seek sex. You demand time; I seek sequence. You examine the end; I seek the beginning. Certainly the end depends on the beginning, not the beginning on the end.

**73.** “Everything that is born,” you say, “has a beginning; and therefore, because he is Son, he has a beginning and began to exist in time.” Let this have been spoken by their own mouths. I confess that the Son was born; the rest of this impiety fills me with horror. You confess him to be God, human being, and yet confine him within such an accusation? May God avert this madness.

## CHAPTER XII

The repeated objection against the Son is answered again by turning it against the Father also. Since the Father requires neither place, time, nor any other creature, such requirements must likewise not be attributed to the Son, whose generation is unique—not only from the Father but also from the Virgin. Since sex and similar conditions had no place in the latter generation, they had no place in the former either.

[Col. 0545D]

**74.** Again they object: “Then he is not a son if he does not possess what sons possess.” May the Father forgive me, may the Son forgive me, and may the Holy Spirit forgive me, as I undertake to raise this question out of piety.

[Col. 0545D]  
*Note:* One manuscript of Teller reads: “the question concerning the property.”

Certainly there is a Father, and he remains forever; there are also creatures according to the divine dispensation. Is there, then, anything belonging to creatures that is not subject either to places, times, creation, or some cause or author? Certainly not. What, then, do you say? Is there anything among these things of which the Father is in need? It is impious to say so. Either cease applying to divinity what belongs to creatures, or, if you insist on making comparisons, consider where your impiety leads—a place God forbid should ever enter even our thoughts.

**75.** We, for our part, maintain the pious answer. God is almighty, and therefore the Father needs none of those things. He has none of the change or development that we require, whose weakness gains progress from such things. But one who is almighty is certainly uncreated, without place, and above time.

[Col. 0545D]  
*Note:* Some manuscripts read: “to say that there is something is a serious matter.”

For nothing exists before God; indeed, to say that anything—including the Word itself—exists before God is a serious matter. Therefore, if this is so, since none of those things that signify development exists in God the Father, because he is God, none of them can be applied to the Son of God either, so that he might receive either a beginning or development, because he is true God from true God.

[Col. 0546A]

**76.** Therefore, since we find no customary order here, acknowledge, Arius, that the Son’s generation was unique. Acknowledge it, I say; and if you do not believe me, at least blush at the voice of God saying: “To whom have you likened me?” (Isa. 46:5). And again: “For God is not as man” (Num. 23:19).

For if God’s work is unique—because he does not make anything with hands, does not complete it through labor, and does not finish it in days—for “he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. 148:5)—why should we not believe that his generation of the Son is unique, since we recognize his unique creation in his works?

[Col. 0546C]  
*Note:* All editions and a few manuscripts read: “his unique operation”; some others: “his unique generation”; the remaining manuscripts, more correctly, read: “his unique creation,” namely, the active creation by which he created all things through the Son.

It is surely fitting that he should be regarded as having generated the Son in a special and unique manner. Let him possess the glory of an extraordinary generation who possesses the grace of extraordinary power.

**77.** Christ’s generation from the Father is not the only marvelous one; his generation from the Virgin is also marvelous. You say that the latter resembles our conception, and I prove that this too is unlike ours—indeed, I will compel you yourself to confess it. Say how he was born from Mary, by what practice the virginal womb received him, how birth occurred without a man’s seed, whence the virgin became pregnant, how a young woman was a mother before pregnancy [reading uncertain], rather than after experiencing intercourse as a wife.

[Col. 0546D]  
*Note:* Most manuscripts read this way; some others read: “a mother before the fetus, rather than a wife’s intercourse”; finally, the other manuscripts and all editions agree with our reading, except that instead of *fetus* many use the feminine form *feta* (“pregnant woman”).

The cause was absent, yet the Son was generated. Whence, then, this birth under a changed law?

[Col. 0546D]

**78.** Therefore, if the custom of human generation was absent in the Virgin, how can you demand the customary conditions of proper generation in God the Father? Certainly custom belongs to sex, because sex belongs to flesh. Where there is no flesh, how can you demand the weakness of flesh? No one examines what is better; you have been commanded to believe, not permitted to investigate. For it is written: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Gen. 15:6).

Nor does speech fail only concerning the generation of the Son; it also fails concerning the works of God. For it is written: “All his works are in faith” (Ps. 32:4). His works, then, are in faith, but generation without faith? We investigate what we do not see, though we are commanded to believe rather than investigate what we do see.

## CHAPTER XIII

The holy Doctor resolves the question of how the Son was begotten and teaches that revelation must be believed, using the examples of Nebuchadnezzar and Peter. He shows that the eternity and divinity of the Son were signified by the latter’s vision, and therefore that Peter must be believed while philosophers are disregarded, since their credibility had already everywhere been withdrawn. Conversely, the Arians are shown to resemble the Gentiles.

[Col. 0547B]

**79.** Someone will say: “How was the Son generated?”

[Col. 0547D]  
*Note:* All editions read: “The Son—quasi everlasting, quasi Word, quasi splendor of eternal light, because splendor operates simultaneously as it is born.” Nearly all manuscripts more aptly read as we have in the text: “as everlasting, as Word, as splendor of eternal light, because splendor operates simultaneously as it is born.”

As everlasting, as Word, as splendor of eternal light, because splendor operates simultaneously as it is born. This is the Apostle’s example, not mine. Do not, then, believe that there was ever even a moment when God existed without wisdom or light without splendor (Heb. 1:3). Do not, Arius, judge divine things by our standards; believe what is divine where you find nothing human.

**80.** A Gentile king saw in the fire, together with the three Hebrew youths, the form of a fourth, resembling an angel; and because he thought this one greater than the angels, he judged him to be the Son of God, whom he had not read about but believed in (Dan. 3:92). Abraham also saw three and worshiped one (Gen. 18:2).

**81.** Peter saw Moses and Elijah on the mountain with the Son of God, and he did not err either concerning nature or concerning glory. Finally, he asked not them but Christ what he ought to do; for although he was preparing service for three, he was nevertheless awaiting the command of one.

But because he simply thought that the number of tents should be offered to the three, he was corrected by the authority of God the Father, who said: “This is my beloved Son; hear him” (Matt. 17:5). That is: “Why do you associate your fellow servants with your Lord? This is my Son. Moses is not the Son, Elijah is not the Son, but this one is the Son.”

The Apostle understood the correction, fell on his face, overwhelmed by the Father’s voice and the Son’s glory; but he was lifted up by the Son, who is accustomed to raise up those who lie prostrate. He saw one; he saw only the Son of God. For the servant-men withdrew, so that the Lord alone—who alone was designated as the Son—might be seen.

**82.** What, then, was the purpose of that vision? It did not signify an equality between Christ and the servants, but marked out a mystery: namely, that the Law and the Prophets, agreeing with the Gospel, might reveal the everlasting Son of God whom they had announced.

Therefore, when we hear of the Son from the womb and of the Word from the heart, let us believe that he was not fashioned by hands but born from the Father—not the work of an artisan but the offspring of a parent.

**83.** And therefore the one who says, “This is my Son,” did not say, “This is my temporal son”; he did not say, “This is my creature, my work, my servant”; but, “This is my Son,” whom you see in glory.

This is the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob, who appeared to Moses in the bush, of whom Moses said: “He who is has sent me” (Exod. 3:14).

[Col. 0547D]  
*Note:* Compare with this passage what Irenaeus discusses on this question, before the rise of the Arian heresy, in Book IV of *Against Heresies*, chapter 26; and afterward Hilary, Books III and IV *On the Trinity*; Basil, Book II *Against Eunomius*; Augustine, *On the Trinity*, Book II, chapter 7; Prudentius; and others.

The Father was not in the bush, nor the Father in the wilderness, but the Son spoke to Moses. Finally, Stephen said of him: “This is he who was in the assembly in the wilderness with the angel” (Acts 7:38). This, then, is the one who gave the Law, the one who spoke to Moses, saying: “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exod. 3:16). This, then, is the God of the patriarchs; this is the God of the prophets.

[Col. 0548B]

**84.** We read of the Son; let your mind grasp the reading, and let your tongue utter the confession. Remove arguments from here, where faith is sought; let dialectic already be silent in its own gymnasia. I do not ask what the philosophers say; I ask what they do. They alone have remained in their gymnasia.

See how faith outweighs arguments.

[Col. 0547D]  
*Note:* It is clear from this entire passage that many of those who professed philosophy at that time were devoted to idols. As early as the year 362, Julian the Apostate had enacted a law removing Christians from teaching and studying humane letters and philosophy in the public gymnasia. Baronius and others observed that this law was an appendix to Book 3, *On Physicians and Professors*, of the *Theodosian Code*. Christian writers and unbelievers alike protested the injustice of this constitution, as we read in Gregory of Nazianzus, *Oration* 1 *Against Julian*; Jerome, *Chronicle*; Ambrose, *Against Symmachus*; Augustine, *City of God*, Book XVIII, chapter 5; Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XXII; and others. The law, however, is found to have been revoked by Valentinian, as is evident from what follows in sections 6 and 7; on these passages see Gothofredus. Since pagans were not prohibited by the same laws from professing the sciences, they continued to practice them publicly.

Those who argue eloquently are abandoned daily by their companions; those who believe simply increase daily. Philosophers are not believed; fishermen are believed. Dialecticians are not believed; tax collectors are believed. The former bound the world with pleasures and luxuries; the latter stripped it bare through fasts and sufferings. Thus injustice has already begun to attract more people than pleasure.

**85.** Now let us see how far the Arians differ from the Gentiles. The Gentiles call their gods different in sex and unlike in power; the Arians assert a Trinity differing in divinity and unlike in power. The Gentiles maintain that the beginning of their gods was temporal; the Arians falsely say that Christ began in time. Did they not derive the whole coloring of their impiety from philosophy? Yet the Gentiles magnify what they worship, whereas the Arians assert that the Son of God, who is God, is a creature.

## CHAPTER XIV

That the Son of God is not a creature is established from the fact that he did not command the Gospel to be preached to himself; from the fact that the creature is subjected to vanity; from the fact that he created all things; from the fact that he is read of as begotten; and finally from the distinction between generation and adoption that was handed down, in which both natures are declared to exist in him. These many and great testimonies are confirmed by the Apostle’s exposition.

[Col. 0548D]

[Col. 0549A]

**86. [Elsewhere, Chapter VI.]** It has become clear, as I think, holy Emperor, that the Lord Jesus is neither unlike the Father nor temporal. It remains that this other sacrilege also be refuted, and that we prove the Son of God not to be a creature. The oracle of the passage now before us assists us in this: for we heard it read, the Lord saying: “Go into the whole world and preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 16:15). Whoever says “every creature” excludes none.

Where, then, are those who call Christ a creature? For if he were a creature, would he command the Gospel to be preached to himself? Therefore he is not a creature but the Creator, who commands his disciples to undertake the task of teaching the creature.

**87.** Christ is not a creature. For the creature has been subjected to vanity, as the Apostle said (Rom. 8:20). Was Christ, then, subjected to vanity? Again, according to the same Apostle: “The creature groans and labors in childbirth until now” (ibid., 22). Does Christ, then, groan and labor in childbirth, he who freed our groans from death? “The creature,” he says, “will be set free from the slavery of corruption” (ibid., 21).

We therefore see that there is a great distinction between the creature and the Lord, because the creature is in slavery, whereas the Lord is spirit; and “where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Cor. 3:17).

[Col. 0549D]  
*Note:* A number of manuscripts read: “and that there is a distinction between God and …”

**88.** Who introduced this error, that he should call a creature the one who created and made all things? Did the Lord create himself? For if it is read that all things were made through him, and that without him nothing was made (John 1:3), did he make himself?

[Col. 0549D] 462

If it is read—and this cannot be denied—that God made all things in wisdom, can it seem likely that wisdom was made in itself?

[Col. 0549D]  
*Note:* All editions, together with a few manuscripts, read: “because it was from itself”; but many more manuscripts, and more coherently, read: “because it was made in itself.”

**89.** We read that he was begotten, because the Father said: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Ps. 109:3). We read of the firstborn (Matt. 1:25); we read of the Son; we read of the only-begotten (John 1:14): firstborn, because no one existed before him; only-begotten, because no one exists after him. We also read: “Who will recount his generation?” (Isa. 53:8). “Generation,” he says, not “creation.” What can be compared with these many and such great testimonies?

**90.** The Son of God also shows the distinction between generation and grace when he says: “I ascend to my Father and your Father, my God and your God” (John 20:17). He did not say, “I ascend to our Father,” but, “I ascend to my Father and your Father.” This separation shows a distinction: his begetter is our Creator.

[Col. 0550A]

**91.** And he added: “My God and your God,” because although he and the Father are one, and the Father is his Father by the property of nature, the Father began to be our God through the Son—not by right of nature but by grace. Nevertheless, he appears here to signify both natures in Christ: divinity and flesh—divinity from the Father, flesh from the mother; the former before all things, the latter from the Virgin. Finally, he named the Father first as Son, and afterward named God as man.

**92.** Everywhere the testimonies show that he speaks of “his God” from the person of the man: “God, my God, look upon me; why have you forsaken me?” (Ps. 21:1). And elsewhere: “From my mother’s womb you are my God” (ibid., 11). Above, he suffers as a man; below, he is a man who is cast forth from his mother’s womb. Therefore, when he says, “From my mother’s womb you are my God,” he signifies that the one who was always the Father became his God from the moment when he was cast forth from his mother’s womb.

**93.** Since, then, we have read of Christ’s generation in the Gospel, in the Apostle, and in the prophets, how dare they say that he was created or made?

[Col. 0550D]  
*Note:* Some manuscripts read: “And what is the sense in which he was created?”

They ought indeed to consider in what sense they have read that he was created and in what sense that he was made. For it has been taught that the Son of God was begotten from God and born from God. But let them carefully observe the sense in which they have read that he was made: it was not God who was made, but the Son of God who was born as God; afterward, according to the flesh, he was made man from Mary.

**94.** If they do not believe me, let them believe the Apostle, who says: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, made from a woman, made under the Law” (Gal. 4:4). “His Son,” he says—not one of many, not a common son, but his own. When he says “his own,” he signifies the distinctive property of eternal generation.

He afterward asserted that this one was made from a woman, so that the making might be ascribed not to the divinity but to the assumption of the body: made from a woman through the taking on of flesh; made under the Law through observance of the Law. The heavenly generation was before the Law; this one was after the Law (Council of Chalcedon, Act I, *Definition of Faith at Nicaea*).

[Col. 0550C] 463

## CHAPTER XV

The holy Bishop answers the two passages of Scripture in which Christ is said to have been made and created. He declares that these expressions apply to him only according to his human nature, and also makes clear, on the authority of the sacred books, that the past tense has been used for the future.

**95. [Elsewhere, Chapter VII.]** Hence they are also accustomed to boast vainly of what is written: “God made him Lord and Christ.”

[Col. 0550D]  
*Note:* The edition reads: “and made him God … and made him God …”

Let the unlearned read the whole passage and understand it. For it is written: “God made him Lord and made him Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified” (Acts 2:36). It was not the divinity that was crucified, but the flesh. That could indeed be made which could be crucified. Therefore the Son of God was not a creature.

**96.** Let that other passage also disappear, the one with which they customarily slander him, and let them learn how it was spoken: “The Lord created me” (Prov. 8:22).

[Col. 0551D]  
*Note:* The Arians repeatedly made much of this passage, and Ambrose always answers it in the same way—for example, in *Commentary on Psalm 118*, Sermon 5, and below in Book III of this work, chapter 4, where he examines it more carefully. The same solution is found in many passages of Athanasius, Basil and Gregory of Nyssa *Against Eunomius*, Gregory of Nazianzus, Jerome, Augustine, and others. Nevertheless, some interpreted that passage itself differently; on this matter see Petavius, *Theological Dogmatics*, Book II, *On the Trinity*, chapter 1.

He did not say, “The Father created me,” but, “The Lord created me.” The flesh acknowledges the Lord; glory signifies the Father. Our creaturely nature confesses the Lord; charity knows the Father.

[Col. 0552D]  
*Note:* Many manuscripts read: “clarity knows the Father.” This is not at all a bad reading.

Who, then, is unaware that this is said on account of the incarnation? Therefore he says that he was created in that in which he also testifies that he is man, saying: “Why do you seek to kill me, a man who has spoken the truth to you?” (John 7:20). He says “man” in that in which he was also crucified, died, and was buried.

**97.** There is no doubt that he used the past tense for what was future. This is the custom of prophecy: future things are spoken either as though present or as though already accomplished. Thus you read in Psalm 21: “Fat bulls surrounded me” (Ps. 21:13); you also read: “They divided my garments among themselves” (ibid., 19). The evangelist indicates that this was prophesied concerning the time of the Passion. For to God future things are present, and to him for whom all things are foreknown, things that are to come are as things already accomplished, as it is written: “He who made the things that are to come” (Isa. 45:11).

[Col. 0552D]  
*Note:* Some manuscripts read: “future things are completed, as …”

98. Nor is it surprising if he says that he was founded before the ages, since you read that he was predestined before the times of the ages. How clearly this is expressed concerning the incarnation, the following words show: “Wisdom,” he says, “built herself a house, and set up seven pillars, and slaughtered her victims; she mixed her wine in the bowl and prepared her table; and she sent her servants, calling with a most exalted proclamation, saying: ‘Whoever is foolish, let him turn in to me’” (Prov. IX, 1 ff.). Do we not see all these things fulfilled in the Gospel after the incarnation: that he celebrated the mysteries of the sacred banquet, that he sent the apostles, that he cried out with a loud voice, saying, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John VII, 37)? Thus what follows corresponds to what came before, and we see the whole course of the incarnation set forth in an ordered exposition of prophecy.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “Whoever is foolish? Let him turn in to me.”]

99. Many other testimonies of this kind could be produced, showing that such things were spoken concerning the incarnation; but I shall not bury myself in books, lest the treatise appear too diffuse.

## CHAPTER XVI

If “created” and “begotten” mean the same thing to the Arians, they do Christ an injury; but if they believe that the terms differ, the one whom they read of as begotten must not be regarded as a creature. This is confirmed by Paul’s testimony: he forbids service to the creature, yet professes himself Christ’s servant; Paul is therefore to be believed rather than Arius. It is further shown that a creature cannot be in God, since God is simple, and that the Son must not be reduced to the order of creatures, since the Father is well pleased in him.

[Col. 0551D]

100. I now ask the Arians themselves whether they think that “begotten” is the same as “created.” For if they say that they are the same, then there is certainly no difference between begetting and creating. Therefore, since we too have been created, there is no difference between us and Christ, nor between Christ and the elements. But although they are mad, they will nevertheless not dare to say this.

101. Finally, to indulge their folly in what is untrue: if, as they think, there is no difference in the word, why do they not call the one whom they worship by the better name? Why do they not use the word of the Father? Why do they cast away what expresses honor and assume what expresses injury?

102. But if there is a difference between “created” and “begotten,” as I believe, when we read “begotten,” we certainly do not understand “begotten” and “created” to mean the same thing. Let them therefore say that he was generated from the Father and produced from the Virgin; or let them explain how the Son of God can be both begotten and created. One nature—and above all, God—does not admit of diversity.

103. At any rate, let my opinion be set aside; let us question Paul, who, being filled with the Spirit of God and foreseeing these questions, spoke generally against the Gentiles and specifically against the Arians. He says that those who serve the creature rather than the Creator have been condemned by divine judgment. Thus we read: “God gave them over to the desires of their heart, so that they dishonor their bodies among themselves; they exchanged the truth of God for a lie, and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is God, blessed forever” (Rom. I, 24–25).

104. Paul therefore forbids me to serve the creature and admonishes me to serve Christ. Christ is not a creature: “Paul,” he says, “a servant of Jesus Christ” (ibid., 1). And he is a good servant who recognizes the Lord; he himself forbids us to serve the creature. How, then, would he himself serve Christ if he thought Christ a creature? Either, therefore, let them cease worshiping the one whom they call a creature, or let them cease calling a creature the one whom they pretend to worship, lest under the name of worshipers they commit more serious sacrilege. For an enemy within the household is more detestable than an outsider; and it is a graver crime to misuse Christ’s name against Christ.

105. What better interpreter of the Scriptures, then, could we seek than that teacher of the Gentiles, that vessel of election, chosen from among persecutors? He confesses that he had persecuted Jesus. He had certainly read Solomon more thoroughly than Arius and was learned in the Law; and because he had read it, he does not say that Christ was created, but begotten. For he had read: “He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. CXLVIII, 5). Was Christ made by a word? Was Christ created by a command?

106. How, moreover, can a creature be in God? For God is of a simple nature, not joined and composite: [Note: Older editions and some manuscripts read, “to whom nothing happens”; the Roman edition and a larger number of manuscripts read, “… nothing is added.” Below, where our text, with the same Roman edition and more manuscripts, has “interpretable by speech,” or “by utterance,” as in some manuscripts, the remaining manuscripts and editions read “interpretable by action.” There is no serious objection if “by action” has been put for “by deed” or “operation,” from which we interpret and know God.] nothing is added to him, but he possesses in his nature only what is divine; filling all things, yet himself nowhere confused; penetrating all things, yet himself nowhere penetrable; wholly present everywhere, and at the same time present either in heaven, or on earth, or in the farthest depths of the sea; incomprehensible to sight, inexpressible by utterance, immeasurable by understanding, to be followed by faith, to be venerated in religion—so that whatever can be conceived religiously, whatever is more excellent for beauty, whatever is higher in power, you should understand to belong to God.

107. Therefore, because the Father is well pleased in the Son (Matt. XVII, 5), believe that the Son is worthy of the Father; believe that the Son came forth from God, as he himself testifies, saying, “I came forth from God and have come” (John VIII, 42); and elsewhere, “I came forth from God” (John XVI, 27). He who came forth from God and proceeded from God can possess nothing other than what belongs to God.

## CHAPTER XVII

He proves that Christ is the true God from the fact that he is God’s own Son. After first resolving the difficulty that arises, he confirms the same point from the fact that Christ was begotten and that he came forth from God. He then adds the unity of the Father and Son in operation and will. Finally, after adducing the apostles and the Centurion as witnesses in opposition to the Arians, he joins Isaiah and John to them.

108. Hence he is not only God, but also true God, true from the True, and so true that he himself is the truth. [Col. 0553C] Thus, if we seek his name, he is truth; if we seek natural majesty, the Son of God is true to such a degree that he is also his own. [Note: Several manuscripts read, “if we seek natural majesty, he is a groan.”] For it is written: “He who did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us” (Rom. VIII, 32)—handed him over, certainly, according to the flesh. Divinity is characterized by ownness, ownness by truth, piety by mercy, and security by offering.

109. But lest they bring an accusation because it is written, “The Father handed him over,” the Apostle himself said elsewhere: “Peace from God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ, who gave himself for our sins” (Gal. I, 3–4); and elsewhere: “Just as Christ loved us and handed himself over for us” (Eph. V, 2). If, then, he was both handed over by the Father and handed himself over, it is evident that the operation is one and that the will of the Father and the Son is one.

110. If, therefore, we seek natural majesty, he was begotten. Whoever denies that he was begotten denies that he is the Father’s own; whoever rejects his ownness considers him common to the rest. But if we seek the particular character of his generation, he came forth from God. For since in our usage “to come forth” means what is already present and seems to emerge from inward, hidden places, which is what is called “coming forth,” we perceive, even within the limitations of language, the character of divine generation: he did not appear to have come forth from some place, but as God from God, Son from Father; nor did he appear to have begun in time, since he comes forth by being born from the Father, as he himself who was born said: “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High” (Ecclus. XXIV, 5).

[Note: Three manuscripts read, “which already is to come forth from the inward secrets”; one reads, “which already seems to emerge from the inward secrets,” and so forth.]

111. But if they do not recognize the nature, if they do not believe the Scriptures, let them at least believe the works. To whom does the Father say, “Let us make man” (Gen. I, 26), except to one whom he knew to be the true Son? In whom would he recognize his own image, except in the true one? An adopted son and a true son are not the same; nor would the Son say, “We are one” (John XVI, 22), if he were comparing himself with the true one while he himself was not true. The Father therefore says, “Let us make.” The one who said this is true. Can the one who made be untrue, then, and can what is granted to the speaker be denied to the maker?

112. How, moreover, unless he knew the true Son, could he entrust to him the unity of his will and the reality of his work? For since the Son performs the very works that the Father performs, and gives life to whom he wills, as it is written (John V, 19, 21), and since he is not different in power and is free in will, unity is preserved. The power of God lies in the proper possession of divinity; and freedom lies not in some difference but in unity of will.

113. The apostles, troubled on the strait, though they still did not believe in their hearts, when they first saw the Lord’s feet treading upon the waters and beheld without fear the footprints of the Lord walking upon the restless surge of the sea—and when, after he had boarded the boat that the waves had troubled, they saw the waters grow calm and the elements obeying—believed him to be the true Son of God, saying: “Truly, you are the Son of God” (Matt. XIV, 25 ff.).

[Note: Several manuscripts read, “The apostles’ company, though they still did not believe, was troubled on the strait”; one reads, “The heart of the apostles, though they still did not believe, was troubled on the strait.” Other manuscripts and editions, more suitably, have the reading printed in the text.]

114. The Centurion, together with the others who were with him, confesses the same thing when the foundations of the world were shaken during the Lord’s Passion—and you, heretic, deny it! The Centurion says: “Truly this was the Son of God” (Matt. XXVII, 54). “He was,” says the Centurion, while the Arian says, “He was not.” With bloodied hands but devout mind, he affirms both the reality and the eternity of the generation; you, heretic, deny the reality of the generation and assign it a time. Would that you had bloodied your hands rather than your soul! But you are not innocent in hand and are savage in mind; as far as lies within you, you inflict death, since you suppose him weak; or rather—and this is graver—even though divinity cannot feel a wound, you attempt, so far as lies within you, to kill his majesty in Christ, not his body.

115. We therefore cannot doubt that he is the true God whom both the executioners believed to be the true Son of God and the demons confessed. We do not now require their testimonies, but they are nevertheless preferred to your sacrileges. We named them so that you might blush; we also brought forward divine answers so that you might believe.

116. The Lord cries out through Isaiah: “For those who serve me a new name shall be called, which shall be blessed upon the earth; and they shall bless the true God. And those who swear upon the earth shall swear by the true God” (Isa. LXV, 16). Isaiah said this, I maintain, when he saw his majesty. This is indicated in the Gospel: he saw the majesty of Christ and spoke concerning him.

117. Consider, nevertheless, what the Evangelist John also wrote in his letter: “We know that the Son of God has appeared and has given us understanding, so that we may know the Father and be in his true Son Jesus Christ our Lord. This is the true God and eternal life” (1 John V, 20). John calls the Son of God the true God. Therefore, if he is the true God, he is certainly not created, possessing nothing deceptive or counterfeit, nothing confused or unlike.

## CHAPTER XVIII

The errors of the Arians are recalled in the Nicene definition, so that they may not deceive anyone. They are reported together with their anathema, which is said to have been issued not only at Nicaea but also once and again at Ariminum.

118. [Elsewhere, chapter VIII.] “God from God, light from light, true God from true God, born from the Father, not made, of one substance with the Father.”

119. Thus, according to the Scriptures, our Fathers spoke. They also thought it right to insert the sacrilegious doctrines into their decrees so that Arius’s perfidy might betray itself, and not conceal itself as though smeared over with artificial cosmetics and colors. Those who do not dare to explain what they think apply such cosmetics. Therefore Arian impiety is not opened up by exposition but exposed by condemnation, so that the person who eagerly desires to hear it might first recognize that it had been condemned and not stumble, before hearing it explained in order to believe it.

[Note: Ambrose makes clear that the preceding definition of faith is nothing other than a summary of the Nicene Creed. The same is learned from the collectors of the synodal acts, from later councils, including Chalcedon, and from various Fathers—Athanasius in his letter to Jovinian, Basil in Letter 78, and others. It is also evident from the canonical codices of the Roman and African Churches, and finally from the historians Rufinus, book I, chapter 6; Socrates, book I, chapter 8; and Theodoret, book I, chapter 12. The last two also report a letter of Eusebius of Caesarea concerning this matter.]

120. [Elsewhere, chapter IX.] “The Catholic and Apostolic Church anathematizes those,” he says, “who say, ‘There was a time when he was not,’ and, ‘Before he was born, he was not’; and those who say that he was made from nothing, or from another substance or οὐσία [ousia], or that the Son of God is mutable or changeable.”

[Note: Older editions and manuscripts differ only in this: many of them have inquam, “I say,” instead of inquit, “he says”; the Roman edition adds aliquando, “at some time,” after the word “was.” It is indeed found in all the records of this council, but since readers can easily supply it, we think that the holy Doctor omitted it.]

121. You have received, holy Emperor, the lawful condemnation of those who assert such things. It was not through human contrivance, [Note: All editions and some manuscripts read, “not through some composition”; but three hundred and eighteen bishops assembled at the council, as I said above. But …] nor through any contrived arrangement, that the three hundred and eighteen bishops came together in council, as I explained more fully above (Prologue, no. 5). Rather, the Lord Jesus showed that he himself was present at the council through the sign of his Passion and name in their number: the cross is represented by the three hundred, and the name of Jesus by the eighteen priests.

122. The first confession was also made at the Council of Ariminum, and after the Council of Ariminum came a second correction. The confession is attested by the letter sent to the Emperor Constantius; the councils that followed attest the correction.

[Note: This council was held in the year 359 at Ariminum, a coastal city in the Italian province of Romagna. It is therefore highly credible that its acts, which, according to Jerome in Against the Luciferians, were preserved in public and ecclesiastical archives, were available to the people of Milan. Saint Ambrose, however, uses only the testimony of the synodal letter to Constantius, in which the bishops—nearly four hundred and more—inform the Emperor that they had decided that nothing of what had been decreed at Nicaea should be changed. This letter, scarcely surpassed by any more precious relic of antiquity that has come down to us, appears in Athanasius’s On the Councils of Ariminum and Seleucia, and is reported not only by the Greek writers Socrates, Sozomen, and Theodoret, but also by Hilary in the fragments. Yet that splendid confession did not long remain intact. The ten delegates of the council to Constantius first, and then nearly all those bishops, did not correct it but corrupted it: partly frightened by the Emperor and partly deceived by the Arians, they agreed to abolish the terms “substance” and “consubstantial.” No one who has recorded the affairs of the Church fails to remember this act of treachery. Certainly we have already seen what the holy Doctor wrote about it in On Luke, book V, no. 71; he will also discuss it below in book III and in several other places. Finally the true correction followed, which Ambrose calls the second. The councils whose testimony is indicated here are the Alexandrian Council, presided over by Athanasius in 362; the Council of Paris, convened in the same year, whose synodal letter is preserved among Hilary’s fragments; and finally the Roman Council held under Pope Damasus in 369. It would certainly be worthwhile to consult all of them.]

## CHAPTER XIX

He first attributes one of the errors mentioned above to Arius, refuting him with John’s testimony; then, as the occasion arises, he describes the heresiarch’s tragic death. Next he examines and refutes the rest of Arius’s blasphemies one by one.

[Col. 0556C]

123. Arius therefore says, “There was a time when he was not”; but Scripture says, “He was,” and does not say, “He was not.” Thus John wrote: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God” (John I, 1). See how many times he says “was,” and nowhere says “was not.” Whom, then, should we believe: John, who reclined upon Christ’s breast, or Arius, rolling about amid his own spilled entrails? [Note: Athanasius records this foul and horrifying death of Arius in Oration I Against the Arians and gives a fuller account in his Letter to Serapion, where he cites the presbyter Macarius as the guarantor of the story. Epiphanius also mentions it in Heresy 69. As for the ecclesiastical historians, since scarcely any of them omitted it, it would be superfluous to list their names here.] Thus we might recognize that Arius’s perfidy was like that of Judas the betrayer, whom a similar punishment condemned.

124. Arius’s entrails were indeed poured out—shame forbids me to say where—and thus he burst open in the middle, falling face-first, defiled by the foul mouth with which he had denied Christ. For he burst open, just as the Apostle Peter also said concerning Judas (Acts I, 18), because “he acquired a field from the wages of iniquity, and falling headlong he burst open in the middle, and all his entrails were poured out.” His death was not accidental, where, in an equal sacrilege, an equal example of punishment followed, so that the same penalty overtook those who denied the same Lord and those who betrayed the same Lord.

125. Let us proceed to the others. Arius says, “Before he was born, he was not”; but Scripture says that all things came into being through the Son. How, then, did he give being to others who himself did not exist? When the impious man says “when” and “before,” these two words plainly indicate time. How, then, do they deny time before the Son and want things belonging to time to have existed earlier, when the very expressions “when,” “before,” and “at some time” indicate time?

126. Arius says that the Son of God is from nothing. How, then, is he the Son of God? How was he generated from the paternal womb? How is the Word read to have been poured forth from the heart, unless he is understood to have proceeded secretly from the Father’s innermost and immeasurable being, as it is written? For the Son is either a son by adoption or by nature. We are called sons by adoption; he is a Son by the truth of nature. How, then, is he from nothing who made all things from nothing (Ps. XLIV, 1)?

127. Whoever does not know from where the Son is has no Son. Thus the Jews also did not have the Son, because they did not know from where he was. Therefore the Lord said to them: “You do not know from where I come” (John VIII, 14); and below: “You know neither me nor my Father” (ibid., 19). For whoever denies that the Son is from the Father does not know the Father from whom the Son is, nor does he know the Son, because he does not know the Father (Gal. IV, 5).

128. Arius says, “From another substance.” What other substance, then, is equal to the Son of God, so that the Son of God may be from it? Or how do they criticize us because we speak of οὐσία [ousia] in Greek or substantia in Latin when, by saying that the Son of God is from another substance, they themselves thereby affirm that God has substance? [Note: All editions and a substantial number of manuscripts read, “to say that the Son is God”; but other manuscripts, neither fewer nor inferior, read, “to say that the Son is God’s,” which is plainly preferable.]

129. But if they wish to speak about the name of the divine substance or nature, they will easily be refuted, because Scripture frequently mentions οὐσία [ousia] in Greek and substantia in Latin. Peter also wants us, as we read, to become “partakers of the divine nature” (2 Pet. I, 4). If they say that the Son is from another substance, they refute themselves: they confess the word “substance,” which they fear, and they place the Son alongside the creatures whom they pretend to prefer him to.

130. Arius calls the Son of God a creature, though not like the other creatures. But what creature is not unlike another creature? Man is not like an angel, earth is not like heaven, the sun is not like water, light is not like darkness. Thus he granted no preeminence at all; he merely covered the fraud of his impiety with a wretched disguise in order to deceive the simple.

[Note: All editions and some manuscripts read, “What creature is not like another creature?” This is incorrect, for it would mean that every creature is like every other, which does not agree with what follows. Some manuscripts therefore rightly remove the negation, while a larger number double it, as in the text.]

131. Arius says that the Son of God is mutable and changeable. How, then, is he God, if he is mutable, when he himself said: “I am, I am, and I have not changed” (Mal. III, 6)?

## CHAPTER XX

He desires that a Seraphim, as once to Isaiah, fly to him for his cleansing; indeed, he invites Christ himself to come to him, to the Emperor, and to his other readers. Finally, after mystically indicating the Lord’s cup, he asks that Gratian and the other faithful be intoxicated by its power.

[Col. 0558B]

132. But now I must confess that prophetic saying which Isaiah utters before prophesying about the Lord: “Woe is me, for I am pierced in heart; though I have unclean lips and dwell among a people also having unclean lips, I saw the Lord Sabaoth” (Isa. VI, 5). If Isaiah calls himself wretched because he saw the Lord Sabaoth, what shall I say of myself, who, though I have unclean lips, am compelled to discuss the generation of God? What, then, am I about to say concerning things that I fear, when David asks that his mouth be guarded against things he knows (Ps. XXXVIII, 2)? O that one of the Seraphim might also bring me that glowing coal, which he took from the divine altar, carrying it with the tongs of both Testaments, and burn my unclean lips!

133. But because at that time the Seraphim descended to the prophet in a figure (Isa. VI, 6), while you, Lord, after revealing the mystery, came to us in the flesh—not through an ambassador or messenger, but yourself, by your own coming—cleanse my conscience of my hidden faults, so that I, once unclean but now made clean by faith through your mercy, may also sing David’s words: “I will sing to you on the harp, God of Israel; my lips will rejoice when I sing to you, and my soul, which you have redeemed” (Ps. VII, 22–23).

134. Therefore, Lord, leaving your slanderers and enemies, turn yourself toward us; sanctify the ears of Prince Gratian and of all the others into whose hands this little book may come. Make their ears empty for me, so that nowhere the filth of heard perfidy may remain. Cleanse, then, cleanse the ear—not with cups from springs, nor with a draught from a river, nor with the murmur of a passing stream, but with words that work in place of waters, clearer than the brightness of waters and purer than every snow—those words with which you said: “Though your sins be like scarlet, I will make them white as snow” (Isa. I, 18).

135. There is also a cup with which you are accustomed to cleanse the secrets of the mind: a cup not of the old nature, nor from the customary vine, but a new cup brought down from heaven to earth, pressed from that foreign cluster which, as a grape hangs from a vine, so he hung in the flesh upon the wood of the cross. From this cluster, then, comes the wine that gladdens the human heart, intoxicates sobriety, breathes forth the drunkenness of faith and true religion, and pours in the drunkenness of chastity.

[Note: Here and below, on the authority of several more and better manuscripts, we have restored vinum and vino, “wine” and “with wine”; all editions and some manuscripts have poculum and, four times, poculo, “cup” and “with the cup.”]

136. With this wine, therefore, my Lord, cleanse the ears of the August Emperor’s mind, [Note: Several manuscripts read, “Lord, cleanse the ears of the August mind.” This is less suitable.] so that, just as people intoxicated with natural wine love rest, drive away fear of death, do not feel injuries, do not seek what belongs to others, and forget their own concerns, so also he who is drunk with your wine may love peace, secure in the exultation of faith may ignore the death of unbelief, may display the patience of charity, may not retain the sacrileges of others, and may prefer faith even to his own pledges, according to what is written: “Leave all that is yours, and come, follow me” (Matt. XIX, 21).

[Note: We have scarcely any other testimony concerning Gratian’s children than this passage of Ambrose. A passage of Augustine, On the City of God, book V, chapter 25, was indeed cited in older editions with the words, “when he had a little son and a brother”; but in the new edition the particle et, “and,” was removed on the authority of the better manuscripts. Although conjunctions of this kind do sometimes fall out even under the care of the most diligent scribes, full confidence can no longer be placed in that passage. We therefore learn from Ambrose that Gratian had children when this was written. Whether he had one child or more is unknown. Certainly there is no doubt that the offspring mentioned here was not born from his second wife, whom he had recently married, as we explained in the note to the Exposition of Psalm LXI, p. 963, but from the earlier wife, called Constantia. Ambrose’s exhortations are credited with having prevented Gratian, through love for his own offspring, from allowing himself to adopt Theodosius.]

[Col. 0560B] 137. With this wine, Lord Jesus, wash our minds also, so that we may adore you and worship you as Creator of visible and invisible things. You cannot, therefore, fail to be invisible and good, since you have bestowed this also upon your works.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 0559]

471

## PROLOGUE

In this book, which he is adding to the preceding one, Ambrose teaches that the first twelve names of the Son of God, divided into three groups, prove not only the Son’s but also the Father’s eternity. He then briefly compares them with the twelve stones of the priestly vestment and shows, by introducing a new arrangement of them, how necessarily they must be joined together. Returning afterward to the proposed comparison, he praises allegorically the fabric and stones of the garment mentioned. From this point, having also introduced the mystical rationale of a twofold division, he continues to explain the comparison he has begun. From it he gathers faith from works and adds a concise description of faith concerning the Son, showing that it must be joined to works.

[Col. 0559C]

[Col. 0559D] 1. Holy Emperor, I believe that in the preceding book it has been sufficiently demonstrated that the Son of God is eternal, unlike the Father in no respect, begotten and not created. We have also established from the readings of Scripture that the true God is the Son of the true God, and have identified him through the clear indications of his majesty.

2. Therefore, although these arguments are abundantly sufficient for faith—for the greatness of a flowing river is usually estimated from the spring from which it runs—nevertheless, so that our faith may shine more purely, its distinctions appear to be derived in a threefold manner. [Note: The Roman edition alone reads, “For there are certain names that clearly show the ownness …”] There are evident signs that display the ownness of divinity; there are those that display the likeness of the Father and the Son; and there are also those that clearly express the unity of divine majesty. Thus generation, God, Son, and Word belong to ownness; splendor, character, mirror, and image to likeness; and wisdom, power, truth, and life to eternal unity.

3. These signs designate the Son of God in such a way that from them you may also recognize the Father as eternal and the Son as not differing from him. From the One who is comes generation; from the eternal, God; from the Father, Son; from God, Word; splendor of glory; character of substance; mirror of God; image of majesty; goodness from the Good; wisdom from the Wise; power from the Strong; truth from the True; life from the Living. [Note: The phrase “goodness from the Good,” which was not mentioned above, was also omitted in most manuscripts, although it appears in several others and in all editions.] The signs of the Father and the Son therefore correspond, and no one will doubt that they do not differ from one another but belong to one majesty. We would produce examples of each of these names, if we were not constrained by the desire to keep our discourse brief.

4. Like twelve precious stones, these form the pillar of faith. For these are those precious stones (Exod. XXVIII, 17 ff.): sardius, jasper, emerald, chrysolite, and the rest, with which the sacred vestment of holy Aaron—who certainly bears the figure of Christ, the true priest—is woven. The stones are surrounded with gold and engraved with the names of the sons of Israel: twelve stones joined to one another. For if anyone separates and detaches them, the entire structure of faith is dissolved.

[Col. 0561A] 5. The beginning of our faith, therefore, is to know from whom the Son of God was begotten: if he was not begotten, he is not the Son. Nor is it enough to have said “Son,” unless you also designate the only-begotten Son. If he is a creature, he is not God; if he is not God, he is not life; if he is not life, he is not truth.

[Note: On this beginning of faith the Arians, and especially the Eunomians, disputed at length and fiercely with the orthodox, as is discussed more fully in On the Mystery of the Incarnation, chapter 9.]

6. Thus the first three—that is, generation, Son, and only-begotten—principally and properly indicate the Son from God.

7. The next three—that is, God, life, and truth—manifest his power, by which he founded creation and caused it to subsist: “For in him we live and move and are,” as Paul said (Acts XVII, 28). Therefore, in the first three the Son’s ownness is declared; in the other three, the unity of the Father’s and the Son’s operation.

[Col. 0561B] 8. The Son of God is also called image, splendor, and character, because these reveal in the Son the divinity of the Father’s incomprehensible and unsearchable majesty, together with its expressed likeness. These three, too, clearly pertain to likeness.

9. There remains power, wisdom, and justice, so that eternity may be proved through each of these operations. [Note: The Codex Audenensis, the Ebrulensis, and several others read, “wisdom, word.” But neither this reading nor “justice,” which appears in all the other manuscripts and editions, fits this passage adequately. For “Word” belonged to the first series, where “only-begotten” was placed; and justice had not been mentioned. Hence one may conclude that the holy Doctor played more freely with these terms.]

10. This, then, is the garment adorned with precious stones; this is the true vestment of the priest; this is the wedding garment; this is the prophetic weaver who knew well how to interweave these things. Nor is this a worthless fabric, of which the Lord says through the prophet: “Who gave women wisdom for weaving?” (Job XXXVIII, 36). Nor are these ordinary stones—stones, as we read, of completion. For all perfection is in it, if nothing is lacking.

[Note: The Septuagint translators have “the stones of completion … and the compositions”; the Hebrew text has “stones of fullness.” The Chaldean paraphrase has “stones for filling the engravings.” As for what Ambrose adds, “composed stones,” those words must be referred to “the compositions”; they have no corresponding expression in Hebrew or in the other versions, just as “stones of supplementation” in the Vulgate does not.]

The stones are composed and surrounded with gold—that is, with an intelligible nature—if our mind composes them well and a natural understanding joins them together by a reasonable method. Finally, the reading teaches how extraordinary these stones are (Exod. XXXV, 27): although others brought various and lesser things, the devoted leaders nevertheless carried these stones upon their shoulders, from which they made the breastpiece, a woven work (ibid.). The work is woven when the deeds of faith correspond.

11. Let no one think that I am mistaken because above I made a threefold distinction of four each, but below a fourfold distinction of three each. For the sake of a good work, variety of form is more pleasing. Good also is that which the weaving of the priestly garment displays—whether it is the Law or the Church, which made two garments for her husband, as it is written (Prov.
