XXXI, 22 ff.): one of works and the other of the mind, weaving together the coverings of faith and deeds. Thus in one passage, as we read, it first overlays gold and afterward adds hyacinth, purple, scarlet, and fine linen. Elsewhere, again, it first forms little flowers from hyacinth and the other materials, then adds gold, [Note: One manuscript of Thuanus reads, “and there is one,” and so forth. Below, where our text, with Gill in the margin, the Roman edition in the body, and four manuscripts, reads “the series may be arranged,” other manuscripts and editions read “the series is designated”; Erasmus and Gill read “it is designated in series.”] and there is one garment of the priest. Thus, while it gleams with the same colors, the diversity of grace and beauty shines through the diversity of arrangement.

12. Therefore, so that the sequence of the typological interpretation may also be set out, there is no doubt that by the tested gold [Note: Several manuscripts: “and workable silver.”] and silver the sayings of the Lord are signified, upon which faith is established. For it is written: “The sayings of the Lord are pure sayings, silver tested by fire, proved in the earth, purified sevenfold” (Ps. XI, 7). [Note: For our interpretation of these four colors, see our observation in *Exposition of Psalm CXVIII*, sermon 19, no. 22.] Hyacinth resembles the air which we breathe and whose breath we draw in; purple also expresses the appearance of water; by scarlet, fire is understood; earth by linen, for linen is produced from the earth. The human body, moreover, subsists from these four elements.

13. Whether, then, you attach works of the body to the prior harmonious weaving of the mind’s faith [Note: The edition reads, “with preceding harmony”; some manuscripts, “conscience.”]; or whether works come first, and faith, as a religious companion, lends its support to the deeds—this is the religious adornment of the bishop; this is the priest’s veil.

14. Good, therefore, is faith when it shines with the beautiful adornment of works. Concerning it, to state the matter in summary, these are the definitions which cannot be dissolved: if he is from nothing, he is not the Son; if he is a creature, he is not the Creator; if he is made, he is not the Maker of all; if he is learning, he is not the one who foreknows; if he is receiving, he is not perfect; if he is progressing, he is not God; if he is unlike, he is not the image; if he is so by grace, he is not so by nature; if he is without divinity, he is the author of evil: “No one is good except one, God” (Mark X, 18). [Note: All editions and the majority of manuscripts read, “if he is without goodness”; Audoenus, Ebrul., Big., and one Colbert manuscript, however, read, “if he is without divinity.” The latter is more appropriate, as the Scripture text cited below clearly shows. Moreover, since those heretics abused this same testimony in order to strip Christ of his divinity, the Fathers vigorously turned it back against them and argued that the Son’s divinity could not be denied on the basis of that passage without denying his goodness as well. Advancing this argument further, they demonstrated that, according to their view, he would consequently have to be called evil. Ambrose employs this form of argument not only here and above, in Book I, chapter 5, and in his *Exposition of Luke*, Book VIII, nos. 65 ff., but also, besides Hilary and Epiphanius, already mentioned in the cited book and chapter of this work, Basil, Book IV *Against Eunomius*; Gregory of Nyssa, Oration 11 against the same heretic; and Cyril of Alexandria, *Thesaurus*, argue similarly. As for what Petavius writes in volume II of his *Dogmatic Theology*, Book II, *On the Trinity*, chapter 4—that certain ancients, among whom he counts Gregory of Nyssa and Ambrose, not having sufficiently grasped the matter, attacked those heretics too vehemently, as though it followed from their words that the Son of God was evil—the learned man himself does not seem to have considered the matter sufficiently. For if the Son is not good in himself and by his own nature, but only through an external and adventitious goodness, like other creatures, as Petavius himself admits can be deduced from their words, then it properly follows that, considered apart from that precarious goodness, the same Son would in this sense be evil, since he would be imperfect and liable to corruption, error, and finally sin. This was more than sufficient reason for the Fathers to attack the Arians in no other manner than that in which we find them doing so. To this may also be added the fact that Ambrose, in *On Duties*, Book I, chapter 25, no. 117, joins Eunomius with Marcion, as though they held the same view concerning two principles. We have discussed this there.]

## CHAPTER ONE

He resolves the objection of the Arians, who deprive the Son of God of goodness—an objection put forward not without horror—and explains Christ’s saying by distinguishing the persons who speak and by examining the words themselves.

15. I am therefore astonished, holy Emperor, and utterly fail in body and soul, that there are some men—or rather, not men, but beings covered with a human appearance while inwardly possessing bestial insanity—who, after such great and such divine benefits of the Lord, deny that the very author of good things is good.

16. “It is written,” they say, “No one is good except one, God.” I acknowledge that it is written; but the letter contains no error—if only the Arian interpretation did not! The letters themselves are blameless; the meaning is culpable. I acknowledge the saying of the Lord and Savior; but let us consider when he says it, to whom he says it, and with what circumspection he says it.

17. The Son of God speaks, certainly, in the form of a man, and he speaks to a Scribe—namely, to one who would call the Son of God a good teacher while denying that he is God. Christ adds what the man does not believe, so that he may believe the Son of God not as a good teacher, but as the good God. For whenever “one God” is spoken of, the Son of God is by no means separated from the fullness of unity. In the same way, when one good God is named, how can the Only-Begotten be excluded from the fullness of divine goodness? It is therefore necessary either that they deny that the Son of God is God, or that they confess that he is the good God. [Note: Thus the Roman edition, together with many more manuscripts, some of which read: “from the fullness of the divine majesty and goodness”; the older edition and a few manuscripts, however, read: “is separated from the fullness of divinity … from the fullness of divine power,” and so forth.]

18. For this reason, with heavenly circumspection, he did not say, “No one is good except the one Father,” but, “No one is good except one God.” “Father” is the proper name of the one who begets; “one God,” however, in no way excludes the divinity of the Trinity, and therefore it is nature that is being praised. Goodness, then, is in God’s nature, and the Son of God is also in God’s nature; and therefore what is proclaimed is not the property of singularity, but of unity. [Note: The older edition and some manuscripts read, “but what belongs to the Trinity”; the Roman edition and the remaining manuscripts, “but what belongs to unity”; one, however, has, “but what belongs to divinity.” The sense is the same.]

19. Goodness, therefore, is not denied by the Lord; rather, such a disciple is rejected. For when the Scribe had said, “Good Teacher,” the Lord replied, “Why do you call me good?” (Mark X, 18)—that is, if you do not believe me to be God, it is not enough for you to call me good. I do not seek disciples of this kind, who believe me to be a good teacher more according to my humanity than the good God according to my divinity.

## CHAPTER TWO

He proves from his works that the Son of God is good—namely, from his benefits to the Israelites under the Old Covenant and to Christians under the New. Then, when he has shown that it is beneficial to regard him as one’s good Lord and Judge, he adduces the Father’s testimony concerning the Son, and even that of a considerable part of the Jewish people, thereby declaring the Arians worse than the Jews. He concludes all this with an exposition of the Bride’s words, which indicate the same goodness of Christ.

20. But I do not want him to rely upon the prerogative of his nature and the privilege of his power. Let him not be called good by us if he does not deserve it. If he does not deserve it by his works, if he does not deserve it by his benefits, let him be stripped by right of his claim to his own nature and subjected to our judgment. He who is going to judge us does not disdain to be judged, “so that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged” (Ps. L, 6).

21. Is he, then, not good who grants good things to me (Ps. XII, 6)? Is he not good who, when six hundred thousand of the Jewish people were fleeing from their persecutors, suddenly divided the surging waters of the Red Sea by an undivided mass of water (Exod. XIV, 6 ff.), so that the faithful were protected by the waters surrounding them, while the faithless were drowned when the waters returned?

22. Is he not good whose command made the seas solid for those who were fleeing and the rocks wet for those who were thirsty, so that the work might be recognized as that of the true author when moisture hardened and the rock poured forth a flood (Exod. XVII, 6)? To make you recognize the work as Christ’s, the Apostle said: “The rock, however, was Christ” (1 Cor. X, 4).

23. Is he not good who fed so many thousands of the people in the wilderness with heavenly bread, without the burden of labor and with the benefit of repose, lest hunger should assail them (Exod. XVI, 13 ff.)—so that for forty years neither their garments grew old nor their sandals were worn away (Deut. VIII, 4)—thereby showing the faithful an image of the resurrection to come, in which neither the beauty of glorious deeds, nor the splendor of encompassing power, nor the course of human life would perish? [Note: Amerbach and Erasmus, together with the greater number of manuscripts, read *instar infidelibus*, “as a likeness for the unfaithful”; Gill and the Roman edition, together with six handwritten codices, read *instar fidelibus*, “as a likeness for the faithful.” The latter is better, for above the same Israelites are described as those whom the surrounding waters protected as faithful.]

24. Is he not good who made heaven for us what earth is, so that, just as in heaven the spheres of the shining stars gleam as in a kind of mirror, so also throughout the world the choirs of apostles, martyrs, and priests might shine in the place of shining stars?

25. Therefore he is not only good, but also the good shepherd—that is, good not only for himself but also for his sheep: “The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John X, 11). Certainly he laid down his life in order to raise ours; but by the power of his divinity he both laid it down and took it up again, as it is written: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again. No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord” (ibid., 17–18).

26. You see his goodness, because he laid it down willingly; you see his power, because he took it up again. And yet you deny that he is good, although he himself said of himself in the Gospel: “If I am good, why is your eye evil?” (Matt. XX, 15). Ungrateful one, what are you doing? You deny the goodness of the one through whom you hope for good things—if indeed you believe. You deny the goodness of the one who gave us what “eye has not seen and ear has not heard” (1 Cor. II, 9). [Note: The Roman edition alone reads, “What do you say?”]

27. It is advantageous for me to believe that he is good: “It is good to trust in the Lord” (Ps. CXVII, 8). It is advantageous for me to confess the Lord, for it is written: “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good” (ibid., 1).

28. [Note: The older edition reads: “And shall I not believe in the good? For it is good to confess to the Lord. It is advantageous for me to confess the Lord.” Some manuscripts agree with this, except that they omit “and shall I not believe in the good.” The Roman edition alone reads: “It is advantageous for me to confess the Lord … It is advantageous for me to believe that he is good.” The remaining manuscripts agree with our text, except that some read *confiteri* (“to confess”) instead of *confidere* (“to trust”).] It is advantageous for me to regard my Judge as good; for the Lord is a good Judge to the house of Israel. Therefore, if the Son of God is Judge, since God is a good Judge and the Son of God is Judge, the good God is both Judge and Son of God. [Note: All editions and some manuscripts read: “If he is Judge, the Son of God certainly is; since the Lord is Judge and God is good. The Son of God, however, is Judge and God,” and so forth. The Roman edition reads: “… and God is good; but the Son of God is Judge, God,” and so forth. The remaining manuscripts more appropriately have the reading represented in the text.]

29. But perhaps you do not believe others; perhaps you do not believe the Son. Hear the Father saying: “My heart has uttered a good Word” (Ps. XLIV, 1). The Word, then, is good—the Word of whom it is written: “And the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I, 1). Therefore, if the Word is good, and the Son of God is the Word, then the Son of God is certainly the good God, even if this does not please the Arians. Let them at last be ashamed.

30. The Jews were saying, “He is good” (John VII, 12). Although some were saying, “He is not,” others nevertheless said, “He is good”; but you all deny that he is good.

31. He is good who forgives the sin of one person; and is he not good who took away the sin of the world? For it was said of him: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sin of the world” (John I, 29).

32. But why do we hesitate? The Church has already believed him to be good and confessed it, saying: “Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth, for your breasts are better than wine” (Song of Songs I, 1); and elsewhere: “And your palate is like the finest wine” (Song of Songs VII, 9). Good, then, is the one who nourishes us at the breasts of the Law and grace, soothing human cares with heavenly preaching. Yet we deny that he is good, although he is the image of goodness, expressing in himself the likeness of eternal goodness, just as we showed above that it is written: “For he is the spotless mirror of God’s majesty and the image of his goodness” (Wis. VII, 26).

## CHAPTER THREE

That the Son of God is the good and true God, although there is one God.

33. [Elsewhere, chapter II.] But what do you think, you who deny that the Son of God is the good and true God, when it is written that there is no God except one (1 Cor. VIII, 4)? For although there are those who are called gods, do you count Christ among those who are called gods but are not? It is his distinctive property that he always is; and apart from him there is no other good and true God, because God is in him. It is also the distinctive property of the Father that after him there is no other true God, because there is one God—not confusing the Father and the Son, as do the Sabellians, nor separating the Father and the Son, as do the Arians. The Father and the Son have distinction, as Father and Son; they do not have separation of divinity.

## CHAPTER FOUR

The Son of God is shown to be omnipotent by the authority of the Old and New Covenants.

34. [Elsewhere, chapter III.] Since, then, the true and good Son of God is necessarily the omnipotent God, can there be any doubt about this as well? Above, in Book I, chapter 1, we said that it is written that “the Lord Almighty” is his name. Therefore, since the Son is Lord, and the Lord is Almighty, the Son of God is omnipotent.

35. Receive also a passage about which you cannot doubt: “Behold, he comes with the clouds, and every eye shall see him, including those who pierced him; and all the tribes of the earth shall mourn over him. Yes, amen. I am the Alpha [Α] and the Omega [Ω], says the Lord God, who is and who was and who is to come, the Almighty” (Rev. I, 7–8). Who, then, was pierced, and whom do we hope will come, if not the Son? Therefore Christ is the omnipotent Lord and God.

36. Receive something else, holy Emperor; receive Christ speaking: “Thus says the Lord Almighty: After glory he sent me against the nations that plundered you, for whoever touches you is like one who touches the apple of his eye. For behold, I shall lay my hand upon them who plundered you, and I shall rescue you; and those who plundered you shall become plunder, and they shall know that the Lord Almighty sent me” (Zech. II, 8–9). The one who says, “The Lord is Almighty,” is certainly the omnipotent Lord; and the one who sent him is also the omnipotent Lord. Therefore omnipotence belongs both to the Father and to the Son; yet there is one omnipotent God, because there is unity of power.

37. And so that you may know, august Emperor, that it was Christ who spoke both in the Prophet and in the Gospel, as though in the predestination of the Gospel he says through Isaiah: “I am present, I who was speaking” (Isa. LII, 6)—that is, “I am present in the Gospel, I who spoke in the Law.”

38. Then elsewhere: “All things that the Father has are mine” (John XVI, 25). What are “all things”? He was certainly not speaking of created things, for all these things were made through the Son; rather, he was speaking of what the Father has—that is, eternity, majesty, and divinity—which he possessed by being begotten. Therefore we cannot doubt that he who has all that the Father has—“All things that the Father has are mine,” it is written—is omnipotent.

## CHAPTER FIVE

He explains the scriptural passages brought forward against Christ’s omnipotence, dwelling especially on proving that Christ often spoke from the disposition of human nature.

39. Nor do I fear that, because it is written of God, “Blessed and the only powerful one” (1 Tim. VI, 15), the Son of God should be separated from him, since Scripture said that God alone is powerful, not that the Father alone is powerful; and God the Father himself declares through the Prophet concerning Christ: “I have placed help upon one who is powerful” (Ps. LXXXVIII, 20). The Father, therefore, is not alone in being powerful; the Son of God is powerful as well, for the Son is praised in the Father.

40. Let someone certainly show what the Son of God cannot do. Who was his helper when he made heaven? Who was his helper when he founded the world? Did he who had no need of a helper in establishing the angels and dominions need one in order to liberate humanity?

41. “It is written,” they say: “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. XXVI, 39; Luke XXII, 42). And therefore he is omnipotent? How, then, does he hesitate over what is possible? Since I have proved him omnipotent, I have certainly proved that he cannot hesitate about what is possible.

42. “The words are Christ’s,” you say. You speak truly; but observe when he speaks and in what form. [Note: Several manuscripts read, “he bore weakness”; one reads, “he bears nature”; the remaining manuscripts and editions read, “he bore substance”; some also have, “he bears.”] He bore the substance of a man; he assumed the disposition of a man. Indeed, above you have it that, after going a little farther, he fell on his face, praying and saying: “Father, if it is possible.” He therefore speaks not as God, but as man. For would God, since he was God, be ignorant of something being possible or impossible? Or could anything be impossible for God, when it is written: “Nothing is impossible for you” (Job XXII, 17)?

43. [Note: The Master of the Sentences, Book III, distinction 17, section “Furthermore,” cites this passage in such a way that he admits that it contains a considerable difficulty: “Nevertheless,” he says, “it can be understood as having been said in this sense—not because he himself, even insofar as he was man, doubted, but because he adopted the manner of one who doubts and appeared to men to doubt.” Estius, however, was not satisfied with this solution; after applying it to the same passage, he adds: “We shall say more correctly that, for Ambrose, doubt is not an uncertain judgment concerning the truth of a matter, but a certain indifference of the sensory faculty toward following the inclination of nature, or a reasoning that doubts,” and so forth. Yet he does not conceal that he is not entirely satisfied with his own response, since he says that by its aid the passage can be understood “to some extent.” Nevertheless, we wonder why Ambrose’s statement that Christ doubted from human feeling should appear to contain such a great difficulty. For from the entire sequence of his discourse and reasoning it is not difficult to understand that, for our Doctor, Christ’s doubting from human feeling means nothing other than that Christ displayed the same sign of doubt that other human beings customarily display in a similar situation. This is also indicated clearly in *Exposition of Psalm XXXIX*, II, 16, where, explaining the same passage in precisely the same way, he says that Christ “spoke according to human feeling”; he implies that one ought to be cautious and not presume to accomplish easily what one cannot. And below he expresses the human perception of those who think that they have been abandoned by their Lord when they are in danger. It is therefore clear that Estius should not have rejected the Master’s solution—especially since neither in the passages cited, nor in Book IV on Luke, no. 12, where this same text is briefly treated, does he address at all the manner in which Christ, as man, could doubt or be ignorant. Ambrose treats these matters more fully in Book III.]

But what does he doubt about—himself or the Father? Surely about himself, the one who says, “Take it away”; and he doubts from human feeling. The Prophet does not think that anything is impossible for God. The Prophet does not doubt, and do you believe that the Son doubts? Do you place God below human beings? Does God doubt concerning the Father and fear death? Christ, then, is afraid; and while Peter is not afraid, Christ is afraid? Peter says, “I will lay down my life for you” (John XIII, 37); Christ says, “My soul is troubled” (John XII, 27).

44. Both statements are true, and both are fully rational: the one who is lower does not fear, while the one who is higher assumes the disposition of one who fears. The former, as man, is ignorant of the power of death; the latter, as God present in a body, displays the weakness of the flesh, so that the impiety of those who reject the mystery of the Incarnation might be excluded. Finally, he said these things, and Manichaeus did not believe, Valentinus denied, and Marcion judged him to be a phantom. [Note: What Ambrose asserts concerning Manichaeus is also transmitted by many other Fathers: namely, that he denied the truth of the Incarnation and attributed to Christ a phantom-like flesh that deceived the human senses. Athanasius teaches this in *On the Saving Coming of Christ*, p. 365; Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* 66; Augustine, *Against Heresies* 46; and Theodoret in several passages. It is also certain that Valentinus fabricated for Christ a kind of spiritual body that had descended from heaven through the Virgin as through a channel; while Marcion’s impiety was to blasphemously assert that the same Lord was nothing but some sort of apparition. Tertullian, *On the Prescription against Heretics*, chapter 49; Epiphanius, from Irenaeus, *Against Heresies* 31; Augustine, Theodoret, and others testify to this concerning Valentinus; concerning Marcion, Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, chapter 8; Theodoret, Book I of *The Heretical Fables*, chapter 11, and *On the Incarnation of Christ*. Tertullian, in the already cited chapter 30 of *On the Prescription against Heretics*, speaks of both together, recalling their period, philosophical sect, religion, and errors.]

45. He so fully assimilated his feelings to those of the man whose reality he demonstrated by the truth of his body that he said: “Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (Matt. XXVI, 39), although Christ’s willing is certainly the same as the Father’s willing, just as his doing is the same as the Father’s doing. [Note: Macarius and Stephen, in order to defend the Monothelite heresy, cited this passage in the Sixth Ecumenical Council, which is the Third Council of Constantinople, act 4—but mutilated in accordance with the ingenuity of heretics, as the Catholics demonstrated. In act 4, the letters of Agatho, Roman Pontiff, had also been read; in them, among the other testimonies of the Fathers concerning the Gospel words, “Father, if it is possible,” Ambrose’s sentence is placed first. In the following chapter it is read as follows: “Therefore he assumed my will,” and so forth. It was decided to read the passage again in act 10. From this one can see how highly they valued our Doctor.]

46. At this point your question also falls silent—the one you are accustomed to raise because the Lord said, “Not as I will, but as you will,” and elsewhere: “For I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John VI, 38).

## CHAPTER SIX

Taking the opportunity provided by the preceding scriptural passages to digress briefly, he demonstrates first from the fact that the Holy Spirit is likewise said to possess freedom, and then by explicit testimonies in which freedom is attributed to the Son of God.

47. Therefore, so that, as though by an interval inserted for fuller exposition, we may pause briefly, let us show that the Lord was free in his will when he said, “If it is possible.” You have advanced so far in impiety that you deny that the Son of God possesses free will! Yet you customarily detract even from the Holy Spirit, and you cannot deny that it is written: “The Spirit breathes where he wills” (John III, 8). “Where he wills,” it says—not where he is commanded. Therefore, if the Spirit breathes where he wills, does the Son not act as he wills? And certainly the same Son of God says in his Gospel where the Spirit possesses the power to breathe. Does he therefore acknowledge the Spirit as superior, because the Spirit is permitted to do what he is not permitted to do?

48. The Apostle also says that “the one and the same Spirit accomplishes all things, distributing to each one as he wills” (1 Cor. XII, 11). “As he wills,” he says—that is, according to the judgment of free will, not according to obedience to necessity. And the Spirit distributes no ordinary gifts, but those which God is accustomed to perform: the grace of healings and the working of powers. Therefore the Spirit distributes as he wills, while the Son of God does not liberate whom he wills? But hear him also doing what he wills. For he said: “To do your will, my God, I have willed” (Ps. XXXIX, 9). And elsewhere: “I will sacrifice to you willingly” (Ps. LIII, 8).

49. The holy apostle Peter knew that Jesus possessed in his power whatever he willed. Therefore, when he saw him walking upon the sea, he said: “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you upon the waters” (Matt. XIV, 28). Peter believed that, if Christ commanded it, the condition of nature could be changed, so that the waters might submit to human footsteps and the harmony of differing natures might be brought together. Peter asks him to command, not to ask; Christ did not ask, but commanded, and it was done—and Arius contradicts this?

50. What, then, is it for the Son to will what the Father does not will, or for the Son to will while the Father does not will? The Father gives life to those whom he wills, and the Son gives life to those whom he wills, as it is written (John V, 21). Name those whom the Son has given life to and whom the Father was unwilling to give life to. Since the Son gives life to those whom he wills, and the operation is one, you see that not only does the Son do the Father’s will, but the Father also does the Son’s will. What, moreover, is it to give life except through the passion of the Son? The passion of Christ, however, is the will of the Father. Therefore those whom the Son gives life to, he gives life to through the will of the Father. There is therefore one will.

51. And what is the Father’s will except that Jesus should come into this world and cleanse us from vices? Hear the leper saying: “If you will, you can cleanse me” (Matt. VIII, 2). Christ replied, “I will,” and immediately the result of healing followed. You see that the Son is master of his own will, and that Christ’s will is the same as the Father’s. Moreover, since he said, “All things that the Father has are mine” (John XVI, 15), there is no doubt that, since nothing is excepted, the Son has the same will as the Father.

## CHAPTER SEVEN

He returns to the solution of the proposed difficulty and teaches that Christ truly assumed human will and feelings, and consequently that whatever in him does not accord with divinity arises from these and must be referred to the one who was both God and man.

52. There is therefore one will where there is one operation; for in God the sequence of the will is the effect of the operation. But the will of man is one thing and the will of God another. Finally, so that you may know that life is in the human will—since we fear death—but that Christ’s passion was in the divine will, in order that he might suffer for us, when Peter wished to turn him away from his passion, the Lord said: “You do not understand the things of God, but the things of men” (Matt. XVI, 23).

53. Therefore he assumed my will; he assumed my sadness. I confidently name it sadness, because I proclaim the cross. It is my will that he called his own, because as man he assumed my sadness and as man he spoke. Therefore he said: “Not as I will, but as you will” (Matt. XXVI, 39). It is my sadness that he assumed in his own feeling; for no one who is about to die rejoices. He suffers with me, he is sad for me, he grieves for me. Therefore he grieved for me and in me, he who had nothing for which to grieve on his own account.

54. You grieve, then, Lord Jesus, not over your own wounds but over mine; not over your own death but over our weakness, as the Prophet says: “Because he grieves for us” (Isa. LIII, 4). And we, Lord, considered you to be in pain, though you grieved not for yourself but for me.

55. And what is surprising if he grieved for all, who wept for one? What is surprising if, about to die for all, he was distressed, who, about to raise Lazarus, shed tears? Yet there also he is moved by the tears of his devout sister, because he was touched by human feeling; and here he works with profound feeling, so that, just as his death took away death and his bruising healed our wounds, so also his grief might abolish our grief. [Note: The older edition and many manuscripts rightly read, “he touched the human mind”; two have, “they touched.” The Roman edition reads, “they touched the human mind”; the remaining manuscripts have the reading in the text. Immediately afterward, where the older edition and part of the manuscripts read *operabatur effectu*, “he worked by effect,” the Roman edition and other manuscripts read *affectu*, “by feeling.”]

56. As man, therefore, he doubts; as man, he is troubled. His power is not troubled; his divinity is not troubled. Rather, his soul is troubled; it is troubled according to the assumption of human weakness. And because he assumed a soul, he also assumed the passions of the soul. For God, insofar as he was God, could neither be troubled nor die. Finally, he says: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Ps. XXI, 1). He therefore speaks as man, bearing my fears—the fears by which we think that, when placed in danger, we are abandoned by the Lord. As man, he is troubled; as man, he weeps; as man, he is crucified. [Note: Understand here innocent feelings, as well as freedom from the vices by which we lament that our own feelings are corrupted. Although some after Jerome, in his commentary on Matthew, chapter 36, preferred to call these “pre-passions” rather than “passions,” Ambrose nevertheless chose to use this word so that orthodox truth might be set more forcefully against the Arian error. The theologians who followed him, especially the Master in Book III of the *Sentences*, distinction 15, and Thomas Aquinas, Part III, question 15, articles 4 and 6, discuss Christ’s feelings at length.]

57. For the apostle Paul also said: “They crucified the flesh of Christ” (Gal. V, 24). And elsewhere the apostle Peter says: “Christ having suffered according to the flesh” (1 Pet. IV, 1). Therefore it was the flesh that suffered, while divinity was free from death; he allowed the body to suffer according to the law of human nature. But can divinity die, when the soul cannot? “Do not fear,” he says, “those who can kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. X, 28). If, then, the soul cannot be killed, how can divinity be killed?

58. [Elsewhere, chapter IV.] [Note: This passage is cited not only in Letter 134 of Leo the Great to Leo Augustus, but also in act 2 of the Council of Chalcedon and in Letter 24 of the same Pope Leo to Flavian. There is, however, dispute about who added it, together with other patristic testimonies, to the letter mentioned. Garner, in the preface to the scholia on St Cyril, maintains that Theodoret did so; but Quesnel, in his notes on the above-cited Letter 24 of Leo, after refuting Garner’s arguments, contends that those very testimonies were adduced by Leo himself and read in the council under his name. But these matters have little bearing on our purpose.] Accordingly, when we read that “the Lord of majesty was crucified,” let us not suppose that he was crucified in his majesty as such (1 Cor. II, 8), but because the same one is God and man—God through divinity, and the man Jesus Christ through the assumption of flesh—the Lord of majesty is said to have been crucified, because, being a sharer in both natures, that is, the human and the divine, he underwent suffering in the nature of man. Thus, without division, the Lord of majesty is said to be the one who suffered, and the Son of Man, as it is written, is the one who descended from heaven (John III, 13). [Note: The Roman edition reads, “The same one is God and man.” What is said here and below—that, because of the intimate union of the divine and human natures in Christ, the Lord of majesty hung upon the cross, and conversely that the Son of Man descended from heaven—is rightly affirmed. Augustine later taught precisely this in Book I of *On the Trinity*, chapter 13, no. 28, which should be consulted. This is what the Scholastics call the *communicatio idiomatum*, the communication of properties.]

## CHAPTER EIGHT

From the principle established immediately above, he resolves Christ’s statement, “The Father is greater than I.” He shows that these and other statements of the same kind are to be understood according to Christ’s humanity, and confirms by many arguments that the same Lord cannot, according to his divine nature, be called inferior to the Father.

59. Therefore, according to the nature of man, he both doubted and grew weary and rose again; for that which fell is what rises again. According to the nature of man he also says the statement over which they habitually slander him: “For the Father is greater than I” (John XIV, 28). [Note: All editions and some manuscripts read “and grew weary”; the remainder read either “and was distressed” or “and was made weary.”]

60. But since elsewhere it is said: “I came forth from the Father and came into the world; again, I leave the world and go to the Father” (John XVI, 28), how does he go except through death, and how does he come except through resurrection? Finally, he added, to indicate that he had spoken of the assumption of humanity: “Therefore I told you before it happens, so that when it has happened you may believe” (John XIV, 29). For he was speaking of the passion of his body and of the resurrection, through which those who had previously doubted began to believe. God, after all, does not pass from place to place, since he is always everywhere. As man, he is the one who goes; he himself is the one who comes. Finally, elsewhere he says: “Rise, let us go from here” (ibid., 31). Therefore he goes and comes in that which he shares with us.

61. For how can God be lesser, when God is perfect and complete? But he is lesser in the nature of man; and do you wonder if, in the person of a man, he called the Father greater—he who, in the person of a man, said that he was a worm, not a man? For he said: “But I am a worm and not a man” (Ps. 21:7); and elsewhere: “As a sheep he was led to the slaughter” (Isa. 53:7).

[Note: The wording seems rather harsh, since it appears at least verbally to confuse the nature and person of the man. To resolve the difficulty, Petavius, *Dogmatic Theology on the Trinity*, says that “person” here should be understood in the sense in which ordinary speech says that someone speaks or acts “in another’s person,” that is, in another’s place, name, or authority. He judges that several other Fathers likewise use the word “person” in this sense. He could have added that Ambrose himself says below, in chapter 10, no. 81, that the obedience of death belonged to the incarnation, in which Christ assumed both our functions and our names. Whatever may be said about this meaning, since the holy Doctor elsewhere sufficiently distinguishes nature and person throughout this work, it is certain that his orthodox meaning here is that Christ spoke as man, or according to human nature, when he said that the Father was greater; just as in Book IV he says that the same Christ speaks from his assumption of the person of the incarnate man.]

62. If you say that he is lesser in this respect, I cannot deny it. But, to use the language of Scripture, he was not born lesser, but was made lesser (Heb. 2:9)—that is, he became lesser. How, then, was he made lesser, unless because “though he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself” (Phil. 2:6–7)—not relinquishing what he was, but assuming what he was not, because he took the form of a servant?

63. Finally, so that we might know that he was made lesser through assuming a body, he indicated that David prophesied about him as man, saying: “What is man, that you remember him, or the son of man, that you visit him? You made him a little lower than the angels” (Ps. 8:5–6). The Apostle himself interpreted this passage, saying: “We see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels because of the suffering of death, crowned with glory and honor, so that, apart from God, he might taste death for everyone” (Heb. 2:9).

64. Thus the Son of God was made lesser not only than the Father but also than the angels. And if you use this to his detriment, is the Son, in the nature of God, therefore lesser than his own angels, who serve and minister to him (Matt. 4:6)? Thus, while you wish to assert that he is lesser, you fall into impiety by preferring the nature of angels to the Son of God. But “a servant is not above his master” (Matt. 10:24). Indeed, even when he had taken flesh, angels ministered to him. Thus you should recognize that he was diminished in no respect through the nature of his body; for God could not suffer loss in himself, since what he assumed from the Virgin was neither an addition to the divine nature nor a diminution of his power.

65. The Son, therefore, is not lesser according to his divinity, since he possesses the fullness of divinity and glory. Greater and lesser are ordinarily distinguished in bodily things: by rank, fullness, or certainly by age. Such considerations have no place when divine matters are being discussed. A person is commonly called “greater” when he instructs and forms another; but it is not conceivable that God’s Wisdom should have been instructed by another’s teaching, since it itself established all instruction. How well, then, the Apostle said: “So that, apart from God, he might taste death for everyone” (Heb. 2:9), lest we think that the passion belonged to his divinity rather than to his flesh!

66. Therefore, if they have not found a way to prove that he is greater, let them not slander the words but seek the meaning of the words. I ask them, then, whom they think to be greater. If they think him greater because the Father is Father, this does not mean that there is here an age or a period of time, nor that the Father’s gray hair is contrasted with the son’s youth; for such things ordinarily make one a father. Father and son, however, are names of one who generates and one who is born. They do not seem to separate but to join; for the affection of nature is not a loss to nature. Kinship unites human beings to one another; it does not divide them.

67. Therefore, if they cannot bring forward any argument from nature, let them at least believe the testimonies. The Evangelist finally testifies that the Son is not lesser because he is Son; indeed, he indicates that he is equal because he is Son, saying: “For this reason the Jews were seeking all the more to kill him, because he not only broke the Sabbath but also called God his own Father, making himself equal with God” (John 5:18).

68. It is not the Jews who say this; the Evangelist testifies that he made himself equal with God by calling himself the proper Son of God. For it is not written from the standpoint of the Jews, saying, “For this reason we wanted to kill him”; rather, the Evangelist says in his own person: “For this reason the Jews were seeking to kill him.” He explained the reason why the Jews were moved to kill him: because, while he broke the Sabbath as God and claimed God as his own Father, he asserted for himself, not only in breaking the Sabbath the majesty of divine power, but also, in the name of his own Father, the right of eternal equality.

[Note: Codex Tell., “in the name of his own Father …”]

69. To this the Son of God most appropriately replied, proving both that he was the Son of God and that he was equal: “Whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does in the same way” (John 5:19). The Son, therefore, is both called and proved equal to the Father. This is a good equality, for it excludes any difference in divinity and at the same time identifies the Father with the Son, to whom the Son is equal. It is not a different or solitary equality, since no one is equal to himself alone. The Evangelist, therefore, interpreted what it means for Christ to call himself the proper Son of God: it means that he makes himself equal with God.

70. Following this, the Apostle said: “He did not regard equality with God as something to be seized” (Phil. 2:6). Whoever does not possess something attempts to seize it. Therefore, he did not possess equality with the Father as though it were a seizure; he possessed it in his own substance, as God and Lord.

[Note: One edition reads, “which he possessed in his own nature.”]

Hence he added: “He took the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:7).

[Note: Some manuscripts and the old edition read, “the contrary”—that is, “a servant contrary to an equal”; the remaining manuscripts and the Roman edition have the reading in the text. Below, where nearly all editions and manuscripts read *quomodo eadem*, “how could the same [nature],” two manuscripts instead read *quomodo eidem*, “how could the same [thing] to the same,” and so forth.]

A servant is certainly the opposite of one who is equal. He is therefore equal in the form of God, lesser in assuming flesh and in the suffering of man. For how could the same nature be lesser and equal? And if he is lesser, how does he do in the same way the things that the Father does? How could the same operation belong to different powers? Can one who is lesser operate in the same way as one who is greater? Or can there be one operation where there is a different substance?

71. Therefore, understand that Christ cannot be called lesser according to his divinity. He himself speaks to Abraham: “By myself I have sworn” (Gen. 22:16). The Apostle shows that the one who swears by himself cannot be lesser. Thus he says: “When God made his promise to Abraham, because he had no one greater by whom to swear, he swore by himself, saying: ‘Surely, blessing I will bless you, and multiplying I will multiply you’” (Heb. 6:13–14).

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “and multiplying you will be multiplied.”]

Christ therefore had no one greater, and for that reason he swore by himself. The Apostle rightly added: “For human beings swear by one greater than themselves; but God has no one greater” (Heb. 6:16).

[Note: This passage explicitly declares what can be understood from the whole context of the chapter: namely, that the Son, insofar as he is God, can in no way be called lesser than the Father. There is no doubt that this answer overturns and shatters the principal device of the Arian armies. Nevertheless, some of the Fathers did not hesitate to say that the same Son could be called lesser even as God, insofar as complete equality of nature is preserved between the two: the Son possessing this one distinction below the Father, that he is begotten; and the Father this one distinction above the Son, that he is unbegotten and the Son’s origin. On this matter see the Synod of Sardica, in its synodal letter; Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, writing to the Alexandrians, whose letter is cited by Theodoret, Book I, chapter 4; Athanasius, Book II, *Against the Arians*; Gregory of Nazianzus, Orations 5 and 30; Chrysostom, Homily 75 on John; and other Greek Fathers. Among the Latins, see Hilary, Book IX of *On the Trinity*, chapter 31, and Augustine, Book III of *Against Maximinus the Arian*, chapter 14. Ambrose’s distinction nevertheless prevailed among later writers.]

72. Or, if they wish this to be understood as spoken of the Father, the rest does not fit. For the Father was not seen by Abraham, nor did Abraham wash the feet of God the Father, but of him in whom there was a figure of the future man. Finally, the Son of God says: “Abraham saw my day, and rejoiced” (John 8:56). He, therefore, is the one who swore by himself, the one whom Abraham saw.

73. Indeed, how can he have someone greater, when he is one in divinity with the Father (John 10:30)? What is one is not unlike itself; but there is a distinction between greater and lesser. Thus the example of the present reading teaches concerning the Son and the Father that the Father has no one lesser, nor the Son of God anyone greater, since there is no difference of divinity between the Father and the Son, but one majesty.

## CHAPTER IX

When it is objected that the Son is lesser than the Father because he was sent by the Father, the reply is made that he was also sent by the Spirit, yet is not thereby considered lesser. It is further added that the Spirit is sent by the Father and the Son, to signify the unity of their operations. From this we are carefully instructed to distinguish which expressions apply to Christ as God and which to him as man; many examples are then presented and explained.

74. I am certainly not troubled by the argument they commonly bring forward, that he is lesser because he was sent. For if he is not shown to be lesser, and equality of honor is shown—since all honor the Son just as they honor the Father (John 5:23)—it is clear that he is not lesser because he was sent.

75. Do not consider the limitations of human speech, but the clarity of the words; believe the works. Consider that our Lord Jesus Christ said through Isaiah that he had been sent by the Holy Spirit (Isa. 61:1). Is the Son therefore lesser than the Spirit because he was sent by the Spirit? You have it written that the Son says that he was sent by the Father and by his Spirit: “I am the first, and I am for ever; and my hand founded the earth, my right hand established the heavens” (Isa. 48:12–13). And below: “I spoke, and I called; I brought him, and made his way prosperous. Draw near to me and hear these things: from the beginning I have not spoken in secret. When they came to be, I was there; and now the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit” (Isa. 48:15–16).

The one who made heaven and earth himself says that he was sent by the Lord and by his Spirit. You see, therefore, that this is simplicity of expression, not an insult arising from being sent. He who was sent by the Father is himself the one sent by the Spirit.

76. And so that you may recognize that there is no difference of majesty, the Son also sends the Spirit, as he himself said: “When the Paraclete comes, whom I will send to you from my Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from my Father” (John 15:26). Above he also taught that this same Paraclete was to be sent by the Father, saying: “But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name” (John 14:26).

Observe the unity: the one whom God the Father sends, the Son also sends; and the one whom the Father sends, the Spirit also sends.

[Note: The earlier edition, together with one or two manuscripts, reads, “But if they wish”; the Roman edition and the remaining manuscripts read, “But if they do not wish.” This is preferable, since it refers to the final words of the passage cited from Isaiah: “The Lord has sent me, and his Spirit.” For whoever denies that Christ is introduced here as speaking through the prophet must necessarily attribute these words to the Father.]

But if they do not wish the Son to have been sent because we read that the Son is at the Father’s right hand, they will have to admit concerning the Father what they deny concerning the Son—unless perhaps the Arians invent for themselves either another Father or another Son.

77. Let them therefore be silent about their empty disputes over words, since, as it is written, the kingdom of God is not in persuasive speech but in the demonstration of power (1 Cor. 2:4). Let us preserve the distinction between divinity and flesh. One Son of God speaks in both, because both natures are in the same person; and although the same person speaks, he does not always speak in the same manner. Consider in him now the glory of God, now the sufferings of man. As God, he speaks divine things, because he is the Word; as man, he speaks human things, because he was speaking in my substance.

[Note: This passage is attested in precisely this form not only by all the Ambrosian manuscripts and printed editions, but also by the First Council of Ephesus, the third ecumenical council, chapter 24, among the excerpts from the works of the Fathers in volume III of Labbe’s edition, where it is also repeated in act 6 of Baluze’s collection; by the ecumenical Council of Chalcedon, act 1 and 2, volume IV of the same edition of Labbe; and by the letter of Pope Leo to Emperor Leo, both in Labbe, volume III, and in Quenellius’s edition of Leo’s works, within the text of the cited letter. Nevertheless, Quenellius noted in the margin that the Codex Thuaneus reads, “questions of an empty dissertation.” Below, the most diligent Baluze, using ancient copies of the Council of Ephesus, Contius, and the Corbie manuscript of the Council of Chalcedon—which also adds the reading of Rusticus—restored the text to “one spoke in both,” and so forth. He could also have added the Greek text of the Council of Chalcedon in Labbe’s edition: εἷς ἐν ἑκατέρῳ λαλεῖ ὁ τοῦ Θεοῦ Υἱός, “one, the Son of God, speaks in both,” as well as the Greek text of the cited edition of Leo’s letter. In the same Council of Ephesus Baluze therefore restored the reading, “one spoke in both.” In Ambrose, Facundus, and act 5 of the Lateran Council under Pope Martin, as well as in two Colbertine manuscripts, the reading was, “one spoke in both [feminine forms],” and so forth. Nevertheless, apart from the witnesses mentioned by Baluze himself, all our manuscripts, the cited Councils of Ephesus and Chalcedon in Labbe’s edition, and Leo’s letter in the same edition, together with the sequence of the discourse, plainly confirm the reading in the text.]

78. “This is the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6:51). This bread is flesh, as he himself said: “The bread that I will give is my flesh” (John 6:52). This is the one who came down from heaven; this is the one whom the Father sanctified and sent into this world.

[Note: All printed editions and many manuscripts read, “This very wording … did not require divinity”; other manuscripts, together with the Greek text of the Council of Chalcedon in Labbe’s edition, agree with us, except that some manuscripts duplicate the negation, reading, “nor did this very wording … not require divinity.” Baluze preferred this reading on the basis of ancient copies of the Council of Ephesus and two Ambrosian manuscripts. The second negation, however, must certainly be removed, as the meaning itself shows; or, at least, following Mercator and Contius, whom Baluze cites there, one should read: “And this very wording …”]

Nor does the very wording teach us that divinity required sanctification, but that the flesh did. Finally, the Lord himself said: “And I sanctify myself for them” (John 17:19), so that you may recognize that he is sanctified in the flesh for us and that, in his divinity, he sanctifies.

79. This is the same one whom the Father sent, but who was made of a woman and made under the Law, as the Apostle said (Gal. 4:4). This is the one who says: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to evangelize the poor” (Luke 4:18). This is the one who says: “My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me. If anyone wishes to do his will, he will know whether the teaching is from God or whether I speak from myself” (John 7:16–17).

There is therefore one teaching from God and another from man. When the Jews sought his teaching according to his humanity and said, “How does this man know letters, when he has not been taught?” (John 7:15), Jesus answered and said: “My teaching is not mine.” For although he taught without literary education, he seemed to teach not as man but rather as God, who had not learned the teaching but had discovered it.

80. For he discovered every path of instruction, as was read above. The following was certainly said of the Son of God: “This is our God, and no other will be reckoned beside him, who discovered every path of instruction. Afterward he appeared on earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch 3:36 and following).

How, then, does he not possess his own teaching according to his divinity, when he discovered every path of instruction before he was seen on earth? Or how can he be lesser, of whom it was said: “No other will be reckoned beside him”? He is plainly called incomparable, since no one else can be reckoned in comparison with him; but he is so incomparable that he cannot be preferred to the Father. If they think this was said of the Father, they will not escape the impiety of Sabellius by attributing the assumption of human flesh to the Father.

[Note: Epiphanius writes in the *Anacephalaeosis* of Book II of his work that the Sabellians agree with the Noetians in almost everything, except that they deny that the Father himself suffered. What could seem more opposed to Ambrose’s position? Augustine, however, conveniently came to the aid of his teacher. In *Heresy* 41, after citing Epiphanius’s words, he adds: “How can this be understood of the Sabellians, when they are so well known to say that the Father suffered that they are more frequently called Patripassians than Sabellians?” These matters will be reconciled elsewhere.]

81. Let us pursue what follows: “He who speaks from himself seeks his own glory” (John 7:18). Observe the unity, which identifies both the Father and the Son. The one who speaks cannot fail to exist; but the one who speaks cannot be from himself, since in him all things are naturally from the Father.

82. What, then, does “he seeks his own glory” mean? It means glory not divided from the Father; for the Word, who is God, certainly possesses glory. Thus he says: “That they may see my glory” (John 17:24). But the glory of the Word is the same glory as the Father’s, as it is written: “The Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. 2:11). Thus, according to his divinity, the Son of God possesses his own glory, yet the glory of the Father and the Son is one. He is therefore not lesser in splendor, since the glory is one; nor is he lesser in divinity, since the fullness of divinity is in Christ.

83. “How, then,” you ask, “is it written: ‘Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son’?” (John 17:1). “The one who says this,” you reply, “requires glorification.” So far you have eyes; you have not read what follows. For it continues: “So that your Son may glorify you” (John 17:1). Does the Father also require glorification, since he is glorified by the Son?

## CHAPTER X

The objection drawn from the Son’s obedience is resolved. It is shown that the Trinity has one power, divinity, and operation; and it is added that Christ also displayed obedience to his mother, although he certainly cannot be called lesser on that account.

84. In the same way they commonly object to the Son’s obedience because it is written: “And being found in appearance as a man, he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death” (Phil. 2:7–8). The Apostle first mentioned “man” and then said “unto death,” so that we might understand that the obedience belonged not to his divinity but to his incarnation, in which he assumed both our functions and our names.

85. We have therefore learned that the Trinity has one power, which it taught us both in the passion itself and after the passion: the Son suffers through the mystery of the body; the Holy Spirit is poured into the apostles; the spirit is commended into the hands of the Father; and God the Father is also manifested with a loud voice.

[Note: The old edition reads, “which he also taught in the passion itself. For the Son suffers, the spirit is commended into the hands of the Father, and God the Father also [is manifested] with a loud voice”; Gill alone reads, “and he taught after the passion itself. For the Son suffers …,” and so forth. The text is confused and disordered. The manuscripts generally agree with us, except for a few that give the final part as: “the Holy Spirit is poured out; the Father also …,” omitting the intervening words.]

We have learned that the Father and the Son have one image, one likeness, and one sanctification. We have learned that they have one operation, one glory, and also one divinity.

86. There is therefore one and only one God, because it is written: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone you shall serve” (Deut. 6:13). There is one God—not because he is himself both Father and Son, as the impious Sabellius asserts, but because the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one divinity. Where there is one divinity, there is one will and one command.

87. Finally, so that you may know that the Father exists, that the Son exists, and that the Father and Son have one work, follow the Apostle, who said: “May God himself, and our Father, and our Lord Jesus direct our way to you” (1 Thess. 3:11).

[Note: The latest Paris edition reads, “The Father speaks, and the Son speaks,” with a corrupted meaning.]

He speaks of the Father and the Son, but the direction is one, because the power is one. Elsewhere also you have: “May our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God our Father, who loved us and gave us eternal consolation and good hope in grace, console your hearts and strengthen them” (2 Thess. 2:16–17). What unity he displays, so that the consolation is one and not plural! Let faithlessness therefore be silent; or, if it cannot be overcome by reason, let it be softened by humane kindness.

88. Let us consider how humanely the Lord acted, so that he might teach us not only faith but also conduct. For, being established in the form of man, he was subject to Joseph and Mary (Luke 2:51). Was he therefore lesser even than human beings because he was subject? Piety is one thing and power another; but piety does not prejudice power. In what respect, then, do you read that he was subject to the Father? In the body, certainly, in which he was subject to his mother.

## CHAPTER XI

Ambrose proposes to deal humanely with the Arians, following Christ’s example of treating wounds with wine and oil. Inviting everyone to this heavenly medicine, he explains for what purpose and with what benefit Christ assumed flesh. From this he shows how greatly it profits us to have faith, by which we recognize that Christ assumed every weakness for our sake, while his divinity burst forth in the passion. From these considerations it may be understood that the Son of God was sent without any subjection; nor need we fear that this faith displeases the Father, since the Father signifies that he is well pleased in the Son.

89. Let us also act humanely; let us persuade them of what benefits them, and let us entreat and weep before the Lord who made us (Ps. 94:6). For we do not wish to conquer but to heal; we do not act deceitfully but admonish religiously. Humanity often bends those whom neither strength nor reason has been able to overcome. Thus the Lord healed with oil and wine the man who, descending from Jericho, fell among robbers—one whom neither the harsher medicines of the Law nor prophetic severity had cured (Luke 10:30 and following).

90. Let all who wish to be healed therefore come to him. Let them receive the medicine which he brought from the Father and prepared in heaven, compounded from those immortal juices. It does not grow from the earth, for no natural substance contains the ingredients of this preparation. By divine counsel he assumed this flesh, to show that the law of the flesh is subject to the law of the mind. He assumed flesh so that, as man, he might conquer and instruct human beings.

91. What would it have profited me if, like God, he had displayed his power and merely demonstrated his divinity to be inviolable? Or why would he have assumed flesh unless he was to allow himself to be tempted according to the condition of my nature and weakness? He had to be tempted; he had to suffer with me, so that I might know how to conquer when tempted and escape when he had suffered with me. He conquered through self-control; he conquered through contempt for riches; he conquered through faith. He trampled down ambition and drove away excess; he banished wantonness.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “he restrained wantonness”; others, “he will have bound it.”]

92. Peter saw this medicine and abandoned his nets—that is, the instruments and means of making a living—renouncing the desire of the flesh as one renounces a rotten ship, into which, as into a kind of bilge, many passions flow. A great medicine, therefore, which not only cut away the scar of the ancient wound but also cut out the cause of the suffering. O faith, richer than every treasure! O medicine more excellent than all our wounds and sins!

93. Let us consider that it benefits us to believe rightly. It benefits me to know that Christ assumed my weaknesses for my sake and underwent the sufferings of my body (Isa. 53:4). For me—that is, for every human being—he became sin; for me he became a curse; for me and in me he became subordinate and subject; for me he became a lamb, for me a vine, for me a stone, for me a servant, for me the son of a maidservant; for me he was ignorant of the day of judgment; for us he did not know the day or the hour.

94. For how could he be ignorant of the day who made the days and the times? How could he be ignorant of the day of judgment who expressly declared both the hour and the cause of the coming judgment? He became a curse, therefore, not according to his divinity but according to the flesh; for it is written: “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree” (Deut. 21:23).

[Note: Most manuscripts read, “Cursed is the man who …”]

He certainly hung according to the flesh, and therefore he became a curse because he assumed our curses. He wept so that you, a human being, would not weep forever; he suffered insults so that you would not grieve over your own insult.

95. It is a great remedy to have consolation in Christ. He endured these things for us with such patience, and yet we are unable to endure such things patiently for his name! What appetite would not learn to forgive, when Christ prayed even for his persecutors while crucified? Do you see that what you consider Christ’s weaknesses are your virtues? Why do we raise questions against him about the remedies provided for us? Those tears wash us; that weeping cleanses us; and that doubt strengthens us, lest, if you begin to doubt, you despair.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “they free us”; other manuscripts and the printed editions more fittingly read, “they wash us.”]

The greater the insult, the more abundant the grace that is owed.

96. But recognize divinity in the very insults. He hung on the cross, and all the elements served him. The sun withdrew, daylight vanished, darkness was spread and enfolded everything, and the earth trembled; but the one who hung there did not tremble (Matt. 27:51). What else do these events signify but reverence for the Author? You see that he is on the cross, but you do not see that he grants the kingdom of God. You read that he tasted death, but you do not read that he also invited the robber to paradise (Luke 23:43). You look at the women weeping at the tomb, but you do not look at the angels keeping watch (John 20:12). You read what he said, but you do not read what he did. You say that the Lord told the Canaanite woman: “I was sent only to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel” (Matt. 15:24); but you do not say that he did what she had asked of him.

97. From this you should understand that “sent” does not mean that he was compelled by another’s command, but that he exercised his own will voluntarily. Otherwise you display contempt for the Father. For if, as you interpret it, Christ came to Judea as a servant of the Father’s commands, to heal only its inhabitants—and if, as we read, he first freed the daughter of the Canaanite woman—then he was certainly not the executor of another’s command but a free agent acting according to his own will. Where there is freedom of will, there is no violation of the mission.

98. Nor should you fear that what the Son did displeased the Father, since the Son himself says: “I always do what pleases him” (John 8:29); and elsewhere: “The works that I do, he himself does” (John 14:12). How, then, could what the Father himself did through the Son have displeased the Father? For there is one God, as it is written, who justified the circumcised from faith and the uncircumcised through faith (Rom. 3:30).

99. Read everything; attend carefully to everything. You will find that he demonstrated Christ in such a way that God could be seen in man. Do not maliciously interpret the Son as boasting about the Father when you hear that the Father is well pleased in the Son (Matt. 17:5).

## CHAPTER XII

It is investigated whether Catholics or Arians can more fittingly reconcile Christ, considered in the person of the judge, with their position. The objection arising from the judge’s session and the Father’s words is dissolved. It is shown that no subjection is signified in the Son by his sitting at the Father’s invitation, nor any superiority by his sitting at the Father’s right hand. Finally, from the angelic Trisagion it is explained that the Trinity of persons in God, together with the unity of nature, is signified.

100. But if they cannot be moved by humane considerations, let us appeal to the judge. To whom shall we go at last? To the one who possesses judgment, certainly. To the Father? But the Father judges no one; “he has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22). He gave it by begetting, not by bestowing something external. See how unwilling he was to allow you to detract from his Son: he gave you the very judge.

101. Let us therefore see, before the judgment, which of us has the better case: I or you. It is the mark of a prudent advocate first to win the judge’s favor. Do you honor man but not honor God?

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “You do not honor the Lord.”]

What wins over a judge: honor or insult? Suppose that I have sinned—which is not the case; does Christ take offense at his own honor? We all sin. Who, then, will deserve pardon: the one who offers honor or the one who inflicts insult?

102. Or, if reason does not move you, let the very appearance of the judgment at least move you. Raise your eyes to your judge; observe who sits, with whom he sits, and where he sits. Christ sits at the right hand of the Father. If your eyes cannot grasp this, hear the Prophet saying: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand” (Ps. 109:1). The Son therefore sits at the right hand of the Father.

Tell me now, you who think divine things should be assessed according to secular standards: does the one who sits at the right hand seem inferior to you? Is the Father insulted because he sits at the left? The Father honors him, and you regard it as an insult? The Father prefers this to be an example of piety, and you regard it as a command of authority? He rose from death and sits at the right hand of God.

103. “But,” you say, “the Father said it.” Consider also where the Father does not speak and the Son foretells it: “From now on you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power” (Matt. 26:64). He says this concerning the assumption of the body; to him the words are addressed: “Sit at my right hand” (Ps. 109:1).

For if you are asking about the eternal seat of his divinity, when Pilate asked him whether he was the king of the Jews, he said: “For this I was born” (John 18:37). The Apostle therefore teaches that it is useful for us to believe that Christ sits at the right hand of God not as one obeying a command or receiving a favor, but as the beloved Son. Thus you have: “Seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God; set your minds on the things that are above” (Col. 3:1–2).

To set one’s mind on what is above means to believe that Christ, in sitting there, does not obey as one commanded but is honored as the most beloved Son. Therefore, with respect to the body, he says: “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet” (Ps. 109:1–2).

104. If you also twist this into an accusation because the Father said, “I will place your enemies beneath you,” then the Father also draws to the Son those whom the Son raises and gives life: “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him; and I will raise him up on the last day” (John 6:44).

And you say that the Son of God is subject through weakness, although the Father draws to him those whom he will raise on the last day? Does this seem to you a form of subjection in which the kingdom is prepared for the Father, when the Father draws people to the Son, and there is no room for accusation when the Son hands the kingdom over to the Father, nor is anything preferred?

[Note: Codex Albinus reads, “nor is anyone preferred”; Codex Teller reads, “nor is anyone preferred to anyone.”]

These are proofs of piety: the Father hands over to the Son, and the Son to the Father. They hand things over to each other in such a way that neither the one who receives acquires something foreign, nor the one who hands over loses anything.

105. Sitting at the right hand is likewise no superiority, nor is sitting at the left an insult. Divinity knows no rank, is confined by no place, and is defined by no times. We human beings measure such things with narrow minds. There is no difference in love and no division in unity.

106. But why should we wander farther? You have surveyed everything, seen the judge, and noticed the angels proclaiming. They praise, and you criticize! Dominions and Powers venerate, and you slander! All his saints adore him; the Son of God does not adore, the Holy Spirit does not adore. The Seraphim say: “Holy, holy, holy” (Isa. 6:3).

107. What does the threefold repetition under one name of holiness mean? If the repetition is threefold, why is the praise one? If the praise is one, why is the repetition threefold? Why threefold, unless because the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one in holiness? He did not say it once, lest he separate the Son; not twice, lest he pass over the Spirit; not four times, lest he join creatures to the Trinity.

And to show that the Trinity has one divinity, after saying three times, “Holy, holy, holy,” he added in the singular: “The Lord God of hosts” (Isa. 6:3). Holy, therefore, is the Father; holy the Son; holy also the Spirit of God. The Trinity is worshiped; it does not worship. The Trinity is praised; it does not praise. I prefer to believe as the Seraphim do and to worship as all the heavenly Powers and Virtues do.

## CHAPTER XIII
Continuing the allegory of the Lord’s judgment, Ambrose briefly refutes the blasphemous opinions of the Arians, Sabellians, and Manichaeans concerning their judge. Then, having set forth Christ’s reproaches against his other adversaries, he hopes that his own judgment will be more lenient.

**108.** Let us therefore examine your defense, and see how you will reconcile the judge to yourself. Say it plainly—say it, I mean: “I think that you, Christ, are unlike the Father.” He will reply: “Distinguish them, if you can; distinguish, I mean, in what respect you think me unlike him.”

**109.** Say something else: “I consider you a creature.” And Christ will reply: “If the testimony of two men is true, you ought at least to have believed both me and the Father, who called me begotten.”

**110.** “I deny that you are good.” And he will say: “Let it be done to you according to your faith, so that I may not be good to you.”

**111.** “I do not consider you omnipotent.” And he himself will reply: “Then I cannot forgive you your sins.”

**112.** “I say that you are subject.” To this he will answer: “Why then do you ask liberty and pardon from one whom you think subject to servitude?”

**113.** I see that your defense is stuck. I do not press you, because I myself am conscious of my sins. I do not begrudge pardon, because I myself desire forgiveness. I wish to know your request. Behold, I bring your desires before the judge: I do not expose your crimes; I await the series of your requests.

**114.** Say, then, what is contained in the common prayer. Say, I mean: “Lord, make me in the image of God.” He will reply: “In what image? The one you denied?”

**115.** Say: “Make me incorruptible.” He will certainly answer: “How can I make you incorruptible when, by calling me a creature, you chose to regard me as capable of corruption? The dead will rise incorruptible, and you call him corruptible whom you see as God” (1 Cor. 15:52)?

**116.** Say: “Be good to me.” He will say to you: “Why do you ask for what you denied? I wanted you to be good; I said, ‘Be holy, because I myself am holy’ (Lev. 19); and you persist in denying this to me? And you expect forgiveness of sins? But no one can forgive sins except God alone. Therefore, since I am not truly and alone your God, I certainly cannot forgive your sins.”

**117.** Let the Arian and Photinian say this: “I deny,” he says, “that you are God.” The Lord will reply: “The fool said in his heart, ‘There is no God’” (Ps. 52:1). Of whom do you think this was said: of a Jew, a gentile, or the devil? Whoever it was said of, Photinian, the one who kept silent is more tolerable; but you have dared to say it aloud, so that you might prove yourself more foolish than the fool. “You deny God,” he says, “although I have said, ‘You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High’” (Ps. 81:6). And you deny God, whose divine works you behold all around you?

**118.** Let the Sabellian say: “I consider you yourself to be the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.” The Lord will reply: “You do not hear the Father; you do not hear the Son. Is there any confusion here? Scripture itself teaches you that the Father is the one who delivered judgment, and that the Son is the one who judges. Have you not heard me say, ‘I am not alone, but I and the Father who sent me’” (John 8:29)?

[Note: So reads the printed text, together with several manuscripts; others read, “he teaches us”; some, “he teaches you”; and two read, “he does not teach you.” These readings are erroneous unless the statement is understood as a question.]

**119.** Let the Manichaean say: “I believe that the devil is the author of our flesh.”

[Note: That the Manichaeans admitted two principles—one of good and the other of evil—and taught that all bodily things were created by the principle of evil is testified by the authors whom we have already often cited, Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* 76, and Augustine, *Against Heresies* 47. Augustine also adds that they carefully prohibited the killing of animals, lest the princes of darkness be offended.]

He will reply to him: “Then what will you do in the heavenly places? Go to your author. I want those to be with me whom the Father gave me. You think, Manichaean, that you were created by the devil; hurry, then, to his dwelling, where there are fire and sulfur, where his conflagration is not extinguished, so that his punishment may never die.”

**120.** I pass over the other monstrosities of the heretics—not their names, but what their judgment will be, what form their sentence will take. To all of them he will reply in the language of moral reproach: “My people, what have I done to you, or in what way have I grieved you?” (Mic. 6:3). “Did I not lead you out of Egypt and free you from the house of slavery?”

[Note: All printed editions, along with several manuscripts, read *non nomina*, “not their names.” Some others read *qui dies erit judicii*, “what the day of judgment will be”; several read *unus . . . quid gesserit judicii*, “what one . . . has done in judgment.” The remaining witnesses rightly have the reading given in the text, with two exceptions: where *non nomina* is found, they read *non nomine*, “not in name,” without a change of meaning.]

**121.** But it is little merely to have freed you from Egypt and snatched you from the house of slavery; greater still is that I gave myself for you. You will therefore say: “Did I not take upon myself all your insults? Did I not offer my body for you? Did I not embrace death, something that belonged not to my divinity but to your redemption?”

[Note: Several manuscripts read, “in devotion to redemption.”]

“Is this the gratitude that is returned? Did my blood accomplish only this, as I myself once said through the Prophet: ‘What profit is there in my blood, since I have descended into corruption?’” (Ps. 29:10). “This, then, is what it accomplished: that you impiously denied me, for whom I endured these things.”

**122.** But I, Lord Jesus, even though I myself am conscious of grave sins, will nevertheless say: “I did not deny you; you have reason to forgive the weakness of the flesh.
