I confess my offense; I do not deny my sin: ‘If you will, you can cleanse me’” (Matt. 8:2)—for the one who said this earned the right to say it. “Do not, I beg you, enter into judgment with your servant” (Ps. 142:2). I do not ask you to judge, but to forgive.

## CHAPTER XIV

He explains the judge’s sentence; and, after examining the quibbles of his adversaries, makes clear that no appeal from it is possible.

**123.** What do we think Christ will judge? Do I say that he will judge? Rather, he has already judged. We have his sentence: “Let all honor the Son just as they honor the Father. Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him” (John 5:23).

**124.** If you dislike the sentence, appeal to the Father; rescind the judgment that the Father delivered. Say that he has a Son unlike himself. He will reply to you: “Then I lied when I said to the Son, ‘Let us make man in our image and likeness’” (Gen. 1:26).

**125.** Say that he created him. He will reply to you: “Why, then, did you worship one whom you considered a creature?”

**126.** Say that he begot the Son as lesser. He will reply: “Measure him; let us see.”

[Note: The Arians are mocked here. While they boasted that they relied on the principles of philosophy, they introduced a relation of quantity where, philosophically speaking, there ought to be a relation of quality. Cyril of Alexandria likewise attacks the same fallacy of Eunomius in *Thesaurus*, dissertation 11. Ambrose touched on this difficulty in a single word because he had already explained it fully above.]

**127.** Say that you ought not to have believed him. He will answer: “Had I not said to you, ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him’” (Matt. 17:5)? What does “hear him” mean? Surely this: “All things that the Father has are mine” (John 17:10). The apostles heard this, as it is written: “They fell upon their faces and were greatly afraid” (Matt. 17:6). If those who confessed fell down, what will those who denied him do? But Jesus touched those men and raised them up; he will allow you to lie there, so that you may not see the glory that you denied.

**128.** Let us see, then, that the one whom the Son condemns, the Father also condemns. Let us therefore honor the Son as we honor the Father, so that through the Son we may be able to reach the Father.

## CHAPTER XV

He speaks modestly of his work; nevertheless, he says that it is sufficient for faith, since Scripture supports the divine generation in so many places, though the Arians are deaf to it. Showing that their obstinacy is plainly like that of the Jews, he prays that they may love the truth. Finally, he teaches that they should be abandoned as heretics and Antichrists.

**129.** These things, august Emperor, I have set forth piecemeal and briefly, arranging them rather in an unpolished form than explaining them thoroughly. If the Arians consider some things incomplete, I scarcely admit that they have even been begun; if they think that something still remains, I think that almost everything remains—for the unbelieving lack everything, while the faithful abound. In the end, Peter’s single confession was sufficient for faith in Christ: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16:16). For it is enough to know that his generation is divine, not divided, not diminished, not derivative, and not created.

[Note: Quite a few manuscripts read, “not altered.” Although this is not unreasonable, the reading of others and of the printed editions, “not diminished,” is better. This expression, like the following one, is best understood from the following passage of Hilary, *On the Trinity*, Book VI: “He knows no portion in God, but knows the whole God from the whole God; he knows one from one; not cut off, but born; he knows that in the birth of God there is neither diminution of the begetter nor weakness of the one born.”]

**130.** This too is expounded throughout the books of Scripture, yet the impious still do not believe it: “The heart of this people has been made fat, and they have heard heavily with their ears, and they have burdened their eyes, lest they should ever see with their eyes, hear with their ears, and understand with their heart” (Isa. 6:10). For, after the manner of the Jews, the Arians habitually close their ears or stir up disturbances whenever the word of salvation is heard.

**131.** And what wonder is it if unbelievers are unwilling to believe human voices, when they do not believe divine ones? The Son of God was saying, as you have it in the Gospel: “Father, glorify your name.” The Father’s voice was heard from heaven saying: “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again” (Acts 9:4). The unbelievers heard these words but did not believe. The Son was speaking; the Father was answering; and the Jews were saying: “It has thundered for him” (ibid., 29); while others said: “An angel has spoken to him” (John 12:29).

**132.** Paul too, as it is written in the Acts of the Apostles, was being called to grace by the voice of Christ, while several companions were walking along with him; yet he alone said that he had heard the voice of Christ. Thus, holy Emperor, whoever believes, hears—and hears in order to believe; whoever does not believe does not hear, but neither wants nor is able to hear, lest he believe!

**133.** Would that, insofar as lies within my power, they were willing to hear, so that they might believe: to hear with good will and gentleness, seeking the truth rather than attacking it. For it is written that we should not give attention to myths and endless genealogies, which produce questions rather than the building up of God that is in faith. “The end of the commandment is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith.” Some, having strayed from these things, have turned aside to empty talk, desiring to be teachers of the law, though they understand neither what they say nor concerning what they make assertions (1 Tim. 1:4 ff.). Elsewhere the same Apostle says: “Avoid foolish and undisciplined questions” (2 Tim. 2:23).

**134.** The Apostle says that such people are to be abandoned—those who sow questions, that is, heretics.

[Note: So read the more numerous and better manuscripts. Others read partly, as do the editions of Amerbach and Erasmus, “who assert questions, that these are heretics”; partly, as does Gill, “who sow . . . that these are heretics”; one manuscript has, “and that they are heretics”; the Roman edition reads, “that is, that they are heretics.”]

Of these he also says elsewhere that some will depart from the faith, giving attention to deceitful spirits and doctrines of demons (1 Tim. 4:1).

**135.** John too says that heretics are Antichrists, clearly designating the Arians (1 John 2:18). For this heresy arose after all the other heresies and gathered poisons from every heresy. Just as it is written of the Antichrist that “he opened his mouth in blasphemy against God, to blaspheme his name and to wage war against his saints” (Rev. 13:6), so these men detract from the Son of God and have not spared even the martyrs; and—something that perhaps the Antichrist himself will not do—they have falsified the divine Scriptures.

[Note: We have seen Ambrose complain in his *Exposition of Psalm 36* and elsewhere that the Alexandrians made an unsuitable division of the beginning of John’s Gospel; he himself mentions that division more than once below. Yet he clearly indicates there that he did not regard it as a corruption. It is therefore evident that he is referring here to another adulteration. Nor was it a trivial one, as is clear from the fact that he complains of it not only in this work but also in *On the Holy Spirit*, Book II, chapter 6, and at greater length in Book III, chapter 11, where he gives an example of the same corruption.]

Therefore, “whoever says that Jesus is not the Christ—he is the Antichrist”; whoever denies the Savior of the world denies Jesus; whoever denies the Son also denies the Father, because it is written: “Everyone who denies the Son does not have the Father” (1 John 2:23).

[Note: Six manuscripts read, “nor does he have the Father.” The Greek likewise has οὐδὲ τὸν πατέρα ἔχει (“nor does he have the Father”). Nevertheless, all the other manuscripts and printed editions read, “he also denies the Father.”]

## CHAPTER XVI

He promises Gratian victory and relates that it was foretold by Ezekiel. He confirms this hope from the Emperor’s piety, accepting the earlier disasters suffered at the hands of the Eastern heretics. Finally, he beseeches God, now appeased, to bring aid to the faithful army, the region, and its commander.

**136.** Nor ought I, Emperor, to detain you at greater length when you are intent upon war and contemplating victorious trophies over the barbarians. Go forth, fully surrounded by the shield of faith and carrying the sword of the Spirit; go forth to the victory promised in former times and foretold in the divine oracles.

**137.** For Ezekiel, even then, prophesied both the future devastation of our people and the wars of the Goths. Thus you have it: “Therefore prophesy, son of man, and say: ‘O Gog, thus says the Lord: Will you not on that day, when my people Israel is established to dwell in peace, rise up and come from your place, from the farthest regions of the north? And many nations will be with you, all riding horses, a great and mighty assembly and a numerous force; and you will rise up against my people Israel like a cloud covering the earth in the latter days,’ etc.” (Ezek. 38:14 ff.).

[Note: Several manuscripts read, “a numerous gathering, and he will ascend”; the others and the printed editions read as in the text, except that the old edition, together with some manuscripts, has “and he will descend,” while the Roman edition has “and you will ascend.” Ambrose’s interpretation, by which he considers Gog to mean the Goths, is reported by Jerome in the preface to Book XI of his commentary on Ezekiel, and in the *Hebrew Questions or Traditions*, chapter 10. Jerome indicates that he did not find it entirely convincing, though he was reluctant to reject it openly. In the first passage he proposes nothing certain or definite concerning the interpretation, despite naming its author with an expression of respect; in the second he indicates that he would be prepared to follow it if events confirmed it. His observation that the Goths are more properly called Getae by learned men than Gog and Magog is not especially compelling. It is certain that many nations’ names appear one way in the sacred books and another way in Greek or Latin writers. It is therefore plausible that, if Jerome had written after Theodosius’s victory, he would have agreed with Ambrose on this point. When Proclus, bishop of Constantinople, under the younger Theodosius, adapted this same interpretation in a speech delivered from the pulpit to the victory over the barbarians who were ravaging the empire at that time, his hearers responded with tremendous applause, as Socrates testifies in Book VII, chapter 43 of his *History*. Joan Dallaeus ought therefore to have been recalled from this error, so that he would not say in Book II, chapter 3 of *On the Use of the Fathers*: “Ambrose, as we mentioned above, rather carelessly understands Gog and Magog to mean the Goths.” In making this criticism, to say nothing more severe, he showed himself to be rather careless.]

**138.** This Gog is the Goth whom we now see having come forth, concerning whom future victory is promised us, as the Lord says: “They will plunder those who plundered them, and they will strip those who stripped them, says the Lord. And on that day I will give Gog”—that is, the Goths—

[Note: Several manuscripts read, “I will give Gog,” that is, the Goths.]

“a named place, a tomb of Israel, a burial-place of many men who came upon the sea. Around it he will build up the mouth of the valley, and there he will bury Gog and all his multitude; it will be called Ge Polyandrium Gog, and the house of Israel will bury them, so that the land may be cleansed” (Ezek. 39:10 ff.).

[Note: Amerbach’s edition, together with a few manuscripts, reads, “he will build these valleys, this one and them, and there he will bury Gog.” In the same manuscripts, *this one and them* is lacking; in its place the Tellier manuscript has, “and around this valley he will arrange them.” Erasmus and the editions that follow him read, “he will construct the peristome and bury them”; the Roman edition has, “they will construct . . . they will bury.” The remaining manuscripts read as in the text, except that they have *he will construct them* rather than *he will construct the mouth*. The Greek is τὸ περιστόμιον τῆς φάραγγος, “the mouth of the valley.” Further below Erasmus and the subsequent editions have, “And it will be called Polyandrium”; Amerbach and the manuscripts have, “the Valley Polyandrium.” So too do the Septuagint: εἰς Γαὶ τὸ πολυάνδριον. Jerome says that valleys and rugged places are called *gai* or *ge* in Hebrew in his commentary on this passage.]

**139.** Nor is it doubtful, holy Emperor, that we, who have suffered the battle brought on by another’s faithlessness, will have the aid of the Catholic faith now flourishing in you.

[Note: Several manuscripts read, “we have suffered punishment,” which is not unreasonable. Others, and all the printed editions, rightly read, “we have suffered battle,” that is, war inflicted on account of the faithlessness of the Arian emperors Constantius and Valens. This was brought upon them by the Goths, who, driven from their settlements by the Alans, crossed the Danube with Valens’s permission and received part of Thrace for cultivation. Not long afterward, however, they took up arms against that emperor and, after inflicting many defeats upon his generals, devastated the regions mentioned here by Ambrose with slaughter, rape, and fire. Gratian, therefore, when he was preparing to bring aid to Valens against those barbarians, asked our Doctor for these books, evidently so that, as he was about to go to an Arian emperor, he might be fortified with a salutary antidote. You will find this Gothic war carefully described by Ammianus Marcellinus, among others, in Book XXXI, chapters 4 and following.]

For an evident cause of divine indignation preceded: faith was first broken in the Roman Empire precisely where it had been broken toward God.

**140.** I do not wish to recall the deaths of the confessors, their tortures and exiles, the offices of pious priests, and the rewards of traitors.

[Note: All the printed editions and several manuscripts read *tormenta*, “tortures”; others omit the word. For *piorum sacerdotia proditorum munera*, some have “the offices of impious priests” or “of faithless priests.” Some manuscripts read the whole passage as follows: “to recall the exiles of pious priests, the rewards of the faithless,” and so on. The sufferings endured by Catholic bishops under Arian emperors are described elegantly, in addition to the ecclesiastical historians, by Gregory of Nazianzus in his Oration to the 150 Bishops, his Oration against the Arians, and elsewhere.]

Have we not heard that, from the regions of Thrace through Ripensian Dacia and Moesia, and throughout all Valeria of the Pannonias, that entire frontier trembled alike at sacrilegious voices and barbarian assaults? What could so savage a neighborhood bring upon us? Or how could the Roman state have been secure under such a guard?

**141.** But now, almighty God, we have washed away sufficiently and more than sufficiently, through our exile and our blood, the deaths of the confessors, the exiles of the priests, and the outrage of so great an impiety.

[Note: The Roman edition, together with one or two manuscripts, reads “through our destruction”; the old edition and the remaining manuscripts read “through our exile,” which is not inappropriate. Ambrose speaks here in the person of the Catholics, many of whom were certainly driven from their homeland by these barbarian incursions.]

It has become sufficiently clear that those who violated the faith cannot remain safe. Turn back, Lord, and raise up the banners of your faith.

**142.** Here it is not military eagles, nor the flight of birds, that lead the army, but your name and worship, Lord Jesus. Here it is not an unbelieving land, but the land that habitually sends forth confessors—Italy, once tested but never changed—which long ago you defended from the barbarian enemy and have now also avenged.

[Note: Several manuscripts read, “not some religion,” which is less harmonious.]

Here there is no wavering mind in the Emperor, but steadfast faith.

**143.** Now show an evident sign of your majesty, so that he who believes you to be the true Lord of powers and commander of the heavenly host, and who believes you to be the true power and wisdom of God—not temporal and created, but everlasting, as it is written, “the power and divinity of God” (1 Cor. 1:24)—may, supported by the help of your majesty, earn the trophies of his faith.

# BOOK THREE

## CHAPTER ONE

Ambrose first explains why he undertakes to treat more fully in these books matters handled more briefly in the preceding books. He answers the objection that he has used myths by appealing to the example of Scripture, which mentions various poetic subjects, especially the Sirens, figures of pleasures. Christians must be drawn away from them both by Paul’s words and by Christ’s deeds.

**1.** Since, most merciful Emperor, you had commanded me to write something about the faith for your instruction, and since you yourself had encouraged me, even in person, when I was hesitant, I therefore composed, as though standing in battle order, only two little books, in which I might point out certain roads and paths of faith.

**2.** But since the perverse disposition of certain people, intent on sowing questions, challenges me to produce a more copious work,

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads *uberiori configi*, “to be struck down by a more abundant work”; the old edition and several manuscripts read *uberiori confligi*, “to contend with a more extensive work”; the remaining witnesses read as in the text.]

your pious concern and mercy also calls me to other matters, wishing to test in greater things the one whom you approved in small ones. I have therefore decided to develop somewhat more fully what was treated briefly above, lest we appear to have abandoned it through lack of confidence in our assertion rather than presented it with the assurance of faith.

**3.** And since we introduced a comparison with the name of the Hydra and the shore of Scylla (Book I above, chapter 4), in order to show that either the perfidy with its reborn growths must be avoided or its notorious shipwrecks,

[Note: Amerbach and Erasmus read, “the deity of the Hydra . . . the heat of the discussion”; Gill and the Roman edition, “the name of the Hydra . . . the heat of the discussion”; the manuscripts agree with us, except for one Thuan manuscript, which reads, “or the remaining shoots . . . or the wreckage of the ship,” and so forth. By the “color of the discussion” is meant its ornament and charm.]

if anyone thinks it improper that such a rhetorical coloring should be drawn from poetic myths, and, having found nothing to criticize in the faith, finds something to reproach in the language, let him acknowledge that not only the poets’ ideas but even their verses have been inserted into the divine Scriptures.

**4.** For where else does that saying come from, “For we are also his offspring” (Acts 17:28), which Paul uses, instructed by prophetic usage? The prophetic sequence of speech does not shrink from mentioning giants (Num. 13:34) or the Valley of the Titans (2 Sam. 5:18). Isaiah too mentioned Sirens and daughters of sparrows (Isa. 43:20). And Jeremiah, speaking of Babylonia, said that “the daughters of Sirens will dwell there” (Jer. 27:39), to show that the enticements of Babylon—that is, of worldly confusion—are to be compared with the fables of ancient wantonness,

[Note: In place of *lasciviae*, “wantonness,” one manuscript, the Thuan manuscript, has here and below *fallaciae*, “deceit.”]

which, like a certain sweet-sounding but deadly song on the rocky shore of this life, seemed designed to ensnare the minds of the young. Even the wise man is introduced by the Greek poet himself (Homer, *Odyssey* XII) as having passed them by, surrounded by certain bonds of his wisdom. Thus, before the coming of Christ, it was judged difficult for even the stronger not to be captured by the attractions of splendid pleasure!

**5.** [Elsewhere, chapter 2.] But if that poet judged the enticement of worldly wantonness to be destructive to human minds and liable to cause shipwreck, what ought we to think, to whom it has been written: “Make no provision for the flesh in its desires” (Rom. 13:14)? And elsewhere: “I chastise my body and bring it into subjection, lest, after preaching to others, I myself should become disqualified” (1 Cor. 9:27).

**6.** For Christ brought us salvation not through luxury but through fasting. Nor did he fast in order to earn his own grace, but for our instruction. Nor was he overcome by bodily weakness so that he might hunger; rather, by hungering he demonstrated the reality of the body he had assumed, teaching that he had assumed not only a body but also the weaknesses of our body, as it is written: “He himself took our weaknesses and bore our diseases” (Isa. 53:4).

## CHAPTER II

What belongs to the body was assumed by Christ for our sake and must not be attributed to his divinity. In this respect he is the Most High; whoever denies this attributes the incarnation to the Father. When God is said to be alone, or alone to possess immortality, this must also be understood of Christ, both to avoid the impiety just mentioned and because the Son’s operation is asserted to be the same as the Father’s.

**7.** It belongs to the body—that is, it belongs to us—that he hungered; it belongs to us that he wept and was sorrowful even unto death. Why are things that belong to us attributed to the divinity? It belongs to the body that he is also said to have been made. Thus you have it: “Mother Zion will say, ‘A man, yes, a man was made in her, and the Most High himself founded her’” (Ps. 86:5). He says, “A man was made,” not “God was made.”

**8.** Who, then, is both the Most High and man, except the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for us (1 Tim. 2:5–6)? This certainly pertains to the incarnation: our redemption came through blood, forgiveness through power, and life through grace. As the Most High, he gives; as man, he prays. One thing belongs to the Creator, another to the Redeemer. Although distinct, these are benefits of one author; for it was fitting that the one who created us should redeem us.

**9.** Who, then, can deny that Christ is signified as the Most High? For whoever thinks otherwise attributes the mystery of the incarnation to God the Father. But there can be no doubt on this point, since elsewhere he said of the mystery of the Passion: “The Most High gave his voice, and the earth was shaken” (Ps. 17:14). And in the Gospel you have: “And you, child, will be called the prophet of the Most High; for you will go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways” (Luke 1:76). Who is the Most High? The Son of God. Therefore Christ is the Most High God.

**10.** Likewise, when God is said to be alone, the Son of God is not thereby excluded. For the one who is Most High is alone, as it is written: “Let them know that your name is Lord, that you alone are Most High over all the earth” (Ps. 82:19).

**11.** Hence that objection too has been refuted, which they habitually twist into a charge: that it is written of God, “who alone has immortality and dwells in inaccessible light” (1 Tim. 6:16). For this is written of God, a name that is common to the Father and the Son.

**12.** For if, wherever they read “God,” they deny that the Son is also designated, they will both be impious by denying the power of divinity to the Son and seem, with Sabellian impiety, to assert that the Father became incarnate. Let them explain how they can understand without impiety what the Apostle says of the Father: “In whom you were also raised through faith in the operation of God, who raised him from the dead” (Col. 2:12). Let them also observe what follows and what they thereby encounter: “And when you were dead in trespasses and in the uncircumcision of your flesh, he made you alive together with him, forgiving you all trespasses, wiping out the bond written against us in decrees, which was contrary to us; and he took it out of the way, fastening it to the cross, stripping off the flesh” (ibid., 13–14).

**13.** Therefore God the Father alone is not to be understood as the one who raised the flesh, but the Son also, whose temple was raised.

[Note: Several manuscripts read, “Therefore, if God,” which is incorrect unless the words are understood as a question or exclamation, with the conjunction *and* removed.]

The one who raised it certainly also gave it life; the one who gave it life also forgave sins; the one who forgave sins also removed the bond; the one who removed the bond fastened it to the cross; the one who fastened it to the cross stripped off the flesh. But the Father did not strip off flesh, for the Father did not become flesh; rather, the Word became flesh, as we read (John 1:14). You see, therefore, that when the Arians separate the Son from the Father, they fall into the danger of saying that the Father suffered.

**14.** We, however, easily demonstrate that this was said of the Son’s operation. For he himself raised his own body, as he himself said: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19). He himself also gives us life together with his body: “For just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wills” (John 5:21). He himself forgave sins, saying: “Your sins are forgiven you” (Luke 5:20). He himself fastened the bond to the cross, having been crucified through the suffering of his body. No one else stripped off flesh except the Son of God, who clothed himself in flesh. The God who accomplished the work of our resurrection is therefore the one signified here.

## CHAPTER III

The Apostle confirms that the Son must not be separated from the Father, since it is also appropriate to the Son to be blessed, alone powerful, and immortal—by nature, not by grace, by which even the angels are immortal—and to dwell in inaccessible light. After explaining how the final expression is to be understood, he shows how the Father and the Son can alike be called “alone.”

**15.** Therefore, when you read “God,” do not separate the Father; do not separate the Son, because the divinity of the Father and of the Son is one and the same. Thus do not separate them even where you read that he is “blessed and alone powerful.” For this is said of God, as you have it: “I charge you before God, who gives life to all things” (1 Tim. 6:13). But Christ also gives life; therefore the name of God belongs equally to the Father and the Son, since the effect of their operation is also the same.

[Note: The printed editions read, “for it is said of him”; the manuscripts read, “for it is said of God.”]

Let us pursue the rest. “I charge you,” he says, “before God, who gives life to all things, and Christ Jesus.”

**16.** The Word is also in God, as it is written: “In God I will praise the Word” (Ps. 55:11). In God is his everlasting power, Jesus.

[Note: The final word, “Jesus,” has been omitted in most manuscripts.]

Thus, by the name of God, he testified to the unity of divinity; by the name of Christ, to the mystery of the incarnation.

**17.** Finally, to show that he had been speaking of Christ’s incarnation, he added: “Who bore witness to the good confession before Pontius Pilate, so that you may keep the commandment without stain until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ, whom at the proper time the blessed and only powerful one will reveal, the King of kings and Lord of lords, who alone possesses immortality and dwells in inaccessible light, whom no human being has seen nor can see” (1 Tim. 6:13 ff.). These things, then, were written of God, whose name, dignity, and truth are shared by the Son.

**18.** Why, then, is the Son separated here, when all these things also belong to the Son? Or, if they do not belong to him, deny that he is God, so that you may deny what belongs to God.

[Note: Several manuscripts read, “as you deny what follows from God.”]

He cannot be denied as blessed, since he gives blessedness: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven” (Ps. 32:1). He cannot be denied as blessed, since he grants sound doctrine, as it is written: “which is according to the gospel of the glory of the blessed God” (1 Tim. 1:11). He cannot be denied as powerful, for the Father says of him: “I have placed help upon one who is powerful” (Ps. 89:20). And who would dare deny his immortality, when he himself has bestowed immortality even upon others, as it is written of the wisdom of God: “Through her I shall possess immortality” (Wis. 8:13)?

**19.** But his immortality is one thing, and ours another. Fragile things must not be compared with divine things. There is one substance of divinity that does not know how to die. Therefore the Apostle, although he knew that the soul and the angels are immortal, proclaimed that God alone possesses immortality. For the soul also dies: “The soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezek. 18:20). Nor is an angel immortal by nature, since his immortality rests upon the will of the Creator.

20. Nor should you draw an objection from the fact that Gabriel does not die, nor Raphael [Note: Uriel does not die is absent from not a few manuscripts; but since it is found in certain others and in all the printed editions, there is nothing to prevent our regarding it as Ambrose’s own wording. For although the learned J. B. Thiersius, in his letter to Luc Acherius, demonstrated by several arguments—above all by the testimonies of Charlemagne, Haito of Basel, the Council of Orléans, and the Second Roman Council under Pope Zacharias—that this Uriel ought to be expunged from the list of angels, nevertheless, since Ambrose, as Thiersius acknowledges, repeatedly cited the Fourth Book of Esdras as canonical, where that name occurs several times, there is no doubt that here too he could have followed its authority. For what the learned man adds there—that Uriel was perhaps numbered by the Doctor among the reprobate angels—is wholly foreign to his intention. In any case, in this passage the holy Bishop beautifully and wisely distinguishes natural immortality from immortality received by participation: he assigns the former to God alone and reserves it for him, while attributing the latter only to the angels; in this Augustine later followed him as well.] Uriel does not die. For even in them the capacity of nature is liable to defect, though it is not subject to discipline. Every rational creature receives incidental conditions and is subject to judgment. In these incidental conditions there are punishment and the penalty of judgment, corruption, and advancement. Hence Ecclesiastes also says: “For God will bring every work into judgment” (Eccl. XII, 14). Therefore every creature is capable of corruption and death, even if it does not die or sin; and it does not possess this capacity from immortal nature, but from discipline or grace, provided it does not turn itself toward vices in any respect. Thus one immortality is that which is bestowed; another is that which is always without the capacity for change.

21. Is Christ’s divinity denied to be immortal because, in the flesh, he tasted death for all? [p. 501] Gabriel would then be better than Christ, because Gabriel did not die while Christ died. But “a servant is not above his master” (Matt. X, 24); the weakness of the flesh is one thing, the eternity of divinity another: death belongs to the flesh, immortality to power. If divinity prevented the flesh—which by nature was certainly subject to corruption—from seeing corruption, how could divinity itself die?

22. How, moreover, does the Son not dwell in inaccessible light, since the Son is in the bosom of the Father, while the Father is light and the Son himself is also light, because “God is light” (John I, 9)? Or, if we suppose that there is another inaccessible light besides that of the Godhead, surely light is not better than the Father, so that he who, as it is written, is both with the Father and in the Father would not be in the light (ibid., 2). Therefore let them not separate the Son when they read of God alone; nor let them separate the Father when they read of the Son alone.

23. The Son is not without the Father on earth, and do you suppose that the Father is without the Son in heaven? When I say that the Son is in the flesh, or on earth, I speak according to the times of the Gospel; for now “we know Christ no longer according to the flesh” (II Cor. V, 16). Thus the Son is in the flesh, and is not alone, according to what is written: “And I am not alone, because the Father is with me” (John VIII, 16); and do you suppose that the Father is alone in the light?

24. But lest you think this an argument [Note: Erasmus and Gill, in the margin, and the Roman edition in the main text, read “think this a clever argument”; the same Erasmus and Gill in the main text, as well as Amerbach with all the manuscripts, read “think this an argument.” This is entirely correct, since Ambrose can repeatedly be observed using *argumentum* for a proof devised by human ingenuity and cleverness, to which he ordinarily opposes the testimony of Scripture, as here.] receive also the testimony: “No one,” he says, “has ever seen God, except the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father; he has declared him” (John I, 18). How is the Father alone, if the Son is in the Father’s bosom? How does he declare the one whom he does not see? The Father, therefore, is not alone.

25. Now receive both the Father alone and the Son alone. The Father is alone because there is no other Father; the Son is alone because there is no other Son; God is alone because the Trinity has one divinity.

## CHAPTER IV

Christ is narrated as having been made only according to the flesh; for, in order to redeem human beings, he did not need assistance, just as he did not need it in order to raise himself, whereas others required prayer in order to raise the dead. Although he himself prayed, this must be referred to his humanity; his divinity, however, must be judged from the fact that he commanded—in which respect the devil is placed above the Arians. After explaining why the Son is called “powerful,” the argument is brought to its conclusion.

26. [Elsewhere, Chapter III.] It is therefore sufficiently clear both that the Father alone is not God without the Son and that the Son alone is not understood as God without the Father, because the Son of God is read to have been made according to the flesh, not according to divine generation [Note: This clause—“because he was made according to the flesh”—was absent from the ancient edition and from several manuscripts; the first Roman edition restored it. Several of our manuscripts differ from that edition only in reading *factus legitur* (“is read to have been made”) instead of *factus intelligitur* (“is understood to have been made”).]

27. In what respect he was made, he asserted through the mouth of the holy patriarch, saying: “For my soul is filled with evils, and my life has drawn near to hell. I am counted among those who descend into the pit; I have become like a man without assistance, free among the dead” (Ps. LXXXVII, 4ff.). Here too, he says, “I have become like a man,” not like God. “My soul is filled with evils”: the soul, certainly, not the divinity. He was made in that respect in which he was subject to the realm of the dead; he was made in that respect in which he was counted among others, for divinity rejects the likeness implied by comparison. And yet, even in that flesh subject to death, observe the majesty of divinity in Christ. Although he was made like a man and made as flesh, he was nevertheless made free among the dead, and free without assistance.

28. But how does the Son here say that he was without assistance, when it was said above (chap. 2): “I have placed assistance upon the mighty” (Ps. LXXXVIII, 20)? Here, therefore, distinguish the natures. The flesh has assistance; divinity does not. He is free, then, because he knew nothing of the bonds of death—not captured by the underworld, but the one who worked in the underworld. He is without assistance because he saved his people himself, not through a messenger or an ambassador. For how could he seek assistance for raising his own body, when he raised others?

29. And although human beings too have raised the dead, they did not do so by their own power, but in the name of Christ. It is one thing to ask and another to command; one thing to earn and another to bestow.

30. Elijah therefore raised the dead, but he prayed; he did not command (III Kings XVII, 21–22). Elisha raised the dead [Note: Three manuscripts read “conformed to the dead man, by the touch of the body”; one manuscript, however, reads the words that immediately follow in such a way that the sense is: “so that he might be a type of the one who was to come, who, sent in the likeness of sinful flesh, would raise the dead, having himself also been buried in human flesh.”] by being conformed to the dead man; the touch of Elisha’s own dead body also raised a man, so that he might be a type of the one who was to come—sent in the likeness of sinful flesh, and, himself buried, to raise the dead (IV Kings XIII–XIV).

31. Peter too, when he healed Aeneas, said: “In the name of Jesus the Nazarene, arise and walk” (Acts II, 6). He did not say “in his own name,” but “in the name of Christ.” “Arise” is the word of one commanding; but the confidence rests on merit, not presumption of power, and the authority of the command rests on the working of the name, not on his own power. What, then, do the Arians say? In the name of Christ Peter commands, yet they do not want the Son of God to have commanded, but to have asked.

32. But it is written that he asked. Learn the distinction. He asks as the Son of Man; he commands as the Son of God. Do you not grant to the Son of God what even the devil granted, while you detract from him with greater sacrilege? The devil says: “If you are the Son of God, tell this stone to become bread” (Luke IV, 3). He says, “Command”; you say, “Entreat.” He believes that, when the Son of God commands, the nature of the elements and of created things can be changed; you believe that, unless the Son of God asks, even his will is not accomplished. The devil thinks the Son of God must be judged by his power; you, by his weakness. The devil’s temptations are more bearable than Arius’s arguments.

33. Nor should it trouble you that he called the Son of Man powerful, when you read that the “Lord of glory” was crucified (I Cor. II, 2). What power is greater than to have dominion over the heavenly powers (Eph. I, 21)? He possessed it who commanded Thrones, Dominations, and Angels. For although he was among beasts, as it is written (Mark I, 13), angels nevertheless ministered to him, so that you may recognize that incarnation is one thing and power another. According to the flesh, then, he is tempted by beasts; according to his dignity, he is adored by angels.

34. [p. 503] We have therefore learned that he was made a human being, and that this must be referred to the human being. Elsewhere too you have: “Who was made for him from the seed of David” (Rom. I, 3); according to the flesh, certainly, he was made from the seed of David. But as God he was born from God before the ages.

## CHAPTER V

He teaches by examples drawn from Scripture itself that “made” does not always mean the same as “created.” From this he concludes that one must not quibble over the letter in the manner of the Jews, whom he nevertheless proves to be less evil than the heretics; and he again confirms the proposition previously set forth.

35. Yet “made” does not always refer to creation; for it is written: “Lord, you have been made our refuge” (Ps. LXXXIX, 1); and: “You have been made my salvation” (Ps. CXVII, 14). This does not define or declare creation or production; rather, he is said to have been made my refuge and turned toward me for salvation, just as the Apostle also said: “Who was made for us wisdom from God, and righteousness, sanctification, and redemption” (I Cor. I, 30). He said that he was made for us, not created from the Father. Finally, he explained later how he could say that he was made wisdom for us, saying: “But we speak God’s wisdom in a mystery, the wisdom hidden, which God predestined before the ages for our glory, which none of the rulers of this age knew. For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (I Cor. II, 7–8). Here the mystery of the Passion is expressed; the sequence of eternal generation is certainly not being declared.

36. My wisdom, then, is the Lord’s cross; my redemption is the Lord’s death. For we were redeemed with precious blood, as the Apostle Peter said (I Pet. I, 19). With his own blood, therefore, the Lord redeemed us as a human being; and, as God, the same one forgave sins.

37. Let us not therefore set traps in certain words or hunt after verbal snares, interpreting a word that is thought by the ungodly to signify something else according not to what its meaning expresses, but to what the letter displays. Thus the Jews perished, because they despise the depths of meaning and follow the bare words. “For the letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (II Cor. III, 6).

38. And yet, between two grave sacrileges, it is perhaps more detestable to refer to divinity what belongs to the flesh [Note: Some manuscripts read “than to refer to the flesh,” etc.] than to refer to the letter what belongs to the spirit. The Jews were afraid to believe that God had flesh, and therefore lost the grace of redemption, because they reject the cause of salvation. These men, however, bring the majesty of divinity down to the weaknesses of the flesh. The Jews who crucified the Lord’s flesh are detestable; yet I consider those more detestable who believed that Christ’s divinity was subjected to the cross. Finally, the one who often dealt with the Jews said: “Avoid a heretic after the first correction” (Titus III, 10).

39. Nor, without injury to the Father [Note: Amerbach and several manuscripts read “that wisdom was made for us”; the remaining editions and manuscripts read “that he was made,” which is better, since it refers back to the Apostle’s preceding words, “who was made for us wisdom,” etc.], do they transfer by a sacrilegious interpretation to that inexpressible generation of Christ, subject to no times or moments, the statement that he was made wisdom for us. For, apart from the fact that injury to the Son is an insult to the Father, these sacrileges also proceed against the Father, of whom it is written: “Let God be true, and every human being a liar” (Rom. III, 4). Or, if they think this was said of the Son, they do not indeed prejudice the matter of his generation; yet by the authority of this reading they confess what they deny: that God, and true God, is meant.

40. It would be lengthy to enumerate each instance in which we read that something was made, not by nature but by grace. Moses too says: “He was made my helper and protector for salvation” (Exod. XV, 2). David says: “Be for me a protecting God and a house of refuge, that you may save me” (Ps. XXX, 3). Isaiah says: “He was made a helper to every lowly city” (Isa. XXV, 4). The saints certainly do not say to God, “You were created,” but, “By your grace you were made our protector and helper.”

## CHAPTER VI

To refute an objection drawn from John, he first demonstrates that the Arian interpretation gives support to the Manichaeans. He then explains the various ways of distinguishing the words of the same passage and clearly proves that it cannot in any way be referred to the divine substance without injury to the Father; finally, he sets forth the passage’s true meaning.

41. Hence there is no need to fear that statement which the Arians habitually construct by a savage interpretation, saying that the Word of God was made, because, they say, it is written: “What was made in him is life” (John I, 4) [Note: All the printed editions and some manuscripts read “was life”; several other, better manuscripts read “is life.”]

42. First, let them understand that, if they refer “what was made” to the divine substance, they entangle themselves in the questions of the Manichaeans. For the Manichaeans object: If what was made in him is life, then there is something that was not made in him and is death, so that they may wickedly introduce two principles. But the Church condemns this.

43. In the second place, how can they prove that the Evangelist pronounced the words in this way? [Note: That the Alexandrian and Egyptian interpreters are meant can be learned from what the holy Doctor recalls in his Exposition of Psalm XXXVI, no. 35. From these two passages it may be understood that there were two principal ways of reading this text. The first enclosed an absolute sense in the words “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made that was made”; the second allowed the sense to end only with the following words, “what was made.” Nor were there lacking those who extended the sense as far as the words “what was made in him.” Gregory of Nyssa followed this distinction in Book I Against Eunomius, as did Epiphanius in the *Ancoratus*, no. 75, where he sharply criticizes the first reading as injurious to the Holy Spirit; something may perhaps be said about this in Book I *On the Holy Spirit*. Augustine accepts the first reading but distinguishes its second part in this way: “What was made in him was life.” He considers absurd the alternative subdivision of the same part, which places a comma after the words “in him.” See Book V, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chap. 14, and Tractate I on John, no. 16, as well as the commentators on the same passage.] Most learned and faithful interpreters pronounce it this way: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made that was made.” Others read it this way: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.” Finally, they pronounce “What was made,” and then add “in him,” that is: Whatever was made is in him. What does “in him” mean? The Apostle teaches when he says: “For in him we are, and live, and move” (Acts XVII, 28).

44. Yet even if they pronounce it in whatever way they wish, they cannot here slander God the Word if they want to refer “what was made” to his substance, without also slandering God the Father, of whom it is written: “Whoever does the truth comes to the light, so that his works may be made manifest, because they have been done in God” (John III, 21). Here we read that human works have been done in God, yet we cannot refer them to the divine substance. Rather, we either understand them to have been made through him, as in the Apostle’s statement that all things were created through him and in him, “and he is before all things, and all things hold together in him” (Col. I, 16); or, as the testimony of the present reading teaches [Note: The more reliable manuscripts read this way; others, together with all the printed editions, read “the reading of the testimony.” Again, where we, with all the manuscripts, read “chastity, piety,” all the printed editions read instead “charity, piety,” etc.], we must regard as having been made in God the virtues by which the fruit of eternal life is acquired: chastity, piety, religious devotion, faith, and other things of this kind, which have been made in accordance with God’s will.

45. Therefore, just as they were made in the will of God the Father, so also in the will and power of Christ, as we read: “Created in Christ for good works” (Eph. II, 10); and in the Psalm: “Let peace be made in your power” (Ps. CXXI, 7); and elsewhere: “You made all things in wisdom” (Ps. CIII, 24). He says, “You made them in wisdom,” not “You made wisdom.” For since all things were made in wisdom, while Christ is the wisdom of God (I Cor. I, 24)—not an accidental quality, but subsisting and enduring forever—if wisdom was made, it was made in a condition inferior to that of all things, because wisdom could not make itself. Therefore, if “made” is frequently referred to something rather than to nature, “created” too is referred to a cause.

## CHAPTER VII

The statement of Solomon, “The Lord created me,” is shown to signify Christ’s incarnation for the redemption of the Father’s works. This is explained from the words of the Son himself; and he shows that “beginning” may also be understood of instruction in the virtues, of all whose paths the Lord is demonstrated to have opened for us and truly to have initiated.

46. [Elsewhere, Chapter IV.] Hence we understand that what is written concerning the Lord’s incarnation—“The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways, for his works” (Prov. VIII, 22)—signifies that the Lord Jesus was created from the Virgin for the redemption of the Father’s works. There can be no doubt that this was spoken of the mystery of the incarnation, since the Lord assumed flesh for the sake of liberating his works from the service of corruption, so that through the suffering of his body he might destroy the one who held the power of death. The flesh of Christ exists for the sake of the works; his divinity was before the works, because he himself is before all things, and all things hold together in him.

47. The divinity, therefore, was not made for the works; rather, the works were made for the divinity, as the Apostle declared when he said that all things are for the Son of God. Thus you have: “It was fitting for him, through whom are all things and for whom are all things, in bringing many sons to glory, to perfect the author of their salvation through suffering” (Heb. II, 10). Did he not clearly explain that the Son of God, who created all things for the sake of his divinity, later undertook suffering for the salvation of the people, the assumption of flesh, and the acceptance of death?

48. What works he was created from the Virgin for, the Lord himself showed when he healed the blind man, saying: “I must work the works of him who sent me” (John IX, 4). And he added, so that we might believe this was said of his incarnation: “As long as I am in this world, I am the light of this world” (ibid., 5). For as a human being he is in this world for a time; as God, he always is. Elsewhere too he says: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the world” (Matt. XXVIII, 20).

49. Nor does any difficulty remain concerning “beginning,” since, when questioned in the flesh, “Who are you?” he answered: “The beginning, which I am also speaking to you” (John VIII, 25) [Note: The old edition, together with several manuscripts, reads “refers to the eternity of the divine substance.”]. This refers not only to the substance of eternal divinity, but also to the instruction of the virtues. By this he proved himself eternal God, because he is himself the beginning of all things, and the author of every virtue, because he is the head of the Church, as it is written: “For he is the head of the body, the Church; he is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead” (Col. I, 18).

50. It is therefore clear that “the beginning of his ways” was also spoken of the incarnation and must be referred to the mystery of the body he assumed. For this reason he assumed flesh: to lay out for us a path to heaven. Hence he says: “I ascend to my Father and your Father, my God and your God” (John XX, 17). And, so that you may know that the almighty Father prescribed his ways to the Son according to the incarnation, you have in Zechariah the Angel’s words to Jesus dressed in filthy garments: “Thus says the almighty Lord: If you walk in my ways and keep my commandments” (Zech. III, 7). What is that filthy garment except the assumption of flesh?

51. The Lord’s ways, then, are like paths of a good life, directed by Christ, who says: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John XIV, 6). The way above is therefore the power of God; for Christ is our way. It is a good way, which opened the kingdoms of heaven to believers. The Lord’s ways are straight ways, as it is written: “Make your ways known to me, O Lord” (Ps. XXIV, 4). Chastity is a way; faith is a way; abstinence is a way. There is a way of virtue, and there is also a way of iniquity; for it is written: “And see whether there is any way of iniquity in me” (Ps. CXXXVIII, 24).

52. Christ, therefore, is the beginning of our virtue. He is the beginning of integrity, who taught virgins not to await masculine intercourse but to dedicate the integrity of mind and body more holily to the Spirit than to a husband (II Cor. XI, 2). Christ is the beginning of frugality, who became poor although he was rich (II Cor. VIII, 9). Christ is the beginning of patience, who, when cursed, did not curse in return, and when struck, did not strike back (I Pet. II, 23). Christ is the beginning of humility, who took the form of a servant (Phil. II, 7), although in the majesty of his power he was equal to God the Father. From him every virtue received its beginning.

53. And therefore, so that we might learn these kinds of virtue, the Son was given to us, “whose beginning is upon his shoulders” (Isa. IX, 6). That beginning is the Lord’s cross: the beginning of strength, by which the way was opened for the saints and martyrs to the suffering of the sacred contest.

## CHAPTER VIII

The verse recently cited from Isaiah is explained with reference to Christ’s humanity and divinity, and by it various heresies are shown to be overthrown.

54. Isaiah saw this beginning, and therefore said: “A child was born” [Note: All the printed editions and a few manuscripts read here and below, “A child was born for us”; more manuscripts omit “for us,” which is better, as the context shows.], “a Son was given to us.” The Magi saw it too, and therefore, when they beheld the little one in the manger, they worshiped him, saying, “A child was born”; when they saw the star, they proclaimed, “A Son was given to us” (Matt. II, 11). One gift is from earth, another gift from heaven, yet one person is perfect in both: without any diminution of divinity and without any lessening of human nature. They worshiped one person and offered gifts to that same person, showing that he who appeared in the manger was himself the Lord of heaven.

55. Distinguish the force of each word: “A child was born; a Son was given to us.” Although he was born from the Father, he was not born for us but given to us, because the Son did not exist for our sake; rather, we exist for the Son. For he was not born for us who was born before us and is the creator of the whole creation; nor is he now born for the first time, who always existed and was in the beginning [Note: Several manuscripts read, “as he was in the beginning.”]; rather, that which did not exist is born for us. The angel likewise said to the shepherds that he had been born, as you have it written: “For today a Savior has been born for you, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David” (Luke II, 11). Therefore, what did not exist was born for us: the child from the Virgin, the body from Mary. This came after us; the Son came before us.

56. Other codices read: “A child was born for us; a Son was given to us”—that is, he who was the Son of God was born here from Mary as a child for us and was given to us [Note: Several manuscripts read here, “A child was born from Mary,” etc.]. Hear the Prophet saying that he was given: “And give us your salvation” (Ps. LXXXIV, 8). What is above us is given; what is from heaven is given, just as we also read concerning the Spirit: “The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Rom. V, 5).

57. But observe how this passage extinguishes many heresies. “A child was born for us,” not for the Jews; for us, not for the Manichaeans; for us, not for the Marcionites. The Prophet says “for us,” that is, for believers, not unbelievers. In his mercy he was indeed born for all, but the faithlessness of the heretics caused the one who was born for all not to be born for all. The light of day is commanded to rise upon the good and the wicked, but it is not seen by those who do not see it (Matt. V, 15).

58. Therefore, just as the child was not born for everyone but for the faithful, so the Son was not given to the unbelieving but to the faithful. He was given to us, not to the Photinians; for they say that the Son of God was not given to us but was born among us from the beginning. He was given to us, not to the Sabellians; for they do not want the Son to have been given, asserting that the Father and the Son are the same person. He was given to us, not to the Arians; for they too do not have the Son as given for salvation, but as sent because of weakness. They do not have the Counselor, whom they think did not know the future; they do not have the Son, whom they do not think eternal, although it is written concerning the Word of God that he was in the beginning, and elsewhere: “In the beginning was the Word” (John I, 2). Finally, to return to the example at hand: “In the beginning,” he says, before he made the earth, before he made the abysses and before he brought forth the springs of water, “before all the hills he begot me” (Prov. VIII, 23ff.) [Note: “Before he made the abysses” was missing from the printed editions; we have restored it from the manuscripts.].

## CHAPTER IX

Ambrose resolves the difficulty arising from the passage of Solomon cited above, making clear that there the past may also be understood as future and that a twofold nature is signified in Christ.

59. Perhaps you will say: How have I recalled that “The Lord created me” was spoken of Christ’s incarnation, when the world was created before Christ’s incarnation? Consider that it is customary in the divine Scriptures both to speak of future things as though they were past and to signify in Christ a twofold substance, of divinity and of flesh, lest anyone either deny his divinity or deny his flesh.

60. For just as you have in Isaiah, “A child was born for us, and a Son was given to us” (Isa. IX, 6), so here too he first mentioned the creation of the flesh and then added an assertion of divinity, so that you might know that there are not two Christs but one: he who was generated from the Father before the ages and created from the Virgin in the last times. That is: “I am the one created from a human being, created for a purpose, who was generated before the ages.”

61. Finally, when he was about to say, “The Lord created me,” he prefaced it with: “I will recall what has been from the age.” When he was about to say, “He begot,” he prefaced it with: “In the beginning, before he made the earth, before all the hills he begot me.” When “before” is said, it extends backward without limit and without any definition. Hence: “Before Abraham was, I am” (John VIII, 58)—certainly not after Adam; and “before Lucifer” (Ps. CIX, 3)—certainly not after the angels. But when he said “before,” he did not place himself within anything; rather, he said that everything was within him. For this is how the divine Scriptures customarily signify God’s eternity. Elsewhere too you have: “Before the mountains were made and the earth and the world were formed, from age to age you are” (Ps. LXXXIX, 2).

62. Generation, therefore, is before all things; creation is among all things and for the sake of all things. Born from the Father above the Law, made from Mary under the Law.

## CHAPTER X

In resolving the Baptist’s words from which they argued that Christ was made even before the incarnation, he first indicates that they can be referred to predestination; nevertheless, from what precedes he proves that they must be understood of the incarnation. Proceeding from this to mystical matters, he declares that Christ preceded John in dignity and merit—especially since he alone was the Bridegroom of the Church, whose type had been expressed in the history of Ruth, even with Moses excluded; and although he did not entirely neglect the Synagogue, he alone called the Church.

63. [Elsewhere, Chapter V.] But it is written: “After me comes a man who was made before me, because he was before me.” Hence they say: “Behold, he who existed was made.” Let us weigh the words themselves. “After me,” he says, “comes a man” (John I, 30). The one who comes, then, is a man; the one who was made is the same. “Man,” however, is the name of a sex; sex belongs not to divinity but to human nature.

64. I could therefore say: He existed in the foreknowledge of the body, but in the eternity of power; for the Church existed, and the saints were predestined before the ages. But that is not what I say here. Rather, I assert that “made” refers not to divinity but to the nature of the incarnation, as John himself said: “This is the one of whom I said: After me comes a man who was made before me.”

65. Since, as I said above, he had proposed a twofold substance in Christ, so that you might understand both divinity and flesh [Note: Several manuscripts read here, “a definite flesh.”], at this point he began with the flesh. For the divine Scriptures have a fluid customary order: sometimes they begin with Christ’s divinity and descend to the mysteries of the incarnation; sometimes they take their beginning from the humility of the incarnation and rise to the glory of divinity, as frequently in the prophets, the Evangelists, and Paul. Here too, in accordance with the custom just mentioned, he began with the Lord’s incarnation, intending to speak of his divinity—not to confuse human and divine things, but to distinguish them. The Arians, however, like Jewish wine merchants, mix water with wine, because they confuse divine and human generation, referring to deity what was spoken of the flesh.

66. Nor am I troubled by what they appear likely to object: that in the preceding passage the word “man” does not occur. For it reads: “The one who comes after me.” But let them observe what he placed before it there: “The Word became flesh” (John I, 14). Therefore he did not add “man,” because he had said “flesh.” Through “flesh” we understand man there, and through “man” we understand flesh. Thus, because he had said, “The Word became flesh,” it was unnecessary to name “man” here, since he had already indicated him by the expression “flesh.”

67. Following the same example, later he first mentioned the Lamb who would take away the sins of the world; and so that you might understand that the one previously mentioned had become incarnate, he said: “This is the one of whom I spoke earlier: After me comes a man who was made before me” (ibid., 29)—that is, “I said ‘man,’ not ‘God was made.’” But to declare that he was himself incarnate, since he existed before the ages, and to prevent us from believing there were two sons, he said: “Because he was before me.” For if he had referred “was made” to divine generation, what need was there to add a third statement and repeat what he had said above? But because he had previously spoken only of the incarnation—“After me comes a man who was made before me”—he therefore added, “Because he was before me,” since the eternity of divinity had to be expressed. This is the reason for his precedence: the one who is the eternal power of his own Father is rightly seen to have been placed before him.

68. Yet the richness of spiritual understanding allows us to range more widely and to press the Arians to a conclusion, since they want “was made” here to refer not to the man but to divinity. What can they hold on to, when the Baptist said: “After me comes the one who was made before me”? That is: he was made above my merit, above my grace; later in the time of the flesh, venerable in the honor of divinity. “After me he came” refers to time; “he was before me,” to eternity; “he was made before me,” to honor—for even the mystery of the Incarnation is above human grace.

69. Finally, he expressed below what he had connected with this, saying: “After me comes a man whose sandal I am not worthy to carry” (John I, 27), explaining the excellence of dignity [Note: Some manuscripts read “of divinity”; the more appropriate reading in other manuscripts and in all the printed editions is “of dignity”], not the eternity of divine generation. This pertains so fully to the incarnation that he first introduced the type of the mystical sandal among human beings. For, according to the Law, the wife of a deceased man was assigned to his nearest relative or brother, so that he might raise up the seed of his brother or relative (Num. XXXVI, 6). Thus, although Ruth herself was a foreigner, because she had had a husband from among the Jews who had left a surviving relative, and while she was gathering the handfuls of his harvest by which she supported both herself and her mother-in-law, Boaz saw and loved her. Yet he did not take her as wife until he had first removed the sandal of the one to whom, according to the Law, the wife was owed (Ruth IV, 5–7).

70. The history is simple, but its mysteries are profound: one thing was happening, another was being signified. For if we twist the meaning according to the letter, there is nearly something shameful and horrifying in the wording, if we refer its sense and interpretation to ordinary bodily intercourse. What was being signified, however, was the one who was to come from the Jews, from whom Christ is according to the flesh, and who would raise up the seed of his nearest relative—that is, of the dead people—through the seed of heavenly teaching. For him the spiritual prescriptions of the Law bore the nuptial sandal for the Church to be joined to him.

### 71

Moses is not the bridegroom; for it is said to him, “Remove the sandals from your feet” (Exod. 3:5), so that he may yield to his Lord. Nor is Jesus son of Nave the bridegroom; for to him also it is said, “Remove the sandals from your feet” (Josh. 5:16), lest, because of the similarity of the name, he be thought the bridegroom of the Church. There is no other bridegroom, but Christ alone is the bridegroom, of whom John said: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom” (John 3:29). Their sandal, therefore, is removed; his cannot be removed, as John said: “I am not worthy to unfasten the strap of his sandal” (John 1:27).

### 72

Christ alone, then, is the bridegroom to whom she who comes from the nations, the bride—formerly poor and starving, but now enriched by Christ’s harvest—marries. She gathers in her lap the sheaves of the fruitful grainfield and the remnants of the Word with the inner faculty of her mind, so that she may feed with new nourishment that widow exhausted by the death of her son, and that mother impoverished by the death of her people, neither leaving the widow destitute nor seeking another.

### 73

Christ alone, then, is the bridegroom who does not begrudge even the Synagogue itself the sheaves of his harvest. Would that she did not exclude herself! She had those whom she could gather for herself; but because her people are dead, like a woman left needy by the death of her son, she gathered through the Church sheaves by which she might live. Those sheaves, as it is written, “coming, shall come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves” (Ps. 125:6).

[Note: All editions read, “her bridegroom is dead”; all manuscripts read, “her people,” etc. The latter is more appropriate, for it must be referred to the preceding words: “the mother impoverished by the death of her people.”]

### 74

Who else would dare claim the Church as his bride, except the one and only bridegroom who called her from Lebanon, saying: “Come here from Lebanon, bride; come here from Lebanon” (Song 4:8)? Or of whom else could the Church say: “His palate is sweetness itself, and he is altogether desirable” (Song 5:16)?

And since we have taken up the subject of the sandal of the feet, to whom else than the Word of God incarnate does the saying apply: “His legs are marble columns, founded upon golden bases” (ibid., 5:15)? For Christ alone walks through souls and advances in the minds of the saints; in them the footprints of the heavenly Word have been fixed, as though upon golden bases and precious foundations.

### 75

Thus it is clear that both the man and the type refer to the mystery of the incarnation.

## Chapter XI

He returns to the subject at hand and teaches that wherever Christ is said to have been made, this must be referred either to the incarnation or to some cause or accompanying circumstance. He explains this sense through numerous testimonies from the sacred books, especially from Paul; but he dwells above all on persuading us that Christ is the true priest, prefigured in Melchizedek, and that he possesses unity of operation with the Father, not merely a likeness.

### 76

Therefore, when he is said to have been made, this often refers not to the substance of his divinity but to the incarnation, and sometimes also to a cause. For if you refer it to divinity, then God was also made a reproach; for you have it thus: “But you rejected and reduced to nothing; you cast away your Christ” (Ps. 88:39); and below: “And he was made a reproach to his neighbors” (ibid., 42). He says “neighbors,” not citizens, household members, or those who cling to him, because “he who clings to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6:17); whoever is merely a neighbor does not cling to him. And he was “made a reproach,” because the Lord’s cross is “a stumbling-block to the Jews and foolishness to the Greeks” (1 Cor. 1:23). Yet by that same cross he was made higher than the heavens, higher than the angels, and became the guarantor of a better covenant—the very one who existed before the former covenant.

[Note: A number of manuscripts read, “foolishness to the Greeks who are wise.” “By that same cross,” etc.]

### 77

See how I do not avoid these matters, but even heap them up; nevertheless, consider in what manner he was made.

### 78

First, after purification had been accomplished, he sat at the right hand of the Majesty on high, having been made so much greater than the angels (Heb. 1:3–4). Where there is purification, there is a victim; where there is a victim, there is a body; where there is a body, there is an offering; where there is the gift of an offering, there is the sacrifice of the Passion.

### 79

Next, he is the guarantor of a better covenant (Heb. 7:22). Where there is a covenant, the death of the testator must precede it (Heb. 9:16), as is written below. But death refers not to the eternity of divinity, but to the frailty of human nature.

### 80

It is also shown how he was made higher than the heavens: “Immaculate,” he says, “separated from sinners, and made higher than the heavens; he has no daily need, as the priests do, first to offer a sacrifice for his own sins and then for those of the people. For this he did once for all by offering himself, as it is written” (Heb. 7:26–27). No one is said to have been made higher unless he had previously been lower in some respect. In that respect, therefore, he was made higher by sitting at the right hand of the Father—the one who, having been made lower than the angels, submitted himself to suffering (Heb. 2:9).

[Note: All editions read “more excellent”; nearly all manuscripts read “higher.”]

### 81

Finally, the Apostle himself says to the Philippians that, “having been made in the likeness of man and found in appearance as a man, he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death” (Phil. 2:7–8). Observe where he was made: “in the likeness,” he says, “of man,” not in the power of God; and he was “made obedient unto death,” so that he possessed the obedience of a man, but the reign of divinity.

[Note: This is how all editions and many manuscripts read. Some, however, read *obedientia* (“obedience”) instead of *obedientiam* (“obedience” as the object), removing the comma before “the reign of divinity.” A few others have “the reign of dignity” for these words.]

### 82

How many further examples, then, shall we still use to show that the expression “he was made” must be referred to the incarnation or to something else? What is made is also created: “He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. 148:5). “The Lord created me” (Prov. 8:22)—this is said according to the flesh. We also showed above, in the first book, that “created” appears to be spoken of the incarnation (Book 1, chap. 14 and following).

[Note: The Roman edition, with two manuscripts, reads “what was made”; older editions, with the remaining manuscripts, read “he who was made,” referring to Christ. Ambrose then adds that “made” and “created” have the same meaning, namely, the meaning by which they refer to the production of things from nothing. This is entirely true in Greek usage, as Jerome teaches in his commentary on Ephesians 4 and Augustine in Book 1 against the Adversaries of the Law and the Prophets, chapter 23, although the latter also asserts that in Scripture both terms are used indifferently of things made either from some material or from none. As for Latin, those same Fathers note that *creari* and *fieri* are used both of the generation of children and of the appointment of magistrates, which is perfectly clear from the usage of approved writers. Ambrose therefore follows the Greek Fathers most firmly, since they always shrank from calling the divine Word κτίσμα—that is, “a creature”—and he is convinced that all the scriptural testimonies abused by the Arians can be most suitably explained in this way.]

### 83

The Apostle himself, by asserting that the creature must not be served, indicated that the Son is from God not as one created but as one begotten (Rom. 1:25). Yet elsewhere also, in order to show how the words “The Lord created me” are to be understood in Solomon, he indicated what had been created in Christ.

### 84

Let us therefore review the whole sequence of the chapter, for you have it thus: “Since the children share in flesh and blood, he himself likewise shared in the same, so that through death he might destroy him who held the power of death” (Heb. 2:14). Who, then, is the one who wished us to share in his flesh and blood? Certainly the Son of God. How could he become a sharer in what is ours except through flesh? Or through what else than the death of the body did he dissolve the bonds of death? For death’s death was the assumption of death in Christ. He has therefore introduced the subject of the incarnation.

### 85

Let us examine what follows: “For surely he did not assume angels, but the seed of Abraham. Hence he had to be made like his brothers in every respect, so that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest before God, to expiate the sins of the people. For in that which he himself suffered and was tempted, he is able to help those who are tempted” (ibid., 16–17). “Therefore, most holy brothers, sharers in a heavenly calling, consider Jesus, the apostle and high priest of our confession, faithful to his Creator, as Moses also was in all his house” (Heb. 3:1–2). These are plainly the Apostle’s words.

### 86

You see in what respect he says that he was created: “In that,” he says, “he took hold of the seed of Abraham”; he is plainly asserting a bodily generation. In what respect, then, except in the body, did he expiate the sins of the people? In what respect did he suffer, except in the body, as we said above: Christ suffered according to the flesh? In what respect was he a priest, except in that which he assumed from a priestly lineage?

### 87

A priest must offer something, and according to the Law must enter the holy place through blood (Heb. 9:25). Therefore, since God had rejected the blood of bulls and goats, this priest had to enter, through his own blood, as you have read, into the Holy of Holies at the summit of heaven (ibid., 12), so that there might be an eternal offering for our sins.

[Note: All editions and some manuscripts read “the cleansing of sins”; the other manuscripts read “the offering for sins.” The latter is more appropriate, for it means the same as “an offering for sins,” which is the subject here.]

The same person is therefore priest and victim. Yet both priesthood and sacrifice are duties belonging to human condition; for he was led like a lamb to be sacrificed, and he is a priest according to the order of Melchizedek.

### 88

Therefore, when someone sees there the order belonging to human condition, let him not assign to it the right of divinity.

[Note: The edition reads, “assigns the right of divinity.”]

The Church understands that Melchizedek, through whom Abraham offered his sacrifices (Gen. 14:18), was not an angel, as in the Jewish fantasies, but a holy man and priest of God. As a type bearing the figure of the Lord, he is described as being without father, without mother, without genealogy, without beginning, and without end, in order to show that the everlasting Son of God would come into this world: born without a father according to the incarnation, without a mother according to divine generation, and without an account of his generation, because it is written: “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. 53:8).

[Note: Jerome, in Letter 25 to Evagrius, attributes this opinion not to the Jews but to Origen and Didymus.]

### 89

We therefore accept that Melchizedek was a priest of God as a type of Christ: Melchizedek in the type, Christ in truth. The type, however, is the shadow of the truth. Melchizedek was king in the name of a single city; Christ is king in the reconciliation of the whole world, because it is written: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5:19). This means the everlasting divinity—or, if the Father is in the Son as the Son is in the Father, the unity both of substance and of operation is certainly not denied.

### 90

How can they rightly deny this, even if they wish to, when it is written: “The Father who dwells in me himself does the works”; and, “The works that I do, he himself does” (John 14:10)? He did not say, “And he himself does them,” lest you should judge that there was a likeness rather than a unity of work. But by saying, “The works that I do, he himself does,” he plainly left it established that we must believe the work of the Father and the Son to be one.

### 91

Finally, where he wished a likeness of works, not a unity, to be understood, he said: “Whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do” (ibid., 12). Here, by inserting “also,” he suitably granted us a likeness, while nevertheless denying natural unity. The work of the Father and the Son is therefore one, even if this does not please the Arians.

## Chapter XII

The reign of the Father and the Son is one and undivided; likewise, their divinity is one.

### 92

I ask, then, how they wish the reign of the Father and the Son to be divided, when the Lord said, as we showed above: “Every kingdom divided against itself will be destroyed” (Matt. 12:25).
