### 93

And therefore, to exclude the sacrilege of Arian savagery, holy Peter also asserted that the Father and the Son have one dominion, saying: “Therefore, brothers, strive to make your calling and election sure. For if you do these things, you will never fall; for in this way entrance into the eternal kingdom of our God and Savior Jesus Christ will be richly supplied to you” (2 Pet. 1:10–11).

[Note: One manuscript reads “of our Creator”; several others, and all editions, read “of our Savior.” The remaining and more reliable manuscripts read “of our Preserver.”]

### 94

Or if someone thinks that this was said only of Christ’s dominion, and accepts it in this way in order to separate the Father and the Son in power, he will nevertheless acknowledge that the Son’s kingdom is also eternal. Thus they will either introduce two divided kingdoms, making them subject to destruction, even though no kingdoms are comparable to the kingdom of God—which they cannot deny belongs to the Son, however much they wish to—or they will return against their own position and admit that the kingdom of the Father and the Son is the same; or, which is sacrilegious to say, they will assign to the Father the right of a lesser kingdom; or, conversely, they will acknowledge as equal the kingdom of the one whom they impiously declare lesser in divinity.

[Note: All editions, together with some manuscripts, read, “or they will see themselves opposed to their own position.” What could be more ridiculous?]

### 95

But this does not fit, agree, or hold together. Let them therefore say that the kingdom is one, as we say and prove. We prove it not by our own testimony, but by heavenly testimonies.

### 96

First, learn from other examples also that the kingdom of heaven is likewise the kingdom of the Son. For he himself said: “Amen, amen, I say to you, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom” (Matt. 16:28). There can therefore be no doubt that it is the kingdom of the Son of God.

[Note: Older editions and many manuscripts read, “some of those standing here”; the Roman edition reads, “some standing here”; the remaining manuscripts read, “some of these standing here.” The text should certainly be written as it stands here, for in this passage, as also in the passage cited below from Mark, the Greek consistently reads τῶν ὧδε ἑστηκότων, “of those standing here.” Again, where all editions and some manuscripts read, “Therefore it cannot be doubted,” the remaining manuscripts prefer, “Do not doubt.”]

### 97

But understand that the Son’s kingdom is the very kingdom that belongs to the Father: “Amen, I say to you, there are some standing among those present who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God coming in power” (Mark 8:39). The two kingdoms are so entirely one that there is one reward, the same inheritance, the same merits, and the same guarantor.

[Note: All editions read, “the kingdom of the coming God”; the manuscripts read, “the kingdom of God”; one manuscript has, “the Son of God coming,” a reading confirmed also by the idiom of Scripture throughout. Again, where all editions and many manuscripts read, “the same heir,” some others have, “the same men.”]

### 98

How can it not be the same kingdom, especially when the Son himself said of himself: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of my Father” (Matt. 13:43)? What belongs to the Father through the propriety of majesty belongs also to the Son through the unity of the same splendor. Scripture therefore speaks both of the Father’s kingdom and of the Son’s (John 17:5).

### 99

Understand now that when Scripture says “the kingdom of God,” it does not separate the power of the Father or of the Son; under the one name of God it comprehends both the Father’s kingdom and the Son’s, as you have it: “When you see Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob and all the prophets in the kingdom of God” (Luke 13:28).

Do we deny that the prophets are in the Son’s kingdom, when the Lord also answered the thief who said, “Remember me when you come into your kingdom”: “Amen, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:42–43)? Or what does it mean to be in the kingdom of God except not to know eternal death? Those who do not know eternal death see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “in the kingdom of the Son.”]

### 100

How, then, can he not possess authority over what he gives when he says: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 16:19)? Observe the distinction. The servant opens; the Lord bestows. The former does so through himself; the latter through Christ. The servant receives the keys; the Lord appoints the authorities.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “the right of bestowing.”]

The right of the giver is one thing, and the obedient service of the administrator another.

### 101

Learn further that the Father and the Son have one kingdom and one dominion. You have this in the letter to Timothy: “Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ according to the command of God our Savior and of Christ Jesus our hope” (1 Tim. 1:1). The one kingdom of the Father and the Son is therefore clearly declared, just as the Apostle Paul also asserted, saying: “Know this, that every immoral or impure person, or covetous person—which is idolatry—has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God” (Eph. 5:5).

Therefore there is one kingdom and one divinity.

### 102

The Law proved that there is one divinity when it says that there is one God (Deut. 6:4). The Apostle also proved it by saying of Christ: “In him dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily” (Col. 2:9). For if, according to the Apostle, all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily in Christ, they will either acknowledge that the Father and the Son possess one divinity; or, if they wish to separate the divinity of the Father and the Son, since the Son possesses bodily the whole fullness of divinity, what do they think should still be reserved, when nothing is greater than the fullness of perfection? Therefore there is one divinity.

## Chapter XIII

The Son possesses his own majesty, equal to the Father’s; the angels are not his companions but spectators.

### 103

[Elsewhere, chapter 6.] We stated above that there is one image and one likeness (Book 1, chapter 7); it remains for us to teach that the Father and the Son likewise possess one majesty. This will not be difficult, since the Son himself said of himself: “When the Son of Man comes in his majesty, and all the angels with him, then he will sit upon the throne of his majesty” (Matt. 25:31). Here the Son’s majesty is plainly expressed. What is lacking to him whose uncreated majesty they cannot deny? The Son therefore has majesty.

### 104

Let them now accept, so that they cannot doubt, that the majesty of the Father and the Son is one. For the Lord himself said: “Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, the Son of Man will be ashamed of him when he comes in his own majesty and that of the Father and of the holy angels” (Luke 9:26). What does “and of the holy angels” mean except that the servants are honored by the dignity of their Lord?

[Note: The older edition reads, “unless servants too honor the dignity of their Lord as their own.”]

### 105

He therefore referred his own dignity to the Son and the Father—not so that the angels might have equal fellowship with the Father and the Son, but so that they might behold the surpassing glory of God. For the angels do not possess their own majesty, as it is written of the Son: “When he sits upon the throne of his majesty” (Matt. 25:31). Rather, they stand by, so that they may see the glory of the Father and the Son with whatever sight they are able or worthy to possess.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “so that they may see the grace.”]

### 106

Finally, the divine words themselves explain the matter, so that you may understand that the glory of the Father and the Son is not shared with the angels. For you have it thus: “When the Son of Man comes in his majesty, and all the angels with him.” And to teach that there is one majesty and one glory, his own and the Father’s, he says in another book: “The Son of Man will be ashamed of him when he comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels” (Mark 8:38).

[Note: All editions and most manuscripts read, “will be ashamed of him.” The Roman edition alone reads, “will reject him”; the remaining manuscripts read, “will confess him.”]

They are in service; he is in glory. They are in attendance; he is on the throne. They stand; he sits. To use human language, he judges, while they minister.

### 107

He did not first mention the Father’s divine majesty and then add his own and that of the angels, lest he appear to have proceeded from higher things to lower ones and established some order of rank. But since the Father could not be regarded as inferior, he first mentioned his own majesty and then added that of the Father and the angels. Thus, by placing himself between the Father and the angels, he would not appear either to have ascended from the angels to the Father through his own successive advances, or to have descended again from the Father to the angels in an ordered diminution of himself. For we who confess one divinity of the Father and the Son do not posit, as the Arians do, a different order.

## Chapter XIV

The Son is of one substance with the Father; in many scriptural testimonies this must also be understood according to divinity, although in certain others the word is understood either of possessions or of the incarnation.

### 108

What shall I say, most august Emperor, concerning substance, that the Son is of one substance with the Father, when we read that the Son is “the image of the Father’s substance” (Wis. 7:26), so that you may understand him to differ from the Father in nothing according to divinity?

### 109

In accordance with this image he said: “All that the Father has is mine” (John 16:15). Therefore we cannot deny substance in God. For he is not without substance who gave others the ability to possess substance, although the substance of God is one thing and that of creatures another. Nor could the Son of God be without substance, through whom all things subsist.

[Note: Throughout Ambrose, “substance” means the same as the Greek οὐσία, that is, the very nature of a thing, or that by which each thing is what it is. This meaning, which cannot be denied to be thoroughly Catholic, eventually prevailed among the Latins, so that God was said to possess substance and Christ to be consubstantial with the Father. When the Latins referred the word *substantia* to its origin—whether they derived it from *subsistere*, as Augustine does in Book 7 of *On the Trinity*, chapters 4 and 5, or from *substare*, as Boethius does in *On the Two Natures*—they asserted that the word could properly be used only of that which was subject to, supported, or as it were laid beneath, accidents. The same authors may be consulted, as may Marius Victorinus, who flourished in the time of Constantius. He discusses at length the various meanings of this expression and mentions all the passages cited here by our Ambrose. Phoebadius also treats the matter, and from all these writers it can be understood how much they recoiled from the word. Athanasius must not be omitted: in his work *On the Synods*, page 903, reporting the creed of Sirmium, where it was decreed that the terms “substance” and “consubstantiality” should be avoided, he records this fact.]

### 110

And therefore he says: “My bone was not hidden from you, which you made in secret, and my substance in the lowest parts of the earth” (Ps. 138:15). Things accomplished before the foundation of the world or in inscrutable majesty could not be hidden from power and divinity. We therefore read the word “substance.”

### 111

But you will say that “substance” is spoken of the incarnation. For the moment, I have established that the name “substance” is read here, and that it is not read, as you claim, of patrimonies. Now, if you please, let us understand, according to the mystery, that substance was in the lower parts of Christ. For in order to free the souls of the dead through the soul of his own body, to break the bonds of death, and to forgive sins, he worked in hell.

### 112

Yet what prevents you from understanding it as the divine substance, since God is everywhere in such a way that it was said to him: “If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present” (ibid., 8)?

### 113

Finally, he declared through what follows that the meaning must be referred to divine substance, saying: “Your eyes saw my unwrought being” (ibid., 16). The Son is not the product of a work, but the begotten Word of eternal power. For he used the word ἀκατέργαστον, that is, “unwrought” and “uncreated”: the Word born from the Father without the testimony of any creature. Yet we have abundant other testimonies concerning substance. Let substance in this passage be bodily, provided that you too confess that the Son of God is not a work, but his unwrought divinity.

### 114

I know that some say that even the mystery of the incarnation is “unwrought,” because no use of intercourse with a man was involved, since it was the birth of a Virgin. If, then, many have said that in this passage even Mary’s birth was not a work, do you, Arian, think that the Word of God is a work?

### 115

Or do we read the word “substance” only here? Did he not say elsewhere: “The gates of the cities have been broken down, the mountains have fallen, and substance has been revealed” (Nahum 2:6)? Is a creature indicated here as well? Some customarily say that “substance” means a pecuniary estate. If you refer the passage to this meaning, then the mountains fell so that a pecuniary patrimony might be seen.

### 116

But let us remember which mountains fell. They are those of whom it was said: “If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Remove yourself and throw yourself into the sea’” (Matt. 17:19). The mountains, then, are the lofty things that exalt themselves.

### 117

Finally, in Greek the text reads, “and the kingdoms fell” (Nahum 2:6).

[Note: The Septuagint reads καὶ τὰ βασίλεια διέπεσε, “and the kingdoms fell.”]

What kingdoms are these except those of Satan, of whom the Lord said: “How will his kingdom stand?” (Matt. 12:26). We therefore understand those mountains—which are the kingdoms of the devil. When these kingdoms fall from the hearts of the faithful, it is revealed that Christ the Son of God is of the Father’s substance.

What are those same airy mountains from whose midst four chariots proceed (Zech. 6:1)?

### 118

We observe that the height exalting itself against the knowledge of God fell at the word of the Lord, when the Son of God said: “Be silent and come out, unclean spirit” (Mark 1:25). Of this also the prophet said: “Behold, I am against you, corrupt mountain” (Jer. 51:25).

### 119

These mountains therefore fell, and it was revealed that there was divine substance in Christ, when those who saw him said: “He is truly the Son of God” (Luke 4:41). For he commanded the demons not with human power but with divine power.

Jeremiah also says: “Upon the mountains take up mourning, and upon the deserted paths lamentation, because they have failed; because there are no men, they did not hear the voice of substance. From birds to beasts they have trembled and failed” (Jer. 9:10).

### 120

Nor did he omit, elsewhere, when he was explaining the frailties of human condition and showing the weakness of the flesh and the feeling of our mind that he had assumed, to say through the Prophet: “Remember, Lord, what my substance is” (Ps. 88:48). The Son of God was speaking in the nature of human frailty.

### 121

Concerning this, above, in order to reveal the mysteries of the incarnation, he said: “But you, Lord, have rejected and regarded as nothing; you have cast away your Christ; you have overturned the covenant of your servant; you have profaned his sanctuary on earth” (ibid., 39–40). In what respect did he call him a servant except in the flesh? For “he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men, and found in appearance as a man” (Phil. 2:6–7). By my assumption he is a servant; by his own power he is Lord.

### 122

What of the passage you have: “For who has stood in the substance of the Lord?” (Jer. 23:18); and elsewhere: “If they had stood in my substance, and had heard my words, and if they had taught my people, I would have turned them from their wickedness and their devices” (ibid., 22)?

## Chapter XV

The Arians, by calling the Son ἑτεροούσιον, “of a different substance,” plainly acknowledge substance in God; and they avoid this word for no other reason than that they are unwilling to confess him the true Son of God, as Eusebius of Nicomedia indicated. The term ὁμοούσιον, “of the same substance,” was therefore rightly established by the Fathers of Nicaea, since it is opposed to heresy and supported by Scripture; consequently, it must be retained despite the things they fabricate about the Sabellians.

### 123

How can they deny that God has substance? How can they think that the word “substance,” which is exceedingly common in Scripture, must be avoided, when they themselves, by calling the Son ἑτεροούσιον, “of a different substance,” nevertheless do not deny that there is substance in God?

### 124

They therefore flee not from the word but from the force of the word, because they do not wish him to be the true Son of God. Although the sequence of divine generation cannot be comprehended by a human word, the Fathers nevertheless judged that their faith should be marked by this precise expression, in opposition to ἑτεροούσιον, following the authority of the prophet who says: “Who has stood in the substance of the Lord and seen his Word?” The Arians therefore accept the word “substance” when it is used according to their impiety, but reject and repudiate it when it is approved according to the piety of the faithful.

[Note: Amerbach and Erasmus have here the term ἐπιούσιον, “super-substantial,” specifically; Gill and the Roman edition, together with the manuscripts, have the reading in the text, except for two codices, which read “against ὁμοούσιον.” The latter is incorrect.]

### 125

For what else is the reason that they refuse to call the Son ὁμοούσιον, “of the same substance,” with the Father, except that they are unwilling to confess him the true Son of God? Their own author, Eusebius of Nicomedia, disclosed this in his letter, writing: “If we call him the true and uncreated Son of God,” he says, “we begin to confess him ὁμοούσιον with the Father.” When this letter was read at the Council of Nicaea, the Fathers placed this word in the statement of faith, because they saw that it was feared by their opponents, so that, as though by a sword drawn by the opponents themselves, they might cut off the head of their abominable heresy.

[Note: Scholars dispute which letter of Eusebius of Nicomedia Ambrose mentions here. Hermann, in Book 2 of *The Life of Saint Athanasius*, chapter 8, following Cardinal Baronius under the year 325, thinks it is the letter mentioned by Theodoret in Book 1, chapter 8, in Valesius’s edition. Valesius, however, defending that passage of Theodoret, thinks it should be understood not of a letter from Eusebius of Nicomedia but of a statement of faith presented by Eusebius of Caesarea to the Fathers of the council; he adduces various arguments for this view, though they do not seem strong enough to remove every difficulty. Whatever the case may be, it is certain that Ambrose is speaking here not of a formula or statement of faith but of a letter. The fact that Eusebius is called by Ambrose the author of the Arians is not peculiar to this holy man: Athanasius frequently designates the Arians by the name “Eusebians.” Socrates also records, in Book 1, chapter 6, while discussing the letter of Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, that Eusebius did not so much defend the teaching of Arius as seek to propagate his own teaching in writing.]

### 126

They say that they avoid this word uselessly because of the Sabellians, thereby displaying their ignorance. For ὁμοούσιον means “one thing in relation to another,” not “the same thing in relation to itself.”

[Note: This is what Basil writes in Letter 300: “For ὁμοούσιον is not something in relation to itself, but one thing in relation to another.”]

We therefore rightly call the Son ὁμοούσιον with the Father, because this word signifies both the distinction of persons and the unity of nature.

### 127

Can they deny that οὐσία, “substance,” is found in Scripture, when the Lord also spoke of ἐπιούσιον bread (Matt. 6), and Moses wrote: “You shall be to me a λαὸς περιούσιος, a people of special possession” (Exod. 19)? Or what is οὐσία, and from what is it derived, except from οὖσα ἀεί, “that which always remains”? He who is and always is is God; and therefore, because it remains forever, οὐσία is called divine substance.

For this reason, ἐπιούσιος bread is so called because from the substance of the Word it supplies to the heart and soul the substance of abiding strength; for it is written: “Bread strengthens the heart of man” (Ps. 103:15).

128. Let us therefore keep the precepts of our predecessors, and let us not, through the rashness of an inexperienced person, dare to violate hereditary seals [Note: Some manuscripts read “as through the rashness of an inexperienced person,” etc. By “the priestly book” Ambrose here means the definition and creed of the Council of Nicaea. When the Arians sought to overturn it at the Council of Rimini, Valens of Singidunum administered the poison of Arian perfidy to the simple-minded Catholic bishops. In the second creed of that council, amid various propositions agreeing with orthodox faith, this most cunning man inserted the clause by which those who professed Christ to be a creature like the other creatures were condemned by an anathema. By what devices the Arians stirred up this tragedy is related by Sulpicius Severus, book II, and Jerome, *Against the Luciferians*. Ambrose everywhere attacks the impiety of Arius himself.] The prophetic sealed book no elders, no Powers, no angels, no archangels dared to open: the prerogative of explaining it was reserved for Christ alone. Who among us would dare to unseal the priestly book, sealed by confessors and already consecrated by the martyrdom of many? Those who were compelled to unseal it nevertheless sealed it again afterward, once their fraud had been condemned; those who did not dare to violate it became confessors and martyrs. How can we deny the faith of those whose victory we proclaim?

## CHAPTER XVI

Ambrose warns Catholics against the fraudulent devices of the Arians and exposes certain deceptive confessions of theirs. He proves, by collecting arguments, that it is not enough for them occasionally to call the Son God [Col. 0615B], unless they acknowledge him as equal to the Father.

129. Let no one fear, let no one be afraid: he who threatens contributes more to the faithful. The blandishments of the faithless are poisoned; they must be guarded against when they pretend to proclaim what they deny. Those who readily believed were deceived in this way before also, so that they fell into the snares of perfidy precisely where they thought faith was present.

130. “Let him be anathema,” they say, “who says that Christ is a creature like the other creatures.” The simple heard this and believed. For, as it is written, “The innocent believes every word” (Prov. XIV, 15). They heard and believed, deceived first by the sound of the words; and, like birds intent upon the bait of faith, they did not beware of the snare stretched out for them [Col. 0615C]. Thus, while following the faith, they touched the hook of unspeakable fraud. Therefore Scripture says: “Be shrewd as serpents and simple as doves” (Matt. X, 16); shrewdness is set first so that simplicity may be safe.

520. 131. There are, indeed, evangelical serpents who strip off their former way of life in order to put on new conduct, as it is written: “Stripping off the old man with his deeds, and putting on the new, according to the image of him who created him” (Col. III, 9–10). Let us therefore, having laid aside the skin of the old man, learn the ways of the evangelical serpents, so that, after the manner of serpents, we may know how to preserve our head and avoid deceit.

132. It would have been enough to say: “Let him be anathema who calls Christ a creature.” Why, Arius, do you mix poisons with a good confession, so as to contaminate the whole body? By adding “like the other creatures,” you do not deny that Christ is a creature; rather, you say that he is a creature unlike the others. You call him a creature, even though you assert that he is superior to the other creatures. Indeed, Arius, the teacher of this impiety, said that the Son of God was a perfect creature, but not like the other creatures. Do you see, therefore, that you have adopted the hereditary language of your father? It is enough to deny that he is a creature. Why was it necessary to add, “but not like the other creatures”? Cut away what has rotted, lest the infection spread: it contains poison; it brings death.

133. Next, you sometimes call Christ God. But say “true God” [Note: All editions and some manuscripts read: “call him God, as true God, as the fullness,” etc. The other manuscripts, as in the text, are more elegant.], so that you assign to him the fullness of the Father’s divinity. For there are those who are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth. He must not therefore be called God casually, but in such a way that you proclaim the same divinity in the Son that the Father possesses, as it is written: “For as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself” (John V, 26). He granted it, certainly, as to a Son through generation, not as to one lacking it through grace.

[Col. 0616B] 134. “And he gave him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of man.” See what he added, lest you slander him on the basis of the word. You read “Son of man” and accuse him of receiving? Then deny that he is God, if not everything that belongs to God is attributed to the Son. For when he said, “Everything that the Father has is mine” (John XVI, 15), why do you not confess that everything belonging to the divine nature is also in the Son? For the one who says, “Everything that the Father has is mine”—what does he exclude that the Father does not have?

135. What is this that you recall *emphatically*, or rather with language more faithful to the truth: that he raised the dead, crossed the sea on foot, and healed human weaknesses? For he granted these things even to his servants. I marvel more at these things in human beings, namely, that he gave them such great power. I want to hear something about Christ that is peculiarly Christ’s, something that cannot be shared with created things: that he was begotten, that he is the only-begotten Son of God, that he is true God from true God, and that he sits at the Father’s right hand.

136. Wherever I read of the Father and the Son seated together, the Son is always sitting at the right hand. Is the Son therefore better than the Father? We do not say this. But whom the love of God honors, human iniquity disparages. The Father knew that questions would be raised concerning the Son; he gave us something to follow, an example of piety, lest we disparage the Son.

## CHAPTER XVII

Ambrose answers the objection that might arise here and explains why the Lord appeared to Stephen standing. From Stephen’s prayers to the Son he confirms the equality of the Son and the Father and brings the book to a close.

[Col. 0616D] 137. Stephen said that he saw Jesus standing at the right hand of God in only one place (Acts VII, 55). Learn the reason for this too, lest you raise some question on the matter. Why is he shown sitting at the right hand everywhere, yet is read to be standing in one place? He sits as judge of the living and the dead; he stands as advocate for his own. He was therefore standing as a priest when he offered to the Father the sacrifice of the good martyr [Col. 0617A]; he was standing as one who would return the prize of so great a contest to the good combatant.

138. Receive the Spirit of God yourself also, so that you may distinguish these things, as Stephen received him; and say, as the martyr said: “Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of man standing at the right hand of God.” Whoever has the heavens open sees Jesus at the right hand of God; whoever has the eyes of his mind closed does not see Jesus at the right hand of God. Let us therefore confess Jesus at the right hand, so that heaven may be opened for us also. Those who confess otherwise shut heaven against themselves.

522. 139. If some object that the Son was standing, let them show in this passage that the Father was sitting. For although he said that the Son of man was standing, he did not mention in this passage that the Father was sitting.

[Col. 0617B] 140. So that it might be understood more clearly that the Son’s standing involved no dishonor but rather authority, Stephen entreated the Son to commend him more fully to the Father, saying: “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit” (Acts VII, 58). And to show that the Father and the Son possess the same authority, he repeated his prayer, saying: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them” [Col. 0618A] (ibid., 59). The Lord says this in his own passion, as Son of man, to the Father; Stephen, in his martyrdom, prays for this from the Son of God. When the same grace is requested from the Father and the Son, the same power is declared.

141. Or, if they wish to say that Stephen spoke to the Father, let them consider what they themselves signify by their own testimony. Although these things do not trouble us, nevertheless let those who base everything on the letter and on the order of the words observe that the Son is asked first. We, however, even according to their interpretation, demonstrate the unity of the Father’s majesty and the Son’s. For when both the Father and the Son are entreated, the equality of the petition indicates unity. But if they do not approve of the words being addressed to the Son—“Lord”—we see that they are also trying to deny that he is Lord.

[Col. 0618B] 142. But now that the crown of so great a martyr has emerged, let us relax the labors of the contest and keep a holiday from today’s discourse. Let us continue to praise the holy martyr, as was fitting after great struggles: wounded and bloodied by the adversary’s blows, but crowned with Christ’s rewards.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0617]

521. ## CHAPTER I

It is not surprising that human beings should have erred in their knowledge of Christ, but that they did not obey Scripture. Even he was not known by the angels except through revelation, nor by the Forerunner himself. Ambrose describes the triumph of this same Christ as he ascends into heaven and shows how much greater it was than the raptures of certain prophets. After describing the angels’ conversation on this matter, he proves against the Arians that the Son is omnipotent.

1. As I consider, august Emperor, how the human race could have erred so that most people, alas, followed differing opinions concerning the Son of God [Note: This is the reading of several and the better manuscripts. Other manuscripts and editions read “the human race concerning the Son of God, so that most followed different…”; older editions read “the human race.”], it does not seem sufficiently surprising that human knowledge should have erred concerning heavenly things; what is surprising is that it did not yield obedience to the Scriptures.

2. For what is surprising if, through worldly wisdom, human beings could not comprehend the mystery of God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Col. II, 3), when even the angels could not know it except through revelation? [Col. 0617D] [Note: Most manuscripts omit the conjunction in “the mystery of God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.”]

522. 3. Who could have followed the Lord Jesus by opinion rather than by faith, now penetrating the underworld from heaven’s highest heights, now rising from the underworld to the heavenly realms; suddenly emptied, so that he might dwell among us, yet never diminished, since the Son was always in the Father and the Father in the Son?

4. The Forerunner himself doubted, although he was appointed beforehand before the face of the Lord, in the figure of the Synagogue [Note: That is, insofar as he represented the figure and person of the Synagogue. But insofar as he was Christ’s Forerunner, the suspicion of such a great error could not fall upon so great a prophet, as Ambrose himself taught in *Exposition of the Gospel according to Luke*, book V, no. 93, where he treats the matter more fully. Besides Thomas Aquinas, *Summa theologica* II–II, q. 2, art. 7, ad 2, see the sacred interpreters on Matthew XI and Luke VII. As for the angels’ doubt, we have already observed, in *On the Institution of the Virgin*, chapter 5, no. 39, that our Doctor repeats this opinion several times; but nowhere does he discuss it more fully than here.]. Finally, having sent his disciples, he asks: “Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?” (Matt. XI, 3).

5. The angels too were astonished at the heavenly mystery. Therefore, when the Lord rose again, and the heights of heaven could not contain him rising from the dead whom the narrow place of the tomb had shortly before concealed according to the flesh [Note: Some manuscripts of better quality read: “the stars of heaven could not sustain him … uncertain opinion.”], even the heavenly beings were held in uncertainty and wonder.

6. For the Lord, newly victorious and crowned with fresh spoils, was coming into his holy temple. Angels and archangels went before him, marveling at the spoil won from death. Although they knew that nothing could accrue to God from the flesh, because everything is beneath God, nevertheless, as they looked upon the trophies of the cross—whose beginning was upon his shoulders—and the spoils of the eternal victor, they seemed unable to contain the one whom the gates of heaven had sent forth. Although they can never contain his majesty, they sought some broader way for him on his return: so completely had he lost nothing by emptying himself!

7. Yet a new path had to be prepared for the new victor, for the victor is always greater and higher. But because the gates of eternal justice, the gates of both the New and the Old Testament through which heaven is opened, are eternal, they are not changed but raised up [Note: One manuscript of Thuaneus reads: “the same entrances of the New and Old Testament, through which …”]. For it was not one man who was entering, but the whole world in the Redeemer of all.

8. Enoch was transferred (Gen. V, 11), and Elijah was carried away (IV Kings II, 12); but a servant is not above his Lord. For “no one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven” (John III, 13). Although Moses’ body did not appear on earth, we nowhere read that he was in heavenly glory until afterward, when the Lord, as the pledge of his resurrection, broke the bonds of the underworld and raised up the souls of the righteous. Enoch, therefore, was transferred, and Elijah was carried away: both were servants, both with their bodies; but the angels had not seen them after the resurrection, nor with the spoils of death and the triumph of the cross [Note: Quite a few manuscripts read: “after the resurrection, already with the spoils.” This is not a bad reading, for it implies “as Christ afterward ascended.”]

[Col. 0619B] 9. And therefore, seeing the Lord of all coming, the first and only one to triumph over death, they commanded the gates to be lifted for the princes, saying with wonder: “Lift up your gates, you princes, and be lifted up, you everlasting doors; and the King of glory shall enter” (Ps. XXIII, 7).

10. Yet there were still some in the heavenly realms who were astonished and marveled at the new procession, the new glory; and therefore they asked: “Who is this King of glory?” (ibid., 8). But since the angels too make progress in knowledge and have a capacity for advancement, they possess discernment of power and wisdom. God alone is without progress, because in every perfection he is eternally complete.

11. Others—those, certainly, who had been present at the resurrection, those who had seen him or had already come to know him—said: “The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle.”

12. Again the multitude of angels sang in advance in a triumphal procession: “Lift up your gates, you princes, and be lifted up, you everlasting doors; and the King of glory shall enter.”

13. Again others, astonished, said: “Who is this King of glory?” (ibid., 10). “We saw him without form or beauty” (Isa. LIII, 2). If this is not he, then who is this King of glory?

14. Those who knew answered: “The Lord of hosts, he is the King of glory.” Therefore the Lord of hosts is the Son. How then do the Arians call him weak, whom we believe to be the Lord of hosts just as we believe the Father to be? How do the Arians distinguish the power, when we read of the Father as Lord of hosts and of the Son as Lord of hosts? 524 For many manuscripts have the passage written this way also: “The Lord of hosts himself is the King of glory.” The interpreters have rendered *sabaoth* in some places as “Lord of hosts,” in others as “king,” and in others as “omnipotent” [Note: Some manuscripts have “the interpreters in some places rendered it omnipotent.” Since Ambrose argues here from the word “omnipotent,” the other interpretations could be omitted without loss of meaning. But since they occur in other handwritten manuscripts as well as in all the printed editions, we have not thought the other two should be rejected. The first interpretation, by which *sabaoth* is explained as “hosts” or “armies,” is recognized by Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* 26, and, besides other Fathers, by Origen, Gregory of Nazianzus, Augustine, and Jerome, *Letter* 136 to Marcella. Jerome also confirms both this interpretation and the third, according to which the word means “omnipotent,” in *Letter* 142. As for the claim that the word itself can also mean “king,” we have not found it supported by anyone else.]. Therefore, since the one who ascended is the Son, and the one who ascended is the Lord of hosts, the Son of God is certainly omnipotent.

## CHAPTER II

No one can ascend into heaven without faith; and if anyone ascends without it, he must be cast out. Faith must therefore be carefully preserved. There are also heavens within us, whose gates must be opened and raised through confession of Christ’s divinity. The Arians do not raise these gates, nor do those who seek the Son among earthly things. They must therefore be sent back with Mary Magdalene to the apostles, against whom the gates of hell will not prevail. From what has been said it is gathered that the servant must not detract from the dignity of the Lord.

14. What, then, shall we do? How shall we ascend into heaven? There are powers arranged there, princes appointed, who guard the gates of heaven and ask the one ascending: “Who will admit me unless I proclaim Christ omnipotent?” The gates are closed; they are not opened to just anyone. Whoever wishes may not enter unless he believes faithfully. The imperial palace is guarded.

15. But suppose an unworthy person should creep in, evade the princes of the heavenly gates, and recline at the Lord’s banquet. The master of the feast will enter, see that he is not clothed in the wedding garment of faith, and cast him into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth, if he does not preserve faith and peace (Matt. XXII, 11 ff.).

16. Let us therefore preserve the wedding garment we have received, and let us not deny what belongs properly to Christ, whom the angels proclaim omnipotent, the prophets signify, and the apostles testify, as we have already shown above (Book II, chapter 4).

17. Perhaps the Prophet did not speak merely of the gates of this heaven through which he would pass. For the Word of God also penetrates other heavens, of which it is said: “We have a great priest, the high priest, who has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God” (Heb. IV, 14) [Note: The Roman edition reads: “For we have a high priest who has passed through …”; the other editions and the manuscripts read as in the text, except that the older editions, along with the Roman edition, read “has passed through.”]. What are these heavens except those of which the Prophet also says: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps. XVIII, 1)?

18. Christ stands at the door of your mind. Hear him saying: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock; if anyone opens to me, I will enter in to him, and I will dine with him, and he with me” (Rev. III, 20). And the Church says of him: “The voice of my brother knocks at the door” (Song V, 2) [Note: Some manuscripts read: “Behold, I have stood at the door of your mind, and I knock.”]

19. He stands, therefore, and he does not stand alone. Angels precede him, saying: “Lift up your gates, you princes” (Ps. XXIII, 7). Which gates? Those of which he says elsewhere: “Open for me the gates of righteousness” (Ps. CXVII, 19). Open your gates to Christ, therefore, so that he may enter into you. Open the gates of righteousness; open the gates of chastity; open the gates of fortitude and wisdom.

20. Believe the angels when they say: “Be lifted up, everlasting gates, and the King of glory shall enter, the Lord of hosts” (Ps. XXIII, 7) [Note: This is the reading of the majority and better manuscripts. Other manuscripts and editions read: “so that the King of glory may enter into you,” etc.]. Your gate is the melodious confession of a faithful voice; your gate is the door of the word, which the Apostle desires to have opened for him, saying: “That a door of the word may be opened for me to declare the mystery of Christ” (Col. IV, 3) [Note: Some manuscripts read: “the martyrdom of Christ.”]

21. Let your gate therefore be opened to Christ, and let it not merely be opened but also raised up—provided it is eternal and not perishable. For it is written: “And be lifted up, everlasting gates.” The threshold was raised up for Isaiah when the Seraph touched his lips and he saw the King, the Lord of hosts (Isa. VI, 7).

22. Your gates, therefore, will be raised up if you believe the Son of God to be eternal, omnipotent, immeasurable, incomprehensible, and one who knows all past and future things. But if you think him limited in power and knowledge, and subject to another, you do not raise the everlasting gates.

23. Let your gates therefore be raised, so that Christ may not enter you in the Arian conception as a little one, a weak one, a subordinate one; but let him enter in the form of God, let him enter with the Father, let him enter as he is, having surpassed heaven and all things, and let him send the Holy Spirit to you. It is advantageous for you to believe that he ascended and sits at the Father’s right hand. For if, in your impious thought, you detain him among creatures and earthly things, if he does not depart from you, he will not ascend for you, and the Paraclete will not come to you, as he himself said: “For if I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go away, I will send him to you” (John XVI, 7).

24. But if you seek him among earthly things, as Mary Magdalene sought him, beware lest he say to you also: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father” (John XX, 17). For your gates are narrow; they cannot contain me. They cannot be raised up; I cannot enter.

25. “Go therefore to my brothers”—that is, to those everlasting gates which, when they see Jesus, are raised up (ibid.). Peter is an everlasting gate, against whom the gates of hell will not prevail (Matt. XVI, 18). John and James are everlasting gates, being sons of thunder (Mark III, 17). The Churches are everlasting gates. Desiring to proclaim Christ’s praises in them, the Prophet says: “That I may declare all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion” (Ps. IX, 15).

26. Great, therefore, is the mystery of Christ, at which even the angels marveled. You must therefore revere it, and you must not detract from the Lord by treating him as a servant. You are not permitted to remain ignorant; for he descended for this reason, so that you might believe. If you do not believe, he did not descend for you, and he did not suffer for you. “If I had not come,” he says, “and had not spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin. He who hates me hates my Father also” (John XV, 22–23). Who, then, hates Christ except the one who disparages him? For just as it belongs to love to honor, so it belongs to hatred to disparage. The one who hates raises questions; the one who loves gives reverence.

526. ## CHAPTER III

Ambrose first turns back upon the Arians themselves the words, “Christ is the head of every man … but God is the head of Christ.” He then proves from another passage of Scripture, which those same heretics customarily brought forward, that God is the head of Christ considered according to his human nature alone. Nor do they interpret more wisely the opposing text, “The one who plants and the one who waters are one.” After explaining these matters, he shows in what manner the Father is in the Son, the Son in the Father, and the faithful in both.

27. [In some editions, chapter II.] Let us therefore examine some of their other questions. “It is written,” they say: “Christ is the head of every man, the man is the head of the woman, and God is the head of Christ” (I Cor. XI, 3). In this question, I ask them to tell me whether they wish to join these four together or divide them. If they join them and say that God is the head of Christ just as the man is the head of the woman, see what they fall into. For if this comparison is taken as one of equals, and these four—that is, woman, man, Christ, and God—are compared as though they shared the likeness of one and the same nature, then woman and God will begin to be of one nature.

28. If this is displeasing because it is sacrilegious to say so, let them divide the terms as they wish. If, therefore, they wish Christ to stand in relation to God the Father as the woman stands in relation to the man, they necessarily say that Christ and God are of one substance, since woman and man are of one bodily nature (Gen. II, 24); the difference lies in sex. But since there is no difference of sex between Christ and the Father, they will acknowledge what is one between the Son and the Father in nature, while denying what is different in sex.

29. Does this division please them? Or do they wish woman, man, and Christ to be of one substance, while separating the Father? Does this division, then, please them? If so, see what they fall into. They must either confess themselves not only Arians but also Photinians, because they acknowledge Christ as man alone and think that he must be joined only to human nature; or, even against their will, they ought to accept our position, by which we piously and reverently defend what they impiously conceived: Christ is, according to divine generation, the power of God, but, according to the assumption of flesh, he is of one bodily substance with all human beings, while the glory of his incarnation remains unimpaired, because he assumed the reality, not merely the appearance, of flesh [Note: The older edition reads: “who assumed authority, not the image of flesh.” The Roman edition and the manuscripts read as in the text, except that the same edition prefers “who assumed the truth.” One manuscript of Thuaneus reads: “because truth assumed the image of flesh.” This is very poor.]

[Col. 0623A] 30. Let God therefore be the head of Christ according to the human condition. For he did not say “the Father is the head of Christ,” but “God is the head of Christ,” because divinity, as creator, is the head of creation. He rightly said “God is the head of Christ,” so that he might signify both Christ’s divinity and his flesh—that is, his incarnation—in the name “Christ”; and in the name “God,” the unity of divinity and greatness of power.

31. God is said to be the head of Christ according to the incarnation to such an extent that Christ is said to be the head of man according to the incarnation of the Word. The Apostle clearly explained this elsewhere, saying: “For the man is the head of the woman, just as Christ is the head of the Church” (Eph. V, 23). And he added in what follows: “Who gave himself up for her” (ibid., 25). According to the incarnation, therefore, Christ is the head of man, because the giving-up took place according to the incarnation.

32. [Note: All editions read: “Therefore Christ is the head of man, God is the head of Christ.” The manuscripts more aptly omit “Christ is the head of man,” as the immediately following words sufficiently show.] God is therefore the head of Christ, where the form of a servant—that is, of a man, not of God—is being discussed. But nothing prejudices the Son of God if, according to the truth of the flesh, he is like human beings, since in divinity he is one with the Father (John X, 30). This interpretation does not diminish his power; rather, it proclaims his mercy.

33. Who would piously deny the one divinity of the Father and the Son, when the Lord himself, as he was bringing his commandments to completion, said to his disciples: “That they may be one, as we also are one” (John XVII, 11)? It was stated as a testimony of faith, although the Arians twist it into an argument for their perfidy. For since they cannot deny the unity, which they read so many times, they try to weaken it, so that the unity of divinity between the Father and the Son may appear to be of the same kind as the unity of devotion and faith among human beings, although even among human beings there is a unity of nature arising from their common nature.

34. Thus the passage that they customarily bring forward to diminish the Lord’s unity is also resolved most clearly: “The one who plants and the one who waters are one” (I Cor. III, 8). The Arians would not bring this forward if they had any understanding. For how can they try to deny that the Father and the Son are one, when Paul and Apollos are one both by nature and by faith? Yet they cannot be one in every respect, because human things cannot be compared with divine things.

35. God the Father is therefore inseparable from the Word, inseparable in power, inseparable in wisdom, through the unity of the divine substance. He is in the Son, as it is frequently written. Yet he is not in the Son as one sanctifying someone in need [Note: All editions and two manuscripts read “signifying one in need”; the other manuscripts read “sanctifying one in need.” The latter is more suitable. We may also note in passing that this Arian interpretation of the words of John was very common. Besides our Ambrose, it is reported and refuted by Athanasius, *Oration* 4 against the Arians; Hilary, *On the Trinity*, book VIII; Augustine, *Against Maximinus*, book III; Cyril of Alexandria; and others.], nor as one filling what is empty, because God’s power is not empty. Power is not increased by power, because there are not two powers but one power. Divinity does not receive divinity, because there are not two divinities but one divinity. We, however, through the power we have received and which dwells in us, shall be one in Christ [Note: The same manuscript reads: “through the power received and dwelling in us.”]

36. The wording is common, therefore, but the substance is different—divine in one case, human in the other. We shall be one; the Father and the Son are one. We are one according to grace; the Son according to substance. One unity is by conjunction, another by nature. Finally, observe what he said earlier: “That all may be one, just as you, Father, are in me, and I in you” (John XVII, 21).

37. Consider, therefore, that he did not say, “You in us, and we in you,” but “You in me, and I in you,” so that he might separate himself from created things. And he added: “And they in us” (ibid.), so that here too he might distinguish his own power and that of the Father from us; so that our being one in the Father and the Son might not appear to be a matter of nature but of grace, while the Son and the Father are one not because the Son received this through grace, but because he possesses it naturally as Son.

## CHAPTER IV

Ambrose first explains, from the words that follow, the passage cited by the heretics: “The Son can do nothing of himself,” and so forth. Then, examining each word of the complete text, he shows by examples drawn especially from the creation of the world and certain miracles of Christ that these words cannot be understood according to the Arian interpretation without impiety or absurdity.

38. [In some editions, chapter III.] Again they bring forward another objection, asserting that the power of the Son and the Father cannot be one and the same, because he himself said: “Amen, amen, I say to you, the Son can do nothing of himself except what he sees the Father doing” (John V, 19). Thus they say that the Son did nothing from himself and cannot do anything except what he sees the Father doing.

39. O foreknowing wisdom of the unbelievers’ arguments, which placed beside the question what would resolve it, adding what follows: “For whatever he does, the Son also does likewise” (ibid.). This is what follows. Why, then, is it written, “The Son does the same things,” and not “such things” [Note: Some manuscripts read “and not other things”; all the other manuscripts and editions read “and not such things.” The latter is more correct: to do the same things signifies equality, while “such things,” that is, similar things, signifies imitation. Ambrose refutes the objection that the Arians pressed from the preceding passage not only here and in *On the Holy Spirit*, book II, chapter 12, but also in *Hexaemeron*, book II, chapter 5, no. 19, and in the twentieth sermon on Psalm CXVIII, no. 32. The last passage is worth examining.]—unless you should understand in the Son the unity, not an imitation, of the Father’s work?

40. Nevertheless, to examine even their arguments, I ask them to answer whether the Son sees the works of the Father. Does he see them or not? If he sees them, then he also does them. If he does them, let them cease denying the omnipotent one whom they confess capable of doing everything he sees the Father doing.

[Col. 0625A] 41. What, then, does “he sees” mean? Is it some bodily use of the eyes? [Note: Some manuscripts read: “Is there some kind of seeing with the eyes … bodily sight also in the Father, etc.”] But if they wish to say this about the Son, they must also demonstrate a bodily use of operation in the Father, so that the Son may see him doing what the Son himself is going to do.

42. What, then, does “the Son cannot do anything of himself” mean? Let us ask this; let us consider it. Is there, then, something impossible for God’s power and wisdom? For this is the Son of God. He did not receive a strength that was foreign to him; rather, just as he is life, not supported by another’s life-giving but giving life to others because he himself is life, so also he is wisdom—not as though an ignorant being receiving wisdom, but as one who from his own wisdom makes others wise. Likewise he is power, not as though he gained an increase of power through weakness, but himself being power, bestowing power upon the strong.

43. How, then, does power itself say, as though confirming it with an oath: “Amen, amen, I say to you” (John V, 19)—that is, “Faithfully, faithfully, I say”? [Note: Jerome also gives this meaning of the word *amen* in Letter 134 to Sophronius and Letter 137 to Marcella. In those letters he adds two other meanings, namely, where it is used sometimes for “let it be done,” and sometimes for “truly” or “it is true.” Ambrose likewise accepts these meanings, the former in his exposition of Psalm XL, no. 36, and the latter in *On the Mystery*, chapter 9, no. 54, and elsewhere.] You therefore speak faithfully, Lord Jesus, and with a certain repetition of solemn confirmation you affirm that you can do nothing except what you see the Father doing. You made the world. Did your Father make another world for you to receive as a model? The impious must therefore confess either that there are two worlds or certainly many worlds, as some philosophers assert, thus involving themselves in the error of paganism [Note: The holy man refers here to the opinion of certain philosophers concerning the plurality of worlds, which he mentions more than once elsewhere—for example, *Hexaemeron*, book I, chapter 1, no. 3, and book II, chapter 2, no. 5. This opinion was divided in two ways. Some maintained that multiple bodily worlds existed, while others admitted only a pair: the bodily world in which we live and an incorporeal world, also called the archetype. Ambrose appears to be referring to the former in the passages cited, as does the great Augustine in *Against the Academics*, book III, chapter 10, no. 23; *City of God*, book II, chapter 2, and book XI, chapter 5, along with many others. Augustine refers to the latter in *On Order*, book I, chapter 11, no. 32, and *Retractations*, book I, chapter 3; Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, book XI, no. 27, citing book VI of Clement of Alexandria’s *Stromata*, and many others do likewise. Gregory of Nazianzus also attacks the Arians with no less force in Oration 36 for introducing two or even four worlds.]. Or, if they wish to follow the truth, let them say that you made what you made without a model.

44. Tell me, Lord, when have you seen the Father incarnate walking upon the sea (Mark 6:48)? I do not know; I consider it sacrilegious to believe this of the Father, since I have learned that you alone assumed flesh. When have you seen the Father at the wedding turning water into wine (John 2:9)? But I have read that you alone, the only-begotten Son, were born from the Father; you alone I have received as conceived from the Holy Spirit and generated from the Virgin according to the mysteries of the Incarnation (Matt. 1:25). Therefore the things we have mentioned as performed by you were not performed by the Father; but, without a paternal work as your model, you alone, the immaculate one, came forth from the Virgin’s womb to redeem the world’s salvation by your blood.

45. And lest they perhaps think that only the mystery of the Incarnation is to be set aside—for when they say, “The Son can do nothing from himself” (John 5:19), they make no exception, so that one impious man even said, “He cannot make so much as a gnat,” mocking the majesty of heavenly power with such reckless presumption and insolent speech—tell me, Lord Jesus, what land the Father made without you. He did not make heaven without you, for it is written: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established” (Ps. 32:6).

46. Nor did he make the earth without you, for it is written: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3). For if the Father made anything without you, the Word of God, then not all things were made through the Word, and the Evangelist is lying. But if all things were made through the Word, and through you all things that did not exist began to exist, then surely whatever you did not see made by the Father, you yourself made. Unless perhaps they impose upon you, through that Platonic philosophical discussion, certain philosophical ideas as models, though we know that those very ideas were ridiculed by the philosophers themselves. But if you yourself made them, the assertion of the faithless is vain: they attribute to the author of all things, who possesses in himself the mastery of making, an advancement through learning.

[Note: Here, as also in Book I of the *Hexaemeron*, chapter 1, no. 1, Ambrose, following the ancient Fathers—such as Justin Martyr, *Exhortation to the Greeks*; Clement of Alexandria, Book VI of the *Stromata*; Tertullian, *On the Soul*, chapter 8, and *On the Prescription against Heretics*, chapter 7; and others—understands by “ideas” certain incorporeal, eternal, uncreated natures, distinct from God and from the world. Aristotle explains and ridicules them in this sense in various places in the *Metaphysics* and *Ethics*. But many accuse Aristotle of having distorted the teaching of that same philosopher into an absurd sense, whether because he envied his teacher or because he did not sufficiently grasp his meaning; for the divine philosopher understood by “ideas” nothing other than forms existing in the mind of God, according to which he created the world. Besides Eusebius, Book XI of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, no. 53, and Book XV, no. 13, this is how Augustine interprets him in *Eighty-Three Questions*, question 46, and Book I of the *Retractions*, chapter 3, as do many others.]

47. But if they deny that heaven or earth was made through you, let the impious consider into what abyss their madness is plunging them, since it is written: “The gods who did not make heaven and earth—let them perish” (Jer. 10:11). Will he therefore perish, Arius, who both found and redeemed what had perished? But let us return to the matters proposed.

## CHAPTER V

Pressing the exposition of the passage already begun, he explains four reasons why we say that something cannot be done; he demonstrates, after resolving certain objections, that the first three do not apply to Christ; and he deduces that the Son can do nothing from himself solely because of the unity of his power with the Father.

48. How can the Son do nothing from himself? Let us ask what it is that he cannot do. There are many different kinds of impossibility. Something is impossible by nature; something else is possible by nature but impossible through weakness. There is also a third kind: something may be possible through bodily and mental strength, yet impossible through lack of skill or inability. There is also what is impossible to change because of the determination of an unchanging purpose, the steadfast perseverance of the will, and fidelity to friendship.

49. But so that we may perceive these things more clearly, let our discussion proceed by examples. It is impossible for a bird to acquire wisdom’s discipline or any art; it is also impossible for a stone to go anywhere. A stone cannot move unless it is moved by another’s motion; therefore a stone cannot move itself or pass from one place to another. Nor can an eagle be instructed in human disciplines. Here you have one kind of impossibility, whose cause is nature.

50. It is also impossible for a weak person to perform the works of a strong person; but this impossibility has another cause. What one can do by nature, one cannot do through weakness. Weakness, therefore, is also the cause of this impossibility. This is consequently another kind of impossibility, since bodily weakness holds one back from the ability to act.

51. There is also a third cause of impossibility: even if someone could do something by nature and bodily strength, he may nevertheless be unable to do it through lack of skill or inability—for example, an uneducated person or a slave.

52. Which of these causes of impossibility that we have enumerated—for the fourth we shall set aside for the moment—do you think applies to the Son of God? Is he perhaps insensible by nature and immovable, like a stone? A stone indeed he is for the impious, to their ruin, but for the faithful he is the cornerstone. Yet he is not insensible, upon whom the faithful of the peoples, endowed with spiritual perception, are built. He is not the immovable rock: “They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4). Therefore the paternal work is not impossible for Christ because of a difference in nature.

53. Do we perhaps think that something is impossible for him through weakness? But he is not weak, for by an authoritative word he healed the weaknesses of others. Did he seem weak when, commanding the paralytic, “Take up your bed and walk” (Mark 2:11), he was already issuing the command of health while the man was still asking for a remedy for his weakness? Was the Lord of powers weak when he gave sight to the blind, raised up those who were bowed down (Ps. 145:8), raised the dead (Matt. 11:5), caused the effect of healing to precede our requests, healed those who prayed, and cleansed them by the touch of his fringe (Mark 6:56)?

54. Unless perhaps, impious men, you thought that weakness was present when you saw the wounds. Those were indeed wounds of the body, but there was no weakness in that wound from which the life of all flowed forth. Hence the prophet also said: “By his bruising we were healed” (Isa. 53:5). Was he who was not weak in the wound weak in majesty? Consider how. When he commanded demons and forgave the sins of the guilty—or when he entreated the Father?

55. At this point they may perhaps say: How are the Father and the Son one, if the Son now commands and now prays? They are one; he commands and he prays. Yet when he commands, he is not alone; and when he prays, he is not weak. He is not alone, because whatever the Father does, the Son also does in like manner. He is not weak, because although he was made weak in the flesh on account of our sins, that weakness in him was the instruction of our peace, as it is written, not a weakness of his majesty.

[Note: Some manuscripts read “that,” “some,” “that was ours,” and so forth.]

56. Finally, so that you may know that he asks as man and commands as God, you have it in the Gospel that he said to Peter: “I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail” (Luke 22:32). But when Peter had previously said to him, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God,” he replied: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church; and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 16:18). Could he therefore, by his own authority, give the kingdom to the one whose faith he could not strengthen? When he calls him “rock,” did he not indicate the Church’s foundation?

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “he judged him the foundation of the Church.”]

Consider, then, when he prays and when he commands. He prays when he is shown to be about to suffer; he commands when he is believed to be the Son of God.

57. We therefore now see that two kinds of impossibility are excluded, since God’s power can be neither insensible nor weak. Do you produce a third kind, claiming that he could do nothing as though he were unskilled and without a teacher, or a slave without a master? Then you have lied, Lord Jesus, who yourself called yourself both teacher and Lord, and you deceived your disciples when you said: “You call me Teacher and Lord, and you speak rightly; for so I am” (John 13:13).

[Note: Two manuscripts add, “and you do well.”]

But you would not deceive them, O Truth—especially those whom you called friends.

58. Yet if they distinguish you from an artisan as though you were unskilled, let them see whether they are saying that you—that is, the Wisdom of God—lacked skill. Nevertheless, they cannot separate the unity of substance between you and the Father. For ignorance, not nature, distinguishes an artisan from an unskilled person. But there is no craftsmanship lacking in the Father, nor ignorance in you; for Wisdom is not foolish.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “I shall see whether skill was lacking in you,” and so forth.]

59. Therefore, if the Son can be neither insensible by nature, nor weak, nor unskilled, nor a slave, let them consider that the Son is one with the Father both in nature and majesty, and that in operation his power does not differ from the Father’s, since everything the Father does, the Son also does in like manner. For no one can do the same work in the same way as another unless he both lacks inequality of operation and possesses unity of the same nature.

60. Nevertheless, I still ask what it is that the Son cannot do from himself unless he sees the Father doing it (John 5:19). And foolishly I offer certain examples from lower things: “I have become foolish; you compelled me” (2 Cor. 12:11). For what is more foolish than to sift arguments concerning the majesty of God—arguments that provide more opportunity for disputes than for the edification of God, which is in faith (1 Tim. 1:4–5)?

[Note: The Codex Bigot reads, “examples for the weaker,” and so forth.]

Let arguments answer arguments: words may answer their arguments, but for us let there be love, which is in God, proceeding from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith.

[Note: Some manuscripts, following the Apostolic text, omit “in God”; and below, instead of “such an inept proposal,” those same manuscripts prefer “your inept proposal,” and so forth.]

Therefore, in refuting so foolish a proposition, I am not reluctant even to resort to ridicule.

61. How, then, does the Son see the Father? A horse sees a painting, which it cannot imitate by nature; but the Son does not see in that way. A child sees the work of an adult, but cannot imitate it; nor does the Son of God see in that way.

62. Therefore, if the Son can invisibly both see and act through the secret commonality of the same nature that he shares with the Father, and can accomplish whatever he wills through the fullness of divinity, what remains except that, through the inseparable unity of power, we should believe that the Son does nothing except what he has seen the Father doing? For through incomparable love the Son does nothing from himself, since he wills nothing that the Father does not will. This is not weakness, but unity.

[Note: Most and more authoritative manuscripts read as above; others, including some editions, read, “because of the inseparable unity.”]

## CHAPTER VI

He proceeds to the fourth of the arguments mentioned above and clearly proves that the Son does nothing that is not approved by the Father, since the unity of their will and power is perfect; he then removes certain difficulties.

63. Therefore the Son is not rebellious, as we may say also concerning the fourth proposition; for the Son, as counselor, did nothing that was not in harmony with the Father’s will. Finally, the Father saw what the Son had done and approved it, because it was very good. Thus you have it in Genesis: “And God said, ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light; and God saw the light, that it was good” (Gen. 1:3–4).

64. Did the Father say here, “Let there be such light as I myself have made”; or, “Let there be light that did not exist before”; or did he ask what kind of light the Son would make? No: the Son made it as he willed, and the Father willed it to such an extent that he approved it. Therefore it is a new work of the Son.

[Note: All editions and some manuscripts read, “But let there be light . . . or the Son”; the latest Paris edition reads, “But the Son.” This is not inappropriate. The remaining manuscripts read as in the text.]

65. Furthermore, if the Son is criticized according to the Arians’ interpretations because he did what he saw, although according to the Scriptures he both made what he had not seen and brought into existence what did not exist, what do they say about the Father, who proclaimed what he had seen, as though he had been unable to foresee the things that were to be made?

66. The Son therefore sees the Father’s work just as the Father sees the Son’s work. He does not praise it as something alien, but recognizes it as his own: “Whatever the Father does, the Son also does in like manner” (John 5:19), so that you may understand the Father’s and the Son’s work to be the same. Therefore the Son does nothing except what the Father approves, praises, and wills, because he is wholly from the Father—not like a creature, which commits many offenses by repeatedly offending its author’s will through the striving and stumbling of sin. The Son therefore does nothing except what pleases the Father, because there is one will, one judgment, one true love, and one effect of operation.

67. Finally, so that you may know that it is a matter of love that the Son cannot do anything from himself except what he sees the Father doing—for after saying, “Whatever he does, the Son also does in like manner,” he added, “For the Father loves the Son”—the Scripture’s statement that he “cannot” do something refers to the unity of inseparable and indivisible love.

68. If, then, love is naturally inseparable, as it truly is, its operation is naturally inseparable as well; and it is impossible for the Son’s work not to agree with the Father’s will (John 12:50), since what the Son does, the Father also does, and what the Father does, the Son also does; and what the Son speaks, the Father also speaks, as it is written (John 14:10): “My Father who remains in me, he himself speaks; and the works that I do, he himself does.”

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “The words that I speak, as the Father told me, so I speak; and my Father who remains in me, he himself does the works.” These words are indeed found in John at the passages cited. Nevertheless, we make no alteration against the agreement of the manuscripts and the ancient editions.]

For the Father made nothing without his power and wisdom, since he made all things in wisdom, as it is written: “You made all things in wisdom” (Ps. 104:24). Nor did God the Word make anything without the Father.

69. He does not work without the Father; without the Father’s will he did not offer himself to that holy and saving suffering as the sacrificial victim of the whole world; without the Father’s will he did not raise the dead (Heb. 10:10). Finally, when he was about to raise Lazarus, he lifted his eyes upward and said: “Father, I thank you because you have heard me. I knew that you always hear me; but because of the crowd standing around I said it, so that they may believe that you sent me” (John 11:41–42).

[Note: Five manuscripts read, “from the person of a man in the assumption of the flesh”; the others and the editions read as in the text. We have already noted that Ambrose does not always use the word “person” in its strict, scholastic sense. Indeed, here it means nothing other than “insofar as he is man.” As for the unity of will with the Father of which he speaks here, if we understand it as the unity of the human will, it will be nothing other than agreement, submission, and conformity. But there is nothing to prevent us from interpreting it as the true unity of the divine will.]

Thus, although he spoke from the standpoint of the assumed incarnate man, he nevertheless expressed the unity of the Father’s will and operation, because the Father hears and sees everything that the Son wills. The Father therefore sees the Son doing and hears him willing. Finally, he did not ask and then say that he had been heard.

70. Nor can it be thought that the Father does not hear what the Son wills. And so that you may know that he is always heard by the Father—not as a servant, nor as a prophet, but as a Son—he says: “I knew that you always hear me; but because of the crowd standing around I said it, so that they may believe that you sent me.”

71. Therefore he gives thanks on our behalf, lest we believe that the Father and the Son are the same person, when we hear that the Father’s work and the Son’s work are the same.

[Note: All editions and some manuscripts read, “He gave thanks. Therefore, lest we believe . . .”; a greater number of manuscripts, and those of greater authority, read, “He gives thanks, lest we believe . . .” This is preferable. For the reason why he gave thanks on our behalf is explained: namely, so that we should not believe that the Father and the Son are one person, since no one gives thanks to himself.]

For you might know that he did not give thanks as a weak man, but that, as the Son of God, he always claimed divine power for himself: he cried, “Lazarus, come out!” This is the voice of one commanding, not of one praying.

## CHAPTER VII

The doctrine already proposed is confirmed by the fact that the Son is the Father’s Word—not like our word, but living and active—and therefore that his unity of will, power, and substance with the Father cannot be denied.

72. But to return to what came before and bring our argument to its conclusion: as the Word, the Son does the Father’s will. Our word is, of course, an utterance; it consists of syllables and sound. Nevertheless, it does not differ from our understanding and mind, and the things we hold inwardly we signify as a testimony of the Word at work. But our speech does not act. The Word of God alone is neither merely uttered nor what they call *ἐνδιάθετον* (“indwelling” or “inward”), but it acts, lives, and heals.

[Note: We have already noted that the uttered Word, or *προφορικόν*, is opposed to the inner Word, or *ἐνδιάθετον*. No one was so insane as to say that the divine *προφορικόν* Word was syllables or bodily sound in that sense. But the Arians did maintain that it was itself *ἐνδιάθετον* and similar to human dispositions, and therefore accidental and separate from the Father’s nature, as we understand from Basil’s Homily 27 *Against the Arians* and elsewhere. Nevertheless, they also asserted that this Word was uttered in a certain spiritual manner: namely, that it was born from the Father not by the generation of a Word who remains, but as though by the utterance of a flowing speech. Ambrose combats this view throughout the present work.]

73. Do you wish to know what kind of Word this is? Hear him who says: “For the Word of God is living and active and powerful, sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow” (Heb. 4:12).

74. You hear the Word of God, the Son, and do you separate him from the Father’s will and power? You hear that he lives; you hear that he heals. Do not, then, compare him with our word. For if our word speaks of what it has not seen with its eyes and has not heard with its ears—and yet speaks of what it has known through certain inward mysteries of human nature—how impious is anyone who demands, in the Word of God according to his divinity, a bodily kind of sight and hearing, and supposes that the Son cannot do anything from himself except what he has seen the Father doing, when, through the unity of the same substance, as we have said, the same willing, the same refusal, the same ability are present in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit?

75. If human beings, though often differing in the quality of their senses, nevertheless agree through the intention of a single purpose, what should we judge concerning the Father and the Son of God, when divine substance possesses what human love imitates?
