76. Let us nevertheless suppose, as they themselves wish, that the Son acts according to the model in which he has seen the Father acting. This too belongs to the same substance; for no one can carry out another’s imitation of an operation unless he possesses unity of the same nature.

## CHAPTER VIII

He first turns back upon the heretics themselves their objection by which they denied that the Son was equal to the Father because he could not beget another; then, by examples from human beings, he shows that whether someone begets or does not beget has no bearing on power—especially since otherwise the Father himself would have to be called less powerful. From this he concludes that divine realities must not be judged by human realities, but that one must stand by the authority of Scripture. Finally, after showing that omnipotence must either be denied to the Father or granted to the Son, he argues that, if the heretics have not begotten sons, they are less powerful than their own servants who have produced offspring, and therefore that their entire argument is foolish.

[In some editions, Chapter VI.]

It is absurd, august Emperor, that certain people have become accustomed to use even this as an objection to the inequality of God the Father and the Son: they say that the Father is omnipotent because he begot the Son, but deny that the Son is omnipotent, saying that he was unable to beget.

[Note: All editions and some manuscripts omit “It is absurd” and begin immediately, “August Emperor, certain people,” and so forth. Hence many manuscripts also omit “August Emperor.” Other manuscripts, though fewer, preserve it as in the text; this is preferable.]

78. But observe how savage impiety causes the dialectic of the philosophers to convict itself. By this question they must either confess in their own words that the Son is coeternal with the Father, or, if they ascribe some beginning in time to the Son, they must also ascribe a beginning of power to the Father. Thus, while denying that the Son is omnipotent, they begin—as it is impious to say—to assert that the Father began to be omnipotent through the Son.

79. For if the Father is omnipotent through generation, then either the Son is coeternal with the Father—for if the Father has always been omnipotent, the Son is also eternal—or, if there was a time when the Son was not eternal, there was therefore a time when the Father was not omnipotent. For when they wish to say that the Son began at some point, they fall into the position that the Father’s power too did not always exist, but began with the generation of the Son. Thus, while they wish to detract from the Son of God, they grant him more, so that, contrary to all propriety, they seem to declare him the source of the Father’s power, although the Son says: “All that the Father has is mine” (John 16:15)—that is, not things that he himself handed over to the Father, but things that he received from the Father by right of generation.

80. And therefore we say that the Son is eternal power. If, then, his power and divinity are eternal, his power is certainly eternal as well. Whoever therefore detracts from the Son detracts from the Father, offends piety, and violates love. Let us honor the Son, in whom the Father is well pleased; for it pleases the Father that the Son in whom he is well pleased should be praised.

81. Nevertheless, let us answer their intention, lest we appear to have evaded the issue by some rhetorical peroration.

[Note: We have observed that Ambrose uses *epilogus* in the sense of a speech such as orators employ to divert the minds of judges from consideration of the case at hand and to stir and arouse their emotions, in Book VI of the *Hexaemeron*, no. 24. Nor is the word used here in a sense wholly unrelated to that one; it means nothing other than this kind of discourse.]

“The Father begot,” they say; “the Son did not beget.” What argument for inequality is this? Generation belongs to the Father’s property, not to power; and piety makes equal, it does not separate. Finally, we know that even in the ordinary circumstances of our weakness it often happens that the weak have children while the stronger do not; that slaves have them while masters do not; that the poor have them while the powerful do not.

82. But if they say that this too is a weakness, because human beings wish to have children but cannot, then—even though human realities must not be compared with divine realities—let them nevertheless understand that among human beings also, having or not having children belongs not to power but to paternal property. Begetting is not within the control of our will, but depends upon the condition of the body; for if it belonged to power, the more powerful person would surely have many children. Therefore having or not having children is not a matter of power.

83. Is it perhaps a matter of nature? If you regard it as a weakness of nature and appeal to human examples, the Father’s nature is the same as the Son’s. Thus either you call him the true Son and detract from the Father in the Son through the unity of the same nature—for just as the Father is God by nature, so also is the Son; yet the Apostle says that gods are not gods by nature but are so called (1 Cor. 8:5)—or, if you deny that he is a true Son, that is, of the same nature, then he was not begotten. If the Son was not begotten, the Father did not beget.

84. It follows, according to your position, that God the Father is not omnipotent, because he could not beget if he did not beget the Son but created him. But because the Father is omnipotent, and according to your position only the one who begets is omnipotent, he certainly begot the Son rather than creating him. Yet he himself is more worthy of belief than you are. He says, “I have begotten” (Ps. 110:3), and frequently bears witness that he is the one who begot.

85. Therefore Christ’s not having begotten does not constitute any weakness of nature or power, because, as we have often said, generation pertains not to the height of power but to the property of nature.

[Note: Petavius explains this statement of Ambrose in Book II of *On the Trinity*, chapter 5, as follows: “It is something proper to the person, or to the divine nature insofar as it subsists in the Father.” To make the point clearer, one must observe that the Son is generated from the Father’s nature not insofar as it is nature, but insofar as it is in the Father. Thus the Son is simultaneously consubstantial with the Father and personally distinct from him.]

For if the Father is omnipotent because he has a Son, he could have been more omnipotent if he had had several.

86. Or did his power fail in one generation? I shall show that Christ too has sons, whom he begets daily—but by a generation, or rather regeneration, that belongs to power, not to nature. Adoption belongs to power; generation belongs to property. Scripture itself has taught us this. John says: “He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him. He came to his own, and his own did not receive him. But to all who received him he gave power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name” (John 1:10–12).

87. We have therefore learned that it is a matter of power that he made us children of God.

[Note: The Roman edition and some manuscripts read, “We therefore say.” The ancient edition and other manuscripts read, “We have therefore learned.” The latter is more appropriate, since it refers back to the preceding words, “he gave them power,” and so forth. Again, where all the editions and some manuscripts read, “the generation of property,” the Amerbach and Erasmus editions read, “generations”; the remaining manuscripts invert the phrase as follows: “the property of generation.” This is less suitable.]

But the divine oracles declare that generation belongs to property. For the Wisdom of God says: “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High” (Ecclus. 24:5)—that is, not compelled but freely; not subject to power, but born through the mystery of generation, by the privilege of lordship and the right of power.

[Note: Four manuscripts read, “by the right of piety,” which is not inappropriate.]

Finally, concerning that same Wisdom—that is, the Lord Jesus—the Father says elsewhere: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Ps. 110:3).

88. He said this, of course, not to indicate a bodily womb, but to show the property of true generation. For if you refer it to a bodily womb, then the omnipotent Father begot with pain and conception. But far be it from us to measure God by bodily weakness. There is a womb that is the mystery of the Father’s substance, an inward secret that no nature of angels, archangels, powers, dominions, or any creatures could penetrate. The Son is always with the Father and always in the Father: with the Father through the inseparable distinction of the eternal Trinity, and in the Father through the unity of the divine nature.

89. Who, then, is this judge of divinity, who examines the Father and the Son—one asking why he begot, the other why he did not beget? No one condemns a servant or maidservant for not having begotten a child; yet these men condemn Christ for not having begotten, for by their opinion they condemn him when they detract from him. Nor is love diminished or merit taken away when spouses do not beget children with one another; yet these men diminish Christ’s power because he did not beget.

90. “Why,” they say, “is the Son not the Father?” Because the Father is not the Son either. “Why did this one not beget?” Because the other was not begotten. Nor does the Son possess less because he is not the Father, nor the Father less because he is not the Son. For the Son said: “All that the Father has is mine” (John 16:15). Thus generation belongs to the Father’s property, not to the right of power.

91. There is a certain undivided reality of the distinct, incomprehensible, and ineffable substance of the Trinity. We have received the distinction of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, not confusion: distinction, not separation; distinction, not plurality.

[Note: All editions and many manuscripts read as above. Others, with the words joined differently, add: “distinction, not separation; we always receive the divinity that remains, in wondrous mystery, from the Father, always through the Son, always in the Holy Spirit.” One Colbert manuscript reads: “We have learned distinction, not separation, not plurality.” The remainder is as in the text.]

In the divine and wondrous mystery, therefore, we always receive the Father, always the Son, always the Holy Spirit—not two Fathers, not two Sons, not two Spirits. For there is one God, the Father, from whom all things come and we exist for him; and one Lord Jesus, through whom all things come and we exist through him (1 Cor. 8:6). One Lord Jesus was born from the Father, and therefore he is the only-begotten. There is also one Holy Spirit (1 Cor. 12:11), as the same Apostle said. This is how we receive it, how we read it, how we hold it. We know distinction; we do not investigate hidden causes; we preserve the mysteries.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “We know the secrets; we preserve the mysteries.”]

92. It is an outrageous act that those who do not possess the ability to beget offspring should arrogate to themselves and claim the authority to examine divine generation.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “should arrogate to themselves the power to investigate it.”]

Let them therefore deny that the Son is equal to the Father because the Son did not beget; let them deny that the Son is equal to the Father because he has the Father.

If they said this about human beings, some of whom wish to have children but cannot, we would consider it an insult. We would likewise regard it as an insult if, among two persons equal in honor, equality were denied to the one who had children in comparison with the one who did not. And so, I say, this too appears a grave matter even among human beings: that someone should be thought inferior merely because he has a father. Unless perhaps they think that Christ, as though established within a household, grieves because he has not been emancipated from his Father and has no power to administer the patrimony.

[Note: The ancient edition reads, “who distinguished all sacred things”; the Roman edition and the manuscripts read, “who destroyed all sacred things.” It was said that minors were “in sacred things,” as is clear from the Theodosian Code, *On Maternal Property*, laws 1 and 9.]

But Christ is not among the sacred ones who destroyed all sacred things.

93. Nevertheless, let them answer what they wish: is it a true generation, and is the true Son born from God the Father—that is, from the Father’s substance—or is he born from another substance? For if they say that he is from the Father, that is, from God’s substance, then we agree, because they say that the Son is from the Father’s substance.

[Note: All editions read, “it agrees that they say . . .”; the manuscripts read, “it agrees because they say . . .” This is preferable, for it is equivalent to saying, “we agree among ourselves,” or “we do not disagree on this point,” and so forth.]

Therefore, because he is of one substance, he is necessarily of one power. But if the Son is of another substance, how is the Father omnipotent while the Son is not? For what is more excellent if God made the Son from another substance, since the Son too made us children of God from another substance? Therefore the Son is either of one substance with the Father or of one power.

94. Their question therefore comes to nothing, because they cannot judge Christ—indeed, because he conquers when he is judged. Yet those who raise this question deserve their own judgment. For if the Son is not equal to the Father because he did not beget a Son, then let these men admit that, if they do not have sons, even their own servants of that sort ought to be preferred to them, since they cannot be equal to those who have children. But if they do have sons, let them not think that merit is attributed to them, but to the right of their sons.

95. This question therefore does not stand: the Son cannot be equal to the Father because the Father begot a Son while the Son did not himself beget anyone from himself. For a spring begets a river, while a river does not itself beget a spring from itself; light begets radiance, not radiance light; and radiance and light have one nature.

## CHAPTER IX

He presents and refutes the various sophistical objections of the Arians by which they argued that the Son had a beginning. For, apart from the fact that they are shown either to argue against themselves or to accomplish nothing, their reasoning is also defective in human matters, since there can be no beginning before the beginning of all things. Time, therefore, did not precede its author; for if he ever did not exist, then the Father once existed without his power and wisdom. Finally, after showing by human examples that someone may be said to exist before he is born, he condemns the rashness of the heretics.

96. Since, then, they have been unable to prove inequality from the objection based on generation, let them understand that their widely circulated calumnious question has likewise been refuted. [Note: Thus nearly all the manuscripts; the edition, however, reads: “For they are accustomed to object.” In any case, this objection was always one of the principal Arian arguments; but the Eunomians turned it against us with a certain special adaptation of their arguments. Gregory of Nyssa answered them in Book VIII of *Against Eunomius*, Basil in Book IV against the same opponent, Hilary in Book XII of *On the Trinity*, and others as well.] For they are accustomed to put forward this question: “How can the Son be equal to the Father? For if he is Son, he did not exist before he was begotten; or, if he did exist, why was he born?” And do they not customarily deny that they are Arians, those who put forward Arius’s questions?

97. Accordingly, they demand an answer from us, so that if we say, “He existed before he was begotten,” they may slyly reply: “Then he was created before he was begotten, and he differs in no way from the other creatures, since the creature began to exist before the Son.” They add: “Why was he who existed born? Was it because he was imperfect, so that afterward he might become more perfect?” But if we answer that he did not exist, they immediately object: “Then generation gave existence to one who did not exist before he was born,” so that from this they may conclude: “Therefore he existed when the Son did not exist.”

98. But let those who propose this, and who seek to envelop the truth in obscurity, say themselves whether the Father generates temporally or timelessly. For if they say temporally, they will attribute to the Father what they object against the Son, so that the Father may appear to have begun to exist, although previously he did not. If they say timelessly, what remains except that they themselves solve the question they have proposed, and that, while denying that the Father’s generation is temporal, they also acknowledge that the Son’s generation is not temporal?

99. If, then, his generation is not from time, it follows that nothing preceded the Son that is not itself from time. For if something existed before the Son, then not all things that are in heaven or on earth were created in him, and the Apostle is proved false, since he wrote this in his Epistle (Colossians 1:16). But if nothing preceded his generation, I do not see why he is asserted to be later, whom no one preceded.

100. Another of their thoroughly impious objections must be connected with this; it conceals a trick by which it strikes the senses of the simple and pierces their minds. For they ask whether everything that has an end once began. And if they receive the answer that whatever has an end began at some point, they ask in turn whether the Father ceased to beget the Son. When they have secured this answer, with our agreement—if it should be granted—they weave the following conclusion: “Then generation began.” If one does not reject this, it appears to follow that, if generation began, it began in the one who was born; and thus he is said to have been born who previously did not exist. From this they define their conclusion: “Therefore, at some time the Son did not exist.”

101. They add other absurdities of their loquacity, saying: “If the Son is the Father’s Word, and is therefore said to have been begotten because he is the Word; and if what is the Word is not a work—the Father spoke in many ways (Hebrews 1:1)—then he begot many sons, if he did not act but spoke the Word.” Madmen! As though they did not understand the difference between an uttered verbal expression and the Word of God, born from the Father and abiding eternally: born, certainly, not uttered; in whom there is not a syllable formed by composition, but the fullness of eternal divinity and life without end. [539]

102. They append another impiety, asking whether the Father begot willingly or unwillingly. If we say “willingly,” we seem to acknowledge a will older than the generation, and they reply that the Son is not coeternal with the Father, since something preceded him; or that he too is a creature, because it is written: “He has done all that he willed” (Psalm 113:11). Yet this was said not of the Father and the Son, but of those creatures that the Son made. But if we answer that the Father begot unwillingly, we seem to have called the Father weak.

103. But in eternal generation neither willing nor unwilling precedes. Therefore I would call him neither unwilling nor willing, because generation does not lie within the capacity of the will, but appears to belong to a certain right and property of the paternal mystery. For just as the good Father is not good either by will or by necessity, [Note: An old edition reads: “but by nature, so he generates”; several manuscripts and Gill in the margin read: “but over both, so he generates.” The remaining manuscripts and the Roman edition have the reading printed in the text. This was also Arius’s objection, as Epiphanius recorded it in *Heresy* 76.6. The Fathers opposed a twofold answer to it: some acknowledged that the Son was begotten by the will, while denying—as Ambrose does not fail to do here—that the will was prior to generation; others, and more numerous writers, offered precisely the solution given here by our Doctor.] but above both—that is, by nature—so the Father does not generate from will or necessity.

104. Nevertheless, let generation be in the will of the one who generates. When, they ask, did this will exist? If it was at the beginning, then the Son was also at the beginning. If the will was eternal, the Son too is eternal. If the will began, then God the Father must have been displeased with what he was, so that he changed his condition. He was therefore displeased with himself without the Son and began to be pleased with himself in the Son.

105. The consequence is that we must say: If he assumed the inclination to beget according to our custom, then he also assumed according to our custom the other things that ordinarily precede generation. But in our practice of generation there is desire, not will.

106. They thus reveal their impiety, those who wish Christ’s generation to have begun, so that it may appear to be not the generation of the abiding Word but the utterance of flowing speech. Then, by introducing many sons, they deny in Christ the property of the divine nature, so that he is regarded as neither only-begotten nor firstborn. Finally, if he is believed to have received a beginning, he also appears destined to have an end.

107. But the Son of God never at any time assumed a beginning, for he was “in the beginning” (John 1:1); nor will he have an end, since he is the beginning and the end of the universe (John 8:20). For since he is the beginning, how did he receive what he already possessed? Or how will he have an end of himself, since he himself is the end of all things, so that in that end we may remain without end? For since God’s generation is not temporal, it finds neither time before itself nor time within itself.

108. Their cold and empty question, then, has no place even among created things themselves; for even temporal things do not appear in every case to possess a temporal distinction. Light, certainly, generates radiance, yet it cannot be grasped how radiance should be later than light or light older than radiance, because wherever there is light, there is radiance, and wherever there is radiance, there is also light. Thus light cannot exist without radiance, nor radiance without light, because there is light in radiance, and radiance in light. Therefore the Apostle called the Son “the radiance of the Father’s glory” (Hebrews 1:3), because the Son is the radiance of the Father’s light: coeternal because of the eternity of his power, inseparable because of the unity of his brightness.

109. If, then, we cannot comprehend or separate these temporal and material things that we see, can we comprehend God, whom we do not see and who is above every creature, in the very mystery of his generation? Can we separate him from the Son by time, when all time is the work of the Son?

110. Let them cease, then, to say: “Before he was begotten, he did not exist.” For “before” belongs to time, whereas generation is before times; and therefore what is later is not earlier. Nor can a work exist before its author, since works themselves receive their beginning from their maker. For how can the use of a work be considered prior to its maker, when all time is a work and every work received from its maker the fact that it should exist?

111. I still wish to test these men who think themselves clever, so that they may answer concerning our matters, while they slander divine things and flee far from the inscrutable mystery of heavenly generation. Let them establish their question by an example from human generation. They say of the Son of God that before he was begotten he did not exist—that is, they say this of the Wisdom of God, of the Power of God, of the Word of God, whose generation knows nothing before itself. But if he once did not exist, as they wish—which it is sacrilegious to say—then at some time the fullness of divine perfection was not in God, if afterward he received the process of generation. [Note: A certain Paris edition reads: “of the true God.”]

112. Nevertheless, so that they may know how empty and easily refuted their question is, although there is nothing in him that is common to human and divine things, I will nevertheless teach these men that people existed before they were born. Or let them deny that holy Jacob existed before he was born, when, while still placed in the hidden recess of his mother’s womb, he supplanted his brother (Genesis 25:23). Let them deny that Jeremiah existed before he was born, to whom it is said: “Before I formed you in the womb of your mother, I knew you; and before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you and appointed you as a prophet to the nations” (Jeremiah 1:5). What could be clearer than the example of so great a prophet, who was sanctified before he was born and known before he was formed?

113. What shall I say also of John, of whom his devout mother bears witness that, while he was still placed within her womb, he recognized the presence of the Lord in spirit and marked it by exultation, as we remember is written, when his mother said: “For behold, when the voice of your greeting came to my ears, the infant in my womb leaped for joy” (Luke 1:41)? Did he exist, then, who prophesied, or did he not exist? Certainly he existed; for he existed who revered his author, and he existed who spoke within his mother. Finally, Elizabeth was filled with the spirit of her son, and Mary was sanctified by the Spirit of her Son. For you have this written: “The infant in her womb leaped,” and “Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit” (ibid.).

114. [Note: Compare, if convenient, this exposition of the passage with that found in nearly the same words in Book II of the Commentary on Luke.] Observe the proper force of each word. Elizabeth first heard Mary’s voice, but John first sensed the grace of the Lord. Beautifully the oracles correspond with oracles, woman with woman, and pledge with pledge. These women speak of grace; those infants inwardly accomplish the mystery of piety and begin it through their mothers’ progress. By a double miracle, though with different honors, the mothers prophesy through the spirits of their infants. Who, then, is the author of this miracle? Is it not the Son of God, who caused those not yet born to exist?

115. Your question concerning human affairs [Note: The edition reads “our question”; the manuscripts read “your question,” that is, “your objection.”] cannot apply here; can it apply to divine mysteries? What does “Before he was begotten, he did not exist” mean? Did the Father receive some period of conception, so that periods of time preceded the Son? Or, after the manner of female nature, did he labor to bring forth his generation, so that the labor itself would be older than the Son? What is this? Why do we investigate divine mysteries? I have learned the property of divine generation, not its mode.

116. An outrageous crime! Some measure heavenly things by what comes from themselves, although they think that Christ could not be born but could only be made, as though he were one of the eunuchs; or as though the Father adopted as his Son one of the eunuchs whom he was unable to beget.

## CHAPTER X

To those who object, on the testimony of John, that Christ lives because of the Father and therefore should not be regarded as equal to him, the answer is given that the Son’s life according to his divinity neither began in time nor depends on anyone. The passage is shown to be understood of his human life because it had already spoken there of his body and blood. The first of two interpretations of the disputed passage is then referred to his humanity, while the second is shown to signify the Son’s equality with the Father and also his likeness to human beings. Next, after briefly addressing the insult they inflicted upon the Son, he explains in what sense the Son lives because of the Father even according to his divinity. Finally, after explaining what unity our life has with the divine life, he briefly disposes of another objection, namely, that the Son is said to be glorified through the Father.

117. [Elsewhere, Chapter V.] Many also make this an occasion for a question, because it is written: “As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father; and whoever eats me, he too will live because of me.” They say: “How is the Son equal to the Father, when he said that he lives because of the Father?”

118. Let those who propose this first answer what sort of life the Son has: whether it is a life bestowed by the Father upon one who did not possess it. [Note: The latest Paris edition reads: “whether he does not possess the life that the Father bestowed.”] But how could he ever have lacked life, when he himself is life, as he says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (Luke 14:6)? It is certainly eternal life, just as power is eternal (Romans 1:20). Did life, then, at some time—so to speak—not possess itself?

119. Consider what was read today concerning the Lord Jesus: that he died for us, “so that whether we are awake or asleep, we may live together with him” (1 Thessalonians 5:10). Is the divinity of him whose death is life not itself life, when divine life is eternal? [Note: Three manuscripts read: “since divine life is eternal”; one reads: “since he is eternal divinity.”]

120. Or is his life in the Father’s power? Yet he did not even say that the life of his own body was in another’s power, as it is written: “I lay down my life, that I may take it again. No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again. I received this commandment from my Father” (John 10:17–18).

121. Is his life, then, according to his divinity judged to have been placed in another’s power, when his life according to the body was not subject to another’s power? It would have been another’s power if there were not unity of power. But just as he signifies that laying down his life belongs to his own power and free will, so also the fact that he laid it down according to the Father’s command signifies the unity of his own will and the Father’s will.

122. If, then, the Son neither received life at some point in time nor has it subject to another’s power, let us see in what sense he said: “As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father” (John 6:58). Let us explain it as best we can—or rather, let him explain it himself.

123. Consider, then, what he said immediately beforehand. He says: “Amen, amen, I say to you.” He first instructs you how you ought to hear him: “Truly, truly, I say to you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6:54). He first declared that he was speaking according to the Son of Man, and do you suppose that what he said concerning the flesh and blood according to the Son of Man should be referred to his divinity?

124. Finally, he added: “For my flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” (ibid., 56). You hear flesh; you hear blood; you recognize the sacraments of the Lord’s death—and you slander his divinity? Hear him saying: “For a spirit does not have flesh and bones” (Luke 24:39). But whenever we receive the sacraments, which through the mystery of the sacred prayer are transformed into flesh and blood, we proclaim the Lord’s death (1 Corinthians 11:26). [Note: Cardinal Perronius cited a closely similar expression from Book 4 of *On the Incarnation* in Book II, chapter 31, of *On the Sacrament of the Eucharist*, and taught that it signifies the same thing as *vertere* in Virgil’s phrase “He changes himself into every form”—namely, the conversion of the body into another form and shape. Albertinus, attempting to answer him in Book II of *On the Sacrament of the Eucharist*, says that two other meanings of this verb may be added. But these do nothing to support his case. First, he says, it sometimes means the same as “to cause to become,” as when Pliny says of almonds that they are “transformed from sweet into bitter”; nor does he deny that in this sense Christ’s body is offered on the altars to be transformed. In this matter we disagree with him only because he does not conceal that he understands a symbolic body. But that final point is absurd: apart from the fact that the body was already symbolic in the antitypes, it is certain that some real transformation is always indicated, whether of substance, when the subject is substance, or of accident, as in Pliny’s example. He says that the second meaning is one in which a compound expression is used for its simple form, so that “to be transformed into a body” means the same as “to be formed into a body”—that is, in his view, to become the form of a body. But who among mankind has ever spoken in this way? Certainly the examples handed down for these verbs and others do not support this, nor does he anywhere set out his theory of compounds; and even if he stripped the expression of that meaning as far as possible, it would not serve his purpose here. Ambrose, therefore, signifies nothing here except what is stated in Book *On the Mysteries*, chapter 9, section 50: “By the blessing itself, nature is changed.” For the mystery of the sacred prayer is the same as the blessing, as are the Lord’s own words.]

125. After he had made clear that he was speaking according to the Son of Man, and had repeatedly mentioned flesh and blood, he later added: “As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father; and whoever eats me, he too will live because of me” (John 6:58). How, then, do they think this should be understood? For the comparison may appear to be twofold. The first is as follows: “As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father.” The second is: “As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so whoever eats me lives because of me.”

126. If they choose the first interpretation, it means this: Just as I was sent by the Father and descended from the Father, so I live because of the Father. For who was sent and descended, as it were, except the Son of Man, as he himself said above: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man” (John 3:13)? Therefore, just as he was sent and descended as the Son of Man, so, as the Son of Man, he lives because of the Father. Finally, whoever eats him as the Son of Man also lives because of the Son of Man. He thus compared the event of his incarnation with his coming.

127. But if the second interpretation is preferred, do we not clearly gather both the Son’s equality with the Father and his likeness to human beings? For what does “As he himself lives because of the Father, so we live because of him” mean except that the Son gives life to humanity just as the Father gave life to human flesh in the Son? For just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whomever he wishes, as the Lord himself said above (John 5:21).

128. The Son’s equality with the Father is therefore established also through the unity of giving life, since the Son gives life in the same way as the Father. Recognize, then, his eternal life and power. Our likeness to the Son, and a certain unity with him according to the flesh, is also made clear, since just as the Son of God was given life by the Father, so human beings have been given life in the flesh. For it is written (Romans 4:24) that just as God raised Jesus Christ from the dead, so we too, as human beings, are given life by the Son of God.

129. According to this interpretation, therefore, not only is the grace of generosity brought down to the human condition, but the eternity of divinity is also proclaimed: of divinity, because it gives life; of the human condition, because it has been given life, and in Christ.

130. But if someone refers both statements to Christ’s divinity, then the Son of God is compared with human beings, so that the Son lives because of the Father just as we live because of the Son of God. But the Son of God bestows eternal life, whereas we cannot bestow it; therefore, by comparison with us, neither does he bestow it. Let the Arians, then, receive the reward of their faith, so that they may not attain eternal life from the Son.

131. Let us now proceed further. If they are pleased to refer this passage to the perpetuity of the divine substance, let them also accept a third interpretation. [Note: Several manuscripts read: “to the property of the substance.”] Does it not clearly appear to say that just as the Father is living, so the Son also lives? Who would not understand this as referring to the unity of life—that the Father and the Son have the same life? For just as the Father has life in himself, so he also gave the Son to have life in himself (John 5:26). He gave it through unity; he gave it not in order to take it away, but in order that he might be glorified in the Son; he gave it so that he might be pleased; he gave it not so that the Father might guard it, but so that the Son might possess it.

132. But they think an objection should be raised because he had said: “I live because of the Father” (John 6:58). Certainly, if they refer this to his divinity, the Son lives because of the Father: because he is Son from the Father; because he is of one substance with the Father; because the Word has been poured forth from the Father’s heart (Psalm 44:1); because he proceeded from the Father; because he was begotten from the Father’s womb (Psalm 109:3); because the Father is the fountain of the Son; because the Father is the root of the Son.

133. But perhaps they will say: “If you think that the Father and the Son have unity of life, since the Son said, ‘I live because of the Father,’ is there also unity between the Son’s life and that of human beings, since the Son said, ‘Whoever eats me lives because of me’?”

134. On the contrary, just as I acknowledge that the heavenly life of the Father and the Son is one through the unity of the divine substance, so I profess that, with the privilege of either the divine nature or the Lord’s incarnation excepted, we share spiritual life with the Son through the unity of human nature: “As is the heavenly one, so also are the heavenly ones” (1 Corinthians 15:18). Finally, just as we sit at the right hand of the Father in him—not because we sit together with him, but because we sit in the body of Christ, about which we shall speak more fully later (below, Book V)—so, I say, we sit in Christ through unity of body; likewise, we live in Christ through unity of body.

135. Nor am I afraid merely because it is written: “And I live because of the Father”; even if he had said “through the Father,” I would not be afraid.

136. [Elsewhere, Chapter VI.] They also customarily object to the following, because he said: “This illness is not unto death, but for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it” (John 11:4). For the Son is glorified not only through the Father and by the Father, since it is written: “Glorify me, Father” (John 17:5), and elsewhere: “Now the Son of Man has been glorified, and God has been glorified in him, and God has glorified him” (John 13:31–32); the Father is also glorified through the Son and by the Son, because the Truth said: “I have glorified you on earth” (John 17:4). [Note: Some manuscripts read: “but for the glory of God.”]

137. Therefore, just as he is glorified through the Father, so he also lives because of the Father. Hence some have thought that *doxa* (δόξα) means “opinion” rather than “glory,” and have interpreted the passage in this way: “I have glorified you on earth; I have completed the work that you gave me. And now glorify me, Father”—that is, *doxason* (δόξασον). The sense would then be: “I have instilled in human beings this opinion concerning you, so that they may know you to be the true God; and confirm this opinion concerning me in them, so that they may believe me to be your Son and the true God.”

## CHAPTER XI

The distinction that the Arians attempted to construct from the Apostle’s words teaching that all things are “from the Father” and “through the Son” is ridiculed. It is shown that the same omnipotence of the Father and the Son is expressed there; this is confirmed both from other passages and from Paul’s own text. It is demonstrated from the same context that the heretics absurdly refer the passage to the Father, although it belongs to the Son; nevertheless, nothing is taken away from the Son’s power if it is understood of the Father. Finally, he proves that in the expressions “from whom,” “through whom,” and “in whom” something exists, there is no difference, and that all these expressions are said of the three persons.

138. It is ridiculous that some create a distinction of power between the Father and the Son from that apostolic passage. [Note: Some manuscripts read: “because it is written that there is no difference of power, because it is written, ‘All things are from the Father, and all things through the Son, his through him; yet for us one …’” [the reading is uncertain]; other manuscripts and all editions, more suitably, read as in the text.] Because it is written: “Yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and we in him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through him” (1 Corinthians 8:6). For they say that there is a considerable difference in divine majesty because it is said: “All things are from that one” and “all things are through this one.” Nothing, however, could be clearer than that the omnipotent Son is indicated in this passage by an evident argument; for just as all things are from him, so all things are through him.

139. The Father is not “among all things,” to whom it is said: “All things serve you” (Psalm 118:91). The Son is not “among all things,” because all things were made through him (John 1:3), all things subsist in him, and he is above all the heavens (Colossians 1:17). The Son is therefore not among all things but above all things. According to the flesh, he is indeed from the family of the Jews; yet he is also “God over all, blessed forever” (Romans 9:5), whose name is above every name, and of whom it is said: “You have subjected all things under his feet” (Psalm 8:8). By subjecting all things, he left nothing that was not subject to him, as the Apostle said (Hebrews 2:8). If this too was spoken according to the mystery of the incarnation, how can we doubt the incomparable majesty of heavenly generation?

140. It is therefore certain that there is no difference of power between the Father and the Son. Finally, the difference of power is so entirely absent that the same Apostle said that all things are from him through whom all things are, as you have it: “For from him and through him and in him are all things” (Romans 11:33).

141. If, then, according to their opinion, only the Father is signified, he cannot both be omnipotent because all things are from him and not be omnipotent because all things are through him. Either, therefore, by their assertion they will acknowledge the Father to be weak and not omnipotent, or, against their will, they will confess in their own words that the Son too is omnipotent.

142. Let them nevertheless choose whether they think the Father is declared here. If the Father, then all things are also through him. If the Son, then all things are also from him. But if all things are through the Father, nothing is thereby to be taken away from the Son; and if all things are from the Son, the Son must likewise receive the same acknowledgment.

143. And lest they think that we are lying in wait through the surreptitious use of a single verse, let us review the whole passage: “O the depth,” he says, “of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How inscrutable are his judgments and unsearchable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor? Or who has first given to him, and it shall be repaid to him? For from him and through him and in him are all things; to him be glory forever” (ibid., 33 ff.).

144. Of whom, then, do they think this was said—the Father or the Son? If of the Father, the Father is not the Wisdom of God, because the Son is the Wisdom of God. But what is there that Wisdom cannot do, of which it is written: “Although she is one, omnipotent, and abiding, she renews all things in herself” (Wisdom 7:27)? We do not read that she approaches, but that she abides. Thus, according to Solomon, you have omnipotent and abiding Wisdom. You also have her as good, because it is written: “Wisdom is not overcome by wickedness” (ibid., 30).

145. But let us return to the point. “How inscrutable,” he says, “are his judgments!” If, then, the Father gave all judgment to the Son, the Father appears to be declaring the Son, who judges (John 5:22).

146. Finally, so that you may know that he is speaking not of the Father but of the Son, he added: “Who,” he says, “has first given to him?” For the Father gave to the Son; but he gave by right of generation, not by a gift of generosity. And therefore, because it cannot be denied that the Son received from the Father, according to what is written: “All things have been handed over to me by my Father” (Matthew 11:27), nevertheless, by saying, “Who has first given to him?” he did not deny that the Son received by nature from the Father; rather, he declared that the Father cannot be called prior to the Son. For even if the Father gave to the Son, he did not give as to one who was later, because the uncreated and immeasurable Trinity, which possesses one eternity and one glory, admits neither time nor rank, whether of a later or an earlier.

147. But if we think the Greek manuscripts should be followed, which have *tis prosedōken autō* (τίς προσέδωκεν αὐτῷ), “who has added to him?”, you see that one to whom nothing can be added is not unlike one who is full. [Note: The Greek words were absent from the editions of Amerbach and Erasmus. The latter, however, wrote this observation in the margin: τίς προέδωκεν αὐτῷ. The passage is found in this form in Isaiah 40 and likewise in Paul. Ambrose, however, seems to have read *prosedōken* (προσέδωκεν), or *prosethēken* (προσέθηκεν), when he says that nothing can be added to him. The same reading was indicated by whatever traces of the Greek letters remained, although the reading transmitted by the Aldine edition agrees neither with Jerome’s translation nor with the Latin text published under the name of the Septuagint. Similar observations are also found in Estius on Romans 11:35, where it is added that the more authentic reading is *proedōken* (προέδωκεν), because the verb *antapodothēsetai* (ἀνταποδοθήσεται), “shall be repaid,” corresponds to it more appropriately. In any case, what Ambrose discusses in this chapter concerning the distinction between the prepositions “from” and “through” is treated more fully again in Book II of *On the Holy Spirit*, where we shall show that this very argument was taken from Basil.] Therefore, if this entire apostolic passage belongs more appropriately to the Son, we see that it must also be believed of the Son that all things are from him, as it is written: “For from him and through him and in him are all things.”

148. Nevertheless, let them think that it was said of the Father. Let us therefore remember that, just as we read that all things are from him, so also all things are through him; the authority of the Father and the Son is proclaimed with respect to the whole universe of creation. And although we have already proved the Son’s omnipotence by the example of the Father, since their concern is to diminish him, let them consider that they also diminish the Father. If the Son is weak because all things are through him, is the Father also weak because all things are through the Father?

149. But so that they may recognize that there is no distinction between these expressions, I shall demonstrate again that “from whom” something exists and “through whom” something exists refer to the same person, and I shall show that both are read of the Father. For we have this statement: “God is faithful, through whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son” (1 Corinthians 1:9). Let them consider what the Apostle said. We are called through the Father, and there is no question about that; are we created through the Son, and do they regard this as something lower? The Father called us into the fellowship of the Son, and we devoutly accept this as we ought; the Son created all things, and they think that this was not the exercise of a free will but an act of compelled and servile obedience?

150. But so that you may recognize more fully that there is no difference between the power of the Father and of the Son, since we are called through the Father into the fellowship of his Son, this fellowship itself is from the Son, as it is written: “For from his fullness we have all received” (John 1:16). According to the Greek Gospel, however, we should understand this as “from his fullness.”

151. Behold: fellowship is both through the Father and from the Son; yet it is not a differing fellowship, but one fellowship, just as the same John said in his Epistle: “That our fellowship may be with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ” (1 John 1:3).

152. Understand also that Scripture speaks of one fellowship for us not only from the Father and the Son but also from the Holy Spirit: “The grace,” it says, “of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all” (2 Corinthians 13:13).

153. But I ask: in what respect does the one through whom all things are appear inferior to the one from whom all things are? [Note: A few manuscripts read: “Or because he is said to have acted.”] Is it because he is asserted to be the one who acts? But the Father also acts, because he is the true one who said: “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5:17). Therefore, just as the Father works, so also the Son works. The one who acts is not weak or inferior, since the Father also acts; and therefore what the Son shares with the Father ought not to be regarded as belonging to an inferior status because of the Father, lest the heretics rather diminish the Father in the Son.

154. Nor is this a minor point: elsewhere the same holy John, in refuting the questions raised by Arian perfidy, says: “If you know that he is righteous, know that whoever practices righteousness is born of him” (1 John 2:29).

[Note: [Col. 0646D] Some manuscripts: “who justifies righteousness . . . or through whom, as the preceding passages indicate, do we have the promise of life? Thus, therefore, etc.”]

But who is righteous except the Lord, who loved righteousness (Psalm 10:8)? Or whom do we have, as the preceding passages indicate, as the giver of the promise of eternal life, if we do not have the Son? If, then, the Son of God promised us eternal life, and he himself is righteous, we have certainly been born of him. Or, if they deny that we have been born from the Son by grace, they do not confess the Son to be righteous.

[Col. 0646D] 155. You must therefore believe that all things are also from the Son of God, because, just as God the Father, so too the Son is the author and creator of all things. We see, then, that this question is empty, since it is agreed that we must believe of the Son that all things are from him, through him, and in him.

[Col. 0647A] 156. We have explained how all things are from him and how they are also through him. But who could doubt that all things are in him, when it is written elsewhere: “For in him all things were founded in the heavens, and in him they were created; and he is before all things, and all things subsist in him” (Colossians 1:16)? You therefore have grace from him, the one who acts, and in him the foundation of all things.

## CHAPTER XII

What was objected from John—that the Son is compared to a vine and the Father to a vinedresser—is to be understood of the incarnation. Those who take it as referring to the divine generation inflict two injuries on the Son: they place him below Paul and make him equal to other human beings; and they inflict as many injuries on the Father, whom they testify to be not only equal to that same Apostle but even insignificant. After this false interpretation has again been rejected and the true one confirmed, it is asserted that, according to his divinity, the Son too is the vinedresser, while according to his humanity he is the grape. From this the preceding explanation of the Father’s preeminence is established.

[Col. 0647B]

157. They also customarily bring forward, to separate the divinity of the Father and the Son, what the Lord said in the Gospel: “I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinedresser” (John 15:1). They say that the vinedresser and the vine are of different natures, and that the vine is subject to the vinedresser’s power.

158. Thus, then, you want the Son according to his divinity to be like a vine, so that without a cultivator he is powerless and can be abandoned or cut down; and you derive a charge from the letter, because the Lord said that he was the vine, signifying the mystery of his incarnation? Nevertheless, if you are pleased to argue from the letter, I too acknowledge—indeed, I openly profess—that the Son called himself the vine. For woe to me if I deny the mystery of the common salvation!

159. How, then, do you wish to understand that the Son of God called himself the vine? If you take the statement as referring to the divine substance, and believe that there is as much difference in divinity between the vinedresser and the vine as between the Father and the Son, [Note: [Col. 0647D] Not a few manuscripts: “and as [there is] between the vinedresser and the vine.”]

you inflict a double injury on the Son and a double injury on the Father. You injure the Son because, if according to his divinity he is inferior to the vinedresser, then by your assertion he must also be judged inferior to the Apostle Paul, since Paul too said that he was a vinedresser, as you have it: “I planted, Apollo watered, but God gave the growth” (1 Corinthians 3:6). Do you therefore want Paul to be better than the Son of God?

160. You have one injury. Here is the second: if, according to the substance of eternal generation, the Son is the vine, since he said, “I am the vine, you are the branches” (John 15:5), that divine generation too will appear to be of one substance with us. But “who is like you among the gods, O Lord,” as it is written (Exodus 15:11)? And again in the psalm: “For who among the clouds shall be equal to the Lord? Or who shall be like God among the sons of God?” (Psalm 88:7).

[Col. 0648A] 161. Yet you do not disparage the Son alone, but the Father also. For if all the prerogative of paternal power is contained in the name “vinedresser,” and Paul too is a vinedresser, then you compare the Apostle as equal to the Father, whom you deny to have the Son.

162. Moreover, since it is written: “Neither is he who plants anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the growth” (1 Corinthians 3:7), you will place the fullness of the Father’s majesty in that title which you see to be weak.

[Note: [Col. 0647D] Not a few manuscripts, including some of no slight authority: “the height of the Father’s majesty.”] For if he who plants and he who waters is nothing, but God gives the growth, see what your impiety is attempting to assert: that the Father too is to be despised under the name of vinedresser, and that some god must be sought who supplies growth to the Father’s work. They therefore impiously think that the power of God the Father is to be preferred on the basis of the name “vinedresser,” in which God the Father shares a common appellation with a human being.

163. But what is remarkable if he is preferred—as you heretics wish—to the Son, whose divine substance does not differ from the human condition? For if you think that the Son was called the vine according to his divine substance, you judge him not only subject to corruption and the uncertain elements, but also merely a participant in human nature, since the vine and the branches are of one nature. Thus it would seem that the Son of God did not assume flesh through the mystery of the incarnation, but took his beginning from flesh.

164. I, however, will plainly say that his flesh, although through a new mystery of generation, was nevertheless of one nature with us; and that this is the mystery of our salvation, not the beginning of a divine generation. He is the vine because he bears my sufferings; for in him the formerly fragile human condition, supported by him, grew strong again through the fruitful harvests of renewed piety.

165. Yet if the pomp of the vinedresser delights you, tell me, I ask, who it was

[Note: [Col. 0647D–0648D] Some manuscripts: “say it, even against your will.” Shortly after the words “make it known to me,” two codices add “my end,” which is found neither in the others nor in Jeremiah.]

who it was who spoke in the prophet: “Lord, make it known to me, so that I may know; then I saw their designs. I was led like an innocent lamb to slaughter, and I did not know it; against me they devised a plan, saying: ‘Come, let us put wood into his bread’” (Jeremiah 11:19). For if the Son speaks the mystery of the incarnation that was to come, since it is impious for you to believe that this concerns the Father, it is certainly the Son who says above: “I planted you as a fruitful vine; how have you been turned into the bitterness of a strange vine?” (Jeremiah 2:21).

166. Thus you see that the Son too is the vinedresser, sharing one name with the Father, one work, one dignity, and one substance. Therefore, if the Son is both vinedresser and vine, we understand the vine according to the mystery of the incarnation.

[Note: [Col. 0648D] All editions and a few manuscripts read: “and if the Son is vinedresser and vine”; others: “if [the Son] is vinedresser”; one: “if of the vinedresser,” etc.]

167. But he not only said that he was the vine; he also called himself a cluster of grapes in prophetic language, at the time when Moses, at the Lord’s command, sent scouts to the Valley of the Cluster (Numbers 13:14). What is that valley except the humility of the incarnation and the fruitfulness of the Passion? And I think that he was called a cluster because, from that vine transplanted out of Egypt—that is, from the family of the Jews—a fruit useful to the world sprang forth (Psalm 79:9).

[Col. 0649] Some manuscripts: “only a useful fruit,” with no bad sense.

Certainly no one can refer a cluster of grapes to the divine generation. Or whoever does so leaves nothing else for us except to believe that that cluster was born from a vine. Thus the fool ascribes to the Father what he condemns in the Son.

168. But if it can no longer be doubted that the Son of God was called the vine according to the incarnation, you see according to what mystery the Lord spoke when he said, “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28). For after saying this above, he immediately added: “I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinedresser” (John 15:1), so that you might recognize that the Father is greater in this respect: just as the vinedresser is the cultivator of the vines, so the Father is the cultivator of the Lord’s flesh. That flesh could increase with age and be cut down through suffering, so that the entire human race might be sheltered from the harmful heat of worldly pleasures by the shadow spread through the saving arms of the cross.

# BOOK FIVE

[Col. 0649]

## PROLOGUE

“Who, then, is the faithful and prudent servant?” His reward is indicated in Peter, and likewise in Paul, whose authority Ambrose desired to obey when he added this book to the others, since it could not be included in the preceding one. What he is going to discuss in it, and with what purpose: that he should be granted pardon, since the return on the money entrusted to them must be sought from all ministers. The faithful are this return for him; but he will be blessed if he may hope for a reward. Nevertheless, he desires the rewards of the saints less than exemption from punishments, which he urges everyone to earn.

[Col. 0649B]

1. “Who, then, is the faithful and prudent servant whom the Lord appointed over his household, to give them food at the proper time? Blessed is that servant whom, when his lord comes, he finds doing so” (Matthew 24:45–46). This is not an insignificant servant; he must be someone great. Let us consider who he is.

2. It is Peter, chosen by the judgment of the Lord himself to feed the flock, who deserved to hear three times: “Feed my lambs; feed my sheep; feed my little sheep” (John 21:13 and following). Thus, by feeding Christ’s flock well with the food of faith, he wiped away the guilt of his earlier fall. And so he is instructed three times to feed, and three times asked whether he loves the Lord, so that the one who had denied him three times before the cross might confess him three times (Matthew 26:70 and following).

3. Blessed also is that servant who can say: “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food; for you were not yet able to receive it” (1 Corinthians 3:2). For he knows how to feed each person. Who among us can do this? Who among us can truly say: “I became weak to the weak, in order to win the weak” (1 Corinthians 9:22)?

4. And yet that great man, chosen by Christ for the care of the flock, to heal the weak and tend the infirm, immediately rejects a heretic from the flock entrusted to him after one admonition (Titus 3:10), lest the infection of one wandering sheep spread like a festering sore and contaminate the whole flock. Moreover, he commands that foolish questions and disputes be avoided (ibid., 9).

5. What, then, shall we do, imprudent inhabitants placed among the new tares of an ancient harvest? If we remain silent, we will seem to yield; if we argue, we must fear that we too may be judged carnal. For it is written concerning such questions, which produce quarrels: “The servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but must be gentle toward all, teachable, patient, instructing with modesty those who resist” (2 Timothy 2:23–24).

[Note: [Col. 0649D] The Roman edition alone reads: “correcting with modesty.”]

And elsewhere: “If anyone is contentious, we have no such custom, nor the Church of God” (1 Corinthians 11:16). And therefore it was decided that something be written, so that our writings might answer the impiety of the heretics on our behalf, without any disturbance.

[Note: [Col. 0649D] Some manuscripts: “it was God’s judgment.”]

[Col. 0650C] 6. Therefore, revered Emperor, we are preparing to begin this fifth book. For it was also appropriate that the fourth book should end with that discussion of the vine, lest we seem rather to have heaped the same book together with a tumult of questions than filled it with the fruit of the spiritual vineyard; nor was it fitting to leave the harvest of faith unfinished while so many arguments still overflowed.

7. [Note: All editions and some manuscripts read, “Therefore five books”; the other manuscripts, more appropriately, read as in the text.]

In the fifth book, therefore, we set forth the inseparable divinity of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, temporarily setting aside a fuller discussion of the Holy Spirit, prompted by the teaching of the Gospel reading (Matthew 25:15). Thus, by a certain fivefold allotment of these books, we lend at interest to human hearts the five talents of faith entrusted to us; lest, when the Lord comes and finds his money hidden in the earth, he say to me: “Wicked and lazy servant, you knew that I reap where I did not sow and gather where I did not scatter. Therefore you ought to have entrusted my money to the money-changers, so that when I came I might have received what was mine” (ibid., 26–27); or, as it is written in another book: “Then I, when I came, would certainly have demanded it with interest” (Luke 19:23).

[Col. 0650D] Some manuscripts: “with more straightforward discussion.”

[Col. 0650D] Some manuscripts: “that we might lend to human affections.”

8. Forgive, therefore, if the boldness of this rather extended discourse has offended anyone. Consideration of our duty compels us to believe what we have received: “We are stewards of the heavenly mysteries” (1 Corinthians 4:1). We are ministers—not all equally, but, as he says, “to each one as the Lord has given.” “I planted, Apollo watered, but God gave the growth” (1 Corinthians 3:3, 6). Let each person therefore strive to receive a reward according to his labor; for, as the Apostle said, we are God’s fellow workers, God’s cultivation, God’s building (ibid., 9). Blessed, then, is the one who sees such interest from his investment; blessed also is the one who beholds the fruit of his work; blessed too is the one who builds upon the foundation of faith with gold, silver, and precious stones (ibid., 12).

9. You who hear or read these things are everything to us: you are the moneylender’s interest—the interest of the word, not of money; you are the cultivator’s return; you are the builder’s gold, silver, and precious stones.

[Col. 0651D] All editions and some manuscripts read: “you are lenders of interest … you are builders … building upon [the foundation] precious stones.” The greater number of manuscripts, and those of greater authority, read: “you are the lender,” etc. That this is the genuine reading is clearly demonstrated both by the preceding words, “you are everything to us,” and by those that follow, “in your merits lies the full sum of priestly labor,” and so forth.

In your merits the full sum of priestly labor rests; in your souls the fruit of episcopal work shines forth. In your progress the Lord’s gold gleams, and the silver is multiplied, if you hold fast to the divine utterances: “The utterances of the Lord are pure utterances, silver tested by fire, proven on the earth, purified sevenfold” (Psalm 11:7). You, then, will make the lender rich and the cultivator fruitful; you will prove the architect skilled. I do not say this arrogantly, because what I vow is not so much mine as yours.

10. O that I might then safely say of you: “Lord, you gave me five talents, and behold, I have gained five more” (Matthew 25:20), and display the precious talents of your virtues!

[Col. 0651D] The Amberbach edition, Erasmus, and many better manuscripts read “at that time”; Gill’s and the Roman edition, together with others, read “now.” The latter is incorrect, for the subject here is not the present time but the future resurrection.

[Col. 0651C] For “we have this treasure in earthen vessels” (2 Corinthians 4:7). These are the talents which the Lord commands to be lent out spiritually; or they are the two coins of the New and Old Testaments which that Evangelical Samaritan left with the man stripped by robbers, for the treatment of his wounds (Luke 10:35).

11. Nor do I desire these things, brothers, out of greed for a reward, so that I may be placed above many; the reward from your progress is enough for me.

[Col. 0652D] Some manuscripts: “lest I be called greedy; not for that reason,” etc.

Would that I be found not unworthy of what I have received! I do not demand what ought to be assigned to those better than I, although, Lord, you are accustomed to say: “I also wish to give to this last one as to you” (Matthew 20:14). Let him who deserves it receive authority over ten cities (Luke 19:17).

12. Let him be such as Moses, who wrote down the ten words of the Law (Deuteronomy 5:5 and following). Let him be Joshua the son of Nun, who subdued five kings and received the Gibeonites into submission (Joshua 10:22 and following), so that he might be a type of the man who would come bearing that name, by whose command all bodily pleasures would be overcome and the nations converted, so that they might follow the faith of Jesus Christ rather than their former pursuits and desires. Let him be David, whom young women singing met and said: “Saul has triumphed over thousands, David over ten thousands” (1 Samuel 18:7).

13. It is enough for me if I am not thrust into the outer darkness, like the man who hid the talent entrusted to him in a certain earth of his flesh:

[Col. 0652D] All editions and a few manuscripts read “like the leaders”; the greater number and better manuscripts read “like the leader.”

like the leader of the Synagogue and the other leaders of the Jews, who buried the divine utterances entrusted to them in a kind of earth of their own body. Intent on the pleasures of the flesh, they plunged the heavenly investment into a kind of pit of their exalted heart (Matthew 23:14 and following).

14. Let us therefore not hide the Lord’s money within the hiding places of the flesh, nor place that mina in a handkerchief (Luke 19:20). Rather, like good money-changers, let us always weigh it out with a certain sweat of mind and body, with an even and ready disposition, so that “the word may be near you, in your mouth and in your heart” (Deuteronomy 30:14).

15. This word is God’s; it is the precious talent by which you are redeemed. This is the money that must often be seen upon the tables of souls, so that, by being frequently put into circulation, the sound of good coins may go forth throughout the whole earth, through which eternal life may be prepared. This, then, is the eternal life which you bestow, almighty Father: “that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17:3).

## CHAPTER I

How impious the Arians are when they attack that in which human happiness consists. John always joins the Son with the Father, especially where he says: “That they may know you alone as true,” and so forth. There, therefore, “the true God” must also be understood of the Son, since he can neither be denied to be God nor called false—not even merely titular. Once this last point has been demonstrated from the Apostle, it is rightly established that Christ is the true God.

[Col. 0652C]

16. Let the Arians therefore perceive how impious they are, since they raise questions for us about our hope and desire.

[Col. 0652D] Some manuscripts: “And because I am distinguished above the rest.”

And because on this point above all they are accustomed to cry out, saying that Christ is separated from the only true God, let us refute their impious interpretations as far as our strength permits.

17. In this passage they ought rather to understand that this is the benefit, this is the reward of perfect virtue, this divine and incomparable gift: that we know Christ together with the Father, and do not separate the Son from the Father, just as Scripture does not separate them. For this contributes more to the unity than to the distinction of divine power: the same reward grants us one honor through the knowledge of the Father and the Son. No one can possess this reward unless he has known both the Father and the Son; for, just as knowledge of the Father, knowledge of the Son acquires eternal life.

[Col. 0653A] 18. Thus, just as at the beginning the Evangelist joined the Word with God the Father in a pious confession, saying, “And the Word was with God” (John 1:1), so here too, when he wrote the words of the Lord, “That they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17:3), by that conjunction he joined the Father and the Son, so that no one might separate Christ, the true God, from the majesty of the Father. For conjunction never separates.

19. And therefore, by saying, “That they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent,” he destroys the Sabellians and excludes the Jews—those who were listening to him speak—so that the former might not think that the Father was the same as the Son, if he had not added “and Jesus Christ,” or so that the latter might not separate the Son from the Father.

[Col. 0653B] 20 and 21. But I ask why they do not think that what is understood from the preceding words should be supplied: since he first mentioned the Father as the only true God, why should we not also understand Jesus Christ to be the only true God? It was not otherwise necessary to express this, lest he appear to be saying that there are two gods. For we do not say that there are two gods, and we confess that the Son is of the same divinity as the Father.

22. Let us therefore ask in what sense they think that a distinction of divinity has been made here. Do they deny Christ to be God? But they cannot deny it. Do they deny him to be the true God? But if they deny that he is true, let them say whether they judge him to be a false god or merely a titular god. For according to Scripture, he is either the true God, merely titular, or false: true, like the Father; titular, like the saints; false, like demons and idols.

[Col. 0653D] Some manuscripts: “or merely titular, as the saints are”; or “false, as demons are.”

Let them therefore say by what confession they designate the Son of God: do they think that he has falsely assumed the name of God, or that, as a titular god, he possesses only an inspiration of divinity?

[Col. 0653D] The editions and a few manuscripts here and below read “a falsely appropriated name.”

23. I do not think they would say that the name was falsely assumed, lest they involve themselves in a more obvious crime of impiety and, by insinuating that a false name of God was assigned to Christ as to demons and idols, expose themselves. But if they think that he was called God because he possessed an inspiration of divinity, like many holy men—Scripture called them gods (John 10:35), to whom the word of God was addressed—then they do not place him beyond human beings, but consider him comparable to human beings. They think him to be only what he himself granted to human beings, saying to Moses: “He has appointed you as god to Pharaoh” (Exodus 7:1). Hence it is also said in the psalm: “I said, you are gods” (Psalm 81:6).

555 24. Yet Paul excludes this sacrilegious opinion when he says: “For even if there are those who are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth” (1 Corinthians 8:5). He did not say, “There are gods,” but “there are those who are called gods.” But Christ, as it is written, “is the same yesterday and today” (Hebrews 13:8). “Is,” he says—that is, not merely in name, but also in reality.

[Col. 0654A] 25. And rightly it is written: “Yesterday and today he is the same,” so that the impiety of Arius could not find an opportunity for establishing sacrilege. When Arius read in the second psalm the Father saying to the Son, “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Psalm 2:7), he noted the word “today,” not “yesterday,” applying to the eternity of the divine generation what had been said about the assumption of flesh, as Paul says in the Acts of the Apostles: “And we announce to you the promise made to our fathers, that God has fulfilled this for our children, raising up Jesus, as it is written in the second psalm: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you’” (Acts 13:32 and following).

[Col. 0653D] The Roman edition, with one manuscript, reads “for their children”; the other codices read “for our children.” So too do some Greek copies and the Vulgate version; but more Greek codices read τοῖς τέκνοις αὐτῶν ἡμῖν, “to their children—to us.” Moreover, this entire excerpt—from “as Paul says in the Acts …” through “Today I have begotten you”—which was absent from the ancient edition and not a few manuscripts, as were many other passages, was first conjectured among the variant readings of Gill’s edition and later admitted into the text of the Roman edition. We have retained it on the authority of several manuscripts of better age.

Filled, therefore, with the Holy Spirit, the Apostle, in order to destroy that ferocity, says: “Yesterday and today he is the same, and forever”: “yesterday,” because of eternity; “today,” because of the assumption of the body.

[Col. 0654B] 26. Christ therefore is, and he always is; for whoever is, always is. Christ, however, always is—the one of whom Moses says: “He who is has sent me” (Exodus 3:14). Gabriel certainly existed, and Raphael existed, and the angels existed; but those who at some time did not exist are by no means said in the same sense always to be. Christ, however, as we read, was not “yes and no,” but “in him it was yes” (2 Corinthians 1:19). Hence truly it belongs to God alone to be, since he always is.

27. Therefore, if they do not dare to call him a titular god, and it is a greater impiety to call him false, it remains that he is the true God, not unlike but equal to the true Father. Since he justifies and sanctifies whomever he wishes, not by taking sanctifying power from outside himself but by possessing it within himself, how is he not the true God?

[Col. 0654C] For the Apostle certainly called him the true God,

[Col. 0654D] All editions and some manuscripts read “who would naturally be the true God”; in most manuscripts “true” is omitted, as becomes clear to anyone who considers the passage carefully.

who is God by nature, as you have it: “For then,” he says, “when you did not know God, you served those who by nature were not gods” (Galatians 4:8)—that is, those who could not be true gods, since this was entirely lacking to them by nature.

## CHAPTER II

Once it has been proved that the Son is the true God and not inferior to the Father, it is shown that, when Scripture speaks of the Father as “alone,” the Son is not excluded; indeed, this designation belongs above all to him and to him alone. The Trinity alone is not among all things but above all things. The Son alone does what the Father does and alone possesses immortality; therefore he is not to be separated from the Father in disputed expressions. Nevertheless, the passage may be understood as referring to the incarnation. Those finally exclude the Father from the redemption of humanity who wish the Son to be separated from him.

[Col. 0654D]

28. In the preceding books we have abundantly demonstrated from the readings of Scripture that Christ is the true God. Therefore, if Christ, as has been taught, is the true God, let us ask why, when they read of the Father as the only true God, they desire to separate the Son from the Father.

29. If they say that the Father alone is the true God, they cannot deny that the Son also is the only God who is truth, because Christ is truth. Is truth less than the true, since, according to the usage of names, “true” is often derived from “truth,” just as “wise” is derived from “wisdom” and “just” from “justice”? We perceive no such distinction between the Father and the Son, because nothing is lacking in the Father, since the Father is truthful; and the Son, because he is truth, is equal to the true one.

[Col. 0655D] Some manuscripts: “because the Father is truth”; one: “of truth.”

30.
