But so that they may know that, when they read “alone,” the Son is by no means to be separated from the Father, let them remember that God says through the prophet: “I alone stretched out the heavens” (Isaiah 44:24). Yet the Father did not stretch them out without the Son. For the Son himself, who is the wisdom of God, says: “When he prepared the heavens, I was present with him” (Proverbs 8:27). And Paul confirms that the following was said of the Son: “In the beginning, you, Lord, founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands” (Hebrews 1:10).

Whether, then, the Son made heaven, as the Apostle wished it to be understood—and he too certainly did not stretch out heaven alone, without the Father—or, as you have it in Proverbs, “God founded the earth in wisdom, but prepared the heavens in understanding” (Proverbs 3:19), it is shown that neither did the Father make the heavens alone without the Son, nor the Son without the Father; and yet the one who stretched out heaven is called “alone.”

31. That this is also plainly to be understood of the Son, although he is called “alone,” even though he is never believed to have done anything without the Father’s knowledge, you have elsewhere as well,

[Note: [Col. 0655D] Three manuscripts read: “and that he never [did anything] with the Father unaware”; one reads “Father,” etc.]

where it is written: “He alone stretches out the heavens and walks upon the sea as upon a pavement” (Job 9:8). For the Lord’s Gospel taught us that it was not the Father but the Son who walked upon the sea, when Peter asked him, saying: “Lord, command me to come to you” (Matthew 14:28).

But prophecy itself also provides evidence. For holy Job prophesied the Lord’s coming (Job 3:8), concerning whom he truly said that he would overcome the great sea-monster, and it happened: for he struck down and crushed that savage sea-monster—namely, the devil—by the venerable suffering of his body in the last times (Isaiah 27:1).

[Col. 0655D] All editions read “Zabulus”; and certainly Ambrose more often designates the devil by that name. Yet nearly all written codices at this place prefer “the devil.”

32. The Son, therefore, is the only and true God; this prerogative too is granted to the Son. For it cannot properly be said of anything created that it is “alone.” How can something that shares in creation be separated from the rest as though it were alone?

Thus a human being appears to be rational among all earthly animals, but he is not the only rational being; for we know that the heavenly works of God are rational as well, and we confess angels and archangels to be rational. If angels are rational, then a human being is not called rational alone.

[Col. 0656A] 33. But they say that the sun may be called “alone,” because there is no second sun. Yet the sun itself shares many things with the stars: it traverses the heavens (Genesis 1:14), belongs to that ethereal and heavenly substance, is a creature, is counted among all God’s works, serves God with them all, blesses God with them all, and praises God with them all. Therefore it is not properly called alone, since it is not separated from the rest (Psalm 148:3).

34. Since, then, no creature can be compared with the divinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, which alone is not among all things but above all things—and let the exposition concerning the Spirit be reserved for the present—just as the Father is called the only true God, having nothing in common with the rest, so too the Son is the only image of the true God, the only right hand of the Father, the only power and wisdom of God.

35. The Son alone therefore does what the Father does, because it is written: “Whatever I do, he himself does” (John 5:16).

[Col. 0656D] The Roman edition alone reads: “Whatever he himself does, the Son also does likewise.”

Since the work of the Father and the Son is one, it is rightly said of the Father and the Son that God alone acted. Hence, when we call him Creator, we confess both the Father and the Son. For when Paul said, “They served the creature rather than the Creator” (Romans 1:25), he certainly did not deny the Father as Creator, from whom all things are, nor the Son, through whom all things are.

36. It does not appear foreign to this that it is written: “Who alone possesses immortality” (1 Timothy 6:16). For how could he not possess immortality who has life in himself? He possesses it in his nature; he possesses it in his substance. He possesses it not through a temporal grace but through eternal divinity; he possesses it not as a servant through a gift, but as the coeternal Son through the property of his generation. And he possesses it as the Father does: “For just as the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son also to have life in himself” (John 5:16). “As he has,” he says, “so he gave.”

You learned above (Book IV, chapter 6) how he gave it, so that you would not think this was a bestowal of grace where there is the mystery of generation. Since, then, there is no difference in life between the Father and the Son, how can it be thought that the Father alone possesses immortality while the Son does not?

37. Let them therefore understand that here too the Son is not to be separated from the only true God, the Father, since they cannot prove that the Son is not the only and true God. Especially since either, as we said, “Christ” is to be understood here as the only true God, or else one part is to be understood as referring to the divinity of the Father and the Son, and another to the incarnation of Christ. For knowledge is not complete unless it confesses Jesus Christ as the only-begotten true God and Son of God according to eternity, and as one born from a Virgin according to the flesh.

The same Evangelist taught us this elsewhere, saying: “Every spirit that confesses Jesus Christ to have come in the flesh is from God” (1 John 4:2).

[Col. 0657A] Some manuscripts: “to have come in the flesh.”

38. Finally, that it is not foreign to understand the mystery of the incarnation in this passage too, the sequence of the reading itself teaches us. For it says: “Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son” (John 17:1). Since he both mentions that the hour has come and asks to be glorified, how can we judge that he spoke otherwise than according to the assumption of flesh? For divinity has no appointed moments of time imposed upon it, nor does eternal light need glorification.

Therefore, in “the only true God,” the Father, we understand the Son of God also as the only true God according to the unity of divinity; and in the name of Jesus Christ, which he received when he was born from a Virgin, we recognize the mystery of the incarnation.

[Col. 0657B] 39. But if, when they read of the Father as the only true God, they desire to separate the Son, then, when they read concerning the incarnation of the Son, “This is the stone that was rejected by you builders, which has become the head of the corner,” and below, “There is no other name under heaven given among human beings by which we must be saved” (Acts 4:11–12), they must think that the Father too is to be separated from the benefit of granting us salvation.

But there is neither salvation without the Father nor eternal life without the Son.

## CHAPTER III

When the Arians press the objection that two gods are introduced on the basis of unity of substance, the response is that plurality follows rather from diversity, and therefore their accusation falls back upon themselves. Multiple kinds of diversity explain why two human beings cannot be called one human being, although all human beings are called simply “human” when the unity of nature is indicated. In these created things there is only one nature; in the divine persons, however, there is complete unity. Therefore the Son must not be separated from the Father, especially since they do not dare deny that worship is owed to him.

[Col. 0657C]

40. But the Arians assert: If you call the Son, like the Father, the only true God, and confess the Father and the Son to be of one substance, you introduce not one God but two gods. For those who are of one substance appear to be not one God but two gods, just as two human beings, or two sheep, are called plural; whereas a human being and a sheep are not called two human beings or two sheep, but one human being and one sheep.

41. This is what the Arians say, and by this subtle argument they try to ensnare the simpler-minded. Yet if we read the divine Scriptures, we shall find plurality to apply more properly to things that are of different and distinct substance, that is, ἑτερουσία. This is expressly set forth in the books of Solomon, in the passage where he says: “There are three things that are impossible to understand, and a fourth that I do not know: the track of an eagle flying, the ways of a serpent upon a rock, the paths of a ship sailing, and the ways of a man in his youth” (Prov. 30:18–19). Certainly the eagle, the ship, and the serpent are not of one kind or nature, but of different and distinct substance, and yet they are three. Their arguments, therefore, are turned back against them by the testimonies of Scripture.

42. Thus, by saying that the substance of the Father and the Son is distinct, and that their divinity is different, they themselves plainly assert two gods. But we, while confessing both the Father and the Son, and asserting that they possess one divinity, say that there are not two gods but one God. We prove this also by the Lord’s declarations, because wherever there are several, there is a difference either of natures or of wills and operations. Thus, to refute them by their own testimonies, two men are spoken of: although they are of one nature by the law of birth, they nevertheless differ in time, thought, work, and place. Therefore one man cannot be spoken of in the sense and number of two, because there is no unity where there is diversity. But one God is spoken of, and the glory and fullness of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are signified.

43. So great, finally, is the truth of unity that even when only the nature of human generation or flesh is signified, one man is spoken of as consisting of many, as you find: “The Lord is my helper; I will not fear what man can do to me” (Ps. 117:6)—that is, not one individual person, but one flesh and one frailty of human generation. He added: “It is better to hope in the Lord than to hope in man” (ibid., 9). Here, too, he did not designate a particular man, but the human condition in general. Immediately afterward he speaks of many: “It is better to trust in the Lord than to trust in princes” (ibid., 9). Where “man” is spoken of, therefore, the common unity of nature among all people is sometimes signified, as we said above; where “princes” are spoken of, a certain diversity of powers is present.

44. Among human beings, or in human beings, there is unity in some particular matter—whether of love, desire, flesh, devotion, or faith. But universal unity, which embraces everything within itself according to the glory of divinity, belongs solely to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

45. Accordingly, when the Lord was indicating the difference among human beings, who have nothing among themselves that could pertain to the unity of an indivisible substance, he said: “In your law it is written that the testimony of two men is true” (John 8:17). And after stating, “The testimony of two men is true,” when he came to the testimony concerning himself and his Father, he did not say, “Our testimony is true, because it is the testimony of two gods,” but: “I am the one who bears witness concerning myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness concerning me” (ibid., 18). Above, likewise, he said: “Even if I judge, my judgment is true, because I am not alone, but I and the Father who sent me” (ibid., 16). Thus, both below as above, he signified the Father and the Son; he neither introduced plurality nor divided the unity of the divine substance.

46. It is therefore evident that what is of one substance cannot be separated, even if it is not a matter of singularity but of unity. By “singularity” I mean what is called in Greek μονοτής. Singularity pertains to the person; unity pertains to the nature.

Things that are of different substance are accustomed to be called not only one but also several, although this has already become clear from the prophetic testimony; the Apostle himself, however, stated it more explicitly when he said: “For although there are those who are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth” (1 Cor. 8:5).

You see, then, that those who are of different substances, and not of the truth of one nature, are called gods. But the Father and the Son, because they are of one substance, are not two gods but one God: “one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things” (ibid., 6). “One,” he says, “God the Father, and one Lord Jesus”; and above: “One God, not two gods” (ibid., 4); and below: “One Lord,” and not two.

47. Plurality, therefore, is excluded; unity is not set aside. Just as, when we read “the Lord Jesus,” we do not, as we said above (Book II, chapter 5), separate the Father from the right of lordship that he shares with the Son, so, when we read “the one true God, the Father,” we cannot separate the Son from the right belonging to the one true God, which he shares with the Father.

48. Or let them say what else they think or believe when we read: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone you shall serve” (Matt. 4:10). Do they think that Christ is not to be worshiped and that Christ is not to be served? If the Canaanite woman, who worshiped him (Matt. 15:25), deserved to obtain what she asked, and if the Apostle Paul, who declares in the opening of his writings that he is Christ’s servant (Rom. 1:1), deserved to become an apostle—not from men or through a man, but through Jesus Christ—let them say what they think should be followed. Do they prefer to share with Arius in his faithlessness, so that by denying Christ to be the one true God they show that they judge him neither worthy of worship nor of service? Or do they prefer to share fellowship with Paul, who, by serving and worshiping Christ, plainly confessed with voice and affection that he is the one true God, whom he acknowledged by pious service?

## CHAPTER IV

The heretics objected that Christ offered worship to the Father. It is answered that this too must be referred to his humanity, as the examination of the passage makes clear; yet testimonies to his divinity are added there, as we see also in other works of Christ.

49. If anyone should say that the Son also worships God the Father, because it is written, “You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know” (John 4:22), let him consider when, before whom, and with what assumed disposition he speaks.

50. Indeed, it was not without reason stated above that Jesus, wearied from his journey, was sitting and asked the Samaritan woman for a drink, because he was speaking according to the flesh of man. For according to his divinity he could neither grow weary nor thirst (ibid., 7).

51. Then, when the Samaritan woman called him, as it were, a Jew and thought him a prophet, he replied as a Jew who taught the mysteries of the Law spiritually: “You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know.” “We,” he says—that is, he joined himself to human beings. But how could he be joined to human beings except according to the flesh? And to show that he had answered according to the incarnation, he added: “For salvation is from the Jews” (ibid., 22).

52. But immediately afterward he set aside the human disposition, saying: “The hour is coming, and now is, when true worshipers will worship the Father” (ibid., 23). He did not say, “We shall worship.” He would certainly have said this if he had entered into partnership with our service.

53. Yet when we read that Mary worshiped him (Matt. 28:9), we must understand that, according to the same nature, he cannot both worship as a servant and be worshiped as Lord. Rather, because as a human being among human beings he is said to worship, and as Lord he is worshiped by servants.

54. We therefore read and believe many things according to the mystery of the incarnation; but in the very experience of his human nature we may behold the divine majesty. Jesus grows weary from his journey, in order to refresh the weary; he asks for a drink, intending to give spiritual drink to the thirsty; he hungers, intending to give the food of salvation to the hungry; he dies, intending to give life; he is buried, intending to rise again; he hangs trembling upon the wood, intending to strengthen those who tremble; he covers the heaven with darkness, in order to give light; he shakes the earth, in order to make it firm; he disturbs the seas, in order to calm them; he opens the tombs of the dead, in order to show that they are dwelling places of the living; he is born of a Virgin, in order that he may be believed to have been born from God; he pretends not to know, in order to make the ignorant know; he is said to worship as a Jew, in order that he may be worshiped as the true Son of God.

## CHAPTER V

Ambrose answers those who press the Lord’s words to the mother of the sons of Zebedee, explaining that Christ did not wish to afflict her with sorrow, but acted out of clemency. Several reasons for this indulgence are given. The Lord therefore preferred to refer the granting of her request to the Father rather than declare the request itself impossible; nevertheless, it is shown from Christ’s own words and by comparison with other passages that his answer causes him no difficulty.

55. “How,” they ask, “can the Son of God, the one true God, be like the Father, when he himself said to the sons of Zebedee: ‘You shall indeed drink my cup, but to sit at my right or at my left is not mine to give you, but to those for whom it has been prepared by my Father’ (Matt. 20:23)?”

This, then, is the argument for the divine inequality that you allege. Yet you ought rather to venerate the Lord’s clemency in this, and to worship his grace—if only you were able to perceive the deep mysteries of God’s power and wisdom.

56. Consider what she asks with and for her sons. She is a mother, concerned for the honor of her sons; her measure of desire is indeed excessive, but nevertheless deserving of pardon. She was also a mother advanced in age, religious in devotion, and deprived of comfort. At the time when she ought either to have been helped or supported by the assistance of vigorous offspring, she endured the absence of her children, and had preferred to her own pleasure the reward of her sons who followed Christ—sons who, summoned by the Lord’s first call, as we read, left their nets and their father and followed him (Matt. 4:22).

57. Thus, indulgent because of the earnestness of maternal care, she entreated the Savior, saying: “Say that these two sons of mine may sit, one at your right hand and the other at your left, in your kingdom” (ibid., 20:21). It was an error, but an error of devotion; for maternal affection does not know how to be patient. Though greedy for the fulfillment of her desire, her longing was nevertheless pardonable: she was not eager for money, but for grace. Nor was her request shameless, since she was concerned not for herself but for her children. Consider the mother; keep the mother in mind.

58. But it is no wonder if the affection of parents toward their children seems worthless to you, since you also consider the love of the almighty Father toward his only-begotten Son worthless. The Lord of heaven and earth was ashamed—let me speak according to the assumption of flesh and the powers of the soul—he was ashamed, I say, and, to use his own word, embarrassed to deny a mother asking for her sons even a share in his seat. Yet you maintain that the Son of the eternal God sometimes stands in the place of a minister, and sometimes performs ministerial service; that his sitting with the Father derives not from the unity of majesty but from the Father’s command. You deny to the true God, the Son of God, what he himself plainly did not wish to deny to human beings.

59. He considered the mother’s love, by which she consoled her old age with the reward of her sons, and although weary from maternal longing, endured the absence of her dearest children.

60. Consider also that she was a woman—that is, of the frailer sex—which the Lord had not yet strengthened by his own Passion. Consider, I say, the heir of that first woman Eve, falling through the succession transmitted to all of immoderate desire. The Lord had not yet redeemed her with his own blood; by his blood he had not yet washed away the excessive appetite for unlawful honor that had become rooted in the affections of all. The woman, therefore, was sinning through an inherited error.

61. And what wonder if a mother was concerned for her sons—which is more tolerable than being concerned for herself—when even the apostles themselves, as we read, were disputing among themselves about precedence (Luke 22:24)?

62. The physician of all humanity, therefore, ought not to have wounded the bereft mother’s still-sick mind with a reproach of shame, lest, when her request was denied her too harshly, she should grieve as though condemned for an immoderate petition.

63. Accordingly, the Lord, who knew that devotion ought to be honored, answered not the woman but her sons, saying: “Can you drink the cup that I am going to drink?” When they said to him, “We can,” Jesus said to them: “You shall indeed drink my cup, but to sit at my right or at my left is not mine to give you, but to those for whom it has been prepared by my Father” (Matt. 20:22–23).

64. How patient and merciful is the Lord; how profound his wisdom and how good his love! For he wished to show that the disciples were not asking for some trivial matter, but for something they could not obtain, and therefore reserved the privilege of that paternal honor for the Father. He did not fear that this would detract from his own right, since he “did not regard equality with God as robbery” (Phil. 2:6). At the same time, because he loved the disciples—as you find written, “he loved them to the end” (John 13:1)—he did not wish those whom he loved to think that he had denied them what they asked. Holy and good is the Lord, who would rather conceal something of his right than diminish something of his love: “Love is patient, love is kind; it is not jealous, it is not puffed up, it does not seek its own interests” (1 Cor. 13:4).

65. Finally, so that you may recognize that his words, “It is not mine to give you,” arise not from weakness but from indulgence: when the sons of Zebedee ask without their mother, he says nothing about the Father. Thus you find: “It is not mine to give you, but to those for whom it has been prepared” (Mark 10:40). The evangelist Mark states it this way. But where the mother asks for her sons, that is, according to Matthew, he says: “It is not mine to give you, but to those for whom it has been prepared by my Father” (ibid.). Here he added, “by my Father,” because maternal affection was asking for a greater indulgence.

66. If they think that by saying, “For those for whom it has been prepared by my Father,” he either grants more to the Father or detracts something from himself, let them say whether they also think that something was detracted from the Father when the Son said in the Gospel concerning the Father: “The Father judges no one” (John 5:22).

67. If we consider it sacrilegious to believe that the Father so transferred judgment to the Son that he himself does not possess it—for he does possess it, and divine majesty cannot lose what it possesses by nature—then we must certainly consider it sacrilegious to suppose that the Son cannot give whatever human beings can merit or any creature can receive, especially since he himself said: “I am going to the Father, and whatever you ask of him in my name, I will do” (John 14:12–13).

For if the Son cannot do what the Father can give, then Truth has lied, and he cannot do whatever is asked of the Father in his name. He did not therefore say, “For those for whom it has been prepared by my Father,” so that it should be requested only from the Father; for he remembered that he himself gives everything that is requested from the Father. Accordingly, he did not say, “Whatever you ask from me, I will do,” but, “Whatever you ask from him in my name, I will do.”

## CHAPTER VI

Intending to resolve the objection more carefully, Ambrose argues that the request in question, if it was not impossible in itself, would have been possible for Christ, especially since the Father gave him all judgment—something to be understood without any indication of imperfection. Nevertheless, he proves that the request must be counted among impossible things. He teaches that, for it to be possible at all, Christ’s answer must then be understood according to his human nature, and he explains this by examining the passage. Finally, he again confirms his position that this sitting is impossible.

68. I now ask whether they think that what was requested by Zebedee’s wife and sons was possible for human nature or for any creature, or impossible. If it was possible, how could he who caused everything that did not exist to exist lack the power to grant the apostles a seat at his left or right? Or how could he be unable to judge human merits, when the Father gave him all judgment?

69. It is known how he gave it (John 5:22). For how did the Son receive it as one in need, when he created all things from nothing? Did he not possess judgment over those whose natures he had made? The Father gave all judgment to the Son “so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father” (ibid., 23). Thus it is not the Son’s power that increases, but our knowledge; nothing is added to his substance, but what is known by us is added for our benefit, so that by knowing the Son of God we may have eternal life (John 17:3).

70. Since, in the knowledge of the Son of God, there is his honor, whereas the increase is ours and not his, if anyone thinks that God’s power is augmented by that honor, he must also believe that God the Father can be augmented, since he too is glorified through our knowledge, just as the Son is, according to what the Son said: “I have glorified you on earth” (ibid., 4). Therefore, if what was requested was possible, it was certainly within the Son’s power.

71. Nevertheless, let those who think it possible show which human being or other creature sits either at the right or at the left of God. For the Father says to the Son: “Sit at my right hand” (Ps. 109:1). Therefore, if someone sits at the Son’s right hand, then, speaking in human terms, the Son is found between that person and the Father.

72. What was requested, then, was not something possible for a human being. But he did not wish to say that human beings could not sit with him, because he desired that his divine glory should remain concealed and not be disclosed before his resurrection. Earlier, too, when he had appeared in glory among his servants Moses and Elijah, he warned the disciples not to tell anyone what they had seen (Matt. 17:9).

73. Therefore, if human beings or other creatures could not earn this, the Son ought not to seem less powerful because he did not give the apostles what the Father had given neither to human beings nor to other creatures. Or let them say to which of these the Father gave it. Certainly not to the angels, concerning whom Scripture says that all the angels “stood around the throne” (Rev. 7:11). Gabriel likewise said that he stood, as you find: “I am Gabriel, who stand before the Lord” (Luke 1:19).

74. It was not given, then, to the angels, nor to the elders who worship the One seated. They do not sit upon the throne of majesty; rather, as Scripture says, they stand around the throne. There are twenty-four other thrones, as you find in the Apocalypse of John: “And upon the thrones I saw twenty-four elders sitting” (Rev. 4:4). In the Gospel also the Lord himself says: “When the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:28).

He did not say that the apostles could be granted a share in his own throne, but that there are those other twelve thrones. We must nevertheless understand these not as bodily seats but as the succession of spiritual grace.

75. In the Book of Kings the prophet Micaiah said: “I saw the Lord God of Israel sitting upon his throne, and all the host of heaven stood around him, at his right and at his left” (3 Kings 22:19). How, then, while the angels stand at the right and left of the Lord God, and the whole heavenly host stands, will human beings sit at God’s right or left—human beings to whom the likeness of angels is promised as the reward of virtue, as the Lord says: “You shall be like the angels in heaven” (Matt. 22:30)? “Like the angels,” he says, not more than the angels.

76. If, therefore, the Father gave nothing more than the Son, the Son certainly gave nothing less than the Father. The Son, therefore, is not less powerful than the Father.

77. Nevertheless, suppose that what was requested was possible for human beings to obtain. What does he mean when he says: “But to sit at my right or at my left is not mine to give you” (Matt. 20:23)? What does “mine” mean? Above he said: “You shall indeed drink my cup”; below he said: “It is not mine to give you.” Above he said “my,” and below he said “mine”; he did not change the expression. The statements above, therefore, teach why he said “mine.”

78. For when the woman, as though he were a human being, asked him to allow her sons to sit at his right or left, and when she had asked him as though he were merely human, the Lord answered as though merely human concerning his Passion: “Can you drink the cup that I am going to drink?” (ibid., 22).

79. Therefore, because he was speaking according to the flesh about the Passion of his body, he wished to show that according to the flesh he would leave us an example and likeness of undergoing suffering, but according to the human condition he would not grant the companionship of the heavenly seat. This is what he said: “It is not mine,” just as elsewhere: “My teaching is not mine” (John 7:16). He means, “It is not mine according to the flesh,” for what is divine is not an utterance of the flesh.

80. How explicitly he revealed his indulgence toward the disciples whom he loved when he prefaced his reply with: “You shall indeed drink my cup.” Since he ought not to give what they had requested, he proposed something else, first recalling what he would grant them before stating what he would deny, so that they might understand all the more that the defect lay in the suitability of their request, not in the Lord’s generosity.

81. “You shall indeed drink my cup,” he says—that is, “I will not deny you the Passion that belongs to my flesh. What I possess by my human assumption, you can imitate. I have given you the victory of suffering, the inheritance of the cross. But to sit at my right or at my left is not mine to give you.”

He did not say, “It is not mine to give,” but, “It is not mine to give you.” Thus he does not assert that he lacks the power, but that creatures lack the merit.

82. Understand it in another way: “It is not mine to give you”—that is, “It is not mine, who came to teach humility; it is not mine, who came not to be served but to serve; it is not mine, who uphold justice, not favor.”

83. Referring the matter finally to the Father, he added: “For those for whom it has been prepared,” to show that the Father too is accustomed to grant things not according to requests but according to merits, because “God shows no partiality” (Acts 10:34). Hence the Apostle also says: “Those whom he foreknew, he also predestined” (Rom. 8:29). He did not predestine them before he foreknew them; rather, he predestined the rewards of those whose merits he foreknew.

84. The woman is therefore rightly reproved: she requested from the Lord both things impossible and a privilege of a special kind. Yet what he judged should be given to the saints, he bestowed not on two apostles but on all the disciples, even without anyone’s entreaty, by his own willing generosity, as it is written: “You shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:28).

85. Therefore, even if we suppose that what was requested was possible, there is no ground for accusation. Yet when I read that the Seraphim stand (Isa. 6:2), how can I think that human beings sit at the right or left of the Son of God? The Lord sits above the Cherubim, as you find: “You who sit above the Cherubim, appear” (Ps. 79:2). How, then, will the apostles sit above the Cherubim?

86. Nevertheless, I draw this conclusion not from my own ingenuity but from the oracle of the Lord’s voice. For the Lord himself, later commending the apostles to the Father, says: “Father, I desire that where I am, they also may be with me” (John 17:24). If he had judged that the Father would give human beings the divine seat, he would have said: “I desire that where I sit, they also may sit with me.” But he says: “I desire that they may be with me,” not “that they may sit with me”; and “where I am,” not “as I am.”

87. He continues: “That they may see my glory.” Here too he did not say, “That they may possess my glory,” but “that they may see it.” A servant sees; the Lord possesses. David likewise taught this when he said: “That I may see the delight of the Lord” (Ps. 26:4). The Lord himself revealed the same in the Gospel, saying: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8). “They shall see,” he says, not “they shall sit with God above the Cherubim.”

88. Let them therefore cease to judge lesser things concerning the Son of God according to his divinity, lest they also judge lesser things concerning the Father. For whoever believes wrongly about the Son cannot think rightly about the Father. Whoever believes wrongly about the Spirit cannot think rightly about the Son. Where there is one dignity, one glory, one love, and one majesty, whatever you suppose must be detracted from one is detracted from all; for then there will no longer be fullness if you distinguish and divide it into separate portions.

## CHAPTER VII

The objection drawn from the passage, “You loved them as you loved me,” is refuted. First, the impiety of the Arians’ interpretation is exposed; then the same words are compared with similar ones; finally, the entire passage is considered. From this it is inferred that Christ’s being sent, although it must be understood according to the flesh, does him no harm. Once this has been established, the manner of the divine sending is described.

89. Nevertheless, most august Emperor, there are some who, wishing to deny the unity of the divine substance, try to diminish the love of the Father and the Son because it is written: “And you loved them as you loved me” (John 17:23). When they say this, what are they doing except introducing a certain equality of comparison between the Son of God and human beings?

90. Can human beings be loved by God in the same way as the Son, in whom the Father was well pleased? He pleases by himself; we please through him. For in those in whom God sees his Son according to his image, he adopts them through the Son into the grace of sonship, so that just as we exist according to the image through the Image, so through the generation of the Son we may be called into adoption. One love, therefore, is the love of nature, eternal; another is the love of grace.

91. Or if they make an issue of the words because it is written, “You loved them as you loved me,” and think that a comparison has been made, then they must also think that the following was said comparatively: “Be merciful, as your Father who is in heaven is merciful” (Luke 6:36); and elsewhere: “Be perfect, as my Father who is in heaven is perfect” (Matt. 5:48).

If the Father is perfect according to the fullness of his majesty, while we are perfect according to the progress of an acquired virtue, then the Son too is loved by the Father according to the fullness of an ever-abiding love, whereas in us the love of God is earned through the progress of virtue.

92. You see, then, what grace God has given to human beings, and yet you wish to dissolve the natural and indivisible love of the Father and the Son. You still scrutinize the words where you should discern the unity of majesty.

93. Consider the whole passage and from what disposition he speaks. For you have him saying: “Glorify me, Father, with the glory that I had with you before the world existed” (John 17:5).

See that he speaks from the disposition of the first man, since by that request he asks for us what man remembers having been granted in paradise before sin, as he also promised the thief in his Passion: “Truly, truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43). This is the glory that existed before the world.

He spoke of the world with reference to human beings, as you find: “Behold, the whole world has gone after him” (John 12:19); and elsewhere: “So that this world may know that you sent me” (John 14:31).

94. Nevertheless, so that you might know that the Son of God is great, saving, and almighty, he added an indication of his majesty, saying: “All mine are yours, and yours are mine” (ibid., 10). He possesses everything, and yet you turn his being sent into an insult?

95. If you do not understand his being sent according to the flesh, as the Apostle said (Rom. 8:3), and from a simple word construct a prejudice, saying that inferiors are customarily sent by superiors, what will you answer to the fact that the Son was sent to human beings? For if you think the one who is sent is lesser than the one by whom he is sent, learn that a lesser person also sent a greater, and that greater persons were sent to lesser ones.

Tobias sent the archangel Raphael (Tobit 9:3); an angel was sent to Balaam (Num. 22:22); and the Son of God was sent to the Jews (Matt. 21:37).

96. Was the Son of God therefore lesser than the Jews to whom he was sent? For it is written concerning him: “Finally he sent them his only son, saying, ‘They will respect my son’” (Matt. 21:37). Notice that he named the servants first and then the son, so that you may know that, according to the power of his divinity, the only-begotten Son of God neither bears the name of servants nor shares their common condition. He is sent as one to be revered, not to be compared with servants.

97. He rightly added “my,” so that he might be believed to have come not as one of many, nor of a degenerate nature, nor of some lesser power, but as the true one from the true, the image of the Father’s substance.

98. Nevertheless, suppose that the one who is sent is lesser than the one who sends him. Then Christ is also lesser than Pilate, because Pilate sent him to Herod. But the expression does not prejudice power: Scripture, which says that he was sent by the Father, also says that he was sent by the governor.

Textual and editorial notes (supplied apparatus):

- 46. [Col. 0658D] Some manuscripts read: “although also from the prophetic [testimony].”
- 52. [Col. 0659D] The Roman edition reads “the disposition of the name” (*nominis affectum*) in place of “the human disposition.”
- 53. [Col. 0659D] The Amerbach, Erasmus, and Gill editions read, in the margin, “the Lord and the Son”; Gill has this in the text, while the Roman edition, with the written codices, reads “the Lord [is worshipped] by servants.” Again, after three words, some manuscripts read, “we read and believe the mysteries according to the incarnation”; but this is contrary to the authority of the other manuscripts and of all the editions. Nor is there discussion here of mysteries, but of the testimonies of Scripture.
- 54. [Col. 0660D] All editions read, “he asks for a drink, intending to give [spiritual drink]”; almost all handwritten codices, on the contrary, read, “he asks for a drink, being about to give [it].”
- 55. [Col. 0660D] Some manuscripts read: “the mystery of inequality.” This is not quite correct.
- 56. The same manuscripts read: “Consider whatever a mother asks with and for her sons. She is certainly concerned for the honor of her sons. Her measure of wishes is indeed excessive,” etc. [Col. 0661D] They also read: “and the reward of her own wish.” Below likewise: “Thus this mother, devoted in maternal concern but more indulgent toward advantage.” This is not very apt.
- 57. [Col. 0661D] Some manuscripts read “and although greedy for you”; others, “and although greedy there.”
- 58. [Col. 0661D] A few manuscripts read “sometimes to perform service”; the remaining manuscripts and editions more aptly have the reading in the text.
- 61. [Col. 0661D] Three manuscripts omit after “which is more tolerable”: “than for herself”; one supplies instead, “concerned for honor.” Amerbach and Erasmus read, “than if for herself.”
- 63. [Col. 0662D] Two manuscripts read “whom he knew ought to be honored”; one reads “would say,” etc.
- 64. [Col. 0662D] Gill and the Roman edition read “the prerogative for them”; the other editions with the manuscripts read “its prerogative,” namely, that of the thing the apostles requested. Again, where all editions and some manuscripts read “would detract from his own right,” the larger number of manuscripts prefer “would deny his own right.”
- 67. [Col. 0662D] A few manuscripts read: “If you think it sacrilegious to believe.” [Col. 0663D] Some manuscripts read “he will do it”; one, “he may do it.” The remaining manuscripts and all editions, as also sacred codices of every language, read “I will do it.”
- 79. [Col. 0665D] Amerbach, Erasmus, and the latest Paris editions read “according to my flesh.” Gill, the Roman edition, and the manuscripts most aptly read “mine according to the flesh,” namely, the teaching.
- 82. [Col. 0665D] Some manuscripts read: “who came to teach in humility … who uphold justice. For grace, finally, … [he is] accustomed to yield, not to merits.” This is very poor.
- 87. [Col. 0665D] Not a few manuscripts read “the will of the Lord”; but it is often observable that *voluntas* (“will”) and *voluptas* (“delight”) are interchanged in manuscripts.
- 88. [Col. 0666D] “Whoever believes wrongly about the Spirit cannot think rightly about the Son” is lacking in most manuscripts. Moreover, there is nothing surprising in Ambrose’s dwelling rather long in refuting this objection: Basil, *Against Eunomius* IV, p. 107; Epiphanius, *Heresy* 69, no. 58; Cyril of Alexandria, *Assertion* 26; and others record that the Arians were accustomed to press it.
- 91. [Col. 0667D] Some manuscripts read “advancing according to virtues.” Other manuscripts and the editions agree with one another, except that the editions read “of an incidental virtue” in place of “of an advancing virtue.”
- 92. [Col. 0667D] Some manuscripts read “what grace of God.”
- 93. [Col. 0667D–0668D] The words “See that he speaks from the disposition of the first man … because you sent me” are absent not only from all editions but also from all the French manuscripts that could be consulted. They have been restored from one Vatican codex. Besides being wholly consonant with Ambrose’s style, their omission leaves incomplete the saint’s invitation immediately above to examine the whole passage and leaves insufficient coherence with what follows concerning Christ’s sending.
- 94. [Col. 0668D] Two manuscripts read “the judgment of his majesty.”
- 95. [Col. 0668D] The Bigotian codex reads “and greater persons [were sent] by lesser”; some others, “and greater persons [were sent] to lesser persons.” The latter is more suitable.
- 98. [Col. 0668D] The old edition reads, “But Scripture prejudices power”; Gill, the Roman edition, and some manuscripts read, “But it does not prejudice,” etc. The remaining—and better—manuscripts have the reading translated above, except that some read “whom [it says was] sent” for “which says [he was] sent.”

99. Hence, if we form sober judgments about the Son of God—judgments worthy of him—we must understand that he was “sent” because, from that incomprehensible and ineffable depth of profound majesty, the Word of God gave himself to be grasped by our minds according to our capacity, not only when he emptied himself, but also when he dwelt within us, as it is written: “For I shall dwell in them” (2 Corinthians 6:16). Finally, elsewhere also you have the words spoken by God: “Come, let us descend and confuse their languages” (Genesis 11:7). For God did not at some time descend from one place to another—he who says: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jeremiah 23:24)—but he appears to descend when the Word of God penetrates our affections, as the prophet said: “Prepare the way for the Lord; make his paths straight” (Isaiah 40:3), so that, as he himself promised, when he comes with the Father he may make his dwelling among us. It is therefore evident how he comes.

## CHAPTER VIII

That Christ is not “Lord” insofar as he is truly the Son of God, but insofar as he is man, as is shown by his addressing the Father sometimes as “Father” and sometimes as “Lord.” How several heresies are struck down by a single verse of Scripture. The statements applicable to Christ either as the Son of God or as the son of David must therefore be distinguished; only under the latter title is he to be called a servant. Finally, several passages are shown to be capable of being understood only with reference to the Incarnation.

100. Hence it is also evident how he calls him “Lord” whom he knows as Father. For he says: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth” (Matthew 11:25). First Wisdom called him his Father; afterward he called him Lord of creation. Thus the Lord himself shows in his Gospel that there is no lordship where there is true offspring, saying: “What do you think about the Christ? Whose son is he?” They say to him: “David’s.” Jesus says to them: “How then does David, in the Spirit, call him ‘Lord,’ saying: ‘The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand’? And he added: ‘If therefore David calls him Lord in the Spirit, how is he his son?’ And no one was able to answer him a word” (Matthew 22:42 ff.).

101. How carefully, even in this testimony, the Lord safeguarded the faith against the Arians! For he did not say: “The Spirit calls him Lord,” but that David spoke “in the Spirit,” so that he might be believed to be both Lord and God according to his divinity, whose son he is according to the flesh—namely, David’s son. You see, therefore, that the name of filial piety and that of lordship are distinguished.  
[Note: Some manuscripts read: “of the Father and the Lord.”]

102. And rightly the Lord proclaimed his own Father, but the Lord of heaven and earth, so that when you read both “Father” and “Lord,” you understand “Father of the Son” in the one case, and “Lord of creation” in the other. In the one there is the prerogative of nature; in the other, the authority of power. For, taking the form of a servant, he calls him “Lord” precisely in respect of the servitude he assumed: equal in the form of God, a servant in the body. Servitude belongs to the flesh, but lordship to divinity. Hence the Apostle also says: “The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory” (2 Corinthians 1:3), asserting God with reference to the assumed humanity, but “Father” with reference to glory. Did God have two sons, Christ and glory? Certainly not. Therefore, if Christ is the one Son of God, Christ is surely glory. What, then, do you take away from him who is the glory of the Father?

103. If, therefore, the Son is glory and the Father is glory—for “Father of glory” cannot mean anything other than glory—there is not a division of glories, but one glory. Thus glory refers to the proper character of the nature, while lordship refers to the servitude of the body assumed. For if even the flesh is subject to the soul of a righteous person, as it is written: “I chastise my body and bring it into servitude” (1 Corinthians 9:27), how much more is it subject to divinity, of which it is said: “For all things serve you” (Psalm 118:91)?

104. With a single question the Lord excluded the Sabellians, Photinians, and Arians alike. For when he says that “the Lord” said to “the Lord,” Sabellius is excluded, since he wants the Father to be the same person as the Son. Photinus is excluded [Note: That is, he denies that Christ existed before assuming flesh, as we have observed elsewhere.], since he judges according to the flesh; for the Lord of King David could be no one but one who is God. It is written: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Deuteronomy 6:13). Would the prophet, who reigned under the Law, think contrary to the Law?

Arius is excluded, since he hears that the Son sits at the right hand of the Father. If he argues from human custom, he destroys himself and pours back upon himself the poison of his sacrilegious argument: while interpreting the inequality of the Father and the Son according to human practice, he goes astray from the truth in both cases, preferring the one whom he diminishes, since he must confess as prior the one whom he hears sitting at the right hand. The Manichaean is also excluded. For he does not deny that he is the son of David according to the flesh, since, when the blind cried out, “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on us” (Matthew 20:30), he was pleased by their faith, stood still, and healed them. But he denies that this belongs to his eternity if the impious call him merely the son of David.  
[Note: Several manuscripts read: “while interpreting the inequality of God … in both respects,” etc.]

105. For he is the Son of God against Hebion; he is the Son of David against the Manichaeans; he is the Son of God against Photinus; he is the Son of David against Marcion; he is the Son of God against Paul of Samosata; he is the Son of David against Valentinus; he is the Son of God against Arius and Sabellius, heirs of pagan error; he is the Lord of David against the Jews, who, seeing the Son of God in the flesh, believed in their impious frenzy that he was merely a man.  
[Note: Tertullian, *On the Flesh of Christ*, chapter 18, reports that Hebion acknowledged nothing in Christ that was not that of a pure and unqualified man; so also Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* III.21 and 27; Epiphanius, *Heresies* 30; Augustine, *On Heresies* 10; and others. This was also the error of Paul of Samosata, as may be learned from Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* V.28 and VII.27, 29, and 30: he called Christ a mere man. He nevertheless added that the Word, having descended from heaven, dwelt in Jesus, as Epiphanius testifies, *Heresies* 65. Augustine also mentions this same heretic in *On Heresies* 44, as do others.]

106. But according to the faith of the Church, the Son of God and the son of David are one and the same Son, because the mystery of God’s Incarnation is the salvation of all creation, according to what is written: “So that, apart from God, he might taste death for everyone” (Hebrews 2:9)—that is, so that every creature might be redeemed, without any suffering on the part of the divinity, by the price of the Lord’s blood—as it says elsewhere: “Every creature will be freed from the slavery of corruption” (Romans 8:21).

107. It is one thing for the Son to be called such according to the divine substance, and another according to the assumption of flesh. For according to divine generation the Son is equal to God the Father; according to the assumption of the body he is servant to God the Father, because, he says, “he took the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:7). Yet the Son is one and the same. In relation to the holy patriarch David, however, he is Lord according to his glory, but son according to the succession of bodily descent—not failing to be himself, but acquiring for himself the right of our adoption.  
[Note: Hilary, *On the Trinity* II: “The dignity of power is not lost when the humility of the flesh is assumed,” that is, when it is received in the Incarnation. These two clauses correspond so aptly to these two Ambrosian passages that they may serve in place of a commentary on them.]

108. Nor did he assume servitude in the person of man only through David’s lineage [Note: Some manuscripts read: “but also from the Lord.” Not very suitably.], but also through his name, as you have it: “I have found David my servant”; and elsewhere: “Behold, I shall send my servant to you; the Rising One is his name” (Zechariah 3:8; 6:12). The Son himself also says: “Thus says the Lord, who formed me from the womb as a servant for himself, and said to me: ‘It is a great thing for you to be called my child. Behold, I have appointed you as a covenant for my people, as a light for the nations, that you may be salvation to the ends of the earth’” (Isaiah 49:6 ff.). To whom is this said, if not to Christ? Although he was in the form of God, “he emptied himself and took the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:6–7). What is “in the form of God” except in the fullness of divinity?

109. Learn, therefore, what it means that “he took the form of a servant”: the fullness of human perfection, the fullness of obedience. Therefore he says in the thirtieth Psalm: “You have set my feet in a spacious place. I have become a reproach to all my enemies. Shine your face upon your servant” (Psalm 30:9, 12, 17). He is called a servant as man, in whom he was sanctified; a servant as man, in whom he was anointed; a servant as man, in whom he was made subject to the Law and made of a Virgin. To put it briefly, he is called a servant as one who has a mother, as it is written: “O Lord, I am your servant; I am your servant and the son of your handmaid” (Psalm 115:7); and elsewhere: “I am afflicted and humbled exceedingly” (Psalm 37:9).  
[Note: Several manuscripts read: “your servant.” He is a servant in the one who was anointed; he is a servant in the one who was sanctified; he is a servant in the one who was created; and, to put it briefly, etc.]

110. Who was humbled exceedingly except Christ, who came to free everyone through obedience? For just as through the disobedience of one man the many were made sinners, so through the obedience of one the many will be made righteous (Romans 5:19). Who received the cup of salvation (Psalm 115:13): Christ, the chief priest, or David, who possessed neither priesthood nor underwent suffering? Who offered the sacrifice of praise?

111. But if this is insufficient, consider another passage: “Guard my soul, for I am holy” (Psalm 85:2). Would David have said this of himself? Yet he says it who also says: “You will not abandon my soul to the underworld, nor will you permit your holy one to see corruption” (Psalm 15:10). The same person therefore says both things.

112. He added: “Save your servant” (Psalm 85:2); and below: “Give authority to your servant and to the son of your handmaid” (ibid. 16); and elsewhere, namely in Ezekiel: “I shall raise up over them one shepherd, and my servant David will rule them. He himself will feed them and will be their shepherd; and I, the Lord, will be their God, while my servant David will be ruler in their midst” (Ezekiel 34:23–24). David, the son of Jesse, had certainly already died. He therefore speaks of Christ, who for our sake became the son of a handmaid according to the form of man. For according to divine generation he has not a mother but a Father; nor is he the fruit of a bodily womb, but the eternal power of God.

113. Therefore, when we read that the Lord said: “My time has not yet been fulfilled” (John 7:8), and: “I am with you only a little while” (John 13:33), and: “I am going to him who sent me” (ibid.), and: “The Son of Man has been glorified” (ibid. 31), we must refer these statements to the mystery of the Incarnation. But when we read: “And God has been glorified in him, and God has glorified him” (ibid.), what question remains, when the Son is glorified by the Father and the Father is glorified by the Son?

114. Finally, to disclose the faith of unity and the bond of the Trinity, he said that he was also to be glorified by the Spirit, as you have it: “He will receive from what is mine and will glorify me” (John 16:14). Therefore the Holy Spirit also glorifies the Son of God. How, then, did he himself say: “If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing” (John 8:54)? Is the Son’s glory therefore nothing? It is sacrilegious to say so, unless you refer the statement to the flesh, since the Son spoke in the person of man: in comparison with divinity, the glory of the flesh is nothing.

115. Let them therefore cease impiously to bring forward what turns back upon their own unbelief. They say: “It is written: ‘Now the Son of Man has been glorified’” (John 13:31). I do not deny that it is written: “The Son of Man has been glorified”; but let them see what follows: “And God has been glorified in him.” I have an excuse concerning the Son of Man; he has none concerning the Father, because the Father did not assume flesh. I have an excuse, and I do not use it; he has none, and yet he brings accusations. Let him either allow me to understand the passage straightforwardly, or let him refer to the flesh what belongs to the flesh. A pious mind distinguishes what is read according to the flesh and according to divinity; a sacrilegious mind confuses them and twists whatever has been said according to the humility of the flesh into an insult against divinity.  
[Note: The older editions and several manuscripts read: “For it is written—I do not deny it—‘Now the Son of Man has been glorified.’ But let them see what has been added: ‘The Son of Man has been glorified.’ Let them also see what follows,” etc. The Roman edition, together with some manuscripts, has the reading printed in the text. Although its reading is not unreasonable, we would prefer the other if, instead of “Now the Son of Man has been glorified,” the first clause had read: “If I glorify myself,” etc. In that form the syntax and sequence of the discourse would be more coherent.]

## CHAPTER IX

When the Arians object, following Jewish custom, to the order of the words “in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,” the holy man replies, in addition to the answer he has already given, that the Son is often placed before the Father.

116. [Formerly Chapter IV.] What else are the Arians than false and shameless interpreters of divine words in the Jewish manner, when they say that the power of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is so different that it is written: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19), and from the order of the words they manufacture a difference in divine power?

117. Although in the earlier books I have already asserted this very testimony in support of the unity of majesty and name, nevertheless, if they raise a question from it, I can establish from the testimonies of Scripture that in many passages the Son is named first and the Father afterward. Is the Father therefore, because the Son’s designation is placed first, second to the Son by the prejudice of the words, as the Arians wish? Far from it, I say—far from it. Faith knows nothing of such an order; it knows nothing of a distinction in the honor of the Father and the Son. I have read of no such thing, heard of no such thing, and found no rank within God. Nowhere have I read of a second or third God; I have read of the first, and have heard of the first and only one (Isaiah 44:6).

118. If we demand a superstitious adherence to order, the Son ought not to sit at the Father’s right hand, nor ought he to have called himself the first and the beginning. The Evangelist therefore began wrongly with the Word before mentioning God, saying: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God” (John 1:1). For according to human custom and order he ought first to have named the Father. The Apostle also did not know this order when he said: “Paul, servant of Christ Jesus, called as an apostle, set apart for the Gospel of God” (Romans 1:1); and elsewhere: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit” (2 Corinthians 13:13). If we pursue the order of the words, he placed the Son first and the Father second.  
[Note: Several manuscripts read: “the Son at the beginning.”]

But the order of the words is often changed. Therefore you must not raise a question either from order or from rank concerning God the Father and his Son, since according to divinity there is no division within unity.

## CHAPTER X

How the Arians openly pass over to paganism when they object to the words “Whoever believes in me does not believe in me,” and so forth. The true meaning of the passage is explained, lest anyone suppose that the Lord prohibited faith in himself; it is shown that he spoke sometimes as God and sometimes as man. After various effects of the same faith have been brought forward, several other passages are likewise proved to require the same interpretation.

119. Finally, to make it clear that they are not Christians, they deny that one ought to believe in Christ, saying that it is written: “Whoever believes in me does not believe in me but in him who sent me” (John 12:44). I had been waiting for this confession: why were you amusing yourselves with such evasions? I knew that my dispute was with pagans; but they are converted, whereas you are not converted. If they believe, the mystery is preserved; you have lost what you received—or perhaps what you began with was not faith at all, but a fiction.

120. “It is written,” they say, “‘Whoever believes in me does not believe in me but in him who sent me.’” But observe what follows, and observe in what way the Son of God wishes to be understood. For it follows: “And whoever sees me sees him who sent me” (John 12:45)—that is, the Father is seen in the Son. He therefore explained what he had stated earlier: the one believes in the Son who also confesses the Father. For whoever does not know the Son does not know the Father either; everyone who denies the Son does not have the Father, while whoever confesses the Son has both the Son and the Father.

121. What, then, does “does not believe in me” mean? Not in what you see bodily; not in the man alone whom you see. For he did not assert that one should believe in a mere man, but that you should believe that Jesus Christ himself is both the Son of God and man. Hence he says both: “I have not come of myself” (John 7:28); and elsewhere: “I am the beginning, the very one who is speaking to you” (John 8:25). As man, he did not come of himself; as the Son of God, he does not have his beginning from a human being. “But I am,” he says, “the beginning, the very one who is speaking to you” (John 12:46): the things I have spoken are divine, not human.

122. It is not lawful to believe that he denied that one ought to believe in him, since he himself said: “So that everyone who believes in me may not remain in darkness” (John 12:46); and elsewhere: “For this is the will of my Father who sent me, that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him may have eternal life” (John 6:40); and elsewhere: “You believe in God; believe also in me” (John 14:1).

123. Let no one therefore receive the Son without the Father, since we read of the Son. The Son has a Father, but not a temporal father; not one arising from suffering, conception, or grace. I have read of generation, but I have not read of conception. The Father says, “I have begotten,” not “I have created”; and the Son does not call his creator “God” in relation to the eternity of divine generation, but calls him Father.

124. He signifies himself now in the person of man, now in the majesty of God: now claiming for himself unity of divinity with God the Father, now assuming the weakness of human flesh; now indicating that his teaching is not his own, now that he does not seek his own will; now saying that his testimony is not true, now that it is true. For he himself said: “If I testify about myself, my testimony is not true” (John 5:31). And later he says: “Even if I testify about myself, my testimony is true” (John 8:14).

125. How, then, is your testimony not true, Lord Jesus, when the one who believed you, though placed upon a cross and standing amid the punishment of confessed crime, laid aside the criminal’s deserts and obtained the rewards of an innocent man (Luke 23:41 ff.)?

126. Was Paul therefore deceived, who received his sight because he believed—the sight he had lost before he believed (Acts 9:18)?

127. Did Jesus son of Nave also err, when he recognized the commander of the heavenly army? But after he believed, he immediately conquered, worthy to triumph through the battle of faith. In the end, he did not lead bronze-clad ranks into battle, nor did he use a battering ram or other engines of war; rather, at the sound of seven priestly trumpets he brought down the fortifications of the enemy walls. Thus an immense war was brought to an end by the blast of the trumpet and the priest’s mitre (Joshua 6).

128. The prostitute saw this. When she had despaired of any means of salvation amid the destruction of the city, because faith had conquered, she raised up the signs and standards of faith in the Lord’s Passion and tied scarlet thread in the window, so that the appearance of mystical blood, destined to redeem the world, might flourish there (Joshua 2).  
[Note: Several manuscripts read: “Thus the name of the future Jesus was …,” etc., less appropriately.]

Thus outside, the name of Jesus brought victory to those fighting; inside, the image of the Lord’s Passion brought salvation to those in danger. Because Rahab understood the heavenly mystery, the Lord says in the Psalm: “I shall remember Rahab and Babylon, those who know me” (Psalm 86:4).

129. How, then, is your testimony not true, Lord, except according to the weakness of human beings? For “every human being is a liar” (Psalm 115:2).

130. Finally, to show that he had spoken according to his humanity, he said: “The Father who sent me, he himself bears witness about me” (John 8:18). But his testimony is true according to divinity, as he himself says: “And my testimony is true, because I know where I came from and where I am going; but you do not know where I come from or where I am going. You judge according to the flesh” (ibid. 14–15). Those who think that Christ lacked knowledge sufficient to give testimony therefore judge not according to divinity but according to humanity.

131. Therefore, when you hear: “Whoever believes in me does not believe in me,” and: “The Father who sent me himself gave me a commandment” (John 12:49), you have learned how you should understand the statement.  
[Note: Some manuscripts read: “which must be referred to the Father.”]

Finally, he showed what the commandment was when he said: “I lay down my life in order to take it up again. No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord” (John 10:17 ff.). You see that this was said to show that he possessed free power to lay down and take up his life again, as he himself said: “I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it up again. I received this commandment from my Father” (ibid.).

132. Whether it is called a “commandment,” or, as some Latin codices have it, a “precept,” it is given not according to divinity but according to the Incarnation, for the victorious undergoing of the Passion.  
[Note: A few manuscripts read: “the incarnation of the nature to be undertaken,” etc. Where the Latin codices translate the word as *mandatum* or *praeceptum*, the Greek has ἐντολήν (*entolēn*, “commandment”); Grotius observes concerning this word that ἐντέλλεσθαι may also be used where there is no command in the strict sense.]

## CHAPTER XI

That when Christ is read as saying nothing from himself, this must be referred to his humanity. How it is rightly said that, even according to his divinity, he hears and sees the Father; and, through many accumulated arguments, it is proved that the Son of God is not a creature.

133. [Formerly Chapter V.] Are we really to reduce the Son of God to such a state of humiliation that he does not know how to do or say anything except what he has heard, and are we to suppose that a prescribed measure has been set for his actions and speech, because it is written: “I have not spoken from myself” (John 12:49), and below: “As the Father said to me, so I speak” (ibid. 50)? Let these statements be referred either to the obedience of the flesh or to the faith of unity. For many of the more learned understand the Father’s hearing the Son and the Son’s saying something to mean that, through the unity of nature, whatever the Son knows the Father wills through the unity of will, he is said to have heard.

134. Hence what is declared is not a bodily function but an inseparable resolve of cooperation. The passage does not signify any physical hearing of words, but the unity of will and power that exists both in the Father and in the Son. He also recalled that this unity exists in the Holy Spirit elsewhere, saying: “For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak” (John 16:13), so that we might understand that whatever the Spirit speaks, the Son also speaks, and whatever the Son speaks, the Father also speaks, because the Trinity has one judgment and one operation.  
[Note: All editions read this way, but many manuscripts omit the word “cooperation,” in whose place the Laetian manuscript has “is compared.” The omission is erroneous.]

For just as the Father is seen in the Son—not in bodily appearance, but in the unity of divinity—so also the Father speaks in the Son, not with a temporal voice or bodily sound, but through the unity of action. Finally, when he had said: “The Father who dwells in me, he himself speaks, and the works that I do, he himself performs,” he added: “Believe me that I am in the Father and the Father is in me. Otherwise, believe because of the works themselves” (John 12:50; 14:10).  
[Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “As the Father said to me, so I speak; and the Father who dwells in me, he himself performs the works.” The same reading occurs above in Book IV, chapter 6, section 68.]

135. This is our understanding according to the sequence of the divine Scriptures. Let the Arians, however, who refuse to form worthy judgments about God, be refuted by an example suited to their own merits, lest they believe everything carnally: they themselves see the works of their father, the devil, performed incorporeally. As the Lord made clear concerning their associates, the Jews, saying: “You do what you have seen your father doing” (John 8:38)—not because they had seen the devil working, but because they had done what he willed and commanded, and because, invisibly, the devil worked sin in them according to their iniquity. We have stated this, following the Apostle (2 Timothy 3:9), on account of the foolishness of the unbelievers.  
[Note: Some Paris editions read: “according to his will”; other editions and manuscripts more correctly have “according to his wills,” that is, his will and commands.]

136. In any case, it has been sufficiently proved by examples from Scripture that the following pertains to the unity of divine majesty: the Father remains in the Son, and the things spoken by the Son are understood to have been heard from the Father. By what else can we understand the unity of majesty than by the fact that the same honors are rendered to the Father and the Son? For what could be said more excellently than what the Apostle said: “They crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2:8)?

137. The Son, therefore, is both God of majesty and Lord of majesty; but majesty is not subject to creatures. Therefore the Son is not a creature.

138. The Son is “the image of the Father’s substance” (Hebrews 1:3). Every creature is unlike the heavenly substance, but the Son of God is not unlike the Father. Therefore the Son is not a creature.

139. The Son “did not regard equality with God as something to be seized” (Philippians 2:6). No creature is equal to God, but the Son is equal. Therefore the Son is not a creature.

140. Every creature is mutable; but the Son of God is not mutable. Therefore the Son of God is not a creature.

141. Every creature, according to the capacity of its nature, receives qualities both good and evil, and experiences their diminution. But nothing can either diminish or increase in the Son of God with respect to his divinity. Therefore the Son of God is not a creature.

142. “God will bring every work into judgment” (Ecclesiastes 12:14), but the Son of God is not brought into judgment, because he himself judges. Therefore the Son of God is not a creature.

143. Finally, to make you understand the unity, the Savior says concerning the sheep: “No one snatches them from my hand. What the Father has given me is greater than all, and no one can snatch them from my Father’s hand. I and the Father are one” (John 10:29–30).

144. The Son gives life just as the Father does: “For just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whomever he wishes” (John 5:21). The Son raises up as the Father does; the Son preserves as the Father does. If he is not unequal in grace, how is he unequal in power? The Son also does not lose anyone, just as the Father does not. Therefore, lest anyone believe in two gods or introduce a division of power, he said that he is one with the Father. How can a creature say this? Therefore the Son of God is not a creature.

145. To reign and to serve are not the same thing. Christ, however, is both king and the son of a king. Therefore the Son of God is not a servant. Every creature serves, but the Son of God does not serve; rather, he makes sons of God out of servants. Therefore the Son of God is not a creature.

## CHAPTER XII

He confirms the foregoing from the parable of the rich man who went away to obtain a kingdom for himself, and shows that it should not be taken as an insult if the Son is said to hand the kingdom over to the Father and the Father is said to subject all things to him. We are now the kingdom of Christ and are in Christ’s kingdom; one day we shall be in the kingdom of God, where the whole Trinity reigns equally.

146. Accordingly, he introduced that divine parable of the rich man who went away to a distant region to receive a kingdom and return (Luke 19:12), describing himself according to the substance of his divinity and his incorporation. For he himself is rich according to the fullness of divinity; for our sake he became poor, although he was rich, and an eternal king, begotten by an eternal king. He went away into a foreign land according to the assumption of the body, because, entering upon the ways of man as upon a journey into a foreign place, he came into this world to prepare a kingdom for himself from among us.

147. Jesus therefore came to this earth to receive a kingdom from us, to whom he said: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke 17:21). This is the kingdom Christ received; this is what he handed over to the Father. For how could he receive a kingdom who was the eternal king? The Son of Man therefore came to receive the kingdom and to return. The Jews did not wish to receive him, concerning whom he says: “Those who did not want me to reign over them, bring them here and kill them” (Luke 19:27).

148. Let us follow the order of Scripture. He who came will hand the kingdom over to God the Father; and when he has handed over the kingdom, then he himself will also be subject to the one who subjected all things to him, so that God may be all in all (1 Corinthians 15:24, 28). If the Son of God received the kingdom as the Son of Man, then, as the Son of Man, he will also hand over what he received; and if he hands it over as the Son of Man, then as the Son of Man he acknowledges subjection—according to the condition of the flesh, not according to the majesty of divinity.  
[Note: The older editions and many manuscripts read this way, except that the same editions and not a few manuscripts have here and above “as the Son of Man.” We have restored the reading “if as the Son” from the better manuscripts. Some place a comma before *tradit* (“he hands over”), while others place it after *tradit ergo* (“therefore he hands over”). The editions end the sentence with *agnosceret* (“he would acknowledge”), whereas the cited manuscripts have *agnoscit* (“he acknowledges”). Three other codices read: “what he received as the Son of Man. Therefore the Son of God also hands it over. Recognize the assumption of humanity …” The Roman edition does not differ from these except in punctuation: “what he received: as the Son of Man, therefore, the Son of God also hands it over. Recognize the assumption of humanity …”]

149. And you bring forward as an insult the fact that God subjected all things to him, although you hear that the Son of Man hands the kingdom over to God, and although, as we said in the earlier books, you have read: “No one comes to me unless the Father draws him, and I shall raise him up on the last day” (Book II, chapter 4). If we follow the letter, see and consider rather the unity of mutual honor: the Father subjected to the Son, and the Son hands over to the Father. Say which is greater: to draw or to raise up? Is not, according to human usage, the drawing the service of the one who draws, while the raising is the power of the one who raises? Yet the Son draws to the Father, and the Father draws to the Son; the Son raises up, and the Father raises up. Let the sacrilegious notions of distinction depart wherever there is unity of power.

150. [Note: The Roman edition, with a few manuscripts, reads: “Therefore he hands over … Nor does it perish,” etc. But the older editions, with very many more manuscripts, read better: “May he hand over,” etc. Again, whereas all editions and most manuscripts read “while I am on the way,” some other manuscripts read “while I am in life.”]

Does the Son therefore hand his kingdom over to the Father? The kingdom that Christ hands over is not diminished but increased. We are the kingdom, because it was said to us: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke 17:21). We are first the kingdom of Christ, afterward the Father’s, because it is written: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14:6).  
[Note: Some manuscripts read: “while I am in life.”]

While I am on the way, I belong to Christ; when I arrive, I belong to the Father; but everywhere through Christ, and everywhere under Christ.  
[Note: Several manuscripts read: “While I am in life.”]

151. It is good to be in the kingdom of Christ, so that Christ may be with us, as he himself says: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the world” (Matthew 28:20). But it is better to be with Christ: “For to depart and to be with Christ is far better” (Philippians 1:23).  
[Note: All editions read: “while we are in this …”; after this they place a full stop and attach the following words to the preceding sentence. The manuscripts, however, display the reading found in the text.]
