While we are in this world under sin, Christ is with us, so that through the obedience of one the many may be made righteous (Romans 5:19). And if I escape the sin of this world, I shall begin to be with Christ. Finally, he says: “I shall come again and take you to myself” (John 14:3); and below: “I desire that where I am, they also may be with me” (John 17:24).

152. Therefore we are now under the kingdom of Christ while we are engaged in the body and have not yet laid aside the form of a servant, which he received when he emptied himself. But when we have seen his glory, which he possessed before the world existed, we shall be in the kingdom of God, in which are the patriarchs and prophets, concerning whom it is written: “When you see Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob and all the prophets in the kingdom of God” (Luke 13:28), so that we may then enjoy a fuller knowledge of God.  
[Note: Several manuscripts read: “while we are occupied in work and action, while we follow the form of a servant.” This is not sufficiently appropriate.]

153. But in the Son’s kingdom the Father also reigns, and in the Father’s kingdom the Son reigns, because the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father. Where the Son dwells, the Father also dwells; and where the Father dwells, the Son also dwells, as he himself says: “I and the Father will come to him, and we will make our dwelling with him” (John 14:23). Therefore, just as there is one house, so there is one kingdom. The kingdom of the Father and the Son is so entirely one that what the Son hands over, the Father receives, and what the Father receives, the Son does not lose. Therefore, in the one kingdom there is unity of power. Let no one, then, separate the divinity of the Father and the Son.

## CHAPTER XIII
What the subjection of Christ is: after proposing and rejecting various kinds of subjection, he works through the Apostolic text; from it he refutes the impious opinion of the heretics on this matter. The subjection signified as future cannot belong to the divinity, since there has always been the fullest harmony of will between the Father and the Son. Yet everything is truly subject to the same Son according to his divinity; nevertheless, it is said not yet to be subject in this sense because not all human beings obey his commands. After they have become subject to him, Christ himself will then be subjected in them, and the Father’s work will be perfected.

[Col. 0679B]

### 154. [Elsewhere chapter VI.]

But if the Father and the Son share one name and right of God, since the Son of God too is the true God and everlasting King, the Son of God is certainly not subject according to his divinity. Let us therefore consider, august Emperor, how we ought to understand the word “subject.”

### 155.

For how is the Son of God subject? Is he subject as a creature is subject to vanity? But it is impious to think anything of this sort concerning the substance of the divinity.

### 156.

Or is he subject as every creature is subject to the Son of God, since it is likewise written: “You have subjected all things beneath his feet” (Psalm 8:8)? But Christ is not subject to himself.

### 157.

Or is he subject as a woman is subject to her husband, as we read: “Let women be subject to their husbands” (Ephesians 5:22); and elsewhere: “Let a woman learn in silence with complete submission” (1 Timothy 2:11)? But it is sacrilegious to compare either a man with the Father or a woman with the Son of God.

### 158.

Or is he subject in the manner of Peter’s statement: “Be subject to every human institution” [Note: [Col. 0679D] All editions read this way; but, by contrast, nearly all manuscripts have “to every human ordinance.”] (1 Peter 2:13)? Christ is certainly not subject in this way either.

### 159.

Or is he subject as Paul wrote: “Be mutually subject to God and the Father in the fear of Christ” (Ephesians 5:21)? But the Son is subject neither in his own fear nor in that of another Christ, because there is one Christ. Consider the force of these words, for we are subject to the Father while we also fear Christ.

### 160.

How, then, are we to understand “subject”? Let us review the whole Apostolic passage, so that nothing may appear to have been removed by fraud [Note: [Col. 0679D] Some manuscripts read “precluded by stealth.”] or suppressed by concealment:

“If in this life only we have hope in Christ, we are more pitiable than all human beings. But now Christ has risen from the dead, the firstfruits of those who sleep” (1 Corinthians 15:19–20).

You see that the discussion concerns the resurrection of Christ.

### 161.

“For just as through one human being there is death,” he says, “so through a human being there is also the resurrection of the dead. For just as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive. But each in his own order: Christ the firstfruits; then those who belong to Christ, who have believed in his coming. Then the end, when he hands over the kingdom to God and the Father, when he has abolished every principality, authority, and power. For he must reign until he places all his enemies beneath his feet. Last of all, death, the enemy, will be destroyed; for he has subjected all things beneath his feet. But when he says, ‘All things have been subjected to him,’ it is evident that this excludes the one who subjected all things to him. But when all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to the one who subjected all things to him, so that God may be all in all” (1 Corinthians 15:20–28).

The same Apostle also said to the Hebrews: “But now we do not yet see all things subjected to him” (Hebrews 2:8). We have received the sequence of the Apostolic reading.

### 162.

How, then, do we say that he is subject? The Sabellians and Marcionites say that this is the future subjection of Christ to God the Father [Note: [Col. 0679D] Some manuscripts have “subjection,” so that the statement may be resolved as “God the Word into the Father.” Thus: “the Word”; some also have “. . . in the Father.” “God, therefore, the Word”; others, more suitably—and all the editions—as in the text. What is related here concerning the Sabellian dissolution of the Word into the Father, moreover, provides us with a not implausible way of reconciling Epiphanius and Augustine with one another. For above, in Book II, chapter 9, we said that the former had been criticized by another because he maintained that the Father had suffered at the hands of the Sabellians, since they confused the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit into one person. Yet it is credible that they, as often happens with all heretics, wavered in their opinions and answers; and that, in order to escape the designation “Patripassians,” they sometimes professed that the Word had existed as the same person with the Father before the incarnation, but that through the incarnation he had emanated from the Father and, once his passion had finally been completed, had been resolved back into the Father. This agrees not only with this passage of Ambrose but also very well with another passage in Book II, *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 7. It may have happened that Augustine, when criticizing Epiphanius, did not notice this sophistry of certain, perhaps fewer and more obscure, Sabellians.]

—so that the Son may be poured back into the Father. If, then, the subjection of the Word means that God the Word is resolved into the Father, then whatever is subject to the Father and the Son will be resolved into the Father and the Son, so that God may be all in all creatures. But it is absurd to say this. Therefore subjection does not mean a pouring back. For the things that are subjected are one thing—namely, created things—and the one to whom that subjection is made is another. Let the interpreters of that savage dissolution, then, be silent.

### 163.

Would that those others too were silent who, because they cannot prove that the Word of God and the wisdom of God are capable of dissolution, attribute weakness to the divinity, saying that it is written: “But when all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to him” (1 Corinthians 15:28).

### 164.

We see, therefore, that Scripture speaks of him not as already subjected, but as to be subjected. Therefore the Son is not now subject to God the Father. In what respect, then, do you say that the Son will be subject? If according to his divinity, he is neither disobedient, since he is not divided from the Father, nor subject, since he is not a servant but the only Son belonging properly to his Father. Indeed, when he created heaven, founded the earth, and exercised power, he also exercised love. There is therefore no servile subjection in the divinity of Christ. But if there is no subjection, his will is free.

### 165.

And if they think that the Son’s subjection consists in the Father’s doing everything according to the Son’s will, let them learn that this itself is an argument for indivisible power, because it is unity of will—a unity that did not begin in time but always existed. Where there is perpetual unity of will, there is certainly no weakness of temporal subjection. For if he were subjected by nature, he would remain subject forever. But when he is said to be subjected at a particular time, that subjection will belong to the dispensation he assumed, not to perpetual weakness—especially since the everlasting power of God cannot change its condition according to time, nor can the right of power accrue to God the Father in time. For if the Son will at some point change so as to become subject according to his divinity, then God the Father, if he will at some point be able to do more so as to have the Son subject according to his divinity, must necessarily be judged, according to your interpretation, to be able to do less for the present.

### 166.

What guilt, moreover, did the Son incur, so that he should later be believed capable of being subjected according to his divinity? [Note: [Col. 0681D] All editions read “according to his divinity”; all manuscripts, “according to the flesh.” The Roman edition, with a few manuscripts, consequently reads “and, against the Father’s will, claim . . .”; the other and more numerous manuscripts read as in the text.] Did he perhaps seize for himself the right to sit at the Father’s right hand according to the flesh, and, against the Father’s will, claim the privilege of the Father’s throne? But he himself says: “I always do the things that please him” (John 8:29). Therefore, if the Son pleases the Father in all things, why will he be subjected who was not subject before?

### 167.

Let us see, then, whether that subjection belongs not to the divinity but to us, in the fear of Christ—a subjection full of grace and full of mystery. Let us therefore once again weigh the Apostle’s words:

“But when all things have been subjected to him,” he says, “then he himself will also be subjected to the one who subjected all things to him, so that God may be all in all.”

What do you say, then? Are not all things now subject to him? Are not the choirs of the saints subject? Are not the angels, who ministered to him when he was present on earth (Matthew 4:11)? Are not the archangels, who were sent even to Mary as heralds of the Lord’s coming (Luke 1:26)? Is not the whole heavenly army subject? Are not the Cherubim and Seraphim, the Thrones, Dominions, and Powers subject—those beings that venerate and praise him?

### 168.

How, then, will they be subjected? Certainly in the manner the Lord himself said: “Take my yoke upon you” (Matthew 11:29). For it is not the unruly who bear the yoke, but the humble and meek. [Note: [Col. 0679D] This is found in the more numerous and better manuscripts, except that some read *plena* (“full”) instead of *plane* (“clearly”). The remaining manuscripts and all the editions have: “It is clearly not [a subjection] to angels, nor to human beings themselves,” and so forth.]

This is clearly a subjection that is not contemptible even to human beings, but glorious: “so that at the name of Jesus every knee may bow, in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue may confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father” (Philippians 2:10–11). The reason why all things were not previously subject is that they had not yet received the wisdom of God and had not yet borne the yoke of the Word with the neck of the mind made ready for it. [Note: [Col. 0682D] Some manuscripts read “the not-tameable yoke of the Word,” and so forth; this is not a bad reading if *domabili* (“tameable”) is construed with *cervice* (“neck”), not with *jugo* (“yoke”).] But “to all who received him,” as it is written, “he gave power to become children of God” (John 1:11).

### 169.

Someone may say: “Then Christ is already subject, because many have believed?” Not at all, because Christ’s subjection is not found in a few but in all. For just as, if the flesh still desires against the spirit in me, while the spirit desires against the flesh, I do not appear to be subject even though I am subject in part, so, because the whole Church is one body of Christ, as long as the human race remains divided, we divide Christ. Christ, therefore, is not yet subject, since his members are not yet all subject. But when we are not many members but one spirit, then he himself will also be subject, so that through his subjection God may be all in all.

### 170.

And just as Christ is not yet subject, so the Father’s work is not yet perfected, because the Son of God said: “My food is to do the will of my Father who sent me, and to complete his work.”

What question, then, is there here? The Son’s subjection will be in me, in whom the Father’s work is imperfect because I myself am not perfect. Am I, then, who am carrying out the Father’s imperfect work, making the Son subject? But this is not an injury; it is grace. For in the fact that we are subjected, our progress—not that of the divinity—is at issue, so that we may be subjected to the Law and subjected to grace. For previously, as the Apostle himself said, the wisdom of the flesh was hostile to God, “for it was not subject to the Law” (Romans 8:7); but now it has been subjected through Christ’s passion.

## CHAPTER XIV

He pursues the difficulty he has begun and teaches that Christ is subject only according to the flesh; yet, while he was subjected in the flesh, he nevertheless displayed signs of divinity. It is contradictory that he should be subjected according to that divinity. But the humanity he assumed is subjected in us, in such a way that our humanity is exalted in his humanity. Finally, he explains when that subjection of Christ will take place.

[Col. 0682D]

### 171.

And yet, lest anyone bring a false charge, observe what Scripture, divinely inspired, has taken care to guard against. It shows us in what respect Christ will be subject to God, while teaching in what respect he has subjected all things to himself. Therefore it says: “But now we do not see all things subjected to him” (Hebrews 2:8). “We saw Jesus made a little lower than the angels because of the suffering of death.” It therefore shows that he was made lower through the assumption of flesh. What prevents it, then, from signifying subjection likewise through the assumption of flesh, by which he will subject all things to himself, while in that very flesh he himself is subject to God the Father?

### 172.

Let us therefore consider his subjection:

“My Father,” he says, “if you are willing, take this cup from me; nevertheless, not my will but yours be done” (Luke 22:42).

That subjection, then, will be according to the assumption of human nature, because we read: “Found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death” (Philippians 2:8). The subjection is plainly one of obedience; obedience unto death; death belonging to the assumption of humanity. That subjection, therefore, will belong to the assumption of humanity. It is by no means a weakness of the divinity, but this is a dispensation of piety.

### 173.

See how little I fear their propositions. They object that he is to be subjected to God the Father; I read that he was subject to Mary his mother, for it is written of Joseph and Mary: “And he was subject to them” (Luke 2:51). Or, if they think this is what follows, let them say that the divinity was subject to human beings.

### 174.

His being called subject, therefore, should cause no prejudice—just as it causes no prejudice that he is read to be a servant, asserted to have been crucified, and proclaimed to have died. When he was dying, he was living; when he was being subjected, he was reigning; when he was being buried, he was raising the dead. He presented himself as subject to human power, while in another respect he declared himself the Lord of eternal majesty. He stood before a judge, yet as the perpetual Judge he claimed for himself the throne at God’s right hand. Finally, it is written: “From now on you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of the Power of God and coming on the clouds of heaven” (Matthew 26:64).

He was scourged by the Jews, yet commanded the angels. Born from Mary, he was under the Law; before Abraham, he was above the Law (Galatians 4:4). On the cross, he was to be venerated according to his nature. Finally, the sun withdrew, the earth trembled, and the angels fell silent (Matthew 27:51). Did the elements fear to see the passion of the one whose birth they were able to see? And in him whose bodily subjection they could not endure, will they endure the subjection of his venerable nature?

### 175.

But since the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are of one nature, the Father will certainly not be subject to himself. Therefore the Son will not be subject in that respect in which he is one with the Father, lest through the unity of divinity the Father too should appear to be subject to the Son. Thus, just as on that cross it was not the fullness of the divinity but our weakness that was subjected, so afterward the Son will also be subject to the Father through participation in our nature. When the enticements of the flesh have been subjected, wealth, ambition, and pleasure will not rule the heart; rather, God will be everything for us, if in all things we live according to his image and likeness, as far as we are able to receive it.

### 176.

The benefit, therefore, has passed from the individual to the community, because in his own flesh he subdued the nature of the whole human race. And therefore, according to the Apostle: “Just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the heavenly” (1 Corinthians 15:49). This cannot happen except through the inner person.

Let us therefore lay aside all these things—that is, the things we read of: “anger, rage, blasphemy, abusive speech” (Colossians 3:8)—and, as it is said below: “Let us strip off the old person with his actions and put on the new, which is renewed in knowledge according to the image of its creator” (ibid., 9–10).

### 177.

And so that you might know that, when he says “so that God may be all in all,” he does not separate Christ from God the Father, he himself says to the Colossians:

“There is neither male nor female, Jew nor Greek, barbarian nor Scythian, slave nor free; but Christ is all and in all” (Colossians 3:11).

Therefore, when he says likewise to the Corinthians, “so that God may be all in all” (1 Corinthians 15:28), he embraces Christ’s unity and equality with God the Father, because the Son is not separated from the Father. And just as the Father is all and in all, so Christ also works all things in all.

If, then, Christ too works all things in all (1 Corinthians 12:6), he is certainly not subject in the majesty of his divinity, but in us. How, however, is he subject in us, unless in the same way in which he was made lower than the angels—that is, in the mystery of the body? For in this respect all things did not yet appear subject to him, although from the beginning they had certainly been serving their creator.

### 178.

If you ask how he is subject in us, he himself shows it when he says:

“I was in prison, and you came to me; I was sick, and you visited me. Whatever you did for one of these least ones, you did for me” (Matthew 25:36 and following).

You hear “sick,” and you are not moved; you hear “subject,” and you are moved—although he is sick in the same respect in which he is subject, in which he was made sin and a curse for us.

### 179.

Therefore, just as he was made sin and a curse not for himself but for us, so he will be subject in us not for himself but for us—not subject in an eternal nature, nor accursed in an eternal nature. For it is written: “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree” (Galatians 3:13). He was accursed because he took upon himself our curses; he was also subject because he himself took upon himself our subjection—but in the assumption of the form of a servant, not in the majesty of God. Thus, while he showed himself in the flesh to be a sharer in our weakness, he made us, through his divine power, sharers in the divine nature (2 Peter 1:4).

This does not mean either that we have a natural fellowship in Christ’s heavenly generation, or that this subjection in Christ belongs to his divinity. Rather, just as the Apostle said that through that flesh of his—which is the pledge of our salvation—he has made us sit in the heavenly places (Ephesians 2:6), although we are not literally seated there, so he is said to be subject in us through his assumption of our nature.

### 180.

For who would be so insane as to think, as we said above (chapter 5 and following), that the venerable seat at the right hand of God the Father is owed to him [Note: [Col. 0684D] Thus the manuscripts agree by a large consensus; the editions, however, read “is not owed, since even according to the flesh . . .,” and so forth.], when even according to the flesh that seat is bestowed upon Christ by the Father, though he possesses the higher generation and equal power? Angels adore him, and you, with sacrilegious presumption, spread out for yourself the throne of God?

[Col. 0685A]

### 181.

“You will say that it is written: ‘When we were dead in sins, he made us alive together with Christ, by whose grace you have been saved, and he raised us together and made us sit together in the heavenly places, in Christ Jesus’” (Ephesians 2:5–6). [Note: [Col. 0685D] All editions read “they say: ‘When you were dead in sins, he made you alive together with Christ.’” All manuscripts have “you will say: ‘Because . . .’”]

I acknowledge that it is written. But God does not allow human beings to sit at his right hand; rather, he allows them to sit in Christ, because Christ is the foundation of all things and the head of the Church (Ephesians 5:23). In him, the common nature according to the flesh has earned the privilege of the heavenly seat. For in Christ, flesh is honored in God; and in the flesh, the nature of the human race is honored as sharing in all human beings.

### 182.

Therefore, just as we sit in him through the commonality of bodily nature [Note: [Col. 0685D] The old edition has “through the common nature of the body”; the Roman edition: “through . . . the communion of nature”; some manuscripts: “through the common body of nature”; the remaining manuscripts agree with our text.], so he too—who through the assumption of our flesh was made a curse for us, although a curse certainly cannot fall upon the blessed Son of God—will likewise be subject in us through the obedience of all.

This will occur when a Gentile has believed; when a Jew has acknowledged the one whom he crucified; when a Manichaean has adored the one whose coming in the flesh he did not believe; when an Arian has confessed as omnipotent the one whom he denied; and, finally, when in all there has been the wisdom of God, justice, peace, love, and resurrection. Through his works and the diverse kinds of virtues, therefore, Christ will be subject to the Father in us, when, vices having been rejected and sin lying dormant, the one spirit of all peoples begins in a single understanding to cling to God in all. Then God will be all in all (1 Corinthians 15:28).

## CHAPTER XV

He briefly resumes the matters discussed above, skillfully gathering from the unity of divine power in the Father and the Son that whatever is said concerning the Son’s subjection must be referred solely to his humanity. He further confirms this from the love that belongs equally to both.

[Col. 0685C]

### 183.

Let us therefore briefly gather together the conclusion of the whole explanation. The unity of power excludes the notion of an injurious subjection. The abolition of powers and the victory won over death do not diminish the power of the triumphant one. Obedience produces subjection; Christ assumed obedience; obedience led to the cross; the cross led to salvation. Therefore, wherever there is a work, there also is the author of the work.

When all things, then, have been subjected to Christ through Christ’s obedience, so that all knees may bend at his name, then he himself will be all in all. For now, because not all believe, not all appear to be subject. But when all have believed and have done the will of God, Christ will be all and in all. When Christ is all and in all, God will be all and in all, because the Father always remains in the Son. How, then, can the one who redeemed the weak be accused of weakness?

### 184.

And lest you perhaps refer to the Son’s weakness even the statement that God subjected all things to him, learn that he himself also subjected all things to himself. For it is written:

“Our citizenship is in heaven, from which we also await the Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform the body of our humiliation so that it may be conformed to the body of his glory, according to the operation by which he is also able to subject all things to himself” (Philippians 3:20–21).

You have learned, then, that he is able to subject all things to himself—according to the operation of his divinity, certainly.

### 185.

Now learn that he receives all things as subjected according to the flesh, as it is written:

“He who worked in Christ, raising him from the dead and appointing him at his right hand in the heavenly places, above every principality, authority, power, and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come; and he subjected all things beneath his feet” (Ephesians 5:20–21).

All things, therefore, will be handed over to him as subjected according to the flesh, according to which he was also raised from the dead, and according to the human and rational soul in which subjection is found.

### 186.

Most interpret in a divine sense what is written: “Will not my soul be subject to God?” (Psalm 61:1). [Note: [Col. 0686D] Some manuscripts read “by the right of the Lord”; most have “to the Lord.”]

He said “soul,” not “divinity”; “soul,” not “majesty.” And so that we might know that through the Prophet the Lord was speaking of the assumption of human nature, he added: “How long will you assail a human being?” (ibid., 3)—in accordance with what he says in the Gospel: “Why are you seeking to kill me, a human being?” (John 8:40).

And he added: “Nevertheless, they intended to reject my worth; they ran in thirst; with their mouth they blessed, but in their heart they cursed” (Psalm 61:4). For the Jews, when Judas brought back the price, refused to accept it (Matthew 27:6), running in the thirst of madness because they rejected the grace of spiritual drink.

### 187.

This is the pious interpretation of subjection. For since this gift belongs to the Lord’s passion, he will certainly be subject in us in the respect in which he suffered. Why? So that neither angels, nor powers, nor height, nor depth, nor things present, nor things future, nor any other creature may be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:38–39).

From what we have said, we see that no creature has been excepted. Rather, he includes among those he listed above every creature, if there is any such creature.

### 188.

We must also consider that, although above he said, “Who will separate us from the love of Christ?”, below he added: “Neither death, nor life, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus” (ibid., 35).

We therefore see that the love of God is the same as the love of Christ. He did not place the words “the love of God that is in Christ Jesus” without purpose, lest you understand the love of God and Christ as separate. There is nothing that love divides, nothing that eternal divinity cannot do, nothing that escapes the truth, eludes justice, or passes beyond wisdom.

## CHAPTER XVI

The Arians are condemned by David through the Holy Spirit, since they dare to detract from Christ’s knowledge. The passage they cite for this purpose is not free from suspicion of corruption; but even if it were entirely free from it, the word “Son” must be distinguished. For knowledge cannot be lacking to Christ as the Son of God, since he is wisdom; nor can he lack knowledge of any part, since he created all things. He who made the ages cannot fail to know what will happen, and still less can he fail to know the day of judgment. Whether that knowledge is something great or something small, it must not be denied to the Son—and indeed not even to the Holy Spirit. Finally, he adds various indications from which it may be inferred that this knowledge belongs to Christ.

[Col. 0687B]

### 189. [Elsewhere chapter VII.]

From this we must know that those who mention such things are detestable and condemned by the Holy Spirit. For whom else does the Prophet specifically condemn but the Arians, who say that the Son of God does not know times and years? There is nothing that God does not know. Christ, however, is God, and Christ is the Most High; for he himself is God over all.

### 190.

See how the holy David shudders at people of this kind, who detract from the Son of God’s knowledge. For you have this:

“They are not in the labors of human beings, and they will not be scourged with human beings; therefore pride has taken possession of them; they are covered with their iniquity and impiety. Their iniquity has come forth as though from fatness; they have passed over into the disposition of the heart” (Psalm 72:5 and following).

He certainly condemns those who suppose divine things are to be assessed from the disposition of the heart. For God is subject neither to disposition [Note: [Col. 0687D] Some manuscripts have “subject,” nor to the heart.] nor to order, since we see that even the things that occur in human experience and in the succession of the human race [Note: [Col. 0687D] So the old edition and many manuscripts; the Roman edition, with others, has “occur in human succession.”], do not always happen by some established arrangement of reason, but most often unfold through hidden and secret mysteries.

### 191.

“They have thought and spoken wickedness; they have spoken iniquity against the Most High; they have set their mouth against heaven” (ibid., 8).

We see, therefore, that he condemns as guilty of impious sacrilege those who, from the likeness of human nature, arrogate to themselves the ordering of the heavenly mystery.

### 192.

“And they said: ‘How has God known? And is there knowledge in the Most High?’” (ibid., 11).

Do not the Arians repeat this loudly every day, saying that complete knowledge cannot be in Christ? “He himself,” they say, “professed that he was ignorant of the day and hour.”

Do they not say, “How did he know?”—those who assert that he could not know except what he had heard and seen [Note: Some editions have “except what he has learned.”], and who by a sacrilegious interpretation transfer to weakness the things that pertain to the unity of the divine nature?

### 193.

“It is written,” they say: “But concerning that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels of heaven nor the Son, but the Father alone” (Mark 13:32).

First, the ancient Greek codices do not have the words “nor the Son knows.” But it is not surprising if even this has been falsified by those who interpolated the divine Scriptures. The reason why it appears to have been added is revealed by the way it is pressed into the interpretation of so great a sacrilege. [Note: [Col. 0687D] Hilary, *On Matthew*, chapter 26: “By saying that no one knows that day, and that it is unknown not only to the angels but even to himself, he removed concern about the end of the ages from our anxious minds.” Although he argues this way in his commentary on Matthew, this does not at all prove that he read the words “nor the Son” in that evangelist, since he could have reasoned from the other words, “the Father alone,” or certainly have alluded to the passage in Mark where they occur. Ambrose, however, does not appear to have read the same words even in Mark; otherwise this very fact—that they occur in Mark’s Gospel—would have provided the heretics with an easy answer. Jerome likewise indicates something of the sort in his treatment of the same verse, Matthew 24:36. Since the words in question are not found in the Greek copies, especially those of Origen and Pierius, he derives an argument against Arius and Eunomius. If the same words had appeared in Mark, that would have been sufficient for them to neutralize the force of this argument. Erasmus, however, maintains in his discussion of the same passage in Matthew that these words were removed from Matthew’s text because Mark, who abbreviated that Gospel, reports them. Grotius rightly criticizes him at that passage, asserting instead that copyists transferred the words from Mark into Matthew. The reader may consult Grotius himself.]

### 194.

Yet suppose that the evangelists did write it. The name “Son” is ambiguous, for he is also called the Son of Man. Thus he may appear, according to the ignorance involved in our assumption [Note: The Roman edition alone has “according to the unwise assumption of our nature.”], not to have known the day of the future judgment.

For how could the Son of God be ignorant of the day, when in him are hidden the treasures of the wisdom and knowledge of God (Colossians 2:3)?

### 195.

I ask, however, whether he possessed knowledge from substance or from accident. For all knowledge comes either from nature or from instruction. Knowledge comes from nature when, for example, a horse runs or a fish swims; they do these things before they learn them. From instruction, on the other hand, a human being learns to swim; for unless he has learned, he cannot know how.

Since, then, even speechless animals naturally possess the ability to do and know what they have not learned, what do you think of the Son of God? Does he possess knowledge from instruction or from nature?

If from instruction, then he was not born wisdom; he began to become perfect through development, and he did not always exist. But if he possesses natural knowledge, then he was perfect in the beginning and proceeded perfect from the Father; and therefore he did not need foreknowledge of future things.

### 196.

He was not, then, ignorant of the day. For it does not belong to the wisdom of God to know in part and be ignorant in part. How could he be ignorant of a part who made all things, when knowing is less than making?

We know many things that we cannot make, and we do not all know them in the same way; we know them in part. A farmer knows the force of the winds and the courses of the stars in one way, a city-dweller in another, and a helmsman in another. Although not everyone knows everything, they are still said to know. But the one who made all things alone knows them fully.

The helmsman knows at which watch Arcturus rises [Note: [Col. 0689D] Arcturus, also called Boötes and Arctophylax, is a northern constellation. It acquired the first and last of these names because it is positioned behind, as it were at the tail of the Bear; it is also called Boötes because it appears to follow and guide the heavenly wagon. Orion received its name from the abundance of waters, because it rises in winter and is thought to stir up rains and storms. Finally, the Romans called the Pleiades *Vergiliae* because they rise in spring, just as the Greeks called them *Pleiades* because several appear together. Hence Ambrose calls them “clusters,” or, as some manuscripts read, “groupings of the Pleiades.”], and what risings of Orion he should observe; yet he does not know the clusters of the Pleiades [Note: [Col. 0689D] A few manuscripts have “the groupings of the Pleiades.”] or the number or names of the other stars, as does the one “who numbers the multitude of the stars and calls them all by their names” (Psalm 146:4). The power of his own work certainly does not deceive him.

### 197.

How, then, do you suppose that the Son of God made these things? Was he like a seal-ring that does not perceive what it impresses? But “the Father made all things in wisdom” (Psalm 103:24)—that is, he made all things through the Son, who is the power and wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24). It belongs to wisdom to know both the powers and the causes of its works. Therefore the creator of all things could not be ignorant of what he made or fail to know what he himself bestowed. He therefore knows the day that he made.

[Col. 0689B]

### 198.

“But you say that he knows the present day and does not know the future.” Although the proposition is foolish, let me satisfy you from the Scriptures. Learn that he not only made past things but also things that are future, as it is written: “He who made the things that are to come” (Isaiah 45:11).

Elsewhere Scripture says: “Through whom he also made the ages, who is the brightness of his glory and the imprint of his substance” (Hebrews 1:2–3). The ages include the past, the present, and the future. How, then, were future things made, unless the operative power and knowledge comprehended the number of all the ages?

For just as he calls things that are not as though they were (Romans 4:17), so also he made things that are future as though they already were. [Note: [Col. 0690D] One Colbert manuscript has: “not because it happened that they already were, but because”—which is by no means a bad reading.] They cannot fail to be, because the things he commanded to exist are necessarily future. Therefore, he who made future things knew them according to the mode in which they are future.

199. If this is to be believed of the ages, much more must it be believed of the day of judgment, since the Son of God possesses knowledge of it as though it had already been made by him; for it is written: “By your ordinance the day will endure” (Ps. 118:91). [Note: The Roman edition alone reads “the day endures.” Not only does it endure, but it will also endure—for he said “endures” because future things are also present to the prophets in the Spirit—“so that,” etc. But it is evident that this kind of interpolation corrupts Ambrose’s meaning, and that the holy Doctor wrote “the day will endure,” although he himself, in Psalm 118, followed the common reading.] He did not say only “it endures,” but also “it will endure,” so that by its ordering the things that are to come may be governed. Therefore, does he not know what he has ordained? Will he who planted the ear not hear? Will he who formed the eye not perceive? (Ps. 93:9).

200. Let us nevertheless see whether perhaps it is something very great that could have escaped its creator; and let them choose whether they think it something great and more excellent than the rest, or something trifling and contemptible. If trifling and contemptible, then—to speak in accordance with ordinary usage—it is no injury not to know what is cheap and insignificant; for since it belongs to power to know what is greatest, he seems rather to have disdained the baseness of a degenerate work. He is therefore acquitted of disdain, not deprived of power.

201. But if they consider knowledge of the day of judgment great and supreme, let them say what is greater or better than God the Father. He knows the Father, then, as he himself says: “No one knows the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wills to reveal him” (Matt. 11:27). He knows the Father, I say, and does not know the day? Do you therefore believe that he reveals the Father and cannot reveal the day?

202. Further, since you establish certain ranks, preferring the Father to the Son and the Son to the Spirit, tell me whether the Holy Spirit knows the day of judgment; for nothing is written here about him. You certainly deny it. [Col. 0690B] What if I show that he does know it? For it is written: “But God has revealed to us through his Spirit; for the Spirit searches everything, even the deep things of God” (1 Cor. 2:10). Since he searches the deep things of God, and God knows the day of judgment, the Spirit also knows it. For he knows everything that God knows, as the Apostle declares when he says: “For who among human beings knows the things of a human being except the human spirit that is in him? So also no one has known the things of God except the Spirit of God” (ibid., 11). See, then, whether, by denying that the Holy Spirit knows, you also deny that the Father knows—because the Spirit of God has known the things that belong to God, whereas the things that the Spirit of God has not known are certainly not God’s—or whether, by confessing that the Spirit of God knows what you deny the Son knows, you place the Spirit above the Son, contrary to your own assertion. But this is not only a sacrilegious doubt; it is also foolish.

[Note: Thus read by several manuscripts, and by the more authoritative ones. Others, however, and with them Gill and the Roman edition, read: “lest, by denying … you deny also that the Father knows. The things of God … are not God’s. By confessing, therefore, that the Spirit … you prefer the Spirit to the Son.” This is less well expressed. In Amerbach and Erasmus there is a lacuna from the beginning of this section to the passage under discussion.]

203. Let us now consider in what ways knowledge is gathered, and show that the Son himself demonstrated that he also knew the day. For what we know we declare either by time, place, signs, persons, or order. How, then, did he not know the day of judgment, when he expressed both the hour of judgment, its place, its signs, and its causes?

204. Finally, you have this: “In that hour, let the one who is on the housetop not go down to take the vessels from his house; and the one in the field likewise must not turn back” (Luke 17:31). Thus he knew the outcome of future dangers to such an extent that he even showed those in danger the means of safety.

205. Could the Lord have been ignorant of the day when he himself said of himself that the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath (Matt. 12:8)?

[Note: Lest it seem obscure why Ambrose proves that Christ knew the day of judgment from the fact that he is also Lord of the Sabbath, one should note that this is the intention of our Doctor: namely, that Christ cannot possibly be ignorant of those things of which he himself is Lord. That he is Lord of the day of judgment is taught by the fact that he is also Lord of the Sabbath, which is both the most excellent of all days and, as Ambrose often teaches, a figure of the resurrection. The things that follow concerning the destruction of Jerusalem should be understood spiritually, as may be learned from Book X on Luke, section 15 and the following sections.]

[Col. 0691A]

206. He also designated the place elsewhere, when, as the disciples were showing him the buildings of the temple, he said: “Do you see all these things? Amen, I say to you, not one stone will be left upon another that will not be destroyed” (Matt. 24:2).

207. When the Apostles also asked him about the sign, he replied: “See that you are not deceived. For many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am the Christ’” (Luke 21:8); and below: “There will be great earthquakes in various places, and famines and pestilences, and terrors from heaven, and there will be great signs” (ibid., 11). Thus he expressed both the persons and the signs.

208. In what manner, moreover, he says that armies will surround Jerusalem, or that the times of the nations will be fulfilled, and in what order, is disclosed by the testimony of the Gospel reading. Therefore he knew everything.

589

## CHAPTER XVII

That Christ did not wish to reveal the day of judgment because this was provided for our benefit. This is clarified by another saying of the Lord, as well as by a closely parallel passage of Paul. When they press the question why he answered the disciples as though he did not know, other passages are brought forward in which ignorance likewise seems to be attributed to the Father. From these Ambrose argues that, if they admit ignorance or impotence in the Father, they must consequently admit the same substance in the Son as in the Father; unless they prefer to accuse the Son of falsehood, although neither deceiving can be attributed to him nor to the Father, but in the passages mentioned the unity of both is indicated.

209. But we ask for what reason he did not wish to indicate the moments of time (Luke 19:43). If we inquire into it, we shall find that this was not a matter of ignorance, but of wisdom. For it was not beneficial for us to know; so that, while we do not know the fixed moments of the future judgment, we may always avoid the habit of sinning, as though stationed on watch and placed upon a kind of watchtower of virtue, lest the day of the Lord find us amid our vices. For it is not beneficial to know, but to fear what is to come; for it is written: “Do not aspire to lofty things, but fear” (Rom. 11:20).

216. For if he had explicitly indicated the day, he would seem to have prescribed a rule of life for only that generation of human beings which was nearest to the judgment; the earlier age would either have been more lax in righteousness or more secure in sin. For an adulterer cannot cease from the desire to commit adultery unless he fears punishment every day. [Note: The old edition reads: “cannot cease from the desire to commit adultery”; the Roman edition: “cannot abandon it”; but the manuscripts have the reading given in the text.] Nor can a robber abandon the secluded haunts of the passes he besets unless he knows that punishment threatens him at every moment. For those whose incentive is impunity generally find fear burdensome.

211. Therefore I said that it was not beneficial to know; indeed, it was beneficial to be ignorant, so that, being ignorant, we might fear; and, by keeping watch, we might be corrected, as he himself said: “Be ready, because you do not know at what hour the Son of Man will come” (Matt. 24:44). For unless a soldier knows that war is at hand, he does not know how to stand ready in the camp.

212. Hence elsewhere also, when the Lord himself was questioned by the Apostles—who certainly did not understand the matter as Arius did, but believed that the Son of God knew future things, for if they had not believed this, they would never have asked him—when, then, he was asked when he would restore the kingdom to Israel, he did not say that he did not know, but said: “It is not yours to know the times and years which the Father has placed in his own authority” (Acts 1:7). Pay attention to what he said: “It is not yours to know.” Read it again: “It is not yours.” He said “yours,” not “mine”; for he was now speaking not according to perfection, but according to the progress of the human body and our soul. Therefore he said “yours,” not “mine.”

213. The Apostle likewise followed this teaching: “Concerning the times and the moments, brothers, you have no need that we write to you” (1 Thess. 5:1). Thus even the Apostle himself, the servant of Christ, did not say that he was ignorant of the moments, but that the people did not need to be taught them, since they must always be armed with spiritual defenses, so that the power of Christ might stand ready in each person. When the Lord says, “Concerning the times which the Father has placed in his own authority,” he plainly cannot be excluded from the Father’s knowledge, since he is in no way excluded from the Father’s authority; for authority is generated from wisdom and power, and Christ is both.

214. But you ask why he did not deny this to the disciples in such a way as to suggest that he knew but did not wish to speak; instead, he mentioned that neither the angels nor the Son knew (Mark 13:32). I, too, shall ask you why God says in Genesis: “I will go down, then, and see whether, according to the cry that has come to me, they have completed their deeds; and if not, I will know” (Gen. 18:21). Why does Scripture also say of the Lord: “And the Lord came down to see the city and the tower which the sons of human beings were building” (Gen. 11:5)? Why does the Prophet likewise say in the Psalter: “The Lord looked down upon the sons of human beings, to see whether there is anyone understanding or seeking God” (Ps. 52:3)—as though, if God did not descend there, or if the Lord did not look here, he would either be ignorant of human works or unaware of their merits?

215. But in the Gospel according to Luke you also have the Father saying: “What shall I do? I will send my most beloved son; perhaps they will respect him” (Luke 20:13). According to Matthew and Mark, however, you have: “He sent his only Son, saying: ‘They will respect my Son’” (Matt. 21:37; Mark 12:6). In one book he says, “Perhaps they will respect him,” and, as though ignorant, he hesitates; for this is the language of one who hesitates. In the other two books, however, he says: “They will respect my Son”; that is, he confirms the reverence that ought to be shown.

216. But neither is it proper for God to doubt nor to be deceived. He doubts who is ignorant of what will happen; he is deceived who foretells one thing and something else follows. What could be clearer than that Scripture says the Father declared one thing about the Son, while that same Scripture testifies that something else happened? He said: “They will respect my Son”; but the Son was struck, mocked, crucified, and killed (Matt. 27:29 ff.), and suffered in the flesh things far more grievous than those servants who had previously been sent. Was the Father therefore deceived, or was he ignorant, or was he unable to help? But the true God does not know how to deceive; for it is written: “God is faithful and does not lie” (Titus 1:2). How could he have been ignorant, who knows all things (Dan. 13:42)? Or what could he have been unable to do, who can do all things?

217. Yet if he was either ignorant or unable—for you more readily assent to saying that the Father was ignorant than to confessing that the Son knew—you see that, from this very fact, the Son is of one substance with the Father: if, according to your folly, the Son is like the Father, then either he does not know all things or he cannot do all things. For I am neither miserly nor rash concerning the Son’s praises, so as to dare to say that the Son can do more than the Father, since I make no distinction of power between the Father and the Son.

[Note: All editions and a few manuscripts read: “from this very fact that the Son is of one substance with the Father, just as …” The remaining manuscripts agree with us. And rightly so: the adversaries did not assume that the Son was of one substance with the Father, so that Ambrose might argue against them from this that the Son, like the Father, either did not know all things or could not do all things. Rather, he argues conversely that, because they admitted in the Father the same deficiency of knowledge and power that they claimed existed in the Son, it followed that one and the same substance belonged to both.]

218. But perhaps you will say that the Father did not say this, but that the Son falsely represented the Father. You therefore accuse the Son not only of weakness, but also of sacrilege and falsehood. Nevertheless, if you do not believe what the Son says about the Father, do not believe what he says about himself either. For if he wished to deceive us by saying that the Father had doubted, as though he did not know what would happen, then he also wished to deceive us about himself by saying that he did not know future things. It would be far more tolerable to one’s shame if he had first pretended ignorance concerning himself than if what he proclaimed about the Father should appear to have been defeated by the outcome, contrary to his promises. [Note: Some editions read: “on the contrary, the promised event having been frustrated.”]

219. But neither is the Father deceived nor does the Son deceive. Rather, there is this customary manner in the divine Scriptures, as the preceding and many other examples attest: God pretends not to know what he does know. In this matter, therefore, the unity of divinity and the unity of ordering are proved in the Father and the Son, if, just as God the Father pretends not to know what he knows, so the Son, who is the image of God, also pretends not to know what is known to him.

## CHAPTER XVIII

Intending to explain the reason for the Lord’s answer to the Apostles, the holy man first attributes it to Christ’s indulgence; then, after presenting other explanations proposed by certain people, he declares the genuine one to be that the same Lord spoke from human feeling. From this he concludes that the knowledge of the Father and the Son is equal, and therefore that the Son is not less than the Father. Then, after setting against the text that says the Son is less another text in which he is said to be equal, he chastises the rashness of the Arians in judging the Son; and, when they impiously asserted that he was lesser, he shows that he himself is rightly called the stone.

[Col. 0694A]

220. It has therefore been taught that the Son of God was not ignorant of future things. If they admit this, I too, now answering the question why he mentioned that neither the angels nor the Son, but only the Father, knew (Mark 13:32), recognize here his customary love and grace toward the disciples, which ought by now to be known to everyone from its frequent occurrence. For the Lord, inclined toward his disciples by an excessive love, prefers, when they ask about things whose knowledge he judges useless, to appear ignorant of what he knew rather than to refuse them; and he loves to instruct us for our benefit more than to display his own power.

221. Yet many are not so cautious as I am; for I prefer to fear lofty things rather than to understand them. Still, many rely upon what is written: “And Jesus advanced in age and wisdom and grace with God and human beings” (Luke 2:52), and confidently say that, according to his divinity, he could not have been ignorant of future things, but that, according to his assumption of our condition, he said that he was ignorant as the Son of Man before the cross. For when he says “the Son,” he does not speak as though of someone else; for he himself is both our Lord, the Son of God, and the Son of the Virgin. Rather, through an intermediate expression he shapes our understanding, so that he might be believed, as the Son of Man according to his assumption of our ignorance or progress, not yet to have known everything fully. “It is not ours to know what is future.” [Note: All editions and several manuscripts read: “It is not yours to know”; the other manuscripts read: “For it is not ours to know.” The latter is much more coherent, since it gives the reason for the preceding statement: “he shapes our understanding, so that, as though …” The opinion of certain people—that Christ, at the time of his mission, was in fact ignorant of some things according to his human nature and truly advanced in knowledge—he declares not to be acceptable to him as a view dangerous in matters of faith. Those heterodox writers who commonly follow this opinion cannot deny that in this respect they have the holy Doctor against them. Nor need one fear that the dissimulation he admits should appear joined to falsehood. For, apart from the fact that he adapted himself to those whom he addressed, to whom that knowledge was not owed, he himself spoke as a human being—that is, as endowed with a rational soul, to which knowledge of future things was by nature not at all proper, although through union with the Word he was not ignorant of them. In this sense one may also interpret Athanasius, Oration 4 against the Arians; Hilary, Book IX on the Trinity; Basil, Letter 391; Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 36; and others.]

Therefore he seems to be ignorant in the same condition in which he advances; for how could he advance according to his divinity, in whom the fullness of divinity dwells (Col. 2:9)? Or what could the Son of God be ignorant of, who said: “Why are you thinking evil things in your hearts?” (Matt. 9:4). How could he be ignorant of one of whom Scripture says: “But Jesus knew their thoughts” (Luke 6:8)?

222. Let others say these things; but I, returning to what came before, proposed the passage in which the Father said: “Perhaps they will respect my Son” (Luke 20:13). I think this was written because, since the Father was speaking about human beings, he appeared to speak in accordance with human feeling. I think all the more that the Son, who lived among human beings, acted as a human being, and assumed flesh, assumed our feeling, so that he might say that he did not know through our ignorance, not because he himself was ignorant of anything. For although he appeared human in the reality of his body, he was nevertheless life; he was light; and power went out from him, healing the wounds of the afflicted by the authority of his majesty (Luke 6:19).

223. You therefore see that the question has been removed from you: the saying concerning the Son is referred to his assumption of complete human condition, while what is written about the Father was written for this reason, so that you may at least cease calumniating the Son.

224. The Son of God, then, was ignorant of nothing, for there was nothing of which the Father was ignorant. If the Son was ignorant of nothing, then, to conclude, let them say in what respect they wish him to appear lesser. If God generated a lesser Son, he bestowed less upon him; if he bestowed less, then either he willed less or he was able to do less. But the Father is neither weak nor envious, since neither will nor power existed before the Son. For in what respect is he lesser who has everything that the Father has (John 16:15)? He received everything from the Father by right of generation, and fully expressed the Father in the glory of his majesty.

225. “For the Father is greater than I,” they say, is written (John 14:28). But it is also written: “He did not deem it robbery to be equal with God” (Phil. 2:6). It is written that the Jews therefore sought to kill him, because he called God his Father, making himself equal with God (John 5:18). It is written: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). They read “one,” but do not read the many other passages. Can one and the same person therefore be both lesser and equal according to the same nature? One statement refers to divinity, the other to flesh.

226. They call him lesser. I ask who has measured him, who is so lofty in heart as to place God the Father and the Son as though before his tribunal, in order to judge between them concerning precedence? “My heart is not exalted, nor have my eyes been lifted up in vain,” David says (Ps. 130:1). King David feared to exalt his heart in human affairs; we exalt ours against divine secrets. Who, then, judges concerning the Son of God? Thrones, Dominions, Angels, Powers? But the Archangels serve and minister; the Cherubim and Seraphim minister, and they praise. Who, then, judges concerning the Son of God, when he has read that the Father himself knows the Son but does not judge him? “No one knows the Son except the Father” (Matt. 11:27). “Knows,” he says, not “judges.” To know is one thing; to judge is another. The Father possesses knowledge within himself; the Son does not possess authority above himself. And again: “No one knows the Father except the Son”; and he knows the Father just as the Father knows him.

227. But you say that he called himself lesser (John 14:28). He also called himself a stone. You say more, and impiously slander him; I say less, and piously affirm it. You call him lesser and confess him to be above the angels; I call him lesser than the angels, and I do not detract from him, because I am not accusing his divinity but proclaiming his mercy.

## CHAPTER XIX

Turning to God the Father, the holy man explains why he does not regard the Son as lesser than him. He then asserts that it is not his place to measure the Son of God, since only an angel was appointed to measure Jerusalem, and perhaps even Christ as man. But Arius showed himself an imitator of Satan. It is therefore rash to dispute about the divine generation, since only a sign concerning the human nature has been proposed through Isaiah; nor should comparison be made in divine matters. Finally, he demonstrates, by setting various examples from Scripture against it, how greatly the arrogance of Arius must be avoided.

[Col. 0696B]

228. To you now, almighty Father, I turn my words with tears. I readily call you inaccessible, incomprehensible, immeasurable; but I would not dare to call your Son lesser. For when I have read that he is “the radiance of your glory and the image of your substance” (Heb. 1:3), I fear that, by calling the image of your substance lesser, I might seem to call your substance lesser, since the Son is its image, while the whole fullness of your divinity is in the Son. I have often read, and readily believe, that you, your Son, and the Holy Spirit are immense, uncircumscribed, beyond estimation, and ineffable. Therefore I cannot measure you in order that I might examine you.

229. Nevertheless, suppose that with rash spirit and daring I wished to measure you. By what, I ask, shall I measure you? The prophet saw a measuring cord (Ezek. 40:3), with which an angel measured Jerusalem. Yet it was an angel who measured, not Arius; he measured Jerusalem, not God. And perhaps the angel could not even measure Jerusalem, for he was a man. Finally, you have this: “I lifted up my eyes and saw, and behold, a man, and in his hand a measuring cord” (ibid.). He was a man because a type of the assumption of the body was being revealed. He was that man of whom it was said: “After me comes a man whose sandal strap I am not worthy to untie” (John 1:27). Therefore Christ, in the type, measures Jerusalem; Arius measures God. [Note: The old edition reads: “Not Arius, God”; the Roman edition, together with several manuscripts, removed the negation, and we follow that reading. Some other manuscripts, however, retain the negation but do not recognize the word “God,” with no less satisfactory sense.]

230. And Satan disguises himself as an angel of light. What wonder, then, if Arius imitates his master, so as to usurp what is forbidden (2 Cor. 11:14)? Although he presumes, with even more intolerable sacrilege, to claim for himself knowledge of divine secrets and the mysteries of the heavenly generation—something his father the devil did not do by himself— for the devil confessed the true Son of God, whereas Arius denies him.

231. If, then, I cannot measure you, almighty Father, can I discuss the secret of your generation without sacrilege? Can I say that there is something greater or lesser between you and your Son, when he who was born from you said: “Everything that the Father has is mine” (John 16:15)? Who appointed me judge or divider of human affairs? The Son says this, and we claim for ourselves the right to division and judgment between the Father and the Son? Even good piety refuses arbiters in the division of an inheritance. Shall we, then, be arbiters, so that we may divide between you and your Son the substance of uncreated majesty? [Note: Several manuscripts read: “the substance of uncreated majesty.”]

232. “This generation,” he says, “is an evil generation; it seeks a sign, and no sign will be given it except the sign of the prophet Jonah” (Luke 11:29). A sign is given, certainly, not of divinity but of incarnation. Indeed, when he was about to speak of the incarnation, he said: “Ask a sign for yourself.” And when he replied, “I will not ask, nor will I test the Lord,” the answer was given: “Behold, a virgin will receive in the womb” (Isa. 7:11 ff.). Therefore, can we not see a sign of divinity, yet seek a measure? Woe to miserable me! Do we dare impiously to scrutinize one whom we cannot worthily entreat?

233. Let the Arians see what they are doing. If I call you, Father, greater than all, I have insultingly compared you with your works; if I call you greater than the Son, as Arius asserts, I have impiously judged you. That judgment will first concern you, for no precedence can be established except by comparison, and no one can be preferred unless judgment has first been passed concerning him. [Note: Thus the Roman edition reads together with part of the manuscripts. The old edition, however, with other written copies, reads: “Let them see; nevertheless, what they do … the judgment concerning you will come first,” etc.]

234. We are not permitted to swear by heaven (Matt. 5:3); yet we are permitted to judge concerning God. But you have entrusted judgment concerning everything to your Son alone. [Note: All editions read: “to judge concerning the Son of God”; the manuscripts, almost unanimously: “to judge concerning God.”]

235. John feared to baptize the Lord’s flesh. John refused, saying: “I ought to be baptized by you, and you come to me?” (Matt. 3:14). And shall I subject Christ to my judgment?

[Col. 0697C]

235. Moses declines the priesthood; Peter declines the obedience imposed upon him in the ministry. Does Arius search even the deep things of God? But Arius is not the Holy Spirit; rather, “Do not seek what is too high for you” (Eccl. 3:22) was said to Arius and to human beings. [Note: The old edition reads: “Moses excuses himself”; the Roman edition: “Peter excuses himself,” etc. Some manuscripts read: “Moses excuses himself from the priesthood; Peter …” The more numerous and authoritative manuscripts have the reading given in our text. Below, where all editions and most manuscripts read “in the ministry,” some other copies prefer “in the mystery.”]

236. Moses was forbidden to see the face of the Lord (Exod. 33:23); Arius deserved to see the secret. Moses and Aaron were among his priests; Moses appeared with the Lord in glory. That Moses, therefore, saw only the back parts of God in the type; Arius comprehended the whole of God face to face. But no one, he says, can see my face and live (Exod. 33:20).

237. Paul likewise says concerning inferior matters: “We know in part, and we prophesy in part” (1 Cor. 13:9). Arius says: “I have known God wholly, not in part.” Therefore Paul was inferior to Arius: the chosen vessel knows in part, while the vessel of destruction knows everything. Paul says: “I know a man—whether in the body or outside the body I do not know; God knows—that he was caught up into paradise and heard ineffable words” (2 Cor. 12:4–5). Paul, caught up to the third heaven, did not know himself; Arius, rolling in filth, knew God. Paul says of himself: “God knows”; Arius says of God: “I know.”

238. But Arius was not caught up into heaven, although he followed the one who, in damnable boastfulness, presumed upon divine things, saying: “I will place my throne above the clouds, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:14). For just as he said, “I will be like the Most High,” so Arius wants the Son of God, the Most High, to appear like himself: he does not reverence him in the majesty of eternal divinity, but measures him according to the weakness of the flesh.

## [ON THE HOLY SPIRIT]

[Col. 0697]

## INTRODUCTION TO THE BOOKS ON THE HOLY SPIRIT

When the emperor Gratian requested from Ambrose by letter the first two books On the Faith, he also asked him—as we observed in the Introduction to that work above, p. 439—not to decline writing a treatise on the divinity of the Holy Spirit. The holy Bishop could not refuse so pious a request from the emperor; he had asked only for a delay, so that he might meditate more seriously on the discussion he had undertaken (Letter to Gratian). He therefore divided the work into three books, applied the finishing hand, and sent it to the emperor as soon as possible.

At the beginning of the first book he places a preface (Prologue, section 1 ff.) in which he beautifully demonstrates that Gideon not only prefigured Christ by freeing his people, but also signified, through the great prodigy of the dew falling now upon the fleece and now upon the threshing floor, that the outpouring of the Holy Spirit would one day pass from the Jews to the Christians, by whose work so many thousands of people had most recently been brought back into the bosom of the Church (ibid., sections 5, 17). Then, taking up his argument, he proves that the Holy Spirit is truly God and transcends the order of created things (chapters 1, 3), chiefly from the fact that in the Gospel sin against the Spirit is denied forgiveness in this age or in the age to come. He adds that in the sacred books the Spirit is called the Spirit of God, that he spoke through the prophets and Apostles, and that his infinite goodness is made known alike in the sanctification of creatures and in his outpouring, diffused simultaneously through every place and among all people, revealing his immensity, immutability, and eternity (chapters 4, 10). After confirming this by an exposition of the mystical ointment of which Scripture speaks, he discloses the Spirit’s substantial unity with the other two persons (chapter 11). He entirely denies that mission is opposed to this unity (chapter 12), since among all the divine persons there is unity of peace, grace, charity, and the remaining gifts and qualities (chapters 13 ff.).

At the beginning of the second book, after presenting in a few words the history of Samson, he teaches (Prologue) that Samson always acted successfully while the Holy Spirit was with him, but unsuccessfully as soon as he was deprived of that support. After declaring that this very power of the Holy Spirit is the same as that of the Father and the Son, and that his purpose is not different from theirs, he asserts that the life of us all consists no less in knowing the Spirit himself than in knowing the Father and the Son, since by his operation we are given life just as by theirs (chapters 1, 4). After asserting at length that the Spirit is the creator of things and therefore worthy of adoration (chapter 5), and after resolving certain objections, he makes clear that in establishing the Church the Spirit had one will, calling, and command with the Father and the Son (chapters 6, 10). Then, once it has been established that the Spirit is inferior neither to the Father nor to the Son in knowledge (chapter 11), and certain difficulties concerning this matter have been unfolded (chapter 12), he claims for the Spirit prophecy and the apostolate as something shared by him with the other two persons (chapter 13). From this he skillfully concludes that the three have one operation.

The argument begun in the preceding book continues in the third. It is established that not only the mission of the prophets and Apostles but also that of the Lord himself must be referred to the Spirit (chapters 1, 2). Yet this does not mean that any subjection returns to the Son, since the Spirit himself is also sent by the Father and the Son. In this, therefore, nothing is to be understood except the unity of divinity, just as in those expressions in which the Spirit is called a finger, right hand, and hand, and likewise where he is said to accuse, judge, avenge, be grieved, or be tested (chapters 3, 9). A more extended discussion arises (chapters 10, 11) concerning John’s words, “The Spirit is God,” which they had expunged from the Gospel manuscripts with sacrilegious boldness. In this passage, as in certain others supplied by the Pauline Epistles, the divinity of the Spirit is most powerfully established (chapters 12, 14). It is shown (chapters 13, 15) that there is no danger that the three should therefore be called three Gods or Lords, since the three divine persons possess the same holiness and nature (chapters 16, 17). Finally, after gathering together as into a bundle the principal points of the entire treatise, and treating and affirming some of them again, the work is brought to its crown (chapter 18 ff.).

It is plainly evident from what has thus far been explained that this work ought to bear no other title than On the Holy Spirit. Nevertheless, we acknowledge that it is cited under the title On the Trinity by certain writers (Ivo, Decretum, part II, chapter 7; Gratian, etc.), and that in not a few manuscripts the same title is prefixed to these three books, just as it is to the five books above. In both works the same adversaries are opposed, namely the Arians, who asserted that the Spirit was inferior to the Son, although in certain passages he also attacks the Pneumatomachi proper (Book III, chapter 15 and elsewhere). Everyone can see that these books were composed only after the five books On the Faith mentioned above. We add only this: although Athanaric, king of the Goths, who died at Constantinople on the eighth day before the Kalends of February in the year 381, had already died when the holy Doctor published this work, he nevertheless still knew nothing of the death of Peter of Alexandria, nor of the abdication of Gregory, by which he relinquished the patriarchate of New Rome at the Second General Synod held there. Since there is no mention of that synod in these books, it is clear that they were brought to completion around the middle of the year 381.

In truth, however, Jerome’s criticism of the books On the Holy Spirit, which he attacks under a silent omission of the author’s name with a somewhat severe obelus, gives us no small difficulty. Most people think that no one other than Ambrose is designated here. So that everyone may be able to judge the matter more safely, and so that we may not ourselves seem to evade the knot of the difficulty, we present the entire passage here:

“I preferred to be an interpreter of another person’s work rather than, as some do, to adorn an ugly female crow with another’s colors. Long ago I read someone’s little books on the Holy Spirit, and, in accordance with the comic poet’s saying, I saw good things from the Greeks become not good things in Latin. There was nothing dialectical there, nothing manly, nothing forceful—nothing that would compel the reader, even against his will, to assent. Rather, the whole work was slack, soft, polished, and handsome, and here and there perfumed with carefully selected fragrances. But my Didymus, having the eye of the bride … Certainly whoever reads this will recognize the thefts of the Latins and will despise the streams once he begins to draw from the springs” (Letter to Paulinian, prefixed to this work).

Who has ever denounced any treatise in harsher words?

Rufinus, when hostility had arisen between himself and Jerome, attacked him with the greatest indignation on account of that very statement:

> “But since,” he says, “we have promised to prove how he tears to pieces Ambrose, a man worthy of everyone’s admiration, a bishop who was not only a pillar of the Church of Milan but also a kind of pillar of all the Churches and an impregnable tower” (*Book II of the Invectives against Jerome*).

After inserting much material, he continues in this fashion:

> “You have heard how he now again calls the man whom he had earlier called a crow and wholly dark a little crow painting himself with others’ feathers or colors; and how shamefully he tears him to pieces, saying that the man has nothing manly about him—though he was chosen by God for the glory of Christ’s Churches, and spoke in the presence of persecuting kings in testimony to the Lord, and was not put to shame. Saint Ambrose wrote about the Holy Spirit not only with words but also with his own blood. For he offered his blood to his persecutors, who poured it out from him, but God reserved him for further labors. Even if he followed the Catholic Greek writers, our own authors, and appropriated something from their writings, it should not immediately have become your chief concern, your labor, and your preoccupation to translate Didymus’ book *On the Holy Spirit* for this reason, so that his thefts might be recognized . . . . . . If, then, you did not spare so great and such a man as Ambrose, etc.”

Baronius, convinced that Ambrose had borrowed no small portion of his work from Basil, accused Rufinus of slandering Jerome (*Annals*, year 381), on the ground that Jerome had begun his translation of Didymus’ book before those three books were composed. But, to pass over the fact that Jerome’s version was not completed until after the death of Damasus—and therefore after Ambrose’s work had already been in circulation for several years—who could ever believe that Rufinus would have launched so atrocious an accusation against Jerome with such confidence unless he had been perfectly certain and fully informed of the matter itself? Or that Jerome, whose temperament was vehement and not naturally disposed to conceal an insult, would have restrained himself from branding his accuser with the deserved mark of slander, although he nowhere removes the charge laid against him?

But there is no need for these conjectures. Anyone who compares Ambrose’s work with Didymus’ treatise will discover that not a few passages have been transferred from the latter into the former—for example, the discussions of the outpouring of the Holy Spirit (*Book I*, chapters 5 and 7), sanctification (*Book II*, chapters 11 and 12), knowledge and gifts (*Book I*, chapter 13 and following); to these one may also add the passage concerning the prophecy of Amos (*Book II*). Yet our Ambrose was not so devoted to Didymus that he would disdain to pluck from the writings of others whatever he thought suited his subject and insert it into his own work. Thus, when the Fathers of Florence observed that he owed very much to Basil (*Session 22*, chapter 6), especially in *Book II*, chapter 8 and following, they rightly declared that he had expounded Basil’s three books *On the Holy Spirit*. We see that the great Baronius followed their opinion. There are, moreover, proofs drawn from Athanasius, Gregory of Nyssa, and several others, so that anyone may reasonably judge that, while composing his work, our Doctor had before his eyes the finest treatments that had been published on the same subject.

Although he here and there plucks out what he thinks useful to his purpose, he does not, as Jerome relates, rashly and indiscriminately snatch fallen feathers from other birds, after the fashion of Aesop’s little crow. Rather, like a diligent and industrious bee distinguishing the juices of flowers and plants from which it gathers its honey, he takes some things and rejects others, alters some, transposes others, and finally produces many things of his own which are found in none of the other authors.
