Even if nothing were found in these books that had not been read in other authors, it would not therefore follow that everything had been taken from foreign writings. For who does not know that it often happens that those who labor on the same subject, even if they have never communicated their thoughts to one another, nevertheless produce many things strikingly similar—especially if each draws and draws up his proofs from the same sources, such as the utterances of Holy Scripture?

Therefore we frankly admit that Rufinus was carried away by his indignation beyond what was appropriate when he accused Jerome of having translated Didymus’ books into Latin with the sole intention that the latter’s—namely, Ambrose’s—thefts might be recognized (*loc. cit.*). But, on the other hand, we shall not conceal that Jerome’s criticism mentioned above, if it truly concerned Ambrose, went considerably beyond the bounds of exaggeration. Nor do we think that Baronius himself would have disagreed with us, since, in the accusation by which Jerome in the same place censures the Roman Church (*Annals*, year 385), he did not hesitate to acknowledge a manifest hyperbole.

Indeed, it cannot be granted that the holy Bishop plundered Didymus’ treatise in the manner which the Doctor cited above seems to indicate. And certainly, although Didymus may show himself more dialectical than Ambrose, Ambrose’s diction is nobler, his discourse fuller, and his arrangement more harmonious. Whoever weighs the arguments of both with attentive mind will readily recognize that Ambrose achieves and completes his purpose no less effectively than Didymus. It would therefore not be absurd to say that Jerome here did what those are wont to do who, not content to heap excessive praise upon authors to whom they have devoted study and labor, also depress works published by others on the same subject below what truth and fairness allow.

Since this is so, anyone who wishes to pass a true and legitimate judgment on this work of Ambrose should choose as guides more equitable evaluators—namely, the sacred councils (Florence, session 22, and others), and many highly learned men (Cassiodorus, *Institutions of Divine Literature*, chapter 16, and elsewhere), who, by putting forward the testimony and authority of those councils, showed the esteem in which they held them.

Above all, however, we have at hand a bishop of Hippo whom we may set against the presbyter of Stridon: a man exceedingly practiced in polemical works, whose judgment concerning this work is as follows:

> “Saint Ambrose, while treating a great matter concerning the Holy Spirit, in order to demonstrate that he is equal to the Father and the Son, nevertheless uses a subdued style of speech, because the subject undertaken requires evidence of things, not verbal embellishments or devices for bending the minds” (*Book IV of Christian Doctrine*, chapter 21, no. 46).

No one should say that this judgment, which could scarcely conflict more sharply with Jerome’s, was offered by a disciple to win the favor of his teacher. It is, in itself, exceedingly moderate; and Augustine had other passages from Ambrose’s treatises at hand which he could have offered as examples of subdued diction, had he thought this work “flaccid, soft, polished, and beautiful.”

[Col. 0703]

**OF SAINT AMBROSE, BISHOP OF MILAN, THREE BOOKS ON THE HOLY SPIRIT [Note: [Col. 0703C] Written in the year 381.], TO GRATIAN AUGUSTUS. (S)**

[Col. 0703]

# BOOK ONE

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0703A]

In Gideon’s election there was a figure of the Lord’s Incarnation; in the sacrifice of the kid, of the expiation of sins through Christ’s body; in that of the bull, of the abolition of profane sacrifices; and, finally, in the three hundred soldiers, of the redemption that was to come through the cross. The fact that Gideon asked for several signs belonged to the mystery: through the fleece’s dryness and wetness, the infidelity of the Jews and the calling of the nations were signified; through the dew gathered into the basin, the washing of the apostles’ feet. Ambrose prays that the filth of his feet may be cleansed by this, and at the same time praises Christ’s kindness. How useful it is to imitate this! The same water, sent by the Son of God, works marvelous transformations throughout the world; yet it cannot be sent by another, since it is the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, who is not subject to another’s power.

### 1

When Jerubbaal, as we read (*Judges* 6:11), was threshing a harvest of wheat beneath a tree—an oak—with a rod, he received an oracle that he should rescue God’s people from the power of foreigners into liberty. Nor is it surprising that he was chosen for grace, since even then, beneath the shadow of the sacred cross and of venerable wisdom, established in the predestined mystery of the future Incarnation, he was bringing forth from hiding places the visible grains of a fruitful crop and separating the election of the saints from the refuse of empty chaff. [Note: [Col. 0703C] All editions and manuscripts read thus, except that in a few, instead of *qui tamquam*, there is *Et tamquam*; and in the Roman edition, instead of *virga veritatis*, *virga virtutis* is printed.]

They are trained as though by the rod of truth; laying aside the superfluities of the old man together with his deeds, they are gathered, as in a winepress, into the Church. For the Church is the winepress of the eternal fountain, in which the fruit of the heavenly vine overflows.

### 2

[Note: [Col. 0703C] The Roman edition reads *Commotus oraculo*; the old edition and by far the majority of manuscripts, *Quo motus oraculo*; some others, *Quo doctus oraculo*. And indeed, below Gideon is called a learned man, as also in Origen, *Homily on the Same*, where he is called an educated man.]

Moved by this oracle, Gideon, when he had heard that, although the thousands of peoples were failing, the Lord would deliver his people from their enemies through one man (*ibid.*, 14), offered a kid of the goats. According to the angel’s command, he placed its flesh and unleavened bread upon the rock [Note: [Col. 0704C] A few manuscripts read, “and poured sauce over it”; one manuscript of Albinus, “and poured incense over it.”] and drenched them with broth. As soon as the tip of the staff held by the angel touched them, fire burst from the rock, and the sacrifice that was being offered was consumed (*ibid.*, 19 and following).

By this sign it appears to have been declared that the rock represented the body of Christ, because it is written: “They drank from the rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4). This, of course, was referred not to his divinity but to his flesh, which flooded the thirsty hearts of the nations with the perpetual stream of its blood.

### 3

Already then, therefore, it was declared in mystery that the Lord Jesus, crucified in his flesh, would abolish the sins of the whole world—not only the sins of actions but also the desires of souls. The flesh of the kid refers to the guilt resulting from deeds; the broth, to the allurements of desires, as it is written: “The people desired an evil desire, and they said, ‘Who will feed us with meat?’” (Numbers 11:4).

Thus, when the angel stretched out the staff and touched the rock from which fire came forth (*Judges* 6:21), he showed that the Lord’s flesh, filled with the divine Spirit, would burn away all the sins of human nature. Hence also the Lord says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12:49).

### 4

The learned man, therefore, and one who foresaw the future, perceived heavenly mysteries. Accordingly, in obedience to the oracles, he killed the bull assigned by his father to idols, and he himself sacrificed another bull of seven years to God (*Judges* 6:25). [Col. 0704C]

By this act he most clearly revealed that, after the Lord’s coming, all the sacrifices of paganism were to be abolished, and that the one sacrifice of the Lord’s Passion was to be offered to God for the redemption of the people. For that bull was a type of Christ, in whom the fullness of the seven spiritual virtues dwelt, as Isaiah said (Isaiah 11:2). Abraham also offered this bull when he saw the Lord’s day and rejoiced (John 8:56).

This is the one who was offered now under the figure of a kid, now of a sheep, now of a bull: a kid, because it is a sacrifice for sins; a sheep, because it is a voluntary victim; a bull, because it is an immaculate victim.

### 5

Holy Gideon therefore foresaw the mystery. Finally, he chose three hundred men for battle (*Judges* 7:6), to show that the world was to be delivered from the assault of more powerful enemies not by the multitude of a number but through the mystery of the cross.

Yet although he was brave and faithful, he still sought fuller proofs from the Lord of the victory that was to come, saying:

“If you will save Israel by my hand, as you have said, O Lord, behold, I shall place a fleece of wool on the threshing floor. If dew is upon the fleece and dryness upon all the earth, I shall know that by my hand you will deliver your people according to your promises.”

And so it happened (*Judges* 6:36 and following). But afterward he asked that dew should again flow over the whole earth while there was dryness in the fleece.

### 6

Perhaps someone may ask whether he appears to have been almost unbelieving, since, instructed by repeated signs, he still requested more. But how can one appear to have tested the matter in doubt and uncertainty when he was speaking mysteries? He was not doubtful, therefore, but provident, so that we might not doubt.

For how could he have been doubtful when his prayer had an effect? And how could he have confidently undertaken the battle unless he had understood the oracle? For the dew upon the fleece was faith in Judea, because, like dew, the words of God descend (Deuteronomy 32:2).

### 7

Therefore, when the whole world of pagan superstition was parched by unfruitful heat, that heavenly dew of visitation was upon the fleece. But afterward, when the sheep that were “the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matthew 15:24)—from which I think the figure of the Jewish fleece was sketched—when, I say, those sheep denied the fountain of living water (Jeremiah 2:13), the dew of faith dried up in the breasts of the Jews, and that divine fountain diverted its channels into the hearts of the nations (Isaiah 3:2).

Hence the whole world is now moistened with the dew of faith; but the Jews have lost their prophets and counselors.

### 8

Nor is it surprising that those who have been deprived by the Lord God of the abundance of prophetic rain should suffer the dryness of faithlessness, [Col. 0705D] since he says: “I shall command my clouds not to rain upon this vineyard” (Isaiah 5:6).

For the rain of the prophetic cloud is saving, as David also said: “He shall descend like rain upon the fleece, and like drops that drip upon the earth” (Psalm 72:6). The whole of Holy Scripture promised us this rain for the entire world, which would water the earth under the advent of the Lord and Savior [Note: [Col. 0705D] Some manuscripts read, “by the dew of the Spirit’s divine mouth.”] with the dew of the Spirit.

The Lord has therefore already come, and the rain has also come; the Lord has come bearing heavenly drops with him. [Col. 0706A] And therefore we now drink, though formerly we were thirsty, and drink that divine Spirit in an inward draught.

### 9

Holy Gideon therefore foresaw that the nations of the Gentiles also would drink the true and spiritual dew by receiving faith, and for that reason he examined the matter more carefully; for vigilance is necessary among the saints.

Indeed, even Jesus son of Nun, when he saw the commander of the heavenly army, asked: “Are you for us or for our adversaries?” (Joshua 5:13), lest he be deceived by some trickery of the adversary.

### 10

Nor was it without purpose that he placed the fleece neither in a field nor in a meadow, but on the threshing floor, where there is a harvest of wheat: “The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few” (Luke 10:2), because through faith in the Lord there was to be a fruitful harvest of virtues.

[Col. 0706B]

### 11

Nor was it without purpose that he dried up the Jewish fleece and poured its dew into a basin, so that it was filled with water, yet he himself did not wash his feet in that dew (*Judges* 6:39–40). [Note: [Col. 0705D] Thus all editions and many manuscripts; but several others read, not incorrectly, “should claim the ministry.”]

The prerogative of so great a mystery belonged to another. The one who alone could wash away everyone’s filth was awaited. Gideon was not great enough to claim this mystery for himself. For it was not Gideon but the Son of Man who came not to be served but to serve (Matthew 20:28).

Let us therefore recognize in whom these mysteries appear to have been fulfilled. Not in holy Jerubbaal, for at that time they were still only beginnings. The nations were conquered because dryness still prevailed among the nations; Israel conquered because the dew then remained upon the fleece.

### 12

Let us come to the Gospel of God. I find the Lord stripping off his garments, girding himself with a linen cloth, pouring water into a basin, and washing the feet of his disciples (John 13:4 and following). This water was that heavenly dew; this was prophesied—that the Lord Jesus would wash the feet of his disciples with that heavenly dew. [Note: [Col. 0705D] Some manuscripts read, “which by that heavenly work,” etc.]

And now let the feet of our souls be stretched out. The Lord Jesus wishes to wash our feet also; for he says not to Peter alone but to every believer: “Unless I wash your feet, you will have no share with me” (ibid., 8).

### 13

Come, therefore, Lord Jesus; strip off the garments that you put on for my sake. Be naked, so that by your mercy you may clothe us. Gird yourself for our sake with a linen cloth, so that you may gird us with the immortality of your gift. Pour water into the basin; wash not only the feet but also [Note: [Col. 0706D] All editions and not a few manuscripts read “the head.” “And not only . . . I wish to remove the traces of the body,” all editions; but other manuscripts more suitably distinguish the words as in the text.] [Col. 0706D] the head; not only the traces of our body but also those of our mind.

I wish to remove all the filth of our weakness, so that I too may say: “At night I took off my tunic; how shall I put it on? I washed my feet; how shall I soil them?” (Song of Songs 5:3).

### 14

How great is this majesty! You wash the feet of your servants like a servant; like God, you send dew from heaven. You wash not only their feet but also invite us to recline with you, and by the example of your gracious condescension you exhort us, saying:

“You call me Lord and Teacher, and you speak rightly, for so I am. If I, then, the Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet” (John 13:13–14).

### 15

I too wish, therefore, to wash the feet of my brothers. I wish to fulfill the Lord’s command; [Note: [Col. 0707C] Some manuscripts read, “he wanted me not to be ashamed.” A few others add after the three words, “a good ministry of humility.” I have retained the reading here, as have all editions.] I wish not to be ashamed within myself, nor to disdain what he himself first did.

It is a good mystery of humility, because while I wash away another’s filth, I cleanse my own. But not everyone [Note: [Col. 0707C] Some manuscripts read, “could receive this,” etc. As for the statement that follows, that Gideon wished to wash the angel’s feet, we do not know from where it was taken. For the Bibles that exist make no mention of this matter.] could grasp this mystery.

Abraham also wished to wash feet, but out of the affection of hospitality (Genesis 18:4). Gideon too wished to wash the feet of the angel of the Lord who appeared to him; but he wished to wash the feet of one person, and wished to do so as one offering service, not as one granting fellowship.

This is the great mystery that no one understood. Finally he said to Peter: “What I am doing, you do not know; afterward you will understand” (John 13:7).

This, I say, is the divine mystery, which even those who have washed will seek to understand. [Note: [Col. 0707C] Thus the old edition and all manuscripts except a few, which have *coeleste mysterium* (“a heavenly mystery”) instead of *coelestis mysterii* (“of the heavenly mystery”). The Roman edition presents the passage as follows: “For this is simple water, but a heavenly mystery.”]

The water of the heavenly mystery is therefore not merely ordinary water, through which we obtain the privilege of having a share with Christ.

### 16

There is also a certain water which we should pour into the basin of our soul: water from the fleece and from the Book of Judges, water from the Book of Psalms (Psalm 23:2). It is the dew of the heavenly oracle.

Come, therefore, Lord Jesus; let this water enter my soul and my flesh, so that by the moisture of this rain the valleys of our minds and the fields of our inmost heart may grow green (Psalm 72:6). Let your drops come upon me, sprinkling grace and immortality.

Wash the footsteps of my mind, lest I sin again. Wash the heel of my soul, [Note: [Col. 0707C] The manuscript of Theodore reads, “the heel of my enemy.” This is not sufficiently correct. What Ambrose intends by the heel of the soul and its washing is explained in a detailed manner below, in *On the Mysteries*, chapter 6, no. 32.] so that I may wipe out the curse (Genesis 3:15); so that I may not feel the serpent’s bite with my inward foot, but, as you yourself commanded those who follow you, may be able to tread upon serpents and scorpions without harm (Luke 10:19).

You redeemed the world; redeem the soul of one sinner.

### 17

This is the special prerogative of your mercy: that you redeemed the whole world in each individual. Elijah was sent to one widow (1 Kings 17:9); Elisha cleansed one man (2 Kings 5:14). But you, Lord Jesus, have cleansed these thousand today.

How many in Rome, how many in Alexandria, how many in Antioch, and how many also in Constantinople! For Constantinople too has now received the word of God and has merited clear proofs of your judgment.

For as long as it kept the poisons of the Arians enclosed within its own vitals, troubled by neighboring wars it resounded with hostile arms around its walls, [Note: [Col. 0707C] All editions and a few manuscripts read, “the wall resounded with weapons”; several other manuscripts, “it surrounded its walls with weapons.” But the reading adopted by the remaining manuscripts is more harmonious: “it resounded with weapons.” For a city may be said to “resound its walls with weapons” in the same way that a man is said to have “his head struck by an arrow,” and in similar expressions.

It appears that Constantinople is here said, before it expelled the Arians, to have lived in continual fear because of the incursions of the Goths, who ravaged the neighboring regions. Ambrose attributes these disasters also to the Arian heresy. After Eusebius of Nicomedia was intruded into the see of Paul, the patriarch, who had been deprived of his dignity through the greatest injustice, the most depraved heretics and leaders of heresy occupied that Church for nearly forty years. When the emperor Valens was killed, Gregory of Nazianzus was summoned by the orthodox to feed and care for that afflicted flock. He himself explains how much he advanced it in his *Poem on His Life* and in Orations 32 and 48.]

but after it repudiated the exiles from the faith, it saw the very enemy, the judge of kings, whom it had always been accustomed to fear, surrendered to it; it received him as a suppliant, buried him when he died, and possesses him in his burial. [Note: [Col. 0707D] The Roman edition reads, “it saw the very enemy whom the kingdom always . . .” Valesius explains this reading in his notes on Ammianus Marcellinus, book 22, as follows: “the very enemy—that is, King Athanaric with his people—whom the kingdom—that is, the Roman Empire in the East—always . . .”

But the Roman edition would not have imposed this reading on that most learned man had he consulted any old edition or manuscript. For, a little earlier, in connection with Marcellinus’ words in the same chapter, “Athanaric, at that time a most powerful judge,” he had himself added this observation: “Thus the Gothic kings, rejecting the title of king, preferred to be called judges.” Themistius also attests this concerning Athanaric in his *Oration 10 to Valens*, and elsewhere.

Athanaric, driven out by a faction of his own people, was magnificently received at Constantinople by Theodosius, who went a considerable distance to meet him. When he shortly afterward died there, the emperor arranged for him to be buried there in a thoroughly royal manner, as Ammianus in the cited passage, Zosimus in book 4, the Chronicles of Idatius and Marcellinus, and many others have recorded.]

How many, then, have you cleansed in Constantinople, and finally how many throughout the whole world today!

### 18

[Note: [Col. 0708C] “Damasus did not cleanse, Peter did not cleanse” is omitted in some manuscripts. Nevertheless it appears in the others and in all editions, and rightly so: not only is it more common for scribes to omit than to add, especially where several members begin with the same word, as happens here, but it is also customary for the bishops of the principal sees to be named together.

Thus Jerome, in his letter to the presbyter Marcus, and Theodosius, book 11, *On the Catholic Faith*, joined Damasus, the Roman pontiff, with Peter, patriarch of Alexandria. Why should we not suppose that our Ambrose did the same here? Certainly he mentioned the see of each equally, as well as that of Gregory. Nor is it an obstacle that Peter had already died, though he is named among the living; Ambrose may not yet have learned of his death, as was said in the Admonition.

As for the fact that, although he mentioned Antioch, he omitted its bishop, we may reasonably believe that this was done deliberately because of the division between Paulinus and Meletius.]

Damasus did not cleanse, Peter did not cleanse, Ambrose did not cleanse, Gregory did not cleanse; the services are ours, but the sacraments are yours. [Note: [Col. 0708D] Some manuscripts read, “For it is not a human work.”]

For it is not within human power to confer divine things. It is your gift, Lord, and the gift of the Father, who spoke through the prophets, saying: “I shall pour out my Spirit upon all flesh, and their sons and daughters shall prophesy” (Joel 2:21). This is, in figure, that heavenly dew; this is the voluntary rain, as we read: “You set apart a voluntary rain, O God, for your inheritance” (Psalm 68:9). [Alternative: chapter 1.]

For the Holy Spirit is subject neither to another’s power nor to another’s right; he is the arbiter of his own freedom, distributing all things according to the authority of his own will, as we read (1 Corinthians 12:11), “to each one as he wills.”

## CHAPTER ONE

Having begun his argument, Ambrose praises the emperor both for his faith and for the restoration of the Church’s basilica. Then, after saying that the adversaries, if they deny that the Holy Spirit serves, cannot deny that he is above all things, he adds that the same Spirit, when he said, “All things serve you,” sufficiently indicated that he is separate from creatures. This is established also by other testimonies.

### 19

The Holy Spirit is therefore not among all things but above all things. Since you have been so fully instructed concerning the Son of God, most merciful emperor, that you may now teach others yourself [Note: [Col. 0709D] Thus Gill and the Roman edition, together with several better manuscripts. The old edition and the remaining manuscripts differ from them only in reading *quia non* instead of *quoniam illae* and, instead of *ut ipse jam doceas*, *ut ipsi jam instructionem audimus*. In those manuscripts the words are added: “so that the reader may instruct one who desires and demands instruction.” These are merely editorial additions.], I shall not delay one who desires and demands to hear something more explicit concerning him. This is especially so since you recently showed yourself so pleased by an assertion of this kind that you ordered the Church’s basilica to be restored without anyone’s prompting.

### 20

We already possess the grace of your faith and the reward of our own faith; for we can say nothing else except that it was the grace of the Holy Spirit that, while everyone was unaware, you suddenly restored the basilica. This, I say, is the gift and work of the Holy Spirit, who was then being proclaimed by us but was working in you.

### 21

Nor do I lament the losses of the earlier period, since that sequestration of the basilica drew interest from a certain investment. For you sequestered the basilica in order to prove the faith. Your piety therefore fulfilled its purpose: it sequestered it in order to test it, and tested it in order to restore it.

I did not lose the fruit, and I retain the judgment; and it became clear to everyone, in a certain distinction of the deed, that your judgment had never been divided. It became clear, I say, to everyone that the act was not yours when you sequestered the basilica, but was yours when you restored it.

### 22

Let us therefore begin with lower matters, so that our treatise may ascend as though by certain steps, [Col. 0709D] and so that those who do not defer to the faith [Note: [Col. 0709D] Thus the old edition, the manuscripts, and editions of better quality. Several others read, “those who do not betray the faith”; the Roman edition, with some manuscripts, more suitably has, “those who do not defer to the faith.” The first reading should not, however, be rejected, for after the word *faith* the sense may easily supply “yield to the argument of the treatise.”] may be moved even by reason.

For at the outset they may say: “We do not say that the Spirit serves.” But if they say that Christ serves, how can they deny this of the Spirit? If they agree that Christ was in the form of a servant according to the flesh [Note: [Col. 0710D] Many manuscripts read, “that Christ served.”] this is established and agreed.

Therefore, if Christ does not serve according to his divinity, the Spirit also does not serve. But if the Spirit does not serve, while all things serve, then the Spirit is above all things, since he does not serve [Note: [Col. 0710D] In the old edition and in several Paris editions, *sicut omnia* (“as all things”) is added. There follows: “Therefore the Holy Spirit is not among creatures, nor among all things, but above all things. For he is subject neither to another’s power nor to another’s right, but is the arbiter of his own freedom, since he distributes all things according to the authority of his own will, as it is written, to each one as he wills.” But these words are not found in the manuscripts and are plainly an interpolation, stitched together partly from the title of this chapter, as it appears in the manuscripts and old edition, and partly from the text itself, as is clear from the end of the preceding prologue.] as all things.

### 23

Now let us establish the very point we have made by testimonies. The beginning of the discussion is that all things serve. It is clear that all things serve, since it is written: “All things serve you” (Psalm 119:91).

The Spirit spoke this through the Prophet. He did not say, “We serve,” but, “They serve you,” so that you might believe that he himself is exempt from service. Therefore, since all things serve and the Spirit does not serve, the Holy Spirit is certainly not among all things.

### 24

For if we say that the Holy Spirit is among all things, then, when we read that “the Spirit searches the deep things of God” (1 Corinthians 2:10), we deny that God the Father is above all things. Since the Spirit is from God, and is the Spirit of his mouth, how can we say that the Holy Spirit is among all things, when God, whose Spirit he is, is above all things—being of complete perfection and perfect power?

### 25

And lest they suppose that the Apostle was mistaken, let them learn whose authority he followed in making this confident assertion. For the Lord said in the Gospel:

“When the Paraclete comes, whom I shall send to you from my Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness concerning me” (John 15:26).

The Holy Spirit therefore proceeds from the Father and bears witness concerning the Son. He also bears witness concerning the Father, as a faithful and true witness. Nothing could be fuller for expressing the divine majesty; [Note: [Col. 0710D] A certain Paris edition reads, “nothing is clearer concerning the truth,” which is not sufficiently correct.] nothing could be clearer for demonstrating the unity of divine power, since the same Spirit knows what the Son knows, being the witness and indivisible sharer of the Father’s secrets.

### 26

He therefore excluded the fellowship and multitude of creatures from the knowledge of God. By not excluding the Holy Spirit, he showed that the Spirit is not a companion of creation.

Hence the statement that we read in the Gospel—“No one has ever seen God, except the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father; he has declared him” (John 1:18)—concerns an exception for the Holy Spirit. For how could he not have seen God who searches even the deep things of God? How could he not have seen God who knows the things that are God’s (1 Corinthians 2:10)? How could he not have seen God who is from God?

Therefore, since it is stated that no one has ever seen God, while the Spirit has seen him, the Spirit is certainly excepted. He is therefore above all things, since he is excepted from all things.

## CHAPTER TWO

That the Holy Spirit’s being among all things is not proved by the words, “All things were made through him,” since he was not made. Otherwise the Son—and indeed the Father also—would likewise have to be counted among all things. This is the same impiety.

### 27

It appears, most holy emperor, that the reasoning is fully consistent with piety, but it does not appear so to the impious. Observe, then, what they attempt. Heretics are accustomed to say that the Holy Spirit must therefore be counted among all things because it is written concerning the Son of God: “All things were made through him” (John 1:3).

### 28

How badly the accusation is confused, when it does not preserve the truth and is entangled in a perverse order of assertion! [Note: [Col. 0711D] Erasmus and later editions print in the margin, “the argument is confused.” But there is no reason not to retain the reading *actio*, since here, as often elsewhere, that word means the same as “accusation.”]

This would have force if they proved that the Holy Spirit was among all things because he had been made. For Scripture says that all things were made through the Son—namely, all things that were made. But since the Holy Spirit is not taught to have been made, he cannot be proved to be among all things, since he was neither made like all things nor created.

This testimony therefore serves me in both respects: it proves that he is above all things because he was not made, and because he is above all things, he is not to be regarded as having been made or counted among the things that were made.

### 29

But if someone argues that, because the Evangelist stated that all things were made through the Word, he did not except the Holy Spirit—although, speaking through John, the Spirit of God said, “All things were made through him,” not “We were all made,” since the Lord himself showed that the Spirit of God speaks through the Evangelists, saying, “For it is not you who will speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew 10:20)—nevertheless, if someone, as I said, does not except the Holy Spirit at this point but counts him among all things, then neither does he except the Son of God where the Apostle said:

“For us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and we through him” (1 Corinthians 8:6).

But to know that the Son is not among all things, let him read what follows. For when he says, “And one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things” (*ibid.*), he certainly excepts the Son of God from all things, just as he had excepted the Father.

30. To detract from either the Father, or the Son, or the Holy Spirit is the same impiety. For one does not believe in the Father who does not believe in the Son; nor does one believe in the Son of God who does not believe in the Spirit; nor can faith stand without the rule of truth. For whoever begins to deny the unity of power in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit cannot, where there is no division, prove that faith is divided. Therefore, just as it is the unity of piety to believe rightly, so it is the unity of impiety to believe wrongly.

31. Accordingly, those who think that the Holy Spirit ought to be numbered among “all things,” because they read that all things were made through the Son, necessarily also think that the Son must be numbered among all things, because they read: “All things are from God” (II Corinthians 5:18). Consequently, they do not separate the Father from all things either, since they do not separate the Son from all created things; for just as all things are from the Father, so all things are also through the Son. [Note: All editions and some manuscripts read: “The Apostle himself clearly said this above,” etc. Others, more numerous and supported by better authority, read as we have in the text.] Foreseeing this very point concerning the Spirit, the Apostle said lest even the impious should think that he had placed the Son among all things, since they had heard the Son say: “What the Father has given me is greater than all” (John 10:29). [Note: Some manuscripts read: “what he has given me.”]

## CHAPTER III

That when the Apostle said that all things are from the Father through the Son, he did not exclude the Spirit from their fellowship; since things referred to one person are also attributed to the others. Thus those baptized in the name of Christ are counted as baptized in the name of the Father and of the Spirit as well—provided that they have believed simultaneously in the three persons; otherwise there is no baptism. The same applies to baptism invoked in the name of the Holy Spirit. But if, because of this passage, the Spirit were separated from the other persons, then, because of other passages, the Father would have to be said to be subordinate to the Son. The Son is worshiped by the angels, not by the Spirit; for the Spirit is his witness, not his minister. When the Son is placed before all things, this is to be understood of created things. The dignity of the Holy Spirit is proved by the unforgivability of the sin committed against him. The origin of that unforgivability, and how there is one Spirit.

32. But perhaps someone may ask why, when he has said “all things are from the Father and all things through the Son” (I Corinthians 8:6), he remained silent about the Holy Spirit, and may wish to derive a prejudice from this. If he persists in interpreting maliciously, how many passages will he find in which the power of the Holy Spirit is proclaimed, though Scripture expressed nothing there either about the Father or about the Son, but left it to be understood!

40. [Note: In the Benedictine edition the sequence proceeds in this mutilated form, omitting two sets of four numbers. Editors.]

When, therefore, the grace of the Spirit is proclaimed, is the God the Father or the only-begotten Son denied? Not at all; for just as the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father, so also, he says, “the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Romans 5:5). And just as one who is blessed in Christ is blessed in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit—because there is one name and one power—so also, wherever some divine operation of the Father, or of the Son, or of the Spirit is indicated, it is referred not only to the Holy Spirit but also to the Father and the Son; and it is referred not only to the Father but also to the Son and the Spirit. [Note: Some manuscripts read: “so also in the Holy Spirit.” “Love,” he says, “has been poured out”; the other witnesses, including all editions, differ among themselves only in that the word “he says” is absent from them.]

41. Finally, the Ethiopian eunuch of Queen Candace, baptized in Christ (Acts 8:27), received the full mystery. And those who said that they did not know the Holy Spirit, although they claimed to have been baptized in John’s baptism, were afterward baptized (Acts 19:2 and following), because John baptized for the remission of sins, in view of the coming Jesus, not in his own name. For that reason they did not know the Spirit: they had not received baptism in Christ’s name, as John used to baptize. Although John did not baptize in the Spirit, he nevertheless preached both Christ and the Spirit. Thus, when he was asked whether he might himself be the Christ, he replied: “I baptize you with water, but one stronger than I will come, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry; he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire” (John 1:26–27). Therefore, because these people had not been baptized in Christ’s name or with faith in the Holy Spirit, they could not receive the sacrament of baptism.

42. They were therefore baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Their baptism was not repeated but renewed, for there is “one baptism” (Ephesians 4:5). Where the full sacrament of baptism is absent, no beginning or form of baptism is reckoned to exist. [Col. 0714A] It is full, however, if you confess the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. If you deny one, you overthrow the whole. And just as, if in your words you include one—whether the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit—but in faith deny neither the Father, nor the Son, nor the Holy Spirit, the sacrament of faith is complete, so also, although you name the Father, the Son, and the Spirit, if you diminish the power of either the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit, the whole mystery is empty. Finally, those very people who had said, “We have not even heard whether there is a Holy Spirit,” were afterward baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ (Acts 19:5). This added to their grace, because through Paul’s preaching they had by then come to know the Holy Spirit.

[Note: Hardly any other passage of Ambrose has provided theologians with so rich a harvest of disagreement as this one. In commenting on these very words in Acts 19, Bede the Venerable teaches that this was Ambrose’s opinion: that a minister of baptism, by pronouncing only the name of Jesus Christ, truly and validly baptizes; and Bede himself subscribes to this view. Pope Nicholas I appears to have added still greater authority to it by his own judgment, in his *Response to the Consultations of the Bulgarians*, chapter 104. Peter Lombard likewise embraced this opinion without hesitation in Book IV of the *Sentences*, distinction 3, chapter “But what,” and what follows. Nor should we judge Saint Thomas to dissent from them in Part III, question 66, article 6, if we trust Cajetan, who even now maintains that baptism can be efficaciously conferred when only one person of the Trinity is named. Other Thomists, however, try to show that this opinion is foreign to the mind of their master; examining that question is not part of our present purpose. Moreover, Hugh of Saint Victor must unquestionably be counted alongside Pope Nicholas and the Master of the Sentences, in Book I of *On the Sacraments*, chapter 13. Hence one may conclude that this opinion was quite familiar to ancient theologians.

But Bellarmine, prudently, says in *On the Sacrament of Baptism*, Book I, chapter 3: “The principal foundation of all the authors after Ambrose is the authority of Ambrose himself; therefore, if Ambrose did not intend to say what his words appear to mean, the principal foundation of that opinion collapses.” Accordingly, to bring light to the Ambrosian meaning by probing it, the same cardinal first warns that Ambrose is to be understood in the light of Basil, whom he followed. He adds that he joins those who believe that Ambrose, and Bede after him, should not be understood as speaking about the form of baptism, but only about the words of Acts that are pronounced; and that the holy Doctor means nothing else than that, in this passage and similar ones, whenever any one of the divine persons is expressed, the other two are silently included.

Estius, in Book IV of the *Sentences*, distinction 3, §5; Nicholas in his *Observations on the cited passage of Thomas*; Alexander in Part III, Dissertation 13; and Hardouin in *On Baptism in the Name of Christ* propose the same solution. But the last three add a second answer to the first: they say that Ambrose’s passage is to be understood only of the profession of faith that adult candidates for baptism used to make. For, when asked—as we have seen elsewhere—“Do you believe in the Father?” they answered, “I believe,” and likewise concerning the other two persons. Saint Ambrose therefore intends that, even if those being baptized had been asked about only one person of the Trinity and had answered accordingly, they would nevertheless have received legitimate baptism, provided that they retained in their minds the right faith concerning the whole Trinity.

No one should doubt that both explanations are in themselves consistent with the truth; but the latter agrees more closely than the former with Ambrose’s words. For the very sequence of the discourse plainly shows that the divine persons named in baptism are also at issue there. Yet many considerations persuade us that this naming is not the utterance made by the minister simultaneously with the washing. First, if the latter were intended, it would follow that the form was valid upon the naming of the Holy Spirit alone—a view that you will find admitted by no one except the Master of the Sentences. Further, since Ambrose undoubtedly proposed to follow Basil here, and perhaps Didymus as well, it is hardly credible that he intended at this point to depart from men who clearly held that the utterance of all three persons was altogether necessary in the form of baptism.

Consult Basil, *On the Holy Spirit*, chapters 10, 11, and 12, and also Book V, *Against Eunomius*, chapter 3. As for Didymus, he asserts that the divinity of the Holy Spirit is most powerfully demonstrated by the fact that, in administering baptism, the person of the Spirit must be pronounced as necessarily as the Father and the Son; and he explicitly teaches that if the priest omits any one of them, the sacrament is made invalid.

But the argument that ought to be considered much stronger is that Ambrose himself repeatedly asserts, in hundreds of passages, that the utterance of the three persons is necessary for true baptism. Consult him in Book VIII on Luke, no. 67; and in *On the Mysteries*, chapter 4, no. 20, where we have already added some remarks on this subject. To say nothing of the author of *On the Sacraments*, Book II, chapters 5 and 7, in this very work he repeatedly indicates that baptism, whether administered by Catholics or by heretics, is always conferred by the minister with the explicit utterance of the three persons. Thus, following the example of other Fathers, he establishes the divinity of the Spirit.]

43. Nor should it appear contradictory that, although the Spirit is afterward left unmentioned, he was nevertheless believed in; what had been omitted in words was expressed in faith. For when it is said, “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ,” the mystery is completed through the unity of the name. The Spirit is not separated from Christ’s baptism, because John baptized in repentance, whereas Christ baptized in the Spirit (ibid., verse 4).

44. Let us now consider whether, just as we read that the sacrament of baptism is complete in Christ’s name, nothing is lacking to the fullness of the mystery when only the Holy Spirit is named. Let us follow reason: whoever names one has signified the Trinity. If you say “Christ,” you have indicated God the Father, by whom the Son was anointed; the one who was anointed, the Son; and the Holy Spirit, by whom he was anointed. For it is written: “This Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit” (Acts 10:38). And if you say “the Father,” you have likewise indicated his Son and the Spirit of his mouth—provided that you also grasp this in your heart. And if you say “the Spirit,” you have named God the Father, from whom the Spirit proceeds, and the Son, because the Spirit is also the Son’s Spirit.

45. Scripture therefore joins authority to reason and indicates that we may rightly be baptized in the Spirit also, when the Lord says: “You will be baptized in the Holy Spirit” (Acts 1:5). Elsewhere the Apostle says: “For we were all baptized in one body, into one Spirit” (I Corinthians 12:13). [Note: Some manuscripts read: “You will be baptized by the Holy Spirit.”] [Note: The Roman edition reads: “all in one body, in one Spirit”; the earlier edition differs from it and from the manuscripts only in having “in one Spirit,” as does the Roman edition. The Greek text reads: ἐν ἑνὶ πνεύματι … εἰς ἓν σῶμα ἐβαπτίσθημεν, “in one Spirit … we were baptized into one body.” Again, where the manuscripts and the earlier edition read “one work,” the Roman edition thought it should be corrected to “one body.”]

One work, because there is one mystery; one baptism, because there is one death for the world; one unity of preaching, which cannot be divided.

46. But if in this passage the Spirit is separated from the operation of the Father and the Son because it is said, “All things are from God and all things through the Son” (I Corinthians 8:6), then, when the Apostle says of Christ, “who is God over all, blessed forever” (Romans 9:5), he has placed him not only above all created things but also above the Father—which is impious to say. But far from it! The Father is not among all things, nor among some class of his creatures. Every creature is below; above is the divinity of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. The former serves; the latter reigns. The former is subject; the latter rules. The former is a work; the latter is the author of the work. The former worships all; the latter is worshiped by all.

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “All things are from the Father.” Below, where we follow the better manuscripts and read “and where the Apostle,” other manuscripts and all editions prefer: “and there, because the Apostle,” etc.]

47. Finally, it is written of the Son: “And let all the angels of God worship him” (Hebrews 1:6). [Note: All editions read: “all his angels”; all manuscripts read: “the angels of God.”] You do not find: “Let the Holy Spirit worship him.” And further: “To which of the angels did he ever say, ‘Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet’? Are they not all,” he says, “ministering spirits sent out for service” (ibid., 13–14)? When he says “all,” does he include the Holy Spirit as well? Certainly not, because the angels and the other Powers are appointed for ministry and service to the Son of God, that they may serve him.

48. But the Holy Spirit is not a minister; he is the Son’s witness, just as the Son said of him: “He will bear witness about me” (John 15:26). The Spirit, then, is the Son’s witness. One who is a witness knows everything, just as God the Father is a witness. Thus you find later that our salvation was confirmed, “God bearing witness by signs and wonders and various miracles and distributions of the Holy Spirit” (Hebrews 2:4–5). He who distributes as he wills is certainly above all, not among all; for to distribute belongs to the grace of the author, not to the material of the work (I Corinthians 12:11).

49. If the Son is above all, through whom our salvation received its beginning so that it might be preached, then God the Father, who bears witness and confirms our salvation by signs and wonders, is likewise excluded from all things. The same applies to the Spirit, who by his distributions bears witness to our salvation: he is not to be numbered among the multitude of creatures, but is to be reckoned with the Father and the Son. When he distributes, he is not himself divided by any incision; for, being indivisible, he loses nothing when he gives generously to all. So too the Son loses nothing when the Father receives the kingdom, nor does the Father lose anything when he hands it over to the Son. We have therefore learned, with the Lord’s testimony (I Corinthians 15:6), that there is no loss in the distribution of spiritual grace; for he who breathes where he wills (John 3:8) is everywhere without loss. We shall speak more fully of this below.

[Col. 0716B] 50. Since our present purpose is to assert in due order that the Spirit is not to be counted among all things, let us bring forward as the author of this assertion the very Apostle whose words they make the subject of dispute. What those “all things” are, whether visible or invisible, he himself indicated when he said: “For in him all things were created, in the heavens and on earth” (Colossians 1:16). You see that “all things” is said of those that are either in heaven or on earth; for there are also invisible things in heaven, and these too were made.

51. Yet, lest anyone be unaware of what he meant by “all things,” he added: “Whether thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers, all things were created through him and in him, and he is before all things, and all things hold together in him” (ibid., 16–17). Did he therefore include the Holy Spirit among creatures here? Or, when he says that the Son of God is before all things, should he be thought to have said that he is before the Father? Certainly not. For just as here he says that all things were created through the Son and that all heavenly things hold together in him, so there can be no doubt that all heavenly powers exist in the Holy Spirit also, since it is written: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their host” (Psalm 32:6). He, then, is above all, from whom comes all the power of heavenly and earthly things. Therefore, he who is above all does not serve; he who does not serve is free; and he who is free possesses the rights of lordship.

52. If I said this at the outset, it would be rejected. But just as they deny lesser things so that greater things may not be believed, so let us put lesser matters first, so that either they may expose their faithlessness even in lesser matters, or, if they agree to the lesser, we may infer the greater from them.

53. I think, most merciful emperor, that those who dare to count the Holy Spirit among all things have been thoroughly refuted. Nevertheless, so that they may know that they are pressed not only by apostolic testimonies but also by the Lord’s own words, how do they dare to number the Holy Spirit among all things when the Lord himself said: “Whoever blasphemes against the Son of Man will be forgiven; but whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come” (Luke 12:10)? How, then, can anyone dare to count the Holy Spirit among creatures? Or who would so bind himself that, if he detracted from a creature, he would not think that this could be released for him by some pardon? For if the Jews, because they worshiped the host of heaven (II Kings 17:16), were deprived of divine protection, while the one who worships and confesses the Holy Spirit is acceptable to God, and the one who does not confess him is condemned as guilty of sacrilege without forgiveness, then from this it may certainly be judged that the Holy Spirit is not among all things but above all things, since an insult against him is expiated by eternal punishments.

54. But pay careful attention to why the Lord said: “Whoever blasphemes against the Son of Man will be forgiven; but whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come” (Luke 12:10). Is the offense against the Son one thing and that against the Holy Spirit another? For just as there is one dignity, so there is one insult. [Note: Morinus, in Book IX of *On Penance*, chapter 28, citing this passage of Ambrose, does not hesitate to assert that it is to be understood truly and properly of the sin that most of the Fathers regarded as unforgivable. But for his opinion to stand, it would have to be shown that our Doctor’s view is that all who had once denied the divinity of the Holy Spirit were entirely barred from returning to faith and forgiveness; and that would certainly not be easy to prove. Since this matter is not at all examined here—neither whether some sin is truly unforgivable, nor under what conditions it becomes so—anyone wishing to know more about the question should consult what we noted in Book II of *On Penance*, chapter 4, as well as our warning in *On the Fall of a Consecrated Virgin*. We observe in passing that this argument has always appeared most effective against those who attack the divinity of the Holy Spirit, and was therefore treated carefully and at length by Didymus, Basil, Cyril, and others.]

But if someone, deceived by the appearance of the human body, thinks less of Christ’s flesh than is fitting—for that flesh ought not to seem contemptible to us, since it is the chamber of power and the fruit of the Virgin—he is at fault, but he is not excluded from forgiveness, which he may obtain through faith. If, however, someone denies the eternal dignity, majesty, and power of the Holy Spirit, and thinks that demons are cast out not by the Spirit of God but by Beelzebul, there can be no appeal for forgiveness there, where sacrilege is complete; for whoever has denied the Spirit has denied both God the Father and the Son, since the Spirit of God is the same as the Spirit of Christ.

## CHAPTER IV

That the Holy Spirit is one and the same Spirit who spoke in the prophets and in the apostles; that he is the Spirit of God and of Christ; and that Scripture designates him also as the Paraclete, the Spirit of life, and the Spirit of truth.

55. No one will doubt that the Spirit is one, although many have doubted that God is one. [Note: Epiphanius attests this concerning Simon Magus, *Heresy* 21; the Marcionites, *Heresy* 42; and the Manichaeans, *Heresy* 66. Concerning the last of these, Augustine says the same in *On Heresies*, chapter 26.] For many heretics have said that the God of the Old Testament is one and the God of the New Testament another. But just as there is one Father, who, as we read, spoke formerly to the fathers through the prophets and, “in these last days, has spoken to us in his Son” (Hebrews 1:1–2); and just as there is one Son, who, according to the account of the Old Testament, was offended by Adam, was seen by Abraham, and was worshiped by Jacob—so also there is one Holy Spirit, who burned brightly in the prophets, was breathed into the apostles, and was joined to the Father and the Son in the sacrament of baptism (II Peter 1:21; John 20:22; Matthew 28:19). Of him David says: “Do not take your Holy Spirit from me” (Psalm 50:13). Of him he also says elsewhere: “Where shall I go from your Spirit?” (Psalm 138:7).

[Note: The Son is said to have been offended by Adam because Ambrose, like many of the ancient Fathers, customarily attributed the creation of the world and all the appearances of the Old Testament to the Son, as we have had occasion to note more than once above. The present remarks on the unity of the Holy Spirit appear to have been borrowed from Didymus, immediately after the beginning of Book I.]

56. So that you may know that the Spirit of God is the same as the Holy Spirit, we read in the Apostle: “No one speaking in the Spirit of God says, ‘Anathema to Jesus’; and no one can say, ‘Lord Jesus,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (I Corinthians 12:3). The Apostle therefore called him the Spirit of God. He also called him the Spirit of Christ, as you have here: “You are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you. But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him” (Romans 8:9). And below: “But if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you” (ibid., 11). It is therefore the Spirit of God who is the Spirit of Christ.

57. He is also the Spirit of life, as the Apostle says: “For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has set me free from the law of sin and death” (ibid., 2).

58. The Spirit, then, whom the Apostle called the Spirit of life, the Lord in the Gospel called the Paraclete; and he is the Spirit of truth, as you have here: “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, so that he may be with you forever, the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because it neither sees him nor knows him” (John 14:16–17). Thus you have the Paraclete Spirit designated as the same Spirit of truth and invisible Spirit. How, then, do some, as regards divinity, think the Son visible, when the world cannot even see the Spirit? [Note: Augustine reports that this impious opinion belonged to the Arians, in Letter 111, now 148, no. 10, and in Book II of *On the Trinity*, chapter 9. But in Book I *Against Maximinus*, chapter 3, and Book II, chapter 26, he teaches that these heretics tried to use this evasion by saying that lesser beings are seen by greater ones—for example, angels by archangels—and that in the same way the Son is seen by the Father, while the Father alone can be seen by no one. Athanasius reports that this sophistry was proposed by Arius himself in his *Thalia*, in his book *On the Synods*. Petavius asserts in Book VIII of *On the Trinity*, chapter 2, that Ambrose has this Arian distinction in view here, but he states this without evidence or argument.]

59. Now hear the Lord’s own testimony that the Spirit who is the Spirit of truth is the Holy Spirit. At the end of this book you have: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22). Peter also teaches that the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of the Lord when he says: “Ananias, why did it seem good to you to test and lie to the Holy Spirit?” (Acts 5:3). Immediately afterward he says the same to Ananias’s wife: “Why did it seem good to you to test the Spirit of the Lord?” (ibid., 9). By saying “you,” he showed that the Spirit of whom he had spoken to Ananias was intended. It is therefore the Spirit of the Lord who is the Holy Spirit. [Note: Some manuscripts read: “the Holy Spirit, who is the Spirit of God.”]

60. The Lord also made clear that the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of the Father when, according to Matthew, he said that during persecution we should not worry about what we are to say: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew 10:20). According to Luke he says the same: “Do not be anxious about how or what you should answer or say, for the Holy Spirit of God will teach you in that very hour what you ought to say” (Luke 12:11–12). Therefore, although many spirits are mentioned, since it is written, “He makes his angels spirits” (Psalm 103:4), there is nevertheless one Spirit of God.

61. The apostles and prophets therefore received that one Spirit. As the chosen vessel, the teacher of the nations, also says: “We have all drunk of one Spirit” (I Corinthians 12:13)—as of one who cannot be divided but is poured into minds and flows into the senses, extinguishing the heat of worldly thirst.

## CHAPTER V

That the Holy Spirit, although he sanctifies creatures, is neither a creature nor changeable; that he is always good, since he is given by the Father and by the Son; that he is not to be numbered among those said to turn aside; that he is the source of goodness, the Spirit of God’s mouth, the corrector of evils, and necessarily to be confessed as good; finally, that since he is affirmed to be good in Scripture and joined to the Father and the Son in baptism, his goodness can in no way be denied; yet he is not said to advance in goodness, but to perfect others—something that distinguishes him from all creatures.

62. The Holy Spirit therefore does not belong to the substance of bodily things; for he pours incorporeal grace into bodily things. But neither does he belong to the substance of invisible creatures; for they too receive sanctification from him, and through him surpass the other works of the world. Whether you name angels, dominions, or powers, every creature awaits the grace of the Holy Spirit. For just as we are free through the Spirit, because “God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father.’ Therefore you are no longer a slave but a son” (Galatians 4:6–7), so also every creature awaits the revelation of the children of God, whom the grace of the Holy Spirit has made children of God (Romans 8:19). Therefore the whole creation itself will be changed by the revelation of spiritual grace and will be freed from slavery to corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God (ibid., 21).

63. Every creature is therefore changeable—not only that which has already been changed by some sin or by the condition of the elements, but also that which can be subject to corruption through a defect of nature, even if it has not yet been changed through the pursuit of discipline. For, as we taught in the preceding books (Book III, *On the Faith*, chapter 2), it is clear that even the nature of angels could be changed. It is reasonable to judge that what is true of the nature of one is true of the others as well. The nature of the others is therefore changeable, though their discipline is better.

64. [Elsewhere, chapter V.] Every creature, then, is changeable; but the Holy Spirit is good and unchangeable. For he cannot be changed by any fault, since he removes the faults of all and forgives sins. How, then, can he be changeable who changes others by sanctifying them to grace, while he himself is not changed? [Note: Some manuscripts read: “who changes others by sacrificing.”]

65. How can he be changeable who is always good? The Holy Spirit, through whom good things are administered to us, was never evil. Thus the two evangelists, in one and the same passage, expressed the same meaning in different words. In Matthew you have: “If you, though you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him?” (Matthew 7:11). According to Luke, however, it is written: “How much more will your Father from heaven give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him?” (Luke 11:13). We therefore perceive, by the Lord’s judgment and the evangelists’ testimony, that the Holy Spirit of the Lord is good, since one evangelist names “good things” in place of the Holy Spirit, and the other names the Holy Spirit in place of “good things.” If, then, the Holy Spirit is what is good, how is he not good?

[Note: Some manuscripts read “the good Spirit”; but the more numerous and older witnesses, like all editions, read “the Holy Spirit.” The Greek codices likewise have πνεῦμα ἅγιον, “Holy Spirit,” rendered in the Latin translation of the Syriac version as “Spirit of holiness”; in the Ethiopic version as “the good gift of the Holy Spirit”; and, more simply, in the Persian as “Holy Spirit.” Didymus too observed this same reading in Matthew and Luke, and a similar treatment of the preceding arguments is found in him.]

66. Nor does it invalidate the point that some manuscripts have, also according to Luke: “How much more will your Father from heaven give a good gift to those who ask him!” This good gift is spiritual grace, which the Lord Jesus poured out from heaven after he had been fastened to the cross, carried away the triumphal spoils of death that had been emptied of its power, and, conquering death, rose from the dead, as it is written: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to human beings” (Psalm 67:19). [Note: Three manuscripts read: “he made captivity captive”; the rest and all editions read: “he led captivity captive,” etc. The Greek expression ἠχμαλώτευσας means “you made captive,” “you reduced to captivity,” or something similar.] He rightly said “gifts”; for just as the Son was given, of whom it is written, “A child is born to us, a Son is given to us” (Isaiah 9:6), so spiritual grace also was given. Why should I hesitate to say that the Holy Spirit was also given, when it is written: “The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5:5)? [Note: Some manuscripts read “the grace of God”; the others and the editions read “the love of God.” The Apostle’s text is ἡ ἀγάπη τοῦ θεοῦ, “the love” or “affection of God,” etc.] Since captive hearts could not receive him, the Lord Jesus first led captivity captive, so that he might pour out the gift of divine grace upon those made free.

67. He beautifully said: “Captivity captive.” For Christ’s victory is the victory of freedom, which claimed all people for grace and bound no one to injury. Therefore, in the liberation of all, no one is captive. And because, at the time of the Lord’s Passion, the injury alone was idle, having lost all the captives whom it had held, captivity itself, returning upon itself, became captive—not now enslaved to Belial but to Christ, for to serve him is freedom. For “he who was called in the Lord as a slave is the Lord’s freedman” (I Corinthians 7:22). [Note: Some manuscripts read: “He is the Lord’s free man”; all the rest and all editions read: “He is the Lord’s freedman.” The Apostle also has ἀπελεύθερος τοῦ Κυρίου, “the Lord’s freedman.”] [Note: Many manuscripts read: “the injury alone was struck”; two read: “the injury alone was idle,” somewhat better; some read: “he alone was struck by injury,” which is less suitable. It is therefore preferable, with the other manuscripts and all editions, to read “the injury alone was idle,” that is, it was useless and could no longer harm anyone.]

68. But to return to our subject: “All have turned aside,” he says; “together they have become useless; there is none who does good, not even one” (Psalm 13:3). If they exclude the Holy Spirit, they themselves confess that he is not among all things; if they do not exclude him, then let them admit that he too turned aside among all.

69. But let us see whether he possesses goodness, since he is the source and beginning of goodness. For just as the Father possesses goodness and the Son possesses goodness, so also the Holy Spirit possesses goodness. The Apostle also taught this when he said: “The fruit of the Spirit is peace, love, joy, patience, goodness” (Galatians 5:22). Who can doubt that he is good whose fruit is goodness? For “a good tree produces good fruits” (Matthew 7:17).

70. Therefore, if God is good, how is he not good who is the Spirit of his mouth (Psalm 32:6), who even searches the depths of God (I Corinthians 2:10)? Can the contagion of evil enter into the depths of God? From this we may also understand how mad those are who deny the Son of God to be good, when they cannot deny the Spirit of Christ to be good. Concerning him the Son of God says: “Therefore I said, he will take from what is mine” (John 16:15). [Note: Some manuscripts read: “the thought of evil.”]

71. Is the Spirit not good who makes good people out of the worst, removes sin, destroys evil, excludes guilt, pours in the good gift, makes apostles out of persecutors, and priests out of sinners? “You were once darkness,” he says, “but now you are light in the Lord” (Ephesians 5:8). [Note: Ambrose says the same in Sermon 10 on Psalm 118, no. 17: “We have received the Holy Spirit, who not only forgives our sins but also makes us his priests, so that we may forgive sins to others.”]

72. But why do we delay them? [Note: The Roman edition, with several manuscripts, reads *deferimus eos* (“why do we defer them?”); older editions, with others, read *differimus eos* (“why do we put them off?”), that is, “why do we not answer immediately?”] For if words demand it, while they do not reject the facts, let them accept that the good Spirit is written of; for David said: “Your good Spirit will lead me into the right way” (Ps. 142:10). For what is the Spirit except full of goodness? Although inaccessible by nature, he is nevertheless receivable by us because of his goodness, filling all things with power, yet participated in only by the righteous; a simple substance, rich in virtues, present to each person, distributing from himself to each, and wholly present everywhere.

73. And rightly the Son of God said: “Go, baptize the nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19), not disdaining the fellowship of the Holy Spirit. Why, then, do some now take offense that the Spirit, whom the Lord did not disdain in the sacrament of baptism, is joined to the Father or the Son by our devotion?

74. The Spirit, therefore, is good—but good not as acquiring goodness, rather as imparting it. For he does not receive from creatures; the Holy Spirit is received. Just so, he is not sanctified, but himself sanctifies: the creature is sanctified, whereas the Holy Spirit sanctifies. Although there is a verbal commonality here, there is nevertheless a distinction of nature. For both the human being who receives holiness and God who bestows holiness are called holy, since we read: “Be holy, because I also am holy” (Lev. 19:2). Sanctification and corruption, therefore, cannot belong to one and the same nature; and consequently the grace of the Holy Spirit and the creature cannot be of one substance.

75. Since, then, every other invisible nature apart from the Trinity—whose rational and incorporeal substance some rightly consider it to be—does not impart spiritual grace but acquires it, and does not participate but assumes, the creature’s association must certainly be separated from fellowship with the Holy Spirit. Let them therefore believe that the creature is not the Holy Spirit; or, if they consider him a creature, why do they associate him with the Father? If they judge him a creature, why do they join him to the Son of God? But if they do not regard him as separable from the Father and the Son, let them not consider him a creature; for where there is one sanctification, there is one nature.

## CHAPTER VI

Although we are baptized in water and in the Spirit, the Spirit is nevertheless far superior to water; and therefore he must not be separated from the Father and the Son.

76. There are nevertheless many who, because we are baptized in water and in the Spirit, do not think that the gifts of water and of the Spirit differ, and therefore do not think that their natures differ. They do not understand that we are buried in that element of water so that, renewed through the Spirit, we may rise again. For in water there is the image of death; in the Spirit, the pledge of life. Through water the body of sin dies, since water encloses the body as though in a kind of tomb; through the power of the Spirit we are renewed from the death of sin, reborn in God.

77. And therefore these three are one, as John said: “Water, blood, and Spirit” (1 John 5:8)—one in the mystery, not in nature. Water, then, is the witness of burial; blood, the witness of death; the Spirit, the witness of life. If, therefore, there is any grace in water, it is not from the nature of water but from the presence of the Holy Spirit.

78. Do we live in water as we live in the Spirit? Are we sealed in water as we are in the Spirit? For in him we live, and he is the pledge of our inheritance, as the Apostle also says in writing to the Ephesians: “In whom, when you believed, you were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise, who is the pledge of our inheritance” (Eph. 1:13–14). [Note: Some manuscripts read: “Therefore we have been sealed according to the Spirit, not by the creature,” and so forth.] We have therefore been sealed with the Holy Spirit—not by nature, but by God—for it is written: “God, who anointed us and who sealed us and gave us the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts” (2 Cor. 1:21–22).

79. We have therefore been sealed with the Spirit by God. For just as we die in Christ so that we may be reborn, so also we are sealed with the Spirit so that we may retain his splendor, image, and grace. This is truly a spiritual seal. For although we may be sealed outwardly in the body, nevertheless we are sealed in truth within the heart, so that the Holy Spirit may imprint in us the likeness of the heavenly image.

[Note: Older editions, with several manuscripts, read “we are sealed with the Spirit”; the Roman edition, with the remaining witnesses, more suitably reads “we are sealed in appearance.”]

80. Who, then, would dare to say that the Holy Spirit is separated from God the Father and Christ, when through him we are deemed worthy to exist according to the image and likeness of God, and through him it comes about, as the Apostle Peter said (2 Pet. 1:4), that we are “partakers of the divine nature”? Here there is not the inheritance of carnal succession, but the spiritual exchange of the grace of adoption. And so that we may know that this is more truly the seal of our heart than of our body, the Prophet teaches when he says: “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us, O Lord; you have given gladness in my heart” (Ps. 4:7).

## CHAPTER VII

The Holy Spirit is not a creature, since he is unbounded and has been poured into the Apostles scattered throughout all the regions; indeed, he sanctifies the angels themselves, to whom he makes us equal. Mary was filled by him, as was Christ the Lord, and likewise all things above and below. From his operation, represented by the stirring of the pool, all blessing has its origin.

81. Since every creature, then, is bounded by the fixed limits of its nature—for even those invisible works that cannot be comprehended by places and boundaries are nevertheless confined by the particular property of their substance—how would anyone dare to call the Holy Spirit a creature, when his power is not bounded or delimited? For he is always in all things and everywhere, which is properly characteristic of divinity and lordship: “The earth is the Lord’s, and its fullness” (Ps. 23:1).

81*. Therefore, when the Lord sent out his humble servants, the Apostles, so that we might recognize that a creature is one thing and spiritual grace another, he sent them to different places, because they could not all be everywhere at once. But he gave the Holy Spirit to all, and although the Apostles were separated, the Spirit poured into them the inseparable gift of grace. The persons were therefore different, but the effect of the operation was one in all, because the Holy Spirit is one. Of him he said: “You will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and throughout all Judea and Samaria and to the ends of the earth” (Acts 1:8).

82. The Holy Spirit, therefore, is unbounded and infinite. He poured himself into the minds of the disciples across the separations of their distinct regions and into the distant boundaries of the whole world; nothing can elude or deceive him. Hence holy David says: “Where shall I go from your Spirit, or where shall I flee from your presence?” (Ps. 138:7). Of what angel does Scripture say this? Of what Dominion? Of what Power? Whose angelic power will we find diffused through so many people? Angels were sent to a few, whereas the Holy Spirit was poured into peoples. Who, then, can doubt that what is poured simultaneously into many and is not seen is divine, whereas what is seen by individuals and held by them is corporeal?

[Note: Some manuscripts read “simultaneously into their breasts,” which is less suitable.]

83. But just as the Spirit who sanctifies the Apostles does not share human nature, so also the Spirit who sanctifies Angels, Dominions, and Powers does not share the nature of the creature. If some think that the holiness of angels is not spiritual, but a certain other grace belonging to the property of their nature, they will certainly judge angels inferior to human beings. For since they themselves admit that they would not dare to compare angels with the Holy Spirit, while they cannot deny that the Holy Spirit is poured into human beings—and since the sanctification of the Spirit is a divine gift and endowment—they will necessarily find that human beings possess a better sanctification and must be preferred to angels. But since angels descend to assist human beings (Heb. 1:14), it must be understood that the angelic creature is indeed superior and receives more spiritual grace; nevertheless the gift of the same Author toward both us and them is one.

[Note: Some manuscripts read “above the property of their nature.”]

[Note: Amerbach and Erasmus, with part of the manuscripts, read “nor could they forbid it”; Gill and the Roman edition, with another part, read “nor can they deny it.” The manuscripts are divided between these readings.]

84. What a great grace it is that even makes the creature of human condition, though inferior even to the rewards of angels, equal to the angels, as the Lord himself promised when he said: “You will be like the angels in heaven” (Matt. 22:30). Nor is this difficult: for he who made them angels in the Spirit will also, through the same grace, make human beings like angels (Ps. 103:4).

[Note: The latest Paris edition reads “he himself previously promised.” Below, where we, together with the ancient editions and nearly all the manuscripts, read “he made in the Spirit,” the Roman edition substituted “he made spirits.”]

85. Of what creature can it be said that it has filled all things, as is written of the Holy Spirit: “I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh” (Joel 2:28)? This cannot be said of an angel. Indeed, Gabriel himself, sent to Mary, said: “Hail, full of grace,” thereby declaring the spiritual grace in her: the Holy Spirit had come upon her, and her womb, full of grace, was to be inhabited by the heavenly Word.

86. For it belongs to the Lord to fill all things, as he says: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. 23:24). If, then, it is the Lord who fills heaven and earth, who can judge the Holy Spirit to be excluded from dominion and deprived of divine power, when he filled the world and, beyond the whole world, filled Jesus, the Redeemer of the entire world? For it is written: “Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan” (Luke 4:1). Who else, then, could fill the one who fills all things except he who possessed the same fullness?

[Note: Some manuscripts read “deprived of divine power.”]

87. But let them not object that this was said according to the flesh; although that one alone was greater than all, and power went out from his flesh that healed all. Nevertheless, just as the Lord fills all things, so also it is written of the Spirit: “Because the Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world” (Wis. 1:7).
