You also have it said of all who had gathered with the Apostles that, “filled with the Holy Spirit, they spoke the word of God with confidence” (Acts 4:31). You see that the Holy Spirit gives both fullness and confidence; his operation the archangel announces to Mary, saying: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you” (Luke 1:35).

88. You also have it in the Gospel that an angel descended at a certain time into the pool, and the water was stirred; and whoever went down first into the pool became well (John 5:4). What did the angel signify in this figure except the descent of the Holy Spirit, which in our times was to consecrate the waters when invoked through priestly prayers? That angel, therefore, was a messenger of the Holy Spirit, because through spiritual grace a remedy was to be brought to the illnesses of our souls and minds. The Spirit therefore has the same ministers as God the Father and Christ. Thus he fills all things, thus he possesses all things, thus he operates all things and in all things, just as God the Father and the Son also operate.

[Note: All editions and some manuscripts have this reading; the others variously read “which in our times would consecrate the waters that were to be invoked by priestly prayers,” or “which, invoked by priestly prayers, would consecrate the waters destined for our times.”]

89. What, then, is more divine than the operation of the Holy Spirit, when God himself bears witness that the Spirit presides over his blessings, saying: “I will place my Spirit upon your offspring, and my blessings upon your children” (Isa. 44:3)? For there can be no complete blessing except through the infusion of the Holy Spirit. Hence the Apostle found nothing better to wish for us, as he himself said: “We do not cease praying and asking for you, that you may be filled with the knowledge of his will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding, walking worthily of God” (Col. 1:9). He therefore taught that this is the will of God: that, walking more fully in good works, words, and thoughts, we should be filled with the will of God, who places the Holy Spirit in our hearts. If, then, the one who has the Holy Spirit is filled with the will of God, there is certainly no difference of will between the Father and the Spirit.

## CHAPTER VIII

The Spirit is given by God alone; nevertheless, he is not given in his entirety to individuals, since no one except Christ was able to receive him in his fullness. Through the Spirit, love is poured out; this love, prefigured by the mystical ointment, is shown to have nothing in common with creatures. Since the Spirit is said to proceed from the mouth of God, he must not be counted among created things, nor among divisible things, since he is eternal.

90. Observe also that God gives the Holy Spirit (Rom. 5:5). This is not a human work, nor is he given by a human being; rather, the one invoked by the priest is bestowed by God, in which act the gift belongs to God and the ministry to the priest.

[Note: Some Paris editions and manuscripts read “God’s hand.”]

For if the Apostle Paul judged (Eph. 5:18) that he could not give the Holy Spirit by his own authority, and considered himself so unequal to this office that he wished us to be filled with the Spirit by God, who is so great as to dare to claim for himself the transmission of this gift? The Apostle therefore brought forward a wish in prayer, not a right claimed by any authority; he desired to obtain it, not presumed to command it. Peter likewise says that he was not capable of either compelling or preventing the Holy Spirit. For he said: “If, then, God gave them the same grace as he gave us, who was I that I could hinder God?” (Acts 11:17).

[Note: A few manuscripts read “he brought forward the wish through preaching.”]

91. But perhaps they are not moved by apostolic examples; let us therefore employ divine oracles. For it is written: “Jacob is my servant; I will receive him; Israel is my chosen one; my soul has accepted him; I have given my Spirit upon him” (Isa. 42:1).

[Note: Older editions and a few manuscripts read “my beloved Israel.”]

The Lord also said through Isaiah: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me” (Isa. 61:1).

92. Who, then, would dare to say that the substance of the Holy Spirit is created, when, once he has shone in our hearts, we see the beauty of divine truth and recognize the distinction between creature and divinity, so that the work is separated from its Author? Or of what creature has God spoken in such a way that it pours out Dominions or Powers or Angels? But of the Spirit, he says: “I will pour out from my Spirit” (Joel 2:28). He does not say “the Spirit,” but “from the Spirit.” For we cannot receive the fullness of the Holy Spirit; we receive only as much as the arbiter of our condition, according to his will, apportions from himself.

Just as the Son of God “did not consider it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself” (Phil. 2:6–7), so that we might be able to receive him with our minds, he emptied himself not because he was empty of his fullness, but so that, for me, who could not bear his fullness, he might be poured out according to what I could receive. So also the Father says that he pours out from the Holy Spirit upon all flesh. For he did not pour out the whole Spirit, but what he poured out abounded for all.

93. Something of the Spirit, therefore, has been poured out upon us. But upon the Lord Jesus, when he was in the form of a human being, the Spirit remained, as it is written: “Upon whom you see the Spirit descending from heaven and remaining upon him, this is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit” (John 1:33). Toward us there is the generosity of the giver, flowing from abundant provision; in him the fullness of the entire Spirit remains eternally. What he judged sufficient for us, he poured out; and what was poured out was neither separated nor cut off, but possesses the unity of fullness, illuminating the sight of our heart according to the capacity of our virtue. In the end, we receive as much as the progress of our mind acquires. The fullness of spiritual grace is inseparable, but it is shared with us according to the capacity of our nature.

94. God therefore pours out from the Spirit, and the love of God is also poured out through the Spirit. Here we must recognize the unity of operation and grace. For just as God poured out from the Holy Spirit, so also “the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit” (Rom. 5:5), so that we may understand that the Holy Spirit is not a work, but the arbiter and overflowing fountain of divine love.

[Note: Some manuscripts read “that we are the work of the Holy Spirit.”]

95. Likewise, so that you may believe that what is poured out cannot be common to creatures but is something special to divinity, the name of the Son is also poured out, as you have it: “Your name is ointment poured out” (Song 1:2). Nothing can be more excellent than the force of this expression. For just as ointment enclosed in a vessel confines its fragrance—the fragrance, so long as it is restrained by the narrowness of that vessel, cannot reach many, although it preserves its power—but when the ointment is poured out from the vessel in which it was enclosed, it spreads far and wide, so also Christ’s name, before his coming, was confined among the people of Israel, as though in a vessel, within the minds of the Jews: “God is known in Judah; his name is great in Israel” (Ps. 75:1). This is the name that the vessels of the Jews held, confined within their own narrowness.

96. The name was indeed great even then, when it remained within the narrow confines of the weak and the few; but it had not yet poured its greatness through the hearts of the nations and to the ends of the whole world. Afterwards, however, when through his coming he shone throughout the entire world, he extended that divine name of his through the whole creation—not filled by any addition, for fullness knows no increase, but filling what was empty—so that his name might be wondrous throughout all the earth. The pouring out of this name therefore signifies an overflowing abundance of graces and a lavishness of heavenly blessings; for whatever is poured out flows over from abundance.

[Note: Some manuscripts read “overflowing with a certain abundance, signifying the power of graces,” followed by a lacuna; others continue with “and so, just as the creature …”]

97. Therefore, just as the wisdom that proceeds from the mouth of God cannot be called created, nor the Word that is uttered from the heart, nor the power in which there is the fullness of eternal majesty, so also the Spirit who is poured forth from the mouth of God cannot be considered created. God himself has shown such unity that he says he pours out from his own Spirit. From this we understand that the grace of God the Father is also the same as that of the Holy Spirit, and that it is divided among the minds of individuals without incision or diminution. What is poured out from the Spirit of God is neither cut up nor comprehended in bodily parts, nor divided.

98. [Elsewhere, Chapter VIII.] For how is it believable that the Spirit is divided by means of some cutting instruments? John says of God: “By this we know that he remains in us, from the Spirit that he gave us” (1 John 3:24).

[Note: This is the reading of the more numerous and better manuscripts. Some manuscripts and all editions, however, read: “But what remains is always present, and is not changed.” Two lines later, where the older editions and a much larger number of manuscripts read “subject to corruption,” the Roman edition, with some other codices, reads “subject to vanity.”]

What always remains certainly does not change. Therefore, if it does not undergo change, it possesses eternity. The Holy Spirit, then, is everlasting; but the creature is subject to corruption and therefore mutable. What is mutable cannot be everlasting (Rom. 8:20). Consequently, there can be no fellowship between the Holy Spirit and the creature, because the Spirit is everlasting, whereas every creature exists in time.

99. The Apostle also demonstrates that the Holy Spirit is everlasting: “For if the blood of bulls and goats and the ashes of a heifer, sprinkled upon those who are defiled, sanctify for the cleansing of the flesh, how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the everlasting Spirit offered himself unblemished to God, cleanse your conscience” (Heb. 9:13–14)! The Spirit, therefore, is everlasting.

## CHAPTER IX

The Holy Spirit is rightly called the ointment of Christ and the oil of gladness, and for what reasons. Christ himself is not the ointment, since he was anointed with the Holy Spirit. It should not seem strange, however, if the Spirit is called ointment, since both the Father and the Son are also called Spirit. Yet there is no confusion among them, since Christ alone died in the body, whose saving cross is proclaimed.

100. Many have thought that the Holy Spirit is the ointment of Christ.

[Note: Some manuscripts read “who anoints well.”]

And rightly ointment, because he is called the oil of gladness, fragrant with a bond of many graces. Almighty God the Father anointed him as the chief priest, who was not anointed like others according to the figure prescribed by the Law, but, anointed according to the Law in the body and, in truth, above the Law, is full of the power of the Holy Spirit from the Father.

101. This is the oil of gladness of which the Prophet says: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. 44:8).

[Note: Some manuscripts read “before your companions.”]

Peter accordingly says that Jesus was anointed with the Spirit, as you have it: “You know what happened throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee after the baptism that John preached: Jesus of Nazareth, how God anointed him with the Holy Spirit” (Acts 10:37–38). The Holy Spirit, therefore, is the oil of gladness.

102. He aptly called it the oil of gladness, so that you would not consider it a creature; for it is the nature of oil of this kind that it does not mix at all with the moisture of another nature. Gladness, too, does not anoint the body but illuminates the innermost heart, as the Prophet said: “You have given gladness in my heart” (Ps. 4:7). It is therefore a waste of effort for anyone who wishes to mingle the oil with the more liquid creature, since, because the nature of oil is lighter than the others, when the other substances settle, it rises and remains separate.

[Note: Some manuscripts read “the moisture of another, more liquid nature.”]

How, then, do these most depraved tavernkeepers think that they can, by their fraud, mingle the oil of gladness with the other creatures, when corporeal things cannot be mixed with incorporeal things, nor created things with uncreated things?

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “Since the nature of oil is more fluid, while the others resist it, it is seen raised above the others and set apart.”]

102*. And rightly he is called the oil of gladness with which Christ was anointed. It was not necessary to seek for him ordinary oil such as is used either to heal wounds or to relieve heat, since he did not seek worldly healing as a treatment for his wounds, nor did eternal power require refreshment for an exhausted body.

[Note: Some manuscripts read “cleansing health”; several others, more suitably, “the health of the world”; the remainder and all editions read “worldly health.”]

103. Nor is it surprising that he possesses the oil of gladness, who made the dying rejoice, stripped the world of sadness, and abolished the mournful stench of death. Hence the Apostle says: “For we are the good fragrance of Christ before God” (2 Cor. 2:15), clearly indicating that he was speaking of spiritual things. And when the Son of God himself says: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me” (Luke 4:18), he signifies a spiritual ointment. The Spirit, therefore, is the ointment of Christ.

[Note: Amerbach and Erasmus, with part of the manuscripts, read “the stench of death in majesty”; Gill and the Roman edition, with another part, read as in the text, “the stench of mournful death.”]

104. Or, since “your name is ointment poured out” refers to the name of Jesus, if they wish Christ himself to be understood there under the name of ointment, rather than the Spirit of Christ, nevertheless, since the Apostle Peter said that the Lord Jesus was anointed with the Holy Spirit, it is entirely clear that the Spirit too is called ointment.

105. But why should this be surprising, when the Father and the Son are also said to be Spirit? We will discuss this more fully when we begin to speak about the unity of the name (below, chap. 14). Yet since a most beautiful passage has arisen here as well, let us not seem to pass it by without a concluding ornament. Let them understand that the Father too is called Spirit, as the Lord said in the Gospel: “God is Spirit” (John 4:24); and that Christ is called Spirit, because Jeremiah said: “The Spirit before our face is the Lord Christ” (Lam. 4:20).

106. The Father, therefore, is Spirit, and the Son is Spirit, because whatever is not the body of a creature is spirit. But the Holy Spirit is not confused with the Father and the Son; rather, he is distinct both from the Father and from the Son. For the Holy Spirit is not dead, since he could not die: he did not assume flesh and could not be subject to death, being eternal divinity. But Christ died according to the flesh.

107. He died in that which he received from the Virgin, not in that which he had from the Father; he died in that in which Christ was crucified. The Holy Spirit could not be crucified, because he had neither flesh nor bones; but the Son of God was crucified, having assumed flesh and bones, so that on that cross the temptations of our flesh might die. For he assumed what he was not in order to conceal what he was; he concealed what he was so that he might be tempted in that nature, and that what was not might be redeemed, so that he might call us to what he was through what he was not.

108. O divine mystery of that cross, on which weakness clings, power is free, vices are nailed fast, and trophies are raised!

[Note: The Bigot codex reads “in which weakness was present.”]

Hence a certain holy man says: “Nail my flesh with fear of you” (Ps. 118:120). He says not with iron nails, but with the nails of fear and faith; for the constriction of power is stronger than that of punishment.

[Note: Some manuscripts read “the constriction of fear.” Below, where the text reads “punishment does not release,” those manuscripts have “power does not release.”]

Thus, when Peter followed the Lord as far as the courtyard of the high priest (Matt. 26:58), although no one had bound him, faith had bound him; and the one whom faith bound, punishment did not release. Again, when he was being bound by the Jews, devotion released him, and punishment did not hold him, because he did not withdraw from Christ.

109. Therefore, you too must crucify sin, so that you may die to sin; for the one who dies to sin lives for God. Live for him who did not spare his own Son, so that in the Son’s body he might crucify our sufferings. For Christ died for us so that we might live in his risen body. Therefore, what died in him was not our life but our guilt: “He bore our sins in his body upon the tree, so that, separated from our sins, we might live for righteousness; by whose wounds we have been healed” (1 Pet. 2:24).

110. That wood of the cross, therefore, is a kind of conveyance for the ship of our salvation, not a punishment.

[Note: All editions and some manuscripts have this reading; others variously read “for there is another salvation, the passage of eternal salvation,” or “for such a ship is the passage,” and so forth.]

For there is no other salvation except the conveyance of eternal salvation. While I desire death, I do not feel it; while I despise punishment, I do not suffer it; while I disregard fear, I do not know it.

[Note: Some manuscripts read “while awaiting death.”]

111. Who, then, is he by whose wounds we have been healed, except Christ the Lord? Of him Isaiah prophesied that his wound is our healing (Isa. 53:5). Of him the Apostle Paul wrote in his Epistles: “He who knew no sin was made sin for us” (2 Cor. 5:21).

[Note: Many manuscripts read “because he was made sin for us.” Again, where all editions read “the nature of the body,” nearly all manuscripts read “the creature of the body.”]

This is truly divine in him: the flesh did not commit sin, nor did the creature of the body he assumed sin.

[Note: Editions read “the nature of the body did not sin.”]

For what is surprising if divinity alone did not sin, since it possesses no incitements to sin? But if God alone is without sin, then every creature, by its own nature, as we have said, can be subject to sin.

## CHAPTER X

The Spirit forgives sins; in this he shares with the Father and the Son, but not with the angels.

112. Say, then, whoever you are who deny the divinity of the Holy Spirit: the Spirit could not be subject to sin, since he rather forgives sins. Does an angel forgive? Does an archangel? Certainly not; the Father alone, the Son alone, and the Holy Spirit alone forgive (Luke 5:21). But no one who is able to forgive is unable to avoid it.

[Note: Amerbach and Erasmus, with not a few manuscripts, read: “But no one who cannot forgive can avoid it.” This is erroneous, since the sense would then be the same as if one wrote: “All who cannot forgive can avoid it.” Gill’s reading, followed here, is better; the Roman edition differs from it only by doubling the negation: “cannot fail to avoid it.”]

113. But perhaps someone may say that a Seraph also said to Isaiah: “Behold, this has touched your lips, and it will remove your iniquities and cleanse your sins” (Isa. 6:7).

[Note: All editions read “and it removed … it cleansed”; all manuscripts read “and it will remove … it will cleanse,” agreeing here with the Hebrew and the Greek and Latin versions.]

“It will remove,” he says, “and it will cleanse.” I will not remove them, but that fire from the altar of God will do so—that is, spiritual grace. For what else can we piously understand the altar of God to be except the grace of the Spirit? Certainly not wood from the forests, nor soot and charcoal. Or what is more pious than to understand according to the mystery that it was revealed in Isaiah’s mouth that all human beings would be cleansed through the passion of Christ, who, like a coal according to the flesh, burned away our sins, as you have it in Zechariah: “Is this not a brand plucked from the fire?” And he was Jesus, clothed in filthy garments (Zech. 3:2–3).

114. Finally, so that we may know that this common mystery of redemption was most clearly revealed through the Prophets, you also have it said in this passage: “Behold, he has taken away your sins” (ibid., 4). This does not mean that Christ laid aside his own sins—he committed no sin—but that in the flesh of Christ the whole human race was absolved from its sins.

115. But even if the Seraph had taken away the sin, he would have been assigned to this mystery as one of God’s ministers. For Isaiah said: “Because one of the Seraphim was sent to me” (Isa. 6:6).

## CHAPTER XI

The Spirit is sent to all and does not pass from one place to another, since he is confined neither by place nor by time. Thus he proceeds from the Son just as the Son himself proceeds from the Father, in whom he always remains; yet he comes to us when we receive him. He comes in the same way as the Father himself, from whom he can never be separated.

116. [Elsewhere, Chapter X.] The Spirit is indeed said to be sent, but the Seraph to one person and the Spirit to all (John 16:7). The Seraph is sent for ministry; the Spirit performs the mystery. The Seraph carries out what is commanded; the Spirit distributes as he wills (1 Cor. 12:11). The Seraph passes from place to place, for he does not fill all things and is himself filled by the Spirit. The Seraph descends with a movement appropriate to his nature; but we cannot conceive this of the Holy Spirit, of whom the Son of God says: “When the Paraclete, the Spirit of truth, comes, whom I will send to you, who proceeds from the Father” (John 15:26).

117. For if the Spirit proceeds from one place and passes to another, then the Father and the Son too will be found in a place. If the Spirit whom the Father—or the Son—sends goes out from a place, then, as he passes and proceeds, he seems, according to impious interpretations, to leave both the Father, as a body, and the Son.

[Note: All editions and some manuscripts have this reading; others variously read “as does the Son” or “and likewise the Son.” In place of *utique*, nearly all have *itaque*.]

118. I say this in response to those who claim that the Spirit has a downward movement. But the Father, who is above all—not only corporeal nature but also invisible creation—is not bounded by any place. Nor is the Son, the Maker of the whole creation, confined by the places and times of his works, since he is above every creature. Nor is the Spirit of truth, as the Spirit of God, bounded by any bodily limits (Wis. 7:23). Since he is incorporeal, he surpasses every intelligible creature of substance by the ineffable fullness of divinity; he breathes where he wills (John 3:8), and he inspires as he wills, possessing power over all things.

119. Therefore the Spirit is not sent as though from one place, nor does he proceed as though from one place, when he proceeds from the Son, just as the Son himself says: “I proceeded from the Father and came into the world” (John 16:28). By this he destroys every opinion according to which movement from place to place can be conceived, as it can in the case of certain bodily things. Likewise, when we read that God is either within or outside, we certainly do not confine God within some body, or separate him from some body; but, weighing this with profound and ineffable consideration, we understand the mystery of the divine nature.

[Note: Here and at the end of the following section Ambrose uses the word “proceed” to signify the temporal mission of the Spirit. It is therefore surprising that Estius wrote in Book I of the *Sentences*, distinction 14: “It should be known that it is not easily found among the Fathers that the mission of the Holy Spirit is signified by the name ‘procession,’ except in Bede,” and so forth.]

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “we confine him within some body.”]

120. Finally, Wisdom says that she proceeded from the mouth of the Most High (Ecclesiasticus 24:5), not in such a way as to be outside the Father, but with the Father, because “the Word was with God” (John 1:1)—and not only with the Father, but also in the Father. For he says: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 14:10). Yet when he goes forth from the Father, he does not depart from a place, nor is he separated as body from body; nor, when he is in the Father, is he enclosed in him as body within body. Likewise, when the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, he is not separated from the Father or from the Son. For how could he be separated from the Father, when he is “the Spirit of his mouth” (Psalm 32:6)? This clearly expresses both the sign of eternity and the unity of divinity.

121. Therefore he exists and always remains who is the Spirit of the mouth; but he seems to descend when we receive him, so that he may dwell in us and we may not be alienated from his grace. He seems to descend for us—not because he descends, but because our mind ascends to him. We would speak of this more fully if we did not remember that in the preceding books it had already been stated (*On the Faith*, Book V, chapter 7) that the Father also said: “Let us go down and confuse their languages” (Genesis 11:7); and that the Son said: “Whoever loves me will keep my word, and my Father will love him; and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14:23).

122. Thus the Spirit comes in the same way as the Father comes, because where the Father is, there also is the Son; and where the Son is, there is the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit, therefore, must not be thought to come separately. He comes not from place to place, but from the ordering of creation to the salvation of redemption, from the grace of vivification to the grace of sanctification, so that he may transfer us from earth to heaven, from dishonor to glory, and from servitude to the kingdom.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “from the underworld to glory.”]

123. Thus the Spirit comes in the same way as the Father comes. For the Son said: “I and the Father will come, and we will make our dwelling with him.” Did the Father come bodily? In the same way, therefore, the Spirit comes; and when he comes, the full presence of both the Father and the Son is present in him.

124. Who, then, can separate the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son, when we cannot even call upon the Father and the Son without the Spirit? For “no one can say, ‘Lord Jesus,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Corinthians 12:3). Therefore, if we cannot call Jesus Lord without the Spirit, certainly we cannot proclaim him without the Spirit. But if the angels also proclaim the Lord Jesus, whom no one can proclaim without the Spirit, then the gift of the Holy Spirit is at work in them as well.

125. We have therefore proved that the presence of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one, and that their grace is one—so heavenly and divine that the Son gives thanks to the Father for it, saying: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and have revealed them to infants” (Matthew 11:25).

## CHAPTER XII

The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit have one peace and one grace; likewise one love, which appeared especially in the redemption of humanity; and finally one communion of the three.

126. [In other editions, chapter XI.] Therefore, since there is one calling, there is also one grace. For it is written: “Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 1:7). Here we have it that the Father and the Son have one grace, and that the Father and the Son have one peace. Yet this grace and peace is the fruit of the Spirit, as the Apostle himself taught, saying: “The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience” (Galatians 5:22). And good and necessary is that peace, so that no one may be disturbed by the uncertainties of disputes, nor be shaken by the storm of bodily passions, but that, in the simplicity of faith and tranquility of mind, his devotion may persevere calmly in the worship of God.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “so that we may neither suffer the passion of bodily storms”; others, “so that we may not suffer the storm of passions”; the rest, together with the editions, read as in the text.]

127. We have proved this concerning peace. Concerning grace, the prophet Zechariah says that God promised to pour out upon Jerusalem “the Spirit of grace and mercy” (Zechariah 12:10); and the Apostle Peter says: “Repent, and let each of you be baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of sins; and you will receive the grace of the Holy Spirit” (Acts 2:38). Therefore, just as there is the grace of the Father and the Son, so also there is the grace of the Holy Spirit. For how can grace exist without the Spirit, since all divine grace is in the Holy Spirit?

128. [In other editions, chapter XII.] We read not only of the peace and grace of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, but also of love and communion, faithful Augustus. For it is said: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God” (2 Corinthians 13:13). We have received the Father’s love. The love that belongs to the Father also belongs to the Son. For he himself said: “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him” (John 14:21). For what is the love of the Son except that he offered himself for us and redeemed us with his blood (Ephesians 5:2)? And the same love is in the Father, because it is written: “For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son” (John 3:16).

[Note: Three manuscripts read, “the communion of faithful eternity.”]

129. Therefore the Father handed over the Son, and the Son himself handed himself over. Love is preserved, and piety is not injured; for there is no injury to piety where there is no misery in the handing over. The Father handed over one who was willing; he handed over one who offered himself—not, of course, to punishment, but to grace. If you examine the merit of the act, ask what it is called in the language of piety. The chosen vessel clearly demonstrates this unity of divine love, because the Father handed over the Son and the Son himself handed himself over. The Father handed him over, who “did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all” (Romans 8:32). Of the Son also he says: “Who handed himself over for me” (Galatians 2:20). “He handed him over,” he says. If it was an act of grace, why do I accuse him? If it was an injury, my debt is greater.

130. But just as the Father handed over the Son, and the Son himself handed himself over, understand that the Spirit also handed him over. For it is written: “Then Jesus was led by the Spirit into the desert, to be tempted by the devil” (Matthew 4:1). Therefore the loving Spirit also handed over the Son of God. For just as the love of the Father and the Son is one, so we have declared that this love of God is poured out through the Holy Spirit (Romans 5:5), and that it is the fruit of the Holy Spirit, because “the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience” (Galatians 5:22).

131. [In other editions, chapter XIII.] It is clear that communion belongs both to the Father and to the Son, because it is written: “Our communion is with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ” (1 John 1:3); and elsewhere: “The communion of the Holy Spirit be with you all” (2 Corinthians 13:13). Therefore, if there is one peace, one grace, one love, and one communion of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, then certainly there is one operation. And where there is one operation, there cannot be a divided power or a distinct substance. For how could the grace of the same operation be harmonious?

## CHAPTER XIII

Ambrose demonstrates from the Scriptures that the three divine Persons have one name; and especially that the Son and the Holy Spirit have the unity of one name, since each is called both Paraclete and Truth.

132. [In other editions, chapter XIV.] Who, then, would dare deny the unity of the name when he sees the unity of the operation? But why should I establish the unity of the name by arguments, when the clear testimony of the divine voice is that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit have one name? For it is written: “Go, baptize the nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19). He said “in the name,” not “in the names.” Therefore the name of the Father is not one, the name of the Son another, and the name of the Holy Spirit another, because there is one God—not several names, because there are not two gods or three gods (1 Corinthians 8:4).

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “not several divinities,” which does not make good sense.]

133. And to make clear that there is one divinity and one majesty, because the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit have one name, and that the Son did not come in one name while the Holy Spirit came in another, the Lord himself says: “I have come in my Father’s name, and you did not receive me; if another comes in his own name, him you will receive” (John 5:43).

133*. Scripture declares that what is the Father’s name is also the Son’s name, because in Exodus the Lord said: “I will go before you in my name, and I will call upon the Lord in my name before you” (Exodus 33:19). The Lord therefore said that he would call upon the Lord in his own name. The Lord’s name, then, belongs both to the Father and to the Son.

[Note: Thus read the old edition and several manuscripts; the Roman edition differs only by omitting the preposition *in*. Some manuscripts give the final portion thus: “I will call upon you, Lord, by my name,” and so forth. The Septuagint, however, reads: “I will pass before you with my glory, and I will call by my name, ‘Lord,’ before you” (some manuscripts read, “by the name of the Lord”). Augustine translates this in *Questions on the Old Testament*: “I will pass before you, my glory; and I will call upon the name of the Lord in your sight.”]

134. Since, then, the Father and the Son have one name, understand that the Holy Spirit also has the same name, since the Holy Spirit comes in the name of the Son, as it is written: “But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things” (John 14:26). Whoever comes in the name of the Son certainly also comes in the name of the Father, because the Father and the Son have one name. Thus it follows that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit have one name. For there is no other name under heaven given among human beings by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12).

[Note: In the Benedictine edition, two sets of ten chapter numbers are omitted, so that the sequence printed there corresponds to the sequence restored here as follows: 135 corresponds to 155, 136 to 156, and so on to the end of Book I. EDD.]

135. At the same time he taught that the unity of the divine name, not dissimilarity, must be believed, since Christ comes in the unity of the name, whereas Antichrist will come in his own name, as it is written: “I have come in my Father’s name, and you did not receive me; if another comes in his own name, him you will receive” (John 5:43).

136. From these passages, therefore, it has been taught that there is no diversity of name in the Father, the Son, and the Paraclete Holy Spirit; and that what is the Father’s name is also the Son’s name; likewise, that what is the Son’s name is also the Holy Spirit’s name, since the Son too is called Paraclete, just as the Holy Spirit is. Therefore the Lord Jesus says in the Gospel: “I will ask my Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, to be with you forever, the Spirit of truth” (John 14:16). He rightly said “another,” lest you understand the Son himself to be the Spirit himself; for there is unity of name, not the Sabellian confusion of Son and Spirit.

[Note: The old edition reads, “the confusion of the Spirit, which is Sabellian”; two manuscripts read, “the Spirit whom Sabellian confusion calls”; one, “as Sabellian confusion admits.” The remaining manuscripts and the Roman edition read as in the text.]

137. [Benedictine edition; in other editions, chapter XV.] Thus the Son is one Paraclete and the Holy Spirit another Paraclete. For John also called the Son a Paraclete, as you have it: “If anyone sins, we have a Paraclete with the Father, Jesus Christ” (1 John 2:1). Therefore, just as there is unity of name, so also there is unity of power; for where the Paraclete Spirit is, there also is the Son.

138. For just as the Lord says here that the Spirit will be with the faithful forever, so elsewhere he shows that he too will be with the apostles forever, saying: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20). The Son and the Spirit, therefore, are one. The Trinity has one name and one inseparable presence.

139. And just as we have shown that the Son is called Paraclete, so also we have shown that the Spirit is called Truth. Christ is Truth; the Spirit is Truth. For you have it in the Epistle of John: “Because the Spirit is truth” (1 John 5:6). Therefore the Spirit is called not only the Spirit of truth, but also Truth, just as the Son is proclaimed to be Truth, who says: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).

## CHAPTER XIV

The sacred books show that each Person of the Trinity is light; and that the Spirit is also signified as fire in Isaiah, whose fire was prefigured in Moses’ bush, in the tongues of flame, and in Gideon’s jars. The divinity of the same Spirit cannot be denied, since his operation is the same as that of the Father and the Son, and the light and fire of the Lord’s face are likewise proclaimed.

140. [In other editions, chapter XVI.] What more shall I establish than that just as the Father is light, so also the Son is light, and the Holy Spirit is light? This is certainly a matter of divine power. For God is light, as John said: “God is light, and there is no darkness in him” (1 John 1:5).

141. The Son too is light, because “the life was the light of human beings.” And to show that the Evangelist had spoken of the Son of God, he said concerning John the Baptist: “He was not that light, but came to bear witness to the light. He was the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1:8–9). Therefore, since God is light, and the true light is the Son of God, without doubt the Son of God is true God.

142. Elsewhere also you have it that the Son of God is light: “The people who sat in darkness and in the shadow of death saw a great light” (Isaiah 9:2). And what could be clearer than this: “For with you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light” (Psalm 36:9)? This means that with you, almighty God the Father, who are the fountain of life, in your Son’s light we shall see the light of the Holy Spirit. The Lord himself shows this when he says: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22); and elsewhere: “Power went out from him” (Luke 6:19).

[Note: All editions and several manuscripts read as in the text. Some others read, “in the light of your Son we shall see,” and some: “In your light we see the Son’s light and that of the Holy Spirit.”]

143. Who could doubt that the Father himself is light, since it is written concerning his Son that he is “the radiance of eternal light” (Hebrews 1:3)? Whose radiance is the Son except that of the eternal Father, since he is always with the Father and always shines forth not with a different, but with the same, brightness?

144. Isaiah indicates that the Holy Spirit is not only light but also fire, saying: “And the light of Israel will become a fire” (Isaiah 10:17). Thus the prophets called him a burning fire, because in these three forms we perceive the majesty of divinity most clearly: sanctifying belongs to divinity; illuminating is proper to fire and light; and the divine is customarily expressed or seen in the form of fire. For “God is a consuming fire,” as Moses said (Deuteronomy 4:24).

145. Moses himself saw fire in the bush and heard God when a voice came to him from the flame of the fire, saying: “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exodus 3:15). There was therefore a voice from the flame, and a flame in the bush, and the flame was harmless. The bush was burning but was not consumed, because through that mystery the Lord signified that he would come to illuminate the thorns of our body, not to consume those afflicted, but to soothe their afflictions—the one who would baptize “in the Holy Spirit and fire” (Matthew 3:11), so that he might bestow grace and consume sins. Thus, in the form of fire, God preserves his purpose.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “not consuming afflictions but soothing them; he who …”]

146. In the Acts of the Apostles also, when the Holy Spirit had descended upon the faithful, he appeared in the form of fire. For you have it: “Suddenly there came from heaven a sound as of a mighty rushing Spirit, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting; and divided tongues as of fire appeared to them” (Acts 2:2–3).

147. Hence, when Gideon was about to overcome Midian, he ordered three hundred men to take jars, to have burning torches in the jars, and to hold trumpets in their right hands (Judges 7:16). Our ancestors, having received this interpretation from the apostles, have preserved it for us: the jars are our bodies, formed from clay, which know no fear when they are kindled by the fervor of spiritual grace and testify to the passion of the Lord Jesus with the proclamation of a ringing voice.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “marked out from clay, which do not know how to hold works except through fervor”; others, “delicate through a work of clay, which do not know swelling if through fervor”; the remaining manuscripts and editions agree with our reading. This interpretation of the jars and torches used by Gideon is also found in Origen, Homily 9 on the Book of Judges; Augustine, *Question 49* on the same book; and Gregory the Great, Book XXX of the *Moralia*, and elsewhere.]

148. Who, then, would doubt the divinity of the Holy Spirit, when wherever the grace of the Spirit is, there the form of divinity appears? By this testimony we gather not diversity but unity of divine power. For how can there be a distinction of power where the effect of the operation is one in all things? Nor can there be grace of the sacraments except where there is forgiveness of sins.

149. What, then, is this fire? It is not fire gathered from lowly brushwood, nor the crackling blaze of forest straw, but that fire which improves good deeds as gold is improved and consumes sins as straw. This is certainly the Holy Spirit, who is called both the fire and the light of the Lord’s face.

[Note: The Albinus manuscript adds, “and the light,” because “the light of God’s face is the light of the Holy Spirit.”]

He is light, as we said above: “The light of your face has been marked upon us, O Lord” (Psalm 4:6). What, then, is this marked light except that spiritual seal in which believers have been sealed, as he says, “with the Holy Spirit of promise” (Ephesians 1:13)?

150. [In other editions, chapter XVII.] And just as the divine face is light, so also fire flashes forth from God’s face, because it is written: “Fire shall burn before him” (Psalm 50:3).

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “For the grace of God shines forth in judgment”; the rest read as the edition does, except that some have “on the day of judgment.”]

For grace shines brightly on the day of judgment, so that acquittal may follow and reward the service of the saints. O the great abundance of the Scriptures, which no human understanding can comprehend! O the greatest sign of divine unity! How many things are signified in these two little verses!

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “How many things, as we have said, are signified by these two verses! Because it is light,” and so forth.]

## CHAPTER XV

The Holy Spirit is life just as the Father and the Son are; indeed, whether the Father is understood as the one with whom is the fountain of life, or the Son, that fountain is nothing other than the Spirit.

151. [In other editions, chapter XVIII.] We have said that the Father is light, the Son is light, and the Holy Spirit is light. Let us also accept that the Father is life, the Son is life, and the Holy Spirit is life. For John said: “What was from the beginning, what we have heard, what we have seen, what our eyes have looked upon, and what our hands have handled, concerning the Word of life—and the life appeared, and we have seen and testify and proclaim to you concerning the life that was with the Father” (1 John 1:1–2). He spoke both of the Word of life and of life, in order to signify both the Father and the Son as life. For what is the Word of life except the Word of God? Therefore both God and the Word of God are life. And just as the Word is called the Word of life, so also the Spirit is called the Spirit of life. For it is written: “The Spirit of life was in the wheels” (Ezekiel 1:20). Therefore, just as the Word of life is life, so also the Spirit of life is life.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “And consequently the Word of God is also life, and just as …” A little later they have: “it ought to be understood that the Son is remembered as the fountain of life.”]

152. [In other editions, chapter XIX.] Understand now that just as the Father is the fountain of life, so also many have understood the Son to be signified as the fountain of life, since the psalm says: “With you, almighty God, your Son is the fountain of life”—that is, the fountain of the Holy Spirit—because the Spirit is life, as the Lord says: “The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life” (John 6:63), because where there is the Spirit, there is life, and where there is life, there is also the Holy Spirit.

[Note: This holy Doctor could not have expressed more clearly the procession of the Spirit from the Son. In this connection it should not be overlooked that he did not claim this opinion as a private one, but declared it to be shared by many. There can be no doubt that he included Athanasius among them; for in his book *On the Human Nature Assumed*, when citing the verse of David to which Ambrose alludes here, Athanasius says: οἶδε γὰρ παρὰ τῷ Θεῷ Πατρὶ ὄντα τὸν υἱὸν πηγὴν τοῦ ἁγίου Πνεύματος—“For he knows that with God the Father the Son is the fountain of the Holy Spirit.”]

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads, “because where there is the Spirit, and where there is life, there is also the Holy Spirit.”]

153. Nevertheless, many wish the Father alone to be signified by the fountain in this passage, although they see what Scripture has recorded: “With you,” it says, “is the fountain of life” (Psalm 36:9)—that is, with the Father is the Son, because the Word was with God, was in the beginning, and was with God.

154. But whether one understands the Father or the Son as the fountain in this passage, we certainly understand the fountain not as that of this water, which is a creature, but as the fountain of that divine grace—that is, of the Holy Spirit—for he himself is living water. Therefore the Lord says: “If you knew the gift of God, and who it is that says to you, ‘Give me a drink,’ you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water” (John 4:10).

155. David’s soul thirsted for this water (Psalm 42:2). The deer longs for this fountain of waters, not thirsting for the serpents’ poisons. For the water of spiritual grace is living, because it purifies the inward parts of the mind, washes away every sin of the soul, and cleanses the error of hidden things.

## CHAPTER XVI

The Holy Spirit is a great river, by whose gift mystical Jerusalem is watered. He is equal to his fountain, that is, to the Father and the Son, and is signified as such in Scripture. The holy Doctor thirsts for his water; but, so that it may be preserved in us, he warns that the devil, desire, and heresy must be avoided, since our vessels are fragile. He also advises that we abandon broken cisterns, so that, following the example of the Samaritan woman and of the patriarchs, we may find the Lord’s water.

156. [In other editions, chapter XX.] But lest anyone perhaps disparage the Spirit as something small, and from this attempt to create some difference in magnitude because water appears to be a small portion of a fountain—although examples drawn from creatures seem altogether unsuitable to divinity—let them nevertheless learn, lest they derive any prejudice even from this comparison with a creature, that the Holy Spirit is called not only water but also a river, according to what is written: “From his belly will flow rivers of living water.” This he said concerning the Spirit, whom those who were going to believe in him were beginning to receive (John 7:38–39).

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “as though it were a smallness.”]

[Note: Likewise Gregory of Nazianzus, after recounting in Oration 37 the comparisons by which Catholics sought, in some measure, to make the knowledge of the divine Persons more accessible, professes that he used them not without a certain fear and scruple.]

157. Therefore the Holy Spirit is a river, and a very great river, which, according to the Hebrews, flowed from Jesus on earth, as we have received through the prophetic word of Isaiah (Isaiah 66:12). This great river flows continually and never fails.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “and does not ebb away.”]

And it is not only a river, but also a rushing current, overflowing in its greatness, just as David said: “The rushing of the river makes glad the city of God” (Psalm 46:4).

[Note: All editions and several manuscripts read as in the text. Some others read, “which flows from the inward parts of Jesus.” Immediately afterward, the editions of Amerbach and Erasmus and some manuscripts read, “as we often received from the mouth of the prophets”; the remaining manuscripts and editions read as in the text.]

158. For that heavenly city, Jerusalem, is not washed by the course of some earthly river; rather, the Holy Spirit, proceeding from the fountain of life, of whom we are satisfied by a brief draught, appears to flow more abundantly among those heavenly Thrones, Dominions, and Powers, Angels and Archangels, boiling forth in the full course of the seven spiritual virtues. For if a river, poured over the high banks of its channel, floods beyond them, how much more does the Spirit, surpassing every creature, when he touches the remaining fields of our mind as though they were lower regions, gladden that heavenly nature of created beings with a more abundant richness of sanctification!

159. Nor should it disturb you that here he speaks of rivers (John 7:38), or elsewhere of seven spirits (Revelation 5:6); for by these expressions the fullness of the seven spiritual virtues is signified, as Isaiah said (Isaiah 11:2): the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of God. There is therefore one river, but many channels of spiritual gifts. This river, then, proceeds from the fountain of life.

160. Again, do not turn your understanding toward lower things because there seems to be some difference between a fountain and a river. Divine Scripture has nevertheless provided for everything, lest human weakness be ensnared by the poverty of words. You may set before yourself any river you wish: it comes from a fountain, yet it is of one nature, one brightness, and one grace. Say likewise that the Holy Spirit has one substance with the Son of God and God the Father, one brightness and one glory. I shall grasp the faithful brevity of the unity of power and shall not fear any question concerning difference of magnitude. For Scripture has also provided for us in this matter. The Son of God says: “Whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John 4:14). This fountain is certainly spiritual grace, a river proceeding from a living fountain. The Holy Spirit, therefore, is also the fountain of life.

161. You perceive, then, from his own words that the unity of divine greatness is signified, and that Christ cannot even be denied to be the fountain by the unbelieving, since the Spirit too is called a fountain. And just as the Spirit is called a river, so also the Father said: “Behold, I will flow toward you like a river of peace and like an overflowing torrent of the glory of the nations” (Isaiah 66:12). Who, then, would doubt that the Son of God is the river of life, from whom the rivers of eternal life flowed?

[Note: Most and better manuscripts read as in the text. Some others, as well as the old edition, read, “I will flow upon you”; the Roman edition, on the basis of the sacred books, reads, “I will flow upon them.”]

162. Good, therefore, is the water, spiritual grace. Who will give this fountain to my breast? Let it spring up in me; let the giver of eternal life flow in me. Let this fountain overflow in us, not flow away. Wisdom says: “Drink water from your own vessels and from the fountains of your wells, and let your waters overflow in your streets” (Proverbs 5:15–16). How shall I retain this water so that it does not flow away or slip out? How shall I preserve my vessel, so that through some crack of sin the moisture of eternal life does not drip away? Teach us, Lord Jesus; teach us as you taught your apostles, saying: “Do not store up treasures for yourselves on earth, where rust and moth destroy, and where thieves break in and steal” (Matthew 6:19).

[Note: All editions and several manuscripts read as in the text. Some others read, “so that water penetrating the crack may not …”]

163. He clearly signifies that the thief is the unclean spirit, who cannot creep upon those walking in the light of good works, but who, in the darkness of worldly desires and amid the pleasures of earthly delights, strips anyone whom he captures of every flower of eternal virtue.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “if he has seized anyone rolling about.”]

And therefore the Lord says: “Store up treasures for yourselves in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys, and where thieves do not break in or steal. For where your treasure is, there also will your heart be” (Matthew 6:20–21).

164. Our rust is wantonness; our rust is lust; our rust is luxury. These cover the sharpness of the mind with the filth of shameful acts. Our moth, again, is Arius; our moth is Photinus. By their impiety they tear the holy garment of the Church; seeking to separate the indivisible unity of divine power, they gnaw with sacrilegious bites at the precious veil of faith. The water is poured out if Arius presses in his tooth; it flows away if Photinus drives his sting into someone’s vessel. We are a worthless piece of clay and quickly feel the effects of vices. Yet no one says to the potter: “Why have you made me thus?” (Romans 9:20). For although our vessel is worthless, one vessel is nevertheless for honor and another for dishonor. Do not, then, open your cistern; do not dig into it through vices and crimes, lest someone say: “He opened a pit and dug it, and he fell into the ditch that he made” (Psalm 7:15).

165. If you seek Jesus, abandon the broken cisterns. Christ is accustomed to sit not at a cistern but at a well. There the Samaritan woman found him—the woman who believed, the woman who desired to draw water (John 4:6). Although you ought to come in the morning, even if you come later, at the sixth hour you will find Jesus wearied from the journey. He was wearied—but in you, because he sought you for a long time, and your unbelief wearied him for so long. Yet he is not offended if only you come now: he asks for a drink, intending to give one. He drinks not the water of a passing stream, but your salvation; he drinks your devotion; he drinks the cup—that is, that passion which redeems your sins—so that you may quench the thirst of this world with the blood of the sacred drink.

166. Thus Abraham won God’s favor after he had dug a well (Genesis 21:30). Thus Isaac, while walking toward the well (Genesis 24:62), received as his wife the woman who came, in a type of the Church (ibid., 67). The faithful woman is found at the well; the unfaithful at the cistern. Finally, Rebecca, as we read, found her suitor at the spring, while the prostitutes washed themselves in the blood of Jezebel at the cistern (1 Kings 22).

[Note: Quite a few manuscripts read, “Rebecca, as we read, found the petitioner”; three read, “found the one who was going to petition.”]

# BOOK TWO

## PROLOGUE

The three divine Persons were not unknown either to the ancient judges or to Moses; and their equality with one another is declared, especially in the case of the Son with the Father. The Holy Spirit was present with Samson, whose remarkable history is then reviewed and applied to various mysteries of the Church. When that same Spirit departed, Samson fell into manifold calamities. Ambrose explains this so that these calamities may not be attributed merely to the cutting of his hair, and he sets forth the spiritual meanings of those events.

1. Although in the first book, in the reading of the ancient history, it has been disclosed [Note: [Col. 0743D] Thus all editions and many manuscripts; but several others read: “if we pay close attention, it has been disclosed.” Some omit “if we pay close attention.” Both this phrase and the word “we find” were probably added by those scribes who depended on the wording of earlier manuscripts and failed to notice that the sense was incomplete. Although we do not deny that a defect entered the received reading through the omission of some word in certain manuscripts, we prefer to leave it defective rather than attach to it a clause that we judge foreign to it.]—if we pay close attention, we find that even among the judges of the ancient Jews the sevenfold grace of the Spirit shone forth, and that through the Holy Spirit the mysteries of heavenly sacraments were revealed, whom Moses knew to be eternal. Indeed, at the very beginning of the world—or rather, before the beginning—he joined him to God, knowing him to be everlasting before the world’s beginning. For if anyone observes carefully, he will recognize the Father, the Son, and the Spirit at the beginning. Of the Father it is written: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Gen. 1:1–2). Of the Spirit it is said: “The Spirit was borne over the waters” (ibid., 4). And fittingly, at the beginning of creation the figure of baptism is marked out, by which creation was destined to be cleansed. We also read of the Son that he is the one who separated the midst of light from darkness; for there is one God the Father who commands, and one Lord Jesus who acts.

2. But lest you again think that the Father’s command makes him arrogant in commanding, or that the Son’s obedience makes him inferior, the Father confesses the Son to be his equal through the unity of their work, saying: “Let us make man according to our image and likeness” (ibid., 26). For what else do the common image, operation, and likeness signify than the unity of the same majesty?

[Note: [Col. 0743D] There were ancient Fathers, both before and after the Council of Nicaea, who acknowledged that the Father commanded the Son: for example, Irenaeus, book III, chapter 8, and book IV, chapter 75; Marius Victorinus, book I of *On the Creation of Things*; Athanasius, *On the Decree of the Council of Nicaea*; and Basil, *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 16. Yet they consider the Father’s command to be authoritative, not despotic, and believe that it introduces no servitude in the Son, as Basil explains clearly in the cited work, chapter 8, Cyril of Alexandria in his commentary on this passage of Genesis, and Gregory of Nazianzus, *Oration* 36. See also what we have already noted in our book *On the Faith*.]

3. Yet, so that you may recognize more fully the equality of the Father and the Son: just as the Father spoke and the Son acted, so the Father acts and the Son speaks. The Father acts, as it is written: “My Father is working until now” (John 5:17). You have the saying addressed to the Son: “Speak the word, and he will be healed” (Matt. 8:8). And the Son says to the Father: “I desire that where I am, they also may be with me” (John 17:24). The Father did what the Son said.

4. Abraham, too, was not ignorant of the Holy Spirit. Indeed, he saw three and worshiped one (Gen. 18:2–3), because there is one God, one Lord, and one Spirit. Therefore there is unity of honor, because there is unity of power.

5. And why should I speak of each one individually? Samson, born through a divine promise, had the accompanying Spirit; for thus we read: “Because the Lord blessed him, and the Spirit of the Lord began to accompany him in the camp” (Judg. 13:24–25). And therefore, foreseeing the future mystery, he sought a wife from foreigners (Judg. 14:1 ff.); his father and mother, as it is written, did not know that this was from the Lord. And rightly he was considered stronger than the others, because the Spirit of the Lord directed him. Under that guidance, now alone he put foreign peoples to flight, and now, with a bite that could not be resisted and with strength that could not be overcome, he tore apart a lion and divided it with his hands (ibid., 5 ff.). If only he had been as careful to preserve grace as he was strong in overcoming the beast!

6. Perhaps this was not only a miracle of strength but also a mystery of wisdom and an oracle of prophecy. For it does not seem meaningless that, as he was approaching the mystery of marriage, a roaring lion met him, which he tore apart with his hands; and in its body, as he was about to obtain the desired marriage, he found a swarm of bees and took honey from its mouth, giving it to his father and mother to eat (ibid., 8 ff.).

[Note: [Col. 0744D] Amerbach and Erasmus read: “as he was about to seek the desired marriage”; some manuscripts: “as he was about to seek the desired union”; several others, together with the Gill and Roman editions, read as in the text.]

The people of the nations who believed had honey. Formerly that people had been savage; now it belongs to Christ.

7. Nor is the question he proposed to his companions devoid of mysteries, when he said: “Out of the eater came forth food, and out of the strong came forth sweetness” (ibid., 14).

[Note: [Col. 0744D] Thus the old edition and by far the majority of manuscripts, except that some prefer *dulcedo* (“sweetness”) to *dulce* (“sweet”); but the Roman edition, with several other manuscripts, reads “and out of the mighty came forth sweet,” rather than “and out of the strong,” etc.]

It was mystical to such a degree that its revelation was sought for three days, and could come only through the faith of the Church. It was to be revealed on the seventh day, when the period of the Law had been completed, after the Lord’s Passion. For thus you have it: the apostles did not understand because Jesus had not yet been glorified (John 7:39).

8. “What,” they said, “is sweeter than honey, and what is stronger than a lion?” To them he replied: “If you had not plowed with my heifer, you would not have discovered my riddle” (Judg. 14:18). O divine mystery! O evident sacrament! We escaped the destroyer; we conquered the powerful one. There is now the food of life where previously there had been the wretched hunger of death. Danger is turned into salvation, bitterness into sweetness. Grace proceeded from offense, power from weakness, life from death.

9. Yet there are some who think, on the contrary, that the marriage could not have been established unless the lion from the tribe of Judah had been killed; and therefore, in his body—that is, in the Church—

[Note: [Col. 0744D] Several manuscripts read: “bees were found, which stored up honey.” Again, where all the editions, together with one or two manuscripts, read “and in it honey in figure,” the remaining manuscripts read “but in it,” etc.]

bees were found, storing up the honey of wisdom, because after the Lord’s Passion the apostles believed more fully. Samson, therefore, as a Jew, killed this lion, but in him he found honey, as a figure of the redemption of the inheritance, so that the remnant might be saved according to the election of grace (Rom. 11:27).

10. “And,” he says, “the Spirit of the Lord rushed upon him, and he went down to Ashkelon and struck thirty men there” (Judg. 14:19–20).

[Note: [Col. 0745D] After the words “thirty men,” four manuscripts add: “he completed thirty years.”]

For he could not fail to hold the victory who perceived the sacraments. Thus those who solve and announce the riddle receive the reward of wisdom in robes, the distinction of an upright way of life.

11. Again, other mysteries arise here: his wife is taken away, and therefore the foxes set the foreigners’ sheaves on fire (Judg. 15:1 ff.).

[Note: [Col. 0745D] Several manuscripts read: “For there are those who customarily deceive people with their cunning against the divine sacraments.”]

For with his own cunning he has been accustomed to deceive those who contend against the divine sacraments. Hence he says again in the *Song of Songs*: “Catch for us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards, so that our vineyards may blossom” (Song 2:15).

[Note: [Col. 0745D] The Thuaneus, Colbertinus, and one Albian manuscript read: “It is good: little vineyards.” The Tellinian manuscript and the old edition read: “It is good: little foxes.” The Roman edition and several manuscripts read as in the text.]

He rightly said “little,” because they could not destroy the larger vineyards, although the devil too, despite his strength, is little.

12. Therefore he—so that we may summarize the history, since the exposition of the entire reading must be reserved for its proper time—was invincible as long as he possessed spiritual grace, like that people of God chosen by the Lord, that Nazirite under the Law. Samson, then, was invincible and so unconquerable that with the jawbone of an ass he struck down a thousand men; and he was so full of heavenly grace that, when thirsty, he even found water in the jawbone of an ass (Judg. 15:15 ff.). You may regard this either as a miracle or turn it into a mystery: among the humility of the Gentile people there would be both rest and triumph. In accordance with what is written: “To the one who strikes you on the cheek, offer the other also” (Matt. 5:39).

[Note: [Col. 0745D] Several manuscripts read: “through this patience in injuries, by which we are instructed”—some, “by which we are instructed”—“we triumph over certain goads of anger, so that we may receive the sacraments of baptism”; others: “you may see baptism”; others: “he says that the Savior was baptized at thirty years.” In the thirtieth year of his incarnation the Lord Jesus is killed by the Jews; so that after the death he suffered—several manuscripts and the editions read “after death had been suffered”—there might be rest. There is here a clear imitation of that passage of Virgil from book X of the *Aeneid*:

> After death had been suffered, figures of what kind, as rumor tells, fly about.

We have displayed the foregoing variants so that this example may show how much scribal boldness sometimes allowed itself.]

Through this patience in injuries, by which the sacraments of baptism instruct us, we triumph over certain goads of anger, so that, after death has been suffered, we may attain the rest of the resurrection.

13. Was that, then, the Samson who dissolved woven cords of sinews and new ropes as though they were soft threads? Was that the Samson who, as long as he possessed spiritual grace, did not feel the bonds fastened to his hair by a fixed stake? I mean the same man who, after the Spirit of God departed from him,

[Note: [Col. 0746D] There is also here an evident imitation of Virgil, book II of the *Aeneid*. For there he writes:

> How greatly changed from that Hector who returned wearing the spoils of Achilles.]

far changed from that Samson who returned wearing the spoils of the Philistines, degenerate from his strength on a woman’s knees, touched and captured,

[Note: [Col. 0746D] Thus the old edition and several manuscripts; but the Roman edition, with several others, reads: “bound and captured.”]

was shorn of his sacred hair (Judg. 16:9 ff.)?

[Note: [Col. 0746D] Some manuscripts read: “his unconquered hair is shorn.”]

14. Did the hair of his head, then, possess such importance that, while it remained, his unconquered strength endured, but when his head was shorn the man’s entire power was suddenly dissolved?

[Col. 0746A] It is not so: we must not suppose that bodily hairs possessed such force. There are hairs of religion and faith: the hairs of the Nazirite, perfected under the Law and consecrated in frugality and abstinence. By these, the woman who prefigured the Church and had poured oil over the Lord’s feet wiped the traces of the heavenly Word (John 12:3); for at that time she also knew Christ according to the flesh.

These are the hairs of which it is said: “Your hair is like flocks of goats” (Song 4:1), springing from that head of which it is said: “The head of a man is Christ” (1 Cor. 11:3); and elsewhere: “His head is gold, pure gold, and his locks are like black fir trees” (Song 5:11).

[Note: [Col. 0746D] The old edition reads: “And good are the fir trees, the ships of Tarshish”; the Roman edition: “And rightly the ships of Tarshish are made from fir”; but the manuscripts agree with us, except for a few that read: “And good are those bringing ships,” etc.]

And good are the ships of Tarshish made from fir, which float above the waves of the world and provide a safe means of navigation for salvation.

15. Therefore, signifying in the Gospel that there are certain visible hairs of the head and certain intelligible ones, our Lord says: “But even the hairs of your head are all numbered” (Matt. 10:31), evidently signifying the deeds of spiritual virtues. For God does not concern himself with our bodily hairs. Yet it is not unreasonable to think that, because of the divine majesty, nothing can be hidden from him.

16. But what benefit is it to me

[Note: [Col. 0746D] Several manuscripts read: “if almighty God knows my hairs”?]

that God himself knows all my hairs? It benefits and profits me if he, the ever-watchful witness of good works, grants the reward of eternal glory. Indeed, Samson himself declares that these are not bodily but intelligible hairs, saying: “If I am shorn, my strength will depart from me” (Judg. 16:17). This is about the mystery; now let us consider the sequence of the reading.

## CHAPTER ONE

That the Spirit of the Lord is also Lord and power, and is not inferior in this respect to the Father or the Son

17. Above you have: “The Lord blessed him, and the Spirit of the Lord began to accompany him” (Judg. 13:24–25). Below he says:

[Note: [Col. 0746D] The Roman edition alone reads: “and rushed upon him”; several manuscripts read: “and fell upon him,” which is not inappropriate. For in certain Greek copies it reads καὶ κατήλαυνεν ἐπὶ αὐτὸν, “and he rushed upon him,” although in more copies we find καὶ ἤλατο, “and he leapt upon him and rushed upon him,” etc.]

“And the Spirit of the Lord directed him” (Judg. 14:6). He likewise says: “If I am shorn, my strength will depart from me” (Judg. 16:17). After he was shorn, see what Scripture says: “The Lord,” it says, “departed from him” (ibid., 20).

18. You see, then, that the one who accompanied him is the one who departed from him. The Lord, therefore, is the same as the Spirit of the Lord—that is, Scripture called the very Spirit of God “Lord,” just as the Apostle also says: “The Lord is the Spirit; and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Cor. 3:17). Thus you have the Holy Spirit also called Lord. For the Holy Spirit and the Son are not one person, but they are one.

19. In this passage he also called him “power” and signified the Spirit. For just as the Father is power, so the Son is power, and the Holy Spirit is power (1 John 5:7). You have read that Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Cor. 1:24). We also read that the Father is power, as it is written: “You will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of the Power of God” (Matt. 26:64). Here he certainly called the Father “Power,” at whose right hand the Son sits, as you have it: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand” (Ps. 109:1).

The Lord himself also called the Holy Spirit “power,” saying: “You will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you” (Acts 1:8).

[Note: [Col. 0747D] The Roman edition, with several manuscripts, reads here and in book I, chapter 7: “You will receive power, the Holy Spirit coming upon you.” The old edition here, with several other manuscripts, reads: “of the Holy Spirit coming upon you.” The same old editions, at the cited passage in book I, and more manuscripts in both places, read: “when the Holy Spirit comes upon you.” The last two readings correspond equally to the Greek words ἐπελθόντος τοῦ ἁγίου Πνεύματος, “when the Holy Spirit has come upon you.”]

## CHAPTER TWO

That the counsel of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one

20. For the Spirit himself is power, because you have read: “The Spirit of counsel and power” (Isa. 11:2). And just as the Son is the Angel of great counsel, so the Spirit is also the Spirit of counsel, so that you may know that the counsel of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one.

[Note: [Col. 0747D] The Thuaneus manuscript reads: “so that you may know that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one counsel,” not “counsel,” etc.]

This counsel concerns not uncertain matters but matters foreknown and determined.

21. You may also recognize from this that the Spirit is the arbiter of the divine counsel.

[Note: [Col. 0747D] Some manuscripts read: “This too must be recognized from the fact that above,” etc.]

For since above (book I, chapter 6) we taught that the Holy Spirit is the arbiter of baptism, and since we have read that baptism is God’s counsel, as you have it: “But the Pharisees rejected God’s counsel for themselves, not having been baptized by him” (Luke 7:30), it is plainly clear that, since baptism cannot exist without the Spirit, God’s counsel likewise does not exist without the Spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0748D] The Thuaneus manuscript, *Exposition on Luke*, book VI, no. 4, reads: “God’s counsel is in the baptism of John; who, then, would doubt that God’s counsel is in Christ’s washing? This is the counsel that the Angel of great counsel found, which no one knew. For who has known the mind of the Lord,” etc.]

22. And so that we may know more fully that the Spirit is power, we must understand that he is the one who was promised when the Lord said: “I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh” (Joel 2:28). Therefore the one who was promised to us is power, just as the same Son of God also declared in the Gospel, saying: “And I send upon you the promise of my Father; but you remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24:49).

23. The Evangelist signifies that the Holy Spirit is power to such a degree that he records him descending with great force, saying: “And suddenly there came from heaven a sound, as though the Spirit were being borne along by a mighty force” (Acts 2:2).

24. But lest you again think that this must be referred to sensible and bodily things, understand that the Spirit descended in the same manner in which Christ will descend. For he too will descend with power, as you have it: “They will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with great power and majesty” (Matt. 24:30).

25. For how could there not be one and the same power and authority, when the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one work, one judgment, one temple, one giving of life, one sanctification, and one kingdom?

## CHAPTER THREE

Just as it is life to know the Father and the Son, so it is life to know the Holy Spirit; therefore he must not be separated from the divinity of the Father

26. Let them say in what respect they think the divine work is dissimilar. For just as it is life to know the Father and the Son, as the Lord himself declared, saying: “This is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3), so it is also life to know the Holy Spirit. For the Lord says: “If you love me, keep my commandments; and I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, that he may remain with you forever, the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because it does not see him or know him; but you know him, because he remains with you and is in you” (ibid. 14:15 ff.).

27. Therefore the world did not have eternal life, because it had not received the Spirit. But where the Spirit is, there is eternal life; for he is the Spirit who produces eternal life.

[Note: [Col. 0748D] A few manuscripts read: “Hence I sometimes marvel.”]

Hence I marvel that the Arians raise a question concerning the only true God. For just as eternal life is to know the only true God, so eternal life is to know Jesus Christ, and so eternal life is to know the Holy Spirit. The world does not see him in the same way that it does not see the Father; it does not know him in the same way that it does not know the Son.

[Note: [Col. 0748D] Several manuscripts read: “in the same way that it does not know the Father.”]

But whoever is not of this world possesses eternal life, and the Spirit remains with him forever—the Spirit who is the light of eternal life.

28. Therefore, if knowledge of the only true God confers what knowledge of the Son and the Spirit confers, why do you separate the Son and the Spirit from the honor due to the true God, when you do not separate them from the greatness of the benefit? For either you must believe that this supreme gift belongs to the only true divinity, and confess that the only true divinity belongs, as to the Father, so also to the Son and the Spirit; or, if you say that the one who is not the true God can also confer eternal life,

[Note: [Col. 0748D] Some manuscripts read: “the one who is not the true God can confer eternal life; will you not thus fall into the position of seeming,” etc.]

you will appear to derogate still more from the Father, whose work you will think is not the special work of the only true divinity but something to be compared with the works of a creature.

## CHAPTER FOUR

That the Holy Spirit, no less than the Father and the Son, gives life through an operation that is not different
