29. What wonder, then, if the Spirit is the giver of life, since he gives life as the Father does and as the Son does (John 5:21)? Who would deny that giving life belongs to eternal majesty? For it is written: “Give life to your servant” (Ps. 118:17). Thus the one who is a servant—that is, a human being—is given life: previously he did not possess life, but in order to possess it, he received it.

30. Let us therefore see whether the Spirit is given life or gives life himself. But it is written: “The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3:6). Therefore the Spirit gives life.

31. But so that you may understand that the giving of life by the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is not divided, understand that there is also unity in the giving of life, since God gives life through the Spirit himself. For Paul said: “He who raised Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies because of his Spirit dwelling in you” (Rom. 8:11).

## CHAPTER FIVE

That Scripture signifies the Holy Spirit as creator, just as it does the Father and the Son. This is also shadowed forth by pagan writers, but demonstrated most clearly in the mystery of the incarnation; after Ambrose has touched upon some aspects of it, he confirms the argument begun from the fact that the worship owed to the creator alone is also owed to the Spirit

32. Who, then, can doubt that the Holy Spirit gives life to all things, since he too, like the Father and the Son, is creator of all things,

[Note: [Col. 0749D] Several manuscripts read: “and that almighty God the Father is never understood to have acted except with the Spirit.”]

and almighty God the Father is not understood to have acted without the Holy Spirit, since even at the beginning of creation “the Spirit was borne over the water” (Gen. 1:1)?

33. Therefore, while the Spirit was borne over it, creation possessed no grace; but after this world’s creation also received the Spirit’s operation, it deserved all the beauty of grace by which the world shone. Finally, the Prophet declared that the grace of the universe cannot remain without the Holy Spirit, saying: “When you take away their Spirit, they fail and return to their dust. Send forth your Spirit, and they will be created, and you will renew the face of the earth” (Ps. 103:29–30). Thus he taught not only that all creation cannot stand without the Spirit, but also that the Spirit is the creator of the whole creation.

34. And who can deny that the earth was made by the work of the Holy Spirit, when its renewal is also his work? For if they wish to deny that it was created through the Spirit, while they cannot deny that it is renewed through the Spirit, they will defend the position that the operation of the Holy Spirit is better than that of the Father and the Son, whom they seek to separate from it. That is abhorrent to the truth; for there is no doubt that the renewed earth is better than the earth as created.

Or, if the Father and the Son first made the earth without the operation of the Holy Spirit, and afterward the operation of the Holy Spirit was joined to it, what was made would appear to have needed the assistance of what was added. But may no one suppose this, so that the divine operation might be thought to possess the variation of a creator that Manichaeus introduces.

[Note: [Col. 0749D] What the Manichaeans understood by “the variation of the creator” can be learned clearly from Epiphanius. For in *Heresy* 66, no. 25, when he recounts the ravings that Manichaeus had borrowed from Archelaus, he provides much that illuminates this passage of Ambrose.]

35. Or do we suppose that the substance of the earth exists without the work of the Spirit, without whose work even the vaults of heaven do not endure? For it is written: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power” (Ps. 32:6). Observe what he says: he refers all the power of the heavens to the Spirit. For how could the one who was borne over the waters before the earth existed be idle when the earth was being made?

[Note: [Col. 0749D] Amerbach, Erasmus, and several manuscripts read: “was not borne”; Gill and the Roman edition, with more manuscripts, read: “was at rest.”]

36. The Gentiles,

[Note: [Col. 0749D] Gregory of Nazianzus, *Oration* 37, testifies that the operation of the Holy Spirit in governing the world was represented under certain veils of names by those pagans who flourished in the greater reputation for theology and approached nearer to us—namely, Aristotle, Anaxagoras, and Hermonymus, as Elias of Crete interprets it. There is no doubt that Ambrose follows Gregory of Nazianzus here; but because he was writing for Latin readers, he wished to indicate an authority more familiar to them. That authority was taken from book VI of Virgil’s *Aeneid*, where it is sung:

> In the beginning, the Spirit within nourishes heaven and earth, the liquid plains,  
> the shining globe of the moon and the Titanic stars;  
> infused through its limbs, Mind moves the whole mass  
> and mingles itself with the great body.]

following us in a kind of shadow because they could not draw in the truth of the Spirit, inserted into their verses that the Spirit within nourishes heaven and earth, and even the globes of the moon and the gleaming stars. Thus they do not deny that the power of creation subsists through the Spirit, while we, who read this, deny it? But you think that by “spirit” they meant a material breath. If they declared a material spirit to be the author of all things, do we hesitate to say that the Spirit of God is the creator of all things?

37. But why linger over foreign writers? Let them receive an evident proof that nothing can exist which the Holy Spirit is denied to have made. Nor can it be doubted that angels, archangels, thrones, and dominions subsist through his operation, since the Lord himself, according to the flesh, whom angels served, was born when the Spirit came upon the Virgin. Thus, according to Matthew, the angel said to Joseph: “Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary your wife; for what has been begotten in her is from the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 1:20). And according to Luke he said to Mary: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you” (Luke 1:35).

38. The Virgin’s childbirth, therefore, is the work of the Spirit. The fruit of the womb is the Spirit’s work, according to what is written: “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb” (ibid., 42). The flower of the root is the Spirit’s work: that flower, I mean, of which it was rightly prophesied: “A shoot will come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower will rise from his root” (Isa. 11:1). Jesse’s root is the patriarchal family of the Jews; the shoot is Mary; Mary’s flower is Christ. He was to spread the good fragrance of faith throughout the whole world and therefore sprang from a virginal womb, as he himself said: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song 2:1).

39. A flower preserves its fragrance even when cut, and increases it when crushed; nor does it lose it when plucked. So too the Lord Jesus, on that gallows of the cross, neither withered when crushed nor vanished when torn away. Cut by the thrust of the spear, he blossomed more beautifully in the sacred color of the blood poured forth, himself knowing nothing of death,

[Note: [Col. 0751C] Several manuscripts read: “and having died,” which is not sufficiently correct.]

and breathing forth to the dead the gift of eternal life. In this flower of the royal shoot, therefore, the Holy Spirit rested.

40. The good shoot, as some think, is the Lord’s flesh. Rising from an earthly root toward heavenly things, it spread throughout the world the fragrant fruits of sacred religion, pouring forth the mysteries of divine generation and grace upon the heavenly altars.

41. We therefore cannot doubt that the Spirit is creator, since we recognize him as the author of the Lord’s incarnation. For who could doubt this when, at the beginning of the Gospel, you have it that Christ’s generation was as follows: “When Mary had been betrothed to Joseph, before they came together, she was found to have conceived in the womb from the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 1:18)?

[Note: [Col. 0751C] Several manuscripts read: “from the Holy Spirit.” Although most do not have this wording, the Greek nevertheless reads, etc. Augustine explains very clearly the difference between the prepositions *ex* and *de* in chapter 27 of *On the Nature of the Good*. Discussing the Apostle’s text “because from him and through him,” which had been brought forward against the Manichaeans, he says: “From him” does not mean the same as “of him.” What is “of him” may be called “from him,” but not everything that is “from him” is rightly called “of him.” Heaven and earth are from him because he made them, but they are not of him, because they are not of his substance, etc. Likewise, in the *Acts with Felix the Manichaean*, book II, when the heretic asked whether the rational soul was truly from God, Augustine replied: “From God, not of God.” Nevertheless, good authors do not always speak with such strictness, but frequently use these particles interchangeably and in the same sense. Indeed, in the Vulgate translation, where the translator is generally more cautious, he rendered almost every place where the Greek manuscripts have ἐκ with *de*. Ambrose himself sometimes disregarded this distinction, as will appear below in chapter 9, no. 94 ff.; for there, to prove that “from him” can also apply to the Holy Spirit, he freely adduces testimonies in which *de* is used for *ex*, and above, in no. 88, explicitly affirms that all things are “of the Spirit.”]

42. Although most copies have “of the Spirit,” the Greek text from which the Latins translated says ἐκ Πνεύματος ἁγίου, that is, “from the Holy Spirit.” What is from something is either from its substance or from its power. It is from its substance in the case of the Son, who says: “From the mouth of the Most High I came forth,” as is also the case with the Spirit, who proceeds from the Father (Sir. 24:5). Of the Spirit the Son says: “He will glorify me, because he will take from what is mine” (John 16:14). It is from power in the case of the saying: “There is one God, the Father, from whom are all things” (1 Cor. 8:6).

43. How, then, did Mary have in her womb something from the Holy Spirit? If it was as from his substance, did the Spirit therefore change into flesh and bones? Certainly not. If the Virgin conceived as a result of his operation and power, who can deny that the Spirit is creator?

44. What of Job, who plainly shows the Spirit to be his creator, saying: “The divine Spirit who made me” (Job 33:4)? In a single verse he demonstrated both that the Spirit is divine and that he is creator. [Elsewhere, chapter 6.] If, therefore, the Spirit is creator, he is certainly not a creature; for the Apostle distinguished creature and creator, saying: “They served the creature rather than the Creator” (Rom. 1:25).

45. At the same time he admonishes us to serve the Creator, condemning those who serve the creature, since we owe service to the Creator.

[Note: [Col. 0751D] Some manuscripts read: “At the same time he admonishes us to serve the Creator, showing that those who serve [the creature] are condemned. And since the Spirit is creator, he teaches us to serve him,” etc.]

And because he knew the Spirit to be creator, he teaches that he must be served, saying: “Beware of the dogs, beware of the evil workers, beware of the mutilation; for we are the circumcision, who serve the Spirit of God” (Phil. 3:2–3).

[Note: [Col. 0752C] Seven manuscripts read thus; all editions and a few manuscripts read “who serve God in the Spirit”; still others, fewer in number, read “who serve God with the Spirit.” Augustine, in book III of *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, chapter 7, reports three readings of this passage but does not say which he prefers. In book I of *On the Trinity*, chapter 6, however, he observes that in all or nearly all Greek copies and in many Latin ones it is written “who serve the Spirit of God,” while the reading “who serve God with the Spirit,” found in some copies, is an error. Since shortly before this he clearly appears to designate Ambrose—understood not only from the fact that Augustine is known to have read these books, but also because the same testimonies from Paul and Matthew cited here are likewise cited in the mentioned chapter of book I of *On the Trinity*—we may infer that the corruption of which the Arians are accused consisted in replacing “the Spirit of God” with “God with the Spirit.” The legitimate reading, therefore, is the one we adopt. Although the editions of Erasmus and those following him, as well as several manuscripts, give the Greek words as οἱ Πνεύματι Θεῷ λατρεύοντες, many manuscripts and Amerbach give only Πνεύματι λατρεύοντες. Erasmus himself, in his note on this passage of the Apostle, acknowledges that our reading is Ambrose’s. Zezerus follows the same reading and defends it not only on Ambrose’s and Augustine’s authority but also on Salvian’s.]

46. If anyone disputes this on the basis of the variation among Latin manuscripts, some of which the treacherous have falsified, let him examine the Greek copies and observe that they contain: οἱ Πνεύματι Θεοῦ λατρεύοντες, which the Latin translates: “who serve the Spirit of God.”

47. Therefore, since the same Apostle says that the Spirit must be served, while asserting that service is owed not to a creature but to the Creator, he plainly shows that the Holy Spirit is creator and is to be venerated with the honor of eternal divinity, because it is written: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Matt. 4:10).

## CHAPTER SIX

To those who object from Amos’s words that the Spirit is created, it is answered that the word there is to be understood of the wind, which is often created; but this cannot be said of the Holy Spirit, since he is eternal and cannot be dissolved by death or by heretical transfer to the Father. If they press more stubbornly that the same passage was written about the Holy Spirit, one must return to the spiritual interpretation: Christ, by his coming, established the thunder—that is, the force of the divine words. The human soul is signified by the Spirit, just as the flesh assumed by Christ is also signified. Since each person of the Trinity is truly creator, it follows that the Spirit is likewise the author of the Lord’s incarnation, having already been asserted to be the creator of all things.

48. [Elsewhere, chapter 7.] I am not unaware that heretics have been accustomed to object that the Holy Spirit appears to be created because many of them enlist, in support of their impiety, the passage in which Amos spoke of the breath of the winds, as the prophetic speech itself makes clear. Thus you have it: “Behold, I am the one who establishes thunder and creates the spirit, and announces his Christ to human beings, making light and mist, and ascending upon the heights; the Lord God almighty is his name” (Amos 4:13).

49. If they raise the question from this passage because he said that the Spirit was created—since Esdras taught us that the Spirit is created, saying [Note: [Col. 0753D] Nearly all old editions and manuscripts have this in the Third Book. Indeed, there is nothing to prevent this reading from being Ambrose’s; for we observed in our Admonition to the book *On the Good of Death* that these books of Esdras are variously divided in different manuscripts.] in the Fourth Book: “And on the second day you again created the spirit of the firmament” (IV Esdr. VI, 41)—nevertheless [Note: [Col. 0753D] Several manuscripts, as you have proposed: “let us adhere,” etc.] so that we may adhere to what has been proposed, namely, to what Amos said, does not the sequence of the statements clearly testify that the prophet was speaking of this creation of the world?

[Col. 0753C] 50. Finally, he began in this way: “I am the Lord, who establishes thunder and creates the spirit.” Let the order itself teach us; for if he had wished to speak of the Holy Spirit, he certainly would not have mentioned thunder first. For thunder is not older than the Holy Spirit—although they are impious, they nevertheless do not dare to say this. Further, when we see that what follows concerns light and cloud, is it not clear that this should be understood as having been said of the creation of the world? For whenever storms arise in this world, we know from daily experience and observation that thunder comes first, blasts of wind follow, the sky grows dark with clouds, and light is poured back out of the darkness. The blasts of winds are also called “spirit,” as it is written: “Fire and brimstone and the spirit of storms” (Ps. X, 7).

51. And so that you might know that he spoke of this spirit, he says: [Col. 0753D] “establishing thunder and creating the spirit”; for these things are frequently created when they occur. But the Holy Spirit is eternal; and even if someone dares to say that he was created, he nevertheless cannot say that he is created every day, as are the gusts of wind. Finally, Wisdom herself, speaking according to the mystery of the body assumed [Note: [Col. 0753D] The same manuscripts: “having spoken of the assumption of the body,” etc.], says: “The Lord created me” (Prov. VIII, 22). Although she was prophesying what was to come, nevertheless, because the coming of the Lord and Savior had been predestined, she did not say, “He creates me,” but “He created me,” so that they would believe that Jesus’ body was to be generated from the Virgin Mary not repeatedly, but once.

52. Therefore, this too, which the prophet described as a daily work of God in the establishment of thunder and in the creation of the spirit, it is impious to understand as though we should attribute anything of the kind to the Holy Spirit. Even the impious cannot deny that he existed before the ages; and so we affirm in faithful testimony both that he always exists and that he always remains. For he who was borne over the waters before the world (Gen. I, 2) cannot be thought to have begun after the world; nor is it right to suppose that there are many Holy Spirits, generated as though by daily generation. Far be it that anyone should pollute himself with such impiety [Col. 0754B] as to say that the Holy Spirit is frequently created, or ever created. For I do not understand why he should be thought to be created frequently—unless perhaps they also believe that he frequently dies and is frequently created. But how can the Spirit of life die? Therefore, if he cannot die, there is no reason why he should need to be created repeatedly.

53. [Note: [Col. 0753D] Several manuscripts read: “But those who think in this way.”] But those who think otherwise fall into the sacrilege of failing to distinguish the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0754D] We have made some observations on this return of the Word into the Father in chapter 13 of Book V of *On the Faith*, no. 162. Here, however, we shall note that what is argued throughout this chapter in response to the objection drawn from the passage in Amos was also argued by Didymus, as well as by Basil in Book III *Against Eunomius*; nor is it unrelated to Jerome’s exposition of the same passage of the cited prophet.]—those who think that the prolative Word returns into the Father and that the prolative Spirit is poured back into God—so that there is one return and a kind of alternation in something repeatedly changing itself into different forms, whereas the distinction of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit remains always immutable and holds the unity of its power.

54. Nevertheless, if someone thinks that the prophetic statement should be referred to an interpretation concerning the Holy Spirit because it says, “announcing his Christ to human beings” (Amos IV, 13), he will more readily refer it to the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation. For if you are troubled because he said “spirit,” and therefore do not think that this should be referred to the mystery of the assumption of humanity, follow the Scriptures, and you will find that it agrees perfectly with Christ. It is fitting to understand that he established the thunders by his coming—that is, the force and sound of the heavenly Scriptures, by whose thunder, so to speak, our minds are struck with awe, so that we may learn to fear and show reverence to the heavenly oracles.

55. Finally, in the Gospel the Lord’s brothers were called “sons of thunder”; and when the Father’s voice came, saying to the Son, “I have glorified, and I will glorify again” (John XII, 28), the Jews said, “Thunder has occurred for him” (ibid., 29). Although they could not draw in the grace of truth, nevertheless, unwillingly and unknowingly, they confessed it and spoke the mystery, because the Father’s great testimony concerning the Son resounded. In the Book of Job also Scripture says: “Who knows when he will make the firmament of his thunder” (Job XXVI, 14)? Certainly, if this referred to the thunders of heavenly disturbances, he would have said that their firmaments were future, not that they had been made.

56. Therefore, we understand “thunders” in this passage as referring to the Lord’s words, whose sound has gone out into all the earth; but “spirit” as referring to the soul that he assumed, rational and perfect. For Scripture frequently designates the human soul by the term “spirit,” as you have it: “Who creates the spirit of a human being within him” (Zech. XII, 1). Thus the Lord too, signifying his soul by the designation “spirit,” says: “Into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke XXIII, 46).

57. And so that you might know that he had spoken of the Lord Jesus’ descent, he added that he would announce his Christ to human beings [Col. 0755B] (Amos IV, 13). For he announced him at the baptism, saying: “You are my most beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. III, 17). He announced him on the mountain, saying: “This is my beloved Son; listen to him” (Matt. XVII, 17). He announced him in the passion, when the sun withdrew and the seas and earth trembled. He announced him through the centurion, who said: “Truly this was the Son of God” (Matt. XIV, 33).

58. Therefore, we must refer this entire passage either to the literal understanding of this breath, which is inhaled in living, or to the mystery of the Lord’s body. For if he had said here that the Holy Spirit was created, Scripture could certainly have declared the same elsewhere, just as we frequently read concerning the Son of God that, according to the flesh, he was both made and created (Rom. I, 3).

[Col. 0755C] 59. Nevertheless, we ought to contemplate his majesty in the very fact that he assumed flesh for us, so that we may see divine power in that assumption of the body itself [Elsewhere chapter VIII]. For just as we read that the Father created the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation, so also that the Spirit created it; and we likewise read that Christ himself created his own body. The Father created it, according to what is written: “The Lord created me” (Prov. VIII, 23); and elsewhere: “God sent his Son, [Note: [Col. 0755D] Several manuscripts: “born of a woman.” And below: “having been conceived in the womb from the Holy Spirit.”] made of a woman, made under the Law” (Gal. IV, 4). The Spirit also created that entire mystery, according to what we read: “Mary was found to be with child from the Holy Spirit” (Matt. I, 18).

60. You have it that the Father created and that the Spirit created. Accept also that the Son of God created, when Solomon says: [Col. 0755D] “Wisdom built herself a house” (Prov. IX, 1). Therefore, how can the Holy Spirit, who created the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation—a mystery surpassing all creatures—be a creature?

61. We have shown above (above, chapter 5) that, with respect to the general principle, the Holy Spirit is our creator according to the flesh in the outward human being [Note: [Col. 0755D] The same manuscripts: “Now let us show in the inward being. The Father created thus, and the Son created thus, and the Holy Spirit.”]; now let us show that he is also our creator according to the mystery of grace. And just as the Father creates, so also the Son creates, and so also the Holy Spirit creates, as we read in Paul’s words: “It is God’s gift, not from works, so that no one may boast; for we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works” (Eph. II, 8 ff.).

## CHAPTER VII

That the Spirit is no less the author of spiritual creation, or regeneration, than the Father and the Son. What that creation consists in, and its excellence; and how the sacred books’ statements that appear to attribute members and a body to God should be understood.

62. [Elsewhere chapter IX.] Therefore the Father creates us for good works; the Son also creates, because it is written: “But to all who received him he gave power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name—who were born not from bloods, nor from the will of the flesh, nor from the will of a man, but from God” (John I, 12–13).

63. Likewise, the Lord himself testifies that we are reborn from the Spirit according to grace, saying: “What is born from flesh is flesh, because it is born from flesh; and what is born from spirit is spirit, because God is spirit. Do not marvel that I said to you: You must be born again. The Spirit breathes where he wills, and you hear his voice, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes; so is everyone who is born from the Spirit” (John III, 6 ff.).

64. It is therefore clear that the Holy Spirit is also the author of spiritual generation, because we are created according to God so that we may be God’s children. Therefore, when he has taken us into his kingdom through the adoption of sacred regeneration, do we deny him what belongs to him? He has made us heirs of heavenly regeneration; do we claim the inheritance but reject its author? But the benefit cannot remain when its author is excluded; neither is there an author without a gift, nor a gift without an author. If you claim the grace, believe in the power; if you reject the power, do not seek the grace. [Note: [Col. 0755D] All editions and not a few manuscripts: “Who denied Christ immediately also lost the name”; but eight other manuscripts, more elegant, as in our text.] Whoever denied the Spirit immediately denied the gift as well. For if the author is worthless, how can the gifts be precious? Why do we begrudge ourselves our own gifts, diminish our hope, reject our dignity, and deny the Comforter?

65. But we cannot deny him [Note: [Col. 0756D] Several manuscripts: “we cannot.” “Do we deny him? Far be it.” Less elegantly.]. For far be it from us to deny what is greatest, since the Apostle says: “But you, brothers, are children of the promise according to Isaac; but just as then the one born according to the flesh persecuted the one born according to the Spirit” (Gal. IV, 28–29). Here too, what was said above is evidently understood: “the one born according to the Spirit.” Therefore, whoever is born according to the Spirit is born according to God. We are reborn when our disposition is renewed inwardly and we put off the oldness of the outward human being [Note: [Col. 0756D] Many manuscripts: “we put off the old desires.”]. And therefore the Apostle says again: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new human being, who was created according to God in truth, righteousness, and holiness” (Eph. IV, 23–24). Let them hear how Scripture marks the unity of divine operation: whoever is renewed in the spirit of his mind puts on the new human being, who was created according to God.

66. This regeneration, then, is the more excellent work of the Holy Spirit; and the Spirit is the author of this new human being, who is created in the image of God. No one will doubt that this is better than our outward human being. Indeed, the Apostle indicates that one is heavenly and the other earthly, saying: “As is the heavenly one, so also are the heavenly ones” (I Cor. XV, 48).

67. Therefore, since spiritual grace makes us heavenly, we must also understand by reason that it can create what is earthly, even though we lack examples [Note: [Col. 0757D] The edition: “although we believe by examples.”]. For holy Job says elsewhere: “The Lord lives, who judges me, and the Almighty, who has brought my soul to bitterness; but the divine Spirit, which is in my nostrils” (Job XXVII, 2–3). Here he certainly did not designate the vital breath or bodily respiration by “spirit,” but signifies by “nostrils” the inward human being, by which he inhaled the scent of eternal life and drew in the grace of heavenly ointment through a kind of twofold sense.

68. For there are spiritual nostrils, as we read, which the Bride of the Word possesses, to whom it is said: “And the scent of your nostrils” (Song VII, 8); and elsewhere: “The Lord smelled the fragrance of sweetness” (Gen. VIII, 21). There are therefore certain inward members of the human being, whose hands are understood in action, ears in hearing, and feet in a certain progress of good work [Note: [Col. 0757D] The Roman edition alone: “hands in touching.” But nothing should be changed in the common reading; for the hand is not only for touching, but much more for acting and working.]. Thus, from their functions, we gather what may be called figures of the members; for it is not fitting for us to think of anything in the inward human being according to bodily categories.

69. [Elsewhere chapter X.] And there are some who think that God is formed bodily [Note: [Col. 0757D] All editions and several manuscripts: “to be formed.” Not incorrectly, for this is equivalent to being expressed by an image or figure. But other manuscripts more simply read: “to have been formed,” that is, configured and composed in outward appearance. Ambrose appears here to be attacking the Anthropomorphites, or Vadiani, concerning whom see Epiphanius, *Heresies* 70, and Augustine, *On Heresies*, chapter 5.] when they read of his hand or finger. They do not perceive that these things were not written on account of the form of a body, since there are neither members nor parts in the Godhead, but were expressed on account of the unity of the Godhead, so that we may believe that it is impossible for either the Son or the Holy Spirit to be separated from God the Father, since the fullness of divinity dwells, as it were bodily, in the substance of the Trinity. Therefore the Son is also called the Father’s right hand, as it is written: “The right hand of the Lord has done powerfully; the right hand of the Lord has exalted me” (Ps. CXVII, 16).

## CHAPTER VIII

He refutes the subtle argument of the heretics who would insist that God is to be glorified “in the Spirit,” but not “with the Spirit,” in order to infer from this that the Spirit is inferior. He makes clear why the particle “in” can also be applied to the Son, and even to the Father; conversely, he shows that it can be attributed also to creatures without any injury to divinity, and therefore that in these same prepositions the conjunction of the divine persons is to be simply recognized.

70. But what wonder if foolish people make an issue of words, [Note: [Col. 0757D] There is no doubt that the people Ambrose here identifies are the same who gave Basil the occasion to write his book *On the Holy Spirit*, namely the Aetians. Basil relates that when he sometimes concluded prayers in the Church’s assembly by offering glory to God the Father, at times “with his Son,” and at times “through the Son in the Holy Spirit,” some were offended by that prayer as strange to Christian ears. He therefore refuted their error—which he says had arisen partly from Aetius’ arguments and partly from the opinions of pagan philosophers—in the work mentioned. Ambrose follows this doctrine throughout this and the following chapter.] when they make an issue even of syllables? There are those who think that a distinction must be made on this basis: they say that God is to be proclaimed “in the Spirit,” not “with the Spirit”; and they think that some significance regarding the Godhead should be inferred from a single syllable or from a particular usage. They argue that if they say that God is to be proclaimed “in the Spirit,” they appear to indicate the ministry of the Holy Spirit; but if they say that God’s power or glory is “with the Spirit,” they appear to designate a certain fellowship and communion of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

71. But who can separate what cannot be separated? Who can divide the fellowship that Christ showed to be indivisible? “Go,” he says, “baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII, 19). Did he here change either a word or a syllable concerning the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit? Certainly not. Rather, he says, “in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” The same thing is heard concerning the Spirit as concerning the Father and himself. Therefore, when “in the Spirit” is said, it is understood not as any ministry of the Holy Spirit, but rather as a sharing in honor or work.

72. Consider here also that this prejudice of your opinion extends to the Father and the Son, because he did not say, “with the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,” but “in the name.” Yet this syllable does not express some ministry of the Trinity, but power.

73. Finally, so that you may know that the syllable does not prejudice faith, but that faith commends the syllable [Note: [Col. 0758D] The old edition: “but that faith convinces the syllable”; the Roman edition and several manuscripts: “but that the syllable commends faith”; the remaining manuscripts, including the more numerous and better ones, as in the text.], Paul too speaks “in Christ.” Nor is Christ therefore lesser because Paul spoke “in Christ,” as you have it: “We speak before God in Christ” (II Cor. II, 6). Just as the Apostle says, “we speak in Christ,” so also it is said, “we speak in the Spirit,” as the Apostle himself said: “No one says, ‘Lord Jesus,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (I Cor. XII, 3). Therefore, what is designated here is not the subordination of the Holy Spirit, but a bond of grace.

74. And so that you may know that the distinction does not depend on the syllable, he says elsewhere also: “And such were some of you; but you were washed, but you were sanctified, but you were justified in the name of Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God” (I Cor. VI, 11). How many examples can I produce from this! For it is written: “You are all one in Christ Jesus” (Gal. III, 26); and elsewhere: [Note: [Col. 0759D] The Roman edition: “sanctified in Christ Jesus.” And again: “so that we might become the righteousness of God … Thus may your thoughts fall away from chastity.” The old edition and certain manuscripts: “sanctified in Christ Jesus.” And again: “so that we might be … so that they may fall away from faith.” The remaining manuscripts agree with us, except that one has “fall away from truth” instead of “fall away from chastity.] “sanctified in Christ Jesus” (I Cor. I, 2); and again: “so that we might be the righteousness of God in him” (II Cor. V, 21); and elsewhere: “so that they may fall away from the chastity that is in Christ Jesus” (II Cor. XI, 3).

75. But what am I doing? While I say that the same thing is written concerning the Son as is written concerning the Spirit [Col. 0759B], I expose myself even more to their objection: that what is religiously said concerning the Spirit is not so because it is written concerning the Son, but because the same thing is written concerning the Spirit, they claim that it has been derogated from the Son on account of the Spirit [Note: [Col. 0759D] Thus the old edition with very many manuscripts; but the Roman edition with a few others: “they object that it should be diminished.”]. For they say: “Is it perhaps written concerning God the Father?”

76. But let them accept that it is also said concerning God the Father: “In the Lord I will praise the word” (Ps. LV, 5); and elsewhere: “In God we will perform power” (Ps. LIX, 14); and: “In you is my remembrance always” (Ps. LXX, 16); and: “In your name we will rejoice” (Ps. LXXXVIII, 17) [Note: [Col. 0759D] The Roman edition: “they will rejoice”; other editions and manuscripts: “we will rejoice”; some, however: “we rejoiced.”]; again elsewhere: “so that his works may be revealed, because they have been done in God” (John III, 21); and Paul says: “In God, who created all things” (Eph. III, 9); and again: “Paul and Silvanus and Timothy to the Church of the Thessalonians in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (I Thess. I, 1); and in the Gospel: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John XIV, 10); and: “The Father who remains in me” (ibid.). It is also written: “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord” (II Cor. X, 17); and elsewhere: “Our life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. III, 3). Did he here honor the Son more than the Father by saying that we are in God with Christ? Or does our condition claim more for itself than the grace of the Spirit, so that we can be with Christ but the Holy Spirit cannot? And when Christ wishes to be with us, as he himself said, “Father, I will that where I am, they also may be with me whom you have given me” (John XVI, 24), would he disdain to be with the Spirit? It is also written: “When you assemble, and my spirit, with the power of the Lord Jesus” (I Cor. V, 4) [Note: [Col. 0759D] Several manuscripts: “in the power of the Lord Jesus.” Incorrectly.]. Therefore, we assemble with the power of the Lord, and yet we dare to say that the Lord Jesus does not wish to assemble with the Spirit, although he does not disdain to assemble with us.

[Col. 0760A] 77. The Apostle therefore considers that there is no distinction depending on whether you use one syllable or the other. For the syllable signifies conjunction, and conjunction does not make separation; indeed, if it divided, it would not be called conjunction.

78. Why, then, does it trouble you to say that glory, life, power, magnificence, and authority belong to God the Father or to his Christ “in the Holy Spirit,” while you are unwilling to say “with the Holy Spirit”? Is it because you fear that you would appear to associate the Spirit with the Father and the Son? But hear what is written concerning the Spirit: “For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus” (Rom. VIII, 2). And elsewhere God the Father says: “And they will worship you, and in you they will pray” (Isa. XLV, 14). God the Father says that we ought to pray in Christ; and you think that the Spirit is diminished if it is said that the glory of Christ is in him?

[Col. 0760B] 79. Hear that the Apostle did not fear to claim for himself what you fear to confess concerning the Spirit. He says: “To be dissolved and to be with Christ is much better” (Phil. I, 23). With whom, then, is the Apostle? You deny that the Spirit is with the one with whom the Apostle merited to be through the Spirit.

80. What reason is there, then, for preferring to say that the glory of God or of Christ is “in the Spirit” rather than “with the Spirit”? Is it because, if you say “in the Spirit,” the Spirit is declared to be lesser than Christ? [Note: [Col. 0759D] All editions and many manuscripts: “Christ is declared lesser than the Spirit”; nevertheless, seven manuscripts of better quality have the reading in the text. The sense most clearly requires this reading.] Although it is plainly objectionable to make the Lord greater and the Spirit lesser, nevertheless, since it is written: “Christ was made sin for us, so that we might be the righteousness of God in him” (II Cor. V, 21), he is found to be most powerful in whom we are most lowly [Note: [Col. 0760D] All editions and many manuscripts have this reading; some others: “he is found in whom we are powerful, not weak”; some: “he is found in whom we, above all, are weak”; others differ from the editions only in adding the word “placed” to “we are.”]. So also you have it elsewhere: “For all things subsist in him” (Col. I, 17), that is, in his power. Those things that subsist in him cannot be compared with him, since they receive their substance from his power in order that they may subsist.

81. Do you therefore wish God to reign “in the Spirit” in such a way that the Spirit’s power should furnish God’s reign with its beginning, as though it were some source of substance? But this is impious. And therefore our predecessors, in order to declare the one power of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, used to say that the glory of Christ is “with the Spirit.”

82. For how is the Holy Spirit separated from the Son, when the Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit that we are children of God? “But if children, then heirs—heirs indeed of God, and co-heirs of Christ” [Col. 0760D] (Rom. VIII, 16–17). Who, then, could be so insane as to separate the everlasting conjunction of the Spirit and Christ, when through the Spirit we become co-heirs of Christ, and the Spirit even joins together what is separated?

83. “If indeed we suffer with him, so that we may also be glorified with him” (ibid.). Therefore, if through the Spirit we are glorified together with Christ, how can we refuse to say that the Spirit himself is glorified together with Christ? We separate the life of Christ and the Holy Spirit, although the Spirit says that we shall live together with the Son of God. For the Apostle says: “But if we have died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live together with him” (Rom. VI, 8); and elsewhere: “For if we suffer together,” he says, “we shall also live together; and not only shall we live together, but we shall also be glorified together; and not only shall we be glorified together, but we shall also reign together” (II Tim. II, 11–12).

84. There is therefore no distinction in these syllables; for both syllables signify conjunction. Finally, we often find one inserted and the other understood in the Scriptures, as it is written: “I will enter your house with burnt offerings” (Ps. LXV, 13), that is, “with burnt offerings”; and elsewhere: “He brought them out,” it says, “in silver and gold” (Ps. CIV, 37), that is, “with silver and gold.” Elsewhere also it says: “You will not go out in powers with us” (Ps. XLIII, 10), in place of “with powers.” Therefore, since there can be no calumny in ordinary usage of speech, and no calumny ought to be raised against divinity from speech, it is necessary that one believe unto righteousness with the heart, and that confession be made with the mouth unto salvation from faith in the heart (Rom. X, 10). But those who do not believe with the heart construct calumny with words.

## CHAPTER IX

He explains the apostolic passage that the heretics abused in order to introduce a distinction among the divine persons. Having exposed the impiety of the heretical interpretation, he shows that the passage in its entirety can rightly be said of each individual person; nevertheless, he asserts that it properly concerns the Son. Finally, what he had affirmed—that all the parts of the same passage apply to each person—he confirms with many testimonies; and from the very fact that it belongs to the Father to be said to be “from him are all things,” he skillfully concludes that “through him” and “in him” can likewise be attributed to the same person.

85. Finally, the same is true of the statement in which they say that there is a distinction because it is written: “But for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and we are for him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we are through him” (I Cor. II, 6). For when it says “from him,” they want matter to be designated; when it says “through him,” they want either an instrument of the work or a ministry to be indicated; but when it says “in him,” they want either the place or the time in which all things appear to have been made to be signified.

86. Thus they desire to prove a certain difference of substance, striving to separate an instrument from its proper worker or author, and to distinguish time or place from the instrument. Is the Son therefore alien in nature from the Father because an instrument is alien from its proper worker or author? Or is the Son alien from the Spirit because a place or time is separated from the category of an instrument?

87. Now compare our assertions. They want matter to be “from God,” as though from God’s nature, so that, just as one says that an ark is made from wood and a statue from stone, so matter proceeded from God, and that same matter was made through the Son as through some instrument. Thus they indicate that the Son is not so much the worker as the instrument of the work; and they say that all things were made “in the Spirit,” as though they were made in some place or time. They assign each thing to a separate person and deny all things in common.

88. But we show that all things are so from God the Father that God the Father has not lost anything by the fact that all things are through him and in him, nor are all things from him as from matter. Likewise, all things are through the Lord the Son in such a way that he is not deprived of the fact that all things are from the Son [Note: [Col. 0761D] “And are in him” is lacking in all editions and in not a few manuscripts; nevertheless, we have restored it from six other manuscripts of better quality. A little later, where all manuscripts and the old edition read “all things from God,” only the Roman edition has “all things from the Father.”.], and are in him. And all things are in the Spirit in such a way that we teach that all things are through the Spirit and all things are from the Spirit.

89. For these syllables, like those of which we spoke above, signify one another. The Apostle did not say: “All things are from God, and all things are through the Son,” in order to indicate that the substance of the Father and Son is separable, but in order to teach, without confusion, that the one is the Father and the other the Son. These syllables are therefore not mutually hostile, but allied and harmonious, so that they often apply to one person, as it is written: “For from him and through him and in him are all things” (Rom. XI, 36).

90. If you truly consider where this statement was taken from, you will not doubt that it was said of the Son. For the Apostle speaks according to the prophecy of Isaiah: “Who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?” (Isa. XL, 13). And he added: “For from him and through him and in him are all things.” Isaiah said this of the maker of all things, as you have it: “Who measured the waters with his hand, and heaven with a span, and the whole earth with a closed hand? Who established the mountains on a scale and the hills on a balance? Who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?” (Isa. XL, 12).

91. And the Apostle added: “Because from him and through him and in him are all things.” What does “from him” mean? That the nature of all things is from his will, and that he is the author of all things that began to exist. What does “through him” mean? That constitution and continuance have been imparted to all things through him. What does “in him” mean? That all things look upon the author of life and the dispenser of his grace and gift with a certain marvelous longing and indescribable love, according to what is written: “The eyes of all hope in you”; and: “You open your hand and fill every living thing with good according to your will” (Ps. CXLIV, 15).

92. If you say the same concerning the Father—“from him,” because from him is the Wisdom that works, which gave existence, from its own will and the Father’s, to all things that did not exist; “through him,” because all things were made through his Wisdom; “in him,” [Note: [Col. 0763D] All editions and some manuscripts: “because he is in him”; a great number of other manuscripts: “because he is himself.”] because he is the source of life-giving substance, in whom we live and exist and move—

93. and if you say the same concerning the Spirit, so that, formed through him, established through him, and strengthened in him, we may receive the gift of eternal life [Note: [Col. 0763D] Some manuscripts: “that we may receive eternal life.”—]

94. when these things therefore appear to apply either to the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit, it is certain that nothing lowly is demonstrated in them; for we say that most things are from the Son, and many through the Father, as you have it said concerning the Son: “That we may grow in him in all things, who is Christ the head, from whom,” he says, “the whole body, joined and connected through every supporting joint according to the measure of each part, produces the body’s growth for its building up in love” (Eph. IV, 15–16). And again, in Colossians, concerning those who did not possess knowledge of the only-begotten Son of God: “They do not hold fast to the head,” he says, “from whom the whole body, supplied and joined together through its joints and connections, grows with the growth of God” (Col. II, 19). For we have stated above that Christ is the head of the Church (Col. I, 18). And elsewhere you have it that “from his fullness we have all received” (John I, 16). The Lord himself also said: “He will take from what is mine and announce it to you” (John XVI, 14). And above he said: “I knew that power had gone out from me” (Luke VIII, 46).

95. Likewise, so that you may recognize the unity, it is also said concerning the Spirit: “Whoever sows in the Spirit will reap eternal life from the Spirit” (Gal. VI, 8). And John says: [Col. 0763C] “By this we know that he is in us, because he has given us from his Spirit” [Note: [Col. 0763D] Several manuscripts: “because he is in us, from his Spirit whom,” etc.]. And the angel says: “What will be born from her is from the Holy Spirit” (Matt. I, 20). And the Lord says that “what is born from the Spirit is spirit” (John III, 6).

96. Therefore, just as we read that all things are from the Father, so we are taught by testimonies that all things can also be said to be from the Son, through whom all things are, and that all things are from the Spirit, in whom all things are.

97. Now let us consider whether we can teach that something is through the Father. But it is written: “Paul, servant of Christ, through the will of God” (I Cor. I, 1); and elsewhere: “Therefore he is no longer a servant, but a son; and if a son, also an heir through God” (Gal. IV, 7); and elsewhere: “Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father” (Rom. VI, 4). And elsewhere God the Father says to the Son: “Behold, proselytes will come to you through me” (Isa. LIV, 15).

98. You will find many other things, if you inquire into what has been done through the Father. Is the Father therefore lesser because we read that many things are in the Son and from the Son, and find in the heavenly Scriptures that very many things have been done [Note: [Col. 0764D] All editions: “or spoken”; all manuscripts: “or given.”] or given through the Father?

99. But we likewise read that many things have been done through the Spirit, as you have it: “But God revealed them to us through his Spirit” (I Cor. II, 10); and elsewhere: “Guard the good deposit through the Holy Spirit” (I Tim. I, 14); and to the Ephesians: “To be strengthened through his Spirit” (Eph. III, 16); and to the Corinthians: “To one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom” (I Cor. XII, 8); and elsewhere: “But if through the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live” (Rom. VIII, 13); and above: “He who raised Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you” (ibid., 11).

100. But perhaps someone will say: “Show me specifically where it is read that all things are from the Son, or all things are from the Spirit.” But I reply by asking that they show me where it is read that all things are through the Father. Yet when we have proved that these expressions apply to the Father, or to the Son, or to the Holy Spirit, and that no distinction of divine power can arise from such syllables, there is no doubt that we must understand “through whom are all things” to mean “from whom are all things,” and “from whom are all things” to mean “through him are all things,” and “in whom are all things” to mean “through him [possibly: from him] are all things.” For every creature exists both from the will, through the operation, and in the power of the Trinity, as it is written: “Let us make man according to our image and likeness” (Gen. I, 26); and elsewhere: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power” (Ps. XXXII, 6).

## CHAPTER X

Intending to prove that the Trinity has one will, one calling, and one command, he teaches that, just as the Father and the Son called the Church, so also the Spirit called it. He demonstrates this from the election of Paul and Barnabas, but especially from Peter’s mission to Cornelius. Here, briefly touching upon the power of the same Spirit and Peter’s threefold confession, he declares that the calling of the Gentiles was foreshadowed in the vision of that apostle; although previously like wild beasts, they laid aside their savagery through the Spirit’s work. Then, having established the foregoing from another passage, he shows that in Jeremiah—when he was lowered into a cistern by the Jews and then brought out by Abdemelech—a symbol had gone before of the Holy Spirit, held in contempt by those same Jews but honored by the Gentiles whom he purified.

101. [Elsewhere ch. XI.] Not only is the operation of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit everywhere one, but their will, calling, and command are likewise one and the same. This can be observed in that great and salutary mystery of the Church. For just as the Father called the Gentiles to the Church, saying, “I will call the one who was not my people, my people, and the one who was not beloved, beloved” (Hos. II); and elsewhere, “My house shall be called a house of prayer for all nations” (Isa. LVI, 7), so also the Lord Jesus says that Paul was chosen by him to call forth and gather the Church, as you find the Lord Jesus saying to Ananias: “Go, for this man is a vessel of election for me, to carry my name before the Gentiles” (Acts IX, 15).

[Note: Several manuscripts read “and not chosen, chosen.”]

102. Therefore, just as God the Father called the Church, so Christ also called it; and just as Christ called, so the Spirit also called, saying: “Set apart for me Paul and Barnabas for the work to which I have called them.” Then, he says, “after fasting and praying, they laid their hands on them and sent them away.” They, sent ahead by the Holy Spirit, arrived in Seleucia (Acts XIII, 2 ff.). Thus Paul received his apostleship not only by the command of Christ but also by the command of the Holy Spirit, and he hastened to gather the Gentiles.

103. Nor was it Paul alone, but also Peter, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles. While he was praying, he saw heaven opened and a certain vessel, tied at its four corners, like a sheet, in which were all kinds of four-footed animals, wild beasts, and birds of the air. A voice came to him: “Rise, kill, and eat.” And Peter said: “By no means, Lord; I have never eaten anything common or unclean.” And the voice came to him again: “What God has cleansed, do not call common.” This happened three times, and the vessel was taken back into heaven (Acts X, 11 ff.). Therefore, while Peter was silently pondering this within himself, and the servants of Cornelius, sent by the angel, had come to him, the Spirit said to him: “Behold, men are seeking you. Rise, then, go down, and go with them; do not hesitate, because I have sent them” (ibid., 19–20).

104. How clearly did the Holy Spirit display his power! First of all, because he inspired the one who was praying and was present with the one who was entreating; then because, when Peter was called, he answered, “Lord,” and therefore deserved a second, clearer oracle, since he confessed the Lord. But Scripture makes clear who this Lord is: the one responding was speaking to the one to whom he had responded. The following words show that it was the Spirit who had been revealed, because the one who was foreshadowing the mystery was himself revealing the mystery.

105. Observe also that, by repeating the figure of the mystery three times, he expressed the operation of the Trinity. Therefore, in the mysteries the interrogation is made threefold and the confirmation is celebrated threefold; no one can be cleansed except by a threefold confession. Hence Peter himself is questioned three times in the Gospel (John XXI, 15) whether he loves the Lord, so that by a threefold response the bonds which he had contracted by denying the Lord—and with which he had bound himself—might be released.

[Note: Some more reliable manuscripts read: “so that by a threefold response he might release the bonds which he had tied by denying the Lord” (others, including the editions: “which he bound by denying the Lord”; the old edition: “which he bound”; the Roman edition: “with which he bound himself”).]

106. Then, because an angel is sent to Cornelius, the Holy Spirit addresses Peter (Acts X, 3): “For the eyes of the Lord are upon the faithful of the earth” (Ps. C, 6). Nor is it without significance that, after he had earlier said, “What God has cleansed, do not call common” (Acts X, 15), the Holy Spirit suddenly fell upon the Gentiles, so that he might cleanse them. From this it is shown that the Spirit’s operation is a divine operation. Peter, sent by the Spirit, did not await a command from God the Father; rather, he confessed that the oracle belonged also to the Spirit and testified that the grace belonged to the Spirit himself, saying: “If, therefore, God granted them the same grace as he granted us, who was I that I could hinder God?” (Acts XI, 17).

107. It is therefore the Holy Spirit who cleansed us from that Gentile filth. In those kinds of four-footed animals, wild beasts, and birds was an image of human nature, which appears to have put on a beastly savagery after the manner of wild animals, unless it is softened by the sanctification of the Spirit. Good, therefore, is the grace which changes bestial rage into spiritual simplicity.

[Note: Some manuscripts read “which changes through the Spirit and simplicity.”]

“For we too were once foolish, disobedient, deceived, enslaved to various desires and pleasures; but now, through the renewal of the Spirit, we have begun to be heirs of Christ and fellow heirs with the angels” (Titus III, 3).

108. Thus the holy prophet David, seeing in the Spirit that we would become like the heavenly beings rather than wild beasts, says: “Rebuke the beasts of the forest” (Ps. LXVII, 32), signifying by “forest” not one resounding with the rush of wild animals or bristling with the groans of beasts, but that forest of which it is written: “We found it in the fields of the forest” (Ps. CXXXI, 6). In it, as the Prophet said, “the righteous shall flourish like the palm tree and shall multiply like the cedar that is in Lebanon” (Ps. XCXI, 13). That is the forest from which the nourishment of the heavenly Word poured down when the crowns of the prophetic trees were shaken. That is the forest into which Paul entered as a ravening wolf but came out as a shepherd: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth” (Ps. XVIII, 5).

109. We were therefore wild beasts, and for this reason the Lord says: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves” (Matt. VII, 15). But through the Holy Spirit the fierceness of lions, the spotted nature of leopards, the cunning of foxes, and the rapacity of wolves have now disappeared from our dispositions. Great, therefore, is the grace that has changed earth into heaven, so that, as the Apostle said (Phil. III, 20), our manner of life is in heaven, although previously, like wild beasts, we wandered in the forests.

110. Nor did the apostle Peter demonstrate only here, but also elsewhere in the same book, that the Church was built by the Holy Spirit. For you find him saying: “God, who knows the hearts of men, bore witness by giving them the Holy Spirit, just as he did to us; and he made no distinction between us and them, cleansing their hearts by faith” (Acts XV, 8–9). Here we must observe that, just as Christ is the cornerstone who joined together the unity of both peoples, so also the Holy Spirit did not distinguish between the hearts of the two peoples but united them.

111. Therefore, do not, as a Jew, despise the Son whom the prophets announced; do not despise the Holy Spirit; do not despise Isaiah; do not despise Jeremiah, whom that man, taken up by the Lord from the cistern of the Jewish household, lifted out with rags and ropes (Jer. XXXVIII, 10). For the Jewish people, despising the prophetic word, had thrown him into the cistern. Yet no one among the Jews was found to lift up the prophet; only an Ethiopian, Abdemelech, did so, as Scripture testifies.

[Note: The Roman edition here and below reads “with rough rags.” The other editions and the manuscripts omit “rough”; in the Bibles the word is “old” or “rotten.”]

112. In this name there is a most beautiful figure: the prophetic word, which the Jews had thrust down as though into the mud of their mind and flesh, we sinners from the Gentiles—formerly black with sins and once unfruitful—have lifted from the depths (ibid., 11). Therefore it is written: “Ethiopia shall lift up her hands to God” (Ps. LXVII, 32).

[Note: Some manuscripts read “prevailed”; one reads “will offer first”; the others and the editions read “will lift up first.” The Greek has προφθάσει, “will anticipate,” “will precede,” and so forth.]

In this the figure of the holy Church is signified. She says in the Song of Songs: “I am black and beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem” (Song I, 4): black through guilt, beautiful through grace; black by nature, beautiful through redemption;

[Note: The manuscripts read: “or perhaps black through guilt.”]

or certainly black from the dust of her labor. She is black while she fights; she is beautiful when she is crowned with the insignia of her victory.

113. And rightly is the prophet lifted by ropes, for the faithful man said: “The ropes have fallen for me in splendid places” (Ps. XV, 6). And rightly by rags, because the Lord himself, when those who had first been invited to the wedding made excuses, sent messengers to the exits of the roads so that all whom they found, both good and bad, might be invited to the wedding (Matt. XXII, 9–10). With these rags, therefore, he lifted the prophetic word from the mud.

## CHAPTER XI

We shall imitate Abdemelech if we believe that the Son and the Holy Spirit know all things. Scripture attributes this knowledge to the Spirit; it attributes the same to the Son. The Son is glorified by the Spirit, just as the Spirit is glorified by the Son. Likewise, from the fact that we read that the Father, Son, and Spirit speak and reveal the same things, we must recognize in them unity of nature and knowledge. Finally, the Spirit’s searching of the deep things of God does not imply ignorance, since the Father and the Son are also called searchers, and Paul, although chosen by Christ the Lord, was nevertheless instructed by the Spirit.

114. You too, then, will be an Abdemelech—that is, one taken up by the Lord—if you lift the Word of God from the depths of Gentile ignorance; if you believe that he is not deceived; that the Son of God is not passed over and does not fail to know what is to come; and that the Holy Spirit also is not deceived, of whom the Lord says: “When that Spirit of truth has come, he will lead you into all truth” (John XVI, 13). When he says “all,” he omits nothing—not the day, not the hour, neither past nor future things.

115. And so that you may know that he also knows all things and announces the future, and that he has one knowledge with the Father and the Son, hear what the Truth of God says about him: “For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will announce to you the things that are to come” (ibid.).

116. Thus, so that you may understand that he knows all things, when the Son said, “But concerning that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels of heaven” (Mark XIII, 32), he excluded the Holy Spirit. But if the Holy Spirit was excluded from ignorance, how was the Son of God not also excluded?

117. But you say that he numbered the Son of God among the angels. He did indeed number the Son, but he did not number the Spirit. Either, then, admit that the Holy Spirit is superior to the Son of God, so that you now speak not only like an Arian but also like a Photinian; or recognize how you ought to understand the statement that he said the Son did not know.

[Note: Thus read the editions and many more manuscripts. Others read: “Would that he had said not only … the Son of God.”]

For, as man, he who was created could be numbered among creatures.

118. But if you wish to learn that the Son of God knows all things and possesses foreknowledge of all future things, then whatever you think was unknown to the Son, the Holy Spirit received from the Son. He received it through unity of substance, just as the Son received from the Father: “He will glorify me,” he says, “because he will receive from what is mine and announce it to you. Everything that the Father has is mine; therefore I said that he will receive from what is mine and announce it to you” (John XVI, 14–15). What could be clearer than this unity? What the Father has belongs to the Son; what the Son has, the Spirit also received.

119 and 120*. Nevertheless, accept that the Son knows the day of judgment. It is written in Zechariah: “And the Lord my God will come, and all the holy ones with him. On that day there will be no light, but cold and frost; and there shall be one day, and that day shall be known to the Lord” (Zech. XIV, 5). This, then, is the day known to the Lord, who will come with his holy ones to enlighten us at his second coming.

121. But let us pursue what we began concerning the Spirit. For in the example cited above you have the Son saying of the Spirit: “He will glorify me.” The Spirit therefore glorifies the Son, just as the Father also glorifies him; but the Son of God also glorifies the Spirit, as we said above. He is not therefore weak who returns glory in mutual exchange through the unity of eternal light; nor is he inferior to the Holy Spirit, by whom he himself is glorified.

122. You too will be taken up, then, if you believe that the Spirit spoke what the Father spoke and what the Son spoke. Finally, Paul was taken up for this reason: because he believed and taught in this way, because “what eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, the things God has prepared for those who love him, he revealed to us through his Spirit,” as it is written (I Cor. II, 9–10).

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “Paul was taken up by God.”]

And therefore the Spirit is called the Spirit of revelation, as you find: “For God gives the Spirit of wisdom and revelation to those who prepare themselves for the recognition of him” (Isa. LXIV, 4).

[Note: Some manuscripts add after “for the recognition of him”: “For just as the Father knows the Son, so the Son knows the Father, and so the Spirit knows God the Father; and just as the Father reveals to us what belongs to him, so also the Son, and so the Holy Spirit has revealed.” Since the same words occur elsewhere in certain other manuscripts, while in others they are not part of the text but serve as headings, just as in the old editions—where they appeared there with slight changes, at the beginning of chapter 12—we have decided to place them only in the margin, so that you may learn how carelessly or arbitrarily scribal copyists behaved in such matters.]

123. There is therefore unity of knowledge: just as the Father reveals, who gives the Spirit of revelation, so also the Son reveals, because it is written: “No one knows the Son except the Father; nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wills to reveal him” (Matt. XI, 27). He said more about the Son—not because the Son has more than the Father, but lest he be thought to have less. And it is not without reason that the Father is revealed in this way by the Son, because the Son knows the Father in the same way that the Father knows the Son.

124. Now accept that the Spirit also knows God the Father. For it is written: “Just as no one knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man that is in him, so also no one has known the things of God except the Spirit of God” (I Cor. II, 11). “No one,” he says, “has known them except the Spirit of God.” Is the Son of God therefore excluded? Certainly not, because neither is the Holy Spirit excluded when it is said: “Nor does anyone know the Father except the Son.”

125. Therefore the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one both in nature and in knowledge. Nor is the Spirit to be numbered among all the things that were made through the Son, since he knows God the Father, whom, as it is written (Matt. XI, 27), no one can know except the Son. But the Holy Spirit also knows him. What follows, then? When the totality of creatures is mentioned, the Holy Spirit is not included.

126. Now let them answer: what is there in man that knows the things of man? Certainly it is the rational faculty, which surpasses the other powers of the soul and by which the distinctive nature of man is judged. What, then, is the Spirit who knows the deep things of God, through whom Almighty God is revealed? Is he inferior in the fullness of divinity, although this example also proves him to be of the same substance as the Father? Can he be ignorant of anything who knows God’s counsels and his mysteries hidden from the beginning? What could he not know who knows all that belongs to God? For the Spirit also searches the deep things of God (I Cor. II, 10).

127. And lest you think that he searches what is unknown and searches it in order to learn what he does not know, he first stated that God revealed to us through his Spirit:

[Note: Some manuscripts read “his Spirit.” The reading “He first stated that God revealed to us, so that you might learn at once …” is less suitable.]

at the same time, so that you might learn that the Spirit knows the things revealed to us through that Spirit, he says later: “For who knows the things of a man except the spirit of man that is in him? So also no one has known the things of God except the Spirit of God.”

[Note: Most manuscripts read: “except the spirit of man that is in him,” and so everywhere.]

Therefore, if the spirit of man knows the things of man, and knows them before it searches them, can there be anything belonging to God that the Spirit of God does not know? Concerning him the Apostle did not say casually: “The things of God no one has known except the Spirit of God”—not that he came to know them by searching, but that he knows them by nature; not that knowledge of divine things is accidental in him, but that it is natural knowledge.

128. But if it troubles you that he said “searches,” accept that this too is written of God, since he is the searcher of hearts and kidneys. For he himself said: “I am he who searches hearts and kidneys” (Jer. XVII, 10). You also have concerning the Son of God in Hebrews: “He is the searcher of the mind and thought” (Heb. IV, 12). Hence it is clear that no inferior being searches the inner things of a superior; for it belongs solely to divine power to know hidden things. Likewise, then, the Holy Spirit is a searcher, as is the Father; likewise the Son is a searcher. This is expressed by the particular character of the language, so that it may be seen that there is nothing he does not know, and that nothing escapes him.

129. Finally, he who was chosen by Christ was instructed by the Spirit. For, as he himself testifies, having attained knowledge of the divine mystery through the Spirit, he shows that the Spirit knows God and that the Spirit revealed to us the things of God, just as the Son also revealed them. And he added: “We have not received the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God, so that we may know the things given to us by God. These things we also speak, not in words taught by human wisdom to persuade, but in a demonstration of the Spirit and of the power of God” (I Cor. II, 12–13).

## CHAPTER XII

Having proved that the Spirit reveals just as the Father and the Son do, he explains how that same Spirit does not speak from himself. He shows that bodily organs must not be imagined in him, nor any inferiority fabricated from the fact that he is said to hear, since the same would have to be attributed to the Son; indeed, also to the Father, since the Father too hears the Son. The Spirit is therefore said to hear and glorify the Son in the sense that he revealed him to the prophets and apostles. From this the unity of the operation of the three persons is established; and since the Spirit performs the same works, it is likewise declared that he and the Father have the same substance.

130. It has therefore been proved that, just as God revealed to us the things that belong to him, and the Son revealed the things that belong to God, so also the Spirit revealed them. From one Spirit, through one Son, our knowledge proceeds to the one Father; and from one Father, through one Son, goodness, sanctification, and the sovereign right of eternal power are transmitted to the one Holy Spirit. Where, therefore, there is a manifestation of the Spirit, there is the power of God;

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “there is the power of God,” which may constitute a distinct reading.]

and there can be no distinction where the work is one. Therefore, what the Son speaks, the Father also speaks; what the Father speaks, the Son also speaks; and what the Father and the Son speak, the Holy Spirit also speaks.

131. Hence the Son of God said concerning the Spirit: “For he will not speak from himself” (John XVI, 13), that is, not without communion with me and the Father. For the Spirit is not divided or separated, but he speaks what he hears—hearing, that is, through unity of substance and through the particularity of knowledge. For he does not receive hearing through bodily openings, nor does a voice resound through certain bodily modes of divine utterance, nor does he hear something he does not know. Among human beings, hearing often produces knowledge; yet even among human beings speech is not always bodily address or bodily hearing: “The one who speaks in tongues,” he says, “does not speak to men but to God. For no one hears him, but in the Spirit he speaks mysteries” (I Cor. XIV, 2).

132. Therefore, if hearing is not always bodily even among human beings, do you demand in God the sound of human weakness and certain bodily organs of physical hearing, when he is said to hear so that he may be understood to know? We know what we have heard, and first we hear so that we may be able to know. But in God, who knows all things before they occur, knowledge precedes hearing. Thus, so that we may say that the Son does not fail to know what the Father wills, we speak of his having heard; but in God there is no sound or syllable such as ordinarily signifies an indication of the will. Rather, the unity of will is understood through divine mysteries, while among us it is signified by outward indications.

133. What, then, does “he will not speak from himself” mean? It means that he does not speak without me, because he will speak truth and inspire wisdom. He does not speak without the Father, because he is the Spirit of God; he does not hear from himself, because all things are from God.

134. The Son received all things from the Father, because he himself said: “All things have been handed over to me by my Father” (Matt. XI, 27). The Son possesses all the things of the Father, because he says again: “All things that the Father has are mine” (John XVI, 15). And what he himself received through unity of nature, the Spirit also received from him through the same unity, as the Lord Jesus himself declares when speaking of his Spirit: “Therefore I said, he will receive from what is mine and announce it to you” (ibid.). What the Spirit speaks belongs to the Son; what the Son gave belongs to the Father. Thus neither the Son nor the Spirit speaks from himself, because the Trinity speaks nothing outside itself.

135. But if you attempt to refer this to some weakness of the Holy Spirit or to a certain resemblance to bodily baseness, you will also refer it to an insult against the Son, because the Son also said of himself: “As I hear, I judge”; and, “The Son cannot do anything else except what he sees the Father doing” (John V, 30).

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “The Son cannot do anything else.”]

For if it is true—as it certainly is true—that the Son said, “All things that the Father has are mine” (ibid., 19), and if according to his divinity the Son is one with the Father, one through natural substance, though not one person according to Sabellian impiety, then this unity, which exists through the property of substance, cannot be separated. Therefore the Son cannot do anything except what he has heard from the Father, because the Word of God remains forever (Ps. CXVIII, 89), and the Father is never divided from the Son’s operation. What the Son does, he knows the Father wills; and what the Father wills, the Son knows how to do.

136. Finally, lest you think that there is any difference of work between the Father and the Son either in time or in order, but believe in the unity of the same operation, he says: “The works that I do, he himself also does” (John V, 17). And again, lest you perceive any distinction in the differentiation of works, but judge that the Father and the Son have the same will, do the same things, and possess the same power, Wisdom says to you concerning the Father: “Whatever he does, the Son does likewise” (ibid., 19). The act is therefore neither prior nor second for either of them, but the effect of one and the same operation. Thus the Son is said to be able to do nothing from himself because his operation cannot be separated from the Father’s. Likewise, the operation of the Holy Spirit is not separated. Hence he too is said to hear the things that he speaks from the Father.

137. What if I show that the Father also hears the Son, just as the Son hears the Father? For you have it written in the Gospel that the Son says: “Father, I thank you because you have heard me” (John XI, 41). How did the Father hear the Son, when earlier the Son had said nothing to the Father concerning Lazarus? And lest you think that the Son was heard by the Father only once, he added: “And I knew that you always hear me” (ibid., 42). Therefore the hearing is not one of subordinate obedience, but of eternal unity.

138. Likewise, then, the Spirit is said to hear from the Father and to glorify the Son. He glorifies him because the Holy Spirit taught us that the Son of God is the image of the invisible God, the radiance of his glory, and the impress of his substance (Col. I, 15; Heb. I, 1–2).
