For the Spirit spoke both in the patriarchs and in the prophets; and finally the apostles began to become more perfect after they had received the Spirit. There is therefore no distinction in divine power or grace. For although there are divisions of graces, the Spirit is the same; and although there are divisions of ministries, the Lord is the same; and although there are divisions of operations, the God who works all things in all is the same (I Cor. XII, 4 ff.).

[Note: Three manuscripts read: “and although there are divisions of mysteries.”]

There are divisions of gifts, not separations within the Trinity.

139. Finally, it is the same God who works all things in all, so that you may know that there is no distinction of operation between God the Father and the Holy Spirit, since the Father, who works all things in all, also performs the works that the Spirit performs. For although the Father works all things in all, “to one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith in the same Spirit, to another gifts of healings in the one Spirit, to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another discernment of spirits, to another kinds of tongues, to another interpretation of tongues. But all these things the one and same Spirit works, distributing to each as he wills” (ibid., 8 ff.).

140. There is therefore no doubt that the things the Father performs are also performed by the Spirit. Nor does he operate by command, as one who hears bodily operates, but by will, since he possesses free choice and is not the servant of another’s power. He does not obey as one commanded; rather, as the giver, he governs his own generosity.

141. Consider for the moment whether you will say that the Spirit performs all the things that the Father performs. Yet you cannot deny that the Father performs what the Holy Spirit performs;

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “Now consider … but it cannot nevertheless be denied.”]

otherwise the Father would not perform all things if he did not perform the things that the Spirit performs. But if the Father also performs the things that the Spirit performs, and the Spirit distributes his own operations according to his will, you must either say that the Spirit distributes them according to his own will against the will of God the Father, or, if you say that the Father wills the same thing as the Holy Spirit, you must confess—whether unwillingly and not in your heart, yet at least with your mouth—the unity of the divine will and operation.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “the one will of the divine operation.”]

142. But if the Holy Spirit has one will and one operation with God the Father, then he also has one substance, since the Creator is recognized from his works. “The same Spirit,” he says, “the same Lord, the same God” (ibid., 5). Whether you say “Spirit,” he is the same; whether you say “Lord,” he is the same; whether you say “God,” he is the same. Not the same in the sense that the Father himself, the Son himself, and the Spirit himself are one and the same person, but because the Father and the Son also have the same power. He is therefore the same in substance and power, because in divinity there is neither Sabellian confusion, nor Arian distinction, nor earthly and bodily change.

## CHAPTER XIII

Prophecy came not only from the Father and the Son but also from the Spirit. The same command and operation of the Spirit with them is signified in the apostles; and from this the unity of command, establishment, and generosity in the three is to be understood. Nevertheless, no prejudice need be feared from this fellowship, since it has no place even in human friendship. Finally, it is confirmed that this is the inheritance of apostolic faith by the fact that the apostles are said to have obeyed the Holy Spirit.

143. Accept another example, holy Emperor, a powerful example familiar to you. “In many portions and in many ways God also spoke to the fathers in the prophets” (Heb. I, 1). And the Wisdom of God said: “I will send prophets and apostles.” And, as it is written, “to one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith in the same Spirit, to another gifts of healings in the one Spirit, to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy” (Luke XI, 49; I Cor. XII, 8 ff.). Therefore, according to the Apostle, prophecy came not only through the Father and the Son but also through the Holy Spirit; and so there is one gift and one grace. You have, therefore, that the Spirit too is the author of prophecies.

[Note: Thus read the majority of the more authoritative manuscripts. Others, together with all the editions, insert the word “example.” We think there is no other reason for removing it than that “example,” when speaking of testimonies from Scripture, seemed too inappropriate. Nevertheless, anyone who examines this treatise more carefully will find the same word used in this sense more than once.]

144. The apostles also said: “It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us” (Acts XV, 28). When they say “it seemed good,” they show that the Spirit is not only the worker of grace but also the author of the execution of what was commanded. For just as we read concerning God, “It pleased God,” so also, when it is said that it seemed good to the Holy Spirit, he is shown to be the arbiter of his own power.

145. And how could he not be its arbiter, who speaks what he wills and commands what he wills, just as the Father commands and the Son commands? For just as Paul heard a voice saying to him, “I am Jesus whom you are persecuting” (Acts XVI, 7), so also the Spirit forbade Paul and Silas to go into Bithynia. And just as the Father spoke through the prophets, so Agabus says concerning the Spirit: “Thus says the Holy Spirit: The man whose belt this is will be bound in this way in Jerusalem” (Acts XXI, 11). And just as Wisdom sent the apostles, saying, “Go into all the world and preach the Gospel” (Mark XVI, 15), so the Holy Spirit says: “Set apart for me Paul and Barnabas for the work to which I have called them” (Acts XIII, 2). Thus, sent ahead by the Holy Spirit, as Scripture indicates below, they had no distinction from the other apostles, as though some were sent in one way by God the Father and others in another way by the Spirit (ibid., 4).

146. Finally, when Paul had been sent by the Spirit, was the vessel of Christ’s election, and acknowledged that God had worked in him, saying, “For he who worked in Peter for the apostleship to the circumcised also worked in me for the Gentiles” (Gal. II, 8), since the same one worked in Paul who worked in Peter, this plainly shows that, since the Spirit worked in Paul, the Holy Spirit also worked in Peter. But Peter himself also testifies that God the Father worked in him, as it is recorded in the Acts of the Apostles: “Men and brothers, you know that from the early days God chose among us that the Gentiles should hear the word of the Gospel from my mouth” (Acts XV, 7). Behold, then, God worked the grace of preaching in Peter. Since he was chosen and taken up through Christ, who would dare deny the operation of Christ, when the Lord himself says: “Feed my little lambs” (John XXI, 15)?

147. The operation of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is therefore one—unless perhaps you think, you who deny the unity of their work toward the apostles, that the Father and the Spirit worked in Peter in whom the Son had worked because the Son’s operation contributed nothing to his grace. Thus, as though the powers of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit had been added and combined, you would make their operation multiple, lest Christ’s operation alone prove insufficient to strengthen Peter.

148. Not only is there found one operation of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit in Peter, but the unity of the divine operation is also revealed in all the apostles [Col. 0774D], together with a certain authority of heavenly appointment. For divine operation has command, not ministry; for when God operates, he does not force anything out by labor or by craft, but “he spoke, and they came to be” (Ps. 32:9). He said, “Let there be light,” and there was light (Gen. 1:3); for in God’s command lies the effect of his operation.

[Col. 0775A] 149. If we wish to observe this royal power, which has also been conferred upon the Holy Spirit by the testimony of Scripture, we can easily find it; and it will be revealed that all the apostles were not only disciples of Christ, but also ministers of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Thus also the Teacher of the Gentiles instructs us, saying: “God has appointed some in the Church: first apostles, second prophets, third teachers; then powers, gifts of healings, helps, administrations, kinds of tongues” (1 Cor. 12:28).

150. Behold: God appointed apostles, appointed prophets and teachers, gave the gift of healings—which above you have seen to be given through the Holy Spirit—and gave kinds of tongues. Yet not all are apostles, not all prophets, not all teachers. “Not all,” he says (ibid., 10), “have the gift of healings,” nor, he says, “do all speak in tongues.” For all divine gifts cannot exist in each individual person: according to his capacity, each receives what he either desires or deserves. But the power of the Trinity is not like this weakness, for it is the munificent source of all graces.

151. Finally, God appointed the apostles. Those whom God appointed in the Church, Christ chose and appointed as apostles, and he sent them throughout the world, saying: “Go into the whole world and preach the Gospel to every creature. Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved; but whoever does not believe will be condemned. These signs will accompany those who believe: in my name they will cast out demons, [Col. 0775C] they will speak in new tongues, they will pick up serpents; and if they drink anything deadly, it will not harm them. They will lay hands on the sick, and they will be well” (Mark 16:15 ff.). Behold: the Father appointed teachers, and Christ too appointed them in the Churches; and just as the Father gives the gift of healings, so also does the Son; just as the Father gives the gifts of tongues, so also has the Son bestowed them.

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads, “and he named them apostles.”]

152. Likewise, we learned above concerning the Holy Spirit that he bestows the same kinds of graces. For, he says, “through the Spirit the gift of healings is given to one, kinds of tongues to another, prophecy to another” (1 Cor. 12:9–10). Therefore the Spirit gives the same gifts that the Father gives, and the Son also gives. Let us now receive more explicitly what we touched upon above: the Holy Spirit also commands the same office as the Father and the Son, and appoints the same ministers. For Paul said: “Pay attention to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has appointed you bishops [Note: Some manuscripts read, “to govern the Church of the Lord.”] to rule the Church of God” (Acts 20:28).

153. There is therefore unity of command, unity of appointment, and unity of bestowal. For if you separate appointment from power, what reason would there be that those whom Christ appointed as apostles, God the Father should appoint, and the Holy Spirit should appoint as well—unless perhaps they feared, as men, some prejudice arising from a partnership in possession or right [Note: Some manuscripts read, “they feared a prior claim”; others, more numerous and authoritative, and all editions read, “they feared prejudice.” Below, where all editions and a few manuscripts read “the command was destroyed,” the more numerous and better manuscripts more aptly read “the command was distributed.”]? And so the operation was divided and the command distributed.

154. Such distinctions are narrow and trivial among human beings, who nevertheless often agree in will even when they do not agree in action. Hence, when someone was asked what a friend was, he replied, “Another self.” [Note: We have no doubt that Ambrose here means Cicero. We have cited this saying, taken from Cicero’s *On Friendship*, in the final chapter of Ambrose’s *On Duties*, book III, where friendship and friends are discussed.] If, then, a human being defined a friend by saying that he was another self—namely, through unity of love and grace—how much more ought we to esteem the unity of majesty in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, since through the same operation and divinity there is expressed either unity or, indeed, something greater, ταυτότης (*tautotēs*), as it is called in Greek? [Note: Some manuscripts read τὸ αὐτοῦ; an old edition reads ταυτὸν; the Roman edition and other manuscripts more correctly read ταυτὸ, “the same,” from which comes ταυτότης, which philosophers call “identity,” and to which ἑτερότης, “difference,” is opposed.] For ταυτὸ means “the same,” because the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit possess the same thing: thus their willing and their ability are not matters merely of affection or will, but belong to the substance of the Trinity.

155. This is the inheritance of apostolic faith and devotion [Note: Three manuscripts read, “the faith of the apostles and the inheritance of devotion.”], which may also be considered from the Acts of the apostles themselves. Paul and Barnabas therefore obeyed the commands of the Holy Spirit. All the apostles obeyed as well, and immediately appointed those whom the Spirit had ordered to be separated: “Separate for me Paul and Barnabas,” he says (Acts 13:2). Do you see the command of the one who orders? Consider the merits of those who serve.

156. Paul believed; and because he believed, he cast away the zeal of a persecutor and carried off the crown of righteousness. He who had devastated the Churches believed; but, converted to the faith, he preached in the Spirit what the Spirit commanded. The Spirit anointed his athlete and, having shaken off the dust of impiety, presented him as an unconquerable champion against unbelievers in various encounters with the impious; and through diverse sufferings trained him for the prize of the heavenly calling in Christ Jesus (Acts 9:20 ff.).

[Note: Three manuscripts read, “what God commanded.”]

157. Barnabas also believed, and because he believed, he obeyed. Thus, chosen by the command of the Holy Spirit—a command that redounded to him as a distinction of every kind of merit—he was not unworthy of so great a fellowship. For one grace shone forth in those whom the one Spirit had chosen.

158. Nor was Paul inferior to Peter, although Peter was the foundation of the Church, while Paul was a wise architect who knew how to lay the footsteps of believing peoples [Col. 0776D]; nor, I say, was Paul unworthy of the college of the apostles, since he could easily be compared with even the foremost and was second to no one. For the one who knows himself not inferior makes himself equal.

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 0777]

## CHAPTER ONE

Not only the prophets and apostles, but also the Son of God, were sent by the Spirit. This is proved from Isaiah and the Evangelists; and the reason why Luke wrote that the same Spirit descended like a dove and remained upon Christ is explained. Thereafter, Christ’s same mission having been confirmed, it is inferred that the Son is sent by the Father and the Spirit, just as the Spirit is sent by the Father and the Son.

1. In the preceding book (chapter 12), we demonstrated by clear testimonies of Scripture that the apostles and prophets were appointed by the Holy Spirit—those to prophesy, these to evangelize—just as they were appointed by the Father and the Son [Note: So Ambrose and Erasmus, with part of the manuscripts; Gill and the Roman edition, with another part, read “designated.” Moreover, the old editions make everything from the beginning of this chapter to the words “And the Lord sent me, and his Spirit,” found below in section 7, a preface. Then, after adding the title “Because the Spirit is upon Christ; and just as the Son sent the Spirit, so the Spirit sent the Son of God,” they begin chapter 1 with the words “Who is it that says,” and so forth. The Roman edition, however, following the greater number of manuscripts, much more coherently combined that preface with the following chapter into a single chapter. Some manuscripts also contain a brief preface, but one comprising only a few lines; it ends after the words in section 1, “they cannot doubt.” Then, in place of the title, the words that follow in the text are supplied, namely, “That the Spirit is upon Christ, and that just as he sent the Spirit, so the Spirit sent the Son of God.” Since these words are absent from several other manuscripts, and in the remainder agree with the title mentioned above just as they do in the editions, we regard them as considerably suspect.]—now we add what all must rightly marvel at and cannot doubt: that the Spirit is upon Christ, and that just as he sent the Spirit, so the Spirit sent the Son of God. For the Son of God says: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me; for this reason he anointed me, he sent me to evangelize the poor, to proclaim release to captives and sight to the blind” (Isa. 61:1). When he read this from the book of Isaiah, he said in the Gospel: “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” (Luke 4:21), indicating that it had been spoken of him.

2. Can we then be surprised that the Spirit sent both prophets and apostles, when Christ said: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me” (ibid., 18)? And he rightly said, “upon me,” because he was speaking as the Son of Man. As the Son of Man he was both anointed and sent to preach the Gospel.

3. But if they do not believe the Son, let them also hear the Father speaking, because the Spirit of the Lord is upon Christ. [Note: Five manuscripts read, “For John says.”] He says to John: “Upon whom you see the Spirit descending from heaven and remaining upon him, this is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit” (John 1:33). God the Father said this to John: John both heard and saw and believed. He heard from God, he saw in the Lord, and he believed that it was the Spirit who descended from heaven. For it was not a dove, but “as a dove,” that descended; thus it is written: “And I saw the Spirit descending from heaven like a dove” (Mark 1:10).

4. Just as John said that he had seen it, so Mark also wrote; but Luke added that the Holy Spirit descended in bodily form, like a dove (Luke 3:22), so that you would not think that it had been an incarnation, but a form. He therefore presented a form so that the one who did not see the Spirit might believe through the form, and so that through the form he might declare that the Spirit shared with the Father and the Son one honor in command, one operation in the mystery, and one gift in baptism [Col. 0778A]—unless perhaps we believe that it is ineffective for the servant to be baptized in the one in whom the Lord was baptized.

5. Beautifully, however, he said, “remaining upon him” (John 1:33), because whenever the Spirit wished, he either inspired the prophets with a word or acted through them; but he always remained in Christ.

6. Nor should it trouble us again that he said “upon him”; for he was speaking of the Son of Man, since he was baptized as the Son of Man. According to his divinity, however, the Spirit is not upon Christ but in Christ; for just as the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father, so the Spirit of God and the Spirit of Christ is both in the Father and in the Son, because he is the Spirit of the mouth. He remains in God who is from God, as it is written: “But we have not received the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God” (1 Cor. 2:12). And he remains in Christ, who received from Christ; and he is in Christ, because it is written again: “He will receive from what is mine” (John 16:14) [Note: Some manuscripts read, “He will receive from me.” But whether one reads “from me” or “from what is mine,” the sense is the same, since the Greek has ἀπ’ ἐμοῦ, “from me.”]; and elsewhere: “For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has freed me from the law of sin and death” (Rom. 8:2). Therefore, according to Christ’s divinity, the Spirit is not upon Christ, because the Trinity is not above itself but above all things; it is not above itself, but in itself.

7. Who, then, could doubt that the Spirit sent prophets and apostles, when the Son of God says: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me” (Luke 4:18)? And elsewhere: “I am the first, and I am forever; my hand founded the earth, and my right hand established heaven. I will call them, and they will stand together, and they will all be gathered and hear. Who declared these things to them? Loving you, I did your will against Babylon, so that the seed of the Chaldeans might be removed. I spoke, and I called; I led him and made his way prosperous. Draw near to me and hear these things. From the beginning I have not spoken in secret; when they were happening, I was there. And now the Lord God has sent me, and his Spirit” (Isa. 48:12 ff.). Who is it that says, “The Lord God and his Spirit sent me,” except the one who came from the Father to save sinners? When you hear that the Spirit also sent him, do not, when you read that the Son sends the Spirit, believe that the Spirit possesses an inferior power.

8. Therefore the Father sent the Son, and the Spirit did as well; the Spirit also was sent by the Father and the Son. The Father sent him, because it is written: “But that Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name” (John 14:26). The Son sent him, because he said: “But when that Paraclete comes, whom I will send you from the Father, the Spirit of truth” (John 15:26). If, then, the Son and the Spirit send one another, just as the Father sends, this is not an injury of subjection but a community of power.

## CHAPTER TWO

The Son is given in the same manner as the Spirit; hence not subjection but one divinity is demonstrated by their operation.

9. The Father not only sent the Son but also gave him, just as the Son himself gave himself. For we read: “Grace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, who gave himself for our sins” (Gal. 1:3–4). If they think that he was subordinate because he was sent, they cannot deny that he is the source of grace because he was given. He was given by the Father, as Isaiah said: “A child is born for us, a Son is given to us” (Isa. 9:6); but he was given, I dare say, also by the Spirit who was sent by the Spirit [Note: The Thuan manuscript reads, “and by the Spirit, who was sent by Christ.”]. Since the prophet did not specify by whom he was given, he showed that he was given by the grace of the Trinity; and since the Son himself gave himself, he certainly could not, according to his divinity, be subordinate to himself. Therefore, his being given could not be a matter of divine subjection.

10. The Holy Spirit also was given, because it is written: “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete” (John 14:16). The Apostle also says: “Therefore, whoever rejects these things rejects not a human being but God, who has given his Spirit in us” (1 Thess. 4:8). Isaiah likewise shows that both the Spirit and the Son were given: “Thus says the Lord God, who made heaven [Note: The Roman edition reads, “and fixed it.” The Greek idiom does indeed have καὶ πήξας αὐτόν, “and fixed it,” but the Hebrew, the Syriac version, and the common Latin version read “and stretched it out,” while the Arabic has “and raised it up.” This makes it clear that the reading of this passage varies.] and formed it, who established the earth and the things that are in it, and gives the Spirit to the people who are upon it, and the Spirit to those who tread upon it” (Isa. 42:5). And concerning the Son: “I, the Lord God, have called you in righteousness, and I will hold your hand and strengthen you; and I have given you as a covenant for my people, as a light to the nations, to open the eyes of the blind and to lead out those who are bound from their chains” (ibid., 6–7). Since, then, the Son was both sent and given, and the Spirit likewise was sent and given, they necessarily possess unity of divinity, since they possess unity of operation.

## CHAPTER THREE

The same unity is also recognized from the fact that the Spirit is called the finger and the Son the right hand; human speech assists the understanding of divine things. The tablets of the Law are shown to have been written by this finger and later broken, and the reason for this is explained; finally, Christ is shown to have written with the same finger. Yet no inferiority is to be admitted in the Spirit on the basis of bodily comparison.

11. Hence the Spirit is also called the finger of God, because the communion of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is undivided and inseparable. For just as Scripture called the Son of God the right hand of God, as we read: “Your right hand, Lord, has been glorified in strength; your right hand, Lord, has shattered the enemies” (Exod. 15:6), so the Holy Spirit is called the finger of God, as the Lord himself says: “But if I cast out demons by the finger of God” (Luke 11:20). [Col. 0780A] In another book of the Gospel, at the same place, he called this finger the Spirit of God, as you have it: “But if I cast out demons by the Spirit of God” (Matt. 12:28).

12. What, then, could have been said more explicitly to signify the unity of divinity or operation—which, according to divinity, belongs to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—than that we should understand that the fullness of eternal divinity would seem to be divided even more than our own body, if someone separated the unity of substance and multiplied the powers, when the eternity of the same divinity is one? [Note: Some manuscripts read, “this body of ours, rather than the fullness of the eternal…”]

668 13. It is often appropriate to estimate what is above us from our own speech; and because we cannot see those things, let us draw conclusions from what we can see. “For his invisible attributes,” says the Apostle, “are understood and perceived from the creation of the world through the things that have been made” (Rom. 1:20). He added: “And also his eternal power and divinity” (ibid.). One of these seems to have been said concerning the Son, the other concerning the Holy Spirit: just as the Son is called the eternal power of the Father, so also the Spirit, because he is divine, is believed to be eternal divinity. The Son too, because he always lives, is eternal life. This finger of God, therefore, is both eternal and divine. For what belongs properly to God that is not eternal and divine?

13. By this finger, as we read, God inscribed those stone tablets that Moses received (Exod. 31:18). God did not form the letters and characters that we read with a bodily finger; rather, he gave the Law through his Spirit. Therefore the Apostle said: “For the law is spiritual,” and it is certainly not written with ink but “with the Spirit of the living God,” not on stone tablets but “on tablets of hearts of flesh” (2 Cor. 3:3). For if the Apostle’s letter is written in the Spirit, what prevents us from believing that the law of God also was written not with ink but with the Spirit of God—a law that does not stain but illuminates the secrets of our heart and mind?

14. It was written on stone tablets (Exod. 32:19), because it was written symbolically; but the tablets were first broken and cast from Moses’ hands, because the Jews fell away from prophetic works. And rightly the tablets were broken, while the writing was not erased. Take care, too, that your tablet not be broken, lest your mind and spirit be divided. Is Christ divided? He is not divided, but is one with the Father; let no one separate you from him. If faith fails, the tablet of your heart is broken. The firmness of the spirit is shattered if you do not believe in the unity of divinity in the Trinity.

Your faith too is written, and your guilt too is written, just as Jeremiah said: “Your guilt, Judah, is written with an iron stylus and with a diamond point” [Note: The Roman edition alone reads, “with an iron stylus and on a diamond point.” Although the Vulgate version reads this way, the other editions and the manuscripts of Ambrose, together with the Chaldean and Syriac versions, more correctly read “…and with a diamond point”; for, as Grotius observes in his note on the same passage, the “point” is the very sharp edge of the diamond, customarily used for writing or engraving. This passage is absent from the Greek idiom.]. And, he says, “it is written upon your breast and upon your heart” (Jer. 17:1). There, then, is guilt where grace is also found; but guilt is written with a stylus, while grace is marked by the Spirit.

15. By this finger also, mystically, the Lord Jesus, with head bent, was writing on the ground when the adulterous woman was brought by the Jews (John 8:6), signifying figuratively that when we judge another’s sins, we ought to remember our own.

16. And lest, because God wrote the Law by his Spirit, we should again believe that the Spirit was something inferior, as though part of his ministry, or should suppose, by comparison with our body, that the Spirit of God was some small and limited portion, the Apostle says elsewhere (2 Cor. 2:13) that he does not speak in words of human wisdom, but in words taught by the Spirit, comparing spiritual things with spiritual things. He says that the natural person does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God; for he knew that one who compared divine things with bodily things would be counted among natural persons, not among spiritual people. “For it is foolishness to him,” he says (ibid., 14). And because he knew that such questions would arise among natural people, foreseeing the future, he says: “For who has known the mind of the Lord, that he may instruct him?” (ibid., 16). But we have the mind of Christ.

## CHAPTER FOUR

To those who contend that the Spirit is lesser because he is called the finger, he replies that this too turns into an insult against the Son, who is called the right hand. These names, therefore, must refer only to the unity of divinity. Hence Moses sang that the whole Trinity acted in the crossing of the Red Sea. Nor is it surprising that the Spirit’s operation was present there, where there was a figure of baptism, since Scripture teaches that the three Persons operate and sanctify equally in this.

17. [Elsewhere chapter 3.] But if someone still clings to carnal ambiguities and wavers over bodily examples, let him consider that he cannot think correctly about the Son if he thinks incorrectly about the Spirit. For if they think that the Spirit of God is some small and limited portion because he is called the finger of God [Note: Some manuscripts read, “because the Spirit of God is called…”], then they likewise say that there is a small and limited portion in the Son of God because he is called the right hand of God.

18. But the Son is called both the right hand and the power. Therefore, if we weigh our words, no perfection can exist without power; and let them beware of thinking—a wicked thing to say—that the Father, imperfect in his own substance, received perfection through the Son, and let them cease denying that the Son is coeternal with the Father. For when was the power of God absent? But if they think that the power of God did not exist at some time, they will at some time deny that fullness existed in God the Father, since they think that power was at some time lacking in him.

19. But these things, as I said, have been written so that we may refer them to the unity of divinity and believe what the Apostle said (Col. 2:9): that the fullness of divinity dwells bodily in Christ, and dwells in the Father, and dwells in the Holy Spirit; and that just as there is unity of divinity, so also there is unity of operation.

20. This can also be gathered from the Song of Moses. For when he had led the Jewish people across the sea, he confessed the operation of God the Father, the Son, and the Spirit, saying: “Your right hand, Lord, has been glorified in strength; your right hand, Lord, has shattered the enemies” (Exod. 15:6). You have it that he confessed both the Son and the Father, whose right hand the Son is. And below, so as not to pass over the Holy Spirit, he added: “You sent your Spirit, and the sea covered them; and by the Spirit of your anger the water was divided” (ibid., 10) [Note: Several manuscripts, and Ambrose and Erasmus with them, have this reading. Gill, with several other manuscripts, omits everything following the words “the sea covered them” up to “You see, therefore.” The latter portion, namely from the words “By this the unity is signified,” was restored by the Roman edition; but there is no reason why it should have rejected the former portion.]. By this is signified the unity of divinity, not inequality within the Trinity.

[Col. 0782B] 21. [Elsewhere chapter 4.] You see, therefore, that the Holy Spirit also acted together with the Father and the Son, so that, as though the waves had frozen in the middle of the sea, a kind of wall of water might rise for the passage of the Jews, and then, flowing back again through the Spirit, overwhelm the Egyptian people (Exod. 14:22). Hence many also understand the pillar of cloud to have gone before the Jewish people by day, and the pillar of fire by night, so that spiritual grace might protect its people (Exod. 13:21).

670 22. The Apostle also declared that this operation of God, which the whole world rightly admires, did not occur without the work of the Holy Spirit, saying that the truth of a spiritual mystery preceded in that figure. Thus you have it: “For all our fathers were under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea; and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink” (1 Cor. 10:1 ff.).

23. For how could the type of the sacrament have existed without the operation of the Holy Spirit, whose entire reality is in the Spirit? The Apostle also taught this when he said: “But you were washed, but you were sanctified, but you were justified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God” (1 Cor. 6:11).

24. You see, therefore, that the Father operates in the Son, and the Son [Note: Some manuscripts read, “and the Spirit operates.”] operates in the Spirit. Therefore, in accordance with the sequence of Scripture, do not doubt that what was in the figure existed in reality, since reality itself has declared it. For who would deny his operation in the bath of baptism, in which we experience his operation and grace?

25. [Elsewhere chapter 5.] For just as the Father sanctifies, so the Son also sanctifies, and the Holy Spirit sanctifies. The Father sanctifies, as it is written: “May the God of peace sanctify you, so that your spirit and soul and body may be preserved blameless on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Thess. 5:23). And elsewhere the Son says: “Father, sanctify them in the truth” (John 17:17).

[Col. 0783A] 26. Concerning the Son, the same Apostle said: “He was made for us by God wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption” (1 Cor. 1:30). You see that he was made sanctification? But he was made so for us—not that he changed what he was, but that he might sanctify us in the flesh.

27. The Apostle teaches that the Holy Spirit also sanctifies. For he says: “We ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers beloved by the Lord, because God chose you as firstfruits for salvation, in the sanctification of the Spirit and faith in the truth” (2 Thess. 2:13).

28. Therefore the Father sanctifies, the Son also sanctifies, and the Holy Spirit sanctifies; but there is one sanctification, because there is one baptism and one grace of the sacrament (Eph. 4:5).

## CHAPTER FIVE

[Col. 0783B]

He gathers together the argument begun above and confirms that unity is signified by the finger and the right hand from the fact that the works of God are the same as the works of his hands, and that the works of his hands are also the same as the works of his fingers; finally, he shows that “hand” applies to the Son and the Spirit just as “finger” applies to the Spirit and the Son.

29. [Elsewhere chapter 6.] But why is it surprising that he sanctifies individuals, when he himself does not need sanctification but overflows with it, since, as I said, we have received such majesty from him that the Holy Spirit appears inseparable from God the Father, as a finger is inseparable from the body?

30. But if someone thinks that this should be referred to diminution rather than to unity of power, he will surely fall into such madness that he will seem to fashion the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit into something like a single bodily form and to portray certain distinctions of limbs.

31. But let them understand, as I have often said, that this testimony signifies not inequality but unity of power, since the works that are God’s are the same as the works of his hands, and we read that those same works are also the works of his fingers. For it is written: “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament announces the works of his hands” (Ps. 18:1); and elsewhere: “In the beginning you founded the earth, Lord, and the heavens are the works of your hands” (Ps. 101:26). The works of the hands, then, are the same as the works of God. Therefore there is not a distinction of operation according to the bodily character of limbs, but unity of power.

32. The works of the fingers, too, are the same as the works of the hands, because it is likewise written: “For I shall see your heavens, the works of your fingers, the moon and the stars that you founded” (Ps. 8:4). What less, then, is the finger reported to have done here than the hand, when the fingers did the same thing as the hand? Thus it is written: “For you have delighted me, Lord, in your work, and I shall rejoice in the works of your hands” (Ps. 91:5).

[Col. 0784A] 33. And yet, because we read that the Son is the hand—“Did not my hand make all these things?” (Isa. 66:2), and elsewhere, “I will place you in the opening of the rock, and I will protect you with my hand; I have placed my hand beneath the covering of the rock” (Exod. 33:22)—which refers to the mystery of the incarnation, because the eternal power of God assumed the covering of the body [Note: Three manuscripts read, “because we read one…”], it is certainly clear that Scripture speaks of the hand both in relation to the Son of God and in relation to the Holy Spirit.

34. And again, because we read that the Spirit is the finger of God (Luke 11:20), we understand that they were called “fingers” in order to signify the Son and the Spirit. Finally, to recall that he possesses the sanctification both of the Son and of the Spirit, a certain holy man said: “Your hands made me and fashioned me” (Job 10:8).

## CHAPTER SIX

The Spirit reproves just as the Father and the Son do; indeed, judges cannot judge without him. This is shown by the judgments of Solomon and Daniel, which are briefly explained in passing; and it is shown that no other spirit inspired Daniel than the Holy Spirit.

35. [Elsewhere chapter 7.] Why do we reject similarity of wording when we assert unity of power, since the unity of power extends so far that the Spirit reproves just as the Father reproves and the Son reproves? For it is written: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor correct me in your wrath” (Ps. 6:1). Then in the forty-ninth Psalm the Lord says: “I will rebuke you and set your sins before your face” (Ps. 49:21); and likewise concerning the Holy Spirit the Son said: “But when I depart, I will send the Paraclete to you; and when he comes, he will reprove the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment” (John 16:7–8).

36. But where does the madness of impious people lead us, that we should seem to be arguing from something doubtful that the Holy Spirit reproves [Note: All editions and some manuscripts read, “so that we seem to be establishing what the Spirit reproves as though it were uncertain”; other manuscripts, more numerous and better, read more smoothly, “so that we seem to be establishing that the Spirit reproves, as though…”], when judges themselves cannot judge except through the Spirit? Finally, that famous judgment of Solomon, arising amid the uncertainty of litigants—when one woman, having crushed the infant whom she herself had borne, wished to claim another’s child as her own, while the other defended her own son—detected both the deceit hidden in their very thoughts and the maternal affection in their wombs. This plainly shone forth through the gift of the Holy Spirit [Note: Thus all editions and many manuscripts; some, however, read, “this gift was manifested through the Holy Spirit”; one manuscript reads, “he learned this by the gift of the Holy Spirit.”]. For no other power would have penetrated the hidden conscience of the women except the sword of the Holy Spirit, concerning which the Lord said: “I have not come to bring peace, but a sword” (Matt. 10:34); for the inner mind is penetrated not by iron but by the Spirit. “For the Holy Spirit of understanding is one, manifold, subtle, mobile” (Wis. 7:22); and below: “Observing all things” (ibid., 23).

37. See what the prophet says: he observes all things. Therefore Solomon also perceived all things, so that he ordered that sword to be brought (1 Kings 3:24); for, pretending that he wished to divide the child, he considered that the true mother would care more for her child than for her own consolation, and would prefer grace to legal right rather than legal rights to grace. But the woman who pretended maternal affection, blinded by her desire to prevail, would think little of the child’s death [Note: Some manuscripts read, “would care little about its fate”], since she did not understand the loss of compassion.

Thus that spiritual man, who “judges all things” (for “the spiritual person judges all things,” 1 Cor. 2:15), sought nature in the affections, which lay hidden in the words; and he questioned compassion so that it might disclose the truth. The mother therefore prevailed through the affection of love, which is a fruit of the Spirit.

38. The Spirit judges in the prophet, because the word of wisdom is given through the Spirit. How, then, can it be denied that the Holy Spirit can reprove the world concerning judgment, when he removes the uncertainty of judgment and grants its outcome?

### 39 and 40

Daniel, too, unless he had received the Spirit of God, could never have detected the adultery of lust and the falsehood of deceit. For when Susanna, assailed by the conspiracies of the elders, saw that the people’s judgment had been swayed by their regard for the elders, and, deprived of every support, alone among human beings conscious of her chastity, prayed to God as judge, Scripture says: “The Lord heard her voice when she was being led away to perish, and the Lord stirred up the holy Spirit of a young adolescent, whose name was Daniel” (Dan. 13:44–45). Thus, in accordance with the grace of the Spirit he had received, he detected the wavering testimony of the treacherous. For it was plainly an operation of divine power that their own voice should betray those whose disposition remained hidden.

> [Note: Erasmus and later editions read “among enemies”; Amerbach and the manuscripts, with great agreement, read “among human beings.”]

### 41

Understand, then, the sacred and heavenly miracle of the Holy Spirit. She preferred to remain chaste for herself rather than for the people; she preferred to undergo the danger of innocence rather than of modesty. When accused, she was silent; when condemned, she kept silence, content with the judgment of her conscience. She preserved the reverence due to modesty even amid dangers, lest those who had been unable to extort her chastity should appear to have extorted her immodesty. When she called upon the Lord, she obtained the Spirit, who revealed the hidden conscience of the elders.

### 42

Let chaste women learn not to fear slander. For she who placed the chastity of her life above her life itself neither suffered the loss of life nor failed to receive the glory of chastity. So, too, Abraham, once commanded to go abroad, was deterred neither by the danger threatening his wife’s chastity nor by the terror of the death set before him; and he preserved both his own life and his wife’s chastity.

> [Note: Amerbach reads “to approach a foreign woman”; Erasmus and later editions, “to approach a foreign land”; all the manuscripts read as in the text.]

No one, therefore, ever repented of having trusted God.

> [Note: Three manuscripts read “No one ever repented of having believed in the Lord.”]

Chastity increased devotion in Sarah, and devotion increased chastity.

### 43

And lest anyone perhaps suppose that, when Scripture says, “God stirred up the holy Spirit of the young adolescent” (Dan. 13:45), the spirit in him was a human spirit rather than the Holy Spirit, let him read further on and discover that Daniel received the Holy Spirit and therefore prophesied. Indeed, the king preferred him because he possessed spiritual grace. For he says:

“You, Daniel, are able, because the holy Spirit of God is in you.”

And further Scripture says:

“Daniel was set over them, because an extraordinary Spirit was in him” (Dan. 6:3).

But the Spirit of Moses, too, was divided among those who were to judge (Num. 11:25).

## Chapter VII

**That the Son himself neither judges nor takes vengeance without the Spirit; hence the same Spirit is called the sword of the Word. But since, conversely, the Word is called the sword of the Spirit, the complete unity of power in both is thereby recognized.**

### 44

But why should we speak of the others? We have learned that the Lord Jesus himself not only judges in the Spirit but also takes vengeance. For he would not take vengeance upon Antichrist unless he had first judged his merits—that is, the one whom, as we read, “the Lord Jesus will destroy with the Spirit of his mouth” (2 Thess. 2:8).

> [Note: Some manuscripts read, “Through the Lord Jesus himself, the Spirit not only…”]

> [Note: In some copies this chapter is numbered VIII.]

Here the grace is not something acquired, but the unity remains indivisible, because neither can Christ exist without the Spirit, nor the Spirit without Christ. The unity of the divine nature cannot be separated.

### 45

And since the example has been introduced that the Lord Jesus “will destroy him with the Spirit of his mouth,” the Spirit is understood as a certain sword of the Word (Eph. 6:17). Indeed, the Lord Jesus himself says in the Gospel: “I have not come to bring peace, but a sword” (Matt. 10:34).

For he came to give the Spirit, and therefore there is also upon his mouth a two-edged sword, namely spiritual grace (Rev. 19:15). The Spirit, therefore, is the sword of the Word.

### 46

And so that you may know that there is no inequality but unity of nature, the Word, too, is the sword of the Holy Spirit. For it is written:

“Take up the shield of faith, with which you may extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one, and receive the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the Word of God” (Eph. 6:16–17).

### 47

Since, therefore, the sword of the Word is the Holy Spirit, and the sword of the Holy Spirit is the Word of God, there is plainly unity of power.

## Chapter VIII

**The foregoing unity is proved by the fact that, just as the Father is said to be grieved and tempted, so also the Son is said to be grieved and tempted. The Son was also tempted in the desert, where the figure of the cross was raised in the bronze serpent; but the Apostle likewise says that the Spirit was tempted there. From this Ambrose concludes that the Israelites were guided into the promised land by the same Spirit, and that his will and power are one with those of the Father and the Son.**

### 48

This unity may also be considered in other passages of Scripture. For when Ezekiel says to the Jewish people, “And you grieved me in all these things, says the Lord” (Ezek. 16:43), Paul says to the new people in his letter, “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed” (Eph. 4:30).

Again, when Isaiah says of those same Jews, “But they did not believe, and they provoked the Holy Spirit” (Isa. 63:10), David says of God, “And they provoked the Most High in the wilderness, and tested God in their hearts” (Ps. 77:17–18).

### 49

Receive also the fact that, although Scripture elsewhere says that the Spirit was tempted and that God was tempted, it likewise says that Christ was tempted. For the Apostle says to the Corinthians:

“Let us not tempt Christ, as some of them tempted him and perished by serpents” (1 Cor. 10:9).

It was a just punishment that those who did not revere the author should experience the serpents’ venom.

### 50

And appropriately the Lord, with the bronze serpent suspended, commanded the wounds of the wounded to be healed (Num. 21:9). For the bronze serpent is an image of the cross. Although Christ was suspended in his flesh, nevertheless in him he himself was crucified to the world, and the world was crucified to him:

“For me the world has been crucified, and I to the world” (Gal. 6:14).

That world was crucified in its own allurements. Therefore the serpent suspended was not a real serpent but a bronze one, because the Lord assumed the likeness of the sinner in the truth of his body but without the reality of sin. By imitating the serpent through the slippery weakness of human nature, and then laying aside the coverings of the flesh, he destroyed the craft of the true serpent.

Through the Lord’s cross, therefore, which comes to our aid in the punishment of temptation, I recognize the offense against the Trinity committed by the faithless, since I receive the Trinity’s remedy.

### 51

Since, then, you have in the book of Moses that the Lord, when tempted, sent serpents upon the Jewish people (Num. 21:6), you must either acknowledge the unity in the divine majesty of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; or else, since apostolic Scripture says that the Spirit was tempted, you must understand him under the name “Lord.”

The Apostle, writing to the Hebrews, says that the Holy Spirit was tempted. For thus you read:

“Therefore, as the Holy Spirit says: ‘Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts, as in the provocation, on the day of temptation in the wilderness, where your fathers tempted me, tested me, and saw my works. For forty years I was near that generation, and I said: They are always erring in heart; but they have not known my ways. As I swore in my wrath, they shall not enter into my rest’” (Heb. 3:7ff.).

> [Note: The Roman edition and the Florentine manuscript read “when they tempted the Lord,” which makes poor sense. The apostolic Scripture referred to is clearly the passage that follows, where the Holy Spirit says, “Your fathers tempted me.” From this it is plainly established that Paul calls the same one “Spirit” whom Moses in the book of Numbers calls “Lord.”]

## 52

According to the Apostle, therefore, the Spirit was tempted. If he himself was tempted, then he himself was guiding the Jewish people into the promised land, as it is written:

“He led them through the abyss like a horse through the wilderness, and they did not grow weary; like cattle through the plain, the Spirit descended from the Lord and guided them” (Isa. 63:13–14).

And he himself, surely, supplied the clear rain of heavenly nourishment; he himself fertilized with fruitful rain the daily harvest that the earth had not produced and that no farmer had sown.

### 53

Let us now examine the details. God had promised the Jews rest; the Spirit calls that rest his own (Exod. 16:12). God the Father recalls that he was tempted by the faithless; the Spirit likewise says that he was tempted by them, because there was one temptation by which the one divinity of the Trinity was tempted by sacrilegious people.

God condemns the Jewish people (Num. 14:8), so that they cannot reach the land flowing with milk and honey—that is, the rest of the resurrection. The Spirit condemns them by the same sentence, saying:

“They shall not enter into my rest” (Ps. 94:11).

There is, therefore, one sentence of will and one excellence of power.

## Chapter IX

**That the Holy Spirit is confirmed to be provoked by Peter’s words. It is shown, from other passages and from the statement of the same Apostle concerning Ananias and Sapphira, that the Spirit of God and the Spirit of the Lord are one and the same. Hence Ambrose argues either for the Holy Spirit’s conjunction with the Father and the Son or for his proper divinity.**

### 54

Perhaps, however, someone might say that this example cannot be applied to the proper identity of the Holy Spirit, unless the Apostle Peter had also taught us elsewhere that the Spirit can be tempted by our sins. For thus he speaks to Ananias’s wife:

“Why did you agree together to tempt the Spirit of the Lord?” (Acts 5:9).

Indeed, the Spirit of the Lord is himself the Spirit of God, because there is one Holy Spirit, as the Apostle Paul also taught when he said:

“But you are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you. But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him” (Rom. 8:9).

He first mentioned the Spirit of God and immediately added that he is the same as the Spirit of Christ. And after he had spoken of the Spirit, so that we might understand that where the Holy Spirit is, there Christ is, he added:

“But if Christ is in you” (Rom. 8:10).

### 55

Then, just as he shows here that where the Spirit is, there Christ is, so elsewhere he shows that where Christ is, there also is the Holy Spirit. For after saying, “Do you seek proof of the Christ who speaks in me?” (2 Cor. 13:3), he says elsewhere:

“For I think that I too have the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 7:40).

The unity, therefore, is inseparable, because wherever the Father, Christ, or the Spirit is indicated, Scripture testifies that there is the whole fullness of the Trinity.

### 56

Peter himself, moreover, in the example we have proposed, first mentioned the Holy Spirit and afterward said “the Spirit of the Lord.” For thus you read:

“Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit and to keep back part of the price of the land? While it remained, did it not remain yours, and when it was sold, was it not in your power? Why have you put this deed in your heart? You have not lied to human beings but to God” (Acts 5:3ff.).

And afterward he said to his wife:

“Why did you agree together to tempt the Spirit of the Lord?” (Acts 5:9).

### 57

First, we understand that he called the Holy Spirit the Spirit of the Lord. Then, since he first mentioned the Holy Spirit and added, “You have not lied to human beings but to God,” you must understand either the unity of divinity in the Holy Spirit, since when the Spirit is tempted, God is deceived; or, if you attempt to exclude the unity of divinity, then, according to the words of Scripture, you must believe that the Spirit himself is God.

> [Note: All editions and some manuscripts read “you believe the Spirit of the Lord.” The other manuscripts, and more appropriately, read “you believe the Spirit to be God.” This clause corresponds to the later one, “confess the divinity of the Holy Spirit,” since in both places the argument against the heretics is that, if they refuse to confess the unity of divinity in the three persons, they will at least be forced not to deny the divinity of the Holy Spirit.]

### 58

For if we understand the statement to refer both to the Spirit and to the Father, then in God the Father and the Holy Spirit we recognize a unity of truth and knowledge, because the lie is detected by the Holy Spirit just as by God the Father.

But if we take both statements as referring to the Spirit, why do you, faithless man, try to deny what you read? Either confess the unity of divinity of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, or confess the divinity of the Holy Spirit. Whichever you say, you have said both in God, because unity establishes divinity, and divinity establishes unity.

> [Note: The Roman edition alone reads “of the Father and the Son in the Holy Spirit.” Immediately afterward the same Roman edition, together with the earlier edition and some manuscripts, reads “or confess the divinity of the Holy Spirit in the Father and the Son.” The more numerous and better manuscripts do not recognize “in the Father and the Son.”]

## Chapter X

**That the divinity of the Holy Spirit is established from a passage in John. The passage was indeed removed by the heretics, but to no purpose, since their unbelief can be refuted more easily from it. The sequence of the text is examined to show that this passage concerns the Spirit. The one who is reborn from the same Spirit is born from the Spirit, from whom Christ himself is believed to have been born and reborn. The divinity of the Spirit is again gathered from two testimonies of John, and finally it is explained how the Spirit, water, and blood are called witnesses.**

### 59

Not only in this passage does Scripture plainly testify to the θεότης—namely, the divinity—of the Holy Spirit; the Lord himself also said in the Gospel:

“Because God is Spirit” (John 3:6).

Arians, you so expressly testify that this passage concerns the Spirit that you remove it from your copies. Would that you removed it from your own copies and not also from the copies of the Church!

At the time when Auxentius, through impious unbelief, had occupied the Church of Milan with arms and an army, or when the Church of Sirmium was being attacked by Valens and Ursacius, with their wavering bishops, this falsehood and sacrilege of yours was discovered in the ecclesiastical books. Perhaps you did this also in the East.

> [Note: Some manuscripts read “the impious unbelief of Auxentius.” This intrusion by Auxentius occurred in 355 and was carried out by the emperor Constantius with the same armed terror and violence by which he drove the holy Dionysius from his see into exile, as we learn from Athanasius’s *Letter to the Solitaries* and Hilary’s book against Constantius. As for the disturbance of the Church of Sirmium, there is no doubt that the Sirmian councils are meant. At the first, held in 351, they deposed Photinus from that see and issued a formula of faith that bore the appearance of orthodox doctrine, so that Hilary attempted to defend it in his book *On the Synods*, although Athanasius condemned it in his book *On the Synods of Ariminum and Seleucia*. But those same men, who seemed to have benefited the Church by deposing the heresiarch, obtained from Constantius the appointment of Germinius, or Garminius, a heretic of the Arian party, to the vacant see. At the second synod held there in 357 they proposed the formula which the great Hosius, overcome by fear, weariness, and the weakness of his failing age, signed, thereby causing immense grief to all Catholics. Finally, at the third synod, convened in 359, they promulgated another formula, dictated by Mark of Arethusa, no less hostile and destructive to the Catholic faith. Hence it may be understood that “wavering priests” here means bishops insufficiently firm in their adherence to the true faith. If anyone, against Petavius, Valesius, and other modern scholars, wishes to hold that there were not three councils but only one, from which those three formulas proceeded, what Ambrose says here can nevertheless be referred to that council.]

> [Note: All editions read “this false and simultaneously sacrilegious image”; almost all the manuscripts instead read “this falsehood and your sacrilege.” This is quite acceptable, for it is equivalent to saying, “your falsification or corruption and adulteration, together with your sacrilege, has been detected.” But what does “sacrilegious image” mean?]

### 60

You were able to erase the letters, but you could not remove the faith. That erasure exposed you all the more; that erasure condemned you all the more. For you could not smear the truth, but that erasure was scraping your names from the book of life.

Why was the statement “Because God is Spirit” removed, if it did not refer to the Spirit? If you wish it to refer explicitly to God the Father, then you also deny God the Father, whom you suppose should be erased.

> [Note: The Roman edition reads, “you denied the Father whom you thought should be erased.” Immediately afterward several manuscripts read, “Choose whichever you wish,” and so forth.]

Choose whichever you wish: in either case the noose of your impiety will bind you, if you confess yourselves heathens by denying either the Father as God or the Spirit as God. Your confession is therefore held against you: you erase the oracle because you fear the example.

### 61

You erase it, indeed, in your breasts and minds; but the divine oracle is not erased. The Holy Spirit is not erased, but he turns away from impious minds. Grace is not erased, but iniquity is, because it is written:

“I am, I am he who blots out your iniquities” (Isa. 43:25).

Finally, Moses, pleading for the people, says:

“Blot me out of your book, if you will not spare this people” (Exod. 32:32).

Yet he was not blotted out, because he did not possess iniquity but overflowed with grace.

### 62

You have therefore been convicted by your own confession, since you cannot say that what you did was done wisely but rather craftily.

> [Note: Some manuscripts read, “but was done cunningly. You recognized…”]

For cunningly you recognized that the testimony of this passage convicted you and that your arguments could not stand against its testimony. Where else could the meaning of this passage be directed, since the entire sequence of the reading concerns the Spirit?

### 63

Nicodemus asks about regeneration, and the Lord replies:

“Amen, amen, I say to you, unless someone is born through water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:5).

And to show that one generation is according to the flesh and another according to the Spirit, he added:

“What is born from the flesh is flesh, because it is born from the flesh; and what is born from the Spirit is spirit, because God is Spirit” (John 3:6).

Follow, therefore, the whole sequence of the reading, and you will find that the Lord has excluded your impiety by the fullness of his assertion. He says:

“Do not marvel that I said to you, ‘You must be born again.’ The Spirit breathes where he wills, and you hear his voice, but you do not know where he comes from or where he goes; so it is with everyone who is born from the Spirit” (John 3:7–8).

> [Note: Several manuscripts read “through water and the Holy Spirit.” Further on they read “what is born from flesh is flesh.” Moreover, the words that follow—“because it was born from the flesh”—are absent from the Bibles of all languages just as are the words under discussion, “because God is Spirit.” Yet, just as there can be no doubt that the latter words were erased from the sacred pages by the heretics, it is sufficiently remarkable that they have nowhere been restored to their proper place. Perhaps someone may ask why these words were deleted from chapter 3, since they remain intact in chapter 4, verse 24. Our Ambrose gives a sufficient reason: the heretics thought that the words in chapter 4 could be twisted to refer to the Father.]

### 64

Who is born from the Spirit and is made spirit except the one who is renewed in the spirit of his mind? This is plainly the one who is regenerated through water and the Holy Spirit, because through the washing of regeneration and renewal by the Holy Spirit we receive the hope of eternal life.

Elsewhere the Apostle Peter says:

“But you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit” (Acts 11:16).

Who is baptized with the Holy Spirit except the one who is reborn through water and the Holy Spirit?

Therefore the Lord said of the Holy Spirit:

“Amen, amen, I say to you, unless someone is born through water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.”

And therefore, later on, he defined us as being born from the one through whom, earlier above, he said that we are reborn. This is the Lord’s statement: I rely on the written text, not on an argument.

> [Note: Ambrose says that he relies on the written text rather than on an argument because human testimony too commonly yields to arguments, as he himself writes in *On the Faith*, book I, chapter 11, section 70. See likewise what we noted on book III, chapter 3, section 24.]

### 65

Yet I ask why, if it is not doubted that we are reborn through the Holy Spirit, it should be doubted that we are born from the Holy Spirit, since the Lord Jesus himself was both born and reborn from the Holy Spirit.

If you confess that he was born from the Holy Spirit (Matt. 1:20), because you cannot deny it, but deny that he was reborn (Matt. 3:16), this is great folly: you confess what is unique to God and deny what is common to human beings.

Therefore it is rightly said to you, as it was said to the Jews:

“If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things?” (John 3:12).

> [Note: A few manuscripts read “that we are born,” rather than “that we are reborn.”]

### 66

Nevertheless, in Greek we find both passages written in such a way that he did not say “through the Spirit” but “from the Spirit.” Thus it reads:

**Ἀμὴν, ἀμὴν, λέγω σοι, ἐὰν μή τις γεννήθη ἐξ ὕδατος καὶ Πνεύματος**

—that is, “from water and the Spirit.”

Since, therefore, it ought not to be doubted that the phrase “what is born from the Spirit” is written concerning the Holy Spirit, there is no doubt that the Holy Spirit is God, according to what is written: “God is Spirit.”

### 67

Elsewhere, too, so that the same Evangelist might disclose that this was written concerning the Holy Spirit, he says:

“Through water and the Spirit Christ Jesus came, not in water only but through water and blood. And the Spirit gives testimony, because the Spirit is truth; for there are three witnesses: the Spirit, the water, and the blood, and these three are one” (1 John 5:6ff.).

> [Note: The old edition and some manuscripts read “and blood, and the Spirit’s testimony, because the Spirit is truth … these three are one in Christ Jesus.” The other manuscripts agree with us, except that instead of “the Spirit is truth,” some, along with the Vulgate alone, read “Christ is truth.”]

### 68

Hear how they are witnesses. The Spirit renews the mind; the water benefits us in the washing; the blood concerns the price.

For the Spirit made us children of God through adoption; the water of the sacred font washes us; the Lord’s blood redeemed us.

Thus, through the spiritual sacrament, we obtain one invisible testimony and another visible testimony, because “the Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit” (Rom. 8:16).

Although the fullness of the sacrament exists in both, there is nevertheless a distinction of function. Therefore, where there is a distinction of function, there is certainly not equality of testimony.

## Chapter XI

**It was objected that John’s words, “The Spirit is God,” should be referred to God the Father, since afterward Christ declares that God is to be worshiped in Spirit and truth. First it is answered that the word “spirit” sometimes signifies spiritual grace. Then, if they wish the person of the Holy Spirit to be understood by the words “in spirit,” and consequently deny that worship is due to him, it is shown that the argument applies equally to the Son. Yet countless examples prove that the Son is to be worshiped, and therefore the same must be understood concerning the Spirit. What is the footstool of the feet commanded to be worshiped? This signifies the Lord’s body; and since the Spirit is its author, it follows that he too must be worshiped, though it does not follow that Mary is to be worshiped. The worship of the Spirit is therefore not abolished; rather, his conjunction with the Father is expressed when the Father is said to be worshiped in the Spirit. This is confirmed by similar expressions.**

### 69

Perhaps, however, someone may reply that later in this very book the Lord again called the Spirit God, but meant God the Father. For thus you read in the Gospel:

“The hour is coming when true worshipers will worship the Father in Spirit and truth. For the Father also seeks such people to worship him. God is Spirit, and those who worship him must worship in Spirit and truth” (John 4:23–24).

Not only by this example do you wish to deny the divinity of the Holy Spirit; you also interpret “worship God in Spirit” as implying the subjection of the Spirit.

### 70

I shall answer this passage briefly: “spirit” is often used for spiritual grace, just as the Apostle says:

“The Spirit himself pleads for us with unutterable groanings” (Rom. 8:26),

that is, spiritual grace—unless perhaps you have been able to hear the groanings of the Holy Spirit.

Here, therefore, God is worshiped not in the wickedness of the heart but in spiritual grace. For “wisdom does not enter into a malevolent soul” (Wis. 1:4), because no one can say, “Lord Jesus,” except in the Holy Spirit (1 Cor. 12:3).

Immediately afterward he added:

“There are varieties of graces” (1 Cor. 12:4).

### 71

This, therefore, cannot refer either to the fullness or to a portion of the Spirit, because neither can the human mind contain his fullness, nor is he divided into any sections of himself. Rather, he pours out the gift of spiritual grace, in which God is worshiped, just as he is worshiped in truth. For no one worships unless he piously receives the truth of his divinity.

Nor, of course, does one apprehend Christ personally, or the Holy Spirit personally.

### 72

Or, if you think that the phrase concerning the Spirit appears to have been spoken personally, and likewise the phrase concerning Christ, then God is similarly worshiped in truth just as he is worshiped in the Spirit.

Either there is therefore a similar subjection—which, God forbid, you should believe, since then the Son too would not be worshiped—or, as is true, there is a similar unity of grace, and the Spirit is worshiped.

### 73

Let us therefore gather together and conclude the impious questions of the Arians here. If they deny that the Spirit is to be worshiped because God is worshiped in the Spirit, then let them deny that truth is to be worshiped because God is worshiped in truth.

For although there are many truths, since it is written, “Truths have been diminished by the children of men” (Ps. 11:1), they have nevertheless been given by the divine Truth, who is Christ and who says:

“I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).

If, therefore, they understand “truth” in this passage according to ordinary usage, let them likewise understand “spiritual grace,” and there is no difficulty. But if they take “truth” to mean Christ, let them deny that Christ is to be worshiped.

### 74

But they are refuted by the deeds of the devout and by the sequence of Scripture. Mary worshiped Christ, and therefore she was sent to the apostles as the herald of the resurrection, breaking the inherited bond and the monstrous offense of the female race.

For the Lord accomplished this in a mystery: where sin had abounded, grace might also abound (Rom. 5:20). And appropriately a woman was sent to men, so that she who had first announced guilt to a man might be the first to announce the Lord’s grace.

### 75

The apostles also worshiped him (Matt. 28:17), and therefore, because they bore testimony to the faith, they received the teaching of the faith.

The angels also worshiped him, of whom it is written:

“Let all his angels worship him” (Heb. 1:6).

### 76

They worship not only his divinity but also the footstool of his feet, as it is written:

“Worship his footstool, for it is holy” (Ps. 98:5).

Or, if they deny that the mysteries of the Incarnation are also to be worshiped in Christ—mysteries in which we discern, as it were, certain traces of divinity and certain paths of the heavenly Word—let them read that the apostles also worshiped him when he rose again in the glory of his flesh (Matt. 28:17).

> [Note: The holy Doctor discusses here somewhat more fully, and not without reason, the question of the worship of Christ even according to his humanity. For the Apollinarists, in order to establish their impious doctrine of one nature in Christ, used to assert, on the basis of a spurious letter of Pope Julius, that if Christ had not one nature but two, Catholics ought to worship one and not the other, and that they were baptized into the divine nature but not into the human. Hence they used to give orthodox Christians the malicious name ἀνθρωπολάτραι, “worshipers of a human being,” and wrote on their doors that one should worship not a man who bears God but a God who bears flesh. Athanasius, in his book *On the Incarnation of Christ* and his *Letter to Adelphius*, Epiphanius in *Ancoratus*, section 51, Leo of Byzantium, Ambrose here and in *On the Sacrament of the Incarnation*, and others vigorously refuted these errors. After the Council of Chalcedon, Constantinople V established that Christ according to both natures is to be honored with one and the same worship.]

### 77

Therefore, if it detracts nothing from Christ that God is worshiped in Christ—because Christ too is worshiped—it detracts nothing from the Spirit that God is worshiped in the Spirit, because the Spirit too is worshiped, as the Apostle says:

“We serve the Spirit of God” (Phil. 3:3).

For the one who serves also worships, as was said above:

“You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone you shall serve” (Deut. 6:13).

### 78

But lest someone appear to evade the example we have proposed by asking how the Prophet’s statement, “Worship his footstool” (Ps. 98:5), can pertain to the mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation, let us consider it.

We must not judge the footstool according to human usage. For God is neither corporeal nor finite, so that we should suppose a footstool placed beneath him as a support for his feet.

Nor do we read that anything except God is to be worshiped, because it is written:

“You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone you shall serve” (Deut. 6:13).

How, then, could the Prophet, nourished under the Law and instructed in the Law, command something contrary to the Law?

The question is therefore not a trivial one, and for that reason let us consider more carefully what the footstool is.

For elsewhere we read:

“Heaven is my throne, but the earth is the footstool of my feet” (Isa. 66:1).

But neither is the earth to be worshiped by us, because it is God’s creation.

79. Let us see, however, whether the Prophet means that that earth is to be adored which the Lord Jesus assumed in taking flesh. Thus, by the footstool, earth is understood; and by earth, the flesh of Christ, which even today we adore in the mysteries and which the apostles adored in the Lord Jesus, as we said above. For Christ has not been divided, but is one (1 Cor. I, 13); nor, when he is adored as the Son of God, is he denied to have been born of the Virgin. Since, then, the sacrament of the Incarnation is to be adored, and the Incarnation is the work of the Spirit, as it is written: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; and the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke I, 35), undoubtedly the Holy Spirit also is to be adored, when he is adored who, according to the flesh, was born of the Holy Spirit.

[Note: It is astonishing how much this passage has perplexed modern heterodox writers. The cardinals Bellarmine, book III, chapter 12, and Perronius, likewise book III of *De Eucharistia*, chapter 14, proposed it as exceedingly strong evidence for proving that the highest worship—what they call *latria*—is owed to Christ in the eucharistic liturgy and that, in fact, it had already been customary to offer it from those happy days of the flourishing Church. Plessis and Albertinus, on the other hand, attempted in their replies either to break its force, if not entirely, or at least to weaken it.

The former gives two replies. First, Ambrose speaks of adoration in the same sense in which he speaks of eating; and of eating in the same sense in which he speaks of touching or handling. Yet, he says, Ambrose, when discussing Mary Magdalene in his *Exposition of Luke*, asserts that Christ is now touched not bodily but through faith. Nothing, however, could be more inept than this reply. For the holy Doctor so far from denying that Christ can be touched after the resurrection clearly affirms that the other Mary held Christ’s feet in her embrace. Moreover, even if we cannot handle Christ in the Eucharist by bodily touch, but only the accidents with which he is clothed, what prevents us from recognizing through faith that one who is truly present, though hidden, is worthy of veneration through true and external adoration?

His second reply is that Christ is adored in the mysteries, but that the mysteries in the sacrament are not adored, nor the sacrament itself. He chiefly tries to prove this because, in certain passages, the Fathers and Ambrose himself call the sacrament a creature. But since there “sacrament” means either the matter of the sacrament before consecration, or the sacramental types or appearances, this consideration advances his case not at all.

Nor is he more successful when he explains “Christ is adored in the mysteries” as referring not to the particular adoration offered to Christ as present, but to that common adoration by which, in every act of religion—for example, in baptism or some similar rite—we venerate him seated at the Father’s right hand. Such evasions and side paths are sought in vain. For it is clear that this is the one purpose of our Ambrose: to prove that adoration cannot be denied to the Spirit on the ground that Christ’s flesh, whose author is that same Spirit, is truly adored. To show that this is so, he asserts that the same flesh was adored by the apostles at the resurrection and is still adored by us in the mysteries.

Who, then, does not understand that Christ is adored in the mysteries because he is present there for us, just as the apostles adored him at the resurrection because they were looking upon him as present? Albertinus nevertheless insists that there is no reason here to understand by “mysteries” the Eucharist rather than the sacrament of baptism, since many Fathers command us to offer the same worship to Christ in baptism. But anyone who examines the words of the passages he cites will easily see that they do not concern the special veneration offered to the Lord’s flesh, but only that common worship by which we can adore Christ wherever we are.

That this passage is to be interpreted specifically of the Eucharist is confirmed, besides what we have already said, by Augustine, Ambrose’s most faithful disciple. In explaining the verse of Psalm XCVIII cited above by Ambrose—“Adore his footstool”—so as to apply it to the sacrament of the altar, he borrowed not only Ambrose’s ideas but even his very words.]
