80. And lest anyone should transfer this to the Virgin Mary: Mary was the temple of God, not the God of the temple. Therefore only he is to be adored who was at work in the temple.

[Column 0795B] 81. Nothing, then, detracts from the fact that God is adored in the Spirit, because the Spirit also is adored. Yet if we consider the very words, what else should we understand in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit but the unity of one and the same power? For what does “one must adore in Spirit and truth” mean (John IV, 24), if you do not refer this to spiritual grace and to true faith of conscience, but, as we have said, understand it personally—if indeed this is a word worthy to express the divine majesty—as referring to Christ and to the Spirit?

[Note: Amerbach and Erasmus have: “Unless you never refer this to spiritual grace”; several manuscripts: “Unless you refer this only to grace,” and so forth. Gill and the Roman edition, together with many more manuscripts, have the reading in the text. The qualification he adds to the word “personally”—“if indeed this is a word worthy …”—indicates that when human beings are compelled to explain divine things in human words, they cannot express anything fully worthy of God’s majesty. Augustine likewise uses the word “person” with no less caution and hesitation in book VII, chapter 4, of *On the Trinity*, as do Vincent of Lérins and others.]

82. What, then, does “the Father is adored in Christ” mean, except that the Father is in Christ, the Father speaks in Christ, and the Father remains in Christ? Certainly not as a body in a body—for God is not a body—nor as something confused within something confused, but as the true in the true: God in God, light in light, the eternal Father in the coeternal Son. Thus the insertion of one body into another is not meant, but the unity of power. Therefore, through the unity of power, Christ is co-adored in the Father, when God the Father is adored in Christ. In the same way, through the unity of that same power, the Spirit is co-adored in God, while God is adored in the Spirit.

83. Let us examine more carefully the force of this expression and of the argument, and gather its proper meaning from other passages. “You made all things,” he says, “in Wisdom” (Ps. CIII, 24). What, then, do we understand here? Is Wisdom excluded from the works? Yet “all things were made through him” (John I, 3). And David says: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established” (Ps. XXXII, 6). Therefore, he who calls the Son of God the author even of the heavenly things certainly spoke of all things as having been made in the Son in such a way that, in the restoration of creation, he did not in the least separate the Son from the Father, but joined him to the Father.

[Note: Gill and the Roman edition, with the greater number of manuscripts, have: “He himself, who calls the Son … the author.” Amerbach and Erasmus, with other manuscripts, have: “He himself indeed [calls] the Son … the author.”]

84. Paul also says: “For in him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible” (Col. I, 16). When he says “in him,” did he deny “through him”? Certainly not; rather, he affirmed it. Again, elsewhere he says: “One Lord Jesus, through whom are all things” (1 Cor. VIII, 6). Therefore, when he says “through him,” did he deny that all things were created in him, through whom he says all things exist? These expressions—“in him” and “with him” (Col. I, 16)—have this force: that they are to be understood as one and alike, not contrary. He made this clear also in what follows when he said: “All things were created through him and in him” (ibid.). These three expressions—“with him,” “through him,” and “in him”—are one in Christ, as Scripture testifies, as we said above (Book II, chapters 8–9). For you have it that all things were created through him and in him.

85. Hear also that the Father was with him, and he was with the Father, when all things were being created. Wisdom says: “When he prepared the heavens, I was with him; when he established the fountains of the waters” (Prov. VIII, 27). And in the Old Testament the Father, by saying “Let us make” (Gen. I, 26), showed that the Son was to be adored with him, as the creator of all things. Therefore, just as creatures are said to have been created in the Son, of whom the Son is understood to be the creator, so, when God is said to be adored in truth, the expression should be understood according to the same manner, since the proper force of the word is frequently used in that way: the Son also is to be adored. In the same way, then, the Spirit also is adored, because God is adored in the Spirit. Therefore the Father is adored both with the Son and with the Spirit, because the Trinity is adored.

[Note: Amerbach and Erasmus have “creation is discussed”; the other editions and all the manuscripts have “creatures are said to have been created.” Again, where all the editions and the majority of manuscripts have “when God is adored in truth,” several others read “when [God is adored] in the Son, in truth.”]

686 CHAPTER XII.

From the fact that Paul indicated that the light of the divinity of the Trinity—which the three apostles adored in Christ—was present, it is also declared that the Spirit is to be adored. It is shown from the very words that the Spirit is designated by the Apostle. The divinity of that same Spirit is proved from the fact that he has a temple in which he dwells not as a priest but as God; and also from the fact that he is adored together with the Father and the Son, from which the unity of their nature is understood.

86. Does anyone deny that the divinity of the eternal Trinity is to be adored, when the divine Scriptures express the incomprehensible majesty of the Trinity? As the Apostle says elsewhere: “For God, who said, ‘Let light shine out of darkness,’ has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Cor. IV, 6).

[Note: The Bigot manuscript has “of the charity of God.” Against this stand not only all the others and the editions, but also the authority of the apostolic text.]

87. The apostles saw this glory when the Lord Jesus shone on the mountain with the light of his divinity: “The apostles saw,” he says, “and fell on their faces” (Matt. XVII, 6). Do you suppose that they adored him even as they fell, when they could not endure the radiance of the divine light with their bodily eyes, and the splendor of eternal light obscured the sight of mortal vision? Or what else did those who saw his glory say at that time but: “Come, let us adore and fall down before him” (Ps. XCIV, 6)? [In some copies, chapter XIII.] For “God has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Cor. IV, 6).

88. Who, then, is he who shone so that we might know God in the face of Christ Jesus?

[Note: Several manuscripts have: “so that we may know the Lord.”]

For he said: “God has shone, so that the glory of God might be known in the face of Christ Jesus.” Whom do we think is meant here other than the Spirit who has been declared? Or who is there besides the Holy Spirit to whom the power of divinity should be ascribed? For those who exclude the Spirit must necessarily introduce another who receives the glory of divinity together with the Father and the Son.

89. Let us therefore repeat the same words: “It is God who has shone to give the light of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.” You have Christ clearly expressed. Whose glory, then, is said to enlighten, unless it is the Spirit’s? He expressed him as God, because he said “the glory of God.” If this is the Father’s glory, then it remains that he who said “Let light shine out of darkness” and “has shone in our hearts” must be understood as the Holy Spirit; for we cannot venerate another together with the Father and the Son. If, then, you understand the Spirit, and the Apostle called him God, you must therefore acknowledge the divinity of the Spirit, you who deny it.

90. But how shamelessly you deny it, when you read that the Holy Spirit has a temple! For it is written: “You are the temple of God, and the Holy Spirit dwells in you” (1 Cor. III, 16). God, then, has a temple; a creature does not truly have a temple. But the Spirit has a temple, since he dwells in us. For it is written: “Your members are the temple of the Holy Spirit” (1 Cor. VI, 15).

91. In the temple he dwells not as a priest or as a minister, but as God, since the Lord Jesus himself said: “I will dwell in them and walk among them; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people” (Lev. XXVI, 12). And David says: “The Lord is in his holy temple” (Ps. X, 5). Therefore the Spirit dwells in his holy temple, just as the Father dwells, and the Son also dwells, who said: “I and the Father will come, and we will make our dwelling with him” (John XIV, 23).

91*. We therefore recognize that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit remain in one and the same [temple] through the unity of the same nature. Therefore the one who dwells in the temple is of divine power. For just as we are the temple of the Father and the Son, so also we are the temple of the Holy Spirit: not many temples, but one temple, because it is the temple of one power.

92. The Father, however, remains in us through the Spirit whom he gave us. How, then, can a different nature remain at the same time? It certainly cannot. The Holy Spirit remains with the Father and the Son. Therefore the Apostle joined the grace of Jesus Christ and the love of God to the communion of the Holy Spirit, saying: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Spirit be with you all” (2 Cor. XIII, 13).

CHAPTER XIII.

When Catholics are accused of introducing three gods by attributing divinity to the Spirit, the accusation is turned back upon the accusers: for the same reason they introduce two gods unless they deny divinity to the Son. The orthodox doctrine is then explained.

92*. [In some copies, chapter XIV.] But what are you afraid of—that which you are accustomed to bark out, lest you make three gods? Far from it. For where one divinity is understood, one God is named. When we call the Son God, we do not call two gods. For if, when you confess the divinity of the Spirit, you think that three gods are being named, then, when you call the Son divine—since you cannot deny it—you introduce two gods. Therefore, according to your own position, if you think that “God” is the name of one person and not of one nature, you must either speak of two gods or deny that the Son is God.

[Note: The greater number and better manuscripts have: “if, when you confess the divinity of the Spirit, you think that we are speaking of three gods.” Several others, as well as all the editions, have: “if, when you confess the divinity of the Spirit, you think that three gods are being named.”]

93. But let us excuse you for ignorance, even if we do not excuse you for guilt. According to our position, there is one God, one divinity, and a unity of power. Just as we speak of one God, confessing the Father under the name of divinity without denying the Son, so also we do not exclude the Holy Spirit from the unity of divinity, and we do not assert three gods but deny them; for plurality is produced not by unity but by division of power. How could the unity of divinity admit plurality, when plurality belongs to number, while the divine nature does not admit number?

CHAPTER XIV.

In addition to the testimonies already given, other passages can be brought forward to prove the rule of the three persons. Two are brought from the letters to the Thessalonians, and, by comparison with other scriptural texts, it is shown that dominion is attributed to the Spirit just as to the other persons. Finally, after another, even clearer passage from the second letter to the Corinthians has been cited, it is inferred both that the Spirit is Lord and that where the Lord is, there is the Spirit.

94. [In some copies, chapter XV.] There is therefore one God, while the majesty of the eternal Trinity is preserved, as the example proposed makes clear. Nor do we see the Trinity expressed by the name of divinity only in that passage. In many places, as we said above, and especially in the letters which the Apostle wrote to the Thessalonians, he most clearly declared the divinity and dominion of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Thus you have: “May the Lord multiply you and make you abound in love for one another and for all, as we do for you, so that he may strengthen your hearts blameless in holiness before our God and Father at the coming of our Lord Jesus” (1 Thess. III, 12–13).

[Note: Several manuscripts have: “which the Apostle addressed.”]

95. Who, then, is the Lord who multiplies us and makes us abound before our God and Father at the coming of the Lord Jesus? He named the Father and he named the Son. Whom, then, did he join with the Father and the Son besides the Spirit? Who is the Lord who strengthens our hearts in holiness? For holiness is spiritual grace,

[Note: Several manuscripts of no inferior authority have: “is spiritual grace.”]

as he also said below: “In sanctification of the Spirit and faith in the truth” (2 Thess. II, 12).

96. Whom do you think is meant here as Lord, other than the Spirit who has been named?

[Note: Gill and the Roman edition, with several manuscripts, have: “Was this God the Father?” Amerbach and Erasmus, with many more manuscripts, have: “Nor was it God the Father.” This is not inappropriate, for it is a question combined with a certain indignation and reproach.]

Nor could God the Father have taught you this, who said: “The one upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit” (John I, 33). For the Spirit descended in the form of a dove (Luke III, 22), both to bear witness to wisdom, to fulfill the sacrament of spiritual washing, and to show that he carried out one operation with the Father and the Son.

97. And lest you think that something escaped the Apostle through inadvertence, but rather that he knowingly and prudently, filled with the Holy Spirit, signified the Lord whom he understood to be God, he repeated the same point in the second letter to the Thessalonians, saying: “May the Lord direct your hearts into the love of God and the patience of Christ” (2 Thess. III, 5).

[Note: Several manuscripts have: “If the direction is from God and from Christ … it must be shown who directs if it is love,” and so forth.]

If there is love of God and patience of Christ, it must be shown who the Lord is who directs, if we deny the direction of the Holy Spirit.

98. But we cannot deny it, since the Lord said of him: “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. When that Spirit of truth comes, he will lead you into all truth” (John XVI, 12–13). And David says of him: “Your good Spirit will lead me into the right way” (Ps. CXLII, 10).

99. [In some copies, chapter XVI.] See what the Lord’s voice has resounded concerning the Holy Spirit. The Son of God came, and because he had not yet poured out the Spirit, he declared that certain little ones among us were living without the Spirit.

[Note: The Thuane manuscript has: “He declared us degenerate without the Spirit.”]

He said that the Spirit would come, who would make the little ones stronger, through the growth, namely, of spiritual maturity. He said this not to place the Spirit’s power above his own, but to show, in the knowledge of the Trinity, that the fullness of power is present.

100. Therefore you must either name some fourth being whom you ought to recognize besides the Spirit, or else judge that there is no other Lord than the one designated as the Spirit.

101. But if you demand an explicit expression of the words by which Scripture calls the Spirit Lord, you could not have been unaware of it, since it is written: “The Lord is the Spirit” (2 Cor. III, 17). The entire sequence of the reading shows that this was said of the Holy Spirit. Let us therefore consider the apostolic words: “Whenever Moses is read,” he says, “a veil lies over their heart; but when they turn to the Lord, the veil will be taken away. The Lord is the Spirit; and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (ibid., 15–16).

102. He therefore not only called the Spirit Lord, but also added: “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.” Thus we all, with unveiled face beholding the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord (ibid., 18). That is, having first turned to the Lord, so that with spiritual understanding we might see the glory of the Lord as though in a mirror of the Scriptures, we are now transformed from the glory that turns us toward the Lord into that heavenly glory.

Therefore, since the Lord is the one to whom we turn, while the Lord is the Spirit by whom we are transformed, and since we have turned to the Lord, the Holy Spirit is clearly designated as Lord. For he receives those who have turned and transforms them.

[Note: Several manuscripts have: “How could one transform what one had not received?”]

103. Yet why do we seek an explicit expression of the word when we see an explicit expression of unity? Even if you distinguish between Lord and Spirit, you still cannot deny that where the Lord is, there also is the Spirit, and that whoever has turned to the Lord has turned to the Spirit. If you attack the letter, you do not deny the unity; if you wish to separate the unity, you confess the Spirit himself as Lord of the power.

CHAPTER XV.

Although the Spirit is called Lord, this does not thereby introduce three Lords; for, since the Son, no less than the Father, is called Lord in various passages of Scripture, two Lords are not thereby introduced. Dominion exists in divinity, and divinity in dominion; these belong indivisibly to the three persons.

104. [In some copies, chapter XVII.] But perhaps you will say again: “If I call the Spirit Lord, I shall declare three Lords.” When you call the Son Lord, do you either deny the Son or confess two Lords? Far from it. For the Son himself said: “You cannot serve two lords” (Matt. VI, 24). Yet he certainly did not deny either himself or the Father as Lord. He also called the Father Lord, as you have it: “I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth” (Matt. XI, 25). And he referred to himself as Lord, as we read in the Gospel: “You call me Lord and Teacher, and you do well; for so I am” (John XIII, 13).

[Note: The Roman edition, with one or two manuscripts, has: “and you say well.”]

But he did not speak of two Lords. Rather, he showed that he had not spoken of two Lords when he warned them beforehand: “You cannot serve two lords.” For there are not two lords where there is one dominion, because the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father;

[Note: Several manuscripts have: “and therefore there is one Ruler.”]

and therefore there is one Lord.

105. The Law likewise taught this: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one Lord” (Deut. VI, 4). That is, he is unchanging, always remaining in the unity of power, always the same, changed neither by addition nor by diminution. Thus Moses spoke of one, and yet he remembered that the Lord rained from the Lord (Gen. XIX, 14).

[Note: Several manuscripts have: “The Apostle also distinguishes them: ‘May the Lord grant him mercy,’” and so forth.]

The Apostle also says: “May the Lord grant him to find mercy from the Lord” (2 Tim. I, 18). The Lord rains from the Lord; the Lord gives mercy from the Lord. The Lord is not divided there, where he rains from the Lord, nor is he separated here, where he shows mercy from the Lord; rather, in both passages the unity of dominion is expressed.

106. In the Psalms also you have: “The Lord said to my Lord” (Ps. CIX, 1). He did not thereby deny that the Father was his Lord because he said that the Son was his Lord. Rather, he called the Son his Lord so that you would not believe that the Son was the prophet’s son, but the Lord—a point which the Lord himself made clear in the Gospel when he said: “If David, in the Spirit, calls him Lord, how is he his son?” (Matt. XXII, 43). David says “Lord” in the Spirit; the Spirit does not say “Lord.”

Or, if they attack this point because he called the Spirit Lord, then by an equally sacrilegious argument they must appear to assert that the Son of God is also the Son of the Holy Spirit.

107. Therefore, just as we do not speak of two Lords when we designate both the Father and the Son, so neither do we speak of three Lords when we confess the Spirit as Lord. For just as it is sacrilege to speak of three Lords or gods, so also it is wholly sacrilegious to speak of two Lords or gods, because there is one God, one Lord, and one Holy Spirit; and whoever is God is Lord, and whoever is Lord is God, because divinity is in dominion and dominion is in divinity.

108. Finally, you have read of the Father as both Lord and God: “Lord my God, I will call to you; hear me” (Ps. CXL, 1).

[Note: This is the reading of the old editions and several manuscripts. The Roman edition and the Colbert manuscript differ from these only in preferring *I called* instead of *I will call*; the remaining written copies have: “I will call to you, and you heard me.”]

And you have the Son as both Lord and God, as you read in the Gospel, for when Thomas touched Christ’s side he said: “My Lord and my God” (John XX, 28). Therefore, just as the Father is God and the Son Lord, so the Son is God and the Father Lord. The devout designation is alternated; the divine nature is not alternated, but grace remains unchanging. These are not comparative judgments of generosity, but natural determinations of love,

[Note: The Thuane manuscript has: “the settled truths of love.”]

because unity possesses distinctiveness, and distinctiveness possesses unity.

688 CHAPTER XVI.

The Father is holy, and likewise the Son and the Spirit, and for this reason they are celebrated with the same threefold hymn. God cannot be proclaimed by us more worthily than by calling him holy; hence it is clear that the Holy Spirit must not be diminished. Everything that belongs to God is present in him: he is named together with the Father and the Son in baptism, and the Father has given him what is greater than all things, which no one can take from him. Thus, from the passage in John from which the heretics constructed their accusation, the equality and unity of the Trinity in divinity are established. Finally, after it has been explained in what manner the Son receives from the Father, the way in which various heretics are refuted at the cited passage is revealed.

109. [In some copies, chapter XVIII.] Therefore the Father is holy, the Son is holy, and the Spirit is holy; but not three holy ones,

[Note: The same point is expressed in precisely the same way in the Creed attributed to Athanasius: “Not three eternal ones, not three uncreated ones, not three immeasurable ones.” Augustine likewise says in Book XI, chapter 24, of *The City of God*: “One God, because of the inseparable divinity, just as one omnipotent, because of the inseparable omnipotence; yet, when each is asked about separately, each one of them is answered to be God and omnipotent, while, when all are considered together, they are not three gods or three omnipotents, but one God omnipotent. So great is the inseparable unity in the three, which has willed to be proclaimed in this way.” Nothing agrees more closely with Ambrose’s view. For just as our Saint gives as the reason why it is not permissible to say “three holy ones” that there is one true and natural holiness, so Augustine denies that they can be called three omnipotents because there is one omnipotence. It is evident here that the terms “omnipotent” and “holy” are taken in the concrete sense, as theologians call it—that is, for the reality itself which is holy and omnipotent. Perhaps those who, following St. Thomas, *Summa* I, question 39, article 3, say that these same terms are taken substantively do not differ greatly from us. On this matter, see the commentators on that passage.]

because there is one holy God, one Lord. For there is one true holiness, just as there is one true divinity: that one true, natural holiness.

110. Therefore all these things that we believe to be holy proclaim that one holiness alone. The Cherubim and Seraphim praise him with unwearied voices and say: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts” (Isa. VI, 3). They do not say it once, lest you understand singularity; they do not say it twice, lest you exclude the Spirit; they do not say “holy ones,” lest you suppose plurality. Rather, they repeat it three times and say the same thing, so that in the hymn you may understand both the distinction of the Trinity and the unity of the divinity. When they say this, they proclaim God.

111. We too find nothing more precious by which we can proclaim God than to call him holy. Whatever else is said is inferior to God, inferior to the Lord. Therefore consider from this point also whether anything should be detracted from the Holy Spirit, whose name is the praise of God. The Father is praised in this way, and the Son is praised in this way, just as the Spirit is named and praised. The Seraph praises him; the entire choir of the blessed praises him, calling God holy, the Son holy, and the Spirit holy.

112. How, then, does he not possess everything that belongs to God, who is named with the Father and the Son by priests in baptism; who is invoked with the Father and the Son in the offerings; who is proclaimed by the Seraphim in heaven with the Father and the Son; who dwells in the holy; who is poured into the righteous and breathed into the prophets? Hence in divine Scripture everything is called θεόπνευστος (*theopneustos*, “God-breathed”) because God inspires what the Spirit has spoken (2 Tim. III, 16).

113. Or, if they do not want him to possess everything that belongs to God and to be able to do everything, let them say what he does not possess and what he cannot do. For just as the Son possesses everything, and the Father does not begrudge giving everything naturally to the Son, to whom he gave what is greater than all things, as Scripture testifies: “What the Father has given me is greater than all” (John X, 29), so also the Spirit of Christ possesses what is greater than all things, because righteousness knows no envy.

114. Therefore, if we pay careful attention, here too we understand the unity of divine power. “What the Father has given me,” he says, “is greater than all, and no one can snatch them from the hand of my Father. I and the Father are one” (ibid., 30). For if we correctly showed above (Book III, chapter 3) that the hand of God is the Holy Spirit, then that same hand is certainly the Father’s hand and the Son’s hand, since the Spirit of the Father is the Spirit of the Son. Therefore, just as whoever among us has received eternal life in the name of the Trinity cannot be snatched from the Father, so he cannot be snatched from the Son, nor can he be snatched from the Spirit.

115. From the very fact that the Father is said to have given and the Spirit to have received from the Son—for it is written, “He will glorify me, because he will receive from what is mine and will announce it to you” (John XVI, 14)—which seems to have been said more concerning the function of his dispensation than concerning the right of divine power, since the Spirit received those whom the Son redeemed in order to sanctify them—from these very words, I say, on which they base their accusation, the unity of divinity is discerned, not any neediness in the giver.

116. The Father gave through generation, not through adoption. He gave as what existed in him by the right of divine nature, not as a gift of generosity, as though it had been lacking. Therefore, because the Son acquired peoples in the same way as the Father and gives life in the same way as the Father, he expressed his equality with the Father through the unity of power, saying: “I and the Father are one.” When he says “I and the Father,” equality is revealed; when he says “are one,” unity is declared. Equality excludes confusion; unity excludes separation. Equality distinguishes the Father and the Son; unity does not separate the Father and the Son.

[Note: Several manuscripts have: “He expressed his unity of power with the Father by his equality.”]

117. Therefore, when he says “I and the Father,” he repels Sabellius, because he said that he was one and the Father another; he repels Photinus, because he joined himself to God the Father. He repels the former by the words above, “I and the Father,” and the Arians by the words below, “We are one.” Yet in both the earlier and the later expressions he cuts down the heretical violence of the Sabellians, because he said “we are one,” not “I am one,” and of the Arians, because he said “I and the Father,” not “the Father and I.”

[Note: Several manuscripts have: “He cuts down their blindness.” This is less suitable. Apart from the fact that “to cut down blindness” is somewhat inelegant, the word “violence” is familiar to Ambrose when he is speaking of heretics. Yet we do not know whether, wherever *saevitas* (“violence,” “savagery”) is written in him, *scaevitas* (“perversity,” “inauspiciousness”) might not instead have been intended, so as to signify not so much the cruel and savage mind of the heretics as its sinister and disastrous character.]

This was not an act of defiance but of piety and foreknowledge, lest we should suppose there to be an error in the order. Unity knows no order, equality knows no rank; nor can it be attributed to the Son of God, who is himself the teacher of piety, that he injured piety through defiance.

690 CHAPTER XVII.

Ambrose shows by examples that, for understanding the Lord’s words, the places in which they were spoken are useful. He teaches that Christ spoke the sentence cited from John in Solomon’s portico, by which the soul of the wise person is signified; for he denies that Christ would have uttered these words in the heart of a foolish or disturbed person, and explains why. He adds that those who lack faith stone Christ with the same words; and that, just as Peter was given the keys of heaven because he confessed them, so Judas Iscariot perished miserably because he did not believe them. On this occasion he attacks the Jews, who bought and sold the Son of God, Joseph. He explains mystically the prices paid in both cases; and, after expounding in the same way the traitor’s complaint about Mary Magdalene’s ointment, he adds that Christ is bought in one way by heretics and in another by Catholics, and that they vainly claim the name of Christians if they divide the Spirit from the Father.

118. It is therefore worth noting in what place the Lord discussed these matters, for his declarations are frequently assessed according to the qualities of the places in which he stayed. When he was about to fast, he was led by the Spirit, as we read (Matt. IV, 1), into the desert, so that he might empty out the devil’s temptations. For although it is praiseworthy to have lived temperately amid an abundance of resources, temptation’s lure is nevertheless more frequent amid riches and pleasures. Finally, the tempter promises abundance in order to tempt, while the Lord nourishes hunger in order to conquer.

I do not deny that continence can exist amid riches; but even if someone who sails the sea often escapes harm, he is nevertheless more exposed to danger than one who has refused to sail.

119. Let us look at the rest. Jesus, intending to promise the kingdom of heaven, ascends a mountain (Matt. 5:1). Elsewhere [Col. 0805B] he leads his disciples through the grainfields (Matt. 12:1), intending to sow in their affections a heavenly harvest of teachings, so that the harvest of souls might ripen abundantly. As he was completing the duties assumed in taking flesh, when he already saw perfection in the disciples whom he had established through the root of his words, he enters a garden (John 18:1), [Note: [Col. 0805D] Quite a few manuscripts read “to plant fresh shoots of vegetables”; one has “to have planted”; two, “planted”; some, “of the flowering palm.”] in order to plant young olive trees in the house of the Lord, and to water with the stream of his blood the righteous man, flowering like a palm, and the fruitful vine (Ps. 127:3).

120. In this place too Christ was walking in Solomon’s portico on the day of the Dedication, as we read (John 10:23)—that is, he was walking in the breast of the wise and peaceful man, intending to dedicate that man’s affection to himself. The Prophet teaches what this portico is when he says: “I walked in the innocence of my heart in the midst of your house” (Ps. 100:2). [Note: [Col. 0805D] Thus read most manuscripts; several others, as well as all printed editions, have “of my house.” Although the sacred codices favor this reading, it nevertheless seems that the other should be preferred, as the following words immediately show: “Therefore we have within us the house of God.”] Therefore we have within us the house of God; we have courts, we also have porticoes, and we have streets as well, because it is written: “And in your streets let your waters overflow” (Prov. 5:16). Enlarge, then, this portico of your heart with the Word of God, who says to you: “Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it” (Ps. 81:11).

121. Therefore, as the Word of God walks in the heart of the wise 691 and peaceful man, let us hear what he says: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). He will not say this in the breast of a disturbed and foolish man, because “the natural man does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God; for they are foolishness to him” (1 Cor. 2:14). The narrow breasts of the impious cannot contain the greatness of faith. Accordingly, when the Jews heard, “I and the Father are one,” they took up stones to stone him (John 10:31).

[Col. 0805D] 122. Whoever cannot hear this is a Jew; whoever cannot hear this stones Christ with the harsher stones of his unbelief—and, if you believe me, wounds Christ. For although he cannot now feel a wound: “For now we know Christ no longer according to the flesh” (2 Cor. 5:16), nevertheless he is stoned by the impiety of the Arians, while he rejoices in the piety of the Church.

[Col. 0806A] 123. “The law of your mouth is good for me, Lord” (Ps. 119:72); I keep your commandment. You yourself said that you are one with the Father. Because Peter believed this, he received the keys of the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 16:19), and, secure in his own standing, forgave sins; because Judas did not believe this, he strangled himself in the noose of his impiety (Matt. 27:5). O hard stones of the unbelieving against the words! O the misshapen noose of the betrayer—and the still more deformed price of the Jews! O wicked silver, by which the just man is either bought for death or sold! Joseph was sold (Gen. 37:28), Jesus Christ was bought (Matt. 26:15): the one for slavery, the other for death. Detestable inheritance, fatal sale, which either sells a brother to injury or bids for the Lord’s destruction—the Redeemer of all.

[Col. 0806B] 124. Thus Judaism violated the two things that are superior to all others, faith and piety; and in both cases, Christ, the author of faith and piety. For Christ was typified in the patriarch Joseph, and Christ is present in the truth of his body: he “did not regard being equal with God as something to be seized, but took the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:6–7), assuming slavery because of our falls, and not shrinking from suffering.

125. [Note: [Col. 0806D] Concerning the sale of Christ, Ambrose recalls elsewhere, in Book VI on Luke, no. 31, that he had said more; it is likely that he was referring either to this very chapter or to chapter 3, “On the Patriarch Joseph,” II.14, where much is found that is very similar to what we read here.] In one place he is bought for twenty pieces of gold, in another for thirty. For how could his true price be grasped, whose worth cannot be defined? The price goes astray because the devotion goes astray. In the Old Testament he is sold for twenty pieces of gold, in the Gospel for thirty; for truth is more precious than its type, grace is more generous than discipline, and the present reality is richer than the Law, because the Law promised [Col. 0806C] his coming, while the Law of his coming brought fulfillment.

126. The Ishmaelites buy him for twenty pieces of gold; the Jews, for thirty. Nor is the symbolism here insignificant. The faithless are more generous toward sacrilege than the faithful toward salvation. Yet it is fitting to consider the character of both transactions. Twenty pieces of gold are the price of slavery; thirty pieces of gold are the price of the cross. Although the mysteries of his assumption of flesh and of his passion are equally wondrous, the fullness of faith is nevertheless found in the sacrament of the passion. I do not value less the birth of the holy Virgin; but I embrace more gratefully the sacrament of the blessed body. What is more merciful than that he gave me his own injuries? 692 Yet what he has bestowed upon us is fuller: he who could not die, because he was God, died by our death, so that we might live by his Spirit.

[Col. 0806D] 127. Finally, it was not without significance that Judas Iscariot valued that ointment at three hundred denarii (John 12:5): by fixing that price, he seemed to indicate the Lord’s cross. Hence the Lord also says: “She poured this ointment on my body to prepare me for burial” (Matt. 26:12). Why, then, did Judas value it more highly? Because forgiveness of sins costs sinners more, and pardon appears more precious. Thus you have it written: “He to whom more is forgiven loves more” (Luke 7:47). Therefore sinners themselves confess the grace of the Lord’s passion, which they have lost, and bear witness to Christ—even those who persecuted Christ.

128. Or perhaps, because “wisdom does not enter a malevolent soul” (Wis. 1:4), the betrayer’s disposition was saying this as well: he valued the passion of the Lord’s body more highly in order to draw everyone away from faith by the enormity of the price. Therefore the Lord offered himself freely, so that the necessity of poverty might not turn anyone away from Christ. The patriarchs sold him cheaply so that all might buy him. Isaiah said: “All you who have no silver, go, buy, and drink; eat without silver” (Isa. 55:1). [Note: [Col. 0807D] The Ambrosian and Erasmian editions have: “Come, buy and drink. And they ate and were satisfied in the desert”; Gill’s and the Roman edition: “Come, buy and drink; eat” (the Roman edition: “buy”) “without silver”; several manuscripts: “Come, drink, and eat,” and so forth; but the majority and better manuscripts read as in the text.] so that the one who had no silver might acquire him. O betrayer Judas, you value his ointment of passion at three hundred denarii, yet sell his passion for thirty denarii (Matt. 26:15)! Rich in valuation, worthless in crime.

129. Therefore not everyone buys Christ at the same price. Photinus buys him in one way, buying him for death; the Arian in another, buying him for insult; the Catholic in another, buying him [Note: [Col. 0807D] The Floriac manuscript reads “for glory,” since for some he is “the odor of death unto death,” while for others “the odor of life unto life.” But the reading is “buys,” and so forth.] for glory. Yet he buys him without money, according to what is written: “He who has no money, let him buy without price” (Isa. 55:1).

130. “Not everyone,” he says, “who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 7:21). Although many call themselves Christians, they usurp the name, but not all receive the reward. Cain too offered a sacrifice (Gen. 4:3), and Judas received a kiss (Luke 22:48), but he heard: “Judas, are you betraying the Son of Man with a kiss?” [Note: [Col. 0807D] Book X on Luke, no. 63: “That is, you complete a crime by the pledge of love, shed blood under the pretext of charity, and inflict death by the instrument of peace.”] that is, you consummate crime by the pledge of love, sow hatred by the instrument of peace, and inflict death by the service of charity.

131. Therefore let the Arians not flatter themselves by usurping the name, because they call themselves Christians. The Lord will answer them: “You invoke my name, yet deny my substance. But I do not acknowledge my name where my eternal divinity is absent. It is not my name when it is divided from the Father and separated from the Spirit. I do not acknowledge my name where I do not acknowledge my doctrine; I do not acknowledge my name where I do not acknowledge my Spirit.” For the Spirit of the Father does not recognize that he can be compared with the servitudes that he created. We have already said much about this (Book I, chapter 1 and following).

693 CHAPTER XVIII

Intending to confirm the divinity of the Holy Spirit from what has been argued thus far, he takes up several matters again—namely, that the Spirit does not have sins but forgives them; that he is not a creature but the Creator; and finally, that he does not adore but is adored.

132. [Elsewhere chapter XIX.] To sum up, however, so that at the end we may gather more explicitly what has been said in scattered places, the glory of his manifest divinity is established above all from these four considerations: God is recognized either because he is without sin, or because he forgives sins; or because he is not a creature but the Creator; or because he does not adore but is adored. [Note: [Col. 0807D] Some manuscripts: “of manifest divinity.”]

133. Thus no one is without sin except the one God, because no one is without sin except the one God. [Note: [Col. 0808D] All printed editions read: “Therefore no one is without sin, because no one is without sin except …,” from which words some manuscripts remove “because no one is without sin.” The remainder, however, numerous and ancient, agrees with us. Indeed, the words “because no one is without sin” seem to be cited as the text of Scripture itself and introduced as a proof of what precedes. Since they do not appear in this precise form in the biblical books, it is credible that the passage referred to is Matt. 19:17, “No one is good except God alone.”] No one also forgives sins except the one God, because it is likewise written: “Who can forgive sins except God alone?” (Luke 5:21). The Creator of all, too, can be none other than he who is not a creature; and whoever is not a creature is without doubt God, because it is written: “They served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever” (Rom. 1:23). God also does not adore but is adored, because it is written: “You shall adore the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Deut. 6:13).

134. Let us therefore consider whether the Holy Spirit possesses any of these things that bear witness to divinity. First, then, let us discuss the claim that no one is without sin except the one God, and let them demonstrate what sin the Holy Spirit has.

135. But they cannot demonstrate it, and they demand authority, so that we may teach from the reading that the Holy Spirit did not sin, just as it is written concerning the Son that he “committed no sin” (1 Pet. 2:22). Let them accept that we teach this by the authority of Scripture: for it is written: “In Wisdom is the Spirit of understanding, holy, unique, manifold, subtle, readily mobile, eloquent, undefiled” (Wis. 7:22). Scripture calls him undefiled. Did it lie about the Son, so that you should believe that it lied about the Spirit? For in the same passage the prophet says of Wisdom that nothing defiled enters into her. She herself is undefiled, and her Spirit is undefiled. Therefore, if the Spirit has no sin, he is God.

136. But how can he be guilty of sin who himself forgives sins? Therefore he did not sin; and because he is without sin, he is not a creature. For every creature is subject to the possibility of sin, whereas the eternal divinity alone is free from sin and undefiled.

[Col. 0808D] 137. Now let us see whether the Spirit forgives sins. There can be no doubt about this, since the Lord himself said: “Receive the Holy Spirit: whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven” (John 20:22). Behold, sins are forgiven through the Holy Spirit. Human beings offer their ministry for the forgiveness of sins; they do not exercise the right of some independent power. For they forgive sins not in their own name but in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. They ask; divinity grants. The service is human, but the generosity belongs to heavenly power.

138. It is also beyond doubt that sins are forgiven through baptism; and in baptism there is the operation of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Therefore, if [Note: [Col. 0809D] All printed editions and many more manuscripts read “does not have sin”; the Ebrulph and Aud. codices read “forgives sin.” Quite rightly, for Ambrose is not here proving that the Spirit has no sins, but is now arguing that he himself forgives sins.] the Spirit forgives sin, since it is written: “Who can forgive sins except the one God?” (Mark 2:7), then surely he who cannot be separated from the unity of the natural name cannot be separated from God’s power either. But if he is not separated from God’s power, how is he separated from God’s name?

139. Let us now see whether he is a creature or the Creator. But since above we have proved the Creator most clearly—because it is written: “The divine Spirit who made me” (Job 33:4), and “by the Spirit” the face of the earth is renewed (Ps. 104:30), and it has been shown that everything languishes without the Spirit—it is evident that the Spirit is the Creator. Who could doubt this, when, as we showed above, even the generation of the Lord from the Virgin, which is superior to all creatures, did not occur without the operation of the Spirit?

140. The Spirit, therefore, is not a creature but the Creator; and whoever is the Creator is certainly not a creature. And because he is not a creature, he is without doubt the Creator, who cooperates with the Father and the Son in all things. [Note: [Col. 0809D] Thus read most manuscripts; some, as well as all printed editions: “the Creator of all, who cooperated with the Father and the Son in all things.”] But if he is the Creator, then, when the Apostle condemns paganism by saying, “They served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever” (Rom. 1:23), and when, as we have taught above (Book II, chapters 5–6), he urges that the Holy Spirit must be served, he both demonstrates that the Spirit is the Creator and shows that, because he is the Creator, he must be called God. This is also contained in the Epistle written to the Hebrews, where it says: “The one who created all things is God” (Heb. 3:4). Let them say, then, what was created without the Father, the Son, and the Spirit—or let them confess that the Spirit too possesses one divinity with the Father and the Son.

141. He also taught that the Spirit must be adored, when he called him Lord and God. For whoever is God and Lord of the universe must certainly be adored by all; for it is written: “You shall adore the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Deut. 6:13).

142. Or let them say where they have read that the Spirit adores. For it is said of the Son of God: “Let all his angels adore him” (Heb. 1:6); it is not written, “Let the Spirit adore.” For how can he adore who is not among servants and ministers, but with the Father and the Son has the services of the righteous subject to him? For it is written: “We serve the Spirit of God” (Phil. 3:3). [Note: [Col. 0810D] The latest edition reads: “We serve the Spirit God.”] Therefore we must adore him whom the Apostle taught us to serve; and whoever we serve, we also adore, according to what is written—and let us repeat it often: “You shall adore the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve.”

143. Yet the Apostle did not omit this point either, for he also declared that the Spirit is to be adored. Since we have taught that the Spirit is in the prophets, and no one can doubt that prophecy is given through the Spirit, [Note: [Col. 0810D] Some manuscripts: “therefore, when we serve God, the one who is in the prophets is adored—that is, the Spirit is adored.”] then certainly, when the one who is in the prophets is adored, the same Spirit is adored. Thus you have it: “If the whole Church assembles together in one place and all speak in tongues, but an uninstructed person or an unbeliever enters, will he not say that you are mad? But if all prophesy, and an uninstructed person or an unbeliever enters, he is convicted by all and judged by all. The secrets of his heart are also made manifest; and so, falling on his face, he will adore God, declaring that God is truly among you” (1 Cor. 14:23 ff.). Therefore it is God who is adored, God who remains and speaks in the prophets; but the Spirit remains and speaks. Therefore the Spirit too is adored.

CHAPTER XIX

From the fact established above that the Spirit both remains and speaks in the prophets, he concludes that the Spirit knows all that belongs to God, and therefore is one with the Father and the Son. He confirms this again by showing that the Spirit possesses everything God possesses—namely, divinity, knowledge of the heart, truth, the name above every name, and the power to raise the dead—the last of which he assigns to the Spirit from Ezekiel, in whom he also proves the Spirit equal to the Son.

[Col. 0810C] 144. Therefore, just as the Father and the Son are one because the Son possesses everything the Father possesses (John 16:15), so the Spirit is one with the Father and the Son because he too knows everything that belongs to God (1 Cor. 2:10). He did not extort these things, lest their loss be an injury to the one who lost them; he did not seize them, lest there be damage to the one from whom they seemed to have been taken. He did not seize them through need, nor extort them through the superiority of a stronger power; rather, he possesses them through the unity of power. Therefore, since he performs all these things, because “it is the one and the same Spirit who works all things” (1 Cor. 12:11), how can he not be God, who possesses everything God possesses?

145. Or let us consider what God has that the Holy Spirit does not have. God the Father has divinity; the Son has it too, in whom the fullness of divinity dwells; and the Spirit has it as well, because it is written: “The divine Spirit who is in my nostrils” (Job 17:3).

146. God has the power to search hearts and kidneys, because it is written: “God, who searches hearts and kidneys” (Ps. 7:10). The Son has it too, for he said: “Why are you thinking evil in your hearts?” (Matt. 9:4). Jesus knew their thoughts. The Spirit also has it, for he reveals even the secrets of another’s heart to the prophets, as we said above (Book II, chapter 13): “The secrets of his heart are made manifest.” And why should we wonder that he searches the secrets of human beings, when he even searches “the depths of God” (1 Cor. 2:10)?

147. God has the quality of being truthful, because it is written: “Let God be true, and every man a liar” (Rom. 3:4). Elsewhere it is written: “God is faithful, who does not lie” (Titus 1:2). Does the Spirit lie, who is the Spirit of truth—or rather, whom we have shown to be called truth, since John also called him truth, just as he called the Son truth (John 16:13)? And David says in the psalm: “Send forth your light and your truth; they themselves have led me and brought me to your holy mountain and to your tabernacles” (Ps. 43:3). If you understand the Son as the light, then the Spirit is truth; or if you understand the Son as truth, then the Spirit is light.

148. God has a name above every name, and he gave the Son this name, as we read (Phil. 2:9), so that all might bend their knees in the name of Jesus. Let us consider whether the Spirit has this name. It is also written: “Go, baptize the nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Mark 16:15). Therefore he has a name above every name. What the Father and the Son possess, the Spirit possesses as well through the unity of the natural name.

149. [Elsewhere chapter XX.] God has the power to raise the dead: “For just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whomever he wills” (John 5:21). The Spirit also raises the dead, through whom God raises them, because it is written: “He will give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you” (Rom. 8:11). Yet lest you think his grace weak, hear that the Spirit also raises the dead. The prophet Ezekiel says: “Come, Spirit, and breathe upon these dead, and they shall live. And I prophesied as he commanded me, and the Spirit of life entered into them, and they lived and stood upon their feet, an exceedingly great assembly.” [Note: [Col. 0811D] Several manuscripts read “many assemblies.”] (Ezek. 37:9–10). And below God says: “You shall know that I am the Lord, when I open your graves, to bring my people out of their graves; and I will put my Spirit in you, and you shall live” (ibid., 13–14).

150. When he says “my Spirit,” did he perhaps designate someone other than the Holy Spirit? For he would not call the spirit that gives breath his own spirit, nor could this spirit come from the four quarters of the world. The breath of the winds that we see belongs to one region, not to the whole; and the spirit by which we live belongs to individuals, not to all. But the Holy Spirit is such that he is both over all and in all. Thus from the prophetic words one can observe how the bones, once scattered after the dissolution of their limbs, return through the life-giving Spirit to the form of a restored body; and how the ash gathers into its limbs, animated with the sense of joining together before it has been reshaped into the appearance of living.

151. Do we not recognize, in the likeness of the deed, the unity of divine power? The Spirit raises the dead just as the Lord raised them in his own passion, when suddenly, in the twinkling of an eye, the graves of the dead were opened and restored bodies rose from the tombs (Matt. 27:52); the stench of death was wiped away and the fragrance of life restored, and the ashes of those who had breathed their last received again the appearance of the living.

152. Therefore the Spirit possesses what Christ possesses; he therefore possesses what God possesses, because everything the Father possesses the Son also possesses. Hence he said: “Everything that the Father has is mine” (John 16:15).

CHAPTER XX

The Spirit is represented by the river flowing from the throne of God; by the waters mentioned by David, heavenly powers are signified. The kingdom of God is the work of the Spirit; nor is it surprising that the Spirit reigns together with the Son, since Paul promises that we too shall reign together with the Son.

153. [Elsewhere chapter XXI.] Nor is it an insignificant matter that we read of a river issuing from the throne of God. For John the Evangelist says: “And he showed me a river of living water, bright as crystal, proceeding from the throne of God and of the Lamb; in the midst of its street, and on either side of it, the tree of life, bearing twelve fruits, yielding its fruit each month; and the leaves of the tree are for the healing of all nations” (Rev. 22:1–2).

154. This is certainly the river proceeding from the throne of God—that is, the Holy Spirit, whom the one who believes in Christ drinks, as Christ himself says: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.” This he said about the Spirit (John 7:37–38). Therefore the Spirit is a river.

155. He is therefore at the throne of God; for water does not wash the throne of God. Accordingly David did not say that the waters are above the throne of God, but above the heavens, whatever water you may understand: “And the waters that are above the heavens, let them praise the name of the Lord” (Ps. 148:4). He said “let them praise,” not “let it praise.” For if he had wished the element of water to be understood, he would certainly have said “let it praise”; by using the plural, he intended powers to be understood.

156. And what is surprising if the Holy Spirit is at the throne of God, when the kingdom of God itself is the work of the Spirit, as it is written: “The kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit” (Rom. 14:17)? The Savior himself also says: “Every kingdom divided against itself will be destroyed” (Matt. 12:25). Then, by adding, “But if I cast out demons by the Spirit of God, surely the kingdom of God has come upon you” (ibid., 28), he showed that the kingdom of God is indivisible with the Spirit.

157. What, then, is more foolish than for anyone to deny that the Holy Spirit reigns together with Christ, when the Apostle even says that we shall reign together with Christ in Christ’s kingdom: “For if we have died together with him, we shall also live together with him; if we endure, we shall also reign together with him” (2 Tim. 2:11–12)? But we reign through adoption, he through power; we by grace, he by nature.

158. Therefore the Holy Spirit also shares the kingdom with the Father and the Son, since he is of one nature, one lordship, and one power with them.

CHAPTER XXI

Isaiah was sent by the Spirit, and therefore saw that same Spirit. What is meant by the moving wheels and the various wings; and why, when the Spirit is proclaimed by the Seraphim as God Sabaoth, only the impious can deny this name to him.

159. [Elsewhere chapter XXIII.] Since the Spirit shares the kingdom, what prevents us from understanding him as the one by whom Isaiah was sent? We cannot doubt this when Paul is our authority, whose judgment Luke the Evangelist so confirmed in the Acts of the Apostles that he wrote as follows. Thus you have it, Paul saying: “The Holy Spirit spoke well through Isaiah the prophet to our fathers, saying: ‘Go to this people and say: You will hear with your ears and not understand; and seeing, you will see and not perceive’” (Acts 28:25–26).

160. Therefore it was the Spirit who sent Isaiah. If the Spirit sent him, then the Spirit is surely the one whom Isaiah saw when King Uzziah died, saying: “I saw the Lord Sabaoth sitting upon a high and exalted throne, and the house was full of his majesty; and the Seraphim stood around him: six wings for one and six wings for the other; with two they covered his face, with two they covered his feet, and with two they flew; and they cried out to one another and said: ‘Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God Sabaoth; the whole [Note: [Col. 0813D] Some manuscripts: “the whole earth is full of the glory of his majesty.”] earth is full of his majesty’” (Isa. 6:1 ff.).

161. If the Seraphim were standing, how were they flying? If they were flying, how were they standing? If we cannot comprehend this, how do we wish to comprehend God, whom we do not see?

162. But just as the prophet saw one wheel within another wheel moving (Ezek. 1:16)—which certainly does not refer to the form of a bodily vision but to the grace of both Testaments, because the life of the saints is round and so harmonious that what follows answers to what came before—so likewise the wings were standing and the wings were flying. The wheel within the wheel is life under the Law and life under grace, because Judaism is within the Church and the Law is within grace. For the Jew who is one inwardly is within the Church, and circumcision of the heart is a sacrament within the Church. But this is the Judaism within the Church of which it is written: “God is known in Judah” (Ps. 76:1). Therefore, just as one wheel runs within another wheel, so the wings were standing and the wings were flying.

163. Likewise the Seraphim covered their face with two wings, their feet with two, and flew with two. Here too there is a sacrament of spiritual wisdom. Times stand; times fly. The past stands; the future flies. And like the wings of the Seraphim, they cover God’s face and feet, because in God, who has neither beginning nor end, the entire course of time is directed away from knowledge of his beginning and end. [Note: [Col. 0813D] The edition of the Society of Jesus and the editions following it, together with some manuscripts, read: “because in God the course of time is carried onward . . .” (the Roman edition: “toward God”); the Ambrosian edition, together with many more manuscripts, reads as in the text, except that some have “thought” instead of “knowledge.” The sense is that, in God, who enjoys unchanging eternity, the succession of times has no place.] Thus the past or future stands, while the present flies. Do not seek the mysteries of his beginning or end, which do not exist. You have the present: praise him, but do not scrutinize him.

164. The Seraphim praise him with tireless voices, and you scrutinize him? By doing this, they show us that God is not to be scrutinized at some times but praised always. Therefore the Lord Sabaoth is also the Holy Spirit. [Elsewhere chapter XXIII.] Unless perhaps the impious dislike the teacher whom Christ chose; or can they deny that the Holy Spirit is the Lord of hosts, who himself gives whatever powers he wishes?

CHAPTER XXII

To establish the unity of the kingdom in the three Persons, the passage cited from Isaiah is examined; and it is shown that there is no difference of meaning among those who have interpreted it of the Father, the Son, or the Spirit. Moreover, the Spirit’s majesty is affirmed from the fact that the crucified one is called the Lord of majesty; and his equality with the Father and the Son is shown to be so great that the Arians will never be able to overthrow it.

165. Now we may recognize the unity of majesty and kingdom in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. For many say that Isaiah saw God the Father at that time (Isa. 6:1), while Paul said that it was the Spirit, Luke confirmed this (Acts 28:25), and John the Evangelist referred it to the Son. For it is written concerning the Son (John 12:36): “Jesus said these things, and he departed and hid himself from them. Although he had performed so many signs before them, they did not believe in him, so that the word of Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled, which he said: ‘Lord, who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?’” (Isa. 53:1). “Therefore they could not believe, because Isaiah said again: ‘He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, so that they might not see with their eyes, understand with their heart, turn, and I would heal them’” (Isa. 6:10). Isaiah said this when he saw his majesty and spoke about him.

166. John explicitly said that Isaiah had spoken these very words, and clearly revealed that the Son’s majesty had appeared to him; Paul, however, recalled that the Spirit had spoken these things. How, then, is this difference to be understood?

167. The difference is one of words, not of meaning. Although they said different things, none of them erred, because the Father is seen in the Son, who said: “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John 14:9). And the Son is seen in the Spirit, because just as no one says “Lord Jesus” except in the Holy Spirit (1 Cor. 12:3), so Christ is seen not with bodily eyes but through spiritual grace. Hence Scripture says: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine upon you” (Eph. 5:14). And when Paul had lost his sight, how could he see Christ except in the Spirit (Acts 9:8)? Hence the Lord also says: “For I have appeared to you for this purpose, to appoint you a minister and a witness of the things in which you have seen me and of those in which you will see me” (Acts 26:16). For the prophets too received the Spirit and saw Christ.

168. Therefore there is one vision, one command, one majesty. Or do we deny that the Holy Spirit too is the Lord of majesty (1 Cor. 2:12), when the Lord of majesty was crucified—the one who was born from the Holy Spirit of the Virgin Mary? For Christ is not another but one: before the ages he was born from the Father as the Son of God, and in the age of the world he was generated as man through the assumption of flesh.

169. Why should I say that, just as the Father and the Son are undefiled and almighty, so also is the Spirit (Wis. 7:22)? For Solomon said in Greek παντοδύναμον, πανεπίσκοπον—“almighty” and “overseeing all”—as was shown above from the Book of Wisdom (chapter 18, no. 135). Therefore the Spirit too possesses honor and majesty.

170. Consider now whether anything perhaps does not befit him; or, if you dislike him, Arian, remove him from fellowship with the Father and the Son. But if you try to remove him, you will see the heavens turning back above you. [Note: [Col. 0815A] All printed editions and some manuscripts read “you will see the heavens overturned above you”; the remaining manuscripts more suitably read “you will see the heavens turn back above you”; some have “overthrown,” that is, “falling upon you.”] For all their power is from the Spirit (Ps. 33:6). If you try to remove him, you must first lay your hand upon God, because “God is Spirit” (John 4:24). But how will you remove him, [Note: [Col. 0816A] Some manuscripts: “who is the searcher of God.”] who searches the depths of God (1 Cor. 2:10)?

[ON THE MYSTERY OF THE LORD’S INCARNATION.]

[Col. 0815]

INTRODUCTION TO THE BOOK ON THE MYSTERY OF THE LORD’S INCARNATION

[Col. 0815]

[Col. 0815A] It is the customary practice of heretics that, however thoroughly they may be cast down and overthrown by the force of arguments and truth, they nevertheless never consent to proceed calmly, much less to admit that they have been defeated. Ambrose, who knew this character of theirs very well, judged that the errors of the Arians had been sufficiently refuted in five books On the Faith and had resolved to add nothing further for the future (chapter 7, no. 62). Nevertheless, their tricks and devices brought it about that, compelled by weighty circumstances, he could neither decline nor avoid entering the arena with them again.

Two Arians, chamberlains of the Emperor Gratian (Pauline, Life of Ambrose), drew him into this dispute. They had ambitiously and arrogantly proposed objections against the Lord’s incarnation, and he had promised that on the following day he would answer them in the Portian Basilica before the entire assembly of the faithful. The space seemed too limited to suffice for preparing a discourse on matters so serious, especially since it was highly probable that the heretics would flock there in great numbers to criticize and disparage anything that might have been said with insufficient caution or reflection. Nevertheless our Ambrose did not fail to keep his promises. When he saw that the aforementioned courtiers had not arrived at the appointed time—although he suspected that they were deliberately delaying in order to throw him into confusion by an unexpected appearance—he nevertheless immediately began to speak (chapter 1, no. 1).

Yet, in order still to leave them the opportunity of approaching him, he took the occasion supplied by the history of the sacrifice offered by the two first brothers, which had been read aloud at the Church’s frequent assembly (No. 2), and briefly disclosed with what fault Cain’s sacrifice had been tainted (No. 3 and following). Then he teaches that this terrible sentence, by which Cain himself was struck from God’s own mouth, extends also to all heretics (Chapter 2, no. 6 and following), but especially to those whose succession he traces down to the Apollinarists, who held erroneous views concerning Christ’s human soul. Finally, after earnestly exhorting his hearers never to allow themselves to be torn away from the bosom of the Church (No. 13), he elegantly and forcefully proves against the Arians that Christ is eternal and truly God (Chapters 3 and 4). From these he turns to the Apollinarists, though he spares their name (Chapter 5); and he also accuses the author of a certain book—whom we believe to have been Apollinarius himself—of blasphemy, while likewise suppressing his name (Chapter 6, no. 51). Afterwards, in Chapter 6, continuing to press their remaining errors, having warned that one must carefully distinguish between what belongs properly to Christ’s divinity and what pertains to his humanity (Chapter 4, no. 23 and following), he destroys, with the most invincible force of argument, one of the principal fantasies of these men: that the Lord’s divinity and flesh were of one substance (Chapter 6, no. 49 and following). In this matter we may rightly affirm that he made excellent and highly skilled use of Athanasius’ letter to Epictetus (published among his works and in Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* 77). Nor did he overthrow with less intellectual power their other opinion, which deprived the Lord of a rational soul (Chapter 7). Since this error is also reported to have belonged to the Arians (Augustine, *On Heresies*, chapter 55; Theodoret, *Compendium of Heretical Fables*, book IV, chapter 1), no one will be surprised that these same chamberlains of the emperor, attached and enrolled to the Arian party, had raised it against the Arians.

Here the blessed Bishop had ended his sermon. But when he was arranging it into a book, he decided to append at the end a solution of the difficulty that had been proposed to him after the sermon had been delivered (Chapter 8 and following). For since the heretics, who had never ceased to lie in wait for Gratian’s piety, had not heard Ambrose speaking in the Portian Basilica, as has been said, they boasted before him with great confidence that the Father, who was unbegotten, could not be of the same substance as the Son, whom no one denied to have been begotten. The Arian heresy turned upon this objection as upon a principal hinge, as we understand from the books of those who defended the Catholic faith with singular distinction. Ambrose therefore resolved the objection, which had been reported to him by the Emperor, with such solidity that nothing at all is left for us to desire. Finally, after resolving another difficulty, but one much lighter, concerning Christ’s omnipotence, the book is closed (Chapter 10, no. 111 and following).

Moreover, we cannot refrain from highly praising here the prudence and moderation of the holy Bishop. Although, when he reduced his sermon to book form, he was less ignorant than anyone else of the grievous end of the two chamberlains whom we have mentioned, nevertheless, lest he should appear in any way to be yielding to agitation, he allowed no word on that matter to escape him. The incident was too remarkable to be omitted; but since it has been elegantly and accurately described by Paulinus, the historian of our Ambrose’s life, we shall reproduce it in his own words:

“There were also at that time two chamberlains of the Emperor Gratian, belonging to the Arian heresy, who proposed a question for the Bishop to discuss. They promised that on the following day they would all be present at the Portian Basilica to hear him. The question concerned the Incarnation of the Lord. But on the appointed day the pitiable men, filled with the swelling of pride and mindful neither of their promises nor of God, whom they despised in his priest, and giving no consideration to the injury done to the waiting people—forgetful also of the Lord’s words, that ‘whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble, it is necessary that a millstone be hung around his neck and that he be plunged into the depths of the sea’—mounted a carriage, as though for the sake of being conveyed, and left the city, while the priest waited and the people remained assembled in the church. But I shudder to relate what the end of this obstinacy was. For suddenly they were thrown from the carriage and gave up their souls, and their bodies were handed over for burial. Saint Ambrose, however, unaware of what had happened and unable to keep the people waiting any longer, ascended the tribunal and began to speak on the question that had been proposed, saying: ‘Brothers, I am concerned to discharge a debt, but I do not find my creditors of yesterday’; and the rest is written in the book entitled *On the Incarnation of the Lord*.”

Thus Paulinus, whose final words also disclose the book’s title. We find this same title in other writers as well, by whom the same little work was later cited with approval (the Synod against the Tragedian, Irenaeus, in the collections of Councils by Baluze and Christ. Lupus, and elsewhere). Some additionally append the words “against the Apollinarists” (Theodoret, *Polymeron*). There were also those who, moved by the work’s opening, wished to cite it under the title *Sermon on Cain and Abel* (Ivo, *Decretum*, part II, chapter 7; Gratian, *On Consecration*, distinction 2). But unquestionably the best title of all is the one borne not only by very many and highly authoritative manuscripts, as well as by the old editions, but also indicated by Ambrose himself (Chapter 7, no. 63), namely, *On the Sacrament of the Lord’s Incarnation*—or, as the Roman editors preferred, together with certain authors, *On the Mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation*.

As for the date of the same book: just as nothing is more certain than that it is later than the books *On the Faith* (ibid., no. 62), so it is not easy to determine by how many years those books preceded it. In citing them, the holy Doctor once uses the word “formerly” in this work (Chapter 8, no. 79); but in other passages where he mentions them, he always employs expressions indicating that they had been published not long before. Nevertheless, since the books *On the Faith* were not completed until the year 379, as has been shown, whereas Paulinus reports that this work itself was composed while the Emperor Gratian was still alive—he died in 383—the word “formerly” scarcely permits us to suppose that it was composed before the year 382; nor does Gratian’s death permit us to place it much later than that year.

[Col. 0817]

**ONE BOOK OF SAINT AMBROSE, BISHOP OF MILAN, ON THE SACRAMENT OF THE LORD’S INCARNATION**  
[Note: [Col. 0817] Written around the year 382.]

703 **CHAPTER ONE**

[Col. 0817]

Having indicated the occasion for his discourse, Ambrose turns to the sacrifices of Cain and Abel. He investigates what displeased God in the former’s offering. Then, after briefly explaining Abel’s burnt offering [Col. 0818], he teaches whom the sentence pronounced against Cain strikes.

**1.** “Brothers, I desire to discharge a debt, but I do not find my creditors of yesterday, unless perhaps they thought that by an unexpected gathering they could throw us into confusion. But true faith is never thrown into confusion.”

[Note: [Col. 0817] Thus the old edition and several manuscripts, except that *brothers* is absent in many; the Roman edition and several other manuscripts read, “Brothers, I take care”; the rest, “Brothers, I believe,” and so forth.]

**2.** Therefore, while those men perhaps are coming, let us turn aside to these farmers who have been proposed: one of them, namely Cain, offered the Lord produce from the fruits of the earth; the other, Abel, offered a sacrifice from the firstborn of his sheep (Genesis IV, 3–4). I find nothing in the outward form of the gifts to criticize, except that Cain learned that his gifts were displeasing, and the Lord said: “If you offer rightly, but do not divide rightly, you have sinned” (ibid., 7).

**3.** Where, then, is the crime? Where is the fault? Not in the offering of the gift, but in the disposition of the one offering it. Some think, and rightly so, that the difference was this: one had selected what he would offer, while the other offered what he had that was less valuable. But our spiritual understanding is not so impoverished that we should suppose that the Lord was seeking a bodily sacrifice, not a spiritual one. Therefore he added, “Be quiet” (ibid.), indicating that it is more tolerable to abstain from bringing gifts than to offer a gift with faithless devotion. For whoever does not know how to divide does not know how to discern; but the spiritual person judges all things (1 Corinthians II, 15). And for this reason Abraham divided the sacrifice that he was offering (Genesis XV, 10).

**4.** Abel also knew how to divide: he offered a sacrifice from the firstborn of his sheep (Genesis IV, 4), teaching that it was not the gifts of the earth—gifts that had degenerated in the sinner—that would please God, but those in which the grace of the divine mystery might shine forth.

[Note: [Col. 0819C] Several manuscripts read: “in which the divine grace might shine forth in the mysteries.”]

He therefore prophesied that we would be redeemed from guilt through the Lord’s Passion, concerning whom it is written: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sin of the world” (John I, 29). Hence he offered from the firstborn, so that he might designate the firstborn. He therefore showed that we would be the true sacrifice of God, of whom the Prophet says: “Bring to the Lord the sons of rams” (Psalm XXVIII, 1).

[Note: [Col. 0819C] All editions and by far the majority of manuscripts read: “And rightly it is confirmed by God’s judgment, which sentence, etc.” Some others read: “And rightly this is shown, which sentence, etc.” We have restored the passage from one Victor manuscript, two Colbert manuscripts, and one Sorbonne manuscript.]

And rightly this is confirmed by God’s judgment.

**5.** But to him who was rejected it is said, “Be quiet.” I think that this sentence was pronounced generally against all who stand outside the Church; for here I discern a figure of many peoples, whom the divine sentence encompasses, whose gifts he then already rejected in that Cain (Genesis IV, 5).

[Note: [Col. 0819D] Several manuscripts read: “I see here a future multitude of peoples.”]

**CHAPTER II**

[Col. 0820A]

After enumerating the various classes of people who, under the false covering of the Christian name, almost ravage the Church and are subject to the sentence just mentioned, he warns us how we must avoid that same sentence.

**6.** For this is a general sentence against all the impious. Therefore, if a Jew offers—one who separates the Son of the Virgin Mary from God the Father—it is said to him: “If you offer rightly, but do not divide rightly, you have sinned; be quiet” (ibid., 7).

**7.** If an Eunomian offers—one who proceeds from the fountain of Arian impiety and, through the overflowing filth of his faithlessness, slips into the mire, asserting that Christ’s generation, which is above all things, must be gathered from the traditions of philosophy—then, since the order of creatures is one thing and the power of divine secrets another, it is said to him also: “If you offer rightly, but do not divide rightly, you have sinned; be quiet.”

**8.** This is said to the Sabellian, who confounds the Father and the Son. This is said to the Marcionite, who thinks that the God of the New Testament is one and the God of the Old Testament another.
