This is said to the Manichaean and the Valentinian, who did not believe that Christ assumed the reality of human flesh.

[Note: [Col. 0819D] Paul of Samosata blasphemously held Christ to have been a mere man, as we observed in book V of *On the Faith*, chapter 8, no. 105, although he did not deny that the divine Word dwelt in him. Basilides, however, attributed to Christ only an illusory body and, in its place, deliriously claimed that Simon of Cyrene had been nailed to the cross, after the eyes of the Jews had been seized and deceived, as Irenaeus reports in book I, *Against Heresies*, chapter 23; Epiphanius, *Heresy* 24, no. 3; and others after them. Hence Theodoret, *Dialogues* 2, p. 52, numbers Basilides and the Samosatene among two classes of heretics who fight each other face to face. What reason, then, could Ambrose have had for joining such divergent men together? Perhaps, however, they were linked not because of the similarity of their opinions but because of the similarity of their sentence—that is, their condemnation. Nevertheless, we can detect this affinity between their doctrines: according to the mind of both, the Word or God could in no way be said to have suffered or died; for the one did not acknowledge true flesh in Christ, while the other denied hypostatic union in him, or even introduced two persons. But since this last claim rests upon certain letters of Dionysius of Alexandria, whose authority is unstable and suspect, we do not present it as certain and established. On this matter, consult Garnerius, Dissertation 1, *On Heresies*, and the books of Nestorius, Alexander of the third century, part 1.]

Paul of Samosata and Basilides also are numbered among those sharing the same sentence.

**9.** Likewise, by the authority of this same sentence, those who denied the divinity of the Holy Spirit are condemned.

[Note: [Col. 0820D] Understand this as referring to the Pneumatomachi, and to those against whom the preceding books *On the Holy Spirit* were published.]

For some are either Jewish Arians or Arian Jews; for just as the former separate the Son from the Father, so the latter separate the Spirit from God the Father and the Son of God.

[Col. 0820C] **10.** To Novatian, Donatus, and all who have eagerly sought to divide the body of the Church, it is said individually: “If you offer rightly, but do not divide rightly, you have sinned.” For the sacrifice offered to God belongs to the Church, to which Paul said: “I beseech you, brothers, by the mercy of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God” (Romans XII, 1). They therefore divided the sacrifice wrongly by tearing the members of the Church apart.

**11.** This sentence also strikes those who separate the rational soul from the mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation, wishing to separate human nature from the human being.

[Note: [Col. 0820D] He refers to the followers of Apollinarius of Laodicea. As Jerome records in his *Chronicle* under the year 379, Apollinarius, obstinately asserting certain errors through an ostentatious display of intellect, established the heresy bearing his name; Damasus condemned it after holding a council at Rome. His principal error was that he maintained that the Word had not assumed a soul together with the flesh, but that the Word himself supplied the place of a soul to the flesh, as may be learned from Gregory of Nazianzus, letter to Cledonius; Augustine, *On Heresies*, chapter 55; Leontius of Byzantium, Act IV; Vincent of Lérins, *Commonitory* I, chapter 17; Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History* II, chapter 46, in the edition of Valesius; and many others. These authors also indicate, however, that the heresiarch later conceded a soul to Christ, though deprived of mind or reason—that is, only the sensitive part of the soul. Hence Suidas, not inelegantly, says under the entry “Apollinarius”: “He said that the Lord assumed flesh endowed with the soul of a calf, but did not admit our mind.” He also devised other erroneous opinions concerning the Incarnation, about which below, in chapter 6. Here we shall add only that he likewise held an un-Catholic opinion concerning the Trinity. For Gregory of Nazianzus, in letter 1 to Cledonius, explicitly says that Apollinarius imagined the Trinity as composed of the great, the greater, and the greatest; Theodoret follows him in book IV, chapter 8, of his *Compendium of Heretical Fables*. Basil also accuses him in letter 59 of confusing the persons of the Trinity with one another; the same is found in Theodoret at the cited passage. Yet, besides the fact that Basil, in letter 293, suggests that this accusation may have originated with Apollinarius’ adversaries, Vincent of Lérins and Leontius of Byzantium defend him in the cited passages. Epiphanius may also be added, *Heresy* 77, where, recounting the disputation of Vitalis the Apollinarist against Paulinus, he reports that Vitalis accused Paulinus of the Sabellian doctrine—something he surely would never have done had he himself been attached to Sabellius’ opinions. Ambrose himself sufficiently indicates that he did not regard the Apollinarists as wholly suspect concerning errors about the Trinity, when he adds: “And these perhaps offer rightly to the Trinity.” By these words he makes it sufficiently clear that he means not the Arians, who likewise denied that Christ had assumed a human soul, but the Apollinarists.]

And these perhaps offer rightly to the Trinity; but they do not know how to distinguish human nature from divine nature. For God’s nature is simple, whereas the human being consists of a rational soul and a body. If you remove one of the two, you have removed the whole nature of the human being.

**12.** This sentence, therefore, is directed against all heresies that persecute the Church under the name of brotherhood, but not in a brotherly manner. For under the adoption of the Christian name and a certain merely nominal kinship of faith—

[Note: [Col. 0822D] The Roman edition and a few manuscripts read “under an opinion”; the old edition, together with the more numerous manuscripts, reads “under an option.” This is not inappropriate, for it has the same meaning as “under the choice and adoption” of the Christian name, which they falsely and adulterously impose upon themselves.]

—they desire to wound us with parricidal swords.

[Note: [Col. 0822D] Some manuscripts read: “with parricidal hatreds they seek to wound us,” and so forth.]

For “our turning is toward them,” and sinners rule over us in the world.

[Note: [Col. 0822D] The old edition, with a few manuscripts, reads: “Our conversion is from God”; the Roman edition, with the rest, more appropriately reads: “… is toward them.” The allusion is to Genesis III, 16, according to the Septuagint: *καὶ πρὸς τὸν ἄνδρα σου ἡ ἀποστροφή σου, καὶ αὐτός σου κυριεύσει*—“and your turning shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule over you.”]

For the sinner rules in the world, but the righteous person in God’s kingdom.

**13.** Let us therefore beware lest anyone attempt to separate us from the chamber of the eternal King and from the inner sanctuary of Mother Church, into which that soul signifies in the *Song of Songs* that it has introduced the Word of God (Song of Songs III, 4).

[Note: [Col. 0822D] He alludes not inelegantly to the royal chamber, on account, that is, of the emperor’s chamberlains who, as we explained in the Admonition, furnished the occasion for this writing.]

Let us beware lest we separate the substance of the Only-Begotten Son from the bosom of the Father, from a kind of paternal womb, and from the secret nature; and lest, by the words through which the truth of the assumed Incarnation is established, we undertake to introduce prejudices against the divine generation. Otherwise it may also be said to one of us: “If you offer rightly, but do not divide rightly, you have sinned; be quiet”—that is: if we do not know how to distinguish what belongs properly to eternal divinity from what belongs to the Incarnation; if we compare the Creator with his works; if we say that the Author of the ages began after the ages. For it cannot be that the one through whom all things exist should be one among all things.

**CHAPTER III**

Having rebuked those who would not accept John’s testimony concerning the eternity of the Word, and having praised the same Evangelist, he examines the passage in which, he teaches, not only the eternity and divinity of the Word are signified, but also that these same attributes are shown to belong to the Father. Nothing bodily is to be conceived in the Word; and although we scarcely grasp his nature, John’s authority ought to be sufficient for us, as is explained by what John saw concerning the Word.

**14.** “I do not ask that we be believed; let Scripture be recited. I do not say on my own authority, ‘In the beginning was the Word’ (John I, 1), but I hear it. I do not fabricate it, but read it—what we all read, though we do not all understand it. When it is read, we all hear it, but not all listen: ‘For the heart of some has grown thick, and their ears have heard heavily’ (Acts XXVIII, 27)—the ears, that is, of the inner disposition. It is not the flesh that sins, for it performs its proper function and receives the sound,

[Note: [Col. 0822D] Some manuscripts read: “but the mind, hard of hearing.”]

but the mind, though capable of pure hearing, is a wicked interpreter, refusing to hear what is said and understand what is read. Why do you close your ears as though with wax and lead, and yet cannot shut out the Lord’s benefits and the functions of nature? You hear unwillingly; you hear with disgust; you hear so that you cannot excuse yourself by saying that you did not hear.”

707 **15.** “You hear, therefore, when it is read: ‘In the beginning was the Word’ (John I, 1). Who says this? That fisherman, John, certainly; but he does not say it as a fisherman, but as a fisherman of the human race, who would no longer catch fish but bring human beings to life (Luke V, 10). What he says is not his own, but belongs to him who granted him the power to give life. As a fisherman, he had been more silent than the fish he formerly caught, and regarding divine mysteries he was even more mute, since he did not know the author of his voice. But, made alive by Christ, he heard the voice in John and recognized the Word in Christ.”

**16.** “And therefore, full of the Holy Spirit, knowing that ‘beginning’ does not mean time but is above time, he left the ages behind and, ascending in spirit beyond every beginning, said: ‘In the beginning was the Word.’ In other words, let heaven remain; for it did not yet exist when the Word was in the beginning. Even if heaven has a beginning, God does not. Finally, ‘In the beginning God made heaven and earth’ (Genesis I, 1). ‘He made’ is one thing; ‘he was’ is another. What is made begins; what was does not receive a beginning but precedes it.

“Let the times remain also, since time follows heaven. Let the angels and archangels remain as well.

[Note: [Col. 0822D] Augustine discusses at length the time at which the angels were created in *The City of God* XI, chapters 9 and 32, and XII, chapter 15; but in the end, following his teacher’s example, he defines the matter only hesitantly.]

“Even if I cannot find their beginning, there was nevertheless a time when they did not exist. For those who at some point began did not exist before. If, then, I cannot find the beginning of those whom I know certainly to have a beginning, how can I find the beginning of the Word, from whom every beginning—not only of all creatures but also of all our thoughts—is preceded?”

**17.** “Thus he had plainly expressed the Word’s everlasting divinity. But lest anyone separate the eternity of the Word from the Father, so that we might believe the Word’s eternity to be the same as the Father’s, that good fisherman added: ‘And the Word was with God’ (John I, 1). What he had said must be understood in this way: ‘The Word was’ just as the Father was, since he was always with the Father, was in the Father, and was beside the Father. Indeed, just as we read concerning the Father, ‘he was,’ so we read concerning the Word, ‘he was.’”

[Col. 0823B] **18.** “Why do you distinguish the meaning when you do not distinguish the hearing? The Word’s being is with the Father; the Father’s being is with the Word. For we read that ‘the Word was with God.’ Therefore, if according to your opinion he once did not exist, then according to your opinion the one with whom the Word was also did not exist in the beginning. Through the Word I hear; through the Word I understand that ‘the Word was God.’ For if I believe—and I do believe—that the Word is eternal, I cannot doubt the Father’s eternity, whose Son is eternal.

“If I consider his generation temporal, he begins to share our condition, so that the Father may seem to have begun to exist. But if you do not doubt concerning the Father, because it is not possible for God to begin to exist, if you do not doubt concerning the Father because it belongs to God to possess eternal perfection—lest perhaps you should slip through the customary usage of human speech, when you hear ‘Word’ and ‘Son’—he added: ‘And the Word was God’ (ibid., 1).”

**19.** “He has, of course, what the Father has, because he was God. How do you deny the eternity of the one who has the one name of God together with the Father? Do not let sound and similarity of speech deceive you. There is another word that has times, that is gathered into syllables and composed of letters. The Son is not such a Word, because the Father of the Word is not such.”

**20.** “We must therefore beware lest even there we appear to introduce a question concerning a bodily voice.

[Note: [Col. 0823C] The editions of Gill and Rome, with one or two manuscripts, read: “lest we also introduce it to him”; Amerbach and Erasmus, with many more manuscripts, read: “lest we introduce it to you”; other manuscripts, though few, more appropriately read: “lest we introduce it there also,” that is, into John’s passage. Again, where all editions and most manuscripts read “lest we appear to bring forward,” some others read “lest we appear to introduce.”]

“God is incorporeal; therefore an incorporeal being certainly does not have a bodily voice. If there is no bodily voice in the Father, neither is the Son a bodily word. If there is no body in the Father, neither is there time in the Father. If there is no time in the Father, then there is none in the Word. And if there is no time of beginning in the Word, then neither is there number nor rank in the Word. For if there is number in the Word, there are many words. If there are many words, there are also many sons. But there is one Word, which excludes both rank and number: one according to nature.”

**21.** “Do not ask what sort of nature it is. ‘I do not know’ is much better here than ‘I know.’ This alone I know well: that I do not know those things which I cannot know. ‘What we have seen and what we have heard,’ John says (1 John I, 3). He said that he knew this alone well: what he had heard and what he had seen—he who reclined upon Christ’s breast. For him, then, it is enough to have heard; for me it is not enough.”

[Note: [Col. 0823D] Some manuscripts read: “This sort of nature, he asks? I do not know, I do not know,” and so forth. The others, and all the editions, agree among themselves, except that the editions, with a few manuscripts, prefer *of this kind*, while in several others *what sort* is read. Some of these manuscripts repeat the word “I do not know”; some omit it, which is much better than “I know.”]

**22.** “But what he heard, he told me; and what he heard from Christ, I cannot deny to be true concerning Christ. Therefore, what he heard, I heard; and what he saw, I saw. He saw what he saw—not, of course, the divinity, which according to its nature cannot be seen. But because it could not be seen according to its nature, he assumed what was beyond the nature of divinity, so that he might be seen according to the nature of a body. Finally, the Holy Spirit too was seen in a form, like a dove (Luke III, 22), because divinity could not be seen in the truth of its own splendor.”

**CHAPTER IV**

It is not enough to believe that Christ has true flesh unless we exclude from it every confusion and every other weakness of divinity; nor is it enough to call him the God of both covenants unless we profess the Word himself to be coeternal; nor, finally, is it enough to acknowledge that he began before the Virgin unless we proclaim him older than every beginning. Peter’s confession is commended; and it is explained why he remained silent while the others were speaking and how beautifully he later answered.

**23.** “Therefore do not interpret according to nature what lies beyond the nature of divinity. For even if you believe that true flesh was assumed by Christ and offer a body to be transformed upon the altars,

[Note: [Col. 0823D] The same meaning is plainly expressed in book IV of *On the Faith*, chapter 10: “We receive the sacraments, which through the mystery of sacred prayer are transformed into flesh and blood.” There we defended these words against the tricks of the sacramentarians, who twist them away from their proper and natural meaning. But this passage itself deserves particular attention. First, none of the ancient authors by whom it is cited—namely Theodoret, Ivo, and Peter Lombard—did not fail to understand it in a simple, literal sense (*κατὰ λέξιν*, “according to the wording”). We do not think that the last two would resist this interpretation; but the words of the first, by which he renders Ambrose’s statement in Greek, must be considered. They are as follows: *κᾂν γὰρ πιστεύσῃς ὡς ἀληθὲς εἴη τὸ σῶμα τοῦ Χριστοῦ, καὶ προσκομίσῃς τῷ θυσιαστηρίῷ πρὸς μεταποίησιν*—“For even if you believe that Christ’s body is real and bring it to the altar for transformation,” and so forth. Who could persuade himself that these words signify only a figurative change? Or rather, who would not recognize there the unmistakable testimony of the Greeks’ faith concerning the reality of the Eucharist? Furthermore, since in the first clause the words “true flesh was assumed” are used in their natural sense, the sequence itself warns that in the following clause the word “body” should not be understood differently. The words that follow are still more effective: “yet do not distinguish the nature of divinity and of the body,” where it is clearer than noonday that true divinity is set over against the body. Finally, the meaning that Ambrose’s opponents impose upon him is exceedingly absurd. It is the same as though the holy Bishop had written: “It is not at all enough for you to believe that Christ hung nailed to the cross; nor is it enough for you to believe that his figure was a bronze serpent, unless you also believe that Christ himself died in it, and not his divinity.” Everyone sees that this reasoning is utterly foolish. On the contrary, a most beautiful gradation results if Ambrose’s words are not diverted from their natural meaning.]

“Yet do not distinguish the nature of divinity and of the body; and it is said to you: ‘If you offer rightly, but do not divide rightly, you have sinned’ (Genesis IV, 7). Divide what is mine; divide what belongs to the Word as his. I did not possess what was his, and he did not possess what is mine. He assumed what is mine in order to impart what is his. He assumed it not to confuse it, but to fill it. If you believe in the assumption, you imagine confusion. You have ceased to be a Manichaean, but you have not yet begun to be a son of the Church.”

**24.** “If you believe in the assumption of a body, add compassion to divinity. You have avoided a portion of faithlessness, not faithlessness itself. For you believe what you presume will benefit you; you do not believe what is worthy of God.”

[Col. 0825B] **25.** “Again, if you believe that the same God is God of both the New and the Old Testament, but place times and moments before his Word, Valentinus is more tolerable, for he believes that not ages precede God, but gods do—that is, that the ages are gods.

[Note: [Col. 0826D] Concerning this absurdity of Valentinus, besides Epiphanius, *Heresy* 31, and Augustine, *On Heresies*, chapter 11, see Irenaeus, book I, *Against Heresies*; Tertullian, *Against Valentinus*; and others.]

“For it is a lesser sacrilege to join ages to divinity than to place them before it.”

**26.** “If, again, you believe that Christ did not take his beginning from the Virgin, but nevertheless think that some beginning existed before Christ, then, in terms of temporal distinction, the dispute is about impiety.

[Note: [Col. 0826D] The Roman edition reads: “there is agreement,” which gives an evident sense but lacks all authority.]

“For you have denied that he is coeval with the Virgin, not that he is coeval with time. But I will not deny that he is coeval with the Virgin according to the assumption of his body, and I will confess him to be the Creator of time. For what do you gain if you say that Christ is this or that creature? The creature is changed; divinity is not worshiped.”

[Note: [Col. 0826D] All editions and several manuscripts read: “divinity is worshiped”; the remaining manuscripts read: “divinity is not worshiped.” The latter is better, since the meaning here is that when you say Christ is one creature rather than another, you change the creature but do not worship his divinity.]

**27.** “Christ did not wish to be recognized in this way, nor to be judged only by those achievements that are above humanity. Accordingly, when he asked, ‘Who do people say that I am?’ (Matthew XVI, 13), while some said Elijah, others Jeremiah, or one of the prophets, he praised no one’s opinion. But when Peter said, ‘You are the Christ, the Son of the living God’ (ibid., 16), he rightly praised this one alone.”

**28.** “John says it; Peter says it; Christ approved it; and you do not approve it, Arian? Do you think that John and Peter should not be believed—men whom our Lord Jesus Christ himself deemed sufficient, even if they alone, as witnesses to his glory, for the faith of all? Finally, as witnesses to the Old and New Testaments, Moses is brought forward together with Elijah, and Peter is frequently brought forward together with John (Matthew XVII, 1).”

[Col. 0826A] **29.** “Peter says, ‘You are’ (John XIII, 23); he does not say, ‘You began to be.’ Peter says, ‘You are the Son of God’; he does not say, ‘You are a creature.’ John said this. If you still have not believed because you did not understand the mystery of the one reclining above wisdom, Peter repeated it. Christ commended both: the one by judgment, the other by mystery. He added this so that you might read that he reclined upon Christ’s breast and understand that his head, in which the chief seat of all the senses is found, was filled with a certain hidden wisdom. But if you do not think the mystery should be understood, at least do not attack the judgment. Peter is praised because he believed the Son of God whom he saw, because he separated himself from the still-rude opinions of the uneducated crowd. Accordingly, when the Lord asked what people thought concerning the Son of Man, while the opinion of the crowd was being reported, Peter remained silent.”

**30.** “You are silent, then, Simon, and while the others answer, you remain silent still (Matthew XVI, 14), although you are the first to ask even when you have not been asked. Do you not fear being reproved by the Lord because you do not answer the one who asks? ‘For this reason,’ he says, ‘I do not answer: I am not being asked for my own opinion, but for another’s. For I have read: “So that my mouth may not speak the works of men” (Psalm XVI, 4).” Now it is the work of faithless men to proclaim faithlessness. Therefore I remain silent, because I am not yet being asked what I feel. I will not bring forth with my lips what my mind has not approved. The time will come when I shall answer. I too shall be asked what I think; then at last I shall answer what is mine. It is mine to speak faith, assert devotion, and proclaim grace.”

**31.** “He is not silent, then, as though slow in understanding or tardy in speech, nor does he delay the obedience of his voice as though he were disdainful. Rather, as one cautious, he avoids the danger of popular opinion.

[Note: [Col. 0822D] Some manuscripts read: “cautious of danger.” He avoids popular opinions. Below, only the Roman edition reads: “you have it in the preceding passages.”]

“He who did not avoid the danger to salvation. Later you find that he leapt from the boat to meet the Lord (Matthew XIV, 29), not eager for glory but prompt in obedience.”

32. This, then, is Peter, who had previously remained silent in order to teach us that we ought not even to repeat a word of the ungodly. This, I say, is the one who, when he heard, “But you—who do you say that I am?” (Matt. 16:15), immediately, mindful of his position, took the first place: the first place, certainly, in confession, not in honor; the first place in faith, not in rank. This is what he means: “Now let no one surpass me; now it is my turn. I ought to make amends for having been silent; my silence ought to prove useful. My tongue has no thorns; faith must come forth without hindrance.” While the others are clearing away the mud—alien, to be sure, but nevertheless mud—of the impiety they had uttered, when they said that Christ was either Elijah, or Jeremiah, or one of the prophets (Matt. 16:14)—that utterance had mud, that utterance had thorns—while the others, I say, are washing away this mud, while those thorns are being disentangled in the others, let our voice resound: “the Son of God, Christ.” My speech is pure; impiety, when expressed, has left no thorns in it.

[Note: Amerbach, Erasmus, and some manuscripts read *in hoc labant coenum*, “in this they stumble over the mud”; Gill and the Roman edition read *in hoc lavant coenum*, “in this they wash away the mud”; but the better reading, found in more manuscripts, omits *in*.]

33. This, then, is Peter, who answered on behalf of the other apostles, or rather, before the others (ibid., 16). And for this reason he is called the foundation, because he knows how to preserve not only what is his own but also what is shared by all. [Note: Some manuscripts read, “Christ addressed him.”] Christ supported him in this; the Father revealed it. For the one who proclaims the true generation from the Father received it from the Father; he did not derive it from the flesh.

## CHAPTER V

That this faith is and remains the foundation of the Church against all heresies: namely, the belief that in Christ there is both a divine and a human generation. That these two generations do not hinder one another, but that what belongs to each remained intact even in his passion and burial. Therefore the weaknesses of the body must not be attributed to the divinity, since the latter is independent of place and time; and the divine Word could suffer nothing except according to the flesh.

34. Faith, then, is the foundation of the Church. For it was not said of Peter’s flesh, but of his faith, that the gates of death would not prevail against him; rather, his confession conquered hell (ibid.). And this confession excluded not merely one heresy. Since the Church, like a good ship, is often battered by many waves, the foundation of the Church must stand firm against all heresies.

35. The day would fail me sooner than the names of the heretics and the various sects; yet this general faith is directed against them all: that Christ is the Son of God, eternal from the Father, and born from the Virgin Mary. The holy prophet David depicts him as a kind of giant, because he is one, yet a participant in divinity and in the body, possessing a twofold and double nature: “Like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber, he rejoiced like a giant to run his course” (Ps. 18:6). He is the bridegroom of the soul according to the Word; a giant of the earth, because, traversing the duties of our human condition, while he was always the eternal God, he assumed the mysteries of the incarnation—not divided, but one, because he is one in both and one in each: that is, whether in divinity or in the body. For one did not come from the Father and another from the Virgin; rather, it is the same one, differently from the Father and differently from the Virgin.

36. One generation does not prejudice the other, nor does the flesh prejudice the divinity; for neither the pledge prejudiced the Father, nor the will the passion, nor the passion the will. [Note: Athanasius, in his Letter to Epictetus, found among his works and also in Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* 77, writes: “And it was paradoxical that he himself was the one who suffered and did not suffer,” and so forth. Consult the passage itself and compare it with this passage of Ambrose.] The same one was suffering and not suffering; he was dying and not dying; he was being buried and not being buried; he was rising and not rising. For he was raising up his own body: what fell is what rises; what did not fall does not rise. He was therefore rising according to the flesh, which, having died, rose again; he was not rising according to the Word, which had not been dissolved into the earth but always remained with God.

37. Thus he was dying according to the assumption of our nature, but was not dying according to the substance of eternal life; and he was suffering according to the assumption of the body, so that the reality of the assumed body might be believed, but was not suffering according to the impassible divinity of the Word, which is wholly free from pain. Finally, he himself said: “God, my God, look upon me; why have you forsaken me?” (Ps. 22:1), because the one who according to his flesh was forsaken could not according to his divinity either be abandoned or forsaken.

38. He says the same thing also: “Far from my salvation are the words of my sins” (ibid.). That is, whoever hears, “Why have you forsaken me?” must not misunderstand it, but must recognize that these words are spoken according to the flesh and are far removed from the fullness of divinity. The words of sins are alien to God, because sins of words are also alien to him. But since I assumed alien sins, I also assumed the words of alien sins, so that I might say that I had been forsaken by God the Father, although I am always with God.

39. He was therefore immortal in death and impassible in suffering. For, as God, the anguish of death could not contain him, while, as man, the underworld saw him. Finally, “he gave up his spirit” (Matt. 27:50), and yet, as the arbiter of laying aside and taking up the body, he gave up his spirit but did not lose it. He hung upon the cross and moved all things. He trembled on the wood, at whom this whole world trembled. He was amid torments, receiving wounds, and granting the heavenly kingdom. Having been made the sin of all, he washed away the sins of the human race. Finally, he died—and I say it exultantly and triumphantly a second and a third time: he died—so that his death might become the life of the dead.

[Note: A considerable number of manuscripts read, “he was expiating the wounds.”]

40. Nor is even his tomb without its miracle. For when he had been anointed by Joseph and buried in Joseph’s tomb (Luke 23:53), by a new kind of work he himself, though dead, opened the tombs of the dead. His body indeed lay in the tomb, but he himself, free among the dead, granted forgiveness to those placed in the underworld, once the law of death had been dissolved. His flesh was therefore in the tomb, but his power was at work from heaven. He was shown to all through the reality of his body: the Word was not flesh, but the flesh was the Word’s. The flesh indeed tasted death, but the power of God remained impassible; and although he laid aside the body, God suffered no loss through the body.

41. Why do you attribute the body’s sufferings to the divinity and join the weakness of human pain to the divine nature? “Now my soul is troubled,” he says (John 12:27). The soul was troubled, not Wisdom; for Wisdom remained unchangeable, even though it was surrounded by a garment of flesh. For in that form of a servant there was the fullness of the true light; and when he emptied himself, he was still light. Finally, he said: “Walk while you have the light” (John 12:35). And when he was in death, he was not in darkness. Indeed, even to those placed in the underworld he poured forth the light of eternal life. There too the true light of Wisdom shone; it illuminated the underworld, but was not confined by the underworld. For what place can contain Wisdom? Hence the righteous man says: “But where is Wisdom found? And where is the place of understanding? Man does not know its way, nor is it found among human beings” (Job 28:12–13).

42. Wisdom, therefore, is neither in time nor in place, and this itself signifies that it does not belong to time. But how could that which was in the beginning be in time? How could that which was with God be in a place? If the Only-begotten Son is sought, he is found, in the Gospel’s language, in the bosom of the Father. Do you suppose that the bosom of the Father is a place? And do you ask how he was born, when the prophetic man says: “Man does not know its way” (Job 28:13)? Do you judge his origin according to human beings, when Job says that it was not found among human beings? And do you attribute death to Wisdom, of which the abyss says, “It is not in me,” and the sea says, “It is not with me” (ibid., 14)? Heaven does not say, “It is not in me”; the abyss says, “It is not in me.” For he did not say to the abyss, but to the Father: “Into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23:46). Even if that soul was in the abyss, it is no longer there, because it is written: “For you will not leave my soul in the underworld, nor will you permit your holy one to see corruption” (Ps. 16:10).

43. The sea therefore says, “It is not with me”—that is, our life, troubled by the waves of the world, says this. His flesh is not among human beings, because “according to the flesh we now know Christ no longer” (2 Cor. 5:16). The earth says, “It is not with me,” because he has risen. Hence the angel says: “Why do you seek the living among the dead?” (Luke 24:5). And the sea rightly said, “It is not with me,” because he was above the sea. Indeed, he walked upon the sea with bodily footsteps when, with the sea beneath him, he commanded Peter also to walk upon the sea (Matt. 14:29). Although Peter faltered, he faltered not through weakness in the one who commanded, but through weakness in the one who obeyed.

44. Do not therefore mix the ink of our nature with the splendor of glory, nor cast the cloud of human flesh over the light. Again, if, in proclaiming the passion, you fail to recognize what is capable of suffering, you have rejected the Lord’s piety and denied your salvation. We must therefore consider those people insane who, hearing the Son of God say, “Why do you strike me?” (John 18:23), thought that he was, according to the nature of the divinity, subject to insult. He said, “Why do you strike me?”; but the divine nature did not feel the blows. He said: “I gave my back to scourges and my cheeks to blows; but I did not turn my face away from the shame of spitting” (Isa. 50:6). He mentioned the back, the cheeks, and the face—that is, parts of the human body. For what the flesh of the Word suffered, or while remaining in the flesh, the Word of God suffered in the flesh, as it is written: “Christ having suffered in the flesh” (1 Pet. 4:1). In himself, therefore, he referred to it on account of the assumption of the body, so that he himself might take upon himself what belongs to us and clothe human things with his own.

45. The flesh therefore rightly suffered according to its own nature, and through that bodily suffering the nature of the Word was not changed. [Note: Some manuscripts read, “its nature was changed”; this yields an absurd sense unless *immutata* is taken there in the sense of “changed.” The matters discussed in this chapter and throughout the following chapter, however, have such close affinity with Athanasius’s letter mentioned above that it is difficult to imagine anything more closely related.] For our resurrection is real, and therefore Christ’s passion is proclaimed as real.

## CHAPTER VI

The refutation of all those heretics who say either that Christ suffered only in appearance or that he comprised two persons in himself, as well as those who either distinguish the Word from the Son of God, or fail to distinguish the divinity from the flesh, or subject the divinity, as though it were imperfect, to the body’s injuries. Ambrose shows that the authors of all these errors—those who fancied that the Lord’s divinity and flesh were of one nature—falsely claim the authority of the Council of Nicaea, making clear that Scripture narrates Christ as having suffered only according to his humanity. He adds that Christ assumed flesh in order to redeem in himself what had sinned, since God and sin can have nothing in common. Finally, he exposes how absurd are the consequences that follow from the opponents’ position.

46. For he did not suffer in appearance, as some say, because he did not walk upon the sea in appearance either—although the disciples are reported in the Gospel to have thought that he did (Matt. 14:26). But they are excused because “the Spirit had not yet been given” (John 7:39); for Jesus had not yet been glorified (Rom. 5:5). Christ has now been crucified and has risen for us; the Spirit has now been given to us, and he is the defender of truth. The disciples sometimes erred so that we might not err afterward. Their error therefore benefits us. They erred as human beings; they believed as disciples.

47. We must therefore condemn both those who proclaim that Jesus came only in appearance and those who, by the opposite line of error, deny that there is one and the same Son of God. They say that one was born from God the Father and another was generated from the Virgin, although the Evangelist says that “the Word became flesh” (John 1:1), so that you might believe in one Lord Jesus, not two.

48. Some have also believed that the Word of God is one thing and the Son of God another, although the Evangelist testifies that the very one who was the Word in the beginning with God the Father came to what was his own (ibid., 11). There are also those who have thought that the Word came to Christ as it came to one of the prophets, rather than that Christ himself is the Word of God. But it was not said of any prophet that “the Word became flesh.” No prophet took away the sins of the world. Of no other was it said: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3:17). Of no prophet do we read that he is the Lord of glory, of whom the Apostle said that “the Jews crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8).

49. But while we refute these people, others emerge who say that the Lord’s flesh and divinity are of one nature. What underworld has vomited forth such sacrilege? The Arians are already more tolerable, for through these people the strength of the Arians’ impiety grows, enabling them to assert with greater determination that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not of one substance—because these people have attempted to say that the Lord’s divinity and flesh are of one substance. Moreover, when they say that the Word was converted into flesh, hair, blood, and bones, and was changed from its own nature, they provide them with an opportunity to twist the weakness of the flesh into a weakness of the divinity, by alleging that the divine nature itself underwent a change.

50. There are also those who have advanced so far in impiety as to think that the Lord’s divinity was circumcised and that the perfect became imperfect; and that on the cross it was not flesh that hung there, but that divine substance which works all things, coagulated in the appearance of flesh. Who would not shudder? Who could listen to the claim that the Word of God made for himself passible flesh not from the Virgin Mary but from the divine substance? By asserting this, they go so far as to maintain that the Lord’s body was not assumed in time, but had always been coeternal with the Word of God.

51. The authors of all these errors are those who said that the Lord’s divinity and flesh were of one nature. I read what I would not have believed unless I had read it myself. I read, I say, in the books of a certain person the statement that in Christ both the instrument and the one who moved the instrument were of one nature. [Note: Leontius of Byzantium, in his *Book against the Frauds of Apollinaris*, reports these very words as coming from a discourse of Apollinaris himself, whom Ambrose here identifies as their author. He thereby makes the source plain.] I have included this so that the author’s name may be discovered from his writings, and so that they may understand that even the most refined arguments and ornamented language cannot conceal the force of truth.

52. This man also frequently declares that he adheres to the teaching of the Council of Nicaea. But in that teaching our fathers said that not the flesh, but the Word of God, is of one substance with the Father; and they confessed that the Word proceeded from the Father’s substance, while the flesh came from the Virgin. How, then, is the name of the Council of Nicaea used as a pretext, and new doctrines introduced that our ancestors never held, when Scripture says that Christ suffered according to the flesh (1 Pet. 1:2), not according to the divinity? Scripture says: “The Virgin will conceive in the womb and will bear a Son” (Isa. 7:14). For she received the power and bore the Son, whom she received from herself.

[Note: All editions and a few manuscripts read, “whom she herself also received”; somewhat more numerous manuscripts read, “whom she received from herself,” which is not unsuitable if *from herself* is referred to the power. Most manuscripts, however, have *from herself*, that is, from her own substance, a sense supported by what follows.]

53. Finally, Gabriel also declares this in his own words, saying: “And the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35). “From you,” he says, so that you might understand that, according to his humanity, the one who was born was born from her. Mary herself generated him from herself, so that what was generated from her might possess a true bodily nature, while the prerogative of the Lord’s generation remained intact. [Note: Some manuscripts read, “with the prerogative of the Lord’s incarnation preserved,” but this is not sufficiently correct, since the prerogative of the eternal generation is intended.] Paul likewise says that he was predestined for the Gospel of God: “which he had promised beforehand through his prophets concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Rom. 1:2–3). And to the Galatians: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, made from a woman” (Gal. 4:4). And to Timothy he said: “Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, from the seed of David” (2 Tim. 2:8).

54. Therefore he received from us what he could offer on our behalf, so that he might redeem us from what was ours; and what was not ours he bestowed upon us from what was his, by his divine generosity. He offered himself, therefore, according to our nature, so that he might work beyond our nature. The sacrifice is from what is ours; the reward is from what is his. In the same person you will find many things both according to nature and beyond nature. According to the condition of the body, he was in the womb, was born, was nursed, and was placed in a manger; but beyond the condition of nature, a Virgin conceived and a Virgin gave birth, so that you might believe that he was God, who was renewing nature, and that he was man, who according to nature was born from a human being.

55. For the nature of the Word itself was not changed, as some have interpreted it; it is always unchangeable, just as he himself said: “See, see that I am, and I have not been changed” (Mal. 3:6). Paul also said: “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever” (Heb. 13:8). That is, he was not changed according to the nature of the flesh, but remained unchangeable even within the changeable condition of human nature.

56. You have therefore learned that he offered a sacrifice from what was ours. For what was the reason for the incarnation except that the flesh which had sinned might be redeemed through itself? What had sinned was therefore redeemed. The divinity of the Word was not sacrificed, because the divinity of the Word had not sinned; and therefore the nature of the Word was not changed into the nature of flesh, because the divinity, free from sin, ought not to offer itself for a sin it had not committed. Christ offered in himself what he assumed, and he assumed what he had not previously possessed. He did not therefore assume the divinity of his divinity, in whom there was the fullness of eternal divinity; rather, he assumed flesh in order to strip off the spoils of the flesh and, in himself, both to crucify the devil’s spoils and to raise the trophies of his power.

57. Therefore, if the flesh of all human beings, including Christ’s, was subject to injury, how can you say that it is of one substance with the divinity? If the Word and flesh are of one substance, and flesh derives its nature from the earth, why should the Word and the soul—which he assumed as a complete expression of human nature—be said to be of one substance? The Word, however, is of one substance with God, according to the Father’s declaration and the Lord’s own assertion, when he says: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). Thus the Father is proclaimed to be of one substance with an earthly body. And yet you are still indignant with the Arians because they say that the Son of God is a creature, when you yourselves say that the Father is of one substance with creatures?

[Note: The older edition reads, “if all flesh, and in Christ”; the Roman edition, “if flesh and in Christ all”; but the manuscripts, with strong agreement, read, “if the flesh of all,” which gives the best sense. The point is that Christ’s flesh and the flesh of all human beings are of the same substance and nature, and therefore one is subject to the same injuries as the other.]

58. What else do you accomplish by saying this except either to compare Adam’s clay and our earth with the divine substance, or at least to transfer the divinity into the sphere of earthly corruption’s injury? For by saying that the Word became flesh and bones, you are saying that it was converted into earth, since flesh and bones are from the earth.

59. “So it is written,” they say, “that the Word became flesh” (John 1:14). It is written, I do not deny it; but consider what follows. It follows: “And he dwelt among us”—that is, the Word that assumed flesh dwelt among us, that is, dwelt in human flesh. For this reason he was called Emmanuel, which means “God with us” (Matt. 1:23). Therefore, “the Word became flesh” means that he became man. So also Joel said: “I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh” (Joel 2:28). The promise is not of an outpouring of spiritual grace upon irrational flesh, but upon human beings.

[Note: This objection was conspicuously advanced by the Apollinarists. This may be inferred not only from the care with which Ambrose refutes it, but also from the fact that Athanasius refutes it with no less diligence in his Letter to Epictetus, although the two follow somewhat different lines of reasoning.]

60. But if you insist upon the literal sense, and think that because it is written that the Word became flesh, the Word of God was converted into flesh, do you deny that it is also written of the Lord that he committed no sin but was made sin (2 Cor. 5:21)? Was the Lord therefore converted into sin (Gal. 3:13)? Certainly not. Rather, because he assumed our sins, he was called sin. He was also called accursed—not because the Lord was converted into a curse, but because he himself assumed our curse: “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree” (Deut. 21:23). Are you therefore surprised that it is written, “The Word became flesh,” when flesh was assumed by the Word of God, although it is written of sin, which he did not possess, that he was made sin? This means not that he became sin by the nature or operation of sin—since he was made in the likeness of sinful flesh—but that he might crucify our sin in his flesh, he undertook for us the assumption of the infirmities of a body of flesh already subject to sin.

61. Let them therefore cease to say that the nature of the Word was changed into the nature of the body, lest, by the same interpretation, the nature of the Word seem to have been changed into the contagion of sin. For what he assumed is one thing, and what was assumed is another. Power came upon the Virgin, just as the angel also said to her: “The power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1:35). But a body was born from the Virgin; and therefore the descent was heavenly, but the conception was human. The nature of the flesh and the nature of the divinity could not, therefore, be the same.

## CHAPTER VII

He explains why he added this book to the preceding books. Then, after demonstrating the foolishness of those who denied that Christ assumed a soul, he establishes the assumption of the soul by testimonies from Scripture. He next explains why the Lord ought not to have omitted the soul from his assumption and shows that these same people are troubled by a groundless fear. He discusses in what sense Christ is said to fear or to make progress, while there is nevertheless no danger that he should be divided or appear to have a *tetras* introduced; this last charge he turns back against those very people.

62. I could pursue the subject at greater length, but I fear that these matters may seem to some either superfluous or excessively long. Perhaps someone might say: “Did you not promise that you would complete your discussion of the divinity of the Father and the Son in the five books you wrote?” But what am I to do when they sow new questions every day? The promise is not set aside; the objection binds me. For how can an answer have an end if the objections have no limit?

63. Nevertheless, I had promised above that I would complete my response concerning the divinity of the Father and the Son. In this book, however, a fuller treatment, as was necessary, has been arranged concerning the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation. Since what the Lord says—“My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. 26:38)—and below, “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (ibid., 39)—refers not to the compassion of the Holy Spirit but to the assumption of a rational soul and to the affect of human nature, it follows that, by affirming the Lord’s mystery, we must establish that the fullness of human nature was present in Christ, and separate the Holy Spirit from any presumption of weakness. For the one who is not subject to passion is not subject to weakness.

64. I therefore ask on what grounds some think that a soul was not assumed by the Lord Jesus. Is it because they fear that Christ might be overcome by a human emotion? They say, in fact, that “the desire of the flesh opposes the law of the mind” (Rom. 7:23). But the one who said this was far from thinking that Christ had been led into the bonds of sin by the law of the flesh. Rather, while placed amid the turmoil of human weakness, he believed that help could come to him through Christ, saying: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (ibid., 24–25). Could the one who rescued others from the slippery path of the flesh fear that he himself might be overcome by the dominion of that flesh?

65. But if, as they wish, he feared the allurements of this flesh, he ought also to have avoided assuming flesh, lest he be drawn into the slippery error. But how could he fear the slipperiness of sin, who came to remit sin? And therefore, since he assumed human flesh, it follows that he assumed the perfection and fullness of the incarnation; for nothing in Christ is imperfect. He therefore assumed flesh in order to raise it up; he assumed a soul—indeed, he assumed and received a perfect, rational, human soul.

66. For who can deny that he assumed a soul, when he himself says: “I lay down my soul for my sheep”? And again: “For this reason the Father loves me, because I lay down my soul, so that I may take it up again” (John 10:15, 17). This is not said as a parable, nor with a superficial meaning in which one thing is said and another understood, as in the statement: “Your new moons and your Sabbaths my soul hates” (Isa. 1:13). Although even that passage can be referred to Christ’s soul, which was set forth in order to abolish the error of Jewish superstition and establish the truth of the one sacrifice.

67. They may doubt the prophetic passage, but they cannot refute this evangelical statement as referring to the soul’s proper reality, since it was spoken concerning the Lord’s death and resurrection. Finally, he adds: “No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord. I have power to lay down my soul, and I have power to take it up again” (John 10:18). He therefore lays down the very soul that he assumed. I say that he assumed it; for the living Word of God did not itself become, in his flesh, a substitute for our soul. Rather, just as he assumed our flesh, so also, by assuming human nature, he assumed our complete soul. He assumed, I say, a soul in order to bless the mystery of his incarnation; he assumed my emotional life in order to correct it.

68. What need was there to assume flesh without a soul, when insensible flesh and an irrational soul are neither subject to sin nor worthy of reward? He therefore assumed for our sake that which was more greatly endangered in us. What benefit would it be to me if he did not redeem me wholly? But he redeemed me wholly, who said: “You are indignant with me because I made the whole man well on the Sabbath” (John 7:23). He redeemed me wholly, because in the faithful the complete man, not merely part of him, rises again as a perfect human being.

69. Let these compassionate people therefore cease to fear that Christ could not govern his own flesh, or a perfect soul and human understanding, when he even governed the colt of a donkey on which no one had previously sat (Luke 19:30). “He who planted the ear, will he not hear?” (Ps. 94:9). Could the one who governed others not govern himself? Could the one who forgave sins himself commit sin? Let these people, excessively anxious as though they were Christ’s tutors, cease to fear that even in him the desire of the flesh might have overcome the law of the mind, which it did not overcome in Paul but merely opposed (Rom. 7:23). The athlete of Christ counts the victories of his mind; they tremble lest the flesh should have faltered in the Lord, although it conquered in his servant.

70. Christ does not wish us to fear on his behalf; the Lord does not wish us to weep on his behalf. Hence he says: “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me; weep for yourselves” (Luke 23:28). And to these people he says: “Do not fear for me; fear for yourselves.” Have you not heard David say: “The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? The Lord is the defender of my life; from whom shall I tremble?” (Ps. 27:1). And elsewhere: “I will not fear what man can do to me” (Ps. 118:6); and elsewhere: “I will not fear what flesh can do to me” (Ps. 56:5).

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “what flesh can do to me. Therefore [he could fear] a fall”; two read, “God [could fear] a fall … could fear.”]

71. He therefore says: “Could I fear the fall of human nature, when man himself did not fear it? As God before the flesh, and God in the flesh, I assumed the perfection of human nature. I assumed human understanding, but I was not puffed up by the understanding of the flesh. In human understanding I said that my soul was troubled; in human understanding I hungered; in human understanding I prayed, although I am accustomed to hear those who pray.” [Note: This teaching of Ambrose concerning Christ’s progress in wisdom seemed so problematic to Peter Lombard that he declared it alien from the teaching of the other Fathers and even from the mind of the Church, unless it is understood of an external progress and according to the judgment of other people: “For he so appeared and acted,” he says, “as though he were without knowledge.” Yet Estius and other theologians are not unjustified in finding this answer unsatisfactory, since it would concede the point to the opponents. For what could be more convenient for them than to ascribe that apparent progress merely externally to the divinity, which, they maintained, supplied the place of Christ’s soul? Petavius, *On the Incarnation*, book XI, chapter 2, writes that the Fathers did not all hold the same opinion on this matter, since some admitted human progress in Christ while others denied it. Concerning our holy Doctor he says: “Ambrose, however, appears to affirm more strongly than nearly all the others that Christ truly made progress and increased both in age and in wisdom and in grace.” This is the statement with which he supports his opinion, citing the words of the following paragraph: “How did he make progress?” Nevertheless, Ambrose himself prevents us from agreeing entirely with this distinguished scholar. For when, in book V of *On the Faith*, chapter 18, section 221, he had reported that many people professed that the Lord knew all things according to his divinity but truly was ignorant of certain things according to his humanity, in the following section he openly indicates that this opinion is not acceptable to him. Yet he does not therefore regard such people as heretics in any way; indeed, we may reasonably infer from his own words that they were Catholics. We would therefore readily allow ourselves to be persuaded that, since the same opinion was held by many Catholics and was useful for refuting the inventions of the Apollinarists, the holy Doctor is arguing here on behalf of that opinion rather than expressing his own; we have already observed more than once that this sometimes occurs in his writings. Nevertheless, it seems to us quite probable that whatever is argued here concerning Christ’s progress should be accommodated and attributed to that third kind of knowledge which theologians admit in him in addition to blessed and infused knowledge, under the name of acquired or experiential knowledge. They say that this is the knowledge by which our holy Doctor says Christ progressed through human understanding—namely, through knowledge of things received by the senses—not because ignorance preceded that knowledge, but because he learned by a new mode of knowing, that is, through experience acquired with the advance of age, what he had previously known. Augustine recognizes something similar in Adam, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book VIII, chapter 8. But the reason we must not suppose that the minds of Ambrose and certain other Fathers have been fully understood in this matter is that, in order to affirm that the Lord possessed a human soul, they saw that it was sufficient to demonstrate some kind of progress—whatever its nature—from Scripture. Accordingly, they did not devote much effort to investigating the nature of that progress. You may easily observe something similar in Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* 77.26, Theodoret, *Compendium of Heretical Myths* V.13, and others.]

“I progressed through human understanding, as it is written: ‘And Jesus progressed in age and wisdom and grace before God and human beings’” (Luke 2:52). [Note: A few manuscripts read, “before God and before human beings.” The progress in age and the progress in wisdom are human. Let the order of the words teach you how the Wisdom of God progressed. For this reason he first mentioned age, and so forth.]

72. How did the Wisdom of God progress? Let the order of the words teach you. There was progress in age, and progress in wisdom—but it was human wisdom. He mentioned age first so that you might understand that the statement was made according to the human condition, for age belongs not to divinity but to the body. Therefore, if he progressed in human age, he progressed in human wisdom. Wisdom progresses through understanding, because wisdom comes from understanding. Now Jesus progressed in age and wisdom. What understanding progressed? If it was human, then it too was assumed; if it was divine, then it was changeable through progress. For whatever progresses is certainly changed for the better; but what is divine is not changed. Therefore what is changed is certainly not divine. Human understanding, then, was progressing; therefore he assumed human understanding.

### 73

And that we may know that he was speaking as a human being, he prefaced it above by saying: “But the child grew and became strong, being filled with wisdom; and the grace of God was with him” (ibid., 40). “Child” is the name of our age; neither could God be strengthened, nor could God grow, nor could the height of God’s wisdom, nor the fullness of divinity, be filled. What was therefore being filled was not God’s wisdom, but ours. For how was he being filled who descended in order to fill all things (Eph. IV, 10)?

[Note: Two manuscripts read, “ascended, in order to fill”; an incongruous and contrary sense.]

### 74

But in what sense did Isaiah say that the child did not know father or mother? For it is written: “Before the child knows father or mother, he will receive the power of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria” (Isa. VIII, 4). The wisdom of God is not deceived by future and hidden things; but infancy, lacking knowledge and possessing human ignorance, does not know what it has not yet learned.

### 75

“But it must be feared,” you say, “that if we attribute to Christ two principal faculties of understanding, or a twofold wisdom, we divide Christ.” Do we divide Christ when we worship both his divinity and his flesh? Do we divide him when we venerate in him the image of God and the cross? Certainly the Apostle, who said of him, “For although he was crucified through our weakness, yet he lives through the power of God” (II Cor. XIII, 4), himself declared that Christ is not divided. Do we also divide him when we say that he assumed a rational soul capable of understanding (I Cor. I, 13)?

### 76

For it was not God the Word himself who was present in his flesh in place of a rational soul capable of understanding; rather, God the Word assumed a rational soul capable of understanding—and a human soul, of the same substance as our souls—and flesh like ours, of the same substance as our flesh, and thus was also perfect man, yet without any stain of sin; for he himself did not commit sin, but for our sake was made sin, so that we might become the righteousness of God in him (II Cor. V, 21).

[Note: Some manuscripts read “in himself.” Thus they say that his flesh was of the same substance as our flesh, and likewise his soul and flesh were of the same substance as ours.]

His flesh, therefore, and his soul are of the same substance as our soul and flesh.

### 77

Nor do I fear that I may seem to introduce a tetrad; for we who assert this truly worship the Trinity alone. I do not divide Christ when I distinguish the substance of his flesh from that of his divinity; rather, I proclaim one Christ with the Father and the Spirit of God. I shall show that those who say that Christ’s flesh is of one substance with his divinity introduce a tetrad even more than we do. For what is of the same substance is not “one” as a single person, but is one in unity; certainly, when confessing the Son to be of the same substance as the Father in the proceedings of the Council of Nicaea, they believed not one person but one divinity in the Father and the Son.

### 78

Therefore, when they say that his flesh was of the same substance as that of which the Son of God was, they themselves fall into the absurdity of their vain assertion which they bring against us, namely, that they divide Christ. Thus they introduce a fourth uncreated being for us to worship, although only the divinity of the Trinity is uncreated.

## CHAPTER VIII

Against the Catholic position that the Son who was begotten is equal to the Father who begot him, the opponents object that the begotten cannot be of the same nature as the unbegotten. It is answered that the terms “begotten” and “unbegotten,” which are not found in Scripture, are introduced by them, although they reject the words “nature” and “substance” precisely because they deny that these occur in the same Scriptures. It is also demonstrated from the sacred books that God possesses nature and substance.

### 79

I had concluded the book; but it was a matter of religious duty that we should not seem to have passed over something we could not resolve.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “lest, having passed over it, we should divide”; some others, “lest we should seem to pass it by.” Many, including the Gill and Roman editions, read as in the text. The manuscripts mostly, and the ancient editions, read “to differ through zeal”; the text has been emended from the Remigius manuscript to “to be distracted by zeal,” that is, to be distracted, tossed about, and agitated by passion.] For some people had heard us say earlier that the Son of God who was begotten cannot be unequal to the Father who begot him, although the one was begotten and the other begot him, because generation belongs not to power but to nature. They think that, against this question, they have had their voice stifled; but, in a blameworthy evasion, they turn their steps in the same place, imagining that the question is changed by changing the wording. They say: “How can the unbegotten and the begotten be of one nature and substance?”

### 80

Therefore, most merciful Emperor, to answer the question you have proposed to me, I find first of all that “unbegotten” is nowhere found in the divine Scriptures: I have not read it, nor have I heard it. What sort of inconsistency is it, then, in people of this kind that they accuse us of using words that are not written, when we speak of what is written—and they themselves object to us with what is not written? Do they not contradict themselves and undermine the authority of their own accusation?

### 81

For they say that it is not written that God is substance and nature, although Scripture certainly testifies that the Son of God is “the radiance of the Father’s glory and the imprint of his substance” (Heb. I, 3); and in another book we have shown at fullest length that many passages speak of divine substance (On the Faith, Book III, chapter 4).

### 82

Who, moreover, would deny that there is a divine nature, when the Apostle Peter wrote in his letter that the Lord’s mercy worked through the passion of the cross in order, he says, “to make us partakers of the divine nature” (II Pet. I, 4)? Paul also wrote elsewhere: “But at that time, when you did not know God, you served those who by nature are not gods” (Gal. IV, 8). For so we also find it in the Greek manuscripts, whose authority is greater.

### 83

What, then, are those people doing who deny that there is a divine nature, except that they now slander not only the Son but also the Father? For if it is denied that God is God by nature, then he is so by grace, like human beings; or else he is falsely believed to be God, like the demons, whose images are given the name of gods. But let us follow apostolic authority and say that the images do not possess a divine nature. If it is not in the images, then it is not in the demons; it remains, therefore, that in God there is a divine nature and substance (I Cor. X).

### 84

We have therefore taught, on apostolic authority, that it is rightly said of God the Father that he is God by nature. Let them now accept that the nature of God the Father is the same as that of the Son, and likewise the same as that of the Holy Spirit, lest they perhaps say in the same way: “We read that the nature is divine, but we do not read that there is unity of the divine nature.”

But when the Son himself said, “I and the Father are one” (John X, 30), he proved the unity of divinity. When he said, “All things that the Father has are mine” (John XVI, 15), and below, “Father, all mine are yours, and yours are mine” (John XVII, 10), he asserted unity. When he said, “The Father who dwells in me, he himself does the works that I do” (John XIV, 10), he made unity most plainly evident.

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads, “he himself does the works.” It also reads, “As the Father gave me commandment, so I do.”]

### 85

Furthermore, Peter shows that there is one divine nature: “that he might make us,” he says, “partakers of the divine nature” (II Pet. I, 4). He could have spoken otherwise, if he had judged differently; he could, I say, have said: “that he might make us partakers of divine natures,” especially since through the Son we enter into participation in the divine nature. Can one give what one does not possess? There is therefore no doubt that he gives from what he has; and consequently the one who grants participation in the divine nature possesses the divine nature.

### 86

The Apostle Paul likewise, by saying “those who by nature are not gods” (Gal. IV, 8), shows that the true God has one nature. For he too could have said, “those who by natures are not gods,” if he knew that there was a plurality of divine natures, so that one were in the Father, another in the Son, and another in the Holy Spirit. By saying, therefore, “by nature they are not gods,” he expressed the unity of the divine nature.

### 87

What does it mean for God to be God by nature, except that he is the true God? Thus he said to the Thessalonians: “How you turned to God from idols, to serve the living and true God” (I Thess. I, 9). For those beings are falsely said to be gods, whereas by nature God is living and true. In ordinary usage also we distinguish an adoptive son from a true son. We do not say that an adoptive son is a son by nature; rather, we say that the one who is a true son is a son by nature.

### 88

We have therefore proved by the reading of Scripture that nature and substance are divine; apostolic authority has also demonstrated that the divine nature is one, not plural.

## CHAPTER IX

The heretics, wishing the unbegotten Father—which they have not read in Scripture—to be granted to them, reveal their contentious spirit. Yet it must be admitted that the term is written—but in Arius, against whom the Apostle is set. Their objection is turned back against them, and the term “unbegotten” is shown to be applicable even to a creature. After explaining the opponents’ argument, Ambrose replies that the terms “begotten” and “unbegotten” signify not nature but a quality. He proves this at length with examples, dwelling especially on the possibility that the same substance can arise from different beginnings.

### 89

Now let them show where they have read of the Father as unbegotten. But if, in the manner of dialecticians, they demand that they be granted the right to use what has not been read as though it had been read, they reveal that they are being driven by a contentious zeal and are not seeking knowledge of the truth.

For even in dialectic, unless what they demand to have granted them is granted—that by which they desire to find an opening for contention—they cannot find the starting point of their dispute. And this is so in a matter where the contest is more about the subtleties of disputation than about an examination of the truth. For this is the glory of dialecticians: to appear to defeat and refute the truth by words. The rule of faith, on the contrary, is that truth, not words, should be weighed. Finally, simple truth belonging to fishermen excludes the words of philosophers.

[Note: Many manuscripts read “defend with zeal”; others, “defer with zeal,” which is not inappropriate if *deferre* is understood as “yield” or “comply”; several others and the Roman edition read “bring forward arguments.” The sense is plain. But since the reading “differ with zeal” is found in very many manuscripts and ancient editions, we have corrected the text from the Remigius manuscript to “be driven apart by zeal,” that is, “to be distracted, tossed about, and agitated by passion.”]

### 90

What sort of assertion is this, then, when, unless I grant them the word “unbegotten,” they cannot find the beginning of their assertion? Let them show, therefore, where they have read it.

### 91

It had slipped my mind; now I recall it. “It is written,” they say, “for Arius called the Father unbegotten, and the Son begotten and created.”

[Note: Some manuscripts read “the Son.” On what authority do they contend against apostolic writings?]

There you have the authority on which they contend against apostolic writings. Let them contend, then, provided that they admit they are disciples of Arius. For how do they deny the master whose invention they follow?

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “If they say this, because Arius judged more rightly, I ought to say what the Apostle said.” Ambrose appears here to have imitated Basil, *Against the Arians*, Oration II.]

### 92

But if they say what Arius said, I ought more rightly to say what the Apostle said (Eph. III, 14). He named the Father; he did not call him “unbegotten.” He named the Son, and he called him the begotten Son. What I read, I do not deny; indeed, I gladly use it. What I have not read, I ought not to use. Yet let them use it, even though we would not do so in dialectic—unless perhaps they also say that, just as we do not read that the Father is begotten as the Son is, we ought therefore to consider him unbegotten.

### 93

That is understood, then; it is not read. But if it is understood, I have not read that the Holy Spirit is begotten either. Therefore, since he is not begotten, according to your position he too must be called unbegotten. If, then, you say that the unbegotten and the begotten cannot be of one substance, it remains that you should not deny the unity of divine nature and substance between the Father and the Holy Spirit, since we read neither that the Father nor that the Holy Spirit is begotten.

For if the whole force of your argument lies in this—that the unbegotten and the begotten cannot be of one nature—then one who is not begotten is of one nature and substance with another who is not begotten.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “And if for this reason we think the Father …”]

And if you think that the Father is greater because he is not begotten, is the Holy Spirit also greater than the Son?

### 94

Many examples, indeed countless ones, can be supplied in which something that has not been begotten is called unbegotten. For many have said that the world is unbegotten, and they have likewise maintained that the matter of all things—which the Greeks call *hyle*, as though it were a material forest—is unbegotten.

They therefore see that this word cannot possess some special prerogative of power, unless perhaps they think they honor God by a word with which philosophers thought the world ought to be honored. Is the Father unbegotten, then, in the same way as the world? Certainly not. Or is this expression alone suitable for God, when God lies beyond the scope of every expression? Nothing, therefore, is precious to God in a word that can be common to other beings.

### 95

Yet let us grant, as you wish, that the prerogative of this expression is immeasurable—a prerogative designated not by any authority but estimated according to your own judgment. What does it accomplish, then, that you wish to make a difference of nature and a difference of power between the Father and the Son on the basis of a word?

“Unbegotten and begotten,” he says, “cannot be of one nature and substance”; or, as they sometimes say, “The unmade and the made are not of one nature.” For they do not distinguish between the unbegotten and the unmade, nor do they wish there to be a difference between the begotten and the created, provided only that they call the Son a creature.

### 96

They say, therefore, that because the Father surpasses every cause—that is, *aitia* (αἰτία), as the Greeks say—and was not created from another, he is not a son; since he is a substance that does not have from elsewhere the beginning or cause from which he exists. And for that reason, they say, another substance of this kind cannot exist, because all things receive from God the Father the cause of their subsistence.

Hence they say it is not plausible that the Son, because he is from the Father and does not possess from himself the cause of his existence but receives it from the Father, should be like the Father—since the Father has the cause of his existence from no other, whereas the Son, as they allege, could not exist unless he received this very fact of existing from the Father.

### 97

And so they say that the unbegotten and the begotten are unlike, as though—as I have often said elsewhere—generation belonged to power and not to nature. When I say “begotten,” I have expressed not a property of nature but the meaning of generation; and I shall establish this by clearer examples.

For if I say simply “son,” without adding whose son, it may mean a son of a human being, a son of iniquity, a son of pestilence, or a son of the devil, as Scripture testifies concerning the Jews (John VIII, 44); and, in ordinary usage, the offspring of cattle or the young of pigeons. Therefore, the designation “sons” does not express a particular nature. But if I wish to designate nature, I shall name a human being, a horse, or a bird, so that the nature may be understood.

### 98

Thus, if I wish to designate the divine nature, I ought to name the true God. But when I say “Son,” I signify one who has been begotten; when I also say “Father,” I declare that he has begotten. Do not therefore make this a distinction of nature, since it signifies the one who begets and the one who is begotten. Such terms signify a quality of substance: there are many sons, but the sons differ—one by nature, another by grace.

### 99

There are many invisible and visible creatures: invisible creatures, such as Principalities and Powers, Thrones and Dominions; visible creatures, such as the sun, moon, stars, human beings, and earth. Thus there are different species and different substances of creatures.

Therefore, if you wish to express the distinctive nature of some creature, you will name the sun, the moon, or the stars; and in this way it is understood what you intend to signify.

### 100

But if you say “made” or “created”—terms which they sometimes apply to the Son—because many things have been made and created, you appear to have signified not a property of substance but a kind of quality. For substance is one thing and quality another.

Finally, we said elsewhere that the Latins have translated *ousia* (οὐσία) by the word *substantia*. But when God’s *ousia* is mentioned, what else is signified except that God always is?
