The letters themselves express this, since the divine reality, being always (*ousa aei*, οὖσα ἀεί), is called *ousia* (οὐσία), with the order of one letter altered for the sake of sound, brevity, and elegance of expression.

Thus *ousia* signifies that God always is. But the designation “unbegotten,” or “begotten,” as you wish, declares how something exists—that is, that the Father is not from another, whereas the Son is not from himself.

[Note: The editions read “declares what it is”; the manuscripts read “declares how it is,” that is, it signifies not substance but mode. This is entirely appropriate, for it is taken from Basil’s words in Book IV *Against Eunomius*: “The unbegotten is a mode of existence, not a name of substance.” Observe also that a few words later *species* is used for an individual; Ambrose’s elsewhere attested usage shows that this is not unprecedented.]

The species here appears to be different. The species is indeed distinct, but the divinity is undivided.

### 101

You ask how this can be proved? I shall also show, among created things, that there are different species and different beginnings in many cases, yet one substance; and I shall bring forward examples from Scripture. Therefore, if this can occur in mortal things, how do they impose a law of necessity of this kind upon the divinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit?

[Note: This argument is treated not only in Book IV of Basil’s *Against Eunomius*, chapter 2, but also in Athanasius’s *On the Decrees of the Council of Nicaea*, Book II of Gregory of Nyssa’s *Against Eunomius*, and elsewhere.]

### 102

All flying creatures that appear to belong to the same genus are likewise of the same nature: thus there is one genus and one nature of eagles, similarly of vultures, and likewise of other flying creatures according to their genera.

Yet when we investigate how flying creatures began to exist, we find three kinds and read of different causes of their origin. For it is written that God said: “Let the waters bring forth creeping things with living souls, and flying things that fly” (Gen. I, 20). A little later, when God had made paradise and placed the human being in it, it is written that “God formed from the earth the beasts of the field and the birds of the sky” (Gen. II, 19). The birds are therefore here said to have been formed from the earth.

Above also you read that God said to the birds, “Increase and multiply” (Gen. I, 22), certainly commanding the increase of generation through the union of male and female. We therefore observe that creatures of one genus began to exist in different ways: some from the waters, others from the earth, and others through the generation of male and female. Yet all are of one nature and do not differ in substance.

### 103

What, indeed, is as much of one nature as our flesh and the reality of the Lord’s body? Yet the two came into being through different causes and arose from different beginnings. The Lord’s flesh was generated when the Spirit came upon the Virgin (Luke I, 35), without awaiting the customary intercourse of male and female. Our flesh, however, cannot be formed within the mother’s womb unless the male and female sexes cover the seeds in their natural furrows. Yet although the cause of generation is different, the flesh of Christ has one nature with all human beings.

### 104

The Virgin’s childbirth did not change nature; it renewed the manner of generation. Finally, flesh was born from flesh. The Virgin therefore possessed something of her own to give. The mother did not give something alien, but contributed from her own womb what was hers, in an unusual manner but through the customary function. The Virgin therefore possessed flesh which, by the law of ordinary nature, she transferred into the child.

Thus the nature of Mary, the one who generated according to the flesh, and of the one begotten, is the same; nor is he unlike his brothers, since Scripture says that he was made like his brothers in every respect (Heb. II, 17). The Son of God is like us, not according to the fullness of divinity, but according to the reality of a rational soul and, to put it more explicitly, of a human body belonging to us.

[Note: Some manuscripts and editions read: “Let us say, of a human nature belonging to us,” and so forth.]

### 105

What, moreover, shall we say of Adam himself? Although he was formed from the clay of the earth, he certainly begot sons who shared his nature, participated in his race, and inherited his succession (Gen. II, 17). The beginnings in the sons and in their parent were indeed different, but the nature of the human condition was one. Yet the difference of their origin did not prejudice the similarity of their substance.

The son is therefore like the father even in those respects in which, because of the frailty of the human condition, they could not possess the fullness of likeness. How, then, can the true Son be unlike God the Father?

## CHAPTER X

Those who acknowledge that the Son is like the Father but deny that he is of the same substance do not differ from the foregoing. For there can be no accidental or partial likeness between them, since likeness of this sort is attributed even to mere human beings in relation to God; but the Son’s likeness to the Father is a likeness of nature, and the Son is also the Father’s perfect image. The term “unbegotten” therefore poses no obstacle to Catholics; rather, it exposes the perfidy of the heretics, who, while using a term unknown to Scripture, denied the omnipotence attributed there to those persons.

### 106

But many who follow the same sect think that they differ in their manner of argument from those who say that the Son is unlike the Father in every respect. We shall therefore also examine the absurdity of those who say that the Son is like the Father but is not of one substance with him.

### 107

Things that are not of one nature are necessarily different and distinct; and things of a different nature consequently cannot be alike—unless perhaps you call them alike in appearance but unlike in reality. Milk, snow, and the swan have the same appearance of whiteness, but they preserve the difference of their distinct natures; the difference of their natures is not disguised by similarity of appearance.

### 108

How, then, do these people call the Father and the Son alike while denying unity of substance? Do they think them alike in form, figure, or color? But these belong to bodies and indicate a certain composition. How can we apply likeness according to color or form to what is invisible? Or how can a creature be like the uncreated?

[Note: All editions, except the last two Paris editions, which read “in the invisible . . . we apply,” read “we desire the latter things.” The manuscripts agree almost unanimously with the latter reading, except that they omit *in*; nevertheless, the common reading adopted here is preferable.] How can he be “the radiance of his glory and the imprint of his substance” (Heb. I, 3), if—as they say—different glory means different substance?

### 109

“They are alike,” they say, “according to glory and operation, and for this reason the Son is called the image of God.” Therefore, if he is like in some respects but not in all, he is partly like and partly unlike. It follows from this proposition that, if he is like in part and not in the whole, the image of God is composite in part; and consequently the one whose image is composite also appears to be composite. But if the composite image preserves likeness only in part, it cannot itself be partly like the one whose image it is.

### 110

Those who deny that he is like according to unity of nature therefore consider him like other beings. They are accustomed to say: “Why do you think that Scripture has given the Son anything great by calling him an image, when God himself said to human beings, ‘Be holy, because I also am holy’ (Lev. XIX, 2), and the Son said, ‘Be perfect, just as your Father who is in heaven is perfect’ (Matt. XVI, 48)?”

They do not understand that this very comparison establishes that the Son is like the Father not according to a part but according to the fullness and perfection of divinity. Finally, if there are many who are alike, why alone is the Son called “the image of the invisible God” and “the imprint of his substance,” unless it is because in him there is unity of the same nature and an expression of the same majesty?

[Note: Three manuscripts read, “in him is the nature of the same unity, and of the same …”; two read, “in his nature is the unity of the same …” The remaining manuscripts and all editions agree with the reading adopted here.]

### 111

For one likeness is according to imitation, and another according to nature. The words of the examples proposed also indicate this. Scripture says, “Be holy,” so that they may become holy through imitation. Thus it is said to human beings, “Be,” because they are not yet holy; but God says of himself, “I am holy,” not as though he became holy by progress, but because his nature remains.

Then Wisdom says, “Be perfect,” so that they may begin to possess what they do not have. But of the Father it says, “As your Father who is in heaven is perfect.” The Father is perfect because he always is. Therefore his *ousia* is called in Greek *ousia*, because he always is; or in Latin *substantia*, because he remains in himself and does not subsist through another’s assistance.

[Note: Up to this point Ambrose has argued against the pure and rigorous Arians, such as the Aetians, Eunomians, and Anomoeans. We understand from Theodoret, *Heretical Fables*, Book IV, chapter 3, that all of them were commonly called Troglites or Troglodytes because they held their meetings and assemblies in caves. He now turns to the more moderate party, namely those who rejected the term *homoousios* (ὁμοούσιος), established at the Council of Nicaea, and substituted *homoiousios* (ὁμοιούσιος). Epiphanius calls these people Semi-Arians in *Heresy* 73, as does Augustine in *On Heresies*, chapter 58. As for the division of the Arians into several streams, Ambrose had already touched on it in *On the Faith*, Book I, chapter 6, section 45.]

### 112

The Father is therefore holy and perfect; the Son also is holy and perfect, as the image of God. He is the image of God because all that belongs to God is seen in the Son: eternal divinity, omnipotence, and majesty. What God is, such he appears in his image. Therefore you must believe the image to be such as God is.

For if you diminish the image, it will appear that you have diminished the one whose image it is. If you believe the image to be lesser, God will appear lesser in the image. Whatever you judge the image to be, such will the one whose invisible image it is necessarily appear to you.

The image said, “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John XIV, 9). And whatever you judge the one to be whose image you believe the Son to be, such must the Son necessarily be judged. Therefore, because the Father is uncreated, the Son is uncreated; because the Father is not lesser, the Son is not lesser; because the Father is omnipotent, the Son is omnipotent.

### 113

It has therefore been said—even if they use what they do not read, in calling him unbegotten—that this word in no way prevents us from believing Christ to be of one nature and substance with the Father. And if he is of one nature, he is certainly of one power.

### 114

This passage is by no means difficult for refuting the efforts of the faithless. How can they deny that Christ is omnipotent, when Scripture says so, while they wish to use a term which Scripture does not teach? We have already shown that Christ is omnipotent (Book II *On the Faith*, chapter 3), and this is signified in the Apocalypse of John the Evangelist, in the prophecy of Zechariah, and in the Gospel.

If anyone thinks these passages should be reviewed, let him turn back to the preceding discussion and read it again.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “and in the prophet Zechariah.”]

### 115

Yet what I almost passed over there because of the accumulation of testimonies, let them say of whom they think Amos was speaking when he prophesied. For it is written: “The Lord who touches the earth and makes it tremble, and all who dwell in it shall mourn. And he shall rise like the river of Egypt, for he builds his ascent above heaven and confirms his promise above the earth; he calls the water of the sea and pours it out upon the face of the earth. The Lord Almighty is his name.”

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “And his consummation shall rise like a river, and descend like the river of Egypt. Because he builds …”]

Do they not understand that all these things apply to the Son, who, descending, touched the earth, shook it in his passion, ascended from the earth into heaven, and descended from heaven to earth, just as he himself had promised?

### 116

But why labor over the Son, when Scripture also testifies that the Spirit is omnipotent? For it is written: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their strength” (Ps. XXXII, 6).

And it is written of Wisdom that she possesses within herself the omnipotent Spirit. Solomon says: “Wisdom taught me, she who is the craftsman of all things” (Wis. VII, 12). For in her there is a Spirit of understanding, holy, unique, manifold, subtle, readily moving, articulate, undefiled, manifest, inviolable, loving what is good, sharp, provident, capable, bountiful, benevolent, steadfast, whole, free from anxiety, all-powerful, all-seeing, and penetrating all things, including intelligible spirits.

[Note: The older edition and quite a few manuscripts read “subtle, good, mobile”; the Roman edition and the remaining manuscripts read “subtle, readily mobile.” Where all editions and most manuscripts read “sharp, provident, capable,” some manuscripts read “sharp, impassible.” Finally, in place of “of invisible spirits,” which occurs in all editions and most manuscripts, some read “spirits of invisible things.”]

## AMBROSIAN FRAGMENT TAKEN FROM THEODORET, *DIALOGUE II OF THE POLYMORPH* (C, S)*

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following fragment are printed in parallel in Migne.]

### Of Saint Ambrose, Bishop of Milan, in the *Exposition of the Faith*

We confess our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, the Only-Begotten, begotten from the Father without beginning before all the ages according to his divinity; but in the last days the same one was incarnate from the holy Virgin Mary, and assumed a perfect human being consisting of a rational soul and a body, consubstantial with the Father according to divinity and consubstantial with us according to humanity.

For an ineffable union of two perfect natures has taken place. Therefore we confess one Christ, one Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, knowing that, while he is coeternal with his own Father according to divinity—and according to that divinity he is also the creator of all things—he deigned, after the holy Virgin’s consent, when she said to the angel, “Behold the will of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word,” ineffably to build for himself from her a temple and unite it to himself from the very conception—not a coeternal body brought down from heaven from his own substance, but taking it from the mass of our substance, that is, from the Virgin, and uniting it to himself.

God the Word was not changed into flesh, nor did he appear as a phantom; rather, preserving his own substance without change or alteration, he took the firstfruits of our nature and united them to himself. God the Word did not take his beginning from the Virgin; rather, while existing coeternally with his own Father, he deigned, through his immense goodness, to unite to himself the firstfruits of our nature—not by being mixed with it, but appearing as one and the same in both substances, as it is written: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John II, 19).

For Christ God is destroyed according to my substance, which he assumed; and the same one raises up the destroyed temple according to the divine substance, according to which he is also the creator of all things.

He never, after the union which he deigned to unite to himself from the very conception, either departed from his own temple or was able to depart because of his ineffable love for humanity. Rather, he is the same one, capable of suffering and incapable of suffering: capable of suffering according to his humanity, incapable of suffering according to his divinity. “For see, see me, that I am, and I do not change.”

Therefore God the Word raised up his own temple, and in it accomplished the resurrection and renewal of our nature. Showing this to his disciples, he said: “Touch me and see that a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I am—not existing, but possessing them”—so that, by considering both the one who possesses and that which is possessed, you might perceive not a mingling, transformation, or alteration, but a union that has taken place.

For this reason he also showed the marks of the nails and the piercing of the spear, and ate in the presence of his disciples, so that in every way he might assure them that the resurrection of our nature had been renewed in himself.

And although, according to the blessed substance of his divinity, he remained unchangeable, unalterable, incapable of suffering, immortal, and lacking nothing, he permitted every suffering to be inflicted, by concession, upon his own temple; he raised it by his own power, and through his own temple accomplished the complete renewal of our nature.

But the Catholic and Apostolic Church anathematizes those who say that Christ was merely a human being; or that God the Word was capable of suffering; or that he was changed into flesh; or that he possessed a body consubstantial with himself; or that he brought it from heaven; or that he was a phantom; or who say that, because God the Word was mortal, he needed resurrection from the Father; or that he assumed a body without a soul; or a human being without a mind; or that the two natures of Christ, having been mingled together by blending, became one nature; and those who do not confess that in our Lord Jesus Christ there are two natures without confusion, but one person, according to which he is one Christ and one Son.

### Saint Ambrose, Bishop of Milan, in the *Exposition of the Faith*

We confess our Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, begotten from the Father without beginning before all the ages according to his divinity; but in the last days the same one was incarnate from the holy Virgin Mary, and assumed a perfect human being consisting of a rational soul and a body, consubstantial with the Father according to divinity and consubstantial with us according to humanity. For an ineffable union of two perfect natures has taken place.

Therefore we confess one Christ, one Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, knowing that, while he exists coeternally with his own Father according to divinity—and according to that divinity is also the creator of all things—he deigned, after the holy Virgin’s consent, when she said to the angel, “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word” (Luke I, 38), ineffably to build for himself a temple from her and unite it to himself from the very conception—not a coeternal body brought down from heaven from his own substance, but taking it from the mass of our substance, that is, from the Virgin, and uniting it to himself.

God the Word was not changed into flesh, nor did he appear as a phantom; rather, preserving his own substance without change or alteration, he united to himself the firstfruits of our nature that he had assumed. God the Word did not take his beginning from the Virgin; rather, while existing coeternally with his own Father, he deigned, through his immense goodness, to unite the firstfruits of our nature to himself—not by being mingled, but appearing as one and the same in both substances, as it is written: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John II, 19).

For Christ God is destroyed according to my substance, which he assumed; and the same one raises up the destroyed temple according to the divine substance, according to which he is also the creator of all things.

[Col. 0848D] Never, after the union which he deigned to unite to himself from the very moment of conception, did he either withdraw from his temple or, through his ineffable goodness, have the power to withdraw from it. Yet he is both passible and impassible: passible according to his humanity, impassible according to his divinity. For “See, see that I am he, and I do not change” (Malachi 3:6). After God the Word had therefore raised up his temple, and in it had perfected the resurrection and renewal of our nature, showing this to his disciples, he said: “Touch me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I am not [a spirit], but have [flesh and bones]” (Luke 24:39); so that, considering both the one who possesses and that which is possessed, you may understand that there was neither mixture, conversion, nor alteration, but union.

[Col. 0850A] For this reason he also displayed the marks of the nails and the wound of the spear, and ate in the presence of his disciples, so that in every way he might persuade them that the resurrection of our nature had been renewed in himself. And although, according to the blessed substance of his divinity, he was free from change and alteration, impassible, immortal, and in need of nothing, he permitted all sufferings to be inflicted upon his temple, raised it up by his own power, and through his temple accomplished the perfect renewal of our nature.

But those who say that Christ is a mere man, or that God the Word was subject to suffering, or that he was changed into flesh, or that he possessed a consubstantial body, or brought it down from heaven, or was a phantom; or who say that God the Word, being mortal, needed to be raised by the Father, or that he assumed an inanimate body, or a man without a mind, or that the two natures of Christ, confused through mixture, became one nature; and those who do not confess that in our Lord Jesus Christ there are two unconfused natures, but one person, insofar as Christ is one and the Son is one—the catholic and apostolic Church anathematizes them.

[Note: [Col. 0849B] Although this fragment contains such clear statements against the heresies of Nestorius and Eutyches that someone might, not without an appearance of truth, persuade himself that it was composed by an author later than the Councils of Ephesus and Chalcedon; nevertheless, since the passage is found complete in Theodoret at the place cited, and since the final part of the same fragment, beginning with the words “But those who say,” etc., is copied in Leo of Byzantium, Book I, Against the Heretics Mentioned Above, we more willingly judge it to have been excerpted from some commentary by Ambrose which the hostility of time has destroyed. Accordingly, because of its affinity with the books On the Faith, and especially On the Sacrament of the Incarnation of the Lord, we believe that nowhere could it be displayed more appropriately than here; therefore we reproduce this same passage here in Theodoret’s words, together with our own translation, from the latest Paris edition.]

[EPISTLES.]

[Col. 0849B]

## ADMONITION CONCERNING THE EPISTLES OF SAINT AMBROSE, ARRANGED IN A NEW ORDER

[Col. 0849B] It is beyond doubt that all writers imprint an image of themselves both in all their works generally and especially in their letters. Yet no one will deny that Saint Ambrose, more than others, everywhere stamped certain marks and characteristics of his virtues upon all his writings, and that in this collection of letters above all he left behind an image of himself that is both vivid and breathing.

Indeed, in this work—for we shall remain silent here for the moment about his other writings—those distinguished virtues by which Ambrose came to be regarded as a perfect model of bishops shine forth, each in its proper place. The petitions or letters presented to Valentinian testify to the love with which he was impelled to defend the dignity of the Christian religion. What he wrote in the affair of the basilicas reveals the ardor with which he burned to defend catholic doctrine and to pour out his blood for its integrity. Elsewhere we admire his magnanimity in pardoning injuries and bestowing benefits upon those who were most hostile to him; elsewhere we are astonished at his steadfastness before emperors and tyrants.

There are letters in which his pastoral solicitude is evident—a solicitude embracing not only the diocese of Milan but also other dioceses, however distant. There are others in which his learning, prudence, holiness, and estrangement from every taint of avarice break forth. Led by these qualities, deacons, priests, and bishops consulted him as the common oracle of his age; and not only private persons but also men of princely rank entrusted the most serious affairs to his integrity and skill.

Finally, throughout these letters the piety, charity, mercy, modesty, equity, and tireless perseverance of the holy bishop in vigils and pious labors can be seen everywhere with no little admiration. Thus we seem to behold not a faint and schematic portrait of Ambrose, but a lifelike and solid representation—indeed, Ambrose himself restored to life.

We are entirely convinced that great benefit will accrue to the reader from these most beautiful letters. In order that the benefit might be still greater, we devoted our efforts not only to explaining passages which we judged to require an advocate, but also to establishing an entirely new arrangement of the work.

Certainly, it would have been highly desirable for us not to depart from either of the published arrangements, since nothing in this field can be changed without causing some inconvenience to those who wish to consult in their proper sources the various testimonies which earlier authors either indicate or cite. Nevertheless, the disorder of both arrangements is so great, and their confusion so extensive, that we found it altogether necessary to devise another.

The older editions, apart from lacking very many letters which the Roman editors added, present a series of letters arranged neither according to time nor according to subject. The Roman edition, while attempting to remedy this defect, confused everything still further. It forcibly transferred several letters—if the expression may be allowed—from their native soil to a foreign one; nor did it pay any attention to distinguishing dates, although this was of the greatest importance. We shall say nothing for the moment about how unsuccessfully it arranged the subject matter: letters which ought to have been joined were often separated, while those which ought to have been separated were joined.

Nor could we take refuge in the manuscripts. For, in addition to the faults with which we have said the editions suffer, the manuscripts differ considerably from both published arrangements, although less from the older editions; and they themselves differ so greatly from one another that a letter which is number 30 in the Thuaneus manuscript is number 69 in the Longipontinus, while the letter numbered 36 in the Longipontinus is placed as number 48 in the Thuaneus, with the same situation occurring in many other cases.

Therefore, since we were compelled to sort out such vast confusion, nothing seemed more convenient than to distribute, according to the order of time, all those letters whose date we were able to establish, following the chronology which we know to be chiefly approved by learned scholars.

From this arise two classes, although the first greatly exceeds the second. So that readers may understand what principles we followed in assigning each letter its place and number, we shall briefly present, in continuous order, the arguments by which their dates are established.

Some other letters could indeed have been added to this first arrangement if we had judged the affinity of their style or subject with certain others sufficient for determining their date. But such supports seem to us too weak for us to believe that we can safely rely on them alone.

As for the second class, we decided to establish it in the following manner: letters concerned with the exposition of the sacred books were to be placed first; they would be followed by those dealing with some serious and religious subject; finally, several short letters which could not suitably and neatly be assigned to either group would close the series.

We have already noted that many letters absent from the older editions were published in the Roman edition. Nevertheless, we are no less certain that many more have perished, or at least are still wrestling with moths in some unknown corner of a library.

For just as it is entirely certain that Ambrose sent a considerable number of letters to his brother Satyrus and to some other very close friends (*On the Death of Satyrus*), so it can likewise be learned from the letters that remain that several others which the holy bishop wrote to his sister Marcellina, to the emperor Theodosius, to the tyrant Eugenius, to Alypius, to Phoebadius, and to Delphinus are missing.

Since our efforts to bring them out of darkness, undertaken with all the care of which we were capable, achieved nothing in this respect, the one task remaining to us was to devote ourselves diligently to adorning the surviving letters, which we judge to be the finest of all those written by the holy bishop.

Accordingly, besides what we have already mentioned as having been undertaken by us, we employed a large number of manuscripts for their correction, most of which preserve a very ancient and excellent hand. In addition, we separated several spurious letters from the rest; the grounds for this, so that no one may think it was done rashly, will be given in their proper places.

Finally, to lighten as far as possible the labor of those who would need to consult in our edition passages cited from other editions, we have arranged to append three catalogues, comparing all the editions with one another according to their three orders, and have added a fourth, alphabetical catalogue. With their help every obstacle and difficulty will be smoothed away.

But first the chronology of our first class must be demonstrated.

[Col. 0854]

## THE ORDER OF THE EPISTLES DISTRIBUTED ACCORDING TO CHRONOLOGICAL SEQUENCE IS ESTABLISHED

[Col. 0851]

## FIRST CLASS

[Col. 0851A]

**[Ann. 379.]** The first epistle is addressed to the emperor Gratian, whose letter is also prefixed. In it Ambrose excuses himself for not having met the emperor when he was returning from the East. Since this return of Gratian can most conveniently be understood as that particular return by which, after Valens—his uncle, whom he had gone to support—had been defeated by the Goths and burned in a peasant’s hut on the third day before the Kalends of September in the year 378, Gratian returned to the West in the following year, we have not unreasonably assigned the year 379 to this epistle.

**II.** This letter, addressed to Constantius as a new bishop in order to instruct him in the duties of his office, also commends to him the Church of Imola [Col. 0852A] and warns him to beware of the Arians coming from Illyria. Since this is understood to refer to the incursions of the Goths, who, as has already been said, were ravaging those provinces after the death of Valens, and since the letter mentions the approaching days of Lent, we infer that it was written during Lent of the year 379.

**[Ann. 380.] III and IV** are inscribed to Felix. Their date can be inferred from the fact that the latter, which is known to have been sent only a few days after the former, invites that bishop of Como to the dedication of a basilica constructed by Bassianus, bishop of Lodi. Ughellus reports that its consecration took place in the year 380 [Col. 0853A], in volume II of *Italia sacra*. Moreover, if this date is correct, it must also be added that this very letter was dated on the day before the Kalends of November, since it clearly discloses that day.

**V and VI** were written to Syagrius, bishop of Verona. In them Ambrose informs him that the judgment which he had rendered against the virgin Indicia had been rescinded by Ambrose at a gathering of bishops.

Although those who wish this to have occurred in the year 380 give no reason for their opinion, we nevertheless have reasons not to depart from them. First, it is sufficiently clear that these events took place at the very beginning of Syagrius’s episcopate, since Indicia—who had received the veil from his predecessor Zeno many years earlier—was accused of a crime especially fitting, as is customary, to younger years and an immature mind [Col. 0853B]. Second, that Nicetus mentioned in this letter is thought to be the same Nicetus whom Law 11, *Ne sanctum baptisma*, etc., mentions as having been issued in the year 377.

**VII and VIII** are believed to have been sent to Justus, the thirteenth bishop among the bishops of Lyon. Since he is said never afterward to have returned to Lyon after the Council of Aquileia, which he attended together with Ambrose in the year 381, but to have withdrawn into the deserts of Egypt, it follows that both letters preceded that synod.

**[Ann. 381.] IX, X, XI, and XII** are the letters occasioned by the Council of Aquileia held in the case of Palladius and Secundianus. We have included them in this edition together with the acts of that council not merely because they had been published in the Roman edition and are found among Ambrose’s works in certain manuscripts [Col. 0853C], but much more because the holy bishop is known to have assisted the Fathers of Aquileia both with his skill in debate and with his hand in writing.

The date of the council is clearly established, since its acts bear at their head the names of Syagrius and Eucherius as consuls, and there is no doubt that their consulship fell in the year 381.

Yet what shall we do with Father François Chifflet, who contends that these acts are spurious and were fabricated by Vigilius of Thapsus, who wrote toward the end of the fifth century? Chifflet not only arranged for them to be published among Vigilius’s legitimate works, but also defended his judgment in a special dissertation.

To make clear why we could not agree with him, we shall examine his principal arguments [Col. 0853D], as briefly as we can.

He relates that Vigilius was led to fabricate that synod because he thought that the Arians—whom he certainly did not dare openly to attack under his own name—could more easily be refuted by invoking the authority of a council. He supports this by observing that the same Vigilius had also attributed other books composed by himself to Athanasius and Ambrose.

But even if that latter attribution were entirely certain, there is an enormous difference between assigning the name of an ancient author to some recently composed pamphlet and substituting a false council for a genuine one whose acts had long since been published and preserved in the archives of churches and learned men [Col. 0854A].

The first practice is not especially unusual and is not easily detected, particularly if an author who wrote in a foreign language is adopted. The second is almost unheard of and could scarcely be attempted except by a madman.

Who, then, could persuade himself that an educated bishop would expose his own reputation and the cause of the catholic Church to the insults and ridicule of the Arians to such an extent? For, since Vigilius possessed the complete council itself, retaining even its date, its subscriptions—although corrupted in some places—and part of its synodal letters, as Chifflet himself writes, how could he flatter himself so greatly as to believe that this same synod was preserved nowhere else—not in Africa, not in Gaul, not even in Italy [Col. 0854B]?

Indeed, why did he not himself publish the genuine records, which would undoubtedly have had greater force against the heretics than fabricated ones? Add to this that nothing occurs in the same acts which does not fit the arguments and the persons engaged in debate extemporaneously and with a kind of sudden heat.

Chifflet nevertheless presses the matter further. He criticizes the fact that Valerian is there consistently placed before Ambrose, contrary to the honor and dignity of the see of Milan, and that Anemius, by claiming for himself the primacy of Illyricum, sins equally against modesty and truth.

But if Vigilius had the genuine acts of the council, as Chifflet states, why would he have wanted to alter precisely those features by which his fraud and imposture could most easily be exposed? We shall demonstrate in their proper places that nothing was admitted there which deserves reproach [Col. 0854C].

The same author raises several other objections to the points we have reported, but they are even weaker; some not only do nothing for his case but can be turned against him with greater force.

We therefore do not hesitate to judge these acts genuine. Our one wish would be that they had reached our own age intact. As for the pamphlet on the divinity of the Son which Chifflet tried to force upon us as a supplement to this work, we shall show in its proper place that it departs from every appearance of truth as completely as anything could.

**[Ann. 381 and 382.] XIII and XIV**, which we have joined to the Ambrosian letters, are inscribed in the name of the Italian bishops; we shall explain there why we have done so [Col. 0854D].

The first concerns both the schism of Antioch and the ordinations of Maximus the Cynic and Nectarius. The latter was elevated to the see of Constantinople at the universal synod held there only in March of the year 381, or, as others maintain, at one reconvened in the year 382.

Therefore, if anyone prefers the former view, nothing prevents him from thinking that this letter was written at the Council of Aquileia. As for Epistle XIV, since it thanks Theodosius for the response he had given to the preceding letter, it is clear that it cannot have been sent from a council convened before the year 382.

**[Ann. 383.] XV and XVI**, which concern the death of Saint Ascholius and the appointment of Anysius to his see, seem to belong to no other year than 383 [Col. 0855A].

Ascholius had attended the Roman synod held in the year 382, and Anysius was already succeeding him while Damasus, whose death is assigned to the year 384, was still alive. Accordingly, while Ascholius was returning to Thessalonica and Anysius was informing Ambrose of his death, the final months of 382 and the first months of 383 necessarily elapsed.

**[Ann. 384.] XVII and XVIII** were written against the *Report* of Symmachus. Their date can be discovered without difficulty. Since Symmachus, while Valentinian was still under the guardianship of his heretical mother and Gratian had been destroyed by the fraud and crime of Maximus, thought the opportunity especially favorable for restoring the worship of fictitious deities, he presented his *Report* to Valentinian.

Ambrose replied as soon as he was able—namely, in the very year 384, when he had returned to Italy from his first embassy to the tyrant Maximus and Symmachus was administering the prefecture of the City [Col. 0855B].

In this contest the pagan orator was so far inferior to the Christian that he obtained neither the restoration of the Altar of Victory nor that of the other ceremonies. Hence Ennodius aptly sang of this event:

> Victory takes the palm of eloquence from her friend:  
> She passes over to Ambrose; the goddess’s anger favors him more.

**[Ann. 385.] XIX** gives instructions concerning the episcopal office to Vigilius, who had been elevated to the bishopric of Trent a few months earlier.

According to his own acts, Vigilius presided over that Church for twenty years. His martyrdom is said to have occurred under the consulship of Stilicho, who, as we know, held that dignity in the years 400 and 405. Therefore the new bishop could have begun his episcopate only in the year 380 or 385.

Since the acts of the Council of Aquileia testify that Abundantius, his predecessor, was still alive in 380 and also in the following year, it is clear that this did not happen in 380; it remains, therefore, that it happened in 385.

We are not unaware that our Mabillon, in the Preface to the fifth century of the Benedictine history, stated that he had seen certain acts of this same Vigilius which attributed to him not twenty years of episcopate but only twelve. Yet the reason discouraging us from trusting these later acts is that, on this hypothesis, Vigilius’s episcopate would have had to begin in 388 or 393, and this letter would consequently belong to one of those later years [Col. 0855D].

Nevertheless, we recognize that it was written before Theodosius’s law prohibiting marriages between Jews and Christians, that is, before the year 388. For since the letter is chiefly concerned with such marriages, Ambrose—who could not have been ignorant of that law—would unquestionably have invoked its authority in this matter if it had already existed.

**[Ann. 385 and 386.] XX and XXI**, together with the Sermon appended to them, arose from the persecution which Ambrose suffered from the empress Justina and the other Arians.

It is agreed that the holy bishop was harassed at this time in such a way that, when the persecution had been quieted in the same year in which it began, it broke out again in the following year.

Baronius maintains that the first year of this persecution fell in the year 386 of the Christian era, when our saint first sent his pamphlet or Epistle XXI to Valentinian; and that in the immediately following year the Sermon *On the Basilicas* was delivered on Palm Sunday, with the letter to Marcellina written on the following day.

Yet it is not obscure that the matter was otherwise. When he delivered that Sermon, the basilica had already been surrounded by soldiers for many days, and Ambrose was being guarded there by the people day and night lest he be seized. On the contrary, the letter to Marcellina indicates that on that very Sunday he had returned to his own house to sleep, prepared to go into exile if ordered.

From this you may also learn that on the Friday and Saturday immediately preceding he had gone from his house to the church and from the church to his house with complete freedom [Col. 0856B].

Add to this the many matters mentioned in the Sermon but omitted from that letter: the law promulgated in favor of the Council of Ariminum, the order to come to the imperial court, and, when the holy bishop had refused to obey it, the order to leave Milan, as well as the hymns he composed.

Nor can it reasonably be objected that he communicated all these things to his sister in other letters. For even if, according to Baronius himself, Epistle XX and the sermon mentioned were not from the same year, in both he vehemently attacks that detestable law.

Finally, since a comparison of the two demonstrates that the letter and the sermon are contemporaneous, the very fact that the same Cardinal separated them shows how weak his opinion is [Col. 0856C].

Nor is it an easier matter to assign the year 387 of the Christian era to the later persecution. This storm raged chiefly around the Easter season; after it had subsided, Ambrose was sent as envoy to Maximus; another embassy then followed; and finally that same tyrant invaded Italy with an army, an event which some report to have taken place in August.

Scarcely anyone would believe that so short a period was sufficient for all these events. Moreover, Augustine, as determined by the calculations of the more learned, was reborn in the sacrament of the baptismal water during the Easter festivals of the year 387. He himself testifies that this did not happen in the year of so many and such great disturbances, but in the year immediately following [Col. 0856D].

What led Baronius and others into error was their belief that the law enacted in 386 on behalf of the Council of Ariminum had provided the occasion for harassing the Catholics.

We also know from Mabillon that, because the Gospel concerning Christ’s entry into Jerusalem was once read in many churches on the first Sunday of Advent, and the same custom still continues at Milan, it is possible to assign the two letters and the Sermon to that same year in such a way that the letter to the sister was written at Easter, while the other letter and the Sermon were moved to the following Advent.

But, to say nothing of the fact that the Gospel was read at that time not according to custom but by some accidental circumstance, Ambrose assigns two years to the persecution; and the law so frequently mentioned, which is brought forward against Baronius, also argues for this view [Col. 0857A].

We must therefore acknowledge that the wicked Justina raged during two distinct years. Nothing prevents us—indeed, everything persuades us—from believing that this persecution, whose source lay solely in the empress’s unchecked power, began already at the Easter festivals of the year 385.

The holy bishop informed his sister of it at the very beginning. When Justina was distressed that the persecution had produced no effect, she was stirred up by her customary hatred and arranged for a law to be enacted at the beginning of the following year in favor of the Council of Ariminum.

When even this course did not advance her cause sufficiently, she then wished Ambrose to be summoned so that he might engage in a contest with Auxentius at the palace [Col. 0857B]. But when the holy Teacher rejected this condition, that woman finally broke out into open violence and folly.

Thus, while Ambrose was being besieged in the basilica, he delivered the Sermon to the people. We did not wish to separate it from these letters, both because the sequence of events is more readily understood from their connection and because we have no doubt that Ambrose sent it to Marcellina, to whom he likewise sent two other sermons enclosed in the following letter.

**[Ann. 386.] XXII** is wholly occupied with composing a description of the discovery and translation of the bodies of the martyr brothers Gervasius and Protasius.

The Roman editors had unjustly removed the other of the Sermons which, as we stated above, are contained in this letter from its proper place [Col. 0857C]. We have restored it to that place by right of return.

Since this discovery brought the persecution to an end, Baronius assigns the letter to the year 387, whereas we assign it to 386.

The Roman Martyrology reports the translation of these bodies on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July. A Sermon by Augustine on the same subject, delivered on that day, also survives; hence some have convinced themselves that the sacred relics were transferred by Ambrose on that very day.

Nevertheless, the conclusion of the persecution—which they themselves assign to the Easter festivals—sufficiently teaches us that the celebration of the translation was postponed to another time on account of the Easter solemnities.

**XXIII** replies to certain bishops who had consulted Ambrose concerning the difficulty posed by Easter, which fell on the seventh day before the Kalends of May in the year 387 [Col. 0857D].

Bucherius assigns this letter to the year 381 after Christ because it testifies that two years earlier Easter Sunday had been celebrated on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, on which date it is agreed that the same feast occurred in the year 379.

But Bucherius is contradicted by the fact that Ambrose would not have been speaking about an Easter which would not return for six years when it was in fact going to occur in the immediate future; nor would those who consulted him have been troubled by such premature concern.

Add to this that in the letter which Bucherius himself claims was written in 381, the words “in times somewhat earlier,” which could refer only to the year 380, would sound absurd, whereas under our hypothesis they are properly understood of both that year and 383.

The year 386 must therefore be assigned to this letter [Col. 0858A]. An error must be recognized in the word “two years,” and its origin may be conjectured from the fact that, in the numeral VII written in these characters, the first character, V, was worn away, leaving only the two following figures, namely II.

François Balbus traces the origin of the error elsewhere, as will be seen in its proper place, where another paschal cycle will also have to be discussed.

**[Ann. 387.] XXIV** was written upon Ambrose’s return from the second embassy which he undertook to Maximus; he recounts its circumstances and sequence to the younger Valentinian.

The holy bishop had departed shortly after the disturbances which Justina had stirred up against him had been quieted. The same tyrant then followed him back into Italy with an army in the year 387 of the Christian era.

**XXV** replies to Studio, who was uncertain whether it was permissible to condemn anyone to capital punishment [Col. 0858B].

The whole question turned on the fact that there were certain clerics who deprived from communion those who ordered that a criminal be executed. Saint Ambrose acknowledges that the difficulty was increased by the fact that even among bishops there were some who pursued the punishment of criminals before secular judges.

Since he identifies the Ithacians—the authors of the execution of Priscillian, who was beheaded in the year 385—as the persons responsible for such punishment, but does not indicate that they had yet been expelled from the fellowship of the orthodox—a measure that was finally taken not long after the execution of Maximus, in the year 388—it necessarily follows that this letter was sent during the interval between the years 385 and 388.

[Col. 0858C] **XXVI** is a continuation of the preceding letter. In it he considers at greater length the Lord’s judgment concerning the adulterous woman, which above he had only touched upon. Hence it is known that both letters were sent at the same time and to the same person, although there is some variation in their inscriptions.

**XXVII** is shown to be the first, or at least one of the first, among all those addressed to Irenaeus by the words in which Ambrose says: “Do not be ashamed to question your father.”

We infer the year in which it was written from the fact that the persecution indicated by the words “he suffered for Christ” seems most conveniently understood as the persecution of Justina. We therefore think that it should be assigned either to this year, 387, or to the preceding year, 386 [Col. 0858D].

Indeed, the affinity and agreement between the matters treated in it and the subject of the second letter to Simplicianus are so great that each in a certain manner demonstrates and confirms the date of the other.

**XXVIII** is connected and joined quite neatly with the preceding letter. For after the preceding letter explained how we must flee the company and fellowship of the wicked, this one advances Irenaeus to a higher level, making clear that, as one enrolled in the service of the Church, he ought to surpass other Christians in holiness of life.

From this you may understand that this letter is only a short time later than the preceding one.

[Col. 0859A] **XXIX** gives Irenaeus instructions concerning still greater perfection. It shows that he ought to aspire to such perfect union with the highest Good that he would never return to lower things, which for this reason must be abandoned.

There is therefore no doubt that this letter followed the preceding two shortly afterward. The mournful death of Gratian, which is plainly indicated there, further confirms this.

**XXX** is concerned with explaining a passage from Haggai. Ambrose testifies that he wrote it immediately after sealing Epistle XXIX and handing it to the courier, as is shown by its opening words.

**XXXI, XXXII, and XXXIII** are linked together in the following manner.

When the holy bishop had answered the question posed to him by Irenaeus in Epistle XXXI, Irenaeus found in the words of Deuteronomy cited near its conclusion an occasion for proposing a new question. The saint answered him in the letter which ought to have been numbered XXXII.

But since, before he had received Irenaeus’s final letter, Ambrose had appended another letter to Epistle XXXI, the letter which ought to have been numbered XXXII was relegated to the position of XXXIII.

The Roman editors did make a change in the inscription of XXXII, but it will be explained more satisfactorily by notes added there.

To investigate the date of these letters, we should observe that in XXXIII the statement “Every saint is a firstborn” is discussed much more fully than in the book *On Cain and Abel*. Hence we conjecture that in *On the Blessing of the Patriarchs*, chapter 11, section 55, where the same argument is treated, readers are referred to this letter by the words “as we have shown elsewhere” [Col. 0859C].

It is very probable that Ambrose did not write letters of this kind with the intention that they should be read only by those to whom they were addressed in their inscriptions, but that they should also be shared with others.

If this conjecture is admitted, it will be necessary to regard this letter as earlier than that same book, which we believe was published around the year 387. Since the letter itself was not written until after XXVII, the first of the responses to Irenaeus, it follows that these letters must be assigned to the same period as the preceding ones.

In any event, what we have said here sufficiently demonstrates that Ambrose’s letter *To Apollinarius*, in which mention is made near the end of Jeremiah’s partridge, still survives, contrary to Hermann’s opinion.

**[Ann. 387.] XXXIV, XXXV, and XXXVI** reveal from their very first words how little time separates them from one another [Col. 0859D].

They answer the doubts of Horontianus. In the third, however, the holy bishop complains that opportunities for martyrdom had been taken away from him when he had almost reached the fulfillment of his desire.

Everyone can see that this cannot be referred more suitably to anything than to the cruel period of Justina’s persecution. Although it is not easy to determine whether these events had already occurred long before, the holy man speaks in terms that in a certain way more clearly indicate an opportunity close at hand.

**XXXVII and XXXVIII** were sent to Simplicianus, who succeeded Ambrose in the episcopate.

Both in the Life of Ambrose and in the *Ecclesiastical Annals* under the years 375 and 385, Baronius asserts that all Ambrose’s letters to Simplicianus were written by the holy bishop during the first years of his episcopate, as we shall explain in connection with Epistle LXV [Col. 0860A].

The principal reasons which draw us away here from the opinion of that most learned Cardinal are these:

1. It is understood from the very opening of Epistle XXXVIII that when Ambrose wrote it he was in the midst of the course of his sermons.

2. He undertakes to prove, as a deliberate thesis, that pagan philosophers borrowed many things from our sacred authors—not as though they were engaged in another task, but according to a definite plan. He treats this argument especially in the *Exposition of Psalm 118* and in the books *On the Patriarchs*.

It is therefore quite probable that all those commentaries directed against the proud and ignorant men who foolishly boasted that the sacred authors had drawn from profane sources—as Saint Augustine testifies—should be assigned to approximately the same period [Col. 0860B].

Finally, the kinship of this Epistle XXXVII with the book *On Jacob and the Blessed Life*, in its diction, its ideas, and its entire subject, is so great that everyone may easily assign them to the same period.

As for XXXVIII, since it is a continuation of the preceding letter, it is clear that no long interval elapsed between the two.

### XXXIX

This letter was intended for Faustinus, who was grieving the death of his sister beyond measure. To console him by the example of common calamities, it recalls the ruins of cities half destroyed. Although Baronius refers these destructions of cities to the invasion of Italy by the tyrant Maximus, he relies on the authority of Pacatus. Yet the passage of Pacatus which he seems to cite concerns not Italy but Gaul. Since, however, it is no less difficult to refer those same destructions of noble cities to the war against Eugenius than to that against Maximus, we do not depart from Baronius’s opinion, and, since nothing more probable presents itself, we think that this letter was written toward the end of the year 387.

### XL

*[Ann. 388 or 389.]*

This letter is entirely devoted to persuading Theodosius to revoke the edict ordering that a certain Jewish synagogue at Callinicum be rebuilt by the bishop, and that the monks who had burned a shrine of the Valentinian heretics, after being provoked by their insults, be punished. Gothofredus maintains that this letter refers to no other law than Law 4 *On the Jews*, enacted at Constantinople on 29 September 393, and therefore assigns the letter itself to that year. In support of his opinion, he might further have added that Ambrose mentions both the episcopal house previously burned at Constantinople and the pardon granted by Theodosius to the people of Antioch.

Nevertheless, Paulinus’s authority is more persuasive to us in all these matters, since he was an eyewitness to the affairs of his teacher. Here he expressly states that the letter was written after Maximus had been destroyed and Theodosius had established himself at Milan, while Ambrose was bishop at Aquileia. And in fact Ambrose speaks at length there of Maximus, sufficiently indicating by the manner in which he discusses him that Maximus had not long before been defeated by Theodosius’s arms. It follows that the law which occasioned this letter was issued not at Constantinople but at Milan, and was therefore entirely different from the one proposed by that same Gothofredus.

As for the pardon granted to the people of Antioch, Sozomen, in Book VII, chapter 23, assigns it to the time when Theodosius was preparing to make war on the tyrant Eugenius; but everyone acknowledges that he is mistaken on this point. As for the episcopal house at Constantinople that was burned—the event which Socrates says occurred in 388—it certainly does not prevent the adverb “some time ago” from being properly used in a letter of that same year, as we shall demonstrate in its proper place.

We must therefore conclude that this letter was written when the emperor, after overthrowing Maximus, returned to Milan. Now, from the Theodosian Code it is understood that on 20 September 388 he had not yet departed from Aquileia, whereas by 10 October of the same month he had already arrived at Milan, where he remained until May of the following year. From this it is clear that, during this very interval, the holy Bishop, who had gone to Aquileia on his own business, wrote to Theodosius about the revocation of the aforementioned edict.

### XLI

Ambrose wrote this letter so that his sister might learn how the case of the bishops and monks, discussed in the preceding letter, had reached a favorable conclusion. He also appended to it the speech which, after returning to Milan, he delivered before Theodosius on the same matter. No one, therefore, can deny that this letter followed the preceding one after only a short interval. There is no reason to doubt that, as soon as he was able, Ambrose returned to his see in order to bar access to those who might deceive the emperor’s religious conscience, and to obtain in person the outcome he so earnestly desired.

### XLII

This is a reply to Siricius. When the heresy of Jovinian had openly broken out at Rome, that pope held a council of the Roman clergy and subjected its author and adherents to the penalty of anathema. He then wrote a synodal letter to the Milanese so that the same heretic—whom he knew to have fled from a monastery situated not far from the walls of Milan and governed under Ambrose’s supervision—might be suffocated in that city like a snake in its own lair.

After receiving Siricius’s letter, Ambrose arranged for the same heresy to be condemned at a synod convened at Milan, and, in the name of the bishops present, reported this to the pope, while at the same time refuting the heresy with powerful arguments.

We can determine the date of this letter from these words of his: “the impiety of the Manichaeans, which the most merciful emperor has abhorred.” Gothofredus refers these words to Law 20 *On Heretics*, promulgated in 391. Since, however, that law contains no mention of the Manichaeans, we think with Baronius that they allude to Law 18 *On Heretics*. Since this latter law is reported to have been enacted on 27 June 389, we do not think it inappropriate to assign the council and the letter to that year, or rather to 390.

### XLIII and XLIV

*[Ann. 389.]*

These letters are addressed to Horontianus. After reading the *Hexaemeron*, he had written to Ambrose because he had not found it sufficiently explained there why man, the last of all created things, had been created by God, and he asked Ambrose to clarify the matter for him. After the holy Bishop had answered his first questions, Horontianus again proposed another difficulty that had arisen from reading the same work. Ambrose resolved this one as well; these two letters consist of those responses.

It is therefore certain that both letters are later than the *Hexaemeron*, that is, later than the year 389, around which time we have shown that the work was published. It is likewise demonstrated that they followed it after no long interval: since Horontianus was bound by the closest relationship to Ambrose, by whose hands he had been ordained deacon or priest, there can be no doubt that, as soon as the *Hexaemeron* was published, he received and read it from him.

### XLV

This letter begins the series of those said to have been written to Sabinus. That Sabinus was the bishop of Piacenza who signed the Council of Aquileia; a certain miracle of his is related in Book V, chapter 10, of the *Dialogues* of Saint Gregory, and his name is commemorated in the Roman Martyrology on 11 December.

The reading of the *Hexaemeron* had likewise raised a difficulty for him, because nothing was discussed there about paradise. When Ambrose learned of this doubt from Sabinus’s letter, he explained that he had passed over that subject because he had already treated the same topic several years earlier. Hence it may be understood that this letter followed the book *On Paradise* by several years, but followed the book *Hexaemeron* only after a short interval.

### XLVI and XLVII

These too are said to have been sent to Sabinus. The first was occasioned by some Apollinarian who had traveled through lands and seas in order to spread his heresy. When he came to Milan, he began to criticize certain points in Ambrose’s books; in this letter the holy Teacher announces that he had publicly refuted him.

In the following letter, after briefly mentioning the book which he had arranged to have sent to Sabinus, written more distinctly than the earlier one, Ambrose discusses at length the usefulness of an exchange of letters in which something from Scripture is chiefly examined. Since it is altogether probable that the works of Ambrose which that Apollinarian dared to attack, and which Ambrose says he had sent in a more carefully written copy, are the same as the books *On the Faith* and *On the Incarnation of the Lord*, and since he also speaks of himself as already an old man, we do not think that either letter can more suitably be assigned to another year than to 389 or thereabouts.

### XLVIII

This letter is connected with the preceding ones both in subject and in date. For we believe that the booklets which Ambrose here says were returned to him are the same ones said above to have been sent to Sabinus. This may also be inferred from the fact that the blessed Bishop does not omit, in this letter either, to mention his advanced age.

### XLIX

This letter likewise depends on the preceding one. Since our Ambrose frequently declares there that he will devote himself more diligently to letters, especially to those in which something from the sacred books is examined, he surely fulfills that promise in this letter, which is almost entirely concerned with divine teachings. No one, therefore, will deny that it ought not to be detached from the others.

### L

This letter was granted to the prayers of Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia, who had begged Ambrose to send him, by way of friendly correspondence, some discussion drawn from the sacred books. To satisfy his wishes, our Saint chose as his subject the prophecy of Balaam. We have therefore placed this letter in the series of the preceding ones because it too contains a mention of his old age.

### LI

*[Ann. 390.]*

This letter was sent to the emperor Theodosius when he was coming to Milan after the massacre at Thessalonica, in order that Ambrose might explain why he had not awaited the emperor’s arrival. It is universally acknowledged that the massacre occurred in the year 390.

### LII

*[Ann. 392.]*

This letter reveals that it was sent at the time when Rufinus was made consul and prefect of the praetorium after having been master of the offices. Since there is no doubt that he attained these offices in 392, it follows that this letter was delivered to Titianus in that same year.

### LIII

This letter affectionately mourns the premature and grievous death of the younger Valentinian, and Ambrose also appeals to Theodosius to hasten his burial. It is certain that this same Valentinian died on 15 May 392; hence we understand that the letter was sent not long afterward.

### LIV and LV

These letters were addressed to Eusebius, who was the head of a noble Bolognese family. One concerns a certain attendant and the cough of the boy Faustinus; in the other, our Ambrose cleverly announces that the same boy, together with his father Faustinus, had gone to him at Bologna, while Ambrose and Ambrosia had remained with him at Milan.

Since he calls this Ambrosia a “spiritual dove” for no other reason than that he had consecrated her with the virginal veil, as is noted in the book *On the Institution of the Virgin*, it follows that these letters are later than that book, which we assign to the year 392.

### LVI

This letter is a reply to Theophilus of Alexandria. The subject of the writing was the Antiochene schism, about which more will be said in connection with Ambrose’s letter. Meanwhile, it should be observed that Flavian is censured in it for having fortified himself against the authority of the Council of Capua by rescripts obtained from Theodosius, who had then returned to the East.

After spending nearly three years in Italy, the emperor did not return to Constantinople until 26 November 391. The synod, therefore, must have been held between that date and 15 May of the following year, the day on which we have said that Valentinian was killed. After that time episcopal assemblies could no longer be held in Italy because of the wars provoked by the tyrant Eugenius.

When the synod ended, the Fathers of Capua informed Theophilus of what had been decided there concerning the aforementioned dispute. Later, when Theophilus sent a letter to Ambrose for the same reason, he elicited from the holy man the letter under discussion here. Who, then, can deny that it could scarcely have been written before the end of 392?

We have placed after the preceding letter another one concerning the case brought against the Bonosian heresy. The entire matter had already been treated at the Council of Capua, which we have just mentioned, and its examination had been entrusted to the bishops neighboring that heretic, so that they might investigate it more promptly and carefully.

When those bishops consulted the author of this letter and appeared to entrust the judgment to him, he replied that the matter belonged not to him but to them, since the council had assigned it to them. At the same time he powerfully refuted the Bonosian error concerning the perpetual virginity of the Mother of God.

These facts clearly show that this letter was contemporary with the preceding one and that, in the Roman edition, it was wrongly detached from it—not only because of this chronological connection but also because it forms a second part of the Council of Capua. It is more difficult to determine to which author this letter should be attributed. There are substantial arguments on both sides, which we shall examine in their proper place.

### LVII

*[Ann. 393.]*

This letter explains to the tyrant Eugenius why Ambrose had withdrawn from Milan when Eugenius approached it. It is exceedingly probable that this tyrant did not attack Italy immediately after Valentinian was killed on 15 May and Arbogast placed Eugenius on the throne, but that he had first completed certain other campaigns.

We learn this both from Paulinus in the *Life of Ambrose* and from Severus Alexander in Gregory of Tours, *History*, Book II, chapter 9, as well as from this very letter, in which Ambrose testifies that Eugenius had written to him at the beginning of his reign and that Ambrose later wrote to him whenever some necessity arose.

Led by these considerations, we think that the tyrant’s invasion occurred no earlier than the end of 392, or rather the beginning of 393, and therefore assign this letter to that period.

### LVIII

This letter concerns a subject of great renown. Nothing at that time was more illustrious than Paulinus’s renunciation and withdrawal from his ancestral and personal honors. Yet the letter was not written after he had already withdrawn to Nola—that is, in 394—as Baronius seems to have thought.

For, apart from the fact that the letters of Paulinus himself to Alypius and Augustine, as well as the letters of both men to Paulinus, fairly clearly suggest that he came to Nola in 393, this very letter sufficiently indicates that, when Ambrose wrote it, he had never yet seen Paulinus. He saw him afterward at Florence, when he was traveling to Rome and was about to return from there to Nola.

Moreover, during the first years Paulinus spent at Barcelona, he did not publish and sell all his possessions at once, but gradually disposed of them in several stages. Therefore, since Ambrose testifies that after all those possessions had been sold Paulinus had by then become poor, we think that, when our Saint wrote these words, Paulinus was already preparing for his journey. Hence it is clear that this letter cannot more suitably be assigned than either to the final months of 392 or the beginning of 393.

### LIX

This letter deserves notice because it makes clear in what year of Ambrose’s life it was sent. The holy Bishop expressly states that he had completed his fifty-third year when he wrote it.

Yet the words presented somewhat earlier cause far more difficulty. They read as follows: “Exposed to barbarian disturbances and the storms of war, we are in the midst of the straits of war.” Baronius, in the *Life of Ambrose* and in his *Annals*, Ughellus in *Sacred Italy*, and the Bollandists in the *Acts of this holy man Severus*, refer this passage to the wars of the tyrant Maximus. From this they infer both that this letter must be assigned to the year 387 and that Ambrose’s fifty-third year coincided with that date.

They further add that, since the holy Bishop extended his life to April 387, he had completed sixty-four years. They think that their opinion is strongly supported by the fact that far more blood was shed in the war against Maximus than in that against Eugenius.

But their reasoning proves nothing. In the letter under discussion, barbarian disturbances and the storms of war are mentioned; no one can establish from this that the wars in question were more savage than others. Hermann prefers to understand the passage of Ambrose as having been written about the war against Eugenius, and argues that this accords better with the history of Ambrose’s life, which he denies extended beyond his fifty-seventh year.

This, however, is not entirely clear. We must therefore acknowledge that, whether the words are applied to the war of Eugenius or to that of Maximus, the result is the same. One point may perhaps favor Baronius’s opinion more: in several passages of the preceding letters Ambrose repeatedly mentions his old age, something less appropriate to a man whose life ended at fifty-seven than to one who lived to sixty-four.

Nevertheless, we know that Basil and certain other saints also had the habit of speaking of themselves as already old, even though they died at a less advanced age. We therefore wish to leave the judgment of the matter to the reader. We do point out, however, that this difference changes nothing in the years of Ambrose’s episcopate, but only in the events before his episcopate; even so, Baronius seems to extend those events too far.

### LX

This letter warns Paternus not to marry his son to his daughter’s granddaughter—that is, an uncle not to marry his sister’s daughter. In dissuading him, our Ambrose relies chiefly on the arguments that such a marriage is contrary to the divine laws and is prohibited by a constitution of Theodosius, from whom, he says, Paternus had received the highest honor.

Since these words cannot be more suitably applied than to the office of *comes sacrarum largitionum*, which Paternus is known from many letters of Symmachus to have held, and since Law 14 *On Metals* indicates that he administered that office in 393, these considerations persuade us to assign this letter also to the year 393.

As for the prohibition of Theodosius mentioned above, it has not survived to our time, but it is mentioned elsewhere, as we shall explain in its proper place.

### LXI

*[Ann. 394.]*

This is a reply to Theodosius, from whom the holy man had received a letter concerning the thanksgiving which was to be rendered to God for the tyrant Eugenius’s defeat, achieved not without a miracle. Ambrose therefore informs the emperor of what he himself had done in carrying out the emperor’s requests.

The letter thus speaks for itself: it was sent in no other year than 394, since that tyrant suffered punishment in September of that very year.

### LXII

This letter was written to the same prince, at the same time, and on a similar subject. In it Ambrose asks the emperor to pardon those who, after following the tyrant, had fled into the churches after his death in order to avoid punishment for their crime.

### LXIII

*[Ann. 396.]*

This letter occupies the final place in our first class. The reason for writing it was as follows. After the death of Limenius—not, as some think, of Eusebius, whom Jerome states in his *Chronicle* and in *On Ecclesiastical Writers* to have ceased living in 371—the diocese of Vercelli was left without a bishop.

Our Ambrose wished to cut off the source of so great an evil, namely, the dissensions of the clergy and people, and therefore sent this letter to them. It is beyond doubt that it is later than the Council of Aquileia of 381, which Limenius himself signed. But it must be assigned to no year other than 396 by anyone unwilling to reject the testimony of the *Acts of Gaudentius of Novara*, which Mombritius and Bollandus assign to 22 January.

For in those Acts we read that, a few months before his death, Ambrose went to Vercelli to settle a certain dispute. We shall understand this journey most conveniently if we say that, when his letters had achieved little with stubborn minds, the holy Bishop went there in person at last to overcome their obstinacy.

Those who think that this letter is spurious because it mentions Venetia fail to observe that the same word is used both by other writers of the same period and by Ambrose himself in certain works—see Letter 18, section 21.

With greater plausibility, perhaps, they might argue that large fragments from other works of our Teacher were transferred and inserted into this letter; we shall identify those passages individually in their proper places. Yet this is not contrary to Ambrose’s custom. Even if he nowhere else used this practice, it would nevertheless not be surprising if he again assembled and sharpened against Sarmatio and Barbatianus, the fiercest enemies of these virtues, what he had already discussed elsewhere with diligence concerning continence, fasting, and vigils.

In any case, whatever is said about these heretics clearly confirms the date of this letter; its diction, character, and subject matter most powerfully assert Ambrose as its true author.

## SECOND CLASS

In the *Admonition* we indicated that the second class of letters would be divided into three groups: letters composed either to explain the Scriptures, or dealing with some serious subject, or containing merely expressions of familiar courtesy and obligation.

The first series consists altogether of thirteen letters. It should be noted that the one placed at the head of the others and entitled “To Irenaeus” could appropriately have been placed after Letter XXVII. Both letters were written to the same Irenaeus and concern passages from the same book of Exodus.

Likewise, Letters LXX and LXXI, sent to Horontianus and explaining both the return of the soul fallen into sin to good conduct and virtue and its various advances along the path of virtue, could have been joined to Letter XXXIV, in which the spirituality of that same soul is discussed with the same Horontianus—if we had considered such an affinity by itself sufficient evidence for establishing their date.

Letter LXXI, addressed to Constantius, resolves various difficulties raised by pagans and heretics concerning the institution and abolition of circumcision. Since three Constantiuses are found at that time, all honored with episcopal dignity—one of Orange, one of Siscia, and another of uncertain see, as we shall observe in the *Acts of the Council of Aquileia*—it cannot easily be determined to which of them, or indeed whether to any of them at all, the letter was sent.

We nevertheless lean more willingly toward the view that it was written to the same man to whom the second letter of this edition was sent. Since this Constantius, as we have seen, consulted the holy Teacher as a father concerning the ordering of his life and the administration of his office, it is likely that, whenever another difficulty arose, he would not have hesitated to lay it before Ambrose.

This letter could not seem to be placed more suitably elsewhere than here, since it may be referred partly to the ancient covenant, in which circumcision was instituted, and partly to the new covenant, in which it was abolished.

Finally, Letters LXXIV and LXXV bear various inscriptions at their head, as will be more conveniently explained elsewhere.
