We shall say only this here: as far as may be inferred from their style, these two letters were sent at the very beginning of Ambrose’s episcopate, when the holy Bishop was especially occupied with reading the works of Origen.

The second series of this class contains only eight letters, but all were elaborated on great matters and in a serious style. In them Ambrose sometimes shows the dignity of the new covenant to surpass that of the old; sometimes he earnestly urges the prompt administration of the sacraments of baptism. Elsewhere he strengthens clergy who are losing heart in their duty; elsewhere he makes clear, by word and example alike, how the peace of households should be safeguarded. Finally, he does not allow holy and just actions and deliberations to be deprived of their due praise.

Since nothing occurs in these letters that cannot be explained more appropriately in the notes attached to them, we shall say no more about them here.

The third series yields to the others both in the small number and brevity of its letters, though not in seriousness. It contains only seven short letters written in a familiar style to some friends; nevertheless, they display not only the Saint’s courtesy but also a pleasantness expressed in honorable humor.

## NEW ORDER OF THE LETTERS OF SAINT AMBROSE COMPARED WITH THOSE PREVIOUSLY PUBLISHED

[In this index, as in what follows, the Arabic numerals designating the columns of the new edition correspond to the numbers which we have printed in heavier type within the text.]

Four have been relegated to the appendix, and one omitted.

## ORDER OF THE ROMAN EDITION COMPARED WITH THE OLDER EDITIONS AND THIS NEW EDITION

# LETTERS OF SAINT AMBROSE, BISHOP OF MILAN, DIVIDED INTO TWO CLASSES

The first contains those which it was possible to arrange in chronological order; the second embraces the remaining letters, distinguished according to their subject matter.

## FIRST CLASS

### 751. LETTER OF GRATIAN TO AMBROSE

*[Written in the year 379.]*

He invites Ambrose to come to him so that he may be strengthened in the faith concerning the divinity of the Son and the Holy Spirit. He also requests a book, and asks that another on the Holy Spirit be joined to it.

**Gratian Augustus to Ambrose, the religious priest of almighty God**

#### 1

*[Some manuscripts read: “I greatly desire the one whom I remember absent, so that, when [lacuna], I may be present in body.”]*

I greatly desire to be bodily present with the one whom I remember as absent and with whom I am present in mind. Therefore hasten to me, religious priest of God, so that you may teach me the truly believing doctrine. *[Some manuscripts and earlier editions: some read *doctrinam veram credentem* (“the true doctrine believing”); others, like our text, read *doctrinam vere credentem* (“the doctrine truly believing”).]*

I do not seek controversy, nor do I wish to embrace God more with words than with the mind; but I wish that the revelation of the divinity may settle more deeply in a heart that has been opened more fully. *[A few manuscripts read: “that the revelation of the divinity may enter a breast laid open.”]*

#### 2

For he will teach me—the one whom I do not deny, whom I confess to be my God and Lord—not charging him with the created nature which I see in myself, since I confess that I can add nothing of myself to Christ. *[That is, he does not turn against Christ’s divinity the fact that he believes that Christ assumed his own human nature.]*

Yet I wish also to commend myself to the Father by proclaiming the Son. *[Some manuscripts read: “yet I would wish . . . to commend myself.”]*

I shall not fear envy in God; I shall not think myself such a praiser as could increase the divinity by words. I, weak and fragile, proclaim as much as I can—not as much as the divinity itself is.

#### 3

I ask you to give me the treatise which you had given me, adding there a faithful discussion of the Holy Spirit. *[He means the first two books of *On the Faith*, as was explained in the *Admonition* to those books and in the preface to the work *On the Holy Spirit*. Some manuscripts read: “so that you may treat the subject itself.”]*

Convince me by the Scriptures and by arguments that he is God. May the Divinity preserve you for many years, father and worshiper of the eternal God whom we worship, Jesus Christ.

## LETTER ONE

*[Written in the year 379.]*

Ambrose excuses himself to the Caesar for not having come. After praising the emperor’s humility, faith, and piety, he writes that he is sending the requested books and promises to satisfy his wishes by composing treatises on the Holy Spirit.

**To the most blessed Augustus Gratian, and the most Christian prince, Ambrose, bishop**

*[Ambrose indicates that it was not customary to give emperors the title “most Christian.” At the beginning of the letter, when he again addresses Gratian by that title, he immediately adds the reason: “For I have nothing . . .” Yet he was rightly called most Christian, since he had remained untouched by the Arian plague, which had infected his uncle Valens, his stepmother Justina, and other rulers, and since he demanded with such ardor to be instructed in the true faith, whose most zealous champion he always was. In the same way Ambrose calls Valentinian “most Christian” in the heading of his first letter against Symmachus, thereby indicating that this title bound him to defend the Christian faith.]*

#### 1

I was not lacking in affection, most Christian of princes—for I have nothing more truthful or glorious to say than this. I say, then, that I was not lacking in affection, but that modesty held back my affection and prevented me from going to meet your Clemency.

*[Understand this as referring to Gratian’s return from the East to Germany; see what we have observed in the *Admonition* to the books *On the Faith*.]*

Yet although I did not meet you in person upon your return, I met you in spirit and in prayer, in which the duties of a priest are greater. “I met you,” I say? When, indeed, was I absent from one whom I followed with my whole affection, to whom I was attached in mind and heart? And certainly the presence of souls is the greater.

I read the course of your daily journey. Night and day I was stationed in your camp in care and thought, standing guard with the sentinels of prayer; and although weak in merit, I was diligent in affection.

### 2

And indeed, when we were conveying these things for your safety, we were acting on our own behalf. There is no flattery here—flattery is something you do not seek, and I regard it as alien to our office—but there is an abundance of gratitude, which you have bestowed. He himself knows, the Judge of our affairs whom you acknowledge and in whom you devoutly believe, that my inmost being is renewed by your faith, your safety, and your glory; and that I offer not only the prayers due from me in my public office, but also those prompted by private affection.

[Note: From this passage it may reasonably be inferred that public prayers for emperors departing on campaign were customarily offered at the command of bishops. Baronius, under the year 379, persuades himself that this demonstrates Ambrose was not the only one who commended Gratian’s arms to God in public prayers, because in Ausonius’s speech on his consulship, delivered in that year to the same emperor, we read: “The forum and basilica, once full of business, are now full of vows and vows undertaken for your safety; for under your rule, who is not secure?” But the great Cardinal has not sufficiently noticed that Ausonius’s word *basilica* is not used here for a sacred building, in the sense in which it frequently occurs in Jerome, our Ambrose, and other ecclesiastical writers, but for some spacious place where councils and trials, banquets, games, and similar activities took place, as Cicero and others use the word. This is clear not only because Ausonius joins it with the forum, but also because he speaks of both together as formerly “full of business.” The added statement that public security rests upon the emperor’s safety agrees beautifully with those words of Ambrose above: “And indeed, when we were conveying these things for your safety,” and so forth.]

For you restored peace to me in the Church, and closed the mouths—and, would that you had closed the hearts as well—of the faithless; and you did this with no less authority of faith than of power.

[Note: We have no doubt that this refers to certain vexations which the holy Bishop suffered, at the very beginning of his episcopate, from the supporters of Auxentius. Certainly, in Book I of *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 1, mention is made of a certain basilica which Gratian later restored to the Catholics, after it had first been taken from them, doubtless through Justina’s prayers and influence. But these events belong after the date of this letter.]

### 3

For what shall I say of your recent letter? You wrote the entire letter with your own hand, so that the very letters themselves might speak of your faith and piety. Thus Abraham once slaughtered a calf with his own hands (Gen. XVIII, 7) in order to serve it to his guests at table; nor did he seek the assistance of others in that religious service. But he, a private man, was paying homage either to the Lord and the angels, or to the Lord in the angels; while you, Emperor, honor a lowly priest by your royal condescension. Yet the honor is offered to the Lord when a humble servant is honored; for he himself said: “Whatever you did for one of these least ones, you did for me” (Matt. XXV, 10).

### 4

But I merely praise in an emperor that humility which is exalted; and I do not attribute to you a faith greater than what you declared with a mind truly conscious of your merit, a faith taught you by him whom you do not deny. For who else could have taught you not to reproach him for possessing the creature which you see in yourself? Nothing more morally appropriate, nothing more explicit, could have been said. To call Christ a creature is an insult, not a confession of reverence. Furthermore, what could be more insolent than to regard him as being what we are? Thus you have taught me, though you profess that you wish to learn from me: I have never yet read or heard anything like this.

### 5

How pious, how admirable, is the fact that you do not fear envy in God! You presume a reward from the Father for your love of the Son, and, in praising the Son, you confess that you cannot add anything to him; rather, you wish also to commend yourself to the Father through your proclamation of the Son. He alone, surely, taught you this, who said: “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father” (John XIV, 21).

### 6

To this you added that, since you are weak and frail, you did not regard yourself as such a praiser that you could increase divinity by your words; rather, you proclaimed as much as you were able, not as much as divinity itself is. This weakness is stronger in Christ, as the Apostle also said: “When I am weak, then I am strong” (II Cor. XII, 10). This humility excludes frailty.

### 7

[Note: Someone may ask whether Ambrose really went to Gratian. Baronius, under the year 379, thinks that this happened. Nor does the view seem entirely incredible, since Ambrose so explicitly promised this journey and Gratian anticipated him with such gracious courtesy. Nevertheless, we consider the contrary opinion more probable, both for other reasons and because he did not personally bring the books requested of him to Gratian, but sent them; and also because we find that in August of this same year the emperor was back at Milan.]

I shall certainly come, and I shall hasten, as you command, so that I may hear these things in person and read them in person when they proceed from your mouth. I have also sent two little books; and since they have already been approved by your clemency, I shall fear no danger. As for the work *On the Spirit*, however, I meanwhile ask pardon for my writing, since I have learned what sort of judge I am to have for my discourse.

### 8

Meanwhile, your judgment and faith concerning the Lord and Savior, drawn from your confession concerning the Son of God, overflow into a most abundant defense by which the eternal divinity of the Holy Spirit also comes to be believed. Thus you do not reproach him with possessing the creature which you see in yourself, nor do you suppose that God the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ envies his own Spirit. Whatever has no communion with a creature is divine.

[Col. 0879A]

### 9

If the Lord is favorable, I shall also satisfy the desire of your clemency, so that you may esteem him whose grace you have received as plainly worthy, in his own name, of preeminence in the glory of God.

### 10

May God Almighty, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, deign to preserve you, most blessed and flourishing, through a long life; to establish your kingdom in the highest glory and in perpetual peace; august lord Emperor, chosen by divine judgment, most glorious of princes.

[Note: The words “chosen by divine judgment,” which were lacking in the edition based on the Milan manuscript, have been restored. They signify that princes are established even in hereditary succession not without divine judgment. But they also seem to indicate the extraordinary election of the nine-year-old Gratian, which Ammianus describes in Book XXVII: how it was carried out by his father Valentinian with the common consent of the army.]

## LETTER II

He advises Constantius, recently elected bishop, to govern the Church upon the sea and among the rivers, explaining what each signifies. He urges him to gather the waters with which he may irrigate the minds of the people; and, after teaching what sort of discourses he should deliver and what virtues he ought to command, he treats of the balance by which speech is to be weighed. In order to show the usefulness of humility, he adduces the example of blessed Joseph. Having demonstrated the vanity of present things through the histories of Joseph and David, he instructs him to encourage the people to acquire true riches for themselves. Finally, commending to him the Church of Forum Cornelii, he adds something about prudence toward heretics, justice toward neighbors, and humanity toward servants.

[Note: Thus read the old edition and the manuscripts, except for the single manuscript Longipontanus, where “Ambrose to Constantine” is written. We also learn that another manuscript has the same inscription because Ughellus, in volume II of *Italia Sacra*, p. 633, quoting a passage from this letter, calls it “to the Emperor Constantine.” But this is a gross error, since at that time there could have been no Emperor Constantine, and the fact that the person to whom this letter was sent was a bishop is declared even by its opening words: “You have undertaken the office of the priesthood,” and so forth. The Roman editors would therefore not have been wrong to prefix “Ambrose the bishop to Constantius his brother” as the heading, unless they had designated him in the summary of the letter as bishop of Arausio. We shall discuss this below.]

### AMBROSE TO CONSTANTIUS

### 1

You have undertaken the office of the priesthood, and, sitting in the Church’s ship, you steer the vessel against the waves. Hold the rudder of faith, so that the storms of this age may not be able to disturb you. The sea is indeed great and spacious, but do not be afraid, because he himself founded her upon the seas and prepared her upon the rivers (Ps. XXIII, 2). Therefore, not without reason, amid so many straits of the world, the Church of the Lord, built as it were upon the apostolic rock, remains immovable and endures upon an unshaken foundation the assaults of the raging brine (Matt. XVI, 18). She is washed by the waves, but not shaken; and although the elements of this world frequently strike against her with a great crash and rebound, she nevertheless has a most secure harbor of salvation in which to receive those who labor.

### 2

Yet although she is tossed upon the sea, she runs among rivers. See whether she does not rather run in those rivers of which it is said: “The rivers have lifted up their voice” (Ps. XCII, 3). For there are rivers which will flow from the belly of the one who has received drink from Christ and has drawn from the Spirit of God (John VII, 38). These rivers, therefore, when they overflow with spiritual grace, lift up their voice. There is also a river which flows down upon his saints like a torrent (Isa. LXVI, 12). There is also the rushing of a river which makes glad the peaceful and tranquil soul (Ps. XLV, 5). Whoever receives from the fullness of this river, like John the Evangelist, like Peter and Paul, lifts up his voice; and just as the apostles spread the voice of evangelical preaching throughout the whole world’s boundaries with resonant proclamation, so this man too begins to proclaim the Lord Jesus. Receive, therefore, from Christ, so that your sound may also go forth.

### 3

The sea is divine Scripture, containing profound meanings and the depth of prophetic mysteries; into this sea many rivers have flowed. Thus there are sweet and clear rivers, and there are snowy springs which leap up into eternal life (John IV, 14); there are also good words, like honeycombs (Prov. XVI, 24), and gracious sayings which irrigate the minds of their hearers with a kind of spiritual drink and soothe them with the sweetness of moral instruction. The streams of the divine Scriptures are therefore various. You have what you may drink first, what you may drink second, and what you may drink last.

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads “living springs.” This is not inappropriate, unless the agreement of the other editions and manuscripts should prevail. The springs should therefore be understood as “snowy,” not as gathered from snow, but as cold; or certainly as pure and bright, as is said immediately before of the rivers.]

### 4

Gather Christ’s water, the water that praises the Lord (Ps. CXLVIII, 5). Gather water from many places, the water poured out by the prophetic clouds (Eccl. XI, 3). Whoever gathers water from the mountains and draws it toward himself, or draws it from the springs, himself also sprinkles like a cloud.

[Note: Some editions and manuscripts read “and he himself waters,” as the clouds do.]

Therefore fill the bosom of your mind, so that your land may grow moist and be irrigated by domestic springs. Whoever reads and understands much is filled; whoever has been filled irrigates others. Hence Scripture says: “When the clouds are filled, they will pour out rain upon the earth” (ibid.).

### 5

Let your discourses therefore flow freely; let them be pure and lucid, so that by moral discussion you may pour sweetness into the ears of the people and charm the congregation with the grace of your words, so that it may follow willingly wherever you lead. But if there is any obstinacy or fault either in the people or in certain individuals, let your discourses be such as to prick the hearer and pierce the conscience of one who knows himself to be guilty: “The words of the wise are like goads” (Eccl. XII, 11). The Lord Jesus also goaded Saul when he was a persecutor. Consider how salutary that goad was: it made an apostle from a persecutor, when he said: “It is hard for you to kick against the goad” (Acts IX, 5).

### 6

There are also discourses like milk, which Paul poured into the Corinthians (I Cor. III, 2); for those who cannot partake of stronger food exercise the infancy of their understanding with the nourishment of milk.

### 7

May your addresses be full of understanding. Hence Solomon also says: “The lips of the wise are weapons of understanding” (Prov. XIV, 3); and elsewhere: “Let your lips be bound with understanding” (Prov. XV, 5).

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “Let them be bound to understanding.”]

That is, may the expression of your discourses shine forth, may understanding flash, and may your address and exposition require no external assertion; rather, may your discourse defend itself with its own weapons, and may no word of yours go forth in vain or emerge without meaning. For there is a bandage which ordinarily binds up the wounds of the soul; whoever rejects it reveals that his own salvation is hopeless (Isa. I, 6). Therefore, toward those who are afflicted by a serious ulcer, use the oil of speech with which to soothe the hardness of their minds; apply a poultice, add the bandage of a saving commandment, so that you may not allow those who wander and fluctuate concerning the faith or the observance of discipline to perish with a spirit relaxed and a vigor slackened.

### 8

Therefore admonish the Lord’s people, and entreat them to abound in good works, to renounce their vices, and not to kindle the conflagrations of flames—not, I say, on the Sabbath, but at any time—lest they burn their own body. Let there be no fornication or impurity among God’s servants, because we serve the immaculate Son of God (Eph. V, 3). Let each person know himself and possess his own vessel (I Thess. IV, 4), so that, having subdued the soil of his own body, he may await its proper fruits, and his land may not produce thorns and thistles (Gen. III, 18), but that he himself may say: “The earth has yielded its fruit” (Ps. LXXXIV, 13); and that, amid this formerly thorny fragility of the passions, grafted virtues may burst into flower.

[Note: Most manuscripts read: “But let the earth itself say,” and so forth.]

### 9

Teach and instruct them also to do what is good, and let each person not interrupt a praiseworthy work, whether it is seen by many or done without a witness; for a wealthy conscience is sufficient witness to itself.

### 10

Let him also flee evil and reproach.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “evil things and reproaches.”]

Even if he believes that he cannot be convicted. For even if he is shut in by walls and covered by darkness, without a witness and without anyone who knows, he nevertheless has the judge of his deed, one whom nothing deceives and to whom all deeds cry out. In the end, the voice of blood also cried out (Gen. IV, 10).

[Note: The editions read: “Each person has himself.”]

Each person has himself and his own soul as a severe judge of himself, an avenger of wickedness, and a vindicator against crime. Thus Cain wandered about in fear and trembling (ibid., 14), paying the penalty for his parricidal deed; so that his death became a remedy for him, since through death it freed him from the terror of death which he feared at every moment as a wandering exile. Let no one, therefore, whether alone or with another, do anything shameful or dishonorable. And if anyone is alone, let him be ashamed before himself above all others, since he ought especially to fear himself.

### 11

Let no one covet many things, because even a few things are many to him; for poverty and riches are names for want and satiety. He is not rich who lacks anything, nor poor who lacks nothing. Let no one despise a widow, defraud an orphan, or cheat his neighbor. For woe to him who has wealth gathered by deceit and builds a city upon blood (Hab. II, 6)—that is, his own soul!

For the soul is what is built like a city (Ps. CXXI, 3). Avarice does not build this city but destroys it; lust does not build it but burns it up and sets it on fire. Do you wish to build the city well? “Better is a little with the fear of God than great treasures without fear” (Prov. XV, 16). A man’s riches ought to advance the redemption of his soul, not its destruction. A treasure is redemption if someone uses it well; but it is also a snare if someone does not know how to use it (Prov. XIII, 8).

For what is money to a man except a kind of provision for a journey? Much becomes a burden, moderation is useful. We are travelers through this life. Many walk, but it is necessary for a person to pass through well; for the Lord Jesus is with the one who passes through well. Therefore you read: “If you pass through the water, I am with you; the rivers will not overwhelm you, nor will fire burn your garments if you pass through” (Isa. XLIII, 2). But whoever binds fire to his own body—the fire of lust, the fire of immoderate desire—does not pass through, but burns up this covering of his soul (Prov. VI, 27).

A good reputation is more excellent than money, and good favor is better than all heaps of silver (Prov. XXII, 1). Faith itself is sufficient for itself, rich enough and more than enough in its own resources. To the wise person nothing is foreign except what is inconsistent with virtue; wherever he goes, he will find everything his own.

[Note: Many manuscripts, and with them all the editions, read: “Wherever he goes, all things are his.” But the reading found in more and better manuscripts is “he will find all things his.”]

The whole world is his possession, since he makes use of the whole of it as though it were his own.

### 12

Why, then, is a brother defrauded? Why is a laborer cheated? “Not great gains,” says Scripture (Prov. VI, 26), “from the wages of a prostitute”—that is, from this slippery fragility.

This prostitute is not a particular woman but a public one; not one woman alone, but all wandering desire is a prostitute. Every faithlessness, every deceit, is a prostitute—not only she who prostitutes her body, but every soul that sells its hope and seeks shameful profit and degenerate payment.

We too are laborers, who work for a reward and expect from our Lord and God the reward of this work of ours. If anyone wishes to know how we are laborers, let him hear the one who says: “How many loaves my father’s laborers have in abundance, while I perish here from hunger!” (Luke XV, 17); and below: “Make me,” he says, “like one of your laborers” (ibid., 19).

All are laborers; all are workers. Yet whoever expects the fruit of his labor should consider that he who has defrauded another of his due wages will himself be defrauded of his own. This lending at interest incurs offense, and afterward it will repay with an increased measure. Therefore, whoever does not wish to lose what is eternal should not take away from another what is temporal.

### 13

Let no one speak deceitfully to his neighbor. There is a snare in our lips, and often a person is not disentangled by his words but entangled in them (Prov. VI, 2). The mouth of the malicious is a deep pit: a great precipice for innocence, but a greater one for malice (Prov. XXII, 14). The innocent person, while easily believing, quickly falls (Prov. XIV, 15); yet this fall can be followed by rising again. The slanderer, however, is plunged by his own devices into a place from which he will never leap or escape.

Let each person therefore weigh his words, without fraud or deceit: “A false balance is detestable before God” (Prov. XI, 1).

[Note: The old edition, together with part of the manuscripts, reads: “which weighs out another’s wage”; the Roman edition, together with another part, reads: “which weighs out another’s merchandise.”]

I do not mean that balance which weighs out another’s merchandise—for, even in cheap goods, deceit is costly—but the balance of words itself is detestable before God: it puts forward the appearance of the weight of sober seriousness and attaches to it the artifices of fraud.

[Col. 0883B]

God especially condemns this: when someone deceives his neighbor by the graciousness of his promises and oppresses him with fraudulent injustice after lending at interest, gaining nothing for himself from the devices of his cunning. For what does it profit a man if he gains the wealth of the whole world but defrauds his soul of the payment of eternal life? (Matt. XVI, 26).

### 14

There is another balance for pious minds to consider, in which the deeds of individuals are weighed. In this balance sins generally incline toward judgment, or good deeds outweigh sins. Woe to me if vices come first and, with their deadly weight, incline toward the sentence of death! It is more tolerable if they follow afterward; yet all things are manifest to the Lord, even before judgment: neither good deeds nor things full of offense can be hidden (I Tim. V, 24).

### 15

How blessed is the one who has been able to cut out avarice, the root of vices! Such a person will certainly not fear this balance. For avarice generally dulls human understanding and perverts judgments (I Tim. VI, 10), so that people think profit to be piety and money to be the reward of prudence.

But the great reward of piety, and the profit of sobriety, is to have enough of what is useful. For what benefit do the excesses of riches provide in this world, when they bring neither any assistance at birth nor any hindrance at death? We are born into this world without clothing, and we depart without provisions for the journey; we are buried without an inheritance.

### 16

The balance of our merits hangs before each of us, and is often inclined this way or that by the slightest moments of either a good work or a degenerate vice. If evil deeds incline it—alas for me! If good deeds do so, pardon is at hand. No one is free from sin; but when good deeds incline the balance, sins are lifted up, overshadowed, and covered.

Therefore, on the day of judgment, either our works will help us, or they themselves will sink us into the depths, as though we had been weighed down by a millstone. For iniquity is heavy, supported as it were by a leaden talent; avarice is intolerable, as are all pride and foul deceit (Zech. V, 7). Therefore exhort the Lord’s people to hope more in the Lord and to abound in the riches of simplicity, in which they may walk without a snare and without impediment (II Cor. VIII, 2).

### 17

The sincerity of pure speech is also good and rich before God. Even if it walks among snares, nevertheless, because it knows not how to set ambushes or fasten bonds for others, it is not itself bound.

### 18

It is also of the greatest importance that you persuade them to know how to humble themselves, to understand the true appearance of humility, and to know its nature. Many possess the appearance of humility but not its virtue. Many display it outwardly but attack it inwardly; they put it forward as a disguise, deny it when truth is concerned, and reject it when grace is at issue. “There is one who humbles himself wickedly, while his inward parts are full of deceit” (Eccl. XIX, 23). And there is one who lowers himself excessively through excessive humility.

Humility, therefore, exists only without disguise and without fraud. It is true when it possesses a pious sincerity of mind (Rom. V, 19). Its virtue is great. Through the disobedience of one man, death entered; and through the obedience of one Lord Jesus Christ, the redemption of all was accomplished.

### 19

Holy Joseph knew how to humble himself. Although he had been sold into slavery by his brothers or bought by merchants (Gen. XXXVII, 28), and, as Scripture says, humbled in fetters (Ps. CIV, 18), he learned the virtue of humility and rejected weakness.

Accordingly, when he had been bought in the regions of Egypt by a royal servant, the chief of the cooks (Gen. XXXIX, 1 and following), he did not, with a consciousness of noble ancestry—as a shoot of the Abrahamites—despise household service or disdain his degraded condition. Rather, he showed himself diligent and faithful to his master’s authority, contemplating with profound wisdom that it made no difference in what condition a person displayed himself as praiseworthy; the end of good conduct was that one should be approved in whatever condition one was found. The chief point was that character should make a condition honorable more than the condition should make character honorable. Indeed, the lower the condition, the more conspicuous the virtue.

He therefore displayed himself as such a person, so diligent, that his master entrusted his entire household to him and committed everything to him.

### 20

Hence his master’s wife also cast her eyes upon him (ibid., 7 and following), captivated by the beauty of his appearance. It makes no difference to us whether age or beauty is sought by wanton eyes. Let artifice be absent, and there is no guilt in beauty; let seduction be absent, and appearance is blameless, as is the grace of form.

Thus, stirred and raging in mind, she accosted the young man, and, compelled by lust and overcome by the goads of passion, confessed her crime. But he rejected the outrage,

[Note: On this subject consult Philo, Book *On Joseph*, in the final Paris edition, p. 533.]

saying that it was contrary to the customs of the Hebrews and to their laws to violate another’s marriage bed. Their concern was to preserve chastity, so that men of integrity might be joined in marriage with undefiled virgins, and that no one should consort with a woman who did not know the lawful use of the marriage bed. He also regarded it as a religious obligation not to be drunk with shameful intemperance and, ungrateful for his master’s kindness, to inflict a serious insult upon the one to whom he owed obedience.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “lest he, a Hebrew, be drunk,” which is less elegant.]

### 21

Was he ashamed to call that man, though vile, his master, and to confess himself a servant? On the contrary, when the woman pressed him, even begged him, perhaps out of fear that she would be betrayed, or poured out tears of love in order to force him into submission, he was moved neither by pity to consent to the outrage nor compelled by fear. He resisted her pleas and did not yield to her threats, preferring dangerous honorableness to rewards, rather than a shameful recompense to chaste modesty.

Again the woman attacked him with greater attempts (Gen. XXXIX, 11 and following). When she saw that he was inflexible and immovable even a second time,

[Note: All editions read: “also, for a second time, immovable through passion, with savage shamelessness,” and so forth. All the manuscripts read as in the text, except that many rightly omit *et* before *impudentia*.]

with savage passion and shamelessness supplying her strength, she attacked the young man, seized his garment, dragged him toward the bed, and offered him her embrace. She had almost captured him, had Joseph not stripped off the garment by which he was held—so that he would not strip off the clothing of humility, the garment of modesty.

### 22

Thus the man who had been humbled even to prison knew how to humble himself. When he endured false accusation, he preferred to bear a false charge rather than report a true one. He knew, I say, how to humble himself, because he was humbled for the sake of virtue.

He was humbled as a type of the one who was to humble himself even to death, and death on a cross; the one who was to come in order to awaken this life from sleep and teach that this manner of living is a dream. In it, the various changes of circumstances, as though drunken, pass by; and, seeing nothing solid or stable, like a sleeper’s dream, we do not see though we look, we do not hear though we listen, we are not satisfied though we eat, we do not rejoice though we celebrate, and we do not arrive though we run.

Vain are the hopes of people in this age, who think that things which are not are to be pursued as though they were. Thus empty and hollow appearances of things came and went like a dream: they stood before us and vanished. They were spread around us and scattered; they seem to be held, but they are not held.

At last, when someone hears the one who says, “Rise, you who sleep” (Eph. V, 11), and rises from the sleep of this age, he understands that all these things are false. He awakes, and the dream flees; power flees, concern for patrimony departs, the beauty of appearance, and the pursuit of honors. These are dreams, by which those who are awake in heart are not moved, but by which sleepers are tormented.

### 23

Let holy Joseph bear witness that my discourse is true: the things of this age are neither perpetual nor lasting. Though noble in birth from the beginning and rich in wealth, he suddenly became a lowly servant; and, what made the very degradation of servitude more bitter, he became a purchased slave bought with money by a base master. It is considered less degrading to serve a free man; servitude is doubled when one serves household slaves.

Thus he was a slave of illustrious birth, poor though descended from a rich father, passing from love to hatred and from favor to punishment; then again from prison to the court and from accusation to judgment. He was neither broken by adversity nor elated by prosperity (Gen. XLI, 39 and following).

[Col. 0886A]

### 24

Holy David also bears witness that the changes of circumstances are momentary, through the frequent alterations of his condition. He was despised by his father but precious to God; noble in triumph but base in the eyes of envy (I Sam. XVI, 11 and following); summoned to royal service and chosen for kinship (I Sam. XVIII, 2 and following); finally, with his face and appearance changed, an exile from the kingdom and a fugitive from parricide. At one time he lamented his own offenses, and again removed those of others; reconciled with the heir, he became more noble than when disfigured (II Sam. XII, 1 and following).

Having experienced everything, he said beautifully: “It is good for me that I was humbled” (Ps. CXVIII, 71).

### 25

Although this may also be referred to the one who, though he was in the form of God and could easily bend the heavens, nevertheless descended and, taking the form of a servant, bore our infirmities (Phil. II, 6), who, foreseeing that his saints would not seize honor for themselves as though it were a possession by robbery but would subject themselves to their equals and place others before themselves, said: “It is good for me that I was humbled.” It is good for me that I subjected myself, so that all things might be subjected to me, and God might be all in all (I Cor. XV, 27–28).

Pour this humility into the minds of individuals, and offer yourself as an example to all, saying: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (I Cor. XI, 1).

### 26

Let them learn to seek the riches of good works and to be rich in character. The beauty of riches is not in the purses of the wealthy but in the nourishment of the poor. Riches shine more nobly in the sick and needy.

Let the wealthy therefore learn to seek not what is theirs but what belongs to Christ, so that Christ may also seek them and bestow his own gifts upon them. He spent his blood for them (Rom. VIII, 32), poured out his Spirit upon them, and offered them his kingdom. What more will he give, who offered himself? Or what is the Father not going to give, who handed over his only Son to death for us?

Therefore admonish them to serve the Lord in sobriety and grace, to raise their eyes to heavenly things with the whole diligence of their minds, and to count nothing as gain except what belongs to eternal life. For all the profit of this world is the loss of souls.

In the end, the man who wished to gain Christ suffered the loss of everything (Phil. III, 8). Yet, although he said this wonderfully, he expressed less than he had received. He was speaking of what belonged to others; Christ, however, said: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself” (Luke IX, 23), so that he himself may become his own loss, by which Christ’s gain is made.

[Note: Many manuscripts read: “without loss, without gain”; the other manuscripts and all editions, more correctly, read as in the text.]

All these things are fleeting, with loss and without gain; the only gain is where the fruit is perpetual and the reward is eternal rest.

### 27

I commend to you, my son, the Church which is at Forum Cornelii, so that you may visit it frequently, being close at hand, until a bishop is appointed for it. Because I am occupied by the approaching days of Lent, I cannot travel so far.

[Note: It would be difficult to find among the ancients a bishop addressed by another bishop with the title “son.” Nor does any other reason occur to us why Ambrose called Constantius by this name, unless he had been taken from the Milanese clergy and raised to the episcopate, or had immediately after his consecration entrusted himself to Ambrose’s instruction in the principles of the spiritual life. Whatever the case may be, the whole course of the letter declares that he was truly a bishop; and therefore the Roman edition wrongly wrote in its summary that he was merely a bishop-designate. Nor does it more successfully assign the see of Arausio to him there. How could that be, when in this very passage the Church of Forum Cornelii is commended to the same bishop for frequent visitation, since it was nearby? The city once called Forum Cornelii is now called Imola, as we learn from Paul the Deacon, Book II of *The Deeds of the Lombards*, chapter 18, whom later geographers followed. Today it is subject to the metropolitan of Ravenna. At this same time there was another Constantius who signed, together with the bishop of Arausio, the Council of Aquileia; he was bishop of Sciscia. But since modern geographers identify Sciscia with Segesta, which was situated in Pannonia, this letter could not have been addressed to that Constantius either. Since, apart from these two, we encounter no other bishop of that name who flourished at that time, we frankly confess that the see of our Constantius is unknown to us.]

### 28

You have there Illyrians infected with the evil doctrine of the Arians. Beware their tares; let them not approach the faithful, and let adulterous seeds not spread. Let them consider what happened to them because of their faithlessness, and let them be silent so that they may follow the true faith.

Certainly, minds imbued with the poisons of unbelief can hardly remove the glue of their impiety. If that disastrous venom has taken root in them, do not think that they should easily be trusted. For it is a sinew, and one of the limbs, of wisdom not to believe rashly—especially in a matter of faith, which is rarely perfect among human beings.

[Note: No other calamity is doubtless indicated here than that by which, after Valens, the Arian emperor, had been defeated and burned, those provinces were dreadfully devastated by the victorious Goths.]

### 29

Yet if there is someone whose weakness is suspect and whose disposition is wavering, but who wishes to clear himself of the opinion formed about him, allow him to think that he has given satisfaction; show some indulgence. For when a person’s opportunity to give satisfaction is excluded, his disposition is alienated.

Even physicians, when they see familiar illnesses, as they themselves call them, do not yet apply medicine but nevertheless await the proper time for treatment. They do not abandon the invalid; rather, with gentler words or whatever soothing remedies they can employ, they handle him carefully, lest either an illness left untreated grow worse through despair of mind, or a disease that is too raw reject the medicine, since it cannot reach maturity if the physician applies his hands to such matters while they are still undigested.

[Note: Perhaps we should read “the signs of illness,” so that the meaning would be that medicine is not applied as soon as the first indications of illness are detected; namely, according to the Hippocratic saying, “Treat and move what has ripened, but not both at once” (*Pépona pharmakeúein, kai kineîn, mē hama*). This agrees beautifully with Ambrose’s words below, “or the disease, being too raw, may reject the medicine.” Nevertheless, by “recognizable illnesses” we may also understand customary and not excessive diseases; for in extreme and unusual cases, when delay is dangerous, immediate treatment is necessary. Therefore nothing should be changed in the reading found in all the manuscripts and editions.]

For even an unripe fruit, if it is shaken, quickly perishes.

[Col. 0887C] **30.** And since we have taken our example from the field, instruct them to preserve inviolate the rights of the boundary, to guard the ancestral limits which the Law protects. Frequently, the neighbor’s favor ranks above brotherly love (Deut. 19:14); for the brother is often far away, whereas the neighbor is near, a witness of one’s whole life and an arbiter of one’s conduct. Let him take pleasure in seeing the unconfined cattle roam through the neighboring spaces and, lying down in green grass, enjoy secure leisure.

**31.** Let the master also hold slaves, subjected to him by the law of servitude, under the discipline of restraint, as though they were partners of his soul. For he is called the father of the household, so that he may govern them as sons; since he too is God’s servant and calls the Lord of heaven, the ruler of all powers, his Father. Farewell, and love us, as you do; for we love you.

## LETTER III

[Note: Written around A.D. 380.]

He praises Felix’s little gift, but reproves him for not having visited him for a long time; he asks that he not postpone it so long again.

### AMBROSE TO FELIX

**1.** You sent me truffles, and indeed of astonishing size, so large that they were a marvel. [Note: There are many proverbial expressions derived from the bosom, by which something hidden is signified—for example, “to rejoice in one’s bosom” and “to be in one’s bosom.” See Erasmus, *Adagia*, book I, century 3, proverb 13.] I did not wish, as they say, to hide them in my bosom, but preferred to display them to others as well. Accordingly, I sent part to my friends and kept part for myself.

**2.** It was a pleasant gift, [Note: The editions and some manuscripts read “but not so overpowering.”] though not so powerful as to suppress my justly aroused complaint that you, who love us, have not visited us for so long. And take care hereafter that you do not discover greater truffles of pain. [Note: All the editions read *invehas* (“bring in”); all the manuscripts read *invenias* (“find”). Neither reading is unsuitable. But the latest Paris edition, against the testimony of the others and of the manuscripts, printed *grata in mente* (“welcome in the mind”) instead of *grata in munere* (“welcome as a gift”). This is foreign to the author’s meaning: the truffles, which he indicates were welcome to him as a friend’s gift, being gifts of the earth, are likewise presented as unpleasant when they signify a swelling of the body caused by a wound or the distress of a swelling spirit.] For the meaning of the name is different: just as they are welcome as a gift, so in the body and in the emotions they are unpleasant. Obtain this from yourself, that I may grieve less at your absence; for the cause of my agitation is my longing for you. If you can, arrange to be less welcome.

**3.** I have stated the matter and established the cause. That missile-like, [Note: The expression “missile-like sentence” is used metaphorically, from a spear (*hasta amentata*) bound with a certain strap called an *amentum*, so that it could be hurled more surely and powerfully. See Junius, *Adagia*, century 3, proverb 12.] non-manipular [Note: That is, “profitable,” because it brought with it a kind of revenue in little gifts.] sentence must be hurled. You were certainly afraid; but see how moved I am, that it delights me to jest. Nevertheless, do not excuse yourself afterward. For although this excuse of yours is a profitable one to me, [Note: *Vectigalis* means “profitable,” since it has brought with it a kind of tax or revenue in the form of gifts.] it nevertheless judges you badly—and does not judge me any better—if you think that your absence can be compensated by gifts, or that I can be bought off with gifts. Farewell, and love us, who love you.

## LETTER IV

[Note: Written in A.D. 380.]

He says that he was refreshed by Felix’s conversation, especially because he hoped Felix would come for the consecration of the basilica after they had celebrated the anniversary of his episcopal consecration. He promises his prayers for this purpose and asks Felix for reciprocal prayers when he enters the Holy of Holies. [Col. 0889A] Then, having mystically described what is contained there, he praises Felix’s administration and promises that assistants will not be lacking.

### AMBROSE TO FELIX

[Note: All the editions read “To Felix, bishop of Como”; the manuscripts, however, agree with the text, “Felix, greetings,” except for a few in which *salutem* is omitted and the Theodorian manuscript, which reads *Feliciano*. The former reading is not sufficiently correct. The context of this letter clearly proves that this Felix presided over the diocese of Como; that he is the same person to whom the preceding letter was addressed is shown not merely by the name but chiefly by the similarity of subject. Since the earlier letter was sent to Felix when he was excusing his failure to come, this one likewise makes unmistakable mention of the same excuse. Moreover, both letters are recognized as having been written to a very close acquaintance who was not at a great distance. This Felix, whose name deserved to be entered in the catalogue of the saints, is commemorated on the day before the Ides of July in these words: “At Novocomum, Saint Felix, the first bishop of that city.” Ughelli asserts that Ambrose appointed him bishop of the Church of Como not as metropolitan but as an apostolic legate, since this see had never been subject to Aquileia. Yet he offers no argument for his view. His denial that Felix was the first to sit at Novocomum may, however, be refuted—not without reason—from the final part of this letter. Consider it, reader, and decide.]

**Greetings to Felix.**

**1.** Although I was weak in bodily health, when I read your speech, filled with the unanimity of your heart toward me, I received no small help toward recovery, as though refreshed by some pennyroyal [Note: Where the edition reads *pulegio*, the manuscripts have partly *poleio* and partly *puleio*. *Pulegium* and *puleium* are in fact the same herb; for in the Glosses of Philoxenus we read *puleium*, Greek βλήχων or γλήχων. There is also an herb called *polium*, named from its gray color, παρά τῆς πολιότητος. Consult Dioscorides and others concerning the properties of both.] of your conversation. At the same time, you announced that a day memorable to us both was approaching—the day on which you assumed the helm of the high priesthood—about which I had just been speaking with our brother Bassianus. [Note: The Laetian and Carolinian manuscripts read *Bassiliano*; the others and the editions read *Bassiano*. He subscribed to the Council of Aquileia and to the letter to Siricius, and in both places, as also in Paulinus’ *Life of Ambrose*, he is called bishop of Lodi. Ughelli mentions a basilica founded by him, as stated in the Preface. His name is inscribed in the roll of the saints on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February.]

For our conversation turned to the dedication of the basilica which he founded in the name of the Apostles, and this gave the conversation its direction, since he indicated that he was earnestly seeking your holy presence.

**2.** Then I wove into our conversation the day of your birth, [Note: Ambrose here calls the anniversary of episcopal consecration the “birthday,” just as he did in book VIII of the *Exposition of the Gospel according to Luke*, no. 73. Since something has already been said there about the custom of celebrating that day, it seemed sufficient to add only this here. Anyone wishing to learn more about the custom will find much in Casaubon’s notes on Spartianus, p. 10, no. 45.] which fell at the very beginning of the Kalends of November; and I said that, unless I was mistaken, it had drawn near and was to be celebrated the following day, so that afterward you would have no excuse. Therefore I made a promise about you, since you are equally permitted to make one about me; I made the promise to him and exacted it from myself. For I take it for granted that you will be present, because you ought to be present. Your resolve, then, will bind you no less than my promise, since you have determined [Note: The edition reads, “you have resolved in your mind.”] to do what is fitting. You see, therefore, that I promised my brother not so much with the boldness of one who promises as with consciousness of your intention. Come, then, lest you rebuke two priests: yourself, for not having come, and me, for having promised so readily.

**3.** We shall celebrate your birthday with our prayers, and may you not forget us in your petitions. [Col. 0889C] Our spirit will accompany you. When you enter the second tabernacle, which is called the Holy of Holies (Exod. 26:35 ff.), see that, following our custom, you bring us in with you. When, in spirit, you burn incense at that golden censer, do not omit us; for that is what is in the second tabernacle, from which your prayer, full of wisdom, is directed like incense toward heaven.

**4.** [Note: Just as the Ark of the Covenant here signifies the book of the holy Gospels, so the golden vessel filled with manna signifies the sacred pyx in which the Eucharist, worthy of adoration, was kept.] There is the Ark of the Covenant, covered on every side with gold—that is, the teaching of Christ, the teaching of the wisdom of God. There is the golden vessel containing manna, the receptacle of spiritual nourishment and the storehouse of divine knowledge. There is Aaron’s rod, the insignia of priestly grace. It had withered before, but in Christ it blossomed again. There are the Cherubim above the tablets of the Covenant, signifying knowledge of sacred reading. There is the mercy seat, above which, in the heights, is God the Word, the image of the invisible God (Col. 1:15), who says to you: “I will speak with you from above the mercy seat, from between the two Cherubim” (Exod. 25:22). For he speaks with us in such a way that we understand his speech—or because he speaks not earthly but intelligible things, as he says: “I will open my mouth in parables” (Ps. 77:2). For where Christ is, there is everything: his teaching, the forgiveness of sins, grace, and the separation of the dead from the living.

**5.** Aaron once stood in the midst of them, interposing himself so that death would not pass from the corpses of the dead to the ranks of the living (Num. 16:47–48). But here, as the Word, he always stands within each person. Though we do not see him, he separates within us rational virtues from the corpses of deadly passions and pestilential thoughts. He stands here as one who came into this world to blunt the sting of death, to close its devouring mouth, to give the living the eternity of grace, and to grant resurrection to the dead (Heb. 2:14–15).

**6.** You serve this one as a good soldier (1 Tim. 1:18); you guard his deposit; you lend out his money at interest, according to what is written: “You shall lend to the nations” (Deut. 15:6). It is a good interest-bearing loan of spiritual grace, which the Lord, when he comes, will demand with interest; and when he finds that you have administered it well, he will give you more in return for less. It will be my sweetest reward that my judgment concerning you is confirmed. [Note: Observe that an ordained bishop is never found without the laying-on of hands by another bishop. This custom has been rashly abolished by heretics.] The ordination you received through the laying-on of my hands and the blessing in the name of the Lord Jesus will not be condemned (2 Tim. 1:6). Do good work, therefore, so that on that day you may find your reward, and that both I in you and you in me may find rest.

**7.** Christ’s harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few; and it is difficult to find those who will help. [Note: The Belvacian manuscript reads, “who may announce.” Immediately afterward the Albinian manuscript has *verum*. The word is old; Boyer has, “But this is true among us.”] Yet this is an old saying. The Lord is powerful enough to send laborers into his harvest (Matt. 9:37). Certainly, in that community of Como, most have already begun to believe in your teaching and have received the word of God through your instruction. But he who has given believers will also give assistants, so that the necessity of your excusing why you visited us so late may be removed, and so that the grace of your presence may be poured out upon me more frequently. Farewell, and love us, as you do.

## LETTER V

[Note: Written around A.D. 380.]

Defending the judgment he rendered in the case of Indicia, he criticizes Syagrius’ judgment because the proper legal procedure was not observed. Maximum, the author of the tragedy, did not appear before him; Syagrius ordered the virgin to undergo a most insulting examination, although other means were available by which a virgin ought to be judged. The examination was uncertain and useless, since the office of midwives was something else. The case, therefore, should not be decided in this way, especially since Indicia was said to have given birth. In what cases an examination might be tolerated is explained. Syagrius offers a vain excuse; Maximum was truly the accuser. Finally, after the accusation and witnesses have again been censured, the testimony of Marcellina and others on behalf of Indicia is reported, after which Ambrose’s judgment is presented.

### AMBROSE TO SYAGRIUS

[Note: All the editions read “to Syagrius, bishop of the Church of Verona”; the manuscripts, contrary to them, agree with the text. There is no doubt, however, that the man to whom Ambrose replies held the helm of that Church.]

**1.** In your own letter you wrote that care must be taken lest our beloved Veronese speak against our judgment. I do not think they will; at least, it is not their custom. Or, if they do speak against it, there is no doubt what they are accustomed to criticize: they come here exasperated and return to you peacefully, especially since our judgment was reached in consultation with our brothers and fellow priests. You, however, without the advice of any brother, thought that this judgment had to be made by you alone. [Note: Thus the manuscripts; the editions read, “you thought that it had to be judged.” Zeno, by whose judgment Indicia is said to have been approved and consecrated, is not, according to Baronius in his notes, the same person whose memory is commemorated on the day before the Ides of April in the Roman Martyrology. He argues that the other Zeno was also a bishop of Verona but lived later, and that his sermons were published under the name of Zeno the martyr. Yet others maintain, on the contrary, that this Zeno was Syagrius’ predecessor and the only bishop of Verona of that name in this period; they suggest that he was called a martyr in the collection of sermons compiled from the works of various Fathers and attributed to him because he may have suffered something under the apostate Julian.] In this matter, however, you prejudged the case before judging it: you considered that a girl approved by the judgment of Zeno, of holy memory, and sanctified by his blessing many years earlier, should be brought into danger of conviction without an author of the charge, without an accuser, and without anyone formally presenting the accusation. [Note: Some manuscripts read “without one declaring that he had withdrawn”; some others have an incomplete reading, “without a declamation”; the remaining manuscripts and all the editions have an incomplete reading, “without a report.” The latter is more correct. Nevertheless, the manuscripts that read *professore* (“one making a formal declaration”) instead of *professione* (“formal declaration”) are not entirely unacceptable.] The calumny against her had been concocted by worthless people, by heretics—as they themselves claim—by depraved persons seeking freedom for their own disgraceful behavior through crime, greed, and intemperance, and finally by those who had been expelled and driven from her house, because they were weaving works of varied color beneath the outward face of their profession [Note: Some manuscripts add “they wove beneath it a work of varied color.”] beneath what they had displayed at the outset of their profession.

**2.** You placed such accusers and such witnesses before your tribunal—people who dared neither to accuse nor to bind themselves by the obligation of a formal charge—and nevertheless you decided that a virgin who had no accuser and no informer ought to be subjected to examination. Where was the solemnity of this judicial inquiry? Where was such a formula of judgment? If we consult the public laws, they demand an accuser. If we consult the Church, it says: “Every word shall be established by two or three witnesses” (Matt. 18:16)—but by witnesses who had not been enemies yesterday or the day before yesterday, lest, in their anger, they should wish to harm someone or, having been injured, seek revenge.

**3.** The witnesses’ freedom from hostile feeling must therefore be sought, but in such a way that the accuser first comes forward. Even those priests of the Jews (Dan. 13:34 ff.) first laid their hands upon Susanna’s head, formally made their accusation, and likewise added the authority of testimony, which the imprudent people, misled by error, had accepted. But through the prophet the almighty God exposed and reproved them by divine judgment, so that it became clear to everyone that they wished to sow prejudice beforehand against an innocent woman in danger. [Note: Some manuscripts read “who had failed”; one reads “who were failing.”] For, lacking the grounds of accusation and supporting proof, they reckoned that, if prejudice assailed people’s minds after their ears had been preoccupied, it would bring a pre-judgment to the examination of the truth. For when reports precede the facts, they block the ear and occupy the mind, so that proof is no longer sought and rumor is treated as a proven crime.

**4.** We therefore demanded an accuser and judged that Maximum, the author of the whole spectacle, must be pressed. But he abandoned by a formal declaration the accusation he had deliberately composed and verbally presented; nevertheless, in feeling he pursued it and in practice carried it out. He fled from the name because he distrusted the proof. Finally, after spreading rumors and also composing and sending letters, he sought to intensify the hatred attached to the accusation. But integrity could not be overwhelmed or entrapped. For if he had possessed proofs, he would never have demanded an examination by your sentence.

**5.** What, then, was your purpose, and where were you aiming, when you thought that a midwife should be employed? Is it to be permitted for everyone to accuse, and, once they have abandoned proof, to make it lawful for them to demand an examination of the genital secrets? Are sacred virgins always to be handed over to such mockeries—things horrible and shameful both to see and to hear? Indeed, even in your own letter there is no small embarrassment in the expression you attempted. If things that cannot be uttered in the ears of others without damage to modesty may be spoken of, can they be examined in a virgin without injury to her modesty?

**6.** You found yourself a cheap slave girl, a shameless household servant. Why should you not abuse her modest service and expose her modesty, especially since nothing is more sacred in a virgin than modesty? A sacred virgin is not sought merely to be physically intact, but also to preserve her unoffended modesty in every respect. The virgin of the Lord relies upon her own supports for her vindication and needs no external advantages to prove herself a virgin. It is not the examination of hidden and concealed parts, but modesty evident to everyone, that bears witness to integrity. The woman whom the gravity of her own conduct does not prove is not pleasing to God. She is not approved by the Lord if she requires the testimony of a single midwife—a testimony usually purchased for a price. Does such a woman seem to you wealthy in credibility, when she can be bought and deceived, so that she may excuse the guilty and conceal the crime—or, if she does not know what has occurred, may be unable to detect the disgrace?

**7.** Nor do I think that what you included in your letter is just: that unless she is examined, her integrity will be endangered and she will remain uncertain about herself. Are all women who have not been examined therefore in danger of losing their modesty? Are women who are about to marry to be examined first, so that they may marry with better proof? Are those who are to be veiled likewise to be subjected first to such handling? For they are not merely visited but handled. And according to your judgment, it is more proper to examine one who has not been approved than one who has been consecrated.

**8.** What shall we say when even the leading physicians say that the reliability of such an examination cannot be established with sufficient certainty, and that the ancient teachers of medicine held the same opinion? We too have learned this by experience: differences and disputes have often arisen among midwives, so that there has been more doubt concerning a woman who submitted herself to examination than concerning one who was not examined. We recently discovered this in an actual case. A woman of servile status was examined and rejected at Altinum; later, at Milan, not by my order but at the will of Nicentius, former tribune and notary, her master or patron, she was examined by a woman highly skilled and well provided with the resources of this art. [Note: Some manuscripts read *saltim* or *saltem inspecta* (“examined at least”). This is not sufficiently correct. Altinum was a respectable municipality of Italy, whose ruins, as is believed, were leveled to the ground by Attila; some remains are still visible, as Leander Albertus reports in the *March of Treviso*. Again, where all the editions read “Nicentius, former tribune and notary,” all the manuscripts read “Nicentius, from the tribune and notary”—a rather harsh expression but not wholly incongruous. Paulinus mentions this Nicentius in his *Life of Ambrose* and considers him to be the same as Nitentius, mentioned in law 11 of the year 377, *That Holy Baptism Be Not Repeated*.] Although all the circumstances that might have been required were present—neither the midwife’s poverty making her testimony suspect nor her lack of education making her incompetent—the question nevertheless remains.

**9.** What, then, did it accomplish to examine her, when condemnation remains? Anyone may assert, as he pleases, that the woman was an unskilled practitioner or that she had been bought. Thus the injury of the examination remains without any result. What will happen next? Whenever someone appears who does not believe, will the virgin be handled again? [Note: The Amerbach edition and some manuscripts read, “the virgin will be disparaged.” The meaning is not bad.] For if she ever refuses to be examined, according to your claim she will confess the crime. It is easier for her to refute something she never did than something she did. The midwives will therefore be changed repeatedly, lest any particular favor be suspected. Among the many midwives—although even in great cities there are few who practice this form of medicine—there will be one who is either malicious or incompetent, who passes beyond the barriers of modesty and, through incompetence, brands an innocent modesty with a mark of shame. You see into what danger you bring the virginal profession by thinking that a midwife should be employed: the virgin will now be endangered not only by the loss of her modesty but also by the uncertainty surrounding the midwife.

**10.** Let us now consider what the office of a midwife is. We read even in the Old Testament of midwives, but not of female examiners. They entered the presence of women in labor, not of virgins; they received births, not examined modesty. Hence they were called *obstetrices*, either because they stand against pain, or at least because they stand by the child, lest, when the womb’s generative barriers have been loosened, it fall to the ground. [Note: After mentioning this origin of the word, Vossius adds that he prefers the explanation that *obstetrix* is derived as though from *assestrix*, because she sits beside the woman giving birth. We do not know whether many have approved this opinion; certainly it has not won our approval.]

In two further passages of Scripture we find midwives employed, but always for childbirth and never for examination. First, when Rachel is in labor (Gen. 35:17); then, when Tamar gives birth (Gen. 38:27); and third, when Pharaoh orders the Hebrew midwives to kill the male children (Exod. 1:15 ff.). They replied that Hebrew women did not give birth in the manner of Egyptian women, but that Hebrew women gave birth before the midwives entered to them. In its earlier part this passage is useful for the salvation of the Hebrews; in what remains, however, it is damaging to the credibility of the midwives, who learned to lie for salvation’s sake and to deceive for excuse.

**11.** Why, then, do we grasp at things that are suspect and doubtful, when there are other, greater documents and testimonies for examining the truth, in which the signs of violated modesty are more evident? What is more public than an offense against modesty and the deflowering of virginity? Nothing, surely, reveals itself more plainly than the loss of chastity. The belly swells, and the burdens of her fetus weigh upon her as she walks—to say nothing of the other signs by which a silent conscience betrays itself.

**12.** Perhaps, under the pretext of sterility, a disgrace could be concealed in some cases. But here, when the child had been born and exposed—or killed, while concern was shown more for hatred than for proof—and the matter had been spread through the ears of everyone, the freedom for slander was strangled, if she had given birth. She had lived at Verona and was frequently visited by virgins and married women, for she was always held in honor. Priests also visited her because of their reverence for her chastity and because she was an example of gravity. How, then, could she conceal a crime that would betray itself even by its appearance? How could she conceal her womb? How could she fail to shrink from the sight of women and the eyes of those who greeted her? How could she suppress her voice in labor? Pain does not permit this. Indeed, Scripture calls the pains of a woman in labor the greatest pains (Gen. 3:16). “So,” it says, “the day of the Lord comes suddenly and unexpectedly, like the pain of childbirth,” which closes every avenue of escape for remaining concealed (Isa. 13:8–9).

**13.** This is the more reliable testimony of the evidence, from which even women themselves shrink. Thus Elizabeth concealed herself for five months because, though barren, she had conceived in old age (Luke 1:24). By these signs, even Mary’s virginity was suspected of disgrace by those ignorant of the mystery. Hence Joseph, to whom the virgin was betrothed, suspected wrongdoing while he still did not know the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation (Matt. 1:18).

**14.** Are we therefore denying that virgins should be examined? Since I have nowhere read of such a practice, I neither assert it nor consider it true. But because we do many things for appearance rather than for truth, and frequently put forward numerous pretexts because of error—for there are people who do not know how to do what is right except through fear of punishment—let us leave this to those whom modesty does not restrain from falling, but whom fear of injury alone deters; those who have no concern for modesty or love of chastity, but only fear punishment. Let us leave it to servants, who are more afraid of being caught than of having sinned. Let it be far from a sacred virgin to know a midwife: childbirth is presumed, and the relief of pain is intended, not an examination of modesty.

Let us also leave it to those women who, if attacked by serious slanders, overwhelmed by testimony, and strangled by arguments, flee to the expedient of submitting themselves to examination, so that the guarded condition of their bodies may be proved—if indeed it can be detected in those whose sense of modesty and discipline of integrity are wavering. [Note: Cyprian likewise says this in the previously cited letter to Pomponius. Although he recognized that this method of investigating virginity was uncertain, when the case concerned girls who confessed that they had lain with men but denied having experienced anything sexual, he ordered that they be examined: “Let the virgins,” he says, “in the meantime be carefully examined by midwives.”] Yet the case is in a bad state when the prerogative of the flesh is preferred to that of the mind. I prefer virginity to be expressed by the seal of character rather than by the enclosure of the body.

**15.** There is also this remarkable point in what you wrote: that certain persons had intimated to you that they would not communicate with you if you believed that she should be received without a visitation. So you accepted a formula for judgment. What sort of people are they, who wish to prescribe to priests what we must follow? We have therefore freed you from the necessity of undertaking an extremely burdensome inquiry, so that you would not be compelled to carry out the formula they imposed. What, then, will become of us, who have not obeyed their zeal?

**16.** Nevertheless, I know that many there fear the Lord. For we too recently saw here, and discovered that there are such people there, who complain that this accusation was fabricated. They are said to have favored Maximum because this virgin did not go around their houses, greet their matrons, or court their favor. What, then, shall we do? How shall we strip her of so grave a crime? How shall we persuade her to take up new practices and abandon her own?

Surely the reading teaches that Mary was found at home when the archangel Gabriel came to her (Luke 1:28). Susanna is portrayed as fleeing the crowds (Dan. 13:15 ff.). Indeed, when she was bathing, she ordered Paradise to be closed. What, especially in a virgin whose chief work is modesty, is more excellent than privacy? What is safer than privacy, and more conducive to every action? [Note: The old edition reads: “modesty, which is private, is safer in privacy for every action and more readily available.” The Roman edition and some manuscripts have the reading used in the text. The other manuscripts also read, not unacceptably: “modesty, which is safer in privacy, is more readily available in privacy for every action.”] For she has assumed the duties of modesty, not of running about. But I shall consider other matters later; for now I must answer your letter.

**17.** I am astonished, brother, that you defend Maximum so insistently as not having been an accuser, but as having grieved with a parent’s pain at the odium of a rumor that had been spread. He could not deny that, as an enemy and hostile litigant, having already initiated a quarrel, he had attempted judicial proceedings against the sacred virgin; that he had separated his wife’s house from the virgin’s by placing a wall between them; that he had divided the bond of sisterly fellowship between the women; [Note: All the editions read, “and other things—alas!—and that the virgin …”; the manuscripts, on the contrary, unanimously agree with the text.] and that he had other grounds for grieving because the virgin, in the territory belonging to his family, had withdrawn from his association.

How, then, was he not an accuser—the man who had long exercised the feelings of an accuser, who brought an accusation in his speech, filled your ears with his outcry, and produced witnesses of hearsay, [Note: “Witnesses of hearsay” are those who affirm that they received a matter only by hearing it and from rumor, rather than seeing it with their own eyes. Yet, as Plautus says:

“One eyewitness is worth more than ten who have heard:

Those who hear report what they have heard; those who see know the truth.”]

and demanded an inquiry?

**18.** However elaborately you argued, you could not deny what you wrote to Indicia: that Maximum, whether prompted by others or moved by personal grief, had lodged a serious accusation. That letter alone is sufficient evidence of an accusation. I did not think that I should press you with the letters you had sent to me; but when I read those you had sent to the virgin, I noticed that what you had written to me was different. Nevertheless, since your letters did not agree with one another, I thought you should be consulted, not accused.

What, then, is the meaning of that argument of yours—that he had reported what you had written to me, namely, that she had been accused of a disgraceful crime, so that he asserted that a child had been born and buried? As though you had written that to Indicia rather than to me. When she heard from your letter that Maximum was being withdrawn from the accusation, she produced your letter, by which she proved him to be the informer of the crime. She had not read the letter addressed to me and did not know what it contained.

**19.** From the beginning I recoiled from the slander, because I saw that the object was not to pursue a crime but to inflict an injury upon the virgin. What was demanded was her examination and visitation, not the presentation of any disgraceful act. Who would not judge that this whole story, fraudulently contrived from the beginning, was entirely inconsistent and incoherent?

Low-born women had run to the monastery and proclaimed the birth of a child by a virgin and the killing of the infant; from the monastery the rumor had been spread among the people and had reached the ears of Maximum, her new relation by marriage. He himself had appealed to the bishop; the women who were said to have spoken were dismissed and forced to flee, as became clear before us. Those who claimed to have heard the matter came to the Church and brought forward Renatus and Leontius, those two men of iniquity whom Jezebel set forward (1 Kings 21:10), whom Daniel rebuked (Dan. 13:15 ff.), and whom the Jewish people suborned (Matt. 26:59–60), so that they might falsely pursue the life of an innocent person by their testimony.

Yet although they had composed the disgrace together, entered upon the same path together, and, not to omit anything, joined Maximum, accompanied—as Leontius said—by those who had spread the rumor, when they stood before my tribunal and I first asked about the origin of the case, they produced different and contradictory accounts—not separated by distance but divided by lies.

**20.** Since they did not agree with one another, they had sent away Mercury and Lea, persons of the lowest status and most detestable wickedness; Theodule had fled, being well aware that she could be charged with the crime of having previously lain alone in Renatus’ bed; another maidservant was present who said that she had been defiled by the same Renatus. On the very day appointed for the inquiry, they withdrew from the assembly of the bishops, although Renatus himself had suddenly declared the day before that they were going to leave.

**21.** For this reason I prescribed a date for the hearing. Yet, although there was no accuser and no testimony pressing the case, I informed the holy sister that you were asking for the virgin in question to be examined and visited in her presence.
