But she piously refused the examination while not declining to testify. She said that she had discovered nothing in Indicia except what belonged to virginal modesty and holiness: that Indicia had lived at Rome in our house while we were absent and had not given herself over to the intimacy of any men; and that she hoped to receive with her from the Lord Jesus a share in the kingdom of God.

22. I also questioned our daughter on her father’s side, who is accustomed never to leave her, and whose affection is evidence of her life. Therefore, although what she said under oath ought to have been accepted as testimony, nevertheless, under solemn adjuration, she declared that she was wholly innocent of the charge brought against her, and that she knew nothing in her of any conduct lacking in good character.

23. We also questioned her nurse, a woman of free status. Her social standing, by no means compromised by degrading servitude, gave her liberty to speak the truth; her loyalty and age supported her testimony; and her office as nurse gave her knowledge of the secret. She too declared that she had seen nothing dishonorable, and that no act deserving reproach had been entrusted to her by the virgin as to a parent.

24. Moved by these statements, we pronounced Indicia an innocent virgin and acquitted her of the charge. The sentence, however, included Maximus, Renatus, and Leontius in such a way that Maximus was left hope of restoration if he corrected his error; but Renatus and Leontius were to remain excommunicated unless, after their repentance had been proved and their prolonged lamentation for this deed, they should show themselves worthy of mercy. Farewell, brother, and love us, because we love you.

## EPISTLE VI

*[Written around A.D. 380.]*

When Syagrius had, by his judgment, subjected Indicia to an insulting examination, Ambrose remonstrates with him as a friend. Setting before his eyes the most atrocious vengeance which the Israelites exacted for the violation of chastity in the wife of the Levite, he elegantly recounts the entire sequence of events.

### AMBROSE TO SYAGRIUS

1. You retain the knowledge of what was done in our court; and therefore I now address you as though you were a part of my own soul, since you have before you a familiar and grieving complaint concerning the insult offered to chastity. Was it right that the case of an uncharged and unheard virgin should be adjudicated in such a way that she could not be acquitted? That is, unless, at the cost of her own injury, unless she were dragged from honorable modesty into the indecent exposure of her body, thereby bringing upon herself a grave testimony, so that she might be exposed to ridicule and branded with shamelessness. What privilege, then, did you grant to integrity? What sort of honor did you confer upon it, so that those who think such a service ought to be received might rejoice when they are provoked or invited to it; so that they should lose the freedom of making a common defense, and should not be able to defend themselves by right, whether under holy law or public law; so that no accuser need be demanded, no prosecutor pressed—but that she should merely put on shamelessness and throw herself open to injury?

2. Our ancestors did not regard chastity as something contemptible. They paid it such reverence that they thought war ought to be undertaken against those who dared to violate modesty. Indeed, their zeal for vengeance was so great that all the men of the tribe of Benjamin were destroyed, except the six hundred who survived the battle because the naturally higher ground protected them. Thus the matter is set out in the sequence of the divine text, whose wording it is appropriate to review.

*[Note: Many manuscripts read “except five hundred”; several of these also read only three hundred, rather than four hundred, for the virgins preserved from the destruction of Jabesh. But the other manuscripts and all editions read better, as in the text.]*

3. A Levite man, greater in spirit than in possessions, lived in the region of Mount Ephraim.

*[Note: Not everything that follows is found in the sacred codices; nevertheless, it is read in Josephus, Jewish Antiquities, Book V, chapter 2. Some manuscripts read “greater in spirit than in morals.”]* The place had fallen to him by lot as his tribal portion, given to him as an inheritance of land. He took for himself a wife from Bethlehem of Judah. And, as happens at the beginning of unions, he burned with an excessive passion for the young woman; and because he did not enjoy her company, he burned more and more with the desire to possess her, and seethed beyond measure.

*[Note: All editions read, “He burned more intensely, and”; the great majority of manuscripts read, “his possession burned more intensely, and.” The Laetian manuscript reads best, as in the text.]* Since, on the woman’s side, there was no corresponding response—whether because of the fickleness of love or the force of grief—which would have led her to settle the matter with him at an equal price, he quarreled with her.

Hence frequent disputes arose. The woman, offended, returned the keys and went back to her father’s house.

*[Note: “She returned the keys.” This is taken from Roman law. If a man divorced his wife, he ordered her to keep or manage her own property and at the same time took the keys away from her, as Sigonius and others show from Cicero, Philippic 2, in Book I, chapter 9, of On Roman Civil Law and Its Antiquities.]*

4. But he, overcome by love—for he had nothing else in which to place his hope—when he saw that the fourth month was already passing, went there, trusting that the young woman’s spirit might be softened by the counsel of her parents. His father-in-law met him at the door and brought him inside; he reconciled him with his daughter; and, wishing to send them away more happily, kept him for three days, as though restoring the marriage. When he wished to leave, he postponed his departure for a fourth day under the pretext of hospitality, prolonging the delay. In the same way, when he wished to add a fifth day to the preceding ones, and no new reasons for delay remained, the father’s affection nevertheless did not lack the desire to retain his daughter. He postponed the promised opportunity for departure until midday, so that they might set out after strengthening themselves with food. After the meal, he wished to add a further delay because evening was already approaching; and although reluctantly, he yielded to his son-in-law’s entreaties.

5. The Levite continued his journey in good spirits because he had recovered the woman he loved. Accompanied by only one servant, and with the day already declining, they hurried along the road at a rapid pace. The woman rode on an animal, while the man felt no weariness, since the satisfaction of his desire, together with the woman’s varied conversation with the servant, made the journey easier.

When they drew near Jerusalem, which was thirty stades away and was then held by the Jebusites, the servant suggested that they turn aside into the city, because at nightfall even places that were safer should be regarded with suspicion, and the uncertainties of darkness should be avoided—especially since the inhabitants of the region were not Israelites. They should therefore turn aside first, lest hostile men bring ambushes against them, since the obscurity of night was highly suitable for those seeking an opportunity to carry out a crime.

But his master did not at all approve the suggestion that they should lodge among foreigners, since the cities of Gibeah and Ramah in Benjamin were not far away. His own judgment prevailed, and he disregarded the servant’s advice, as though the counsel were judged by the servant’s status, and not as though even the lowliest condition might be elevated by sound advice. The sun was already setting; scarcely, in fact, did he reach the city before evening overtook him.

*[Note: Some manuscripts read “the lowly condition might be strengthened.”]*

6. The Gabaonites were inhospitable, harsh, and unbearable—yet more bearable in every respect than they would have been had they received anyone as a guest.

*[Note: The old edition reads, “yet more tolerable in every respect”; the Roman edition and all the manuscripts read better, “yet more tolerable in all respects.” Certain Paris manuscripts substitute “all” for “everything.” Incorrectly: the phrase here is elliptical, “more tolerable in all respects,” just as Horace says *caetera laetus* (“cheerful in other respects”), and similarly elsewhere.]* Indeed, it would have been better for this Levite man if he had found no lodging in Gibeah. But, so that no offense might be lacking, at his first entrance he found no lodging. As he stood in the public place and sought the mercy of strangers, he encountered an old man returning from the countryside, whom evening had forced to leave his agricultural work and come into the city.

When the old man noticed him and asked where he was going and from where he had come, he replied: “I am returning from Bethlehem of Judah and am making for Mount Ephraim, and the woman is with me. But behold, I have turned aside here, and there is no one who will receive me as a guest and provide a place for rest. It is not that I or my animal lack food or drink; rather, we are prevented from obtaining lodging under a roof. These provisions are available; what is lacking is shelter.”

The old man replied with great kindness and calm: “Peace be with you. Come in as both guest and fellow citizen, for I too come from the region of Mount Ephraim, and this is a hospitable dwelling. Yet long residence has established my home here.” He then received them into his house and supported them with his own service and the resources of hospitality.

*[Note: Some manuscripts read “he cherished him according to his strength.”]*

7. The old man urged them to be cheerful and pressed them to drink repeatedly, so that wine might erase the memory of their cares. Suddenly the Gabaonites surrounded them—young men surrendered to every form of lust, possessing nothing measured or restrained. The woman’s beauty had attracted them and was driving them into complete madness. Captivated by her appearance, and taking advantage of the old age of their host and the weakness of his means of assistance, they conceived the hope of possessing her, demanded the woman, and pounded on the door.

8. The old man therefore went out and begged them not to defile the hospitable table with a disgraceful outrage, and not to suppose that the venerable right of hospitality could be violated even among the untamed peoples of barbarous nations. The Levite was a fellow tribesman, an Israelite man joined in a lawful marriage; yet they were inflicting upon him, with the indignation of the heavenly Judge, such an insult.

When he saw that this achieved little, he added that he had a virgin daughter, and that he would offer her, at greater grief to a parent but with less damage to the obligations of hospitality, considering public disgrace more tolerable than private dishonor.

*[Note: The Roman edition reads, “public disgrace is considered more tolerable than private dishonor.” The sense is good and clear, but since this reading is opposed not only by all the other editions but also by all the manuscripts, we do not prefer it to such unanimous agreement. But what if one should read “less tolerable”? Certainly the alteration would be lighter than in the common reading.]*

But they, driven on by the heat of fury and inflamed by the stimulus of lust, burned all the more intensely for the young woman’s beauty precisely because she was refused to them. Deprived of justice, they mocked words of fairness and despised the old man’s daughter because she was offered with less resentment against the crime.

9. Therefore, when pious prayers achieved nothing and the old host stretched out his hands in vain, the woman was seized as hope of assistance had disappeared, and throughout the entire night the outrage was completed. When daylight put an end to their excess, she returned to the hospitable door—not because she sought the sight of the man, whom, in the shame of her misery, she thought she ought rather to avoid, but so that she might report to her husband what had happened, having lost her chastity, and display before the hospitable door, in a pitiable form, the funeral of her dishonor.

The Levite went out and found her lying there. He supposed that shame prevented her from raising her face at all, and began to console her, saying that she had yielded to such an outrage not willingly but under compulsion. He urged her to rise and return home with him. But when she gave no answer, he raised his voice further, as though she were sleeping, to awaken her from sleep.

10. When the certainty of her final death became clear, he placed her remains on the animal, carried them home, and sent the woman’s dismembered limbs in twelve parts throughout the tribes of Israel. Moved by this, the whole people assembled at Mizpah. When the Levite’s complaint had been heard there, all burst into war, deciding that no man should be permitted to enter the tabernacle until vengeance had been taken on the authors of so great a crime.

They rushed toward battle in their anger. But the judgment of the wiser men prevailed: they should not rashly fight against fellow citizens, but should first investigate the crime by words and impose penalties proportionate to the offense. It did not seem just that the price of a few men’s crimes should reach everyone, or that the private sins of young men should undermine the condition of public safety.

They therefore sent men to announce to the Gabaonites that they should surrender the perpetrators of so great an outrage. Otherwise, they should understand that defending such a crime was no less criminal than committing it.

11. But when the men of Gibeah returned a proud answer, the counsels of peace were changed into war. Even though many were being overwhelmed by a few in the first and second engagements, the Israelites did not think that they should yield to their adverse battles. Four hundred thousand fighting men were contending against twenty-five thousand men of the tribe of Benjamin and seven hundred Gibeahite youths experienced in war.

Although two battles had already fallen to their disadvantage, their ready spirit did not abandon Israel’s confidence of victory or its anticipated hope of vengeance.

12. But because, though superior in number and in the justice of their cause, they had withdrawn with an unfavorable outcome in battle, they judged that they had offended God and sought reconciliation with heavenly grace through fasting and the greatest lamentation.

*[Note: Many manuscripts read “with an inferior outcome in battle.”]* After praying for the Lord’s peace, they returned to the war with greater intensity, since an oracle had given courage to them and increased their hope.

They then pretended to retreat from the front and arranged ambushes during the night behind the city where the enemy force was stationed. While the Israelites withdrew and the enemy pursued, an opportunity was created to attack the now-empty city. Soon fire was brought near and the blaze was kindled; the roar and raging heat of the flames revealed that the city had been captured. This broke the courage of the Israelites and raised the spirits of their enemies.

The men of Benjamin, thinking themselves shut in and surrounded, began to disperse and flee toward the desert before they were attacked from the rear. The Israelites, on the other hand, pressed them with a double line and pursued them as they scattered.

13. Twenty-five thousand were therefore killed—that is, nearly all the men of Benjamin—except for the six hundred who seized the stronghold of a rocky crag. Partly because of the site’s natural strength and protection, and partly because their desperation inspired terror in the victors, they survived.

Prosperity should remind one to be cautious; in adversity, vengeance is counted as victory. Nor were the women spared from this great disaster. The entire tribe of Benjamin—women, children, girls, and people of every age—was destroyed by sword or fire. An oath was also added that no one should give his daughter in marriage to a man of that tribe, so that every succession by which the name might be restored would be abolished.

14. When the war ended, anger also ended, and fury turned into repentance. Laying down their weapons, the men of Israel assembled together, wept bitterly, and kept a fast, grieving that one tribe had perished from among their brothers and that a strong branch of their people had been destroyed.

They had rightly made war as the price of the crime against the defenders of the outrage; yet, miserably, they had turned the people against their own entrails and afflicted both sides in civil war.

*[Note: “They had turned the people against their own entrails,” that is, the people had turned against themselves and against the destruction of the related tribe. This imitates Lucan, Book I, On the Civil War: “And the powerful people, turned by their victorious right hand against their own entrails.”]*

The outpouring of tears aroused compassion, and moved their feelings; consideration of their cruelty followed.

*[Note: The editions read, “struck their feelings.”]* Envoys were sent to those six hundred men of Benjamin who had defended themselves for four months on the exposed crags, or who had been sustained by the scarcity of the desert, which would have endangered the multitude of their besiegers.

The envoys lamented the common distress: the Benjaminites had lost fellow tribesmen, while the Israelites had lost relatives and allies. Yet the succession by which the tribe might be restored had not been entirely cut off. They would therefore consider together how both the oath might remain valid and one tribe might not perish, severed from the body.

15. An altar was then erected, and a sacrifice of reconciliation and peace was offered. Because the people of Jabesh-gilead were liable to punishment and the curse—for all Israel had bound itself by a solemn oath that anyone who did not go up with them to punish the outrage should be put to death—twelve thousand fighting men were sent against them, so that all the men and women might be destroyed by the sword, while only the young women who had not known a man in marriage would be spared.

*[Note: Some manuscripts read “twenty-two thousand fighting men.”]*

After all the people of Jabesh-gilead had been killed, four hundred virgins alone survived the destruction of the others.

*[Note: The Regius manuscript reads: “three hundred virgins … among four hundred young men.”]*

Israel took these women and decided that the men of Benjamin should lay aside their fear of war and take the untouched girls as wives, preserving both their youth and their chastity. The girls would have a legitimate reason before their husbands, since none of their people had taken up arms against them; and they would also be objects of affection, since they had been rescued from the ultimate punishment for the sake of the Benjaminites. In this way, marital partners were obtained for four hundred young men.

16. But since two hundred men remained without wives, we learn that provision was also made for them without violating the oath. A festival was celebrated every year at Shiloh. There the virgins were accustomed to rejoice and perform dances in honor of religion; some would go before their mothers, and the entire road would be filled by the procession of those journeying to the festival.

One of the elders said: “If those two hundred men of the tribe of Benjamin were to station themselves in ambush among the vineyards until the entire female crowd had poured out, and each man, rising from the vineyards, were to seize as his wife whichever woman chance brought before him, this would not constitute fraud. The people favor restoring the succession of the tribe, but because of the oath they cannot give their daughters in marriage. Yet it would not appear to violate the oath if they did not consider it necessary to prevent the seizure, since the oath would impose neither the necessity of compelling nor of prohibiting them. The Benjaminites should therefore provide for themselves without fear.

“If the girls’ parents should demand vengeance, they will recall them partly by entreaty and partly by turning the blame for the failure of careful guardianship back upon the parents themselves, since they had come out with their daughters knowing that the men of Benjamin lacked wives. That tribe, having suffered enough, now deserves not punishment but mercy. They have been treated with sufficient severity, and a part of their own body has been subdued. The people burned too fiercely in their desire to extinguish the succession of the tribe and destroy its own members. God is pleased that a tribe should not perish from the people, and that provision should not be made so harshly because of one woman.”

17. The Israelites approved this plan. The men of Benjamin carried it out: stationed in the vineyards at a suitable place and time, they occupied the roads filled with the female procession. The solemnity of the religious festival provided them with the occasion for marriage.

The daughters, torn from their fathers’ embraces, seemed to be handed over by their parents themselves into the men’s power; it was as though they were not being taken away from their mothers’ laps but were coming forth from them as women already betrothed. Thus the tribe of Benjamin, which had nearly been destroyed and wiped out, soon flourished again, providing a lesson that vengeance for chastity brings great destruction upon those who act insolently, and that retribution for violated chastity is severe.

18. Scripture teaches this not only here but in many places. In Genesis too we read that the Egyptian king Pharaoh was afflicted with punishments because he had attempted to violate Sarah, although he did not know that she was another man’s wife.

*[Note: “Punishments” means torments and tortures of suffering.]*

19. The Lord therefore wills that chastity be protected; how much more, then, does he will that integrity be defended? Consequently, no injury should be inflicted upon sacred virgins. For those who do not marry, and those who do not take wives, are regarded as being like the angels of God in heaven.

Therefore let us not inflict bodily insult upon heavenly grace, since God is powerful: neither can transgression escape him, nor can the bitter and grievous insult offered to a gift accepted by him and to consecrated virginity fail to move him. Farewell, brother, and love us, because we love you.

## EPISTLE VII

*[Written before A.D. 381.]*

Justus had asked what was signified by the command that half a didrachm be offered for redemption. Ambrose replies that faith and mercy, in which redemption consists, are signified by it. The same price was prescribed for all, corresponding to the manna, whose measure is explained in relation to wisdom and the blood of Christ. It also corresponds to the paschal lamb, which, being distributed equally, indicated that an equal redemption was granted to each person; and to this the same reward promised in the Gospel also refers.

He then adds that Christ is our redemption. Although he had no need of redemption for himself, he commanded that the stater be given not for his own sake but for ours. Ambrose explains what is signified by this stater and why the Jews failed to understand it, though Christians should not imitate them. He adds that half a didrachm represents those who devote part of their life to the world, which the Hebrew boys did not do. Finally, after explaining why the Lord paid what he did not owe, he unfolds certain mystical meanings suitable for the formation of moral conduct.

### AMBROSE TO JUSTUS, GREETING

*[Note: This is how the manuscripts read; the editions add nothing at all to the name Justus. Augustine, Jerome, Leo, and others commonly adorn the name of the person to whom they write with a title of dignity or profession. Ambrose, however, generally avoids such titles except in letters addressed to emperors. Hence it is more difficult to identify the recipients unless the context itself indicates them. Moreover, since the entire sequence of this letter breathes a certain familiarity, and since Justus himself is called “brother” by Ambrose—a term with which bishops in former times rarely honored anyone except bishops—we may infer that he possessed the same dignity. Since the holy Justus mentioned in the Roman Martyrology on September 2 was bishop of Lyons at that time and also attended the Council of Aquileia, having doubtless been invited by Ambrose, its principal organizer, no other Justus occurs to us to whom this letter could more appropriately have been addressed.]*

1. You do well, brother, to remind me that we should apply the stories exchanged in letters, and the conversation of absent friends, to the interpretation of the heavenly oracle, by asking me what that didrachm signifies, half of which a Hebrew is commanded to offer for the redemption of his soul.

*[Note: Among the Hebrews, the didrachm was equal in weight to the shekel. Thus, just as there was a double shekel—one profane, containing two drachmas or ten obols, and another ecclesiastical, containing four drachmas or twenty obols—so too a double didrachm must be recognized: the ordinary one, consisting of ten obols, and the sacred one, consisting of twenty. Hence what Ambrose calls half a didrachm is translated by the Vulgate as half a shekel; and what he calls a didrachm of twenty obols is rendered by the same Vulgate as a shekel of twenty obols. Münster, Fagius, and Vatablus discuss these weights further in their comments on this passage, as does Gualperius on Matthew 17.]*

For what is more congenial than to weave conversation about divine matters?

2. Half a didrachm is a drachma; and the redemption of the soul is faith. Faith, therefore, is the drachma which, as we read in the Gospel, the woman diligently seeks after losing it, lighting a lamp and sweeping her house; and when she finds it, she summons her friends and neighbors, asking them to rejoice with her because she has found the drachma that she had lost.

For the loss of the soul is great if someone loses faith, or the grace that he acquired for himself through the price of faith. You too, therefore, should light your lamp. “Your lamp is your eye”—that is, the inner eye of the mind. Light this lamp, which receives spiritual oil and shines throughout your whole house. Seek the drachma, the redemption of your soul. Whoever has lost it is troubled; whoever has found it rejoices.

3. There is also a redemption of the soul in mercy. “The ransom of a man’s soul is his wealth,” by which mercy is performed, since it helps the poor at its own expense.

*[Note: The old edition reads: “Faith, therefore, is grace; grace is mercy; mercy is redemption.” Several manuscripts differ from this only in reading “grace of mercy” and omitting the following word, namely “mercy.” But the Belvacensis manuscript and several others preserve the true reading, which we adopt.]*

Faith, then, grace, and mercy are the redemption of the soul, which is expended as a drachma—that is, as the full price of the complete sum. For it is written, when the Lord says to Moses:

“When you take the census of the children of Israel in their visitation, each shall give the Lord the redemption of his soul, and there shall be no destruction among them in their visitation. This is what all who pass through the census shall give: half a didrachm, which is according to the sacred didrachm. A didrachm is twenty obols; half a didrachm is an offering to the Lord. Everyone who enters the census from twenty years of age and above shall give an offering to the Lord. The rich man shall not add to it, and the poor man shall not diminish it from half a didrachm. When they begin to give the offering to the Lord, they shall make atonement for their souls. You shall take the money of the offering from the children of Israel and give it for the service of the tabernacle of testimony; and it shall be a lawful memorial for the children of Israel before the Lord, to make atonement for your souls” (Exodus 30:12 ff.).

*[Note: The manuscripts agree substantially with the old edition in this text of Exodus. The Roman edition, however, altered several expressions, which we display here together: “the price of redemption … in their plague … the offering of the didrachm … shall enter the census … shall give the offering … shall not diminish … the money of the offering … a memorial for Israel … to make atonement for their souls.”]*

4. Would the rich therefore have been lacking, if he could have offered more, or the poor, if he had possessed less, if this half-didrachm had consisted in money rather than in virtue? We must therefore understand that this is not a material but an intelligible drachma, which is considered something to be contributed equally by all.

Finally, we also read that the heavenly food—for the food and delight of heavenly nourishment is wisdom, with which those placed in paradise were fed, and which was the unfailing food of the soul, called manna by the divine word—was distributed to each soul in such a way that the division was equal:

“They gathered according to the command of Moses, both he who gathered much and he who gathered little, and they measured it with the gomor. He who had gathered much had nothing extra, and he who had gathered little lacked nothing” (Exodus 16:17–18).

Each gathered a gomor for every person according to the number of souls who were in his tents.

*[Note: The gomor is a measure equal to three Attic chenices, according to Jerome. Josephus says that it contains τρεῖς ἡμισυκοτύλους—three and a half cotylae. A cotyla and a hemina are the same, according to Fannius. It therefore contains one hemina and half of another. Nannius gives this account, and Fagius does not differ from him in his commentary on Exodus 16.]*

A gomor, therefore, is a measure of wine, as the interpretation states.

*[Note: The Roman edition alone reads, “a gomor, that is, a measure or completion.” Jerome, in On Hebrew Names, indeed explains gomor as “taking,” “completion,” or “perfection.” But that meaning is not at issue here; nothing is indicated except the kind of measure denoted by the term. For this reason Ambrose adds below: “A gomor, therefore, is a measure, and a measure of wine.”]*

6. There is also a measure of wisdom, which, if it exceeds the measure, does harm, since it is written: “Do not be excessively wise” (Ecclesiastes 7:17). Paul too taught that the distribution of graces is given according to measure, when he says:

“To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good: to one, a word of wisdom; to another, a word of knowledge; to another, faith of wisdom through the Spirit of knowledge according to the same Spirit; faith in the same Spirit” (1 Corinthians 12:7 ff.).

The grace is distributed according to the will of the Spirit. The fact that he distributes belongs to equity; the fact that he distributes according to his own will belongs to power. Or, it is because he wills to give each person what he knows will be beneficial.

*[Note: The manuscripts agree extensively in this reading. All the editions, however, retaining the common text of the Apostle, give it as follows: “To another, the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another, faith in the same Spirit; to another, gifts of healings in one Spirit,” and so forth.]*

7. A gomor, then, is a measure, and a measure of wine “that gladdens the heart of man” (Psalm 103:15). What is the joy of the heart except the delight of the drink of wisdom? This is the wine which Wisdom mixed in the bowl and offers for drinking, so that we may acquire sobriety and prudence. It ought to be poured equally into our senses and thoughts and into all the movements within this house of ours, so that we may know how to abound in everything and lack nothing.

8. More fully, however, this is understood of the blood of Christ, from whose grace nothing is diminished and nothing added. Whether you take little or drink deeply, the same perfect measure of redemption is given to all.

*[Note: This passage is cited by the Church of Lyons at the end of the book On Holding Fast to the Truth of Scripture, although the work from which it was taken is not identified.]*

9. The Fathers are likewise commanded to celebrate the Lord’s Passover—that is, the lamb—in such a way that they feast according to the number of their souls, neither more nor fewer. No one is to receive more and another less, but each according to the number of his souls, lest the stronger take more or the weaker less.

Grace is divided equally among all; redemption is divided; the gift is divided. There ought not to be more, lest someone depart empty of hope and redemption. There are more when some fall outside the number; but all the saints have been numbered, even the hairs of their heads, for the Lord knows those who are his. Nor ought there to be fewer, lest the weaker person be unable to receive because of the greatness of grace.

10. Therefore he commanded all to bring an equal devotion and faith to the Lord’s Passover—that is, to the crossing-over. Passover occurs when the soul lays aside irrational passion and assumes a good compassion, so that it may suffer with Christ and receive his passage into itself, so that he may dwell in it, walk in it, and become its God.

Grace, therefore, is equal among all, but virtue differs in each. Let each person therefore take a portion suited to his strength, so that the stronger may not lack and the weaker may not be burdened.

11. You have this in the Gospel: an equal payment is made to all who labor in the vineyard. But few reach the prize, few the crown, and few say: “The crown of righteousness has been laid up for me” (2 Timothy 4:8). The reward of generosity and grace is one thing; the payment of virtue is another—the recompense of labor.

*[Note: The Roman edition reads “another reward for labor,” but neither the old edition nor any manuscript recognizes the word “another.” The text is better as it stands, since the reward of virtue and labor is neatly set against the gift of grace and generosity, whereas “the recompense of labor” would be opposed to “the payment of virtue,” even though here virtue is understood as existing in labor. The same edition places “Christ” before “from death” and adds “of sin” after “from slavery,” but both expressions are absent from the manuscripts and ancient editions and are in no way necessary to the sense.]*

12. The didrachm, then, is redemption—or rather, half a didrachm. He redeemed us from death; he redeemed us from slavery, so that we would not be subject to the world, which we have renounced.

Therefore the Lord says to Peter in the Gospel that he should go to the sea, cast a hook, take the stater found in the mouth of the fish, and give it for the Lord and for himself to those who demanded the didrachm.

*[Note: The stater was the name of a Doric coin, and that it had the same value as the shekel, or greater didrachm, is shown not only by this letter of Ambrose but also by comparing Exodus 30 in the translation of the Seventy with the Vulgate translation of the same chapter. Thus, when Origen says in his commentary on Matthew 17, “The Savior commands a stater to be given, in which there were two didrachms,” he appears to be speaking not of the temple didrachms but of the ordinary ones. Nannius therefore wrongly criticizes Budaeus in his notes on this letter for teaching that the stater was worth four drachmas; if he meant the smaller drachmas, he did not depart from the correct value. Consult Budaeus himself.]*

*[Note: The manuscripts and the old edition read this way here and twice below. Not without reason, since the word occurs twice in the cited passage of Matthew, τὰ δίδραχμα, in the plural nominative; nevertheless, the singular “drachma,” which follows immediately, shows the intended usage. The Roman edition therefore everywhere substituted “didrachm.”]*

This, then, is the didrachm that was demanded according to the Law. But the Son was not obliged to pay it; the outsider was. For why would Christ redeem himself from this world, when he had come to take away the sin of the world? Why would he redeem himself from sin, when he had descended in order to forgive sin to all? Why would he redeem himself from slavery, when he had emptied himself in order to grant freedom to all? Why would he redeem himself from death, when he had assumed flesh so that by his death he might obtain resurrection for all?

### 13

The Redeemer of all certainly had no need of redemption. But just as He received circumcision in order to fulfill the Law (Luke 2:22), and came to baptism in order to fulfill righteousness (Matthew 3:15), so also He did not refuse to pay the didrachma demanded of Him; rather, He immediately ordered a stater to be given for Himself and Peter (Matthew 17:26). For He preferred to pay more than the Law required rather than deny what belonged to the Law.

He also showed that the Jews acted contrary to the Law when they demanded a didrachma from one person, although Moses prescribed that half a didrachma should be demanded. Therefore He ordered a single drachma—one for Himself and one for Peter—to be paid in the stater. A good census-payment of Christ, which is paid in a stater, because the stater is righteousness, and righteousness is above the Law. Finally, Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes (Romans 10:4).

This stater is found in the mouth of the fish—the fish whom the fishers of men catch; the fish who weighs his words, so that he may bring them forth tested by fire (Psalm 17:31).

[Note: The Roman edition reads “who weighs with the stater”; all the others, together with the manuscripts, omit the word “stater.”]

### 14

The Jews did not know this stater, which they gave to the betrayer. The Law, however, demands half a didrachma for the redemption of a soul, assigning that drachma to God, because it could not claim the whole didrachma. For scarcely could any portion of devotion be discerned in a Jew.

But whoever is truly free, a true Hebrew, belongs wholly to God; everything he possesses belongs to freedom. He has nothing belonging to the one who refuses freedom, saying: “I have loved my master, my wife, and my children; I will not go out free” (Exodus 21:5).

This refers not only to the master but also to the weakness of the man who has subjected himself to the world because he loves the world—or his own mind, that is, the νοῦς, the author of this will.

[Note: The older edition reads “or his own mind,” that is, “not.” The Roman edition had restored νοῦν, but had inverted the order of the words; we have restored it from all the manuscripts. This passage will receive considerable illumination if you compare it with Book I of *On Paradise*, chapter 2, section 11.]

It refers not only to the wife but also to the pleasure that takes up domestic concern, not that eternal concern. Therefore his master pierces this man’s ear at his threshold and door, so that he may remember his own statement by which he chose slavery.

### 15

And therefore, Christian, do not imitate this man.

[Note: Some manuscripts read “do not imitate Christ.” This is less correct, for it is certain that “this man” refers to the slave mentioned immediately beforehand. Observe also that it is not very customary for someone writing privately to a friend to sprinkle his letter with moral instructions concerning others, as Ambrose does here and at the end. Nevertheless, similar exhortations may be found in Jerome, for example in Letters 128, to Fabiola, and 129, to Dardanus. Hence one may infer that either both saints foresaw that their letters would be made public, or perhaps had decided to make them so.]

For it is written to you not that you should offer half a didrachma to God, if indeed you wish to be perfect, but that you should sell all that you possess and give to the poor (Matthew 19:21). Nor are you to reserve a portion of your servitude for the world; rather, you must deny yourself entirely, take up the Lord’s cross, and follow Him.

### 16

We have therefore understood why half a didrachma is demanded by the Law: because half was reserved for this worldly kind, that is, for secular conduct, domestic use, and posterity, for which it was necessary that a portion should also be designated from the inheritance.

[Note: The Vatican, Thuane, and Belvian manuscripts read *sortem exsortem*, that is, “a lot without a lot,” namely, something vain and useless, since it is earthly—just as the Greeks say βίος ἀβίωτος, “a life without life,” χάρις ἄχαρις, “grace without grace,” and δῶρον ἄδωρον, “a gift without a gift.” The other manuscripts and all the editions read *sortem ex sorte*, namely, a portion of that possession which, in the first division and allotment, was assigned to each tribe.]

Hence, when the Pharisees tested the Lord with the deceptive question whether He advised paying the census-tax to Caesar, He replied: “Why do you test Me, hypocrites? Show Me the coin of the census-tax” (Matthew 22:18–19). They offered Him a denarius bearing Caesar’s image. He said to them: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (ibid. 22:21), showing that they were so imperfect, although they thought themselves perfect, that they paid Caesar before God. For those whose first concern was the world were bound to pay first what belonged to the world. Hence He says, “Render”—that is, “you render”—the things that are Caesar’s (Daniel 2:17), among whom Caesar’s figure and image are found.

### 17

Those Hebrew boys, therefore—Ananias, Azarias, and Misael (Daniel 3:18), and that wiser Daniel (Daniel 1:8)—who did not worship the king’s image, who did not receive it, and who took nothing from the king’s table, were not bound to pay tribute. For they possessed nothing of what belonged to the earthly king (Deuteronomy 18:2). Therefore their imitators do not pay tribute, since God is their portion.

Hence the Lord says: “Render”—that is, “you render,” you in whom Caesar’s image is found, because you have brought it forth. But I owe nothing to Caesar, because I possess nothing of this world: “For the prince of this world is coming, and he will find nothing in Me” (John 14:30).

Peter owes nothing, nor do My apostles, because they are not of this world, although they are in this world. I sent them into this world, but they are no longer of this world, because they are with Me above the world.

### 18

What belongs to the divine Law is therefore commanded to be paid, not what belongs to Caesar. Yet even the perfect man—that is, the preacher of the Gospel—no longer owed this payment, since he preached more. The Son of God did not owe it, nor did Peter, adopted by the Father through grace. But, “lest they be scandalized,” He said, “go to the sea, cast a hook, and take the first fish that comes up; when you have opened its mouth, you will find a stater. Take it and give it to them for Me and for you” (Matthew 17:26).

O great mysteries! He gives the half-didrachma that the Law commanded, and does not deny what belongs to the Law, as though He had been made from a woman, made under the Law (Galatians 4:4). I have spoken of what was made according to the Incarnation: “from a woman” according to sex. Woman is sex; a virgin is a species. Sex belongs to the genus; virginity to integrity.

In what respect, then, He came under the Law, in that respect He was made from a woman—that is, in the body. And therefore He commands that the didrachma be paid for Himself and Peter, because both were born under the Law. He therefore commands payment according to the Law, in order to redeem those who were under the Law (Galatians 4:5).

### 19

Yet He commands that a stater be given, with which they might place a restraint upon their mouths, lest they commit sin through excessive speech. He commands that the stater found in the fish’s mouth be given, so that they might recognize the Word.

For since they demanded what belonged to the Law, why did they not know what belonged to the Law? They ought not to have been ignorant of the Word of God, because it is written: “The Word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart” (Deuteronomy 30:14).

He therefore pays the whole didrachma to God who has reserved nothing for the world. For righteousness is paid to God, and righteousness is sobriety of mind; the guarding of speech is paid to God, and that is sobriety of speech. For “with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10:10).

### 20

The drachma may also be understood as the Old Testament, and the didrachma as the price of both Testaments. For according to the Law each person was redeemed through the Law; but whoever is redeemed according to the Gospel pays the drachma according to the Law and is redeemed by the blood of Christ according to grace, possessing a twofold redemption, both of devotion and of blood.

For faith alone is not sufficient for perfection unless one also obtains the grace of baptism and, redeemed by the blood of Christ, receives [it].

[Note: Thus read the older edition and almost all the manuscripts. Some manuscripts, together with the Roman edition, read: “redeemed by the blood of Christ, he should take up the cross.”]

Therefore the drachma that is paid to God is good.

[Note: Whether the drachma and denarius were equal in value is disputed among Budeus, Alciatus, and Rudolph Agricola, as Nannius observes in his scholia. We refer students of this subject to them, as well as to Villalpando, Brerewood, and Walton.]

The drachma is not the denarius; they are different. For on the denarius is Caesar’s image, but on the drachma is God’s image (Matthew 22:21), because it belongs to the one God, for imitation of Him. It begins from one and spreads into infinity; and again, from the infinite number all things return to one, as though to their end, because God is both the beginning and the end of all things.

Hence those concerned with such matters called one not a number, but the element of number.

We have said this because it is written: “I am the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last” (Revelation 1:8); and: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deuteronomy 6:4).

### 22

You, therefore, also, in the likeness of God, be one and the same: not sober today and drunk tomorrow; peaceful today and quarrelsome the next day; temperate today and incontinent the next. For each person is changed by the variety of his conduct and becomes another person; in him what he was is no longer recognized, and he begins to be what he was not, degenerate from himself.

It is a serious matter to be changed for the worse. But be like the image on the drachma, unchanging, preserving the same character every day. When you see the drachma, pay attention to the image; that is, when you see the Law, pay attention in the Law to the image of God, Christ, because He is the image of the invisible and incorruptible God. Let Him shine for you as in a mirror of the Law (Colossians 1:15).

Confess Him in the Law, so that you may recognize Him in the Gospel. If you have known Him in the commandments, recognize Him in His works.

Farewell; and if you think that this didrachma entrusted to me has not been entrusted fruitlessly, do not hesitate to entrust me again with whatever you may have.

## LETTER VIII

[Note: Written before the year 381.]

He argues against those who denied that the sacred authors wrote according to an art, maintaining that they derived their principles from those very authors who taught about the same art. Then, after presenting several passages from the sacred books, he carefully proves that the rules of expression are observed in them.

### AMBROSE TO JUSTUS

[Note: It is highly probable that, when Ambrose had given Justus permission in the final words of the preceding letter to ask again about anything concerning the Scriptures, Justus asked him what he thought about the style and manner of expression followed by the writers of both Testaments; and that Ambrose satisfied him with this answer.]

### 1

Many deny that our authors wrote according to an art.

[Note: That many denied that the sacred authors composed their writings according to the precepts of an art should surprise no one. For, with regard to the Old Testament, although part of it was written by Moses, who was highly skilled in Egyptian wisdom, and part by others, many of whom are known to have been cultivated by extensive learning, nevertheless, because of their rare knowledge of the original language of those books, they were read almost exclusively in translations, and translations that rendered the words almost literally. They therefore necessarily displayed little elegance, being deprived of the natural qualities of their own language as well as of the advantages of a foreign one.

As for the New Testament, since its writers were rustic and unlearned—apart from Luke and Paul, who nevertheless denies that he made use of the attractions of human wisdom—how could we reasonably suppose that they would polish their writings with studied and artificial brilliance?

When Ambrose says that many denied that our writers wrote according to an art, this should therefore be understood not only of outsiders and unbelievers, among whom this accusation was frequently made, but also of Christians themselves, who recognized the truth of the objection. To omit many others, Origen, in Book I Against Celsus, speaks of the apostles as follows: “There was in them no force derived from the art of speaking or of delivery; nor did they employ any sort of dialectical or rhetorical order or method such as might attract their hearers according to the devices of the Greeks.”

Arnobius too, in Book I Against the Nations, does not deny that the sacred volumes were composed by unlearned and unpolished men. He calls their language not merely commonplace and sordid, but does not even contradict those who claim that our doctrines are burdened with barbarisms and solecisms. He is content to turn that barbarism to the advantage of the Christian cause, as Origen also does in the book cited above.

What, then, you may ask, does our teacher assert? Against the authority of so many men, does he maintain that the sacred books were fashioned according to grammatical canons or adorned with rhetorical flowers and embellishments? Certainly not. His sole contention is that the sacred authors expressed those matters that chiefly had to be explained for the understanding of each subject in such a way that they left posterity a form from whose observance an art could be constructed. This is entirely compatible with simplicity of style, or even with barbarism.]

Nor do we object. For they did not write according to an art, but according to grace, which is above every art. They wrote what the Spirit enabled them to speak. Yet those who wrote about art discovered art in their writings and composed commentaries and manuals of art from them (Acts 2:4).

### 2

Finally, the principal requirements of an art are that there be an αἴτιον, ὕλη, and ἀποτέλεσμα—that is, a cause, material, and result. Since, therefore, we read that holy Isaac said to his father, “Behold, the fire and the wood; but where is the victim?” (Genesis 22:7), what is lacking among these things?

For the one who asks is in doubt; the one who answers the questioner declares the matter and resolves the doubt. “Behold the fire”—that is, the αἴτιον, the cause; “and the wood”—that is, the ὕλη, which in Latin is called *materia*, material. What third thing remains except the ἀποτέλεσμα, the result, which the son asked about and the father reported in his answer? “Where is the victim?” “God,” he said, “will provide Himself a sacrifice, my son” (ibid. 22:8).

### 3

Let us unfold the mystery for a little while.

[Note: The Roman edition reads “Let us discuss it briefly”; the others, together with almost all the manuscripts, read “Let us set it aside.” This is by no means inappropriate, for it means the same as “let us unfold it,” or as though drawing it out into several parts.

Again, where the older edition reads “that the sacrifice of righteousness is also wisdom, and prudently,” and the Roman edition “that of righteousness is wisdom prudently,” the manuscripts agree with us, except that some read “patience” instead of “wisdom,” while others have both. Finally, for “Therefore the sacrifice of righteousness is, as it is, of wisdom,” which is read in all the editions and manuscripts, the Belvian manuscript alone has “Therefore righteousness, therefore wisdom.”]

God shows a ram hanging by its horns (Genesis 22:13). The ram is the Word full of tranquility, moderation, and patience. By it is shown that wisdom is a good sacrifice, and that it is good to know the prudent means of making satisfaction and obtaining reconciliation. Hence the prophet says: “Sacrifice the sacrifice of righteousness” (Psalm 4:6). Therefore it is the sacrifice of righteousness, just as it is the sacrifice of wisdom.

### 4

Behold, then, the mind, hot and burning like fire, which performs its work. Behold also intelligible things—that is, material. Where is the third element, understanding?

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “Behold sight, air, color; where is seeing? Behold sense, behold sensible things; where is sensing?” This is taken from the book of Philo cited above, where we read: “Behold sight, behold color; where is the seeing? And, in general, behold sense, the criterion, but also sensible things, the materials; where, then, is sensing?”]

Behold color; where is seeing? Behold sensible things; where is sensing? For material is not seen by everyone. Therefore God gives the gift of understanding, sensing, and seeing.

### 5

The Word of God, therefore, is the ἀποτέλεσμα, that is, the definition and completion of the argument, which is poured into the wiser and confirms what is doubtful.

Beautifully, even those who did not believe in Christ’s coming refute themselves, so that they confess what they think must be denied.

[Note: Ambrose’s meaning is easily understood if one observes that, after Philo had said that it belongs to God Himself to provide the victim, he adds shortly afterward: “But a ram is found held fast—that is, the Word remaining quiet and restraining,” and so forth, which was rendered above in section 3.]

For they call the ram the Word of God, yet do not believe the mystery of the Passion, although the Word of God is present in that mystery in which the sacrifice was fulfilled.

### 6

Let us therefore first kindle in ourselves the fire of the mind, so that it may work within us. Let us seek the material that nourishes the soul, as though we were searching for it in darkness.

For even the Fathers did not know what manna was. “They found manna,” he says, “saying that it was speech and the Word of God” (Exodus 16:15–16). From this source all disciplines continually flow and derive their nourishment.

[Note: All the editions and some manuscripts read “supplying material”; the other manuscripts read partly “of the one supplying,” and partly “of the one supplying material”; Laetus alone reads “nature.” Two verses later, where the older edition, together with all the manuscripts, reads “they found,” the Roman edition alone corrected it to: “But finding manna, they learned that it was the Word of God.” We would not strongly object if, in the received reading, it had merely changed “saying” into “learning,” for scribes could easily have erred here, and Philo supports the latter wording in a later passage, where he writes: “Having found, they learned the word of God and the divine Word,” and so forth.]

### 7

This is the heavenly food. It is signified in the words of the one who says: “Behold, I will rain bread upon you from heaven” (ibid.). The αἴτιον, then, is that God is at work, watering minds with the dew of wisdom. The ὕλη is that souls, seeing and tasting, take delight and ask where something brighter than light and sweeter than honey comes from.

The answer is given in the sequence of Scripture: “This is the bread that the Lord has given you to eat” (ibid. 16:15). This is the Word of God, which God arranged and ordered. By it the soul of the wise is nourished and delighted. It is bright and sweet, illuminating the souls of its hearers with the splendor of truth and soothing them with the sweetness of virtues.

### 8

The prophet had learned within himself what the αἴτιον of a completed undertaking was. When he was sent to the king of Egypt to liberate the people of God, he said: “Who am I, that I should go and bring the people out from the power of the king?” The Lord replied: “I will be with you” (Exodus 3:11–12).

Moses asked again: “What shall I say to them if they ask, ‘Who is the Lord who sent you, and what is His name?’” The Lord said: “I am Who I am. You shall say, ‘He Who is has sent me’” (Exodus 3:13–14). This is the true name of God: to be always.

Hence the Apostle says of Christ: “For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who was preached among you through us—through me and Silvanus and Timothy—was not ‘Yes’ and ‘No’; but ‘Yes’ has been in Him” (2 Corinthians 1:19).

Moses replied: “If they do not believe me or obey my voice, saying, ‘The Lord has not appeared to you,’ what shall I say to them?” (Exodus 4:1 and following). He gave him signs to perform, so that they might believe that he had been sent by the Lord.

Moses said a third time: “I am not worthy; I have a weak voice and a slow tongue. How will Pharaoh listen to me?” (ibid. 4:10). He was answered: “Go, and I will open your mouth and teach you what you must say” (ibid. 4:12).

### 9

Those questions and answers contain, in their midst, seeds of wisdom and θεωρία, contemplation. Yet the ἀποτέλεσμα, the result, is pleasing, because He says: “I will be with you” (Exodus 3:12).

Although He gave Moses signs to perform, when Moses again expressed doubt—so that you may know that signs are for those who do not believe, but the promise is for those who believe—He answered Moses’ weakness, whether of merit or of desire: “I will open your mouth and teach you what you must say.” Thus the perfect ἀποτέλεσμα was preserved.

### 10

You have this also in the Gospel: “Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you” (Matthew 7:7).

Ask ἀπὸ τοῦ αἰτίου—that is, seek from the author. You have ὕλη, intelligible things, with which you may seek. Knock, and God opens the Word to you.

The one who asks is the mind, which works like fire. Intelligible things are the material in which the ardor of the mind works, as fire works in wood. God opens to you the Word, which is the Ἀποτέλεσμα.

We have this elsewhere in the Gospel also, when the Lord says: “When they hand you over, do not worry about how or what you are to speak; for what you are to say will be given to you in that hour. For it will not be you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew 10:19–20).

### 11

You have this also in Genesis.

[Note: Ambrose has the same material in *On Isaac*, chapter 8, but explains it at somewhat greater length. There, after noting that it imitates Philo’s *On the Fugitive*, we add here that the Jew teaches that the type and image of those who discover knowledge not by laborious inquiry but by the force and acuity of their intellect is set before us in the patriarch Jacob. Philo proves this by noting that when Isaac marveled at the speed of his son, the son immediately attributed its cause to the divine will, from which the diversity of intellects arises.

By ὅροι below, one should understand not only precise definitions but also all formulas and methods by which anything is clearly explained.]

Isaac said: “What is this? What have you found so quickly, my son?” He replied: “The Lord your God delivered it into my hands” (Genesis 27:20).

The Ἀποτέλεσμα is the Lord. Whoever seeks through the Lord finds. Laban, however, did not seek through the Lord, because he sought idols; therefore he did not find them (Genesis 31:33 and following).

### 12

Beautifully, he preserved what they call ὅροι, definitions. The first ὅρος is: “Go and bring me some of your game, so that I may eat” (Genesis 27:24). By the kindling and fanning of his exhortation, as though by a certain fire, he rouses his mind to work and seek.

The second ὅρος is: “What is this that you have found so quickly?” This occurs in the form of a question.

The third ὅρος is in the answer: “The Lord your God delivered it into my hands” (ibid. 27:20).

The Ἀποτέλεσμα is God, who concludes and completes all things; concerning Him there can be no doubt.

### 13

There is also that ὅρος concerning spontaneous growth:

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “You shall not sow, nor shall you reap the spontaneous growth. And if you say, ‘If we do not sow, we shall not reap,’ the answer will be given to you, as it is written: ‘I will send you My blessing in the sixth year, and it will produce fruit for three years.’ This is certainly true. For …” The older editions, together with all the manuscripts, read: “If you do not sow, you shall not reap,” which is closer to Philo’s words, where one reads only: “You shall not sow, nor shall you reap its spontaneous growth.”]

“If you do not sow, you shall not reap” (Leviticus 25:11 and following). For although cultivation calls forth the seeds, nature nevertheless works within them by a kind of spontaneous power so that they may spring up.

### 14

Hence the Apostle says: “I planted, Apollo watered, but God gave the growth. Therefore neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth” (1 Corinthians 3:6–7).

God gives to you in the spirit, and the Lord sows in your heart. Act, therefore, so that He may breathe upon you and sow, so that you may reap. If you have not sown, you will not reap. You are warned, as it were, to sow: you did not sow, you will not reap. This is the sentence. The end corresponds to the beginning: the beginning is seed, the end is harvest.

### 15

“Learn from Me,” He says. Nature assists the learner; God, however, is the author of nature. It is also God’s gift that we learn well, because it belongs to nature to learn thoroughly; for the hard-hearted do not learn.

Growth comes through nature, which possesses the grace of a divine gift; but God gives completion and perfection—that is, that most excellent and divine nature and substance of the Trinity.

Farewell, and love us as you do, because we love you.

## RECORDS OF THE COUNCIL OF AQUILEIA AGAINST PALLADIUS AND SECUNDIANUS, THE HERETICS

The assembly of the Fathers, and Ambrose’s address to them concerning the preparation of the records.

[Note: Aquileia, where the synod was held in the year 381, was the metropolis of the region of Carnia, as Binius observes, and was so called from its waters; he adds several further remarks about it in his notes on this synod. Ughelli, following Strabo, reports that it was also named from the eagle. This council was convened against Palladius and Secundianus, supporters of Arian impiety. It is established that they were bishops in Dacia and Moesia, as the Fathers indicate in their letter to the emperors, although it is uncertain which diocese they belonged to. Ambrose mentions Palladius in Book I of *On the Faith*, chapter 6, section 45, as a man especially devoted to the Arian party. We also have a certain Palladius, opponent of Germinius, and Secundianus, an Illyrian priest and minister of Ursacius and Valens; but it is more probable that those men were different from these.

The bishops by whom these heretics were condemned, although they did not sit in very large numbers, were at least distinguished by outstanding merit. Their sees, together with their votes, will be found below for the most part; if anything concerning the more illustrious among them appears worth noting, we shall add it briefly.]

### 1

In the consulship of the most illustrious men Syagrius and Eucherius, on the third day before the Nones of September, at Aquileia, in the church, with the bishops seated—Valerian of the city of Aquileia, Ambrose, Eusebius, Limenius, Anemius, Sabinus, Abundantius, Artemius, Constantius, Justus, Philaster, Constantius, Theodore, Almachius, Domninus, Amantius, Maximus, Felix, Bassianus, Numidius, Januarius, Proculus, Heliodorus, Jovinus, Felix, Exuperantius, Diogenes, Maximus, Macedonius, Cassianus, Marcellus, and Eustathius—Bishop Ambrose said:

[Note: The Roman edition and Labbé read “on the Nones of September”; the Tellian and Chifflet manuscripts read “on the third day before the Nones of September.” Certainly, it was easier here to omit something or substitute a whole number for a fractional one than the reverse. But immediately below, where the same manuscript, Labbé, and Chifflet read “with the bishops,” the Roman edition alone omits “with,” with no small difference of sense.]

[Note: The Roman edition and Labbé read “Anemius and Sabinus”; Chifflet and the Tellian manuscript read “Anemius Sabinus,” with the Tellian manuscript reading “Sav[in]us.”]

[Note: The Tellian and Labbé editions add “Felix Bassianus … Marcellus Eustathius.”]

### 2

“We have discussed matters for a long time without committing them to records. Since such great sacrileges are being thrust upon our ears by Palladius and Secundianus that scarcely anyone can believe they could blaspheme so openly, and lest they later attempt by some trick to deny what they have said—although the testimony of such great priests cannot be doubted—nevertheless, since it is pleasing to all the bishops, let records be made, so that no one may be able to deny his own profession. What, then, holy men, is your judgment? It must be declared.”

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “For a long time, brother fellow priests, we have discussed our disputes without records. But because such great and open matters …”]

All the bishops said: “It is pleasing.”

[Note: The same Roman edition reads: “Let the records be written; it is pleasing … Our controversy must be confirmed and published by imperial rescript, so that it may be cited. Let the rescript therefore be read, if it is pleasing.” All the bishops said: “It is pleasing.”]

Bishop Ambrose said: “Our disputes must be confirmed in writing by the imperial rescript, so that they may be cited.”

The imperial document is read aloud in the council.

### 3

“Deacon Sabinianus read:

[Note: Before the following words of the rescript, the Roman edition inserts: “Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius, emperors …”]

‘Desiring to ascertain as soon as possible that priests should not disagree through ambiguous reverence for doctrines, we had ordered the bishops to assemble in the city of Aquileia, entrusted to the excellence of your authority on account of its merits.

[Note: The Roman edition similarly reads: “Nor could controversies of doubtful opinion be more correctly clarified than if we had appointed the bishops themselves as interpreters of the dispute that had arisen.”]

For controversies of doubtful judgment could not be resolved more appropriately than if we appointed the bishops themselves interpreters of the dispute that had arisen, so that the conflicting disagreements in instruction might be settled by those from whom the principles of doctrine proceed.

### 4

‘Nor do we now command anything different from what we commanded before. We are not reversing the wording of the order, but recalling the excessive number of those summoned.

[Note: The same edition reads: “cutting back the excessive number.”]

For Bishop Ambrose of the city of Milan, distinguished both by the merit of his life and by God’s favor, suggests that a multitude is unnecessary where truth would not struggle among many if it had been entrusted to a few. He also suggests that he and the priests of the neighboring cities of Italy would be fully sufficient to answer the assertions of those who stand opposed.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “For this reason we judged that the venerable men should be spared the fatigue of travel, lest anyone who was weighed down by advanced age, exhausted by bodily weakness, or of modest means because of praiseworthy poverty should be compelled to visit unfamiliar lands.”]

We have therefore judged that the venerable men should be spared fatigue, lest anyone burdened by advanced age, worn out by bodily weakness, or of modest means through praiseworthy poverty be required to travel to unfamiliar lands. And so forth.’

Ambrose asks that Arius’s letter, once read, be condemned by Palladius. Palladius evades the demand and denies that he will answer unless it is a general council. The Fathers strike with an anathema those who deny either the divinity or the eternity of the Son of God.

Palladius seeks an escape by repeatedly claiming that he confesses Christ to be truly the Son of God. His fraud consists in confessing Him while refusing to acknowledge that He is the same God and the Only-Begotten.

The discussion then moves to Christ’s immortality, and from that to His wisdom, and likewise from wisdom to goodness; here Palladius attempts, as usual, to make a mockery of the matter. He is then pressed on whether he acknowledges the Son of God to be omnipotent and also judge. After much evasion, he makes full use of his customary appeal to a general council.

At this point Altalus is condemned, since he too refused to answer. Palladius asks that lay hearers be admitted, and he is condemned.

### 5

Bishop Ambrose said:

“Behold what a Christian emperor has established. He did not wish to wrong the priests; he appointed the bishops themselves as interpreters. Since, therefore, we are seated in a priestly council, answer what is put to you.

Arius’s letter has been read; it will be read again now, if you wish. From the beginning it contains blasphemies: he said that the Father alone is eternal. If you think that the Son of God is not eternal, assert this in whatever manner you wish. If you think it should be condemned, condemn it.

The Gospel is present, and the Apostle; all the Scriptures are at hand. Establish your case from whatever source you wish, if you think that the Son of God is not eternal.”

[Note: Some editions read “assert.” The sense is: “But do you think it should be condemned? Condemn it.”]

### 6

Palladius said:

“It has happened through your deliberate action, as the sacred reading brought forward by you dictates, that this is not a general and complete council. Since our colleagues are absent, we cannot answer.”

[Note: Chifflet reads “as the sacred reading produced by you indicates”; the Roman edition reads “as the imperial sanction dictates”; the Tellian manuscript and Labbé read “the sacred reading.” The sense is not materially different. Below, where the same edition and Chifflet read “our colleagues,” the Tellian manuscript and Labbé read “our fellow priests.”]

Bishop Ambrose said: “Who are your colleagues?”

Palladius said: “The Eastern bishops.”

### 7

Bishop Ambrose said:

“In the past, councils were held in such a way that the Easterners, established in the East, had their council in the East, and the Westerners in the West. We, established in the regions of the West, have assembled in the city of Aquileia in accordance with the emperor’s command.

[Note: The Roman edition, Labbé, and Chifflet read “the command of the emperors”; the Tellian manuscript more correctly reads “the command of the emperor,” namely Gratian, whose name alone is repeatedly mentioned here.]

Indeed, the prefect of Italy also sent letters saying that, if the Easterners wished to assemble, they had the authority to do so. But because they knew the established custom—that the council of the Easterners was held in the East, and that of the Westerners within the West—they thought they ought not to come.”

### 8

Palladius said:

“Our emperor Gratian ordered the Easterners to come. Do you deny that he ordered this? The emperor himself told us that he had ordered the Easterners to come.”

Bishop Ambrose said:

“Certainly he ordered it, since he did not forbid them to come here.”

Palladius said:

“But your request caused them not to come. Under the appearance of a false intention, you obtained this and delayed the council.”

[Note: The Roman edition reads “under the appearance of pious but false piety.”]

### 9

Bishop Ambrose said:

“There is no need to wander any longer. Answer now. Was Arius right to say that the Father alone is eternal? Did he say this according to the Scriptures, or not?”

Palladius said:

“I will not answer you.”

Constantius, bishop, said: “You do not answer, [Note: [Col. 0918D] Since you blasphemed for so long, refer these words to those above: ‘For a long time we discussed the matter outside the official record,’ by which we are taught that the dispute had already previously been conducted on both sides.] you who have blasphemed for so long?”

Eusebius, bishop, said: “But you ought straightforwardly to disclose the freedom of your faith. If a pagan demanded from you how you believed in Christ, you ought not to be ashamed to confess it.”

### 10

Sabinus, bishop, said: “You requested that we answer. Today, at your will and under your pressure, we have assembled, and we did not wait for the remaining brothers who were able to come. Therefore it is not permitted for you to wander off into evasions. Do you say that Christ was created? Or do you say that the Son of God is eternal?” [Col. 0918D]

Palladius said: “[Note: [Col. 0918D] The Roman edition reads: ‘I tell you that we said this to you for that reason: that we would come so that you also might assemble; for we were awaiting our associates, but you did not act rightly in stealing in secretly.’ Labbé and Chifflet agree sufficiently with the Tellier manuscript, except that Chifflet alone has *we wrote* instead of *we said*; and instead of *we would prove* he reads, with Labbé, *we would assemble*. Finally, where we, together with both, have *steal in secretly*, the Tellier manuscript has *steal away*. Perhaps this is not entirely unsuitable, since the same sense is expressed below by *you stole away*.] I told you that we said this to you [Col. 0919A] so that we would come and prove that you had not acted rightly in stealing away from the emperor.”

Ambrose, bishop, said: “Let Palladius’s letter be read, whether he gave us this instruction; and it will be shown that even now he is deceiving us.”

Palladius said: “Certainly, let it be read.”

The bishops said: “When the emperor was present at Sirmium, did you appeal to him, or did he himself compel you?” And they added: “What do you answer to this?”

Palladius replied: “He said to me: ‘Go.’ We said: ‘Have the Easterners been summoned?’ [Note: [Col. 0919D] He says: ‘They have been summoned’; this was lacking in the Roman edition, and we have restored it from the Tellier manuscript, Labbé, and Chifflet.] He said: ‘They have been summoned.’ Surely, if the Easterners had not been summoned, would we have assembled?”

### 11

Ambrose, bishop, said: “Let the case of the Easterners be set aside; today I seek your judgment. [Col. 0919B] Arius’s letter has been read to you. You customarily deny that you are an Arian. Either condemn Arius today, or defend him.”

Palladius said: “It is not within your authority to demand this from me.”

Eusebius, bishop, said: “We do not believe that the devout emperor said anything other than what he wrote. [Note: [Col. 0919D] The same edition reads: ‘He ordered the Western bishops to assemble.’] He ordered the bishops to assemble; he could not have told you alone, contrary to his written order, that the case should by no means be argued without the Easterners.”

Palladius said: “Were only the Italians ordered to assemble?”

Evagrius, presbyter and legate, said: “He said four days beforehand, and two days beforehand, that he would be present. What, then, were you awaiting? The opinion of your associates among the Easterners, as you say? [Note: [Col. 0919D] The Roman edition reads *their presence*; Tellier, Labbé, and Chifflet read *their opinion*, which was to be awaited.] You ought to have given that instruction, not promised a confrontation.”

Palladius said: “Because I had come as if to a full council, I saw that my associates had not assembled; [Note: [Col. 0919D] The Roman edition reads: ‘But I judged that I should assemble according to the command, in order to say that you should do nothing to the prejudice of the future council.’] I therefore assembled in order to say that, according to the command, you were acting to the prejudice of the future council.”

### 12

Ambrose, bishop, said: “You yourself demanded that we sit today. Indeed, today you yourself said that we Christians had come to Christians. Thus you acknowledged us to be Christians. You promised that you would engage in a confrontation; you promised that you would bring forward or accept an argument. [Note: [Col. 0920D] Thus the Tellier manuscript reads, except that, through a copyist’s error, *you will bring forward* is written as *you will take away*; the printed edition omitted the phrase or read *you will accept*.] We therefore gladly accepted your preliminary statement. We wished you to come as a Christian. I presented to you the letter of Arius, written by Arius, whose name you say is frequently used to wrong you. You say that you do not follow Arius. [Col. 0919D] Today your position must be clear: either condemn him, or establish his position by whatever readings you may use.” And he added: “Therefore, according to Arius’s letter, is Christ, the Son of God, not eternal?”

Palladius said: “We said that we would prove ourselves Christians, but in a full council. We absolutely do not answer you to the prejudice of the future council.”

[Col. 0920A] Eusebius, bishop, said: “Without deceit, you ought to set forth your profession of faith.”

Palladius said: “And what are we reserving for the council?”

### 13

Ambrose, bishop, said: “By every voice condemnation has been pronounced against the one who would deny that the Son of God is eternal. Arius denied it; Palladius follows him, since he does not wish to condemn Arius. Consider, therefore, whether this man’s position is to be approved, and it may be understood whether he speaks according to the Scriptures or against the Scriptures. For it has been read: ‘The eternal power and divinity of God.’ The power of God is Christ (1 Corinthians 1:24). If, therefore, the power of God is eternal, then Christ is certainly eternal, because Christ is the power of God.”

[Col. 0920B] Eusebius, bishop, said: “This is our faith; this is the catholic understanding. Whoever does not say this, let him be anathema.”

All the bishops said: “Anathema.”

### 14

Eusebius, bishop, said: “He expressly says that the Father alone is eternal and that the Son began at some point.”

Palladius said: “I have neither seen Arius nor know who he is.”

Eusebius, bishop, said: “Arius’s blasphemy has been brought forward, in which he denies that the Son of God is eternal. Do you condemn this perfidy together with its author, or do you assert it?”
