Palladius said: “Where the authority of a full council is absent, I do not speak.”

### 15

Ambrose, bishop, said: “After the divine judgments have been pronounced, do you hesitate to condemn Arius, although he has burst apart in the midst?” And he added: “Let the holy men who are legates of the Gauls speak as well.”

Constantius, bishop and legate of the Gauls, said: “We have always condemned that man’s impiety, and now we condemn not Arius alone, but also anyone who does not say that the Son of God is eternal.”

Ambrose, bishop, said: “What does my lord Justus also say?”

Justus, bishop and legate of the Gauls, said: “Let anyone who does not confess the Son of God to be coeternal with the Father be held anathema.”

All the bishops said: “Anathema.”

### 16

Ambrose, bishop, said: “Let the legates of the Africans speak as well, [Note: [Col. 0920D] The Roman edition and Chifflet have ‘who brought here the opinions of all the priests of Africa’; Tellier and Labbé read as in the text.] who have brought here the opinions of all their fellow citizens.” [Col. 0920D]

Felix, bishop and legate, said: “If anyone denies that the Son of God is eternal, and denies that he is coeternal, I, the sole legate of the entire African province, do not condemn him alone; the whole chorus of priests who sent me to this most holy assembly has also already condemned him.”

[Col. 0921A] Anemius, bishop, said: “The head of Illyricum is none other than the city of Sirmium; I therefore am the bishop of that city. I pronounce anathema upon the one who does not confess the Son of God to be eternal and coeternal with the Father, which means everlasting. [Note: [Col. 0921D] Chifflet reads thus, and Tellier and Labbé do not differ from him, except that they read the first clause as follows: ‘but also that one, indeed, who does not confess.’ The entire passage in the Roman edition reads: ‘And also, as it has been recited, I pronounce anathema upon the one who confesses the Father alone to be eternal, alone without beginning, alone true, alone possessing immortality, but not the Son as equal.’ Ambrose, bishop, said: ‘And in this I condemn him.’] But I also pronounce it upon those who do not confess the same.”

### 17

Ambrose, bishop, said: “Hear what follows.”

And it was recited: “The one eternal, the one without beginning, the one true, the one possessing immortality.”

Ambrose, bishop, said: “Condemn also in this respect the one who denies that the Son is the true God. For since he himself is the truth, how is he not the true God? [Note: [Col. 0921D] The Roman edition alone has ‘the true God.’ Palladius said: ‘Who does not call the Son true?’]” And he added: “What do you say to this?”

[Col. 0921B] Palladius said: “Who does not call the Son true?”

Ambrose, bishop, said: “Arius denied it.”

Palladius said: “Since the Apostle says that Christ is God over all, can anyone deny the true Son of God?”

### 18

Ambrose, bishop, said: “So that you may know how simply the truth is required from us, behold, I say what you say—but I have an incomplete answer. [Note: [Col. 0921D] The Roman edition alone has ‘I have an answer.’] For when you speak in this way, you appear to deny the true God; but if you confess plainly ‘the true God, the Son of God’ [Note: [Col. 0922D] The same edition reads: ‘I say the true Son of God.’], establish it in the order that I propose.”

Palladius said: “I speak to you according to the Scriptures; I call the true Son of God Lord.”

Ambrose, bishop, said: “Do you call the Son of God the true Lord? [Note: [Col. 0922D] Here and in several passages below, where the Roman edition has *God*, the other witnesses and the Tellier manuscript consistently have *Lord*.]”

Palladius said: “Since I call him the true Son, what more is there?”

Ambrose, bishop, said: “I am not asking merely that you call him the true Son, but that you call the true Lord the Son of God.”

### 19

Eusebius, bishop, said: “Is Christ the true God, according to everyone’s faith and the catholic confession?”

Palladius said: “He is the true Son of God.”

Eusebius, bishop, said: “For we too are sons by adoption, but he is so according to the particularity of divine generation” (Galatians 4:7). And he added: “Do you therefore confess that the true Son of God is the true Lord according to birth and property?” [Note: [Col. 0922D] Chifflet alone adds ‘according to divinity.’]”

[Col. 0921D] Palladius said: “I call him the true, only-begotten Son of God.”

Eusebius, bishop, said: “Do you therefore think it contrary to the Scriptures if Christ is called the true God?”

[Col. 0922A]

### 20

When Palladius remained silent, Ambrose, bishop, said: “The one who calls him only the true Son of God and does not wish to call him the true Lord [Note: [Col. 0922D] Thus Tellier, Labbé, and Chifflet; the Roman edition instead reads ‘the true God,’ and seems to deny that he is God.] appears to deny him. Let Palladius therefore confess him in this order, if indeed he confesses him, and say whether he calls the true Lord the Son of God.”

Palladius said: “When the Son says, ‘That they may know you, the only true Lord, and Jesus Christ whom you sent’ (John 17:3), is this said as an expression of affection or in truth? [Note: [Col. 0922D] The Roman edition reads: ‘He says it with human affection, or in truth?’]”

Ambrose, bishop, said: “John said in his letter: ‘This is the true God’ (1 John 5:20). Deny this.”

Palladius said: “When I call him the true Son, I also profess true divinity.”

[Col. 0922B] Ambrose, bishop, said: “And here lies the deception. For you customarily speak of one and true divinity in such a way that you say it belongs only to the Father, not that the Son also possesses true and one divinity. Therefore, if you wish to speak openly, since you appeal to the Scriptures, say what the evangelist John said: ‘This is the true God’; or deny that it was said.”

Palladius said: [Note: [Col. 0922D] The same Roman edition adds: ‘Apart from the Son, there is no other begotten one.’] “Apart from the Son there is no other begotten one.”

### 21

Eusebius, bishop, said: “Is Christ the true God according to everyone’s faith and the catholic confession, or, according to your position, is he not the true God?”

Palladius said: “He is the power of our God.”

Ambrose, bishop, said: “You do not have the freedom to profess it; and therefore, anathema to the one who does not confess the true Lord, the Son of God. [Note: [Col. 0922D] The same edition reads ‘the true God, the Son of God.’]”

All the bishops said: “Let the one who does not say that Christ, the Son of God, is the true Lord be anathema. [Note: [Col. 0922D] The same edition reads ‘does not say that he is the true God.’]”

### 22

Again he added: “The only true one, the only one possessing immortality.”

Ambrose, bishop, said: “Does the Son of God possess immortality, or does he not possess it according to his divinity?”

Palladius said: “Do you accept the Apostle or not? ‘The King of kings, who alone possesses immortality’” (1 Timothy 6:16).

Ambrose, bishop, said: “What do you say about Christ, the Son of God?”

Palladius said: “Is the name ‘Christ’ divine or human?”

### 23

Eusebius, bishop, said: “According to the mystery of the flesh he is indeed called Christ, but he is the same God and human being.”

Palladius said: “Christ is a name of the flesh; Christ is a human name. And you answer me.”

Eusebius, bishop, said: “Why do you linger over irrelevant matters? When Arius’s impiety was being read—he says of the Father that he alone possesses immortality—you brought forward testimony agreeing with Arius’s impiety, saying from the Apostle: ‘He who alone possesses immortality and dwells in inaccessible light’ (1 Timothy 6:16). But if you understand it, he expressed the dignity of the whole nature in the name of God, since in the name of God the Father and the Son are designated.”

Palladius said: “And you were unwilling to answer what I asked.”

### 24

Ambrose, bishop, said: “I ask you openly for your position: does the Son of God possess immortality [Col. 0923B] according to divine generation, or does he not?”

Palladius said: “According to divine generation he is incorruptible, and through the flesh he died.”

Ambrose, bishop, said: “It was not the divinity that died, but the flesh died.”

Palladius said: “Answer me first.”

Ambrose, bishop, said: “Does the Son of God possess immortality according to his divinity, or does he not? [Note: [Col. 0923D] The Roman edition reads: ‘But have you not now revealed your deceptions and traps according to Arius’s profession,’ and so forth. The sense is more harmonious if some other support were available to him.] But have you not now revealed your deceptions and traps according to Arius’s profession?” And he added: “What do you think of the one who denies that the Son of God possesses immortality?”

All the bishops said: “Let him be anathema.”

### 25

Palladius said: “The divine offspring [or: ‘divine seed’] is immortal.” [Col. 0923C]

Ambrose, bishop, said: “This too is an evasive formulation, so that you do not state anything clearly about the Son of God. I say: The Son of God possesses immortality according to his divinity—or deny that he possesses immortality.”

Palladius said: “Did Christ die, or did he not?”

Ambrose, bishop, said: “According to the flesh. Our soul does not die, for it is written: ‘Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul’ (Matthew 10:28). Since, then, our soul cannot die, do you think that Christ died according to his divinity?”

Palladius said: “Why do you shrink from the designation of death?”

Ambrose, bishop, said: “Indeed, I do not shrink from it; I confess [Col. 0923D] it according to the flesh. For it is through him that I have been released from the bonds of death. [Note: [Col. 0923D] Thus the Tellier manuscript and the editions of Labbé and Chifflet; the Roman edition left the passage as follows: ‘that Christ died according to the flesh. For by his death, having been bound with the bonds of the devil, I have been rescued from the power of death.’ [Col. 0924D] It should be observed that the word *bound* in this context entails a negation, like *unclosed*, *uncovered*, and similar forms; the Roman editors do not seem to have noticed this.]”

Palladius said: “Death is caused by the separation of the spirit. For Christ, the Son of God, assumed flesh, and through the flesh he died.”

Ambrose, bishop, said: “It is written that Christ suffered. [Note: [Col. 0924D] The Roman edition reads ‘having suffered in the flesh . . . he is an Arian’; the other witnesses, together with the Tellier manuscript, omit ‘in the flesh’ and prefer ‘he is the devil.’] Therefore he suffered according to the flesh, [Col. 0924A] while according to his divinity he possesses immortality. Whoever denies this is the devil.”

Palladius said: “I do not know Arius.”

### 26

Ambrose, bishop, said: “Then Arius spoke wrongly, since the Son of God also possesses immortality according to his divinity.” And he added: “Did he therefore speak well or badly?”

Palladius said: “I do not agree.”

Ambrose, bishop, said: “With whom do you not agree? Anathema to the one who does not explain the freedom of his faith.”

All the bishops said: “Anathema.”

Palladius said: “Say what you wish; its divinity is immortal.”

Ambrose, bishop, said: “Whose—the Father’s, or the Son’s also?” And he added: “Arius piled up many impieties. But let us move on to other matters.”

### 27

And it was recited: “The one wise.”

Palladius said: “The Father is wise from himself; but the Son is not wise.”

Ambrose, bishop, said: “Then the Son is not wise, although he himself is Wisdom (1 Corinthians 1:24)? For we too say that the Son was born from the Father.”

Eusebius, bishop, said: “Is there anything so impious, so profane, as the denial that the Son of God is wise?”

Palladius said: “He is called Wisdom; who could deny Wisdom?”

Ambrose, bishop, said: “Is he wise, or is he not?”

Palladius said: “He is Wisdom.”

[Col. 0924C] Ambrose, bishop, said: “Then he is wise, since he is Wisdom.”

Palladius said: “We answer you according to the Scriptures.”

Ambrose, bishop, said: “As I see it, Palladius has also attempted to deny that the Son of God is wise.”

Eusebius, bishop, said: “Let the one who denies that the Son of God is wise be anathema.”

All the bishops said: “Anathema.”

### 28

Eusebius, bishop, said: “Let Secundianus also answer on this matter.”

When Secundianus remained silent, Ambrose, bishop, said: “The one who is silent wishes to retain a complete judgment.” And he added: “When he says ‘the Father alone is good,’ did he confess or deny the Son?”

Palladius said: “We read: ‘I am the good shepherd’ (John 10:11); and do we deny it? Who would not call the Son of God good?”

Ambrose, bishop, said: “Then Christ is good?”

Palladius said: “Good.”

[Col. 0925A] Ambrose, bishop, said: “Then Arius spoke wrongly of the Father alone, since the Son of God also is God, good to all. [Note: [Col. 0925D] The Roman edition and Chifflet read ‘since the Son of God is the good God.’ Tellier and Labbé have an ellipsis: ‘since he is good to all.’ Two lines later, where the edition reads ‘Christ good,’ the Tellier manuscript has ‘Christ the good God,’ which fits the following context better.]”

Palladius said: “Whoever does not call Christ good speaks wrongly.”

### 29

Eusebius, bishop, said: “Do you confess Christ to be good? For I too am good. He said to me: ‘Well done, good servant’ (Matthew 25:20), and: ‘The good man brings good things out of his good treasure’” (Luke 6:45).

Palladius said: “I have already said that I will not answer you until the full council.”

Ambrose, bishop, said: “The Jews were saying that he is good (John 7:12), while Arius denies that the Son of God is good.”

Palladius said: “Who can deny this?”

[Col. 0925B] Eusebius, bishop, said: “Then God the Son of God is good.”

Palladius said: “The good Father begot a good Son.”

### 30

Ambrose, bishop, said: “He also made us good (Genesis 1:31), but not according to divinity. Do you say that the Son of God is the good God?”

Palladius said: “The Son of God is good.”

Ambrose, bishop, said: “You see, then, that you call Christ good, a good son, but not the good God—which is what is being asked of you.” And he added: “Anathema to the one who does not confess the good Son of God as God. [Note: [Col. 0926D] The Roman edition reads: ‘who does not confess the Son of God as good.’]”

All the bishops said: “Anathema.”

### 31

He likewise recited: “The only powerful one.”

[Col. 0925C] Ambrose, bishop, said: “Is the Son of God powerful, or is he not?”

Palladius said: “He who made all things—is he not powerful? He who made all things—is he less powerful?”

Ambrose, bishop, said: “Then Arius spoke wrongly.” And he added: “Do you condemn Arius on this point as well?”

Palladius said: “How do I know who he is? I answer for myself.”

Ambrose, bishop, said: “[Note: [Col. 0926D] The same Roman edition reads: ‘Is the Son of God, God, powerful, or is he not?’ And below: ‘Then the Son is the good God.’] Is the Son of the Lord God a powerful God?”

Palladius said: “Powerful.”

Ambrose, bishop, said: “Is he the good God?”

Palladius said: “I have already said that the only-begotten Son of God is powerful.”

Ambrose, bishop, said: “The powerful Lord.”

[Col. 0925D] Palladius said: “The powerful Son of God.”

### 32

Ambrose, bishop, said: “Human beings too are powerful, for it is written: ‘Why do you boast of wickedness, you who are powerful in iniquity?’ (Psalm 52:3). And elsewhere: ‘When I am weak, then I am powerful’ (2 Corinthians 12:10). What I require from you is that you confess Christ, the Son of God, to be the powerful Lord; or, if you deny it, establish your denial. For when I say that the Father and the Son have one power, I say that the Son of God is powerful just as the Father is. Do you therefore hesitate to confess that the Son of God is the powerful Lord?”

Palladius said: “I have already said that, according to the debate, we answer you as we are able. You alone wish to be judges; you wish to be the litigants. We do not answer you now, but we shall answer you in a general and full council.”

Ambrose, bishop, said: “Anathema to the one who denies that Christ is the powerful Lord.”

All the bishops said: “Anathema.”

### 33

It was likewise recited: “The only powerful one, judge of all.”

Palladius said: “The Son of God is the judge of all. [Note: [Col. 0926D] The Roman edition reads: ‘I profess the Son of God; but the Father is the one who gives, and the Son is the one who receives.’] There is one who gives, and there is one who receives.”

[Col. 0926B] Ambrose, bishop, said: “Did he give it by grace or by nature? Judgment is also given to human beings.”

Palladius said: “Do you say that the Father is greater, or not?”

Ambrose, bishop, said: “I shall answer you later.”

Palladius said: “I will not answer you if you do not answer me.”

Eusebius, bishop, said: “Unless you condemn Arius’s impiety in due order, we shall not give you the opportunity to ask questions.”

Palladius said: “I do not answer you.”

Ambrose, bishop, said: “Is the Son of God, as it has been read, judge or not?”

[Col. 0926C] Palladius said: “If you do not answer me, I, treating you as an impious man, will not answer you.”

### 34

Ambrose, bishop, said: “You have my profession, by which I shall answer you. Meanwhile, let Arius’s letter be read.” And he added: “In Arius’s letter you will also find this sacrilege that you are attempting.”

Palladius said: “I am the one asking questions, and you do not answer?”

Eusebius, bishop, said: “We say that the Son of God is God equal to the Father.”

Palladius said: “You are the judge; your recorders are here.”

Ambrose, bishop, said: “Let your own men write, if they wish.”

### 35

[Col. 0926D] Palladius said: “Is the Father greater, or is he not?”

Eusebius, bishop, said: “According to divinity, the Son is equal to the Father. You have in the Gospel that the Jews persecuted him because he not only broke the Sabbath but also called God his own Father, making himself equal to God (John 5:18). What the impious persecutors confessed, we believers cannot deny.”

Ambrose, bishop, said: “Elsewhere also you have: ‘Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings, becoming obedient unto death’ (Philippians 2:6–8).” And he added: “You see that he is equal in the form of God? And, he says, he took the form of a servant (ibid.). In what respect, then, is he lesser? Certainly according to the form of a servant, not according to that of God.”

Eusebius, bishop, said: “Just as, when constituted in the form of a servant, he was not inferior to a servant, so, when constituted in the form of God, he could not be inferior to God.”

### 36

Ambrose, bishop, said: “Either say that the Son of God is lesser according to divinity. [Note: [Col. 0927D] Thus Tellier and Labbé; the Roman edition and Chifflet read ‘the Son is lesser than the Father.’ Immediately afterward, instead of ‘the Father is greater,’ the Roman edition alone has ‘the Father, he says, is greater than I.’]”

Palladius said: “The Father is greater.”

Ambrose, bishop, said: “According to the flesh.”

[Col. 0927B] Palladius said: “‘He who sent me is greater than I’ (John 14:28). Was the flesh sent by God, or was the Son of God?”

Ambrose, bishop, said: “Today we prove that you falsify the divine Scriptures. For it is written: ‘My peace I give you; my peace I leave you. [Note: [Col. 0927D] ‘Let not your heart be troubled,’ as well as the words ‘I said, I am going’ [Col. 0928D] before the phrase ‘I go to the Father,’ are missing in the Roman edition.] Let not your heart be troubled; not as the world gives do I give to you. If you loved me, you would rejoice because I said, “I am going to the Father,” because the Father is greater than I.’ He did not say: ‘He who sent me is greater than I’” (ibid.).

Palladius said: “The Father is greater.”

Ambrose, bishop, said: “Anathema to the one who adds anything to the divine Scriptures or takes anything away.”

[Col. 0927C] All the bishops said: “Anathema.”

### 37

[Note: [Col. 0928D] This entire line is missing in Chifflet.] Palladius said: “The Father is greater than the Son.”

Ambrose, bishop, said: “According to the flesh the Son is lesser than the Father; according to divinity he is equal to the Father. Read, therefore, that the Son of God is equal to the Father, just as the copies now produced also testify (Psalm 115:16). According to the flesh, however, why are you surprised that he is lesser, since he said that he was a servant (Matthew 21:42), since he called himself a stone, since he called himself a worm (Psalm 22:6), since he said that he was lower than the angels, because it is written: ‘You made him a little lower than the angels’ (Psalm 8:5)?”

Palladius said: “I see that you are making impious assertions; we do not answer you without hearers.”

Sabinus, bishop, said: “Let no one seek a judgment from one who has blasphemed in so many judgments.”

Palladius said: “We do not answer you.”

### 38

Sabinus, bishop, said: “Palladius has now been condemned by everyone; Arius’s blasphemies are far less serious than Palladius’s. And when Palladius had risen and wished to go outside, he said: ‘Palladius has risen for this reason: because he sees that he is to be refuted by the clear testimonies of Scripture, just as he has already been refuted. For it has been read that, according to divinity, the Son is equal to the Father. Let him accept that the Son of God has no one greater according to divinity. It is written: “When God made his promise to Abraham . . . because he had no one greater by whom to swear, he swore by himself” (Hebrews 6:13). You therefore see from Scripture that he has no one greater by whom he could swear. But it is the Son of whom it is said that he appeared to Abraham; hence he also says: “Abraham saw my day, and rejoiced” (John 8:56).’”

Palladius said: “The Father is greater.”

Eusebius, bishop, said: “When he spoke as God, he had no one greater; when he spoke as a human being, he had someone greater.”

### 39

Palladius said: “The Father begot the Son; the Father sent the Son.”

Ambrose, bishop, said: “Anathema to the one who denies that the Son is equal to the Father according to divinity.”

All the bishops said: “Anathema.”

Palladius said: “The Son is subject to the Father; the Son keeps the Father’s commands.”

Ambrose, bishop, said: “Subject according to the condition of the flesh. Besides, you yourself remember that you have read: ‘No one comes to me unless the Father draws him’ (John 6:44).”

Sabinus, bishop, said: “Let him say whether he is subject to the Father according to divinity or according to the incarnation.”

### 40

Palladius said: “Then the Father is greater.”

[Col. 0928C] Ambrose, bishop, said: “And elsewhere it is written: ‘Faithful is God, through whom you were called into fellowship with his Son’ (1 Corinthians 1:9). I say that the Father is greater according to the assumption of the flesh, which the Son of God assumed, not according to divinity.”

Palladius said: “What comparison is there with the Son of God? Can the flesh say, ‘God is greater than I’? Was it the flesh that spoke, or the divinity, since the flesh was there?”

Ambrose, bishop, said: “Flesh does not speak without a soul.”

Eusebius, bishop, said: “God was speaking in the flesh according to the flesh when he said: ‘Why are you persecuting me, a human being?’ (John 8:40). Who said this?”

[Col. 0928D] Palladius said: “The Son of God.”

Ambrose, bishop, said: “Then the Son of God is God according to divinity, and he is human according to the flesh.”

Palladius said: “He assumed flesh.”

Eusebius, bishop, said: “Then he used human words.”

Palladius said: “He assumed human flesh.”

### 41

Ambrose, bishop, said: “Let him say that the Apostle did not say ‘subject’ according to divinity [Note: [Col. 0928D] The Roman edition reads: ‘he said, becoming obedient unto death.’], but according to the flesh; for it is written: ‘He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death’ (Philippians 2:8). In what respect, then, did he taste death?”

Palladius said: “Because he humbled himself.”

Ambrose, bishop, said: “It was not the divinity but the flesh that was humbled and subjected.” And he added: “Did Arius speak well or badly in calling him a perfect creature?”

Palladius said: “I do not answer you, since you have no authority.”

Ambrose, bishop, said: “Do you profess whatever you wish?”

Palladius said: “I do not answer you.”

### 42

Sabinus, bishop, said: “[Note: [Col. 0929D] The same Roman edition reads: ‘You answer on behalf of Arius, but you do not answer our questions.’] You do not answer on behalf of Arius, and you do not answer the questions?”

Palladius said: “I did not answer on behalf of Arius.”

[Col. 0929B] Sabinus, bishop, said: “You answered to such an extent that you denied the Son of God to be powerful and denied him to be the true God.”

Palladius said: “I do not tolerate you as a judge, since I accuse you of impiety.”

Sabinus, bishop, said: “You yourself compelled us to sit.”

Palladius said: “I instructed you to sit so that I might accuse you. Why did you steal away from the emperor? To prevent a full council, you obstructed it.”

Ambrose, bishop, said: “When Arius’s impieties were being read, your impiety too was condemned, since it agreed with Arian impiety. [Note: [Col. 0929D] Thus Tellier, Labbé, and Chifflet, except that they have in this final passage: ‘during the reading of the letter, to put forward what you wished.’ The entire passage in the Roman edition reads: ‘It pleased you that Arius’s letter be read; it was said that you should raise the doubt you wished; you raised the proposition that the Father is greater than the Son . . . because the Son of God said that the Father is greater.’] It pleased you, during the reading of the letter, to raise the proposition that you wished. You were answered concerning how the Son said that the Father [Col. 0929C] was greater, namely because the Father is greater than he according to the assumption of the flesh. You also proposed that the Son of God is subject; and you were answered on this point as well, namely that the Son of God is subject according to the flesh, not according to divinity. You have our profession; now hear the rest. Since you have been answered, answer [Note: [Col. 0930D] The Roman edition reads ‘answer the following questions.’] the matters that are being read.”

### 43

Palladius said: “I do not answer you, because whatever I have said is not written down; only your words are written down. I do not answer you.”

Ambrose, bishop, said: “You see that everything is being written down. Indeed, what has been written provides abundant evidence for the judgment of your impiety. [Note: [Col. 0930D] The Roman edition and Labbé read ‘for the judgment of your impiety.’]” And he added: “Do you call Christ a creature, or do you deny it?”

Palladius said: “I do not answer.”

[Col. 0929D] Ambrose, bishop, said: “Less than an hour ago, when it was being read that Arius called Christ a creature, you denied it. You were given the opportunity to condemn the perfidy, but you refused. At least now say whether Christ was born from the Father or created.”

[Col. 0930A] Palladius said: “If you wish, let our recorders come, and let everything then be recorded.”

Sabinus, bishop, said: “Let him bring his recorders.”

Palladius said: “We shall answer you in a full council.”

### 44

Ambrose, bishop, said: “Attalus signed the proceedings of the Council of Nicaea. Let him deny the fact, since he came to the council. Let him say today whether he signed the proceedings of the Council of Nicaea or not.” When Attalus remained silent, Ambrose, bishop, said: “Although the presbyter Attalus is among the Arians, he nevertheless has authority to speak. Let him freely profess whether he signed the proceedings of the Council of Nicaea under his bishop Agrippinus or not.”

Attalus said: “You have already said several times that I have been condemned; [Col. 0930B] I do not answer you.”

Ambrose, bishop, said: “Did you sign the proceedings of the Council of Nicaea or not?”

Attalus said: “I do not answer you.”

### 45

Palladius said: “Do you now wish a full hearing to be held, or not?”

Chromatius, presbyter, said: “[Note: [Col. 0930D] The Roman edition reads: ‘You did not deny that the Son is a creature.’] You did not deny that he is a creature; you denied that he is powerful. You denied everything that the catholic faith professes.”

Sabinus, bishop, said: “We are witnesses that Attalus signed at the Council of Nicaea and now refuses to answer. What does everyone think?”

When Attalus remained silent, Ambrose, bishop, said: “Let him say whether he signed the proceedings of the Council of Nicaea or not.”

### 46

Palladius said: “Let your recorder and ours stand here, and let them write everything.”

Valerian, bishop, said: “Everything you have said and everything you have denied has already been written down.”

Palladius said: “Say what you wish.”

Ambrose, bishop, said: “Since Palladius repeatedly wishes to be condemned, although he has already frequently been condemned, I shall read Arius’s letter, which he refused to condemn. State what you think.”

All the bishops said: “Let it be read.”

And it was recited: “But not merely in appearance was he born,” and the rest.

Ambrose, bishop, said: “I answered you concerning the greater; I answered you also concerning subjection. Now answer yourself.”

### 47

Palladius said: “I will not answer unless the hearers come after the Lord’s Day.”

Ambrose, bishop, said: “You came to conduct the proceedings, but after I confronted you, you saw Arius’s letter, which you were unwilling to condemn, yet you cannot assert. Therefore you now withdraw and quibble. I shall read it out in full, point by point. [Note: [Col. 0930D] Thus the Tellier manuscript, which Labbé and Chifflet follow, except that Tellier places the period after the word *I recite*, while Chifflet places it before the adverb *whether*. The Roman edition would also fit this reading, except that it substitutes *you dare* for *you can* and repeats the word *again* before *I recite*.] Say whether Christ appears to have been created, whether there was a time when he was not, or whether he was always the only-begotten Son of God. [Col. 0931A] When you have heard Arius’s letter, either condemn it or approve it.”

### 48

Palladius said: “Since I accuse you of impiety, I do not use you as my judge. You are a transgressor.”

Sabinus the bishop said: “State what impieties you allege against our brother and fellow priest Ambrose.”

Palladius said: “I have already told you: I shall answer in a full council and in the presence of the hearers.” [Note: Tell. and Labb.: “with the recorders present.” Not sufficiently correctly.]

Bishop Ambrose said: “I desire to be refuted and challenged in the assembly of my brothers. So state what I have said impiously; but do I seem impious to you because I assert piety?”

Bishop Sabinus said: “Then does he seem impious to you who charges Arius’s blasphemies?” [Note: The Roman edition adds after *arguit*: “and I profess the good God, the Son of God.”]

[Col. 0931B] 49. Palladius said: “[Note: Cod. Tell.: ‘I did not deny him; I said that the Son of God is good.’] I did not deny the good Son of God.”

Bishop Ambrose said: “Then do you say that Christ is the good God?”

Palladius said: “I do not answer you.”

Bishop Valerian said: “Do not press Palladius too much; he cannot simply confess our truth. For his conscience is confused by a twofold blasphemy: he was ordained by the Photinians, and he was condemned together with them; and now he shall be condemned more fully.” [Note: Roman edition: “now, as an Arian, he will be condemned more completely.”]

Palladius said: “Prove this.”

Bishop Sabinus said: “He could not deny Christ to be the true God in any other way than by following his teachers.” [Note: The same edition: “deny Christ to be the true God”; certain Paris editions: “commit perjury.”]

[Col. 0931C] 50. Bishop Ambrose said: “You have alleged that I am impious; prove it.”

Palladius said: “We shall bring forward our exposition; but when we have brought it, then there will be a disputation.” [Note: Thus Tell. and Chifl.; Labb. has instead “then there will be an arrangement”; the Roman edition, “then there will be a proof.”]

Bishop Ambrose said: “Condemn the impiety of Arius.”

When Palladius remained silent, Bishop Eusebius said: “He is lingering over matters that are superfluous. Palladius has refused to condemn so many of Arius’s impieties; indeed, by asserting them, he has rather confessed them. Whoever does not condemn this man is like him and must rightly be called a heretic.”

All the bishops said: “Let Palladius be anathema from us all.”

51. Bishop Ambrose said: “Do you consent, Palladius, that the remainder of Arius’s writing be read?” [Col. 0931D]

Palladius said: “Provide hearers; let recorders come from both sides. You cannot be judges if we do not have hearers; and unless those who will hear come from both sides, we shall not answer you.” [Note: Roman edition: “If they do not have recorders.”]

Bishop Ambrose said: “Which hearers are you seeking?”

Palladius said: “Many distinguished men are here.”

Sabinus the bishop said: “After so many blasphemies, are you asking for hearers?”

Bishop Ambrose said: “Priests ought to judge laymen, not laymen priests. Nevertheless, state whom you are asking to be judges.”

Palladius said: “Let the hearers come.”

Chromatius the presbyter said: “Without prejudice to the priestly condemnation, indeed, let even the material belonging to Palladius now be read aloud publicly.” [Note: Roman edition: “let them also now be heard”; other editions, including Tell., have the wording as in the text.]

52. Palladius said: “They are not permitted to speak. Let the hearers come, and recorders from both sides; and these men will answer you in a general council.”

Bishop Ambrose said: “Although he has been found involved in many impieties, we shall nevertheless be ashamed that one who claims the priesthood should appear to have been condemned by laymen. For this reason also, and in this very matter, he must be condemned: he awaits the judgment of laymen, whereas priests ought rather to judge laymen. In accordance with what we have heard Palladius profess today, and in accordance with what he has refused to condemn, I declare him unworthy of the priesthood [Note: Chifl.: “and to be treated”; Tell. and Labb.: “and to be deprived.” The latter expression has the same form as the formula by which they said that he should be abstained from; it means “to be deprived,” the final wording used by the Roman edition.] and to be deprived of it, so that a Catholic may be ordained in his place.”

All the bishops said: “Anathema to Palladius.”

[Col. 0932C] 53. Bishop Ambrose said: “The most merciful and Christian emperor said that he had entrusted the case to the judgment of the priests and had established them as arbiters of the dispute.” [Note: Thus Labb. and Chifl.; Tell. differs only in reading the first part as: “and also so that he himself might be the arbiter,” which the Roman edition likewise presents; but it additionally omits *inquit* and, after *constituissemus*, adds *commisit*.]

“Since, therefore, it appears that judgment has been entrusted to us as interpreters of the Scriptures, let us condemn Palladius, who refused to condemn the opinion of the impious Arius; and because he himself denied that the Son of God is eternal, along with the other matters contained in the record. Therefore let him be held anathema.”

All the bishops said: “We all condemn him; let him be held anathema.”

### Condemnation of Palladius by the individual fathers

54. Bishop Ambrose said: “Since all these Christian men, brothers approved by God and our fellow priests, are present, let each one state his judgment.” [Col. 0932D]

[Note: Valerian, who is always named first in this council and is mentioned after Pope Damasus in two Roman councils—one of the year 370 and the other of 382—is believed to have succeeded Fortunatianus in the episcopate of Aquileia, being an Arian who became Catholic. His chief distinction is that he trained his clergy extremely well, so that afterward very many bishops were chosen from it as though from a sacred seminary. Jerome wished to be formed there in piety; Rufinus, for his part, relates that he was educated there in the monastery. Hermannus also believes that the emperor’s rescript was addressed to this same Valerian. He thinks the reason why Valerian is placed before Ambrose here was either that he was in fact metropolitan of Dalmatia, or at least that, while the see of Milan was occupied by Auxentius, the Italian bishops had recourse to him as metropolitan. Ambrose, therefore, was unwilling to strip him of this honor, especially in his own church. For more on the dignity of that same church, see Ughellus.]

Bishop Valerian said: “It is my judgment that whoever defends Arius is an Arian, and whoever does not condemn his blasphemies is himself a blasphemer. Therefore I judge that such a man must be excluded from the fellowship of the priests.”

Palladius said: “You have begun to play; play on. Without an Eastern council we shall not answer you.”

55. [Note: After the death of Germinius, who had seized the church of Sirmium, Anemius was ordained there by Ambrose against the will of Justina, who was striving by every means to have an Arian elected. Paulinus records a notable miracle that occurred at this ordination in his Life of Ambrose. As for Anemius’s earlier designation of Sirmium as the capital of Illyricum, this must either be understood of western Illyricum; or, if it refers also to eastern Illyricum, it must be said that the see of Thessalonica had not yet been raised by Damasus to metropolitan dignity, as Hermannus wisely observes in his Life of Ambrose.]

Anemius, bishop of Sirmium, said: “Whoever does not condemn the Arian heresies must necessarily be an Arian. Therefore we judge that this man must once again be excluded from our communion and deprived of the priestly assembly.” [801]

[Note: We have already observed, in the note on Letter 2, that the Roman editors wrongly added “to Constantius” the words “to the bishop of Orange,” although the same letter was addressed to Constantius. As for the bishop of Orange, one may infer his authority from the fact that we find him participating in several synods.]

Constantius, bishop of Orange, said: “Palladius, a disciple of Arius, whose impieties were long ago condemned by our fathers in the Council of Nicaea and today, when they were reviewed, were individually approved by Palladius—because he was not ashamed to say that the Son of God is alien to God the Father, since he confesses Him to be a creature; since he says that He began in time, he denies the true Lord—I judge him worthy of eternal condemnation.” [Note: The Roman edition alone has: “because he was not ashamed to say that the Son of God … and when he confesses Him to be a creature, when he says that He began in time,” and so forth.]

56. [Note: Since it is highly probable that this Justus is the same man to whom two letters of Ambrose are extant, we think that we have said enough about him there.]

Bishop Justus said: “I judge that Palladius, who refused to condemn the blasphemies of Arius and appears rather to confess them, can no longer be called a priest or counted among the bishops.”

[Note: The editions of the Councils by Binius and Labbé read *Citiniensis* in the text and *Tiniensis* in the margin; the Regius manuscript and Chifl. read *Ticiniensis*, from Divio. This strongly confirms Baronius’s conjecture that this Eventius was bishop of Ticinum, whose feast is celebrated under the name Juventius or Eventius on 6 February. His apparent rejection of that opinion on the authority of the Roman edition, where he is called bishop of Cenetum, is not based on a very firm argument, since the authority of the manuscripts and other editions contradicts that reading.]

Eventius, bishop of Ticinum, said: “I judge that Palladius, who refused to condemn the impiety of Arius, must be permanently removed from the fellowship of the priests.”

57. Abundantius, bishop of Trent, said: “Since Palladius defends manifest blasphemies, let him know that he has been condemned by the Council of Aquileia.”

[Note: We certainly believe that there is no obstacle to identifying this Eusebius with the man whom Ambrose calls, in *On Virginity*, chapter 20, no. 129, the fisherman of the Church of Bologna, suited to this kind of fishing—that is, to persuading girls to undertake sacred virginity. Under his leadership, Bologna possessed flourishing communities of consecrated women, which Ambrose praises in Book I of *On Virgins*, chapter 2, no. 60.]

Bishop Eusebius of Bologna said: “Because Palladius not only refused to condemn the impieties of Arius, written in a diabolical style and not fit even to be admitted to the ears, but also became their defender by denying the Son of God to be the true Lord, the good Lord, the wise Lord, and the eternal Lord, I judge, both according to my own opinion and the judgment of all Catholics, that he has rightly been excluded from the priestly assembly.” [Note: The Roman edition and Labbé read: “the true God, the good God, the wise God, the eternal God.”]

58. [Note: We have already said in the introductory note that this Sabinus, or Savinus, appears to be the same Sabinus to whom several letters of Ambrose are extant; accordingly, there will again be an opportunity to speak of him.]

Sabinus, bishop of Piacenza, said: “Since it has been made plain to everyone that Palladius, who is an author of Arian perfidy, also embraces its impiety, which is contrary to the evangelical and apostolic ordinances, the sentence brought against him by the entire council is just. Although he has already been deprived of the priesthood according to the judgment of my own insignificance, he must rightly be expelled from this most holy assembly.” [Note: Thus Tell. and Labb.; the Roman edition has: “Palladius, who is an author … and is its defender”; Chifl. has *assertorem*, “defender.”]

Felix and Numidius, legates of the Africans, said: “Anathema to the sect of the Arian heresy, in which Palladius was declared at the Synod of Aquileia. We also condemn those who resist the truth of the Council of Nicaea.” [Note: The Roman edition: “of which Palladius was declared a defender.”]

59. [Note: We briefly mentioned Limenius in the introductory note, and perhaps we shall add something concerning him in the note on the letter to Vercellae.]

Limenius, bishop of Vercellae, said: “It is clear that Arian doctrine has often been condemned. Therefore, since Palladius was summoned before this holy Synod of Aquileia and refused to correct or reform himself, but rather approved what was reprehensible and stained himself with the perfidy which he publicly confessed that he held, I too declare, by my sentence, that he must be deprived of the priestly fellowship.” [Note: Chifl.: “he contaminated himself with demonstrable perfidy.”]

Maximus, bishop of Emona, said: [Note: Sacred Geography places the city of Emona in the province of Istria under the metropolitan see of Aquileia. Valesius, however, believes it to be the city called Ema by Herodian and listed as the first of the cities of Italy.]

“Palladius, who not only refused to condemn the blasphemies of Arius but rather confessed them himself, has been justly and deservedly condemned; God knows it, and the conscience of the faithful has condemned him.” [Col. 0935A]

60. Exuperantius, bishop of Dertona, said: “Since Palladius refused to condemn the sect or doctrine of Arius, but defended it, just as my other fellow priests have condemned it, I too condemn him.”

[Note: This Bassianus, or Bassilianus, as he is called in Cod. Tell., is mentioned in the second letter to Felix of Como, no. 1; we made several observations there as well.]

Bassianus, bishop of Lodi, said: “I heard, as did my other fellow priests, the impieties of Arius, which Palladius not only did not condemn but confirmed. Let him be anathema, and let him be deprived of the priesthood.”

61. [Note: Philaster left behind a memorial of his learning, a little book *On Heresies*, but a much more illustrious remembrance of his holiness in the ecclesiastical diptychs, where he is commemorated on 18 July.]

Philaster, bishop of Brescia, said: “Together with all the others, I have condemned the blasphemies and iniquity of Palladius, who follows and defends Arian doctrine.” [Col. 0935B]

[Note: This Constantius is called “of Sciscia” from Sciscia, a city situated on the borders of Pannonia. Hence it may be inferred that he is not the man to whom the preceding letter to Constantius was written, since Sciscia is at a very great distance from Imola, which is described as near the church of that Constantius.]

Constantius, bishop of Sciscia, said: “Like my other fellow priests, I too judge that Palladius, who did not condemn the blasphemies and impieties of Arius, must be condemned.”

[Note: We have the doctrine and piety of Heliodorus recorded in several letters of Jerome; his name is also read in the catalogue of the saints on 5 July.]

Heliodorus, bishop of Altinum, said: “Together with my other fellow priests, I condemn the perfidy of Arius and of all the heretics whose associate Palladius is—Palladius, whose foolish heart has not confessed the truth.”

62. [Note: The episcopal see of Felix of Jadera, or Jadertum, was Jadera, a city of Dalmatia, today Zara Vecchia.]

Felix, bishop of Jadera, said: “I condemn Palladius, who speaks blasphemies against the Son just as Arius did, together with all the others.”

Theodorus, bishop of Octodurum, said: “We judge Palladius, who denied Christ to be the true God, coeternal with the Father, to be neither a Christian nor in any way a priest.” [Col. 0935C]

Dominus, bishop of Gratianopolis, said: “Like my brothers, I too judge that Palladius, who persists in the perfidy of Arius, must be condemned forever.”

63. Proculus, bishop of Marseille, said: “Palladius, who by refusing to condemn Arius’s blasphemies defended them under a certain impious inheritance, has been designated a blasphemer by the sentence of many already venerable priests and declared alien to the priesthood. Accordingly, my judgment likewise designates him as condemned forever.”

Diogenes, bishop of Genoa, said: “Together with my other fellow priests, I judge that Palladius, who does not confess Christ the Lord to be the true God, like and equal to the Father, but rather denies it, must incur condemnation.” [Col. 0936A] [Note: Cod. Tell.: “that he must share his condemnations with my other brothers or fellow priests”; but the editions agree among themselves, except that the Roman edition has “with the priests” instead of “with his fellow priests.”]

64. Amantius, bishop of Nice, said: “Since Palladius did not destroy the sect of Arius, I too condemn him according to the judgment of my fellow priests.”

Januarius the bishop said: “Just as all my fellow priests condemned Palladius, so I too judge by the same sentence that he must be condemned.”

### Secundianus, when questioned about acknowledging Christ as the true God, attempts to mock the fathers with the same evasion as Palladius

[Col. 0936B] 65. When Secundianus had withdrawn for a while, [Note: The Roman edition alone: “When Secundianus had slipped away briefly and later returned.”] Bishop Ambrose said: “You have heard, Secundianus, the kind of sentence Palladius, the impious man, received after being condemned by the priestly council. Although we were displeased that you did not recoil from his madness—that is, Palladius’s madness—I nevertheless ask you certain questions specifically. Do you say that our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, is the true God or not the true God?”

Secundianus said: “Whoever denies that the Father of our Lord and God Jesus Christ is God is not a Christian; [Note: The same edition alone adds: “nor is he a Christian who denies Christ to be the true Son of God.” And below: “I call the only-begotten Son the true Son of God.”] nor is he a Christian who denies the true Lord, the Son of God.”

Bishop Ambrose said: “Do you confess the Son of God to be the true God?”

Secundianus said: “I call Him the true Son of God, the true only-begotten Son of God.” [Col. 0936C]

66. Bishop Ambrose said: “Do you call Him the true Lord?”

Secundianus said: “The true only-begotten Son. Who denies the true Son of God?”

Bishop Eusebius said: “It is not enough that you confess the only-begotten Son of God, for everyone confesses this. What matters is that Arius called the Father alone Lord, alone true, and denied the Son of God to be the true Lord. Do you simply confess the Son of God to be the true God?” [Note: Thus Tell., Labb., and Chifl.; the Roman edition has: “It is not enough that you confess the true Son of God …” It continues: “This chiefly moves us: Arius called the Father alone God, alone good; but he denied the Son of God to be the true God. Therefore, simply …”]

Secundianus said: “I do not know who Arius was; I do not know what he said. You are speaking with me, a living man, to a living man. I say what Christ said: ‘the only-begotten One who is in the bosom of the Father’ (John 1:18); therefore He asserts Himself to be the Father’s only-begotten Son. The only-begotten Son, then, is the true Son of God.” [Col. 0937A]

67. Bishop Ambrose said: “Is He the true God, the true Son of God, God?” [Note: The Roman edition similarly has: “Is He the true Son of God?” He replies, “And he adds: In the divine readings it is written that those who swear …” Two lines later: “Therefore we confess the Son of God to be true …”]

“And it is written in the divine books: ‘Those who swear upon the earth shall swear by the true God’ (Isaiah 66:16). There can be no doubt that this concerns Christ. We therefore profess the true God; this is our faith and our confession: the only-begotten Son of the Father is the true God. You too speak of the true God, and then of the Son as the true God.”

Secundianus said: “Concerning the true God.”

804 68. Bishop Ambrose said: “Is the Son of God the true God?”

[Col. 0937B] Secundianus said: “[Note: Tell. and Labb.: “Then the only-begotten Son is a liar.” And below: “But the only-begotten God.” In what follows they omit the word *true* once and again.] “Then He is a liar.”

Bishop Ambrose said: “You are practicing deception here, so as not to say ‘the true God,’ but ‘the true only-begotten God.’ Therefore say simply: ‘The only-begotten Son of God is the true God.’”

Secundianus said: “I said that He is the only-begotten Son of God.”

69. Bishop Eusebius said: “Photinus does not deny this; Sabellius confesses it.”

Bishop Ambrose said: “And whoever does not confess this is rightly condemned. Thus I question you again and again, although by evasions you have denied the truth. I am not asking you merely to call Him the true only-begotten Son of God, but also the true God.”

Secundianus said: “I profess myself a servant of the truth. What I say is not being written down, whereas what you say is written down. I call Christ the true Son of God. Who denies that He is the true Son of God?” [Col. 0937C]

70. Bishop Ambrose said: “[Note: Tell. and Labb. likewise: ‘Whoever denies the only-begotten …’] ‘Whoever denies the true God, the only-begotten Son of God, let him be anathema.’”

Secundianus said: “The true God, the only-begotten Son of God—[Note: Roman edition: “What are you presenting to me?”] what are you professing to me that is not written?”

Bishop Ambrose said: “It is manifest sacrilege that Arius denied Christ, the Son of God, to be the true God.”

Secundianus said: “I call Jesus Christ, the Son of God, God—the one who is called Christ, the true Son of God; I call Him the Son of God, but ‘true God’ is not written.” [Note: Roman edition alone: “I call Jesus Christ, the Son of God—for Christ is called the Son of God—the true Son of God; but ‘true God’ is not written.”]

[Col. 0937D] 71. Bishop Ambrose said: “Have you still not come to your senses?” And he added: “So that he may not appear to have had anything slipped past him, let him confirm his own judgment. Let him therefore say that the only-begotten Christ, the Son of God, is the true God.”

Secundianus said: “I have already said it. What more do you wish to extort from me?”

Bishop Ambrose said: “What did you say? Certainly, even if you had said ‘true’ many times, you would still have to answer; for what is said gloriously must often be repeated.” [Note: The same Roman edition: “If you had said ‘true’ many times, you would still have to answer. For whatever is said with glory …”]

Secundianus said: “It has been said: ‘Let your word be yes, yes; no, no’ (Matthew 5:37).”

72. Bishop Ambrose said: “Whoever says that the Father Himself is the Son is sacrilegious. What I ask of you is that you say that, from the true God, the true God, the Son of God, was born.”

Secundianus said: “I say that the Son was begotten by God, who Himself says, ‘I have begotten you’ (Psalm 109:3); and I say that He is the one who confesses Himself to have been begotten.” [Col. 0938B] [Note: The Roman edition: “the Father saying, ‘Today I have begotten you,’ and confessing that He has begotten Him, I say that He is the true only-begotten Son of God.”]

73. Bishop Ambrose said: “Is He the true God from the true God?”

Secundianus said: “And when you add ‘true’ even to the name, you hear what sort of faith there is in you, and whether you are a Christian?”

Bishop Eusebius said: “Who denied Him to be the true God? Arius and Palladius denied it. If you believe Him to be the true God, you ought to designate Him plainly.”

74. Bishop Ambrose said: “If you do not say that the true God was born from the true God, you have denied Christ.”

Secundianus said: “When questioned about the Son, I gave an answer; I answered as I ought to profess. [Col. 0938C] [Note: Roman edition: “We have our exposition … it shall be read.”] We have your exposition; we shall bring it forward; let it be read.”

Ambrose said: “You ought to have brought it today; instead, you are trying to evade the matter. [Note: Tell. and Labb.: “Demand a profession from me.”] You demand a profession from me, and I demand a profession from you. Is the Son of God the true God?”

Secundianus said: “He is the only-begotten God, the Son of God. [Note: Roman edition: “the true Son of God. And I ask you …”] And I ask Him: Is He the only-begotten One?”

75. Bishop Ambrose said: “[Note: Thus Tell. and Labb.; the Roman edition has: “Let reason move us, and not impiety”; Chifl.: “Let impiety move us by reason.”] Let reason, and your impiety and foolishness, move us. [Note: Roman edition: “When you say ‘the true only-begotten Son’ … so that you may dissolve this. But without anyone’s support.”] When you say ‘the true only-begotten God,’ you do not say ‘the true God,’ but ‘the true only-begotten One.’ Therefore, to remove this question, answer thus: ‘Is the true God from the true God?’”

Secundianus said: “Then did God not beget God? [Col. 0938D] [Note: The same edition: “Did He not beget the Son? Is that true God who exists? And what is ‘begot,’ unless it means that God is one?” And below: “I say the true only-begotten One, and the true God”; the other editions, including Tell., have the wording as in the text.] The true God who exists, who is what He is, begot; did He beget one true, only-begotten Son?”

[Col. 0939A] Ambrose said: “You do not confess the true God, but wish to say ‘the true only-begotten One.’ I too say ‘the only-begotten One,’ but also ‘the true God.’” [Note: The same edition: “I say the true only-begotten One and the true God.”]

Secundianus said: “I say that He was begotten by the Father; I say to everyone that He was truly begotten.”

### Names of the bishops and presbyters who attended the council

76. Valerian, bishop of Aquileia.

Ambrose, bishop of Milan.

Eusebius, bishop of Bologna.

Limenius, bishop of Vercellae.

Anemius, bishop of Sirmium in Illyricum.

Sabinus, bishop of Piacenza.

Abundantius, bishop of Trent.

[Col. 0939B] Philaster, bishop of Brescia.

Constantinus, bishop of Orange, legate of the Gauls.

Theodorus, bishop of Octodurum.

Dominus, bishop of Gratianopolis.

Amantius, bishop of Nice.

Maximus, bishop of Emona.

Bassianus, bishop of Lodi.

Proculus, bishop of Marseille, legate of the Gauls.

Heliodorus, bishop of Altinum.

Felix, bishop of Jadera.

Eventius, bishop of Ticinum.

Exsuperantius, bishop of Dertona.

Diogenes, bishop of Genoa.

[Col. 0939C] Constantius, bishop of Sciscia.

Justus, bishop of Lyon, another legate of the Gauls.

Felix, legate of the Africans.

Numidius, legate of the Africans.

[Note: It is not stated from what nation Evagrius came as legate to the Synod; perhaps he represented some private bishop. For when the votes of the nations were being collected, he remained silent.]

Evagrius, presbyter and legate.

Artemius, Almachius, Januarius, Jovinus, Macedonius, Cassianus, Marcellus, Eustathius, Maximus, [Note: We spoke in the introductory notice of this Chromatius, who later became bishop of Aquileia, and perhaps we shall say something about him again.]

Chromatius, presbyter.

806 **LETTER IX**

The Council gives thanks to the bishops of Gaul and writes to them concerning the condemnation of Palladius and Secundianus.

The Council that convened at Aquileia, to its most beloved brothers, the bishops of the Gallic provinces of Viennensis and First and Second Narbonensis. [Note: Cod. Tell.: “Letter of the Council of Aquileia to the bishops of Italy.” But the copyist contradicts himself by adding: “The Council … to the bishops of the province of the Viennenses and Narbonenses,” and so forth.]

[Col. 0939D]

1. We give thanks to your holy unanimity because, in our lords and brothers Constantius and Proculus, you have granted us the presence of all of you; and, following the ordinances of our forefathers, you have added no slight weight to our judgments, since the profession of your holiness agrees with them, most beloved lords and brothers. Therefore, just as we gladly received the holy men named above into your fellowship and ours, so we dismiss them with abundant thanksgiving.

2. How necessary this assembly has been will become clear from the facts themselves, since Palladius and Secundianus—the adversaries and enemies of God, defenders of the Arian sect and heresy, the only two who dared to come to the Council—received, while present, the sentence they deserved, having been convicted of impiety. Farewell. May our almighty God protect you unharmed and flourishing, most beloved lords and brothers. Amen.

## LETTER X

[Col. 0940B] It gives thanks to the emperors for convening the synod; explains who attended it; recalls the evasions, blasphemies, and obstinacy of the heretics; and finally implores the emperors’ faith, so that the decrees of the council may be put into execution by their authority and certain other heretics may also be restrained.

To the most merciful and Christian emperors and most blessed princes Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius, the holy Council that convened at Aquileia.

1. Blessed be God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who gave you the Roman empire; and blessed be our Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, who in His goodness guards your kingdom. Before Him [Note: The Roman edition alone: “we give thanks for you … because our faith also …”] we give thanks to you, most merciful princes, because you have shown devotion to the faith and have endeavored to assemble a priestly Council in order to remove disputes, while preserving honor for the bishops through your gracious favor, so that no willing man might be absent and no unwilling man might be compelled. [Note: The Roman edition had moved everything from “might be compelled unwillingly” through “burdened by old age” to the later passage concerning “the needy and poor.”]

2. Accordingly, in obedience to the command of your gentleness, we assembled without envy of numbers and with a willingness to debate. No bishops from the heretics were found except Palladius and Secundianus, names of an ancient perfidy, on whose account they demanded that a council be assembled from the farthest regions of the Roman world. Behold, no man burdened by the years of old age, whose venerable gray hair alone would have commanded respect, was compelled to come from the remotest shore of the Ocean; [Note: The Roman edition omits the words “and nothing was lacking from the Council.”] nothing was lacking from the Council. [Col. 0940D] No one dragging along a feeble body weighed down by the cost of fasts was forced, through the hardship of travel, to lament the losses caused by diminished strength; finally, no one who gloried in poverty among priests groaned because he had been deprived of assistance for making the journey. Thus, most merciful Prince Gratian, what divine Scripture praised has been fulfilled in you: “Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and the poor” (Psalm 40:2). [Col. 0941A]

3. But how grievous it would have been if, on account of only two men, [Note: Thus Cod. Reg. and Tell., as well as the editions of Labbé and Chifl., except that Tell. originally had *curiosos*, and Reg. alone reads *summis destitui* instead of *suis destitui*. At the end of the whole sentence, where Tell. and Chifl. have “following the ordinances of our forefathers,” Cod. Regius has “the rescripts,” while Labbé has “the commands of our forefathers.” The Roman edition reads the passage as follows: “May your clemency consider that, while curious priests from throughout the world came here in the faith, the churches were deprived of their chief pastors. Nevertheless, although some were unable to come because of the length of the journey, all from nearly every western province were present through legates, who by their attestations … and who testified to what accords with the teaching of the Council of Nicaea, as the writings make clear. Therefore, now let the votes of the peoples resound throughout your empire, just as the defenders of the faith were not absent here according to your will. Finally, although … those who opposed …”] priests devoted to perfidy should leave the churches throughout the world deprived of their chief priests! Although they could not come because of the length of the journey, nevertheless nearly all were present from the western provinces through legates whom they had sent; by clear attestations they declared that they held what we assert and that it accords with the teaching of the Council of Nicaea, as the documents appended below show. Therefore, the prayers of the peoples now sound in harmony everywhere under your rule, and yet the defenders of the faith were not lacking here at your command. For although the ordinances of our forefathers had been set forth clearly, and it is impious and sacrilegious to deviate from them, we nevertheless offered an opportunity for debate.

4. First, therefore, we examined the very beginning of the controversy that had arisen, and we decided that the letter of Arius should be read. He is found to be the originator of the Arian heresy, from whom the heresy also received its name. We did this so that, since they were accustomed to deny that they were Arians, they might either condemn Arius’s blasphemies by denouncing them, defend them by asserting them, or at least not refuse the name of the man whose impiety and perfidy they followed. But because they could not condemn their author and did not wish to approve him, [Note: The Roman edition alone adds: “nor could they approve him, nor did they wish to condemn him.” But we do not alter the reading found in the other editions and manuscripts.] although they had challenged us to debate three days earlier at a fixed place and time, they came forward before the appointed meeting and suddenly began to flee the encounter and avoid the debate, even though they had said that, because they were Christians, they would easily prove their position. [Col. 0941C] We gladly accepted this claim and wished them to prove it.

5. Nevertheless, we had a lengthy exchange with them. The divine Scriptures were placed before us, and patience was granted for debating from the beginning of the day until the seventh hour. If only they had said little—or at least if we could erase what we heard! For when Arius, in sacrilegious words, wished to imply that the Father alone is eternal, alone good, alone the true God, alone possessing immortality, alone wise, and alone powerful, while the Son was deprived of these qualities, [Note: Thus Tell. and Chifl.; Labb. has “with impious agitation,” while Cod. Reg. and the Roman edition have “with impious commendation”; perhaps *commentatione*, “with impious theorizing,” should be read. As for the Roman edition’s *voluisset intelligere*, “had wished to make understood,” no manuscript supports it.] these men preferred to follow Arius rather than confess the Son of God as the eternal God, the true God, the good God, the wise and powerful God, and the one possessing immortality. We wasted many hours without result. Their impiety increased, and it could not be corrected in any way.

6. Finally, when they saw themselves overwhelmed by the sacrileges of Arius’s letter (which we therefore appended, so that Your Clemency too might recoil from it), they withdrew from the reading of the middle of the letter and asked us to respond to their propositions. Although it was neither orderly nor reasonable for us to interrupt the propositions—and although we had replied that they should condemn the impieties of Arius and that we would respond to whatever points they wished, preserving the proper order, place, and sequence—nevertheless we yielded to their perverse desire. Thereupon, falsifying the written words of the Gospel, they presented to us as though the Lord had said: “He who sent me is greater than I,” whereas the sequence of the Scriptures teaches otherwise.

[Note: [Col. 0942D] Tellier and Labbe: “They asked for a choice from the middle of the letter.”]

7. When reproved for the falsehood, they admitted it, yet were not corrected by reason. For when we said that the Son is called less than his Father according to the assumption of flesh, but that according to divinity he is proved by the testimonies of Scripture to be equal and coequal with the Father; and that there can be no distinction of rank or degree of greatness wherever there is unity of power [Note: [Col. 0942D] The Regius manuscript reads: “distinction of degree.”], they not only refused to correct their error but even began to increase their madness, saying that the Son was subject to the Father according to divinity—as though there could be any subjection of God according to his divinity and majesty. Finally, they refer his death not to the mystery of our salvation but to some weakness of divinity.

8. We shudder, most merciful emperors, at such dreadful sacrileges and wicked teachers; and, so that they might not continue deceiving the peoples whom they held, we judged that they ought to be deprived of the priesthood, since the petitions submitted below echoed their impieties. For it is not fitting that they should claim for themselves the priesthood of one whom they denied. We implore your faith and your glory: show reverence to the author of your imperial authority, and decree that the defenders of impiety and adulterers of the truth are to be barred from the thresholds of the Church by letters of Your Clemency addressed to the competent courts, and that, in place of the condemned, holy priests be installed through the legates of our insignificance.

[Note: [Col. 0942D] Thus the Regius manuscript. The Tellier manuscript and the Roman, Labbean, and Chifletian editions instead read: “whom they held in the priesthood, we think they should be deposed.” For it is not fitting, etc.]

9. The same sentence also includes Attalus the presbyter, who confessed his betrayal of his office and clung to the sacrileges of Palladius. [809]

[Note: [Col. 0943C] The Roman and Labbean editions, together with the Tellier manuscript, read “and openly involved in sacrileges …”; Chiflet, with the Regius manuscript, reads as in the text. Below, where Attalus’s teacher is named, only the Regius manuscript has “Julian Valens”; the first name is omitted in the Tellier manuscript and in the three editions. He should apparently not be confused with Valens of Mursa, Ursacius’s colleague, who probably ceased to live before this year. Rather, he was another, younger man who, having been intruded by the Arians at Patavium in Pannonia into the see of Mark, a pious and Catholic bishop still living—for *superpositus* indicates this—was shortly afterward expelled and fled to Italy, where he stirred up the disturbances mentioned in this and in the final letter of this Council.]

For what shall we say about his teacher, Julian Valens? Although he was nearby, he avoided the council of priests, lest he be compelled to plead before the priests the causes of his ruined homeland and of his treacherous citizens.

[Note: [Col. 0943C] The Roman edition reads: “to plead the causes of the citizens.”]

He also dared, as is reported, defiled by Gothic impiety and clad in the manner of the Gentiles, to appear before the Roman army wearing a torc and an armlet.

[Note: [Col. 0943D] The Regius manuscript reads: “and Gothic armlets, profaned,” etc.]

This is unquestionably sacrilege not only in a priest but also in any Christian.

[Note: [Col. 0943D] The Tellier manuscript and Labbe read: “which is abhorrent to a Christian according to Roman custom”; the Roman edition: “…… and Roman”; the Regius manuscript and Chiflet read as in the text.]

Indeed, it is abhorrent to Roman custom. Unless, perhaps, this is how the priestly idolaters of the Goths usually appear.

10. May the priestly name, which that sacrilegious man disgraces, move your piety; for he is accused even by the voices of his own people, if any of them can still remain. At any rate, let him return to his own home and not contaminate the cities of flourishing Italy—he who now associates with himself men like himself through unlawful ordinations and seeks, through every kind of depraved person, to leave behind a seedbed of his impiety and treachery.

[Note: [Col. 0943D] The Roman edition reads: “so that he may win over every depraved person to himself”; the other editions and manuscripts agree among themselves, except that where *derelinquere* occurs, the Tellier manuscript has *derelinqueret*, and Labbe has *delinqueret*.]

He never even began to be a bishop. For first he had been set over the holy man Mark, a priest of admirable memory, at Patavium; but after he had been disgracefully expelled by the people, the man who could not remain at Patavium is now wreaking havoc at Milan after the ruin—let us call it the betrayal—of his homeland.

[Note: [Col. 0943D] The editions read *ne dicamus* (“not to say”); the manuscripts read *dicamus* (“let us say”). Where the Regius manuscript and the Roman edition have *latet*, Labbe reads *inquietavit* (“disturbed”), and Tellier and Chiflet *inequitavit* (“mounted upon”). The meaning is scarcely different, but the latter verb is more characteristic of Ambrose. Again, where the Regius manuscript and Roman edition read *nobis consulere* (“to advise us”), Labbe, Chiflet, and the Tellier manuscript have *consolari* (“to console”).]

11. Therefore, in all these matters, may Your Piety deign to provide for us, lest we appear to have assembled in vain while obeying the statutes of Your Tranquillity. For it must be guarded against not only that our decrees but also yours should be disgraced.

[Note: [Col. 0943D] The Regius manuscript reads *laedantur* (“be harmed”); Chiflet *ludantur* (“be mocked”); the Roman edition *infirmentur* (“be weakened”); Tellier and Labbe *infamentur* (“be disgraced”). Again, where the Roman edition reads *opportune redire* (“to return at a suitable time”), the other two editions and both manuscripts have *maturius redire* (“to return sooner”). This agrees more closely with the mind of the councils, which invariably condemned the prolonged or unnecessary residence of bishops in the imperial court. [Col. 0944C]]

We therefore ask that Your Clemency deign also to hear the legates of the council, holy men, and order them to return promptly with the effective fulfillment of what we request, so that you may receive a reward from the Lord God Christ, whose churches you have cleansed from every stain of sacrilege.

12. You also decreed under the previous law that the Photinians should not be permitted to hold any assemblies, and you abolished the law issued concerning the convocation of a council of priests. We ask that, since we know that they are still attempting to hold an assembly at the town of Sirmium, Your Clemency, by now also prohibiting that gathering, order that reverence be shown first to the Catholic Church [810] and then to your laws, so that, with God as your protector, you too may triumph, since you care for the peace and tranquillity of the churches.

[Note: [Col. 0944C] The Roman edition alone reads: “as the sentence against them has already been passed by the council of priests. We further ask that …” If anyone wishes to accept this reading, the “council of priests” mentioned in this letter may reasonably be understood as one of those councils in which Photinus was condemned, as Hilary records in the fragments, pp. 343–344; there he also mentions the Council of Milan held in 347, to which these bishops might be alluding. Yet that heretic was condemned in other councils as well, among which Epiphanius places the Council of Sardica in *Heresy* 71, though not all authorities agree with him.

Since, however, two manuscripts and an equal number of printed editions present a wholly different reading, the question now is which law is said to have been enacted against these same heretics. Baronius, under the year 381, holds that it was the sixth law *On Heretics*, issued on the fourth day before the Ides of January of that year, which forbids the Photinians to hold assemblies in the cities. Against this opinion it may be objected, first, that it is not probable that a law enacted in the East would be cited there; and second, that the sixth law applies not only to Photinians but also to certain other heretics. Nevertheless, the first objection could easily be answered by saying that this very law might have been adopted by Gratian; and the second by observing that the Photinians were the first and chief persons against whom the same law was promulgated. But since this letter testifies that the law it cites repealed another law—a fact not found in the sixth law itself—it is understood that the council is referring to some other law that has not survived.]

**LETTER XI**

They inform the emperors what took place in the council and warn them not to allow Ursinus to insinuate himself among them, since he was the author of the disturbances and was also accused of an infamous crime. Finally, they ask them to provide for the safety of the Roman clergy and of everyone else.

To the most merciful emperors and Christian princes, the most glorious and blessed Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius, the Council that assembled at Aquileia.

[Col. 0944C]

1. Provision has indeed been made, most merciful emperors, by the statutes of Your Tranquillity, so that the perfidy of the Arians may no longer be able either to lie hidden or to spread; for we think that the council’s decrees will by no means fail to have effect.

[Note: [Col. 0945C] Thus the Regius manuscript and Sirmond. The Roman edition adds: “and not without reason.”]

For, as far as the western provinces are concerned, only two have been found who dared to oppose the council with profane and impious words—men accustomed scarcely to disturb a corner of Ripensian Dacia.

2. There is another matter that causes us even greater anxiety, and since we have assembled, it had to be properly dealt with, lest it should be able to disturb the whole body of the Church, spread throughout the entire world, and trouble everything.

[Note: [Col. 0945C] The Roman edition reads: “now accustomed to disturb it. But there is another matter that causes us even greater anxiety … and to defile everything.”]

Although we have often assembled, we have not been able to prevent Ursinus from insinuating himself into Your Piety—although he allows nothing to remain peaceful and, amid so many military necessities, an untimely intrusion is being attempted.

[Note: [Col. 0945C–D] Ursinus, or Ursicinus, who had been made a presbyter by Liberius and assigned to the ministry of the Julian Basilica, was elected bishop by those who had adhered to Liberius, in opposition to Damasus, who had supported the party of Felix and ministered at the Laurentian Basilica. This schism brought innumerable conflicts and killings among the faithful. The schismatics Marcellinus and Faustinus attempted to place the blame for them on Damasus, and Ammianus, an open enemy of the Christian religion, also came to their aid. Yet everyone can see how much weight should be given to the testimony of such men.

Damasus is amply freed from blame by the judgments both of Joventius and Praetextatus, prefects of the City, and of Valentinian himself, who expelled Ursinus from Rome; especially by the judgments of the Roman councils and of this Council of Aquileia, by the praises of the saints Ambrose and Jerome, and finally by the testimony of Rufinus, Socrates, and other historians.]

Nevertheless, lest your holy mind and tranquillity of spirit, which seeks to care for everyone, be swayed by the feigned flattery of an importunate man, we judge that—if you deem it worthy—we must beseech and implore you, not only taking precautions against the future but also shuddering at the past, which has already been brought about by his recklessness. For if he should find any path for his audacity, what would he not throw into confusion?

3. But if pity for one man can bend you, much more should the prayer of all the priests move you. For who among us will join himself to him in the fellowship of communion, when he has attempted to usurp a rank not owed to him and could not reach it lawfully, and when he is attempting most importunately [811] to reclaim what he sought most importunately?

[Note: [Col. 0945D] The Regius manuscript reads: “He still attacks those condemned so many times … who, as most men …”]

Although so often condemned for disturbances, he still proceeds as though he were not to be feared because of the examples of the past. For, as we have learned and seen in this council, he was commonly allied and joined with the Arians when he was attempting to disturb the Milanese Church by a detestable assembly with Valens:

[Note: [Col. 0945D–Col. 0946D] The Roman edition omits “with Valens.” It is not to be understood as Valens of Mursa, as Labbe warns in a marginal note, but as the man from Patavium mentioned in the preceding letter.]
