now before the doors of the synagogue, now in the houses of the Arians, he held secret councils and joined his own followers to them; and because he could not openly appear in their gatherings, he instructed and trained them in how the peace of the Church might be disturbed. He drew breath from their fury, because through them he might acquire supporters and associates.

[Note: [Col. 0945D–Col. 0946D] To make it easier to understand what period is meant here, note that Ursinus, whom Joventius expelled in 366 to extinguish the fire of the sedition, as has already been said, was recalled the following year by Praetextatus. But when, in that same year, he was sent by the same prefect of the City into Gaul, he remained there in exile until 371, when he obtained permission to extend the boundaries of his exile. Finally, when in 378 he attacked Damasus with false accusations through Isaac, a Jew and deserter from the Christian rites, and Isaac was ordered to remain in exile in Gaul, Ursinus himself was banished to Spain; after that, he is not found to have returned.

It must therefore be said that this scoundrel, during the interval in which he was allowed to wander more freely, abused the opportunity by stirring up disturbances in various places and by joining himself to the Arians at Milan, especially after the death of the elder Valentinian, as is stated here. Nor is it at all implausible to believe that Ambrose is indicating that these very disturbances were suppressed by the authority of Gratian, since his first letter gives Gratian thanks for restoring peace to the Church.]

[Note: [Col. 0946D] The Roman edition remodelled the passage as follows: “He could not; he instructed and trained those whose favor allowed him to breathe, so that he might more fully earn supporters and associates, in how the peace of the Church should be disturbed.” Sirmond and the Regius manuscript read as in the text, except that Sirmond printed *sperabat* (“hoped”) instead of *respirabat* (“drew breath”).]

4. Since it is written, “Avoid a heretic after one admonition” (Titus 3:10), and since another man, speaking by the holy Spirit, said that such beasts must be avoided and not received even with a greeting (2 John 10), nor met in person, how can it be that we should not judge him an advocate of perfidy when we have seen him inserted into their fellowship?

Even if he were absent, ought not Your Clemency nevertheless to have been implored so that he would not be permitted to disturb the head of the entire Roman world, the Roman Church, and that most holy apostolic faith? For from there the rights of venerable communion flow out to all. Therefore we ask and entreat you to deign to remove from him the opportunity to insinuate himself.

5. We know the holy modesty of Your Clemency. May it remember that he should not bring before your hearing matters unworthy of it, should not interrupt with matters alien to the office and name of a priest, and should not speak to you shamelessly. He ought to have a good reputation even among outsiders (1 Timothy 3:7); let Your Clemency remember what sort of testimony his own citizens have brought against him.

For we are ashamed to say, and it is immodest to recount, how disgraceful a reputation has wounded him through their accusations. At least, constrained by that shame, he ought to have kept silent; and if he possessed any priestly conscience, he would have preferred the peace of the Church and concord to his ambition and zeal. But being far removed from all modesty, he sends letters through the mutilated man Paschasius, the standard-bearer of his fury, sowing disturbances and attempting to rouse pagans and depraved men of every kind. [812]

6. We therefore pray that you grant security both to the Roman people, who since the report of the prefect of the City remain in uncertainty, and to us priests, by rejecting this most importunate man.

[Note: [Col. 0946D] The Roman edition reads: “grant us security by your intervention. Once this has been obtained from Your Clemency, may we give thanks to God the almighty Father and to Christ his Son, God and Lord, and celebrate your merits in perpetual prayer.” The Regius manuscript and Sirmond read as in the text, except that here, instead of “the Lord God,” they read “his Son, the Lord God.”]

Once this has been obtained, may we continually offer thanks to God the almighty Father, and to Christ, the Lord and God.

**LETTER XII**

Thanks are given to the emperors for restoring tranquillity to the Church, and the bishops’ prayers are promised to them. Then, after certain schisms among Catholics have been reported, the same princes are asked to order a council to assemble at Alexandria and not to disdain to lend it their assistance, thereby conferring a great benefit upon the bishops.

To the most merciful and Christian emperors, and the glorious and blessed princes Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius, the holy Council that assembled at Aquileia.

[Col. 0947B]

1. Even if our thanksgiving overflowed with every possible expression of gratitude, we could never equal the benefits of Your Piety, most merciful, blessed, and glorious emperors, Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius, beloved by God the Father and by his Son, our Lord Jesus Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0947C] The Roman edition reads: “after many dangers.”]

For after so many years and the various persecutions which the Arians inflicted upon the Catholics—especially that Lucius, who raged in the impious slaughter of monks and virgins—and that dreadful head of perfidy, Demophilus—

[Note: [Col. 0947D–Col. 0948D] Demophilus is appropriately joined to the same Lucius, for he was one of the principal leaders of the Arian party. When he was bishop of Berrhoea in Thrace, he attended the Council of Ariminum in that capacity. Later, while Liberius was exiled in that same city, Demophilus offered him the creed of Sirmium and the condemnation of Athanasius for his signature, and was no small cause of his lapse. After the death of Eudoxius, the Arian bishop of Constantinople, Demophilus was appointed by the same faction to replace him in 370. A decade later Theodosius expelled him into exile. Nevertheless, in 383, he is found attending Constantinople with the leaders of various sects whom Theodosius had summoned there in the hope of composing, if possible, a reconciliation. He finally died in that city in 386. Ambrose mentioned him in book 1, chapter 6 of *On the Faith*, and ecclesiastical historians have remembered him extensively and in competition with one another.]

[Note: [Col. 0947D] The same edition reads: “especially that Vellutius, who raged in the impious slaughter of monks and virgins, as did Demophilus”; the Regius manuscript reads as in our text. Sirmond’s edition likewise differs only in reading “especially Lucius … and Domophylus.” The learned editor evidently observed that this passage concerns no one other than Lucius, who, after Athanasius’s death, criminally seized the Church of Alexandria and sent certain pious monks into exile after violently dragging them from their caves, as Theodoret relates in book 4, chapter 21 of his *Ecclesiastical History*. As for the slaughter of the virgins, how shamefully, by the order of that same Lucius, they were stripped naked by pagan soldiers in the church and dragged through the city, and how inhumanly not a few of them died from the ferocity of the blows inflicted upon them, this is recalled in the letter of Peter of Alexandria in the following chapter of Theodoret.]

peace and tranquillity have been restored to all the churches of God, especially to the Catholic churches throughout the East; while in the western provinces scarcely two heretics have been found who can oppose the holy council. Who could think himself an adequate spokesman for your thanksgivings?

[Note: [Col. 0948D] Thus the Regius manuscript and Sirmond. The Roman edition reads: “so that peace and tranquillity may at last be restored through Your Clemency to all the churches of God, especially to the Catholic churches throughout the East.”]

2. Yet although we cannot express your benefits in words, we wish to repay them through the prayers of the council. Though in each church we daily keep watch before our God on behalf of your imperial power, nevertheless, gathered into one—as we think nothing more beautiful can be offered [813]—we give thanks to our almighty God both for your rule and for your peace and safety, because through you peace and concord have thus been poured back upon us.

[Note: [Col. 0948D] The Roman edition reads: “so that it may thus be poured back, because through the western churches, etc.”]

3. In the western provinces, it seemed that the faith was obstructed only in two corners, that is, in the region of Ripensian Dacia and Moesia; and now, after the council’s sentence, we think that, through the favor of Your Clemency, provision should immediately be made for them. Throughout all districts and regions, and in the secluded villages as far as the ocean, the communion of the faithful remains one and undefiled.

In the eastern provinces, however, we have learned with the greatest joy and gladness that, after the Arians who had violently invaded the churches were expelled, the holy temples of God are frequented solely by Catholics.

4. Yet since the envy of the devil is never accustomed to rest, we hear that frequent dissensions and unsettled discord exist among the Catholics themselves. We are utterly distressed that we have learned that so many things have been renewed and that those who ought to have been assisted are now being burdened—men who have always remained in our communion.

Finally, Timothy, bishop of the Church of Alexandria, and Paulinus of Antioch, who have always preserved an undefiled harmony of communion with us, are said to be pressed by the dissensions of others, whose faith in earlier times was wavering. If it can be done, and if full faith commends them, we desire that they be joined to our fellowship; but in such a way that the established precedence of the partners of the ancient communion be preserved. Our concern for them is not superfluous: first, because the fellowship of communion ought to give offense to no one; and second, because we have received letters from both parties, especially from those who were in dispute in the Church of Antioch.

[Note: [Col. 0948D] Timothy was chosen bishop of Alexandria after the death of Peter, who had succeeded Athanasius there and had placed Maximus the Cynic philosopher—infected with the errors of Apollinaris—above Gregory of Nazianzus. These matters, as well as Paulinus of Antioch, will be discussed more conveniently in the following letter.]

5. Indeed, unless a hostile invasion had intervened, we had arranged to send some from our number there, who might serve as mediators and arbiters for restoring peace, if that were possible. But because our efforts could not then achieve their purpose amid the public disturbances, we believe that the prayers we previously offered to Your Piety should be renewed: in accordance with the agreement between the parties, we asked that, when one of the two died, the rights of the Church should remain with the survivor and that no forcible superordination should be attempted.

[Note: [Col. 0949C] The Roman edition reads: “we renew to Your Piety our prayers, in which we asked …”; Labbe and the Regius manuscript read as in the text. Valerius thinks that *partium factum* should be read *partium pactum* (“the agreement of the parties”). Indeed, the conditions of that agreement are immediately set out.]

Therefore, we ask you, most merciful and Christian princes, to decree that a council of all the Catholic priests assemble at Alexandria, so that they may discuss and determine more fully among themselves to whom communion is to be granted and for whom it is to be preserved.

[Note: [Col. 0949C] Thus the Regius manuscript and Sirmond. The Roman edition reads: “for whom it is to be observed.” It also adds below, after the word “fellowship,” “up to the present time.”]

6. [814] For although we have always maintained the arrangement and order of the Church of Alexandria, and, according to the custom and practice of our ancestors, have preserved its communion in an unbreakable fellowship up to the present time, nevertheless, lest some appear to have been passed over—those who, even by the agreement that we wish to uphold, asked for our communion—or lest the advantages of that peace and fellowship of the faithful be neglected, we beseech you to provide that, after they have discussed the matter among themselves in a fuller assembly, your Piety also lend assistance to the decrees of the priests.

[Note: [Col. 0949C] The Roman edition reads: “and that it be brought to your attention,” etc.]

And decree that the matter be reported to us, lest we waver in anxious uncertainty; rather, joyful and secure, may we give thanks to Your Piety before almighty God, not only because perfidy has been excluded but because faith and concord have been restored to the Catholics. This is what the churches of Africa and Gaul entreat you through their legates: that throughout the world you make all bishops your debtors. It is no small debt that is owed to your virtue.

[Note: [Col. 0949C] The same edition reads: “which is owed to your virtue for the peace of the entire Roman world,” etc.]

7. To plead for Your Clemency and obtain what we request, we have sent our brothers and fellow priests as legates. We ask that you deign to hear them graciously and decree that they return promptly.

**LETTER XIII**

[Col. 0950A]

After giving thanks to Theodosius for restoring the orthodox to their basilicas and expressing his grief over the disturbances of the Church, Ambrose complains that, after Meletius’s death, another bishop has been installed at Antioch. He asks that Nectarius, who was ordained at Constantinople after Maximus, yield his place, or that a synod at Rome pronounce upon the ordination of both.

To the most blessed emperor and most merciful prince Theodosius, Ambrose and the other bishops of Italy.

[Note: [Col. 0949C–D] Jacobus Sirmond was the first to publish this and the following letter from the manuscripts of the Royal Library in the appendix to his edition of the Theodosian Code; Labbe then transferred them into his edition of the Councils. Since they had not yet appeared among Ambrose’s works, we have nevertheless judged that they should be admitted into our edition because it cannot reasonably be denied that they belong to Ambrose no less than the letters of the Council of Aquileia. It is unknown at which council they were written, although it is rightly said that it was an Italian council.]

1. We knew that your holy mind was devoted to almighty God with pure and sincere faith; but you have increased your benefits by restoring the Catholics to their churches, Augustus Emperor. Would that you had also restored the Catholics themselves to the ancient reverence, so that they might undertake nothing contrary to the prescriptions of their ancestors, neither rashly abolishing what ought to be preserved nor preserving what ought to be abolished.

Thus, Emperor, we perhaps groan more sorrowfully than imprudently. It was easier to expel the heretics than for the Catholics to reach agreement. For the extent of the recent confusion cannot be explained.

[Note: [Col. 0949D–Col. 0950B] These words are thought to indicate the sixth law of Theodosius concerning heretics, by which they were forbidden to hold assemblies and the churches were ordered to be restored to the Catholics. How the Arians yielded the churches that they occupied at Constantinople is described by Socrates, book 5, chapter 7, and Sozomen, book 7, chapter 5.]

2. Long ago we wrote that, since the city of Antioch had two bishops, Paulinus and Meletius, whom we thought agreed in faith [815], either peace and concord should be established between them while the ecclesiastical order remained intact, or, if one of them died while the other survived, no one should be substituted in the place of the deceased while the other remained alive.

[Note: [Col. 0949D–Col. 0950C] The preceding letter of the Fathers of Aquileia to Theodosius, no. 5, makes exactly the same points concerning the agreement between Paulinus and Meletius; Socrates, book 5, chapter 5, and Sozomen, also book 5, chapter 3, may likewise be consulted. As for Theodoret’s account, book 5, chapter 3, that Paulinus rejected the terms of this agreement when Meletius offered them, since it departs here from the testimony of all the others, it is not unjustly attributed to his partiality toward Meletius and Flavian.]

But now, after Meletius’s death, while Paulinus survives—a man whose remaining in our communion is attested by the fellowships that our ancestors carried on without offense—it is asserted that, contrary to law and ecclesiastical order, someone has been installed in Meletius’s place, or rather superimposed upon it.

[Note: [Col. 0950C] The person who was substituted in Meletius’s place is not named here. It is established, however, that the person intended is Flavian, whom we know to have been elected by the faction of the younger men against his own oath, despite the dissent of Gregory of Nazianzus. His election is therefore rejected not only in this synodical letter but also by Ambrose in his letter to Theophilus.]

3. This act is said to have taken place with the consent and counsel of Nectarius, although we do not see what order his ordination followed. For recently, in the council, when Maximus had shown—after the letters of Peter, a man of holy memory, were read—that the communion of the Church of Alexandria remained with him, and when he had clearly testified that he had been kept in a private house, because the Arians still occupied the basilicas of the Church, with bishops acting under instructions and ordaining him, we had nothing, most blessed of princes, on which to base doubt concerning his episcopate, since he had also testified that force had been inflicted upon him while he resisted, even by many of the people and clergy.

[Note: [Col. 0950C–Col. 0952B] Valerius, in his observations on Sozomen, book 7, chapter 9, argues that the text should read: “that he had been appointed by order, with three bishops ordaining him.” This is an excellent correction, though it cannot be admitted into the text without manuscript support.

Since falsehoods are interwoven with truths here in the account of Maximus, the narrative must be taken up somewhat earlier so that the two may more easily be distinguished. He was an Alexandrian by birth and attempted to combine the shamelessness of the Cynic philosophers with Christian practices. He travelled through various cities, from which he was expelled as soon as possible because of his immoral character. Finally, when he came to Constantinople, he insinuated himself so deceitfully into the mind of Bishop Gregory that Gregory praised him in a public speech.

Shortly afterward, however, Maximus rose up against Gregory and advanced his cause by his usual arts to such an extent that bishops from whom he could receive the laying-on of hands were sent by Peter, bishop of Alexandria. He was ordained in the house of a certain flute-player, not because the basilicas were occupied by the Arians, as he falsely persuaded the Latin bishops, but so that the Catholics would not prevent his ordination. Here another falsehood of his is exposed: he claimed that force had been used against him so that he might be consecrated. Indeed, after he had seized the Church of Saint Anastasia by night, he was expelled from it by the clergy and people.

Thus compelled to leave Constantinople, he went to Thessalonica and approached Theodosius. When Theodosius rejected him, he went to Alexandria, where his shamelessness reached the point that he threatened Peter that he would invade his see unless Peter restored him to Constantinople. But after the prefect of Egypt expelled him from there, he was forced to remain quiet for a time, until he learned that a council had been summoned in Italy.

He then came to the council—for Valerius’s opinion that he merely sent letters seems less consistent with the words of this letter—and, having brought with him letters from Peter of Alexandria, who possessed the greatest authority among the Latins, he was admitted by the Fathers into communion. Yet, so that they would not make a decision after hearing only one side while remaining unaware that the history of this impostor was well known to Damasus and the others, they sent this letter concerning the matter to Theodosius.

It may be asked whether Maximus came to this council or to some earlier one. It seems more probable that he came to an earlier council, as both the adverb *recently* used here and the fact that the letter came from Peter, who is nevertheless stated here to have already died, sufficiently show.]

4. Yet, lest it should appear that, with the parties absent, we had presumptuously determined something, we thought it necessary to inform Your Clemency by letter, so that the matter might be addressed in the interest of public peace and concord; for we were in fact observing that Gregory was by no means claiming the priesthood of the Church of Constantinople in accordance with the tradition of the Fathers. Therefore, in the synod we judged that nothing should be rashly decided concerning what seemed to have been prescribed by the 816 bishops of the whole world. [Note: Labbe places in the margin, “But then”: not inappropriately. Yet his indication there that the ecumenical synod mentioned here was the same one which Palladius so often alleges was prohibited by Ambrose at the Council of Aquileia does not present as great an appearance of truth. For how could those who had been responsible for preventing that synod from being general reproach the Easterners for having refused to attend it? Nevertheless, the following makes it clear that a synod held in the West is being discussed.] At that very time, then, those who avoided a general council are said to have been conducting matters at Constantinople. For when they learned that Maximus had come to this gathering [Col. 0952A] to plead his case before the synod (which—even if no council had been summoned—he had the right and ancestral custom to do, just as Athanasius of holy memory, Peter not long before, bishops of the Church of Alexandria, and many of the Easterners had done; so that he might be seen to have sought the judgment of the Roman Church, Italy, and the whole of the West); when, as we have said, they discovered that he wished to bring his case against those who had denied his episcopate, they ought surely also to have awaited our judgment concerning him. We do not claim a prerogative in the examination, but there ought nevertheless to have been a sharing in the common decision.

5. Finally, it ought first to have been established whether his priesthood should be annulled before another was conferred, especially by those against whom Maximus complained that he had been either abandoned or unjustly attacked. Therefore, when they received Maximus the bishop into communion, our association with them was justified, since it was established that he had been ordained bishop by Catholic bishops, [Note: It can be recognized from canon 16 of the Synod of Antioch, which Dionysius Exiguus renders as follows, that Gregory had by no means been placed over the see of Constantinople according to the ecclesiastical canons: “If any bishop, while a church is vacant, rushes into a vacant church and seizes its see without a full and complete council, he must be deposed, even if the entire people whom he has plundered should choose to have him.” Add canon 1 of the Synod of Sardica and canon 15 of Nicaea I, as well as Jerome’s letter to Oceanus. Nevertheless, after Gregory’s transfer had been approved by the universal council, it became legitimate by virtue of the same Antiochene canon; but the Westerners could not yet have learned this.] nor did we think that he should be excluded from seeking the episcopate of Constantinople. We judged that his claim should be weighed in the presence of the parties. [Note: Valesius, followed by Hermannus, thinks that “Gregory” should be read, not “Nectarius.” And indeed the historical circumstances fit very well. For when Meletius and the other Fathers of the Council of Constantinople had placed Gregory over that Church, after Meletius had died, the prelates appointed Nectarius to the position when Gregory voluntarily gave way. Nevertheless, it is scarcely credible that Nectarius should have entered all the manuscripts in place of Gregory. First, it is certain that this entire letter is concerned chiefly with Nectarius, and that what is said below—that the one who was elected first should be restored to Constantinople—makes sense only with reference to Nectarius. Second, Nectarius’s deposition may be referred to the fact that, when Theodosius chose Nectarius, who had not yet received baptism, several bishops initially resisted, if we are to believe Sozomen, book VII, chapter 8, who asserts this. Finally, this too may have been one of Maximus’s impostures, devised by him so that he might draw the Latins more effectively to his side.] But since our modesty had recently learned that Nectarius had been ordained at Constantinople [Col. 0953A], we do not see how our communion can remain joined with the Eastern regions, especially since Nectarius is said to have been immediately deprived by those same men of communion with whom he had been ordained.

6. Here, then, is no slight difficulty. We are not distressed by some dispute arising from personal affection and ambition, but by the disruption and disunion of communion. Nor do we see how it can otherwise be settled, unless either the one who was ordained first is restored to Constantinople, or at least a council of our Eastern colleagues and ourselves is held in the city of Rome concerning the ordination of the two men.

7. For it does not seem unworthy, Augustus, that the bishop of the Roman Church and the neighboring and Italian bishops [Note: The Codex Regius reads, “should not undergo examination.”] should undergo examination, [Note: Hermannus, in book X, chapter 5 of his Life of Gregory of Nazianzus, conjectures that these words should be referred to the history of the Council of Constantinople, where it is said that the bishops—apparently divided in the dispute between Meletius and Paulinus—sent letters hastily to the Egyptian and Macedonian prelates and invited them, trusting that concord could be restored through their authority, especially that of Acholius of Thessalonica. That Acholius is the same man who baptized Theodosius in 380 and whose virtues Ambrose praises in Letter 15.] who thought that the judgment of a single bishop, Acholius, ought to be awaited in such a way that he was thought to have to be summoned from the Western regions to Constantinople. If something was reserved for this one man, how much more ought it to be reserved for several!

8. We, however, admonished by the most blessed prince, the brother of Your Piety, to write to Your Clemency’s imperial authority, ask that, where there is one communion, Your Clemency may wish there also to be a common judgment and harmonious agreement.

## LETTER XIV

[Note: Written around the year 382.]

Having commended Theodosius for having worked to restore unity between the Eastern and Western Churches, the bishops explain why they had written the preceding letter concerning that matter. They add that they had also been concerned that the supporters of Apollinaris should be condemned. Finally, they assert that, in requesting a council, they had done no one an injustice and had nowhere departed from the custom of their ancestors.

To the most blessed emperor and most merciful prince THEODOSIUS, AMBROSE and the other bishops of Italy.

1. The knowledge of your faith, spread throughout the whole world, has deeply delighted our hearts; and, so that this glory too might be created for your reign—that you might appear to have restored unity to the Churches of the West as well as of the East—we have thought it right both to beseech Your Clemency and to instruct you by our letter concerning ecclesiastical affairs, most tranquil and faithful Emperor. For it was a source of grief that the bonds of sacred communion between the Easterners and Westerners had been severed.

2. We now keep silent about whose error or whose fault it was, lest we seem to be spreading tales and engaging in empty conversation. Nor do we regret having attempted what would have become a fault had it remained unattempted. For we were often accused on this ground: that we appeared to slight fellowship with the Easterners and reject their favor.

3. We even thought that a labor had to be undertaken by us—not on behalf of Italy, which has long been peaceful and secure from the Arians and is troubled by no disturbance of heretics; not, I say, on our own behalf, because we seek not what is ours but what belongs to all; not on behalf of Gaul and Africa, which enjoy the harmonious fellowship of all the bishops; but so that those matters which had disturbed our communion from the Eastern side might be examined in a synod, and every difficulty removed.

4. For we were moved not only by the matters concerning which Your Clemency deigned to write, [Note: From this passage, and from what is read below, you may understand that the emperor replied to the first letter of the bishops with an august and authoritative response, and indicated both the sequence of Nectarius’s ordination and the deceptions and crimes of Maximus, as well as the matters relating to the case of Paulinus and Flavian. As for what is added concerning the Apollinarists, there is no mention of them in the preceding letter; and it seems in a way to be indicated that this heresy had only recently become known to them, although Pope Damasus had already condemned it.] but also by many things concerning those who are attempting to introduce into the Church some doctrine—I know not what—said to be that of Apollinaris. These matters had to be cut away while the parties were present, so that, convicted of the new doctrine and refuted in their error, they might not hide under the general name of the faith; but that, since they did not hold to the authority of doctrine, they might immediately lay down both their office and the title of bishop, and that no remnants or contrivances of trickery might afterward remain for those wishing to deceive. For anyone who has not been convicted in the presence of the parties will always seize the handle of the question that must be referred back. [Note: The Codex Regius reads: “will always seize the apostolic question for reference.”]

5. For this reason we requested a priestly council, [Note: This passage responds to the words of the preceding letter, section 6: “that a council of ourselves and the Easterners be held in the city of Rome concerning the ordination of the two.” For they insist that their mind had been free from fault in requesting a council and that they could not rightly be accused; similarly, in the preceding letter, they had anticipated the grounds on which they might be charged, in more than one place.] so that no one might be permitted to fabricate a lie against an absent person, and so that the truth of the matter might be examined in council. Thus no suspicion of ill intention or carelessness falls upon those who observed everything in the presence of the parties.

[Col. 0955A] 6. Certainly, we set out the allegations not for the purpose of deciding, but of informing; and although we requested judgment, we do not impose a prejudgment. Nor should it be regarded as any insult when bishops were invited to the council—bishops whose absence had often been more effective than their presence when the common good was being considered. Indeed, we ourselves did not regard it as an insult when a presbyter of the Church of Constantinople, named Paul, [Note: Labbé adds this in the margin: “Expelled in the year 342, when Hermogenes was killed by the people, and Constantius placed Macedonius on the see of Constantinople.”] requested within Achaea a synod of Easterners as well as Westerners.

7. Your Clemency recognizes that the request was not unreasonable, since it had also been sought from the Easterners. But because Illyricum was viewed with suspicion, maritime and safer routes were sought. Nor did we innovate anything as though following a new rule: [Note: We understand these words in the same sense as the words of the preceding letter: “by right and ancestral custom, as did Athanasius of holy memory,” and so forth.] rather, while preserving the decisions established in councils by Athanasius of holy memory, who was as it were a pillar of the faith, and by the ancient holiness of our fathers, we do not uproot the boundaries set by our fathers; nor do we violate the rights of inherited communion. Instead, while reserving the honor due to your imperial authority, we have shown ourselves devoted to peace and quiet.

## LETTER XV

[Note: Written in the year 383.]

Ambrose has learned of the death of Acholius, though not without a certain miracle: he was not so much dead as transferred to a happier life; his deeds had earned him comparison with Elisha, while the successor whom he made heir of his spirit persuades us to say that he also represented Elijah. Acholius’s first meeting with Ambrose had been most pleasing to him, and his death was deeply mourned by many; yet the desire for the holy man is eased by the virtue of his successor.

AMBROSE to ANATOLIUS, NUMERIUS, SEVERUS, PHILIPPUS, MACEDONIUS, AMMIANUS, THEODOSIUS, EUTROPIUS, CLARUS, EUSEBIUS, and TIMOTHEUS, [Note: Some manuscripts of better quality read, “to Munerius.”] the lords and bishops, [Note: The old edition reads, “lord bishops”; the Roman edition and some manuscripts, “of the Lord, the bishops”; in many others both words are omitted. Immediately afterward, however, where all editions read “to the clergy of the people of Thessalonica,” almost all manuscripts support our reading.] and to all the beloved clergy and people of Thessalonica, greetings.

1. While I always desire to keep the holy man fixed in my mind and examine all his actions as though stationed on a watchtower, I have drawn, through an excessive scrutiny born of anxiety, the bitterness of the earliest report; and I have learned what I would still prefer not to know: that the man whom we sought on earth now rests in heaven. [Note: The editions add “the holy Acholius” after “the man”; some more recent manuscripts include one or the other of these words, while many older ones include neither. Those who think that Ambrose silently indicates in what follows that Acholius appeared to him after death in a vision are not unreasonable.]

2. You ask who announced this, since your letter had not yet arrived? I do not know who brought the news. It is indeed customary for us not willingly to retain a message of sorrow; nevertheless, although the sea was closed at that time and the lands were occupied by barbarian invasion, when there was no one who could arrive, there was still someone who could report it. Thus it seems to me that the holy man himself announced to us that he had already received forever the reward of his labor and, released from the bonds of the body, was clinging to Christ amid the ministry of the angels, wishing to free his beloved from his mistaken hope, lest we should pray for a long continuation of this life for one to whom the rewards of eternal life were already being presented.

3. He departed, therefore; he did not die. The veteran of Christ Jesus emigrated from us, changing only this earth for heaven, and, clapping his spiritual wings and oars, saying: “Behold, I have fled far away” (Psalm 54:8). For long before, in the spirit of the Apostle, he desired to leave the earth; but he was held back by the wishes of everyone, as we read concerning the Apostle (Philippians 1:23–24), because for him to remain longer in the flesh was necessary for the Church. For he lived not for himself but for all, and was a minister of eternal life to the people, so that he might first obtain its fruit in others before attaining knowledge of it in himself. [Note: We have restored “knowledge,” a word absent from the editions, from the manuscripts.]

4. He is now, therefore, an inhabitant of the realms above, a possessor of that eternal city, Jerusalem, which is in heaven. There he sees the immeasurable dimensions of its city, pure gold, precious stone, and everlasting light without the sun. Though he had long known all these things, he now sees them manifested face to face and says: “As we have heard, so also we see in the city of the Lord of hosts, in the city of our God” (Psalm 47:9). Placed there, therefore, he calls upon the people of God, saying: “O Israel, how great is the house of God, and how vast the place of his possession! Great, and it has no end” (Baruch 3:24–25).

5. But what is this? While I consider the man’s merits, follow his departing spirit as though accompanying it, and mingle among the choirs of the saints who escort him, I have almost forgotten myself—not through any merit, but through affection. Has the wall of faith, grace, and holiness therefore been snatched away from us—he whom the barbarian weapons of the Goths, though their forces attacked us so often, could never penetrate, nor the warlike fury of many nations overcome? Indeed, while they laid waste the other places, there they asked for peace; and when they wondered what could resist them without any army, the wiser among them told them that an imitator of Elisha, equal to him in age but not inferior in spirit, dwelt within. They should beware lest blindness overtake them too, as it had the Syrian army (2 Kings 7:1 ff.). [Note: Baronius states that this occurred in the year 378, when, after Valens had been killed, the victorious Goths carried out exceedingly cruel devastations and massacres, of which we have spoken more than once. Yet there is nothing to prevent the following years from also being indicated here; for the adverb “so often” plainly testifies that the same thing happened repeatedly.]

6. Yet Christ’s gifts are different in relation to his disciples. Elisha led captive armies of Syrians into Samaria; but holy Acholius, by his prayers, caused the victors to flee from the regions of Macedonia. Do we not understand that this too belonged to a higher virtue: that where no soldier was present, they were driven away without a soldier? Is it not also blindness that they fled though no one was pursuing them? Yet holy Acholius pressed them and fought—not with swords, but with prayers; not with weapons, but with merits.

7. Is it unknown to us that the saints fight even when they are inactive? Was Elisha idle? [Col. 0957B] Idle in body, certainly; but he wielded his spirit and fought in prayer when, in the Syrian camp, the sound of horsemen and the sound of a great force were heard. The Syrians thought that armies of other kings were coming against them to aid the people of Israel; struck with terror, they fled in great fear, so that four lepers, who had gone out desiring death, plundered the enemy camp. Did the Lord not perform similar or almost greater wonders in Macedonia through the prayers of holy Acholius? For the Goths were not disturbed and terrified by an empty fear or a needless suspicion, but by a raging disease and burning pestilence. Finally, they fled then in order to escape; afterward they returned to ask for peace, so that they might live.

8. Thus, in the merits of so great a man, we saw former ages and gazed upon the works of the prophets that we had read. Like Elisha among weapons and armies, he lived amid conflict, settling battles by his merits. Finally, when security had been restored to those dwelling with him—something harder for him than war itself—he breathed out his holy spirit. Like Elijah, he was lifted up to heaven (2 Kings 2:11), not indeed by a fiery chariot or fiery horses—unless perhaps we did not see those things—nor amid a disturbance of the air, but in the will and peace of our God, and amid the joy of the holy angels, who rejoiced that so great a man had passed over to them.

9. Certainly, we can in no way doubt these things, since the rest corresponded. For at the very moment when he was still being raised up, as though he had cast off the garment of his own melotis, he clothed his holy disciple Anysius and vested him with the insignia of his priesthood. [Note: A melotis is nothing other than a sheepskin, since the Greek word μῆλον means “sheep.” Although Ambrose chiefly alludes here to Elijah’s cloak, which the Septuagint calls μηλωτή, there is nothing to prevent us from thinking that he used the word also to indicate that Acholius retained his monastic clothing even in the episcopate. Athanasius writes that Antony used this kind of garment, and Cassian, Palladius, Socrates, and others show that it was also common among the Egyptian monks.] I do not hear of his merit and grace for the first time now, nor did I learn of them in your letters; rather, I recognized them in your correspondence. For, as though foreseeing that he would succeed him, although he concealed it under promises, he nevertheless pointed him out by indications, mentioning that he had been assisted by his care, labor, and service. Thus he already seemed to declare him his associate—the man who would not come as a newcomer to the highest priesthood, but as an old executor of the priesthood. To him the Gospel saying aptly applies: “Well done, good and faithful servant, because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things” (Matthew 25:23).

10. These things concerning holy Acholius I share with you; but this is particular to me: I am bound to the man of blessed memory because he granted me the opportunity not to remain ignorant of him. For when he came to Italy, and I was weakened by illness so that I could not go to meet him, [Note: Not without probability, some say that Acholius’s first meeting with our Ambrose occurred in the year 382, when he came to Italy and was to be present at the council held at Rome toward the end of that year, which they also say Ambrose attended.] he himself came to me and visited me. With what eagerness and affection he rushed upon me, and I upon him! With what groaning we lamented the evils of this age and the things that happened here! We drenched our garments in a flood of tears while we enjoyed the most desired greeting, mutual longing, and a long-awaited embrace. Thus what had been my wish became his kindness, because I was able to see him. For although the greater part, and the fuller knowledge, consists in seeing those whom we love in the spirit, [Note: All the editions read, “to see in the spirit those whom we love”; all the manuscripts omit the verb “to see,” while the more authoritative ones have “by which we love” instead of “those whom we love.”] nevertheless we also desire to see them in the form of the body. Thus once the kings of the earth sought to see the face of Solomon and to hear his wisdom (1 Kings 10:24).

11. He therefore departed from us and left us on this sea. But what was useful for him is more grievous to many because of the barbarian fury: it drove him away, but who will be able to restore him to us? The Lord restores him, and restores him in his disciple. Your judgments restore him, to whom it was said: “Give manifest signs of him to Levi, and his truth to the holy man” (Deuteronomy 33:18). You have given his manifest sign, since you were founded upon his instruction; you have given an imitator of the man who said to his father and mother: “I did not see you” (ibid., 9), who did not acknowledge his brothers and did not recognize his sons; who guarded the word of the Lord and observed his covenant. “The peoples will recount his righteousness” (Ecclesiasticus 44:15).

12. Such was the life of the man, such is his inheritance, such his conduct, such his succession. As a boy he devoted himself to monasteries, and, shut up in a narrow hut within Achaea, nevertheless traversed the divisions of many lands by his grace. When the Macedonian peoples entreated him to accept the highest priesthood, he was chosen by the bishops, so that where previously the faith had been enclosed by a priest, there afterward the priest might confirm the walls and foundations of the faith. [Note: Observe that here the people are granted the right not to choose or appoint a bishop, but only to entreat and petition for one. We discuss this more fully below in the letter to Vercellus.] [Note: Many manuscripts read, “was closed off by the priest”; but this seems no less corrupt than the reading “was enclosed by the priest.” What, then, if we should read claudicabat (“limped”)? It would certainly correspond more neatly with the following clause, “the foundations of the faith would be confirmed.” Yet claudebat can also have the same meaning, from claudeo or claudo, forms which Vossius shows are not entirely unknown.]

13. Nor was his disciple otherwise in imitation of him, for he too said to his father and mother: “I did not see you” (Deuteronomy 33:9 ff.). He did not see them through preference, nor did he see them through affection; and he did not acknowledge his brothers, because he desired to know the Lord. He too recognized the word of the Lord, guarded his covenant, and will always place honor upon his altar. Bless, Lord, his faith, holiness, and diligence. May your blessing come upon his head and upon his neck. May he be honored among his brothers; may there be in him the appearance of a bull, so that he may scatter the hearts of his enemies, soothe the minds of the saints, and make the judgment of your priests flourish in him like a lily (ibid., 16 ff.). Farewell, brothers, and love me, because I love you.

## LETTER XVI

Ambrose congratulates Anysius, recently appointed in the place of Acholius, and, praising his predecessor’s holiness, his youth spent in a monastery, his virtue-filled manhood, and his fruitful old age, prays that Anysius may become the successor to the same merits.

AMBROSE, bishop, to his brother ANYSIUS.

1. I have long held you in mind, although I am reading [your letter] only now for the first time; and by his merits I know one whom I had not seen with my eyes. I grieve that the former event occurred, but I rejoice that this has followed, because although, while I was still alive, I would not have wished that to happen, I nevertheless hoped that, after the departure of that holy man, only one such as you could worthily succeed him. We therefore regard you as the disciple of Acholius of holy memory from long ago, and now as his successor and heir both of his honor and of his grace. Great is your merit, brother. I rejoice for you, since not even for a moment was there doubt that so great a man would have a worthy successor. And great is the burden, brother: you have taken upon yourself the weight of so great a name, so great a standard, and so great a measure. Acholius is sought in you; and just as he was in your affection, so in your duties his virtue, his discipline, and the image of his strength of soul are desired in such an aged body.

2. I saw the man, I confess—for I owe to his merits even the fact that I saw him. I saw that he was in the body in such a way that I thought him to be outside the body. I saw the image of the one who, whether in the body or outside the body, did not know, but had been caught up into paradise (2 Corinthians 12:2). For he traversed everything in frequent journeys—Constantinople, Achaea, Epirus, Italy—so that younger men could not keep up with him. Those stronger in body gave way, because they knew that he was without the body’s impediment; he used it only as a covering, not as an instrument; certainly for service, not for support. For he had so disciplined his body that in it he crucified the world, and himself to the world.

3. Blessed is the Lord, and blessed is his youth, which he spent in the tents of the God of Jacob, placed in monasteries. When his parents or relatives sought him there, he said: “Who are my brothers, or who is my mother?” (Matthew 12:48). “I do not know father, mother, or brothers of mine, except those who hear the word of God and do it.” Blessed also was the progress of his youth, in which he was chosen for the highest priesthood, already proved by the mature reward of his virtues. For he came like David to restore peace to the people (2 Samuel 5:3). He came like that ship carrying with it intelligible gold, cedar wood, and precious stones (2 Chronicles 9:21), and those silvered wings of the dove, among whose divisions he slept in the sleep of peace and tranquility (Psalm 67:14). [Note: Some manuscripts read, “he was raised to the priesthood.”] [Note: The manuscripts and the old edition read this way, except that in place of “and these” they have “as”: “as that dove having silvered wings.” The Roman edition alters the passage in this manner: “so that that dove, having silvered wings…”]

4. For even the sleep of the saints is active, according to what is written: “I sleep, and my heart is awake” (Song of Songs 5:2). And just as holy Jacob, while sleeping, saw divine mysteries (Genesis 28:13) that he had not seen while awake—a passage open to the saints from heaven to earth, with the Lord looking down and promising his land as a possession—so, sleeping a short sleep, he obtained what his inheritance later acquired through great labor. For the sleep of the saints is at rest from all bodily pleasures and all disturbance of mind; it brings tranquility to the mind and peace to the soul, so that, as though released from the body’s bond, it may rise up and cling to Christ.

5. This is the sleep and life of the saints, which holy Acholius lived; and blessed was his old age as well. That is truly venerable old age which grows white not through gray hairs but through merits (Wisdom 4:8). For that is reverend hoariness which is the hoariness of the soul, shining forth in white thoughts and deeds. What is truly the age of old age except an unstained life (ibid., 9), which is extended not through days or months but through ages, whose duration is without end and whose longevity is long without weakness? For the longer it endures, the stronger it is; and the longer one lives that life, the more strongly one grows into a perfect man.

6. May the Lord therefore prove you to be his successor not only in honor but also in character, and deign to establish you in the highest grace, so that the peoples too may gather to you, concerning whom you may say: “Who are these who fly like clouds and like doves with their young?” (Isaiah 60:8). May they also come like the ships of Tarshish (2 Chronicles 9:21), which receive the grain bestowed by the true Solomon—twenty measures of wheat. May they receive Solomon’s oil and wisdom, and may there be peace between you and the people; may you guard the covenant of peace. Farewell, brother, and love us, because we too love you.

[Note: The Longobardic codex: “The booklet of Saint Ambrose to the Emperor Valentinian the Younger against Symmachus.” And indeed Ambrose himself, replying to this same report of Symmachus, cites this writing under the name of a booklet. But since in all the other manuscripts and in every edition it is called a letter, not a booklet, we did not think that the customary title ought to be changed.]

## LETTER XVII

It is the duty of emperors to protect religion, and restoration of superstition must not be sought from them. Thus no account is to be taken of those who demand anything contrary to the honor of the Christian faith. The petition was falsely presented in the Senate’s name, since the Christian senators did not consent to it. The matter ought to be referred to Theodosius and to the bishops. Valentinian, if he grants privileges to unbelievers, is to be excluded from the Church and will also inflict an injury upon the memory of his brother and father; they are introduced as protesting this vehemently.

AMBROSE, bishop, to the most blessed prince and most Christian emperor VALENTINIAN.

[Col. 0961B] 1. Although all men who are subject to Roman rule serve you, emperors and princes of the earth, you yourselves serve almighty God and the sacred faith. For salvation cannot otherwise be secure, unless each person truly worships the true God—that is, the God of the Christians, by whom all things are governed; for he alone is the true God, who is worshiped in the inmost mind. For, as Scripture says: “The gods of the nations are demons” (Psalm 95:5). [Note: Thus the old edition and some manuscripts; the Roman edition reads: “the God of the Christians, by whom all things are governed—for he alone is the true God—should worship with his inmost mind.” Many manuscripts also omit the words “by whom all things are governed.” But this variation seems to have arisen solely because they did not believe that *veneretur* could be used in a passive sense, though attentive reading will show that Ambrose uses it thus more than once.]

2. Whoever therefore serves this true God and receives him to be worshiped with inward affection expends not dissimulation or connivance, but zeal of faith and devotion. Finally, even if he does not do these things, he ought at least to offer no assent whatever to the worship of idols and to the profane rites of ceremonies. For no one deceives God, to whom even all the secrets of the heart are manifest.

3. Therefore, since faith must be shown by you, most Christian Emperor, to the true God, and since the faith itself requires zeal, vigilance, and devotion, I wonder how some have conceived the hope that you ought by your command to restore altars to the gods of the nations and also provide expenditure for the uses of profane sacrifices. For what has long since been claimed either by the treasury or by the public chest, you will seem rather to bestow from your own than to restore to them from theirs. [Note: Very many manuscripts read “either by the treasury or by the public chest”; a few others, “either by the treasury or by money.” The latter is not wholly bad, since it means the same as confiscation or purchase. Nevertheless, we do not depart from the other reading and from all the editions.]

4. And those complain of losses who never spared our blood, who even demolished the buildings of the Churches. They ask also that you confer privileges upon them—those who, by a recent law of Julian, denied our people the common use of speaking and teaching—and those privileges by which even Christians have often been deceived. For they wished to entangle some in those privileges, partly through imprudence and partly in order to evade the burdens of public obligations; and, because not all are found steadfast, very many fell away even under Christian emperors. [Note: We have already noted, at Book I of *On the Faith*, chapter 13, section 84, that Julian forbade Christians to teach the more liberal disciplines. He perhaps means the following law, the last promulgated by that emperor.]

### 3.

But if these things had not already been removed, I would approve their being taken away by your authority. Yet since they have been prohibited and banned throughout almost the whole world by numerous emperors before your time, and since at Rome they were removed by your brother, Gratian of august memory, in accordance with the true faith, and rendered obsolete by issued rescripts, I beg you neither to overturn measures faithfully established nor to rescind your brother’s commands. In civil matters, no one thinks that what has been decreed should be rashly disturbed; yet the command concerning religion is trampled underfoot.

[Note: [Col. 0962C] The emperors designated here are undoubtedly Constantine the Great and his sons. Certainly, the law of Constantius concerning the pagans still survives, by which he decreed that the temples of idols be closed, sacrifices abolished, and the resources assigned to this sacrilegious worship confiscated for the treasury. But when Julian, as Sozomen reports in Book IV, chapter 3 of his *History*, restored all these things to use, Valentinian, Valens, and Gratian again proscribed the profane religions of fictitious deities, their property being assigned to the treasury, as can be learned from Law 20, “Concerning the Pagans,” and Law 8, “Concerning the Right of the Treasury.” Moreover, Godefridus, in Law 3, “Concerning Interrogations,” says that those who want the altar of Victory to have been overturned in the year 382 are commonly mistaken; he asserts that this had happened much earlier, namely in 376, when Jerome in Letter 7 and Prudentius in Book I *Against Symmachus* state that it occurred under Gracchus, prefect of the city. Yet although neither of them specifically mentions that same altar of Victory, it is nevertheless established that it was removed several years before 382, since in that very year they undertook an attempt to restore it; and Gratian had already ceased to govern Italy and Rome from the year 379 onward.]

### 6.

Let no one take advantage of your youthful age. If he is a pagan who is requesting these things, he ought not to bind your mind with the fetters of his superstition; rather, by his own zeal he ought to teach and admonish you how you should pursue the true faith, when he defends falsehood with such agitation. I too advise that consideration be shown to the merits of distinguished men; but it is certain that God must be preferred to everyone.

### 7.

If military affairs are under consideration, the opinion of a man experienced in battles should be awaited and his counsel approved. When religion is being discussed, think of God. No injustice is done to anyone when almighty God is preferred to him. He has his own opinion. You do not compel anyone unwilling to worship what he does not wish to worship. May the same be permitted to you, Emperor, and may each person patiently endure it if he does not force upon the emperor what he would be distressed to have the emperor force upon him. Even pagans have usually disapproved the disposition of a turncoat; each person ought freely to defend the faith of his mind and preserve his chosen course.

[Col. 0962C]

### 8.

But if some people who call themselves Christians think that something of this kind ought to be decreed, let neither bare words seize your mind nor empty names deceive you. Whoever advises this is sacrificing, and whoever decrees it is sacrificing. Yet one person’s sacrifice is more tolerable than the fall of everyone. The entire senate of the Christians is put at risk.

[Col. 0963A]

### 9.

If today some pagan, God forbid, were to set up an altar with images and compel Christians to assemble there, so that they might be present at the sacrifices, so that ash from the altar, embers from the sacrilege, and smoke from the funeral pyre might fill the breath and mouths of the faithful; and if he were to give his vote in that senate-house where men sworn at the altar of the image were compelled to vote—for this is why they interpret the altar as having been placed there: so that, by its oath, as they suppose, each member of the assembly might deliberate for the common interest, when the senate-house is already filled with a greater number of Christians—would not a Christian who was compelled by such a choice to come to the senate believe this to be persecution? This is often what happens; for they are compelled to attend even amid insults. Then, while you are emperor, will Christians be compelled to swear at an altar? What is swearing except confessing the divine power of the one whom you invoke as the guardian of your faith? While you are emperor, this is being requested and demanded: that you order the altar to be raised and public funds to be provided for profane sacrifices.

[Col. 0963B]

### 10.

But this cannot be decreed without sacrilege. Therefore I beg you not to decree or establish it, nor to subscribe to decrees of this kind. As a priest of Christ, I appeal to your faith. All of us bishops would have approached you,

[Note: [Col. 0963C] From this we infer that Symmachus’s report was secretly presented to the emperor, perhaps so that either the bishops would not intervene before Valentinian granted his requests, or Christian senators would not protest by submitting a counter-petition—as Ambrose testifies had already happened in a similar case.]

unless something so incredible and sudden had reached the ears of men: that such a thing had either been proposed in your council chamber or requested by the senate. But heaven forbid that this should be said to have been requested by the senate: a few pagans make use of the common name. For nearly two years earlier, when they attempted to request this, the holy Damasus, priest of the Roman Church, chosen by God’s judgment, sent me a petition which the Christian senators—indeed, very many of them—had submitted, declaring that they had commissioned no such thing, that they did not agree with petitions of this kind from the pagans, and that they did not give their assent.

[Note: [Col. 0963D] Several manuscripts read, “to give our consent to their petitions.”]

They also publicly and privately complained that they would not assemble in the senate-house if anything of this kind were decreed.

Is it fitting for your times—that is, for Christian times—that the dignity of Christian senators should be taken away so that the profane will of pagans may be fulfilled? I sent this petition to your brother’s clemency; from it it became clear that the senate had not commissioned its envoys to request anything concerning the expenses of superstition.

[Col. 0964A]

### 11.

But perhaps someone will say: Why did they not previously attend the senate when these matters were being requested? Those who did not attend make their wishes sufficiently clear; those who spoke before the emperor have spoken sufficiently. Yet we are astonished that, while they take away from private citizens the freedom to resist in Rome, they do not want you to be free not to command what you do not approve, but to preserve what you do approve.

[Note: [Col. 0963D] Thus read the manuscripts of better quality. Several others, together with the printed editions, read “not to preserve what you do not feel”; the rest disagree among themselves about the placement of the negations, but with a corrupt meaning.]

### 12.

And therefore, mindful of the embassy recently entrusted to me, I appeal again to your faith; I appeal to your mind: do not think either that a reply should be given in accordance with such a petition of the pagans, or that you should add the sacrilege of your signature to replies of this kind. At least refer the matter to the emperor Theodosius, the father of your clemency, whom you have been accustomed to consult concerning almost all the more important affairs. Nothing is greater than religion; nothing is more sublime than faith.

[Note: [Col. 0963D] He refers to the embassy entrusted to him by Pope Damasus, namely that he should act before Gratian so that he would not grant the petitions of the unbelievers. He does not say, “I appeal to your faith again,” as though he had already appealed to Valentinian, but because he himself had already once discharged a similar office, though before another emperor. Likewise, when he says that this same embassy was recently entrusted to him, he means that he had undertaken only this one after completing the former, just as we have seen that the preceding law was perhaps called by Ambrose “the last” on this account, because it was the last of the emperor Julian.]

### 12*

If this were a civil matter, a reply would be reserved for the opposing party; it is a matter of religion, and I, a bishop, appeal to you.

[Note: [Col. 0963D] Several manuscripts read, “I appeal to the bishops.” The expression occurring not long afterward, “the parent of your clemency,” does not use *parent* in its natural sense, but as a title of honor and affection. Valentinian is thus, as a young man still under maternal guardianship, being urged to regard Theodosius with the love and reverence of a son.]

[Col. 0964C]

Give me a copy of the report that was sent, so that I may reply more fully; and, having been consulted about everything, let the parent of your clemency give his answer. Certainly, if anything else is decreed, we bishops cannot endure and disregard it with equanimity. You will be permitted to come to the Church; but there you will not find a priest—or you will find one who resists.

### 14.

What will you answer to a priest who says to you:

[Note: [Col. 0964D] Since Valentinian was still only a catechumen and was not permitted to attend the Eucharist of the faithful, these “gifts” cannot be understood as the offerings which the same faithful presented in order to receive them from the priest after consecration. They must instead be understood as the various donations which Christians had long contributed for the adornment of churches, the sustenance of ministers, and other similar purposes. Thus Marcellinus, seizing an opportunity to slander the Roman pontiffs, declares that it is no wonder if they seek the pontificate: “Once they have obtained it,” he says, “they will be so secure that they will be enriched by the offerings of matrons,” and so forth. For the rest, who would not marvel not only at the courage Ambrose displays here, but also at the episcopal courage which he testifies to have shone in other bishops? Happy the times that produced such priests!]

“The Church does not seek your gifts, because you have adorned pagan temples with gifts? The altar of Christ rejects your offerings because you made an altar for images; for your voice, your hand, and your signature are your work. The Lord Jesus refuses and rejects your service because you have served idols; for he said to you: ‘You cannot serve two masters’ (Matthew 6:25). Your privileges are not possessed by virgins consecrated to God, while the virgins of Vesta claim theirs? Why do you seek the priests of God, to whom you have preferred the profane petitions of the pagans? We cannot assume fellowship with another’s error.”

### 15.

What will you answer to these words? That you fell because you are a boy? Every age is mature for Christ; every age is full of God. Youth is no excuse where faith is concerned: even little children have confessed Christ with fearless speech before persecutors.

[Note: [Col. 0965D] All the printed editions and most manuscripts read, “Christ is.” The wording “Every childhood is approved as full of faith in God,” and the restoration of the passage as it appears in the text, are found in the Belv., Thuan., Reg., and Carol. manuscripts. Observe here also a clear allusion to the apostolic passage, 1 Corinthians 14:20: “Do not become children in your thinking,” and so forth. The pagans considered this an opportune time to obtain the restoration of their sacred rites, not only because the emperor’s youth generally made the government weaker, but also because of the tyrant Maximus, from whom a bloody war threatened Italy.]

### 16.

What will you answer to your brother? Will he not say to you:

“I did not believe that I had been defeated, because I left you as emperor; I did not grieve to die, because I had you as my heir; I did not lament my withdrawal from imperial power, because I believed that my commands—especially those concerning divine religion—would endure through all ages. I had raised these monuments of pious virtue; these were my spoils from the world, these my trophies from the devil; these were the spoils I offered after victory over the enemy of all, in which eternal victory resides. What more could my enemy have taken from me? You have revoked my decrees—something even the man who took up arms against me has not done. Now I receive a more grievous wound than one inflicted on my body, because my measures are condemned by my brother. In the better part of me I am endangered before you; for one was the death of my body, the other of my virtue. Now my imperial power is revoked, and what is more grievous, it is revoked by your people and by mine; what is revoked is that which even my opponents praised in me. If you yielded willingly, you condemned my faith; if you yielded unwillingly, you betrayed your own. Thus—and this is more grievous—I am endangered in you as well.”

### 16*

What will you answer even to your father, who will address you with greater anguish, saying:

“You have judged me most wrongly, my son, if you thought that I had shown indulgence to the pagans. No one reported to me that there was an altar in that Roman senate-house. I never believed that such an outrage had occurred: that, in that common assembly of Christians and pagans, pagans should sacrifice—that is, insult Christians who were present—and that unwilling Christians should be compelled to attend the sacrifices. Many different crimes were committed while I was emperor; I avenged whatever was discovered. If something then remained hidden, must one therefore say that I approved what no one reported to me? You have judged me most wrongly if you think that a foreign superstition, rather than my faith, preserved my imperial power.”

[Note: [Col. 0965D] Baronius, under the year 371, thinks that these words were spoken more in a rhetorical effort to sway the mind of the boy Valentinian than in accordance with the truth. The elder Valentinian could not have been unaware of the matter; nor is it surprising if he pretended not to know, since he had even promulgated laws in favor of the freedom of pagan religion. Yet, with due respect to so great a man, it hardly seems consistent with Ambrose’s prudence that he should have said things whose falsity he knew could easily be exposed by his opponent. And certainly, although that emperor could not have been unaware that this altar had been placed in the senate-house, it is nevertheless highly credible that nothing had been reported to him about the sacrifices, at which Christians were compelled to be present there, or about the oaths which the unbelievers customarily exacted from them.]

[Col. 0966A]

### 17.

Since you therefore understand that, if you decree anything of this kind, injuries are inflicted first upon God, then upon your father and your brother, I beg you to do what you understand will benefit your salvation before God.

[Col. 0966D]

*Written in the year 384.*

## REPORT OF SYMMACHUS, PREFECT OF THE CITY

In the name of the senate, he entreats the emperors that the ancient religions be restored and the altar of Victory repaired, so that oaths may be sworn at it according to ancient custom. For the earlier emperors should not be imitated in removing it, but in not removing other rites. Rome requests this from them, and it can plainly be granted without damage to the treasury. It should, however, be considered unjust that property bequeathed to the Vestals and to the sacrificial priests should be forbidden to reach them—a matter for which the gods are said to have taken vengeance by sending famine. Finally, he denies that what he requests should be called a public expense, and he closes his speech by urging the emperors to grant his petitions.

### 1.

“When the most distinguished senate, ever yours, recognized the vices subjected to the laws and saw the reputation of recent times cleansed by pious emperors, following the authority of a good age, it disgorged the grief it had long suppressed and once again ordered me to be the envoy of its complaints.

[Note: [Col. 0966D] From these words we learn that the same Symmachus had been chosen by the pagan senators two years earlier to attempt to obtain the restoration of their sacred rites, about which Ambrose speaks in the preceding letter, section 12.]

[Note: [Col. 0966D] The entire passage beginning ‘to whom therefore the hearing of the divine emperor … ever august’ was excised in the Roman edition. It is found not only in the other editions and all the manuscripts, but was also the formula used in petitions.]

The hearing of the divine emperor was therefore denied to him by wicked men because justice would not be lacking, O emperors Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius, illustrious, victorious, triumphant, ever august.

### 2.

“Thus fulfilling a twofold office, both as your prefect pursuing public affairs and as the envoy commending the instructions of the citizens, I have no conflict of purposes here. For people have now ceased to believe that they gain distinction through the favor of courtiers by disagreeing. To be loved, honored, and cherished is greater than imperial power. Who could tolerate private quarrels harming the commonwealth? The senate rightly pursues those who have placed their own power above the reputation of the emperor.

[Note: [Col. 0966D] Thus read the manuscripts and the Roman edition. Amerbach, Erasmus, and Gill instead read, “have ceased to believe.” Some manuscripts read, “the servants of certain kings are compelled to show zeal.” Below, the old edition together with most manuscripts reads, “laws and deeds.”]

### 3.

“Our labor, however, keeps watch on behalf of your clemency. For whom does it profit more that we defend the institutions of our ancestors, the laws and destinies of our fatherland, than the glory of the present age—which is greater precisely when you understand that, contrary to the custom of your ancestors, nothing is permitted to you? We therefore request the restoration of the condition of the religions, which long benefited the commonwealth. Certainly, let the emperors of both sects and both opinions be counted: the nearest predecessor honored the ceremonies of the fathers; the more recent did not remove them.

[Note: [Col. 0967C] “Nearest” means Julian; “more recent” means Valentinian, who is also indicated, together with his brother Valens, by the term “nearest” in the following sentence. Observe how little prudence Symmachus displays in this report, since he speaks everywhere about his deities and sacrifices to a Christian emperor as though he were speaking to a worshiper of idols.]

If the religion of former times does not provide an example, let the dissimulation of those nearest to you provide one.

### 4.

“Who is so friendly with the barbarians that he would not demand the altar of Victory? We are cautious about the future and avoid omens of this kind. Nevertheless, let at least honor be paid to the name, though it has been denied to the deity.

[Note: [Col. 0967C] A few manuscripts read, “at least honor to the man.”]

Your eternity owes much to Victory, and will owe still more. Let those who have gained nothing from it reject this power; you must not abandon the patronage that has been friendly to your triumphs. This power is the object of everyone’s prayers; let no one refuse to honor what he professes to desire.

### 5.

“But if the avoidance of this omen were not justifiable, it was nevertheless fitting at least to spare the ornaments of the senate-house.

[Note: [Col. 0967C] The Reg. edition reads, “there would not even be a just avoidance of this omen.” Several manuscripts differ from this only in reading *non esset* for *non est etiam*. The others present the passage as, “there would not be a just visitation of this man.” That is not sufficiently correct. Onuphrius Panvinius follows another reading in his book *On the City*, changing *hujus hominis* (“of this man”) to *hujus numinis* (“of this deity”) and *visitatio* (“visitation”) to *vitatio* (“avoidance”), while also indicating that *usitatio* (“customary use”) was written somewhere. We think our reading is preferable, with the following sense: even if it were not just to avoid the evil omen derived from the removal of the altar of Victory, nevertheless, and so forth.]

I beg you to ensure that what we received as boys we leave to posterity as old men. The love of custom is great. The deed of the divine Constantius did not long endure.

[Note: [Col. 0967D] Thus read all the editions and manuscripts except one Long. manuscript, which has “the deed of Constantine.” Baronius, under the year 346, recommends reading “the deed of Constans,” as though Symmachus were reproaching Constans for the brevity of his reign and for having been removed by Magnentius because of his prohibition of the rites of the gods. He thinks this conjecture is strongly confirmed by what follows below: “But the divine Constantius.” The same argument is repeated under the year 356. Godefridus follows Baronius in Laws 2 and 3, “Concerning the Pagans,” which he regards as laws of Constans; in the latter place he thinks that Symmachus’s “deed of Constans” silently contrasts with the deed of Magnentius, who restored the rites of the gods. Then, after presenting three laws of Constantius by which access to temples and the use of sacrifices were forbidden, he states in the third that during this period, namely in the year 356, Constantius destroyed the altar of Victory, and that this is proved by the writings of Symmachus and Ambrose. Yet their arguments are not strong enough to make us abandon Constantius here against the authority of so many manuscripts and all the editions. What prevents us from saying that his action did not last long, since his immediate successor, Julian, later rendered it obsolete? Moreover, the fact that Symmachus mentions Constantius again is not inconsistent with the practice of orators, who repeat the same matter from time to time whenever they think it serves their purpose. Add to this what is said below: “who would not have undertaken anything of this kind if someone else before him had deviated.” How could these words fit Constantius, according to Symmachus’s meaning, if Constantius knew that his brother had enacted laws concerning this matter and that Magnentius had overturned them? It is therefore credible that Constans prohibited only nocturnal sacrifices, which Magnentius is known to have restored.]

You should avoid every example that you soon learned had been removed. We are concerned for the eternity of your reputation and name, lest a future age find anything that needs correcting.

### 6.

“Where shall we swear by your laws and words? By what religion shall a false mind be restrained from lying in its testimony? Everything indeed is full of God, and no place is safe for the treacherous; but the very presence of religion being brought to bear has great force in producing fear of wrongdoing. That altar holds together the harmony of all; that altar summons each person to faith. Nothing gives greater authority to our decisions than that our entire order, as though sworn, makes its decisions there. Will a profane seat therefore lie open to perjuries? And will my illustrious emperors, who are protected by a public oath, judge this acceptable?

[Col. 0968A]

### 7.

“But the divine Constantius is said to have done the same thing. Let us rather imitate the other deeds of that emperor, who would not have undertaken anything of this kind if someone before him had gone astray. For the fall of a predecessor corrects the successor, and improvement arises from criticism of the earlier example.

[Note: [Col. 0968D] The Roman edition alone reads, “and from the example of the preceding detection.”]
