It was permissible for that parent of your clemency, in a matter still new, not to guard against hostility. Can the same defense apply to us if we imitate what we remember to have been condemned?

### 8.

“Let your eternity receive other deeds of the same emperor, which it may more worthily put to use. He took nothing away from the privileges of the sacred virgins; he filled the priesthoods with noblemen; he did not deny expenditures for Roman ceremonies; and, following the joyful senate through all the streets of the eternal City, he looked upon the shrines with a peaceful expression, read the names of the gods inscribed on the pediments, asked about the origins of the temples, and admired their founders.

[Note: [Col. 0968D] Several manuscripts read, “the names of the gods.”]

Although he himself followed other religions, he preserved these by imperial authority; for each person has his own custom, each his own rite. The divine mind has distributed different guardians and forms of worship among cities.

[Note: [Col. 0968D] All the printed editions and manuscripts read this way; nearly all omit the negation, and several also omit the word *cultus* (“worship”). In place of it, Panvinius, already cited above, reads “among all cities.”]

Just as souls are assigned to those who are born, so fated spirits are assigned to peoples.

[Note: [Col. 0968D] Epictetus, *Enchiridion*, chapter 38: “For where the useful is, there also is the pious” (ὅπου γὰρ τὸ σύμφερον, ἐκεῖ καὶ τὸ εὐσεβές). Both therefore make utility the foundation of piety, but they define it in different ways.]

Utility also contributes, and this above all asserts the gods to mankind. For since the whole rational explanation lies hidden, from where can knowledge of the deities arise more properly than from the memory and records of successful events?

[Note: [Col. 0968D] Several manuscripts read, “since the whole matter is in the open”; one reads, “since the whole matter is accomplished.”]

If long antiquity gives authority to religions, then faith preserved through so many ages must be maintained, and we must follow our ancestors, who successfully followed theirs.

### 9.

“Let us now imagine Rome standing before us and addressing you in these words:

‘Best emperors, fathers of your country, revere my years, to which pious worship has brought me. I shall use the ceremonies of my ancestors; nor do I regret it. I shall live according to my custom, because I am free. This worship brought the world under my laws; these sacred rites drove Hannibal back from my walls and the Senones from the Capitol. Was I preserved for this purpose, to be condemned in my old age? I shall see to what is thought necessary; but the correction of old age, however late, is nevertheless insulting.’

### 10.

“Therefore we ask peace from the ancestral gods and the native gods.

[Note: [Col. 0969C] A good number of manuscripts read, “from the ancestral gods, the native gods”; some corruptly read *indigentibus* (“needy”) for *indigetibus* (“native”). Virgil, in Book I of the *Georgics*, does indeed place together *dii patrii indigetes* (“ancestral native gods”); but nothing prevents Symmachus from separating the two nouns. Although the native gods are rarely understood as the same as those whom the Greeks call θεοὶ πατρῷοι καὶ ἐγχώριοι (“ancestral and native gods”), they are nevertheless often understood as heroes translated among the gods and dwelling among them. See also the other meanings of the term in Vossius, *Etymologicon*, Joseph Laurentius, Book II of the *Polyhistor*, dissertation 49, and others.]

It is just that whatever all worship should be regarded as one. We all look upon the same stars; the sky is common to us all; the same universe surrounds us. What difference does it make by what wisdom each person seeks the truth? One road cannot lead to so great a mystery. But this is a discussion for people with leisure; now we offer prayers, not disputes.’

[Note: [Col. 0969D] Thus read the old edition and the manuscripts, except a few, which also read “now disputes.” The Roman edition instead reads “we offer prayers, not disputes.” By “disputes” one should not understand battles fought with weapons, but the contests of argument which he has just said belong to people with leisure.]

### 11.

“What advantage to your sacred treasury has been gained by removing the privilege of the Vestal virgins? Under the most generous emperors, is what the most frugal provided to be denied? In that apparent stipend there is only the honor of chastity. Just as honor is made an adornment of their life, so it is considered a distinction to be free from the obligations of sacrifice.

[Note: [Col. 0969D] The Roman edition alone reads, “to be free from the duties of the priesthood.”]

They seek, in a certain sense, the bare name of immunity, since poverty protects them from expense. Thus those who take something away from their property contribute more to their praise; for virginity dedicated to the public welfare gains in merit when it lacks a reward.

### 12.

“Let such savings be absent from the purity of your treasury. Let the treasury of good emperors be increased not by the losses of priests but by the spoils of enemies. Can any profit compensate for resentment? And since avarice does not enter into your character, those whose ancient supports have been taken away are all the more pitiable. For under emperors who abstain from what belongs to others and resist greed, what does not stir the desire of the taker is removed only to the injury of the one who loses it.

### 13.

“The treasury also lays claim to fields bequeathed by the intention of the dying to virgins and ministers.

[Note: [Col. 0969D] He calls those who are failing—whose lives are yielding under the burden of old age—“the dying”; Ambrose commonly calls them “the weakened.” Such persons’ wills are especially sealed in circumstances of this kind.]

I beg you, priests of justice, to restore private succession to the sacred rites of your city. Let them make their wills securely, and let them know that under non-avaricious emperors what they have written will be secure. Let this happiness of the human race delight you. The example of this case has begun to trouble the dying. Are Roman religions therefore not subject to Roman laws? What name shall be given to the seizure of property which no law and no circumstance has made forfeitable? Freedmen receive legacies; slaves are not denied their rightful allowances under wills.

[Note: [Col. 0969D] He calls them “rightful advantages” because slaves were not permitted to receive either an entire inheritance or just any legacies, but only a *peculium*—that is, a modest sum of money—or some allowance, such as produce, clothing, and so forth. We understand from Suetonius, Juvenal, and others that *commoda* could be used for an allowance assigned to priests, soldiers, and others.]

Are only noble virgins and ministers of the fated rites excluded from estates acquired by inheritance? What benefit is there in dedicating a chaste body to the public welfare, supporting the eternity of the empire with heavenly defenses, joining friendly virtues to your arms and eagles, undertaking effective prayers on behalf of all, and not possessing the same legal rights as everyone else? Is the servitude rendered to human beings therefore better? We injure the commonwealth, for it is never advantageous to it to be ungrateful.

### 14.

“Let no one think that I am defending the cause of the religions alone.

[Note: [Col. 0970C] It was an old and familiar accusation of the pagans that the empire never suffered any calamity without attributing it to the Christian religion. Tertullian expresses it elegantly in *Apology*, chapter 40: “If the Tiber rises to the walls, if the Nile does not rise into the fields, if the sky stands still, if the earth moves, if there is famine, if there is plague, immediately: ‘Christians to the lion!’” Besides Tertullian in this same *Apology* and our Ambrose in the following discussion, other defenders of Christian innocence also refuted these slanders, among whom Augustine won the palm by publishing his books *On the City of God*.]

All the misfortunes of the Roman people have arisen from crimes of this kind. The law of our ancestors had honored the Vestal virgins and the ministers of the gods with modest sustenance and rightful privileges. The integrity of this provision lasted until degenerate money-changers converted the nourishment of sacred chastity into payment for base porters. Public famine followed this deed, and the sickly harvest disappointed the hopes of all the provinces. These are not faults of the earth. We do not blame the stars. Neither rust harmed the crops nor did oats destroy the grain; the year dried up because of sacrilege. For it was necessary that everything perish because what belonged to the religions was denied.

[Col. 0970C]

### 15.

“Certainly, if this evil has some precedent, let us attribute such great famine to the power of the years. A severe wind compressed this sterility. Life is prolonged among wild shrubs, and once again the poverty of the rural populace has fled to the oaks of Dodona.

[Note: [Col. 0970D] Some manuscripts read, “to suitable trees.” Incorrectly: the trees of Dodona are oaks, whose acorns are said to have sustained the earliest human beings. The severity of the famine is therefore indicated by saying that the poor were compelled to eat acorns because milder crops were lacking.]

What province has ever endured anything like this when public honor nourished the ministers of the religions? When have oaks been shaken for human use, when have the roots of plants been torn up, when has the mutual fertility of regions failed to compensate for alternating shortages, when grain was shared by the people and the sacred virgins? The produce of the earth commended the sustenance of the priests, and was a remedy rather than a largesse. Is it doubtful that what the present scarcity of all has exacted was always given for the abundance of all?

### 16.

“Someone may say that public expenditure was denied for the costs of a foreign religion. Far be such an opinion from good emperors, so that what was assigned to some from the common fund should appear to belong to the treasury.

[Note: [Col. 0971C] Several manuscripts read, “so that what is common”; the others, together with the printed editions, read, “so that what comes from the common fund”; the old edition reads, “what formerly came from the common fund.”]

For since the commonwealth consists of individuals, what proceeds from it should again become the property of individuals. You govern everything, but preserve each person’s own property; justice has greater power with you than license. Consult your own generosity: do you want these things to be regarded as public which you have transferred to others? Once savings have been granted to the honor of the city, they cease to belong to those who granted them; what was initially a benefaction becomes, through use and time, an obligation. Thus anyone who asserts that, unless you incur the odium of withdrawing these grants, you bear the obligation of continuing to provide them attempts to instill an empty fear into your divine mind.

[Note: [Col. 0971D] Some manuscripts read, “to have the presence of those who provide.” Incorrectly: “to incur the obligation of the providers” means to be as bound as if they were continuing to provide, unless they withdraw the grants.]

### 17.

“May the hidden protections of every sect favor your clemency; and may those especially which once helped your ancestors defend you and be worshipped by us. We seek the condition of the religions which preserved the imperial power of your divine father and supplied legitimate heirs to that fortunate emperor.

[Note: [Col. 0971D] The Roman edition reads, “which preserved the imperial power of your father, the summit of your family,” and so forth. When he says that the rule of the elder Valentinian was preserved by the religions of his gods, this should be understood in the sense not that Valentinian followed those religions, but that he did not abolish them, as Symmachus said above. For this same reason the pagan Marcellinus commends that emperor in Book XXX, chapter 9. Indeed, Valentinian himself testified by Law 9, “Concerning Malefices,” that he had left each person free to follow whatever religion he chose. This is also why Ambrose says of the younger Valentinian in his funeral eulogy: “What his father lacked, he added; what his brother established, he preserved.”]

That elder divine emperor looks from his starry citadel upon the tears of the priests and considers himself blamed for a custom violated which he himself willingly preserved.

[Col. 0971C]

### 18.

“Provide also your divine brother with a correction of another’s counsel. Conceal the deed which he did not know had displeased the senate, since it is clear that the embassy was excluded precisely so that public judgment would not reach him. It is appropriate to the reputation of former times that you should not hesitate to abolish what has been shown not to have been the emperor’s own approval.”

[Col. 0971D]

*Written in the year 384.*

## LETTER XVIII

Ambrose replies to the report of Symmachus and, after securing the goodwill of Valentinian, attacks three principal points in that report. First, he opposes to the personification in which Rome was represented as demanding the restoration of her ancient rites another personification of the same Rome demanding contrary things. He compares the sacred virgins and priests of Christ with the Vestals and sacrificial priests. Finally, he demonstrates by irrefutable arguments that the claim that famine had exacted vengeance for the abolition of those ceremonies was groundless.

Ambrose, bishop, to the most blessed prince and most clement emperor, Valentinian Augustus.

[Note: [Col. 0971D] Several manuscripts read, “and most Christian emperor.”]

1. When the most illustrious prefect of the city, Symmachus, had referred to Your Clemency that the altar which had been removed from the senate house of the city of Rome should be restored to its place—and when you, Emperor, although still flourishing in the youthful training of your early years, were nevertheless a veteran in the strength of faith and did not approve the petition of the pagans—I presented a memorandum at the very moment, as I learned, when the report was submitted. Although I had included in it whatever seemed necessary for the proposal, I nevertheless requested that a copy of the report be given to me.

   [Note: The title “most illustrious” is attributed not so much to the honor of the person as it is a title and indication of rank, as we have already observed elsewhere. See also, if you have time, Alciatus, *Book III of the Disputations*.]

2. Accordingly, I answer the assertions of the report in this address—not uncertain of your faith, but watchful in prudence, and confident in your dutiful judgment—asking only this: that you should look for the force of the matter, not the elegance of the words.

   [Note: The Roman edition reads “which ought to be weighed”; the other editions and manuscripts read “which ought to be awaited,” except for one Vatican manuscript, which has “which ought to be sought.”]

   For, as divine Scripture teaches (Ecclesiastes 6:11), the tongue of learned wise men is golden. Adorned with embellished expressions and flashing, as it were, with the gleam of a precious color reflected from shining eloquence, it captures the eyes of minds and dazzles them with the appearance of beauty.

   [Note: Two manuscripts read “with a beautiful appearance, and it strikes the sight”; one reads “it strikes with the appearance of beauty”; the others, together with the printed editions, read “with the appearance of the beautiful,” while the Roman edition has “and it strikes the sight.”]

   But if you handle this gold more carefully, outwardly it has the value of gold, but inwardly it is mere metal.

   [Note: Supply: “Outwardly it displays the value of gold; inwardly it is metal,” namely bronze or iron; the name of the genus is being used for an inferior species.]

   Turn over and examine, I beg you, the sect of the pagans: they make precious and grand sounds, but defend things drained of truth. They speak of God, yet worship an image.

3. The most illustrious prefect of the city therefore put forward three points in his report which he thought powerful: first, that Rome, as he says, demands the restoration of her ancient rites; second, that allowances should be granted to her priests and Vestal virgins; and third, that when the allowances of the priests were withheld, a public famine followed.

4. In his first argument, lamenting Rome weeps through the language of her complaint, demanding, as he says, the ancient rites of her ceremonies.

   “These sacred rites,” he says, “drove Hannibal back from the walls and the Senones from the Capitol.”

   [Note: Everyone knows that Hannibal, the Carthaginian commander, intensely hostile to the Roman people, brought Roman affairs into the greatest danger. Eventually softened by the pleasures of Apulia and weakened by Fabius’s delay, he was compelled to withdraw from Italy and was later defeated by Scipio Africanus. The Senones, after crossing from Celtic Gaul into Italy, seized the city itself by force. But when they were about to occupy the Capitol, they were detected by the honking of geese, after the guard of dogs had failed, and were thrown down from the Tarpeian Rock by Manlius.]

   And so, while the power of the sacred rites is being proclaimed, their weakness is exposed. Hannibal therefore mocked the Roman sacred rites for a long time, and while the gods were supposedly fighting against him, he reached the walls of the city by a series of victories. Why did they allow themselves to be besieged, when the weapons of their gods were fighting on their behalf?

5. For what should I say about the Senones? The Roman survivors would not have withstood them as they penetrated the hidden places of the Capitol, had a frightened goose not betrayed them by its clamor. Behold what sort of guardians the Roman temples possess. Where was Jupiter then? Was he speaking through the goose?

6. But why should I deny that the rites of the sacred institutions fought on behalf of the Romans? Hannibal also worshipped the same gods. Let them choose, then, which alternative they want. If the sacred rites prevailed among the Romans, then they were defeated among the Carthaginians; if they triumphed among the Carthaginians, they certainly did not benefit the Romans either.

7. Let that odious complaint of the Roman people therefore be dismissed:

   [Note: All the printed editions read, “Rome did not order this”; several manuscripts read, “Rome did not order this matter”; the remaining manuscripts, more appropriately, read, “she did not order this …,” with “complaint” understood.]

   “Why do you stain me every day with the blood of a harmless flock wasted for no purpose? Trophies of victory are found not in the entrails of cattle but in the strength of warriors. I subdued the world by other disciplines.

   “Camillus fought; after recovering the standards taken to the Capitol and slaughtering the conquerors of the Tarpeian Rock, he brought them back in triumph. Virtue overthrew those whom religion had not driven away.”

   [Note: Camillus was appointed dictator five times and, because of his outstanding services to the Republic, was called another Romulus. Having gathered the remnants of the Romans, he routed and crushed the Senones, who were intent on plunder; Ambrose mentions him chiefly for this reason.]

   “Why should I speak of Atilius, who devoted even his death to military service?”

   [Note: Atilius Regulus, captured by the Carthaginians in war, was sent to the Senate to negotiate an exchange of prisoners. After strongly dissuading the exchange, he returned to Carthage to face certain and cruel death.]

   “Africanus found triumph not among the altars of the Capitol but amid Hannibal’s battle lines.

   “Why do you bring before me examples from antiquity? I hate the rites of the Neros. What shall I say of emperors who lasted only two months, and of kings whose ends were joined to their beginnings? Or perhaps it is something new that barbarians have exceeded their own boundaries?

   “Were those men Christians, whose rites, by the wretched and unprecedented example of one emperor held captive and, under the other, a captive world, revealed themselves false in what they had promised of victory?”

   [Note: Nannius says that these words undoubtedly refer to Licinius Valerian and his son Gallienus. Their father, captured by the Persian king Sapor, grew old in miserable slavery, with Sapor using his neck as a mounting block whenever he mounted his horse; the other ruined the world through luxury and depravity, to such an extent that thirty tyrants seized the provinces and even women assumed the diadem against him.]

   [Note: Several manuscripts read, “and deceived what promised victory,” which is less suitable.]

   “Was there no altar of Victory then either? I regret my error. Ancient gray hair has drawn the blush of shame for its disgraceful bloodshed. I am not ashamed to change with the whole world in its old age. It is certainly true that no age is too late to learn thoroughly. Let old age be ashamed if it cannot correct itself.

   “It is not the grayness of years that has been praised, but of conduct” (Wisdom 4:9).

   [Note: All the printed editions and a few manuscripts read, “gray hair is to be praised.”]

   “There is no shame in passing over to better things. This alone I had in common with the barbarians: formerly I did not know God. Your sacrifice is a rite sprinkled with the blood of beasts. Why do you seek the voice of God in dead cattle? Come and learn the heavenly warfare on earth: here we live, and there we serve as soldiers. Let God himself, who created heaven, teach me its mystery—not a man who did not know himself. Whom should I believe about God more than God? How can I believe you, when you admit that you do not know what you worship?”

8. “One cannot reach so great a mystery by a single road,” he says. “What you do not know, we have learned through the voice of God. What you seek through conjectures, we know from the very wisdom and truth of God.

   “Your practices therefore do not agree with ours. You beg emperors to grant peace to your gods; we ask Christ to grant peace to the emperors themselves. You worship the works of your own hands; we consider it an insult that anything made should be thought to be God. God does not wish to be worshipped in stones. Finally, even your own philosophers laughed at these things.”

9. But if you deny that Christ is God because you do not believe that he died—

   [Note: Some manuscripts read, “because you believe that he died”; the others, and all the printed editions, read, “because you do not believe that he died.” The latter is preferable, as the following makes clear: they do not believe that Christ could have died.]

   —you do not know that his death was a death of the flesh, not of the divinity, which brought it about that no believer now dies—how much more foolish are you, who worship your own god with insult and detract from him with honor? For you think your god is wood. O insulting reverence! You do not believe that Christ could have died. O honorific obstinacy!

10. “But,” he says, “the ancient altars must be restored to the images, and their ornaments to the shrines.”

   Let these things be demanded by the partner of superstition; the Christian emperor has learned to honor the altar of Christ alone. Why do they compel pious hands and faithful lips to offer service to sacrilegious sacrifices?

   [Note: A few manuscripts read, “to offer service to sacrifices.”]

   Let the voice of our emperor resound with Christ, and let him speak of him alone, whom he recognizes, because “the heart of the king is in the hand of God” (Proverbs 21:1). Did a pagan emperor raise an altar to Christ? While they demand the restoration of what once existed, they themselves show by their example how much reverence Christian emperors ought to show toward the religion they follow, since pagans deferred everything to their superstitions.

11. “We have only just begun,” they say, “and now those who were excluded are following.”

   [Note: The old edition reads, “While we have begun, let us follow those excluded”; the Roman edition and the manuscripts agree with us, except that it retains *sequamur*, “let us follow,” where they nearly unanimously have *sequuntur*, “they follow.”]

   We glory in blood; they are troubled by expense. We count these things as a victory; they consider them an injury. They never contributed more to us than when they ordered Christians to be scourged, proscribed, and killed. Religion made into a reward what unbelief thought was punishment. Look at their greatness of spirit. Through injuries, poverty, and punishment we grew;

   [Note: All the printed editions read, “we believe”; all the manuscripts read, “we grew.”]

   they do not believe that their ceremonies can remain without profit.

11. “Let the Vestal virgins,” he says, “retain their exemption.”

   [Note: On the Vestals, see what we observed in Book I *On Virgins*, chapter 4, no. 15. What is said below, “the Vestals are captured,” alludes to the formula by which the pontiff received a new virgin: “I take you, beloved.”]

   Let those who do not know how to believe that virginity can be without payment say this; let those who distrust virtue entice people with profits. Yet how many virgins have promised rewards produced for them?” Scarcely seven Vestal girls are recruited. Behold the entire number produced by the fillets binding their heads, the purple trimmings of their clothing, the pomp of the litter surrounded by the retinue of attendants, the greatest privileges, enormous profits, and finally the prescribed duration of chastity.

12. Let them raise the eyes of mind and body; let them see a people of modesty, a multitude of integrity, an assembly of virgins. Their heads are adorned not with fillets but with a veil ignoble in its use and noble in chastity;

   [Note: The printed editions and a few manuscripts read, “a veil noble in its use” or, in the Roman edition, “noble in use”; the more numerous and better manuscripts have the reading reproduced in the text.]

   not with carefully cultivated but renounced allurements of beauty; not with those ornaments of purple or the luxury of pleasures, but with the practice of fasting; not with privileges or profits. In short, everything is of such a kind that one might think they were being called back from their pursuit while they perform their duties. But while the duty is performed, the pursuit is encouraged. Chastity is increased by its own losses.

   It is not virginity when it is bought at a price and not possessed through devotion to virtue. It is not integrity when it is bid for at a money auction for a time, for the profit to be gained.”

   [Note: All the printed editions read, “as though at an auction … it is solicited”; all the manuscripts agree with us, except that one reads “action” and another “security” instead of “auction.”]

   The first victory of chastity is to overcome the desire for possessions, because the pursuit of profit is a temptation to modesty. Let us suppose, nevertheless, that financial support should be granted to virgins. What gifts would remain for Christian women? What treasury would be sufficient for such wealth? Or if they think that it should be granted only to Vestals, are they not ashamed that those who claimed everything for themselves under pagan emperors should not think that, under Christian rulers, we ought to share the same lot?

[Col. 0976A]

13. They also complain that public provisions are not owed to their priests and attendants. What a tumult of words has arisen from this! On the contrary, recent laws deny us even the profits of private inheritance, and no one complains.

   [Note: Ambrose is understood here to be referring to Valentinian’s twentieth law, addressed to Pope Damasus, concerning bishops and others, by which clerics were in fact forbidden to receive anything by testament from pious women who had attached themselves to them. In declaring that he is not troubled by the loss which this law imposed on clerics, Ambrose agrees beautifully with Jerome; but here he does not conceal his profound grief that the avarice of clerics provided the occasion for the law. See his second letter *On the Life of Clerics*.]

   For we do not consider it an injury, since we do not grieve over the loss. If a priest seeks the privilege of avoiding the curial burden,

   [Note: The burden of the curial office will be discussed more appropriately in the letter to Theodosius.]

   he must surrender his native city, his ancestral property, and the possession of all his goods. How greatly would the pagans intensify this complaint, if they possessed it: that a priest purchases freedom for the holidays of his ministry at the cost of his entire patrimony, and, at the loss of every private advantage, buys the exercise of a public service; that, while pleading the watches required for the common safety, he consoles himself for domestic poverty with this recompense, because he has not sold his ministry but acquired favor.”

14. Let him compare the cases. You want to excuse a decurion,

   [Note: Understand this as referring to Theodosius’s law 104 concerning decurions; there will also be an occasion to discuss it in the letter mentioned above.]

   while it is not permitted to excuse a priest from the Church. Wills are written for the attendants of temples; no layperson is excluded, no one of the lowest condition, no one prodigal of modesty.” Of all people, only the cleric is denied the common right—he alone from whom the common vow is received on behalf of all, and to whom the common duty is entrusted. No bequests from grave widows, no gift. And even when no fault is found in his conduct, a penalty is prescribed for his office. What a Christian widow bequeaths to the priests of a shrine is valid; what she gives to the ministers of God is not.

   I have recorded this not to complain, but so that they may know what I do not complain about. For I would rather that we be poorer in money than in grace.

[Col. 0976C]

15. But they report that what has been donated or left to the Church has not been violated. Let them themselves say who stripped the temples of their gifts—

   [Note: It is established that this plundering of the churches took place under Julian. See Sozomen, *Ecclesiastical History* V.5; Theodoret III.12; and the *Tripartite History* VI.32.]

   —a deed that was done to Christians. If such things had been done to pagans, the injury would have been restored rather than inflicted. Is justice only now being claimed, and equity demanded? Where was this judgment then, when all Christians’ possessions had been plundered, when they begrudged them even the breath of life and everywhere withheld from the dead the last offices of burial?”

   Those whom the pagans threw into the sea were returned by the sea. This is a victory of faith: even they now criticize the deeds of their ancestors, whose actions they condemn. But what, in heaven’s name, is the logic of their seeking the gifts of those whose actions they condemn?

[Col. 0977A]

16. Yet no one denied gifts to shrines or bequests to soothsayers; only the estates were removed, because they were not using religiously what they defended by the right of religion. Those who use our example—why did they not also use our service? The Church possesses nothing for itself except faith. These are the revenues it provides, these are its fruits. The Church’s property is the expenditure of the needy.

   [Note: Ambrose testifies here that the whole Church is bound by this law. How perfectly he himself fulfilled it, you will learn from what we observed in Book II *On Duties*, chapters 15 and 28.]

   Let them count the captives whom the temples have redeemed, the nourishment they have supplied to the poor, and the exiles for whom they have provided the means of living.

   [Note: Two manuscripts read, “Therefore, once the prey had been seized.” After the second verse, where the old edition and several manuscripts have *quod*, “what,” some read *quae triste piare nefas*, “which would expiate the grievous crime”; the Roman edition, more appropriately, with the others reads *quae triste piaret nefas*. This imitates the verse from Book II of the *Aeneid*: “They set up the image, which would expiate the grievous crime.”]

   Therefore the estates were seized, not rights.

[Col. 0977C]

17. Behold what happened: the public famine, they say, avenged the grievous crime, since what had served the interests of the priests began to serve the use of everyone. Therefore, after the groves had been stripped, they say, trees deprived of bark licked the mouths of the starving with their wretched sap.” Therefore, exchanging the grain of Chaonia for acorns, they were once more reduced to the pasture of cattle and recalled to the nourishment of an unhappy diet; shaking the oak, they consoled their wretched hunger in the forests.

   [Note: Here the manuscripts and printed editions agree, except that some manuscripts omit the word *glande*, “acorn.” Nevertheless, the wound in these words is by no means obscure. Besides the clear allusion to Virgil’s verse in Book I of the *Georgics*: “They exchanged Chaonian acorns for rich grain,” the word *Chaonian* derives from the region of Epirus in which the city of Dodona was founded. Not far from it stood a grove sacred to Jupiter, entirely of oaks; hence Symmachus in his *Report*, and Ambrose below, call the trees “Dodonaean oaks.” The text should therefore read either “exchanging the Chaonian acorn for grain,” or “exchanging grain for Chaonian acorns,” and so forth.]

   [Page 838]

   New wonders, evidently, of the earth—things that had never happened before—although pagan superstition was raging throughout the world!

   [Note: A few manuscripts read, “we were consoling miserable hunger”; this too alludes to Virgil’s verse from the work already cited: “And with the shaken oak you shall console hunger in the forests.”]

   Indeed, when before did the harvest ever disappoint the farmer’s hopes in empty ears,

   [Note: Virgil, in the work cited: “The expected crop mocked the empty fields with barren oats.”]

   or the grain sought by the furrows ever leave the hope of the peasant people unfulfilled?

18. And from where did the Greeks obtain the prophecies of their oak,

   [Note: The manuscripts have this reading; the printed editions have “the prophecies held by the oak.” The source is Virgil, *Georgics* II, where we read: “… and the oak whose prophecies were sought by the Greeks.” It is clear that the Dodonaean oaks are meant. Besides the commentators on Virgil concerning the cited verse, Erasmus may also be consulted, *Adages* I.1.7.]

   unless they thought that the remedy of forest nourishment was a gift of heavenly religion? For such are the gifts they believe their gods bestow. Who but the people of the nations worshipped the Dodonaean trees, when they honored the sad fodder of the field with the dignity of sacred groves?

   [Note: All the printed editions read, “the sad fodder of the sacred grove”; all the manuscripts have the reading reproduced in the text.]

   It is not credible that their gods, in anger, imposed as punishment what they were accustomed, when appeased, to confer as a gift.

   But what justice is there in their grieving because nourishment was denied to a few priests while they themselves denied it to everyone, when the vengeance was more severe than the offense? It is therefore not an adequate cause to have brought about so great a distress in a deceived world: that, while the crops were green, the ripe hope of the year suddenly died.”

[Col. 0978A]

19. And certainly the rights of temples were abolished throughout the world many years ago. Is it only now that the pagan gods have thought of avenging their injuries? For this reason the Nile did not swell in its accustomed course to avenge the losses of the city priests,

   [Note: Just as Rome is called “the City” by antonomasia, so Ambrose here calls the Roman priests “city priests.”]

   who did not avenge the losses of their own?

20. Yet suppose they think that the injuries of their gods were avenged in the previous year. Why were they despised in the present year? For now the peasant people do not feed on plucked roots of herbs, nor seek the solace of wild berries,

   [Note: Some manuscripts read, “nor does food taste from the thorn bushes.” The following sense is also a parody of Virgil, *Georgics* I: “And Gargara itself marvels at its harvests.”]

   nor snatch food from brambles. Rather, rejoicing in the work of happy abundance, while the rustic people themselves marvel at their harvests, they have filled their fasting with the satisfaction of their desire.” The earth has returned to us harvests that yield interest.

[Col. 0978B]

21. Who, then, would be so unfamiliar with human affairs as to wonder at the changing fortunes of the years? And yet we know that even in the previous year most provinces overflowed with produce. What should I say of Gaul, richer than usual? Pannonia sold grain that it had not sown; and Second Raetia learned the envy of its fertility.

   [Note: All the printed editions read, “and fertile Raetia”; all the manuscripts read, “and Second Raetia.” Today that region is divided into Upper and Lower Raetia; it is not known to us whether in Ambrose’s time it was distinguished as First and Second. See its location in Ptolemy, Book II, and in more recent geographers.]

   For she, who was accustomed to be safer from famine, provoked an enemy against herself by her fertility. The harvests of autumn nourished Liguria and Venetia. Therefore that year did not wither through sacrilege, and this year has blossomed with the fruits of faith. Let them deny also that the vineyards overflowed with abundant growth. Thus we have received a harvest that has paid interest, and we possess the benefits of a more generous vintage.

[Page 839]

22. The final and greatest point remains: whether you, emperors, ought to restore the supports that have benefited you. For he says: “Let them defend you; let us worship them.”

   This, most faithful Princes, is what we cannot endure: that they reproach us by saying that they entreat their gods in your name, and, although you have not ordered it, commit enormous sacrilege, interpreting your silence as consent. Let them keep their own defenses for themselves; let those defenses protect their own people, if they can. For if those by whom they are worshipped cannot help them, how can they defend you, by whom they are not worshipped?

23. “But,” he says, “the rite of our ancestors must be preserved.” What of the fact that everything has subsequently advanced toward improvement? The world itself, which either had first solidified when the seeds of the elements were driven together through the void, forming a tender sphere, or while the work was still confused and unorganized, had been dark with horror—did it not afterward, when heaven, sea, and earth had been distinguished from one another, receive the forms of things by which it appears beautiful? Once freed from its moist darkness, the earth marveled at the new sun. Day does not shine forth fully at its beginning; as time proceeds, it gleams with an increase of light and blazes with heat.

[Col. 0979B]

24. The moon itself, by which the Church is represented in prophetic oracles, when it first rises and is renewed through its monthly phases, is hidden from us in the darkness.

   [Note: Several manuscripts read, “is hidden in the darkness of night.”]

   Gradually filling out its horns, or releasing itself from the region of the sun, it shines with the brightness of a clear radiance.

25. In earlier times they did not know how to cultivate the fruits of the earth. Later, when the diligent farmer began to rule the fields and clothe the shapeless soil with vineyards, people of wild disposition shed their wildness, softened by civilized cultivation.”

   [Note: Ambrose has also borrowed this passage from Virgil, *Georgics* I: “And he frequently works the earth and commands the fields.” Other verses from Book II have also been expressed here; you can easily detect them yourself.]

26. The first age of the year itself, which colored us with an equal usage at the impulse of growing things—

   [Note: The Roman edition reads, “bare of things that grow,” which makes excellent sense, but the manuscripts and the old edition read, “deprived of the supports of things that grow.” The meaning is nevertheless the same: “at the will of growing things,” or according to their choice or law.]

   —in the course of time blossoms as its flowers fall, and reaches maturity in its final fruits.

27. We too, inexperienced in age, have the understanding of infancy;

   [Note: All the printed editions read, “we possess infancy”; nearly all the manuscripts read, “we possess the understanding of infancy.”]

   but as our intelligence changes with the years, we lay aside the beginnings of immaturity.

[Col. 0979C]

   Let them therefore say that everything ought to have remained in its beginnings, and that they disapprove of the world because it has been lit by the splendor of the sun. How much more pleasing it is to have driven away the darkness of the mind than that of the body, and to have caused the radiance of faith to shine forth rather than that of the sun!

   Therefore the first beginnings of the world, like those of all things,

   [Note: The printed edition, with a few manuscripts, reads, “changed their primitive course”; many manuscripts read, “shone in their primitive state”; the remaining manuscripts, more appropriately, read, “wavered in their primitive state,” that is, they faltered through weakness.]

   wavered, so that the old age of venerable, hoary faith might follow. Let those whom this displeases condemn the harvest, because its fertility comes late; let them condemn the vintage, because it comes at the decline of the year; let them condemn the olive, because its fruit comes last.

28. Therefore our harvest is the faith of souls; the Church’s grace is the vintage of merits. It was green among the holy from the rising of the world, but in the final age it spread among the peoples, so that all might understand that faith in Christ had not stolen into untutored minds—for no victory has a crown without an adversary—but that, once the opinion which had previously grown strong had been driven out, what was true has rightly been given precedence.

   [Note: The Roman edition reads, “the faith of souls, and grace in the Church …”; all the printed editions read, “what was true has rightly been preferred”; the manuscripts variously have “what was true becomes rightly preferred,” “preferred to injury,” or “preferred in law.” It might perhaps be read, “that it has rightly been preferred.”]

30. If the ancient rites were pleasing, why did Rome itself adopt foreign rites? I pass over the earth hidden beneath costly materials, and the shepherds’ huts resisting gold of debased quality. But, to answer the very complaint they make: did they not, as rivals of another people’s superstition, accept the images of captured cities, conquered gods, and foreign rites of sacred worship?

   [Col. 0980B]

   Where, then, is the precedent by which Cybele washes her chariot in the simulated waters of the Almo?

   [Note: Several manuscripts read, “her courses.” As Nannius observes, the Almo is a river of Rome in the first region, beside which the Romans once performed the rites of Cybele according to the same ritual by which the Gallic priests acted in Phrygia. After quoting several verses of Ovid and Juvenal concerning this river, he adds: “When sacred rites are performed elsewhere in imitation of this, they pretend that the nearby river is the Almo, since it is customary for things that cannot really be included among sacred rites to be represented as though they were; this is treated as though they were real.” Virgil, *Aeneid* IV: “And he had sprinkled the simulated waters of the Avernian spring.” Nannius adds that, concerning the foreign sacred rites adopted at Rome, Pope Leo also speaks elegantly in Sermon I *On the Apostles*: “When it held sway over nearly all nations, it served the errors of all nations,” and so forth. Nevertheless, we know that edicts were often issued to expel foreign religions from the City.]

   Where did the Phrygian seers come from, and the divinities of Carthage, always hated by the Romans as an unequal enemy? The Africans worship the Heavenly Goddess, the Persians Mithras, and many Venus—different names, not different gods.

   [Note: This is taken from Herodotus: “They have also learned to sacrifice to the Heavenly Goddess, having learned it from the Assyrians and Arabians. The Assyrians call Aphrodite Mylitta, the Arabians Alilat, and the Persians Mithra.” Thus Nannius.]

   So they believed Victory also to be a goddess, although victory is a gift, not a power: it is bestowed, not dominant; the favor of legions, not the force of religions. What a great goddess, then, whom the multitude of soldiers claims for itself, or whom the outcome of battles grants!

31. They ask that her altar be erected in the senate house of the city of Rome—that is, in the place where more Christians gather. There are altars in all the temples, and even an altar in the temple of Victories.

   [Col. 0980C]

   Because they delight in numbers, they celebrate their sacrifices everywhere. What is this except an insult to the faith, to claim the sacrifice of one altar? Is it to be tolerated that a pagan sacrifice while a Christian is present?

   “Let them drink,” he says, “let them drink, even unwillingly, smoke with their eyes, the symphony with their ears, ash with their throats, incense with their nostrils, and let the raised embers of our fires sprinkle the faces of those who turn away, however much they recoil.”

   [Note: The Amerbach edition, with not a few manuscripts, reads “and of those opposing”; the others, with the remaining manuscripts, read “and of those turning away.”]

   Are the baths, porticoes, and streets occupied by images not enough for them? Will there also be no common condition in that common assembly? The pious portion of the Senate will be constrained by the voices of those who protest and by the oaths of those who adjure them. If it refuses, it will seem to expose a lie; if it gives in, it will confess sacrilege.

32. “Where,” he says, “shall we swear to your laws and words?” Then does your mind, enclosed and bound by the laws, gather support from the ceremonies of the pagans and bind its faith to them? Now not only the faith of those present but also of those absent—and what is more, that of the emperors—is being assaulted. For you compel them if you command it.

   Constantius, of revered memory, not yet initiated into the sacred mysteries, thought himself polluted if he saw that altar. He ordered it removed; he did not order it restored. The former possesses the authority of an action; the latter possesses no authority of an order.

   [Note: The Long and Laetian manuscripts read “Constantine.” But “Constantius” must certainly be read, concerning whose baptism Socrates writes in Book II, chapter 47, as do others.]

33. Let no one flatter himself because of absence.

   [Note: Above, in Letter 14.6, Ambrose writes: “whose absence was often more present”; this sentiment was very familiar to the holy bishop.]

   The one who implants himself in minds is more present than the one who makes a display before the eyes. For it is more to be joined in mind than to be united in body. The Senate has you as presidents of the assembly that must be convened; it assembles for you.”

   [Note: In nearly all the manuscripts, *vobis coit*, “it assembles for you,” is absent.]

   It offers its conscience not to the gods of the pagans, but to you; it places you before its children, though not before its faith. This is the love to be desired, this is the love greater than imperial power: that the faith which preserves the empire may remain safe.

34. But perhaps someone might be troubled that so faithful a ruler was thus abandoned—as though the worth of merits were measured by the fleeting circumstances of the present. For what wise person does not know that human affairs are placed in a kind of cycle and circuit, since they do not always have the same outcomes, but conditions vary and fortunes change?

35. Whom did the Roman temples send forth more blessed than Gnaeus Pompey? Yet after he had encircled the world with three triumphs, driven from the field, a fugitive from war, and exiled from the boundaries of his own empire, he fell by the hand of the eunuch of Canopus.

   [Note: After Pompey lost the battle of Pharsalus, he fled to the king of Egypt. When he stepped from his ship onto Egyptian soil, the royal eunuch Achillas treacherously murdered him, as Plutarch records in his *Life of Pompey*, Suetonius in the *Life of Julius Caesar*, and others. Ambrose calls the eunuch “of Canopus” because Canopus was an Egyptian city 120 stadia from Alexandria.]

36. Whom did they produce more noble than Cyrus, king of all the lands of the Persian East? He too, after defeating powerful rulers who opposed him and sparing the defeated,

   [Note: Herodotus, Book I of the *Histories*, Justin, Book I, and others write about Cyrus, king of the Persians, who had treated the defeated Croesus with great humanity and in a thoroughly royal manner, but was captured and beheaded by Tomyris.]

   perished, overcome by women’s arms. And that king who had even honored the defeated with a place at his table became, after his head had been cut off and enclosed in a vessel full of blood, a plaything of female commands, being ordered to satisfy himself with it.

   [Note: “Being ordered to satisfy himself” is absent from nearly all the manuscripts, but occurs in all the printed editions.]

   Thus, over the course of his life, events of unequal and utterly different kinds are reported, not equal things corresponding to equal things.

[Col. 0982A]

37. Whom do we find more devoted to sacrifices than Hamilcar, the Carthaginian commander? While he stood amid the battle lines during the whole engagement, he was offering a sacrifice. When he learned that part of his forces had been defeated, he threw himself into the very fires that he was feeding, so that with his own body he might extinguish the fires which he had discovered had been of no help to him.

   [Note: Thus all but a few manuscripts, in which *restringeret* (“might restrain”) stands in place of *restingueret* (“might extinguish”); all the printed editions read, “might extinguish with his own blood.”]

38. For what should I say about Julian? Because he foolishly trusted the predictions of the soothsayers, he deprived himself of the means of retreat.

   [Note: The imprudence of the apostate Julian, when he undertook war against the Persians and, after burning the ships, cut off the hope of return for himself and the Roman army, is described by Sozomen, Book VI, chapter 1; Theodoret, Book III, chapter 25; and others.]

   Therefore, in a common misfortune there is no common offense; for our promises have deceived no one.

39. I replied to those who challenged me as though I had not been challenged; for my concern was to refute the Report, not to expound superstition. Nevertheless, Emperor, let their very report make you more cautious. For when he had woven together the account of the earlier emperors, saying that the earlier group had observed their fathers’ ceremonies and the later had not removed them, he added: “If the example of the ancients’ religion does not persuade, let the dissimulation of those nearest to us do so.” By this he clearly taught what you owe both to your faith, so that you do not follow the example of the pagans, and to piety, so that you do not violate your brother’s decrees. For if they praised the dissimulation of those emperors only in their own interests—emperors who, although Christians, nevertheless did not remove the decrees of the pagans—how much more ought you to defer to fraternal affection, so that, although you ought to dissimulate even something you perhaps did not approve, lest you detract from your brother’s decrees, you may now hold to what you judge suitable both to your faith and to the bond of kinship.

[Note: Written in the year 385.]

## LETTER XIX

[Col. 0982C]

Ambrose to Vigilius, recently chosen for the episcopate, who had begged him to provide him with a model for his formation. He warns him not to allow the faithful to enter into marriages with unbelievers; to deter the people from fraud and usury; and to exhort them to hospitality. Above all, however, he urges him more effectively to prohibit the marriages of Christians with pagans already mentioned, and for this purpose he goes through and expounds the whole history of Samson.

AMBROSE TO VIGILIUS.

[Note: The Roman edition has “to Vigilius, his brother”; below it seems that “he should be admonished” ought to be understood. We have already indicated in the Admonition to the book On Tobit that the Vigilius to whom this letter was sent was none other than Vigilius, bishop of Trent; no one has disagreed with us on this point. The Roman Martyrology, announcing his death on 25 June, relates that he was stoned by pagans while attempting to destroy the remnants of idolatry; the collection of Usuard and the Acts mentioned in Mabillon’s Preface to his tenth century agree with this account. It is therefore readily apparent why Ambrose so strongly dissuaded Vigilius from permitting marriages between the faithful and pagans.]

1. You asked me for the marks of your formation, since you have newly been called to the priesthood. And since you have built up yourself, as was proper, having been judged worthy of so great an office, it seems necessary to indicate how you should build up others also.

2. First of all, recognize the Church of the Lord entrusted to you. Therefore always beware lest any offense creep in and it become, as it were, a common body through admixture with pagans. Hence Scripture says to you: “Do not take a wife from the daughters of the Canaanites, but go to Mesopotamia, to the house of Bethuel,” that is, “to the house of wisdom;” “and acquire her union for yourself” (Gen. 28:1–2).

Mesopotamia is a region in the eastern parts, enclosed there by two very great rivers, the Euphrates and the Tigris, whose source is in the regions of Armenia.

[Note: Mesopotamia is therefore called this tract of land because it is μέσος ποταμῶν, “between rivers.”]

They flow by different courses into the Red Sea.

[Note: The Roman edition has “into the Persian Sea”; but it is preferable to tolerate an error in geography than to depart from all the manuscripts and editions.]

Therefore, under the name Mesopotamia, the figure of the Church is signified: the Church, with the mighty streams of prudence and the channels of justice, waters and makes fertile the minds of the faithful, into whom it pours the grace of holy baptism—whose type preceded it in the Red Sea—and washes away guilt. Teach the people, therefore, to seek the union of marriage not from foreigners but from Christian households.

[Note: The Roman edition alone adds, “and from the daughters of Laban for you,” and so forth.]

3. Let no one cheat a hired worker of his due wage, because we too are hired workers of our God and await from him the reward of our labor (Lev. 19:13). And you, whoever you are, merchant, deny your hired worker a monetary wage—that is, something cheap and perishable—yet the reward of the heavenly promises will be denied to you. Therefore, as the Law says, “You shall not cheat a hired worker of his wage” (Deut. 24:14).

[Note: The holy man gave the same command to Constantius in Letter 2, §12; indeed, he gave it to all Christians in On Tobit, ch. 24, §92.]

4. You shall not lend your money at interest, because it is written that the one who has not given his money at interest will dwell in God’s tabernacle (Ps. 14:5).

[Note: Thus the manuscripts, with only two exceptions. In those, the first hand had written supplantator, “one who supplants,” which is read in all the editions. But it is more probable that supplantatur is used here in an active sense, “is supplanted.” In any case, the command to lend money without hope of receiving it back is very similar to what is prescribed in On Tobit, ch. 2, §8; ch. 14, §49; and ch. 16, §54.]

For the one who seeks the profits of interest is a cheat. Therefore, if a Christian has money, let him give it as though he were not going to receive it back—or at least as though he were going to recover only the principal that he gave. In this he possesses no small interest of grace. Otherwise, this is deception, not assistance.

[Note: In the same sense, On Tobit, ch. 4, §13: “What is more unjust to you,” and so forth. Likewise, ch. 3, §11: “You give less and demand more,” and so forth. Finally, ch. 14, §48: “It is harsh to demand repayment,” and so forth.]

For what is harsher than to give your money to someone who does not have it and then demand double from him? If he did not have even the single sum with which to repay you, how will he repay double?

5. Let Tobit be our example. He never demanded the money he had given except at the end of his life (Tob. 4:21).

[Note: In the cited book On Tobit, ch. 2, §6: “Not so much desiring to reclaim what had been entrusted,” and so forth.]

He did so more to avoid defrauding the heir than to compel the recovery of the money he had deposited.

[Note: The Long manuscript reads, “The peoples established interest for themselves”; the others and the editions read as in the text, except that a few manuscripts have se conciderunt instead of saepe conciderunt, “often fell.” No other peoples are meant here than those Chuni of whom Ambrose said in On Tobit, ch. 11, §39, that more of them perished by their own blows than by those of the enemy.]

Peoples have often fallen through usury, and it has become the cause of public ruin. Therefore we priests must take particular care to cut away those vices that seem to creep among very many people.

6. Teach a guest that hospitality ought to be voluntary rather than compelled, lest, in offering hospitality, he reveal an inhospitable disposition of mind and, in the very reception of the guest, violate grace through injury. Rather, let grace be cultivated through the practice of service and some ministry of kindness.

[Note: Ambrose plainly says the same thing in Book I of On Abraham, ch. 5, §35: “The guest does not demand riches from you,” and so forth.]

For rich gifts are not demanded from you, but voluntary services, full of peace and fitting concord. Vegetables are better with friendship and goodwill than a banquet adorned with exquisite dishes if the affection of goodwill is absent (Prov. 15:17). We read that peoples were destroyed by a grave catastrophe because the rights of hospitality had been violated (Judg. 20:44). Terrible wars were also undertaken because of lust (Gen. 34:25).

[Col. 0984C] 7. But scarcely anything is more serious than to be joined to a foreign woman, where incitements to lust and discord, together with the crimes of sacrilege, are kindled. Since marriage itself ought to be sanctified with a priestly veil and blessing, how can a marriage be called a marriage where there is no harmony of faith? Since prayer ought to be shared, how can there be a common marital love between those differing in devotion?

[Note: Nothing is more widely known than that among pagans women customarily covered their heads with a veil of saffron-colored cloth when they were led to their husbands. We learn from ecclesiastical writers that this custom was also received among Christians from the earliest times. Tertullian, in On the Veiling of Virgins, ch. 11, and Ambrose, in Book I of On Abraham, ch. 9, trace its origin to the imitation of Rebecca, who, when she saw the husband toward whom she was journeying, immediately veiled herself, as the divine Scriptures relate. Ambrose teaches that this veiling signifies that modesty ought to precede marriage. Isidore, in Book II of On Ecclesiastical Offices, ch. 19, says that it signifies the wife’s subjection to her husband. Moreover, when Ambrose uses the words “with a priestly veil,” he seems to indicate that the veil was customarily placed by the priest himself, something not easily found in another author. As for the blessing, not only do Innocent I, in his letter to Victricius; the Fourth Council of Carthage, canon 13; Isidore, Book II of On Ecclesiastical Offices, ch. 19; and others show that its use was customary in the early Church, but even before them Tertullian, in Book II To His Wife, ch. 9, and Siricius, Letter I to Himerius, ch. 4, speak of it. Siricius says: “That blessing which the priest places upon those about to marry is, among the faithful, like a kind of sacrilege if it is violated by any transgression.” Tertullian joins an offering to the blessing; nor is this surprising, since among most unbelievers marriage was not celebrated without sacrifice.]

Many have often been captured by love of women and betrayed their faith, as the people of the fathers did at Baal-peor. Therefore Phinehas seized a sword and killed the Hebrew man and the Midianite woman (Num. 25:8), and he appeased the divine anger so that the whole people would not be destroyed.

8. Why should I speak of many examples? I shall bring forward one from among many, and through its recollection it will become clear how destructive it is to take a foreign woman in marriage. Who was stronger, and from his earliest beginnings more fortified by the Spirit of God, than Samson the Nazirite? Yet he too was betrayed, and through a woman he was unable to preserve his own grace (Judg. 16:18ff.). We shall recount in historical prose the whole sequence of his birth and life according to the contents of the sacred book, as follows—not in the sequence of its wording, but in its meaning.

9. For many years the Philistines held the Hebrew people subject and subordinate, because it had lost the privilege of faith by which its fathers had gained victory. Yet the distinction of election before its author and the cord of inheritance had not been wholly cut off. But because they were often lifted up by the arrogance of prosperity, he usually handed them over to the power of their enemies, so that, in keeping with human nature, they might seek from heaven a remedy for their troubles. For we are subject to God when we are pressed by some adversity; prosperity exalts the mind. This has been proved by experience on other occasions, but especially in that reversal of affairs by which, in turn, dominion passed back from the Philistines to the Hebrews.

10. For when the hearts of the Hebrews had been so crushed by the long injustice of prolonged subjection that no man dared to raise his spirit toward freedom with a manly resolve, Samson arose for them, predestined by divine oracle: a great man, not to be counted among the many but outstanding among the few, and, beyond all dispute, easily first of all in bodily strength.

From the beginning, therefore, he is a spectacle for our profound admiration—not because of those splendid marks of temperance and sobriety by which he abstained from wine from childhood onward,

[Note: Some editions and manuscripts read, “abstaining from wine from childhood.”]

nor because of those sacred observances that, as a Nazirite, he long preserved with unshorn head, but because from adolescence—the softer age in others, but in his case extraordinary—he accomplished deeds of perfect virtue, astonishing and beyond human measure. Through these he soon revealed the truth of the divine oracle, showing that such grace had gone before him in no superficial way: an angel descended and announced to his parents, beyond their expectation, his birth, his future rule and his protection for his people.

[Note: All editions read futurum regimen, “future rule”; the manuscripts, by contrast, read futurus regimen, which is grammatically defective, except for one or two that have futurum regimen. As for Ambrose’s calling the Philistines Palaestini, whereas the Septuagint and Vulgate call them Philistines, he follows not Josephus alone but also the Hebrew text, to which the Syriac and Arabic versions likewise agree.]

For they had long been oppressed by the harsh rule of the Philistines.

11. His father was from the tribe of Dan, a God-fearing man (Judg. 13:2ff.), born in no ignoble station and distinguished above others. His mother was barren in the womb but not barren in the virtues of her spirit. She was worthy to receive a vision of an angel by admitting him into the hospitality of her mind; she kept the command and fulfilled the oracle.

Yet she did not allow herself to know the divine secret without her husband. She told him that a man of God, of splendid appearance, had appeared to her and had brought prophecies concerning their future offspring. By this promise she conveyed to her husband the confidence that they shared in the faithfulness of the heavenly promises. When he learned this, he piously prayed to God, asking that the grace of the vision might also be granted to him, and saying: “Lord, let your angel come to me also.”

12. Hence I think that he did not, as someone supposed, harbor any suspicion because of jealousy toward the woman, who was of remarkable beauty,

[Note: No one other than Josephus is designated by these words. In Book V of his Antiquities, ch. 10, after praising the extraordinary beauty of Samson’s future mother, he adds shortly afterward: “He was also violently impassioned with love for the woman and therefore excessively jealous” (ἦν δὲ καὶ μανιώδης ὑπ᾽ ἔρωτος ἐπὶ τῇ γυναικὶ καὶ διὰ τοῦτο ζηλότυπος ἀκρατώς). Finally, after mentioning the first appearance of the angel, he adds: “When she came to her husband, she recounted to him what she had learned from the angel, marveling at his beauty and stature; as a result of her praises, he fell into jealous astonishment and into the suspicion prompted by such a passion.” (ἡ δὲ τῷ ἀνδρὶ παραγενομένῳ τὰ παρὰ τοῦ ἀγγέλου ἐκδιηγήσατο, ἐκθαυμάζουσα τοῦ τε τὸ κάλλος, τὸ μέγεθος, ὡς ἐκεῖνον, ἐκ τῶν ἐπαίνων εἰς ἔκπληξιν κατὰ ζηλοτυπίαν, περιστῆναι, καὶ ὑπόνοιαν τὴν ἐκ τοιούτου πάθους κινουμένην).]

but rather that he was provoked by zeal for divine grace and wished to share in the sight of the sacred gift. For, had his mind been perversely affected by vices, he would not have found such favor with the Lord that the angel would return to his house. After giving the instructions that the use of the oracle required, the angel suddenly withdrew, lifted up in the appearance of a powerful flame. This terrified the man, but the woman interpreted it more auspiciously, turning it into joy and removing his anxiety, since seeing God is an indication of prosperity, not of adversity.

13. Once he had grown up, commended by such marks from heaven, he turned his mind to marriage—either because he recoiled in spirit from the wandering and familiar habit of slippery lust that was common among young men, or because a reason was already being sought by which he might turn the power and harsh rule of the Philistines away from the necks of his people.

Accordingly, as he went to Timnah (this is the name of a city situated in that region, which at that time was frequented by Philistine inhabitants), he saw a virgin of pleasing appearance and attractive countenance. He asked his parents, whose company supported him as he traveled, to seek her for him in marriage.

But they, unaware of where his intention was leading, thought that a foreign woman ought to be avoided. They did not understand that his purpose was to become more hostile to the Philistines if they refused, or, if they consented, to gain an opportunity to inflict injury upon his subjects—since, through the union, equality of rank and the favor of companionship would justly increase, and, if anything offensive occurred, the pursuit of vengeance would extend farther. When they had tried in vain to bend his mind by presenting the claims of legitimate offspring, they willingly yielded to his decision.

14. Once his request had been accepted, Samson went to see the woman who had been promised to him. He turned aside briefly from the roadway, and immediately a wild lion from the forest confronted him, savage in its untamed freedom. He had no companion and no weapon at hand. Shame forbade retreat, while conscious strength gave him confidence. He rushed upon it, embraced it with his arms, and killed it. Having strangled it with the knot of his arms, he threw it beyond the road over the woodland growth and left it there.

The place was pleasant, rich in grassy pasture and planted with vineyards. Therefore he thought that the remains of the beast would soon be of no consequence to his beloved bride, since occasions of this kind are made more attractive not by frightening spoils but by gentle pleasures and festive foliage. Finally, when he returned by the same road, he found a honeycomb in the lion’s body and took it away,

[Note: Several manuscripts read, “a gift for the girl’s parents.”]

intending it as a gift for the parents and the girl; such gifts suit a bride. After tasting the honey, he gave the honeycomb to those mentioned above to eat and suppressed the explanation of its origin.

15. But one day, as it happened, a wedding feast was being celebrated.

[Note: Josephus, in the passage cited, has: “As the drinking proceeded and there was merriment, as commonly happens on such occasions” (τοῦ ποτοῦ προβαίνοντος, καὶ παιδιᾶς οὔσης, οἷα φιλεῖ παρὰ τοῖς τοιούτοις καιροῖς). From this you may observe how ancient was the custom of mingling verbal license with wedding banquets, and from what source the freedom of the thalassian and Fescennine songs arose.]

The young men, cheerful at the banquet, invited one another to play through their exchanges of speech. As one teased another with sharper wit, as is customary in such situations, the contest kindled the general merriment. Samson then proposed this question to the young men who were feasting with him: “From the eater came forth food, and from the strong came forth sweetness.” He promised a reward to those who solved it, as payment for their wisdom: thirty linen garments and an equal number of robes, corresponding to the number of the banqueting men, or a penalty for those who failed to understand.

16. Since they could neither unravel the tangled question nor distinguish its ambiguity, they drove his wife, partly by threats and partly by wearisome entreaties, to ask her husband to solve the riddle, presenting this as a distinguished token of marital favor and a reward for love.

She, whether frightened in spirit or bent by feminine cunning, began, as though in pious complaint, to cloak her resentment of marital hostility with the claim that she, his companion and confidante throughout life, had not learned her husband’s secret and had been treated like the others, as though he did not trust her with his private mystery: “You hate me,” she said, “and do not love me, since you have hidden this from me until now.”

17. [Note: All editions read, “His spirit, certainly unconquered by these and similar things”; all manuscripts, as in our text, read, “His spirit, unconquered by these and all other things,” except that some omit ad before caetera.]

Though his spirit remained unconquered by these and all such things, it was softened by the woman’s caresses. He revealed to his beloved the question he had proposed, and she revealed it to her fellow citizens. At last, on the seventh day—the day appointed for solving the riddle—before sunset, they discovered the answer and reported it in this form:

“What is stronger than a lion? What is sweeter than honey?”

And he replied:

[Note: Josephus has “nor is anything more deceitful than a woman” (οὐδὲ γυναικὸς εἶναί τι δολερώτερον). Since these words are absent from the sacred books, the holy Doctor translated them from the same historian.]

“Nor is anything more deceitful than a woman. For if you had not plowed with my heifer, you would never have understood my riddle.”

Immediately he went down to Ashkelon and killed thirty men. Taking their garments, he gave the promised reward to those who had solved the riddle.

18. He abstained from marrying the girl whose treachery he had discovered and withdrew to his native home. The young woman, disturbed in spirit and dreading with justified fear the resentment of the injured man and the violence of the strongest of men, which she thought would become her ruin, entered into marriage with another man—the very man whom Samson, when he married her, had taken as his paranymph, or trusted companion.

Yet even by this pretended marriage she did not avert the danger of offense. For when the matter was revealed and he was prevented from returning to his wife because her father said that she had married another man, he added that Samson might marry her sister if he wished. Wounded by the provocation of the insult, Samson devised a public vengeance, taking up the indignation caused by a private injury.

He seized three hundred foxes. It was late summer, when the grain in the fields was already ripe. He tied them together in pairs, tail to tail, placed a burning torch between them, and fastened it with an unbreakable knot. Then, as an avenger of the injury, he released them among the bundles of the grain harvest that the Philistine inhabitants had cut.

Terrified by the fire, wherever they rushed and rolled headlong they spread the flames and burned their grain. Disturbed by this loss, since all the produce of their lands had been destroyed, they reported what had happened to their rulers. Those rulers sent men to Timnah to surround with fire the woman who had changed her marital allegiance, together with her entire household and parents, because she was the cause of their devastation and injury. They declared that the man ought not to have been harmed, since he could avenge himself by bringing public disaster upon them.

19. Yet Samson did not grant the Philistine people forgiveness for their offense, nor was he content with this limit of vengeance. He slaughtered them in a massive massacre, and very many of them perished by the sword. He himself withdrew to Etam, to the torrent in the wilderness. There was a rock there that served as a stronghold for the tribe of Judah.

But the Philistines, who did not dare to attack him and could not overcome the steep and precipitous defenses of the stronghold, declared war on the tribe of Judah and pressed it into battle. Seeing that reprisals were justly being made, they judged that it was by no means true, equitable, or advantageous to the public interest that their subjects and tributaries should be destroyed—especially on account of another man’s crime.

[Note: The words “when they saw that what was just was being exacted” are absent from all the editions, but are restored from all the manuscripts.]

After conferring together, they demanded that the perpetrator of so great a crime be handed over to them, and thus what he had committed would be without harm to them.

[Note: The editions and some manuscripts read “just and equitable.” Below, however, some manuscripts read “the perpetrator of so great a crime.”]

20. Once this condition had been imposed upon them, the men of the tribe of Judah gathered three thousand of their own number and went up to Samson. They first declared that they were subjects of the Philistines, whom they were obliged to obey not by free choice but through fear of danger. They thereby shifted the odium of their action onto those who possessed the right to compel them.

Then he said:

“What kind of justice is this, people of Abraham’s race? Must I exact a ruinous vengeance for a wife first deceived and then taken away, and is it forbidden me to avenge a domestic injury without danger? Have you inclined your minds so far toward the shameful obedience of slaves that you offer yourselves as agents of another’s insolence and turn your hands against yourselves? If I must perish because I gave free rein to my grief, I would rather perish at the hands of the Philistines.

“My household was attacked and my wife was solicited. If I was not allowed to live without their treachery, at least let me die without the crime of my own people. Did I return an injury I had received, or did I inflict one? You judge whether the retaliation was deserved. They complain about the loss of their crops; I complain about the loss of my wife. Compare bundles of harvested grain with a companion of the marriage bed. They themselves approved my grief, since they avenged the injuries done to me.

“See to what service they consider you suited. They want you to put to death the man whom they themselves judged worthy of vengeance against those who had injured him, and for whom they furnished the means of revenge. But if you carry your necks so submissively beneath the proud, hand me over to the hands of my enemies; do not kill me yourselves. I do not refuse death, but I flee your contagion.

[Note: “I flee your contagion” must here be interpreted as: “I take care lest you contract the contagion of sin through my death.”]

“But if you yield through fear to insolent men, bind my hands with ropes. Even unarmed, they will find weapons in the loosened knots. Certainly they thought the condition imposed would be sufficiently fulfilled if you handed me over alive.”

21. When they heard this (ibid., 13ff.), although three thousand men had gone up against him, they gave their oath that they would inflict no violence upon his life. He would merely submit to bonds, so that they might accomplish his surrender and thus clear themselves of the crime of which they were accused.

22. Having received this pledge, Samson emerged from the cave and abandoned the protection of the rock. When he saw the Philistines approaching to receive him, with two ropes fastened upon him, he roared in spirit and tore all the bonds apart. Then he seized the jawbone of an ass lying there and struck down a thousand men, putting the others to flight in a great display of courage. Armed armies yielded to one unarmed man. Those who dared to engage him at close quarters were easily cut down without effort; flight saved the others from destruction.

Therefore, even today the place is called Agon,

[Note: The Roman edition reads, “Siagon is the name of the place ... he accomplished it through the exceptional strength of an ass’s jawbone.” Yet although in the sacred pages and in Josephus the place is called Maxilla, “Jawbone,” and Elevation of the Jawbone, all the manuscripts and ancient editions write Agon, and explain the name by saying that a contest was completed there, omitting mention of the ass’s jawbone. We do not doubt, therefore, that our reading is also Ambrose’s.
