It is likely that in Josephus’ words, “It is now called Siagon because of Samson’s manly deed performed there” (ὁ Σιαγὼν καλεῖται νῦν διὰ τὴν Σαμψῶνος ἀνδραγαθίαν ἐπ᾽ αὐτῷ γενομένην), Ambrose read, “It is called Agon” (ὁ Ἀγὼν καλεῖται), and so forth. What follows concerning Samson’s spirit being elated by his victory and forgetful of the divine gift was likewise taken from the same historian.]

because Samson completed there a glorious contest through his outstanding courage.

[Note: The Roman edition reads, “He completed it with exceptional strength, using an ass’s jawbone.”]

23. Would that he had been as moderate in victory as he was strong against the enemy. But what commonly happens occurred: an insolent spirit, puffed up by prosperity, which ought to have attributed the outcome of the battle to divine favor and protection, claimed it for itself, saying: “With an ass’s jawbone I destroyed a thousand men.”

He neither built an altar to God nor offered a sacrifice. Neglecting sacrifice and assuming the glory, he called the place “the Slaughter of the Jawbone,” as though he might consecrate his triumph forever through its name.

24. Soon he began to burn intensely with severe thirst. There was no drink, and he could no longer bear or endure it. Understanding, therefore, that nothing belonging to human strength was so easy that it could be accomplished without divine assistance,

[Note: Thus the ancient edition and all manuscripts except one, which has “nothing belonging to human work,” a reading that is not at all bad. The Roman edition, however, emended it to “nothing belonging to human aid.” Yet “of human aid” can rightly be retained, provided it is construed as: “nothing of human aid—that is, of human strength—was so easy that ...”]

he cried out and begged that almighty God not turn against him the fact that, in an imprudent and careless utterance, he had attributed something to himself.

Indeed, he ascribed that victory to God, saying: “You have given this great salvation into the hand of your servant, and now help me, because behold, I am dying of thirst and, through the necessity of thirst, am being delivered into the power of those over whom you granted me so great a triumph.”

By God’s mercy, when he had thrown away the jawbone, God opened a fissure in it, and a spring burst forth from it. Samson drank and recovered his spirit, and he called the place “the Invocation of the Spring,” because he had corrected the boastfulness of his victory by the prayers of invocation.

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads, “the spring of invocation.” Josephus relates that this flowed not from the jawbone itself but from a nearby rock.]

Thus contrary judgments were promptly rendered: arrogance quickly incurred offense, while humility reconciled itself without any offense.

25. When he had brought the war against the Philistines to an end, he withdrew from the cowardice of his own people and despised the hostile hand. He went to Gaza, a city in the territory of the Philistines, and stayed there in an inn.

When the Gazites learned this (Judg. 16:1ff.), they did not let it pass through concealment. They hurried to surround his lodging and block all the entrances to the house, lest he arrange a flight during the night.

When Samson learned what was being prepared, he anticipated their ambush at midnight. He seized the pillars of the house with his hands, supported all the timber and the mass of the roof with his powerful neck,

[Note: The same Roman edition reads, “anticipating the gates of the city, and embracing both doorposts in his hands, with all the timber and the bar upon his neck,” and so forth. The old edition, together with all the manuscripts, reads as in the text, except that one manuscript has maceriem, “wall,” instead of materiem, “timber.” This is not sufficiently correct, since materiem totam, “all the timber,” renders Josephus’ words ὅση τε ἄλλη περὶ αὐταῖς ἦν ξύλωσις, “all the other woodwork around them.” As Ambrose omits the bars of the gate, so he alone mentions the mass of the roof.]

and transported it to the summit of the highest mountain overlooking the city of Hebron, which was inhabited by the Hebrew people.

26. But when he transgressed in free and unrestricted fashion not only the boundaries of his ancestral territory but also the limits of conduct prescribed by the observance of his forefathers, he found in this the source of his impending ruin.

Although he had learned by experience how little trustworthy the first marriage to a foreign woman was, and ought therefore to have been cautious afterward, he again failed to avoid union with Delilah, a prostitute. Because he loved her passionately, he offered himself as an opportunity for hostile deceit.

For the Philistines came up to her and promised to give her eleven hundred denarii each if she would reveal to them where he placed his confidence in his strength, so that, once this was known, he could be surrounded and captured.

27. But she, who had once prostituted herself for money, cleverly and cunningly, amid drinking and the allurements of love, began to ask him—as though admiring the greatness of his strength—by what means he surpassed the strength of all others. At the same time, pretending to be fearful and anxious, she begged him to entrust to his beloved the secret by which he might be bound and subjected to another’s power.

Still sober and strong in spirit against the blandishments of the prostitute, he answered deceit with deceit, saying that if he were bound with fresh, green vines and not withered ones, the weakness of his body would make him like other men.

When the Philistines learned this through Delilah and surrounded the sleeping man with vine bonds, he was awakened as though unexpectedly. They found him not inferior to his known and customary strength; once the bonds were loosened, his free strength resisted and overcame them, numerous though they were.

28. But after a short time Delilah, as though she had been mocked and complaining, did not cease to repeat her devices and demand proof of his love.

Samson, still strong in judgment and laughing at the deceit, told her that if he were bound with seven ropes not yet used, he would fall into the power of his enemies. But this too was in vain.

A third time, as though drawing the answer from a mystery and now nearer to falling, he said that if the seven locks of hair on his head were loosened and woven together as though into a cord, his strength would depart from him.

[Note: The Belvedere manuscript reads “nearer to slipping.” The expression below, in cubitum, appears to mean the same as licio or in licium, “into a cord,” as it is read in Scripture. Yet it was also a kind of bond called ἀγκωνόδεσμος, “an elbow-bond,” to which Ambrose may have been referring.]

This too deceived the makers of the ambush.

29. But finally, when the shameless woman had lamented that she had been mocked so many times and grieved that she had been judged unworthy to be entrusted with the secret of her beloved, and when she saw that what she sought as a remedy was suspected as a means of betrayal, she compelled him by her tears to give her credence.

At the same time, the man’s unconquered strength up to that point made it seem necessary that he should fall into distress. Wounded in spirit, he revealed his secret: he said that the strength of God was upon him, that he was consecrated to the Lord, and that, according to the Lord’s command, he allowed his hair to grow. If it were cut, he would cease to be a Nazirite and would lose the use of his own strength.

When the Philistines learned through the woman of the man’s weakness, they brought her the payment for her crime, so that, bound by the price, she might carry out the deceit.

30. She, however, exhausted by her harlot’s caresses, forced him into the sleep of love. She summoned a barber and, applying the razor, cut off the seven locks of his head. Immediately his strength was diminished through the transgression of the prohibition.

When he awoke from sleep, he said: “I shall do as I usually do and shake myself free upon my adversaries.” But he recognized neither the alertness of his mind nor his strength; neither vigor remained nor grace.

Therefore, reflecting that he had rashly entrusted himself to women and, thinking himself deceived, that if he attempted anything further he was condemned by weakness, he gave his eyes to blindness and his hands to bonds. Bound in fetters, he entered a prison unknown to him for many years.

[Note: All editions read: “Reflecting how rashly he had entrusted himself to the woman of his enemies, and, having been shorn, condemned by weakness, he could not attempt anything further; he gave his eyes to blindness.” Erasmus and Gill read: “Having been blinded in his eyes, he gave his hands to bonds,” and so forth. The manuscripts, however, present our reading with broad agreement, except that many join the words calvi ratus into calviratus, a word that does not exist in Latin. To understand the final part easily, interpret it as follows: calvi ratus, “thinking himself deceived”; tentare ulterius aliquid, “if he should attempt anything further”; and damnatum infirmitatis, equivalent to “since he had been condemned by weakness,” and so forth.]

### 31

And now, as time passed, his hair began to grow again (Judges 16:22 ff.). When a celebrated banquet was being held, Samson was brought out of prison and placed in the sight of the people. There were nearly three thousand men and women; they assailed him with grievous insults and mocked him with derision. This was endured all the more harshly, and beyond the very condition of captivity, by a man conscious of his innate strength. For to live and die is a function of nature, but to be made an object of mockery is considered a disgrace.

Desiring, therefore, either to relieve so great an outrage by vengeance or to forestall it thereafter by his death, he pretended that, because of the weakness of his body and the shackles on his feet, he could not support himself. He asked the boy who guided his steps to bring him near the columns by which the whole building was supported. When he had been brought there, he grasped with both hands the supports of the entire structure. While the Philistines were intent upon the sacrificial festival that they were offering to their god Dagon—through whom they believed their enemy had been delivered into their power—and were counting the tricks of a treacherous woman among heaven’s benefits, he cried out to the Lord, saying:

“Lord, remember your servant once more, so that, in requital for my two eyes, you may grant me vengeance upon these nations. Let them not give glory to their gods, saying that, with their help, they have taken me into their power. I do not value my life more highly. Let my soul die with the Philistines, so that they may recognize that my weakness was no less deadly to them than my strength.”

### 32

He then shook the columns with great force, and broke and shattered them. The collapse of the upper structure followed, engulfing him also and throwing down all those who were looking on from above. There a great multitude of men and women alike perished,

[Note: Two manuscripts read “and a quiet triumph”; two others read “and a great triumph.”]

and the triumph he sought was achieved by his death, with an end in no way inferior or dishonorable when compared with all his earlier victories. For although, up to that time and thereafter, he was inviolable and incomparable among men experienced in warfare in this life, nevertheless in death he conquered himself and displayed an unconquerable spirit, scorning and treating as virtually nothing the end of life that all fear.

### 33

It was therefore an act of courage that he closed the day with the number of his victories increased, and found not a captive but a triumphal end. That he was overcome by a woman should be attributed to nature rather than to his personal character, since the human condition is weaker than guilt;

[Note: All printed editions read “the human condition is greater, guilt is less,” a statement without meaning or, indeed, absurd. All the manuscripts therefore rightly exclude the word “greater,” so that the human condition is said to be subject to guilt. Josephus’s words also support our correction. At the end of the passage mentioned so often above he says: “And as for being overcome by a woman, this must be attributed to the nature of human beings, which is less powerful than sins” (Καὶ τὸ μὲν ὑπὸ γυναικὸς ἁλῶναι, δεῖ τῇ φύσει τῶν ἀνθρώπων προσάπτειν ἥττονι ἁμαρτημάτων οὔσῃ, etc.).]

for it is pressed down and yields to the allurements of wrongdoing. Thus, since Scripture testifies concerning him that he killed more people in his death than he had killed during the course of his life, he seems to have been captured more for the destruction of his enemies than in order that he himself should be cast down or diminished. For he did not prove himself inferior to them, since his burial was more glorious than his power. In the end he was not crushed and buried beneath weapons but beneath the corpses of his enemies, covered by his own triumph, leaving a glorious memorial to posterity: he had ruled his people, whom he found in captivity, according to his own judgment for twenty years in freedom, and when buried in his ancestral soil he left them heirs to liberty.

### 34

This example therefore makes it clear

[Note: Ambrose proscribes marriages between Christians and persons of another sect not only in this letter, but also in various passages of the earlier volume—namely, Book II *On Abraham*, chapter 9, section 84; the *Exposition of Psalm 118*, sermon 20, section 48; and Book VIII *On Luke*, section 2. There is, however, considerable controversy among the older and newer scholastics as to whether our Doctor holds that such disparity of worship, as they call it, prevents a marriage from being contracted and also invalidates and dissolves a marriage already contracted. Gratian, Peter Lombard, and others defend the affirmative position; Bellarmine, Estius, and the rest of the more recent writers stand on the negative side. They are chiefly led to this conclusion because Ambrose places heretics in the same class as pagans and Jews; and therefore they argue that this impediment became dissolving by custom and tacit agreement rather than by any law. We admit that Ambrose did not speak so clearly on this matter that all possibility of doubt is removed. Nevertheless, if one examines closely the testimonies already indicated, one will find that he prohibits all such kinds of unions in a manner sufficiently indicating that they are to be regarded as null. As for imperial constitutions, we have the law of Theodosius issued in A.D. 388, which imposed the penalty of adultery—that is, capital punishment—upon Christians and Jews who entered into marriage with one another. Before that time, however, it is credible that different customs concerning the same matter were observed in different places.]

that the companionship of foreigners must be avoided, lest the snares of treachery take the place of the love proper to marriage. Farewell, and love us, because we love you.

[Note: Written in the year 385.]

## LETTER XX

He relates to his sister what happened at Milan over several days on account of the basilica that the Arians were demanding, and how he himself was summoned by Valentinian’s officials while the people protested. He then relates how, when decans had been sent to seize the basilica, Castulus the Arian was carried off by the people; on his account, although he had been freed through his own intervention, various condemnations followed. After these events the holy bishop was again addressed in the emperor’s name and replied with great steadfastness. He adds that on the following day, after the basilica had been occupied, the soldiers promised to go over to the Catholics, and that the people had yielded nothing of their courage. He adapts to the circumstances of the time the temptations of Job, especially those which he is read to have suffered through a woman. Meanwhile the basilica was freed, but a notary brought him harsh messages, by which he was in no way moved. Finally he applies the prophecy of Jonah to present events, and adds the people’s joy at the liberation of the basilica and the remission of the fine imposed on the merchants, Valentinian’s words to the counts, and his own reply to Calligonus’s threats.

### 1

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “Ambrose, bishop, to his sister Marcellina.”]

Since in nearly all your letters you anxiously inquire about the Church, hear what is happening. The day after I received your letter, in which you had indicated that your dreams were troubling you, a mass of grave anxieties began to stir. No longer was the Portiana—that is, the basilica outside the walls—

[Note: Our Mabillon, *Italian Journey*, p. 17: “The Basilica of Saint Victor, outside the walls in Ambrose’s time, was called Portiana after its founder.”]

being demanded, but the new basilica—that is, the one inside the walls, which is larger.

### 2

The leading officers,

[Note: “Leaders of the forces” is absent from many manuscripts, but is found in some manuscripts and in all printed editions. Perhaps Ambrose calls the *principes virtutum* nothing other than the *magistri militum* and the *principes agentium in rebus*. Consult J. C. Bulengerus, *On the Roman Empire*, Book III, chapter 12, and Book VI, chapter 44, concerning their offices. The *comites consistoriani* were those who attended the emperor’s consistory. On them see the same Bulengerus, Book III, chapter 2, *On the Roman Emperor*, and Book II, chapter 9, *On the Roman Empire*. One may also add Godefridus, under the law concerning the *Comites Consistoriani*.]

namely, the counts of the consistory, came to me first, asking both that I surrender the basilica and that I ensure that the people caused no disturbance. I replied that it was contrary to established order for a priest to surrender the temple of God.

### 3

The following day there was an acclamation in the Church. The prefect also came there

[Note: There were various kinds of prefects, concerning which see the Bulengerus cited above, *On the Roman Empire*, in various places, as well as Godefridus. Since the prefect is called simply “the prefect” here, we understand him to be the prefect of the praetorium, whose office the same authors explain in many places.]

and began to urge us either to surrender the Portiana basilica. The people protested. Thus we departed at that time, with him saying that he would report the matter to the emperor.

### 4

The next day, which was Sunday, after the readings and the exposition, when the catechumens had been dismissed, I was delivering the creed to certain candidates for baptism in the baptisteries of the basilica.

[Note: That is, after the reading of the sacred texts and the discourse, namely, the sermon or exposition of the reading. When he says that he had delivered the creed to the candidates, we explained above, in Book I *On Elijah*, chapter 10, section 34, who were called *competentes*. The time at which they received the creed is expressly indicated here. Isidore also says in Book I *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 27, speaking of Palm Sunday: “On this day the creed is delivered to the candidates.” We infer, however, that this custom did not continue for long from the fact that Alcuin, when discussing the same matter, uses the imperfect form “was accustomed” rather than the present form. Indeed, from Augustine we understand that even in Ambrose’s time the same day was not assigned everywhere for the delivery of the creed. Consider his Sermon 59 on Matthew, Sermon 212 *On the Delivery of the Creed*, and others.]

There I was informed, on reliable report, that they had sent decans from the palace to the Portiana basilica and were hanging the curtains, and that part of the people was proceeding there.

[Note: Godefridus, under the law concerning decans, asserts that their office was the same as that of lictors: “For apprehending the accused, and likewise for hanging royal veils or curtains in places claimed for the treasury, the decans performed this service.” To demonstrate this he cites this very passage. Bulengerus also cites it, Book VI, chapter 73; consult him.]

Nevertheless, I remained at my duty and began to celebrate the Mass.

[Note: It seems that *missam facere coepi* refers not to the dismissal of the candidates but to the sacrifice itself. Otherwise, since he had already dismissed the catechumens, he would have used the verb *coepi*—“I began”—quite improperly.]

### 5

While I was offering the sacrifice, I learned that a certain Castulus had been seized by the people, a man whom the Arians called a presbyter. They had encountered him in the street as he was passing by. I began to weep most bitterly and to pray to God during the offering itself, asking him to come to our aid, lest anyone’s blood should be shed in the cause of the Church;

[Note: The old edition and not a few manuscripts read “and not this man’s blood.” This is not wholly unreasonable if it refers to Castulus. The Roman edition, together with several manuscripts, reads better: “lest anyone’s blood.” Nannius names Costerus as the first author of this correction; nevertheless, he says that the passage still seems corrupt because in Latin one does not say that blood “is made.” He therefore thinks that *flueret*—“should flow”—should be read instead of *fieret*—“should be shed.” Gronovius, in his *Observations in Eccle.* 25, removes Nannius’s scruple by citing passages from Livy. Yet even he, when he holds that the reading should be “lest anyone’s blood,” proposes *ne quis sanguis*—“lest any blood”—and reasons more subtly than is appropriate.]

and certainly that my own blood might be poured out for the salvation not only of the people but also of the impious themselves. Why say more? I sent presbyters and deacons and rescued the man from injury.

### 6

The gravest condemnations were immediately decreed, first against the entire body of merchants. Thus, during the holy days of the final week,

[Note: Ambrose himself, in his *Exposition of Psalm 118*, Sermon 15, section 7, speaking of the oil of mercy, says: “This oil shines at the solemn celebrations of the Church.” In particular, Gregory of Nyssa, *Oration 3 on the Resurrection of the Lord*, Chrysostom, *Oration 6 to the People of Antioch*, and others testify that prisoners were formerly accustomed to be released at the Paschal solemnity. Many laws were also enacted concerning this matter, for example Laws 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, and 8 *On the Remission of Crimes*. It is easy to see that our saint is alluding here chiefly to Laws 3 and 4, issued by Valentinian I in A.D. 367 and 368.]

when the chains of debtors were customarily loosened, chains clattered and were placed around the necks of the innocent; two hundred pounds of gold were demanded

[Note: Thus the manuscripts read, and the printed editions do not depart from them except that they substitute *intra*—“within”—for *infra*—“during,” and that the Roman edition has suppressed the word *totum*—“the whole.” Immediately afterward, where all the printed editions and a few manuscripts read “Some reply,” the more numerous and better manuscripts prefer “They reply otherwise.”]

within the space of three days. They replied that they would pay only that amount or double it, if it were demanded, provided that they kept their faith. The prisons were full of merchants.

### 7

All the palace offices—that is,

[Note: “All the offices” means “very many offices,” namely, those signified here, although he may perhaps have left some unmentioned. The *memoriales* were those in charge of the memorial archives; see Bulengerus, Book IV *On the Roman Empire*, chapter 13. The title *agentes in rebus* appears in Book XII of Justinian’s Code. They are also frequently mentioned in the Theodosian Code, especially Book VI. Some think that this is a general designation for those who administer the emperor’s affairs, whether they were imperial procurators or commissioners sent through the various provinces to the legates with enlarged authority; hence, in later books, some are called *ducenarii*, others *centenarii*. Nannius, following Alciatus, holds this view; but while refuting it he says that he conjectures the *agentes in rebus* to be those who lead an order, that is, military magistrates. He thinks this is proved by the laws of Theodosius and Justinian, where they are contrasted with the palace soldiery. *Apparitores* were those who obeyed various magistrates; concerning them see Bulengerus, cited work, chapter 17. The same author discusses the counts in so many places that it would take too long even to list them; it is therefore preferable to refer the reader to him, as also to Godefridus. Finally, something has already been said about the *honorati* in Book II *On Duties*, chapter 29, section 150. To that we add only that Alciatus, in Book I of his *Praetermissa*, defines them as those who possess palace rank but abstain from administration; Nannius considers them the same as those who in Rome were called senators and in the municipalities decurions. To demonstrate this he cites Theodosius, Book XVI, title 4, law 44. See also Godefridus under the law concerning the office of the civil judge.]

memorial officials, agents in affairs, and attendants of various counts—

[Note: One Paris manuscript reads: “attendants of the opposing counts.”]

were ordered to hold back from advancing, ostensibly so that they would be prohibited from taking part in the sedition. They threatened the *honorati* with many extremely severe penalties unless they surrendered the basilica. The persecution was raging; and, if they had opened the gate, they seemed ready to break out into every kind of crime.

### 8

I myself was summoned by counts and tribunes so that the basilica might be surrendered without delay. They said that the emperor was exercising his lawful right, since everything was in his power. I replied that, if he demanded from me what was mine—that is, my estate, my silver, or anything of that kind belonging to me—I would not resist, although everything that belonged to me belonged to the poor. But what belongs to God is not subject to imperial authority. If my patrimony is demanded, invade it; if my body is demanded, I will meet you. Do you wish to drag me into chains? Do you wish to put me to death?

[Note: Nearly all the manuscripts read “it is my will”; all the printed editions more aptly read “it is my delight,” and so forth.]

It is my delight. I will not surround myself with a multitude of people, nor cling to the altars while pleading for my life; rather, I shall be sacrificed more gratefully on behalf of the altars.

### 9

I was indeed horrified in spirit when I learned that armed men had been sent to occupy the basilica of the Church, lest, while they claimed the basilica, some massacre should occur and turn to the destruction of the whole city. I prayed that I might not survive the funeral pyre of so great a city, or of all Italy.

[Note: That is, I was more horrified lest the resentment and offense caused by another’s blood should return upon me than lest my own blood should be shed.]

I loathed the blame of shedding blood and offered my throat. Gothic tribunes were present, and I addressed them, saying: “For this reason did Roman possession receive you, that you should make yourselves the agents of public disturbance? Where will you go if these things are destroyed?”

### 10

I was required to restrain the people. I replied that it was within my power not to stir them up, but that it was in God’s hand to calm them. Finally, if they supposed me to be an instigator,

[Note: All the printed editions read “if they thought me an instigator … into whatever regions they wished”; all the manuscripts read “if he thought,” referring either to the emperor or, more probably, to Justina, his mother.]

then punishment ought already to be inflicted upon me, or I ought to be carried away into whatever desert regions they wished. After saying this, they departed. I spent the entire day in the old basilica. From there I withdrew home to sleep, so that if anyone wished to take me away, he would find me ready.

### 11

Before dawn, as soon as I stepped across the threshold, the basilica was surrounded and occupied by soldiers. It is said that the soldiers sent this message to the emperor: if he wished to come out, he would have the opportunity; nevertheless, they would remain present if they saw him meeting with the Catholics. Otherwise, they would go over to that assembly which Ambrose was convening.

### 12

No one among the Arians dared to come out, since there were no citizens among them, only a few members of the royal household and some Goths. Just as in former times the wagon was their dwelling, so now the Church is their wagon. Wherever this woman proceeds, she carries all her assemblies with her.

[Note: The Goths are believed to be a Scythian people who live in wagons; they are called *ἀμαξόβιοι* (*amaksobioi*) and *ἀμαξοβίται* (*amaksobitai*), “wagon-dwellers.” The settlements of the Goths—both of the eastern Goths, that is, the Ostrogoths, and of the western Goths, that is, the Visigoths—are located in the Baltic Sea near Sweden. I think their name was derived from goodness, that is, *goeth*, just as another people called themselves Quadi from evil, that is, *quaeth*; and as the Franks were called *urii anchen*, that is, “young unmarried men, not yet husbands.” Thus Nannius. Ambrose therefore suggests that the Arian assemblies were itinerant.]

I learned from the people’s groaning that the basilica was surrounded. But while the readings were being delivered, I was informed that the new basilica too was full of people; that the congregation seemed larger than when everyone was free; and that a reader was being urgently requested. What more need be said? The very soldiers who seemed to have occupied the basilica, when they learned that I had ordered that they be excluded from communion, began to come to this assembly of ours.

When the women saw them, they became agitated, and one woman rushed out. The soldiers themselves, however, said that they had come to pray, not to fight. Someone among the people shouted. How moderately, how steadfastly, how faithfully they demanded that we go to that basilica! It is also reported that in that basilica the people were demanding my presence.

### 14

Then I began this address:

“You have heard, my children, that I read the Book of Job,

[Note: The Roman edition alone adds: “The Book of Job was read today.”]

which has been completed according to the customary service and season. The devil knew from experience that this book would also be proclaimed, in which the whole strength of his temptation is exposed and revealed; and therefore today he shook himself with greater violence. But thanks be to our God, who has strengthened you so firmly in faith and patience. I had gone up expecting to see one Job; I found all the Jobs whom I could admire. In each one of you Job came to life again; in each one the patience and virtue of that holy man shone forth.

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “For what more fitting thing could be said?” The reading *praesentius*, however, should by no means be changed; the meaning is the same as if one were to write: “What words could have been uttered by a mind more present and free from passions?”]

For what could have been more fitting than what the Holy Spirit has spoken today through Christian men? ‘We ask, Augustus; we do not fight. We are not afraid, but we ask.’ This is fitting for Christians: that they desire the tranquility of peace, and that steadfastness in faith and truth should not be recalled even by the danger of death. For the Lord is the ruler who will save those who hope in him” (Psalm 16:7).

### 15

“But let us come to the readings that were proposed. You see that the devil is given permission to tempt (Job 1:12), so that the good may be tested.

[Note: All the printed editions read: “The enemy envies”; all the manuscripts read, with no worse sense: “The wicked man envies.”]

The wicked man envies the progress of the good and tests them in various ways. He tested holy Job in his possessions; he tested him in his children; he tested him in bodily pain. The stronger man is tested in his own body, the weaker in another’s. He wanted to take away from me the riches that I possess in you and to scatter this patrimony of your tranquility. He longed to tear from me you yourselves, my good children, for whom I renew the sacrifice every day; he tried to involve you in the ruins of public disturbance. I have therefore already endured two kinds of temptation. And perhaps because the Lord God knows me to be weaker, he has not yet given him power over my body. Even if I desire it, even if I offer myself, perhaps he still judges me unequal to this contest and exercises me through different labors. Nor did Job begin with this conflict; rather, he completed his course in it.

### 16

“Job was tested by messengers bringing calamities upon calamities; he was also tested through a woman, who said: ‘Say something against God, and die’ (Job 2:9). You see how many things are suddenly stirred up: Goths, weapons, Gentiles, fines imposed on merchants, and punishment for the holy. You understand what is being commanded when it is ordered: ‘Surrender the basilica’—that is, ‘Say something against God, and die.’ Not only speak against God, but also act against God. The command is: ‘Surrender the altars of God.’

### 17

“We are therefore pressed by royal commands, but we are strengthened by the words of Scripture, which replied: ‘You have spoken as one of the foolish women speaks’ (ibid., 10). This, then, is no insignificant temptation; for we have learned that the harsher temptations are those that come through women. In the end, Adam too was overthrown through Eve (Genesis 3:6), and this caused him to depart from the heavenly commands. Once he recognized this error, guilty of a transgressing conscience, he wished to hide, but he could not hide. Therefore God said to him: ‘Adam, where are you?’ (ibid., 9)—that is, ‘What were you before? Where have you now begun to be? Where had I placed you? Where have you crossed over by your own act?’ You acknowledge that you are naked because you have lost the good garments of faith. These are the leaves with which you now seek to cover yourself. You rejected the fruit and wish to hide beneath the leaves of the Law, but you are exposed. You desired to withdraw from the Lord your God for the sake of one woman; therefore you flee from the one whom you had sought to see. You preferred to hide yourself with one woman, leaving behind the spectacle of the world, the dwelling-place of paradise, and the grace of Christ.

### 18

“What shall I say about the fact that Jezebel also persecuted Elijah with bloodshed (1 Kings 19:1 ff.), and that Herodias caused John the Baptist to be killed (Matthew 14:3 ff.)? Each woman acted against one man; but the less my merits are by comparison, the more grievous are the temptations. The strength is weaker, but the danger greater. Women succeed one another; hatreds alternate; schemes change; the elders are summoned; the king’s injury is made the pretext.

What explanation is there, then, for this more serious temptation against this little worm,

[Note: Thus the majority of the manuscripts, including the better ones. Others read: “more serious temptations”; to make that reading fit, the printed editions added the word “to be moved.”]

unless it is because they are persecuting not me but the Church?

### 19

“The command is finally given: ‘Surrender the basilica.’ I answer: ‘It is neither lawful for me to surrender it nor expedient for you to receive it, Emperor. You have no legal right to violate a private man’s house; do you think the house of God should be taken away?’ It is alleged that the emperor may do everything, that everything belongs to him. I reply: ‘Do not burden yourself, Emperor, by thinking that you possess any imperial right over what belongs to God.

[Note: The holy Doctor had already stated above that emperors have no right over the Church and divine matters, and below he repeats the same truth in his own pamphlet addressed to Valentinian. Many most holy men have defended this truth through countless labors and sometimes even with their own blood. Others have vigorously championed it in published works. Among them Facundus, in his work against the book of the Emperor Justinian *Against the Three Chapters*, argues with powerful reasoning about the courage with which bishops must defend the rights of the Church, especially in Book XII; consult that work.]

Do not exalt yourself. But if you wish to rule longer, be subject to God. It is written: ‘Render to God the things that are God’s, and to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s’ (Matthew 22:21). Palaces belong to the emperor; the Churches belong to the priest. You have been entrusted with authority over public walls, not over sacred things.’

It is said again that the emperor ordered: ‘I too ought to have one basilica.’

[Note: “I answered: ‘You may not have it’” is absent from nearly all the manuscripts. Since, however, it appears in all the printed editions and seems by no means unnecessary to the sense, we have not thought it should be removed from the text.]

I answered: ‘You may not have it. What have you to do with an adulteress? For she is an adulteress who has not been joined in the lawful marriage of Christ.’”

### 20

While I was discussing these matters, I was informed that the royal curtains had been gathered up, but that the basilica was crowded with people and was demanding my presence. I immediately directed my speech there, saying:

“How lofty and profound are the oracles of the Holy Spirit! In the morning, as you remember, brothers, we read words to which we replied with the deepest anguish of heart: ‘O God, the nations have entered into your inheritance’ (Psalm 78:1). And in truth the nations have entered—and more than nations have entered. For Goths and men of different peoples have come; they have come with weapons and, surrounding the basilica, have occupied it. We, ignorant of your greatness, were grieving over this,

[Note: Several manuscripts read: “but our shamelessness was thinking otherwise.” This is not entirely correct.]

but our imprudence was thinking otherwise.

### 21

“The nations have come, but they have truly come into your inheritance. For those who came as nations have become Christians. Those who came to invade the inheritance have become fellow heirs with God. I have defenders whom I thought were enemies; I hold as allies those whom I regarded as adversaries. That saying has been fulfilled which the prophet David sang concerning the Lord Jesus: ‘His place has been made in peace,’ and, ‘There he broke the horns of bows, shield, sword, and war’ (Psalm 75:3–4).

“For whose gift is this, whose work, if not yours, Lord Jesus? You saw armed men coming toward your temple; from one side you saw the people groaning and present in great numbers,

[Note: All the printed editions read: “lest the basilica of God should be surrendered. From the other side, force was being imposed upon the soldiers and the emperor; death was before my eyes.” The manuscripts read as in the text, except that two have: “so that death might be before the soldiers of the emperor.” One manuscript reads: “You restrained the armed men, the commanders, and the prefects. If weapons clash, if they are shut up in my temple …”]

lest the basilica of God should appear to be surrendered; from the other side you saw force being imposed upon the soldiers. Death was before my eyes, lest fury be permitted to do anything amid these events. You inserted yourself, Lord, between them and made both one (Ephesians 2:14). You restrained the armed men, saying, surely: ‘If they rush to arms, if those shut up in my temple are stirred up, what profit is there in my blood?’ (Deuteronomy 32:36).

[Note: Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read: “If a quarrel is stirred up.” This is less elegant. Some manuscripts read: “If swords are stirred up.” Below, where all the manuscripts read “having marveled at the emperor’s …,” all the printed editions have “having supposed the emperor’s …”]

Therefore thanks be to you, Christ. It was not an envoy or messenger, but you, Lord, who saved your people. You tore off my sackcloth and girded me with gladness” (Psalm 29:10, 12).

### 22

I was saying these things, marveling that the emperor’s disposition could be softened by the soldiers’ zeal, the counts’ entreaty, and the people’s prayer. Meanwhile I was informed that a notary had been sent to deliver commands.

[Note: There were three kinds of officials whom emperors used to convey secret commands, namely notaries, tribunes, and counts. These dignities, however, sometimes came together in one man; Godefridus supplies many examples of this under the first law *On Imperial Commands*, and we shall find one below in Ambrose’s own pamphlet. Bulengerus discusses the notary in Book VI, chapter 5.]

I yielded for a little while, and he announced the command. “What possessed you,” he said, “to act contrary to the order?”

I replied: “I do not know what the order was, nor am I certain what is alleged to have been rashly done.”

He said: “Why did you send presbyters to the basilica? If you are a tyrant, I want to know, so that I may know how to prepare myself against you.”

I replied that I had done nothing to the prejudice of the Church. When I had heard that the basilica was occupied by soldiers, I had merely uttered a freer lament; and when many urged me to go there, I had said: “I cannot surrender the basilica, but I ought not to fight.” Later, when I learned that the royal curtains had been removed from there, and when the people demanded that I go there, I sent presbyters. I myself did not wish to go, but said: “I believe in Christ that the emperor himself will act with us.”

### 23

“If these things seem tyrannical, I have weapons—but in the name of Christ. I have power to offer my own body. Why did he delay striking, if he thought me a tyrant?

[Note: Under the ancient covenant, Samuel anointed Saul and David, and the prophet Nathan anointed Solomon. The kings Saul and Uzziah, however, fell under God’s grave displeasure when they usurped priestly office.]

By ancient right, empires were bestowed by priests, not usurped; and it is commonly said that emperors desired the priesthood more than priests desired the empire. Christ fled lest he be made king (John 6:15). We have our own tyranny. The priest’s tyranny is weakness: ‘When I am weak,’ he says, ‘then I am strong’ (2 Corinthians 12:10).

“Yet he must beware lest he make himself a tyrant, since God has not raised up an adversary against him.

[Note: This must be understood of the earlier embassy, as we explained in the *Admonition*.]

Let it not be considered the greatest matter that I am Valentinian’s tyrant, since he complains that he was unable to cross into Italy because of my embassy. I added that priests have never been tyrants, but have often suffered tyrants.”

### 24

That entire day was spent in our sorrow. Nevertheless, the royal curtains were torn down by the mocking boys. I could not return home, because soldiers were surrounding and guarding the basilica. With the brothers we recited psalms in the smaller basilica of the Church.

### 25

The next day the Book of Jonah was read according to custom. When it had been completed, I began this address:

“The book has been read, brothers, in which it is prophesied that sinners will return to repentance. It has been received in such a way that it was hoped its fulfillment would occur in the present. I added that the righteous man would even have wished to incur an offense, so that he might neither witness nor announce the destruction of the city. And since that saying was sorrowful, he was also saddened that the gourd had withered. God also said to the prophet: ‘Are you sad because of the gourd?’ Jonah replied: ‘I am sad.’ The Lord said that if Jonah grieved because the gourd had withered, how much more must the salvation of so great a multitude matter to him. Therefore he removed the destruction that had been prepared for the whole city.”

### 26

Without delay it was announced that the emperor had ordered the soldiers to withdraw from the basilica, and that the merchants should also be repaid what had been exacted from them in the condemnation.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “what had been exacted as part of the condemnation.”]

What joy there was then among the whole people! What applause from the entire populace! What thanksgiving! It was the day on which the Lord delivered himself up for us, the day on which penance is remitted in the Church. The soldiers vied with one another to announce this, rushing to the altars and signifying the token of peace with kisses. Then I recognized that God had struck the worm before dawn so that the whole city might be saved.

### 27

These things happened—and would that they were already finished! But imperial words, full of agitation, indicate that more serious disturbances are to come. I am called a tyrant, and something more than a tyrant. For when the counts begged the emperor to come out to the Church, and said that they were making this request at the soldiers’ urging, he replied: “If Ambrose orders it, you will hand me over to him in chains.” Consider what remains after these words. All were horrified at the utterance, but he has people by whom it may be aggravated.

28. Finally, even in an explicit statement [Note: [Col. 1001D] Bulengerus explains what the dignity of the chamberlain was in book III, chapter 13, of *On the Roman Empire*. See also Godefridus, under “On the Chief of the Sacred Bedchamber.” As for the exceedingly insolent threats of this eunuch, as well as Ambrose’s free and noble reply, the same saint touches upon them discreetly in *On Joseph*, chapter 6, no. 33, as also upon his bloody punishment; [Col. 1002C] yet he does so with such great restraint that nothing could be further from an insulting manner. Concerning his punishment, see what we said from Augustine in the Admonition to that same book.] Calligonus, [Col. 1002C] the chief of the chamber, dared to order me: “While I am alive, do you despise Valentinian? I will take your head.” I replied: “May God permit you to fulfill what you threaten; for I shall suffer what bishops [Note: [Col. 1002C] Thus the old edition, where after the word *bishops* one should mentally supply [Col. 1002D] “are accustomed to suffer”; and similarly after the word *eunuchs*, “are accustomed to do” should be supplied. By this expression he may have alluded to that Egyptian Achillas, by whom Pompey was killed, whom Ambrose identifies in his booklet against Symmachus’s *Relatio*. The Roman edition, however, has *of a eunuch* here instead of *eunuchs*, and immediately adds only: “I do not fear your threats; for you can kill the flesh, but you cannot kill the soul. You can take away this bodily life, but you cannot extinguish merit. For the soul that is subject to God is not subject to human power. Do you think you can harm me? Rather, you provide me a great benefit. You take away temporal life, so that everlasting life may follow.”] eunuchs do. And would that God turn them away from the Church and make them direct all their weapons against me, and satisfy their thirst with my blood! [Note: [Col. 1002D] The Roman edition adds: “Complete their thirst with my blood. Farewell, sister, in the Lord.”]

860 [Note: [Col. 1002D] Written in the year 386.] LETTER XXI

Ambrose excuses himself for not coming when summoned to the consistory, asserting that in a matter of faith or ecclesiastical order no one ought to judge except priests; nor was he contumacious in refusing to inflict an injury upon his own order. He adds that Auxentius might choose Jews or unbelievers as judges, that is, the bitterest enemies of Christ; and that he did not refuse to discuss these matters in the Church or in a synod. He would have said these things in person, had he not been prevented by his fellow bishops and the people.

[Note: [Col. 1003C] In one Vatican manuscript and in the Long manuscript this heading is prefixed: “A booklet of Ambrose himself to the emperor Valentinian against Auxentius.” Ambrose himself likewise subscribes: “I, Ambrose, bishop, have presented this booklet,” etc.]

To the most merciful emperor and most blessed Augustus Valentinian, Ambrose, bishop.

1. Dalmatius [Note: [Col. 1003C] We said in the preceding letter to Marcellina that emperors used notaries and tribunes for confidential orders.] summoned me, as he stated, by your clemency’s command. He requested that I too choose judges, just as Auxentius had chosen them. Yet he did not disclose the names of those who had been requested; he merely added that the contest would take place in the consistory, with your pious judgment as arbiter.

2. To this matter I reply, as I think, suitably. No one ought to judge me contumacious when I assert that your father, of august memory, not only [Note: [Col. 1003C] Sozomen, book VI, chapter 7, reports that when the bishops of the Hellespont and Bithynia asked Valentinian to permit them to assemble for the correction of the teaching of the faith, the emperor replied: “Since I am established among the order of laymen, it is not lawful for me to examine such matters too closely; but let the priests, whose concern these matters are, assemble separately wherever they wish.” These words harmonize beautifully with those of Ambrose. One might also add what is reported by Theodoret, book IV, chapter 6, as well as what Marca discusses in book II, chapter 6, of the *Concordia*, and what he argues concerning Ambrose’s ordination. As for the laws indicated here, Baronius, under the year 369, thinks that Ambrose refers to Valentinian’s law 20, “On Appeals.” Godefridus, however, refutes him under that same law. We therefore think it more likely that the law to which Ambrose refers no longer exists. There is, however, another law issued in the name of Gratian in the year 376, namely law 23, ordering that if there are matters arising from certain disagreements and minor offenses belonging to religious observance, they should be heard in their proper places and by the synods of their own dioceses. See Godefridus under that same law.] declared this in words, but also established it by his laws: “In a matter of faith or of any ecclesiastical order, the person who is neither unequal in office nor different in legal status ought to judge.” These are the words of the imperial rescript: that is, he wished priests to judge priests. Moreover, if a bishop were accused in some other respect and his conduct had to be examined, he wished even this matter to belong to episcopal judgment.

3. Who, then, has replied contumaciously to your clemency? He who wishes you to be like your father, or he who wants you to be unlike him? Unless perhaps the judgment of so great an emperor is considered worthless by certain people—an emperor [Note: [Col. 1004C] An allusion is made here to that noble act of the elder Valentinian: while he was numbered among Julian’s prefects, he struck in the face a minister who had sprinkled him with lustral water.] whose faith was proved by the steadfastness of his confession and whose wisdom is praised for the progress by which the state was improved.

4. When, most merciful Emperor, have you heard of laymen judging a bishop in a matter of faith? Are we therefore so bent by a kind of flattery that we forget the rights of the priesthood, and think that what God has given me should be entrusted by me to others? If a bishop is to be taught by a layman, what will follow? Let a layman debate, and let the bishop listen; let the bishop learn from a layman. But certainly, whether we review the sequence of the divine Scriptures or ancient times, who would deny [Note: [Col. 1004D] The Colbertine manuscript has *annuat*, “assent,” which does not make good sense.] that in a matter of faith—of faith, I say—bishops have usually judged Christian emperors, not emperors bishops?

5. By God’s favor, you will advance further into the maturity of old age, and then you will judge what sort of bishop he is who subjects priestly authority to laymen. Your father, by God’s favor a man of more mature years, used to say: “It is not mine to judge between bishops.” Now your clemency says: “I ought to judge.” He, baptized in Christ, considered himself unequal to the weight of so great a judgment; your clemency, for whom the sacraments of baptism are still reserved to be acquired, arrogates judgment concerning the faith, although you do not know the sacraments of that faith.

6. We may leave the kind of judges he has chosen to public estimation, since he is afraid to disclose their names. Let them come plainly, whoever they are, to the Church. Let them listen with the people—not so that anyone may sit as judge, but so that each person may examine his own inclination and choose whom he will follow. The matter concerns the priest of this Church. If the people hear him and think that he argues better, let them follow his faith; I shall not begrudge it.

7. I say nothing of the fact that the people themselves have already judged. I am silent about the fact that they requested from your clemency’s father the man whom they now possess [Note: [Col. 1004D] The more extraordinary circumstances surrounding Ambrose’s election are touched upon here with great modesty. You will find them treated more fully by Paulinus in his *Life of Ambrose*.]. I am silent about the fact that the father of your piety promised that there would be peace if the chosen man accepted the priesthood. I followed the faithfulness of these promises.

8. But if he boasts of the approval of certain foreigners, let him be bishop there, wherever those people come from who think he should be honored with the name of bishop. [Col. 1004C] For I neither know him as a bishop nor know where he is from.

9. Where, then, do we stand, Emperor, when you yourself have already declared your judgment—indeed, have even issued [Note: [Col. 1004D] Here the holy bishop refers to law 4, *On the Catholic Faith*, which both granted the Arians permission to assemble in the churches and threatened the penalty of death not only against those who violently resisted that constitution, but also against those who presented the emperor with petitions against it. Sozomen, book VII, chapter 13, has elegantly described how that law was promulgated.] laws, leaving no one free to judge otherwise? What you prescribed for others, you prescribed also for yourself; for an emperor issues laws which he himself first observes. Do you wish me, then, to test whether those chosen as judges will either oppose your judgment or at least excuse themselves on the ground that they were unable to resist an emperor’s command so severe and so absolute?

10. But this would be the conduct of a contumacious, not a modest, priest. Behold, Emperor, you are already rescinding your own law in part; would that it were not in part but altogether! For I would not want your law to stand above God’s law. God’s law has taught us what we are to follow; human laws cannot teach this. They can extort change from the timid, but they cannot inspire faith.

862 11. Who, then, upon reading that throughout so many provinces an order has been issued in an instant that whoever opposes the emperor is to be struck down by the sword, and that whoever does not surrender the temple of God is immediately to be killed—who, I say, could say, whether alone or among a few, to the emperor: “I do not approve of your law”? Is this forbidden to priests but permitted to laymen? And will someone who either hopes for favor or fears displeasure judge concerning the faith?

12. Shall I then undertake to choose lay judges who, once they have upheld the truth of the faith, will either be proscribed or killed, as the law issued concerning the faith decrees? Shall I therefore expose people either to treachery or to punishment?

13. Ambrose is not so important that the priesthood should be cast down for his sake. The life of one man is not as valuable as the dignity of all priests [Note: [Col. 1005C] From this you may understand that, immediately after Valentinian issued the law, the bishops assembled at Ambrose’s initiative, so that, at this critical juncture, they might see that the Church suffered no harm.], with whose counsel I wrote these things. They informed me that perhaps one of those chosen by Auxentius might even be a pagan or a Jew; if we entrusted judgment concerning Christ to such men, we would be handing them a triumph over Christ. What else could they enjoy hearing from such people except an insult to Christ? What else could please them except—God forbid—that Christ’s divinity be denied? Such men plainly agree with the [Arian] who says that Christ is a creature, something which pagans and Jews also readily confess.

14. This was written at the Council of Ariminum; and rightly I abhor that council, following the teaching [Note: [Col. 1005C] Ambrose uses the testimony only of the Council of Nicaea, not of Constantinople, perhaps because the authority of the latter would not have been accepted in the West. Thus it may plausibly be said that, in support of the divinity of the Holy Spirit, which he touches upon incidentally, he put forward not the canons of that council but the confession of Gaul and Spain.] of the Council of Nicaea, from which neither death nor the sword will be able to separate me. Theodosius, the most blessed emperor and kinsman of your clemency, both follows and approves this faith. Gaul holds this faith, and Spain holds it, and they preserve it together with their devout confession of the divine Spirit.

15. If the matter is to be discussed, I have learned to discuss it in the Church, as my predecessors did. If there is to be debate concerning the faith, that debate ought to belong to priests, as was done [Note: [Col. 1005D] Socrates, book I, chapter 22, speaks as follows on this matter: “Then, after Constantine had spoken at length concerning peace and concord, he left the subsequent, more careful investigation of the doctrines of our religion to the bishops’ judgment and authority.” See also Athanasius, *Oration against the Arians*.] under Constantine, the emperor of august memory, who did not issue any laws beforehand but granted the priests free judgment. It also happened under Constantius, the emperor of august memory and heir to his father’s dignity; but what began well was completed otherwise. For the bishops had first written a sincere statement of faith; but when certain people wished to judge concerning the faith within the palace, they contrived that, through evasions, the bishops’ judgments should be altered. Yet they immediately recalled their distorted decision. And certainly [Note: [Col. 1005D] The latest Paris edition has “the smaller number,” which agrees less well with the history of the Council of Ariminum. For although the bishops there initially embraced the Nicene faith with great unanimity, later, after the representatives whom they had sent to Constantius had been bent from their purpose, almost all subscribed to the articles of Valens. Finally, when the larger number considered the damage inflicted upon the faith by that subscription, they came to their senses and rejected the Arian formula. On this matter consult what we observed in book I, chapter 18, no. 122, of *On the Faith*.] the larger number at Ariminum approved the faith of the Council of Nicaea and condemned the [Arian] decrees.

863 16. If Auxentius appeals to a synod in order to debate concerning the faith—although it is not necessary [Note: [Col. 1006D] The same is found in the Letter to Gratian attached to the Council of Aquileia, no. 3: “How serious it would have been if, because of only two priests who were diseased with treachery, the churches throughout the world had been deprived of their chief priests!”] to weary so many bishops on account of one man, who, even if he were an angel from heaven, ought not to be preferred to the peace of the churches—when I hear that a synod is being assembled, I too shall not be absent. Remove the law, then, if you want there to be a contest.

17. I would have come, Emperor, to your clemency’s consistory to present these matters in person, if either the bishops or the people had permitted me [Note: [Col. 1006D] Several manuscripts read “if either the bishops or the people had released me.”], saying that a matter of faith ought to be discussed in the Church before the people.

18. And would that, Emperor, you had not ordered [Col. 1006C] me to go wherever I wished! Every day I went out, and no one guarded me. You ought to have sent me wherever you wanted, since I was offering myself to everyone. Now the priests say to me: “It makes little difference whether you leave willingly or surrender the altar of Christ; for once you have left, you will have surrendered it.”

19. And would that it were plainly clear to me that the Church would in no way be handed over to the Arians! I would willingly offer myself to the judgment of your piety. But if I alone am the cause of disturbance, why has an order also been issued to seize all the other churches? Would that it be confirmed that no one is to trouble the churches! I desire that a judgment be pronounced concerning me, whatever it may appear to be.

20. Therefore, Emperor, graciously accept the reason why I could not come to the consistory. [Note: [Col. 1007D] Nannius writes concerning this passage: “He tacitly reproaches him for having been twice compelled, as an ambassador to Maximus, to stand in the consistory contrary to episcopal dignity: once when he was sent there for peace, and once to bring back the remains of Gratian, his brother.” The consistory is the emperor’s tribunal, where he administers justice. Thus far Nannius; but the learned man is mistaken in thinking that both of Ambrose’s embassies preceded this letter, whereas only the first can be so understood, as is demonstrated in the Admonition.] I have learned to stand in the consistory only on your behalf; and I cannot contend within the palace, since I neither seek nor know the palace’s secret chambers.

21. I, Ambrose, bishop, have presented this booklet to the most merciful emperor and most blessed Augustus Valentinian.

SERMON AGAINST AUXENTIUS ON THE SURRENDER OF THE BASILICAS

He removes the people’s anxiety caused by the imperial order by explaining his reply, and adds that he did not go to the consistory because he feared that the basilica would be handed over. [Col. 1007B] Then, after challenging his opponents to debate in the Church, he declares that he is not frightened by weapons; and, recalling his response concerning the sacred vessels, he testifies that he is ready for conflict. God’s decree cannot be evaded, nor can his protection be overcome; yet he wishes to suffer in his servants. Since Ambrose had not previously been seized, it is clear how vainly the heretics are making a tumult. Then, after adapting the history of Naboth and Christ’s entry into Jerusalem to the present matter, he attacks Auxentius’ cruel law; after answering the Arians’ objections, he declares that he would gladly debate before the people. Auxentius, he says, has already been condemned by the pagans whom he had chosen as judges, as well as by Paul and Christ himself. The same heretic appealed to Caesar, forgetting the preceding year; and the Arians, while stirring up hatred against Christ’s servants, are much worse than the Jews. For the Church prefers the image not of Caesar but of Christ. After adding a few remarks about his response and his hymns, he declares that he is not disobedient but the emperor’s son in the Church, while Auxentius is worse than a Jew.

1. I see that you have suddenly become more agitated than usual, and are guarding me. [Note: [Col. 1007D] Some manuscripts read: “I am surprised that this has happened . . . you saw me”; others, “you heard me.” In several manuscripts the latter words are expressed thus: “but the others”—while the remaining manuscripts and editions have the more speech-like reading found in the text.] I wonder what this means, unless perhaps it is because through the tribunes you saw or heard that an imperial order had been issued summoning me, so that I might leave from here wherever I wished, and that anyone who wished might have permission to follow. Did you fear, then, that I would abandon the Church and, while worrying about my own safety, leave you? But you could also have observed what I myself ordered: that I could not possibly have any intention of abandoning the Church, because I feared the Lord of the world more than the emperor of this age. Certainly, if force were to drive me away from the Church, my flesh could be expelled, but not my mind. I am ready that, if he does what belongs to royal power, I should undergo what is customary for the priesthood.

2. Why, then, are you troubled? I shall never abandon you willingly; when compelled, I do not know how to resist. I may grieve, I may weep, I may groan; against weapons, soldiers, and even Goths, my tears are my weapons, for such are the defenses of a priest. Otherwise I neither ought nor can resist. But I am not accustomed to flee and abandon the Church, lest someone interpret my action as prompted by fear of a harsher punishment. You yourselves know that I am accustomed to defer to emperors, not yield to them; to offer myself willingly to punishments and not fear what is being prepared.

3. Would that I were certain that the Church would in no way be handed over to heretics! I would gladly go to the emperor’s palace, if that were compatible with the priestly office, so that I might contend in the palace rather than in the Church. But in the consistory Christ is not usually the accused but the judge. Who would deny that a case concerning the faith should be conducted in the Church? If anyone has confidence, let him come here. Let him not seek either the judgment of the emperor, already bent—as he has revealed by issuing a law that attacks the faith [Note: [Col. 1008D] The preceding letter dealt at length with this law.]—or the hoped-for support of certain ambitious people. I will not allow anyone to sell an injury to Christ.

4. The soldiers surrounding us [Note: [Col. 1008D] The Roman edition has “the clatter of weapons.”], the clash of arms with which the Church has been enclosed, do not frighten my faith; but they agitate my mind, lest, while you hold me, something harmful arise for your salvation. I have already learned not to fear; but I have begun to fear for you more. Permit your priest, I beg you, to engage the enemy. We have an adversary who provokes us: our adversary is the devil, who, as the Apostle said, goes about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour (1 Peter 5:8). Without doubt he has received—he has received it; we are not mistaken, but warned—the power to attempt this, lest perhaps by wounds to my body I might be drawn away from my purpose concerning the faith. You too have read that the devil tested holy Job with many such wounds. [Note: [Col. 1008D] All editions read “he tested him with many others”; some manuscripts, “he tested him with many”; many others, and manuscripts of better authority, “he tested him with many such wounds,” namely wounds of the body. What follows at the end—“he asked for and received the power”—proves this temptation; it is not an explanation of another temptation.] Finally, he asked for and received such power, so that he might test his body, which he covered with sores.

865 5. When it was proposed [Note: [Col. 1008D] There were two kinds of vessels in the churches: consecrated vessels, which served the sacred mysteries, and those which were counted among the ornaments because of their value or workmanship. This is explained more fully in *On Duties*, book III, chapter 28, no. 136.] that we should now surrender the vessels of the Church, I gave this reply: If anything of mine were demanded—an estate, a house, gold, or silver—I would willingly offer what belonged to me. But I could not take anything away from the temple of God, nor surrender what I had received to guard, not to surrender. Moreover, I was also concerned for the emperor’s safety, since it would benefit neither me to surrender nor him to accept. Let him hear the voice of a free priest: if he wishes to be preserved, let him withdraw from injuring Christ.

6. These words are full of humility and, as I think, full of that devotion which a priest owes the emperor. But our struggle is not only against flesh and blood; it is also, and more seriously, against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places (Ephesians 6:12). That tempter, the devil, through his ministers increases the conflict and thinks that it must be tested by wounds to my body. I know, brothers, that these wounds which we receive for Christ are not wounds [Note: [Col. 1009D] All editions read “by which life is lost”; the manuscripts, on the contrary, read “by which life is not lost.” The latter is better, since conjunctions such as “for” or “inasmuch as” must be understood.] by which life is lost, but by which it is extended. Permit the contest, I beg you; you ought to be spectators. Consider that if a city possesses an athlete or an expert in some other noble art, it desires to offer him for competition. Why do you reject in greater matters what you are accustomed to desire in lesser ones? He does not fear weapons or barbarians who does not fear death and is held back by no pleasure of the flesh.

7. Certainly, if the Lord has assigned us to this contest, you have kept watch and maintained guards through so many nights and days in vain. The will of Christ will be fulfilled. For our Lord Jesus is almighty; this is our faith. Therefore what he commands to happen will happen, and it is not fitting for us to oppose the divine judgment. [Note: [Col. 1009D] Several manuscripts read: “nor is it fitting for you to oppose the divine judgment.”]

8. You heard what was read today: the Savior ordered the apostles to bring him the colt of a donkey, and commanded that if anyone resisted, they should say: “The Lord needs its service” (Luke 19:35). What if even now he has ordered this colt of a donkey to be brought to him—that is, this animal accustomed to carrying a heavy burden, as is the human condition, to which he says: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke, because it is easy” (Matthew 11:28)? What if, I say, he has now ordered this colt to be brought to him, sending those apostles who, already stripped of their bodies, bear before our eyes the incomprehensible form of angels? If anyone resists, will they not say: “The Lord needs its service”? What if the desire for this life resists, if flesh and blood resist, if bodily existence resists because perhaps we seem pleasing to some people? But he who loves us here will love us much more if he allows us to become Christ’s sacrifice, because to depart and be with Christ is far better, even though to remain in the flesh is more necessary for your sake (Philippians 1:23). Therefore there is nothing for you to fear, most beloved brothers. I know that whatever I suffer, I shall suffer for Christ. And I have read that I ought not to fear those who can kill the flesh. I have also heard him say: “Whoever loses his soul for my sake will find it” (Matthew 10:39).

9. Therefore, if the Lord wills it, it is certain that no one will resist. But if he is still postponing our contests, why are you afraid? It is not bodily custody but the Lord’s providence that is accustomed to enclose Christ’s servant.

10. You became troubled because you found two open doors, which, it is said, a certain man, blinded in his eyes, opened while returning to his own lodging. From this learn that human guarding provides no assistance. Behold: one man who had lost the gift of sight has undone all your defenses and mocked your guards; but the Lord has not lost the protection of his mercy. Do you not remember that two days ago it was also discovered that on the left side of the basilica there was an accessible entrance which you thought had been closed and fortified? Armed men enclosed the basilica; they examined these and those entrances. They were covered with blindness, so that they could not see what was open. Thus you know that it remained open through many nights. Stop worrying, then, because what Christ commands will happen, and what is expedient will happen.

11. Finally, I shall bring before you examples from the Law. Elisha was being sought by the king of Syria, and an army had been sent to capture him; he was surrounded on every side. His servant began to be afraid, because he was a servant—that is, he did not possess a free mind and free authority. The holy prophet asked that his eyes be opened and said: “Look, and see how many more are for us than against us.” He looked and saw thousands of angels (2 Kings 6:14 and following). You have therefore observed that Christ’s servants are guarded more by those who are unseen than by those who are seen. But even those unseen guardians, if they protect them, do so as advocates summoned by your prayers. For you have read that those very men who were seeking Elisha entered Samaria [Note: [Col. 1009D] Some manuscripts read: “with the very man as their leader.” This is not at all a bad reading.] to find the very man whom they were eager to capture. They not only could not harm him; they were preserved through the intercession of the very man against whom they had come.

12. The apostle Peter also offers you an example of both matters [Note: [Col. 1009D] The Roman edition reads: “gave you an example.”] (Acts 12:4 and following). When Herod sought and seized him, he had him placed in prison [Note: [Col. 1010D] Nannius wonders whether “to receive into prison” means the same as “to store away” or “to confine.” Yet the legal formula is customary in this matter. Ulpian, *Digest*, book 48, title 3, law 1, says: “Whether the person should be received into prison.” Callistratus, in the same title, law 10, writes: “When they had been received into prison,” etc.]. For the servant of God had not withdrawn but had stood firm, ignorant of fear. The Church prayed for him, but the apostle rested in prison, which is evidence that he was not afraid. An angel was sent to awaken him as he slept; through that angel Peter was led out of prison and escaped death for a time [Note: [Col. 1010D] The Roman edition, together with a few manuscripts, reads “escaped death”; the others, along with the remaining manuscripts, insert the words “for a time.”].

13. Later, after defeating Simon, the same Peter was sowing God’s commandments among the people and teaching chastity. He stirred the minds of the pagans; when they sought him, the Christian souls entreated him to withdraw for a little while. Although he desired martyrdom, he was nevertheless moved by consideration for the praying people, for they asked him to remain in order to instruct and strengthen them. What more need be said? At night he began to leave by the walls, and when he saw Christ meeting him at the gate and entering the city, he said: “Lord, where are you going?” Christ replied: [Note: [Col. 1011C] Thus read the old edition and nearly all manuscripts, except that a later hand added “to Rome” in one place, and the Roman edition admitted that word into the text. Apart from Hegesippus, book III, Ambrose here, and Gregory in *Psalm IV on Penance*, scarcely any other ancient writer is found to mention this appearance of Christ to Peter. As for Peter’s arrival at Rome and his victory over Simon Magus, both events are celebrated by such abundant testimony from the ancient Fathers that we would be embarrassed even to linger over a list of their names; yet certain heterodox writers are still not embarrassed to deny a matter which Calvin and Blondel themselves, compelled by the force of the evidence, acknowledged and confessed.] “I am coming to be crucified again.”

Peter understood that the divine reply referred to his own crucifixion. Christ could not be crucified again, since through the passion of death he had put off the flesh he had assumed: “For the death that he died, he died to sin once for all; but the life that he lives, he lives to God” (Romans 6:10). Peter therefore understood that Christ would be crucified again in his servant. Thus he willingly returned. When the Christians questioned him, he gave them his answer, and immediately he was seized; through his own cross he glorified the Lord Jesus. [Col. 1011B]

14. You therefore see that Christ wishes to suffer in his servants. What if he says also to this servant: “I wish him to remain; but you, follow me” (John 21:22), and wishes to taste the fruit of this tree? For if his food was to do the will of the Father (John 4:34), likewise his food is to feast upon our sufferings. To take an example from the Lord himself: when he wished, he suffered, and when he was sought, he was found. But when the hour of his passion had not yet come (John 7:30), he passed through the midst of those seeking him, and although they saw him, they could not seize him. This clearly shows that when the Lord wills, each person is found and seized; but when he postpones it, even if he comes before the eyes of those seeking him, he is not seized. [Note: [Col. 1011D] All editions read: “But when he postpones it, even if he comes into the hands and before the eyes of those seeking him”; all manuscripts agree with us, except that one Colbertine manuscript reads: “even if he is sought, he is not held by the eyes of those seeking him.”]

[Col. 1011C] 15. Therefore, did I not go out every day, whether to visit or to proceed to the martyrs? Did I not pass by the royal palace [Note: [Col. 1011D] Nannius says that *praetexebam* means “did I not pass by the palace road on the way there and back?” This is understood to mean that Ambrose did not seek detours or turn aside from his route while going to the martyrs, so that he would not pass by the palace [Col. 1012C].] as I went and returned? Yet no one seized me, although—as they later revealed—they had intended to drive me out, saying: “Leave the city and go wherever you wish.” I confess that I was expecting something great: either a sword for Christ’s name or a fire. But they offered me luxuries instead of sufferings; Christ’s athlete demands not luxuries but his sufferings. Therefore let no one trouble you because they prepared either a carriage or the harsh words, as they seemed to him, uttered by Auxentius himself, who calls himself a bishop.

16. Many were saying that executioners had been sent ahead and that the punishment of death had been decreed. I do not fear that, and I do not abandon this cause. For where shall I go when everything is full of groaning and tears, since throughout the churches Catholic priests are ordered to be expelled, those who resist are to be struck with the sword, [Note: [Col. 1012C] “Curiales” were those who served as magistrates and in municipal offices. On them see Bulengerus, *On the Roman Empire*, book VII, chapters 3 and 5, and Godefridus.
