As for the enactment of the law in favor of the Council of Ariminum—which Ambrose asserts was dictated and written by Auxentius himself—Rufinus, *History*, book II, chapter 16; Gaudentius, Preface to the *Sermons*; and Sozomen, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, chapter 13, testify that Benevolus, prefect of the record offices, when ordered to dictate and subscribe it, refused with great firmness and was consequently driven into exile by Justina.] and all the curiales are to be proscribed unless they carry out the order? And all this was written by the hand and dictated by the mouth of a bishop who, in order to prove himself most learned, did not omit an ancient example. For we read in the prophet that he saw a flying sickle (Zechariah 5:1). Imitating this, Auxentius sent a flying sword through all the cities. And Satan disguises himself as an angel of light, and in evil imitates his power (2 Corinthians 11:14).

[Col. 1012B] **17.** You, Lord Jesus, redeemed the world in a single moment; Auxentius, in a single moment, will slaughter so many peoples—as far as it lies within him—some by the sword, others by sacrilege? He seeks my basilica with bloodstained mouth and hands. To him the reading appointed for today rightly replied: “But to the sinner God said: Why do you recite my ordinances?” (Psalm 49:16)—that is, it is incompatible with peace and fury, incompatible with Christ and Belial (2 Corinthians 6:15). You also remember what was read today about Naboth (22, q. 8, c. *Convenior*, § *Nabuthe*), a holy man who possessed his own vineyard and was approached with a royal request that he give up his vineyard, so that the king, having cut down the vines, might plant cheap vegetables there. He replied: “Far be it from me to give up the inheritance of my fathers.” The king was grieved that a right belonging to another had been denied him by a just reply, but he was deceived by a woman’s counsel. Naboth defended his vines even with his own blood (1 Kings 21:1 ff.). If he did not surrender his vineyard, shall we surrender Christ’s Church?

[Note: [Col. 1012D] Several manuscripts read “I sent the basilica”; others, and all printed editions, “my basilica,” that is, one of my basilicas; for there were quite a few in Milan.]

**18.** What, then, was my contumacious reply? I said in the assembly: “Far be it from me to surrender Christ’s inheritance.” If he did not surrender the inheritance of his fathers, shall I surrender Christ’s inheritance? But I added this also: “Far be it from me to surrender the inheritance of my fathers”—that is, the inheritance of Dionysius, who died in exile on account of the faith; the inheritance of Eustorgius the confessor; the inheritance of Myrocles; and the inheritance of all the faithful bishops of former times.

[Note: [Col. 1012D] The names of these bishops are written variously in the manuscripts. In some, *Extorgi* or *Euxtorgi* appears instead of *Eustorgii*, just as *Metrocli* and *Merocli* appear instead of *Myroclis*. Myrocles was, if Ughellus is to be believed, the eighth bishop of Milan; but if we follow the most ancient catalogue published in the *Museo Italico*, p. 110, he was the seventh after Saint Barnabas, as the catalogue is said to have been supplemented by a more recent hand. Eustorgius is numbered tenth both by Ughellus and by Mabillon. Dionysius, however, who is placed only thirteenth in the *Italia Sacra*, follows Eustorgius in the catalogue published in the cited *Museo*. Rufinus, *History* I.19, Socrates II.36, and others report that, because he refused to condemn Athanasius at the Council of Milan, this Dionysius was driven into exile by Constantius and died there.]

I replied with what belongs to a priest: “Let the emperor do what belongs to the emperor. Let him take my life before he takes my faith.”

**19.** But to whom shall I surrender it? The Gospel reading appointed for today should teach us what is being sought and from whom it is being sought. You heard, indeed, that when Christ was seated upon the foal of a donkey, the children cried out, and the Jews were displeased (Luke 19:35). Finally, they appealed to the Lord Jesus, asking him to make them keep silent. He replied: “If these are silent, the stones will cry out” (ibid., 40). Then he entered the temple and drove out the money-changers, the sellers of doves, and the chairs from the temple of God.

This reading was not recited because of any arrangement of ours, but by chance; yet it is well suited to the present circumstances. The praises of Christ are always blows against the faithless. And now, when Christ is praised, the heretics say that sedition is being stirred up; the heretics say that death was being prepared for these people—and truly they have death in Christ’s praises. For how can they endure the praises of one whose weakness they proclaim? Thus today also, when Christ is praised, the madness of the Arians is beaten.

**20.** The Gerasenes could not endure Christ’s presence (Luke 8:37); these men are worse than the Gerasenes, for they cannot endure even the praise of Christ. They see Christ’s children singing his glory, because it is written: “From the mouth of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise” (Psalm 8:3). They mock this tender age, filled with faith, when they say: “Look at what they are shouting!” But Christ replied to them: “If these are silent, the stones will cry out” (Luke 19:35)—that is, the stronger will cry out; the young will cry out; the more mature will cry out; the old will cry out.

[Note: [Col. 1013D] Quite a few manuscripts read: “and these old men, praises to him,” and so forth.]

These stones have already been made solid in relation to that Stone of whom it is written: “The stone which the builders rejected has become the cornerstone” (Psalm 117:22).

**21.** Invited, then, by these praises, Christ enters his temple, takes up a whip, and drives the money-changers from the temple (John 2:15). For he does not tolerate money’s servants in his temple; he does not tolerate in his temple those who sell chairs. What are the chairs except honors? What are the doves except simple minds, or souls following a white and pure faith? Shall I therefore bring in one whom Christ excludes? The one who sells dignities and honors is ordered to leave; the one who wishes to sell the simple minds of the faithful is ordered to leave.

[Col. 1013D] **22.** Therefore Auxentius is expelled; Mercurinus is excluded. It is one monster with two names. For, so that he might not be recognized, he changed his name; because an Arian bishop named Auxentius had formerly been here, he called himself Auxentius in order to deceive the people whom that former man had held.

[Note: [Col. 1014D] All printed editions read “he called himself Mercurinus”; all manuscripts read “Auxentius.” The correction is certainly required by the sense. Ambrose is indicating here that the man who had become hateful under the name Mercurinus adopted the name Auxentius so that, through the similarity of names, he might more easily insinuate himself into the minds of the Milanese Arians, whose last pseudo-bishop had been Auxentius.]

He therefore changed his name, but he did not change his perfidy: he stripped off the wolf, but put on the wolf. It does him no good to have changed his name; what he is can be recognized. In one place he was called one thing, here he is called another; he has names according to the regions. He now has two names; and if he goes from here elsewhere, he will have a third. How can he bear to retain a name that serves as evidence of so great a crime? He committed lesser offenses in Scythia, and was so ashamed that he changed his name; here he has dared more atrocious deeds, and will he wish, wherever he goes, to be exposed by his own name? Will he write the blood of so many peoples with his own hand and still be able to stand firm in spirit?

**23.** The Lord Jesus expelled a few people from his temple; Auxentius left no one. Jesus drives them from his temple with a whip; Auxentius with a sword. Jesus with a whip; Mercurinus with an axe. The merciful Lord thrusts sacrilegious men out with a whip; the wicked man persecutes the devout with steel.

You rightly said today of him: “Let him take his laws away with him.” He will take them, even if he does not wish to; he will take his conscience, even if he does not take the document; he will take his soul inscribed with blood, even if he does not take the letter inscribed with ink. “Your guilt, Judah, is written with an iron stylus and an adamantine claw; it is written upon your breast” (Jeremiah 17:1)—that is, it is written there from which it came forth.

**24.** Does this man, full of blood and gore, even dare to mention discussing the matter?

[Note: [Col. 1014D] Only the Roman edition reads “of revisiting the matter.” Perhaps this should be understood as “of discussing it again,” since they had already discussed it the previous year. But there is no reason to alter the text on that account.]

He thinks that those whom he could not deceive by speech must be struck down with the sword. He dictates bloody laws with his mouth, writes them with his hand, and thinks that a law can impose faith upon human beings. He did not hear what was said today: “A person is not justified by works of the Law” (Galatians 2:16), or: “Through the Law I died to the Law, so that I might live for God” (ibid., 19)—that is, through the spiritual law he died to the bodily interpretation of the Law. Let us also die, through the law of our Lord Jesus Christ, to this law that establishes decrees of perfidy.

It was not the Law that gathered the Church, but the faith of Christ. “The Law is not based on faith; rather, ‘the righteous person lives by faith’” (Galatians 3:11). Faith, then, not the Law, makes a person righteous, because righteousness does not come through the Law but through the faith of Christ. Whoever rejects faith and prescribes the rights of the Law testifies against himself that he is unjust, because “the righteous person lives by faith.”

**25.** Should anyone follow this law by which the Council of Ariminum is confirmed, at which Christ was called a creature? But they say: “God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the Law” (Galatians 4:4). Therefore, they read “made”—that is, created. Do they not consider the very statement they have advanced? Christ is said to have been made, but from a woman: that is, he was made according to the Virgin’s childbirth, while according to his divine generation he was born from the Father.

They also read today that Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law, having become a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). Was Christ a curse according to his divinity? But the Apostle teaches you why he is called a curse, saying that it is written: “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree” (ibid.)—that is, he took our flesh in his flesh, our weaknesses and our curses in his body, in order to crucify them. He was not accursed in himself, but was accursed in you. Elsewhere, finally, you have: “He who knew no sin was made sin for us,” because he took upon himself our sins in order to abolish them through the sacrament of his passion (2 Corinthians 5:21).

**26.** I would discuss these matters more fully before him in your presence, brothers; but, knowing that you are not ignorant of the faith, he shrank from your examination and chose for himself four or five gentile men, approximately, as judges—if indeed he chose any.

[Note: [Col. 1015D] *Cognitor* is often the judge himself, the one who hears a case; often the advocate in a lawsuit, to whom a case is entrusted by a litigant present before the judge; and often also one who claims to recognize others disputing about their status and declares their birth and homeland. Cicero, *Against Verres*: “A Roman citizen who had appointed honorable men as cognitors was taken away and crucified.” Thus Nannius.]

I wish they were present in the assembly of all—not to judge Christ, but to hear Christ’s majesty. Yet they have already passed judgment concerning Auxentius, to whom they did not believe when he spoke daily. What condemnation of him could be greater than that he was defeated before his own judges without an opponent? Therefore we already hold their judgment against Auxentius as well.

[Col. 1015C] **27.** And because he chose gentiles, he deserves condemnation by right, since he abandoned the Apostle’s instructions, when the Apostle says: “Does any one of you, having a case against another, dare to be judged before the unjust and not before the saints? Or do you not know that the saints will judge the world?” (1 Corinthians 6:1–2). And below he says: “Is there no wise person among you who can judge between brothers? Instead, brother goes to court against brother—and this before unbelievers” (ibid., 5–6). You see that what he proposed is contrary to the Apostle’s authority. Choose whether we ought to follow Auxentius or Paul as our teacher.

**28.** But what need is there for me to speak of the Apostle, when the Lord himself cries out through the prophet: “Hear me, my people, you who know judgment, whose heart contains my law” (Isaiah 51:7)? God says: “Hear me, my people, you who know judgment.” Auxentius says: “You do not know judgment.” You see that he now despises God in you, since he rejects the sentence of the heavenly oracle.

“Hear me,” he says, “my people,” says the Lord. He does not say: “Hear, gentiles.” He does not say: “Hear, Jews.” For the people who had been God’s people had already become the people of error; and the people who had been the people of error began to be God’s people because they believed in Christ.

This, then, is the people who judge—the people whose heart contains the divine law, not the human law: a law written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God; engraved not on paper but sealed upon the heart; the law of grace, not of blood (2 Corinthians 3:3). Who, then, does you an injury: the one who refuses your hearing, or the one who chooses it?

**29.** Hemmed in on every side, he fled to the cunning of his fathers. He wishes to stir up resentment against the emperor, saying that a young catechumen, ignorant of sacred learning, ought to judge, and that judgment should take place in the imperial council. As though last year, when I was summoned to the palace, and the matter was being discussed before the leading men in the presence of the imperial council, while the emperor wished to seize the basilica, I had been broken by consideration of the royal court, failed to maintain a priest’s constancy, or departed with my rights diminished!

Do they not remember that, when the people learned that I had gone to the palace, they rushed in such a way that those present could not withstand their force?

[Note: [Col. 1016D] A few manuscripts read: “could not withstand them.”]

When the military commander went out with lightly equipped troops to disperse the crowd, did they not all offer themselves to death for the faith of Christ? Was I not then asked to soothe the people with a long speech?

[Note: [Col. 1016D] The Roman edition alone reads “with gentle speech.”]

Was I not asked to pledge my faith that no one would invade the basilica of the Church? And although my service was requested as a favor, nevertheless, because the people had gone to the palace, resentment was stirred up against me. They therefore want me to return to that resentment.

**30.** I recalled the people, and yet I did not escape resentment. I judge that this resentment should indeed be moderated, but not feared. For what should we fear on Christ’s behalf? Unless perhaps this ought to trouble me, that they say: “Then the emperor ought not to receive a single basilica in which he may proceed; Ambrose wants to have more power than the emperor, so that he denies the emperor the ability to proceed.”

When they say this, they eagerly seize upon our words, like the Jews who tested Christ with crafty speech, saying: “Teacher, is it lawful to pay tribute to Caesar or not?” (Matthew 22:17). Is resentment against the servants of God always stirred up by the mention of Caesar? Does impiety summon the imperial name as a pretext for its slander? And can these men say that they do not share the sacrilege of those whose teaching they imitate?

**31.** Yet see how much worse the Arians are than the Jews. The Jews asked whether they thought the right of tribute should be paid to Caesar; these men wish to give the emperor the right over the Church.

[Note: [Col. 1016D] A few manuscripts read “do not wish to give,” which produces the opposite sense.]

But just as the faithless follow their author, so let us answer according to what the Lord and our author taught us. For Jesus, considering the Jews’ deceit (ibid., 18 ff.), said to them: “Why are you testing me? Show me a denarius.” When they had given him one, he said: “Whose image and inscription does it bear?” They replied: “Caesar’s.” And Jesus said to them: “Give back to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s.”

Therefore I too say to those who reproach me: “Show me a denarius.” Jesus saw Caesar’s denarius and said: “Give back to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s.” Can they offer Caesar’s denarius for the seizure of the Church’s basilicas?

**32.** But in the Church I know one image: the image of the invisible God, concerning which God said: “Let us make the human being according to our image and likeness” (Genesis 1:26); that image of which it is written: “Christ is the radiance of his glory and the image of his substance” (Hebrews 1:3).

In this image I behold the Father, as the Lord Jesus himself said: “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John 14:9). For this image is not separated from the Father; it taught me the unity of the Trinity when it said: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30); and below: “Everything that the Father has is mine” (John 16:15). And concerning the Holy Spirit, he says that the Spirit is Christ’s and receives from Christ, as it is written: “He will take what is mine and declare it to you” (ibid., 14).

**33.** What, then, have we replied that is not humble? If he demands tribute, we do not refuse it.

[Note: [Col. 1017D] It is not surprising that Ambrose affirms that the Church’s lands were subject to taxation and paid tribute to the emperors. For there are laws in the *Theodosian Code* promulgated by Constantine and his successors—for example, law 1, *On the Grain Supply and Taxes*, and others under the title *On Bishops and Clerics*—by which the Church’s possessions are subjected to taxes. As for the clergy, it is certain that their property was liable to tribute, and often their persons also to public obligations, as Ambrose says in *Against Symmachus*.]

The Church’s fields pay tribute. If the emperor desires the fields, he has the power to claim them; none of us intervenes. The people’s contribution may flow to the poor. Let them not make the fields a cause for resentment; let them take them, if the emperor wishes. I do not give them as a gift, but I do not refuse them.

They seek gold; I can say: “I do not seek silver and gold.” But they create resentment because gold is distributed. Nor do I shrink from this resentment. I have treasury-assessors: my treasury-assessors are Christ’s poor. This is the treasure I know how to gather.

[Note: [Col. 1017D] Nannius says that one was called *aerarius* who, being a commoner, was entered by the censors on the registers of Caere and consequently struck from the roll of his century, so that he could no longer earn pay. When this was done by the emperor, they were called “ruined by the treasury.” Livy, third decade, book 9, included the name of a colleague among those whom he left as *aerarii*. But soldiers who received pay were also sometimes called *aerarii*, in the opposite sense; they were called μισθοφόροι, “mercenaries.” Cicero, *To Atticus*: “Soldiers not so much *aerarii* as, as they are called, *aerati*.” This is the sense intended here, for he called the poor who lived from the Church’s stipend “Christ’s *aerarii*.”]

Would that they always charge me with this crime: that gold is distributed to the poor! If they object that I seek defense from them, I do not deny it; I even seek it eagerly. I have a defense, but it is found in the prayers of the poor. Those blind and lame, the weak and the elderly, are stronger than vigorous warriors. In the end, the gifts of the poor bind God, because it is written: “Whoever is generous to the poor lends to God” (Proverbs 19:17). The protection of warriors often does not earn divine favor.

**34.** They say also that I have deceived the people through the verses of my hymns. Certainly, I do not deny this either. This is a great song, more powerful than anything. For what is more powerful than the confession of the Trinity, which is celebrated daily by the mouth of the entire people? All eagerly strive to confess the faith; they know how to proclaim the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit in verse. Thus everyone has become a teacher who could scarcely have been a disciple.

**35.** What, then, can be more obedient than to follow the example of Christ, who, appearing in human form, humbled himself and became obedient unto death (Philippians 2:7–8)? In the end, he freed everyone through obedience: “For just as through the disobedience of one person the many were made sinners, so through the obedience of one the many will be made righteous” (Romans 5:19).

If he was obedient, then let them accept the teaching of obedience to which we cling, saying to those who stir up resentment against us on account of the emperor: “We pay back to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s” (Matthew 22:21). Caesar’s tribute is not denied (23, question 8, c. *Conventior*, § *Tributum*); the Church of God certainly must not be handed over to Caesar, because the temple of God cannot be Caesar’s property.

**36.** No one can deny that this was said with honor toward the emperor. For what is more honorable than to say that the emperor is a son of the Church? When this is said, it is said without sin and with grace.

[Note: [Col. 1018D] All printed editions read: “For the emperor is a good man”; all manuscripts omit “good,” although the following sentence consistently contains the word.]

The emperor, then, is within the Church, not above the Church. For a good emperor seeks the Church’s assistance; he does not reject it. Just as we say these things humbly, so we explain them firmly.

But some threaten fires, the sword, and deportation.

[Note: [Col. 1018D] Deportation is the harshest form of exile, in which someone is confined on a remote island.]

We, the servants of Christ, have learned not to fear. Terror is never burdensome to those who do not fear. Finally, it is written: “The arrows of infants have become their wounds” (Psalm 63:8).

[Col. 1018C] **37.** It therefore seems that sufficient answer has been given to the points proposed. Now I ask them what the Savior asked: “Was the baptism of John from heaven or from human beings?” (Luke 20:4). And the Jews could not answer him.

If the Jews did not nullify John’s baptism, does Auxentius nullify Christ’s baptism? This baptism is not from human beings but from heaven; it was brought to us by the Angel of great counsel (Isaiah 9:6), so that we might be justified before God.

Why, then, does Auxentius think that faithful peoples baptized in the name of the Trinity must be rebaptized, when the Apostle says: “One faith, one baptism” (Ephesians 4:5)? And why does he claim to be an adversary of human beings rather than of Christ, when he despises God’s counsel and condemns the baptism that Christ gave us for the redemption of our sins (Luke 7:30)?

[Note: [Col. 1019C] Written in the year 386.]

# LETTER XXII

[Col. 1019A]

Having announced the discovery of the bodies of the martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, he reports that he said to the people: that the martyrs are heavens, just as the apostles are; that the day had also been their confession; that they had first been humbled by the Lord and then raised from the earth; and that this was their resurrection, since they had performed so many miracles. He gave thanks to God for so great a protection and enlarged upon it through the deeds of Elisha. Finally, the description of the relics and the plan for their translation were received with popular applause. He adds the sermon of the following day, in which, after recalling the Catholics’ joy, he attacked the envy of the Arians, showing that, while they denied an evident miracle, they were like the Jews and believed otherwise than the martyrs had believed; and that, since they did not acknowledge the Trinity confessed even by demons, they were worse than the demons themselves.

[Note: [Col. 1019C] Thus the old edition and the manuscripts read, except that in some manuscripts *atque oculis* (“and with the eyes”) appears as *atque osculis* (“and with kisses”), the word *Ambrosius* is added after *frater*, and in one manuscript *praetermittere* occurs instead of *praeterire*. The Roman edition, however, recast the whole passage in this form: “Ambrose the bishop to his sister Marcellina: Since I am accustomed to conceal from your holiness nothing of what happens here in your absence, know also, dearest sister,” and so forth.]

To his sister, to be preferred to life and to his very eyes: her brother.

**1.** Since I am accustomed to omit nothing from what happens here in your absence, know also that holy martyrs have been found by us. For when I had dedicated the basilica, many began, as if with one voice, to appeal, saying: “Dedicate it as you dedicated the Roman basilica.”

[Note: [Col. 1019C] The Roman edition alone reads: “I wished to dedicate . . . as in the Roman basilica you will dedicate this basilica.” In this second part the old editions and manuscripts vary. Where the former, together with a few manuscripts, read: “Thus you will dedicate in the Roman basilica,” other manuscripts read partly: “Thus into the Roman basilica”; partly: “Do you thus dedicate the Roman basilica?”; and others: “Thus also the Roman,” or “As you dedicated the Roman basilica.” The last reading seems the strongest. The sense is that, after Ambrose had dedicated the church but had not yet placed relics in it, the people, distressed by this, insist that he not omit this ceremony either, since he had not omitted it at the consecration of the Roman basilica.

Samuel Petit, *Observations* III.8, says that some infer two things from this passage: first, that there was a Roman district in Milan, from which the Roman basilica received its name; second, that the basilica whose dedication is discussed here was the same as the Roman basilica. The same writer attempts to overturn both conclusions. The second is in itself untenable, for from the sequence it is clear that the basilica into which the bones of Saints Gervasius and Protasius were transferred was the Ambrosian basilica, since it is clear from Paulinus that the body of blessed Nazarius had been deposited in the Roman basilica.

As for his denial that the name “Roman” came from the district, on the ground that it is not said to have been in the Roman district but is itself called Roman, this argument is too weak to require refutation. Nor are the reasons he offers for this name much stronger: he conjectures that the basilica derived its name either from the Roman rite perhaps observed there or from Peter, to whom it was dedicated, the first father of the Roman faith and see. We reject this conjecture. Since it is established that this church was built by the gate called Roman, it is more plausible that it received its name from its proximity. See Herman, *Life of Ambrose* IV.17; Ughellus, *Italia Sacra*; and others.]

I replied: “I will, if I find the martyrs’ relics.” Immediately there arose, as it were, a certain ardor of presage.

[Note: [Col. 1020C] Augustine, *Confessions* IX.7, says that these relics were revealed to Ambrose through a vision; and in *City of God* XXII.8, that they were made known through a vision. Hence it may be inferred not only that the holy bishop was alerted to them by that inward inspiration, but also by an apparition. It is clear, however, that not everything that happened is recounted here, from what follows: “What more need be said?”]

**2.** What more need be said? The Lord granted his grace. Although the clergy were afraid, I ordered the ground to be excavated at the place before the screens of Saints Felix and Nabor.

I found signs corresponding to the matter. When those upon whom we were to lay hands had also been brought near, the holy martyrs began to emerge in such a way that, while we were still silent, a coffin was seized and laid face down toward the place of the holy tomb.

[Col. 1019C] We found two men of astonishing stature, as the ancient age was accustomed to produce. All the bones were intact, and there was a great deal of blood. A vast crowd gathered throughout those two days.

What more need be said? We wrapped the remains intact and arranged them in order; as evening was already approaching, we transferred them to the basilica of Fausta. There were vigils there throughout the night, and the laying on of hands.

[Note: [Col. 1020C] All printed editions read: “We buried them intact and transferred them in order. As evening was already approaching, we came to the basilica of Fausta.” Since this reading was defective, the Roman edition supplied *venimus* (“we came”) as a supporting verb. All manuscripts, however, agree with our reading, except that the Belvedere manuscript has “of the vigil in order”; the others more appropriately reject *vigiliae*, since *in order* there has the same meaning as *in due sequence*.]

On the following day we transferred them to the basilica called Ambrosian.

[Note: [Col. 1020D] That basilica was called Ambrosian after its founder and is still called the greater basilica of Saint Ambrose. The basilica Ambrose calls Fausta now bears the title of Saints Vitalis and Agricola. The basilica from which the sacred relics of Gervasius and Protasius were dug up, which Paulinus says was called that of Saints Nabor and Felix, is now called Saint Francis. On these matters see Ughellus, in his discussion of the relics preserved at Milan, and Mabillon, *Italian Journey*, p. 15.]

As we were transferring them, a blind man was healed. My sermon to the people was as follows:

**3.** When I considered the extraordinarily large and unprecedented attendance of your assembly, and the gifts of divine grace that shone forth in the holy martyrs, I confess that I judged myself unequal to this task. It seemed impossible that I could express in speech what we can scarcely hold in our minds or comprehend with our eyes.

But when the sequence of the holy Scriptures began to be read, the Holy Spirit, who spoke through the prophets, granted that we might bring forth something worthy of so great an assembly, of your expectation, and of the merits of the holy martyrs.

**4.** “The heavens,” he says, “declare the glory of God” (Psalm 18:2). When this psalm is read, it occurs to us that not so much the material elements as the heavenly merits seem to offer God a proclamation worthy of him. Yet today’s chance reading has made clear which heavens declare the glory of God.

Look to my right; look to my left at the most sacred relics.

[Note: [Col. 1020D] Thus all the manuscripts read, with a few exceptions in which *videtis* (“you see”) appears instead of *videte* (“look”); all printed editions, however, read: “You see . . . gazing,” and so forth.]

Behold men of heavenly conduct; gaze upon trophies of exalted spirit. These are the heavens that declare the glory of God; these are the works of his hands that the firmament announces. For it was not worldly allure but the grace of divine action that raised them to the firmament of the most sacred passion. Long beforehand, by examples of conduct and virtue, it announced in them the martyrdom that they would undergo, since they remained steadfast against the slipperiness of this world.

**5.** Paul was a heaven, for he said: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20). James and John were heavens; indeed, they are called “sons of thunder” (Mark 3:17). Therefore, like heaven, John saw the Word with God (John 1:1).

The Lord Jesus himself was the heaven of perpetual light when he declared God’s glory—but the glory that no one had seen before. Therefore he said: “No one has ever seen God except the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father; he has declared him” (John 1:18).

If you seek the works of God’s hands, hear Job say: “The divine Spirit who made me” (Job 33:4). And so, strengthened against the devil’s temptations, he preserved the mark of untroubled steadfastness. But let us come to what follows.

**6.** “Day,” he says, “pours forth the word to day” (Psalm 18:3). Behold true days, which no darkness of night interrupts. Behold true days, full of light and eternal radiance, which poured forth the word of God—not in a superficial speech, but from the depths of their hearts—steadfast in confession and persevering in martyrdom.

**7.** Another psalm that was read says: “Who is like the Lord our God, who dwells on high and looks upon the lowly, in heaven and on earth?” (Psalm 112:5). God truly looked upon the lowly when he revealed the relics of the holy martyrs of his Church, hidden beneath an obscure mound—their souls in heaven, their bodies on earth: “raising the needy from the earth and lifting the poor from the dung heap” (ibid., 7). You see how he has placed them with the princes of his people.

Who else should we regard as the princes of the people except the holy martyrs? Their names, long unknown, Protasius and Gervasius, are now placed among them.

[Note: [Col. 1021D] The Thuan manuscript alone reads: “whose names, long before unknown”; with the other manuscripts it has *praeferuntur* (“are placed before”), where all printed editions read *proferuntur* (“are brought forth”).]

They have made the Milanese Church, once barren of martyrs, rejoice in her own passion’s titles and examples, so that she is now the mother of many children.

**8.** Nor is this contrary to the true faith: “Day pours forth the word to day” (Psalm 18:2)—soul to soul, life to life, resurrection to resurrection. “And night declares knowledge to night”—that is, flesh to flesh, since their passion has declared the true knowledge of faith to all.

Good nights, luminous nights, which have stars. For “as star differs from star in glory, so also is the resurrection of the dead” (1 Corinthians 15:41).

**9.** Not without reason, then, do many call this the resurrection of the martyrs. I shall see whether the martyrs have risen for themselves or for us; certainly, they have risen for us.

[Note: [Col. 1021D] All printed editions and a few manuscripts read *Videro* (“I shall see”); some manuscripts read *video* (“I see”) and *videbo* (“I shall see”). Some, however, are uncertain whether the words refer to themselves or to us: “certainly, the martyrs”; others have: “I shall see whether for themselves or for us—certainly, martyrs,” and so forth; still others read as in our text.]

You yourselves have recognized—or rather, you have seen—that many have been cleansed from demons; that many, when they touched the martyrs’ garments with their hands, were freed from the infirmities from which they suffered; that the miracles of former times have been restored. You see many healed, as though by the shadow of the martyrs’ bodies, by that grace which, at the Lord Jesus’ coming, had poured itself upon the earth with greater force.

[Note: [Col. 1021D] Here *oraria* means handkerchiefs or cloths; otherwise *oraria* also refers to articles of priestly clothing.]

How many handkerchiefs are being thrown about! How many garments are being requested and laid upon the most sacred relics, so that they may be made medicinal by the very touch! Everyone rejoices to touch the outermost hem; and whoever touches it will be saved.

10. I give you thanks, Lord Jesus, that at this time you have raised up for us such spirits of the holy martyrs, [Note: [Col. 1021D] This refers to the persecution of the empress Justina, as we have already explained in the Introduction. It should also be noted in passing that the sentence below—“Such defenders I seek”—was made more famous in the memory of our fathers when Saint Charles ordered it inscribed on a banner marked with images of the saints Gervasius and Protasius, which was carried in a public procession to bring an end to the plague, as is recorded in his Life.] when your Church is seeking greater protection. Let all recognize what sort of champions I require: men able to defend, not accustomed to attack. These are the men I have acquired for you, holy people, men who benefit all and harm no one. Such defenders I seek, such soldiers I have, [Note: [Col. 1022D] Latinius conjectures that *milites habeo* should be read as *milites aveo*, “I desire soldiers.” The verb *habeo* is absent from some manuscripts, but is found in many more and in all printed editions. The words that follow—“that is, not soldiers of the world … I fear envy”—had been omitted from the editions but are restored from all the manuscripts. Again, where all editions and a few manuscripts read “those who envy me,” many manuscripts insert the pronoun *eos*, “them,” which is not inappropriate.] that is, not soldiers of the world, but soldiers of Christ. I fear no envy on account of such men, whose protection is safer the greater it is. Indeed, I desire their protection even for those very people who envy me because I have them. Let them come, then, and see my guards; I do not deny that I am surrounded by such weapons:

> These trust in chariots, and those in horses;  
> but we shall glory in the name of the Lord our God.  
> (Psalm XIX, 8)

11. The succession of the divine Scriptures relates that, when Elisha was surrounded by the army of the Syrians, he said to his frightened servant that he should not be afraid: “For,” he said, “there are more with us than against us” (IV Kings VI, 16). And, to demonstrate this, he asked that the eyes of Gehazi be opened; when they were opened, he saw that innumerable armies of angels were present with the prophet. Although we cannot see them, nevertheless we perceive them. These eyes were closed so long as the bodies of the saints lay hidden beneath the earth. The Lord opened our eyes; we saw the aids by which we have often been defended. We did not see these things, but nevertheless we possessed them. Thus, as we trembled, the Lord seemed to say: “See how many martyrs I have given you.” With our eyes opened, therefore, we contemplate the glory of the Lord, which is manifested in the martyrs’ past suffering and present activity. Brothers, we have escaped no small burden of shame: we had patrons and did not know it. We have found this one thing by which we may seem to surpass our forebears. We have attained knowledge of the holy martyrs, which they had lost.

12. Noble relics are brought forth from an ignoble tomb; trophies are displayed to heaven. [Note: [Col. 1023C] Gregory of Tours, *Book I of the Miracles*, chapter 47, relates this event. He denies that it was recorded in the history of Saints Gervasius and Protasius, but says that he learned it from someone’s account: when a tablet fell from the chamber during the sacred rites and struck the martyrs’ heads, blood flowed from them until all the linens and ecclesiastical veils had been abundantly stained with it.] The tomb is wet with blood; signs of triumphal bloodshed appear; the inviolate relics are found in their proper place and order, and the head, torn from the shoulders. Now the elderly recall having once heard the names of these martyrs and having read their inscription. The city had lost its own martyrs, though it had seized those belonging to another. [Col. 1023B] Although this is God’s gift, I cannot deny the grace that the Lord Jesus has bestowed in the days of my priesthood; and because I am not worthy to be a martyr myself, I have acquired these martyrs for you.

13. Let the triumphant victims take their place [Note: [Col. 1023D] We do not see what could be said more explicitly here to prove the true and bodily presence of Christ upon the sacred altar. Let the sectarians weigh every one of his words; if there is any sincerity and good faith in them, they will acknowledge the fact.] where Christ is the victim. He is upon the altar, the one who suffered for all. They are beneath the altar, those who were redeemed by his suffering. I had destined this place for myself, for it is fitting that the priest should rest where he was accustomed to offer; but I yield the place on the right to the sacred victims. This place was owed to the martyrs. Let us therefore enclose the most holy relics and bring them into worthy buildings [Note: [Col. 1023D] All editions and a few manuscripts read *dignis aedibus*, “worthy buildings”; most manuscripts, however, read *dignis sedibus*, “worthy places.”], and let us celebrate the whole day with faithful devotion.

14. The people cried out that the deposition of the martyrs should be postponed until the Lord’s Day [Col. 1023C]; but permission was finally obtained for it to take place on the following day. On the following day I again addressed the people in this manner.

15. [Note: [Col. 1023D] This final section has been severed from the body of this letter and placed among the sermons in all editions, but the reader may judge how inappropriately.] Yesterday I discussed the verse, “Day pours forth speech to day” (Psalm XVIII, 3), as far as my understanding allowed. Today, however, divine Scripture seems to me to have prophesied not only of the earlier time but also of the present. For when I see the continuous celebration of your holiness extending through days and nights, those days have declared themselves to be the oracles of the prophetic song—yesterday and today—of which it is most fittingly said: “Day pours forth speech to day”; and those nights, about which it is most appropriately said: “Night reveals knowledge to night.” For what else have you poured forth during these two days except the word of God from the depths of your devotion, and what else have you demonstrated except that you possess the knowledge of faith?

16. Yet there are people who habitually envy your celebration. And because they cannot bear your celebration with an envious spirit, they hate the cause of the celebration. They go so far in their madness as to deny the merits of the martyrs, whose works even the demons confess. But this is not surprising, since the treachery of unbelievers is so great that the devil’s confession is often more tolerable. For the devil said: “Jesus, Son of the living God, why have you come before the time to torment us?” (Matthew VIII, 29). Yet although the Jews heard these words, they themselves denied that he was the Son of God. And now you have heard the demons crying out and confessing to the martyrs that they cannot endure their punishments, saying: “Why have you come to torment us so severely?” [Note: [Col. 1023D] Thus the manuscripts; the editions insert “before the time” between “to torment” and “us.”] And the Arians say: “These are not martyrs; they can neither torment the devil nor free anyone,” although the demons’ torments are proved by their own voices, and the martyrs’ benefits are demonstrated by the cures of those who are healed and by the signs of those who have been set free. [Note: [Col. 1023D] Some manuscripts read *voce prodantur*, “are revealed by their voice”; others have *probantur*, “are proved”; still others, together with the editions, have *probentur*, “may be proved.” Again, where all editions and some manuscripts read “by remedies for the blind,” others partly read “by remedies of the saints” and partly “by remedies of those who have been healed”; the latter reading is preferable.]

17. They deny that the blind man was given sight, but he does not deny that he was healed. He says: “I see, though I did not see before.” He says: “I have ceased to be blind,” and he proves it by the fact. These men deny the benefit, though they cannot deny the deed. [Note: [Col. 1024C] Nothing is more certain or better attested than this miracle—not only because of the very great authority of Ambrose and the fact that it was known to all the people of Milan whom this same bishop was addressing, but also because of the eyewitness testimony—if the expression may be forgiven—of Augustine, which can be read in *The City of God*, Book XXII, chapter 8, and even more explicitly in the sermon on the feast of the martyrs Gervasius and Protasius. The same miracle, together with others mentioned in this letter, is related by Paulinus in the Life of Ambrose, who likewise could have been an eyewitness. It is therefore astonishing that the Arians were so obstinate that they regarded such evident miracles as inventions, or even—as Paulinus reports—as fraudulent acts performed for money. From Augustine and Paulinus alike, however, we learn that the heretics’ obstinacy was at least weakened, if not broken, by the manifestation of the martyrs, and that the persecution subsided. For this reason we are even more surprised that among the heterodox of our own time—who scarcely display greater veneration toward any other Father than toward our Ambrose—someone should nevertheless have been found to revive the ancient Arian slander, though under certain veils of wording.] There is a well-known man named Severus, a butcher by trade, who, when he was able, was employed in public service. He had laid aside his occupation after he had been afflicted with a disability. He summons as witnesses the people whose support had previously sustained him; he calls forward as judges of his recovery those whom he had as witnesses and arbiters of his blindness. He cries out that, as soon as he touched the fringe of the martyrs’ garment with which the sacred relics are clothed, his sight was restored.

18. Is this not like what we read in the Gospel? For we praise the power of one author; and it makes no difference whether the act is a work or a gift, since he both gives in the work and works in the gift. What he grants others to do, his name accomplishes in the work of others.

We read in the Gospel that, when the Jews saw the remedy of healing in that blind man, they sought testimony from his parents. They asked: “How does your son see?” When he said: “Though I was blind, now I see” (John V, 35). This man also says: “I was blind, and now I see. Ask others, if you do not believe me; ask strangers, so that you will not think that my parents are supporting me.” Their obstinacy is more detestable than that of the Jews. When the Jews doubted, they at least questioned the parents; these men question secretly and deny openly. They are now unbelievers not merely toward the work, but toward its author.

19 and 20. But I ask what it is that they do not believe: whether some people can be visited by the martyrs? This is not to believe in Christ, for he himself said: “And you will do greater things than these” (John XIV, 12). Or do they disbelieve that these martyrs—whose merits have long flourished—can do so, when their bodies have long since been discovered?

Here I ask whether they envy me or the holy martyrs. If they envy me, do any miracles occur through me? Do they occur by my work or in my name? Why, then, do they envy me for what is not mine? If they envy the martyrs—for if they do not envy me, it remains that they appear to envy the martyrs—they show that the martyrs possessed a faith different from the one they themselves hold. For they would not otherwise envy the martyrs’ works unless they judged that the martyrs possessed the faith that these men do not possess. This is the faith confirmed by the tradition of our forefathers, which even the demons cannot deny, but which the Arians deny.

21. Today we heard those upon whom hands were being laid say that no one can be saved unless he believes in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; that the person who denies the Holy Spirit and does not believe in the omnipotent power of the Trinity is dead and doomed. [Note: [Col. 1025D] All editions read: “that no one can be saved who denies the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, who denies the Trinity,” etc. The manuscripts, without exception, restore the passage as it appears in the text.] The devil confesses this, but the Arians do not wish to admit it. The devil says: “Let him who denies the divinity of the Holy Spirit be tormented as he himself was tormented by the martyrs.”

22. I do not accept testimony from the devil, but confession. [Col. 1025D] The devil spoke unwillingly, compelled and tortured. What wickedness suppresses, suffering extorts. [Note: [Col. 1025D] *Extorquet injuria* means “suffering,” that is, torment and pain, extorts it. Thus in Book II *On Abraham*, chapter 8, section 5: “let him be subdued by suffering,” meaning by labor and blows.] The devil yields to blows, while the Arians still do not yield. How much have they suffered, and how, like Pharaoh, are they hardened by their own evils?

The devil said, as we read in Scripture: “I know who you are: you are the Son of the living God” (Mark I, 24). The Jews said: “We do not know who he is” (John IX, 29). Today and yesterday, or last night, the demons said: “We know that you are martyrs.” The Arians say: “We do not know; we do not wish to understand; we do not wish to believe.” The demons say to the martyrs: “You have come to destroy us.” The Arians say: “The demons’ torments are not genuine, but fabricated and contrived mockeries.”

I have heard that many things can be fabricated, but no one has ever been able to invent something that would make a demon pretend to be a demon. [Note: [Col. 1025D] The old edition reads *ut daemoniacum*, “to appear demoniacal”; some manuscripts read *ut daemonium*, “to appear as a demon”; more manuscripts and the Roman edition read *ut daemonem*, “to appear as a demon.”] What of the fact that we see those upon whom hands are laid being so violently agitated? Where is there room here for fraud? Where is there suspicion of pretense?

23. But I do not invoke the demons’ voices as support for the martyrs. Let the sacred passion be proved by its benefits. It has judges, but judges who have been purified; it has witnesses, but witnesses who have been set free. Better is the voice spoken by the health of those who came infirm; better is the voice uttered by blood. For blood has a clear and resonant voice that reaches from earth to heaven.

You have read God saying: “The blood of your brother cries out to me” (Genesis IV, 10). Here too the blood cries out by the evidence of its color; the blood cries out by the proclamation of its activity; the blood cries out in the triumph of its suffering. [Note: [Col. 1025D] This translation of the sacred relics is recorded in the Roman Martyrology on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July. We have discussed it in the Introduction.] Your request has been granted: we have postponed the burial of the relics from yesterday until today.

[Note: [Col. 1025D] Written in the year 386.]

## LETTER XXIII

[Col. 1026C] Having set forth both the difficulty and the necessity of determining the date of Easter, Ambrose proves that observing particular days is permissible provided superstition is absent, and explains his own advice. He discusses what must be considered concerning the Law and how it is to be observed. After demonstrating that the day of the Passion and the day of the Resurrection must be distinguished, and resolving the difficulties by examples from earlier times, he declares that we are not bound to the letter of the text. Having confirmed the whole argument, he briefly touches upon the virtues necessary for celebrating Easter.

Ambrose, bishop, to his most beloved lords and brothers, the bishops established throughout Aemilia.

### 1

Divine Scripture and the tradition of our forefathers teach us that it requires no ordinary wisdom to determine the day of the Easter celebration. Those who gathered for the Council of Nicaea, among its decrees that were as true as they were admirable in matters of faith, also considered the celebration of Easter. They assembled the most skilled calculators and worked out a cycle of nineteen years, establishing, as it were, a circle from which an example might be generated for the following years. They called this circle the *enneadecateris*, following the principle that we ought not to waver in uncertainty over such a celebration because of some empty opinion, but, having discovered the truth by sound calculation, should ensure that everyone’s devotion converges, [Note: [Col. 1027D] Observe the custom of the ancient Church, according to which the sacrifice was offered during the privilege of Easter at the very time consecrated by Christ’s resurrection.] so that everywhere, on one night, the sacrifice may be brought forward for the Resurrection of the Lord. [Note: [Col. 1027D] Two manuscripts read “may be offered for the Resurrection of the Lord.”]

[Note: [Col. 1025D] Beda and several others attribute the nineteen-year cycle not to the Council of Nicaea but to Eusebius of Caesarea; Baronius, under the year 325, criticizes the Ambrosian text on the authority of this passage. He could also have added the testimony of Dionysius Exiguus from his first letter. Bucherius, however, accuses Dionysius of error; he proves that Ambrose spoke less clearly in this letter from the fact that below he does not expressly say that the cycle of the *enneadecateris* was established, but uses the words “if anyone carefully considers, they thought it should be established.”

We do not agree with Bucherius that Ambrose borrowed from Theophilus what he says here about the celebration of Easter, nor that this letter was written in the year 381 after Easter and after Theophilus of Alexandria had published his Easter calendar. It seems more probable to us that this letter itself is earlier than that calendar. As for the *enneadecateris*, Bucherius himself does not deny that it was mentioned in some way at the Council of Nicaea; nevertheless, we do not think that it was decreed and established so definitively that the controversy over the celebration of Easter was thereby made entirely clear. We are led to this opinion not only by the words of Ambrose quoted above, but also by the difficulties that certainly emerged both from this letter itself and later from Cyril, Leo the Great, and others.

We therefore believe that the Council determined, first, that the Greeks and Latins should celebrate Easter, the Resurrection, on the same day; second, that, in distinction from the Jews, this day should be the Sunday immediately following the fourteenth day of the moon of the month of March; and third, that the nineteen-year cycle should be admitted. Certain matters necessary for the use of the cycle, however, were not sufficiently explained, and hence later difficulties arose. On this subject see the notes of Franciscus Balbus on this letter, published among the minor works of Nicolaus Faber.]

### 2

Most beloved lords and brothers, we must not depart so far from the truth or differ so wildly in our thinking that some requirement concerning this celebration should be imposed upon all Christians, since the Lord himself chose the day on which he would celebrate the Passover, and that day agrees with true observance. For it is written:

> The day came when it was necessary for the Passover to be sacrificed, and he sent Peter and John, saying, “Go and prepare the Passover for us, so that we may eat it.” They said to him, “Where do you wish us to prepare it?” And he said to them, “Behold, when you enter the city, a man carrying a jar of water will meet you. Follow him into the house he enters, and you shall say to the master of the house: ‘The Teacher says to you: Where is the guest room where I may eat the Passover with my disciples?’ He will show you a large upper room furnished; prepare it there.”  
> (Luke XXII, 10 and following)

### 3

We understand, therefore, that we ought not to descend to earthly things, but to seek the large furnished room above, so that we may celebrate the Lord’s Passover. We must also wash our minds with a certain spiritual water from the eternal fountain, maintain the measure of a devoted celebration, and not investigate particular lunar days according to popular opinion, since the Apostle says: “You observe days, months, seasons, and years; I fear that I have labored among you in vain” (Galatians IV, 10). For it begins to be contradictory.

### 4

It is one thing to observe days in the pagan manner—to judge, according to the moon, what should be undertaken, for example, to avoid the fifth day and to begin nothing on it—[Note: [Col. 1028C] Ambrose discussed pagan superstitions concerning the observance of the fourth day in Book IV of the *Hexaemeron*, chapter 9. What he says here about the fifth day undoubtedly refers to Virgil, *Aeneid* I:

> The moon herself assigned different days to different works:  
> avoid the fifth, and so forth.

[Col. 1028D]] to recommend various phases of the moon for conducting business, or to avoid certain days, as many have been accustomed to avoid the “following days” or the Egyptian days. [Note: [Col. 1028D] Gill reads *pastores dies*, “shepherd days.” This is a printer’s error, though it was nevertheless accepted in the Paris edition of 1586. Bucherius explains “following days” as follows: “The days that followed the Kalends, Nones, or Ides were considered unlucky by the Romans” (Gellius, Book V, chapter 17). As for the Egyptians, Augustine also mentions them in his commentary on the Apostle’s words quoted above by Ambrose, but he does not explain which days they were. Cangius, reviewing various recent opinions concerning these days under the word *dies*, says that there were two unlucky days in each month for beginning undertakings. See also Abulensis on Exodus XII.]

It is another thing to direct the observance of a religious mind toward the day of which it is written: “This is the day that the Lord has made” (Psalm CXVII, 24). For although it is written that the Lord’s Passover ought to be celebrated on the fourteenth day of the first month, and although we truly ought to seek the fourteenth moon for celebrating the sequence of the Lord’s Passion, nevertheless we can understand from this that, for such a solemnity, either the perfection of the Church or the fullness of clear faith is required, as the prophet said when speaking of the Son of God: “His throne shall remain forever before me like the sun, and like the perfect moon” (Psalm LXXXVIII, 38).

### 5

For this reason, when the Lord had performed marvelous works on earth, as though the faith of human minds had already been founded, he mentioned that the time of his Passion had come, saying: “Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son, so that your Son may glorify you” (John XVII, 1). Elsewhere he teaches that the glory required for celebrating the Passion is this, saying: “Go and tell that fox: Behold, I cast out demons today and tomorrow I complete healings, and on the following day I am brought to completion” (Luke XIII, 32). Jesus is brought to completion in those who begin to be perfect, so that by their faith they may believe in the fullness of his divinity and redemption.

### 6

Therefore we seek both the day and the hour, as Scripture instructs us. The prophet David also says: “It is time for action, Lord” (Psalm CXVIII, 126), asking to receive understanding for knowing the Lord’s testimonies. Ecclesiastes likewise says: “There is a time for every matter” (Ecclesiastes III, 1; Jeremiah VIII, 7). Jeremiah cries out: “The turtledove, the swallow, and the sparrows of the fields have recognized the times of their coming” (Jeremiah VIII, 7). What could seem clearer than the statement made concerning the Lord’s Passion: “The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master’s manger” (Isaiah I, 3)? Let us therefore recognize this manger of the Lord, in which we are nourished, fed, and refreshed.

### 7

We must therefore know above all the time when harmonious prayer for the sacred night is poured out throughout the whole world, because prayers too are commended by their proper time, as it is written: “In an acceptable time I have heard you, and on the day of salvation I have helped you” (Isaiah XLIX, 8). This is the time of which the Apostle said: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (II Corinthians VI, 2).

### 8

For this reason it was necessary that, even after the calculations of the Egyptians and the determinations of the Alexandrian Church, many bishops of the Roman Church should still await my opinion in letters concerning what I thought should be written about the day of Easter. [Note: [Col. 1029C] It may be disputed whether the noun “bishop,” together with its adjective and verb, is to be connected with *exspectant*, “await,” or whether it stands in the genitive and refers to the word τὸ *definitiones* (“determinations”). The latter seems more probable to us, since an adverb can also connect what follows with the preceding sentence, and it would not seem entirely correct to say that many bishops of the Roman Church still awaited Ambrose’s opinion, unless one prefers to understand “Roman Church” here as “the Roman metropolitan church.” But apart from the fact that this expression is less usual, why would those bishops seek the opinion of the metropolitan of Milan rather than that of the Roman metropolitan? We therefore understand “bishop” indefinitely, in the sense of “bishops,” since it is well known that several Roman pontiffs had issued regulations concerning the Easter feast before that time. Indeed, we can learn from Saint Leo’s later letter to the emperor Marcian that the same difficulty which compelled our Ambrose to write on this subject arose again afterward. Compare the two letters and you will find a considerable affinity between them.]

Although the question concerned the date of the coming Easter, we will also explain what should be observed thereafter, should a similar question arise.

### 9

There are two things to be observed in the solemnity of Easter: the fourteenth moon and the first month, which is called the month of new grain. Therefore, lest we seem to depart from the Old Testament, let us review the passage concerning the day on which Easter is to be celebrated. Moses admonishes the people, saying that the month of new grain must be observed and proclaiming it to be the first month. For he says:

> This month shall be for you the beginning of months; it shall be the first among the months of the year. And you shall celebrate the Passover to the Lord your God on the fourteenth day of the first month.  
> (Exodus XII, 11)

### 10

The Law, certainly, was given through Moses; but grace and truth came through Jesus Christ (John I, 17). Therefore he who spoke the Law, later coming through the Virgin in the last times, brought the fullness of the Law to completion, because he came not to abolish the Law but to fulfill it (Matthew V, 17). He celebrated the Passover in the week in which the fourteenth moon fell on Thursday. On that very day, as the preceding discussion teaches, he ate the Passover with his disciples; on the following day, that is, Friday, he was crucified, on the fifteenth moon. On the Sabbath, that great day, it was the sixteenth moon; and consequently he rose from the dead on the seventeenth moon. [Note: [Col. 1029D] Some manuscripts read: “who spoke through the Law.”]

### 11

Therefore this law of the Passover must be observed by us, so that we do not observe the fourteenth moon on the day of the Resurrection, but rather on the day of the Passion, or at least on one of the immediately preceding days, since the celebration of the Resurrection takes place on Sunday. We cannot fast on Sunday, because we rightly condemn the Manichaeans for fasting on that day. [Note: [Col. 1029D] On the Sunday fast practiced by the Manichaeans, see Augustine’s Letter 36 to Casulanus, sections 27 and 29. Proterius also says something about it in his letter to Leo.]

For one does not believe in Christ’s Resurrection if one prescribes the law of fasting for the day of the Resurrection, since the Law says that the Passover is to be eaten with bitterness (Exodus XII, 8), that is, with grief, because the author of salvation was put to death by so great a sacrilege of men. On Sunday, however, the prophet teaches us to rejoice, saying: “This is the day that the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it” (Psalm CXVII, 24).

### 12

Therefore we must observe not only the day of the Passion but also the day of the Resurrection, so that we may have both a day of bitterness and a day of joy: on the former let us fast, on the latter let us be refreshed.

Thus, if—as will soon be the case—the fourteenth moon of the first month falls on a Sunday, because we ought neither to fast on Sunday nor to break the fast when the thirteenth moon falls on Saturday, since the fast is especially to be offered on the day of the Passion, the celebration of Easter must be postponed to the following week. For the fifteenth moon follows, on which Christ suffered, and it will be Monday; Tuesday will be the sixteenth moon, on which the Lord’s flesh rested in the tomb; and Wednesday will be the seventeenth moon, on which the Lord rose. [Note: [Col. 1030D] This was the central difficulty on which Ambrose had been consulted: when Easter fell on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May, it was uncertain whether it could be transferred to the seventh day before the Kalends of May, for the reasons proposed here by Saint Ambrose and by Proterius in the letter cited. Incidentally, one may observe that what we said in the Introduction to the book *On Elijah and Fasting* concerning the fast of Holy Saturday is clearly confirmed here.]

### 13

Since that sacred three-day period therefore falls in the final week immediately ahead, within which he suffered, rested, and rose again—and concerning which he said, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John II, 14)—what can cause us the trouble of doubt? For if the matter causes scruple because we are not celebrating the actual day of either the Passion or the Resurrection on the fourteenth moon, the Lord himself did not suffer on the fourteenth moon but on the fifteenth, and he rose on the seventeenth moon. [Note: [Col. 1030D] All manuscripts read: “But what if it causes scruple … on which day,” etc.]

But if it causes concern that, passing over the fourteenth moon—which falls on Sunday, that is, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May—we advise restoring the celebration on the following Sunday, there is authoritative precedent for this.

### 14

For in times not much earlier, when the fourteenth moon of the first month had fallen on a Sunday, the solemnity was celebrated on the following Sunday. [Note: [Col. 1030D] The old edition reads “in the eighty-ninth and ninety-third year”; the Roman edition retains only “and in the ninety-third year.” Franciscus Balbus and Bucherius more correctly read “in the eighty-ninth year.” Balbus says that he finds the nineteenth-year cycle there, with the thirteenth year of the nineteen-year cycle, the dominical letter F, and Easter extended to the day before the Kalends of April. Bucherius reports that this year was 373 after the restoration of salvation. Both corrections are confirmed by Proterius’s letter and by the era of Diocletian, which they hold to have begun on the fourth day before the Kalends of September in the year 284 after Christ.]

In the eighty-ninth year from the beginning of Diocletian’s reign, when the fourteenth moon was on the ninth day before the Kalends of April, we celebrated Easter on the day before the Kalends of April. The Alexandrians and Egyptians likewise, as they themselves wrote, when the fourteenth moon had fallen on the twenty-eighth day of the month Phamenoth, celebrated Easter on the fifth day of the month Pharmuthi, which is the day before the Kalends of April, and thus agreed with us. [Note: [Col. 1031B] So the Roman edition and the manuscripts, together with the calculations of Proterius, Balbus, and Bucherius. The old edition, however, reads “on the twenty-eighth day of Pharmuthi.”]

Again, in the ninety-third year from the beginning of Diocletian’s reign, when the fourteenth moon fell on the fourteenth day of Pharmuthi, which is the fifth day before the Ides of April and which was a Sunday, Easter was celebrated on Sunday, the twenty-first day of Pharmuthi, which according to our reckoning was the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May. [Note: [Col. 1031B] The old edition reads “the fifteenth”; the Roman edition restores “the sixteenth.” It is plainly evident that, since the preceding Sunday fell on the fifth day before the Ides of April, the following Sunday fell not on the fifteenth but on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May.] Since both calculation and precedent support us, nothing concerning this matter ought to trouble us.

### 15

Now the matter that seems to require explanation is that many think we will celebrate Easter in the second month, although it is written: “Observe the first month of new grain” (Deuteronomy XVI, 1). This cannot happen—that Easter should be celebrated outside the month of new grain—unless one observes the fourteenth moon so literally that one celebrates only on that very day.

Indeed, the Jews will soon celebrate Easter in the twelfth month, not the first—that is, according to our reckoning, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April. [Note: [Col. 1031C] The ancient edition reads “on the third day before the Kalends of April”; the Roman edition, together with the manuscripts, reads “on the thirteenth,” and so forth. Balbus observes that this confirms the change from Pharmuthi to Phamenoth mentioned above.]

According to the Egyptians, however, it will be on the twenty-fourth day of the month Phamenoth, which is not the first month but the twelfth. [Note: [Col. 1031C] So the Roman edition; the old edition reads “but the twelfth, and it begins on the sixth.” This is erroneous. It is certain that the month Phamenoth begins on the fifth day before the Kalends of March and ends on the seventh day before the Kalends of April; accordingly, the month Pharmuthi begins on the sixth day before the Kalends of April. It should be observed, however, that when Ambrose calls Pharmuthi the first month, he means the first month of new grain, which was the first month of the year according to the Law. Among the Egyptians the first month was called Thoth and corresponded to our September. See Lactantius Firmianus, Book I, chapter 6.]

For the first month among the Egyptians is called Pharmuthi; it begins on the sixth day before the Kalends of April and ends on the seventh day before the Kalends of May. Therefore, according to the Egyptians, we will celebrate the Lord’s Easter in the first month, namely, on the seventh day before the Kalends of May, which is the thirtieth day of the month Pharmuthi.

### 885

**16.** Nor do I consider it absurd that we should derive an example for determining the month from the place where the first Passover was celebrated. Hence our predecessors, in their discussion of the Council of Nicaea, considered that this same Enneadecateris, or nineteen-year cycle, should be established,[Note: [Col. 1031C] The old edition reads, “that day, the Endecateris”; the Roman edition, “the same, namely the month, Enneadecateris.” This is an excellent [Col. 1031D] correction; for Ambrose here teaches that the Nicene Fathers decreed that the nineteen-year cycle should begin with the month of new grain and end in it, because in that same month the Passover was first celebrated of old by the Jews.] and rightly observed the month of new grain, because in Egypt fresh grain is cut in this first month. This month, moreover, is both the first according to the Egyptian harvest and the first according to the Law, [Col. 1032B] but the eighth according to our custom. [Note: [Col. 1031D] It is principally from this passage that chronologists assert that Ambrose was the first of the Latin Fathers to mention indictions. Yet they would have gathered this more properly from *On Noah and the Ark*, ch. 17, no. 60, where he sufficiently indicates that their use had begun not long before. It may be questioned, however, which indiction he designates in both passages: the Constantinopolitan, which began on the Kalends of September; the Constantinian, whose beginning was the eighth day before the Kalends of that month; or, finally, the Roman, Antiochene, or some other among those mentioned by writers. The more knowledgeable agree, however, that Ambrose should be understood to mean the Constantinian indiction. Although Baronius declares its institution a matter of extreme obscurity, the more generally accepted opinion assigns it to A.D. 312, under the rule of Constantine the Great. A substantial argument for this view is that Athanasius, in *On the Synods*, states that the gathering of the Arians held at Antioch convened, with Constantius present, in the fourteenth indiction. Those who, on the basis of this passage of Ambrose, attribute the indictions to Theodosius are thereby plainly refuted. Indictions are frequently mentioned in the Theodosian Code; Godefridus presents their table immediately at the beginning. See also the *Chronicle of Marcellinus* and the Alexandrian Chronicle, although the latter is disfigured by countless errors.]

For the indiction begins in the month of September. Thus the Kalends of April fall in the eighth month. But this month begins not according to ordinary usage, but according to the custom of experts, at the equinox, which is the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, and it ends on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May. Accordingly, within these thirty-one days, the days of Passover have often been celebrated. [Note: [Col. 1032C] Three manuscripts read “often celebrated”; one, which is also the oldest, and all printed editions read “often celebrated,” except certain Paris manuscripts, where we find “is often celebrated.” Moreover, when Ambrose says “within these thirty-one days,” there seems to be an error here as well: there are thirty-two days from the twelfth day before the Kalends of April to the eleventh day before the Kalends of May.]

**17.** But although [Note: [Col. 1032C] Balbus rightly observes that what follows cannot agree with “two years”; for it agrees with no year other than the ninety-fifth of the Diocletian era, that is, A.D. 379. Hence he concludes that “two years” arose from what had been written as “six years.” Nothing is more probable than this conjecture. Nevertheless, Bucherius retains the common reading and believes that the year designated by the words “two years ago” was A.D. 369. But that calculation does not accord with what is said here about the Passover of the year 387, which is described as imminent, since Bucherius considers this letter to have been written in 381. And, when a similar difficulty later arose concerning the Passover of the year 355, Saint Leo did not think that experts should be consulted until the year 553. Hermannus, moreover, reports that it may have happened that a different cycle was observed by Victorinianus; and in fact Bucherius published another, still older one, in which the resurrection-Passover of the year 384 is placed on the twelfth day before the Kalends of May—that is, on the eleventh—since in that author’s calendar the feast of Easter is consistently advanced by one day from the year 378 onward. Yet that same canon is found to be riddled with so many errors that we dare not trust it.] we celebrated the Lord’s Passover six years ago on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May—that is, on the thirtieth day of the month, according to our calculation—we ought not to be troubled if we are likewise going to celebrate the Lord’s Passover soon on the thirtieth day of the month Pharmuthi. But if someone thinks that this is a second month because the Sunday of Passover will occur three days after the completion of the month, which appears to be completed on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, let him consider that the fourteenth lunar day in question will fall on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May—that is, within the prescribed number of the month. The Law, however, requires the day of the Passion to be celebrated within the first month of new grain.

**18.** Satisfaction has therefore been made according to the fullness of the moon, for three further days remain before the month is completed. It does not therefore fall into another month when Passover is celebrated within that same month, which is the first. We ought not, however, to be bound by the letter, although the custom of celebrating Passover itself instructs us in this; the Apostle also teaches us when he says: “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (1 Cor. 5:7).

The passage set before us likewise teaches that the letter is not to be followed. For it reads as follows: “And you shall celebrate the Passover to the Lord your God on the fourteenth day of the first month” (Exod. 12:18). He speaks of the day in terms of the moon; and therefore even the most learned, according to the Law, calculate the month by the lunar course. Since, moreover, the lunar course begins for many with the Nones of the moon—that is, with the first day—[Note: [Col. 1033D] The Roman edition reads, “You see, on the day before the Nones of May”; the old edition reads, “You see, on the Nones of May.” The latter is a suitable reading. Since, as Balbus notes, the new moon of the first month may begin, according to the Alexandrian cycle, on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, it follows that the Nones of May may sometimes be included in the first lunar month. Perhaps, however, the Roman editors did not think that the Nones could belong to the preceding month, since Festus says that the Nones are so called from the new moon, because the beginning of the moon falls on them; Macrobius says that they are so called because they are, as it were, the beginning of a new reckoning. Such etymologies, however, are not sufficiently weighty. Ambrose is certainly right to say here “since the lunar course begins for many with the Nones,” rather than “for all.”] you see that even the Nones of May can still be reckoned as belonging to the first month of new grain. Therefore, in accordance with the meaning of the Law, this is also the first month. Finally, the Greeks call the moon *mēnē* (μήνη), and hence they call months *mēnes* (μῆνας); and the natural usage of foreign peoples calls the moon “days.”

**19.** The sequence of the Old Testament also shows that the day of the Passion and the day of the Resurrection are to be celebrated on different days. For it reads as follows:

“There shall be for you a lamb without blemish, clean, perfect, a year-old male; you shall take it from the sheep or the goats, and it shall be kept by you until the fourteenth day of this month.
