Then the whole assembly of the congregation of the children of Israel shall slaughter it toward evening, [Note: [Col. 1033D] One Vatican manuscript reads “with the whole multitude of the synagogue.”] and they shall take some of its blood and place it on the two doorposts and on the lintel of the door of the house in which they shall eat it among themselves. They shall eat this flesh roasted by fire during the night.” And below:

“And you shall eat it with anxiety, for it is the Lord’s Passover. For I will pass through the land of the Egyptians on that night, and I will strike every firstborn in Egypt, from man to beast; and throughout the land of Egypt I will execute judgment—I am the Lord. The blood shall be for you as a sign on the houses in which you are; and I will see the blood and protect you, [Note: [Col. 1033D] Three manuscripts read, “and there shall not be for you a plague.”] and the plague of destruction shall not be upon you. I will strike the land of Egypt, and this day shall be for you memorable and solemn; you shall celebrate it as a feast to the Lord throughout your generations, an everlasting ordinance. You shall celebrate it as a feast” (ibid., 5 ff.).

**20.** We observe that the day of the Passion is also described in fasting, since the lamb is to be slaughtered toward evening. We may, however, understand the final period as “evening,” according to John, who says: “Children, it is the last hour” (1 John 2:18). In accordance with the mystery, too, it is clear that he was killed in the evening of the day, when darkness immediately fell. It is therefore right that the fast be observed on that day, since it says: “You shall eat it with anxiety”; for anxiety accompanies those who are fasting.

But on the day of the Resurrection there is the rejoicing of nourishment and gladness—the day on which the people appear to have gone forth from Egypt, after the firstborn of the Egyptians had been killed. [887] The later passages make this clearer, where Scripture says that after the Jews had celebrated the Passover as Moses commanded, it happened around midnight that the Lord struck every firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh onward. Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron during the night and said to them: “Rise and go out from my people, [Note: [Col. 1033D] The editions read, “you and the children of Israel.”] both you and your children; go and serve the Lord your God” (Exod. 12:29–31).

The Egyptians pressed the people, hurrying to drive them out as quickly as possible. Thus the Israelites departed in such haste that they had no opportunity to leaven the unleavened dough; for the Egyptians drove them out, and they could not wait, [Note: [Col. 1033D] The old edition, together with three manuscripts, reads, “they could not wait for the provisions they had prepared”; the Roman edition reads, “they could not wait, nor did they prepare provisions.” The latter correction is supported by the words of Exodus 12:39: καὶ οὐχ ἠδυνήθησαν ἐπιμεῖναι, οὐδὲ ἐπισιτισμὸν ἐποίησαν—“they could not wait, nor did they prepare provisions,” and so forth. Nevertheless, since one Vatican manuscript supplies a reading not far removed from that text, we have judged that it should be admitted into the text.] for the provisions they had prepared for the journey.

**21.** It has therefore been established that the day of the Resurrection is to be observed after the day of the Passion. That day of the Resurrection should not be the fourteenth lunar day, but a later one, as the Old Testament indicates; [Note: [Col. 1034D] One Vatican manuscript reads, “because the days of the Passion are those when, departing,” and so forth.] for the day of the Resurrection is the day on which, as the people were going out from Egypt and were baptized in the sea and in the cloud, as the Apostle says (1 Cor. 10:2 ff.), they conquered death, receiving spiritual bread and drawing spiritual drink from the rock. The Lord’s Passion cannot be celebrated on the Lord’s Day; and if the fourteenth lunar day falls on a Sunday, another week must be added, as also happened in the seventy-sixth year from the beginning of Diocletian’s reign.

For at that time we celebrated the Lord’s Passover without any uncertainty on the twenty-eighth day of Pharmuthi, which is the ninth day before the Kalends of May, [Note: [Col. 1034D] All editions read, “on the thirtieth day of the month Pharmuthi, which is the seventh day before the Kalends of May.” But Balbus and Bucherius recognized that the passage required correction and accordingly proposed restoring “on the twenty-eighth day … which is the ninth day before the Kalends of May.” This is an excellent correction, since the passage concerns the year 360 of the era of salvation; otherwise the details cannot agree with one another.] in accordance with the unquestioned tradition of our predecessors. The course and calculation of the moon also support this, since Passover was to be celebrated on the twenty-first lunar day; for the customary reckoning extends as far as the twenty-first lunar day.

**22.** Since so many indications of the truth converge, let us celebrate the feast of the public salvation with joy and exultation, following the examples of our predecessors, coloring our doorposts—where the door of the word is found, which the Apostle asks to have opened for him—by faith in the Lord’s Passion [Note: [Col. 1035C] One Vatican manuscript reads, “celebrating in faith the Lord’s Passion.”] (Col. 4:3). David also speaks of this door: “Set, O Lord, a guard over my mouth, and a door of restraint around my lips” (Ps. 140:3), so that we may speak of nothing except the blood of Christ, by which we conquered death and by which we were redeemed.

Let the fragrance of Christ burn within us. Let us hear him himself; let us direct toward him the eyes of both mind and body, marveling at his works and proclaiming his benefits. Upon the lintel of our door let the confession of sacred redemption shine. [Col. 1035B] With fervent spirit let us receive [Note: [Col. 1035C] One manuscript reads, “the sacrament of the image of sincerity.”] the sacrament in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth, singing together in devout teaching the glory of the Father [Note: [Col. 1035C] One manuscript reads, “and the majesty of the Son and the indivisible harmony of the Holy Spirit.”] and the majesty of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, indivisible.

[888] [Note: [Col. 1035C] Written in the year 387.]

### LETTER XXIV

After explaining why he gives an account of his embassy—how, having been compelled to enter the council chamber, he refused to kiss Maximus, and how he turned back upon Maximus the accusations by which the latter claimed that Ambrose had deceived him and that barbarians had been sent against him by Bauto—he narrates how freely he opposed Valentinian’s clemency to Maximus’ cruelty and insisted that Gratian’s body be returned. Finally, after reproaching the tyrant for the killing of Vallio, he was expelled, and he adds that his concern was not so much for his own danger as for the exile of Hyginus.

**AMBROSE TO THE EMPEROR VALENTINIAN**

[Col. 1035C]

**23.** Although the reliability of my previous embassy has been so approved by you that no account of it is demanded from me—for it became sufficiently clear from the very fact that I was detained for several days within Gaul—[Note: [Col. 1035D] The Amerbach edition and the manuscripts read *aliquot, me violenti a Maximo*; the subsequent edition reads *me violentiam a Maximo*. Neither produces a suitable meaning. Other manuscripts partly read *me volente a Maximo*, and partly *me volentia Maximo* or *me volentia Maximo*, which is the true reading. Tacitus writes similarly: “These and such things were pleasing to the people” (*haec atque talia plebi volentia fuere*). Sallust also uses the expression. Ambrose therefore indicates that, in matters pleasing to Maximus, he either did not accept them or did not promise that he would carry them out; for the verb *recepisse* may be explained in either way. Again, where we, with the old edition and many manuscripts, read *ad pacem protenderent*, the Roman edition and certain manuscripts read *propenderent*, and one reads *praetenderent*. Two manuscripts read *me voluntatem Maximi*.] and had not accepted what was pleasing to Maximus, nor supported measures that inclined more toward his will than toward peace—in short, you would not have entrusted me with a second embassy unless you had approved the first. But since, as I was returning, he imposed upon me the necessity of deciding the matter with him, I thought that in this letter I should make an account of my embassy known, lest anyone’s speech should weave falsehoods into the truth before my return had been fully and clearly marked by the seal of genuine truth. [Note: [Col. 1035D] The old edition and not a few manuscripts read *viri prius vana*; some read *veri prius vana*. This is not unsuitable, since Ambrose is not unaccustomed to calling things empty of truth, in imitation of Virgil, *veri vana*. Several manuscripts and the Roman edition, however, read as in the text.]

**2.** When I had reached Trier, I went to the palace on the following day. A Gallic man came out to me, Gallicanus, the chief of the bedchamber, the imperial eunuch. I asked for permission to approach you. He asked whether I had a rescript from your Clemency. I replied that I did. He reported that I could not be seen except in the council chamber. I said that this was not the sacerdotal custom, and that there were certainly matters about which I ought to speak seriously [Note: [Col. 1036C] The Roman edition reads, “about which I ought to speak alone, in private.”] with his sovereign. What more is there to say? He consulted him, but thought that the same response should be brought back, so that it might be clear that the earlier responses too had been drawn from his judgment. Nevertheless, I said that this was indeed foreign to our office, but that, having accepted the duty, I would not fail to discharge it. I considered humility pleasing to me, especially in your matter and, to speak truthfully, in the matter of fraternal devotion.

**3.** When he had taken his seat in the council chamber, I entered. He rose to give me a kiss. I stood among the members of the council. [Note: [Col. 1036D] Two manuscripts read *inter consistoria non fleti* (“not wept among the councilors,” an uncertain reading).] Some began to urge me to come forward; he called me. I replied: “Why do you kiss one whom you have not acknowledged? For if you had acknowledged me, you would not see me in this place.”

“You are agitated, Bishop,” he said.

“No,” I replied, “but from embarrassment at standing in another’s place.”

“And you entered the council chamber during your first embassy.”

“Nor was that my error,” I said. “The fault was in the one who summoned me, not in the one who entered.”

“Why did you enter?” he asked.

“Because then I was asking peace as an inferior, but now as an equal.”

“By whose favor are you equal?” he asked.

I replied: “By the favor of almighty God, who preserved for Valentinian the kingdom that he had given him.”

**4.** Finally he burst out, saying: “Since you and that Bauto [Note: [Col. 1036D] Our holy bishop mentions the count Bauto again in his letter to Theodosius. Philostorgius reports that Bauto’s daughter married the emperor Arcadius in Book XI of his *History*. Zosimus, however, praises him at such length that he nearly gives rise to the suspicion that Bauto was devoted to the superstition of idols. They also thought that this man was none other than the Bauto who was consul at the time when Augustine delivered his panegyric at Milan, as Augustine himself wrote in Book III, ch. 25, of *Against the Letters of Petilianus*.] have deceived me—that Bauto who wanted to claim the kingdom under the pretext of the child and who also sent barbarians against me—as though I do not have men whom I can bring forward, since so many thousands of barbarians serve under me and receive their provisions from me. And if I had not been detained at the time when you came, who would have opposed me and my valor?”

**5.** To this I replied gently: “There is no need for you to become agitated, since there is no cause for agitation; but listen patiently to what is being reported to you. I too came for this reason: during my first embassy, while you trusted me, you asserted that you had been deceived by me. This too is glorious for me, on behalf of the safety of the child-emperor. For whom ought bishops to protect more than wards? It is written: ‘Judge for the orphan, and justify the widow, and rescue the one suffering wrong’ (Isa. 1:17); and elsewhere: ‘The judge of widows and the father of orphans’ (Ps. 67:6).”

**6.** Yet I will not reproach Valentinian with my service. To speak the truth, when did I oppose your legions and prevent you from invading Italy? With what rocks? In what battle line? With what troops? Did I really close the Alps against you with my own body? [Note: [Col. 1037D] With what sincere affection Ambrose performed this service for the boy Valentinian in undertaking these two embassies, he himself also recalls in the funeral panegyric of that prince, to which the reader may refer.] If only that had been my achievement! I would not fear your objection or dread your accusations. By what promises did I deceive you into accepting peace? Did not Count Victor [Note: [Col. 1037D] It is clear that the Victor mentioned here is different from Victor, the son of Maximus, whom Arbogastes, sent into Gaul by Theodosius after the death of Maximus, killed.] meet me within Gaul near the city of Mainz, having been sent by you to ask for peace? In what way, then, did Valentinian deceive you, when peace was requested from you before he asked for it? In what way did Bauto deceive you, when he displayed loyalty to his own emperor? Was it because he did not betray his sovereign?

**7.** “In what way did I circumvent you? When I first came, and you said that Valentinian ought to come to you as a son to his father, I replied that it was not reasonable for a child with his widowed mother to cross the Alps in the harsh season of winter; and that without his mother he ought not be entrusted to so long a journey amid uncertain circumstances. We had been entrusted with an embassy concerning peace, not with a promise of his arrival [Note: [Col. 1037D] Several manuscripts read, “an embassy concerning peace promised to you”; others, and the editions, with better sense, read, “an embassy concerning peace entrusted to us.”] It is certain that we could not promise what had not been commanded. I certainly promised nothing, so much so that you said: ‘Let us await what response Victor brings back.’

“It is clear that he reached Milan while I was being detained, and that what he requested was denied him. The efforts of both sides were directed toward peace alone, not toward the emperor’s arrival, which ought not to have been brought about. I was present when Victor returned. How, then, did I recall Valentinian? Envoys were again sent to Gaul to deny his arrival; they found me at Valence in Gaul. Returning, I encountered soldiers of both sides guarding the mountain passes. Which of your armies did I recall? Which eagles did I turn back from Italy? Which barbarians did Count Bauto send?

**[Col. 1037D] 8.** And what wonder if Bauto had done this, being of Transrhenan [Col. 1038A] origin, when you threatened the Roman Empire with barbarian auxiliaries and transborder squadrons, whose provisions were paid for by the taxes of the provinces? [Note: [Col. 1037D] The Roman edition, together with a few manuscripts, reads “of the provinces.”] Consider, however, the difference between your threats and the gentleness of the boy Augustus Valentinian. You demanded that, surrounded by columns of barbarians, you should pour into Italy; Valentinian [Note: [Col. 1037D] It is likely that the Huns, after they had been defeated together with the Goths by Theodosius, as Zosimus records in Book IV, maintained peace with the Romans until this time. As for the Alans, Gratian was so fond of that people that, for this reason, he alienated the minds of the Romans from himself and gave Maximus an opportunity to usurp power.] turned back the Huns and Alans, who were approaching Gaul through the lands of the Alemanni. What cause for resentment is there if Bauto made barbarians fight barbarians? While you occupied the Roman soldier, while he was being deployed against himself on both sides, the Juthungi were ravaging the Rhaetias in the heart of the Roman Empire; and for this reason a Hun was summoned against the Juthungus. But because the same Hun was also devastating Alemannia from the neighboring territory [Note: [Col. 1038D] The Erasmus and later editions read, “and now the neighborhood”; the Amerbach edition and all the manuscripts read, “and now from the neighborhood.”] and the danger already pressed upon Gaul from nearby, he was compelled to abandon his triumphs so that you might not be afraid. Compare the actions of the two of you. You caused the Rhaetias to be invaded; Valentinian bought peace for you with his own gold.

**9.** Look also at the man standing beside you on your right, whom Valentinian, although he could have avenged his own grief, sent back to you with honor. He held him in his own territory and restrained the impulse to act even when he received news of his brother’s death. He did not repay you in kind—even though the dignity was not equal, the relationship was nonetheless the same. Compare, then, the actions of both, with you as judge. He sent your brother back to you alive; you should at least return him dead. Why do you deny him his brother’s remains, when he did not deny you assistance against himself?

[Note: [Col. 1038D] The holy Bishop does not say how this man was called; but Marcellinus clearly reveals in the *Panegyric of Theodosius* that his name was Pacatus.]

**10.** But you fear that the return of the remains will renew the soldiers’ grief; for this is your excuse. The man whom they abandoned alive—will they defend him when dead? Why do you fear him dead, whom you killed when you could have preserved him? “He was my enemy,” you say; “I killed him.”

“He was not your enemy,” I reply, “but you were his. He no longer feels your defense; consider your own case.” If someone today should think that imperial power ought to be usurped in these regions, I ask whether you would call yourself his enemy, or him yours. Unless I am mistaken, the usurper brings war, while the emperor defends his rightful claim. So you deny the remains of the man whom you ought not to have killed? Let the emperor Valentinian have at least his brother’s remains as hostages of your peace.

And how could you claim that you had not ordered him killed when you prohibit his burial? Can it then be believed that you did not begrudge him life, when you begrudge him even burial?

**[Col. 1038D] 11.** But let me return to my own case. I hear that you complain that those who are with the emperor Valentinian have gone over rather to the emperor Theodosius. What did you expect would happen when you demanded that they be punished as they fled from you and killed them when captured, while Theodosius enriched them with gifts and bestowed honors upon them?

“Whom did I kill?” he asked.

I replied: “Vallio.” [Note: [Col. 1039C] The name of this count appears in various forms. All editions write *Balio*; some manuscripts *Ballio*; many others, and by far the majority, *Vallio*. The last is entirely correct. Thus Pacatus says of the same man in the *Panegyric* mentioned above: “Vallio the triumphant … after the highest magistracies, the consular purple, and the accumulation of a senate of honors within a single household, was compelled to take his own life.”]

“But what kind of man was he? What sort of warrior? Was this a just cause for his death—that he kept faith with his emperor?”

“I did not order him to be killed,” he said.

“I heard,” I replied, “that he was ordered to be killed.”

“But,” he said, “if he had not inflicted violence upon himself, I had ordered him to be taken to Chalon and burned alive there.”

“Then,” I replied, “that is why it was believed that you had killed him. For who would think that he ought to be spared when a vigorous warrior, a faithful soldier, and a useful count had been killed?”

I then departed, while he said that he would deal with the matter.

**12.** Later, when he saw that I was abstaining from the bishops who maintained communion with him, or who were seeking the death of certain men, even though they were deviating from the faith, he was angered by them and ordered me to return without delay. I, however, gladly set out, although many did not believe that I would escape the ambushes. My only grief was that I discovered that the aged Bishop Hyginus was being led into exile, when nothing remained to him except his final breath.

When I pleaded with his attendants on his behalf, asking that they not allow the old man to be driven out without clothing and without a quilted mattress [Note: [Col. 1039D] A *plumarium* was a feather-filled cushion or mattress, so that the limbs of that good old man might lie somewhat more gently after being broken. Baronius, under the year 387, suspects that this Hyginus was the same as Adiginus, the bishop of Córdoba, whom Severus, in Book II of his *History*, says first stirred up the bishops against Petilianus. Yet according to that same historian, Adiginus—or Iginus, as he is called below—admitted the Priscillianists into communion, which is incompatible with the nobility of our Hyginus, unless perhaps, deterred by the harshness of the proposed exile, he abandoned his former steadfastness. Ambrose, still on the road home, could in no way yet have learned of such a change.] I myself was expelled.

**13.** This is the account of my embassy. Farewell, Emperor, and be more secure against a man who conceals war beneath the covering of peace.

[892] [Note: [Col. 1040C] Written after the year 385 and before the year 387.]

### LETTER XXV

When Studius asks whether he may pronounce judgment against criminals, Ambrose replies that although the use of the sword has indeed been permitted to him, it is nevertheless expedient that he exercise clemency. For this purpose he brings forward the example of Christ, who acquitted the adulterous woman, and he explains why communion ought not to be denied to judges who impose capital sentences.

[Col. 1039C]

**AMBROSE TO STUDIUS**

[Note: [Col. 1040C] The editions read *Ambrose the bishop to Studius*; the manuscripts, *Ambrose to Studius*; the Gembloux manuscript, *to Studious*. There was a certain Studius who was a count of the Roman state in the year 401, according to Law 17, *De Bonis Proscriptorum et Peculatus*, and in the year 404, according to Law 13, *De Episcopis*. Whether he was the same man to whom this and the following letter were addressed cannot be determined with certainty.]

[Col. 1040A]

**1.** I recognize the affection of your pure mind, your devotion to the faith, and your fear of our Lord Jesus Christ. Even I would hesitate to give a response concerning this matter, constrained on one side by what has been entrusted to you for the preservation of the laws, and on the other by mercy and grace, were it not that you possess apostolic authority for this: “For he who judges does not carry the sword without cause” (Rom. 13:4); for he is God’s avenger against those who do evil.

**2.** Yet even though you knew this, you did not think it useless to ask. For there are some, [Note: [Col. 1040C] The manuscripts agree almost unanimously in this reading. The old edition would not differ from us except that it inserts the negation, “for there are not”; the Roman edition likewise rejects the negation but at the same time removes from the text the following words, “outside the Church, however”—wrongly, since the words below plainly demonstrate that Catholics did not maintain such excessive severity: “And therefore our predecessors preferred to be more lenient toward judges,” and so forth. Innocent I also clearly defined the same matter in Letter 3 to Exsuperius, whose words we omit. We therefore think it likely that the persons designated here are none other than the Novatians, who, among the other features of stricter discipline that they promoted, added the rule that a judge who had justly condemned a defendant to death should be excluded from communion at the altar.] outside the Church, however, who do not admit to communion in the heavenly sacraments those who have judged that a capital sentence should be imposed upon certain persons. Many also abstain voluntarily; and they are indeed praised, nor can we refrain from commending them, while we observe the Apostle’s authority to the extent that we dare not deny them communion.

**3.** You see, therefore, what authority grants and what mercy advises. You will have an excuse if you do it; praise if you do not. But if you cannot do so, do not nevertheless crush the guilty with the squalor of prison; instead, release them, and I will approve you all the more as a priest. For it may happen that, once the case has been examined, a defendant is admitted to judgment, and afterward either asks pardon for himself or, at any rate, without severe harshness—as someone has said—dwells in prison.

I know, however, that many pagans have been accustomed to boast [Col. 1041A] that they brought back from their administration of the provinces an unsullied axe. [Note: [Col. 1041C] These men are said in Greek to administer power ἀναιμακτὶ, “without bloodshed,” as Vespasian is reported to have done; his saying was that he would rather perish than destroy. Thus Nannius. He might also have added the statement made by Capitolinus about Antoninus Pius: “Almost alone among all rulers, he lived entirely without civil or enemy bloodshed, so far as it depended on him.” Lampridius likewise attributes an ἀναίμακτον, “bloodless,” rule to Severus, but under a false title.] If pagans do this, what ought Christians to do?

**4.** In every matter, however, accept the Savior’s answer (John 8:3 ff.). When the Jews had found an adulterous woman, they brought her to the Savior, seeking to entrap him: if he acquitted her, he would appear to violate the Law, although he had said, “I have not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it” (Matt. 5:17); if he condemned her, he would appear to have come contrary to the purpose he had set before himself.

Foreseeing this, therefore, the Lord Jesus bent his head and wrote on the ground. What did he write, except the prophetic saying: “Earth, earth, write down these men as rejected” (Jer. 22:29), which is recorded concerning Jeconiah by the prophet Jeremiah?

**5.** When the Jews appeal to him, the names of the Jews are written on the earth; when Christians approach, the names of the faithful are not written on earth but in heaven. On earth are written those rejected by their own father, who test their father and heap insults upon the author of salvation.

When the Jews appeal, Jesus inclines his head; and because he has nowhere to lay his head, he raises it again, as though about to pronounce judgment, and says: “Let the one who is without sin be the first to stone her” (Matt. 8:20). Then, bending his head again, he wrote on the ground.

**6.** Hearing this, they began to leave one by one, beginning with the elders (John 8:7)—either because those who had lived longer had more crimes, or because, being wiser, they first understood the force of the sentence and began rather to mourn their own sins, since they had come as accusers of another’s crime.

**7.** When they had gone away, Jesus remained alone. Raising his head toward the woman, he said: “Where are those who accused you? Has no one stoned you?” [Note: [Col. 1041D] The Roman edition reads, “No one has condemned you”; the other editions, together with all the manuscripts, read, “No one has stoned you.”]

She replied: “No one.”

Jesus said to her: “Neither will I condemn you. Go, and from now on see that you do not sin again” (ibid., 10–11).

He does not condemn, as redemption; he corrects, as life; as a fountain, he washes clean. And because Jesus inclines himself when he inclines in order to raise up those who are fallen, therefore he says the forgiveness of sins: “Neither will I condemn you.”

8. You have an example to follow. For it may happen that this guilty man can still have hope of correction: if he is without baptism, that he may receive remission; if baptized, [Note: [Col. 1041D] The labors of canonical repentance were formerly so great and so prolonged that they could not without reason be imposed in place of capital punishment, as a kind of more burdensome death.] [Col. 1042A] that he may do penance and offer his body for Christ. How many roads there are to salvation!

9. And therefore the ancients preferred to be more lenient toward judges, so that, while their sword was feared, the fury of crimes might be restrained rather than provoked; whereas, if communion were denied, the punishment of criminals would seem to have been exacted. Our predecessors therefore preferred that the law should rest more on the will of one who abstains than on compulsion. Farewell, and love us, because we too love you.

---

## 894 EPISTLE XXVI

After repeating the subject of the preceding letter, Ambrose returns to the Jews who brought an adulterous woman before Christ, comparing them with bishops who pursued the death of criminals. From this he explains the place [Col. 1042B] where the woman was brought forward and discusses at length the remission of sins. Finally, he reviews and elucidates each part of the same story from the Gospel.

### AMBROSE [Note: [Col. 1041D] All editions read *Studio*; all manuscripts read *Irenaeo*, except the Corbie, German, and Fulda codices, in which the opening sentence is omitted and the text continues with the letter to Bellicius, numbered 75 in the old edition and 45 in the Roman edition. It is certain from the subject that this letter was written to no one other than the person to whom the preceding letter is addressed; yet for that very reason it is more credible that the editors substituted *Studio* for *Irenaeo* than that scribes substituted *Irenaeo* for *Studio*. Since the recipient of these letters could have been called Studius Irenaeus, there is nothing to prevent the first letter from having been addressed under the first name and the later one under the second.] TO IRENAEUS

1. Although in my preceding letter I already resolved the little question which you proposed, nevertheless, since you seek something fuller, I have not refrained from bringing it forward and carving it out for you as for a son.

2. This question has always been famous, and the woman’s acquittal celebrated: she was brought before Christ as guilty of adultery in the Gospel according to John (John 8:11). The Jews devised this evasive maneuver so that, if she were acquitted contrary to the Law, the Lord Jesus’ sentence would be held contrary to the Law; but if she were condemned according to the Law, Christ’s grace would appear void.

3. The issue became more pressing after bishops began, in public tribunals, to accuse men guilty of the gravest crimes [Note: [Col. 1042D] The Corbie, German, and Fulda manuscripts read: “some accused and pressed them … others [approved] such accusations”; the German manuscript reads: “they began to disapprove of such accusers.” What most accords with the truth is the view held by Hermann, *Life of Ambrose* book V, chapter 4, and book VII, chapter 1, as well as by Thomassin, volume I, part I, book II, chapter 11: namely, that the bishops designated here were the Ithacians. At their instigation the tyrant Maximus ordered Priscillian to be executed, as Sulpicius Severus records in book II. How greatly the very gentle spirit of Ambrose recoiled from their cruelty is clear not only from this and the preceding letter, but also from what he wrote in *Exposition of Psalm 118*, sermon 8, number 41, and *On the Duties*, book II, chapter 21.], while others began to press them all the way to the sword and ultimate death, and still others to approve such accusations and the bloody triumphs of priests. What else are these men saying than what the Jews said: that those guilty of crimes should be punished by the public laws, and therefore that even priests ought to accuse in public tribunals those whom, as they assert, the laws required to be punished? The cause is the same, but the number is smaller—that is, the question of judgment is not different, [Col. 1043A] but the resentment over the punishment is different [Note: [Col. 1043D] The old edition and some manuscripts read: “but almost different resentment.”]. Christ did not allow one woman to be punished according to the Law; these men assert that a smaller number has been punished.

4. But in what place does Christ pass this judgment? [Note: [Col. 1043D] Ambrose had said the same thing, in precisely this sense, in *On the Holy Spirit*, book III, chapter 17: “It is therefore worth observing in what place the Lord discussed these matters; for his declarations are often assessed according to the character of the places in which he stayed.”] For he generally shaped his discussions according to the character of the places in which he deigned to teach his servants. Thus, walking in Solomon’s portico—that is, the portico of the wise—he said: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30); and in the temple of God he said: “My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me” (John 7:16). He also exercises this judgment while situated in the temple, as is written later; for you have this: “Jesus spoke these words in the treasury, teaching in the temple, and no one seized him” (John 8:20). [Col. 1043B] What is the treasury? The contribution of the faithful, the expense of the poor, the refuge of the needy. Accordingly, while sitting there, Christ—as you find in Luke—judged the widow’s two coins preferable to the gifts of the rich (Luke 21:2), preferring, by divine testimony, to the rewards of lavish generosity [Note: [Col. 1043D] The Corbie, German, and Fulda manuscripts read: “the devotion of diligent freedom.”] the devoted affection of careful liberality.

## 895

5. Let us see what he himself, who had such a judgment, was contributing while situated near the treasury; for he did not prefer the woman who cast in two coins without purpose. That poverty is precious, rich in the mystery of faith. These are the two coins which that Gospel Samaritan left with the innkeeper for the care of the wounds of the man who had fallen among robbers (Luke 10:35). Thus, in this figure also, he considered that the widow—who represents the Church—should contribute to this sacred treasury, so that the wounds of the poor might be healed and the fasts of travelers relieved.

6. Therefore you must now consider spiritually what Christ is contributing. He was distributing among the peoples silver tested by fire, the words of heaven, and was counting the money bearing the royal image among the affections of the peoples (Psalm 11:6). No one put in more than the one who gave everything. He satisfied the hungry, filled the needy, enlightened the blind, redeemed captives, raised up paralytics, restored the dead to life, and, what is greater, granted acquittal to the guilty and forgave sins. These are the two coins which the Church sent [Note: [Col. 1044D] The Thuanus manuscript adds: “after she received Christ.”] after she received them from Christ. For what are the two coins except the price of the New and Old Testaments? [Col. 1043D] The price of Scripture is our faith, for what is read is valued according to the judgment of the understanding. The remission of sins, therefore, is the price of both Testaments, [Note: [Col. 1044D] Four manuscripts read: “which was announced in figure through the lamb throughout the year,” etc.] announced in figure through the lamb and completed in reality through Christ.

7. Hence you have the fact that the purification of seven days does not exist without the purification of three days (Exodus 12:3). The seven-day purification is according to the Law (Leviticus 12:2), which, in the figure of the present Sabbath, announced the spiritual Sabbath; the three-day purification is according to grace, which is signified by the testimony of the Gospel (Luke 24:7), because the Lord rose on the third day. Where punishment is prescribed, there must be repentance for sins; where remission is granted, there is grace. Repentance comes first; grace follows. Therefore neither repentance exists without grace nor grace without repentance; for repentance must first condemn sin, so that grace may abolish it. Hence John, receiving the Law’s figure, baptized for repentance, while Christ baptized for grace (Matthew 3:11).

8. [Note: [Col. 1044D] See what Ambrose discusses in *Exposition of Luke*, book VII, number 49, and what we have noted there.] The seventh day, therefore, signifies the mystery of the Law, and the eighth the resurrection, as you have in Ecclesiastes: “Give a portion to seven, and also to eight” (Ecclesiastes 11:2). In the prophet Hosea, too, you read that he was told: “Take for yourself a prostitute for fifteen denarii” (Hosea 3:1), since, by the twofold coin of the Old and New Testament—that is, by the complete price of faith—that woman is taken in, supported by a wandering and meretricious retinue of foreign nations.

9. “And I took her,” he says, “for a homer of barley, and half a homer, and a nevel of wine” (ibid., 2). By barley he signifies that he would call the imperfect to faith in order to make them perfect: the homer signifies a full measure, and the half-homer a half-full measure. The full measure is in the Gospel; the half-full measure is in the Law, whose fullness is the New Testament. For the Lord himself says: “I have not come to abolish the Law, but to fulfill it” [Col. 1044C] (Matthew 5:17).

10. Nor is it without purpose that we read of David’s fifteen psalms of ascents, and of the sun ascending fifteen steps when Hezekiah, the righteous king, received a prolongation of this life (Isaiah 38:8). For it signified that the sun of righteousness was to come (Malachi 4:2), illuminating the fifteen steps of the Old and New Testaments by the light of his presence, by which our faith ascends to eternal life. Hence I think that what was read today from the Apostle (Galatians 1:18) is also mystical, because he remained with Peter for fifteen days. It seems to me that, as the holy apostles exchanged among themselves in varied speech their interpretation of the divine Scriptures, a brightness of full light shone forth and the shadow of ignorance departed. But now let us come to the acquittal of this adulterous woman.

11. She had been brought before the Lord Jesus by the scribes and Pharisees as guilty of adultery (John 8:3 and following), and she was brought forward with this stratagem: if he acquitted her, he would appear to abolish the Law; but if he condemned her, he would appear to alter the purpose of his coming, since he came to forgive the sins of all. Indeed, above he says: “I judge no one” (John 8:15). So, when they brought her forward, they said: “We found this woman openly committing adultery. For it is written in the law of Moses that every adulteress should be stoned. But what do you say about her?” (Leviticus 20:10).

12. While they were saying these things, Jesus, with his head bent, was writing with his finger on the ground. When they continued waiting to hear him, he raised his head and said: “Let the one among you who is without sin be the first to stone her.” What is as divine as this sentence: that the one who is himself free from sin should punish sins? For how could you tolerate someone who avenges another’s crime while defending his own? Does he not condemn himself more severely when he condemns in another what he himself commits?

13. Having said this, he wrote on the ground. What did he write? Certainly this: “You see the splinter that is in your brother’s eye, but you do not see the beam that is in your own eye” (Matthew 7:3). Lust is like a splinter: it is quickly kindled and quickly consumed. The sacrilege of faithlessness—by which the Jews denied the author of their own salvation—was resounding with the magnitude of its crime [Note: [Col. 1045D] Some manuscripts read: “the faithlessness toward the author of salvation,” etc.].

14. [Note: [Col. 1045D] Three manuscripts read: “Sinners are written on earth, the righteous in heaven.”] He was writing on the ground with the finger with which he had written the Law (Exodus 31:18). Sinners are written on earth, but the righteous in heaven, as he said to the disciples: “Rejoice, because your names are written in heaven” (Jeremiah 17:13). He wrote a second time so that you might know that the Jews were condemned by the twofold Testament (Luke 10:20).

15. When they heard this word, they went out one by one, beginning with the elders, and they sat there considering themselves [Col. 1045C] (John 8:6). Jesus alone remained, and the woman standing in the midst. He rightly says that they went out, since they did not wish to be with Christ. Outside is the letter; inside are the mysteries. They were following certain things in the divine readings like the leaves of trees, not the fruit: they lived in the shadow of the Law and could not see the sun of righteousness.

16. Finally, when they had departed, Jesus alone remained, and the woman standing in the midst. When he is about to grant forgiveness of sin, Jesus remains alone, as he himself says: “Behold, the hour is coming, and has already come, when you will be scattered, each to his own, and you will leave me alone” (John 16:32); for it was not an ambassador or messenger, but the Lord himself, who saved his people (Isaiah 63:8). He remains alone because no human being can share with Christ this power of forgiving sins. This is Christ’s sole prerogative, for he took away the sin of the world (John 1:29). The woman also deserved to be acquitted: when the Jews departed, she remained alone with Jesus.

17. Then Jesus raised his head and said to the woman: “Where are they who accused you? Has no one stoned you?” And [Col. 1046A] she replied: “No one, Lord.” And Jesus said to her: “Neither will I condemn you; go, and from now on be careful not to sin” (John 8:10–11). Observe, reader, the divine mysteries and Christ’s mercy. When the woman is accused, Christ bows his head; but he raises it when the accuser is absent. Thus he wishes no one to be condemned, but all to be acquitted.

18. In brief, he destroys all the questions of the heretics when he says: “Has no one stoned you?” [Note: [Col. 1045D] The Roman edition has *condemned*, *condemned*, and *to condemn*, whereas the other editions and all the manuscripts have *stoned*, etc.]—those who say that Christ does not know the day of judgment, or who quote him as saying: “But to sit at my right hand or at my left is not mine to grant you” (Matthew 20:23). Behold, here too he says: “Has no one stoned you?” How does he ask about what he sees? He asks for our sake, so that we might know that she had not been stoned. It is also a habit arising from human feeling that we very often ask about what we see. And therefore the woman replied: “No one, Lord”—which is to say: “Who can stone one whom you yourself do not condemn? Who can punish another under the condition of such a sentence?”

19. The Lord replied to her: “Neither will I condemn you.” Notice how he tempered his own sentence, so that the Jews could find nothing to accuse him of regarding the woman’s acquittal, but would turn the accusation back upon themselves if they wished to complain: the woman is dismissed, not acquitted, because there was no accuser [Note: [Col. 1045D] The edition reads: “not because she was proved innocent.”]. What complaint, then, could they make, when they themselves had first ceased prosecuting the charge and carrying out the punishment?

20. He also added to the woman who had gone astray: “Go, and from now on be careful not to sin.” He corrected the guilty woman; he did not acquit the crime. For guilt is condemned by a more severe sentence if each person hates his own crime and begins to condemn the offense in himself. When a guilty person is killed, it is the person rather than the guilt that is punished; but when guilt is laid aside, the acquittal of the person becomes the punishment of the sin. What, then, does “Go, and from now on be careful not to sin” mean? It means: Since Christ has redeemed you, let grace correct what punishment could not reform but only chastise. [Note: [Col. 1045D] The Corbie and Fulda manuscripts read: “let grace correct what punishment could not”; with these words they conclude the letter.] Farewell, son, and love us as a son, because we love you as parents.

---

## 898 [Note: [Col. 1046D] Written around A.D. 387.] EPISTLE XXVII

He teaches Irenaeus that the Egyptians’ abominations were livestock; from this it is understood that piety and virtue displease the wicked, and consequently that good men ought to persist in pursuits opposed to theirs. This is illustrated by the example of Jacob’s wives, who agreed to flee from their father and follow their husband. Through this allegory it is explained what those approaching the Church ought to practice.

### AMBROSE [Note: [Col. 1046D] It is uncertain who that Irenaeus was to whom so many of Ambrose’s letters are extant. Nevertheless, we conjecture that he was a deacon, or rather a priest of the second rank: first, because in the following letter our saintly author gives him instructions concerning the priestly life; and second, because from Letter 33 we learn that he consulted Irenaeus about difficulties in Scripture. Since Ambrose greets the same man as “son” at the end of the letters and praises him for enduring persecutions for Christ’s glory with steadfast courage, it may perhaps reasonably be inferred that he lived among the clergy of Milan during the persecution stirred up by Justina.] GREETS IRENAEUS

1. You indicated to me that you were troubled because you had read: [Col. 1047A] “Let us sacrifice to God what is abominable among the Egyptians” (Exodus 8:26). [Note: [Col. 1047D] The Roman edition reads: “For we shall sacrifice to the Lord God the abominations of the Egyptians.” The Pratensis and Gembloux codices read: “what is abominated among the Egyptians, sacrificed to God”; the others, together with the old edition, read: “let us sacrifice to God.” The same Roman edition, with one Vatican codex, again reads: “that you might resolve this”; the other editions, more suitably, read: “by which you might resolve this.”] But you had the means by which to resolve this, because it is written in Genesis that the Egyptians abominated a shepherd of livestock (Genesis 46:34)—not, of course, because of the man, but because of the livestock. They turned the soil with the plow; but Abraham and Jacob, and later Moses and David [Note: [Col. 1047D] After “shepherds,” the Roman edition alone repeats “of livestock”; whereas the old edition and by far the majority of the manuscripts read: “assuming a discipline in this office.” The same Roman edition, with only two codices, reads: “indicating a discipline.” “Entering upon” would not be objectionable, but we do not detract from the more widely received reading.] were shepherds, taking up in this office a kind of royal discipline.

2. [Note: [Col. 1047D] Thus the old edition and the manuscripts; the Roman edition, however, reads “spotless sacrifices.” This is evidently drawn from Philo’s *On Fugitives*, where he writes, *τέλεια γὰρ καὶ ἄμωμα ἱερεῖα αἱ ἀρεταί* (“for the virtues are perfect and unblemished sacrificial victims”); similar words also occur in *On Sacrifices*. But perhaps “sacrifices offered” here means the same as “perfect,” since their perfection required that they be sprinkled with salted meal, from which the word for sacrificing (*immolandi*) is derived.] The Egyptians therefore hated sacrificed victims—that is, perfect pursuits of virtue, complete in discipline. What the vicious hate is therefore pure and pious among the good. The luxurious glutton recoils from the work of virtue [Note: [Col. 1048D] All editions and some manuscripts read: “the luxurious glutton, the Egyptian, avoids”; thus the body, etc. The other manuscripts, which are also the more reliable, read as in the text. Philo confirms this reading in the cited book *On the Flight from the World*, from which much has been transferred here. He writes there: “The pleasure-loving Egyptian abominates the body” (*Τὸ φιλοπαθὲς Αἰγύπτιον βδελύττεται σῶμα*).] and avoids it. Thus the Egyptian body, which loves enticements, turns away from the virtues of the soul, abominates authority, recoils from the disciplines of virtue, and rejects all works of this kind.

3. Whatever, then, the Egyptian avoids—that Egyptian who is not truly human—you should embrace, since you possess knowledge of humanity. But shun what he follows and chooses, because prudence and folly cannot agree with one another. Just as prudence and self-control reject whatever belongs to the category of imprudence and intemperance, so every fool and incontinent person is excluded from what belongs among the goods and inheritance of the wise and self-controlled.

4. Finally, those holy women, Leah and Rachel—one laborious, the other a strong aspiration—rejected not kinship of race but difference of character. When they had been instructed by their husband Jacob that he wished to depart in order to escape the envy and laziness of Laban and his sons, they replied: “Have we still a portion or an inheritance in our father’s house? Are we not regarded by him as strangers? For he sold us and devoured our price” (Genesis 31:14–15). Behold, first, that the lazy and envious man alienates from himself and avoids the laborious woman who is steadfast in discipline, and wants to separate himself from her, because he sees her as a burden to him; he thinks he has made a profit by alienating her, and judges that this is her price and the fruit of his pleasure.

5. Now let us hear how virtue possesses what laziness does not [Col. 1048A]. For they say: “All the wealth and glory that God took from our father shall be ours and our children’s” (ibid., 26). They rightly say that it was taken away by God’s judgment, because he is the author of good things, by whose grace the lazy are stripped; for the wicked and weak cannot grasp the beauty of the divine inheritance. But the one who is attentive succeeds within, possessing a strong spirit in himself. Who, however, is strong except God alone, who restrains and governs all things?

6. To such people, therefore, God’s inheritance is due. Hence Isaiah also says: “There is an inheritance for those who believe in the Lord” (Isaiah 54:17). Beautifully he says: “There is an inheritance”; for it alone is inheritance—there is no other. A blind treasure is not inheritance, nor does everything that passes away possess the benefit of inheritance; that inheritance belongs only to those for whom God is their portion. [Note: [Col. 1048D] The Roman edition alone reads: “Hence holy David invites us.”] Therefore the holy one of the Lord says: “The Lord is my portion” (Psalm 118:57); and elsewhere: “I have become heir to your testimonies” (ibid., 111). You see what the righteous man possesses: God’s commands, his utterances, and his precepts. In these he is rich, in these he feeds, in these he delights, as though in all riches.

7. Possessing these things, Leah and Rachel did not seek their father’s wealth, in which there was counterfeit money, irrational appearance, and no spiritual vigor. Finally, like women who were rich and free, they considered him not rich but needy. Everyone who shares in good and liberal disciplines [Note: [Col. 1048D] Cicero argues in the last of his *Paradoxes* that only the wise man is rich; the same opinion is repeated by Philo in the book already cited; consult it.] considers no fool rich, but poor and needy, even rejected—although he may overflow with royal riches and proudly boast of his power in gold.

8. The company of such people must therefore be avoided, even if some bond of kinship unites one to them. Association with fools is harmful: it infects and discolors a sober mind. For just as “with the holy you will be holy,” so “with the perverse you will be perverse” (Psalm 17:26–27). [Note: [Col. 1048D] After the words “you will be perverse,” the Roman edition adds, “as it is written.”] It frequently happens that someone who, despite his own resolve, listens to an incontinent person is colored by the dye of folly, even though he himself wishes to maintain the discipline of self-control. Therefore discipline and insolence are rightly contrary and opposed to each other.

9. When the husband, experienced in discipline, asked their opinion, they raised a voice already proved by long practice of virtue: “Have we still a portion or an inheritance in our father’s house?” (Genesis 31:14)—that is, [Col. 1049A] “Are you asking us whether we wish to leave him?” [Note: [Col. 1049D] Many manuscripts read: “As though you did not know us.”] As though you did not know that we have no desire at all for his company, and that no sweet desire for the riches of worldly things or joy in luxury holds us [Note: [Col. 1049D] The old edition and all the manuscripts read this way; the Roman edition has removed the words “by many”]. These are the things which we have regarded as wretched and alien to us; these are what we consider full of poverty and want.

10. They add the reason for their separation: Laban had lost true glory and the abundance of a good treasure, in which we are born. [Note: [Col. 1049D] All editions and some manuscripts read: “in which the greatest vigor was given … because he lost the spiritual coin, because …” But besides the fact that three times as many manuscripts establish our reading, clarity of sense also supports it.] The vigor of the mind and the good coin of the image and likeness of God had been given him, because it was spiritual coin. He lost it because he chose what was more splendid in the world rather than what was true and useful for his life. Their beauty passes by one who is deprived of divine goods, since in what he considers beautiful he deceives and misleads himself. [Col. 1049B] Hear his words, therefore, and judge.

11. He followed holy Jacob and his daughters, lest perhaps he should find in them something of his own vices and thus retain authority to call them back to himself. Rebuking the righteous man, although he had been refuted with reason and could find nothing to say or allege by which he ought to hold him, he said: “If you had told me, I would have sent you away” (ibid., 27). In this he revealed what the righteous man had fled: lest Laban pursue him, escort him, or send him away accompanied by such a retinue. First, Jacob ought not to have subjected himself to the bondage of many masters, so that he would be dismissed by Laban like a little slave. Then, because the man intent upon discipline and seeking the true way to virtue did not seek a human guide to escort him, but heavenly oracles. “They,” he says, “commanded me to depart from here, and now accompany me as I travel.”

12. “But how would you have sent me away? With your joy, surely, which is full of sorrow—with tambourines and organs [Note: [Col. 1049D] The Roman edition alone reads: “with unmodulated musicians playing”; the others and the manuscripts read: “excessive,” and some of these: “with musicians playing excessively.” Below, where all editions except Amerbach’s read “with silent voices,” nearly all the manuscripts prefer “with many voices.” This must be attributed to the scribes’ lack of understanding; Ambrose was referring here to Philo’s *κτύπων ἀνάρθρων καὶ ἀλόγων* (“of inarticulate and irrational sounds”).] playing without restraint, with the sweet sounds of pipes producing unpleasant echoes, with discordant sounds, clashing rattles, silent voices, and cymbals striking the soul? Did you think I could take delight in these things? That I could be recalled by them? These are what I fled; nor do I fear the resentment provoked by your words. I fled lest such things follow me, lest I depart carrying away anything of yours.”

13. For one does not reach the Church of Christ by such escorts, the Church toward which Jacob was heading, so that he might lead there the armies of peoples, bring in the riches of nations, and pour forth posterity—fleeing the shadows of empty things, preferring the living beauty of virtues to senseless images, and serious matters to things that win applause. You see how the pagans adorn banquets and announce festivals; but these are more hostile to pious minds, because many are deceived by them and captivated by sweet banquets, captivated by dancers’ choruses, while they flee our fasts, regard them as harsh, and think them harmful and burdensome to the body.

14. Did you suppose that I desired your gold? But you do not possess gold tested by fire, by which the righteous are proved (Psalm 11:7). Or did I desire silver? But you do not possess silver, [Note: [Col. 1050D] The same Roman edition adds: “because you have cast away the splendor of heavenly speech.”] since you do not possess the splendor of heavenly speech. Perhaps I hoped that you would add your little slaves to serve me? [Col. 1050B] But I seek free men; I flee slaves of sin. Perhaps companions for the journey and guides along the roads were necessary? If only they could follow! I would show them the Lord’s ways. But since you do not know God, how do you know his ways? The chosen enter his ways; not everyone enters them, but no one is excluded.

15. Let the one who is prepared follow; let him enter the road that leads to Mesopotamia, so that the one who seeks it may cross the waters—the waters of the Tigris and the Euphrates, of strength and righteousness—through the tears of repentance and the baptism of grace. [Note: [Col. 1050D] All editions read: “in it there is virtue”; all manuscripts: “in it there is a road.”] In it is the way of God’s army; for all who are in the Church serve as soldiers for God. In it is that distinguished flock of diverse virtues which Jacob chose for himself. Every soul without a mark is ignorant and untrained, knowing nothing of discipline; but the soul that bears a mark is likewise rich in works and abundant in graces.

16. Whoever comes to it must first reconcile an angry brother [Col. 1050C]. Whoever comes to it must inhabit that precious and active Shechem—the workshop of virtues—in which violated chastity receives severe retribution. Whoever comes to it must wrestle with God, so that he may train himself in imitation of him and enter into the humility and sufferings of Christ. Let him take up his cross and follow Christ (Matthew 16:24). Finally, the good wrestler does not envy or become swollen with pride; indeed, he blesses the one who wrestles against him with such a gift.

17. Let us therefore follow holy Jacob and his ways, so that we may arrive at those sufferings and those struggles, [Note: [Col. 1050D] The old edition and all the manuscripts read: “Let us reach the wall”; the Roman edition reads: “Let us reach the shoulder.” We could not but retain this correction. It is obvious that Shechem is designated here, a name which Ambrose invariably interprets as “shoulder.” Consult the preceding volume, *On Abraham*, book I, chapter 2, number 5; book II, chapter 3, number 8; *On Joseph*, chapter 3, number 9; *On the Blessing of the Patriarchs*, chapter 3, number 11, and elsewhere.] let us reach the shoulder; let us reach patience, the mother of the faithful, and Father Isaac—that is, one capable of joy and overflowing with gladness. Where there is patience, there is joy, because after tribulations comes patience, and patience produces testing, in which there is hope—hope by which we are not put to shame. For whoever is not ashamed of the cross of Christ will not have Christ put to shame in him (Romans 5:3). Farewell, son, and do not be ashamed to question your father, since you are not ashamed to glory in the sufferings of Christ.

---

## 902 [Note: [Col. 1051C] Written around A.D. 387.] EPISTLE XXVIII

The Pythagorean maxim that the common road ought to be avoided is shown to have been taken from the sacred writings; from this it is inferred that the priestly life ought to shrink from ordinary life. Hence Ambrose urges Irenaeus to flee popular opinions and desires, to enter the Lord’s gates and the narrow road leading upward, and to tread it.

### AMBROSE GREETS IRENAEUS

1. We find a Pythagorean injunction [Note: [Col. 1051C] We understand this to refer to no one other than Philo, who, at the beginning of his book *That Every Good Person Is Free*, aptly and elegantly explains the Pythagorean saying *ταῖς λεωφόροις μὴ βαδίζειν ὁδοῖς* (“not to walk on the broad public roads”), which he calls *ἱερώτατον θίασον* (“a most sacred association”). Erasmus also includes the same saying among the Pythagorean symbols [Col. 1051D] and, following Jerome, explains it in precisely the same sense. Laertius, book VIII; Justin, book XX; Arnobius, book I *Against the Nations*; and others relate how the Pythagoreans observed this injunction and how, because the vast majority of them aroused the hatred of the other people whom they avoided, they were destroyed by slaughter.] celebrated in the writings of certain men: Pythagoras prohibited his disciples from entering the common and customary road used by the people. But where he took this is not unknown. Since, as most believe, he traced his origin to the Jewish people, he derived the precepts of his teaching from their discipline as well. And rightly he was regarded as great among philosophers; he scarcely found an equal, as they say. [Note: [Col. 1051D] The old edition and all the manuscripts read this way; the Roman edition reads: “one scarcely finds his equal,” indicating in a marginal note that it was taken from Virgil’s epigram. It is true that among the epigrams attributed to Maro there is one, also found among Ausonius’ *Idylls*, containing that half-line; but it reads *reperit* (“he finds”), not *reperis* (“you find”). Nevertheless, one should not say that Ambrose was referring to that passage, but either to Josephus, who in book I *Against Apion* awards Pythagoras the palm of piety and wisdom, or to Ovid’s testimony in book XV of the *Metamorphoses*, where he sings of the same philosopher:

> In mind he approached the gods, and what nature denied  
> To human eyes, he grasped with the eyes of his heart.

Or finally to some other ancient passages in which Pythagoras is frequently praised.] He had therefore read in Exodus that Moses had received this divine command by oracle: “Remove the sandal from your feet” (Exodus 3:5). He had read the same command given to Joshua [Note: [Col. 1051D] There is considerable disagreement among the ancients about Pythagoras’ birthplace, as may be learned from Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, book I; Diogenes Laertius, book VIII; and others, to which we add the learned Huet, *Demonstratio Evangelica*, book I, proposition 4, chapter 2. As for the statement here that Pythagoras drew extensively from Jewish sources, we add nothing to what we noted on this matter in the preceding volume, in *Exposition of Psalm 118*, sermon V, and elsewhere.] (Joshua 5:15), namely, that those who desired to walk on the Lord’s road should put aside the dust of the worn and popular road. He had read the command given to the same Moses that he should ascend the mountain with the priests, while the people stood apart (Exodus 24:13–14). He therefore separated the priests from the people and afterward commanded Moses himself to enter within the cloud.

2. Do you see the distinctions? Nothing plebeian, nothing popular, nothing common with the pursuits, habits, and customs of the uncultivated multitude is required in priests. The priestly dignity claims for itself sober gravity before the crowds, a serious life, and singular weight. For how can someone who has nothing secret or distinct from the people be respected by the people, someone who differs in nothing from the multitude? What would they admire in you if they recognized their own ways in you? What if they saw nothing in you beyond themselves, or encountered in you—the one they consider worthy of reverence—the very things of which they are ashamed in themselves?

3. Let us therefore rise above plebeian opinions, and turn aside from certain tracks of herd-like conduct and the ruts of a well-worn road; let us avoid the ground of the common path, along which runs the man whose life is lighter than a runner’s, of whom it is said: “He passed by, and did not see” (Job 9:25).

[Note: The latest Paris edition reads *transivi, et non vidi* (“I passed by, and did not see”). Below, where our text, together with the older edition and several better manuscripts, reads *fumo iniquitatis* (“with the smoke of iniquity”), the Roman edition, along with other manuscripts, has *fimo iniquitatis* (“with the dung of iniquity”). The sense is not unfavorable. Some manuscripts, instead of *oblitus* (“covered”), prefer *obligatus inscitiae* (“bound by ignorance”).]

Let us seek for ourselves a way inaccessible to the speech of the arrogant, untrodden by the works of the ignorant, which no defiled person may wear down—defiled, that is, by the filth of his own sloth—

[Note: The Roman edition has *et fimo iniquitatis oblitus* (“and covered with the dung of iniquity”).]

—and covered with the smoke of iniquity, ruined by darkness and by certain crumbling walls of the soul, who has never tasted the sweetness of virtue, or who at least has thought that it should be viewed obliquely rather than received with direct affection and an open heart; and—what most people who seem witty and urbane are fond of doing, transforming the beauty of wisdom into the disgrace of cleverness—not beholding true grace, as though placed in the night, he does not believe those who live in the day. For he belongs to the number of the Temanites and Sabeans who fail and turn away from the truth, of whom Job says:

“Look at the roads of the Temanites and the paths of the Sabeans: they will fall into confusion, those who place their hope in cities and riches. Thus you have risen against me without mercy; therefore, when you see my wound, be afraid” (Job 6:19 and following).

4. Let us therefore abandon these wandering paths of those who turn aside, and that dust of those who fail, who, through their own desire, have often fallen in the wilderness. Let us turn instead and follow the way of wisdom, which the sons of those who glorify and boast of themselves have not trodden,

[Col. 1052C]

which destruction does not know and death does not recognize, because God has directed it:

“The abyss said, ‘It is not in me’; the sea said, ‘It is not with me’” (Job 28:14).

But if you seek the way of wisdom and discipline, to worship God and to be subject to him is wisdom; to refrain from sins is discipline.

5. What, then, have we to do with the way of this age, in which there is temptation—or rather, human life itself is temptation—and with a life more fleeting than a tale: dwelling in houses of clay,

[Col. 1053A]

spending days and nights on profits, always thinking about profits, and seeking a day-laborer’s daily wage, and, as they say of cicadas, feeding upon a certain breath of the desires? Truly like cicadas, because they live from day to day,

[Note: The old edition has *quaestuque*; the Roman edition, *questuque*; several manuscripts omit the conjunction *-que*, not improperly. Yet they pronounce *quaestu* with a diphthong less elegantly. Here there is a clear allusion to Virgil, *Georgics* 3:

“And the plaintive cicadas will split the groves with song.”

As for the holy Bishop’s assertion that these same cicadas live on air, he may have had in mind either Aristotle, *History of Animals* 1.7, or Pliny, *Natural History* 2.26, but especially Virgil, *Eclogues* 5, where we read:

“While bees feed on thyme, while cicadas feed on dew.”

It is certain, however, that here he is imitating Philo, from the cited book, *That Every Good Person Is Free*, near the beginning.]

they are worn out by their own gain. For what else are men without weight, without discipline, except that they seem like cicadas, born for a single day and death, making more noise than speech? They soothe themselves amid the heat of burning desires with a song harmful to themselves, and soon perish, bearing no fruit and possessing no grace.

The paths of such people are therefore harmful and crooked like those of serpents, which drag themselves along with the poisonous movement of their bodies and gather themselves into a spiral of wickedness,

[Note: Several manuscripts have *in sphaeram* (“into a sphere”); others, together with the editions, have *in spiram* (“into a spiral”). Virgil, *Georgics* 2:

“The scaly serpent gathers itself into a spiral by its winding movement.”]

and cannot raise themselves toward heavenly things.

6. Let us enter the gates of the Lord, the gates of righteousness; when the righteous person has entered them, he gives thanks to the Lord (Psalm 117:19). But this entrance belongs to few, as the Lord says: “For narrow is the gate and constricted the way that leads to life, and few are those who find it” (Matthew 7:14). But the wide gate and broad way, along which many walk, leads to death and brings its travelers there.

904

7. Let our way therefore be narrower, our strength more abundant, our track more confined, our faith more exalted, our path more constricted, our mental vigor overflowing, and our paths straight; for the footprints of virtues are unbending. Hence Solomon says: “O those who have abandoned straight paths!” (Proverbs 2:13).

8. Let our step be directed upward, since it is better to ascend. Indeed, as has been read today: “Woe to those who go down into Egypt” (Isaiah 31:1)! It is not, of course, a crime to cross into Egypt; but it is a crime to cross into the customs of the Egyptians, to cross into the violence of their faithlessness and the deformity of luxury.

[Note: The old edition and not a few manuscripts have “their faithlessness, their appetite for food, and their luxury”; some have “their greed and the deformity of luxury”; Pratell and Gem have “the violence of faithlessness, the appetite for food, and the deformity of luxury”; others, together with the Roman edition, have “the savagery of faithlessness”; Albin has “blindness,” and so forth.]

Whoever crosses over there descends; whoever descends falls. Let us therefore avoid the Egyptian man, and not God. For even the king of the Egyptians himself had been handed over to the power of his own vices; in comparison with him Moses was considered a god, ruling kingdoms and subjecting powers to himself. Hence we read that he was told: “I have made you a god to Pharaoh” (Exodus 7:1).

Farewell, and love us as a son, as you do.

[Note: Written about the year 387.]

# LETTER XXIX

He urges the pursuit of the beauty of the highest good, promising that our eye will be refreshed by it and our soul nourished, since this is the soul’s food, the knowledge of which God reveals to the saints and which David eagerly sought. This good must be held fast with care, since it is the very good announced by the Evangelists, namely Christ. Whoever receives this good with desire will attain to knowledge of the mysteries and will already neglect the things of the body, to which the Apostle exhorts us. The soul must therefore be raised above its affections, so that it may be borne toward that good in which the fountain of life is found, and to which we are brought only by virtue. Yet perseverance and constancy are necessary for this work.

**AMBROSE TO IRENAEUS, GREETING.**

1. While reading, when I had rested my mind for a little while,

[Note: The edition reads, “not because he is approved as innocent.”]

[Col. 1054B]

because I had stopped my nocturnal labor,

[Note: The passage concerns the first vigils, which were completed immediately at the first hour of the night. Jerome also speaks of them in Letter 7 to Leta, in these words: “And, with the lamp lit, let her grow accustomed to offering the evening sacrifice.” From the lamp came the term *lucernarium* (“lighting of the lamp”), mentioned by Epiphanius in the *Anacephalaeosis*, Basil in *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 29, and Chrysostom in Homily 19 to the Antiochenes. Of the other two vigils, held at midnight and at sunrise, Ambrose speaks clearly in *On Abraham* 1.9, *On Elijah and Fasting* 15, on Psalm 36, verse 25, and on Psalm 118, Sermon 19.]

I began to turn over in my mind that verse which we had used in the evening at the vigils:

[Note: The editors interpret this verse commonly as referring to Christ’s bodily appearance, whereas the ancient Fathers understood it of his inward beauty alone, considering the lowliness of his bodily form to belong to the humility of the Incarnation. On this matter see Rigaltius’s dissertation *On the Beauty of Christ*.]

“Beautiful in beauty beyond the sons of men” (Psalm 44:3).

“How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim him” (Isaiah 52:7).

And truly nothing is more beautiful than that highest good, whose proclamation also is exceedingly beautiful, especially in the continuous progression of its discourse and in the traces, as it were, of apostolic preaching. But who can equal those preachers? Those to whom God granted not only to announce Christ, but also to suffer for him.

2. Let us, as far as we can, direct our minds toward him and be in him; let us hold in our minds that which is beautiful, honorable, and good, so that through its illumination and radiance our soul may become beautiful and our mind bright. For if our eyes are covered by some dimness, they are nourished by the greenness of the fields and the beauty of the woodland, or of a grassy hill, which dispels every unevenness of the ailing gaze; and the pupils and orbs themselves seem to be colored by a certain healthful beauty. How much more does this eye of the mind, when it beholds that highest good, dwells in it, and feeds upon it, shine and sparkle, so that what is written may come to pass:

“Let my soul be filled as with marrow and fatness” (Psalm 21:21)!

Indeed, the one who knowingly recognizes the souls of his flock takes care to provide meadow grasses, so that there may be abundant pasture for him; for with sweeter grasses the lambs become fatter and the milk’s yield healthier. The rich who ate and worshiped made use of such pastures (Psalm 22:1); for these are the pastures of faith in which God’s holy one is placed.

3. There is therefore also hay with which flocks of sheep are nourished—sheep that produce the fleeces of wisdom and provide a garment of prudence. Perhaps this is the mountain hay upon which the words of the prophets descend:

“As snow upon the hay” (Deuteronomy 32:2);

and which the wise man diligently gathers, so that he may have sheep for clothing, namely, for a spiritual covering (Proverbs 27:25). The soul that clings to that highest good, which is divine, therefore possesses both its food and its clothing. The Apostle Peter urges us to seek this good, so that through acquiring knowledge of it we may become partakers of the divine nature (2 Peter 1:4).

[Col. 1055B]

4. God, who is good, opens the knowledge of this good to his saints and gives it from his good treasure, as the sacred Law bears witness, saying:

“Because the Lord swore to your fathers that he would give you and open for you his good treasure” (Deuteronomy 28:11–12).

[Note: Several manuscripts have “to your fathers, that he might open the treasure.”]

From this heavenly treasure he gives rain to his land, to bless all the works of your hands. This is the rain of the utterance of the Law, which waters the soul that is fertile and fruitful in good works, so that it may possess the moisture of grace (Deuteronomy 32:2).

5. David sought knowledge of this good, as he himself indicates, saying:

“One thing I asked of the Lord, this I will seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, and behold the delights of the Lord and contemplate his temple” (Psalm 26:4).

He immediately added in the same psalm that this is the highest good:

“I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (ibid., 13).

Here it is sought; there it will be seen fully, face to face. This good is in the house of God, in his secret place and retreat. Hence he says again:

“We shall be filled with the good things of your house” (Psalm 64:5).

Elsewhere also he expressed that this is the summit of blessing, saying:

“May the Lord bless you from Zion, and may you see the good things of Jerusalem” (Psalm 127:5).

Blessed, therefore, is the one who dwells there at the entrance of faith, in the lodging place of the mind, in the dwelling of devotion, and in the practice of virtue.

6. Let us therefore be in him and remain in him, of whom Isaiah also says:

“How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace, who proclaim good things” (Isaiah 52:7)!

[Note: The Roman edition alone has “of whom the Apostle also speaks.”]

Who are those who proclaim the gospel, except Peter, Paul, and all the apostles? What do they proclaim to us except the Lord Jesus (1 Corinthians 1:1)? He is our peace; he is that highest good, because he himself is good, proceeding from the Good—for from a good tree, a good fruit is read to come (Matthew 7:18). His Spirit also is good; receiving from him, it leads God’s servants along a straight way (Psalm 142:10). Who, possessing God’s Spirit within him, would deny that he is good, when he himself says: “Or is your eye evil because I am good?” (Matthew 10:15).

Let this good come into our soul and into the inmost parts of our mind—the good which God in his mercy gives to those who ask him.

[Col. 1056A]

He is our treasure, our way, our wisdom, our righteousness, our shepherd—and the good shepherd. He is our life. Do you see how many goods there are in the one Good?

7. The Evangelists proclaim these goods to us. Seeking these goods, David says:

“Who will show us good things?” (Psalm 4:6).

And he shows that he himself is the good, adding:

“The light of your countenance has been marked upon us” (ibid.).

Who, then, is the light of the Father’s countenance except “the radiance of glory and the image of the invisible God” (Hebrews 1:3), in whom the Father is seen and glorified, just as he himself glorifies his Son (John 17:5)?

8. The Lord Jesus himself, therefore, is the highest good, announced to us by the prophets, proclaimed by angels, promised by the Father, and preached by the apostles (1 Timothy 3:16).

[Col. 1056B]

He came to us as maturity; and not merely as maturity, but as maturity upon the mountains, so that there might be nothing bitter, nothing immature in our counsels, nothing harsh or rough in our works and conduct—he who was the first to proclaim good things. Hence he says:

“The one who spoke, behold, I am here,” that is, “the one who spoke in the prophets” (Hebrews 1:1), “I am here in the body which I assumed from the Virgin; I am here as the inner image of God, the impress of his substance; and I am here as man.”

[Note: Some manuscripts have “the one who spoke, I am here,” that is, “the one who spoke,” and so forth.]
