But who recognizes me? They saw a man, but believed him, on account of his works, to be above man. Was he not man when he wept for Lazarus (John 11:35), and again above man when he raised him? Was he not man when he was scourged, and again above man when he took away the sin of the whole world (John 1:29)?

9. Let us therefore hasten to him in whom the highest good is found; for he is goodness itself, he is the expectation of Israel, who calls you to repentance, so that you may not come into judgment but receive the forgiveness of sins. “Repent,” he says (Matthew 4:17). He is the one of whom the prophet Amos cries:

“Seek the good” (Amos 5:14).

He is the highest good, who needs nothing and abounds in all things. He easily abounds in whom the fullness of divinity dwells bodily (Colossians 2:9). He easily abounds, from whose fullness we have all received and in whom we have been filled, as the Evangelist says (John 1:9).

10. When the soul has tasted this true and highest good as that which it desires and delights in,

[Note: Several manuscripts have *sicut illo* (“as that [object]”); some have *in illo, concupiscibili suo* (“in that object of its desire”).] and has drunk it in through these two affections, excluding pain and fear, it burns with incredible fervor. For when it has kissed the Word of God, it knows no measure and is never satisfied, saying:

“You are sweet, Lord, and in your delight teach me your justifications” (Psalm 118:68).

Having kissed the Word of God, it desires him above every beauty, loves him above every joy, delights in him above all spices, longs to see him often and gaze upon him repeatedly; it longs to be drawn, so that it may be able to follow. “Your name,” it says, “is poured-out ointment” (Song of Songs 1:2); therefore we love you, young women; therefore we strive, but we cannot grasp you. Draw us, so that we may run, so that through the fragrance of your ointments we may receive the strength to follow.

907

11. The soul also hastens to see the inner mysteries, the very rest of the Word, the dwelling itself of that highest good, its light and its splendor. In that paternal bosom and retreat it hastens to hear his words; and when it has heard them, it receives them as surpassing every sweetness. Let the Prophet teach you, who tasted them and said:

“How sweet are your words to my palate, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth” (Psalm 118:113)!

For what else does the soul desire once it has tasted the sweetness of the Word and once seen his glory? Moses, placed upon the mountain and receiving the Law for forty days, did not seek bodily food (Exodus 34:28). Elijah, hastening toward that rest, asked that his soul be taken from him (1 Kings 19:4). Peter, himself gazing upon the glory of the Lord’s resurrection on the mountain, did not wish to descend, saying:

“Lord, it is good for us to be here” (Matthew 17:4).

What, then, must be the glory of the divine substance, what the goods of the Word, into which angels long to look (1 Peter 1:12)!

12. The soul that sees this therefore does not seek this body and understands that it ought to have the least possible familiarity with it. It renounces the world, withdraws itself from the bonds of the flesh, and strips itself of all the chains of these pleasures. Thus Stephen saw Jesus and was not afraid to be stoned; indeed, while being stoned, he prayed not for himself but for those by whom he was being killed (Acts 7:55 and following).

Paul likewise, caught up to the third heaven, did not know whether he was in the body or outside the body; caught up, I say, into paradise, he no longer experienced the use of his own body. Hearing the words of God, he was ashamed to descend to the infirmities of the body (2 Corinthians 12:2).

13. Knowing, therefore, what he had seen or heard in paradise, he cried out, saying:

“Why do you still make decrees, as though living in the world? Do not touch, do not handle, do not taste those things which by their very use are all destined for corruption” (Colossians 2:20 and following).

He wanted us to exist in the image of this world, not in its possession and use; so that we might use this world as though we did not use it, as passing through it, not as settling in it; walking as though in an image of the age, not in desire,

[Note: Nannius calls the wording obscure. “I think,” he says, “the meaning is this: He wanted us to move about in the world as in an imaginary thing, which possesses no solid existence.” I think he was alluding to 1 Corinthians 7: “For the form of this world is passing away”; afterward he adds, “walking as though in the image of the age.”]

so that with the swiftest possible discourse we may pass through the very image of this world.

[Note: The editions of Erasmus and Gill, together with two manuscripts, have *velocissima dispositione* (“with the swiftest arrangement”); the Roman edition has *velocissima praeteritione* (“with the swiftest passing”); Amerbach and the other manuscripts have “... disputatione” (“... discussion”). The sense is appropriate, for Ambrose expresses nothing else than his desire to discuss the image of the world in as few words as possible. Again, two verses below, where our text, together with several manuscripts and editions, has *aderat Domino* (“he was present to the Lord”), the Roman edition has *sed aderat Domino* (“but he was present to the Lord”); one manuscript has *adhaeserat Domino* (“he had clung to the Lord”), another *adhaerebat Deo* (“he was clinging to God”).]

He himself, walking by faith and not by sight, was a sojourner away from the body and was present with the Lord; and while he was on earth, he lived not in earthly things but in heavenly things.

14. Let our soul, therefore, which wishes to draw near to God, raise itself above the body, cling always to that Highest One, to that good which is divine, which always is, which was in the beginning, and which was with God—that is, the Word of God. He is that divine one in whom we live, and move, and exist (Acts 17:28). He is the one who was in the beginning; he is the one who is. For Jesus Christ, the Son of God,

[Col. 1058D]

“is in you,” he says; in him there was no “Yes” and “No,” but “Yes” was present in him (2 Corinthians 1:19).

[Note: The Roman edition alone has “who is in you, he says, was not in him”; the old edition and the manuscripts have the reading in the text, except that instead of *in vobis* (“in you”), the old edition preferred *in nobis* (“in us”).]

He is the one who told Moses to say: “He who is has sent me” (Exodus 3:14).

908

15. Let our soul therefore be with this one, and, if possible, always be; so that someone may also be able to say of us:

“My soul is always in your hands” (Psalm 118:109).

It will be so if it is not in the flesh but in the Spirit; it will be so if it does not mingle with earthly things. For when it turns back toward carnal things, then the allure of the body creeps upon it; then it burns with anger and indignation; then it is afflicted by sadness; then it is upturned through arrogance;

[Note: He describes the face of a proud person, who raises his lofty countenance toward heaven. The opposite is the downcast person, who lowers his face toward the earth. Thus Nannius.]

then it is oppressed by grief.

16. These are the grave illnesses of the soul, by which it is often driven toward death, while its eyes are blinded so that they do not see the light of true glory and the riches of the eternal inheritance. But if it always directs them toward God, it will receive from Christ the radiance of wisdom, so that it may have a gaze enlightened by the knowledge of God; it will see the hope of our calling and behold that which is good, pleasing, and perfect.

For what is good is pleasing to the Father; what is pleasing is perfect, as you have it in the Gospel, where the Lord says:

“Love your enemies, so that you may imitate the Father, who makes his rain fall upon the just and the unjust” (Matthew 5:44 and following).

This is surely goodness. And afterward he concludes, saying:

“Be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect” (Romans 13:10).

For charity is perfect; indeed, it is the fullness of the Law. And what is as good as charity, which thinks no evil?

17.

[Note: The Royal manuscript has: “And therefore flee earthly things.”]

Therefore flee the earth, where there is envy, ambition, and strife. Let your soul make itself capable of that good, so that it may fly above the clouds, be renewed like the eagle, and put forth wings like the eagle; so that, with the oars of its renewed wings,

[Note: Since wings serve birds what oars serve ships, poets—especially Virgil—derived this metaphor; Ambrose transferred it here.]

it may not fear to seek high things, and may leave this dwelling behind; for an earthly dwelling weighs down the soul (Wisdom 9:15).

Let it strip off the old things, cast away the desires of error, and wash its eyes, so that it may see that fountain of true wisdom, that fountain of eternal life, which flows and overflows for all and lacks nothing. For who has given anything to him, since from him, through him, and in him are all things (Romans 11:35)?

18. The highest good, therefore, is the fountain of life, from which the substance of living is supplied to all; but it possesses abiding life in itself. It receives from no one as though it were needy; it bestows goods upon others and takes nothing for itself from elsewhere, for it does not need us. Hence, speaking in the person of man, he says:

“Because you do not need my goods” (Psalm 15:2).

What, then, is more beautiful than to draw near to him and cling to him? What pleasure could be greater? If one has seen him and freely tasted from the fountain of living water, what else could one desire? What kingdoms? What powers? What money?—when one realizes how wretched even here is the condition of kings, how changeable the state of power, how brief the spaces of this life, and how many forms of servitude exist within power itself, since they live according to the will of others, not their own.

19. But who passes into eternal life furnished with personal wealth, unless supported by the wealth of virtues—a wealth declared to be received by all but impossible for the rich (Matthew 19:26)? It is therefore not blessed to use these things, but to see that by which you may despise them, refute vain things by the truth,

[Note: Several manuscripts have “and reject them as though they were empty”; some have “and reject empty things as true things” (one has “truly reject”); more correctly, the others and all the editions have *et vana veri*, “and refute vain things by the truth,” etc., a phrase concerning which we have already spoken.]

and judge them empty and worthless, while loving the beauty of naked truth, which exposes these most deceptive vanities of the age.

20. Raise your eyes, therefore, O soul—those eyes of which the Word of God says to you:

[Note: The Greek word *ἐκκαρδίωσας*, which Ambrose here translates, has, as Nannius observes, a stronger emphasis; it means something like “you have torn out the heart.” The old translator rendered it, “You have wounded my heart,” and so forth.]

“You have captured our heart, my sister, my bride; you have captured our heart with one glance of your eyes” (Song of Songs 4:9).

Climb the palm tree; conquer the world, so that you may grasp the height of the Word. Leave this image of the world outside; leave wickedness outside. Bring in instead the goodness of the mind, which possesses grace in the tree of life, if it washes its robe and enters the city, which is true grace for the saints, in which the tabernacle of God is found, around which the scribes of the Lord pitch their tents,

[Note: *Praetendunt* means “they pitch their tents before others,” surrounding them with their guards, as Nannius aptly notes; we remember having observed this elsewhere.]

where neither day, nor sun, nor moon provide light, but the Lord himself is its light, illuminating the entire city (Revelation 21:23). For he is the light of the world (John 8:12), not visible light, but the intelligible brightness of souls that are in this world, into which he pours himself with the shining light of rational wisdom, as it is proclaimed in the Gospel (Luke 24:32),

[Note: The edition reads, “and as it is proclaimed in the Gospel.”] inflaming with the vapor of incorporeal power the hidden places of minds and the innermost chambers of souls.

21. If anyone therefore begins to be a citizen of that heavenly city—namely, a citizen in conduct and character—let him not depart from it or go out; let him not turn back his step, not the step of his body, I mean, but the step of his mind;

[Col. 1060A]

let him not return backward. Behind us are luxury and impurity. Thus Lot, ascending the mountain, left the crimes of Sodom behind; but she who looked back could not escape to higher things (Genesis 19:30). Let it not be your feet, therefore, but your conduct that turns back. Let your hands not become slack, nor the knees of your devotion and faith grow weak. Let there be no relapse of weakness in your will, no interruption caused by sins. You have entered—remain. You have arrived—stand firm. “Save your soul alive” (Genesis 19:17).

22. As you ascend, raise your step along the straight path; no one safely returns from there. On this side is the way; on that side, ruin. On this side, ascent; on that side, a precipice. The labor of ascending is great, but the danger of descending is great also. Yet the Lord is powerful, and he can keep you established there, enclosed by prophetic walls and apostolic towers.

Therefore the Lord says to you:

“Enter, tread, for the vintage is ready” (Joel 3:13).

Let us be within, not outside. In the Gospel the Son of God says:

“Let the one who is on the roof not go down to take away his vessels” (Luke 17:31).

He is not speaking of this roof, but of that one:

“He stretches out heaven like a chamber” (4 Esdras 16:60).

23. Be within, therefore, within Jerusalem, within your soul, peaceful, gentle, and tranquil. Do not leave it, nor, by descending, exalt this vessel of yours through honors, riches, or arrogance. Be within, so that foreigners may not pass through you, so that sins, empty works, and empty thoughts may not pass through your soul. They will not pass through if you sanctify war as the struggle of devotion and faith,

[Col. 1060C]

as the contest for truth against the allurements of the passions; and if you take up the armor of God against spiritual wickedness and the cunning of the devil, who tests our senses through fraud and deceit.

[Note: Some manuscripts have “him who, while remaining an old soldier, ...”]

The gentle warrior easily tramples him down—the warrior who does not sow quarrels but, as befits a servant of the Lord, teaches the faith with modesty and rebukes those who oppose it. Scripture says of this:

“Let the gentle person rise up as a warrior” (Joel 3:9);

and let the weak person say:

“I can do all things in him who strengthens me” (Philippians 4:13).

24. Relying on this faith, even the weak person will prevail, and his soul will be holy. The prophetic or apostolic mountains will drip sweetness for him (Joel 3:18), and the hills will flow with milk. What a hill that is which gave the Corinthians milk to drink (1 Corinthians 3:2)! And waters will flow for him from his own vessels and from the springs of his wells; or, from his belly, living waters—namely, spiritual waters—which the Holy Spirit supplies to his faithful. May he also deign to water your soul, so that the fountain of water springing up into eternal life may abound in you (John 4:14).

[Col. 1061A]

Farewell, and love us as a son;

[Note: The final Paris edition has “love us as sons ... as we love you as a parent,” a meaning rendered in the wrong order.]

for we love you as parents.

[Note: Written about the year 387.]

# LETTER XXX

He teaches that one must not dwell in low-lying places in the manner of the luxurious, but, like the saints, in higher places, where a temple must be built for the Lord—namely, in one’s own minds. The luxurious do not build this temple, whose summit we measure with the aid of righteousness. Who are denied the right to build tombs for themselves and to ascend into the house of God? And in what manner are they roused, by threats and promises alike, to build it?

**AMBROSE TO IRENAEUS, GREETING.**

1. When I had finished my preceding letter and handed it over to be delivered to you, I remembered what the Lord spoke through the hand of the prophet Haggai, saying:

“Is it time for you to dwell in paneled houses?” (Haggai 1:4).

[Note: In Greek it reads *ἐν οἴκοις κοιλοστάθμοις*, that is, “in hollowed-out houses”; hence Nannius thinks that by the words “in paneled houses” Ambrose intended to signify that underground chambers existed in those buildings. Nevertheless, he also acknowledges that Ambrose says below “paneled houses” and “paneled silver.”]

What, then, does this mean except that one must dwell in higher places, not in valleys and underground dwellings? For those who live beneath the earth cannot build the temple of God, and they say:

“The time has not come for the house of the Lord to be built” (ibid., 2).

At the same time, it belongs to the luxurious to seek underground chambers, pursuing coolness in summer because, relaxed by pleasures, they cannot otherwise bear or endure the heat, and therefore seek shady recesses; or because the idle spend their sluggish leisure beneath the earth. Moreover, dark and obscure places delight them more, because they think that their crimes are concealed by them, according to the saying:

“Darkness surrounds me like walls: whom do I fear?” (Ecclesiasticus 23:26)?

[Note: “Hypogaea,” says Nannius, are subterranean places where innkeepers and prostitutes customarily lodge; because of their resemblance to the lairs of wild animals, the Romans call them *lustra*. A prostitute is indeed called in Greek *χαμαιτύση* and *χαμεταίρις*.]

But they hope for this in vain, since God sees the depths of the abyss and hidden things, and apprehends everything before it comes to be (Wisdom 8:8).

2. But Elijah did not dwell in underground chambers, nor did Elisha. One of them, in fact, carried the widow’s dead son up to the upper room where he was accustomed to sit, and there he restored him to life (1 Kings 17:22). Likewise, that great woman of Shunem prepared an upper room for the other, as Scripture bears witness (2 Kings 4:16 and following), and there, although she had no child, she received the privilege of conceiving offspring and witnessed the miracles of the child restored to life.

What shall I say of Peter, who, ascending to the upper room at the sixth hour, learned the mysteries concerning the baptism of the Gentiles (Acts 10:9 and following)?

[Note: Amerbach, together with several manuscripts, has “at the ninth hour.” The phrase “ascending to the upper room” indicates the ancient custom of the Jews of climbing to the upper part of the house when they were about to pray.]

But the parricide Absalom set up a monument for himself in the King’s Valley and, after he was killed, was thrown into a pit (2 Samuel 18:17). The saints therefore ascend to the Lord, while the wicked descend into vices;

[Col. 1062A]

the saints are in the mountains, the criminals in the valleys; for God is the God of the mountains and not the God of the valleys (1 Kings 20:20).

[Note: The Roman edition adds after these words, “He says therefore: Set your hearts now upon your ways; ascend the mountain.” But this has no support from any manuscript or printed witness.]

3. Those who therefore dwelt there—that is, in houses situated in the valleys, where God does not dwell—could not have the house of God within themselves. For the Lord was seeking this house from them: that they might build themselves and raise up within themselves the temple of God with living stones of faith.

He was not seeking constructions of earthly walls or roofs of woodland timber,

[Note: Some manuscripts have “the wooden summits.” But the reading of the others and of the editions should be retained, since “the timber of the roofs” here signifies the same thing as “the timber of the mountains.”]

which, once they existed, hostile hands would destroy. Rather, he was seeking that temple which would be built in the minds of human beings, to whom it would have to be said:

“You are the temple of God” (1 Corinthians 3:16).

In that temple the Lord Jesus would dwell, and from it he would proceed for the redemption of all, so that a sacred palace might be found in the Virgin’s womb, in which the King of heavenly things would dwell, and the human body would become the temple of God—a body which, even after it had been dissolved, would be raised again in three days.

### 4

But the luxurious do not build this house—those who inhabit paneled houses (Haggai 1:4) and delight in paneled silver; for pure silver is sordid in their eyes, and so too the place of a simple dwelling is sordid to such people (Isaiah 5:8). They enlarge the spaces of their houses, and by adding to them they continue adding, joining house to house and estate to estate; they dig out the earth, so that even the element itself may yield to their dwellings, and, like sons of the earth, they may be placed within its womb and hidden in its belly. These are plainly the people of whom Jeremiah says: “Woe to him who builds his house without justice” (Jeremiah 22:13)! For whoever builds with justice does not build upon earthly things, [Col. 1062C] but upon heavenly ones.

### 5

“You have built a house,” he says; “measure its upper chambers, furnished with open spaces and windows, and paneled with cedar and painted with vermilion” (ibid., 14). He measures the upper chambers who, having contemplated God’s judgment, judges the judgment of the humble and the judgment of the poor. But whoever fixes his attention upon avarice and upon the blood of the innocent does not build the upper chambers with judgment, nor does he keep to the proper measure, because he does not possess Christ. He does not seek to have the divine breath of grace blow upon him, nor does he seek the splendor of full light; nor does he have upper rooms painted with vermilion, to whom it cannot be said: “Like a scarlet thread are your lips” (Song of Songs 4:3).

### 6

“Such a man,” he says, “shall not be buried” (Jeremiah 22:19); for whoever buries himself alive beneath the earth and, as it were, has buried himself in a tomb, has deprived himself in death of the repose of burial. Thus, having been placed in the valley of bodily pleasures, he does not find a tomb from which he can rise again. Such a man, therefore, does not build a temple for God either, because he does not know the time of his correction. For how can such people build a temple, when, like wild beasts and animals, they take refuge in caves and hiding places of wild beasts and animals, plunge themselves into pits in the manner of serpents, and bury themselves according to the habit of a deceitful fox?

### 7

Nor does he prepare a tomb for himself who dies before his time; for while living, he is dead (1 Timothy 5:6). Nor does he hear the voice of Haggai—that is, of the feaster, as the interpretation makes clear.

[Note: [Col. 1063D] Haggai is commonly interpreted as “festive,” “solemn,” and “circling”; but perhaps Ambrose rendered the name as τὸ *epulantem* (“the feaster”), because feasting customarily forms no small part of solemn celebrations.]

For he does not enter the tabernacle of God with “the voice of rejoicing and confession,” the sound of one feasting (Psalm 41:5). For how can he hear his voice who does not see his works? If he saw them, he would hear the word that was made in his hand, delighted by the deeds with which he knocked; and it would be opened to him and descend into his soul, so that he might feast upon the foods of sincerity and [Col. 1063D] truth.

[Note: The old edition and many manuscripts read “the food of truth.” This is not sufficiently correct unless one takes *epuletur* passively, as “let him be eaten.”]

### 8

Therefore, because he did not listen, the word again comes by the hand of Haggai, and says:

[Note: The Roman edition alone has: “and he says: Go up to the mountain, cut wood, and build the house,” as though he were saying, “Rise,” and so forth.]

“Rise from your paneled houses, depressed by wickedness, and go up to the mountain of the heavenly Scriptures; cut down the wood of wisdom, the wood of life, the wood of knowledge. Make your ways straight; order your actions, so that they may possess their proper order, which is necessary and useful for building the Lord’s house” (Haggai 1:8).

### 9

“For if you do not do this, neither will heaven give its dew” (ibid., 10)—that is, the heavenly word, which descends like dew upon the grass, will not temper the heated movements of bodily passions, nor extinguish the fiery darts of various desires. Nor will its earth—that is, [Col. 1063D] the soul—give fruit.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “the soul will give its shoots.”]

This is because it withers unless it is filled with the irrigation of God’s word and drenched with heavenly dew, through the abundance of spiritual grace.

### 10

And because he knew that the inhabitants of underground chambers and little pleasure-houses were idle:

[Note: Thus the old edition and the manuscripts, except that they omit *Jesus* before *Josedech*. The Roman edition corrected the passage as follows: “The Lord stirred up for them the spirit of Zerubbabel … and the spirit of Jesus son of Josedech, the high priest.”]

“I will stir up for them,” he says, “the spirit of Zerubbabel from the tribe of Judah, and Jesus Josedech the high priest” (ibid., 24), so that they may be urged to build the divine house. “Unless the Lord builds the house for himself, those who build it labor in vain” (Psalm 126:1).

He himself is Zerubbabel, perpetual overflow, being the fountain of life and the Word of God, through whom all things exist, from whom all things come, and in whom all things consist (Colossians 1:16–17). This Overflow says: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7:37)—that is, the outpouring of an unfailing stream.

We also read of a nocturnal outflow, Zebulon, which is prophetic.

[Note: The old edition reads: “We read of Zebulon, which is prophetic, and also of that itself.” The Roman edition has: “We read of Zebulon, which is prophetic, and of that itself.” The manuscripts, in strong agreement, support our reading.]

But it too has now shone brightly through the infusion of this stream, by which that stream of vanity in Jezebel disappeared. She, hostile to the truth and opposed to the utterances of the prophets, was so torn apart by dogs’ bites that no trace of her remained, but she was destroyed with her entire body and all the insignia of her descendants (2 Kings 9:33ff.).

Thus Zerubbabel from the tribe of Judah is himself the great priest Jesus, designated both by tribe and by name. Two persons seem to be signified, while one is expressed, because the same one—like a mighty man born from the Mighty One, like a redeemer born from a virgin—fulfilled the truth of the one Son of God, a saving giant, in the divided diversity of both natures.

### 11

Therefore, intending to raise holy Zerubbabel from the dead, he says:

[Note: The Roman edition alone removes the words *from the dead* from the text.]

“Once again I will shake heaven and earth, the sea and the wilderness” (Haggai 2:22).

He had shaken them before, when he delivered his people from Egypt (Exodus 14:22ff.), when there was a pillar of fire in heaven (Exodus 13:21), the earth amid the waves, a wall in the sea, a road in the water, and, in the wilderness, a daily harvest multiplied from heavenly produce; when the rock was opened into springs of water.

But he also shook them afterward in the passion of the Lord Jesus (Luke 23:44), when heaven was covered with darkness, the sun withdrew, rocks were split, tombs were opened, the dead were raised, and the dragon, conquered amid its own waves, saw fishers of men not only sailing upon the sea but also walking without danger.

### 12

The wilderness too was shaken when the unfruitful people of the nations began to grow golden with the harvest of devotion and faith. The agitation of the wilderness and of the nations became so great that the preaching of the apostles whom he sent to call the nations was so extensive and so forceful that “their sound went out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Psalm 18:5).

So great, I say, was the agitation of the wilderness that “more were the children of the desolate woman than of her who had a husband” (Isaiah 54:1); and the wilderness blossomed like a lily (Isaiah 35:1). The chosen of the nations entered among the remnant of the people, so that the remnants might be saved according to the election of grace (Romans 11:6).

### 13

“And I will fill this house,” he says, “with my silver and gold” (Haggai 2:8)—with heavenly utterances, which are “like silver tested by fire” (Psalm 11:7), and with the brightness of true light, shining like spiritual gold in the hidden minds of the saints.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “This house with glory, says the Lord of hosts. The silver is mine and the gold is mine.” Thus: “I have filled it with silver,” and so forth.]

He bestows these riches upon his Church, by which intelligible treasures are filled and the glory of the house is increased beyond its former glory, which the chosen people possessed.

[Note: Certain manuscripts read: “and the house is increased in glory beyond the former glory.”]

[Note: The same edition adds: “For this is what follows: ‘The latter glory of this house shall be greater than the former, says the Lord of hosts; and in this place I will give peace.’ For peace …”]

### 14

For peace and tranquility of soul surpass every glory of the house, because “peace surpasses all understanding” (Philippians 4:7). This is the peace beyond peace that will be given after the third shaking of heaven, sea, earth, and wilderness, when he destroys all Powers and Principalities.

For “heaven and earth will pass away” (Matthew 24:35), as will the entire appearance of this world; and each person will rise against his brother with a sword—that is, with a word penetrating the marrow of the soul (Hebrews 4:12)—so that everything opposed may be destroyed: the chariot from Ephraim and the horse from Jerusalem, as Zechariah said (Zechariah 9:10).

Then there will be peace throughout all things, with no bodily passions or obstacles of an unbelieving mind standing in the way, so that Christ may be all things in all, presenting the hearts of all in submission to the Father (1 Corinthians 15:28).

### 15

Therefore it is also said mystically to him alone:

“I will take you, Zerubbabel, and set you like a seal, because I have chosen you” (Haggai 2:24).

For when our soul has become peaceful, so that it may be said to it, “Return, return, O Shulammite” (Song of Songs 6:12)—which signifies “the peaceful one,” or, to use your name, *εἰρηνικήν*, “the peaceful one”—then it will receive Christ within itself like a seal, that is, the image of God, so that it may exist according to the image; for “as is the heavenly one, so also are the heavenly ones” (1 Corinthians 15:48).

And we must bear the image of the heavenly one—that is, peace.

### 16

And so that we may know this to be true, you have in the Song of Songs, at the very end, what is said to the already perfected soul, and what the Lord Jesus also says to you:

“Set me as a seal upon your arm” (Song of Songs 8:6),

so that peace may shine in your heart, Christ in your works, and wisdom, righteousness, and redemption may be formed in you.

Farewell, my son, and love us, because we love you.

[Note: Written around A.D. 387.]

## LETTER XXXI

To Irenaeus, who asks whether God loves differently those who believe immediately from childhood and those who believe later, when they are more advanced in age, the holy Bishop responds that Scripture indicates that God grieved over the fall of the Synagogue, which had previously been faithful; nevertheless, he afterward transferred his love to the Church. This is signified by David’s two wives and also by Moses’ account of the captive woman.

### Ambrose sends greetings to Irenaeus.

### 1

You wisely thought it necessary to inquire whether there is any difference before God between the love shown to those who have believed from childhood and that shown to those who have advanced through youth [Note: The Roman edition reads: “or more advanced age.”] or later life. For divine Scripture has not passed over this matter or left it untouched.

Indeed, the Lord our God says not without purpose through the prophet Joel:

“Lament before me over the Bride, girded with sackcloth for her virginal husband” (Joel 1:9).

[Note: Several manuscripts read: “girded and over her husband”; the edition reads: “girded with sackcloth over her husband.”]

He grieves over the Synagogue, which had formerly been betrothed in her virginity to the Word of God—or certainly over the soul that had fallen away from good merits.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “from the good things of the mind.”]

She had stumbled into the offense of sins to such an extent that she incurred hatred and, worn out with the filth of impiety and faithlessness, became a pitiable object of contempt, greatly changed from the grace of that Bride who had previously deserved to hear:

“I will betroth you to myself in faith, righteousness, and mercy” (Hosea 2:19).

### 2

She is rightly declared worthy of lamentation, since she had lost the value of such great gifts and suffered so grievous a loss of her bridal virtues that her virginal Bridegroom was taken away from her.

For according to our merits the Word of God either lives or dies for us. If our purposes and works are good, the Word of God lives and works in us; but if our thoughts and works are dark, “the sun of righteousness” dies for us (Malachi 4:2).

Therefore he commanded that lamentation be made for that soul. For just as those with whom the Bridegroom is present should rejoice and feast, so the soul from which the Bridegroom has been taken away should mourn, as it is written in the Gospel concerning the apostles:

“When the Bridegroom is taken away from them, then they will fast in those days” (Matthew 9:15).

### 3

That soul, therefore, had previously possessed joy and exultation, when it possessed a *παρθενικὸς λόγος*, a virginal Word. And so it did not fast, because the days were days of feasting and refreshment, while the Bridegroom was present, bringing to those whom he accompanied an abundance of fertility, supplies of heavenly nourishment, and an outpouring of wine, by which human hearts are gladdened.

[Note: All editions and several manuscripts read: “an abundance of heavenly nourishment, drenched with a supply of wine”; other manuscripts, including ours with few exceptions, read: “an abundance of fertility, drenched with a supply of heavenly nourishment and wine”; the Long manuscript reads: “drenched with wine.” The last reading is not very suitable, since *rigatus* is in the accusative and means “irrigations.”]

But after she lost the Bridegroom through her deeds, she is commanded to do penance for her sins in sackcloth and to mourn for herself, because Christ, who is the *παρθενικὸς λόγος*, the virginal Word, died and was crucified for her (Psalm 103:15).

[Col. 1066C]

### 4

If this occurred from the first age, and the other soul does not seem to have experienced such a union, but from the beginning dedicated the flower of her virgin faith to Christ, and, having been joined to him through the first mysteries of devotion, received sacred observances as a young woman, she is the Israelite soul of the ancient lineage.

[Note: Two manuscripts read: “of the lineage of truth”; two others, more correctly, “of the lineage of truth”; one reads: “of the lineage of devotion.” The latter is less elegant.]

She is descended from the race of the patriarchs. If she had preserved the course of her faith without stumbling, she would have been the Bride of the virginal Word, of great merit, like the one who “grasped righteousness, and it will meet her like a mother, and like a woman from her virginity she will receive it” (Sirach 15:2).

### 5

There is also another soul acquired from the nations, and both are the Bride of one Word, which is a great mystery.

This is demonstrated to you in the Book of Kings (1 Samuel 25:39), since David had two wives: Ahinoam the Jezreelite and Abigail, whom he acquired afterward. The former was stricter; the latter was a soul full of mercy and grace, hospitable and generous, who saw the Father with unveiled face and contemplated his glory. She received that divine dew of the Father’s grace, as the interpretation of her name indicates.

But what is the dew of the Father except the Word of God?

[Note: The Boyer manuscript reads: “which has infused the hearts of all with the moisture of grace and faith.”]

The Word of God infused the hearts of all with the moisture of faith and righteousness.

### 6

Beautifully, therefore, the true David says to this soul what was said to Abigail:

“Blessed is the Lord God of Israel, who sent you today to meet me, and blessed is your character” (ibid., 32ff.).

And again he says to her:

“Go up in peace to your house. Behold, I have heard your voice, and I have respected your face” (ibid.).

Finally, these words of the Bridegroom to the Bride are also found in the Song of Songs:

“Show me your face, and let me hear your voice” (Song of Songs 2:14).

### 7

At that time she was dismissed, because she had another husband, who was called Nabal in Hebrew and, in Latin, “foolish,” harsh, inhospitable, inhuman, and ungrateful—one who did not know how to return services.

[Note: The Amberst edition and six manuscripts add: “in Latin, foolishness.”]

But after her husband died, the prophet David, because she was released from the law of her husband, took her as his wife.

Through this union the mysteries of the Church that would believe from the nations are signified. After losing the husband to whom she had previously been joined, she passed over to Christ, rich in pious resources and endowed with the wealth of humility, faith, and mercy.

[Note: The Boyer manuscript reads: “the mysteries believed by the Church are signified.” For “rich in pious resources,” the same manuscript has: “rich in resources.”]

### 8

But in this passage it is not she who is lamented, but Ahinoam, who was wickedly strong against her brother; and therefore the brother became a cause of agitation for her. Hence it is said in their person:

“You have made us a proverb among the nations, a shaking of the head among the peoples” (Psalm 43:15).

When the devil found her wavering, he tore her down like a lion and took away her delight (Micah 4:4). He overturned her vineyard and her fig tree, beneath which she had formerly been accustomed to rest, and caused her fruit to wither.

### 9

Taking pity on those who were dry and white with excessive desiccation, God says to the prophet:

“Lament before me over the Bride girded with sackcloth, and over her virginal husband” (Joel 1:9),

that is, over the dead husband of such a soul or of the Synagogue.

In another passage, reproaching her, he says that she had forgotten her purpose, forgotten love, become unmindful of grace, strayed from discipline, and lost the former affection of a wife (Hosea 4:6). Rightly, therefore, he rebukes her in his words, recalling and unfolding the expressions of affection and the names of devotion that belonged to her:

“You did not call me as your household servant, as father, and as the initiator of your virginity.”

### 10

Therefore, for this soul, whose intemperance has caused the Word of God to die, and in whom that *παρθενικὸς λόγος*, that virginal Word, has died, he enters into mourning.

[Note: The final Paris edition reads: “he fell into mourning.”]

He brings forward an intercessor, so that she may be called to repentance and thus be able to merit mercy.

But the other soul, good in understanding and exceedingly beautiful in appearance, like Abigail acquired in war, after her adversaries had been conquered and her husband had died—he had been surrounded by spiritual wickedness and resisted and opposed her, lest his beautiful wife be taken away (1 Samuel 25:30)—is received by the victorious and loving Bridegroom.

He bestows joy and grace upon her, cleansing her of every impediment to her beauty and stripping off the garments of captivity. Thus, after laying aside all the hair of her head—that is, the little locks of sins, which seem like superfluities upon our body, for “if a man lets his hair grow long, it is a disgrace to him” (1 Corinthians 11:14)—she strives to attain “the unity of faith,” “the perfect man,” and “the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ” (Ephesians 4:13).

She is to lay aside every disturbance of mind, be established in love, grow in the Lord Jesus, and “obtain increase for the whole body.”

[Note: All editions and some manuscripts read: “and obtain every increase for the body.” Many other and better manuscripts read: “and obtain increase for the whole”; some have: “increases for the body.”]

### 11

This is the soul whom the Law sets before you under the figure of a good woman:

“If you see her among the captives and desire to take her as your wife, you shall bring her into your house” (Deuteronomy 21:11ff.).

You are to entrust to her the whole interior of your house, the possession of all your inward parts; you are to remove her superfluities, cut away her lapses, and, with a razor not overly sharp lest it cause injury, cut away the remnants of your passions and trim your empty thoughts.

Therefore he says: “You shall shave her head,” so that no obstacles may obstruct the eyes of the wise, which are in her head.

“And she shall sit,” he says, “in your house for thirty days” (Ecclesiastes 2:14), mourning the sins of her own birth and the contrivances of the most wicked father, the devil, who wishes to gather what he did not beget (Jeremiah 17:11).

Thus, cleansed by the purification of this mystical number, she may obtain the keys of marriage.

### 12

Beautifully he says: “Afterward you shall go in to her,” so that you may enter wholly into your soul, gather yourself within it, dwell in it, remain with it, and have your entire way of life in it; so that you may be not in the flesh but in the spirit, and propose to join her to yourself as a companion in life, knowing that she will share her good things with you.

Then, having benefited from her grace, you may say:

“I was a child of good understanding, and I received a good soul” (Wisdom 8:19).

And she may answer you:

“I will take you and bring you into the house of my mother, and into the chamber of her who conceived me” (Song of Songs 3:4).

That good mother of souls is the Jerusalem that is in heaven.

### 13

She will therefore be your wife, and, finding you, she will kiss you.

“And if afterward she does not please you” (Deuteronomy 21:14)—because she chastises her body and brings it into subjection—you shall not permit her to serve, that is, to serve the pleasures of the body; you shall not subject her to the flesh, but allow her to remain free.

Nor shall you alienate her—that is what “sell” means—nor shall you despise her. Instead, you shall permit her to serve her God in the chastity of faith and the sobriety of good works.

Farewell, and love us, because we love you.

[Note: Written around A.D. 387.]

## LETTER XXXII

He teaches that Satan is represented under the figure of the partridge by deceit and lust. How, by crying out, it gathered peoples to itself, and how Christ likewise, by crying out, called them back to himself; and in what way this accords with the nature of the partridge. From this he concludes that Christ did not cry out in vain and that, after the devil has been utterly stripped, that foolish one whom God chose will be saved.

[Note: This is the reading of a large number of manuscripts and of the old edition. One Vatican manuscript, the Long manuscript, the Laetian manuscript, and, with them, the Roman edition read: “Ambrose to Sabinus.” We shall examine this heading shortly.]

### Ambrose sends greetings to Irenaeus.

### 1

“The partridge cried out; it gathered what it did not hatch” (Jeremiah 17:11).

[Note: The Roman edition alone adds: “May I take the beginning of the following letter from the end of the preceding letter to Irenaeus concerning the mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation against Apollinarius.” It is evident that the editors inserted these words to indicate that the beginning of this letter should be referred to the end of the preceding one, which concludes: “The partridge was left behind, which cried out in order to gather what it did not hatch,” and so forth.]

[Note: In the ancient edition the heading of this final letter reads “To Irenaeus.” But since all the manuscripts, as well as the Roman edition itself, present the same letter as addressed to Sabinus, it is surprising that the same edition says that it was written to Irenaeus. It seems to have happened that, just as the letter addressed to Sabinus was given the heading “To Irenaeus” in the old edition because the editors thought that it was intended for the same person to whom this letter was addressed, so also the present letter was labeled “To Sabinus” in the three manuscripts mentioned above because the copyists persuaded themselves that it was intended for the same person as the other. Yet the very arrangement preserved in each letter makes us think that they were written separately. In the one, Ambrose speaks with Sabinus as with a man of exceptional merit and authority; in this one, however, he speaks more familiarly with Irenaeus, whom our holy bishop does not hesitate to address in the subscription as “son.” Therefore, since a much larger number of manuscripts and all the old editions indicate that this letter was addressed to Irenaeus, and since its opening words can appropriately be referred to those at the end of the preceding section—“the contrivances of the most wicked devil, who wishes to gather what he did not beget”—we have judged that its proper order and heading should be restored.]

For it is permissible for me to borrow the opening of the following letter from the end of the preceding one. The question is a very celebrated one; and therefore, if we are to resolve it, let us consider what history tells us about the nature of this bird.

[Note: Understand this as referring to Aristotle’s *History of Animals*, book 9, chapter 6, where the partridge’s cunning in misleading hunters is described; or to Pliny’s *Natural History*, book 10, chapter 33. Basil also says something about this matter in Homily 8 on the *Hexaemeron* and more in Homily 13 of the *Exhortation to Baptism*. Aldrovandus discusses it extensively in book 13 of his *Ornithology*, and Huet in his notes on Origen’s *Commentary*, pages 16–17. Consult these works.]

For it is no small mark of prudence to consider this matter, since Solomon also knew the natures of animals and spoke of cattle, birds, reptiles, and fish (1 Kings 4:33).

### 2

This bird is said to be full of deceit, fraud, and trickery. It knows the ways of deceiving the hunter and understands the arts by which it may draw him away from its young. It omits no attempt of cunning by which it may lead the hunter away from its nest and its hiding places.

Certainly, if it notices that the hunter is pressing upon it, it deceives him for as long as it can give its offspring a signal and opportunity to flee. When it senses that they have escaped, it too withdraws, leaving the ambusher deceived by its slippery art.

### 3

It is also said to be promiscuous in its mating, so that the males rush upon the females with the greatest rivalry and grow heated in wandering lust.

[Note: The Colbertine manuscript reads: “as though the males were females.”]

For this reason the impure, malicious, and fraudulent animal is thought to be comparable to the adversary and deceiver of the human race, the most deceitful one and author of impurity.

### 3*

“Therefore the partridge cried out,” receiving its name from “destroying.” It is that Satan who is called in Latin “the Adversary.”

[Note: Aldrovandus says that this etymology of *partridge* was invented by more recent writers; from this one may understand that he did not encounter this passage of Ambrose. We do not dispute his claim that the etymology is ridiculous, since for Ambrose’s purpose it was enough that it had been accepted in his own time. Dalechamp says in his notes on Pliny that the word derives from the verb *πέρδειν*, “to fart,” while others have devised other origins for the same word.]

He cried out first in Eve (Genesis 3:4–5); he cried out in Cain; he cried out in Pharaoh (Exodus 5:2), in Dathan, Abiram, and Korah (Numbers 16:2). He cried out among the Jews when they demanded that gods be made for them while Moses was receiving the Law (Exodus 32:1).

He cried out again when they said of the Savior, “Let him be crucified, let him be crucified,” and, “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matthew 27:23, 25).

He cried out when they demanded that a king be made for them, so that they might depart from the Lord God who was their king (1 Samuel 8:5).

He cried out in every vain and faithless person.

### 4

By these cries he gathered peoples to himself whom he had not created. For God made human beings in his own image and likeness (Genesis 1:27), while the devil, by the deceit of his voice, had joined human beings to himself.

He gathered the peoples of the nations to himself, making riches without judgment. Hence the proverb about the greedy rich man: this partridge gathers riches without judgment.

But my Jesus, like a good judge, does everything with judgment. He came, as it is written, saying:

“I speak righteousness and the judgment of salvation” (Isaiah 63:1).

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “the judgment of the Savior.”]

### 5

By this grace, therefore, he plundered that partridge, the devil. He took away from him the wealth he had gathered wickedly, the multitude he had assembled, and he called back the souls of the nations from error, together with the minds of peoples who had strayed.

And because he knew that they had been deceived by the devil’s voice, he too cried out—first in Abel, whose blood cried out (Genesis 4:10)—in order to loosen the bonds and knots of their ancient error.

He cried out in Moses, to whom he said, “Why do you cry out to me?” (Exodus 14:15). He cried out in Joshua son of Nun (Joshua 1:1). He cried out in David, who said, “I cried out to you; save me” (Psalm 118:146). He cried out in all the prophets.

Therefore he also says to Isaiah, “Cry out”; and Isaiah says, “What shall I cry?” (Isaiah 40:6).

He cried out in Solomon, calling people to wisdom with the loftiest proclamation:

“Come, eat of my breads and drink the wine that I have mixed for you” (Proverbs 9:5).

[Note: All editions read: “with a proclamation to wisdom”; one Vatican manuscript reads: “with proclamation and wisdom”; the other manuscripts, more correctly, have the reading adopted in the text.]

He also cried out in his own body, like a scarab in wood (Habakkuk 2:11).

He cried out in order to deceive and outwit the ambusher, saying:

“My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46).

He cried out in order to strip him, answering the thief:

“Amen, amen, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43).

Therefore, when Jesus cried out, that partridge was immediately abandoned by those whom it had gathered, in the middle of its days.

### 6

For this reason some have thought that this too should be applied to the nature of the partridge, since it steals the eggs of another bird, warms them with its own body, and by this deceit tries to acquire offspring that belong to another.

But, as the saying goes, “a crow’s eye” [Note: The edition reads “the eye of a crow”; the manuscripts read “a crow’s eye,” as Cicero also has it in his speech for Lucius Flaccus. Ambrose seems to allude to a Greek proverb mentioned by Macrobius in book 7 of the *Saturnalia*: “a crow plucks out a crow’s eye,” meaning that a cunning person defeats by a more cunning art the trick by which another cunning person was trying to deceive him. See Erasmus, *Adages*, chiliad 1, centuria 3, proverb 75.], for birds too have their own arts.

When the bird whose eggs have been stolen, nest invaded, or young deceived by an error of resemblance and an imitation of appearance—

[Note: This is the reading of Erasmus and later editions, together with several manuscripts. The Amberst edition and some others read: “deceived by the likeness of error and by imitation of appearance.” The Colbertine manuscript has: “deceived by imitation of appearance.” The Pratensian and Gemblacensian manuscripts read: “deceived by error, likeness, appearance, imitation.” This reading is not displeasing.]

—even though it is weaker in strength, it puts on and arms itself with cunning. When all the labor spent in feeding and rearing has exhausted the bird that is raising the young, and the chicks have begun to grow, the partridge then gives out a cry, like a trumpet of affection, and calls its offspring.

The young, stirred by a kind of natural hearing, recognize their parent and abandon the impostor. Thus, when it wishes to gather what it did not hatch, it loses those whom it thought it was raising.

### 7

Jesus therefore did not cry out in vain. The people of the entire world had strayed from their own creator, deceived by the voice, flatteries, art, and appearance of the partridge. Following its slippery arts, they were called back by the voice of their true parent, so that they might abandon the deceiver and leave the fraudulent one in the middle of his days—that is, before the end of this age, from which the Lord Jesus rescued us and called us to eternal life.

Therefore, now that we are dead to the world, we live for God (Romans 6:8).

### 8

When, therefore, this partridge has been utterly abandoned by its false children, then that foolish one whom God chose will be saved, because “God chose the foolish things of the world.” Therefore, if anyone seems wise in this age, let him become foolish so that he may be wise (1 Corinthians 1:27).

Farewell, my son, and love us, as you do; because we love you.

[Note: Written around A.D. 387.]

## LETTER XXXIII

To Irenaeus, who expressed fear that someone might infer from the scriptural passage concerning two wives that there are two souls in one and the same human being, Ambrose writes that different qualities of the soul are indicated there. In the beloved wife the soul devoted to pleasure is represented; in the hated wife, the soul pursuing stricter virtues. He explains that the firstborn belong to the latter, both from another passage and from the passage under discussion.

### Ambrose sends greetings to Irenaeus.

### 1

In the preceding letter we wrote that our soul must be freed from its adversaries and undertake with it the companionship of an inseparable life.

Because our discussion took its example from Deuteronomy (Deuteronomy 21:16), where the subject is a man who had two wives, one hated and the other loved, you seem not to have been moved casually to fear that someone might understand this as saying that the man had taken two souls to himself. This is entirely impossible.

### 2

But you yourself are not unaware that Scripture sometimes speaks allegorically, referring one thing to the Synagogue and another to the Church; one thing to the soul and another to the mystery of the Word; and still other things to the various kinds and qualities of souls. These distinctions are discerned by the one who judges spiritually.

Therefore, in the following chapter of the Law, I think that not two souls but different qualities of one soul are included.

There is a beloved type of soul that desires pleasures, flees labor, avoids remorse, and neglects God’s judgment. It is beloved because it seems sweet and pleasant for a time: it does not afflict the mind but delights it.

But the other soul is sadder. It is consumed by zeal for God, as a strict wife would neither want nor tolerate nor permit her spouse to commit adultery. It indulges the body in nothing, relaxes nothing for pleasure or delight, rejects hidden disgrace, and pursues the hardships of labor and the burdens of danger.

### 3

“If both of them bear children,” he says, “he may not set the firstborn son of the beloved wife before the firstborn son of the hated wife when establishing the inheritance, since he knows that the son of the hated wife is the firstborn.”

In this, I do not think that simple precedence is being signified, as though the issue were merely between two firstborn sons. Rather, the expression indicates that the son of the hated wife possesses the prerogative of the firstborn.

For the firstborn is the one born first, and the firstborn are holy, because “every male that opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord” (Exodus 13:2; Luke 2:23).

Yet not every firstborn is holy. Esau, who was certainly the firstborn, was not holy.

**4.** Saints, however, are the firstborn; finally, you have this in Numbers:

> “Behold, I have taken the Levites from among the sons of Israel in place of every firstborn who opens the womb, from the sons of Israel. For mine are they; on the day when I struck down every firstborn of Egypt, I sanctified every firstborn of Israel” (Num. 3:12).

**[Note: [Col. 1072D]]** You will find this passage also treated in *Cain and Abel*, Book II, chapter 2, section 7. Whether Ambrose, when discussing the same passage from Numbers in *The Blessing of the Patriarchs*, referred the reader to that work or to this letter, we examined in the *Admonition*.

Thus the Levites were received in place of the firstborn, as though they were holy; for we know from the Letter written to the Hebrews that the firstborn are holy, where we read:

> “But you have approached Mount Zion and the city of Jerusalem, and ten thousand angels; and the church of the firstborn” (Heb. 12:22).

Therefore, just as the firstborn of the Church are holy, so also are the Levites, since they too are firstborn. For they are not holy by the order of their birth, but by the gift of sanctification; Levi was the third son of Leah, certainly not the first (Gen. 29:34).

[Col. 1073A] **5.** Whoever is sanctified is the one who opens the womb. What womb? Hear him who says:

> “Sinners went astray from the womb” (Ps. 57:4).

Since you have understood “the firstborn who opens the womb,” understand the womb of a good mother, from which the saints do not go astray, but sinners do. The Levites, moreover, are taken away from the midst of Israel, because they have nothing in common with the people whose worldly firstborn are destroyed. For the firstborn of the world belong to another mother, from whose womb Paul was separated when he was called to the grace of God (Gal. 1:15). And therefore, separated from the midst of the people, he received the Word, which is in the midst of our heart. Hence also it was said:

> “But one stands in your midst whom you do not see” (John 1:26).

**6.** Our excursion, then, from Law to Law was not pointless, since we were demonstrating that the firstborn is not the son of that agreeable woman—that is, of the more indulgent and pleasure-loving one—even though the words of the passage under discussion express this, when Scripture says:

> “He will not be able to put the son of the agreeable woman first, since he knows that the son of the hated woman is the firstborn” (Deut. 21:17).

He is truly the firstborn who is the holy offspring of a holy mother, just as she is the true mother from whose womb true sons do not go astray, but sinners do. Therefore the former is not the son of a true mother, nor truly the firstborn; he is assisted as though he were the firstborn, so that he may not lack, but he is not honored in order to make him rich. The latter, however, received a double portion of everything, so that he might abound. Likewise, in Genesis you find that the patriarchs were each given two garments as a gift by their brother Joseph when they were sent back to their father (Gen. 45:22),

**[Note: [Col. 1073D]]** All editions and manuscripts read this; some, so as to indicate “their brother”; others, though more numerous and more reliable, read “to indicate to their father.”

so that they might signify to their father that Joseph, whom their father had believed dead, had been found.

**7.** The firstborn therefore received the prerogative of the inheritance, as Scripture says:

> “This is the beginning of his sons, and to him belong the rights of the firstborn” (Deut. 21:18).

From the firstborn Son of God, therefore, come the holy firstborn; and from that Beginning—because he himself is the beginning and the end (Rev. 1:8)—the beginning is called holy: the beginning is the son to whom belongs the prerogative of the firstfruits, in accordance with what was said to Abraham:

> “Cast out the slave woman and her son; for the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac” (Gen. 21:10).

**8.** The divine oracle teaches that this pertains more to the inheritance of virtues than of money, when the Lord says:

> “Whatever Sarah tells you, listen to her voice, because in Isaac your offspring shall be called” (ibid., 12).

What other inheritance was there in Isaac except the inheritance of holiness, which ennobled his father? He placed the son of the slave woman over the nations, as though conferring on him a single portion of the patrimony; but he gave Sarah’s son a double portion, to whom not only temporal things but also heavenly and everlasting things were granted. Farewell, and love us, because we love you.

**[Note: [Col. 1073D]]** Written around the year 387.

# LETTER XXXIV

When Horontian asks whether the soul, about which the philosophers hold erroneous opinions, is of heavenly substance, Ambrose first refers him to the books of Ezra; then, demonstrating its dignity by Paul’s testimony, he explains how all creation is said there to groan and again to be set free.

**AMBROSE TO HORONTIAN, GREETING.**

**1.** You asked me whether the soul appears to be of heavenly substance.

**[Note: [Col. 1073D]]** Ambrose gathers together almost all the philosophers’ opinions about the soul. For Xenocrates, the soul is mind without body; for Zeno, fire; for Aristotle, a certain fifth essence, which he calls *entelecheia*; for Aristoxenus, a certain tension of the body; for Empedocles, blood poured around the heart; for Euripides, God; for Pythagoras, numbers; for Dicaearchus, an empty name; for Democritus, atoms. These are the views reported by P. Nannius, who also prefaced them with the observation that the opinion of Plato cited by the holy Bishop was taken from Book V of *The Laws*. See also *Noah and the Ark*, chapter 25, section 92, and Cicero, Book I of the *Tusculan Disputations*.

For you do not think that the soul is either blood, fire, or the harmony of the nerves, as the common run of philosophers interprets it; nor, as that patrician lineage among them—Plato—argues, do you think that the soul is “that which moves itself and is not moved by another.” Or perhaps, following Aristotle, who with his keen intellect introduced a certain fifth kind of element, you have approved of *entelecheia* (ἐντελέχεια), from which you might compose and, as it were, fashion the substance of the soul.

**2.** On this subject I advise you to read the book of Ezra,

**[Note: [Col. 1074D]]** The Fourth Book of Ezra is indicated here; its authority is discussed in the *Admonition* to *The Good of Death*.

which both despised those philosophical trifles and, with the deeper wisdom he had gathered from revelation, touched upon the fact that souls belong to a higher substance.

**3.** The Apostle, although he did not state it explicitly,

**[Note: [Col. 1074D]]** Erasmus and the editions following him read “did not express”; Amerbach and all the manuscripts read “not explicitly.”

nevertheless left us to understand it, like a good teacher and spiritual farmer, awakening the minds of his disciples by the hidden seeds of doctrine: namely, that our souls belong to a higher creation and to a certain most excellent nature. For when he says that creation was subjected to futility, not willingly but because of him who subjected it in hope, “because creation itself will be set free from the slavery of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God” (Rom. 8:20–21), he shows that the grace of souls is no ordinary thing. By their power and virtue the human race rises to adoption as children of God, possessing within itself what was granted to it according to the likeness and image of God.

Souls are neither grasped by any touch nor seen by bodily sight; and therefore they display the likeness of that incorporeal and invisible nature, and in their substance surpass bodily and sensible quality. For the things that are seen are temporal, signify temporal things, and cling to temporal things; but the things that are not seen cling to that eternal and highest Good, and in him they live, exist, and move (Acts 17:18). If they choose what is good, they do not allow themselves to be separated or divided from him.

[Col. 1075A] **4.** Every soul, therefore, seeing itself confined in this bodily hovel, yet not having degenerated through sharing in this earthly dwelling, groans, burdened by its union with this body; for “the corruptible body weighs down the soul” (2 Cor. 5:4), and “the earthly dwelling presses down the mind burdened with many thoughts” (Wis. 9:15). At the same time, recognizing that it walks by faith and not by sight, it wishes to depart from the body and be present with the Lord (2 Cor. 5:7).

**5.** Let us therefore consider how creation was subjected to futility (Rom. 8:20), not by its own will, but by the divine ordinance by which it was determined that souls ought to be joined to bodies for the sake of their hope, so that while they hope for good things they may show themselves worthy of heavenly recompense:

> “For we must all appear before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive the things proper to the body” (2 Cor. 5:10).

Therefore each soul should foresee that the merits of its way of life will be repaid to it. And he says beautifully, “what belongs to the body” (Rom. 8)—that is, what it undertook to govern—so that if it governed well, it may receive the reward for which it was subjected in hope; and if badly, punishment, because it did not hope in God, nor strive toward that adoption as children and the freedom of true glory.

**6.** The Apostle therefore taught that the creation of the human race was subjected to futility.

**[Note: [Col. 1075C]]** All editions read: “For what is so subjected to futility as man, and as his soul?” All manuscripts read: “For what is so man as his soul?” This is not unsuitable; for it is from this that man is shown to be subject to futility: his soul, in which he most especially consists, is subject to the same condition.

For what is so truly man as his soul? Of its companions he says:

> “While we are in this body, we groan, being burdened” (2 Cor. 5:4).

David also says:

> “Man has become like futility” (Ps. 143:4);

and:

> “All is futility; every living man” (Ps. 38:6).

The life of man in this age, therefore, is futility. The soul is subjected to this futility. Thus when the holy person does what belongs to the body, he does not do it willingly or by his own choice, but “because of him who subjected it in hope” (Rom. 8:20),

**[Note: [Col. 1075C]]** The Roman edition alone reads: “he does it in hope, so that he may obey him,” and so forth.

he does it in order to obey him. From this example of the soul let us proceed to the remaining creatures.

**7.** Consider the sun, moon, and stars. Although they shine with splendid brilliance as the lights of heaven, they are nevertheless creatures, and for daily service they either rise or set,

**[Note: [Col. 1075D]]** Some Paris editions read: “by the ordinance of the Creator … with which they are clothed; therefore by day,” and so forth.

serving the arrangement of the eternal Creator, supplying the radiance with which they are clothed and shining out by day and by night. How often is this sun covered by clouds? How often, when the earth is deprived of it by obstruction,

**[Note: [Col. 1075D]]** The older editions, together with the Regius manuscripts, read “bring about an obstruction to the earth”; several manuscripts read “bring about the earth by an obstruction.” In some of these, however, the verb *bring about* is omitted, in place of which one Vatican manuscript has, not inappropriately, “as they report.” The Roman edition, together with four manuscripts, has the equally reasonable reading “an obstruction is brought about for the earth.” Immediately afterward, where the older editions and manuscripts read “when opposite to it,” the Roman edition has “when opposite to the moon.” A little later, instead of “they arise for themselves,” the editions read “as he says,” while the manuscripts variously have “they arise for them,” or “they arise from them, as he says.” One Vatican manuscript restores the passage as “eclipses arise,” and so forth. Finally, the Psalmist’s passage, given in the ancient editions and all the manuscripts as “the moon knows its settings,” is rendered by the Roman edition from the sacred books in these words: “He made the moon for appointed times; the sun knows,” and so forth.

when its ray of light has been reflected from the opposite direction, eclipses occur. As Scripture says:

> “The moon knows its settings” (Ps. 103:19).

It knows when it shines with its full sphere and when it is emptied. The stars also, covered with mist, vanish. They endure the uses of this worldly service, certainly not willingly but in hope,

**[Note: [Col. 1076C]]** This passage gave some people occasion to think that Ambrose attributed rational souls to heaven and the stars, following Origen’s opinion. On this matter one may consult Dionysius Petavius, Book I of *The Work of the Six Days*, chapter 12, and Daniel Huetius, Book II of *Origenian Questions*, question 8. Apart from the response made by some that the holy Doctor is here employing a certain personification, it is worth noting that in those times there were not a few who thought that the heavenly spheres possessed rational souls. Ambrose is speaking here within that hypothesis and opinion, which had not yet been condemned by the Church. Yet that he did not hold this opinion as true and certain may be understood from the fact that in the following letter he proposes another view and leaves Horontian free to follow whichever he considers more authoritative. We cannot gather the holy Bishop’s opinion on this matter better from elsewhere than from Book II of the *Hexaemeron*, chapter 4, section 17, where he distinctly denies that the heavens and the firmament praise God as certain spiritual powers, but says that they do so only as the works of the world. Examine that passage and compare it with the similar passage in Basil, *Homily 3 on the Hexaemeron*.

because they also hope for the reward of this labor from him who subjected them. Therefore they endure it on his account—that is, on account of his will.

**8.** Nor is it surprising that they patiently endure this, since they know that their Lord and the Creator of all things, whether in heaven or on earth, took upon himself the frailty of our body and the servitude of our condition. Why, then, should they not patiently endure the slavery of their corruption, when the Lord of all humbled himself for the whole world even unto death, took the form of a servant (Phil. 2:7), and became sin—and even a curse—for us (Gal. 3:13)?

Imitating his goodness, therefore, the heavenly creatures, although they groan because they have been subjected to the futility of this world, nevertheless console themselves with the knowledge that they will be set free from the slavery of corruption into the freedom of glory, when the adoption of the children of God arrives, which is the redemption of all:

> “For when the fullness of the nations has entered, then all Israel will be saved” (Rom. 11:25).

For whom will he not forgive among the people, who forgives even that persecutor of his own who said:

> “Crucify him, crucify him” (John 19:6);

and:

> “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27:25)?

But since the heavenly creation too has been subjected to futility (Rom. 8:20), although this is in hope, the piety and redemption of the truth will permit even their faithlessness and drunkenness—fallen through the futility of this world—to have a share in forgiveness.

**9.** To conclude, then: that great and mighty sun, that moon which the darkness of night does not cover, and those stars which are the ornaments of heaven now endure the slavery of corruption, because every body is corruptible. Indeed, the heavens will pass away, and heaven and earth will pass away (Matt. 24:35). But afterward the sun, moon, and the other lights of the stars will rest in the glory of the children of God, when God will be all in all (1 Cor. 15:28)—may he also be in you and in us through his fullness and mercy.

**10.** Or do we believe that even the angels themselves, who in the labors of this world endure various ministries, as we read in John’s *Apocalypse* (Rev. 3:1 and following), do not groan when they are employed as ministers of punishments and destructions?

**[Note: [Col. 1077D]]** Although God chiefly employs reprobate angels to exact the penalties of crimes, as the executioners and agents of his justice—we read, for example, in Psalm 77:49, “sending evil angels”—he sometimes also uses good angels for this ministry, as we understand not only from various passages of the *Apocalypse*, but also from 4 Kings, chapter 19, and Daniel, chapter 10. As for Ambrose’s testimony that these same angels groan, it should be understood in the sense in which he indicates in the following letter that they suffer with the body of the Church, like superior members suffering with inferior members. Augustine teaches in several places, especially in *The City of God*, that their happiness is not impaired by this compassion; later theologians agree.

They possess a blessed life and would certainly prefer to return to that former state of their tranquility rather than have it interrupted by the avenging punishments of our sins.

**[Note: [Col. 1077D]]** Some manuscripts read, “who do not have …”; this is less suitable. Below, where the older editions and many more manuscripts read *interpolari* (“be interrupted”), the Roman edition, with a few other manuscripts, prefers *interpellari* (“be troubled”). But, as Nannius says, *interpolari* occurs so frequently in these books in place of *interpellari* that it is doubtful whether Saint Ambrose uses the two words interchangeably.

For those who rejoice over the redemption of a single sinner (Luke 15:10) certainly groan over the afflictions of so many sinners.

**11.** If, therefore, even the heavenly creatures and Powers endure the slavery of corruption, though in hope, so that later they may rejoice for us and with us, let us too console ourselves amid the sufferings of this present time through hope and expectation of future glory. Farewell, my son, and love us, because we love you.

259 **[Note: [Col. 1078D]]** Written around the year 387.

# LETTER XXXV

In this letter the first question is why, although the Apostle’s words do not say that all creation is subject to corruption, all creation is nevertheless said to groan together. Then, from what follows there, the discussion proceeds to the Spirit of adoption, the greatness of the heavenly rewards, the groaning of the saints, the firstfruits of the Spirit, the adoption of children, and saving hope.

**AMBROSE TO HORONTIAN.**

**1.** The preceding letter answered your inquiry; this is a portion of my answer which does not dissolve the former answer but completes it. For as I reviewed what follows, I confess that I was troubled because he added:

> “For we know that all creation groans” (Rom. 8:20);

whereas in the preceding passage he had said without qualification:

> “Because creation was subjected to futility.”

For he did not say that all creation, but that creation which was subjected. And again he says:

> “Because creation itself will be set free from the slavery of corruption” (ibid., 21).

But thirdly he added that all creation groans together (ibid., 22).

**2.** What, then, does this addition mean, unless perhaps it is because not all creation is subject to futility; and because not all is subject to futility, not all will be set free from the slavery of corruption? For what could be set free if it is free and exempt from subjection to futility and from its slavery of corruption?

All creation, however, groans together not in its own labor but in ours, and perhaps is in travail with that spirit of salvation, the spirit of joy, awaiting the adoption of the children of God, so that it may share the common joy and exultation of the redemption of the human race. Either all creation groans because of its love for us, or because of the member of its body whose head is Christ. But whether you understand it in the way we have described, or simply understand him to have said that all subjected creation groans and suffers the pains of childbirth, interpret it as you wish.

**[Note: [Col. 1078D]]** The Greek word ὠδίνω means both “to suffer the pains of childbirth” and “to be in pain.” Saint Ambrose alludes here to both meanings, which are not present in the Latin expression *parturio*. Thus Nannius.

**3.** Now let us consider what he added:

> “Not only that, but we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly, awaiting the adoption of children, the redemption of our body” (Rom. 8:23).

What adoption of children means is taught on the preceding page; and therefore, for the sake of explaining the meaning, we must return to that page.

**4.** “Those who by the Spirit,” he says, “put to death the deeds of the flesh will live” (ibid., 13). Nor is it surprising that they live, since they become sons of God—those who have the Spirit of God. So truly is he a son of God that he does not receive the spirit of slavery but the Spirit of adoption as children, so that the Holy Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit that we are children of God.

The witness of the Holy Spirit is that he himself is the one who cries in our hearts, “Abba, Father,” as it is written to the Galatians (Gal. 4:6). There is also that great testimony that we are children of God: for we are heirs of God, but co-heirs with Christ. He is a co-heir who is glorified together with him; but he is glorified together with him who, by suffering for him, suffers with him (Rom. 8:16 and following).

**[Note: [Col. 1078D]]** The editions and most manuscripts read “but he is glorified”; other codices read “but [he is glorified] with him,” which produces a more elegant gradation.

**926 5.** To encourage us to suffer, he adds (ibid., 18) that all the things we suffer are less than, and unworthy of, the future reward of such labors—the reward of good things that will be revealed in us,
