when, having been reformed according to the image of God, we shall have deserved to behold his glory face to face.

**6.** To exalt the greatness of the future revelation, he added that creation too awaits this revelation of the children of God. Creation is now subjected to futility, not willingly but in hope, because it hopes for the grace of its ministry from Christ; or because it too will be set free from the slavery of corruption, so that it may be received into the freedom of the glory of the children of God, so that there may be one freedom of creation and of the children of God when their glory has been revealed.

But now, while the revelation is delayed, all creation groans together, awaiting the glory of our adoption and redemption, already in travail with that spirit of salvation and wishing to be set free from the slavery of futility.

**7.** The Apostle joined to this also the groaning of the saints who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, for they too groan. Although they are secure concerning their own merit, they nevertheless suffer with us because the redemption of the entire body of the Church is still future. For while some members of their body are still suffering, how could other members, even though they are superior, fail to suffer with the suffering members of one body?

**8.** Hence I think the Apostle said (1 Cor. 15:28) that then the Son himself will also be subject to him who subjected all things to him. Those who are still suffering are not yet subject: in them Christ perhaps still thirsts, still hungers, and in them he is naked, because they do not fulfill the word of God and do not put on Christ, who is the clothing of believers and the garment of the faithful.

But those in whom he is sick still need medicine; and therefore they are not yet subject. For this subjection is one of virtue, not of weakness. In the strong, then, and in those who fulfill God’s commandment, the Son of God is subject. But now he suffers more in those who do not help the suffering than in those who ask to be helped. This is the pious and true interpretation of the subjection of the Lord Jesus: he will subject himself in order to be God all in all.

**[Note: [Col. 1079D]]** The Roman edition alone reads, “the Son will be subject to him who subjected all things to him.”

**9.** We have traversed the Apostle’s meaning; now let us consider who those are who have the firstfruits of the Spirit (Rom. 8:13). Let us therefore question the Law about what it declares under the name of firstfruits or beginning. It says:

> “You shall not delay the firstfruits of your threshing floor and of your winepress” (Exod. 22:29);

and below:

> “You shall bring the firstfruits of your firstfruits into the house of the Lord your God” (Exod. 34:26).

Firstfruits and tenths are different: firstfruits belong to a greater grace and to the most careful observance of sanctification. Abel therefore pleased God because he did not delay his offering, but offered from the firstborn of his sheep (Gen. 4:4).

Although some wish there to be a distinction between firstfruits and firstborn—that is, what is born first—on the grounds that, once the seeds have been gathered, the beginnings are offered from the whole threshing floor, nevertheless whatever is first taken from the harvest is offered to the Lord; but we shall discuss this elsewhere.

**[Note: [Col. 1079D]]** In the margin of the Roman edition there was a reference to *Cain and Abel*, Book II, chapter 1; and indeed sections 5 and 6 there contain a mystical discussion of firstfruits and beginnings. It seems more credible to us, however, that our Doctor promises Horontian that he will sometime write to him more fully on this subject than that he refers him to that work. Nannius explains the meaning of this Ambrosian passage as follows: Saint Ambrose makes this distinction between firstfruits and beginnings: firstfruits come from the harvest, beginnings from threshing; firstfruits include the ears of grain, while beginnings consist of the pure seed; what is first reaped he calls “firstfruits,” and what is first collected after the grain has been beaten out he calls “beginnings.” It may also be added that “beginnings” are properly so called because they have been initiated and consecrated to God; thus firstfruits belong to the making of vows, and beginnings to the fulfillment of vows. So far Nannius.

The whole harvest of the threshing floor seems to be sanctified by the offering of the firstfruits, but the firstfruits themselves are holier.

**10.** Similarly, the saints are the Lord’s firstfruits, especially the apostles. For God first placed apostles in the Church; they both prophesied many things and preached the Lord Jesus, because they received him first (1 Cor. 12:28). The prophet Simeon received him (Luke 2:28), as did the prophet Zechariah, his son John, and Nathanael, in whom there was no deceit (John 1:47); therefore he rested beneath the fig tree; and Joseph, who was called righteous, who buried him (Luke 23:53).

These are the firstfruits of our faith. Yet the nature of the other seeds is the same as that of the firstfruits, although in some there is a lesser grace:

> “For God is able from stones to raise up children for Abraham” (Matt. 3:9).

**11.** Here is an example from the Lord Jesus himself. In the resurrection of the dead he is called “the firstborn from the dead” (Col. 1:18). The Apostle himself signified him as the firstfruits when he said:

> “In Christ all will be made alive, but each in his own order: Christ the firstfruits, then those who are Christ’s, who believed in his coming” (1 Cor. 15:22).

The truth of the body in him is the same as in us; yet he is called both the firstborn from the dead, because he was the first to rise, and the firstfruits, because he is holier than all fruits and has sanctified the other fruits that share in his fellowship.

He is also the beginning of those who are according to the image—indeed, the image of the invisible God (Col. 1:15)—in whom, according to divinity, there is nothing bodily and nothing temporal, because he is the radiance of the Father’s glory and the image of his substance (Heb. 1:3). We have extended this epistolary discourse because we wished to explain what the firstfruits are.

**12.** Our firstfruits, therefore, are the apostles, chosen from all the fruits of that present time,

**[Note: [Col. 1080D]]** The Roman edition had removed the word “present,” which occurs both here and elsewhere and in all the manuscripts; it does not appear at all useless to the sense. We have attached *scilicet* (“namely”) to this phrase on the authority of the principal manuscripts.

to whom it was said:

> “You will do greater things than these” (John 14:12),

for the grace of God poured itself out upon them. These, I say, were groaning, awaiting the redemption of the whole body, and they still groan, because many are still laboring and wavering.

**[Note: [Col. 1080D]]** The same Roman edition reads, “And if someone should raise himself toward the things above”; other editions and a manuscript read, “And if”; several manuscripts more appropriately read, “So that if someone should stand …”; the Albinus manuscript reads “raise himself,” and would rightly be preferred to the others if it were supported by even one additional witness.

So that if someone stands upon the higher shore and is still struck by the waves through the middle of his body, he groans and suffers the pains of childbirth until he escapes entirely. He certainly groans who still says to us:

> “Who is weak, and I am not weak?” (2 Cor. 11:29).

**13.** Therefore let us not be troubled by what is written:

> “We who have the firstfruits of the Spirit groan inwardly, awaiting the adoption of children, the redemption of our body” (Rom. 8:23).

The meaning is clear: those who have the firstfruits of the Spirit groan while awaiting the adoption of children. This adoption of children is the redemption of the whole body, when, face to face, like a son of God by adoption, a person will see that divine and eternal Good.

There is an adoption of children in the Lord’s Church when the Spirit cries, “Abba, Father” (Gal. 4:6), as you find in the Letter to the Galatians. But that adoption will be perfect when all who are worthy to see God’s face rise in incorruption, honor, and glory. Then the human condition will truly judge itself redeemed.

Hence the Apostle glories, saying:

> “For in hope we have been saved” (Rom. 8:24).

For hope saves, just as faith does, of which it is said:

> “Your faith has saved you” (Luke 18:42).

**14.** Therefore the creation that was subjected to futility not willingly but in hope (Rom. 8:20) is saved by hope. So too was Paul, who knew that it would be gain for him to die and, released from the body, be with Christ, yet remained in the flesh for the sake of those whom he would gain for Christ (Phil. 1:21). What, then, is hope except expectation of future things? Hence he says:

> “But hope that is seen is not hope” (Rom. 8:21).

For it is not the things that are seen, but the things that are not seen, that are eternal:

> “For what does someone hope for if he sees it?”

We seem to possess the things we see; how, then, can we hope for what we possess? Nothing, therefore, of the things hoped for is seen:

> “Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2:9).

**15.** Therefore, if what is seen cannot be hoped for, some people are not reasoning correctly. For:

> “What does someone see, and what does he hope for?”

**[Note: [Col. 1081D]]** All manuscripts read this way, while the editions read, “unless perhaps you understand it in this way.” A little later, where all editions and most manuscripts read, “Because that is true,” several manuscripts read, “What else? It is true,” and so forth.

Unless perhaps it is understood in this way: “What does someone see, and what does he hope for?” or “What does he await?” For this is true: we hope for what we do not see; and therefore, although it seems to be absent from us, we await it with patience:

> “Waiting, I waited for the Lord, and he regarded me” (Ps. 39:2).

Therefore we wait patiently because the Lord is good to those who endure him (Lam. 3:25). And it seems fitting that he says, “he repaid me through patience”: We await what we hope for, and we do not see it. For a person does something great when he hopes for and awaits what is not seen; and therefore, because he directs his mind toward that which is all things, he endures.

**16.** Beautifully, then, it is said:

> “But hope that is seen is not hope” (Rom. 8:24),

concerning the powers of this age, its dignities, and its riches. You see someone conspicuous in fasces and chariots; he has no hope in the chariots that are seen.

Nor is hope in the element of heaven itself, but in the Lord of heaven. **[Note: [Col. 1081D]]** Ambrose attacks the vanity of the Chaldeans so frequently in the preceding volume that we find it more convenient to refer readers to the index than to list those passages here.

Nor does the Chaldean place his hope in the stars that he observes; nor the rich man in his possessions, nor the miser in his interest. Rather, he has hope who places his hope in him whom he does not see—that is, in the Lord Jesus, who stands in our midst and is not seen (John 1:26). Finally:

> “Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, what the Lord has prepared for those who love him.”

929 **[Note: [Col. 1081D]]** Written around the year 387.

# LETTER XXXVI

When someone asks which spirit Paul said “intercedes for us with inexpressible groanings,” the answer is that no other is meant than the Holy Spirit, who both directs our prayers and groans for our sins with an inexpressible—that is, heavenly—groaning.

**AMBROSE TO HORONTIAN.**

[Col. 1082B]

**1.** Our letters are linked together, so that we seem to be conversing as though we were present with one another. Thus I receive from your question, and you from my explanation, material for writing letters.

**2.** You indicated that you were troubled about which spirit is meant by the statement:

> “For he intercedes for us with inexpressible groanings” (Rom. 8:26).

Let us therefore return to what precedes, so that the reading may reveal what we seek:

> “Likewise,” he says, “the Spirit also helps the weakness of our prayer” (ibid.).

Does it not seem to you that this is the Holy Spirit, since he is our helper, like the one to whom it is said:

**[Note: [Col. 1082D]]** Some manuscripts read, “Be my helper.”

> “You are my helper; do not abandon me or despise me, my saving God” (Ps. 26:9).

**3.** For what other spirit could teach Paul what he ought to pray? The Spirit of Christ teaches, just as Christ also taught his disciples to pray (Luke 11:1). Who could teach after Christ except his Spirit, whom he himself sent to teach and direct our prayers? For:

> “We pray with the Spirit, and we pray with the mind” (1 Cor. 14:15).

So that the mind may pray well, the Spirit goes before it and leads it along the right path (Ps. 142:11), lest carnal things, lesser things, or even things beyond its strength creep in:

> “To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good” (1 Cor. 12:7).

Finally, it is written:

> “Ask for great things, and small things will be added to you. Ask for heavenly things, and earthly things will be added” (Matt. 6:33).

4. Therefore he wants us to ask for greater things, and not linger over earthly ones. Yet he knows what he grants, distributing to each as he wills (I Cor. XII, 11). For at times, knowing the measure—which we do not know—he says: “You cannot receive these things now.” I ask for the passion of martyrdom; “the spirit is willing” [Note: All editions and some manuscripts read *spiritus promptus est* (“the spirit is willing”), but more and better manuscripts add *τὸ sanctus* (“holy”); this word is entirely compatible with the sequence of the discourse.] (Matt. XXVI, 41). But seeing the weakness of my flesh, lest, while desiring greater things, I lose lesser ones, he says: “You cannot receive these things.” [Note: Consider the opportunities I had—my embassies to the tyrant Maximus, as well as Justina’s persecution. If you read more attentively what the holy Bishop wrote about it, you will acknowledge that it was not he who lacked martyrdom, but martyrdom that lacked him.] What opportunities I had—and how nearly I was recalled from the very threshold of the end! For the good physician knows what food is suited to each weakness and to each time for the restoration of health. Sometimes the timely administration of food restores health; but if someone takes it at an unsuitable time, or takes what is not appropriate, he becomes exposed to danger.

[Note: Compare this passage of Ambrose with several Augustinian passages, especially those in Book I, *To Simplicianus*, Question 2, and in *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 14, where the fittingness of divine calling is discussed; you will find no slight affinity of doctrine between teacher and pupil.]

5. Therefore, because we do not know what we ought to pray for, or how we ought to pray, the Holy Spirit “intercedes for us” (Rom. VIII, 26); for he is the Spirit of our advocate, Jesus. And he intercedes with unspeakable groanings; for Christ also grieves on our behalf (Isa. LIII, 4). God the Father too says: “My belly, my belly, I am in pain” (Jer. IV, 19). And we frequently read that he is indignant and grieving. He groans in order to take away our sins and teach us to practice repentance. For his is a pious groaning, full of authority, of which the Prophet says: “And my groaning is not hidden from you” (Ps. XXXVII, 10). [Col. 1083B] For he did not hide as Adam did, but said: “Behold, I am the shepherd, and what has this flock done wrong? I have sinned; exact punishment from me” (I Chron. XXI, 17).

6. From this, then, comes the groaning of the Spirit of God; [Note: Some manuscripts read: “and that groaning indeed.”] and that groaning of the Prophet is rightly called unspeakable, because it is heavenly. For the things that Paul heard in heaven (II Cor. XII, 4), he heard as unspeakable things, things which human beings ought not to utter; but what is hidden from human beings is known to God. For he knows everything, being the searcher of the heart; yet he searches those things which the Spirit has cleansed (Rom. VIII, 27). God therefore knows what the Spirit asks [Note: A few manuscripts read: “and what the wisdom of the Spirit is.”] and what the Spirit’s wisdom is, the Spirit who intercedes for the saints, as you have it: “For the Spirit also intercedes for us” (ibid.). For those for whom Christ suffered, and whom he cleansed with his blood, the Spirit also intercedes.

Farewell, and love us as a son; for we love you.

[Note: Written about the year 387.]

## LETTER XXXVII

When Simplicianus had assured Ambrose that he would be doing something useful if he expounded some passage from the Apostle before the people, the holy man promises that he will comply with his wishes, especially since he knows that his friend will act as his judge in the matter. He therefore sends him what he had discussed in his absence: namely, that our freedom consists in wisdom, a position which he says the philosophers have vaunted with ambitious display. Yet he establishes this doctrine as having been handed down by the Fathers, both from Solomon and from the examples of Jacob and Joseph. From these examples he shows that a person becomes free not by being sold, but by wisdom. Having thereby demonstrated who is free and who is not, he defines as being master of himself only the person who is not compelled; hence he concludes that servitude can sometimes be joined with freedom. What follows contains certain examples and descriptions of the truly free, to which is added the assertion that only the person who lives according to the laws enjoys freedom. Then, after several arguments against the philosophers, he contrasts Christians with their heroes. Finally, after affirming that those who serve wicked passions are not free, he teaches how our members serve righteousness.

**AMBROSE to SIMPLICIANUS, greetings.**

1. Recently, when a familiar conversation was taking place between us in the intimacy born of our long-standing affection [Note: Gill’s edition reads: “an inward conversation was believed to be taking place.”], you let me know that you would be pleased if I undertook to discuss before the people something from the writings of the Apostle Paul—writings whose profundity in their counsels can scarcely be grasped, but whose sublimity in their sayings lifts up the hearer and kindles the speaker. This was especially so because in most passages he explains himself in his own words so fully that the person who expounds him finds nothing of his own to add; and if he wishes to say something, he performs more the office of a grammarian than of a disputant. [Note: The Roman edition alone adds: “from the mysteries of the Psalmist, or from the writings of Paul … whose depth … they themselves explain in their own discourses.” It is clear that the Roman editors interpolated these and similar words into this letter for no other reason than to insert it among the expositions of the Psalms. As for the obscurity of certain Pauline passages, Augustine speaks of it in precisely the same way in his *Letter to the Romans*. Indeed, Peter himself acknowledges the same difficulty in his second Letter, chapter 3, verse 16.]

2. Nevertheless, because I recognize in you both the affection of an old friendship and—what is more—the love of paternal grace (for old age has something associable with many people, whereas paternal love has no such limitation), and because you judged that I had not already acted without substance in what you request, I shall obey your wishes. I am especially encouraged and challenged by my own example, which is not difficult for me to imitate; for I shall imitate not some great man but myself, when I return to use among my own people something that is not great.

3. As for the counsels, when the image and likeness of the blessed life were being expressed in our discourse, we think that the composition was made in such a way that it would not displease many others—and certainly would not displease you, who love us. Although it is more difficult to avoid displeasing your judgment than that of many people, you lighten the weight of your judgment by your affection, and I take comfort in that.

4. Since this letter finds you absent [Note: The Roman edition alone adds: “It concerns Psalm 104, which was read today, and the sayings …”], it concerns the sayings of the Apostle Paul, who calls us from servitude into freedom, saying: “You were bought at a price; do not become slaves of human beings” (I Cor. VII, 23). He shows that our freedom consists in knowledge of wisdom. [Note: All editions read “that our freedom is in the wisdom of Christ”; the most numerous manuscripts read “that our freedom is in the wisdom that is in Christ”; one manuscript, together with the editions of Erasmus and Gill in the margin, reads “that our freedom is in the knowledge of wisdom.” We have no doubt that the latter is the genuine reading, while supposing that the other arose from the word “knowledge” being erased in an ancient exemplar. For whether one reads “in the wisdom that is in Christ,” which produces a somewhat unsuitable sense, or “in Christ’s wisdom,” which seems a little more elegant, how could the holy Doctor then add that this opinion had been proclaimed with great insistence by the philosophers? On the contrary, the Stoics advertised with great display that freedom consists in knowledge of wisdom, or simply that the wise person alone is free. This subject is treated in Cicero’s *Paradox* 5, and also, though not very differently, in Book 6. Clement of Alexandria, in Book III of the *Paedagogus*, chapter 6, asserts that the Christian alone is rich; Philo likewise demonstrates that every good person possesses freedom in a work published under that title, from which our Ambrose transferred no small amount into this letter, just as he borrowed certain material in Book I of *Jacob and the Blessed Life*, chapters 7 and 8, and Book II, chapters 1 and 3, where the same argument is treated, as we noted in the commentary on those books.] This opinion has been vigorously debated and loudly proclaimed by the philosophers through an elaborate effort of disputation: they say that every wise person is free, but every foolish person is a slave. [Note: The Roman edition reads: “but every foolish person is a slave.” In the following verse, however, instead of “David’s son says,” many more manuscripts read “David says,” while a few read “Solomon says.” As for the reason Ambrose attributes Ecclesiasticus to Solomon, we discussed it in volume I, page 807. Concerning the philosophers’ many plagiarisms, he discusses them in so many passages, both in the earlier volume and in this one, that we think it unnecessary to list them.]

5. But David’s son said this much earlier, when he declared: “The fool changes like the moon” (Eccl. XXVII, 12). For the wise person is not broken by fear, not changed by power, not elated by prosperity, and not overwhelmed by sorrows. Where there is wisdom, there is strength of spirit, steadfastness, and courage. The wise person, therefore, remains the same in spirit; he is neither diminished nor increased by changes in circumstances. Nor does he sway like a child, “tossed about by every wind of doctrine”; rather, he remains perfect in Christ, founded upon charity and rooted in faith. The wise person therefore knows nothing of the decline of circumstances [Note: All editions read: “he does not know a changeable spirit”; but most manuscripts read: “he does not know the various vicissitudes of the spirit.” Some read: “he does not know movement”; others: “the spirit is not various”; and the Boyer manuscript: “he does not know that the spirit is various.” This is not inappropriate.], and is ignorant of the spirit’s various vicissitudes; but “he will shine like the sun of righteousness,” which shines in the kingdom of his Father (Matt. XIII, 43).

6. Let us consider, then, from what source Philosophy—concerning which the discipline and prudence of the Fathers have taught—has drawn this doctrine more fully. Was not Noah the first, when he noticed that his son Ham had foolishly laughed at his father after seeing him naked, to curse him, saying: “Cursed be Ham; he shall be a household servant to his brothers” (Gen. IX, 25)? And did he not set over him as masters his brothers, who wisely thought that their father’s old age ought to be honored? [Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “Cursed be Canaan.” Certainly the Septuagint writes ἐπικατάρατος Χάμ (“Cursed be Ham”), which Ambrose evidently followed here, as elsewhere.]

7. Was not Jacob also that fountain of every discipline who poured the richness of this whole argument into the hearts of all, and who was preferred on account of his wisdom to his older brother (Gen. XXVII, 29)? Finally, the pious father, who had to contend in paternal affection between his two sons, [Note: The old edition reads: “but differed in judgment.”] yet differed in judgment—for affection is conferred according to relationship, whereas judgments are formed according to merit—when he divided grace between one and mercy between the other, gave grace to the wise and mercy to the foolish. Since the latter could not raise himself to virtue by his own strength, nor lift his steps forward spontaneously, he blessed him so that he would serve his brother and be his servant. He thus showed that folly is worse than servitude, so that servitude might serve as a remedy for him; for the fool cannot govern himself, and unless he has a guide, he is cast headlong by his own desires. [Note: The same edition reads: “that folly is worse than servitude”; but there is no reason why the word “servitude” should have been removed.]

8. Therefore, as a father who was attentive and concerned for his welfare [Note: Some manuscripts read: “and consoling him, he made him …”], he made him the servant of his brother, so that he might be governed by his counsel. For this reason, among peoples lacking counsel, wise men are appointed as rulers, to govern the folly of the common people by their own strength; so that under the appearance of power they may exercise dominion, and by the authority of their power subject even the unwilling to obedience to the wiser and to submission to the laws. He therefore placed a yoke upon the foolish man as upon an untamed creature, and denied freedom to him of whom he had said that he would have to live by his sword; lest he fall through recklessness, he set over him a brother, under whose authority and guidance, while subject, he might advance toward conversion. And because servitude admits of distinction—for one person is weaker through necessity but stronger through will, since the good that is done not from necessity but from free will is more beautiful—he first imposed upon him the yoke of necessity, and afterward bestowed upon him the blessing of voluntary submission.

9. Nature, then, does not make a person a slave, but folly; nor does manumission make a person free, but discipline. Esau was born free and became a slave; Joseph was sold into slavery (Gen. XXXVII, 28), and was chosen for authority (Gen. XLI, 41), so that he might rule over those who had bought him. Yet he did not disdain the service of diligent obedience; he retained the height of virtue, preserved the freedom of innocence, and maintained the authority of integrity. Hence the Psalmist beautifully says: “Joseph was sold into slavery; they humbled his feet in fetters” (Ps. CIV, 18). He says “he was sold into slavery,” not “he was made a slave.” “They humbled his feet,” not his soul.

10. For how could the soul have been humbled of which he says: “Iron passed through his soul”? While sin passes through the souls of others—for sin is like iron, since it can penetrate them—the soul of holy Joseph was so impervious to sin that it rather pierced sin itself. Finally, he was not bent by the allurements of his mistress, nor without reason did he fail to feel the flames of lust, because he was burning with the greater ardor of divine grace. Hence this too was beautifully said of him: “The word of the Lord tested him” (Ps. CIV, 19), by which he quenched the flaming arrows of the devil.

11. How could this man be a slave, when he instructed the rulers of the people in that administration of grain, so that they might take thought for and provide against the coming scarcity? Or how could he be a slave when he acquired the whole land and reduced the entire Egyptian people to servitude (Gen. XLVII, 20)? He did not do this to impose the dishonor of a servile condition, but to establish a tribute, while nevertheless exempting the property of the priests from taxation, so that priestly religion might also be held inviolable among the Egyptians.

12. Sale, then, did not make him a slave; for he had indeed been sold to merchants. But if you consider the price, you will find many who have bought young girls of distinguished beauty for themselves and, captivated by love for them, have surrendered themselves to shameful servitude. Apeme, the concubine of King Darius, was seen sitting at his right hand, taking the diadem from his head and placing it upon her own, striking his face with her left hand, while the king gazed at her with open mouth, rejoicing whenever the woman smiled at him; but if she became angry, he considered himself wretched and afflicted. Thus, having laid aside his authority, he sought by caresses to soothe her anger and begged that she be reconciled to him (III Esdras IV, 29–30). [Note: The Boyer manuscript reads: “that she might cover his anger with flattery.”]

13. But why do we cite these examples with such elaborate argument? [Col. 1087B] Do we not often see parents who have fallen into the power of pirates or savage barbarians redeemed by their children with money? [Note: Thus read the editions and by far the majority of manuscripts, except that all editions and a few manuscripts omit the word “money.” The Boyer manuscript, however, gives the passage as follows: “redeemed. Do the laws of nature lie subject to money? Is filial devotion summoned into slavery?”] Are the laws of money more powerful than the laws of nature? Is filial devotion summoned into servitude? Many people buy lions, yet they do not rule the lions; rather, they are in turn subjected to them, so that if they see the lions, enraged, shaking the manes from their necks, they flee and hide. Money, therefore, has no decisive power, although it often buys masters for itself; nor do auction records, by which the buyer is frequently awarded and assigned ownership. A contract does not change a person’s kind, nor does it take away the freedom of wisdom. Indeed, as it is written (Prov. XVII, 2), many free people serve a wise servant; and there is an intelligent slave who governs foolish masters.

14. Whom, then, do you consider more free? Wisdom alone is free. It places the poor over the rich and makes slaves lend to their own masters—not money, but understanding; not money, but the talent of that Lord’s eternal treasure, which never perishes and whose interest is precious. It makes them lend that intelligible silver of heavenly utterances, concerning which the Law says: “You shall lend to the nations, but you shall not borrow” (Deut. XV, 6). The Hebrew lends to the nations; he himself does not receive doctrine from the peoples, but gives it. The Lord has opened his treasure to him, so that he might make the nations moist with the rain of his word and become ruler of the nations, while having no ruler above himself.

15. The wise person, then, is free, bought at the price of heavenly oracles—with that gold, that silver, of the divine word; bought at the price of blood (for it is no small thing to recognize the buyer); bought at the price of grace. He has heard and understood the one who says: “You who thirst, go to the water; and whoever has no silver, go, buy, drink, and eat” (Isa. LV, 1).

16. The person is free who, going forth to war, sees a woman beautiful in appearance, and, after plundering the wealth of his enemies, desires the woman whom he has found there, removes what is superfluous, takes off her garment of captivity, and joins her to himself as a wife—no longer as a slave, but as a free woman (Deut. XXI, 10–11). For he understands that prudence and discipline are not subject to servitude. Therefore the Law says: “She shall not be sold for money” (ibid., 14); for no price is worthy of her. And Job says: “Draw wisdom into your inner being” (Job XXVIII, 18). The topaz of Ethiopia cannot be compared with it [Note: The Boyer manuscript reads: “gold from Ethiopia and topaz”], although topaz is regarded as more precious than gold and silver.

17. Yet not only is that person free who has not endured a master bidding at auction [Note: Two manuscripts read “who has not endured a litigating master”; one reads “a bidder.” Neither is satisfactory. For “he did not endure a bidder” means the same as “he was not bought at auction.” The addition “nor saw one raising his finger” refers to an ancient custom by which purchasers raised a finger as a sign that they were bidding. Cicero, *Against Verres* III: “The buyers rush up at the appointed time; the bidder raises his finger.”], nor seen one raising his finger; rather, that person is more free who is free within himself, who is free according to the laws of nature, knowing that the law prescribed by nature concerns morals, not conditions, and that the measure of duties is determined not by human judgment but by the disciplines of nature. Do you therefore consider such a person merely free, or do you also regard him as a kind of censor and superintendent of morals? Hence Scripture truly says that the poor will be placed over the rich, and those without property over those who administer it (Prov. XXII, 7).

18. Does the person who buys support for himself with money seem free to you? The person who seeks the applause of the crowd more than the judgment of the wise? Is that person free who is moved by popular ears, or the one who fears the hissing of the mob? Yet this is not the freedom that a manumitted person receives and acquires when he is presented with the lictor’s palm [Note: Nannius thinks that the lictor’s palm is the same as the praetor’s *vindicta* in Horace. But the *vindicta*, or, as others call it, the rod, was a staff whose end—whether wielded by the praetor or, at his command, by a lictor—touched the head of the person being asserted into freedom. We prefer, however, to understand “palm” as the hand of the master or lictor, with which a slap was inflicted upon the person being manumitted. See Book II of Phaedrus, fable 36.]. For I do not consider generosity, but virtue, to be freedom. It is not conferred by the votes of others, but claimed and possessed by one’s own greatness of spirit. The wise person is always free, always honored, always one who presides over the laws. Finally, the law is not laid down for the just but for the unjust (I Tim. I, 9); for the just person is himself a law to himself and does not need to seek from elsewhere the pattern of virtue, since he carries it enclosed in his heart, having the work of the law written on the tablets of his heart. To him it is said: “Drink water from your own vessels, and from the springs of your own wells” (Prov. V, 15). For what is as close to us as the word of God? This is the word in our heart and in our mouth, which we neither see nor grasp.

19. The wise person is therefore free, because whoever does what he wishes is free. But not every good will is the will of the wise person alone; rather, the wise person wills everything that is good. For he hates evil because he has chosen what is good. Therefore, if he has chosen what is good, he is free as the arbiter of choice and as the chooser of action, because he does what he wishes. The wise person, therefore, is free. The wise person does everything well. Whoever does everything well does everything rightly; and whoever does everything rightly does everything without offense, irreproachably, without harm, and without disturbance to himself. Whoever possesses the ability to do everything without offense, irreproachably, without disturbance, and without harm does nothing foolishly, but does everything wisely. Whoever acts wisely has nothing to fear, for fear belongs to sin. Where there is no fear, there is freedom; where there is freedom, there is power to do what one wishes. Therefore the wise person alone is free.

20. For whoever can neither be compelled nor prevented is in no way a slave. But it belongs to the wise person neither to be compelled nor to be prevented; therefore the wise person is not a slave. A person is prevented when he does not do what he desires. But what does the wise person desire, except the things that belong to virtue and discipline, without which he cannot exist? These are within him and are not torn away from him. If they are torn away, he is no longer wise, since he is without the practice and discipline of virtue, from which he deprives himself if he is not a willing interpreter of virtue. And if he is compelled, it is clear that he acts unwillingly.

In all actions there are either corrections arising from virtue, falls arising from wickedness, or things that are intermediate and indifferent. The wise person is not a compelled but a willing executor of virtue, since he does everything that pleases him while fleeing wickedness and admitting not even its dream. With respect to indifferent things, he is so unmoved that, unlike the mass of humanity, he does not incline now here, now there at every moment; rather, his mind hangs as evenly balanced as on a scale, so that it does not lean toward pleasures, nor does it incline even slightly toward things that ought to be shunned. His affection remains immovable. It is therefore clear that the wise person does nothing unwillingly and is not compelled; for if he were a slave, he would be compelled. The wise person, then, is free.

21. The Apostle also defines the matter in this way when he says: “Am I not free? Am I not an apostle?” (I Cor. IX, 1). So free was he that, when certain people had entered in order to test his freedom, he did not yield even for an hour to subjection, as he himself says (Gal. II, 5), so that the truth of the Gospel might be proclaimed. Since he did not yield, he preached willingly. Where there is willingness, there is the reward of willingness; where there is necessity, there is obedience to necessity. Willingness, therefore, is better than necessity. To will belongs to the wise person; to obey and serve belongs to the foolish.

22. This too is the Apostle’s definition, when he says: “If I do this willingly, I shall have a reward; but if unwillingly, I have been entrusted with a stewardship” (I Cor. IX, 17). The reward, therefore, is conferred upon the wise person, while the wise person acts voluntarily; hence, according to the Apostle, the wise person is free. Therefore he himself also cries out: “You were called to freedom; only do not use freedom as an opportunity for the flesh” (Gal. V, 13). He removes the Christian from the law, lest he appear to submit to the law unwillingly; he calls him into the Gospel, which people both proclaim and practice willingly. The Jew is under the Law, the Christian through the Gospel; in the Law there is servitude, in the Gospel freedom, where there is knowledge of wisdom. Therefore everyone who receives Christ is wise; and whoever is wise is free. Every Christian, therefore, is both free and wise.

23. Yet the Apostle taught me that there is something beyond freedom itself: that serving is freedom. “Though I was free from all,” he says, “I made myself the servant of all, that I might win the more” (I Cor. IX, 19). What is beyond freedom except possessing the Spirit of grace and possessing charity? Freedom makes people free; charity makes them friends of God. Hence Christ says: “But I have called you friends” (John XV, 15). Good is the charity of which it is said: “Through charity serve one another” (Gal. V, 13).

Christ also served in order to make everyone free. “His hands served with the basket” (Ps. LXXX, 7). He “did not regard it as robbery to be equal with God,” but “took the form of a servant” (Phil. II, 6), and became all things to all people in order to bring salvation to all (I Cor. IX, 22). Paul imitated him; for the benefit of those whom he desired to win, he was as though under the Law and as though living without the Law. To the weak he willingly became weak, in order to strengthen them; he ran in order to obtain the prize; and he disciplined his body in order to triumph in Christ over the powers of the air.

24. For the wise person, then, even serving is freedom. From this it follows that for the fool even ruling is servitude; and, what is worse, while he presides over a smaller number, he serves more numerous and more oppressive masters. He serves his own passions; he serves his desires, whose dominion he can escape neither by night nor by day, because he has masters within himself and suffers within himself an intolerable servitude. There is a twofold servitude: one of the body and another of the soul. The masters of the body are human beings; the masters of the soul are wickednesses and passions. The wise person is rescued from these by the freedom of his spirit alone, so that he may escape their servitude.

25. Let us therefore seek the truly wise and truly free person who, although he lives under the dominion of many, says freely: “Who is there who will contend with me in judgment? You alone, withdraw your hand from me; from your presence I cannot hide myself, and let not your fear terrify me” (Job XIII, 19ff.).

26. Following him, King David says: “Against you alone have I sinned” (Ps. L, 6). Supported by the height of royal power, as though he were master of the laws and not subject to them, he was nevertheless held accountable to God alone, who is Lord of all powers.

27. Hear another free man: “For me it is a very small thing that I should be judged by you or by a human day; indeed, I do not even judge myself. For I am conscious of nothing against myself … but the one who judges me is the Lord” (I Cor. IV, 3–4). This is the true freedom of the spiritual person, because he judges all things but is himself judged by no one—not by any fellow creature, but knowing himself to be subject to God alone, who alone is without sin (I Cor. II, 15). Of him Job says: “The Lord lives, who judges me in this way” (Job XXVII, 2); for he alone can judge the righteous, before whose presence heaven is not clean and the pure and bright lights of the stars are not without stain.

28. Who is there who can bring forward among the many others the Sophoclean verses which say: “Jupiter rules over me, but no human being”? How much more ancient is Job; how much older is David? Let them therefore acknowledge that whatever superior things they have said they have received from our people.

29. Who, then, is wise except the person who has reached the very secrets of divinity and has come to know the hidden things of wisdom once they have been revealed to him? The wise person alone, therefore, is the one who has used God as his guide in learning the inner chambers of truth; and mortal human beings have become heirs and successors of the immortal God through grace, and in a certain sense participants in his joy, as it is written: “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. XLIV, 8).

30. If anyone looks more closely into the workings of these matters, he will recognize how many aids there are for the wise person and how many hindrances for the foolish [Note: A few manuscripts read: “how great are the aids of wisdom.”], and that what is an aid to the one—freedom—is an impediment to the other—servitude. For the wise person rises up like a victor after subduing and triumphing over lust, fear, cowardice, sorrow, and the other vices, until he drives them from possession of his mind and repels and excludes them from all his boundaries and limits. For an experienced commander knows how to avoid the sallies of brigands and certain stratagems of war [Note: Understand “stratagems,” which he calls “the thefts of war,” imitating Sallust and Virgil in several passages], which the most wicked adversaries of our soul often attempt with flaming darts [Note: A few manuscripts read: “which they always attempt with darts.”]. For we have battles even in peace, and peace in war. Hence he says: “Outside were conflicts, inside fears. But in all these things we conquer because of him who loved us” (II Cor. VII, 5). [Note: The editions read: “He says that neither in distress … nor in danger of death is he terrified”; the manuscripts agree with our text, except for the Boyer manuscript, which supports the editions.] He says that he is terrified neither by distress, nor by persecutions, nor by hunger, nor by danger, nor by death (Rom. VIII, 37).

31. But the person who fears these things, who dreads death—how is he not a slave? He certainly serves, and serves a wretched kind of servitude; for nothing so utterly reduces the soul to every form of slavery as the fear of death. How can a cast-down and contemptible, base and ignoble mind raise itself up, plunged into every abyss of weakness by its desire for this life? See how much a slave he is: “I will hide myself,” he says, “and I shall be groaning and trembling upon the earth; and everyone who finds me will kill me” (Gen. IV, 14). Thus, like a slave, he received a mark, yet even so he could not escape death. The sinner therefore serves fear; he serves desire, he serves greed, he serves lust, he serves wickedness, he serves anger, and yet he seems free to himself. Rather, he serves more than if he were placed under tyrants.

32. But those who live according to the laws are free. The true law is the right word; the true law is not carved on tablets or engraved in bronze, but impressed upon minds and fixed in the senses. Thus the wise person is not under the law, but is himself a law to himself, containing the work of the law in his heart, formed for himself by a natural stylus and a kind of inscription (Rom. II, 14–15). Is our blindness so great that we do not see the clear representations of things and the images of virtues? And how disgraceful it is that upright peoples obey human laws in order to share in freedom, while whole peoples obey human laws in order to share in freedom, and the wise neglect and abandon the true law of nature, expressed in the image of God, and the true reason that bears the standard of freedom—although there is such freedom in it that, while we are children, we do not know how to serve vices, being strangers to anger, excluded from greed, and ignorant of lust! How wretched, then, that although we are born in freedom, we die in servitude!

33. But this happens through fickleness of spirit and weakness of character, because we turn over empty cares and perform useless labors. The heart, action, and work of the wise person ought to be rooted and immovable. Moses taught this when his hands became heavy, so that Jesus the son of Nun could scarcely support them. Therefore the people prevailed when the actions being performed were not superficial, but full of weight and virtue—not marked by a wavering spirit or faltering affection, but by the stability of a firmly established mind (Exod. XVII, 12).

The wise person therefore stretches out his hands, while the fool draws them together, as it is written: “For the fool folds his hands together and consumes his own flesh” (Eccl. IV, 5), thinking more about carnal than spiritual things. But not the daughter of Judah, who, stretching out her hands, cried to the Lord: “You know that they bear false witness against me” (Dan. XIII, 43). She judged it better not to sin, even if she fell victim to the slanders of her accusers, than to commit sin under the cloak of impunity. Thus, by despising death, she preserved her innocence. Nor was it otherwise with the daughter of Jephthah, who confirmed her father’s vow concerning her sacrifice by her own assent, willingly and encouragingly (Judg. XI, 36).

34. I do not derive my discussion of contempt for death from the books of the philosophers, nor from the Indian gymnosophists, whose Calanus is especially praised for his reply to Alexander when Alexander ordered him to follow him:

“By what praise,” he said, “do you summon me as worthy to go to Greece, if I can be compelled to do what I do not wish?”

Truly, the saying is full of authority, but the mind was even fuller of freedom. Finally, he also wrote a letter:

“Calanus to Alexander.

### 35

“Friends are persuading you to use force and to impose necessity [Col. 1092D] upon the Indian philosophers [Note: [Col. 1092D] Several manuscripts and the old editions read: “upon the Indian philosopher.” But, after a few intervening words, where all the manuscripts and old editions read, “For you will transfer bodies,” etc., the Roman edition presents the passage thus: “You will transfer bodies [lacuna] you will no more compel souls to do what they do not wish than stones,” etc. Moreover, in the cited book Philo also adduces the example of the philosopher Calanus, which Plutarch likewise discusses in his *Alexander the Great*.], who do not see our works even in dreams.. For you may transfer bodies from place to place, but you will not compel souls to do what they do not wish, [Col. 1093A] any more than you can compel stones and pieces of wood to emit a voice. [Note: [Col. 1093D] The Roman edition alone reads: ‘The greatest fire … inflicts pain and produces corruption.’] The greatest fire inflicts pain upon living bodies and produces corruption; we are above this fire, for while alive we are being burned. There is no king or prince who can extort from us the doing of what we have not resolved to do. Nor are we like the philosophers of Greece, who meditated words instead of realities for the sake of popular reputation: among us realities are joined to words, and words to realities; our actions are swift and our speeches brief; in virtue we possess blessed freedom.”

### 36–37

Splendid words—but only words; [Note: [Col. 1093D] The same edition reads, ‘splendid steadfastness, and the man’s splendid letter’; the other editions and manuscripts read as we have in the text, much more elegantly. It is clear that *man* is placed here to distinguish his steadfastness and greatness of spirit from those of the girls about whom he will speak shortly. Ambrose also seems to pass over in silence what Cicero, Valerius Maximus, Plutarch, and others recorded about Calanus’s death: they say that he climbed alive onto a burning pyre. But since such a death must be attributed to pride and ostentation, it is not surprising that the holy Bishop counted it as nothing.] splendid steadfastness, but a man’s; a splendid letter, but a philosopher’s. Among us, however, even girls, in their longing for death, raised the steps of virtue to the heights of heaven. What shall I say of Thecla, Agnes, and Pelagia, who, sprouting like noble shoots [Note: [Col. 1093D] The metaphor is taken from trees, in which shoots and suckers sprout; these are called *μοχεύματα* by the Greeks. The examples placed here and below were extremely familiar to the holy Doctor, so that there is no need to add anything about them. Concerning Pelagia, we merely note that what was observed about her near the end of Book III *On Virgins* may be consulted.], hastened toward death as toward immortality? A virgin exulted among lions [Note: [Col. 1094D] The Amerbach and Roman editions, together with not a few manuscripts, read “awaited the roaring beasts”; Erasmus and Gill read “awaited the beasts coming forth”; several manuscripts more suitably read “watched the roaring beasts”; one has “looked upon them.”’.], and fearlessly watched the roaring beasts.

And, to compare our examples with the Indian gymnosophists: what that man boasted in words, Saint Lawrence proved by deeds, so that, being burned alive and surviving the flames, he could say, “Turn it over; eat.” He was no unworthy rival of the descendants of Abraham and of the Maccabean boys, some of whom sang amid the flames, while others, as they were being burned, did not ask to be spared but assailed their persecutor so that he would kindle the fire more fiercely (II Maccabees 7:5 ff.). The wise man is therefore free.

### 38

What, then, is more sublime than Saint Pelagia? Surrounded by persecutors, yet before she came into their sight [Col. 1093C], she said: “I die willingly. No one shall touch me with his hand; no one with a wanton eye shall violate the virgin. I shall carry my modesty with me; with me I shall carry my chastity unharmed. The plunderers shall gain no profit from their insolence. Pelagia will follow Christ. No one shall take away her freedom; no one shall see a captive woman who is free in faith, distinguished in chastity, and marked by an illustrious ancestry of prudence. Whatever is servile shall remain here, bound for no purpose.”

Great, therefore, is the freedom of holy virginity: enclosed by the ranks of persecutors and amid the greatest dangers to her chastity and life, she was in no way bent.

### 39

But not free is the man ruled by anger, for he is subjected to the yoke of sin; an angry man also digs up sin (Proverbs 29:22): “Whoever commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 8:34).

Nor is he free who serves greed; for he cannot possess his own vessel. Nor is he free who, serving desires and pleasures, drifts about in wandering error. Nor is he free who bows before ambition; for he serves another’s command.

But free is the man who can say: “All things are lawful for me, but not all things are beneficial; all things are lawful for me, but I will not be brought under the power of anything.” “Food is for the stomach, and the stomach for food” (1 Corinthians 6:12). Free is the man who says: “Why should our freedom be judged by an unbelieving conscience?” (Ibid., 13).

### 40

Freedom, therefore, belongs to the wise, not to the foolish; for “he who binds a stone in a sling is like one who gives glory to a fool” (Proverbs 26:8): he wounds himself and, while hurling the missile, brings danger upon himself. Certainly, just as the force of the projectile is intensified and the harm of a stone’s fall is doubled, so the fool’s downfall in freedom is more violent. [Note: [Col. 1094D] The latest Paris editions read “belongs to the wise,” omitting “not to the foolish.”].

The fool’s power must therefore be cut back, not freedom added to him; slavery is what suits him. Hence it is also said: “Thorns are born in the hand of a drunkard, but slavery in the hand of the imprudent” (Ibid., 9). For just as the drunkard is wounded by his own cups, so the fool is wounded by his own deeds. The one inserts himself into sin by drinking; the other condemns himself to guilt by acting, and by his deeds is dragged into slavery.

Paul saw himself being dragged into captivity by the law of sin (Romans 7:23); and therefore, in order to be freed, he fled to the grace of freedom.

### 41

Fools, then, are not free, to whom it is said: “Do not become like a horse or a mule, which have no understanding. Bind their jaws with bit and bridle, lest they approach you. Many are the scourges of sinners” (Psalm 31:9 ff.). Many scourges are needed, therefore, to restrain their lack of understanding. Discipline requires this, not cruelty.

Finally, “whoever spares his rod hates his son” (Proverbs 13:24), since each person is scourged more severely by his own sins. The burdens of offenses are heavy, the blows of crimes grievous; they weigh upon the soul like a heavy load, inflict scars upon it, and make the wounds of the mind fester (Psalm 37:5–6).

### 42

Let us therefore lay down so heavy a burden of slavery. Let us renounce luxury and pleasures, which bind us with certain chains of desire and fasten us with fetters. “Pleasures profit nothing for a fool,” and whoever has given himself over to pleasures from childhood will remain in slavery, so that though alive he is dead.

Let luxury therefore be cut away [Note: [Col. 1094D] The Boyer manuscript alone reads: “Let riches be cut back.”]; let pleasures be pruned. If anyone has been luxurious, let him bid farewell to what went before. A vine that has been cut back bears fruit; one that has been half-pruned puts forth foliage; one that is neglected grows wild.

Hence it is written: “Like a field is the imprudent man, and like a vineyard is the man lacking understanding; if you leave him, he will become desolate” (Proverbs 24:30). Let us therefore cultivate this body of ours, discipline it, and bring it into slavery; let us not despise it.

### ### 43

[Note: [Col. 1095D] Perhaps it will not be unwelcome to compare what follows through the final section with the discussion in Book I *On Jacob and the Blessed Life*, chapter 3, section 10.]

Our members are weapons of righteousness, but they are also weapons of sin.. If they are raised up, they are weapons of righteousness, so that sin does not rule in them. If our body has died to sin [Note: [Col. 1095D] The Boyer manuscript reads this way; all the others and all the editions omit “our body,” which gives a less satisfactory sense.], guilt will not reign in it, and our members will be free from sin.

Let us therefore not obey its desires, nor present our members to sin as weapons of iniquity. If you have looked upon a woman in order to desire her, your members are weapons of sin. If you have spoken to entice her, your tongue and mouth are members of sin. If you have removed the boundaries established by our fathers, your members are weapons of sin. If you have hastened with swift feet to shed innocent blood, your members are weapons of iniquity.

### 44

Conversely, if you have seen a needy person and brought him into your house, your members are weapons of righteousness. If you have rescued one who was suffering injustice, or someone being led to death; if you have torn up a debtor’s bond, your members are weapons of righteousness.

If you have confessed Christ—for ““wise lips are weapons of understanding.”” (Proverbs 14:7) [Note: [Col. 1095D] The Roman edition and a few manuscripts read “the lips of the wise man”; the older sources and many more manuscripts read “the lips of wisdom”; perhaps the latter is correct, since the Greek has ὅπλα δὲ αἰσθήσεως χείλη σοφά, “but the lips of wisdom are weapons of understanding.”]—your lips are members of righteousness. Whoever can say, “I was the eye of the blind, the foot of the lame, the father of the weak” (Job 29:15), possesses members that are members of righteousness.

### 45

Freed from sin, therefore, as though purchased by the price of Christ’s blood, let us not be subjected to the slavery of human beings or of passions. Let us not be ashamed to confess our sin. See how free was the man who could say: “I did not fear the multitude of the people, so as not to proclaim my sin in the presence of all” (Job 31:33).

For whoever confesses to the Lord is stripped of slavery. “The righteous man is his own accuser at the beginning of his speech” (Proverbs 18:17). He is not only free but also righteous. Righteousness is in freedom, and freedom is in confession; as soon as someone has confessed, he is acquitted.

Thus he says: “I declared my injustice against myself to the Lord, and you forgave the impiety of my heart” (Psalm 31:5). Delay in acquittal, therefore, lies in confessing; forgiveness of sins follows confession. The wise man is the one who confesses; he whose sin has been forgiven is free, no longer contracting any debts of sin. Farewell, and love us as you do, because I too love you.

[Note: [Col. 1096D] Written around the year 387.]

## LETTER XXXVIII

That the wise man is rich, and that no sex is excluded from this, Ambrose learned from Peter’s letter, whose passage he explains. Peace and other virtues are rich, and Enoch and Elijah are to be counted among the order of the rich. After comparing Ahab and Naboth, he confirms the problem proposed.

**AMBROSE TO SIMPLICIANUS, GREETING.**

### 1

Recently we seemed to have fallen into philosophical disputation when, taking our starting point from the Apostle Paul’s letter, we were discussing that every wise person is free. But afterward, when I was reading the letter of the Apostle Peter, I noticed that every wise person is also rich, and that he excluded no sex, since he wrote that women should possess their entire adornment not in precious jewelry but in good morals:

“For,” he says, “not outwardly in the braiding of hair, or in the putting on of gold, or in the clothing of garments, is the adornment, but the hidden man of the heart” (1 Peter 3:3–4). [Note: [Col. 1096D] The manuscripts and editions read this way, except that the Roman edition prefers, “of which,” he says, “there should not be …”; the Boyer manuscript renders the whole passage as follows: “Not,” he says, “is the outward braiding of the hair, or the putting on of gold, or the style of clothing an adornment, but the hidden man of the heart.”]

### 2

There are therefore two things: that a human being exists within a human being, and that the one is rich who requires the use of no riches for himself. He aptly called him “the man of the heart,” because he is wholly hidden in wisdom, just as wisdom itself is not seen but understood.

No one before Peter used such an expression as “the man of the heart.” The outward man has many members within him; but the inward man of the heart is wholly full of wisdom, full of grace, full of beauty.

### 3

“In incorruptibility,” he says, “of a quiet and modest spirit, which is rich before God” (Ibid.). And truly rich is the one who can appear rich in God’s sight, before whom the earth is small and the world itself narrow. Yet God knows only that person to be rich who is rich in eternity, who stores up the fruits not of wealth but of virtues.

Who, then, is rich before God except the quiet and modest spirit, which never perishes? Does he not seem rich to you who possesses peace of mind and the tranquility of repose, desiring nothing, agitated by no storms of passion, neither despising old things nor seeking new ones, and by continually desiring becoming poor amid the greatest riches?

### 4

That is truly rich peace which surpasses every understanding (Philippians 4:7). Rich is peace, rich is modesty, rich is faith; for “to the faithful the whole world is a possession” (Proverbs 17:6). Rich is simplicity. There are also riches of simplicity, which investigates nothing, considers nothing constrained, suspicious, or deceitful, but pours itself out in pure affection.

### 5

Rich is goodness. Whoever preserves it is nourished by the riches of the heavenly inheritance. To use examples from the earlier Scriptures, it says:

““Blessed is the man whom the Lord reproves. Do not reject the admonition of God [lacuna] In famine he will deliver you from death; in battle he will deliver you from the hand of the sword, and from the scourge of the tongue he will hide you [lacuna] Wild beasts will be at peace with you, and you will know that your house will be in peace”” (Job 5:17).

For when the vices and passions of this flesh, which commonly wage war against the soul, have been subdued, your tents will be without disturbance, your house without offense, your offspring without failure, [Note: [Col. 1097D] This alludes to Genesis 27:27, “Behold, the smell of my son is like the smell of a full field,” and also to Job 5:26, “You will enter the grave in abundance, as a heap of grain is gathered in.”] your posterity like the scent of a full field, and your burial like a harvest.

For when others consider their own decline [Note: [Col. 1097D] The Boyer manuscript reads “consider their own fruit.”], then the heap of your grain, ripe for the heavenly storehouses, is brought in [Note: [Col. 1097D] Nannius says that wherever something is stored, the place is called an *apotheca*; today, however, we use the term for the shops of apothecaries.].

### 6

Rightly, then, the righteous person is always lending, while the wicked person is in need. [Note: [Col. 1097D] The Roman edition reads, “he lends acts of righteousness by God’s command”; the other editions and manuscripts read, “he lends acts of righteousness, God’s command.” The verb “lends” is doubled only in the Boyer manuscript, though it is at least understood in the others.] He lends righteousness;; he lends God’s commandment to the poor and needy. But the fool does not truly possess even what he thinks he has.

Do you suppose that he possesses anything who clings day and night to his treasure and is tormented by greedy and wretched anxiety? He is truly needy, even if he seems rich to others; he is poor to himself, because he does not use what he has, while he continues to seize some things and desire others. Where there is no limit to greed, what benefit are riches?

No one is rich who cannot take away with him what he possesses here. Whatever is left here is not ours but belongs to another.

### 7

Rich was Enoch, who carried away with him what he possessed and brought the whole account of his goodness into the heavenly storehouses (Genesis 5:25))—for this reason he was taken away, lest evil change his heart (Wisdom 4:11).

Rich was Elijah, who, lifted up in a fiery chariot, carried the treasures of his virtues into the heavenly dwellings (2 Kings 2:11). Yet he left no small riches to his heir, riches that he himself would not lose.

Who would have called him poor even when, lacking the food of daily life, he was sent to a widow to be fed by her? At his word heaven was closed and opened; at his command the jar of flour and the vessel of oil did not fail for three years but abounded. Their contents were not diminished by use but replenished (1 Kings 17:9 ff.).

Who would call him poor at whose will fire descended (2 Kings 1:14), whom rivers impassable to others did not obstruct (2 Kings 2:8), but which returned to their own source so that the prophet might cross on dry foot?

### 8

Ancient history describes two neighboring men (1 Kings 21:1 ff.), King Ahab and the poor man Naboth. Which of them do we believe was poorer, and which richer?

One, endowed with the royal support of wealth, insatiable and incapable of being satisfied with his resources, desired the poor man’s little vineyard. The other, despising in his mind the many golden fortunes of kings—βασιλέων τὰς πολυχρύσους τύχας—and the imperial treasures, was content with his own vine.

Does he not seem more truly rich, more truly a king, who possessed enough for himself and ruled his desires so that he desired nothing belonging to another? But the other was utterly needy: his own gold seemed worthless to him, while another’s vine was reckoned most precious.

Learn why he was utterly needy: because riches unjustly amassed are vomited out (Job 20:15), whereas “the root of the righteous remains” (Proverbs 12:12) and flourishes like a palm tree (Psalm 92:12).

### 9

Is not the man who passes away like a shadow poorer than the poor man (Psalm 144:4)? Today the impious man is exalted; tomorrow he will not be, and his place will not be found (Psalm 37:35–36).

What, then, is it to be rich except to abound? But who abounds if he is narrow in spirit? Whoever is narrow in spirit is certainly confined. What abundance, then, is there in confinement? The man who does not abound is not rich.

Hence David beautifully says: “The rich have become poor and hungry” (Psalm 34:10). Although they possessed the treasures of the Scriptures, those who did not understand became poor, and those who tasted no food of spiritual grace became hungry.

### 10

Nothing, therefore, is richer than the disposition of the wise, and nothing poorer than that of the foolish. Since the kingdom of God belongs to the poor (Matthew 5:3), what could be richer?

Therefore the Apostle says splendidly: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God!” (Romans 11:33). David also speaks splendidly: he rejoiced in the way of the heavenly testimonies as in all riches (Psalm 119:14).

Moses speaks explicitly when he says: “Naphtali is the fullness of those who receive” (Deuteronomy 33:23). In the Latin interpretation, Naphtali signifies abundance or expansion [Note: [Col. 1098D] The same Boyer manuscript says that, according to the meaning of the Latin translation, it signifies abundance or expansion. With regard to this meaning, the allusion is to the words of the cited passage from Deuteronomy: “Naphtali will enjoy abundance and will be full of blessings.” Otherwise, the word would more correctly be interpreted as comparison, turning back, or crookedness, as is commonly done.].

There is abundance, therefore, where there is satiety. But where there is hunger for desires and insatiable appetite, there is poverty. Yet because scarcely any desire for money or for this world ever possesses satiety, he added: “And he will be filled with blessing” (Ibid.). [Note: [Col. 1098D] The Boyer manuscript alone reads: “Therefore it is said of the righteous.”]

### 11

In accordance with this, the Apostle Peter defined adornment as existing not in gold, silver, or women’s clothing, but in the hidden and concealed man of the heart (1 Peter 3:3). From this no woman should strip herself of the garment of piety, the ornament of grace, and the inheritance of eternal life..

Farewell, and love us, because we love you.

[Note: [Col. 1098D] Written not long after the year 387.]

## LETTER XXXIX

Ambrose reproves Faustinus, who was fleeing human society because of his sister’s death, warning him that this was an insult to his sister and that death is common not only to human beings but also to cities. Nothing, therefore, is now owed her except prayers. The Apostle forbids us to know anyone according to the flesh, but directs us toward the new creation. What that new creation is, and how Ambrose himself is obliged to console Faustinus, is examined.

**AMBROSE TO FAUSTINUS, GREETING.**

### 1

I knew that you would grieve over the death of your sister with bitter sorrow; yet not so that you would remove yourself from us, but so that you might return yourself to us. For even if consolations are less pleasant to those who mourn, they are nevertheless sometimes necessary.

But you have gone away into the mountain fastnesses and dwell among the caves of wild beasts, having renounced all intercourse with human society [Note: [Col. 1099D] Several manuscripts and old editions read “having renounced the use of society.”].”]—and, what is more serious, having renounced your own judgment.

### 2

Did your sister deserve so much from you that, because of her, the human condition—which ought to have been held in such high regard by you because it had borne so distinguished a woman—should be of less worth in your eyes?

Certainly, as she was leaving this life, she consoled herself with the thought that she was leaving you alive: a parent to her grandchildren, a guardian to the little ones, and a helper to those left without support. Yet you deny yourself to both your grandchildren and us, so that we cannot experience the fruit of her consolation.

Those dear pledges call you not to grieve but to console them. When they see you, they do not believe that their mother has died [Note: [Col. 1099D] The Boyer manuscript reads: “do not believe that she is absent.”]. In you they recognize her; in you they retain her presence; in you they believe that her life remains for them.

### 3

But you grieve because she, flourishing so recently, suddenly perished. Yet this is something we share not only with human beings but also with cities and with the earth itself.

As you came from the city of Bologna, you were leaving behind Claterna, Bologna itself, Mutina, and Regium; on your right was Brixillum; before you appeared Placentia, still proclaiming its ancient nobility in its very name. On your left, you looked with pity upon the uncultivated Apennines and considered the fortresses of peoples once most flourishing, rereading them in sorrowful emotion.

Did so many half-ruined cities, and the funerals of lands displayed beneath the same view, not remind you that the departure of one woman—holy and admirable though she was—should be regarded with consolation, especially since those cities lie forever prostrate and destroyed, whereas she, though taken from us for a time, is spending a better life there? [Note: [Col. 1099D] This imitates Servius Sulpicius’s letter to Cicero concerning the death of his daughter Tullia: “Returning from Asia, as I was sailing from Aegina toward Megara, I began to look around at the regions. Behind me was Aegina, before me Megara, on the right the Piraeus, on the left Corinth—towns that were once most flourishing, but now lay prostrate and ruined before my eyes. I began to think to myself: ‘How strange! We little human beings are indignant if one of us dies or is killed, while in one place the corpses of so many cities lie scattered.’” So Nannius.]

### 4

I therefore think that she should not so much be mourned as accompanied by prayers, nor her soul be made sorrowful by your tears [Note: [Col. 1100D] The Boyer manuscript reads: “I think her soul should be commended not by your tears but rather by prompt offerings.”], but rather commended to the Lord by offerings.

### 5

Perhaps you will assert that you are secure concerning her merits and faith [Note: [Col. 1100D] The Boyer manuscript alone reads: “secure in faith concerning her merits.”], yet that you cannot endure your longing because you no longer see her according to the flesh, and that this causes you the greatest grief.

Does the apostolic saying not move you: “For from now on we know no one according to the flesh. And even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him” (2 Corinthians 5:16)?

Our flesh cannot be perpetual and lasting. It must die in order to rise; it must be dissolved in order to rest, [Note: [Col. 1100D] Some manuscripts read “and become a certain [thing],” while the Boyer manuscript alone reads “it must fix certain boundaries for sin.”] so that there may be an end to sin.

We have therefore known many according to the flesh, but now we no longer know them. “We knew the Lord Jesus,” says the Apostle, “according to the flesh; but now we no longer know him.” For he had already laid aside the garments of the flesh; he was no longer seen in the appearance of a human being; he had already died for all, and all had died in him, so that, renewed and brought to life through him by the Spirit, they might live no longer for themselves but for Christ.

Hence the same Apostle says elsewhere: “I live, yet now it is no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20).

### 6

Rightly, therefore, the man who had formerly known Christ according to the flesh, now recognizing his works invisibly and examining not his flesh but his power—he who had formerly persecuted the disciples of the man and the followers of the flesh with hostile hatred—afterward became the teacher of the nations and began to instruct and train the worshipers of Christ’s majesty for the preaching of the Gospel.

And therefore he added: “If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation” (2 Corinthians 5:17). That is, whoever is perfected in Christ is a new creation, because whoever is flesh is imperfect.

Finally, the Lord himself says: “My spirit shall not remain in these human beings, because they are flesh” (Genesis 6:3). The carnal person, therefore, is not in Christ. But if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation, formed not by a newness of nature but by grace.

The old things that belonged to the flesh have therefore passed away; all things have been made new. What are these things except those which the learned scribe in the kingdom of heaven knows (Matthew 13:52), like the householder who brings forth new and old from his treasure—not the old without the new, nor the new without the old?

Therefore the Church also says: “I have kept the new and the old for you” (Song of Songs 7:13). The old things have passed away—that is, the hidden mysteries of the Law—and in Christ all things have been made new.

### 7

This is the new creation of which the Apostle says to the Galatians: “For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision counts for anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creation,” through which the flesh, now renewed, blossoms and finds the fruit of grace, though previously it bore the thorns of an old offense (Galatians 5:6).

Why, then, should we grieve if it is now said to the soul: “Your youth will be renewed like the eagle’s” (Psalm 103:5)? Why should we sigh for the dead, since the reconciliation of the world with God the Father has already been accomplished through the Lord Jesus (2 Corinthians 5:18)? [Note: [Col. 1100D] The Long manuscript reads “what we may deserve,” which is not sufficiently correct.]

### 8

Since, then, we hold the benefits of Christ, we act as ambassadors for Christ, both before everyone and especially before you (Ibid., 20), so that you may know that his gifts are irrevocable and believe what you have always believed. Do not bring your conviction into doubt through excessive grief, because the Lord Jesus was made sin in order to take away the sin of the world (John 1:29), and so that we might all be the righteousness of God in him (2 Corinthians 5:21): no longer subject to guilt, but secure in the reward of righteousness.

Farewell, and love us, because we love you.

[Note: [Col. 1101D] Written toward the end of the year 388.]

## LETTER XL

He asks to be heard by the emperor, asserting that accessibility is praised in a ruler; that he cannot remain silent without danger to both of them; that kings do not dislike frankness; that the emperor, though pious, can be deceived; and that the decision to rebuild the synagogue is dangerous, since it exposes the bishop either to martyrdom or to betrayal. He refutes the reasons for the imperial rescript by proposing the example of Julian, especially because the Jews had burned a number of churches. He then discusses the Valentinian temple and the gifts said to have been removed, showing that by minimizing these matters the door is opened to Jewish accusations and a triumph over Christ is granted. On this subject he makes an allegorical appeal to the Lord. After warning Theodosius by the example of Maximus not to seek vengeance against Jews or heretics, he again urges him toward clemency.

[Note: [Col. 1101D] This is the reading of all editions and by far the majority of manuscripts. Some, however, prefix only: “Ambrose to the emperor Theodosius.” Paulinus mentions this letter and recounts the occasion, subject, and outcome of its composition; all these matters were discussed sufficiently in the notice assigning its date.]

**AMBROSE, BISHOP, TO THE MOST CLEMENT PRINCE AND MOST BLESSED EMPEROR, THE AUGUSTUS THEODOSIUS.**

### 1

I am almost always occupied with unremitting cares, most blessed Emperor [Note: [Col. 1101D] Some manuscripts read: “I am always devoted to unbroken exercises, or cares, most blessed Emperor.” This is not bad, but the larger number of manuscripts and all editions support our reading, except that the Roman edition removes the adverb “always.”].
