Yet never have I been in such a fever of anxiety as now, when I see that care must be taken lest something be charged against me, including the danger of sacrilege.

I therefore ask you to hear my speech patiently. For if I am unworthy to be heard by you, I am unworthy to offer for you, to whom you entrust your vows and prayers. Will you not, then, hear the man whom you wish to be heard on your behalf? Will you not hear one speaking for himself whom you have heard speaking for others? Do you not fear your own judgment, lest, when you consider me unworthy to hear, you make me unworthy to be heard on your behalf?

### 2

Nor is it imperial to deny freedom of speech, nor priestly to fail to say what one thinks [Note: [Col. 1101D] All editions and some manuscripts read: “not to say what he thinks.”].

For nothing is so popular and so beloved in you emperors as loving freedom even in those who are subject to you in military service [Col. 1102A]. Indeed, this distinguishes good from bad rulers: good rulers love freedom, wicked ones slavery.

Nor is anything more dangerous before God or more shameful before human beings in a priest than not freely proclaiming what he thinks. For it is written: “I spoke of your testimonies in the presence of kings, and I was not ashamed” (Psalm 119:46). And elsewhere: “Son of man, I have appointed you as a watchman for the house of Israel. If,” he says, “the righteous turns away from his righteousness and commits sin, because you did not distinguish for him”—that is, because you did not tell him what must be avoided—“his righteousness will not be remembered, and I will require his blood from your hand.

““But if you warn the righteous so that he does not sin, and he does not sin, the righteous man shall surely live, because you warned him; and you will save your own soul”” (Ezekiel 3:17–19). [Note: [Col. 1102D] The Regius manuscript reads “that is, you did not distinguish,” and below “because you distinguished.” Conversely, where this manuscript agrees with many others and all editions in reading “if you distinguish for the righteous,” the Prat and Gem manuscripts read “if you tell the righteous.”]

### 3

I would therefore rather, Emperor, have you with me among the good than in fellowship with the wicked.. For this reason, the silence of a priest ought to displease your clemency, while his freedom should please you. You are involved in the danger of my silence, but helped by the benefit of my freedom.

I do not therefore thrust myself forward improperly or intrude into matters belonging to others; I obey what is owed and obey the commands of our God. I do this first out of love for you, for your sake, and out of concern to preserve your salvation.

If this is either not believed or forbidden to me, I speak plainly out of fear of offending God [Note: [Col. 1102D] The Regius manuscript alone reads: “mindful of divine displeasure. For if … you should drink it in.”]. If my danger would free you from danger, I would patiently offer myself for you, though not willingly; for I would rather that you be acceptable to God and glorious without the danger I incur.

But if the fault of my silence and dissimulation weighs me down without freeing you, I would rather that you judge me importunate than useless or shameful. For it is written by the holy Apostle Paul, whose teaching you cannot refute: “Insist in season and out of season; reprove, entreat, rebuke, with all patience and instruction” (2 Timothy 4:2).

### 4

We therefore also have one whom it is more dangerous to displease, especially since emperors do not dislike each person’s fulfilling his own duty, and you patiently listen when each person offers advice according to his office. Indeed, you correct him if he does not follow the proper order of his service [Note: [Col. 1102D] In this passage and at the beginning of the letter—namely, in the words “those who are subject to you in military service”—he seems to use *militia* not only for military pay and service in the army, but for any function, ministry, or office. So Nannius.].

What you gladly accept from those who serve you, then, can this be offensive in priests, when we speak not what we wish but what we are commanded?

You know what has been read: “When you stand before kings and governors, do not consider what you will say; for it will be given you in that hour what you should say. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew 10:19–20).

And yet, if I speak in matters of the commonwealth, although justice must also be preserved there, I am not bound by so great a fear if I am not heard. But in God’s cause, whom will you hear if you do not hear the priest? In whose case is sin committed at greater risk if you do not hear him?? Who will dare tell you the truth if a priest does not dare?

5. I know you to be devout, merciful, gentle, and calm, having faith and fear of the Lord in your heart; but often certain things deceive us. Some have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge (Rom. 10:2). I therefore think we must be cautious lest this also creep into faithful minds. I know your devotion toward God and your gentleness toward human beings; I am bound by the benefits of your indulgence. And for that very reason I fear more and am more anxious: lest you later condemn me by your own judgment because you did not avoid a lapse through my dissimulation or flattery [Col. 1103B]. If I saw that an offense was being committed against me, I ought not to remain silent; for it is written:

[Note: [Col. 1103C] The Regius manuscript alone reads: “But if your brother sins against you, go and rebuke him between yourself and him. If he listens to you, you have won your brother; but if he does not listen to you, take with you one or two more, so that every word may stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses. But if he does not listen to them, tell the Church.” You see, therefore, Emperor, that I cannot conceal God’s cause. What then? “God’s cause,” etc.]

“If your brother sins against you, rebuke him first, then reproach him, before two or three witnesses” (Matt. 18:15 ff.). If he does not listen to you, tell the Church. Shall I then be silent about God’s cause? Let us consider, therefore, what it is that I fear.

6. It has been reported by the commander of the eastern military forces [Note: [Col. 1103C] Cedrenus, in his History, calls this magistrate Honoratus, evidently the prefect of Constantinople, where he says this action took place. But he errs so greatly concerning the truth of the matter that no account can be taken of him. Valesius, discussing the Count of the East in his edition of Ammianus Marcellinus, p. 4, says: “Since this was a civil authority, I am surprised that St. Ambrose should write in his letter to Theodosius: ‘It has been reported by the Count of the East of the military forces ...’; but more expert scholars will untie this knot.” Godfrey was more successful in resolving it. In his Chronology of the Theodosian Code and in his Commentary on title 9, “Concerning the Jews,” he teaches that the man whom Ambrose calls “the Count of the East of the military forces”—whom the cited law designates as “Count and Master of both military forces in the East,” to distinguish him from the other Count of the East of the civil forces, whom Zosimus describes in Book 5—was the military Count of the East. Bullengerus, Book 4, On the Roman Empire, chapter 25, although he does not seem to distinguish the two offices sufficiently, clearly indicates that military authority also belonged to the Count of the East, in these words: “Because the Persians were ravaging Armenia and Mesopotamia, the Illustrious Count of the East was placed over it with an army, as vicar of the praetorian prefect.” A little later: “The Illustrious Count and Master of the Soldiers in the East.” Book 8, “On Billeting.” In the following chapter he likewise reports that there were two military Counts in the East; consult him. These considerations sufficiently dispel Valesius’s doubt. As for Godfrey’s contention, against Baronius, that this letter was written in the year 393, we have already examined it in its proper place.]

that the synagogue had been burned, and that this was done at the instigation of a bishop. You ordered the others to be punished, but ordered the synagogue itself to be rebuilt by the bishop. [Note: [Col. 1104C] Several manuscripts read: “I do not assert.” Nannius explains the noun “assertion,” which follows, in this way: “Assertion,” that is, defense. The metaphor is taken from a civil action, in which an *assertor*, or defender, had to appear to vindicate the liberty of another person claimed for slavery. So he. But perhaps it would be more correct and simpler to say that “the bishop’s assertion,” or affirmation, is the testimony by which he would declare whether or not he had done that deed. The words “I do not affirm” contain a rhetorical omission, by which what is most strongly being said is denied as having been said.]

I do not assert that the bishop’s testimony ought to have been awaited; for priests are regulators of disturbances and lovers of peace, unless they themselves are moved by an injury to God or an insult to the Church. [Note: [Col. 1104C] All editions and most manuscripts read, “Let someone be”; a few others, “Let it be to some.” The Regius manuscript and Latinius’s conjecture read, as in the text, “Let it otherwise be.”]

Let this bishop, then, be more ardent in the burning of the synagogue but more timid at the trial. Do you not fear, Emperor, that he might acquiesce in your judgment? Are you not afraid that he might become a colluder?

7. Do you not also fear what will happen—that he might resist your count in words? It will therefore be necessary either to make him a colluder or a martyr: both are foreign to your times, and either would resemble persecution, whether he is compelled to collude or is forced to undergo martyrdom. [Note: [Col. 1104C] Nannius wants “to collude” here to mean the same as “to fall into idolatry”; he likewise takes “colluder” to mean what is now called an apostate. In secular writings, however, a colluder is one who conspires with the accused and betrays the case to the opponent.]

You see toward what the outcome of the case is tending. If you think the bishop is courageous, beware the martyrdom of the stronger man; if you think him unstable, avoid the fall of the weaker. For the person who has compelled a weak man to fall is held more tightly accountable.

8. Given this situation, I think the bishop will say that he himself [Note: [Col. 1104D] The Council of Elvira, held in the year 305, prohibited in canon 60 that anyone killed for destroying an idol should be admitted to the catalog of martyrs. But the burning at issue here did not seem unlawful, under the law of retaliation and the law of nations, as is said below.]

spread the fires, stirred up the crowds, [Note: [Col. 1104D] The old edition reads, “shut in the peoples.”] and gathered the people, lest he lose the opportunity for martyrdom and subject the stronger man on behalf of the weak. [Note: [Col. 1104D] “O blessed lie!” says Nannius. Understand this in the same sense in which the Church sings, “O happy fault!”—namely, because of its effect; in itself, a lie is always evil. See, if you wish, what we noted in the first volume, Book 1, On Abraham, chapter 8, no. 71.]

O blessed lie, by which he gains the absolution of others, for his own sake! This is what I too have asked, Emperor: that you punish me more severely; and if you considered this a crime, that you attribute it to me. Why order judgment against absent men? You have here one who is present; you have a defendant confessing. I proclaim that I burned the synagogue—or at least that I ordered them to burn it—so that there might be no place in which Christ was denied. If it is objected to me, “Why did you not burn this one here?” it has already begun to be burned by divine judgment; my work has ceased. And if the truth is sought, I was slower to act because I did not think this ought to be punished. What should I have done, when there would have been neither an avenger nor a reward? These words touch upon shame, but they recall grace, lest an act be done that incurs the offense of the Most High God. [Note: [Col. 1104D] All editions read, “lest it become an act”; the manuscripts, on the contrary, omit “act.”]

9. Nevertheless, let no one bring a bishop to account for this duty [Col. 1104C], for I have pleaded with your clemency; and although I have not yet read that this order has been revoked, let us consider it revoked. What if other, more timid men, fearing death, offer to rebuild the synagogue from their own resources? Or what if the count, once he learns that this was first ordered, himself commands it to be rebuilt from the property of Christians? You will have a colluding count, and you will entrust victorious standards to him, the labarum to him—that is, the standard consecrated by the name of Christ [Note: [Col. 1105C] The Roman edition adds, “the sign,” after the words “consecrated by the name of Christ.” Apart from the fact that no other edition or manuscript recognizes this word, the labarum was not properly a solid standard—that is, it was not made of solid material—but an imperial banner. Eusebius, in Book 1 of the Life of Constantine, chapter 31, describes at length both the occasion on which it was instituted and its form; later historians eagerly repeated the same description. Since Eusebius also records, in Book 2, chapter 8, that Constantine selected fifty men from the protectores, whose sole duty was to guard with their escort the banner they carried alternately on their shoulders, and since Theodosius the Younger orders in one of the laws of the Theodosian Code that those placed over it be called *labari praepositi*—for that is what the Greeks call the labarum—and be recruited from the schools of the domestici, it may perhaps seem strange that Ambrose, omitting these matters, here mentions an absent count. Nevertheless, it may be that Theodosius either left that banner with this count when departing from the East or wished him to return with it after the victory; just as Sozomenus reports that Stilicho took that same banner with him when he traveled to Constantinople after the death of Arcadius.]

who will restore a synagogue that does not know Christ? Command the labarum to be carried into the synagogue; let us see whether they do not resist.

10. Will a place for Jewish faithlessness therefore be made from the spoils of the Church? Will property acquired for Christians through the favor of Christ be transferred to the offerings of the faithless? We read that temples were formerly founded for idols from the spoils of the Cimbri, and from the plunder of other enemies. [Note: [Col. 1105D] A few manuscripts read, “from the hands of the Cimbri ... from the hands of Christians.” This is not sufficiently correct, for *manubiae* are either money obtained by selling enemy booty or the booty itself. On the Cimbri, destroyed by Marius, consult Florus, Book 3, chapter 3; Paterculus, Book 2; and others.]

The Jews will write this inscription on the front of their synagogue: “A temple of impiety made from the spoils of Christians.”

11. [Note: [Col. 1105D] One Regius manuscript reads, “discipline and reason”; the others and the editions agree among themselves, except that the Roman edition has “may move” for “moves,” less appropriately.]

But concern for discipline moves you, Emperor. What, then, is more important: the appearance of discipline or the cause of religion? Censure must yield to devotion.

12. [Note: [Col. 1106C] The sense is, as Nannius says: “Have you not heard, Emperor, that those who were clearing the arena, digging out the ruins and unstable material so that a new temple might rise there by Julian’s command, were burned by heavenly fire?” For in Theodoretus, Book 3 of Ecclesiastical History, chapter 20, we read that fire burst from the foundations and burned the workmen. So he. He could have added a witness beyond all objection in this respect: Ammianus, Book 23, chapter 1, and the author of the Tripartite History, Book 6, chapter 43.]

Have you not heard, Emperor, that when Julian ordered the temple at Jerusalem to be restored, those who were carrying out the cleansing were consumed by divine fire? Do you not fear that the same thing may happen now? So far from your having had to give this order, Julian gave such an order!

13. What, then, moves you? Is it because some public building has been burned, or because it was the site of a synagogue? If you are moved by the burning of a most worthless building—for what could there have been in so insignificant a fortress? [Col. 1105C]—do you not remember, Emperor, how many houses of prefects have been burned at Rome, and no one was punished? Indeed, if any emperor wished to censure the deed more severely, he aggravated the case of the man who had been struck by so great a loss. [Note: [Col. 1106C] The Long manuscript reads, “he attended to the case.” Godfrey, in the place cited, establishes on the authority of Ammianus, Zosimus, and the *Notitia Imperii* that the fortress of Callinicum was situated in Osrhoene, a province of the East.]

What, then, would have been more deserving of punishment, if punishment were necessary: the burning of some part of the buildings of the fortress of Callinicum, or the burning of the city of Rome? [Note: [Col. 1106C] From Socrates, Book 5, chapter 17, we learn that the house of Nectarius was burned, and that this happened when Theodosius Augustus and Cynegius were consuls—that is, in the very year which we assign to this letter. Nor does it hinder us that Ambrose says the same house had been burned long before. In this passage he is acting just as someone defending at trial a person who had committed homicide through carelessness and was immediately compelled to suffer punishment might compare him with another who had earlier committed murder by ambush and had suffered no serious penalty: “You have already passed sentence on this innocent man, while you have decreed nothing severe against that criminal by whom a citizen was brutally slaughtered long ago.” You see here that he departs in no way from common usage.]

The house of the bishop in Constantinople was burned long ago, and your son interceded with his father so that you would not punish either the injury done to him—that is, to the emperor’s son—or the burning of the priestly house. Do you not consider, Emperor, whether, if you order this also to be punished, he himself may again intervene to prevent its punishment? But that matter was well secured by the father for the son; for it was fitting that the son himself should first forgive the injury done to him. It was well divided with a distinction of grace, so that the son was asked to intercede for his own injury, and the father for the injury to his son. You therefore have nothing to reserve for your son; and take care that you do not detract from God.

14. The cause, then, is not sufficient to justify such agitation, so that a population should be punished with such severity because a building was burned—much less because a synagogue was burned: a place of faithlessness, a house of impiety, a refuge of madness, which God himself condemned. For we read this through the mouth of Jeremiah, when our Lord God says:

“I will do to the house upon which my name has been invoked, in which you trust, and to the place which I gave to you and to your fathers, as I did to Shiloh; and I will cast you away from my presence, as I cast away all the race of Ephraim, your brothers. And you, do not pray for this people, and do not ask mercy for them, and do not approach me on their behalf; for I will not hear you. Or do you not see what these people are doing in the cities of Judah?” (Jer. 7:14 ff.) [Col. 1107A]

[Note: [Col. 1106D] The manuscripts have this reading; the edition of Amerbach, following the Septuagint, writes “Selo”; Erasmus and later editions, following the Vulgate, write “Silo.” Below, instead of “your brothers,” some manuscripts have “your fathers.”]

God forbids anyone to plead for those whom you think ought to be punished.

15. But certainly, if I were acting according to the law of nations, I would say how many basilicas of the Church the Jews burned during the reign of Julian. [Note: [Col. 1107C] On these burnings of basilicas, consult Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 19 against Julian; Chrysostom, Oration 4, volume 1; Cyril of Alexandria; and others.]

Two at Damascus, one of which was scarcely restored, and then at the expense of the Church, not of the synagogue; the other basilica still bristles with shapeless ruins. Basilicas were burned at Gaza, Ascalon, Beirut, and almost all those places, and no one sought vengeance. A basilica was also burned at Alexandria by pagans and Jews, a basilica that surpassed the others alone. The Church was not avenged, but the synagogue will be?

16. Will the shrine of the Valentinians, which was burned, also be avenged? For what is it but a shrine, in which there is an assembly of pagans? Although the pagans call twelve gods [Col. 1107B], these people worship thirty-two Aeons, whom they call gods. [Note: [Col. 1107C] The Roman edition reads, “they worship thirty Aeons.” In fact, they acknowledge that many—thirty in number—according to Irenaeus, Book 1 Against Heresies; Tertullian, Against the Valentinians; Epiphanius, Heresy 31; Theodoretus; Paulinus in the Life of Ambrose; and Augustine, On Heresies, chapter 11. But since the last of these states that the Valentinians taught all those Aeons to have been generated from Bythus and Sige, the agreement of the manuscripts and old editions leads us to think that Ambrose counted both of them among the other thirty. Certainly, in his own book On the Incarnation of the Lord, chapter 4, no. 2, where he touches on the madness of these heretics, he does not specify the number of the Aeons. Moreover, by the twelve gods mentioned in the preceding line, Nannius rightly understands the “council gods,” because they were believed to attend the councils of Jupiter and were so called, each being assigned to a particular month. Their names are given in this couplet by Ennius:

Juno, Vesta, Minerva, Ceres, Diana, Venus, Mars,

Mercury, Jupiter, Neptune, Vulcan, Apollo.]

For I have also learned that a report was made and an order issued concerning them, that punishment should be inflicted upon the monks who, when the Valentinians tried to prevent them from going—as was their custom and ancient practice, singing psalms—to the festival of the martyrs of the Maccabees, were provoked by their insolence and burned their shrine, hastily constructed in a certain rural village.

17. [Note: [Col. 1107D] All editions read, “How many offer themselves ... him because he overturned the altar”; all manuscripts, “How much they offer themselves”; but most have only “him who overturned the altar.” One Regius manuscript also places the name “Capitolinus” before “him.” Nevertheless, if Baronius’s opinion at the year 362, as well as Hermann’s, Book 5 of the Life of Ambrose, chapter 13, is accepted—and it certainly seems highly plausible to us—this very martyr was named Emilianus. For both writers attribute to him what Jerome reports in his Chronicle concerning the martyrdom of Emilianus of Dorostorum, as does Theodoretus, Book 3 of his History, chapter 7, where he says that the judge’s name was Capitolinus. As for the statement that afterward no one refused to kiss that judge, we understand this chiefly of the kisses with which the Apostles commanded Christians to greet one another and which, especially during the celebration of the sacred rites, they offered individually to one another. On this matter see Baronius at the year 45; Albaspinaeus, Observations and Book 2 of On Ancient Ecclesiastical Polity, chapter 15 and following; Cardinal Bona, Book 2 of On Liturgical Matters, chapter 16; and others.]

How many will offer themselves for such an option when they remember that, in Julian’s time, the man who overturned an altar and disrupted a sacrifice, after being condemned by the judge, achieved martyrdom? Thus that judge who heard him was never regarded except as a persecutor; no one thought him worthy of an encounter, no one ever thought him worthy of a kiss. If he were not already dead, I should fear, Emperor, that you would exact vengeance upon him, although he did not escape heavenly vengeance, surviving his own heir. [Note: [Col. 1108D] “Heir” here means, says Nannius, not one who succeeded the deceased in law, but one who was expected to succeed him, so that you understand that the son died before the father.]

18. But it is reported that the investigation was entrusted to a judge, and that it was written that he ought not to report the matter [Note: [Col. 1108D] This is the reading of by far the majority of the manuscripts; some others and all the editions read, “but to punish.” The words “the offerings must be sought,” to omit other matters, indicate that in those times the Church possessed a large supply of valuable goods and vessels.] but to punish it; and that the stolen offerings should also be recovered. I shall omit other matters: the basilicas of the Churches were burned by the Jews, and nothing was restored, nothing reclaimed, nothing investigated. But what could the synagogue have possessed in a remote fortress, when everything there is not much, nothing precious, nothing abundant? What, moreover, could have been carried off in the fire by Jews lying in wait? [Note: [Col. 1108D] Some manuscripts read, “to be seized by foolish Jews.”]

These are the devices of Jews who wish to bring accusations, so that, while these things are being complained of, an extraordinary military investigation may be ordered and a soldier sent—perhaps to say what someone once said here before your arrival, Emperor: “How can Christ help us, when we are fighting on behalf of the Jews against Christ?” [Note: [Col. 1108D] All editions read, “who are sent to punish their own people, the Jews,” etc.; all the manuscripts have the better reading found in the text.] “who are sent to punish the Jews? They have destroyed their own armies; they wish to destroy ours.”

19. Into what further accusations will those men not leap who have also slandered Christ with false testimonies? Into what accusations will men who are liars even about divine matters not leap? Whom will they not declare to have been authors of sedition? Whom will they not attack, even those whom they do not recognize, so that they may behold countless ranks of chained men from the Christian people, see the necks of the faithful populace led captive, see God’s servants consigned to darkness, struck with axes, given to the flames, and handed over to the mines, lest their punishment end quickly?

20. Will you give the Jews this triumph over the Church of God? This trophy over the people of Christ? These joys to the faithless, Emperor? This celebration for the synagogue, these mournings for the Church? The Jewish people will record this solemnity among their festivals and will surely number it among those on which they triumphed over the Amorites and Canaanites, or were delivered from Pharaoh, king of Egypt, or from the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. They will add this celebration, signifying that they have triumphed over the people of Christ.

21. Although they themselves deny that they are bound by Roman laws, so that they regard the laws as crimes, now they think that they should be avenged as though by Roman laws. Where were those laws when they themselves burned the roofs of the consecrated basilicas? If Julian did not avenge the injury to the Church because he was a colluder, will you, Emperor, avenge the injury to the synagogue because you are a Christian?

22. And what will Christ say to you hereafter? Do you not remember what he commanded holy David through the prophet Nathan (2 Sam. 7:8 ff.)?

“I chose you as the younger among your brothers and made you emperor from a private citizen. From the fruit of your seed I placed you upon the imperial throne. I subjected barbarian nations to you; I gave you peace; I led your enemy captive into your power. You had no grain to feed your armies; by the hand of the enemies themselves I opened the gates and unlocked the granaries for you. Your enemies gave you the provisions they had prepared for themselves. I confused the plans of your enemy, so that he exposed himself. I bound the usurper of the empire himself and shackled his mind so that, although he still had an opportunity to flee, he nevertheless shut himself in with all his men, as though afraid that any of them might perish for you. [Col. 1109B]

I gathered his count and army from the other part of the natural world, whom I had previously scattered so that they would not join together for war, and assembled them to complete your victory. [Note: [Col. 1109C] Nannius understands this to mean that the fleet of the admiral whom Maximus had placed in command of the naval war was scattered by a storm. Some people call earth and water the two parts of nature; they do not regard air and fire as elements, but as things composed of elements, having been born from something else rather than being the first principles or seeds of nature’s things. So Nannius. In any event, several historical matters are touched upon here, and it would not be useless to compare them with the accounts of historians of the same period. See likewise what we observed on Psalm 61, no. 62.]

I ordered your army, composed of many untamed peoples gathered from various nations [Note: [Col. 1109D] A few manuscripts read, “of nations gathered from everywhere.”], to preserve the loyalty, peace, and concord of a single people, as though it were one nation. When there was the greatest danger that the treacherous plans of the barbarians might penetrate the Alps, I gave you victory within the very barrier of the Alps, so that you could conquer without loss. I therefore made you triumph over your enemy, and you give my enemies a triumph over my people.”

23. Was it not for this reason that Maximus was abandoned? A few days before the expedition, when he heard that the synagogue at Rome had been burned, he had sent an edict to Rome, as though he were the defender of public discipline. Hence the Christian people said: “No good awaits this man. This king has become a Jew.” [Note: [Col. 1109D] The entire passage, beginning “we heard this defender ...” and ending “he died for sinners,” is missing from one Regius manuscript; perhaps not without reason.]

“We heard that he was the defender of discipline, but Christ soon proved him, Christ who died for sinners” (Rom. 5:6). If this was said concerning a speech, what will be said concerning vengeance? He was therefore immediately defeated by the Franks, by the people of the Saxons, in Sicily, [Note: [Col. 1109D] The Long manuscript reads “Scythia”; other manuscripts and the editions more correctly read “Siscia,” a name improperly printed in the editions as “Sicia.” Siscia was an episcopal see of some importance in Upper Pannonia. Below, where all editions and many more manuscripts read “and by which the defeated man was offended,” some manuscripts display “you too, defeated, were offended.”] at Siscia, at Poetovio; in the end he was defeated everywhere on earth. What has the devout man in common with the faithless? Examples of impiety must be abolished together with the impious. What harmed that man, what offended him when he was defeated, must not be followed but condemned by the man who conquered.

24. I have therefore not recounted these things to you as though you were ungrateful, but have counted them as benefits rightly conferred, so that, reminded by them, you may love more the one upon whom more has been bestowed. [Note: [Col. 1109D] The sense is somewhat obscure because of the transposition of the words. They should be arranged more easily as follows: “You should love more the one upon whom more has been bestowed.”]

Finally, the Lord Jesus said this to Simon when he answered: “You have judged rightly” (Luke 7:44). Then, turning to the woman who anointed his feet with perfume, representing the type of the Church, he said to Simon: “Therefore I say to you: her many sins have been forgiven, because she loved much. But the one to whom little is forgiven loves little” (ibid., 47). This is the woman who entered the Pharisee’s house and cast out the Jew but acquired Christ. For the Church excluded the synagogue. Why is it being tried again, so that in the house of Christ’s servant—that is, from the breast of faith, from the house of Christ—the synagogue may exclude the Church?

25. These things, Emperor, I have gathered into this address out of love and concern for you. For I am indebted to your benefits, by which, at my request, you have freed many from exile, from prisons, and from the penalties of ultimate death; [Note: [Col. 1110C] Hermann attributes this to the victory over Eugenius that followed these events and says that, at the request of the holy Bishop, many were freed from exile and extreme punishment. But apart from the fact that, on the basis of Orosius and Pacatus, he himself acknowledges that Theodosius used his victory mercifully, we have already observed that Ambrose obtained many such concessions from Theodosius. Certainly, we have repeatedly observed that it belongs to bishops to approach emperors on behalf of the unfortunate, and this may also be seen from several of Augustine’s letters.]

so that I ought to prefer, for the sake of your safety, not to fear even offending your spirit. No one acts with greater confidence than one who loves from affection; certainly no one who looks after his own interests ought to cause injury. I fear lest I lose in a single moment the favor of every priest that has been built up over so many years. [Note: [Col. 1110D] All editions read, “of whatever priesthood”; the manuscripts, almost unanimously, read, “of whatever priest.” Those who prefer the former reading may understand it thus: “Lest I lose the favor and approval acquired for my priesthood, whatever it may be, whether worthy or unworthy.” The latter reading may be interpreted in this sense: “Lest I lose the favor of whatever priest”—that is, of all the bishops—through which they have long been accustomed to obtain the indulgence of rulers toward the accused.]

[Note: [Col. 1110D] The Colbertine manuscript reads, “And yet I implore the gift of grace.” But what danger to salvation there is, Emperor, in your not considering something to be sought or punished, etc. Below, instead of “your faith,” the same manuscript has “our faith.”]

And yet I do not deprecate the loss of favor, but the danger to salvation.

26. Nevertheless, how great a matter is it, Emperor, that you should not regard as requiring investigation or punishment what no one to this day has investigated and no one has ever punished? It is a serious matter for your faith to be endangered on behalf of the Jews. When Gideon had killed the consecrated calf (Judg. 6:31), the pagans said: “Let the gods themselves avenge their injury.” Who has the power to avenge the synagogue? Christ, whom they killed, whom they denied? Or will God the Father avenge those who do not receive the Father because they did not receive the Son? Who has the power to avenge the Valentinian heresy? [Col. 1111A] How does your devotion avenge it, when you have ordered them to be excluded and have not permitted them to claim the opportunity to assemble (2 Kings 22:2)? [Note: [Col. 1111C] One Regius manuscript reads: “Although, above all others, you yourself know how you avenge them, since you have ordered them to be excluded”; the other manuscripts and all editions read as in the text, except that some manuscripts have “in whatever way” instead of “how.” There are several laws in the Code, under the title “Concerning Heretics,” by which the assemblies of all heretics are prohibited, although the Valentinians are not specifically named.]

If I set before you Josiah, a king approved by God, you will condemn in these people precisely what was approved in him.

27. Certainly, if little trust is placed in me, order those whom you judge to be bishops to be present; let it be considered, Emperor, what ought to be done while the faith remains safe. If you consult your counts about financial matters, how much more ought it to be considered fitting for you to consult the priests of the Lord in a matter of religion!

28. Let your clemency consider how many plotters the Church has, how many investigators. If they encounter even a slight crack, they will drive in their barb. I am speaking in human terms; but God is feared more than human beings, and he is rightly preferred even to emperors. [Note: [Col. 1111C] Several manuscripts read, “But God is feared more than all.”]

If someone thinks that a friend, a parent, or a relative should be given precedence, I have rightly judged that precedence should be given to God and that he should be preferred to everyone. Look to your own interests, Emperor, or allow me to look to mine.

29. What will I answer later if it is discovered that, on the authority granted here, some Christians were killed by the sword, clubs, or leaden weapons? How will I clear this deed? How will I excuse it before the bishops who now groan and write that, after serving for thirty and more years [Note: [Col. 1111C] Several manuscripts read, “some of the presbyterate,” etc. The duties of the municipal curia were especially burdensome to clerics, since they included responsibility for taxes and public buildings. They would have been still more burdensome if clerics had been required to supervise pagan spectacles, as Innocent I seems to indicate in his decretal to Victricius of Rouen, chapter 13, ed. Quesnel, as well as in Letter 4 to the bishop of Nocera, chapter 3, and Letter 23 to the bishops of the Council of Toledo. It is more probable, however, that the same pontiff is speaking of lay curiales, whom he forbids to be adopted into the clerical rank. At least there can be no doubt that clerics were not subject to those pagan services when our Ambrose wrote these words; otherwise he would never have passed over so disgraceful a matter so lightly. As for the other duties of the curiae, Constantine the Great had desired clerics to be exempt from them by Law 2, “Concerning Bishops.” But not only did Julian the Apostate abolish all clerical exemptions, as Sozomenus reports in Book 5, chapter 5; other emperors also partly restored them and partly restricted them with various conditions, as may be learned from the various laws of the Theodosian Code. See likewise above, Letter 18, nos. 13 and 14.]

some priests have held office, or served as ministers of the Church, they are being withdrawn from sacred service and assigned to the curia, and are grievously lamenting? [Note: [Col. 1111D] The Regius manuscript reads: “For if anyone serves you, he is protected for a fixed period of military service ... it must be considered”; the other manuscripts and editions substantially agree, except that they read, “For when those who ...” Fornerius, Part 3, Selection 7, thinks that *serventur*, as found in the editions, or *servantur*, as most manuscripts read, should be emended to *ferientur*, “they will be struck,” a not unreasonable suggestion. In this passage Ambrose refers to Law 88, “Concerning Decurions,” and Law 100 under the same title, by which, after five years of military service or thirty years of palatine office, exemption from these duties was granted. See likewise Law 12, “Concerning the Privileges of Those Who Serve in Sacred Office,” etc., by which Theodosius himself reduced the period of palatine service to ten years.]

For if those who serve you are protected for a fixed period of military service, how much more ought you to take account of those who serve God! How, I ask, will I excuse this before the bishops who complain about clerics and write that the churches are being devastated by oppressive demands?

30. I nevertheless wished this to come to the attention of your clemency; you will deign, as you think best, to consider and moderate the matter by your judgment. But exclude and cast out what distresses me—and rightly distresses me. You yourself do whatever you have ordered to be done; or, if that man will not do it, I would rather that you be more merciful than that he fail to do what he was ordered to do. [Note: [Col. 1112C] The Regius manuscript reads, “what you ordered.”]

31. You have reasons still to invite and earn the Lord’s clemency concerning the Roman Empire; [Note: [Col. 1112C] Understand this as referring to the children of Theodosius.] you have those in whom you may hope for more than you do for yourself: may their favor and their safety move you in this appeal. [Note: [Col. 1112C] All editions and most manuscripts read, “let it reach my address, lest the case”; one Colbertine manuscript reads, “let it reach you.” The Regius manuscript has, as in the text, “I warn you not to entrust the case.”]

I fear that you may entrust your case to another’s judgment. Everything is still intact for you. In this matter I bind myself before our God on your behalf, [Note: [Col. 1112C] That is, sometimes it is contrary to one’s duty to keep an oath, as the holy Doctor himself teaches in Book 1 of On Duties, chapter 50, no. 264.] and you need not fear an oath. Can what is corrected for the sake of God’s honor possibly displease God? Certainly change nothing in that letter, whether it has been sent or not yet sent; order another to be dictated, one full of faith and full of devotion. It is within your power to correct; it is not within mine to conceal.

### 32

[Note: [Col. 1112D] Zosimus, Sozomen, and other writers have recorded that the statues of the empress Flaccilla and even of Theodosius were overthrown at Antioch during a riot. On this occasion, since the people of Antioch were in the greatest fear, Chrysostom, still a presbyter, delivered to console them the most beautiful speeches *On the Statues*. But when Theodosius finally turned to milder counsels, the same Chrysostom, in *Oration 20 to the Antiochenes*, splendidly commended his clemency.]

You pardoned the Antiochenes their offense; you recalled the daughters of your enemy and entrusted them to a relative for upbringing; you sent your enemy’s mother provisions from your treasury.

[Note: [Col. 1112D] The Belvacensis, Thuaneus, and Carolinus manuscripts read: “you recalled the sons of your enemy to be brought up,” etc. If that reading were true, Theodosius would deserve still greater praise for sparing the male children of his enemy despite the danger to his own security. Yet, apart from Victor, whom Zosimus relates was killed by Andragathius, we do not find that Maximus had male offspring.] Such great piety, such great faith toward God, will be darkened by this deed. You, therefore, who spared armed enemies and preserved your foes—do not, I beg you, think that Christians should be punished with such zeal.

### 33

Now, Emperor, I beg you not to receive with disdain one who is anxious both for you and for himself; for it is the voice of a holy man: “Why was I made to see the affliction of my people?” (1 Maccabees 2:7), so that I should incur God’s displeasure? For my part, I have done what could be done with the greatest honor: I acted so that you would hear me more readily in the palace, lest, if necessity required it, you should hear me in the church.

[Note: [Col. 1113D] Written in the year 388.]

## LETTER XLI

He informs his sister about the events that had occurred on account of the synagogue and temple mentioned above; he relates how, after explaining the passage from Jeremiah concerning the words of the priests, he expounded the Gospel reading and showed that the Lord’s mercy is there commended, the imitation of which he likewise requires from us. He also teaches how we represent the sinful woman of the Gospel by washing, wiping, anointing, and kissing the Lord’s feet; otherwise we shall be subject to the prophet’s rebuke. Finally, he explains how, turning his speech toward Theodosius, he eventually obtained the revocation of the edict.

[Note: [Col. 1113D] The Roman edition, in which this letter was first published, gives it the heading: “Ambrose, bishop, to his sister Marcellina.” The Regius manuscript, the only one in which it could likewise be found, more simply prefixes: “A brother to his sister.” Moreover, Paulinus marks this very letter so distinctly and explicitly that no one can doubt that it is genuinely Ambrosian.]

## A BROTHER TO HIS SISTER

[Col. 1113B] **1.** You have deigned to write to me that your holy self is still anxious, because I had written that I was anxious; and so I am surprised that you did not receive my letter in which I had written that my security had been restored. For when it was reported that the synagogue of the Jews had been burned by Christians at the instigation of a bishop, and that the meeting-place of the Valentinians had likewise been burned, an order was given—while I was at Aquileia—that the synagogue should be rebuilt by the bishop and that vengeance should be taken upon the monks who had burned the Valentinian building. Then I, after accomplishing little by repeated efforts, gave a letter to the emperor and sent it at once. When he proceeded to the church, I delivered this sermon:

[Note: [Col. 1113D] The Regius manuscript reads: “When it had been reported to the emperor that the synagogue of the Jews in the eastern regions had been burned … and the grove of the Valentinians … who had burned the place.”]

**2.** It is written in the prophetic book: “Take for yourself an almond rod” (Jeremiah 1). We must consider why the Lord said this to the prophet; for it was not written without purpose. Indeed, we also read in the Pentateuch that the almond rod of Aaron the priest, after it had long been laid aside, blossomed (Numbers 17:8).

[Note: [Col. 1113D] The Roman edition reads: “It signifies that the prophetic utterance, and so forth, ought to be straight.”]

For the rod seems to signify that prophecy or priestly authority ought to be upright, so that it persuades not merely what is pleasing but what is beneficial.

**3.** Therefore the prophet is commanded to take an almond rod, because the fruit of that tree is bitter in its rind, hard in its shell, but fruitful within; so, in imitation of it, the prophet too should present what is bitter and hard, and not shrink from announcing sad things. Likewise the priest, because his instruction, though it may for a time seem bitter to some, and, like Aaron’s rod, may long be laid aside in the ears of those who pretend not to hear, nevertheless blossoms at some point when it is thought to have dried up.

[Col. 1114A] **4.** Hence the Apostle also says: “What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love and in a spirit of gentleness?” (1 Corinthians 4:21). First he spoke of the rod and, like an almond rod, struck those who had gone astray, so that afterward he might console them with a spirit of gentleness. Thus the one whom the rod excluded from the heavenly mysteries, gentleness restored.

To his disciple also he gave such instructions, saying: “Reprove, exhort, rebuke” (2 Timothy 4:2). Two are hard and one is mild; but they are hard for this reason: so that they themselves might make the hearers gentle. For just as, in bodies sick from excessive bile, the bitterness of food or drink becomes sweet, while, conversely, the pleasantness of delicacies is bitter, so when the soul is wounded it grows sick from the pampering of flattering pleasure, and again is tempered by the bitterness of correction.

[Note: [Col. 1114D] Roman manuscripts read: “of voluntary correction.”]

[Col. 1114B] **5.** Let these remarks suffice as a taste of the prophetic reading. Let us also consider what the Gospel reading contains:

“A certain Pharisee asked Jesus the Lord to eat with him; and he entered the Pharisee’s house and reclined at table. And behold, a woman who was a sinner in the city, when she learned that Jesus was reclining in the Pharisee’s house, brought an alabaster jar of ointment; and standing behind him at his feet, she began to wet his feet with her tears” (Luke 7:36 and following).

[Note: [Col. 1114D] The Regius manuscript reads: “She was wetting his feet with her tears.” After omitting what follows, it recites the rest up to the passage “Your faith has saved you; go in peace,” and continues the whole sequence of the Gospel text to the end of the chapter. Having completed this, it adds: “How simple in its words,” and so forth.]

And he recited the rest up to the passage: “Your faith has saved you; go in peace.” “How simple in its words,” I added, “how profound in the counsels of the Gospel reading! Therefore, since it is the speech of the great Counselor, let us consider its depth” (Isaiah 9:6).

**6.** Our Lord Jesus Christ judged that people could be bound more effectively by benefits and summoned to do what is right by them than by fear; and that love contributes more to correction than terror.

[Note: [Col. 1114D] The same manuscript reads: “and if we discharged toward one another the duties owed in return for graces, perhaps we would repay them.”]

Therefore he sent grace beforehand, coming through the Virgin’s childbirth, so that in baptism he might forgive sins and make people more grateful to him. Then, if we rendered suitable services in return for the gifts freely given, he declared in this woman what reward the same grace would bring. For if he had merely remitted our first debts, he might seem more cautious than merciful, and more provident in correction than magnificent in reward.

[Note: [Col. 1114D] The handwritten manuscript reads this way; the Roman edition has only “more provident.” It is characteristic of a narrow spirit to entice without advancing. Therefore, and so forth.]

It is the mark of a narrow spirit merely to entice by cunning; but it is fitting for God that those whom he has invited through grace should be advanced by increases of that same grace. Therefore he gives to us beforehand through baptism, and afterward bestows more abundant gifts upon those who serve well. Thus Christ’s benefits are both incentives to virtue and rewards.

[Col. 1115A] **7.**

[Note: [Col. 1115D] The Roman edition adds at the beginning: “There were two debtors to a certain moneylender,” which is omitted in the Regius manuscript.]

But let no one recoil from the word “moneylender.” Previously we were under a harsh moneylender, who could neither be satisfied nor appeased except by the death of the debtor (Luke 7:41). The Lord Jesus came and saw us bound by a heavy debt at interest.

[Note: [Col. 1115D] The Regius manuscript reads: “bound by a heavy debt of death”; perhaps it is better to read “of interest.”]

No one could pay off his debt with the capital of his innocence. I had nothing of my own from which I could free myself; he brought me a new kind of acquittal, so that I might change creditors, since I had no interest with which to repay the debt.

It was not nature but guilt that made us debtors; for by our sins we contracted heavy debts, so that we became liable though we had been free. A debtor is one who has received something from a moneylender’s funds. Sin, however, comes from the devil: as though in his estate the impious man possesses these riches. For just as Christ’s riches are virtues, so the devil’s riches are crimes.

He had reduced the human race to perpetual captivity under the heavy interest of a liability-bound inheritance, which its indebted originator had transmitted to his descendants through an interest-bearing succession.

[Note: [Col. 1115D] The Roman edition reads: “an inheritance subject to liability,” which is not entirely correct. But again, where the manuscript reads “worked,” the reading “made a debtor,” found in the edition, is preferable.]

The Lord Jesus came and offered his death for the death of all; he shed his blood for the blood of everyone.

**8.** We have therefore changed creditors; we have not escaped—or rather, we have escaped, for the debt remains but the interest has been abolished. The Lord Jesus says to those who are in chains: “Come out,” and to those who are in prison: “Come forth.” Therefore your sins have been forgiven (Isaiah 49:9).

He forgave everyone, and there is no one whose debt he did not release. For it is written that he “forgave all trespasses, erasing the bond that stood against us with its decrees” (Colossians 2:13–14).

Why do we retain the bonds of others and wish to exact what belongs to others, when we ourselves make use of indulgence for our own debts? He who forgave everyone demands this from everyone: that each person, remembering what has been forgiven him, should himself forgive another.

**9.** See to it that you do not begin to have a heavier case as a creditor than as a debtor. In the Gospel, the master forgave a man his entire debt; afterward that man began to demand from his fellow servant what he himself had not repaid. Therefore his master, enraged, exacted from him with the harshest punishments what he had previously forgiven him (Matthew 18:27 and following).

[Note: [Col. 1116D] The same edition reads: “the entire debt.” For since he had not repaid it, his master, angered, demanded from him what he had previously forgiven, and so forth. But there was no reason for him to be “slaughtered” with the utmost injuries; as we have already noted more than once, Ambrose uses “injuries” to mean torments and punishments.]

Let us therefore beware lest this happen to us: by refusing to remit what is owed to us, we may begin to pay what has been remitted to us. For it is written, the Lord Jesus saying: “So also my heavenly Father will do to you, if each of you does not forgive his brother from your hearts” (Matthew 18:34).

Let us therefore forgive the small debts, since greater ones have been forgiven us; and let us understand that we shall be more acceptable to God the more we forgive, because we are more grateful to God in proportion to what has been forgiven us.

**10.** Finally, when the Pharisee was questioned by the Lord, he said: “Who, then, loves him more?” He replied: “I suppose the one to whom he forgave more.” The Lord said to him: “You have judged rightly” (Luke 7:42–43).

The Pharisee’s judgment is praised, but his disposition is reproved. He judges correctly concerning others, but he himself does not believe what he thinks concerning them. You hear a Jew praising the discipline of the Church, proclaiming its true grace, and honoring the priests of the Church; you urge him to believe, but he refuses. Thus he does not follow what he praises in us.

[Note: [Col. 1116D] The Regius manuscript reads: “You urge him to believe, and what is in us,” and so forth.]

His praise, therefore, is not complete, because he heard Christ say: “You have judged rightly.” Cain too offered correctly, but he did not divide correctly; therefore God said to him: “If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, you have sinned; be still” (Genesis 4:7).

So this man too offered correctly, because he judged that Christ ought to be loved more by Christians, since he had forgiven us many sins; but he did not divide correctly, because he thought that the one who forgives human beings their sins could be unaware of them.

[Col. 1116B] **11.** Therefore he said to Simon: “Do you see this woman? I entered your house; you gave me no water for my feet, but she has wet my feet with her tears” (Luke 7:44).

We are all one body of Christ, whose head is God and whose members we are (1 Corinthians 12:12). Some may perhaps be his eyes, such as the prophets; his teeth, such as the apostles, who poured the food of the Gospel proclamation into our breasts. Hence it is rightly written: “His eyes are bright with wine, and his teeth whiter than milk” (Genesis 49:12).

There are also his hands: those who are seen to carry out good works. There is also his belly: those who distribute the strength of nourishment to the poor. Therefore there are also some who are his feet—and may I be found worthy to be his heel!

He therefore pours water on Christ’s feet who grants forgiveness even to the lowest persons; and while he frees the common people, he nevertheless washes Christ’s footprint.

**12.** He too pours water on Christ’s feet who cleanses his conscience from the filth of sins; for Christ walks in the breasts of individuals. Take care, therefore, that you do not have a polluted conscience and begin to defile Christ’s feet. Beware lest the thorn of wickedness in you wound the heel of Christ as he walks within you (Luke 7:44).

For this reason the Pharisee did not give water for Christ’s feet: he did not possess a mind cleansed from the filth of faithlessness. How could he cleanse his conscience when he had not received Christ’s water?

The Church, however, has both water and tears: the water of baptism and the tears of repentance. For faith, which mourns former sins, is accustomed to avoid new ones.

Therefore Simon the Pharisee, who had no water, certainly had no tears either. For how could he have tears when he did not repent? And because he did not believe in Christ, he had no tears. If he had had them, he would have washed his eyes so that he might see Christ, whom, though he reclined at table with him, he still did not see. For if he had seen him, he certainly would not have doubted his power.

[Col. 1117A] **13.** The Pharisee had no hair, because he could not know the Nazarene; the Church had hair, because she sought the Nazarene.

[Note: [Col. 1117D] The Roman edition reads: “which sought the Nazarene.”]

Hair is counted among the superfluities of the body; yet when it is anointed, it gives off a good fragrance and adorns the head. If it is not anointed with oil, it weighs the head down. So riches too are a burden if you do not know how to use them, if you do not sprinkle them with the fragrance of Christ.

But if you shelter the poor, wash their wounds, and wipe away their filth, then you have indeed wiped Christ’s feet.

**14.** “You gave me no kiss, but she, from the moment I entered, has not ceased kissing my feet” (Luke 7:45).

A kiss is evidently a mark of love. How, then, could a Jew have a kiss, when he did not recognize peace and did not receive peace from Christ, who said: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John 14:27)?

The Synagogue has no kiss; the Church has one. She waited, loved, and said: “Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth” (Song of Songs 1:1). She wished by his kiss to quench drop by drop the ardor of her long desire, which had been kindled by expectation of the Lord’s coming, and thus to satisfy her thirst by this gift.

Therefore the holy Prophet says: “You will open my mouth, and it will proclaim your praise” (Psalm 50:17).

Whoever praises the Lord Jesus kisses him; whoever praises him surely believes. Finally, David himself says: “I believed, and therefore I spoke” (Psalm 115:10); and above: “Let my mouth be filled with your praise, and let me sing your glory” (Psalm 70:8).

**15.** The same Scripture also teaches you about the pouring out of special grace: he kisses Christ who receives the Spirit, as the holy prophet says: “I opened my mouth and drew in the Spirit” (Psalm 118:131).

He therefore kisses Christ who confesses him: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10:10).

He kisses Christ’s feet who, reading the Gospel, learns of the deeds of the Lord Jesus and marvels at them with devout affection; and so, with a reverent kiss, he as it were kisses the traces of the Lord as he walks.

[Note: [Col. 1117D] The same manuscript reads: “Let us kiss Christ,” and so forth. Here we may observe the trace of that reverent silence by which the ancient Fathers concealed the mystery of the Eucharist whenever they spoke before the uninitiated.]

Let us therefore kiss Christ with the kiss of communion: “Let the reader understand” (Matthew 24:15).

**16.** How could a Jew have this kiss? He who did not believe in his coming did not believe in his passion either. For how could he believe that he suffered, when he did not believe that he had come?

The Pharisee therefore had no kiss, except perhaps the kiss of the betrayer Judas. But Judas too did not possess one. Therefore, when he wished to present the promised kiss to the Jews as a sign of betrayal, the Lord said to him: “Judas, are you betraying the Son of Man with a kiss?” (Luke 22:48).

That is: you offer a kiss although you do not possess the love of a kiss; you offer a kiss although you do not know the mystery of the kiss. It is not the kiss of the lips that is sought, but that of the heart and mind.

**17.** But you say: “He kissed the Lord.” True, he kissed him with his lips. This is the kiss that the Jewish people possess; therefore it was said: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Matthew 15:8).

Therefore he does not possess the kiss who has neither faith nor love; for in a kiss the force of love is impressed.

[Note: [Col. 1117D] The Roman edition reads: “The force of love is expressed.” The handwritten manuscript is more apt: “is impressed”—that is, it is not merely displayed outwardly but also conveyed and infused.]

Where there is no love, there is no faith and no affection. What sweetness can there be in kisses?

**18.** The Church, however, does not cease kissing Christ’s feet; and therefore in the Song of Songs she asks not for one kiss but for many (Song of Songs 1:1). Like holy Mary, she is attentive to all his words, receives all that he says, and, when the Gospel or the prophet is read, keeps all his sayings in her heart (Luke 2:51).

The Church alone, therefore, possesses kisses, like a bride; for a kiss is, as it were, a pledge of marriage and a privilege of wedlock.

How could a Jew have kisses, when he does not believe in the Bridegroom? How could a Jew have kisses, when he does not yet know that the Bridegroom has come?

[Col. 1118B] **19.** He not only has no kisses; he also has no oil with which to anoint Christ’s feet (Luke 7:46). For if he had oil, he would first have softened his own neck.

Finally, Moses says: “This people is stiff-necked” (Exodus 34:9). And the Lord says that the Levite and the priest passed by, and none of them poured oil or wine into the wounds of the man struck by robbers (Luke 10:31–32). They had nothing to pour in; for if they had possessed oil, they would have poured it into their own wounds as well.

But Isaiah cries out: “There is no ointment to apply, neither oil nor bandage” (Isaiah 1:6).

**20.** The Church, however, has oil with which she soothes the wounds of her people, lest the hardness of the wound spread deeply. She has oil, which she received secretly.

[Note: [Col. 1118D] After “received,” the Roman edition adds the adverb “secretly”; the manuscript does not recognize it.]

With this oil Asher washed his foot, as it is written: “Blessed is the son of Asher; he shall be acceptable to his brothers, and he shall dip his foot in oil” (Deuteronomy 33:24).

With this oil, therefore, the Church anoints the necks of her people so that they may receive Christ’s yoke. With this oil she anointed the martyrs, so that she might wipe away from them the dust of the world. With this oil she anointed the confessors, so that they would not yield to toil, fall exhausted, or be overcome by the heat of this world. Therefore she anointed them so that she might refresh them with spiritual oil.

[Note: [Col. 1118D] The Regius manuscript reads: “so that spiritual oil might refresh them.”]

**21.** The Synagogue does not have this oil. She has no olive tree, and she did not understand the dove that brought back an olive branch after the flood (Genesis 8:11).

That dove later descended when Christ was baptized and remained upon him, as John testifies in the Gospel, saying: “I saw the Spirit descending from heaven like a dove, and it remained upon him” (John 1:32).

How, then, could he have seen the dove who did not see the one upon whom the Spirit descended like a dove?

**22.** The Church therefore both washes Christ’s feet, wipes them with her hair, anoints them with oil, and pours ointment upon them; for she not only heals the wounded and comforts the weary, but also sprinkles them with the fragrance of gracious favor.

She pours this same grace not only upon the rich and powerful but also upon people of the common household. She examines everyone with an equal balance, receives everyone into the same bosom, and cherishes everyone in the same lap.

**23.** Christ died once; he was buried once. Nevertheless, he wishes ointment to be poured daily upon his feet.

Upon whose feet, then, do we pour Christ’s ointment? Those are Christ’s feet of which he himself says: “Whatever you did for one of the least of these, you did for me” (Matthew 25:40).

The woman of the Gospel refreshes these feet and waters them with her tears (Luke 7:38), whenever forgiveness is granted to the lowliest, guilt is washed away, and pardon is bestowed.

He kisses these feet who loves even the lowliest members of the sacred people. He anoints these feet with ointment who imparts even to the humblest the grace of his gentleness.

In these the martyrs, in these the apostles, and in these the Lord Jesus himself declares that he is honored.

[Col. 1119B] **24.** You see how moral the Lord is, urging you by his example toward piety; he is moral also when he reproves.

Finally, accusing the Jews, he says: “My people, what have I done to you? Or in what have I saddened you? Or in what have I troubled you? Answer me. For I brought you up from the land of Egypt and freed you from the house of slavery” (Micah 6:3–4).

And he added: “I sent before you Moses and Aaron and Miriam” (Numbers 23:2 and following).

Keep in mind what Balak had planned against you—that is, the man who sought the aid of magical art—yet I did not allow him to harm you.

You were oppressed as you wandered in exile through foreign lands and were burdened by heavy hardships.

[Note: [Col. 1119D] The handwritten manuscript reads: “You were oppressed by deceitful schemes.”]

“I sent before you Moses and Aaron and Miriam.” First, the one who had stripped the exile was himself stripped (Exodus 14:29).

You, who had lost your own possessions, acquired those of others. Freed from enemies who surrounded you, and safe amid the waters, you witnessed the slaughter of your enemies, when the same water that had borne you along as it surrounded you overwhelmed the enemy as it flowed back.

Did I not, when you came through the desert and lacked food, provide you with nourishing rain and supplies flowing around you wherever you went? (Exodus 16:4 and following.)

Did I not, after all your enemies had been defeated, bring you into the region of Botryon? (Numbers 13:24.)

Did I not hand over to you Sihon, king of the Amorites (Numbers 21:26)—that is, the proud leader who provoked you?

[Note: [Col. 1119D] The same manuscript reads: “Did I not offer you the living leader, whom you transfixed,” and so forth.]

Did I not deliver the king of Ai alive into your hands, whom, after you had hanged him and lifted him up on the accursed cross, you condemned under the ancient curse (Joshua 8:23 and following)?

What shall I say of the armies of the five kings whom you slew, though they tried to deny you the lands owed to you (Joshua 10:26)?

And now, for all these things, what else is required of you, O man, except that you do justice and righteousness, love mercy, and be ready to walk with the Lord your God? (Micah 6:8.)

[Col. 1120A] **25.** And what reproach did the pious and gentle King David receive through the prophet Nathan?

“I,” he says (2 Samuel 12:7 and following), “chose you as the lesser among your brothers. I filled you with the spirit of gentleness. Through Samuel, in whom I was present and my name was present, I anointed you king.”

[Note: [Col. 1119D] The Regius manuscript reads: “I, after removing that earlier king who was of your party,” and so forth.]

“I, after removing that earlier king whom an evil spirit tormented so that he persecuted the priests of the Lord, made you, an exile, a triumphant man. From your offspring I placed an heir on your throne—not merely as heir but as your companion. I also subjected foreigners to you, so that those who attacked you might serve you.

“And you will deliver those who serve me into the power of my enemies? And you will take away what belonged to my servant, thereby bringing sin upon yourself, while my adversaries will have something over which to boast?”

**26.** Therefore, Emperor—to turn my words now not only concerning you but also toward you—since you understand how gravely the Lord is accustomed to reprove, know that the more glorious you have become, the more you owe to your author.

For it is written: “When the Lord your God has brought you into a foreign land and you have eaten foreign fruits, do not say: ‘My strength and my righteousness have given this to me.’ Rather, say: ‘The Lord God has given it; Christ, in his mercy, has bestowed it.’”

Therefore, by loving his body, that is, the Church, give water for his feet and kiss his feet (John 12:3), so that you may not only absolve those who have been caught in sins, but also grant them the peace of reconciliation and release them into tranquility.

Pour ointment upon his feet, so that the whole house in which Christ reclines may be filled with your ointment, and all who recline with him may rejoice in your fragrances.

[Note: [Col. 1119D] The Regius manuscript reads: “with fragrances”—that is, honor the lowliest in such a way.]

Honor the lowliest in such a way that the angels may rejoice in their absolution, just as they rejoice over one sinner who repents (Luke 15:10); let the apostles rejoice and the prophets delight.

For the eye cannot say to the hand, “I do not need your work,” nor the head to the feet, “You are not necessary to me” (1 Corinthians 12:21).

Therefore, since all are necessary, protect the entire body of the Lord Jesus, so that he too may guard your kingdom by his heavenly favor.

[Col. 1120C] **27.**

[Note: [Col. 1119D] Everything from this number through the next is restored from the Regius manuscript. Besides the sequence of the argument and the similarity of expression, what Paulinus relates about the holy bishop’s conversation with the emperor and his officials also persuades us that this material is Ambrosian.]

“When I came down,” he said to me, “you had spoken about us.”

I replied: “I discussed what would be to your advantage.”

Then he said: “In fact, I had ruled too harshly concerning the rebuilding of the synagogue by the bishop, but it has been corrected. The monks commit many crimes.”

Then Timasius, master of the cavalry and infantry, began speaking even more vehemently against the monks. I replied to him: “I am dealing with the emperor as is proper, because I know that he possesses the fear of the Lord. But with you, who speak so harshly, I must deal differently.”

**28.** Then, after I had remained there for some time, I said to the emperor: “Let me offer security for you; release my mind from anxiety.”

[Note: [Col. 1120D] The Regius manuscript reads: “While he was seated, though he did not openly … he said that he would correct it. I began to stand.” Read: “I began to press him.”]

While he was seated and nodding, but was not openly promising, and while I remained standing, he said that he would amend the rescript.

I immediately began to say that he should remove all judicial inquiry, lest on the occasion of this inquiry some count should oppress Christians with an injury.

[Note: [Col. 1121C] The Roman edition reads: “lest on the occasion of this inquiry the magistrates should inflict some injury upon Christians.” He promised that he would do this. The manuscript reading is more pleasing, and we follow it.]

He promised that it would be done.

I said to him: “I am relying on your word,” and I repeated: “I am relying on your word.”

[Note: [Col. 1121C] The Regius manuscript reads: “Proceed,” he said. “In reliance on my word,” and so on.]

“Proceed,” he said, “in reliance on my word.”

And so I approached the altar, unwilling to approach it unless he had fully promised me this. Truly, such grace accompanied the offering that I myself perceived it to be more acceptable to our God, and that the divine presence had not been absent.

[Note: [Col. 1121C] The same manuscript reads: “I perceived it to be more acceptable, and the divine …”]

Everything, therefore, turned out according to our desire.

[Note: [Col. 1121C] Written at the end of the year 389, or the beginning of 390.]

## LETTER OF POPE SIRICIUS TO THE CHURCH OF MILAN

He teaches the Milanese that the devil acted out of envy in causing new heresies to creep into the Church. He reveals how destructive they are, and reports that in an ecclesiastical assembly their authors, whose names are individually listed, were condemned.

“SYRICIUS [Note: [Col. 1121C] In the codex of the Canons and Constitutions of the Roman Church first published through Quesnel’s efforts, this letter and the following one were printed with various readings, which we shall present here. There its heading is: “To all the bishops of Italy” (Thuaneus manuscript: “to various bishops”), concerning the condemnation of Jovinian and the other heretics who detract from virginity. But we do not depart from the edition of Ambrose’s Works and from Labbe’s Councils, in which the same lemma is prefixed.] TO THE CHURCH OF MILAN.

**1.** “I should always wish, dearest brethren, to announce joys to the sincerity of your love and peace, so that through letters passing back and forth we might in turn be strengthened by the assurance of your well-being.

[Note: [Col. 1121D] Quesnel: “might be strengthened by the indication of your well-being.”]

But because the ancient enemy does not allow us to be free from his assault in peace—he who was a liar from the beginning, an enemy of truth, a rival of humankind, who first deceived himself in order to deceive humankind, an adversary of chastity and master of luxury—he feeds upon cruelties and is punished by abstinence. Through his ministers he proclaims fasting superfluous, having no hope for the future, struck down by the Apostle’s saying: ‘Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die’ (1 Corinthians 15:32).

[Note: [Col. 1121D] The edition of Ambrose’s Works and the Councils reads: “because he does not permit us to remain undisturbed from his assault”; the Roman edition adds “never” in place of “because.” Quesnel’s reading, which we adopt, is more elegant.]

[Note: [Col. 1121D] This is the reading of the Roman edition and Quesnel; the old edition and the Councils have “to be punished by abstinence”; some Roman codices, “is punished.” This is not bad; nevertheless, if we permitted conjectures, we should very gladly restore “indigestions” (*cruditatibus*) in place of “cruelties” (*crudelitatibus*) in the preceding clause. Both the sense and the similarity of the writing support this change; similar scribal slips are frequently found in manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 1121D] The Roman edition alone reads: “he says that these things are superfluous. … struck down by the saying.” By the devil’s ministers are here meant Jovinian and his followers, against whose errors Jerome wrote two books and three Apologies. In the former of those books, chapter 2, he enumerates the same errors; Augustine also briefly lists them in *On Heresies*, chapter 82. Moreover, in various places in his works Augustine supplies much that concerns Jovinian’s heresy, for example, book II of *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, chapter 23, likewise book II, and chapter 23 of the *Retractions*, and elsewhere.]

**2.** “O unhappy audacity! O cunning of a desperate mind! Already the unfamiliar utterance of heretics was creeping like a cancer within the Church, so as, once it had seized the breast, to hurl the whole person into death. And unless the Lord of Sabaoth had broken the snare which they had prepared, the spectacle of so great an evil and its public hypocrisy would have drawn many simple hearts into ruin; for the human mind is easily led toward the worse part, preferring to fly through broad spaces rather than to traverse with labor the path of the narrow way.

[Note: [Col. 1122C] So the old edition, and also the Roman, except that it substitutes “walk” for “fly.” Labbe and Quesnel read: “wishing to fly through broad spaces”; the former has in the margin: “to fly through the broad way.”]

**3.** “For this reason, dearly beloved, it was quite necessary to make known to your consciences what has been done here, lest, through the ignorance of any priest, the contagion of these most wicked men, entering the Church under a religious name, should defile it. As it is written, the Lord says: ‘Many come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves; by their fruits you will know them’ (Matthew 7:15–16).

These are indeed those who, under the cheapness of their clothing, boast themselves to be Christians; so that, advancing under the veil of a pious name and entering the house of prayer, they may pour forth discourse of serpentine disputation, shoot in darkness at the upright in heart (Psalm 10:3), and, turning them away from Catholic truth, lead them after the manner of the devil into the frenzy of their own teaching and defraud the simplicity of the sheep.

[Note: [Col. 1122D] The old edition reads: “those, it seems, who boast that they know us through Christ’s advantage”; the Roman and Labbe: “who boast themselves as Christians.” Quesnel’s reading, which we place in the text, is by far the best.

All editions and Labbe’s text read “turning away from Catholic truth”; the Roman edition, “perverting.” Labbe’s margin and Quesnel’s text support our reading, except that the latter reads “forestalling.”]

4. “Indeed, we have learned and tested the malignity of many heresies from the apostles down to the present day; but never have such dogs wearied the Church’s mystery with their barking as these men now suddenly bursting in, with the doctrine of faithlessness springing up, enemies of the faith, whose disciples they are they have revealed by the fruits of their words. For while other heretics, through misunderstanding, have proposed particular kinds of questions by which to tear down and rend the divine institutions, these men, having no wedding garment, wound Catholics by perverting, as I have said, the coherence of the Old and New Testaments, and by interpreting them in a diabolical spirit. By seductive and counterfeit speech they have already begun to ravage some Christians and join them to their madness, not containing within themselves the poison of their wickedness; rather, as though chosen, they have exposed their blasphemies in a reckless written statement and, driven by the fury of a desperate mind, have publicly proclaimed them everywhere in favor of the pagans.

[Note: The Roman edition and Labbé in the margin read “from apostolic times until now.” Immediately afterward, where the same Roman edition, together with Labbé and Quesnel, reads “we have proved,” the old edition has “we have abolished.”]
