[Note: The Thuanus manuscript reads, “such barking has wearied the mysteries of the Church.” A little later, where our text with Quesnel reads “having sprung up,” the old edition and Labbé have “polluted,” while the Roman edition has “polluted” in a different form.]

[Note: Quesnel alone reads, “they began to ravage several Romans,” and so forth.]

[Note: The old edition, omitting the negation *non* after the word “within,” continues: “But, enticed by their blasphemies … everywhere, in the fury of the pagans, publicly by the faithful,” and so forth. The Roman edition likewise omits the negation and emends the passage as follows: “Putting themselves forward as though chosen, they nevertheless published their blasphemies in a rash written statement … everywhere they revealed themselves in favor of the pagans.” Labbé has the first part as in the old edition; Quesnel has the second in these words: “They publicly proclaimed the fury of the pagans.” We have placed in the text the first part of the former and the latter part of the latter.]

5. “Their madness, through a horrifying written statement, seems suddenly to have been conveyed to my humility by faithful Christians, men of excellent birth and distinguished religion, so that, exposed by priestly judgment, it may be destroyed by a spiritual sentence as contrary to the divine law. We certainly do not disdain the vows of marriage, which we attend under the veil; but we honor with greater reverence virgins whom marriage produces as dedicated to God.

[Note: So Quesnel reads, except that we have retained “to the divine law” from other editions. The other editions do not recognize “But their madness”; their minor variations are not significant and do not produce a sufficiently coherent sense.]

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads, “we who were present at the veiling”; but the same edition, as well as the old edition, continues, “but virgins devoted to God,” and so forth. Labbé and Quesnel give the better reading, as in our text. We have discussed the wedding veil, or *flammeum*, elsewhere.]

6. “When the presbyteral council had been convened, it became clear that their opinion was contrary to our teaching, that is, to Christian law. Therefore, following the command of the Apostle, because they were proclaiming something other than what we had received, we excommunicated them (Galatians 1:8).

[Note: All editions of Ambrose and the Councils read, “to be contrary.” Hence, etc. Nannius explains what is meant by “when the presbyteral council had been convened”: “It is as if you were to say, ‘when the senate had met’; for *presbyterium* (πρεσβυτήριον) is an assembly of elders, just as *gerousia* (γερουσία) is an assembly of senators among the Lacedaemonians. For presbyters were in the Church what senators were in the republic. Both received their name from their more advanced age.”]

“Know, therefore, that there was one judgment among all of us—presbyters and deacons, as well as the entire clergy—that Jovinianus, Auxentius, Genialis, Germinator, Felix, Prontinus, Martianus, Januarius, and Ingeniosus, who were found to be instigators of a new heresy and blasphemy, should remain forever condemned outside the Church by divine sentence and our judgment.

[Note: The old edition of Ambrose and the Councils reads, “they were proclaiming to all of us … one judgment was raised”; the Roman edition has, “one judgment was issued”; Labbé in the margin, “it is established that one judgment was made.” Quesnel’s reading, as in the text, is best.]

7. “Because I do not doubt that your holiness will preserve this, I have sent these writings through my brothers and presbyters, Crescentius, Leopardus, and Alexander, who may fervently fulfill their religious duty in the spirit of faith.

[Note: Labbé and Quesnel read, “and my fellow presbyters … fulfill it fervently.”]

[Note: Written around the year 389.]

## LETTER XLII

The Synod of Milan praises Siricius because he defended the Church from wolves. These men rage against virginity while pretending to defend marriage, although Paul commands that virginity be preferred to it. The same heretics, denying that Christ could have been born of a Virgin, are refuted by testimonies from Scripture. After adding a few remarks in praise of widowhood and abstinence, which these men opposed, the Fathers testify that they anathematized them as Manichaeans.

To the most beloved lord and brother, Pope SYRICIUS:

AMBROSE, SABINUS, BASSIANUS, and the others.

[Col. 1124A]

1. “We have recognized in the letter of Your Holiness the watchfulness of a good shepherd, who faithfully guards the gate entrusted to you and watches over Christ’s fold with devout solicitude (John 10:7 ff.), worthy of being heard and followed by the Lord’s sheep. And because you know Christ’s little sheep, you easily detect the wolves and meet them as a watchful shepherd, lest these men scatter the Lord’s fold by the savagery of their faithlessness and their wild howling.

[Note: Labbé and Quesnel read, “who diligently …” Quesnel alone has, “because you are at the gate against the little sheep …”; the Thuanus manuscript reads, “because we, who are perhaps in the fold, between you and the little sheep of Christ and the wolves …”]

2. “We praise this, dearest lord and brother, and celebrate it with our whole affection. Nor do we wonder that the Lord’s flock shuddered at the wolves’ madness, since it did not recognize in them Christ’s voice. For it is the howling of beasts to preserve no grace of virginity, no order of chastity; to wish to confuse everything indiscriminately; to abolish the ranks of different merits; and to introduce a kind of poverty into the heavenly rewards—as though Christ had only one crown to bestow, and not many titles of reward.

3. “These men pretend to bestow honor upon marriage. But what praise can there be for marriage if virginity has no glory? Nor do we deny that marriage has been sanctified by Christ, when the divine voice says, ‘The two shall be one flesh’ (Matthew 19:5), and shall be one in spirit. But what we have been born as is prior to what we have become, and the mystery of the divine work is far more excellent than the remedy for human weakness.

“A good wife is rightly praised, but a devout virgin is preferred as better, since the Apostle says: ‘He who joins his virgin in marriage does well; and he who does not join her does better. For the one thinks about the things of God, the other about the things of the world’ (1 Corinthians 7:38). The one is bound by marital ties; the other is free from ties. The one is under the law; the other under grace.

“Marriage is good, through which the succession of the human race has been produced; but virginity is better, through which the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom has been acquired and a succession of heavenly merits has been found. Through a woman, care entered the world; through a virgin, salvation came. Finally, Christ chose virginity as a special gift for himself, displayed the gift of integrity, and represented in himself what he had chosen in his mother.

[Col. 1125A]

[Note: All editions of Ambrose read, “presented it in himself”; Labbé and Quesnel rightly read, “represented it in himself.”]

4. “What madness of these deadly barkings, that the same men should say that Christ could not be generated from a Virgin, while they assert that virgins remain virgins after giving birth to human children? Does Christ possess for others what, as they say, he could not possess for himself? Yet although he assumed flesh and became human in order to redeem humanity and recall it from death, he came to earth by an extraordinary path, as God, so that, just as he had said, ‘Behold, I make all things new’ (Isaiah 43:19), he might also be born through the birth of an immaculate Virgin, and, as it is written, might be believed to be God with us.

[Note: All editions of Ambrose, Labbé, and the Thuanus manuscript read as in the text. Quesnel preferred, “But they are exposed as having strayed from the way of truth.”]

“But they are exposed as saying, ‘The Virgin conceived, but the Virgin did not give birth.’ A virgin, therefore, could conceive but could not give birth, although conception always precedes and birth follows?

[Note: The heresy which professed that Mary remained a virgin after conception but not after childbirth is not mentioned by Siricius in his letter, perhaps because the Jovinianists had not dared to spread it in Rome. Augustine nevertheless mentions it in *On Heresies*, chapter 8, and in Book 1 of *Against Julian*, chapter 2. Ambrose attacks it below with the same arguments that he uses not only in *On the Institution of Virginity*, chapters 8 and 9, and in *Exposition of Luke*, Book 2, section 75, but also in *On the Mysteries* and in the letter to Vercellae. Here *generatio* is frequently used for the birth itself, although strictly speaking it is equivalent to conception; for generation is no more exclusively feminine than masculine.]

[Note: The old edition reads, “who assumed his flesh, although he became man”; Labbé, “who thus assumed flesh, although,” etc.; the Roman edition, “thus assumed flesh, thus became man.” Quesnel’s reading, which we have adopted in the text, is preferable.]

5. “But if the teachings of priests are not believed, let the oracles of Christ be believed; let the messages of the angels be believed, who say, ‘For no word shall be impossible with God’ (Luke 1:37). Let the Apostles’ Creed be believed, which the Roman Church has always kept and preserved inviolate.

[Note: There is no doubt that *symbolum* derives from the Greek *symballein* (συμβάλλειν). This word has two meanings, one referring to the mind and the other to the body. In the first sense, *symballein* means to conjecture or judge; thus the *symbolum* is nothing other than a sign and a kind of pledge by which Christians recognized and distinguished themselves from heretics, just as soldiers distinguish themselves from enemies by a military password. The second meaning of the same word is “to contribute” or “to gather together.” Hence some say that the Creed was so called because, after the Lord’s ascension, the individual apostles met to establish a formula of faith, each contributing what he believed, and thus composing the Creed.

Rufinus gives both explanations, but the latter has been sharply attacked by more recent writers. Their principal arguments are: first, that no mention of a creed occurs in the Acts of the Apostles; second, that the Fathers of the first three centuries of the Church are entirely silent about it; and third, that the earliest creeds differ somewhat in wording. From this they conclude that it was not the apostles themselves but the early bishops who composed the Creed from the principal articles of faith.

It is not our task to settle this dispute. Nevertheless, we cannot refrain from saying here that both the word *symbolum* and its meaning are of very ancient standing in the Church. It is mentioned not only by Augustine (*Sermons* 59, 212, and 214), Jerome in his letter to Pammachius, and Ambrose in several places, but also by Tertullian, near the beginning of *On the Veiling of Virgins*, in *On the Prescription against Heretics*, chapter 13, and in *Against Praxeas*.

Nor should we conceal that Jerome writes of this Creed that, although it was handed down by the apostles, it is not written on paper and with ink, but on the fleshy tablets of the heart. This supplies a substantial argument against those who maintain that it was composed by the apostles themselves and committed to writing.

Finally, when Ambrose says that the Apostles’ Creed is preserved inviolate by the Roman Church, Rufinus asserts precisely the same thing. The time when that sacred password was formerly handed over to candidates for baptism and recited by them is explained in the letter to Marcellus, section 4.]

“Mary heard the angel’s voice. When she had earlier asked, ‘How shall this happen?’ (Luke 1:34), not questioning the faith of the generation, she afterward replied, ‘Behold, I am the handmaid of the Lord; let it happen to me according to your word’ (Luke 1:38). This is the Virgin who conceived in the womb; the Virgin who bore a son. For it is written: ‘Behold, the Virgin shall receive in her womb and bear a son’ (Isaiah 7:14). He did not say merely that a virgin would conceive, but also that a virgin would give birth.

[Col. 1126A]

6. “What is that sanctuary gate, that outer gate facing east, which remains closed? ‘No one,’ he says, ‘shall pass through it, except the God of Israel’ (Ezekiel 44:2). Is this not Mary, through whom the Redeemer entered this world? This is the gate of righteousness, as he himself said, ‘Allow us to fulfill all righteousness’ (Matthew 3:15). This gate is blessed Mary, of whom it is written that ‘the Lord shall pass through it, and it shall remain closed’ (Ezekiel 44:2) after childbirth, because she conceived and gave birth as a virgin.

[Note: Quesnel alone reads, “No one has passed through it, but the God of Israel alone has passed through it.” Later he reads, “He passed through it, and it shall remain closed,” because she conceived and gave birth as a virgin.]

7. “What is so incredible if Mary gave birth contrary to the ordinary course of nature’s origin and remained a virgin, when, contrary to nature’s course, the sea saw and fled, and the streams of the Jordan returned to their source (Psalm 113:3)? It does not therefore exceed belief that a virgin gave birth, when we read that a rock poured out water (Exodus 17:6), and that a wave of the sea was solidified like a wall (Exodus 14:22). It does not exceed belief that a human being came forth from a virgin, when we read that a rock poured forth a flowing spring (Numbers 20:11), that iron floated upon the waters (2 Kings 6:6), and that a human being walked upon the waters (Matthew 14:26).

“Therefore, if a wave carried a human being, could a virgin not give birth to a human being? But what human being? The one of whom we read: ‘The Lord will send them a man who will save them, and the Lord will make himself known to the Egyptians’ (Isaiah 19:20).

“In the Old Testament, therefore, the Hebrew virgin led the army through the sea; in the New Testament, the virgin of the King was chosen as the heavenly palace for salvation.

[Note: The Roman edition and Quesnel read “the rod of the Hebrews”; the old edition and Labbé more aptly read “the virgin of the Hebrews,” namely, Moses’ sister. Again, where the old edition reads “the virgin of the race” and the Roman edition “the king’s rod,” Labbé and Quesnel more correctly read “the virgin of the King,” as Ambrose does more than once in *Exhortation to a Virgin* and *On the Institution of Virginity*.]

8. “And what of this? Let us also add the praises of widowhood, since in the Gospel, after the Virgin’s most celebrated childbirth, Anna the widow appears, who had lived with her husband for seven years from her virginity, and was a widow of eighty-four years. She did not depart from the temple, serving with fasts and prayers night and day (Luke 2:36–37).

9. “And deservedly widowhood is despised by those who are accustomed to observe fasts—fasts by which, they complain, they were once afflicted for some time—and who seek to drive away the hardship of abstinence through daily banquets and a life of luxury. They do nothing more rightly than condemn themselves with their own mouths.

[Note: Ambrose’s statement that Jovinianus and his associates had afflicted their flesh with fasts refers to the fact that they had spent some time in the monastery at Milan practicing these holy exercises, which they later regretted. Hence Jerome and Augustine occasionally call them Epicureans.]

10. [Note: Quesnel reads, “But let them fear God, lest he reckon that fast to them.”]

“But they also fear that that fast may be reckoned to them. Let them choose what they wish: if they have ever fasted, then let them repent of their good deed; if never, then let them themselves confess their intemperance and luxury.

[Note: Quesnel likewise has, “and let them also say that Paul …”]

“And therefore they say that Paul was a teacher of luxury. But who will be a teacher of sobriety if he was a teacher of luxury—the man who disciplined his body and brought it into servitude, and who remembered that through many fasts he had rendered Christ the observance owed to him (1 Corinthians 9:27)? He did not do this to praise himself and his own conduct, but to teach us what we should follow.

“Did that man teach luxury who said, ‘Why, as though you were living in this world, do you make judgments? Do not touch, do not handle, do not taste—which things all lead to corruption’ (2 Corinthians 6:5)? He also said that we must live ‘not in indulgence of the body, not in any honor that leads to the satisfaction and cultivation of the flesh, not in the desires of error, but in the Spirit, by whom we are renewed’ (Colossians 2:19 ff.).”

[Col. 1127C]

11. “If what the Apostle said is insufficient, let them hear the Prophet saying, ‘I covered my soul in fasting’ (Psalm 68:11). Therefore, whoever does not fast is uncovered and naked, exposed to injury. Finally, if Adam had clothed himself in fasting, he would not have become naked (Genesis 3:7).

[Note: Quesnel alone reads, “naked he was cast out.” Immediately afterward the old edition reads, “The love of fasting freed Nineveh”; Quesnel, together with the Roman edition and Labbé, reads as in the text.]

“Nineveh freed itself from death by fasting (Jonah 3:5). The Lord himself says, ‘This kind of demon cannot be cast out except through prayer and fasting’ (Matthew 17:20).

12. “But why say more before that master and teacher, when those men have already received the fitting reward of their faithlessness—those who have come all the way here so that no place might remain in which they were not condemned? They have truly proved themselves Manichaeans by not believing that Christ had indeed come from a Virgin.

[Note: Baronius, relying on this passage of Saint Ambrose, maintains that Jovinianus agreed in part with the Manichaeans at this time. Yet since Jovinianus accused Catholics of the heresy of the Manichaeans because they professed that the Mother of God preserved her virginity even after childbirth—as may be read in Augustine, Book 1 of *Against Julian*, chapter 2—it seems much more credible that the holy Doctor is here charging Jovinianus with nothing more than the logical consequence of his errors, as commonly happens in debate. Thus the crime that Jovinianus wrongly accused the orthodox of is justly and deservedly turned back upon himself.]

“What madness equal to that of the new Jews is this? If it is not believed that he came, neither is it believed that he assumed flesh. Therefore he appeared as a phantom and was crucified as a phantom. But he was crucified for us in truth; in truth he is our Redeemer.

13. “He is a Manichaean who denies the truth, who denies Christ’s flesh; and therefore there is no forgiveness of sins for them. But there is the impiety of the Manichaeans, which even the most merciful emperor has condemned, and all who saw them avoided them as though they were contagious. Our brothers and fellow presbyters Crescentius, Leopardus, and Alexander bear witness to this. Burning with the Holy Spirit, they expelled them from the city of Milan as fugitives, condemned by the execration of all.

[Note: It is uncertain which imperial edict is indicated here. Three laws occur in the *Theodosian Code*, title “On Heretics.” The first prohibits the Manichaeans from holding any assemblies; the second and third order that these heretics be expelled. Since the first was issued by Valentinian the Elder as early as 372, it is generally agreed that Ambrose’s passage does not refer to it. Baronius refers it to the second, enacted on 17 June 389, whereas Gothofredus argues that the passage should be understood of the third law, assigned to the year 391. The foundation for Gothofredus’s view is too weak to support it, and we regard Baronius’s opinion as more certain, as observed in the Admonition.

As for the law against the Jovinianists which the same Cardinal thinks was issued in the year 390 under the title “On Monks,” it is clear that it was not enacted because of these heretics, since it concerned only monks of the East and was repealed not long afterward. As for Law 53 “On Heretics,” enacted in 412, which orders Jovinianus to be beaten with lead and deported to the island of Boa, it seems contrary not only to Jerome’s testimony, according to which Jovinianus had died in 409, the year in which Jerome wrote against Vigilantius, but also plainly conflicts with Gothofredus’s chronology in his commentary on the *Theodosian Code*, although Gothofredus accepts the law as genuine.]

[Note: All the editions of Ambrose and Labbé include Leopardus; Quesnel omits him.]

[Note: Quesnel alone reads, “they left them as though fugitives.” Shortly afterward, Quesnel agrees with Labbé in reading “Plotinus,” whereas the editions of Ambrose had “Prontinus.”]

14. “Therefore know that Jovinianus, Auxentius, Germinator, Felix, Plotinus, Genialis, Martianus, Januarius, and Ingeniosus, whom Your Holiness condemned, have likewise been condemned among us according to your judgment. May our almighty God protect you, our most beloved lord and brother, safe and flourishing.”

[Note: The Roman edition gives the following subscription: “I, Ambrose, bishop of Milan, have subscribed. Eventius, bishop of Cenetum, sends greetings … Maximus, bishop of Emona; Felix, bishop of Jadera; Bassianus, bishop of Lugdunum; Theodorus, bishop of Octodurum; Constantius, bishop of Arausio; Sabinus, bishop of Piacenza. At the command of … Eustasius, bishop, and all the orders subscribed.” Since the names of the sees of the individual bishops are absent from the old edition, Labbé, and Quesnel, this is substantial evidence that they were repeated from the Council of Aquileia, especially since two bishops to whom no sees are assigned here are not found at that council. All the other editions agree sufficiently with one another, except that Eustasius is duplicated in the old edition and Labbé, and that Labbé and Quesnel have “all in order” instead of “all the orders.”]

Item: subscription.

[Col. 1129A]

Eventius, bishop, sends greetings to Your Holiness in the Lord, and I have subscribed to this letter.

Maximus, bishop.

Felix, bishop.

Bassianus, bishop.

Theodorus, bishop.

Constantius, bishop.

At the command of the lord Bishop Geminianus, who was himself present. I, Aper the presbyter, have subscribed.

Eustasius, bishop, and all the orders subscribed.

[Note: Written around the year 389.]

## LETTER XLIII

Horontianus asks why, although man far surpasses other creatures, he was created later than they, and why neither Ambrose himself nor Moses has disclosed the reason for this matter. Ambrose replies that Moses did not wish to mix conjectures into the divine books, and adds that he will propose suitable explanations. He uses the example of a banquet prepared for the sake of a human being; then that of a contest, in which the human athlete must undertake various struggles; and finally declares that it is customary to place the most excellent things at the beginning and the end. Since heaven was created first, he teaches that man was created last. After man’s comparison with heaven, the gifts granted to him are disclosed, as well as his dominion over the elements and beasts; from these facts it is inferred that the other creatures were appropriately created beforehand.

AMBROSE TO HORONTIANUS

1. “You indicated to me that you were troubled, after reading the *Hexaemeron* which I wrote, because, when you observed how much divine Scripture, and the style of my discourse, had attributed to man—more than to any living creature on earth—you noticed that all the winged creatures, land creatures, and creatures in the waters had been produced by earth or water before man, for whose sake they had been created; and you asked me to explain why man was generated last, a matter about which Moses was silent and which I had not dared to touch.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “the things that are in the waters, which earth or water had produced, and for what reason they were created, so that man would be generated last.” The other manuscripts and all editions have the more elegant reading found in the text. In passing, we should warn the reader that Ambrose drew several things in this letter from Philo’s *On the Creation of the World*. He transformed them, however, into a form more suited to piety and the Christian religion.]

2. “Perhaps that interpreter of the divine oracle kept silent deliberately, lest he appear to offer himself as the arbiter and counselor of the heavenly plan. For it is one thing to speak what was infused by the Spirit of God, and another to interpret God’s will. We, however, not as interpreters of God but as gathering seeds of reason from ordinary human experience, think that we may infer from what the Lord himself has infused into human use in other matters why it was fitting that man should be created last.

[Note: The editions and two manuscripts read, “we think that we can.”]

3. “For whoever prepares a banquet, like that rich man in the Gospel—for we must compare divine things with divine things, so that we may gather the meaning more clearly—first prepares everything, kills the bulls and the fattened animals, and then invites his friends to dinner. First, therefore, the lighter things are prepared, and then the more honored guest is invited.

“Thus the Lord first prepared a feast for man from the other animals, and then called him, as a friend, to his own banquet; truly as a friend, as one who shares in divine love and is an heir of glory. Finally, he says to him, ‘Friend, how did you come in here to the wedding?’ (Matthew 22:12). The things that come first, therefore, are the servants; the friend is the one invited last.”

[Col. 1130B]

4. “Consider another example. What is the world except a kind of arena full of contests? Hence the Lord says in the Apocalypse, ‘To the one who conquers I will give the crown of life’ (Revelation 2:10); and Paul says, ‘I have fought the good fight’ (2 Timothy 4:7); and elsewhere, ‘No one is crowned unless he has competed lawfully’ (2 Timothy 2:5).

“Almighty God is surely the organizer of this contest. Whoever undertakes the contest in this age, does he not prepare everything necessary for the contest, and then call the athletes, with the wreaths of reward prepared, to strive for the crown? He does this so that the one who conquers may not have to wait, but may depart after receiving his reward. The rewards of man, therefore, are the fruits of the earth and the lights of heaven: the former for the use of the present life, the latter for the hope of eternal life.

5. “Like an athlete, therefore, man enters the arena last. He raises his eyes to heaven and sees that the heavenly creation too has been subjected to futility, not willingly but because of him who subjected it, in hope (Romans 8:20). He sees that every creature groans together, awaiting redemption. He sees that all things remain in toil.

“He raises his eyes and sees crowns of lights; he considers the orbs of the moon and stars: ‘For the righteous who have conquered shall be like the stars in heaven’ (Daniel 12:3). He disciplines his body, lest it oppose him in the contest; he anoints himself with the oil of mercy; he exercises daily in the arena of virtue; he covers himself with dust; he runs toward the turning-post of the course—not as though uncertain, he directs his blows, he flexes his muscles, but not in vain. He strikes the adversary whom he does not see, because he attends only to the one before whom all things yield, including those who are unseen, and in whose name the powers of the air were diverted.

“He balances the blow, and Christ strikes; he raises his heel, and Christ directs it into the wound. Finally, although Paul did not see whom he was striking, he did not strike the air as though aimlessly (1 Corinthians 9:26), because in preaching Christ he wounded all the spiritual forces of wickedness that opposed him. It is not without reason, therefore, that man entered the arena last, for whom the crown was prepared, so that heaven might precede him as his reward.

[Note: The note may allude either to Ariadne’s crown or, generally, to the stars scattered here and there like flowers, which he calls crowns—namely, from which starry crowns can be made. So Nannius.]

[Note: All editions and several manuscripts read, “he covers himself with dust from the stadium and runs,” and so forth. The Belvacuensis and Albinus manuscripts read, “he covers himself with dust and runs in the stadium”; the Laetian manuscript, “he runs the stadium.” Pratensis and Gemblacensis finally have the reading found in the text. We explained elsewhere what it means to cover oneself with dust, in *On Elijah and Fasting*, chapter 21, section 79.]

6. “But our struggle is not only against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places; it is also against flesh and blood (Ephesians 6:12). A struggle against satiety, a struggle with the very fruits of the earth, a struggle with wine, by which even the righteous man was intoxicated (Genesis 9:21), and by which the entire army of the Jews was overthrown (Exodus 32:6); a struggle with wild beasts; a struggle with the birds of heaven, by which flesh, once fattened, is not brought into servitude; a struggle with the dangers of journeys and the dangers of rivers, as Paul says (2 Corinthians 11:29); a struggle with the branches of trees, with which the apostles were beaten (Acts 16:22).

“You see how many contests there are. The earth, therefore, is man’s training ground; heaven is his crown. Either, as a friend, the servants should have gone before him, or, as an athlete, the rewards.

[Note: Nannius says that *exercitium* means the same as *palaestra*, namely, the place where boxers train themselves. Or Ambrose alluded to Genesis 3, where the Lord sent him out to work the ground. That is his interpretation.]

[Note: All manuscripts have this reading; the editions, conversely, have “as an athlete, the crown and rewards.”]

7. “Consider another point. In everything, the beginnings and the ends are the most excellent. If you consider a house, its foundations and roof are better than everything else; if a field, sowing and harvest, planting and vintage. How delightful are grafted trees, and how pleasing are the hoped-for fruits!

“Thus heaven was created first and man last, as a kind of heavenly creature upon earth. For although in body he is compared with the beasts, in mind he is numbered among heavenly beings. Just as we have borne the image of the earthly, so we also bear the image of the heavenly (1 Corinthians 15:49). How could he not be heavenly who was made in the image and likeness of God (Genesis 1:26)?

8. “Therefore, in the creation of the world, heaven was first, and heaven was last—that is, God, who is the God of heaven and what lies beyond heaven. Hence the statement is more properly understood of him: ‘Heaven is my throne’ (Isaiah 66:1). For God does not sit above an element, but in the human heart. Hence the Lord also says, ‘We shall come to him and make our dwelling with him’ (John 14:23). Heaven, therefore, is the beginning of the world’s work; man is its end.

9. “Heaven is from the world; man is above the world. The former is a portion of the world; the latter is an inhabitant of paradise and Christ’s possession. Heaven is thought incorruptible, yet it passes away; man is considered corruptible, yet he puts on incorruption. The form of heaven perishes; man rises again as though immortal.

[Note: The Roman edition reads, “its form passes away.”] Nevertheless, both were made by the hands of the Lord, according to the authority of Scripture.

“For just as we read of the heavens, ‘The heavens are the work of your hands’ (Psalm 102:26), so man says, ‘Your hands made me and fashioned me’ (Psalm 118:73).

[Note: The Roman edition likewise reads, “and prepared me.”]

“Similarly, ‘The heavens declare the glory of God’ (Psalm 18:1); and just as the heavens shine with the splendors of the stars, so human beings shine with the lights of their merits, whose works shine before their Father who is in heaven (Matthew 5:16).

“The upper firmament is the firmament of heaven; there is also another firmament not unlike it, of which it was said, ‘Upon this rock I will build my Church’ (Matthew 16:18): the former is the firmament of the elements, the latter of virtues.

“Indeed, the latter is more excellent: ‘He sucked oil from the flinty rock’ (Deuteronomy 32:13), for the rock is Christ’s flesh, which redeemed heaven and the whole world (1 Corinthians 10:4).

10. “Why should I add those other things and, as though running the entire course, press you further? God has made man a participant in the divine nature, as we read in Peter’s letter (2 Peter 1:4). Hence someone rightly says, ‘For we are indeed his offspring’ (Acts 17:28). He has given us a share in his kinship, and in rational nature, so that we may seek that divine reality which is not far from each one of us, in whom we live and move and have our being.

[Note: The same editions read, “from knowledge of himself.” This is not correct, as the preceding words indicate.]”

11. Since he had bestowed upon man what is the greatest of gifts, God granted to him, as to a most beloved and familiar creature, all the things that are in this world (Gen. I, 28), so that he would lack nothing necessary either for life or for a good life. Some of these things, namely, the abundance of earthly resources, would provide for the satisfaction of pleasure; others—the knowledge of heavenly mysteries—would inflame the human mind with love and desire for learning, by which we might be able to enter that sublime inner sanctuary of divine things. Thus both gifts were supremely excellent: man was to have all the riches of the world subject to him—all flying creatures, land animals, and even fish—as well as the use of the sea, like a king of the elements; without labor or want, in imitation of and likeness to his venerable Creator, he was to abound in everything, live in complete abundance, and open paths for himself and advance by stages through which he might ascend to the royal palace of heaven.

12. On this difficult journey you will easily find as a traveler that man who has been so formed in disposition and will that he has little familiarity with his own body and enters into no companionship with any vice; he is not smoothed and polished by the words of flatterers.[^c0108-1] [Note: **[Col. 1132D]** All editions read, “you will not easily find a traveler”; almost all manuscripts more elegantly delete the negation.] Nor, placed upon the wheels of prosperous times, does he disdain the lowly, flee from sorrow, or shake off and diminish the praises of the holy; nor does he burn away every desire of hope through passion for glory or presumed wealth. His spirit is not bent by sadness, broken by injury, troubled by suspicion, stirred by lust [Note: **[Col. 1132D]** Erasmus’s edition and those following read “is not agitated”; Amerbach and the manuscripts read “is not stirred.”], conquered by bodily passions, or disturbed by the appetite for vanities and the allurements of pleasures. If you add the virtues—chastity, sobriety, and self-control—he is readily able to restrain the immoderate impulses of fickle passions, impose a measure upon his pleasures and desires, distinguish doubtful matters with equity, and settle uncertainties with tranquility of mind. And, as though he had composed all the quarrels of body and mind, like a good arbitrator he preserves undisturbed harmony between the outer and inner man, reconciling them within himself. If circumstances require it, no evil counselor turns him back through fear from the crown of suffering;[^c0108-2] such a man will be received by the Father not merely as a friend but even as a son, so that he may attain the riches of His glory and inheritance.

[^c0108-1]: **[Col. 1132D]** Some manuscripts read “the abundance … for the fulfillment of the will” (*abundantiam … ad voluntatis perfunctionem*), followed by “others, knowledge,” and so forth.

[^c0108-2]: **[Col. 1132D]** The metaphor is taken from pumice stone, which craftsmen use for smoothing and polishing; flatterers imitate this by their caresses and fondling.

[^c0108-3]: **[Col. 1133D]** Some manuscripts and all printed editions read “let fear call him back from the crown of suffering.”[^c0108-4]

13. Rightly, then, man was formed last, as though he were the consummation of nature, to be an arbiter of justice among all other living creatures. And, if it is permissible to summon an example, just as Christ is “the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. X, 4), so are we, in the Lord’s contemplation, like beasts of burden. For the Prophet says: “Κτηνώδης ἐγενέθην παρά σοι”—that is, “I was regarded as a beast before you” (Ps. LXXII, 23).[^c0108-5] Yet what comparison is there, when He redeemed those who were perishing, while we sacrifice? He called servants to freedom, while we impose captivity upon the free? But “who is like God?” (Ps. LXXXVIII, 9).

[^c0108-5]: **[Col. 1133D]** The Prat manuscript and the Gem edition read: “and yet with an equal comparison.”

14. Nevertheless, man, the last of all creatures, came forth—pleasing in appearance, sublime in mind—so that he might be a marvel to every creature. In him, after the likeness of the eternal God, the νοῦς (*nous*, mind or intellect) was invisible, clothed in human form.[^c0108-6] This νοῦς is the vigor of the soul, claiming for itself, as a ruler, authority over soul and body. Although the other animals do not see it, they nevertheless fear it, just as we fear God, whom we do not see; and we fear Him all the more because we do not see Him.[^c0108-7]

[^c0108-6]: **[Col. 1133D]** Nannius wonders why Saint Ambrose retained the Greek word. Was it because Latin writers render it variously, sometimes as *mens* (“mind”) and sometimes as *animus* (“spirit”)? Or because he preferred its Greek etymology—that νοῦς is said to derive from νοεῖν, “to understand,” whereas *mens* derives from *meminisse*, “to remember,” and *animus* is called ἄνεμος (“wind”)? The force and nature of these words are well expressed by νοῦς. Or was it because Anaxagoras said that all things are preserved by matter and νοῦς? There was no reason for the learned man to debate these matters so anxiously; this passage should simply be referred to Philo’s imitation, for in the cited work he philosophizes in precisely the same way.

[^c0108-7]: **[Col. 1134D]** All printed editions and a few manuscripts read “whom, because we do not see, we fear.” Many more and better manuscripts omit *because*: we do not fear God on account of not seeing Him, but because we know Him to be just and omnipotent.

15. For, to dare to speak of him according to God’s image and likeness, as it is written (Gen. I, 26): while God pours Himself forth in the fullness of His majesty and sees all things—embracing everything and penetrating each thing, heaven, air, earth, and sea—so that nothing escapes Him, and nothing exists that is not established in Him, depends upon Him, and is full of Him, as He Himself says, “I fill heaven and earth, says the Lord” (Jer. XXIII, 24), so the human νοῦς sees everything and is not itself seen. Possessing an invisible substance of its own, through learning, deliberation, and the senses it comprehends hidden things; it penetrates the secrets of the sea and the concealed recesses spread throughout all lands. It investigates both natures, after the likeness of the supreme God whom it imitates and follows, whose image is represented in separate things in limited portions. It also raises itself into the air and passes beyond its clouds; through the pursuit of knowledge and the ardor of wisdom it directs itself toward the heights of heaven. There, for a little while, astonished by the wonder of the heavenly stars and delighted by the brightness of the lights, it looks down upon worldly things below; it turns its attention also toward Hesperus, Arcturus, and the other ἀπλανεῖς πλανῆται—“fixed wandering stars”—and, seeing that their wandering is harmless, perceives how they seem to move everywhere without error, weaving their course and wandering about.[^c0108-8] With still greater desire it raises itself toward the very bosom of the Father, in whom is the only-begotten Son of God, declaring the secrets of God, and later to be raised to see Him face to face (John I, 18). Even now, however, He reveals these things in part to those whom He deigns to favor, and pours forth, in a riddle, from His Spirit and countenance a radiance of light like a torrent, so that the one illumined by it may say: “There was a flaming fire in my bones, and I was dissolved on every side and could not endure it” (Jer. XX, 9). David also says: “Let my judgment proceed from your face” (Ps. XVI, 2).

[^c0108-8]: **[Col. 1134D]** Prat and Gem read ἀπλανεῖς, “fixed stars,” followed by *atlantides*. But the latter word is a gloss that entered the text in place of the word expelled from it; for Ambrose explains why the planets, that is, the wandering stars, are nevertheless free from error: their wandering is harmless. Amerbach, with many manuscripts, reads *eum infensus* (“hostile to it”), but this is very poor; the correct sense is *inoffensus* (“harmless” or “untroubled”).

16. By this vigor of mind—to return to the point from which I digressed—man both subdues external things and sees what is separate and distant; he subjects animals stronger than himself in bodily power and has infused into the others such reverence for him that, as if competing with one another, they obey him like a king and comply with his voice. Although they are irrational, they recognize reason and imprint upon themselves the discipline that nature did not give them.[^c0108-9] Thus, when wild animals see his gentleness, they are tamed by his command. They have often suspended their bites when the sound of a human voice recalled them. We see hares caught without injury by the harmless teeth of dogs; lions themselves abandon their prey when a human voice resounds; leopards and bears are stirred up and recalled by voices; horses snort at the applause of men, soften their pace at silence, and often pass by without being struck, though they have been struck—the lash of the tongue drives them on more powerfully.

[^c0108-9]: **[Col. 1134D]** Some manuscripts read: “and they imprint discipline upon themselves,” with *reason* understood.

17. What shall I say about the gifts animals offer? The ram grows a fleece to please man and plunges into the river to increase its luster. Sheep also choose better pastures so that, being heavy with young, they may distend their udders with milk of sweeter flavor; they undergo the pains of childbirth so that they may bring their gifts to man.[^c0108-10] Bulls groan all day beneath the plow pressed into the furrows.[^c0108-11] Camels, besides submitting to the burden they must carry, present themselves to be shorn like rams, so that different animals may bring their tribute to man as to a king and pay their annual tax. The horse, exulting in so great a rider, gathers its proud steps and, curving its back to receive its master, spreads its back beneath the lordly saddle.[^c0108-12]

[^c0108-10]: **[Col. 1135D]** Nannius observes that this is Virgilian, specifically from the *Georgics*: “Let the bull then begin to groan for me beneath the pressed-down plow.”

[^c0108-11]: **[Col. 1135D]** This too, says the same Nannius, is Virgilian: “To leap upon the ground and gather proud steps.” Servius explains this as meaning “so that it may proceed with discipline.”

[^c0108-12]: **[Col. 1135D]** Let no one be disturbed by the fact that man was made last; the same horse teaches us that this should be understood not as contempt but as honor. It carries its rear rider and does not despise him but fears him, carrying him about through various places by its own labor. In a single moment a man traverses distant places and travels across far-off regions, sometimes on single horses and sometimes in triumphal quadrigas.[^c0108-13]

[^c0108-13]: **[Col. 1135D]** This refers to using one horse for racing, as the Greeks call such horses κέλητες (*keletes*); they do not draw two horses, as in the case of riders who leap from one horse to another, nor are they joined in a yoke, as happens with pairs and four-horse chariots. So Nannius.

18. Since I have mentioned triumphal quadrigas, I must add to them Elijah’s chariot, by which he was carried through the air (IV Kings II, 11), and the elephants, upon which a victorious man stands and, although he is last, governs those who are ahead. So too the helmsman sits at the stern of a ship and guides the whole vessel. Hence I think it is not without significance in the Gospel that the Lord Jesus was sleeping in the stern: when awakened, He commanded the wind and the sea and calmed the storm (Matt. VIII, 24), showing that He came last because He came as helmsman. Therefore the Apostle says: “The first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam a life-giving spirit. But not first was that which is spiritual, but that which is natural, and afterward that which is spiritual” (I Cor. XV, 45–46); and he adds: “The first man was of the earth, earthly; the second man from heaven, heavenly” (ibid., 47).

19. Rightly, therefore, man is last, as though he were the sum of the whole work, as though he were the cause of the world, for whose sake all things were made; as though he were the inhabitant of all the elements. Among wild animals he lives, with fish he swims, above birds he flies, with angels he associates, on earth he dwells, and in heaven he serves; he plows the sea, feeds upon the air, cultivates the soil, travels the deep, fishes in the waves, hunts birds in the air, and is an heir in heaven, a co-heir with Christ. This is according to his diligence (Rom. VIII, 17).

20. Receive also what transcends man’s nature. Moses walked at the bottom of the sea (Exod. XIV, 29); the apostles, at its surface (John XXI, 8). Habakkuk flew without wings (Dan. XIV, 35). Elijah conquered on earth and triumphed in heaven (IV Kings II, 11). Farewell, my son, and love us, because we love you.

[^c0108-14]: **[Col. 1135D]** Written around the year 389.

# LETTER XLIV

Ambrose to Horontianus

Moses rightly indicated what distinction exists between God and the world: he signified the former as impassible and invisible, and the latter as corruptible and corporeal. The six days of the world’s creation are not attributed to God because He needed time, but so that an ordered arrangement might be expressed. The dignity of the number seven is explained, though the number eight is preferred to it, since eight is the number of the New Testament, as seven is of the Old. The passage from Hosea is expounded in this connection, and, by continuing to commend the same ogdoad, the letter concludes with praises of the new covenant.

## AMBROSE TO HORONTIANUS

1. You have admirably observed the prophetic division—or rather, the divine division—for Moses did not write these things from himself, but what had been infused and revealed to him, especially those concerning the establishment of the world. This division distinguished the Maker from His works (Gen. I, 1 ff.). For since one thing was impassible and another receptive of suffering, Moses referred what was impassible to God, the Maker; but what was passible, without soul or self-directed motion, receiving motion, soul, and form from its Creator, he assigned to this world. It was not fitting that this world, once made, should be left without a governor and, as it were, a father to defend it. Therefore he most clearly describes the invisible God as the ruler and, as it were, guardian of this visible world. “What is invisible is eternal; what is seen is temporal” (II Cor. IV, 18).

2. Moses therefore represents the world as having been made in six days—not because God needed time for its establishment, since within a moment He is able to make whatever He wishes (for “He spoke,” says the Psalm, “and they were made,” Ps. CXLVIII, 5)—but because things that are made require order, and order generally requires both time and number. This is especially so because, intending to give us a pattern for our work, God observed the number and sequence of days. We need time in order to accomplish something with due maturity, lest we rush our plans and works or omit their proper order. When we read that God, as Scripture shows, made all things with wisdom, with a certain counsel and arrangement (Ps. CIII, 24), it is consistent with reason that He first made heaven, which is most beautiful. We ought first to raise our eyes toward it, to believe that we must strive toward it, and to regard that seat as superior to all earthly things.[^c0108-15]

[^c0108-15]: **[Col. 1136D]** An old edition and several manuscripts read “and in order, so that He might first make heaven.”

3. Thus He created the world in six days and rested from His works on the seventh day (Gen. II, 2). The number seven is good.[^c0108-16] We do not treat it in the Pythagorean manner or according to the custom of the other philosophers, but according to the pattern and divisions of spiritual grace. For the prophet Isaiah comprised the seven principal virtues of the Holy Spirit (Isa. XI, 2). This hebdomad, like the venerable Trinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, is without time and without sequence; it is the source of number and is not bound by the law of number. Therefore, just as heaven, earth, and seas were formed for the grace of the eternal Trinity, as were the sun, moon, and stars, so also we recognize a certain sevenfold ministry of the planets, corresponding to the circuit and sphere of the seven spiritual virtues and outstanding in the power of divine activity, by which this world is illuminated. Their host is said to correspond to the number of those stars that are called fixed stars, or, as the Greeks say, ἀπλανεῖς.[^c0108-17] The northern constellation likewise received its Latin name from the fact that seven stars shine within it; toward it, especially, helmsmen are said to direct their gaze as toward a guide.

[^c0108-16]: **[Col. 1136D]** The Pythagoreans, as Stobaeus observed (*Ecclesiastical Physics*, book I, chapter 11), were certainly more devoted than all other philosophers to the study of numbers. The Platonists also appear to have attached great importance to them. Hence the ancient Fathers, who generally embraced that philosophical school, customarily treated the explanation of numbers seriously. Ambrose frequently does so, as may be seen from the indexes to both volumes under the word “number.” It may be added that in this letter, as elsewhere, he imitates in several places Philo’s *On the Creation of the World* and book I of *Allegorical Interpretation of the Laws*, near the beginning.

[^c0108-17]: **[Col. 1137D]** Some manuscripts read “which they call ineffable stars.” This is incorrect, as the following word ἀπλανεῖς clearly shows.

4. This distinction of privilege descends from heaven to earth. To pass over the sevenfold grace of our head, consisting in two eyes, two ears, two nostrils, and the mouth through which we perceive great sweetness, what a marvel it is that in most cases legitimate human formation begins in the seventh month, and that the child who is born then receives the course of a viable generation? In the eighth month, however, we observe that the natural law forbids the time of childbirth; and if, by chance, a fatal necessity should open the barriers of delivery, danger hastens upon both the mother who gives birth and the child.[^c0108-18]

[^c0108-18]: **[Col. 1137D]** Aulus Gellius, book III, chapter 16, discussing variation in the timing of childbirth, writes from medical and philosophical authorities that a human being is rarely born in the seventh month, never in the eighth, often in the ninth, and very often in the tenth. Consult Gellius himself, as well as what we said on Psalm CXVIII, sermon 15, section 16.

5. Yet the one born in the seventh month, even if born safely, is born for labor; whereas whoever receives the mysteries of regeneration on the eighth day is consecrated through grace and called to the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom. Great is the grace of the hebdomad in the virtues of the Holy Spirit; nevertheless, the same hebdomad signifies the ogdoad and consecrates it. In the former there is sound; in the latter, fruit. Therefore, when paradise was opened on the eighth day, the grace of the Spirit restored those whom their guilt had made exiles.

6. The Old Testament knows this ogdoad, which we call “the eighth” in Latin, for Ecclesiastes says: “Give a portion to seven, and indeed to eight” (Eccles. XI, 2). The hebdomad of the Old Testament is the eighth of the New, when Christ rose again and the day of new salvation dawned for all. This is the day of which the Prophet says: “This is the day that the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it” (Ps. CXVII, 24). On that day the radiance of full and perfect circumcision poured itself upon sinful humanity. Therefore the Old Testament also gave a portion to the eighth in the solemnity of circumcision. But that reality still lay hidden in shadow. The Sun of righteousness came (Mal. IV, 2), and through the completion of His own Passion revealed the rays of His light, which He uncovered for all and by which He opened the brightness of eternal life.[^c0108-19]

[^c0108-19]: **[Col. 1137D]** Some manuscripts read “by which He rewove everything,” and so forth. This is not inappropriate.

7. These, then, are the seven and the eight of which Hosea also says that with this number he hired her for himself and acquired the fullness of faith. For the passage reads: “And I went and hired her for myself for fifteen silver pieces, and a *cor* of barley, and half a *cor* of barley, and a *nevel* of wine” (Hos. III, 2).[^c0108-20] In the preceding passage the Lord had commanded him to hire a prostitute; therefore it is clear that he hired her and even specified the amount of her payment. The fifteen silver pieces consist of seven and eight; they therefore signify the hebdomad and the ogdoad. Thus the prophecy received the consummation of faith at the price of the two Testaments, that is, at the price of complete faith, and the Church received its fullness. For in the first Testament the people of Israel were acquired; in the second, the peoples and nations. Therefore the prostitute is hired in the fullness of faith, whether she is one of the nations seeking union with her husband, or one of the adulterous Jewish people who had abandoned their Lord and the author of virginal faith, while spreading their assemblies throughout the whole world.

[^c0108-20]: **[Col. 1137D; 1138D]** The Prat manuscript has *oephy* in the gloss; Gem has *noephy* or “wine” in the text. Neither reading is satisfactory. Jerome translates the passage: “And I acquired her for myself for fifteen silver pieces, and a *cor* of barley, and half a *cor* of barley.” The Septuagint reads: “And I acquired her for myself for fifteen silver pieces, and a *gomor* of barley, and a *nevel* of wine.” Ambrose’s version differs somewhat from both. In the gloss he says that *gomor* and *cor* are measures of the same size, namely, thirty *modii*, and that *nevel* is half a *cor*. So P. Nannius.

8. When he said, “in a *cor* and in half a *cor* of barley,” the *cor* signifies the fullness of measure, and the half-*cor* a half-full measure. There is fullness in the Gospel and partial perfection in the Law [Note: **[Col. 1138D]** The Roman edition alone reads “partial fulfillment in the Law.”], just as we read the Lord saying: “I have not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it” (Matt. V, 17). Elsewhere we read that the Lord spoke through the prophet Micah, saying that there would then be peace in the land of Israel when the Assyrian came into its land, and seven shepherds and eight bites of men rose up against him (Mic. V, 5). Then there is full peace for the faithful people, freed from every temptation and vanity, when peace and grace have excluded the vanity of this world from our hearts: peace belonging to the Old Testament, grace to the New.

9. The seven shepherds are the precepts of the Law, by which the flock, still like an irrational creature, was led and governed through the wilderness by the staff of Moses (Exod. IV, 20). The eight bites are the commandments of the Gospel and the words spoken by the Lord’s mouth: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. X, 10). They are good bites, by which we have tasted the gift of eternal life, devouring the forgiveness of sins in the body of Christ. In the Old Testament there is the bitter bite of death; therefore it is said: “Death has devoured mightily” (Isa. XXV, 8). In the New Testament there is the sweet bite of life, which swallowed death. Therefore the Apostle says: “Death has been swallowed up in its victory. Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting?” (I Cor. XV, 54–55).

10. To use apostolic testimonies: when God made man, He rested from all His works on the seventh day (Gen. II, 2). But because the Jewish people contemptuously disobeyed the commandments of their God, the Lord said: “They shall not enter into my rest” (Hebr. IV, 3). Therefore God appointed a further day, of which He says: “Today, if you hear my voice” (Ps. XCIV, 8). Scripture embraces two general days, yesterday and today, concerning which it says: “Imitate the faith of Jesus Christ. He is the same yesterday and today, and forever” (Hebr. XIII, 7–8). In the earlier day there is the promise; in the following day, its fulfillment. But since neither Moses nor Joshua brought the people into rest on yesterday’s day, Christ brought them in on today’s day. To Him the Father said: “Today I have begotten you” (Ps. II, 7); for through His resurrection Jesus obtained rest for the people. Our rest is the Lord Jesus, who said: “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke XXIII, 43). Rest is in heaven, not on earth.

11. Why, then, should I investigate the risings and settings of the stars, at whose rising the untilled fallow fields are split by hard plowshares, or at whose setting the joyful harvest lies down (Apoc. XXII, 16)?[^c0108-21] One star is enough for me in place of all the others, the bright and morning star. At its rising a harvest was sown—not of crops, but of martyrs—when Rachel wept for her children (Jer. XXXI, 15), so that she might offer the infants, washed in her tears, for Christ. At the setting of that star, not the ashes of senseless things but the triumphant sheaves of breathing dead were raised from their tombs.[^c0108-22]

[^c0108-21]: **[Col. 1139C–D]** Nannius says that this has been shaped from Virgilian words: “Daphnis, why do you look up at the ancient risings of the constellations? Nor do we watch the settings and risings of the stars in vain.” The editions read “untilled fallow fields” (*inarata … novalia*); the manuscripts, conversely, read “untilled fallows” (*inaratae … novales*), evidently from Virgil, *Georgics* I: “Meanwhile, let the shorn fallows rest in alternation.”

[^c0108-22]: **[Col. 1139D–1140D]** The reference shows that Ambrose gladly mentions the Holy Innocents. He not only recalls them with praise in book II of his commentary on Luke, section 49, but also in book I of *Duties*, chapter 41, section 213, where we have noted several matters that should be consulted. The Roman edition reads “not the ashes of sensible things”; the other editions and all manuscripts read “not the ashes of insensible things,” with some manuscripts having “ashes of embers.” Nannius explains *cremium* as derived from *cremare*, “to burn.” Some grammarians hold that *cremium* is what adheres, burned, around the edges of a frying pan when food is fried, and they cite Psalm CI: “My bones have dried up like a *cremium*.” The Septuagint has καὶ τὰ ὀστᾶ μου ὡσεὶ φρύγιον συνεφρύγασαν—“and my bones have been scorched like dry wood.” Hesychius interprets φρύγιον as ξύλον ξηρόν, “dry wood” or “a log.” Here, however, *cremia* unquestionably signifies funeral pyres, that is, the bones remaining after cremation, which we sometimes call relics.

12. Let the hebdomad therefore be celebrated, because through seven stages of life human life runs onward to old age, as Hippocrates, the master of medicine, explained in his writings. The first age is infancy, the second childhood, the third adolescence, the fourth youth, the fifth manhood, the sixth the maturity of life, and the seventh old age. Thus there are the infant, child, adolescent, young man, man, veteran, and old man.[^c0108-23]

[^c0108-23]: **[Col. 1140D]** What is said here concerning the various ages of man was borrowed by Ambrose from Hippocrates and Solon through Philo’s *On the Creation of the World*, but he adapted it to Christian meaning.

13. Solon, however, established ten divisions of life in periods of seven years. The first age, infancy, lasts until the emergence of the teeth, with which a child prepares food and distinguishes speech, so that he may become capable of speaking.[^c0108-24] Childhood continues until the years of puberty and the first signs of generation; adolescence lasts until the down of the beard; youth continues until the attainment of full virtue. The fifth age is manhood, suitable for marital unions throughout the entire hebdomad. The sixth hebdomad is likewise assigned to manhood, fit for advancement in prudence and energetic in action. The seventh hebdomad, and the eighth, reveal a mature age, vigorous in understanding and likewise endowed with speech not lacking in pleasantness of address. The ninth hebdomad still retains some remnants of strength, while the tongue and wisdom are gentler. The tenth hebdomad completes the measure; whoever reaches it will knock at the late vestibules of death.[^c0108-25]

[^c0108-24]: **[Col. 1140D]** Some manuscripts read “so that he may appear affable.” A few more read “generative testaments” below. This is not entirely inappropriate, since *testamenta* may be taken in the same sense as signs and indications; nevertheless, the received reading is preferable.

[^c0108-25]: **[Col. 1140D]** Three manuscripts read “the deadly vestibules”; one reads “the severe vestibules of death.”

14. Hippocrates and Solon therefore knew either seven ages or hebdomads of the ages. In those ages the hebdomad takes precedence; the eighth introduces one single, perpetual age, in which we grow into a perfect man, in the knowledge of God and the fullness of faith, in which the measure of legitimate maturity is fulfilled (Eph. IV, 13).

15. The grace of the hebdomad is also discernible in our inward parts. For they say that we have seven internal organs: the stomach, heart, lungs, spleen, liver, and two kidneys. We also have seven external parts: the head, the buttocks, the belly, two hands, and two feet.

16. These things are most excellent, but subject to pain. Who, however, would doubt that the gift of the eighth is greater, since it renewed the whole human being so that he could no longer suffer? Thus the seventh age of the world was concluded; the grace of the eighth dawned, making man no longer belong to this world but to be above the world. For now we live not our own life but Christ: “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Phil. I, 21). Therefore we live no longer in the flesh but in the faith of Christ. The Apostle says: “From this we infer that the day of the world has been brought to its conclusion” (Gal. II, 2). Finally, the last hour has come: the Lord Jesus died for us, and we all died in Him, so that we might live for God (I John II, 18). Therefore it is not we who once existed who live, but Christ lives in us (II Cor. V, 15).[^c0108-26]

[^c0108-26]: **[Col. 1141D]** The old edition and several manuscripts read “and to die is gain.” The Roman edition reads “to die is gain”; many other manuscripts read, “to die is gain; it is flight from sin.” The latter reading may be understood, but the former is preferable.

17. The hebdomad has therefore departed; the eighth has come. Yesterday has departed; today has come—that “today” which was promised, by which we were admonished to hear and follow the voice of God. The day of the Old Testament has departed; the new day has come, on which the New Testament was brought to completion. Concerning it He says: “Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will confirm a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah—not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt” (Hebr. VIII, 8–9). He adds why the covenant was changed: “Because they did not remain in my covenant, and I disregarded them, says the Lord” (ibid., 9).[^c0108-27]

[^c0108-27]: **[Col. 1141D]** The Roman edition alone reads “and I will complete … so that I might lead them out.” Amerbach, with several manuscripts, adds “yet it was changed.”

18. The priests of the Law have departed, as have the tribunals of the Law.[^c0108-28] Let us approach the new priest (Hebr. IV, 14), the throne of grace, the visitor of our souls, a priest chosen not according to the law of a carnal commandment but according to the power of an unfailing covenant.[^c0108-29] For He did not seize the honor for Himself but was chosen by the Father (Hebr. V, 4), as the Father Himself says: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX, 4). We therefore see what the new priest has offered. Other priests offered for themselves and for their own people; but because He had no sin for which to offer on His own behalf, He offered Himself for the whole world and entered the holy places through His own blood.

[^c0108-28]: **[Col. 1141D]** The Prat manuscript and Gem read: “The priests of the Law have approached the tribunals of the king.”

[^c0108-29]: **[Col. 1141D]** The Roman edition alone reads “according to the power of an indissoluble covenant”; the old edition and several manuscripts read “according to the power of an unfailing covenant.” Other manuscripts have the reading found in the text, except that Prat and Gem give “the power of unfailing life.” In the other manuscripts *covenant* is more appropriately understood from the preceding phrase, where the word is expressed.

19. This, then, is the new priest and the new sacrifice—not from the Law but above the Law; the advocate of the world, the light of the age, who said, “Behold, I come,” and came (Apoc. XXII, 7). Let us approach Him in the abundance of faith, worshiping, beseeching, and hoping in Him whom we do not see with our eyes but hold fast with affection. To Him belong all honor and glory forever. Farewell, my son, and love us, because we love you.

[^c0108-30]: **[Col. 1141D]** Written around the year 389.

# LETTER XLV

Ambrose to Sabinus

In response to Sabinus, who asks whether Ambrose had written about paradise and what his opinion of it was, Ambrose replies. After briefly touching upon the description of the place according to the historical sense, he passes to a mystical exposition. Having therefore taught that paradise is in the principal part of the soul, he explains what is signified by the things that existed there and what human beings imitate in the serpent. He declares the extent of human weakness and the greatness of God’s love for humanity, and exhorts us to flee the delights of the senses.

## AMBROSE TO SABINUS

1. After reading the *Hexaemeron*, you thought you should ask whether I had appended anything concerning paradise, and what opinion I held about it; you indicated that you wished earnestly to know this. I, however, wrote about it long ago, when I was not yet a veteran priest.

2. I have discovered that many people hold different opinions about it. Josephus, as a historiographer (*Antiquities*, book I, chapter 2), says that the place was filled with very many trees and shrubs and was watered by a river that divided into four rivers. For although the waters had been gathered together into one collection, the earth did not wholly empty itself or deprive us of its streams; even today it bursts forth into springs and leads out channels of rivers by which, like a devoted mother, it nourishes her offspring at full breasts.

3. Others offer other accounts, but all agree that in paradise (Gen. II, 9) there was a deeply rooted tree of life and a tree of knowledge that distinguishes good and evil, along with other trees full of vigor and full of life—breathing and rational.[^c0108-31] From these things it is concluded that paradise itself cannot be understood as earthly, located in some particular place, but in our principal part, which is animated and quickened by the virtues of the soul and by the infusion of the Spirit of God.

[^c0108-31]: **[Col. 1142D]** Philo the Jew, *On the Creation of the World*, p. 35: κατὰ δὲ τὸ θεῖον παράδεισον ἔμψυχα καὶ λογικὰ τὰ φυτὰ πάντα εἶναι συμβέβηκε—“In the divine paradise it has come about that all the plants are living and rational,” and so forth.

[^c0108-32]: **[Col. 1142D]** The Roman edition alone reads: “paradise may be seen in our principal part, which is animated … and through the infusion of the Spirit.” Then follows “Finally, therefore,” and so forth. This alteration was evidently introduced so that Ambrose would not appear to deny the reality of the earthly paradise. But it was unnecessary. The blessed Doctor everywhere either acknowledges or presupposes the historical truth, as was observed in book II of *Paradise*, chapter 2, section 1. Otherwise, how could he assert here that all agreed that the trees were living and rational, if he intended this to be understood while excluding the natural sense, which he knew many people accepted? Certainly, much near the end of this letter plainly cannot be understood as spoken by the holy Doctor according to the historical sense alone.

### 4

Finally, Solomon clearly declared in the Spirit that paradise is in the human being. And because he expresses the mysteries either of the soul and the Word, or of Christ and the Church, therefore he says of the virginal soul—or of the Church, which he wished to present as a chaste virgin to Christ (II Cor. 11:2):

> “A garden enclosed is my sister, my bride; a garden enclosed, a sealed fountain” (Song 4:12).

### 5

In Greek, *paradisus* is called “garden” in Latin. Finally, Susanna was in a garden, and so it is read in Latin [Col. 1143A] (Dan. 13:7). Adam too was in a garden, and so we read (Gen. 2:8). Therefore, do not be troubled by the fact that some Latin manuscripts have “garden,” while others have “paradise.”

### 6

Therefore, the chaste wife is there where the virgin is. Although the virgin, as an exception, has her own barriers and seals, both are in paradise, so that she may be cooled against the heat of the body and the burning of the flesh by the shade-giving shelter of the virtues.

### 7

Therefore, paradise is in our ruling faculty, overgrown with plantings of very many opinions. In it God chiefly established the tree of life—that is, the root of piety. For this is the substance of our life, if we render devoted worship to the Lord and our God.

### 8

He also established there a seedbed of the knowledge of good and evil; for among all the other earthly living creatures, the human being alone possesses knowledge of good and evil. There were also other diverse plantings there [Col. 1143B], whose fruits are the virtues.

### 9

But because God knew that the human inclination was capable of knowledge and would more quickly incline toward cunning than toward the highest prudence—for the Judge who established definite limits in our soul could not be unaware of the quality of his own work—he wished, as the provident author of our salvation, to remove cunning from paradise and to instill devotion to life and the discipline of piety. Therefore he commanded the human being to taste of every tree that is in paradise, but not to taste of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil (Gen. 3:2–3).

### 10

But because every creature is subject to passion, pleasure slipped into human inclinations as though by the serpent’s stealthy movement. Accordingly, holy Moses not without reason represented pleasure under the likeness of a serpent. [Col. 1143C] For it is prone upon its belly like a serpent, proceeding not on feet or raised upon any legs, but slippery through the winding curve of its entire body. Earth is its food, as it is for the serpent, since it knows no heavenly nourishment. It feeds upon bodily things, is changed into various forms of desire, and winds itself through twisting, crooked coils.

[Note: The word *angulatur* (“winds itself through angles”) alludes to the etymology of *anguis* (“snake”), which turns itself around and becomes entangled in coils—coils that Prudentius and Cicero call “the windings of the Maeander.” Thus Nannius.]

It has poison in its teeth, with which every sensualist tears himself apart, the glutton destroys himself, and the debauchee perishes. How many has wine broken? Drunkenness has dissolved them; indigestion has distended them.

### 11

Now I understand why the Lord God breathed into the face of the human being: there is every sense there, there is the seat and enticement of pleasure—in the eyes, ears, nostrils, and mouth—so that he might make our senses stronger against pleasure (Gen. 2:7). [Col. 1143D] This pleasure, then, like a serpent, has instilled cunning in us. For it is not pleasure, but labor and prolonged meditation, together with the grace of God, that gives perfect prudence.

### 12

Yet because the inheritance of the human race is entangled in the serpent’s frauds [Col. 1144A], [Note: You will find a passage closely parallel to this in *On Psalm* 37, no. 8, and in *On Psalm* 118, Sermon 6, no. 15.] let us follow the serpent’s cunning in this respect: let us not thrust our head into dangers, but guard it intact above all else. “Our head is Christ” (I Cor. 11:3).

Let it remain unharmed, so that the serpent’s poisons may not harm us. For “wisdom is good with an inheritance” (Eccl. 7:12)—that is, with faith, since it is the inheritance of those who believe in the Lord.

### 13

But if that first human being, who spoke with God while placed in paradise (Gen. 2:15), could fall so easily—created from virgin earth, which had recently been formed and created at the utterance of God, not yet hardened by the blood of parricidal slaughter, not yet polluted by crimes and disgrace, not yet condemned in our flesh to the curse of an inherited condition—[Col. 1144B] how much more easily afterward did the slippery path toward sin bring a greater precipice upon the human race, when a worse condition succeeded a more tolerable one through the succession of generations?

[Note: All the printed editions read this way; on the other hand, nearly all the manuscripts read *caeterorumque concreta* (“hardened by the blood of the others”), and two have *caeterarumque* (“of the others,” feminine).]

### 14

[Note: The Roman edition reads, “if the magnet stone”; the old edition and all the manuscripts read, “if the stone of the magnet,” while some have “magnet, the stone.” This example, which—as several other passages were—was transferred here from Philo’s *On the Creation of the World*, declares without ambiguity that the contagion of original sin is transmitted through the propagation of concupiscence. Augustine likewise explains that mournful inheritance everywhere in his work against Julian, never having recourse to that covenant devised by more recent theologians. Moreover, Philo himself, in the work cited, acknowledges that the same concupiscence is the source and origin of all the evils of the human race. Consult the work itself, p. 35.]

For if a magnet stone has such power in nature that it draws iron to itself and transfers itself into its likeness, so that, when several iron rings are brought near that stone by those wishing to test it, it holds them all in the same manner; and if, after the stone has adhered to one ring, you bring another ring near that ring, and then substitute each one in turn, although the force of nature penetrates through all of them in sequence, nevertheless it binds the earlier ones with a stronger bond and the later ones with a weaker bond—how much more has the condition and nature of the human race fallen from a purer state into a worse one [Col. 1144C], when it reached a more depraved condition!

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “how much more depraved”; others, more suitably, and all the printed editions read, “when it reached a more depraved condition.”]

### 15

For if nature is diminished through those forms that are not capable of guilt, how much more is its strength weakened through minds and limbs stained by the pollution of crimes! Hence, because wickedness had increased and innocence had been abolished, “there was none who did good, not even one” (Ps. 13:1). The Lord came to restore the grace of nature—or rather, to increase it—so that where sin abounded, grace might abound still more.

Therefore it is evident both that God is the author of the human being and that God is one, not many gods: one who made the world, and one world, not many worlds, as the philosophers say.

### 16

First, therefore, he created the world, and then the inhabitant of the world, for whom the whole world would be a homeland. For if today a wise person is a citizen wherever he goes, understands everything as his own everywhere, and considers himself nowhere a stranger or a guest, how much more was that first human being an inhabitant of the whole world and, as the Greeks say, a *cosmopolitan* [*kosmopolitēs*], “a citizen of the world,” a recent work of God, an unfailing conversational companion, [Col. 1145A] a fellow citizen of the saints, planted together with the virtues, set over all earthly living creatures, marine creatures, and birds. He considered the whole world his possession. The Lord protected him as his work, and, as a good parent and creator, did not abandon him.

Finally, he cherished the one whom he had created to such an extent [Col. 1145A] that he redeemed him when disowned, received him when cast out, and raised him from the dead through the passion of his only-begotten Son. Therefore God is the author of the human being, and the good creator loves his work; nor does the good Father abandon him whom, like a wealthy head of a household, he redeemed with the resources of his own inheritance.

[Note: *Cosmopolites*, that is, “a citizen of the world,” says Nannius. [Col. 1145D] Some philosophers gave a similar answer when asked what countrymen they were; hence also arose the poet’s saying:

> “Every soil is a homeland to the brave, as the sea is to fishes.”

Nannius identifies no other author for the earlier reply than Socrates; see Erasmus, *Adages* 2.2.93.]

### 17

Therefore let us beware lest that woman—that is, the passion of our senses—make this human being, that is, the *mind* (*nous*), effeminate through pleasure, even though she herself has been deceived and deluded, and draw him, once ensnared, into her own laws and judgment.
