Let us flee pleasure as a serpent. It has many arts, especially in the human being. Other living creatures are captured by eagerness for food; but the more senses of eyes and ears a human being possesses, the greater the dangers.

Farewell, and love us, as you do; for we love you.

[Note: Written around A.D. 389.]

## LETTER XLVI

Ambrose writes to Sabinus that a slanderous Apollinarian had been publicly refuted; that he had treated him humanely, although the Apollinarian did not admit a servile form in Christ; and that the words which especially displeased him—namely, that God is the Father of the Son and Lord of creation—agree with the words of David. After this, he demonstrates through numerous testimonies of Scripture that the same Son, without injury to his divinity, was made not only a servant but also a curse, reproach, and sin.

[Note: The old edition reads, “Ambrose to Irenaeus”; the Roman edition, together with the manuscripts, reads, “Ambrose to Sabinus, bishop,” although many of these omit “bishop.” Nevertheless, it is no less certain that Sabinus possessed that dignity, since there was no other Sabinus who was bishop of Piacenza and is found to have attended the Council of Aquileia, whose intimacy with Ambrose is attested by several letters from the latter to him. Leo the Great cited this letter as written to Sabinus, *Letter* 134, formerly 97, as did Leontius of Byzantium.]

## AMBROSE TO SABINUS

[Col. 1145C]

### 1

The man whom you described as a sower of slanderous speech is most frivolous; he has now received the payment for his poison. For he was answered publicly, and what he had sown privately he reaped openly.

I had previously regarded him merely as vain and envious. But when this speech reached my ears, I immediately replied that he had been infected by the poison of Apollinaris, who cannot hear that our Lord Jesus assumed servitude for us in assuming this body, although the Apostle cries out that he took the form of a servant (Phil. 2:7). This is the defense, this is the hedge of our faith. Whoever destroys it will himself be destroyed, as it is written: “The serpent will bite the one who breaks through the hedge” (Eccl. 10:8).

[Note: Some manuscripts read “he is most truthful”; one has “most wicked,” perhaps “most depraved.”]

### 2

At first I addressed him gently: “Why do you do a good thing with an evil intention?” For I count it a benefit if someone, after reading my writings, tells me what seems troubling to him. First, because I can be mistaken even in matters that I know. [Col. 1146A] Many things escape notice, and many sound different to different people. If it can be done, it is a fine thing to take precautions against everything.

Moreover, I ought not to be displeased when many people raise numerous questions about the apostolic writings and the very words of the Gospel and of the Lord, if they find in my writings something that they think ought to be disputed. For many indulge their own zeal, like this man, who traveled throughout the world for the purpose of finding someone to criticize, not someone whom he might regard as worthy of imitation.

[Note: Amerbach and a few manuscripts read “many rightly pass over”; Erasmus and Gillius, with others, read “many, however, pass over.” The Roman edition has “many, nevertheless, pass over.”]

### 3

Thus, in order to gnaw away at something in my writings, he found himself a broad opportunity: in the passage where the Lord Jesus said, “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth” (Matt. 11:25), we said that this was spoken so that we might understand him to be the Father of the Son and the Lord of creation.

Although in the Psalm the Son plainly called the Father “Lord”:

> “They saw me and shook their heads; help me, Lord, my God” (Ps. 108:25–26).

For, speaking according to the form of a servant, he called “Lord” the one whom he knew as Father. Equal in the form of God, he proclaimed himself a servant according to the substance of the flesh: servitude belongs to the flesh, while lordship belongs to divinity.

### 4

You therefore perceive, with your admirable prudence, that the things spoken in the Gospel are to be referred to the time of the Gospel, when the Lord Jesus lived among human beings in human form. For now we no longer know Christ according to the human condition (II Cor. 5:16). Let him have appeared and been known in this way to the ancients; the old things have passed away, and everything has become new (ibid., 17).

Yet everything is from God, who reconciled us to himself through Christ. We were dead, and therefore one was made a servant for all (Phil. 2:7). What shall I say—“a servant”? He was made sin, reproach, and a curse. For the Apostle said that “he was made sin for us” (II Cor. 5:21), because the Lord Jesus “was made a curse” (Gal. 3:13).

He said that when he has subjected all things to himself, then he himself also will be subject. Peter too said, “In the name of Jesus the Nazarene, rise and walk,” in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 3:6). He said there that God “glorified his servant Jesus” (ibid., 13), and no one raises a charge on account of the time.

In the Apocalypse John also called him a lamb (Rev. 5:12). In the Psalm he was called “a worm and not a man” (Ps. 21:7). He became all these things in order to blunt the sting of our death, remove our servitude, and erase curses, sins, and reproaches (I Cor. 15:55).

[Note: The manuscripts unanimously have “What shall I say, servant?” The printed editions add *factus est* (“was made”) after *servus*; below, after *walk*, they omit these words in the Acts of the Apostles.]

### 5

Since Scripture contains these and other things—things that you wrote in response to a certain inquirer, and many more besides [Col. 1147A]—how could anyone hesitate to say what has been piously written, since it concerns the glory of Christ, not his diminution?

For when it is said concerning his gift, that is, the manna, that “the one who gathered less did not have less, and the one who gathered much did not have more” (Exod. 16:18), could he himself either be diminished or increased? What was diminished in him who had assumed our servitude and our weaknesses?

He was humbled; he was in the form of a servant, but he was the same in the glory of God the Father. He was a worm on the cross, but he was the same one who forgave even the sins of his persecutors. He was a reproach [Col. 1147B], but he was also the majesty of the Lord, as it is written: “The majesty of the Lord will be seen, and all flesh will see the salvation of God” (Isa. 40:5).

What did he lose, in whom nothing was lacking? He indeed had neither appearance nor beauty, but he possessed the fullness of divinity. He was considered weak, but he had not ceased to be the power of God. He was seen as a human being, but divine majesty and the glory of the Father shone forth upon earth.

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads “because they were written piously”; below, together with the others, we read “from which it could have come,” whereas the Roman edition has “from which it could not have come.”]

### 6

Therefore the Apostle beautifully used a repetition of the same expression when he said of the Lord Jesus:

> “Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:6–7).

What is “in the form of God” except in the fullness of divinity, in that expression of divine perfection? Therefore, although he was in the fullness of divinity, he emptied himself and assumed the fullness of human nature and perfection. Just as nothing was lacking in God, so nothing was lacking for the completion of humanity, so that he might be perfect in both forms.

Hence David also says:

> “Beautiful in form beyond the sons of men” (Ps. 44:3).

### 7

The Apollinarian is cornered and has nowhere to turn; he is trapped in his own nets. For he himself had said, “He took the form of a servant; he is not read as a servant.” [Col. 1147D]

Therefore I ask again: What is “in the form of God”? He replies: “In the nature of God.” For, the Apostle says, there are those who are not gods by nature (Gal. 4:8).

I ask what it means that he took “the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:7). Without doubt, it means the perfection of human nature and condition, as I said, so that he might be in the likeness of human beings.

And it is beautifully said not “the likeness of flesh” but “the likeness of human beings,” because he was the same in the flesh. But because he alone was without sin, whereas every human being is in sin, he appeared in human form.

Hence the prophet says:

> “He is a man, and who will know him?” (Jer. 17:9).

A human being according to the flesh, but beyond a human being according to divine operation.

Finally, when he touched the leper, he appeared to be a human being; but he was beyond a human being when he cleansed him. And when he wept for Lazarus, who had died (John 11:33, 44), he wept as a human being; but he was above a human being when he commanded the dead man to come out with his feet bound. He appeared to be a human being when he hung upon the cross; but he was above a human being when, after the tombs were opened, he raised the dead (Matt. 27:52).

[Note: Leo’s letter reads, “he was not spoken of as a servant”; but the printed editions and the Ambrosian manuscripts read better, “he is not read as a servant.” This is known to have been the principal foundation of the Apollinarian error, which our Ambrose here very forcefully overturns.

Nor should one suppose that Ambrose taught something contrary to Pope Hadrian I in his letter to the Council of Frankfurt, where he denies that the Lord should be called by the name “servant,” or contrary to that council itself, where it says, following Augustine: “Our Lord, even in the form of a servant, was not a servant, but, even in the form of a servant, was Lord.”

For those statements must be understood as directed against the heresy of Elipandus and others who blasphemously claimed that Christ was the Son of God only by adoption and therefore was a servant not through a servitude freely assumed and belonging to another, but through a proper and natural servitude. This is utterly foreign to Ambrose’s thought.]

### 8

Nor should the poison of Apollinaris flatter itself because it is written, “He was found in appearance as a human being” (Phil. 2:7). Jesus was not denied to be a human being, since Paul elsewhere says of him, “The mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus” (I Tim. 2:5); rather, this was confirmed.

For it is the usage and custom of Scripture to signify matters in this way, just as we read in the Gospel:

> “We saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father” (John 1:1).

Therefore, just as he is called “as the only-begotten” without denying that he is the only-begotten Son of God, so he is called “as a human being” without denying that the perfection of humanity was present in him.

### 9

Although, therefore, he was in the form of a servant, humbled even unto death, he was nevertheless in the glory of God. What harm, then, did servitude do to him?

He is read as having been made a servant because he is read as having been made from a Virgin and created in the flesh. For every creature serves, as the prophet says:

> “All things serve you” (Ps. 118:91).

Hence God the Father also says:

> “I have found David my servant; with my holy oil I have anointed him. He will call me: You are my Father, the God of my salvation. And I will make him firstborn” (Ps. 88:27–28).

And in another Psalm:

> “Guard my soul, for I am holy; save your servant” (Ps. 85:2);

and later in the same Psalm:

> “Give power to your servant, and save the son of your handmaid” (ibid., 16).

I have brought together the words of the Father and of the Son, so that divine oracles rather than human arguments might answer him.

### 10

Elsewhere he says:

> “Into your hands I commend my spirit” (Ps. 30:6);

and:

> “You have set my feet in a spacious place” (ibid., 9);

and:

> “I have become a reproach beyond all my enemies” (ibid., 12).

And in the same Psalm:

> “Shine your face upon your servant” (ibid., 17).

Through Isaiah the Son of God himself also says:

> “From my mother’s womb the Lord called my name, and he made my mouth like a sharp sword, and under the covering of his hand he protected me. He made me like a chosen arrow and concealed me in his quiver; and he said to me: You are my servant, Israel” (Isa. 49:2–3).

For the Son of God is called both God’s servant and Israel, just as elsewhere:

> “Jacob is my servant, Israel is my beloved” (Isa. 44:1).

For he alone truly not only saw God the Father but also declared him (John 1:18).

### 11

And it continues:

> “In you I shall be glorified. And I said: I have labored in vain, and I have spent my strength for nothing; therefore my judgment is before the Lord, and my sorrow before my God. And now thus says the Lord, who formed me as a servant for himself from the womb, to gather Jacob and Israel” (Isa. 49:4–5).

Who gathered the people of God except Christ? Who was glorified before the Lord? Who is the power of God? To whom did the Father say, “It is a great thing for you to be called my servant”? And to whom does he say:

> “Behold, I have appointed you as a covenant for my people, as a light for the nations, so that you may be salvation to the ends of the earth” (ibid., 6)?

Concerning him Ezekiel also spoke through his mouth, saying:

> “I will raise up over them one shepherd, and my servant David will rule them, and he will be their shepherd; and I, the Lord, will be their God, and David will be prince in their midst” (Ezek. 34:23–24).

David the king had already died. Therefore the true David—the truly humble, truly gentle, truly strong-handed Son of God—is announced under this name.

He is also signified in the book of the prophet Zechariah, when God the Father says:

> “Behold, I will send my servant; ‘Rising’ is his name” (Zech. 3:8).

Did the sun of his righteousness lack the splendor of his divinity merely because he wore filthy garments?

### 12

And what more need be said? Do we think servitude is something weaker than sin, than a curse, than reproach, than the weaknesses that he assumed for us so that they might be turned away from us? For he was made all these things in order to empty them all of their power.

But they do not accept that he was made a servant, reproach, sin, and a curse because they assert that the Word and the flesh have one substance. They say: “Therefore, because he redeemed us, he was called a servant, and he ought to have been called sin.”

They do not understand that this is Christ’s glory: he assumed servitude in his body in order to restore freedom to all; he bore our sins in order to take away the sin of the world.

[Note: This error is refuted by Athanasius in his *Letter to Epictetus*, by Epiphanius in *Against Heresies* 77, and also by Ambrose himself in *On the Sacrament of the Incarnation of the Lord*, chapter 6, as well as by others whom we have discussed at length there and in the preface to that work.]

### 13

He was made a servant, sin, and a curse so that you might cease to be a servant of sin and so that he might release you from the curse of the divine sentence.

He therefore assumed your curse:

> “Cursed is everyone who hangs upon a tree” (Gal. 3:13).

He became a curse upon the cross so that you might be blessed in the kingdom of God. He was dishonored and despised, counted as nothing. [Col. 1150A] He said, “I have labored in vain” (Isa. 49:4), through whom Paul deserved to say, “I have not labored in vain” (Phil. 2:16), so that he might confer upon his little servants the fruit of good work and the glory of evangelical preaching, through which all might be released from the burden of labor.

### 14

Having heard these things, the partridge that cried out to gather what she had not brought forth was abandoned in the middle of her days (Jer. 17:11), and was overwhelmed by the voice of the Lord Jesus. Finally, he takes to flight.

[Note: Hermann believes that, after this heretic had come from Milan to Piacenza, he was refuted by Sabinus at the request of someone who had consulted him, and that the bishop then reported the matter to Ambrose. Yet the sequence of the letter seems rather to indicate that the Apollinarian came from Piacenza to Milan, and that Ambrose, having been informed by Sabinus through a letter of what had happened there, in turn wrote back to him concerning what had taken place in the same matter at Milan. The final words clearly confirm this view.]

Farewell, and love us; for we love you.

[Note: Written around A.D. 390.]

## LETTER XLVII

Ambrose explains to Sabinus why he sent him a more clearly written copy of his book, and why he prefers writing to dictation. He then invites him to make reciprocal use of letters, [Col. 1150B] showing what benefit results from this.

## AMBROSE TO SABINUS

### 1

I have sent the requested codex, written more clearly and distinctly than the writing I sent previously, so that its ease of reading might present no obstacle to your judgment. For the copy was written not for appearance but for necessity. [Col. 1150D] We do not dictate everything, especially at night, when we do not wish to be burdensome or troublesome to others. Moreover, what is dictated rushes forth in a kind of impulse and is carried along in a flowing stream.

[Note: These words agree sufficiently with those of Paulinus: “Nor did he avoid the labor of writing books with his own hand, except when some illness weakened him.” His adding another reason why he wrote himself, beyond the care of refining his style—namely, to spare another person’s fatigue—beautifully demonstrates the holy man’s exceptional humanity. Jerome likewise testifies in more than one place that he was accustomed to dictate at night. Nor is it unknown that, while Origen dictated, several scribes at once used to take down his words, with another Ambrose supplying the expense.]

### 2

But for us, who take care to distinguish an elderly man’s speech through familiar use down to the smallest detail and to fix it with a kind of slow step, it seems more suitable to attach our own hand to our pen [Col. 1150C], so that we may seem not so much to pour something out as to conceal it. Nor should we be ashamed to have another write for us; rather, conscious of ourselves, without any judge, we should weigh what we write not only with our ears but also with our eyes.

[Note: The Belley codex reads *familiarius ad unguem*, etc.; less suitably.]

For the tongue is faster than the hand, as Scripture says:

> “My tongue is the pen of a swiftly writing scribe” (Ps. 44:2).

[Note: Here *deflare* means to pour out suddenly and impulsively whatever comes to one’s mouth.]

### 3

But perhaps you will say that the text refers the speed to the writer. Yet you are not mistaken about what is signified: only the speed of a swiftly writing scribe can receive the words of the prophetic tongue.

The Apostle Paul also wrote with his own hand, as he himself says:

> “I have written to you with my own hand” (Gal. 6:11).

He did so for the sake of honor; we do so for the sake of modesty.

### 4

Nevertheless, while you still exercise judgment concerning books, let us interrupt them with letters, whose use is of such a kind that, though separated by intervals of place, we remain joined in affection. In letters, the image of presence shines among the absent, and written conversation unites those who are separated. In them we also mingle our spirit with a friend and pour our mind into him.

### 5

Now, if, as you encourage, letters also give off something of the writings of the ancients, souls do not merely seem to be joined together through progress in true doctrine; the appearance and form of a fuller conversation are also expressed. Thus, through a reciprocal contest undertaken in turns of asking and answering, friends who challenge and embrace one another through such an exchange seem to be brought together in one place and set face to face.

### 6

Why should I produce the examples of our predecessors, who infused faith into the minds of peoples through their letters and wrote to entire, densely gathered populations? They indicated that they were present when they wrote while absent, as the holy Apostle says (I Cor. 5:3): he was absent in body but present in spirit—not only when he wrote but also when he judged.

Finally, while absent, he condemned through a letter and likewise absolved through a letter. For Paul’s letter was a kind of image of his presence and a form of his work.

### 7

For his letters were not like those of others, “weighty and strong, but his bodily presence weak and his speech contemptible” (II Cor. 10:10). Rather, the Apostle’s letter was such that the form of his command was such as the substance of his action: “For as we are in word through a letter when absent, so also we are in action when present” (ibid., 11).

He expressed an image of his presence in his letters and signified their fruit and testimony in his work.

[Note: Most manuscripts read this way; some, as well as all the printed editions, read “the fruit of testimony.”]

Farewell, and love us, as you do; for we also love you.

[Note: Written around the year 390.]

## LETTER XLVIII

He begs Sabinus to examine his books with strict scrutiny and explains the advantages that result from this. He adds, however, that harshness of expression must be tolerated so long as the profession of faith remains intact. He contrasts his professions of faith with those of various heresies and finally promises that in the future he will devote himself especially to writing letters.

## AMBROSE TO SABINUS

### 1

You have sent back to me the little books, which I shall regard as more approved by your judgment. Therefore I sent others, attracted not by the favor of your judgment but by the truth promised by you and requested by me. For I would rather have your judgment correct whatever troubles you before it goes out into public view, from which there would be no possibility of recalling it, than be praised by you for something that others would criticize.

Accordingly, I asked you to be the judge of the things you request. I did not wish you merely to read what I sometimes distribute to the public, but desired that it should come under the reckoning of your judgment.

[Note: These words have been transferred here from Cicero’s *Letters*, book 3, letter 9, where it reads: “The judgment and delay of the long bench, as our Pompey calls it.”]

This judgment and delay will not be “of the long bench,” as the ancient saying has it. It is easy for you to judge our work.

### 2

For my part, I thought I ought to come forward at your invitation. It is your task to decide clearly and to examine critically what you should correct, lest they charge you with fault for things that may have slipped past us.

For somehow, apart from the cloud of inattention that surrounds me, everyone is deceived by his own writings, and they pass over his ear. And just as even deformed children delight their parents, so a writer’s unbecoming expressions flatter him. Something is usually said too carelessly, something is received too maliciously, and something emerges ambiguous.

Moreover, things must be examined by another’s judgment. We ought not to weigh and investigate every scruple of malice according to our own opinion more than according to another person’s.

[Note: These words of Ambrose have often been mentioned with praise, especially by Baronius in the *Roman Martyrology*, where he discusses Saint Sabinus.]

### 3

Therefore lend the ear of benevolence to cunning and handle everything; [Note: The old edition reads “winnow the expressions”; the Roman edition, together with the written codices, reads “pinch the expressions.” To pinch means to test by hand whether something firmly adheres to another thing or can easily be pulled away. This makes clear the metaphorical sense intended here.] pinch the expressions. See whether they contain not courtroom flatteries and persuasive words, but sincerity of faith and sober confession.

[Note: It was the custom among the ancients that those who received other people’s books for examination indicated, by placing certain marks, what ought to be removed or changed. Horace writes in *The Art of Poetry*:

> “[lacuna] He marks the unpolished lines with black by a transverse stroke of the pen. [lacuna]”]

Place a mark beside a word of doubtful weight and deceptive balance, lest an adversary interpret anything as supporting his case. Let it be refuted if he begins the contest. A book is in a bad state if it cannot defend itself without a defender.

Therefore the one who proceeds without an interpreter speaks for himself.

[Note: The interpreter here is what we commonly call a mediator—that is, a conciliator. Cicero writes in *Against Verres*: “Those who are accustomed to be intermediaries or interpreters for corrupting a judgment.” Likewise in his letters: “The interpreter whom I most recently used with Lepidus.” Thus Nannius.]

Yet this book of ours will not leave us unless it has received authority from you. Therefore, when you order it to proceed under the protection of your faith, it will commit itself to you.

### 4

Nevertheless, since the kingdom of God is not in speech but in power (I Cor. 4:20), if the word gives offense, inquire into the power of the profession. The profession of faith is a statement which, against the Sabellians and Arians, we hold to have been handed down by our predecessors in this form [Col. 1152D]: we venerate God the Father, his only-begotten Son, and the Holy Spirit. We hold that this Trinity is of one substance, majesty, and divinity. In the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit we baptize, as it is written (Matt. 28:19).

We therefore confess that the Son, coeternal with the Father, assumed flesh, was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, and is equal to the Father according to divinity, in the form of God—that is, in the entire fullness of divinity, which dwells in him bodily, as the Apostle said (Col. 2:9). In the person of a human being he took the form of a servant and humbled himself even unto death (Phil. 2:8).

[Note: We have already observed several times how highly Ambrose valued the ancient traditions of the Church; nor will we hesitate to point out this passage as well. As for the Sabellians, Arians, and Photinians, we have sufficiently discussed their inventions and errors in *On the Faith* and *On the Incarnation*.]

5. Accordingly, our position against Photinus is this; against Apollinaris, however, a legitimate caution is required: we must confess that, just as in the form of God nothing was lacking in him of the divine nature and fullness, [Note: [Col. 1153D] We observed in Book *On the Incarnation of the Sacred Mystery*, chapter 2, section 11, that the Apollinarians’ principal error was their denial either that Christ assumed a human soul or that he assumed one possessing mind and reason. In the same work, chapter 7, Ambrose also employs the very argument which he uses here.] so in that human form nothing was lacking in him whereby he might be judged an imperfect man—for he came to save the whole man. For it was not fitting that he who had completed a perfect work in others should allow this work to be imperfect in himself. For if anything was lacking in him, he did not redeem the whole; if he did not redeem the whole, then he deceived us who said that he had come for this very reason, to save the whole [Col. 1153B] man. But since it is impossible for God to lie (Hebr. VI, 18), [Note: [Col. 1153D] The Roman edition has, “for God to lie”; the Greek likewise has Ψεύσασθαι Θεὸν (“for God to lie”). Nevertheless, because of the agreement of the manuscripts and older editions, we think that Ambrose has here employed a hyperbaton, which should be restored as follows: “It is impossible for God to lie.”] he did not deceive us. Therefore, since he came in such a way as to redeem and save the whole, he assumed everything that belonged to human perfection.

6. Our position is of this kind, as you remember. If some expressions cause offense, they do not prejudice the faith; for an undoubting mind overshadows an uncertain expression and protects it from error.

7. These are preliminary remarks I have made with you. If you approve, I shall include them in the collection of our letters and assign them a place there, so that they may be commended by your name, and so that mutual love through the Lord may be increased by your letters to us and ours to you. Read them, then, in order to judge them; and whatever moves you, write to me about it. For true love is proved by steadfastness. I am now pleased with what is easier for old men: to weave letters in daily and familiar speech, and, if something from the divine Scriptures happens to present itself, to append it. Farewell, brother, and love one who loves you; for I love you very much.

[Note: [Col. 1153D] Written around the year 390.]

## LETTER XLIX

He is never less alone than when, being alone, he writes to a friend; he teaches by examples the benefits of solitude, especially that then one may have God present through writing and open one’s mind to him.

### AMBROSE TO SABINUS

1. Since you too have come to appreciate the use of our letters, [Note: [Col. 1154D] The Roman edition has, “in which indeed.” Less aptly.] in which there is, as it were, conversation between absent persons, I shall more frequently address you in my writings when I am alone. [Col. 1153D] [Note: [Col. 1154D] This paradox was treated in Book III of *The Duties*, chapter 1, section 2; there we also indicated its source. Nor shall we omit to mention here Francis Petrarch, *On the Solitary Life*, Book II, section 3, chapter 2, where he recalls how dear solitude was to Ambrose and describes his suburban retreat, citing this very testimony from the present letter.] For I am never less alone than when I seem to be alone, nor less at leisure than when I seem to be at leisure. [Col. 1154A] Certainly, at my own discretion I summon those whom I wish and bring to myself those whom I love most or whom I consider most suitable. No one interrupts, no one breaks in upon the conversation. Then I hold you more closely, confer with you about the Scriptures, and together we prolong our conversation.

2. Mary was alone, and she spoke with the angel (Luke I, 28). She was alone when the Holy Spirit came upon her and the power of the Most High overshadowed her. She was alone, and she brought about the salvation of the world, [Note: [Col. 1154D] So the older edition reads, together with several better manuscripts; the Roman edition, with some other codices, has “and conceived the Redeemer.” But Mary may certainly be said to have conceived redemption in the same way that she is said to have brought about salvation, namely, insofar as she gave birth to the world’s mediator and restorer. This manner of expression is by no means uncommon in Ambrose.] and conceived the redemption of all. Peter was alone, and he came to know throughout the whole world the mysteries of the sanctification of the nations (Acts X, 10 ff.). Adam was alone (Gen. II, 9), and he did not transgress, because his mind clung to God. But after the woman was joined to him, he could no longer remain attached to the heavenly commandments; [Col. 1154B] and therefore he hid himself when God was walking in paradise (*On Repentance*, distinction 2, chapter “When Adam”).

3. And even now God walks in paradise (Gen. III, 8) when I read the divine Scriptures. Genesis is paradise, in which the virtues of the patriarchs spring up; Deuteronomy is paradise, in which the commandments of the Law put forth shoots; the Gospel is paradise, in which the tree of life bears good fruit and spreads the commandments of eternal hope among all peoples.

4. Hearing, then, “Love your enemies” (Matt. V, 44); hearing, “Sell all that you have and follow me” (Matt. XIX, 21); hearing, “To the one who strikes you on the cheek, offer the other also” (Luke VI, 29); yet not doing these things, scarcely loving one who loves me, refusing to give up what I possess, and wishing to avenge an injury and wrest back what has been taken from me, although Scripture says something else—that is, that one must grant more than what has been asked for or seized—I see that I am acting against God’s commandments. And when I open the eyes of my conscience, I recognize that God is present and walking with me. I want to hide myself; I want to cover myself; but I am naked before God, before whom all things are naked and exposed (Hebr. IV, 13). Ashamed, then, I desire to cover the shameful parts of my sins, as though they were members of my body. But because God sees everything, and because, covered with leaves and hidden in a refuge, I appear to myself concealed, I think that I am hidden because I am clothed in a body. This is the very garment of skin with which Adam was expelled from paradise (Gen. III, 23): neither protected from the cold nor covered against disgrace, but exposed both to injury and to [Col. 1154D] guilt.

5. It is therefore clear from these things that when we are alone, [Col. 1155A] then we offer ourselves to God, then we open our minds to him, then we strip off the garment of deceit. Adam was alone when he was placed in paradise; he was alone also when he was made in the image of God. But he was not alone when he was expelled from paradise. The Lord Jesus was alone when he redeemed the world (John XVI, 32). For it was not an ambassador or messenger, but the Lord himself alone, who saved his people—although he is never alone in whom the Father is always present. Therefore let us also be alone, so that the Lord may be with us. Farewell, and love us; for we love you.

[Note: [Col. 1155C] Written around the year 390.]

## LETTER L

That God cannot lie is not a weakness; yet God has a certain “weakness” that is stronger than human beings, namely, the cross. That it is not surprising that God infused prophecy into Balaam, since he did not withhold it even from a leader of the Synagogue who persecuted Christ, so that he might draw testimony from his enemies. How greatly Balaam corrupted his prophecies through unbelief and greed, and especially what treachery he displayed in persuading others to sin. Thus it follows that God was not changeable toward him, since he had perceived his wickedness.

### AMBROSE TO CHROMATIUS

1. Does God perhaps lie? But he does not lie, because it is impossible for God to lie. Is this impossibility perhaps a weakness? Certainly not; for how could he be all-powerful if he were unable to accomplish something? What, then, is impossible for him? [Note: [Col. 1155D] The same Roman edition has: “That, certainly, which is contrary to his nature, not that which is difficult for his power.” But we do not see what this transposition and alteration is intended to accomplish. Observe in passing how much more perceptively and wisely Ambrose argues here than Pliny, *Natural History* II, 7, who infers that God cannot do everything from the fact that he cannot inflict death upon himself.] Not what is difficult for his power, but what is contrary to his nature. [Col. 1155C] “It is impossible for him,” he says, “to lie.” This impossibility is not a weakness but a matter of power and majesty, because truth does not admit falsehood, nor God’s power the error of fickleness. Therefore, “Let God be true, and every human being a liar” (Rom. III, 4).

2. [Note: [Col. 1155D] Quite a few manuscripts have “Therefore he is true”; some have “certainly true”; the remaining manuscripts and the editions read as in the text.] Truth, therefore, is always in him; he remains faithful; he cannot change or deny himself. For if he denies that he is true, he lies; but to lie belongs not to power but to weakness. Nor can he change himself, because his nature does not admit weakness. This impossibility, then, belongs to his fullness, which can neither diminish nor increase itself—not to weakness, which is feeble in that by which it increases itself. From this it follows that God’s impossibility is supremely powerful. For what is more powerful than to be ignorant of whatever belongs to weakness?

3. Yet there is another “weakness” of God that is stronger than human beings, and a “foolishness” of God that is wiser than human beings (I Cor. I, 25). The one concerns the cross, the other divinity. If, then, what is weak in him is power, how can what belongs to power be weak? Let this, therefore, be established for us: God does not lie.

4. But neither is there an augur or diviner in Israel, according to the law of God (Deut. XVIII, 10). How, then, does Balaam—who was an augur—say that he was forbidden by a divine oracle (Num. XXII, 31 ff.) to go and curse the people of Israel, and yet go; and how did the angel of the Lord, who had forbidden him to proceed, meet him and stand in the way of his donkey, which was carrying him? Nevertheless, he himself also told him to go, but to say what would be infused into him? [Note: [Col. 1156C] The Roman edition alone has: “If there is no divination, etc.”] If there is no augur in Israel, how did this man, who was an augur, receive a divine oracle that revealed the future? If he was speaking God’s oracle, from where had he acquired the merit of divine inspiration?

5. But do not be surprised that the Lord infused into an augur what he was to speak, when you read in the Gospel that he also infused it into one of the leaders of the Synagogue who was among those persecuting Christ: “It is expedient that one man should die for the people” (John XI, 50). In this there was not the merit of prophecy but an assertion of truth, so that it might be revealed through the testimony of Christ’s adversaries, and so that the unbelief of those who did not believe might be refuted by the words of their own diviners. [Note: [Col. 1156D] All editions have “that Chaldean Balaam”; Nannius says that this alludes to the fact that astrologers and horoscope-casters are called “Chaldeans” because of the vice of that nation. Nevertheless, since almost all manuscripts prefer “that Chaldean Abraham,” it is more likely that the gift of Abraham’s faith, bestowed upon one who came from Chaldaea, is introduced to prove what is here said concerning the prophecy granted to Balaam.] Thus that Chaldean Abraham is brought forward as an example of faith, so that the superstition of the Chaldeans might fall silent. It is therefore not the merit of the one who confesses, but the oracle of the one who calls, [Note: [Col. 1156D] So the manuscripts read, except for one or two; those have, as do all the editions, “by the grace of God revealing.” What, then, did he acquire, etc.?] namely, the grace of God who reveals.

6. What offense, then, did Balaam incur (Num. XXII, 12), except that he said one thing while plotting another? For God requires a clean vessel, not one polluted with uncleanness and filth. Balaam was therefore being tested, not approved; for he was full of deceit and trickery. Finally, when he had first asked whether he ought to go to that foolish people and had been forbidden, he made excuses. Later, when more distinguished ambassadors had been sent, with richer promises and more abundant gifts, [Col. 1157A] he was enticed (Num. XXII, 19) and thought that he should consult again— as though God could be swayed by a price or by gifts.

7. He received an answer as though he were a greedy man, not as though he were seeking the truth, so that he might be mocked rather than instructed. He began to go; the angel met him in a narrow place (ibid., 24). He showed himself to the donkey but did not show himself to the augur. He revealed himself to the donkey and crushed this man; nevertheless, so that Balaam might eventually understand, he opened his eyes. He saw, yet still did not believe the evident oracle; and although he ought to have trusted even his eyes, he replied in obscure and ambiguous language.

8. Then the Lord, indignant, said through the angel: “Go, but whatever I inspire into you, that you shall say” (ibid., 35)—that is, not what you wish, but what you are compelled to speak. Like an empty instrument, you will produce a sound for my words. I am the one who will speak, not you, who will merely echo what you hear and will not understand. You will gain nothing by going, [Note: [Col. 1157D] A few manuscripts have, “you will remain without payment.” This is not sufficiently correct.] because you will return without monetary reward and without spiritual benefit. Accordingly, his first utterance is: “How shall I curse one whom the Lord has not cursed?” (Num. XXIII, 8), so that he might show that the blessing of the Hebrew people lay not in his own will but in God’s grace.

9. “From the highest mountains,” he says, “I shall behold him” (Num. XXIII, 9), because I cannot comprehend with my eyes this people who will dwell alone—not marking out their boundaries by possession of territory, but spreading through the eternal ages by inhabiting virtue and possessing singular customs. For who among the other nations can be counted with it, since it surpasses the fellowship of neighboring peoples by the sublimity of its righteousness? Who can gather up the constitution of its generation? We perceive, indeed, that their bodies were formed and fashioned from human seed, but their souls sprang up from higher and wondrous seedbeds.

10. “Let my soul die with their souls” (ibid., 10): let it die to this bodily life, so that in the souls of the righteous it may attain the grace of that eternal life. In this, even then, the majesty of this heavenly mystery and of holy baptism was revealed. Through its operation, human beings die to their former guilt and to the works of the wicked, so that, transformed by the newness of life into fellowship with the righteous, they may rise again into their manner of life. And what wonder is it that human beings die to sin in order to live to God?

11. When Balak heard this, he was indignant, [Note: [Col. 1157D] The Roman edition alone has: “saying, ‘What have you done to me? I called you to curse my enemies, and behold, you have blessed them with a blessing.’”] saying: “I brought you to curse them, and you bless them.” He replied: “I suffer a false accusation concerning what I do not know, for I say nothing of my own; I merely return a sound like a clanging cymbal.” Again he was led from one place to another, and whenever he wished to curse, he blessed: [Note: [Col. 1157D] The same edition has: “There will be no labor in Jacob, nor pain in Israel. The Lord their God is with them.”] “There is no labor in Jacob, nor pain in Israel” (ibid., 21). The Lord protects him. And afterward he ordered seven altars and sacrifices to be prepared. Certainly Balaam ought to have departed, but through weakness of mind and fickleness of judgment he thought that he could turn God’s will aside. In the frenzy of his mind, he desired one thing and spoke another.

12. “How beautiful,” he says, [Note: [Col. 1157D] The Roman edition has: “Your dwellings, Jacob; your tents, Israel.”] “are your dwellings, O army of the Hebrews! Your tents are like shady groves, like a paradise beside a river, and like a cedar beside the waters” (Num. XXIV, 5–6). “A man shall come forth from Jacob and shall possess many nations, and his kingdom shall be raised on high; on earth, too, he shall extend his dominion [Col. 1158B] into Egypt. Those who bless him shall be blessed, and those who curse him shall be cursed” (ibid., 9). Whom does this signify, then, except the people of Christ? [Note: [Col. 1157D] The older edition and several manuscripts have: “He signifies, and God blesses him” [some have “blessed him”]; in some manuscripts “God” is omitted; the Roman edition has: “whom God has blessed”; the remaining manuscripts read as in the text.] God blesses this people, into whose marrow the word of God descends, even to the division of soul, joints, and marrow (Hebr. IV, 12). Balaam would have possessed the Lord’s grace if he had done this according to the inclination and purpose of his own heart. But since an evil mind is exposed by its own counsels, and the hidden things of the soul are revealed by their outcome, his mind is disclosed by the plots that follow.

13. Therefore he found a fitting reward for his malice. For when he perceived that, placed in a frenzy of mind, he could not curse, he gave the king this advice: [Note: [Col. 1158D] All editions and most manuscripts have, “Let these be the oracles”; Prat and a few others more aptly have, “Let these be the oracles of those.”] “These may be the oracles that God has commanded; accept counsel against the oracles [Col. 1158C] of God. This people is righteous and has God’s protection, because it has not devoted itself to divinations and auguries but to the eternal God alone; therefore it surpasses the others in faith. Yet at times faithful minds also slip through the allurements of the body and the enticement of beauty. You have many women, and most of them are not lacking in beauty. The male sex is never more slippery than when it is quickly captured by feminine beauty, especially if the ardor of their minds is inflamed by frequent conversations and burns as though by torches; if they drink in the hope of possession and prolong their desire. Let your women therefore cast hooks with their words. Let them not make their first approaches difficult, but let them move about, easy to see and approachable in speech, [Note: [Col. 1158D] Nannius says that Maro’s line is more accurate, with a slight alteration:

‘Neither easy to see, nor agreeable in speech to anyone.’] and surround the whole army. Let them deal with these men by such craft that they do not yield to intercourse unless, through the fellowship of sacrilege, they have confirmed the pledge of mutual love. For in this way they will be able to deprive themselves of heavenly protection, if they themselves turn away from the Lord their God through sacrileges.”

14. Balaam was therefore not righteous, since he was an adviser of fornication and sacrilege, as is also clearly written in the Apocalypse of John the Evangelist, where the Lord Jesus says to the angel of the Church of Pergamum: “You have there those who hold the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to place a stumbling block before the children of Israel, to eat things sacrificed to idols and to commit fornication. So you also have those who hold the teaching of the Nicolaitans” (Apoc. II, 14–15). From this it is evident that Manes’ Manichaean sacrileges consist in mixing and joining [Note: [Col. 1159D] The disgraceful practices to which Ambrose says that the Manichaeans joined sacrilege are explained by Augustine in *On Heresies*, chapter 46.] sacrilege to disgrace.

15. Therefore neither was God unjust, nor was his judgment changeable. For he detected Balaam’s mind and the secrets of his heart, and therefore he tested him as a diviner but did not choose him as a prophet. Certainly, the grace of so many oracles and the sublimity of the revelations ought to have converted him. But his mind, full of wickedness, uttered words without offering faith, wishing by its counsels to undermine what it had announced as future. And because he could not defraud the oracles, he supplied fraudulent counsels, by which [Note: [Col. 1159D] The edition, together with some manuscripts, has, “by which the frivolous people of the Jews were tempted.” More numerous and better manuscripts have, “by which the frivolous people of the Jews were indeed tempted”; this is by no means incorrect.] the frivolous people of the Jews were indeed tempted, but not overcome. For the righteousness of one priestly man dissolved the whole plot of the criminal man (Num. XXV, 11)—and it was far more wondrous that the army of the fathers could be delivered through one man than that it could be deceived.

16. I have sent this little gift to your holy mind, since you wish me to set down something concerning the interpretations of the ancient writers. I, for my part, have undertaken to append letters in familiar speech, letters that give off something of the character of the fathers. If you approve their flavor, I shall not be embarrassed to send you more of this kind hereafter. For I would rather, in senile words, ramble with you about heavenly matters—what the Greeks call ἀδολεσχῆσαι, “to indulge in idle talk.” [Note: [Col. 1159D; 1160D] Because Greek words are written ignorantly and without sufficient distinction in handwritten codices, Amerbach extracted from them a reading that was not only barbarous but wholly devoid of sense. Accordingly, in order to apply a remedy to the manifest sore, Erasmus substituted, as though it were genuine: “the Greeks call it ἀδολεσχίαις γηραλαίαις περὶ τῶν ἄνω ἀδολεσχεῖσθαι” (“to ramble in senile chatter about heavenly things”). This did not satisfy the Roman editors; after mutilating several words, they presented only: “the Greeks call it ἀδολεσχῆσαι.” But a closer examination of the characters in which this passage is written in the Royal manuscript discloses the true reading, which we have restored. Ambrose discussed the word ἀδολεσχῆσαι and its meaning in *On Isaac and the Soul*, chapter 1, section 1; in his exposition of Psalm XVIII, sections 13 and 14; and elsewhere.] “Isaac went out into the field to indulge in idle talk” [Ἐξῆλθεν ἄρ᾽ Ἰσαὰκ εἰς τὸ πεδίον ἀδολεσχῆσαι]—as Rebecca was coming, seeing in spirit the mysteries of the future Church, than seem to have abandoned the art [Note: [Col. 1160D] All editions and a few manuscripts have “to have ceased from the art”; some others have “to have given up the art”; the remaining manuscripts more correctly have “to have abandoned the art,” namely, the interpretation of Scripture, so that he might work something out by his own effort.] and, in greater haste, breathe out something that is now suited neither to our studies nor to our strength. Farewell, and love us; for I love you.

[Note: [Col. 1160D] Written around the year 390.]

## LETTER LI

He declines his arrival not from an ungrateful feeling, but lest he should be forced to remain silent or provide grounds for offense. Theodosius is prone to anger but readily appeased by his own nature; therefore Ambrose excused himself on the grounds of illness so as not to provoke him. The bishops groaned over the massacre at Thessalonica; accordingly, in cleansing that offense, the emperor must imitate the repentance of the saints, without which sin is not removed. The devil, who envied him, must be conquered. Ambrose does not dare to offer the sacrifice in the emperor’s presence, since he was divinely deterred from doing so; yet repentance itself is a sacrifice. He grieves that he did not forestall the emperor’s deed, since he truly loves him.

### TO THE MOST AUGUST EMPEROR THEODOSIUS, FROM AMBROSE, BISHOP

1. I have a sweet recollection both of our old friendship and of the favors that, through my frequent intercessions, you have bestowed on others with the greatest generosity. From this it can be understood that I could not previously have avoided your arrival—always most eagerly desired by me—out of any unwilling feeling. But I shall briefly explain why I did so.

2. In your [Note: [Col. 1160D] As Nannius observes, *comitatus* means the emperor’s household, together with its officials and attendants; this was formerly called a cohort.] retinue I alone seemed to have been deprived of the natural right to hear, and thus to be deprived of the power to speak as well. For you were frequently moved when certain matters that had been decided in your council reached me. I therefore found myself excluded from ordinary practice, although the Lord Jesus says that nothing is hidden that will not be revealed (Luke VIII, 17). Accordingly, I satisfied the imperial will as best I could out of reverence, and I took care that either you yourself should not have grounds for anger because I had acted to prevent any imperial decisions from being reported to me, or that, when present, I should either fail through fear to hear everything and incur the reputation of one who connived, or hear in such a way that my ears were open but my voice closed—so that, having heard, I could not speak, lest I harm those who had fallen under suspicion of treason and were in danger.

3. What, then, was I to do? Should I refuse to hear? But I could not close my ears with the wax of ancient fables. Should I betray what I heard? But what I feared in your commands I would have to guard against in my words, lest anything bloody be committed. Should I remain silent? But—what would have been the worst of all—my conscience would be bound and my voice taken away. And what of this? “If a priest does not warn the one who is going astray, the one who has gone astray will die in his guilt, and the priest will be liable to punishment because he did not warn the one who was going astray” (Ezek. III, 19).

4. Hear this, august emperor. I cannot deny your zeal for the faith; I do not dispute your fear of God. But you possess a natural impulse which, if someone seeks to soothe it, you quickly turn toward mercy; if someone provokes it, you stir it up still further, so that you can scarcely recall it. Would that, if no one calms it, no one might inflame it! I gladly entrust it to you: you yourself recall yourself, and through devotion to piety you conquer the impulse of nature.

5. I preferred to entrust this impulse secretly to your thoughts rather than perhaps provoke it publicly by my actions. Therefore I preferred to fall short somewhat in my duty rather than in humility, and to have others seek from me the authority of a priest rather than have you miss in me [Note: [Col. 1161D] So all editions read, but the passage seems somewhat corrupt. It might perhaps be easily corrected by substituting *amantissimo* (“for one most loving”) for *amantissime* (“most lovingly”).] the honor due to one most loving; so that, with the impulse restrained, the freedom to choose a course of action might remain intact. I pleaded serious bodily illness, one that could scarcely be relieved except by gentler men. Yet I would have preferred to die rather than fail to await your arrival for two or three days. But what else could I do? There was no alternative.

6. Something happened in the city of the Thessalonians that no memory records, something that I could not prevent from happening—indeed, something I had declared beforehand would be most atrocious, when I so often pleaded against it. And what you yourself later considered a grave act when belatedly attempting to revoke it, I could not minimize. When it was first heard, [Note: [Col. 1161D] The Roman edition alone has “when, because of the arrival of the Gallic bishops, etc.” But the sense is no worse without the adverb *cum*. There is also dispute concerning which synod is intended by the words that follow. Baronius thinks it was the synod at which Jovinianus and his followers were condemned. Although Hermannus states in his *Elucidations* that he has noticed nothing by which that opinion can either be established or refuted, in Book VII, chapter 1, of the *Life of Ambrose* he nevertheless thinks that this assembly of bishops met because of the Ithacians and Felix, whom they had imposed upon the diocese of Trier. But he himself offers no support for his view. We shall have to speak again elsewhere about this latter synod.] a synod had assembled because of the arrival of the Gallic bishops. Everyone groaned; no one received the news with indifference. Your acquittal was not possible within Ambrose’s communion, and the odium of the offense would have been increased against me if no one had said that reconciliation with our God was necessary.

7. Are you ashamed, Emperor, to do what David, the prophet-king and ancestor of Christ according to the flesh, did? He was told that a rich man who possessed many flocks had, because a guest had arrived, seized and killed the one sheep belonging to a poor man. When he learned that he himself was being accused because he had done this, he said: “I have sinned against the Lord” (II Sam. XII, 13). Therefore, Emperor, do not bear impatiently being told: “You have done this thing,” as the prophet said to King David. For if you listen carefully and say, “I have sinned against the Lord”; if you say the royal prophetic words, “Come, let us worship and fall down before him, and let us weep before the Lord our God, who made us” (Ps. XCIV, 6); then it will also be said to you: “Because you repent, the Lord forgives your sin, and you shall not die” (II Sam. XII, 13).

8. Again, when David had ordered the people to be counted, he was struck in the heart and said to the Lord: “I have sinned greatly in doing this, and now, Lord, take away the iniquity of your servant, for I have sinned greatly” (II Sam. XXIV, 10). Then the prophet Nathan was sent to him again and offered him three possible conditions, so that he might choose whichever he wished: three years of famine in the land, or three months of fleeing before his enemies, or three days of death in the land. David replied: “These three things are exceedingly grievous; nevertheless, let me fall into the hand of the Lord, for his mercies are very abundant, and let me not fall into the hands of man” (ibid., 14). His guilt consisted in wishing to know the number of the entire people who were with him, something that ought to have been reserved for God alone.

9. And when, he says, death was spreading among the people, on the very first day, around the hour of the midday meal, David saw the angel striking the people and said: “I have sinned, and I, the shepherd, have acted wickedly; but what has this flock done? Let your hand be against me and against my father’s house” (ibid., 17). Therefore the Lord repented and ordered the angel to spare the people, while David was to offer a sacrifice. At that time there were sacrifices for sins; now there are sacrifices of repentance. Thus David became more acceptable to God through that humility. For it is not surprising that a human being sins; what is blameworthy is not recognizing that one has gone astray and not humbling oneself before God.

10. Holy Job, who was himself powerful in the world, said: “I did not hide my sin, but proclaimed it before all the people” (Job XXXI, 33). Jonathan, the son of the monstrous king Saul, said to him: “Do not sin against your servant David” (I Sam. XIX, 4); and, “Why do you sin by killing David, who is innocent, without cause?” (ibid., 5). For although Saul was king, he was sinning if he killed an innocent man. Finally, when David had already obtained the kingdom and heard that Abner, an innocent man, had been killed by Joab, the commander of his army, he said: “I and my kingdom are innocent forever from the blood of Abner son of Ner” (II Sam. III, 28), and he fasted in his grief.

11. I have written these things not to shame you, but so that the examples of kings may spur you to remove this sin from your kingdom. You will remove it by humbling your soul before God. You are a human being, and temptation has come upon you; conquer it. Sin is removed only by tears and repentance. Neither an angel nor an archangel can remove it; only the Lord himself, who alone can say, “I am with you” (Matt. XXVIII, 20), forgives us when we sin, provided that we bring repentance.

12. I advise, I beg, I urge, I admonish you, because it grieves me that you, who were an example of unheard-of piety, who held the summit of clemency, who did not permit individual guilty persons to perish, should not grieve that so many innocent people have perished. Even if you have acted most successfully in battle and are praiseworthy in other matters, yet the summit of your deeds has always been your piety. The devil envied you this, the thing you possessed above all. Conquer him while you still have the means by which you can conquer. Do not add another sin to your sin, so that you may seize what has harmed many who have seized it.

13. Certainly, although in all other matters I am indebted to your piety, to which I cannot be ungrateful—a piety that I preferred to that of many emperors and equated with that of one—I have no grounds for defiance toward you, but I do have grounds for fear. [Note: [Col. 1163C] Here blessed Ambrose tempers episcopal authority with dutiful indulgence. Elsewhere we have observed him acting more severely toward the younger Valentinian, when he threatened that the bishops would bar him from entering the church and reject his gifts. Indeed, he rebuked Theodosius himself more harshly when he suspected that the emperor wished to enter the church by force, as Paulinus recounts in his *Life*. But it was customary for holy bishops both to display indulgence toward the humble and repentant and to exercise severity against the obstinate. Thus Cyprian, Letter 55, in the older editions: “But if there are some who think that they can return to the Church not by prayers but by threats … let them know for certain that against such the Lord’s Church stands closed.”] I do not dare to offer the sacrifice if you wish to be present. Is what is not permitted in the case of the blood of one innocent person permitted in the case of many? I do not think so.

14. Finally, I write in my own hand what you alone should read. So may the Lord free me from all tribulations: for I perceived that the prohibition was issued to me openly, not by man or through man. For when I was anxious, [Note: [Col. 1163D] The ancient Fathers did not reject all dreams or nocturnal visions. Indeed, we have observed Ambrose repeatedly speaking of many apparitions as sent by God; and likewise Cyprian in several passages, Augustine in his books *On the City of God* and elsewhere, Gregory in Book IV of the *Dialogues* and in the *Homilies*, and many others whom we pass over.] on the very night when I was preparing to set out, you seemed indeed to have come to the church; but I was not permitted to offer the sacrifice. I pass over other matters, insofar as I was able to avoid them; but I endured them, as I think, out of love for you. May the Lord grant that everything proceed in peace. In many ways our God warns us—by heavenly signs, by the commands of the prophets; he even wishes us to understand through the visions of sinners—so that we may ask him to remove disturbances, preserve peace under your rule, and ensure that the faith and tranquility of the Church endure, since it benefits her that her emperors should be Christian and devout.

15. Certainly you wish to be approved by God. There is a proper time for everything, as it is written: “It is time,” he says, “to act, O Lord” (Eccles. III, 1); and: “It is the time of favor, O God” (Ps. CXVIII, 126). You will offer then, when you have received permission to sacrifice, when your offering is acceptable to God. [Col. 1163C] Would it not please me to enjoy the emperor’s favor, so that I might act according to your will, if the circumstances allowed it? And a simple prayer is also a sacrifice: this brings pardon, that brings offense; for the former contains humility, [Col. 1164A] the latter contempt. For it is God’s own declaration that he prefers his command to be obeyed rather than sacrifice to be offered. God cries this out; Moses announces it to the people; Paul proclaims it to the peoples. Do what you understand to be more important at the proper time. “I desire mercy rather than sacrifice,” he says (Matt. IX, 13). Why should those not be more Christian who condemn their own sin than those who think they should defend it? For “the just man is an accuser of himself at the beginning of his speech” (Prov. XVIII, 17). Whoever accuses himself when he has sinned is just, not the one who praises himself.

16. Would that, Emperor, I had trusted myself sooner rather than trusting your customary conduct. I thought that you quickly forgive and quickly recall your decision, as you have often done; and you were forestalled, while I did not avoid what I ought not to have failed to guard against. But thanks be to the Lord, who wishes to chastise his servants lest he destroy them. This I share with the prophets, and you will share with the saints.

17. Would I not place Gratian’s father before my own eyes? [Note: [Col. 1163D] It may be questioned which Gratian is meant here. Certainly a very learned man recently wrote that from this passage of Ambrose, as well as from words of Gregory of Nyssa, he had discovered, besides Honorius and Arcadius, the sons of Theodosius, another pair of children about whom authors are almost entirely silent—namely, Gratian and Pulcheria. There is no dispute concerning Pulcheria, whom Baronius [Col. 1164C] and many others acknowledge; but it will not be so easy to pronounce concerning Gratian. For the passage of Gregory found near the end of his *Oration on the Funeral of Flaccilla*, in which that author persuades himself that Theodosius had four children—three males and one daughter—can conveniently be explained in this way: of the three children, Flaccilla left her husband two who were male, as suitable for the defense of the empire; while she herself retained only the daughter. As for what Ambrose says here about Gratian, it must not be understood of a true son begotten by blood and physical descent; for Ambrose repeatedly indicates that emperors advanced in age were accustomed to be called fathers of younger emperors, even when the latter were born of another father, and that younger emperors were called sons of those senior rulers. Thus, in Letter 17, no. 12, he calls Theodosius the father of Valentinian II; in Letter 24, no. 7, he reports that the tyrant Maximus complained that Valentinian had not come to him as a son to a father; and much more clearly, in Letter 53, no. 5, he calls the same Valentinian, although already dead, the son of Theodosius. From this one may infer how Theodosius can here be called Gratian’s father.] Your holy other children ought to receive pardon. I have placed that beloved name first; I have shown them affection alike. I love them, cherish them, and accompany them with my prayers. If you believe, follow; if, I say, you believe, acknowledge what I say; if you do not believe, pardon what I do, in which I place God first. May you, august Emperor, enjoy with your holy children the fullest blessedness and perpetual tranquility.

[Note: [Col. 1164D] Written around the year 392.]

## LETTER LII

He congratulates Tatianus that the cause which he feared to face in court together with his granddaughter has been removed, and urges him to make himself readily available for settlement.

[Note: [Col. 1164D] The Roman edition alone reads, ““the bishop to Titianus.”.” That man, Titianus or Tatianus—for we find him called both in the Theodosian Code and elsewhere—was a man of great merit and authority. He held the dignity of praetorian prefect under the emperor Theodosius, under whom his son Proclus or Proculus was also honored with the office of prefect of Constantinople. But when both fell under the hatred of Rufinus, the latter arranged for the father to be driven into exile and the son to suffer capital punishment, as Zosimus relates in Book IV.]

### AMBROSE TO TITIANUS

1. An innocent victory has come to you, so that you may enjoy the security of victory without the bitterness of a wish fulfilled. For Rufinus, having been made praetorian prefect from master of the offices during his consulship, has thereby begun to wield greater power, but can now do you no harm; he is prefect of another jurisdiction. [Note: [Col. 1165D] The later Paris editions read, “he began to have greater power.” The statement that Rufinus, from master of the offices, was made praetorian prefect during his consulship should be understood to mean that he was heaped with the highest offices of the empire. Bullengerus discusses the consuls in Book I of *On the Roman Emperors*, chapter 18; the master of the offices in Book I of *On the Roman Empire*, chapter 13; and the praetorian prefect in Book III, chapter 2. Yet all his numerous and high offices did not prevent him from paying the penalty for his crimes. On this matter see Book XI of Philostorgius and others.] How glad I am for him, as for a friend, because, enriched by honor, he has been relieved of envy; and for you, as for a son, because you have been freed from one whom you regarded as a harsh judge. Thus, if you settle the matter with your granddaughter, it will be an act of filial devotion, not of fear. [Note: [Col. 1165D] The Roman edition reads, “I rejoice with him,” and so forth.]

2. Therefore be more ready for a settlement, whose hope is stronger and whose outcome is more agreeable. Its hope is stronger because the father of your granddaughter, who had greatly flattered himself on account of that man’s judgment, now has nothing to hope for from him: he is occupied with other matters and has set aside his former concerns, or laid them down together with the office he then held. The other man considers the merits of his case, not a patron of his judgment. The outcome is more agreeable because the gratitude for the settlement will be assigned to you: you were able to disdain it, yet did not disdain it, looking to the affection of kinship rather than the goad of resentment. Farewell, and love us as a son, because we love you as parents.

[Note: [Col. 1165D] Some manuscripts, almost unanimously, read “your granddaughter.” What should be made of them? “He had greatly flattered himself,” and so forth. But the true reading is supplied by other editions.]

[Note: [Col. 1165D] Written in the year 392.]

## LETTER LIII

Explaining the reason for his silence, he mourns the death of Valentinian, chiefly because of his great devotion to God and his affection for Ambrose. Then, having announced that marble is available for his burial, he urges that the matter be expedited for the sake of Valentinian’s sisters.

### AMBROSE TO THE EMPEROR THEODOSIUS

1. Your clemency’s message broke my silence; for amid such sad circumstances I had resolved to do nothing better than, if possible, hide myself away. But because I could neither conceal myself in some retreat nor withdraw from the priesthood, I hid within myself, at least in silence.

2. I grieve, I confess, with bitter grief—not only because Valentinian Augustus died at an untimely age, but also [Note: [Col. 1165D] These words agree remarkably with what the same Ambrose says in the funeral oration for this very Valentinian, especially near the end of the speech. They also accord with what Theodoret writes in Book V, chapter 15, of his *History*, as well as with Suidas in the *Excerpta on the Lives of the Caesars*, where he discusses the younger Valentinian.] because, instructed in the faith and formed by your teaching, he had acquired such devotion toward our God and had become so deeply attached to me that he now loved the man whom he had previously persecuted, and regarded as a father the man whom he had previously rejected as an adversary. [Col. 1166A] I have not brought this up to recall an old injury, but as testimony to his conversion. The former disposition was alien to him; this one was his own, infused into him by you and held so firmly that it excluded his mother’s persuasion. He used to claim that he had been nourished by me; he longed for me as for a devoted father; and when some falsely announced my arrival, he impatiently awaited me. Indeed, even during those days of public mourning, [Note: [Col. 1166D] At that time Gaul was flourishing with bishops of outstanding holiness of life, such as Martin of Tours, Delphinus of Bordeaux, Victricius of Rouen, and others.] although he had within Gaul holy and eminent priests of the Lord, he thought it necessary to write so that he might be initiated by me into the sacraments of baptism. Though this was not reasonable, it nevertheless showed, in an affectionate way, his devotion toward me.

3. Shall I not, then, embrace him with my inmost breath and with the secret depths of my mind and heart? Shall I consider him dead to me? Rather, he is more dead to me. [Note: [Col. 1166D] All editions read “more alive”; all manuscripts read “more dead.” The latter makes no less sense, for the meaning is the same as if he had said: “All these things make me feel more keenly that he has been taken from me.”] What thanks I offered to the Lord because he had so turned toward me, so amended himself, as though he had assumed the character of a more mature age! What thanks I offered to your clemency because you had not only restored him to the kingdom, but also—and this is greater—had instructed him in the disciplines of your faith and devotion! Shall I not, then, mourn that he died suddenly, whole in years, before he could attain the grace of the sacraments he desired? You refreshed my spirit by deigning yourself to bear witness to my grief. You, Emperor, I regard as the judge of my affection, you as the interpreter of my mind.

4. But there will be no lack of occasions for weeping later. For now, concerning his burial, since your clemency has written that it should be arranged here [Note: [Col. 1166D] The edition reads “it must be arranged.” But “if he departed without baptism, I have now suppressed what I had learned” is found in the manuscripts; the editions differ, unless “I did not suppress” is intended.]—if he departed without baptism, I have now suppressed what I had learned—there is here a very beautiful porphyry basin, highly suitable for such a use; for Maximianus, the colleague of Diocletian, was buried in the same manner. There are very valuable porphyry slabs with which the cover may be clad, so that the imperial remains may be enclosed. [Note: [Col. 1166D] So read most manuscripts; but the edition and some manuscripts read, “with which the cover of the basin was clad.”]

5. This had been prepared, but your clemency’s rescript was awaited. Its receipt revived your holy daughters, the sisters of your son Valentinian, [Note: [Col. 1166D] Justa and Grata, the sisters of this Valentinian, persevered in virginity.] who are afflicted in grievous ways; and they were still more distressed because nothing had been written to them for so long. Hence they received no small consolation. Yet, while the remains remain unburied, they do not spare themselves at all; for they seem to themselves to be holding the daily funeral of their brother. And truly, since they are never without great weeping and profound grief, whenever they approach him they return bloodless. Provision will therefore be made both for them and for the beloved remains if the burial is expedited, lest they be entirely dissolved by the summer heat; for we have scarcely passed through the previous summer.

6. I preserve your command and commend you to the Lord. May the Lord love you, because you love the Lord’s servants.

[Note: [Col. 1167C] Written around the year 392.]

## LETTER LIV

He informs Eusebius that the offense against the apparitor has been forgiven, and that the cough of Faustinus has worsened again.

### AMBROSE TO EUSEBIUS

[Note: [Col. 1167C] The memory of Eusebius of Bologna is recorded in the Roman Martyrology on the sixth day before the Kalends of October. He is likewise mentioned in the Council of Aquileia, p. 801, where we noted that he did not appear to us to be the same person whom Ambrose praises at the beginning of *On the Institution of a Virgin*. But we believe that the man to whom this and the following letter are addressed is a different person, as stated in the note to *On the Institution of a Virgin*. Thus, the fact that some manuscripts and editions write “to Eusebius the bishop” in the heading is attributable to the error of those who made one person out of the two Eusebiuses. Certainly, in the following letter he is not greeted as a bishop, nor is he called “brother” at the end of either letter, which is how Ambrose usually addresses bishops.]

1. The apparitor of the prefecture, who incurred offense because of the services performed at Portus, is now sailing into port. [Note: [Col. 1167D] Bulengerus carefully explains what *apparitor*, *apparere*, and *apparitum* mean, how many kinds of officials bore this name, and which magistrates they formerly served, in Book VI of *On the Roman Empire*, chapter 17. He also relates several things about the apparitors of the praetorian prefect, one of whom was the man discussed here. Observe also how cleverly our Ambrose plays upon proverbs derived from “port”: he applies to the contractor responsible for repairing the ports the sayings “to sail into port” and “to strike against the port” or “to suffer shipwreck,” about which see Erasmus, *Adagia*, chiliad 1, centuria 1, adage 46, and chiliad 1, centuria 5, adage 76.] He arrived at an opportune time. For as soon as I received your letter, I saw the prefect and pleaded for him. He immediately forgave him and ordered the letter withdrawn which he had dictated concerning the confiscation of his property. If he had come later, no one would have shown more clearly that the difficult task of repairing the port was impossible than this man, who had suffered shipwreck there, unless he had had you as his pilot; otherwise he could not have escaped from there except naked.

[Note: [Col. 1167D] Some editions read, “as soon as he received … I ordered it to be withdrawn.” Neither reading is particularly apt.]

2. Little Faustinus is suffering from a cough. [Note: [Col. 1167D] “To the holy sister,” that is, to a consecrated virgin; this will be discussed in the following letter.] He came to the holy sister to be treated, and he came willingly, for he has discovered that it is better for his stomach to be treated. [Note: [Col. 1168C] All manuscripts read, ““and he considers [him] a physician;”];” but all editions have “he thinks me the physician.”] In fact, he considers me a physician as well and awaits luncheon. Thus he is treated here twice a day, and he had begun to recover beautifully. But while they are eager to make him abstain out of excessive affection, he has begun to cough more from his stomach; and he will continue to suffer unless he returns to his medicines. Farewell, and love us, because we love you.

[Note: [Col. 1168C] Written around the year 392.]

## LETTER LV

Mentioning that some of Eusebius’s offspring have remained with him and some have gone to Eusebius, he adorns the two Faustini with blessings adapted to the family of Noah; and, in greeting Valentinian, applies to him the figures of Canaan and Nimrod.

### AMBROSE TO EUSEBIUS

[Note: [Col. 1168C] There is no doubt that this Eusebius is precisely the man to whom the preceding letter is addressed—the father of one Faustinus and the grandfather of the other, who was reported to be suffering from a cough. Nor will anyone doubt that both are designated here. Yet Father Nannius was considerably mistaken when he interpreted Ambrose’s “pledge” as though our Ambrose himself, together with another Ambrose—namely, his father—were intended. It is certain, however, that the reference is only to the boy Ambrose and the virgin Ambrosia, for whose sake the book *On the Institution of a Virgin* was published. He is no less mistaken when he understands the following sentence as though the holy man meant his own father Ambrose by “in the father,” and his younger brother Parthenius by “in the younger son.” But who would dream that this Eusebius was our Ambrose’s grandfather? These are trifles and mere nonsense.]
