1. Both Faustini have been restored to you; for us, both Ambrosi have remained as pledges. You yourself possess what is foremost in the father and what is most delightful in the younger son, because you hold the summit of virtue and display the grace of humility; we possess what lies between the father and the younger son. With you is the highest dignity of the whole household and the unbroken succession of the name. [Note: [Col. 1168D] The Codex Vindobonensis reads “and the perpetuation of the name”; the Roman edition, “and for the perpetuity of the name.” The other manuscripts and editions read as in the text.] With us is modest mediocrity, which hangs upon the highest and rests upon the later one. With you, therefore, lies the repose of both of us; when this repose is shared with us, it wipes away all anxiety from our minds. With you is the man who, through his character, deeds, and such offspring, has found favor with our Lord. With you is the man who, amid the storms of this world, nourished a spiritual dove—understand Ambrosia, as we explained in the note to *On the Institution of a Virgin*—so that it might bring him the fruits of peace (Gen. VIII, 11 ff.), anointed with the olive of integrity. With you is the man who built an altar to God, whom God blessed together with his sons, saying: “Increase and multiply” (Gen. IX, 9), and with whom he established a covenant of peace, so that it might be for him and his sons unto an everlasting generation.

2. You therefore possess an heir of divine blessing, a sharer in grace, [Note: [Col. 1168D] So read the old edition and several manuscripts; but the Roman edition, with some other manuscripts, reads “a prince of righteousness.”] a participant in righteousness. But see, I beg you, that this Noah of ours, a farmer and good planter of a fruitful vineyard, once he has been intoxicated with the cup of your love and favor, does not, like one drunk with wine, give himself over too long to rest. And if he should happen to fall asleep, may the longing for our Shem awaken him.

3. There is also there a younger Japheth among the brothers (Gen. IX, 23), who, out of reverent devotion, clothes his father—the father sees him even while asleep and never releases him from his heart, but always holds him in his eyes and embrace—and, when he awakens, understands what his younger son has done for him. Japheth is called *latitudo* in Latin, “breadth,” because grace is spread upon his lips and in his character. Therefore the Lord blessed him, because he, [Note: [Col. 1169C] The old edition reads “like a good man”; the Roman edition adds “the crab,” perhaps because the text below says “returning backward,” which suits a crab or *cancer*. The true reading, however, is found in the manuscripts: “as though returning to Bologna”; some have “Bologna,” less correctly, since the passage concerns the boy Faustinus, who returned to Bologna together with his father. Immediately afterward the same Roman edition reads *latificet* (“make broad”) instead of *laetificet* (“make joyful”); this would not be objectionable if even one manuscript supported it.] as though returning backward to Bologna, covered his father with the pious garment of charity (Gen. IX, 26) and paid honor to devotion. Of him the father also says: “May God make Japheth joyful in the tents of Shem” (ibid., 27). Hence, in the enumeration of the generations (Gen. X, 1 ff.), he is preferred to his elder brother, yet is substituted for him in the blessing: he is preferred because of the honor of his name, but substituted because of the precedence of elder age and the honor due to nature.

4. Shem, however, is called *nomen* in Latin, “name.” And rightly this Ambrose of ours is a good name, in whose tents [Note: [Col. 1169D] Thus the Roman edition, together with many more manuscripts; the old edition, with one or two manuscripts, reads “may Japheth rejoice.”] Japheth is enlarged, because “a good name is better than many riches” (Prov. XXII, 1). Let this man, then, also be blessed, and let his grace be greater than gold and silver; let the seed of Abraham be his portion; [Note: [Col. 1169D] The old edition and a few manuscripts read “let them be in blessing”; the Roman edition reads “let every person be blessed”; a large number of manuscripts read as in the text.] let every blessing rest upon the descendants and the whole household of the just man. But let no one be accursed: let all be blessed, for blessed is the fruit of Sarah.

5. The Ambrosi greet you; the sweetest Parthenius greets you; Valentinian greets you, prepared for humility—what is called *Chanaan* in Hebrew, as though “the boy of his brother,” [Note: [Col. 1169D] Some manuscripts read “to whom he also succeeded in name.”] to whom he also yielded in his own name. And therefore, like Nimrod, a giant bearing a twin name, an outstanding hunter upon the earth, of whom it is said: “Like Nimrod, a giant hunter before the Lord” (Gen. X, 9). For rustic in intelligence but strong in bodily power, he surpasses in strength those whom he cannot equal in intelligence, so that he may seem to carry the Comacine rocks with him and, “nearer to a bull in face,” to express their appearance in his countenance, [Note: [Col. 1169D] Some Paris editions read, “and the face of a bull in his own appearance.” The sense is clear, but this differs from the manuscripts and other editions. The true reading, which we adopt, alludes to Virgil, *Georgics* III:

> “And nearer to a bull in face, and all that is steep.”

Ambrose uses “face” for the outward appearance of the region and as an image of its roughness. Nannius conjectures that the Comacine rocks are that part of the Alps overlooking Como, to which Pompeius Strabo, the father of Pompey the Great, led a colony. But, he says, this is conjecture.] indignant at having been placed second and stripped of his paternal name, a metropolitan man made subject to one from Bologna; for he does not know the caresses of infancy, and he shook himself unharmed from the nurse’s lap. [Note: [Col. 1170C] All editions and most manuscripts read “into the sore”; some others read “unavenged,” which suits the context better.] Farewell, and love us, because we love you.

[Note: [Col. 1170C] Written in the year 392.]

## LETTER LVI

Ambrose is saddened that the Council of Capua was unable to bring the disputes between Evagrius and Flavian to an end. He censures Flavian because he presented petitions to the emperor, but does so in such a way that he does not wish this to injure Flavian’s rights. Finally, he advises Theophilus how to exercise the judgment entrusted to him by the Council of Capua, especially urging him to refer the matter to the Roman pontiff.

### AMBROSE TO THEOPHILUS

1. Evagrius has nothing with which to press his case, while Flavian has something to fear, and therefore avoids examination. Let the brothers pardon a justified grief, because the whole world is shaken on their account, yet they do not sympathize with our grief. [Note: [Col. 1170D] Some manuscripts read, “let them at least endure calmly to be touched.” Below, Nannius appropriately observed that *intentione* has the same meaning as *contentione* and obstinacy.] Let them at least calmly endure being reproached by those whom they see to have been harassed for so many years by their obstinacy. For between these two, who choose nothing that pertains to the peace of Christ, a grave discord has stood throughout the world.

2. To the shipwreck of this good peace the holy Synod of Capua had at last offered a harbor of tranquility: communion was to be granted throughout the East to all who confessed the Catholic faith, while the case of these two men was to be examined by you, with our brothers and fellow priests from Egypt sitting alongside you. We considered this to be a true judgment, since, by granting communion to neither party, it would incline toward neither through favoritism.

3. Since, then, we hoped from these most equitable decrees of the synod that a remedy had now been provided and an end brought to the discord, your holiness writes that our brother Flavian has again returned to the aid of petitions and the support of imperial rescripts. The labor of so many priests has therefore been poured out in vain. Once again we must return to the judgments of this age; once again to rescripts; once again elderly priests will be harassed; they will cross the seas; once again men weak in body will exchange their homeland for foreign soil; once again the most holy altars will be abandoned, so that we may set out for distant places; once again crowds of poor men, the bishops, who formerly did not find poverty burdensome, and are in need of external support, [Note: [Col. 1171B]] The later Paris editions read, “in need of eternal assistance.” Concerning the following sentence Nannius writes: “I am uncertain whether the text is quite correct, so that the meaning would be that, by collecting contributions from the poor, they seek travel provisions; for here nothing means travel food except provisions. What if, instead of *inopum*, one should read *inopem*, so that they are either compelled to lament their poverty or, if they do not lament it, to endure it? I would adopt this reading, unless *usurpare* is properly used when we seize what is not ours—which happens when priests take away the poor man’s food for their own use.” Costerius rightly corrected *gerere* to *gemere*.] will be compelled to lament their poverty, or at least to appropriate the food of the poor for their journey.

4. Meanwhile, Flavian alone, as he thinks, an outlaw, does not come when we all assemble. Creditor and debtor meet one another; these men cannot meet each other. Flavian alone, as he wishes, is excluded from the fellowship of the priesthood, and he does not present himself either to the imperial decrees or to the assembly of priests.

5. Yet even moved by this grief, we grant brother Evagrius the appearance of a good cause.. He seems to himself more defensible because Flavian avoids him, or because he regards himself as having an equal rival; yet each relies more on the defects of the other’s ordination than on his own. [Note: [Col. 1171C] So read all editions and some manuscripts; many others read “than relying on his own.” Neither seems entirely satisfactory to us. For who could be said to rely on his own defects? But although the manuscripts offer no support, the sense sufficiently indicates that the word *bonis* (“good qualities”), which follows immediately, has been omitted by scribes.] We nevertheless call them back to a better path, preferring that they be defended by their own merits rather than by another’s fault.

6. Since, then, you have written in your own letter that some means may be found by which the discord of the brothers can be removed, and since the holy Synod has entrusted the right of hearing the case to your unanimity and to our other fellow priests from Egypt, you must again summon our brother Flavian. If he persists in refusing to come, then, while preserving the decrees of the Council of Nicaea and also those of the Synod of Capua, and while maintaining the undisturbed peace of all, you must take such counsel that we do not seem to destroy what has been built: “For if I destroy what I built, I make myself a transgressor; and if I build again the things I destroyed” (Gal. II, 18). Let the grace of the peace granted among all therefore be preserved; nevertheless, the withdrawal of the other party must not be able to frustrate its effect.

7. We certainly think that the matter should be referred [Note: [Col. 1171C] Observe how ancient it is to refer major cases to the judgment of the Roman pontiff. On this subject consult the letters of Innocent I and Leo I, as well as the *Concordia* of Marca and others.] to our holy brother, the priest of the Roman Church, since we presume that you will judge matters which cannot displease him. The decision will thus be useful, and the security of peace and quiet will be assured, if your council establishes what brings no disagreement to our communion. Then we too, after receiving the series of your decrees, when we learn that what was done has undoubtedly been approved by the Roman Church, may joyfully obtain the fruit of such an examination. [Note: [Col. 1171C] Some Paris editions read “may obtain”; Cardinal Nicholas of Cusa reads “we approve”; the remaining editions and manuscripts read “may we obtain.”]

## LETTER CONCERNING THE CASE OF BONOSUS, TO BE JUDGED ACCORDING TO THE DECREE OF THE SYNOD OF CAPUA

In response to inquiries about what should be decided in the case of Bonosus, the author replies that the judgment no longer belongs to him but to those to whom it was entrusted by the assembly at Capua. He adds, however, that Bonosus was rightly censured concerning the sons of Mary, and briefly asserts that Mary had only one son.

1. “You sent us a letter concerning Bonosus the bishop, in which you wished to inquire of our opinion either out of a concern for truth or out of modesty. But since the judgment of the Council of Capua was such that judges were assigned from among Bonosus’s neighbors and his accusers—and especially Macedonians, who, together with the bishop of Thessalonica, were to inquire into his deeds or writings— [Note: [Col. 1173D] All editions and manuscripts read “whether they should investigate”; some others omit the word *vel* (“whether”). Longueval alone preserves the word *scriptis* (“from writings”). As for this Bonosus, we have discussed him at length in *On the Institution of a Virgin*, chapter 5, no. 35, and chapter 10, no. 65; it is enough here to have reminded the reader.] we have recognized that the form of judgment appropriate to us could not be applied. For if the Synod still existed in its entirety, we could rightly decide matters contained in the sequence of your writings. It is therefore your task, since you have accepted this judgment, to give sentence on everything and to allow neither the accusers nor the accused any opportunity to withdraw or evade it; for you have taken the place of the Synod, having been chosen by the Synod to conduct the examination.”

[Note: [Col. 1171D] In all editions this letter was prefaced with “Ambrose to Theophilus and Anysius”; the Roman edition adds “bishops.” In all the manuscripts, however, instead of these names appears “Concerning Bonosus the bishop.” The Carolinian and Thuanean manuscripts alone add “Ambrose to Theophilus.” The question therefore arises whether this letter is truly by Ambrose and to whom it was sent. First, despite the agreement of all the editions and two manuscripts, as mentioned above, the doctrine and arguments presented here have such complete affinity with certain undisputed writings of Ambrose that they seem to attest that this letter belongs to the holy bishop. Nevertheless, since the agreement of many more manuscripts is opposed to the authority of the editions, and since these letters mention “our brother Ambrose” in the words, “when Bonosus had sent to our brother Ambrose,” it is much more likely that they were written by someone else. Those who have attributed them to Ambrose therefore acted with good reason. Yet they disagree considerably among themselves about identifying the author. Holstenius, in his *Roman Collation*, attributes them to Siricius; but it remains uncertain whether he followed the authority of some manuscripts or Baronius’s conjecture, and whether he intended to add the title proper to Siricius. Jacob Almainus cites the same letters as if they came from Damasus, and Cajetan does not differ from him in his *Apology for the Book on the Comparative Authority of the Pope and the Council*. Chronology, however, proves both claims false, as does Nicholas of Cusa in Book II, chapter 18, of *On Catholic Concord*, where, after presenting many passages from the same letter, he adds: “That pope, I believe, was Saint Damasus”—whose name, he says above, was not found in his manuscript—“who wrote this reply, since, as is shown by the immediately following Letter 73, Damasus was pope at that time.” But the words which this author quotes there are taken from Letter 17, no. 10, which is known to have been written around the year 384; this does not support his conjecture at all. Nor, therefore, should Robert Cocus be heard, when in Book III, chapter 14, he assigns it to the same pontiff and records that it was so affirmed at the Council of Basel on the authority of Aeneas Sylvius, Book I. But what if someone wished to regard the letter in question as belonging to another of the metropolitans of Italy? What if it was written by Ambrose himself, but in the name of some synod held after Capua, over which he presided? For our part, amid such dense darkness, we define nothing. As for the persons to whom the same letter was addressed, although Theophilus is joined to Anysius in all editions, and appears alone in two manuscripts, since he is omitted in the others as well as by Cusa and Almainus, it is clear that the scribes prefixed his name for no other reason than that the preceding letter is addressed to Theophilus. Moreover, his diocese was so remote that he could not conveniently decide Bonosus’s case himself. Nor do we think that the letter was addressed to Anysius alone; otherwise, how could it write to him about the very man—[the text is incomplete here]—with the bishop of Thessalonica, and so forth?? Holstenius therefore did not make a bad inscription: “To the most beloved brothers Anysius and the other bishops established throughout Illyricum.” Cusa and Almainus, however, assert that the letter is a reply to writings sent by those to whom the judgment of Bonosus had been entrusted by the Council of Capua. Finally, all editions begin this letter, “I received your letter concerning Bonosus the bishop,” whereas all manuscripts begin it, “You sent concerning Bonosus”—namely, letters. More manuscripts read *direxit* (“he sent”), but this is incorrect.]

[”.”]

2. “Finally, when Bishop Bonosus, after your judgment, had sent to our brother Ambrose to consult his opinion, and had burst into and entered the Church from which he had been barred, he was told that nothing rash ought to be attempted, but that everything should be conducted moderately, patiently, and orderly, and that nothing should be attempted against your decision; that you should determine what seemed appropriate to justice, since the Synod had granted you this authority. Therefore, the first requirement is that those to whom the power of judging has been given should judge; for you, as we have written, decide in the place of the entire Synod. [Note: Some manuscripts read, “you discern in the place of the Synod.”] It is not fitting for us to judge as though by the authority of the Synod.

[Note: A few manuscripts have “patiently, in an orderly manner”; others, together with the printed editions, have the reading in the text. Here someone may perhaps wonder why Bonosus’s case was remitted by the Synod of Capua to the same judges by whom he had already been condemned. It is, however, credible that the earlier sentence was not what is called definitive. It may also have happened that the Synod added other judges to the first. But since the acts of that Synod have perished, nothing can be proposed except hesitantly. Nevertheless, Launoius discusses that council at length in volume I of his letter to Samboeuf; his discussion is well worth consulting.]

3. “Certainly, we cannot deny that the matter of Mary’s sons was rightly censured, and that your Holiness rightly recoiled from the claim that another birth proceeded from the same virginal womb from which Christ was born according to the flesh. For the Lord Jesus would not have chosen to be born through a virgin if He had judged her likely to be so incontinent that intercourse with human seed would defile that generative organ of the Lord’s body, that palace of the eternal King. Whoever asserts this asserts nothing other than the perfidy of the Jews, who say that He could not have been born of a Virgin. Now, if they receive authority for this from the priests, so that Mary may appear to have borne many children, they will strive with even greater zeal to overthrow the truth of the faith.

4. “And where is that which is written, when the Lord said to His mother concerning John the Evangelist, ‘Woman, behold your son’; and again to John concerning Mary, ‘Behold your mother’ (John 19:26–27)? What does this mean—that, while the Lord hung upon the cross and was taking away the sin of the world, He also pronounced judgment concerning His mother’s integrity? What else is meant except that perfidy should close its mouth and fall silent, lest it dare to assail the Lord’s mother with any insult? The same judge and defender of maternal modesty is therefore witness that she was betrothed only to Joseph, yet knew nothing of the rights of the marriage-bed through any marital intercourse (Matt. 1:18). For He would not have wished to separate her from her husband’s companionship if she were to receive children from Joseph.

5. “But if this is insufficient, the Evangelist added his testimony, saying that the Disciple ‘received her into his own’ (John 19:27). [Note: All the printed editions and a few manuscripts read *in suam*, understanding “as his mother”; but several older and better manuscripts have *in sua*, evidently from the Greek εἰς τὰ ἴδια, “into his own things,” as we have already seen Ambrose cite it more than once. It may be useful to compare carefully the arguments by which Mary’s perpetual virginity is defended here with those by which Ambrose defends the same doctrine in the cited passages of *On Virginity*. It will thus easily be seen that those who assigned both writings to the same author were not so greatly mistaken.] Did he therefore divorce her? Did he take her away and remove her from her husband? Therefore, whoever reads this in the Gospel, why does he stagger and toss about like a shipwrecked man?

6. “This, then, is the Son’s testament concerning His mother’s integrity; this is Mary’s rich inheritance of inviolate modesty; this is the completion and consummation of the whole matter. Finally, He said this and gave up His spirit (ibid., 30), bringing every mystery to its completion through a good ending of devotion.

7. “We have also read and reviewed everything, both what concerns Senecio, who was given to our brother and fellow bishop Bassus as a partner in governing the Church, and the other matters concerning which we await the standard of your judgment.”

[Note: Written toward the end of the year 392 or at the beginning of 393.]

## LETTER LVII

He explains to Eugenius why he did not await him at Milan. Then, after reviewing what had taken place under Valentinian and Theodosius on the occasion of Symmachus’s report, he freely reproves the same tyrant because, by granting expenditures to pagan temples, he had kept neither the fear of God nor the opinion others would form of him before his eyes. Setting against his transgression the example of the Hebrews, he says that this was the reason he did not write back to him; nevertheless, he says that in future he will use with him the same freedom that he had employed with other emperors.

**Ambrose, bishop, to the most merciful emperor Eugenius.**

1. [Note: Paulinus states in Ambrose’s Life that, upon hearing of Eugenius’s arrival, Ambrose withdrew to Bologna and there explained to him the reasons for his withdrawal; we also noted this in the *Admonition to the Exhortation of the Virgin*.] The fear of the Lord was the reason for my withdrawal. I have been accustomed to direct all my actions toward Him, insofar as I can, never to turn my mind away from Him, and never to value anyone’s favor more highly than Christ’s. For I do no one an injury if I prefer God to everyone; and, trusting in Him, I do not fear to tell you emperors what I think according to my understanding. Therefore, what I did not keep silent before other emperors, I shall not keep silent before you either, most merciful Emperor. And, to preserve the order of events, I shall briefly review what pertains to this matter.

2. When Symmachus, a man of the highest distinction, was prefect of the City, he had reported to Valentinian, the emperor of august memory, the younger prince, asking that he order the temples that had been taken away to be restored. He acted according to his office, in keeping with his zeal and devotion. Certainly, I too, as a bishop, had to recognize my own duty. I gave the emperors two petitions, in which I explained that a Christian could not restore the expenses of sacrifices, and that, although I had not been the one responsible when they were removed, I had become responsible for preventing their restoration; and then, because by giving them he himself would seem to be offering them to images rather than restoring them. What he himself had not taken away, he was not restoring as though he himself had taken it away; rather, he was distributing it at his own discretion for the expenses of superstition. Finally, if he had done so, either he would not come to the Church, or, if he came, he would either find no priest or find one resisting him in the Church. Nor could it be pleaded in his defense that he was a catechumen, since even catechumens are not permitted to supply expenses for idols.

[Note: The Roman edition has “two petitions to the emperor”; the Regius manuscript, in which we find this letter alone, has “two petitions to the emperors.” Perhaps this is because he arranged for copies of the same petitions to be delivered also to Theodosius, or because what was offered to one emperor was regarded as offered also to his colleagues, as we have observed elsewhere. These two petitions are nothing other than Letters 17 and 18, presented above.]

[Note: Another edition reads, “responsible for preventing them from being decreed, because he would be giving the prices of sacrifices”; the Regius manuscript has the reading in the text. Here he gathers together, as if into a single bundle, the arguments he used before Valentinian in Letter 17.]

3. My petitions were read in the council chamber. There were present the highly distinguished Bauto, a count and master of military rank, and Rumoridus, himself of the same dignity and devoted from his earliest childhood to the worship of the pagan peoples.

[Note: St. Ambrose does not clearly indicate here that Bauto was devoted to the worship of idols. Nevertheless, we noted in Letter 24, section 4, that the praises with which Zosimus commends him almost suggest that he was alien to Christian worship. If this is not true, then his exceptional virtue must be acknowledged—virtue approved by so great a detractor of Christians.]

Valentinian at that time heard my representation and did nothing except what the principle of our faith required. His companions also acquiesced in him.

4. Later I also plainly explained the matter to the most merciful emperor Theodosius, and did not hesitate to speak to his face. When the senate’s embassy had brought such a request before him—even though the entire senate had not demanded it—he finally yielded to my petition. Thus I did not approach him for several days, and he did not take offense, because I was not acting for my own advantage but for what benefited both him and my soul. I was not ashamed to speak in the presence of the King (Ps. 118:46).

[Note: Baronius conjectures that this occurred in 388, when Theodosius returned to Milan after Maximus had been defeated, and, after so great a victory, was more ready, as they themselves believed, to hear kindly the petitions of the pagans.]

5. Again, when an embassy was sent by the senate within Gaul to Valentinian, the emperor of august memory, it could extort nothing; and certainly I was absent and had written nothing to him at that time.

[Note: After Theodosius had returned to the East, they presented new petitions to Valentinian around the year 392, believing that they would finally overcome his youth; but their attempt was fruitless, as Ambrose testifies here and in the funeral oration for the same emperor. From this we recognize that these petitions were entirely different from those which Paulinus mistakenly conflates in Ambrose’s Life.]

6. But after your Clemency assumed the government of the empire, it later became known that those privileges had been granted to prominent men in public affairs who were devoted to pagan observance; and perhaps it might be said, August Emperor, that you yourself had not restored the temples but had given them as gifts to men who had deserved well of you. Yet you know that, for fear of God, one must act steadfastly, as is often done for the sake of freedom—not only by priests, but also by those who serve you in the army or are counted among the provincials. Under your rule envoys asked you to restore them to the temples, but you did not do so; later others made the same request, and you resisted; afterward you decided to give them to the very men who had made the request.

7. Although imperial power is great, consider, Emperor, how great God is. He sees everyone’s hearts, questions the inner conscience, knows everything before it happens, and knows the hidden things of your breast (Acts 1:24; Dan. 13:42). You do not allow others to deceive you, and do you wish to hide anything from God? [Note: The Regius manuscript reads, “Do you wish to hide anything from Him? Nothing entered your mind. If they were acting…” The same passage is nevertheless reported in this form by Paulinus, who transcribed several other passages from this letter almost word for word.] Did this not enter your mind? Although they were acting with such persistence, was it not your duty, Emperor, to resist all the more persistently out of reverence for the supreme, true, and living God, and to refuse what was an offense against the sacred law?

8. Who envies you because you gave to others what you wished to give? We are not examiners of your generosity, nor envious of other people’s advantages; we are interpreters of faith. How will you offer your gifts to Christ? Few will judge what you have done; everyone will judge what you intended. Whatever they do will be yours; whatever they do not do will be theirs. Although you are emperor, you ought to be more subject to God. How will Christ’s priests distribute your gifts?

9. A similar question arose in earlier times; yet the persecution itself yielded to the faith of the fathers, and paganism gave way. For when a quinquennial contest was being held in the city of Tyre, and the most wicked king Antiochus had come to watch it, Jason appointed officials for the sacred rites so that the Antiochenes might bring three hundred didrachmas of silver from Jerusalem and give them for the sacrifice of Hercules. [Note: Understand the Olympic games, once famous throughout Greece, which were called quinquennial because they were celebrated every fifth year. From Eusebius, Xiphilinus, and others, we learn that such games were established not only at Elis but elsewhere as well.] But the fathers did not give the money to the pagans. They sent faithful men and protested that it should not be spent on a sacrifice to the gods, since that was inappropriate, but should be used for other expenses. It was decreed that, although he had said the silver was sent for the sacrifice of Hercules, it ought indeed to be accepted for the purpose for which it had been sent; but because those who had brought it resisted, out of their zeal and devotion, so that it should benefit not the sacrifice but other necessities, the money was handed over for the construction of ships.

[Note: The Regius manuscript reads, “He appointed Antiochene spectators who were to bring drachmas from Jerusalem. And he sent it for the sacrifice…” Another reading is: “They protested that it should not be spent on the sacrifice … although he had said that it had been sent for the sacrifice of Hercules … that what had been sent ought to be used.”]

Although they had sent it under compulsion, they sent it not for the sacrifice but for other public expenses.

10. Finally, those who had brought it could certainly have kept silent; but they were injuring the faith because they knew where it was being taken. Therefore they sent men who feared God to act so that the money would be assigned not to the temple but to the expenses of the ships for which it had been sent. They entrusted the money to those who would plead the cause of the sacred law; the judge of the matter was the one who acquitted the conscience. If, when placed under another’s power, they took such precautions, there can be no doubt what you ought to have done, Emperor. You, whom no one compelled and whom no one held under his power, ought to have consulted a priest.

[Note: The Roman edition reads, “Finally, those who had brought it certainly could have kept silent”; the Regius manuscript reads, “Finally, they obtained it, and, as far as they could, they kept silent,” and so forth.]

11. Certainly, when I resisted at that time—even though I resisted alone—I did not wish to do so alone, nor did I alone advise it. Since, therefore, I am held accountable for my words both before God and before all people, I understood that I could neither do nor ought to do anything else except look to my own responsibility, because I could not prudently trust you. For a long time I suppressed and concealed my grief; I thought that nothing should be disclosed to anyone. Now I am not permitted to dissemble, and it was not free for me to remain silent. Therefore, even at the beginning of your reign, I did not write back when you wrote to me, because I foresaw that this would happen. Finally, when you demanded a letter and I did not write back myself, I said: “This is the reason: I think it must be wrested from him.”

12. Nevertheless, when the occasion arose for me to perform my duty on behalf of those who were concerned for themselves, I both wrote and pleaded, to show that in matters involving the fear of God I possessed a just sense of responsibility, and that I valued flattery less than my own soul; but that, in matters in which it is proper for you to be petitioned, I would also display the diligence owed to authority, just as it is written: “Honor to whom honor; tribute to whom tribute” (Rom. 13:7). For if I rendered honor to a private person from the depths of my heart, how could I fail to render it to an emperor? But you who wish honor to be rendered to you must permit us to render it to Him whom you wish to be acknowledged as the author of your empire.

[Note: Written around the year 393.]

## LETTER LVIII

He recounts the withdrawal of Paulinus and Therasia after distributing their possessions among the poor, as well as the future accusations of the pagans on that account, whose superstition and blindness he deplores. Then, proving by examples that nothing should be considered shameful for religion’s sake, he gives a mystical interpretation of David’s dancing and Elijah’s nakedness, and defends them.

**Ambrose to Bishop Sabinus.**

1. I have learned that Paulinus, second to none in the splendor of his lineage in the region of Aquitania, sold both his own property and his wife’s and devoted himself to this way of life for the sake of faith, so that he might give to the poor what he had converted into money. Having himself become poor from being rich, as though relieved of a heavy burden, he bids farewell to his household, his country, and even his family, so that he may serve God more zealously. He is said to have chosen the seclusion of the city of Nola, where, fleeing disturbance, he may spend his life.

[Note: Few doubt that Paulinus was born at Bordeaux in Aquitania, nor does Baronius himself oppose this. There was therefore no reason for the great Cardinal to suspect that the words of this passage had been transposed by copyists, and to arrange them thus: “Paulinus, second to none in the splendor of his lineage, sold his possessions in the region of Aquitania.” The integrity of the passage is demonstrated not only by the agreement of the manuscripts and editions but also by the meaning of the words themselves. Ambrose is not denying that the same Paulinus was descended from Roman ancestors on both his father’s and his mother’s side, since he belonged to the senatorial order through both lines; rather, he assigns him Aquitania as his native country. If, however, the passage were to be interpreted according to Baronius’s view, we would admit a hyperbaton in it, a figure by no means unusual in our author.]

2. His wife also comes very near to him in virtue and devotion and does not diverge from her husband’s purpose. Finally, after transferring her estates into the ownership of others, she follows her husband and, content with her husband’s small plot of land there, consoles herself with the riches of religion and charity.

[Note: The Roman edition, together with a few manuscripts, reads, “she consoles herself with the riches of religion and simplicity”; the old edition, together with the remaining codices, has the reading in the text, except that in place of *charitatis* the Longobard manuscript has *castitatis*, “chastity.” By “plot of land” the holy Doctor indicates some small estate scarcely sufficient to support Paulinus and his wife.]

[Note: Paulinus testifies in poem 32 that a son born to him in Spain died on the eighth day and was buried at Complutum in the basilica of the Martyrs.]

They have no offspring, and therefore the hoped-for posterity of their merits is lacking.

3. When the leading men hear this, what will they say? “A man from that family, that lineage, and that character, endowed with such eloquence, has withdrawn from the senate; the succession of a noble family has been cut off. This cannot be endured.” And while they themselves shave their heads and eyebrows whenever they undertake the rites of Isis, if perhaps a Christian man, more devoted to the most holy religion, changes his clothing, they call it an outrageous deed.

[Note: The worship of Isis—called Io by some and Ceres by others—was once celebrated in Egypt, especially at Alexandria. When her rites were transferred from there to Rome, they were eventually expelled from the City, because of the disgracefulness of the worship and ceremonies, during the consulship of Piso and Gabinius; later they were restored, as we learn from Tertullian, *Apology* 6. They shaved not only the hair of the head and eyebrows but also the hair of the entire body, to show their grief at the death of Osiris, Isis’s husband. This was one reason why Christian emperors prohibited women from being shaved bald through many laws. More concerning Isis may be found in Diodorus Siculus, book I; Apuleius, *Milesian Tales*, final chapter; Plutarch, *On Isis and Osiris*; and others.]

4. I grieve indeed that there is such scrupulous observance in falsehood and such negligence in truth, so that most people are ashamed to appear more devoted to the most holy religion, without considering the words of Him who says: “Whoever is ashamed of me before men, I also will be ashamed of him before my Father who is in heaven” (Mark 8:38).

[Note: “Here he calls an idol or the worship of an idol ‘falsehood,’ using ecclesiastical language; elsewhere they call it ‘vanity.’ See 1 Kings 16:26, ‘provoking God by their vanities’; Psalm 4: ‘Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?’; Jeremiah 8: ‘Why have they provoked me to anger with their carved images and vanities.’” So Nannius.]

But Moses was not ashamed. Though he had been adopted into the royal household, he considered the reproach of Christ preferable to the treasures of Egypt. David was not ashamed, for he danced before the Ark of the Testimony in the sight of all the people (2 Sam. 6:20). Isaiah was not ashamed, for he went naked and barefoot among the peoples, proclaiming heavenly oracles (Isa. 20:2).

5. What is as deformed a spectacle as contorting one’s gestures like an actor and softening one’s limbs in a feminine manner? Wanton dancing is the companion of pleasure and the sport of luxury. What of the words he himself sang: “All nations, clap your hands” (Ps. 46:2)? If we consider bodily things, we suppose that he clapped his hands as though mingling with women’s dances and applauding with a shameful sound. It is also said to Ezekiel: “Clap your hand and stamp your foot” (Ezek. 6:11).

6. Yet what is shameful when done according to bodily appearance is worthy of reverence when contemplated in the light of the most holy religion, so that those who criticize these things may themselves lead their souls into the snares of criticism. Michal, for example, criticized David as he danced and said to him: “How glorious was the king of Israel today, when he uncovered himself today before the eyes of his maidservants!” David answered her: “Before the Lord I will play, who chose me instead of your father and instead of all his house, to appoint me ruler over the people of the Lord, over Israel. I will play before the Lord, and I will humble myself still further, and I will be contemptible in my own eyes; and with the maidservants whom you mentioned, with them I shall be honored” (2 Sam. 6:20ff.).

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “These things must be revealed.”]

7. David therefore was not ashamed of women’s opinions, nor did he blush to endure reproaches among women in the service of religion. For he was playing before the Lord, his master; and he pleased Him all the more because he humbled himself before God in such a way that he placed royal majesty second and offered God the service of a lowly servant. Finally, the woman who criticized such dancing was condemned to sterility and bore no royal offspring, lest she produce the proud; and, what is true, she obtained no succession of descendants or of merits.

8. If anyone still doubts, let him accept the testimony of the Gospel. The Son of God said: “We sang to you, and you did not dance” (Matt. 11:17). The Jews, therefore, who did not dance and did not know how to clap their hands, were abandoned; the nations, who gave God spiritual applause, were admitted. For “the fool folds his hands together and consumes his own flesh” (Eccles. 4:5)—that is, he entangles himself in bodily affairs and consumes his own flesh like an overwhelming death, and therefore will not find eternal life. But the wise man raises up his works so that they may shine before his Father who is in heaven (Matt. 5:16); he does not consume but raises his own flesh even to the grace of the resurrection. This is the glorious dance of the wise man, which David danced; and therefore, through the loftiness of spiritual dancing, he ascended as far as the seat of Christ, so that he might see and hear the Lord saying to his Lord: “Sit at my right hand” (Ps. 102:1).

9. Therefore, if you judge that this interpretation of dancing has not fallen absurdly upon us, do not yet shrink from the labor of reading (Isa. 20:2), but review with me also what you know well concerning Isaiah: that he was stripped naked in the sight of the peoples who came to meet him, not disgracefully but most gloriously, since he was proclaiming the Lord’s oracles with his own mouth.

[Note: A few manuscripts read, “that he sang to us,” which is less apt.]

10. But perhaps someone may say: “Then it was not shameful for a man to go completely naked among the peoples, when both men and women came out to meet him? Did not the sight itself offend the eyes of everyone, especially of the women? Do we not ourselves usually shrink from looking upon naked people? For this very reason the genitals of human beings are covered with clothing, lest an unsightly sight strike and wound the gaze and vision of those looking.”

[Note: All the editions and a few manuscripts read, “that he went entirely naked.”]

11. I agree as well. But consider what the action signifies and what such an appearance represents: that the boys and virgins of the Jews would walk naked when led into captivity. “As my servant Isaiah,” he says, “goes naked and barefoot” (ibid., 3). He could indeed have expressed this in words, but he preferred to intensify it through an example, so that the appearance itself might inspire greater horror, and so that they might fear for themselves what they recoiled from in the prophet’s body. Where, then, is the greater horror of shame: in the prophet’s body, or in the sin of the faithless, which brought upon them such a calamity of captivity as a consequence of their merits?

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “but preferred to heap it up through an example.”]

[Note: “Appearance,” says Nannius, means the sight and vision of the thing itself, from the ancient verb *specere*, “to see.”]

12. What if there was no disgrace in the prophet’s body? He was not intent upon bodily things but upon spiritual ones. For, in the ecstasy of his mind, he does not say, “I shall hear what I will speak,” but “what God will speak in me” (Ps. 84:9). Nor does he consider whether he is naked or clothed. Adam, for example, was naked before sin (Gen. 2:25), but he did not know that he was naked because he was clothed with virtues. After he committed sin, however, he saw that he was naked and covered himself. Noah was naked (Gen. 9:21), but he was not ashamed because he was full of joy and spiritual gladness. Finally, the one who mocked him as naked remained subject to perpetual reproach for his shame. Joseph, on the other hand, lest he be shamefully stripped, left his garment behind and fled naked (Gen. 39:12). Who, then, was shameful—the woman who held another’s garment, or the man who removed his own?

13. But so that it may be clearer that the prophets do not look at themselves or at the things near their feet, but at heavenly things: Stephen was being stoned, yet he saw the heavens opened and Jesus standing at the right hand of God (Acts 7:55). Therefore he did not feel the blows of the stones and did not consider the wounds of his body; his eyes were fixed upon Christ, and he clung to Him. Thus Isaiah also did not see himself naked but offered himself as an instrument of the divine voice (Isa. 20:2), so that he might bring forth what God was speaking through him.

14. But suppose he did see himself: could he fail to do what he was commanded? Could he consider shameful what God ordered? Sarah was charged with unbelief because she laughed (Gen. 18:2); Abraham was praised because he did not hesitate at the word of God, and he received the greatest reward because, at God’s command, he believed that even parricide could be carried out piously (Gen. 15).

[Note: That is, as Nannius observes, the slaughter of his son; for every killing of a relative is called parricide, and especially killing those who have earned the title “father of their country.”]

15. What modesty, then, would there have been for the prophet when one thing was being enacted and another signified? The Jews, abandoned by the Lord God because of their crimes, had begun to be conquered by their enemies. They wanted to turn to the Egyptians so that they might protect them against the Assyrians, although, if they had taken good counsel, they ought rather to have returned to the faith. The angry Lord signifies that they were entertaining a vain hope: they thought that an offense against the Lord could be relieved by a greater sin, even though the very people in whose aid the Jewish nation trusted would themselves be conquered. This is the historical meaning.

16. The figurative meaning is this: one who trusts in the Egyptians is a person devoted to luxuries and enslaved to wantonness. No one gives himself over to luxury unless he has departed from the commandments of the true God. Once someone begins to indulge in luxury, he begins to deviate from the true faith. Thus he commits two greatest crimes: the disgraces of the flesh and the sacrileges of the mind. Whoever does not follow the Lord his God stuffs himself with luxury and lust, with the body’s deadly passions. Whoever stuffs and plunges himself into such mire incurs the snares of perfidy. For “the people sat down to eat and drink” (Exod. 32:6), and demanded gods to be made for them.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “and plunges himself into the mire”; another reads, “and plunges himself into pleasures.”]

Thus the Lord teaches that whoever gives his soul over to these two kinds of wrongdoing is stripped of his garment—not a woolen garment but the garment of living virtue, whose covering is not temporal but eternal. Farewell, and love us, because we love you.

[Note: Written around the year 393.]

## LETTER LIX

Upon hearing that the presbyter James had withdrawn from Persia to Campania, he praises the tranquillity of that region and contrasts it with the disturbances by which Milan was being shaken.

**Ambrose to Bishop Severus.**

[Note: The name of Severus, bishop of Naples, is entered in the register of the saints on the day before the Kalends of May. Symmachus, although a pagan, also mentions him with great honor in book VI, Letter 51. After Baronius, Ughellus in volume VI of *Italia Sacra*, and the Bollandists on the date mentioned, identified this man as the recipient of Ambrose’s letter; there they published the life of that holy bishop.]

1. Our brother and fellow presbyter James, having departed from the remotest part of Persia, has chosen the shores of Campania for his rest and your pleasant surroundings. You see in what regions he has presumed that security could be available to him, as though this place were free from the storms of the world, where, after long labors, he might spend the remainder of his life.

[Note: It is unclear whether these words refer to some shore of the Persian Gulf itself or to a more distant region of Persia.]

[Note: Most manuscripts read, “as though free from the emptiness of this world.”]

2. For the remoteness of your shore pours tranquillity into the senses, not only because it is removed from dangers but also from every disturbance; it leads minds away from terrifying and savage storms of cares to honorable rest. Thus that common saying concerning the holy Church seems especially suited and applicable to you, which David says: “He founded it upon the seas and prepared it upon the rivers” (Ps. 23:2). For a mind free from barbarian incursions and the bitterness of battles is available for prayer, devoted to God, concerned with the things of the Lord, and cherishes what belongs to peace and tranquillity.

3. We, however, exposed to barbarian movements and the storms of war, are caught in the midst of the strait of every affliction, and for these labors and dangers we gather still heavier dangers for the life to come. Hence that prophetic saying seems to be sung concerning us: “Because of the labors I saw the tents of the Ethiopians” (Hab. 3:7).

[Note: Baronius, followed in this by Ughellus and other recent writers, as well as by the continuators of the Bollandists, maintains that this passage refers to the war of the tyrant Maximus. On the contrary, the author of the vernacular Life of Ambrose argues that the same words should be referred to Eugenius’s arrival in Italy. We have discussed the matter sufficiently in the *Admonition*.]

4. For in the darkness of this world, by which the truth of future perfection is overshadowed, I have now completed my fifty-third year, situated in this body in which we have long endured such heavy groans. How could we not be encamped and dwelling in the tents of the Ethiopians, together with the inhabitants of Midian? Because of the consciousness of their dark deed, they even fear to be judged by mortal man (Ps. 119:5). “The spiritual person judges all things, but he himself is judged by no one” (1 Cor. 2:15). Farewell, brother, and love us, as you do, because we love you.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “when I have already extended [my life] to the year …”]

[Note: The Roman edition reads, “with the tents of Kedar.”]

[Note: Written around the year 393.]

## LETTER LX

He deters Paternus, who is considering giving his granddaughter through his daughter in marriage to his son, from his intention by considering the very names involved. He denies that this conforms to divine law, as well as to filial piety and the constitutions of the Caesars; then, after answering certain objections, he confirms that such a marriage is inexpedient.

**Ambrose to Paternus.**
1. I have read the greeting of my like-minded Paternus, [Note: [Col. 1183C] A good many manuscripts read “consolation,” which is not sufficiently correct. Nannius explains the purpose of this letter as follows: “Formerly it was permitted for a paternal uncle to marry his brother’s daughter, as is clear from fragments of Ulpian, whose words are these: ‘Among collateral relations, formerly marriages could not be contracted down to the fourth degree; now, however, it is permitted to marry within the third degree, provided that it is a brother’s daughter, not also a sister’s daughter, or a paternal aunt, or a maternal aunt, although she is in the same degree. The first among the Romans to use this kind of marriage was Claudius Caesar, who married Agrippina, his brother’s daughter. Paternus now considered that the same right applied in an equal degree, and asked whether what was permitted to a paternal uncle was also permitted to a maternal uncle: if marriage with a brother’s daughter was not incestuous, it seemed that marriage with a sister’s daughter should not be incestuous either. Saint Ambrose refutes this in the present letter.’ Thus far Nannius. But there is nothing in the whole letter from which it can be inferred that this was the cause of Paternus’s doubt. On the contrary, the entire sequence of argument makes clear that our Doctor regarded the marriage of a paternal uncle with his brother’s daughter as no less unlawful than that of a maternal uncle with his sister’s daughter.”] but by no means a paternal consultation: you wish to join your son in marriage to your niece by your daughter—but this is worthy neither of a grandfather nor of a father. Therefore consider what you have consulted about; for whatever we intend to do, we must first ask what name belongs to the deed, and then assess whether it deserves praise or blame.

For example, intercourse with a woman is pleasurable to some, [Note: [Col. 1183D] Several Paris editions read “even those skilled in medicine,” but this is incorrect; among the Greeks, medical apprentices themselves are called *medici*, as we have observed elsewhere.] and even physicians’ apprentices regard it as beneficial to the body. But one must consider whether she is a wife or a stranger, and then whether she is married or unmarried. If someone has intercourse with a woman betrothed and given to him, he calls it marriage; [Note: [Col. 1183D] The Roman edition alone reads “is free from marriage”; but there is no reason to depart from the other editions and all the manuscripts.] whoever violates the modesty of another commits adultery, a name whose mere utterance usually restrains the boldness of attempting it (27, q. 2, c. *Quis desponsata*). To strike an enemy is victory; to strike a guilty man is justice; to strike an innocent man is homicide. If anyone considers this attentively, he withdraws his hand. Therefore, you too, I ask, reconsider with yourself what you are proposing.

2. You wish to arrange a marriage between our children. I ask whether those to be joined are equals or unequal. But, unless I am mistaken, they are usually called “matched.” Whoever yokes oxen to the plough or horses to the chariot chooses equals, so that their age corresponds and their appearance, neither their nature differs nor their dissimilarity disfigures them. [Note: [Col. 1184C] Several manuscripts read “neither separates nor discolors.” Nannius not unreasonably observes that Ambrose is alluding to Ovid:

> How badly unequal bullocks come to the plough,

> so the younger wife is oppressed by a great husband.]

You are preparing to join your son to your niece by your daughter—that is, to have him marry his sister’s daughter, although he was born of a different mother from the one who bore his mother-in-law. Ask what sanctity lies in the names: this man is her maternal uncle, and she is called his niece. [Note: [Col. 1184C] Casaubon observed in his notes on Spartianus, p. 6, no. 12, that Ambrose uses the word *neptis* in this letter both in its ancient sense of “daughter’s daughter” and in its more recent sense of “brother’s daughter,” a usage that eventually became the only one current among Italians and Gauls. We add that our bishop, while discouraging the proposed marriage by considering the names, seems to have imitated the tragedies of Sophocles and Seneca, in which Oedipus’s marriage to his mother Jocasta is shown to deserve execration by means of the terminology of kinship—terminology confused here in a similar way. Consult the final act of Sophocles’ *Oedipus Tyrannus* and the opening of Seneca’s *Thebaid*.]

Does not even the sound of the names deter you, when this man’s name evokes “grandfather,” while she applies to her maternal uncle the name that refers to a grandfather? What further confusion there is among the remaining terms! [Col. 1184B] You will both be called grandfather and father-in-law; she too will be called by different names, both niece and daughter-in-law. The brothers will borrow different titles, so that she will be her brother’s mother-in-law, and he her sister’s son-in-law. Let a niece marry her maternal uncle, and let the affection of unstained children be changed into seductive love.

3. You say that on this matter you await the judgment of your holy bishop. [Note: [Col. 1184D] All the editions read “I do not think that the judgment is awaited”; all the manuscripts, on the contrary, read as we have printed it.] I do not think so, nor do I believe it. For if that were the case, he himself would have thought it necessary to write. By not writing, he indicated that he considered the matter in no way doubtful. What could be doubtful, when divine law even forbids cousins—children of two brothers—to enter into marital union, although they are related in the fourth degree? Here, however, the relationship is of the third degree, which also appears to be excluded from marriage by civil law.

4. But first let us inquire into the ordinances of sacred law. In your letter you maintain that such a marriage is considered permitted by divine law because it is not forbidden. I, however, assert that it is forbidden; for since the prohibitions concerning cousins are less severe, I judge that this relationship, which is bound by a closer tie, is much more certainly prohibited. Whoever binds lesser things does not release greater ones; rather, he binds them.

5. If you think it is permitted because it is not expressly forbidden, you will not find it stated in the words of the Law that a father may not take his daughter as wife. Is it therefore lawful because it is not forbidden? Certainly not. It is forbidden by the law of nature; it is forbidden by the law written in the hearts of individuals; it is forbidden by the inviolable rule of piety and by the title of kinship. How many things of this kind will you find not prohibited by the law issued through Moses, and yet prohibited by a certain voice of nature!

[Col. 1185B] 6. There are many things which it is lawful to do but which are not expedient; “all things are lawful,” but not all things are expedient (1 Cor. 6:12); “all things are lawful,” but not all things build up. If the Apostle therefore recalls us even from things that do not build up, how can we think that something should be done which is both unlawful according to the pronouncement of the Law and does not build up, while it conflicts with the order of piety? And yet those very ancient things, which had been harsher, have been tempered through the Gospel of the Lord Jesus: “The old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new” (2 Cor. 5:17).

7. What is more solemn than the kiss between a maternal uncle and his niece—the kiss which he owes her as though she were his daughter and she owes him as though he were her parent? [Note: [Col. 1185C] Adrian Turnebus observes from Cicero that it was once the Roman custom for relatives to greet their female relatives with a kiss, unless any of them were notorious.] By contemplating such a marriage, you will make this innocent kiss of affection suspect, and you will deprive dear children of a most sacred bond.

[Col. 1185C] 8. But if divine laws are passed over, at least the commands of the emperors—through whom you received the highest honor—should not have been disregarded. [Note: [Col. 1185C] These words of Ambrose show that Paternus had been adorned with great dignities. Hence those who think that he was the same man to whom the law of Theodosius on mines, 14, was addressed under the title *comes sacrarum largitionum*, and to whom five letters of Symmachus in Book V are addressed, are not conjecturing unreasonably. The constitution of Theodosius referred to here has been lost; but it is mentioned in two laws of his sons. One is Arcadius’s law 3, *De incestis nuptiis*; the other, *Si nuptiae ex rescripto petantur*, was issued by Honorius. Others too mention the same prohibition: Libanius in his speech *On the Angariae*, edited by Godefroy; Augustine, *City of God*, Book XV, chapter 16; Paul the Deacon, Book XIII; and others.]

For the emperor Theodosius prohibited even cousins and first cousins from entering into marriage with one another, and imposed the severest punishment if anyone dared to violate the sacred bonds of brothers. Yet those persons are equal to one another in relationship; only because they are bound by the tie of kinship and the fellowship of brothers did he require them, in piety, to respect the fact that they had been born.

[Col. 1186A] 9. But you say that an exception was granted to someone. [Note: [Col. 1185D] This was evidently the objection raised from the law of Honorius cited above, whose words are: “except those whom he did not forbid to petition …” An example of this relaxation may be found in Symmachus, Book X, Letter 11, or 14 of Juretus’s appendix. See likewise Cassiodorus, Book VII of the *Variae*, Form 46.] Yet this does not prejudice the law; for what is established generally benefits only the person to whom the relaxation appears to have been granted, whereas a very different resentment applies to the rest. [Note: [Col. 1186C] Some Paris editions read “in the common fellowship”; the others, and all the manuscripts, read “in common.” Neither expression is satisfactory unless the negation is prefixed to the verb *statuitur*. Again, where all the editions read “a different injury,” we have restored from all the manuscripts “a different envy.”]

We read, nevertheless, that in the Old Testament someone called his wife his sister; but it is unheard-of that anyone should take his niece as wife and call her his spouse.

10. Now what you denied is especially remarkable: that your niece could enter into union with her maternal uncle, your son, because she is not joined to him by agnatic kinship. [Note: [Col. 1186C] All the editions read “by a closely related seed”; the manuscripts variously read “to the seed of a relative,” “by the seed of a relative,” and, in several others, “to closely related seed.” Immediately afterward the editions of Erasmus and those following him read “that she might be joined to him by the legitimate right of agnation, but by the title of cognation,” whereas Amerbach, together with all the manuscripts, gives the reading printed here.]

As though uterine brothers—that is, those born of the same mother but different fathers—could therefore enter into marriage with one another if they were of different sexes, since they too cannot possess the right of agnation but are joined to one another only by the title of cognation.

[Col. 1186B] 11. Therefore you ought to abandon that intention which, even if it were lawful, would not extend your family. For our son ought to give you grandchildren, and your dearest niece ought to give you great-grandchildren. Farewell, together with all your family.

[Note: [Col. 1186D] Written around the year 394.]

## LETTER LXI

Ambrose explains why he withdrew from Milan and soon returned there, and, after giving thanks to God for the assistance granted to Theodosius, promises to obey the emperor’s will. While warmly commending his piety, he asks him to exercise clemency.

[Note: [Col. 1186D] Thus the Regius manuscript; the Roman edition reads, “The bishop Ambrose to the most august emperor Theodosius.”]

### AMBROSE TO THE EMPEROR THEODOSIUS

1. Most blessed emperor, you thought—as I have learned from your august letter—that I was far away from the city of the Milanese because I believed that your affairs had been abandoned by God. But I was not so imprudent, nor so forgetful of your courage and merits, as to fail to presume that heavenly aid would attend your piety, by which you would rescue the Roman Empire from the savagery of a barbarian brigand and from the throne of an unworthy usurper.

2. [Note: [Col. 1186D] The Regius manuscript reads: “I hastened to return … I had thought that he should be avoided; I had learned that he had departed from Milan.”] I therefore hastened to return immediately after I learned that the man whom I had rightly thought should be avoided had departed. For I had not abandoned the Milanese Church, entrusted to me by the judgment of the Lord; [Col. 1187A] [Note: [Col. 1187C] He means Eugenius, who was approaching Milan after granting permission to restore the sacrilegious pagan ceremonies. On his arrival, see Letter 57, to Eugenius himself, and what we observed there from Paulinus in the *Life of Ambrose*.] I was avoiding the presence of one who had involved himself in sacrilege. I returned, therefore, around the Kalends of August, and from that day remained here. Here, Augustus, your letters concerning your clemency found me.

3. Thanks be to our Lord God, who answered your faith and piety and restored the form of ancient holiness. [Note: [Col. 1187D] The Roman edition reads, “restored ancient holiness.” Here Ambrose is referring to the wholly extraordinary miracles by which God marked Theodosius’s victory over the tyrant Eugenius. They will be discussed more fully in the following letter.] In our own time we saw what we marvel at when reading the Scriptures: such a presence of divine assistance in battle that no mountain peaks delayed your advance and no hostile weapons offered any impediment.

4. You think that for these things I ought to give thanks to our Lord God. I shall gladly do so, conscious of your merit. It is certain that an offering presented in your name is pleasing to God—and what evidence of devotion and faith this is! [Note: [Col. 1187D] Thus the Regius manuscript; the Roman edition reads, “and what an indication of devotion and faith it is … in commemoration of the victory,” which is less elegant.] Other emperors at the beginning of a victory order triumphal arches or other insignia of triumph to be prepared; your clemency prepares an offering to God and desires that an oblation and thanksgiving be celebrated before the Lord by priests.

5. Although I am unworthy and unequal to so great a duty and to the celebration of so many prayers, I shall nevertheless write what I did. I brought your pious letter with me to the altar, placed it upon the altar, and carried it in my hand when I offered the sacrifice, so that your faith might speak through my voice and the emperor’s letter might perform the office of a priestly offering.

6. Truly the Lord is favorable to the Roman Empire, since he has chosen such a ruler and father of rulers, whose courage and power, established at so great a height of imperial triumph, are supported by such humility that he has conquered emperors by courage and priests by humility. What should I hope for? What should I desire? [Note: [Col. 1187D] The Roman edition reads: “You have everything, and, to sum it up …”] You have everything. From what is yours, then, I shall take the sum of my prayers: you are pious, Emperor; you possess the greatest clemency.

7. Yet again and again I wish you an increase of piety, than which the Lord has given nothing more excellent, so that through your clemency the Church of God may rejoice not only in the peace and tranquility of the innocent but also in the acquittal of the guilty. [Note: [Col. 1187D] The latest Paris editions read, “in their absolution,” which does not make good sense. Below, where the Roman edition reads, very appropriately, “those who have not sinned before”—that is, those who had not previously rebelled with Maximus—the Regius manuscript has the no less satisfactory “those who have also sinned against you.” In that manuscript the letter ends with these words. Nevertheless, the ending found in the editions is not objectionable, provided that the word “Amen” is removed from there.] Above all, forgive those who have not sinned before. May the Lord preserve your clemency. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 1188C] Written toward the end of the year 394.]

## LETTER LXII

Ambrose excuses himself for not having written to Theodosius earlier. He announces that he is sending the deacon Felix to him and asks that the emperor accept his petitions on behalf of certain persons who have taken refuge in the sanctuary of the Church.

[Note: [Col. 1188C] Thus the Regius manuscript; the Roman edition reads, “To the most clement ruler and most blessed emperor, the august Theodosius, Ambrose the bishop.”]

### AMBROSE TO THE EMPEROR THEODOSIUS

1. Although I recently wrote to your august clemency, even twice, it was still not enough for me merely to return, as though in equal measure, the service of a letter, since I am so deeply indebted to the frequent benefits of your clemency that I cannot repay by any services what I owe, most blessed and most august Emperor.

2. Therefore, since the first opportunity had not to be neglected—an opportunity in which, through your chamberlain, I could give thanks to your clemency and present the duty of my greeting— [Col. 1188B] I had to ensure that the fact that I had not written earlier should not be thought to have resulted from excessive idleness rather than necessity. I therefore had to seek a reason by which I might offer your piety the due service of a greeting.

3. Rightly, then, I sent my son, the deacon Felix, [Note: [Col. 1188D] It is a common and quite probable opinion that this was the same Felix who was later appointed to govern the Church of Bologna.] to deliver my letter, both to represent me in the duty I owed you [Note: [Col. 1188D] The Roman edition reads, “to represent me and my remembrance of you.”] and to commend to you those who had fled for refuge to the Church, the mother of your piety, asking for mercy. I could not endure their tears without anticipating, through my supplications, the arrival of your clemency. [Note: [Col. 1188D] The Regius manuscript reads, “who would anticipate the arrival of your clemency through our entreaties.” But the reading of the editions is preferable.]

4. Great is what we ask, but we ask it of one to whom the Lord has granted things unheard-of and marvelous, of one whose clemency we know and whose piety we hold as a pledge. Therefore we confess that we expect more from you, since, just as you conquered by courage, so you must also conquer yourself by your piety. Your victory is judged to have been bestowed upon you, in the ancient manner and through ancient miracles, such as those granted to holy Moses, holy Joshua, Samuel, and David—not by human estimation but by an outpouring of heavenly grace. [Note: [Col. 1188D] The same manuscript reads, “is reckoned by an outpouring.” Paulinus relates that this victory over the tyrant Eugenius, reported by the emperor Theodosius, gave rise to these words of Ambrose, as was observed in the *Admonition*. Since we have noted something about the prodigies that assisted Theodosius’s cause in *Exposition on Psalm 36*, no. 25, we add nothing here.] Here we ask for an equal piety, by whose merit such a victory itself was sought.

[Note: [Col. 1188D] Written in the year 396.]

## LETTER LXIII

Ambrose laments that the Church of Vercelli has long been deprived of a bishop because of internal disputes. He praises the harmony by which Eusebius was once elected and urges that the same Church strive to have Christ standing in its midst. He then attacks Sarmatio and Barbatianus, who, having fled from a monastery, envied others the abstinence and virginity they themselves had abandoned. He adds that the world was restored through abstinence and that these heretics were worse than Epicurus himself; by their teaching, man is transformed into a brute and even cast below certain animals. The virtues mentioned are praised and proposed for observance. The qualities to be considered in choosing a bishop are set out, as is the danger of either choosing an unworthy man or refusing obedience to a worthy one. The election must be divine; the chosen man must be free from anger and outstanding in self-restraint. The excellence required in the Church of Vercelli is described, where Eusebius had joined monastic life to the clerical life. The praises of Eusebius and Dionysius and a comparison of clerical and monastic life follow. Afterward, splendid precepts of virtue are given to the people of Vercelli.

[Note: [Col. 1189C] This superscription seems contrary to Ambrose’s practice, and nowhere else do we find him using a similar one. We would readily attribute it to the boldness of scribes if it were not found in every manuscript. We therefore think it more likely that the holy bishop used it because he considered it appropriate to write in a pastoral manner to the Church entrusted to him.]

### AMBROSE, CALLED THE SERVANT OF CHRIST AND BISHOP, TO THE CHURCH OF VERCELLI AND TO THOSE WHO CALL UPON THE NAME OF OUR LORD JESUS CHRIST

May grace from God the Father and from his only-begotten Son be fulfilled in you in the Holy Spirit.

1. I am consumed with grief because the Church of the Lord that is among you still has no priest. [Note: [Col. 1189D] It was not the death of Eusebius, who had long since died, but that of Limenius—whom we have seen signing the acts of the Council of Aquileia together with Ambrose—that had left the see of Vercelli vacant at that time.] Alone now among all Liguria and Aemilia, [Col. 1189A] and among Venetia and the other neighboring regions of Italy, it lacks such an office. [Note: [Col. 1189D] Those who think from these words that this letter should be denied to Ambrose understand nothing. The reference is not to the city of Venice, which had not yet been built, but to the region of Venetia, which is known to have been familiar not only to much earlier writers but also to Ambrose himself, who mentions it in Letter 18, no. 21.] Other Churches used to seek such a bishop from it; and, what is more shameful, your dispute is attributed to me as an obstacle. [Col. 1189C] [Note: [Col. 1189D] As Nannius observes, “dispute” here means nothing other than contention—that is, the obstinacy of each side in its own opinion. This was charged against Ambrose because, by virtue of his metropolitan authority, he was obliged to quiet and settle it.] For since there are dissensions among you, how can we either decide anything, or you elect anyone, or anyone consent to undertake an office that is scarcely endured even among those who are united?

2. This is the institution of a confessor; this is the offspring of righteous fathers, who, when they saw and approved the holy Eusebius, whom they had never previously known, preferred him to their fellow citizens. [Note: [Col. 1190C] Ughellus states in Book IV of *Italia sacra* that this Eusebius was the first of the bishops of Vercelli whose names have come down to us. Ambrose does not say where he was from, but Jerome testifies that he was a Sardinian in these words: “Eusebius, a Sardinian by birth and, from a reader of the city of Rome, bishop of the Church of Vercelli, was exiled to Scythopolis and from there to Cappadocia by the emperor Constantius because of his confession of faith; under the emperor Julian he returned to his Church … he died while Valentinian and Valens were reigning.” Jerome places his death in the sixth year of those emperors in his *Chronicle*, which Baronius shows to have fallen in the year 371 of the era of salvation.] How much did it matter that he should be approved, and how much that he should be seen? Such a great man rightly emerged, whom the whole Church elected; rightly was he believed to have been chosen by divine judgment, whom all had requested. [Col. 1190A] [Note: [Col. 1190D] Here our saint appropriately distinguishes election from petition, evidently indicating that the former belonged to the clergy and the latter to the people, just as he clearly separated the two in Letter 15, no. 12, speaking of Saint Acholius: “Requested by the peoples of Macedonia, elected by the priests.”]

It is therefore fitting that you follow the example of your fathers, especially since, having been instructed by a holy confessor, you ought to be better than your fathers to the extent that a better teacher instructed and educated you. [Note: [Col. 1190D] The Gembloux manuscript reads, “a better author instructed.”] Give an outstanding example of your modesty and concord by agreeing together in requesting a priest.

3. For if, according to the Lord’s saying, “Whatever two of you agree upon on earth concerning anything they ask, it will be done for them by my Father who is in heaven; for where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them” (Matt. 18:20), how much more, where the assembly is complete in the name of the Lord and the petition of all agrees, should we have no doubt that the Lord Jesus will be there as the author of the will, the judge of the petition, and the director—or giver of grace—of the ordination!

4. Make yourselves therefore worthy to have Christ in your midst. For where there is peace, there is Christ, because Christ is peace (Eph. 2:14); where there is justice, there is Christ, because Christ is justice (1 Cor. 1:30). Let him be in your midst, so that you may see him; otherwise it may be said to you also: “There stands among you one whom you do not see” (John 1:26). The Jews did not see the one in whom they did not believe; we behold him through devotion and see him through faith.

5. Let him therefore stand in your midst, so that the heavens may be opened for you—those heavens that declare the glory of God—and so that you may do his will and perform his work (Ps. 18:2). For the one who sees Jesus has the heavens opened to him, as they were opened to Stephen when he said: “Behold, I see the heavens opened and Jesus standing at the right hand of God” (Acts 7:55). Jesus stood as an advocate; he stood as one concerned, to assist Stephen, his athlete, while he fought; he stood as one prepared to crown his martyr.

6. Let him stand for you also, so that you will not fear him sitting; for when he sits, he judges, as Daniel says: “Thrones were set, and the books were opened, and the Ancient of Days sat down” (Dan. 7:9). In the eighty-first Psalm it is written: “God stood in the assembly of the gods; but in the midst he judges among the gods” (Ps. 81:1). Sitting, therefore, he judges; standing, he judges among them. He judges the imperfect, but among the gods he judges. Let him stand for you as your defender, as the good shepherd, lest fierce wolves attack you.
