7. Our admonition turns toward this matter for good reason. For I hear that Sarmatio and Barbatianus have come to you—men who speak emptily and say that abstinence has no merit, that frugality has no merit, that virginity has no grace; that all are valued at the same price; and that those who discipline their flesh with fasts in order to make it subject to the mind are delirious. The Apostle Paul would never have done this or written to instruct others if he had thought it madness. He therefore boasts, saying: “I discipline my body and bring it into subjection, lest, after preaching to others, I myself should be found reprobate” (1 Cor. 9:27). Therefore those who do not discipline their bodies but wish to preach to others are themselves regarded as reprobates.

8. For what is more reprobate than what provokes luxury, corruption, and wantonness—than an incitement to lust, a lure of pleasure, fuel for lack of self-control, and the kindling of desire? What new school has sent these Epicureans among us? Not, as they themselves claim, a school of philosophers, but one of ignorant men who praise pleasure, encourage indulgence, and think chastity useful for nothing. “They were with us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2:20); nor should we be ashamed to say what the evangelist John says. But when they were placed here, they first fasted and remained disciplined within the monastery; there was no place for luxury, and freedom for frivolous disputation was forbidden.

9. These delicate men could not endure this. They went out; afterward, when they wished to return, they were not received. I had heard most of the things that I ought to guard against; I had warned them, but had accomplished nothing. [Note: [Col. 1191D] Thus the old edition and the manuscripts, except that some of the latter have *plerumque* (“for the most part”) instead of the Greek τὸ *pleraque* (“most things”); the old editions read *deberent* (“they ought”) instead of *deberem* (“I ought”), as does the Roman edition, which also reads *caveri* (“that precautions should be taken”). I had warned them, but accomplished nothing. These words indicate that Ambrose himself had charge of the monastery in which Sarmatio and Barbatianus had lived, although he had appointed a priest over it as well, as Augustine testifies in *On the Morals of the Catholic Church*, chapter 33. This should be compared with what Augustine records about the same asceterium in *Confessions*, Book VIII, chapter 6.] And so, boiling over, they began to spread such ideas that they became miserable inciters of every vice. They certainly lost the benefit of their fasting; they lost what they had gained by restraining themselves for a time. Now, with diabolical zeal, they envy the good works of others, whose fruit they themselves have forfeited.

10. What virgin could hear that there is no reward for purity and not groan? Let her not easily believe it—or, at any rate, let her not abandon her endeavors or turn aside the purpose of her mind. What widow, when she learns that widowhood bears no fruit, would prefer to keep faith with her marriage and remain in sorrow rather than entrust herself to happier prospects? What woman bound by the discipline of marriage, if she hears that chastity has no honor, could fail to be tempted into carelessness through weakness of body or mind? [Note: [Col. 1191D] All the editions and a few manuscripts read “when she has conceived”; other manuscripts more elegantly read “when she has discovered.” Below, the Regius manuscript reads “the faith toward a spouse … or through weakness of mind.”] Therefore the Church daily proclaims, in sacred readings and in the discourses of priests, the praise of modesty and the glory of purity.

11. The Apostle therefore says in vain: “I wrote to you in my letter not to associate with fornicators” (1 Cor. 5:9). And lest they perhaps say, “We are not speaking of all the fornicators of the world, but of one who has been baptized in Christ, who should no longer be regarded as a fornicator, whatever his life may be, being acceptable to God,” the Apostle added: “Not at all meaning the fornicators of this world”; and below: “If anyone bearing the name of brother is a fornicator, or greedy, or serves idols, or is a reviler, or a drunkard, or a robber, with such a one do not even take food. For what have I to do with judging those who are outside?” (1 Cor. 5:10–12). [Note: [Col. 1192D] The Roman edition reads, “if one who is called a brother is a fornicator.”] And to the Ephesians: “But fornication and every impurity and greed must not even be named among you, as is fitting for saints” (Eph. 5:3). He immediately adds: “For know this: no immoral or impure person, or greedy person—which is idolatry—has an inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God” (Eph. 5:5). [Note: [Col. 1192D] All the editions and some manuscripts read “who is an idolater”; a great many others read “which is idolatry.”]

It is clear that this is said of the baptized; for those who are baptized into the death of Christ receive the inheritance, and are buried with him so that they may rise with him (Rom. 6:3). Therefore they are heirs of God and coheirs of Christ: heirs of God because God’s grace is inscribed upon them; coheirs of Christ because they are renewed into his life; heirs also of Christ because through his death, as that of a testator, an inheritance is given to them. [Note: [Col. 1192D] The Roman edition reads “because it is transmitted”; the others, together with nearly all the manuscripts, read “because it is inscribed.”]

12. These people, therefore, ought to pay greater attention to themselves, since they have something they can lose, than those who possess nothing. [Note: [Col. 1192D] Thus the old edition and the majority of the better manuscripts; the Roman edition, with some others, reads “they ought to act with greater vigilance.”] They ought to exercise greater vigilance, to beware of the enticements of vice and the provocations of error, which arise especially from food and drink. In the end, “the people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play” (Exod. 32:6).

13. Even Epicurus himself, whom these men think they should follow rather than the Apostles, although he is an advocate of pleasure and denies that pleasure is the discoverer of evil, does not deny that certain things arise from pleasure from which evils are generated. Indeed, he does not regard the life of the luxurious as blameworthy if it is filled with delights, unless it is shaken by fear of pain or death. How far this is from the truth can also be recognized from the fact that he asserts that pleasure was principally created in man by God the creator, just as Philomarus, a follower of his sect, argues in his epitomes; and he cites the Stoics as authorities for this opinion. [Note: [Col. 1193D] There is remarkable variation in the spelling of this name. The old edition has *Philuminaris*, the Roman edition *Philomarus*, while the manuscripts have *Filominus*, with some reading *Filuminus*. Since no one among the Epicureans can be found with this name, we would not hesitate to believe that it is the same person whom Diogenes Laertius initially calls Philodemus, and whom Cicero also mentions in Book II of *On Ends*, though not without some variation: some editions and manuscripts have *Polydemus*, others *Philodamus*. Gassendi thinks he was that Philodemus of Gadara mentioned by Strabo in Book XVI.] [Note: [Col. 1193D] The old edition reads “he cites historians”; the Roman edition and all the manuscripts read “he cites the Stoics.”]

14. But divine Scripture refutes this, for it teaches that pleasure was infused into Adam and Eve through the serpent’s snares and enticements (Gen. III, 1 ff.). Indeed, if the serpent itself is pleasure, then the various slippery passions of pleasure are, as it were, infected with the poison of corruptions. It is therefore clear that Adam, deceived by the appetite for pleasure, fell away from God’s commandment and from the fruit of grace. How, then, can pleasure restore us to paradise, when it alone deprived us of paradise?

[Note: [Col. 1194C] Some manuscripts read partly “the pleasure infused and introduced into Eve,” and partly “that pleasure infused as Eve’s”; the others, and all printed editions, read as in the text. Below, where the editions and some manuscripts read “are the appetite of pleasure,” several manuscripts have “the appetite of pleasure is.” Therefore, by pleasure, etc.]

15. Hence also the Lord Jesus, wishing to make us stronger against the devil’s temptations, fasted in preparation for the struggle (Matt. IV, 2).

[Note: [Col. 1194D] Some manuscripts read, “to make us stronger, he fasted, about to contend.”]

Thus we might know that we cannot otherwise overcome the enticements of evil. Indeed, the devil first hurled the spearpoint of his temptations from pleasure, saying: “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become loaves” (ibid., 3). Therefore the Lord said: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God,” and, though he could have done so, he refused to make the stones into bread, teaching us by his saving command to devote ourselves more to the study of Scripture than to pleasure. And since these people deny that one ought to fast, let them explain why Christ fasted—unless it was so that his fasting might be an example for us. Indeed, later he taught that evil cannot easily be overcome except by our fasting, saying: “This kind of demon is not cast out except by prayer and fasting” (Matt. XVII, 20).

16. What else does Scripture mean when it teaches that Peter fasted, and that, while he was fasting and praying, the mystery concerning the baptism of the Gentiles was revealed to him (Acts X, 10), unless it wished to show that even the saints themselves become more excellent when they fast? Likewise, when Moses fasted, he received the Law (Exod. XXXIV, 28). And so, when Peter fasted, he was instructed in the grace of the New Testament. Daniel also, by the merit of fasting, closed the mouths of lions and saw the affairs of future times (Dan. XIV, 32; IX, 2 ff.). Or what salvation can there be for us unless we wash away our sins by fasting, since Scripture says: “Fasting and almsgiving deliver from sin” (Tob. XII, 8)?

[Note: [Col. 1194D] A Gembloux manuscript reads, “delivers from punishment.”]

17. Who, then, are these new teachers who exclude the merit of fasting? Is this not the voice of the Gentiles, saying: “Let us eat and drink”? The Apostle rightly mocks them, saying: “If I fought with beasts at Ephesus in human fashion, what advantage is it to me if the dead are not raised? Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die” (I Cor. XV, 32)—that is: “What benefit did my struggle unto death bring me, except that I might redeem my own man?”

[Note: [Col. 1194D] All editions and some manuscripts read “that I might redeem”; the remaining manuscripts read “that I might redeem him, who vainly ...” Again, where we, with some manuscripts and the Roman edition, read “the loss of the resurrection,” the old edition, with other manuscripts, prefers “the loss of redemption.”]

For he is redeemed in vain if there is no hope of resurrection. And therefore, with all hope of resurrection abandoned, “let us eat and drink”: let us not lose the enjoyment of present things, since we possess no expectation of future things. It belongs, then, to those who indulge in food and drink to hope for nothing after their death.

17. Finally, the Epicureans, advocates of pleasure, say that death is nothing to us: for what is dissolved is insensible; and what is insensible is nothing to us.

[Note: [Col. 1194D] This statement occurs in Epicurus’s letter to Menoeceus, and even more clearly in his Principal Doctrines; hence Diogenes Laertius reports it. As for this philosopher’s view concerning the mortality of the soul, Jerome, in Book II Against Jovinianus, and Augustine, in Book VI of the Confessions, chapter 16, as well as many others, testify to precisely what Ambrose says.]

[Col. 1194C] By this they show that they live only in body, not in mind; that they perform the function not of the soul but of the flesh alone; for they think that, when the soul and body are separated and dissolved, their entire life’s function perishes, the merits of virtue perish, and all the soul’s vigor perishes—that they wholly fail along with the body’s sensation, and that nothing of the soul remains, although the body itself is not immediately dissolved. The soul, then, is dissolved before the body, although according to their own opinion they ought to consider the flesh and bones that remain after death; while according to the true doctrine they ought not to deny the grace of resurrection.

18. The Apostle therefore rightly reproves them and warns us not to be led astray by such opinions, saying: “Do not be deceived: bad conversations corrupt good morals. Be sober righteously, and do not sin” (I Cor. XV, 33); for some have no knowledge of God. Sobriety, then, is good, because drunkenness is sin.

[Note: [Col. 1194D] Seven manuscripts read, “Be sober and righteous”; the others and all editions read, “Be sober righteously.” The former is better, since the Apostle’s text has ἐκνήψατε δικαίως, “be sober righteously.”]

19. What of the fact that Epicurus himself—the defender of pleasure, whom we mention so frequently in order either to prove that these people are disciples of the Gentiles and followers of the Epicurean sect, or to show that even that philosopher, whom the philosophers themselves exclude from their company as a patron of luxury, is more tolerable than they—what of the fact that he cries out, as Demarchus asserts, that drinking parties, banquets, children, sexual intercourse with women, an abundance of fish, and other such things prepared for the lavish use of a feast do not make life pleasant, but sober discussion?

[Note: [Col. 1195C] What Ambrose reports here from Demarchus is also found in the already cited letter to Menoeceus. Gassendi observes this in Book III of On the Life of Epicurus, where he says that Demarchus is mentioned nowhere else than by our Doctor. It is, however, exceedingly probable that this is none other than Hermarchus, a disciple of Epicurus who succeeded him in the sect and its discipline and published several books against Plato and the Platonists, as can be learned from Diogenes Laertius. Certainly Hermarchus and Demarchus do not differ so greatly that writers could not easily take one for the other.]

He even added that those who use the resources of a banquet moderately are those who do not seek them immoderately. Whoever willingly uses only juice and bread, or water, despises the banquets of delicacies, because many troubles arise from them. They also say elsewhere: “It is not immoderate feasting or drinking that produces the sweetness of pleasure, but a life of self-restraint.”

20. Since philosophy has rejected those people, does the Church not exclude these? Indeed, they frequently attack themselves with their own arguments, as bad causes do.

[Note: [Col. 1195D] Erasmus and the editions following him read, “because he has a bad case”; the Amerbach edition and all manuscripts read, “because bad cases have [this].” This is not inappropriate, for it means the same as “what happens in bad cases is customary,” and so forth.]

1028

For although their principal doctrine is that they consider no pleasure genuine except what is perceived through food and drink, yet, realizing that they could not pursue so reprehensible a definition without the greatest disgrace and could not avoid being abandoned by everyone, they wished to cloak it with a kind of plausible argumentation. Thus one of them said:

[Col. 1195C] “While we pursued pleasure through banquets and songs, we lost that pleasure which is poured into us through the perception of the Word, by which alone we can be saved.”

21. Do these people not appear to us unequal and discordant in this many-sided argument? Scripture condemns them so thoroughly that it did not overlook those whom the Apostle rebuked, as Luke says in the Acts of the Apostles, writing that book in historical style:

[Note: [Col. 1195D] Some manuscripts read, “lest the Apostle pass them by.” Below, where all editions and the great majority of manuscripts read “in historical style,” some have “in Stoic style.” This is incorrect, for Ambrose elsewhere observes that blessed Luke’s style is historical.]

“But some Epicurean and Stoic philosophers discussed with him, and some said: ‘What does this babbler wish to say?’ Others said: ‘He seems to be a proclaimer of new demons’” (Acts XVII, 18).

22. Yet the Apostle did not leave this group without the benefit of grace. For Dionysius the Areopagite also believed, together with Damaris his wife and many others.

[Note: [Col. 1195D] All editions and most manuscripts read thus, except the Roman edition, which has “with his wife”; some other manuscripts also read, instead of Damaris, partly “Damalis” and partly “Damale.” [Col. 1196C] Thus readily did scribes err in proper names. Ambrose makes Damaris the wife of Dionysius the Areopagite here and elsewhere.]

Thus those who believed made clear, by their example, that the gathering of the most learned and eloquent people had been defeated by a simple argument. What, then, do these people intend, who attempt to corrupt those whom the Apostle acquired and whom Christ redeemed with his blood?

[Note: [Col. 1196C] All editions read, “What is it that they assert?” whereas the manuscripts omit “what is it”; some, instead of “what they assert,” read “who assert.” Below, where all editions and most manuscripts read “by the admixture of a man,” some manuscripts have “by the loss of a man.” The latter does not have a bad sense.]

They assert that the baptized ought not to apply themselves to the discipline of virtue; that banquets and abundance of pleasures do them no harm; that those who abstain from them are fools; that virgins ought to marry and bear children; that widows likewise ought to repeat what they once experienced through sexual intercourse with a man; and that, even if they are able to remain continent, those who do not wish to repeat the intercourse are in error.

23. What, then? Shall we cast off humanity and put on the animal? Shall we strip off Christ and clothe ourselves—or cover ourselves—with the garment of the devil? Yet since even those teachers of the Gentiles did not think that honor ought to be joined with pleasure, because they seemed to be enclosing an animal with a human being, are we to pour bestial practices into the human breast and inscribe the irrational rites of beasts upon the rational mind?

[Note: [Col. 1196D] The Roman edition alone reads, “Shall we pour even bestial practices into the human breast and inscribe them upon the rational mind?” This is not a bad reading, but our text is no less elegant, since it expresses an exclamation with a certain indignation.]

24 and 25. Although there are many kinds of animals that, once they have lost their mate, do not know how to indulge in intercourse and spend their lives as though in solitude, and although many feed on simple herbs and know no other way to quench their thirst than from a pure spring,

[Note: [Col. 1196D] Saint Ambrose means the turtledove, which he praises beautifully for such remarkable continence throughout chapter 19 of Book I of the Hexaemeron, and more briefly in Sermon 19 on Psalm CXVIII, section 13, and elsewhere.]

[Col. 1196C] you may also frequently see dogs accustomed to abstaining from forbidden food, holding back their mouths in hunger when abstinence is commanded.

[Note: [Col. 1196D] The Amerbach edition reads, “and no other than from a spring”; Erasmus and the editions following him, “and from no other,” and so forth; but nearly all manuscripts read as in the text. Below, where all editions and some manuscripts read “and we see dogs,” many more manuscripts agree with us.]

Are human beings, then, called back from a practice which even mute beasts have learned from human beings not to transgress?

26. What is more beautiful than abstinence, which even makes the years of youth grow old, so that there may be an old age of character? For just as an excess of food and drunkenness inflames even more mature age, so the frugality of meals tempers the fierceness of youth, as does the flowing spring.

[Note: [Col. 1196D] All editions read, “and the outer fire by the pouring in of water from a flowing spring”; the manuscripts read variously, “and by a flowing spring the outer fire,” and “by a flowing spring and infusion”; others support our reading.]

[Col. 1197A] The outer fire is extinguished by the infusion of water. It is therefore not surprising if the inner heat of the body is also cooled by drinking from a stream.

[Note: [Col. 1197D] A Laetian manuscript reads, “is cooled and abates; for the flame is nourished by food, since,” and so forth.]

For hay, straw, wood, oil, and things of this kind are food for fire, by which it is nourished. If you remove or fail to supply them, the fire too is quieted. Likewise, then, the body’s heat is nourished or diminished by food: it is stirred up by food and extinguished by food. Luxury, therefore, is the mother of lust.

27. What of the fact that moderation is in harmony with nature and with that divine law which, at the very origin of all things, gave the springs for drinking and the fruits of trees for eating? After the flood the righteous man discovered wine as a test of himself (Gen. IX, 20). Let us therefore use the natural food of moderation—if only we were able to do so! But because not all are strong,

[Col. 1197B] the Apostle says: “Use a little wine because of your frequent infirmities” (I Tim. V, 23). We must not drink, then, for pleasure, but because of infirmity. Let us therefore drink sparingly as a remedy, not abundantly for luxury.

28. Finally, Elijah, whom the Lord was instructing toward the perfection of virtue, found a collyrida at his head and a vessel of water, and therefore, through the strength of that food, fasted for forty days (III Kings XIX, 6).

[Note: [Col. 1197D] In Greek, κολλύρα and κολλυρίς, this is a cake-like bread baked under the ashes. See Vossius, Etymology, under “Collyrium.”]

When our fathers crossed the sea on foot, they drank water, not wine (Exod. XVII, 6). Daniel and the Hebrew youths lived on their ancestral food and drank water: he restrained the fury of lions, while they saw the blazing fire harmlessly feeding around their bodies (Dan. I; XIV; III).

29. And why should I speak of men? Judith, not at all swayed by the banquet of the luxurious Holofernes, under the banner of sobriety alone won a victory despaired of by manly arms; she freed her homeland from siege and killed the military commander with her own hands (Judith XIII).

[Note: [Col. 1197D] The old edition and some manuscripts read, “not at all swayed by Holofernes’ abuse”; some others, “not unhappily delighted by Holofernes’ banquet”; still others and the Roman edition read as in the text. In place of “in the strength of manly arms,” some manuscripts read “by the strength of the arm.” This is not particularly bad.]

This is a clear example: luxury softened that terrifying warrior of the peoples, while temperance in food made this woman stronger than men. Nature was not defeated here in her sex; she conquered in her food. Esther bent the proud king by her fasts (Esth. IV, 16). Anna, after eighty-four years in widowhood, serving in the temple day and night with fasts and supplications, recognized Christ (Luke II, 37), whom John, the teacher of abstinence and a kind of new angel of the earth, announced (Matt. III, 4).

[Note: [Col. 1197D] The Remigius and Regius manuscripts read “eighty-three.”]

30. O foolish Elisha, who fed the prophets on wild clumps (IV Kings IV, 39)! O Ezra, forgetful of the Scriptures, who restored the Scriptures to memory (II Esdras VIII, 2)! O foolish Paul, who glories in fasts (II Cor. XI, 27)—if fasts are of no benefit!

[Note: [Col. 1197D] The old edition and some manuscripts read, “who fed them with wild branches”; the Roman edition has a lacuna; the other manuscripts read best, “with wild berries.” For anything small is called a “berry” or “cluster,” whence Ambrose himself, in his book On Elijah and Fasting, chapter 6, section 18, says in the same sense: “The wild vine burdened the tables with its little clusters.”]

31. But how can they be of no benefit, when by them vices are cleansed? If you offer them with humility and mercy, as Isaiah spoke by the divine Spirit, “your bones shall grow fat, and you shall be like a watered garden” (Isa. LVIII, 11). Your soul, then, grows fat, and its virtues are enriched by the spiritual fat of fasting; your fruits multiply through the abundance of your mind, so that there may be in you a sober intoxication,

[Note: [Col. 1198D] The edition reads, “a sober intoxication in you.”]

as there is in that cup of which the Prophet says: “And your cup, intoxicating, how excellent it is!” (Ps. XXII, 5).

[Col. 1198B] 32. But not only that moderation which is sparing of food is praiseworthy; so also is moderation in desire. For it is written: “Do not follow your desires, and turn away from your pleasure. If you give your soul its desire, it will make you a joy to your enemies” (Eccl. XVIII, 30); and below: “Wine and women cause even the wise to apostatize” (Eccl. XIX, 2). Hence Paul also teaches moderation even within marriage (I Cor. VII, 2 ff.); for an incontinent person in marriage is, as it were, an adulterer who transgresses the Apostolic law.

33. And why should I speak of the greatness of the grace of virginity,

[Note: [Col. 1198D] All editions read, “the glory of virginity”; all manuscripts, “the grace of virginity.”]

which deserved to be chosen by Christ, so that she might also be the bodily temple of God, in which, as we read, “the fullness of divinity dwelt bodily” (Col. II, 9)? A virgin gave birth to the salvation of the world; a virgin brought forth the life of all. Should virginity alone, then, not exist, when it has benefited everyone in Christ? A virgin bore him whom this world cannot contain or sustain. When he was born from Mary’s womb, he nevertheless preserved the barrier of genital modesty and the inviolate seals of virginity.

[Note: [Col. 1198D] Nearly all manuscripts read thus; some, as well as some editions, read “he nevertheless preserved his generative,” and so forth. Observe in passing how plainly Ambrose affirms the continued bodily integrity of Mary after childbirth; consult also our observations on Book II of Luke, section 57, and on Letter 42, section 4.]

Thus, in the Virgin, Christ found what he wished to be his, what the Lord of all would take for himself. Through a man and a woman, flesh was cast out of paradise; through a virgin, it was joined to God.

34. What shall I say of Mary, the other sister of Moses, who, leader of the womanly ranks, crossed the sea on foot (Exod. XV, 20)? And by what merit was the venerable Thecla revered even by the lions, so that the beasts, lying unfed at the feet of their prey, prolonged their sacred fast and violated the virgin neither with a wanton eye nor with a rough claw?

[Note: [Col. 1198D] The Roman edition alone reads, “that they might offer their sacred fasting”; the remaining editions and manuscripts read, “that they might offer a sacred fast.” Some read “postpone,” which is not at all bad, since it has the same sense here as “prolong.” As for Thecla’s example, and the arguments that follow, being characteristic of Ambrose in a similar context, we consider it unnecessary to point this out.]

[Col. 1199A] For the sanctity of virginity is violated even by the gaze itself.

35. Finally, with what reverence did the holy Apostle speak of virginity: “Concerning virgins I have no commandment of the Lord, but I give advice, as one who has obtained mercy from the Lord” (I Cor. VII, 25). He has no commandment, but he has advice; for what is above the law is not commanded, but is rather recommended by advice once given. Authority is not presumed, but grace is demonstrated; nor is it demonstrated by just anyone, but by one who obtained the Lord’s mercy. Whose counsels, then, are better than those of the Apostles? The Apostle says: “I give advice”; these people think that they ought to dissuade anyone from pursuing virginity.

[Note: [Col. 1199D] Some manuscripts read, “He says: ‘I give advice’; these people think that they ought to dissuade.”]

36. We ought to recognize how great a praise the prophet—or rather Christ in the prophet—expressed in a brief verse:

[Col. 1199B] “A garden enclosed is my sister, my bride, a garden enclosed, a sealed fountain” (Song IV, 12).

Christ says this to the Church, which he wishes to be a virgin, without spot and without wrinkle. A beautiful garden is virginity, bearing many fruits of good fragrance. “A garden enclosed,” because it is surrounded on every side by the wall of chastity. “A sealed fountain,” because virginity is the fountain and source of purity, preserving inviolate the seals of integrity. In this fountain the image of God shines, because bodily purity is joined with purity of simplicity.

37. No one can doubt that the Church is a virgin, since the Apostle Paul betrothed her, even among the Corinthians, to present a chaste virgin to Christ (I Cor. VII, 26). In the earlier letter, therefore, he gives advice and considers virginity a good gift, so that it may be disturbed by no necessities of the present age, stained by no defilement, or shaken by any storms. In the later letter he is Christ’s guarantor, that he can present the Church’s virginity in the integrity of that people (II Cor. XI, 2).

38. Answer me now, Paul: why do you give advice because of the present necessity (I Cor. VII, 26)? “The unmarried man,” he says, “is concerned with the things of the Lord, how he may please God” (ibid., 32). And he adds: “The unmarried woman and the virgin think about the things of the Lord, so that she may be holy in body and spirit” (ibid., 34). She therefore has her wall against the storms of this world, and, fortified by the enclosure of divine protection, she is disturbed by no blasts of the age.

[Note: [Col. 1200D] Some Paris editions read, “fortified by the perfection.”]

[Col. 1199D] A good counsel, because there is usefulness in counsel, but a snare in a commandment. Counsel invites the willing; a commandment binds the unwilling. If someone follows the counsel and does not regret it, she has gained its benefit. But if someone regrets it, she has no grounds to accuse the Apostle; she ought to have judged her own weakness. She is therefore guilty with respect to her own will, since she bound herself with a snare and knot more burdensome than she could bear.

39. Thus, like a good physician, who wishes both to preserve stability of virtue in the strong and to provide health for the weak, he gives advice to some and points out a remedy to others:

[Col. 1200A] “The weak person should eat vegetables” (Rom. XIV, 2)—let him take a wife; the stronger should seek the stronger food of virtue.

[Note: [Col. 1200D] Some manuscripts read, “let him await the food of virtue.”]

And rightly he added: “He who has firmly resolved in his heart, having no necessity but possessing authority over his own will, and has judged in his heart to keep his virgin, does well. Therefore he who gives his virgin in marriage does well, and he who does not give her in marriage does better. A woman is bound by the law as long as her husband lives. But if her husband dies, she is free: let her marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord. Yet she will be happier if she remains as she is, according to my advice; for I think that I too have the Spirit of God” (I Cor. VII, 38 ff.). To have the counsel of God means to examine everything carefully, to recommend what is better, and to point out what is safer.

40. A prudent guide displays many roads, so that each person may proceed along whichever one he wishes and considers suitable for himself, provided that he reaches the place where he can take his stand in the camp. The road of virginity is good, but lofty and arduous; it requires the stronger. The road of widowhood is also good, not as difficult as the former, but rough and harsh, and it requires the more cautious. Marriage too is good; it is level and direct, though by a longer circuit it reaches the camp of the saints, and it receives many. There are therefore rewards for virginity, merits for widowhood, and a place also for conjugal chastity. Each has its own steps and advances in virtue.

41. Stand firm, then, in your hearts, lest anyone overthrow you, lest anyone be able to subvert you. The Apostle taught us what it means to stand—that is, what was said to Moses:

[Col. 1200C] “The place on which you stand is holy ground” (Exod. III, 5).

No one stands except one who stands by faith, unless one stands fixed in the judgment of one’s heart. Elsewhere also we read: “But stand here with me.” Both statements were spoken by the Lord to Moses: “Where you stand is holy ground” (Deut. V, 31), and “Stand here with me”—that is, you stand with me if you stand in the Church. For that place is holy; that land is fertile in holiness and rich in harvests of virtues.

42. Stand, therefore, in the Church; stand where I appeared to you, and there I am with you. Where the Church is, there is the firmest station of your mind; there is the foundation of your soul, where I appeared to you from the bush. You are the bush; I am the fire—the fire in the bush, I in the flesh. Therefore I am fire, so that I may shine upon you, consume your thorns and your sins, and display my grace to you.

43. Standing, then, in your hearts, drive away the wolves seeking to plunder the Church. Let there be no laziness in you, no perverse mouth, no bitter tongue. Do not sit in the council of vanity, for it is written: “I have not sat in the council of vanity” (Ps. XXV, 4). Do not listen to those who slander their neighbors, lest, while you listen to others, you be provoked to slander your neighbors as well, and it be said to each of you: “Sitting, you slandered your brother” (Ps. XLIX, 20).

44. Those who sit slander, but those who stand bless the Lord; to them it is said:

[Col. 1201A] “Behold now, bless the Lord, all servants of the Lord, who stand in the house of the Lord” (Ps. CXXXIII, 1).

One who sits—speaking of bodily usage—relaxes in the body as though at leisure and loosens the mind’s attention.

[Note: [Col. 1201D] The old edition, with a few manuscripts, reads, “as though the body were relaxed by leisure”; the Roman edition has a lacuna; other manuscripts read partly, “as though the body were relaxed by leisure,” and partly as in our text.]

But one who stands is a prudent watchman, an untiring scout, an ever-watchful guard, who takes his position in the camp. He is also a vigorous warrior who stands in the battle line before the expected battle, wishing to anticipate the plans of his opponent.

[Note: [Col. 1201D] The Roman edition reads, “before the expected battle.” This is less suitable, for the expression refers to the time and plainly imitates Virgil’s verse in Book IV of the Georgics: “Before the expected battle, he stands in ordered camps,” which we already cited in connection with a similar expression in Book On the Flight from the World, chapter 8, section 47.]

45. “Let the one who stands take heed lest he fall” (I Cor. X, 12). The one who stands does not know how to slander; for idle people’s tales are the seedbed of slander and the revelation of malice. Hence the Prophet says: “I hated the assembly of the wicked, and I will not sit with the impious” (Ps. XXV, 5). And in Psalm Thirty-Six, which he filled with moral instructions, he immediately placed at the beginning:

[Note: [Col. 1201D] All editions and some manuscripts read thus; others have “which you fill with precepts,” and some “in precepts,” referring to moral instruction.]

[Col. 1201B] “Do not be malicious among those who are malicious, and do not envy those who commit iniquity” (Ps. XXXVI, 1).

Malice does more harm than wickedness, because malice possesses neither pure simplicity nor open wickedness, but hidden ill will. Hidden things are more difficult to guard against than known things. Hence our Savior also warns us to beware of evil spirits,

[Note: [Col. 1202D] The Bigotian and Gembloux manuscripts read, “from spiritually evil spirits.”]

because they seize us under the appearance of flattering pleasures and through the simulation of other things, when they display the allurements of ambition, honor, greed, wealth, and the pride of power.

46. Therefore, in every undertaking, but especially in the election of a bishop, malice must be absent, since in him the life of all is formed. A man should be chosen with a calm and peaceful judgment—chosen from among all, for the sake of all, and one who may heal all.

[Col. 1201C] “A gentle person is a physician of the heart” (Prov. XIV, 30).

The Lord also spoke of himself as such a physician in the Gospel, saying: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Matt. IX, 12).

47. He is a good physician who took upon himself our infirmities and healed our sicknesses. Yet this same one, as it is written, did not glorify himself to become high priest; rather, the one who spoke to him said: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Hebr. V, 5 ff.). As he says elsewhere: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.”

Because he was to be the type of all future priests, he therefore assumed flesh, so that in the days of his flesh he might offer prayers and supplications to God the Father with a loud cry and tears. And from what he suffered, although he was the Son of God, he seemed to learn the obedience that he would teach us, so that he might become the author of salvation for us (ibid.). Finally, when his sufferings were completed,

[Col. 1202A] being himself perfected, he gave health to all and took away the sin of all.

48. For this reason he himself also chose Aaron as priest (Num. XVII, 8), so that human ambition, rather than the grace of God, might not prevail in the choice of a priest; so that it might not be voluntary offering, nor self-assumption, but heavenly calling. He should offer gifts for sins who is able to feel compassion for sinners, because, as he says, “he himself also bears infirmity.” No one ought to take the honor for himself, but should be called by God, as Aaron was; and so Christ did not seize the priesthood but received it (Hebr. V, 2–3).

49. Finally, when succession traced through Aaron’s lineage favored heirs of blood more than partners in righteousness, the true Melchizedek came, after the pattern of that Melchizedek whom we read about in the Old Testament:

1034

[Col. 1202B] the true Melchizedek, the true king of peace, the true king of righteousness. For this is the interpretation of his name: “without father, without mother, without enumeration of genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life” (Hebr. VII, 2–3).

[Note: [Col. 1202D] Many manuscripts read, “without generation”—or, in the Regius manuscript, “without genealogy”—“without enumeration”; other manuscripts and printed editions read as in the text.]

This also refers to the Son of God, who knew no mother in that divine generation and no father in this birth from the Virgin Mary: born from the Father alone before the ages, born from the Virgin alone in this age, he could not have a beginning of days, since he was in the beginning. How could he have an end of life, when he is the author of life for all? He himself is the beginning and end of all things (Apoc. I, 8). But it also refers to the example, so that the priest should be, as it were, without father and without mother: one in whom not nobility of birth but the grace of character is chosen, and in whom the preeminence belongs to virtue.

[Note: [Col. 1202D] Some manuscripts read, “let the grace of virtues be chosen in him. Let faith be the prerogative in him,” and so forth.]

[Col. 1202C] 50. Let him possess faith and maturity of character—not one without the other, but both united in one person, corresponding with good works and deeds. Hence the Apostle Paul wishes us to be imitators of those who, he says, through faith and patience possess the promises (Hebr. XI, 9 ff.). Through patience Abraham deserved to receive and possess the grace of the blessing promised to him. The holy prophet David warns us that we ought to be imitators of Aaron, whom he set among the saints of the Lord for our imitation, saying: “Moses and Aaron among his priests, and Samuel among those who call upon his name” (Ps. XCVIII, 6).

51. He was plainly a man worthy to be proposed to all as an example to follow. When a dreadful death was spreading among the people because of the rebellious, he placed himself between the living and the dead, so that he might stop the death and prevent more from perishing (Num. XVI, 48).

[Note: [Col. 1202D] Erasmus and the editions following him read, “so that he might make it stop”; the Amerbach edition and the majority of manuscripts read, “so that he might establish it.” We have seen Ambrose use this expression more than once elsewhere.]

Truly he was a man of priestly mind and spirit, who, like a good shepherd, offered himself for the Lord’s flock with devoted affection. Thus he broke the sting of death, restrained its assault, and denied it passage.

[Note: [Col. 1203D] Some manuscripts read, “the merit of devotion helped.”]

Devotion helped his merit, because he offered himself for those who were resisting.

52. Let those who are divided, then, learn to fear the Lord’s anger and to appease the priests. What? Did not Dathan, Abiram, and Korah perish because of their dissension, when the earth’s chasm swallowed them (ibid., 33)?

For when Korah, Dathan, and Abiram incited two hundred and fifty men against Moses and Aaron and rose up to separate themselves from them, they said:

[Note: [Col. 1203D] Some manuscripts read, “forty men ... all the holy ones and the Lord himself.”]

“Let it be enough for you that the whole assembly, all the holy ones, and the Lord himself are among them” (ibid., 3).

53. Therefore the Lord, angered, spoke to the entire assembly.

[Col. 1203B] “The Lord knows those who are his” (II Tim. II, 19),

and he brought the holy ones to himself; those whom he did not choose, he did not bring to himself. And the Lord commanded them to choose small altars (arulae) for themselves, and that Korah and all who had risen with him against Moses and Aaron, the priests of the Lord, should place incense upon them, so that the one whom the Lord had chosen might be confirmed as holy among the Levites.

54. And Moses said to Korah:

“ Hear me, sons of Levi. Is it a small thing to you that God separated you from the assembly of Israel and brought you near to himself, so that you might perform the services of the Lord’s Tabernacle?” (Num. XVI, 9 ff.).

And below: “Do you seek to exercise the priesthood, you and your whole assembly gathered against God? And what is Aaron, that you murmur against him?”

55. When, therefore, the causes of the offense had been considered—that men unworthy to exercise the priesthood wished to do so, and consequently dissented and murmured, rejecting God’s judgment in the choice of their priest—a great fear seized the whole people, and the terror of punishment enveloped everyone.

[Note: [Col. 1203D] The Gembloux manuscript reads, “invaded everyone.”]

Yet when everyone pleaded that the insolence of a few should not cause all to perish, the guilty are identified, and two hundred and fifty men with their leaders are separated from the body of the whole people. The earth roars and splits open in the midst of the assembly; its bosom opens into the depths; the guilty are snatched away and banished from all the elements of this world, so that they might pollute neither the air by breathing, nor the sky by sight, nor the sea by touch, nor the earth by their burial.

56. The punishment ceased, but the wickedness did not. From this very fact the people’s murmuring arose: that the people had perished through the priests [Col. 1203D]. In such indignation the Lord would have destroyed them all, unless he had first been moved by the prayers of Moses and Aaron, and afterward, through the intercession of his priest Aaron, preferred to grant the ungrateful a greater shame of pardon—those who had rejected the grace they were offered.

57. Miriam the prophetess herself, who with her brothers had crossed the stretches of the sea on foot, because she still did not understand the mystery of the Ethiopian woman [Col. 1204A] and had murmured against her brother Moses, bristled with the spots of leprosy; she would scarcely have been freed from so great a contagion unless Moses had pleaded for her (Num. 12:10 ff.). Although that murmuring is understood figuratively of the Synagogue, which, ignorant of the mystery of this Ethiopian woman—that is, of the Church from the nations—murmurs daily with abuse and envies that people whose faith will itself strip her of the leprosy of her faithlessness, according to what we read: “A hardening has come upon part of Israel, until the full number of the Gentiles should enter, and thus all Israel should be saved” (Rom. 11:25).

58. And so that we may understand that in priests divine grace operates more than human favor, one of the many rods that Moses had received from the tribes and stored away—Aaron’s rod—blossomed. Thus the people perceived that the gift of divine judgment was to be recognized in a priest [Col. 1204B], and ceased to claim for themselves by human judgment an equal share in the grace, having previously thought that an equal prerogative belonged to them. What else did that rod signify except that priestly grace never withers, and that, in the deepest humility, it possesses in its office the flower of the authority entrusted to it? Or was this also related to the mystery? We do not think it accidental that this happened near the end of the priest Aaron’s life. It seems to declare that the ancient people, their priestly stock made rotten by the age-old decay of unbelief, would in the last times be reformed through imitation of the Church [Note: Some manuscripts read “into the practices of faithful devotion”] and, through faith and devotion, send forth again the flower long since dead, revived by grace.

59. What does it mean, moreover, that after Aaron’s death God commanded not the whole people but Moses alone, who belongs to the priests of the Lord, to invest his son Eleazar with the garments of Aaron the priest (Num. 20:26), except that we should understand [Note: The holy Doctor expressly shows that episcopal consecration ought to be performed only by priests, that is, bishops; and he also sufficiently indicates, without ambiguity, how little right the people have always had in episcopal election, since he mentions no role for them here] that a priest ought to consecrate a priest and himself clothe him in the vestments—that is, the virtues—of the priesthood? Then, if he observes that nothing is lacking from his priestly attire and that everything fits properly, he should admit him to the sacred altars [Note: “For he is to intercede for the people”]. For one who is going to intercede for the people must be chosen by the Lord and approved by the priests, lest there be anything seriously offensive in one whose office it is to intervene for the offenses of others. Priesthood is no ordinary virtue: one must beware not only of association with grave crimes, but even with the smallest, so that he may be ready for mercy, not reproach one who has made a promise, call back the fallen, sympathize with grief, maintain gentleness, love devotion, and repel or restrain anger. Let him be a kind of trumpet to rouse the people to devotion and to fill them with wonder at tranquility.

60. There is an old saying: “Accustom yourself to be one”—so that your life may express a certain portrait, always preserving the same image it first received. How can a person be one who is now inflamed with anger, now boiling over with intense indignation, now blazing in countenance, now changed by pallor—variable and discolored from moment to moment? But suppose it is natural for him to become angry, or that circumstances usually provoke him. Even so, it belongs to a human being to moderate anger, not to be carried away by a leonine fury [Note: All manuscripts read thus; against them all printed editions read: “to be carried away by fury, not to know how to become gentle, not to raise cries, not to provoke,” and so forth.], so that he does not know how to grow gentle, sow shouting, or aggravate a quarrel with those of his household. For it is written: “An angry man digs up sin” (Prov. 15:18).

He is not one who has a divided heart; nor is he one who does not know how to restrain himself in anger. Of such a man David beautifully says: “Be angry, and do not sin” (Ps. 4:5). He does not command anger, but makes allowance for nature: what a person cannot prevent, he can mitigate. Therefore, even if we become angry, let our emotion receive its movement according to nature, not according to sin, which is contrary to nature. For who could tolerate a man unable to govern himself when he has undertaken to govern others?

61. For this reason the Apostle provided a model, saying that a bishop must be blameless (1 Tim. 3:2); and elsewhere: “For a bishop must be without reproach, as God’s steward, not arrogant, not quick-tempered, not addicted to wine, not violent, not greedy for dishonest gain” (Tit. 1:7 ff.). For how can the mercy of a steward and the greed of one who desires wealth belong together?

62. I have set down what I have learned must be avoided. The Apostle is the teacher of virtues: he teaches that opponents are to be corrected with patience, and commands that a bishop be “the husband of one wife” (ibid.)—not excluding one who has no share in marriage (for that would be beyond the commandment of the law), but requiring him to preserve through marital chastity the grace of his cleansing [Note: One manuscript reads “the grace of absolution”]. Nor is he thereby invited by apostolic authority to beget children again in the priesthood: the Apostle says “having children,” not “begetting them,” and does not permit a second marriage.

63. I have not passed over this point because many argue [Note: The Bigotian manuscript reads: “the husband of one wife can be said of a wife taken after baptism”; others read more correctly as in our text. It would also be worthwhile to compare what is taught here about monogamy and priestly continence with the discussion in *On Duties*, book 1, chapter 50, sections 257 and 258, and to consult the observation appended there] that “the husband of one wife” means one who had a wife after baptism, on the grounds that baptism washed away the fault that had constituted an impediment. Indeed, all vices and sins are washed away, so that if someone had defiled his body with several women to whom he was not joined by any law of marriage, everything is forgiven him. But marriages are not dissolved if someone contracts a second one: the guilt is removed by the washing, not the law. There is no guilt in marriage; it is a law. Therefore what belongs to the law is not forgiven as though it were guilt, but remains binding as law.

For this reason the Apostle also established the rule, saying: “If anyone is without reproach, the husband of one wife” [Note: A reference to Distinction 26, chapter “Qui sine”]. Thus the man who is without reproach, the husband of one wife, is bound by the law governing reception of the priesthood; but one who has entered a second marriage is not guilty of having been polluted, yet is deprived of the priest’s prerogative.

64. We have stated what the law is; let us also state its rationale. But first let us recognize that the Apostle established this not only concerning a bishop and presbyter, but that the Fathers also added, in the proceedings of the Council of Nicaea, that no cleric should be one who had entered a second marriage [Note: The Roman edition and a few manuscripts read “in the proceedings of the Council of Nicaea”; other manuscripts read “in the proceedings held at the Council of Nicaea”; the remaining manuscripts and older editions read “in the proceedings of the Council of Nicaea,” as does the ancient edition of Gratian and others. However one reads this passage, it remains difficult. Since only twenty canons of the Council of Nicaea are known, and none of them says anything about excluding bigamists from the clergy, it is uncertain what Ambrose indicates by these words. Baronius and those who follow him seem to have found a wedge for this knot by asserting that, besides these twenty canons, others were composed by the same synod but did not survive to our time. Yet, with all due respect to such eminent men, the inquiry conducted by the other bishops who, in the time of Boniface and Zosimus, sent envoys to Alexandria and Antioch to seek out the same canons yielded only twenty; the old copies of the same synod likewise contain the same number—for Rufinus’s twenty-two mean nothing, since he made four out of two that had been divided; and finally the testimonies of Theodoret, book 1, chapter 8, and Hincmar of Rheims in his letter to the bishop of Laon plainly show that there were no more than twenty Nicene canons. Accordingly, some do not dispute their number but deny that our Doctor is speaking of canons, maintaining that he bears witness only to proceedings held on this matter at the Council of Nicaea, not to canons enacted there. Yet since Ambrose first stated what the Apostle had established concerning a bishop and presbyter, it is clear that he then added what had been decreed at the mentioned synod concerning a deacon and subdeacon; nor can this passage be understood in any other sense. We therefore find nothing more probable than to say that this canon was added to the Nicene canons in the manuscript used by the holy Bishop, by which he was misled, as others have been in similar matters. Nor should the phrase “nor any cleric” disturb anyone, since it is clear that the word “cleric” is restricted to deacons and subdeacons, just as in the words of Leo the Great, Letter 12 to Anastasius, chapter 4: “For even to those established outside the order of clerics … not even is carnal intercourse granted to subdeacons.” By these words the holy Pope intended to include subdeacons and the higher orders within the class of clerics, but not the lower orders, since marital union with wives was permitted to the latter].

For how can he console a widow, honor her, and exhort her to preserve her widowhood and remain faithful to her husband, if he himself did not preserve fidelity to his first marriage? Or what difference would there be between the people and the priest if they were bound by the same laws? The priest’s life must outweigh the rest, just as grace outweighs it; for one who binds others by his commands must himself observe the lawful commands.

65. How I resisted being ordained! At last, when I was compelled, I at least asked that my ordination be postponed! But the canonical provision [Note: “Canonical provision” here has the force of an ecclesiastical or canonical constitution; “popular pressure” means force and impetus arising from the people] did not prevail; popular pressure prevailed. Nevertheless, Western bishops approved my ordination by their judgment, and Eastern bishops by their example [Note: Ambrose often complains about his election, for example in *Duties*, book 1, chapter 1, section 4; *On Repentance*, book 2, chapter 8, section 72; and elsewhere. As for his statement that Eastern bishops confirmed his ordination by their example, Baronius and those after him think this refers to Nectarius of Constantinople, as discussed more fully in the note on Letter 13, section 3].

Yet the neophyte is forbidden to be ordained (Distinction 61, chapter “Neophytus”), lest he be lifted up by pride. If the ordination lacked delay, that is the force of compulsion; if the humility appropriate to the priesthood is not lacking, then, where no cause of blame remains, the fault is not imputed.

66. If in other Churches such care is taken in ordaining a priest, how much greater care is required in the Church of Vercelli, where the bishop seems to be required to possess two things equally: the discipline of a monastery and the discipline of the Church? [Note: Baronius thinks Eusebius established this institution in the year 328, when he returned from Egypt, to which he had been sent as legate by the Roman Pontiff. But since Ambrose says that Eusebius was guided not by the Egyptian monks, as Baronius asserts, but by the examples of Elijah, Elisha, and John the Baptist, so that he might unite monastic life with the clerical life, there is no reason why we should not suppose that this union preceded that embassy.]

For Eusebius, of holy memory, was the first in the western regions to unite these distinct things: while living in a city, he maintained the practices of monks and governed the Church with the sobriety of fasting. Much assistance is added to the grace of the priesthood if he binds the young to the pursuit of abstinence and to the rule of integrity, and withdraws those living within the city [Note: Some manuscripts read “withdraws them from the city’s way of life”] from the city’s habits and social intercourse.

67. From this discipline came men such as Elijah, Elisha, and John, son of Elizabeth [Note: Several manuscripts and the Roman edition omit “Elizabeth,” but we think the omission arose because they did not notice that the word is in the genitive case; in the Greek phrase it is “John, of Elizabeth,” with “son” understood]. Clothed in garments of skins and coverings of goats, poor and needy, afflicted by hardships and suffering, they wandered in deserted places, among the high and dense mountain ranges, the pathless crags, the dreadful recesses of caves [Note: Some manuscripts read “the storehouses of caves”], and the shallow hollows of pits—men whose way of life the world was not worthy to receive.

From this discipline came Daniel, Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael. Though they were fed in the royal court, they were nourished by fasting as though in the deserts, on coarse food and ordinary drink. And rightly the royal servants [Note: The editions of Amerbach and Erasmus read “they prevailed over kings”; Gill’s and the Roman edition read “they prevailed over the king”; the manuscripts read as in the text] prevailed over kingdoms, despised captivity after shaking off its yoke [Col. 1207C], subdued powers, overcame the elements, extinguished the nature of fire, blunted the flames, turned aside the edge of the sword, and closed the mouths of lions. Where they were thought likely to be weaker, there they were found stronger. They did not shrink from human mockery because they hoped for heavenly rewards; they did not dread the darkness of prison, since the grace of eternal light shone upon them.

68. Holy Eusebius followed these men. He went out from his land, from his kindred, and preferred pilgrimage to the leisure of home. For the sake of the faith he also chose and willingly embraced the hardships of exile [Col. 1208A], taking with him Dionysius, of holy memory [Note: Athanasius himself, in his *Letter to the Solitaries*, together with Hilary in the conclusion of his *Letter to Constantius*, Socrates, Sozomen, Sulpicius Severus, and others, explains how Eusebius of Vercelli and Dionysius of Milan were driven into exile by the emperor Valens because at the Council of Milan they refused to subscribe to the condemnation of Athanasius].

Dionysius had set the emperor’s friendship below voluntary exile. Thus, when the memorable men were surrounded by arms and hemmed in by an army, as they were dragged from the greater church, they triumphed over imperial power. Through earthly insult they purchased strength of mind and the power of the kingdom—things that the armed hand, with all the clamor of weapons, could not wrest from them. They subdued the savagery of a beast-like spirit, which could not harm the saints. For “the king’s anger is like the growling of a lion,” as you read in Proverbs (Prov. 19:12).

69. The man who begged them to change their decision confessed that he had been defeated; but they considered their stronger pen their own iron swords [Note: Nearly all manuscripts read this; the printed editions, however, do not recognize the word “hand”]. Their faithlessness was wounded so that it might kill, but the faith of the saints was not wounded. They did not long for a fatherland’s tomb, for whom a heavenly dwelling was reserved. They wandered throughout the world, “as having nothing, yet possessing everything” (2 Cor. 6:10).

Wherever they were sent was considered a place of delight, for nothing was lacking to those whose faith abounded in riches. Indeed, they enriched others while themselves poor in means but rich in grace. They were tested but not destroyed—in fasting, labors, imprisonment, and vigils. “They escaped from weakness, strong” (Heb. 11:34).

They did not await the allurements of luxury, whom hunger fattened. The scorching summer did not burn them, for the hope of eternal grace refreshed them. The cold blows of frost did not break them, for devotion blossomed like spring within them [Note: The Roman edition and several manuscripts read “whose glory refreshed them … the cold of the blows”; the older edition reads “whose grace refreshed them … the chill of the blows.” Many manuscripts, however, read as in the text]. They did not fear human chains, for Jesus had loosed them. They did not wish to be ransomed from death, for they trusted that Christ would raise them.

70. Finally, holy Dionysius obtained through his prayers that he might lay down his life in exile, lest, on returning, he should find the people or clergy confused by the practices or customs of the faithless. He earned this grace: to bring back with him the Lord’s peace in a tranquil spirit.

Thus, just as holy Eusebius first raised the banner of confession, so blessed Dionysius, in the places of exile [Note: All printed editions and some manuscripts read “with a title nearer to martyrdom” (some, “of martyrdom”); many others read “with the first title,” which seems more suitable here, so that the labors and hardships of his prolonged exile, in which Dionysius ended his life, may be preferred to a bloody but brief martyrdom. Baronius, in the year 375, Ughellus in volume 4, and the continuators of the Bollandists report that he died in the city of Retroia in Cappadocia on 25 May, in the year 371 or 374. As for Eusebius, two sermons published under Ambrose’s name, which Ughellus cites from a manuscript supposedly written a thousand years ago, say that he died amid tortures inflicted on him by the Arians. Yet, as Baronius observes under the year 371, it seems most unlikely that Ambrose would here have either omitted this fact or, following the reading of the older edition, transferred the “first” title from Dionysius to Eusebius, if Eusebius’s exile had been crowned by a bloody end. We shall speak elsewhere of those sermons and of both holy confessors], breathed out his life with a title superior to that of martyrs.

71. This endurance therefore took root in holy Eusebius through the practice of the monastery, and from the habit of stricter observance it drew the capacity to endure labor. For who would doubt that these two things are preeminent in the more devoted Christian life: the duties of the clergy and the practices of monks? [Note: All printed editions and a few manuscripts read “for sociability”; the larger number of manuscripts read “for usefulness,” namely, so that one may serve and accommodate oneself to the needs of one’s neighbors. In Ambrose, “moral character” likewise means ease and accessibility of conduct.]

The former discipline is directed toward usefulness and moral character, the latter toward abstinence and endurance; the former is practiced as though in a theater, the latter in secrecy. The one is seen, the other hidden. Therefore the good athlete says: “We have become a spectacle to the world and to angels” (1 Cor. 4:9). He was truly worthy to be watched by angels: he wrestled to reach Christ’s prize; he contended to establish the life of angels on earth and to repel the wickedness of angels in heaven. For he wrestled against spiritual wickedness. The world rightly watched him, so that the world might imitate him.

72. This life is lived in the arena, the other in a cave; this one against the world’s confusion, the other against the appetite of the flesh; this one subdues bodily pleasures, the other flees them; this one is more pleasing, the other safer; this one governs itself, the other restrains itself. Yet both deny themselves in order to become Christ’s, because it was said to the perfect: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matt. 16:25). He therefore follows Christ who can say: “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2:20).

73. Paul denied himself when, knowing that chains and tribulations awaited him in Jerusalem, he voluntarily offered himself to danger, saying: “I do not account my life of any value to myself, if only I may complete my course and the ministry of the word that I received from the Lord Jesus” (Acts 20:24 ff.). Finally, though many stood around him, weeping and pleading, he did not change his mind. Such ready faith is a severe judge of itself!

74. The one therefore fights, the other withdraws; the one conquers allurements, the other flees them; for the one the world is vanquished, for the other it is an exile; for the one the world is crucified, and he is crucified to the world (Gal. 6:14), while the other is exiled from the world. The one faces more temptations and therefore achieves the greater victory; the other encounters fewer falls and therefore has an easier guardianship.

75. Thus Elijah himself, so that the word of his mouth might be confirmed [Note: Some manuscripts read “so that the word might be strengthened,” and so forth], was sent by the Lord to hide himself by the brook Cherith (1 Kings 17:3). Ahab threatened, Jezebel threatened; Elijah was afraid and arose. Then, strengthened by intelligible food, he walked for forty days and forty nights as far as Mount Horeb, the mountain of God, entered a cave, and rested there. Afterwards he was sent to anoint kings (1 Kings 19:8–9). He was therefore hardened for endurance by dwelling in solitude; and, as though nourished toward the fatness of virtue by rustic food, he advanced stronger.

76. John also grew up in the desert [Note: This is how the older edition and many manuscripts read; the Roman edition, with some other manuscripts, omits “and baptized the Lord”], and baptized the Lord (Luke 3:2, 19). There he first exercised steadfastness, so that afterward he might rebuke the king.

77. Since, in speaking of the dwelling of holy Elijah in the desert, we have not idly passed over the names of the places as though merely filling time, we ought to explain what they signify. Elijah was sent to the brook Cherith. There ravens fed him, bringing bread in the morning and meat in the evening.

It was not without reason that bread was brought in the morning, because bread “strengthens the human heart” (Ps. 103:15). With what food, indeed, except mystical food, was the prophet nourished? In the evening meat was supplied. Understand what you read, for Cherith means “understanding.” Horeb is said to mean “the whole heart,” or something like “heart,” while Beersheba is the Latin interpretation of “the well of the seventh” or “of the oath” [Note: In *On Flight from the World*, chapter 6, section 34, Cherith is explained as “knowledge”; but Horeb—or, as it is written in some manuscripts, Choreb—is said in the same work to mean “drying,” and it is also commonly explained as dryness, desert, destruction, and sword. Ambrose departs considerably from those interpretations here, but plainly follows the authority of another writer. As for the word Beersheba, or Betsheba, all sources offer the explanation given here].

78. First Elijah withdrew to Beersheba for the mysteries of the holy law and the sacraments of divine justice. Afterwards he was sent to the brook, to that rushing stream “which makes glad the city of God” (Ps. 45:5).

You perceive in both one author of the Testament. The ancient Scripture is like a deep and obscure well, from which one draws with labor; it is not yet full, because the one who would fill it had not yet come. Therefore he later says: “I have not come to abolish the Law, but to fulfill it” (Matt. 5:17).

For this reason the Lord commands the saint to cross over to the river (1 Kings 17:3), because whoever drinks from the New Testament finds not merely one river, but “rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John 7:38): rivers of understanding [Note: The manuscripts almost unanimously read this; all printed editions read “rivers of knowledge”], rivers of thought, spiritual rivers. Yet these rivers dried up in the time of faithlessness, lest sacrilegious people drink and the faithless be refreshed.

79. There the ravens recognized the prophet of the Lord, whom the Jews did not recognize. Ravens fed the man whom that royal and noble race persecuted. Who is Jezebel, who persecuted him (1 Kings 17:6), except the Synagogue, flowing vainly and abounding vainly in Scriptures that it neither keeps nor understands?

Who are the ravens that fed him except those whose young call upon him, and to whose beasts he gives food, as we read: “To the young ravens that call upon him” (Ps. 146:9)? Those ravens knew whom they were to feed: they were those who possessed understanding and who carried food to him from that stream of sacred knowledge.

80. The one who understands and keeps what is written feeds the prophet. Our faith gives him its sap; our progress gives him nourishment. He feeds upon our minds and thoughts; his word feasts upon our understanding. We give him bread in the morning when, placed in the light of the Gospel, we offer him the steadfastness of our hearts.

By these things he is nourished; by these things he flourishes; by these things he fills the mouths of those who fast—mouths to which the unbelief of the Jews supplied no food of faith. There the whole prophetic word is hungry: they do not see its inner richness, and it is stripped and thin, unable to fatten their throats.

81. Perhaps for this reason they brought meat in the evening, as stronger food, which the Corinthians, weak in understanding, could not consume; and therefore they were given milk to drink by the Apostle (1 Cor. 3:2). Stronger food was therefore brought in the evening of this world, and bread in the morning.

And because the Lord commanded this nourishment to be supplied, the prophetic saying appropriately applies here: “You will delight the outgoings of morning and evening,” and further: “You have prepared their food; for such is its preparation” (Ps. 64:9–10) [Note: All editions and some manuscripts read as in the text; many others read “morning departures and evenings,” and some “you will delight in morning departures and evening”].

82. But I think enough has been said about the teacher. Let us now pursue the life of the disciples, who have clothed themselves in that praise and make the days and nights resound with hymns. This is truly the service of angels: always to be engaged in the praises of God, to win the Lord’s favor through frequent prayers, and to entreat the Lord [Note: All editions and some manuscripts read “they strive for the Lord through prayer or works”; the more numerous and better manuscripts support the reading in the text]. They devote themselves to reading or occupy their minds with continual works. Separated from the company of women, they provide one another with a secure guardianship.

What kind of life is this, in which there is nothing to fear and so much to imitate? The labor of fasting is compensated by tranquility of mind; it is lightened by practice, sustained by leisure, or relieved by work. It is not burdened by worldly anxiety, occupied by the troubles of others, or harried by the city’s distractions.

83. In fulfilling or teaching this office, you understand what kind of teacher must be appointed. We can find such a teacher if your unanimity inclines toward it, if you give yourselves to one another (Eph. 4:32), if anyone thinks that he has been wronged by another [Note: Erasmus and later editions read “does not think himself wronged”; the negation is absent from Amerbach and all the manuscripts, nor does the sense permit it. For one who does not think himself wronged has nothing to forgive another].

For justice is not expressed only in this form: that you do not harm one who has not harmed you. It is also expressed in this: that you forgive even one who has harmed you. We are usually injured by another’s deceit, by the trickery of a neighbor. Do we think it a virtue to avenge deceit with deceit and repay fraud with fraud?

For if justice is a virtue, it must be free from crime [Note: Some manuscripts read “to be free from crime, to repel wickedness with integrity”; in some, the word “with integrity” is omitted], and it must not repel wickedness with wickedness [Col. 1211D]. What kind of virtue is it for you to do what you punish in another? That is contamination by wickedness, not vengeance. It makes no difference whom you harm—whether a just person or an unjust person—since you ought not to do harm.

Nor does it matter how you are malicious, whether from a desire for vengeance or from a wish to cause harm [Note: The Roman edition alone reads “from a just zeal for vengeance.” Ambrose seems here to touch upon the various causes by which dissension was being fostered in the Church of Vercelli and the election of a bishop delayed], since malice is blameworthy in either form. To be malicious differs in no way from being unjust. Therefore it is said to you: “Do not be malicious among those who are malicious, nor envy those who do injustice” (Ps. 36:1). And above he says the same: “I have hated the congregation of the malicious” (Ps. 25:5). He embraced all of them; he excepted no one. He considered their malice, not their cause.

84. What better model is there than divine justice? For the Son of God says: “Love your enemies” (Matt. 5:44). Again he says: “Pray for those who persecute and slander you.” He carries the demand for perfection so far that he commands love toward those who inflict injury [Note: Many manuscripts read “so that he might fulfill love,” which is not sufficiently correct].

And because he had said in the Old Testament, “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay” (Deut. 32:35), in the Gospel he says that one should pray for those who have inflicted harm, lest he take vengeance upon those for whom he promised to take vengeance. He wishes to leave the matter to your will, in which he is bound by his own promise. If you seek vengeance, you have this: the unjust person is punished more by his own opinions than by judicial severity.

85. Since no one can be without some adversities, let us act [Note: All editions read “by our judgment … can be condemned”; almost all manuscripts, rightly, read “by our fault … is condemned”] so that adversities do not come upon us through our own fault. No one is more severely condemned by another’s judgment than the fool is by his own, since he himself is the author of his misfortunes.

Therefore let us avoid troublesome and contentious business, which yields no fruit and brings impediment [Col. 1212C]. Yet we must act so that we do not have cause to regret our own judgment or our actions. It is the part of the prudent to foresee matters, lest he often have cause to regret himself; for only God never needs to repent.

What fruit of justice is there except tranquility of mind? Or what is it to live justly except to live in tranquility? As is the character of the master, so is the condition of the whole household. If these things are sought in a household, how much more in the Church, where rich and poor, slave and free, Greek and Scythian, honored and common, are all one in Christ (Col. 3:11)?

86. Let no one presume, because he is rich, that more respect is owed to him (Prov. 17:5). He is rich in the Church who is rich in faith; for to the faithful the whole world is wealth [Note: The manuscripts read this; the printed editions read “who is not rich for himself in the poor.” In the Church the faithful person is rich, for the faithful person, and so forth].

What wonder if the faithful possess the world, when he possesses Christ’s inheritance, which is more precious than the world? “You were redeemed with precious blood” (1 Pet. 1:19)—a statement made to everyone, not merely to the wealthy.

But if you wish to be rich, follow the one who says: “Be holy in all your conduct” (ibid., 15). He does not speak only to the rich but to all, because he judges without respect of persons, as his good witness the Apostle says: “And therefore, not in negligence, not in disdain, not in exaltation of heart, but in fear,” he says, “conduct yourselves during this time of your sojourning” (ibid., 17). You have received time on this earth, not perpetuity. Use the time, knowing that you will depart.

87. Do not trust in riches, because all those things will be left here; faith alone will accompany you. Justice too will be your companion, if faith goes before. What do riches flatter you with? You were not redeemed from your vain way of life by gold or silver, by possessions, or by silk garments, but by the precious blood of Christ Jesus (ibid., 18–19).

He therefore is rich who is God’s heir and Christ’s fellow-heir. Do not despise the poor: he made you rich. Do not disdain the needy: “This poor man cried, and the Lord heard him” (Ps. 33:6). Do not reject the destitute: “Christ also became poor, though he was rich; he became poor for your sake, so that by his poverty he might make you rich” [Note: The editions of Amerbach and Erasmus read “and Christ became poor, so that by poverty he might …”; the Roman edition reads “and Christ became poor for you, though he was rich, so that by poverty he might …”; Gill and the manuscripts rightly restore the passage as in the text]. Do not exalt yourself as though you were rich: he sent out his apostles without money.

88. Indeed, the first of them said: “Silver and gold I do not have” (Acts 3:6). He glories in poverty, as though fleeing contamination. “Silver and gold,” he says, “I do not have”—not “gold and silver” [Note: Many manuscripts read this; the editions of Gill and the Roman edition read “I do not have.” One who does not know how to use gold and silver does not know their proper order. Amerbach, Erasmus, and some manuscripts contain a lacuna here].

He does not know the order who does not know the use. “Silver and gold I do not have, but I have faith.” I am rich enough in the name of Jesus, which is above every name (Phil. 2:9). I have no silver, but I do not seek it; I have no gold, but I do not desire it. Yet I possess what you rich do not possess, what even you consider more valuable, and I give it to the poor, so that in the name of Jesus I may say: “Strengthen the weak hands and make firm the feeble knees” (Isa. 35:3).
