89. But if you wish to be rich, be poor. You will then be rich in every respect if you are poor in spirit: “It is not wealth but the mind that makes a person rich” (Matt. 5:3).

90. There are those who humble themselves amid great riches, and rightly and prudently so. For the law of nature is sufficiently rich for everyone; one quickly finds in it what is abundant. But for desires, every abundance of riches is poverty.

In the end, no one is born poor; rather, one becomes poor. Poverty therefore belongs not to nature but to opinion. Thus the person rich by nature is quickly found, while the person rich in desire is difficult to find. For the more each person acquires, the more he thirsts, and he becomes inflamed, as though by a kind of drunkenness, with the desires of his own greed.

91. Why do you seek, as though it were necessary, an accumulation of wealth? Nothing is so necessary as to know what is not necessary. Why do you throw the blame back upon the flesh? [Note: One Colbertine codex reads, “Not the care of the body.”] It is not the body’s stomach but the mind’s greed that makes one insatiable. Has the flesh taken away hope of the future? Has the flesh removed the sweetness of spiritual grace? Has the flesh hindered faith? Has the flesh assigned anything to vain opinions as though to furious masters? The flesh loves moderate frugality more: by it the burden is removed and health is put on, for it lays aside anxiety and takes up tranquility.

92. Yet wealth itself is not blameworthy. Indeed, “the ransom of a man’s soul is his wealth” (Prov. XIII, 8), because one who gives to the poor ransoms his own soul. There is therefore also a place for virtue amid these material riches. You are like helmsmen on the great sea. If someone steers his vessel well, he quickly crosses the strait and reaches the harbor; but whoever does not know how to manage his wealth is sunk by his own burden. Therefore it is written: “The possession of the rich is a very strong city” (Prov. X, 15).

93. What is this possession but Jerusalem, which is in heaven, where the kingdom of God is? It is a good possession, which produces everlasting fruits. A good possession, which is not abandoned here but possessed there. Whoever is in this possession says: “The Lord is my portion” (Ps. CXVIII, 94). He does not say, “My portion extends and stretches from this boundary to that.” He does not say, “My portion is among those neighbors”—unless perhaps he means among the apostles, among the prophets, among the saints of the Lord; for this is the portion of the righteous. He does not say, “My portion is in meadows, not in woods, not in fields”—unless perhaps in the fields of the wood, in which the Church is found, concerning which it is written: “We found it in the fields of the wood” (Ps. CXXXI, 6). He does not say, “My portion is herds of horses,” for “a horse is deceitful for salvation” (Ps. XXXII, 17). He does not say, “My portion is herds of cattle, donkeys, sheep”—unless perhaps he counts himself among those herds that recognize their owner; and wishes to have fellowship with that she-ass which did not shun Christ’s manger (Isa. I, 3); and that sheep is his portion which was led to sacrifice, and that Lamb who stood before the shearer without a sound and did not open his mouth (Isa. LIII, 7), whose judgment was exalted in his humility. Well does he say, “Before the shearer,” because on that cross he laid aside what was superfluous, not what was his own: he divested himself of the body but did not lose his divinity.

94. Therefore, not everyone [Note: Whatever is said in this and the following section has so close an affinity with the exposition of this same verse in Sermon 12 on Psalm CXVIII, sections 38 and 39, that it cannot be denied that Ambrose did here what we often observe him doing elsewhere: namely, that he was accustomed to transfer to another place, as occasion and subject required, material which he considered himself to have treated suitably somewhere else.] says, “The Lord is my portion.” [Col. 1214D] The avaricious man does not say it, because avarice comes and says: “You are my portion; I held you subject, you served me, you sold yourself to me for that gold, you assigned yourself to me in that possession.” The luxurious man does not say, “Christ is my portion,” because luxury comes and says: “You are my portion; you enslaved yourself to me at that banquet, I caught you in those nets of feasting, I hold you bound to your appetite by its contract. Do you not know that the price of your table was dearer to you than the price of your life? I convict you by your own judgment: deny it, if you can—but you cannot deny it. In the end, you kept nothing for life; you spent everything on the table.” The adulterer cannot say, “The Lord is my portion,” because lust comes and says: “I am your portion; you pledged yourself to me in love for that young woman; on that prostitute’s night you passed over to my laws and my rights.” The traitor does not say, “Christ is my portion,” because immediately [Note: The Colbertine codex reads, “evil deceit rushes upon him.”] the wickedness of evil rushes upon him and says: “He deceives you, Lord Jesus; this man is mine.”

95. We have an example (John XIII, 2): when Judas had received bread from Christ, the devil entered his heart, as though claiming his own possession, as though retaining the right of his portion, as though saying: “This man is not yours but mine: certainly my minister, your betrayer; plainly, he is mine. In the end, he reclines with you and serves me; he feasts with you and feeds with me; he received bread from you and money from me; he drank with you and sold your blood to me.” How true these words were, Judas proved. In the end, Christ withdrew from him, and Judas himself also left Jesus, following the devil.

96. How many masters he has who has rejected the one! But let us not reject him. Who would reject the one whom those follow who are bound with chains—but voluntary chains, which loosen rather than bind, chains in which those bound glory, saying: “Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ, and Timothy” (Philem. 1)? We are bound by him more gloriously than we are released and set free by others. Who, then, would flee peace? Who would flee salvation? Who would flee mercy? Who would flee redemption?

97. You see, children, what those who followed these things have become, and how the dead act. Let us strive to acquire the diligence of those whose praise in virtue we admire, and let us silently recognize in ourselves the qualities we proclaim in others. Nothing soft or slack reaches praise: “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. XI, 12). The fathers ate the lamb in haste. Faith is hasty, devotion eager, hope tireless; it does not love the soul’s resistance, but its transfer from fruitless idleness to the fruit of labor. Why do you put it off until tomorrow? You can gain today as well; for you must be careful not to hold on to that day and lose this one. Even a single hour is no small loss: one hour too is a portion of the whole of life.

98. There are young people who want to reach old age quickly, so that they may not remain longer under the authority of their elders; and there are also old people who would like, if they could, to return to youth. I approve neither desire: the young, dissatisfied with the present as though ungrateful, seek a change of life; the old seek delay, although youth can grow old in conduct and old age can flourish in deeds. For age brings moral improvement no more than discipline does. How much more, then, ought we to raise our hope toward the kingdom of God, where there will be newness of life and grace, not a change of age?

99. Reward is not prepared by idleness or sleep. A sleeper performs no work; idleness bears no fruit—rather, it brings loss. Esau lost the primacy of blessing [Note: All editions read, “the primacy of the blessing”; all manuscripts read, “the primacy of blessing.”] because he preferred to receive food rather than seek it (Gen. XXVII, 35). Industrious Jacob found favor with both parents.

100. And yet, although Jacob was superior in virtue and grace, he yielded to his brother’s indignation, since his brother grieved that a younger brother had been preferred to him. Therefore it is written: “Give place to wrath” (Rom. XII, 19), lest another’s indignation drag you also into sin while you wish to resist and to avenge yourself. You can remove guilt both from him and from yourself if you think you ought to yield. Imitate the patriarch, who at his mother’s counsel sought a distant land (Gen. XXVII, 43). And whose mother? Rebecca, of course—that is, patience. For whose counsel could this have been except patience? [Note: The manuscripts agree almost unanimously on this reading. All editions, by contrast, read: “The mother loved her son and, contrary to the affection of pious love, wanted the son to be sent away.” Again, where our text, together with all editions and some manuscripts, reads, “And therefore, because …,” many more codices omit the words “therefore … nevertheless” and the verb “gave.” The sense is not bad, provided the transposition of the words is restored as follows: “And because the good mother bestowed a blessing on both sons”—which should have been supplied—“she gave the blessing that she could preserve for the younger son.”] The mother loved her son; for she preferred that he be exiled from herself rather than from God. And because she was a good mother, she bestowed a blessing on both sons; yet she gave the younger son the blessing she could preserve. For she preferred not son to son, but the diligent to the idle and the faithful to the faithless. Yet she also did no little good for the elder son himself by sending the younger away, lest he commit fratricide.

101. And so, since he was an exile from his parents because of piety, not because of wrongdoing, he spoke with God and increased in wealth, children, and grace. Nor was he elated by these things when he met his brother; rather, he humbled himself and bowed down—not indeed to that harsh, furious, degenerate man, but to the one whom he discerned in his brother. Therefore he bowed seven times, [Note: The holy Doctor calls seven the number of remission because of the Sabbath day and the year of Jubilee; he treats this mystical interpretation of the number in so many places that scarcely anything else occurs more frequently in his writings.] namely, with the number of remission, because he was not bowing to a human being but to the one whom he foresaw in the spirit as coming in human flesh to take away the sins of the world (John I, 29). This mystery is disclosed to you by Peter’s reply, when he says: “If my brother sins against me, how often shall I forgive him? Up to seven times?” (Matt. XVIII, 21). You see that the remission of sins is a type of that great Sabbath, that perpetual rest of grace; and therefore it is bestowed in contemplation of it.

102. But what does it mean that he also arranged his wives, children, and all his possessions, and ordered them also to bow down upon the ground (Gen. XXXIII, 6)? Not, surely, that element which is often filled with blood, in which is the workshop of crimes, or which often bristles with vast rocks, precipitous cliffs, or barren and sterile soil; but that flesh which was to become a protection for us. And perhaps this is the mystery which the Lord taught you when he said: “Not only seven times, but also seventy times seven” (Matt. XVIII, 22).

103. You too, therefore, forgive your injuries, so that you may be sons of Jacob (Col. III, 13). Do not become embittered like Esau. Imitate holy David, who, like a good teacher, left us an example to imitate, saying: “In return for loving me, they slandered me; but I prayed” (Ps. CVIII, 4); and when he was cursed, he prayed. Prayer is a good shield: by it insult is shut out, a curse is repelled, and it is often turned back upon those who cursed, so that they are wounded by their own weapon: “They will curse,” he says, “but you will bless” (ibid., 28). One should court the curse of men when it wins the Lord’s blessing.

104. Finally, beloved, consider that Jesus suffered outside the gate (Heb. XIII, 12), and you too go out from this earthly city, because your city above is Jerusalem. Live there, so that you may say: “But our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III, 20). Therefore Jesus went out from the city [Note: Some manuscripts read, “so that we may be above the world.”] so that, going out from this world, you might be above the world. Moses alone, who saw God, had the tabernacle outside the camp when he spoke with God (Exod. XXXIII, 7 ff.); and although the blood of the sacrifices made for sin was brought to the altars (Exod. XXIX, 12–13), their bodies were burned outside the camp, because no one situated within the vices of this world lays aside sin, nor is his blood acceptable to God unless he comes out from the defilement of this body.

105. Love hospitality, through which holy Abraham [Note: The old editions read, “found favor.” By receiving the son as a guest, Sarah deserved to bear a son; some manuscripts read, “he found Christ, received him as a guest, and Sarah deserved a son”; the remaining manuscripts and the Roman edition have the reading given in the text.] found favor (Gen. XVIII, 3 ff.), received Christ as a guest, and deserved a son from Sarah when she was already worn out by old age. Lot too escaped the fire of the destruction of Sodom (Gen. XIX, 2 ff.). You too can receive angels if you offer your hospitality to those who arrive. What shall I say of Rahab, who by this service found salvation (Josh. II, 1 ff.)?

106. Show compassion to those held bound in chains, as though you were bound with them. Comfort those placed in mourning: “It is better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of joy” (Eccl. VII, 3). In the former, the merit of good service is credited; in the latter, the fault of a fall. Finally, there you hope for a reward; here you have already received it. Feel for those who suffer as though you were suffering together with them.

[Col. 1218A] 107. Let a wife show deference to her husband, not serve him as a slave. Let her offer herself to be guided, not coerced. She is unworthy of marriage who is worthy of quarrels. Let the husband likewise guide his wife like a helmsman, honor her as a companion in life, and share with her as a fellow-heir of grace.

108. Mothers, wean your children and love them; but pray for them that they may be long-lived upon the earth, not in the earth but above the earth. For nothing is long-lived in this land; and whatever lasts long is brief and more slippery. Advise them to take up the Lord’s cross rather than love this life.

109. [Note: Everything contained in this entire section and in the first part of the following one was taken, almost word for word, from Book X on Luke, section 129, and the three following sections.] Mary, the mother of the Lord, stood before her son’s cross; no one taught me this except holy John the Evangelist (John XIX, 25). Others recorded that the world was shaken during the Lord’s passion, that heaven was covered with darkness (Matt. XXVII, 45), that the sun withdrew, and that the thief was received into paradise after his pious confession (Luke XXIII, 43). John taught what the others did not: how, as he hung upon the cross, he addressed his mother, considering it more important that, having conquered his sufferings, he should perform the duties of piety toward his mother than that he should grant the heavenly kingdom. For if the pardon granted to the thief is an act of piety, much richer piety is shown in the way the mother is honored by her son with such affection: “Behold,” he says, “your son … Behold, your mother” (John XIX, 27). From the cross Christ bore witness and divided the duties of piety between mother and disciple. The Lord was composing not only a public but also a domestic testament, and John, worthy as witness of so great a testator, sealed his testament. It was a good testament—not of money, but of eternal life—not written with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God, who says: “My tongue is the pen of a swiftly writing scribe” (Ps. XLIV, 2).

110. Nor was Mary less than was fitting for the mother of Christ. When the apostles had fled, she stood before the cross and watched her son’s wounds with pious eyes, because she was awaiting not the death of her child but the salvation of the world. Or perhaps, because the royal palace had learned that through her son’s death came the redemption of the world, she thought that by her own death she too might add something to the public offering. But Jesus did not need an assistant for the redemption of all, since he saved all without an assistant. Hence he also says: “I have become like a man without help, free among the dead” (Ps. LXXXVII, 5). He did indeed receive the affection of a parent, but he did not seek another’s help.

111. Imitate her, holy mothers, who in her only and dearly beloved son displayed so great an example of maternal virtue. For you do not have children dearer to you, [Note: A considerable number of manuscripts read, “nor did the Virgin seek any consolation …”] nor did the Virgin seek the consolation of being able to bear another son.

112. Command your servants, not as though they were subject to you by condition, but remembering that they are sharers in the same nature as you. [Note: The Roman edition reads, “that you are fellow-sharers”; perhaps this is a compositor’s error, propagated into all subsequent editions.] (1 Pet. II, 18). Servants too, serve your masters willingly; for each person ought patiently to accept the condition in which he was born. Obey not only good masters but also harsh ones. For what credit is there in your servitude if you diligently serve good masters? But if you also win the approval of harsh ones, there is credit. Free people too receive no reward when they are punished by judges for wrongdoing; the reward comes when they are punished even though they have not sinned. So you too, in contemplation of the Lord Jesus, even if you serve difficult masters, will receive a reward if you do so patiently. For the righteous Lord himself suffered at the hands of the unjust, and with wondrous patience fastened our sins to his cross, so that whoever imitates him may wash away his own sins with his own blood.

113. In sum, turn yourselves all to the Lord Jesus. Let there be in you delight in this life through a good conscience, patience in death with hope of immortality, assurance of resurrection with the grace of Christ, truth with simplicity, faith with confidence, abstinence with holiness, diligence with sobriety, conduct with modesty, learning without vanity, sobriety of doctrine, and faithfulness without the drunkenness of heresy. [Note: The old edition, together with many manuscripts, reads, “sobriety of faithful doctrine without the drunkenness of heresy”; with these words they conclude the letter. The Roman edition, together with the remaining codices, agrees with our text, except that in some manuscripts “of Christ” is absent.] The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen.

[Col. 1219]

## SECOND CLASS (C)

[Col. 1219]

### 1049 EPISTLE LXIV

[Col. 1219B] To Irenaeus, who asks why the manna that once rained upon the Israelites does not rain upon Christians, Ambrose replies that the manna was a type of the Lord’s body and therefore, once this present reality was given, the former disappeared. He adds that it also contained an image of wisdom, which is the true food of souls and whose subtlety is commended from various passages of Scripture.

**AMBROSE TO IRENAEUS, GREETING.**

1. You ask me why the Lord God rained manna upon the people of the fathers and does not now rain it. If you understand, he does rain it, and every day he rains manna from heaven upon those who serve him. That bodily manna indeed (De Consecratione, distinction 2, chapter *Corporeum*) is found today in many places, but now it is no longer so great a miracle, because what is perfect has come. The perfect bread, however, is the bread from heaven, the body from the Virgin, about which the Gospel teaches you sufficiently. How much greater are these things than those former ones! [Note: Everything from the first words of this epistle through “superioribus” is cited by Lanfranc, *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, chapter 18, to prove Christ’s substantial presence in the Eucharist.] For those who ate that manna, that is, that bread, died; but whoever eats this bread will live forever (John VI, 5).

2. But there is also spiritual manna, that is, a spiritual rain of wisdom, which is poured from heaven upon the gifted and those who seek it; it bedews the minds of the devout and sweetens their throats. Whoever therefore understands the infusion of divine wisdom delights in it, seeks no other food, and lives not by bread alone but by every word of God (Matt. IV, 4). Whoever is more inquisitive asks what this thing is that is sweeter than honey. The minister of God answers him: “This is the bread that God gave you to eat” (Exod. XVI, 15–16). What this bread is, hear: “The word,” he says, “which God ordained.” This ordinance of God, then, this nourishment, feeds the soul of the wise, enlightens it and sweetens it, shining with the flash of truth and soothing it as with a honeycomb, with the sweetness both of various virtues and of the word of wisdom. “The words of the good are honeycombs,” as it is written in Proverbs (Prov. XVI, 24).

3. But receive the reason why it is small: [1050] because the mustard seed too is small, and it is compared with the kingdom of heaven (Luke XIII, 19); and faith, which is like a mustard seed, can remove mountains and cast them into the sea (Luke XVII, 6). The kingdom of heaven is also like leaven, which a woman hid in three measures of flour until the whole was leavened (Luke XIII, 21). Moses also ground the head of the golden calf as fine as dust, cast it into the water, and gave the people to drink (Exod. XXXII, 20); for their heart had been thickened by the enormity of their faithlessness, so that it might be softened and take on the fineness of faith. Finally, the woman who has ground well will be taken up, but the one who has ground badly will be left behind. [Note: The Roman edition prefixes these words: “Behold, it was fine upon the surface of the desert, like coriander”; they are absent from the other editions and manuscripts.]

4. Grind your faith finely, then, so that you may be like that soul which awakens Christ’s love within itself, which the heavenly powers marvel to see ascending; so that it may ascend without stumbling and rise from this world with joy and gladness, like a vine-shoot, and like smoke lift itself upward, burning with the fragrance of a holy resurrection and with the sweetness of faith, as you have it written: “Who is this who comes up from the wilderness like a vine-shoot, like smoke kindled and perfumed with myrrh and frankincense, with every powder of the perfumer?” (Song III, 6). [Note: Some manuscripts read, “perfumed with the fragrant smoke of incense.”]

[Col. 1220D] 5. Beautifully he expressed its subtlety by comparing it with powder and mentioning perfume, [Note: The Roman edition alone adds: “because in Exodus we read of a finely compounded incense; but that is prophetic incense.”] because in Exodus we read of something fine (Exod. XXX, 8), and because that incense, compounded from many ingredients, is prophetic incense, namely, the prayer of the saints, so that it may be directed before the Lord, as David also says: “Let my prayer be directed like incense before you” (Ps. CXL, 2). Indeed, the Greek says: Κατευθυνθήτω ἡ προσευχή μου ὡς θυμίαμα ἐνώπιόν σου—“Let my prayer be directed like incense before you.” And in the Apocalypse of John we read that an angel stood before the altar, holding a golden censer, and that much incense was given to him from the prayers of all the saints. “And the smoke of the incense of the prayers of the saints,” he says, “rose from the angel’s hand before God” (Rev. VIII, 3–4).

6. The navel and the belly of the soul that ascends to Christ are also subtle; therefore it is praised in the bridegroom’s words: “Your navel is a turned goblet, never lacking mixed wine; your belly is a heap of fine wheat among lilies” (Song VII, 2). [Note: The same reading is found in the Roman edition: “a heap of fortified wheat”; the sacred Scriptures support that reading. On the other hand, not only the manuscripts and editions of Ambrose oppose it, but also the reasoning of Ambrose’s own sense. For the bride’s belly would not be shown to be subtle by being compared with a heap of fortified wheat, but by being compared with a heap of fine and delicate wheat.] For in every teaching there is a turning, and a spiritual drink that does not fail in fullness, together with knowledge of heavenly mysteries. The belly of the soul is also mystical, like the navel: through this belly it takes in not only strong food, by which hearts are strengthened, but also sweet and flowering food, by which they are delighted. Perhaps Moses also taught this through many prayers, and that sacrilege was to be softened by devout petitions.

7. In the Book of Kings also, when the Lord revealed himself to holy Elijah, a voice of a gentle breeze went before him, and immediately the Lord revealed himself to him (III Kings XIX, 12), so that we may understand that bodily things are thick and heavy, while spiritual things are soft and subtle, so that they cannot be grasped by the eyes. Indeed, the spirit of wisdom is also read to be subtle and mobile in the Book of Wisdom (Wis. VII, 22), for in her there is a spirit of understanding, holy, unique, manifold, subtle, and mobile; it first grinds her words, lest anything offend either in thought or in speech. Finally, when that Babylon is destroyed, what will be said? “The sound of the millstone will no longer be heard in you” (Rev. XVIII, 22). [Note: This is the reading of the old edition and most manuscripts. The Roman edition alone has “which will be destroyed”; but, together with the ancient edition and some manuscripts, the text says “when it is destroyed.”]

8. This manna, then, was subtle and was gathered for the day; it was not kept for the following day, because discoveries of wisdom are more pleasing when found at the proper time, and those things discovered over a period of time are not as wondrous as those poured forth by the living quickness of the present mind. Or perhaps it was because future mysteries were being revealed: the manna that had been kept until sunrise could no longer be eaten—that is, it could retain its efficacy only until Christ’s coming. But when the Sun of righteousness rose, and the more splendid sacraments of Christ’s body and blood shone forth, the inferior things would cease, and those perfected things would be given to the people to consume. Farewell, and love us, because we too love you.

### EPISTLE LXV

To Simplicianus, who wishes to know why the blood of the sacrifices was poured partly upon the altar and partly into bowls, Ambrose courteously replies that the part with which the altar was drenched signifies knowledge of the mysteries, while the part poured into bowls signifies knowledge of conduct. He further explains that Christ’s coming, by which he instructed us in both disciplines and redeemed everyone with his own blood, was prefigured in the same sacrifice.

**AMBROSE TO SIMPLICIANUS, GREETING.**

1. You told me that you were perplexed when you read what Moses did after offering sacrifice and slaughtering peace-offerings to the Lord: he put half the blood into bowls and poured half upon the altar (Exod. XXIV, 6). [Note: Baronius appears to rely chiefly on these words in his *Life of Ambrose* to show that Simplicianus was sent by Damasus, Roman Pontiff, to Milan as soon as he learned of Ambrose’s ordination, so that he might serve the new bishop—who had been raised from the administration of the province to the episcopal office—in the place of a father and teacher. Although inferior in rank to his disciple, Baronius says, Simplicianus adopted this method of educating him: he did not act as a teacher but presented himself as though he were his disciple’s disciple, proposing certain questions from sacred Scripture to test his intellectual powers, like an eagle challenging its young to fly. The same Cardinal repeats this account in nearly identical terms in the *Annals* under the years 375 and 385; Ughellus, Ripamontius, and others followed him. Yet although we learn from Augustine’s *Confessions* VIII.2 that Simplicianus lived at Rome under Constantius and contributed to the conversion of the rhetor Victorinus, it cannot be inferred from this either that he was born at Rome or that he was a presbyter of the Roman Church, much less that Damasus sent him to educate Ambrose. Further, even if we granted that Simplicianus’s letter to our saint was written at the beginning of his episcopate, it would by no means follow that Simplicianus wrote it with the intention of teaching him, since he likewise proposed questions to Augustine when the latter had recently been elected to the same dignity, without thereby deciding to assume the role of teacher toward him. The following facts alone are therefore certain concerning that holy old man: that he had served God from his earliest years; that he was highly learned in divine letters; that he traveled through various regions to acquire that knowledge; and finally that he stood to Ambrose as a father in receiving the grace—whether because he instructed him in the first elements of the faith at Rome, or because at Milan, when Ambrose was still a catechumen about to be consecrated bishop, he prepared him to receive consecration properly and piously. Paulinus recounts how he succeeded Simplicianus in the episcopate.] But what is the reason that you yourself are uncertain and ask this of us, when you have traveled through the whole world for the sake of faith and of acquiring divine knowledge, and have devoted all the time of this life to daily reading by night and day, embracing even intelligible things with your keen intellect—especially since you are accustomed to demonstrate how far the books of philosophy have strayed from truth, and how empty many of them are, so that the discourse of their authors in their writings gives out before their life does?

2. Nevertheless, because the exchange of speech, like the exchange of money, is of great use, and the greatest progress toward the common profit of commerce is achieved by it, I cannot keep silent about how marvelous this division of the blood is. One part appears to signify the moral discipline of wisdom, the other the mystical. That which is put into the bowls is moral; that which is poured upon the altar is mystical, because by a divine gift and a kind of inspiration it is poured into human minds, so that they may think about God in ways that are fitting and full of faith.

3. Indeed, those who have spoken of his majesty and of heavenly things—whether apostles or holy prophets—have dared to speak only from revelation shown to them. Hence Paul testified in his letter that he had been caught up into paradise and had heard words that it is not lawful for a human being to speak (II Cor. XI, 4). Stephen also saw the heavens opened and Jesus standing at the right hand of God (Acts VII, 55); and the prophet David saw him seated [Col. 1223B] (Ps. CIX, 1). For why should I speak of Moses, concerning whom Scripture says that no prophet has arisen again in Israel like Moses, who knew the Lord face to face, in all the signs and wonders that he performed in the land of Egypt (Deut. XXXIV, 10–11)? [Note: The manuscripts agree almost unanimously on this reading. The editions, by contrast, have “and Isaiah the prophet.” It is more probable, however, that the editors inserted “Isaiah” because in that prophet, chapter VI, verse 1, we clearly find: “I saw the Lord seated,” and because David was substituted by scribes for Isaiah, to whom Ambrose’s passage refers more obscurely.]

4. Mystical wisdom, therefore, is offered to God, who, by the splendor of divine wisdom—of which he is the father and begetter—kindles the soul’s vigor and illumines the mind. The wisdom of God is Christ, in whose breast John reclined (John XIII, 25), so that he might be shown to have drawn divine mysteries from that primary and secret source of wisdom. Indeed, he himself, conscious of the gift, wrote this: he feared to claim for himself what he had received and to attribute it to his own genius. The Lord himself also said to the apostles, opening his mouth: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John XX, 22); [Col. 1223C] by this he declared that he was the one who had said to Moses: “I will open your mouth and instruct you what you must say” (Exod. IV, 12). Thus this divine wisdom, inexpressible, unmixed, and incorrupt, pours its grace into the souls of the saints and reveals knowledge, so that they may contemplate its glory. [1053]

5. The moral discipline of wisdom, however, is that which is sent into the bowls and received and drawn from them. The bowls, therefore, are receptacles of the senses. The two eyes are bowls; so are the ears, the nostrils, the mouth, and the other parts suited to their functions. The eyes receive and provide sight, the ears hearing, the nostrils smell, the mouth taste, and so forth. Into these bowls the Word, in whom is the primacy of priesthood or prophecy, pours portions of his blood, so that he may give life to and animate the irrational parts and make them rational.

6. Finally, after he had enumerated and proclaimed to the people the precepts of the Law, and was about to speak of the contemplation of that intelligible ark of the testimony, or of the lampstand, [Note: Some manuscripts and the old edition read “or of the incense altar”; others, together with the Roman edition, read “or of the incense altar-vessel.”] he slaughtered victims and offered them, pouring part of the blood upon the sacred altars and putting part into bowls (Exod. XXV, 31 ff.).

[Col. 1224A] 7. Thus there is a division of that mystical, that is, divine and moral, wisdom. Λόγος (*logos*) is the divider of souls and virtues; the *logos*, that is, the powerful and sharp word of God, passes through and penetrates to the division of the soul, and also distinguishes and divides virtues (Heb. IV, 12). Moses, its minister, distinguished the kinds of virtues by the division of the blood.

8. And because nothing is announced in the Law above all else except Christ’s coming, and his passion is prefigured, see whether this is not the saving victim which the Word, God, offered in himself and sacrificed in his own body. First he taught moral discipline in the Gospel, and also in the Law; he displayed it in his patience and in the very act and work of his life, pouring into our conduct and senses—as into bowls—a certain substance, and the very life-giving elements of wisdom, by which he enlivened human minds for the sowing of virtue and the institutions of piety. Then, approaching the altar, he poured out the blood of his victim.

[The supplied source ends here, mid-sentence.]

9. Accordingly, whether you understand these things in this way, the pious interpretation is, as I think, this; or whether you prefer to follow Solomon, the meaning agrees equally well: since the prophet Moses poured blood into bowls, you should recognize that it is the very blood of which it is written that Wisdom mixed her wine in a bowl (Prov. IX, 2), saying that they should abandon folly and seek wisdom. Wisdom is therefore drawn from the bowl; discipline is drawn, understanding is drawn, correction is drawn, reform of life is drawn, moderation of character and counsels is drawn, the grace of piety, the increase of virtue, the fountain of abundance.

[Col. 1224C] 10. As for his pouring the blood upon the altar, [Note: [Col. 1224D] So the manuscripts; the editions, however, read: “it is possible to understand.”] it is possible to understand this as the washing of the world, the remission of all sins. For he pours that blood upon the altar like a sacrifice, to drain away the sins of many. The Lamb is indeed a sacrifice—but not a lamb of irrational nature, rather one of divine power—of whom it was said: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John I, 29). For he not only cleansed the sins of all by his blood, but also bestowed forgiveness by divine power. Does it not seem to you that he poured out his blood, from whose side water and blood flowed above the very altar of his Passion (John XIX, 34)? Farewell, and love us with the affection of a parent, as you do.

## LETTER LXVI

[Col. 1224D] After praising letters, especially those composed on a useful subject, he teaches that by Aaron’s melting the women’s earrings into the head of the calf is signified the removal of the seal of faith from the serpent’s blasts, and that the idolatry of the Jews was foreshadowed; while by Moses’ crushing the calf after breaking the tablets is indicated the destruction of pride and faithlessness. Finally, by his ordering them to rage against their neighbors, we are admonished to put religious duty before our kinsmen and to cut away whatever in us resists God.

### AMBROSE TO ROMULUS

1. There is no doubt that the kind of letter was invented so that we might in some fashion converse with those who are absent. Yet this practice becomes more beautiful through use and example when frequent and delightful conversations are exchanged between parent and children; [Note: [Col. 1225C] Some manuscripts and certain Paris editions read *alloquia cudantur* (“conversations may be forged”); the Roman edition alone has *alloquia conferantur* (“conversations may be exchanged”); many other manuscripts and the old editions have *alloquia caedantur* (“conversations may be cut”). Ambrose had already used this expression in Letter 37, §1; as Nannius observes, it imitates Terence: “But meanwhile,” says the comic poet, “while we cut conversations”; although some also read “forge conversations.” Thus far he.] so that, though separated in body, a certain likeness of presence may truly be reproduced. Through such services love grows, [Note: [Col. 1225D] Not a few manuscripts read: “if by your [lacuna] it is increased by letters”; one reads: “may it be increased by letters,” a reading that is not displeasing.] just as it is increased by your letters to me or mine to you. But I have begun to experience this much more richly in the recent utterances of your affection, by which you thought it necessary to consult me about the meaning of Aaron’s taking gold from the people when they asked him to make gods for them; about the fact that the head of a calf was fashioned from that gold; and about Moses’ being so harshly indignant that he ordered each man to rise up with his sword for the death of his neighbor (Exod. XXXII, 2 ff.). For it is a great thing to allow no loss to intrude upon those who are absent—not merely a loss of affection, but also of shared and generous knowledge. Since, then, you ask what I think about this, I shall speak more in the spirit of sharing than of explaining.

2. While Moses was receiving the Law on Mount Sinai, the people were with Aaron the priest. Although they were often prone to sin, they are not shown to have fallen into sacrilege as long as the Law was being given. But when the divine oracle fell silent, sin crept in, and they asked that gods be made for them. [Note: [Col. 1225D] The Roman edition alone reads: “For they say thus: ‘Rise and make gods for us who shall go before us.’ Therefore, being compelled…”] Aaron, being compelled, asked for their rings and the women’s earrings. He put what was handed over into the fire, and the head of a calf was cast.

[Col. 1225C] 3. We can neither wholly excuse so great a priest nor dare to condemn him. Yet he was not without prudence when he took away the rings and earrings from the Jews; for those who were plotting sacrilege could possess neither the seal of faith nor ornaments for their ears. Finally, the patriarch Jacob also hid the earrings together with the idols of the nations when he concealed them at Shechem (Gen. XXXV, 4), so that no one might hear the superstitions of the Gentiles. Beautifully, then, he said: “Put away the rings and the golden earrings [Note: [Col. 1225D] So the old edition and many manuscripts; some give only “which belong to the women,” while the Roman edition preferred: “which are in the ears of your women.” Nannius discusses this passage as follows: “I was often troubled by the question why Jacob buried earrings, so utterly foreign to idolatrous worship, together with the idols. But our Hebrew scholar Andreas of Balen relieved me of this scruple by answering that the earrings there are so called because priests cover their ears with them in the worship of a deity, like the fillets among the Romans. Nevertheless, we would prefer to understand them as earrings dedicated to some deity and marked with its image or with the figure of a heavenly body”; on this, consult Grotius on the same passage.] which are the earrings of your women” (Exod. XXXII, 2)—not because he would leave the men’s earrings untouched, but because he was showing that men did not have them. It was also fitting that the earrings should be taken away from the women, lest Eve hear the serpent’s voice again.

4. And because they had listened to sacrilege, when their earrings were melted, the image of sacrilege was melted; for one who listens wrongly is accustomed to forge sacrilege. But why the head of a calf emerged, the following events show: it signified what Jeroboam would later introduce, this kind of sacrilege, so that the Hebrew people might worship [Note: [Col. 1226C] All editions and some manuscripts read “golden calves”; many other and better manuscripts read “golden heifers.” The Israelites had inherited this madness of worshiping cattle from the long-standing Egyptian practice of venerating Apis or Serapis under the form of a bull.] golden heifers (III Kings XII, 30); or else because every act of faithlessness has the same monstrous character and bestial folly.

5. Provoked by the disgrace of this deed, Moses broke the tablets, crushed the calf’s head, and reduced it to dust, so that every trace of impiety might be destroyed. [Col. 1226B] [Note: [Col. 1226D] The Roman edition alone reads: “For he says: ‘Moses, angry with anger, threw the two tablets from his hands and broke them beneath the mountain; and taking the calf they had made, he burned it with fire and crushed it,’ and so forth. The first tablets were therefore broken.”] For the first tablets were broken so that the second might be restored; through the preaching of the Gospel, faithlessness was crushed and vanished. Thus Moses dispersed that Egyptian arrogance—*typhus* [Note: [Col. 1226D] Among ecclesiastical authors, *typhus* means pride and arrogance. The word τῦφος (*typhos*), from which it derives, properly means “smoke.”]—and restrained that height which exalted itself, by the authority of the eternal Law. Hence David also says: “The Lord will break the cedars of Lebanon and crush them like the calf of Lebanon” (Ps. XXVIII, 5–6).

6. Therefore the people swallowed up all faithlessness and pride, lest impiety and arrogance swallow them. For it is better that each person prevail over the flesh and its vices, so that it may not be said of him that “death, prevailing, has swallowed him up” (Isa. XXV, 8), but rather: “Death has been swallowed up in victory. Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting?” (I Cor. XV, 54–55). And it was said of the Lord: “He shall drink from the torrent on the way” (Ps. CIX, 7), because he accepted vinegar in order to swallow up the temptations of all.

7. But when he caused neighbors to be killed by neighbors, sons by parents, brothers by brothers, the command was clear: religious duty must be preferred to kinship, piety to familial closeness. For true piety is that which places divine things before human things, and eternal things before temporal ones. Hence Moses himself [Note: [Col. 1226D] So the old edition and all the manuscripts, except that some read *ad Dominum* (“to the Lord”) instead of *a Domino* (“from the Lord”). The Roman edition completely recast the passage as follows: “Moses said: ‘If anyone is for the Lord, let him come to me.’ And all the sons of Levi gathered to him; and he said … ‘Pass through, and return from gate to gate throughout the camp; and let each man kill his brother and each his neighbor,’” and so forth.] said to the sons of Levi: “Whoever is ready from the Lord, let him come to me.” And he said to them: “Thus says the Lord God of Israel: Let each man put his sword upon his thigh and pass through” (Num. XVIII, 6); [Col. 1227A] so that, through contemplation and love of divine reverence, every affection of kinship might be destroyed. Three thousand men are indeed said to have been killed, and we are not moved by aversion to the number; for it is better that all be freed through the punishment of a few than that vengeance be inflicted upon all. Nor does anything harsh seem involved when the vengeance is for an offense against heaven.

8. Finally, the Levites’ ministry was chosen for this task as holier than the rest; God is their portion. For those who know nothing as their own do not know how to spare their own; to the holy, God is everything. There is also that true Levite, the avenger and defender, who puts the flesh to death in order to preserve the spirit; such was the one who said: “I chastise my body and bring it into subjection” (I Cor. IX, 27). What is nearer to the soul than the flesh? What is nearer than the passions of the body? The good Levite puts them to death within himself with the spiritual sword, which is the two-edged and powerful word of God (Hebr. IV, 12).

9. There is also the sword of the spirit, which passes through the soul, as was said to Mary: “A sword will pass through your own soul, so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed” (Luke II, 35). Is not the flesh joined to the soul by a kind of fraternal fellowship? Is not speech also akin and closely related to our mind? When, therefore, we restrain speech so that we do not fall into sin through excessive talking, we sever the right of brotherhood and dissolve the bond of fraternal kinship; and the soul likewise separates its irrational element, as something related to it, by the power of reason.

10. Thus Moses taught the people to rise up against their neighbors, through whom [Note: [Col. 1227D] Two manuscripts read “so that the power of faith might be restored”; two others, “so that faith and virtue might be restored.” But both these four manuscripts and nearly all the others omit *ut desecaretur* (“so that it might be cut away”), although these words are found in all the editions and add something to the coherence of the sense.] faith might be restored and virtue hindered, so that whatever in us was turned aside from virtue, confused by errors and entangled in vices, might be cut away. Through this discipline the people deserved not only to appease the divine indignation and avert the offense, but also to secure grace.

11. Since you consulted me, I have therefore expressed what we think according to our capacity. If you have anything better, [Note: [Col. 1227D] All editions read *nobis comparticipato* (“share it with us”); all manuscripts read *nobiscum participato* (“share it together with us”). Below, where all manuscripts and nearly all editions read *potius eligendum* (“rather to be chosen”), some Paris editions have *potius diligendum* (“rather to be loved”). Since Ambrose treats Romulus as a son while nevertheless indicating that he is skilled in Scripture, it is not difficult to suppose that he was either a deacon or, more likely, some priest entrusted with the administration of a rural church. Certainly, in the second letter addressed to him, he is explicitly said to live in the country.] share it with us, so that from you and from us we may learn what ought rather to be chosen and followed. Farewell, and love us as a son, since we also love you.

## 1057 LETTER LXVII

Having shown that Moses accepted Aaron’s excuse for his sons, the same passage is considered as implying that each person’s judgment concerning his own office is pre-eminent. From this it is inferred that true repentance is rare, for nature and shame hinder it, as does the speed of the emotions; moreover, it cannot take place unless desires have been extinguished and love of justice is vigorous. Hence Judas’s repentance was ineffectual, for God accepts no repentance unless it is sincere; this was represented figuratively by the three goats.

### AMBROSE TO SIMPLICIANUS, GREETING

1. How great each person is in his own office ought to be illustrated by the reading that rightly moved you: Moses, than whom no one saw God more directly (Num. XII, 8), nor did another prophet arise in Israel who saw God face to face as Moses did (Deut. XXXIV, 10); he who was continually with the Lord for forty days and nights when he received the Law on the mountain (Exod. XXXIV, 28); he, I say, to whom God gave the words he was to speak (Exod. IV, 12), is found to have approved Aaron his brother’s counsel rather than his own. Was there ever anyone more prudent and better instructed than Moses? Yet we read that Aaron himself later went astray with Miriam concerning the Ethiopian woman.

2. But examine carefully the point at which Moses surpassed Aaron in knowledge and the point at which Aaron surpassed him in counsel (Num. XII, 1). Moses was the great prophet who said of Christ: “You shall hear him as you hear me” (Deut. XVIII, 15). And concerning him the Lord himself said: “If they do not hear Moses and the prophets, neither will they believe if someone should rise from the dead and go to them” (Luke XVI, 31). Therefore, in a prophetic matter, Moses is preferred as a prophet; but where the matter, office, and duty of the priesthood are concerned, Aaron is preferred as priest. [Col. 1228C] Let us therefore examine the passage itself.

3. A goat had been sacrificed for sin and offered as a burnt offering. Moses later sought it, and it had been burned. Moses became angry with Aaron’s sons Eleazar and Ithamar, who had survived, and said: “Why did you not eat what was sacrificed for sin in the holy place? Since they are holy of holies, I have given this to you to eat, so that you may remove the sin of the congregation; and it must be eaten inside, as I was commanded,” he said. [Note: [Col. 1228D] Most manuscripts read: “what was sacrificed for sin in the place,” and so forth.] When Aaron saw that he was angry, he answered calmly: “If today they have offered their burnt offerings for their sin before the Lord, and such things have happened to me, shall I eat what they offered today for sin? Would it please the Lord?” Moses heard this, and it pleased him (Lev. X, 16 ff.). Let us consider what these things signify. [Note: [Col. 1228D] The Roman edition reads: “Since it is the holy of holies, this is what you must eat in the holy place.” And below: “the burnt offerings before the Lord.”]

4. [Note: [Col. 1228D] Philo the Jew, *On the Fugitives*: “To commit no sin at all belongs to God alone; to repent belongs to the wise person; but this is exceedingly difficult and hard to find.” Many other passages from the same work have been transferred into this letter.] To commit no sin belongs to God alone; to amend, correct an error, and repent of sin belongs to the wise. Yet this is difficult in human life. For what is rarer than finding a person who accuses himself and condemns his own deed? Confession of sin is therefore rare, repentance is rare, and the assertion of its reality among human beings is rare. Nature resists it, and shame resists it: nature, because all are under sin, and whoever bears flesh is liable to guilt. Thus the nature of the flesh and the enticement of the world resist innocence and integrity. Shame also resists it, because everyone is ashamed to confess his own fault while thinking more about present things than future ones.

5. Moses endeavored to find a soul free of sin, so that it might lay aside the spoils of error and depart naked of guilt, without any shame concerning itself. But he did not find one, because irrational impulse quickly rushes ahead, and a certain flame of exceedingly rapid movement devours the soul and burns up its innocence. Present things outweigh future things; violent things outweigh restrained things; many things outweigh the better; pleasant things outweigh serious ones; soft things outweigh harsh ones; joyful things outweigh sad ones; enticing things outweigh severe ones; and things done precipitately outweigh those done slowly. Iniquity is swift, for it suggests opportunities for wrongdoing: “their feet are swift to shed blood” (Ps. XIII, 3). Virtue, on the other hand, is slow and long-enduring, delaying; it judges beforehand and considers what it is about to undertake. Thus the mind, which watches over what is good, examines its own counsels and first tests what is seemly and honorable; but iniquity anticipates thought in action. [Note: [Col. 1229D] All editions read *opere cogitationem* (“in action, thought”); the manuscripts variously read *opera* or *opere* before *cogitationi* (“in action anticipates thought”).] Repentance, therefore, is sluggish and ashamed, because it is weighed down and recalled by shame over present things; it attends only to future things, whose hope is late and whose fruit is slower, and therefore its very request is slower.

[Col. 1229C] 6. In the midst of these efforts of hope and virtue, shamelessness runs ahead; by the appearance of present things repentance is excluded, its affection is, as it were, burned up, and such perception is obliterated. [Note: [Col. 1229D] The old edition and many manuscripts read *aboletur in vitiis* (“is destroyed amid vices”); the Roman edition and some other manuscripts read *aboletur invitus* (“is destroyed unwillingly”); Boyer and one Colbert manuscript more appropriately read *aboletur intuitus* (“the outlook is destroyed”).] The Law seeks repentance and does not find it; for it has been scorched by the heat and smoke of iniquity, and a certain indignation of the Law is aroused. Moses says that repentance ought to have been eaten in the holy of holies, and rebukes the priests as being too sluggish. Aaron replied that priestly judgment ought to be prudent, and that this office should not easily be entrusted to an unsound conscience, lest the error become worse than the first. For oil or wine is easily corrupted and spoiled in a foul vessel.

7. But how could sin be burned up when the fire was alien, and this under the gaze of the Lord, who knows even hidden things? Can it please the Lord if someone, while still living amid iniquities and holding injustice enclosed in his heart, says that he is repenting? It is like a sick person pretending to be well: he will become even sicker, because the pretense of health can do him no good; it is merely shaded by words and supported by no help of virtue.

8. Alien fire, therefore, is lust; alien fire is every blaze of unjust desire; alien fire is every burning of avarice. No one is cleansed by this fire; rather, he is burned up. For when this alien fire is present, if anyone presents himself before the Lord, heavenly fire consumes him, just as it consumed Abiud and Nadab together with the things that had been offered for sin upon the sacred altars. Whoever therefore wishes to cleanse his sin must remove alien fire from himself. Let him offer himself only to that fire [Note: [Col. 1229D] Some manuscripts read: “which burns up guilt in a person.”] which burns up guilt, not the person.

9. Hear what this fire is: “Jesus baptizes in the Holy Spirit and fire” (Matt. III, 11). This is the fire that dried up the flow of blood of the woman who had suffered hemorrhaging for twelve years (Matt. IX, 20). This is the fire that removed Zacchaeus’s sin when he said that he would give half of his possessions to the poor and, if he had taken anything from anyone, would restore it fourfold (Luke XIX, 8). This is the fire that wiped away the robber’s guilt; for it is a consuming fire, and it said to him: “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke XXIII, 43). It healed those in whom it found a simple and pure confession, with nothing malicious and nothing deceitful.

10. Finally, Judas could not reach the remedy when he said: “I have sinned in betraying innocent blood” (Matt. XXVII, 54), because he was carrying alien fire in his breast, and it inflamed him toward the noose. He was unworthy of a remedy because he did not turn inwardly and groan, nor did he practice repentance diligently. For the Lord Jesus is of such great mercy that he would have granted forgiveness even to him, if he had awaited Christ’s mercy.

11. [Note: [Col. 1230D] Observe that Ambrose here requires both a sincere conversion of heart in sinners in order to obtain forgiveness and true authority in priests to remit sin to those who are properly disposed.] Priests therefore do not remove this guilt, nor the sin of one who presents himself deceitfully and is still intent on wrongdoing. They cannot feast upon what is full of deceit and inwardly bears the scar of the serpent; for the priest’s food is the remission of sins. Hence Christ, the high priest, says: “My food is to do [Note: [Col. 1230D] The Roman edition alone reads: “the will of him who sent me.”] the will of my Father who is in heaven” (John IV, 34). And what is the will of God except this: “When you have turned back and groaned, then you shall be saved” (Isa. XXX, 15)? In that deceitful person, therefore, there is no food. Finally, neither can he himself taste the sweetness of the feast in whom there is no sincere and pure conscience; for the bitterness of deceit covers the sweetness of the feast, and a bad conscience does not permit repentance to refresh and nourish the guilty soul.

12. Therefore such an affection, such a request, and such repentance are neither useful nor pleasing to priests. And rightly that goat which was offered for sin as a burnt offering was burned, because it was not a sincere sacrifice (Lev. XVI, 27); for alien fire was found in its sacrifice. The sacrifice is therefore not pleasing or acceptable to God; nothing is acceptable except what has been tested in the riches of sincerity and truth.

13. Therefore elsewhere also you read of two goats: one on which fell the Lord’s lot, the other for removal; the one on which the Lord’s lot fell was to be offered and sacrificed for sin, but the one on which fell the lot for removal was to be sent into the desert, so that it might receive the iniquities of the people or of some sinner (Lev. XVI, 8 ff.). For just as there are two men in the field, one of whom will be taken and the other left (Matt. XXIV, 40), so there are two goats: one useful for sacrifice, the other sent into the desert. The latter is useful for nothing; it is neither to be eaten nor consumed at the priests’ feast. For just as among foods what is good is eaten and what is useless or bad is thrown away, so we call good works “feasting works” [Note: [Col. 1231D] So the old edition and many manuscripts; the Roman edition and several other manuscripts read: “which are useful.”], because they are fit to be eaten.

14. It will therefore not please the Lord if a priest eats a sacrifice in which there is deceit in the offering [Note: [Col. 1231D] The Boyer manuscript reads: “there is deceit in the offering.”] rather than the sincerity of earnest confession. This goat, therefore, must be sent into the desert, where our fathers wandered and erred, and could not reach the land of resurrection, but their memory perished from the earth. Finally, hear what works are fit for feasting: “The sabbaths of the land shall be food for you” (Lev. XXV, 6). For the repose that feasts and refreshes is rest in God, which produces tranquility of soul. Let us therefore also rest in discourse. Farewell, and love us as you do, because we love you.

## LETTER LXVIII

What God threatened against the Jews when he said:

“I will make the sky bronze and the earth iron.”

### AMBROSE TO ROMULUS

1. Since you are in the country, I am surprised that you thought you should ask me why God said: [Note: [Col. 1231D] The Roman edition reads: “I will make your sky like bronze and your land like iron.”] “I will make the sky bronze and the earth iron” (Deut. XXVIII, 23). For the very appearance of the countryside and its present fertility can teach us how great is the kindness of the air and the indulgence of heaven when God deigns to grant abundance; but when there is sterility, everything seems closed, the air thick, as though it had been hardened into the rigidity of bronze. Hence elsewhere you read that in the days of Elijah the heavens were closed for three years and six months (III Kings XVII, 1).

2. The meaning, therefore, is that the bronze sky is closed and denies the earth the use of its benefits. The earth too is iron when it refuses produce and, with hostile hardness, excludes the seeds cast into it from its fertile [Note: [Col. 1231D] All editions read: “excludes them from its womb”; all manuscripts read: “excludes them from the field.”] soil, which it is accustomed to cherish in the lap of a gentle mother. For when does iron bear fruit? When does bronze release rain?

3. He therefore threatens the impious with pitiable famine, so that those who do not know how to show the devotion of children to the common Lord and Father of all may lack the nourishment of the Father’s indulgence. Let the sky be bronze for them, with the air congealed and hardened into the rigidity of metal; let the earth be iron for them, knowing nothing of its offspring, [Note: [Col. 1231D] Erasmus and the editions following him read: “and what poverty usually has.” The Amerbach edition and most manuscripts read: “as impiety usually had”; some manuscripts have *habeat* (“has”); the Belvedere manuscript and several others read as in the text. But so that the passage may be understood more clearly, it seems to be constructed thus: “let it sow quarrels, as though it possessed what poverty usually has.”] sowing discord as poverty commonly does. For those who lack food make use of plunder, relieving their hunger at the expense of others.

4. Now if the offense of the inhabitants is such that, because of divine anger, battles are brought upon them, the earth is truly iron, [Note: [Col. 1232D] Nannius says that these words are composed from allusions to Virgil:

“The harvest bristles with drawn swords,
and the bronze weapons gleam.”] bristling with crops of weapons and stripped of its own fruits, fertile for punishment but barren for nourishment. But where is abundance? “Behold, I will rain bread upon you,” says the Lord (Exod. XVI, 4). Farewell, and love us, because we love you.

## 1061 LETTER LXIX

To one asking why the Law forbids men to wear women’s clothing and women to wear men’s clothing, he replies that this is contrary to nature, as can be understood even from animals; nevertheless, women’s adoption of men’s dress is more tolerable than men’s adoption of women’s attire. But the law, he says, concerns morals rather than clothing. After this he attacks those who curl their hair.

### AMBROSE TO IRENAEUS, GREETING

1. You have reported to me, as a son to his father, that certain people asked you what it means that the Law so severely called those unclean who wore the clothing of the opposite sex, whether men or women. For it is written: “There shall not be a man’s garment upon a woman, nor shall a man put on a woman’s robe; for everyone who does these things is unclean before the Lord your God” (Deut. XXII, 5). [Note: [Col. 1232D] The Roman edition reads: “There shall not be a man’s garment upon a woman, nor shall a man put on a woman’s robe, for everyone who does these things is unclean before the Lord your God,” and so forth.]

2. And if you examine the matter carefully, it is incongruous, something that nature herself rejects. Why do you not wish to appear to be what you were born to be? Why do you assume another’s appearance? Why do you pretend to be a woman—or you, woman, to be a man? Nature clothes each sex in its own garments. Finally, their use, color, movement, gait, [Note: [Col. 1232D] A large lacuna begins here in nearly all manuscripts and editions, after the words “different strength,” unless Erasmus supplied the missing text; only the Laet manuscript would otherwise offer assistance in restoring it.] strength, and voice are different in man and woman.

3. But among the other kinds of living creatures also, the appearance of a lion differs from that of a lioness, as do their strength and sound; a bull’s differs from a heifer’s. Among deer too, as greatly as the sexes differ, so greatly does their appearance differ, so that you can distinguish them even from a distance. Among birds, the comparison between them and human beings comes even closer with respect to clothing; in birds, natural coverings themselves distinguish the sexes. Male peacocks are splendid, while the females are not similarly adorned with the varied beauty of their feathers. Pheasants too have a different color distinguishing the sexes. What of chickens? How melodious is the cock’s voice, performing its customary duty in the watches of the night to awaken and to sing! Do these creatures change their appearance? Why do we desire to change ours?

4. And indeed, following Greek custom, it has become common for women to wear men’s garments, as though in shorter tunics. [Note: [Col. 1233D] Many councils prohibit women from using men’s clothing, such as the Council of Gangra, canon 13, and others. The reason why a similar change is not likewise found prohibited for men is that few men were thought likely to dishonor the dignity of their sex by such disgrace.] Yet suppose that women seem to imitate the nature of the superior sex: why do men wish to counterfeit the appearance of the inferior sex? A lie is shameful in speech, much more so in dress. Finally, in temples, where falsehood is opposed to faith, there is also falsehood against nature. There, for men to assume women’s [Note: [Col. 1233D] The Laet manuscript reads: “they wear a garment and feminine bearing, which is thought to be a woman’s sacred dress”; the reading in the edition is better. Between these three words the Roman edition alone has: “For everyone who does these things is unclean before the Lord your God—that is, a man,” and so forth.] clothing and feminine bearing is considered sacred. Hence the Law says that every man who puts on a woman’s robe is unclean before the Lord.

5. I think, however, that he spoke not so much about clothing as about morals, or about our customs and actions, so that one kind of action should befit a man and another a woman. Hence the Apostle, as an interpreter of the Law, says: “Let your women be silent in the churches” (I Cor. XIV, 34). They are not permitted to speak, but are to be submissive, as the Law says. If they wish to learn anything, let them ask their husbands at home (I Cor. XIV, 35–36). And to Timothy: “Let a woman learn in silence [Note: [Col. 1233D] The manuscripts’ lacuna ends with these words; Amerbachius prefixed: “The Apostle says: ‘Let a woman learn in silence.’”] with all submission. But I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man” (I Tim. II, 11–12).

6. How disgraceful it is for a man to perform women’s work! Let those who curl their hair like women also give birth—let them labor in childbirth. And yet women are veiled, while these men go to war. Let those have an excuse who follow the customs of their fathers, though barbarian customs, such as the Persians, Goths, and Armenians; but nature is greater than one’s homeland.

7. What shall we say about others who think this should be turned toward luxury, keeping attendants with curled hair and necklaces while they themselves wear long beards and let their hair flow? Chastity is rightly not preserved where the distinction of sex is not maintained. In this matter the teachings of nature are obvious, as the Apostle says: “Is it fitting for a woman without a veil to pray to God? Does not nature itself teach you that if a man has long hair it is a disgrace to him, but if a woman has long hair it is a glory to her, because hair has been given to her as a veil?” (I Cor. XI, 13–15). These are the things you should report to those who inquire. Farewell, and love us as a son, because we love you as parents.

## LETTER LXX

[Col. 1233D] Just as it is characteristic of a strong soul to stand firm in goodness, so it is characteristic of a weak one to fall and rise again. Therefore, whereas the progress of the stronger soul is described in the Song of Songs, the conversion of the fallen soul is described in the prophecy of Micah, which he proposes for consideration. After first interpreting the name Micah, he explains the misery of the sinful soul, recounts its inward corrections, adds exhortations and the Lord’s ready help, reveals its blessed transformation, and describes the fruitfulness and tranquility that Christ grants it. Then, after repeating a number of points from earlier discussions, he appends the same soul’s thanksgiving for its deliverance. After this he exhorts Horontianus to perseverance.

### AMBROSE TO HORONTIANUS

1. The prophets indeed announced the gathering of the nations and the future building of the Church. But since within the Church there is not only the continual progress of strong souls, but also the falling and subsequent conversion of the weak, we can therefore gather from the prophetic books how either that splendid and strong soul proceeds without any offense, or the weaker soul falls, or the fallen soul is restored and regains its step.

2. Just as in the Song of Songs we read of the continual advances of that blessed soul, so in Micah, concerning whom conversation with us arose, let us consider the conversion of the fallen soul. For you were not moved without reason by what was said by this prophet: “And you, Bethlehem, house of Ephrathah” (Mic. V, 2). How can there be a house of fury where Christ was born? This is what the names of the places express, but they illuminate the mysteries of their operations. [Note: [Col. 1234D] Ambrose explains and elucidates in *On Isaac and the Soul* the soul’s advances, obscurely sketched in the Song of Songs. When he says here that a conversation with Horontianus about Micah had arisen between them, he sufficiently indicates that the occasion for this letter came from that same conversation.]

3. First, let us consider what meaning “Micah” has in Latin. It signifies “Who is from God”; or, as we find elsewhere, “Who is this”—the son of Morathi, that is, “of the heir” (Mic. 1:1). But who is the heir except the Son of God, who says: “All things have been delivered to me by my Father” (Matt. 11:27)? And although he himself was the heir, he willed us to be co-heirs. Properly, then, “Who is this” means not one of the people, but one chosen for the grace of God, in whom the Holy Spirit speaks, who began to prophesy in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah (Mic. 1:1). This order signifies the progress of the vision: from evil kings it arrives at the times of a good king.

[Col. 1234D] **Note:** Thus the old edition and the Roman manuscripts. The Roman edition, however, reads “son of Morasthi, heir.” Ambrose is alluding to the opening words of this prophet: “The word of the Lord … to Micah the Morasthite,” by which not his father but his native land is indicated. Accordingly, “son of Morasthi,” or “son of Morathi”—for both forms are correctly written—means the same as “born at Morasthi.” As for the meaning of the name, Ambrose entirely agrees with Jerome in the Prologue to his exposition of this same prophecy: “Micah, ὄστις οὖν …, in our language means ‘who, as it were,’ or ‘who, like.’” Besides these interpretations, Micah is also explained as “humbled,” “struck,” and so forth.

[Col. 1234D] 4. And therefore, since the soul afflicted under evil kings previously suffered, it seems necessary to consider what course its conversion takes. It had been destroyed as though it were weaker, and all its fortification had become a road for passers-by and the onslaught of passions; loosened by luxury and crushed by pleasures, it had been banished from the face of the Lord. Its tower was squalid—that tower which, as we read in Isaiah’s song (Isa. 5:2), was set in the midst of a flourishing vineyard. For the tower is squalid when the vine withers, [Col. 1235D] and its sheep strays; but when the vine regains its greenness, or when the sheep returns, it shines forth. [Col. 1235D] **Note:** Some manuscripts read, “and its grape dries up,” and below, “it shines with the greenness of the grape.” Thus in the following passages “grape” is always substituted, but less correctly. Nothing is more squalid than iniquity, and nothing more radiant than righteousness.

[Col. 1234D] **Note:** Other meanings of the name Micah are indicated here. Besides being explained as “who is from God” or “who is this”—interpretations that, provided the first is written *quis adeo* (“who indeed”), rather than *quis a Deo* (“who is from God”), do not differ greatly from Jerome’s statement in the passage cited above, that “Micah, ὄστις οὖν …, in our language means ‘who, as it were,’ or ‘who, like’”—the name is also explained as “humbled,” “struck,” and so forth.

5. The sheep is recalled to this tower when the soul is recalled from its fall, and in that sheep the kingdom of Christ returns. This is the beginning, because he himself is the beginning and the end (Rev. 1:8), or the beginning of salvation. Yet the soul is first rebuked because it has gone so grievously astray, and it is told: “Why did you know evils? Was there not a king for you?” (Mic. 4:9). This means: You had a king to rule and protect you; you ought not to have strayed from the path of righteousness or abandoned the ways of the Lord, who bestowed rational understanding upon you. [Col. 1236D] **Note:** The Roman edition reads, “Or has your counsel perished?”—as though it said: “Where were …?” Where were your thoughts? Where were the plans by which, through the strength implanted in you, you could foresee injustice and drive away iniquities? “Why did pains seize you like a woman in labor?” (ibid.)—so that you might give birth to iniquities and bring forth injustices? No pain is greater than that which wounds the conscience with the sword-point of sin; nor is there any heavier burden than the load of sins and the weight of crimes. It presses down the soul and bends it toward the earth, so that it cannot raise itself up. Heavy, my son—exceedingly heavy—are the weights of sins. Finally, that woman in the Gospel who was bent over, presenting the figure of a suffering soul, could be raised up by Christ alone (Luke 13:11).

[Col. 1236D] **Note:** The Roman edition reads: “And grieve, daughter of Zion, like a woman in labor.”

6. To this soul, therefore, it is said: “Act manfully, [Col. 1236D] and draw near, daughter of Zion, that you may give birth” (Mic. 4:10). For the pains of a woman in labor produce tribulation, tribulation patience, patience testing, and testing hope; “but hope does not disappoint forever” (Rom. 5:3–4). Everything opposed to good morals is expelled and cast out together, lest its remaining seeds bear fruit and sprout again into new births.

7. [Col. 1236D] Nor are horns and hooves given to it without purpose, so that it may crush all the sheaves of the threshing floor, like the calf of Lebanon (Mic. 4:13). Unless the sheaves are crushed and the chaff winnowed, the inner fruit cannot appear or be released. Let the advancing soul therefore first break up and shake off the excesses of its passions, so that it may display its fruits in the very field. How many adversities there are that hinder good births! [Col. 1236A] These must first be uprooted, lest through them the fruitful sowings of the soul be destroyed.

[Col. 1236D] **Note:** The Roman edition reads: “I will make your horns iron, and I will make your hooves bronze.” “Nor without purpose …”

8. Then the provident counselor of the soul also sees to it that he confines it within its pleasures and blocks its desires, so that it may not delight in them. For the chastisements of a parent are useful when he does not spare the rod, so that he may make his son’s soul obedient to saving commands (Prov. 13:24). For the rod visits, as we read: “I will visit their iniquities with the rod” (Ps. 88:33). Thus he who strikes the cheek of the Israelite soul with the rod trains it in the discipline of patience through the Lord’s rebuke. No one who is chastised and reproved should despair; for “he who loves his son chastises him” (Ecclus. 30:1). Let no one lose hope in the remedy.

9. Behold: where the house of the one who sees fury was, there is the house of bread; where there was cruelty, there is mercy; where there was punishment of the innocent, there is the redemption of all, as it is written: “And you, Bethlehem, house of Ephrathah, are not least among the princes of Judah; for from you shall come forth a Ruler in Israel” (Mic. 5:2). Bethlehem is the house of bread; Ephrathah is the house of the one who sees fury. This is the meaning of these names. Christ was born of Mary in Bethlehem; and Bethlehem is the same as Ephrathah (Luke 2:6). Thus Christ was born in the house of fury; and therefore it is no longer the house of fury but the house of bread, because it received him who descended from heaven—the bread (John 6:50). Ephrathah is the house of the one who sees fury because, while Herod sought Christ there, he decreed that the infants should be killed; hence “a voice was heard in Ramah, Rachel weeping for her children” (Matt. 2:18).

10. But now let no one fear, because that rest which David sought (Ps. 131) was heard of in Ephrathah and found in the fields of the forest. At that time the gathering of the nations was still a forest; but after it believed in Christ, it became fruitful (Luke 1:42), because it received the fruit of the blessed womb. Rachel therefore died in childbirth (Gen. 35:19), because even then, like the wife of a patriarch, she saw Herod’s fury, which spared not even the tenderest age. At the same time, because in Ephrathah she gave birth to Benjamin—superior in appearance, but posterior in mystery—namely Paul, who before he was born caused his mother no small pains, persecuting her children. There she died and was buried [Col. 1236D], so that we, having died and been buried with Christ, might rise again in the Church. For by another interpretation Ephrathah signifies either “made fruitful” or “filled with fruits.”

11. [Col. 1236D] Here, that is, in the prophetic book, we find *ὀλιγοστὸς εἶ*—“you are among the few.” In Matthew, however: “And you, Bethlehem, house of Judah, are not among the few” (Mic. 5:2). There it is “house of Judah”; here, “house of Ephrathah.” The discrepancy is in the words, not in the meanings. For inner Judea saw the fury, and outer Judea endured it. “You are among the few,” because few are those who enter the house of bread by the narrow way. And “you are not among the few,” that is, among those who are progressing, because she did not recognize Christ.
