Nor is she least, being the house of blessing and the receptacle of divine grace; yet she is least in the eyes of one who seems to confer anything upon Christ. And whoever desires the Church desires Christ; for in every least person Christ is either harmed or honored, according to what he himself said: “Whatever you did for one of these least ones, you did for me” (Matt. 25:40).

[Col. 1236D] **Note:** Having resolved the principal difficulty—namely, how that town in which Christ chose to be born could be called the house of fury—Ambrose now turns to the divergent reading in which the text proposed in Micah and that in Matthew appear contradictory. After showing that the meaning of both statements beautifully agrees, rather than conflicts, he makes no effort to reconcile the details in which alone he claims the contradiction lies. Jerome, however, in his discussion of this same passage of Micah, notes the discrepancy with its citation in Matthew as it appears both in the Septuagint and in Hebrew, and investigates the causes of so great a difference. Consult him not only on this prophet but also in his letter to Pammachius on the best method of translating, and in his discussions of other interpreters.

[Col. 1237B] 12. That Bethlehem itself is Ephrathah is taught by the reading in Genesis, where it says: “Rachel died and was buried on the road to Ephrathah, which is Bethlehem” (Gen. 35:19). On the road [Col. 1237D] is the burial of holy Rachel, who was a type of the Church, so that passers-by might say: “The blessing of the Lord be upon you” (Ps. 128:8), and: “Those who come shall come with rejoicing” (Ps. 125:6).

[Col. 1237D] **Note:** Thus the majority of the better manuscripts; some others, as well as all the editions, read: “Holy Rachel was buried.”

13. Every soul, therefore, that receives that bread descending from heaven is a house of bread—that is, the bread of Christ—which is nourished by the strength of the heavenly bread dwelling within it and is strengthened in heart. Hence Paul also says: “For we are all one bread” (1 Cor. 10:17). Every faithful soul is Bethlehem, just as Jerusalem is said of the soul that possesses the peace and tranquility of the Jerusalem above, which is in heaven. He is the true bread who, when broken and crushed, [Col. 1237D] satisfies all.

[Col. 1237D] **Note:** The Roman edition alone reads “satisfies all.” The Fifth version … of the other versions. Elsewhere in the same edition the word *traditio* is similarly altered. [Col. 1238D] It should be noted that Ambrose is speaking in these passages of Origen’s Hexapla and Octapla, in connection with which Jerome, when discussing Micah 4, also uses the expression “the Fifth version.” In the same sense Epiphanius uses the word *ἔκδοσις* in *On Weights and Measures*, section 9, and elsewhere. Nevertheless, there is nothing to prevent Ambrose from having preferred the word *traditio* (“version” or “tradition”). On Origen’s Hexapla and Octapla, see Eusebius, Book VI, chapter 17, and Valesius’s notes on that passage, as well as Huet, Book III on Origen, section 4, and others.

14. The Fifth version has “house of bread.” *Beth* means “house,” and *leem* means “bread.” Because of Jewish unbelief, we think that the readings of the other versions were either omitted by the Jews themselves, lest they refute themselves, or removed by others.

15. That Bethlehem also belonged to the tribe of Judah is taught by the reading in the Book of Judges, because that Levite took for himself a concubine from Bethlehem of Judah, and his concubine became angry with him and returned to her father’s house in Bethlehem of Judah (Judg. 19:2).

16. [Col. 1238D] Christ’s going forth was therefore from the days of the world; for the world begins for us at the time when the day of salvation begins, and he went forth to set Israel on its course. [Col. 1238A] “Until the time of the woman in labor” (Ps. 18:7). When Christ comes to someone, fertility comes; birth comes (Mic. 5:3), just as it came to the Church, which bore more children than the woman who had children, and bore seven—that is, legitimate, tranquil, peaceful children. The soul therefore begins to conceive, and Christ is formed in it when it receives his coming and is nourished by his riches, so that nothing is lacking to it, and so that other souls, seeing it, may return to the way of salvation.

[Col. 1238D] **Note:** The Roman edition reads: “And his going forth is from the beginning, from the days of the world.”

17. “And he shall be peace” (Mic. 5:5), but this cannot be proved except through temptations. For then its peace and tranquility will be judged genuine when it has excluded or restrained vain thoughts; when it has subdued all the movements of rising passions; when distress, persecution, hunger, danger, and the sword have increased. [Col. 1238B] “Then,” he says, “there shall be peace,” because “in all these things we conquer through him who loved us,” since we trust that neither death [Col. 1238D] nor the power of temptations will tear us away from and separate us from his love (Rom. 8:35).

[Col. 1238D] **Note:** All editions and some manuscripts read “nor anything whatever of temptations”; other manuscripts of greater authority read “nor the power of temptations.”

Then he will give temptations so that the righteous may be tested. The Lord indeed gives temptations with the intention that he does not wish anyone to be deceived; but because most of the weak are overcome by temptations, those who are strong are tested.

18. Then there will be dew from the Lord for them (Mic. 5:7); then there will be rest. Then the soul of the righteous will be like a lion’s cub [Col. 1238D] in the sheepfolds of the flocks (ibid., 8). I would not hesitate to refer this to Christ by the Gospel example, because he said: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. 13:43). For his chariots—that is, the irrational impulses and movements of this body—will be restrained (Mic. 5:10). “Outward fightings, inward fears” (2 Cor. 7:5) will be quieted. There will be tranquility everywhere, both within and without; and no one will answer or resist the good will, because the obedience of the flesh, once the dividing wall of the barrier has been removed and the two have become one, will abolish all discord (Eph. 2:14).

[Col. 1238D] **Note:** The Roman edition alone reads “in the flocks of the sheep.”

19. But if any weak soul, like Israel according to the flesh, should stumble and, disturbed by persecutions, separate itself somewhat from that love of Christ, it is chastised and reproved [Col. 1238D] as faithless, ungrateful, and unbelieving—having been freed from the vanities of the world, yet having fallen back into them by looking toward them. From it he demanded neither gifts nor sacrifices of bulls, but only that [Col. 1239A] it should know the good and do justice. “It has been announced to you,” he says, “O man, what is good, or what the Lord requires of you, except to do judgment and justice, to love mercy, and to be ready to walk with your Lord?” (Mic. 6:8).

But because that weaker soul did not preserve these things, the Lord says: “Woe is me, for I have become like one who gathers straw at harvest and like a cluster of grapes at the vintage” (Mic. 7:1). Hearing these words, the prophet, in whom God was speaking, says to that soul: “Woe is me, O soul, [Col. 1239D] because one full of fear has not remained on the earth.” Or, if the Lord himself is speaking, he is pitying the punishments that would come because of sins and groaning over our errors.

[Col. 1239D] **Note:** The Roman edition reads: “Woe is me, O soul, because fear has perished from the earth”; the other editions and all the manuscripts have the wording of the text. The Greek, *ἀπώλωλεν εὐσεβής*, is not poorly rendered by Ambrose as “one full of fear has perished,” with “of God” understood.

20. Hearing this, the soul—because it will not gather the fruit of its seeds and, having lost the harvest, will find no support for itself—will press the olive but will have no oil of gladness, nor drink the wine of joy. It also recognizes that all things in the works of the flesh are full of bloodshed, full of deceit, fraud, falsehood, fabricated duties of piety, carefully composed pretenses, and that all who are in the house are its enemies. Therefore the movements of its own body, which are grave adversaries of our soul, must be guarded against. It turns, begins to hope in God, and, understanding that the flesh truly exists as its enemy, says to it: “Do not rejoice over me, my enemy, because I have fallen; but I shall rise. For if I sit in darkness, the Lord will enlighten me” (ibid., 8).

21. Considering also that some power was insulting it and resisting it, lest it follow a better path, [Col. 1239D] and riding upon it because it had been handed over to the destruction of the flesh (1 Cor. 5:5), so that it might be crushed by various evils—whether imposed by the Lord for the expiation of sins or by the wicked one out of envy of its conversion—the soul says further: “I will bear the wrath of the Lord,” who either chastises the one who has fallen or has given you power to afflict me; “because I have sinned, nevertheless I will bear it until he himself justifies my cause” (Mic. 7:9).

[Col. 1239D] **Note:** Some manuscripts read “and disturb it”; but “ride upon it” seems more characteristic of Ambrose.

Unless I confess and pay the price for my iniquities, I cannot be justified. But when I have been justified, paying double for my sins, [Col. 1239D] he will bring forth my judgment, setting aside his indignation, because satisfaction has been made to the sentence.

[Col. 1239D] **Note:** The Roman edition reads: “He will execute my judgment.”

He will bring me out into the light, so that I may see his righteousness (ibid.) and behold his delight. My enemy—that is, the devil’s wickedness—will see this light of my reconciliation, and will be covered with shame, she who now says: “Where is the Lord your God?” (ibid., 10). She will see his mercy in me; she will see his compassion.

22. Therefore, when we are in any adversity of the world—whether there is bodily pain, the loss of children, or that of other loved ones—let us not listen to him saying: “Where is the Lord your God?” I say, let us not listen. His temptations must be guarded against when grievous pain presses hard; then he strives to turn away the sick soul.

23. Therefore the soul that has not listened to him lying in ambush against it, later seeing the wonders of God, seeing itself in heaven while the devil creeps like a serpent on earthly ground, will rejoice and say: “Who is a God like you, taking away sins and transferring iniquities?” (ibid., 18). You did not remember your indignation, but as you plunged all our iniquities into the sea—like Egyptian lead—so you voluntarily returned to mercy, which you bestowed by a twofold gift: forgiving sins and concealing them, according to what is written: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered” (Ps. 31:1).

[Col. 1239D] **Note:** The Carolingian manuscript reads: “like the Egyptian people.” Immediately afterward Pratensis and Gembloux add: “and you restored mercy.”

For you wash away some sins by the blood of your Son, and you grant others to us, so that we may cover our errors with good works and confessions.

[Col. 1239D] **Note:** Observe that the holy Doctor does not say that sins are covered by the external imputation of Christ’s righteousness, as the Calvinists maintain, but by good works proceeding from his freely given grace. You will readily recognize this as Ambrose’s consistent doctrine if you compare this passage with what is discussed in the same sense in *On Noah and the Ark*, chapter 31, section 117, and in *An Apology for David*, chapter 13, section 62, as well as elsewhere.

When he says, “taking away sins,” this refers to forgiveness, because he removes them entirely, so that they are no longer present and he will not remember them. But when he says, “transferring iniquities,” this is because, when we confess our falls and overshadow them with the fruit of good action, they are referred back to the author of guilt and instigator of sin. For what else does one who confesses guilt accomplish except to show that he has been led astray by the deceit and malice of the opposing spiritual power?

24. In this, therefore, that soul gives thanks: because the Lord both takes away sins and transfers iniquities and plunges them into the depths of the sea. This can also be referred to baptism, by which the Egyptian is submerged and the Hebrew rises again; and by which, through the depth of wisdom and the abundance of good works, former sins are covered through the riches of the mercy of our God, who, mindful of his promise to Abraham, did not allow his heir—the soul—to perish.

25. That soul, then, is recalled in this way. [Col. 1240D] At the end of this letter our Ambrose inserted several remarks concerning Horontian’s background. First, he indicates that Horontian was educated and trained among the clergy from earliest boyhood, just as it was once customary to designate boys for ecclesiastical service; this was noted above in *On Repentance*, Book II, chapter 8, section 72. Next, when he says that Horontian was consecrated by the imposition of his hands, he sufficiently declares that he was a cleric of Milan. Finally, he testifies that Horontian demonstrated his faith in the diaconate and thereafter attained a higher rank. For Ambrose requires that the faith which Horontian had previously displayed in sacred ministry—that is, in the diaconate—should also, without doubt, be exhibited in the rank in which he then stood out, evidently the priesthood. From this one may reasonably conjecture that Ambrose appointed him to govern some church situated outside Milan.

But you, my son, who from the first flower of boyhood have been an heir of the Church that received and holds you, persevere in your purpose, mindful of the grace of God and of the gift that you received through the laying on of my hands, so that in this rank, as in sacred ministry, you may demonstrate your faith and diligence, and await the Lord Jesus’ reward. Farewell, and love us as a son, because we love you.

## LETTER LXXI

After the various stages by which the fallen soul restores itself, described above, this letter considers the faithful soul’s reception, instruction, and perfection by Christ; and it shows that the soul’s various advances are signified by Christ’s journeys.

**AMBROSE TO HORONTIAN**

1. In the preceding letter we discussed the soul that had some wandering turns in its journey, like the old Israel according to the flesh, which was wavering; for it too will be saved through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered (Rom. 11:25), although it reformed itself through a conversion involving a lesser error. [Col. 1241D] In this letter, however, let us discuss the daughter of the Church, and consider how the Lord Jesus first received her, instructed her, and perfected her in his Gospel.

[Col. 1241D] **Note:** The Roman edition alone reads “we completed our discussion.” Below, where the same phrase occurs, the old edition and most manuscripts have “through a lesser error,” while some manuscripts read “through a lesser error’s conversion,” and so forth.

2. He first received her to protect her while she was placed in confusion. For, being an exile from paradise (Gen. 3:23), where else could the soul of every human being dwell except in confusion? And he led her into Bethlehem (Matt. 2:1). The progress of the soul that has been received is already signified by the fact that he ascended to the house of bread, where it would know neither the hunger of faith nor barrenness. I am speaking of the class and order of our souls, by which we live and move, not of any particular soul. For we should discuss not the individuality and character of one soul, but the class of souls, as I have said.

3. Christ descended into Egypt (ibid.), carrying the protection and guidance of our soul; from there he returned to Judea. He was in the desert (Matt. 4:1), he was in Capernaum, he was near the borders of Zebulun, around the maritime regions; he passed through the fields; he was in Bethphage and in Ephraim and in Bethany. From there he passed into paradise, where he gave himself up to be captured, and he suffered on Golgotha.

4. All these are stages of our soul, through which, when exercised, it finds the grace of holy instruction. For after the human condition, expelled from paradise in Adam and Eve, had been confined in a fortress, it began to wander here and there, carrying its errant footsteps about without any fixed direction. [Col. 1241D] But at the appointed time the Lord Jesus emptied himself, so that he might receive the exile into himself and restore it to its former grace. Thus, [Col. 1241D] having found it after its return through the winding path of error, he recalled it to paradise, as the Gospel reading teaches.

[Col. 1241D] **Note:** Some manuscripts read “having found it on its return,” “through a winding path,” and so forth. The Roman edition alone, inserting three words, reads: “as the assertion of the Gospel reading teaches.”

5. He led it through the fields so that, while fasting, he might feed it—first in the desert, then in Capernaum, dwelling in a field rather than a city; then near the borders of Zebulun, around nocturnal streams, that is, the more obscure riddles of the prophets. Thus it might learn to extend itself to the borders of the Gentiles, where all would gather, and not fear the waves and storms of this life, because Christ has the ships of Tarshish (1 Kings 10:22)—intelligible ships, of course, which cross the sea and bring pious cargoes for the construction of the temple. In such ships Christ sails, and in the stern he rests upon a tranquil sea like a good pilot. When it is stirred up, he rises and rebukes the winds, so that he may pour tranquility back upon his own (Matt. 8:26). Passing also to the Gentiles, he frees this soul, which had been held by the bonds of the Law, lest it pass into fellowship with the nations.

6. He comes to Bethany, to the place of obedience; therefore the dead man is raised there. For when the flesh has been subjected to the soul, the human condition no longer lies as though dead in its tomb but is raised by the grace of Christ. There also it learns to offer itself to suffering for the name of God (John 11:17 ff.). From the place of obedience, as John teaches (John 12:1), it is led into Ephraim—that is, to the fruitfulness of good fruits. From there it is brought back to Bethany, that is, to obedience; for once it has tasted the fruit of holy submission, it does not at all refuse to preserve it and to be tested in it repeatedly.

7. Hence, now proved, it comes to Jerusalem, worthy to be the temple of God and the dwelling place of Christ. Finally, the Lord Jesus, sitting upon a young donkey, is received with rejoicing and joy by an innocent age (ibid., 14).

[Col. 1242D] **Note:** The Belvedere manuscript reads: “in which the Spirit might dwell.”

8. Afterward, in paradise, it is taught the words of eternal life. Hence the Lord also allowed himself to be captured, as the evangelist John writes (John 18:8), signifying that our soul—or rather, the human condition—having been released from the bonds of error, returned through Christ to the place from which it had been expelled in Adam. Hence also it is said to that confessing thief: “Amen, amen, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:42–43). He had said: “Remember me when you come into your kingdom.” Christ did not answer concerning the kingdom, but addressed the immediate matter: “Today you will be with me in paradise.” That is, what was lost must first be restored; afterward what is to be increased may be bestowed, so that through paradise one may arrive at the kingdom, not through the kingdom at paradise.

[Col. 1242D] **Note:** We noted in *On the Fall of a Virgin*, chapter 8, section 36, that some people, both from certain words written there and from this very passage of the letter, attributed to Ambrose the opinion that some intermediate state was admitted between heavenly blessedness and the punishments of hell. But apart from the fact that nothing certain about Ambrose’s view on this matter can be gathered from the cited book, whose author is not completely established, anyone who examines the words of that book and of this letter more attentively will readily extract a more suitable meaning from them. It must be observed that there the discussion concerns a girl who, having lost the merits of continence maintained for some time, as well as those of other good works, is said to obtain pardon for very grave crimes through the labors of continual repentance. Here, however, the one who is converted only at the moment of death is compared with the one who, enriched with the merits of virtues and pious works, has departed from the living. It will therefore be readily understood that the exemption from punishment, the rest, and the paradise to which Ambrose promises that such penitents will come mean nothing other than the final dwelling in the Father’s house—that is, the lowest degree of blessedness. The kingdom, however, which he asserts is reserved for the saints and those possessing apostolic merit must be understood as the highest summit of heavenly glory. He therefore says most aptly: “Through paradise one arrives at the kingdom,” because it is first necessary for someone to obtain forgiveness for what he has committed before he can deserve a more exalted throne. The same point may also be read in the book *On the Faith of the Resurrection*, concerning which we have written there.

9. What is to be given in greater measure for their labors is reserved for the disciples; therefore he promised them a dwelling but deferred the kingdom. Thus the one who is converted at the moment of death and confesses the Lord Jesus may deserve the dwelling of paradise; but the one who exercised himself long beforehand, served as a soldier for Christ, acquired the souls of peoples, and offered himself for Christ has God’s kingdom prepared in accordance with his services, and may rejoice that he has been granted its reward. Hence it is said to Peter: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 16:19). The thief, converted from robbery, has rest; the one proved in apostleship received authority.

10. This is the Gospel soul; this is the soul from the Gentiles, the daughter of the Church, far better in its course than that one cast out from Judea. It raises itself by good counsels and works toward the Lord Jesus and toward higher things; Christ received it on Golgotha. [Col. 1244D] **Note:** Here Ambrose adapts to his subject the opinion of certain Hebrews and other ancients. He likewise discusses it in Book X on Luke, section 114; we have also made some observations on that passage. Here was Adam’s tomb, so that he might raise that dead man upon his own cross. Therefore, where there was the death of all in Adam, there is the resurrection of all in Christ. Farewell, my son, and love us, because we love you.

## LETTER LXXII

Some people asked why God, having instituted circumcision in the Old Testament, abolished it in the New; why he also enacted a law concerning it at all, since it exposed the boy to danger; and why, finally, he wished it to be performed on that particular part of the body. First, therefore, to satisfy those who were alien to the faith, Ambrose replies that circumcision was practiced by wise men and by very many peoples, and that there was a reason why it was celebrated on the eighth day. Next, he teaches Christians that it contained a sign of redemption and therefore, once the price of this redemption had been paid, it ought to be omitted. Then he shows that heretics who slandered the law because it required the shedding of blood were thereby also condemning the Lord’s Passion. From this he refutes those who accused circumcision of harming faith, as well as those who argued that the part of the body that was natural ought not to be cut away. Finally, after discussing at length the hidden circumcision of Christians, he proves that they are not bound to the external rite.

**AMBROSE TO CONSTANTIUS**

1. A question of no small importance moves many people: why circumcision is commanded by the authority of the Old Testament as though useful, yet rejected by the teaching of the New Testament as though useless (Acts 15:10), especially since Abraham was the first to receive the oracle that circumcision should be practiced (Gen. 17:10)—the same Abraham who saw the day of the Lord Jesus and rejoiced (John 8:56). This is certainly clear, because he looked not to the bodily but to the spiritual things of the divine law; and therefore he perceived the true Passion of the Lord’s body in the immolation of the lamb.

[Col. 1244D] **Note:** The Roman edition reads “in the ram”; the other editions and all the manuscripts read “in the lamb.” But the ram is signified by the lamb, as in Exodus 32 and in the preceding letter by the calf, meaning an ox or bull.

2. What, then, shall we say moved Father Abraham to institute first that which his descendants would not follow? Or why are the bodies of infants circumcised, exposed to danger at the very moment of birth, and subjected to this command by an oracle, so that a matter of religious mystery becomes a danger to salvation? What does this mean? For the true reason is hidden; and either something ought to have been signified by an open mystery, or the indication of the mysteries ought not to have been entrusted to a dangerous sign.

3. But why is the sign of the divine Covenant given on that part of the body which is judged less honorable in appearance? Or for what reason did the very Maker of our body wish, at the beginning of our generation itself, for his work to be circumcised, wounded, bloodied, and cut, and for a part to be removed which he who ordered all things harmoniously had judged should be made, together with the other members, as necessary? Either this portion of our body is contrary to nature, in which case it was not fitting for all human beings to possess something contrary to nature; or it is according to nature, in which case it was not fitting to amputate what had been created according to the perfection of nature—especially since those alien to the portion of the Lord our God have customarily ridiculed this above all.

Moreover, since God’s purpose is, as he himself has frequently testified, to summon more people to observe the sacred religion, how much more would they be invited if some were not deterred by either the danger or the disgrace of circumcision itself?

4. Therefore, to return to the beginning and pursue the order we have proposed, it seems necessary to speak about the nature of circumcision itself. Its defense must be twofold, because the accusation is twofold: one accusation is made by the Gentiles, the other is entertained by those who belong to the people of God. The accusation of the Gentiles is more vehement; they consider men marked by circumcision worthy of reproach and ridicule also because of it.

[Note: [Col. 1244D] We find that Jews, on account of the removal of the foreskin, were customarily called by the profane in mockery *curti*, *verpi*, and *recutiti*—“shortened,” “mutilated,” and “recut.”]

Yet even the wisest among the Gentiles approve circumcision to such an extent that they think their chosen men ought to be circumcised for the purpose of learning about and celebrating the mysteries.

[Col. 1245A] 5. Finally, the Egyptians, who devote themselves both to geometry and to calculating the courses of the stars,

[Note: Thus the old edition and nearly all manuscripts read it. The Roman edition, however, has “who devote their efforts.” Ambrose speaks elsewhere more than once of the Egyptians’ expertise in the mathematical disciplines.]

judge a priest impious if he does not possess the mark of circumcision. For they do not think that the wisdom of magical incantation, or geometry, or astronomy can retain its power without the seal of circumcision.

[Note: The old edition and some manuscripts read “their way”; the Roman edition and several manuscripts read “their power.”]

And therefore, so that they may lend power to their activity of obtaining what they seek, they think that some purification of their diviners should be performed through the mystery of circumcision.

6. We find in the history of the ancients that not only the Egyptians,

[Note: Saint Ambrose reports, on the testimony of certain authorities, that among the Egyptians not only males but females also were customarily circumcised; see *On Abraham*, book II, chapter 11, section 78. Concerning them and the other nations from whom he says in this passage that circumcision was adopted, one may consult Josephus, *Antiquities*, book I, chapter 13, and book VIII, chapter 4; Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* 30, section 30; and Polydorus, chapter 3, who cites Cyprian among other authorities, though he was misled by a sermon wrongly attributed to that Father in his ancient editions.]

but also some of the Ethiopians, Arabs, and Phoenicians used circumcision among their own peoples. They think that they still preserve this as a means of demonstrating their reasoning, because, having been initiated through the first fruits and blood of their bodies, they consider that the snares of demons—which those beings devise against our race—

[Col. 1245B] are destroyed by the consecrations of a small part, so that those who strive to harm the salvation of the whole human being may think their operation weakened by the law or appearance of sacred circumcision. For I think that in former times the prince of the demons himself judged that he ought to cease his arts against the effect of a harmful operation if he attempted to harm someone whom he perceived to have been initiated by the seal of sacred circumcision, or someone who seemed at least in this duty to obey the divine law.

7. Whoever carefully considers the functions of each member will be able to judge that there is a meaningful reason for this little portion of the body: not only is the child circumcised, but he is circumcised on the eighth day, when the mother of the newborn begins to be in pure blood, whereas before the eighth day she is said to sit in unclean blood (Gen. XVII, 12).

[Col. 1245C] These things have been said against those who are joined to us by no unity of faith; hence, as an argument against dissenters, this is a more difficult field for discussion.

8. Let those who believe in the Lord Jesus have the following answer to themselves—something we did not wish to expose while arguing against the opinions of the Gentiles. For if we were redeemed not with perishable silver and gold but with the precious blood of our Lord Jesus Christ (I Pet. I, 18–19), then who was the seller, except the one who already possessed our service, purchased at the cost of our sinful succession?

[Note: The Ambrosian and Roman editions, together with a few manuscripts, read “who already possessed what was ours.” Erasmus and Gill, with the remaining manuscripts, read “who already possessed our service.” It should incidentally be observed that these few words clearly imply the transmission of original sin.]

Without doubt, he himself demanded the price, in order to strip from servitude those whom he held bound. The price of our liberation, however, was the blood of the Lord Jesus, and it necessarily had to be paid to him to whom we had been sold by our sins.

9. Until this price was paid for all human beings—for it had to be paid through the shedding of the Lord’s blood for the absolution of all—there was need for the blood of individuals who followed the precepts of the sacred religion according to the Law and the customary rite. But because the price was paid for all after Christ the Lord had suffered, it is no longer necessary for the blood of each individual to be shed through circumcision. Circumcision of all has been accomplished in the blood of Christ; and on his cross we have all been crucified together with him, and buried with him in his tomb, planted in the likeness of his death, so that we might no longer serve sin: “For he who has died has been justified from sin” (Rom. VI, 7).

[Col. 1246B] 10. But if someone—such as Marcion or Mani—thinks that God’s judgment should be criticized because he either judged that an oracle concerning the performance of circumcision should be issued or gave a law commanding the shedding of blood,

[Note: Since these heretics, as we have already observed, rejected the entire instrument of the ancient covenant—or rather even rejected God as the author of the Law, believing, as Augustine testifies concerning the Manichaeans in *On Heresies*, chapter 4, that he was not the good God but one of the princes of darkness—it followed that they proscribed circumcision as having been established in the Old Law. But since it is characteristic of heretics always to defend every excess opposed to sound doctrine, there were some who professed that this bodily amputation was to be retained even under the Gospel. Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* 30, and Augustine, *On Heresies*, chapters 9 and 10; *Against Cresconius*, book I, chapter 31; and *Against Faustus*, book XIX, chapter 18, as well as Philastrius and others, record that the Ebionites and Symmachians were of this kind.]

then he must also think that the Lord Jesus should be criticized, since he shed not a little but much blood for the redemption of this world, and even today commands us to shed our own blood in so great a struggle for religion, saying: “Whoever wishes to follow me, let him take up his cross and follow me” (Matt. XVI, 24). But if there is no just accusation when someone offers his whole self for devotion and cleanses himself through the shedding of much blood, how can we criticize the Law for requiring a drop of blood, when we proclaim that the Lord Jesus commands the shedding of much blood and the death of the whole body?

11. Nor was the very mark and appearance of circumcision without significance: by it the people of God, marked upon the body as though by a seal, were distinguished from the other nations. Now, however, the one who has been given the name of Christ does not require a bodily sign, since he has obtained the privilege of a divine name. What is absurd about it if, for the sake of devotion, some pain or labor seemed to be imposed, by which dedication might be more fully tested through these struggles? It was also fitting that the mark of religion should grow from the very beginnings of life, and that everyone of more advanced age should be ashamed to yield either to labor or to pain, both of which tender infancy had overcome.

12. But the Christian people no longer need the slight pain of circumcision,

[Col. 1247A] since, bearing the Lord’s death, it inscribes upon its forehead at every moment contempt for its own death,

[Note: In the same sense, in *On the Faith of the Resurrection*: “We are marked by his death; announcing his death, we proclaim it,” and so forth. Tertullian likewise, in *On the Soldier’s Crown*, chapter 3, says that the religious practice of fortifying the forehead with the clear image of the cross, which he teaches came from apostolic tradition, was customary in his time at every individual action. On this matter see similarly Jerome, Letter 22 to Eustochium; Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechetical Lecture* 13; and others.]

since it knows that it cannot have salvation without the Lord’s cross. For who would use a needle for battle when he is equipped with stronger weapons?

13. Everyone can easily see that the following argument must be refuted: that many might have been summoned to obedience to the sacred religion if they had not been turned back by fear of pain or consideration of labor. Could something frighten an adult more when most infants endured it without danger?

Let it nevertheless be granted that some Jewish infants died because they could not endure the pain of the circumcised body and the burning wound. But this neither frightened the others, who were strong in more advanced age, nor made less praiseworthy the one who obeyed the heavenly commands.

[Col. 1247B] 14. If they think that this slight pain was an obstacle to confession, what will they say about martyrdom? For if they criticize the pain of circumcision, let them also criticize the death of the martyrs, through whom religion has been increased, not diminished. So far is the pain of circumcision from having harmed faith that pain makes faith more credible; for the grace of faith is greater if someone despises pain for the sake of religion. Such a person also has a greater reward than the one who chose to undergo the pain of circumcision in order to glory in the Law and seek praise from human beings rather than from God.

15. Circumcision, therefore, had to be performed in part before the coming of the one who would circumcise the whole human being; for the human condition had to become accustomed in part to believing in what is perfect. But if circumcision had to be performed, on which part of the body could it have been more fittingly performed than on that which some consider less honorable? Thus, to those members of our body thought to be more lowly, they might give a more abundant honor, and “those parts of us that are less honorable might have greater honor” (I Cor. XII, 23). For where should a man have been more strongly reminded of his blood than in that part which offers its service to error?

16. Now it is time to answer those who say that, if this part of our body is according to nature, it ought by no means to have been amputated; but if it is not according to nature, it ought not to have been born with us. Since they are so subtle, let them answer me also whether human succession, which grows through generations, is according to nature or contrary to nature.

If it is according to nature, then it should never be interrupted. And how, then, are the integrity of men, the virginity of girls, the abstinence of widows, and the continence of married people praised? No effort, therefore, to seek succession should have been interrupted. Yet the very author of nature did not obey generation, for, while he was established in the body, he offered himself as a teacher

[Col. 1248A] and encouraged his disciples toward integrity, saying: “There are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven; let whoever can accept this accept it” (Matt. XIX, 12).

17. Although the human being is composed of body and soul—for the moment it is sufficient to say this and to be silent about the spirit—

[Note: “We consist of soul, body, and spirit,” says the holy Doctor in *On Cain and Abel*, book II, chapter 2, section 6. One may frequently observe this definition of the human being in his writings.]

the same thing is not according to nature in both. What is according to the nature of the body is contrary to the nature of the soul, and what is according to the nature of the soul is contrary to the nature of the body. Thus, if I say that what is according to nature for the visible is contrary to what is not seen, and that what is according to nature for what is not seen is contrary to the visible, there is therefore nothing incongruous in God’s human beings if some things are done contrary to the nature of the body but according to the nature of the soul.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “the same thing is not according to nature in both; but what pertains to the body . . . is contrary to the nature of the body.”]

[Note: The latest Paris edition reads “in the works of God.” There are also several changes throughout this section in the Roman edition, but they introduce no different meaning.]

18. Those who say that more people would have believed if circumcision had not existed should have this answer: more people would believe if there had been no martyrdoms. But the courage of the few is superior to the laxity of the many. Just as many kinds of baptism were given beforehand because that one true sacrament of baptism in the Spirit and water was to follow, by which the whole human being is redeemed, so the circumcision of many had to precede, because the circumcision of the Lord’s Passion was to follow—the circumcision endured by Jesus as the Lamb of God, “to take away the sins of the world” (John I, 36).

[Note: The same Paris editions read: “the circumcision of many was to be omitted.” Below: “circumcision ought to have been omitted.” Neither reading is suitable.]

19. We have written these things to show that the circumcision which is outward had to precede, so that after the Lord’s coming it might rightly be regarded as excluded. Now, however, the circumcision that is necessary is the circumcision that is hidden, just as the superior Jew is the one who is hidden—in the spirit, not in the letter. For since there are two human beings in one person, concerning whom it is said, “Although our outward human being is being corrupted according to the desires of error, the inward one is renewed day by day” (II Cor. IV, 16), and elsewhere, “I delight in the law of God according to the inward human being” (Rom. VII, 22), our inward human being is the one made in the image and likeness of God, while the outward one was formed from clay. Thus, in Genesis also, he shows you two creations of the human being (Gen. I, 27), signifying a human being created a second time (Gen. II, 7).

20. Just as there are two human beings, so there are also two ways of life: one belonging to the inward human being, the other to the outward. Many actions of the inward human being indeed reach the outward human being, just as the chastity of the inward human being also extends to bodily chastity. Whoever is unaware of adultery of the heart is likewise unaware of bodily adultery; yet it does not follow that one who has not committed adultery bodily has not committed it also in the heart, according to the saying: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. V, 28). For even if he is not yet an adulterer in body,

[Note: The edition reads, “is not an adulterer in body.”]

he is already an adulterer in intention.

There is therefore a circumcision of the inward human being: whoever is circumcised removes all the enticements of the flesh as though they were a foreskin, so that he may be in the spirit and not in the flesh, and by the spirit may put to death the acts of his body.

21. This, then, is the circumcision that is hidden, just as Abraham was previously in the foreskin and afterward came to be in circumcision (Rom. IV, 11). Thus our inward human being, when it is in the flesh, is as though in the foreskin; but when it is no longer in the flesh and is in the spirit, it begins to be in circumcision and not in the foreskin.

Just as the one who is circumcised does not remove the whole flesh but only the foreskin, where corruption is more frequent, so the one who is circumcised in secret removes that flesh concerning which it is written: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass. The grass withers, and its flower falls; but the word of the Lord remains forever” (Isa. XL, 6–7). The flesh that will see the salvation of God remains, as it is written: “All flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Luke III, 6). What flesh this is—cleanse your ears, so that you may understand.

22. Such, then, must the hidden circumcision be that it has no comparison with the circumcision that is outward. Therefore, the one who is a Jew in secret is the superior one: he is from Judah, whose hand is upon the neck of his enemies, who, reclining, rested like a lion and like a lion’s cub, whom his brothers praise (Gen. XLIX, 8). From this Judah the ruler does not fail, because his word makes rulers who are not subjected to worldly enticements or captured by the pleasures of this world.

And because Judas himself came into this generation,

[Note: Thus the Roman edition and several manuscripts. The old edition and some manuscripts, however, read: “therefore many who are afterward born advance toward virtue”; other copies read: “therefore he is preferred to many, so that,” and so forth. The latter is less suitable.]

therefore many who were afterward born are preferred, so that they may rejoice in the leadership of virtues. Let us therefore have circumcision in secret, and in secret the spiritual Jew. For the spiritual person, as a ruler, judges all things, while he himself is judged by no one (I Cor. II, 15).

23. The circumcision prescribed by the command of the Law, which existed only in part, therefore had to cease after the one came who would perform the circumcision of the whole human being and fulfill the circumcision of the Law.

[Note: All editions and a few manuscripts read: “prescribed by command of the Law”; the remaining manuscripts read as in the text.] Who is this, except the one who said: “I have not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it” (Matt. V, 17)?

[Col. 1250A] 24. Yet, if you consider the matter carefully, there is also this reason why the circumcision of the foreskin ought by now to have ceased: the full number of the Gentiles has entered. Circumcision was not commanded to the Gentiles but to the seed of Abraham. Thus you have it in the first oracle:

“And God said to Abraham: ‘But you shall keep my covenant, you and your seed after you throughout their generations. And this is my covenant, which you shall keep between me and you and your seed after you throughout their generations: Every male among you shall be circumcised, and you shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin, and it shall be for a sign of the covenant between me and you. A child eight days old shall be circumcised among you, every male throughout your generations. The native-born servant of your household and the one bought with money from every son of another who is not of your seed shall be circumcised; and it shall be my covenant in your flesh, an everlasting covenant. An uncircumcised male who does not circumcise the flesh of his foreskin on the eighth day shall be cut off from that generation, because he has broken my covenant’” (Gen. XVII, 9 ff.).

[Col. 1250B] [Note: The Roman edition alone reads, “and it shall be my covenant.”]

The Hebrew, indeed, is denied to have “on the eighth day,” as Aquila indicates.

[Note: Ambrose’s familiarity with introducing various readings of Aquila is evident to anyone from other passages as well as from his exposition of Psalm CXVIII.]

But not all authority lies with Aquila, who, being almost a Jew in his attention to the letter, passed over and did not include “the eighth day.”

25. Meanwhile, you have heard both about the eighth day and about circumcision given as a sign. A sign, however, is an indication of a greater reality, an indication of future truth. The covenant was given to Abraham and his seed, to whom it was said: “In Isaac shall your seed be called” (Gen. XXI, 12).

Therefore it was permitted for a Jew to circumcise either one born in his household or one bought with his money. We cannot extend this to a foreigner or proselyte unless they were born in Abraham’s household, bought with his money, or descended from his seed.

Finally, he said nothing about proselytes. When he wished to speak of them, he named them, as you have it:

“And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to Aaron and to his sons and to all the sons of Israel, and say to them: Any man, any man of the sons of Israel and of the proselytes who have joined themselves to you, whoever offers a burnt offering” (Gen. XVII, 12).

Wherever, therefore, he included them, the Law binds them; where they are not signified by the oracle, how do they appear to be bound? Thus you have it also: “Speak to the sons of Aaron” (Lev. XVII, 1 ff.), when he speaks about the priests. You have the same when he speaks about the Levites.

26. It is therefore entirely clear, even according to the letter of the Law—although the Law is spiritual—that according to that same letter the peoples of the nations could not have been bound to circumcision. Circumcision itself was a sign until the full number of the Gentiles should enter and thus all Israel should be saved, circumcised in heart and not merely in a small part of one member. Thus the circumcision of the Jews, which remains even today, has been sufficiently both excused by us and excluded.

27. As for their saying that circumcision was or is a source of reproach among the Gentiles, first, they have no right to reproach or ridicule what others make themselves participants in.

[Note: He means those Gentiles among whom circumcision was in use, as mentioned above in sections 5 and 6.]

Let it nevertheless be granted that there were people who ridiculed it. Why should this move us, when the very cross of the Lord is a stumbling block to Jews, foolishness to Greeks, but to us the power and wisdom of God (I Cor. I, 23–24)? And the Lord himself said:

[Note: Four manuscripts read: “Whoever has confessed me … I also will confess him.” This is not especially suitable here.]

“Whoever has been ashamed of me before human beings, of him I also will be ashamed before my Father who is in heaven” (Luke IX, 26),

teaching us not to be shaken by those things that human beings ridicule, if they are done for the sake of religious devotion.

## LETTER LXXIII

Why the Law was given, when Paul indicates that it does harm: it would have been unnecessary if the natural law, written on our hearts and found even in infants, had been preserved. Once that law had been broken, the written Law became necessary in order to remove excuse by making sin manifest; afterward, this was taken away by the grace of Christ.

### AMBROSE TO IRENAEUS

1. You were not moved superficially when the Apostle’s reading had been completed, because today you heard the passage: “The Law produces wrath; but where there is no Law, neither is there transgression” (Rom. IV, 5). Therefore you thought it necessary to ask why the Law was given, if it was of no benefit—indeed, if it was harmful, since it produced anger and introduced transgression.

[Note: The Prat and Gem manuscripts read: “why this is so, if the Law is nothing,” and so forth.]

2. According to your question, it is certainly true that the Law given through Moses was not necessary. For if human beings had been able to preserve the natural law that God the Creator infused into the breast of each individual, there would have been no need for that law which, written on tablets of stone, bound and tied the weakness of the human race more than it freed and released it.

That there is, however, a natural law in our hearts the Apostle also teaches, when he writes that often the Gentiles naturally do what belongs to the Law, and, although they have not read the Law, they nevertheless have the work of the Law written in their hearts (Rom. II, 14).

3. That law, therefore, is not written but born within us. It is not received through any reading, but flows from a kind of natural fountain, impressed upon each person and drawn up by human minds. We ought to have preserved it either out of fear of the future judgment—for our conscience, which testifies to it, reveals itself before God through silent thoughts, by which wickedness is either convicted or innocence defended.

Thus, although it is always open before the Lord, it will be made especially manifest on the day of judgment, when the hidden things of the heart that were thought to lie concealed will come under examination. Yet the disclosure of these hidden things would in no way harm us if the natural law were present in human hearts; for it is holy, without deceit and without fraud, sharing in justice and free from wickedness.

4. Finally, let us question infancy and see whether any crime is found in it: avarice, ambition, deceit, savagery, arrogance. It knows nothing as its own, claims no honors for itself, does not know how to put itself before another, is ignorant of fraud, and neither wishes nor is able to avenge itself. A pure and simple mind cannot comprehend what arrogance is.

5. Adam broke this law when he wished to claim for himself what he had not received, so that he might be like his creator and maker and seek divine honor. Thus through disobedience he incurred offense and fell into guilt through arrogance.

If he had not broken the command but had obeyed the heavenly instructions, he would have preserved for his own heirs the privilege of nature and of the innocence innate in him. Therefore, because the natural privilege of the law was corrupted and effaced through disobedience, the written Law was considered necessary,

[Col. 1252B] so that the one who had lost everything might retain at least a part, and so that the person who had lost what he had assumed by birth might at least learn and preserve it by instruction.

At the same time, because pride was the cause of his fall, and pride arose from the privilege of innocence, that Law had to be given which would make him subject and submissive to God (Rom. VII, 8). For without the Law sin was unknown, and guilt was less where there was ignorance of guilt. Hence the Lord also says: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse concerning their sin” (John XV, 22).

6. The Law was therefore given, first, to remove excuse, so that no one could say: “I did not know the sin, because no rule had been given concerning what I should avoid.” Second, it was given to make all subject to God through the recognition of sin (Rom. III, 19).

It made all subject because it was given not only to the Jews but also called the Gentiles; for proselytes from the Gentiles were joined to them. Nor can the one who failed to appear after being called seem to have been exempt: the Law both called and bound those whom it summoned.

The guilt of all therefore produced subjection; subjection produced humility; humility produced obedience. Thus, because pride had contracted guilt, guilt, in turn, generated obedience. Hence the written Law, which seemed superfluous, became necessary, so that sin might be dissolved by sin.

7. But lest someone again be frightened and say that sin was increased through the Law, and suppose that the Law not only did no good but even did harm, there is something with which he can console his anxiety: although sin abounded through the Law, grace also abounded (Rom. V, 20). Let us understand what this means.

8. Sin abounded through the Law because through the Law came recognition of sin (Rom. VII, 7), and it began to harm me to know what I could not avoid because of weakness. Foreknowledge is useful for avoiding something; but if I cannot avoid it, knowledge has harmed me.

Thus the Law was turned toward the opposite; nevertheless, through the very increase of sin it became useful to me, because I was humbled. Hence David also said: “It is good for me that I have been humbled” (Ps. CXVIII, 71).

By humbling me, however, it loosened the bond of the former error,

[Col. 1253A] with which Adam and Eve had bound the entire succession of their descendants.

[Note: The old edition and several manuscripts read: “with which Adam and Eve had stripped themselves.” The Roman edition and other manuscripts more appropriately read: “with which they had bound.” The transmission of original sin from Adam to all his offspring is explained so clearly and distinctly in this letter that we must understand Augustine not to have read it, since he nowhere employs its testimony against the Pelagians.]

Therefore the Lord came as though obedient, so that the snare of human disobedience and transgression might be loosened. Just as sin entered through disobedience, so sin was dissolved through obedience. Hence the Apostle also says: “Just as through the disobedience of one human being the many were made sinners, so through the obedience of one human being the many will be made righteous” (Rom. V, 19).

9. You therefore have one answer: the Law was both superfluous and not superfluous. It was superfluous in that it would not have been necessary if we had been able to preserve the natural law. But because we did not preserve it, this Law through Moses became necessary, so that it might teach me obedience and loosen that snare of Adam’s transgression which had bound the whole inheritance.

Guilt indeed increased through the Law, but the pride that was the author of guilt was also dissolved, and this benefited me. Pride discovered guilt, but guilt brought about grace.

10. Receive another answer. The Law through Moses was not necessary. Finally, it “entered alongside” (ibid. 20), which seems to signify not an ordinary entrance but one almost furtive,

[Note: Thus the Roman edition and several manuscripts; the old edition and some manuscripts read “but as though accidental.”]

because it entered into the place of the natural law. Therefore, if the natural law had retained its own place, this written Law would by no means have entered. But because transgression had excluded that law and had almost abolished it

[Note: All editions and some manuscripts read: “had abolished it, in human hearts” (the Roman edition: “in their hearts”); the remaining manuscripts, including some of better quality, read as in the text. Immediately afterward, where the same editions and several manuscripts have “and disobedience,” two manuscripts read “which is disobedience,” and two others “which, through disobedience.”]

from human hearts, pride reigned and disobedience had spread itself abroad. Therefore this Law succeeded it, so that it might confront us in writing and close every mouth, making the whole world subject to God (Rom. III, 19).

The world was made subject through the Law because everyone is convicted by the rule of the Law, and no one is justified by works of the Law. That is, through the Law sin is recognized, but guilt is not forgiven. Thus the Law seemed to have done harm because it had made everyone sinners.

[Col. 1253C] 11. But when the Lord Jesus came, he forgave everyone the sin that no one could escape and erased our written bond by the shedding of his blood (Col. II, 14). This is what he says: “Sin abounded through the Law, but grace abounded through Jesus” (Rom. V, 20). For after the whole world had been made subject, he took away the sin of the whole world, as John testified, saying: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sin of the world” (John I, 29).

Therefore no one should glory in works, because no one is justified by his own deeds. Rather, the one who is righteous has received this as a gift, because he has been justified through the washing. It is faith, therefore, that liberates through the blood of Christ (Rom. IV, 6), because blessed is the one whose sin is forgiven and pardon is granted.

Farewell, my son, and love us, because we love you.

## LETTER LXXIV

Since many denied that the Law should be abolished, on the grounds that God had established it, or inferred from its abolition that the two Testaments could not have come from the same God, this is resolved by the Apostle’s statement: “The Law was our pedagogue,” and so forth. A pedagogue is necessary only for children; therefore the Law was given to the Jews as to the weak. Its precepts were imperfect, but they foretold the perfect realities. Finally, after a brief discussion of avarice, an exhortation is added to accept both Testaments, which are represented by the ox and the ass in Isaiah.

[Note: Thus the old edition and all manuscripts, some of which also add: “A sermon of Saint Ambrose to the people.” This inscription is found alone in the sermon-books of Corbie, Bigot, Germanus, and Fulda, in which we find this same letter. The Roman edition, however, prefixed to this letter: “Ambrose the bishop to Clementianus.” There is no doubt that it substituted Clementianus for Irenaeus because the opening of the following letter makes clear that this and the next letter were written to the same person. Nevertheless, since there is a defect in the inscription of both, it cannot be determined so readily; we have therefore judged that we should not depart from the manuscripts and ancient editions.]

### AMBROSE TO IRENAEUS

1. My son, today you heard it read in the Apostle that “the Law was our pedagogue in Christ, so that we might be justified by faith” (Gal. III, 24).

[Note: The Laud, Corbie, Germanus, and Fulda manuscripts read: “You heard, brother, today it was read,” and so forth.]

By this one statement I think the questions that commonly trouble many people have been settled. For there are those who say: Since God gave the Law to Moses, why is so much found in the Law that now appears to have been nullified by the Gospel? And how can there be one author of both Testaments, when what was permitted in the Law began to be forbidden through the Gospel? Such is bodily circumcision, which, although it was then given as a sign so that the truth of spiritual circumcision might be maintained,

[Note: The same manuscripts read: “although it was then given as a sign, so that spiritual circumcision was itself in the sign. Why is this difference judged?” Then follows: “And further,” and so forth.]

nevertheless, for what reason was it present even in the sign? Why is this difference judged to exist, so that at that time it was considered an act of piety to be circumcised, whereas now it is judged impious (Num. XV, 35)?

Furthermore, the observance of the Sabbath day as a day of rest was required by the Law, to such an extent that if anyone carried a load of wood, he became liable to death. Now, however, we see that the day itself is assigned without penalty both to bearing burdens and to conducting business. There are also many precepts of the Law that appear to have ceased in the present time.

2. Let us therefore consider the reason. The Apostle did not speak idly when he said that “the Law was our pedagogue in Christ” (Gal. III, 24). Whose pedagogue is it—of a mature person or of an adolescent? Certainly of an adolescent or a child, that is, of an age that is weak. For a pedagogue, as the Latin interpretation also indicates,

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “He is the guide of the child, to whom indeed,” and so forth.]

is the teacher of a child. To an imperfect age he cannot apply perfect precepts, which it would not be able to bear.

Finally, through the prophet the God of the Law says: “I will give you commands that are not good” (Ezek. XX, 25), that is, not perfect; for whatever is good is certainly perfect. The same God reserved more perfect things for the Gospel, since he says: “I have not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it” (Matt. V, 17).

### 3.

What, then, is the cause of this difference, except human diversity? He knew that the Jewish people were stiff-necked, unstable through falling, humble, prone to faithlessness, hearing with the ear yet not hearing, seeing with the eyes yet not seeing, light-minded and forgetful of commands through a certain slippery childishness. Therefore he applied the Law as a pedagogue to the unstable disposition and feeble mind of the people, and, regulating the precepts of the Law itself, willed that one thing should be read from the Law and another understood: so that the foolish person might at least observe what he read and not depart from the letter’s prescription; while the wise person might understand the intention of the divine mind, which the letter did not express. The imprudent was to preserve the command of the Law, the prudent its mystery. Thus the Law has the severity of the sword, like a pedagogue’s rod, so that at least by threatening punishment it might frighten the weakness of an imperfect people; but the Gospel has indulgence, by which sins are forgiven.

[Note: The old edition has “fallen, humble, more prone to faithlessness”; the Roman edition has “wanton, unstable, more prone to faithlessness.” Some manuscripts likewise omit *humble*, and some also omit *unstable*. The others read as in the text, except that some have *faithlessness* instead of *of faithlessness*, without a harmful difference of meaning.]

### 4.

Paul therefore rightly says that “the letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3:6).

[Note: All editions and a few manuscripts read, “The letter therefore kills”; the others, including the best witnesses, read: “[lacuna] circumcises.”]

The letter circumcises a small portion of the body; but the spirit, understanding circumcision, guards the circumcision of the whole soul and body. Thus, when superfluities have been cut away—for what is more superfluous than the vices of greed and the sins of lust, which nature did not possess but guilt sought out?—chastity may be maintained and frugality loved. Bodily circumcision is therefore a sign; spiritual circumcision, however, is the truth: the former cuts off a bodily member, the latter sin.

Nature generated nothing imperfect in a human being, nor was anything commanded to be removed as superfluous. Rather, the purpose was that those who cut away a part of their body should understand that sins must be cut away much more, and that those who persuade us to sin must be cut off, even if they were joined to us by a kind of bodily unity, as it is written: “If your right hand causes you to stumble, cut it off and throw it away from you; for it is better for you that one of your members should perish than that your whole body should go into Gehenna” (Matt. 5:30). Thus, just as for children, so also for the Jews, incomplete precepts were commanded—not the whole precepts—and they were instructed to keep one part, as it were, of their member clean, since they could not keep their entire body clean.

### 5.

They were also commanded to celebrate a sabbatical rest on one day of the week (Exod. 31:15), so that they might be subjected to no burden, once released from worldly works—if only they had departed in this way!—so that they might carry with them no burdens of grave sins into that perpetual Sabbath of the ages to come.

But because God knew that the people were unstable, he prescribed for the weaker a portion, in the observance of a single day, and reserved fullness for the stronger. The synagogue observes a day; the Church, immortality. In the Law, therefore, there is a portion; in the Gospel, perfection.

### 6.

The Jewish people are forbidden to carry wood (Num. 15:33), that is, things consumed by fire. He holds to a shadow who flees from the sun. But to you, he did not allow the sun of righteousness to be an impediment, pouring into you the open light of his grace, and saying: “Go, and from now on see that you do not sin” (John 8:11).

To you the imitator of that eternal sun says: “If anyone builds upon the foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, stubble, each one’s work will become manifest. For the day of the Lord will make it manifest, because it will be revealed in fire; and the fire will test what sort of work each one’s is” (1 Cor. 3:12–13 and following). Let us therefore build upon Christ—Christ is our foundation—that which will not be burned up but improved. Gold is improved by fire, and silver is improved.

### 7.

You have heard of gold and silver, and you suppose that this means material wealth; you desire to accumulate it. But you are wasting your effort. This gold and silver bears a burden and produces no fruit. The expense of the heir is a burden to the one who seeks it. This gold, like wood, is burned up; it does not endure. This silver will bring you loss of life on that day, not gain.

Another gold and another silver are sought from you: namely, good understanding and an excellent word.

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads, “an excellent word.” These are the gifts of God, of which David says, “The utterances of the Lord,” and so forth.]

These are the gifts of God: “The utterances of the Lord are utterances that are pure, silver tested by fire, proved upon the earth, purified sevenfold” (Ps. 12:6). The grace of your understanding and the brilliance of pure speech are required: the splendor of faith, not the ringing of silver.

This remains; that perishes. This has a reward and departs with us; that has loss, because it is left here.

### 8.

If some rich person thinks that silver stored up and hidden away can assist him toward life, he carries an empty burden that the fire of judgment will consume. Leave your wood here, you rich, so that your burden may not add fuel to the future fire. If you distribute it, the burden will be diminished; and what remains will not be a burden.

Do not hoard, miser, lest you become a Christian in name only, but a Jew in conduct, when you discover that your burdens are punishment for you. For it has been said to you not through a shadow but in the sun: “If anyone’s work remains, he will receive a reward; if anyone’s work is burned up, he will suffer loss” (1 Cor. 3:14).

### 9.

And therefore, as one perfectly instructed in the Law and confirmed in the Gospel, accept the faith of both Testaments. For “blessed is he who sows upon every water, where the ox and the ass tread” (Isa. 32:20), as was read today—that is, blessed is he who sows among peoples who follow the teaching of both Testaments.

The ox is that plow-animal bearing the yoke of the Law, of which the Law says: “You shall not muzzle the ox while it is threshing” (Deut. 25:4), and which has the horns of the divine Scriptures. In the Gospel the Lord mounted the colt of the ass as a figure of the gentile people (Luke 19:33).

[Note: The final editions of Paris read, “the ox is for those plowmen.”]

### 10.

I think, however, that because the word of God is rich, we should also understand this: the ox has horns full of terror; the bull has fierceness; the ass has gentleness. This applies well to the present matter, because blessed is the one who maintains both severity and gentleness, so that discipline may be preserved by the one and innocence not be crushed by the other. Excessive severity often extorts a lie through fear.

God preferred to be loved rather than feared. The Lord demands love; a servant demands fear, although continual terror cannot exist in a human being. For it is written, as was read today: “Behold, in your fear they themselves will fear, those whom you feared.”

[Note: “Farewell, my son,” and what follows are omitted in the Corbie, German, and Fulda manuscripts.]

Farewell, my son, and love us, because we love you.

# LETTER LXXV

Having set forth the difficulty of extracting Paul’s meaning, Ambrose adds the text of that same Apostle, who affirms that no one becomes an heir except through faith. He then refutes the Jews who claim that the inheritance is owed to them because of the Old Testament, revealing what kind of heirs they should be considered.

## AMBROSE TO CLEMENTIANUS

### 1.

Although I know that nothing is more difficult than to discuss the Apostle’s text—for even Origen himself is far inferior in the New Testament to what he is in the Old Testament—nevertheless, since in the preceding letter I seemed to you to have explained not absurdly why the Law was called a pedagogue, in today’s discourse I shall also attempt to unfold the very force of the Apostle’s argument.

[Note: It is likely that Ambrose, when he professes that there is so much difficulty in explaining the Apostle’s text, was prompted by the two reasons he sets forth in Letter 37, section 1: namely, that the divine counsels are so profound that the human intellect can scarcely grasp them; while elsewhere God explains himself in such a way that he leaves the interpreter nothing to add beyond grammatical exposition. As for Origen, Huet, *Origen*, book 3, chapter 2, section 1, number 7, acknowledges that Ambrose’s judgment concerning him is entirely true. But Huet adds two other reasons for this: first, that the ancient Scriptures had already been illuminated by numerous commentaries, traditions, and treatises, which could assist him; and second, that, since the old ceremonies had there been abolished, he was permitted to indulge his style more freely in allegories.]

### 2.

The earlier portions of his reading contain this: no one is justified by works of the Law, but by faith; “For all who are of the works of the Law are under a curse … but Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law, having become a curse for us” (Gal. 3:10, 13).

The inheritance, therefore, was not given from the Law but from the promise. For promises were made to Abraham and to his seed—which is Christ (ibid., 16). Thus the Law was established because of transgressions until the seed should come to whom the promise had been made (ibid., 19). Therefore all things were shut up under sin, so that the promise might be given to believers through faith in Jesus Christ … But after faith came, we are no longer under the Law (ibid., 25)—that is, we are no longer under the pedagogue.

[Note: The Roman edition reads, “under the pedagogue, that is, under the Law.”]

And because we are sons of God, we are all in Christ Jesus. If, then, we are all in Christ Jesus, we are therefore Abraham’s seed, heirs according to the promise. This is the conclusion of the Apostle’s argument.

### 3.

But there still confronts him someone who might also say as a Jew: “I too am an heir, because I am under the Law. The old Law is called a Testament; and wherever there is a testament, there is an inheritance.”

Although he himself said to the Hebrews that a testament is not valid unless the death of the testator intervenes (Heb. 9:17)—that is, that a testament is not valid as long as the testator lives, but is confirmed by his death—nevertheless, because the Lord spoke about the Jews through Jeremiah and said, “My inheritance has become for me like a lion” (Jer. 12:8), he did not wish to deny that they were heirs.

But there are heirs without the substance, and there are heirs with the substance. Those who are written into a will while the testator is still alive are called heirs, but without the substance.

### 4.

There are also minor heirs, who differ in no respect from a servant, because they are under guardians and stewards. “So also we Jews,” he says, “were serving under the elements of this world. But when the fullness of time came and Christ arrived” (Gal. 4:3), we are no longer slaves but free, if we believe in Christ.

Therefore he gave them the appearance of an inheritance, but denied them possession.

[Note: The Roman edition reads, “He gave them hope of an inheritance.”]

They have the name of heir but not its use. For, like minor heirs, they claim only the bare name of inheritance, not authority; they do not possess the right to command or to use it, because they await the fullness of their age, when they will be freed from their guardians.

[Note: Some manuscripts read “under guardians and authors,” and some even “under guardians and makers.” The latter is less appropriate.]

### 5.

Thus, like minors, the Jews too are under a pedagogue. The Law is a pedagogue; a pedagogue leads one to a teacher. Our only teacher is Christ: “Do not call anyone your master or teacher, because your one master and teacher is Christ” (Matt. 23:10).

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “The teacher instructs; the teacher shows the way of salvation.”]

The pedagogue is feared; the teacher shows the way of salvation. Fear therefore leads to freedom, freedom to faith, faith to love, and love obtains adoption; adoption obtains inheritance.

Where there is faith, therefore, there is freedom. A servant is under fear; a free person is from faith. One is under the letter, the other under grace; one is in slavery, the other in the spirit. “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Cor. 3:17).

If, then, where there is faith there is freedom; where there is freedom there is grace; and where there is grace there is inheritance, then the Jew is in slavery under the letter, not the spirit. Whoever does not have faith does not have the freedom of the spirit. Where there is no freedom, there is no grace; where there is no grace, there is no adoption; where there is no adoption, there is no succession.

### 6.

Thus, as though the tablets were closed, he sees the inheritance but does not possess it; he has no authority over the text.

[Note: Nannius annotated these words as follows: “To see an inheritance means to enter upon an inheritance; for this was the common legal expression. But from the fragments of Ulpian and from book 4, title 1, of the Theodosian Code, I believe that it refers to the time granted to an heir for deciding whether he wishes to enter upon the inheritance. Here, however, *to see the inheritance* means simply to look at it, although the one who looks does not immediately see it in the full sense. For the one who sees recognizes the matter and examines it not less with the mind than with the eyes, as in that prophetic passage: ‘So that hearing they may not hear, and seeing they may not see.’”]

For how does he say, “Our Father” (Matt. 6:9), while denying the true Son of God, through whom adoption is acquired? How does he call it a testament while denying the death of the testator? How does he claim freedom while denying the blood by which he was redeemed?

For this is the price of our freedom, as Peter says: “You were redeemed with precious blood” (1 Pet. 1:19)—not, of course, the blood of a lamb, but of the one who came in gentleness and humility like a lamb and liberated the whole world by the single sacrifice of his body, as he himself says: “I was led like a lamb to be sacrificed” (Isa. 53:7). Hence John also says: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29).

### 7.

Thus the Jew is an heir in the letter, not in the spirit (Gal. 4:2), like a minor under guardians and stewards. But the Christian, who has recognized the fullness of time in which Christ came, made of a woman and made under the Law, so that he might redeem all who were under the Law—the Christian, I say, through the unity of faith and the knowledge of the Son of God, grows into a perfect man, into the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ (Eph. 4:13).

Farewell, my son, and love us, because we love you.

# LETTER LXXVI

At the request of Irenaeus, Ambrose presents a summary of the Letter to the Ephesians. He writes that in it the heavenly inheritance and participation in the heavenly throne with Christ are set before us, through whom we have been claimed for freedom; that the goal of faith, love, by which we are joined to Christ, is shown; and that no other letter is filled with so many blessings, which he briefly and individually expounds.

## AMBROSE TO IRENAEUS, GREETINGS

### 1.

You asked us to impress upon you a summary of the letter written to the Ephesians, which seems obscure unless you collect its divisions. Through these the Apostle thought it necessary to persuade us that we should not despair of the kingdom of God (Eph. 1:5 and following).

### 2.

First, therefore, he set forth what is usually the greatest incentive to the pursuit of virtue among good people: the hope of rewards and the inheritance of heavenly promises, which have drawn near through the passion and resurrection of Christ.

### 3.
