Then he added that not only has our return to paradise been restored through Christ, but that the honor of the heavenly throne has also been bestowed upon this flesh through participation in Christ’s body. Thus you should no longer doubt the possibility of ascending, since you recognize that your participation in the flesh of Christ adheres to the heavenly kingdom.

Through his blood the reconciliation of all things, whether in heaven or on earth, has been accomplished—he who descended for this reason, in order to fulfill all things—through his apostles, prophets, and priests, through the confirmation of all things and the gathering of the nations.

[Note: Erasmus and the editions following him read: “who therefore descended to remove our captivity; therefore he ascended to fulfill all things through the apostles … to complete the gathering of the nations. But the end …” The Roman edition reads: “all things, and through the apostles … to complete the gathering of the nations. But the end …” The manuscripts and Ambrosius agree with our text. Observe that the difficulty of this passage lies in the hyperbaton and ellipsis, which may be explained here as follows: “through his blood”—he who therefore descended in order to fulfill all things—the reconciliation of all things, whether in heaven or on earth, has been accomplished; through his apostles … recognize that the gathering of the nations has been accomplished; and recognize the end, and so forth.]

Recognize, then, the end of our hope: his love, so that we may grow in him in all things. For he is the head of all, and according to the measure of activity we all rise up into one body through its construction in love (Eph. 4:15 and following).

### 4.

There is therefore no reason to despair that the members should adhere to their head, especially since from the beginning we were predestined to adoption as sons of God through Jesus Christ and in him.

He proved this predestination by affirming what had been foretold from the beginning: “A man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Gen. 2:28; Eph. 5:31). This is a sacrament of Christ and the Church.

If, then, the union of Adam and Eve is a great sacrament in Christ and in the Church, it is certain that, just as Eve was bone from the man’s bones and flesh from his flesh, so we too are members of Christ’s body, bone from his bones and flesh from his flesh.

### 5.

No letter has poured out so much blessing upon the people of God as this one. In it (Eph. 1:1 and following) he signifies not only that we have been blessed by God, but that we have been blessed with every spiritual blessing and in the heavenly places. He, a witness richly endowed with divine grace, also signifies that we have been predestined to adoption as sons; that in the Son of God we have been filled with grace and have abounded in it so as to know the mystery of the eternal will.

Moreover, in the fullness of time, when all things in Christ were reconciled—both those on earth and those in heaven—we were established in him by lot, so that the things of the Law and the things of grace might be fulfilled in us.

We were also chosen according to the Law in the age of youth, which is an undefiled life, having nothing of childish wantonness or old age’s weakness. We were taught to wage a vigorous battle not only against flesh and blood but also against every army of spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places (Eph. 6:12).

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “enriched with divine grace.” Others, more numerous, read, “rich witnesses of divine grace.” Finally, the rest, together with all editions, read as in the text, where Paul is designated by the words “a rich witness of divine grace.”]

[Note: Not a few manuscripts read, “against every wickedness.”]

### 6.

Therefore, just as those people received by lot possession of lands captured from the enemy, so the lot of grace has fallen to us, so that we may be God’s possession—he who possesses our kidneys (Ps. 139:13), that is, the seedbed of chastity and self-control.

Do you ask to recognize this lot? Recall the lot that fell upon Matthias, so that he might be appointed to the number of the twelve apostles (Acts 1:26). The prophet David also says: “If you sleep between the two lots” (Ps. 68:13), because the one who stands between the lot of the Old and the New Testament, reclining in both, is admitted to the tranquility of the heavenly kingdom.

The daughters of Zelophehad sought this lot of their paternal inheritance, and their petition was approved by divine judgment (Num. 27:1 and following). But they sought it in shadow, for Zelophehad signifies “shadow of the mouth.” Thus, in the shadow of speech, they sought what was not revealed. The request for the paternal inheritance made by Zelophehad’s daughters was therefore in the shadow of speech; for us, however, it is in the splendor of the Gospel and in the revelation of grace.

### 7.

Let us therefore be God’s possession, and let him be our portion, in whom are the riches of his glory and inheritance. For who is rich except God alone, who created all things?

But he is much richer in mercy, because he redeemed everyone and, as the author of nature, transformed us—who according to the nature of the flesh were children of wrath and subject to disturbance—so that we might be children of peace and love (Eph. 2:4 and following).

For who can change nature except the one who created nature? Thus he raised the dead and made them, having been made alive in Christ, sit in the heavenly places in the Lord Jesus himself (ibid., 8).

[Note: Erasmus and the editions following him read, “and subject to death”; Ambrosius and all the manuscripts read, “and subject to disturbance.”]

### 8.

This does not mean that any human being earned the privilege of sitting upon that seat of God of which the Father said to the Son alone, “Sit at my right hand” (Ps. 110:1). Rather, because in that flesh of Christ, through participation in the same nature, the flesh of the entire human race has been honored.

For just as he is read as having been subject in our flesh (Luke 2:51), through the unity of flesh and the obedience of the body, in which he was obedient unto death (Phil. 2:8), so we too have sat with him in the heavenly places in his flesh.

We have not sat independently, therefore, but have sat in Christ. The Son of Man alone sits at the right hand of God, as he himself said: “From now on you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of God” (Matt. 26:64).

For in Christ Jesus his grace and goodness toward us abounded, so that, though dead in works, redeemed through faith and saved by grace, he might grant us such a gift of freedom. In this gift nature itself, as though raised again, experienced the grace of a new creation, so that we might walk in good works, created in Christ, although previously we had degenerated through the fault of a culpable inheritance.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “we were subject to the inherited fault”; the others, and all editions, more correctly read, “we were subject,” where the propagation of original sin is most clearly expressed.]

### 9.

For, once the hostilities that had previously existed in the flesh had been removed, peace was made for the whole universe in heaven (Eph. 2:14). Thus human beings might be like angels on earth; the nations and the Israelites might become one; and in one human being both the new person and the old might come together, once the wall of the barrier that divided both in hostile opposition had been removed.

For when the nature of this flesh had aroused anger, discord, and dissension, and the Law had bound us with condemned men’s chains, Christ Jesus restrained the insolence and intemperance of the flesh by putting it to death. He nullified the law of commandments in decrees, showing in them that the spiritual teachings of the Law must not be interpreted according to the letter.

He also destroyed the idle rest of the Sabbath and the superfluous bodily practice of circumcision, and opened access to the Father for everyone in one spirit. For how can there be discord where there is one calling, one body, and one spirit?

### 10.

What else did the Lord Jesus accomplish by descending (Eph. 4:8) except to claim us from captivity for freedom, and to make that captivity captive to himself—captivity bound by the chains of faithlessness and fettered with the shackles of wisdom, with every wise person putting his feet into its fetters, as it is written?

And when he had descended and ascended in order to fulfill all things (John 1:16), we all received from his fullness.

### 11.

Therefore, first, he placed in the Church those filled with the Holy Spirit: apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors, and teachers, so that through their exhortations the progress of believers might be brought to completion and the work of faithful ministry might grow.

[Note: A great number of manuscripts read as in the text. Some, together with Ambrosius, read *built* instead of *is built*. Erasmus and the editions following him read, “the work might grow and be built,” and so forth.]

Each person is built up by the edification of virtues to the measure of the inner age, which is the measure of a more perfect, blameless life (ibid., 13), that is, of the perfect man; receiving from Christ’s fullness, he receives fullness of grace.

### 12.

Who is a perfect man except the one who has passed beyond childhood’s childish understanding, adolescence’s uncertainty and instability, and the uncontrolled heat of youth, and has advanced into the firmness of a perfect man, growing into that maturity of character?

Such a person is not easily bent by the address of a wayward disputant, nor cast upon the rocks by a storm of irrational and turbulent teaching, while he seeks remedies for error. He follows the truth not only in speech but also in his actions and receives into himself the building of love.

Thus he attains to the unity of faith and knowledge, and, like a member, does not fail his head, that is, Christ, who is the head of all. From him the whole body of the faithful and wise, through the rational harmony of the Word—that is, being joined together, *συναρμολογούμενον* (*synarmologoumenon*), “bound together by the harmony of the Word”—is fitted, compacted, and joined together.

[Note: The Roman edition reads *jugulaverat*, “had joined,” together with the Greek, *ἁρμονίᾳ τοῦ λόγου δεδεμένον*, “bound by the harmony of the Word.” This is absent from not a few manuscripts. Since, however, it is quite familiar for scribes to omit Greek, we have restored the passage from other manuscripts and editions.]

Through every joint of ministry it produces the growth of the body according to the measure of each part, for its own building up in love, so that one temple of God may rise in all, and one dwelling-place of the heavenly habitation may exist in the spirit of all.

### 13.

In this, I think, we should understand not only the connection of holy human beings and of all believers, but also that of all the higher rational Virtues and Powers. Through a certain harmony of virtues and ministries, one body composed of all spirits of rational nature may adhere to its head, Christ, joined together by such a structure of building that not even by touch does the joint between the individual adherents appear to differ.

For this is what the Greek said: *ἁφὴν τῆς χορηγίας κατ’ ἐνέργειαν ἐν μέτρῳ*—“the contact of the supply according to activity in measure.” It will not be difficult for so great an architect to join everything together according to the measure appropriate to each person’s merits and faith, since the building of love excludes and closes every gap of offense.

[Note: Ambrosius and some manuscripts read “a crack of offense.” The Roman edition and other written copies read “a fissure of offense”; some read “of confession.” The latter is absurd.]

There is therefore no doubt that the fellowship of the heavenly Powers will adhere to this temple in order to build it. For it would be incongruous to understand that the building of human love rises so far into the temple of God that God’s dwelling comes to be in us through the spirit, but not also among the heavenly Powers.

[Note: The passage is transmitted differently. Ambrosius and some manuscripts have *ἁφὴν τῆς χορηγίας κατ’ ἐνέργειαν ἐν μέτρῳ*. Erasmus differs only by transposing the words. The Roman edition restores the longer reading, *διὰ πάσης ἁφῆς τῆς χορηγίας κατ’ ἐνέργειαν ἐν μέτρῳ*. In many manuscripts the Greek sentence is absent.]

### 14.

For this reason, so that such a building might progress more rapidly in us, the Apostle urges us to open the eyes of our heart, lift them to higher things, seek the knowledge of God earnestly, examine the truth, hide God’s commandments in our heart, lay aside the desires of error and the hidden things of disgrace, be renewed through the grace of the sacraments, restrain anger, release resentment before sunset, and beware lest your adversary take possession of your higher faculties—that spirit possessing power which plunged itself into Judas’s heart (John 13:12) and shattered the doors of his soul, so that he could not resist, exclude the thief, turn away the liar, rise from the dead, or assume sobriety.

He urges that a wife should be subject to her husband as the Church is to Christ; that a husband should offer his life for his wife, just as Christ gave himself for the Church (Eph. 5:25).

Finally, like a good soldier, he urges us to take up the weapons of God and always hold them before us, not only against flesh and blood but also against spiritual wickedness (Eph. 6:12), lest we be softened by our own people or captured by strangers.

I have briefly summarized these matters as best I could.

Farewell, my son, and love us, because we love you.

# LETTER LXXVII

To one asking what that inheritance is for which many do not hesitate to meet death, Ambrose replies that it is the very inheritance which we obtain as free people from the promise. For when we serve God through love, we possess true freedom.

He teaches that this was signified in the blessing of Esau. From this he concludes that even from the Law, under which there was slavery, freedom also comes, since the Law led us to faith. He adds that it is not Christ but Moses who will accuse them, and therefore that the Jews are foolish, since they choose as their accuser the one who should be a good judge.

## AMBROSE TO HORONTIANUS

### 1.

You did not think it pointless to ask what the inheritance of divine things is, and why it is valued under so great a name, so that many offer even their lives for it.

[Note: The Roman edition reads, “why it is considered so valuable”; the old edition, “why it is valued so highly.” All manuscripts add “in name,” which is not inappropriate, since here it has the same force as “in price.”]

But if you consider that even in human practice the prospect of a monetary inheritance causes the rights of affection to become more revered—for more deference is shown to parents, lest wounded affection avenge itself by disinheriting or repudiating an insolent child—you will certainly cease to wonder at the great desire for the divine inheritance.

[Note: The Latins say *disinherit*, the Greeks *repudiate*. The distinction between the two is that we repudiate during life and disinherit at death. Once repudiated, a person is immediately denied the parents’ favor and the rights of children; once disinherited, he is denied succession to the goods. By “pledges” here he means children. Thus Nannius.]

### 2.

An inheritance has been set before all Christians. For Isaiah says: “There is an inheritance for those who believe in the Lord” (Isa. 54:17). It is hoped for from the promise, not from the Law.

This is proved by the example of the Old Testament, when Sarah said: “Cast out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac” (Gen. 21:10).

Isaac was Sarah’s son; Ishmael was the slave woman’s son. These events occurred before the Law. Therefore the promise is older than the Law.

We, according to Isaac, are children through the promise; the Jews, according to the flesh, are children of the slave woman (Gal. 4:28). Our mother is the free woman, who did not give birth at first, but afterward, from the promise, poured herself out and bore a male child. Their mother is Hagar, giving birth into slavery.

The one to whom grace is promised is free; the one upon whom the yoke of the Law is imposed is a slave. Therefore the promise came before the Law for us, and, according to nature, freedom is older than slavery.

Freedom, therefore, comes from the promise; slavery comes from the Law. Yet although the promise itself came before the Law, as we have said, and freedom comes from the promise, and love from freedom, nevertheless love is according to the Law, since it is greater than freedom.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “which is the greater freedom.” Others, instead of “Therefore we are not slaves,” read, “Will he then serve?”]

### 3.

“Therefore we are not slaves?” And how is it written: “Praise the Lord, servants” (Ps. 135:1)? How does the Apostle himself say: “As servants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart with goodwill” (Eph. 6:6)?

There is also a free slavery, which is voluntary. Concerning it the Apostle says: “The one who was called while free is Christ’s slave” (1 Cor. 7:22). This is slavery from the heart, not from necessity.

Thus we are indeed servants of our Creator, but we possess the freedom that we have received through the grace of Christ, having been born from the promise according to faith.

Therefore, as those born from a free woman, let us offer the sacrifice of freedom, marked on the forehead as is fitting for free people, so that we may not be ashamed but glory—marked by the spirit, not by the flesh.

To such people it is rightly said: “Stand firm, and do not submit again to the yoke of slavery” (Gal. 5:1). He did not say, “Do not serve,” but “Do not submit to the yoke of slavery,” for the yoke of slavery is heavier than slavery itself.

### 4.

Finally, Isaac said to his son Esau when he asked for a blessing: “Behold, your dwelling shall be from the richness of the earth and from the dew of heaven above; you shall live by your sword, and you shall serve your brother. But it shall come to pass when you have thrown off and loosened his yoke from your neck” (Gen. 27:39–40).

How can this be consistent—that he should serve once he has loosened his brother’s yoke from his neck—unless we understand that there is a distinction in kinds of slavery?

Let the reading itself explain to us what the difference is. Isaac was good, and good also for us, who according to him are born into freedom; and he was a good father to both sons.

Finally, he demonstrated his love for both, showing affection toward one and giving a blessing to the other. For he had said to his elder son that he should bring him food and receive the blessing. But while the elder delayed and sought wild, country food, the younger brother brought food from the household flock of sheep.

### 5.

Christ is the good food of all; faith is good food; mercy is sweet food; grace is delightful food. The people of the holy Church feast upon these foods.

The Spirit of God is good food; the forgiveness of sins is good food. But the food of the Law is exceedingly hard, and its terror consists in punishments; the observance of the letter is wild food, rather than the grace of indulgence.

Finally, that people were under a curse, but we are in blessing. Faith is swift food: “The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart” (Deut. 30:14). The food of the Law is slower. Indeed, while the Law was awaited, the people went astray (Exod. 32:1 and following).

6. The father therefore conferred the blessing upon the diligent and faithful son; but because he was a good father, he preserved a blessing also for the elder son, so that he might make him servant of his brother—not because he wished to reduce his household to degenerate servitude [Note: [Col. 1265D] Quite a few manuscripts read “wished it to degenerate” or “to bring it into servitude.”], but because one who cannot rule and govern himself ought to serve and be subject to the wiser, so that he may be governed by his counsel and not be plunged into ruin or fall through his own folly and rashness. Servitude of this kind, therefore, is bestowed in place of a blessing. Indeed, it is counted among blessings, among the fertility bestowed upon the land and the dew of heaven from above. But because he had said, “You shall live by your sword,” lest presumption of strength or power harm him, he added, “You shall serve your brother,” so that you may both produce abundant fruits of the flesh, attain the dew of divine grace, and follow him who governs by his own direction.

7. But this will happen when you have removed his yoke from your neck, so that you may receive the reward of voluntary service and not suffer the injury of compulsion. Such service is dishonored when it is imposed by necessity; it is honored when it is offered out of devotion. Hence the Apostle says: “If I do this willingly, I have a reward; but if unwillingly, I have been entrusted with a stewardship” (1 Cor. 9:17). The reward of recompense is certainly better than the service of stewardship [Col. 1265D]. Let us therefore not be held by the yoke of servitude, but serve one another through the love of the Spirit, because the Apostle says: “Through love of the Spirit serve one another” (Gal. 5:13). Fear belongs to the Law; love belongs to the Gospel. Thus: “The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord, but the fullness of the Law is love” (Eccles. 1:16). Yet the Law itself also says: “And in this word every commandment is restored” (Rom. 13:8), and, he says, in this one saying it is fulfilled: “You shall love your neighbor” (Gal. 5:14).

8. This, then, is what we have proposed: although servitude comes from the Law, freedom is nevertheless according to the Law; for love is of freedom, while fear is of servitude. There is therefore both love belonging to the Law and servitude belonging to love; but the Law is the herald of love, while the love of the Gospel is the arbiter of devout service.

9. The Law, then, is not superfluous, since it accompanies the weaker like a pedagogue. I mean weakness of character, not of bodies; for they are infants who do not know how to utter the word of God and do not receive his works (Gal. 3:24). For if the age of old age is an unstained life (Wis. 4:9), then certainly the age of adolescence is a stained life. The Law, therefore, was a pedagogue—that is, νόμος (*nomos*, “law”)—until faith should come. [Note: [Col. 1266D] The Roman edition reads, “Νόμος, therefore—that is, the Law—was a pedagogue.”] “And as though we were weak,” he says, “we were guarded by the Law, confined for that faith which was to be revealed” (Gal. 3:23). But after faith came, the Gospel does not say “the faith” but simply “faith”; for that is the one faith which is in the Gospel. Although the righteousness of God is revealed in it, “which is from faith to faith” (Rom. 1:17), nevertheless the faith of the Law is such only if the fullness of faith is added to it. This faith is therefore rightly called, as it were, the only one: without it the former is not faith, while in it the former is confirmed. Thus, when this faith came, fullness came; the adoption of sons came; weakness ceased; infancy departed; we rise up into a perfect man and put on Christ. How, then, can one in whom Christ is the power of God be weak and small? Therefore we have come to perfection and have received the precepts of perfection.

10. You heard read today [Note: [Col. 1266D] There is no doubt that this reading was given in the Church’s assembly. Whether it was at Milan, however, is quite uncertain.]: “I can do nothing of myself; as I hear, I judge” (John 5:30). You heard read: “I do not accuse you; I do not judge you. I do not accuse you; Moses accuses you, in whom you hope” (ibid., 45). You heard read: “If I bear witness concerning myself, my testimony is not true” (ibid., 31). I have learned what sort of judge and what sort of witness I ought to be. He does not say, as though he were weak, “I can do nothing of myself,” but the weak person is the one who understands it in that way. The Son indeed does nothing without the Father, because their operation is common and their power is one; but in this passage he speaks as a judge, so that we may understand that human beings, when judging, must form their sentence not according to their own will and power, but according to equity.

11. Suppose that a defendant has been charged and convicted of a crime, offering no grounds for his defense but begging and throwing himself at the judge’s knees. The judge answers him: “I can do nothing of myself.” Justice, not power, governs judgment. “I do not judge; your deeds judge you. They themselves accuse you and they themselves condemn you. The laws adjudge you; I do not alter them as judge, but preserve them. I bring forward nothing from myself; the form of judgment proceeds from you against you. I judge according to what I hear, not according to what I wish; and therefore my judgment is true, because I do not indulge my will but equity.”

12. Let us therefore consider what the religious principle of judging is. The Lord, judge of heaven and earth and of all things, says: “I can do nothing of myself; as I hear, I judge.” And a human being says to his Lord: “Do you not know that I have power to release you and power to crucify you?” (John 19:10). Why can the Lord not do so? “Because,” he says, “my judgment is true” [Note: [Col. 1267D] The Roman edition alone reads, “my judgment is just.”]. “For I do not seek my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 5:30)—that is: not the will of the man whom you see; not the judgment of the man whom you judge only as a human being; not the will of the flesh, because “the spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matt. 26:41); but the divine will, which is the author of the Law and the arbiter of judgment. Likewise, the true witness is one who bears testimony not to himself but to another; for it is written: “Let your neighbor praise you, and not your own mouth” (Prov. 27:2).

13. Beautifully, however, it is said mystically to the Jews: “I do not judge you”—that is, “I, the redemption of all, I, the forgiveness of sinners, do not judge you,” because you did not receive me. “I do not judge,” who willingly pardon. “I do not judge,” who redeem sinners with my blood (Isa. 43:25). “I do not judge,” who blot out iniquities and will remember them no more. “I do not judge,” who prefer the sinner’s life to his death (Ezek. 18:23). “I do not judge,” who do not condemn but justify those who confess. “Moses accuses you”; he reproves you, “in whom you hope.” He accuses you because he does not possess the power of judgment, which belongs to his author. The one in whom you hope therefore accuses you; the one in whom you were unwilling to hope acquits you.

14. Great was the Jews’ folly [Note: [Col. 1267D] Several manuscripts read “the Jews’ prudence.” Incorrectly.]. They are rightly accused in their crimes because they chose an accuser and rejected a good judge; and therefore acquittal is absent from them, while punishment is not.

15. Rightly, therefore, my son, you began from the Law, and have been confirmed in the Gospel—from faith to faith, as it is written: “For the righteous person lives by faith” (Rom. 1:17) [Note: [Col. 1267D] Hermannus, relying on these words, considers this Horontianus to have been converted from Judaism; we do not disagree with him in this respect. We add, however, that he does not appear to be the same man to whom the preceding letters addressed to Horontianus were sent. For it is clear that the latter was offered to the Church by his parents from childhood, and this question does not seem to have been proposed by a deacon and a man trained in ecclesiastical disciplines, to whom Ambrose sent these letters in order to resolve it.]. Farewell, and love us, because we love you.

## LETTER LXXVIII

That we are justified by faith, like Abraham, through which we are sons of the free woman; that circumcision had power only through Christ, who himself underwent it and rendered it obsolete; and therefore that righteousness is to be expected from faith alone, which, if perfect, is never without love.

[Note: [Col. 1268D] The Roman edition reads, “Ambrose the bishop to Horontianus.” The word “bishop” is absent from the old edition and all the manuscripts, and in several of them the address is entirely omitted.]

### AMBROSE TO HORONTIANUS

1. “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Gen. 15:6). But what is reckoned as righteousness proceeds from unbelief to faith. We are therefore justified by faith, not by works of the Law. Abraham himself had two sons, Ishmael and Isaac, one by a slave woman and the other by a free woman (Gal. 4:22 ff.). The response was such that he expelled the slave woman and the son of the slave woman, for the son of the slave woman was not to be the heir. Therefore we are not sons of the slave woman but of the free woman, with the freedom by which Christ freed us. From this it follows that those who are from faith are more truly Abraham’s sons, for they are heirs of faith rather than of generation. The Law is a pedagogue; faith is free. Let us therefore cast away the works of servitude and hold fast the grace of freedom [Note: [Col. 1268D] Four manuscripts read, “let us leave the shadow for the sun, as we leave Jewish rites; let us leave the circumcision of one member, which profits nothing.”]: let us leave the shadow and follow the sun; let us leave the Jewish rites (Gal. 3:24).

2. Circumcision of one member profits nothing. Hence the Apostle says: “Behold, I, Paul, tell you that if you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Gal. 5:2). Not because he cannot profit you, but because he judges those unworthy of his benefits who abandon his ways.

3. Indeed, Zipporah circumcised her son beforehand and averted the danger that threatened (Exod. 4:25). But Christ then profited, while perfection was still being deferred [Col. 1268B]. When the people of believers were still a child, the Lord Jesus came—not as a child, but perfect in all things. He was first circumcised according to the Law, so as not to abolish the Law; afterward, through the cross, in order to fulfill the Law (1 Cor. 13:10). Therefore what is partial ceased, because what is perfect came; for in Christ the cross circumcised not one member but the superfluous pleasures of the whole body.

4. Perhaps it is still asked why he who had come to display perfect circumcision wished to be circumcised in part. I do not think this requires prolonged deliberation. For if he became sin in order to cleanse our sins (2 Cor. 5:21), and became a curse for us in order to nullify the curses of the Law (Gal. 3:13), then for the same reason he was circumcised for us: to remove the circumcision of the Law and to give the salvation of the cross.

5. The Apostle therefore asserts that through the Spirit and from faith we are to await the hope of righteousness (Gal. 5:5), and that, having been called to freedom, we must not turn our freedom into an opportunity for the flesh. For neither circumcision nor uncircumcision has any power, but only “faith working through love” (ibid., 6). Therefore it is written: “You shall love the Lord your God” (Deut. 6:4). Whoever loves certainly believes, and through believing each person begins to love. Thus Abraham believed, and so began to love; and he believed not partially but in all things. Otherwise he could not have full love, because it is written: “Love believes all things” (1 Cor. 13:7). If it does not believe all things, it does not appear to be perfect love. Perfect love therefore possesses all faith.

6. Yet I would not readily say that every faith immediately possesses perfect love, because the Apostle says: “If I have all faith, so that I remove mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing” [Col. 1269A] (1 Cor. 13:2). For since there are three chief things in a Christian man—hope, faith, and love—“the greatest of these is love” (ibid., 13).

7. But I think that the Apostle said this for the sake of his argument [Note: [Col. 1269D] Some manuscripts read “for the sake of the grace proposed”; others, and all the editions, read “for the sake of the proposition,” that is, for the sake of his argument or in order to serve his argument. The holy Doctor means that the Apostle proposed an impossible hypothesis in order to explain the necessity of love.]. For it does not seem to me that someone who has all faith, so as to remove mountains, can lack love. The same applies to the statement that someone might possess all mysteries and all knowledge: how could he lack love, especially since John says, “Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ is born of God” (1 John 4:7), and he himself had said above, “Whoever is born of God does not sin” (ibid., 3:9)? From this it follows that if the one who believes that Jesus is the Christ is born of God, and the one born of God does not sin, then the one who believes that Jesus is the Christ does not sin. If someone sins, he does not believe; whoever does not believe does not love; whoever does not love is subject to sin [Note: [Col. 1269D] Several manuscripts read, “does not believe and is subject to sin.”]. Therefore the one who sins does not love, for “love covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. 4:8). But if love excludes the inclination to sin—and since it also casts out fear—then love is surely full of perfect faith.

8. Finally, the apostles, who were to become friends, said: “Increase our faith” (Luke 17:5), asking the good physician to heal the faith that was still weak in them. Their faith was still weak when Peter also heard: “You of little faith, why did you doubt?” (Matt. 14:31). Faith, therefore, like a precursor of love, takes possession of the soul and prepares paths for the love that is to come. Thus all faith is present wherever there is the perfection of love.

[Col. 1269C] 9. Therefore I think it is said that “love believes all things” (1 Cor. 13:7)—that is, it makes faith believe all things [Note: [Col. 1269D] In four manuscripts the words “and to have such a soul possess all faith” are omitted; likewise the following words, “there all faith is, just as where there is perfect love.”], and makes such a soul possess all faith. Consequently, where there is perfect love, there is all faith; just as where there is perfect love, there is all hope. For just as love believes all things, so it is written that it “hopes all things” (ibid.). It is therefore greater because it embraces both hope and faith.

10. Whoever possesses this love fears nothing, because love casts out fear; and therefore, with fear banished and stripped away, he bears all things and endures all things. Whoever therefore endures all things through love cannot fear martyrdom. Hence, like a victor, he says elsewhere at the end: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6:14). Farewell, my son, and love us, because we love you.

## 1095 LETTER LXXIX

To Bellicius, who, after believing in Christ, recovered from illness: Ambrose maintains that both his illness and his recovery should be attributed to a visitation by the same Christ; and, in order to retain him and hasten him toward the other sacraments, he exhorts him.

### AMBROSE TO BELLICIUS, GREETING

1. You informed me that, having been afflicted by a serious illness, you had believed in the Lord Jesus and had already begun to recover [Note: [Col. 1269D] The Boyer manuscript reads, “You informed me that you had been struck,” and so forth.]. That illness therefore contributed to your salvation, bringing more goad than danger, because you had long delayed the promise [Note: [Col. 1270D] The same manuscript reads, “more assistance”; the other manuscripts and all the editions more aptly read, “more goad,” namely, because the illness spurred him toward faith. But where all the editions and nearly all the manuscripts read, “you were gnawing at the promise,” we have restored from the Albin manuscript, “you were delaying the promise.”]. This is what he says: “I strike, and I heal” (Deut. 32:39). He struck with illness and healed through faith. For he saw that your inner disposition was not empty of devout desire but was being shaken out of its delays; and therefore he preferred to admonish you in such a way as not to injure your health but to awaken your devotion.

2. For how could he harm the health of one who, as we read in the Gospel, is accustomed to say: “I will come and heal him” (Matt. 8:7)? [Note: [Col. 1270D] The Boyer manuscript reads, “Therefore he awaited an invitation from your family.”] Thus, when your family invited him to visit your house, he undoubtedly said: “I will come and heal him.” And even if you did not hear him, he nevertheless spoke, as God, in an imperceptible manner; and even if you did not see him, there can be no doubt that he visited you incorporeally.

3. But you saw him because you believed in him; you saw him because you received him as a guest in the lodging of your mind. You saw him in spirit; you saw him with the eyes within. Therefore hold fast this new guest, long awaited but received late, in whom “we live and move and have our being” (Acts 17:28). You have tasted, therefore, the first beginnings of faith; let the word not become hidden in your heart. This is all grace; this is the whole gift. No one judges the inner chambers of a house by its entrance, since all the fruit is within [Note: [Col. 1270D] The Boyer manuscript reads, “all display,” which is not at all bad.]; nor is it the mark of a wise man to look into a house through the window, or of a foolish man to listen at the door.

4. There are other mysteries of more perfect sacraments, because “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, what God has prepared for those who love him,” as Scripture says (1 Cor. 2:9). There are other things belonging to the future glory, which the prophets announced, to whom they were revealed, and which the saints proclaimed as good news (ibid.), through the Spirit of God sent from heaven, into which the angels long to look, as the Apostle Peter says (1 Pet. 1:12). There are other things in which are the redemption of the world, the forgiveness of sins, the distribution of graces, and participation in the sacraments. When you have received these, you will then marvel that so great a gift has been given to humanity, so that you will judge that manna, which we marvel to have flowed from heaven for the Jews (Exod. 17:15 ff.) [Col. 1271A], to have been neither so great a grace nor so powerful an operation for salvation [Note: [Col. 1271D] To the words “nor so great a grace” the Boyer manuscript alone adds what is omitted in the other manuscripts and all the editions, not without loss of elegance.]. For all who received that manna in the desert died, except Joshua son of Nun and Caleb (Num. 32:12); but whoever tastes this sacrament will not die forever. May the Lord Jesus heal you. Farewell.

## LETTER LXXX

Where he shows that the healing of the man blind from birth was an act of divine power, rebukes the disciples’ question, and recalls and briefly explains certain parts of the same story.

[Note: [Col. 1271D] Some manuscripts and the old edition have this form; the Roman edition inserted “the bishop,” in Greek τὸ ἐπίσκοπος. The Laetus, Long, and Gem manuscripts, by correction, read “Ambrose to Irenaeus”; the first hand of the Gem manuscript reads “to Horontianus”; five others reject the salutation entirely, replacing it in three manuscripts with “A discourse on the man born blind.” But it is clear from what precedes that this letter should be addressed to Bellicius.]

### AMBROSE TO BELLICIUS

1. You heard, brother, the reading from the Gospel in which it was related that the Lord Jesus, passing by, saw a man blind from birth [Note: [Col. 1271D] The old edition and certain manuscripts read, “blind from his generation.” Therefore we too must not pass him by. Further below: “so that you may recognize that the healing of this man, who was blind from his birth, is not a matter of art,” and so forth.]. Therefore, if the Lord saw him, he did not pass him by (John 9:1); so neither should we pass by the one whom the Lord did not consider it right to pass by, especially since the fact that he had been blind from birth was not stated without purpose.

2. There is a kind of blindness that usually covers the sharpness of the eyes through the force of illness and is alleviated over time. There is a kind of blindness caused by an influx of humors; this too is generally driven away by medical skill once the defect has been removed. Thus you may recognize that the healing of this man, who was blind from birth, was not a matter of medical art but of power. The Lord bestowed health; he did not practice medicine. For the Lord Jesus healed those whom no one else could cure.

3. How foolish were the Jews, who asked: “Did this man sin, or his parents?” (ibid., 2) [Note: [Col. 1271D] The Roman edition reads, “How foolishly the disciples ask”; the other editions and the manuscripts read as in the text, except that a few have “foolish” instead of “foolish men.” Chrysostom likewise calls this question of the disciples absurd in the same sense.], attributing bodily weaknesses to the merits of sins. Therefore the Lord says: “Neither did this man sin, nor his parents, but that the works of God might be manifested in him” (ibid., 3). What nature lacked belongs to the Creator to restore, since he is the author of nature. Hence he added: “As long as I am in the world, I am the light of this world” (ibid.)—that is, all who are blind can see if they seek me as their light [Note: [Col. 1272D] The old edition reads, “all can see because they are blind.”]. “Draw near, and be enlightened, so that you may be able to see” (Ps. 33:6) [Note: [Col. 1272D] The Laud, Corb, Germ, Colb, and Ful manuscripts read, “so that God may be seen.”].

4. What, then, does it mean that the one who restored life by command and gave health by a word—saying to the dead man, “Come forth” (John 11:44), and Lazarus came out of the tomb; saying to the paralytic, “Rise, take up your pallet” (Mark 2:11), and the paralytic rose and began to carry the pallet on which he had lain with all his limbs loosened [Note: [Col. 1272D] Several manuscripts read “loosened”; some, “on which he lay with his limbs loosened.”]—what, I say, does it mean that he spat and made clay, anointed the eyes of the blind man, and said to him: “Go, wash in Siloam,” which means “sent”; and he went, washed, and began to see (John 9:7)? What is the reason for this? A great one, I think; for the one whom Jesus touches sees more clearly.

5. At the same time, observe both his divinity and his sanctification. Like light, he touched and poured himself in; like a priest, through the figure of baptism, he fulfilled the mysteries of spiritual grace. He spat so that you might recognize that the inner things of Christ are light. And truly he sees who is cleansed inwardly by Christ [Note: [Col. 1272D] The Corb manuscript reads, “who is cleansed by Christ on earth.” It is also worth noting that in this healing of the man born blind the Fathers discerned an outstanding figure of baptism. See, among others, Augustine on this passage of John, and you will observe that the disciple follows in the teacher’s footsteps. It should also be noted here that this same Gospel was formerly accustomed to be read in the Church toward the end of Lent, as these words testify: “Come to baptism; the very time is at hand.” From these words it is also clear that this Bellicius had not yet departed from the ranks of the catechumens.]. His saliva washes; his word washes, as you have it: “Now you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you” (John 15:3).

6. What else does it signify that he made clay and anointed the eyes of the blind man (John 9:6), except that you should understand that he himself restored to health the human being upon whom clay had been applied, he who formed humanity from clay (Gen. 2:7), and that this flesh of our clay receives the light of eternal life through the sacraments of baptism? You too, draw near to Siloam—that is, to the one who was sent by the Father—as you have it: “My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me” (John 7:16). May Christ wash you, so that you may see. Come to baptism; the very time is at hand. Come quickly, so that you too may say: “I went, and I washed, and I began to see” (John 9:11); so that you may say: “I was blind, and I began to see” [Note: [Col. 1272D] The Corb, Laud, Colb, Germ, and Ful manuscripts read, “I was in darkness.”]; so that you may say, as this man declared when light was restored to him: “The night has passed, but the day has drawn near” (Rom. 13:12).

7. It was night when there was blindness. It was night when Judas received the morsel from Jesus and Satan entered into him. It was night for Judas, in whom the devil was; it was day for John, who reclined on Christ’s breast (John 13:27). It was also day for Peter when he saw the light of Christ on the mountain (Matt. 17:2 ff.) [Note: [Col. 1272D] The same manuscripts read, “It was night, but he saw the light. For others it was night,” and so forth.]. It was night for the others, but day for Peter. Yet it was night for Peter himself when he denied Christ. Finally, the rooster crowed and he began to weep (Matt. 26:70 ff.), so that he might correct his error; for the day was already drawing near.

8. The Jews asked the blind man: “How did you see?” (John 9:10). Great madness! They were asking what they saw; they were asking the cause while they saw the deed.

9. And they cursed him, saying: “You be his disciple” (John 9:28). Their curse is a blessing, because their blessing is a curse [Note: [Col. 1273D] In quite a few manuscripts and in Amerbach, the words “their curse … his disciple” are absent.]. “You be his disciple,” they say. They are useful precisely when they think they are doing harm [Note: [Col. 1273D] In some manuscripts this letter is joined in a single sequence with the letter we placed as number 26: “They think they are doing harm. The question always sung aloud,” and so forth.]. Farewell, my son, and love us as you do, because we love you.

## LETTER LXXXI

He strengthens certain clergy who are becoming discouraged in spirit because of labor and difficulty, setting before their eyes not only the reward that is to come but also Christ’s prepared protection. For this reason, after explaining several passages of Scripture, he warns them not to allow themselves to be torn away from him.

### AMBROSE TO THE CLERGY

1. It often happens that some slight offense blinds human minds, and if voluntary things do not come to them according to their desire, they withdraw from their duty. This may be tolerated in another class of people, but in those who devote themselves to divine service it is a source of great sorrow.

2. There are some in the clerical office against whom the enemy strives to creep, if he cannot otherwise ensnare them, inserting thoughts of this kind into minds that have been wounded: “What benefit is it for me to remain among the clergy, to suffer insults and endure perpetual labors, as though my field could not feed me, or, if I have no field, as though I could not obtain my expenses by some other means?” [Note: [Col. 1273D] This passage indicates that within the clerical order some possessed certain resources while others possessed none. We discussed this matter in Book I of *The Duties*, chapter 36, no. 184.] Thus even good character is drawn away from its duty by such thoughts—as though the sole concern of a cleric were to provide for his expenses, rather than to secure for himself divine support after death. Yet the one who can safely decide here against the ambushes of so many enemies will abound after death.

3. Hence Ecclesiastes says: “Two are better than one, for they have a good reward for their labor; for if one falls, the other will raise up his companion” (Eccles. 4:9–10) [Note: [Col. 1273D] The old edition here, and we along with the Roman edition and the manuscripts of *On the Institution of a Virgin*, chapter 11, read, “If one falls, the other will raise him.” On this reading see Nobilius. The old edition in the work just cited, and the Roman edition here, read “if one falls, he will raise him.” We place a comma before “one” with the manuscripts, but we do not dare restore “if they fall” instead of “if one falls,” although we conjecture that Ambrose wrote it, on the basis of the Greek words ἐὰν πέσωσι, ὁ εἷς ἐγερεῖ or ἐγείρει, and so forth.]. Where are “two who are better than one,” except where Christ is, and the one whom Christ protects? For if the one who is with the Lord Jesus falls, Jesus raises him.

4. But why did he say, “in their labor”? Does Christ, then, also labor? Certainly he labors, who says: “I have labored, crying out” (Ps. 58:4). He labors [Note: [Col. 1274D] Several manuscripts read, “but not in us,” which produces a faulty sense.], but in us. Indeed, he sat exhausted beside the well (John 4:6). But how he labors, the Apostle taught us by a lesser example when he said: “Who is weak, and I am not weak?” (2 Cor. 11:29). The Lord himself also taught this in his own words: “I was sick, and you did not visit me; I was naked, and you did not clothe me” (Matt. 25:43). He labors in order to raise me when I lie fallen.

5. Hence in Elisha there also preceded a figure of the Lord: he threw himself upon the dead boy in order to raise him (2 Kings 4:34). This signifies that Christ died together with us so that he might rise for us. Christ therefore cast himself down even to the level of our frailty in order to raise us. He cast himself down; he did not fall, but raised his companion. For he made us his companions, as it is written: “He has been anointed with the oil of righteousness above his companions” (Ps. 44:8) [Note: [Col. 1274D] The Roman edition alone reads, “with the oil of gladness.”].

6. Hence Ecclesiastes beautifully says: “For if one falls, he raises his companion” (Eccles. 4:10), not that he himself is raised. Christ was not raised by another’s help and assistance; he himself raised himself. Thus he says: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” He said this about the temple of his body (John 2:19). Nor was he rightly raised by another, since he did not fall; for the one who is raised by a second has fallen, and the one who has fallen needs assistance in order to be raised. The following words also teach this, as Scripture says: “Woe to the one who is alone when he falls and has no second to raise him! And if two sleep together, they have warmth” (Eccles. 4:10–11). We have died together with Christ, and therefore we live together with him (Rom. 6:8). Christ died together with us so that he might warm us, who says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12:49).

7. I was dead, but because I died together with Christ in baptism, I received from Christ the light of life. Whoever dies in Christ receives through Christ the warmth of life and the vapor of resurrection. The boy was cold; Elisha warmed him with his own spirit and gave him the warmth of life (2 Kings 4:34). He lay down beside him so that the warmth of his repose, with which the boy had been buried symbolically, might awaken him. Therefore the one who does not die in Christ is cold; the one whom the burning fire does not approach cannot be warmed; one who does not have Christ with him cannot grow warm toward another [Note: [Col. 1274D] Thus the Roman edition reads with part of the manuscripts; the old edition with the remaining manuscripts reads, “cannot grow strong.”].

8. And so that you may recognize that this was said according to the mystery, not according to number—for “two who are better than one”—he added the mystical statement: “A threefold cord is not quickly broken” [Note: [Col. 1274D] The Roman edition alone reads, “is not quickly broken.”]. For three things that are not composite are not broken. The Trinity, therefore, whose nature is uncompounded, cannot be broken, because God is one and simple and uncompounded, whatever he is; but what is remains and is not subject.

10. It is good, therefore, to cling to another, to insert one’s neck into his collar, to submit one’s shoulder, to carry him, and not to grow weary of the bonds. For from the house of those who were bound came forth the one who was to reign: that child who is above the older and foolish king. Therefore those who follow him are bound with bonds. Thus Paul was “a prisoner of Jesus Christ” (Eph. 3:1). Hence Jesus himself also “led captivity captive” (Eph. 4:8). It was not enough for him to release the captivity imposed by the devil, lest it again invade those who were free and wandering [Note: [Col. 1275D] All editions and some manuscripts read, “free and unoccupied”; several others, and those of better quality, read, “free and wandering.” This is more suitably opposed to what follows, “to put their feet into the fetters of wisdom.”]. Perfect release was judged to consist in dwelling under Christ and putting one’s feet into the fetters of wisdom, being his captive so that one might be free from the adversary.

11. Rightly is he called a child, since “a child has been born for us” (Isa. 9:6); and truly an excellent child, to whom God the Father said: “It is a great thing for you to be called my child” (Isa. 49:5). He is also wise, as the Gospel teaches, because “he advanced in age and wisdom” (Luke 2:52). He is also appropriately poor, because, although he was rich, he became poor in order to enrich us by his poverty (2 Cor. 8:9). Therefore he does not disdain the poor in his kingdom, but hears him and delivers him from all distress and trouble.

12. Let us therefore live under him, so that the older and foolish king [Note: [Col. 1275D] The Roman edition inserts here, “who does not know how to take precautions for the future.”] may have no power over us. When he wishes to reign as though he were master of his own will, and refuses to be under the bonds of the Lord Jesus, he grows old in sins and falls into the deformity of folly. For what is more foolish than, after abandoning heavenly things, to turn one’s attention to earthly things, and, having set aside eternal things, to choose what is perishable and fragile?

13. Let no one therefore say: “We have no portion in Jacob, nor inheritance in Israel” (1 Kings 12:16) [Note: [Col. 1275D] This same edition alone reads, “no portion in David, nor inheritance in the son of Jesse.”]. Let no one say: “I am not among the clergy,” because it is written: “Give Levi his lots” (Deut. 33:8). And again David says: “For he who rests in the midst between two lots, he himself flies upward on spiritual wings” (Ps. 67:14). Do not say of your God: “He is burdensome to me” (Wis. 2:12), nor of your place: “It is useless to me,” because it is written: “Do not leave your place” (Eccles. 10:4). The adversary wishes to take it away; he wishes to lead you away because he envies your hope and envies your gift.

14. But you, whoever you are among the clergy of the Lord, his portion and possession, do not withdraw from the Lord’s possession, so that you may say to the Lord: “You possessed my reins; you received me from my mother’s womb” (Ps. 138:23); and so that he may say to you, as to a good servant: “Come over and recline” (Luke 17:7). Farewell, my sons, and serve the Lord, because the Lord is good.

## LETTER LXXXII
How he came to be appointed judge in the matter of MARCELLUS, Laetus, and their sister, and why he undertook that inquiry in such a way that he preferred to act as arbiter, he recalls; he sets out the state of the dispute and shows that Marcellus ought not to bear his loss with resentment. Then he praises him for having shown himself an exceptionally fair arbiter. He explains why he nevertheless altered something in his arbitration; and finally he declares how each party won without harm to the Church.

## AMBROSE TO MARCELLUS

### 1

The course of your case has reached me—a case which you did not initiate but took up, because both the demands of piety and the desire to demonstrate generosity toward the poor required it. I learned, in accordance with the form of the sacred injunction—which the authority of the blessed Apostle, as well as the pattern and discipline of your teaching and life, imposed upon me [Note: Ambrose calls imperial laws “the form of the sacred injunction,” as Thaumassus reports, *Ecclesiastical Discipline*, part I, book II, chapter 42. Perhaps, however, no other enactment is indicated here except that famous one which Sozomen mentions as having been promulgated by Constantine the Great, *Ecclesiastical History*, book I, chapter 9.]—that, when I myself reproved you because the long-standing quarrel still persisted among you, the parties imposed upon me the necessity of investigating it.

### 2

I confess that I was ashamed to refuse, especially when the advocates of both sides, wearing the toga [Note: Nannius says that *togati*, from the dress and appearance in which they conducted cases, came to be called advocates and lawyers.] and attacking one another in turn, declared that it should be determined under my examination which party had the greater support of law or justice. What more need I say? Since the appointed days had already been concluded, and only a few hours remained—hours during which the prefect nevertheless had other cases to hear—the advocates of the case asked that the time be extended for a few days, so that I might sit as judge. Such was the eagerness of Christian men not to have the prefect judge a matter belonging to a bishop. They also alleged various things that had been dishonorably done, and each, according to his own interest, put forward claims which ought to have been examined by a bishop as judge rather than by the prefect.

### 3

Confused by these circumstances, and at the same time reminded of the apostolic injunction, which says: “Do you not judge those who are within?” (I Cor. 5:12). And again: “If, then, you have secular lawsuits, appoint as judges those who are of no account in the Church. I say this to your shame. Is there really no wise person among you who can judge between his brother? But brother goes to law with brother—and that before unbelievers” (I Cor. 6:4), I accepted the inquiry, but in such a way that I would be an arbiter of a settlement.

For I saw that, if I judged in your favor, he might refuse to accept the decision; whereas, if judgment were given in his favor, your defense and that of your holy sister would obey it. The conditions for deciding were therefore unequal. They might also have regarded the favor of priestly kinship with suspicion. For when does a defeated person consider anyone other than himself fairer? And, in truth, the losses arising from this long-standing quarrel were intolerable to both parties, whether its outcome lacked profit or the consolation of generosity [Note: Thus all editions and several manuscripts read. Others, however, have *furti caret* or *careret*; some even have *fructificaret*. Hence one might not implausibly conjecture that Ambrose wrote *fructi careret*, for Terence and others used *fructi* in the genitive. As for the fact that the holy Bishop uses the word *jurgium*—“quarrel”—instead of *lis*—“lawsuit”—more than once above and also below, Nannius explains that *jurgium* is used for a matter pursued by legal action.]

### 4

Since, therefore, I saw that the judgment was uncertain, the law disputed, and the claims on both sides numerous, while envious petitions [Note: That is, petitions submitted to princes by one of the litigants.] covered even the surreptitious obtaining of rescripts; and since I also observed that, if he won, he would have to proceed under a burdensome condition—concerning double the fruits and the expenses of a lawsuit lasting many years [Note: By the law *De Fructibus et Litibus*, issued by Valentinian the Elder in A.D. 369, it was enacted that one who had unjustly possessed property should not only be expelled from that possession but should also restore double the fruits to the rightful owner, together with the costs of the suit. This last provision was later modified by a law of Honorius promulgated in A.D. 423, which prohibited instituting a new action for litigation expenses.]—whereas it was not consistent with your office to demand the expenses of the quarrel, nor proper for you, as possessor, to seek anything from the fruits which you had received, I preferred to cut short the quarrel by settlement rather than aggravate it by judgment [Note: Erasmus and the editions following him, with a few manuscripts, read *compositione sedare*, “to calm by settlement”; Amerbach, with many more manuscripts, reads *compositione caedere*, “to cut short by settlement.” One may indeed say *litem caedere*, “to cut short a lawsuit,” just as one says *litem secare* or *dirimere*, “to sever” or “settle a lawsuit.”] . For other quarrels would have been stirred up; and, what is most serious, even if the quarrels were removed, hatred would nevertheless remain, which among good people constitutes a loss.

### 5

Placed amid these disturbances, when the office of priest, the dignity of a woman’s sex, the gravity of a widow, and regard for a friend all concurred in addressing me—not superficially, but under a threefold title—I thought I should follow this course: to wish that no one be defeated, and that all should win. Nor did my judgment fail; for you all won—won through kinship, won through nature, won through Scripture, which says: “Why not rather suffer wrong? Why not rather be defrauded?” (I Cor. 6:7).

### 6

But you think that you have been burdened by the loss of a legal right and by financial damage. Such losses are certainly better for priests than the profits of the world: “It is more blessed to give than to receive” (Acts 20:35). But perhaps you say: “I ought not to have suffered fraud, I ought not to have endured wrong, I ought not to have incurred loss.” What then? Would you have wished to inflict it? But even if you did not inflict it, he would say that he had suffered it. Therefore see what the Apostle says: “Why not rather suffer fraud?” It almost seems that the one who does not suffer it has committed it; for the stronger ought to endure.

### 7

But why do I deal with you as though this were my matter and not yours? You yourself offered, as arbiter of the dispute, that your sister should possess a portion of the estate for the term of her life, and that after her death the whole possession should pass to her brother. No one was to approach him in your name or in the name of the Church; he was to retain it for himself, if he preferred, so that he would assign nothing to the Church. When I proclaimed this and praised the generosity infused into your spirit, your brother replied that he approved the offer, provided that the fear of impairing the estate were removed.

For how could a woman—and, what is more, a widow—manage a taxable estate [Note: Nannius thinks the possession is called “taxable” because it pays taxes, which, if not paid on the appointed day, impose heavy penalties upon the owner. It also appears from this that the administration of such an estate was more difficult for a widow, since women were commonly harassed more severely in the distribution and collection of taxes and other burdens, being less able to defend themselves against injustice.] ? What good would it do you to yield the rights of possession to her if she thought that she would have to bear greater losses because of the uncultivated land [Note: Some manuscripts of Longueil have *jura possessionis crederes*, “you would entrust the rights of possession”; the Gembloux manuscript has *jure possessionis decederes*, “you would withdraw by right of possession.”] ?

### 8

This concern moved the advocates of both parties. And so, with everyone agreeing, it was decided that Laetus, a man of senatorial rank, should take over the land and pay your sister each year a fixed quantity of grain, wine, and oil. Thus from your holy sister there passed away not her right, but her anxiety; not the fruits, but the labor of cultivation; not the revenue, but the uncertainty of events—the “hazard,” as it is commonly called.

If violent storms and winds impede the yield, your sister will nevertheless retain her own abundance. If the produce of the region’s fields withers through excessive drought, the fertility of the crops belonging to your sister will nevertheless not diminish [Note: Erasmus and the editions following him read *sorori tamen tuae stata*; Amerbach and the manuscripts have a lacuna; Longueil reads *sanctae*. As for what follows—“Laetus will charge it to himself”—Nannius explains it in this sense: “That is, he will bear the payment at his own risk, will free it from extraordinary burdens, and will pay it after securing it against them.”] . Laetus will assume the conditions of his offer: if the needs of the times and extraordinary exactions arise, your sister, through your generosity and at Laetus’s expense, will be exempt; Laetus, meanwhile, will console himself with ownership of the land.

### 9

Thus everyone has won: Laetus, because he obtained the right to the land, which he did not previously possess; your sister, because she will enjoy annual fruits without litigation or quarrel. Yet no one has won more completely or more gloriously than you, who, while wishing to confirm your generosity toward your sister, made her share in a brotherly relationship with both parties. For you granted ownership to your brother and the usufruct to your sister [Note: Some manuscripts read “the use of the fruits.” From what follows, observe how far it was from Ambrose’s principles to wish the Church to become wealthy through the ruin or disturbance of families.] . Nothing is taken from the Church that is acquired for piety; love is not Christ’s loss but his gain. Indeed, love is the fruit of the Holy Spirit (Gal. 5:22).

The inquiry, therefore, proceeded according to the apostolic pattern. Previously we grieved that you had a lawsuit; the quarrel proved beneficial, since it led you to assume the form of apostolic life and injunction. The former conduct was not fitting for the priesthood; this settlement accords with the apostolic norm.

### 10

Nor should you fear that the Church will be without a share in, or deprived of, your generosity. She has your fruits—and indeed more abundant ones: she has the fruits of your teaching; she has the wages of your life; she has the fertility which you have watered through your instructions. Rich in these revenues, she does not seek temporal things, because she possesses eternal ones.

You have added to her not only apostolic but also evangelical fruits; for the Lord said: “Make friends for yourselves from unrighteous mammon” (Luke 16:9). You too have made friends—and, what is remarkable, out of people who were at odds. You have brought brothers back into the rights of kinship; through this love and grace you have made them secure in the knowledge that they will be received into eternal dwellings.

### 11

Therefore, with Christ as the author, and with two priestly arbiters—you, who first supplied the pattern, and I, who pronounced the judgment—the peace that has been made will not falter, since the support of faith has been so great that faithlessness cannot exist without punishment.

### 12

Laetus will plow for the sister whose alien labors he previously begrudged. Laetus will gather the harvest for the sister whose gifts from another he previously could not bear. He will carry the fruits to his sister’s granaries, and he will do this cheerfully, now fulfilling the meaning of his name as well [Note: “That is,” says Nannius, “he will do it gladly, and will correspond both to the property and to the etymology of his name, which signifies joy.” So far Nannius. We understand from the letters to Paternus, Irenaeus, and Priscus that Ambrose did not dislike such wordplays. Yet this practice is common to him with many other authors, several of whom Casaubon mentions in his notes on Lampridius, no. 23, where he considers these very words of our Doctor somewhat harsh, perhaps being himself a little more delicate in this passage.] .

### 13

Meanwhile, having been conformed to Christ as an apostle and assuming prophetic authority, you will say to the Lord: “You have possessed my reins” (Ps. 138:13). Such possession better befits Christ: that he should possess the virtues of his priest, and receive these fruits, which are integrity and self-restraint, and, what is more, love and tranquility. Farewell, and love us, because we love you.

## LETTER LXXXIII

He commends the pardon granted to a son who had married without consulting his father; and, after recalling certain benefits which the son would derive from it, he shows that by this readiness to forgive he followed the footsteps of the saints.

## AMBROSE TO SISINNIUS

### 1

That you forgave our son at my request, because he had taken a wife without consulting you, I attribute more to piety than to your love for me; for it is a greater thing that piety itself obtained this from you than that anyone’s petition obtained it [Note: The editions following Erasmus read *quam cujusquam*, “than anyone’s”; Amerbach, with the manuscripts, reads *quam cujusce*, “than that of anyone.” But this arose from a scribal error caused by the similarity of sound: the ancients pronounced *cujusce* and *cujusque*, *coce* and *quoque*, in the same way. Hence Cicero’s well-known joke concerning the son of Cocceius, who was a candidate: “I shall favor you, Cocceius.” The wit depended on the ambiguity of pronunciation.] . Certainly a priest obtains more when virtue prevails; for a priest’s petition is an instruction in piety.

Nature therefore obtained it; the son obtained it even more fully, because consideration of a request is usually temporary, whereas the settled disposition of virtue and the constant inclination of the mind endure [Note: “It signifies *philostorgía* (φιλοστοργία),” says Nannius, “namely that affection by which parents are inclined toward their children.” There is also some allusion, as becomes clearer from what follows, to Terence: “For a great offense, a little punishment is enough for a father.”] .

### 2

It was therefore beautifully done that you recognized yourself as a father—especially since your indignation was justified. For I prefer that the fault be acknowledged, so that paternal indulgence may be praised the more. Yet it was itself also a paternal offense, since you ought to have chosen, by your own judgment, the woman who was to come into the place of a daughter and to whom you would become a father.

For we receive children either by nature or by choice: in nature there is chance; in choice, judgment [Note: The Thuane and Carolinian manuscripts read *in natura causa est*, “in nature there is a cause.” This is incorrect. Pliny the Younger speaks in precisely the same sense of the distinction between generation and adoption in his *Panegyric*, where he discusses Trajan’s adoption as a son by the emperor Nerva.] . We are more offended by adopted children than by those born to us, because the degeneration of natural children is attributed to nature, whereas the disgrace of those acquired by adoption or marriage is attributed to our own error.

There was therefore reason for you to be angry with your son, but also reason for you to forgive him, because he chose a wife for himself. You acquired a daughter without the risk of choosing. If he married a good woman, he acquired favor for you; if he was mistaken, by receiving her you will make her better, whereas by rejecting her you will make her worse.

### 3

A girl is indeed handed over to a son by her father after more mature deliberation; but she is led from the son to the father with a greater intention of obedience, and, chosen by her husband, enters her father-in-law’s house. The son fears that his judgment may displease, and the daughter-in-law fears the demands of service.

The privilege of the father’s choice raises and exalts her; fear of offending humbles the other, and modesty makes her bow. The son will have no grounds for reproaching his wife as though he were free from blame if something has perhaps gone wrong in a way that custom permits. Rather, he will work harder to prove himself in both matters: his judgment in choosing his wife, and his obedience.

### 4

You therefore did what good parents do: you forgave quickly, but only after being entreated. Before you were asked, forgiveness would not have been forgiveness but approval of the deed. Moreover, to delay pardon longer would have been bitter for you and useless for them; for paternal entrails could not endure it longer.

### 5 and 6

With the highest devotion, Abraham offered his son as a burnt offering in accordance with God’s oracle. As though he were free from natural feeling, he drew the sword, lest delay stain the sacrifice. Yet when he was ordered to refrain from striking his son, he willingly put away the sword; and he who had hastened, in the intention of faith, to sacrifice his only-begotten son, hastened with a still greater zeal of piety to substitute a sheep for the sacrifice (Gen. 22:6 ff.).

### 7

Joseph also (Gen. 44:15 ff.), in order to retain his younger brother, feigned anger toward his brothers and outrage at the contrived charge of theft [Note: The Roman edition reads, “he was indignant at the theft he had fabricated”; the old edition reads, “the theft fabricated by him”; the manuscripts omit *a se*, “by him.”] . Yet when one of his brothers, Judah, fell at his knees and the others wept, overcome and moved by brotherly affection, he could no longer maintain the appearance of severity. After sending away the attendants, he revealed to his brothers that they were his kinsmen and that he himself was Joseph, whom they had sold; that he did not remember his own injury, excused in brotherly fashion the bitterness of their sale of him, and referred to higher causes what he could reproach—because it had been necessary for it to happen under God’s providence: so that the one who would feed his people, suffering from lack of foreign grain, might pass into Egypt, and might provide assistance for nourishing his father and brothers during the time of famine [Note: A considerable number of manuscripts read *quod oportuisset*, “what had to happen”; some read *quod potuisset*, “what could have happened.”] .

### 8

What shall I say of holy David, who, at the request of a single woman, allowed his paternal heart to soften toward his degenerate son, forgetful of his brother’s blood, and received him back into the house (II Sam. 14:12) [Note: Many manuscripts read “forgetful of fraternal blood”; others, and all the editions, more appropriately read “forgetful of his brother’s blood.”] ?

### 9

The father in the Gospel likewise received his younger son, who had squandered all the property received from his father by living wantonly. When the son returned, the father was moved by the humility of a single confession—that he acknowledged having sinned against his father. He went out to meet him with loving affection, fell upon his neck, ordered the first robe, a ring, and shoes to be brought to him, and, honoring him with a kiss and presenting him with a gift, welcomed him at a marvelous banquet (Luke 15:22).

### 10

You have shown yourself an imitator of these men through paternal piety, by which we draw nearest to God. For this reason I readily urged our daughter to undertake the hardship of the journey even in winter, since she would spend the winter more comfortably not only in lodging but also in paternal affection, now that grace had succeeded indignation. And since you had fully conformed yourself to the likeness and imitation of the saints, you accused those who, through fabricated lies, had thought to stir your mind against your sons. Farewell, and love us, because we love you.

## LETTER LXXXIV

He commends Cynegius for consulting him.

## AMBROSE TO CYNEGIUS

### 1

How candidly you commended yourself by your modesty, since you consulted me about something you did not approve but were accommodating your parent in, so that you would not violate filial piety, secure in the knowledge that I could report nothing except what was fitting for holy relationships.

### 2

I, for my part, gladly took upon myself your burdens, and, as I believe, returned your granddaughter to her grandfather. I do not know under what mistaken idea he wished to make her his daughter-in-law, thereby changing a grandfather into a father-in-law. There is no need to say more, lest this too add to the embarrassment. Farewell, my son, and love us, because we too love you.

## LETTER LXXXV

After thanking Syricius for sending him a letter through the priest Syrus, he praises Syrus’s quick return and adds some remarks about following Christ.

## AMBROSE TO SYRICIUS

### 1

Your letters are welcome to me whenever I receive them. But when you send some of our fellow servants, as you did our brother and fellow priest Syrus, whom you accompanied with your letters, my joy is doubled. Would that his visit had been longer-lived! For as soon as he arrived, he thought he had to return. That greatly diminished my desire, but added much to his favor.

### 2

For I love those priests and deacons who, when they have gone somewhere, do not allow themselves to remain away from their own ministry for long [Note: From these words, as well as from those in Letter 12, section 7, where Ambrose, in his own name and in that of other Italian bishops, begs the emperors to release more quickly the envoys sent by them to the imperial court, and from similar passages, it is clear how alien the holy bishops considered it to ecclesiastical duty for sacred ministers to remain long absent from their sees and stations.] .

The prophet says: “I have not grown weary following after you” (Jer. 17:16). But who can grow weary following Jesus, when he himself says: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11:28)? Let us therefore always follow Jesus and never cease. If we follow continually, we never fail; for he gives strength to those who follow him. Thus, the nearer you are to virtue, the stronger you will be.

### 3

Often, when we follow, our adversaries say to us: “Where is the word of the Lord? Let it come!” (Jer. 17:15). But let us not grow weary in following, nor let ourselves be turned aside by the obstacle of a deceptive question.

This was said to the prophet when he was being sent to prison and cast into the pit of mud: “Where is the word of the Lord? Let it come!” (Jer. 37:15). But he followed all the more, and therefore reached the prize, and therefore received the crown; because he who followed Jesus did not grow weary: “For there is no labor in Jacob, nor shall pain be seen in Israel” (Num. 23:21).
