Farewell, and love us; for we love you, who love us and are our father [Note: The edition reads *ut parentem*, “as a father”; the manuscripts read *et parentem*, “and as a father.” We do not think that the person whom he honors here with this title is different from the one whom he calls “brother” in the following letter, nor perhaps from Pope Syricius of Rome.] .

## LETTER LXXXVI

Concerning letters carried in both directions by Priscus.

## AMBROSE TO SYRICIUS

### 1

You gave letters to Priscus, my friend and equal in age, when he was coming; I too gave him letters to deliver when he returned, as both duty and affection required. He therefore repaid each of us the service owed, restoring your letters to me and mine to you. For this reason he ought to obtain an increased reward for his service. Farewell, brother, and love us, because we love you [Note: Some manuscripts read “and my equal in age.”] .

## LETTER LXXXVII

He praises Polybius, at whose request he says that he wrote two letters, one to Segatius and one to Delphinus.

## AMBROSE TO SEGATIUS AND DELPHINUS, BISHOPS

### 1

Our son Polybius, after returning from Africa, where he had performed the duties of proconsular jurisdiction with great distinction, spent several days with us and poured himself into my heart with the greatest charm.

### 2

Then, when he wished to leave and travel from here, he asked me to write to each of you. I promised that I would. Accordingly, I dictated a letter and gave it to him written in the name of both of you. He asked for another. I said that one letter had been given to both of you [Note: There can be no doubt that the letters which Ambrose mentions here were included in his book of letters, if he ever compiled such a book. Since they now exist nowhere, that book must necessarily have perished. From the following letters as well, we understand that others likewise did not reach us.] , according to our custom and practice, because your holy mind would take pleasure not in the number of letters but in the conjunction of names; nor could it bear the separation of names whose affection was united. This was prescribed for my service, so that I might employ the economy of love.

### 3

What more need I say? He demanded another, and I gave it, so that I would neither deny him what he requested nor alter what had become customary. Thus he has something to give back to each of you; for he makes this sole claim—that, after returning one letter to one of you, he would not be empty-handed toward the other.

And I shall discharge to you the gift of undivided affection without any danger of offense or scruple of division, especially since this form of writing is also apostolic: one person may write to many, as Paul wrote to the Galatians; and two may write to one, as it is written: “Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ, and Timothy, a brother, to Philemon” (Philem. 1) [Note: Most manuscripts read “and Timothy, a brother, to Philemon.”] . I greet you; love us, and pray for us, because I love you.

## LETTER LXXXVIII

He praises Priscus, the bearer of letters between them.

## AMBROSE TO ATTICUS

### 1

You gave letters to my Priscus. My Priscus returned them to me, and I returned them to Priscus. Love your Priscus, as you are accustomed to do—and even more than usual. I urge this because I too esteem my Priscus very highly.

Our old love for him has grown together with us from childhood; but I saw him again only after a long interval, so that he truly came to me as Priscus not only in name but also because of the length of time that had passed [*Priscus* means “old” or “ancient”]. Farewell, and love us who love you, because we love you.

## LETTER LXXXIX

He discusses Alypius’s letters to him and his own letters to Alypius.

## AMBROSE TO ALYPIUS

### 1

Antiochus, a man of consular rank, returned to me letters from your Excellency, and I did not neglect the duty of replying. Through my own people I sent letters, and, if I am not mistaken, when another opportunity arose I sent a second letter.

But since I think that the duties of friendship ought not so much to be measured out as increased [Note: Thus a large number of manuscripts and the Roman edition read. The old edition, together with some manuscripts, reads: “than that insult should not be increased.”] , it was appropriate, especially when the man who had so greatly honored me by your letter was returning, that some service of my words should be returned, so that I might be discharged toward both of you, and he toward you, since he was obliged to return what he had received [Note: The Roman edition alone reads “who honored me with this service.”] . Farewell, and love those who love you [Note: The Gembloux codex reads: “Farewell, brother, and love us, because we too love you.” Pratensis has: “Farewell, brother. Here ends,” and so forth.] .

## LETTER XC

He recalls Antonius’s affection for him and his own affection for Antonius in return.

## AMBROSE TO ANTONIUS

### 1

You are never silent to me, nor will I ever complain that you have passed me over in silence, since I know that I am not absent from your heart. For since you render what is of greater value, how can you deny even that which often flows to many, not so much through the practice of love as through the exchange of duty?

### 2

I also gauge your reciprocal feeling from my own heart, so that I never consider myself absent from you or you from me, since we always cling to one another in spirit. I never think that your letters are lacking to me or mine to you, since I address you face to face each day, directing toward you my eyes, my interests, and all my services.

### 3

It is a delight to meet you in these matters, for your letters, as I speak openly with the intimate companion of my heart, make me feel ashamed. Therefore I ask you to refrain from returning thanks; for the highest reward of my service toward you is that I should think I have not failed in the duty I owe you [Note: Some manuscripts read “if you should consider that I have not failed.”] . Farewell, and love us, because I too love you.

## LETTER XCI

He praises Candidianus and humbles himself.

## AMBROSE TO CANDIDIANUS, HIS BROTHER

### 1

There is great splendor indeed in your speech, but it shines even more brightly for me in your affection; for in your letters I behold the radiance of your mind, most beloved and most blessed brother. May the Lord bless you and give you his grace; for in your letters I recognize your prayers more than my merits. What merits of mine could equal such words of yours? Love us, brother, because we love you [Note: Several manuscripts read “because I too love you.”] .

# ON THE DEATH OF HIS BROTHER SATYRUS

## INTRODUCTORY NOTICE TO THE TWO BOOKS ON THE DEATH OF HIS BROTHER SATYRUS

Besides his sister Marcellina, who had professed a vow of perpetual virginity and, as the books *On Virgins* and Ambrose’s letters to her clearly show, lived mostly at Rome, Ambrose also had a brother, whose death occasioned these little works.

It is established that his name was Satyrus; on the authority of the holy Doctor, the Roman Martyrology therefore enrolled him among the saints under September 17. It is further understood from his epitaph, which Dungalus reports as having been written by Ambrose himself (*On the Cult of Images*, volume IV of the *Library of the Fathers*, part II), that he was also called Uranius. Unless one prefers to assign to *τῷ Uranio* not the force of a surname but merely that of an epithet signifying the blessedness of Satyrus, already received into heaven. We shall leave the matter undecided and append the epitaph after these preliminary remarks.

Satyrus first pleaded cases in the forum (Book I, section 40), and afterward was placed in charge of the administration of provinces (section 58), both of which careers he shared with Ambrose. Yet far more points of likeness than of unlikeness shone forth in them, and each so closely reflected the other in face, bodily appearance, health, intelligence, and character (sections 38, 39, 79), that scarcely any pair of brothers ever existed who agreed so perfectly with each other.

From this arose that intimate and mutual affection which bound them together more closely than nature itself (sections 21, 22). As a result, when Ambrose, unwilling and reluctant, had undertaken the burden of the episcopate, Satyrus took upon himself the entire care of domestic and temporal affairs (sections 20 ff.), intending at least to relieve his brother of this portion of labor and anxiety.

It happened that a certain Prosper, living in one of the provinces of Africa, refused to pay money owed to the brothers (section 24). Satyrus decided to travel there, although his brother strongly opposed him and repeatedly recalled him by letter (section 25). Yet, when the ship in which he was traveling broke apart during the voyage, he reached the intended shore not without extreme danger (sections 17, 27). He settled the matter with Prosper according to his wishes.

But after returning to Italy, and indeed to Milan, he had scarcely been restored to his brother’s embraces when he fell into a very serious illness, by the force and severity of which he died (section 17).

How great a grief Ambrose received from his death, anyone can readily understand from the love and most affectionate companionship of life that existed between the two brothers. Nevertheless, he did not allow himself to be broken by this misfortune. Not only did he order that he himself close the eyes of the lifeless body with his own hand (No. 19), and place his shoulders beneath the bier (No. 1); he also mounted the ambo of the basilica and, before an immense crowd of people, while the face of the corpse lay exposed (No. 78), praised him in the first of these orations, of which we present here the substance.

At the beginning (No. 1 and following) he gives thanks that the danger threatening the Church appears to have been diverted onto his own household; and he declares that he ought not so much to grieve that he has lost his brother as to rejoice that he once possessed him. Above all, it consoles him that all the people’s tears accompany his own (No. 5), and that he need no longer fear ever being separated from his brother (No. 6). Then, after recalling with the tenderest affection the many bonds that united him to his brother (No. 7 and following), he excuses his grief in such a way as to assert that it should be moderated rather than extinguished. He nevertheless gathers certain grounds for consolation, especially (No. 17 and following) that he was permitted to render the final offices of affection to his brother on his return from Africa. Then, recalling the same brother’s services to him, he describes his fear at his absence and the deceptive joy caused by his return (No. 20 and following). Next, comparing the mourning for his brother with the mourning for Tabitha, he explains why it would not have been appropriate for his brother to be restored to life (No. 28 and following). After comparing his own condition with that of his brother [Col. 1287] (No. 31 and following), he returns once more to those things that intensify his longing for him (No. 34 and following). He then turns his discourse to the cardinal virtues, and praises the confidence that his brother placed in the Eucharist and the prudence with which he took care not to receive baptism from a schismatic (No. 42 and following). After commending his eloquence, courage, simplicity, chastity, temperance, and generosity toward the poor, he shows what kind of man he was toward his brothers from the fact that he neither divided the patrimony, nor married, nor made a will (No. 49 and following). Although these things increase the sense of grief, he proposes reasons why the grief should nevertheless be moderated, and promises that he will never lay aside his brother’s memory (No. 63 and following). Finally, after inserting a few remarks for the consolation of Marcellina, he bids his brother a most affectionate final farewell and closes the oration with prayers poured forth for his peace and rest (No. 76 and following).

When seven days had passed (Book II, No. 2), the people returned to Satyrus’s monument to celebrate the customary ceremonies and prayers. There Ambrose delivered the second of these orations, although constrained by lack of time in composing it,, and he pronounced it at considerable length, approximately as follows. After prefacing that in the first book some indulgence had been granted to grief, he promises that in this one he will consider more closely the condition of all human beings (No. 1 and following). He then proposes three matters for discussion: namely, that death is common to all; that through its agency we are made safe from the troubles of this age; and finally, that through it access is given to the resurrection (No. 3). To persuade his hearers that this common law ought to be accepted, he brings forward various examples, such as peoples who accompanied birth with lamentation but death with applause, as well as the Lycians, among whom men were compelled by law to wear women’s clothing in mourning (No. 4 and following). Next, adding several arguments, he severely chastises the helplessness of women at their husbands’ funerals (No. 8 and following), and teaches that patience at the death of friends is no more difficult than patience during their prolonged absence (No. 15 and following).

Soon he proceeds to the second part (No. 18 and following), setting forth the manifold calamities of human life, and proving by the examples of holy men that we cannot be delivered from them except through death (No. 23 and following). When he has enlarged upon how much those same men endured, he concludes from this (No. 44 and following) that death is not to be feared, since in it itself are found rest, gain, remedy, and honor. Finally he moves to the last part, which he supports by three kinds of argument: reason, the example of the universe, and the testimony of an accomplished event (Nos. 50, 52). He touches briefly upon the point that reason requires body and soul to share punishments or rewards together. But after dwelling at length on the second part (No. 53 and following), he philosophizes beautifully about the generations and transformations of nature. Then, after wisely resolving certain doubts, he establishes the resurrection by the examples of the phoenix and of human generation (Nos. 58, 60). After explaining the order and manner of that resurrection, he says that it is unworthy not to believe in it when credence is given both to philosophical delusions about the transmigration of souls into various bodies and to poetic absurdities about the transformation of serpents’ teeth into human beings (Nos. 61, 65, 70). From this he concludes, on the basis of the testimonies of the prophets, whose passages he presents and explains, that greater credence ought to be given to the resurrection (No. 66 and following). Finally he comes to the testimonies of an accomplished event. Here, after relating the history of three dead persons whom Christ restored to life, he does not omit those who were raised by Elijah, Peter, and during the Lord’s Passion (No. 77 and following). The holy Bishop again rises against the philosophers and clearly demonstrates that the resurrection is consonant with reason (No. 86 and following). He adds (Nos. 90, 91) that faith must be given to God and to Christ, who is the cause of the resurrection; and, explaining how Paul will be caught up into the air (No. 92), he teaches that the patriarchs live, piously discussing their virtues (No. 95 and following). After adding the explanation of how Christ is called “free among the dead,” he expounds spiritually what Moses prescribed concerning trumpets (Nos. 95, 117); to these he adds an exposition of certain passages from the Song of Songs and the Apocalypse (No. 118 and following). Finally, gathering the entire oration together as though into a single sheaf, and openly expressing his wishes that he may soon follow his brother, he brings the discourse to an end (No. 130 and following).

There can be no doubt that these two books consist of two separate orations, which Ambrose himself wished to join into a single work, giving it the title of books and perhaps also adding or altering certain things. Hence, at the very beginning of the second book, he writes these words: “In the preceding book we granted something to grief,” and so forth. In manuscripts the work is likewise prefaced by this title: “Here begin the books of Saint Ambrose, Bishop, on the Death of His Brother Satyrus and on the Resurrection of the Dead.” In certain codices, however, there is some variation. For example, in some it is entitled as follows: “The Mournful Lament of Blessed Ambrose, Bishop, on the Death of His Most Beloved Brother”; but in such matters we find that scribes used the greatest freedom.

Of greater authority is the fact that Augustine (Book II of *On Original Sin*, chapter 41) cites the second book in these words: “In the work that he wrote on the Resurrection”; while Ambrose himself (*Exposition of Psalm I*, no. 51) uses this heading for both: “In the Books of Consolation and Resurrection.” We shall discuss the first part of this title in the Admonition to the Oration on the Death of Valentinian; for now we shall merely observe that the common title expresses the subject of the discourse more clearly. As for the title of the second book, it is generally formulated as *On the Faith of the Resurrection*, or *On the Resurrection of the Dead*; and the preceding analysis of the book plainly proves that this title is appropriate and fitting.

No one will deny that the work was composed in the very year in which Satyrus departed to the heavenly realms; but in what year precisely this death occurred is less clear. Baronius thinks that it should be assigned to the same year as the slaying of Gratian, namely 383.. He supports his opinion by arguing that the fear of war and barbarians discussed here cannot be referred elsewhere than to the invasion that Maximus threatened Italy with after the death of that emperor. Yet, apart from the fact that nowhere are Maximus or Eugenius said to have brought with them barbarians of the kind described by the holy Bishop in the first book, how could Ambrose either have omitted mention of so recent a sorrow or have declared so confidently that whatever everyone feared had been diverted onto and expiated in his own household through his brother’s death?

Moreover, since the fact that Satyrus undertook his voyage at the beginning of Ambrose’s episcopate is suggested by Prosper’s attempt to use Ambrose’s office as an occasion for not paying his debt, and since Ambrose says that Satyrus was taken away in the very flower of his age (Book I, no. 31), it is clear that those warlike disturbances and threats of the barbarians fit better with the death of the emperor Valens in the year 378, burned in a hut on the fourth day before the Kalends of September. At that time a great fear of the barbarians invaded Italy and the neighboring provinces. Accordingly, we have no doubt that both books were written in the following year, that is, 379. It also appears that this occurred at the beginning of summer, since Ambrose testifies that his brother sailed through the winter cold and died only a few months after his return.

It was an ancient custom among the Athenians that those who had fallen while fighting bravely for their country should be honored with a public eulogy, as Plato records in the *Menexenus*. The Romans, however, paid the same honor to distinguished men and women; historians observe that this custom originated with the consul Publius Valerius Publicola, who publicly praised his colleague Junius. Yet even more ancient traces of the same rite exist in the sacred books. For what else are David’s lament over Saul and Jonathan, described in the Second Book of Samuel, chapter 1,, or Jeremiah’s lament over King Josiah, mentioned in the Second Book of Chronicles, than funeral eulogies?

It should therefore not seem surprising if so many orations are found among the Fathers of the Greek and Latin Churches in praise of those who either poured out their blood for the faith and name of Christ or adorned the Christian name with the splendor of extraordinary virtues. But perhaps it may seem more unusual that a brother himself undertook to celebrate the praises of his brother. Ambrose, however, has the clearest examples with which to defend himself. To omit the fact that among the pagans it was customary for great men to present themselves as eulogists of the dead who had been bound to them by the closest ties of relationship—for this is recorded of Julius Caesar, who praised his aunt Julia and his wife Cornelia from the rostra according to custom, as Suetonius says in his *Life*—one Gregory of Nazianzus, whose orations delivered at the funerals of his father, brother, and sister survive, would be sufficient patronage for Ambrose. Later Bernard imitated both Gregory and Ambrose in praising his brother Gerard.

Before the worktable is cleared away, we should point out that Dungal, deceived by certain scribes who, because of a certain similarity of subject, copied the book *On Paradise* together with these two books, cited that same book as a third book *On the Death of Satyrus*. Everyone can see that he was seriously mistaken in this. As for the epitaph he mentions, these words of his are not wholly unworthy of our Ambrose (*loc. sup. cit.*):

> For heavenly Satyrus, his brother Ambrose bore the final honor  
At the martyr’s left..

[Note: [Col. 1289] Namely, Saint Victor.]

> This is the reward of his merit: that the moisture of sacred blood,  
> Penetrating nearby, bathes the remains.

[Col. 1289]

# # TWO BOOKS OF SAINT AMBROSE, BISHOP OF MILAN, ON THE DEATH OF HIS BROTHER SATYRUS (C)

[Note: [Col. 1289] Written in the year 379.]

[Col. 1289]

## BOOK ONE

[Col. 1289] 1113 1. We have led away, dearest brothers, my offering, an undefiled offering, an offering pleasing to God, [Col. 1290] my lord and my brother Satyrus.

[Note: [Col. 1289] All printed editions and some manuscripts read *dominum et fratrem* (“my lord and my brother”); several other, more authoritative manuscripts read *domnum et fratrem*. Our Menard observes in chapter 70 of the Rule of Saint Benedict that the word *Dominus* was royal and imperial, and that Augustus Caesar did not wish to be addressed by it. Later, however, writers, wishing to use a humbler term, formed the word *domnus* by syncope from *dominus*. After proving this with examples drawn from Severus Sulpicius and elsewhere, he adds that the same thing occurred among the Greeks with the word κύριος (*kyrios*, “lord”), from which later writers formed κῦρος (*kyros*).. See Hephten on the same Rule, Cangius in the *Glossary*, and elsewhere.]

I remembered that he was mortal, and my expectation did not deceive me, [Col. 1291A] but grace abounded.

[Note: [Col. 1291D] The Vallian Codex reads: “But where sin abounded, grace abounded even more,” and so forth.]

Thus I have nothing for which to complain, and I have something for which to give thanks to God: for I always wished that, if any troubles threatened either the Church or me, they should fall upon me and my household instead. Thanks therefore be to God, because amid this universal fear, when everything is threatened by barbarian disturbances, I have borne the common sorrow in private grief, and whatever I feared for everyone has been turned upon me. And would that the matter may end here, so that my grief may be the ransom of the public grief!

2. Indeed, dearest brothers, in human affairs I possessed nothing more precious, nothing more lovable, nothing dearer than such a brother; but public interests take precedence over private ones. If anyone were to ask what he himself thought, he would have preferred to die for others rather than live for himself.

[Note: [Col. 1291D] Several manuscripts of better quality read *mallet* (“he would have preferred”); some read *malit* (“he would prefer”).]

For this reason Christ died according to the flesh for all, so that we might learn not to live for ourselves alone (II Corinthians 5:15).

3. Furthermore, I cannot be ungrateful toward the divine will: for we ought rather to rejoice that I had such a brother than to grieve that I have lost a brother; the former was a gift, the latter a debt. Thus, as long as I was permitted, I made use of the capital entrusted to me:

[Note: [Col. 1291D] Quite a few manuscripts read *perfruitus sum*; the rest, and all printed editions, read *perfructus sum*. Below, where nearly all manuscripts and the old editions read *commisso mihi fenore* (“the interest entrusted to me”), the Roman edition substitutes *concesso* (“granted”), and so forth.]

the one who deposited the pledge has reclaimed it. It makes no difference whether you refuse to return a deposit or grieve when it is reclaimed. In either case the trust is uncertain, and life is at risk.

[Note: [Col. 1291D] Nannius, after bringing forward the various meanings in which *vita* is used—sometimes for the soul, sometimes for food, sometimes for the span of life, and sometimes for moral character—says that Ambrose uses the word here in this last sense. Nevertheless, although we do not entirely reject this view, we think it more simply means eternal salvation and life.]

If it is a fault to deny money, is it piety to deny the offering, when the lender of money can be cheated but the author of nature and creditor of our relationship cannot be defrauded?

[Note: [Col. 1292D] All manuscripts except three read *pietas est* (“is it piety?”); the three read *impietas est* (“is it impiety?”), which all printed editions have changed to *impietas non est* (“it is not impiety”).]

Therefore, the greater the sum of the loan, the more welcome the interest on the principal..

4. For this reason we cannot be ungrateful concerning our brother, because he returned what belonged to our common nature, and earned what belongs to singular grace.

[Note: [Col. 1292D] All printed editions, with a few manuscripts, read *de fratris morte* (“concerning the brother’s death”); the larger number of manuscripts, and the better sense, read *de fratre* (“concerning the brother”).]

Who would refuse the common human condition? Who would grieve that his own particular pledge had been taken away, when the Father, for our consolation, handed over his only Son to death for us (Romans 8:32)? Who should think himself exempt from the condition of dying who is not exempt from the condition of being born? It is a great mystery of piety that the death of the body was not exempted even in Christ; and although he was Lord of nature, he nevertheless did not refuse the law of the flesh that he had assumed.

I must die; he did not have to die. Could he not have remained in this way, if he had wished, who said concerning his servant, “If I want him to remain until I come, what is that to you?” (John 21:22)

[Note: [Col. 1292D] Some manuscripts read: “He says, ‘I want him to remain in this way.’”]

But if he had so remained, he would have lost the price of the perpetuity of this life for himself and the sacrifice for me. What greater consolation for us, then, than that Christ too died according to the flesh? Or why should I weep more bitterly for my brother, when I know that piety itself could not die?

1115 5. Why should I alone among all weep for the one whom you all weep for? I have dispersed private grief into common grief, especially since my tears do no good, whereas your tears establish faith and bring consolation.

You who are rich weep, and by weeping you prove that hoarded riches contribute nothing to salvation, since death cannot be postponed by the price of money, and the final day carries away the rich and the poor alike. You old men weep because you fear this lot among your children;

[Note: [Col. 1292D] Several manuscripts read *liberam sortem* (“a free lot”). This is not inappropriate, since that lot is truly free which seizes whomever it wishes, whether old or young. Yet it may also have been a scribal error, by which *liberam* was written for *liberum*.]

and because you cannot prolong the life of the body, raise your children not for bodily use but for the practice of virtue. You young men also weep because the end of nature is not the maturity of old age. The poor too wept; and, what is far more precious and far more abundant, they washed his sins with their tears. Those are redeeming tears; those are groans that conceal the pain of death; that is a grief which, through the perpetual abundance of joy, blunts the sensation of former sorrow.

[Note: [Col. 1292D] Some manuscripts read: “softens the feeling of pain.”]

Thus, although the funeral is private, the weeping is public; and therefore the weeping cannot be prolonged when it has been consecrated by the feelings of everyone.

6. For what reason should I weep for you, my most loving brother, when you have been taken from me in such a way as to belong to everyone? I have not lost the use of you, but exchanged it: formerly inseparable in body, now indivisible in affection. You remain with me, and you will always remain.

Indeed, while you lived with us, your homeland never took you away from me, nor did you ever prefer your homeland to me; and now you have provided another one. I have begun no longer to be a stranger here, where the better part of me is. For I was never wholly within myself, but in the other of us lay the greater part of us both; yet both of us were in Christ, in whom lies both the sum of the universe and the portion of each individual.

This tomb is dearer to me than my native soil, because in it there is the fruit not of nature but of my grace. For in this body that now lies lifeless is the more excellent function of my life, because in this body that I myself bear there is also a richer portion of you.

7. Would that, just as we can breathe whatever this is of your memory and grace, we could also breathe whatever this is of your life,,

[Col. 1293A]

and that half of my years might fall away and contribute to the use of yours!

[Note: [Col. 1293D] Some manuscripts read: “that we might be able to hope for what we breathe” (some: “prepare by hope”).]

It was fitting that, since our inheritance of possessions had always been undivided, the time of our lives should not have been divided.

[Note: [Col. 1293D] Some manuscripts read: “that life and time should not be divided.”]

Or at least, since our companionship in life had always been indistinguishable, we should not have had distinct companionships in dying.

[Note: [Col. 1293D] The Tours Codex reads: “distinct associations in dying.”]

8. But now, brother, where shall I go, and where shall I turn? An ox seeks its fellow ox and does not think itself complete, and with frequent lowing gives pious proof of its affection if the one with which it was accustomed to draw the plowshare beside its neck should be missing. And shall I not seek you, brother? Or could I ever forget you, with whom I have always borne the plowshare of this life?

I was inferior in labor, but more closely joined in love; not so much made capable by my own strength as made bearable by your patience. You, ever anxious with pious affection, surrounded my side with your own: with love, as a brother; with care, as a father; with solicitude, as an elder; with reverence, as a younger.

Thus, in the single degree of one relationship, you supplied me with the duties of several relationships, so that in you I must seek not one person but many whom I have lost. In that one man, flattery was unknown and affection was expressed. For you had nothing to add by pretense, since you encompassed everything through devotion; so that you neither received additions nor expected repayment..

1116 9. But in what way, forgetful of duty yet mindful of gratitude, am I advancing through excessive grief? The Apostle recalls me and, as though placing reins upon sorrow, says—as you recently heard:

> “We do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who sleep, so that you may not grieve like the rest who have no hope” (I Thessalonians 4:12).

Forgive me, dearest brothers. For not all of us can say, “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (I Corinthians 4:16); but if you seek an example to imitate, you have one whom you can imitate. Not everyone is fit to teach; would that everyone were ready to learn!

10. Yet we have not incurred a grave fault by our tears; weeping is not always a sign of unbelief or weakness. One kind of grief belongs to nature, another to distrust; and it makes a great difference whether one longs for what one possessed or mourns what one has lost.

Pain is not the only thing that has tears; joy too has its tears. Affection awakens weeping, prayer drenches the bed, and supplication, according to the prophetic saying (Psalm 6:7), washes the couch.

[Note: [Col. 1293D] The Roman edition reads: “and a tear, according to the prophetic saying,” and so forth.]

The patriarchs too wept greatly when their own were buried. [Col. 1293D] Tears, therefore, are signs of affection, not enticements to grief.

[Col. 1294A]

I wept, I confess, but the Lord also wept. He for another; I for a brother (John 11:35). He wept for all in one person; I shall weep for you, brother, in all.

11. He did not weep from his own affection but from ours; for divinity does not have tears.

[Note: [Col. 1293D] Most and better manuscripts, from which the old editions do not depart except that everywhere they prefer *lacrymatus est* (“wept”) to *lacrymavit*, read: “but he wept in that in which he was sorrowful; he wept in that in which he was crucified, who died, who was buried [lacuna]. He wept in that in which he called Zion mother.” Some manuscripts and the Roman edition have this reading.]

Rather, he wept in that in which he was sorrowful (Matthew 26:38); he wept in that in which he was crucified, in which he died, in which he was buried. He wept in that of which the prophet has spoken to us today, saying:

> ““Mother Zion shall say: ‘A man, and a man was made in her, and the Most High himself founded her’”’” (Psalm 86:5).

He wept in that in which he called Zion mother, being born in Judaea and received from a Virgin.. According to his divinity he could not have a mother, because he is the author of his mother. He was made not by divine generation but by human generation; because he was made man, God was born.

[Note: [Col. 1293D] The Remigius and Benignus Codices read: “God-man was born”; other manuscripts and the printed editions read more suitably: “God was born.” Here eternal generation is set against temporal generation. Below, in place of “and born and given,” the same codices read “and made and given.”]

12. Thus elsewhere you read:

> “A child is born to us, a Son is given to us” (Isaiah 9:6).

In “child” there is the name of an age; in “Son,” the fullness of divinity. Made from a mother, born from the Father; nevertheless he was both born and given. Do not regard him as different, but as one.

For there is one Son of God, born from the Father and arising from the Virgin, in distinct order but with the name converging into one, as the present reading also teaches: “A man was made in her, and the Most High himself founded her” (Psalm 86:5)—a man, certainly, in body; the Most High in power.

And although he is God and man by the difference of natures, yet he is the same, not another, in both.. One thing is proper to his nature, another common to us; but in both there is one, and in both he is perfect.

[Note: [Col. 1294D] Most manuscripts read: “but in one name they converge.” Below, instead of “perfect in both,” the same manuscripts read “perfect on either side.”]

13. It is therefore not surprising that God made him both Lord and Christ. He made Jesus, that is, the one who received his name from the body. It is of him also that the patriarch David writes:

> ““Mother Zion shall say: ‘A man, and a man was made in her.’”.’”

[Note: [Col. 1294D] Several manuscripts read: “a man was made in her.”]

The one who was made man is unlike the Father, not in divinity but in body; nor is he separated from the Father, but distinguished in the work entrusted to him, remaining in participation of power and set apart in the mystery of the Passion.

14. The exposition of this passage calls for a fuller treatment, by which we could demonstrate the authority of the Father, the distinct property of the Son, and the unity of the whole Trinity.

[Note: [Col. 1294D] *Tractatus* can sometimes mean a simple exposition; here, however, it has the sense of a discussion or controversial argument. It should not seem absurd that Ambrose considered it not at all foreign to his purpose at this point to touch upon a controversy of the faith. This must be attributed to the arrogance of the Arians, who, while still numerous at Milan, frequently harassed Catholics with their sophistries.]

But today I have undertaken the role of consoling, not of discussing, although directing the mind away from grief by the effort of exposition is itself a use of consolation.

[Note: [Col. 1294D] A few manuscripts read: “but my grief must be restrained.”]

My grief must rather be moderated than my affection diverted, so that my longings may be soothed rather than put to sleep. For I do not wish to go far from my brother or be drawn away by other occupations, since this discourse has been undertaken as though to accompany him, so that I may follow him with my mind for a longer time as he departs, and embrace in thought the one whom I hold before my eyes.

In him I wish to fix the entire power of my sight; with him to linger in every service of the soul; to surround him with every expression of affectionate devotion. My mind is stunned: I do not believe him lost, whom I still see present; nor do I think him dead, whose services I still do not miss, services to which I had devoted the use of my life and the whole duty of breathing.

15. What return shall I make for such great favor and such great labor?? I had made you my heir, brother; you left me as your heir. I wished you to outlive me; you left me as the survivor.

In return for your gifts, to repay your benefits, I offered prayers; now I have lost even my prayers, but I have not lost your benefits. What shall I do, the successor of my heir? What shall I do, the survivor of my own life? What shall I do, deprived of the light that I possess? What thanks, what gifts shall I return to you?

You have nothing from me except tears. Or perhaps, secure in the merit of your life, you do not seek the only tears that remain to me. For even while you still lived, you forbade me to weep; you testified that our grief, rather than your death, was painful to you.

Tears forbid me to go farther, and weeping calls me back. Your affection also forbids me, lest, while we mourn our own loss, we should seem to despair of your merits.

1118 16. Certainly, however, you lessen for us the bitterness of this grief as well. I have nothing to fear, since I used to fear for you; I have nothing left that the world can take from me.

Although our holy sister remains, venerable in integrity, equal in character, and not inferior in service, we both feared more for you; we thought that the pleasure of this life had been placed in you. For your sake it was pleasant to live; for your sake it was not burdensome to die. We both prayed that you would survive us; it did not help us to survive you.

When did the mind not shudder, when fear of this kind touched it? How overwhelmed was my mind at the news of your illness?

[Note: [Col. 1295D] Quite a few manuscripts read: “the mind did not become constricted”; several others: “the mind did not collapse”; the remaining manuscripts and printed editions have the more elegant reading given in the text.]

17. Woe to our wretched expectation! We thought that the one whom we see had been restored, but he had only been delayed.

[Note: [Col. 1295D] The very ancient and widespread practice in the Church of making vows, and the great efficacy of the patronage of the saints both in driving away dangers and in obtaining benefits from God, is attested by Ambrose with the greatest authority. Compare this passage with the very similar one in *Exhortation to a Virgin*, chapter 3, no. 15. Add also what the blessed Doctor teaches concerning the invocation of the same saints in *On Widows*, chapter 9.]

For now we understand that his leave had been obtained through your prayers from the holy martyr Lawrence. Would that you had asked not only for leave but also for a long extension of life! You who were able to obtain leave to come could have obtained many years of life.

[Note: [Col. 1295D] Some manuscripts read: “you could obtain leave to live.” This is less suitable.]

And indeed, almighty and eternal God, I give you thanks that you did not deny us even these final consolations; that you granted us the long-desired return of our most beloved brother from the regions of Sicily or Africa. For he was taken from us so soon after he came that he seemed to have been delayed for this one purpose alone: to return to his brothers.

18. I possess my pledge, which no journey can now tear away from me. I possess relics that I can embrace; I possess a tomb that I can cover with my body; I possess a grave upon which I can lie. I shall believe myself more acceptable to God because I shall rest above the bones of the holy body.

Would that I could have set my own body against your death as well! If you had been attacked with swords, I would have offered myself to be pierced in your place. If I could have called back your departing soul, I would have offered my own instead.

19. It did me no good to draw in your final breaths, nor to breathe my breath into the mouth of the dying. For I thought either that I myself would receive your death or that I would transfuse my life into you.

[Note: [Col. 1295D] The old edition and several manuscripts read: “to breathe my breaths into him”; the Roman edition, with other manuscripts, more suitably reads: “to breathe my breath into his mouth.” Nannius observes that here Ambrose is contending with Virgil’s lament and surpasses the charm of poetry in prose itself. What Nannius adds—that the saint did not here follow the errors of the pagans, who, according to Pythagorean transmigration, received the soul of the dying with open mouth as though they would thereafter live by his spirit—is entirely true, since Ambrose immediately supplies other reasons. The Virgilian verses he cites are from Book IV of the *Aeneid*:

> “And if some final breath still lingers,  
> I shall gather it with my mouth.”

He also adds other verses of Statius from Book II of the *Silvae*, expressing precisely the same idea. Anyone wishing to learn about other ancient rites concerning the dying should consult Joseph Laurentius’s *Polymathia*, Book III, Synopsis 9, as well as the authors cited there.]

O unhappy but nevertheless sweet final pledges of our kisses! O wretched embraces, during which the lifeless body grew rigid and the final breath vanished! I was indeed clasping your arms, but I had already lost the one whom I held; and I gathered your final breath with my mouth, so that I might share in your death.

[Note: [Col. 1296D] Some manuscripts read *ore religabam* (“I bound back with my mouth”); the rest of the manuscripts and the printed editions read *ore relegebam* (“I gathered again with my mouth”); the Roman edition, following Virgil cited above, reads *legebam* (“I gathered”). Below, where all printed editions and a few manuscripts read *morte redolebat* (“it breathed fragrance in death”), the remaining manuscripts in great number prefer *morte redolebam* (“I breathed fragrance in death”).]

1119 But somehow that life-giving breath became life-giving for me and breathed a greater grace even in death itself.

[Note: [Col. 1296D] Quite a few manuscripts read: “I breathed fragrance in death itself.”].”]

Would that, if I could not prolong your life through my own breath, at least the strength of your final breath could have been transferred into my mind, and that our affection might have breathed forth the purity and innocence of your soul! You would have left me this inheritance, dearest brother—one that would not strike my affection with tearful pain,

[Note: [Col. 1296D] Some manuscripts read: “would not wound my affection at the sight.” This gives a scarcely less suitable sense.]

but would commend the heir through memorable grace.

[Col. 1297A] 20. What shall I do now, since I have lost all the sweetnesses of this life, all its consolations, and finally all its adornments? You alone were my comfort at home and my distinction abroad. You, I say, were the arbiter in counsel, a sharer in care, an advocate against anxiety, a banisher of grief; you were the defender of my actions and the protector of my thoughts; finally, you alone were the one in whom domestic concern rested and public care found repose.

I call your holy soul to witness that, in the construction of the churches, I often feared lest I should displease you.

[Note: [Col. 1297D] All printed editions read “in the public works of the Church”; some Paris manuscripts read “in the churches”; but the best manuscripts, almost unanimously, read “in the construction of the Church.” Below, instead of “so that I fear,” as found in all printed editions and some manuscripts, the most numerous manuscripts read “so that I may not fear.” The preceding reference to the construction of the Church should be understood of the building of the basilica that the holy man constructed at Milan. We noted in connection with Letter 22 that this is the same basilica mentioned there by him. Gregory of Tours also mentions it in Book I of *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 47, as does Ughellus in volume IV of *Italia Sacra*, page 34. Nor does it conflict with Ambrose’s testimony in this oration that Satyrus had undertaken responsibility for temporal affairs: Ambrose himself professes in Book II of *Duties*, chapter 21, that whatever pertains to the dignity of the Church is not foreign to the episcopal office.]

Finally, when you returned, you rebuked me for the delay. Thus at home and abroad you were, as it were, the instructor and arbiter of a certain priest, so that you would not allow me to think about domestic matters but judged that I should care for public ones. Yet I shall not fear that I seem to speak arrogantly: this is part of your praise, because without giving any offense you both governed your brother’s household and upheld the priesthood.

### 21

I realize, indeed, that my mind is moved when I recall your services and review your virtues; yet I find rest precisely in this emotion of mine. These recollections, although they renew my grief, nevertheless bring me pleasure. Can I either not think of you, or ever think of you without tears? And could I ever fail to remember so dear a brother, or remember him without a kind of tearful gratitude? For what has ever been pleasant to me that did not proceed from you? What, I ask, was ever a pleasure to me without you, or to you without me? What activity was not shared by us—indeed, what of our very sight, and what sleep, was not almost held in common? What desire was ever separate? What footprint was not common [Col. 1297C]? [Note: [Col. 1297D] Not a few manuscripts read: “Indeed, so that when I raised my step,” etc.] Almost as though, when I lifted my foot, either you seemed to be lifting my body, or I yours.

### 22

But whenever it was necessary to go out without the other, you would think your side uncovered; [Note: [Col. 1298D] Codex Turonensis alone reads *affectum multatum*. In the following verse many manuscripts likewise read: “the accustomed vigor did not repent of being absent from holy grace”; but the better reading, found in the other manuscripts and all printed editions, is as in the text.] you would see the face altered and judge the spirit sorrowful. The accustomed grace did not shine forth; the usual vigor was absent. Solitude aroused everyone’s suspicion that some illness had befallen one of us. Thus it seemed strange to everyone that we should be separated!

For my part, unable to endure and not forgetting my brother’s absence, I would repeatedly turn my neck and look for you, as though you were present; I seemed to speak with you and look upon you face to face. But, as though with my neck bent beneath a yoke, whenever I had fallen short of what I hoped for, I thought that I was dragging myself along: reluctant to proceed, ashamed to be seen, and hurrying back because I had no desire to go on without you.

[Col. 1298A] ### 23

But when we both had to go out, there were not more footprints on the road than words, nor was our walking more frequent than our conversation. We were concerned not with walking but with the pleasure of speaking, for each of us hung upon the other’s lips. We did not read the road with fixed attention, but tested one another’s anxious conversations; we drank in the delight of one another’s eyes and breathed the pleasures of our brother’s image. How silently I admired your virtues within myself! How I congratulated myself that the Lord had given me such a brother—so modest, so capable, so innocent, so simple! So much so that when I thought of your innocence, I despaired of your capability; when I saw your capability, I would not have thought you innocent! Yet by a wondrous virtue you joined both together.

[Note: [Col. 1298D] “Capable,” that is, keen and competent in action, is here opposed to “innocent” and “simple,” because those who possess more blood and heat are more easily carried away by the passions of desire or hatred than others.]

### 24

Finally, what the two of us had been unable to conclude, you completed alone [Col. 1298B]. As I hear, Prosper congratulated himself that, on account of my priesthood, he would not have to return what he had taken away. But he experienced the effectiveness of your single effort as greater than that of two men. Thus he paid everything, neither ungrateful toward your moderation nor mocking your modesty; rather, he was grateful for your restraint and not arrogant toward your effectiveness.

But for whom, brother, did you seek those things? For we wanted the reward of your labors to be the very proof of them. You completed everything, and when you returned after accomplishing it all, you alone—who ought to be preferred to everyone—were taken from us, as though you had postponed death for this very reason: to complete the duty of filial devotion and carry away the palm of effectiveness.

### 25

Nor did the honors of this world themselves delight us, dearest brother, because they separated us from one another [Col. 1298C]. We attained them not because their acquisition was to be desired, but lest our dissembling should seem paltry. [Note: [Col. 1298D] Some manuscripts read: “the acquisition of them was to be awaited.” Below, some read: “partly by your timely death, partly by your more timely death”; others, including the printed editions, read as in the text.] Or perhaps they were bestowed for this reason: because, since your untimely death was to be the occasion of the end of our happiness, we might learn to live without one another.

### 26

And indeed I recognize the foreboding of my mind when I often recall what I wrote. I tried to call you back, brother, so that you would not go to Africa yourself, but would send someone else. I was afraid to commit you to the road and entrust you to the waves, and an anxiety greater than usual had entered my mind. Yet you both arranged the journey and set the matter in order, and, as I hear, entrusted yourself once more to the waves in an old and leaky ship. [Note: [Col. 1298D] *Sentinoso*: a ship into whose bilge a great deal of water flowed through the cracks opened by decay.] For while you sought speed, you neglected caution, eager for our pleasure and concealing your own danger.

[Col. 1299A] ### 27

O deceptive joy! O uncertain course of human affairs! When you had returned from Africa, been restored from the sea, and been saved from shipwreck, we thought that you could no longer be taken from us. Yet, placed on land, we endure more grievous shipwrecks; for the man whom the shipwrecks of the sea could not bring to death—because he escaped them by vigorous swimming—his death began to be our shipwreck.

For what sweetness remains to us, now that so exceedingly sweet an ornament, so bright a light amid the darknesses of this world, has been extinguished—that ornament in which not only the glory of our family but of our entire fatherland has perished?

### 28

I am indeed deeply grateful to you, dearest brothers, holy people, because you consider my grief no different from your own; because you regard this solitude of ours as something that has happened to you; [Note: [Col. 1299D] Some Paris editions read: “you believe this concern of ours”; the other editions and the manuscripts, more correctly, read: “you believe this solitude of ours.” Solitude and bereavement are spoken of concerning the death of close relations. In the third verse, several manuscripts lack the word *vota* (“expressions of grief” or “prayers”). Even without it, the sense remains intact, but something is nevertheless lost from the symmetry.] because, with a new kind of devotion, you offer the tears of the entire city, the prayers of every age and every rank [Col. 1299B].

For this is not the grief of private compassion, but a kind of public duty and gift of affection. Or, if some compassion for me touches you because I have lost such a brother, I have received abundant fruit; I possess a pledge of your affection. I would rather have my brother alive, but nevertheless public duty is more pleasing in prosperity and more welcome in adversity.

### 29

Nor does the merit of so great a service seem to me insignificant. For it was not without purpose that either in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 9:39) the widows are described weeping over the dead Tabitha, or in the Gospel (Luke 7:12) a crowd is introduced accompanying the funeral of a young man, moved by the tears of his widowed mother, to whom resurrection was owed. The widows, however, wept for Tabitha, whereas the entire city wept for this young man [Col. 1299C].

There is therefore no doubt that the patronage of the apostles is procured by your tears. I say, there is no doubt that Christ was moved by compassion when he saw you weeping. Although he did not now touch the bier, he nevertheless received the spirit entrusted to him; and although he did not call the dead man with the voice of his body, by the authority of divine power he freed his soul from the torments of death and from the assaults of spiritual wickedness. [Note: [Col. 1299D] Some manuscripts read: “Yet he received the gift, and although he did not call … he did not sit upon the bed.”]

And although he did not sit upon the bier, where the dead man lay, he nevertheless rested in Christ. And although he did not speak to us, he nevertheless sees the things that are above us, and rejoices that he now sees things better than those we possess. For through what we read in the Gospel, we understand what is to come; and the appearance of present things is an indication of future things.

### 30

He had no need of a temporary resurrection [Note: [Col. 1299D] Some manuscripts read: “bodily resurrection.”] for whom an eternal one was owed. Why should he fall back into this miserable and most wretched corruption and return to this tearful life? Rather, we ought to rejoice that he has been snatched away from such impending and pressing evils.

For if, when the world was at peace and wars had ceased, no one mourned Enoch when he was taken away (Genesis 5:24), but the prophet instead praised him, as Scripture says of him, “He was taken away, lest wickedness should alter his heart” (Wisdom 4:11), [Note: [Col. 1299D] Some manuscripts read: “lest wickedness should change his understanding,” or “lest deceit should deceive his soul.”] how much more rightly must this now be said, when the uncertainty of life is added to the world’s slippery condition!

He was taken away lest he fall into the hands of the barbarians; he was taken away lest he see the destruction of the whole world, the end of the age, the funerals of his relatives, the deaths of his fellow citizens, and finally the defilement of holy virgins and widows—which is more bitter than any death [Col. 1300B].

### 31

For my part, brother, I consider you blessed both in the flower of your life and in the manner of your death. You were not taken from us, but from dangers; you did not lose life, but escaped the dread of the calamities that were closing in. [Note: [Col. 1299D] Several manuscripts and Ambrosius’ edition read: “For since you were compassion toward your own”; some read more suitably: “inclined toward your own.” The more elegant reading, found in other manuscripts and the printed editions, is as in the text.]

For, given the compassion of your holy spirit toward your own, if you knew that Italy was now being pressed by an enemy so near, how deeply you would groan! How you would grieve that the whole of our safety rested upon the barrier of the Alps, and that a wall of chastity was being constructed from felled trees! [Note: [Col. 1299D] Nannius notes that in other manuscripts, instead of *concaedibus*, there is *congeribus*—in some written *congeriebus*—and in others *aggeribus*, that is, piles of fallen trees used to block the roads against the enemy. He adds that he leaves it to others to decide which reading is better, since *concaedibus* can mean many pieces of wood laid together as though by a common felling. This conjecture certainly does not miss the mark, for Tacitus uses the same word in this sense in Book I. Accordingly, where our text, with Gill, the Roman edition, and several manuscripts, reads “with so slight a distinction,” the editions of Amerbach and Erasmus, together with some manuscripts, prefer “your people, held by the enemy in so great a danger.” Other manuscripts, quite numerous, read: “your people being kept by the enemy at so slight a distance, by the impure enemy,” etc. This is by no means a bad reading.]

With what distress you would grieve that your own people were separated from the enemy by so slight a boundary—an impure and cruel enemy who would spare neither chastity nor life!

[Col. 1300C] ### 32

“How,” I ask, “would you endure what we must endure and perhaps, more grievously, be forced to witness: virgins being carried away; little children torn from their parents’ embraces and hurled upon weapons; bodies consecrated to God being violated; and the aged womb of a mature widow returning to the disused purposes of burdens, rather than of children?” [Note: [Col. 1300D] Codex Remigius and Codex Benignus read: “what we must suffer, and—what is more grievous—be forced to endure.” This is less appropriate. Here, however, *perpeti* has the sense of “not prevent,” which is certainly less severe than being forced to look upon such disgrace.]

“How,” I ask, “would you tolerate these things—you who, even with your final breath, perhaps already forgetful of yourself but still mindful of us, repeatedly warned us to beware the barbarian invasion, recalling that you had not said without reason that we must flee?”

Perhaps you did so because you saw that we would be abandoned by your death—not through weakness of spirit, but through devotion; and if you were weak for our sake, you were nevertheless strong for yourself.

When your noble kinsman Symmachus called you back because Italy was said to be ablaze with war, because you were heading into danger and would encounter the enemy, you replied that this very circumstance was your reason for coming: so that you would not be absent from our danger, but would show yourself a sharer in your brother’s peril. [Note: [Col. 1301C] Ambrose calls Symmachus, the father of Satyrus, “your parent” here in the same way as in Letter 17.12, Letter 52.17, and Letter 53.5 Theodosius is called the parent of Valentinian the Younger and Gratian. Likewise, in many laws of the Theodosian Code, earlier emperors, although wholly unrelated by blood, are honored by their successors with the same title, evidently as a mark of respect and veneration, and perhaps here also as testimony that the mind remembered benefits received. From this we infer that Satyrus, on his return from Africa, passed through Rome.]

### 33

[Note: [Col. 1301D] Here, as Nannius observes, there is an evident imitation of this passage of Virgil:

> “And you, O most holy wife,  
> Blessed in your death, and not preserved for this grief.”

]

Blessed, therefore, in so timely a death, because you were not preserved for this grief. Certainly happier than your holy sister, who, deprived of your consolation and anxious for her modesty, recently blessed in having two brothers, now distressed on account of her two brothers, can neither follow one nor abandon the other. Your tomb is her lodging, and your body’s grave is her home.

And would that even this were a safe refuge! Food is amid weeping, drink amid tears; for you have given us the bread of tears and given us drink in tears, in measured portion—or perhaps beyond measure (Psalm 79:6).

[Col. 1301B] ### 34

For what shall I say of myself, who may neither die, lest I leave my sister, nor wish to live, lest I be torn away from you? What can be pleasant to me without you, in whom all our pleasure always consisted? Or what benefit is there in spending longer in this life and lingering on earth, where we lived happily for so long as we lived together?

Even if there were something here capable of delighting us, it could not delight us without you. And even if we had at some time wished to prolong our life eagerly, we would still no longer wish to exist without you.

### 35

These things are unbearable. For what is bearable without you, the great companion of my life, the great sharer of my labors and duties? I could not even anticipate your fall in order to make it more bearable; my mind was so terrified to think of anything of the sort. It was not that I was unaware of the human condition, but that a certain habitual reliance upon our hopes had obscured the perception of our common frailty, so that I knew how to think of nothing concerning you except prosperity.

### 36

Finally, recently, when I was pressed by a serious decline—and would that it had been the last!—this alone grieved me: that you yourself were not sitting beside the bed and, sharing with my holy sister the duty I had wished for, closing the eyes of the dying man with your fingers. [Note: [Col. 1301D] This custom was borrowed from ancient practice, by which the eyes of the dying were closed by the hands of those closest to them. Pliny mentions it and explains its rationale in Book 11, chapter 37, and many others refer to it.]

What had I wished for! What am I repaid with! What hopes fail! What duties take their place! I was preparing one thing but am compelled to perform another. I am no longer the recipient of funeral ministrations, but the minister.

O harsh lights of my eyes, which were able to see my brother dying! O unfeeling and cruel hands, which closed the eyes in which I saw more! [Note: [Col. 1301D] It was also customary among the Romans for the corpses of parents to be carried to the pyre or tomb by their sons, those of relatives by their kinsmen, and those of emperors by the leading senators. In later centuries, too, we know that Saint Louis was carried on the shoulders of Philip, his son and successor, to the tombs of his ancestors. But this is obvious.]

O still harsher neck, which was able to bear so mournful a burden, even in a service that brought consolation! [Col. 1302D]

### 37

You, brother, would more properly have performed these services for me. These were the duties I expected from you; these were the offices I longed for. But now that I survive my own life, what consolation shall I receive without you? You alone used to console me when I grieved, arouse joy, and drive away sadness.

How do I now see you, brother, when you return no words to me and offer no kisses? [Col. 1302B] Yet our mutual love was always so deeply rooted in each of us that it was nourished more by inward affection than displayed through public endearments. We did not seek the testimony of others, since we possessed such great affection for one another.

The manly sap of brotherhood had so infused itself into both of us that we seemed not to prove our love by caresses, but, conscious in our minds of our devotion, to be content with inward affection and have no need of the embellishment of endearments. Our very likeness formed us for mutual love. I do not know with what likeness of mind or with what likeness of body we seemed to see one in the other. [Note: [Col. 1302D] Some manuscripts read: “I do not know what more expressive likeness of mind than of body.” This is not sufficiently correct. From this passage we may understand that the clothing of bishops differed from that of others more by simplicity and modesty than by shape or color. This is beautifully confirmed by a letter of Celestine I to the bishops of the province of Vienne, where he writes: “We are to be distinguished from the people and others by doctrine, not by clothing; by conduct, not by dress; by purity of mind, not by adornment,” etc. See likewise what Possidius records about the clothing customarily worn by Augustine. Some manuscripts read: “I do not know what more expressive likeness of mind than of body we seemed to possess.”]

### 38

Who saw you and would not think that he had seen me? How often have I greeted people who, because they had previously greeted you, would say that they had already been greeted by me! How many people said something to you who remembered that they had said it to me! [Col. 1302C]

What joys and how much frequent delight arose for me from seeing them mistake us for one another! [Note: [Col. 1302D] Nannius says that this too is borrowed in part from Virgil:

> “Daucia, Larides, and Tymber, offspring most alike,  
> Indistinguishable to their own, and a pleasing error to their parents.”

]

What a welcome error, what a delightful slip, what a devout deception, what a pleasing misrepresentation! For there was nothing in your deeds or words that I feared having attributed to me, since I rejoiced that your qualities were ascribed to me.

### 39

Yet if they insisted too strongly, saying that they remembered having confided something to me, I would reply laughing and rejoicing: “Be careful that you have not told my brother.” For although everything between us was shared—one spirit, one affection—there was nevertheless one thing that was not shared: the secrets of our friends. Not because we feared the danger of conferring them with each other, but because we maintained our fidelity in keeping them [Col. 1303A].

Certainly, if a matter had to be weighed by counsel, the counsel was always shared, though the secret was not always shared. For even if friends spoke to one of us in such a way that what they had said would reach the other, I know that the secrecy was generally preserved so faithfully that it was not entrusted even to my brother. [Note: [Col. 1303C] All printed editions read: “would reach each of the two”; all manuscripts read: “would reach the other,” which gives the better sense. In some manuscripts the adverb “generally” is added to *complacitum*, but this plainly seems superfluous. Observe, moreover, how faithful Ambrose was regarding the secrets of his friends, and with what sacred and careful scruple.]

For it was a trustworthy indication that something had not been disclosed to an outsider if it had not been shared with one’s brother.

### 40

With such great and excellent blessings, then, I confess that I was lifted into a kind of ecstasy of mind and ceased to fear for my survival, because I believed him more worthy of life. [Note: [Col. 1303C] An old edition reads: “I would wish to fear”; the Roman edition and the overwhelming majority of manuscripts read: “I had ceased to fear.” Below, where all printed editions read “how unexamined the wounds,” nearly all manuscripts read “how examined the wounds,” which would make no sense.] And for that reason I received a blow that I cannot bear. The pains anticipated in advance are more bearable than wounds that have not been foreseen.

Who will now console me in my sadness? [Col. 1303B] Who will lift me when I am afflicted? With whom shall I share my cares? Who will free me from the commerce and burden of this world? [Note: [Col. 1303C] Thus read the Roman edition and several manuscripts. The old edition, together with some manuscripts, reads: “who will free me through use.” The meaning is not different, for it likewise signifies “free me from the care and business of temporal affairs.” Immediately afterward, where the editions of Gill and Rome, with a few manuscripts, read “manager of affairs,” the edition of Amerbach, Erasmus, and by far the majority of manuscripts read “originator of affairs.”]

For you were the director of affairs, the judge of servants, the arbiter of brothers—not an arbiter of litigation, but of affection.

### 41

For whenever I had to discuss something with my holy sister, we would appoint you judge of which opinion seemed better. [Note: [Col. 1303D] Several manuscripts read: “who would injure no one’s face,” and so forth; other manuscripts and the printed editions, more correctly, read as in the text. It is a Terentian expression from the *Adelphoe*, Act V, scene 4: “To offend no one, to smile upon everyone,” etc.]

You would offend no one, and, eager to satisfy both, you preserved both your affection for love and the moderation of judgment, so that you dismissed each of us pleased and secured the gratitude of each for yourself.

Or if you yourself brought forward something for debate, how welcome was your dispute! How free from bitterness your indignation itself! How unbitter your correction even of the servants, when you learned to defer more to your brothers than to punish them out of affection! Our position restrained our eagerness to correct; or rather, you, brother, drew us away from every desire to correct, promising to vindicate and wishing to soften [Col. 1304A].

### 42

Thus you gave no small testimony to prudence, which the wise define in this way: [Note: [Col. 1303D] Plato seems to be indicated here. In several places, especially Book IV of the *Laws*, he discusses divine worship and the administration of the state. What follows concerning self-knowledge and the proper ordering of life is taken from the First *Alcibiades*.]

The first of good things is to know God and to venerate that true and divine reality with a devout mind; to love with the whole affection of the mind that lovable and desirable beauty of eternal truth.

The second is to derive toward one’s neighbors, from that divine fountain and heavenly nature, the devotion that is owed to them. Even the wise men of the world drew this principle from our laws. For they could not have poured these teachings into human disciplines unless they had drunk from that heavenly fountain of divine law. [Note: [Col. 1303D] The manuscripts of Remigius and Benignus read: “they could not have poured them into discipline unless they had drunk from that fountain.”]

### 43

What, then, should I say about his reverence for the worship of God? Before he had been initiated into the more perfect mysteries, while he was in a shipwreck, when the ship in which he was traveling struck a rocky shoal and was breaking apart under the waves pressing in from both sides, he feared not death but leaving life without the mystery.

He therefore asked those whom he knew to be initiated for that divine sacrament of the faithful—not to thrust curious eyes into the mysteries, but to obtain the aid of faith. [Note: [Col. 1303D–1304C] Several manuscripts read: “not, as a curious person, to insert his eyes into the mysteries.” Many things in this single passage reveal the ancient discipline of the Church. First, here, as frequently elsewhere, you see the Eucharist called the divine sacrament of the faithful. Second, it was carefully kept hidden from the eyes of the uninitiated. Third, it was not accustomed to be consecrated only for present use, but was also preserved for future use. Finally, Christians are shown to have had the custom of carrying it with them in their dangers. We have already spoken more than once about the first two points, sufficiently for present purposes. To confirm the latter points, readers need only be referred to Tertullian, Book II *To His Wife*, chapter 5; Cyprian, *On the Lapsed*, where he recounts the remarkable eruption of fire from the chest in which the same sacrament was enclosed; Eusebius, Book VI of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 44; Gregory the Great, Book III of the *Dialogues*, chapter 33; and John the Deacon, who reports the same event in Book I of the *Life of Gregory*. To these one may add more recent writers: Spencaeus, Book II *On Eucharistic Worship*; Cardinal Bona, Book II *On Liturgical Matters*, chapter 17; Mabillon, Book I *On Gallican Liturgy*, chapter 9; Thiers, *On Frequent Exposition of the Blessed Sacrament*; and others.]

For he had it tied in a cloth and wrapped the cloth around his neck. [Note: [Col. 1304C] Nannius explains *orarium* as follows: “Here *orarium* is the same kind of garment as that which is now called the stole in sacrificial worship, and among the ancients was called an *infula*. Its ends are called ribbons, and even now it is placed upon children being initiated in baptism. It is an emblem both of victims and of priests; I believe that it became customary among Christians because Saint Peter calls the Christian people both royal and priestly.” So far he. But apart from the fact that he confuses many things that are entirely distinct from one another, there is no doubt that he assigns to *orarium* a meaning foreign to this passage. Here *orarium* is exactly the same as above, in Letter 22.9: namely, a sweat-cloth, scarf, or linen cloth intended for wiping the face, a sense in which the word is frequently found in writers of the same period.]

Thus he threw himself into the sea, seeking no plank broken from the ship’s framework upon which he might be supported while floating, since he had sought only the weapons of faith. And so, believing that he was sufficiently covered and protected by these things, he desired no other aids.

### 44

At the same time, one may observe his courage. When the rowing apparatus was failing, he did not take up a plank like a shipwrecked man, but, like a brave man, took assistance from his own virtue [Col. 1305A]. [Note: [Col. 1304D] Some manuscripts read: “he had lain upon a plank . . . in which he had trusted.”] Neither hope abandoned him nor expectation deceived him. Finally, saved first from the waves and carried into the harbor of his earthly station, he recognized his bishop, to whom he had entrusted himself.

Immediately, once he had either rescued his other servants himself or learned that they had been rescued, he disregarded his possessions and did not long for what had been lost. He sought the Church of God in order to give thanks for his deliverance and to learn the eternal mysteries, declaring that no duty was greater than returning thanks. [Note: [Col. 1305C] Some manuscripts read: “that no duty was greater for returning thanks.”]

[Note: [Col. 1305C] Nannius says that this agrees with the Persian law mentioned by Xenophon, according to which those convicted of ingratitude were punished with the highest penalty. He might also have added the ancient law that allowed freedmen who proved ungrateful toward their patrons to be recalled into slavery. Terence alludes to this in the *Andria*, Act I, scene 1, in Simon’s words to the freedman Sosia: “I do not alter what was done.” See likewise what Ambrose discusses concerning the repayment of benefits in Book I of the *Duties*, together with the passages from Cicero’s *Duties* cited there.]

For if failing to repay a human being was judged comparable to homicide, how great a crime is it not to repay God?

### 45

It is therefore the mark of a prudent person to recognize himself and, as the wise have defined it, to live according to nature. For what is so according to nature as to return thanks to the author of all things?

Look upon this sky: does it not return thanks to its author when it is seen? “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament announces the work of his hands” (Psalm 18:2). The sea itself, when it is calm and tranquil, bears witness to the sign of divine serenity; when it is stirred, the heavenly indignation is a terror.

Do we not rightly marvel at the grace of God when we observe that insensible nature restrains its waves by a kind of sensible reason, and that the water recognizes its boundaries? What shall I say of the lands, which, obedient to the divine command, spontaneously provide food for every living creature (Genesis 1:11), and restore what they have received from the fields multiplied and increased as though by growing interest?

### 46

Therefore, he who, guided by nature, had grasped the order of the divine work with the fiery vigor of his mind understood first of all that thanks must be returned to his savior. But because he could not return it, he could possess it. [Note: [Col. 1305C] Ambrose uses the same exchanged construction in Book VI on Luke, section 25. Nannius notes that he borrowed this figure from Cicero’s *Oration for Gnaeus Plancus*. The Ciceronian words are examined by the rhetorician Julianus in Gellius, Book I, chapter 4. Some manuscripts read: “such gratitude of his.”]

For such is the power of gratitude that, even when it is returned, it is possessed; and by possessing it, it is returned. He was therefore returning thanks and presenting faith. For if he had experienced the protection of so great a heavenly mystery wrapped in a cloth, how much did he think he would experience if he took it into his mouth and drew it into the entire secret place of his heart! How much greater did he consider that which was poured into his inward parts, when what had been covered by a cloth had benefited him so greatly!

### 47

But he was not so eager as to be careless; for we know that many, through the eagerness of their zeal, neglect caution. He summoned the bishop to himself (24, question 1, chapter “Advocavit”), and considered no grace genuine except that of true faith. He therefore asked him whether he agreed with the Catholic bishops—that is, with the Roman Church.

And perhaps at that time the Church of that region was in schism. For Lucifer had separated himself from our communion. Although he had gone into exile on behalf of the faith and had left behind heirs of his faith, Satyrus nevertheless did not consider faith to exist in schism. For even if they held faith toward God, they did not hold it toward the Church of God, whose limbs they allowed to be divided and whose members to be torn apart.

Indeed, since Christ suffered for the Church, and the Church is the body of Christ (Ephesians 5:25), those who empty his Passion and tear apart his body do not appear to show faith toward Christ. [Note: [Col. 1305C–1306C] Some manuscripts read: “for that profit.” But this is surely a scribal error.
