As for Lucifer, the Fathers and historians of ecclesiastical affairs have transmitted the following about him. He was a bishop of Cagliari in Sardinia who, when he refused to comply with the Emperor Constantius at the synod of Milan, was sent into exile together with the holy and Catholic bishops Dionysius, Eusebius, Paulinus, and Rhodanius. He remained in exile, moving from place to place, until the time of Julian Caesar. While in exile, he defended Athanasius by publishing distinguished books against Constantius, on account of which the leading men of his age praised him as inflamed with a sincere desire for martyrdom.

However, when he returned to the West and found Antioch, through which he was traveling, divided between the Eustathians and the Meletians, and ordained Paulinus for the party of the former, he provided the occasion for the long dissension discussed above in connection with Letter 56. Saint Eusebius disapproved of Paulinus’ ordination. Interpreting this injury as his own, Lucifer resolved not to accept the Council of Alexandria, although he had subscribed to it through his representative, and separated himself from all who admitted into their communion anyone who had subscribed to any of the Arian formulas. They attribute the origin of the Luciferian schism to this.

There are also those who, against Jerome’s view, attribute it to Lucifer’s hostility toward Eusebius; and others who connect it with the heresy concerning the infusion of the soul. But neither explanation is sufficiently credible. Besides Ambrose in this passage, Lucifer is discussed by Jerome in the *Dialogue Against the Luciferians*, Rufinus in Book I, chapter 19 and following, Augustine in *On Heresies*, chapter 81, and also Socrates in Book III, chapter 5 and following, Sozomen in Book V, chapters 12 and 13, Theodoret in Book III, chapter 5, and others.]

### 48

Thus, although he held the “loan” of grace and feared, as a debtor to so great a name, to sail onward, he nevertheless preferred to cross over to a place where he could safely discharge it. For he judged that repayment of divine grace consisted in devotion and faith; and as soon as a freer opportunity was given by the Church, he did not delay fulfilling it.

[Note: [Col. 1306D–1307D] Ambrose has already indicated more than once that Satyrus had not yet been regenerated by baptism when he entrusted himself to the sea. Nothing was more common in those times than to postpone this sacrament until a more advanced age. Since many did this in order to loosen the reins on their desires more freely, the Fathers reproved the practice severely and emphatically, as may often be observed in our Ambrose.

Yet Satyrus’ life is here described as having been ordered with such piety and holiness that he is entirely freed from this suspicion. Nevertheless, he himself may cautiously have feared this for himself, just as Monica, Augustine’s mother, feared in Augustine’s case: namely, that he might lose baptismal grace—which Ambrose testifies he never lost—if, carried away by some youthful passion, he approached baptism at an even earlier age.

After being warned by the danger of the shipwreck from which he had escaped, he hastened toward baptism with the caution we have seen. Nor was he compelled to observe the customary stages of the catechumens, since we understand that these were accustomed to be omitted whenever danger pressed, from the baptism of those who, afflicted by a serious illness, were initiated by the same sacrament.

As for the place where our Satyrus was baptized, since Ambrose passes over it in silence, the Correctors of the Decretum display excessive confidence when they write that Ambrose relates that Satyrus, after landing in Sardinia, summoned the Sardinian bishop to himself, and so forth. Nevertheless, although Rufinus, when writing about the Luciferian schism in Book I, chapter 30, seems in some way to favor them by saying that it still continues among a few, nothing prevents it from having spread not only as far as Sicily but also to the nearer coasts of Africa.]

He both received the grace of God that he desired and preserved what he had received [Col. 1307A]. Nothing, therefore, is wiser than that prudence which distinguishes divine things from human.

### 49

Why should I speak of his eloquence, tested in the practice of the law courts? With what astonishing admiration he shone in the auditorium of the lofty prefecture! [Note: [Col. 1308D] The prefecture is called “lofty” because it was the tribunal of the praetorian prefect, whose dignity was regarded as the summit of all others. Appeals were made to him from the governors of the provinces, and in his court advocates—at least one hundred in the East—pleaded cases. They were called “most illustrious” and “most distinguished” and were granted various exemptions, as Julius Caesar Bulenger explains in Book III of *On the Roman Empire*, chapter 4.]

But I prefer to praise those things which, after receiving the mysteries of God, he judged superior to human affairs.

50. If anyone wishes to contemplate his courage more fully, let him consider how often, after a shipwreck, with a certain unconquerable contempt for this life, he crossed the seas and traversed distant regions by traveling through them; finally, how at this very time he did not shrink from danger but came to meet it—enduring injury, heedless of the cold, and—if only he had been mindful of caution! Yet he was blessed precisely in this: while he was permitted to use the strength of his body, he fulfilled the duty of youth without hindrance in carrying out whatever he wished, and lived his life without knowing weakness. [Col. 1307B] 1128

51. But with what elaboration shall I describe his simplicity? For it was a certain moderation of character and sobriety of mind. Grant me, I beg, your indulgence, and permit my grief, so that I may speak somewhat more fully about one with whom I am no longer permitted to converse. Certainly it is beneficial for you also to recognize [Note: [Col. 1308D] Some manuscripts read, “not through some weakness upon us,” etc.] that you did not confer this duty upon me through some weakness, but by judgment; that you were moved not by pity for death, but summoned by the honor of his virtues. For every simple soul is blessed (Prov. 11). His simplicity, moreover, was so great that, transformed into a child, he shone with the innocent simplicity of that age, as an image of perfect virtue [Col. 1307C] and as a kind of mirror of blameless conduct. [Note: Some manuscripts read, “and as a mirror of certain innocent manners.”] Therefore he entered the kingdom of heaven, because he believed God’s word; because, like a child, he rejected the art of flattery, gently absorbed the pain of an injury, which he avenged more harshly; was readier for complaint than for deceit, easy to reconciliation, difficult to ambition, holy in modesty—so that you would often praise in him an excessive bashfulness [Note: A few manuscripts read, “which you would think necessary,”] rather than seek a necessary one.

52. Yet the foundations of virtue are never excessive; for modesty does not hinder duty but commends it. Thus, as though suffused with a maidenly bashfulness, he would reveal his feeling in his face if, on coming suddenly upon a married woman, he happened to encounter her; as though bowed down [Col. 1308A] and almost sunk into the earth, although he was by no means out of place in that gathering of men, he was slow to raise his face, lift his eyes, or return a word. He did this through a certain chaste modesty of mind, with which bodily chastity also corresponded. For he preserved undefiled the gifts of holy baptism, pure in body and purer in heart; he shuddered no less at the disgrace of adulterous speech than at that of the body, judging that the reverence owed to chastity should be shown no less through the integrity of words than through bodily purity.

[Note: The mention here of encountering a married woman—“the mother,” that is, the matron, not a virgin—is explained by the fact that women were rarely permitted to go out from their parents’ homes into public, and never without their faces veiled. How much less were they permitted to engage young men in conversation at crossroads!]

53. Finally, he loved chastity so greatly that he did not seek a wife, although in this there was not only a desire for chastity but also a motive of devotion. In a remarkable way he both concealed his avoidance of marriage and shunned self-display; his concealment was so complete [Col. 1308B] that, even when we pressed him, he seemed rather to be postponing marriage than refusing it. This, then, was the one matter he did not entrust even to his brothers—not because of any hesitation caused by indecision, but through the modesty of virtue.

54. Who, then, would not marvel at a man who, between two brothers—one a virgin, the other a priest—middle-aged yet not inferior in greatness of spirit, so distinguished himself between two supreme gifts that he reflected the chastity of the one gift and the holiness of the other, not by the bond of profession but by the duty of virtue? Therefore, if lust and anger are the nurses of the remaining vices, I may rightly call chastity and clemency, as it were, the parents of certain virtues; although devotion also, as it is the chief of all good things, is likewise the seedbed of the other virtues.

[Col. 1308C] 55. For what shall I say of his frugality and a certain chastity in possessing things? The man who preserves what is his does not seek what belongs to another; nor is the man who is content with his own puffed up by excess. He therefore wished only to recover what was his own, more to prevent being defrauded than to become rich. For he rightly called those who sought what belonged to others “hawks of money.” If avarice is the root of all evils, then certainly the person who does not seek money has stripped himself of vices (1 Tim. 6:10).

56. He was never pleased by elaborate banquets or heaped-up dishes, except when he invited friends; he sought only as much as nature required, not as much as remained over for pleasure. And certainly he was not poor in possessions, yet he was poor in spirit. [Note: “Poor in spirit” is added in the ancient edition and in not a few manuscripts, with the words “for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” [Col. 1309D]; but these words were excised in the Roman edition and are absent from many manuscripts. Indeed, this seems to us an interpolation by some copyist, since it does not fit suitably with what precedes and follows.] We ought certainly not to doubt his blessedness. [Col. 1309A] (Matt. 5:3) He did not exult in riches like a wealthy man, nor did he regard the little he possessed as insufficient like a poor man.

57. It remains that, in bringing to completion the cardinal virtues, we should also discern in him the qualities of justice. For although the virtues are related to one another and interwoven, a certain more distinct form of each is nevertheless required, especially of justice. [Note: Thus the ancient edition and most manuscripts; the Roman edition, with some manuscripts, lacks “form and expression.”] In this virtue he is altogether sparing toward himself in outward matters; and whatever he possesses, with a certain severity toward himself, he pours out upon his neighbors, carried away by love of the common good.

58. Yet justice has many forms. One concerns relatives, another everyone, another the worship of God, or assistance to the needy. What he was like toward everyone is shown by the affection of the provincials whom he governed [Col. 1309B]; they said that he had been more truly their father than their judge, a gracious arbiter in matters of dutiful relationship and a steadfast examiner of equitable law. [Note: “Affection,” that is, favor and goodwill. Otherwise it was common enough for provincials to disparage governors after they had left the administration of a province; indeed, they often accused them of extortion.]

59. What he was like among his brothers, although he embraced the whole human race with benevolence, is shown by the undivided inheritance: [Note: Many manuscripts read “neither distributed nor deliberated”; perhaps the reading should be “nor diminished or peeled,” that is, reduced and stripped.] the inheritance was neither distributed nor diminished, but preserved. For he denied that devotion to his brothers was his reason for making a will. He indicated this also in his final speech, when he commended those whom he had loved: he had not been willing to take a wife, lest he be separated from his brothers; nor had he wished to make a will, lest our discretion in any matter be infringed. Finally, although we pleaded and entreated him, he still thought that nothing should be set down; yet he did not forget the poor, merely begging that as much should be given as seemed right to us.

60. By this one act he sufficiently expressed both a sign of divine fear and an example of human religious duty. For what he gave to the poor he gave to God, since “whoever is generous to the poor lends to God” (Prov. 19:17); and by asking that what was just be done, he left not a small portion but everything. For this is the highest justice: to sell what one possesses and give it to the poor. “He scattered abroad; he gave to the poor; his righteousness endures forever” (Ps. 111:9). Therefore he left us stewards, not heirs; for an inheritance is sought for a successor, whereas stewardship is bound to the poor.

61. Hence the Holy Spirit has not unjustly expressed even today, through the voice of a little reader, how great he was: “Innocent in his hands and pure in heart, who has not received his soul in vain, nor dealt deceitfully with his neighbor: this is the generation of those who seek God” (Ps. 24:4, 6). [Note: We have already noted in more than one place the ancient custom by which boys were appointed to the office of reader.] Such a man, then, will ascend the mountain of the Lord and dwell in God’s tabernacle, because, entering without blemish, he practiced justice, spoke truth, and did not deceive his neighbor (Ps. 15:2–3); nor did he lend out his money at interest, since he always wished to recover his hereditary inheritance. I recognize the oracle: what no arrangement ordered, the Spirit revealed. [Note: A few manuscripts read, “no disposition arranged.”]

62. What shall I say, moreover, about the fact that, advancing beyond justice itself through devotion, when he thought that some share of the common fruits should be allotted to a certain occupant [Note: Nannius observes that he is here called an “occupant,” meaning one who was taking possession of the resources belonging jointly to Satyrus and Ambrose; he further notes that Macrobius calls Dionysius of Sicily an “occupant of the palace.”] in consideration of my office, he credited me with being the author of the generosity and contributed the profit of his share to the common partnership?

[Col. 1310B] 63. These things, and others that were then a source of the greatest pleasure to me, now above all intensify the recollection of my grief. Yet they remain, and will always remain; they never pass away like a shadow. The grace of virtue does not perish with the body, nor is the end of nature identical with the end of merit—although the exercise of nature itself does not perish forever but rests through a certain temporary cessation. [Note: All editions read “which were then of the greatest pleasure to me, I have intensified with the recollection of grief”; Gill reads “he intensified”; the Roman edition reads “they intensify.” The manuscripts, like our text, generally read “they intensify,” except that instead of this some read “they bring forward,” and some also read “they intensify grief through recollection.”]

64. Since he was thus accomplished in such virtues and rescued from dangers, I shall mourn him more from longing than from a sense of loss. For death itself, by its appropriateness, urges us to think that he should be accompanied with gratitude rather than mourned; for it is written, in the midst of common grief, that personal grief ought to be set aside (4 Esdras 10:11 and following). Nor is this said in prophetic speech only to that one woman who is represented there, but to each of us, since it appears to have been spoken to the Church.

65. Thus Scripture speaks to me as well, saying: “Is this what you teach? Is this how you instruct the people of God?” [Note: Two manuscripts read, “and thus you instruct God’s people”; two others, “Is this how you establish God’s Church?”] “Or do you not know that your example is a danger to others? Unless, perhaps, you complain that you have not been heard. This is first of all the shameless arrogance of one who wishes to deserve alone what he knows has been denied even to many saints, although you know that God is not a respecter of persons” (Acts 10:34). For although God is merciful, if he always heard everyone, he would seem to act not from free will but from a kind of necessity. Moreover, when everyone prays, if he heard everyone, no one would die. For how many people do you pray every day? Is God’s decree to be overturned out of regard for you? Why, then, do you grieve that something was not obtained when you know that it cannot always be obtained?

[Col. 1311A] 66. “Fool,” he says, “above all women, do you not see our mourning and what has happened to us, because Sion our mother is distressed with universal grief and has been humbled with humiliation? Mourn exceedingly even now, because we all mourn; and be sorrowful, because we have all been made sorrowful. But you are sorrowful for your brother. Ask the earth, and it will tell you that she is the one who ought to mourn, as the survivor of so many offspring that have sprung up upon her. For from her,” he says, “from the beginning, all were born; others will come, and behold, almost all are walking toward destruction, and the multitude of them is destined for annihilation. Who, then, ought to mourn more—she who has lost so great a multitude, or you who grieve for one?” (4 Esdras 10:6 and following). [Note: The Roman edition reads: “Foolish, he says … she is distressed with every grief … and mourns most intensely. And now, since we all mourn and are sorrowful because we have all been made sorrowful, you are sorrowful for your son. Ask the earth … to mourn the downfall of so many offspring springing up upon her.” The ancient edition and manuscripts read as in the text, except that Erasmus and Gill also read “foolish.” We judge, however, that the word “foolishly” should be retained, on the basis of the phrase below, “you are sorrowful for your brother.”]

67. Therefore let common grief absorb our grief and drive out the bitterness of private sorrow. [Col. 1311B] We ought not to mourn those whom we see to have been set free; for it is not without purpose that we recall that at this time such holy souls have been released from bodily bonds. For, as though by divine judgment, we see widows of such gravity die at one and the same time, so that their departure seems to be a kind of departure, not death’s setting, lest chastity, now veteran with its service completed, fall into doubt after modesty had been preserved for so long. What sighs and what grief this bitter recollection awakens in me! And although I was not without sorrows, yet amid my private grief, amid the loss of so many flourishing merits, a certain common condition of human nature consoled me; and, fixed upon one grief, I had concealed the bitterness of the public funeral beneath the appearance of domestic devotion. [Note: Ambrose testifies in more than one place that the death of widows distinguished by the gravity of their life and conduct was accustomed to bring him particular grief.]

68. I therefore return, Holy Scripture, to your consolations; for I find it helpful to dwell upon your precepts and sayings. [Note: [Col. 1312D] Not a few manuscripts read, “Because it is easier … by reason within yourself.”] [Col. 1311C] How much easier it is for heaven and earth to pass away than for one iota of the Law to fall (Luke 16:17)! But let us now hear what is written: “Now keep your grief within yourself, and endure bravely the misfortunes that have come upon you. For if you acknowledge the decree of God, you will receive your son in due time, and you will be praised among women” (4 Esdras 10:15–16). If this is said to a woman, how much more to a priest? If it concerns a son, it is certainly not absurd that similar things should be recalled concerning the loss of brothers—although, if I had had a son, I would never have loved him more. For just as the labors expended and pains undertaken in vain at the death of children seem to increase grief, so among brothers the habits of companionship and fellowship inflame the bitterness of sorrow.

69. But behold, I hear Scripture saying: “Do not make this speech, but consent to be persuaded. What has happened to Sion? Take comfort concerning the grief of Jerusalem. For you see that our holy places have been defiled, and the name that has been invoked over us has almost been profaned; our people have suffered insult, our priests have been burned, our Levites have been in captivity, our women have been defiled, our virgins have suffered violence, our righteous have been carried away, our little ones have been betrayed, our young men have served, and our strong men have been made weak. And what is greater than all these things, the seal of Sion has been broken, because she has been stripped of her glory and has now been delivered into the hands of those who hate us. You, therefore, shake off your great sorrow and lay aside the multitude of your griefs, so that the Mighty One may again be gracious to you and the Most High may grant you rest, a rest from your sorrows” (ibid., 20 and following). [Note: The manuscripts and editions read thus, except that the Roman edition alone has “and the name that has been invoked,” while in the following verse that edition, together with the ancient edition and some manuscripts, reads “and our young men,” where the great majority of manuscripts have “and those of ours.” The latter may perhaps be the correct reading: “and our sons.”]

70. Therefore the tears will cease; for we must obey remedies that bring salvation, since there ought to be some distinction between the faithful and the faithless. Let those weep who cannot possess the hope of resurrection—a hope taken away not by God’s judgment but by the harshness of their faith. Let there be a distinction between Christ’s servants and the worshipers of idols: let the latter weep for their dead, whom they believe to have perished forever; let those have no holiday from tears, no rest from sorrow, who believe that the dead have no rest. But for us, whose death is not the end of nature but the end of this life—since nature itself is restored to something better—let every tear wipe away the circumstances of death.

71. Certainly, if those who regarded death as the end of sensation and the failure of nature found some consolations for themselves, how much more should we, to whom the consciousness of good deeds promises better rewards after death! The pagans have their consolations, because they consider death the rest from all evils; and just as they are deprived of the fruit of life, so they think themselves deprived of all awareness and of the pains of punishments that we endure, severe and constant, in this life. But we, just as we ought to be more uplifted by the reward, should also be more patient through the consolation; for those whom death will not take away but eternity will receive seem not to be lost but sent ahead.

72. Therefore the tears will cease—or, if they cannot cease, I shall mourn you, brother, amid the common lamentation and conceal my domestic sighs beneath the public grief. For how could they cease, when tears steal forth at every sound of your name—whether habit itself awakens the memory, affection presents your image, or recollection renews the pain? When are you absent, since you are represented by so many acts of kindness? [Note: Some manuscripts read, “For you are present, and are always offered before me.”] You are present, I say, and are ever before me; with my whole soul and mind I embrace you, look upon you, speak to you, kiss you, and hold you, whether in the very quiet of night or in the clear light of day, when you deign to revisit and console me in my mourning. Finally, the nights themselves, which seemed more oppressive when you were alive because they denied us the opportunity of seeing one another, have now begun to be sweet; and sleep itself, once the unwelcome interrupter of our conversations, has become dear, because it has restored you to me. We are therefore not wretched but blessed: neither the presence nor the care of those we love is lost; their grace increases. For death is an image resembling sleep. [Note: Ambrose seems to have in mind a passage of Plato near the end of the Apology of Socrates, where, arguing that death is a gain, he compares it with the most peaceful sleep. It is likely that others borrowed the same comparison from him, including Cicero in his work On Old Age and in the first Tusculan Disputation.]

73. And if, during the quiet of night, souls still clinging to bodily bonds and, as it were, confined within the prison-like enclosure of their limbs, can nevertheless perceive higher and separate realities, how much more do they behold these things when, with a pure and ethereal sense, they suffer no impediments from bodily corruption! And when, as the day was already inclining toward evening, I complained that you did not revisit me as I rested, you were wholly and indivisibly present at all times. [Note: All manuscripts and the ancient edition read thus, except that some manuscripts have “as the day was pressing on” instead of “inclining”; the Roman edition, on its own initiative, altered the passage to “as the day, already pressing on, was hastening toward nightfall.” That correction is too bold for us to accept.] Thus, while my limbs were steeped in that sleep, and I was awake for you while you lived for me, I would say: “What is death, brother?” For certainly you were separated from me for no moment. You were so present everywhere that the access to one another which we could not always have during the use of this life is now present to us always and everywhere. For then it was impossible for everything to be present: our embraces, our sight of one another, and the sweetness of bodily kisses could not be available in every place and at every time. The images of our souls were always with us, even when we were not together; and they have not perished now either, but continually fly to us—more abundantly in proportion to the greatness of our longing.

74. I hold you, therefore, brother, and neither death nor time will tear you from me. The tears themselves are sweet, the very weeping is pleasant, by which the heat of the soul is quenched and affection, as though released, evaporates. For I cannot be without you, nor ever fail to remember you, nor remember you without tears. O bitter days, which reveal the breaking of our interrupted union! O mournful nights, which have lost so good a companion of your rest and a companion inseparable from me! What crosses would you bring forth, if the image of your presence did not pour itself upon me, if the visions of the mind did not represent the one whom the appearance of the body denies us?

75. Now, now, brother, dearest to my soul, although you died an untimely death, you are nevertheless blessed: you do not endure these things, nor are you compelled to mourn a lost brother whom you could not bear to be absent for long, but whom you would quickly revisit. If then you hastened to drive away the weariness of my solitude and lessen the sadness of your brother’s mind, how much more frequently now ought you to revisit my afflicted spirit and, having been conceived from you, soften its grief through you!

76. Yet the practice of my office grants me some intervals, and the attentiveness of priestly service draws my mind away. But what will happen to our holy sister? Although she tempers her devotion through divine fear, she nevertheless again kindles the very grief of devotion through her zeal for religion. She lies stretched upon the ground, embracing the tomb with her entire lap; wearied by her painful steps, sad in feeling, she renews her mourning day and night. For although she often suspends her weeping in speech, she renews it in prayer. And although the memory of Scripture, sowing consolations, goes before her, she compensates for the desire to weep through the constancy of prayer, restoring the abundance of her tears especially when no one can interrupt her. Thus you have something for which to pity her, but nothing for which to reproach her; for weeping in prayer is a virtue. And although this is characteristic of virgins, whose sex is softer and whose feelings are more tender, so that at the sight of our common frailty they overflow into tears even without the awareness of domestic grief, nevertheless, when there is greater cause for mourning, an end is placed upon the mourning. [Note: A few manuscripts read, “she recalls it in prayer … the constancy of her prayer through the abundance of her tears.”]

77. The means of offering consolation is therefore lacking, because there is an abundance of grounds for excusing her. For you cannot forbid what you teach, especially since religion supports her tears, not grief, and she conceals the course of common lamentation out of fear of shame. Console her, then, if you can approach her spirit and penetrate her mind. Let her see that you are present and feel that you are not dead, so that, secure in regard to your merit and strengthened by your consolation, she may learn not to grieve heavily for one who has reminded her that there is no cause for grief. [Note: Some manuscripts read, “who has drawn near to the one who does not grieve.”]

78. But why should I delay you, brother? Why should I wait for our prayer to die with you and, as it were, be buried with you? Although the appearance and form of your lifeless body itself usually bring consolation, and the grace that remains and the enduring features soothe the eyes, I say that I will delay no longer. [Col. 1314C] Let us proceed to the tomb. But first, before the people, I offer my final farewell; I proclaim peace; I release the kiss. [Note: This shows that the face of Satyrus’ corpse was exposed.] Go ahead to that home common and owed to all, but now more desirable to me than to others. Prepare companionship for your guest; and just as everything was shared by us here, so there also let us know no divided right.

[Note: Relatives used to cry “Farewell three times” to the dead so that they might not only testify to their affection, but also, if perhaps the spirit believed to have been expelled still lay hidden in the body, awaken it by those words.]

[Note: The same manuscripts read, “the desirable home, the fellowship of lodging … you leave one who longs for it.”]

79. Please do not long delay one who longs for you; await one who hastens; help one who is hurrying; and if I seem to you to linger too long, summon me. For never were we absent from one another for very long, yet you used to revisit me. Now, since you can no longer return to us, we shall go to you: it is right that we repay the duty and take our turn. Our condition in life was never separate: our health or illness was always shared; when one fell ill, the other came down with the sickness, and when one recovered, both rose again. How have we lost our common right? If our sharing in illness existed even now, how did we not share in death?

[Col. 1315A] 80. To you now, almighty God, I commend an innocent soul; [Note: Here too testimony is borne that Catholic prayers were customarily offered for the aid and deliverance of the dead.] to you I offer my sacrifice. Receive graciously and serenely this brotherly gift, this sacrifice of a priest. These libations of mine I now send ahead; with this pledge I come to you—not a pledge of money but of life—so that you may not make me remain longer a debtor for so great a loan. The interest of brotherly love is not small, nor is the capital of nature insignificant, when the increase of virtue compounds it. I can endure it, if I am soon compelled to repay it.

# BOOK TWO: ON FAITH IN THE RESURRECTION

[Col. 1315]

1. In the preceding book we yielded something to grief, lest remedies applied to a wound still burning should aggravate rather than soothe the pain; and also because we repeatedly addressed our brother and held him before our eyes. It was not inappropriate to relax for a little while the feeling of nature, which is nourished by tears, soothed by weeping, and immobilized by astonishment. For the appearance of piety is gentle and tender: it loves nothing insolent, nothing harsh, nothing hard. Patience is proved more by endurance than by resistance.

2. Since, therefore, the day of death ought by now to have inclined our brotherly spirit amid tearful scenes [Note: A few manuscripts read, “to incline the brotherly mind,”]—since it held the whole of it—and since on the seventh day we return to the tomb, a day that is a symbol of future rest, it is helpful to transfer and redirect our mind from our brother toward an exhortation addressed to the whole human race. [Note: These words indicate not only that this speech was delivered on the seventh day after the burial of Satyrus, but also that this day was customarily observed in a particular way in funeral rites. Something of this custom is still retained regarding the seventh, as well as the third, ninth, and thirtieth days. On this subject, see the Funeral Oration for Theodosius.] In this way we will neither be so fixed upon our brother with all our senses that emotion steals upon us, nor, exiled from such devotion and grace, abandon the one we love and thereby increase the injustice of so great a grief, if today he were to die for us not only in reality but also in our speech. [Note: Most manuscripts read, “and die for us in the speech.”]

3. Therefore, dearest brothers, we proposed to console ourselves through what is common to all and not to regard as harsh whatever awaits everyone, and for this reason not to mourn death: first, because it is common and owed to all; then, because it releases us from the afflictions of this age; finally, because, when we have rested from the labor of this world in the likeness of sleep [Note: Not a few manuscripts read, “from labour of this kind.”], renewed vitality is poured back into us. What grief would the grace of resurrection fail to console? What sorrow would it not exclude, if you believe that nothing is destroyed by death—indeed, that the very swiftness of death makes it impossible for anything more to be destroyed? Therefore, dearest brothers, in this common exhortation let us also pay our affection to our brother. We will not seem to have strayed too far from him if, through the hope of resurrection and the sweetness of future glory, he lives again for us today in our speech.

4. Let us begin, then, by showing that we ought not to mourn the death of our own. For what is more absurd than to mourn as something exceptional what you know has been prescribed for everyone? This is to raise the mind above the human condition, refuse the common law, reject fellowship with nature [Note: Some manuscripts read, “reject the fellowship,”] inflate the mind with the flesh, and fail to recognize the measure of the flesh itself. What is more absurd than not knowing who you are and aspiring to be what you are not? Or what is more imprudent than being unable to endure, when it occurs, what you know will happen? Nature herself calls us back and, through a certain consolation of her own, withdraws us from grief of this kind. For what grief is so grave, or what pain so bitter, that the mind is not sometimes relieved within it? Nature has this property: however sorrowful people may be, if only they remain human, they nevertheless for a little while draw the mind away from grief.

5. Some peoples, it is said, even existed who mourned the birth of human beings and celebrated their death. Nor was this foolish; they thought that those who had entered upon this sea of life should be mourned, while those who had emerged from the storms and waves of this world should be accompanied with justifiable joy. [Note: Herodotus, whom Cicero praises in his Consolation on the Death of His Daughter, mentions in Book 5 peoples among whom this custom prevailed. To him one may add Valerius Maximus, Book 2, chapter 6, Solinus, Pomponius Mela, and others. See likewise Cicero near the end of the first Tusculan Disputation, where he derives from verses of Euripides the same explanation of that practice.] We ourselves also forget the birthdays of the dead, and renew with solemn celebration the day on which they died. [Note: Understand “birthdays of the dead” to refer not only to martyrs, whom Cyprian and many others mention, but also to other Christians, whose deaths were customarily commemorated each year by prayers and sacrifices, as may be learned from Tertullian, On Monogamy, chapter 10. Finally, “birthdays” and “birthday celebrations,” besides being applied to martyrs—in which sense the phrase occurs more than once in Paulinus’ poems about Saint Felix—were also applied to other matters. Thus Ambrose says “the birthday of the priesthood” in Book 8 on Luke, no. 73, and in Letter 4 to Felix the Count, no. 2; the latter passage has also been noted by us elsewhere.]

6. Grief, then, should not be endured as something oppressive according to nature, lest we seem either to claim for ourselves some exceptional privilege over nature or to reject what is common to all. For death is equal for everyone, undistinguished among the poor and making no exception for the rich. And therefore, although through the sin of one it passed into all (Rom. 5:18), just as we do not reject the author of our race, so we should not reject death; and just as death came through one, so resurrection should come through one. Let us not reject affliction if we are to arrive at grace. For Christ came, as we read, to save what had perished (Luke 19:10), and so that he might be Lord not only of the living but also of the dead (Rom. 14:9). I fell in Adam, was expelled from paradise in Adam, and died in Adam; how could he call me back unless he found me in Adam, so that, just as in him I was subject to sin and indebted to death, so in Christ I might be justified? (Augustine, On Original Sin, chapter 41.) If death is therefore a debt, its payment ought to be bearable. But this point must be reserved for the later sections.

7. Our present purpose is to maintain that death ought not to occasion more grievous mourning, since nature herself rejects such mourning. Finally, the Lycians are said to have laws requiring men to put on women’s clothing if they indulge in grief, because they judged mourning in a man to be soft and effeminate. [Note: This law, observed in Lycia, a province of Asia Minor, concerning the manner of mourning, is mentioned by Valerius Maximus, Book 2, chapter 6, and by Plutarch in his Consolation to Apollonius.] It is disgraceful for those who, for faith, religion, country, equity of judgment, and the pursuit of virtue, ought to offer their breast to death when it confronts them, to grieve more heavily over another’s death when, if circumstances demanded it, they themselves ought to desire it. For how can you refuse for yourself what you grieve to have happened to another with excessive impatience? Lay aside your grief, if you can; if you cannot, contain it.

8. Pain must either be wholly swallowed up or held in check. Why should reason not soothe your sadness more than time? [Note: Nannius holds that this sentence was modeled upon Terence’s words in the Heautontimorumenos: “Either I was certainly born by nature extraordinarily suited to misery, or that saying is false which I commonly hear, that time takes grief away from people.” He also compares Cicero, Letter 5 of Book 12 to Atticus: “There are many paths of consolation, but the straightest is this: let reason accomplish what time will accomplish.”] What the passage of time would erase, wisdom will mitigate more effectively. Indeed, I consider it irreligious toward the memory of those whom we grieve to have lost if we prefer to forget them rather than be soothed by consolation; to remember them with horror rather than with gratitude; to fear the recollection of those whose image ought to be a source of pleasure; to distrust rather than hope concerning the merits of the dead; and to judge those whom we loved to have been consigned to punishment rather than destined for immortality.

9. But you say: “We have lost those whom we loved.” Is this not something we share with the world itself and with the elements, since we cannot hold forever what has been entrusted to us for a time? The earth groans beneath the plow, is beaten by rains, shaken by storms, gripped by cold, and scorched by the sun, so that, made fertile, it may bring forth its annual fruits; and when it has clothed itself in varied blossoms, it strips and divests itself of its own adornment. How many things does it have that seize these away? Yet it does not complain that it has lost its fruit, which it produced for the very reason that it would lose it; nor does it deny what it remembers is destined to be taken from it.

### 10

The heavens themselves do not always shine with the globes of twinkling stars, by which they are marked out as though with certain crowns. They do not always grow white at the rising of light or gleam with the sun’s rays; rather, through continual alternation, that especially lovely face of the world is darkened by the dreadful dampness of the nights. What is more pleasing than light? What more delightful than the sun? [Col. 1318B] 1138 Yet these set every day;; nevertheless, we do not grieve that they have departed, because we expect them to return. You are taught by these things what patience you ought to display regarding your own losses. If the things above set and cause you no grief, why should you grieve when human beings have set?

### 11

Yet let grief be patient; let there be moderation in sadness, such as is required in prosperity. If it is not fitting to rejoice immoderately, is it fitting to mourn immoderately? For immoderation of grief, or fear of death, is no slight evil. How many has it driven to the noose, armed with the sword, so that in that very act they exposed their madness—unable to endure death, yet desiring death—and what they fled as an evil, they adopted as a remedy?

[Note: Not inappropriately, what Martial says agrees with this passage. Blaming Fannius’ voluntary death, he concludes his epigram with these words:

> Is this not madness, I ask: to die lest you die?]

Since such people could not bear and endure what was consistent with their nature, they fall into the opposite of their desire: they are separated forever from those whom they wished to follow. But such cases are rare, since nature itself recalls them, even if madness has driven them headlong.

### 12

Yet this is common among women: to raise public cries, as though they feared that their misery might go unrecognized; to seek the filth of clothing, as though the sensation of grief lay in it; to moisten their uncombed heads with dirt; finally, as is commonly done in many places, to tear apart their coverings and rip open their garments, exposing their secret modesty, as though they were themselves prostituting their modesty, because they had lost the rewards of modesty.

[Note: Cicero, in Book III of the *Tusculan Disputations*, calls this intemperance of women in mourning “varied and detestable kinds of lamentation,” describing and condemning *paedores* [term uncertain], women’s lacerations, beatings of the knees, breast, thighs, and head, and similar practices.. Yet scarcely anyone has attacked that disgrace more seriously or vehemently than Chrysostom, in Homily 61 on chapter 11 of John, Homily 4 on chapter 2 of Hebrews, and Homily 3 on chapter 1 of Philippians. At that time, however, they had not yet seen or heard anything like what is reported in the accounts of regions discovered not long ago: namely, that the barbarian women of the kingdom of Narsingh, in groups, are either buried alive with their husbands’ corpses or burned, according to the rank of their husbands.]

Thus wanton eyes are provoked, so that they desire and begin to love the exposed limbs; if they did not see them, they would not love them. And would that those soiled coverings of the body obscured not the appearance but the mind! Usually sensuality of mind lies hidden beneath a gloomy garment; the disfiguring horror of the clothing is used to cover the secret impulses of wanton spirits.

### 13

A woman mourns her husband sufficiently piously if she preserves modesty and does not abandon faithfulness. These are the proper services rendered to the dead: that they live in people’s minds and remain in their affections. She has not lost her husband who displays chastity; she has not been widowed from marriage who has not changed her husband’s name.

Nor have you lost an heir, if you assist a co-heir; but in place of a successor among corruptible things, you have exchanged him for a companion among the immortals..

[Note: Most manuscripts read: “you have changed your fellowship for that of immortals.”]

You have someone who may represent the heir to you. Pay the poor what is owed to the heir, so that he may survive not only his mother’s or father’s old age but also his own life. You leave more to your successor if his portion does not serve the luxury of the present but becomes the price of the future.

[Col. 1319B]

### 14

But we miss those whom we have lost. For there are two things that cause the greatest anguish: either longing for those whom we have lost, as I measure it by my own example;

[Note: Tully, Book I of the *Tusculan Disputations*: “Who is there who does not initially mourn the death of his loved ones because he thinks that they have been deprived of life’s advantages? Take away this opinion, and you will have taken away grief,” and so forth.]

or the belief that they have been deprived of life’s sweetness and robbed of the fruits of their labor. [1139] For the touch of love is tender; it arouses an unanticipated affection,, leaving greater opportunity for soothing grief than for excluding it. At the same time, it seems pious to long for what one has lost, and weakness grows under the appearance of virtue.

### 15

But why should you think that woman more patient who has sent her beloved away to foreign lands and has learned that he has crossed the sea for military service, the duties of an office undertaken, or the practice of commerce, than you, who have been abandoned not by chance or personal choice, nor for the sake of money, but by the law of nature?

Yet the hope of recovering him is closed to you, as though anyone had any certainty of returning. And uncertainty usually causes greater distress when the fear of danger remains intact; it is more grievous to fear that something has happened than to endure what you already know has happened.

[Note: Nearly all manuscripts read: “than to grieve that what has already happened…”]

One thing piles up the full weight of fear; the other awaits an end to grief.

### 16

Do masters have the right to transfer slaves wherever they have decided, but God does not?

[Note: All printed editions read *an dominis jus est* (“is there a right for masters”); many manuscripts, however, read *quae non creaverint* (“which they have not created”).]

You are not granted the opportunity to await one who returns; you are nevertheless granted the opportunity to follow the one who has gone before.. Certainly, the brief use of life seems to have taken little from the one who went before, nor does it delay you long who have remained.

### 17

But if you cannot moderate your longing, does it not nevertheless seem unworthy, out of devotion to your longing, to wish to overturn the order of things? Lovers certainly have more ardent longings, yet these are restrained by consideration of necessity; and although they grieve at being abandoned, they do not usually mourn. Those who have been left behind are ashamed to love with greater impatience.

[Note: Many manuscripts read: “even though they grieve at departing.”]

Thus patience in longing is all the more commendable.

### 18

But what shall I say about those who think that the dead are deprived of life’s sweetness? There can be no pleasure amid the bitterness and pains of this life, generated either by the body’s own weakness or by the misfortunes that befall us from outside. Always anxious and hanging even upon the hopes of happier things, we drift in a kind of uncertainty, hoping for doubtful things as though they were certain, misfortunes as though they were prosperity, and perishable things as though they were solid; possessing no power in our own judgment and no firmness in our desires.

But if something happens contrary to our will, we think ourselves ruined; we are broken more by the pain of adversity than we enjoy the fruits of prosperity. From what good, then, are those deprived who are more often snatched away from misfortune?

[Col. 1320A]

### 19

Health, I suppose, helps more when it is good than illness harms; wealth delights more than poverty afflicts; the loving affection of children is greater than the grief of losing them; youth is more pleasant than old age is sad. Yet people are often wearied of their own wishes and regret what they desired, so that they grieve over obtaining what they had feared they might not obtain.

As for exile and the bitterness of other punishments, what homeland can compensate for them? What pleasures? Even when such things are present, they are weakened either by the inability to enjoy them or by fear of losing them.

[Col. 1320B]

### 20

Let it nevertheless be granted that the course of human life [1140] remains untroubled, free from pain, and continuous in its pleasures.. What advantage, however, can the soul gain when enclosed within the framework of such a body and confined within the narrow spaces of its limbs?

If our flesh flees from prison and detests everything that denies it the ability to roam—though it seems to extend beyond itself through the limited senses of hearing and sight—how much more eagerly does our soul desire to escape this bodily prison-house?

[Note: Nannius says that an *ergastulum* is a place where chained slaves are kept “for the works” (*πρὸς τὰ ἔργα*), that is, for labor.]

Free in its airy movement, the soul goes—we do not know where—or comes from where we do not know (John 3:8).).

### 21

Yet we know that it survives the body and, once freed from the barriers of its own senses, sees with an unimpeded gaze what, while situated in the body, it did not see.

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads, “which example.” Below, where that same edition, together with the old edition and some manuscripts, reads “as though the body were buried in quiet,” the Amerbach edition and some manuscripts have “with the body at rest”; the majority of manuscripts alone read “as though the body were buried and raised to higher things.”]

We can estimate this from the example of sleepers, whose minds, as though their bodies were buried in repose, rise toward higher things and report to the body visions of absent things, or even of heavenly things.

Therefore, if death frees us from the miseries of the age through the death of the flesh, it is certainly not an evil: it restores freedom and excludes pain.

### 22

This, then, is the point from which we must begin our argument that death is not an evil, because it is a refuge from all miseries and evils, a trustworthy station of security, and a harbor of rest. For what adversity do we not experience in this life? What storms and tempests do we not endure? By what misfortunes are we not shaken? Whose merits are spared?

### 23

The holy patriarch Israel, exiled from his homeland, brother, and parents, changed his home through exile (Genesis 28:5);); he mourned the rape of his daughter (Genesis 34:2), the death of his sons-in-law (Genesis 49:5), endured famine, and, when dying, was deprived of burial. For he begged that his bones be transferred, so that even in death he might not rest.

### 24

The holy Joseph experienced the hatred of his brothers, the plots of the envious, the service of slaves, the commands of merchants (Genesis 37:4 and following),

[Note: A considerable number of manuscripts read: “the insolence of the queen, the ignorance of the king.”]

the insolence of his mistress, the ignorance of her husband, and even the misery of prison (Genesis 39:12 and following).

### 25

The holy David lost two sons: one incestuous (2 Samuel 13:29), the other a parricide (2 Samuel 18:14). It was a disgrace to have had them, and a grief to have lost them. He also lost a third, a little boy whom he loved. He mourned him while he was alive but did not long for him once he was dead.

For we read that when the child was ill, David pleaded with the Lord on his behalf, fasted, lay in sackcloth, and, while the elders stood by to raise him from the ground, thought he should neither rise nor eat dinner. But when he learned that the child had died, he rose from the ground, immediately washed, anointed himself, changed his clothes, worshiped the Lord, and took food (ibid., 20).

When his servants found this astonishing, he answered them that he had rightly fasted and wept while the child was alive, because he rightly believed that the Lord could have mercy, and that one should not doubt that the Lord could preserve the life of the living, since he could give life to the dead. But once death had occurred, why should he fast, when he could no longer bring back the dead or restore the lifeless? “I shall go to him,” he said; “but he shall not return to me” (ibid., 23).

[1141]

### 26

O greatest consolation for one who longs! O true judgment of the wise!

[Note: A few manuscripts read: “an indication of the wise.”]

O marvelous wisdom of one who serves! Let no one endure with indignation that something adverse has happened to him, or complain that he has been afflicted contrary to his merit.

For who are you, that you should pronounce beforehand concerning your own merit? Why do you wish to anticipate the Judge? Why do you take away the sentence from the one who will judge? This was not permitted even to the saints, nor was it ever claimed by the saints with impunity.

David confesses in his hymn that he was scourged for this reason:

> Behold, these are sinners, and they abound in this age; they have obtained riches. Therefore in vain have I justified my heart and washed my hands among the innocent; and I was scourged all day long,

[Note: All printed editions and some manuscripts read: “and my avenger.” Some other manuscripts, joined by the Roman Psalter of Quinius, read: “and my judge.” Remigius, with the Vulgate, has: “and my chastisement,” which does not differ from the Hebrew, where “and my rebuke” is read. Finally, the remaining manuscripts, with the common Roman Psalter, read: “and my informer” (*καὶ ὁ ἔλεγχός μου*). The Roman edition’s reading *in matutinis* (“in the mornings”), in place of *in matutinum* (“until morning”), departs from the much greater number of manuscripts, the ancient editions, and Augustine’s reading.]

> and my informer until morning (Psalm 72:12 and following).

### 27

Peter too, although full of faithful devotion, because he was not yet conscious of our weakness, presumptuously said to the Lord, “I will lay down my life for you” (John 13:37); before the cock crowed a third time, he underwent the trial of his presumption (John 18:27).

Although that trial became an instruction leading to salvation, so that we may learn not to despise the weakness of the flesh lest, by despising it, we be tempted, nevertheless, if Peter was tempted, who could presume or assert that he cannot be tempted?

Without doubt Peter was tempted for our sake, so that the danger of temptation might not be found in one who was stronger. In him we were to learn how, when resisting in persecutions and tempted by the desire for life, we might nevertheless overcome the sting of temptation by the tears of patience.

### 28

Yet the same David—lest perhaps anyone devoted to Scripture be troubled by the difference in his actions—the same David, I say, mourned his dead parricidal son, although he had not mourned his innocent son.

Finally, when he was weeping and mourning, he said:

> My son Absalom, my son Absalom! Who will grant me death in your place? (2 Samuel 18:33)

Therefore not Absalom alone is mourned: the parricide is mourned, and Ammon is mourned (2 Samuel 13:36). The incestuous son is not only mourned but also avenged: one because he despised the kingdom, the other because of his brother’s exile. The criminal is mourned; the beloved is not.

What is the reason? What is the explanation? There is therefore no ordinary deliberation among the prudent, no ordinary confirmation among the wise. Great is the constancy of prudence amid such diversity of actions; faith is one.

He mourned those who had died, but did not think the dead infant should be mourned: he believed that the former had perished for him, but hoped that the latter would rise again.

### 29

But let us speak of the resurrection later and now return to the subject before us. We have already stated that holy men also endured many serious hardships in this world, without the support of merits, amid the misery of labors.

Therefore David, returning to himself, says later:

> Remember, Lord, that we are dust; man is like grass, his days are as a flower of the field (Psalm 102:15);

and elsewhere:

> Man has been made like vanity; his days pass away like a shadow (Psalm 143:4).

For what is more wretched than we are, [1142],

[Note: Augustine, in Book IV against Julian, chapter 12, quotes almost the same passage from Book III of Cicero’s *On the Republic*; Ambrose seems also to have imitated this passage.]

who, as though stripped and naked, are cast into this life, with a fragile body, an unstable heart, a feeble spirit, anxious when faced with cares, sluggish for labors, and inclined toward pleasures?

### 30

Not to be born, therefore, is by far the best course, according to the judgment of the holy Solomon. Even those who seemed to themselves outstanding in philosophy followed this judgment. For he was earlier than they,

[Note: This is the reading of the editions and manuscripts, except for certain Paris editions, which have “later than us,” and some manuscripts, which read “later than our people.” Remigius has “was not later.” Nevertheless, the common reading may have this meaning: Solomon, who is said to be older than the pagan wise men, may nevertheless be later than many of our own people, such as Job, Moses, and others.

As for the author to whom the pagans attribute the statement mentioned here, Aristotle, according to Plutarch, assigns it to Silenus in the *Eudemus*, or *On the Soul*. Cicero likewise reports it in Book I of the *Tusculan Disputations* and in his *Consolation*. See also Theognis’ epigram on this subject, Sophocles’ *Oedipus at Colonus*, Lactantius Book III, chapter 18, and Ausonius’ *Eclogue on Human Life*.]

yet, later than our people, he spoke in Ecclesiastes:

> And I praised all the dead who are already dead, more than the living who are still alive. And better than both is he who has not yet been born and has not seen the evil work that is done under the sun. And I saw all labor and every excellence of this work, because one person is envied by another. This too is vanity and presumption of spirit (Ecclesiastes 4:2 and following).

### 31

And who said this except the one who asked for and obtained wisdom (Wisdom 7:7), so that he might know the structure of the world, the power of the elements, the courses of the year, and the arrangements of the stars; so that he would not be ignorant of the natures of animals, might gather the rage of beasts, and discern the force of winds and the thoughts of human beings?

Since the heavenly things did not escape him, how could mortal things escape him? He investigated the thought of the woman who claimed for herself a child that belonged to another (1 Kings 3:27); he learned the natures of animals that he had not received through divine grace inspiring him (Wisdom 7:20). Could he have erred or lied about the condition of his own nature, which he had experienced within himself?

### 32

But he was not the only one who thought this, even if he alone expressed it. He had read that the holy Job said:

> Let that day perish on which I was born (Job 3:3);

and he understood that birth is the beginning of all evils. Therefore he wished the day on which he was born to perish, so that the origin of misfortunes might be removed; and he wished the day of his generation to perish, so that he might receive the day of resurrection.

He had also heard Solomon’s father say::

> Make known to me, Lord, my end and the number of my days, so that I may know what I lack (Psalm 38:5).

For David knew that what is perfect cannot be comprehended here, and therefore he hurried toward the things that are to come. Now we know in part and understand in part; but then what is perfect will be comprehended, when, with our face unveiled, not a shadow but the truth begins to shine upon us for the contemplation of the divine majesty and eternity (1 Corinthians 13:12).

### 33

Yet no one would hasten toward the end unless he were fleeing the troublesomeness of this life. Therefore David also explained why he hastens toward the end, saying:

> Behold, you have made my days old, and my condition is as nothing before you;

[Note: The Roman edition, together with a few manuscripts, reads: “and my substance.” The old edition and many more manuscripts read: “and my condition.” The Greek is *καὶ ὑπόστασίς μου*, that is, nature, constitution, and so forth.]

> nevertheless, every human being who lives is complete vanity (Psalm 38:6).

Why, then, do we delay [1143] fleeing vanity?? Or what delights us in being vainly troubled in this world, storing up a treasure of money and not knowing for which heir we are gathering it?

Let us ask that the blows be removed from us, that we be snatched from the foolish world, that we be freed from a long exile, and return to that homeland and natural home. For in this land we are strangers and sojourners (Ephesians 2:19).

[Note: Some manuscripts read *remigandum* (“we must row back”); others, and the editions, more correctly read *remigrandum* (“we must migrate back”).]

We must return there from which we descended. We must seek and implore this not superficially but earnestly, so that we may be freed from the deceits and iniquity of those who speak much.

Even the one who knew the remedy groans over his prolonged sojourn and laments that he dwells with sinners and the wicked (Psalm 119:5). What shall I do, who both possess sin and do not know the remedy?

### 34

Jeremiah too laments that he was born, saying in these words:

> Alas for me, mother! Why did you give birth to me, a man who brings a cause of judgment upon the whole earth? I have benefited no one,

[Note: Many manuscripts read: “nor has anything benefited me.” Others, and all the editions, more closely follow the prophet’s words: “… no one has benefited me.” Philo Judaeus, in *On the Confusion of Tongues*, quotes the whole passage somewhat differently:

> “O mother, what a man you have borne me, a man of strife and a man of hatred to the whole earth; I have not benefited, nor have they benefited me” (*Ὦ μῆτερ, ἡλίκον με ἔτεκες ἄνθρωπον μάχης, καὶ ἄνθρωπον ἀηδίας πάσης τῆς γῆς· οὐκ ὠφέλησα, οὐδὲ ὠφέλησάν με*).]

> nor has anyone benefited me; my strength has failed (Jeremiah 15:10).

If holy men therefore flee life, whose life, although useful to us, is nevertheless judged useless to them, what ought we to do? We who can benefit neither others nor ourselves feel that this life is like borrowed money, becoming heavier each day through the accumulating interest of sins.

### 35

“I die daily,” says the Apostle (1 Corinthians 15:31). This is certainly better than those who said that the contemplation of death is philosophy.

[Note: Cicero, in the *Tusculan Disputations*, attributes this statement to Plato; and indeed you find in Plato’s *Phaedo* the passages quoted by the Orator in the *Tusculan Disputations*. Nevertheless, we learn from Jerome’s *Apology against Rufinus*, Book III, that Plato was not the first author of this saying but that it came from Pythagoras.]

They proclaimed the study of death; he actually exercised death itself.. And they did so for their own sake, whereas Paul, already perfect, was dying not for his own weakness but for ours.

What is the contemplation of death except a kind of separation of body and soul, since death itself is defined as nothing other than

[Note: Some manuscripts read “the succession of body and soul,” and some “the cutting-off of body and soul,” which is somewhat better; but the reading preserved here is found in the other manuscripts and all the editions. The definition of death given by the holy bishop is presented in Plato’s *Gorgias* as follows:

> “Death happens to be, as it seems to me, nothing other than the dissolution of two things: soul and body” (*Ὁ θάνατος τυγχάνει ὢν, ὡς ἐμοὶ δοκεῖ, οὐδὲν ἄλλο ἢ δυοῖν πραγμάτοιν διάλυσις, τῆς ψυχῆς καὶ τοῦ σώματος*).

Similar definitions are found in several passages of the *Phaedo*.]

the separation of body and soul? But this is according to common opinion.

### 36

According to the Scriptures, however,

[Note: Ambrose had defined three kinds of death in Book 9 of *On the Good of Death*, and also in Book VII of his commentary on Luke. It will not be unpleasant for the reader to compare this passage with those places.]

we understand death to be threefold.

One is when we die to sin and live for God (Romans 6:10). Blessed, therefore, is the death that flees guilt, is devoted to the Lord, separates us from mortality, and consecrates us to immortality.

Another death is the departure from this life, by which the patriarch Abraham died, the patriarch David died, and they were buried with their fathers, when the soul is released from the bond of the body.

The third death is the one of which it is said: “Let the dead bury their own dead” (Matthew 8:22). By this death not only the flesh but also the soul dies: “The soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezekiel 18:4). It dies to the Lord, not through the weakness of nature but through guilt.

But this death is not the completion of this life,

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “this is not the superficial passing of this life.”]

but the fall of error.

### 37

One death, therefore, is spiritual; another is natural; the third is penal. But natural death is not itself penal death, for the Lord gave death not as a punishment but as a remedy.

Thus, for Adam when he sinned, one thing was prescribed as punishment and another [1144] as remedy.. As punishment:

> Because you have listened to the voice of your wife and eaten from the tree concerning which I commanded you, saying that you alone should not eat from it, cursed is the earth in your labors. In sorrow you shall eat its fruit all the days of your life. It shall produce thorns and thistles for you, and you shall eat the plants of the field. By the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread, until you return to the earth from which you were taken (Genesis 3:17 and following).

### 38

You have a respite from punishments: amid the thorns of this world, its anxieties, and the pleasures of riches—which exclude the Word and enclose punishment—death was given as a remedy, as though it were the end of evils.

For he did not say: “Because you have listened to the woman’s voice, you shall return to the earth.” That would have been a penal sentence, just as this is one: “The earth shall produce thorns and thistles for you.” Rather, he said: “You shall eat your bread in sweat until you return to the earth.”

Do you see that death is rather the boundary of our punishments, by which the course of this life is cut short?

### 39

Therefore death is not only not an evil; it is also a good. Accordingly, it is sought as a good, as it is written:

> People will seek death and will not find it (Revelation 9:6).

Those will seek it who will say to the mountains, “Fall upon us,” and to the hills, “Cover us” (Luke 23:30). The soul that sins will also seek it. The rich man placed in hell seeks it, wishing that his tongue might be refreshed by Lazarus’ finger (Luke 16:24).

### 40

We see, therefore, that this death is gain and that life is punishment. Hence Paul also says:

> For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain (Philippians 1:21).

What is Christ, except death of the body and life of the spirit? Therefore let us die with him, so that we may live with him.

Let there be in us a daily practice and disposition of dying, so that through that separation from bodily desires which we have mentioned, our soul may learn to withdraw itself from them. Placed, as it were, on high, where earthly desires cannot approach it or glue themselves to it, let it take on the image of death, lest it incur the punishment of death.

For the law of the flesh resists the law of the mind and subjects it to the law of error,

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “the law of God.”]

as the Apostle revealed when he said:

> I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin (Romans 7:23).

We are all assaulted; we all feel it; but we are not all freed. And therefore: wretched man that I am, unless I seek a remedy!

### 41

But what remedy? Who will free me from the body of this death?

> The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord (ibid., 24–25).

We have a physician; let us follow the remedy. Our remedy is the grace of Christ, and the body of death is our body.

Therefore let us live as strangers to the body, lest we become strangers to Christ; and although we are in the body, let us not follow the things that belong to the body,

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “nor desire the rights of nature.”]

nor [1145] abandon the rights of nature, but prefer the gifts of grace::

> For to be dissolved and to be with Christ is much better; but to remain in the flesh is more necessary for your sake (Philippians 1:23–24).

### 42

But it is not necessary for everyone, Lord Jesus; not for me, who am useful to no one. For me, to die is gain, lest I sin further. To die is gain for me, who am driven by the very book with which I console others, as by a more forceful admonition, toward longing for my lost brother, because it does not allow me to forget him.

Now I love him more and long for him more intensely. I long for him when I speak; I long for him when I read again; and therefore I think this should rather be written, lest I ever be torn away from his memory.

I do not do this contrary to the Scriptures, but I think in harmony with the Scriptures, so that I may grieve more patiently and long more impatiently.

[Col. 1326C]

### 43

You have granted me, brother, that I should not fear death. Would that my soul might die in your soul! For Balaam, endowed with the Spirit for prophecy, desires this as the greatest good:

> May my soul die in the souls of the righteous, and may my seed become like the seed of these men (Numbers 23:10).

[Note: The old edition and many manuscripts read: “like the seed of the righteous.” The Roman edition and other manuscripts, as in the text, are more correct. For where the Hebrew and Vulgate have “and may my end be like theirs,” the Septuagint translators render it: “and may my seed become like the seed of these men” (*καὶ γένοιτο τὸ σπέρμα μου ὡς σπέρμα τούτων*).]

And truly he desires this according to the prophecy. For the one who had seen Christ’s rising also saw his triumph; he saw death and, in him, the perpetual resurrection of human beings. Therefore he does not fear death, since he will rise again.

Let my soul, then, not die in sin,

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “and let it not receive the iniquity of sin within itself.”]

nor let it receive sin within itself; but let it die in the soul of the righteous, so that it may receive his righteousness. Indeed, whoever dies in Christ becomes a participant in his grace through the washing.

### 44

Death, therefore, is not fearful, nor bitter to the needy,

[Note: All editions and many manuscripts read: “nor pleasing to the rich,” which, although true in itself, is entirely foreign to this passage. The reading of Benignus, Remigius, and other codices, although not many, is therefore much better: “nor more burdensome to the rich.”]

nor more burdensome to the rich, nor unjust to the elderly, nor cowardly for the strong, nor everlasting for the faithful, nor unexpected for the wise.

[Note: Nannius includes among those who covered the shamefulness of their lives with an honorable death Cato’s son and the emperor Otho; concerning the latter he also cites verses of Ausonius and testimony from Suetonius. He could, however, have added quite a few others who, as Ambrose indicates, bought fame with blood shed easily and whom one encounters throughout the monuments of literature. Regarding what follows about peoples freed by the death of one person, see *Exposition on Luke*, Book VI, section 108, and our note on that passage.]

How many have consecrated life by the mere title of death! How many were ashamed to live, but benefited by dying? By the death of one person, we have often received the liberation of great peoples; by the death of an emperor, enemy armies have been put to flight, armies whom he could not have defeated while alive.

### 45

By the death of martyrs religion has been defended, faith increased, and the Church strengthened. The dead have conquered; the persecutors have been conquered. Therefore, although we do not know the lives of these people, we celebrate their deaths.

Hence David also exulted prophetically in the ecstasy of his mind:

> Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints (Psalm 115:15).

He preferred death to life. The death of martyrs itself is the reward of life. By death, too, the hatred of enemies is dissolved.

### 46

Why say more? By the death of one, the world was redeemed. Christ could have avoided death if he had wished; but he did not regard death as something cowardly that ought to be avoided, nor could he have saved us [1146] better than by dying..

Therefore his death is the life of all.

[Note: Here he intended to indicate both the practice of marking the forehead and breast with the cross and the unambiguous distinction between sacrifice and prayers. We have already observed both practices more than once in Ambrose.]

By his death we are marked; in our prayers we proclaim his death; in offering it we preach his death. His death is victory; his death is a sacrament; his death is the world’s annual solemnity.

What more should we say about his death, when we prove by the divine example that death alone sought immortality and that death itself redeemed itself?

Death, therefore, is not to be mourned when it is the cause of universal salvation; death is not to be fled when the Son of God did not disdain it and did not shrink from it. The order of nature must not be dissolved, for what is common to all cannot be excluded in individuals.

[Col. 1327C]

### 47

Death, indeed, was not in nature, but it was changed into nature. For God did not establish death from the beginning but gave it as a remedy.

Let us consider whether this may seem contradictory. If death is good, why is it written that God did not make death, but that death entered the world through the malice of human beings (Wisdom 1:13; 2:24)?

In truth, death was not necessary for God’s work, since, when they were placed in paradise, a continual succession of every good flowed upon them. But after condemnation through transgression, human life became miserable through prolonged labor and intolerable groaning. An end to evils had to be given, so that death might restore what life had lost.

[Note: He seems to allude to the story of Tithonus. When the gift of immortality had been granted him through the favor of Tethys, he became so weary of life that he preferred to be transformed into a vile little creature rather than remain subject any longer to human troubles and miseries.]

Immortality is more a burden than a benefit unless grace gives it support.

### 48

And if you examine the matter carefully, this death is not death according to nature but according to malice; nature remains, while malice dies. What existed rises again—and would that, just as it is now free from sinning, it were also free from its former guilt!!

But this itself shows that death is not natural, because we shall be the same people we were. Therefore we shall either pay the penalties for our sins or obtain the reward of our good deeds. For the same nature will rise again, now more honored through the wages of death.

Indeed, the dead who are in Christ will rise first; then, he says, we who are alive will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet Christ in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord (1 Thessalonians 4:15–16).

They come first; the living second. They come with Jesus; the living through Jesus. For them life is sweeter after rest; for the living, although their shortcut is welcome, the remedy remains unknown.

### 49

There is therefore nothing in death that we should fear, nothing that we ought to grieve, if either life is repaid to nature when it asks back what was received, or if it is devoted to the duty that demands it, in which there is either the practice of religion or the exercise of virtue.

For no one wished that he should remain forever in this condition.

[Note: In Sermon 20, section 12, on Psalm 108, he mentions that some people doubted John’s death, in such a way that he clearly shows himself to have been certain about it.]

It was thought that John had received a promise that he would not die, but it was not believed. We retain the words but transfer the meaning. In his own book he denies that he was promised he would not die, lest an empty hope should infect anyone through his example.

But if it is an insolent hope to wish this, how much more insolent is it to grieve beyond measure over what has not happened beyond measure?

[1147]

### 50

Pagans generally console themselves either through the commonality of misery, through the law of nature, or through the immortality of the soul.

[Note: Here he briefly gathers together whatever pagan authors have handed down concerning the reasons for bearing death with equanimity. On this subject one may consult Cicero, Book I of the *Tusculan Disputations*, and his *Consolation* on the death of his daughter; Plutarch’s *Consolation to Apollonius*; and others.]

Would that their doctrine were consistent, rather than transforming the wretched soul into the various mockeries and shapes of monsters!!
