What, then, ought we to do, whose reward is resurrection? Since most people cannot deny its grace, they reject the faith. Therefore let us establish it, as far as we can, not by one argument alone but by several methods.

### 51

Indeed, everything is believed either through experience, reason, example, or because, since it is fitting that things should be so, they are believed to be so; and each of these contributes support to faith.

Experience: because we are moved.

Reason: because it is right to judge that what moves us belongs to another power..

Example: because the field has produced crops, and therefore we expect that it will produce them again.

Fitness: because, even where we do not expect fruit, we nevertheless believe it fitting that we should by no means abandon the works of virtue.

### 52

Each point, then, is established by its corresponding evidence. Yet faith in the resurrection is gathered more clearly from three considerations, which encompass everything: reason, the example of the universe, and the testimony of an accomplished event—for very many have risen.

The argument is evident: since the whole practice of our life consists in the partnership of body and soul, while resurrection is either the reward of good action or the punishment of evil action, the body whose actions are being weighed must necessarily rise. For how will the soul be summoned to judgment without the body, when an account must be rendered for the conduct of both, in their companionship?

### 53

Resurrection has been assigned to all; but it is therefore difficult to believe because it is not our merit but God’s gift. The first evidence for resurrection, then, is the customary order of the world and the state of all things: the succession of generations, the alternation of successions, the settings and risings of the heavenly signs, and the daily succession of day and night, as though they were continually restored to life.

The proper balance of this generative earth could not otherwise be maintained unless divine providence restored by nightly dew as much of the moisture by which all earthly things are generated as the heat of the daytime sun had dried up. For why should I speak of fruits? Do they not seem to you to die when they fall, and to rise again when they grow green once more? What has been sown rises again; what has died rises again; and it is reshaped into the same genera and the same species. In these fruits the earth first restored its produce; in them our nature first imitated the appearance of resurrection.

[Col. 1329D] Some manuscripts read, “because it is God’s gift beyond our merit.”

### 54

Why do you doubt that body will rise from body? A grain is sown; a grain rises again. An apple falls; an apple rises again. But the grain is clothed with a flower and covered with a husk. “This mortal must put on immortality, and this corruptible must put on incorruption” (I Cor. 15:53). The flower of resurrection is immortality; the flower of resurrection is incorruption. For what is richer than perpetual rest? What is more abundant than enduring security? This is the manifold fruit, through whose increase the human race springs forth more fruitful after death.

### 55

But you marvel at how what has putrefied is made solid again, how what has been dispersed comes together, and how what has been consumed is restored; yet you do not marvel at how seeds, loosened by the vapor and pressure of the earth, grow green. For the seeds themselves too are dissolved and putrefy through their union with the soil; and when, darkened and killed beneath the soil, the generative sap has enlivened them, through a certain vital warmth they breathe out a kind of spirit of green vegetation.

Then, little by little, it raises the tender youth of the developing ear upon its stalk, and nature, like a diligent mother, encloses it within certain sheaths, lest harsh frost scorch it as it matures, and protects it from excessive heat of the sun. The grain itself, while still bursting forth as though from its first cradle, and later when mature, it customarily encloses within a rampart of awns, lest rain beat it down, wind scatter it, or the bites of small birds destroy it.

[Col. 1329D] The old edition reads *occata soli* (“struck by the soil”); the Roman edition, *occata et mortua soli* (“struck and killed by the soil”); all the manuscripts, by contrast, read *occaecata*, and so forth. This is not at all inappropriate: by the harrowing of the grain it comes about that the grain, as though darkened and oppressed by darkness, dies beneath the clod. Below, instead of *herbae viridantis* (“of the green herb”), which is found in all the printed editions and some manuscripts, many more manuscripts read *herbae viridantes* (“of green herbs”), and some *virides* (“green”). For a comparison of this passage with what is stated in Book III of the *Hexaemeron*, chapter 8, no. 34, concerning the germination of herbs, students will not be displeased.

### 56

[Col. 1330A] Why, then, do you marvel if the earth restores human beings whom it has received, when it gives life to, raises up, clothes, fortifies, and protects every body of seed that it has received?

Cease, then, to doubt that the earth’s trust will return what has been entrusted to it from the human race: it returns the seeds committed to it multiplied by a kind of usurious increase. For why should I speak of the kinds of trees, which “rise from the seed once planted,” revive their loosened fruits through renewed fertility, and restore them to their ancient form and likeness, while some trees, their bodies renewed, pass through many generations, so that by enduring they conquer the ages?

We see a grape-seed putrefy and the vine rise again; a shoot is grafted, and the tree is reborn. Is divine providence concerned with restoring trees but unconcerned with human beings? And will the one who did not allow the things he gave for human use to perish permit the human being to perish whom he made in his own image?

[Col. 1329D] The allusion is to Virgil, *Georgics* II:

> “Others rise from seed once planted,” and so forth.

### 57

But it seems incredible to you that the dead should come to life again. “Foolish man, what you sow does not come to life unless it first dies” (ibid., 36). Sow any dried-up fruit: it is revived.

“But it has sap.” Our body too has its blood; it has its moisture. This is the sap of our body. Hence I judge that the objection some make—that a dried-up shoot cannot come back to life—and that they attempt to transfer as a prejudice against the flesh, is likewise to be dismissed. For flesh is not dry: all flesh comes from mud, mud is in moisture, and moisture comes from the earth.

Indeed, many plants are born even in soil that is continually dry and sandy, because the earth itself supplies them with moisture.

[Col. 1330D] Some manuscripts read, “I think it should be taken as an example.”

[Col. 1330D] Thus the old edition and many manuscripts. The Roman edition, however, and some manuscripts read *humo arido, arenosoque* (“from dry, sandy soil”), which it also insists should be the reading. Nannius supports this, citing Priscian. Latinius, on the contrary, thought that *humi arido arenosoque* (“in dry, sandy soil”) should be restored; no manuscript supports this reading, although some have *humi arida, arenosaque* (“in dry, sandy soil”).

[Col. 1330C] Some manuscripts read, “Does the earth therefore deny this to human beings?” Others have *denegaret* (“would deny”).

Does the earth, which habitually regenerates everything, then degenerate in the case of human beings? Hence it is clear that one should not doubt what is more in accordance with nature than contrary to it: for it is natural that all things which are born should rise again, while it is contrary to nature that they should perish.

### 58

What follows is what usually disturbs the Gentiles: how can it be that the earth should restore those whom the sea has swallowed, wild beasts have torn apart, and animals have devoured? The issue must therefore be approached in such a way that the question concerns not faith in the resurrection but a particular circumstance.

Suppose, then, that the bodies of those who have been torn apart do not rise; the rest rise. Nor is resurrection destroyed if an exception is made for a particular condition. Yet I wonder why they think even these cases should be doubted, as though everything that comes from the earth did not return to the earth and dissolve into the earth (Eccles. 3:20).

The sea itself, too, usually casts upon neighboring shores whatever human bodies it has submerged. If this were not so, I imagine it would be difficult for God to join what has been scattered and unite what has been dispersed. The world obeys him, the mute elements comply, nature serves him. Is it really a greater miracle to give life to mud than to join it together?

[Col. 1330D] The Remigius manuscript reads, “which birds have torn apart.” A little later, this same manuscript, together with several others, reads, “which is thus finally found.”

[Col. 1330D] Quite a few manuscripts read, “do not rise”; nevertheless, the resurrection is not destroyed, with a sensible qualification.

[Col. 1331C] Some manuscripts read, “It would not be difficult for God.”

### 59

In the region of Arabia there is a bird called the phoenix. When it has died, it comes back to life, restored through the renewed moisture of its flesh. Do we alone not believe that human beings are raised?

Yet through frequent report and the authority of written accounts we know that this bird is said to have been allotted a lifespan of five hundred years. When, by a certain prophetic discernment of its nature, it recognizes that the end of its life is approaching, it prepares for itself a chamber from frankincense, myrrh, and other perfumes. When the work and the appointed time have been completed, it enters the chamber and dies. From its moisture a worm is said to arise; gradually the worm gathers itself into the form of the same bird, and its shape is formed. Then, supported by the oars of its wings, it begins the functions of renewed life as an act of filial devotion.

For it carries that chamber—either the tomb of its body or the cradle of the one rising again, in which, as it declines, it dies, and, dying, rises again—from Ethiopia to Lycaonia. Thus, when this bird rises again, the inhabitants of those regions understand that the period of five hundred years has been completed.

For that bird, the five-hundredth year is the year of resurrection; for us, it is the thousandth: for the bird, within this age; for us, at the consummation of the world. Many also believe that the bird itself kindles its funeral pyre and then comes back to life from its own ashes and embers.

[Col. 1331C] The Roman edition reads, “and by the authority of writers”; the other editions and all the manuscripts read, “and by the authority of the Scriptures.” Yet one should not suppose that Ambrose attributes to the sacred Scriptures what he had read concerning the phoenix among pagan or, at any rate, ecclesiastical authors, as Dallaeus mockingly argues in Book II, chapter 3, of *On the Use of the Fathers*. For when, in Book V of the *Hexaemeron*, chapter 23, no. 79, he explains that the phoenix is a figure of resurrection, he says nothing at all about Scripture; although, among the Christians to whom he was writing, that would have carried the greatest weight. Here, since he is arguing against pagans, why would he mention the divine Scriptures, which would have had no authority among them? He therefore uses the expression “the voice of the Scriptures” to designate the writings of authors, whether secular or ecclesiastical, and joins these with “frequent report,” that is, oral testimony.

Nor should it seem surprising that the ancient Fathers used the example of the phoenix to prove the resurrection of bodies: Tertullian, *On the Resurrection*, chapter 13; Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechetical Lecture* 18; Clement of Rome, *First Letter to the Corinthians*; Basil, Homily 8 on the *Hexaemeron*; Epiphanius, *Ancoratus*, no. 85, and *Physiologus*, chapter 11; and many others. For, leaving the poets aside, historians wrote about the same bird in great numbers—for example, Herodotus in *Euterpe*, Cornelius Tacitus, *Annals* VI, Pliny, *Natural History* II, chapter 2, and others. Some of them even testified that they had seen it at a specified time and place. Those devout men therefore wisely chose to use a common belief in order to explain and affirm the resurrection, a matter especially difficult to grasp.

Today, however, the phoenix is relegated to the realm of fables, as can be seen in more recent writers on ornithology. But it is entirely foreign to the reverence owed to the holy Fathers to declare that those who believe in the existence of the phoenix are thinking contrary to the authority of Scripture.

[Col. 1332D] Ambrose seems here to speak in the same sense as Augustine wrote in Book XX, chapter 7, of *The City of God*; or else he has used “a thousand years” for all the years of this age, so that a complete number might signify the fullness of time itself. The latter interpretation is supported by what follows below, in no. 63: “The ages of the world are one year,” and so forth. If anyone nevertheless prefers to understand these words according to the opinion of the Chiliasts, let him consult what we noted in the previous volume, in the exposition of Psalm I, no. 54.

### 60

But perhaps the more discriminating character of nature may also bring discrimination to faith. Let our mind return to the origin and beginning of the generation of human beings. You are men and women; you know what is human. And if some of you do not know, do you suppose that what is born comes from nothing?

From how small a beginning we rise to such greatness! Even if we do not state it explicitly, you nevertheless understand what we mean—or rather, what we do not wish to say. From where come this head and this remarkable face, whose craftsman we do not see, though we see the work, formed for various functions and uses? From where comes the more upright form, the elevated posture, the power of action, the vigor of sensation, the ability to walk?

The organs of nature are certainly unknown to us, but its operations are known. You too were once seed, and your body is the seed of the one who will rise again. Hear Paul and learn that you are seed:

> “It is sown in corruption; it will rise in incorruption. It is sown in dishonor; it will rise in glory. It is sown in weakness; it will rise in power. It is sown an animal body; it will rise a spiritual body” (I Cor. 15:42 and following).

You too, then, are sown like the other things. Why do you marvel if you rise like the other things? But you believe those things because you see them; you do not believe these because you do not see them: “Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed” (John 20:29).

[Col. 1332D] Some manuscripts read, “but the mysteries are known.”

[Col. 1332D] The Roman edition and some manuscripts read, “since from a small thing we rise to such greatness.”

### 61

Yet before the appointed time arrives, even those things are not believed; for not every season is suitable for reviving seeds. Wheat is sown at one time and born at another. At one time the vine is grafted; at another its budding branches grow mature, its foliage luxuriates, and its grape is formed. At one time the olive is planted; at another, like a womb heavy and laden with offspring of berries, it bends beneath the abundance of its fruit.

Before the proper time arrives for each thing, its offspring is more restricted; nor does that which generates, though it generates, have control over the time of generation. At one time you may see the common mother of all things shapeless in her desolation; at another, naked of offspring; at another, green with flowers; at another, herself dry.

Certainly she would wish to clothe herself in every season and never put off the golden garment of the crops or the green garments of the meadows. Yet she is herself in need, and, having poured her produce into others, is left without resources from her own abundance.

[Col. 1332D] Some manuscripts read, “at one time shapeless in her desolation, at another fertile; at one time green with flowers, at another lacking them.”

[Col. 1332D] Some manuscripts read, “she bends beneath the burden.”

### 62

Therefore, if you do not believe in our resurrection by faith, and do not believe it by example, you will believe it by experience. For other fruits—the vine, the olive, and various apples—the end of the year is suitable for ripening; for us also, the consummation of the world, like the end of the year, has appointed the proper season for rising again.

And rightly the resurrection of the dead occurs at the consummation of the world, lest after resurrection we should have to fall back into this evil age. For this reason Christ suffered: to free us from this evil age, lest the trials of this age should again overthrow us, and rebirth should be harmful if we were reborn for sin.

### 63

We therefore know both the reason and the time of resurrection: the reason, because nature corresponds to itself equally in all its offspring and does not degenerate only in the succession of human beings; the time, because everything is generated at the end of the year.

The ages of the world are one year. And why is it surprising that there is one year, when there is one day? For on one day the Lord hired workers for the vineyard, saying: “Why do you stand here idle all day?” (Matt. 20:6).

### 64

The causes of origins are seeds. The Teacher of the Gentiles declared that the human body is seed (I Cor. 15:42). There is therefore a substance for rising again, since there is a succession of sowing.

But if there were no substance or cause, someone might think it difficult for God to regenerate human beings from whatever source or in whatever manner he wished—he who commanded the world to exist from no material and no substance, and it came into being.

Look at the heavens; behold the earth. From where come the fires of the stars? From where the sphere and rays of the sun? From where the globe of the moon? From where the peaks of the mountains, the hardness of rocks, the wooded forests? From where the widespread air, or the waters poured within and spread over everything?

But if God made all these things from nothing—for “he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. 148:5)—why should we marvel that what has existed can be born again, when we see that what did not exist has been born?

### 65

What is astonishing is that, although they do not believe in resurrection, the Gentiles nevertheless, with a certain kindly benevolence, take thought lest the human race perish; and therefore they say that souls pass over and migrate into bodies, lest the world perish. But let them say for themselves which is more difficult: for souls to pass over or to return; to reclaim what is their own or to seek what is new.

[Col. 1333D] It is one thing, and a very different thing, to believe in the immortality of souls and to believe in the resurrection of bodies. Many philosophers maintained the first belief. Cicero, near the beginning of Book I of the *Tusculan Disputations*, Lactantius in Book VII of *The Blessed Life*, no. 8, Augustine in Letter 137 to Volusianus, no. 11, and many others report that Pherecydes was the first teacher of it, from whom Pythagoras, Plato, and others derived this opinion.

As for the second truth, since only those who did not fail to know the true God possessed knowledge of it, the pagan philosophers differed most seriously among themselves concerning the state of the soul once freed from bodily bonds. Their most celebrated opinion was that souls migrated from one body into another. Herodotus, in *Euterpe*, says that Pythagoras learned this doctrine from the Egyptians. Ambrose, in this book, and Augustine, in Book X, chapter 30, of *The City of God*, testify that Plato likewise gave his name to this same madness. Many, however, assigned the soul a nobler condition after the dissolution of the body. On this subject consult Cicero’s *Dream of Scipio* and elsewhere; Plutarch, Book V, chapter 7, of *On the Opinions of the Philosophers*; indeed Plato himself, in the *Phaedo* and elsewhere.

### 66

Let those who have not learned doubt; but for us, who have read the Law, the prophets, the apostles, and the Gospel, doubt is not permissible. For who could doubt when he reads:

> “At that time all your people will be saved, those who are written in the book; and many of those sleeping in the hollows of the earth will rise at one opening, some to eternal life and others to reproach and everlasting confusion. And those who understand will shine like the splendor of the firmament, and many of the righteous like the stars forever” (Dan. 12:1 and following).

He therefore aptly called death the rest of those who sleep, so that you might understand that death is not perpetual: it is entered for a time in the manner of sleep and for a time shut out. He also showed that the future development of that life which follows death is better than the life spent before death in grief and sorrow. The former is compared with the stars; the latter is given over to distress.

[Col. 1334D] Thus the edition of Gill, the Roman edition, and part of the manuscripts. The other manuscripts have “those buried in the earth.” In place of this, Amerbach and Erasmus read “those thrust into the earth,” an unusual expression which Nannius would not have failed to note if he had not neglected to consult the manuscripts.

### 67

For why should I gather together those things written elsewhere: “You will raise me up, and I will confess to you”? What of the holy Job, who experienced the injuries of this life and, by the patient strength of his virtue, overcame every adversity, and promised himself compensation for his present evils through the resurrection, saying: “You will raise up this body of mine, which has suffered many evils” (Job 19:26)?

Isaiah also, announcing the resurrection to the peoples, said that he was the messenger of the Lord’s response. For you have this:

> “For the mouth of the Lord has spoken, and they will say on that day” (Isa. 25:8).

What the peoples will say that the mouth of the Lord has spoken is explained later, where it is written:

> “Because of your fear, Lord, we conceived and gave birth to the spirit of your salvation, which you poured out upon the earth. Those who inhabit the earth will fall, but those who are in the tombs will rise. For the dew that comes from you is healing for them, but the land of the impious will perish. Go, my people, and enter your chambers. Hide yourselves for a little while, until the anger of God has passed” (Isa. 26:18 and following).

[Col. 1334D] The Roman edition alone reads, “surpassing all adversities by the virtue of patience.”

### 68

How well he designated the tombs of the dead as chambers, in which we are hidden for a little while, so that we may pass more tolerably into the judgment of God, which, on account of our crimes, will assume the justice of deserved indignation!

The one who is hidden and rests is therefore alive, as though withdrawing and retreating from the midst of things, lest the distress of this world entangle him in tighter snares. The prophetic oracles promise that the joy of resurrection is stored up there, and that the health of bodies dissolved will be restored by divine dew.

And rightly dew is signified, since by it all the generative seeds of the earth are revived. Why, then, should it be surprising if even the ashes and embers of our decaying body are enriched by the fatness of heavenly dew, and, after receiving vital moisture, the form of our limbs is reshaped into its own structure?

### 69

The holy prophet Ezekiel also teaches this and describes it in a full exposition: how vigor is poured back into dry bones, sensation returns, movement is added, and, as the sinews return, the structure of the human body grows firm; how the exceedingly dry bones are clothed with renewed viscera, and the openings of the veins and the rivulets of blood are covered by the extended covering of the skin.

As we read the prophetic words themselves, the harvest of human bodies seems to rise again to life; and you can see the broad spaces of the fields sprouting with new seeds.

[Col. 1335D] We have already explained elsewhere that “viscera” signifies flesh. The same word is used here and once again below in this sense.

### 70

But if the ancient sages believed that a crop of armed men sprang up from the teeth of a serpent in the Theban region, although it is certain that seeds of one nature cannot be transformed into another nature, nor can a birth contrary to its own seeds be produced—so that human beings should be born from a serpent and flesh arise from teeth—how much more should we believe that whatever has been sown rises again in its own nature, that crops do not differ from their sowing, that soft things do not come to life from hard things nor hard things from soft, and that poisons are not converted into blood, but flesh is restored from flesh, bone from bones, blood from blood, and moisture from moisture?

You Gentiles, then, can you deny the restoration of nature, when you can assert its transformation? Can you refuse to believe the oracles, the Gospel, and the prophecies, while believing empty fables?

[Col. 1335D] There is a clear allusion to these verses of Virgil from *Georgics* II:

> “No bulls breathing fire from their nostrils ploughed these fields, nor did a crop bristle with the teeth of a monstrous serpent, with the helmets and dense spears of men.”

Ambrose is also referring to what the poets relate about Cadmus, founder of Thebes; see Ovid, *Metamorphoses* III, fable 1, and Natalis Comes, *Mythologia* VIII, chapter 23, and IX, chapter 14. Ovid sings similarly about Jason in Book VII, fable 1, as do others who treated the Argonauts; Natalis Comes may also be consulted, Book VI, chapter 8.

### 71

But let us now hear the prophet himself. For he says:

> “The hand of the Lord came upon me, and the Lord led me out in the spirit and placed me in the middle of a plain, and it was full of human bones. He led me around them, and behold, there were very many bones upon the face of the plain, and they were exceedingly dry. And he said to me: ‘Son of man, will these bones live?’ And I said: ‘Lord, you know.’ And he said to me: ‘Prophesy over these bones, and say to them: Dry bones, hear the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord to these bones: Behold, I am bringing the spirit of life into you; I will put sinews upon you, bring viscera upon you, stretch skin over you, and put my Spirit into you; and you will live, and you will know that I am the Lord.’ And I prophesied as he commanded me. And when I prophesied all these things, behold, there was a great earthquake” (Ezek. 37:1 and following).

### 72

Now observe how he first shows hearing and movement in the bones, before the spirit of life is poured back into them. Above, the dry bones are commanded to hear, as though they possessed the sense of hearing; and here the approach of each bone to its own joint is indicated by the prophetic word:

> “And the bones were coming together, each bone to its own joint. And I saw, and behold, sinews and viscera were growing upon them, and skin was rising over them from above; but there was no spirit in them” (ibid., 7 and following).

### 73

Great is the Lord’s grace, that the prophet is appointed as a witness of the future resurrection, so that we too might see it through his eyes. For not everyone could be appointed as a witness; but in one person we are all witnesses, because falsehood cannot be found in a holy man, nor such error in a prophet.

### 74

Nor should it seem too improbable that, at God’s command, bones are reformed into their own structure, when we have countless examples in which the nature of things has obeyed heavenly commands: the earth was ordered to produce food, and it produced it (Gen. 1:11); at the touch of a rod, a rock vomited water for thirsty peoples (Num. 20:11); and, through divine compassion, streams poured forth from hard rocks parched by heat (Exod. 4:3).

The rod changed into a serpent. What else did this signify except that, when God wills it, sensible things can be generated from insensible things? Do you really think it more incredible that bones come together when commanded (Ezek. 37:7) than that waters flow backward and seas retreat? For the prophet testifies:

> “The sea saw and fled; the Jordan turned backward” (Ps. 114:3).

Nor can there be any doubt that the course of the waters was halted and restrained for the salvation of one people and the death of another, while the same waters surrounded some and flowed back against others to destroy some and preserve others (Exod. 14:22 and following).

What of the Gospel itself? Did the Lord not prove there that a wave is quieted by a word (Matt. 8:26), that the clouds of heaven are driven away, the blasts of the winds yield, and the mute elements serve God upon peaceful shores?

[Col. 1336D] Most manuscripts read, “the salvation of one, the death of another is confirmed.” This is not satisfactory unless, before the two words, one reads *quo* (“by which”) instead of *quod* (“that”); a simple scribal error could easily have occurred.

[Col. 1336D] Quite a few manuscripts read, “so that they might dash others against the shore”; some have “injure.”

### 75

But let us pursue the rest, so that we may understand how the dead are animated by the spirit of life, how those lying down rise, and how the tombs are opened. He says to me:

> “Prophesy, son of man, and say to the spirit: Thus says the Lord: Come from the four winds of heaven, O spirit, and breathe upon these dead, and let them live. And I prophesied as he commanded me, and the spirit of life entered into them, and they lived and stood upon their feet, an exceedingly great assembly. And the Lord spoke to me, saying: Son of man, these bones are the whole house of Israel. For they say: ‘Our bones have become dry, our hope has perished, we shall perish.’ Therefore prophesy and say: Thus says the Lord: Behold, I am opening your tombs, and I will lead you out of your tombs into the land of Israel; and you will know that I am the Lord, when I open your graves and lead my people out of the graves. I will put my Spirit in you, and you will live, and I will place you upon your own land, and you will know that I am the Lord. I have spoken, and I will act, says the Lord” (Ezek. 37:9 and following).

[Col. 1336D] Most manuscripts, together with the Septuagint, have this reading. Other codices and all the printed editions, following the Vulgate, read: “and you will know that I am the Lord who has spoken, and I will act.” In the following clause, instead of “the joints are restored,” as found in the old edition, two manuscripts read “the unions are restored”; the others, including the Roman edition, have the reading in the text.

### 76

We have observed how the exchanges of the vital spirit are restored; we have learned how the dead are raised when the tombs split open. Is it really surprising that, at the Lord’s command, the tombs of the dead are opened, when the whole earth is shaken within its boundaries by a single thunderclap, the sea overflows its limits, and yet restrains the course of its waves?

Finally, the one who has believed that “in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet—for the trumpet will sound—the dead will rise” (I Cor. 15:52) “will be caught up among the first in the clouds to meet Christ in the air” (I Thess. 4:16). The one who has not believed will be left behind and will submit himself to judgment through his own faithlessness.

[Col. 1337D] All the editions read: “who has believed that when the last trumpet sounds the dead will rise, he will be caught up first”; the manuscripts agree with us, except that some omit *canet enim tuba* (“for the trumpet will sound”) and have “the dead will rise first; they will be caught up.” This is not sufficiently correct. Below, where the Roman edition reads “and will subject himself to faithlessness,” the old edition and some manuscripts have “and will subject himself to his own faithlessness”; the remaining manuscripts have “and his faithlessness,” and so forth.

### 77

Our Lord Jesus Christ also showed you in the Gospel how you will rise, if we now come to examples. He did not raise only Lazarus, but raised the faith of all. If you believe this when you read it, your mind too, which had been dead, comes back to life in that Lazarus.

What does it mean that the Lord approached the tomb and cried out in a loud voice, “Lazarus, come out!” (John 11:44), except that he offered a glimpse and set forth an example of the future resurrection? Why did he cry out with his voice, as though he were not accustomed to act by the spirit, as though he were not accustomed to command silently? He did this to show what is written:

> “In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet, and the dead will rise incorruptible” (I Cor. 15:52).

For the sound of trumpets corresponds to the elevation of the voice. And he cried, “Lazarus, come out!” Why is a name added, unless perhaps to prevent one resurrected person from being mistaken for another, or to prevent the resurrection from appearing accidental rather than commanded?

[Col. 1337D] Amerbach and some manuscripts read, “so that he might present an image”; the Remigius and Benignus manuscripts, “so that he might present hope.”

[Col. 1337D] A few manuscripts read, “as though he were not accustomed to command.”

### 78

The dead man therefore heard and came out of the tomb, his feet and hands bound with strips, and his face wrapped in a cloth (John 11:44).

Understand, if you can, how he makes his way with his eyes closed, directs his step with his feet bound, and advances with a gait that cannot be separated, yet with a movement in which his progress is divided. The bonds remained, but did not hold him. His eyes were covered, but he saw. The one who was rising saw; the one who was walking saw; the one who was leaving the tomb saw.

For when the power of the divine command was at work, nature did not require its customary function. As though transported beyond itself, it no longer served its own order but the divine will. The bonds of death were broken before those of burial; movement was effected before it was prepared.

[Col. 1337D] A few manuscripts read, “he separates his step.” In the received reading, however, there is no fault, says Nannius, but great obscurity. The meaning is: How does he direct his course with his feet bound, his legs tied together, and yet walk as though they were spread apart, advancing with an alternating movement of the feet? So far Nannius.

[Col. 1338D] The strips here are the burial bandages called by John *κειρίαι* (*keiriai*), or more properly *κηρίαι* (*kēriai*), from *κήρ* (*kēr*), meaning death or fate. Nannius thinks David alludes to them where we read, “The cords of death came before me; the ropes of the underworld surrounded me”; for the Jews bound corpses smeared with unguents so that they would not come apart through decay. Yet ordinary strips are also meant by *institas*. Indeed, it also denotes a kind of women’s garment edged with such a band or border, as Nannius himself and Vossius observe concerning the same word.

### 79

If you marvel at these things, learn who commanded them, so that you may cease to marvel. Jesus Christ is the power of God, life, light, and resurrection of the dead. His power raised up the one lying down; life lifted up his step; light drove away darkness and restored sight; resurrection restored the grace of living.

[Col. 1338D] Thus all the editions and some manuscripts. Many others read, “the way, the light … raised up the step.”

### 80

Perhaps it troubles you that Jews remove the stone and Jews loosen the strips, so that you too may be anxious about who will remove the stone from your tomb (ibid., 41). As though the one who could pour the spirit back into the body could not remove a stone; or the one who made a bound man walk could not break bonds; or the one who gave light to covered eyes could not uncover the face; or the one who could restore nature could not split a rock!

But this was done so that those who were unwilling to believe with their minds might at least believe with their eyes. They remove the stone, see the corpse, smell the stench, and tear apart the strips. They cannot deny that he was dead, whom they behold rising again; they see the signs of death and the gifts of life.

What if, while they strive, they are themselves corrected by the very labor? What if, while they hear, they are made to believe by their own ears? What if, while they look, they are corrected by their own eyes? What if, while they break the bonds, they loose their own minds? What if, while Lazarus is stripped, the people are freed? While they permit Lazarus to depart, do they themselves return to the Lord?

Finally, many who had come to Mary, when they saw what had happened, believed (ibid., 45).

### 81

Nor did our Lord Jesus Christ give only this example; he also raised others, so that we might believe through still more abundant examples.

He raised a young man, moved by the tears of his widowed mother, when he approached and touched the bier, saying: “Young man, I say to you, arise.” And the one who had been dead sat up and began to speak (Luke 7:14). As soon as he heard, he immediately sat up, immediately spoke. Here, then, was another grace of power and another order of nature.

### 82

For why should I speak of the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, at whose death the crowds wept and the flute players sounded? Indeed, a funeral procession is displayed as evidence of death. How quickly, at the Lord’s voice, the spirit is changed, the restored body rises, and food is taken, so that it might be believed that life had returned.

### 83

And why should we be surprised that, at the voice of God, the soul is restored and the entrails return to the bones, when we remember that a dead man was raised through the prophetic touch of a body (2 Kings 13:21)? Elijah prayed and raised the dead child [Col. 1338D] (1 Kings 17:22); Peter commanded Tabitha, in the name of Christ, to rise and walk, and the poor, when she had been restored to them, rejoiced and believed in return for their nourishment (Acts 9:40); and do we still not believe for the sake of salvation?

[Note: Most manuscripts give this passage in abbreviated form as follows: “Do we not believe? Our Lord Jesus Christ himself also enacted this very sequence of the resurrection.” Nevertheless, the other manuscripts and all editions have the text as above.]

They redeemed another’s resurrection with their tears; are we not to believe in our own because of Christ’s passion? When he gave up his spirit, to show that he had died for our resurrection, he enacted that very sequence of the resurrection. For at the same moment that, crying out again with a loud voice, he gave up his spirit, the earth was shaken, the rocks were split, the tombs were opened, and many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep arose; and, coming out of the tomb after his resurrection, they entered the holy city and appeared to many (Matthew 27:51–52).

### 84

If these things happened when he gave up his spirit, [Col. 1339B] why do we regard them as incredible when he begins to return for judgment? Especially since this resurrection is a demonstration of that resurrection and an example of the truth that is to come; yet an example is less than the reality.

Who, then, during the Lord’s passion opened the tombs, gave a hand to those rising, and showed them the way by which they should go to the holy city? If no human being did so, surely divine power was at work in the bodies of the dead. Do you seek human assistance where you see the work of God?

### 85

Divine mysteries do not need human services.

[Note: All editions and a few manuscripts read “divine mysteries do not need human mysteries”; the remaining manuscripts read “divine mysteries do not need human ministries,” which plainly fits better with what follows.]

God commanded heaven to come into being, and it came into being; he decreed that the earth should be created, and it was created (Genesis 1:6ff.). Whose shoulders carried the rocks together? Who amassed the expenses? Who supplied his labor to the God who was at work? These things were made in an instant. Do you wish to know how briefly? ““He spoke, and they were made” [Col. 1339C] (Psalm 143:5).). If the elements rise at a word, why should the dead not rise at a word?

Although the dead are dead, they once lived; they possessed the spirit by which they perceived, and they possessed powers by which they acted. There is a great difference between something that never possessed a soul’s capacity and something that remained lifeless.

The devil said, “Tell this stone to become bread” (Luke 4:3). He confesses that, at God’s command, nature can be changed; yet you do not believe that, at God’s command, nature can be restored?

### 86

Philosophers dispute about the course of the sun and the structure of heaven, and there are people who think that they should be believed, although they do not know what they are talking about. They did not ascend into heaven, measure its axis, and scrutinize the world with their eyes. For none of them was with God in the beginning; none of them said of God: “When he prepared heaven, I was with him, and I was with him arranging all things; I was the one in whom he rejoiced” (Proverbs 8:27, 30).

[Note: Several manuscripts read “in whom he applauded”; some manuscripts and the edition read “in whom he rejoiced.”]

If they are believed, then God is not believed—God who says:

“Just as the new heaven and the new earth that I make will remain before me, says the Lord, so shall your name and your offspring remain. And it shall be month after month, and sabbath after sabbath; and all flesh shall come before me to worship in Jerusalem, says the Lord God. And they shall go out and see the limbs of the men who transgressed against me. For their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be extinguished; and they shall be a spectacle to all flesh” (Isaiah 66:22ff.) [Col. 1339D–1340A].

### 87

If earth and heaven are renewed, why should we doubt that human beings can be renewed, for whose sake earth and heaven were made? If the transgressor is preserved for punishment, why should the just person not be perpetuated for glory? If the worm of sinners does not die, how will the flesh of the righteous perish?

For this is the resurrection, as the very sound of the word expresses it: what has fallen shall rise again; what has died shall live again.

### 88

This is the complete and just rationale, if I am not mistaken: since body and soul act together—for what the soul conceives, the body carries out—both shall come to judgment, and both shall either be handed over to punishment or reserved for glory.

For it seems almost absurd that, when the law of the flesh attacks the law of the soul, and the mind often does what it hates, when sin dwelling in a person works through the flesh, the soul should be subjected to an injury caused by another and made guilty of another’s fault, while the flesh, the author of misery, enjoys repose; or that the one who did not err alone should alone be crushed, or that the one who did not serve grace alone should alone receive glory.

[Note: “Be subjected to an injury,” that is, to punishments and torments.]

[Note: Some manuscripts read “who did not serve the glory.”]

### 89

The reasoning is full and just, I think. But I do not demand reasoning from Christ. If I am convinced by reasoning, I reject faith.

“Abraham believed God” (Genesis 15:6); let us also believe, so that, being heirs of his race, we may also be heirs of his faith. David also believed, and therefore he spoke (Psalm 115:10); let us also believe, so that we may be able to speak, knowing that “he who raised the Lord Jesus Christ will also raise us with Jesus” (2 Corinthians 4:14).

This was promised by God, who never lies (Titus 1:2). Truth itself promised it in the Gospel, saying: “This is the will of him who sent me: that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me, but should raise it up on the last day” (John 6:39).

He did not think it enough to say this once; he also confirmed it by repeating the statement.

[Note: All editions read “he confirmed it with a repeated expression”; all manuscripts read “he marked it,” that is, confirmed it.]

For it continues:

“For this is the will of my Father who sent me: that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him should have eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day” (ibid., 40).

### 90

Who says this? Surely the one who, though dead, raised many bodies of the dead [Col. 1340D]. If we do not believe God, do we not believe the example either? Do we not believe what he promised, when he even accomplished what he did not promise?

What reason would he have had for dying, unless he also had a reason for rising? For, since God could not die, Wisdom could not die; but what was not dead could not rise. Flesh was assumed, which could die, so that when what normally dies was dying, what had died might rise again.

[Note: The old edition and several manuscripts read: “Since the Wisdom of God could not die”; the Roman edition, together with the remaining manuscripts, has the reading printed in the text.]

For there could be no resurrection except through a human being, since “as through a human being came death, so through a human being comes the resurrection of the dead” (1 Corinthians 15:21).

### 91

Therefore a human being rose again, because a human being had died: a human being was raised, but God was the one who raised him. Then he was human according to the flesh; now in every respect he is God. For now we no longer know Christ according to the flesh, but we retain the grace of the flesh, so that we may recognize him as the first fruits of those who sleep, himself the firstborn from the dead.

The first fruits are certainly of the same kind and nature as the remaining fruits, whose richer yield brings first offerings to God: a sacred offering on behalf of all, and, as it were, certain first libations of restored nature.

[Note: Several manuscripts read “whose more abundant produce”; one has “for the more joyful harvest.”]

Christ, then, is the first fruits of those who sleep. But is he the first fruits of his own dead, who are held in a kind of sweet sleep as though exempt from death, or of all the dead? “For just as all die in Adam, so also all will be made alive in Christ” (1 Corinthians 15:22). Therefore, just as Adam is the first fruits of death, so Christ is the first fruits of resurrection.

### 92

All rise again, but no one should despair, nor should the righteous grieve over the common fellowship of resurrection, since he awaits the special fruit of virtue. All indeed will rise, but each one, as the Apostle says, “in his own order” (ibid., 23).

The fruit of divine mercy is common to all, but the order of merits is distinct. The day shines for everyone; the sun warms all peoples; rain makes everyone’s possessions fertile with a more abundant shower.

### 93

We are all born, and we shall all rise again; but in both cases the grace of living or living again is unequal, and the condition is different. “In an instant, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet, the dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed” (ibid., 52).

Indeed, even in death some rest while others live.

[Note: In Ambrose, “rest” and “life,” freedom from punishment and the throne in the kingdom, are everywhere to be understood in the same sense that we explained they should be understood in Letter 71 to Horontius. Those who fabricate from such expressions an intermediate state between glory and punishment are therefore mistaken. For in countless passages he directly opposes immortality to punishments, as in this very discourse, section 8, where he says that those condemned to punishment are owed immortality. Had Jean Daillé considered this more carefully, he would have reproduced the same expressions with less hostility in book 2, chapter 4, of *De Usu Patrum*.]

Rest is good, but life is better. Finally, Paul awakens the one who rests to life, saying: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine upon you” (Ephesians 5:14).

Here, then, he is awakened so that he may live, so that he may be like Paul, so that he may be able to say: “For we who are alive will not precede those who have fallen asleep” (1 Thessalonians 4:14). He is not speaking of the ordinary use of life and the exchange of breath, but of merit for resurrection.

For after he had said, “The dead who are in Christ will rise first” [Col. 1341D] (ibid., 15), he added: “Then we who are alive, together with them, shall be caught up in the clouds to meet Christ in the air.”

### 94

Paul certainly died and, through a venerable passion, exchanged bodily life for immortal glory. Did he therefore deceive us when he wrote that, as one living, he would be caught up in the clouds to meet Christ?

We read this of Enoch (Genesis 5:24), and of Elijah as well (2 Kings 2:11). But you too will be caught up in spirit. Behold Elijah’s chariot; behold the fires—even if they are not visible, they are being prepared—so that the righteous may ascend, the innocent be transferred, and your life may know no death.

Finally, the apostles did not know death; hence it was said: “Amen, amen, I say to you, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom” (Matthew 16:28).

The one who has nothing in himself that must die is alive; he has no Egyptian sandal or bond. He removes it before laying down the service of this body. Enoch, therefore, is not the only one who lives, because he is not the only one who was caught up: Paul too is caught up to meet Christ [Col. 1342B].

### 95

The patriarchs also live. For God would not otherwise be called the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, unless the dead were living; “for he is not God of the dead but of the living” (Luke 20:38).

We too shall live if we are willing to imitate the deeds and conduct of our ancestors. We marvel at the patriarchs’ rewards; let us imitate their service. We proclaim grace; let us follow obedience. Let us not, enticed by foods, cut through the snares of the world..

Let us seize the opportunity of the time, the prescription of the Law, the mercy of the call, and the desire for suffering. The patriarchs went out from their land, and let us go out deliberately from the power of the body. Let us go out deliberately; they went into exile. But they did not consider it exile, because devotion undertook what necessity did not command.

They exchanged one land for another; let us exchange earth for heaven. They did so in habitation; let us do so in spirit. Let wisdom display to them a heaven illuminated by stars; may the true knowledge of that same wisdom illuminate the eyes of our heart.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “Wisdom showed [it],” while ours reads, “May the true knowledge of that same wisdom illuminate the eyes of our heart.”]

Thus the type converges with the truth, and the truth with the type.

### 96

Abraham was ready to receive guests (Genesis 18:2), faithful to God, diligent in service, prompt in duty. In a type he saw the Trinity; he enriched hospitality with religious devotion, looking upon three and worshiping one. While preserving the distinction of the persons, he nevertheless called them one Lord, offering the honor of a gift to three and signifying one power.

In him it was not instruction but grace that spoke. He believed better what he had not learned than we who have learned. For no one had falsified the type of the truth; therefore he sees three but venerates unity.

He brings out three measures of fine flour and sacrifices one calf, believing firmly that there is one sacrifice, a gift of three, one offering, and the grace of three.

[Note: Thus all editions and most manuscripts read. Others have: “a threefold gift, one offering of three graces.” A few lines later, where we, with the Roman edition and all manuscripts, read “abstinent in triumph,” and retain one manuscript reading “and vigorous in triumph,” the ancient edition had “abstaining in triumph.”]

For, in the episode of the four kings (Genesis 14:1ff.), who would not understand that, as a sign of the Lord’s prefigured passion, he subjected the elements of material nature and all worldly things to himself?? He was faithful in war and abstinent in triumph, preferring not to become rich through human gifts but through God.

### 97

The old man believed that he could beget a son; the father judged that he could sacrifice his son (Genesis 22:11). Nor did paternal affection tremble, when devotion strengthened the old man’s right hand. For he knew that a sacrificed son was more acceptable to God than a sound one.

Thus he leads his beloved son to the sacrifice; the one whom he had received late he offered early. Nor is he recalled by the name of father, when the one called him “father” and the other “son.” Dear pledges of their names, but God’s commands were dearer.

[Note: The Roman edition reads “but more extensive commands”; the others and the manuscripts read “but more lovable commands”; the Benedictine edition reads “God’s commands.”]

Thus, although their hearts sympathized with one another, their vows endured. With a father’s hand he drew the sword over his son and, in a textually difficult phrase, struck with paternal feeling, lest the penalty fail [Col. 1343B].. He trembled lest the blow go astray, lest his right hand fail. He felt the affection of piety, but did not abandon the task of devotion; he hastened to obey even when he heard the oracle.

Therefore let us also put God before everyone whom we love—before father, brothers, and mother—so that he may preserve our loved ones for us, just as we see him rewarding Abraham more abundantly as a recompense-giver than as a servant.

[Note: The same Roman edition reads “so that the beloved may be preserved for us”; the old edition and the manuscripts agree with one another, except that they prefer “that we may be preserved,” where we, with the manuscripts, read “that our loved ones may be preserved for us.”.”]

### 98

The father did offer his son, but God is pleased not by blood but by devotion. He showed a ram in the wood in place of the man, so that he might return the son to his father without allowing the victim to perish before the priest.

Thus Abraham was not stained with parricide, nor was God deprived of a sacrifice. The prophet saw this and neither sought ostentation nor maintained obstinacy: he exchanged a ram for a man.

This shows all the more clearly how devoutly he offered the one whom he received back so willingly. You too, if you offer your gift to God, do not lose it. But we are greedy. God offered his only Son to death for us (Romans 8:32); we deny him our own.

Abraham saw this and recognized the mystery: that salvation would come to us through the wood. It was not hidden that, in one and the same sacrifice, one thing appeared to be offered and another could be killed.

### 99

Let us therefore imitate Abraham’s devotion, Isaac’s goodness, and his chastity. He was plainly a good and modest man, devoted to God and chaste toward his wife. He did not return injury; he yielded to those who excluded him and received back those who repented. He was neither insolent in defiance nor harsh in granting favor.

He avoided litigation when he departed; he was ready to forgive when he received them back; he was more lavish in goodness when he pardoned. When fellowship was requested, he added a feast of joy.

### 100

Let us also imitate in Jacob the type of Christ; let there be in us some likeness to his deeds. We shall be his companions if we are his imitators.

He obeyed his mother, yielded to his brother, served his father-in-law, and sought his reward from profits, not from dividing the flocks. There is no greedy division where the portion is profitable.

Nor was the ladder from heaven (Genesis 28:12) an idle sign: it indicated that through Christ’s cross there would be a future fellowship of angels and human beings. His thigh was made powerless (Genesis 32:29), so that in his thigh he might recognize the heir of his generation, and so that the disabling of the thigh might prophesy the passion of the heir.

### 101

We see, then, that heaven is open to virtue, and that this is not reserved for a few: “Many will come from the east and from the west and from the north and from the south, and they will recline in the kingdom of God” (Matthew 8:11), expressing the enjoyment of perpetual rest after the movements of their souls have been buried.

Let us follow Abraham in our conduct, so that he may receive us into his bosom and, as the heir of his humility, like Lazarus (Luke 16:23), enfolded in his own virtues, cherish us in a devout embrace.

[Note: A very similar explanation of what we should understand by “Abraham’s bosom” can be found in the *Exposition on Psalm 38*, section 11, if you do not object to consulting that passage.]

For it is not in a bodily bosom that the holy patriarch’s succession, approved by God, cherishes us, but in a kind of covering formed by good deeds.

“Do not be deceived,” he says; “God is not mocked” (Galatians 6:7).

### 102

We perceive how grave a sacrilege it is not to believe in the resurrection. For if we do not rise, then Christ died for nothing; therefore Christ did not rise (1 Corinthians 15:13). If he did not rise for us, then he certainly did not rise—for what reason would he have had to rise for himself?

The world rose again in him; heaven rose again in him; earth rose again in him. For there will be a new heaven and a new earth (Revelation 21:1).

But where was resurrection necessary for him, whom the bonds of death could not hold? Even though he died according to the human condition, he was nevertheless free among those in the underworld.

### 103

Do you wish to know how free?

“I became like a man without help, free among the dead” (Psalm 87:5).

And rightly free, since he could raise himself, according to what is written: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19).

And rightly free, since he had descended to redeem others. He became like a man—not fashioned merely in appearance, but formed in reality—because he is both human, and “who will know him?”

“For he was made in the likeness of human beings, and was found in appearance as a human being; he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death” (Philippians 2:7–8), so that through that obedience we might see his glory, “glory as of the only-begotten from the Father,” according to the holy John (John 1:14).

[Note: The Roman edition omitted the words “according to the holy John”; we have restored them from other editions and manuscripts.]

Thus the figure of Scripture is preserved, so that both the glory of the only-begotten and the nature of the perfect human being may be preserved in Christ.

### 104

Therefore he did not need a helper. He did not need one when he made the world, that he should need one when he redeemed it. “Not an ambassador, not a messenger, but he himself saved him.” “He spoke, and they were made” (Psalm 32:9).

“He himself saved him”: he himself everywhere, because all things are through him (Colossians 1:17). Who would help the one in whom all things were created and in whom all things hold together? Who would help the one who makes all things in an instant and raises the dead at the last trumpet (1 Corinthians 15:52)?

This is not because he could not do so at the first, second, or third trumpet; rather, the order is preserved—not an order in which difficulty is overcome only after delay, but a legitimate number that must be unfolded.

[Note: The old edition and the manuscripts almost unanimously read as above; the Roman edition, with one or two manuscripts, has “so that the number may be vindicated.”]

### 105

I think that the time has come to speak about the figure of the trumpets, since the discourse is drawing toward its end, so that the trumpet of our own completed discourse may also serve as a sign.

We read in John’s Apocalypse of seven trumpets, which seven angels took up (Revelation 8:2). There we read that, when the seventh angel sounded his trumpet, a loud voice came from heaven saying: “The kingdom of this world has become the kingdom of our God and of his Christ, and he will reign forever and ever” (Revelation 11:15).

The trumpet is also understood as a voice, since we read: “Behold, a door was opened in heaven, and the first voice that I heard was like a trumpet speaking with me and saying: ‘Come up here, and I will show you what must happen next’” (Revelation 4:1).

We also read: “Blow the trumpet at the beginning of the month” (Psalm 80:4); and elsewhere: “Praise him with the sound of the trumpet” (Psalm 150:3).

### 106

We must therefore attend with every spiritual power to what the symbolism of the trumpets means.

[Note: Origen discusses the trumpets of Scripture in *Homily 30 on Matthew*, though more briefly; nevertheless, he quotes there in full the passage from Numbers that Ambrose cites below. Our teacher may therefore have derived what he argues here from that source and, as was his custom, expanded it.]

We must not endanger ourselves by accepting the matter like an old woman’s tale, if we fail to perceive meanings worthy of spiritual doctrine and suited to the majesty of Scripture.

For when we read that our battle is not against flesh and blood but against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places (Ephesians 6:12), we must understand that the weapons are not carnal but powerful through God (2 Corinthians 10:4).

It is not enough merely to see the trumpet or hear its sound unless you understand the character of the sound. For if the trumpet gives an uncertain sound, how will anyone prepare for battle?

Therefore we must know the power of the trumpet’s voice, lest we seem barbarians when we hear or speak of such trumpets.

[Note: The Romans used the trumpet in military affairs, just as barbarians used drums and pipes. On this subject, consult Justus Lipsius, *De Militia Romana*, book 2, dialogue 10.]

And therefore, when we speak, let us pray that the Holy Spirit may interpret these trumpets for us.

### 107

Let us therefore seek in the ancient Scriptures what we have read concerning the kind of trumpets, recognizing that the solemnities prescribed by the Law for the Jews are shadows of higher celebrations and heavenly festivals.

[Note: All editions read “knowing them”; some manuscripts read “conjecturing them,” others “proclaiming them,” and still others “agreeing with them.” The last reading seems preferable.]

Here there is a shadow; there the truth. Let us strive to arrive at the truth through the shadow.

This figure is also expressed elsewhere in the following manner. For we read that the Lord spoke to Moses:

“Speak to the children of Israel, saying: In the seventh month, on the first day of the month, you shall have rest, a sacred memorial of trumpets. It shall be holy for you. You shall perform no servile work, and you shall offer a burnt offering to the Lord” (Leviticus 23:24).

[Note: The Roman edition reads “a sacred day called a memorial of trumpets to the Lord.” The old edition agrees with the manuscripts and the sacred codices, except that it places the comma after “called,” which is unsuitable.]

But in Numbers:

“The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Make two trumpets for yourself; make them of beaten silver. They shall be for you for summoning the assembly and for moving the camps. When you blow them, the whole assembly shall gather at the door of the tent of testimony.

“If you blow one trumpet, all the princes and leaders of Israel shall come to you. When you blow the first signal, the camps shall move forward and shall be stationed toward the east. When you blow the second signal, the camps shall move forward and shall be stationed toward Lebanon.

“When you blow the third signal, the camps shall move forward and shall be stationed toward the north. When you blow the fourth signal, the camps shall move forward and shall be stationed toward the north.

[Note: Erasmus and Gill read “toward the slopes”; the Roman edition reads “toward the south.” The sacred codices support both readings, some having *paremballousai liba* (“stationing toward Lebanon”), others *noton* (“the south”). Nevertheless, there is no doubt that the reading of the Ambrosian edition and the manuscripts, namely “toward Lebanon,” is correct, since the same reading occurs below, in section 115, and in section 119 the Bridegroom invites the bride from Lebanon. Again, where we, with the old edition and all the manuscripts, read “toward the north,” the editions read “toward the sea.” In this matter not only the Septuagint supports them, but Ambrose himself below, in section 115, applies the third trumpet’s signal to the sea. Nevertheless, it is difficult to depart from all the manuscripts and the ancient edition. Observe also that neither the Hebrew nor any version except the Septuagint contains anything about a third and fourth trumpet signal; and instead of the wording found everywhere in the sacred writings, “the camps that were stationed,” Ambrose seems to have read “the camps that will be stationed.”]

“Let them blow the trumpet as a signal for their movement. When you gather the assembly, blow the trumpet, but not as a signal. The sons of Aaron, the priests, shall blow the trumpets, and it shall be a perpetual ordinance for you throughout your generations.

“When you go out to war in your land against enemies who resist you, you shall signal with the trumpets; and you shall be remembered before the Lord, and you shall have deliverance from your dead.”.

[Note: The Roman edition alone adds “and you shall have deliverance from your enemies.” It thought this necessary to restore from Scripture, but we have observed several times already that the copy used by the holy Doctor differs in many places from the versions currently circulating.]

“On your days of rejoicing, on your festivals, and on your new moons, you shall sound the trumpets over your burnt offerings and your sacrifices of salvation; and they shall be for you as a memorial before the Lord,” says the Lord (Numbers 10:1ff.).

[Note: Some manuscripts read “when the trumpet sounds,” instead of “at their movement.” Other manuscripts have “Aaron the priest shall sound the trumpet.”]

### 108

What, then? Shall we regard the festival days as consisting in drink and feasts? But let no one judge us in eating; for we know that the Law is spiritual (Romans 7:14).

Therefore let no one judge us in food or drink, or with regard to a festival, a new moon, or a sabbath. These are a shadow of things to come, but the body belongs to Christ (Colossians 2:16).

Let us therefore seek the body of Christ, which the voice of the Father from heaven, as though a final trumpet, revealed to you when the Jews were saying that “it had become thunder for him” (John 12:28).). The body of Christ, which the final trumpet will reveal to us again, for the Lord himself will descend from heaven at the command of the archangel and at the trumpet of God, and the dead who are in Christ will rise (1 Thessalonians 4:15).

“For where the body is, there the eagles will gather” (Luke 17:37). Where the body of Christ is, there is the truth.

### 108

The seventh trumpet of the week therefore seems to signify rest. Rest is reckoned not only in days, years, and periods—hence the number of the jubilee was also consecrated—but also includes the seventieth year, when the people who had endured seventy years in captivity returned to Jerusalem.

Nor is observance of the sacred number neglected in hundreds and thousands. For God did not speak idly when he said: “I have left to myself seven thousand men who have not bent the knee before Baal” (1 Kings 19:18).

Thus the shadow of future rest is represented in days, months, years, and the duration of the world itself. Therefore, through Moses, the children of Israel are commanded that in the seventh month, on the first day of the month, everyone should have rest as a memorial of trumpets, and that no servile work should be performed, but a sacrifice should be offered to God. For at the very end of the week, as on the world’s sabbath, spiritual rather than carnal works are demanded of us.

What is carnal is servile, because the flesh serves the mind; innocence makes one free, while guilt makes one a household slave.

[Note: Some manuscripts read “innocence makes free, guilt makes one a servant”; one has “makes one saleable.” A household slave (*vernaculus*) is a servant born in the house.]

### 109

Spiritual realities therefore had to be made known through a mirror and in a mystery: “Now we see through a mirror, in an obscure manner; then face to face” (1 Corinthians 13:12).

Now we wage war according to the flesh; then we shall see divine mysteries in the spirit. Therefore let the character of the true Law be expressed in our conduct, since we walk in the image of God. For the shadow of the Law has already passed: a shadow for the carnal Jews, an image for us, and truth for those who will rise again.

[Note: Many manuscripts read “a shadow for the carnal, an image for us, and truth for us who will rise again.” The reading in the text is preferable and is expressed in the same terms in the *Exposition on Psalm 38*, section 25, and *On the Duties*, book 1, chapter 48, section 248.]

We know that, according to the Law, there are these three things: shadow, image, and truth—the shadow in the Law, the image in the Gospel, and the truth in judgment.

But all things belong to Christ, and all things are in Christ. We cannot now see him according to truth, but we see him as in an image of the things to come, whose shadow we perceived in the Law.

Christ, therefore, is not a shadow but the image of God—not an empty image but the truth. Thus the Law came through Moses, because the shadow came through a human being, the figure through the Law, and the truth through Jesus (John 1:17). For truth could come from nowhere except from truth.

### 110

If anyone desires to see this image of God, he must love God so that he may be loved by God. Let him no longer be a servant but a friend, one who has fulfilled God’s commands, so that he may be able to enter the cloud where God is (Exodus 24:15).

Let him make for himself two rational trumpets, beaten from tested silver (Numbers 10:1)—that is, composed and adorned with precious speech. Let no hoarse rebuke, with terrifying sound, break in with a murmur; rather, let lofty thanksgivings be poured out to God in continual jubilation..

For at the sound of such trumpets the dead are raised—not animated by the clatter of bronze, but by the word of truth. Perhaps these two trumpets are those through which Paul, in the divine Spirit, sounded forth, saying:: “I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the mind; I will sing psalms with the spirit, and I will sing psalms with the mind” (1 Corinthians 14:15). For one without the other does not seem to provide a complete summons.

### 111

Nor is it everyone’s task to blow both trumpets, nor is it everyone’s task to gather the whole assembly. This privilege is granted only to the priests and ministers of God who blow them (Numbers 10:2ff.).

Whoever hears should follow them to where the glory of God is, and should hasten to assemble at the tent of testimony; there he may behold divine works and earn that legitimate and eternal dwelling for the succession of his posterity.

Then the battle is completed and the enemy is put to flight, when the grace of the Spirit and the diligence of the mind sound together.

[Note: Some manuscripts add “and follows them,” but this is not entirely correct.]

### 112

There are also those saving trumpets: if you believe with your heart and confess with your mouth, “For one believes with the heart unto righteousness, but confession is made with the mouth unto salvation” (Romans 10:10).

By this twofold trumpet one reaches that holy land, namely the grace of the resurrection. Therefore let them always sound together for you, so that you may always hear the voice of God. Let the declarations of angels and prophets always awaken and stir you [Col. 1348C], so that you may hasten to higher things.

[Note: The old edition and many manuscripts read “so that you may hasten to higher things, to the place of the wonderful tabernacle.” Gill indicated that the lacuna could be supplied in the variant readings; from this, the Roman edition restored the passage, and many of our manuscripts confirm that restoration.]

### 113

David revolved this intention in his heart when he said:

“For I shall pass into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God, amid the voice of rejoicing and confession, the sound of one feasting” (Psalm 41:5).

For it is not only enemies who are conquered by the sound of these trumpets; pleasures, festivals, and new moons cannot exist without them either. No one can rejoice with joy, or celebrate festivals or new moons in which he desires to be emptied of bodily grace and worldly occupation and filled with the light of Christ, unless he drinks in the promises of divine speech and believes the oracles as they resound.

Even sacrifices approved by God cannot be offered unless the confession of the voice breathes upon them, the confession that, through priestly offering, customarily arouses peoples to implore God’s grace.

### 114

Let us therefore be preachers of the Lord and praise him with the voice of the trumpet (Psalm 150:3), not holding small or contemptible opinions of his power, but those capable of filling the ear of the mind and penetrating the secret places of the deepest conscience.

Let us not think that what belongs to the body should be attributed to divinity. Let us not measure the greatness of divine power by human capacities, asking how someone rises, with what sort of body he comes, or how dissolved things come together and fallen things are restored. For as soon as these things are decreed by God’s will, they are accomplished.

The audible sound of trumpets is not awaited; rather, the invisible power of heavenly magnificence performs the work. For with God, to will is to accomplish. We should not seek the exertion required for resurrection, but await its fruit.

This will be celebrated more readily if, emptied of vices, we attain the fullness of the spiritual mystery, if renewed flesh receives grace from the spirit, and if the soul receives from Christ the radiance of eternal light.

[Note: The Roman edition and most manuscripts read as above. The old edition, together with other manuscripts, has “and let the soul merit [the radiance] from Christ.”]

115. But these mysteries belong not only to individuals, but also to the whole community. For observe, according to the pattern of the Law, the order of grace. When the first trumpet sounds, it gathers those from the east, as the foremost and elect; at the second, those equal in merit who, dwelling toward Lebanon, have abandoned the mockeries of the nations; at the third, those who, tossed about as though on the sea by this world’s strait, have wavered amid the waves of this age; at the fourth, those who have been altogether unable sufficiently to soften the hardness of their minds by the instruction of spiritual eloquence, and therefore have been called from the north—for according to Solomon, the north wind is harsh (Prov. XXVII, 16).

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads, “situated toward the south.” But below that same edition, together with the old edition and several manuscripts, reads, “by the breath of this world”; whereas the majority and better manuscripts have, “by the strait of this world.”]

116. Therefore, although all are raised in an instant, all are nevertheless raised according to the order of their merits. And so the first to rise are those who, coming forward with the mature readiness of devotion and with a kind of dawn-like rising of faith, received the rays of the eternal sun. I may rightly understand this either of the patriarchs, according to the sequence of the Old Testament, or of the apostles, according to the Gospel. The second are those who, abandoning the rites of the nations, passed from sacrilegious error into the discipline of the Church. And so the former are first among the fathers, the latter second among the nations: from the former the light of faith began; in the latter, once received, it endured until the setting of the world.

[Note: All editions and most manuscripts read, “The third are raised, those who are from the south,” which is more harmonious. The Corbie and Benignus manuscripts of Remigius read as in the text.]

The third are raised, and the fourth—the former from the south, the latter from the north. By these four the earth is distinguished; within these four the year is contained; by these four the world is filled; by these four the Church is gathered. For all who, joined to the holy Church and reckoned under the name of God, will obtain the privilege of resurrection and the grace of eternal delight, since they will come from east and west, from north and south, and will recline in the kingdom of God (Luke XIII, 29).

[Col. 1349D] 117. For Christ does not encompass his world with a scanty light, since “his going forth is from the highest heaven, and his circuit reaches to its highest point; and there is no one who can hide himself from his heat” (Ps. XVIII, 7). He enlightens all in his goodness. He does not wish to reject the weak, but to correct them; nor does the Church desire to exclude the hardened, but to soften them.

[Note: The Roman edition reads, “And therefore Christ invites them in the Gospel.” Below it adds, “Recognize the voice of the one inviting in the Song of Songs.” But the old edition and all the manuscripts agree with us, except that in place of “recognize,” some read “hear.”]

And therefore, in the Song of Songs the Church, and in the Gospel Christ, invites them, saying: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matt. XI, 28–29).

118. Recognize also the voice of the Church inviting; for she says: “Arise, north wind, and come, south wind; blow through my garden, and let my perfumes flow forth. Let my brother come down into his garden and eat the fruit of his fruit trees” (Song IV, 16; V, 1).

[Note: Several manuscripts read, “and toward the fruit,” which is less suitable.]

For she already knew that the works of such people would also be fruitful for you, and therefore promised Christ fruit from them. And she who first said that she had been brought into the King’s chamber, loving breasts more than wine, when she loved the one who loved her, sought the nursing child, and scorned dangers for the sake of religion.
