119. Then you are asked to come from Lebanon, bride, still wholly beautiful and wholly without reproach in the judgment of the Lord. For it is written: “You are wholly beautiful, my near one, and there is no reproach in you. Come here from Lebanon, bride; come here from Lebanon” (Song IV, 7–8).

120. Later, no longer fearing any streams of water or descending torrents from Lebanon, you yourself summon the north wind and the south wind, desiring that your garden be blown through, so that your perfumes may flow forth in some, and in others you may offer Christ the manifold fruits of your fertility.

121. And therefore blessed is the one who keeps the words of this prophecy (Rev. XXII, 7), which revealed the resurrection to us through clearer testimonies, saying: “And I saw the dead, great and small, standing before the throne, and the books were opened; and another book was opened, which is the book of life; and the dead were judged from what had been written in the books, according to their deeds. And the sea gave up the dead who were in it, and Hades gave up the dead who were in it” (Rev. XX, 12).

[Note: Most manuscripts read, “the dead described in the books”; several others, together with the old edition, read, “the dead from the writings in the books.” In Greek: ἐκ τῶν γεγραμμένων ἐν τοῖς βιβλίοις, “from what had been written in the books,” which the Roman edition elegantly rendered from the Vulgate.]

Do not, then, doubt how they rise, when Hades vomits them forth and the sea restores them.

122. Hear also when the future grace of the righteous is promised: “And I heard,” he says, “a great voice from the throne saying: Behold, the tabernacle of God is with human beings, and he will dwell with them; and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God. And he will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death will be no more; neither will there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore” (Rev. XXI, 3–4).

123. Compare now, if you please, and set this life against that life; and choose, if you can, perpetual bodily life amid the labor and miserable distress of so many changes, the weariness of desires, and the disgust of pleasures. If God wished to perpetuate these things, would you not choose that other life? For if life itself is to be fled from, so that it may be an escape from troubles and a rest from distress, how much more ought that rest to be desired which will be followed by the perpetual joy of the future resurrection, where there is no succession of crimes and no enticement to sin?

124. Who is so patient in pain that he does not pray for death? Who is so steadfast in illness that he does not prefer to die rather than live in weakness? Who is so strong in sorrow that he does not desire to end it, even by dying? And if we ourselves displease ourselves while we live, when we know that an end has been appointed to our life, how much more would this life weary us if we saw that the labors of this body were destined to remain without end?

Who, then, would wish to be exempt from death? Or what is more grievous than miserable immortality? “If in this life,” he says, “we have hope in Christ only, we are more miserable than all human beings” (I Cor. XV, 19)—not because it is miserable to hope in Christ, but because Christ has prepared another life for those who hope in him. This life is subject to sin; that one is reserved for reward.

124. How much disgust, we see, even the brief courses of our lives bring us? A boy longs for adolescence; an adolescent measures out for himself the years of a greater age; a young man, ungrateful for the benefit of his flourishing years, desires the dignity of old age. Thus, by nature, everyone wants to be changed, because he regrets what he is. Finally, even the things we desired after they have been obtained become wearisome; and what we wished to deserve, once we have deserved it, we cast aside.

[Note: Some manuscripts, and from them all editions, had inserted the following interpolation: “against the philosophical sects, who say either that the soul alone endures after the death of the body or believe in μετεμψύχωσιν [transmigration of souls].” But apart from the fact that it is absent from many more and better manuscripts, the very sequence of the argument plainly rejects this addition. In what follows, instead of “because we regret what we are,” the Thuan manuscript has, “because we regret what we know.” This is not sufficiently correct.]

125. Hence the holy men also, not without reason, often lamented that their sojourn had been prolonged (Ps. CXIX, 5): David lamented, Jeremiah lamented (Jer. XX, 17), Elijah lamented (III Kings XIX, 4).

[Note: Several manuscripts read: “If these too are believed to be wise … if we are raised according to the judgment of the rest”; one has, “if they are raised.”]

If we trust the wise, and those in whom the divine Spirit spoke were hastening toward better things; if we inquire into the judgments of others, to discover that all agree in one opinion, how many preferred death to sorrow, how many preferred death to fear? Clearly, they judged the fear of death more grievous than death itself. So little is death feared for its own evils that it is preferred to the miseries of life, when the end of the dying is desired and the fear of the living is avoided.

126. But let it be granted that resurrection is preferred to this life. What have the philosophers themselves discovered after death, some condition which will delight us more than resurrection? Those who say that souls are immortal cannot sufficiently console me, since they redeem only part of me. For what grace can there be when I have not escaped whole? What life is there if God’s work in me perishes? What justice, if death is the end of nature and is common to the sinner and the righteous? What truth is there in believing the soul immortal because it moves itself and is always in motion?

[Note: By “the end of nature,” understand the dissolution of the naturally composite being, not the destruction of both its constituent parts; for he is arguing against those philosophers who admitted the immortality of the soul, that is, the Platonists. Yet he seems especially to have Cicero in view, who in Tusculan Disputations I, having rejected the poets’ fictions concerning punishments in the underworld, concludes by this dilemma that no one ought to fear death: “How, then, or why do you say that death seems evil to you, which will either make us blessed while our souls remain, or will not make us miserable if we are without sensation?”]

That what we have in common with beasts belongs to the body, while what takes place before the body is uncertain; and that truth is not established from opposites, but destroyed.

127. Or do you approve the opinion of those who say that our souls, when they have departed from this body, pass into the bodies of wild beasts and various living creatures?

[Note: Irenaeus, Against Heresies II, chapter 59, makes Plato the first author of this error. It cannot indeed be denied that this philosopher followed this opinion in the Phaedo, the Timaeus, and Book X of the Republic; but what we observed above at section 55—that the opinion originated with him—is entirely refuted.]

But certainly the philosophers themselves are accustomed to explain that these are the fictions of poets, composed through the allurements of Circe’s potions; and they say that it was not those who supposedly underwent these transformations, but the minds of those who invented them, that were changed, as though by a Circean cup, into various monstrous beasts.

[Note: The old edition reads, “like Circean peoples”; the Roman edition and the manuscripts more suitably read, “like a Circean cup.” The famous story concerns Circe, the daughter of the Sun, and her sorceries; see Homer, Odyssey XII; Ovid, Metamorphoses XIV, fable 1; Augustine, City of God XVIII, chapter 17; and others.]

For what is as much like a prodigy as the belief that human beings could be changed into the form of beasts? How much greater a prodigy it would be for the soul that governs a human being to assume the nature of beasts, hostile to the human race, and for a being capable of reason to pass into an irrational animal, than for the body’s appearance to be changed! You yourselves destroy these claims by what you teach. For you have transmitted, through magical incantations, the forms of this monstrous transformation.

128. Poets make these things into playthings; philosophers condemn them. And what they consider fictitious concerning the living, they judge true concerning the dead. Yet those who invented these tales wished not to prove their own story, but to mock the errors of the philosophers—those who think that the same soul which, with a gentle and humble purpose, was accustomed to overcome anger, assume patience, and abstain from bloodshed could, inflamed by the roaring movement of a lion, impatient of anger and unrestrained in madness, thirst for blood and desire slaughter;

and that the soul which moderated the diverse roars of peoples by a kind of royal judgment and soothed them with rational speech could afterward, amid trackless places and deserts, submit to howl in the manner of wolves;

or that the soul which, groaning beneath an unjust burden, bellowed with pitiable complaint under the harsh labors of the plow could afterward, changed into human form, seek horns upon a smooth brow.

[Note: Nannius says that “smooth” is the opposite of “rough.” Virgil, concerning the daughters of Proetus: “And often she would seek horns upon her smooth forehead.”]

Or that the soul which previously was borne aloft by swift wings to the heights of heaven through the upper air by the oarage of its wings would afterward seek flights no longer its own and grieve that it had grown sluggish under the weight of a human body.

129. Perhaps this is also why you lost that Icarus: the youth, led astray by your arguments, had perhaps first believed that he himself had been a bird. Thus also many old men were deceived, credulous of the swan-tales, while they thought that by soothing themselves with mournful melodies they could change their white hair into white feathers and linger in grievous sorrow.

[Note: All editions and some manuscripts read, “so that they might remain in grievous sorrow”; two have, “so that they might die of sorrow”; the rest, more harmoniously, read as in the text. By “swan-tales” he refers to the transformation of Cygnus, overcome with grief at the death of his kinsman Phaethon, into the bird bearing his name. See Ovid, Metamorphoses II, fable 4; similarly, concerning Icarus, Book VIII, fable 3.]

130. How unbelievable these things are! How deformed! How much more fitting it is to believe according to nature, to believe according to the use seen in other fruits, to believe according to examples of deeds, the oracles of the prophets, and Christ’s heavenly promise. What, indeed, is more excellent than to judge that God’s work does not perish, and that those made according to the image and likeness of God cannot be transferred into the forms of beasts, since the image of God is not bodily, but spiritual?

For how could a human being, to whom the remaining classes of living creatures are subject, migrate in his better part into an animal subject to him? Nature does not permit this; and if nature did permit it, grace would not.

131. But I shall see what opinion you, nations, hold concerning yourselves. For it ought not to seem surprising that you believe yourselves capable of being changed into beasts, since you worship beasts. I would nevertheless prefer that you judge yourselves according to your merit more favorably, so that you may believe yourselves destined not among the companies of beasts, but among the fellowship of angels.

[Note: The old edition reads, “believe that you will be there, and that your souls, from this winding course of life, strive … and thus that it belongs to the saints to arrive.” The Roman edition cut off this final portion. But the manuscripts establish our reading with complete agreement, except that some read, “to ascend to heavenly things.”]

132. From this winding course of life and the filth of the earthly body, the soul has the power to depart and strive toward those heavenly assemblies, and, since it belongs to the saints to arrive there, to sing praise to God—as we learn from the prophetic reading that those who played the cithara sang (Rev. XIV, 2): “For great and wondrous are your works, Lord God Almighty; your ways are just and true, King of the nations!

[Note: The Roman edition, following the Vulgate, reads, “King of the ages”; all the manuscripts and the old edition read, “King of the nations”; the Greek is ὁ βασιλεὺς τῶν ἁγίων, “King of the holy ones.” Below, where all editions and many manuscripts read “to see” and “to see the bridal chambers,” several manuscripts have “to behold” in both places. This is not sufficiently correct, for those infinitives depend on the preceding sentence, “the soul has the power …”]

Who will not fear and glorify your name? For you alone are holy, because all nations will come and worship before you.”

To see also your wedding, Jesus, at which the bride is led from earthly things to heavenly things amid the songs of universal joy; for all flesh will come to you (Ps. LXIV, 3), no longer subject to the world but joined to the Spirit; to see the bridal chambers adorned with fine linen, roses, lilies, and crowns.

[Note: All editions and most manuscripts read, “For whose other wedding are they thus adorned with the purple of confessors?” The Roman edition has “with the labor of confessors”; but the Turon, German, and Victor manuscripts more suitably read as in the text. Ambrose uses “purple” here for the violet color, which he considers characteristic of confessors; see Commentary on Luke VII, section 128.]

For whose other wedding are they adorned in such a way? They are adorned with the purple of confessors, the blood of martyrs, the lilies of virgins, and also the crowns of priests.

133. This is what holy David desired above all else, that he might look upon and behold these things. Finally he says: “One thing I have asked from the Lord; this I will seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, and behold the delight of the Lord” (Ps. XXVI, 4–5).

134. It is pleasing to believe this; it is delightful to hope for it. Certainly, not to have believed is punishment; to have hoped is grace. And if I am mistaken in this, because I prefer to be joined after death to angels rather than to beasts, I gladly make this mistake, nor will I ever, while I live, allow myself to be deprived of this belief.

135. For what consolation remains to me except that I hope to come to you, brother, more quickly, and that there will not be long separations between us after your departure; and that through your intercessions it may be granted that you summon me sooner, as I long for you? Who is there who ought not to desire this above all else for himself: that this corruptible body may put on incorruption and this mortal body put on immortality (I Cor. XV, 53), so that we who now succumb to death through the frailty of the body, being raised above nature, may no longer be able to fear death?

[Note: Several manuscripts read, “that he may be above nature, so as to fear death,” and so forth.]

## Consolation on the Death of Valentinian

[Col. 1355]

### Prefatory Notice to the Consolation on the Death of Valentinian

[Col. 1355]

The younger Valentinian was preparing to return from Gaul to Italy, where fear of the threatened invasion of the barbarians was calling him, when he was removed from the living through the treachery of the count Arbogast on the Ides of May in the year 392, on the eve of holy Pentecost. His body was brought back to Milan not long afterward and was kept there in his palace until the emperor’s instructions concerning his burial could be received. When the emperor’s letter on this matter finally arrived, Valentinian’s funeral rites were celebrated. On that occasion Ambrose delivered the following speech in honor of the prince, who had been taken from imperial power and life in the twentieth year of his age.

After briefly explaining the reasons that led him to speak (section 1), he says that Valentinian had come (section 2), but surrounded by the tears of all who mourned him as a public parent (section 3). Then (sections 3 and following), borrowing laments from Jeremiah in order to mourn the prince, he asserts that Valentinian, who had united the maturity of counsel with the bloom of youth and had drawn even barbarians into reverence for himself, was mourned by all Italy in common; yet that this grief especially concerned the Church (sections 5 and 6), since by the deaths of Gratian and Valentinian she had been struck on both cheeks.

After showing how rare it is for the young either to keep themselves entirely from vices or to return promptly to a better way of life, he demonstrates (sections 9 and following) that Valentinian had submitted his neck to the yoke of the Lord while still a young man; and that if there had been anything in his conduct which might have provided an opportunity for detraction, it had been erased by such rapid correction (sections 14 and following) that the mouths of his slanderers were silenced. Then turning his discourse to the virtues of this prince, he praises his piety magnificently, bringing forward the most beautiful examples of that virtue (sections 18 and following). To this he adds (sections 21 and following) his love for the peoples, whom he could neither be induced to burden with new taxes nor fail to defend from the barbarians, even at evident risk to his life.

There the holy man, recalling Valentinian’s affection toward himself (sections 23 and following), and elegantly explaining how ardently the prince had desired to be baptized by him and to use him as his guarantor before Arbogast, allows the tenderest emotions of his love and grief to break forth, so that he might openly reveal the vows and plans he had formed for the benefit of that prince, who loved him in the place of a parent. Thereafter he skillfully enlarges upon the great benevolence with which the emperor embraced his friends and the great affection with which he embraced his sisters (sections 35 and following). Turning his speech to the sisters, he undertakes to teach them what measure should be observed in mourning a brother’s death (sections 41 and following). He treats with particular care the circumstance that they grieved him all the more because he had died before receiving baptism (sections 51 and following).

From that consolation he turns to prayers, earnestly begging and imploring divine mercy not to separate Valentinian from Gratian, and exhorting his hearers to appease God on behalf of both through their common prayers (sections 54 and following). After this, wishing to illuminate the virtues of both with greater splendor, he applies several passages from the Song of Songs to them; yet he employs such caution and reverence there (sections 58 and following) that he removes every opportunity for offense or calumny. Finally, after solemnly declaring that no forgetfulness of these princes could ever enter his prayers or sacrifices, he again gives free rein to his grief (sections 77 and following). But here too, taking refuge in God, he implores him (section 81) not to allow him to be separated from them in the age to come, and to compensate for their untimely death by granting them an earlier resurrection.

From this speech we can readily recognize that it was delivered when the funeral rites were being performed for Valentinian. As for the year and day on which he was buried, their determination depends entirely upon knowing the year and day on which that prince was killed. But Marcellinus Comes is not once free from error in establishing these matters. For he writes in his Chronicle: “In the consulship of Tatianus and Symmachus, the emperor Theodosius, leaving Italy, returned to Constantinople. The emperor Valentinian died at Vienne, strangled by the treachery of Arbogast, on the Ides of March.”

His first error here is that he places the killing in the consulship of Tatianus and Symmachus. For it is established that in the year 391, when they held that office, Theodosius was still at Milan on the Ides of April, and that Valentinian, who had accompanied him to Aquileia, had not yet departed in July. Marcellinus errs again in saying that Arbogast’s crime occurred on the Ides of March; for that date cannot in any way agree with what Ambrose says in Letter 53 (section 5) about the summer heat.

For this reason learned authorities prefer the testimony of Epiphanius, who asserts that the same killing took place on the Ides of May, in the consulship of Arcadius for the second time and Rufinus for the first, on the day before Pentecost (On Weights and Measures, section 20)—that is, as we have already said, in the year 392, on May 15. Therefore, if you add the two months during which Ambrose says that Justa and Grata mourned their brother’s death (sections 49 and 50) to Epiphanius’s reckoning, you will understand that the funeral of this emperor was postponed until the Ides of July while the command of Theodosius was awaited.

Nevertheless, a certain doubt may arise even from this opinion, because when Ambrose writes in the letter mentioned above that Valentinian’s burial should be hastened, he gives this reason: “lest the remains of the dead prince should completely dissolve in the summer heat; for we have scarcely passed through the preceding summer” (section 5). It must indeed be admitted that, if these words are interpreted according to common usage, they indicate not so much the middle of July as the beginning of autumn. Yet it is more certain that Valentinian was found with his throat crushed on the Ides of May and remained unburied for no more than two months than that his funeral can be postponed until autumn. We must therefore say that the expression “the preceding summer” means nothing more than that part of the summer heat which had already passed.

In the old editions, the title of this little work was: Funeral Speech on the Death of the Emperor Valentinian. In the Roman edition it is: Funeral Sermon on the Death of Valentinian the Younger, Augustus. The manuscripts also vary in the wording of the title. Some present it in this form: Here Begins the Treatise on the Death of the Emperor Valentinian the Younger; but in many more it is expressed thus: Here Begins the Consolation of Valentinian—“Letter of Consolation” in some manuscripts—and in some places τὸ junioris [“of the younger”] is added.

From this it is clear that in the headings of works copyists often add material according to their own inclination; but amid these minor variations the genuine title is easily recognized. In this matter Ambrose had great authors whom he could follow. Cicero’s composition on the death of his daughter is prefaced by the title Consolation. Plutarch also published a book entitled Consolation to Apollonius. But no author has more writings marked by this title than the philosopher Seneca, who gave the same heading to three little books.

[Col. 1357]

## Saint Ambrose, Bishop of Milan: Consolation on the Death of Valentinian

[Note: Written in the year 392.]

[Col. 1357]

1. Although writing about the one whose loss we mourn increases our grief, nevertheless, because we often find rest in recalling the person whom we mourn as lost—for when we direct our mind toward him in writing and fix our attention upon him, he seems to revive for us in speech—it seemed important to record something about the final days of the younger Valentinian. I did not wish either to appear to have effaced in silence the memory of one who had deserved well of us and to have left our pledge of affection unhonored, or to have shrunk from the stimulus to grief, since having grieved is often a consolation to the grieving. At the same time, when I speak about him or to him, my speech is as though he were present or as though I were speaking to one who is present.

[Note: Throughout this little work Ambrose speaks of Valentinian as of a most beloved son. That he was likewise regarded by this prince in the name and place of a parent is clear both from the following conclusion and from Letter 53 to Theodosius, as noted there.]

2. What, then, shall I mourn first? What shall I first lament in bitter complaint? The days of our hopes have been turned for us into tears, since Valentinian came to us—but not as he was expected. Yet even by his death he wished to fulfill his promise; but his presence, which we had desired, became most bitter to us. Would that he were still absent from us, so that he might live for himself! But when he heard that the Alps of Italy were being threatened by a barbarian enemy, he preferred to put himself in danger by leaving Gaul rather than fail us in our danger.

[Note: All editions and a few manuscripts read, “a great danger.” It is likely, however, that scribes were led to place the word “danger” by the preceding word “danger,” whereas the reading of the majority of manuscripts, which have “crime,” gives a more suitable sense. It is not easy to say who the barbarians were from whom danger threatened the empire, for it is mentioned below that there were also others who were well disposed toward the emperor and his empire.]

We recognize the emperor’s great crime: he wished to come to the aid of the Roman Empire! This is a cause of death filled with praise. Let us pay tears as tribute to the good prince, because he paid us even the tribute of his death.

3. Yet no exhortation to weep is necessary. Everyone weeps: the unknown weep, those who feared him weep, the unwilling weep, the barbarians weep, and those who seemed to be enemies weep.

[Note: This is an imitation of Virgil, Aeneid VI, where one reads:

“How many groans of men did that field drive toward the great city of Mars?”]

How many groans did he draw from the peoples along the entire course of his journey from Gaul to this place? For all, weeping with the grief of a household, shed tears over him as though a public parent had died, and all mourn their own funerals. We have lost an emperor in whom two things equally intensified our grief: the immaturity of his years and the old age of his counsels.

[Note: Ambrose repeatedly testifies that Valentinian was killed in the flower of youth, and he likewise says this of Gratian in more than one place. Certainly, the authorities agree that the former died in the twentieth year of his age; as for the latter, although Fulgentius Victor places his death in the thirty-eighth year of his age, Baronius maintains that “twenty-eighth” should be read there. Indeed, some even deny that he was older than twenty-four when he died. See Socrates V, chapter 11; Sozomen VII, chapter 13; and others.]

In this I weep as the Prophet said: “My eyes have grown dim from weeping, because he who consoled me has been taken far from me” (Lam. I, 16). Not only the eyes of my body but also those of my mind have been weakened, and every sense has been covered with a kind of blindness, because he has been taken from me who turned my soul and recalled me from the deepest despair concerning affairs to the greatest hope.

4. Hear, all peoples, and see my grief. “My virgins and my young men have gone into captivity” (ibid., 18); but when they learned that they were on Valentinian’s side, they returned free.

The barbarian enemy served the youthful emperor and, forgetting his victory, remembered imperial reverence. He voluntarily released those whom he had captured, apologizing that he had not known they were Italians.

We were still preparing to add a wall to the Alps. Valentinian’s favor did not await the barrier of the Alps, the currents of rivers, or the ramparts of snow; but, having crossed the Alps and the rivers, it protected us with the wall of his empire. Therefore I seem to need the opening of the prophetic Lamentations: “How Italy mourns, which abounded in joys! Weeping, she wept in the night, and her tears are upon her cheeks. There is no one to comfort her among all those who love her. All who love her have despised her. All her people groan” (ibid., II).

5. And because it was said of Jerusalem, “Weeping, she wept in the night,” our Jerusalem also—that is, the Church—“wept in the night,” because he who made her brighter through his faith and devotion has fallen. Rightly, therefore, she wept as she wept, and still her tears are upon her cheeks.

[Note: Several manuscripts read, “It was said: She wept. And our …”]

The abundance of tears is usually revealed by the moisture poured over the face, when the cheeks are bedewed with tears; but since it is written, “His cheeks are like bowls of spices producing perfumes, his lips are lilies distilling full-flowing myrrh” (Song V, 13), the mystical grace of the weeping Church is understood, for at Valentinian’s death she poured out the good perfume of her grief and celebrates his life by proclaiming it. Death could not harm him, because the fragrance of his proclamation, celebrated by the mouths of all, wiped away every stench of death.

[Note: So read the majority and better manuscripts. The old edition and some manuscripts have, “mystically, the grace of the Church”; the Roman edition has, “mystical myrrh,” and so forth.]

### 6

The Church therefore weeps for her pledge, and her tears are upon her cheeks. Hear what “cheek” means: “If anyone strikes you on the cheek, offer him the other also” (Luke 6:29), because he is patient in his sufferings so that the one who strikes may repent. You were struck, O Church, upon one cheek when you lost Gratian; you offered the other when Valentinian was taken from you. Rightly, then, your tears are not upon one cheek only but upon both, because in pious grief you mourn both brothers. You weep, therefore, O Church, and in your weeping your cheeks overflow like flowing drops of piety. What are these cheeks of the Church? Those of which Scripture says elsewhere: “Your cheeks are like the rind of a pomegranate” (Song of Songs 6:6). These are the cheeks upon which modesty commonly shines and beauty gleams; upon which there is either the flower of youth or the mark of mature age.

[Note: Nannius understands the reference to be to the beard itself, which is the distinguishing mark of mature age; hence the subsequent mention of Aaron’s beard.]

At the death, therefore, of faithful emperors there is a certain modesty of faith, a certain shamefastness of the Church; and in the exceedingly premature death of pious rulers the entire beauty of the Church is made more mournful.

### 7

The Church weeps in her wise men, who are like the head of the Church—for “the eyes of the wise man are in his head” (Ecclesiastes 2:14). She weeps in her eyes, that is, in her faithful, because it is written: “Your eyes are like doves, apart from your silence” (Song of Songs 4:1), since they see spiritually and know how to keep silent about the mysteries they have seen.

She weeps in her priests, who are like the cheeks of the Church, upon which is Aaron’s beard (Psalm 132:2)—that is, the priestly beard, upon which the anointing oil descends from the head. These are the ones in whom the Church’s beauty resides, in whom her flower is more gracious, in whom her age is more mature. Like the rinds of pomegranates, they display beauty outwardly through bodily abstinence, while inwardly they nourish with spiritual wisdom the people entrusted to them, of every age and sex—exposed to the world’s injuries, yet dividing its inner mysteries.

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “but inwardly dividing the mysteries.” P. Nannius observes that there is an allusion to the rind or husk of pomegranates, by which the seeds within are divided.]

She weeps in her virgins, who are like lilies—lilies full of myrrh—displaying the whiteness of integrity and the glory of mortified bodily desire.

### 8

In these, then, she weeps, as it is written: “The roads of Zion mourn; her priests groan; her virgins have been carried away, and she herself is indignant within herself” (Lamentations 1:4). Within herself indeed she is indignant; but to Valentinian she says: “I will take you and bring you into the house of my mother, and into the chamber of her who conceived me. “I will give you to drink of wine from the ointment of much labor and rich fragrance, from the flow of my pomegranates” (Song of Songs 8:2);; so that he may drink the wine “that gladdens the human heart” (Psalm 103:15), and so that the flow of the pomegranates may pour over him, in which there is abundant and varied fruit.

[Note: Thus read all the manuscripts; the older edition differs only in reading *unguenti* (“of ointment”) instead of *unguento* (“ointment”). The Roman edition judged that both words should be omitted.]

For the discourse of many meanings, abounding in passages from diverse Scriptures—the discourse of angels, apostles, and prophets, whom holy Church encloses within one kind of rind—is the flow of the pomegranates.

### 9

Seeing these things, Valentinian, full of perfect grace, replies: “It is because of the Lord’s mercies that we have not perished, because his compassions have not come to an end. He will renew them like the morning light” (Lamentations 3:22–23). “My sighs are many, and my heart has failed. The Lord is my portion, I said; therefore I will wait for him. The Lord is good to those who wait for him, to the soul that seeks him. It is good to hope in the salvation of the Lord. It is good for a man, when he has borne the heavy yoke in his youth, to sit alone and keep silence, because he has borne the heavy yoke” (ibid., 24 and following).

He consoles himself with the reward of his virtues, since in his youth he absorbed labors and endured many dangers. He preferred to bear the heavy yoke of a more disciplined purpose,

[Note: One manuscript reads “of an intended reform”; another, “of a more elevated purpose.”]

rather than that soft yoke, full of delights,

[Note: The older edition and some manuscripts read “the envy of the mind’s delights”; the Roman edition reads “the enticements of delights.” A large number of manuscripts, as in the text, read “the mind’s neck bent beneath the riches of the world,” with a few exceptions.]

upon the vigorous neck of his mind.

### 10

Clearly blessed is the one who, even in old age,

[Note: The Codex Regius reads: “rose from error.”]

corrected his error; blessed is the one who, even at the moment of death, turned his mind away from vices. “Blessed are those whose sins are covered” (Psalm 31:1), because it is written: “Turn away from evil and do good, and dwell forever and ever” (Psalm 33:15).

Whoever, therefore, ceases from sins and turns toward better things at whatever age will obtain pardon for his former sins, whether he has confessed them through a penitential disposition or has turned away from them through the resolve to correct himself.

Yet this man must earn fellowship in obtaining pardon with many others;

[Note: Cicero, *Oration for Marcus Caelius*: “And many … were great men and distinguished citizens, whose youthful desires, once they had cooled, gave rise to extraordinary virtues when their age had already become established.” It may safely be said that Ambrose was looking to these words.]

for there are many who have been able in old age to withdraw from sins and the slippery ways of youth, but rare is the person who in youth has borne the heavy yoke with serious sobriety. This is the yoke of which the Lord says in the Gospel: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you; take my yoke upon you” (Matthew 11:28–29).

If, therefore, before being weighed down by the heavy burden of sins, someone bears the yoke in youth, he will sit alone—not to be compared with the multitude, but with the one who can say: “For you alone have established me in hope” (Psalm 4:10).

### 11

But perhaps you will say: How does Jeremiah call it a heavy yoke, when in the Gospel the Lord says: “My yoke is easy and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:29)?

First, learn that the Greek text has merely *yoke* and does not add *heavy*.

[Note: Ambrose’s habit of consulting various versions of Scripture can be recognized not only from this passage but from many others. In the Septuagint the text reads only: Ἀγαθὸν ἀνδρὶ ὅταν ἄρῇ ζυγὸν—“It is good for a man when he bears a yoke”—but the Latin Fathers commonly admit the word *heavy*, as, for example, Hilary in his exposition of Psalm 118, letter Beth, and Cassiodorus on the same psalm, verse 147. Ambrose seems to have followed them in Sermon 9 on this very psalm, where he has the same wording.

Nobilius, reporting the distinction Ambrose here draws between that prophetic yoke and the evangelical yoke—“How could Jeremiah say ‘a heavy yoke’ when the Lord says, ‘My yoke is easy’?”—adds: “The translator of Theodoret: because he takes the heavy yoke upon himself.”.”]

Yet observe this also: even if the passage in Lamentations reads thus (Lamentations 3:27), in the Gospel he nevertheless called the yoke easy and the burden light—not the yoke light. The yoke of the Word may indeed be heavy, yet easy: heavy for an adolescent, heavy for a young man whose age is in its flower, so that he may be unwilling to offer his neck for the yoke of the Word. The yoke of the Word may also seem heavy because of the burdens of discipline, the severity of correction, the weight of abstinence, and the restraint of wantonness; yet it is sweet through the fruit of grace, the hope of eternal reward, and the sweetness of a purer conscience.

[Note: All editions read “seem heavy because of the weight of discipline, austerity,” and so forth; all the manuscripts, on the contrary, read as in the text.]

Nevertheless, he called the yoke of the Word easy and the burden of obedience light, because for the one who receives the yoke of the Word upon a patient neck, the burden of discipline cannot be heavy.

### 12

Whoever, then, bears the yoke from youth will sit alone and keep silence, rejoicing that the eternal mysteries of divine reward have been revealed to him. Or certainly he will keep silence because he has no need to excuse his sin, having forestalled it through mature confession and laid it aside through prompt correction.

It will not be said to him: “What you did not gather in youth, how will you find in old age?” (Ecclesiastes 25:5).

This may also be understood in the following way: whoever quickly bears the yoke of the Word—that is, from youth—will not mingle with young men, but will sit apart and keep silence,

until he has trained himself in the fullness of virtue and clothed his soul with great patience. He will offer his cheek to the one who strikes it, even despising the injury of a beating,

[Note: All editions read “content with the injury”; some manuscripts read “contented with the injury,” while the greater number and better manuscripts read “despising the injury.”]

so that he may obey the heavenly commandments.

### 13

For it is a great thing either to abstain from the vices of youth or to abandon them at the very threshold of youth and turn toward more mature pursuits;

[Note: Thus read the manuscripts, except for one or two, which have “toward higher things”; all the editions, however, give “toward healthier things.” Although the latter reading may seem more usual, *ad seriora* may be understood as meaning “toward more serious pursuits,” or at least “toward later pursuits”—that is, the pursuits of old age..]

for the ways of youth are slippery and tangled. Finally, Solomon says: “There are three things that are impossible for me to understand, and a fourth that I do not know: the track of an eagle flying, the way of a serpent upon a rock, the path of a ship sailing, and the way of a man in his youth” (Proverbs 30:18–19).

David, however, says: “Remember not the sins of my youth and my ignorance” (Psalm 25:7). For a young man slips not only because of the treacherous weakness of his age, but often sins also through ignorance of the heavenly commandments. Yet the one who pleads ignorance quickly obtains pardon.

The prophet therefore says: “Remember not the sins of my youth and my ignorance.” He does not say: “Remember not the sins of my old age and my knowledge”; rather, like a prophet who quickly corrected and amended the vices of youth, he pleads his age and his ignorance.

### 14

Valentinian likewise, even in his sin, says in imitation of the prophet: “Remember not the sins of my adolescence and my ignorance.” Nor did he merely say this; he corrected his error beforehand, before he learned that he had fallen into any error. Therefore he says: “Remember not the correction of my youth.” Error is found in many; correction in few.

### 15

And what shall I say now of the others, since he even thought that the amusements of youth ought to be renounced, the license of age cut away,

[Note: Some manuscripts read “the joyfulness of age.” Here too, we believe that there is an allusion to the Ciceronian oration cited above.]

the harshness of public severity softened, and the gentleness of old age extended to another’s years for the one who was summoned to face the danger of an established accusation?

He was initially reported to enjoy the circus games. He removed this tendency so completely that he did not even consider the circus spectacles appropriate for the solemn birthdays of emperors or for the honor of the imperial office.

[Note: This passage reveals Philostorgius’ hostile attitude toward this emperor. Speaking of him in Book 11, he says: “While he was using bears and lions, in the twentieth year of his life he was deprived at once of life, empire, and the hunting of wild beasts.” But what clearer sign of Valentinian’s reform could he have given than abstaining from such spectacles even on the most solemn days and ordering the beasts themselves killed—animals which, as has been noted in Book 2 of *Duties*, chapter 21, section 109, were customarily brought from Africa and more distant regions?]

Some said that he was occupied with the hunting of wild beasts and that his attention was being drawn away from public affairs. He ordered all the beasts killed in a single moment.

### 16

He heard cases in the council chamber and, with the spirit of Daniel, rendered a youthful yet senile judgment in matters about which old men were uncertain or were swayed by the presence of some individual.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “and even matters in which they were led … so that you might see him, with Daniel’s spirit, bearing a senile judgment as a young man.” The older edition and the manuscripts agree with our text, except that only a few manuscripts add the particle *que* after *senilem*.]

The envious spread the charge that he requested his midday meal prematurely. He began to practice fasting so regularly that he would often, while still fasting, provide the customary banquet for his Counts, thereby satisfying both sacred religion

[Note: This fasting was ecclesiastical rather than merely voluntary, since the text below says: “by which he might also satisfy sacred religion.” Nevertheless, it was not open to the emperor to refuse his commanders the banquets customarily provided on the days of that fast, especially since many among those same commanders still followed the pagan religion.]

and the emperor’s humaneness.

[Note: Several manuscripts read: “and that the emperor’s humaneness, in some theatrical form and with its decorum, should not perish. At Rome a noble youth was reported … he ordered, etc.” This is less satisfactory. The *Theodosian Code*, law 5 on stage performers, from the year 389, survives; by it this same Valentinian forbids a *thymelica*—that is, a female stage performer who performs music and dances on the *thymele*, a part of the orchestra—from being taken away from the City. Godefroy believes that this law was issued at Ambrose’s urging, and he is probably right to connect it with this history.]

### 17

It was reported that certain young nobles at Rome were being ruined by the beauty and grace of a stage performer. He ordered her to come to the imperial court. The messenger, corrupted by a bribe, returned without accomplishing the order. He sent another messenger, lest he appear to have wished to reform the young men’s vices but been unable to do so. This gave some people an opportunity to criticize him; yet, once she had been brought there, he neither watched her perform nor saw her privately.

[Note: Either he watched her, namely on the stage, or he saw her, that is, privately.]

Afterward he ordered her to return, both so that everyone might recognize that his command had not been ineffectual and so that he might teach the young men to restrain themselves from love of a woman whom he himself, though able to keep her under his authority, had despised.

He did this while he still had no wife, and yet displayed a chastity as though he were bound by marriage. Who was ever so much master of a servant as he was of his own body? Who was ever so much the judge of others as he was the censor of his own age?

### 18

What shall I say of his piety? When men of noble birth,

[Note: Some manuscripts read “men wealthy in ancestry.” Here the more serious difference lies in the division of the clauses than in the words themselves. All the editions punctuate the following as: “which quickly tends to stir envy of royal ambition, when the accuser pressed the charge,” whereas the manuscripts punctuate it: “which quickly tends to stir envy, when the accuser pressed the charge of royal ambition.” The latter meaning is clearly superior, since in the former the substance of the crime or accusation is not stated, whereas in the latter it is—the accusation of royal ambition, that is, of an attempted seizure of the throne and royal title.

That the emperor denied he would allow anything bloody to be decreed on holy days is beyond dispute; the reference is to the Easter holidays, which were called by this name because of the preeminence of the feast. Ambrose speaks of them in Letter 20, section 6: “Therefore, on the holy days of the last week, when the bonds of debtors used to be loosened,” and so forth.

Valentinian’s reverence for these days was all the more praiseworthy because not only were persons guilty of various crimes ordered to be released at this feast by Law 3 on Criminal Pardons, enacted by Valentinian the Elder, with the exception of those guilty of treason; this Valentinian himself also promulgated three other laws, in the years 381, 384, and 385.]

and wealthy lineage—which is apt quickly to stir envy—were being pressed by an accuser on a charge of royal ambition, while the prefect pressed the case, he replied that nothing bloody should be decreed, especially on holy days..

When, after several days, the accuser’s written charge was read, he declared it calumnious

[Note: The Roman edition, together with the earlier editions, reads “about to declare it calumnious”; in the following line it alone reads “he ordered the same person to appear.” The manuscripts, in both places, read as in our text.]

and ordered that the accused man should remain at liberty until the prefect had investigated the matter. Neither before nor afterward did anyone, under a youthful emperor, fear the envy aroused by so serious a charge. The young man laughed at what robust emperors fear.

### 19

Rome had sent ambassadors to recover the rights of the temples,,

[Note: Some manuscripts read “the privileges of the priests.” At two different times the pagans sought from the younger Valentinian the restoration of their religious practices. The first was in the year 384, when Symmachus was prefect of Rome; Ambrose replied to his report in Letters 17 and 18.

Since they obtained nothing at that time, they later repeated their attempt, believing that they had found a more favorable opportunity—namely, when Theodosius had returned to Constantinople and Valentinian had been almost reduced to servitude in Gaul by Arbogast—but again without success. This passage concerns the latter petition, which, as Ambrose indicates below, was presented shortly before the emperor’s death.

He distinguishes both petitions admirably in Letter 57, addressed to Eugenius. From that letter Paulinus’ error is exposed: Paulinus had attributed to the embassy sent to the Caesar in Gaul two works by Ambrose, as we observed in the notes to that letter.

Ambrose’s silence here concerning the earlier report is due both to modesty, lest he appear to praise himself, and to honor toward Valentinian, to whom all the glory of rejecting the second petition belonged.]

the profane privileges of the priesthood, and the rites of their sacred worship. More seriously still, they claimed to act in the name of the senate. And when everyone present in the council chamber, Christians and pagans alike, said that these things ought to be restored, he alone, like Daniel (Daniel 13:45), stirred by God’s Spirit within him, accused the Christians of treachery and opposed the pagans, saying: “How do you suppose that I should restore what my pious brother took away, when in doing so both religion and my brother would be injured, and he would not wish to be surpassed by me in piety?”

### 20

When they appealed to the example of his father, saying that no one had taken these things away under his father, he replied: “You praise my father because he did not take them away; nor did I take them away. Did my father restore them, so that you demand that I restore them? Finally, even if my father had restored them, my brother had taken them away, and in this matter I would prefer to imitate my brother. Or was my father an Augustus and my brother not? Equal reverence is owed to both, and both have shown equal concern for the state. I will imitate both: I will not restore what my father could not restore, because no one had taken it away; and I will preserve what was established by my brother.

“Let Rome, as a parent, ask for anything else she desires. I owe affection to my parent, but I owe greater obedience to the author of salvation.”

### 21

What shall I say of his love for the provincials—of the love with which he himself embraced them, or of the love they returned to their counselor, since he never allowed any impost to be imposed upon them?

““They cannot pay the arrears,” he said; “will they be able to bear new burdens?”?”

[Note: Understand this as referring to the apostate Julian, from whose remissions to the provincials we learn something in Law 11 on Exemptions from Obligations, Law 1 on Remission of Debts, and likewise Law 1 on the Gold Crown. Pagan writers praise this emperor’s generosity to an astonishing degree. Consult Libanius, Mamertinus in his panegyric, and Ammianus, Book 25 of the *History*, chapter 4. Valesius admits that this passage is difficult to reconcile with what Ammianus had said in Book 16, chapter 5.]

For this the provinces praise Julian: he in the strength of manhood, this man while advancing through adolescence; he found very much and exhausted everything, whereas this man found nothing and abounded in everything.

### 22

While he was stationed in the regions beyond the Alps, he heard that barbarians had approached the borders of Italy. Anxious lest his kingdom be attacked by a foreign enemy, he hastened to come, eager to abandon the leisure of Gaul and take upon himself our dangers.

### 23

These matters I shared with others. The following were personal to me: he often called for me while I was absent,

[Note: The older edition, together with part of the manuscripts, reads “and that he had been initiated by me.” The Roman edition, together with another group, reads “and that he was to be initiated by me”—a reading that is preferable, as what follows clearly persuades us.. One may also add what the holy man writes to Theodosius in Letter 53, section 2.]

and preferred to be initiated by me into the sacred mysteries. Indeed, when a certain rumor reached the city of Vienne—that I was going there in order to invite him to Italy—how delighted he was, how he rejoiced that I would soon be with him as he desired! My delay in arriving seemed too long to him. And would that no messenger had preceded my arrival!

### 24

I had already promised that I would set out, replying both to the honorable men who requested it and to the prefect that, although modesty prevented me from intruding unnecessarily in order to provide for Italy’s tranquillity, I would not fail in the face of necessity.

[Note: Who are meant by the “honorable men” was explained in Book 2 of *Duties*, chapter 29, section 150. His statement that modesty restrained him from approaching the emperor agrees fully with Letter 1 to Gratian, section 1.]

This had been confirmed: behold, on the following day came letters concerning the preparation of stopping places, the conveyance of royal ornaments, and other such things indicating that the emperor was about to begin his journey.

[Note: Several manuscripts read: “Behold, after three days.” Immediately afterward, however, the reference to preparing the stopping places clearly means certain public lodgings prepared for emperors undertaking a journey, for governors, and even for the soldiers themselves when they set out on campaign. See Cassiodorus, Book 12 of the *Variae*, Letters 18 and 19.]

For these reasons, the embassy was suspended by the very people who had requested it.

### 25

I seemed guilty to myself because my hoped-for presence had not been fulfilled. But would that I owed you this guilt while you were still alive! I would excuse myself on the grounds that I had heard nothing of your dangers, received none of your letters, and could not have met you with my own animals, even if I had already begun the journey.

Thus, confident of pardon, while I counted the days and traced the course of your arrival, behold, I received a rescript telling me that I should proceed without delay, since you wished me to be a guarantor of your loyalty before your Count.

[Note: To this rescript we should refer what Ambrose writes in Letter 53, section 2: “He thought that I should initiate him through baptism.” It is therefore fairly probable that the reference is not to a rescript in the strict sense but to a letter written in Valentinian’s own hand, of the kind Ambrose says he received from Gratian in Letter 1, section 3.

In Letter 53 no reason is given for the emperor’s desire for the holy man’s arrival except that he was to be baptized. In this funeral oration, however, another reason is given first: Ambrose was to act as the emperor’s guarantor before Arbogast.

Certainly Arbogast’s hidden resentments had broken out into open hostility, as Gregory of Tours, drawing on the contemporary historian Severus Alexander, relates in Book 2 of his *History*, chapter 10, and as Zosimus, Book 4, and Philostorgius, Book 11, chapter 1, also report.

No one could have been more suitable than our Bishop for reconciling the Caesar and the Count, as is evident from what Paulinus relates in Ambrose’s *Life* concerning the high esteem in which Ambrose was held by that same Count.]

Did I resist? Did I delay? The message added that I should hasten more quickly and should not suppose that the reason for my journey was the synod of the Gallic bishops,

[Note: It is indeed established that those disagreements had nothing whatsoever to do with the substance of the faith. Ambrose, who always burned with such zeal in defending it, would never have withdrawn his presence from synods of this kind. They were either disputes that had arisen between the bishops of Arles and Vienne, as Quesnel judges in his *Dissertation on Saint Hilary of Arles*, or disturbances provoked on their occasion by those who had entered into communion with the Ithacians. We discussed this matter in the notes to Letters 24 and 26.]

on account of whose frequent disagreements I had repeatedly excused myself; rather, the reason was that he himself was to be baptized.

### 26

As soon as I set out, I was able to perceive indications of what had already happened, but in my eagerness to hurry I could pay attention to nothing. I was already crossing the Alpine passes when, behold, a bitter message came to me and to everyone concerning the death of so great an emperor.

I turned back from my journey and washed it with my tears. With what hopes of everyone was I setting out? With what grief of everyone was I returning? For they did not think that an emperor had been taken from them, but their salvation.

How deeply was I myself afflicted by grief—first because so great a ruler, my cherished pledge, so eager for me, had died! What agitation of his did I discover during those two days in which he survived the letter he had sent me? In the evening a *silentarius* set out;

[Note: Many laws concerning the *silentarii* exist in the *Theodosian Code*, under the title “On Decurions and Silentarii.” Their duty was to keep watch at the doors while the emperor was in council or conferring with his own people or with outsiders. Sometimes, however, men were selected from their corps to carry out the emperor’s commands, as can be learned both from this passage and from Philostorgius, Book 7, chapter 7.]

on the morning of the third day he was already asking whether the man had returned, whether I was now coming. Did he thus imagine that some deliverance would come to him?!

### 27

O excellent young man, would that I could have found you alive! Would that some delay had preserved you for my arrival! I make no promise concerning any virtue of mine, nothing concerning my ability or prudence; but with what care between you and your Count, with what diligence, would I have restored harmony and favor!

How I would have offered myself on behalf of your loyalty; how I would have taken upon myself those whom he said he feared!

[Note: Thus read the older edition and all the manuscripts. The Roman edition inserted the preposition *a* before *quibus*, producing an entirely opposite meaning. According to the older reading, Arbogast is represented as pretending to fear that the emperor might endanger certain men of his party; according to the Roman reading, the Count is represented as fearing violence or treachery from certain imperial attendants.]

Certainly, if the Count had not yielded, I would have remained with you. I assumed that you would listen to me if you saw that I had not been heard on your behalf.

### 28

I had many things that I could hold on to; now I have nothing except tears and weeping. Every day you grow greater to me in grief; you increase my lamentation.

[Note: Several manuscripts read: “You grow toward grief and groaning.” All testify how much you did for me.]

Everyone bears witness to how highly you valued me; everyone calls my absence the cause of your death. But I am not Elijah, nor am I a prophet, so that I could have known the future. I am only a voice crying out in grief, by which I can mourn the past.

What better thing can I do for you than repay with tears such great affection as you showed me? I received you as a little child,

[Note: It is established that Ambrose undertook two embassies to Maximus, concerning which the holy Bishop speaks at length in various letters. See Letter 20, section 23; Letter 21, section 20; and Letter 24, together with the observations on it.]

when I was going as an envoy to your enemy. I embraced you when you had been entrusted to the maternal hands of Justina. I went again as your envoy to Gaul, and that service was dear to me—first for your safety, then for the peace and piety with which you sought your brother’s remains: not yet secure on your behalf, and already anxious about the honor of your brother’s burial.

### 29

But let us return to the Lamentations and enter into the very depths of grief: “What shall I testify to you,” he says, “or to what shall I compare you, daughter of Jerusalem? Who will save you, and who will console you, virgin daughter of Zion? For your ruin has become great. Who will heal you?” (Lamentations 2:13).

But who will console me, from whom others seek the office of consolation? “He has filled me with bitterness; he has made me drunk with gall. I grieve in my belly; I grieve in my belly” (Lamentations 3:15; Jeremiah 4:19), to use the prophet’s language, because I have lost the one whom I was about to bring forth in the Gospel..

### 30

But he did not lose the grace he sought,

[Note: Perhaps no other Catholic Father asserts more strongly than Ambrose, in various passages—and especially in Book 2 of *On Abraham*, chapter 11, section 84; Sermon 3 on Psalm 118, section 14; and *On the Mysteries*, chapter 4, section 20—the absolute necessity of receiving baptism.

Nevertheless, those testimonies must be understood in such a way that they do not deny that baptism of desire, when baptism in water cannot be received, suffices for salvation. This is made clear by what is said here and below concerning that desire for baptism.

Pope Innocent III, in a letter to the bishop of Cremona, confirms on the testimony of our Doctor that a sincere desire for the sacrament, when it cannot be received in fact, brings salvation. Bernard says that he embraces this opinion on the authority both of Ambrose and of Augustine in his treatise addressed to Hugh of Saint-Victor.

Finally, this very passage from the oration is commonly cited in support of that position by Hugh of Saint-Victor, *On the Sacraments*, “On Baptism,” chapter 5; blessed Thomas, Part III, question 68, article 2; the Master of the Sentences, Book 4, distinction 4, section “There are also others”; and, after them, the general body of the scholastic theologians.]

for he has risen today for me in the discourse with which I was addressing the people. For when I had begun to expound the appointed reading, namely, that the poor people should bless God,

[Note: Observe, reader, with what zeal the holy Bishop devoted himself to preaching the divine word, since on the very day when he was to deliver the emperor’s funeral oration he did not omit first to interpret the Gospel to the people. We have already observed elsewhere that he sometimes spoke from the pulpit once and again on the same day.]

I began to ask who this people was and to distinguish between the two peoples: one rich, the other poor—the rich people of the Jews, the poor people of the Church. The former was rich in the oracles entrusted to it; the latter, poor because it borrowed the oracles of others.

Poor indeed, because it was gathered by the one who became poor, although he was rich, so that we might be enriched by his poverty: “For he emptied himself so that he might fill all” (2 Corinthians 8:9).

### 31

But how is he poor who possessed the riches of eternity and the fullness of divinity? Finally, he was in the flesh and said: “From now on you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power” (Matthew 26:64). Elsewhere he says to Peter: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 16:19).

So this is the poor man who bestowed the heavenly kingdom? But hear how he is poor: “Take my yoke upon you,” he says, “because I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matthew 11:29).

Therefore his people too are poor—not through want, for I see them richer than that rich people, since they have deserved to possess not only the prophetic oracles but also the commandments of the apostles, poured forth by the divine Spirit.

### 32

He is poor, then, not through want but poor in spirit, to whom it is said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5:3). Truly blessed are the poor who received what the rich did not have.

Among this number is that prophetic poor man of whom it is written: “This poor man cried, and the Lord heard him” (Psalm 34:6). From this people comes the one who says: “Silver and gold I have none, but what I have I give you: in the name of Jesus of Nazareth, rise and walk” (Acts 3:6).

That poor man,

[Note: Some manuscripts read “the author of the poor people.”]

the founder of the poor people, says: “God, do not be silent about my praise, for the mouth of the sinner and the mouth of deceit have been opened against me. They spoke against me with a deceitful tongue; they surrounded me with words of hatred and attacked me without cause. In return for loving me, they slandered me; but I prayed” (Psalm 109:2 and following).

Prayer is a good shield, by which all the flaming arrows of the adversary are driven back (Ephesians 6:16). The Lord Jesus therefore prayed, and Valentinian, his imitator, prayed.

### 33

But perhaps someone will say: What benefit did his prayer bring him? Behold, he was killed at the very beginning of his life’s course.. I speak of the swiftness of his death, not of its manner—for I do not speak in accusation but in grief.

Yet the Lord also prayed, and he was crucified; for this was what he prayed: that he might take away the sin of the world. Let us therefore hear what the disciple of Christ prays for: certainly what the Teacher taught.

He taught us to watch and pray, lest we enter into temptation—that is, lest we fall into sin. For this is the Christian’s temptation: to slip into danger to his own soul. But to fear death is not the mark of perfection.

### 34

But one ought also to ask for one’s enemies and to pray for those who persecute, just as the Lord prayed, saying: “Father, forgive them; for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). Observe the greatness of his mercy. They were persecuting their own author, while he was forgiving even grave sins committed by his adversaries; indeed, he excused the deed by the veil of ignorance, saying: “For they do not know what they are doing.” For if they had known, they would not have persecuted their Lord, in whose power and jurisdiction they would have understood their salvation to lie. And because Christ’s persecutors were not content with his death alone, they added curses and insults, as he himself says: “They shall curse, but you shall bless” (Psalm 108:28). He taught us that we ought by no means to fear the curses of our persecutors, since we have the author of blessing; nor ought their insults to disturb us, where there is a protector who can remove the curses.

### 35

What of the fact that he did not fear death? Rather, he offered himself for all, saying that the innocent were being made objects of hostility in vain, and that others were being imperiled on his account in vain; instead, he wished for death himself, lest he should be the cause of death to others. This is that Gospel saying of the Lord at the very moment of his arrest: “If you seek me, let these men go” (John 18:8). Thus he died for all whom he loved, for whom his friends thought it a small matter if all should perish.

[Note: From this you may understand that Arbogastes demanded the execution of certain friends of Valentinian as men hostile to him; and perhaps this is what moved the Roman editors, above, at no. 27, to restore the reading “from whom he said he was afraid,” as was observed there.]

### 36

We have observed what disposition he had toward his friends; let us consider what affection he had toward his sisters. In them he found repose, in them he consoled himself, in them he relaxed his mind, and soothed his heart, wearied by cares. He asked them that, if they seemed to have been offended by their brother through some youthful lapse or by some word, they would forgive him and beseech pardon for him from the Lord God. He kissed the sisters’ hands and heads, forgetful of imperial power and mindful of brotherhood; and the more he surpassed others by right of authority, the more humbly did he present himself to his sisters. He asked them not to remember the injury, but to remember his kindness.

[Note: Valentinian is reported to have had three sisters, Justa, Grata, and Galla. Since the last of these, who had married Theodosius, was already dead, only the first two remain as having been present at this address. We noted in connection with Letter 53 that they had preserved their resolve of perpetual virginity.]

### 37

It happened that he heard of a legal matter concerning some property of theirs; for he was such a man that the provincials might perhaps have judged him an impartial arbiter even in his sisters’ case. Although his affection might incline him toward his holy kindred, he would nevertheless temper his devotion with justice. He heard that the matter concerned not ownership but possession of an estate. On one side affection for his sisters, on the other compassion for the orphan’s case, contended, so that he might intervene with his sisters on the latter’s behalf. He referred the matter to the public judge, lest he violate either justice or affection. Privately, however, as we infer from the resolve of the noble maidens, he impressed upon his holy sisters a pious feeling, so that they might indicate their willingness to relinquish the estate. Truly worthy sisters of so great a brother, who preferred to relax from their own right what their mother had left them rather than have their brother suffer embarrassment in his own case.

[Note: All editions read “which a mother had left to her”; the manuscripts, better, read “which that mother had left to her.”]

### 38

This is your inheritance, holy souls, more precious: your brother’s praise and glory. This pious brother made you nobler and richer, for he did not burden your heads with jewels, but with kisses; he did not surround your hands so much with royal ornaments as he kissed them with his imperial lips. He placed all his consolation in the joy of your presence, so that he did not even greatly long for a wife. He postponed marriage because affection for your grace nourished him more fully.

[Note: All editions and some manuscripts read “because his piety nourished him”; the remaining manuscripts read “because your grace nourished him more,” which is preferable.]

May these things be more a cause of longing than of sorrow for you, so that your brother’s glory may refresh your minds more than grief torments them. Tears themselves often nourish and lighten the mind; weeping cools the breast and consoles a sorrowful affection.

### 39

You see indeed a grievous funeral; yet holy Mary also stood beside the cross of her Son and gazed upon the passion of her only-begotten. I read that she stood; I do not read that she wept. Therefore the Son said to her: “Woman, behold your son.” And he said to the disciple: “Behold your mother” (John 19:26–27), leaving them the inheritance of his love and grace.

In you, pious pledges, since I did not deserve to preserve your brother because of my sins, I desire to show a father’s affection. I behold him in you, I hold him, I think him present to me; indeed, I behold both brothers, whom I regard as though my eyes had been torn out.

[Note: Gratian and Valentinian are meant, toward whom Ambrose never fails to express his love whenever occasion arises. As for the threats of Maximus, which are mentioned immediately afterward, see Letter 24, addressed to this Valentinian.]

How much happier for me was it when emperors persecuted bishops than when they loved them! In Maximus’s hatred there was praise; in the love of these brothers, the inheritance of a funeral punishment.

[Note: “Deadly punishment,” that is, funerary punishment, says Nannius. *Feralis* here does not derive from *fera*, “wild beast,” but from *feriae*, that is, the funeral rites of the dead. Here *feralis haereditas* means the same as “funeral inheritance,” since whatever pertains to the dead is called *feralia*. Thus he explains it.]


Would that I had been permitted to pour out this spirit for you, my sons! I had found a shortening of my grief, and it would have been more glorious for me to die for such precious pledges.

### 40

But I shall return to console you, holy daughters, although the bitterness of what has happened absorbs all power of consolation. If consolation is brief, it brings nothing that can soothe a sorrowful affection; if it is longer, it brings a longer admonition of grief.

For the longer you are, the more you will afflict in consoling the one whom you wish to console, and the longer you will hold his sorrow.

### 41

I shall not, then, wipe away your tears with some sort of brush of speech; nor would I wish to do so even if I could. For there is even a certain pleasure in weeping for pious affections, and often a heavy sorrow evaporates in tears. But this I ask: do not tear your brother, fixed in your hearts, away with harsh lamentations; do not turn him away with mourning; do not awaken him as he rests. Let him remain in your hearts, let him live in your breasts, let him cling to your pious embraces as he used to; let him press brotherly kisses upon you; let him always be before your eyes, always in your kisses, always in your conversations, always in your minds. Let him now be such that you fear nothing for him as you did before. Forget his distress; retain his grace. Hope that he will assist you; let him stand as your protector through the nights; let sleep no longer exclude him from you.

[Note: Although a *penicillus* properly consists of little brushes, that is, animal tails, with which painters apply colors, it is nevertheless not uncommon for such objects to be used for sponges, as in Terence’s *Eunuchus*, act 4, scene 7. So explains P. Nannius.]

For his sake, let rest delight you, so that it may return to you more pleasantly. It lies with you, daughters, that no one can now take your brother away from you.

[Note: Thus all manuscripts; all editions, however, read “that you may relieve [him] with harsh groans,” an absurd sense. For what does it mean to be relieved by harsh groans?]

### 42

But you desire to hold his body; gathered around the tomb, you hold him there. Let that tomb of your brother be your dwelling; let it be your palace hall, in which his beloved limbs will rest.

### 43

And if you call me back to that grief—that he departed life so soon—I do not deny that he died at an immature age, whom we wished to support during the years of our own life, so that he might live from our years, since he could not complete his own.

[Note: This alludes to the customary acclamation, about which Tertullian writes in the *Apologeticum*: “May Jupiter add years to your years from ours.”]

### 44

But I ask whether there is any consciousness after death, or none. If there is, he lives; indeed, because there is consciousness, he now enjoys eternal life. For how can he lack consciousness whose soul lives and flourishes and will return to the body, making it live again when it has been restored to it? The Apostle cries out: “We do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who sleep, so that you may not grieve like the rest who have no hope. For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, so also God will bring with Jesus those who have fallen asleep” (1 Thessalonians 4:12–13). Life therefore remains for those whom resurrection awaits.

### 45

But if the nations, which have no hope of resurrection, console themselves by this one thought—that they say there is no consciousness of the dead after death, and therefore no consciousness of pain remains—how much more ought we to receive consolation, because death is not to be feared, since it is the end of sins; while life is not to be despaired of, since it is restored by resurrection?

Job also teaches that death is not to be feared, but rather desired by the godly, saying: “Would that you would guard me in the underworld and hide me until your anger is appeased, and appoint for me a time at which you will remember me. For if a human being dies, he will live. Having completed the days of my life, I will wait until I come to be again. Then you will call, and I will answer you; but do not despise the works of your hands” (Job 14:13–14).

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “He will live, completing the days of his life. I will wait,” and so forth. This reading agrees with the Septuagint. The old edition and the manuscripts, however, agree among themselves, except that the manuscripts generally read *consumas* rather than *consummans*; this is a copyists’ error. The present reading comes closer to the Hebrew text and to our Vulgate.]

### 46

Let it nevertheless be granted that we should grieve because he died at the beginning of life; we should still rejoice that he departed as a veteran in the service of the virtues. For the reform of his life during that entire slippery period of adolescence was so great, and the praise of his character so great, that it covers over all remembrance of grief. That he died is a matter of frailty; that he was such a man is a matter of admiration.

[Note: In very few words Saint Ambrose has gathered together the complete praise of Valentinian; nevertheless it is not permissible to bring it under any suspicion of flattery, since many others likewise testify to the virtues of that emperor. See Sozomen, book 7, chapter 22; Nicephorus, book 12, chapter 38; and others.]

How blessed would the state have been if it had been able to preserve him longer! But because the life of the saints is not here on earth but in heaven—for to the righteous, to live is Christ and to die is gain, because to depart and be with Christ is much better (Philippians 1:21, 23)—we should grieve that he was snatched from us so soon, but take consolation that he has passed to better things.

### 47

Finally, David wept for his son who was about to die, but did not grieve for him once he was dead (2 Samuel 12:20). He wept lest the son be taken from him, but ceased to weep once he had been taken, because he knew that he was with Christ. And, so that you may know that what I assert is true, he wept for his incestuous son Amnon after he had been killed (2 Samuel 13:36); he grieved for the parricide Absalom after he had been slain, saying: “My son Absalom, my son Absalom” (2 Samuel 18:33). He did not think an innocent son ought to be mourned, because he believed that those had perished for their crime, while this one would live because of his innocence.

### 48

You therefore have nothing in your brother over which you should grieve exceedingly. He was born a human being and was subject to human frailty. No one has redeemed himself from death—not the rich, not kings themselves; indeed, kings are subject to more serious dangers. Job said: “The years allotted to the mighty are numbered, and terror is in his ears; when he seems to have peace, then his overthrow will come” (Job 15:20).

You too must patiently endure that such bitter things have happened to you, since you see that you share them with the saints. David also was left bereft when he lost his sons; he would have wished them to die such as the brother taken from you was. He grieved their crimes, not the death of his sons.

[Note: Likewise, in book 2 of *On the Death of Satyrus*, no. 3, he denies that a brother’s death should be mourned on the ground that death is common to all. Both passages refer to what Telamon says in Cicero, book 3 of the *Tusculan Disputations*: “When I groaned, I knew that he would die.”]

### 49

But let it be granted that mourning was necessary. How long are the periods of grief to be prolonged? For two months you have enclosed yourselves in daily embraces of your brother’s funeral.
