In Scripture only Jephthah’s daughter asked for a period of mourning, after learning that her father, who was going forth to battle, had vowed to offer to the Lord whatever should first meet him when he returned victorious. His daughter met him as he returned from victory, ignorant of piety and ignorant of the vow. He saw her and groaned, saying: “Alas for me, my daughter! You have hindered me and become a goad of sorrow to me. For I have opened my mouth concerning you to the Lord, and I cannot turn back.” She said to him: “Father, if you have opened your mouth concerning me, do to me as has gone forth from your mouth” (Judges 11:35). And again she said: “Leave me for two months, and I will go and weep in the mountains over my virginity, I and my companions” (ibid., 37). When the two months had passed, she returned and fulfilled the offering. By decree of the people of Israel, the women of that people mourned her for four days each year.

[Note: All editions and some manuscripts read “ignorant of piety”; the manuscripts of better quality read “aware of piety,” which gives excellent sense. Since she came out to meet her returning father first of all, how can she be said to have been ignorant of the piety owed by children to their parents?]

### 50

The daughter of Jephthah therefore judged that two months were enough to mourn the flower of her virginity—and resurrection had not yet come. She thought that, in that period of time, she had been mourned sufficiently by a few. All peoples have mourned with you; all the provinces have groaned; and do you still think these sufferings of yours small?

Even if you could redeem your brother by your own death, he would not wish to be restored to life by your affliction, because he believed himself to live better in you. He preferred to die himself rather than see your injury, he who was gladly prepared to offer himself for you, and who, on that very day of our grief, is said to have uttered only this one cry: “Woe to my wretched sisters!”

[Note: Thus all the handwritten copies read this, except one; all the editions read “on the day of your grief.”]

Thus he grieved more over your bereavement than over his own death.

### 51

But I hear that you grieve because he did not receive the sacraments of baptism. Tell me, what else is there in us but willingness and petition? Yet he had long possessed this desire: even before he came to Italy, he wished to be initiated, and recently he indicated that he wanted to be baptized by me. For that reason he thought I ought to be summoned before all other considerations.

Does he not therefore possess the grace that he desired? Does he not possess what he requested? Certainly, because he requested it, he received it. And what of the saying: “The righteous person, by whatever death he is overtaken, will be at rest” (Wisdom 4:7)?

### 52

Therefore, holy Father, bestow upon your servant the gift that Moses received because he saw it in the Spirit, and that David merited because he learned of it by revelation. Bestow, I say, upon your servant Valentinian the gift he longed for—the gift he requested while healthy, strong, and unharmed. Even if illness had caused him to postpone it, he would not have been wholly estranged from your mercy, since he would have been deprived by the speed of time, not by his will.

[Note: Nannius says that the meaning of the following words is this: “Bestow upon Valentinian the grace of baptism and Christianity, since he was always devoted to you.” From what is added concerning the refusal to restore pagan religions, he thinks Ambrose is showing that Valentinian had always been devoted to Christ. Nannius certainly erred in this, however, by referring the emperor’s refusal of the privileges of the temples before the day of his death to the rejected *Relation* of Symmachus. Enough has already been said about this elsewhere.]

Bestow, then, upon your servant the gift of your grace, which he never denied, since before the day of his death he denied the privileges of the temples, even when those whom he might have revered were pressing him.

[Note: The old edition and some manuscripts read “when those pressing him …”; the Roman edition and the remaining manuscripts read “when these were pressing him.”]

A crowd of pagan men stood by; the senate pleaded. He did not fear displeasing human beings, so that he might please you alone in Christ. He who possessed your Spirit—how could he fail to receive your grace?

### 53

Or, if it troubles anyone that the mysteries were not solemnly celebrated, then let martyrs not be crowned either if they were catechumens; for they are not crowned if they are not initiated. But if they are washed in their own blood, then his piety and his willingness have washed him also.

[Note: This was the opinion of all Christian antiquity concerning martyrs baptized by their own blood alone. And certainly, lest Ambrose seem here to be speaking merely for effect, see what he teaches in Sermon 3 on Psalm 118, no. 14. Tertullian had preceded him in this in *On Baptism*, chapter 16; Cyprian, Letter 73, to Jubaianus; and others. Augustine and later writers followed them in this matter.]

### 54

I beg you, Lord, do not separate him from his brother, nor allow this bond of pious brotherhood to be broken. Gratian, already yours and vindicated by your judgment, is now placed in greater danger if he is separated from his brother, if he does not deserve to be with him, through whom I deserved to be vindicated. What hands is he now raising to you, Father, for his brother? With what embrace does he cling to him? How does he refuse to let him be torn away from him?

### 55

The father also is present—the man who, under Julian, despised military service and the honors of the tribunate for love of the faith.

[Note: We read in Socrates, book 1 of his *History*, chapter 1, that Valentinian, the father of our Valentinian, when he was a tribune under Julian the Apostate, was ordered to sacrifice to idols but threw off his military belt rather than renounce the religion of Christ. Sozomen writes, in book 6, chapter 6, that the same Valentinian, when accompanying the emperor into a certain shrine, was sprinkled by a priest with lustral water; when Caesar saw this, Valentinian immediately cut away the part of his cloak that had been wetted and railed against the priest. Theodoret, book 3, chapter 16, even reports that he struck the priest with his fist. As for the indication that the rights of the temples were not removed by him, we have discussed this fully in connection with the *Relation* of Symmachus and Letters 17 and 18.]

Give to the father his son, to the brother his brother—both of whom he imitated: the one in faith, the other equally in devotion and piety in denying the privileges of the temples. He added what the father lacked; he preserved what the brother established. And to this man also I add my intercession, for whom I confidently anticipate a reward.

### 56

[Note: Nannius observes that souls, once they had departed from their bodies, were called *lares* if believed good, *lemures* if bad, and *manes* if it was uncertain to which order they should be assigned. He adds, however, that this distinction was soon effaced, and that the name was attributed to all souls, indeed even to infernal gods. For more on *manes*, see Vossius, *Etymologicon*, under the same word. Nannius further notes that this may perhaps imitate Virgil’s words, *manibus date lilia plenis*—“give lilies to the shades with full hands”; thus *manibus* here may derive not from *manes* but from *manus*, “hand.” On this below.]

Give the holy mysteries with your hands; with pious affection let us ask rest for him. Give the heavenly sacraments; let us accompany the soul of the nephew with our offerings.

[Note: The editions of Amerbach and Erasmus read “the pious soul of the mother with offerings”; Gill’s and the Roman edition read “the pious soul with our offerings”; but the manuscripts read “the soul of the nephew,” and so forth. There is no doubt that this is the genuine reading. What follows concerning flowers clearly shows that Ambrose is alluding to Virgil’s verses, which immediately follow the half-line cited above in book 6 of the *Aeneid*:

> I will scatter purple flowers, and the soul of my nephew  
> With these gifts at least I will heap …

For it was customary to sprinkle flowers upon the tombs of the dearest dead, as Jerome indicates, among many others, in Letter 26, to Pammachius.]

“Lift up your hands in the holy place, peoples, with me, so that by this gift at least we may repay his merits” (Psalm 133:2). I shall not sprinkle his tomb with flowers, but I shall drench his spirit with the fragrance of Christ. Let others scatter lilies from full baskets; for us, the lily is Christ. With this I shall consecrate his remains; with this I shall commend his grace. I shall never separate the names of pious brothers, though I shall distinguish their merits. I know that this commemoration wins the Lord’s favor and that this union delights him.

### 57

Let no one suppose that anything was taken from their merits by the swiftness of their deaths. Enoch was taken away (Genesis 5:24), lest wickedness change his heart (Wisdom 4:11); and Josiah, in the eighteenth year of his reign, celebrated the Lord’s Passover in such a way that he surpassed all former rulers in devotion, yet did not live longer in proportion to the merits of his faith. Rather, because grave destruction was impending over the Jewish people, the just king was taken away beforehand (2 Kings 23:21).

[Note: This is the reading of the old edition and Amerbach’s edition, together with all manuscripts. Gill’s and the Roman edition read “in the eighth year of your reign.” This is incorrect, as Baron noted under the year 392. Since he was proclaimed emperor on the tenth day before the Kalends of December in the year 375 and was killed on the Ides of May in 392, he died in the eighteenth year of his reign, although the first and last years were incomplete; the comparison established with King Josiah also confirms this.]

I fear, then, that you too were taken from us because of some offense of ours, so that, like the just man, you might escape the bitterness of impending evil in the eighteenth year of your reign.

### 58

But now I shall embrace your beloved remains and commit them to their appointed tomb; first, however, I shall examine each limb. My Valentinian, my young man, “white and ruddy” (Song of Songs 5:10), bearing within himself the image of Christ; for in these words the Church portrays Christ in the *Song of Songs*.

Nor should you think it an injury: servants are marked with the Lord’s brand, and soldiers are marked with the emperor’s name. Finally, the Lord himself said: “Do not touch my anointed ones” (Psalm 104:15), and: “You are the light of the world.” Jacob also said: “Judah, your brothers shall praise you” (Genesis 49:8). He was speaking to a son, yet revealing the Lord. And when it was said of Joseph: “My son is growing, my son is growing, Joseph” (ibid., 22), it signified Christ.

[Note: Some manuscripts read “may they praise you,” and two read “they praise you.” This is not only contrary to the consensus of the sacred books but also contrary to the passage as Ambrose himself cites it in book 4 of *On the Blessing of the Patriarchs*, no. 16.]

[Note: In former times both slaves and soldiers were branded with certain marks: slaves, so that another person might not claim them as his own; soldiers, so that they would not be permitted to desert military service. Erasmus refers Paul’s words in Galatians 6:17—“I bear the marks of the Lord Jesus in my body”—to the former inscription, while Grotius thinks that they allude to the marks of the latter. On the branding of soldiers, see Lipsius, book 1, dialogue 9; on that of slaves, consult Joseph Laurentius, book 1 of the *Polymathia*, dissertation 9.

Furthermore, we cannot refrain here from charging Dallaeus with maliciousness against Ambrose. With what sincerity does he assert in book 2 of *On the Use of the Fathers* that Ambrose applies Scripture to playful purposes, and that he accommodates to Gratian and Valentinian what is said of Christ and the Church in the sacred *Song of Songs* with the freedom poets use? Who does not see that one who overlooks the great caution and reverence with which the holy man softened this adaptation writes not so much in pursuit of truth as in derision of the Fathers? Anyone who examines the thread of the discourse with even moderate attention will readily recognize that our teacher applies these texts to Valentinian only as an imitator of Christ.]

### 59

It is therefore permitted for me also to mark the servant with the Lord’s brand: “My young man, white and ruddy, chosen out of ten thousand” (Song of Songs 5:10). My son was chosen when, after his father’s death, he was taken into the imperial office while still a child.

[Note: Writers agree that this happened on the tenth day before the Kalends of December in the year 375, when he was only four years old.]

“His head is gold, *cephas* [reading uncertain]; his eyes are like doves beside abundant waters” (ibid., 11).

[Note: “There we sat and wept,” said those who came from there (Psalm 136:1).]

### 60

“His belly is an ivory casket” (Song of Songs 5:14), which received the oracles of Scripture, so that he could say: “I am in pain in my belly,” as the prophet said (Jeremiah 4:19). For the one who says these things is an imitator of Christ.

### 61

“His cheeks are like bowls of spices” (Song of Songs 5:13), into which the ointment of Christ flowed.

### 62

“His lips are lilies, dripping with abundant myrrh. His hands are wrought of gold, full of Tharsis” (ibid., 13–14).

[Note: The Roman edition and a few manuscripts read “dripping with full myrrh,” which is also found in the sacred pages and is cited in this way by Ambrose himself in his commentary on Psalm 118. Nevertheless, the old edition agrees with us, together with the greater and better manuscripts. In the following, all editions and manuscripts agree fairly well, except that some manuscripts read *tornatae auro*, “turned with gold.”]

This was because justice shone forth in his words and grace gleamed in his deeds and works; his speech was full of royal virtue and authority, and its steadfastness was not bent by any fear of death. The correction of his actions was precious and disciplined; for every good worker is the hand of Christ.

[Note: The latest Paris editions read “the precious things of the saints,” and so forth.]

### 63

“His throat is sweetness itself, and he is altogether desirable” (ibid., 13).

[Note: Some manuscripts read “sweetnesses, and altogether desirable.”]

How sweet all his judgments clung to the throats of everyone! With what grace each of his words was repeated! How you are longed for by the peoples, my son! You have certainly impressed upon me those final words which I hold in my heart, by which you asked me to become your surety. You left testimony concerning me in a glorious judgment. I could not offer you the pledge of faith that I was preparing; nevertheless, I spoke in your absence, and Christ heard me speaking my pledge for you. My promise is held in heaven, even though it is not held on earth. I am bound to God, even though I could not be bound to human beings.

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads: “surely you impressed yourself, who [in] body …”]

### 64

I have spoken of your body; now I shall address your soul, worthy of prophetic ornaments. I shall therefore use the same opening words: “Who is this one who looks forth like the dawn, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun?” (Song of Songs 6:9).

I seem to see you shining; I seem to hear you saying: “For me it is dawn, Father. Earthly night has passed, and the heavenly day has drawn near” (Romans 13:12). You therefore look upon us, holy soul, from a higher place, gazing down upon what is below. You have come out of the darkness of this age; you shine like the moon and gleam like the sun. And rightly like the moon, because before, too, although in the shadow of this body, you shone forth and illuminated the darkness of the earth; now, transformed by the light of the Sun of Justice, you lead in the bright day.

I seem, therefore, to see you as you depart from the body and, having cast off the darkness of night, rise at dawn like the sun, drawing near to God; and, with swift flight like an eagle, leaving behind the things that belong to earth.

### 65

“Turn, O Shulamite, turn, and we shall see you” (Song of Songs 6:12). Turn toward us in peace, so that you may show your glory to your sisters and they may begin to console themselves in the security of your rest and grace. Turn toward us just once, so that we may see you; then turn again and hasten with complete devotion toward that Jerusalem, the city of the saints.

Or, since Christ says this to a devout soul, he commands her to turn for a little while, so that her glory and the rest that will be hers with the saints may appear to us; afterward he orders her to hasten to that heavenly fellowship of the saints.

### 66

“What will you see in the Shulamite,” he says, “who comes like the ranks of armies?” (Song of Songs 7:1)—that is, in her who fought many battles in the body and against many adversaries. For she fought against foreign enemies; she fought against the slippery changes of the world; she fought against the frailties of the body and against manifold passions.

She heard from the Lord: “Turn, O Shulamite” (Song of Songs 6:12).

[Note: This is the reading of the old edition and the manuscripts, except that some read *commonitione*, “admonition,” instead of *communione*, “communion.” The Roman edition gives the passage as follows: “Turn toward peace. Once she turned in the world; she turned again through communion.”]

She turned once toward peace in the world; she turned again through communion toward the grace of Christ. Therefore her turning in the world was beautiful, and her progress and flight into heaven most beautiful.

### 67

Hence she deserves to hear: “How beautiful are your steps in your sandals, daughter of Aminadab” (Song of Songs 7:1)—that is, daughter of the prince.

[Note: All editions read: “For she is beautiful in her progress; you dwelt in the body,” and so forth. All manuscripts, on the contrary, have the reading adopted by us in the text.]

For your progress in the body was beautiful, as though you used it as a sandal, not as a covering; as though, being higher and more eminent, you carried your foot wherever you wished without any impediment.

Or certainly, you would remove that sandal, as Moses did, to whom it was said: “Remove the sandal from your feet” (Exodus 3:5).

[Note: The old edition and some manuscripts read “that you remove it”; the Roman edition and several other manuscripts read “remove it”; the remaining codices, more appropriately, read “that you might remove it.”]

### 68

Now Father Aminadab himself, that prince of the people, says to you: “Hear, daughter, and see, for the king has desired your beauty” (Psalm 44:11). “How beautiful, therefore, are your steps in your sandals, daughter of Aminadab.” “The curves of your thighs are like necklaces” (Song of Songs 7:1)—that is, grace and moderation harmonized with themselves in all your deeds and equaled the insignia of great triumphs.

Finally, through your moderation and peaceful tranquility, Gaul did not feel the enemy, while Italy drove back the enemy who threatened its borders.

[Note: Among the rewards with which victorious soldiers were presented, necklaces are also reported to have been included; see J. Lipsius, book 5 of *Roman Military Matters*, dialogue 17.]

There can be no doubt that necklaces are marks of victory, since those who have fought bravely in war are honored with necklaces.

### 69

“Your navel is a turned bowl, never lacking mixed wine. Your belly is a heap of wheat enclosed among lilies. Your neck is like an ivory tower. Your eyes are like the pools in Heshbon” (ibid., 2 and following).

[Note: Some manuscripts read here and below “never lacking must”; the remaining manuscripts and all editions, better, read “never lacking mixed wine”; the Septuagint has μὴ ὑστερούμενος κρᾶμα, “not lacking mixed wine.” Immediately afterward, some manuscripts read *minuti* for *muniti*, but that variant has already been discussed.]

A soul’s navel is good when it is capable of every virtue, like a bowl turned by the very author of faith. For Wisdom mixed her wine in a bowl, saying: “Come, eat my bread and drink the wine that I have mixed for you” (Proverbs 9:5).

[Note: The Codex Remigius reads: “Therefore, if the navel should remain adorned,” and so forth.]

This navel, then, turned with every adornment of virtue, does not lack mixed wine. Its belly was filled not only with justice, as with grain for food, but also blossomed with the sweetness and grace of the lily.

[Note: Thus read the manuscripts, with one exception, except that many omit *sicut*, “as.” The editions, however, read: “with the sweetness of grace, which blossomed”; the old editions also omit *sicut*. As for what all editions and some manuscripts have a little farther on—“rational thoughts,” and so forth—many manuscripts give it as: “rational thoughts of faith, the fragrance of circumcision, the attention of adornment, a glorious head.” This is less well arranged.]

His neck too was white and pure, willingly subjected to the yoke of Christ; there were rational thoughts, the fragrance of faith, the attention of circumcision, and the adornment of a glorious head—not crowned with royal diadems but with the marks of the Lord’s blood.

### 70

Rightly, then, as a king victorious over sin and girded with a heavenly crown, he ascended. Of his soul the Word of God says: “How beautiful and how sweet you have become, O love, in your delights!” (Song of Songs 7:6). Beautiful through the adornment of virtue, sweet through grace. Tall like the palm, which is the reward of the victor.

### 71

As this soul ascended, her brother Gratian met her, embraced her, and said: “I belong to my brother, and his turning is toward me” (ibid., 10)—either because he desires him to cling to himself, or because, through brotherly affection, he stands beside him as an advocate, saying that his return is to be preferred even to his own grace.

[Col. 1379D] 72. “Come,” he says, “my brother; let us go out into the country, let us rest in the villages, let us rise early for the vineyards” (ibid., 11–12)—that is, you have come to the place where the fruits of various virtues are presented according to the merits of each, where the rewards of merits abound. Let us therefore go out into the country, where labor is not fruitless but yields a fruitful harvest of graces. What you sowed on earth, reap here; what you scattered there, gather here. Or certainly, come into that field which is the fragrance of Jacob; that is, come into Jacob’s bosom, so that, just as Lazarus the poor man rested in Abraham’s bosom, so you too may rest in the patriarch Jacob’s tranquility; for the bosom of the patriarchs is a certain retreat of eternal rest (Luke 16:22). Jacob’s field is therefore rightly fruitful, as the patriarch Isaac testified, saying: “Behold, the fragrance of my son is like the fragrance of a full field which the Lord has blessed” (Gen. 27:27).

[Col. 1380B] 73. “Let us rest,” he says, “in the villages” (Song 7:11), showing that there is a safer rest there, fortified and enclosed by the protection of heavenly refuge, so that it is not harassed by the assaults of worldly beasts.

74. “At our doors,” he says, “are all kinds of fruits, new and old; my brother, I have stored them up for you” (ibid., 13).

[Note: [Col. 1380D] The Roman edition alone has here and below: “Who will grant that you are a brother.” The holy Bibles omit “a brother.”]

“Who will give you, brother, to me as a brother, nursing at the breasts of my mother?” Finding you outside, I will kiss you; and indeed they will not despise me. I will take you and lead you into the house of my mother and into the chamber of her who conceived me. I will give you a drink of wine from the laboriously prepared ointment, from the juice of my pomegranates. His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me” (Song 8:11 and following). Gratian of august memory promises his brother that the fruits of various virtues are ready for him;

[Note: [Col. 1380D] Ambrose is not alone in celebrating Gratian’s virtues; for Rufinus, in Book 2, chapter 13 of his History, Paulinus of Aquileia, in Book 12 of his History, and Ausonius in his Panegyric, have recorded no less about them than he.]

[Col. 1380C] for he himself was faithful in the Lord, pious and gentle, pure in heart. He was also chaste in body, since, apart from marriage, he knew no intimacy with another woman.

75. Therefore, at the doors of his dwelling he has fruits prepared, not to be sought from afar. He offers his brother what he has stored up, new and old—that is, the mysteries both of the Old Testament and of the Gospel—and he says: “Who will give you, brother, to me as a brother, nursing at the breasts of my mother?” That is, not just anyone, but Christ enlightened you with spiritual grace; he baptized you, because human assistance was lacking to you. He gained more who, you thought, had lost less. What are the breasts of the Church except the sacraments of baptism? And he rightly says “nursing,” as though speaking of one who, having been baptized, seeks the nourishment of snow-white milk. “Finding,” he says,

[Col. 1380D] “you outside, I will kiss you”—that is, finding you outside the body, I will embrace you with the kiss of mystical peace. No one

[Col. 1381A] will despise you; no one will exclude you. I will lead you into the inner chambers and secrets of Mother Church, and into every secret of the mystery, so that you may drink the cup of spiritual grace.

76. Having therefore embraced his brother, he began to lead him to his own dwelling;

[Note: [Col. 1381B] Most manuscripts read “and because of his duty.” This is not at all unsuitable.]

and because he had advanced farther in his dutiful service, he began to ascend with his brother, asking that the greater love there might increase both for him and for his brother, since human vices—in particular envy and boasting, which in many people are accustomed to empty the rights of fraternal affection—had come to an end.

77. Seeing them, whether angels or other souls, those who, as though forming their retinue, accompanied and escorted these brothers in their duty, ask them, saying: “Who is this who ascends white, leaning upon her brother?” (Song 8:5). Let us too have no doubt about the merits of Valentinian, but now let us believe, even on the testimony of the angels, that he ascended washed clean, his stain of sin removed; his faith washed him, and his petition consecrated him. Let us also believe—as others have it—that he ascended from the desert; that is, from this arid and uncultivated place to those flower-filled delights where, joined with his brother, he enjoys the pleasure of eternal life.

78.

[Note: [Col. 1381B] There is an obvious allusion here to those two verses of Virgil from Book 6 of the Aeneid:

“Fortunate both! If my songs have any power,

No day will ever remove you from the memory of time.”]

“Blessed are both, if my prayers will have any power! No day will pass you by in silence; no oration of mine will pass you by without honor,”

[Note: [Col. 1381C] Some manuscripts read “no voice”; others, and the editions, more suitably read “no night.” For here the holy Bishop promises that he will pray for Valentinian’s repose not only by day but also by night. Since there are so many passages both in the books On the Death of Satyrus and in this and the following Oration in which the practice of prayers and sacrifices instituted for the dead is affirmed, even if the others were absent, this one passage alone would suffice to establish the same truth. Ambrose, however, is not the only witness to it: other Fathers likewise attest it in such abundance that the heterodox were compelled to acknowledge the antiquity of this practice, attempting only to obscure its effect and purpose and to entangle it in various evasions. They once replied that the Fathers had yielded to the common opinion of their own age; but when it appeared entirely contrary to faith that men so enlightened by the clear lights of the Christian religion, and so zealous to preserve it from every stain and blemish, had failed to detect this error—if indeed it were an error—or, having detected it, had not concealed it through cowardly and disgraceful prevarication so much as confirmed it, that response was abandoned by more recent writers. Accordingly, the English editors of Cyprian’s works labored much, but in vain, to evade the authority of this saint on the matter. There is a passage from Letter 1 of their edition in which the holy man writes as follows: “What our predecessors, the bishops, decreed was that no brother should appoint a cleric as guardian or administrator; and if anyone did so, no offering should be made for him, nor should a sacrifice be celebrated for his repose.” From these words it is clear that Cyprian and his predecessors admitted some place in which the souls of the living might be helped by prayers. What do the editors say to this? They concede that prayers and offerings were customarily made for the dead as a token of faith, hope, and charity, but they deny that they were instituted for their assistance or as relief from the burning of purgatorial fire. Yet to demonstrate that their response is wholly at odds with the mind of the holy Fathers, although it would be sufficient simply to ask readers to consider the passages of Ambrose with minds free from prejudice, it is nevertheless worthwhile to cite two Fathers, one of the Greek and one of the Latin Church, and to set their judgment against the opinion of the English. The first will be Epiphanius, who, in Heresy 75, no. 3, while enumerating the errors of Aerius, reports the words of that heretic as follows: “He continues: ‘And what reason is there, he says, for naming the dead after their death? For if a living person prays or distributes his goods among the poor, what does the dead person ultimately gain from this?’” Here you have the Protestant opinion listed among the heresies by Epiphanius. But this would be insufficient unless he also established the Catholic position; therefore, to explain the benefit of prayers for the dead, he adds: “For we make mention both of the righteous and of sinners: of sinners, indeed, that we may implore mercy for them from the Lord; but of the righteous … that, honoring the Lord Jesus Christ with a singular honor, we may separate them from the order of other human beings,” and so forth. Here you have orthodox teaching set forth clearly and distinctly. Augustine, however, explains it still more openly in chapter 110 of the Enchiridion, no. 29. After asserting that it must not be denied that the souls of the dead are relieved by the piety of their living relatives when the sacrifice of the Mediator is offered for them or alms are given in the Church, he teaches which of them are believed to benefit from these acts. Dividing the dead into three classes—the first consisting of the very good, the last of the very wicked, and neither of whom, he says, are helped by prayers and petitions—he adds that there is a middle class, neither very good nor very wicked, whom the piety of the living benefits. Thus offerings and alms for the very good are thanksgivings; for those who are not very wicked, acts of propitiation; and for the very wicked, consolations of the living of whatever kind. Nor should you say that our Ambrose speaks here and elsewhere of Valentinian as already blessed. His words concerning Valentinian, Satyrus, or Theodosius must be understood only as the speech of one moved by a pious belief, as when he says, “I anticipate his reward,” in section 47. Nothing prevents us, even now, from offering prayers for the benefit of many of the dead.]

“No night will pass without my weaving some thread of my prayers for you; I will frequent you with every offering. Who will forbid me to name the innocent? Who will forbid me to embrace you in the continuation of my commendation? If I forget you, holy Jerusalem—that is, holy soul, pious and peaceful brotherhood—may my right hand forget me; may my tongue cling to my palate, if I do not remember you, if I do not remember Jerusalem at the beginning of my joy” (Ps. 136:5 and following). I will forget myself sooner than I forget you; and if speech ever falls silent, affection will speak; and if the voice fails, grace will not fail, for it is fixed in my inmost heart.

79. How have the mighty fallen? How have both fallen beside those rivers of Babylon? How much swifter were the courses of both your lives

[Note: [Col. 1382D] Some manuscripts read: “The courses of both men were swifter?”]

than the streams of the Rhône? O Gratian and Valentinian, handsome and most dear to me, with what august an end you closed your lives! How near to you were the boundaries of death! How close your tombs! Gratian and Valentinian, I say, it is pleasant and delightful to cling to your names and to rest in your remembrance. O Gratian and Valentinian, handsome and most dear to all! Inseparable in life, you were not separated in death (2 Sam. 1:23). The tomb did not divide you whom affection did not divide.

[Col. 1383A] 1195 The cause of death did not separate those whom a common devotion joined. Difference in virtues did not make unlike those whom a single religion cherished. More guileless than doves, lighter than eagles, more gentle than lambs, more innocent than calves. Gratian’s arrow did not turn back, and Valentinian’s justice was not empty or vain. How have the mighty fallen without a struggle?

79. I grieve over you, my son Gratian, exceedingly dear to me. You gave many tokens of your devotion. In the midst of your dangers you sought me; in your final moments you called for me; you grieved more over my grief for you. I grieve also over you, my son Valentinian, exceedingly handsome to me. Your love for me had become like the love of a cherished son. Through me you thought you would be snatched from danger; you loved me not only as a parent but also hoped in me as your redeemer and

[Col. 1383B] deliverer. You used to say: “Do you think I shall see my father?” Your beautiful desire concerning me was not matched by effective expectation. Alas for me, the vain hope placed in a human being! Yet you sought the Lord in the priest. Alas that I did not recognize your wish earlier! Alas that you did not send for me secretly beforehand! Alas for what cherished pledges I have lost! How have the mighty fallen, and the weapons worth desiring perished (2 Sam. 1:27)?

80.

[Note: [Col. 1383B] All editions and a few manuscripts read, “And because no one”; more and better manuscripts read, “Lord,” and so forth.]

Lord, since no one has anything that he gives to another more than he desires for himself, do not separate me after death from those whom I experienced as most dear in this life. Lord, I ask that where I am, they too may be with me (John 17:24), so that there at least I may enjoy their everlasting union, since here I could not enjoy a longer companionship with them. I entreat you, supreme God, to raise and resurrect these most dear young men in a timely resurrection,

[Note: [Col. 1384B] Thus nearly all the manuscripts read; the editions, however, have “and compensate an untimely … by a timely resurrection.”]

so that by a more timely rising you may compensate for this untimely course of their life. Amen.

[ON THE DEATH OF THEODOSIUS: AN ORATION.]

[Col. 1383]

NOTICE CONCERNING THE ORATION ON THE DEATH OF THEODOSIUS THE EMPEROR.

[Col. 1383]

After Theodosius the Great died at Milan, his son Honorius—whom, when he was suffering from his final illness, he had summoned to himself from the East—decided that his body should be taken back to Constantinople and buried there in the tomb of the former emperors. Therefore, in order to perform the customary rites for his father’s memory before the body was removed, he arranged for the parental celebration to be held with solemn observance on the fortieth day after the emperor’s death. While the final honors were being offered to that prince, Ambrose, in the presence of Honorius himself, whom his father had appointed emperor of the West, commended the virtues of the deceased in this oration.

Beginning with the prodigies that seemed to have foretold Theodosius’s death, he asserts that Theodosius had not fallen from his kingdom but had exchanged an earthly one for a heavenly one (section 1). He adds (section 2) that his sons’ bereavement should not be mourned, since he had left them the inheritance of his virtues, the grace of Christ, and the loyalty of the army. Then, comparing the funeral procession with which Honorius accompanied his father on the fortieth day with the honors Joseph rendered to his father’s corpse (section 3 and following), he shows that Theodosius was more fortunate than Jacob, since he had overthrown tyrants and idolatry. From there (sections 5 and 6), turning to the prince’s testament—which granted his subjects relief from taxes and pardon to those who had taken up arms on behalf of Eugenius—he infers that all these people should repay their emperor’s benefits to his sons. Addressing the soldiers in this connection, he exhorts them to defend the youth of the emperor’s sons by their loyalty, just as Theodosius’s faith had defended them (section 7 and following), stimulating them both by the victory divinely won over Eugenius and by the memory of the various virtues of so great a prince (section 12 and following). He further adds (sections 15 and 16) that Arcadius and Honorius were no older than Josiah and Asa when they assumed the government of peoples; and that Theodosius would obtain from God an even more abundant protection for them, since he had surpassed the parents of those kings by a far greater piety. Then, beginning an exposition of Psalm 114 (section 17 and following), he employs it to illuminate the virtues of the same emperor (section 25 and following), namely, his piety, clemency, justice, and profound humility in undertaking the yoke of public penance. He adds other qualities that had drawn his own goodwill and affection toward him (section 33 and following); then he pronounces a common prayer for him, composed from the verses of the aforementioned psalm (section 36 and following), even though he repeatedly testifies that Theodosius is enjoying in heaven the rewards of his virtues. He declares him blessed there because he now enjoys the company of Gratian, his other children, and his wife Flaccilla, as well as that of Constantine, the first of the Christian emperors, under whose rule the wood of the Lord’s cross was discovered by his mother, Saint Helena (section 39 and following). He says that through the protection of this wood the arrogance of the tyrants was broken and the faith and piety of the Christian Caesars confirmed, especially those of Gratian and Theodosius, whose glory, he asserts, far surpasses the glory with which they flourished while alive (section 52). Finally (section 53), after demonstrating that Theodosius had been pressed beneath a heavy yoke—first when his father was subjected to a cruel death, again when he assumed the burden of empire, and finally when he went to war against Maximus and Eugenius—he consoles Honorius (section 54) because public necessity does not permit him to accompany his father’s body to Constantinople. He declares that the body must be taken there in the noblest procession and that the city will be made blessed by possessing so august a pledge (section 55).

In some manuscripts this oration is prefaced by the following title: “Psalm 114, on the Death of Theodosius the Emperor,” undoubtedly because an exposition of that psalm is inserted there; but the title found in the majority of manuscripts, both written and printed, is preferable. Since it is established that the same oration was delivered on the fortieth day after Theodosius’s death, and it is equally certain that this prince died on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of January in the year of salvation 395, we understand that it was delivered on the sixth day before the Kalends of February. It must nevertheless be acknowledged that the Magdeburg Centuriators (Century 4, chapters 4 and 13), along with several others, have questioned whether this funeral oration should be attributed to Ambrose. They provide not even the slightest reason for their doubt; and against them the sequence of historical events woven into the work, its style, and its method of interpreting and adapting Scripture to the subject argue decisively.

[Col. 1385]

ORATION OF SAINT AMBROSE, BISHOP OF MILAN, ON THE DEATH OF THEODOSIUS [Note: [Col. 1385C] Written in the year 375.] (C)

[Col. 1385]

[Col. 1385A] 1197 1. These severe earthquakes, these unceasing rains, and the gloom darker than usual beyond what is customary foretold to us that the most merciful emperor Theodosius was about to depart from the earth.

[Note: [Col. 1385C] Marcellinus records in his Chronicle that, after Eugenius had been defeated, the earth was shaken by continuous earthquakes from September through November in certain regions of Europe, when Arcadius was consul for the third time and Honorius for the second—that is, in the year 394, which preceded Theodosius’s death.]

The elements themselves therefore mourned his departure. The sky was covered with darkness, the air was continually made dreadful by gloom, the earth was shaken by earthquakes, and was filled by floods of waters. Why should the world itself not mourn that a prince was soon to be taken away through whom the harshness of this world was accustomed to be tempered, since indulgence anticipated the punishments of crimes?

2. Yet he departed to receive a kingdom for himself,

[Note: [Col. 1385C] The old edition reads, “he departed to his kingdom, which”; the Roman edition and some manuscripts read, “he departed, and the kingdom”; other manuscripts, as in our text, read “he departed to receive a kingdom,” except the Beauvais manuscript, which has: “And indeed he did not lay down the kingdom,” and so forth.]

a kingdom which he did not lay down but changed, having been received into Christ’s tabernacles by right of piety, into that heavenly Jerusalem where, now placed, he says: “As we have heard, so have we seen, in the city of the Lord of hosts, in the city of our God, which God founded forever” (Ps. 47:9). But he left many, as though deprived of a father’s protection, and above all his sons. Yet those whom he left as heirs of his piety are not deprived; those for whom he obtained the grace of Christ

[Note: [Col. 1385C] When Theodosius pardoned those who had embraced Eugenius’s cause, he bound them forever to himself and to his sons. Zosimus, in Book 4 of his History, was compelled to acknowledge this; and Claudian, whom Orosius also identifies as a pagan, testifies to the same matter in his Panegyric on the Fourth Consulship of Honorius, in words that could agree with Ambrose’s no more closely. He writes:

“From this came love; from this, strength made firm by a devoted soldiery;

From this, enduring loyalty toward his sons,” and so forth.]

and the loyalty of the army. This was proof that God favors piety and avenges treachery.

[Col. 1386A] 3. We therefore recently lamented the death of that prince, and now celebrate the fortieth day, with the emperor Honorius attending at the sacred altars; for just as holy Joseph rendered the rites of burial to his father Jacob for forty days, so this son has paid the customary honors to his father Theodosius. And because

[Note: [Col. 1385D] The Roman edition alone reads “the third day”; others have “the thirtieth day,” others “the seventh,” and others “the fortieth.” Nothing needs to be changed in the common reading, provided that in the first clause “the third day” and “the thirtieth,” and in the second “the seventh” and “the fortieth,” are taken disjunctively. The Author of the Apostolic Constitutions, Book 8, chapter 42, mentions the third and fortieth days; but Augustine, Questions on Genesis 172, seems to differ from him concerning the ninth day, denying that Christians should observe mourning for the dead for nine days because of the pagan novendial festival, while he establishes the seventh day from the divine Scriptures. Menardus, in the Concord of the Rule, observes that Augustine disapproved not the observance of nine days but of the ninth day. Palladius, in the Lausiac History, chapter 26, mentions the fortieth day and, according to some manuscripts, also the third. Gregory the Great treats the third, seventh, and thirtieth days together in the Sacramentary, where he discusses a Mass for the dead; he also treats the thirtieth day in Book 4 of the Dialogues, chapter 55. Menardus, cited above, Cottelerius in the cited passage of the Apostolic Constitutions, and several others discuss these rites carefully.]

some customarily observe the third and thirtieth days, and others the seventh and fortieth, let us consider what the reading teaches. “When Jacob had died,” it says, “Joseph commanded the gravediggers to bury him. And the gravediggers buried Israel, and they fulfilled forty days for him; for so the days of burial are counted. And Egypt mourned him

[Note: [Col. 1386C] Gratian reads, “Israel for seven days.” Although the correctors of the decree acknowledge that this reading is contrary not only to all the Ambrosian manuscripts but also to the Septuagint and the Vulgate, they nevertheless contend that it can be defended, both because it is found in all Gratian’s manuscripts and because the same chapter of Genesis mentions Joseph and the other sons of Israel completing seven days. The first argument proves only that Gratian used a less complete copy of Ambrose. As for the second, it is beyond doubt that the passage in which the Bible consistently reads “seventy days” is cited here by Ambrose, not the passage indicated by the correctors.]

for seventy days” (Gen. 50:2). This solemnity, then, is to be followed, since the reading prescribes it. But it is also written in Deuteronomy: “The children of Israel mourned Moses for thirty days, and the days of mourning were completed” (Deut. 34:8). Both observances therefore have authority, because the necessary duty of piety is fulfilled.

4. Good Joseph, then, who gave form to this pious duty, whom his father loved and to whom he said: “May my God help you and bless you with the blessing of a land possessing all things, because of the blessing of breasts and womb, the blessings of your mother, and because of the blessings of your father” (Gen. 49:25)—a good offspring of a pious father. He therefore celebrates his father Jacob’s fortieth day, Jacob the supplanter; and we celebrate Theodosius’s

[Note: [Col. 1387B] Some manuscripts read: “the fortieth day of him who, together with Jacob, supplanted.”]

fortieth day, Theodosius who, imitating Jacob, supplanted

[Note: [Col. 1387B] It is beyond dispute that the tyrants Maximus and Eugenius are designated here. As for the statement that Theodosius “concealed the images of the nations,” Godofredus thinks this should be referred to Law 12, On Pagans, by which all sacrifices and the worship of the gods were prohibited. But since that law was issued on the sixth day before the Ides of November in the year 392—that is, after Eugenius had occupied Valentinian’s throne following Valentinian’s death on the Ides of May—we have no doubt that Ambrose’s words should be referred not only to that law but also to all the events that followed the death of that tyrant. For not only do Augustine, Book 5 of The City of God, chapter 26, Theodoret, Ecclesiastical History, Book 5, chapter 21, and other Christian authors testify that all images and every kind of sacrificial victim were removed by Theodosius after the victory, but Zosimus, Book 4 of his History, also describes the same matter at length.]

the treachery of the tyrants, who concealed the images of the nations; for his faith concealed all the worship of idols and effaced all their ceremonies. He also grieved that the indulgence he had granted to those who had sinned against him had perished,

[Note: [Col. 1387C] We have already seen from Zosimus’s own testimony that Theodosius spared those who had taken Eugenius’s side. Claudian also celebrates this in his Panegyric on the Fourth Consulship of Honorius, in these verses:

“After the battles, he who also set an end to hatred and arms.

It helped the defeated to be captured by the victor,” and so forth.

Orosius, however, explains it more distinctly in Book 7, chapter 35: apart from Eugenius, who was captured and killed, and Arbogast, who turned his own sword upon himself, no one among the defeated was killed. Augustine likewise, in Book 5 of The City of God, chapter 26, after praising Theodosius’s clemency toward the sons of those who had fallen in battle, adds that he did not permit private enmities to prevail after the victory. Nevertheless, from this passage of Ambrose we understand that the pardon granted by the emperor was prevented from reaching certain people by the intervention of others. Certainly, pardon was not granted immediately to everyone, as the holy Bishop himself bears witness in Letters 61 and 62, in which he prays and pleads for the emperor’s clemency toward certain persons. Paulinus also bears witness to this in his Life, where he reports that many were granted pardon by the emperor through Ambrose’s prayers. But the pious Bishop modestly chose to pass over this in silence.]

and pardon had been denied. But the sons will not deny what their father granted; they will not deny it even if someone has tried to interfere. For they cannot deny what he granted to all in common, since they are releasing what he gave to individuals.

[Col. 1387B] 5. Nothing more glorious marked the end of so great a prince,

[Note: [Col. 1387D] Theodosius created Arcadius Augustus on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February in the year 393, as Socrates, Sozomen, and Marcellinus report. He had declared Honorius emperor after the defeat of Eugenius, on the fourth day before the Ides of January of the same year, as we learn from Hydatius, Prosper, and others.]

who had already handed everything over to his sons—the kingdom, the power, the name of Augustus. Nothing, I say, more splendid was reserved for him in death

[Note: [Col. 1388B] All editions and several manuscripts read, “than that which was monstrous in magnitude”; Gill, in various readings, has “than that which was monstrous in quantity”; one Regius manuscript has “than that which was in years,” which, together with one or another manuscript, reads “while he delays” instead of “while he dies,” without an unsuitable meaning. In the first part, however, we have restored from one Vatican manuscript “than that which was in some measure”—namely, in grain, wine, oil, or similar goods; for the grain allowance was demanded in kind, as is clear from many laws in the title On the Grain Supply and Taxes. Bulengerus discusses the grain supply at greater length in Book 6 of On the Roman Empire, chapter 1 and following. As for the opinion of some that what is said here should be referred to the tax of Tatianus, that seems quite obscure; it is more credible that Honorius fulfilled his father’s wish. Nor should these verses of Claudian, in the Fourth Consulship of Honorius, be understood of anything else:

“Let the impious increases of the perpetual tax cease;

Let no unfortunate tablets, no spear fixed again,

Sell your wealth to greedy buyers; let no purchaser be summoned by a call;

Nor let your treasury grow through the losses of private persons.”]

than that the promised relaxation of the collection of grain provisions was granted in certain items while he still lingered, and his successor was made heir to his acts of clemency; and the one who wished to obstruct this brought hatred upon himself,

[Col. 1388A] yet the abundance of such grace was not taken away from Theodosius. Nor without reason: if the final wishes of private persons and the wills of those who die possess perpetual validity,

[Note: [Col. 1388C] One Regius manuscript reads, “wishes for making a will.”]

how can the testament of so great a prince be invalid?

[Note: [Col. 1388C] Some manuscripts read, “Theodosius is also more glorious,” and so forth.]

Theodosius is more glorious in this respect also, since he did not make a will according to ordinary law. He had nothing new to establish concerning his sons, to whom he had given everything, except that he should commend them to a parent who was present;

[Note: [Col. 1388C] Someone has thought that the words “to a parent who was present” were spoken of Ambrose himself, because of the words of Paulinus: “Nor was the emperor Theodosius of blessed memory long in this life after receiving his sons in the Church and handing them over to the priest.” Yet it is more probable that Stilicho is designated there, since Theodosius appointed him not only guardian of Honorius, as Zosimus testifies in Book 4 of his History, but also intended him to be that prince’s father-in-law, Maria, Stilicho’s daughter, having been betrothed to Honorius, as Claudian sings in the wedding poem of the two. Although historians assert that Rufinus was appointed guardian of Arcadius by Theodosius, nothing prevents Theodosius from commending both sons to Stilicho’s trust, as Ambrose says here; the poet cited also supports him in Book 2 Against Rufinus, with these verses:

“Now Roman power rests upon your care, Stilicho,

And the summit of affairs is entrusted to you; to you is committed

The majesty of both brothers,” and so forth.]

and he ought to have made a testament concerning his subjects and those entrusted to him, so that he might leave bequests and designate trusts. He ordered a law of indulgence to be issued, which he left in writing. What could be more worthy than that the emperor’s testament should be a law?

6. So great an emperor has departed from us, but he has not departed altogether; for he left us his sons, in whom we ought to recognize him and in whom we both see and hold him. Let not their age disturb you: the faith of the emperor’s soldiers is a completed age; for age is complete wherever virtue is complete. These things are reciprocal, because the faith of the emperor is also the soldiers’ virtue.

7. You recognize, surely, what triumphs the faith of Theodosius won for you.

[Note: [Col. 1388D] Rufinus, in Book 2 of his History, chapter 32, explains most brilliantly, and especially in a manner suited to Ambrose’s meaning, with what piety Theodosius prepared himself for this war, with what faith he sought divine help in the battle itself, and how many prodigies he obtained from God. Socrates, Book 5, chapter 25; Sozomen, Book 7, chapter 24; and Orosius, Book 7, chapter 35, also describe the event carefully. Add to these what we have noted in the Exposition of Psalm 36, section 25.]

When the army’s column was somewhat delayed in entering the battle because of the narrowness of the terrain and the obstacles presented by the baggage train, and the enemy seemed to be taking advantage of the delay in the battle, the emperor leaped from his horse and, advancing alone before the battle line, said: “Where is the God of Theodosius?” In saying this he was already near to Christ. For who could say this except one who knew himself to cling to Christ? By these words he roused everyone and armed everyone by his example. He was already advanced in age, certainly, but strong in faith.

8.

[Note: [Col. 1389D] The words “Therefore Theodosius’s faith … let it be your strength” are lacking in our manuscripts, but, conversely, they are found in all the editions.]

The faith of Theodosius, therefore, was your victory; let your faith be the strength of his sons. Faith, then, increases age. In the end, neither Abraham, when he was to father a son in old age, considered his age, nor Sarah, when she was to give birth. Nor is it surprising that faith increases age, since it makes the future present. For what is faith except “the substance of things hoped for” (Heb. 11:1)? Thus the Scriptures teach us. Therefore, if faith is the substance of things hoped for, how much more is it the substance of things seen? It is a good faith, of which it is written: “The righteous person lives by faith” (Heb. 10:38). But if he draws back, my soul will not be pleased with him.

9. Let us not, however, draw back to the ruin of our soul, but cling to faith for the acquisition of our soul, since in this warfare of faith our elders Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob obtained testimony. Therefore they left us the inheritance of faith. Abraham was faithful, justified not by works but by faith, because he believed God; Isaac was faithful, who through faith did not shrink from the sword of his father as it was about to strike; Jacob was faithful, who, intent upon the footsteps of his father’s faith, saw the army of angels while traveling

1201

[Note: [Col. 1389D] The Roman edition alone reads, “and called it the Camp of God.”]

and called it the assembly of God (Gen. 32:1).

10. Elsewhere also—that is, in the Books of Kings—Elisha was inside Samaria, and suddenly an army of Syrians surrounded and besieged him. Gehazi saw them and said to his master: “Alas, my lord, what shall we do?” And the prophet Elisha said: “Do not fear, for there are more with us than with them.” And he prayed that the Lord would open Gehazi’s eyes. His eyes were opened, and he saw the mountain full of horses and chariots around Elisha. And Elisha prayed that God would strike them with blindness; and they were struck, and they entered the city they were approaching, seeing nothing (2 Kings 6:15 and following). You have certainly heard this, soldiers who are surrounded: where treachery is, there is blindness. The army of the unbelieving was therefore rightly blind. But where there is faith, there is an army of angels.

[Col. 1390A] Good, then, is faith, which frequently operates even in the dead. In the end, the adversary and his legions are tormented by the daily virtue of the martyrs. Hence I think that the strings of a cithara are called “faiths” for this reason: because even when dead, they produce sound.

[Note: [Col. 1389D] Vossius says that this etymology is witty rather than true in his entry on the word *fido*. He also rejects the etymology by which Festus holds that the strings of a cithara are called “faiths” because they agree among themselves as faith does among human beings, and he offers a genuine derivation.]

11. Therefore we must strive more and more not to be ungrateful in this office of living;

[Note: [Col. 1389D] Some manuscripts read, “in this duty of living, let us be sufficiently ungrateful.”]

rather, as pious persons, let us show diligent and fatherly affection toward the pledges of the emperor. Pay his sons what you owe their father. You owe more to the dead than you owed to the living. For if the rights of minors are violated in the children of private persons only at the cost of grave guilt, how much more in the sons of an emperor?

12. Let there be added whose emperor he was: a pious emperor, a merciful emperor, a faithful emperor, concerning whom Scripture has spoken in no ordinary terms, saying: “A merciful man is great and honorable; but to find a faithful man is difficult” (Prov. 20:6). If it is a great thing to find any merciful or faithful man, how much greater a thing to find an emperor, whom power impels toward vengeance, but compassion nevertheless recalls from vengeance? What is more excellent than the faithfulness of an emperor whom power does not exalt, pride does not raise up, but piety inclines? Of him Solomon beautifully says:

> “The threat of an unjust king is like the roaring of a lion; but as dew upon the grass, so is his cheerfulness” (Prov. 19:12).

[Note: The old edition reads *Iniqui regis imitatio* (“the imitation of an unjust king”); some manuscripts have *minatio* (“threat”), others *minitatio* (“threatening”). The Roman edition accepted *minitatio*, but deleted *iniqui*. Nevertheless, although the word is absent from the sacred manuscripts that we now use, it is credible that Ambrose read it in his copy, on account of the agreement of the manuscripts of this treatise.]

How great, then, is it to lay aside the terror of power and to prefer the gentleness of grace?

13. The emperor Theodosius of august memory considered it a favor when he was asked to forgive; and he was nearer to pardon when he had been more greatly stirred to anger.

[Note: One Regius manuscript reads *commotior* (“more stirred”). Greater anger was a prerogative of forgiveness. It was desired that he should be indignant at that which was feared in others, and so forth—not entirely correctly. Since this passage concerns Theodosius’ inclination toward anger and his readiness to be appeased, it is worthwhile to compare what is said on this subject in Letter 51, section 4, and also to consult what Aurelius Victor recorded in the *Epitome* concerning this emperor’s same emotions.]

His indignation was a prerogative of forgiveness; and in him what was feared in others was desired, namely, that he should become angry. This was a remedy for the guilty; for, although he possessed power above all others, he preferred to remonstrate like a father rather than punish like a judge. We often saw those whom he rebuked trembling, and those convicted of crime, after they had despaired, released from their guilt. For the judge of equity and not the arbiter of punishment wished to conquer, not to chastise; he never denied pardon to one who confessed, or, if there was something concealed by a hidden conscience, he reserved it for God. People feared this utterance of his more than punishment: so great was the emperor’s modesty in acting that he preferred to bind people to himself by religious reverence rather than by fear.

14. The greatest philosopher, they say, granted impunity for crimes committed in anger; but divine Scripture speaks more rightly: “Be angry, and do not sin” (Ps. 4:5). He preferred to cut off sin rather than excuse it. It is better to find praise for clemency in indignation than to be stirred by anger toward vengeance.

[Note: The Roman edition had written in the margin “Aristotle, *Ethics*, book VII, chapter 6.” But apart from the fact that what Ambrose says here is not found very clearly in that passage, it was entirely unusual at that time for the Fathers to refer to Aristotle so honorifically. Certainly Ambrose’s words could be referred no less appropriately to Plato’s *Laws*, book IX, if Ambrose intended to indicate a passage read by him.]

15. Who, then, will doubt that his sons will have the greatest protection with the Lord? With the Lord’s favor, the emperor Arcadius is already strong in youth; Honorius is continually knocking at the gates of adolescence, more advanced in age than Josiah.

[Note: The old edition reads “has already been found strong”; some Paris manuscripts read “already a strong young man”; the Roman edition and the manuscripts agree with our text. Baronius states that Arcadius was twenty years old when he was deprived of his father, although others assign him only seventeen years; you may learn that Honorius was ten years old from the fact that Socrates, Hydatius, and Marcellinus record him as having been born in the consulship of Richomer and Clearchus, that is, in A.D. 384.]

Josiah, having been deprived of his father, began his reign and carried his life onward to the thirty-first year of his reign, and pleased the Lord, because, more than the other kings of Israel, he celebrated the Lord’s Passover and abolished the errors of the ceremonies (IV Kings 22:1 ff.). Asa also, while still weak in bodily strength, when he had undertaken the course of kingship, reigned forty years in Jerusalem.

[Note: The Roman edition alone reads “he reigned forty-one years.” The sacred books also prefer this reading, but Ambrose wished to give the complete number.]

When he was hard pressed by the Ethiopians with an immense and innumerable multitude, he hoped that he could be saved by the Lord even with a few.

[Note: All editions have this reading; but nearly all manuscripts have a lacuna from *speravit* (“he hoped”) to *postulavit* (“he sought”). Pratensis, Gemblacensis, and Albius attempted to repair it as follows: “He hoped in the Lord, he sought, and he conquered, and he employed physicians.” This is not an altogether bad restoration.]

Would that he had remained as faithful in his progress as he was devoted at the beginning! For although he had been saved with a few and had conquered, afterward he sought aid from the Syrians, abandoning the Lord, and employed physicians for the pain in his feet. After receiving so great a sign of divine favor, he ought not to have abandoned his helper, but to have held fast to him. Therefore physicians did not benefit him, and, as though unbelieving, he fulfilled his death.

16. But their fathers, Abijah and Amon, were both faithless. Theodosius, however, full of the fear of God and full of mercy, we hope will stand before Christ as a protector for his children, if the Lord is favorable to human affairs.

A merciful man is good: while helping others, he takes thought for himself, and in another’s remedy he heals his own wounds. For he recognizes himself to be a human being who knows how to forgive; and he follows the ways of Christ, who, having assumed flesh, preferred to come into this world as Redeemer rather than as Judge.

17. Therefore the Psalmist beautifully said: “I loved, because the Lord will hear the voice of my prayer” (Ps. 114:1). As this psalm is read, we seem to hear Theodosius himself speaking. “I loved,” he says: “I recognize a devout voice, whose testimony I recognize.” And truly he loved, who fulfilled his duties with greater diligence; who preserved his enemies; who loved his enemies; who forgave those by whom he had been attacked; who did not permit those aspiring to the kingdom to perish.

This is not the voice of an ordinary person, but of one perfect in the Law, to say, “I loved.” For “the fullness of the Law is love” (Rom. 13:10). But let us hear whom he loved.

[Note: The old edition reads: “When it is silent, love urges us”—plainly, by the grace of divine love. The Roman edition reads: “When it is silent, it urges us—plainly, by the grace of divine love.” A large number of manuscripts have: “When the kind of love is not stated, the grace of divine love is signified,” and so forth. Best of all is one Regius manuscript, as in the text.]

When the kind of love is not stated, the grace of divine charity is signified—the love by which we love that which is desirable above all desirable things, concerning which it is written: “You shall love the Lord your God” (Deut. 6:5).

18. Therefore, as the devout soul, filled with the Holy Spirit, was departing from the earth and rising toward the heights and heavenly things—as though in answer to those who met it—it said: “I loved.” Nothing is fuller; nothing is more expressive.

The angels or archangels asked: “What did you do on earth?” For God alone is the knower of hidden things. It said, “I loved”—that is, “I fulfilled the Law; I did not pass by the Gospel.” This is to say: “I offered myself to death, and all day long I was reckoned as a sheep for slaughter” (Ps. 43:22). And therefore I trust that “neither death nor life, nor angels nor powers, nor height nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Rom. 8:38–39).

19. The Lord Jesus teaches that this commandment of the Law must also be observed in the Gospel, when he says to Peter: “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” And he answered: “You know, Lord, that I love you.” Again he said: “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” And again he answered: “Yes, Lord, you know that I love you.” And when questioned a third time he said: “Lord, you know all things; you know that I love you” (John 21:15 ff.).

Thus the threefold answer confirmed charity, or abolished the error of the threefold denial. And if we seek a threefold answer here, we find it: “I loved, because the Lord will hear the voice of my prayer” (Ps. 114:1 ff.). “I loved, because he inclined his ear to me, and I shall call upon him throughout my days. I loved, because I found tribulation and grief, and for the name of my God I did not flee the perils of hell, but waited for them to seize and find me.”

20. And beautifully he says, “I loved,” because he had now completed the course of this life. Therefore the Apostle, already placed in suffering, also says: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith; what remains is the crown of righteousness laid up for me” (II Tim. 4:7–8).

Great is the Lord, who has given us contests by which the victor may deserve to be crowned. “I loved,” he says, confident that the Lord will hear the voice of my prayer.

21. “I loved,” and therefore he inclined his ear to me, in order to raise up the one lying down and resurrect the dead. God does not incline his ear in order to hear bodily, but in order to accommodate himself to us, so that he may deem us worthy to be heard and may lift up the substance of our weakness.

[Note: Many manuscripts read “and our weaknesses”; some have “and to lift up the weakness of our judgment.”]

He inclines himself to us so that our prayer may rise to him. He has no need of a voice who bestows mercy; for he had no need of a voice when he heard Moses while Moses was silent, and said that Moses, not speaking but crying out to him through unspeakable groanings, was calling to him (Exod. 14:15).

God also knows how to hear blood (Gen. 4:10), although it has no voice and no tongue to speak; but he accepted it as a voice under the title of sacred suffering. It cried out in martyrdom; it cried out in fratricide, which he endured as a sacrifice.

22. “I loved,” he says, and therefore, loving, I did the will of the Lord, and I called upon him not on a few days, but on all the days of my life. For to call upon him on certain days but not on all is the practice of one who is disdainful, not of one who hopes; and to return the payment of thanks for the customary abundance of benefits, not out of a devotional affection.

Therefore Paul says: “Give thanks in all things” (I Thess. 5:17). For when do you lack what you owe to God? Or when are you without God’s gift, since the daily use of life comes from the Lord? “What do you have that you did not receive?” (I Cor. 4:7). Therefore, because you always receive, always call upon him; and because what you have is from the Lord, recognize that you are always in his debt. Yet I prefer that you pay your debt as one who loves rather than as one compelled.

23. Do you hear him saying: “The pains of death surrounded me” (Ps. 114:3)? Yet even in the pain of death I loved the Lord. The perils of hell found me—not, certainly, fearing, but loving and hoping that no distress, no persecution, no danger, and no sword would separate me from Christ.

Finally, he willingly found tribulation and grief, knowing that “tribulation produces endurance, endurance produces character, and character produces hope.” For, like a good athlete, he sought contests in order to find the crown; yet he knew that it had been given to him not by his own strength but by the Lord’s aid. For he could not have conquered unless he had called upon him who helps those engaged in the contest.

24. A wretched man enters the contest in order to conquer; and he himself rushes into danger unless the Lord’s name is present, unless, when he fears, he prays, saying: “O Lord, deliver my soul” (Ps. 114:4).

Hence comes the Apostle’s statement: “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive to the law of sin which is in my members. Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 7:23 ff.).

25. He conquers who hopes in the grace of God, not he who presumes upon his own virtue.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “who hopes in the grace of God.”]

For why should you not presume upon grace when you have as the leader of the contest one who is merciful? “For the Lord is merciful and just, and our God has mercy” (Ps. 114:5).

[Note: This is the reading of the old edition and the manuscripts, except that, where the editions and a few manuscripts have *misericordiam* (“mercy”), we have restored *misericordem* (“merciful”) from the much larger number of manuscripts. The Roman edition interpolated the passage with the following: “For it is written: ‘Now mercy triumphs over judgment.’ And elsewhere: ‘Merciful.’” The editors were led into this error because they did not see that Ambrose is giving a continuous exposition of Psalm 114 and applying it to Theodosius.]

He mentioned mercy twice and justice once: justice stands in the middle, enclosed within a double fence of mercy. For sins abound; therefore let mercy abound. In the Lord there is an abundance of every virtue, because he is the Lord of virtues (Ps. 23:10).

Yet justice is not without mercy, nor is justice without compassion, because it is written: “Do not be excessively just” (Eccles. 7:17).

[Note: One Regius manuscript reads: “What is beyond measure is harmful,” and so forth. The other manuscripts and editions agree with one another, except for certain Paris editions, which incorrectly read *festines* (“you should hasten”) instead of *sustines* (“you can bear”).]

What is beyond measure, even if it is good, you nevertheless cannot bear. Keep to the measure, so that you may receive according to the measure.

26. Mercy nevertheless did not obstruct justice, because mercy itself is justice: “He distributed; he gave to the poor; his justice remains forever” (Ps. 111:9). For the just person knows that he ought to help the weak and needy.

Therefore, when the Lord came to baptism in order to forgive sins to us who were weak, he said to John: “Let it be so now; for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness” (Matt. 3:15).

[Note: The Regius manuscript reads: “Allow us to fulfill,” and so forth.]

It is therefore clear that justice is mercy and mercy is justice. For if God’s mercy did not sustain us, how would we live as infants at the very beginning, when, expelled from the womb, we are cast from warm places into cold, from moist places into dry, like fish whom, as shipwrecked persons, some wave of nature has spewed into this life?

[Note: Philo, *On the Creation of the World*: “Therefore also the infant weeps …” (*Διὸ καὶ ἀποκλαίεται τὸ βρέφος* …).]

Reason is lacking, but divine grace does not fail. He therefore guards the little ones (Ps. 114:6), or at least those who humbly confess themselves to be little ones.

27. Good, therefore, is humility, which frees those in danger and raises up those lying down. He knew it who said: “Behold, I am here; I have sinned, and I, the shepherd, have acted wickedly; but what have these sheep done? Let your hand be against me” (II Sam. 24:17).

He says this well who subjected his kingdom to God, performed repentance, and, having confessed his sin, sought pardon. Through humility he reached salvation. Christ humbled himself in order to raise everyone up; the one who follows Christ’s humility reaches Christ’s rest.

28. And therefore, because the emperor Theodosius presented himself as humble and, when sin had crept in, sought pardon, his soul was turned into its rest, as Scripture says: “Return, my soul, to your rest, because the Lord has dealt bountifully with you” (Ps. 114:7).

He beautifully says to the soul, “Return,” as though it had been exercised by the long-continued labor of every work, so that it might turn from toil to rest.

[Note: The Pratensis and Gemblacensis manuscripts read: “The horse, exercised by long use … turns toward salvation.”]

A horse returns to the stable when it has completed its course; a ship returns to port when, for secure anchorage, it is withdrawn from the mass of the waves. But what does he mean by “to your rest” unless you understand it according to what the Lord Jesus said: “Come, you blessed of my Father; inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25:34)?

[Note: The same manuscripts and some others read: “It is an inheritance from which we receive what has been promised to us,” and so forth.]

As an inherited possession, then, we receive what has been promised to us; for God is faithful, and what he has once prepared for his servants he does not withdraw. If our faith remains, the promise also remains.

[Note: One Regius manuscript reads: “The possession remains.” But the reading should unquestionably be *sponsio* (“promise”).]

29. See, O human being, the grace of Christ around you: you are still tossed about on earth, yet you possess heaven. Let your heart therefore be where your possession is.

This is the rest owed to the just and denied to the unworthy. Therefore the Lord says: “As I swore in my wrath, they shall not enter into my rest” (Ps. 94:11); for those who did not know the ways of the Lord do not enter the Lord’s rest.

But to the one who has fought the good fight and completed the course (II Tim. 4:7), it is said: “Return to your rest” (Ps. 114:7).

Good is the rest that passes beyond the things of the world and rests in those things above the world, in heavenly fellowship and the secrecy of divine things. This is the rest toward which the prophet hastened, saying: “Who will give me wings like a dove’s? I shall fly away and rest” (Ps. 54:7).

This is the holy rest that he knew as his own; toward this rest he says that his soul must be turned.

[Note: Several manuscripts read: “He says that his soul must be turned.”]

The soul was therefore in its rest, to which he says it must return. This is the rest of the great Sabbath, so that each of the saints may be above the perceptible things of the world, wholly intent upon and clinging to God in that intelligible secrecy.

[Note: We have explained elsewhere what is called the great Sabbath.]

This is that Sabbath rest on which God rested from all the works of this world (Gen. 2:2).

30. Theodosius rejoices that he has been rescued from the cares of this age, released from them as from a holiday, and he raises his soul and directs it toward that perpetual rest.

[Note: Many manuscripts read: “And raising his soul toward that rest,” and so forth.]

He rightly declares that God has acted for his good, because God has rescued his soul from death—the death which he often endured amid the slippery instability of this age, troubled by the waves of sins. God has also rescued his eyes from tears (Ps. 114:8), for “pain and sadness and groaning will flee away” (Isa. 35:10).

Elsewhere we read: “He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more; neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain” (Rev. 21:4).

If death will not exist, then the one established in that rest cannot experience a fall; but he will please God in the land of the living. For he will not be there as a human being here, wrapped in a body subject to death, falls, and sins.
