Therefore that region is the land of the living, where the soul exists, which was made in the image and likeness of God, not the flesh formed from clay (Gen. 1:27). Therefore the flesh returns to the earth, while the soul hastens to the heavenly rest, to which it is said: “Return, my soul, to your rest” (Ps. 114:9).

31. Into this rest Theodosius hastened to enter, and to enter the city Jerusalem, concerning which it is said: “And the kings of the earth will bring their glory into it” (Rev. 21:24).

That is the true glory which is received there; that is the most blessed kingdom which is possessed there. Toward it the Apostle hastened, saying: “Therefore we are confident, and we desire rather to depart from the body and be present with the Lord” (II Cor. 5:6); and therefore “we strive, whether absent or present, to please him” (ibid., 9).

32. Thus, released from the uncertain struggle, Theodosius of august memory now enjoys perpetual light and enduring tranquility, and rejoices in the fruits of divine recompense for what he accomplished in this body. Therefore, because Theodosius of august memory loved the Lord his God, he deserved the fellowship of the saints.

33. And I, to conclude my speech with a sort of peroration, loved a merciful man, humble in the exercise of imperial power, endowed with a pure heart and a gentle breast, such as the Lord is accustomed to love, saying: “Upon whom shall I rest, if not upon the humble and gentle?” (Isa. 66:2).

[Note: The old edition and most manuscripts read: “That indeed … through prayer.” The Roman edition and some other manuscripts read: “That indeed … in the peroration.” The latter is the best reading; it means the same as if he said: “To conclude this part of my speech with a recapitulation of Theodosius’ virtues,” as is customary in a peroration.]

34. I loved a man who approved one who reproved rather than one who flattered.

[Note: All writers who have transmitted to posterity, with deserved praise, the splendid humility of Theodosius in undertaking public penance agree fully with what Ambrose says here. See, if you wish, Paulinus, *Life of the Holy Bishop*; Rufinus, *History*, book II, chapter 18; Augustine, *City of God*, book V, chapter 26; Sozomen, *History*, book VII, chapter 25; Theodoret, book V, chapter 18; and others. Ambrose’s Letter 51 may also be joined to these, so that you may understand how the holy bishop prepared the emperor for repentance.]

He laid down every royal insignia that he wore; he publicly mourned in the Church the sin that had crept upon him through the deceit of others; with groaning and tears he prayed for pardon. What private persons are ashamed of, the emperor was not ashamed to do publicly: to perform penance. Nor was there afterward any day on which he did not grieve over that error.

What more? Although he had won a glorious victory, nevertheless, because enemies had been struck down in battle, he abstained from communion in the sacraments until the Lord’s grace toward him was manifested by the arrival of his sons.

[Note: This abstention of Theodosius from communion after the defeat of Eugenius may be referred solely to his reverence toward the divine mysteries, or perhaps also to Ambrose’s exhortation. Since killing adversaries in war is just and worthy of praise, as Athanasius states in his letter to Ammonius the Monk, and since the Fathers did not count deaths occurring in wars as ordinary killings, as Basil teaches in Letter to Amphilochius, canon 13, it remains that what Ambrose writes in Letter 25 concerning judges in capital cases applies here as well: “Our fathers preferred that the matter rest more in the will of one who abstains than in the necessity of the law.” For although the cited letter of Basil recommends that those whose hands are not clean abstain from communion for only three years, Balsamon testifies that this practice was not received in the Church.]

35. I loved a man who, in his final moments, sought me with his last breath. I loved a man who, when he was already being released from the body, was more troubled about the condition of the Churches than about his own dangers.

Therefore I loved him, I confess, and for this reason I grieved my grief in the deepest part of my being, and thought it should be consoled by a more extended continuation of my speech. I loved him, and I presume from the Lord that he will receive the voice of my prayer, by which I accompany the devout soul.

36. “The pains of death surrounded me; the perils of hell found me” (Ps. 114:3). For many are in danger, but few have remedies. The priest is endangered in all; he is distressed on behalf of all the guilty. What others suffer, he himself bears; and again he is freed when those held by dangers are freed.

My heart is crushed, because a man has been taken from us whom we can scarcely find again.

[Note: The Roman edition reads: “Such a man as we can scarcely find.”]

Yet you alone, Lord, must be invoked; you alone must be entreated, so that you may restore him to us in his sons. You, Lord, who even in this humility guard the little ones,

[Note: The Vindobonensis manuscript and some others read: “You will save those who hope in you.” Below, instead of “your saints,” one Colbertinus manuscript reads “your servants.”]

save those who hope in you (Ps. 114:5–6). Give perfect rest to your servant Theodosius, that rest which you have prepared for your saints.

[Note: The Colbertinus manuscript reads: “The rest which you have prepared for your servants.”]

May his soul return there from which it descended; where it cannot feel the sting of death; where it may recognize that this death is not the end of nature but of sin. For “the one who has died has died to sin” (Rom. 6:10), so that henceforth there may be no place for sin; but he will rise again, so that life may be restored, renewed by a more perfect gift.

37. I loved him, and therefore I accompany him as far as the land of the living. I will not abandon him until, with tears and prayers, I bring the man, where his merits summon him, to the holy mountain of the Lord: where there is perpetual life, no corruption, no defilement, no groaning, no pain, and no fellowship with the dead; the true land of the living, where “this mortal puts on immortality, and this corruptible puts on incorruption” (I Cor. 15:54).

Great is the rest that fulfills the desire of one who loves; most beautiful is the promise. Therefore the one hundred and fourteenth psalm is entitled “Alleluia.”

[Note: This is found in one Regius manuscript; in all the others and in all the editions *alleluia* is omitted, inconveniently. The Vindobonensis manuscript instead has “in the hundred and eleventh psalm” for “in the fourteenth psalm.”]

For earlier, in the fourteenth psalm, we received the perfection of the human being. But there the human being was formed and, though perfect, was still subject to sin, because he lives in the world. Here there is true perfection, where guilt has already ceased and the grace of perpetual rest has shone forth.

38. Therefore the one hundred and fourteenth psalm concerns the recompense of love. Hence the Lord’s Passover received the form of its celebration on the fourteenth day of the moon, because whoever celebrates Passover ought to be perfect and ought to love the Lord Jesus, who, loving his people with perfect love, offered himself to suffering.

Let us also love in such a way that, if necessary, we do not flee death for the Lord’s name; let us consider no pain significant and fear nothing. For “perfect love casts out fear” (I John 4:18).

Great is the mystery of the number, when the Father delivered his only Son for us all while the moon shone with the full circle of its light. Such is the Church that devoutly celebrates the Passover of our Lord Jesus Christ: like the full moon, it remains forever.

Whoever celebrates the Lord’s Passover well here will be in perpetual light. Who celebrated it more splendidly than the one who removed sacrilegious errors, closed the temples, and destroyed the images? In this respect King Josiah surpassed those who came before him (IV Kings 23:25).

39. Theodosius therefore remains in the light and rejoices among the assemblies of the saints. There he now embraces Gratian, who no longer grieves over his wounds because he has found an avenger. Although he was taken away by an undeserved death, he possesses rest for his soul.

[Note: Amerbach has “overtaken and seized by an undeserved death”; Gill and Erasmus have “overtaken and snatched away.” The Roman edition reads “killed by an undeserved death”; the very frequent manuscripts have the reading used in the text.]

There the two good men, interpreters of piety, delight in fellowship, generous in their mercy. Concerning them it is rightly said: “Day pours forth the word to day” (Ps. 18:3).

But Maximus and Eugenius are in hell; night, as it were, declares knowledge to night, teaching by their pitiable example how harsh it is to raise arms against one’s own emperors. Concerning them it is beautifully said: “I saw the wicked man exalted and raised up like the cedars of Lebanon; and I passed by, and behold, he was not” (Ps. 36:35).

For the pious man passed from the darkness of worldly affairs into eternal light, and the wicked man was no more, having ceased to be unjust.

40. Now Theodosius of august memory knows that he reigns, since he is in the kingdom of the Lord Jesus Christ, and he beholds his temple. Now he is a king to himself, when he also receives his son Gratian and Pulcheria, his sweetest children, whom he had lost here;

[Note: The old edition reads: “his son Gratian and the beautiful and sweetest one”; the Roman edition reads: “his son Gratian, and the most beautiful and sweetest one.” The manuscripts likewise have this reading, except for one Vatican manuscript and the Thuanus and Bellovacensis manuscripts, which read: “his son Gratian and Pulcheria, the sweetest one,” and so forth. We have explained elsewhere, in connection with Letter 51, how Gratian could have been called Theodosius’ son. If anyone, following Baronius, should think that this Gratian is properly and truly called Theodosius’ son, it must at least be said against that same Cardinal that this Gratian was not born of Flaccilla, to whom Gregory of Nyssa assigns only three children in her funeral oration, but of Galla, the second wife of that emperor, who, according to the historians, died in childbirth a few days before he came to Italy to wage war against Eugenius. Ambrose did not mention this Galla, perhaps because, having been raised by her Arian mother, she had contracted some contamination from her, so that her faith was considered less than whole. Nor do we think Philostorgius should be believed when he writes that she was entirely devoted to the Arian party. As for Flaccilla, we know that she was endowed with supreme virtue and religious devotion; concerning her, see Theodoret, book V of the *History*, chapter 19.]

when Flaccilla, a soul faithful to God, clings to him; when Gratian rejoices that his father has been restored to him; and when Gratian clings to Constantine.

Although the grace of baptism forgave Constantine all his sins when he was at the point of death, nevertheless, because he was the first of the emperors to believe and left behind him an inheritance of faith for the emperors who followed, he found a place of great merit.

[Note: Ambrose could not express his opinion concerning Constantine’s baptism in clearer words. Yet other writers no less clearly testify that this emperor received that sacrament only at the end of his life, such as Eusebius, *Life of Constantine*, book IV, chapters 61–62; Jerome, *Chronicle*; Socrates, *History*, book I, chapter 39; Sozomen, book II, chapter 34; Theodoret, book I, chapter 32; and others. It is therefore surprising that some still obstinately defend the claim that Constantine was baptized by Pope Sylvester on the basis of apocryphal Acts, which they themselves are compelled to acknowledge as corrupted in many respects.]

In his time the prophetic word was fulfilled: “On that day there shall be upon the bridle of the horse, ‘Holy to the Lord Almighty’” (Zech. 14:20). His mother Helena of holy memory revealed this to him after being filled with the Spirit of God.

41. Blessed is Constantine in such a parent, who sought for her imperial son the aid of the divine gift, by which he might stand secure even amid battles and not fear danger.

[Note: This passage also gives us a remarkable testimony to the veneration with which ancient Christians honored sacred relics and to the devout confidence that they placed in their protection. But why, you may ask, does such an excursus on the discovery of the cross occur in a eulogy of Theodosius? We reply that it was very characteristic of Ambrose to depart from his subject whenever a pious occasion invited him to do so. Such an occasion was the mention of Constantine, who was the first of the Caesars to order the standard of the cross to be carried before him in wars. Theodosius imitated him in this respect in his war against Eugenius, as may be learned from Theodoret, book V, chapter 24, and Orosius, book VII, chapter 36.]

A great woman, who found far more to give the emperor than she had received from the emperor. An anxious mother for her son, to whom the rule of the Roman world had fallen, hastened to Jerusalem and searched out the place of the Lord’s Passion.

### 42.

[Note: [Col. 1400C] Ambrose calls Helena a “stable-woman,” because she was believed to have been born to a father who received travelers in a public lodging-house. Yet we are not unaware that Baronius, under the year 306, writes that Constantine’s mother was the daughter of a certain Coel, one of the rulers of Britain, and that this was handed down by the ancient historians of that nation. But since all the historians of Roman affairs call Helena the concubine of Constantius and assert that Constantine was born of an unequal union, it is credible that the opinion reported by Baronius should be regarded as a fable. See, if you wish, the Chronicles of Eusebius and Cassiodorus; Orosius, *History*, book VII, chapter 16; Eutropius, book X; Zosimus, book II; Nicephorus, book VII, chapter 18; and among more recent writers, Morinus, book II, *On the Freedom of the Church*, chapter 6.]

They assert that she was originally a stable-woman, and that she became known in this way to the elder Constantius, who later obtained the throne. A good stable-woman, who so diligently sought out the Lord’s manger! A good stable-woman, who did not fail to recognize that stable-man who healed the wounds of the man wounded by robbers (Luke 10:34). A good stable-woman, who preferred to be accounted refuse, in order to gain Christ (Philippians 3:8).

[Note: [Col. 1400D] One manuscript of Regius: “who regarded everything as refuse.”]

Therefore Christ raised her from refuse to the throne, according to what is written: “He raises the needy from the dust and lifts the poor from the refuse heap” (Psalm 112:7).

### 43.

Helena therefore came and began to revisit the holy places. The Spirit inspired her to seek the wood of the cross. She approached Golgotha and said: “Behold the place of battle—where is the victory? I seek the standard of salvation, and I do not find it. I,” she said, “am in palaces, and the Lord’s cross in the dust? I am among gold ornaments, and Christ’s triumph amid ruins? He is still concealed, and is the palm of eternal life also concealed? How can I consider myself redeemed if redemption itself cannot be seen?”

### 44.

“I see what you have done, devil, so that the sword by which you were slain might be blocked.”

[Note: [Col. 1400D] The Colbertine manuscript: “But she dug out what had been blocked … and did not allow the water to remain concealed.”]

“But Isaac dug out the wells that had been blocked by foreigners, and did not allow the water to remain concealed (Genesis 26:18). Let the ruin therefore be removed, so that life may appear; let the sword be brought forth, by which the head of the true Goliath was cut off (1 Samuel 17:51); let the earth be opened, so that salvation may shine forth (Isaiah 45:8). What did you do, devil, by hiding the wood, except ensure that you would be conquered again? Mary conquered you, she who bore the triumphant one; she who, without diminishing her virginity, brought forth him who, crucified, would conquer you, and, dead, would subdue you. You are conquered today as well, so that a woman may detect your snares. She bore the holy Lord, as it were; I shall seek out his cross. She taught that he had been born; I shall proclaim that he has risen. She caused God to be seen among human beings; I shall raise the divine standard from the ruins for the healing of our sins.”

### 45.

She therefore opens the earth and brushes away the dust. She finds three crosses confused together, which the ruin had covered and the enemy had hidden. But Christ’s triumph could not be obliterated. She hesitates in uncertainty; she hesitates like a woman, but the Holy Spirit inspires a certain means of investigation, since two robbers had been crucified with the Lord. She therefore seeks the middle cross. Yet it could have happened that the accident of the ruin had confused the crosses with one another and reversed their order.

[Note: [Col. 1401C] All printed editions: “had changed and reversed the accident.” All manuscripts: “had reversed the accident.”]

She returns to the Gospel reading and discovers that on the middle cross there had been placed an inscription: “Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews” (John 19:19). From this the sequence of truth was gathered, and by the inscription the saving cross was revealed. This is what Pilate replied to the Jews when they demanded it: “What I have written, I have written” (ibid., 22)—that is, “I did not write what would please you, but what a future age would recognize. I did not write for you, but for posterity.” He was almost saying: “Let Helena have something to read, by which she may recognize the Lord’s cross.”

[Note: [Col. 1401C] What the holy Bishop says here—that the Lord’s cross was distinguished from the robbers’ crosses by its inscription—seems indeed to differ from the opinion of other writers. Some report that the dead man was restored to life; others, that a noble woman was healed of an illness; others finally, that both miracles served as the sign by which it was discerned which of the three crosses was the Lord’s. Yet it is by no means unusual among historians that, while handing down the same event, some should mention or omit different circumstances. In any event, the discovery of the saving cross is asserted by the testimony of so many writers that scarcely anything in history is more firmly established. See Cyril of Jerusalem, letter to Constantius and *Catechesis* IV; Paulinus, letter to Severus, new edition, number 31; Sulpicius Severus, *History*, book II, chapter 48; Rufinus, book II, chapters 7 and 8; Socrates, book I, chapter 17; and others. Nor should Eusebius Pamphilus’s silence be brought as an objection. For, apart from the fact that what he relates in various places in book III of the *Life of Constantine* concerning the discovery of the Lord’s tomb seems to presuppose the discovery of the cross, the omission of one writer must yield to the assertions of so many others.]

### 46.

She therefore finds the inscription and adores the King—not, of course, the wood, for that is the error of the pagans and the vanity of the impious—but him who hung upon the wood, written in the inscription. I mean him who, like a beetle, cried out so that he might forgive the sins of his persecutors:

[Note: [Col. 1401D] “Father” is absent from all printed editions and from many more manuscripts; we have restored the word from the Regius manuscript. Observe here the true Catholic doctrine concerning the veneration due to the holy cross or to images: it does not terminate in the sign itself, but is referred by the mind to what is signified. From this you may see how honestly the Magdeburgians wrote that many superstitious things, violently insulting to Christ’s merit and contrary to the faith, are recounted by the author of this Oration. Yet to those men all things that oppose their unbelief appear contrary to the faith.]

“Father, forgive them” (Luke 23:34).

The eager woman hastened to touch the remedy of immortality; she feared to trample upon the sacrament of salvation. With joyful heart and trembling step, she did not know what to do. Nevertheless she pressed on to the bedchamber of truth; the wood shone forth, and grace glittered. And because Christ had already visited a woman in Mary, the Spirit visited Helena. He taught her what a woman did not know and led her onto a path that a mortal could not have known.

### 47.

She sought the nails with which the Lord had been crucified, and she found them. She ordered one nail to be made into a bridle; from another she had a diadem fashioned: one for adornment,

[Note: [Col. 1402C] One Regius manuscript: “the other for protection.” As for the matters related here concerning the sacred nails, they are also reported by Rufinus, book II, chapter 8; Socrates, book I, chapter 17; Sozomen, book II, chapter 1; Theodoret, book I, chapter 18; and Paulinus of Aquileia, book XI of his *History*.]

and the other she turned to devotion. Mary was visited so that Eve might be freed; Helena was visited so that emperors might be redeemed.

She therefore sent her son Constantine a diadem adorned with gems, whose gems the more precious gem of divine redemption, fastened with the iron of the cross, would bind together. She also sent him a bridle. Constantine used both and transmitted the faith to succeeding kings. Thus the beginning of believing emperors is sanctified by what is above the bridle (Zechariah 14:20): from that time faith came, so that persecution might cease and devotion succeed it.

[Note: [Col. 1402C] Jerome rejects this interpretation of the passage in Zechariah as follows: “I heard from someone a statement pious in meaning but ridiculous: that the nails of the Lord’s cross, from which the emperor Constantine made bridles for his horse, should be called ‘holy to the Lord.’” By these words we do not doubt that he silently reproaches Ambrose. Yet despite this criticism, many later writers embraced Ambrose’s explanation, including Cyril of Alexandria on the same words of Zechariah, Sozomen, Theodoret, Paulinus of Aquileia in the passages cited, and Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 6. We also see that Ambrose here proposed the moral exegesis preferred by Jerome, in these words: “But I ask why it is holy upon the bridle,” and so forth.]

### 48.

Helena acted wisely, placing the cross in the royal diadem upon the head, so that Christ’s cross might be adored in kings.

[Note: [Col. 1402D] Some manuscripts and printed editions read: “Wise was Helena, who raised the cross … to the throne.”]

This is not arrogance but piety, when honor is offered to sacred redemption. A good nail, therefore, is that of the Roman Empire, which rules the whole world and clothes the foreheads of rulers, so that those who were accustomed to be persecutors may become preachers. Rightly is the nail on the head, so that where understanding is, there protection may be. A crown is on the head; a bridle is in the hands.

[Note: [Col. 1402D] By far the majority of manuscripts read: “in the hands is faith.” They have: “They have a crown from the cross … they also have from the cross”; but other manuscripts, and all printed editions, give the reading followed in the text.]

A crown from the cross, so that faith may shine; a bridle also from the cross, so that power may rule; and let there be just restraint, not unjust command.

[Note: [Col. 1402D] Several manuscripts read: “not unjust prayer.” And below: “You placed upon my head.”]

Let rulers also have this granted to them by Christ’s generosity, so that, in imitation of the Lord, it may be said of the Roman emperor: “You placed upon his head a crown of precious stone” (Psalm 21:3).

### 49.

From that time the Church rejoices, while the Jew blushes—not merely blushes, but is also tortured, because he himself is the author of his own confusion. While he insulted Christ, he confessed him to be king; while he called him “King of the Jews,” he confessed his own sacrilege in not believing.

“Behold,” they say, “we crucified Jesus, so that Christians might arise after death and reign when dead. We crucified the one whom kings adore; the one whom we do not adore, they themselves adore. Behold, the nail too is honored; and the one whom we drove into death is a remedy of salvation and, by some invisible power, torments demons. We thought we had conquered, but we confess that we have been conquered. Christ has risen again, and the rulers have recognized that he has risen. He lives again, although he is not seen. Now our struggle with him is greater; now the battle against him is more violent. We despised the one whom kingdoms serve and to whom power is subject—how shall we resist kings? Kings are bent beneath the iron of his feet. Kings adore him, while the Photinians deny his divinity?

[Note: [Col. 1403D] We have dealt sufficiently with the Photinians, as with the Arians, in various passages of the books *On the Faith* and *On the Holy Spirit*.]

Emperors display the nail of his cross upon their diadem,

[Note: [Col. 1403D] Several manuscripts read: “they carry it before their diadem.”]

while the Arians diminish his power?”

### 50.

But I ask: Why is it holy upon the bridle, unless to rein in the arrogance of emperors and restrain the license of tyrants, who might neigh like horses after their lusts, as though it were permitted them to commit adultery with impunity?

[Note: [Col. 1403D] What could have been holy or inviolate for Nero, who, as Suetonius and Tacitus report, filled brothels with distinguished women, and who, according to Suetonius, in addition to corrupting freeborn youths and cohabiting with married women, even violated the Vestal Virgins? As for Caligula, it will not seem surprising that he engaged in adultery with noble matrons, since he did not even spare his own sisters, whom he violated in wicked incest, as the Suetonius cited above records.]

What of the crimes of the Neros, the Caligulas, and the others that we have learned of—what was holy for them upon the bridle?

### 51.

What else, then, did Helena’s work accomplish by directing the bridles, except that she seemed, by the Holy Spirit, to say to all emperors: “Do not become like a horse or a mule” (Psalm 32:9), but “with bridle and bit constrain the jaws” of those who did not recognize themselves as kings in order to govern their subjects?

For power, inclined toward vice, was carried away, and, like beasts, they polluted themselves with wandering lust. They did not know God. The Lord’s cross restrained them and called them back from the fall of impiety. It lifted their eyes, so that they might seek Christ in heaven. They stripped off the bit of unbelief and accepted the bridles of devotion and faith, following him who said: “Take my yoke upon you … for my yoke is easy and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:30).

From that time came the other Christian rulers, except Julian, who abandoned the author of his salvation when he surrendered himself to the error of philosophy. From that time came Gratian and Theodosius.

### 52.

The prophecy therefore did not lie when it said: “Kings shall walk in your light” (Isaiah 60:3). Certainly Gratian and Theodosius, more than the other rulers, shall walk in it—not now covered by soldiers’ weapons, but protected by their merits; not clothed in purple attire, but wrapped in glory.

When they delighted here in the acquittal of many, how much more do they there console themselves by recalling their mercy, as they reckon that they spared the greater number? Now they enjoy a shining light and have obtained dwelling places there far better than those they possessed here, saying: “O Israel, how great is the house of God, and how vast the place of his possession—great and without end!” (Baruch 3:24).

And, having completed the greatest labors, they say to one another: “It is good for a man when he has borne a heavy yoke from his youth; he shall sit alone and be silent, because he has borne a heavy yoke” (Lamentations 3:27). For whoever has borne a heavy yoke from his youth rests afterward; removed from the crowd, he possesses a distinguished place of rest, saying: “For you, Lord, have established me alone in hope” (Psalm 4:10).

### 53.

The poor Lazarus bore a heavy yoke from his youth; therefore he rests alone in Abraham’s bosom, as the testimony of the divine reading declares (Luke 16:24).

Theodosius bore a heavy yoke from his youth, when those who had killed his victorious father plotted against his safety.

[Note: [Col. 1403D] Theodosius the elder, father of the emperor Theodosius, after he had defeated Firmus in battle and compelled him to die, and after he had achieved the greatest successes in Africa, was condemned by the elder Valentinian, who lent his ears to calumny, and ordered him to be killed by the sword, as Paulus Orosius carefully describes in book VII, chapter 33. There is no doubt that his son Theodosius, still very young, was also harassed by his father’s enemies, as Ammianus reports in book XXIX, chapter 6. It is therefore credible that he withdrew to Spain in order to make room for their hatred, as Theodoret reports in book V, chapter 5. From Themistius’s Oration 16, book IV of Zosimus, and other sources, one may learn under how dangerous circumstances he was called to share the empire.]

He bore a heavy yoke when he underwent a pious exile; when barbarians had poured into the Roman Empire, he assumed the imperial power. He bore a heavy yoke in order to remove tyrants from the Roman Empire. But because he was in labor here, he is now in rest there.

### 54.

But now let us come to the conveying of the august body.

You weep, Honorius, august scion, and by your tears bear witness to your pious affection, since you convey your father’s body—still without the honor of a tomb—across so many regions.

The patriarch Jacob too, in order to free the people who were being pressed by the grave danger of a dreadful famine, left his home in old age and hastened to a foreign land. When he died there, he was escorted to his ancestral tomb for several days, with his son accompanying him (Genesis 49:50). Nothing was taken away from his merits; rather, his praise was increased, because, lacking the proper lot of his own home, he wandered in a kind of exile for his final burial.

[Note: [Col. 1404D] All printed editions read: “lacking the allotted destiny of his house, he wandered in a certain exile”; several manuscripts: “lacking the destiny due to his house, he wandered in a certain …”; other manuscripts give the better reading followed in the text.]

### 55.

You also weep, august emperor, because you yourself do not accompany the revered remains all the way to Constantinople.

[Note: [Col. 1404D] One Regius manuscript reads: “august emperor Arcadius.” But the name Arcadius was plainly inserted by some ignorant person who, seeing that Honorius had been addressed above, thought these words should be referred to Arcadius. Yet what would have prevented Arcadius from accompanying his father’s funeral to Constantinople, which was the capital of his empire?]

You share the same reason as we do: we all follow with fitting grief, and, if it were possible, we would all wish to be escorts with you. But Joseph went only to a neighboring province; here, many divisions of territory intervene, and seas must be crossed.

Nor would this burden be difficult for you, if the Republic did not hold you back—the Republic that good emperors have preferred to parents and children. Indeed, for this reason your father made you emperor and the Lord confirmed you: so that you would rule not only over soldiers as a father, but over everyone.

### 56.

Nor should you fear that the triumphal remains will appear dishonored wherever they arrive.

Italy does not think so, for it has witnessed glorious triumphs and, liberated once more from tyrants, celebrates the author of its freedom. Constantinople does not think so either, for it sent the ruler to victory for the second time, and, although it wished to keep him, it could not.

It was indeed awaiting his return with triumphal ceremonies and titles of victory.

[Note: [Col. 1405A] The Pratense and Gembloux manuscripts: “the whole world was awaiting him.”]

It was awaiting the emperor of the whole world, surrounded by the Gallic army and supported by the strength of the whole world. But now Theodosius returns there more powerful, now more glorious: he is escorted by a company of angels, and a throng of saints accompanies him.

Blessed indeed are you, for you receive a dweller in paradise and will hold as your guest the inhabitant of that heavenly city in the august lodging of his buried body.

[Note: [Col. 1405A] The Amerbach edition and two manuscripts: “in the narrowness of the buried body”; manuscripts: “of the body of the tomb”; the Vatican manuscript: “in the august marble tomb”; the other manuscripts and all printed editions agree with us, except that in some of them *sepulcri* is read instead of *sepulti*.]

## Hymns

### Notice on the Hymns of Saint Ambrose

It is known to everyone that Ambrose composed hymns. He himself indicates this in his sermon against Auxentius, in these words: “They say that the people were deceived by the songs of my hymns. I certainly do not deny it. That is a great song, and nothing is more powerful than it. For what is more powerful than the confession of the Trinity?” and so forth (*Sermon on the Basilicas*, number 34).

Paulinus also bears witness to this in his *Life of the same Bishop*. While recounting Justina’s persecution of him in her madness, he says: “At that time antiphons, hymns, and vigils first began to be celebrated in the Church of Milan. The devotion of this observance has remained to the present day, not only in that Church but throughout all the Churches of the West.”

Saint Augustine, an eyewitness, describes the beginning of this institution in exactly the same way in book IX, chapter 7 of the *Confessions*. Elsewhere also, as will be cited below, he frequently and willingly uses verses from these hymns to confirm the matter he is discussing.

It is therefore established by the authority of so many witnesses that the practice of singing hymns was propagated from the Church of Milan into all the Western Churches, and that their subject and material customarily concerned the explanation of the mystery of the divine Trinity.

It is no less certain that Saint Ambrose composed other hymns after that Arian storm had ceased to rage, as may be learned from Augustine, Cassiodorus (*Book on Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 6), Isidore, the Fourth Council of Toledo (canon 13), Bede, and others.

The chief difficulty, therefore, is to separate the genuinely Ambrosian hymns from those of others—namely, from the hymns composed by Hilary of Poitiers, Sedulius, Prudentius, Fortunatus, Elpis, the wife of Boethius, Gregory, Theodulf of Orléans, Alcuin, and Paul the Deacon.

Gillotius was the first to publish separately a collection of hymns issued under Ambrose’s name, gathered in an appendix to his edition. He accepted sixteen as Ambrosian. The Roman editors increased this number by adding eighteen others; subsequent Parisian editions enlarged it still further.

But since all these editions include hymns such as “The Royal Banners Forward Go,” “Come, Creator Spirit,” and others that no one recognizes as Ambrose’s, it is clear that no discrimination was exercised in their judgment. Whatever hymns bearing Ambrose’s name came into the editors’ hands were admitted indiscriminately.

In fact, neither Gillotius nor the Roman editors produce any guarantor whose testimony they considered trustworthy. Those responsible for the Parisian editions cite witnesses of such a kind that, with the single exception of Bede, no confidence can be placed in them. For who would judge any hymn to belong among the Ambrosian hymns merely because it appeared to those editors in some choral manuscript, or because Radulphus of Tongres (*On the Observance of the Canons*, proposition 13), who wrote at the beginning of the fifteenth century, affirmed that it was found in ancient hymnaries at Rome or even in the Ambrosian Office? It has not been sufficiently proved that none of the hymns contained in those books was wrongly inscribed with Ambrose’s name.

Dionysius the Carthusian compiled a catalogue of the hymns he regarded as Ambrosian (*Expositions of the Hymns*). But, except in the case of the hymn “God, Creator of All,” he offers no reason for assigning them to our Doctor, unless it is that he claims to recognize Ambrose’s phraseology and style in some of them. Whenever that is the sole argument, you can easily understand how unsafe it is in this matter.

Clicthove was no more careful in producing arguments for the hymns he lists under Ambrose’s title (*Elucidatory*). Apart from the hymn “Eternal Maker of the World,” which he thinks was taken from the *Hexaemeron* because of its affinity with it, he cites no other reason for proving the others than common opinion.

The same must be said of Gavanti’s authority (*Commentary on the Rubrics*, section 5, chapter 6), since, in examining the Ambrosian hymns, he does not apply a touchstone but merely proposes to follow the judgments of the already cited Radulphus of Tongres, Dionysius the Carthusian, Clicthove, and even other writers of a later age.

We possess an earlier testimony concerning the hymns of our Doctor in the Rule of Saint Benedict. When this holy man prescribes in the Rule the manner of the divine Office (chapters 9, 12, 16, and 17), he orders an Ambrosian song—which elsewhere he also calls a hymn—to be sung at each hour.

Yet those who wrote commentaries on the same Rule interpret the word “Ambrosian,” following Radulphus, in such a way that it designates either hymns composed by Ambrose or others composed in imitation of the Ambrosian hymns. Otherwise, it is not sufficiently established whether the same hymns that we still use in the Church were already customarily sung from the time of Saint Benedict.

In this great difficulty of distinguishing the hymns of our Ambrose from those of others, we have thought it best to admit no hymn as Ambrosian unless it is asserted by the authority of some substantial witness. We judge it preferable to give a place in this volume to fewer but more certain hymns than to multiply their number and indiscriminately confuse genuine and spurious works together.

The first of those we publish here we rightly declare to be Ambrose’s. We have Saint Augustine as our witness, whose following words are read: “In this book I said in one place concerning the Apostle Peter that the Church was founded in him as upon a rock. This meaning is also sung by many mouths in the verses of the blessed Ambrose, where, speaking of the crowing cock, he says: ‘When the cock sang, that very rock washed away its guilt’” (book I of the *Retractions*, chapter 21). It has also been observed by many authors after Bede (*On the Art of Meter*) that this same hymn was taken from the *Hexaemeron* (book V, chapter 24).

The second hymn is also indicated by Augustine, when he recalls his grief at his mother’s death: “I was alone,” he says (book IX, chapter 12), “in my bed, remembering the truthful verses of your Ambrose: ‘You are God, creator of all.’” We do not doubt that this is also the hymn designated in book VI of *On Music*, chapter 9.

The same teacher mentions the third hymn as follows (book *On Nature and Grace*, chapter 63): “The bishop mentioned above also urges that this Spirit be obtained by prayers … where in his hymn he says: ‘And by persistent prayers grant that we may deserve the Holy Spirit.’” This hymn is likewise listed among the Ambrosian hymns by the venerable Bede in the passage cited above, and it is found both in the Cistercian Breviaries and in the latest Paris editions of Ambrose’s works. From these we have transferred it here.

There is no more reason to doubt the fourth hymn than the three preceding ones. We find its first stanza attributed to Ambrose in a Roman Synod held in 430, as preserved in the Baluze Collection; Ildephonsus also cites it more than once in *On the Perpetual Virginity of Blessed Mary*. Its fourth stanza may be read not only in Cassiodorus (*On Psalm 8*, in the conclusion, and *On Psalm 71), but also in Faustus of Riez, who, as bishop, speaks of it in these words in a letter to a deacon: “Receive also, in the hymn of the holy bishop and confessor Ambrose, which the Church sings throughout all the regions of Italy and Gaul on the Lord’s birthday: ‘Come forth from your bridal chamber,’” and so forth.

Cassiodorus indicates the fifth hymn when he says (*On Psalm 74*): “So that the streams of the fountains might receive the redness of wine, their nature having been changed, although nature had not possessed it. Hence blessed Ambrose, in the hymn of the holy Epiphany, proclaimed this wonderfully in words of the most brilliant light.”

Of the two hymns in which the mystery of the Epiphany is celebrated and which are still used, one, sung by the Church in the Office of that day, belongs to Sedulius; the other appears in the Breviaries of the Cistercian Order and in the latest editions of Ambrose’s works. Since Cassiodorus’s words fit it perfectly, we did not hesitate to admit it among the legitimate offspring of so great a Doctor.

We present the sixth hymn—or rather a fragment of a hymn—on the authority of the same Cassiodorus (*On Psalm 101*), for his testimony concerning it reads as follows: “From this also, according to the Apostle, the rosy hymn of Saint Ambrose at the sixth hour breathes fragrance; for he says: ‘I shall pray to the Lord with my mind,’” and so forth.

Nor is this hymn unworthy of the Senator’s praise, if only its meaning is considered. Nevertheless, it may reasonably be questioned whether it was truly composed by Ambrose, since the laws of verse are entirely neglected in it. For, from all that we have already said, it is clearly shown that the holy Bishop was more skilled in this genre than to stumble so frequently. Yet we did not think that Cassiodorus’s authority should be denied, so that this very pleasing little poem might be received among the songs of our Ambrose.

The first verse of the seventh hymn is remembered by Bede (*On the Art of Meter*) as follows: “But the Ambrosian hymns run especially in this way: ‘Splendor of the Father’s glory.’” After adding to this verse the first three verses of the three hymns already discussed, he continues in this manner: “And many others, among which the hymn of the blessed martyrs is composed with most beautiful elegance: ‘Eternal gifts of Christ,’” and so forth.

This testimony does not seem capable of a more appropriate interpretation than that we understand him to attribute that hymn to Ambrose by this designation. We have therefore admitted it as the eighth hymn.

The ninth, tenth, and eleventh hymns were indicated to us by Hincmar, bishop of Rheims (*On the Non-Triple Trinity*). We follow his authority in this matter insofar as the hymns seem worthy of so great a name, or no reason compels us to depart from his judgment.

For example, Hincmar’s authority does not persuade us that the hymn “Now, Holy Spirit, Come to Us,” which is sung at the third hour, originated with Ambrose, since we possess another hymn that is known to have been composed by the holy Bishop for singing at that same hour.

The others whose verses, or even stanzas, he sometimes cites as Ambrosian are stained with so many errors that they are far removed from that man’s elegance. Some of them also display none of the harmony by which, as Bede testifies, Ambrose was accustomed to enclose a single meaning in each verse.

We owe our knowledge of the twelfth hymn to blessed Ildephonsus, who once and again, in his sermon *On the Childbearing and Purification of Blessed Mary the Virgin*, cites its first stanza as composed by Ambrose. From there it was transferred into later editions of the holy Doctor’s works. We copied the second and third stanzas from the book of George Cassander, *On Ecclesiastical Hymns*, where the same hymn is read without its author’s name.

Although prosody is occasionally violated in it, we do not therefore judge it unworthy of Ambrose, since errors of this kind can be found in his indisputably genuine hymns, though not frequently.

The hymn “Praise Is Due to You” is called Ambrosian in book I of the *Miracles of Saint Richarius*, but in what sense it is so called is not entirely clear. Since it is not composed in meter, it must have been made neither by Ambrose nor according to the Ambrosian form.

As for the Eucharistic song “We Praise You, God,” it would be tedious to discuss it anxiously here. No one in our time who is not altogether uneducated denies that the story is a fable which once circulated—that after the great Augustine had been baptized, he and Ambrose sang the same hymn antiphonally in alternation.

We do not deny that some of the hymns circulated in the earlier editions, especially those sung at the daytime hours and at weekday Vespers, may belong to Ambrose. But since distinguishing them from the works of others is the task and labor of this work, we have omitted them with the less hesitation because they are found in nearly all Breviaries and in other books that are especially common.

[Note: [Col. 1409] See the Appendix to volume II of the Benedictine edition (*Patrologia*, volume XVII), where, at the end of the second part, more than fifty hymns inscribed with Ambrose’s name may be read.]

## Hymns of Saint Ambrose, Bishop of Milan

### Hymn I

Eternal Maker of the world,  
who govern night and day,  
and grant seasons to the seasons,  
to relieve weariness,

already the herald of day sounds;  
the vigilant watchman of deep night,  
the nocturnal light for travelers,  
separating night from night.

At his sound the morning star,  
awakened, dissolves the darkness of heaven;  
at his sound the whole host of errors  
abandons the way of harm.

At his sound the sailor gathers strength,  
and the waters of the sea grow calm;  
at his sound the very rock of the Church,  
when the cock sings, washes away its guilt.

Let us therefore rise courageously.  
The cock awakens those who lie sleeping  
and rebukes the drowsy;  
the cock reproves those who deny.

When the cock sings, hope returns;  
health is restored to the sick;  
the robber’s sword is sheathed;  
faith returns to those who have fallen.

Jesus, look upon those who stumble,  
and correct us by looking upon us.  
When you look, the fallen rise,  
and guilt is dissolved by tears.

Shine upon our senses as light,  
and dispel the sleep of our minds.  
Let our voice sound first to you,  
and let us fulfill our vows to you.

### Hymn II

God, creator of all,  
ruler of heaven, clothing  
the day with beautiful light  
and the night with the grace of sleep,

so that rest may restore  
relaxed limbs to the use of labor,  
may lighten weary minds,  
and loosen anxious griefs,

now that the day is complete,  
and with the coming of night our prayers arise,  
we offer hymns, singing with vows,  
that you may aid the guilty.

Let the depths of our hearts sing to you;  
let our melodious voice resound to you;  
let chaste love cherish you;  
let a sober mind adore you.

So that when deep darkness  
has closed the day in nights,  
faith may know no darkness,  
and night may shine through faith.

Do not allow the mind to sleep;  
let guilt know how to sleep.  
Let watchful, refreshing faith  
temper the vapor of sleep.

Freed from slippery sensation,  
let the heights of our hearts dream of you;  
and let the fear of the envious enemy  
not disturb those who rest.

Let us beseech Christ and the Father,  
and the Spirit of Christ and the Father:  
O Trinity, powerful in all things,  
cherish those who pray.

### Hymn III

Now the third hour rises,  
at which Christ ascended the cross.  
Let the mind think of nothing improper;  
let it direct its affection to prayer.

Whoever receives Christ in the heart  
bears an innocent mind  
and by persistent prayers  
is granted to deserve the Holy Spirit.

This is the hour that brought an end  
to the dreadful lethargy of sin,  
dissolved the reign of death,  
and removed guilt from the age.

From this point blessed times began  
through Christ’s grace.  
Truth filled the Churches  
throughout the whole world with faith.

From the lofty summit of his triumph  
he was speaking to his mother:  
“Behold, mother, your son”;  
“Behold, apostle, your mother.”

Teaching a profound mystery  
through the bonds of betrothal set before the bride,  
so that the sacred birth of the Virgin  
might not violate the mother’s modesty.

Jesus gave it credibility  
through heavenly miracles;  
the impious crowd did not believe,  
but whoever believed would be saved.

We believe that God was born,  
and that the sacred Virgin gave birth  
to him who bore the sins of the world  
and sits at the Father’s right hand.

### Hymn IV

[Note: [Col. 1409] The Cistercian Breviary gives this hymn a first stanza, found nowhere else, as follows:

“Attend, you who rule Israel,  
who sit upon the cherubim;  
and appear before Ephraim; awaken  
your power and come.”

But from where this was taken, who could guess?]

Come, Redeemer of the nations;  
show forth the Virgin’s birth.  
Let every age marvel:  
such a birth befits God.

Not from human seed,  
but from a mysterious breath,  
the Word of God became flesh,  
and the fruit of the womb blossomed.

The Virgin’s womb swells;  
the enclosure of modesty remains.  
The standards of virtue shine;  
God moves about within the temple.

[Note: [Col. 1411] Faustus of Riez: “Coming forth from his bridal chamber.”]

Coming forth from his bridal chamber,  
the royal hall of modesty,  
the Giant of twofold substance,  
joyfully to run his course.

His coming forth from the Father,
His return to the Father;

His journey even to the underworld,

His return to the seat of God.

Equal to the eternal Father,

Gird yourself with the trophy of the flesh,

Strengthening the weakness of our body

By enduring through your power.

Now your manger shines,

And the night breathes forth a new light,

Which no night may interrupt,

And which may shine with unbroken faith.

## HYMN V

Most High, who illumines

The spheres of the twinkling stars,

Peace, life, light, and truth—

Jesus, favor those who pray.

Whether by the mystical baptism

You once, on the third sacred day,

Turned back the streams of the Jordan,

Reversing their course in your presence;

Or whether, shining in heaven,

You marked the Virgin’s birth with a star,

And on this day led the Magi

To adore the manger.

Or whether you infused

The taste of wine into jars full of water:

The servant, who knew the secret, tasted

What he himself had not filled.

Seeing the waters change color,

And the rivers be made drunk,

The changed elements are astonished

To pass into other uses.

Thus, while you divide five loaves

Among five thousand men,

The food grew in the mouths

Beneath the teeth of those who ate.

It increased all the more

By the very expenditure of the bread: 1222  
Who, seeing this, will marvel

At the perpetual courses of springs?

Among the hands of those breaking it,

The bread flows forth in abundance;

The fragments that they had not broken

Steal forth to the men.

## HYMN VI

I shall pray to the Lord with my mind;

I shall pray also with my spirit,

Lest only my voice sing to God

While our understanding, led elsewhere,

Wanders uncertainly,

Distracted by empty circumstances.

## HYMN VII

Splendor of the Father’s glory,

Bringing forth light from light,

Day illuminating day

At the beginnings of the new light.

True sun, descend upon us,

Shining with perpetual radiance,

And pour the brightness

Of the Holy Spirit into our senses.

With our vows let us call upon the Father,

The Father of everlasting glory,

The Father of mighty grace;

May he drive away slippery guilt.

May he shape our vigorous deeds,

Blunt the teeth of envy,

Make harsh misfortunes favorable,

And grant the grace to bear them.

May he govern and direct the mind;

With a chaste and faithful body,

May faith burn with warmth

And know nothing of the poisons of deceit.

May Christ be our food,

And faith our drink;

Joyfully let us drink

The sober intoxication of the Spirit.

May this joyful day pass away,

Let modesty be like the dawn,

Faith like midday,

And let the mind know no twilight.

The dawn advances on its course;

May the whole Son come forth,

Wholly in the Father,

And the whole Father in the Word.

## HYMN VIII

The eternal gifts of Christ

And the victories of the martyrs,

Let us sing with joyful hearts,

Offering the praises that are their due.

Princes of the churches,

Triumphal commanders in battle,

Soldiers of the heavenly court,

And true lights of the world.

Having conquered the terror of the age 1223  
And scorned the punishments of the body,

By the shortening of sacred death

They possess blessed life.

The martyrs are handed over to the fire

And to the teeth of wild beasts;

The armed hand of the insane torturer

Rages with its claws.

Their exposed entrails hang forth,

Their consecrated blood is poured out,

Yet they remain unmoved

By the grace of everlasting life.

The devoted faith of the saints,

The unconquered hope of believers,

The perfect love of Christ—

These triumph over the prince of the world.

In them the Father’s glory,

In them the Son’s will,

In them the Spirit rejoices;

Heaven is filled with joys.

Now, Redeemer, we beseech you:

Join us, your praying servants,

To their fellowship

Forever and ever. Amen.

## HYMN IX

[Col. 1412]

With our limbs refreshed by sleep,

We rise, having rejected our couch;

As we sing to you, Father,

We beg you to be present with us.

Let the tongue sing of you first;

Let the ardor of the mind surround you,

So that, in the deeds that follow,

You, Holy One, may be their beginning.

Let darkness yield to light,

And night to the daylight star,

So that the guilt brought by night

May fade through the gift of light.

We, your suppliant petitioners, pray

That you remove all offenses,

Lest you be praised forever

By the mouths of those who sing to you.

Grant this, most loving Father,

Only-begotten, equal to the Father, 1224  
Reigning with the Spirit, the Paraclete,

Throughout every age.

## HYMN X

Companion of the Father’s light,

Light yourself and day of light,

By singing we break the night;

Be present to those who ask.

Take away the darkness of our minds;

Put the hosts of demons to flight;

Drive away drowsiness,

Lest it overwhelm us in our laziness.

Thus, Christ, may you pardon us all

Who believe in you,

So that what we sing in anticipation

May benefit those who entreat you.

## HYMN XI

O blessed Light of the Trinity,

And principal Unity,

The fiery sun is now withdrawing;

Pour light into our hearts.

In the morning, with a hymn of praise,

In the evening, we beseech you:

May our suppliant glory

Praise you throughout all ages.

## HYMN XII

The accessible gate of Christ is made,

Filled and overflowing with grace;

The King passes through and remains,

Closed, as it was, forever.

The offspring of heavenly light

Came forth from the Virgin’s chamber:

Bridegroom, Redeemer, Creator,

The Giant of his own Church.

The mother’s honor and joy,

The boundless hope of believers,

Through the dark cups of death,

Released our sins.

[Col. 1413]

## LIST OF THE MANUSCRIPTS AND EDITIONS OF THE BOOKS BY WHICH THE WORKS OF SAINT AMBROSE CONTAINED IN THIS SECOND VOLUME WERE COLLATED AND CORRECTED

[Col. 1413]

Almost all the works in this volume were corrected from the variant readings collected from manuscripts in the Vatican Library, as was stated regarding the individual treatises of the first volume. They were also emended with the aid of the same editions by which the first volume was corrected; since these were already discussed in that volume’s list, we shall add nothing here.

### THREE BOOKS ON DUTIES

They were collated with the following manuscripts:

One Thuane manuscript, now Colbert, about 1,000 years old. Three Vatican manuscripts of excellent quality. One Benignian manuscript, 800 years old. Two Laudun manuscripts, one 700 years old and the other 500. One Crespian manuscript, 700 years old. One Bigotian manuscript, 700 years old. One Tellerian manuscript, 600 years old. One Fulian manuscript, 600 years old. One Compendian manuscript, approximately 600 years old. Two Sorbonian manuscripts, one 600 years old and the other approximately 400. Two Royal manuscripts, one 600 years old and the other 400. Three Victorine manuscripts, 600, 500, and 400 years old. Four Colbertine manuscripts, 600, 500, 400, and 300 years old. One Carnutian manuscript, approximately 500 years old. One Dionysian manuscript of nearly the same age. One Theodorician manuscript, 500 years old. One Sagian manuscript, 500 years old. One Vallis-Lucent manuscript, 500 years old. One Germanian manuscript of the same age. One Pratellian manuscript, also of the same age. One Corbeian manuscript, 400 years old. One Lyran manuscript, 300 years old. One Laudin manuscript, 300 years old. One Gemetician manuscript, not much more recent.

### THREE BOOKS ON VIRGINS

They were corrected from the following manuscripts:

One Remensian manuscript, given by Hincmar to his church, 800 years old. Two Gemetician manuscripts, one 800 years old and the other mutilated, 700 years old. One Pratellian manuscript, 700 years old. One Fiscan manuscript, but mutilated, 700 years old. One Sagian manuscript, also mutilated, 600 years old. One Albinian manuscript, 600 years old. One Tellerian manuscript, 600 years old. Two Colbertine manuscripts, one 600 years old and the other 400. One Royal manuscript, 500 years old. One Carnutian manuscript, from the Abbey of Saint Peter in the Valley, but mutilated, 500 years old. One Floriacian manuscript, 500 years old. One Theodorician manuscript, 500 years old. One Vallis-Clara manuscript, 500 years old. One Vallis-Lucent manuscript of the same age. One Sorbonian manuscript, 400 years old.

### THE BOOK ON WIDOWS

It was emended from the following manuscripts:

One Gemetician manuscript, 700 years old. One Fiscan manuscript, 700 years old. One Pratellian manuscript of the same age. One Tellerian manuscript, 600 years old. Two Colbertine manuscripts, one 600 years old and the other 400. One Albinian manuscript, 600 years old. One Royal manuscript, 500 years old. One Vallis-Clara manuscript, 500 years old. One Sorbonian manuscript, 400 years old.

### THE BOOK ON VIRGINITY

It was collated with nearly all the manuscripts against which the three books on virgins were corrected.

### THE BOOK ON THE INSTITUTION OF A VIRGIN

It was collated with the following manuscripts:

Two Gemetician manuscripts, approximately 700 years old. One Pratellian manuscript of the same age, but mutilated. One Albinian manuscript, 600 years old. [Col. 1414] One Vallis-Lucent manuscript, 500 years old. One Carnutian manuscript, 500 years old.

### EXHORTATION TO VIRGINITY

It was emended from the following manuscripts:

Two Gemetician manuscripts, approximately 700 years old. One Fiscan manuscript, also 700 years old. One Pratellian manuscript of nearly the same age. One Sagian manuscript, 600 years old. One Albinian manuscript, 600 years old. Two Colbertine manuscripts, one 600 years old and the other 400. One Royal manuscript, 500 years old. One Carnutian manuscript, 500 years old. One Vallis-Lucent manuscript of the same age. One Sorbonian manuscript, 400 years old.

### THE BOOK ON THE FALL OF A CONSECRATED VIRGIN

It was corrected from the following manuscripts:

One Gemetician manuscript, 700 years old. One Floriacian manuscript, 600 years old. One Michaelian manuscript, 600 years old. One Albinian manuscript of the same antiquity. Three Colbertine manuscripts, 600, 500, and 400 years old. One Royal manuscript, 500 years old. One Victorine manuscript, 500 years old. One Regiomontane manuscript, approximately 500 years old. One Sorbonian manuscript, 400 years old.

### THE BOOK ON THE MYSTERIES

It was collated with the following manuscripts:

One Benignian manuscript, 800 years old. One Claromontane manuscript, 800 years old. Two Remensian manuscripts, one belonging to Hincmar and 800 years old, the other 500 years old. One Gemetician manuscript, approximately 700 years old. One Pratellian manuscript, also 700 years old. One Vincentian manuscript—that is, one belonging to Saint Vincent of Le Mans—600 years old. One Albinian manuscript, 600 years old. One Michaelian manuscript, 600 years old. One Illidian manuscript—that is, one belonging to Saint Illidius of Clermont—600 years old. Two Tellerian manuscripts, approximately 600 years old. A fragment of one Germanian manuscript, 600 years old. Two Royal manuscripts, one 500 years old and the other 400. One Laetian manuscript, 500 years old. One Alnetian manuscript of the same age. Three Colbertine manuscripts, two 500 years old and the third 400. One Victorine manuscript, 400 years old. One Sorbonian manuscript of approximately the same antiquity.

### SIX BOOKS ON THE SACRAMENTS

They were reviewed against the same manuscripts with which the book on the Mysteries was collated, and in addition against one Germanian manuscript, 500 years old, and one Vallis-Lucent manuscript of the same age.

### TWO BOOKS ON PENANCE

They were collated from the following manuscripts:

One Benignian manuscript, 800 years old. One Claromontane manuscript, 800 years old. One Laudun manuscript, 700 years old. Two Germanian manuscripts, one 800 years old and the other 500. Two Colbertine manuscripts, one 600 years old and the other 400. One Floriacian manuscript, approximately 600 years old. One Michaelian manuscript, 600 years old. One Albinian manuscript, also 600 years old. One Fulian manuscript, 600 years old. One Remensian manuscript, 500 years old. One Cistercian manuscript, 500 years old. One Sorbonian manuscript, approximately 400 years old.

### THE BOOKS ON THE FAITH, TO GRATIAN

They were emended from the following manuscripts:

One Remensian manuscript, given by Hincmar to his church, 800 years old. Seven Colbertine manuscripts, 800, 600, 500, and 400 years old. One Albinian manuscript, 600 years old. One Bigotian manuscript, approximately 600 years old. One Tellerian manuscript, 500 years old. One Audoenian manuscript, 500 years old. One Ebrulphian manuscript, 500 years old. One Theodorician manuscript, 500 years old. One Laetian manuscript of the same age. One Sorbonian manuscript, approximately 400 years old.

It should be observed, however, that in several manuscripts of the five books on the Faith only the first two are contained.

### THREE BOOKS ON THE HOLY SPIRIT

They were reviewed against the following manuscripts:

One Remensian manuscript, 800 years old. One Remigian manuscript, approximately 600 years old. Four Colbertine manuscripts, 800, 500, and 400 years old. Two Albinian manuscripts, 600 and 500 years old. One Audeonian manuscript, 500 years old. One Theodorician manuscript, 500 years old. One Laetian manuscript, 500 years old. One Sorbonian manuscript, approximately 400 years old. A fragment of an ancient Floriacian manuscript.

### THE BOOK ON THE LORD’S INCARNATION

It was collated with the following manuscripts:

One Remigian manuscript, 800 years old. One incomplete Corbeian manuscript, 800 years old. One fragment of a Thuane manuscript, also 800 years old. Two Albinian manuscripts, 600 and 500 years old. One Victorine manuscript, 600 years old. One Floriacian manuscript, approximately 600 years old. Three Colbertine manuscripts, 600, 400, and 300 years old. One Audoenian manuscript, 500 years old. One Theodorician manuscript, 500 years old. One Sorbonian manuscript, approximately 400 years old.

### THE BOOK OF LETTERS

It was purged and corrected from the following manuscripts:

One Belvacian manuscript, approximately 800 years old. One Pratellian manuscript, also 800 years old. One Thuane manuscript, 800 years old. One Vindocinian manuscript, 700 years old. One Royal manuscript, 600 years old. One Albinian manuscript, approximately 600 years old. One Tellerian manuscript of approximately the same age. One Gemetician manuscript, more than 500 years old. One Longipontian manuscript, 500 years old. One Caroli-Locus manuscript, 500 years old. Two Pontinian manuscripts of no different antiquity. One Laetian manuscript, also 500 years old. One Michaelian manuscript of the same age.

Each of these manuscripts contains all, or nearly all, of Ambrose’s letters. In the manuscripts that follow, however, not all the letters were reviewed, but only certain ones, namely:

The Thirteenth Letter: one Boyerian manuscript—that is, from the library of D. Boyer, president [Col. 1416] in the Senate of Dijon—approximately 800 years old.

The Seventh: one Corbeian manuscript, also 800 years old; one Laudun manuscript, 700 years old; one Thuane manuscript, approximately 500 years old; one Germanian manuscript, also of the same age; and two Colbertine manuscripts, one approximately 600 years old and the other 400.

The Ninth: one second Royal manuscript, approximately 400 years old.

The Council of Aquileia: one second Tellerian manuscript, approximately 600 years old; and the editions of Chifflet in his *Vigilius*, as well as Labbe’s editions in the *Councils*.

Finally, certain others were reviewed partly against a third Royal manuscript, partly against a third Tellerian manuscript, partly against one Fulian manuscript, one manuscript of Saint Mary of Rheims, and one Remigian manuscript.

### THE BOOK ON THE DEATH OF SATYRUS

It was reviewed against the following manuscripts:

One Corbeian manuscript, 800 years old. One Benignian manuscript, 800 years old. One Laudun manuscript, 700 years old. One Remigian manuscript, approximately 600 years old. One Albinian manuscript of the same age. One Royal manuscript, 500 years old. One Germanian manuscript, 500 years old. One manuscript of Saint Gatian of Tours, 500 years old. One Longipontian manuscript, 500 years old. One Vallis-Clara manuscript, 500 years old. One Vallis-Lucent manuscript of the same age. One Colbertine manuscript, 400 years old. One Victorine manuscript, also 400 years old.

### THE BOOK ON THE FAITH OF THE RESURRECTION

It was corrected against all the manuscripts listed above, except the Royal manuscript and that of Saint Gatian; in addition to those, it was examined against one Thuane manuscript, 500 years old, and a fragment of an 800-year-old manuscript of the College of Clermont.

### ORATION ON THE DEATH OF VALENTINIAN

It was collated with the following manuscripts:

Two Thuane manuscripts, 800 and 500 years old. One Corbeian manuscript, 700 years old. One Tellerian manuscript, 600 years old. One Bigotian manuscript, 600 years old. One Remigian manuscript, 500 years old. One Theodorician manuscript, 500 years old. Two Royal manuscripts, 500 and 400 years old. One Longipontian manuscript, 500 years old. One Vallis-Lucent manuscript, 500 years old. One Colbertine manuscript, 400 years old.

### ORATION ON THE DEATH OF THEODOSIUS

It was corrected against the following manuscripts:

Two Thuane manuscripts, 800 and 500 years old. One Pratellian manuscript, 700 years old. One Bellovacian manuscript of approximately the same age. One Vindocinian manuscript, 700 years old. One Albinian manuscript, 600 years old. One Gemetian manuscript of the same age. Two Colbertine manuscripts, one 700 years old and the other 400. Two Royal manuscripts, 500 and 400 years old. One Longipontian manuscript, 500 years old.

## Volume back matter

## INDEX OF SUBJECTS AND STATEMENTS

[Note: [Col. 1415] This index employs two sets of numerical references: for each entry, the first number refers to column numbers printed in the text in bold type; the second number refers to section numbers.]

[Col. 1415]

This index employs a twofold numerical notation: the first, corresponding to the heavier type, indicates the columns of the Benedictine edition continuously inserted in the text; the second indicates the numbers of the sections.

A
[Col. 1415] **AARON**, plainly a man worthy to be proposed to everyone for imitation, truly a man of priestly mind and spirit, who, like a good shepherd, would offer himself for the Lord’s flock with devoted affection, 1034, 51. Aaron surpasses Moses in counsel, Moses in knowledge, 1057, 2. Therefore God himself chose that priest, so that in choosing a priest human desire should not prevail, but the grace of God; not voluntary offering or self-assumption, but heavenly calling, 1033, 48. How blessed he must have considered himself when he stood between the living and the dead, 73, 11. He did not unwisely take rings and earrings from the Jews, 1054, 3 and following. Although he was such a priest that he cast the golden head of the calf, we can neither excuse him nor dare condemn him, 1054, 3. What does it mean that he removed the gold from the people [Col. 1416] who demanded that gods be made for them, and that the head of a calf was fashioned from that gold, or that Moses was so harshly indignant? 1054, 1 and following. He bears the figure of Christ, 471, 4. What his priestly garment signifies; same place and following. Aaron’s rod, an emblem of priestly grace, had previously withered, but in Christ it blossomed again, 764, 4. What it signified, 956, 2 and following; 1035, 58.

**ABDEMELECH**, that is, “taken up by the Lord,” 656, 114. What he prefigured, 655, 111 and following.

**ABEL** pleased for this reason: he did not delay his offering, but offered from the firstborn of the sheep, 926, 9. Who taught us his sacrifice and prophesied it? 703, 4. Abel’s fruit was better than Cain’s: in him the redemption of the world is announced, through the other the ruin of the world; in him the sacrifice of Christ, in him the devil’s parricide, 287, 36.

[Col. 1417] **ABIMELECH**, for the duties of the grace of hospitality, considered that one ought rather to undergo death oneself than betray a fleeing friend, 138, 124.

**ABNEGATION.** Whoever denies himself is himself just and himself worthy of Christ, 38, 142.

**ABRAHAM**, a Chaldean, is summoned at the end so that the superstition of the Chaldeans might fall silent, 994, 5. First in faith, outstanding in righteousness, vigorous in battle, not greedy in victory, hospitable at home, attentive to his wife, 30, 110. He believed not in part but in everything, 1094, 5. Faithful in war, temperate in triumph, he preferred to become rich through God’s gifts rather than through those of men, 1159, 96. What the four kings conquered by him prefigured, same place. He was not ignorant of the Holy Spirit, 635, 4. Abraham was granted the greatest reward because, at God’s command, he believed that even parricide could be piously performed, 1016, 14. He knew that a son offered in sacrifice was more acceptable to God than one kept unharmed; and the child whom he had received late he offered quickly, 1160, 97. How, in one act of his—that of wishing to sacrifice his son—were all four virtues present? 32, 119. He who hastened to sacrifice his only son in the intention of faith hastened with greater devotion to substitute a sheep for the sacrifice, 1104, 5. In the sacrifice of the lamb he saw beforehand the true passion of the Lord’s body, 1071, 1. Why God permitted Abraham’s parricide, but not Jephthah’s, 215, 7 and following. The difference between the two, 216, 9. When Abraham confessed himself to be dung and ashes, he found God’s grace through the greatest humility, 416, 4. How did he present desire obedient to reason? 29, 107 and following. How was prudence present in him? 31, 117. Ready to receive guests, faithful to God, diligent in service, prompt in duty, he saw the Trinity in a type, and in him it was not doctrine but grace that spoke, 1159, 96. As the reward of hospitality he received the fruit of posterity, 95, 104. By the sign of the Lord’s cross and name, having subdued the strength of five kings and their victorious troops, he both avenged his neighbor and earned his brother’s son and triumph, 444, 3. Let us imitate his devotion, 1160, 99. Those are more truly Abraham’s children who are so through faith, 1093, 1. We are not sheltered in the bodily bosom of the holy Patriarch, but his succession, approved by God, cherishes us in a kind of covering of good works, 1161, 101.

**ABSENT PERSONS.** To allow no loss to creep in for the absent is a great matter not only of kindness but also of communication and generous knowledge, 1054, 1.

**ABSOLUTION.** Delay in confessing is delay of absolution; forgiveness of sins follows confession, 941, 45. Who can be absolved if he is not innocent even in his own regard? 13, 45.

**ABSTINENCE.** Abstinence from drink and food teaches one to know no vices by teaching one to know nothing of the causes of vices, 159, 53. Abstinence makes even the years of youth grow old, 1029, 26. Certain persons celebrated for abstinence in the Old Testament are listed, same place, 28 and following. Do not fear weakness resulting from fasting and abstinence, 298, 79. Those who attack the merit of fasting and abstinence are refuted, 1024, 7 and following; 1026, 15 and following. See **FASTING**.

**ABUNDANCE** is where there is satiety, 943, 10.

**ABUNDANTIUS**, bishop of Trent, 786, 1; 805, 76. His condemnation of Palladius, 801, 57.

**AHAB**, the poorest amid royal treasures—and why, 943, 8.

**ACHOLIUS** gave himself as a boy to monasteries and, confined within a narrow hut in Achaea, nevertheless traversed the regions of many lands through grace; he was entreated by the peoples of Macedonia to accept the highest priesthood and was chosen by the priests, 821, 12. He frequently traveled through Constantinople, Achaea, Epirus, and Italy, 822, 2. What was reserved to the judgment of other bishops? 817, 7. Blessed was his old age, 823, 5. Although he concealed it by promises, he indicated through signs that Anysius would succeed him, as though foreseeing it, 821, 9. Having set aside a kind of cloak of his own *melotis*, he clothed his disciple Anysius and vested him in the insignia of his priesthood, 821, 9. His blessed death and outstanding virtues are proclaimed, 819, 3 and following. When the chains of the Goths repeatedly threatened, Saint Acholius, through his prayers, caused them to be driven from the regions of Macedonia as vanquished, 820, 5 and following. He did similar things to Elisha, or nearly greater ones, same place, 7. See **GOTHS**, **AMBROSE**.

**ACTION.** In every action one must seek what suits the persons, the time, and the ages, 57, 222. What you intend to do at length, sometimes you should not do at all, 178, 17.

**ADAM**, created from virgin earth, 983, 13. Why God breathed into his face, 982, 11. He was an inhabitant of the whole world and, as the Greeks say, *kosmopolítēs* (κοσμοπολίτης, “citizen of the world”); a recent work of God, a constant conversationalist, a citizen of the saints, planted together with virtues, set over all living creatures, 983, 16. Why God commanded him not to taste of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, 982, 9. He was alone and did not transgress, because his mind adhered to God; but after the woman was joined to him, he could not cling to the heavenly commandments, 992, 2. He was alone when he was placed in paradise; he was alone also when he was made in the image of God; but he was not alone when he was expelled from paradise, 992, 5. Before sin he was naked, but he did not know himself to be naked, because he was clothed with virtues, [Col. 1418] 1015, 12. He violated the natural law, and through disobedience incurred offense and fell into guilt through insolence, 1078, 5. The cause of his downfall was pride, and pride arose from the privilege of innocence, 1078, 5. Desire for pleasure shows that he was deceived and fell from God’s commandment and from the fruit of grace, 1026, 14. If he had covered himself with fasting, he would not have been made naked, 968, 11. The reproach of his guilt and hiding place, 856, 17. Immediately after his guilt God separated him from delights so that he might do penance; immediately he clothed him in a tunic of skins, not silk, 437, 99. His tomb is on Golgotha, so that Christ might raise him, dead, in his own cross, 1070, 10. See **ORIGINAL SIN**.

**ADOLESCENCE.** What the duties of an adolescent are, 18, 65. Adolescence is close to falls, 189, 12. It is useful for adolescents to follow distinguished and wise men, 93, 97. The beautiful union of the old and the young, 94, 100. See **MODESTY**, **WINE**.

**ADOPTION** belongs to power, generation to property, 536, 86. The adoption of sons is the redemption of the whole body, which will be completed when all, after the resurrection, deserve to see the face of God, 927, 13. Those in whom God sees his Son according to his image he adopts through the Son into the grace of sons; so that, just as through the image we are made according to the image, so through generation we may be called from being sons to adoption, 566, 90.

**ADORATION.** No one adores God unless he drinks in the truth of his divinity with devout affection, 679, 71.

**ADVERSITY.** When we are anointed with certain adversities, then we are subject to God, 844, 9. Blessedness begins with divine judgment where human misery is assessed, 17, 59. Do not weigh the merits of a just person by the misfortunes of this age, 301, 91. Holy men endured grievous and many things in this world without the support of their merits, amid the misery of labors, 1141, 29. Thanks be to the Lord, who wishes to chastise his servants lest he lose them, 1000, 16. Evils not yet examined break the spirit more, 51, 189. We are broken more by the pain of adversity than we enjoy the fruit of prosperity, 1139, 18. Let us be neither softer in sufferings nor more elated in prosperity, 49, 185. In adverse circumstances vengeance is counted as victory, 775, 13. A friend is tested in adversity, for in prosperity everyone appears to be a friend, 139, 129. See **FORTITUDE**.

**ADULATION.** To present oneself as a flatterer or as one who is flattered is, respectively, a matter of cunning and of vanity, 60, 235. To appear softened by flattery is a sign of cowardice, 56, 218. Just as friendship ought to flee flattery, so too it ought to flee another’s insolence, 140, 133. There is no true friendship where there is deceitful flattery, 140, 134.

**ADULTERY** is committed not only by the pollution of the act but also by the intention of the gaze, 69, 265. If anyone assaults the modesty of another man’s wife, he commits adultery; the mere name of this crime often restrains the daring to attempt it, 1018, 1. Once the betrothal has been concluded before ten witnesses and the marriage consummated, any woman commits adultery only at great peril, 310, 20. An incontinent man in marriage is like a kind of adulterer, 1030, 32. An adulterer cannot say, “The Lord is my portion,” 1045, 94.

**ADVERSARY.** There is no crown of victory without an adversary, 840, 28.
