**ILLNESS.** Illness of the flesh repels sin, but lust of the flesh aggravates guilt, 407, 63. What the serious illnesses of the soul are, 908, 15 and following.

**EGYPT.** In Egypt, in the first month, new grain is cut, 885, 16. It is not criminal to cross into Egypt, but to cross into the customs of the Egyptians—to cross into the harshness of their faithlessness and the deformity of their luxury, 904, 8.

**EGYPTIANS** devote themselves to geometry and to calculating the courses of the stars, 1072, 5. Some are accustomed to examine the Egyptian days, 881, 4. The Egyptians abominated shepherds of livestock, not because of the man but because of the animals, 898, 1. They hated sacrificial offerings—that is, perfected pursuits of virtue and things filled with discipline, 898, 2. See **AMBROSE**, **MONTH**, **THEOPHILUS**.

**EQUALITY** knows no rank; unity knows no order, 689, 117.

**EQUINOX.** The day of the equinox is the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, 885, 16.

**EQUITY** strengthens commands; injustice dissolves them, 93, 95.

**RUST** is our wantonness; our rust is our lust, which covers the sharpness of the mind with the filth of shameful acts, 633, 183.

**AESCULAPIUS.** They credit him with restoring the dead, but he himself, struck by lightning, did not escape, 176, 7.

**AGE.** Every age is suitable for God and perfect in Christ, 223, 40; 827, 15. No age is too late for thorough learning, 834, 7. Age is perfect where virtue is perfect, 1200, 6. Faith increases age, same place, 7.

**ETERNITY.** The manner in which Scripture signifies God’s eternity, 508, 61. See **GOD**.

**ETHIOPIANS.** See **CIRCUMCISION**.

**AFFABILITY** ought to be sincere and sober and without flattery, 93, 96. How much affability and gentleness win the favor of the people, 78, 30 and following.

[Col. 1419] **AFFECTION.** Your affection gives a name to your work: just as it proceeds from you, so it is judged, 39, 147. Affection makes a rich or poor gift and assigns value to things, 40, 149. No one uses greater confidence than one who loves from affection, 954, 25. Affection is conveyed by intimacy; judgments are formed by merits, 952, 7. When divine things flow in, bodily affection wanders abroad and the use of the outward man grows obsolete, 228, 60.

**AFRICA** and Gaul possess all their priests in a common fellowship, 818, 3.

**AFRICANUS** found triumph amid Hannibal’s battle lines, 834, 7.

**AGENTES IN REBUS** (“imperial agents”), 854, 7.

**FIELD.** A field is better in proportion as its fruit is more abundant, 178, 17. The fields of the Church. See **CHURCH**.

**HAGGAI**, that is, “feasting,” as the interpretation declares, 912, 7. Nothing should be undertaken that we cannot carry out, 50, 186.

**AGNES**, a virgin, 307, 10. Even her name was not without the radiance of praise, 147, 5. She protected chastity and exchanged salvation for immortality, 54, 213. She is said to have suffered martyrdom at twelve years of age, 147, 7. That event is described, same place and following. Because of her age she was not yet able to be mistress of herself, 148, 8. She hastened to death as though to immortality, 939, 37. Greater than the Pythagorean virgin, 151, 19. Her feast day, 147, 5.

**LAMBS** grow fatter on sweeter grasses, and the milk’s yield is healthier, 905, 2.

**AGRICOLA.** His martyrdom is described, 279, 5. His remains. See **AMBROSE**, **RELICS**, **VITALIS**. Laborious farmers are to be imitated, 416, 3.

**Αἵπον** (“goat” [uncertain]), 783 and following.

**ALANS** and Huns approaching Gaul, Valentinianus held back through the lands of Alamannia, 890, 8.

**ALEXANDER**, our fellow presbyter, 969, 13.

**ALEXANDER**, king of the Macedonians, was sacrificing when the boy who was kindling a light for him remained motionless, though his body was burned, 177, 12. Calanus’s letter to Alexander, and his authoritative speech addressed to that same Alexander, 938, 35 and following.

**ALEXANDRIA.** The basilica there, which surpassed all the others, was burned by Gentiles and Jews in Julian’s time, 957, 15. The Fathers of the Council of Aquileia always maintained the arrangement and order of the Alexandrian Church, 814, 6.

**ALMACHIUS**, bishop, 786, 1; 805, 76.

**ALMON**, river, 840, 30.

**ALTAR** is the form of the body, 366, 7. What is an altar except the form of Christ’s body? 374, 7. See **AMBROSE**.

**ALTINUM**, 767, 8.

**ALYPIUS** gave Antiochus a letter for Ambrose, 1107, 1.

**AMANTIUS**, bishop of Nicea, 786, 1; 803, 76. His condemnation of Palladius, 803, 64.

One who is bent by canvassing is not free, for he serves another’s command, 939, 39.

**AMBROSIA**, the Lord’s sacred ambrosia, 249, 1.

**THE AMBROSIANS** greet Eusebius, 1005, 5.

**AMBROSE.** Both Ambroses remained for us as a pledge, 1004, 1. The Ambrosian basilica, 875, 2.

The people demanded Ambrose as bishop from Valentinian, 861, 7. Valentinian promised future peace if Ambrose accepted the priesthood, same place. Ambrose was called to the priesthood from the uproar of legal disputes and from the public terror of administration, 431, 67. He had not been raised in the bosom of the Church, nor trained from boyhood; he was snatched from the tribunals, drawn away from the vanities of this age, and accustomed by the herald’s voice to the psalmist’s song, 432, 72. He undertook some labor for the Church, same place, 73. The burden of the priesthood was imposed upon one who resisted it, 2, 2. He was snatched from the tribunals and the insignia of administration into the priesthood, 3, 4. How he resisted being ordained, and at last, when compelled, at least sought that his ordination be delayed; but the prescription did not prevail, the pressure prevailed. Finally the Western bishops approved his ordination by their judgment, and the Eastern bishops by their example. If delay was absent from the ordination, it was because of the force of the compulsion, 1037, 65.

Ambrose was a distinguished bishop of the city of Milan both by the merit of his life and by God’s favor, 787, 4. The burden of teaching was imposed upon him, 2, 2. He began to teach before he began to learn, 3, 4. Every day he renewed the sacrifice, 856, 13. In the Church’s buildings he was often afraid of displeasing Satyrus, 1119, 20. What he asked from God at the altars and temple that he dedicated, 302, 94. He incurred envy because he broke the Church’s vessels to redeem captives, 103, 136. He loved those whom he begot in the Gospel no less than if he had received them in marriage, 8, 24. He loved those presbyters or deacons who had advanced in some way and would by no means allow them to remain away from their office for long, 1106, 2. Everything that belonged to him belonged to the poor, 854, 8. He commends himself to the prayers of Bishop Felix, 763, 3. The case of Bishop Marcellus, together with his brother Laetus and the cause of their sister, was referred to Ambrose’s judgment, and he himself pronounced on it, 1100, 1 and following. Because of the frequent disagreements of the bishops he had excused himself from going to Gaul, [Col. 1420] 1181, 25. He did not admit one man to the clergy, and ordered another, who had been admitted, not to precede him, because the bearing and gait of both were unbecoming, 20, 72. He undertook the case of the virgin Indicia and absolved her by episcopal judgment, 765, 1 and following. He grieved that many distinguished widows had died at one time, 1131, 67. He undertook many struggles against royal attacks on behalf of widows, indeed on behalf of all persons who had entrusted property to him, 106, 150. The bishop of the Church of Ticinum, after consulting Ambrose, defended a widow’s deposit, 106, 150 and following. He has no reason to be displeased that I spared him nothing, since I spare myself nothing either, 203, 65. He is blamed because he prohibited unlawful marriages, 216, 10, and because he prohibited consecrated girls who had preserved their integrity from marrying, 219, 26. He was accustomed to show deference to emperors without yielding, and willingly to offer himself to punishments, 864, 2. What opportunities for martyrdom did he have, and how was he recalled from the very brink? 929, 4. He dissuaded a father who wished to join his granddaughter by his daughter to his son, 1017, 1 and following. He was pressed by a serious illness, 1123, 36. He presented as an illness a truly serious bodily condition, 998, 5. Though weakened in bodily appearance, he received no slight grace toward recovery from Felix’s speech, 763, 1. When he was held confined by illness, Acholius visited him, 821, 10; 822, 2. He had already completed fifty-three years, situated in this body, 1018, 4. The place he had predetermined for his burial, 877, 13. See **FELIX**, **COUNCIL OF NICAEA**.

Ambrose and Satyrus attained the honors of the world, lest an appearance of lowliness seem contemptible, 1120, 25. Yet these honors did not delight them, because they separated them from one another, same place. Ambrose so resembled Satyrus in bodily appearance that many said something to Satyrus which they later recalled having said to Ambrose, 1124, 37 and following. Their health or illness was always shared: when one fell ill, the other fell into sickness, and when one recovered, both rose again, 1134, 79. Thus Ambrose’s mutual love with Satyrus always remained so deep that it was nourished more by inward affection than displayed by public flattery, 1124, 37. How inseparable Ambrose was from his brother Satyrus, 1133, 73 and following. How restless he was whenever he had to go out without Satyrus, 1119, 22. Their patrimony and resources were always undivided, 1115, 7. Although everything was common to them, the only thing not held in common was the friends’ private confidence, 1124, 39. If Ambrose had had a son, he would never have loved him more than he loved his brother Satyrus, 1132, 68. Satyrus was for Ambrose at home his sole consolation, outside his adornment, in counsels his arbiter, a participant in his cares, an intercessor for his anxieties, a banisher of grief, an advocate of his actions, a defender of his thoughts; in him domestic concern rested and public care found repose, 1119, 20. Ambrose drew in the last breath of his brother Satyrus and breathed his breath into the dying man’s mouth, 1118, 19. Through the intercessions of the dead Satyrus he hopes to come quickly to him, 1170, 135. He wishes that his soul might die in the soul of his brother Satyrus, 1145, 43. He followed his dead brother Satyrus with a public funeral oration, 1113, 1 and following. He bade Satyrus a final farewell before the people, 1134, 78. He commended Satyrus’s soul to God, 1135, 80. See **SATYRUS**.

Ambrose’s sister was venerable for her integrity, equal to Satyrus in character and not inferior in duties, 1118, 16. See **MARCELLINA**.

Ambrose excused himself to Gratian for not having come, 752, 1. He presented him with a petition of Christian senators against the Gentiles’ request, 826, 10. See **GRATIAN**. Ambrose presented Valentinian with a petition against Symmachus. In it one should look not for elegance of words but for force of substance, same place. He gave the emperors two petitions against Symmachus, indicating that a Christian could not restore the expenses of sacrifices, 1010, 2. The petitions were read in the consistory, and Valentinian did nothing other than what the interest of our faith demanded, same place, 3. Ambrose asked Valentinian not to permit the restorations of Gentile superstitions as they had requested, 824, 1 and following. He informed Valentinian that if he restored the expenses of sacrifices to the pagans, he would either not come to the Church, or, if he came, would find either no priest or one resisting him in the Church, 1010, 3. The pagans, through an embassy announced by the Senate, asked Theodosius to restore the expenses of sacrifices; but when he refused this, he granted assent to Ambrose’s representation, 1011, 4.

The account of the persecution raised against Ambrose by the Arians at Milan, 852, 1 and following. During the very offering he began to pray to God that no one’s blood should be shed in the Church, or at least that his own blood might be poured out for the salvation not only of the people but also of the impious themselves, 853, 5. His speech during the persecution, 855, 14 and following. He refused the emperor’s request for the Church’s vessels, 865, 5. He refused to hand over the basilica to the Arians, 868, 18. He spent the whole day in the old basilica, 855, 10. From there he withdrew home to sleep, so that if anyone wished to lead him away, he might find him ready, same place. He could not return home and recited psalms with the brothers in the Church’s smaller basilica, 858, 24. He was called a tyrant and more than a tyrant, 859, 27. What did he reply to Caligonus, the chamberlain? 859, 28. When summoned to the Consistory to dispute against Auxentius with the emperor as judge, he refused to go, 860, 1 and following. He would not be absent if a synod were convened for that reason, 863, 16. He dictated a letter to the emperor Valentinian concerning the counsel of the priests, 862, 13. He would have come to the consistory to speak to the emperor in person if the bishops or people had permitted it, 863, 17. The emperor announced to Ambrose that he might go wherever he wished, 863, 18. Although those who wished were permitted to follow him, 864, 1. Ambrose indicated that he could not entertain the intention of abandoning the Church, because he feared the Lord of the world more than the emperor of this age, 864, 1. The people of Milan maintained watch and vigil for him day and night, 865, 7. The carefully guarded doors of the Church were found open, 866, 10. In the previous year he came to the palace when summoned, and what happened there at that time, 871, 29. Some threatened fire, the sword, and deportation, 873, 36. He shuddered at heart when armed men were sent to seize the Church’s basilica and offered his throat, 854, 9. Against arms, soldiers, and even Goths, his weapons were tears, 864, 2. He feared not for himself but for his people, same place, 4. Neither death nor the sword could separate him from the teaching of the Council of Nicaea, 862, 14. During the persecution he went out daily either to visit people or to proceed to the martyrs, passing by the imperial palace on his way there and back, 867, 15. He expected either the sword for Christ’s name or fire. A cart had been prepared; many reported that executioners had been sent ahead and that the death penalty had been decreed. But he feared none of these things, 867, 15 and following.

Ambrose discovered the bodies of Saints Gervasius and Protasius, 874, 2 and following. His speech on this subject to the people, 875, 3 and following. Such defenders surround him, 876, 10. Ambrose dedicated the basilica, 874, 1. He was asked to dedicate it as he had dedicated the Roman basilica, same place. Ambrose was invited to a banquet at Bologna, where the translation of a martyr had been celebrated, 277, 1. Where and how were the relics of the martyrs Vitalis and Agricola found and raised by Ambrose? 279, 7 and following. He gathered their triumphant blood and the wood of the cross, 280, 9. He placed them beneath the sacred altars, 280, 10.

Ambrose’s first embassy to Maximus was approved by Valentinian, 888, 1. He explained to Valentinian the circumstances of his second embassy to Maximus, same place and following. When he had reached Trier, he proceeded to the palace the next day; by whom and how was he received there? same place, 2. When Maximus rose to give him a kiss, what did Ambrose reply? same place, 3. What conversations did he then have with him? 4 and following. He kept away from bishops who communicated with Maximus or who sought the death of some persons, even if they had strayed from the faith, 891, 12. For that reason Maximus ordered him to return without delay, same place. He set out on the journey, although many believed he would not escape ambushes, same place. Maximus threatened Ambrose; to be hated by him was praise, 1185, 39. The envoys sent again to Gaul found Ambrose near Valence in Gaul, 890, 7. Within Gaul, Count Victor met Ambrose near the city of Mainz, 889, 6. See **MAXIMUS**.

Ambrose mourned the deaths of Gratian and Valentinian, 1194, 79 and following. He considered the death of both as though his own eyes had been torn out, 1185, 39. He promises to follow them with his prayers and offerings, 1194, 78. What he asks God on their behalf, 1196, 80. Ambrose had received the young Valentinian, had gone as envoy to his enemy, had embraced him after he had been entrusted to the maternal hands of Justina, and again went as envoy to Gaul for peace and to request Gratian’s relics, 1182, 28. His embassy prepared for Vienna to see Valentinian was interrupted, and why, 1180, 23 and following. He was given as a hostage to Valentinian’s count, same place, 25. He entrusted himself to the journey and was crossing the Alpine passes when, on receiving news of Valentinian’s death, he turned back, same place, 26. Valentinian requested that he become his surety, 1190, 63. Ambrose bound his pledge before God on Valentinian’s behalf, 1190, 63. Valentinian thought that through him he would be rescued from dangers; he loved him not only as a parent but hoped in him as his redeemer and liberator, 1195, 79. Valentinian sent him a letter two days before his death, 1181, 26. Ambrose grieved Valentinian’s death with bitter sorrow, 1002, 1 and following. With what words did he address the soul of the dead Valentinian? 1190, 64 and following. He wished the dead Valentinian to be joined to his brother Gratian, 1188, 54, and to his father, same place, 55. Theodosius wrote to him concerning Valentinian’s burial, 1003, 4.

Ambrose did not reply when Eugenius wrote to him at the beginning of his reign; nevertheless, when a matter involving his duty arose, he wrote and made his request, and why, 1012, 12. Ambrose wrote to Eugenius explaining why he had avoided him when he came to Milan, 1010, 1 and following. He freely rebuked him because he had granted expenses to the temples of idols, 1011, 7 and following. Ambrose returned to Milan around the Kalends of August, when Eugenius had departed, 1020, 1 and following.

Ambrose was at Aquileia when the synagogue of the Jews was burned by Christians, as was the meeting place of the Valentinians, [Col. 1422] 956, 1. What did he do in this matter? same place. He wrote about it to the emperor Theodosius, 946 and following. What did Theodosius say to Ambrose as he descended from the platform concerning the burned synagogue and the monks, and what did Ambrose reply? 963, 27 and following. Afterwards Ambrose approached the altar, and how great a grace of offering did he experience? same place, 28. Ambrose asked Theodosius to hasten the burial of Valentinian’s body, lest it completely dissolve in the summer heat, 1003, 5. Ambrose explained to Theodosius why he had avoided his arrival, 997, 7 and following. When he was anxious because of the massacre at Thessalonica, on the very night when he was preparing to depart, Theodosius seemed to have come to the Church, but Ambrose was not permitted to offer the sacrifice, 1000, 14. He did not dare offer the sacrifice if Theodosius wished to attend after the Thessalonican massacre, 1000, 13. See **THEODOSIUS**.

Ambrose complained that only he had been deprived of the natural right within Theodosius’s retinue, so that he was deprived of the opportunity to hear and speak, 997, 2. Theodosius was frequently disturbed because certain matters decided in his consistory had reached Ambrose, 997, 2. Ambrose preferred that something be lacking in his official duty rather than in humility, and that authority be sought from him by other priests rather than honorific treatment be desired from Theodosius, 998, 5. He told Theodosius that he had done what could be done most honorably: to hear him more readily in the palace, lest, if necessary, he should hear him in the Church, 955, 3. He wrote to Theodosius in his own hand, so that he alone might read it, 1000, 14. He was not ashamed to speak in Theodosius’s presence what benefited Theodosius’s soul, 1011, 4. He said to him: “If I am unworthy to be heard by you, I am unworthy to offer on your behalf, to whom you entrust your vows and your prayers,” 946, 1.

Ambrose received letters from the emperor Theodosius, 1020, 1 and following. To give thanks to God for the victory won over Eugenius, he brought this letter with him to the altar, placed it upon the altar, and carried it in his hand while offering the sacrifice, 1021, 5. He asked Theodosius for the absolution of those accused who had fought with Eugenius, 1021, 7, and for those who had fled to the Church seeking mercy, 1022, 3. In his final moments Theodosius sought Ambrose with his last breath, 1207, 35. How deeply Ambrose grieved the death of the emperor Theodosius, 1207, 35 and following. See **THEODOSIUS**.

Ambrose was overwhelmed with grief that the Church of Vercellae had no priest, 1022, 1. He teaches the people of Vercellae what they ought to do in choosing a bishop, 1023, 2 and following. Ambrose thought it more suitable to attach his own hand to his own pen, and why, 988, 2. He did not dictate everything, especially at night, and for what reasons, 988, 1 and following. Instead, he wrote books with his own hand, same place. He sent Sabinus a requested codex written more clearly and plainly, 988, 1. He wrote the *Hexaemeron*, 970, 1. He wrote *On the Earthly Paradise* while still an inexperienced priest, 981, 1. Why did he undertake to write *On Duties*? 8, 23 and following. To whom does he address his discourse *On Duties*? 76, 25. While not yet three years a priest, he wrote the books *On Virgins*, 172, 39. Why did he write *On Virgins*? 163, 5. He spoke on virginity in frequent books, 253, 15. He sent the emperor Gratian two booklets on the faith, 754, 7. Meanwhile he asks indulgence for writing *On the Spirit*, same place. He sets this discussion aside, 552, 7; 557, 34. He wishes a Seraph to fly to him for purification as to Isaiah, so that he may treat of God’s generation, 469, 139 and following. Why he wrote other books after the two books *On the Faith*, 497, 1 and following. He wrote five books on the divinity of the Father and the Son, 717, 62. He delivered daily discourse on moral matters, 325, 1. After the Egyptian calculations and the definitions of the Alexandrian Church, many bishops of the Roman Church also awaited Ambrose’s opinion by letter concerning the day on which Easter should be celebrated, 882, 8. “I shall include them in the books of our letters,” he says, “so that they may be commended by your name,” 991, 7. He undertook to append the letters in familiar speech, redolent in some measure of the customs of the Fathers, 996, 16. Simplicianus delighted when Ambrose took up something from the writings of the apostle Paul for discussion before the people, 930, 1. When Vigilius was appointed to the episcopate, he handed him a model of instruction, 842, 1 and following. He wrote one and the same letter to the bishops Segatius and Delphinus, 1107, 2. What impelled him to write about Valentinian’s death? 1173, 1. How did he refute a certain Apollinarist? 984, 1 and following.

**AMEN**, that is, “faithfully,” 528, 43.

**AMENTATA**, a non-manipular sentence, 762, 3.

**FRIENDSHIP.** The laws of friendship, 138, 125 and following. Christ gave a model of friendship for us to follow—and what that model is, 141, 135. It ought to be constant, 139, 127. It cannot exist between dissimilar characters, 140, 132. It knows no pride, 139, 128. That friendship is commendable which protects honesty, and it must certainly be preferred to wealth, honors, and powers, 138, 124. The duties of friendship ought not so much to be reduced as increased, 1108, 1. The antiquity of friendship has something that can be shared with many; patriotic love does not, 931, 2. Friendships of the poor are generally better than those of the rich, 140, 134. Friendship is a virtue, not a source of profit, 140, 133. It is a support of life, 139, 128. It is the guardian of devotion and the teacher of equality, 140, 132. Nothing among human affairs is more beautiful than friendship, 140, 131. Reproofs are welcome in friendship, 46, 173. No one is more detestable than one who has injured friendship, 141, 136. See **ADULATION**.

**FRIEND.** What is a friend except a partner in love, so that you wish to make one person out of two? 140, 133. A friend is another self, 664, 154. No one can be a friend to a human being if he has been faithless to God, 140, 132. Great weight of charity is added to the power of loving: approve those whom you love, and love those whom you have chosen, 8, 24. A faithful friend is medicine for life and a gift of immortality, 139, 128. A friend must not be abandoned in necessity, 139, 128. Correct a friend who is going astray; do not abandon an innocent friend, 139, 127 and 129. Often enmities must be endured for the sake of a friend’s innocence, 139, 129. Job’s friends’ reproaches are reserved for the final contest, 301, 90. An enemy can be avoided; a friend cannot, if he wishes to lie in wait, 142, 136. See **ADVERSITY**.

**LOVE.** True love is proved by constancy, 991, 7. Nature is not more powerfully disposed to love than grace is, 8, 24. Those deprived of love blush more impatiently, 1139, 17. The touch of love is tender, awakening an unexpected affection, 1138, 14. What is so implanted in nature as that you should love one who loves you? 79, 37. For the incitement of common charity, it is greatly beneficial if one repays those who love, 79, 37. Nothing is so useful as being loved; nothing so useless as not being loved, 77, 29. Although a greater portion and fuller knowledge are in the spirit through which we love, nevertheless we desire to see even in the bodily form, 821, 10. See **AFFECTION**.

**AMINADAB** is referred as a figure to Christ, 236, 94.

**AMMIANUS**, bishop, 819.

We read the fifteen Davidic psalms of the *Anabathmoi*, 895, 10.

**ANATOLIUS**, bishop, 819.

**ANEMIUS**, bishop of Sirmium in Illyricum, 786, 1; 790, 16; 805, 76. His condemnation of Palladius, 800, 55.

**ANGELS.** Although I do not find their beginning, nevertheless there was a time when they were not, 707, 16. An angel is not naturally immortal, 500, 19. In him the capacity of nature is subject to defect, but not subject to discipline, same place, 20. The nature of angels could be changed, 613, 63. They stand by in order to see the glory of the Father and the Son, with whatever modes of vision they can or deserve—
515, 105. They possess stages of knowledge and the capacity for progress; they possess discernment of virtue and prudence, 523, 10. They could not know the mystery of God the Father and of the Lord Jesus Christ except through revelation, 521, 2. Seeing Christ rise again, they were perplexed by uncertainty of opinion: why, and what did they then say? 334, 36; 522, 5 and following. They were ignorant of Christ’s resurrection, 258, 39. The words of angels are the commandments of the Lord, 218, 16. They descend to assist human beings, 618, 83. They guard Christ’s little servants, as advocates for their prayers, 866, 11. The angels are in attendance, the Son of God in glory; they are in the retinue, he on the tribunal; they stand, he sits; he judges, they minister, 516, 106. An angel descending into the pool announced the descent of the Holy Spirit into the waters of baptism, 618, 88. The angels undertake various ministries amid the labors of this world, 924, 10. They groan when they are employed as ministers of punishments and destructions, 924, 10. Though possessing life, they would prefer to return to that higher state of their tranquility rather than be interrupted by the avenging punishments of our sins, 924, 10. As he made the angels in the Spirit, so also through the same grace he will make human beings like the angels, 618, 84. The likeness of angels is promised to human beings as the reward of virtue, 564, 75. Whoever announces Christ appears to be enrolled in the place of the angels, 351, 7. Because of intemperance the angels fell from heaven into the world, 159, 53. See VIRGINS.

ANIMA. The soul has no sex; why, then, did it receive a feminine name? 236, 93. Scripture frequently designates the human soul by the term “spirit,” 644, 56. What is so truly human as one’s soul? 923, 6. Whether the soul appears to be of heavenly substance, 921, 1 and following. Souls are grasped neither by any touch nor seen by bodily sight, and therefore they transcend bodily substance and sensible quality, 922, 3. The Apostle, like a good teacher and spiritual cultivator, left us to understand that our souls are of a superior creation and of a certain most excellent nature, through the hidden seeds of his teaching, 922, 3. See ESDRAS. What the common run of philosophers thinks about the soul, 922, 1. Aristotle judged the soul to be ἐντελέχεια, “entelechy,” 922, 1. Plato says that the soul is that which moves itself and is not moved by another, 922, 1. What truth is there in the belief that, because it moves itself and is always in motion, it is immortal? 1168, 126. See ΝΟῦΣ. The presence of souls is greater, 752, 1. He who enters more deeply into souls is more present than he who displays himself to the eyes, 841, 23. Our soul does not die, 792, 25. We know that the soul survives the body and, once freed by laying aside the barriers of its proper senses, sees with unimpeded gaze what, while situated in the body, it did not see, 1140, 21. If in the quiet of night souls can penetrate to higher things and discern what is distinct, how much more do they behold these things when, with a pure and ethereal sense, they suffer no impediments from bodily stain! 1133, 73. Philosophers who say that souls are immortal do not sufficiently please me when they deny the resurrection of bodies, 1168, 126. How empty and incredible is the opinion of those philosophers who assert that our souls, once they have departed from this body, pass into the bodies of beasts and various living creatures, 1168, 127 and following. It ought not to seem strange if you Gentiles believe that human beings can be changed into beasts, since you worship beasts, 1169, 131. The soul received the body to govern it, so that, if it governed well, it might receive a reward; if badly, punishment, 922, 5. Soul and flesh must be joined together in peace with one another, 252, 11. The soul advances beautifully when it uses the body as a kind of shoe, 268, 87. The strength of the soul is brought to completion through the weaknesses of the flesh, 406, 61. Our mind is the author of guilt; the flesh is innocent, but for the most part it serves sin, 409, 73. The flesh cannot be corrupted unless the mind has first been corrupted, 308, 11. Who would not consider bodily defect or loss of patrimony lighter than defect of character and damage to one’s reputation? 113, 24. How the soul is subjected to vanity, 922, 5. Christ recalled the soul, found in exile from paradise, to paradise by retracing the winding path of error, 1069, 4. How Christ received, instructed, and perfected the soul in the Gospel, 1069, 1 and following. When the soul has cleansed the heart, it finds the Word and sees God, 236, 92. Once it has tasted the fruit of devout submission, Christ does not refuse to preserve it and to test himself repeatedly in it, 1070, 6. The soul that sees Christ as the highest good does not require this body; it renounces the world, withdraws itself from the bonds of the flesh, and strips itself of all the chains of these pleasures, 907, 12. In each individual soul it weds the Word of God, without any turning aside from modesty, as to an eternal bridegroom, 154, 31. Having kissed the Word of God, it desires him above all beauty, loves him above all joy, delights in him above all perfumes, longs frequently to see him and often to contemplate him; it longs to be drawn, 906, 10. When the soul begins to conceive and Christ begins to be formed in it, 1066, 16. The soul possesses joy and exultation when it possesses a παρθενικὸς λόγος, a “virginal word,” 915, 3. The soul that from the beginning dedicated to Christ the virginal flower of its faith, and the soul acquired for him from the Gentiles, are both brides of the one Word, ibid., 4 and following. We read of the soul’s continual progress in the Song of Songs, 1062, 2. Let the soul that wishes to draw near to God lift itself above the body and cling always to that highest good, to that good which is divine and eternal, 907, 14. Let the progressing soul first diminish and shake off the excesses of its passions, so that it may display its fruits in the very field, 1064, 7. Its excellence consists in two things: being exercised in good thoughts and not wavering amid any desires, 51, 200. Each person possesses his own mind as a stern judge of himself, an avenger of wrongdoing and punisher of crime, 756, 10. Faith, grace, mercy, and redemption are the soul’s salvation, 778, 3. Let the soul not die in sin, but let it die in the soul of the righteous, so that it may receive that soul’s righteousness, 1145, 43. The conversion of the fallen soul is explained from the prophet Micah, 1062, 2 and following. How much more gratifying it is to drive away the darkness of the mind than that of the body, and to make the radiance of faith shine forth rather than that of the sun, 839, 27. The soul has its own food and clothing, 905, 3. On what better things do souls feast than good deeds? 43, 163. The garden of the Word is the affection of a flourishing soul, and in its fruit-bearing trees is the fruit of virtue, 227, 54. The Son of God poured out an ointment by which our entire soul ought to be penetrated, 229, 65 and following. See CHRIST. The soul has spiritual flights, 239, 107. It has wings by which it can rise freely from earthly things, 241, 115. By what things the soul’s flight is nourished and increased, 240, 109. Philosophers borrowed from us the chariot of the soul, its horses, and its wings, 240, 11. The four animals of the soul’s chariot are its four affections, 241, 113. Namely, anger, desire, pleasure, and fear—and the manner in which they must be governed, 239, 95 and following. The soul’s chariot rolls smoothly and roundly, without any obstruction, 236, 97. Enter wholly into your soul, gather yourself within it, and dwell in it; remain with it; let all your conduct be in it, so that you may be not in the flesh but in the spirit, 917, 12. Cast out from the city of your soul the image of the devil and raise up the image of Christ, 64, 254. See HARLOT. Disturbance of the soul removes steadfastness; abandonment reveals cowardice and exposes sluggishness, [Col. 1425] 61, 238. The soul cannot be tested except through temptations, 1066, 16. The soul’s emptiness amid anguish, and what it is, 49, 185. Not to be moved by the indignity of circumstances is judged not virtue but sluggishness and laxity, 27, 96. See APPETITE, FLESH. What that soul is which the Law portrays in the form of a good woman, 916, 10 and following. Which souls are like a beloved wife and which like a hated wife, 920, 2. Every faithful soul is Bethlehem, just as it is called Jerusalem when it possesses the peace and tranquility of the Jerusalem above, which is in heaven, 1065, 13.

ANIMALS. All kinds of animals are naturally capable of being gathered together, 34, 128. In all living creatures there is implanted first the instinct to preserve themselves, avoid what harms them, and seek what benefits them, 34, 128. We understand the four forms of the four animals as figuratively corresponding to the distinctive features of the Gospel books, 241, 113. See BEASTS, HUMAN BEING.

ANNA. Her lodging was in the temple, her conversation in prayer, and her life in fasting, 191, 22. She teaches what sort of women widows ought to be, 191, 21. It is a distinction of widowhood that in the Gospel, after the Virgin’s celebrated childbirth, the widow Anna is introduced in succession, 968, 8.

HANNIBAL. For a long time he insulted the sacred rites of the Romans, 834, 4.

RING. A ring does not perceive what it expresses, 587, 197. It is a pledge of faith and the seal of the Holy Spirit, 420, 18.

BEFORE. When “before” is said in Scripture, it extends backward indefinitely, without any specification, 508, 61.

ANTIOCH. The city of Antioch had two bishops, Paulinus and Meletius, 814, 2. The Church of Antioch had sent a letter to the fathers of the Council of Aquileia, 813, 4. See PAULINUS. The martyrdom of an Antiochene virgin and a Christian soldier, who had exchanged clothing with each other, is described, 167, 22 and following. The noble deed of Damon and Pythias, the Pythagoreans, is inferior to the martyrdom of the Antiochene virgin, 171, 34.

ANTIOCHUS. A man of consular rank, 1107, 1. See ALYPIUS.

ANTONY. Ambrose commends Antony’s love for himself, 1108, 1 and following.

ANYSIUS. Formerly a disciple of Acholius, now his successor and heir either of his honor or of his favor, 822, 1. There was not even a moment’s doubt about his election as bishop and successor to Acholius, ibid. How admirably he imitated Acholius, by whom he was designated as successor, 821, 9. See ACHOLIUS.

APEME. The concubine of King Darius, 933, 12.

APER. A presbyter who subscribed, 969, 14.

THE MYSTERY OF OPENING. The mystery of opening in baptism, and why it occurs, 325, 3 and following; 349, 2 and following.

BEE. When it suspects disturbances in the air, it often rises with pebbles lifted up and balances itself amid the empty clouds, 239, 106.

APOLLINARIANS. They assert that the Word and the flesh are of one substance, 988, 12. Against Apollinaris we confess that, just as in Christ, in the form of God, nothing was lacking to the divine nature and its fullness, so in that form of a human being nothing was lacking by which he could be judged an imperfect human being, 991, 5. The objection of the Apollinarians, drawn from the words “The Word became flesh,” is refuted, 716, 59 and following. Certain people are attempting to introduce into the Church some unknown doctrine of Apollinaris, 818, 4.

APOLLINARIAN. He could not bear to hear that Christ had assumed servitude for us in assuming this body, 984, 1. For this reason he traveled throughout the world, seeking someone whom he might criticize, 985, 2. He wished to gnaw at something in Ambrose’s writings, ibid. He prepares his flight, 988, 14. To the Apollinarian’s objection that Christ “received the form of a servant,” but was not chosen as a servant, the answer is given, 986, 7 and following. And to what he objected again—“found in appearance as a human being”—the answer is given, ibid. See AMBROSE.

APOPHORETA. Those invited to a great banquet customarily carry away apophoreta, “gifts to be carried away,” with them, 277, 1. Triumphal apophoreta, ibid.

APOSTLES. All the apostles are disciples not only of Christ but also of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, 662, 149. They sometimes went astray, so that we might not go astray afterward; and their error benefits us, 714, 46. They began to be more perfect after they had received the Holy Spirit, 660, 138. The saints are the firstfruits of the Lord, especially the apostles, 927, 10 and 12. Just as globes of shining stars gleam in heaven, so the choirs of apostles, martyrs, and priests illuminate the whole world, 475, 24. The one converted from a bandit has rest; the one tested in the apostleship received authority, 1070, 9. The apostles still groan, because the labor of many still wavering remains, 927, 12. It seems to me that, as they discussed the interpretation of the divine Scriptures among themselves in varied speech, a radiance full of light shone forth for them, 896, 10. The Apostles’ Creed, which the Roman Church has always preserved and guarded inviolate, 967, 5. Ἀποτέλεσμα, “result” or “completion,” 783, 1 and following. Ἀποτέλεσμα: God is the one who brings all things to conclusion and completion, 786, 12.

ATTENDANTS. Attendants of various officers, 854, 7. An attendant of the prefecture, who had incurred an offense because of port services, sails in the harbor, 1003, 1.

APPETITE. Appetite and the movement of the mind ought to follow reason, not run ahead of it, 60, 237 and following. If it obeys reason, what is fitting can easily be preserved in all duties, 29, 105. When the mind is disturbed, it spreads more broadly and farther, 61, 238. In what way the movements of thoughts and appetite differ, [Col. 1426] 27, 98. A more serious appetite arises from excessive indignation, 61, 240.

AQUILA. A Jew. Not all authority rests upon his translation, 1077, 24.

EAGLE. Once it has died, it is reborn from its own remains, 418, 8.

COUNCIL OF AQUILEIA. The Council of Aquileia was convened in accordance with the emperor’s command, 788, 7; 806, 2. The acts of the Council of Aquileia, 786, 1 and following. An imperial rescript is read in it, 787, 3. It gives thanks to the emperor Gratian, 806, 1 and following. It writes to the bishops of Gaul, 806, 1. See ALEXANDRIAN CHURCH, BISHOPS OF GAUL.

ARABS. See CIRCUMCISION.

ARCADIUS. At the death of Theodosius, he was already vigorous in the strength of youth, 1202, 15. See THEODOSIUS.

ARCHYTAS OF TARENTUM. To his steward he said, “O unhappy man, whom I would punish if I were not angry.” David did something much greater, 26, 94.

RAM. The word “ram” is full of tranquility, moderation, and patience, 783, 3. What it signifies, ibid. and following.

COUNCIL OF ARIMINUM. The first confession and the second correction of the Council of Ariminum, 468, 122. It was written there that Christ is a creature, 862, 14; 870, 25. The law by which that council is confirmed, ibid. The greater number at Ariminum approved the faith of the Council of Nicaea and condemned the Arian decrees, 862, 15.

ARISTOTLE. He thinks that God is content with his own boundaries and lives according to the prescribed limits of his rule, 15, 50. He asserts that God’s providence extends down as far as the moon, 14, 48. He is refuted, ibid. See SOUL.

ARIUS. The author of the Arian heresy, from whom it also received its name, 807, 4. He said that the Father was unbegotten, and that the Son was begotten and created, 723, 91. By saying that the Father alone was eternal, alone good, alone the true God, alone possessing immortality, alone wise, and alone powerful, he impiously wished it to be understood that the Son was deprived of these qualities, 808, 5. He says, “Before the Son of God was born, he did not exist.” But this is refuted, 468, 125. He says that the Son of God came from nothing. But this is refuted, 469, 126 and following. He says that the Son of God is from another substance. But this is refuted, 469, 128 and following. He calls the Son of God a creature—not like the other creatures—and says that he is mutable and changeable, 469, 130 and following. The devil confessed the true Son of God; Arius denies him, 594, 230. It is open sacrilege when Arius denied that Christ the Son of God is the true God, 804, 70. He wishes the highest Son of God to appear like himself, 596, 238. He says, “I have known God wholly, not in part,” 594, 237. He and Sabellius are heirs of pagan error, 570, 105. Let us not, like Arius, by believing in several and dissimilar powers, make several gods according to pagan error, 445, 6 and 10. His letter begins with blasphemies; he called only the Father eternal, 787, 5. It was read at the Council of Aquileia, 798, 46 and following; 807, 4. It was sent to the emperor, 808, 6. Arius is a moth, and Photinus a moth: by their impiety they tear the Church’s holy garment and, with sacrilegious gnawing, consume the precious veil of faith, 633, 183. The devil’s temptations are more tolerable than Arius’s arguments, 502, 32. Arius is refuted by the words of John, 454, 57; 468, 123. He burst open in the middle, 790, 15. Like Judas the betrayer, his entrails spilled out—one is ashamed to say where—and, thrown face down, he polluted his filthy mouth with the very things by which he had denied Christ, 468, 124. He wallowed in excrement, 595, 237.

ARIANS. The blasphemous propositions of the Arians against Christ, 450, 34 and following. The Arian heresy began after all the other heresies and gathered poisons from every heresy, 494, 135. The Arians drew all the coloring of their impiety from philosophy, 468, 85. They agree well with the Gentiles and the Jews in calling Christ a creature, 862, 13. The Arians place all the force of their poisons in dialectical argument, 457, 42. According to their impiety they accept the word “substance” when it is used in their favor; according to the piety approved by the faithful, they reject and refute it, 518, 124. They deny the faith confirmed by the tradition of their ancestors, which even the demons themselves cannot deny, 879, 19. The devil yields to blows, but they still do not yield: how much they have suffered, and how, like Pharaoh, they are hardened by their own evils, 880, 22 and following. They do not deny the Son before the ages, but say that the Father existed before the Son, 455, 59. This is refuted, ibid. They say, “Whoever says that Christ is a creature, in the same sense as the other creatures, let him be anathema.” How fraudulent this was! 519, 130 and following. They deny to the true God’s Son what he plainly did not wish to deny to human beings, 562, 58. By separating the Son from the Father, they fall into the danger of asserting that the Father suffered, 499, 13. Do not separate the Father and the Son according to their teaching, 476, 33. If the Arians consider the Son alien from the Father, why do they worship him? 457, 69; 493, 125. Let them cease to worship one whom they call a creature, or let them cease calling a creature the one whom they pretend to worship, 464, 104. They denied that the Son of God is omnipotent, 583, 182. They diminish Christ’s power, 1212, 49. They are refuted when they say that the Son of God is not good, 473, 15 and following. They deny that Christ possesses free power, 479, 47. They think that in the Son there was not the choice of a free will, but the obedience of a compelled and servile operation, 548, 143. The Arian prefers to have an imperfect and degenerate creator rather than a true and perfect one, 31, 117. Although divinity cannot suffer a wound, nevertheless, so far as lies in it, it attempts to kill its own majesty in Christ, not the body, 466, 114. The Arians do not have the Son of God given for salvation, but sent because of weakness; they do not have a counselor whom they suppose to have been ignorant of the future; they do not have a Son whom they do not consider eternal, 507, 58. By a sacrilegious interpretation, they refer the claim that Christ was made wisdom for us to his ineffable generation, 504, 39. The Arian sometimes calls Christ God, 520, 133. The Arians customarily detract from the Holy Spirit, 479, 47. They think that they detract from the Holy Spirit if they call him the Paraclete, “Comforter”; but in vain, 382, 10. The Arians deny that the Holy Spirit knows the day of judgment, 588, 202. In the Jewish manner they customarily close their ears, 494, 130. How much worse they are than the Jews, 872, 31. Like Jewish wine merchants, they mix water with wine, because they confuse the divine and human generation, 509, 65. The Arians have now divided themselves into several forms: some follow Eunomius or Aëtius; others Palladius or Demophilus, and Auxentius; others follow still others, the heirs of this faithlessness, 452, 45. Some say that the Son is unlike the Father in every respect; others say that he is like him but is not of one substance with the Father, 727, 106. These are refuted, ibid., 108 and following. The Arians flee the person of Eunomius but assert his faithlessness and carry out his impiety, 452, 45. The Arians falsified the divine Scriptures, 494, 135. They interpolated the same Scriptures, 586, 193. How absurdly the Arians removed from their own books and those of the Church the Gospel passage “God is Spirit,” 676, 59 and following. The Arians deny that miracles were performed through the benefit of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, 818, 16. Nor did they spare the martyrs, 494, 135. They wish to give the emperor authority over the Church, 872, 31. When the Arians demanded a basilica, Ambrose opposed them with all his strength, 852, 1 and following. The younger Valentinian issued a law in favor of the Arians, 861, 9 and following. These words, “I and the Father are one,” slaughter the heretical savagery of the Arians, Sabellians, and Photinians, 689, 117; 690, 120 and following. How their blasphemies will be refuted by Christ at the last judgment, 491, 108 and following. If they appeal to the Father, what answer will he give them? 493, 123 and following. How much better a case the Catholic will have before Christ, the judge of all, than the Arian, 490, 101 and following. When Christ is praised, the madness of the Arians is scourged, 869, 19. The various objections of the Arians drawn from the Son’s generation are resolved, 539, 96 and following. The objection drawn from the words “begotten” and “unbegotten” is resolved, 721, 79 and following; 724, 93 and following. Another objection—that the Son could not beget another, and therefore was neither omnipotent nor equal to the Father—is resolved, 535, 77 and following. The objection drawn from the word “alone” is resolved, 534, 16 and following. The objections drawn from the words “who alone possesses immortality,” and so forth, are resolved, 498, 11 and following; 557, 36 and following. The objection drawn from the words “Blessed and only powerful” is resolved, 477, 39 and following. Likewise, the objection drawn from the words “Father, if it is possible,” and so forth, ibid., 41 and following. The objection drawn from the Son of God’s subjection is resolved, 578, 154 and following. The objection drawn from Christ’s obedience and subjection is resolved, 486, 84 and following. The objection drawn from the worship that the Son offered to the Father is resolved, 560, 49 and following. The objection drawn from the Son’s mission is resolved, 567, 95 and following. The objection drawn from Christ’s sitting at the right hand of the Father is resolved, 489, 100 and following; 491, 108 and following. The objection drawn from the claim that the Son is said not to speak from himself is resolved, 574, 133 and following. All the questions of the heretics who say that Christ does not know the day of judgment are briefly destroyed, 897, 18. A response is given to the Arians’ objection that Catholics introduce two gods, 558, 40 and following. The objection of the Arians drawn from the words “Baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” is resolved, 264, 65; 572, 116 and following. The objection drawn from the words “The Father is greater than I” is resolved, 481, 59 and following; 592, 225 and following. The objection drawn from the words “What has been made, in him is life” is resolved, 504, 41 and following. The objection drawn from the words “After me comes a man who was made before me,” and so forth, is resolved, 508, 63 and following. The objection drawn from the words “Behold, I see the heavens opened and Jesus standing,” and so forth, is resolved, 521, 137 and following. The objection drawn from the words “The head of every man is Christ … but the head of Christ is God” is resolved, 526, 27 and following. The objection drawn from the words “that they may be one, just as we are one” is blown away, 527, 33 and following. How wrongly they object to the words “The one who plants and the one who waters are one,” 527, 34. The objection drawn from the words “The Son can do nothing from himself,” and so forth, is resolved, 528, 38 and following. The objection drawn from the words “He lives because of the Father” is resolved, 542, 117 and following. The objection drawn from the words “That his Son may be glorified through him” is resolved, 545, 130 and following. The objection drawn from the words “For us there is one God, from whom are all things, and we,” and so forth, is resolved, 546, 132 and following. The objection drawn from the words “I am the true vine, and my Father is the cultivator” is resolved, 549, 151 and following. In the words “that they may know you, the only true God,” and so forth, the Son is not separated from the only true God, 554, 19 and following. The objection drawn from the words “To sit at my right hand is not mine to give you” is resolved, 561, 55 and following. The objection drawn from the words “You loved them as you loved me” is resolved, 566, 89 and following. The objection drawn from the words “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth” is resolved, 568, 100 and following. The objection drawn from the words “Now the Son of Man has been glorified” is resolved, 571, 115. The objection drawn from the words “Who believes in me does not believe in me, but in him who sent me,” and from other similar expressions, is resolved, 572, 119. The objection drawn from the words “But concerning that day and hour no one knows; neither the angels of heaven nor the Son of Man,” and so forth, is resolved, 586, 193 and following. The objection against the divinity of the Holy Spirit drawn from the words “In Spirit and truth one must worship” is resolved, 679, 69 and following. I do not wish to recall the deaths, tortures, and exiles inflicted by the Arians upon confessors, nor the priestly offices of the devout and the gifts of traitors, 496, 140 and following. Let the Illyrians take notice of what happened to them because of their faithlessness concerning the Arians’ false doctrine, and let them be quiet so that they may follow the true faith, 761, 28. How many in the city of Rome, how many in Alexandria, how many in Antioch, and how many even in Constantinople Christ cleansed from the Arian stain, 603, 17. There was no Arian among the citizens of the city; there were a few from the royal household and some Goths, for whom, as wagons were once their dwelling, so now the Church is a wagon, 855, 12.

ARROGANCE. It is characteristic of shameless arrogance to wish to die alone, when you know that this has been denied even to many saints, 1131, 65.

ARTEMIUS. A bishop, 786, 1; 805, 76.

ASA. If only he had been as faithful in his progress as he was devoted at the beginning, 1202, 15.

DONKEYS. The Lord mounted the colt of a donkey as a figure of the Gentile people, 1083, 9.

ATHANASIUS. A bishop of Alexandria, of holy memory, 816, 4. Athanasius of holy memory was, as it were, a pillar of the faith, 818, 7. See ROME.

ATHLETES. The common people often customarily crown with the victors those who have frequently been defeated, once their contests have been approved, 395, 19.

ATTALUS. A presbyter who confessed his deviation and persisted in the sacrileges of Palladius; he was condemned by the Council of Aquileia, 808, 9. The presbyter Attalus among the Arians, 798, 44.

ATTICUS. He gave Priscus a letter for Ambrose, 1107, 1.

ATTILIUS. He devoted himself to the military service of death, 834, 7.

TO HEAR. One who enjoys hearing provokes another to speak, 21, 76.

EAR. The sole adornment of the ears is to hear what is beneficial, 232, 79.

GOLD AND SILVER. Gold and silver are a burden but have no fruit: they are the burden of the one who seeks them and the expenditure of the heir, 1082, 7. People consider the one who cannot be moved by gold to be more than human, 85, 66. Why should gold and silver be sought from a Christian? 1082, 7.

AUXENTIUS. He occupied the Church of Milan with arms and an army, 676, 59. Auxentius, an Arian bishop, was also called Mercurinus: one portent, two names, 869, 22. One was said to be in the regions of Scythia; another is called here. He has names according to the regions, ibid. He committed lesser offenses in Scythia and was so ashamed that he changed his name; here he dared more criminal acts, ibid. He dares to mention conducting proceedings, full of blood, full of gore, dictating bloody laws with his mouth, writing them with his hand, and thinking that law can impose faith upon human beings, 870, 24. A law was written by his hand ordering Catholic priests to be expelled from the churches, those who resisted to be struck with the sword, and he sent it throughout all the cities, 867, 16. By it the Council of Ariminum is confirmed, 870, 25. In a single moment he will slaughter so many peoples—as much as depends on him—some by the sword, others by sacrilege; and he seeks the basilica with a bloody mouth and bloodstained hands, 868, 17. If he boasts of the approval of certain foreigners, let him be bishop there, wherever those people are who think he ought to be honored with the name of bishop, 861, 8. He chose judges to dispute against Ambrose in the emperor’s palace, 860, 1. He chose four or five pagan judges before whom he was defeated without an opponent, 870, 26. He thinks that the faithful peoples, baptized in the name of the Trinity, ought to be rebaptized, 874, 37. See COUNCIL.

AUXENTIUS. A Jovinianist condemned, 969, 14.

GREED. How old and ancient greed is, 101, 130. How deadly and seductive it is, ibid., 132. Deadly greed and seductive money, which contaminates those who possess it and does not benefit those who do not possess it, 101, 132. How vain it is to accumulate wealth, 64, 251 and following. Contempt for money is a form of justice, 102, 133. Greed is the first thing to weaken justice, 36, 137. Nothing is so contrary to courage as being conquered by profit, 52, 202. Greed generally dulls human understanding and distorts judgments, so that people consider profit piety and money almost a reward for wisdom, 758, 15. Judas the betrayer, through devotion to greed and desire for money, fell into the noose of betrayal, 76, 24. See GOLD, MONEY. Greedy one, do not hoard, lest you become a Christian in name only but a Jew in deed, when you realize that your possessions are a punishment for you, 1082, 8. The greedy person does not say, “The Lord is my portion,” 1045, 94. There is a proverb about the rich miser, because this partridge gathers riches without judgment, 918, 4. He who preserves what is his own does not seek what belongs to another; nor is one who is content with his own inflated by excess, 1129, 55. Let his treasures not possess the eminent man, nor let one who rules free people serve money, 86, 67. To fast and be continent is the achievement of a few; not to desire what belongs to another is not rare, 110, 10.

UNCLE AND NIECE. Between an uncle and his niece there is a third degree of relationship, which also appears to be excluded by civil law from the fellowship of marriage, 1018, 3. This is prohibited by divine law, ibid., 4 and following. What is as customary as the kiss between an uncle and his niece—the kiss which he owes her as though she were his daughter, and she owes him as though he were her parent? 1019, 7.

## B

**BABYLON** is the daughter who ceased to be the daughter of God, 439, 106.

The history and blessing of **BALAAM** are explained, 993, 4 ff. The blessing of the Hebrew people did not depend on their own will but on God’s grace, 994, 8. In a state of mental ecstasy he desired one thing but said another, 995, 11. It is not surprising that what he said and prophesied was infused into him by God, 993, 4 ff. God tested him as though he were divine, but did not choose him as a prophet, 996, 15. While he lived, he did not share in the deeds of those with whom he desired to die in spirit, 279, 7. In his words the magnificence of holy baptism was revealed, 995, 10.

The **BAPTISMS** of the Jews were in some cases superfluous and in others figurative, 355, 2. Many kinds of baptism were set forth beforehand because that one true sacrament of baptism in Spirit and water was to follow, by which the whole human being is redeemed, 1075, 18. There are many kinds of baptism, but one baptism: they are washings, and cannot be called baptisms, 355, 2. Through John the sacraments of baptism were set forth beforehand, 399, 34. John, taking up the type of the Law, baptized for repentance; Christ, for grace, 895, 7. Figures of baptism, 134, 106 ff.; 327, 9 ff.; 352, 12 ff.; 353, 20 ff.; 355, etc. At the beginning of creation the figure of baptism is rightly marked out, by which creation was to be cleansed, 634, 1. The type of baptism preceded in the Red Sea, 843, 2. See **BALAAM**.

Nicodemus was the first to merit hearing the mystery of the washing, 228, 61. Why there is one baptism and not several, 418, 10 ff. There is one baptism because there is one death for the world, 609, 45. The words of Paul, “It is impossible for those who have once been enlightened,” etc., are to be understood of baptism, 417, 8 ff. Unless a catechumen has been baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, he cannot receive remission of sins, 330, 20. Faith alone is not sufficient for perfection unless one also obtains the grace of baptism and receives the blood of Christ by which one has been redeemed, 782, 20. See **CATECHUMEN**. The efficacy of baptism in the desire for it, 1188, 51 ff. See **MARTYRS, VALENTINIAN**.

Why baptism was discovered and instituted, 358, 17 ff. Whence does baptism come, if not from the cross and death of Christ? 356, 6. In baptism the priest consecrates the waters, 327, 8. With what ceremonies, 353, 18. The baptizing priest comes to the font, invokes the name of the Father and the presence of the Son and the Holy Spirit, and uses heavenly words, 357, 14. The descent of the Holy Spirit, invoked over the waters by sacerdotal prayers, consecrates them, 618, 88. The water of the heavenly mystery is not ordinary water, through which we obtain the privilege of deserving to have a share with Christ, 603, 15.

Why is the baptismal font like a tomb? 359, 19. In the water there is an image of death; in the Spirit, a pledge of life, 616, 76. The water is a witness of burial, the blood a witness of death, and the Spirit a witness of life, 616, 77. In the mysteries a threefold question is put and a threefold confirmation is performed; no one can be cleansed except by a threefold confession, 654, 105. What those being baptized were to answer, 332, 28. Renunciation of the devil and the world in baptism, 326, 5 ff.; 350, 5 ff. The mystery of the opening, 325, 3 ff.; 349, 2 ff. The Creed delivered to the candidates in the baptisteries of the basilica, 853, 4. Triple immersion in baptism with a triple interrogation, 359, 20. What immersion signifies, 360, 23. You have been baptized in the name of the Trinity, 381, 5.

In those who were baptized in the name of Jesus Christ, baptism was not repeated but renewed, 608, 42. Just as we read that the sacrament of baptism is complete in the name of Christ, so also when only the Holy Spirit is named, nothing is lacking for the fullness of the mystery, 609, 44 [Col. 1430]. The washing of the feet in baptism, 332, 31; 362, 4 ff. The Roman Church did not observe this custom, ibid., 5. After immersion the baptized person was anointed, and with what words, 360, 14. Anointing of the head in baptism, 332, 29; 350, 4. The baptized person receives μύρον (*myron*), that is, ointment, on the head, 361, 1. White garments in baptism, and why, 333, 34 ff. The baptized receive a spiritual seal, by which the Father seals, Christ confirms, and the Holy Spirit gives a pledge, 336, 42; 363, 8. “God has anointed you; Christ has sealed you; you receive a spiritual seal,” 381, 7 ff. The newly baptized approach the Eucharist, 336, 43 ff.; 364, 11; 366, 15, etc.

On the day of Easter the sacraments of baptism are celebrated throughout the whole world, 288, 42. In baptism the Holy Spirit descends, 358, 14. The Spirit renews the mind, the water contributes to washing, and the blood pertains to the price: the Spirit has made us children of God through adoption, the water of the sacred font washes us, and the Lord’s blood has redeemed us, 678, 68. Who would deny the operation of the Holy Spirit in the washing, in which we perceive his operation and grace? 670, 23. Water in baptism does not cleanse without the Spirit, 330, 19. Christ gave baptism to us for the redemption of our sins, 874, 37. Through baptism the Lord takes away sins and transfers iniquities, plunging them into the depths of the sea, 1068, 24. In baptism the plant is washed, so that hereditary sins may be removed; for our own sins are forgiven through baptism, 333, 32. So that a greater aid of sanctification may be added, 363, 7. See **CONSTANTINE**.

Through the washing we are renewed, through which we are reborn, 417, 8. In the sacrament of baptism we are truly regenerated, 342, 59. What regeneration is, 361, 2. Why it takes place in water, ibid., 3. Through baptism we are renewed like eagles by the washing away of sin, 366, 7. “I was dead, but because in baptism I died with Christ, I received the light of life from Christ,” 1098, 7. In the one being baptized the Son of God is crucified, 418, 9. Whoever dies in Christ becomes a participant in his grace through the washing, 1145, 43. Those baptized are heirs of Christ, because through his death, as that of a testator, an inheritance is given to them, 1025, 11. They ought therefore to act with greater vigilance and avoid the enticements of vices and the provocations of error, ibid., 12. All righteousness has been established in baptism, 353, 15. In it, do not consider the merits of persons but the duties of priests, 332, 27. A comparison between the Probatica pool and baptism, 355, 3 ff. The baptism of the faithless does not heal or cleanse but pollutes, 330, 23. Not every water heals, but only that which possesses the grace of Christ, 352, 15. In baptism there is the presence of divinity, 327, 8 ff.; 33, 27. See **CHURCHES**.

**BARBATIANUS** and **SARMATIO**, new Epicureans, initially practiced fasting and self-restraint within the monastery, 1024, 8. They went outside and then, wishing to return, were not received, ibid., 9. From this point, growing heated, they began to spread heresy, ibid. Their errors are refuted, ibid. ff. They think Epicurus should be followed more than the apostles, 1025, 13. As men with a bad cause do, they frequently attack themselves with their assertions, 1028, 20. They say that there is no merit in abstinence, no grace in frugality, and no grace in virginity; that all are valued at the same price; and that those who chastise their flesh with fasts and make it subject to the mind are delirious, 1024, 7; 1028, 22.

Exposed to barbarian disturbances and storms of war, we find ourselves amid the sea of every affliction, 1017, 3.

**BARNABAS**, chosen by the command of the Holy Spirit—a distinction that redounds to his entire record of merits—was not unworthy of the company of the apostles, 664, 157.

**BASILICA:** the Roman basilica, 874, 1. The Basilica of Fausta, 875, 2. The old basilica, 855, 10. The lesser basilica of the Church, 858, 24. The dedication of a basilica under the name of the apostles, 763, 1. See **FELIX**. How many basilicas of the Church the Jews burned during the reign of Julian: two at Damascus, others at Gaza, Ascalon, Berytus, Alexandria, and nearly all those places; and no one avenged it, 950, 15 ff. The new basilica full of people, 855, 18. Soldiers surrounded and guarded the basilica, 858, 24; 864, 4. The emperor ordered the soldiers to withdraw from the basilica, 859, 26. See **BASSIANUS, CHURCH**.

**BASILIDES** did not believe that Christ had assumed the reality of human flesh, 705, 8.

**BASSIANUS**, bishop of Lodi, 786, 1; 805, 76. His condemnation of Palladius, 802, 60. The signature of Bishop Bassianus, 969, 14. Bishop Bassianus spoke with Ambrose about the dedication of the basilica he had founded in the name of the apostles, 763, 1.

**SENEcio** was given to Bishop **BASSUS** as his associate in governing the Church, 1009, 7.

**BAUTO**, a count of the highest distinction and holder of the rank of master of the soldiery, [Col. 1431] 1010, 3. By birth a Transrhenane, he made the barbarians fight against barbarians, 890, 8.

The divine Scripture placed the **BLESSED LIFE** in the knowledge of divinity and in the fruit of good action before the philosophers did so, 71, 5 ff. The blessedness of individuals is not to be judged according to public prosperity but according to the inner conscience, 13, 44. Which philosophers placed it in freedom from suffering; which in pleasure or the absence of pain; which in moral virtue and bodily and external goods? 71, 4. It receives no increase from bodily pleasure or the enjoyment of advantages, 73, 13. Poverty, hunger, and pain are not an impediment but an aid to the blessed life, 74, 15 ff. All that we suffer is slight and unworthy of comparison with the great reward of future goods that will be repaid for our labors, 926, 5. The blessed life excels even amid sufferings, 73, 9 ff. Innocence and knowledge make one blessed, 72, 8 ff. The blessed life is the fruit of present things, whereas eternal life is the hope of future things, 74, 18. Through Christ our return to paradise has not only been restored to us, but also the honor of the heavenly throne has been bestowed on our flesh through participation in the flesh of Christ, 1085, 3. The marriage of the Lamb is adorned with the bruises of confessors, the blood of martyrs, the lilies of virgins, and also the crowns of priests, 1170, 132. Although the saints are secure regarding their own merit, nevertheless, because the redemption of the whole body of the Church is still future, they suffer together with it, 926, 7.

**BELLICIUS**, afflicted by a severe illness, believed in the Lord Jesus and began to recover, 1095, 1.

In **WAR**, justice and faith must be preserved, 37, 140. In military courage there is no small form of honor and dignity, 54, 211. We have certain battles even in peace, and peace in war, 937, 30. Then the battle is completed and the enemy is put to flight, when the grace of the Spirit and the diligence of the mind sound together, 1164, 111. See **COURAGE**.

**BENEFICENCE** is divided into goodwill and generosity, 38, 143. There is no beneficence where there is no goodwill, 38, 144.

By **BENEFITS**, Christ judged that human beings could be bound and urged more effectively to do what is right than by fear; and that love contributes more than dread to correction, 957, 6. We must strive to bind many people to us by benefits and services and preserve the favor we have bestowed, 98, 121. Our benefits should preferably be conferred on those who cannot repay them to us, 100, 126. Not to be superior in returning a benefit to one's conferring of it is to be inferior, 42, 160. In returning a benefit, the spirit accomplishes more than wealth; goodwill outweighs the ability to return the gift, 44, 166. A benefit cannot remain when its author is excluded; nor can there be an author without a gift, or a gift without an author, 646, 64.

**GOODWILL** surpasses generosity itself, 44, 166 ff. Generosity without goodwill, and goodwill without generosity, is not perfect, 40, 151. Goodwill contains courage within itself, 46, 172. It is increased by the gathering of the Church, fellowship in faith, association in initiation, the bond of receiving grace, and communion in the mysteries, 45, 170. It makes one person out of many, 46, 173. Its other advantages and effects, 43, 173 ff. It is so powerful that it generally overcomes the bonds of nature, 46, 174. It also produces similarity of character, 45, 171. No food is sweeter than goodwill and devotion, 412, 84. Everyone trusts more in the counsel of one who is benevolent than of one who is wise, 44, 167. Take goodwill from human society, and you will have taken the sun from the world, 44, 167. What its effects are, ibid. ff.

The vengeance exacted from the **BENJAMITES** for the violation of chastity in the Levite’s wife is elegantly described, 772, 3 ff. How great was the concern for honor in the war undertaken against the tribe of Benjamin to avenge the injury done to chastity, 135, 110 ff.

The utmost **KINDNESS** is needed to protect public government and private rights, 93, 95.

**BERSABEE** is the Latin interpretation of “the well of seven” or “of the oath,” 1041, 77.

How great the services and benefits that **BEASTS** confer on human beings are, 975, 17. See **ANIMALS, WILD BEASTS**.

**BETH** means “house”; *leem* is said to mean “bread,” 1065, 14.

**BETHANY** means “place of obedience”; therefore the dead man is raised there, 1069, 6.

**BETHLEHEM**, where Christ was born, is the same as Ephrata, 1064, 9. In Matthew it is called “the house of Judah,” and in Micah “the house of Ephrata”; the difference is one of wording, not of meaning, 1065, 11 ff.

One must drink, not for pleasure but because of weakness; sparingly as a remedy, not excessively for luxury, 1029, 27.

Even men who were **BIGAMISTS** before baptism cannot be admitted to sacred orders, 66, 257.

Coming from **BONONIA**, you were leaving Claterna behind you, along with Bononia, Mutina, and Rhegium; Brixillum was on the right [Col. 1432], Placentia confronted you from the front, and on the left you pitied the uncultivated Apennines and the corpses of half-ruined cities, 944, 3. See **VIRGINS**. The fisherman of the Church of Bononia, 245, 129. A metropolitan man subject to Bononia, 1005, 5. The virgins of Bononia, having left their parents’ home, dwell in the sanctuary of virginity, 161, 60. What they do there, ibid.

**GOODNESS** is popular and pleasing to everyone, 77, 29. Leniency is not to be censured, but goodness is to be praised, 125, 68.

The **GOOD** is certainly perfect, 1081, 2. The good that is done not from necessity but from the will is more beautiful, 932, 8. What is good must not be avoided; what is better must be chosen, 205, 72. The habit of good has abandoned the practice of former wickedness, 227, 56. What else can so readily fill the minds of the just as the conscience of a good deed? 43, 163. Virtue is the highest and only good, 74, 18. Nothing is more splendid than that highest good, whose proclamation is also exceedingly splendid, as are the sustained development of its discourse and certain traces of apostolic preaching, 904, 1. When the eye of the mind gazes upon the highest good, dwells in it, and feeds upon it, it shines and glows, 905, 2. If the soul tastes the true and highest good with its desire and delight, excluding pain and fear, it burns with extraordinary ardor, 906, 10. The highest good is the fountain of life, from which the substance of living is supplied to all, 908, 18. To disregard the judgments of the good is either arrogance or dissolution, 60, 236. It is greatly beneficial for each person to be joined to the good, 93, 97. What the vicious hate is sincere and devout among the good, 898, 2.

What persons are concerned by the judgment of **BONOSUS**, bishop, 1008, 1 ff. His error concerning the sons of Mary is refuted, 1009, 3 ff.

What the marriage entered into between **BOAZ** and **RUTH** prefigured, 510, 69 ff.

For a priest and a Christian to wear a **BRACELET** and a torque in the manner of the Gentiles is sacrilege, 809, 9.

**BRIXILLUM**, 944, 3.

## C
CABILLONUM, 891, 11. CADAVERS of half-ruined cities, 944, 3. What is meant by CADES? 289, 45. The healing of the man born blind is a figure of baptism, 1096, 5ff. The crime of CAIN the sacrificer lies not in the offering of the gift but in the disposition of the offerer, 703, 3. What Cain’s rejection of the gift prefigured, 704, 5. His death served him as a remedy: through death it stripped the wandering exile, terrified at every moment by the dread of death, of that condition, 756, 10. CALANUS. See ALEXANDER. The insults of CALIGULAE, 1212, 50. What CALLIGONUS, the chamberlain, dared to order Ambrose to do, 859, 28. A fire in part of the buildings of the fortress of CALLINICUS, 950, 13. CAMILLUS recovered the standards removed from the Capitol, after the triumphal victors of the Tarpeian Rock had been slain, 834, 7. The remote shore of the Campanian coast pours tranquility not only free from dangers but also from every disturbance, 1016, 2. Ambrose praises CANDIDIANUS’s letter, 1108, 1. GREY HAIR is worthy of reverence—namely, the grey hair of the soul, shining forth in grey thoughts and deeds, 823, 5. It is not the grey hair of years that is praised, but of character, 834, 7.

HAIR is a natural covering, 59, 232. Curls of hair are not ornaments for Christ but offenses: allurements of beauty, not precepts of virtue, 230, 71. “Let those who curl their hair like women conceive and give birth,” 1062, 6. There are certain hairs of religion and faith, 637, 14. What the hair with which Mary wiped the Lord’s feet signifies, 439, 69.

This is truly captivity, where souls captive to sin are led to death and possessed by diabolical domination, 306, 4.

What the CAPUAN SYNOD had decreed concerning the dispute between Evagrius and Flavianus of Antioch, 1006, 2. See FLAVIANUS, THEOPHILUS.

FLESH is joined to the soul by a kind of fraternal fellowship, 1056, 9. Our flesh cannot be perpetual and everlasting; it must die in order to rise again; it must be dissolved in order to rest, 945, 5. When the flesh resists, the mind ought to be intent upon God, 439, 105. We are pressed most severely when the flesh gives way, ibid. He who does not fear death and is held by no pleasure of the flesh fears neither weapons nor barbarians, 865, 6. “Let the flesh sleep, let faith keep watch; let the allurements of the body sleep, let prudence of heart keep watch; let your limbs breathe the cross of Christ and the fragrance of burial,” 293, 58. It is not irrelevant if it is said to perish in such a way that it is understood to be restrained rather than destroyed, 416, 96. Let it die to desires; let it be captive and subject, and let it not resist the law of our mind, but die subjected to good servitude, 406, 61. The case is in a bad state when the prerogative of the flesh is stronger than that of the mind, 769, 14. What is carnal is servile, 1163, 108.

The divinities of CARTHAGE were not always equally hated by the Romans, 840, 30. CASSIANUS the bishop, 786, 1; 805, 76.

The threefold virtue of CHASTITY: one conjugal, another of widowhood, the third of virginity, 192, 23. I should rightly call chastity and clemency, in a certain sense, parents of the virtues, 1129, 54. The commandment is chastity; the counsel is integrity, 206, 75. See WIDOWHOOD, VIRGINITY. Chastity is restrained not by punishment but increased by religion and preserved by faith, 222, 35. “She is not chaste who is compelled by fear; nor honorable who is hired for a reward; nor is that modesty honorable which, exposed daily to the reproach of intemperate eyes, is beaten by disgraceful looks,” 150, 15. We ought to be chaste, not weak: to have modest eyes, not powerless ones, 207, 76. Modesty is a good companion for governing chastity, 20, 69. Chastity seeks solitude, 201, 57. It is heaped with its own losses, 836, 12. Its first victory is to conquer the desire for possessions, because the pursuit of profit is a temptation to modesty, 836, 12. Chastity does not know how to redeem what it is accustomed to sell, 150, 15. The homeland of chastity and virginity is in heaven, 151, 20. Chastity made angels: whoever preserved it is an angel; whoever lost it is a devil, 159, 52. Our ancestors showed such reverence for purity that they thought war ought to be undertaken against its violators, 772, 2.
