The reward of chastity is above toil, its grace above use, its recompense above the deed, 208, 82. See SELF-CONTROL.

CASTULUS, whom the Arians called a presbyter, was seized by the people, 853, 5. He was rescued when Ambrose sent presbyters and deacons, ibid.

When the CATECHUMEN gave his name, Christ took clay and spread it over his eyes, 364, 12. The catechumens were dismissed after the readings and the exposition, 853, 4. See BAPTISM.

Κατόρθωμα, that is, a perfect and complete duty, proceeds from the true source of virtue, 110, 10.

The more excellent the CAUSE, the more attentive ought its care to be, 58, 227. The CAUTION of the saints is necessary, 601, 9. The CHALDEAN has no hope in the stars he observes, 928, 16.

CHARITY belongs to the Law, and there is a servitude of charity, 1091, 8. Fear belongs to the Law; charity to the Gospel, 1091, 7. From where does it arise? 34, 127. Is there any difference between the charity of those who believed from childhood and that of those who came to believe in youth or later age? 914, 1ff. Charity cannot exist without faith, 226, 53. Through faith one reaches charity, 80, 39. Perfect charity possesses all faith, 1094, 5ff. Yet I would not readily say that every faith immediately possesses perfect charity, ibid., 6ff. See FAITH. The Lord demands charity; the servant, fear, 1083, 10. The building up of charity excludes and closes the breach caused by offense, 1088, 13. Charity is the first means of commending ourselves, 79, 39. Liberty makes human beings free; charity makes them friends of God, 936, 23. What profit is there in the distribution of patrimony without the grace of charity? 434, 83. The bonds of charity are also its wounds, 293, 60ff. These are the darts of charity, by which Christ wounds those who seek him, 293, 60. The good wounds of charity are to be preferred even to kisses, 221, 333; 274, 111. See LOVE.

CHORATH is interpreted as “understanding,” 1041, 77. CHOREB is said to mean “every heart,” or something like “heart,” 1041, 77.

Although many call themselves CHRISTIANS, they appropriate the name, but not all possess its reward, 692, 130. When Jews plead their case, their names are written on earth; when Christians approach, their names are written in heaven, 803, 5. Every Christian is free and wise, 936, 22. The senate-house is now filled with a greater number of Christians, 825, 9. By a recent law Julian denied Christians the common use of speaking and teaching, 824, 4. It is fitting for Christians both to desire the tranquility of peace and to maintain the constancy of faith and truth, undeterred even by the danger of death, 855, 14. “Through injuries, through poverty, through punishment we have grown,” 835, 11. The pagans never benefited us more than when they ordered Christians to be scourged, proscribed, and killed, ibid. See PERSECUTION.

The name CHRIST was enclosed before his coming among the people of Israel, as though in some vessel, within the minds of the Jews, 620, 95. How afterward it was extended through all creation, ibid., 96. By this name Christ is proclaimed as the true David, the truly humble, the truly meek, the truly mighty in hand, the Son of God, 987, 11. He is called the Word because he is immaculate; Power because he is perfect; Son because he was begotten from the Father; Wisdom because he is one with the Father—one in eternity and one in divinity, 447, 16. If you say “Christ,” you have designated God the Father, by whom the Son was anointed; the one who was anointed, the Son; and the Holy Spirit, by whom he was anointed, 609, 44. God is the one who anoints, and God is the one who is anointed according to the flesh, the Son of God, 448, 24. Christ, as the Son of Man anointed and sent to preach the Gospel, 665, 2. The anointing of Christ is the Holy Spirit, 622, 103. In the name of Christ Paul testified to the mystery of the incarnation, 500, 16. Exposition of the Catholic faith concerning Christ, 730ff. Imperfect confessions of faith concerning Christ, 709, 24ff. There are those who thought that the Word came to be in Christ as in one of the prophets, rather than that Christ himself is the Word of God, 714, 48. See APOLLINARIS, ARIUS.

Christ is proved to be the Most High God, 498, 9. Paul confessed Christ alone as the true God, both in word and affection, 560, 48. He is the one whom the Father begot before the Morning Star, as eternal; whom he generated from the womb, as Son; whom he brought forth from his heart, as Word, 175, 3. From the Father, with the Father, in the Father, born not made and not degenerate, 218, 18. We are sons by adoption; Christ is Son by the truth of nature, 469, 126. In him there is the son’s distinctiveness of divinity, the truth of identity, the mercy of devotion, and the offering of security, 465, 108. It is enough to know that the divine generation is neither divided, diminished, derivative, nor created, 493, 129. Christ expressed the whole of whatever divinity he received from the Father, 158, 48. He is a simple image of God, proceeding from the Father and expressed from the fountain, 453, 49. He is not a shadow but the image of God; not an empty image but the truth, 1164, 109. He is the image of God, not mute, because he is the Word; not insensible, because he is Wisdom; not empty, because he is Power; not vacant, because he is Life; not dead, because he is the Resurrection, 453, 50. “Image” teaches that he is not unlike; “character” signifies that he is an expressed likeness; “splendor” indicates that he is eternal, 453, 49. He is the true God, not unlike but equal to the true Father, 555, 27. Christ is proved against the Arians not to be unlike the Father, 451, 43ff. He is proved to be like him, 453, 48ff. Christ is proved to be the eternal Son of God, 454, 54ff. The Father remains in Christ, as the true in the true, God in God, light in light—as the eternal Father in the coeternal Son, 681, 82. Those who wish to deny that the Son is eternal wish to teach that the Father has changed, 455, 61. Since all things were made in Wisdom, and Christ is the Wisdom of God, he is certainly not accidental but remains forever, 505, 45.

Christ’s will is the same as the Father’s, 479, 50ff. Christ’s willing is likewise what the Father wills, just as his doing is what the Father does, 478, 45. If he was handed over by the Father and also handed himself over, then the operation and will of both are one, 465, 109. Christ is proved by various arguments to possess free authority, 479, 47ff. We see that the love of God is the same as Christ’s, 585, 188.

Christ is proved to be omnipotent, 728, 114ff. The angels announce him omnipotent, the prophets signify it, and the apostles testify to it, 524, 16. Christ is omnipotent; this is our faith, 865, 7. Anathema upon him who denies that the Lord Christ is powerful, 794, 32. At Christ’s command even insensible nature usually obeys, 428, 56. Christ is worshiped together with the Father through the unity of power, when God the Father is worshiped in Christ, 681, 82. In Christ also are the mysteries of the incarnation to be worshiped, 680, 76ff. By the footstool of God’s feet the earth is understood; by the earth, the flesh of Christ, which even today we worship in the mysteries, 681, 79. We worship both his divinity and his flesh, 720, 75. When you prejudge Christ, you judge the Father, 458, 71. According to divinity, the Spirit is not above Christ but in Christ, 666, 6. It was not the Father whom Abraham saw, nor did he wash the feet of God the Father, but of him in whom there is a figure of the future man, 484, 72. It was not the Father in the bush or the Father in the wilderness, but the Son who spoke to Moses; he gave the Law, 460, 83. Christ spoke in the Law, in the prophet, and in the Gospel, 477, 37. Let us preserve the distinction between divinity and flesh: the Son of God speaks as one in both, but he does not speak in one manner, 485, 77. To call Christ a creature is to do so as an object of insult, not as a confession of reverence, 753, 4. What do you accomplish if you say that Christ is this or that kind of creature? The creature changes; divinity is not worshiped, 789, 26.

In what sense Christ was made, 501, 27ff.; 511, 76ff. In what sense it was said of Christ, “The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways, for his works,” 505, 46ff.; 508, 59ff.; 643, 51. He who according to divine generation was born from the Father was made according to the Virgin’s childbirth, 870, 25. He who was within was made manifest outside, 251, 6. In Christ, “making” must be attributed not to divinity but to humanity, 462, 94. He was made under the Law according to the incarnation, from a woman according to sex, 781, 18. Some say that the mystery of the incarnation was inoperative; and why? 517, 114.

Christ, and the passage in which he says that the Father is greater than he, 482, 61ff. He calls him whom he naturally has as Father “God,” because of the mystery of the body assumed, 219, 23. As the Most High he gives; as man he prays: one action belongs to the Creator, another to the Redeemer, 498, 8. He asks as the Son of Man; he commands as the Son of God, 502, 32. Nor when he commands is he alone; nor when he prays is he weak, 531, 55. As God he commands the disease; as man he visits the sick, 202, 60. A command or precept is given to Christ not according to divinity but according to the incarnation, 574, 132.

Christ doubts with human feeling, 478, 43. As man he doubts, as man he is troubled; his divinity is not troubled, but he is troubled through the assumption of human weakness, 480, 56. Most people confidently say that Christ, according to the assumption of our condition, declared before the cross that, as the Son of Man, he was ignorant, 591, 221. He pretends not to know in order to make believers know, 561, 54. How he is said to have been ignorant of the day of judgment, 591, 222. In Christ there was growth in age and growth in wisdom, but this was human, 719, 72ff. Those who think Christ lacked the knowledge needed for bearing witness judge not according to divinity but according to humanity, 574, 130.

What is sanctified in the flesh for us sanctifies through divinity, 485, 78. A devout and true interpretation of Christ’s subjection, 926, 8. Speaking according to the form of a servant, he called “Lord” the one whom he knew as Father, equal in the form of God; proclaiming himself a servant according to the substance of the flesh, 985, 3. Subject to the Father in the body in which he was subject to his mother, 487, 88. How he is subject in us, 580, 167ff. Through his works and the various kinds of virtues he will be subject to the Father in us, 583, 182. This is the defense and hedge of our faith: that for us he assumed servitude in assuming this body, 984, 1. For us he became servant, sin, and curse, in order to remove our servitude and erase curses, sins, and reproaches, 985, 4; 988, 12ff. He served in order to make everyone free, 936, 23. He received the form of a servant, that is, the fullness of human perfection and the fullness of obedience, 570, 109. See SON OF GOD, FATHER, TRINITY, WORD OF GOD.

Although Christ was in the fullness of divinity, he emptied himself and received the fullness of human nature and perfection: just as nothing was lacking to God, so too nothing was lacking to the completion of humanity, so that he might be perfect in both forms, 986, 6. He is one, born before the ages from the Father as the Son of God, and in the age of the world generated as man through the assumption of flesh, 700, 168. Although Christ’s flesh and soul are of the same substance as our soul and flesh, I do not therefore fear lest I seem to introduce a tradux [derivative origin; reading uncertain], 721, 77. Christ became man; he was born God, 116, 11ff. Christ is “yesterday” because of eternity and “today” because of the assumption of the body, 555, 25. Nothing could be added to God from the flesh, 522, 6. God could suffer no loss to himself, since what he assumed from the Virgin was neither an addition to divine nature nor a diminution of power, 482, 64. In Christ’s incarnation, the nature of the Word was not changed, as some have interpreted it; it is always unchangeable, 716, 55. I read in someone’s books that both the instrument and the one who moved the instrument are of one nature in Christ, but this is refuted, 715, 51ff. Those who say that the Lord’s divinity and flesh are of one nature—how many authors of errors are they? 715, 51. Those who say that the Lord’s flesh and divinity are of one substance are shown to be worse than the Arians, 714, 49. They are refuted, 716, 57ff.

Christ did not relinquish what he was but assumed what he was not, 482, 62. According to divine generation Christ is the power of God; according to the assumption of flesh, he is of one substance in the flesh with all human beings, while the glory of his incarnation remains intact, because he assumed the reality, not an image, of flesh, 526, 30; 353, 17; 393, 12. He was formed like a man, not merely in appearance but in reality, 1161, 103. There are those who think that the Lord’s divinity was circumcised and hung on the wood coagulated in the form of flesh, 715, 50. They are refuted, 716, 56ff. The divinity that could not be seen according to its own nature assumed what was beyond the nature of divinity, so that it might be seen according to the nature of the body, 708, 22. Christ was shown to all through the reality of his body, because the Word was not flesh, but the flesh was the Word’s, 412, 40.

It is customary for the divine Scriptures to signify a twofold substance in Christ, divinity and flesh; and why? 508, 59ff. The divine Scriptures have a varied practice: sometimes they begin with Christ’s divinity and descend to the mystery of the incarnation; sometimes they take their beginning from the humility of the incarnation and rise to the glory of divinity—as frequently in the prophets and evangelists, and in Paul, 509, 65. Nothing is announced in the Law above all else except Christ’s coming, and his passion is prefigured, 1053, 8. The great mystery of Christ, at which the angels were astonished, 525, 26. Not only his generation from the Father is wondrous; his very generation from the Virgin is wondrous also, 459, 77. You were commanded to believe it, not permitted to investigate it, ibid., 78.

Christ is first according to divinity, second according to flesh, 265, 72. First, because all things are through him; last, because the resurrection is through him, 266, 73. Christ is firstborn, not first-created, so that he may be believed both begotten by nature and first in perpetuity, 453, 48. Those who think that the Lord Jesus did not assume a soul are refuted, 718, 64ff.; their objections are answered, ibid. Those who separate a rational soul from the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation are struck down by the divine judgment, 706, 11. Because Christ assumed a soul, he assumed the passions of the soul, 480, 56. The Word of God was not present in Christ’s flesh in place of a rational soul capable of understanding, 720, 76. Christ laid down and took up his soul according to the power of his divinity, 475, 25. “He assumed my will; he assumed my sadness,” 480, 53. Nothing in Christ was imperfect, 718, 65. The perfections of Christ, 174, 2ff. If anything human was lacking in Christ, he did not redeem the whole human being, 991, 5. In Christ Wisdom remained unchangeable, although it was surrounded by a garment of flesh, 412, 41. In Christ as God there is flesh; in the flesh the nature of the human race is honored as sharing in all human beings, 583, 181.

What was the cause of the incarnation except that the flesh which had sinned might be redeemed by itself? 716, 56. Christ came into this world to blunt the sting of death, close its devouring mouth, give the living the eternity of grace, and grant the dead resurrection, 764, 5. He assumed what is mine in order to impart what is his, 709, 23. From us he received what he could offer on our behalf, so that he might redeem us from what was ours; and what was not ours he bestowed on us from what was his, by his divine generosity, 715, 54. Because wickedness had increased and innocence had been abolished, the Lord came to restore—indeed, to increase—the grace of nature, 983, 15. He came into the bitterness of human weakness so that the bitterness of our condition might be sweetened, tempered by the sweetness and grace of the heavenly Word, 257, 34. He assumed flesh so that, as man, he might conquer, while teaching human beings, 488, 90. Because of his works, which were to be freed from the service of corruption, he assumed flesh, 505, 46. At Christ’s coming it is no longer a shadow that heals individuals but the truth that heals all, 331, 24. See INCARNATION.

Christ was born from the Father before the ages, but born from the Virgin for the sake of the ages, 152, 21. There is one Son of God, both born from the Father and arising from the Virgin—different in order, but joined in one name, 1116, 12. Born as man from the Virgin, generated from the Father before all things, he would resemble his mother in body and his Father in power, 174, 2. He is not one from the Father and another from the Virgin, but the same one—differently from the Father and differently from the Virgin, 711, 35. We must condemn those who say that one was born from God the Father and another generated from the Virgin, 714, 47. In that divine generation he knew no mother; in this birth from the Virgin Mary he knew no father: before the ages born from the Father alone; in this world arising from the Virgin alone, 1034, 49. According to divinity he could not have a mother, because he is the author of his mother, 1116, 11. Born from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin, he assumed an immaculate body, 394, 13. The Lord was born and reborn from the Holy Spirit, 678, 64. Those who say that Christ could not be generated from the Virgin are refuted, 966, 4. They proved themselves Manichaeans by not believing that Christ came from the Virgin, 969, 12. He is created from the Virgin so that he may be believed to be born from God, 561, 54. He chose virginity as a special gift for himself, displayed the gift of purity, and represented in himself what he chose in his mother, 966, 3. From heaven he chose a vessel through which he might descend, and consecrated the temple of modesty, 257, 33. He could find no purer generation of his flesh than to dedicate the Virgin’s palace as the heavenly dwelling of his own habitation, 272, 105. Coming through a Virgin to give salvation to the world, he undid the woman’s fall by a virgin birth, 284, 26. Christ is the Παρθενικὸς Λόγος, the Virginal Word, 915, 3. Christ is the Virgin’s bridegroom and, if it may be said, Christ of virginal chastity: virginity belongs to Christ; Christ does not belong to virginity, 152, 22. The root is Jesse, the patriarch’s family is the Jews, the branch is Mary, and the flower is Christ, 641, 38. See MARY.

Christ is seen in the manger as man and worshiped as Lord: he lies in swaddling clothes but shines among the stars; the cradle indicates the one being born, and the stars the one who rules; it is flesh that is wrapped, but divinity that is served by angels, 450, 32. Let us recognize the Lord’s manger, in which we are nourished, fed, and refreshed, 882, 6. He was circumcised first, so as not to abolish the Law; afterward through the cross, so as to fulfill the Law, 1093, 3. He was circumcised in order to confer the circumcision of the Law and to give the salvation of the cross, ibid., 4. Why was he baptized? 352, 15ff. And why did the Holy Spirit descend like a dove? 331, 24. Christ fasted so that his fast might be an example for us, 1026, 15. When he teaches without literary training, he appears to teach not as a man but rather as God, 486, 79. Christ is not among the sacred things, since he destroyed all sacred things, 538, 92. What the Lord’s transfiguration signified, 460, 81ff. In the transfiguration the little servants withdrew, so that the Lord alone—he who alone was designated “Son”—might be seen, ibid.

Christ preferred to relax the Law in a matter above the Law rather than deny what belonged to the Law, 780, 13. He became poor so that all might buy him and so that especially the needy might be enriched by his poverty, 268, 85. He satisfied the hungry and filled the needy; he illuminated the blind, redeemed captives, raised paralytics, restored the dead to life, and, what is greater, granted acquittal to the guilty and forgave sins, 895, 6. Man according to the flesh, but beyond man according to divine operation: when he touched a leper, he appeared to be man, but was beyond man when he cleansed him; when he wept over dead Lazarus, he wept as man, but was above man when he commanded the dead man to come out with his feet bound; he appeared to be man when he hung upon the cross, but was above man when, with the tombs opened, he raised the dead, 986, 7. He preferred to overlook something of right rather than abandon charity, 562, 64. He granted healing; he did not practice medicine, for he healed those whom no one could cure, 1096, 2. How many and how great are the kinds of healings he possesses, 202, 62. Everywhere he cures, everywhere he heals—in the journey, in the house, in the wilderness, 224, 42. Whoever is healed by Christ knows no impediment, 202, 63. One is the grace of his power; another is the order of nature, 1156, 81. Christ’s benefits are both incentives to virtue and rewards, 957, 6. He who gave to all demands from all that each, remembering what was forgiven him, forgive another, 958, 8. Christ kindly enlightens everyone; he does not wish to reject the weak but to correct them, 1166, 117. While silent in the Gospel, he worked the salvation of human beings, 4, 9. He generally deigned to shape his discussions according to the qualities of the places in which he taught his servants, 894, 4. Christ prefers to promote our benefit rather than display his own power, 591, 220. He wept with our feeling, not his own, 1116, 11.

Christ wrote on the ground with the finger with which he had written the Law, 896, 14. What his writing on the ground signified figuratively, 668, 14. When he bends down, he bends down in order to raise up those who lie fallen, 893, 7. The woman deserved to be absolved, since, when the Jews departed, she remained alone with Jesus, 897, 16. Why he remained alone when he was about to forgive the sin, 896, 16. He does not condemn, as redemption; he corrects, as life; as a fountain, he washes, 893, 7. How greatly he desires that no one be condemned and all be absolved, 897, 17.

Christ is the chief priest, 571, 110. He is the true Melchizedek, 337, 46; 367, 12. The true Melchizedek, the true king of peace, the true king of righteousness, has come, 1034, 49. He is a new priest and a new sacrifice, not from the Law but above the Law; advocate of the world and light of the age, 981, 17. The same is priest and sacrifice, 513, 87. He was to be a type of all future priests, 1033, 47. He did not claim the priesthood but received it, ibid., 48. He alone can forgive sins, 418, 9.

He plundered the partridge, the devil, taking from him the wealth he had wickedly gathered from the multitude; he recalled the souls of the nations and the minds of wandering peoples from error, 918, 5ff. Christ grows weary from the journey in order to refresh the weary; he asks for a drink in order to give spiritual drink to the thirsty; he dies in order to give life; he is buried in order to rise again, 561, 54. He became weary, but for your sake, because he sought you for a long time; your unbelief wearied him for so long, 634, 184. He asks for a drink in order to give, ibid. He labors, but in us, so that he may raise me when I lie fallen, 1098, 4.

Christ, as light, touched the man born blind and poured in light; as priest, through the figure of baptism he discovered the mysteries of spiritual grace, 1096, 5. Christ as man when he wept for Lazarus; again above man when he raised him; as man when he was scourged; again above man when he took away the sin of the whole world, 906, 8. In the resurrection of Lazarus there is the power of God, life, light, and resurrection of the dead: power raised up the fallen; life lifted up his step; light drove away darkness and restored sight; resurrection renewed the grace of living, 1155, 78.

Christ cried out in Abel, cried out in Joshua the son of Nun, cried out in Solomon, and cried out in his own body, 918, 5. He came in order to be hidden from this world, 117, 36. He desired his divine glory to be concealed and not publicized before he rose again, 564, 72. The praises of Christ are always the scourges of the faithless, 869, 19.

Christ had to be tempted and had to suffer with me, so that I might know how to conquer when tempted and to escape when suffering with him, 488, 91. He assumed what he was not in order to conceal what he was; he concealed what he was so that in him what he was not might be tempted and redeemed, and so that through what he was not he might call us to what he was, 622, 107. Christ’s various struggles and crowns, 270, 96ff. According to the flesh he is tempted; according to his dignity he is worshiped by angels, 502, 33. You see that those things you think are Christ’s weaknesses are your virtues, 489, 95.

In what sense Christ is called a curse, 870, 25. He is called a curse because he assumed our curses: he wept so that you, a human being, might not weep for long; he suffered insults so that you might not grieve over your own insult, 488, 94. Why he is called sin and a curse, 717, 60.

Christ ate the Passover with his disciples on the very day of Passover; on the following day, that is, Friday, he was crucified; the great Sabbath was also the sixteenth day; and therefore on the seventeenth lunar day he rose from the dead, 883, 10ff. He wishes to wash the feet not of Peter alone but of every believer, 602, 12. The prices for which Joseph and Christ were sold are compared with each other, 691, 125ff. Not all buy Christ at the same price, 692, 129. The Lord offered himself freely, so that the necessity of poverty might turn no one away from Christ, 692, 128. Why he entered the garden when he was about to die, 690, 119.

Christ drank the cup—that is, the passion redeeming your crimes—so that you might quench your thirst for this world with the blood of the sacred drink, 634, 184. The wood of the cross is our conveyance, like the transport of a kind of ship of our salvation, 623, 110. The Lord’s hands were extended on the cross in the manner of a flying creature, 241, 115. From the cross Christ bore witness and divided between his mother and the disciple the duties of affection, 1048, 109. See the great clemency of Christ, when he prayed for his persecutors, 1183, 34. He received vinegar in order to release all temptations, 1055, 6. He received a voice under the title of sacred passion; he cried out in martyrdom and cried out in parricide, which he endured as a sacrifice, 1204, 21. He was wounded by a spear so that he might heal us with the blood of the sacred wound, 158, 47. Blood and water came forth from the wound, and he breathed out his spirit: water for the washing, blood for the drink, spirit for the resurrection, 180, 22. He could have avoided death if he had wished, 1145, 46. Christ did not suffer, as some say, in a phantom, 714, 46.

He hung on the cross and moved all things; he trembled on the wood, he at whom the whole world trembled; he was amid punishments and granted the heavenly kingdom; having become the sin of all, he washed away the sins of the human race; he died so that his death might become the life of the dead, 712, 39. He both suffered and did not suffer; he died and did not die; he was buried and was not buried; he rose and did not rise, 711, 36. He was in the form of a servant, but the same in the glory of God the Father; he was a worm on the cross, but the same one who forgave the sins even of his persecutors; he was a reproach, but the same one was the majesty of the Lord. What did he lose, for whom nothing is diminished? 985, 5. When he died, he lived; when he was subjected, he reigned; when he was buried, he raised the dead, 581, 174. He was immortal in death and impassible in passion, 712, 39.

Christ alone was present when he redeemed the world, 992, 5. Christ’s passion needed no assistance, 261, 49. The Redeemer of all did not need redemption, 780, 13. He did not need a helper for the redemption of all, who saved all without a helper, 1048, 110. He needed no helper when he made the world, nor when he redeemed it, 1161, 104. In Christ it was not our life that died but our guilt, 623, 109. He died in what he assumed from the Virgin, not in what he had from the Father, 622, 107. In him flesh suffered according to its nature, and the nature of the Word was not changed by that bodily suffering, 713, 45. If he stripped off the body, there was nevertheless no loss to God from the body, 412, 40.

How the Lord of majesty is said to have been crucified, 481, 58. It was not divinity that was crucified but flesh, 463, 95. It was the death of the flesh, not of divinity, 835, 9. He suffered according to the flesh and possesses immortality according to divinity; whoever denies this is the devil, 793, 25. Christ offered himself according to our nature in order to work beyond our nature: from what was ours came the sacrifice; from what was his came the reward; and in him you will find many things according to nature and beyond nature, 715, 54.

Through the cross Christ was made higher than the heavens, higher than the angels, and became the guarantor of a better covenant, 511, 76. Although the mysteries of Christ’s assumption and passion are admirable in similar ways, the fullness of faith lies in the sacrament of the passion, 691, 126. The Redeemer preferred to come into this world rather than the judge, 1203, 16. Christ’s death is the life of all: by his death we are marked; proclaiming his death, we pray; offering his death, we preach it. His death is victory, his death is sacrament, his death is the annual solemnity of the world, 1146, 46.

It is a great mystery of devotion that the death of the body was not excluded even in Christ, 1114, 4. By the perpetuity of life he would have lost the price for himself and the sacrifice for me, ibid. With admirable patience he fastened our sins to his cross, 1049, 112. He condemned the sin which he did not experience by being born and crucified by dying, 394, 13. When his passions were completed, as though he himself were completed, he gave health to all and took away the sin of all, 1033, 47. The assumption of death in Christ became the death of death, 512, 84. He offered his death for the death of all and poured out his blood for the blood of all, 958, 7.

The rock is Christ’s flesh, which redeemed heaven and the whole world, 972, 9. He is a lamb, but one of divine power: he not only cleansed the sins of all with his blood but also bestowed grace by divine power, 1054, 10. Sometimes he was offered under the type of a kid, sometimes of a sheep, sometimes of a calf: a kid because he is a sacrifice for sins; a sheep because he is a voluntary victim; a calf because he is an immaculate victim, 600, 4. He stripped himself of flesh in order to triumph for you over the dominations and powers of this world, 227, 55.

Nothing is diminished from, and nothing added to, the grace of his blood: whether you take little or much, the same perfect measure of redemption is given to all, 779, 8. “He handed himself over for me: if it is grace, what can I object? If it is an injury, I owe more,” 627, 129. He paid the blood-price; you owe blood. He paid for you; pay for yourself, 244, 126. How Christ’s divinity is recognized amid the very insults of the cross, 489, 96.

Gideon chose three hundred for battle to show that the world would be freed from the attack of more powerful enemies not by the multitude of numbers but through the mystery of the cross, 601, 5. See ABRAHAM. In Christ’s cross the weakness of all human beings is lifted up, 357, 10. The divine mystery of the cross: in it weakness clings, power is free, vices are fastened, and trophies are raised, 622, 108. “Turn the cross of the Lord Jesus in your hands, raising it up in your deeds,” 290, 48. It is the beginning of the strength by which the way has been opened for the holy martyrs to the suffering of the sacred contest, 506, 53.

The Church rejoices at the discovery of Christ’s cross; the Jew is ashamed and tormented, 1212, 49. The nail with which Christ was fastened to the cross is held in honor, is a remedy of salvation, and by some invisible power torments the demons, 1212, 49. See HELENA. Christ’s tomb is not without a miracle: by a novel work of some kind, the dead man himself opened the tombs of the dead, 712, 40. The victor over death had no tomb of his own, and why, 217, 14. See ADAM. Christ penetrated the underworld, but incorruptible he escaped corruption, 245, 128. Although he died according to his humanity, nevertheless within the underworld itself he was free, 1161, 102. Christ was not raised by another’s help and power, but raised himself, 1098, 6. What reason would he have had for dying, unless he had also had a reason for rising again, 1158, 90. Why he is called the firstborn from the dead, the firstfruits, and the beginning, 927, 11. Christ’s victory is the victory of freedom, which claimed all for grace and bound no one to injury, 614, 67. According to the flesh, all things will be handed over to him, 584, 185. What kingdom Christ received and handed over to the Father, 576, 147 ff. Christ’s kingdom does not perish when he hands it over to the Father, but advances, 577, 150. We did not sit, but sat together with Christ, who alone sits at the right hand of God’s power, 1087, 8. Just as Christ is read to have been subject in our flesh, so we have sat together with him in his flesh in the heavenly places, 1087, 8. In Christ’s kingdom we shall reign together with Christ: we by adoption, he by power; we by grace, he by nature, 697, 157. We are his kingdom first, afterward the Father’s, 577, 150. Christ judges while seated; standing, he passes judgment, 1024, 6. In the Holy Spirit he not only judges but also vindicates, 673, 44. In what sense he does not judge, 1092, 13.

Christ is the foundation of all things, 583, 181. Why Paul placed Christ as the foundation, 38, 142. We are all Christ’s body, though some may be the higher members, 429, 62. We are all one body of Christ, whose head is God and whose members are we: some are perhaps the eyes, such as the prophets; the teeth, such as the apostles, who poured the nourishment of evangelical preaching into our breasts; and there are also his hands—those who appear to be executors of good works, 959, 11. Just as Eve was bone from the man’s bones and flesh from his flesh, so may we also be members of Christ’s body: bone from his bones and flesh from his flesh, 1086, 4. Every good worker is Christ’s hand, 1190, 62. Who are Christ’s feet, in whom he indicates that the martyrs, the apostles, and the Lord Jesus himself are honored, 961, 23. Who pours water on Christ’s feet? 959, 11 ff.

Christ is the supreme good, announced to us by the prophets, proclaimed by the angels, promised by the Father, and evangelized by the apostles, 906, 8 ff. See ANIMA. Let us refer all our words and deeds to Christ, 180, 24. Let us not be ashamed of any service that advances the worship and reverence of Christ, 426, 42. While I am on the way, I belong to Christ; when I arrive, I belong to the Father—but everywhere through Christ and everywhere with Christ, 577, 150.

Christ loves to be sought for a long time and repeatedly, 234, 84; 293, 60. How can you deserve that Christ should seek you? 227, 54 ff. To have sought Christ where one ought not is a wound, 225, 47. Where Christ should be sought, 225, 49 ff.; 292, 56. He is never absent from those by whom he is sought, 218, 17. He cannot be found at the end, 225, 46. When should he be sought? 293, 58. How can he be sought except day after day? 224, 43 ff. It is impossible for him to be absent from those who seek him, 292, 57. When you seek Christ, you see God the Father, 233, 82. How does one who seeks Christ reach the angels? 235, 87 ff. Although you ought to come in the morning, even if you come later, at the sixth hour you will still find Jesus wearied from the journey, 634, 184. To whom does Christ seem to delay? 230, 69. Whoever sees Jesus has heaven opened to him, 1023, 5. When does Christ enter through an open door? 231, 74. It is good that our inner beings should be disturbed at the Lord’s coming, 228, 60 ff. How he should be held, 232, 77 ff.

Christ walks in the breasts of each individual; therefore beware lest, while you have an impure conscience, you begin to defile Christ’s feet, 959, 12. As long as we follow Christ, we do not labor, 238, 103. Who can labor while following Jesus? 1106, 2. Why are those who follow him bound with chains? 1099, 10. He reaches Christ’s rest who has followed Christ’s humility, 1205, 27. Where these three are whole—spirit, soul, and body—there Christ is in their midst, 253, 14. Where there is peace, there is Christ; where there is justice, there is Christ, 1023, 4. Where Christ is, there is everything, 764, 4. We have everything in Christ, 237, 99. Christ is everything: if you desire to heal a wound, he is the physician; if you burn with fevers, he is the fountain; if you are burdened by iniquity, he is justice; if you need help, he is strength; if you fear death, he is life; if you desire heaven, he is the way; if you flee darkness, he is light; if you seek food, he is nourishment, 237, 99. He is our rest, 979, 8. He is the beginning of our virtue, 506, 49 and 52. In him are both the fullness of the universe and the portion of each individual, 1115, 6. Where Christ is, there is the protection of our salvation, 169, 29. It is a great remedy to find consolation in Christ, 488, 95. We have one faith, hope, and love: hope in the resurrection, faith in the washing, and love in the sacrament, 180, 22. Where Christ’s body is, there is truth, 1163, 108. How can one in whom Christ, the power of God, is present be weak and little? 1091, 9. No carnal person is in Christ; but if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation—not formed by a newness of nature, but by grace, 945, 6. If the one who is with the Lord Jesus falls, Jesus raises him, 1098, 3. Whoever praises the Lord Jesus kisses him, 960, 14. He kisses Christ who confesses him, ibid., 15. We are bound more gloriously by Christ than we are released and set free by others, 1045, 96. How can Christ’s yoke be easy when it is also said to be heavy? 1177, 11. There is a soul that spiritually gives birth to Christ, 218, 20. See ANIMA.

Christ is the true Naboth, 285, 30. Why David describes Christ as a giant, 711, 35. Why Christ is white and red, 157, 46. He is a lily for us, 1189, 56. He is a vine because he bears my sufferings, 550, 158. Why he is called a cluster of grapes, 550, 161.

**CHROMATIUS**, presbyter, 805, 76; 798, 45; 800, 51.

**FOOD.** Faith is good food; mercy is sweet food; grace is delightful food, 1090, 5.

**CICADAS** live from day to day, are burst apart by their own song, and what people they resemble, 903, 5.

**CIMBRI.** We read that temples were formerly built from the spoils of the Cimbri for idols, 949, 10.

**CIRCUS GAMES**, 1178, 15.

**CIRCUMCISION.** It was necessary for circumcision to take place in part before the coming of him who would circumcise the whole person, 1074, 15; 1076, 23. Marcion and Manichaeus think God’s judgment deserving of criticism because they supposed that the oracle concerning the observance of circumcision had to be proclaimed; but they are refuted, 1073, 10 ff. Circumcision was not performed without purpose on this part of the body and on the eighth day, 1071, 3; 1081, 4 ff. So far from the pain of circumcision having harmed faith, the pain makes faith more credible, 1074, 14. Why is circumcision commanded as useful on the authority of the Old Testament, yet rejected as useless under the teaching of the New Testament? 1071, 1 ff. Why was it then considered piety to be circumcised, but now judged impiety? 1080, 1 ff. According to the literal sense, the peoples of the nations could never have been bound to Jewish circumcision, 1077, 26. We find in the history of the ancient Ethiopians, Arabs, and Phoenicians that some practiced circumcision among their own peoples, 1072, 6. The Egyptians judge a priest impious if he entirely lacks the mark of circumcision; nor do they consider the wisdom of magical incantation, geometry, or astronomy to possess its power without the seal of circumcision, 1072, 5. Circumcision is a matter of the inner person, and what it ought to be, 1075, 19 ff. The sign is bodily circumcision; spiritual circumcision, however, is the reality: the former cuts off a bodily member, the latter sin, 1081, 4.

**CLARUS**, bishop, 819.

**CLATERNA**, 944, 3.

**CLERGY.** Whoever you are in the clergy, you are the Lord’s portion and possession; do not withdraw from the Lord’s possession, 1099, 14. The priest should consider who is best suited to read distinctly, who is most pleasing in singing the psalm, who is most attentive in exorcising those afflicted by an evil spirit, and who is most suitable for the sacristy, 57, 225. From the cleric alone a common vow is undertaken for all, and a common office is entrusted, 837, 14. The public reputation ought to bear witness to the works of the ministers of the altar, 66, 256. It is not enough for a cleric merely to provide for his own expenses; rather, he should secure for himself divine assistance after death, 1098, 2. Those who enter upon the offices of the Church ought to despise human affairs, 48, 183. A churchman ought to abstain from every use of commerce and be content with the produce of his little field, if he has one; if he does not, with the income of his stipends, 49, 184. The Apostle established this not only concerning a bishop and presbyter, but the Fathers at the Council of Nicaea also added in their deliberations that no cleric should be one who had entered into a second marriage, 1037, 64. Only one marriage, and not a repeated union, is permitted to the ministers of the altar, 66, 257. Even before baptism, ibid. It is fitting for churchmen, and especially for those holding offices, to avoid the banquets of outsiders, 24, 86. Those constrained by offense ought not to withdraw from their office, especially clerics, 1097, 1 ff. A cleric is denied the right to make a will, 837, 14. See ECCLESIASTICUS, EPISCOPUS.

**CELIBACY.** The pagans established penalties for celibacy and widowhood, 209, 84. See CASTITAS, VIDUITAS.

**HEAVEN.** Heaven is the beginning of the work of the world, and humanity its end, 972, 8. Heaven is considered incorruptible, yet passes away; humanity is considered corruptible, yet puts on incorruption, 972, 9. What is beyond heaven is the God of heaven, 972, 8. Heaven is where guilt has ceased; heaven is where crimes are struck down; heaven is where there is no wound of death, 377, 20. Earth is humanity’s place of exercise; heaven, its crown, 972, 6. May God himself, who created heaven, teach me its mystery—not a human being who did not know himself, 835, 7. Let your heart be where your possession is, 1205, 29. Who is that man who can open roads for himself and bring up steps by which he may ascend to heaven’s palace? 973, 11 and 12. The Apostle denies you earthly companionship and teaches that you must fly to heaven on spiritual wings, almost beyond the limits of nature, 233, 83. Let us lift our eyes to heaven, judge that we must strive toward it, and consider that seat preferable to all earthly things, 976, 2. The course upward is safe; the descent downward is dangerous, 236, 96. Let the step be toward higher things, because it is better to ascend, 904, 8. See MUNDUS. Paul was heaven; James and John were heavens; the Lord Jesus himself was the heaven of the perpetual human being, 875, 5. What is the airy heaven? 1060, 1 ff.

**THOUGHTS.** The thoughts of the prudent are free: the more they raise themselves toward higher and more divine things, the more freely they move without any hindrance from earthly weight, 139, 107. The highest praise lies in good thoughts, an unstained affection of love, and the intention of a sincere conscience, 249, 2. See APPETITUS.

**KNOWLEDGE OF SELF.** To know oneself is characteristic of the prudent person, as is living according to nature, as the wise have defined it, 1126, 45. What is more absurd than not knowing who you are while striving for what you are not? 1136, 4. It is more serious to know what you should do and not to have done what you recognized ought to be done, 72, 7. Foreknowledge is useful for avoiding something; but if I cannot avoid it, knowing it has harmed me, 1079, 8. They condemn more severely when, after discovering something, they abandon it, 397, 26. See SCIENTIA.

**DOVE.** The dove that carried an olive branch after the Flood later descended when Christ was baptized, 961, 21.

**PILLAR.** What did the pillar of light and the pillar of cloud signify? 354, 22.

**HAIR**, see CAPILLI.

**COMACINE ROCKS**, 1005, 5.

**RECOMMENDATION.** The rule of truth is this: do nothing for the sake of recommending yourself by which another is diminished, 99, 123.

Most of the **COMENSIANS** were converted to the Christian faith, 764, 7.

**COUNT** of the eastern military divisions, 948, 6. The victorious standards and the Labarum were entrusted to the count, 949, 9.

Whoever harms another for his own advantage violates nature, 113, 24 ff. One should seek not one’s own goods and advantages but those of others, 110, 13 ff.

**COMMON.** What belongs to everyone cannot be excepted as belonging to individuals, 1146, 46.

**COMMUNION.** Fellowship ought not to contain any offense, 813, 4. Through the kiss of communion we kiss Christ, 960, 15. Those who think that abstaining from the heavenly sacraments is their punishment are harsher judges of themselves: they prescribe a penalty for themselves and avoid the remedy, 435, 89. No one placed in sin ought to claim for himself the authority or usurpation of the sacraments, 438, 103. Participation in sacred communion must not be granted to those defiled by unclean impurities, 435, 87. Those who demand penance in such a way that they want communion restored to them immediately do not so much desire to release themselves as to bind the priest, 434, 87.

**COMPETENTES**, see BAPTISMUS.

**COUNCIL.** The three hundred and eighteen priests, chosen as Abraham’s men were chosen, victorious through the harmony and strength of their faith, raised up the Council as a trophy after the unfaithful had been subdued throughout the whole world, 444, 5. The Fathers of the Council of Italy do not claim a prerogative of examination but participation in a common judgment, 816, 4. The custom was that in the East there should be a council of Easterners, and within the West one of Westerners, 788, 7. Because of one Auxentius, it is not necessary to weary the bishops by requiring them to come to a synod, 863, 16. A synod had assembled because of the arrival of the Gallic bishops, 998, 6.

**PREACHING.** How the voice should be composed in public addresses, 29, 104. Every day in sacred readings and in the discourses of priests, the Church resounds with praise of chastity and glory of integrity, 1025, 10. See SERMO.

**CONCUBINE.** The word is derived from sexual intercourse, 135, 111.

**TO COVET.** Whoever covets more is always in need, no matter how much he acquires, 41, 155.

**COVETOUSNESS**, see TEMPERANTIA.

**CONDITION.** No condition creates an obstacle to commending a person, 278, 3.

**CONFESSION.** Confession of error is a medicine, 255, 27. A modest confession of sins loosens the bonds of crimes, 426, 40. Let us not be ashamed to confess our sins to the Lord, 416, 5. See CONVERSIO.

**ASSEMBLY.** An evil assembly cannot produce good fruit, 422, 25. We need to be gathered together, and through gathering together we are emptied, 187, 5.

**MARRIAGE.** It is not the defloration of virginity that makes a marriage, but the marital agreement, 259, 41. If someone has sexual relations with a woman betrothed and given to him, he calls it marriage, 1017, 1. Marriage is good, yet the word is derived from a yoke, and from the yoke of the world, 221, 33. Marriage itself is a bond, 283, 21. That a father should take his daughter as wife is forbidden by the law of nature and forbidden by the inviolable prescription of piety, under the title of kinship, 1019, 5. Divine law forbids paternal cousins, who are related in the fourth degree, to join in marital intercourse, 1018, 3. See AVUNCULUS, PATERNUS.

Marriages with foreigners should be avoided, lest the snares of betrayal replace the affection of marriage, 852, 34. The bishop should teach the people that a marriage union should be sought not with foreigners but from Christian households, 843, 2. There is almost nothing more serious than joining oneself to a foreigner, where incentives to lust and discord and the crimes of sacrilege are brought together, 844, 7. This is proved by examples, especially that of Samson, ibid. and following. Marriage ought to be sanctified by the priestly veil and blessing, 844, 7. With more mature deliberation a girl is handed over by her father to her bridegroom, but with a greater purpose of obedience she is led by the bridegroom to the father, and, having been chosen by her husband, enters the house of her father-in-law, 1104, 3. The memorials of marriage are weapons of chastity, 196, 38. It is almost no lesser virtue to abstain from a marriage that once gave pleasure than never to have known the delights of marriage, 185, 1. Although marriages are good, they nevertheless contain things for which the spouses themselves should be ashamed before one another, 287, 36. Slaves are purchased under almost better conditions than marriages, 283, 23. See MATRIMONIUM, NUPTIAE, PATER, VIDUA, VIRGO.

**CONSCIENCE.** Conscience, a wealthy and abundant witness for itself, abounds, 756, 9. Do not fear the sound of words if your conscience is clean, 300, 85. For the wise person, the public disclosure of a crime is not so shameful as the conscience, 115, 29. What punishment is more severe than the inner wound of conscience? 113, 24. So serious is the guilt of conscience that, without a judge, it punishes itself, 438, 103.

**COUNSEL AND COMMANDMENT.** The difference between counsel and commandment, 205, 73. Counsel invites the willing; commandment binds the unwilling, 1031, 38. A commandment is issued to subjects; counsel is given to friends. Where there is a commandment, there is law; where there is counsel, there is grace. A commandment recalls one to nature; counsel summons one to grace, 205, 72. Counsel is given to the good; correction restrains those who err, 40, 151. The use of counsel is especially effective in winning people over—and why? 80, 41. What should the person who gives counsel to another be like? 91, 86 ff. Who can give useful counsel? 85, 66. We entrust our case to the most prudent person and seek counsel from him more readily than from others, 82, 50. In acquiring counsel, uprightness of life, the precedence of virtues, the practice of goodwill, and the grace of gentleness contribute greatly, 84, 60. The counsel of a just man prevails, and frequently outweighs even the judgment of the wisest, 82, 50. If you join both together, the healthfulness of the counsel will be great, ibid., 51. How can you judge someone superior in counsel whom you see inferior in conduct? 84, 62. An evil mind is refuted by its own counsels, 995, 12. To have the counsel of God means carefully to investigate everything, recommend what is better, and point out what is safer, 1032, 41.

**CONSOLATION.** Why is consolation difficult for those who grieve deeply? 1185, 40. The person who consoles himself in some sorrow is strong, 48, 179.

**CONSTANTINOPLE.** Constantinople had already received the word of God; and as long as it fostered the poisons of the Arians, it was disturbed by wars with neighboring peoples and its walls resounded with hostile arms. After it rejected the exiles from the faith, it saw the very enemy, having become judge of kings, surrendered, received as a suppliant, overwhelmed in death, and possessed in burial, 603, 17. Was it awaiting the triumphal ceremonies and titles of victory at Theodosius’s return? 1214, 56. The sepulchral dwelling of his august body will hold him, ibid. Not long ago the bishop’s house at Constantinople was burned, and Theodosius’s son intervened so that he would not retaliate for his own injury or for the burning of the priest’s house, 950, 13.

**CONSTANTINE**, emperor of august memory, granted the priests freedom of judgment, 862, 15. The grace of baptism, when he was at the point of death, forgave him all sins, 1209, 40. See HELENA.

**CONSTANTIUS**, of august memory, not yet initiated into the sacred mysteries, ordered the altar of Victory to be removed, 841, 32. What had begun well under him, heir to his father’s dignity, was completed otherwise, 862, 15.

**CONSTANTIUS**, recently elected bishop: what he ought to do is explained, 754, 1 ff. Ambrose commends to Constantius the Church at the Forum of Cornelius until a bishop is appointed for it, 761, 27.

**CONSTANTIUS**, bishop of Sciscia, 786, 1; 805, 76. His condemnation of Palladius, 802, 61.

**CONSTANTIUS**, bishop of Arausio, envoy of the Gauls, 786, 1; 790, 15; 805, 76; 806, 1. His condemnation of Palladius, 801, 55.

The subscription of Bishop Constantius, 969, 14.

Continence is produced by the will, not by weakness, 206, 75. See CASTITAS, EPICURUS.

**CONTRACTS.** A contract does not change one’s kind or take away the freedom of wisdom, 933, 13. In contracts, and generally in all things, deceit must be absent, 124, 67.

**CONTRARY.** The contrary attacks itself; what is different usually has a distinct rationale, 417, 7.

**ASSOCIATIONS.** Associations with foolish people are harmful: they infect and discolor the mind, 899, 8.

**CONVERSION.** Conversion is found among the few, error among the many, 1178, 14. The Lord awaits our conversion, so that he too may return to grace, 396, 22. It is not surprising that a human being sins; but it is reprehensible if he does not recognize that he has gone astray and humble himself before God, 999, 9. There is no shame in passing over to better things, 834, 7. A crime is lighter when a person voluntarily confesses his sin and repents, 315, 37. Can what is corrected for the sake of God’s honor be displeasing to God? 955, 31. Whoever accuses himself after sinning is just—not the one who praises himself, 1000, 15. While we grieve over what has been committed, we exclude what would otherwise be committed, and a discipline of innocence is formed from the condemnation of guilt, 436, 92. Anticipate your accuser: if you yourself accuse your sins, you will fear no accuser, 428, 53. Whoever strives to correct the vices of human weakness ought himself to bear that very weakness and, in a way, weigh it upon his shoulders, 389, 2. Whoever is converted under the stroke of death and confesses the Lord Jesus deserves a dwelling in paradise; but whoever disciplined himself long beforehand and offered himself for Christ has a kingdom prepared in proportion to his labors, 1070, 9. Blessed is the person who corrected his error even in old age; blessed is the person who, even under the stroke of death, turned his soul away from vices, 1176, 9. When the mind is wounded, it sickens under the fostering warmth of pleasurable flattery and is again tempered by the bitterness of correction, 957, 4. Fables tell of a young man who went abroad because of his love for a prostitute; when, after his love had been extinguished, he returned and encountered his beloved woman saying, “It is I,” he replied, “But I am not myself,” 453, 96. It is serious to be changed for the worse, 782, 22. Be one and the same in the likeness of God: not sober today and drunk tomorrow; peaceful today and quarrelsome tomorrow, ibid. See ANIMA, POENITENTIA.

**IN ABUSE**, one should keep silent, 7, 20 ff.

**HEART.** The inner person of the heart is wholly full of wisdom, full of grace, full of beauty, 941, 2. No one before Peter used such an expression as “the person of the heart,” ibid. Stand firm in your heart, lest anyone overthrow you or be able to subvert you, 1032, 41. David taught us to walk in our heart as though in a spacious house and to live with it as with a good companion, 107, 1. Let the heart keep watch while the flesh sleeps, lest it begin to keep watch over sins in an evil way, 274, 111. Christ loves to be in the heart, 244, 123. God gives you in the spirit, and the Lord sows in your heart, 786, 14. God is appeased by a contrite heart, 225, 51. The heart of a man is deep when there is nothing shallow in it, 243, 121.

**BODY.** The natural beauty of the body ought to be simple and unadorned, more neglected than sought, 23, 83. There is a certain voice that is the movement of the soul expressed through the body, 20, 71. Grace is greater in bodily weakness than in health, 406, 61. The body that loves enticements turns away from the virtues of the soul, abhors its rule, flees the disciplines of virtue, and rejects every work of this kind, 898, 2. Let us cultivate this body of ours, discipline it, and bring it into subjection; let us not despise it, 940, 42. Afflict your body as though dying every day, so that by dying you may live again, 201, 56. What harms the body benefits the spirit, 407, 65. Let us live as strangers to the body, lest we become strangers to Christ; and although we are in the body, let us not follow the things of the body. Let us not abandon the rights of nature, but prefer the gifts of grace, 1144, 41. See MENS.

**CORRECTIONS.** Corrections are generally better than silent friendship, 139, 127.

**ROYAL CURTAINS.** The royal curtains were gathered up, 857, 16. They were torn by mocking boys, 858, 24.

**COSMOPOLITAN.** A *cosmopolite*—a citizen of the world, 983, 16.

**CREATURES.** Some creatures are visible, others invisible, 725, 99. Every creature is bounded by the limits of its own nature, 617, 81. Whatever lacks communion with creatures is divine, 754, [Col. 1444] 8. Every creature exists by the will, through the operation, and in the power of the Trinity, 653, 100. It is also mutable, 613, 64. By its very nature it can be subject to sin, 623, 111, and to the capacity for sins, 693, 136. That cannot be the truth but only an appearance, 331, 25. Why does Paul say that every creature is subject to corruption, yet not say that every creature groans together? 925, 1 ff.

**CRESCENS**, our fellow presbyter, 969, 13.

**CRIME.** A multitude of associates does not make crimes go unpunished, 316, 41. The experience of pain drives away the extravagance of crime and the delights of error, 436, 92. Not to have seen something is itself a crime, but one must beware lest it become the origin of a crime, 408, 69. Just as Christ’s riches are virtues, so the devil’s riches are crimes, 958, 7.

**CROSS.** At every moment the Christian inscribes upon his own forehead contempt for his own death, since he knows that he cannot have salvation without the Lord’s cross, 1073, 12. See CHRISTUS.

**BEDCHAMBER.** Your bedchamber is the inner secret place; your bedchamber is your conscience, 251, 7.

**GUILT.** When a guilty person is killed, the person rather than the guilt is punished; but when guilt is put away, there is acquittal of the person and punishment of the sin, 897, 20. The greater the guilt, the greater the aids that must be sought, 401, 42. It is better to bear another’s guilt than to expose your own, 201, 58. Guilt is there where grace is; but guilt is written with a stylus, whereas grace is marked by the Spirit, 668, 14. Guilt benefited us more than it harmed us, 272, 104. The guilt of all worked subjection; subjection worked humility; humility worked obedience, 1079, 6. See PECCATUM.

**CUM AND IN.** The prepositions *cum* and *in* do not denote inequality among the divine persons, 647, 70 ff. Both syllables belong to the conjunction, 650, 84. See PER.

**DESIRE.** A desire is pardonable when it is not greedy for money but for grace, 561, 57. In the midst of desires, every abundance of riches is poverty, 1044, 90. Whoever does not know how to control his desires is like someone carried away by untamed horses: he is rolled about, trampled, torn apart, and afflicted, 175, 5. See DIVITIAE.

**CARE.** Not to care about what you have done is the height of cruelty, 14, 48.

**CYBELE.** Cybele washes her chariot in the supposedly sacred river Almo, 840, 30.

**NINETEEN-YEAR CYCLE**, 881, 1.

**CYRUS**, king of the Persians: after his head had been cut off and enclosed in a leather bag full of blood, he was ordered to be satiated within it and made a laughingstock of a woman’s commands, 841, 36.

## D

**DALMATIUS**, tribune and notary, 860, 1. He delivered the emperor’s mandate to Ambrose, ibid. **DAMASUS**, priest of the Roman Church, chosen by God’s judgment, 826, 10. He sent Ambrose the petition of the Christian senators against the pagans’ request, ibid. **DAMON.** See **THE ANTIOCHENE VIRGIN**.

**DANIEL**, a captive, corrected the present by his counsels and announced the future, 83, 55. Why he became remarkable to everyone, ibid., 58. He and the three Hebrew boys possessed nothing of what belonged to the earthly king, 781, 17. Unless he had received the Spirit of God, he could never have detected adulterous lust or the falsehood of deceit, 672, 39.

**DAVID** had two wives, Achinoam the Jezreelite and Abigail; the mysteries contained in this are explained, 915, 5 ff. How great his grief was at the death of his sons, 1140, 25 ff. Why he mourned his dead sons Ammon and Absalom, but not another infant, 1141, 28; 1187, 47. He merited such great grace that from his family a virgin was chosen who would give birth to Christ for us through her own childbearing, 431, 69. The benefits conferred upon him by God are recalled, 961, 25.

The transitory nature of human circumstances is shown by the frequent changes in holy David’s condition: despised by his father, precious to God; noble in triumph, lowly through envy; nobler when the heir had been reconciled than when he had been disgraced, 760, 24. No mother mourned an only son so deeply as he mourned an enemy, 123, 62. In forgiving injuries he was not inferior to Paul, 62, 245. When they insulted him, he kept silent, 7, 21. In word and deed he surpassed Archytas of Tarentum, 26, 94 ff.

David was strong in battle, gentle in rule, patient under insult, more ready to bear injuries than to return them, 78, 32 ff. Parents preferred him to their sons, and sons to their parents, 79, 36. David was strong in war, patient in adversity, peaceful in Jerusalem, gentle in victory, grieving in sin, prudent in old age; through the individual tones of his successive ages he preserved the appropriate modes and changes of time, 31, 114. He never waged war unless provoked, 47, 177. Nor did he do so without first consulting the Lord, ibid.

Although a king was, as it were, master of the laws, he was not liable to the laws, but was held answerable to God alone, 936, 26. He did not prefer his own safety to innocence, 116, 33 ff. He became more acceptable to God through humility, 999, 9. By silence he imposed upon himself the law of innocence, 3, 6. David kept silent? 10, 34. By dancing before the ark [Col. 1445] he pleased God all the more because he so humbled himself before God that he set royal dignity aside and offered God the service of a lowly servant, 1014, 7. He wished all people to be judges of his offenses, 298, 77. Now he rejoices more because he wept more, 436, 93.

**DEBBORA** rules peoples, leads armies, chooses commanders, arranges wars, and commands triumphs, 198, 44 ff. In a mystical sense she revealed to us the future rise from the nations of the Church, 198, 47.

**DEBTORS.** It was not nature but sin that made us debtors, 957, 7. He who owes God has more means of repayment than he who owes a human being, 434, 81. No one is poor who owes God, unless he has made himself poor, ibid. Since what you have is from the Lord, always recognize yourself as a debtor, 1204, 22. On the holy days of the final week, the bonds of debtors used to be released, 853, 6.

**DECANS**, sent from the palace to the Portian Basilica, were hanging curtains, 853, 4.

**TITHES** are one thing, firstfruits another: firstfruits belong to greater grace and the most conscientious observance of sanctification, 926, 9.

**DECORUM** is of two kinds, general and particular, 59, 231 ff. It is decorous to live according to nature, 59, 232. Decorum, in Greek πρέπον, “what is fitting,” is placed first in our Scriptures, 9, 30. Decorum is joined to moral goodness in such a way that it cannot be separated from it, 58, 228. There is a certain distinction between moral goodness and decorum, which is easier to understand than to explain, 76, 22. Whatever is decorous is always useful, 129, 88. What order Cicero established concerning decorum, 23, 82. At every age one must ensure that one’s actions are becoming, 23, 82. Dignity is like gracefulness and beauty, 58, 229.

**THE DEAD.** Duties are properly performed toward the dead when they live on in our minds and remain in our affections, 1138, 13. See **THE DEAD**.

**DELIGHT.** Moses not without reason represented delight by the likeness of a serpent, 982, 10. God breathed into the human face in order to make our senses stronger against delight, 982, 11. The thief is the unclean spirit who, amid the darkness of worldly desires and the allurements of earthly pleasures, strips anyone whom he captures of every flower of eternal virtue, 633, 182. Cast down into the valley of bodily delights, he does not find a tomb from which he can rise again, 912, 6.

**DELPHINUS**, bishop, 1107, 2. See **AMBROSE**.

**DEMARCHUS** reports Epicurus’ opinion concerning pleasure, 1027, 19.

**DEMOPHILUS**, an Arian, the dreadful head of perfidy, 812, 1.

**A DEPOSIT.** To preserve and return a deposit is a duty—and is it always so? 68, 263. Deposits, especially those belonging to widows, must be kept inviolate, 105, 144 ff. It makes no difference whether you renounce a deposit or grieve over one that has been returned, 1114, 3.

**IN THE DESERT**, John first practiced steadfastness so that later he could rebuke the king, 1040, 77. Do not listen to those who disparage their neighbors, lest, while listening to others, you be provoked to disparage your own neighbors as well, 1032, 43. If you think that no one should be disparaged, you will not fear the scourges of another’s tongue, 300, 84.

**GOD.** “Lord” and “God” are names of magnificence, names of power, 445, 7. “Lord and God” means either that he rules over all things or that he observes all things and is feared by everyone, 445, 7. This is the true name of God forever, 785, 8. God’s name is sanctified in us when Christian people are proclaimed, 385, 24.

There are evident indications that express the property of deity; others, the likeness of the Father and the Son; and others, the manifest unity of divine majesty. The indications of property are generation, “God,” “Son,” and “Word”; of likeness, splendor, character, mirror, and image; of eternal unity, wisdom, power, truth, and life, 471, 2.

According to the Scriptures, God is either true, merely titular, or false: true, as the Father; titular, as the saints; false, as demons and images, 554, 22. God is recognized either because he is without sin or because he forgives sins; either because he is not a creature but the Creator; or because he does not worship but is worshiped, 693, 132. We must compare divine things with divine things, so that we may understand them better, 970, 3. God must be judged not by the assertions of others but by his own words, 396, 21. Whom should I believe more concerning God than God himself? 835, 11.

God lies beyond the scope of every discourse, 724, 94. To God alone truly belongs being, since he always is, 555, 26. He who is and always is is God, 519, 127. God alone exists without progression, because he is eternally perfect in every perfection, 523, 10. One God, one name, one divinity, one majesty, 265, 68. Many heretics have said that the God of the Old Testament is one and the God of the New Testament another, 611, 55. Many have doubted that there is one God, ibid. Common nature testifies to one God; faith declares one God; grace testifies to one Holy Spirit; the prophets speak of one God, the apostles hear of one God, and the Magi believed in one God, 449, 31. The unity of the Godhead is indicated through the unity of works, 448, 25. The one God in no way excludes the deity of the Trinity, 474, 18.

The divine nature does not admit number, 684, 93. Whatever God is, he is one, simple, and uncompounded, 1099, 8. God is of simple nature, filling all things while himself nowhere confused; penetrating all things while never himself penetrable; incomprehensible to sight, [uninterpretable in speech—uncertain reading], immeasurable to perception, to be followed by faith and revered in religion. Whatever can be conceived more religiously, whatever is more excellent in beauty, whatever is more sublime in power—understand that this belongs to God, 465, 106.

Let us not apply to the Godhead things appropriate to the body, nor measure the greatness of divine goodness by human powers, 1165, 114. In the Godhead there are neither limbs nor parts, but these are expressed on account of the unity of the Godhead, 647, 69. Perhaps it is more detestable to refer things belonging to the flesh to the Godhead than to refer things of the spirit to the letter of Scripture, 503, 38. The image of God is not bodily but spiritual, 1169, 130.

God does not pass from place to place, since he is always everywhere, 481, 60. It cannot be that the one through whom all things exist is one of all things, 706, 13. Examples drawn from creatures seem entirely unsuitable to the Godhead, 631, 176. With the Lord there is an abundance of every virtue, 1205, 25. Perfect divinity does not admit inequality, 175, 4. God is subject neither to arrangement nor to order, 585, 190. The divine majesty possesses, and cannot lose, what it possesses naturally, 563, 67.

That God knows all things and that nothing escapes his knowledge is demonstrated, 15, 51 ff. In God, knowledge precedes hearing, 659, 132. In God there is a certain womb, an inner mystery of the Father’s wisdom, which neither angels nor any created nature could penetrate, 537, 88. Those who fear that their secrets will be exposed do not want to grant God knowledge of hidden things, 15, 54. I am naked before God, before whom all things are naked and uncovered, 992, 4. To God future things are present, 463, 97. It is the custom of the divine Scriptures for God to pretend not to know what he does know, 591, 219. No one deceives God, 824, 2. Neither doubting nor being deceived belongs to God, 590, 216. Truth is always in God; he remains faithful and cannot change or deny himself, 993, 2 ff. It is impossible for God to lie; but this impossibility is not weakness—it is power and majesty, 993, 1 ff. The author of nature and creditor by reason of relationship cannot be defrauded, 1114, 3. See **THE WICKED**.

For God, willing is equivalent to doing, 1165, 114. In God there is one eternal love of nature and another of grace, 567, 90. God is just in all things, wise above all things, perfect in all things, 110, 11. We find nothing more precious by which to praise God than to call him holy, 688, 111. God is not unjust, nor is his judgment changeable, 996, 15. Divinity is eternal life, 543, 119. God is one and almighty, because power is one, 477, 36. God’s impossibility is most powerful, 993, 2. For God, “impossible” does not mean something difficult for his power, but something contrary to his nature, 993, 1. God is not evil; nothing is impossible for God; God is not temporal; God is not lesser, 447, 14.

Divine operation exercises authority; it does not perform service, 662, 148. Divine things do not need human services, 1156, 85. The Lord, who forgave all sins, exempted no offense, 391, 5; 393, 10. He who is the Father of Christ according to divine generation is our Father according to adoption, 219, 23.

Those who think that God does not care about human affairs or does not know what we do in secret are mistaken, 12, 40. Those who think that God has no concern at all for the world are refuted, 14, 48. Moses most clearly describes the invisible God as ruler and, as it were, guardian of this visible world, 975, 1. Nothing contributes more to an upright life than believing that God will be the judge—one whom hidden things do not deceive, disgraceful things offend, and honorable things delight, 33, 124.

Let us prefer God to all whom we love—to father, brothers, and mother, 1160, 97. No injury is done to anyone when the almighty God is preferred to him, 827, 7. I do no one an injury if I prefer God to everyone, 1010, 1. God is feared more than human beings, since he is preferred even to emperors, 954, 28. Honor must be paid to the merits of distinguished men, but it is certain that God must be preferred to all, 825, 6. If failing to repay a human being has been judged similar to murder, how great a crime is it to fail to repay God? 1126, 44.

How good is the Lord, for whom injuries are sweet and death welcome! 294, 61. Let us love the Lord in such a way that, if necessary, we do not flee death for his name, consider no pain too great, and fear nothing, 1208, 38. Why is the inheritance of divine matters valued so highly that many offer even their own death for it? 1089, 1 ff.

To know God and worship him with a devout mind—the wise men of the world learned from our laws that this is the first of good things; the second is to derive piety toward one’s neighbors from that divine source, 1125, 42. This is the substance of our life: that we offer due worship to our Lord and God [Col. 1446], 982, 7. To worship God and be subject to him is wisdom; to abstain from sins is discipline, 903, 4. God does not wish to be worshiped in stones, 835, 8.

God is more inclined to mercy than tenacious of severity, 393, 11; 394, 15 ff. The Lord’s indignation is not the execution of vengeance but rather the working of absolution, 396, 22. We fear God all the more because we do not see him, 974, 14. To see God is an indication of prosperity, not of adversity, 845, 12. If God speaks with someone, that is more than if he speaks with himself, 108, 2. What is as close to us as the Word of God? 934, 18. God seems to descend when the Word of God penetrates our affections, 568, 99. What is as sociable as weaving a discourse about divine matters? 777, 1.

God does not sit above the elements but in the human heart, 972, 8. We have within us God’s house; we have its courtyards, its porticoes, and its streets, 690, 120. Let us be God’s possession, and let him be our portion, 1086, 7. If God reigns in us, virtue reigns, chastity reigns, devotion reigns, 385, 24. Who could say that the Lord is his portion? 1044, 93. In God there is a banqueting and restoring repose, which produces tranquility of spirit, 1060, 14.

When the Lord wills, each person is found and captured; but when he delays, even if the person being sought comes before the seekers’ eyes, he is not seized, 867, 14. Let those who desire to walk the Lord’s way lay aside the dust of the worn and popular road, 902, 1. Whoever seeks through the Lord finds, 785, 11. Not everyone enters the Lord’s ways, yet no one is excluded, 901, 14. The Lord is accustomed to give his own a reward beyond the merit of their labor, 289, 44.

He who completely casts God out of his heart is dead; therefore he who does not cast him out completely but denies him for a time under the pressure of tortures is half-alive, 404, 52. See **DEBTORS**.

**DEVOTION.** Censure ought to yield to devotion, 949, 11. Blessed is the one who dwells at the entrance of faith, in the lodging of the mind, the dwelling of devotion, and the conduct of virtue, 905, 5. Peter labors in us when our devotion labors, and Paul labors also, 244, 125. Whoever receives God into his inmost affection to be worshiped offers not dissimulation or connivance but zeal for faith and devotion, 824, 2.

**DIANA**, the best huntress—not of wild beasts but of lusts, 175, 6.

**THE DEVIL** possessed the service purchased by the tribute of our sinful succession, 1073, 8. The wicked one envies good progress and tests it in various ways, 856, 15. The devil’s envy is never accustomed to rest, 813, 4. When Christ commands, the devil himself becomes the guardian of his own prey, or, unwillingly, obeys heavenly commands, 407, 66. He is little in the eyes of the strong, 636, 11. Whoever entrusts himself to God does not fear him, 380, 30. He destroys himself when he makes the human being whom he strives to overthrow by temptation stronger than before, 407, 63. I have heard many things being fabricated, but no one has ever been able to invent this: to pretend to be a demon, 880, 22.

**DIALECTIC.** The disputation of philosophers is defined as not possessing the force of establishing anything but as devoted to the work of destroying, 451, 42. This is the glory of dialecticians: to appear to defeat and refute the truth by arguments, 723, 89. Philosophers are not believed; fishermen are believed. Dialecticians are not believed; tax collectors are believed, 461, 84.

**DIDRACHM.** What is the didrachm that was demanded according to the Law? 779, 12. Why did Christ not refuse to pay it when they demanded payment? 780, 13 ff. What does the didrachm signify, half of which a Hebrew is commanded to offer for the redemption of his soul? 777, 1 ff.

**DAYS.** We ought not to investigate certain lunar days according to pagan custom, 881, 3 ff. “Day” is used of the moon, 886, 18. The seventh day is a symbol of the future rest, 1135, 2. To whom does the night belong, and to whom the day? 1097, 7. Why do you put it off until tomorrow? You can gain today as well. Take care lest you hold on to neither that day nor this one, 1046, 97.

**OF DIGNITY.** Contemplation of beauty and dignity is free among us, 29, 106. See **FAITH**.

**OF LOVE.** It is good to have the testimony of many concerning one’s love, 79, 38. See **LOVE**, **CHARITY**.

**DILIGENCE.** Faith is swift, devotion alert, hope tireless, 1046, 97.

**THE YEARS OF DIOCLETIAN.** See **EASTER**.

**DIOGENES**, bishop of Genoa, 786, 1; 805, 76. His condemnation of Palladius, 802, 63.

**DIONYSIUS**, in exile, died for the cause of faith, 868, 18. With Eusebius he preferred voluntary exile to the emperor’s friendship and obtained by his prayers that he might lay down his life in exile; thus, with the earlier title of the martyrs, he breathed out his life, 1039, 68 ff.

**THE MOCKERY OF THE GODS BY THE TYRANT DIONYSIUS**, 171, 36 ff.

**DISCIPLINE.** The first purpose of instruction is to turn away from sin; the second is to instill virtue, 189, 12. Discipline and insolence are contrary and opposed to one another, 899, 8.

**DISCIPLES.** The rejection of disciples is a loss to teaching, 55, 214. Christ gave everything to his disciples; but where the grace of the divine gift is at work, no human power exists among them, 400, 35.

**LOSS.** It is a matter without loss that is wholly loss, 41, 154.
