**DIFFERENT.** See **CONTRARY**.

**THE RICH.** Who is truly rich? 295, 65; 941, 3 ff. Who is rich except God alone? 1086, 7. God considers only that person rich who is rich in eternity, who stores up not the fruits of wealth but of virtues, 941, 3. In the Church, the person rich in faith is rich, 1043, 86. Then you will be rich in all things if you are poor in spirit, 1044, 89. The rich person is the one who requires the use of no riches for himself, 941, 2. Wealth does not make a person rich; character does, 1044, 89. He is not rich who does not abound, 843, 9. Nor is the person rich who needs something, nor the person poor who needs nothing, 756, 11. No one is rich who cannot take with him what he possesses here, 942, 6. The rich person is the heir of God and co-heir with Christ, 1043, 87. Every wise person is rich, 941, 1 ff. Nothing is richer than the affection of the wise, nothing poorer than that of the foolish, 943, 10. Every companion of good and liberal studies considers no foolish person rich, even if he abounds in royal wealth, 899, 7. The righteous person, even if he appears poor to another, is rich to himself, 109, 7. It was an ancient custom to consider no one worthy of honor unless he was rich, 101, 129. Let no one presume that, because he is rich, more deference is owed to him, 1043, 86. See **ELIJAH**, **ENOCH**.

**WEALTH.** Wealth itself is not blameworthy; rather, it is in wealth that there is an opportunity for virtue, 1044, 92. Wealth ought to advance the redemption of the soul, not its destruction, 757, 11. The good riches are innocence and simplicity, 295, 65. In Christ, your riches are chastity and the insignia of purity, faith, devotion, and mercy, 384, 21. Wealth provides no assistance for the blessed life, 74, 15 ff. In wealth there is neither assistance for birth nor impediment to death, 758, 15. In wealth and pleasures the allure of temptation is more frequent, 690, 118. Where there is no limit to greed, what benefit is there in wealth? 942, 6. Wealth is a burden if you do not know how to use it, if you do not sprinkle it with the fragrance of Christ, 959, 12. Whoever does not know how to govern his property is overwhelmed by his own burden, 1044, 92. The beauty of wealth lies not in the bags of the rich but in the nourishment of the poor, 760, 26. The redemption of a person’s soul is his wealth: through it mercy is shown, and through expenditure the poor are helped, 777, 3. It is an ancient evil that money should be an honor and that people’s minds should be captivated by admiration for riches, 96, 108. Among the saints of the Lord it is scarcely found that wealth is held in contempt, 100, 128. Admirable is the person who despises wealth, 85, 96. See **GREED**, **DESIRE**, **MONEY**.

**FOR TEACHING.** Not everyone is suited to teach; would that everyone were capable of learning! 1116, 9. Whatever no one taught you, God as its author certainly infused, 443, 2. The teacher ought to excel the one being taught, 163, 1. Nor can you forbid what you teach, 1134, 77.

**OF A GOOD TEACHER.** It belongs to a good teacher to keep away the material of sin, 189, 12. The grace of the Church is the teacher’s praise, 98, 122. It is a wound to seek Christ in the houses of men who falsely assume the title of teachers, 225, 47.

**GRIEF.** Grief does not diminish the pleasure of virtue, 73, 13. Griefs anticipated are more bearable than wounds that have not been examined, 1124, 40. Immoderate grief or fear of death is no small evil, 1138, 11. Let grief be patient, ibid. Grief must either be wholly absorbed or restrained, 1137, 8. The Lycians are said to have laws commanding men to put on women’s clothing if they indulge in mourning, 1137, 7. Why should reason not soothe your sadness rather than time? 1137, 8. See **CRIME**.

**THE DODONAEAN TREES** were worshiped by the peoples of the nations, 838, 18.

**DECEIT** ought to be absent from everything, 124, 67.

**MASTERS.** Command your servants not as though they were subject by condition, but remember that they share the same nature as you, 1048, 112. How many masters does the person have who has fled from one? 1045, 96. See **SERVANT**.

**DOMINUS**, bishop of Grenoble, 786, 1; 805, 76.

**GIFTS.** How can gifts be precious if their giver is worthless? 646, 64. The minds of sleepers, their bodies resting as though buried, raise themselves toward higher things and withdraw from the body, 1140, 21.

**HOUSE.** A good house ought to be recognized at the very vestibule, 164, 7.

**Δόξα (Opinion/Glory).** Some have thought that it means opinion more than glory, 545, 131.

**DRACHMA.** A drachma is not a denarius but something different, 782, 21. The image of God is on the drachma, ibid. The drachma that the woman carefully seeks after losing it is faith, 777, 2.

## E
### E

**DRUNKENNESS**—excellent when it produces sobriety of mind, 376, 17. Where the flesh becomes drunk, the mind staggers, the spirit reels, and the heart wavers, 410, 76.

**CHURCH.** The woman who anointed Christ’s feet with ointment represents the Church, 953, 24. The figure of the Church appears in the woman touching the fringe of Christ’s garment, 399, 31. The woman hiding leaven in flour is a type of the Church, 411, 81 and following. The widow who put two small coins into the treasury was a type of the Church, 895, 5. What are the two small coins that the Church sent after receiving them from Christ? 895, 6. See **DEBORAH**, **ELIJAH**.

The moon is the Church; the stars are the saints, shining with heavenly grace, 286, 25. The prophets announced the future building of the gathering of the nations and of the Church, 1062, 1. The Church consists of everyone, 204, 70. The congregation of the holy Church rises into one body through the unity of faith and charity, 112, 19. It was not the Law that gathered the Church, but the faith of Christ, 870, 24. Just as God the Father called the Church, so did the Son and the Holy Spirit, 653, 102. Peter demonstrated that the Church was built by the Holy Spirit, 655, 110.

The Church is a ship which, with the full sail of the Lord’s cross and the breath of the Holy Spirit, sails safely in this world, 242, 118. Amid the many straits of the world, the Church of the Lord remains immovable, as though built upon the apostolic rock, and persists upon an unshaken foundation against the assaults of the sea, 755, 1. Three things are, as it were, the Church’s guarantors: hope, faith, and charity. When hope has gone before, faith has been founded, charity is ordered, and the Church is joined together, 226, 53. The foundation of the Church must prevail against all heresies, 711, 34. Christ asserts that those who separate the Church, such as heretics and schismatics, use a diabolical spirit, 421, 24. Even if an angel from heaven were involved, he ought not to be preferred to the peace of the Churches, 863, 16. Drive away the wolves seeking to carry off prey from the Church, 1032, 43.

How peacefully orthodox faith and the faith of the faithful flourished in the Western and Eastern Church! 813, 3. All who are in the Church serve God, 901, 15. What ought the person who comes to the Church to provide? 901, 16. Christ alone is the bridegroom, and the Church, coming from the nations, marries him as a needy and fasting bride, 510, 72 and following. The Church does not cease kissing Christ’s feet, 960, 18. It alone possesses the kiss, as a bride, ibid. She is an adulteress who is not joined in Christ’s lawful marriage, 857, 16.

Who are, as it were, the head, cheeks, and jaws of the Church? 1175, 6 and following. The wise men of the Church are, as it were, its head, 1176, 7. What are the breasts of the Church except the sacraments of baptism? 1193, 75. The Church is virgin, married, and widow, 190, 16. She is a virgin in chastity and a mother in offspring, 154, 31. No one can doubt that she is a virgin, 1031, 37. Why is she beautiful among virgins? 295, 67. She is black through guilt and beautiful through grace; black by condition and beautiful through redemption; black while she fights, but beautiful when she is crowned with the insignia of her victory, 655, 112.

Her glory is within, in her faculties or in the inner sanctuaries of the sacraments, 250, 5. Through the Church eternal life is bestowed, 255, 24. The Church is the winepress of the eternal fountain, in which the fruit of the heavenly vine overflows, 599, 1. The grace of the Church is the harvest of merits, 840, 28. Where the Church is, there your mind has its firmest station; there is the foundation of your spirit, 1032, 42. The fruits of the good tree are the children of the Church, 422, 25. See **MARTYRS**.

The Church is wounded not in herself but in us, 225, 48. The Church confesses her wounds and desires to be healed, 399, 31. The Church has oil with which she soothes the wounds of her members, with which she anointed martyrs and confessors, 961, 20. The Church’s weapons are faith and prayer, 199, 49. The Church prays together, works together, and is tested together, 38, 142. Above all, there ought to be fairness and equality in the Church, 99, 124.

The Church washes Christ’s feet and dries them with her hair, because she pours the same grace not only upon the rich and powerful but also upon men of plebeian families; she examines everyone with an equal balance, receives everyone into the same bosom, and cherishes everyone in the same womb, 961, 22. In the Churches there is the ark of the Testament, containing the golden jar with manna, Aaron’s rod, the cherubim above the tablets, and the mercy seat, 763, 4. The synagogue observes a day; the Church observes immortality, 1082, 5.

The vessels of the Church are the adornment of the sacraments and the redemption of captives, 103, 138. When is it permissible even to break up, melt down, or sell the vessels of the Church that have been consecrated? 104, 142. See **AMBROSE**. The Church possesses nothing except faith, 837, 16. The Church’s possession is the support of the needy, ibid. The Church has gold not to preserve it but to distribute it and assist in times of need, 103, 137. Support must be assigned to those expelled from the Church, 88, 77. The bishops write that the Churches are being devastated by severe oppression, 955, 29.

The lands of the Church pay tribute; if the emperor desires the lands, he has the power to reclaim them: I do not give them as a gift, but I do not deny them, 872, 33. The Church’s field is fertile in various resources, 221, 34. Those who, under a tumultuous impulse of mind rather than through settled judgment, transferred their wealth to the Church and later thought it should be reclaimed received judgment as their first reward and sacrilege as their second, 434, 85. Nothing is taken from the Church that is acquired for piety, 1102, 9. The Jewish people are rich, the Church poor—and in what sense? 1183, 30 and following. Christ bestows these riches upon his Church, and by them the heavenly treasures are filled, 913, 13.

The Church of God ought not to be handed over to Caesar, because the temple of God cannot belong to Caesar by right, 873, 35. See **AMBROSE**, **BASILICA**.

The Church rightly claims the authority to bind and loose sins, 392, 7. The Church preserves obedience in both respects, so as to bind and release sin: heresy is harsh in one respect and disobedient in the other; it wishes to bind what it does not release and refuses to release what it has bound, 391, 7. The Lord willed that there be equal authority both to release and to bind, ibid. The Novatians wrongly deny that sins can be forgiven in the Church, 399, 33. The authority to bind and loose has been entrusted to priests alone, 392, 7.

Through the Holy Spirit sins are forgiven. Human beings, however, offer their ministry for the forgiveness of sins; they do not exercise the authority of any power. These people ask; divinity grants. The service is human, but the generosity belongs to heavenly power, 693, 137. The Church has both water and tears: the water of baptism and the tears of repentance, 959, 12. Christ granted to the Church that she might redeem one person through all, 411, 80. The Church takes upon herself the sinner’s burden, 421, 81. The Church desires not to exclude harshly, but to soften, 1166, 117. See **PRIEST**, **NOVATIAN**, **PRESBYTER**.

**ECCLESIASTICAL.** Ecclesiastical life appears more obscure in adolescence, 58, 227. One must strive toward ecclesiastical honor through good deeds and sincere purpose, 98, 119. In ecclesiastical office one finds nothing rarer than someone who follows the institution of the Fathers—and why? 58, 227. The duties of the Church’s ministers, 25, 89. A minister of the Church should devote the times when he is free from Church duties to reading, 25, 88. See **AMBROSE**, **CLERIC**, **JOKES**, **JULIANA**, **WIDOW**.

Ecclesiastical judgment. See **BISHOP**, **FAITH**, **EVIDENCE**, **PRIEST**, **WITNESSES**. Pious emperors benefit the Churches. See **EMPERORS**. At their death, the Church’s grief and tears. See **EMPEROR**, **VALENTINIAN**.

**ECLIPSES** arise whenever the sun is covered by clouds, whenever it is removed from the earth by an intervening object, or when its ray of light has been reflected from the region opposite it, 923, 7.

**ELEAZAR.** What does it signify that, after Aaron’s death, God commanded Moses alone to clothe his son Eleazar in Aaron’s garments? 1036, 59. Eleazar was buried with his triumph, 53, 207. He left peace as heir to his virtue, ibid., 208.

**ALMSGIVING.** No one gave more than the person who gave everything, 895, 6. The Lord does not wish wealth to be poured out all at once but to be distributed, 40, 149. The poor person asks for what you have; he does not ask for what you do not have, 159, 54. See **RICH**, **GENEROSITY**, **POOR**.

**ELEGANCE.** The value of words is outwardly; inwardly they are metal, 833, 2.

**ELIJAH** was hardened for endurance by dwelling in solitude, and, as though nourished toward the fatness of virtue, advanced stronger on rustic food, 1040, 75. He was happier the poorer he was, 74, 14. He was rich because, raised aloft in a fiery chariot, he carried the treasures of his virtues into heavenly dwellings, 942, 7. The Lord lifted Elijah to heaven, intending to restore him to the earth at a favorable time, 399, 34. He conquered on earth and triumphed in heaven, 976, 29. What great virtue belonged to the widow to whom he was sent! 186, 3 and following. She was a figure of the Church, 189, 14 and following.

**ELIZABETH.** Elizabeth was filled with the spirit of her son; Mary was sanctified by the spirit of her Son, 541, 113.

**ELISHA**, inactive in body, wielded the spirit and fought through prayers when the Syrians, struck with great fear, fled, 820, 7. He conducted himself toward the Syrian army more nobly and honorably than the Greeks did toward the Persians, 129, 86 and following. In Elisha, who threw himself upon the dead man to raise him, there is a figure of the Lord, 1098, 5 and following.

**ENNEADECATERIS.** The Fathers of Nicaea established the cycle of nineteen years, 881, 1; 885, 16.

**ENOCH** was rich because he carried away with him what he possessed and brought the whole account of his goodness into heavenly receptacles, 942, 7.

**ἐντελέχεια (entelecheia)**—a certain fifth kind of element, 922, 1.

**EPHRATHA** is said to mean “house having fury,” 1064, 9.

**EPHRAIM.** Parts of the mountain of Ephraim fell by lot to the tribe of Levi, 772, 3.

**EPICURUS**, according to Demarchus, teaches that pleasant living is produced neither by drinking, banquets, nor intercourse with women, but by sober discussion and a restrained life, 1027, 19. Although he denies that pleasure is the originator of evil, he nevertheless does not deny that certain things arise from it from which evils are generated, 1025, 13. The Epicureans think that God cares nothing about us, 14, 47. The advocates of pleasure, who say that death has nothing to do with us, are refuted, 1027, 17 and following.

In the **election of a bishop**, malignity ought above all to be absent, since the life of everyone is formed in him, 1033, 46. Everyone ought to agree in giving assent to his being requested, 1023, 2. How ought he to be the husband of one wife? 1036, 62. Most people argue that “husband of one wife” refers to a wife taken after baptism; but that interpretation is refuted, 1037, 63 and following.

What a newly elected bishop ought to do is explained, 755, 2 and following. The bishop’s duty is to teach, 2, 2. His greatest responsibility is to lend to the minds of the people the words of God entrusted to him, 145, 1. What and how he ought to teach his people, and what sermons he ought to deliver to them, 755, 5 and following. Nothing is more dangerous before God or more shameful before human beings in a priest than to feel something and not proclaim it freely, 945, 2.

This discussion belongs to priests, if the matter under discussion concerns faith, 862, 15. In a matter of faith bishops ordinarily judge Christian emperors, not emperors bishops, 861, 4. In God’s cause, whom will you hear if you do not hear the priest? 947, 4. Who will dare tell you the truth if the priest does not dare? ibid. The emperor did not wish to injure the priests; he appointed the bishops as interpreters, 787, 5.

If a bishop were accused and the case concerned an examination of morals, Valentinian wished such matters to belong to episcopal judgment, 860, 2. See **VALENTINIAN**. A bishop judges the case of another bishop together with his brother and sister, according to the form of the sacred command, 1100, 1. See **PRIEST**.

There was an eagerness among Christian men that a prefect should not judge a bishop’s case, 1100, 2. Some bishops began to accuse persons guilty of very serious crimes in public courts and even to press the matter as far as the sword and ultimate death; others began to approve such accusations and the bloody triumphs of priests, 894, 3. But these practices are condemned, ibid. and following. See **FAITH**.

The absence of bishops was often more effective than their presence, when he consulted them collectively, 818, 16. It is fitting that a buried priest should rest where he was accustomed to offer, 877, 13. A bishop must first of all avoid becoming, as it were, a common body through the admixture of pagans with the Church, 842, 2. If we have been provoked against anyone, a layman has a lighter case than a bishop, 433, 76. Who would tolerate a person unable to govern himself when he has undertaken to govern others? 1036, 60.

In your merits lies the full measure of priestly labor; in your spirits the fruit of episcopal work shines forth, 552, 9. A bishop should use clerics as his own members, especially ministers, 102, 134. What cannot be healed he should cut away with grief, ibid., 135. Whomever he sees as suitable for a particular office, he should assign to it, 102, 134. See **CLERIC**.

Whom ought bishops to protect more than orphans? 889, 5. They are governors amid disturbances and lovers of peace, except when they themselves are moved by an injury to God or an insult to the Church, 948, 6. A bishop of moderate means, distinguished by praiseworthy poverty, 787, 4. Crowds of poor bishops, for whom poverty was not burdensome, 1006, 3. A priest or steward ought to assist the poor and report their needs to the bishop, 86, 79. See **POVERTY**.

Their profession restrained bishops’ eagerness to punish, 1125, 41. If someone does not obey the bishop, he proudly deviates from the truth, 99, 123. Emperors persecute bishops more successfully than they love them, 1185, 139. The anniversaries of bishops’ deaths. See **AMBROSE**, **FELIX**.

**LETTERS.** The genre of letters was invented so that we might have some conversation with the absent and so that, although separated in body, a certain image of presence might be conveyed, 1054, 1; 991, 1. The purpose of letters is that, separated by distances of place, we may remain joined in affection, 989, 4. How great is their usefulness if something of the divine Scriptures breathes through them! ibid., 5 and following. Our ancestors infused faith into the minds of peoples through their letters, ibid., 6. See **PAUL**.

For old men it is easier through daily practice and familiar speech to compose letters and to append whatever happens to arise from the divine Scriptures, 991, 7.

**BANQUETS** of detestable people must be avoided, 182, 31. It belongs to those who indulge in food and drink who hope for nothing after their death, 1027, 18.

**HORSES.** A horse learns to love the sound of its neck being stroked, and becomes accustomed to the word of wantonness before the lash of discipline, 173, 41.

**ISAIAH** was sent by the Holy Spirit, 697, 159. It is shown that he was stripped before the assembled peoples not disgracefully but most gloriously, 1015, 9 and following.

**FOOD.** Food sometimes restores health when taken at the appropriate time, 929, 4. All foods that generate heat should be used sparingly, 176, 8.

**EZRA.** The Book of Ezra despised the philosophers’ trifles about the soul and taught that it belongs to a higher substance, 922, 2.

**ESTHER** bent the proud king through her fasts, 1030, 29.

**ETRUSCAN.** An Etruscan youth carved his face with brands so that no woman could love him, 299, 83.

**EUCHARIST.** Figures of the sacrament of the Eucharist, 373, 1 and following. The sacrament of the Eucharist is older and more excellent than manna, 337, 44 and following; 372, 24. It is also different from the sacraments and mysteries of the Jews, 367, 10 and following.

There are mysteries of more perfect sacraments; there are others that the prophets announced concerning future glory; and there are others in which the redemption of the world, the forgiveness of sins, the distribution of graces, and participation in the sacraments are found. When you have received these, you will marvel that manna possessed neither such grace nor such efficacy for salvation, 1095, 4.

Wine and water are placed in the chalice, 373, 2. What does the mixture of water signify? ibid. Wine and water are placed in the chalice, but through the consecration of the heavenly word it becomes blood, 370, 20. The sacrament of the Eucharist is effected by Christ’s word, 339, 52; 368, 14. By what words are Christ’s body and blood consecrated? 371, 21 and following.

In the Eucharist the bread is ordinary before the sacramental words; when consecration has taken place, bread becomes Christ’s body, 368, 14. Christ’s word is effective: it makes what existed continue to exist and changes it into something else, 369, 15. In the Eucharist one form is named before the blessing of the heavenly words; after consecration the body is signified, 339, 54. After consecration it is already Christ’s body, 369, 16; 371, 23; 378, 24.

That in the Eucharist the nature is changed by the blessing, and that it is not what nature formed but what the blessing consecrated, and that Christ’s true body is received, is proved by various arguments, 338, 50 and following; 369, 17 and following. The transfigured body is offered upon the altars, 709, 23. After consecration one says “Amen,” 340, 55. Christ’s body is on the altar, 366, 7.

Just as he is truly the Son of God, so his flesh, which we receive, is true, and his drink is true, 379, 1. The Lord himself testifies to us that we receive his body and blood, 371, 23. So that there might be no horror of blood, you receive the sacrament in likeness, but truly attain the grace of nature and of the powers, 380, 3. When you receive the flesh, you participate in his divine substance through that food, 381, 4.

Whenever we receive the sacraments which, through the mystery of sacred prayer, are transformed into flesh and blood, we proclaim the Lord’s death, 543, 124. When the Eucharist is received, the priest says to you, “The body of Christ,” and you say, “Amen,” that is, “true,” 372, 25. During the mystery refrain from groaning, spitting, coughing, and laughter, 177, 13.

The protection and effects of the Eucharist, 1126, 46. Whenever you drink Eucharistic wine, you receive forgiveness of sins and are made drunk in the spirit, 376, 17. The Eucharist supplies the substance of eternal life and is Christ’s body, 337, 47. Whoever receives Christ’s body will never hunger, 375, 12. In the Eucharistic bread there is no bitterness but every sweetness, 376, 17.

How often we ought to receive the Eucharist, 372, 28; 378, 25. The Greeks were accustomed to receive the Eucharist after a year, 378, 25. Satyrus, not yet initiated into the mysteries, when he was caught in a shipwreck, asked the initiated for the divine sacrament of the faithful; he had it tied in a scarf, wrapped the scarf around his neck, and thus threw himself into the sea, 1125, 43. How much protection he hoped to receive from it, 1126, 46. The sacrament of the Eucharist is not disclosed to those for whom it is not appropriate, 340, 55.

**EUCHERIUS**, consul, 786, 1.

When the envoys of the pagans asked the emperor **EUGENIUS** to restore the sacred rites to the temples, he did not do so. They asked again on another occasion, and he resisted; later he thought that the very people who had asked ought to be granted their request, 1011, 6. Ambrose freely rebuked him for this, ibid., 7 and following. Although he then resisted alone, others nevertheless gave the same advice, 1012, 11. Maximus and Eugenius teach by their pitiable example in hell how harsh it is to take up arms against one’s own rulers, 1209, 39. See **AMBROSE**.

**EUNOMIUS.** Arius or Aetius was Eunomius’s teacher, 457, 44. Marcion and Eunomius prefer to have God evil rather than good, 31, 117. Eunomius is refuted by the opening words of John, 455, 57. See **ARIANS**.

**EUNOMIAN.** Proceeding from the source of Arian impiety, he asserts that Christ’s generation must be inferred from philosophical traditions, 704, 7.

**EUNUCHS** who castrated themselves are to be condemned, 206, 76.

**EUPHRATES.** Its source is in the regions of Armenia, 843, 2.

**EUSEBIUS**, bishop of Bononia, 803, 66 and following; 786, 1; 788, 10; 789, 11; 805, 76 and following; 791, 10 and following. His condemnation of Palladius, 801, 57.

The entire Church chose Eusebius, bishop of Vercellae, whom they had never previously known, preferring him to their fellow citizens; and it was rightly believed that the man whom everyone had requested had been chosen by divine judgment, 1023, 2. He left his country and his kindred and preferred pilgrimage to the leisure of home; for the faith he also deliberately chose and embraced the hardships of exile—and what he did in exile, 1038, 68.

Eusebius of holy memory was the first in the western regions to unite things that seemed opposed to one another, so that, while living in a city, he might retain the institutions of monks and govern the Church with the sobriety of fasting, 1038, 66. He first raised the banner of confession; through his endurance the monastery was strengthened by practice, and from the custom of stricter observance he drew endurance of labors, 1039, 70 and following. See **DIONYSIUS**.

**EUSEBIUS**, bishop, 819.

**EUSEBIUS OF NICOMEDIA.** His letter was read at the Council of Nicaea, 518, 125.

**EUSTATHIUS**, bishop, 786, 1; 805, 76.

**EUSTORGIUS**, confessor, 868, 8.

**εὐσχημόνως (euskhēmonōs)**—what it signifies, 59, 230.

**EUTROPIUS**, bishop, 819.

**EVE.** A woman has an excuse in sin; a man does not, 255, 25 and following. See **WOMAN**.

**EVAGRIUS** has no argument with which to press his case against Flavian, 1006, 1. Both Evagrius and Flavian relied more on the faults of another’s ordination than on their own, 1007, 5. Evagrius seemed more defensible to himself because Flavian avoided him, ibid. Because of Evagrius and Flavian the whole world is shaken, 1006, 1. It was a source of grief among Easterners and Westerners that the bonds of sacred communion had been broken, 817, 1. We think that the case of Flavian and Evagrius should be referred to our holy brother, the bishop of the Roman Church, 1007, 7. See **THEOPHILUS**.

**EVAGRIUS**, presbyter and envoy, 789, 11; 805, 76.

The Holy Spirit speaks in the **EVANGELISTS**, 606, 29. See **ANIMALS**.

In the **GOSPEL** there is fullness; in the Law, partial perfection, 978, 6. The full measure is in the Gospel; it is half-full in the Law, whose fullness is the New Testament, 895, 9. Here is shadow, here image, there truth. Shadow in the Law, image in the Gospel, truth in heavenly things, 63, 248. We know that, according to the Law, there are these three things—shadow, image, and truth: shadow in the Law, image in the Gospel, truth in judgment, 1164, 109. Shadow for carnal Jews, image for us, truth for those who will rise again, ibid.

The Law has severity; the Gospel has indulgence, by which sins are forgiven, 1081, 3. In the Law there is slavery; in the Gospel, freedom, 936, 22. The person to whom grace is promised is free; the person upon whom the yoke of the Law is imposed is a slave, 1089, 2. In the Law there is sacrifice; in the Gospel, mercy, 405, 54. Thanks to the Gospel, through which, when we read Christ’s deeds, we seem to be present with Christ, 202, 61. See **LAW**.

Various ways of reading the opening of the Gospel according to John, 504, 43. See **JOHN**. The Gospel was read in the Church, 865, 8. The reading was recited, but by accident, 868, 19.

**EVENTIUS**, bishop of Ticinum, 805, 76. His condemnation of Palladius, 801, 56.

**EVENTIUS’S** episcopal subscription, 969, 14.

“From whom” and “through whom” are not syllables struggling against one another but associated and harmonious, 651, 89. “From whom something is” and “through whom something is” involve no distinction, 547, 143 and following. Whatever is from someone is either from his substance or from his power, 642, 42.

**EXCOMMUNICATION.** It is rightly said that the person separated from Christ’s body is handed over to Satan, 410, 78. He comes with the rod who removes a convicted person from sacred communion, ibid. A person who has fallen seriously ought to be separated from the sacraments, 411, 79. Soldiers were commanded to abstain from participation in communion, 855, 13. The person who sells dignities and honors, or wishes to sell the simple minds of the faithful, is expelled from the temple, 869, 21.

There are still people outside the Church who refuse to summon to communion in the heavenly sacraments those who have judged that a capital sentence ought to be imposed on certain persons, 892, 2. Are they to be praised for this? ibid. and following.

**EXAMPLES.** One makes greater progress through examples—and why? 163, 2. We admire the praise of whatever virtues; let us strive to acquire their diligence, and let us silently recognize in ourselves the virtues we praise in others, 1045, 97. See **PAUL**.

**EXERCISES** undertaken at home and in one’s own sphere increase everything, 10, 33.

**TO GO OUT.** What does *exire* mean according to our usage? 466, 110.

**EXILE.** The patriarchs did not regard as exile what devotion undertook, rather than necessity commanded, 1159, 95.

**EXSUPERANTIUS**, bishop of Dertona, 786, 1; 805, 76. His condemnation of Palladius, 802, 60.

**EXTREME UNCTION.** The Novatians lay on hands and believe that it is an act of blessing if a sick person should perhaps recover, 400, 36.

**EZEKIEL** still sees, is still vigorous, and will remain so, 242, 117. See **GOTHS**.

### F
FABRICIUS: The Roman commander’s celebrated deed: when a physician promised the king that he would give him poison, Fabricius sent the physician back, 130, 91.

FACTUM (“made”): Does not always refer to creation, 503, 35. See CHRIST.

DEEDS: In all deeds there are either corrections arising from virtue, lapses arising from vice, intermediate acts, or indifferent acts, 935, 20.

FAME. See Judgments concerning the good.

FAMINE: In the preceding year, but only in certain regions, 837, 17 and following.

FAUSTA’S BASILICA, 875, 2.

FAUSTINUS: Both Faustini were restored to Eusebius, 1004, 1. Faustinus nourished the spiritual dove, ibid. The young Faustinus suffered from a cough and came to his holy sister to be cured, 1004, 2. Ambrose consoles Faustinus, grieving bitterly over the death of his sister, 944, 1 and following. [Col. 1454]

FELIX AND NABOR, 874, 2.

FELIX: Received ordination through the laying on of Ambrose’s hands, 764, 5. Through his ministry many of the people of Como began to believe, and through his teaching they received the word of God, ibid. The feast day of Bishop Felix falls at the beginning of the Kalends of November, 763, 2. It is named from the dedication of the basilica, ibid.

FELIX: The subscription of Bishop Felix, 969, 14.

FELIX: Bishop of Jadera, 786, 1; 805, 76. His condemnation of Palladius, 802, 62.

FELIX: Bishop and envoy of the Africans, 786, 1; 790, 16; 805, 76. His condemnation of Palladius, 801, 58.

FELIX: Deacon sent by Ambrose to deliver a letter to Theodosius, 1021, 3.

FELIX: A Jovinianist, condemned, 969, 14.

FELIX: Sent Ambrose mushrooms of remarkable size, 762, 1. Ambrose rebukes him for not visiting him at all, ibid., 2.

FELIX: Ambrose commends himself to Felix’s prayers, 763, 3.

THE FEMALE SEX: It should not be accused on the grounds that it introduced the cause of error, 253, 16 and following. Without a woman a man has no praise; in a woman he is praised, 254, 22. Following the Greek custom, it has become common for women to wear men’s garments, as though with shorter tunics, 1061, 4. Women should seek ornaments of the inner person more earnestly, 295, 64. How could a woman—and, even more, a widow—administer taxable property? 1101, 7.

USURY: Peoples have often fallen through it, and it was the cause of public ruin, 843, 4. A good interest is the profit of spiritual grace, 764, 6.

WILD ANIMALS: They are tamed by human authority, 974, 16.

FABRICATED AND PRETENDED: Nothing fabricated or feigned possesses true virtue, nor is it usually lasting, 97, 112 and following.

FAITH: Its definition is that truth, not words, should be weighed, 723, 89. Faith alone is undifferentiated for either sex: the wealth of men and the dowry of virgins, 281, 13. Faith cannot stand without the rule of truth, 606, 30. The sinews and certain joints of wisdom consist in not believing rashly, especially in matters of faith, 761, 28. Remove arguments where faith is sought, 460, 84. If I am convinced by reason, I reject faith, 1157, 89. In exhortation to faith, confession is religious; in disputation, it is incautious presumption, 444, 4. Believe divine things where you find no human explanation, 460, 79. In the fullness of the Church, truth is gathered not by a sign but by faith, 358, 15. The patriarchs left us the inheritance of faith, 1200, 9. That alone is faith which is found in the Gospel, 1091, 9. Our declaration of faith, or creed, is set forth, 445, 6. What is the confession of faith that we hold, handed down by our forefathers against the Sabellians, Arians, and Photinus? 990, 4 and following. In a Christian man, faith comes first, 349, 1. God seeks not money but faith, 488, 82. Anathema to him who does not explain the freedom of faith, 793, 26. True faith is never disturbed, 703, 1. Fear does not compel faith; affection displays it, 79, 38. Whoever believed in Christ, even though placed upon the cross and subjected to the punishment of one who had confessed his crime, cast off the thief’s deserts and earned the rewards of the innocent, 573, 125. Whoever believes possesses his own grace; but he possesses another as well if his faith is crowned through sufferings, 404, 50. Faith’s grace is greater if someone despises suffering for religion’s sake, 1074, 14. Faith is a good substance in which the patrimony of our hope lies, 419, 15. Faith, as though preceding charity, takes possession of the soul and prepares paths for the love that is to come, 1094, 8. Whoever loves certainly believes, and by believing each person begins to love, 1093, 5. This is charity greater than authority: that faith remain secure, the faith that preserves authority, 841, 23. Ready faith is a strict judge of itself, 1040, 73. Nothing is more exalted than faith, 826, 11. It is the foundation of the Church, 711, 34. It is the foundation of justice, 38, 142. Faith, not noble birth, brings merit, 278, 3. Faith, not the Law, makes a person just, 870, 24. The slave is under fear, the free person comes from faith; the former is under the letter, the latter under grace; the former is in servitude, the latter in the Spirit, 1084, 5. Where there is faith, there is freedom; where there is freedom, there is grace; where there is grace, there is inheritance, ibid. Faith is richer than all treasures, 488, 92. O faith richer than all treasures! O faith stronger than all bodily virtues! O faith more salutary than all physicians! 237, 100. Without the protection of faith, good works cannot endure, 72, 7. Good faith shines with the beautiful adornment of works, 473, 14. The work is woven together when the deeds of faith correspond, 472, 9. Of the two Testaments—that is, through the price of complete faith—prophecy received its fulfillment, and the Church its fullness, 978, 5. It is faith that liberates through Christ’s blood, 1080, 11. To believe in Christ is the gain of life, 405, 53. In all things faith is beautiful, justice pleasing, and the measure of equity delightful, 124, 66. Faith is an eternal inheritance; money is temporary, 351, 8. Mercy is more generous where faith is more ready, [Col. 1455] 216, 9. Faith obtains as though from a written bond, 434, 80. Faith itself abounds in itself, rich enough and more than rich in its own resources, 757, 11. Our harvest is the faith of souls, 840, 28. Through the Lord’s faith there was to be a fruitful harvest of virtues, 602, 10. There are pastures of faith in which the holy person of God is placed, 905, 2. No one has regretted having believed God, 673, 42. Whoever thinks that faith is present in all things judges all things well, 125, 68. So great is the grace of faith that where a dead man stank before the day, there the whole house is filled with a good fragrance, 430, 63. They surpass the heirs of birth as heirs of faith, 1093, 1. This is faith’s victory: that those whom the gentiles cast down, the seas should restore, 837, 15. Good faith, which often works even in the dead, 1201, 10. The unity of piety is to believe rightly, and the unity of impiety is to believe wrongly, 606, 30. See AGE.

It is a great loss to the soul if someone loses faith, or the grace acquired at the price of faith, 777, 2. A clear cause of divine indignation preceded this: that the Roman Empire’s faith was first broken where faith toward God had been broken, 496, 139. It became sufficiently clear that those who violate faith cannot be secure, 496, 141. Such is the treachery of unbelievers that often even the devil’s confession is more tolerable, 878, 16. See CHARITY, FOOD, CHURCH.

The cause of faith must be conducted in the Church, not in the palace, 864, 3. Matters of faith should be discussed in the Church before the people, not in the emperor’s council chamber, 863, 17. He must rightly be condemned who chose gentiles as judges in a matter of faith, 871, 27 and following. See AMBROSE, BISHOP.

THE FAITHFUL: In Rome, those who have been baptized are called the faithful, 349, 1. Let no one regard as faithful to him those whom he has supposed he could bind to himself either by money or by flattery, 98, 118. Why are the strings of a lyre called *fides* (“faith”)? 1201, 10.

THE SON OF GOD: Twelve indications and names of divinity belong to the Son of God, 471, 3 and following. The dignity and truth of the divine name are shared by the Son, 500, 17. What are the definitions concerning the Son of God that cannot be refuted? 473, 14. He is “firstborn” because no one precedes him; “only-begotten” because no one follows him, 462, 89. The Son is the Word of God, born, not spoken forth, 539, 101. Some have believed that the Word of God is one thing and the Son of God another, 714, 48. Anathema to whoever denies that the true God is the only-begotten Son of God, 804, 70. Anathema to whoever denies that the Son is equal to the Father according to divinity, 796, 39. Anathema to whoever does not confess the goodness of the Son of God, 794, 30. Anathema to whoever denies that the Son of God is wise, 793, 27. Whoever says that the Son of God alone is true, but does not wish to say that he is the true Lord, seems to deny him, 791, 20. Anathema to whoever does not confess this, ibid., 21.

By a mass of accumulated arguments it is demonstrated that the Son of God is not a creature, 575, 137 and following. The same truth is proved by other arguments, 461, 86 and following. He makes an exception for everyone by making an exception for the Son of God—and for the Father as well, 606, 29. According to the power of divinity, the Son of God possesses neither name nor common fellowship with slaves, 567, 96. By various arguments it is proved that the Son of God is truly God, 465, 108 and following, and that he is a good God, 473. That he is of one substance with the Father is proved by various testimonies of Scripture, 516, 108 and following. The Father and Son possess one divinity, as is proved by various testimonies of Scripture, 447, 20 and following. In the Father and the Son there is no difference of divinity, but one majesty, 484, 73. The Son is one with the Father by natural substance, not one according to Sabellian perfidy, 659, 135. The Son of God was given to us, not to the Sabellians, who assert that the same one is Father and Son, 507, 58. The Son is both called and proved equal to the Father, 483, 69. Equality distinguishes the Father and Son; unity does not separate the Father and Son, 689, 116. The Son is the radiance of the Father’s light, coeternal because of the eternity of his power, inseparable because of the unity of his splendor, 541, 108. The Father and Son have one glory, 486, 82. See FATHER.

This is the benefit and reward of perfect virtue, this divine and incomparable gift: that we know Christ with the Father and do not separate the Son from the Father, 554, 17. When God is called “alone,” the Son of God is not thereby separated, 498, 10 and following. The Son must not be separated from the Father where it is written, “Blessed and only Potentate,” 499, 15 and following. The Son is always with the Father and in the Father: with the Father through the indissociable distinction of the eternal Trinity, and in the Father through the unity of the divine nature, 537, 88. Whoever believes in the Son believes also in the Father, 573, 120. The Son is not diminished because he is not the Father, nor is the Father diminished because he is not the Son, 537, 90. The Father gave to the Son not as though he were later by the right of generation, nor as a gift of generosity, 547, 140. The Father gave to the Son as to a Son through generation, not as to one in need through grace, 520, 133. The perfect Father is believed to have begotten a perfect Son, 445, 9. The Son has a Father, but not a temporal one, not through passion, conception, or grace, but through generation, 573, 123. The Son is generated as eternal, as the Word, as the splendor of eternal light—and why? 459, 79. The Son of God received all things from the Father by right of generation and fully expressed the Father in the glory of his majesty, 592, 224. The Son of God possesses immortality in nature and in substance; he possesses it not through temporal grace but through eternal divinity, not as a slave through a gift but as a coeternal Son through the propriety of generation, 557, 36.

That we are one in the Father and Son is not a matter of nature but of grace; that the Son and Father are one is not something the Son received through grace, but naturally, as the Son possesses it, 528, 37. The Son possesses all that the Father possesses—eternity, majesty, and divinity—which he acquired by being born, 477, 38. There is an explicit distinction of generation between the Father and Son, 447, 16. If I wish to designate the divine nature, I must name the true God; but when I say “Son,” I signify one who has been begotten; and when I also say “Father,” I declare that he has begotten, 725, 98. The beginning of our faith is to know that the Son of God was begotten, 472, 5. We may know that the Son was born, but we may not investigate how he was born: I may not deny the former, while fear forbids me to inquire into the latter, 456, 65. Divine generation is above all things, extends beyond all bounds, and rises above every thought and sense, 456, 63 and following. Generation belongs to the Father’s property, not to his power, 536, 81 and following; 537, 90; 540, 103. In divine generation, nothing precedes, neither willing nor refusing, 540, 103. The Son went forth from the Father as God from God, 466, 110. When we read “God from God,” we do not speak of two gods, 448, 23. Whoever proceeded from God and went forth from God can possess nothing other than what belongs to God, 465, 107. The Father is the Son’s fountain; the Father is the Son’s root, 545, 126. Why is the Son of God called the image of the Father? 728, 112.

The Son of God knows all things and possesses foreknowledge of everything, including the day of judgment, 656, 117 and following. The Son of God demonstrated that he knew the day of judgment, 588, 203 and following. The Father hears the Son just as the Son hears the Father, 660, 137. To show that the Son does not fail to know what the Father wills, we speak of his having heard, 659, 132. That the Father and Son possess one majesty is proved by various testimonies of Scripture, 515, 103 and following. The unity of the power and majesty of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is proved from the Scriptures, 674, 48 and following. What belongs to the Father by the property of majesty belongs also to the Son through the unity of the same splendor, 514, 98. The Son’s eternity is the distinguishing mark of the Father’s majesty, 455, 61. The Son is the power of God and therefore coeternal, 669, 18. The Son neither received a beginning nor will have an end, 540, 107. Although God is Father, he is not prior to the Son, 457, 68 and following. The Son, like the Father, received neither beginning nor increase, 459, 75. The Father and Son have the same life, 545, 125. Many have understood the Son as signified by the fountain of life, and as the fountain of the Holy Spirit, 631, 172. The Son’s equality with the Father is established through the unity of their life-giving power, 544, 128. The Father is in the Son, not as sanctifying one in need or filling one who is empty, 527, 35.

By various arguments it is proved that the Son of God is omnipotent, 476, 34 and following, and that no impossibility belongs to him, 530, 52 and following. It is certain that there is no difference of power between the Father and Son, 546, 134. Through nature and majesty the Son is one with the Father, and in operation he does not differ, 532, 59. When the same grace is requested from the Father and Son, the same power is declared, 522, 140 and following. The Son does nothing without the Father, because there is a common operation and unity of power, 1092, 10. The Father’s act is not prior to, nor the Son’s act secondary to, the other; rather, the effect is the same, belonging to one operation, 660, 136. The work of the Father and Son is one, even if the Arians are displeased, 513, 91. Through the unity of their work, the Father confesses the Son to be his equal, 634, 2. You must believe that all things come from the Son of God, because, like the Father, he is both author and creator of all things, 548, 149. The Father did not make the heavens alone without the Son, nor the Son without the Father, 556, 30. It is impossible for the Son’s work not to accord with the Father’s will, 533, 68 and following. The Son made the world without a model, 529, 44; 532, 61 and following. Whoever possesses the glory of an unprecedented generation possesses the grace of unprecedented power, 459, 76. The Son of God caused those who had not been born to exist, 542, 114. By various testimonies it is proved that the Father and Son have one dominion, 513, 92 and following. So completely one is the kingdom of the Father and Son that what the Son hands over the Father receives, and what the Father receives the Son does not lose, 577, 153. The Father and Son hand over the kingdom to one another in such a way that neither does the one who receives acquire something foreign, nor does the one who hands it over lose it, 490, 105. Just as the Son loses nothing when the Father receives the kingdom, so the Father does not lose anything when he hands over his kingdom to the Son, 610, 49. Do not think the Father arrogant when he speaks of his dominion, or imagine that he devalues the Son’s obedience, 634, 2. The Son is called the Paraclete, just as the Holy Spirit is, 628, 156 and following. See CHRIST, TRINITY, WORD.

It is shown that the Son is not inferior to the Father because he was sent, 484, 74 and following. In what sense is he said to have been sent? 568, 99. How, and in what respect, is he subject to the Father? 578, 154 and following. We must judge insane those who thought that the Son of God, according to the nature of his divinity, was subject to degradation, 713, 44. According to the sequence of the Old Testament, the Son of God was offended by Adam, seen by Abraham, and worshiped by Jacob, 612, 55. Many say that the Father God was seen by Isaiah; Paul said it was the Spirit; Luke proved it; and John the Evangelist referred it to the Son, 698, 165. Some think the Son of God visible according to divinity, 612, 58. Where are those who say that the Son of God existed from the time of Melchizedek? 373, 1.

According to the flesh, the Son is inferior to the Father, 796, 37 and following. We frequently read that the Son of God was made and created according to the flesh, 645, 58 and following. In what respect was he born, and in what respect was he made? 462, 93. In what respect was he created? 463, 96. He was not born for us but given to us—and why? 507, 55. From Mary he was born for all through his mercy, but the heretics’ perfidy caused him not to be born for all, although he was born for all, ibid., 56 and 57. According to the Church’s faith, the Son is the same and one Son of God the Father and of David, 570, 106. The Son alone, immaculate, came forth from the Virgin’s womb to redeem the world’s salvation by his blood, 529, 44. Nothing is added to the substance of the Son of God; rather, something is added for our benefit in what is made known to us, 564, 69. No understanding can pass to the Father except through the Son, 456, 63.

Just as I confess that the unity of heavenly life exists in the Father and Son through the unity of the divine substance, so—apart from the privilege either of the divine nature or of the Lord’s incarnation—I profess that fellowship with us in the Son’s spiritual life exists through the unity of human nature, 545, 128. See ARIUS, ARIANS, CHRIST.

Through the Son we pass into fellowship with the divine nature, 722, 85. How does he say “Our Father,” who denies the true Son of God, through whom adoption is acquired? 1085, 6. This is the great testimony that we are God’s children: because we are heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ, 925, 4. Who would grieve at having his own pledge taken away, when God, for our consolation, handed over his only Son for us to death? 1114, 4.

CHILDREN: Since you are unable to live forever, train your children not for bodily use but for the service of virtue, 1115, 5. We offend more readily in adopted children than in natural children, 1103, 2. See MOTHERS.

END AND BEGINNINGS: In all things, beginnings and endings are of greater importance, 972, 7.

THE WICKED: They think that God does not know human actions or that he is an unjust judge, 14, 47.

FLAVIANUS: He has nothing to fear, 1006, 1. After the judgment of the Council of Capua, Flavianus returned to the assistance of prayers and the support of imperial rescripts, 1006, 3 and 6. Flavianus alone, as he himself wishes, is excluded from priestly fellowship, since he presents himself neither before imperial decrees nor before the assembly of priests, 1007, 4. See COUNCIL OF CAPUA, EVAGRIUS.

WEEPING: Weeping over present things is the reward of future things, 179, 21. Weeping, ready to meet the eyes’ need, wins compassion, lessens toil, eases pain, and preserves modesty, 195, 36. See TEARS.

FEAR: Where there is none, there is freedom, 935, 19.

FORNICATION: Let there be no fornication or impurity among God’s servants, because we serve the immaculate Son of God, 756, 8.

FORTE AND FORSITAN: In Greek, τάχα (*tacha*), “perhaps,” these words in Scripture are not the utterance of someone ignorant or doubtful, 423, 30 and following.

FORTITUDE: It is considered in two forms: by despising external bodily things and by pursuing those things that are supreme, 48, 181. It is divided into military and domestic affairs, 46, 175. In military matters it appears through greatness of spirit; at home it also excels and surpasses in bodily strength, 31, 115. Military virtue was not absent from our people in the Old Testament, 52, 205 and following. See WAR.

The fortitude of the Christian athlete, 48, 182. Fortitude possesses a certain force of fierce virtue and contempt for death, 241, 114. Fortitude without justice is material for wrongdoing, 47, 176. This is true fortitude: that through devotion of mind it surpasses the use of nature and the weakness of sex, 195, 37. Fortitude is called such when each person conquers himself, 48, 180, and his disordered impulses, ibid. One must fight against all vices, 51, 202 and following. One must neither be tested by desires nor broken by fear, 52, 203. See BENEVOLENCE.

A man is courageous when he provides for the future, 51, 189. The law of virtue lies not in inflicting injury but in driving it away, 47, 178. Fortitude is proved not only in prosperity but also in adversity, 53, 209. The fortitude of the few is superior to the relaxation of the many, 1075, 18. See AVARICE.

THE FORUM: It must be avoided, and the streets must be avoided, 225, 46.

UTERINE BROTHERS: That is, born of different fathers but the same mother, 1020, 10.

BROTHERLY LOVE: The return of brotherly love is no small thing, nor is the lot of nature insignificant when the increases of virtue enrich it, [Col. 1458] 1136, 80. Envy and boasting commonly empty the rights of brotherly affection in many people, 1193, 76.

FRAUD: Every fraud is disgraceful, 123, 65. The wise person does nothing except sincerely and without fraud, 115, 29. No fraud should be employed in selling inheritances, 125, 70 and following. See SINCERITY.

MODERATION: The flesh loves measured moderation, by which it is stripped of burdens and clothed with health, 1044, 91.

GRAIN DEALERS: Those who seek to profit from the price of grain are rebuked, 117, 38 and following.

COSMETIC ADORNMENT: It is not pleasing, 21, 75. Those who do not dare to explain what they think apply cosmetic concealment, 467, 118.

THEFTS: The secret thefts of slaves are public plunder by the rich, 113, 22.

FUTURE THINGS: It is customary in the divine Scriptures to speak of future things as though they were past, 508, 59. The appearance of present things is an indication of future things, 1121, 29. What is more foolish than to know that something will happen and then, when it happens, be unable to endure it? 1136, 4.

## G

GABAONITES: Inhospitable, harsh, and intolerable, 773, 6. Their vengeance for the violation of chastity in the Levite’s wife, ibid. and following.

THE BISHOPS OF GAUL: They sent envoys to the Council of Aquileia, 806, 1. They were gladly received by it, ibid. The synod of the bishops of Gaul, 1181, 25. Their frequent disagreements, 1181, 25. See AFRICA, COUNCIL, COUNCIL OF NICAEA.

GAZOPHYLACIUM: The contribution of the faithful, the expense of the poor, and the refuge of the needy, 894, 4.

GIDEON: What does his election signify? 599, 1. What else does his sacrifice signify, in which he offered the kid upon the rock? ibid., 2 and following. He was not doubtful but provident, so that we would not be doubtful, 601, 6. He foresaw that the nations of the gentiles too would drink the true and spiritual dew through the reception of faith, 601, 9. He wished to wash the feet of the Angel of the Lord who appeared to him, 602, 25. What did the jars in which he ordered torches to be lit signify? 630, 167. See FLEECE.

GEMINIANUS: Bishop, 969, 14.

GROANS: Pious and full of authority, 930, 5. What are the groaning of Christ and the groaning of the Holy Spirit? ibid. and following.

GENERATION: It belongs not to power but to nature, 721, 79. It is proved by clearer examples that “begotten” expresses not the property of nature but the meaning of generation, 724, 97. See SON OF GOD.

GENIALIS: A Jovinianist, condemned, 969, 14.

GENTILES: They utter grand and precious-sounding words while defending things devoid of truth: they speak of God but worship an image, 833, 2. The gentiles show reverence to their idols by silence, 177, 12. Estates belonging to the shrines of the gentiles were confiscated, 837, 16. See PAGANS.

GERMINATOR: A Jovinianist, condemned, 969, 14.

GERVASIUS AND PROTASIUS: Their bodies are discovered by Ambrose, 874, 2. Men of remarkable stature, 875, 2. All their bones and a great quantity of blood are found, ibid. They are transferred, as evening was already approaching, to the Basilica of Fausta, ibid. On the following day they are transferred to the basilica called Ambrosiana, and a blind man is healed. Miracles are then performed by them, 876, 9. Cloths and garments are thrown over the most sacred relics, and healing is sought through the very touch, ibid. The tomb is wet with blood; bloody signs of triumph appear; the inviolate relics are found in their proper place and order, with the head torn from the shoulders, 877, 12. The people acclaimed that the martyrs’ deposition should be postponed until the Lord’s Day; but they obtained only that it take place on the following day, 878, 14; 880, 23. Ambrose’s sermon to the people concerning this matter, ibid., 15 and following. A blind man named Severus, a butcher by occupation, is healed through the martyrs’ favor, 872, 2; 878, 17. The Arians denied this, ibid. Their blood cries out by the evidence of its color; their blood cries out by the proclamation of its efficacy; their blood cries out through the triumph of their suffering, 880, 23. Gervasius and Protasius caused the Milanese Church, barren of martyrs but now the mother of many children, to rejoice in the titles and examples of its own suffering, 876, 7. The demons acknowledge them, but the Arians refuse to acknowledge them, 880, 22. See MIRACLES.

BY ANOTHER’S SWORD: It is more tolerable to perish by another’s sword than by our own, 6, 15.

GLORY: Glory deferred flees and is not easily grasped, 107, 153. Those whom glory awaits, injury also awaits, 17, 60. Desire for glory has often done harm when sought immoderately, and always when usurped, 52, 203. The more glorious you have become, the more you should know that greater honor is due to your author, 962, 26.

GOG: He is a Goth, 495, 138. Roman possession received Gothic tribunes, 855, 9. Ezekiel prophesied the wars of the Goths, 495, 137. Ambrose promises Emperor Gratian victory over the Goths, 495, 136 and following. The Goths were driven from Macedonia by the prayers of Saint Acholius, 820, 6. Disturbed and terrified by a raging plague and burning pestilence, they fled; later they returned and requested peace, 820, 7. See ACHOLIUS.

GRATA. See JUST.

GRACE: The Lord’s grace is conferred not as though from the merit of a reward, but as though from his will, 289, 43. Grace is the gift of the one who bestows; penitence is the remedy of the one who has sinned, 426, 44. Through John came penitence, through Christ grace: the former he announces as a servant, the latter he gives as Lord, ibid. How can grace exist without the Spirit, since all divine grace is in the Holy Spirit? 626, 127. Grace proceeded from offense, power from weakness, and life from death, 635, 8. Pride found guilt, but guilt produced grace, 1079, 9. Let us not abandon the rights of nature, but prefer the gifts of grace, 1145, 41. Our remedy is Christ’s grace, and the body of death is our body, 1144, 41. There are increases through nature, which possesses the grace of a divine gift, 786, 15. Grace is a greater virtue than nature, 339, 52. The victor is the one who hopes in God’s grace, not the one who presumes upon his own virtue, 1204, 25. It is fitting for God that those whom he has invited through grace he should also advance through increases of that same grace, 957, 6. We are servants of our Creator, but we possess the freedom that we received through Christ’s grace, 1090, 3. Good is the water of spiritual grace, 633, 182. The fullness of spiritual grace is inseparable, but it is shared with us according to the capacity of our nature, 620, 93. All divine gifts cannot exist in each individual person; according to his capacity, each person receives what he either desires or deserves, 663, 150. Since Christ redeemed you, let grace correct the one whom punishment would not reform but would chastise, 897, 20.

GRACE: It is returned precisely in the act of possessing it, 44, 166. It is discharged by being possessed, and retained by being discharged, 100, 127. Its force is such that, when it is returned, it is possessed, and by possessing it one returns it, 1126, 46. What is more according to nature than to return grace to one’s author? 1126, 45. No duty is greater than returning grace, 1126, 44. To proclaim what you have received is not pride but devotion, 377, 19. It is scarcely permissible not to give to anyone; but it is not permissible not to repay, 42, 141. To confer a favor is good; but whoever does not know how to return it is utterly hard-hearted, 43, 162. If failure to return a favor to a human being has been judged similar to homicide, how great a crime is it not to return one to God! 1126, 44. See GLORY, DUTY.

GRATIANUS: Of august memory, 825, 5. He is called a holy emperor, 451, 43 and following; 452, 47; 606, 27; 661, 143. He is called the faithful Augustus, 626, 128. Augustus of the whole world, 443, 1. From his earliest beginnings he always cherished the faith with pious devotion, ibid., 2. He wrote his entire letter to Ambrose in his own hand, 753, 3. He requested a statement of faith from Ambrose, 444, 3. Ambrose hopes that his ears may be cleansed so that he will read his statement and place faith before all things, 470, 134 and following. In Emperor Gratian there was no fickle mind but steadfast faith, 496, 142. He restored peace to Ambrose and the Church, 753, 2. He showed himself so pleased by the declaration of faith that he ordered the Church’s basilica to be restored without any prompting, 604, 19. He had set aside the basilica in order to test the faith; he tested it in order to restore it, ibid., 21. He was faithful in the Lord, pious, gentle, pure of heart, and so chaste that apart from marriage he knew no intimacy with another woman, 1193, 74. He cleansed the churches of every stain of sacrilege, 809, 11. He abolished the privileges and worship of the gentiles at Rome, 825, 5; 842, 39; 1180, 20. He calls Ambrose his father and invites him to himself, 751, 1 and following. The Council of Aquileia gives him thanks, 806, 1 and following. Gratian is comforted by the recollection of his piety as he recounts that he spared many, 1213, 52. The man who raised arms against him had not yet abolished his decrees, 827, 16. Gratian sought Ambrose amid his dangers and called for him at the end of his life, 1195, 79. Gratian was taken away by an undeserved death, 1208, 39. Maximus denies Gratian’s relics to Valentinian, 890, 9. The tomb did not separate Gratian and Valentinian, whom affection did not separate; the cause of death did not divide those whom one piety joined; a difference of virtues did not make unlike those whom one religion cherished, 1194, 79. Theodosius avenged Gratian, 1208, 39. The dead Gratian embraces him, ibid. He meets Valentinian’s ascending soul, and the words with which he addressed it, 1192, 72. See AMBROSE, GOTHS, THEODOSIUS, VALENTINIAN.

GREGORIUS: He claims no priesthood for himself according to the tradition of the Fathers of the Church of Constantinople, 815, 4.

GOVERNOR: He knows at what watch Arcturus rises and what kinds of risings of Orion he should observe, 586, 196.

GYGES’ RING, 115, 30.

GYMNOSOPHISTS: The Indian gymnosophists, 938, 34 and following.

## H
## H

**HABAKKUK** flew without wings, 976, 20.

**HERESIES**, under the option of the Christian name and a certain nominal kinship of faith, seek to wound us with parricidal swords, 705, 12. Heresy, like a certain Hydra of fable, grew through its own wounds, or like the monstrous Scylla of legend, divided into various forms of perfidy, [Col. 1460] while using the name of the Christian sect as a superfluous pretext, 452, 46. Our fisherman John excluded all heresies in the opening words of his Gospel, 454, 57. Heretics truly possess death in the praises of Christ, 869, 19. Every sin concerns individuals, but the sin of heretics and schismatics concerns everyone, 421, 24. My day will fail sooner than the names of heretics and of the various sects, 711, 35.

**HAMILCAR** cast himself into the very fires that he had kindled, 841, 37.

**HEBION.** Christ is the Son of God, against Hebion, 569, 105.

**HEBREW.** The true Hebrew belongs wholly to God; everything he possesses is a matter of freedom, 780, 14.

**HELENA**, mother of the emperor Constantine, is said originally to have been a servant of a stable, and thus to have become known to the elder Constantius, 1209, 42. How she sought the wood of Christ’s cross, 1210, 43 et seq. How she found it, ibid., 45. She found the inscription and worshiped the King, not the wood, 1211, 46. She found the nails and ordered one to be made into a bridle and from the other wove a diadem; she sent these to her son Constantine, and he thereafter used both, ibid., 47. She placed the cross upon the heads of kings, so that Christ’s cross might be worshiped in kings, ibid., 48.

**HELIODORUS**, bishop of Altinum, 786, 1; 805, 76. His condemnation of Palladius, 802, 61.

The sprouting of herbs, 1148, 55.

**HEIRS** exist without property, and also with property, 1084, 3. Minor heirs assume the bare name of inheritance, not its authority; they have neither the right to command nor the right to use, 1084, 4. By human custom, monetary inheritance makes the inheritance more venerable, so that the rights of affection may become more honored, 1089, 1. You leave more to your successor if his portion does not serve the luxury of the present, but the price of the future, 1138, 13. You have someone who can present the heir to you: pay the poor person what is owed to the heir, ibid.

**INHERITANCE.** That alone is inheritance in which God is a portion, 899, 6. Where are true inheritance and true riches situated? 899, 5 et seq. The wicked and the weak cannot receive the beauty of the divine inheritance, ibid.

**HEROD.** See **OATH**.

**ESTHER** pursued the honor of chastity at the risk of her life, 138, 123 et seq.

**HIPPOCRATES**, master of medicine, explained the seven ages of human life, 979, 10.

The fabulous death of **HIPPOLYTUS**, 175, 6.

**SPAIN.** See **COUNCIL OF NICAEA**.

**HUMAN BEING.** The name *homo* is derived from *humus* [earth], and what does this itself teach? 111, 16. He came forth last of all creatures, pleasing in appearance and lofty in mind, so that he might be a wonder to every creature, 974, 14. Why was the human being created after all the other creatures? 970, 1 et seq. Why was he not praised immediately after being created by God? 253, 17 et seq. Whether man or woman, a person ought to know that he is made in the image and likeness of God, and should pursue the beauty of the soul, not of the body, 295, 68. The human being was generated for the sake of the human being, 36, 134. Formed as though for the completion of nature, for justice, and as the arbiter of justice among the other animals, 973, 13. God created the human being as an inhabitant of the world, for whom the whole world would be a homeland, 983, 16. God granted the human being everything that exists in the world, so that he would lack nothing necessary either for life or for a good life, 972, 11. His rewards are the fruits of the earth and the lights of heaven: the former for the use of the present life, the latter for the hope of eternal life, 971, 4. The human being is, as it were, a heavenly creature on earth, 972, 7. By the power of his mind alone, the human being infused his own strength into the other animals, so that they seem to obey him like a king in rivalry with one another and attend to his voice, 974, 16. We are not flesh, but spirit, in the substance of the soul and the power of the mind, 295, 68. In the human being, made in the likeness of God, there is an invisible *νοῦς* (*nous*, intellect or mind), 974, 14 et seq. In him there is nothing lower than what is visible, 253, 17. What is visible serves; what is invisible rules, ibid. The human being is, as it were, an inhabitant of all the elements: he lives among wild beasts, swims with the fish, flies above the birds, associates with angels, inhabits the earth and serves in heaven, plows the sea, is nourished by the air, cultivates the soil, travels the deep, fishes in the waves, hunts birds upon the sea, is an heir in heaven, and a co-heir with Christ, 975, 19. The ages of human life according to Hippocrates and Solon, 979, 11 et seq. Poured from the womb from warm places into cold, from moist into dry, we are tossed about like fish whom, as shipwrecked, the waves of nature have, so to speak, spewed into this life, 1205, 26. What is more miserable than we, who are cast into this life as though stripped and naked, with fragile bodies, unstable hearts, weak minds, anxious in the face of cares, sluggish for labor, and inclined toward pleasures? 1142, 29. The human being is truly a friend of God, as though a sharer in divine love and an heir of glory, 971, 3. Heaven belongs to the world; the human being is above the world: the former is a part of the world, the latter an inhabitant of paradise and Christ’s possession, 972, 9. God so cherished the human being whom he had created that he redeemed him when rejected, received him when cast out, and raised him from death through the passion of his only-begotten Son, [Col. 1461] 983, 16. The old and the new human being, 252, 13. The inner human being is made in the image of God, not the external one, 254, 20. The grace of others is outward; that of the human being is inward, 253, 18 et seq. The hidden human being of the heart, who is poor to the world, is rich to God, 295, 64. There are certain members of the inner human being, whose hands are judged by action, ears by hearing, and feet by a certain progress in good work, 647, 68. Guard your inner human being; do not neglect or despise him as though he were worthless, because he is a precious possession, 5, 11. Remain within, inside your peaceful, gentle, tranquil soul; do not leave it in order to raise this vessel of yours through honors, riches, or arrogance, 910, 23. See **SOUL**.

Among human beings there is unity of nature, arising from the commonality of nature, 527, 33. We are a worthless creature and quickly experience vices, 634, 183. The condition and nature of the human race fell from a purer state into a worse one when it reached a more depraved condition, 983, 14.

**HONORABLE CONDUCT** is like good health, 58, 229. No one has doubted that the blessed life rests upon honorable conduct, 69, 1. Nothing is to be sought except what is honorable, 115, 29. Nothing is more disgraceful than to have no love of honorable conduct, 122, 57. The wise person is recalled from wrongdoing not by fear of punishment but by the rule of honorable conduct, 115, 31. Utility always embraces honorable conduct, and honorable conduct utility, 130, 90. What is honorable is useful; what is useful is honorable; what is useful is just; and what is just is useful, 76, 25. What is honorable is useful, and what is useful is honorable, and conversely, 110, 9; 121, 52 et seq. We often find this asserted in the divine Scriptures, 76, 23. What is shameful cannot be useful; nor, conversely, can what is honorable be useless, 130, 90. See **UTILITY**. The teachers of the nations did not even think that honorable conduct should be joined with pleasure, 1028, 23. The less honorable conduct follows glory, the more it rises above it, 70, 2. Honorable conduct is hindered by no adversity; it shines forth in adversity and excels more greatly there than in prosperity, 132, 98. How great was the concern for honorable conduct shown by the four lepers during the siege of Samaria? 136, 117 et seq. See **DECORUM**.

**HONORATI**, 854, 6.

**HONORIUS**, when Theodosius was dying, was knocking at the doors of adolescence, though more advanced in age than Josiah, 1202, 15. He wept because he was not accompanying the revered remains of his father Theodosius all the way to Constantinople, 1214, 55. Ambrose consoles him, ibid. et seq. See **THEODOSIUS**.

**HOUR.** The loss even of a single hour is not insignificant; one hour is a portion of the whole of life, 1046, 97.

**HORONTIANUS**, an heir of the Church from the first flower of childhood, which received him through the laying on of Ambrose’s hands, 1068, 25. He asks Ambrose why the human being was created last, after all the other creatures, 970, 1. He began with the Law and was confirmed in the Gospel, 1092, 15.

**HOSPITALITY** is a public form of humaneness, 95, 103. The commandment of hospitality must be observed, 186, 4 et seq. In acts of hospitality, every form of kindness should indeed be shown, but more abundant honor should be offered to the just, 95, 107. Hospitality is to be cherished—and why? 1047, 105. We read that peoples were destroyed in a grievous catastrophe because they violated the rights of hospitality, 844, 6. One ought to be a guest by choice rather than from necessity, 843, 6.

**ENEMIES** were called strangers in the ancient custom, 38, 141. Moses was remarkable in this respect: by divine intervention, through his own virtue he even turned away from the enemy punishments that had been threatened, 130, 93. Justice must be preserved even toward enemies, 37, 139. To strike an enemy is victory, 1018, 1.

**HUMANENESS** is the human being’s distinctive and domestic virtue—and from where does the name come? 111, 16. See **HOSPITALITY**. Humaneness often bends those whom neither virtue nor reason could overcome, 488, 89.

**HUMILITY** consists in claiming nothing for oneself and considering oneself inferior, 102, 134. Christ is the beginning of humility: he accepted the form of a servant, although in the majesty of virtue he equaled God the Father, 506, 52. Christ is the flower of humility and simplicity, 226, 57. There is no humility unless it is without pretense and without deceit; true humility possesses a devout sincerity of mind, 758, 18. Not an ignorant humility, but one that possesses modesty and self-knowledge, is praised, 92, 90. The more humble person is more praiseworthy; the more abject person is more just, 436, 91. Humility increases grace, 86, 67. It delivers those in danger and raises those who have fallen, 1205, 27. No one can see divine things more clearly than the person who, conscious of his humility, does not know how to exalt himself, 202, 62.

**HUNNUS** was summoned against the Juthungi, 890, 8. He was compelled to abandon his triumphs, ibid. See **CHUNNI**, **ALANS**.

The **HYDRAS**, with their many teeth, were believed to have bristled in the Theban region like a crop of armed men, 1152, 70. See **HERESIES**.

**HYGINUS**, an aged bishop, for whom nothing remained except his last breath, was led into exile without clothing and without a mattress, 891, 12.

A **HYMN** is addressed particularly to God, 59, 230. They say that the people were deceived by the verses of my hymns; plainly, I do not deny even this, 873, 34.

## I

**ICARUS** lost what he had previously perhaps believed himself to be: a bird, 1169, 129. What did the flight of Icarus signify? 242, 116.

It is not permitted even for catechumens to supply expenses for idols, 1010, 2. The sacrifice of one person is more tolerable than the falling away of everyone, 825, 8. See **PAGANS**, **VALENTINIAN**.

**IDLENESS** does not possess what it possesses, 899, 5.

**ALIEN FIRE** is lust; alien fire is every blaze of unjust desire; alien fire is every burning of avarice. No one is cleansed by this fire, but is burned up, 1058, 8.

The person who pleads ignorance quickly deserves pardon, 1178, 13. The fault was less serious where there was ignorance of the fault, 1078, 5.

The devastation of Illyricum and Thrace, 86, 70. The Church redeemed the captives taken there, ibid. The coast of Illyricum is suspect, 818, 7.

**IMMODESTY.** Human immodesty is so great that many do not know how to offer to religious minds what they offer to the pleasure of the ears, 177, 14.

**IMMORTALITY.** One kind belongs to the divine nature, another to ours, 500, 19. What is heavier than wretched immortality? 1167, 124. Immortality is a burden rather than a benefit unless grace gives it support, 1146, 47.

**EMPERORS** of two months, 834, 7. The emperor issues laws that he himself is the first to observe, 861, 9. This is the difference between good and bad rulers: good rulers love freedom, while the wicked love servitude, 946, 2. A usurper brings on war; an emperor protects his rightful claim, 891, 10. Although you are emperor, you ought to be subject to God all the more, 1011, 8. Emperors, who want honor to be shown to you, allow us to show it to him whom you wish to be acknowledged as the author of your empire, 1012, 12. At the death of faithful emperors there is a certain reverence of faith, a certain modesty of the Church; and at the premature death of pious rulers, the whole beauty of the Church is more sorrowful, 1175, 6. The emperor is within the Church, not above the Church, 873, 36. It benefits the Church that emperors be Christian and pious, 1000, 14. Emperors serve almighty God and the sacred faith, 824, 1. What is more excellent than the faith of an emperor whom power does not exalt, pride does not raise up, but piety inclines? 1201, 12. Victory is usually sought more through the faith of the emperor than through the valor of the soldiers, 444, 3. The Christian emperor has learned to honor the altar of Christ alone, 835, 10. Divine things are not subject to imperial dignity, 854, 8; 857, 16. The emperor has been entrusted with authority over public walls, not sacred ones, 857, 16. Palaces belong to the emperor; the churches belong to the priest, ibid. By ancient right, empires were bestowed by priests, not usurped, 858, 23. It is commonly said that emperors have desired the priesthood more than priests have desired the empire, ibid. Is envy of Caesar always stirred up against the servants of God? 872, 30. See **EQUITY**, **SOLDIER**.

**IMPIETY** invokes this against him as a charge, so that it may use the imperial name as a pretext, 872, 30.
