The **IMPIOUS PERSON** is punishment for himself, 14, 46. The examples of impiety must be abolished together with the impious person, 953, 23. The divine judgment has this habit: those who have committed impious acts condemn themselves by their own confession, 181, 28.

Three differences of impossibilities are explained, 530, 48 et seq. See **CHRIST**, **GOD**.

What is the difference between a wicked person and an envious person? 107, 152.

The preposition **IN**. See **PER**.

The mystery of God’s **INCARNATION** is the salvation of the whole creation, 570, 106. We recognize the Holy Spirit as the author of the Lord’s incarnation, 641, 41; 645, 59. Just as the Father created the sacrament of the Lord’s incarnation, so the Holy Spirit created it, and Christ himself also created it, 645, 59 et seq. See **CHRIST**.

Do not reject the Lord’s **REBUKES**, because they arise from love and grace, 300, 84.

**INDIANS.** See **GYMNOSOPHISTS**.

**INDICIA**, a virgin consecrated by Saint Zeno, 765, 1. She was always honored at Verona and was visited by virgins and priests, 768, 12. At the house of Syagrius she was summoned to trial without an author of the accusation, without an accuser, and without anyone formally presenting the charge, and was ordered to be subjected to inspection, ibid. et seq. What the causes of this accusation were, 769, 16 et seq. Of what crime was she accused? 770, 18 et seq. Renatus and Leontius were her accusers, ibid., 19. They withdrew from the assembly of the bishops, 771, 20. Indicia was truly accused by Maximus, 766, 4; 770, 17 et seq. Ambrose’s sister, Paterna, and Indicia’s nurse bear witness to her integrity, 771, 22 et seq. She is acquitted by Ambrose in the assembly of the bishops, 771, 24. See **SYAGRIUS**.

The **INDICTION** begins in the month of September, 885, 16. [Col. 1463]

**INDIGNATION.** See **ANGER**.

Industry increased grace through imitation of nature, 22, 78. If there is any defect in nature, industry should correct it, 21, 75.

**INFANTS** are those who do not know how to speak the word of God and do not receive his works, 1091, 9.

**INGENIOSUS**, a Jovinianist, is condemned, 969, 14.

I nowhere find the term **UNBEGOTTEN** in the divine Scriptures, 721, 80. The designation “unbegotten” declares that the Father is not from another, nor the Son from himself, 725, 100. The word “unbegotten” in no way prevents us from believing that Christ is of one nature and substance with the Father, 78, 113. Many and countless examples can be supplied in which what has not been begotten is called “unbegotten,” 724, 94.

Let each person know his own **TALENT** and apply himself to what he has chosen as suitable for him, 57, 224. Whatever each person’s talent leads him toward, or whatever duty suits him, is fulfilled with greater grace, 57, 225.

We must pray **FOR ENEMIES AND PERSECUTORS**, 1183, 33. It is a virtue, if, having been injured, you forgive, 122, 59. This is not the only form of justice: not to injure someone who has not injured you; there is also this, to forgive the person who has injured you, 1042, 83. The person who knows how to forgive recognizes that he is human, 1203, 16.

Nothing is more squalid than **INIQUITY**, nothing more splendid than justice, 1063, 4.

There are three classes of people who receive injury—and what are they? 61, 242. The person who disregards an injury is better than the one who grieves over it, 7, 22. The person who does not endure an injury seems almost to have inflicted it, 1101, 6. Forgive your injuries, so that you may be sons of Jacob, 1047, 102.

To be **INNOCENT** means to be ignorant of what causes harm, 125, 68. God commands us to live in simplicity of heart and innocence, 126, 75. For the wise person, hope of impunity is not a hiding place, but innocence, 115, 31. To strike the guilty is equity; to strike the innocent is homicide, 1018, 1. The Lord is praised where there is a clean possession and an innocent discipline of the household, 66, 256.

**INNOCENT CHILDREN** received the palm before they received the understanding of nature, 54, 213. The innocent martyrs, 979, 9.

**FOLLY** makes a person a slave, not nature; nor does manumission make him free, but discipline, 932, 9. No one is condemned more severely by another’s judgment than the fool is by his own, since he is himself the author of his misfortunes, 1043, 85. See **WISE PERSON**.

**ENVY.** See **WICKED PERSON**.

**ANGER.** They say that most philosophers granted impunity for crimes committed in anger, 1202, 14. But sacred Scripture pronounced better concerning this, ibid. If we become angry, our emotion should receive movement according to nature, not sin, which is contrary to nature, 1036, 60. It is better to find praise for mercy in indignation than to be stirred by anger toward vengeance, 1202, 14. Anger must be avoided—and how? 25, 90 et seq. It must be moderated, 298, 77. At all times, insofar as possible, a Christian man ought to moderate his anger, and especially when he approaches prayer, 383, 19.

**IRENAEUS** is not ashamed to glory in the sufferings of Christ, 901, 17.

What the sacrifice of **ISAAC** prefigured, 1160, 98. Let us imitate his goodness; let us imitate his chastity, 1160, 99. What else was in him but an inheritance of holiness that ennobled his father? 921, 8. When Rebecca came, he perceived in spirit the mysteries of the future Church, 997, 16. He received the woman who was coming as a type of the Church as his wife, 634, 184.

Those who receive the sacred rites of **ISIS** shave their heads and eyebrows, 1013, 3.

**ITALY**, which customarily sends confessors: Italy has sometimes been tested, but never changed, 496, 142. Italy is pressed by an impure and cruel enemy who would spare neither chastity nor safety, 1122, 31. Italy has long been quiet and secure from the Arians and is troubled by no disturbance from heretics, 818, 3. The bishops of Italy, by letters sent to Theodosius, ask that he order a council to be convened, 818, 2 et seq. Italy celebrates Theodosius as the author of its freedom, 1214, 56. Italy’s mourning at the death of the younger Valentinian, 1175, 4.

## J
## J

**JACOB.** Accepted at home by his parents; a shepherd faithful to the master of the flock; a diligent son-in-law to his father-in-law; tireless in labor; frugal at table; foremost in making amends; generous in recompense, 30, 111. A man intent upon discipline and seeking the way to pursue virtue sought not a human guide but heavenly oracles, 900, 11. How many adversities he endured, 1140, 23. Since he was exiled from his parents on account of piety, not wickedness, he spoke with God and increased in wealth, children, and favor, 1046, 101. He showed that folly is worse than slavery, so that slavery is its remedy, 932, 7. In worshiping Esau seven times, he was not worshiping a man, but worshiping in spirit the one whom he knew would come in human flesh, 1047, 101. Jacob’s ladder is not without significance: through Christ’s cross, the future fellowship of angels and human beings was prefigured, 1160, 100. Sleeping a brief sleep, he obtained [Col. 1464] what his descendants afterward acquired through great labor, 823, 4. He was reaching toward the Church, in order to lead there the forces of peoples, bring in the riches of nations, and pour forth posterity, fleeing the shadows of empty things, preferring the living beauty of virtues to senseless images, and serious matters to things that win applause, 900, 13. Jacob was the fountain of all disciplines, 931, 7. In him were the four cardinal virtues, 32, 120. Let us follow him and his ways, so that we may arrive at patience, the mother of the faithful, 901, 17. Let us imitate in him the type of Christ; let there be in us some likeness of his deeds. We shall be his companions if we become his imitators, 1160, 100.

**JACOBUS**, our brother and fellow presbyter, sheltered from the farthest recess of Persia, chose for himself the shores and pleasant places of Campania as a place of rest, where, after his long labors, he might spend the remainder of his life, 1016, 1.

**BOASTING** is seductive, which even Paul fears; slippery, which is also guarded against in Paul, 238, 106. It must be avoided, 139, 106. Christ teaches that it ought to be far from the perfect, 224, 44. See **GENEROSITY**, **WISDOM**.

**JANUARIUS**, bishop, 786, 1; 805, 76. His condemnation of Palladius, 803, 64.

**JANUARIUS**, a Jovinianist, is condemned, 969, 14.

**JAPHETH** is called *latitude* in Latin, 1005, 3. In the enumeration of the generations he is preferred to his elder brother; in the blessing he is substituted for him, ibid.

**FASTING.** Through the spiritual fat of fasting the soul grows rich, and its virtues and fruits multiply through the abundance of your mind, so that there may be in you a drunkenness of sobriety, 1030, 31. The saints themselves become more excellent when they fast. When Moses fasted, he received the law; Peter was taught the grace of the New Testament; Daniel closed the mouths of lions and saw the affairs of future times, 1026, 16. Christ brought us salvation not through luxury but through fasting, 498, 6. Whoever does not fast is unprotected and naked, exposed to injury, 968, 11. What salvation can there be for us unless we wash away our sins through fasting? 1026, 16. Christ taught that evil cannot easily be conquered except through our fasting, 1026, 15. Anxiety clings to those who fast, 886, 20. Women fast every day and perform fasts that have not been prescribed, 256, 31. Anyone who prescribes a fast on the day of the resurrection does not believe in Christ’s resurrection, 883, 11. We cannot fast on the Lord’s Day, ibid. See **ABSTINENCE**, **ADAM**, **NINEVEH**.

**JEPHTHAH.** The deed of one who sacrificed his daughter is not to be approved, 215, 6. Jephthah’s promise was harsh, and its fulfillment harsher, 127, 78. Jephthah’s daughter paid for her father’s rash offering with her blood, 291, 51. He caused what had happened accidentally through impiety to become a sacrifice of piety, 128, 81. His deed was more excellent and more ancient than that of the two Pythagoreans, 127, 80 and following. See **ABRAHAM**.

**JEREMIAH** could not bear the fire of charity with which he was inflamed for the prophetic office, 294, 61.

**JEROBOAM.** The hand that had immediately withered through sacrilege was healed through religious devotion, 172, 38.

**JERUSALEM**, that good mother of souls which is in heaven, 917, 12.

**THE NAME OF JESUS** was outwardly present to those fighting for victory; inwardly, the form of the Lord’s passion was present to those in danger, for salvation, 574, 128. Jesus came to this earth to receive a kingdom from us, 576, 147. If you seek Jesus, abandon the broken cisterns, 634, 184. See **CHRIST**.

**JESUS SON OF NUN** was worthy to triumph in the battle of faith, 574, 127. Jesus son of Nun was a type of Christ, 553, 12.

**JEZEBEL.** What does the name signify? 285, 30. Jezebel is the Synagogue, flowing vainly and abounding vainly in the Scriptures, which she neither keeps nor understands, 1041, 79.

**JOHN THE BAPTIST** was an angel, 351, 7. A teacher of abstinence and a kind of new angel of the earth, 1030, 29. Elizabeth heard Mary’s voice first, but John first sensed the Lord’s grace, 542, 114. He was devoted before he was born, 165, 12. Although he did not baptize in the Spirit, he nevertheless preached both Christ and the Spirit, 608, 41. The forerunner himself doubted concerning Christ, although this was in the type of the Synagogue, 522, 4. It was not without reason that he remained bodily undefiled: for three months the Lord’s mother exercised him with a certain oil of her presence and an ointment of her purity, 262, 50. He preferred honor to safety, 129, 89. All the circumstances of his murder are described with the greatest eloquence, 181, 26 and following. See **BAPTISM**, **DESERT**, **ELIZABETH**.

**JOHN.** In relation to the divine mysteries, he was quieter than the fish he had previously caught; brought to life by Christ, he heard the voice in John and recognized the Word in Christ, 707, 15. The Lord’s mother would not have gone over to John except as the possessor of grace, where Christ had his dwelling, 286, 33. John reclined on Christ’s breast so that it might be shown that he had drawn divine mysteries from the chief and hidden source of wisdom, 1052, 4. He reclined on Christ’s breast so that you might understand that his head was filled with wisdom by a certain hidden means, 710, 29. With a kind of greater trumpet he poured forth eternal mysteries, 364, 11. He wrote more mystical things, 260, 46. Why did Christ entrust his mother to him from the cross? 285, 32. He is subscribed to Christ’s testament, 261, 48. John sealed Christ’s testament, a witness worthy of so great a testator, 1048, 109. It was thought that he had been promised not to die, but this was not believed, 1146, 49. I do not wonder that he spoke the divine mysteries more than the others, since Mary was present to him, the court of heavenly sacraments, 262, 50. He excluded all heresies in the opening words of his Gospel, 454, 57. See **MARY**.

**JOB.** Strengthened against the devil’s temptations, he preserved an unblemished record of steadfastness, 875, 5. The devil tempted him in many ways; at last he received power to tempt his body, 864, 4. He tempted him in his possessions, tempted him in his children, tempted him in his body, 856, 15. Job was irreproachable in both prosperity and adversity, 30, 113. It is explained how nothing was lacking in him by way of virtue, nor did anything sinful creep in, 52, 204. He was exceedingly strong, 48, 179. And blessed was he, from whose house the poor never departed empty-handed, 12, 39. No one loved Christ more; he loved him even amid the tortures of his own body, 294, 61. He first discovered what Plato and Cicero said much later, 13, 44.

**JESTS.** All jests are to be entirely avoided by ecclesiastical men, 28, 102 and following.

**JONATHAN**, out of piety, avoided neither his father’s displeasure nor danger to his safety, 138, 124.

**THE BOOK OF JONAH** was read according to custom, 858, 25.

**JOSEPH.** His prudence and other virtues are commended at length, 89, 82 and following. His virtues, especially his modesty, 19, 66. His soul was so inaccessible to sin that it rather penetrated sin itself, 932, 10. So that he would not be shamefully exposed, he left his garment behind and fled naked, 1015, 12. When accused, he kept silent, so that innocence rather than his tongue might defend him, 300, 88. How many adversities he endured, 1140, 24. The sale did not make him a slave, 933, 12. Slavery was wretched, but he who was placed in slavery was not wretched, 75, 20. How submissive in slavery, how steadfast in virtue, how kind in prison, wise in interpretation, moderate in power, provident in abundance, just in famine, and so forth, 30, 112. He knew how to humble himself and learned the virtue of humility; he rejected weakness, 759, 19; ibid., 22 and following. As one sold, he was a type of Christ, 691, 123 and following. He was humbled as a type of Christ, 759, 22. When he endured slander, he preferred to undergo a false accusation rather than report a true one, 759, 22. By the counsel of providence he helped Pharaoh more usefully than if he had contributed money, 87, 74. He did not wish to appear to have lavished what belonged to another, 89, 79. Why did he show himself pleasing to all by acquiring for the king the rights of the lands? 89, 80. His fertile spirit made the barrenness of time fruitful through a certain abundance of counsel and heart, 84, 59. He was neither broken by adversity nor elated by prosperity, 760, 23.

**JOSEPH**, Mary’s husband, suspected her of wrongdoing while he still did not know the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation, 768, 13. Christ’s brothers could have been brothers through Joseph, not through Mary, 260, 43.

**JOSEPHUS**, the historiographer, 981, 2. What opinion he held concerning the earthly Paradise, ibid.

**JOSIAH** did not survive beyond the eighteenth year of his reign by the merits of his faith, 1189, 57. The same king was preferred to all those before him, 1208, 38.

**JOSHUA** was a great man in the miracles of faith and great in triumphs: Moses’ deeds were more august, Joshua’s more successful, 94, 99.

**JUPITER.** They attribute to Jupiter thunderbolts which he did not possess, so that they may testify to the reproaches which he did possess, 176, 7.

**JOVINIAN** is condemned, 969, 14.

**JOVINUS**, bishop, 786, 1; 805, 76.

**JUBILEE** is a sacred number, 1163, 108.

**JUDAS MACCABEUS** found a more glorious place in death than in triumphs, 54, 209.

**JUDAS THE TRAITOR.** Why was he entrusted with the money box? 18, 64. The Lord Jesus is of such great compassion that he would even have granted Judas forgiveness if he had awaited Christ’s mercy, 1059, 9. By God’s pity he could not have been excluded from forgiveness if he had done penance before Christ, not before the Jews, 422, 27. The devil claimed Judas as his own possession, 1045, 95. See **AVARICE**.

**JUDAEA** is within the Church; the Law is within grace, 698, 162. He violated the two things superior to all others, faith and piety; but in both, Christ, the author of faith and piety, 691, 124.

**THE JEWISH PEOPLE.** Although frequently prone to fault, nevertheless, as long as the Law was being given, they are not shown to have erred through sacrilege, 1054, 2. The benefits bestowed on them by God in the desert are recalled, 961, 24. It is much more marvelous that the army of the fathers could have been freed through one man than that it could have been deceived, 996, 15. The promise was made to us before the Law was given to the Jews, 1089, 2. The one who is a Jew inwardly is the one who excels, 1076, 22. The Jew separates the son of the Virgin Mary from God the Father, 704, 6. The Jews, through a civic kind of blemish of envy, refused to believe in the Son of God and were therefore disowned, 191, 20. They perished while despising the depths of meaning and following the bare words, 503, 37. Liars concerning divine matters, 952, 19. They deny that they are bound by Roman laws, so that they consider the laws crimes, ibid., 20. The Jewish people are unstable through their lapsing, humble, more ready for treachery, fickle, and forgetful of the commandments, 1081, 3. Like children, the Jews too are under a pedagogue, 1084, 5. In a Jew scarcely any portion of devotion could be found, 780, 14. The Jews are rightly accused in their crimes, because they chose an accuser and rejected a good judge, 1092, 14. What the Jew praises in us, he himself does not follow, 958, 10. He sees the inheritance but does not possess it, 1084, 6. He was therefore abandoned, because he neither did penance nor accepted grace, 426, 44. He is under a curse; we are in blessing, 1090, 5. Through his offense there is salvation for the nations; through his negligence victory has been preserved for us, 198, 47. Let us abandon Jewish rites; let us abandon the shadow and follow the sun, 1093, 1.

**JUDGE.** Is one who justly condemns a guilty person to death to be deprived of communion in the sacraments? 892, 2 and following. What made this question more difficult? 894, 3. Our ancestors preferred to be more lenient toward judges, 893, 9. Whoever issues commands must always observe the measure of decrees; and whoever distributes tasks must preserve fairness in his examination, 207, 78. In judgment, let favor be absent; let the merits of the case decide, 99, 125. In judging, we must form our sentence not according to our will and power but according to equity, 1092, 10. No suspicion of bias or laxity falls upon those who observe everything in the presence of the parties, 818, 5. When does a defeated person think anyone other than himself more just? 1100, 3. I know that many pagans are accustomed to boast that they brought back an unstained axe from the administration of a province, 892, 3. In the council chamber Christ is not usually the accused but the judge, 864, 3. A distinguished example of ecclesiastical judgment in the case of the virgin Indicia, 765, 1 and following. See **BISHOP**. He condemns himself more severely who condemns in another what he himself commits, 896, 12.

**THE DAY OF JUDGMENT.** It would not have benefited us to know the day of judgment, and why? 589, 209 and following. The grace of the day of judgment shines forth, so that acquittal may follow and reward the service of the saints, 630, 170.

**JUDITH.** Her courage and other virtues are praised, 196, 37 and following. By pursuing honor, she found advantage, 128, 84. With a noble contempt for her own safety, she ended the danger of the siege and gained public advantage through her own honor, 129, 88. Solely under the title of sobriety, she brought back a victory won by the strength of a man, 1029, 29. Her two triumphs, 128, 82.

**JULIANA** urges her children to vow themselves to virginity, 282, 17 and following. With what address did she exhort her son and daughters? 281, 13 and following. She offered to God all that she had—namely, sons and daughters, 291, 54. She prepared and offered to the Lord the temple that we dedicate today, 280, 10. She was worthy of honor, 280, 11. She lamented more deeply the minister taken from the sacred altars than a spouse taken from herself or a father taken from her children, 280, 12. Her husband, a minister of the sacred altar, died suddenly, 284, 24. The reward of Juliana, who piously gave the whole gift of her offspring to the Lord, 302, 93.

**JULIAN**, the emperor, abandoned the author of his salvation when he devoted himself to the error of philosophy, 1213, 51. Since he wrongly trusted the responses of the haruspices, he deprived himself of the means of returning, 842, 38. When he ordered the temple at Jerusalem to be restored, those who were carrying out the divine work of cleansing were consumed by fire, 949, 12. In his time, the man who overturned the altar and disrupted the sacrifice, after being condemned by the judge, achieved martyrdom, 951, 17. But the judge did not escape heavenly vengeance, ibid. Julian is praised because he relaxed the taxes imposed on the provincials, 1180, 21.

**JULIAN VALENS**, a priest, allegedly profaned a necklace and a Gothic armlet and, dressed in the manner of the pagans, dared to appear before the Roman army, 809, 9. Since he was nearby, he avoided the priestly council at Aquileia, ibid. How greatly the priestly name is disgraced in Italy, ibid., 10.

**AN OATH.** For Herod, perjury would have been more tolerable, 127, 77. What is swearing except confessing the divine power of the one whom you call the guardian of your faith? 826, 9. Do not swear, lest you begin to commit perjury, 297, 74.

**RIGHT.** Nature generated common right; appropriation made right private, 35, 132.

**JUSTA AND GRATA.** What great mourning they displayed at the death of their brother Valentinian! 1184, 36 and following. They attended his funeral oration, ibid. Ambrose consoles them, ibid., 38, 40 and following. They passed the course of two months in the daily embrace of their brother’s funeral, 1187, 49.

**JUSTICE** has many forms, 1129, 57. Philosophers say that the first form of justice is that no one should harm anyone unless provoked; this is nullified by the authority of the Gospel, 35, 131. Justice is sparing toward itself but wholly given outwardly; whatever it possesses, through a kind of severity toward itself, pours into its neighbors while it is seized by love of the common good, 1129, 57. It is directed toward the fellowship of the human race and toward the common good, 35, 130. It assigns to each person his own, does not claim what belongs to another, and neglects its own advantage in order to preserve common equity, 31, 115. Great is the splendor of that virtue which is born more for others than for itself, 36, 136. Born more for others than for itself, it seeks not so much its own advantages as public benefits, 241, 114. The piety of justice is first toward God, second toward one’s country, third toward parents, and likewise toward all, 34, 127. Justice is rendered to God through sobriety of mind, 782, 19. Justice cannot exist without prudence, 34, 126; 80, 43. Justice is the higher virtue; generosity is the more pleasing, 35, 130. Justice excellently commends men placed in charge of an office; injustice removes and attacks them, 92, 93. This is the highest justice: to sell what you have and give it to the poor, 1130, 60. Desire for power makes the manly form of justice effeminate, 36, 138. See **AVARICE**.

**THE JUST MAN** regards common things as his own and his own things as common, 32, 118. He considers nothing except what is steadfast and honorable, 109, 7. He is a law unto himself and does not need to seek from elsewhere the form of virtue that he carries enclosed in his heart, 934, 18. He is his own source of favor, 14, 46. He is never alone who is always with God, 109, 7. He possesses God’s commandments, his oracles, and his precepts; in these he is rich, in these he is nourished, in these he delights as though in every kind of wealth, 899, 6. These are the weapons of the just man: that by yielding he may conquer, 7, 20. He fears not betrayal of a crime but contamination by it, 251, 7. He always lends at interest; the unjust man is in need, 942, 6. Why do we readily entrust our safety and reputation to a just and prudent man? 80, 43. It is characteristic of the just man to entrust more to the judgment of good people than to the insolence of an accuser and to be content with the dignity of his own conduct, 6, 18.

**JUSTUS**, bishop of Lyons, another envoy of the Gauls, 786, 1; 790, 15; 805, 76. His condemnation of Palladius, 801, 56.

**JUTHUNGI** were ravaging Rhaetia, 890, 8. See **HUN**.

**YOUNG MEN.** Discontented with the present, as though ungrateful, they demand a change of life, 1046, 98. Many have been able to withdraw from sins and the instability of youth in old age; but rare is the person who in youth has borne the heavy yoke with serious sobriety, 1177, 10. The fickleness of youth is subject to the desires of the world, 242, 116. It is a great thing to abstain from the vices of youth, or to abandon them at the very threshold of youth and turn toward more serious matters, 1178, 13. Youth can grow old in conduct, and old age can flourish in deeds, 1046, 98.

## L

**LABARUM.** A standard consecrated in the name of Christ, 949, 9. It was entrusted to a commander, ibid.

**LABOR.** A change of labor is a truce of rest, 178, 16. God is accustomed to give his people a reward beyond the merit of their labor, 289, 44.

**TEARS** are indicators of piety, not incitements of grief, 1116, 10. Grief alone does not have tears; joy also has its tears, piety arouses weeping, and prayer moistens the bed, ibid. There is also a certain pleasure in weeping for pious affections, and usually grief evaporates heavily through tears, 1185, 41. Tears often nourish and lift up the mind; weeping cools the breast and consoles a sorrowful feeling, 1185, 38. Let us wash away the sins of the body with the tears of repentance, 179, 21. In them are the wages of charity and the duties of piety, 195, 36. There is no doubt that the patronage of the apostles can be obtained through your tears, 1121, 29. Tears are redemptive: when poured out for the dead, they benefit the living, 195, 36. Tears are the priest’s defenses, 864, 2. See **WEEPING**.

**LAETUS.** His disagreement with Marcellus. See **AMBROSE**.

**THE FALLEN.** Forgiveness is to be granted to the fallen, 396, 24 and following. This is beautifully proved by comparison, 397, 25. Jesus glories more greatly in the fallen when he receives those who return, 397, 26.

**GENEROSITY.** There are two kinds: one of liberality, the other of extravagant spending, 96, 109. In giving, one must consider age and weakness, and sometimes also modesty, 42, 158. Generosity is not approved if one extorts from one person what one gives to another, 39, 145. No one should be ashamed to become poor from being rich while giving to the poor, 40, 151. Those who seek the beauty of generosity solely for display seek the reward of the present age and do not store it up for the future, 434, 84. See **LIBERALITY**.

**LEWDNESS** usually lies hidden beneath a mournful garment of mind, 1138, 12. See **RUST**, **LUXURY**.

**A ROBBER.** If a Christian encounters an armed robber who strikes him, he cannot strike back, 114, 27.

**PRAISE.** A man’s praise is not at the beginning but at the end, 254, 21. In praises, one usually commends the homeland and parents, so that, by recalling the origin, the dignity of the succession may be magnified, 151, 20. No one is more praiseworthy than the one whom everyone can praise, 147, 6.

**LAURENCE** demonstrated that the poor are the treasures of the Church, 104, 140. The consecration of the Lord’s blood was entrusted to him, 55, 214. With what words did he begin to address Bishop Xystus, who was being led [Col. 1468] to martyrdom? 54, 214. Placed upon the gridiron, he said: “It is roasted; turn it over and eat,” 56, 216. What Calanus the Indian gymnosophist boasted in words, Laurence proved by deeds: that he might be burned alive and, surviving the flames, say, “Turn it over and eat,” 939, 37. See **SATYRUS**.

**LAURENCE**, the son of Juliana, was obtained by his parents after they vowed him to the martyr Laurence, 281, 15. The vows of his parents shaped him, 291, 52. Before he was born, they consecrated and promised him to the temple and service of God, 291, 52. Juliana found her son Laurence in the Church, proclaiming the oracles of the sacred readings, 292, 55.

**BATHING.** It was an ancient custom in the city of Rome and in most cities that adult sons did not bathe with their parents, nor sons-in-law with their fathers-in-law, 22, 79.

**LAZARUS**, the poor man, bore the yoke from his youth; therefore he rests uniquely in Abraham’s bosom, 1213, 53. In the resurrection of Lazarus, the resurrection of sinners is explained, 428, 54 and following. What we read about Lazarus we ought to believe concerning every converted sinner, 430, 63. The resurrection of bodies is proved by the example of Lazarus’s resurrection, whose circumstances are examined, 1154, 77 and following.

**READINGS** in the Church, 1130, 61. Readings in the Church during the morning hours, 857, 20. Readings are conducted in the new Basilica, 855, 13. A lector is urgently requested, ibid. The series of the sacred Scriptures began to be read, 875, 3. By an accidental reading, ibid., 4. The book of Job was read through in the Church as a solemn observance and at the proper time, 855, 14. The history of Naboth was read in the Church, 868, 17. See **JONAH**, **LAURENCE**. Whoever reads much from the Scriptures and understands it is filled; whoever has been filled waters others, 755, 4.

**LECTOR**, a child, 1130, 61.

**LEONTIUS AND RENATUS**, two men of iniquity, accusers of the virgin Indicia, 770, 19. Condemned by Ambrose’s episcopal judgment, 771, 24. See **INDICIA**.

**LEOPARDUS**, our fellow presbyter, 969, 13.

**LEVITE.** He is called “my very own” or “the one who is for me,” 65, 255. Moses did not divide the land among the Levites, whose dwelling was not earthly but higher; instead, without earthly labor, he assigned them the stipends of sacred service, 287, 37. The Levites are removed from the midst of Israel because they have nothing in common with the people, whose secular firstborn are destroyed, 920, 5. Just as the saints are the firstborn of the Church, so too are the Levites, since they also are firstborn—not holy by the order of birth but through the gift of sanctification, 920, 3. He is the true Levite, avenger and defender, who puts the flesh to death in order to preserve the spirit, 1056, 8. The office of the Levites is no small one, 67, 259. What that office is, ibid., 260 and following. How necessary it is that they not be held by earthly desires, 65, 255. Why is a Levite chosen to guard the sanctuary? 69, 265. Levites and priests must be strangers to all marital intercourse, 66, 258. The Levite is Christ’s possession, since he claims nothing earthly for himself, 288, 41. Christ’s lot is his Levitical lot; his lot is virginity; his lot is widowhood, 287, 39.

**THE LAW OF NATURE** is assumed through customs, not conditions, 934, 17. It is not written but born within us; it is not learned through any reading, but is expressed in each person through a kind of flowing spring of nature and imbibed by human minds, 1078, 3. How many things will you find that were not prohibited by the law given through Moses and yet are prohibited by a certain voice of nature? 1019, 5. See **BOOK**.

Moses’ Law entered in place of the natural law, 1079, 10. The first tablets of the Law were broken so that the second might be restored; through the preaching of the Gospel, faithlessness was shattered and vanished, 1055, 5. Since God gave the Law to Moses, why are there many things in the Law that now appear to have been rendered void by the Gospel? 1080, 1 and following. How can the same author of both Testaments have caused what was permitted in the Law to become impermissible through the Gospel? ibid. Why did the Law of Moses have to be imposed? 1078, 5 and following. Why was the Law given if it produced wrath and introduced transgression? 1077, 1 and following. The Law was not superfluous, since, like a pedagogue, it attends upon the weaker, 1091, 9. How the Law was our pedagogue in Christ, 1080, 1 and following. They followed certain things from the divine readings like leaves of trees, not fruit; they lived in the shadow of the Law, 896, 15. In the Law there is a portion; in the Gospel, perfection, 1082, 5. See **GOSPEL**.

The law of God taught us what to follow; human laws cannot teach this. They are accustomed to extort compliance from the fearful, but they cannot inspire faith, 861, 10. The true character of the law is expressed in our conduct, when we walk in the image of God, 1163, 109. What is relaxed for someone does not prejudice the law, 1019, 9. Whoever binds the lesser does not release the greater but binds it, 1019, 4.

**A BOOK** does not blush, 145, 1. A book is in a bad state if it is not defended by an advocate, 990, 3. Everyone is deceived by his own writings, and they pass by the ear; just as even deformed children please their parents, so a writer’s unseemly words flatter him, 990, 2. See **WRITINGS**.

**LIBER.** In the orgies of Liber, the mystery of religion is an incitement to lust, 150, 16.

**FREE** is the person who does what he wishes, 934, 19. He is freer who is free within himself, who is free under the laws of nature, knowing that the law of nature is prescribed through customs, not conditions, 934, 17. Innocence makes one free; guilt makes one a slave, 1163, 108. Where there is freedom, there is the power to do what one wishes, 935, 19. I consider freedom to be not munificence but virtue, because it is not conferred by the votes of others but claimed and possessed through one’s own greatness of spirit, 934, 18.

**LIBERALITY.** There are very many kinds, and what are they? 86, 79 and following. One assists through the use of money; another, much more splendid, is expended through the contribution of works, 87, 73 and following. Liberality must have a measure, lest it become useless, 88, 76 and following. Why? 89, 78. Beautiful is liberality toward the poor themselves when it keeps a measure, so that you may abound for many, 96, 110. Liberality is to be approved when you do not despise those born from your own seed if you know that they are in need, 40, 150. Yet not so that they may wish to become richer, ibid. Liberality should be neither excessive toward the importunate nor restricted toward the needy, 86, 68. The foremost form of liberality is to ransom captives, especially from a barbarian enemy, 87, 71. When liberality is perfect, 39, 147 and following. Liberality is defined not by the size of one’s patrimony but by the disposition to give, 193, 27. No one gives more than the person who has left nothing for himself, ibid. Money from a small sum is more abundant than a treasure from a great one, ibid. Why did God prefer the widow’s two small coins to the gifts of the rich? 40, 149. The one who gave first is superior in time and first in humanity, 42, 160. Nor do I deny that sins can be diminished through gifts made to the poor, but only if faith commends the expenditures, 434, 83. For a good man to relax something of his legal right is not only an act of liberality but often also of convenience, 95, 106. Liberality is not perfect if you give more for the sake of display than of mercy, 39, 147. See **BENEFICENCE**, **GENEROSITY**.

**THE SERMON OF LIBERIUS** to Ambrose’s sister, 173, 1 and following. He explains the formation and duties of virgins, ibid.

**FREEDOM.** According to nature, it is older than slavery, 1089, 2. Neither slavery detracts nor freedom assists, 278, 3. In Christ, slavery and freedom are weighed on an equal scale, 278, 3. The Apostle taught that there is something beyond freedom: that serving is freedom, 936, 23. The true freedom of the spiritual person, 936, 27. How wretched it is that those who are born in freedom should die in slavery! 938, 32.

**LUST** is like a straw: it catches fire quickly and is quickly consumed, 896, 13. It is fed by banquets, nourished by delicacies, kindled by wine, and inflamed by drunkenness, 410, 76. We read that savage wars were undertaken because of lust, 844, 6.

**LIGURIA** was nourished by the grain of autumn, 838, 21.

**THE LILIES OF CHRIST.** Who are they? 269, 93.

**LIMENIUS**, bishop of Vercellae, 786, 1; 805, 76. His condemnation of Palladius, 801, 59.

**YOUR TONGUE** must be subject to your mind, 5, 13. We are scourged not only by another’s tongue but also by our own, 300, 86. See **SPEAKING**.

**LITIGATION.** To be free from the expense of a lawsuit is no small profit, 95, 106.

**LOGOS (Λόγος)** is the divider of souls and virtues; *logos* is the powerful and sharp Word of God, 1053, 7.

**THE MANNER OF SPEAKING** is the first duty, 10, 35. How one should speak, 5, 14. Those who wish to learn caution in speaking should not deny what belongs to nature but practice what belongs to restraint, 10, 33. Before speaking, the wise person considers what he should say, or to whom, in what place, and at what time, 11, 35. Do not utter any word from your mouth that you might wish to recall, 176, 11. Bind your speech, lest it become extravagant, grow wanton, and gather sins for itself through excessive talk, 5, 12. If one senses that an adversary is present, he ought then to exercise still greater watchfulness over his mouth, 6, 16. Human speech is the beginning of human error, 3, 6. Our speech is the adversary’s snare, 6, 15. Often each person is not explained but entangled by his own words, 757, 13. I have seen very many fall into sin by speaking, scarcely anyone by keeping silent, 3, 5. Death enters through your door if you speak falsely, shamefully, brazenly, or when you ought not to speak, 233, 81. It is rare for anyone to keep silent when speaking would not benefit him, 11, 35. A mind that is not doubtful overshadows doubtful speech and protects it from a fall, 991, 6. See **SPEECH**, **SILENCE**, **WORD**.

**LOT’S WIFE** lost her nature because, although she had chaste eyes, she looked back at immodest things, 169, 29.

**LUKE** wrote the book of the Acts of the Apostles in historical style, 1028, 21.

**LUCIUS**, an Arian, raged in the impious slaughter of monks and virgins, 812, 1.

**LUCIFER** had separated himself from our communion, although he had been exiled for the faith and had left heirs to his faith, 1127, 47.

**TO BE A LAUGHINGSTOCK** is considered a disgrace, 851, 31.

**THE MOON** is represented in prophetic oracles as a figure of the Church, 839, 24. See **DAY**, **MONTH**.

**LUXURY** is the mother of lust, 1029, 26. How bitter is the fruit of luxury! 317, 46. He who is devoted to luxury and enslaved to wantonness places his trust in the Egyptians, 1016, 16. See **RUST**, **LUST**.

The luxurious seek underground chambers, courting coolness in summer, 910, 1. The luxurious add house to house and estate to estate and excavate the earth, so that their element may yield to their dwellings and, like sons of the earth, they may be buried within its womb, 911, 4. The luxurious person hates the work of virtues; the glutton shuns it, 898, 2. The luxurious person does not say, “The Lord is my portion,” 1045, 94. When someone begins to live luxuriously, he begins to deviate from the true faith; thus he commits two very serious crimes: offenses of the flesh and sacrileges of the mind, 1016, 16.

**THE PRECEPTS OF THE LYCIANS**, 1137, 7.

## M
### M

**MACEDONIUS**, bishop, 786, 1; 805, 76. **MACEDONIUS**, bishop, 819.

**THE MACCABEES’ seven boys** won no lesser triumphs over the proud king than their own parents, 54, 211. See **MONKS**.

**THE MAGI** brought gold, frankincense, and myrrh in supplication to Christ’s cradle: with gold confessing him to be king, with frankincense venerating him as God. For gold is the treasure of a kingdom, frankincense the sacrifice of God, and myrrh the sign of burial, 449, 31. The Magi, declaring the king’s power with gold, venerating God with frankincense, and confessing the resurrection of the body with myrrh, 194, 30.

**TEACHERS.** The nobility of the teacher is the first ardor for learning, 164, 7. A tutor is feared; a teacher shows the way of salvation, 1084, 5.

**THE MAGNET.** If you bring several iron rings up to a magnet stone in succession, it grips the earlier ones with a stronger bond and the later ones with a weaker one, 983, 14.

**GREATER** is commonly said of one who instructs and forms someone, 482, 65. Are the rites of our ancestors to be preserved? 839, 23 ff. What is greater than I am must be entrusted to better men; I do not demand it, 553, 11.

**EVILS** must sometimes be avoided, 50, 186.

**THE CURSE OF MEN** should be sought, since it obtains the Lord’s blessing, 1047, 103.

**ILL WILL** is a great precipice for innocence, 757, 13.

**MALIGNITY** does more harm than malice—and why? 1033, 45. To be malignant differs in no respect from being unjust, 1042, 83.

**A COMMANDMENT** has a twofold form: one prescriptive, the other voluntary, 205, 73. It is God’s voice that he prefers his commandment to be carried out rather than sacrifice to be offered: God cries this aloud, Moses announces it to the people, and Paul proclaims it to the nations, 1000, 15. Whoever ceases to sin and renounces wrongdoing must keep the Lord’s commandments, 405, 56. There is a distinction between those who have rendered perpetual obedience to the heavenly commandments and those who have fallen at some time either through error or necessity, 405, 58. See **COUNSEL**, **PRECEPT**.

**A MANICHAEAN** did not believe that the Son of God had come in the flesh, 583, 182. Nor did he accept the sacrament of the Incarnation, 478, 44. He did not believe in the reality of the human flesh assumed by Christ, 705, 8. He is a Manichaean who denies Christ’s flesh, 969, 13. See **CIRCUMCISION**. The Manichaeans introduce two principles, 504, 42. Whence flow the sacrileges of the Manichaeans, who mingle and join sacrilege with the sacrilege of shamefulness, 996, 14. We rightly condemn the Manichaeans for fasting on the Lord’s day, 883, 11. The Manichaean says to the devil, “You are my father,” 31, 117. How is the Manichaean excluded? 569, 104. He is refuted by the opening words of John, 455, 57. How he will be refuted at Christ’s final judgment, 492, 119. The most merciful emperor execrated the impiety of the Manichaeans, 969, 13.

**MANNA.** Why did the Lord rain it upon the people of the fathers, and why does he not rain it now? 1049, 1 ff. Why was it small? 1049, 3. Why was it fine, and why was it gathered each day? 1050, 5 ff. Bodily manna is found even today in many places, 1049, 1. What spiritual manna is, 1049, 2. It is the discourse and Word of God, 784, 6. It is bread from heaven, the body from the Virgin, 1049, 1. See **EUCHARIST**.

**GENTLENESS.** Blessed is the one who maintains both gentleness and severity, so that discipline may be preserved on the one hand and innocence not oppressed on the other, 1083, 10. One who is dear does not possess harshness but gentleness, 415, 93. See **AFFABILITY**.

**THE LAYING ON OF HANDS**, 875, 2. We see those upon whom hands are laid being violently agitated, 880, 22.

**THE VIRTUES OF MARCEL­LINA**, Ambrose’s sister, 178, 15 ff. Ambrose’s sister, at the nativity of the Savior, before the Apostle Peter, with several maidens of God standing by, marked her profession of virginity by changing her clothing, [Col. 1471] 173, 1. Concerned about her brother, 956, 1. She frequently writes to Ambrose for the same reason, 852, 1 ff. Her testimony on behalf of the virgin Indicia, 771, 21. The depth of her grief at the death of her brother Satyrus, 1123, 33; 1134, 76 ff. See **AMBROSE**, **LIBERIUS**, **SATYRUS**.

**MARCELLUS**, bishop, 786, 1; 805, 76. Marcellus, bishop, watered the Church with his institutions, 1101, 10. See **AMBROSE**.

**MARCION** judged Christ’s body to be an apparition, 478, 44. See **CIRCUMCISION**, **EUNOMIUS**.

**A MARCIONITE** thinks that the God of the New Testament is one and the God of the Old Testament another, 704, 8. Christ is the Son of David, against Marcion, 569, 105. The Sabellians and Marcionites say that Christ’s future subjection to God the Father will consist in the Son being poured back into the Father; but this is rejected, 579, 162.

**MARCUS OF PETAVIO**, a priest of admirable memory, 809, 10.

**THE SEA** is divine Scripture, containing within itself profound meanings and the depth of prophetic mysteries, 755, 3. Scripture knows no deep sea, 243, 121.

**THE ETYMOLOGY OF MARIA**, 257, 33 ff. Beautiful things have been prophesied concerning Mary in the figure of the Church, 268, 89. The virtues of Mary the Virgin are described with artistry, 164, 7 ff. She is proposed as an example to virgins, ibid. What is nobler than the Mother of God? What is more radiant than she whom Radiance chose? What is more chaste than she who generated a body without bodily contamination? ibid. To whom would the Lord assign greater merit or reserve a greater reward than to a mother? 260, 45. She was such that the life of this one woman might be the discipline of all, 166, 15. She became more humble when she learned that she had been chosen by God, 165, 12. She was a virgin not only in body but also in mind, 164, 7.

Mary’s virginity boiled like a cauldron and rained Christ’s grace upon the earth like a cloud, 267, 81. The Lord preferred that some should doubt his own ancestry rather than his mother’s chastity, 259, 43. Mary raised the sign of sacred virginity and erected for Christ the holy banner of undefiled integrity, 257, 35. So great was her grace that she not only preserved within herself the grace of virginity but also bestowed the insignia of integrity upon those whom she visited, 261, 50. In Mary there were the secret of modesty, the banner of faith, the obedience of devotion: a virgin within the house, a companion in service, a mother at the temple, 166, 15. How great was her modesty! 20, 69. She seemed less alone to herself when she was alone, 165, 10.

She was alone, and she spoke with the angel. She was alone, and she accomplished the salvation of the world and conceived the redemption of all, 992, 2. Nowhere else is she found, when she is sought, except in her chamber, 296, 71. See **ELIZABETH**.

Mary gave birth to Christ without diminishing her virginity, 1210, 43. When Christ was born from Mary’s womb, he nevertheless preserved the barrier of birth-giving modesty and the seals of undefiled virginity, 1030, 33. The Virgin’s childbirth did not change nature but renewed the manner of giving birth, 726, 104. Never before Mary, and never afterward, did a virgin give birth, 259, 39. It was a lesser thing for a man to have risen again than for a virgin to have given birth, ibid.

Mary was a closed gate because she was a virgin, through which Christ came forth without loss of virginity, 262, 52 ff. Before and after the Lord’s passage it always remained closed, 263, 55. It is the eastern gate through which Christ alone passed, and it remained closed after childbirth, 967, 6. The Word is like a king seated in the royal hall of the virginal womb, 266, 79.

There were those who denied that Mary remained a virgin, and the arguments they used, 257, 35. They are answered, 258, 36 ff. It is proved that she remained a virgin, 260, 44 ff. Those who say that the Virgin conceived but did not give birth as a virgin are refuted, 967, 4 ff. When Mary crowned Christ, 270, 98. Mary was the temple of God, not the God of the temple, 681, 88. See **CHRIST**.

I read that Mary stood beside the cross of her Son; I do not read that she wept, 1185, 39. She stood before the cross of her Son; no one taught me this except Saint John the Evangelist, 1048, 109. How undaunted was the mind of Mary standing before the cross! 261, 49. John considered it more important that Christ, victorious over suffering, should perform filial duties toward his mother than that he should grant the heavenly kingdom, 1048, 109.

From the cross the Lord Jesus bears witness to Mary’s virginity and delays public salvation for a little while, lest he leave his mother dishonored, 261, 48. Mary was not lesser than was fitting for Christ’s mother, 1048, 110. Even by his own death she thought she would add something to the public service, ibid. When Christ commended his mother to John from the cross, he certainly was not divorcing her, nor was Mary abandoning her husband, 261, 48.

Mary is a light cloud, 285, 31. She is the rod bringing forth a flower—and why? 285, 31. In the Virgin’s womb there simultaneously grew both a sheaf of wheat and the grace of the lily’s flower, 269, 91. See **JOHN**.

**THE MURMURING OF MIRIAM**, Moses’ sister, is referred to the type of the Synagogue. Ignorant of the mystery of the Ethiopian woman—that is, of the Church from the nations [Col. 1472]—it murmurs daily with reproach and envies that people by whose faith it too will be stripped of the leprosy of its faithlessness, 1035, 57.

**MARY**, the sister of Lazarus, was rightly preferred to Simon, who gave the Lord a meal, 431, 68. She provided instruction to all who wish to merit forgiveness, ibid. Mary worshiped Christ and was therefore sent to the apostles as the herald of the resurrection, breaking the ancestral bond and the monstrous offense of the female sex, 680, 74.

**MARTIANUS** is condemned for Jovinus’ mixture, 969, 14.

**MARTYRS.** The unbaptized are washed in their own blood, 1188, 52. Whoever desires the glory of martyrdom should not rashly expose himself to dangers, 50, 186. Yet one must not yield because of cowardice, ibid., 187. What should be thought about virgins who threw themselves from a height or drowned themselves in a river so as not to fall into the hands of persecutors? 182, 32. It is said that many martyrs restored themselves again after a fall, 403, 49 ff.

Christ is upon the altar, having suffered for all; the bodies of the martyrs are beneath the altar, having been redeemed by his suffering, 877, 13. The martyrs’ palms are the triumphs of Christ our ruler, 277, 1. The martyr of Christ is the treasure of the Church, 242, 119. By the death of the martyrs religion was defended, faith increased, and the Church strengthened: the dead conquered, while the persecutors were conquered, 1145, 45. The death of the martyrs itself is a reward, ibid. Through the martyrs religion has been increased, not diminished, 1074, 14. The Adversary and his legions are tormented by the daily virtue of the martyrs, 1201, 10. Whoever endures everything through love cannot fear martyrdom, 1094, 10. Virginity is not praiseworthy because it is also found among martyrs, but because it itself makes martyrs, 149, 10. See **GOD**, **PERSECUTION**.

**MATTER.** They maintained that the matter of all things, which the Greeks call *hylē* (ὕλη), as though it were a material forest, was unbegotten, 724, 94.

**MOTHERS.** How should mothers imitate the Blessed Virgin in their love for their children? 1048, 111. Maternal entrails do not know patience, 561, 57.

**MARRIAGE.** The marital union is to be avoided not as though it were a fault, but as a burden of necessity, 208, 81. Long ago the Church condemned those who dared to dissolve the marital bond, 221, 34. The good path of marriage reaches the camp of the saints by a level and direct road, though by a longer circuit, 1032, 40. See **CONJUGAL UNION**.

In **MAURITANIA** all the families are in chains, 161, 59. See **VIRGINS**.

**MAXIMIAN**, the associate of Diocletian, was buried in a porphyry sarcophagus, 1003, 4.

**MAXIMUS**, bishop of Emona, 786, 1; 805, 76. His condemnation of Palladius, 802, 59. The subscription of Maximus, bishop, 969, 14.

**MAXIMUS**, bishop of the Alexandrian Church, informed the bishops of Italy, after reading the letters of Peter, a man of holy memory, that communion with him continued, 815, 3. He testified that force had been applied to him, as bishop, by many even from the people and clergy, ibid. The same Fathers received him into communion, 816, 5. The Fathers of the council of Italy ask Theodosius that, concerning the ordination of Maximus and Nectarius, a council of the eastern bishops and of those of Italy should be held in the city of Rome, 817, 6 ff.

**MAXIMUS** caused raids to be made into Rhaetia, 890, 8. His brother Honoratus was dismissed by Valentinian, who could have avenged in him the killing of his brother Gratian, 890, 9. He threatened the Roman Empire with barbarian auxiliaries and trans-border troops, to whom the provincials paid provisions and taxes, 890, 8. How he received Ambrose as an envoy, and what conversations he had with him, 888, 3 ff. He sent Victor to Valentinian to ask for peace, 889, 6. He complained that, because of Ambrose’s embassy, he had been unable to cross into Italy, 858, 23.

The tyrant Maximus was defeated by the Franks, by the Saxon people, in Sicily, at Siscia, at Petovio—in short, everywhere on earth, 953, 23. A few days before the expedition, when he had heard that the synagogue at Rome had been burned, he had sent an edict to Rome, as though he were the avenger of public discipline, ibid. See **AMBROSE**, **EUGENIUS**.

**MAXIMUS**, accuser of the virgin Indicia, 769, 17 ff. Why was he so hostile to Indicia? 766, 4. What judgment Ambrose pronounced against him, ibid. and 771, 24.

**A PHYSICIAN.** A good physician knows what food is suited to which illness and to which season for the improvement of health, 929, 4. How can one whom you regard with distaste present himself to you for treatment, if he thinks that the physician will regard him not with compassion but with contempt? 389, 2. Medicine must not be neglected in any place or at any time, 224, 42.

**THE PEOPLE OF MILAN**, disturbed and watching over Ambrose so that he would not be driven from the city, 863, 1. See **AMBROSE**.

**MELCHIZEDEK** is called in Latin interpretation “king of justice” and “king of peace,” 337, 45; 367, 10. The Church understands not an angel, according to the Jewish mockeries, but a holy man and priest, and a type of Christ, 513, 88. [Col. 1473]

**THE DISPUTE BETWEEN MELETIUS AND PAULINUS**, how it was settled, 814, 2. See **ANTIOCHENE**.

**THE BETTER MAN.** No one examines the better man, 459, 78.

**OUR LIMBS** are weapons of righteousness and weapons of sin; this is shown by examples, 940, 43 ff.

**MEMORIALS**, 854, 7.

**A LIE** is shameful in speech, much more so in dress, 1061, 4. O blessed lie, by which one obtains the acquittal of others for one’s own sake, 948, 8.

**A GOOD MIND** is a good possession, 5, 11. Sobriety of mind has its own reins, 5, 12. The disposition of the mind is visible in the condition of the body, 20, 71. To be joined in mind is more than to be united in body, 841, 23. Let us kindle within ourselves the fire of the mind, so that it may work in us, 784, 6.

**THE MONTH** is calculated by the most learned according to the lunar course and the Law, 886, 18. The Greeks call the moon **μήνην** (*mēnēn*), whence they call months **μῆνας** (*mēnas*) in Greek, 886, 18. The first month among the Egyptians is called *pharmuthi*; it begins on the sixth day before the Kalends of April and ends on the seventh day before the Kalends of May, 884, 15. The first month according to the Egyptian harvest and according to the Law is the eighth according to our custom, 885, 16. It may still be possible to count the Nones of May as belonging to the first month of the new crops, 886, 18. See **EGYPT**.

**MEASURE.** Keep to the measure, so that you may receive according to the measure, 1205, 25. Even in cheap goods, cheating with the balance and fraudulent measurement is abominable, 123, 65.

**MERCHANTS.** Condemnations against the entire body of merchants, 853, 6. Much concerning merchants, 856, 16. The emperor orders that what had been exacted from the merchants in the condemnation be returned, 859, 26.

**WAGES.** The reward of wages is better than the service of stewardship, 1091, 7.

**HIRED WORKERS.** We are all hired laborers, all workers, 757, 12. Let no one defraud a hired laborer of the wage owed, because we too are hired laborers of our God, 843, 3.

**A HARLOT** is every soul that sells its hope and seeks shameful profits and a degenerate payment, 757, 12.

**MERITS.** God is accustomed to defer to merits, not petitions, 565, 83. Just as the sky shines with the brighter lights of the stars, so human beings gleam with the lights of their merits, 972, 9. The former is the firmament of the elements; the latter, of virtues, ibid. See **DEATH**.

**THE WELL OF MERRHA**, what did it signify? 257, 34.

**MESOPOTAMIA** is a region in the eastern lands, enclosed by the rivers Euphrates and Tigris, 842, 2. Under the name of Mesopotamia the figure of the Church is signified, 843, 2.

**FEAR** is found in sin, 935, 19.

**MICHAEAS** means “Who is from God?” or “Who is this?” 1063, 3.

**MICHAL**, who reproved David’s dancing, was condemned to barrenness and did not produce royal offspring, lest she create the proud, 1014, 7.

**A SOLDIER** is prohibited by human laws from undertaking litigation, conducting legal business, and selling merchandise, 49, 184. Soldiers are signified by the name of the emperor, 1189, 58. The faith of the emperor’s soldiers is perfect maturity, 1199, 6.

**MILITARY SERVICE.** Many enter military service because their parents served, 58, 226. If military matters are to be consulted, the judgment of a man experienced in battles must be awaited, 825, 7.

**MINORS.** The Jews are reported to have injured the Lord in no matter more seriously than by violating the grace of widows and the rights of minors, 189, 13.

**MIRACLES** of divine power are not something everyone can merit, but belong to those whose zeal for religious devotion gives them support, 191, 20. The miracles performed by Saints Gervasius and Protasius cannot be denied by the Arians, 879, 19. Human beings who raised the dead did not do this by their own power but in the name of Christ, 502, 29.

**COMPASSION.** The Lord magnifies what belongs to compassion and diminishes what belongs to vengeance, 395, 16 ff. The Spirit of God is more ready for mercy than for severity, 392, 9. It is better to endure hatred for the sake of mercy than to put forward mercilessness, 102, 136. Mercy itself is justice, 1205, 26. Although mercy is owed to all, it is owed more abundantly to the just, 39, 148. Through sacrifice the just person is commended; through mercy the sinner is redeemed, 405, 54. Mercy makes people perfect, and nothing commends a Christian soul so much as mercy, 11, 38–39. To grieve with sinners is the highest virtue, 432, 73. The redemption of the soul is mercy, 777, 3. A merciful person is good: while helping others, he helps himself, and in another’s remedy he heals his own wounds, 1202, 16. See **NEIGHBOR**.

**MASS.** I began to celebrate Mass, 853, 4. Prayers in the canon of the Mass, 371, 21 ff.; 372, 27 ff. What does the priest say after the Lord’s Prayer? 385, 24. I think that a deceased sister should not so much be mourned as accompanied with prayers; her soul should not be saddened with tears but rather commended to the Lord through offerings, [Col. 1474] 944, 4. See **EUCHARIST**.

**SENT** does not mean that someone has been compelled by another’s authority, but that he has carried out his task by voluntary choice, 489, 97. In divine mission there is not the injury of subjection but a sharing of power, 666, 8. See **THE SON OF GOD**.

**THE PRAISE OF MODERATION**, 389, t. Moderation ought to temper justice, 389, 2.

**MODESTY**, whence is the word derived? 22, 78. What should it be like in one’s walk? 21, 73 ff. It is rich before God, 20, 70. It raises up the adornment of one’s whole life, 58, 228. See **REVERENCE**.

**MEASURE.** To preserve a proper measure in each matter is no small thing, 58, 228.

**MOGUNTIACUM** is a city within Gaul, 889, 6.

**THE MONAD** was called by those concerned with such matters not a number but the element of number, 782, 21.

**THE MONASTIC AND CLERICAL LIFE**, an excellent comparison, 1039, 71 ff. The exercises of the monks who were disciples of Eusebius of Vercellae, 1042, 82. The monks, singing psalms according to ancient custom and practice, proceeded to the celebration of the Maccabean martyrs, 957, 16. See **AMBROSE**, **EUSEBIUS**, **OF VERCELLAE**.

**Μονότης** (*monotēs*, “singleness”), 559, 46.

**THE SON OF MORATHI**, that is, “of the heir,” 1063, 3.

**DEATH** is threefold according to Scripture: one spiritual, another natural, and the third penal, 1143, 36 ff. Death is nothing other than the separation of body and soul, 1143, 35. It was not in nature but was transformed into nature, 1146, 47. It is equal for all, without distinction among the poor and without exception for the rich, 1136, 6. No one can ransom himself from death—not the rich, not even kings; indeed, they themselves are subject to heavier burdens, 1187, 48. Who should think himself exempt from the condition of dying when he is not exempt from the condition of being born? 1114, 4. Death cannot be delayed by the price of money, and the final day carries away rich and poor alike, 1115, 5.

The gentiles say that the dead have no sensation after death, 1186, 45. The gentiles consider death the rest from all evils, 1132, 71. By what arguments gentile men console themselves concerning death, 1147, 50. For Christians, death is not the end of nature but of this life, 1132, 70. The end of nature and of merits is not the same, 1130, 63. Christians have far greater consolations concerning the death of their own people than the gentiles do, 1132, 70 ff.

Nothing casts the soul down into every form of slavery so much as fear of death, 937, 31. No one rejoices when about to die, 480, 53. Death is not an evil, since it restores freedom and removes pain, 1140, 21. It is not merely not an evil, but is also a good, 1144, 39. It is neither frightening nor bitter to the needy, neither heavier for the rich, nor unjust to the old, nor cowardly for the brave, nor everlasting for the faithful, nor unforeseen by the wise, 1145, 44. There is nothing for us to fear in death, nothing that we ought to grieve, 1146, 49. This is because it is the end of sins, 1186, 45.

It should not be mourned, because it is common and owed to all; because it frees us from the hardships of this age; because, in the likeness of sleep, we rest from the labor of this world and a more vigorous vitality is poured back into us, 1135, 3 ff. To fear death is not perfection, 1183, 33. It is not feared for its own evils but is preferred to the miseries of life, 1167, 125. How many have preferred death to grief, and how many to fear, judging the fear of death more grievous than death itself, 1167, 125. Many consecrated their lives by the mere title of death, 1145, 44. By the death of one person we have often received the liberation of great peoples; by the death of an emperor, armies have been put to flight, ibid.

When an opportunity for a praiseworthy death is given, it must be seized immediately, 107, 153. Death should not be fled from, since the Son of God did not disdain it and did not flee from it, 1146, 46. This death is not a death of nature but of malice, 1146, 48. Death is the refuge from all hardships and evils, a trustworthy station of security and a harbor of repose, 1140, 22. For me, to die is gain, so that I may not sin further, 1145, 42. Death was given as a remedy, as it were the end of evils, 1143, 37 ff.; 1146, 47. See **EPICURUS**, **SLEEP**.

What is meditation on death except a certain separation of body and soul? 1142, 35. Paul speaks better when he says, “I die daily,” than those who called meditation on death philosophy, 1143, 35. Let there be in us a certain daily practice and disposition of dying, 1144, 40. Certain peoples are said to have existed who mourned human births and celebrated deaths, 1136, 5. The excessive mourning of women at the deaths of their husbands, 1138, 12 ff. Why should we groan for the dead, since the reconciliation of the world with God has already been accomplished through the Lord Jesus? 945, 7. We forget the birthdays of the dead and renew with solemn celebration the day on which they died, 1136, 5. Some have been accustomed to observe the third and thirtieth day for the dead, others the seventh and fortieth, 1198, 3. See **THE DEAD**, **SATYRUS**, **THEODOSIUS**.

**MORTIFY** your members in the manner of a drum, 289, 47. Mortification. See **BODY**. [Col. 1475]

**CHARACTER.** Through variety of character each person is changed and becomes another, 782, 22. Age contributes no more to the correction of character than discipline does, 1046, 98.

**MOSES.** No one saw God more clearly, 1057, 1. Blessed in his sufferings, 73, 10 ff. How wise he was, 33, 123. In silence he spoke, and in leisure he worked, 108, 2. He thought it honorable that, when asked, he should pray; when injured, bless; when solicited, forgive, 130, 93. Mindful of everyone and forgetful of himself, he did not fear to offend God by praying, so that he might strip and free the people from the danger of offense, 402, 42. They loved Moses more for his gentleness than they admired him for his deeds, 78, 31. He dispersed the Egyptian arrogance and restrained every height that exalted itself by the authority of the eternal law, 1055, 5. By comparison with the Egyptian king, Moses was called God, ruling kingdoms and subjecting powers to himself, 904, 8. Why is he found to have approved his brother Aaron’s counsel more than his own? 1057, 1 ff.

He saw spiritual circumcision, the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth, and the Passion of the Lord, 67, 260. He wrote not his own words but what had been infused and revealed to him, especially what concerns the creation of the world, 976, 1. A comparison of Moses with Peter and John, 246, 132 ff. Although Moses’ body did not appear on earth, we nowhere read of him in heavenly glory until after the Lord, by the pledge of his resurrection, broke the bonds of hell and raised up the souls of the righteous, 523, 8. How Moses’ rod signified the divine Word, 130, 94.

**THE WORD “WOMAN”** is not a term of corruption but a designation of sex, 258, 36; 781, 18. The dignity, chastity, and good conduct of a woman have such power that she can call her husband to faith and devotion, 384, 21. The woman’s voice of modesty, speech of dignity, restraint of caution, guardianship of faith, and discipline of chastity breaks her bonds, 409, 72. For this reason a woman covers her head with a veil, so that her modesty may be safe even in public, 408, 69. The vanity of women’s adornments, 160, 55. A woman is uglier precisely because she strives to please, 159, 51. Against women who disfigure their natural appearance with cosmetics, various colors, and ornaments, 153, 28 ff. We have learned that the harsher temptations are those that occur through women, 856, 17. Nothing is more treacherous than a woman, 847, 17. The virtues of women are compared with the last rank of virgins, 153, 25 ff.

**VERBOSITY** contains abundant sin, 176, 11. See **SPEECH**.

**THE WORLD.** Many have said that the world was unbegotten, 724, 94. Philosophers assert that there are many worlds, 529, 44. There are not many gods but one God, who made the world; and there is one world, not many worlds, as the philosophers say, 983, 15. Why is the world said to have been made in six days? 976, 2. The times of the world are one year, 1151, 63.

The seventh age of the world has been completed; the eighth has dawned—the grace that made the human being no longer belong to this world but to be above the world, 980, 14. What is the world except a kind of contest full of struggles? 971, 4. What and how great are these struggles? ibid., 6. This age is a sea in which we must be like fish, 362, 3. All the commerce of this age is the loss of souls, 761, 26. The things of this age are neither everlasting nor long-lasting, but a mere dream, 759, 22 ff. We must learn to be above the world in this world, 239, 108. Conquer the age, so that you may grasp the height of the Word; leave this image of the world outside—leave wickedness outside, 909, 20.

What is more foolish than, after abandoning heavenly things, to focus on earthly ones, and, having set heavenly things aside, to choose what is fleeting and fragile? 1099, 12. What have we to do with the road of this age, seeking a day laborer’s daily wage and, as they say of cicadas, feeding on some breeze of desires? 903, 5. For this reason Jesus went out of the city, so that you, going out from this world, might be above the world, 1047, 104. It is written not that you should reserve some portion of servitude for the world, but that you should deny yourself entirely, 781, 15. You will praise God if no desire for marriage or concern for the world turns you away from him, 290, 50. That world has been crucified in its own allurements, 674, 50. See **HEAVEN**.

“World” is said with reference to human beings, 567, 93.

**TO BE CHANGED.** The desire to change comes to everyone from nature, because we regret being what we are, 1167, 124. See **CHARACTER**.

**MUTINA**, 944, 3.

**MYROCLES**, bishop, 868, 18.

### N
## N

**NABAL**, in Latin, means foolish, hard, inhospitable, inhuman, ungrateful, 915, 7. **NABOR**, 874, 1. What does the word **NABUTHE** mean? 285, 30. Nabuth was poor, yet rich in himself: he governed his desires and was richer than King Ahab, 943, 8. He defended his vines even with his own blood, 868, 17. Nothing was the cause of his death except his regard for uprightness, 123, 63.

**TO BE BORN** is the beginning of all evils, 1142, 32. Not to be born is by far the best course, 1142, 30 and following.

**NATURE** and substance are spoken of in Scripture, 722, 81 and following. One nature—and especially God—does not admit diversity, [Col. 1476] 464, 102. Whatever is beyond nature comes from the author of nature, 148, 8. Who can change nature except the one who created nature? 1087, 7. It is no less to give new things to reality than to change natures, 339, 52. What nature lacked belongs to the Creator to restore, since he is the author of nature, 1096, 3. That things belonging to one kind and nature can have different principles is proved by various examples, 725, 102 and following. The organs of nature are unknown to us, but its functions are known, 1150, 60. Nature is better than one’s homeland, 1062, 6. Nature assists the learner, 786, 15. Nature itself assigns us our person and appearance, which we ought to preserve, 59, 232. The activity of nature does not perish forever, but rests in a kind of temporary cessation, 1130, 63. Habit quickly bends nature, 24, 85. See **CUSTOMS**.

**NECESSARY.** Nothing is more necessary than to know what is not necessary, 1044, 91.

The bishops of the Italian council do not see what procedure was followed in the ordination of Nectarius, bishop of Constantinople, 814, 3. Nor, therefore, do they hold that his communion is connected with the Eastern parts, 816, 5. See **MAXIMUS**.

The fire of the sacrifice in Nehemiah was a type of the Holy Spirit: how so? 133, 102.

**THE NEGLIGENT:** Christ quickly abandons them, 231, 76.

**NEPHTHALIM** signifies “abundance,” or “expansion,” according to the Latin interpretation, 943, 10.

**NIECE.** See **UNCLE**.

They attribute dominion over fury to Neptune in order to support the charge of incestuous love, 176, 7.

What disgraceful deeds of the Neros we have learned, 1212, 50.

The Fathers of the Nicene Synod, concerning the celebration of Easter, gathered the calculations of nineteen years from the most expert calculators and established, as it were, a certain cycle, 880, 1. The definition of faith at the Council of Nicaea by the three hundred and eighteen Fathers, 467, 118 and 120. Why did the Fathers of the Council of Nicaea place the word **ὁμοούσιον** (*homoousion*, “of the same substance”) in the treatment of the faith? 518, 125. Confessing the Son to be of the same substance as the Father, they believed not in one person but in one divinity in the Father and the Son, 721, 77. They said that it was not the flesh but the Word of God that was of one substance with the Father; and they confessed that the Word proceeded from the Father’s substance, while the flesh was from the Virgin, 715, 52. The priestly book of the Council of Nicaea, signed by confessors and already consecrated by the martyrdom of many: those who were compelled to unseal it later signed it again after their fraud had been condemned; those who did not dare violate it became confessors and martyrs, 519, 128. How steadfastly the faith of the Nicene Council is preserved by Ambrose, the emperor Theodosius, and the Gauls and Spaniards, 862, 14. Gaul and Spain hold the faith of the Council of Nicaea and preserve it with a devout confession of the divine Spirit, 862, 14. See **AMBROSE, COUNCIL, EASTER**.

**NICENTIUS**, former tribune and notary, 767, 8.

**NICODEMUS.** See **BAPTISM**.

Nineveh freed itself from death by fasting, 969, 11.

In **NOAH** there were the four cardinal virtues, 32, 121. He was naked but did not feel shame, because he was full of joy and spiritual gladness, 1015, 12.

**NAOMI** found consolation in grief and assistance in poverty, 195, 33.

A notary was sent to convey the orders, 858, 22.

**Νοῦς** (*nous*) is the vigor of the soul, claiming for itself, as a ruler, the leadership of soul and body, 974, 14. The **νοῦς** of a human being sees everything but is not seen, possessing an invisible substance of its own, 974, 15. Let us beware lest woman—that is, the passion of our senses—effeminate the human being, that is, the **νοῦς**, by pleasure, and draw it, once circumscribed, into her own laws and judgment, 984, 17.

We rightly condemn everything new that Christ did not teach, 220, 28.

**NOVATIAN**—inflamed by grief over the episcopate he had lost—organized a schism, 412, 85. He thought that penance should be granted to no one, 393, 10. He stained Christ’s servants with the pollution of repeated baptism, 398, 30.

The **NOVATIANS** wish to deprive people of hope, so that among the despairing they may more easily persuade them to accept repeated baptism, 424, 34. The teachers of the Novatians call themselves pure, 390, 3. Their pride is humbled, 400, 38. In a manner somewhat like the Stoics, they think all sins must be judged by equal measures, 391, 5. Wickedly they deny that sins can be forgiven in the Church, 399, 33. They do not accept the keys of the kingdom, denying that they ought to forgive sins, 399, 32. They deny that communion should be restored to those who have fallen through transgression, 391, 5. “What wonder, Novatians, if you deny salvation to others, when you refuse your own, although those who seek penance from you differ in nothing from you?” 422, 27. They said that such people ought not to be admitted into the Church, because through penance the hope of repentance had been granted to those who had fallen, 412, 85. Those for whom Christ intercedes, Novatian accuses; those whom Christ redeemed for salvation, Novatian condemns to death, 394, 14. The Novatians say against Novatian that, except in the case of graver crimes, they grant pardon for lesser ones, 393, 20. They are refuted, ibid. and following. They prescribe penance, which they do not release, 390, 4. They are refuted from the parable of the prodigal son, 419, 13 and following. The Novatians’ objection, drawn from the immutability of God, is answered, 395, 21 and following. The objection of the Novatians, drawn from these words—“If anyone sins against another person,” and so forth—is answered, 401, 40 and following. The objection drawn from these words—“There is a sin unto death; I do not say that he should pray for it”—is answered, 402, 45 and following. The objection drawn from these words of the Apostle—“It is impossible for those who have once been enlightened,” and so forth—is answered, 417, 6 and following. The objection drawn from these words of Peter—“Lest perhaps,” and so forth—is resolved, 423, 29 and following. The objection drawn from these words—“Every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven people; but the blasphemy of the Spirit,” and so forth—is answered, 420, 20. What is more proud and harsh than the Novatians? 390, 4. They are prouder than that lawyer who wished to tempt Christ, 398, 27. Like the priest and Levite who passed by the Samaritan, ibid. “It would be more tolerable for you, Novatian, to release than to bind,” 392, 9. The Novatians are successors of those who wanted to kill Lazarus, 429, 59. They resemble the man who grieved that his brother had been received, 412, 85. The voice of the Novatians is the voice of the Pharisees speaking to Judas, 422, 27.

**OF THOSE WHO MARRY.** The word is derived from “clouds,” 286, 34. Marriages should not be condemned but approved, 221, 31. The Apostle commended marriage as a remedy; he did not prescribe it as a choice, 189, 12. They should neither be condemned nor discouraged, 155, 34. It accords with Hebrew customs and laws that whole men should be joined to whole virgins in marriage, 759, 20. It was fitting that those who had broken up another’s union should themselves lose the solemnity of marriage, 135, 110. The pitiable condition of a woman about to marry, 160, 56. If a virgin about to marry chooses a husband, it is a crime; if she does not choose one, it is an insult, ibid. The troubles of marriage, 221, 32. Marriage is both a bond and servitude, 203, 69. Marriage bonds are good, but they are nevertheless bonds, 221, 33. A woman who marries is sold into servitude for her own money, 283, 23. The troubles and disadvantages of married women are described, 153, 25 and following. The apostolic precepts do not condemn second marriages, 188, 10. “We do not forbid second marriages, but we do not recommend them. I say more: we do not forbid second marriages, but we do not approve of those repeated frequently,” 203, 68. Second marriages are genuine servitude, 210, 88. How unbecoming it is for a woman to have children younger than her grandchildren! 201, 59. The banquet of a wedding feast, 845, 15. See **AMBROSE, UNION, MARRIAGE, FATHER, WIDOW, VIRGIN**.

**NUMERIUS**, bishop, 819.

The number seven is good.
