We do not treat it in the Pythagorean manner or according to that of the other philosophers, but according to the form and divisions of spiritual grace, 976, 3 and following. The number of remission is seven, 1047, 101. The week belongs to the Old Testament; the eighth day to the New, when Christ rose again, 977, 5. See **SEVENTH**. The great mystery of the number fourteen, 1208, 38. In the number 318 there is a sign of the Passion and of the name of Jesus, 467, 121. In the hundreds and thousands there is a sacred observance of number, 1163, 108.

**NUMIDIUS**, legate of the Africans, 786, 1; 805, 76. His condemnation of Palladius, 801, 58.

## O

**OBEDIENCE.** It is not fitting for us to oppose the divine judgment, 865, 7. Because pride had incurred guilt, guilt, conversely, produced obedience, 1079, 6.

**OBJECTIONS.** If there is no limit, how can there be an end to the reply? 717, 62.

**OFFERING.** It is more tolerable to abstain from presenting gifts than to offer a gift with disloyal zeal, 703, 3. If you offer your gift to God, you have not lost it, 1160, 98.

Why are midwives so called? 767, 10.

Hidden things are more difficult to guard against than things that are known, 1033, 45. It belongs to divine power alone to know hidden things, 658, 128.

The eighth day comes; the week has passed, 980, 15.

When our eyes are covered with some dimness, they are nourished by the greenness of the fields; and the appearance of a grove or grassy hill drives every unevenness from an ailing gaze, while the pupils and orbs themselves seem to be colored by a kind of healthful beauty, 904, 2. We see more with the mind than with the body, 409, 70. Our own eyes themselves are nets for us, 409, 73. See **CRIME**.

Hatreds are harmful to good morals, 1101, 4.

**DUTY** is derived from *efficere*, “to accomplish,” 9, 26; or from doing those things that harm no one, ibid. Is the word “duty” found in Scripture? 8, 25. Duty is divided into three parts: the honorable, the useful, and what is superior to these, 9, 27. How is it divided among Christians? ibid. and following. Every duty is either ordinary or perfect, 11, 36. The perfect duty is called **κατόρθωμα** (*katorthōma*) by the Greeks, ibid., 37. Some duties are primary, others intermediate: primary duties are shared with few people, intermediate duties with many, 110, 10. [Col. 1478] The same duties are not always owed to everyone, 46, 174. The measure of duties must correspond not to human judgment but to the disciplines of nature, 934, 17. David discussed duty before Panaetius and Aristotle, 10, 31. Prudence is the first source of duty, 34, 126. Public duty is more pleasant in prosperous circumstances and more welcome in adversity, 1121, 28. Rich gifts are not demanded from you, but voluntary services, 843, 6. What is so contrary to duty as not returning what you have received? 42, 160. See **GRATITUDE, VIRTUES**.

**OMNIPOTENT.** He is everywhere, uncreated, without location, and above time, 458, 75. See **GOD**.

What is **ὁμοούσιον** (*homoousion*), and why was it placed in the Nicene Creed? 518, 125 and following.

The measure of a burden ought to correspond to the capacity of the person carrying it, 204, 70.

Let your works shine and bear the image of God, in whose image you were made, 336, 41. If you have recognized God in his commandments, recognize him again in his works, 782, 22. Blessed is the one whose sin is covered by good works, 424, 35. The grace of a good work is more pleasing when expressed in diverse forms, 472, 11. On the day of judgment our works will either assist us or plunge us into the abyss, 758, 16. See **FAITH, PRAYER**.

**OPTATA.** See **VOWS**.

What are prayer, entreaty, petition, and thanksgiving? 251, 9. Do not think it a virtue of minor importance to know how you ought to pray, 376, 18. The order of good prayer is described, 251, 8 and following. The first prayer ought to contain praise of God, the second supplication, the third petition, and the fourth thanksgiving, 384, 22. All these are found in the Lord’s Prayer, 385, 23. Prayer ought to begin with the praise of God, 384, 22, and end with it, 385, 23. So that the mind may be able to pray well, the Spirit goes before it and leads it along the right path, lest carnal things, lesser things, or even things too great for its powers creep in, 929, 3. If you wish to make your prayer effective, lift pure hands through innocence, 383, 18. Let your conduct speak what you pray for; let faith assist it and works commend it, 296, 70. Let your prayer not proceed from your lips alone: direct your whole mind to it; enter into the recesses of your heart; enter wholly within, 382, 13. Since you are always receiving from God, invoke him always, 1204, 22. To invoke God on fixed days but not on all days is the behavior of one who is weary, not of one who hopes, ibid. The Lord wishes to be asked, wishes us to hope in him, wishes to be entreated, 427, 48. The service of the angels is always to be engaged in God’s praises, to win his favor by frequent prayers, and to entreat the Lord, 1042, 82. Prayers are also commended by their timing, 882, 7. Why ought we to pray secretly rather than with shouting? 383, 16 and following. In prayer, great modesty is pleasing and beneficial, 20, 70. The priest imposed silence on the frogs, so that reverence might be shown to prayer, 177, 14. We cannot tolerate women praying in the church with such loud cries, 383, 17. To weep in prayer is a virtue, 1134, 76. When you raise your hands in prayer, should you display the Lord’s cross to the nations? 383, 18. Where ought we to pray? 382, 11 and following. The Lord’s Prayer is brief and full of every virtue, 377, 18. Its exposition, 377, 19 and following. The Lord’s Prayer contains everything; it need not be made commonplace, 252, 10. Where prayer is present, the Word is present; desire is driven away and lust departs, 202, 63. Through the frequent prayers and merits of the prophets, heavenly assistance often came to the fathers, 199, 48. The forgiveness of graver sins ought to be reserved for the prayers of the righteous, 402, 45. “I have a defense, but it is in the prayers of the poor,” 873, 33. Christ desires that many should pray for one, 436, 92. Simple prayer is a sacrifice, 1000, 15. Prayer, tears, and fasting are the good debtor’s sound account, 434, 81. What a good shield prayer is! 1047, 103; 1183, 32. Let frequent prayer commend us to God, 178, 18. God bends down to us so that our prayer may rise to him, 1204, 21. Why does God incline his ear to us? ibid. Why does God not hear everyone? 1131–65. See **MOUTH**.

Solemn prayers with thanksgiving ought to be offered when we rise from sleep, when we go out, when we prepare to eat, when we have eaten, at the hour of incense, and finally when we go to bed, 178, 18. In bed itself, psalms should frequently be recited together with the Lord’s Prayer, ibid., 19. See **TEARS**.

How should the orators of the world formulate a speech before judges? 384, 23.

**ORDER** generally requires time and number, 976, 2. The sacred orders. See **CLERIC, ECCLESIASTICAL**.

The story of Orestes and Pylades, 55, 216.

Origen is far less important in the New Testament than in the Old, 1083, 1.

What is **ὁρμή** (*hormē*, “impulse”)? 60, 237.

The wastefulness of ornaments, 230, 68. See **WOMEN**.

**Ὅρος** (*horos*, “definition” or “boundary”), 783, 12.

Our mouth is our gate; it ought to be opened almost exclusively for Christ, and it should not be opened unless the Word of God has first knocked, [Col. 1479] 233, 80.

A kiss is a sign of sacred peace, 420, 2, and of charity, 431, 69; 959, 14. It is, as it were, a pledge of marriage and a prerogative of wedlock, 960, 18. Whoever does not have faith and charity has no kiss; for through a kiss the force of love is impressed, 960, 17. See **UNCLE**.

The tales of idle people are those by which slander is sown and malice revealed, 1033, 45.

The leisure of the prophets is compared with the leisure of others, 109, 6. I am never less alone than when I seem to be alone, nor less idle than when I am idle, 992, 1. Wages are earned neither through idleness nor through sleep, 1046, 99.

From where is **οὐσία** (*ousia*, “substance”) derived? 519, 127. It is found in Scripture, ibid. The Latins call **οὐσία** “substance,” 725, 100. Scripture frequently mentioned **οὐσία** in Greek, and *substantia* in Latin, 469, 129. When the substance of God is mentioned, what else is signified except that God always exists? 725, 100; 728, 111.

## P
PACIFIC: The river’s current gladdens a peaceful and tranquil soul, 755, 2.

PAEDAGOGUE: As the Latin translation has it, he is the teacher of a boy, 1081, 2.

PAGANS never spared our blood; they even demolished the very buildings of the churches, 824, 4. The privileges of the gentiles had been restricted and prohibited by several earlier emperors, 825, 5; and were removed at Rome by Gratian, ibid. Christians were often deceived by the privileges of the pagans, 824, 4. The pagans petitioned the emperor Valentinian that the altars of the gods of the nations be restored by his command, and that funds also be supplied for profane sacrifices, 824, 3; that their privileges be upheld, ibid., 4; and that oaths be sworn at the altar, 824, 9. See AMBROSE, EUGENIUS, GENTILES, GRATIAN, VALENTINIAN.

PALATINE OFFICES, that is, memorial secretaries, agents in public affairs, and attendants of various counts, 854, 7.

Palladius and Secundianus: Two priests rotten in treachery, 807, 3.. Palladius’s statements and replies at the Council of Aquileia, 788, 6 ff. The sacrileges of Palladius and Secundianus are thrust upon our ears, 786, 2. Palladius and Secundianus say that the Son of God is subject according to his divinity, and refer his death not to the mystery of our salvation but to a certain weakness of divinity, 808, 7. Anathema against Palladius, 799, 50; 800, 52. He is condemned by the Fathers of the Council of Aquileia, 800, 54 ff. He received the sentence he deserved, 806, 2.

PALM: The victor’s reward, 1192, 70.

PANNONIA: They sold grain which they had not sown, 838, 21.

PARADISE: In Greek, *paradeisos*; in Latin, “garden.” Nor should it trouble you that some Latin manuscripts of Scripture have *garden*, others *paradise*, 981, 5. Various opinions concerning the earthly Paradise, 982, 1 ff. What did Josephus think about it? ibid. Through Paradise one reaches the kingdom, not through the kingdom Paradise, 1070, 8.

PARSIMONY: Christ is its foundation, for he became poor although he was rich, 506, 52.

PARENTS. See LIBERALITY, FATHER.

PARTHENIUS, “the sweetest,” greets Eusebius, 1005, 5.

BIRTH: A child born in the seventh month is viable; one born in the eighth is fatal to the mother and the child, 977, 4.

PASSOVER: That is, “passing over,” 352, 12. The Fathers of the Synod of Nicaea followed the practice that everywhere, on one night, the sacrifice for the Lord’s resurrection should be offered, 881, 1. Hence the Lord’s Passover took the form of a festival on the fourteenth day of the moon, 1208, 37. The Law requires that the day of the Passion be celebrated within the first month of the new produce, 885, 17. The sequence of the Old Testament shows that one day is to be observed for the Passion and another for the Resurrection, 886, 19 ff. It is no small difficulty to determine the day of the Paschal celebration, 880, 1. The observance of the day of Passover must be examined by a devout mind, 881, 4 ff. Above all, we must know the time at which harmonious prayer for the holy Paschal night is offered throughout the world, 882, 7. The day of Passover was often celebrated within thirty-one days, 885, 16. If the fourteenth day of the first month falls on a Sunday, the celebration of Passover must be postponed to the following week, 883, 12. This happened in times not much earlier, 884, 14; 887, 21. In the seventy-sixth year from the beginning of the reign of Diocletian, we celebrated the Sunday of Passover, without any doubt on the part of our predecessors, on the twenty-eighth day of the month Pharmuthi, which is the ninth day before the Kalends of May, 887, 21. In the eighty-ninth year from the beginning of Diocletian’s reign, when the fourteenth day of the moon fell on the ninth day before the Kalends of April, we celebrated Passover on the first day of the Kalends of April, 884, 14. The Alexandrians and Egyptians agreed with us in this, ibid. In the ninety-third year from the beginning of Diocletian’s reign, when the fourteenth day of the moon fell on the fourteenth day of Pharmuthi, which is the fifth day before the Ides of April, and that day was a Sunday, Passover was celebrated on the Sunday of Pharmuthi, the twenty-first day, which according to us was the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May, 884, 14. Six years earlier we celebrated the Sunday of Passover on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, 885, 17. Passover is to be celebrated on the twenty-first day of the moon, 887, 21.

When the day of Passover comes, the sacraments of baptism are celebrated throughout the world and virgins are veiled, 288, 42. In accordance with the command of our predecessors, let us celebrate the feast of public salvation, Passover, joyfully and exultantly, coloring our doorposts with faith in the Lord’s Passion, so that we may speak of nothing other than the blood of Christ, 887, 22. On the day of the Resurrection there is exultation, refreshment, and joy; on that day the people seem to have gone out from Egypt, when the firstborn of the Egyptians had been slain, 886, 20. For the solemnity of Passover either the perfection of the Church or the fullness of clear faith is sought, 882, 4. All are commanded to bring equal devotion and faith to the Lord’s Passover, that is, to the passing over, 779, 10. Passover occurs when the soul lays aside irrational passion and takes up good compassion, so that it may suffer with Christ and receive his passing over within itself, ibid. See AMBROSE.

PASCHASIUS: A severed man, 811, 5.

PASSION: Whoever is not subject to passion is not subject to weakness, 718, 63. The adversary lies in wait especially when he sees that passions are arising in us, 6, 15. Christ, as the Word, always stands in each person, separating within us rational virtues from the corpses of passions and destructive thoughts, 764, 5. It is blessed not to be in passion but to be victorious over passion, 75, 19. See SOUL.

FATHER: The proper name of the one who begets, 474, 18. It is God’s praise that he is proclaimed Father; in this lies the glory of his loving devotion, 385, 24. The Father himself is the source of life-giving substance, 651, 92. The Father and the Son are one, not by confusion of person but by unity of nature, 445, 9. God could not beget a lesser Son, 592, 224. The Father does not beget by will or by necessity, 540, 103. The Father wills to be entreated through the Son, and the Son wills the Father to be entreated, 446, 12. Why? ibid., 13. You will find many things accomplished through the Father, 652, 98. See TRINITY.

A father ought to choose his daughter’s future place according to his own judgment, 1103, 2. The disadvantages suffered by parents who give their daughters in marriage, 155, 33. A vow is the will of parents, 291, 51. Jephthah’s daughter ought to teach us how great the force of parents’ vows is, 291, 51. By the merits of virgins, the sins of parents are redeemed, 154, 32. Everyone loves to follow the life of his parents, 58, 226.

PATERNA: Testimony on behalf of the virgin Indicia, 771, 22..

PATERNUS received the highest honor from the emperors, 1019, 8. He consulted Ambrose about whether he could marry his granddaughter through his daughter to his son, 1017, 1. Ambrose proves that this could in no way be done, ibid. and following.

PATIENCE: Christ is its foundation: when he was cursed, he did not curse in return; when he was struck, he did not strike back, 506, 52. Patience is proved more by enduring desire, 1139, 17. Patience is proved more by bearing than by resisting, 1135, 1. Where there is patience, there is joy, 901, 17. See JACOB.

HOMELAND: To have warded off the destruction of one’s country is considered more gratifying than one’s own dangers, 113, 23.

PATRIARCHS: They were shepherds, assuming a certain royal discipline in this office, 898, 1. The modesty of the patriarchs, 19, 66. We marvel at the patriarchs’ rewards; let us imitate their obedience. We preach grace; let us follow obedience. Thus the type and the truth correspond, and the truth joins itself to the type, 1159, 95. The bosom of the patriarchs is a kind of retreat of eternal rest, 1192, 72.

IN THE DIVISION OF AN ESTATE: True piety avoids arbitrators, 594, 231.

PAULINUS, second to none in the splendor of his family in the regions of Aquitania, is said, after selling both his own property and even his wife’s, to have chosen the seclusion of the city of Nola, 1013, 1. They had no children, ibid., 2. Ambrose defends this action of Paulinus against his detractors, ibid., 2 ff.

PAULINUS’S disagreement with Meletius, 815, 2. See ANTIOCHENE, MELETIUS.

PAULINUS OF ANTIOCH’S disagreement with Timothy of Alexandria, 813, 4. See TIMOTHY.

PAUL: He received the apostleship not only by the command of Christ but also by that of the Holy Spirit, 633, 102. What more could Christ have contributed to our zeal for correction than by converting and giving us, from a persecutor, a teacher? 417, 5. Paul could not have attained such great grace in his apostleship if he had been bound to the companionship of marriage, 283, 22. The Holy Spirit anointed Paul, his athlete, and, having shaken off the dust of impiety, presented him, the unconquerable vanquisher of unbelievers, in various encounters with the impious, 664, 156. Carried up into Paradise, he no longer perceived the use of his own body, 907, 12. Paul’s letter was a kind of image of his presence and a representation of his work, 989, 6 ff. Nothing is more difficult than to discuss the Apostle’s reading, [Col. 1481] 1083, 1. Paul’s depth in counsel is scarcely comprehended; his loftiness in his statements raises the listener and kindles the debater. In most passages he explains himself in his own words so clearly that the expositor performs more the office of a grammarian than of a disputant, 930, 1. The general meaning of the Letter to the Ephesians, 1085, 1 ff. Though absent, Paul condemned and absolved through his letter, 989, 6. The one whom Paul had excluded he later restored to the sacraments, 411, 78. The one whom Paul’s rod had excluded from the heavenly sacraments, gentleness restored, 957, 4. Those whom Paul joined together for punishment he likewise wished to belong together in pardon, 416, 95. He teaches that those who have committed a sin unto death are not to be abandoned, but rather restrained by loaves of tears and drink of lamentation, 406, 59. Paul learned to heal in the same way in which he himself had been healed, 410, 77. Paul challenges by his honor, teaches by his instruction, and invites by his example, 245, 130. He died and, through a venerable passion, exchanged bodily life for immortal glory, 1159, 94. Paul was not inferior to Peter: he could easily be compared with him and was second to none, 664, 158. Those who call Paul a teacher of licentiousness are refuted, 968, 10. See ON LEISURE.

PAUL, presbyter of the Church of Constantinople, requested a synod of both the Eastern and Western churches, 818, 6.

PAUL OF SAMOSATA did not acknowledge the reality of the human flesh assumed by Christ, 705, 8. Christ is the Son of God, contrary to Paul of Samosata, 569, 105.

POVERTY: It belongs not to nature but to opinion, 1044, 90. It is precious, rich in the mystery of faith, 895, 5. Chaste poverty is preferable to dowry-based wealth, 161, 62. The minister of Christ was not ashamed of poverty, since the one who redeemed him was poor, 288, 41. Poverty is glorious in priests, 807, 2. See BISHOP. Where there is hunger for desires and insatiable appetite, there is certainly poverty, 943, 10. Which poor people should be helped before others? 88, 76 ff. That poor man who does not see you ought to be looked for; that man who is ashamed to be seen ought to be sought, 88, 77. The physically strong poor have no cause except to wander, 88, 76. Christ does not despise a poor person in his kingdom, but hears him and delivers him from every anxiety and trouble, 1099, 11. If you feed the poor, wash their wounds, and wipe away their filth, you have certainly wiped Christ’s feet, 959, 13. The tears of the poor are redeeming tears; they are groans that conceal death, a sorrow that, through the lasting abundance of joy, covers over the memory of former pain, 1115, 5. The gifts of the poor bind God, 873, 33. Would that they always charge me with this crime, because gold is distributed to the poor! ibid. The poor are my treasury; they are Christ’s poor. I know how to gather this treasure, 872, 33. Do not despise the poor person: he made you rich, 1043, 87. The poor truly are the treasures of the Church, 104, 140. A benefit bestowed on the poor helps more than one bestowed on the wealthy, 100, 127. No one is a pretender toward the poor, 140, 134. An inheritance is sought for a successor, but its administration binds one to the poor, 1130, 60. See INHERITANCE.

ORIGINAL SIN: We are all born under sin, and our very birth is in fault, 394, 13. We have degenerated through the fault of an inherited condition, 1087, 8. I fell in Adam, was expelled from Paradise in Adam, and died in Adam. How can God restore me unless he finds me in Adam—just as subject to guilt and liable to death in him, so justified in Christ? 1137, 6. Adam and Eve bound the entire succession of their own lineage in the chain of error, 1079, 8 ff. The devil had reduced the human race to perpetual captivity through the heavy interest of inherited bondage; the debtor-originator transmitted it to his descendants through an inheritance that had been lent at interest, 958, 7. See DEVIL.

The day of sin is called the day of confusion, 425, 37. Sin is iron, because it is penetrating, 932, 10. No pain is greater than that which wounds the conscience with the sword of sin; nor is there any heavier burden than the load of sins and the weight of crimes, 1063, 5. Nothing causes such profound grief as for someone held captive under sin to remember where he fell and from where he descended, 438, 102. Those placed in captivity under sin must be reverent, not usurpers, 440, 107. Sins are burned up by fire, 134, 104 ff. Whoever thinks about sin strives to shut himself within his own conscience, 432, 71. Why should those who condemn their sin not be more Christian than those who think they should defend it? 1000, 15. What is so divine as this judgment: that the one who is himself free from sin should punish sins? 896, 12. Whoever wishes to cleanse his sin should remove alien fire from himself and entrust himself only to that fire which burns away the fault, not the person, 1058, 8 ff. God washes away some sins for us by the blood of his Son; others he grants to us to cover our errors by good works and confessions, 1068, 23. The Holy Spirit removes all vices and pardons sins, 613, 64. [Col. 1482] God is powerful, whenever he wills, to forgive us sins—even those which we think cannot be forgiven, 418, 12. The forgiveness of sins is the price of both Testaments: announced figuratively through the lamb, it was completed in reality through Christ, 895, 5. The one whose sin has been forgiven has no reason to be ashamed, 429, 58. The death of sin is gain, and its life is punishment, 1144, 40. See GUILT.

SINS: By whom they may be forgiven. See CHURCH, PRIEST.

SINNER: The sinner rules in this world; the just person in God’s kingdom, 705, 12. Why do sinners abound in riches and other goods? 16, 57 ff. Clearly, so that no excuse may be left to them, 18, 63 ff. The sinner has no inheritance, 14, 46. Why is there no peace for sinners? 318, 47. The sinner serves fear, desire, greed, lust, and wickedness; indeed, he serves them more than if he were placed under tyrants, 937, 31. If human nature is diminished by those forms that are incapable of guilt, how much more is its virtue blunted through minds and limbs polluted by the stain of crimes! 983, 15. The sinner’s conscience reeks more heavily than any tomb, 13, 46. Sinners are written on earth, the just in heaven, 896, 14. One must have compassion on the sinner with weeping, prayer, and grief, 411, 81. If the sinner does not spare himself, God will spare him, 315, 36. Forgiveness of sins costs sinners more, and indulgence appears more precious to them, 692, 127.

MONEY: What is money to a person except a kind of provision for the journey? Much of it is a burden; a moderate amount is useful, 757, 11. Those who seek what belongs to others are rightly called “hawks of money,” 1129, 55. Whoever does not seek money has certainly stripped off vices, 1129, 55. Let a Christian give money as though he would not receive it—or at least as though he would receive back the portion he gave, 843, 4. See RICHES, GREED, THE GREEDY.

WASHING THE FEET: A mystery of faith and a mark of humility, 227, 57.

PELAGIA: Surrounded by ranks of persecutors and amid the greatest dangers to chastity and life, she was in no way overcome; and what were her words at that time? 938, 38. The martyrdom of Pelagia the virgin, her mother, and her sisters is elegantly described, 183, 33 ff.

PENTATEUCH, 956, 2.

THROUGH HIM, IN HIM, AND WITH HIM: These expressions have the force that one and the same—not something different or contrary—is understood in them, 682, 84. See FOR.

PARTRIDGE: It received its name from *perdere*, “to destroy,” 918, 3. Its deceit and trickery in misleading hunters, and its lust, 917, 2 ff. It is compared with the devil, ibid. It steals the eggs of others and incubates them with its own body, 919, 6.

TRAVELERS: During a famine they must not at all be expelled from the cities, 119, 45 ff. The prefect of the City performed an outstanding act in this matter, while another disgraceful deed was committed at Rome, ibid.

PERFECTION: There are two forms: one has partial numbers, the other complete numbers; one belongs here, the other there; one accords with human possibility, the other with the perfection of the future, 110, 11. There is complete perfection when nothing is lacking, 472, 9. All perfection is in truth, 63, 248. No one can be perfect without God’s favor, 418, 11.

TREACHERY: How harmful it is, 295, 66. Where there is treachery, there is blindness, 1201, 10. It is necessary to proclaim the treacheries of the treacherous, 710, 30. The flatteries of the treacherous are poisoned; they must be guarded against when they pretend to proclaim what they deny, 519, 129.

DANGERS: They belong to many, but remedies to few, 1207, 36. It is considered glorious if someone seeks the tranquillity of all through his own dangers, 113, 23.

PERSECUTORS: We must not fear their curses, 1184, 34. Christ wishes to suffer in his servants, 867, 14. It is his food to take pleasure in our sufferings, ibid.. He contributes more to the faithful who threatens them, 519, 129. The case is not the same for one who willingly denies Christ and one whom tortures have bent toward sacrilege: in the latter there was no intention, 395, 19 ff. See ADVERSITY, CHRISTIANS, GOD, MARTYRS.

PETER: He received the apostleship not only by the command of Christ but also by that of the Holy Spirit, 653, 103 ff. While seeking his profit at sea, he found the life of all and abandoned his boat. He found God; he left the oar and found the Word; he loosened the nets and bound faith; he folded the nets and raised up human beings; he despised the sea and gained heaven, 246, 131. While the sea was being tossed, he established minds wavering in their shifting station upon the rock, ibid. He faltered upon the sea, not through the weakness of the one commanding but through the weakness of the one obeying, 713, 43. He leapt from the boat to meet the Lord, not desirous of glory but eager for obedience, 710, 31. The less credibility is granted to the fisherman, the more one believes that what Peter said was divine, 216, 132. He answered on behalf of the other apostles, indeed, before the others, 711, 33. Why did he have to wash the foot? 333, 32; 363, 6 ff. It was night for Peter when he denied Christ, 1097, 7. How great a lesson for our salvation Peter’s temptation was, [Col. 1483] 1141, 27. For this reason Christ immediately forgave Peter, because he wept most bitterly, 436, 92. Peter’s threefold reply confirmed his love or erased the error of his threefold denial, 1203, 19. By feeding Christ’s flock well with the food of faith, Peter erased the guilt of his earlier fall, 551, 2. Peter was alone, yet he came to know the mysteries of the consecration of the nations throughout the whole world, 992, 2. He did not shut off hope of pardon from Simon Magus, whom he invited to repentance, 421, 23. Peter, whom no one had bound, was bound by faith; and the one whom faith bound, punishment did not release, 623, 108. Having gone out through the walls by night, he met Christ. When Christ said to him, “I am coming to be crucified again,” he voluntarily returned and honored the Lord through the cross, 867, 13. Peter is the Church’s foundation, 238, 105. When Christ calls Peter a rock, he indicates the foundation of the Church, 531, 56. Peter held the primacy of confession, not of honor; the primacy of faith, not of rank, 710, 32. They do not possess Peter’s inheritance who do not possess Peter’s seat, which they tear apart through impious division, 399, 33. The feast day of Saints Peter and Paul: and what was read on it? 244, 224. Peter’s mother-in-law seems to represent the affection of the will, 202, 64. See DEVOTION.

PETER OF ALEXANDRIA, bishop, 814, 41. Peter, bishop of the Church of Alexandria, a man of holy memory, 815, 3. See ROME.

PHILASTER, bishop of Brescia, 786, 1; 805, 76. His condemnation of Palladius, 802, 61.

PHILIPPUS, bishop, 819.

PHILOMARUS, a follower of Epicurus: what does he discuss concerning pleasure in his epitomes? 1026, 13.

PHILOSOPHY: One clothed in the mantle of philosophy cannot see Christ while wearing, so to speak, the garb of secular wisdom, 235, 92. The man who first discovered the name “philosophy” ordered a flute-player each day, before going to bed, to play softer melodies, 179, 19. Those who seemed to excel in philosophy followed Solomon, 1142, 30. Philosophers borrowed from our Scriptures, 35, 133; 48, 179. Let philosophers and poets acknowledge that whatever better things they have said come from our writings, 937, 28. Philosophers alone have remained in their schools; each day they are abandoned by their companions. Those who believe simply grow each day, 460, 84. See SOUL, DIALECTIC.

PHOENIX: In what year of its life, and how, does it die and rise again? 1149, 59. For it, the year of resurrection is the five-hundredth; for us, the thousandth, ibid.

PHOENICIANS. See CIRCUMCISION.

PHOTINUS: He argues that the Son began from the Virgin, 445, 6. He judges according to the flesh; and how is he excluded? 569, 104. He is refuted by the first words of John, 454, 57. See ARIUS.

PHOTINIANS: They confess Christ to be merely human, 526, 29. They deny Christ’s divinity, 1212, 49. The Son of God was given to us, not to the Photinians, who say that he was not given to us but was born among us from the beginning, 507, 58. How will the blasphemy of the Photinians be refuted at Christ’s final judgment? 492, 117. By imperial law they are not to hold assemblies, 809, 12. The emperors are asked to prohibit them from the town of Sirmium, where they were still attempting to hold assemblies, ibid. See ARIANS.

PHRYGIAN PROPHETS, 840, 30. In the Phrygian sacred rites, sexual immorality is a religious discipline, 150, 16.

PIETY: True piety is that which places divine things before human things and eternal things before temporal things, 1055, 7. As it is the chief of all virtues, so it is also the seedbed of the other virtues, 1129, 54. The form of piety is soft and tender; it loves nothing insolent, nothing harsh, nothing severe, 1135, 1. Through fatherly piety we approach God most closely, 1105, 10. It is not a detriment to nature, 483, 66. Let it train you in justice, self-restraint, and gentleness, 49, 184. The Lord gave nothing more excellent than piety, 1021, 7. No reward is better for God than one that possesses the gifts of piety, 194, 32.

PILADES. See ORESTES.

PLACENTIA, 944, 3. Placentia, 160, 57.

Πλανῆται ἀπλανεῖς: “Wandering stars, unwandering,” 974, 15; 977, 3..

PLATO’S: A certain patrician lineage of philosophers, 922, 1. We know that the Platonic Ideas were mocked even by the philosophers themselves, 529, 46. See SOUL.

FULLNESS: It knows no increase, 620, 96.

PLOTINUS is condemned as a Jovinianist, 969, 14.

RAIN: The divine Scriptures promised rain for the whole world, which would water the earth under the advent of the Lord and Savior through the dew of the Spirit, 601, 8.

REPENTANCE: It is necessary for those who have fallen, just as medicines are necessary for the wounded, 313, 33. Never to repent belongs to God alone, 1043, 85. To commit no sin belongs to God alone; to amend, correct an error, and undertake repentance for sin belongs to the wise, 1057, 4. How greatly does God wish us to mourn our sins? 427, 49 ff. Sin is not removed except by tears and repentance, 999, 11. We ought to repent of sin daily, 436, 95. Rare confession of sin, rare repentance, and rare assertion of his word among human beings, 1057, 4 ff. Good is the repentance which, if it did not exist, would cause everyone to postpone the grace of cleansing until old age, 437, 98. If I have no water, I have tears; while I wash Christ’s feet with them, would that I might wash myself clean! 431, 67. How should repentance be practiced—with what zeal, feeling, intention of mind, inward shaking of the entrails, and conversion of the heart? 427, 46 ff. Priests do not take away the sin of one who presents himself deceitfully and is still intent on sinning, 1059, 11. Repentance must be practiced not only carefully but promptly, 415, 2. It must be practiced when the wantonness of guilt has cooled, 440, 107. It must not be postponed, 437, 98 ff. You who followed the one who was straying, follow the one who is correcting himself, 256, 31. Cling to repentance as to a plank among shipwrecked people, 315, 38. Greater crimes are cleansed by greater weeping, 393, 10. One must grieve more intensely where the sin is more grievous, 315, 37. What must the penitent do? 437, 96. Whoever practices repentance must not only wash away his sin with tears but also cover and conceal his earlier offenses with more reformed actions, 424, 35. Faith that mourns earlier sins is accustomed to avoid new ones, 959, 12. It is better to remain quiet when one cannot perform works of repentance, lest something be done in repentance itself that later requires repentance, 439, 104. Those who practice repentance should have only one regret: that they should not come to regret their repentance itself, 434, 86. I have more easily found those who preserved innocence than those who practiced repentance suitably, 436, 96. If repentance is once undertaken but neither lawfully performed nor properly celebrated, it obtains no fruit from the earlier act and takes away the possibility of a later one, 439, 104. Repentance is a remedy for sin, not an incentive to sin, 435, 90. How wrongly some people, having resolved to practice repentance, think that the hope of repentance has extended to them permission to sin! ibid. Repentance is practiced because of hope of pardon, 419, 16. No one can practice repentance well unless he has hoped for indulgence, 390, 4. God, who requires repentance, promises pardon, 403, 46. The one who reserves himself for pardon does not humble himself with his whole heart, 396, 23. He awaits our groans, but temporal ones, in order to forgive eternal ones; he awaits our tears in order to pour out his compassion, 396, 22. The apostles taught repentance, promised pardon, and released guilt, 424, 35. So great is the medicine of repentance that God seems to change his sentence, 427, 48. There is one mystery of the forgiveness of sins in baptism and repentance, 400, 36. Repentance precedes, grace follows; neither repentance exists without grace nor grace without repentance. Repentance must first condemn sin so that grace may abolish it, 895, 7. If repentance perseveres, it will dare to hope, if not for glory, at least certainly for release from punishment, 314, 36. See CONVERSION.

Just as there is one baptism, so there is one repentance—yet one that is performed publicly, 436, 95. Those who think repentance should be practiced repeatedly are rightly criticized, ibid. Let the mother Church weep for you and wash your guilt with tears; let Christ see you mourning. He loves it when many pray for one, 436, 92. If someone has hidden crimes and diligently practices repentance for Christ’s sake, let him hope for pardon. Let him ask for it with tears, with groans, with the weeping of the entire people; let him beg that he be forgiven. And when his communion has been postponed a second and third time, let him believe that he has pleaded too mildly; let him increase his weeping, return later in greater misery, clasp the feet with his arms, kiss them with kisses, and wash them with tears, 414, 90. Someone living a solitary life ought to pray for one who has sinned against the Lord, 401, 42. Shame must not recall us from public repentance, 435, 91 ff. Those who seek repentance but, after receiving it, are recalled by shame from public supplication seem to have sought repentance for their evil deeds but to practice it for their good deeds, 434, 46. I have known some who furrowed their faces with tears in repentance, plowed their cheeks with continual weeping, and, with fasting mouths and pale faces, displayed the appearance of death in a body breathing out death, 414, 91. Public repentance of a fallen virgin, 314, 35; and of her corrupter, 316, 40. What the prayers and feelings of that virgin ought to be, 317, 43 ff. She ought daily to recite Psalm 50, ibid. Where punishment is prescribed, there repentance for sins ought to be; where forgiveness is granted, there is glory, 895, 6. The Lord’s command applies even to those guilty of the gravest crime: if they practice repentance with their whole heart and open confession of sin, the grace of the heavenly sacrament is to be poured back upon them, 420, 19. It was the day on which the Lord handed himself over for us, on which repentance is released in the Church, 859, 26. See EXCOMMUNICATION, NOVATIANS, PAUL.

POETS. See PHILOSOPHERS.

POLYBIUS admirably exercised proconsular jurisdiction in the regions of Africa, 1106, 1.

POMPEY, after having girded the world with three triumphs, was driven from the battlefield, a fugitive from war and an exile from the boundaries of his own empire, and fell by the hand of the eunuch of Canopus, [Col. 1485] 841, 25.

FRUIT: When an unripe fruit is shaken, it quickly perishes, 762, 29.

PEOPLE: How can someone who has nothing hidden from the people, who is unlike the multitude, be observed by the people? 902, 2.

PORTIANA, that is, the basilica outside the walls, was not being demanded by the Arians; rather, they demanded the new basilica, that is, the one inside the walls, which is larger, 852, 1. Ambrose opposed them, ibid. and following.

POSSESSION: A pure person is a precious possession, 5, 11. We possess what we use, 101, 132.

POWERS: They must not be provoked, 56, 217. Power is begotten from wisdom and virtue, 590, 213.

PRECEPTS: Whoever binds others by his precepts ought himself to observe lawful precepts, 1037, 64. See COUNSEL, COMMANDMENT.

PREDESTINATION: God did not predestine before he foreknew; rather, he predestined the rewards of those whose merits he foreknew, 565, 83.

PREFECTS: The houses of the prefects at Rome were burned, and no one sought vengeance, 950, 13.

REWARDS: The hope of rewards and the inheritance of heavenly promises is usually the greatest incentive for the good to pursue virtue, 1085, 2.

THE PRESENT: Many prefer present things to future ones, 58, 227. The reward of present things is evidence of future things, 414, 89.

PRESUMPTION: It is closer to arrogance than to petition, 434, 80.

THE FEELING OF A TRANSGRESSOR: It customarily displeases even the gentiles, 825, 7.

PRESBYTERS: It is more fitting for presbyters or ministers to maintain humility, 98, 122. The Lord granted his priests, without any exception, the authority to release sins, 393, 10. Presbyters who have served in their rank for thirty or countless years, or ministers of the Church, are withdrawn from sacred office and assigned to the civil administration; they groan bitterly, 954, 29. See PRIEST.

PRICES: To seek increases in prices is a matter not of simplicity but of cunning, 117, 37.

FIRSTFRUITS: Dedicate the firstfruits of your vigils to Christ; offer the firstfruits of your actions to Christ, 230, 69. Some wish there to be a distinction between firstfruits and firstborn, 926, 9.

FIRSTBORN: The firstborn is the firstfruit, 920, 2. He is truly the firstfruit who is the holy offspring of a holy mother, 921, 6. The saints are firstborn, though not every firstborn is holy, 920, 2 ff. From the firstborn Son of God come the holy firstborn; and from him, “beginning,” the one called “beginning” is holy—the Son to whom the privilege of firstfruits is owed, 921, 7.

BIRTHDAYS OF PRINCES, 1178, 15.

PRISCUS: From childhood onward he grew up in age together with Ambrose, 1107, 1.

AMBROSE COMMENDS PRISCUS TO ATTICUS, 107, 1.

PRIVILEGES. See PAGANS.

PROCULUS, bishop of Marseille and legate of the Gauls, 786, 1; 805, 76; 806, 1. His condemnation of Palladius, 802, 63.

THE ONE WHO IS PREVENTED: Whoever does not enjoy the things he desires is prevented, 395, 20..

PROMISE: One must not rashly violate a promise, 215, 6. Not all promises must always be fulfilled, 127, 79. Sometimes it is contrary to duty to fulfill a promise and to keep an oath, 68, 264. It is more tolerable not to make a promise than to do something shameful, 127, 76.

PROPHETS: They received the Spirit and saw Christ, 700, 167. The prophets do not look at themselves or at the things near their feet, but at heavenly things, 1015, 13. He feeds the prophet who understands and keeps what has been written, 1041, 80. It is the custom of prophecy that future things be described either as though present or as though already accomplished, 463, 97.

WHAT IS ONE’S OWN: For those who have nothing, nothing at all is lacking, 187, 5.

PROSPER: He congratulated himself that, because of Ambrose’s priesthood, he would not have to return what he had taken, 1120, 24. Nevertheless, the effectiveness of Satyrus settled everything, ibid.

PROSPERITY: Prosperous circumstances lift up the mind, 844, 9. It easily happens that the mind becomes unfamiliar with adversity through the use of prosperous circumstances, 849, 23. See HONESTY, PROSPEROUS CIRCUMSTANCES.

PRODIGALITY: Even in expenditures on good works one must not be immoderate, 96, 109.

PROTASIUS. See GERVASIUS.

NEIGHBOR: A neighbor is one whom not only a like nature has joined to us but whom compassion has also united to us, 398, 28. It is not kinship of blood but kinship of virtue that makes neighbors, 200, 54. You cannot be a neighbor unless you show mercy, 404, 52. This is the law of nature and of the Lord, which binds us to a common humanity, so that, like parts of one body, we may show mutual concern for one another, 112, 19 ff. To help one who has nothing is humanity; to exact more than you have given is harshness, 112, 20. No one has anything to offer another more than what he wishes for himself, 1196, 79. Let us understand that we will be more acceptable to God insofar as we give more, because we are more grateful to God insofar as more has been forgiven us, [Col. 1486] 958, 9. Let us forgive a little, we to whom more has been forgiven, ibid.. No one ought to harm another while looking after himself, 954, 25. Whoever does not repel injury from a companion, when he can, is as much at fault as the one who inflicts it, 47, 178. How can you fail to recoil from something happening to you when you grieve that it has happened to another even more impatiently? 1137, 7. God condemns this above all: if someone deceives his neighbor through the neighbor’s kindness and, through fraudulent injustice, crushes one weighed down by debt, 758, 13. Whoever rejoices at another’s fall rejoices at the devil’s victory, 433, 78. The one who has compelled a weak person to fall is more tightly bound by guilt, 948, 7.

PRUDENCE: It is occupied with the investigation of truth, 31, 115. It is placed first among the principal virtues, ibid. Our predecessors defined prudence as consisting in knowledge of the truth, 32, 118. Prudence belongs to human reason, 241, 114. There is nothing wiser than that prudence which distinguishes divine things from human things, 1127, 48. Labor and prolonged meditation, together with God’s grace, produce perfect prudence, 982, 11. It is possessed not in the forum or in the streets but in the Church, 235, 88. It has fellowship with all good things, 85, 66. The abundance of prudence flows back upon itself, and the more beautifully it has flowed out, the more practiced becomes everything that remains, 88, 75. No one is prudent who does not know God, 31, 117. It is the prudent person’s task to foresee that he may not often have to repent of himself, 1043, 85. The flights of the prudent are secure through the course of life, 242, 116..

IN PSALM EIGHT: All the virtues of prayer are present, 386, 25. In Psalm fourteen we have received the perfection of the human being, 1208, …

37. The thirty-sixth is filled with moral precepts, 1033, 45. The twenty-second is suited to the heavenly sacrament of the Eucharist, 375, 13. Why the one hundred and fourteenth is inscribed “Hallelujah,” 1208, 37. It is shown how we may hear Theodosius speaking, as it were, in Psalm 114, 1203, 17 and following. See VIRGIN.

PUBLIC. A man who could avenge himself by inflicting public harm ought not to have been injured, 847, 18.

CHASTITY. To integrity of speech no less reverence must be shown than to bodily chastity, 1128, 52. See SHAME.

MODESTY. Good is that modesty which is accustomed so to restrain the eyes of the body that often we do not even see what we see, 409, 70. Good is the modesty commended by silence, 300, 86. Solitude teaches modesty, and a secluded place is the training ground of modesty, 296, 71. A good guardian of modesty is the sorrow of piety, 199, 51. Modesty must be the inseparable companion of virginity, 166, 14. It does not withdraw, but commends duty, 1128, 52. Modesty is not a dowry that stands alone, 273, 109.

THREE BOYS. For the three boys in the fiery furnace there was present, in the form of an angel, one who admonished them that praise of the one power should be rendered in the number of the Trinity: God was blessed; in the Angel the Son of God was seen; and holy, spiritual grace spoke through the boys, 450, 33.

BEAUTY AND COMELINESS. Whether beauty and physical attractiveness have a place among the virtues, 23, 83. If artifice is absent, there is no offense in beauty; if enticement is removed, appearance and the grace of form are blameless, 759, 20. Beauty that is heard of but not seen is desired the more, 167, 22.

PYTHAGORAS. Held in high esteem among philosophers, he scarcely found an equal, as they say, 902, 1. Since, as most believe, he derived his lineage from the Jewish people, he also derived from their discipline the principles of teaching, 902, 1. He was older than Socrates, 10, 31. Following the prophet David, he gave his followers a law of silence, 10, 31. The Pythagorean injunction by which he forbade his disciples to enter the common and customary path of the people, 902, 1. From where this was taken, ibid. When a Pythagorean virgin was compelled by a tyrant to reveal a secret, she bit off her tongue and spat it into the tyrant’s face, 151, 17.

## Q

**QUADRAGESIMA (Lent).** Something ought to be added during the days of Lent, 178, 18.

## R

**RACHEL** preserved the duty of modesty and did not neglect the affection owed to piety, 176, 10. In holy Rachel, the figure of the mystery was more important than the order of marriage, 210, 90. She bore the type of the Church, 235, 91; 1065, 12.

**RAGUEL** was in this respect more honorable than the philosophers: he preferred that his daughter remain unmarried to him rather than that outsiders run risks on account of her marriage, 131, 96 and following.

**RAHAB**, raising up the signs of faith and the banners of the Lord’s Passion, tied a scarlet cord in the window, 574, 128.

**FROGS.** Silence was imposed upon them, 177, 14. See **PRAYER**.

**REASON** ought to restrain desire and make it obedient to itself, 60, 237.

**REBECCA:** why she preferred Jacob to Esau, 1046, 100. [Col. 1487]

**REDEMPTION** is through blood, forgiveness through power, and life through grace, 498, 8. Faith is the redemption of the soul, 777, 2.

**RELAPSE.** Let neither your feet turn back nor your conduct return; let there be no relapse into weakness of will, no recurrence of sins, 909, 21.

**THE KINGDOM OF GOD** comes when you have obtained his grace, 378, 221.

**RELIGION:** whence it derives its name, 159, 52. Religion is to be preferred to family obligation, piety to kinship, 1055, 7. The salvation of children must be placed after the service of religion, 215, 7. Christ teaches us not to be moved by what appears objectionable to human beings, if any accusations are brought on account of religious observance, 1077, 27. Things that are shameful in bodily appearance are to be revered in contemplation of sacred religion, 1014, 6. A great duty of piety, but a richer one of religion, 185, 6. Nothing is greater than religion, nothing more sublime than faith, 826, 11. Whatever is offered to religion ought to be wholly fitting, 426, 42. Religion made into a reward what unbelief thought was a punishment, 835, 11. He who feared religion did not know how to sow disputes, 449, 29. In the vine there is religion, in the olive peace, and in the rose the modesty of consecrated virginity, 157, 46. The fragrance of consecrated religion has arisen from every part of the world, 158, 47. Lions taught the Christian religion when they worshiped the martyr. See **MARTYRS**.

**RELICS**, the most sacred remains of the martyrs, 875, 4. The applause of Jews and Christians at the exaltation of the relics of Saints Vitalis and Agricola, 279, 8. See **AMBROSE**, **GERVASIUS**.

**REMEDY.** God is not offended by a remedy, 183, 33.

**RENATUS.** See **LEONTIUS**.

**OUR REST** is in heaven, not on earth, 979, 8. Good rest is to pass beyond the things of the world and to rest, in heavenly fellowships of mysteries, with those things that are above the world, 1206, 29.

**RESURRECTION** is no more incredible than the miracles of Moses and the other events recorded in the Gospel, 1153, 74. Why should we wonder that what once existed can be born again, when we see that what did not exist has been born? 1151, 64. It belongs to nature for all things that are born to rise again; it is contrary to nature for them to perish, 1149, 57. How serious a sacrilege it is not to believe in the resurrection, 1161, 102. The future resurrection of our body is proved by reason, by the example of the universe, and by the testimony of an accomplished event, 1147, 52 and following. It is also proved by the Old Testament, especially by the prophet Ezekiel, 1151, 66 and following. If the elements rise at God’s command, why do the dead not rise at his command? 1156, 85. Christ promises the resurrection of bodies, and we ought to believe him, 1157, 89 and following. Christ raised several people from the dead so that we might believe through more abundant examples, 1156, 81. This is the order and reason of justice: since body and soul share in action, both must come to judgment; both must either be handed over to punishment or reserved for glory, 1157, 88. If the transgressor is preserved for punishment, why is the righteous not preserved forever for glory? If the worm of sinners does not die, how will the flesh of the righteous perish? 1157, 87. The flesh must rise again, since it is destined to receive the reward of its deeds, 295, 59. The Gentiles cannot deny the resurrection of bodies, since they have believed that human beings could be born from the sown teeth of the Hydra, 1152, 70. The objection of the Gentiles against the resurrection of bodies is refuted, 1149, 58. It is easier for bodies to rise again than for souls to pass from one body into other bodies, 1151, 65. See **LAZARUS**.

All who are joined to the most holy Church and are reckoned under the name of God will obtain the privilege of resurrection and eternal joy, 1166, 116. As death had its first fruits in Adam, so resurrection has its first fruits in Christ, 1158, 91. We are all born, and we will all rise again; but in both cases the grace and condition of living or returning to life are different, 1158, 93. In what order of merits shall we be raised? 1165, 116. We should not seek the exertion of resurrection, but its fruit, 1165, 114. The flower of resurrection is immortality; the flower of resurrection is incorruption, 1148, 54. What grief does the grace of resurrection not console, what sorrow does it not drive away? 1135, 3. The year of resurrection for us is the thousandth, 1149, 59.

**KING.** David taught that one should keep faith with one’s own king, neither usurp power nor fail to revere it, 122, 60. How wretched here is the condition of kings, how changeable the state of power, how brief the spaces of this life, how great the servitude within power itself, since they live according to another’s will, not their own? 908, 18. The endings of kings are joined with their beginnings, 834, 7. See **DAVID**.

**REVELATIONS.** See **SUSANNA**.

**RHEGIUM**, 944, 3.

**RHAETIA**, the second, learned the envy provoked by her fertility: by her fruitfulness she aroused an enemy against herself, 838, 21. See **JUTHUNGI**, **MAXIMUS**. [Col. 1488]

**THE RHONE**, its waters swift, 1194, 79.

Immoderation in laughter, 297, 76.

**RITES.** See **ANCESTORS**.

**THE ROMAN CHURCH** is the head of the entire Roman world, 811, 4. From it the rights of venerable communion flow out to all, ibid. Thus Saint Athanasius and Peter, bishops of the Alexandrian Church, and many of the Eastern bishops acted, so that they appeared to have taken refuge in the judgment of the Roman Church, of Italy, and of the whole West, 816, 4. The Catholic bishops, that is, the Roman Church, 1127, 47. See **SATYRUS**.

Dew removes the nightly droughts of heaven; the dew of our Lord Jesus Christ poured the moisture of eternal life into the night and the worldly darkness, 230, 70. The dew on the fleece was faith in Judaea; afterward it dried up in the breasts of the Jews and flowed into the hearts of the Gentiles, 601, 7. See **GIDEON**.

**THE BUSH** that burned without being consumed signified that the Lord would come to illuminate the thorns of our body, not to consume those afflicted but to soften their afflictions, 629, 165.

**RUFINUS**, having previously been master of the offices, became praetorian prefect during his consulship, 101, 1. Ambrose rejoices that he has been advanced in honor, ibid.

**RUMORIDUS**, a count devoted to the worship of pagan nations from the earliest years of his childhood, 1010, 3.

**RUTH.** See **BOAZ**.

## S
### SABAOTH

Interpreters have rendered *Sabaoth* in some places as “Lord of hosts,” in others as “king,” and in others as “almighty,” 524, 13.

### SABBATH

The rest of the great Sabbath, 1206, 29.

### SABELLIUS

Sabellius’ impiety attributes the assumption of human flesh to the Father, 486, 80. He wants the Father to be the same person as the Son, 569, 104. We must not, like Sabellius, confuse the Father and the Word, 445, 6. There is one God, but not such that he himself is both Father and Son, as the impious Sabellius asserts, 487, 86. He is refuted by the opening words of John, 454, 57. See ARIUS.

The Sabellian confuses the Father and the Son, 704, 8; 476, 33. How will the blasphemy of the Sabellians be refuted at Christ’s final judgment? 492, 118. See MARCIONITES.

### SABINIANUS

The deacon Sabinianus, 737, 3.

### SABINUS

Sabinus returned some booklets to Ambrose, and Ambrose in turn sent others to Sabinus, so that he might examine them with a strict judgment, 990, 1 ff. He begs him to place a mark beside a word of doubtful weight and of a deceptive balance, ibid., 3.

After reading the *Hexaemeron*, Sabinus asked Ambrose about the earthly paradise, 981, 1. He wrote to Ambrose concerning a certain Apollinarian, 984, 1 ff. See AMBROSE.

### SABINUS

Sabinus, bishop of Placentia, 786, 1; 798, 10; 805, 76; 796, 37 ff. His condemnation of Palladius, 801, 58.

### PRIEST

A priest ought to be as though without father and without mother: not nobility of lineage, but the grace of conduct and the precedence of virtues should be chosen in him, 1034, 19.

We priests have a nobility of our own, to be preferred to prefectures and consulships, 299, 82.

A priest ought to consecrate a priest, and he himself ought to clothe him in garments—that is, in priestly virtues, 1036, 59.

What should the one who ministers to Christ be like? 203, 65.

What should priestly virtue be? 1036, 59.

Priestly dignity claims for itself sober gravity apart from the crowds, a serious life, and exceptional weight, 902, 2 ff.

This possession suits Christ better: that he should possess the virtues of his priest and reap the fruits of integrity, continence, charity, and tranquillity, 1103, 13.

Let the priest observe, and assign as a duty whatever is appropriate to each person, 57, 225.

Some priests wore linen breeches, 23, 80. See AARON.

It is especially fitting for a priest to adorn God’s temple with appropriate honor, 96, 111.

A priest who reserves something of his own patrimony for himself does not appear imperfect, 41, 152.

It is the priest’s duty to harm no one and to wish to benefit everyone; but to be able to do so belongs to God alone, 122, 59.

It is fitting for him frequently to undertake suitable expenditures of mercy, and for the people to whom …, 96, 111.

The generosity of priests ought to be sober, not for show, but for justice, 88, 76.

Most priests, the more they contributed, the more they abounded, 88, 78.

Losses of worldly things are better for them than worldly profits, 1101, 5. See VIRGIN.

If a priest seeks the privilege of avoiding the municipal burden, he must renounce his native and ancestral property and the possession of all his resources, 836, 13.

By recent laws even the benefits of private succession are denied to priests, and no one complains, 836, 13.

When Joseph established the tax for the Egyptians, he reserved the priestly possession free from taxation, so that priestly religion too might be held inviolable among the Egyptians, 933, 11.

Throughout the churches, orders are given that Catholic priests be expelled, that those who resist be struck with the sword, and that all municipal officials be proscribed unless they fulfill the emperor’s command, 867, 16.

The tyranny of a priest is weakness, 858, 23. Priests have never been tyrants, but they have often suffered tyrants, ibid.

Christ granted his apostles that sins be forgiven through repentance; this was transmitted from the apostles to the duties of priests, 419, 12.

The Holy Spirit is invoked by the priest and given by God; in this, the gift is God’s, while the ministry is the priest’s, 619, 90.

The gift of the Holy Spirit is the priest’s office, but the right of the Holy Spirit is to loose and bind sins, 392, 8.

It was not Damasus who cleansed, nor Peter, nor Ambrose, nor Gregory; for the sacraments are not our services but yours, O Christ, 603, 18.

The priest’s food consists in the remission of sins, 1059, 11. See CHURCH.

A priest must first be healed, so that he may be able to minister, 203, 65.

In office, neither harsh severity nor excessive leniency is appropriate, 98, 120.

Although a priestly admonition may seem bitter for a time, like Aaron’s rod, nevertheless, when it is thought to have withered, it flowers again, 956, 3.

It is fitting for the priest to favor people by his benefactions or judgments, 98, 12.

We priests are interpreters of the faith, 1011, 8.

If an emperor consults his companions about monetary matters, how much more ought priests to be consulted in a matter of religion! 954, 27.

Valentinian wanted priests to judge priests, 860, 2.

Priests ought to judge laypeople, not laypeople priests, 800, 57. See CONSTANTINE, BISHOP.

To intervene in monetary cases is not the priest’s task, 122, 59.

A priest may remain silent only in a monetary matter; but in God’s cause, where there is danger to communion, even to conceal sin is no slight offense, 99, 125.

It is neither imperial to deny freedom of speech nor priestly not to say what one thinks, 946, 2.

A priest will be liable to punishment because he did not admonish the one who was in error, 998, 3.

Priestly authority should persuade what is useful rather than what is merely pleasing, 956, 2.

Priests should make it their chief concern to cut away those vices that appear to be spreading among very many people, 843, 5.

Priests cannot enter into partnership with another’s error, 227, 14.

In everything the priest is endangered and distressed; whatever others suffer, he himself bears, 1207, 36.

Christ must be sought in the heart of a prudent priest, 226, 50.

The priest’s petition is a teaching of piety, 1103, 1.

The priest obtains more readily when virtue prevails, 1103, 1.

From the example of Dathan, Abiram, and Korah, let dissenters learn to fear the Lord’s anger and to appease priests, 1034, 52 ff.

Everyone is anointed into the priesthood and is also anointed into kingship; but the kingship is royal and the priesthood spiritual, 365, 3.

Priests are like the cheeks of the Church, in which her flower is more pleasing and her age more mature, 1176, 7. See LEVITE.

### SACRAMENTS

Who is the author of the sacraments, except the Lord Jesus? 368, 13.

The sacraments of Christians are more divine and more ancient than those of the Jews, 351, 11.

There cannot be the grace of the sacraments unless there has been forgiveness of sins, 630, 168.

To explain the meaning of the sacraments to those not yet initiated would, I should think, be to betray rather than to expound them, 325, 2.

His cunning is accustomed to deceive those who contend against the divine sacraments, 636, 11.

### SACRIFICE

A sacrifice pleasing and acceptable to God is only one that has been tested in the riches of sincerity and truth, 1059, 12.

You shall offer when you have received the opportunity to sacrifice, when your victim is acceptable to God, 1000, 15.

Sacrifices cannot be approved by God unless confession by the voice accompanies them, as the priestly offering customarily rouses the people to implore God’s grace, 1165, 113.

What does Moses’ action mean when, after offering sacrifice and sacrificing salutary victims to the Lord, he put half the blood into bowls but poured half upon the altar? 1051, 1 ff.

### SOLOMON

Solomon’s noble judgment shone forth through the gift of the Holy Spirit, 672, 36.

How noble was Solomon’s judgment! 213, 1 ff.

The women litigating before him were figures of faith and temptation, 214, 3.

It was not without reason that God’s understanding was thought to be present in Solomon’s judgment, 80, 44 ff.

Solomon’s bed was a figure of our body, 179, 21. See PHILOSOPHERS.

### SALPHA

*Salpha* signifies “shadow of the mouth,” 1086, 6.

The daughters of Salpha, as the interpretation teaches, are “the shadowing of the mouth,” 287, 37.

### DANCING

Lascivious dancing is the companion of pleasure and the sport of lust, 1014, 5.

Where extreme dancing is the companion of pleasure, modesty is unsafe and seduction suspect, 180, 25.

The slippery movements of theatrical dancing are vicious even in a young girl, 426, 42.

No one dances while sober, unless he is insane, 180, 25.

How glorious is the wise man’s dance—the dance that David danced! 1014, 8. See MICHAL.

### SALVATION

Salvation cannot otherwise be secure unless each person truly worships the true God, 824, 1. See ANIMALS.

### SAMARITAN

He is called a guardian, 404, 57.

### SAMSON

Samson’s father did not, as some have thought, harbor any suspicion out of jealousy concerning his wife, who possessed remarkable beauty, 845, 12.

His story is adapted to the various mysteries of the Church, 635, 5 ff.

The account of his conception and the whole sequence of his life is narrated in an orderly historical style, 844, 8 ff.

Predestined by a divine oracle, he was a great man—not to be numbered among the many, but outstanding among the few—easily foremost of all in bodily strength, 845, 10.

He was rightly considered stronger than the others because the Spirit of the Lord guided him, 635, 5.

Would that he had been as chaste in preserving grace as he was strong in overcoming the beast! ibid.

That he was outwitted by a woman should be attributed to nature rather than to guilt, 852, 33.

In death he conquered himself and displayed an unconquerable spirit, 851, 32.

He did not prove himself inferior, he whose burial was more notable than his power, 852, 33. See MARRIAGE.

### SANCTIFICATION

Sanctification is not handed over but infused, 443, 2.

It is spiritual grace, 685, 95.

### THE SAINTS

The life of the saints is not here on earth but in heaven, 1186, 46.

The stars are saints shining with heavenly grace, 286, 25.

The holier someone is, the more secure he is, 158, 51.

The saints require careful vigilance, 601, 9.

The life of the saints is harmonious and so consonant with itself that later things answer to earlier things, 698, 162.

Those who know nothing as their own do not know how to spare what is their own, because for the saints God is everything, 1056, 8.

The saints ascend to the Lord; the wicked descend to vices. The saints are on the mountains, criminals in the valleys, 911, 2.

The sleep of the saints is also active, 823, 4.

The sleep of the saints is free from all bodily pleasures and every disturbance of the mind; it brings tranquillity to the mind and calm to the soul, 823, 4.

Christ alone walks within souls and moves through the minds of the saints, 511, 74.

It is not unknown to us that the saints fight even while they rest, 820, 7.

You have the saints near you to pray for you, 200, 54.

The angels and martyrs, who can pray for our sins, should be entreated, 200, 55. See BEATITUDE.

Love Peter’s nearness and Andrew’s kinship, so that they may pray for you and your desires may depart, 200, 54. See ARROGANT.

### WISDOM

Wisdom says that it came forth from the mouth of the Most High, not so as to be outside the Father, but with the Father, 625, 120.

Divine wisdom, ineffable, unmixed, and incorruptible, pours its grace into the souls of the saints and reveals knowledge, so that they may behold its glory, 1053, 4.

Whoever understands the infusion of divine wisdom rejoices and seeks no other food, 1049, 2.

Wisdom possesses an indivisible fellowship with the virtues, 85, 65.

It cannot exist without justice, 81, 48.

Wisdom is the foundation, but justice is the work, 68, 261.

Where there is wisdom, there is strength of soul, constancy, and courage, 931, 5.

Wisdom grows cold without grace, 361, 1.

There is a measure of wisdom; if it exceeds its measure, it does harm, 778, 6.

The sons of those who glorify and boast of themselves have not trodden the way of wisdom, which destruction does not know and death does not perceive, 903, 4.

How great is the beauty of wisdom! 85, 64.

The more exalted a virtue is, the more we must strive to attain it, 33, 124.

Wisdom is more precious than gold and silver; death does not know it, 290, 50.

Wisdom alone is free: it makes the poor superior to the rich and makes slaves lend at interest to their own masters, 933, 14.

Wisdom is the unfailing food of the soul, with which those placed in paradise fed; the divine Word called it manna, 778, 5.

There is a sacrifice of wisdom, just as there is of justice, 783, 3.

“My wisdom is the cross of the Lord; my redemption is the death of the Lord,” 503, 36.

To the wise person nothing is foreign except what is inconsistent with virtue; wherever he goes, he will find everything that is his, 757, 11.

The wise person is not broken by fear, diminished by power, lifted up by prosperity, or overwhelmed by sorrow. He is always the same in spirit; he remains perfect in Christ, founded in charity and rooted in faith, 931, 5.

Every wise person is free, but every foolish person is a slave, 931, 4 ff.

The philosophers drew this opinion from the sacred Scriptures, ibid., 6 ff.

The wise person is not a compelled but a voluntary executor of virtue, 935, 20.

He is no longer wise who is without the practice and discipline of virtue, ibid.

It belongs to the wise neither to be compelled nor to be forbidden, 935, 20.

For the wise person, even servitude is freedom, 936, 24.

The power of the foolish must be cut back, not freedom added to it; for servitude is appropriate to him, 939, 40.

The heart, conduct, and work of the wise person ought to be rooted and immovable, 938, 33.

It belongs to the wise to desire everything that is good, 934, 19.

The only wise person is the one who has used God as his guide in knowing the chambers of truth and has become, by grace, God’s heir and successor, 937, 29.

Can a wise person, placed in a shipwreck, take a plank away from a foolish shipwrecked man? 114, 27. See RICH.

### SARAH

Sarah rightly denied it because she had laughed, although her laughter was full of gravity and modesty, 297, 76.

Chastity increased Sarah’s devotion, and devotion her chastity, 673, 42.

### SARMATIO

See BARBATIANUS.

### SATAN

In Latin, *Satan* means “adversary,” 918, 3.

### SATISFACTION

When the satisfaction of someone is excluded, his disposition is turned away, 761, 29.

A great wound requires deep and prolonged medicine; a great crime necessarily requires great satisfaction, 315, 37.

### SATYRUS

Satyrus stood between two siblings, one a virgin and the other a priest; midway between them in age, he was not inferior in greatness of spirit, 1129, 54.

Satyrus shared an undivided patrimony with his brothers, 1130, 59.

How great was his devotion toward the worship of God! 1125, 43 ff.

He shone forth with incredible admiration in the audience hall of the prefecture, 1127, 49.

He did not exult in riches as a wealthy man, nor, as a poor man, judge the little that he possessed to be scant, 1129, 56.

He was not poor in resources but in spirit, ibid.

The provincials over whom he presided said that he had been more truly their father than their judge, 1129, 58.

How greatly did he excel all in justice! ibid. ff.

How great was his simplicity! 1128, 57.

How great were his modesty and chastity! ibid., 52 ff.

How prudently did he avoid marriage? 1129, 53. Why? 1130, 59.

His temperance, 1129, 56.

He joined innocence to effectiveness with a remarkable virtue, 1120, 23.

Satyrus, always solicitous with pious affection, surrounded Ambrose with his own side: with charity, as a brother; with care, as a father; with concern, as an elder; with reverence, as a younger man, 1116, 8.

The director of affairs, censor of servants, arbiter between brothers—not an arbiter of litigation but of piety, 1124, 40.

He was judge between Ambrose and his sister, ibid., 41.

He governed his brother’s household without giving any offense and commended the priesthood, 1119, 20. See AMBROSE.

Ambrose recalled Satyrus by letter, so that he would not himself go to Africa but would send someone else instead, 1120, 26.

To gain speed, Satyrus entrusted himself a second time to the waves in an old and leaky ship, ibid.

How great was his courage in the shipwreck! 1125, 44. And after the shipwreck, 1127, 50.

Saved from the waves, he sought the Church in order to give thanks to God, 1126, 44.

He refused to receive the sacrament of baptism except from one who was in communion with the Catholic bishops—that is, with the Roman Church, 1127, 47.

He preserved the gifts of holy baptism undefiled, pure in body and purer in heart, 1128, 52. See EUCHARIST.

We now learn that, in answer to Satyrus’ vows, a passage was obtained through the holy martyr Lawrence, 1118, 17.

A nobleman, his kinsman Symmachus, recalled him so that he would not come to Milan, because Italy was said to be aflame with war, 1122, 32.

The God of Satyrus granted his long-desired return from the regions of Sicily and Africa, 1118, 17.

Satyrus declared that Ambrose’s grief, rather than his own death, was the source of his sorrow, 1117, 15.

He did not make a will, yet he did not forget the poor, 1130, 59.

Satyrus died before his time, 1133, 75.

He died when Italy was known to be pressed by an enemy close at hand—an impure and cruel enemy who spared neither chastity nor life, 1122, 31.

Everyone mourned his death, 1115, 5; 1121, 28.

Christ freed Satyrus’ spirit from the tortures of death and from the assaults of spiritual wickedness; he now beholds the things that are above us, 1121, 29.

On the seventh day we returned to Satyrus’ tomb, 1135, 2.

On that same day Ambrose again delivered a public sermon, ibid. ff.

### SCHISM

Those who are in schism do not appear to offer faith to Christ, 1127, 47. See CHURCH.

### KNOWLEDGE

All knowledge comes either from nature or from instruction, 586, 195.

This alone I know well: that I do not know what I cannot know, 708, 21.

I am not sure whether the pursuits of knowledge without deeds entangle more deeply, 34, 125.

### SCIPIO

Scipio was not the first to know that he was not alone when alone, nor less occupied than when at leisure, 107, 2.

### WRITINGS

I count it as a favor if someone, while reading my writings, tells me what seems to move him and why, 984, 2.

What is required in the art of writing? 781, 2.

Christian writers may take something from profane authors, 497, 3 ff. See BOOK.

### SCRIPTURE

Why is divine Scripture called θεόπνευστος (*theopneustos*), “God-breathed”? 688, 112.

The authority of the Greek manuscripts of sacred Scripture is greater, 722, 82.

Some Latin manuscripts of Scripture were deceitfully falsified, 642, 46.

Anathema to the one who adds anything to or subtracts anything from the divine Scriptures, 795, 36. See ARIANS.

Most people deny that our sacred writers wrote according to the rules of art, 783, 1.

Yet those who wrote about art discovered the art from their writings and composed treatises on art and learning, ibid. ff.

It is the custom of divine Scripture to support the subject it has undertaken and postpone an incidental matter, 258, 37.

The Apostle placed intention and diligence concerning the divine Scriptures last among the duties of the saints, 3, 3.

Christ’s oracles are frequently assessed according to the qualities of the places in which he stayed, 690, 118.

The Old Scripture is like a deep and obscure well, from which one draws water with labor, 1041, 78.

Divine Scripture is a banquet of wisdom: each book is a separate dish, 43, 165.

Whoever has drunk from the New Testament is not merely a river; rivers of living water will also flow from his belly, 1041, 78.

The great abundance of the Scriptures cannot be comprehended by human judgment, 630, 170.

This is the rain of the utterance of the Law, which sprinkles the fertile and fruitful soul with good works, so that it may possess the moisture of grace, 905, 4.

Outside is the letter; within are the mysteries, 896, 15.

God now walks in paradise when I read the divine Scriptures, 991, 3.

Genesis is paradise, in which the virtues of the patriarchs spring forth; Deuteronomy is paradise, in which the precepts of the Law germinate; the Gospel is paradise, in which the tree of life produces good fruits and spreads the commandments of eternal hope among all peoples, 992, 3.

The value of Scripture is our faith, for what is read is assessed according to the judgment of the understanding, 895, 6.

### SECRETLY

What is safer and more convenient for every action than secrecy? 769, 16.

The hidden things of the soul are revealed by its outcome, 995, 12.

### PROSPERITY

Prosperous circumstances warn us to be cautious, 775, 13. See PROSPERITY.

### SECUNDIANI

The statements and responses of the Secundiani at the Council of Aquileia, 803, 65 ff.

He was condemned there, 896, 2. See PALLADIUS.

### SEGATIUS

Bishop Segatius, 1107, 2.

### SEM

“Sem” is said to be a name in Latin, 1005, 4.

### SEMI-ARIANS

The Semi-Arians—that is, those who say that the Son is like the Father but not of one substance with the Father—are refuted, 727, 106 ff.

### OLD AGE

That is truly venerable old age which grows white not with gray hairs but with merits, 823, 5.

An unstained life is the reward of good old age, 94, 101.

Just as the company of equals is sweeter, so that of the old is safer, 57, 221.

Let old age blush if it cannot correct itself, 834, 7. See YOUTH.

### THE SENONES

The Roman remnant would not have withstood the Senones as they penetrated the secret places of the Capitol, unless a frightened goose had betrayed them with its honking, 834, 5.

### SENSE

The more senses of sight and hearing a person has, the greater are his dangers, 984, 17. See CRIME.

### OPINION

A sharpened judgment, 762, 3.

As many people, so many opinions, 172, 39.

### NORTH

The North received its name because the radiance of seven stars shines there; toward it helmsmen especially direct their gaze, as though toward a guide, 977, 3.

### SEVENTH

The seventh day signifies the mystery of the Law, the eighth the resurrection, 895, 8. See NUMBER.

### SPEECH

Speech is divided into conversation and into discussion and debate concerning faith and justice, 28, 99.

What should be done or avoided in each? ibid. ff.

Speech is akin and closely related to our mind, 1056, 9.

Let there be gravity in thought, weight in speech, and restraint in words, 5, 13.

Let agreeable speech accompany it, so that it may win the affection of its hearers, 60, 235.

The exchange of speech, like money, is of great use, 1052, 2.

One pays God by guarding speech, which is sobriety of speech, 782, 19.

If an account is demanded for an idle word, how much more is punishment exacted for a speech of impiety! 4, 7. See SPEAK, WORD.

### SERPENTS

The Gospel serpents cast off their former habit in order to put on new ones, 520, 131.

The image of the cross is the bronze serpent, 674, 50.

### SERVITUDE

Servitude is twofold: one of the body, the other of souls. Human beings are masters of the body, but vices and passions are masters of souls, 936, 24.

There is a free servitude, which is voluntary: servitude arising from the will, not from necessity, 1090, 3.

Servitude compelled by necessity is dishonored; that offered out of piety is honored, 1091, 7.

Servitude is counted among good things, 1090, 6.

The yoke of servitude is heavier than servitude itself, 1090, 3. See FREEDOM.

It is considered less degrading to serve a free person; but servitude is doubled when one serves household slaves, 760, 23.

There is no greater dignity than to serve Christ, 278, 3.

The servant of Christ is accustomed to perceive that he is guarded not by bodily custody but by the Lord’s providence, 866, 9.
