Those who are not seen guard Christ’s servants more than those who are seen, ibid., 11. See CHRIST.

### SLAVES

How slaves ought to serve their masters, 1048, 112.

A master should keep slaves subject to him by the law of servitude, as a means of restraint, regarding them as sharers in the same soul, 762, 31.

Slave boys are inscribed with the mark of their master, 1189, 58. See LORD, WISE.

### SEVERITY

Excessive severity generally extorts a lie through fear, 1083, 10.

It is clear that those who think harsh things should be followed instead of gentle ones, and proud things instead of humble ones, are not to be counted among Christ’s disciples, 390, 3. See MERCY.

### SEVERUS

Severus, blind, was healed by the relics of Protasius and Gervasius, 872, 2; 878, 17.

Severus, bishop, 819.

### SEX

Where the distinction of sex is not maintained, chastity is rightly not observed there, 1062, 7.

This is to preserve the beauty of living: to render to each sex and person what is appropriate, 24, 84.

### SIGNS

There is no need for me to investigate the rising and setting of signs, 979, 9.

### SILENCE

What must we learn above all else except to be silent, so that we may be able to speak? 3, 5.

The wise person is the one who knows how to be silent, ibid.

It is no small virtue to be silent, 250, 3.

What does it mean to be silent about good things? 7, 18.

When should silence be practiced most intensely? 6, 17.

Silence ought not to be perpetual or idle, 4, 9.

If the fault of my silence and concealment weighs me down without freeing you, I would rather have you judge me importunate than useless or disgraceful, 947, 3. See BANQUET, DAVID, SPEAK.

### SIMPLICIANUS

For the sake of faith and acquiring divine knowledge, Simplicianus traveled through the whole world and devoted all the time of his life to daily reading, by night and by day; grasping intelligible matters with a keen intellect, he used to demonstrate how far the books of philosophy had strayed from the truth, 1052, 1.

In Simplicianus, Ambrose recognizes both the affection of an old friendship and, what is more, the love of fatherly grace, 931, 2. See AMBROSE.

### SIMPLICITY

Simplicity is a certain temperance of conduct and sobriety of mind, 1128, 51.

The simple person seems rich to himself if he has enough for food, 295, 65.

Rich is the simplicity that examines nothing and considers nothing contrived, suspect, or fraudulent, but pours itself out with pure affection, 942, 4.

Straightforward simplicity of mind is abundant for every purpose, 98, 119.

Purity of simplicity agrees with bodily cleanliness, 1031, 36.

Everything elicited by artifice and contrived by fraud lacks the merit of simplicity, 122, 58. See FRAUD.

### PRETENSE

See FICTION.

### SINGULARITY

“Singularity,” in Greek μονοτής (*monotēs*), pertains to the person; unity pertains to nature, 559, 46.

### SIRENS

The Sirens were figures of pleasures, 497, 4.

### SIRMIUM

The Church of Sirmium was attacked by Valens and Ursacius while its priests wavered, 677, 59.

### SISINNIUS

At Ambrose’s request, Sisinnius forgave his son, who had taken a wife without consulting him, 1103, 1.

He accused those who thought that his mind should be aroused against his sons by fabricated lies, 1105, 10.

### SOBRIETY

Sobriety of mind and speech, 782, 19.

To regard as sufficient for use whatever is enough is the gain of sobriety, 758, 15.

### SUN

The sun, moon, and stars now endure the servitude of corruption; afterward they will rest in the glory of the children of God, 924, 9.

### SOLEMNITIES

The solemnities prescribed to the Jews by the Law are shadows of the celebrations above and of the heavenly festivals, 1162, 107.

### SOLON

Solon divided the ages of human beings into ten periods of seven years each, 979, 11.

### ALONE

The word “alone” in Scripture by no means separates the Son from the Father, 556, 28 ff.

Let the one who is alone be ashamed before himself, whom he ought especially to reverence, 756, 10.

Accustom yourself to be one, 1036, 60. See ADAM, MARY, IDLE, SCIPIO.

### SLEEP

The image of sleep resembles death, 1133, 72.

### SOPHOCLES

The verses of Sophocles, 936, 28.

Job is older than Sophocles, David more ancient, 937, 28.

### LOT

Just as in the Old Testament the land was divided by lot, so in the Gospel we are assigned to the Lord by a kind of lot, 287, 39 ff.

### SOTHERIS

The martyrdom of Sotheris, who was the parent of the holy Marcellina, 184, 39.

Ordered by the persecutor to be struck with open hands, she offered her face, so that the sacrifice of martyrdom might take place there where the trial of modesty usually occurs, 299, 82.

She was greater than the Etruscan youth whom the stories say scarred his face with marks so that women would not love him, ibid., 83.

### FORM

Sometimes “form” must be understood as “truth,” 331, 25.

### TO HAVE HOPED

To have hoped is grace; not to have believed is punishment, 1170, 134.

### HOPE

What is hope except expectation of future things? 928, 14 ff.

Weak is the hope entrusted to time, 435, 90.

Spiritual things are soft and subtle, so that they cannot be grasped by the eyes, 1051, 7.

### SPIRITUAL SEAL

What the spiritual seal is, 616, 79.

“Spirit” is often used for spiritual grace, 679, 70.

### THE SPIRIT

If you say “Spirit,” you have named both God the Father, from whom the Spirit proceeds, and the Son, because the Spirit also belongs to the Son, 609, 44.

The Spirit of the Lord is himself the Spirit of God, 675, 54 ff.

The Holy Spirit is called Lord, 637, 18.

The Gentiles spoke, in a certain shadowy way, about the Holy Spirit, 640, 35.

It is proved that the Holy Spirit is one and the same, 612, 55 ff.

He cannot think rightly about the Son who can think wrongly about the Spirit, 669, 17.

Those who denied the divinity of the Holy Spirit are either Jews of the Arians or Arians of the Jews, 706, 9.

Scripture clearly testifies that the Spirit possesses θεότης (*theotēs*), that is, deity, 676, 59 ff.

This is proved from two passages of the Apostle Paul, 683, 86 ff.

The Holy Spirit is proved to possess everything that God possesses—namely, divinity, knowledge of the heart, truth, the name above every name, and the power to raise the dead, 695, 144 ff.

What the Son received from the Father through unity of nature, the Spirit also received from him through the same unity, 659, 134.

Just as the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father, so the Spirit of God and the Spirit of Christ are both in the Father and in the Son, 666, 6.

The divinity of the Holy Spirit is proved by the fact that he has a temple, 683, 90 ff.

The Holy Spirit’s one dominion with the Father and the Son is proved from Paul’s Epistles to the Thessalonians and Corinthians, 685 ff.

The Holy Spirit is proved to be eternal, 621, 98.

Moses joined the Holy Spirit with God before the beginning of the world, having recognized that he was eternal before the world’s beginning, 633, 1.

The Holy Spirit, who was borne over the waters before the world, cannot be thought to have begun after the world, 644, 52.

The Holy Spirit is not among all things but above all things, 604, 19.

This is proved by various arguments, ibid. ff.

He does not serve, and all things serve him, 605, 22 ff.

Likewise, because he is above all things and blasphemy against him will never be forgiven, 611, 53 ff.

Again, because he is above all things, because he searches the depths of God, and because he is excluded from all things, 605, 24 ff.

By various arguments it is proved that the Holy Spirit is neither a creature nor mutable, 613, 62 ff.

It is proved that the Spirit is not a creature because he is uncircumscribed, 617, 81 ff.

The Holy Spirit is inaccessible in nature but can be received by us; he fills all things by his power, is shared only by the just, is simple in substance, rich in virtues, present to each person, and wholly everywhere, 615, 72.

The divinity of the Holy Spirit is proved from his mission, 624, 116 ff.

This mission is not a procession from place to place, 624, 119.

Nor is it separation from the Father or the Son, ibid., 120.

Just as the Son of God sent the Holy Spirit, so the Holy Spirit sent the Son of God, 665, 1 ff.

The Spirit was given and sent, as was the Son; and in this they possess the unity of divinity, 666, 9 ff.

The Holy Spirit knows all things and possesses one knowledge with the Father and the Son, 656, 115 ff.

Knowledge of divine things is not accidental in the Holy Spirit but natural cognition, 658, 127.

The Holy Spirit is called truth, just as the Son is, 628, 158.

The Holy Spirit commands what he wills, just as the Father and the Son do, 661, 145; 663, 151 ff.

The Spirit divides as he wills; therefore he is above all things, not among all things, 610, 48.

The Holy Spirit breathes where he wills according to the judgment of free will, not in obedience to necessity, 479, 48.

If the Holy Spirit has one will and operation with God the Father, he also has one substance, 661, 142.

The kingdom of God is indivisible with the Holy Spirit, 697, 156 ff.

Scripture proves that the Holy Spirit is almighty, 729, 115.

Like the Father and the Son, the Holy Spirit too is immaculate and almighty, 700, 169.

The Holy Spirit descended in the form of a dove, both to bear witness to wisdom, to fulfill the sacrament of spiritual baptism, and to show that he has one operation with the Father and the Son, 685, 96.

The operation of the Father and of the Holy Spirit is the same, 660, 139 ff.

Our ancestors declared the power of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit to be one when they said that Christ’s glory is with the Spirit, 649, 81.

Through the unity of the same power, the Spirit is worshiped together with God, since God is worshiped in the Spirit, 682, 82.

It is proved that the Holy Spirit must be worshiped, 680, 77 ff.

The Holy Spirit, like the Father and the Son, is the creator of all things, 640, 32 ff.; 645, 59 ff.

The Holy Spirit gives life, like the Father and the Son, 639, 29 ff.

Through the Spirit we read that many things were made, 652, 99.

The Holy Spirit is above all things; from him comes all the power of heavenly and earthly things, 610, 51.

The Holy Spirit filled Jesus, the redeemer of the whole world, 618, 86; 620, 93.

The birth from the Virgin is the work of the Holy Spirit, 641, 38 ff. See INCARNATION.

The Holy Spirit is good, the source and beginning of goodness, 614, 65 ff.

He does not acquire goodness but imparts it, 615, 74.

The Holy Spirit possesses everything that belongs to God. He is named with the Father and the Son by priests in baptism, invoked with the Father and the Son in offerings, proclaimed with the Father and the Son by the Seraphim in heaven, dwells with the Father and the Son in the saints, is poured into the just, and inspires the prophets, 688, 112 ff.

There is one Holy Spirit: he burned forth in the prophets, was breathed into the apostles, and was joined to the Father and the Son in the sacraments of baptism, 612, 55.

The Holy Spirit is the author of spiritual generation, as are the Father and the Son, 645, 62 ff.

His divinity is proved from the outpouring of the Holy Spirit upon creatures, 619, 90 ff.

The divinity of the Holy Spirit is proved by the fact that he forgives sins, 623, 112 ff.

The Holy Spirit is proved to be God because he is without sin and forgives sins; because he is not a creature but the creator; and because he does not worship but is worshiped, 693, 133 ff.

The Holy Spirit gives the same kinds of graces as the Father and the Son, 663, 152.

When the grace of the Spirit is proclaimed, the grace of God the Father or of the only-begotten Son is not denied, 607, 40.

The grace of God the Father is the same as that of the Holy Spirit, 621, 97.

Prophecy comes not only through the Father and the Son but also through the Holy Spirit; therefore the gift is one and the grace is one, 661, 143.

Those whom the Son redeemed, the Spirit also received in order to sanctify, 689, 115.

He himself is the Spirit who effects eternal life, 639, 27.

He has the same ministers as God the Father and Christ, 618, 88.

Just as the Son is the Angel of the great counsel, so also the Spirit is the Spirit of counsel, 638, 20.

The unity of power is so complete that the Spirit rebukes just as the Father rebukes and the Son rebukes, 671, 35 ff.

The Spirit of Christ teaches his disciples to pray, just as Christ does, 929, 3.

Where the Spirit is, there is Christ; and where Christ is, there is the Spirit, 675, 54 ff.

The Holy Spirit is not only light but also fire, 629, 164 ff.

The Holy Spirit is living water, 631, 174 ff.

He is called not only water but also a river, ibid., 176 ff.

And he is the fountain of life, 632, 180.

The Holy Spirit is the river proceeding from the throne of God; whoever believes in Christ drinks from it, 697, 154.

The Holy Spirit is the oil of gladness, 621, 101 ff.

From this it is proved that he is not a creature, ibid., 102.

The Holy Spirit is the sword of the Word, and the sword of the Holy Spirit is the Word of God, 673, 45 ff. See TRINITY.

Why did the Holy Spirit descend as a dove? 358, 14.

The Holy Spirit descended in bodily form, so that you would not think that this was an incarnation, but an appearance, 665, 4.

And that he might declare that he is of one honor in dominion, …
that he shares in one operation in baptism with the Father and the Son, ibid. Thus the Spirit descended in the same manner in which Christ is to descend, 638, 24. The Holy Spirit does not come from one place to another, but from the arrangement of constitution to the salvation of redemption, from the grace of vivification to the grace of sanctification, so that he may transfer us from earth to heaven, from dishonor to glory, and from servitude to kingship, 625, 122. The heretics’ objection against the divinity of the Holy Spirit, drawn from the words of the prophet Amos concerning the blowing of the winds, is refuted, 643, 48 ff. From these words, “He will receive from what is mine,” etc., by which the heretics construct their slander, the unity of divinity in the Spirit is discerned, not any lack of generosity, 689, 115. In what sense it is said of the Holy Spirit, “He will not speak from himself,” 659, 131 ff. When Scripture says that the Spirit was tested, it also says that God was tested, 674, 50 ff. The heretics’ objection against the divinity of the Holy Spirit, taken from the Apostle’s words, “from whom are all things … through whom are all things,” is refuted, 650, 85 ff. When the Apostle says that all things are from the Father and all things through Jesus, he does not exclude the Holy Spirit, 607, 32. The heretics’ objection that there would be three Lords if the Holy Spirit is Lord is refuted, 686, 104 ff. The objection that there would be three gods is refuted, 684, 92 ff. The objection of the heretics who say that God is to be preached in the Spirit, not together with the Spirit, is refuted, 647, 70 ff. The objection that the Holy Spirit is among all things, because all things were made through the Son, is dispelled, 606, 27 ff. Why the Holy Spirit is called the finger of God, 667, 11 ff. With this finger God inscribed those stone tablets which Moses received, 668, 13. With this finger Christ was writing on the ground, 668, 15. Nor is the Holy Spirit therefore inferior, 669, 17 ff. Rather, the unity of his power with the Father and the Son is demonstrated, 670, 29 ff. I do not hesitate to say that the Holy Spirit was given, 614, 66. Whether you call them Angels, Dominions, or Powers, every creature awaits the grace of the Holy Spirit, 613, 62. The Holy Spirit, proceeding from the fountain of life, appears to flow more abundantly among the Angels, burning with the full current of the seven spiritual virtues, 632, 178. Is not the Holy Spirit good, who makes good people out of the wicked, abolishes sin, destroys evil, excludes guilt, infuses a good gift, makes apostles out of persecutors and priests out of sinners? 615, 71. How does the Holy Spirit descend upon us? 625, 121. The Holy Spirit is not sanctified, but himself sanctifies, 615, 74. We are born and reborn both through the Holy Spirit and from the Holy Spirit, 678, 65. Just as we die in Christ so that we may be reborn, so we are marked with the Spirit so that we may be able to retain his splendor, image, and grace, 616, 79. Whoever is born according to the Spirit is born according to God, 646, 65. The nature of the Holy Spirit is far superior to that of the water in which we are baptized, 616, 76 ff. We were wild beasts, but through the Holy Spirit the ferocity of lions, the spotted nature of leopards, and the cunning of foxes have disappeared from our dispositions, 655, 109. Where the grace of the Holy Spirit is, there the form of divinity appears, 630, 168. There can be no complete blessing except through the infusion of the Holy Spirit, 619, 89. We receive from the outpouring of the Holy Spirit only as much as the progress of our mind acquires, 620, 93. There can be no prayer for pardon where, by denying the Holy Spirit, the fullness of sacrilege is present, 611, 54.

**BETROTHAL.** See **ADULTERY**.

**THE STATĒR** found in the fish’s mouth: what it signifies, and why Christ commanded that it be paid for himself and for Peter, 780, 13 ff.

**STATUS.** The lower the station, the more eminent the virtue, 759, 19. The chief point is this: that character should commend one’s station more than station should commend one’s character, ibid.

**STARS.** They expect the reward of their labor from him who subjects them, 923, 7. See **SUN**.

**STEPHANUS.** He was being stoned, and for Christ he received his wounds, as wounds of charity, with devout affection, [Col. 1496] 294, 61. He saw the heavens opened and Jesus standing at the right hand of God; and therefore he did not feel the blows of the stones and did not consider the wounds of his body, 1015, 13. Jesus stood as an advocate; he stood as one concerned, to aid his athlete in the contest; he stood as one prepared to crown his martyr, 1023, 5. He stood as a priest when he offered the sacrifice of the good martyr to the Father; he stood as though about to award the prize of so great a contest to the good combatant, 521, 138. Stephanus was the first martyr, 242, 119. Let us pursue the praise of the holy martyr, bloodied indeed by the wounds inflicted by his adversary, but crowned with Christ’s rewards, 522, 142.

**STOLE.** It is a nuptial garment, 420, 18.

**STRONG.** It is not sex but virtue that makes people strong, 198, 44.

**STUDY.** People are impelled toward something either by rewards or by benefits; but every zeal grows sluggish through delay, 413, 88.

**TO COMMAND A FOOL.** It is slavery, 936, 24.

**SUBSTANCE.** That is called substance which remains in itself and does not subsist by the aid of something else, 728, 111. The term “substance” is extremely frequent in Scripture, 516, 108 ff. Substance is one thing, quality another, 725, 100. What is of the same substance is not one person but one thing, 721, 77. See **FRIENDSHIP**, **NATURE**.

**PRIDE.** See **ADAM**, **GRACE**, **BOASTING**.

**SUPPLICATIONS.** Full of envy, 1101, 4.

**PUNISHMENT.** It is better for all to be exempted from the punishment of a few than for vengeance to be exacted against everyone, 1056, 7.

**ABOVE US.** Whatever things are above us are matters for wishing rather than for teaching, 152, 23.

**SUSANNA.** She was silent so that, through silent modesty, she might speak more effectively, 300, 87. Her silence was active, 4, 9. While she devoted herself to honor, she also preserved her life, 130, 90. She considered the loss of modesty more serious than the loss of life, 19, 68. She preferred chastity to life, yet did not suffer the loss of life; she attained the glory of chastity, 673, 42.

On the holy day of the Lord’s Resurrection, Susanna offered herself at the divine altar to be veiled; in the solemn assembly of the Church of God, amid the brilliant lights of the neophytes and among the candidates for the heavenly kingdom, she proceeded as though she were going to marry the King, 309, 19. What address was made to her on this day? ibid. She went over to the monastery of virgins, 312, 28. In order to obtain from her parents permission to vow virginity, she said that terrifying revelations had been given to her, 309, 17. Her fall is mourned, 306, 5 ff. A vehement attack is made against her, 306, 6 ff. Her crime, 308, 12 ff. That matter is assailed, ibid., 14 ff. There was an evil rumor about her three years before she fell, 311, 25. She was said to have secretly killed her own son, 314, 34.

**SYAGRIUS**, bishop of Verona, thought that he alone should claim for himself the judgment concerning the virgin Indicia, without the counsel of any brother, 765, 1. He decided that Indicia should be subjected to examination, ibid., 2. Ambrose disapproves of this judgment, 766, 5 ff. In a letter sent to Ambrose, Syagrius defended himself, 766, 4 ff. What he brought forward in his own defense, 769, 15. He wrote to Indicia, 770, 18. Ambrose replied to his letter, 769, 16. He rescinded Syagrius’s judgment and acquitted Indicia, 771, 24. See **INDICIA**.

**SYAGRIUS**, consul, 786, 1.

**CREED.** We ought especially to recite it daily before dawn as the seal of our heart; whenever we are terrified by anything, we should also have recourse to it, 179, 20. See **BAPTISM**.

**SYMMACHUS**, a most illustrious man and prefect of the City, 833, 1. He presented a report to Valentinian, asking that the altar which had been removed from the senate-house of the city of Rome be restored to its place, ibid. In that report he made three points: that Rome demanded the restoration of her ancient rites; that allowances should be granted to the priests and Vestal virgins; and that, when the allowances of the priests had been withheld, public famine had followed, 833, 3 ff. He begs the emperor that the ancient religious practices of the pagans and the altar of Victory be restored, 828, 1 ff. Likewise, when he was prefect of the City, he had reported to the emperor Valentinian that he should order the temples which had been removed to be restored, 1010, 2. See **AMBROSE**, **SATYRUS**.

**SYNAGOGUE.** It is rightly called beautiful among women, not among virgins, 295, 67. The Church excluded it, 953, 24. The laughter of the Jews set it ablaze for eternity, 297, 76. The synagogue has already begun to be consumed by divine judgment, 949, 8. After it had been burned at the bishop’s instigation, Theodosius ordered it to be rebuilt by the very man responsible and demanded that the others be punished, 948, 6; 956, 1. Ambrose proves and pleads that this command ought to be revoked, ibid. ff. This synagogue, built in the last fortress, possessed nothing costly and nothing abundant, 951, 18. The synagogue is the place of faithlessness, the house of impiety, the refuge of madness, which God himself condemned, 950, 14.

**SYRACUSANS.** Their gardens were fraudulently sold by a Sicilian, 125, 71 ff.

**POPE SYRICIUS.** His vigilance is praised, 965, 1 ff.

**SYRICIUS.** He gave Priscus a letter for Ambrose, 1106, 1. [Col. 1497]

**SYRUS**, a presbyter, as soon as he arrived, thought that recourse should immediately be had, 1106, 1.

# T

**TO BE SILENT.** See **BANQUET**, **SILENCE**.

**SUCH** let us be as we wish to be regarded; and whatever feeling we have, let us reveal such as it is, 93, 96.

**Identity** (*ταυτοτής*), 664, 154.

**TEMPERANCE** preserves the measure and order of everything that we judge should be done or said, 31, 115. What is chiefly sought in temperance? 56, 219. Bound by the bond of sacred charity and by the contemplation of heavenly mysteries, it neglects bodily pleasures, 241, 114. Not only is she praiseworthy who is sparing in food, but also she who is sparing in desire, 1030, 32. It accords with nature and with the divine law, 1029, 27. It is the virtue of women, 196, 40.

**TEMPLE.** God has a temple; a creature does not possess a true temple, 683, 90. Since we are God’s temple, let us cast away material concerns from ourselves, 240, 110. Gifts were taken away from the temples of the Christians, 837, 15.

**TIMES**, days, years, and rivers pass away in the same manner, 90, 83. You have received time in this land, not perpetuity: make use of time, knowing that you will depart, 1043, 86. Whoever does not wish to lose what is eternal should not take away from another what is temporal, 757, 12.

We do not regret having attempted it, lest what was left unattempted should fall into guilt, 817, 2.

**TEMPTATIONS** of the devil must then be guarded against when severe bodily pain presses upon us, or the loss of children or of other loved ones, 1067, 22. This is the Christian’s temptation: if he slips into danger to his own soul, 1183, 33. The stronger person is tempted in his own body, the weaker in another’s, 856, 15. We ourselves spread the nets in which we are entangled and ensnared; we ourselves weave our bonds, 409, 73. Because most of the weak are overcome by temptations, the strong are tested, 1066, 17. You are a human being, and temptation has come to you: overcome it, 999, 11. See **FLESH**, **DEVIL**.

Flee the lands in which there is envy, where there is ambition, where there is strife, 908, 17. See **HEAVEN**. What is the iron earth? 1060, 1 and following.

What witnesses are required in an ecclesiastical judgment? 765, 2.

The grace of the New Testament, the peace of the Old, 978, 6. The day of the Old Testament has passed; the new day has come, on which the Testament has been brought to completion as the New Testament, 980, 15. A testament has no force as long as the testator lives, but is confirmed by his death, 1084, 3. Nevertheless, those who have been named in the will are called heirs while the testator is alive, but without possession, ibid. Where there is a testament, there is an inheritance, ibid. See **CLERIC**.

**THAMNATA**, a city frequented by Palestinian inhabitants, 845, 13.

**THECLA**, a virgin, 307, 10. Her virginity and martyrdom, 166, 19. Neither the weakness of the flesh could mutilate her, nor the cruelty of tyrants cast her down through various tortures, 307, 10. Through the gift of virginity she was venerable even to lions, so that the beasts, fasting at the feet of their prey, might offer a sacred fast and not harm the virgin either with a wanton eye or with a claw, 1030, 34. Among the lions the virgin exulted and gazed fearlessly upon the roaring beasts, 399, 37. It was not old age but virtue that proved her, 223, 40.

How deeply the synod lamented the slaughter of the Thessalonians, 998, 6.

**THEODORUS**, bishop of Octodurus, 786, 1; 805, 76. His condemnation in the case of Palladius, 802, 62. The subscription of Bishop Theodorus, 969, 14.

**THEODOSIUS**, bishop, 819.

Those who had killed his father, the triumphant emperor, plotted against the safety of Theodosius, 1213, 53. He underwent exile for the sake of piety, ibid. When barbarians had poured into the Roman Empire, he assumed the imperial power, ibid.

Truly the Lord was favorable to the Roman Empire, since he chose as its ruler and as the father of rulers such a prince, whose virtue and power, established at the highest summit of imperial triumph, were supported by such great humility that in virtue he conquered emperors and in humility priests, 1021, 6.

The most blessed emperor Theodosius both follows and approved the faith of the Council of Nicaea, 862, 14. What triumphs did the faith of Theodosius acquire? 1200, 7. In battle it was said: “Where is the God of Theodosius?” ibid. In his struggles he knew that the crown had been granted to him not by his own strength but by the Lord’s help, 1204, 23. How greatly did he love God? 1203, 17 and following. The summit of his works was always piety, 1000, 12.

After the victory, because the enemies had been overthrown, he abstained from communion in the sacraments, 1207, 34. He was a pious emperor, a merciful emperor, a faithful emperor, 1201, 12. Full of the fear of God, full of mercy, 1202, 16. Humble in his imperial office, endowed with a pure heart and a gentle breast, 1207, 33.

Theodosius restored the Catholics to their churches, 814, 1. He restored unity to the churches of the West as well as those of the East, 817, 1. He effaced all the ceremonies of idols, 1199, [Col. 1498] 4. He closed the temples and destroyed the images, 1208, 38. See **AMBROSE**.

Theodosius prohibited paternal first cousins and maternal cousins from entering into marriage with one another, and established the severest punishment if anyone dared to violate the sacred bonds of brothers, 1019, 8.

If someone has not been convicted in the presence of the parties, then, as his clemency determined in a truly august and authoritative judgment, he will always seize upon the handle of the question to be referred, 818, 4.

He preferred to bind people to himself by religion rather than by fear, 1202, 13. He possessed zeal for the faith and fear of God; but he also possessed the natural impulse that quickly turned either toward mercy or toward anger, 998, 4. He approved one who rebuked him more than one who flattered him, 1207, 34.

Ambrose urges Theodosius to repentance on account of the slaughter at Thessalonica, 998, 6 and following. He sets before him the example of the repentant David, 998, 7 and following, and those of others, 999, 10.

Theodosius humbled himself and, when sin had crept in, asked pardon, 1205, 28. What private persons are ashamed to do, the emperor was not ashamed to do publicly: he laid aside every emblem of royalty that he used, and publicly mourned his sin in the church, 1207, 34. See **AMBROSE**.

Father of Gratian, 1001, 17. Ambrose offered him thanks because he had not only restored Valentinian to the throne but had also instructed him in the disciplines of faith and piety, 1002, 3.

Theodosius overthrew the treachery of the tyrants, 1199, 4. What great benefits God bestowed upon him when he fought against Maximus the tyrant? 952, 22.

Theodosius forgave the Antiochenes their offense, recalled the daughters of his enemy, gave them to be raised in the household of a relative, and sent the mother of his enemy expenses from his own treasury, 955, 32. At Ambrose’s request, he freed very many from exile, prisons, and sentences of ultimate death, 953, 25. He spared armed enemies and preserved his adversaries, 955, 32. He preserved his enemies, loved those who opposed him, forgave those by whom he had been attacked, and did not allow claimants to the throne to perish, 1203, 17. He considered it a benefit received when he was asked to forgive; and he was then nearer to pardon when the disturbance of anger had been more severe, 1201, 13. In him people wished for what they feared in others: that he should become angry, ibid. He grieved that the indulgence he had shown to those who had sinned against him had perished, 1199, 4. In recalling his acts of piety, he consoles himself by remembering that he had spared many, 1213, 52.

The victory of Theodosius over Eugenius is judged to have been bestowed, according to ancient custom and ancient miracles, through an outpouring of heavenly grace like that granted to the holy Moses, the holy Joshua son of Nun, Samuel, and David, 1022, 4.

For the victory won over the tyrant Eugenius, he desired that an offering and thanksgiving should be celebrated to the Lord by the priests, 1021, 4.

The death of Theodosius was foretold by violent earthquakes, continuous rains, and darkness more oppressive than usual, 1197, 1. When he was already being released from the body, he was more anxious about the condition of his churches than about his own dangers, 1207, 35. Before his death he ordered the taxes to be relaxed, 1199, 5. In dying he did not lay down the kingdom but changed it, 1197, 2. As he died, he commended his sons to their present father, 1199, 5. He did not leave those whom he had won for the grace of Christ and the loyalty of the army destitute, 1197, 2. He had handed over to his sons the kingdom, power, and the name of Augustus, 1199, 5. We ought to recognize the dead man in his sons, 1199, 6. Pious and filial service ought to be rendered to them, 1201, 11.

We celebrate the fortieth day after the death of Theodosius, with the emperor Honorius assisting at the sacred altars, 1198, 3 and following. His body is carried to Constantinople, 1214, 55 and following. Where he is buried, ibid., 56. See **CONSTANTINOPLE**.

After death, Theodosius receives his son Gratian and Pulcheria, his sweetest treasures, whom he had lost here, 1209, 40. He is joined to his Flaccilla, ibid., and to the emperor Constantine, ibid. He now enjoys everlasting light and enduring tranquility, and rejoices in the fruits of divine recompense for what he accomplished in this body; he has deserved the company of the saints, 1206, 32. See **AMBROSE**, **HONORIUS**, **COUNCIL OF NICAEA**.

The case of Evagrius and Flavian is referred from the Synod of Capua to Theophilus and the bishops of Egypt, 1006, 2.

**THRACE.** See **ILLYRICUM**.

**TICINUM**, church of, 106, 150.

**TIGRIS**, see **Tygris**.

The dispute between Timothy, bishop of Alexandria, and Paulinus of Antioch, 813, 4. To settle it, the Fathers of the Council of Aquileia beseech the emperor by letter to order a council to convene at Alexandria, ibid., 5. Timothy, bishop, 819.

**FEAR** is the beginning of wisdom and the producer of blessedness, 2, 1. Charity is freedom; fear is slavery, 1091, 7. Fear leads to freedom, freedom to faith, faith to charity, charity obtains adoption, and adoption obtains inheritance, 1084, 5. Temporal fear keeps watch as a protection; it does not know the guardianship of permanence, 79, 38. For the most part, to those for whom impunity is an incentive, fear is a burden, 589, 210. The Lord prefers to be loved rather than feared, 1083, 10. We have learned that Christ’s servants must not fear, 873, 36. It is more grievous to fear that something may happen than to endure what you already know has happened, 1139, 15. Terror is never grievous to those who do not fear, 873, 36.

The innocent victory of Titianus in the case of his granddaughter, 1001, 1.

**TOBIAS** never asked for the money he had given until the very end of his life—and why? 843, 5.

**TORQUES**, collars, are insignia of victory, 1191, 68. Victors in secular battles customarily load the necks of brave men with torques bestowed as rewards, 268, 89.

**TRANQUILITY.** What is it to live justly, if not to live with tranquility? 1043, 85.

**TREATISE.** When a treatise concerns religion, think of God, 825, 7.

Those whose portion is God do not pay tribute, 781, 17. See **WOMAN**.

**TRINITY** cannot be corrupted, being of an uncompounded nature, 1099, 8. Whoever has said “one” has marked the Trinity, 609, 44. It is proved that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one name, 627, 132 and following.

We confess the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, so that in the perfect Trinity there may be both the fullness of divinity and the unity of power, 445, 10. In the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit there is unity of majesty and, what is more, **identity** (*ταυτοτής*), 664, 154. The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one in nature and in knowledge, 657, 124.

It is proved from the Scriptures that the nature of God the Father is the same as that of the Son, and that the nature of the Holy Spirit is also the same, 722, 84 and following. The uncreated and ineffable Trinity, which is of one eternity and glory, admits neither time nor rank, whether of a later or an earlier member, 547, 140. That venerable Trinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is without time and without order; it is the author of number, not bound by the law of number, 977, 3.

In the divinity there is neither Sabellian confusion, nor Arian distinction, nor earthly and bodily change, 661, 142. In it there is neither confusion of what is one nor multiplicity of what is undifferentiated, 447, 17. There is a certain indistinct distinction of the incomprehensible and ineffable substance of the Trinity: we have received distinction of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, not confusion; distinction, not separation; distinction, not plurality, 537, 91. The Father and the Son have distinction as Father and Son, but they do not have separation of divinity, 476, 33. There is unity of the Trinity, distinguished neither by order nor by time, 264, 64. The kingdom of the Trinity is not divided, 446, 11. The Holy Spirit also shares the kingdom with the Father and the Son, 697, 158.

What the Father has belongs to the Son; what the Son has, the Spirit has also received, 656, 118. The Father is seen in the Son, and the Son in the Spirit, 699, 167. We have the image of the Father in the Son, and the seal of the Son in the Spirit, 158, 48. Wherever the Father, Christ, or the Spirit is indicated, as Scripture testifies, there is the fullness of the Trinity, 676, 55.

It is proved that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one will, one calling, and one command, 653, 101 and following. It is proved that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one holiness, 688, 109 and following. Through the unity of the same substance, the same willing and the same refusing, the same ability, are found in the Father, in the Son, and in the Holy Spirit, 534, 74. As the Father is power, so also are the Son and the Holy Spirit, 637, 19 and following. We have learned that the Trinity has one power, which Christ taught us both in himself and after his passion, 487, 85. Just as we read that all things are from the Father, so also from the Son and from the Holy Spirit, 652, 96.

The unity of divinity and operation in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is proved from the Song of Moses, 669, 20 and following. The Trinity has one judgment and one operation, 575, 134. The Trinity is the beginning of all things, and the primacy of the Trinity is over all things, 265, 68. See **INCARNATION**.

As the Father is life, so the Son is life and the Holy Spirit is life, 630, 171 and following. As it is life to know the Father and the Son, so also it is life to know the Holy Spirit, 638, 26 and following.

The Father sent the Son, and the Spirit; the Father and the Son also sent the Spirit, 666, 8; 485, 76. As the Father sanctifies, so the Son sanctifies, and the Holy Spirit sanctifies, but there is one sanctification, 670, 25 and following.

The Son descended, and all things were filled with the new fragrance of the Word. The heart of the Father poured forth the good Word; the Son spread fragrance; the Holy Spirit breathed forth and diffused himself through all hearts, 229, 63.

It is proved that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one peace and one grace, 626, 126 and following. Likewise, that they have the same charity and communion, ibid., 128 and following. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one grace and one presence, 626, 125. As the Father is light, so also are the Son and the Holy Spirit, 629, 160 and following.

The Spirit glorifies the Son, just as the Father also glorifies him; but the Son of God also glorifies the Spirit, 657, 121. As the Father is a river, so also are the Son and the Holy Spirit, 632, 181. From Christ the breasts do not fail; brightness is from God, and the river from the Spirit: this is the Trinity that waters its Church—the Father, Christ, and the Spirit, 152, 22.

It is the same impiety to detract from the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit, 606, 30. They fall into sacrilege who suppose that the “prolative Word” returns to the Father and the “prolative Spirit” is poured back into God, so that there is one pouring-back and a certain alternation of one thing repeatedly changing into various forms, 644, 53. Whoever believes wrongly about the Son cannot think rightly about the Father; whoever believes wrongly about the Spirit cannot think rightly about the Son, 566, 88. The Trinity speaks nothing outside itself, 659, 134.

What is more powerful than the confession of the Trinity, which is celebrated daily by the mouth of the whole people? 873, 34. See **CHRIST**, **GOD**, **FATHER**, **SON OF GOD**.

In sorrow let there be the moderation that is required in prosperity, 1138, 11. It happens that we do not gladly receive a message of sorrow, 819, 2. Although consolations are less pleasing to the grieving, they are nevertheless sometimes necessary, 944, 1.

The mystical meaning of the trumpets that Moses had commanded to be used is explained, 1161, 105 and following. The Romans used a trumpet in military service, ibid.

**TUBERS**, of extraordinary size, 762, 1. The various derivation of this name, ibid.

**TYGRIS** has its origin in the regions of Armenia, 843, 2.

**TYMASIUS**, master of cavalry and infantry, particularly hostile to the monks, 963, 27.

**TYPE** is the shadow of truth, 513, 89.

The perjuries of tyrants are more tolerable than their oaths, 181, 28. Whoever bears the image of a tyrant is liable to condemnation, 64, 254.

# U

**ULCER**, although swollen, when it has been opened and evaporates, provides cooling relief, 305, 1.

**Matter** (*ὕλη*), 383 and following.

**VENGEANCE.** Christ so completely removes from the perfect the desire for vengeance that he commands them to love those who injure them, 1042, 84. Nothing seems harsh in avenging a heavenly injury, 1056, 7. See **ENEMY**.

**UNITY** is not number, but itself the beginning of all things, 447, 19. It is neither divided nor split; therefore it is neither subject to corruption nor to age, 446, 11. What is not one is divided, ibid.

**URIEL** does not die, 500, 200.

**URSICINUS.** See **VALENS**.

**URSINUS**, attempting to usurp a rank not due to him and joined with the Arians, was trying to disturb the Church of Milan, 810, 2 and following.

**USURY.** Nothing is harsher than lending money at interest, 843, 4. The more abundant the sum of interest, the more welcome is the usury of the principal, 1114, 3.

**UTILITY** is twofold: one bodily, the other belonging to piety, 77, 27. Nothing should be judged useful unless it benefits the common good, 114, 25. Utility is the same as moral goodness, 77, 28. There is no utility when more is taken away from moral goodness than is added to utility, 119, 44. We do not measure utility by the assessment of monetary profit, but by the acquisition of piety, 76, 23. Whoever is useless to everyone cannot be useful to himself, 114, 25. See **MORAL GOODNESS**.

**WIFE.** Let a man guide his wife as a helmsman guides his ship; let him honor her as a partner in life and share with her as a co-heir of grace, 1048, 107. Let the woman defer to her husband, not serve him; let her present herself to be governed, not constrained. She is unworthy of marriage who is worthy of quarrelling, ibid. Let a wife please more by moral integrity than by beauty, 256, 30. A good wife is rightly praised, but a pious virgin is preferred as better, 966, 3. If a wife is a temptation, be more cautious; seek a remedy against the danger of temptation, 256, 31.

# V
VALENS, joined with Ursicinus, was attempting to disturb the Church of Milan, 811, 3. It is shameful to say how grievously his reputation was wounded by the disgraceful infamy of his abuse, ibid., 5.

VALENTIA of Gaul, 890, 7.

VALENTINIAN THE ELDER, under Julian, despised military service and the honors of the tribunate out of love for the faith, 1188, 55. His faith was proved by the steadfastness of his confession, and he is praised for the wisdom by which the commonwealth was improved, 860, 3. He responded not only in speech but also confirmed it by his laws: in a case concerning the faith, or any ecclesiastical order, the judge should be one who was neither unequal in office nor different in legal standing; that is, he wished priests to be judged by priests, 860, 2 and 5. After he had been baptized, he said: “It is not mine to judge between bishops,” 861, 5. See BISHOP.

No one reported to him that there was an altar in the Roman senate-house at which sacrifices were offered to idols, 828, 16.

VALENTINIAN THE YOUNGER, a most Christian emperor, 824, 3. He was still a child when, after his father’s death, he was elevated to the imperial power, 1190, 59. How great was Valentinian’s love for the provincials? 1180, 21. He lightened their taxes, ibid. He fought against foreign enemies; he fought against the slippery changes of the age; he fought against the frailty of the body and against manifold passions, 1191, 66. In him there was the maturity of years and the old age of counsel, 1174, 3. How great was his piety, 1179, 18. He replied that nothing bloody should be decreed, especially on holy days, ibid. He imitated his father and his brother, the one in faith, the other in devotion, 1189, 55. A second embassy was sent to him by the pagans in Gaul, asking that he order the expenses of sacrifices to be restored; it was able to extort nothing from him, 1011, 5. When the Roman envoys petitioned in the name of the Senate that the rights of the temples, the profane privileges of the priesthoods, and the worship of sacred things be restored, he refused, 1179, 19; 1188, 52. See AMBROSE, SYMMACHUS.

What disposition Valentinian had toward his friends, 1184, 35 and following. What affection he had toward his sisters, 1184, 36 and following. What he did in their dispute with an orphan, ibid., 37. How concerned he was for the honor of his brother’s burial, 1182, 28. He listened to affairs in the council chamber and, although a young man, gave an opinion appropriate to an old man, 1178, 16. As a young man he laughed at what sturdy princes fear, 1179, 18.

He restrained the Huns and Alans, 890, 8. A barbarian enemy was still waging war against him when he was a young man; forgetting his victory, he voluntarily released those whom he had captured, excusing himself on the ground that he had not known they were Italians, 1175, 4. Through his moderation and peaceful tranquillity, neither Gaul felt the enemy nor Italy repelled the enemy, 1191, 68. By his moderation he equaled the insignia of great triumphs, ibid. He bought peace from Maximus with his own gold, 890, 8. See VICTOR.

How great a reform of life took place in Valentinian, 1186, 46. Envious people complained that he asked for breakfast too early; he began to practice fasting so frequently that, often having eaten nothing himself, he provided a solemn banquet for his companions, 1178, 16. At first he was said to take pleasure in the circus games; he wiped this away so completely that he did not think circus games should be celebrated even on the solemn birthdays of emperors or in honor of the imperial office, 1178, 15. Some said that he was occupied with hunting wild beasts and that his attention was being drawn away from public duties; he ordered all the animals to be killed in a single moment, ibid. What he did concerning a theatrical woman distinguished by beauty and elegance, 1179, 17. See AMBROSE.

The law he issued, by which he made known his changed judgment, attacks the faith, 864, 3. He had previously persecuted Ambrose, but now loved him; he preferred to say that he had been nourished by him, longing for him as for a devoted father. Although he had holy and eminent priests, he nevertheless judged that he should write to Ambrose to be initiated by him into the sacraments of baptism, 1002, 2.

Theodosius was Valentinian’s kinsman, 826, 11. He customarily consulted him about nearly all important matters, ibid. The adornment of his head was glorious, because it was crowned not with royal diadems but with the insignia of the Lord’s blood, 1192, 69.

Valentinian, still sound in age before he obtained the grace of the sacraments he desired, died a sudden death, 1002, 3. He did not lose the grace of baptism, which he had requested, 1182, 30; 1188, 51. With what joy he awaited Ambrose’s arrival, so that he might be initiated by him into the sacred mysteries, 1180, 23 and 25; 1188, 51. Christ baptized Valentinian, because human ministry was lacking to him, 1193, 75. His faith washed him, and his petition consecrated him, 1194, 77.

What he said as he was dying about his sisters, 1188, 50. He did not fear death; rather, he offered himself for everyone, 1184, 35. His steadfastness was not bent by any fear of death, 1190, 62. He died at the beginning of life’s course, 1183, 33; 1185, 43 and 46. He died in the eighteenth year of his reign, 1189, 57. The cause of his death was full of praise, because he wished to aid the Roman Empire, 1174, 2. Hearing that barbarians had approached the borders of Italy, he wished to abandon the leisure of Gaul and undertake our dangers, 1180, 22.

How deeply Valentinian’s sisters were affected by his death, 1003, 5. How great was Ambrose’s grief at his death, 1182, 28 and following. The Church mourned at his death, 1175, 5 and following. The Church had been struck on the cheek when it lost Gratian; it offered the other cheek when Valentinian was taken from it, 1175, 6. At Valentinian’s death everyone thought that what had been taken from them was not an emperor but their salvation, 1181, 26. Everyone wept tears of domestic grief, as though a public parent had died, not merely an emperor, 1174, 3. How blessed the commonwealth would have been if it had been able to preserve him longer, 1186, 46. We must grieve that he was snatched from us so soon, but take comfort that he passed to better things, 1186, 46.

A porphyry sarcophagus was prepared for Valentinian’s burial, 1003, 4. The reply of Theodosius was awaited concerning this, ibid. Valentinian now enjoys eternal life, 1186, 44. As his soul departed from the body, having repelled the night, it approached God like the sun, 1191, 64. In what words Ambrose addresses it, ibid. and following. See AMBROSE, GRATIAN, ITALY.

Valentinian, prepared for humility, greets Eusebius, 1005, 5.

VALENTINUS does not think that there are ages before God, but that there are as many gods as there are ages, 709, 25. Valentinus denied the sacrament of the incarnation, 478, 44. He did not believe in the reality of the human flesh assumed by Christ, 705, 8. Christ is the Son of David, against Valentinus, 570, 105.

The Valentinians worship thirty-two Aeons, whom they call gods, 951, 16. Theodosius ordered them to be excluded and forbade them the opportunity to assemble, 954, 26. A shrine of the Valentinians, hastily erected in a certain rural village, was burned by monks, 951, 16; 956, 1. The emperor ordered vengeance to be taken upon the monks, ibid. See AMBROSE.

VALERIAN, bishop of Aquileia, 786, 1; 805, 76; 798, 46; 799, 49. His judgment concerning Palladius, 800, 54.

VALLIO, a vigorous warrior, faithful soldier, useful companion, ordered to be killed by the tyrant Maximus, 891, 11.

In a VESSEL that is foul, either oil or wine is readily corrupted and deteriorates, 1058, 6.

What the fleece of Gideon, dried out, and the dew poured into a basin signify, 602, 11 and following. What Gideon’s fleece prefigured, 190, 18 and following.

These are the better VEILS: those which are garments of virtues, 273, 109.

The autumn crops fed VENETIA, 838, 21.

VENUS. What the Africans worship as Caelestis, the Persians as Mithras, and most people as Venus, according to the diversity of the name, not according to a diversity of deity, 840, 30.

I know the nature of the divine WORD much better than I know it, 708, 21. To be of the Word is to be with the Father; to be of the Father is to be with the Word, 707, 18. The Word the Son is not like the word gathered together from syllables, because the Father of the Word is not such, 708, 19. According to nature it is one, and this excludes both rank and number, 708, 20. The eternity and divinity of the Word are asserted from the opening words of John’s Gospel, 706, 14 and following. Our speech does not act; only the Word of God acts—not an uttered word, nor what they call the inward word (ἐνδιάθετον), but the Word that acts, lives, and heals, 534, 72 and following. See CHRIST, SON OF GOD.

The Word of God is the Father’s dew, 915, 6. According to our merits, the Word of God either lives or dies for us, 914, 2. The Word of God wounds but does not ulcerate, 235, 91. How good a sword it is, 214, 3. It runs; it is not seized by disgust, nor held back by negligence, 231, 74. It is a treasure within us, 243, 119. See SOUL.

The soothing power of words is more dangerous: they intoxicate the mind with a certain wine of the Sodomite vine, 410, 76. The mirror of the mind generally shines forth in words, 19, 67. Let us not set traps in words or hunt for the snares of expressions, 503, 37. See SPEAK, SPEECH.

The VERCELLI Church, because of dissensions, was deprived of a bishop for a long time, 1023, 1. With what care a priest is sought for ordination in the Church of Vercelli, where two things seem equally to be required of a bishop: the continence of a monastery and the discipline of the Church, 1038, 66. See AMBROSE, EUSEBIUS.

A beautiful and pleasing grace of MODESTY is present in actions and even in speech, 19, 67; and in silence, ibid., 68. It must be maintained in movement itself, in gesture, and in gait, 20, 71. How nature itself is the teacher of modesty, 22, 78. Just as gravity is commended in the aged and liveliness in the young, so modesty is commended in adolescents, 19, 65. In the ordering of life, certain first foundations must be laid from modesty, 56, 220. It is the companion of chastity, 20, 69. Its reefs, 24, 85.

To investigate the TRUTH is implanted in all human beings according to human nature, 33, 125. What must be observed in the investigation of truth, 33, 122. Truth does not deceive, justice does not circumvent, virtue does not mislead, 162, 64. Truth proceeds from nowhere except truth, 1164, 109. Those things are perpetual and solid which are true, 97, 116. Popular usage does not prejudice the truth, 258, 36.

The people of VERONA, most dear when they arrive exasperated, return in peace, 765, 1.

The virgins of VESTA and the priestesses of Pallas do not possess moral chastity but the chastity of years: those who are ordered to be chaste as young women are unchaste as old women, 150, 15. They were taken by force, 217, 113. Scarcely seven girls are captured, 836, 11. The fillets binding their veiled heads, the purple dyes of their garments, the pomp of their litters surrounded by the retinue of attendants, their greatest privileges, immense profits, and finally the prescribed periods of chastity compelled them, ibid.

CLOTHING. Nature clothes each sex in its own garments, 1062, 2. Why did the Law so severely call those unclean who wore the clothing of the opposite sex? 1061, 1 and following. Litigation in the Church is often provoked by the expense of golden clothing and other ornaments, 230, 68.

GARMENTS that were not worn out in the desert signify, like an image, the resurrection for the faithful—and in what way? 475, 23.

We must follow the WAYS of the Lord and guard our own ways, 4, 7.

The favor of NEIGHBORS is often greater than brotherly love, 762, 30.

VICTOR, a companion sent by Maximus to Valentinian to ask peace from him, 889, 6. He met Ambrose near the city of Mainz, ibid. While Ambrose was detained, he reached Milan, and what he requested was denied him, ibid., 7. Ambrose was present when Victor returned, ibid.

They believed VICTORY to be a goddess, although it is a gift and not a power, 810, 30. He said that an altar to her ought not to be erected in the senate-house of the city of Rome, ibid., 31. Victory is not glorious unless there have been arduous struggles, 17, 56.

You are preparing to conquer, you who worship Christ; you are preparing to conquer, you who defend the faith, 444, 3.

Those who despise WIDOWHOOD are refuted, 968, 9. The persecutors of the faith were persecutors of widowhood, 209, 85.

What kind of WIDOW should be chosen for the profession of widowhood, 188, 9 and following. The Apostle did not think younger women should be recalled from devotion to widowhood, 189, 12. The duties of widows, 187, 7 and following; 189, 11 and following. A widow’s strength is not merely bodily chastity but a great and abundant discipline of virtue, 188, 11. It is defined not merely by bodily abstinence but designated by virtue, 185, 7. What her life should be, 191, 21 and following. Widows should instruct their daughters-in-law, so that they may be able to find in them support in mature old age, 194, 33. How merciful and generous a widow should be toward the poor, 193, 27. She must first be chaste from wine, so that she may be chaste from adultery, 196, 40. Pleasures are more slippery for her than serious matters, 200, 53. Who among the clergy should visit the homes of widows and virgins, and how, 24, 87 and following. They must take greater care not to leave room for unfavorable opinion, and why, 192, 26. When they seem to lack a reason for marrying, eagerness should be absent, 203, 67. In a certain sense the teaching of virginity gains strength from the examples of widows, 185, 1. We see many grave widows dying at one time, 1131, 67. It is useless to think that widows should renew marriages in order to have children, 209, 86 and following. How rightly that widow who put two small coins into the treasury was preferred to everyone else, 139, 27 and following. The various goods of widowhood, 199, 51. Such abundant honor is paid to widows that they are honored even by bishops, 188, 8. A good widow does not know want, 195, 34. What her treasures are, 194, 30 and following. The way of good widowhood is good, but rough and difficult, and requires greater caution, 1032, 40. See AMBROSE, DEPOSIT.

VIGILS throughout the night, 875, 2. The verse which we had used in the evening at the vigils, 904, 1. Fewer came to the vigils on the feast day of Saints Peter and Paul, 244, 125. See FIRSTFRUITS.

VIGILIUS, bishop, asked Ambrose for the distinguishing marks of his instruction, 842, 1.

BONDS. “Have compassion on those who are held bound in chains, as though you yourselves were bound with them,” 1047, 106.

You are the Lord’s VINEYARD; you are the vintage: planted as a vineyard, you have produced fruit as a vintage, 376, 16.

It is permissible to drink WINE, but excessive drinking is not fitting, 203, 68. Two things inflame: wine and youth, 175, 5. After the Flood, the righteous man discovered wine as a temptation for himself, 1029, 27. How great is its power, that wines could strip the man whom the Flood had not stripped naked? 159, 53. Wines so loosen men that they are overcome by women, 196, 40.

Who is the perfect MAN? 1088, 12. How disgraceful it is to make a man perform women’s work, 1062, 6. See WIFE.

The name of VIRGIN is a title of modesty, 147, 6. The name of virgin is not recognized where the author of virginity is denied, 168, 24. What is virginal chastity except integrity free from contamination? 151, 21. Merit is produced not by bodily virginity alone but also by integrity of mind, 207, 15. It is more tolerable to have a virgin mind than a virgin body, 168, 24. Truth is virginity; corruption is falsehood, 289, 44. It seems disgraceful to be unmarried, whether as a maiden, virgin, or widow, 289, 45.

Those who barred virginity from the Church of God are reproved, 217, 13. The state of virginity is shown to be neither improper nor new, 220, 27 and following. Nor is it useless, 222, 35 and following. Virginity possesses such power to inspire wonder that even lions marvel at it, 167, 20. Among the pagans virginity is customarily venerated among altars and hearths, 217, 13. It is sought by the nations, but when consecrated it is violated; it is attacked by barbarians and unknown to the rest, 150, 14. The pagans do not possess a sacred virgin, 150, 16. Virginity has the authority of antiquity from the age, and the fullness of its profession from Christ, 150, 13. We do not easily find virgins on earth until God descended into these limbs of earthly bodies, 149, 11. Virginity flowed from heaven, ibid. Its author is the immaculate Son of God, 151, 21. It deserved to be chosen by Christ so that it might also be the bodily temple of God, 1030, 33. Christ is the beginning of integrity: he taught virgins to dedicate the integrity of mind and body to the Holy Spirit rather than to a husband, 506, 52. Nothing more could have contributed to the celebration of the glory of virginity than that God should be born from a Virgin, 272, 104.

Virginity is not commanded, since it is above the law; rather, it is commended by a counsel that is offered. Authority is not presumed, but grace is demonstrated; and it is demonstrated not by just anyone but by one who has obtained the Lord’s mercy, 1031, 35. It cannot be commanded, but may be desired, 152, 23. It alone can be encouraged, not commanded, 282, 17. It is more a matter of a vow than of a command, 282, 17. Why it is encouraged rather than commanded, 204, 70 and following; 207, 78 and following. It is not an integrity common and ordinary among the majority; nor is it allowed on account of weakness, but granted on account of virtue, 220, 29.

Virginity is the praise of youth; it does not seek the assistance of years, since it is the fruit of every age: it suits adolescence, adorns youth, and magnifies old age, 192, 25. That adolescent girls can profess virginity, 223, 39 and following. It must be a matter of priestly caution that a girl not be veiled rashly, 223, 39. He always sought to stir up the desire for virginity through the grace of priests, 200, 26. Mothers who forbid their daughters to profess virginity are reproved, 160, 58 and following. It is more glorious if virgins embrace virginity despite their parents’ resistance, 161, 62 and following. The memorable deed of a certain noble and pious virgin who wished to profess virginity despite her parents’ resistance, 162, 65 and following.

A virgin who publicly professed chastity, 318, 48. Offering her hair to be consecrated under the sacred veil, 273, 108. Virgins were veiled on Easter Day, 288, 42. With what words Ambrose offers a sacred virgin to God at the altar, 872, 107 and following. The people subscribe to the virgin’s profession, saying “Amen,” 309, 20. She who has pledged herself to Christ and received the holy veil has already married; she has already been joined to an immortal husband, 310, 21. If a consecrated virgin, after her profession, wishes to marry according to the ordinary law of marriage, she commits adultery and becomes a handmaid of death, 310, 21. See MARCELLINA, SUSANNA.

Consecrated virgins come from Piacenza, from Bologna, and from Mauritania, to be veiled at Milan, 160, 57 and following. How many virgins the Church of Alexandria, of the whole East, and of Africa was accustomed to consecrate, 222, 36. So great was the number of virgins that they formed a people of modesty, a populace of integrity, an assembly of virginity, 836, 12. This age deserved to have virgins but could not retain them, 159, 52. Angels fell from heaven into the world because of their intemperance; virgins passed from the world into heaven because of their chastity, ibid., 53. In sacred virgins we see on earth the life of angels, which we had once lost in paradise, 272, 104. Virginity displays the life of angels, 283, 19. It is no wonder that virgins are compared with angels, since they are joined to the Lord of angels, 149, 11. Virginal chastity deserves the protection of angels, whose life it deserves, 159, 51. Through man and woman the flesh was expelled from paradise; through a virgin it was joined to God, 1030, 33. Christ has assigned more abundant gifts to none than to virginity, 260, 45. Virgins have rewards in heaven superior to those of others, 282, 17.

The pursuit of integrity is to be preferred to marriage, 221, 31. Married women are unequal to sacred virgins, 155, 36 and following. Marriage is honorable, but integrity is more honorable, 205, 72. The head of a woman is her husband; the head of a virgin is Christ, 169, 29. A married woman belongs to the world; a virgin is Christ’s possession, 288, 40. Marriage is for remedy, virginity for reward, 289, 46. Marriage is good, through which offspring was discovered for the succession of the human race; but virginity is better, through which a heavenly inheritance is acquired and the succession of heavenly merits is found, 966, 3. In a married woman and a widow the fruit is slower; in a virgin it is more mature, 192, 24. Virgins have greater beauty and more fortunate fertility than married women, 154, 30. Where the pursuit of virginity is more frequent, there too the number of human beings is greater, 222, 36. A virgin has children without the pain of childbirth, 288, 42. The way of virginity is good but lofty and arduous, and requires the stronger, 1032, 40.

What virtues a virgin should possess, 271, 100 and following. In passing over to heavenly things, she should pass beyond earthly things, 285, 28. She must know Christ whom she loves and recognize in him both the mystery of his innate divinity and the mystery of the incarnation he assumed, 157, 46. She must persist in prayers, and her face must grow pale through continual supplication, 296, 70. Her mouth should resound with praise of the Lord, with gratitude to the Bridegroom, and with confession of the cross, as she recites the Creed and sings psalms in her chamber, 293, 58. Let simplicity be in her heart, restraint in her words, modesty toward everyone, devotion toward relatives, and mercy toward the needy and poor, 274, 112. She must be gentle, humble, and meek, 269, 93. The virgin’s modesty, meeting everyone openly, bears witness to her integrity, 766, 6. Modesty, sobriety, and restraint should gird the hair of sacred virginity, 273, 109. An unworthy veil for ordinary use, a noble one for chastity; the practice of fasts; finally, everything of such a kind that one might think she was being called back from her pursuit while she was performing her duties, 836, 12.

Virgins are more becoming when they reject concern for adornment; even the fact that they do not adorn themselves is itself an adornment, 160, 54. Above all else, the pursuit of sobriety excels—and what kind of sobriety? 298, 81. Many, while professing a zeal for chastity, seek aids to beauty more than is fitting for the sacred servants of the Lord, 299, 81. It is not beauty, but a reputation for good works exposed to no misfortune, that constitutes adornment, [Col. 1505] 158, 47.

A virgin should first be announced by her seriousness, by evident modesty, a sober gait, and a restrained expression, 177, 13. A woman does not please God if the seriousness of her conduct does not approve her, 766, 6. She herself must be the guardian of her conduct, 165, 9. In a virgin there is a modesty liable to harm, 170, 32. In virgins, modesty adorns age, and silence commends modesty, 176, 9. Nothing is holier in a virgin than modesty, 766, 6. Modesty is a kind of dowry of virginity, commended by silence, 250, 5. Even speaking good things is often a fault in a virgin, 300, 86. I would rather a virgin lack speech than have too much of it, 176, 9. What is more excellent in a virgin than reserve? 769, 16. Even freer merriment is not fitting for virgins, 297, 75. The very going out to church should be rarer for adolescent virgins, 296, 71. Virgin, especially one of sacred profession, let no going out of yours occur without your mother, who should be an anxious guardian of modesty, ibid. I wish visits to younger virgins to be less frequent, 176, 9. What need has a virgin to approach even a neighbor easily? 296, 72. The regular attendance at banquets must be avoided, and greetings must be shunned, 176, 8. She must be far from dances, 180, 25; 182, 31. If she loves, she sins in mind; if she is loved, she sins in deed, 176, 10. She is not sufficiently worthy of approval if she is sought after when she is seen, 177, 13. There will be more from whom a virgin may learn if she teaches herself, since she possesses virtues as teachers, 165, 9.

The bishop explained the hymn of virginity to virgins, 312, 29. In the church the virgins stood in a place separated by screens, bearing inscriptions, where devout and noble matrons asked kisses from them, 311, 24. Good is the virginity that not only absolved both sexes from crime but also summoned them to grace, 253, 16. Divine Scripture brought many women into the light, but gave the palm of public salvation to virgins alone, 284, 28. Virgins deserved to see the Lord’s resurrection before the apostles, 217, 14. Among us girls, through their desire for death, raised the steps of virtue high to heaven, 939, 37. Virgins are prepared to die in order to preserve their integrity, 219, 24. They were stronger than the Pythagoreans, 151, 19. If the Lord wills that chastity be protected, how much more does he will that integrity be defended, 776, 19. This is clearly proved by the example of the Benjamites, 773, 6 and following. No injury should be inflicted upon sacred virgins, 776, 19. The holiness of virginity is violated by the mere sight, 1031, 34. It is not virginity when it is bought for a price and not possessed through the pursuit of virtue, 836, 12.

She is a virgin who marries God; she is a prostitute who has made gods, 159, 52. Do you wish to know how great is the beauty of her who is loved by the King, approved by the Judge, called the Lord’s, consecrated to God, always a bride, always unmarried—so that neither love may have an end nor modesty suffer loss? 156, 37. She is God’s gift, a parent’s offering, the priesthood of chastity, 154, 32. She breathes immortal grace, like the flowers of a garden, like temples through religion, like altars through a priest, 166, 18. How virginity is a closed garden and a sealed fountain, 1031, 36. You are paradise, virgin; beware of Eve, 264, 60. Sacred virgins are especially daughters of Christ, 269, 93. They are like a daughter full of myrrh, displaying the brightness of integrity and the glory of mortified bodily allurements, 1176, 7. The vine is in some sense the fruit of virginity; marriages, like garden vegetables, quickly fall away, 285, 29. Virginity is compared with bees, 156, 40 and following. See MARTYRS.

It was grievous to all good people that anything shameful should be said or believed about God’s virgin, 311, 25. How uncertain in faith is the inspection and visitation of virgins? 766, 8 and following. This is proved by the example of a woman of servile condition, ibid. When and for whom should such inspection be used? 766, 5 and following; 768, 14. There are other proofs and testimonies by which virginity may be examined, 768, 11 and following. I prefer virginity to be expressed by the mark of conduct rather than by the confinement of the body, 769, 14.

The fall of a consecrated virgin is mourned with the greatest bitterness, 305, 3 and following. The fall of a consecrated virgin stained the Church, and from it every Christian soul received a grievous wound, 305, 3. How great and what kind of penance is necessary for a fallen virgin? 314, 34 and following. He who corrupted a sacred virgin certainly committed both adultery and sacrilege, 315, 39. What penance must he undergo? 316, 40. See SUSANNA.

Every VIRTUE receives its beginning from Christ, 506, 52. He is the author of every virtue, 506, 49. All virtues belong to the Holy Spirit, but some are, as it were, cardinal and principal virtues, 363, 9. The definition of the four cardinal virtues, 31, 115. From these arise the kinds of duties, 31, 116. How the cardinal virtues are distinguished from one another in popular judgment, 82, 49. In every wise man, the Greeks identified the rational (λογιστικὸν), spirited (θυμητικὸν), appetitive (ἐπιθυμητικὸν), and discerning (διορατικὸν) faculties; the Latins, however, identified prudence, fortitude, temperance, and justice, 241, 114. Where one virtue is present, the others converge, 80, 43. They are related to one another, 35, [Col. 1506] 129. They are not compatible with vices but remain consistent with one another, 52, 204. Although the virtues are related to and united with one another, a more pronounced form of each individual virtue is nevertheless desired, especially of justice, 1129, 57. There are degrees and progressions of the individual virtues, 1032, 40. The practice of perfect virtue does not require instruction but itself instructs, 159, 51. We do not call virtue an appendage of age, but age an appendage of virtue, 223, 40. Virtue relies more upon its own strength than upon external coverings, 47, 177. There is sufficient protection for everyone if virtue is not absent from the soul, 199, 51. The closer you are to virtue, the stronger you will be, 1106, 2.

Every virtue is slow, deliberate, and long-suffering: it judges beforehand and examines what is to be undertaken, 1058, 5. As you ascend, raise your step directly; no one returns safely from there. On this side is the road, on that side the ruin; on this side ascent, on that precipice; the labor is in ascending, but the danger is in descending, 909, 22. Let our road be narrower, our virtue more abundant, our path more confined, our faith higher, our track more elevated, our mental strength overflowing, and our path straight, because the footprints of virtue are inflexible, 904, 7. The constraint of virtue is more severe than punishment, 623, 108. The grace of virtue does not die with the body, 1130, 63.

Our INTERNAL ORGANS are seven inward and seven outward, 980, 13.

VISION. God warns us in many ways, even through visions granted to sinners, 1000, 14. See APPARITION.

The use of LIFE is brief, and the one who went before did not seem to have taken much from it, nor does he delay you for long who have remained behind, 1139, 16. How little joy can exist amid the bitterness and pains of this life of ours! 1139, 18. This life is subject to sin; another life is reserved as a reward, 1167, 124. If life in itself must be fled, so that it may be an escape from troubles and a rest from hardships, how much more desirable is that rest to which the perpetual joy of the future resurrection will succeed! 1167, 123. Not without reason holy men have often grieved that their dwelling in this life was prolonged, 1167, 124. Three things must be observed in the conduct of life, 29, 105.

The martyrdom of VITALIS is described, 279, 4. The Jews persecuted him while he was alive but honored him when he was dead. See AMBROSE, RELICS, 279, 7.

How FLYING CREATURES came to exist, of which we find three species, 725, 102.

Where there is WILL, there is the reward of the will; where there is necessity, there is the service of necessity. Will is therefore better than necessity, 935, 21. Everyone’s will is the author of his posterity, 202, 64.

PLEASURE alone expelled us from paradise, 1026, 14. Before Christ’s coming, it was difficult to judge that even the stronger could not be captured by the allurements of beautiful pleasure, 497, 4. See ADAM, EPICURUS, TEMPERANCE.

VOW. It is better not to vow than to vow what the one to whom it is promised would not wish to be fulfilled, 127, 79. How often a person grows weary of his vows and repents of what he desired, so that he grieves at having obtained what he feared not obtaining, 1139, 19. After their use, vows themselves become burdensome; and what we desired to earn, once we have earned it, we renounce, 1167, 124. See SATYRUS, VIRGIN.

VOWS OF PARENTS for their children. See LAURENCE, PARENTS.

The VOICE should be neither subdued nor drawn out, 24, 84. Our voice is heard at greater danger to modesty than it is read, 145, 1. See SERMON.

A WOUND of good love; there are wounds of charity, 235, 91. The wounds that we receive for Christ are not wounds by which life is lost, but by which it is extended, 865, 6.

X

The words of XISTUS to Laurence, 55, 215.

Z

The petition of the mother of the sons of ZEBEDEE is examined, 561, 51 and following. Let there be the zeal of God, not that human zeal which envy generates, 108, 154.

ZENON, bishop of holy memory, consecrated the virgin Indicia with a blessing, 765, 1.

From the tribe of Judah, ZERUBBABEL; he himself was Jesus the great priest. Two things seem to be signified, while one is expressed, because he is at once, as it were, the powerful one born from the Powerful One and the redeemer born from the Virgin, 913, 10.

[Col. 1507]

INDEX OF WORDS, SENTENCES, MORE DIFFICULT DOCTRINES, ANCIENT RITES, ETC., EXPLAINED IN THE NOTES.

[Col. 1507]

The bosom of Abraham, 1161. Absence more present, 841. The judgment of Bishop Acholius awaited by the Easterners, 817. In what year did Ambrose’s encounter with him occur? 821. Acholius appeared to Ambrose after his death, 819. Where was Adam’s tomb situated? 1070. “You have been babbling” (Ἀδολέσχησαι), 997. What is adorea? 191. With what penalty were adulterers punished? 310. A wife’s adulterer is put to death, 221.. Egyptian days, 881. The Egyptians used to circumcise males and females, 1072. Who were called *aerarii*? 872. Who was Aetius—his pursuits, errors, and fortunes, 451. Aetius, the teacher of Eudoxius, 451. The argument of the Aetians refuted, 647. *Agentes in rebus*, 106 and 854. Haggai—that is, “feasting,” 911. The name Agnes is not devoid of praise, 147. She suffered martyrdom at the age of twelve, ibid. *Agon* is a name for a contest, 848. The quinquennial contest, 1012. In what year did Agricola and Vitalis suffer martyrdom at Bologna? 278. Ambrose celebrated at Bologna the solemn translation of the bodies of Vitalis and Agricola, 275. He brought some of their relics to Florence for the consecration of a basilica, 275. Albertinus refuted, 63. How dear the Alans were to Gratian, 890. The oars of wings, 908. The river Almo, beside which the Romans once performed the rites of Cybele, 840. “Addresses are cut down,” 1053. A furnished altar, 336. The altar as the form or figure of Christ’s body, 374. Altinum, a municipality of Italy, 767. An absurd judgment, 762. The virgin Ambrosia, 247 and 1004. The pledge of Ambrosius, 1004. Ambrose was snatched from the tribunals and raised to the priesthood, 3 and 342. He was not nourished in the bosom of the Church, 431. The more remarkable circumstances attending his election are touched upon with the greatest modesty, 861. His ordination was confirmed by the example of the Eastern bishops, 1038. He tempered episcopal authority with gracious indulgence, 1000. His prudence and moderation, 701. How diligently did he fulfill the office of teaching? 2. With what zeal was he accustomed to devote himself to preaching the divine Word? 1183. How great was his trustworthiness regarding the private affairs of his friends? 1124. The church built by him, 1119. How greatly did he despise riches? 434. When the master demanded the Church’s gifts that had been offered and handed over, he declared himself ready to restore them, 434. He undertook labor for the Church, 432. It was not martyrdom that he lacked, but martyrdom lacked him, 929. His love for Gratian, whom he calls his son, 751. Did he go to meet Gratian on his return from the East? 753. Pope Damasus entrusted him with an embassy to act with Gratian so that he would not grant the requests of the unbelievers, 826. Ambrose speaks of Valentinian as of a son, and Valentinian of Ambrose as of a parent, 1173. The vexations he suffered from the supporters of Auxentius, 753. He was offered the choice either of disputing in the palace or of withdrawing from the city, 863. His embassies to Maximus on behalf of the boy Valentinian, 889, 1182. Nannius’s judgment concerning both of Ambrose’s embassies, 863. The plots laid against him by the tyrant Maximus, 891. A vessel was handed over by the emperor in the presence of Arbogast, 1181.
