At his request many were freed from exile and extreme punishment, 953. On hearing of Eugenius’s arrival, he withdrew to Bologna, 1009. Ambrose wrote his books in his own hand, and why? 988. Jests and not-too-harsh plays on names, 1103. The agreement between passages in Ambrose and in Augustine, 929. He differs from Cicero, 25. His words were cited at the ecumenical Council of Ephesus and by Leo the Great, 851. Also by the Council of Chalcedon and by the same Leo the Great, 481 and 486. Also by the Third Ecumenical Council of Constantinople, 478. Interpretations of the word “Amen,” 528. Everything is common among friends, 185. A friend is another self, 664. Anemius, bishop of Sirmium, ordained by Ambrose, not without a miracle, 800. When were the angels created? 707. Ambrose admitted as probable a threefold opinion concerning the sin of the angels, [Col. 1508] 159. The angels’ uncertainty concerning Christ’s resurrection, 522. The angels were ignorant of Christ’s resurrection, 259.. They did not know when Christ ascended into heaven, 334. How do they groan on our behalf? 924. Are they ministers of punishments? 924. “It is angular with winding turns,” 982. The soul. The philosophers’ opinions concerning the soul, 921. The human condition is lower than guilt, 851. Peace between the Huns and the Romans, 890. See “Chuni.” Hyginus, an old bishop, led into exile, 891. The obscurity of *hyperbatus* is removed, 391. Subterranean chambers, 910. What are the Platonic Ideas? 530. One who destroys idols is not admitted to the catalog of martyrs, 948. Those who preserved the faith inwardly but offered incense to idols through fear of torture are called half-alive, 404. Why were banquets provided by the emperor for the counts on fast days? 1178. The devastation of Illyricum and Thrace, 86. An image in the Gospel does not exclude truth, 63. What worship is to be offered to images of the saints and to the holy cross? 1211. What were the images of emperors among the Romans? 64. Sacrificial victims, 898. Emperors are honored by their successors with the name “parents,” 1122. The emperor has no imperial right over divine matters, 857. Three kinds of officials for conveying the emperors’ commands, 858. Emperors who reigned for two months, 834. One emperor a captive, under another the world captive, ibid. The power of love is impressed, 960. What is an impression? 1038. The earrings that Jacob buried, 1055. An incidental cause,
358. Let him place incense, 70. The hour of incense, 179. An incubator of fruits, 1130. By sacred evidence, 132. The use of indictions did not begin long before Ambrose; and what does he mean by the term? 885. The gods called *Indigetes*, 830. What does *inequitare* signify? 62. Why is Eleazar called unarmed? 53. What is an *infula*, and to whom was it appropriate? 3. Punishments for ingratitude, 1126. Injuries—that is, torments and tortures—958. Injury—that is, torment and pain—879. By injuries—that is, by rigid and harsh chastisement—314, 1157. Unjust—that is, excessive and beyond one’s strength—204. Innocent infants counted among the martyrs, 54. Frequent mention of them by Ambrose, 979. To appropriate the sustenance of the poor, 1006. A mark of modesty, 1. What do *institae* signify? 1155. Intention—that is, obstinacy of mind—1023. Who were the intercessors? 106. What does *interpellare* mean? ibid. Who was Irenaeus, to whom Ambrose wrote so many letters? 897. Where the rites of Isis were celebrated, prohibited, and restored, 1014. The bishops of Italy request that a council be convened, 818. The letter of the emperor Theodosius to the bishops of Italy, 817. Who the Ithacians were, and how greatly the very gentle spirit of Ambrose recoiled from their cruelty, 893. Ambrose abstains from communion with the tyrant Maximus and the Ithacian bishops, 891. Job, the most ancient of all writers, 13. Are jokes permissible to ecclesiastical men in familiar speech or in a sermon? 28. John of Elizabeth, 1038. Did John the Baptist doubt concerning Christ? 521. John the Evangelist died, 1146. The words “God is Spirit” erased from the Gospel of John, 677. The General Epistle of John, 403. Egypt mourned Joseph for seventy days, 1198. Who were the sons of Joseph, Mary’s husband? 260. Joseph’s opinion rejected by Ambrose, 845. He borrows some things from him, 346 and following. Jovinian and his associates devoted themselves for some time to fasting in a monastery at Milan, 968. Judges. Which gentiles, after administering a province, brought back the bloodless axe? 892. *Jugalis* used for *jugarius*, or charioteer, 173. The widow Juliana built an Ambrosian basilica, 275. Who was Julian Valens? 808. The apostate Julian remitted certain obligations for the provincials, 1180. When he ordered the temple of Jerusalem to be rebuilt, those who were carrying out the work were consumed by divine fire, 950. The war against the Persians caused by the imprudence of the eastern emperor, 842. Justa and Grata, sisters of Valentinian, 1003. They attended his funeral oration, 1184. The persecutions stirred up against Ambrose by the empress Justina: in what year did they occur? 737. Her persecution is indicated, 876. Is justice to be preferred to wisdom according to the philosophers? 67. Who was Justus, to whom Ambrose writes? 777, 801. Are the Juthungi the same as the Vithungi? 890. What the *labarum* was, on what occasion it was instituted, and by whom it was carried, 949. *Laboris lucrum*—that is, exemption from labor—17. Explanation of the jars used by Gideon, 629. Stones supplied as substitutes, 472. Reading in the Church’s assembly, 1091. Readings from sacred Scripture in the Church, 853. To the haruspices of the laws, 837. “Levi, give his men,” 70. “He is called my Levite,” or “he himself is for me,” 65. The practice of handing books over to others for examination, 989. Several books entitled *On Consolation*, 1171. Is the book *On Cain and Abel* cited in the letter to Horontianus? 927. Ambrose wrote several books *On Virginity*, 253. Agreement between the books *On the Institution of the Virgin* and *On the Sacraments*, 252. And with other books of Ambrose, 260 and 272. That the book *On Widows* was genuinely composed by Ambrose, and at what time, 185. The occasion of the book *Exhortation to Virginity*, 275. Who was the author of the books *On the Sacraments*? 341. In what respect the books *On the Sacraments* differ from the book *On the Mysteries*, 341. The book *On the Sacraments* was drawn from the book *On the Mysteries* and from *On the Institution of the Virgin*, 347. The book *On Penance* contains similarities to the *Commentary on Luke*, 426. In Book IV *On the Faith* the same things are read about John as in the *Commentary on Luke*, 541. In Book III *On the Holy Spirit* the same things occur as in Book X *On Luke*, 692. What Ambrose borrowed from Didymus and others in the books *On the Holy Spirit*, 598. Why Liberius the supreme pontiff is called “of blessed memory” and “a holier man,” and in what year he died, 173. Living and rational trees, 981. Limenius, bishop, 802. At his death the Church of Vercelli was deprived of its bishop, 1022. The lighting of lamps, 904. The vigils performed in the Church immediately at the first hour of the night were called *lucernarium*, ibid. The schism of Lucifer of Cagliari, 1127. Lucius, usurper of the Church of Alexandria and persecutor of monks and virgins, 812. The Church of Lyons cites a passage of Ambrose, 779. The moon. Pagan superstitions concerning observation of the fourth and fifth lunar days, 881. The Lycians ordered men to put on women’s clothing if they gave themselves over to mourning, 1137.

The ancient veneration of the Maccabean martyrs, 951. What is a *maforte*? 162. Did Christ appear first to Mary Magdalene after the resurrection? 217. Manichaeus introduces diversity in the Creator, 639. He denied the truth of the Incarnation, 478. He condemned circumcision, 1073. The Manichaeans believe the devil to be the author of our flesh, 491. They are accused of condemning marriage, 155. They add sacrilege to disgrace, 996. They fasted on the Lord’s Day, 883. By what imperial edict were they forbidden to hold any assemblies? 969. Lodgings to be prepared, 1181. “With your hands, give the holy mysteries,” 1189. Marcellinus, brother of the tyrant Maximus, 890. Marcion said that Christ’s body was an apparition, 478. He condemned circumcision, 1073. Interpretation of the name Mary, 257. The principle by which Mary’s undefiled conception is defended, 260. Ambrose defends Mary’s virginity, ibid. In being born, Christ did not break the barriers of virginity, 262. How Mary formed Christ without any activity of her own, 269. Virginity after childbirth, 1030. The heresy of those who professed that Mary remained a virgin after conception, but not after childbirth, 966. Arguments by which Mary’s perpetual virginity is vindicated, 1009. Mary brought about the salvation of the world, 992. Martyrs who took their own lives to preserve chastity, 181. Marriage entered into by children without the knowledge or consent of their parents: whether it is to be regarded as valid and binding, 1103. Whether disparity of worship, according to Ambrose’s judgment, dissolves a marriage both before and after it is contracted, 851. See *Conjugium*, *Nuptiae*. Maximus complains that, because of the embassy of Ambrose, he was unable to cross into Italy, 858. He threatened Ambrose, 1185. Theodosius recalled the daughters of the tyrant Maximus, 956. See *Ithaciani*. Who was Maximus the Cynic, and what were his frauds and lies? 815. The sons of physicians, 1017. By whom Melchizedek was called an angel, 513. The Melchizedekians, 373. The agreement of Meletius and Paulinus that, while one survived, no one should be substituted in the place of the deceased, 814. Who was substituted in Meletius’s place? 815. The meaning of this name, ibid. *Militia* signifies not only military service but also forensic profession, 241. Soldiers are marked with the emperor’s name, 1189. In former times soldiers were forbidden commerce, undertaking lawsuits, and pursuing business in the forum, 49. “I began to celebrate Mass”—that is, to offer the sacrifice, 853. The preface of the Mass and the first prayer of the Canon, 364. The subsequent prayers of the Canon, 371, 372. What does the priest say after the Lord’s Prayer? 385. *Missio* used to signify a procession, 625. Monasteries had not yet been established at Milan, but they had at Bologna, 154. The monastery at Verona, 770. In former times infants offered by their parents to monasteries were compelled to observe the monastic life permanently, 291. From where this custom arose, 292. The prominence of monastic discipline, 951. The conjunction of monastic and clerical life, 1038. The monastic garment, 821. What color clothing did monks wear? 23. What is morality? 1040. The three kinds of death, 1144. The definition of death, ibid. Death is like sleep, 1133. On what grounds the gentiles proved that death should be endured with equanimity, 1147. Prayers for the assistance and deliverance of the dead, 1135. How ancient is the practice of prayers and sacrifices for the dead? 1193. Cyprian’s opinion on this matter is defended, ibid. The efficacy of the living’s intercessions for the dead, 1121. Women’s empty ornaments, 160. Why it was formerly forbidden for women to shave their heads, 1014. Women’s immoderate mourning at the death of their husbands, 1137. Most people said that the world was uncreated, 724. Various philosophical opinions about the plurality of worlds, 529. Myrocles, bishop of Milan, 868.

Nicaea. The number of bishops who attended the First Ecumenical Council of Nicaea, 444. In their number, according to the Greek characters, there is an expression of the Lord’s cross and name, 443. The definition of faith written by the general Council of Nicaea, 467. The number of the Nicene canons, 1037. Why Ambrose uses the authority of the Nicene rather than the Constantinopolitan synod, 861. See *Cyclus*. “From our knots let a flower sprout,” 145. Marked illnesses, 762. Who was Novatian? 385. He wrote a notorious pamphlet against Pope Cornelius, 387. The cause and origin of the Novatian schism, 412. Novatus was a presbyter, not a bishop, 385. He devotes himself to Novatian, 387. Νοῦς, the power of the soul, 973. The Pythagoreans and Platonists were exceptionally devoted to the science of numbers, and after them many of the holy Fathers, 976. Ancient customs concerning marriage, 173. It accords with Hebrew customs and laws that the intact should be joined in marriage to virgins who are intact, 759. Ambrose’s moderate judgment concerning second marriages, 188. Ambrose does not approve marriages repeated many times, but neither does he condemn them, 203.

The offering for sins, 513. From where was the midwife so called? 768. “He goes out with watchful gaze,” 10. Money was entrusted to the Church’s steward or dispenser: and for what purpose? 88. The acceptance of office, 8. Its etymology, 9. How Aristotle discussed duty, 10. An unjustified avoidance of this omen, 829. Ὁμοούσιον (*homoousion*): one thing to one person and another to another; it is not the same in itself, 519. *Opus* used for a natural thing or element, 352. The ancient custom of the Jews of climbing to the upper part of their houses when they were going to pray, 911. Christians praying raised their arms in the form of a cross, 384. The minor orders were not all customarily conferred on everyone, but one on each individual, 58. The impediment of bigamy to sacred orders is extremely ancient, 65. Whether one who had taken one wife before baptism and another after baptism was bound by the law of bigamy, ibid. See *Clerici*. Orestes and Pylades, 56. Orgies, 150. Origen’s self-castration, 206. Origen is far less extensive in the New Testament than in the Old, 1083. Origen’s *Hexapla* and *Octapla*, 1066. Ambrose drew from Origen, 1161. What is Orion? 586. What does ὅρος (*horos*) signify? 785. What kind of kisses were those with which Christians, at the apostles’ command, greeted one another? 952. [Col. 1519]

The pagans attributed the calamities of the empire to the Christian religion, 831. The laws of Constantine the Great and the later emperors against them, 825. On two different occasions they requested from Valentinian the restoration of their religions, 1180. Again they requested the restoration of sacrifices by an embassy sent to him within Gaul, 1011. Palladius, an Arian bishop, 786. The lictor’s palm, 934. Who were Panaetius and his son? 7. In what year did Panaetius live? 10. Ambrose everywhere either assumes or acknowledges the reality of the earthly paradise, 981. With what dignities was Paternus advanced? 1019. Human birth in the seventh, eighth, and sometimes tenth month, 977. Birth as a bodily necessity, 458. Whether Easter, falling on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May, could be transferred to the seventh, 883. Whether Ambrose borrowed anything from Theophilus concerning the manner of celebrating Easter, 880. The sacrifice at the Easter vigil, 881. Nothing bloody should be instituted during the Easter days, and with what degree of veneration those days should be observed, 1179. Ambrose, with Cicero, orders the fatherland to be preferred to one’s parents, 33. The homeland of Paulinus, bishop of Nola, 1013. He had a son, but the child was taken from the living on the eighth day after birth, ibid. Irreligious men maliciously reviled Paulinus’s withdrawal, ibid. Paulinus. See *Meletius*. Paul’s celibacy, 245. Nothing is more difficult than discussing the Apostle’s reading, 1083. The obscurity of certain passages of Paul, 930. What do his words “Would that those who unsettle you would mutilate themselves” refer to? 207. The error of Paul of Samosata concerning Christ, 705. Why Ambrose joins him with Basilides, ibid. The transmission of original sin through the propagation of concupiscence is taught by the example of the magnet stone, 983. The succession of original sin, 1073, 1079, 1087. Whether Ambrose considered any sin irremissible, 421, 611. Those accused before a bishop of hidden crimes were afflicted with heavier punishments, 315. How remission of lesser sins may be obtained, 402. The forgiveness of graver sins is to be reserved for the prayers of the righteous, 401. Sin is covered by improved conduct and satisfaction, 424. In what sense it is said to be covered, 1067. Pelagia the martyr, 182. The death of Pelagia the virgin, 939. The Pentateuch, 956. The etymology of *perdix*, 918. The cunning of that animal toward hunters, ibid. The word *personaliter* cautiously used of divine matters, 682. Peter’s arrival at Rome, his victory over Simon Magus, and Christ’s appearance to him, 867. Peter, the Church’s support and foundation, 237. Who was Philaster, bishop of Brescia? 802. Ambrose drew from Philo’s book *On the Fugitive*, 784, 785. And from other books of his, 898 and following; 903, 931, 976. What distinction is there between the two? 935, 1057. Whatever Ambrose took from Philo, he transformed into a form more suited to piety and the Christian religion, 970. Who was Philomarus, a disciple of Epicurus? 1026. Philosophy is meditation on death, 1143. The greatest of the philosophers, 1201. The philosophers drew from our sacred Scriptures, 932. In Ambrose’s time pagan philosophers publicly professed philosophy in gymnasia, 461. The arguments and fallacies of philosophers must be avoided, 450. Philostorgius’s hostile attitude toward Valentinian, 1178. By what scriptural authority does Ambrose prove the resurrection of the phoenix? 1149. On its example many Fathers proved the resurrection of bodies, ibid. Who was Photinus, and what were his errors? 445. He said that the Word was not substantial and ἐνδιάθετον (*endiatheton*, indwelling), but passing and προσφορικόν (*prosphorikon*, externally uttered), 454. He is condemned in the councils, 809. He judges according to the flesh, 569. Phrygian rites, 149. Piety is joined to justice, 33. “Let neither the veil of Pinea nor the cypresses prevail,” 273. Plato denies that poets who tell unworthy fables about the gods should be heard, 14. What is a *plumarium*? 891. The Pneumatomachi are refuted, 705. Penance for graver and lesser sins, 436. In a person performing penance, whatever is superfluous is purged, as it were, by a certain collective admixture of manly mercy or compassion, 411. The stations of public penance, 428. Works, 437. And exercises are prescribed, 313. How severe were the labors formerly imposed? 893. Public penitents were required to abstain from marital intercourse, 437. Whether public penance should be undertaken for killings committed in war, 1207. Or whether it should be undertaken by some people less promptly, 438. Once performed, it cannot be repeated, 436. Good works brought to death by mortal sin revive through penance, 423. See *Preces*. Poets must not be heard, 14. See *Plato*. Pompey was slaughtered by Achillas, 841. The days following, 881. *Pone accidere*, 75. “He sails in the harbor,” 1003. Posterity is like the scent of a full field, 940. *Potestas* used for nature, 449. The various kinds of prefects, 853. What was the dignity of the chamberlains? 859. What is *praescriptio*? 1038. Whether *praesentius* should be referred to the mind, 856. “They put forward,” 909. *Praetexebam*—that is, “I was passing across,” 867. What does *praevaricari* mean? 948. Who is called a *praevaricator*? 919. Protasius. See *Gervasius*. Public prayers and tears for penitents, and with what ceremonies they were poured forth, 411. Public prayers for emperors departing on campaign, 753. See *Supplicationes*. The presbyterium, 965. Men who are leaders in the virtues, 853. By what death did Proclus, or Proculus, son of Titianus, die? 1002. The gift of prophecy is not granted for the sanctification of those who possess it, 994. For the sake of the purpose, 1093. The definition of prudence according to the wise, 1125. The singing of the psalmists, 432. Psalms to be sung privately at home, 230. At what age are girls their own mistresses and competent to give testimony? 148. Nourished by pennyroyal, 763. “Let it be polished by speeches,” 973. Pylades. See *Orestes*. The homeland of Pythagoras, 901. He scarcely found an equal, 902. In what year did he live? 10. He and his followers delighted in music, 179. The Pythagorean maxim “The common road must be avoided”: in whose books is it found? 901. The Pythagorean virgin, 151. Pythias. See *Damon*.

A question—that is, an objection—542. By questions—that is, by tortures and agonizing pains—776. To receive into prison, 866. An accuser of royal ambition, 1179. From where did religion receive its name? 159. It is to be preferred to the duties of piety, 187. The veneration of sacred relics among ancient Christians, 1210. Miracles performed through the relics of the saints, 878. A rescript, 105. The more direct form of a rescript, 106. The thousandth year of the resurrection is ours, 1150. The various philosophical opinions concerning the resurrection of bodies, 1151. Revelations were not rare in the fourth century, 309. Raetia Secunda, 838. Rivetus is refuted, 387. Rome had adopted foreign religions, 840. The Roman basilica at Milan, 873. Romulus, a deacon or priest in a rural church, 1056. Rufinus falsely accused of slander against Jerome, 598. Interpretations of the word *Sabaoth*, 523. The rest of the great Sabbath, 289. The fast of Holy Saturday, 885. The errors of Sabellius: where and when did he begin to spread them? 445. The Sabellians attribute the assumption of human flesh to the Father, 486. The opinions of Augustine and Epiphanius concerning the Sabellians and Patripassians are reconciled, 579. Sabinus of Piacenza, 801, 984. The high priest, 326. The priests of Urbicius, 838. The Holy Spirit makes priests out of sinners, 615. Levites and priests are bound to continence, 66. Priestly continence, 1037. Priestly monogamy, ibid. The priest’s authority to forgive sins, 1059. Which priests should be consulted? 225. By ancient law, empires were bestowed by priests, 858. “Do not fear the sacrament,” 955. Who were the keepers of the sacristy or secretariat? 69. The sacrifice distinguished from prayers, 1146. Ambrose writes to Saebadius, bishop of Agen, 1106. What does *saevitas* or *scaevitas* mean for Ambrose? 689. “This sea of life,” 1135. What is the Holy of Holies? 325. The saints. Ambrose appears to have regarded the doctrine of invoking the saints as orthodox, 185, 200. The assistance of the saints for living and dead human beings, 1121. “It would become blood,” 835. Sarmatio. See *Barbantianus*. Wisdom. Our freedom consists in the knowledge of wisdom, or only the wise person is free, 931. “To hand over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh,” 407. Satisfaction for sins, 424. Satyrus, Ambrose’s brother: was he called Uranius? 1109. His likeness to Ambrose in spirit and body, the principal events of his life, and his death, ibid. In what year did he die? 1111. Books published by Ambrose on this matter, ibid. The epitaph of Satyrus, ibid. Where he was baptized, 1128. At Satyrus’s funeral his face was uncovered, 1134. The address delivered by Ambrose on the seventh day after his burial, 1135. What is a *scamma*? 17. A conceived crime, 305. Σκευοφυλάκειον (*skeuophylakeion*), 69. An example of the audacity of scribes, 636. Each person's own writings deceive him, 989. “I rely on writing, not argument,” 678. Whether the sacred writers composed their writings according to the rules of art, 783. Ambrose used a manuscript of sacred Scripture that differed considerably from ours, 296. The exemplar of sacred Scripture used by Ambrose differed from others in many respects, 1163. Ambrose was accustomed to consult various readings of Scripture, 1177. Secundianus, an Arian bishop, 786. Who were the Semi-Arians? 728. When the city was captured, the Senones were detected by the cackling of geese, 833. A bilge-filled ship, 1120. The number seven as the number of remission, 1047. “Speeches that pluck,” 989. Severus, bishop of Naples, 1016. Slaves were marked with their master’s insignia, 1189. Sichima—that is, shoulder—901. What is a *siclus*? 777. The duties of the silentarii, 1181. Was Simplicianus sent by Pope Damasus to instruct Ambrose? 1057. Who was that Simplicianus? 1052. To hide in the bosom, 762. Why was Sirmium the capital of Illyricum? 800. The persecution of the Church of Sirmium, and the councils held at Sirmium and their formulas of faith, 675. Siscia, an episcopal see in Pannonia, 953. In what year did Socrates live? 10. “I am never less alone than when I seem to be alone; nor less at leisure than when I am at leisure,” 991. Solitude—that is, bereavement—1121. A widow’s taxable property is burdensome, 1102. Vigilius, bishop of Trent, was killed by pagans; and why Ambrose so strongly dissuades him from allowing marriages between the faithful and unbelievers, 842. On what day, and with what ceremonies, were they veiled and did they make their profession? 309. The public profession of virginity, 318. Various rites pertaining to virgins living in monasteries, 311. What color clothing did they wear? 23. Was their hair ever cut? 313. How great a love of solitude was required of them? 296. Men entered the monasteries of virgins, 312. The examination and testing of virgins’ integrity is uncertain and dangerous, 767. Whether it was ever lawful, 769. The punishment of a virgin who breaks her vow, 311. Virgins as witnesses of the Lord’s resurrection, 217. The hymn of virginity, 312. The Hebrew virgin, 968. ## INDEX OF THE SUBJECTS CONTAINED IN THIS PART OF THE LATER VOLUME

[Col. 1523]

Preface to this volume. 9  
Admonition concerning the three books *On Duties*. 17

## THREE BOOKS ON THE DUTIES OF THE MINISTERS

### BOOK I

23. Chapter I.—The bishop’s proper duty is to teach; he must at the same time be taught and learn himself. Ibid.  
Chapter II.—The manifold danger involved in speaking, and the remedy indicated by Scripture. 25  
Chapter III.—What sort of silence must be observed, and concerning the guarding of mouth and heart. 26  
Chapter IV.—That speech ought to proceed from right reason. 27  
Chapter V.—The adversary must be overcome by silence, so that due humility may be preserved. 28  
Chapter VI.—David’s silence and humility are to be imitated by us. 29  
Chapter VII.—How beautifully Psalm 18 was employed as a preface, whereby the holy man was led to undertake writing on duties. 30  
Chapter VIII.—The etymology of *officium* (“duty”). 31  
Chapter IX.—Duty is derived from what is honorable and useful, and also from the comparison of the two with each other; and the particular reason why this treatise confers great benefit upon Christians. Ibid.  
Chapter X.—Pythagoras borrowed the law of silence from David, and in what respect the former discipline is to be preferred. 32  
Chapter XI.—Scripture shows that every duty is either perfect or intermediate. 34  
Chapter XII.—That God cares for human actions, and concerning the misery of the wicked even amid riches. 35  
Chapter XIII.—The philosophers who deny Providence either wholly or in part are refuted. 37  
Chapter XIV.—That God knows all things. 38  
Chapter XV.—Concerning the reality of punishments and rewards in the other life. 40  
Chapter XVI.—Confirmation of the same argument. Ibid.  
Chapter XVII.—The duties of a young man. 42  
Chapter XVIII.—Concerning modesty and its remarkable effects. The story of two clerics is offered as an example. 43  
Chapter XIX.—How propriety is defined by the orator, and whether, and to what extent, physical beauty contributes to virtue. 47  

[Col. 1524]

Chapter XX.—What must be avoided, and in what leisure one may indulge, in order to preserve modesty. 49  
Chapter XXI.—How anger must be controlled. The saying of Archytas. 50  
Chapter XXII.—Concerning thoughts and desire, and concerning the preservation of propriety of speech in conversation. 52  
Chapter XXIII.—Even respectable jesting is prohibited among ecclesiastical men. 54  
Chapter XXIV.—Three things especially to be observed in the actions of life, and that the saints of the Old Testament excelled in the cardinal virtues. 53  
Chapter XXV.—It is demonstrated that the cardinal virtues existed among the ancient Fathers. 57  
Chapter XXVI.—Concerning the philosophers’ contradiction; the extent to which Moses surpassed their wisdom is explained. 59  
Chapter XXVII.—The first source of duty is prudence. How closely the other three virtues are connected with it. 60  
Chapter XXVIII.—Piety consists in justice and beneficence. Revenge and private possession are contrary to the Gospel. The Stoics borrowed from Scripture the principles of common ownership and mutual assistance. 61  
Chapter XXIX.—Justice must also be observed in war; its foundation is faith, and its form is found in the Church. 63  
Chapter XXX.—Concerning beneficence, goodwill, and generosity. 65  
Chapter XXXI.—A benefit received must be repaid with a more generous hand. The passage concerning Solomon’s banquet is explained spiritually. 69  
Chapter XXXII.—Various ways of repaying a benefit. 71  
Chapter XXXIII.—Goodwill must especially endure in the Church, and among people possessing the same or related virtues. 72  
Chapter XXXIV.—Other advantages of goodwill are recalled. 74  
Chapter XXXV.—Concerning courage in war and at home. Ibid.  
Chapter XXXVI.—Various duties of courage. 75  
Chapter XXXVII.—How and when peace of mind must be preserved. 78  
Chapter XXXVIII.—The mind must be strengthened by exercise against future misfortunes. 79  
Chapter XXXIX.—Courage must fight against all vices. 80  

[Col. 1525]

Chapter XL.—Our people too were not lacking in military courage. 81  
Chapter XLI.—The steadfastness of the martyrs is placed before our eyes through praise of the courage of Judah and Jonathan. 82  
Chapter XLII.—The authorities must not be provoked, nor should ears be lent to flattery. 86  
Chapter XLIII.—Concerning prudence and its principal parts. Ibid.  
Chapter XLIV.—Everyone ought to strive for the duty suited to him. 87  
Chapter XLV.—Concerning the beautiful and the honorable. 88  
Chapter XLVI.—A twofold division of propriety is proposed. 89  
Chapter XLVII.—What one ought not to do if that propriety is to shine forth in our life. 90  
Chapter XLVIII.—Concerning the restraint of anger; David and the Apostle are set before us as examples. The distinction between this life and the life to come. 92  
Chapter XLIX.—The image of the virtues must be preserved in us; that of the Devil and of the vices must be erased. 94  
Chapter L.—Concerning the virtues, dignity, and duties of clerics. 96

### BOOK II

103. Chapter I.—The blessedness of life is acquired through moral goodness. Ibid.  
Chapter II.—The philosophers’ various opinions concerning blessedness, and where it truly consists. 104  
Chapter III.—The definition of blessedness according to Scripture, and that it depends not at all upon external goods or evils. 105  
Chapter IV.—Confirmation of the same argument. 106  
Chapter V.—What are thought to be goods are impediments to blessedness; what are thought to be evils are material for the virtues. 107  
Chapter VI.—Concerning the useful—not that which is profitable, but that which is just and honorable—which is sought even through losses. 109  
Chapter VII.—That usefulness is the same as honorableness. Nothing is more useful than love. The examples of Moses and David are adduced. 111  
Chapter VIII.—The power of counsel; counsel derives its force from justice and prudence. 114  
Chapter IX.—Although justice and prudence are inseparable, one must nevertheless accommodate oneself to the understanding of the common people, who distinguish the cardinal virtues. 116  
Chapter X.—The power arising from the union of justice and prudence is demonstrated by the examples of Solomon, Joseph, and Daniel. Ibid.  
Chapter XI.—It is shown that the third condition which wins a person’s trust shone forth in Moses, Daniel, and Joseph. 118  
Chapter XII.—No one should seek counsel from a person contaminated by vice, but from one whose kind of example we have in Scripture. Ibid.  
Chapter XIII.—Having demonstrated by divine testimonies the beauty of wisdom, he proves its fellowship with the other virtues. 119  
Chapter XIV.—Prudence is joined with the other virtues, and especially with contempt for riches. 120  
Chapter XV.—Concerning generosity, and how it can also be practiced by a poor person. Ibid.  
Chapter XVI.—The proper measure in generosity must be observed; yet alms must not be given too sparingly or timidly. 123  
Chapter XVII.—What virtues must be present in the person whom we consult. 126  
Chapter XVIII.—The great harm brought by unjust counselors is proved by the example of the schism of the ten tribes. 128  
Chapter XIX.—Many people are won over by justice and affability; but the latter must be sincere. Ibid.  
Chapter XX.—The usefulness of good companionship, and that people unequal in age may sometimes be equal in virtue. 129  
Chapter XXI.—A man’s greatest commendation is to defend the weak, receive strangers, and so forth. Avarice is censured; extravagance is condemned in priests. 130  
Chapter XXII.—A proper balance must be established between excessive leniency and severity. 133  
Chapter XXIII.—Those who have been bought off by money or ambition have an unstable loyalty. 134  
Chapter XXIV.—One must strive for honors through good arts, especially ecclesiastical honors; but once the office has been obtained, it must be administered wisely and moderately. Ibid.  
Chapter XXV.—Benefits should be conferred upon the poor rather than the rich, and why. An exhortation to contempt of money follows. 136  
Chapter XXVI.—The ancient evil of avarice and the futile possession of money. 137  
Chapter XXVII.—In contempt for money there is a pattern of justice; this virtue, as well as the others, should be pursued above all by clerics. 138  
Chapter XXVIII.—Mercy should be exercised generously even at the cost of incurring personal unpopularity. To this is related the memorable story of Ambrose’s making of sacred vessels for the redemption of captives. What are the true treasures of the Church. The rules to be observed in melting down and expending consecrated vessels. 139  
Chapter XXIX.—The deposits of widows, indeed of all the faithful, must be defended in the Church even at personal risk. 142  
Chapter XXX.—An exhortation to flee the envious and to pursue prudence, faith, and the other virtues. 144

### BOOK III

145. Chapter I.—The manner of conversing with our own heart. The leisure of the prophets is compared with the leisure of others. The righteous man is never in a confined situation. Ibid.  
Chapter II.—For Christians nothing is useful except what is just. Which duties are perfect and which intermediate. The just man must always seek the advantage of others. 147  
Chapter III.—Concerning the failure to seek one’s own gain, and how disgraceful it is to diminish another’s advantage. 149  
Chapter IV.—What is useful to one person is not truly useful; and the question proposed by the philosophers concerning two shipwrecked men has no place among Christians, for whom charity and humility must be practiced everywhere. 151  
Chapter V.—The just man must do nothing contrary to duty; this is confirmed both by the tale of Gyges’ ring and by the examples of David and John the Baptist. 153  
Chapter VI.—Personal gain must not prevail among us. The Gospel parable concerning those who seek profit from grain, as well as Solomon’s sayings, are brought against them. 156  
Chapter VII.—Strangers must by no means be driven away in a time of famine; this question is discussed. 158  
Chapter VIII.—Those who place the honorable before the useful are approved by God. Ibid.  
Chapter IX.—Fraud and shameful profits are especially unbecoming to clerics; they ought by no means to intervene in monetary cases, though the situation is different in capital cases. They must not harm anyone, even when provoked. Ibid.  
Chapter X.—Even in the sacred Scriptures, provision is made that fraud is to be avoided in every contract. 164  
Chapter XI.—After introducing, through rhetorical silence, certain examples of fraud, it is shown that these and all other frauds are condemned more openly in Scripture. 165  
Chapter XII.—Nothing dishonorable should be promised; nor, if one has sworn to something unjust, should one keep the oath. 167  
Chapter XIII.—After undergoing many dangers for the sake of honor, Judith is said to have gained manifold humility. 169  
Chapter XIV.—How honorable and useful Elisha’s action was. A comparison of it with the celebrated deed of the Greeks. John laid down his life for honor. Ibid.  
Chapter XV.—After recounting the Romans’ noble counsel, it is declared that Moses had the greatest concern for honor. 171  
Chapter XVI.—After briefly introducing Tobit, it is proved that Raguel surpassed the philosophers. 172  
Chapter XVII.—With what devotion to honor the ancient Fathers, when they were about to go into captivity, concealed the sacred fire. Ibid.  
Chapter XVIII.—The Holy Spirit and the baptism of Christians are signified by the account of the preceding event, and especially by the sacrifice offered by Noemia. 174  
Chapter XIX.—The outrage committed by the citizens of Gibeah against the wife of a certain Levite is recounted, and from the vengeance taken for it is inferred how deeply those ancients cherished the cause of honor. 176  
Chapter XX.—After Samaria’s dreadful siege had been ended through Elisha’s prophecy, the concern for honor shown by the four lepers is narrated. 178  
Chapter XXI.—Esther pursued the glory of honor at the risk of her life, and even the barbarian king, after the death of his most beloved man; for friendship must always be joined to honor. 179  

Conclusion. 184  
Admonition concerning the three books *On Virgins*. 183

## THREE BOOKS ON VIRGINS

### BOOK I

187. Chapter I.—The opening, in which the motives for writing and the many grounds for hoping for the work’s success are set forth with great skill. Ibid.  
Chapter II.—The praise of Saint Agnes, based especially on the fact that, scarcely twelve years old, she rejected threats and terrors as well as promises. 189  
Chapter III.—The commendation of virginity, especially because it was able to draw the Word from heaven to earth. 191  
Chapter IV.—Virginity is denied to the pagans and also to the philosophers; and concerning the Pythagorean virgin. 192  
Chapter V.—Heaven is the homeland of virginity, and the Son of God its author. The Church’s endowments. 194  
Chapter VI.—The holy man compares women’s disadvantages with the privileges of virgins, while declaring that he does not thereby condemn marriage. 195  
Chapter VII.—He exhorts parents to train their daughters for virginity; then he defends marriage against heretics and explains certain passages of the *Song of Songs* morally. 198  
Chapter VIII.—He explains the following passage of the *Song of Songs*, “Dripping honeycomb,” and so forth, using it as an occasion to compare holy virgins with bees. 200  
Chapter VIII.—He explains other passages from the *Song of Songs*, exhorting the virgin to seek Christ and comparing her with the angels. 200  
Chapter IX.—The final praise of virginity is presented, namely, freedom from avarice. How great is the happiness of the virgin who is not compelled to conform to luxury and vanity. 203  
Chapter X.—He refutes by examples those who claim that Ambrose’s exhortations to virginity produce no result. 204  
Chapter XI.—Virginity must be preferred to the favor of parents and even to inheritance. 205

### BOOK II

207. Chapter I.—As he is about to discuss the formation of virgins’ character, he gives an account of his purpose and of the envy arising from the presumption attributed to him. Ibid.  
Chapter II.—Mary is proposed as an example to virgins, and her virtues are especially commended. 208  
Chapter III.—Just as Mary is the model for ordering one’s life, so Thecla is called the model for undergoing death. How she was worshiped by the beasts. 211  
Chapter IV.—Concerning the twofold martyrdom of the Antiochene virgin condemned to a brothel, and of the Christian soldier who, after changing clothes with her, freed her. 212  
Chapter V.—The memorable deed of two friends from the Pythagorean sect is recounted with praise. Concerning Dionysius’ mockery in stripping the idols, and concerning the weakness of the gods. 216  
Chapter VI.—The conclusion of the second book; and that before giving the more severe commands, he ought to soothe the souls of the virgins with the sweetness of prayer and examples. 217

### BOOK III

219. Chapter I.—The prayer of Liberius, who consecrated Marcellina after giving her the veil of virginity, is reported and commended. Ibid.  
Chapter II.—Beginning the instruction of the virgin with sobriety, he recounts and ridicules the legendary death and revival of Hippolytus. 221  
Chapter III.—Visits must be avoided by virgins, modesty must be preserved, and silence observed during the celebration of the mysteries. 222  
Chapter IV.—After reciting Liberius’ exhortation, Ambrose praises his sister’s virtues and supplies her with various counsels concerning moderating fasting for a while, frequent prayer, and so forth. 224  
Chapter V.—He exhorts her to shed tears. How Christ took upon himself a body subject to suffering and turned it as it lay in weakness. 226  
Chapter VI.—Having introduced the mention of the holy Forerunner, he describes and amplifies all the circumstances of his slaughter with the greatest eloquence. 227  
Chapter VII.—What is to be thought of those who inflict violence upon themselves so as not to fall into the hands of persecutors. Examples. 229  

Admonition concerning the book *On Widows*. 231

## ONE BOOK ON WIDOWS

Chapter I.—The relation of widowhood to virginity connects the present treatise with the preceding one. The widow of Zarephath is proposed as an example, and her hospitality is commended. 233  
Chapter II.—The precepts for a true widow are given from the Apostle; on this occasion it is denied that Paul condemned second marriages. In what sense it is said to be better to marry than to burn. How great is the dignity of widows. 236  
Chapter III.—That the widow of Zarephath was a figure of the Church, while Elijah was a figure of Christ. 239  
Chapter IV.—He reveals what the life of widows ought to be by the example of Anna. The threefold degree of chastity, and a threefold example of that virtue in Mary, Anna, and Susanna. 241  
Chapter V.—The example of generosity toward the poor is presented in the Gospel widow, in whose two small coins both Testaments were signified. An exhortation to widows concerning good works. 242  
Chapter VI.—In Naomi is proposed the example of a widow receiving fruit from a daughter-in-law whom she had herself trained in virtue. The sadness of widowhood is abundantly compensated by hope of future joys; and concerning the usefulness of tears. 244  
Chapter VII.—It is shown by the example of Judith that widows are not lacking in courage; her preparation against Holofernes is described, as well as her chastity, wisdom, and modesty. 245  
Chapter VIII.—Concerning Deborah and the outstanding lessons she provided for widows. That she prefigured the Church’s struggles and triumphs. 247  
Chapter IX.—After refuting objections concerning the necessity of obtaining support and preserving property, he demonstrates that it is most unbecoming for a widow whose daughters are already marriageable to marry again. 250  
Chapter X.—Christ’s kindness in approaching the afflicted, and that calling upon so great a physician is immediately followed by healing. A moral interpretation of the will which, he teaches, was expressed in Peter’s mother-in-law. 252  
Chapter XI.—After refuting the arguments commonly brought forward in favor of repeating marriage, he declares that he does not condemn second marriages, and chastises the heretics who disapprove of them. 254  
Chapter XII.—The distinction between a precept and a counsel is illustrated by the example of the rich young man mentioned in the Gospel. 256  
Chapter XIII.—Those who are involuntarily eunuchs are not especially to be praised; those who have laid hands upon themselves in order to become such are to be condemned. No one is to be praised except the person who has conquered himself through self-restraint. 257  
Chapter XIV.—How frequent and important is the counsel of widowhood. He attacks its opponents. 260  
Chapter XV.—He responds to widows who object that they desire children, especially addressing those who have had sons from their first marriage. 261  

Admonition concerning the book *On Virginity*. 263

## ONE BOOK ON VIRGINITY

Chapter I.—A historical, philosophical, and moral explanation of Solomon’s judgment. 259  
Chapter II.—A commentary on the history of Jephthah. The deed is to be condemned, but faithfulness in fulfilling a vow is approved. Why God did not prevent Jephthah’s parricide. 267  
Chapter III.—From the history of Jephthah he takes occasion both to chastise the opponents of virginal continence and to defend himself because he forbade a sacred virgin to marry. 268  
Chapter IV.—Taking occasion from the doubting Magdalene, he exhorts virgins to faith, explaining spiritually Christ’s conversation with her. 270  
Chapter V.—Returning to his own defense, he declares that he desires also to recall women intending to marry to the pursuit of virginity. 272  
Chapter VI.—To encourage virginity is neither wrong, nor new, nor useless; nevertheless marriage is not to be condemned. 272  
Chapter VII.—That virginity is not harmful. He responds both to those who objected that it thereby made marriage more difficult for the young and to those who maintained that virgins should receive the veil later. 275  
Chapter VIII.—Just as every age is suited to seeking Christ, so every place is suitable for that purpose. Concerning following Christ by day. 277  
Chapter IX.—Christ is to be sought in the mountains of spices and in the desert; the latter’s fertility is described, together with the reason Christ is called the flower and the lily. 279  
Chapter X.—What must be done to deserve Christ’s coming to us. What the washing of the feet signifies, and what the Bride says: “How shall I defile them?” 280  
Chapter XI.—It is good to tremble and hasten at Christ’s approach. The words of the *Song of Songs* are applied to Christ: “But my hands dripped with myrrh,” and so forth. 281  
Chapter XII.—Christ is to be awaited by all, and especially by virgins. What it means when the Bridegroom says that his locks are wet. Tempters are to be despised. 283  
Chapter XIII.—By what means the Bridegroom can be held, and through what window the Bridegroom is said to put out his hand. Silence is the companion and guardian of virginity. 285  
Chapter XIV.—How the Bride is to enter the heavenly Jerusalem. The light, walls, gates, and citizens of that city are explained. How it is understood that the soul is stripped by the holy angels. 287  
Chapter XV.—Why the soul is designated by a feminine term. The soul’s movements are compared with horses. 290  
Chapter XVI.—The Bridegroom’s invitation into the walnut garden is explained spiritually. The wondrous effects of faith, to which humble confession is shown to be necessary. 291  
Chapter XVII.—He advises the avoidance of boasting by the example of the little bee. Christ and the apostles are to be imitated by us. 293  
Chapter XVIII.—What the poets attribute to the soul—chariots, horses, and wings—they took from Ezekiel. The four forms of the living creatures, by which the four evangelists are represented, are also figures of the four cardinal virtues. How the soul ought to fly. 294  
Chapter XIX.—A mystical explanation of Peter’s fishing. An exhortation that we show ourselves worthy of Christ’s benefit. 298  
Chapter XX.—Ambrose, as though he were about to cast a net, asks the Lord for a second catch. How useful it was for John to abandon everything for Christ. A comparison of fishermen with Moses. 300  

Admonition concerning the book *On the Institution of a Virgin*. 301

## ONE BOOK ON THE INSTITUTION OF A VIRGIN

Chapter I.—Parents rightly have greater concern for a consecrated virgin than for their other children; and silence is especially fitting for virginity. 305  
Chapter II.—Prayer ought to begin with the praises of God and end in thanksgiving. A Gospel passage concerning prayer is explained. 307  
Chapter III.—The female sex is not to be blamed, since God has bestowed such great gifts upon it. God did not approve the human being until after woman had been created, because the union of woman with man was to express the figure of a great mystery; she herself is shown to have received her name from this. 309  
Chapter IV.—It is asserted that the woman’s sin was lighter than the man’s. Remedies against women’s temptations. 311  
Chapter V.—In Sarah, but especially in Mary, Eve’s sentence of condemnation was as though revoked. The opponents of Mary’s virginity are refuted. 313  
Chapter VI.—How absurd it is to suppose that Christ denied his mother the gifts of virginity. 316  
Chapter VII.—Once it has been proved that Mary persevered in virginal integrity, this is confirmed by the fact that she was given as mother to the disciple; her purpose of virginity could not have been changed, since such steadfastness shone forth in her Son’s passion and such virtue in the Baptist’s exultation. 317  
Chapter VIII.—Ezekiel’s testimonies, and especially his statement concerning the door that was not to be opened, apply to Mary, through whom Christ passed without opening it. 319  
Chapter IX.—How virginity is signified by various symbols, and what sacred virgins ought to learn from each of them. 321  
Chapter X.—Virginity is a crown in the Lord’s hand. The Catholic faith concerning the Trinity is asserted against the heretics. Ibid.  
Chapter XI.—One ought not to labor for Christ alone. He is not read to be second except insofar as he is human. 323  
Chapter XII.—Christ is understood in certain passages as the “second young man” designated by Ecclesiastes; he is therefore the one who is described both as having passed through the gate and as having eaten while sitting in it. 324  
Chapter XIII.—Mary’s virginity is beautifully signified by the pot and the light cloud. Virgins ought to gather the rain of this cloud and the perfume of the pot. 325  
Chapter XIV.—What is said mystically about the Church also applies to Mary. 326  
Chapter XV.—How virgins are prefigured by lilies, while Christ is prefigured by a heap of wheat surrounded by lilies. 327  
Chapter XVI.—How virgins must depart with Christ. His divinity must not be doubted; and a virgin must put on Christ and all the ornaments of virtue together. 328  
Chapter XVII.—Thanks are given to God that the angelic life once lost in paradise now shines forth in virgins. Ambrosia is commended to God and offered to him. 330  

Admonition concerning the exhortation to virginity. 333

## ONE BOOK ON THE EXHORTATION TO VIRGINITY

Chapter I.—The opening is taken from the relics of Saints Agricola and Vitalis, which he had brought from Bologna, and from their discovery. 335  
Chapter II.—He magnifies the value of the relics; then he asserts that the widow Juliana is worthy to receive them. 339  
Chapter III.—An exhortation to Juliana’s children. 340  
Chapter IV.—“The dignity of chastity, the disadvantages of marriage, and the Apostle’s judgment concerning marriage.” 342  
Chapter V.—“To virgins in both Covenants the palm of public salvation has been assigned. Virginity is represented by the figure of a garden and a vineyard, just as marriage is represented by the figure of vegetables. Therefore he exhorts his children, rejecting the spiritual Ahab and Jezebel, to embrace the true Naboth, accused and slain for us.” 344  
Chapter VI.—“He teaches his children by what means they themselves can become light clouds through virginity, and give true sons to Levi. What is the distinction between the Lord’s allotment and that of Moses?” 346  
Chapter VII.—“The praise of the virgin’s barrenness. The temptations of virgins; what remedy must be sought against them.” 348  
Chapter VIII.—“To press more earnestly upon his offspring, already promised to God by their parents, he recounts the obedience of Jephthah’s daughter in fulfilling her father’s vow. Then he gives thanks for the holy eagerness of his devout offspring.” 350  
Chapter IX.—To add his own holy exhortation to the mother’s, the holy bishop urges the holy widow’s daughters to seek Christ in the reading of Scripture, in good works, and in nightly prayers. 352  
Chapter X.—The passage in Ecclesiastes concerning clothing is shown to be appropriate to virginity; but what it adds about carrying oil on the head is understood both of humility of mind and of modest arrangement of the body. How the Synagogue says to the Church, “Where do you pasture?” and so forth, while the latter receives these words of Christ: “Unless you know yourself,” and so forth. 355  
Chapter XI.—He exhorts them to avoid the readiness to swear oaths, to prefer tears to joy, and so forth. 358  
Chapter XII.—He commands a good reputation to be acquired, but especially requires sobriety in a virgin. The example of Saint Soteris is proposed. 359  
Chapter XIII.—He reminds virgins to preserve the divine image in themselves. How, and to what extent, the scourge of another’s tongue is not to be feared. The examples of Susanna, Joseph, Daniel, and Job. 361  
Chapter XIV.—One must not judge anyone’s merit from the misfortunes of the world. He declares that the crown preached by Paul is reserved for that widow who offered God a twofold sacrifice: her widowhood and her children’s virginity. 362  

Admonition concerning the book *On the Fall of a Consecrated Virgin*. 363

## THE BOOK ON THE FALL OF A CONSECRATED VIRGIN

Chapter I.—He rouses everyone to grieve, both for themselves and for the Church, over so great a fall. 367  
Chapter II.—He addresses the corrupted woman, describing the condition of her soul before and after the crime. 368  
Chapter III.—How wretched is the woman who now has no access to God, indeed not even to human beings themselves. 369  
Chapter IV.—After refuting the excuses which corrupted women commonly put forward, he pities the fate of the virgin’s parents and of her entire family. 370  
Chapter V.—After recalling the solemnity of consecration and the vows, he resolves the objections drawn from the Apostle’s words. 372  
Chapter VI.—Having recalled the reasons by which she ought to have been recalled from disgrace, he marvels at her madness. 373  
Chapter VII.—He asserts that he had provided her with all the care required by episcopal duty; but she not only gained nothing from it, she also inflicted grave scandal upon others. 375  
Chapter VIII.—The method and difficulty of applying the remedy. The inward acts and outward signs of true repentance are commended. The severity of the future judgment. 376  
Chapter IX.—He rebukes the violator of the virgin and moves him to repentance. 379  
Chapter X.—He supplies the fallen virgin with vivid sentiments of repentance. 380  

Admonition concerning the book *On the Mysteries*. 383

## THE BOOK ON THE MYSTERIES

Chapter I.—He promises to append an exposition of the mysteries to the treatises he had previously delivered on morals. Then, after explaining why he had not worked it out earlier, he undertakes the mystical exposition, which he demonstrates was once celebrated by Christ himself. 389  
Chapter II.—What those entering the Church for initiation promised, in whose presence they made the promise, and why they turned toward the East. 390  
Chapter III.—In the water and the ministers, the operation of the Godhead must be considered. 391  
Chapter IV.—It is declared that water does not cleanse without the Spirit, and it is shown that the Holy Spirit truly descended at Christ’s baptism. 394  
Chapter V.—It is confirmed that Christ is present in baptism. The confession of the Trinity customarily made by the baptized is examined. 397  
Chapter VI.—Why, after emerging from the baptismal font, anointing is performed on the head; and why the washing of the feet also follows baptism. 398  
Chapter VII.—The white garments signify the removal of sins: through whose work the Church was able to call herself both black and beautiful. The beauty of Christ’s Bride, who is the Church, and Christ’s affection toward her. 399  
Chapter VIII.—Concerning the mystical banquet of the Lord’s altar, which is shown to be older than the sacred rites of the Synagogue. 403  
Chapter IX.—Concerning the truth of Christ’s body in the Eucharist, and also the effects of this sacrament and the dispositions required for receiving it. 405  

Preface to the books *On the Sacraments*. 409

## SIX BOOKS ON THE SACRAMENTS
# BOOK ONE

417 **CHAPTER ONE.**—Having first stated that he would treat of the sacraments, which ought not previously to have been explained, he proceeds to the mystery of the opening, which he teaches was signified by Christ in the healing of the deaf and mute. Ibid.

**CHAPTER II.**—He explains the anointing of the Christian athlete; and, in order to encourage him to preserve the faith of his renunciation, magnifies the dignity of the witnesses in whose presence it was made. 419

**CHAPTER III.**—Although the neophytes saw only the font and the ministers, he shows that the things they do not see are greater. 420

**CHAPTER IV.**—The sacraments of Christians are more divine and more ancient than those of the Jews. On the meaning of the word *Pascha* [Passover]. Ibid.

**CHAPTER V.**—In the account of Naaman’s healing, the power of baptismal water is signified. On the descent of the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove when Christ was baptized. 421

**CHAPTER VI.**—Baptism was prefigured both by the crossing of the Red Sea and by the Flood. 423

# BOOK TWO

Ibid.

**CHAPTER ONE.**—He resumes his explanation of the Flood, showing in it a figure of true baptism. Ibid. [Col. 1531]

**CHAPTER II.**—The account of the Pool of Bethesda, stirred by an angel and restoring health to the one who first descended into it, is expounded, together with the paralytic’s reply to Christ. 425

**CHAPTER III.**—After recounting certain matters from the story of Naaman, the Author briefly touches upon several other figures of the same sacrament. 426

**CHAPTER IV.**—The Author proposes two other figures of baptism: the iron that floated at Elisha’s command, and the spring whose waters were sweetened. Ibid.

**CHAPTER V.**—The Trinity is present at the priest’s prayers. 427

**CHAPTER VI.**—After the sentence of death had been pronounced upon human beings because of sin, baptism was devised to raise them again to life. 428

**CHAPTER VII.**—An example of the threefold questioning and immersion existed in Peter’s threefold response. There is one name in which we must be saved, and he explains in what manner we die together with Christ. 429

# BOOK THREE

431 **CHAPTER ONE.**—Why those who have been submerged and given life in baptism receive ointment upon the head, and what regeneration is. On the mystery of the washing of the feet. Ibid.

**CHAPTER II.**—The baptized person is sealed with the Holy Spirit. By the placing of clay upon the baptized man’s eyes, the confession of sins is signified. 433

# BOOK FOUR

435 **CHAPTER ONE.**—The Tabernacle of the ancient Law, and the practices customarily observed there, are adapted to the baptistery and to the effects of baptism. Ibid.

**CHAPTER II.**—The human condition in baptism is a matter of wonder even to the angels. 437

**CHAPTER III.**—Our sacraments are more ancient than the sacraments of the Jews. 438

**CHAPTER IV.**—On the truth of Christ’s body in the Eucharist, and why his blood is given under another appearance. 439

**CHAPTER V.**—By the Lord’s own words his body and blood are consecrated and truly brought into being. 443

# BOOK FIVE

445 **CHAPTER ONE.**—Melchizedek is a figure of Christ, and his sacrifice a figure of the Eucharist. Two reasons why water is mixed into the chalice. Ibid.

**CHAPTER II.**—How the one who has been cleansed is invited by Christ and himself aspires to the sacrament’s immeasurable sweetness. 447

**CHAPTER III.**—The fruit of the Eucharist, and how Christ responds to the Church as she longs for the multitude of her banqueters. 448

**CHAPTER IV.**—In order to instruct the new believers in the manner of prayer, he briefly explains the Lord’s Prayer set before them like a mirror. 450

# BOOK SIX

453 **CHAPTER ONE.**—We do not participate in the divine substance in the Eucharist. Ibid.

**CHAPTER II.**—In all the sacraments the operation of the Trinity and the equality of the divine Persons can be discerned. 455

**CHAPTER III.**—As he is about to hand down the manner of prayer, he reconciles the words of Christ and of the Apostle. 456

**CHAPTER IV.**—Why one should pray secretly and in every place, and in what sense the words “lifting up pure hands” were spoken. 457

**CHAPTER V.**—On the disorderly disputation of those who pray, and with what modesty women ought to pray; also on the beginning, middle, and end of prayer. 458

## Admonition concerning the books *On Penance*. 461

# THE TWO BOOKS ON PENANCE

465 **CHAPTER ONE.**—The praise of moderation. How necessary this virtue is for those placed over the Church. From this he takes the occasion to criticize the Novatians. Ibid.

**CHAPTER II.**—The contradiction of the Novatians both with Scripture and with themselves. The right of binding and loosing is wrongly claimed by heresy, but rightly exercised by the Church. Ibid.

**CHAPTER III.**—He continues to criticize the Novatians’ merciless doctrine concerning the remission of sins. 469

**CHAPTER IV.**—How great divine mercy is, and that those who denied Christ must not all be regarded in the same way. 471

**CHAPTER V.**—An answer is given to the objection drawn from God’s immutability; and it is added that those who sinned in a certain sense unwillingly obtain greater mercy. 472

**CHAPTER VI.**—The Novatians are more ruthless than the hypocrites rebuked in the Gospel. 474

**CHAPTER VII.**—Because of their excessive severity, the Novatians cannot have a share with Christ. 475

**CHAPTER VIII.**—What Christ bestowed upon his disciples. The Novatians, when they lay on hands and confer baptism, are refuted by their own actions. 476

**CHAPTER IX.**—The words of Scripture, “But if a man sins against the Lord, who will pray for him?” are explained in their proper sense. 478

**CHAPTER X.**—John did not absolutely and simply forbid prayer to be made for those guilty of sin unto death. 480

**CHAPTER XI.**—John’s preceding statement is illuminated by another testimony of his; and the Novatians are refuted. 481

**CHAPTER XII.**—Another passage from John’s Gospel is explained in confirmation of the same argument, and an answer is given to those who object that God’s commandments must be kept. 483

**CHAPTER XIII.**—Those who have committed sin unto death must not be abandoned, and the meaning of being “handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh” is explained. 484

**CHAPTER XIV.**—What Ambrose said above—that the flesh, handed over to Satan for destruction, is eaten by the serpent—is explained. Instructions are given for guarding the eyes and the mind. 486

**CHAPTER XV.**—What it means to come “with a rod” or “in a spirit of gentleness.” The proper conduct toward one who has fallen gravely. How all the Church’s flour should be kneaded together and nourished with the food of charity, lest the members become like the Novatians. 489

**CHAPTER XVI.**—The Novatians are compared with the Apostle. How well the Lord’s words suit them: “You do not know whose spirit you are.” Their doctrine concerning penance is refuted. 492

**CHAPTER XVII.**—Piety must be added to severity. It is asserted, against the Novatians’ quibbles, that the Corinthian was initiated by baptism. The word “destruction” does not signify annihilation, but only the chastisement of the flesh. 494

# BOOK TWO

495 **CHAPTER ONE.**—As Ambrose is about to append new instruction to the precepts of the preceding book, he allegorically indicates the necessity of undertaking penance promptly. Ibid.

**CHAPTER II.**—He resolves the apostolic passage brought forward by the heretics and shows that it is to be understood of the repetition of baptism. 497

**CHAPTER III.**—He confirms the preceding solution. 499

**CHAPTER IV.**—He turns back upon the Novatians themselves another objection drawn from blasphemy against the Holy Spirit. 501

**CHAPTER V.**—He resolves the objection drawn from the fact that Peter does not appear to have promised forgiveness expressly to Simon Magus. Then he adds that the apostles handed down to us penance, whose fruits are shown in David. 504

**CHAPTER VI.**—As he urges those who have fallen from faith or innocence to repent, he teaches from Isaiah what they should expect from God and what they themselves ought to offer. Against dances and choreographed revelry. What conditions penance ought to possess. 507

**CHAPTER VII.**—He urges people to weep over and confess their sins. Against the Novatians, he teaches that the complete justification of every sin was represented by the fragrance of the ointment poured by Mary upon Christ’s feet. 510

**CHAPTER VIII.**—In the action of the penitent Magdalene, a pattern of penance was handed down. One must not insult sinners, for whom Christ died. 512

**CHAPTER IX.**—How faith is necessary for penance. How many aids to release are also available to each person. Prayer, tears, and fasting are better than money. The defects of penance are indicated. 516

**CHAPTER X.**—The usefulness of prayers uttered by the whole Church together. The difficulty of true penance. 518

**CHAPTER XI.**—Against those who postpone baptism until death. 521

## Admonition concerning the books *On Faith*. 523

# THE FIVE BOOKS ON FAITH

## Prologue

Ibid.

**CHAPTER ONE.**—He distinguishes the Catholic faith from the errors of heretics and unbelievers. An interpretation of the terms “God” and “Lord.” Against the Arians, he asserts the distinction of the Persons and the unity of nature. 530

**CHAPTER II.**—Having exhorted Gratian to zeal for the faith, he proves Christ’s divinity from the fact that he has one operation with the Father. The divine attributes also belong to Christ, and various names applied to him are discussed. 531

**CHAPTER III.**—Scripture proves the unity of the Father and the Son. 533

**CHAPTER IV.**—On the unity of God and on the gifts of the Magi. 535

**CHAPTER V.**—Various blasphemies of the Arians against Christ are reported. Before answering them, Catholics are warned to beware of the sophistries of philosophers, since the heretics placed their chief hope in them. 536

**CHAPTER VI.**—As he is about to prove that Christ is not unlike the Father, he accuses the leaders of the Arian heresy of dissension and points out the protection afforded by the Scriptures against them. 537

**CHAPTER VII.**—From Paul, the prophets, and the Gospel, Christ is asserted to be like the Father. 539

**CHAPTER VIII.**—From the established likeness of the Son to the Father, the Son’s eternity must also be inferred; this, however, he establishes by particular testimonies of Scripture. 540

**CHAPTER IX.**—Against the heretics, he asserts that Christ is in no way later than the Father, and that eternity must be attributed to both. 541

**CHAPTER X.**—Again on Christ’s eternity, and that divine generation must not be measured according to the pattern of human generation. 542

**CHAPTER XI.**—It cannot be proved that the Father is prior to the Son. 544

**CHAPTER XII.**—The repeated objection against the Son is answered by turning it back upon the Father. There is nothing human in Christ’s generation from Mary; therefore there is nothing human in his generation from the Father. 545

**CHAPTER XIII.**—The question how the Son was begotten is resolved, and it is shown that the divinity and eternity of the Son were signified in Nebuchadnezzar’s vision. 547

**CHAPTER XIV.**—The Son of God is not a creature. The arguments for this are confirmed by the testimony of the Apostle. 549

**CHAPTER XV.**—The sense in which the two passages of Scripture in which Christ is said to have been “made” and “created” are to be understood. 550

**CHAPTER XVI.**—The Arians do Christ an injury if they confuse “begotten” and “created”; but if they do not, they must deny that the one whom they read of as begotten was created. Nothing in God is created, nor can the Son be called a creature, in whom the Father was well pleased. 551

**CHAPTER XVII.**—Christ is true God. The Father and the Son have one and the same operation. 553

**CHAPTER XVIII.**—The Arian errors are recalled in the Nicene definition so that they may deceive no one. They are reported together with their anathema, which is said to have been pronounced not only at Nicaea but also once and again at Ariminum. 555

**CHAPTER XIX.**—After first attributing to Arius one of the errors mentioned above, he refutes it by the testimony of John and describes his tragic death. 556

**CHAPTER XX.**—He longs for the Seraphim to fly to him for his cleansing, as once they flew to Isaiah. He invites Christ to himself, to the emperor Gratian, and to his readers; and finally urges the Emperor and the other faithful to be intoxicated with the heavenly table. 558

# BOOK TWO

559 **Prologue.** Ibid.

**CHAPTER ONE.**—He resolves the Arians’ objection, by which they deprive the Son of God of goodness. 563

**CHAPTER II.**—The Son of God is proved to be good by his works. The words of the Bride of Christ that signify goodness are explained. 564

**CHAPTER III.**—The Son of God is true and good God. 566

**CHAPTER IV.**—The Son of God is omnipotent. Ibid.

**CHAPTER V.**—The passages of Scripture brought forward against Christ’s omnipotence are answered; and he dwells especially on proving that Christ often spoke from the affections of human nature. 567

**CHAPTER VI.**—Freedom is vindicated for Christ. 569

**CHAPTER VII.**—Whatever in Christ does not correspond to divinity arises from the humanity he assumed. 570

**CHAPTER VIII.**—An explanation of the words: “The Father is greater than I.” 571

**CHAPTER IX.**—The objection that the Son was sent by the Father is resolved. One must carefully distinguish which expressions apply to Christ as God and which apply to him as man. 575

**CHAPTER X.**—The objection drawn from the Son’s obedience is dispelled. 578

**CHAPTER XI.**—For what purpose and with what benefit Christ assumed flesh. How useful it is to possess faith, and that the Son of God was sent without any subjection. 579

**CHAPTER XII.**—It is investigated whether Catholics or Arians better make Christ their ally when he is considered as judge. The objection drawn from the Father’s invitation to the Son to sit at his right hand is resolved. 581

**CHAPTER XIII.**—Continuing the allegory of the Lord’s judgment, he refutes the Arians’ blasphemous opinions. 583

**CHAPTER XIV.**—He explains the judgment pronounced by Christ the Judge; and, after dismantling the quibbles of his opponents, shows that no appeal is granted from it. 585

**CHAPTER XV.**—A comparison of Arian and Jewish obstinacy. Ibid.

**CHAPTER XVI.**—Promising victory to Gratian, he recounts that it was foretold by Ezekiel, and beseeches God to bring aid to the faithful army, its commander, and its territory. 587

# BOOK THREE

589 **CHAPTER ONE.**—He dispels the objection to his use of fables by the example of Scripture, mentioning other poetic material and especially the Sirens, who are figures of pleasures from which both Paul’s words and Christ’s deeds ought to draw Christians away. Ibid.

**CHAPTER II.**—The things belonging to the body, which Christ assumed for us, must not be attributed to divinity. What is read—that immortality belongs to God alone—is also to be understood of Christ. 591

**CHAPTER III.**—From the Apostle it is confirmed that the Son must not be separated from the Father. 592

**CHAPTER IV.**—Christ is said to have been made only according to the flesh, and his prayer must be referred to his humanity. Why he is called “Son of Man” and “powerful.” 594

**CHAPTER V.**—In Scripture, “made” does not always mean the same thing as “created.” 596

**CHAPTER VI.**—He refutes an objection drawn from John, directed against the Manichaeans. 598

**CHAPTER VII.**—Solomon’s statement, “The Lord created me,” and so forth, signifies Christ’s incarnation; and the word “beginning” can be understood of the teachings of the virtues, of which Christ was both teacher and beginning. 599

**CHAPTER VIII.**—Isaiah’s verse, “A Son has been given to us,” and so forth, is explained of Christ’s humanity and divinity. 600

**CHAPTER IX.**—He resolves the difficulty arising from the passage of Solomon cited above. 602

**CHAPTER X.**—He resolves the Baptist’s words from which the heretics argued that Christ was made even before the incarnation, and explains in what sense they should be understood. Ibid.

**CHAPTER XI.**—Whenever Christ is said to have been made, he teaches that this refers either to the incarnation or to some cause or circumstance. Christ is the true priest, prefigured in Melchizedek. 605

**CHAPTER XII.**—The kingdom of the Father and the Son is one and indivisible; likewise, the divinity of both is one. 608

**CHAPTER XIII.**—The Son possesses his own majesty, equal to the Father’s; his companions are not angels but spectators. 610

**CHAPTER XIV.**—The Son is of one substance with the Father. 611

**CHAPTER XV.**—The force and appropriateness of the term ὁμοούσιον (*homoousion*, “of the same substance”) against the heretics. 613

**CHAPTER XVI.**—Catholics are forearmed against the Arians’ deceitful confessions. 615

**CHAPTER XVII.**—The reason why the Lord appeared to stand before Stephen is explained; and from Stephen’s prayers to the Son, the Son’s equality with the Father is confirmed. 616

# BOOK FOUR

617 **CHAPTER ONE.**—It is not surprising that human beings should have erred in the knowledge of Christ, but it is surprising that they did not obey Scripture. Even Christ was known to the angels only through revelation. What a triumph Christ’s ascent into heaven was. Ibid.

**CHAPTER II.**—No one will ascend into heaven without faith; or, if anyone has ascended, he must be cast out. There are also heavens within us, whose gates must be opened and raised through confession of Christ’s divinity. Against the Arians. 620

**CHAPTER III.**—The words “The head of every man is Christ . . . and the head of Christ is God,” and the other words, “He who plants and he who waters are one,” are explained against the Arians. 622

**CHAPTER IV.**—The text brought forward by the heretics, “The Son can do nothing of himself,” and so forth, is answered. 624

**CHAPTER V.**—Pressing the exposition of the passage already begun, he explains four reasons why we say that something cannot be done, and demonstrates that the first three do not apply to Christ. 626

**CHAPTER VI.**—He proceeds to the fourth of the reasons mentioned above; and, proving that the Son does nothing that is not approved by the Father, removes certain difficulties. 629

**CHAPTER VII.**—The doctrine already proposed is confirmed by the fact that the Son is the Father’s Word—not like our word, but true and effectual. 631

**CHAPTER VIII.**—He turns back upon the heretics themselves the objection by which they argued that the Son is unequal to the Father because he cannot beget another. Divine things must not be judged by human things; the authority of Scripture must be followed. Omnipotence belongs no less to the Father than to the Son. 632

**CHAPTER IX.**—He sets forth and demolishes the various petty arguments by which the Arians argued that the Son had a beginning. 636

**CHAPTER X.**—An answer is given to those who object that Christ is said to live because of the Father. 639

**CHAPTER XI.**—The distinction which the Arians attempted to derive from the Apostle’s words—who teaches that all things are from the Father and all things through the Son—is ridiculed. 643

**CHAPTER XII.**—The objection drawn from John, where the Son is compared to a vine and the Father to a cultivator, is to be understood of the incarnation. The Son is also a cultivator according to his divinity, but not according to his humanity. 647

# BOOK FIVE

649 **Prologue.** Ibid.

**CHAPTER ONE.**—How impious the Arians are when they attack that in which human happiness consists. John always joins the Son with the Father; hence true divinity is asserted for the Son. 652

**CHAPTER II.**—When the word “alone” is used of the Father in Scripture, the Son is not excluded. The Trinity alone is not among all things but above all things. The Son must not be separated from the Father. 654

**CHAPTER III.**—When the Arians press the claim that two gods are introduced by the unity of substance, the answer is that plurality follows rather from diversity; consequently, their accusation falls back upon themselves. On the unity of the Persons of the Holy Trinity. 657 [Col. 1535]

**CHAPTER IV.**—The objection that Christ worshiped the Father is answered. 659

**CHAPTER V.**—The objection drawn from Christ’s words to the mother of the sons of Zebedee is dispelled. 660

**CHAPTER VI.**—He persists in resolving the proposed objection more carefully. 663

**CHAPTER VII.**—Another objection, drawn from the passage “You loved them as you loved me,” is resolved. 666

**CHAPTER VIII.**—Christ, insofar as he is truly the Son of God, does not have a Lord; he has one insofar as he is man. In a word, one must carefully distinguish what applies to Christ as God from what applies to him as man. 668

**CHAPTER IX.**—The Jewish ordering of the words “In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” is answered when it is brought forward as an objection. 672

**CHAPTER X.**—The Arians openly pass over to the pagans when they object with the words, “He who believes in me does not believe in me,” and so forth. The true sense of the passage is explained. 673

**CHAPTER XI.**—When Christ is read as saying that he speaks nothing from himself, this must be referred to his humanity. In what sense he is also rightly said, according to his divinity, to hear and see the Father. 675

**CHAPTER XII.**—He confirms the preceding arguments from the parable of the rich man who departed to seek a kingdom for himself. We are here Christ’s kingdom. 677

**CHAPTER XIII.**—On Christ’s subjection to the Father, and on the subjection of all things to Christ. 679

**CHAPTER XIV.**—He continues the discussion of Christ’s subjection. 682

**CHAPTER XV.**—He briefly resumes the preceding discussion, concluding from the unity of divine power in the Father and the Son that whatever is said about the Son’s subjection must be referred solely to his humanity. 685

**CHAPTER XVI.**—The Arians are condemned by the Holy Spirit through David, since they dare to detract from Christ’s knowledge. As the Son of God, Christ cannot lack knowledge. 687

**CHAPTER XVII.**—The fact that Christ did not wish to reveal the day of judgment was intended for our benefit. Hence it is absurd to attribute ignorance to the Son. 691

**CHAPTER XVIII.**—The knowledge of the Father and the Son is equal, and therefore the Son is not less than the Father. The Arians’ recklessness is struck down. 693
