**CHAPTER XIX.**—How rash it is to discuss divine generation, and how greatly Arius’s arrogance must be avoided. 696

## Admonition concerning the books *On the Holy Spirit*. 697

# THE THREE BOOKS ON THE HOLY SPIRIT

# BOOK ONE

703 **Prologue.** Ibid.

**CHAPTER ONE.**—He praises Gratian both for his faith and for restoring the basilica to the Church. If the opponents deny that the Holy Spirit serves, they cannot deny that he is above all things. 709

**CHAPTER II.**—It is not proved from the words “All things were made through him” that the Holy Spirit is among all things. 711

**CHAPTER III.**—When the Apostle says that all things are from the Father and through the Son, the Holy Spirit is not excluded from their fellowship. The Son is worshiped by the angels, but not by the Spirit; for the Spirit is his witness, not his minister. The dignity of the Holy Spirit is evident from the fact that sin committed against him is declared unforgivable. 712

**CHAPTER IV.**—The Holy Spirit is one and the same Spirit who spoke in the prophets and in the apostles, who is the Spirit of God and of Christ, and whom Scripture also identifies as the Paraclete, the Spirit of life, and the Spirit of truth. 717

**CHAPTER V.**—Since the Holy Spirit sanctifies creatures, he is neither a creature nor changeable; he is always good. 719

**CHAPTER VI.**—Although we are baptized in water and in the Spirit, the Spirit nevertheless surpasses water by far, and therefore must not be separated from the Father and the Son. 722

**CHAPTER VII.**—The Holy Spirit is not a creature, since he is unbounded and was poured into the apostles scattered throughout all the regions. Mary was filled with the same Spirit, as were also the Lord Christ and, indeed, all things above and below. 723

**CHAPTER VIII.**—The Spirit is given by God alone, yet not wholly to each individual. Through the Spirit charity is poured out. He must not be numbered among created things. 726

**CHAPTER IX.**—The Holy Spirit is rightly called Christ’s ointment and the oil of gladness. Christ himself is not the ointment; yet it should not seem strange if both the ointment and the Spirit are so called, since the Father and the Son are also called Spirit. 728

**CHAPTER X.**—The fact that the Spirit forgives sins is something he shares with the Father and the Son, but not with the angels. 731

**CHAPTER XI.**—The Spirit is sent to all and does not pass from one place to another. [Col. 1536] 731

**CHAPTER XII.**—The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one peace and one grace; likewise one charity, and finally one fellowship among the three. 734

**CHAPTER XIII.**—Scripture also demonstrates that the divine Persons have one name. 735

**CHAPTER XIV.**—The Scriptures show that each Person of the Trinity is light, while the Spirit is also signified as fire. The divinity of the Spirit cannot be denied. 736

**CHAPTER XV.**—The Holy Spirit is life just as the Father and the Son are. 738

**CHAPTER XVI.**—The Holy Spirit is the great river whose service irrigates the mystical Jerusalem. He is equal to his own fountain, that is, to the Father and the Son. 739

# BOOK TWO

741 **Prologue.** Ibid.

**CHAPTER ONE.**—The Spirit of the Lord is also Lord and power, and in this respect is not inferior to the Father or the Son. 746

**CHAPTER II.**—The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one counsel. 747

**CHAPTER III.**—Just as it is life to know the Father and the Son, so it is life to know the Holy Spirit; therefore he must not be separated from the Father’s divinity. 748

**CHAPTER IV.**—The Holy Spirit gives life, just as the Father and the Son do, through an operation that is not different. 749

**CHAPTER V.**—The Holy Spirit is signified in Scripture just as the Father and the Son are. This same truth was also outlined by pagan writers, but it is demonstrated most clearly in the mystery of the Incarnation. Ibid.

**CHAPTER VI.**—An answer is given to those who object from the words of Amos that the Spirit is created. 752

**CHAPTER VII.**—The Spirit is no less the author of spiritual creation, or regeneration, than the Father and the Son. The nature and excellence of that creation, and how the sacred books’ attribution of members and a body to God ought to be understood. 756

**CHAPTER VIII.**—He dispels the heretics’ sophistry, by which they repeatedly claimed that God is to be glorified in the Spirit but not with the Spirit. 757

**CHAPTER IX.**—He expounds and explains the apostolic passage that the heretics misused in order to introduce a distinction among the divine Persons. 761

**CHAPTER X.**—The Trinity has one will. The calling of the Gentiles was foreshadowed in Peter’s vision. In Jeremiah, the episode in which Jeremiah was lowered by the Jews into a pit and brought out by Ebed-melech anticipated a symbol: the Holy Spirit, held in contempt by those same Jews, would be honored by the Gentiles. 764

**CHAPTER XI.**—Ebed-melech is proposed to us as an example. The unity of nature and knowledge in the Trinity must be recognized from Scripture. 767

**CHAPTER XII.**—Having proved that the Spirit reveals just as the Father and the Son do, he explains in what sense the same Spirit does not speak from himself. The Spirit hears and glorifies the Son in the sense that he revealed him to the prophets and apostles. 770

**CHAPTER XIII.**—The unity of authority, establishment, and generosity in the three Persons must be recognized. 773

# BOOK THREE

777 **CHAPTER ONE.**—Not only the prophets and apostles but also the Son of God was sent by the Spirit. Why Luke wrote that the same Spirit descended upon Christ like a dove. Ibid.

**CHAPTER II.**—The Son is given just as the Spirit is given; hence not subjection but one divinity is demonstrated by their operation. 779

**CHAPTER III.**—The same unity is also recognized from the fact that the Spirit is called a finger and the Son the right hand. Ibid.

**CHAPTER IV.**—Those who argue that the Spirit is lesser because he is called a finger are refuted. 781

**CHAPTER V.**—He confirms that unity is signified by the finger and the right hand from the fact that God’s works are the works of his hands, and that the works of his hands are likewise the works of his fingers. 783

**CHAPTER VI.**—The Spirit, just as the Father and the Son, can accuse and indeed judge; judges cannot do so without him. 784

**CHAPTER VII.**—The Son himself does not judge or avenge without the Spirit; hence the same Spirit is called the sword of the Word. 786

**CHAPTER VIII.**—The unity mentioned above is proved by the fact that, just as the Father is read to have been grieved and tempted, so also the Son is read to have been grieved and tempted. The Son was also tempted in the desert, where the figure of the cross was erected in the bronze serpent. Ibid.

**CHAPTER IX.**—The Holy Spirit’s conjunction with the Father and the Son, or his own divinity, is asserted. 788

**CHAPTER X.**—The divinity of the Holy Spirit is established from a passage in John. The passage had indeed been deleted by the heretics, but in vain, since their treachery can be more easily convicted from it. The Spirit’s divinity is again inferred from two testimonies of John, and finally the meaning of the statement that the Spirit, water, and blood are witnesses is explained. 789 [Col. 1537]

**CHAPTER XI.**—Those who object that John’s words, “The Spirit is God,” must be referred to God the Father are refuted. 792

**CHAPTER XII.**—Since Paul signified that the light of divinity, which the three apostles worshiped in Christ, exists in the Trinity, the Spirit too is shown to be worthy of worship. From the very words, it is shown that the Spirit is designated by the Apostle. His divinity is proved by the fact that he has a temple in which he dwells not as a priest but as God. 797

**CHAPTER XIII.**—An answer is given to those who object that Catholics, by attributing divinity to the Spirit, introduce three gods. 798

**CHAPTER XIV.**—By comparing the Epistles to the Thessalonians with other passages of Scripture, it is shown that lordship is claimed for the Spirit just as for the other Persons. 799

**CHAPTER XV.**—Although the Spirit is called Lord, this does not consequently introduce three Lords. 801

**CHAPTER XVI.**—The Father is holy, and likewise the Son and the Spirit; hence the same *trisagion*—“Holy, Holy, Holy”—is celebrated for all three. We cannot proclaim God more worthily than by calling him holy. From the passage of John that the heretics twisted into a calumny, the equality and unity of the Trinity’s divinity are established. 802

**CHAPTER XVII.**—Ambrose shows by examples how passages in which the Lord’s words were spoken assist in understanding them. He teaches that Christ spoke the statement cited from John in Solomon’s Portico, by which the soul of the wise is signified. Against the Jews, who bought and sold the Son of God—Joseph. 804

**CHAPTER XVIII.**—As he is about to confirm the Holy Spirit’s divinity from what has been discussed thus far, he takes up several matters again: namely, that the Spirit does not possess sins but forgives them; that he is not a creature but the Creator; and finally, that he does not worship but is worshiped. 807

**CHAPTER XIX.**—From what was proved above—that the Spirit remains and speaks in the prophets—he concludes that the Spirit recognizes all that belongs to God, and therefore is one with the Father and the Son. He confirms the same point again from the fact that the Spirit possesses everything that God possesses. 810

**CHAPTER XX.**—The river flowing from the throne of God contained a figure of the Holy Spirit; the waters mentioned by David signify heavenly powers. The kingdom of God is the work of the Spirit; nor is it surprising that the Spirit reigns together with the Son, since Paul promises that we too shall reign together with the Son. 812

**CHAPTER XXI.**—Isaiah was sent by the Spirit, and therefore saw the same Spirit. What is to be understood by the moving wheels and the various wings. Why the Holy Spirit God should be called *Sabaoth*, “of Hosts.” 813

**CHAPTER XXII.**—In order to prove the unity of the kingdom in the three Persons, the cited passage of Isaiah is examined; and it is declared that there is no difference of meaning in the interpretations by which it is explained of the Father, the Son, or the Spirit. 814

## Admonition concerning the book *On the Mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation*. 815

# ON THE MYSTERY OF THE LORD’S INCARNATION

## ONE BOOK

817 **CHAPTER ONE.**—On the sacrifices of Cain and Abel: against whom the sentence passed upon Cain is directed. Ibid.

**CHAPTER II.**—After enumerating various kinds of people who, while falsely hiding under the Christian name, tear apart the Church and are subject to the sentence just mentioned, he warns how we must avoid that same sentence. 820

**CHAPTER III.**—Having rebuked those who would not accept John’s testimony concerning the eternity of the Word, and having also praised that evangelist, he examines the passage in which he teaches that not only the eternity and divinity of the Word are signified, but that the same attributes are demonstrated in the Father. 821

**CHAPTER IV.**—It is not enough to believe that Christ has true flesh unless we exclude every confusion of that flesh with divinity; nor is it enough to call him the God of both covenants unless we also profess the Word himself to be coeternal. 824

**CHAPTER V.**—This faith is the foundation of the Church and is effective against all heresies: in Christ, both a divine and a human generation are believed. Bodily weaknesses must not be attributed to divinity. 827

**CHAPTER VI.**—All those heretics are briefly addressed who say either that Christ suffered only in appearance or that he comprised two persons in himself, as well as those who either distinguish the Word from the Son of God, fail to distinguish divinity from the flesh, or subject divinity, as though it were imperfect, to bodily injuries. 830

**CHAPTER VII.**—He excuses having added this book to the preceding books. Against those who denied that Christ assumed a soul. How Christ is said to fear or to make progress. 834

**CHAPTER VIII.**—In answer to the opponents who, against the Catholic position that the Son who was begotten is equal to the Father who begot him, object that one who is begotten cannot be of the same nature as one who is unbegotten. 838 [Col. 1538]

**CHAPTER IX.**—When the heretics wish the unbegotten Father—of whom they did not read in Scripture—to be conceded to them, they reveal their eagerness for contention. The word “unbegotten” is also asserted to be applicable to a creature. 840

**CHAPTER X.**—Those who acknowledge that the Son is like the Father but deny that he is of the same substance do not differ from the preceding opponents. The word “unbegotten” presents no obstacle to Catholics, but exposes the heretics’ treachery. 844

# AMBROSIAN FRAGMENT TAKEN FROM THEODORET 847

## Admonition concerning the Letters of Saint Ambrose arranged in a new order. 849

The order of the Letters arranged according to chronology is affirmed. 851

The new order of the Letters of Saint Ambrose compared with those previously published. 867

The order of the Roman edition compared with the older editions and with this new edition. 869

The order of the older editions compared with the Roman edition and with this new edition. 871

Alphabetical index of the Letters. 873

# LETTERS DIVIDED INTO TWO CLASSES
## FIRST CLASS

875

**Letter of Gratian to Ambrose.**—He invites Ambrose to visit him, so that he may strengthen him in the faith concerning the divinity of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. **Ibid.**

**Letter I.**—Ambrose excuses himself to the Caesarean for not having come, and promises that he will satisfy his wishes by composing treatises on the Holy Spirit. 876

**Letter II.**—To Constantius, recently elected bishop, he gives instruction concerning the chief duties and virtues of the priesthood. 879

**Letter III.**—He praises Felix’s little gift, but reproves him for not having visited him for a long time and asks that he not delay so long. 888

**Letter IV.**—He says that he has been refreshed by Felix’s conversation, especially because he hoped that Felix would come to the consecration of the basilica after they had celebrated the anniversary of his episcopal ordination. He promises him his prayers for this purpose and asks the same from him in return. **Ibid.**

**Letter V.**—Defending the judgment he himself delivered in the case of Indicia, he criticizes Syagrius’s decision because the proper legal procedure had not been observed in it. Syagrius had decreed an exceedingly insulting examination of the virgin. In what circumstances an examination is to be tolerated. After censuring the accuser and the witnesses, Marcellina’s testimony and that of others on Indicia’s behalf are reported, after which Ambrose’s judgment is appended. 891

**Letter VI.**—He reproaches Syagrius for having subjected Indicia to an insulting examination; and, placing before his eyes the most terrible vengeance that the Israelites exacted for the violation of the Levite’s wife’s chastity, he describes the entire course of the affair. 898

**Letter VII.**—Ambrose replies to Justus, who had asked what he meant by the command that half a didrachm be offered as a ransom. 904

**Letter VIII.**—He refutes those who denied that the sacred authors wrote according to the rules of the art. 912

**Proceedings of the Council of Aquileia against the heretics Palladius and Secundianus.** 916

**Letter IX.**—The council gives thanks to the Gallic bishops and writes to them concerning the condemnation of Palladius and Secundianus. 939

**Letter X.**—He gives thanks to the emperors for convening the synod; explains who attended it; recalls the evasions, blasphemies, and obstinacy of the heretics; and finally implores the emperors’ support, so that the council’s decrees may be carried out by their authority and certain other heretics may also be restrained. 940

**Letter XI.**—The bishops inform the emperors what was done in the synod and warn them not to allow Ursinus to insinuate himself into their presence, asserting that he was the author of the disturbances and had also been accused of an infamous crime. 944

**Letter XII.**—They thank the emperors for restoring peace to the Church and promise them the prayers of the bishops. Then, after reporting certain dissensions among Catholics, they ask the same rulers to order a council to meet at Alexandria and not to disdain to provide it with their assistance. 947

**Letter XIII.**—After thanking Theodosius for restoring the orthodox to the basilicas and expressing his grief over the disturbances in the Church, Ambrose complains that another bishop has been installed at Antioch in place of the deceased Meletius; he asks that Nectarius, appointed at Constantinople after Maximus, yield his place, or that a synod at Rome pronounce judgment concerning the ordination of both men. 950

**Letter XIV.**—After commending Theodosius for having worked to restore unity between the Eastern and Eastern Church, the bishops explain why they had previously written the letter concerning this matter. They add that they had also been concerned [Col. 1539] to have the supporters of Apollinaris condemned. Finally, they assert that by requesting a council they had injured no one and had nowhere departed from the practice of their forefathers. 953

**Letter XV.**—He says that he learned of Acholius’s death, and not without a certain miracle; that Acholius was not so much dead as transferred to a happier life; and that his actions had earned him the likeness of Elisha. He adds that Acholius should also be said to represent Elijah, a point especially demonstrated by his successor, whom he made heir of his spirit. 956

**Letter XVI.**—He congratulates Anysius, recently appointed to Acholius’s place, and, while praising his predecessor, prays that Anysius may become the successor to his merits. 959

**Letter XVII.**—It is the emperors’ duty to protect religion, and the restoration of superstition ought not to be requested from them. A petition was falsely presented in the name of the senate, since the Christian senators had not consented to it. The matter ought to be referred to Theodosius and to the bishops. If Valentinian grants privileges to unbelievers, he is to be rejected by the Church. 961

**Report of Symmachus, Prefect of the City.**—In the name of the senate he supplicates the emperors that the ancestral religions be restored and the altar of Victory repaired, and that an oath be exacted before it according to the ancient custom. 966

**Letter XVIII.**—Ambrose replies to the report of Symmachus. 971

**Letter XIX.**—Vigilius, recently appointed to the episcopate, begged Ambrose to provide him with a pattern for his formation; Ambrose gives him various instructions. 982

**Letter XX.**—He recounts to his sister what happened at Milan over several days because of the basilica that the Arians were demanding. 994

**Letter XXI.**—Ambrose excuses himself for not having come to the consistory when summoned, asserting that in a matter of faith or ecclesiastical discipline no one ought to judge except priests, and that he is not obstinate in refusing to inflict an injury upon his order. He adds that Auxentius might perhaps choose Jews or unbelievers as judges in their place; and he says that he does not refuse to discuss these matters in church or in a synod. 1003

**Sermon against Auxentius.**—On the surrender of the basilicas. 1007

**Letter XXII.**—On the discovery of the bodies of Gervasius and Protasius, and on the martyrs. 1019

**Letter XXIII.**—After setting forth the difficulty and necessity of determining the date of Easter, he proves that observing particular days is permissible provided superstition is absent, and explains his own opinion. 1024

**Letter XXIV.**—He explains why he gives an account of his embassy; he recounts how, compelled to enter the consistory, he refused Maximus’s kiss, and how he turned back upon Maximus the accusations by which Maximus charged that he had been deceived by Ambrose and that barbarians had been sent against him by Bauton. 1035

**Letter XXV.**—He replies to Studius, who had asked whether he was permitted to pronounce a sentence against the accused. 1039

**Letter XXVI.**—Repeating the argument of the preceding letter, he compares bishops pursuing the death of the accused with the Jews presenting the adulterous woman to Christ. He then explains the passage where the woman was brought forward and discusses at length the forgiveness of sins. 1042

**Letter XXVII.**—He teaches Irenaeus that the abominations of the Egyptians signify beasts; from this it is understood that piety and virtue displease the wicked, and therefore good men ought to devote themselves to opposite pursuits. He illustrates this by the example of Jacob’s wives, who agreed to flee from their father and follow their husband. He explains allegorically what ought to be done by those who approach the Church. 1046

**Letter XXVIII.**—The Pythagorean maxim that the common road must be avoided was taken from the sacred pages; from this it may be inferred that the priestly life ought to shun the ordinary way of life. Ambrose therefore urges Irenaeus to avoid popular opinions and desires and to enter the narrow way. 1051

**Letter XXIX.**—He advises that the beauty of the supreme good be sought, promising that it will refresh our eyes and nourish our soul. We are brought to this good only through virtue. 1054

**Letter XXX.**—He teaches that one ought not to dwell in low places, after the manner of the luxurious, but, like the saints, in higher places, where the temple of the Lord is to be built—namely, in one’s own minds. This temple is not built by the luxurious; its summit is measured by the aid of righteousness. 1061

**Letter XXXI.**—Ambrose replies to Irenaeus, who asked whether God loves differently those who believe immediately from childhood and those who believe only when already advanced in age. 1065

**Letter XXXII.**—He says that Satan is represented by the partridge’s deceit and lust. He explains how Satan gathered peoples to himself by crying out, and how Christ likewise called them back to himself. 1068

**Letter XXXIII.**—Irenaeus had expressed his fear that someone might infer from the passage of Scripture concerning the two wives that there are two souls in one [Col. 1540] person; Ambrose replies to him. 1071

**Letter XXXIV.**—Horuntian asked whether the soul about which philosophers think wrongly belongs to a heavenly substance. Ambrose first refers him to the books of Ezra; then, demonstrating the soul’s dignity from Paul’s testimony, he explains in what sense all creation is said there to groan and again to require liberation. 1074

**Letter XXXV.**—This letter asks why, although the Apostle’s words do not say that all creation is subject to corruption, all creation is nevertheless said to groan together. He then discusses, from what follows in the same passage, the Spirit of adoption, the greatness of the heavenly rewards, the groaning of the saints, the firstfruits of the Spirit, and related matters. 1077

**Letter XXXVI.**—In reply to the question which spirit Paul meant when he wrote that it pleads for us with inexpressible groanings. 1082

**Letter XXXVII.**—When Simplicianus had assured Ambrose that he would act usefully if he expounded something from the Apostle before the people, the holy man promises to comply with his wishes. 1083

**Letter XXXVIII.**—He learned from Peter’s letter that the wise man is rich and that no sex is excluded; the relevant passage is explained. 1095

**Letter XXXIX.**—He reproves Faustinus for avoiding human society because of his sister’s death. 1098

**Letter XL.**—He asks to be heard by the emperor, affirming that accessibility is praised in a ruler; that he cannot remain silent without danger to both sides; and that freedom does not displease kings. Although the emperor is pious, he can nevertheless be deceived. The proposal to restore the synagogue is dangerous, since it exposes a bishop either to martyrdom or to apostasy. Against the Valentinians. 1101

**Letter XLI.**—He reports to his sister how, after explaining a passage from Jeremiah concerning the words of the priests, he expounded the Gospel reading and showed that it commends the Lord’s mercy, whose imitation he likewise requires of us. He also taught how we may represent the Gospel sinner by washing, wiping, anointing, and kissing the Lord’s feet. 1113

**Letter of Pope Siricius to the Church of Milan.**—He teaches the Milanese that, through the devil’s envy, new heresies had crept into the Church. He exposes how pernicious they are and reports that their authors, whose names are listed individually, were condemned in an ecclesiastical assembly. 1121

**Letter XLII.**—The Synod of Milan praises Siricius because he defended the Church against wolves. These men rage against virginity under the pretended defense of marriage, although Paul commands that virginity be preferred to it. The same heretics, who denied that Christ could have been born of a virgin, are refuted by testimonies from Scripture. After adding a few remarks in praise of widowhood and abstinence, to which these men were hostile, the Fathers testify that they had struck them with an anathema as Manichaeans. 1123

**Letter XLIII.**—He replies to Horontian, who asked why man, though created superior by far to other things, was created later, and why neither Ambrose himself nor Moses had disclosed the reason for this. 1129

**Letter XLIV.**—Moses correctly indicated the distinction between God and the world. The six days are assigned to the creation of the universe not because God requires time, but so that the order of the work might be expressed. The dignity of the number seven is explained, although the number eight is preferred to it, since eight is the number of the New Testament, just as seven is that of the Old. 1134

**Letter XLV.**—Ambrose replies to Sabinus, who asked whether he had written about paradise and what his opinion of it was. 1142

**Letter XLVI.**—Ambrose writes to Sabinus that an abusive Apollinarist had been publicly refuted. Although the man did not admit a servile form in Christ, Ambrose treated him humanely. But the words that especially displeased him—namely, that God is the Father of the Son and the Lord of creation—agree with the words of David. 1145

**Letter XLVII.**—Explaining why he sent Sabinus a book written in a more explicit form, he explains why he prefers writing to dictation. He then invites him to the mutual exchange of letters, showing what benefit results from it. 1150

**Letter XLVIII.**—He begs Sabinus to examine his books rigorously and explains the advantages that result from this; nevertheless, he adds that harshness of expression must be tolerated so long as the profession of faith remains intact. He sets his own professions of faith against various heresies. 1151

**Letter XLIX.**—Writing to a friend, he says that he is never less alone than when he is alone, and teaches the benefits of solitude by examples. 1153

**Letter L.**—That God cannot lie is not a weakness; nevertheless, there is something weak belonging to God, but it is stronger than human beings—namely, the cross. It is not surprising that God infused Balaam with prophecy, since God did not deny it even to the [Col. 1541] priest who persecuted Christ, so that he might draw testimony for himself from his enemies. Balaam corrupted his prophecies with immense unfaithfulness and greed. 1156

**Letter LI.**—He says that he avoided Theodosius’s arrival not from unwillingness, but lest he be forced to remain silent or provide grounds for offense. Theodosius was quick-tempered but naturally inclined to reconciliation; therefore, lest he disturb him, Ambrose excused himself on grounds of ill health. The bishops mourned the massacre at Thessalonica; accordingly, in cleansing it away, the repentance of the saints must be imitated, without which sin is not removed. The devil, who envied him, must be overcome. You would not dare, in the emperor’s presence, to offer the sacrifice, since even divine intervention had deterred him from it; yet repentance itself is a sacrifice. He grieves that his action did not anticipate Theodosius’s act, since he truly loves him. 1159

**Letter LII.**—He rejoices with Tatianus that the reason for fearing a trial involving his niece has been removed, and urges him to make himself readily available for a settlement. 1164

**Letter LIII.**—Explaining the reason for his silence, he mourns Valentinian’s death, especially because of Valentinian’s great piety toward God and goodwill toward Ambrose. Then, after announcing that the marble for his burial is ready, he urges that it be hastened for the sake of his sisters. 1165

**Letter LIV.**—He informs Eusebius that the offense against the apparitor has been forgiven and that Faustinus’s cough has flared up again. 1167

**Letter LV.**—Mentioning that some of Eusebius’s offspring have remained with him and some have gone to Eusebius, he adorns the two Faustini with blessings suited to Noah’s family; and, in greeting Valentinian, assigns him the roles of Canaan and Nimrod. **Ibid.**

**Letter LVI.**—Ambrose laments that the council at Capua could not bring the disputes between Evagrius and Flavian to an end. He censures Flavian for having submitted petitions to the emperor, but does so in such a way that he does not wish this to prejudice Flavian’s right. Finally, he instructs Theophilus on how to exercise the judgment entrusted to him by the Council of Capua. 1170

**Letter concerning the case of Bonosus.**—He replies to those asking what should be decided in Bonosus’s case. 1172

**Letter LVII.**—He explains to Eugenius why he did not wait for him at Milan. Then, after reviewing what had been done under Valentinian and Theodosius on the occasion of Symmachus’s report, he freely reproves the same tyrant because, by granting expenditures to temples of idols, he had shown no regard either for fear of God or for the opinion others would form of him. 1174

**Letter LVIII.**—He recounts the withdrawal of Paulinus and Therasia after they had distributed their possessions among the needy, as well as the future accusations of the pagans on that account, whose superstition and blindness he laments. Then, proving by examples that nothing done for religion ought to be considered shameful, he explains and defends mystically David’s dancing and Elijah’s nakedness. 1178

**Letter LIX.**—He announces the withdrawal of the presbyter Jacob from Persia into Campania and praises the peace of that region, contrasting it with the disturbances that had shaken Milan. 1182

**Letter LX.**—Paternus was considering giving his granddaughter by a daughter in marriage to his son. Ambrose immediately deters him from the plan with a little reflection. He denies that it accords with divine law, with piety, or with the imperial constitutions; then, after resolving certain minor objections, he confirms that such a marriage is inexpedient. 1183

**Letter LXI.**—After explaining why he withdrew from Milan and returned there soon afterward, and after giving thanks to God for the assistance granted to Theodosius, he promises to comply with the same ruler’s wishes. 1186

**Letter LXII.**—He reproaches Theodosius for not having written to him earlier and, announcing that he is sending a deacon to him, asks that he admit Ambrose’s petitions on behalf of certain persons who had taken refuge in the Church. 1188

**Letter LXIII.**—Grieving that the Church of Vercellae had been deprived of a bishop for so long because of internal disputes, he praises the harmony by which Eusebius had once been elected and urges the same Church to strive to have Christ standing in its midst. **Ibid.**

## SECOND CLASS

Ambrose replies to Irenaeus, who asked why the manna that once rained upon the Israelites does not rain upon Christians. 1219

**Letter LXV.**—Ambrose explains to Simplicianus, who wished to know why the blood of the victims was poured partly upon the altar and partly into bowls. 1222

**Letter LXVI.**—After first praising letters, especially those composed on a useful subject, he teaches that Aaron’s casting of the women’s earrings into the head of the calf signifies that the seal of faith was snatched away by the serpent’s breaths and foreshadows the idolatry of the Jews. The fact that Moses ground the calf to pieces after breaking the tablets indicates that pride and faithlessness must be destroyed. Finally, the command that one’s neighbor be attacked does not mean that we should place our kindred after religion, but that we should cut away whatever in us resists God. 1224

**Letter LXVII.**—After showing that Moses accepted Aaron’s excuse concerning his sons, he considers the same passage as implying that each person’s judgment concerning his own office takes precedence. 1227

[Col. 1542]

**Letter LXVIII.**—What God threatened against the Jews when he said: “I will make the heaven like bronze and the earth like iron.” 1231

**Letter LXIX.**—He replies to Irenaeus, who asked why the law forbids men to wear women’s clothing and women to wear men’s clothing. 1232

**Letter LXX.**—Just as it is a sign of a strong soul to remain steadfast in goodness, so it is a sign of a weak soul to fall and rise again. Therefore, since the progress of the stronger soul is described in the Song of Songs, while the conversion of the fallen soul is described in the prophecy of Micah, he proposes that these passages be considered. 1234

**Letter LXXI.**—After the various stages by which the fallen soul repairs itself, described above, the faithful soul’s reception by Christ, instruction, and perfection are considered here. It is shown that Christ’s journeys signify the soul’s different stages of progress. 1241

**Letter LXXII.**—Some asked why God, after instituting circumcision in the Old Testament, abolished it in the New; why he gave a law concerning it when it exposed the child to danger; and finally why he wished it to be performed on that particular part of the body. Ambrose replies to these questions in a letter to Constantius. 1243

**Letter LXXIII.**—He replies to the question why the Law was given when Paul indicates that it is absent. 1251

**Letter LXXIV.**—Many denied that the Law could be abolished, since God had established it, or inferred from its abolition that the two Testaments were not from the same God. This is resolved from the Apostle’s statement: “The Law was our pedagogue,” and so forth. 1254

**Letter LXXV.**—After setting forth the difficulty of extracting Paulinus’s meaning, he adds the Apostle’s text affirming that no one becomes an heir except through faith. He then refutes the Jews, who claimed that the inheritance was owed to them because of the Old Testament. 1257

**Letter LXXVI.**—At Irenaeus’s request, Ambrose gives an outline of the Letter to the Ephesians. He writes that a heavenly inheritance and participation in a heavenly throne are set before us there, through Christ, by whom we have been claimed for freedom. The goal of faith, charity, by which we are joined to Christ, is also shown. No other letter is filled with more blessings, which he briefly discusses one by one. 1259

**Letter LXXVII.**—He replies to the question what that inheritance is for which many do not hesitate to face death. 1263

**Letter LXXVIII.**—Like Abraham, we are justified by faith, through which we are sons of the free woman. Circumcision had force only through Christ, who himself underwent it and brought it to an end. Righteousness, therefore, is to be expected only from faith, which, if perfect, is never without charity. 1267

**Letter LXXIX.**—He tells Bellicius, who had recovered from illness after believing in Christ, that both his illness and his recovery must be attributed to the visitation of that same Christ. He exhorts him to retain Christ and hasten on to the other sacraments. 1269

**Letter LXXX.**—After showing that the healing of the man blind from birth was an act of divine power, he reproves the disciples’ question. He recalls and briefly explains several parts of the same narrative. 1272

**Letter LXXXI.**—He encourages certain clergy who had lost heart because of their labor and difficulties. He places before their eyes not only the reward that awaits them but also Christ’s ready protection. For this reason, after explaining several passages of Scripture, he warns them not to allow themselves to be separated from him. 1273

**Letter LXXXII.**—He recalls how he was appointed judge in the case of Marcellus, Laetus, and their sister, and why he undertook the inquiry in such a way that he preferred to act as arbitrator. He explains the state of the dispute and shows that Marcellus ought not to regard the loss as intolerable. 1275

**Letter LXXXIII.**—He commends Sisinnius for granting forgiveness to his son, who had married without consulting him; and, after mentioning certain advantages that the son would derive from this, he shows that by this readiness to forgive Sisinnius had followed in the footsteps of the saints. 1279

**Letter LXXXIV.**—He commends Cynegius for seeking his advice. 1282

**Letter LXXXV.**—After thanking Syricius for sending him a letter through the presbyter Syrus, he praises the latter’s prompt journey and adds some remarks about following Christ. **Ibid.**

**Letter LXXXVI.**—Concerning letters carried in both directions by Priscus. 1283

**Letter LXXXVII.**—He praises Polybus and states that, at Polybus’s request, he wrote two letters to Segatius and Delphinus. **Ibid.**

**Letter LXXXVIII.**—He praises Priscus, who carried the letters in both directions. 1284

**Letter LXXXIX.**—He speaks of Alypius’s letters to him and of his own letters to Alypius. **Ibid.**

**Letter XC.**—He recalls Antony’s affection for him and his own reciprocal affection for [Col. 1543] Antony. 1284

**Letter XCI.**—He praises Candidianus and humbles himself. 1280

**Preface to the two books on the death of his brother Satyrus.** 1285
